### Volume front matter

### Series title page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library, complete, uniform, convenient, economical, of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed through the first twelve centuries of the Church, most carefully corrected according to the most accurate editions and collated with one another and with certain manuscript codices; continuously illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the fullest editions completed in the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following individual volumes or authors of some importance; with chapters properly arranged within the text itself and with titles of individual pages set at the upper margin and indicating the subject treated; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal which nevertheless possess some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two ample general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which the reader may see at a glance whatever each of the Fathers wrote on any theme; the other of Holy Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented on individual scriptural texts and in what places in their works. A most accurate edition, easily to be preferred to all others if one considers the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of works reprinted, the extremely convenient form of the volumes, constant throughout the whole course of the work, the modest price, and especially this one methodical and chronological collection of six hundred fragments and short works hitherto scattered here and there, now for the first time gathered in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.**

**Second Series, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III.** Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Clergy Library, or Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning. The Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. Two hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; three hundred volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for one thousand eight hundred francs. The purely Latin series embraces all Western authors and Eastern authors as well; the latter, however, are provided in it only in Latin translation.

## In the year of the Lord 1150: Venerable Hervé, monk of Bourg-Dieu

[Column 9]

## Notice

(R. P. Bernard Pez, introductory dissertation in vol. III of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, p. IV.)

Hervé, whom Jean Mabillon, in volume III of the *Annals of the Benedictine Order*, p. 357, places at the end of the eleventh century, and Casimir Oudin, in the supplement to Bellarmine's *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 394, says flourished about the year 1130, was the illustrious glory and ornament of the monastery of Déols, or Bourg-Dieu, in the diocese of Bourges. Lucas d'Achery, in the preliminary observations to volume II of the *Spicilegium*, and the aforementioned Mabillon, p. 358, briefly and sorrowfully describe the fortunes of this monastery. There he records that it was destroyed in 1623 at the request of the most serene prince of Condé, Henri de Bourbon, who established in its place, and in that of the monastery of Saint-Sauveur, two colleges of canons—an excellent reform indeed—one within the palace of Châteauroux, the other at Déols. As for a fuller account of the life Hervé spent there, it is supplied by the admirable and extensive circular letter of the monks of Déols concerning his death, published by d'Achery from a manuscript codex of the abbey of Clairvaux in the above-cited volume of the *Spicilegium*, p. 515. Because, owing to the rarity of d'Achery's work in these realms, it has been seen by very few, it seemed right to reproduce it here word for word. Here it is:

“When the prophet says, ‘The Lord will declare to his people the power of his works,’ if he himself recounts his own praises, not for his own benefit but for the salvation of his hearers, how shall we, whose whole salvation lies in his praises, dare to keep silent about his great deeds, which he has deigned to show us in our own times? Let whoever is about to hear or read these things know that we do not at all wish to exalt the dead with empty or false praise, but, for the praise and glory of Christ and the salvation of the hearers, to set down in a truthful style a few things concerning a lover of truth, out of love for truth itself.

“There was then a man venerable alike for life and teaching, named Hervé, a monk of the monastery of Déols. For about fifty years he lived there, proclaiming the excellence of morals. A native of the country of Le Mans, he left among us many memorials of his faith and wisdom, and also of his innocence. For while still young, and from childhood abundantly imbued with the disciplines of the schools, upon entering the aforesaid monastery he devoted his whole self to the study of Holy Scripture. He began to frequent the Catholic expositors—Augustine, Jerome, Ambrose, Gregory, and the rest—and never ceased to apply himself day and night to their reading and to serve meditation. No obstacle whatever could tear him from the search for truth. Since he possessed singular intelligence and an inestimable memory, he began to store up in the vessel of his heart much that would be useful; like a dove, to choose the better grains; and to retain them in his memory and commit them to writing.

“Accordingly, he first produced a remarkable exposition of the book of Blessed Dionysius, *On the Angelic Hierarchies*.

“Then he expounded the whole book of the prophet Isaiah, the *Lamentations* of Jeremiah, and the final part of Ezekiel, beginning where Pope Saint Gregory had left off and carrying it through to the end.

“At the same time he also expounded the Deuteronomy of Moses, the *Ecclesiastes* of Solomon, the book of Judges, the little book of Ruth, and the book of Tobit, showing by irrefutable reasoning that all things in those books which, to less understanding minds, seem to convey the letter alone attest and proclaim the mysteries of Christ and the Church.

[Column 11] “Moreover, he expounded the Epistles of the Apostle Paul with such an abundance of wisdom that those who read them declare they have never known commentaries comparable to them, and that expositions made with such care can scarcely, or never, be found anywhere.

“Finally, when the fame of his learning had spread on every side, and when, as those who truly knew him testify, no one was held to surpass him in knowledge of the canonical Scriptures, he expounded the book of the Twelve Prophets and the book of Genesis in their entirety with so wonderful an understanding that we have not yet been able to find an exposition of them that could be compared with his.

“Meanwhile, he composed very many expositions of the readings from the holy Gospels and of the canticles that are read in church.

“He also composed a little book on the connection of certain readings, showing that in some churches they are read differently from the way they stand in sacred history. One example that follows will suffice. In Lent a certain reading from the book of Esther is read, and in some lectionaries the reading from Esther thus begins: ‘Esther prayed to the Lord, saying: O Lord God, almighty king, all things are placed under your power.’ From the author of the sacred history he proves there that Esther did not offer that prayer, but Mordecai did; and therefore one should not read, ‘Esther prayed,’ but rather, ‘Mordecai prayed.’ He makes many similar observations there.

“He also wrote a sizeable book on the miracles of Saint Mary, Mother of God, which that same inviolate Virgin performed in his time in the church of Déols. As soon as they had happened, he wrote them down without any delay, as he heard them from the very persons in whom they occurred and from the monk who guarded the monastery.

“Finally, although he felt that the approaching term of his end was drawing near as his strength gradually failed, he nevertheless could not be without his customary work of writing. Asked by several persons to explain what the *Supper of Saint Caecilius Cyprian, bishop of Carthage*, a work compiled from almost all the canonical books, signified—he who retained all the Scriptures in memory beyond everyone else—a matter that until then had been unknown among us—he granted their request and said that, while writing, he might perhaps end his present life together with that work. Since the earlier book of his expositions had dealt with the sayings of the holy Fathers, namely Dionysius the Areopagite, this latter book would likewise deal with the sayings of the same holy Fathers. And so it happened. For when he had expounded the same *Supper* as far as the place where it says, ‘Elizabeth was confounded, Mary was astonished, Sarah saw the deed,’ at which point it ended among us, he and Lord Abbot Girbert, who had assigned this task to him as to his monk and son, judged that no great part of it remained. They were awaiting the part that was lacking from the abbot of Saint-Savin, who said he had it and had promised to send it to them. For he might perhaps have removed much from it or added much to it; he left it as it stood, in an unfinished state.


“And when he had completed the time of Lent in the greatest vigor of mind and in greater bodily strength than he had recently possessed, amid much abstinence, many daily strokes of the rod, devout and unremitting prayers, and the reverent daily celebration of the most holy sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, with the cheerfulness and joy of the Holy Spirit; when, on the day of the holy Supper of the Lord, he had refreshed us in chapter with the honey-sweet bread of the Word of God, he served as weekly celebrant at Mass on holy Easter day and delivered an address in chapter. On Monday he sang Mass in the convent, and afterwards, seized by weakness, he was anointed on Wednesday. But then he could not receive communion. Later, when he had recovered a little, he maintained that this had happened by divine providence, saying that the Lord ought not to come to him, but he to the Lord. Thus on the following day—the Mass of which he had not heard on the preceding day—he heard that day’s Mass; and, after confession, he most devoutly received the most holy mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood as a safeguard for his soul, soon to depart. So throughout the whole week, having heard Mass daily, which he did not wish to omit in any way, and greatly desiring to see Lord Abbot, who then happened to be absent, before he departed, after the abbot’s arrival he was visited and absolved by him. In the hands of the man to whom he confessed himself, he began to be afflicted by a severe indeed, but very brief, pain unto death, passing from this life on the Sunday within the octave of Easter and ascending, as we believe, to the starry realms.

“So that the letter may not be drawn out too long, let us say briefly concerning the whole course of his life that in our days we have known none more eminent in abstinence, more spotless in chastity, sounder in counsel, loftier in humility, more constant in silence, more circumspect in speech and wholly free from vanity, or purer and more fully Catholic in teaching, and none more distinguished in every moral excellence. We write these things to you because he was a brother, that you may rejoice over so great a brother and faithfully render what you promised him, hoping to be joined with him in the kingdom of God, to which we trust he has flown. Farewell.”

Thus far the funeral letter of the monks of Déols concerning the life, character, and teaching of Hervé. It is now useful to make some observations on the catalogue of his works composed by them, as we have seen. Of all Hervé’s works here listed, none has yet been submitted to the press except the commentary on the Epistles of Paul, which the venerable and generous lord René de Châtaigner rescued from neglect and squalor as a genuine work of Saint Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, a man most holy and learned alike, and first published in folio at Cologne from the press of Eucharius Cervicornus in 1533, with a preface by Godfrey Hittorp, citizen of Cologne. John Picard, a regular canon of Saint-Victor at Paris, subsequently published it more carefully and more fully under the name of the same Saint Anselm, in volume II of the works of Saint Anselm, issued in folio at Cologne from the Cholin press in 1612. Yet all learned men now acknowledge that it is not Anselm’s, but the genuine offspring of Hervé of Déols. For more on this, see Labbé, vol. I of the *Dissertations on Ecclesiastical Writers*; Bellarmine; Casimir Oudin in the *Supplement*, p. 395; William Cave in his *Literary History* under the year 1130; and other recent bibliographers in various places. This is also why these commentaries were omitted from the newest and most exact edition of Saint Anselm’s works, prepared at Paris in 1675 by the most learned Gabriel Gerberon of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, and were not reprinted even among the spurious works of the archbishop of Canterbury.

Hervé’s other work, which will henceforth be counted among those published, is his most extensive commentary on Isaiah, divided into eight books, which occupies the entire first part of this volume. To publish it accurately and correctly, we have used two fine parchment manuscript codices in folio. The library of the most celebrated Austrian monastery of Holy Cross, of the Cistercian Order, supplied us with the first; there our studies were energetically assisted by the Reverend and distinguished Daniel, an excellent man to whom scholars will shortly owe still more. This codex is six hundred years old. The other was sent to us from the library of the renowned monastery of Garsten near Steyr, the noble city of Upper Austria, of our Order, by the Reverend Father Peter Oberhueber, its subprior, our friend and a most zealous supporter of our studies. Nor is this one much younger than the Holy Cross codex. From both we restored the text, placing the variant readings, though very few, in the margin. A third manuscript copy of this work also survives in a five-hundred-year-old parchment folio codex in the library of Campilily; it is doubtless the very copy praised in a catalogue compiled at Campilily four hundred years ago under the name of Curveius, on Isaiah. Finally, Cave, relying on Labbé, reports that Hervé’s work addressed to John, abbot of Déols, is preserved in manuscript in the Clermont library at Paris. To him must be added Oudin, who affirms that it is also held in the library of Longpont, of the Cistercian Order, in the bishopric of Soissons. In any event, the learned world owes the publication of this splendid commentary, so full of Hervé’s character and genius as the monks of Déols depicted it above, to the Reverend Father Godfrey Depisch, our fellow religious and companion. By a persistent and truly laborious effort he transcribed it in full from the cited codices and prepared it for the press with singular industry and diligence. Nor would he have declined the labor of bringing to light Hervé’s remaining works, if the codices in which learned men say they are contained had been sent to us.


Oudin, in the *Supplement*, p. 395, testifies that he saw Hervé’s brief manuscript postils on Deuteronomy at Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris. The most illustrious Saint Edmund Martène, in part I, p. 57, of his *Literary Journey*, published in French, writes that he found Hervé’s commentaries on the minor prophets in the Premonstratensian monastery of Saint-Marien at Auxerre. But we are separated from those places by too great a distance to expect anything from them. As for Hervé’s other works, whether and where they survive even today, we have learned nothing of them so far, not even by report.

[Column 13]

## Second notice

(*Literary History of France*, by Benedictine religious, vol. XII, p. 344.)

Hervé was born at Le Mans, not in Brittany [Note: [Column 13] *Fabr. Bibl.*, vol. III], as Genebrard believed [Note: [Column 13] Under the year 1110], nor in Limousin, as Father Le Long asserts [Note: [Column 13] *Bibl. Sacr.*, vol. II, p. 773]. A lively and penetrating mind, together with a great love of study, were the first traits to develop in him and characterized him throughout his life. After promising early displays of his talents, he entered the abbey of Bourg-Dieu, or Bourg-Déols, in Berry, about the year 1100. The circular letter concerning his death guarantees this date, saying that he ended his days in his fiftieth year of religious life under Abbot Gilbert; according to Father Pagi, this comes to 1149 (no. 4), or, according to the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* (vol. II, p. 151), to 1150. From his entry into the cloister, Hervé studied only the sacred books and whatever could facilitate his understanding of them—that is, the sacred interpreters, especially Saint Ambrose, Saint Jerome, Saint Augustine, and Saint Gregory. He spent all [Column 15] the time between the regular exercises in this occupation, with nothing capable of distracting him from it: *Nec quolibet impedimento ab inquisitione veritatis avelli potuit* [“No obstacle whatever could tear him from the search for truth”]. The rich store of knowledge he thereby acquired enabled him to undertake considerable works on Scripture, which won him great renown. His literary labors were ennobled by the purest motives of Christianity, and in him piety kept pace with learning. This is the testimony of the authors of the circular letter already cited. He died on the Sunday of the octave of Easter after redoubling the fasts, vigils, and other austerities in which he had spent Lent to prepare himself for that terrible moment, of which there is reason to believe he had some foreboding. On the preceding Holy Thursday he preached in chapter, and on Easter Day he still had strength to celebrate high Mass and exhort the community.

The circular letter of the religious of Bourg-Dieu credits Hervé with the following works: an explanation of the book *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, attributed to Saint Dionysius; commentaries on the entire prophecy of Isaiah, on the *Lamentations* of Jeremiah, and on the final part of the prophet Ezekiel—that is, on all that Saint Gregory the Great had not explained; other commentaries on Deuteronomy, Ecclesiastes, and the books of Judges, Ruth, and Tobit; an exposition of the Epistles of Saint Paul, regarded as his masterpiece and winning him the reputation of the foremost man of his century in understanding the sacred books; commentaries on the twelve minor prophets; and several explanations of the readings from the holy Gospels and of the chants sung in church.

Hervé also made a kind of concordance, or rather a critique of the differences found in several passages of Scripture, whose readings varied among different churches, where the sacred text had sometimes been altered. For example, he showed that instead of reading, *Oravit Esther ad Dominum, dicens: Domine Deus Rex omnipotens* [“Esther prayed to the Lord, saying: O Lord God, almighty King”], as certain lectionaries had it, one must read, *Oravit Mardochaeus* [“Mordecai prayed”]. This book bore the title *De connexione quarumdam lectionum* [“On the connection of certain readings”]. But might this title itself be corrupt, and should one not instead read *de correctione* [“on correction”]?

He further composed a collection of miracles that God worked in his time in the church of Bourg-Dieu through the intercession of the Blessed Virgin.

Finally, as he approached the end of his course, he was induced by his abbot Gilbert and some of his brethren to comment on a work concerning the Supper attributed to Saint Cyprian. But death did not permit him to finish this task.

These are Hervé’s writings, arranged in the order given them by the authors of the circular letter. It may be presumed that they followed chronological order.

The commentary on the books attributed to Saint Dionysius may be considered lost.

His commentary on Isaiah was published through the care of Dom Bernard Pez, who gave it a place in the third volume of his *Anecdotes* (p. 776 and following); but it lacks the dedicatory letter which, according to Dom Liron, is found in the manuscripts of France [Note: [Column 15] *Historical Singularities*, vol. III, p. 40]. It is divided into eight books, furnished with a preface addressed to John, his abbot. We shall not examine whether this was John I, who governed from 1103 to 1138, or John II, his successor; that question, no less obscure than frivolous, does not deserve the trouble required to clarify it. This commentary shows wide reading in the Fathers, whose substance the author has, so to speak, expressed in his explanations. He speaks of grace as a true disciple of Saint Augustine, and of the Church as a man strongly attached to its unity. His zeal often breaks out in complaints against the pastors of his time, whom he depicts in colors that do no credit to either their learning or their virtue. On the subject of the last times, he says that Elijah will come to reform the abuses seen multiplying daily among Christians; that, as the Church had the apostles at its birth, toward its end it will have Elijah, Enoch, and other excellent doctors who will not be inferior to apostolic men. Hervé regards it as an article of faith that the persecution of Antichrist will last only three and a half years, but he does not think that Antichrist’s death must be immediately followed by the Last Judgment.


The monk Alberic greatly praises this work [Note: [Column 15] *Chronicle*, under the year 1156, p. 328], but he mistakes the author’s name. “Master Henry,” he says—he should have said Hervé—“living in Berry, a monk of the black order, produced a noble work on Isaiah and many others.”

Hervé’s commentary on the Epistles of Saint Paul was made public under the name of Saint Anselm by René de Chataigner, at Paris in 1533, in one folio volume, from Poncet le Preux. The same error of attribution was copied in the two new editions made of it, one at Venice in quarto in 1547, the other at Paris in folio in 1549, by the Marnef brothers; and finally in several collections of the works of Saint Anselm, beginning with that published by Melchior Hittorp at Cologne in 1533, by Eucharius Cervicornus. Sixtus of Siena [Note: [Column 15] *Bibliotheca*, book IV, p. 223] was the first to observe that the old manuscript copies of this commentary bore the name of the monk Hervé. In consequence of this observation, the Jesuit Francisco Ribera began to doubt, according to the report of Cornelius a Lapide, that it came from the archbishop of Canterbury. Bellarmine [Note: [Column 15] *Scriptors*, p. 289] then decisively determined that it did not belong to him. But, because he had not consulted the ancient manuscripts, he fell into another error by assigning this work to Hervé Nédellec, general of the Dominicans, who died in 1323. His authority misled other critics on this point. Finally, after Father Labbé discovered the source of the error, all scholars joined him in restoring this commentary to our author.

The expositions of some of the Gospels of the year long had the same fate as the commentary on Saint Paul: they too passed as works of Saint Anselm. They appear among the genuine works in all the old editions, including that of Father Théophile Raynaud [Note: [Column 15] They also occur in Gerberon’s edition, which we reprinted in volume CLVIII of the *Patrology*, but under the title *Homilies and Exhortations*. See the *Censure of the Works of Saint Anselm of Canterbury* prefixed to that volume, col. 26], under the title *Divi Anselmi in aliquot Evangelia enarrationes* [“Expositions of the divine Anselm on certain Gospels”].

Hervé’s other writings have remained in obscurity. Several libraries preserve copies of them. Dom Rivet had seen in the library of Clairvaux the exposition of the final vision of Ezekiel, [Column 17] in a fine twelfth-century folio manuscript bearing the title: *Liber quem Herveus composuit super ultimam visionem Ezechielis prophetae* [“The book which Hervé composed on the final vision of the prophet Ezekiel”]. He had also seen there the commentary on Deuteronomy, which begins: *Addabarim, id est Deuteronomium liber iste vocatur* [“Addabarim, that is, this book is called Deuteronomy”]. The same work occurs at Saint-Germain-des-Prés under the title *Short Postils on Deuteronomy*.

Hervé’s notes on the book of Judges, on Ruth, on the twelve minor prophets, on the *Lamentations* of Jeremiah, and on Ecclesiasticus form part of the manuscripts of the abbey of Vauluisant in the diocese of Sens. Portions of them are also found at Pontigny.

At Tours cathedral, a five-hundred-year-old manuscript contains, after the letters of Saint Cyprian, Hervé’s commentary on the sermon concerning the Supper attributed to that Father [Note: [Column 17] “One may observe on this occasion,” says Dom Liron (*Historical Singularities*, vol. III, p. 38), “how little criticism there was in those times; for this sermon attributed to Saint Cyprian is a pitiful work. It was already old in Hervé’s time, for I learn that a certain Maurus, a copyist, once dedicated it to Lothair, king of France, who died in 986.”]. It is the last fruit, though not the best, of our author’s pen: this commentary bears the marks both of the defects of the text and of the languid state in which Hervé composed it. As has been said, death overtook him during this work and did not allow him to put the finishing hand to it. The same work is still at Clairvaux, preceded by our author’s notes on the canticles of Hannah and Habakkuk.

To the literary productions of Hervé detailed in the circular letter already mentioned, Dom Gerberon [Note: [Column 17] Preface to Anselm’s Works] adds a commentary on Saint Matthew, another on the *Song of Songs*, and a third on the Apocalypse. This learned man had even proposed to publish them, together with all Hervé’s other writings on the sacred books. We do not know on what basis he attributes these last three to our author. For our part, it appears certain to us that they belong to Anselm of Laon, and we have proved this in the tenth volume of this *History* [Note: [Column 17] See volume CLXII of the *Patrology*, under Anselm of Laon].

Finally, so as to omit nothing concerning our author’s writings, we observe that the circular letter which should serve as the rule for distinguishing them has been printed three times: in volume II of the *Spicilegium*, in volume II of D. Pez’s *Anecdotes*, and in volume VI of the *Benedictine Annals*.

[Column 17]

## Eight books of the commentaries on Isaiah by Venerable Hervé, monk of Bourg-Dieu

(Extracted by the Reverend Father Godfrey Depisch, Benedictine of Melk, from a manuscript codex of the renowned monastery of Holy Cross, of the Cistercian Order in Austria, and collated with a codex of the renowned Benedictine monastery of Garsten near Steyr; edited by the Reverend Father Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. III, part I, p. 2. Augsburg and Graz, at the expense of the Veith brothers, 1721, folio.)


## Book I

## Chapter I

[Column 17A]

**Verse 1.**—“The vision of Isaiah son of Amoz, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.”

At the beginning, “This is” is to be understood, so that the complete sense is: “This is the vision of Isaiah son of Amoz.” It is the manner of prophetic speech first to describe the person, kingdom or city, and time, and afterwards to begin speaking the mysteries of prophecy, so that, in order to demonstrate the truth more firmly, it may first set down the root of history and then bring forth the fruits of the Spirit by signs and allegories. Isaiah, therefore, first declares his own person when he says: “The vision of Isaiah.” In order to identify the person properly, he also relates his lineage when he adds: [Column 18A] “son of Amoz.” He announces the kingdom and city concerning which he is chiefly about to speak, saying: “which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem.” He also describes the time, adding: “in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.”

Nor should it trouble us that he does not say “my vision,” but “the vision of Isaiah.” For it is the custom of Holy Scripture that those who write in it speak of themselves as though of others, showing that they themselves are not speaking, but the Holy Spirit. Thus Moses says: “Moses was a man most meek above all the men that dwelt upon the earth” (Num. 12:3). Since he did not say “I was,” but “he was,” he clearly indicates that another was speaking through him concerning him. [Column 19A] Thus John also says: “That disciple whom Jesus loved” (John 13:23). Therefore, because the writers of the sacred word are moved by the impulse of the Holy Spirit, they bear witness in it concerning themselves as though concerning others. Thus the Holy Spirit spoke through Moses about Moses; the Holy Spirit through John about John; the Holy Spirit through Isaiah about Isaiah. Therefore the man full of God rightly says “the vision of Isaiah,” and not “my vision,” because, carried beyond himself by being filled with the Holy Spirit, he becomes, as it were, outside himself and pronounces judgment about himself as about another; in this too he avoids seeming to speak boastfully. He saw this vision concerning Judah and Jerusalem because, although he prophesied concerning the twelve tribes, he nevertheless prophesied especially concerning the tribe of Judah and the royal city in which [Column 19B] the Temple stood.

But we must ask why he began by saying, “The vision of Isaiah son of Amoz,” and does not seem to add what he saw or to indicate what this vision is.

The answer is that there are three kinds of vision: bodily, spiritual, and intellectual. Consider that in this one command, when we read, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 5:43), three kinds of vision occur. One is through the eyes, by which the letters themselves are seen; another through the human spirit, by which one thinks of one’s neighbor even when absent; the third through the gaze of the mind, by which love itself is apprehended. Of these three kinds, the first is manifest to human beings. For by it heaven and earth are seen, and all things in them that are visible [Column 19C] to our eyes.

Nor is it difficult to indicate the other kind, by which absent bodies are thought. Even while situated among heaven, earth, and the things that we can see in them, we think of them where, seeing nothing with bodily eyes, we nevertheless behold in the mind bodily images: either true images, as we saw the bodies themselves and retain them in memory, or fictive images, as thought can form them. One thinks of Rome, which one has seen, differently from Jerusalem, which one has not seen.

The third kind, by which understood love is beheld, contains things that have no images like themselves, which are not what they themselves are. A man, tree, sun, and whatever other bodily things, [Col. 0019D] heavenly or earthly, are seen when present in their forms and thought when absent through images impressed on the mind. They produce two kinds of vision: one through bodily senses, the other through spirit, in which those images are held. But is love seen one way when present in the form it is and another way when absent in an image like itself? Certainly not. As far as it can be seen by the mind, love itself is seen more by one person and less by another. If some bodily image is thought, love itself is not seen. It is seen not imaginally but properly, not through the body but in a mind cleansed from every stain of vice and filled with the grace of that very love.

[Col. 0020A] These are the three kinds of vision. Let us call the first bodily, because it is perceived through the body and presented to bodily senses; the second spiritual. Whatever is not body but is nevertheless something is rightly called spirit. The image of an absent body is not body, although it resembles body; neither is the very gaze by which it is seen. The third is called intellectual from intellect. Spiritual vision, by which likenesses of bodies are seen in spirit rather than mind, is superior to bodily vision, by which bodies themselves are seen through bodily eyes. Intellectual vision is superior to both, because divine things are seen by the pure mind not through any sign figured spiritually or bodily, but by the pure and keen intellect of the mind.

[Col. 0020B] Of these three kinds, the second and third occur in Isaiah’s vision. His vision is intellectual and sometimes spiritual as well. In images formed in spirit he saw “the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up” and the seraphim standing around him (Isaiah 6:1); but by the mind’s keenness he understood what he saw, as belongs to prophets’ minds. Signs are shown in spirit through likenesses of bodily things, but the mind’s office is added so that they are understood. The spirit of man is a power of the soul lower than mind, in which likenesses of bodily things are impressed but not understood by the mind’s vitality. What is seen not imaginally but properly, and not [Col. 0020C] through body, is seen by mind alone: justice, truth, wisdom, and similar things. Isaiah’s vision is therefore intellectual and perhaps at times spiritual and intellectual together. He calls what is described in this volume his vision. Thus it is clear why he begins, “The vision of Isaiah, son of Amos,” and adds nothing about bodily vision: the meaning of the heavenly oracle which he expounds is itself the intellectual vision he narrates. Prophets were called seers because of visions of this sort—that is, understanders.

Beginning to narrate his vision, he says:

## Verse 2

“Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken: I have nourished and exalted sons, but they have despised me.”

All who held the office of preaching in the Synagogue are rightly called heavens, because they were believed to know heavenly things. The Jewish people is called earth. Thus Moses, stirring priests and people to the words of his warning, said: “Hear, O heavens, the things I speak” (Deuteronomy 32:1), calling the ranks of superiors heavens and the subject people earth. Isaiah addresses heavens and earth for the same reason. He commands heavens to hear but earth to give ear. In holy Scripture hearing is not the sound that reaches the ear but what is received by the heart. Thus the Lord says, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matthew 11:15). He hears who [Col. 0021A] receives words of truth by understanding them in the ear of the heart; he gives ear who hears the sound of words with bodily ears but does not grasp their inward sense. Because priests and teachers must understand mysteries, while the people draw only the bare surface of history through bodily hearing, heavens are commanded to hear and earth to give ear. This is to be observed in all Scriptures whenever these two expressions are joined.

The heavens are therefore warned to hear and earth to give ear because God complains: “I have nourished and exalted sons, but they have despised me.” Whom does he call sons except the Jews, of whom Moses says: “The Lord saw and was provoked to anger because his sons and daughters provoked him” (Deuteronomy 32:19)? He nourished them, feeding them manna in the wilderness forty years; [Col. 0021B] he exalted them in the land promised to their fathers, as Paul says: “The God of the people Israel chose our fathers and exalted the people” (Acts 13:17). But they despised him because they rejected his law, sacrificed to demons, and finally dishonored his only Son.

## Verse 3

“The ox knew its owner, and the ass its lord’s manger; but Israel did not know me, my people did not understand.”

What was the ox except the Jewish people, whose neck the yoke of the law wore down? What was the ass except the Gentiles, whom any deceiver who found them, like a brute animal offering no rational resistance, subjected by error wherever he wished? The ox knew its owner and [Col. 0021C] the ass its lord’s manger, because the Hebrew people found God, whom it worshipped yet did not know, and the Gentiles received the fodder of law which they had not possessed. The manger here fittingly means holy Scripture, in which holy animals are fed with the food of the Word; the Psalmist says of them, “Thy animals shall dwell therein” (Psalm 67:11).

The Lord too, when born, was found by shepherds in a manger (Luke 2:16), because his Incarnation is recognized in the Scripture through which prophets refresh us.

Thus the Hebrew people, tamed under the yoke of the law, knew its owner, Christ present in the flesh. The ass, the Gentile people, given to pleasures and [Col. 0021D] more stupidly brutish [Note: both codices explicitly have this reading], knew its lord’s manger: God’s Scripture, in which it received the food of life. But Israel, that part of the Jewish people which preferred to persist in unbelief, did not know the same owner. “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8). The people who were God’s peculiar possession did not understand the majesty hidden in flesh. Above all others they ought to have understood him; while others recognized him, it alone, having lost the light of the heart, did not understand God’s hidden coming.

It must not be passed over that the great Isaiah prophesies the same Savior’s coming not only in voice and person [Col. 0022A] but also in his own name. Isaiah means “salvation of the Lord,” Christ, of whom the Lord himself promised: “My salvation is near, that it may come” (Isaiah 56:1). Isaiah’s father was called Amos; Amos means strong or mighty. Who is strong and mighty except the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ? Amos also means “tearing away a people.” God the Father tore the Jewish people from their land because of the Savior’s killing and scattered them captive among all nations. Thus Isaiah, son of Amos, signifies the only-begotten Son of the supreme Father.

Isaiah saw a vision over Judah and Jerusalem. Christ saw a vision over us—that is, he foresaw our salvation and looked upon us by the illumination of his grace—when, praying for disciples, he added: “I pray not for these only, [Col. 0022B] but also for those who will believe in me through their word” (John 17:20). Judah means confessing or confession. The Lord saw a vision over Judah when he said: “Everyone who confesses me before men, the Son of Man also will confess before the angels of God” (Luke 12:8). Jerusalem means vision of peace. The Lord contemplated a vision over Jerusalem when he said that “many shall come from east and west and sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 8:11), and “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). There will be the perfect and perpetual vision of peace when we see without end the very fountain of peace.

[Col. 0022C] He saw this vision in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah. These four kings fittingly signify the four Evangelists, of whom John says: “The first living creature was like a lion, the second like a calf, the third had a face as of a man, and the fourth was like a flying eagle” (Revelation 4:7). Uzziah, meaning “strength of the Lord,” may mystically be the creature like a lion. Jotham, meaning “consummated,” is like the calf, because the calf was customarily consumed in God’s sacrifice. Ahaz, meaning in our language “continent,” is the creature with a human face, because it belongs to man to be continent and chaste. [Col. 0022D] Hezekiah, meaning “grasping the Lord,” is like the flying eagle: the fourth Evangelist grasped the Lord by probing more deeply the secrets of his incomprehensible divinity, just as the eagle flies higher than all other birds and looks into the reflected rays of the sun. These living creatures—the holy Evangelists—are rightly called kings of Judah because through them holy Church is ruled until the end of the world.

In their days Isaiah, our Savior, sees the vision over Judah and Jerusalem as said, because while living bodily on earth [Col. 0023A] he raised the eyes of mercy over all who would believe. His vision is unfolded in this prophetic book because this book sufficiently foretold whatever he decreed to do for believers of the New Testament. Every mystery of evangelical grace is foretold in this volume [Note: the Cruciger codex reads “announced beforehand”]. As Isaiah bore the Savior’s type by person and name, so he prefigured him by preaching. Thus the Savior immediately begins through him to open his vision: “Hear, O heavens, what I speak, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken: I have nourished and exalted sons, but they have despised me.”

He narrates a vision when he speaks what he saw or heard with the Father. Since he descended from heavenly things to lowly things for us, he shows this descent at the beginning of his speech. [Col. 0023B] He who from the beginning teaches angels in the heights has now come to teach humans on earth; therefore he beautifully begins, “Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth.” By heavens are signified angelic spirits made in heavenly places; by earth, human nature, which is from earth. Thus in our prayer we are taught to say in the Savior’s voice, “Thy will be done as in heaven and on earth” (Matthew 6:10), that God’s will may be done in humanity as it is by higher nature and observed by human weakness.

[Col. 0023C] Heavens can also signify the minds of the elect, raised by inward love above every earthly contagion. Though their bodies dwell below, their hearts already cling above, truthfully saying, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20). Earth can signify sinners, because to sinful man it was said, “Thou art earth, and to earth thou shalt go” (Genesis 3:19). Or it can signify not the sinful and reprobate but those occupied in earthly actions who arrive at eternal life through alms and tears. Thus heaven and earth mean angelic and human nature, or just and sinners, or contemplative and active persons [Note: the Cruciger codex reads “thus angelic and human”]. All are commanded to hear God’s complaint about ungrateful children, so that every rational creature may witness their depravity.

[Col. 0023D] For he says: “I have nourished and exalted sons, but they have despised me.” Whom does he call sons except those whom the Church begets through water and Spirit? He himself nourishes them in faith and heavenly teaching and exalts them so that they seek “the things above, not the things upon earth” (Colossians 3:1). “He has raised us up together and made us sit in heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:6). Yet after benefits so great, alas, we despise him because we scorn the words of his preachers, through whom his only-begotten Son says: “He who hears you hears me; and he who despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16).

Thus those carnal people who are reckoned by the [Col. 0024A] Christian name, but seek to dishonor the prelates of the Church rather than obey them, are themselves the ungrateful sons of whom the Lord complained that he was despised by them. What follows can also fittingly be understood of them.

“The ox knew its owner, and the ass its lord’s manger; but Israel did not know me, my people did not understand.” For the one whom the Hebrew and Gentile peoples quickly recognized as God and to whose grace they readily hastened from their former observance, this people of false Christians—nourished with the milk of the flesh from the breasts of holy Church and born of Christian parents—was unable to know. For “he who says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 2:4); and “He who does not love does not know God, because God is love” (1 John 4:8). [Col. 0024B] This multitude of people, then, which has faith without charity and good works, by no means sees God [Note: the Garsten codex reads “by no means knew the Lord”]; nevertheless it is called Israel, that is, “seeing God,” because the one whom it does not know through love and good works it sees to some extent through faith. Here it is fittingly added, whether in the voice of the prophet or of the Lord:

VERS. 4.—“Woe to the sinful nation, to a people weighed down with iniquity, to an evil seed, to wicked sons.”

“Woe” denotes everlasting grief and groaning [Note: [Col. 0024D] Garst. codex: “or groaning.”], and the bitterness of eternal punishment. Although he declares that there is no difference between sin and iniquity when he says, “Everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity, and iniquity is sin” (1 John [Col. 0024C] 3:4), nevertheless, in ordinary speech iniquity conveys more than sin; every person freely admits himself a sinner, but is sometimes ashamed to call himself unjust. Wickedness, moreover, is so called from *nequicquam* (“to no purpose”), because through it each person tends toward non-being. Crime, however, exceeds the weight of sin, since we ordinarily call murderers and similar offenders criminal. By every sin a person offends God, to whom every sin is displeasing; by iniquity he is burdened as with a load of great weight; by wickedness he fails away, becomes far from the true being of God, cools from eternal love, and burns in the desire of temporal things; by crime he practices cruelty. To the people of Jews [Col. 0024D] or Christians entangled in such faults, therefore, the woe of unending torment and eternal bitterness is promised. Hence he adds:

“They have forsaken the Lord, they have blasphemed the Holy One of Israel; they have become estranged backward.” The Jews forsook the Lord, as it was said to them through Jeremiah: “You have all forsaken me, says the Lord” (Jeremiah 2:29). Christ is the Holy One of Israel, to whom the crowds sang: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel!” (John 12:13). For he is by nature the Holy of holies, “whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world” [Col. 0025A] (John 10:36). The Jews blasphemed him, saying, “He has a demon and is mad” (ibid.). For blasphemy is that by which false things are said concerning God himself. They too became estranged from God backward, as at last they say to him when repenting: “We have become as at the beginning, when you did not rule over us, nor was [Note: [Col. 0025D] Garst. codex: “nor was [not] invoked.”] your name invoked over us” (Isaiah 63:19).

But many who are reckoned by the Christian profession also forsake the Lord, when, abandoning heavenly things, they seek earthly things. For, having deserted love for the Creator, they love the creature; having abandoned heavenly joys, they delight in weak things; and, having left the things above, all that they thirst for is earthly. Of these, then, it may truly be said that they have forsaken the Lord. They have also blasphemed [Col. 0025B] the Holy One of Israel, because they speak many foolish things concerning God, frequently dare to criticize his judgments, and say that many things are not well ordered and are not rightly done by him. And they are estranged backward, because they return to their former iniquities and are alien from God [Note: [Col. 0026D] Garst. codex: “become alien.”]. For them it would be “better not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them” (2 Peter 2:21). He rebukes them when he adds:

VERS. 5.—“For what shall I strike you further, as you add transgression?”

“For what,” that is, for what sin, “shall I strike you further,” he says—that is, by what fault shall I try to amend you with blows—you who do not improve by the blow, but multiply your faults still further and add transgressions to transgressions? For whoever, when reproved for his fault, murmurs, adds transgressions; so does the person who, instead of abandoning the vices for which he was reproved, is inflamed all the more by the fires of impatience because of the evils he undergoes for correction. Hence it follows:

“Every head is sick, and every heart sorrowful.” The head of the inward person is the mind. Mind differs from heart, because a certain higher power of the soul is called mind, where reason abides and truth is seen. The heart, however, is in a manner fleshly, because there human will and affection properly have their place. [Col. 0025D] Thus the head of transgressors is sick, because the mind of those who willingly commit forbidden acts is weakened by the sickness of sin. And where the head is sick, the heart becomes sorrowful; for if the mind has lost its health and, through sloth and acedia, its desire begins to languish from its attention to heavenly things, immediately the heart becomes sorrowful and sad because of what it suffers for its correction, and murmurs against the scourges. The heart cannot grieve amid adversities unless the mind is sick; rather, with Paul it will glory in tribulations. But in these of whom he speaks, when the head is weakened, sickness has invaded all the limbs, because once their mind has been debilitated by the disease of sin, [Col. 0026A] every member of their actions is weakened by the same spiritual disease. For it follows:

VERS. 6.—“From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no soundness in him.”

And what is signified by the sole except every lowest thing and the smallest action? What, indeed, is expressed by the crown except the height of faith? Thus Jeremiah says to such a soul: “Even the sons of Memphis and Tahpanhes [al., Taphnes] have violated you unto the crown” (Jeremiah 2:16). To be violated unto the crown is, after the practice of evil works, to be corrupted even in the very height of faith. When most wicked spirits entangle a person’s soul in perverse works but cannot injure the integrity of faith, they pollute, as it were, the lower limbs only and do not reach the crown. But whoever is corrupted in faith is now violated unto the crown. For the malignant spirit reaches from the lower members, as it were, to the summit when, defiling the active life, it corrupts the chaste loftiness of faith by the sickness of unbelief. Fitly, therefore, it is said of each such person that from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no soundness in him, because the sickness of sin has occupied everything from his lowest action to the highest loftiness of faith. To those who pursue in conduct what they venerate in belief, divine judgment often grants that by living wickedly they lose what they believed soundly. For they continually defile themselves with perverse [Col. 0026C] actions and, in addition, distrust that the retribution of judgment can be exacted. And often, though they understand how to live well, they lapse into faithlessness even when no one persecutes them. For those who do not believe that a strict judgment is impending, who suppose that they may sin with impunity, how can they either be or be called faithful? To have lost faith is to disbelieve that fitting punishments can be rendered for uncorrected evil works. The people of the Jews also lost faith, because, while they scorned to perform works worthy of faith, blinded by their malice they did not believe that the Redeemer whom they had believed would come had come. Thus whether it is understood of the people of the Jews or of false Christians, or of each individual among them, the saying is fitting: From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no soundness in him. For [Col. 0026D] the ancient serpent spreads its deadly poison through all the limbs of his actions, beginning with the smallest and gradually reaching to the highest. But that sickness grows strong beyond remedy because no medicine has been applied to it. For it follows:

“A wound and a bruise and a swelling sore have not been bound up, nor treated with medicine, nor softened with oil.” Their bodies, he says, either gape with wounds, grow black-and-blue with blows, or swell with sores. What should be understood by the name of wound except the blow of lust, of which it is written, “He has wounded my loins” (Job 16:14)?—“For she has cast down many wounded, and all the strongest have been cast down by her,” as Solomon [Col. 0027A] says (Proverbs 7:26). What, indeed, is denoted by the word bruise except envy, which makes the mind livid while it is inwardly tortured by another’s goods? And what is the swelling sore except the sickness of pride, which makes the mind wounded and puffed up? Let us assign each thing to each, and say: the wound has not been bound up, nor the bruise treated with medicine, nor the swelling sore softened with oil.

The wound is bound up when lust, which wounds both conscience and flesh, is restrained by continence, as the Lord commanded: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35). On the contrary, this prophet reproaches one who has lost chastity: “There is no longer a girdle for you” (Isaiah 23:10). The bruise of wasting envy is cured by the medicine of benevolence when Paul says: “Let all bitterness, and anger, and indignation, and clamor, and blasphemy be taken away from you, with all malice; but be kind to one another, compassionate” (Ephesians 4:31–32). And the swelling sore of pride is softened with oil so that it may recover health—that is, with the sweet soothing of sacred admonition—when the Lord gently says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29; the source prints ‘I, 29’). But the wound, bruise, and swelling sore of the Jews or of this multitude of carnal Christians is neither bound up nor treated with medicine nor softened with oil, because no superior in the Synagogue, and now scarcely any at all in the Church, is found who seeks the salvation of the souls [Col. 0027C] of the flock entrusted to him and endeavors to apply spiritual medicines to wounds of the mind. For as spiritual physicians, priests ought by restraining and binding on every side to bind up the wound of fornication, to cure the bruise of envy with the medicine of the Scriptures, and to soften with oil—that is, with a sweet and gracious admonition which soothes and anoints the mind—those who, puffed up by the understanding of their flesh, bear within their breast the swelling sore of pride or vain glory. This does not mean that the proud person, when occasion requires, ought not to be struck with hard rebuke; but that one who is high-minded and cannot otherwise be touched should be calmed, as it were, by certain charms of sacred admonition, so that he may be healed by the gentleness of humility.

[Col. 0027D] But if the individual words are not assigned to their individual meanings as has been shown, and someone perhaps understands something else by the names wound, bruise, and swelling sore, every wound of sin must first be bound up by checking and restraining it; next it must be treated with the sharp medicine of repentance; and, when the sinner has afflicted himself in repentance, he must be softened with the oil of merciful consolation lest he despair. Thus the Samaritan, that is, the Lord Jesus, intending to heal the wounded man, that is, the human race, “bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine” (Luke 10:35). He bound up the wounds by forbidding sins; he poured in the wine of sharpness by terrifying sinners with the punishment of future condemnation. The evils of the wicked are still being described when he adds:

[Col. 0028A] VERS. 7.—“Your land is desolate; your cities are burned with fire.”

And what is signified by land except the flesh, which was made from the earth? Hence it is sung in the psalm: “Truth has sprung up from the earth” (Psalm 84:12), that is, Christ was born of the Virgin. The land of our body ought to be cultivated by the exercise of sacred disciplines, so that it may produce the fruit of good works; all its members ought to be devoted to divine acts and serve the command of their Creator. If these things are lacking in us, then it may also be said to us: Your land is desolate. For their land is desolate whose flesh is not occupied with sacred disciplines and actions.

What, however, are the cities of this land except the senses [Col. 0028B] of the body—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch? Thus the Lord says to the faithful servant: “Be you over five cities” (Luke 19:19). The cities, then, are burned with fire when the flame of vices burns up the five senses of the body: when the eyes willingly gaze on women’s forms and the ears delightfully hear wanton words; when the mouth eagerly takes unlawful tastes, the nostrils feed on forbidden fragrances, and the hands delight in touching what belongs to sin. The cities of those whose senses are thus inflamed by the heat of desires are certainly burned with fire. Still worse things are shown to happen to them when he adds:

“Strangers devour your region before your eyes, [Col. 0028C] and it shall be made desolate as in an enemy’s devastation.” What is expressed by the name of region except the breadth of their way of life? Of such regions it was said to the apostles: “Lift up your eyes and see the regions, for they are already white for harvest; and he who reaps receives a reward and gathers fruit unto eternal life” (John 4:35–36). The strangers are malignant spirits, eternally estranged from the lot of the elect. These strangers devour their region before their eyes because malignant spirits now wholly plunder their way of life, no longer lying in ambush secretly while they are unaware. For they use violence against some who know it, since they often take away good works in such a manner that the one suffering the violence sees with grief that he is losing them. Often the soul groans; yet, overcome by pleasures of the flesh, it loses the good things it had done though it loves them; it considers the losses it suffers, yet cannot resist the violence of demons plundering its goods. Against others it is unnecessary for them to use violence, because they always find them ready to obey their will. Thus strangers devour this people’s region before their eyes, because unclean spirits consume all the goods of their way of life while they see it.

And that region of their way of life shall be desolated as in an enemy’s devastation, because the ancient enemy rushes upon it with the whole army of vices, in order to destroy and scatter with barbarous cruelty whatever green or fruitful thing remains in it, whatever beautiful or useful, whatever just and good. It follows:

VERS. 8.—“And the daughter of Zion shall be left as a shelter [Col. 0029A] in a vineyard, and as a hut in a cucumber field, and as a city that is laid waste.”

Because Zion means “watchtower,” the daughter of Zion is the soul that used to dwell on high as on a watchtower and, foreseeing the approach of temptations by watchful circumspection, repelled them. For it watched and provided for itself in this way while it had Christ dwelling within, who makes the minds he inhabits watchful and solicitous for their own guarding. But now it is said to be left as a shelter in a vineyard and as a hut in a cucumber field. In the vineyard shelter a keeper stays to guard it by day and night, and when he departs the shelter remains empty. Likewise this daughter of Zion had God the indwelling keeper within her, while her actions, which can be understood by the vineyard, abounded in good fruits. But because strangers now devour the region of her way of life and she ceases to have the fruit of righteousness in her actions, she is left by God, as the vineyard shelter is deserted by its keeper. “For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit and withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding, and will be reproved by the coming iniquity” (Wisdom 1:5). And she shall be left as a hut in a cucumber field because, just as the keeper leaves the hut in the morning once the cucumbers have failed from the garden, so God will leave her because the sweetnesses of spiritual fruits, like cucumbers, now fail in her life and conduct.

She will also be left as a city that is laid waste. For just as the inhabitants [Col. 0029C] who can escape flee from a city seized by enemies and leave it to the enemy to be destroyed without resistance, so the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit depart from this soul when the ancient enemy enters it and leave it to be plundered and destroyed by demons. Every soul that through its own negligence is invaded by malignant spirits and abandoned by Christ suffers such things. Then immediately the voice of those who have suffered them is added, saying:

VERS. 9.—“Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have been as Sodom and like Gomorrah [Note: [Col. 0029D] Codex G.: “a seed, we would have been as Sodom and Gomorrah.”].”

For all the Sodomites and Gomorrheans “were sinners and exceedingly wicked” (Genesis 13:13), and therefore deserved to perish together. If, then, in this [Col. 0029D] multitude of carnal persons there were only reprobate sinners, whom the fire of Gehenna will devour, this people would be as Sodom and Gomorrah. But lest it become altogether like Sodom and Gomorrah, a seed is left to it, because from the multitude of evil people some good ones are born and reserved to furnish an example of holiness. Therefore, lest all religion in this people perish together as it did among the Sodomites and iniquity alone reign, a seed is left to be saved. For though the multitude of reprobates always abounds excessively in this world, especially near the end of the world [Note: [Col. 0030D] Codex G.: “the world’s end.”], nevertheless the elect are never all withdrawn so that only [Col. 0030A] the perverse remain, as in Sodom; rather, in every age righteous persons are left to show the others examples of goodness.

He calls God the Lord of hosts because he exercises every judgment upon human beings through angels; and at his command not only the host of good angels serve, to watch over and raise up the elect, but also that of evil angels, to deceive and oppress the impenitent and reprobate. The prophet has spoken these things concerning the wickedness of those who, ceasing to seek heavenly things, fall away from good works and, pursuing only what belongs to the world for the sake of the present life, become entangled in countless sins. For in the earlier parts of this volume he says much about those who look behind them and turn back.

[Col. 0030B] Historically, from the words “Your land is desolate” to those “As a city that is laid waste,” the destruction of the Jewish homeland, carried out by the Romans, was foretold: when under Vespasian their land was made desolate, their cities burned, and their entire region devoured before them by an army of foreigners; when Jerusalem, besieged and captured by his son Titus, was left like a hut in a cucumber field and like a city being laid waste. And unless the Lord of hosts had left them a seed, they would have been as Sodom or Gomorrah; for unless Christ had left there after his Passion the apostles and those who believed through their word, only reprobates would have remained there, as in Sodom. But because their perversity grew to such a degree that they expelled [Col. 0030C] all believers from their borders, the prophet adds and addresses them thus:

VERS. 10.—“Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; give ear to the law of our God, people of Gomorrah.”

Priests, Pharisees, and scribes were therefore rightly called princes of Sodom, and the Synagogue the people of Gomorrah. For just as the Sodomites “surrounded the house of holy Lot, from boy to old man, the whole people together” (Gen. 19:1), and, so that they themselves might be destroyed from the earth, righteous Lot with his wife and daughters was led out from their midst; so too all these men assailed the primitive Church in a united conspiracy, and, so that they alone who were to perish might remain, they caused Christ with all his followers to depart from them [Col. 0030D]. And because in their blindness they thought that they were doing these things, as it were, out of zeal for the Law, they are rightly summoned to hear the Law. For the lawgiver had said concerning Christ: “For the Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren, like myself; you shall hear him according to all things whatsoever he shall say to you” (Deut. 18:15). And he whom the lawgiver commanded to be heard in all things says: “The Law and the Prophets were until John; from that time the kingdom of God is preached” (Luke 16:16). They are therefore rightly commanded to hear the word of the Lord and receive the Law with their ears, and are reproved from the Law as transgressors—those who still wished to observe carnally the Law which he teaches to have been brought to its end, he whom Moses teaches must be heard in all things whatsoever he should say. Hence, immediately rejecting all the things customarily offered and celebrated according to the Law, the Lord adds:

**VERSE 11.**—“What is the multitude of your victims to me? says the Lord. I am full,” etc.

Why, he says, do you bring me the multitude of your carnal victims? I have no need of your gifts, because I am full of every good thing. The remaining words now added concerning the rejection of such offerings and solemn observances, since they are evident, we judge it superfluous to expound according to the letter. For these sacrifices were once necessary in their own time because of the meaning of the prophetic mysteries which they contained. But since the Law and the Prophets have ceased to prophesy, and the things that had been prophesied have appeared, they now confer no benefit, but rather provoke God to wrath; and thus they are rejected, because, when the sun comes, the shadow flees away. Setting these matters aside, therefore, let us return to the spiritual understanding. For he says:

“Hear the word of the Lord, princes of Sodom; receive with your ears the Law of our God, people of Gomorrah.” And whom he now calls princes of Sodom and people of Gomorrah is clear from what precedes: namely, those of whom he said above, “Woe to the sinful nation, a people burdened with iniquity, an evil seed, wicked sons”; and: “From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no soundness in it” [Col. 0031A], and the other things which he there said. Those who are such are rightly designated by so abhorrent a name, because they have lost all holiness and are filled with every wickedness, being devoted to their iniquities both privately and publicly. Yet they are commanded to hear the word of the Lord and receive his Law with their ears, so that there they may recognize that they, together with all that they do, stand condemned. For these words are not spoken to those who wholly do not know God, but rather to those who “profess that they know God, but deny him by their works, being abominable, unbelieving, and reprobate for every good work” (Titus 1:16).

Yet it often happens that men of this kind give themselves to fasts and afflict themselves in many ways. But because both their mind and conscience are defiled, and they do nothing with a single-hearted purpose, none of their abstinences, afflictions, or works can please God. Hence the rebuke follows: “What is the multitude of your victims to me? says the Lord. I am full.” They sacrifice a multitude of victims who subdue the flesh in many ways. But where crimes reign in the heart, or even sometimes in deeds, the inward Judge of minds and inspector of hidden acts cannot approve outward decency. For he does not accept the gifts of outward conduct when he condemns their hearts, nor praise works displayed externally when he condemns what has taken place in secret; and he who is full of his own good things is not fed by an outward gift. He further adds:

“I have not desired the holocausts of rams, and the fat of fatlings, and the blood of calves, lambs, and he-goats.” In our language *holocaust* means “wholly burned.” For *holon* means “whole,” and *caustis*, “burning”; from these compounded parts comes *holocaust*, that is, “wholly burned.” Therefore he offers a holocaust who kindles his whole self in prayer with the fire of compunction. But God has not desired holocausts of rams. Rams indeed rule the flocks. And what are now figured by rams except those who, placed among innocent and simple people as among sheep, consider themselves better than them, set themselves above them, and desire to claim for themselves something like dominion among them? Their striving is exceedingly perverse, because, while they seek to show or set themselves above others, they imitate him who, despising the common life of the angels, wished through pride to become higher than all, saying: “I will exalt my throne above the stars of God” (Isa. 14:13)—that is, above the angels [Col. 0032B].

The holocausts of rams are therefore rejected, because the prayers of the proud are not received, even when they sometimes set themselves wholly aflame for an hour with the fire of compunction. For prayer, if it is to be received by God, must rise from the root of humility, and the heart must thereafter persevere in humility. The leaders of heretics may also be understood by the rams; if they offer the holocausts of which we have spoken, they are not received. For the subject is not now evil Catholics only, but also certain heretics [Col. 0032C].

What, moreover, is expressed by the fat of fatlings except the tears of those who pray? For whoever does not weep in prayer offers a lean victim; but whoever pours forth tears in prayer sacrifices a fat victim. And among heretics there are some who appear more religious, seeming to occupy themselves with prayers and tears. But the Lord makes clear that he does not at all approve their weeping and supplications when he testifies that he has not desired the fat of fatlings. He has not desired the blood of calves, lambs, and he-goats either. The blood of victims used always to be offered to the Lord, while their flesh was eaten. And since sin is customarily understood by blood [Col. 0032D], what is signified by the pouring out of blood that was offered except confession of sin?

By calves, we may understand proud powers of this world, oppressors of the humble, and those abandoned to harmful freedom; for Jeremiah says to the Chaldeans: “You rejoice and speak proudly, plundering my inheritance, because you have poured yourselves out like calves upon the grass and bellow [variant: *mugistis*, “you have bellowed”] like bulls” (Jer. 50:11). By lambs, the wanton; for Solomon, speaking of a prostitute, adds concerning the lustful man: “Immediately he follows her like an ox led to sacrifice, and like a frolicking lamb” (Prov. 7:22). By he-goats, any sinners whatever; for the Judge “will set the sheep indeed at your right hand, but the goats at the left” (Matt. 29:33). God therefore has not desired the blood of calves, lambs, and he-goats: that is, he has never approved the confession of those who are abandoned to harmful freedom like calves grazing upon others’ goods, who follow wantonness like lambs, or of the rest of the sinners signified by goats [Col. 0033A]. For they customarily confess their sins in such a way that they do not wish wholly to abandon them, but only to interrupt them for a time and afterward repeat them; or they still retain some sins in their heart while confessing others; or their mind is held captive by some error. Therefore, when they bring these and similar sacrifices to the Church, as follows, the Lord says to them:

**VERSE 12.**—“When you come before my sight, who has required these things from your hands, that you should walk in my courts?”

For it was said above concerning this people that from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head—that is, from the least and most external action to the height of faith—there is no soundness in it. These words are therefore now suitably understood as addressed to those who perform infirm deeds and do not hold sound faith: namely, to followers of the heresy of Simon, who sell or buy ordinations, churches, and other sacred things, or consent to dealers in such matters. For when they have assembled in a purchased Church and offered their oblations, the Lord says to them, as has been stated: “When you come before my sight, who has required these things from your hands, that you should walk in my courts?” For God never requires or accepts these things from their hands. “For without faith it is impossible to please God” [Col. 0033C] (Heb. 11:6). Hence he adds:

**VERSE 13.**—“Do not bring sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0033D] Codex G: *sacrificia*, ‘sacrifices’.] any longer in vain.”

“Any longer,” that is, after you have seized this place through the simoniacal heresy, do not now offer sacrifice in it, because it has been profaned. Or “any longer,” that is, after you have been infected by Simon’s poisons, do not bring sacrifice, because I shall no longer receive it from your hands, since you are always regarded as reprobate in the priesthood. It follows:

“Incense is an abomination to me.” The incense offered by such persons in such a place is detested by the Lord. Likewise, he shows that he abhors all their solemn observances, adding: “The new moon, the Sabbath, and other festivals I will not endure: your assemblies are iniquitous.”

**VERSE 14.**—“Your calends and your solemnities my soul has hated; they have become burdensome to me; I have laboured in bearing them.”

For what is expressed by the new moon, the Sabbath, the calends, and solemnities, except everything which is celebrated festively by such persons? Let Simoniacs or other heretics then hold ever so great and frequent solemnities [Note: [Col. 0033D] Manuscripts: “solemnities, because they are exceedingly hateful to God,” etc.]; beyond doubt they are exceedingly hateful to God. For the assemblies of those gathered in their festivals are iniquitous, because all are infected by the poison of heretical impiety [Col. 0034A], and therefore whatever they do is abominated by the Lord.

We may, however, apply these things to evil Catholics. For by the name of incense the power of prayer is expressed, as the Psalmist says: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight” (Ps. 140:2). Thus, rejecting the prayer of the wicked, the Lord says: “Incense is an abomination to me.” For according to Solomon: “He who turns away his ear lest he hear the Law, his prayer shall be execrable” (Prov. 28:9).

Now *Neomenia* is a Greek word: *neon* (νέον) means “new,” while *mēnē* (μήνη) means “moon.” Hence, by the compound name *Neomenia* is called the feast of the new moon, which the Hebrews [Note: [Col. 0034D] Codex G: “Jews.”] observe at the beginning of the months. Thus *Neomenia* means “new moon” [Col. 0034B]. And what is the new moon except a new life? There are some who, apparently struck by the voice of preaching, change their dress but not their disposition; they put on religious clothing, yet do not trample underfoot their former vices; they grow proud because of certain good things displayed before human eyes; they eagerly seek the gains of this present world; and from the outward habit alone which they have assumed, they derive confidence in holiness. The new moon of such persons—that is, the pretence of a new manner of life—is burdensome to God.

What should be understood by the Sabbath except cessation from evil works? (Exod. 31:15.) For on the Sabbath one was commanded to cease from outward action. But one who outwardly rests from a perverse deed while inwardly labours under wicked desires has a Sabbath burdensome to God [Col. 0034C]. He also keeps a festival who praises God with an exulting heart. But the festival of praise of the man concerning whom it is written, “He will praise you when you have done well to him” (Ps. 48:19), is not pleasing to God, because he praises in prosperity and murmurs in adversity, loving God more on account of present goods than future ones. The Lord therefore rightly says to those who, under an appearance of righteousness, serve their vices—“having indeed the appearance of godliness, but denying its power” (2 Tim. 3:5)—that he will not endure their new moon, Sabbath, and other festivals, and that his soul, that is, his will, has hated their calends and solemnities. Or, since God is exterior to all bodies and interior to all minds, that very power of his by which he penetrates and orders all things is called his soul [Col. 0034D].

This distinction may, however, be made between calends and the new moon: the new moon is a new manner of life, whereas the calends are a beginning. But when he says, “My soul has hated your calends,” he execrates the beginnings of those who turn to faith as Simon Magus did (Acts 8), or who turn to the common life as Ananias and his wife did, who committed fraud concerning the price of their land (Acts 5). He detests the beginnings of those who purchase monastic life or a canonry [Note: [Col. 0034D] Codex G: *canonicam*, “canonical [life/office].”] or ordination. He condemns the beginnings of those who come to the monastic order not with the intention of pleasing God but for some other purpose [Col. 0035A]. In short, he rebukes all who begin a good work with an evil intention. Thus he execrates the evil beginnings of all such persons when he declares that he hates their calends.

Nor does he abominate only the calends of such beginnings, but also the solemnities of their subsequent thoughts, by which they rejoice that they have begun in this manner, or rejoice to retain what they began in this way and to persevere in the same evil. By contrast, it is said of the penitent: “For the thought of man shall confess to you, and the remnant of thought shall celebrate solemnities for you” [Note: [Col. 0035D] Elsewhere: “shall keep a festival day for you.”] (Ps. 75:11). The first thought of the penitent, therefore, is that which condemns the former life and begins to confess; but the remnant of thought is that which celebrates solemnities to God, so that one who has been freed from sins may always give thanks to the Deliverer, remembering the evils from which he has been delivered [Col. 0035B]. Therefore, just as the first thought of one confessing is pleasing to God, and the remnant of thought celebrates solemn thanksgivings for his deliverance, so the calends of these persons’ evil beginning and the solemnities of thoughts continuing in the same intention are hateful to him.

He also declares that he has laboured, because for a long time he has borne their stubborn perversities. In himself he remains always tranquil and unchangeable; yet, as has been said, he says that he has laboured because he has long endured their stubborn iniquities with weariness. They also sometimes make lengthy prayers, yet are not corrected from their perversities. Hence it follows:

**VERSE 15.**—“When you stretch forth your hands, I will turn my eyes away from you; and when you multiply prayer, I will not hear: for your hands are full of blood.”
