Those who pray customarily stretch their hands on high. But God does not deign to look upon the stretching forth of wicked hands, and refuses to hear their prayer, however much it is multiplied. For he hears prayer not because of its length but because of pure devotion. Hence he commands his own in the Gospel: “When praying, do not speak much as the heathen do; for they think that they shall be heard because of their many words. Therefore do not be like them” (Matt. 6:7) [Col. 0035D]. Prayer is therefore multiplied in vain by wicked people, because the Lord weighs not the speech of the mouth but the affection of the heart, and their life stands in the way of their prayers being heard. For their hands are full of blood: their works cause their prayers to be rejected by the Lord, and the hands of their actions are full of the blood of the souls whom they kill. To these persons God has thus far spoken in his wrath; but from this point he begins to speak according to mercy, saying:

**VERSE 16.**—“Wash yourselves; be clean; take away the evil of your thoughts from before my eyes.”

Wash yourselves through repentance; be clean through continual observance of purity. For he is washed and clean who both laments past sins and admits none that need lamentation; but he is washed and not clean who laments what he has done but does not abandon it, and after tears repeats the things for which he had wept. For after washing, whoever does not preserve innocence of life after tears neglects to remain clean. Thus they are washed and by no means clean who do not cease to weep for sins committed, but again commit sins which must be wept for [Col. 0036A].

The evil of perverse thoughts must likewise be removed from before his eyes, so that a person may be most pure in his sight not only in action but also in heart. “No human being,” says Gregory (*Morals*, Book XXV, ch. 5), “sees the hidden paths of our mind; yet before the eyes of God we take as many steps as we stir affections. We stumble before him as often as we limp from the straight path with the foot of weak thought. Unless this continual fall of our minds increased before his sight, he would never cry: ‘Take away the evil of your thoughts from before my eyes.’ In saying this, he plainly testifies that he is, as it were, unable to bear the force of our concealed wickedness, which cannot be concealed from him, since whatever is illicitly thought by us in secret is importunately thrust before his sight” [Col. 0036B]. The Lord further indicates what must be done, adding: “Cease to do perversely.”

**VERSE 17.**—“Learn to do good; seek judgment; aid the oppressed; judge for the orphan; defend the widow.”

**VERSE 18.**—“And come, and rebuke me, says the Lord.”

Cease now, he says, from perverse actions, and learn from the teaching of truth to do good. Seek judgment from the wise, lest, if judgment is not rendered between disputants, the wicked prevail against the just. Mercifully aid the oppressed, and judge for the orphan—that is, defend his cause in judgment. And when you have done these things, come and rebuke me. We rebuke one whom we restrain by the authority of reason. What, then, does the Lord mean by commanding us to do holy things and adding [Note: [Col. 0036D] Codex G: “adding an admonition.”], “Come and rebuke me,” except that he plainly indicates how great a confidence good deeds confer? It is as though he openly said: Act rightly, and meet the motions of my judgment not now by the groaning of supplication but by the confidence of authority [Col. 0036D]. Thus John says: “If our heart does not rebuke us, we have confidence toward God” (1 John 3:21). Hence the Lord complains that he had one to rebuke him when he says through the prophet: “I sought among them for a man who would set a hedge and stand opposed before me, lest I should destroy it, and I found none” (Ezek. 22:30; Vulgate: “for the land”). To rebuke God, therefore, is to withstand his wrath confidently and restrain the onset of his judgment. He further indicates what those who perform the aforesaid works of mercy will receive, saying to them:

“If your sins are as scarlet, they shall be made white as snow; and if they are red as the worm, they shall be white as wool.” *Coccinum* (“scarlet”) or *coccus* is the same as *vermiculus* (“little worm,” the crimson dye-worm). When David was repenting of incest and murder, he said: “Deliver me from bloods” (Ps. 50:16). And just as enormous sins are denoted in David by the term “bloods,” so now in Isaiah they are denoted by the blood-red colour of the worm and scarlet. Snow and white wool signify the cleansing of sins and the brightness of righteousness. For the same Psalmist then says: “You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (ibid., 9). Thus, when he promises that red sins shall be made white [Col. 0037B], he undoubtedly promises that great offences will be changed into the brightness of righteousness. It follows:

**VERSE 19.**—“If you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the land.”

If, he says, you have a good will and obediently hear me, you shall eat the good things of that land of which it is said: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26:13). For while all the elements are in motion, the earth alone remains immovable and solid; therefore, by earth is suitably denoted the solidity of eternal rest. The good things of this land are the delightful joy of the heavenly country, the society of angels, the presence of the divine vision, and all the other things which neither “eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man” [Col. 0037C] has been able to conceive. The souls of the righteous eat these things when they delight in them all without end. Then the opposite is added:

**VERSE 20.**—“But if you are unwilling and provoke me to wrath, the sword shall devour you.”

If, he says, you are unwilling to do good, he does not add, “and deserve my wrath,” but, “and provoke me to wrath.” For to deserve God’s wrath is to sin even unknowingly; but to provoke him to wrath is knowingly to oppose his commands: to know the good and despise it, to be able to do it and not wish to do it. The sword signifies either the sentence of the Judge or the torment of everlasting death. For by the name of sword is understood whatever kills, whatever torments, whatever punishes, and whatever burns [Col. 0037D]. The sword, therefore, shall devour those who provoke God to wrath when they hear from him: “Depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire” (Matt. 25:41). For then, as it is written, “they shall enter into the lower parts of the earth; they shall be delivered into the hands of the sword” (Ps. 62:10). Since the holy man did not say these things from himself but heard them from God, he suitably adds: “For the mouth of the Lord has spoken.” The mouth of the Lord is heavenly inspiration, which formed in the prophet’s mind, without the sound of words, all that he himself recounted outwardly. It follows:

**VERSE 21.**—“How has the faithful city become a harlot, full of judgment? Righteousness dwelt in her, but now murderers.”

[Col. 0038A] Jerusalem was a faithful city while she faithfully awaited Christ her king, who was to come in the flesh. She was also full of judgment while right judgment was commonly practised in her. But she became a harlot when she refused to receive the King and Bridegroom whose coming she had awaited, and admitted the ancient corrupter of the soul. For she rejected her lawful husband and received an adulterer.

Righteousness once dwelt in her; but now there are murderers, who killed the Saviour himself. This was said of the period which elapsed from the Lord’s Passion to the destruction of Jerusalem, to which the following is added:

**VERSE 22.**—“Your silver has been turned into dross; your wine has been mixed with water.”

[Col. 0038B] The refuse and impurities of metals are called dross; it may also be called rust. Silver is the brightness of sacred utterance, since “the utterances of the Lord are pure utterances, silver tried by fire” (Ps. 11:7); and “the tongue of the just is choice silver” (Prov. 10:20). Dross, however, signifies the traditions of the Pharisees. Jerusalem’s silver was thus turned into dross, because sacred utterances were obscured among the Jews by the filthy interpretation of the scribes and Pharisees. Wine is the spiritual meaning of divine Scripture, by which the minds of hearers are inebriated; water is the carnal understanding of the same Scripture, as the Evangelist indicates where he relates that the Lord changed water into wine (John 2). Jerusalem’s wine was therefore mixed with water because [Col. 0038C] the meaning of the Scriptures among the Jews was diluted by the admixture of carnal understanding. It follows:

**VERSE 23.**—“Your princes are unfaithful, companions of thieves; all love gifts and pursue rewards. They do not judge for the orphan; the widow’s cause does not come before them.”

Your princes are unfaithful because they keep faith neither with God nor with man. They are companions of thieves because they are both their associates and sharers in thefts. All love gifts because they are full of avarice. They pursue rewards because they seek to receive a return from those to whom they give some benefit. They do not judge for the orphan: that is, they do not uphold his side in judgment. And the widow’s cause does not come before them because they do not deign to hear her or defend her against injuries, since she has no gifts to offer [Col. 0038D]. Such were the rulers of the Synagogue when the Saviour lived bodily upon the earth. It follows:

**VERSE 24.**—“Therefore says the Lord [Note: [Col. 0037D] Elsewhere: ‘the Lord God of hosts.’] of hosts, the Mighty One of Israel: Alas! I shall be consoled over my enemies and take vengeance on my foes.”

The Lord took vengeance upon his Jewish enemies through the Romans. Hence he calls himself the Lord of hosts, because the Roman armies, though unknowingly, served him when they killed and exterminated the Jews for his murder. He took vengeance upon them also after they were killed, because he delivered them to the punishments of Gehenna. In this vengeance the hosts of angels likewise served him [Col. 0039A]. They also experienced him as mighty whom they had considered weak in his Passion. He declared that he would be consoled in their punishment because their evil deeds grieved him. But in saying, “Alas! I shall be consoled,” he shows that he did not desire such consolation. Hence elsewhere he says: “Is the death of the wicked my will, says the Lord, and not rather that he should turn from his ways and live?” (Ezek. 18:23). For he acts unwillingly when he compels sinners by just judgment—he “who wills all men to be saved” (1 Tim. 2:4). What he says next to Jerusalem pertains only to that portion of the Israelite people which was to believe through the new preaching.

**VERSE 25.**—“And I will turn,” he says, “my hand upon you, and refine your dross to purity, and remove all your tin.”

**VERSE 26.**—“And I will restore your judges as they were at first, and your counsellors as in ancient times. After this you shall be called the city of the righteous, the faithful city.”

For he turned his hand upon the chosen portion because, leaving the unbelievers, he powerfully worked signs and miracles through those who believed, for the enlightenment of the rest. “But they went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed” (Mark 16:20).

He refined their dross to purity because, removing the rust of their former understanding, “he opened their minds [Col. 0039C] that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45). And he removed all their tin because he gradually took away from them the practice of Judaizing. For tin, which has the colour of silver but is a cheap metal, signifies the teaching of the Pharisees, which appeared similar to divine utterances. The teaching of those concerning whom it is written was tin: “But certain persons who had believed from the sect of the Pharisees rose up, saying: It is necessary to circumcise them and command them to keep the Law of Moses” (Acts 15:5). But the Lord removed this tin when Peter said: “Why do you test God by placing a yoke upon the neck of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?” (ibid., 10).

[Col. 0039D] And he restored the judges of the Church as they had been at first, because she who formerly had patriarchs, judges, and prophets received apostles, prophets, and teachers in their place. Hence elsewhere it was said to her: “Sons have been born to you in place of your fathers; you shall appoint them princes over all the earth” (Ps. 46:17). After this, no longer the Synagogue of the Jews but the city of the righteous was called such—that is, the Church of Christ, of whom it is sung that “the Lord is righteous in all his words” [Note: [Col. 0039D] Codex G: “in all his ways.”] (Ps. 144:17). He is also faithful, because the Lord is faithful in all his words. Or his city is faithful because it keeps the whole faith for its king. It follows:

[Col. 0040A] **VERSE 27.**—“Sion shall be redeemed in judgment, and they shall bring her back in righteousness.”

Sion, which means “watchtower,” is the people of the Jews [Note: [Col. 0040D] Codex G: “Hebrews.”] who awaited Christ’s coming. Christ himself, when he came, redeemed her with his blood in that judgment of discernment of which it is said: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” (Ps. 42:1); or: “Now is the judgment of the world, and now shall the prince of this world be cast out” (John 12:31). And after she was redeemed, the apostles brought her back to the grace of the Redeemer. They did this in righteousness, because it was just that the things promised to the fathers should be fulfilled in their children. Peter strove to bring her back in this righteousness when he said: “You are the children of the prophets and of the covenant which God made with our fathers, saying to Abraham: ‘And in your seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed.’ God, having raised up his Son, sent him first to you, blessing you, that each one may turn from his wickedness” (Acts 3:25–26) [Col. 0040B]. But concerning those who would not turn, the following is added:

**VERSE 28.**—“And he shall crush the wicked and sinners together.”

For the wicked—that is, those who killed the Lord—and the other sinners of that people were together crushed in the siege of Jerusalem by pestilence, famine, and swords. For he calls murderers “wicked.” Concerning those also who had abandoned the temple of the Lord and turned to idols, it follows: “And those who have forsaken the Lord [Col. 0040C] shall be consumed.”

**VERSE 29.**—“For they shall be confounded by the idols to which they sacrificed.”

For these too were consumed by the sword of the Babylonians and Assyrians, and were confounded by their idols when they could not be helped by them in time of need. Addressing them directly, he adds: “And you shall be ashamed of the gardens which you chose.”

**VERSE 30.**—“When you have become like an oak whose leaves fall away, and like a garden without water.” They had chosen gardens in whose pleasantness they might sacrifice to idols. But they were then ashamed of them when they became like an oak from which leaves fall, and like a garden not watered. For when an oak casts off its leaves, it has neither fruit nor the greenness of leaves; and a garden without water produces nothing green, but whatever had been green in it withers [Col. 0040D]. Thus they too, through the Assyrians and Chaldeans, lost all the beauty of their former adornment, the flower of glory, the freshness of vigour, and the fruit of their good things; nor did they afterward recover them in full. It follows:

**VERSE 31.**—“And your strength shall be like the ashes of tow, and your work like a spark; and both shall be kindled together, and there shall be none to quench them.”

While the Chaldeans fought and besieged Jerusalem, the strength of the Jews was crushed and dry like the ashes of tow [Col. 0041A]; and the work of their rebellion produced, like a spark, the fire by which they themselves were burned. For if they had submitted their necks to the yoke of the Chaldeans, they would not have perished. Hence Jeremiah says: “He who remains in this city shall die by sword, famine, and pestilence; but he who goes out and deserts to the Chaldeans who besiege you shall live, and his life shall be to him as spoil” (Jer. 21:9). Their work, therefore, made a fire like a spark, which burned their strength as tow; because, while they remained in Jerusalem to defend themselves, they so offended the Chaldeans that they deserved no mercy. And in that tribulation both were kindled together—their strength and their work—and there was none to quench the fire of that tribulation; instead, they were allowed to be consumed in it for a very long time [Col. 0041B]. Yet it is pleasing to reconsider the matters we have discussed.

“How,” he says, “has the faithful city, full of judgment, become a harlot? Righteousness dwelt in her, but now murderers.” The faithful city is the Church, which keeps her faith for Christ her king. She is, or was, full of judgment, judging all things rightly and weighing each thing in an even balance. “For the spiritual person judges all things” (1 Cor. 2:15). This Church, certainly, has not wholly become, nor ever will become, a harlot. But because, as the end of the world approaches, the multitude of reprobate persons is now so great within her that scarcely any righteous person appears in her, the prophet marvels how the mind of so great a multitude could be corrupted and lose the chastity which is in Christ; and he bursts into a cry of grief [Col. 0041C] and astonishment, saying: “How has the faithful city, full of judgment, become a harlot?” For the overwhelming multitude of this people that bears the name of Christianity has become a harlot, because, abandoning her lawful husband, Christ, she commits fornication with her lovers: she refuses to do the divine will and wantonly prostitutes herself in pleasures and sins to the desires of unclean spirits.

For the prophet subsequently indicates why he called her a harlot: righteousness once dwelt in her, when she was full of observance of the heavenly commandments. But now she abounds in murderers, who either strike others with the sword or hate them. For “everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” [Col. 0041D] (1 John 3:15), and every murderer is without charity. Therefore the people who have expelled righteousness from themselves and are full of murderers are rightly said to have become a harlot, because they have abandoned the charity of the Bridegroom, who is Christ, and ardently clung to adulterers, who are demons. Some priests also, who ought to correct her morals, have now been corrupted by a similar perversity, so that they themselves nourish the vices of those subject to them. Hence it follows:

“Your silver has been turned into dross; your wine has been mixed with water.” For often a teacher who dares to teach what he neglects to do, when he has ceased to speak the good things which he despised to practise, begins to teach his subjects the evil things that he does, so that by God’s just judgment he may no longer have a good tongue, since he refused to have good conduct; and thus, while he applies himself to the love of earthly things, he may always speak of earthly things and hold the place of governance as though for the profit of pleasure, not for the exercise of labour. Therefore the silver of his preaching has been turned into the dross of foul speech, because he speaks earthly things in place of heavenly, carnal things in place of spiritual, evil things in place of good.

His wine also, by which he might intoxicate others, has been mixed with water, because he softens the spiritual meaning of Holy Scripture by his own interpretation, so as to please his hearers rather than correct them; nor does he set them aflame with the fire of charity, but allows them to remain benumbed in the chill of his own sensuality. [Note: Col. 0041D, Cod. G.: “insensibility.”]

[Col. 0042B] Or rather, it is said to the people: “Your silver has been turned into dross; your wine has been mixed with water,” because now scarcely anyone speaks the divine utterances to God’s people without an admixture of falsehoods and of things which do not contribute to edification. For modern preachers do not strive to observe what Peter says: “If anyone speaks, let him speak as the utterances of God” (1 Pet. 4:11). And the silver of this people is called the silver of sacred speech, which it receives from its teachers. What follows also clearly portrays the character of those whom we now see endowed with secular power.

“Your rulers are faithless,” and the rest. For these secular rulers are faithless, because they now keep faith with scarcely anyone, but deal deceitfully with all. They are also companions of thieves, whom they protect and with whom they divide what those men steal. All not only accept but also “love gifts,” because they take thought for their subjects or help them, not out of love for justice but out of greed for money. For “they pursue recompense,” because they do good only to those from whom they hope for repayment—whereas the elect are commanded to surpass this by acts of kindness, when they hear: “If you do good to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you? For sinners also do the same. And if you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what credit is that to you? For sinners also lend to sinners, that they may receive the like in return” (Luke 6:33–34). This is to pursue recompense.

[Col. 0042D] But the aforesaid rulers “do not judge for the orphan, and the widow’s cause does not come before them,” because, while they do everything for gifts, they neglect to defend the innocence of the poor, from whom they do not hope to gain earthly profit. “Therefore,” says the Lord of hosts, the Mighty One of Israel, “Alas! I will take consolation over my enemies, and I will avenge myself upon my foes!” He who is now provoked by their evil deeds will take vengeance upon them when he is avenged upon them. Hence he is called the Lord of hosts, because he executes vengeance through angels. He is also called the Mighty One of Israel, because his mighty power will save the humble who are now afflicted and condemn the powerful who do not help them. [Note: Col. 0042D, C. Cruc.: “powers, who.”] For, as it is written, “Mercy will be granted to the lowly; but the mighty shall mightily suffer torments, and a stronger punishment awaits the stronger” (Wisdom 6:7, 9). These rulers are his enemies and foes because of the evils described as committed by them, for which the judgment of condemnation, as it is written, hangs over them. Yet these evils which he has thus far portrayed, and which we see daily multiplied among this Christian people, will, as we believe, be corrected through Elijah, because the Saviour says in the Gospel: “Elijah is to come, and he will restore all things” (Matt. 18). Hence he adds here:

“And I will turn my hand against you, and I will smelt away your dross until it is pure,” etc. For he seems to have withdrawn from this people, which now commits so many evils, the hand of his holy operation. [Note: Col. 0043D, Cod. G.: “action.”] But when Elijah comes and restores all things, he will turn his hand toward it again, that it may work holy deeds wonderfully, as of old. “And through Elijah,” he says, “I will smelt away your dross until it is pure”: that is, I will cleanse away from the Scriptures the rust of secular understanding. “And I will remove all your tin”: that is, whatever false doctrine you may possess; for Elijah will restore all things.

“And I will restore your judges as they were at first, and your counsellors as in ancient times,” so that, as at the beginning you had the apostles, at the end you may have Elijah and Enoch, like the apostles, and other eminent teachers not inferior to those who came after the apostles. After this—that is, after I have given you these—you will be called the city of the righteous and the faithful city, though you are now accused [Col. 0043C] of having become a harlot. As we have said, the vast multitude of this people became a harlot because it prostituted itself to the devil in pleasures. But after Elijah, who will restore all things, has brought it back to the chaste love of its lawful husband, it will no longer be called a harlot but the city of the righteous, that is, the people of God. And because the day of judgment will then come, he fittingly adds:

“Zion shall be redeemed in judgment,” etc. For Zion—that is, the Church of the righteous—will be redeemed from those miseries in that judgment, concerning which redemption the Saviour himself says: “Look up and lift up your heads, because your redemption draws near” (Luke 21:28). And the angels will bring her back in righteousness, because “the Son of Man will send his angels with a trumpet and a loud voice, and they will gather his elect from the four winds” (Matt. [Col. 0043D] 24:31). Then he will crush the wicked together, that is, the murderers of the saints and other sinners; and those who, deceived by Antichrist, forsook the Lord will be consumed by eternal punishments. For they will be put to shame by the idols to which they sacrificed. They are said to have sacrificed to idols because, according to the faith of John’s Apocalypse, “they worshipped the dragon who gave authority to the beast, and they worshipped the beast and its image” (Rev. 13:4 ff.); or they had its mark upon their right hand and upon their foreheads, or its name, or the number of its name (Rev. 14:9). To such idols they sacrificed their most wicked [Col. 0044A] actions; but by these they will be put to shame at the Judge’s coming. It follows:

“You shall blush because of the gardens which you chose, when you become like an oak whose leaves are falling, and like a garden without water.” Whoever wholly gives himself over to passing pleasures chooses gardens. Those chose gardens who, in the book of Wisdom, say with their like: “Come, let us enjoy the good things that exist, and use creation swiftly as in youth. Let us fill ourselves with costly wine and perfumes, and let no flower of the season pass us by. Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither. Let there be no meadow through which our luxury does not pass; let no one be excluded from our pleasure. Everywhere let us leave signs of merriment, for this is our portion and this our lot” (Wisdom 2:6 ff.). Behold how they chose the delights of gardens, and what it means to choose gardens. They will blush grievously over these when they stand, full of shame, before the tribunal of the eternal Judge. For then they will be like an oak from which the leaves fall: they will no longer have any fruit of past delight; stripped entirely of all beauty, they will remain naked and dry, fit for burning.

They will also be like a garden without water, because the sun of righteousness, appearing in judgment, will terrify them and dry up all their moisture and greenness. Hence James says: “The sun rose with burning heat and dried up the grass; its flower fell, and the beauty of its appearance perished” (James 1:11). And he added: “So also the rich man withers in his ways” (ibid.). It follows:

“Your strength shall be like the ash of tow, and your work like a spark; both shall burn together, and there shall be none to quench them.” The strength of the wicked, who trust in their own power and stoutly endure so many labours for the desires of this life, will at the resurrection be crushed and dry, fit for burning like the ash of tow. Hence it is elsewhere said: “Tow gathered together is the synagogue of sinners, and their end is a flame of fire” (Ecclus. 21:10). And their work will be like a spark when the memory of the evils that they committed begins to set them on fire, since it is written: “They will come trembling at the thought [Col. 0044D] of their sins, and their iniquities will confront and accuse them” (Wisdom 4:20). For just as a spark is nourished among tow and sets it ablaze, so the memory of their sins will become for these people the beginning of everlasting burning. And after they have heard, “Depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire” (Matt. 25:41), both will burn together in Gehenna: namely, they themselves and their work. “For what has been made will suffer punishment with the one who made it” (Wisdom 14:10), as the wise man says. And there will be none to quench it, because “their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. 66:24).

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0045A]

**VERSE 1.—**“The word which Isaiah son of Amos saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem.”

As he is about to begin a new discourse, he sets before it a new title, in order to distinguish what follows from what preceded. He says not that he heard the word, but that he saw it; because when the Lord speaks not through a subordinate creature but through himself, the heart of the hearer is taught concerning his word without words and syllables. For God’s speaking words to us, as it were, is secretly to make known those things which are to be done, and suddenly to render the uninstructed human heart learned concerning hidden things by the discourse of eternity, without the use of sound. For hearing does not grasp all at once the things which are said to it, since it receives causes through words and words bit by bit through syllables; [Col. 0045B] but sight apprehends all at once and simultaneously that toward which it is directed. Therefore God’s speech, made inwardly to us, is seen rather than heard, because, while it reveals itself without delay of utterance, it illuminates the darkness of our ignorance with sudden light. Rightly, then, did the prophet testify that he had seen the word, because in the secret realm of heavenly visions, by the most lucid perception of his mind, he knew at once the whole which he could not utter outwardly all at once. He saw, moreover, concerning Judah and Jerusalem, because he knew by divine revelation what was to come upon both Synagogue and Church. Judah first signifies the Jewish people and afterwards the Christian people; Jerusalem first signifies the Synagogue and afterwards the Church. The prophet, beginning to recount [Col. 0045C] what he had seen, adds:

**VERSE 2.—**“And it shall be in the last days: the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared upon the summit of the mountains, and it shall be exalted above the hills.”

But it must be asked why he begins by saying, “And it shall be,” rather than simply, “It shall be.” For *and* is a connective conjunction, and we know that a following statement is not joined except to a preceding statement. Yet what he now says at the beginning of this account cannot be continued from the preceding words, because the insertion of the superscription separates it from them. Why, therefore, does he begin by saying, “And it shall be,” when there is no statement to which this is joined? But in this matter we must know that, as we see bodily things, so the minds of prophets see spiritual things; and those things which seem absent to our ignorance are present to them. Thus it comes about that inward things are as connected with outward things in the minds of prophets as they themselves see both at once, and that both the word which they hear within and that which they speak without occur in them simultaneously. The reason, therefore, is clear why he began by saying, “And it shall be”: he joined the word which he uttered outwardly to the word which he had heard inwardly. Thus he continued the words that he uttered outwardly with the inward vision; for this reason he began by saying, “And it shall be in the last days.” For he joins what he begins to say outwardly as though that also were outward which he sees inwardly. By “the last days” he means the time of Gospel preaching. For we are those “upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10:11).

[Col. 0046A] “In the last days, the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared upon the summit of the mountains.” The house of the Lord was the Israelite people. Therefore he is called the mountain of the house of the Lord who deigned to be incarnate from the Israelite people. In that same people, moreover, there were holy men who could rightly be called mountains, because by the merit of their lives they drew near to heavenly things. But the incarnate Only-begotten was not equal to those mountains, because in his divinity he surpassed the merits of all. Hence he is rightly called a mountain above the summit of the mountains, because by his divinity he was found above even the heights of the saints, so that those who accomplished much in God could scarcely touch his footprints from the summit of their thought. Therefore he was prepared upon the summit of the mountains because he appeared among human beings above all the loftiness of prophets [Col. 0046B] and apostles; and he was exalted above the hills because he appointed also seventy-two other disciples (Luke 10:1), who indeed were lofty, but nevertheless inferior to the apostles, as hills are to mountains. For he is exalted above those who receive the faith. All the eminent saints also who followed the apostles may be called hills in comparison with them. It follows: “And all nations shall flow to him.”

**VERSE 3.—**“And many peoples shall go and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us his ways, and we shall walk in his paths.”

Because through the aforesaid mountains and hills the whole world was to be converted to Christ, it is rightly added: “Nations shall flow to him, and many peoples shall go.” And because very many of those who were converted exhorted one another in turn to conversion, they are fittingly recorded as about to say: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob”—that is, to Christ and to the Church—“and he will teach us his ways.” His way, moreover, is peace; his way is humility; his way is patience. For he came into the world for reproaches, insults, and suffering; he bore adversities with equanimity, strongly avoided prosperity, and invited people to the rewards of eternal life. Therefore he taught these his ways to those who afterwards came to faith, that they might follow his footsteps. “For whoever says that he abides in him ought himself also to walk as he walked” [Col. 0046D] (1 John 2:6). But lest it should be unknown how this understanding would come to the nations, so that they might flow to Christ, it is added:

“For the law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.” For the law of Moses and the word of Gospel preaching went forth from Jerusalem through the apostles into the whole world and taught all nations his ways. It follows:

**VERSE 4.—**“And he shall judge the nations and rebuke many peoples.”

The word of the Lord judged the nations because it condemned their wickedness so that they might turn to good; and it rebuked peoples for their unbelief so that they might repent. Or he calls the nations those to be judged because they were to believe. “For whoever does not believe has already been judged” [Col. 0047A] (John 3:18). But the peoples—that is, the Jews—are not to be judged but rebuked because they did not receive the Son of God sent to them. It follows:

“And they shall forge their swords into ploughshares and their spears into sickles.” We see this fulfilled in those who lay aside weapons for Christ and, leading a religious life, till the earth in order to obtain their sustenance from righteous labour. It follows:

“Nation shall not raise sword against nation, nor shall they be trained for war any more.” The unity of faith and charity has made all nations peaceful in Christ, so that nation never takes up sword against nation. For the Church of the righteous, which is among all nations, is forbidden to raise the sword against anyone when it hears from the Lord: “To him who strikes you on one cheek, offer the other also; and from him who takes away your cloak, do not withhold even your tunic. Give to everyone who asks you, and from him who takes what is yours, do not demand it back” [Col. 0047B] (Luke 6:29–30). Therefore nation does not raise sword against nation, because the Church of the saints in all nations keeps these commandments. This saying, indeed, was uttered only concerning the elect, who walk “worthily of the calling to which” they “have been called, with all humility and gentleness, with patience bearing with one another in charity, diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:1–4). But James reproaches the perverse, who seem to bear the name of Christianity and make discord and war for temporal things: “You desire and do not have; you kill and envy, [Col. 0047C] and cannot” [Note: Col. 0047D, another reading: “are not able to.”] “obtain; you quarrel and wage war” (James 4:2). But the Church of the elect, gathered from all nations, does not know how to fight among themselves—the people for whom the Saviour prayed, saying: “That they all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be one in us, so that the world may believe that you sent me” (John 17:21). Of them the Psalmist also says: “Great peace belongs to those who love your law, and there is no stumbling-block for them” (Ps. 118 [119]:165). Rightly, therefore, it was said to the nations called to Christ that nation shall not raise sword against nation, nor shall they be trained for war any more. After this he invites the Jewish people to this newness of grace, adding:

[Col. 0047D] **VERSE 5.—**“House of Jacob, come: let us walk in the light of the Lord.”

That is, let us set the steps of good works in the light of the Gospel. But seeing them persist with obstinate minds in their old state, he suddenly turns to the Lord and indicates why he warned them to come to the light, saying:

**VERSE 6.—**“For you have cast off your people, the house [Note: Col. 0048D, Cod. G.: “house.”] of Jacob.”

That is, you have expelled the Jewish nation because of its unbelief. And he adds the reasons for its casting off, saying: “Because they are filled as of old, and have had diviners like the Philistines, and have clung to foreign children.” [Col. 0048A] They are now filled with wealth, as their fathers were of old. Or they are filled with the filth of iniquity and idolatry, as of old before the Law. And they had diviners, as the Philistine nation had been accustomed to have them, because they consulted magicians and soothsayers like the nations which had not received knowledge of God. And they clung to foreign children because they even sought foreign boys for the commission of that abominable crime. That they are understood to have been filled with riches is now explained: how they were filled as of old is shown when he adds:

**VERSE 7.—**“Their land is filled with silver and gold, and there is no end to their treasures.”

**VERSE 8.—**“And their land is filled with horses, and their chariots are innumerable.”

There is no end to their treasures because the greedy person always lacks—not because the treasures have no limit, but because the mind of their possessor is not filled. “And their chariots are innumerable,” because that which is possessed contrary to God’s command is not worthy of being counted. For the Law forbade the kings of Israel to multiply horses and chariots (1 Sam. 8:11). But the following statement shows how they were filled with iniquities and idolatry as of old: “And their land is filled with idols; they worshipped the work of their own hands, what their fingers made.”

**VERSE 9.—**“And man bowed himself down, and the man of rank was humbled.”

For as they formerly served idols in Egypt, so they did now, and bowed down before images. Yet this must be referred not to the coming of the Lord but [Col. 0048C] to earlier times. For when the Saviour appeared in the flesh, they did not worship idols; rather, they had worshipped them in ancient times, just as they had committed all the other acts that are written. For when the prophet had said that they were cast off by God, he began to show the evils they themselves had already done and the works to which they had devoted themselves when they were cast off, that he might declare them cast off because of the deserving measure of their extreme perversity. Hence, after describing so many iniquities, he adds, addressing the Lord to whom he had spoken thus far:

“Therefore do not forgive them.” For that people offended in such a way that it can no longer obtain remission of sins, because it refused to receive Christ, who alone frees from sins. “For it is impossible for the blood of goats and bulls to take away sins” [Col. 0048D] (Heb. 10:4). Hence the Lord himself says to them: “I told you that you will die in your sins; for if you do not believe that I am, you will die in your sin” (John 8:24).

We may, however, understand the house of Jacob to mean the people of the faithful, because it is said of Christ: “The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever” (Luke 1:32). In that house, namely, evil people are mixed with good, and all are commonly called by the one name of Christianity. But what is now said concerning the house of Jacob must be understood not of the righteous but of this multitude of sinners which still confesses Christ’s name. To them it is rightly said: “House of Jacob, come and let us walk in the light of the Lord,” because “the light came into the world, and people loved darkness rather than light. For everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works be reproved; but whoever does the truth comes to the light, that his works may be made manifest, because they have been done in God” [Col. 0049A] (John 3:10 ff.).

Therefore he says to sinners: “Come and let us walk in the light of the Lord.” As though to say: “Let us cast off the works of darkness” (Rom. 13:12), and “walk as children of light. For the fruit of light consists in all goodness and righteousness and truth” (Eph. 5:8). He says, “Let us walk,” because he speaks to Catholics and therefore exhorts them together with himself to do good. But because they despise to follow his warning and stubbornly persist in the darkness of evil works, he abandons them and, turning to the Lord, immediately pronounces against them a terrible judgment: “You have cast off your people, the house of Jacob, because they are filled as of old.” They are filled with riches, which they have greedily gathered and retain as of old, before they came to Christ, and therefore they have been cast off by him. For he himself, casting them off, says: “Whoever among you does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33).

Other causes are also added for which he cast them off: “Because they had diviners like the Philistines,” that is, they consulted astrologers and diviners like [Col. 0049C] pagans. “And they clung to foreign children,” that is, they were delightfully joined to unclean spirits in the perpetration of evils as though in fornication. Hence the Lord says to Ezekiel: “Oholah played the harlot against me and raved after her lovers, the Assyrians, princes and magistrates who drew near, all young men of desire” (Ezek. 23:5). Now he calls Samaria Oholah. And what is expressed by Samaria except this multitude of sinners? What are her Assyrian lovers except malignant spirits? For *Assyrians* is interpreted as “rebuking” or “convincing”; and demons are called Assyrians because those whom they now make partners with themselves in evil they accuse and convict at the future judgment. Therefore Oholah played the harlot against her husband and raved with desire for her lovers, because this people, which had been betrothed to Christ, despises Christ’s commandments and most willingly fulfils the desires of malignant spirits. These are the princes and magistrates of the hostile party, because “our struggle is not against flesh and blood but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world” (Eph. 6:12).

They are also called young men of desire because they burn for the corruption of souls and, while suggesting wicked pleasures, display themselves as though beautiful to the inward eyes of the deceived mind. “For Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Cor. 11:14). Therefore the malignant spirits, whom Ezekiel calls Assyrians and young men of desire, [Col. 0050A] Isaiah here calls foreign children; and what is said there, “she raved after her lovers,” is what he says here: “And they clung to foreign children.” What he had said—“They are filled as of old”—he subsequently explains, saying: “Their land is filled with silver and gold, and there is no end to their treasures. And their land is filled with horses, and their chariots are innumerable.” It is plain that the people which pursues such things does not seek heavenly things. “For you cannot serve God and mammon” (Matt. 6:24), that is, riches. He then adds mystically:

“And their land is filled with idols.” For what is signified by the name of idols, the Apostle shows: “Covetousness,” he says, “which is the service of idols” (Col. 3:5). Therefore, because this people gathers the aforesaid wealth through covetousness, it is rightly said that its land is filled [Col. 0050B] with idols. It follows: “They worshipped the work of their own hands, what their fingers made.” They worshipped the work of their own hands because the evil which each person especially performs, that he worships as his own god, as do the gluttonous, “whose god is their belly” (Phil. 3:19). It follows:

“And man bowed himself down, and the man of rank was humbled.” Man had been created to behold the heavenly light; but, his sins demanding it, cast outside, he bears the darkness of his mind. He does not seek what is above; he attends to what is below; he does not desire heavenly things; he always turns earthly things over in his mind. Therefore man bowed himself down, and the man of rank was humbled. For every sinner, thinking earthly things and not seeking heavenly things, is voluntarily bent over; because, while following lower desires, he is bent away from the uprightness of his own mind. He who is bent over always looks upon the earth and does not remember at what price he was redeemed, because he seeks low things. For all these reasons it is added: “Therefore do not forgive them.” For all these things are condemnable, and the day of eternal vengeance will suddenly come upon those who do such things. Hence it follows:

**VERSE 10.—**“Enter into the rock, and hide in a pit of earth from the face of the fear of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty.”

The rock signifies the hardness of our heart. We enter the rock when we penetrate the hardness of our heart; and we hide in a pit of earth from the face of the Lord’s fear if, casting out earthly thoughts, [Col. 0050D] we conceal ourselves from the wrath of the strict Judge in the humility of our mind. For the more earth is cast down by digging, the lower the floor is always shown to be. Thus if we more diligently cast earthly thoughts out from ourselves, we find a humbler place within ourselves in which to hide. Behold, because the day of divine judgment hangs over us, the very face of its fear appears as though already present. The more the glory of his majesty draws near, the more terribly each person must fear him. What, then, must be done, and where must we flee? For where can anyone hide from him who is everywhere? But behold, we are commanded to enter the rock and hide in a pit of earth, so that, breaking open the hardness of our heart, we may so escape invisible wrath as we withdraw inwardly in our heart from the love of visible things; so that, when the earth of wicked thought is cast out, the mind may hide itself within itself all the more safely because more humbly. But after the prophet has first given counsel concerning how someone might hide from the wrath of that day, he adds concerning those who neglect thus to hide themselves from it:

**VERSE 11.—**“The eyes of the lofty [Note: Col. 0051D, another reading: “lofty [plural].”] man have been humbled, and the height of men shall be bowed down; but the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day.”

The judgment is still awaited as future, and yet it is already said as though past: “The eyes of the lofty man have been humbled.” But with God the judgment has already taken place. “For whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18). Therefore, although any proud person may still outwardly appear lofty in earthly power, he is nevertheless already inwardly humbled and cast down before God’s eyes. Or what he says, “The eyes of the lofty man have been humbled,” may be understood as said in place of “will be humbled.” And this lofty man may especially be understood as that “son of perdition,” who “opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshipped, whom the Lord Jesus will kill by the breath of his mouth and destroy by the brightness of his coming” [Col. 0051B] (2 Thess. 2:4).

“And the height of men shall be bowed down,” because “everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke 14:11). “But the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day,” because then will be perfectly fulfilled what was said: “You have subjected all things under his feet. But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him” (Heb. 2:8). The prophet, however, who said that the height of men will be bowed down, proves this by enumerating its parts, adding:

**VERSE 12.—**“For the day of the Lord of hosts is upon everyone proud and lofty, and upon everyone arrogant, and he shall be humbled.”

**VERSE 13.—**“And upon all the lofty and towering cedars of Lebanon, and upon all the oaks of Bashan.”

**VERSE 14.—**“And upon all high mountains, and upon all elevated hills.”

**VERSE 15.—**“And upon every lofty tower, and upon every fortified wall.”

**VERSE 16.—**“And upon all the ships of Tarshish, and upon everything beautiful to behold.”

[Col. 0051D] The day of the Lord’s vengeance, he says, is upon every person proud in mind and lofty in power—that is, upon everyone inflated by the eminence of authority—and upon everyone who pursues the boastfulness of arrogance. Cedars are so high that by their height they surpass the stature of all other trees. Lebanon, however, is called “whitening.” And what is signified by Lebanon but the glory of this world? What, then, is signified by the lofty and towering cedars of Lebanon but those who, placed in the most eminent dignities of the world, raise the neck of their mind in pride? Hence it is written: “I saw the wicked highly exalted and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon” [Col. 0052A] (Ps. 36 [37]:35).

Oaks, however, are huge and sturdy trees. Bashan is called “locust” or “fatness.” And what can be understood by the locust, which is almost entirely belly, except gluttony and the greed of the belly? Fatness also arises from the continual abundance of food. What, then, do the oaks of Bashan signify but those who, because of secular power and confirmed haughtiness of heart, are great and hard, and who fatten their flesh through the greed of the belly? Rightly, therefore, the day of vengeance will come upon all the lofty and towering cedars of Lebanon and upon all the oaks of Bashan. High mountains may also be understood as proud kings and emperors, and elevated hills as other haughty consuls and rulers, upon whom due vengeance will come.

What, moreover, is signified by a lofty tower except any proud soul, which towers above others in this world by strong power? And what by a fortified wall except the rich, who are fortified by their wealth and fortify and protect others who do evil? Therefore the day of the Lord will come upon these also. He has designated the proud powers of the world by many names because there are many dignities in this world through which many acquire destruction for themselves.

Tarshish, however, is called “sea.” And what is the sea except this world? What, then, are the ships of Tarshish except the minds of human beings, which are carried through the bitter sea of this world by various desires? Again, Tarshish is interpreted “exploration of joy.” And what are the ships of the exploration of joy except human minds, which in this world experience the joys of present pleasures by satisfying their desires? And what is beautiful to behold except everything desired in the world, while it deceives the eyes of those who look upon it by false or empty beauty? Therefore the day of the Lord will come upon all the ships of Tarshish and upon everything beautiful to behold. Here the preceding sentence is repeated, when he adds:

**VERSE 17.—**“And the loftiness of human beings shall be bowed down, and the height of men shall be humbled, and the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day.”

Then those who now raise themselves proudly will be bowed down, and then the Lord will be exalted, whose humility they now despise. It follows:

**VERSE 18.—**“And idols shall be utterly crushed.”

Then idols will be crushed because the sin of covetousness will be punished by eternal torments. For, as the wise man says: “The offence shall be crushed with the offender” (Ecclus. 27:3). Or thus: the Lord will be exalted, man will be brought low, and idols will be crushed. For human speech seems to possess reason only so long as it has not been compared with divine knowledge. But when falsehood, like straw, has drawn near to the fire of truth, it is swiftly devoured and fails; and all doctrines of falsehood, now called idols because they are feigned and fabricated, will be utterly crushed. And when anyone has been terrified by fear of the Lord, he will first hide these idols in the cave of his breast and in the chasms of the earth, not daring to utter what he had wickedly invented. For God is so perfect that he first casts out these things when concealed and does not permit them to remain within himself. It follows:

**VERSE 19.—**“And they shall enter into the caves of the rocks and into the chasms of the earth, from before the terror of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty, when he rises to strike the earth.”

This is also read thus in the Apocalypse of John: “The kings of the earth and the princes and tribunes, and the rich and the strong, and every slave and free person hid themselves in the caves and rocks of the mountains, and they say to the mountains and rocks: [Col. 0053B] Fall upon us, and hide us from the face of him who sits upon the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb; because the day of their wrath will come, and who shall be able to stand?” (Rev. VI, 15–17.) Therefore, when the near coming of the strict Judge is imminent, when great and terrible signs will frequently appear, “men withering away for fear and expectation of those things which shall come upon the whole world” (Luke XXI, 26), they will enter caves and chasms of the earth, wishing to hide themselves from the face of the evils that are coming. He therefore calls the Judge’s coming his rising up, as blessed Job also does when he says: “For what shall I do when God rises up for judgment?” (Job XXXI, 14.) For now he sits at the right hand of Majesty on high; but then he will rise to strike the earth, when he comes to judge the world.

[Col. 0053C] Yet these things may also be understood of the destruction of the Jewish nation, carried out through the Romans. For he says that the day of the Lord of hosts is upon every proud and lofty person, and so forth. The proud and arrogant may be understood through the cedars of Lebanon and the oaks of Bashan; through the mountains and hills, both the Pharisees and all who held precedence among that people; through the towers and walls, their cities and strongholds; through the ships of Tarshish, those who then fought against the Romans upon the waters, as on the Sea of Galilee; through everything beautiful to behold, generally whatever among them appeared handsome or honourable. For upon all these things the wrath of God then came.

[Col. 0053D] But the Lord alone was exalted on that day—that is, at that time—because “God exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend” (Phil. II, 9). And as the nations came to faith, idols were utterly broken. But the Jews entered into caves of rocks and chasms of the earth from the face of the Lord’s terror, when he rose through the Romans to strike their land; for, once their cities had been captured, they hid in caverns and underground places, as Josephus himself did with his companions. And because at that time every Gentile, having recognized the truth, turned to repentance, the following is rightly added:

[Col. 0054A] **VERSE 20.**—“On that day a man shall cast away the idols of his silver and the images of his gold, which he had made for himself to worship moles and bats.”

**VERSE 21.**—“And he shall enter the clefts [Note: [Col. 0053D] Otherwise, *rifts*.] of the rocks and the caverns of the crags, from the face of the Lord’s terror and from the glory of his majesty, when he rises to strike the earth.”

For “day” is put for that time in which the light of truth shone upon the world through the apostles. A “man” is customarily one who surpasses bestial understanding by reason. Therefore the man—that is, everyone who thinks rationally—at that time cast away idols. For in them he worshipped moles and bats. Moles are blind, dwell beneath the earth, dig up its inner parts, and cast them out. And what [Col. 0054B] are signified by moles except demons, who, lacking the light of inward vision, dig into the hearts of carnal people as into earth by unlawful suggestions, and cause what they wickedly suggest to break forth in speech and action? Bats, however, fly when darkness falls and by night, and often walk upon the ground. So too the malign spirits, lovers of darkness: because they are proud of the subtlety of their nature, they fly; but because, cast down from heaven, they no longer raise themselves by any aspiration toward heavenly hope, they creep upon the earth.

They also chiefly mock the minds of human beings in whom inward light is lacking by these two vices: for they deceive some through pride and others through lust. In those whom they raise up as though knowing lofty things in the arrogance of pride, they fly; but in those whom they cast down through lust, they creep upon the earth. The Gentiles therefore worshipped these moles and bats in their idols; and consequently everyone who thinks rationally cast them away after hearing the preaching of truth, and entered the clefts of the rocks and the caverns of the crags from the face of the Lord’s terror. And Moses was told in Exodus: “I will place you in the hollow of the rock, and I will protect you with my right hand” (Exod. XXXIII, 22).—“But the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 1); the hollow of the rock is the wound in Christ’s side, in which whoever faithfully flees to it is most securely protected.

Therefore, as Christ is signified there by the rock, so in this place the rocks and crags signify the saints; and as the hollow signifies the wound of the Lord’s side, so the clefts [Col. 0054D] of the rocks and caverns of the crags signify the wounds of the holy martyrs. Thus whoever, conscious of sins and fearful of the future judgment, faithfully and humbly seeks the patronage of those whom he knows to have suffered for Christ, and asks to be protected from the wrath to come by their merits and intercessions, enters the clefts of the rocks and the caverns of the crags from the face of the Lord’s terror and the glory of his majesty, which will be revealed when he rises to strike the earth. Or the Lord then rose to strike the earth when he shook the hearts of the Gentiles toward repentance. And every day he himself strikes the earth whenever he troubles the mind of a sinner [Col. 0055A] so that it may turn; and then a man—that is, one wise in a rational manner—enters the aforesaid clefts of the rocks.

Or silver and gold may be understood as speech and understanding, from which idols of perverse doctrines are made. Whoever casts these away enters the clefts of the rocks and the caverns of the crags; and he does not busy himself amid the dust of earth and worthless mud, but proceeds with firm reasoning and finds for himself various openings of virtues through which he may be able to attain the truth. The prophet, however, spoke a little above at length about the destruction of the Jews. Therefore, now considering that they would suffer all these things because of the killing of the Saviour, he warns them to cease persecuting him, saying:

**VERSE 22.**—“Therefore cease from the man whose [Col. 0055B] breath is in his nostrils, for he is accounted exalted.”

What, then, is signified by the nostrils except foreknowledge, and by breath except knowledge? For we often apprehend by smell what we do not see, so that even when certain things lie far off, the fragrance of their quality makes itself known to us; and while we draw breath through the nostrils, we frequently foreknow things not seen. Therefore our Redeemer’s breath is said to be in his nostrils, so that his knowledge may be denoted as existing in foreknowledge; because whatever he made known that he knew in his human nature, he assuredly foreknew before the ages in his divinity. The prophet immediately adds why he had breath in his nostrils, saying: “For he is accounted exalted.” As though he said: He who came down from heavenly things to the lowest places foreknew from above what was to come below. “Cease,” he says, “from this man.” For because of the evil you inflict upon him, hear what follows.

## CHAPTER III

**VERSE 1.**—“For behold, the sovereign Lord of hosts will take away from Jerusalem and from Judah the mighty man and the strong man, every support of bread and every support of water.”

**VERSE 2.**—“The strong man and the man of war, the judge and prophet, the diviner and the elder.”

**VERSE 3.**—“The captain over fifty, the honourable of face, the counsellor, the skilled architect, and the prudent interpreter of mysterious speech.”

All these things happened to the Jewish people after the Lord’s passion. For through the Romans the Lord took away [Col. 0055D] from Jerusalem and from the Jewish people the mighty and strong, every support of bread and every support of water, the strong man and the warrior; so that in that siege they died of hunger and thirst, were finally captured and killed by their enemies, and the survivors were everywhere crushed in miserable slavery. From that time they have had no judge, because, scattered throughout the world, they are governed by no ruler of their own.

The Lord also took away from them the prophet, because he withdrew the word that was accustomed to speak through the prophets. For now there is no one among them who says, “Thus says the Lord” (Exod. V, 1). All have fallen silent, because the word of the Lord departed from them. Nor do they have any diviner—that is, such a prophet [Col. 0056A] as Balaam was (Num. XXII, 5). For he was a diviner, and yet the Lord spoke to him and revealed many of his secrets to him. For future things were often also declared through foreigners, as we read of this Balaam and of the diviners of the Philistines. Thus the diviner—that is, one who announces truth at times and falsehood at times—was taken away from the Jews, since they lost truth and falsehood alike. Nor is there among them an elder, that is, one mature in character. They no longer have even any captain over fifty, because they killed the Lord of Sabaoth, that is, Christ. Nor one honourable of face, because he who is beautiful in form above the children of men did not appear to them to have form or beauty. Nor a counsellor, because Wisdom, which says, “Counsel and equity are mine” (Prov. VIII, 14), forsook them. The angel of great counsel departed from them. There is no longer among them one who can say, “As a wise architect I laid a foundation” (I Cor. III, 10). The architects migrated from them and came to the Church; they laid Jesus Christ as the foundation. From them the Lord also took away the prudent interpreter of mysterious speech, because no teacher was left to them. The interpretation of the Law and the Prophets ceased among them: they read, but do not understand. To this the Lord’s own utterance is added:

**VERSE 4.**—“And I will give boys as their princes; effeminate men shall rule over them.”

For after the Lord’s ascension they had princes who were boys—that is, who thought childish thoughts and acted childishly. And effeminate men ruled over them, that is, those who prostituted themselves in a womanish manner. But let us hear what the populace did.

**VERSE 5.**—“And the people shall rush, man against man, everyone against his neighbour; the boy shall make tumult against the elder, and the base-born against the noble.”

Before Titus besieged Jerusalem, the people within the city fought among themselves; man rushed against man, and everyone killed his neighbour. The boy did not pay honour to the elder, but quarrelled with him; and the base-born dishonoured the noble. But after Jerusalem was captured, when their few survivors again attempted rebellion to their own destruction, let us hear what they did.

**VERSE 6.**—“For a man, he says, shall seize his brother, one of his father’s household: ‘You have clothing; be our leader, and let this ruin be under your hand.’”

For they deserved to have such rulers who said of Christ, as it is written: “We do not want this man to reign over us” (Luke XIX, 14). They judged worthy of leadership the person who was able to possess at least a garment. They preferred him not on account of virtue, but on account of kinship. What is said—“let this ruin be under your hand”—has this sense: Let this misery and calamity be sustained and protected by your aid. But how powerless any such man whom they chose was is shown by his own words as well. For it is immediately added:

**VERSE 7.**—“He shall answer on that day, saying: ‘I [Col. 0057A] am not a physician, and in my house there is neither bread nor clothing; do not appoint me leader of the people.’”

“I am not,” he says, “a physician”: that is, I do not know how to heal your weakness, so that through me you may recover your former health and thus be able, as once you were, to resist your enemies. Here the prophet also adds:

**VERSE 8.**—“For Jerusalem has fallen, and Judah has collapsed, because their tongue and their devices are against the Lord, to provoke the eyes of his majesty.”

Jerusalem fell because it was destroyed by the Roman army; and Judah collapsed because the Jewish people were miserably overcome by them. And this happened for the following reason: because their tongue was against the Lord when they said, “He is guilty of death” (Matt. XXVI, 66)—“Crucify him” (Mark XV, 13); and their devices, when they said, “For we heard him say: ‘I will destroy this temple made with hands, and after three days I will build another not made with hands’” (Mark XIV, 58).

But now, returning to the matter, let us see whether these words may be understood of persons other than Jews as well. “Cease,” he says, “from the man whose breath is in his nostrils.”—“Those who have once been enlightened, have tasted the good word of God [Note: [Col. 0057] Codex G: “have also tasted the heavenly gift, and have been made partakers of the Holy Spirit; have tasted the good word of God,” etc.] and the power of the world to come, and have fallen away,” says the Apostle, “crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and making him a public spectacle” (Heb. VI, 4–6). Thus these too have not yet ceased from the man whose breath is in his nostrils. And, now that the coming of Antichrist is near, they have multiplied to such an extent and infected others with the odour of their pestilence so thoroughly that a true Christian is now rarely found. Hence let us receive with sorrow that this has already been fulfilled in great part. And we do not doubt that what follows is still to be fulfilled more fully:

“Behold, the sovereign Lord of hosts will take away from Jerusalem and from Judah the mighty and strong man, every support of water,” and so forth. For Jerusalem and Judah are this people of believers, now so weakened that it is difficult to find anyone in it mighty and strong for spiritual work. Bread is the body of the Redeemer, received in the mystery; water is sacred knowledge. But the support of bread is taken away, because the power of the sacrament is withdrawn from those [Col. 0057D] who receive it unworthily. Likewise the support of water—that is, the power of knowledge—is taken away from the unworthy; because, if the Spirit is absent, knowledge has no power and cannot grant the capacity to do the good things that you know.

It is now rare to find a warrior faithfully fighting with spiritual arms. An ecclesiastical judge who judges justly, possessing in God’s law the knowledge of judging, is also difficult to find; nearly everything is now vain, passing, and full of error. The prophet too—that is, any teacher proclaiming the future joys of the righteous and punishments of the wicked—has now become exceedingly scarce. For scarcely anyone now dispenses the word of preaching to this people except to obtain money or some other transient thing. And perhaps every such preacher is signified by the diviner. For, just as Balaam the diviner through the superstition of his greed forsook the word of the Lord, so he opposes by his life the good things which he preaches in speech. For Samuel also says: “For resistance is like the sin of divination” (I Sam. XV, 23), that is, refusing obedience and instead resisting. But whoever is such a diviner will suddenly be carried off by the blast of the last persecution.

It is exceedingly difficult to find among this people an elder—that is, one mature through the venerableness of his character. The number fifty, however, customarily signifies repentance and remission of sins. Hence David, repenting in the fiftieth psalm, received remission [Col. 0058B]. Therefore the repentant person is comprised in the number fifty. Who, then, is the captain over fifty—that is, over the penitent—except whoever offers an example of repentance, proclaims repentance, and turns others toward it? John was such a leader: he wore a garment of camel’s hair, ate locusts and wild honey, and commanded others to “produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke III, 8). Indeed Christ also is the leader of repentance and the head of those saved through repentance. Hence the Jews, unwilling that he should be captain over fifty, said to him: “You are not yet fifty years old” (John VIII, 57). But he, knowing himself to be not only the leader of the penitent but also of the righteous, answered: “Before Abraham was made, I am” (ibid., 58).

The honourable of face is one whose inward maturity appears in his face. The counsellor is one who gives counsel concerning how the wiles of demons may be overcome and uprightness preserved. The architect is one who builds up the Church by preaching. The prudent interpreter of mysterious speech is one who prudently understands the mystical utterance of Scripture, or anyone who speaks wisely in a mystical sense. The prudent interpreter of mysterious speech seems to me to be a man learned and practised both in the Law and Prophets and in the Gospel and Apostles. But persons of this sort are daily more and more withdrawn as the time of Antichrist draws nearer, and the wickedness of those who remain grows ever more abundantly. For when Antichrist reigns, if any [Col. 0058D] such men remain, they will either be deceived by him or destroyed. Therefore the Church complains through Jeremiah of that time, saying: “The Lord has removed all my mighty ones from the midst of me; he called a time against me to crush my chosen ones” (Lam. I, 15). It was therefore rightly said that the Lord will take away from Jerusalem and Judah the mighty and strong man, every support of bread and every support of water, the strong man and warrior, judge and prophet, diviner and elder, captain over fifty and honourable of face, counsellor skilled among architects, and prudent interpreter of mysterious speech. These are removed, but useless persons are given in their place.

[Col. 0059A] “I will give,” he says, “boys”—that is, wanton, ungovernable, dissolute persons acting childishly—“as their princes,” that is, their priests and prelates; and effeminate men, that is, lovers of transient praise, will rule over them. For arrogant superiors are effeminate because, while they prostitute their soft hearts to human praises, they are, as it were, corrupted by their lovers. They are effeminate because they are corrupted by the lust of praise. For if they lived manfully, no transient praise would stain them with its corruption. Since they seek not God’s glory but their own, they desire to dominate those subject to them rather than benefit them; and they scarcely deign to speak to them in counsel, but only in domination. By another prophet they are told: “But you ruled them with harshness and with power” (Ezek. XXXIV, 4). They rule with harshness and power, because they hasten not to correct their subjects calmly by reasoning, but to bend them roughly by domination. And such priests and prelates now abound in the Church in many ways because of the sins of the people. For the following words indicate that the people subject to them deserved to have prelates of this kind: “The people shall rush, man against man, everyone against his neighbour”—that is, one will fight against another, injure him, or harm him. And because the wicked strive to dishonour the good, “the boy,” he says, “shall make tumult against the elder”: that is, one possessing wanton and childish conduct will quarrel with one made aged by gravity of character. “And the base-born against the noble”: that is, the sinner against the righteous. The following saying shows how this people receives boys as its leaders.

“For a man shall seize his brother, one of his father’s household: ‘You have clothing,’” and so forth. For what is signified by “man” except any person? And what is understood by “brother” or “member of the household” except any carnal relative or friend? A man therefore seizes his brother to appoint him as leader, because now, with religion declining, it frequently happens that for ecclesiastical rule they choose not the holier person, who is worthy, but some powerful man sets over them the person whom he loves carnally. The Church therefore has boys as its leaders because people are chosen by the powerful not so much on account of the merit of their life as from carnal affection. [Col. 0059D] And it is said to the person thus chosen: “You have clothing; be our leader.” Here “clothing” is understood as a certain outward respectability of conduct, with which some cloak themselves so as to appear blameless to men, though inwardly they have nothing of true or perfect virtue. Such persons are easily chosen by the inexperienced.

“Be our leader,” he says; “and let this ruin be under your hand.” This ruin is the ruin of the inward person; this ruin is death. “Let this ruin be under your hand.” He does not say, “Raise up this ruin,” because he does not care to choose someone who will raise up the fallen, but merely someone who will appear above the rest. Yet the one chosen excuses himself, saying: “I am not a physician, and in my house there is neither bread nor clothing; do not appoint me leader of the people.” Whoever is chosen for pastoral [Col. 0060A] care ought to be a spiritual physician, knowing diligently how to heal the ailments of the inward person; and in the house of his conscience he ought to have the bread of spiritual doctrine, so that, being appointed over his Lord’s household, he may “give them food in due season” (Matt. XXV, 25).

He must also have clothing in his house, so that inwardly he may be clothed with the garment of virtues. Therefore, putting forward necessary grounds for excuse, he says: “I am not a physician, and in my house there is neither bread nor clothing,” although he had been told, “You have clothing,” which we referred to outward conduct. But he answers concerning the inward garment of the heart: “In my house there is no clothing,” as though saying: Although to you I appear clothed with a certain respectability of conduct, I am naked in the eyes of the inward Inspector. Behold, this man is chosen and excuses himself, yet he is not worthy of praise. What then shall we think of those who seek election to such prelac ies in order to magnify themselves before men by means of them? How many, lacking bread and clothing, although they themselves hunger and are naked, neither possessing spiritual food nor keeping Christ’s tunic whole, promise both sustenance and clothing to others, and, though full of wounds, boast that they are physicians! After this the prophetic utterance adds:

“Jerusalem has fallen and Judah has collapsed, because their tongue and their devices are against the Lord, to [Col. 0060C] provoke the eyes of his majesty.” Jerusalem—that is, the Church—has fallen, because near the end of the age the wall of faith and discipline around it has been thrown down and the towers of lofty virtues have collapsed. And Judah—that is, the people of believers—has collapsed, because almost all this multitude has lost the state of uprightness. Their tongue is against the Lord whenever they speak things contrary to God; and their devices are against him whenever they devise new ways of acting wickedly. Thus they provoke the eyes of his majesty, because in their devices they sin deliberately. For every sin is committed either through weakness, ignorance, or deliberate intent. To sin knowingly through weakness is worse indeed than to sin through ignorance; but to sin deliberately is much graver than to sin through weakness. [Col. 0060D] Therefore those who commit evil acts from the deliberate study of wicked contrivances are said not merely to sin in the Lord’s sight but, what is graver, to provoke the eyes of his majesty. It follows:

**VERSE 9.**—“The recognition of their face shall answer them.”

A lustful and undisciplined mind is customarily recognized in the eyes and face; and the glance of the eyes and signs of the face are followed by the commission of wickedness. Hence it is aptly said now: “The recognition of their face shall answer them,” as though it were said: The fault of the heart, which had begun to betray itself through signs in the face, will answer against them through the lust of the flesh in the commission of the deed, so that the foulness of an unclean action may outwardly reveal what they are inwardly. But after such people make such an act habitual, they lose all shame. Hence it is added:

“They proclaimed their sin like Sodom; they did not hide it.” For those proclaim their sin like Sodom who shamelessly or boastfully reveal to others the shameful act which they themselves commit, in order to entice them to a like deed [Note: [Col. 0061D] Codex G: “to like wickedness.”].
