But while they glory in such things, sudden destruction comes upon them; and therefore, as though of the past, it is added:

“Woe to their soul, for evils have been rendered to them.” Their soul receives everlasting evils in return for the evils which they committed in time [Note: [Col. 0061D] Ibid.: *did*.]. Therefore the prophet exhorts us to praise the just Judge, adding:

**VERSE 10.**—“Say to the righteous man that it is well, because he shall eat the fruit of his devices.”

[Col. 0061B] For who is this righteous man except he to whom it is sung: “You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is upright” (Ps. CXVIII, 137)? To him we all ought to say that he acted well in destroying those who proclaimed their sin like Sodom and devoted themselves to evil contrivances. For they shall eat the fruit of their devices, because they shall be punished eternally for their sins. “For sin, when it is consummated, brings forth death” (Jas. I, 15). This is the fruit of sin. But because everyone who still does similar things will afterwards receive a like sentence unless he quickly corrects his actions by repentance, it is rightly added:

**VERSE 11.**—“Woe to the wicked man unto evil; for the recompense of his hands shall be made to him.”

[Col. 0061C] For the happier the wicked man thinks himself when all things come to him according to his desire, the more unhappy he is. For the more he multiplies iniquities, the more he heaps up his own condemnation. For the recompense of his hands shall be made to him, because he will receive according to all that he now does.

But what was said, “Woe to their soul, for evils have been rendered to them,” and so forth, also applies to the Jews. For they received from the Romans the evils which they had inflicted upon Christ; and in eternal punishments they shall eat the fruit of their contrivances by which they falsely accused the Lord. And whoever still persists in the same Jewish impiety: woe to him, because the recompense of his hands shall be made to him. It follows:

[Col. 0061D] **VERSE 12.**—“The exacters of my people have despoiled them, and women have ruled over them.”

Those who exact tribute and other things of this kind are called exacters. Those who demanded payment from the ancient people of God despoiled them, perhaps when they were unable to pay; serving the greed of rulers, they oppressed the people, while the wives of the powerful oppressed them by proud domination. Likewise, we often see this now occurring among this people through exacters and through the wives of rulers. This saying, therefore, is directed against those who despoil and burden believers. But concerning flatterers, who puff them up with excessive favour, it is added:

[Col. 0062A] “My people, those who call you blessed deceive you, and destroy the way of your steps.” For the flatterer deceives the person whom he calls blessed, because he misleads him by a lie and raises him up into vain glory; and he destroys the way of the steps of his action, because while that person believes himself blessed, he believes that the good things he has done suffice for him, and he neglects to hold to the path of his uprightness as he formerly did. Thus many have perished when, near the end, they acted more negligently or turned aside into sins. But lest we be deceived by human favour, we must always think of that terrible judgment of God which still awaits us. For it follows:

**VERSE 13.**—“The Lord stands to judge, and to judge the peoples.”

He does not say that the Lord sits to judge, but that he stands to judge, [Col. 0062B] because he does not yet actually exercise that judgment which is signified by the Judge’s sitting, so as already to condemn sinners. Rather, he still stands: that is, he sees and helps those running or fighting in the course of this life, and preserves for them the rewards prepared. Conversely, he observes those acting wickedly in order to repay them at the end according to their deeds. For he who now stands to judge will at some time sit—that is, he will actually enact the judgment itself. It follows:

**VERSE 14.**—“The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people and with its rulers.”

Who, then, are these elders, except those mature in wisdom and character—that is, all the perfect? “For venerable old age is not long-lasting, nor is it counted by the number of years; but the grey hairs of a man are understanding, and the age of old age is an unstained life” (Wis. IV, 8–9). And who are these rulers except the prophets and apostles, and the good governors of Churches? With these elders and rulers, therefore, the Lord will come to judgment, because he promised them, saying: “You who have left all things and followed me” (Matt. XII, 29), and so forth. He will then come especially in order to punish plunderers and oppressors of believers. Therefore he immediately adds their charge:

“For you have devoured my vineyard.” The Lord’s vineyard is his people; whoever takes away the goods of believers devours it. Therefore he adds more plainly: “The plunder of the poor is in your house”; and, rebuking them, adds:

[Col. 0062D] **VERSE 15.**—“Why do you crush my people and grind the faces of the poor? says the Lord of hosts.”

For those crush the people of God who trouble and afflict his servants; and those grind down, or waste away, the faces of the poor—that is, reduce them to emaciation—who take away their food. Such people therefore kindle God’s wrath fiercely against themselves. It follows:

**VERSE 16.**—“And the Lord said: Because the daughters of Zion have been lifted up, and have walked with outstretched necks, and went with signals of their eyes, and clapped as they walked, and advanced with an affected step in their feet.” [Note: [Col. 0062D] Otherwise, *gait*.]

[Col. 0063A] **VERSE 17.**—“The Lord shall make bald the crown of the daughters of Zion, and the Lord shall lay bare their hair.”

Historically, these things may indeed be referred to Jewish women, who behaved thus in pride and wantonness and who, at the time of Jerusalem’s sudden siege, were made bald and disfigured. But because Zion is interpreted “watchtower,” we may, in a more subtle interpretation, understand the daughters of Zion as faithful souls, which, being as it were placed in a watchtower, customarily foresee approaching temptations with cautious vigilance from the citadel of the mind. Yet such souls are often lifted up into pride and destroy their entire religious way of life.

For since the exaltation of the mind customarily appears also in the face and bodily bearing, after these daughters of Zion were lifted up, they walked with outstretched necks and with signals [Col. 0063B] of their eyes. In contrast holy David, because he had pride neither in heart nor face, professed: “Lord, my heart is not lifted up, nor are my eyes raised” (Ps. CXXX, 1). The daughters of Zion also went—that is, walked about—and clapped with gestures of dissolution, wantonness, and empty joy; and they advanced with an affected step, because they had rejected every discipline of heart and therefore behaved outwardly in this manner. Since, then, the daughters of Zion—that is, Christian souls—did not fear to do such things, the Lord will make bald their crown and lay bare their hair.

What is signified by baldness except the stripping away of shame? For the forehead, exposed in baldness, is the seat of shame. The Lord therefore makes bald their crown when he exposes in them that on account of which their proud [Col. 0063C] minds may blush more grievously, while they are seen by all in ridicule. The Lord also lays bare the hair of their head when he reveals the perverse thought of their hearts. And although this baldness and laying bare often occur even in this life, they will not take place fully “until the Lord comes, who will also bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts” (I Cor. IV, 5). It follows:

**VERSE 18.**—“On that day the Lord will take away every [Note: [Col. 0063D] Otherwise, *every* is absent.] ornament of the footwear and the crescent ornaments.”

**VERSE 19.**—“And necklaces, pendants, bracelets, and mitres.”

**VERSE 20.**—“And hair-dividers, anklets, [Col. 0063D] chains, perfume-vessels, and earrings.”

**VERSE 21.**—“And rings and gems hanging upon the forehead.”

**VERSE 22.**—“And changes of garments and cloaks [Note: [Col. 0064D] Otherwise, *little cloaks*], linen garments, and pins.”

**VERSE 23.**—“And mirrors, fine linen, headbands, and veils.”

By these feminine ornaments, the spiritual ornaments of minds are fittingly signified. Footwear, made from the skins of dead animals and protecting the feet, may signify the examples of the holy Fathers, which secure the steps of our actions upon God’s way. The crescent ornament, a round pendant made like the moon and hanging from the neck upon [Col. 0064A] the breast, signifies a distinguishing mark of some virtue shining in the night of this present life and reaching from action to understanding, as it were from the neck to the breast, according to the saying: “From your commandments I have gained understanding” (Ps. CXVIII, 104). A necklace signifies the wholly complete and beautiful ornament of good action, concerning which Solomon says: “That grace may be added to your head, and a necklace to your neck” (Prov. I, 9). A pendant, by which a bride’s breast is marked and adorned, signifies the seal of spiritual marriage and chaste love. Bracelets, which encircle the upper arms, signify the strong activity of those who work. A mitre signifies restraint of fluctuating thoughts, as though they were hair. A hair-divider, by which the hair is parted, signifies the keenness of discernment which subtly distinguishes good from evil thoughts.

[Col. 0064B] Anklets among women are ornaments for the legs, by which their steps are adorned: namely, gold chains like bracelets, placed about the ankles. What then is signified by anklets except the ornament of virtue at the end of an action? Or because, according to the statement of Genesis, the ancient serpent lies in wait for the woman’s heel (Gen. III, 15)—that is, for the soul’s slipping action—the protective defence of virtue, or the ornament of religious action, placed there, is signified under the name of anklets, where the serpent seeks to inflict a bite.

But a *murenula* is a kind of chain in a winding pattern, woven of gold softened into slender rods in the likeness of a serpent, and fitted for adorning the neck. What, then, should be understood by the *murenula* [Col. 0064C] except the golden teaching of truth, which is regularly bent into manifold senses and so distributed into innumerable propositions, as though into little rods, that it may bind them together in the fastening of one devout intention—possessing serpentine prudence, and constraining and adorning, as it were, the neck, that is, the labor of holy work? Hence also in the Song of Songs it is said to the Bride: “We will make for you golden chains studded with silver” (Cant. I, 10). They are called golden and studded with silver—that is, variegated—because they are sometimes woven with rods of gold and silver, so that wisdom and eloquence may there be signified as mingled together. For wisdom is commonly denoted by gold, and the brilliance of eloquence by silver.

The little scent-vessels, in which [Col. 0064D] perfumes are kept, can represent the hearts of the good, from which the most delightful fragrance of virtues breathes forth. Earrings represent the hearing of the obedient; rings, the seal of secrets, or certainly faith, by which the soul is betrothed to Christ. Gems hanging upon the forehead represent the precious sign of the glorious cross, which we wear upon our foreheads. Changeable garments represent the alternation of religious life, so that one may exercise oneself in those virtues and lead now the contemplative, now the active life. Cloaks represent the outward garb of good works. Linen garments represent the pure and bright adornment of the mind. Needles represent compunction. For the arrangement of hair, adorned with needles, is held in place lest the hair flow too freely and, scattered abroad, become disordered. [Col. 0065A] So too the virtue of compunction does not allow thoughts to drift aimlessly, but binds them together becomingly and in order.

A mirror is the study of sacred reading, in the consideration of which we discover what ugliness or what beauty our inward person possesses. Fine linen represents the subtle garment of the righteousness of those who can say: “I have taken off my tunic” (Cant. V, 3), that is, their former manner of life.

The ribbons which becomingly cover and adorn women’s heads can represent the honorable modesty of the mind.

But a *theristrum* is called, as it were, a summer garment, because summer is called *theri* in Greek. This garment is made of the finest, very delicate linen; and women of Mesopotamia, Arabia, and Spain use it [Col. 0065B] in summer. What, then, is the soul’s *theristrum* except the most subtle and most pure inward clothing of a chaste mind, not allowing it to be heated by the burning of carnal vices, but providing it with the best refreshment amid the heat of temptations?

All these many and great goods, then, belonged to the daughters of Zion—that is, faithful souls—before they were destroyed. But because, after a religious way of life, they are puffed up into pride and dissolved into wantonness, on the day when the Lord shall make their crown bald He will take all these things from them: partly in this age, and entirely on the day of judgment. Thus pride will be the cause and beginning of the loss of so many good works. For no [Col. 0065C] good works can remain where pride rules. For as wind carries off dust, so pride carries away every virtue. Therefore the following is aptly added.

**VERSE 24.**—“And instead of a sweet fragrance there shall be stench; instead of a belt, a rope; instead of curled hair, baldness; and instead of a breast-band, sackcloth.”

For sweet fragrance is the reputation of virtues, concerning which the Apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (II Cor. II, 15). Stench, however, is evil repute and disgrace. Therefore, where virtues are taken away and vices succeed, there is stench instead of sweet fragrance.

The belt signifies the girdle of chastity; the rope, the sin of lust. Hence elsewhere it is written concerning the Lord: “He loosens the belt of kings and girds their loins with a cord” [Col. 0065D] (Job XII, 18). Kings are those who know how to govern well the movements of their members. But when the mind is touched by self-exaltation even on account of continence itself, God often, abandoning its pride, permits it to fall into the uncleanness of deed. He loosens the belt of kings when, in those who seemed to govern their members well, He destroys the girdle of chastity because of the fault of pride. And He girds their loins with a cord, so that, once the girdle of purity has been loosened, the pleasure of sin may rule their members, and so that those whom pride defiles in secret may show publicly how detestable they are. This, therefore, [Col. 0066A] is what is now said of the haughty daughters of Zion: “For instead of a belt there shall be a rope.”

“But instead of curled hair there shall be baldness.” If, according to the customary usage of the Scriptures, the head is understood as the mind, what are the hairs of this head except perceptions and thoughts? Hair, then, is curled when perceptions and thoughts are arranged in beautiful order. But baldness is given instead of curled hair when, in place of an orderly arrangement of rational thoughts in lovely degrees, the shameful and ridiculous nakedness of the mind is displayed in the manifestation of perverse action.

The breast-band is divine love, which restrains the motions of wandering thoughts by the bonds of inward affection. Sackcloth, however, commonly signifies the harshness and piercing of sin. Therefore sackcloth instead of a breast-band [Col. 0066B] occurs when, in place of charity and the discipline of the heart, which was accustomed to bind the mind in the thought of loving God, the harshness of sins and the stings of hatreds tear the mind by the piercing of evil thoughts. [Note: [Col. 0065D] Codex G: “of evil thinkings.”] It follows:

**VERSE 25.**—“Moreover, your most handsome men shall fall by the sword, and your strong men in battle.”

The most handsome men of the Church are those who fight bravely in the spiritual warfare, act manfully, and conduct themselves most honorably in divine religion. Her strong men likewise are those who fight bravely in spiritual warfare. Yet sometimes even such men, while glorying in their own beauty, fall from the state of their uprightness, pierced through by the sword of most wicked pleasure; and those who seemed strong are often overcome and fall in the battle of carnal pleasures [Col. 0066C] [Note: [Col. 0066D] Codex G: “temptations.”]. Hence Jeremiah also says: “Let their young men be pierced by the sword in battle” (Jerem. XVIII, 21). For young men are pierced by the sword in battle when those who walk bravely and eagerly in newness of life are, at the moment of temptation, transfixed by the blade of pleasure.

But if we understand this of the condition of a soul which has sinned after virtues, we take its most handsome men to be good works, which fall by the enemy’s sword; and its strong men to be virtues, which perish in spiritual battle. After so many losses of virtue and such manifold ruin of souls, the following is fittingly added concerning the Church:

**VERSE 26.**—“And her gates shall mourn and lament, [Col. 0066D] and, desolate, she shall sit upon the ground.”

For the gates of the Church are the holy teachers and rulers, through whose ministry each person enters the Church. Amid these losses of virtues, they especially mourn and lament; for as they diligently seek the gain of souls, so they affectionately bewail their loss. Each day they see more and more what they must grieve over more deeply, because days have come and are coming of which the Apostle said that in the last days perilous times will press upon us, and people will be lovers of themselves, greedy, haughty, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without natural affection, without peace, slanderers, incontinent, savage, [Col. 0067A] without kindness, insolent, swollen with pride, traitors, lovers of pleasures rather than lovers of God, having indeed an appearance of godliness but denying its power (II Tim. III, 2–5). For we see all these evils overflowing among the people of this age. Therefore, later, as evils increase still further and Antichrist reigns, the holy Church, desolate, shall sit upon the earth—that is, she shall continue in humility and sorrow, mourning, and in so many evils shall receive no consolation from man. Jeremiah too, beholding this, says: “How does the city sit alone, once full of people? The mistress of nations has become like a widow” (Lam. I, 1).

Morally understood, whoever gives place to the devil and does not guard his heart with all vigilance—his gates mourn; and, with the Bridegroom absent, he is always in grief [Col. 0067B] and, falling from on high, sits in the dust of the earth. Thus far the Prophet has described in many ways the losses of those who, after a religious life, lose the virtues and good things they had done while the devil lays snares. From here he returns his words to the time when the sevenfold Church comes to Christ, saying: “And seven women shall take hold of one man in that day.” But historically, as we began to say above, at the time of Jerusalem’s siege the Lord made the crown of the daughters of Zion bald and took from them the ornament of their footwear, their crescents, necklaces, and the other things described. Therefore, when He was being led to the cross, He said: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep over me, but weep over yourselves and over your children; for days are coming in which they will say: [Col. 0067C] Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that have not borne, and the breasts that have not nursed. Then they will begin to say to the mountains: Fall upon us; and to the hills: Cover us” (Luke XXIII, 28–30). Who can weigh the affliction, weariness of life, and distress which they endured when they said to the mountains: “Fall upon us”? All the things now described, therefore, were fulfilled there. For the most handsome men of the Jews fell by the swords of the Romans; the gates of besieged Jerusalem mourned, when no one could go out or enter; and she sat desolate upon the ground, because in that tribulation she was cast down without a comforter, and at last destroyed. And because, when that old Jerusalem fell, the new one arose, the following is aptly added:

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0067D]

**VERSE 1.**—“And seven women shall take hold of one man in that day, saying: We shall eat our own bread and wear our own garments; only let your name be invoked over us: take away our reproach.”

For what are these seven women except the seven Churches which make one catholic Church? Who is the man except Christ? Therefore seven women shall take hold of one man in that day, because at the time when old Jerusalem was destroyed and the grace of the new preaching shone upon the world, seven Churches clung to Christ, saying: “We shall eat our own bread,” that is, [Col. 0068A] the refreshment of spiritual grace, concerning which the human race, expelled from paradise, says: “I am struck down like grass, and my heart is withered, because I have forgotten to eat my bread” (Ps. CI, 5).

“And we shall cover ourselves with our own garments,” that is, with the clothing of good works, concerning which it is written: “Blessed is he who watches and keeps his garments, lest he walk naked and they see his shame” (Apoc. XVI, 15). For whatever soul neglects to eat invisibly this bread of inward refreshment and to be clothed in these garments of religious actions cannot please this one man, who is the Bridegroom of beautiful souls. “And these things,” they say, “we shall do, provided only that your name be invoked over us”: that you may be called our husband and we your wives; or, that we may be called Christians from [Col. 0068B] Christ and do all things in Christ’s name. “Take away our reproach,” that you may erase every remembrance of our sins, lest, after we have been lawfully joined to you spiritually, it be reproached to us that before we came to you we had committed fornication. It follows:

**VERSE 2.**—“In that day the Branch of the Lord shall be in magnificence and glory, and the fruit of the earth shall be exalted and a rejoicing for those who have been saved from Israel.”

The Branch of the Lord was in magnificence and glory when the eternal Son of God, appearing temporally in flesh, shone brilliantly upon the world through the greatness of His virtues and teaching. The fruit of the earth likewise became exalted when God raised to heaven, in the power [Col. 0068C] of the resurrection, the flesh which He had assumed mortal from our nature, which is of the earth, now made immortal. And then there was rejoicing for those saved from Israel—that is, His disciples—because they were so assured of the glory of His resurrection that, when He ascended to heaven, they were not only touched by no sorrow but were also filled with great joy. For as it is written: “He departed from them and was carried up into heaven; and they, worshipping, returned to Jerusalem with great joy, and were continually in the temple praising and blessing God” (Luke XXIV, 51, 53). The multitude of the remaining faithful Hebrews, whose heart and soul were one, had the same joy. Concerning them it is also added:

**VERSE 3.**—“And everyone who is left in [Col. 0068D] Zion and remains in Jerusalem shall be called holy—everyone who is written for life in Jerusalem.”

**VERSE 4.**—“When the Lord shall wash away the filth [Note: [Col. 0067D] Elsewhere: “filths.”] of the daughters of Zion, and wash from her midst the blood of Jerusalem by a spirit [Note: [Col. 0068D] Elsewhere: “in a spirit,” etc.] of judgment and a spirit of burning.”

“Everyone,” he says, “who was left in Zion in the times of the Apostles, and remained in Jerusalem, that earthly city of the Jews, shall be called holy,” receiving his name from the Holy of Holies—as though he said, “He shall be called a Christian.” Shall Caiaphas, then, be called holy? Shall Annas be called holy? Shall the Pharisees and Scribes be called holy? No. But everyone who is written [Col. 0069A] for life in Jerusalem—that is, all those to whom it is said: “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Matt. V, 12). Understand Jerusalem now as that heavenly city, concerning which it is written: “He who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved for ever” (Ps. CXXIV, 1). Therefore everyone left in Zion in the Apostolic age was called holy who deserved to be inscribed in the book of life, just as the Apostle also says: “At this time a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace. Therefore everyone who is left shall be called holy” (Rom. XI, 5).

“When the Lord shall wash away the filth of the daughters of Zion,” that is, when He shall blot out the sins of the Israelite people and wash away the blood of Jerusalem—that is, the guilt of shedding the Lord’s blood—by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning, [Col. 0069B] as Peter said to those, already pierced in heart, who sought counsel because they understood that they had crucified the Savior: “Repent,” he said, “and let every one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts II, 38). For he speaks of the spirit of judgment when he says, “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized”; he adds the spirit of kindly burning when he says, “and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.” Or rather, since it is by the same Spirit that remission of sins occurs, the Spirit of judgment was first given to the disciples, then the Spirit of burning: the Spirit of judgment when they heard, “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John XX, 22); the Spirit of burning when “there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and one sat [Col. 0069C] upon each of them, and all were filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts II, 3).

When it says, “When the Lord shall wash away the filth of the daughters of Zion,” it seems to speak conditionally, not because this was uncertain to the Lord, but because scarcely any, or only few among many, were found worthy to be washed. For by saying, “When the Lord shall wash away,” it is shown that few from the great multitude would be washed. It follows:

**VERSE 5.**—“And the Lord created [Note: [Col. 0069D] Elsewhere: “will create.”] over every place of Mount Zion, and where He is invoked, a cloud by day, and smoke and the brightness of flaming fire by night.”

By the name Mount Zion the Church is signified, as [Col. 0069D] it is written: “Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion” (Ps. CXXIV, 1). The cloud signifies divine protection, as it is written: “He spread out a cloud for their protection” (Ps. CIV, 39). Day signifies prosperity, and night adversity, as it is sung by the angelic voice: “The accuser of our brethren has been cast down, who accused them before the presence of our God day and night” (Apoc. XII, 10). For the ancient enemy strives to accuse us of making evil use of prosperity and of lacking patience in adversity. Therefore over every place of Mount Zion—that is, wherever the Church is—and where [Col. 0070A] the Lord is invoked—that is, wherever even one of the faithful invokes Him—He has created a cloud of protection and spiritual shade in the day of prosperity. For because the heat of temptation commonly burns the mind more severely in prosperity, there the divine cloud is necessary, continually removing the burning of carnal desires and providing refreshment to the mind.

But in the night of adversity He created smoke and the brightness of fire. What is this fire except that of which He says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire but that it be kindled?” (Luke XII, 49). This fire, then, seems to have smoke for some and brightness for others, according to the Apostle’s saying: “To some indeed we are a fragrance of death unto death, but to others a fragrance of life unto life” (II Cor. II, 16). For when one and the same [Col. 0070B] miracle is seen by many, and some blaspheme while others are converted; or when some attack the word of preaching while others receive it, beyond doubt this fire has smoke by which some are blinded and brightness by which others are enlightened. But the same thought is repeated further when it adds: “For over all glory there shall be protection.”

**VERSE 6.**—“And there shall be a tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0069D] Elsewhere: “there shall be.”] for shade by day from the heat, and for security and a hiding-place from storm and rain.”

For what is every elect person but the glory of God? For He says: “Everyone who calls upon my name, I created him for my glory” (Isa. XLIII, 7). Therefore over all glory—that is, over every elect person—there is protection and a tabernacle for shade [Col. 0070C] in the day of prosperity, from the heat of vices: so that when prosperity smiles and the heat of vices seeks to scorch [Note: [Col. 0070D] Codex G, erroneously.] the mind, divine protection may overshadow us and provide spiritual refreshment. The same protection gives us security from the storm of tribulations; and that tabernacle gives us a hiding-place from the rain of flatteries, so that under God’s protection we may be safe, not fearing storms of adversities, and so that our mind, hidden in the tabernacle of His shade, may not be touched by the rains of seductions and soft words, saying: “For He has hidden me in His tabernacle in the day of evil; He has protected me in the secret place of His tabernacle” (Ps. XXVI, 5). Thus far the divine prophet has delivered the words of the second vision; from here he passes on to others.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0070D]

**VERSE 1.**—“I shall sing,” he says, “to my beloved the song of my cousin concerning his vineyard.”

Moses sang a song of joy after crossing the Red Sea (Exod. XV); Deborah likewise, when Barak had won victory (Judg. V); and David, after being delivered from all his enemies (II Kings XXII). Jeremiah, however, sang a lamenting song, saying: “How does the city sit alone, once full of people?” (Lam. I, 1), and so forth. Moses’ final song also is more a song of sadness than of joy, because the people’s unbelief is foretold in it. Thus Isaiah too is now about to sing a song of mourning: “I shall sing,” [Col. 0071A] he says, “to my beloved,” that is, God the Father, “the song of my cousin,” that is, the Lord Jesus, who by assuming flesh will become my blood-relative—the song, I say, concerning the condition of His vineyard, that is, His people. A *patruelis* is the son of a father’s brother; a *patruus* is the brother of one’s father, as an *avunculus* is the brother of one’s mother. Therefore the Prophet calls Christ his cousin because of nearness of kindred, since He was to assume humanity from that people.

Or Christ is the beloved, to whom the Father says: “You are my beloved Son” (Mark I, 2). And that Beloved made a mournful song about His vineyard, which I shall sing to my beloved people. The song begins thus: “A vineyard was made for my beloved on a horn, the son of oil.” And later it is said: “For the vineyard of the Lord [Col. 0071B] of hosts is the house of Israel.” What does the horn signify except the strength of a kingdom? Therefore a vineyard was made for my beloved on a horn when God’s ancient people advanced into a kingdom. It was made on a horn, the son of oil, because the strength of its kingdom came from the grace of God. It follows:

**VERSE 2.**—“And He fenced it in, selected stones out of it, and planted it as a choice vine.”

He fenced, or fences, it in with angelic guardianships. “And He selected stones out of it,” because He removed the remnant of the Amorites and drove out the adversaries. “And He planted it as a choice vine,” because He chose them for Himself “as His peculiar possession from all nations that are under heaven” (Exod. XIX, 5). It follows:

“And He built a tower in its midst,” that is, [Col. 0071C] the Temple. “And He constructed a winepress [Note: [Col. 0071D] Elsewhere: “a winepress in it.”],” that is, the altar, upon which the blood of victims was poured out, as grapes are pressed in a press. After all these benefits, it adds:

“And He waited for it to produce grapes, and it produced wild grapes.” He waited for His vineyard, according to the sweetness of its nature, to produce grapes—that is, for God’s people to render pleasing and sweet fruits of good works; but, on the contrary, it produced wild grapes—that is, bitter and uncultivated works of paganism. For a *labrusca* is a wild cluster and is called *labrusca* because it grows at the edges (*labra*) of the land, that is, near roads and in hedges, signifying the works of the nations that were around them. The vineyard of the Lord produced wild grapes because [Col. 0071D] Judea, degenerating from the fruit of the patriarchs, produced not the fruit of righteousness but the works of paganism. Then the voice of the master of the household is introduced, saying:

**VERSE 3.**—“Now therefore, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, judge between me and my vineyard,” etc.

At this point what the inhabitants of Jerusalem replied in giving judgment is left unstated. But it is made clear in the Gospel. For they said: “He will destroy the wicked men miserably and lease his vineyard to other husbandmen, who will render him the fruits in their seasons” (Matt. XXI, 41). And when they had condemned themselves by their own judgment, the Lord explained further: “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (ibid.). In the same way He speaks here: “Judge,” He says, “between me and my vineyard.”

**VERSE 4.**—“What more ought I to have done for my vineyard which I did not do for it? Why did I wait for it to produce grapes, and it produced wild grapes?”

Understand: “Ought I not to have done it?” For is it my fault that it produced wild grapes, when I waited for it to produce grapes?

**VERSE 5.**—“Now [Note: [Col. 0072D] Elsewhere: “And now.”],” He says, “I shall show you what I shall do to my vineyard.”

And what He says in the Gospel, “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you” (Matt. XXI, 43), He adds here: “I shall take away its hedge, and it shall be plundered; I shall tear down its wall, and it shall be trampled.”

[Col. 0072B] **VERSE 6.**—“And I shall make it desolate,” etc.

“I shall take away its hedge,” that is, the guardianship of angels and the defense of my protection, and it shall become plunder for the Roman army. “I shall tear down its wall,” that is, the wall of Jerusalem, when Titus besieges it, and it shall be trampled by all passers-by; because “they shall fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive among all nations” (Luke XXI, 24). “And I shall make it desolate,” so utterly uncultivated that it will henceforth bear no fruit of domestic cultivation, but will continually produce wild works.

“It shall not be pruned or dug, and briers and thorns shall grow upon it.” It shall not be pruned, because the branches of vices shall not be cut off from it; rather, they shall die in their sins; nor shall it be dug with the hoe of preaching in order to bear fruit. And briers and [Col. 0072C] thorns—that is, the pricks of sins and crimes—shall grow upon it.

“And I shall command the clouds,” He says, “not to rain rain upon it.” The Apostles say this to that vineyard: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you. But because you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles. For thus the Lord commanded us: I have set you as a light to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII, 46–47). For they are the clouds, because it is said of them: “Who are these that fly like clouds?” (Isa. LX, 8). They were therefore commanded not to rain the shower of preaching upon the unfruitful vineyard, because they were sent to the Gentiles, where they might find fruit. Having spoken mystically thus far, he now plainly [Col. 0072D] declares what this vineyard is, adding:

**VERSE 7.**—“For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the man of Judah His delightful shoot.”

The house of Israel signifies the ten tribes, and the man of Judah the house of Judah, from which the Lord arose. Because of nearness of descent, every man of Judah is His delightful shoot; but the remaining tribes are only His vineyard, that is, His people.

“And I waited for it to render judgment, and behold iniquity; and justice, and behold a cry.” It ought to have rendered judgment between me and Barabbas (Matt. XXVII, 21); but it produced iniquity—that is, transgression of the law—by setting free a murderer whom the law condemns (Num. XXXVIII). For law is called *nomos* (νόμος) in Greek, and from this *anomia* is called iniquity: whatever is without the law or contrary to the law. [Col. 0073A] And I waited for it to render justice by condemning the wicked man, and behold a cry against me, saying: “Crucify, crucify him” (Luke XXIII, 21).

Now let us see whether these things can be understood of those who bear the Christian name. “A vineyard,” he says, “was made for my beloved on a horn, the son of oil.” The Church is God’s vineyard; however many saints it brings forth, it sends out, as it were, so many branches, to whom He Himself says: “I am the vine; you are the branches” (John XV, 5). By the horn—that is, by the corner of a field—the excellent and best part of the land is signified, and through it the chosen part of humankind. Therefore the vineyard was made on a horn, since the Church was planted among the chosen part of humanity. By oil, however, the anointing of the Holy Spirit is signified. Thus he says: “A vineyard was made for my beloved on a horn, the son of oil.” For the son of oil is the faithful people, begotten unto faith in God by the inward anointing of the Holy Spirit. Concerning this oil it is again said: “The yoke shall rot away before the oil” (Isa. X, 27). For the yoke rots away before the oil because, when we are anointed with the grace of the Holy Spirit, we are freed from the servitude of our captivity; and when the proud dominion of evil spirits is driven away, the yoke by which the necks of our freedom were oppressed is broken. Therefore the vineyard was made for my beloved on a horn, the son of oil, because the Church was made for Christ among chosen and spiritual men, who were born from heavenly grace. [Col. 0073C]

“And He fenced it in and selected stones out of it, and planted it as a choice vine.” He fenced it in, as it is written: “The Savior shall be set in it as a wall” (Isa. XXVI, 1). And in Zechariah: “I shall be to her,” says the Lord, “a wall of fire round about” (Zech. II, 5). Or the fortification of discipline may be denoted by the name hedge. He fenced it in, therefore, because He gave it the fortification of discipline. What, indeed, is signified by harmful stones in the vineyard except the hardness of those who remained in unbelief while the world received faith? Therefore He selected stones out of it, because He carefully removed from the midst of the faithful dwelling-place the remnant of unbelievers and everything that could impede the worship of God.

[Col. 0073D] “And He planted it as a choice vine,” because, as it is said elsewhere: “He who sows the good seed is the Son of Man. The good seed, then, are the children of the kingdom” (Matt. XIII, 37–38). Although the enemy has sown tares over it, nevertheless the master of the household sowed nothing but good seed in his field and planted His vineyard as a choice vine.

“And He built a tower in its midst, and constructed a winepress in it.” He built a tower in it because He gave it rulers whose manner of life, like a lofty tower, might rise above it, provide for it, and guard it; concerning whom it is said: “And abundance is in your towers” (Ps. CXXI, 7).

What is signified by the winepress except the pressure of tribulation and the severity of discipline, which cleanses the elect [Col. 0074A] from the filth of vices and separates them from the reprobate, as the grape is strained in the press and oil is separated from dregs? Hence some psalms are entitled “For the winepresses.” Therefore, after receiving so many and such great benefits from God, let us see what man has rendered. It follows:

“And He waited for it to produce grapes, and it produced wild grapes,” because after God had granted it so many goods, cast out the remnant of unbelievers like stones, and given it peace everywhere, it immediately adhered to vices when the multitude of the carnal increased; and in very many who are called Christians it lives like the Gentiles. Not only the Church, but also each one of us, is long awaited by heavenly mercy for doing good. Hence He promises, saying: “If he comes in the second watch, and if he comes in the third watch, and finds them so, blessed are those servants” (Luke [Col. 0074B] XII, 38).

“And it produced,” he says, “wild grapes,” because—alas!—though awaited, we are not ashamed to live carnally, follow the examples of the perverse, and perform the works of unbelievers.

“Now therefore, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, judge between me and my vineyard.” The inhabitants of Jerusalem are those who dwell in the Church. For this is the city of the great King; this is the vision of peace. Peace indeed is multiplied in us, if nevertheless we are children of peace. We too are men of Judah because of Christ, who was born from Judah. The very name Judah also refers to Christ, as it is written: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hand shall be upon the necks of your enemies; the sons of your father shall worship you” (Gen. XLIX, [Col. 0074C] 8). Therefore the discourse is now addressed to the inhabitants of Jerusalem—that is, to those in the Church—and to the men of Judah, undoubtedly to Christians. We may understand this to be said to those who shall sit “upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX, 28). For even now the vineyard of the Lord is judged through them, “because it is time for judgment to begin with the house of God” (I Pet. IV, 17), which is also His vineyard.

“And now,” He says, “I shall show you what I shall do to my vineyard.” I shall take away the hedge of its fortification and defense, because I was a wall around it. And it shall be plundered by greedy robbers—that is, evil spirits who will plunder the good things of virtues. [Col. 0074D] I shall tear down its wall—that is, I shall destroy the fortification of its discipline and its religion. And it shall be trampled, because it shall be trampled in the mire of vices by unclean spirits. Hence elsewhere it is said: “Open it, that those who trample it may come out” (Jerem. L, 26). And I shall make it desolate, so that it may no longer produce any fruit of good work.

“It shall not be pruned or dug, and briers and thorns shall grow upon it.” Pruning is appraisal. For when someone takes up a vine to cleanse it, he prunes—that is, considers and judges what he ought to cut away and what to leave. So God considers the works of His faithful: He preserves the good but cuts away the evil. But those who are continually devoted to evil deeds and with obstinate minds trample His commandments, He does not easily cut away their vices; rather, by terrible judgment He leaves them in their wickedness. And this is what He now threatens: it shall not be pruned or cut back, nor rebuked for the evil it does, but shall be left uncultivated in the horror of its iniquities.

“And I shall command the clouds not to rain rain upon it.” The clouds are holy preachers, who water the parched soil of the human breast with streams of heavenly understanding. But they are commanded to withhold their rain when the soul of the hearer is unworthy of the heavenly shower [Note: [Col. 0075D] Codex Cruc.: “dew.”], as it is said through Solomon: “Do not speak in the ears of fools, because they despise the teaching of your speech” (Prov. XXIII, 9). For because of the excessive sins of subjects, the word of preaching is taken away from teachers. Hence the Lord says to Ezekiel: “I shall make your tongue cling [Col. 0075B] to your palate, and you shall be mute, not like a reproving man, because they are a provoking house” (Ezek. III, 26). Amos also says: “The prudent man shall keep silence in that time, because it is an evil time” (Amos V, 19). This, therefore, is what is said: “I shall command the clouds not to rain rain upon it”—a thing whose excessive fulfillment in our days we lament, because now scarcely anyone speaks the word of God to His people.

“For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the man of Judah His delightful shoot.” The house of Israel is that to which it is said through the Apostle: “But if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s children, heirs according to the promise” (Gal. III, 22). The house of Israel is the Church, which follows the faith of the patriarchs; [Col. 0075C] and the Church is God’s vineyard. Any Christian is a man of Judah, as we showed above; and therefore the man of Judah is His delightful shoot, because God delights in those children “who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (John I, 19).

“‘I expected it to produce judgment, and behold, iniquity; and righteousness, and behold, an outcry.’ To practice God’s judgment and righteousness is this: in every work that you intend to do, first think of God; and, if what you intend accords with God, examine it carefully; and, if it is right before the Lord, carry it out. But if it is found contrary, cut it away from your soul. Yet when those who follow the fickleness of their own will are expected to practice judgment and righteousness, iniquity and outcry break forth. For one who commits lesser sins, as it were, speaks perversities in God’s ears; but one who perpetrates grave evils already cries aloud to the ears of the Almighty. Hence it is written: ‘The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied’ (Gen. 18:20). Such an outcry, therefore, daily rises to God from the wicked. It follows:

VERSE 8.—“Woe to you who join house to house and attach field to field, even to the boundary of the place: shall you dwell [Note: [Col. 0076D] Later editions: “you shall dwell” (*habitabitis*).] alone in the midst of the earth?”

The Prophet now speaks plainly [Col. 0076A] concerning the corrupt morals of his people, interpreting what he had said above allegorically—that the Lord’s vineyard had produced wild grapes. He rebukes the greedy and those devoted to drunkenness; those who draw out iniquities; those who praise evil and blaspheme good; those who arrogantly claim wisdom for themselves; and those who boast greatly of drinking wine. Upon each of these he threatens the woe of everlasting bitterness. But just as up to this point we have shown that what was said about the Jewish people is also said about the Christian people, so now let us understand the prophetic threats to be directed likewise toward those who bear the Christian name and do such things.

Therefore, let all who strive to seize what belongs to others, while desiring to enlarge the extent of spacious dwellings or extend the bounds of their lands, hear what is said: “Woe to you [Col. 0076B] who join house to house and attach field to field, even to the boundary of the place: shall you dwell alone in the midst of the earth?” As though it were said: How long will you keep extending yourselves, as though you could not possibly have companions in the common habitation of the world? It follows:

VERSE 9.—“These things are in my ears, says the Lord of hosts.”

Such deeds, as has been said above, cry out to the ears of the heavenly Judge. In anger he adds: “Unless many houses are made desolate.” This elliptical manner of speaking is a very forceful sign, and most strongly confirms what he threatens. Thus, when the Pharisees tested him by seeking a sign from heaven, “groaning in spirit, he said: Amen, I say to you, if a sign shall be given to this generation” [Col. 0076C] (Mark 8:12). And elsewhere: “As I swore in my wrath, if they shall enter into my rest” (Ps. 54:11). Therefore, angry with those who join house to house, he says: “Unless many houses are made desolate,” because while the greedy persist in multiplying their possessions, they are snatched away by unexpected death. Thus the rich man who said, “I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will gather all my produce and my goods; and I will say to my soul: Soul, you have many goods stored up for many years; rest, eat, drink, feast” (Luke 12:18–19), heard from God: “Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you; and whose will be the things you have prepared?” (ibid., v. 20). This, then, is what he threatens when he says, “Unless many houses are made desolate.” And to what he had said, “You attach field to field,” [Col. 0076D] he adds:

VERSE 10.—“For ten yoke-measures of vineyards shall yield one small flask, and thirty measures of seed shall yield three measures.”

For because they join fields to fields in order to gather an abundance of crops from them, by God’s just judgment their vineyards and fields become barren, so that ten *jugera* of vineyards scarcely yield one little flask of must, and the breadth of fields in which thirty measures of seed have been sown scarcely yields three measures. For barrenness of the earth often occurs because of the iniquity of the greedy. Hence Haggai says: “You looked for much, and behold, it came to little” [Col. 0077A] (Hag. 1:9). After this Isaiah rebukes the excess of drunkards, saying:

VERSE 11.—“Woe to you who rise early to pursue drunkenness, and continue drinking until evening, so that you burn with wine.”

VERSE 12.—“The harp and lyre, tambourine and flute, and wine are at your banquets; but you do not regard the work of the Lord, nor consider the works of his hands.”

These things are clear even without exposition. For those who do not seek the joys of the life to come are corrupted by such pleasures. And while they dissolve themselves in musical sounds and wine, they do not regard the work of the Lord—that is, they do not consider what the Lord commands them to do. Nor do they consider the works of his hands, which he accomplished in the flesh. [Col. 0077B] Hence evil spirits subject them to every servitude of vice. For it follows:

VERSE 13.—“Therefore my people has been led captive, because it had no knowledge; and its nobles have perished through hunger, and its multitude has dried up through thirst.”

For while they devote themselves to feasting and drinking, they die through spiritual hunger and thirst. But the Jewish people was led captive by the Romans among all nations because it did not possess knowledge of the Scriptures, so that, recognizing Christ whom Moses and the prophets had promised to it, it might receive him.

Sacred Scripture is sometimes food for us and sometimes drink. It is food in its more obscure passages, because through exposition it is, as it were, broken like food and swallowed by chewing. It is drink in clearer passages, because it is drunk in just the form in which it is found. The prophet saw food and drink, as it were, lacking to this people when he said:

“Its nobles have perished through hunger, and its multitude has dried up through thirst.” For it belongs to the few to know strong and hidden matters, but to the many to grasp the open meaning of the history. Therefore he declares that the nobles of Judah perished not by thirst but by hunger, because those who seemed to preside, having wholly devoted themselves to external understanding, did not have what they might chew by examining inward things. But because, when the higher ranks fall away from inward understanding, even the understanding of little ones is dried up in external matters, [Col. 0077D] he rightly adds: “Its multitude has dried up through thirst.” It is as though he said plainly: When the common people abandon concern for their life, they no longer seek even the streams of the historical narrative. It follows:

VERSE 14.—“Therefore hell has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth without any limit; and its mighty men, its people, its lofty and glorious ones, shall descend to it.”

Whoever is seized by hell is swallowed into immensity. Wishing to explain its immense breadth, the prophet says: “Hell has enlarged its soul,” that is, its inner parts. “And it has opened its mouth without any limit”—understand, in order to devour the infinite [Col. 0078A] multitude of sinners. For it is said to be enlarged and opened without limit because it draws countless persons to itself and, receiving them into itself, swallows them as though into a certain abyss of its immensity.

Blessed Pope Gregory also writes (*Dialogues*, book IV, ch. 35) that “more than in other places, on the islands of Sicily, pits of torments have opened through the belching forth of fire. As those who know relate, these pits enlarge daily as their openings are loosened, so that, as the end of the world approaches—when it is certain that more persons are to be gathered there for burning—the same places of torment appear to open ever more widely. Almighty God willed this to be shown in this world for the correction of the living, so that unbelievers who do not believe that the torments of hell exist may see the places of torment whose existence they refuse to believe when they hear of them.” Thus it is rightly said [Col. 0078B] that, as the multitude of evildoers increases, hell has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth without any limit. “And,” he says, “its mighty men, its people, and its lofty and glorious ones shall descend to it.”

This was fulfilled especially with respect to the Jews when, as the Romans besieged the city of Jerusalem, an exceedingly great multitude of that unbelieving people perished through hunger, plague, and the sword. Of them it is further added:

VERSE 15.—“And man shall be bowed down, and the man of rank humbled, and the eyes of the lofty brought low.”

VERSE 16.—“And the Lord of hosts shall be exalted in judgment, and the holy God shall be sanctified in righteousness.”

For those who raised themselves against the Romans—or rather, against God—were bowed down in Roman chains after Jerusalem was taken, and were crushed in captivity. And the Lord Jesus was exalted, trampling those who had hitherto trampled him; he who is holy in himself through righteousness, justly condemning his enemies in the sight of men and delivering them to the Romans. When they were destroyed or driven out, the Church’s preaching gained strength. For it follows:

VERSE 17.—“And lambs shall feed according to their order, and strangers shall eat the deserts turned into abundance.”

He calls those “lambs” who are to be fed, concerning whom Peter heard: “Feed my lambs” (John 21:16). And to these the Lord says through Jeremiah: “I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they shall feed you with knowledge and teaching” [Col. 0078D] (Jer. 3:15). Each of them shall be fed according to his order, because, although there are diverse orders in the Church, holy teachers know how they ought to instruct each person.

The sacred Scriptures, which were uncultivated among the Jews because their spiritual sense was not frequented, are called deserts. [Note: [Col. 0077D] Codex G: “their spiritual senses were not frequented.”] But these deserts, transformed into the abundance of spiritual understanding, shall now be eaten by strangers—that is, by the Gentiles.

The Christian people too is spiritually led captive [Note: [Col. 0078D] Codex Cruc.: “is said” (*dicitur*) for “is led” (*ducitur*).], because it neglects to possess knowledge of the Scriptures while it does not learn letters. And its nobles—that is, its priests—have perished through hunger for God’s word, because [Col. 0079A] they themselves, devoted to earthly affairs, do not understand the Scriptures. And its multitude—that is, the simple—suffers thirst for knowledge. Therefore hell enlarges its soul, because places of torment are increased on their account. “And its mighty men shall descend to it,” because “the powerful shall suffer powerful torments” (Wis. 6:7). And its people shall descend, because, as Hosea says, “A people without understanding shall be beaten” (Hos. 40:14). And man shall be bowed down for punishment, who now rises in pride; and the eyes of the lofty shall be humbled. But leaving these matters to be understood, let us pass on to others. It follows:

VERSE 18.—“Woe to you who draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as with the harness-rope of a cart.”

[Col. 0079B] VERSE 19.—“You who say: Let his work hasten and come quickly, that we may see it; let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw near and come, that we may know it!”

Iniquity is drawn with cords of vanity when guilt is prolonged by increase. For the cord of vanity is sin: it binds the sinner and yet is itself nothing, because it has no substance. Hence the Psalmist says: “The cords of sinners have encompassed me” (Ps. 116:61). Since a cord is twisted by adding strands so that it may grow, sin is not unfittingly represented by a cord, for it is always multiplied when defended with a perverse heart.

The harness-rope of a cart is the strap that binds an ox so that it bears the yoke and draws a laden cart. And sin is drawn as with the harness-rope of a cart when the devil’s yoke is borne with a huge burden of iniquities. But those draw out wickedness in this way who do not believe that they will someday suffer penalties worthy of their evil deeds. Therefore they say mockingly: Let his work—that which he will do on the day of judgment—hasten and come quickly. And let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel come, that which he has planned concerning the rewards of the righteous and the recompense of the wicked, and we shall know it. They speak thus because they do not suppose that they will be punished. It follows:

VERSE 20.—“Woe to you who call good evil [Note: [Col. 0079D] Elsewhere: “evil good, good evil,” etc.] and evil good; who make darkness light and light darkness; who make bitter sweet and sweet bitter.”

[Col. 0079D] The fault against which woe is now pronounced can scarcely be avoided by anyone living. For we often call evil—which pleases us—good; and we call good—which we do not want—evil. We often boast that the darkness of our error is the light of knowledge, and call the light of a brother’s counsel the darkness of ignorance. Moreover, we judge sweet the bitterness with which we are filled while we wish to serve our desires, because we love the present age; and we judge the sweetness of spiritual life bitter.

To call good, light, and sweetness by contrary names belongs to the same sin as calling evil, darkness, and bitterness by the names of virtue. This is directed against those [Col. 0080A] who do not regard it as sin if they disparage good, and do not judge it an offense if they praise evil. The Jews especially called evil good and good evil when they said to the Lord: “Do we not rightly say that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” (John 8:48). They made darkness light and light darkness when they said to the blind man: “You are his disciple; but we are disciples of Moses” (John 9:28). They made bitter sweet and sweet bitter when, in the Passion of the Savior, they cried: “Take this man away, and release Barabbas to us” (Luke 23:18). This saying may still be understood in various other ways. But we hasten on to other matters. It follows:

VERSE 21.—“Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent before yourselves.”

[Col. 0080B] The proud person always seems wise to himself and judges that he acts prudently. If one of the brethren gives him counsel and says, “Brother, you ought not to act in this way,” he does not deign to listen, because he considers himself wiser than the other. Hence the Apostle fittingly says that “one who thinks he knows something does not yet know how he ought to know” (1 Cor. 8:9). We must take care lest received wisdom, while it illuminates the darkness of ignorance, take away the light of humility, and so no longer be wisdom—though it shines outwardly by the power of speech, it darkens the speaker’s heart with the veil of pride. For one who arrogantly appears wise to himself is as far from the light of true wisdom as he is not humble in his own judgment. Such were the scribes [Col. 0080C] and Pharisees, who boasted of being wise and persecuted God’s wisdom, which is Christ. It follows:

VERSE 22.—“Woe to you who are mighty in drinking wine and strong men in mixing drunkenness!”

VERSE 23.—“You who justify the ungodly for gifts and take away the righteousness of the righteous from him.”

Saint Timothy was indeed commanded to “use a little wine for the sake of his stomach and his frequent infirmities” (1 Tim. 5:23). But what the righteous person takes sparingly, compelled by necessity, the perverse take immoderately, enticed by pleasure; and they boast that they can drink much wine, by which, when glutted, they lose the steadiness of mind. In judgment, for money, they acquit the guilty; and because the just person does not [Col. 0080D] offer gifts, they condemn him. Such are the works of drunkenness and greed.

What the prophet has so far spoken morally applies both to the Jewish people and to the Christian people. But what he now adds, let us understand of the Jews. For since they performed the deeds he has rebuked up to this point, let us see what he brings forward:

VERSE 24.—“Therefore, as the tongue of fire devours stubble and the heat of flame consumes it, so their root shall be as ashes, and their shoot shall rise like dust.”

This is said of the day of judgment, concerning which Malachi says: “Behold, the day shall come burning like a furnace, and all the proud and all who do iniquity shall be stubble; and the coming day shall set them ablaze, says the Lord of hosts, and shall leave them neither root nor shoot” [Col. 0081A] (Mal. 4:1). Therefore, as stubble is devoured by fire, so their root shall be as ashes. For stubble that is burned is reduced to ashes.

Their root shall become like ashes because it shall both be torn out from the fellowship of the righteous and burned. And their shoot, which does not appear green, shall rise like dust when the Judge cleanses his threshing floor with the winnowing fan. For they shall be like chaff before the face of the wind, and like ashes scattered by a whirlwind. And why?

“For they have cast away the law of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0081D] Elsewhere: “the Lord of hosts.”],” which had been given through Moses; and afterward they “blasphemed the word of the Holy One of Israel”—that is, the preaching of Christ. [Col. 0081B] For if they had not cast away the law of the Lord, they would not have blasphemed the preaching of the Holy One of Israel, who says: “If you believed Moses, perhaps you would believe me also. For he wrote concerning me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?” (John 5:46–47). It follows:

VERSE 25.—“Therefore the wrath of the Lord was angered against his people, and he stretched out his hand over them and struck them; the mountains were troubled, and their corpses became like dung in the midst of the streets.”

Wrath is the most vehement kindling of a stirred mind against one who has done wrong. But God cannot possess wrath in himself, because, being immutable, he is not mentally stirred when angry; rather, in calmness he does what is just. But because he strikes the sinner, he appears [Col. 0081C] as though moved against him by wrath.

The wrath of the Lord was angered against the Jewish people; stretching out his hand against them, he struck them through Vespasian and his son Titus. And the mountains were troubled—that is, the exalted leaders of the Jews. And their corpses became like dung in the midst of the streets, because in the siege of Jerusalem such a multitude of them died from hunger and plague that no one was sufficient to bury them. It follows:

“In all these things his fury has not been turned away, but his hand is still stretched out.” To this day God’s wrath justly persists upon the remnant of the Jews. For his wrath is not like human wrath—that is, a disturbance of an excited mind—but a calm disposition simply established. [Col. 0081D] Because they themselves still remain in wickedness, therefore heavenly wrath still remains upon them. His hand is still stretched out over them, because he still afflicts them. It follows:

VERSE 26.—“And he shall raise a standard among nations far away, and whistle to him from the ends of the earth; and behold, he shall come swiftly and quickly.”

Our King raised the sign of his victory—the sign of the cross—among the nations, in order to gather soldiers to himself from them. And he whistled to it—that is, to the sign of the cross—after the manner of a shepherd gathering his sheep by a whistle; and he gathered them from the ends of the earth, because through the preaching of the apostles he summoned even the furthest recesses of the world to [Col. 0082A] his faith. Hence he says also in Zechariah: “I will whistle for them and gather them, because I have redeemed them” (Zech. 10:8). And once the nations have been gathered to faith, behold, he shall come swiftly and quickly for judgment, in order to render them their reward; for “the day of the Lord is near, and exceedingly swift” (Zeph. 1:14). For the brevity of this life flies past quickly, and Christ soon comes to render the righteous eternal rewards for their labors. Those who faithfully consider these things now bear everything cheerfully and do not fail. Hence it adds:

VERSE 27.—“There is none fainting or laboring.”

There is none fainting in him, because “whoever perseveres to the end, he shall be saved” (Matt. 24:19). Therefore, whoever fails amid adversities is not in our Savior, because he does not have salvation and is not a member of Christ. [Col. 0082B] Nor is anyone laboring in him, because whatever the saints suffer for him is delightful to them. It follows:

“He shall neither slumber nor sleep.” By divine sleep we mean God’s withdrawal, immutable from the things he has foreseen. Conversely, he is awake when he provides aid through teaching or salvation for those who pray for it. Therefore he does not sleep in the great elect, of whom the discourse is now speaking, because he always provides what benefits them and helps them. But neither does he slumber, because he does not close his eyes to their care even in small matters. He may perhaps be believed to sleep when they are torn here by the cruelties of the unjust without vengeance. Yet he watches over his servants all the more when the wickedness [Col. 0082C] of a persecutor unjustly afflicts them. For seeing what they humbly endure here, he surely foresees what he will mercifully repay them there. It follows:

“Neither shall the belt of his loins be loosed, nor the strap of his sandal be broken.” As we read below: “Faith is the belt of his loins” (Isa. 11:5). Therefore the belt of his loins shall not be loosed, because faith shall not be taken away from us. For persecutors have often tried to extinguish his faith and remove it from the world. The sandal signifies evangelical preaching, as the Apostle says: “Your feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace” (Eph. 6:15). Therefore the strap of his sandal shall not be broken, because the bound sandal of evangelical preaching shall not be scattered. For heavenly teaching is bound in the hearts [Col. 0082D] of preachers, as it is written: “Bind up the testimony and seal the law among my disciples” (Isa. 8:16). The strap that binds this evangelical sandal in us is never broken. It follows:

VERSE 28.—“His arrows are sharp, and all his bows are bent.”

What are represented by the bows but the divine Scriptures, from which judgments dart forth like arrows so that the hearts of adversaries may be struck? Therefore his arrows are sharp, because to those whom he corrects through terror he sends pointed, striking, and penetrating judgments of words. And all his bows are bent, because all [Col. 0083A] the divine Scriptures direct threats against all sinners. It follows:

“His horses’ hooves are like flint, and his wheels like the rush of a tempest.” Strength for labor is commonly recognized in a horse’s hoof. Who, then, are God’s horses but holy preachers, seated upon whom he attacks his adversaries? What is signified by horses’ hooves except perfection in virtues, that is, strength in a right course? Therefore his horses’ hooves are like flint, because the power of the Evangelists’ swift progress, by which they run to preach, is most robust. What is expressed by wheels but the rolling movement of preaching? [Note: [Col. 0083D] Codex G: “preachings.”] Thus Ezekiel saw “a wheel in the midst of a wheel” (Ezek. 1:16), because the New Testament is within the Old. Therefore his wheels are borne like the rush of a tempest because [Col. 0083B] his preachings strike and trouble the sinner’s mind with mighty force. It follows:

VERSE 29.—“His roaring is like a lion’s; he shall roar like lion cubs; he shall gnash his teeth, seize the prey, and embrace it, and there shall be none to rescue it.”

VERSE 30.—“And on that day he shall resound over him like the sound of the sea.”

His roaring was like a lion’s because he cried out terribly, saying: “Serpents, brood of vipers, how shall you flee from the judgment of Gehenna?” (Matt. 23:33). And: “Every tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. 3:10). He roared like lion cubs because through the apostles, who are the sons of the prophets [Col. 0083C] like lion cubs, he cried out in the desert of this age the terror of the same judgment.

“And,” he says, “he shall gnash his teeth, seize the prey, and embrace it, and there shall be none to rescue it.” He gnashed his teeth when he answered the persecutors: “I am he” (John 18:5). For immediately “they went backward and fell to the ground” (ibid., v. 6). He held the prey which he had seized—that is, the disciples whom he had chosen—adding: “If therefore you seek me, let these go” (ibid., v. 8). There the Evangelist added: “That the word of Jesus might be fulfilled which he had spoken: Of those whom you gave me, I have lost none” (ibid., v. 9). Therefore he held and embraced the prey like a lion confident in his strength, because with one utterance he threw down his enemies and lost none of his chosen disciples. [Col. 0083D] He held the prey when he said of his sheep: “No one shall snatch them from my hand” (John 10:28).

“And there shall be none,” he says, “to rescue it, and he shall resound over him.” Who shall resound? The one who will vainly try to snatch the prey away from him—that is, the Jewish people. It shall resound over him like the sound of the sea, that is, crying with a tumultuous and confused multitude: “He is guilty of death; crucify him, crucify him” (John 19:6). Those who sought to take the prey from him so resounded over him because they killed him in order to separate the multitudes of believers from him. Hence it is written elsewhere: “For they thought within themselves, saying: This is the heir; let us kill him, that the inheritance may become ours” (Matt. 21:28).

But because thereafter none of them raised his mind toward the joys of the heavenly homeland, and the desolation of Jerusalem and the captivity of that people followed at Roman hands, he adds in their voice:

“We shall look upon the earth, and behold, the darkness of tribulation; and its light has been darkened in its gloom.” “We shall look,” they say, “upon the earth—we who were accustomed to look toward heaven”; that is, we shall now think only about earthly things. “And behold, the darkness of tribulation shall break forth,” because the whole homeland shall suddenly be destroyed through Vespasian and Titus. “And the light of our mind has been darkened in its gloom,” because counsel, wisdom, and understanding have fled from us amid the confusion and extremity of tribulation. Thus far Isaiah has spoken the things divinely shown to him [Col. 0084B] under King Uzziah; henceforth he will speak of what he saw or heard under King Jotham.

## CHAPTER VI

VERSE 1.—“In the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up, and the things beneath him filled the temple.”

VERSE 2.—“Seraphim stood above it.”

As long as Uzziah held the kingdom, Isaiah could not see the Lord Sabaoth. For Uzziah entered the temple as though a priest, contrary to the will of the divine law, and for this reason was struck with leprosy on his forehead, so [Col. 0084C] that he was cast outside the city and reckoned among the unclean (2 Chron. 26). Therefore, because he entered the sanctuary sacrilegiously, it was fitting that, while he lived, the mystery of the divine vision should not be revealed. For it was a grave offense to open the sanctuary unlawfully. Accordingly, it was fitting that the palace of the divine dwelling should remain closed during his days. Upon his death, therefore, the heavenly palaces stand open and the glory of the divine majesty is seen.

“I saw,” he says, “the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up.” Sitting belongs to one who reigns, because “the Lord shall sit as king forever” (Ps. 28:10). Dominion, moreover, is not merely superiority over subjects, but the most perfect and complete possession of every good and excellent thing, and true and unchangeable [Col. 0084D] stability. Therefore he alone, the highest ruler, is rightly called Lord. His throne is the particular order of angelic spirits properly called Thrones, lofty in its nature and lifted up by divine contemplation.

“And the things beneath him filled the temple.” By the name “temple” is designated the heavenly dwelling above, as John testifies, saying: “I saw, and behold, the temple of the tabernacle of testimony in heaven was opened” (Rev. 15:5). And shortly afterward: “And no one was able to enter the temple until the seven plagues of the seven angels were completed” (ibid., v. 8). Therefore the things beneath him filled the temple, because [Col. 0085A] that heavenly dwelling above is full of the innumerable multitude of many thousands of angels.

Seraphim is the name of the first and highest order of all, which stood above the temple, because even by its position it is above all the remaining orders, so that no other spirits intervene between it and God. Hence another translation says that “the Seraphim stood around him.” And for this reason they are called Seraphim—that is, “the burning ones” or “those who set on fire”—because they burn with greater love for their Creator the more closely they see him. It follows:

“Six wings to one, and six wings to the other. With two they covered his face, with two they covered his feet, and with two they were flying.” Because this order of blessed spirits burns with charity beyond the others, and charity is distinguished in two commandments [Col. 0085B] and is chiefly known between two persons, therefore two Seraphim are spoken of, though they are innumerable. And when it is said, “Six wings to one and six wings to the other,” we should not suppose that a numerical count is indicated, but rather that their first, middle, and final intellectual powers freely and completely fly toward God. Hence they are described as having paired wings around face, middle, and feet, in order to suggest universally their wholly airborne nature, abundantly tending upward toward divine things.

But by God’s face, perhaps, divinity may be understood, and by his feet, his humanity. They cover his face, therefore, because the things that concern God are incomprehensible even to them. They cover his feet because, as Dionysius the Areopagite affirms, according to us “the divine formation of Jesus is beyond all reason, hidden from every intellect, and unknown even to the most excellent of the most honorable angels.”

Or rather, by his face and feet let us understand the higher and deeper things of divine intelligences. For God’s height is this: he is none of the things that exist, nor is he anything known to any existing thing; he is neither word nor name nor knowledge, but is exalted in darkness above all things. His depth likewise is darkness and ignorance incomprehensible to all existing beings. Therefore, when they are said to cover his face and feet and to fly only with the middle wings, we must understand that even the exalted order of the most excellent blessed spirits is reverently fearful concerning the higher and deeper things of divine intelligences, and is raised by its middle wings, in due measure, toward the vision and understanding of God.

By covering his face and feet, they piously hide from themselves knowledge of incomprehensible things beneath a kind of shadowing reverence; and thus they offer us an example of cautious fear, lest at any time we presume to investigate God. Rather, let us always praise him, since they never investigate him but praise him unceasingly. Thus they cover his face and feet and fly with their middle wings, because they do not search beyond measure into the lofty and deep things of divinity, but fly moderately and temperately in the knowledge of God. For the flight of the middle wings is the measure of their unceasing God-imitating actions, and the lofty flight of their continual movement. It follows:

[Col. 0086A] VERSE 3.—“And they cried one to another, saying: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.”

When they are said to cry one to another, let us observe that they abundantly communicate their divine understandings to one another. Hence they are also called Seraphim, which is interpreted “the beginning of their speech.” For those who first speak divine praises and knowledges, and then hand them on to be spoken by the other subordinate orders of angels, are rightly called Seraphim, that is, “the beginning of their speech.”

Therefore they cried one to another, saying: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts.” They cry “Holy” three times, but do not add “Lords” or “gods”; instead, they say “Lord God,” indicating that Father, [Col. 0086B] Son, and Holy Spirit are not three Lords or gods, but one Lord God. He is called Lord of hosts because the entire host of heaven serves his command.

In this hymn we should carefully observe that this first order of blessed angels was taught theological knowledge by God himself; and through it he then, as it were, gave himself as teacher to the rest by crying to them: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God.” Because he himself is three in persons and one Lord God in substance, he extends his providence and goodness over all things that exist, from the supercelestial essences to the lowest parts of the earth, as the beneficent Creator of all; and he governs and sustains everything. “For his wisdom reaches mightily from end to end, and orders all things sweetly” [Col. 0086C] (Wis. 8:1).
