Hence he is called the Lord of the heavenly hosts, and the whole earth is sung to be full of his glory. For thus he rules everywhere, in heaven and on earth. Indeed, “whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth” (Ps. 113:3).

According to Augustine, he sits, as it were, in his own house and temple, in an exalted and hidden seat among the higher spirits united by supreme peace and friendship, fused by a spiritual fire of charity into one will. From there he diffuses himself through all things, first by certain most orderly spiritual motions of creation and then by bodily motions; and he uses all things, whether incorporeal or bodily, rational or irrational spirits, good by his grace or evil through their own will, according to the unchangeable determination of his judgment. [Col. 0086D]

But just as denser and lower bodies are governed in a certain order by subtler and more powerful bodies, so all bodies are governed by the rational spirit of life; the deserting and sinful rational spirit of life by the pious and just rational spirit of life; and that spirit by God himself. Thus the whole creation is governed by its Creator, from whom, through whom, and in whom it has also been made and established.

Accordingly, God’s will is the first and supreme cause of all bodily forms and motions. Nothing visible and perceptible happens unless it is either commanded or permitted, from the inward, invisible, and intelligible court of the supreme Emperor, according to the ineffable justice of rewards and punishments, graces and recompenses, in this vast and immeasurable commonwealth of the whole creation. Thus understand what is sung: “Lord God of hosts, the whole earth is full of his glory.” It follows:

VERSE 4.—“And the lintels of the hinges were shaken by the voice of the one crying.”

What is the door of this temple or house, if not the gate of the kingdom of heaven? And who are the pivots of this door, if not those angelic spirits through whose ministry the entrance into the heavenly homeland is opened or closed to us? “For the Lord cast Adam out, and placed before the paradise of delight cherubim and a flaming, turning sword to guard the way to the tree of life” [Col. 0087B] (Gen. 3:24). And when Christ ascended, it was cried out: “Lift up your gates, O princes” (Ps. 23:7). The gate of life has therefore been entrusted to them, that they may either close or open it. We understand them as pivots because that door turns upon them as upon hinges. But what are the lintels over those pivots, if not the minds of the angels? The lintels of the pivots were therefore shaken by the voice of the one crying out, because, while the greater ones sing, “The whole earth is full of his glory,” the minds of the lesser are bent away from the obstinacy of discord which, on account of the sin of the first parent, they had held against those dwelling on earth.

“And,” he says, “the house was filled with smoke.” Understand: by the voice of the one crying out. John says this also: “And the temple was filled with smoke from the majesty of God and from his power” [Col. 0087C] (Rev. 15:8). For the house or temple is filled with smoke from the majesty of God, because even those angelic spirits who always see him in heaven cannot wholly comprehend the power of his majesty. For “cloud and darkness are round about him” (Ps. 96:2), and “he made darkness his hiding-place” (Ps. 17:12). Moses entered this darkness in order to see there the glory of God (Exod. 20:21). For this darkness, or this smoke, is that inaccessible light in which God is said to dwell. Therefore smoke from God’s majesty fills the house, because every creature is in darkness with respect to knowledge of him. It follows:

**VERSE 5.**—“And I said: Woe is me, because I have been silent; because I am a man with polluted lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people having polluted [Col. 0087D] lips; and I have seen the King, the Lord of hosts, with my eyes!”

He reproves himself for silence and for the pollution of his lips, because he kept silent about certain good things which he ought to have spoken, and spoke certain useless things. The measure of discernment must be maintained: we should speak good things when appropriate, and always take care not to speak or hear empty words. For we are drawn far downward when, by continual conversation, we mingle with worldly matters. The prophet rightly reproves this in himself, now saying: “Woe is me, because I have been silent; because I am a man with polluted lips!” Why he had polluted lips he disclosed when he added:

[Col. 0088A] “I dwell in the midst of a people having polluted lips.” He grieved that he had pollution of the lips; but he indicated whence he had contracted it when he declared that he dwelt among a people with polluted lips. For it is difficult for the tongue of worldly people not to defile the mind which it touches. Since, while we often condescend to them in saying certain things, becoming briefly accustomed to that very manner of speech which is unworthy of us, we retain it even with pleasure, so that we no longer wish to return from that mode of speech to which we had come unwillingly through condescension. Thus it happens that we proceed from idle words to harmful ones, from trivial words to graver ones. But the holy prophet indicates how he knew himself to be polluted in lips when he adds: “And I have seen the King, the Lord of hosts, with my eyes.” For he was enlightened by the divine vision so as to recognize in himself things which he had not previously noticed. It follows:

**VERSE 6.**—“And one of the Seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a stone, which he had taken from the altar with tongs.”

**VERSE 7.**—“And he touched my mouth and said: Behold, this has touched your lips; and your iniquity shall be taken away, and your sin shall be cleansed.”

We maintain, on the strong tradition of the ancient Fathers and of those who had been hearers of the apostles, that the highest angelic powers, which are around God, by no means descend here. Why, then, is a Seraph said to have come to Isaiah? But in this statement of the prophet it is intended that we understand that those spirits who are sent receive the designation of those whose office [Col. 0088C] they perform. [Note: Col. 0087D: the manuscripts read *prophetae*, “of the prophet.”] Since the angel carries a coal from the altar in order to burn away sins of speech, he is called Seraph, a term meaning “burning.” Therefore the angel who was sent was from among the lesser ranks, since those highest powers are believed never to come forth into ministry.

He brought the coal of heavenly ardour in the tongs of twofold love; or a stone—*calculus*—which is a very hard, round, and perfectly smooth stone, signifying the power of the Holy Spirit in that it makes a person strong, perfect, whole, and gentle. But what should we understand the altar, which stands before God piled with these coals, to be, except the hearts of the heavenly powers, where the fire of the Holy Spirit always abounds? [Col. 0088D] From there the coal was sent to the prophet—that is, some portion of that fire sufficient to cleanse the sins of speech. But, having said these things anagogically, let us return to the beginning of the passage and investigate its mystical sense.

Isaiah saw the Lord, not indeed as he is, but in a certain symbolic manner, as the prophet’s vision was to be fashioned. For as long as one lives in this mortal flesh, no one advances so far in the power of contemplation that the faculty of the mind fixes the eyes of understanding upon that unbounded light itself. Nor is almighty God yet beheld in his own brightness; rather, the soul beholds something beneath him, by which, refreshed, it may advance [Col. 0089A] and afterward attain to the glory of his vision. For when the prophet declares that he saw the Lord, saying, “In the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne,” he immediately adds: “And the things which were beneath him filled the temple.” When the proud and presumptuous King Uzziah dies, the Lord is seen, because when the exaltation of this world is cut off from the desire of the mind, then the mind itself contemplates God’s glory.

It should be noted that the Lord sits upon a high and exalted throne. For what is his throne except an angelic or human creature, over whom he presides through the understanding which he has given? He calls this throne high and exalted because human nature advances when elevated to heavenly glory; and angelic creation, when it was established in heaven after many spirits fell, was raised from the very source from which it was made secure against falling. His temple is the same as his throne, because the eternal King dwells where he presides. We, then, are his temple, in whose minds he deigns to dwell.

But the things beneath him filled the temple, because whatever is now seen of him is not yet himself, but is beneath him. Thus Jacob saw an angel and declared that he had seen the Lord (Gen. 32:30), because even when we behold his mysteries, it is already a great thing that we are raised above ourselves. It should further be noted that it says, “filled the temple.” For even if an angel appears, he nevertheless satisfies the desire of a weak mind, so that, if it cannot yet behold what is greater, it may at least marvel at the lesser thing which it sees. [Col. 0089C] Therefore the things beneath him fill the temple because, as has been said, when the mind has advanced in contemplation, it contemplates not what he himself is, but what is beneath him. It follows:

“Seraphim stood above it.” This is what is found in Moses: the two Cherubim stand above the ark of the covenant (Exod. 25:18). For by the temple or ark, the Church is signified; by the two Seraphim or two Cherubim, the two Testaments are represented. They stand above the Church because they protect us and surpass all our understanding. For Seraphim, as we have already said, means “burning,” because the Testaments of God inflame the hearts of hearers with the fire of charity. Hence Jeremiah: “Are not my words like fire, says the Lord?” (Jer. 23:29). And Moses: “At his right hand [was] a fiery law” (Deut. 33:2). And the Psalmist: “Your word is exceedingly fiery” (Ps. 118:140). It follows:

“Six wings to the one, and six wings to the other; with two they covered his face, and with two they covered his feet, and with two they flew.” What is signified by God’s face and feet except what was before the ages and what will be after the end of the age? “With two,” he says, “they covered his face.” For who can know his beginning? What was in the eternity of things before he created this world? When did he create thrones, dominions, angels, and the whole heavenly ministry? [Col. 0090A] “And with two they covered his feet.” For who can know his final things? What will happen after the consummation of the age? What after the human race has been judged? What life will follow? Will there be another earth again, and after its passing, other elements again, or another world and sun to be created? Especially in the case of God, who has neither beginning nor end, every sight is excluded from knowledge of his beginning and end. Do not seek his beginning or the secrets of his end, for they do not exist. You have his present being; praise it, do not investigate it.

“And with two,” he says, “they flew.” We know only the middle things, which are disclosed to us through the reading of the Scriptures: when humanity was formed, when the flood occurred, when the law was given, how all the regions of the earth were filled from one human being, and how in the last time the Son of God took flesh. But the other matters of which we have spoken, those two Seraphim cover in the face and feet. For because the Old Testament, in the Law and the Prophets, conceals what was before the beginning of the world, one Seraph covers God’s face with two wings. And because the New Testament, in the Gospel and the teaching of the apostles, likewise conceals what was before the creation of the age, the other Seraph covers his face with two wings. In the same way, because those two Testaments, in the Law and the Prophets and in the Gospel and the apostles, conceal what will take place [Col. 0090C] after the end of the age, each Seraph covers his feet with a pair of wings; and each flies with the two middle wings, while through the Law and Prophets, and through evangelical and apostolic teaching, the things occurring from the beginning of the age until its end are disclosed to us. Thus there are six wings to the one and six wings to the other. It follows:

“And they cried one to another.” The wording “one to another” is well chosen. For whatever we read in the Old Testament, we find also in the New; and what has been read in the New is derived from the authority of the Old: nothing in them is discordant, nothing different. “And they said: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts.” The Trinity is preached in both Testaments. “The whole earth is full of his glory.” This is said of the time of evangelical preaching. For everywhere are Churches of the blessed, which are his glory. Indeed, in all who glorify God by their manner of life, his glory is present; and thus the whole earth is full of God’s glory. Formerly not the whole earth was full of his glory, but one corner of the earth, when it was said: “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. 75:1). But now the whole world is full of his glory.

But what benefit is it to you if the whole earth is full of glory while you yourself do not share in the fullness of God’s glory? For if what you do and what you say are done for the glory of God; if your speech, your touch, your going forth and entering, your food and drink, and all your actions are done for the glory of God, then you too share in this saying: [Col. 0091A] “The whole earth is full of his glory.” It follows:

“And the lintels of the pivots were shaken by the voice of the one crying out.” In another translation it says: “And the lintel was removed by the voice with which they cried out.” The Lord always spoke to Moses and Aaron at the entrance of the tabernacle (Exod. 29:4 ff.), as though signifying, before the Gospel, that he had not yet brought them into the Holy of Holies, [Note: [Col. 0091D] Codex G: “had brought them in.”] as the Church was afterward brought in, saying: “The King brought me into his chamber” (Song 1:3). Therefore, when the Lord descended to earth, that lintel—that is, a kind of obstacle for those wishing to enter—was removed. Or, when Christ broke the gates of hell, returned victor to the heights with the souls of the saints whom he led forth, and opened the kingdoms of heaven, then the lintel was removed.

But in the wording found in the new edition, “And the lintels of the pivots were shaken by the voice of the one crying out,” let us understand the exhortation thus: the gate of the heavenly temple can be opened for believers while remaining closed for unbelievers. For “from the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence” (Matt. 11:12). Therefore we can use force upon this gate and open it for ourselves, if we wish, because its lintels have been shaken—the lintels which previously held it immovably shut.

And it is rightly said, “by the voice of the one crying out,” not “by the voice of those crying out,” because the gate of the kingdom of heaven is opened through the grace of evangelical preaching alone. For Moses was not told what Peter was granted to hear: [Col. 0091C] “For I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 16:19). It follows:

“And the house was filled with smoke.”—“Our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24). From this fire, therefore, because we cannot receive its whole substance, a certain lighter and, so to speak, more rarefied nature of smoke is dispersed throughout the whole Church. Receiving this, let us say: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part” (1 Cor. 13:9); and, “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma” (ibid., 13:12).

“And one of the Seraphim flew to me,” he says, etc. Since we understand the two Seraphim as the two Testaments, we say that the New Testament was sent to the prophet. Possessing within itself both commandments—that is, both its own and those of the Old Instrument—it contains the fiery word of God in the twofold edge of the commandments; and, having touched the lips, it drove away by the truth of its cleansing whatever ignorance there was—for lips may here be interpreted as uncleanness. Truly the divine word is a coal that makes the tongue clean from sin. But since *calculus* is read in the Hebrew for “coal,” it seems to me that the divine word is signified by the name *calculus*. Just as *calculus* is a kind of very hard, round, and perfectly smooth stone, so the word of God, which cannot yield to the contradictions either of heretics or of all adversaries, is called a *calculus*. It seems to me that the Seventy Interpreters also meant this when they rendered it *anthraca*. For *anthrax*, which we translate “carbuncle,” is a kind of shining and gleaming stone, one which we also find among the twelve stones [Col. 0092A] (Exod. 28:18). Whether, then, we understand a *calculus* or a carbuncle as a stone, in the *calculus* the truth and firmness of the divine word are shown, while in the carbuncle bright and manifest teaching is displayed.

That the Seraph is said to have flown, understand as the swift arrival of the divine word upon the prophet and the sudden knowledge of the New Testament. For where God is the teacher, there is no delay in learning. [Col. 0092B] “And in his hand was a stone.” The stone in the hand is the word in operation. For the New Testament, by grace, causes to be fulfilled in works what the Old could not accomplish through severity. “Which he had taken from the altar.” Because he received the evangelical word of preaching from the altar of the Lord’s cross. And he said: “Behold, this has touched your lips,” etc. Sin is cleansed by the touch of the stone—that is, of the divine word—as the Lord said to the disciples: “You are already clean because of the word which I have spoken to you” (John 15:3). The prophet, therefore, cleansed and kindled from heaven with fire, adds:

**VERSE 8.**—“And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? And I said: Behold, I am here; send me.”

[Col. 0092C] Here too one God is made manifest in a plurality of persons. For just as Genesis says, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:2), so here, I think, it is said: “Who will go for us?” For whom else should “for us” be understood to mean except the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, to whom every person goes who obeys their will? In that the person of one speaker is set forward, the unity of the Godhead is expressed; but in the word “us,” the diversity of persons is indicated.

“And I said,” he says, “Behold, I am; send me.” God “calls the things that are not as though they were” (Rom. 4:17), and said, “I am who I am” (Exod. 3:14). Whomever he calls, he immediately causes to subsist, because all things that are without him are not. Therefore the prophet, cleansed from vices, dared to say: “Behold, I am.” It should be noted, however, how the prophet answered only in part to what the Lord had said: “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?”—“Behold, I am; send me.” He was silent about what followed, understanding that no human being was worthy to go to God, and that the whole of one’s way must be made to be the way of him who sends. Yet, in saying, “Send me,” and desiring through the active life to benefit his neighbours, he seeks the office of preaching. For this is true charity: it hastens to God in such a way that it does not abandon the neighbour. Thus cleansed by the stone of the altar and fervent with charity, he freely offers himself to be sent, [Col. 0093A] so that he might make others participants in the grace which he had received. But though he desired in pious love to benefit those then present, he first appeared to prophesy the evils that would come upon those in the future, and then heard of their good. For it follows:

**VERSE 9.**—“And he said: Go and say to this people: Hear, hearing, and do not understand; and see a vision, and do not know. Blind the heart of this people,” etc.

For this passage pertains to the time when the Lord lived on earth, teaching new things and performing miracles. He then said of the Jews: “Therefore I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear, neither do they understand, so that the prophecy of Isaiah may be fulfilled in them, saying: With hearing you shall hear and shall not understand, and seeing you shall see and shall not see. For the heart of this people has grown fat, and they have heard heavily with their ears, and they have shut their eyes, lest at any time they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and be converted, and I heal them” [Col. 0093B] (Matt. 13:13–15). Therefore, because the Lord spoke parables to Jews who did not understand, and performed signs before them which they did not understand because all their understanding was carnal, the divine judgment had rightly said to them through the rebuke of prophecy: “Hear”—understand, the words of the Savior—“and do not know” what they signify.

**VERSE 10.**—“Blind,” he says, “the heart of this people; make their ears heavy, and close their eyes, lest perhaps [Col. 0093C] they see with their eyes, [Note: [Col. 0093D] Elsewhere: “he sees.”] and hear with their ears, [Note: [Col. 0093D] Elsewhere: “he hears.”] and understand with their heart, [Note: [Col. 0093D] Elsewhere: “he understands.”] and be converted, [Note: [Col. 0094D] Elsewhere: “he is converted.”] and be healed.” [Note: [Col. 0094D] Elsewhere: “I heal him.”]

Who is now represented in Isaiah, who is commanded to blind the Jewish people, except the person of the prophets and of the lawgiver himself? Isaiah, then, is told: “Blind the heart of this people,” because, as the Apostle says, “Moses placed a veil over his face, so that the children of Israel might not gaze upon his face, which is done away; but their senses have been dulled. For until the present day the same veil remains unremoved in the reading of the Old Testament, because it is done away in Christ. But even to this day, when Moses is read, a veil is placed over their heart. But when they turn to the Lord, the veil shall be removed” [Col. 0093D] (2 Cor. 3:13–16). Accordingly, because the Scripture of the Law and Prophets is shadowed by the veil of the letter, and the carnal people of the Jews follows the surface of the letter alone, Isaiah, representing the writers of the Old Testament, is said to blind their heart.

But when it says, “Lest perhaps they see with their eyes,” one must know that God left them in their blindness by abandoning them and not aiding them; and he did this by a judgment not unjust but hidden. For when he aids, he acts mercifully; and when he does not aid, he acts justly, because all things are done not rashly but by judgment. [Col. 0094A] Since they were puffed up not from faith but as though from works, blinded by that very swelling, they stumbled upon the stone of stumbling. But in the addition, “and be converted and be healed,” either the negative must be understood from what precedes, so that it says, “that they may not be converted and not be healed”; or it must be understood as accomplished through the mercy of heavenly medicine: since they were of a perverse and proud will and wished to establish their own righteousness, they were abandoned to their blindness so that they might stumble upon the stone of stumbling, their faces be filled with disgrace, and, humbled, seek the name of the Lord—not their own righteousness, by which the proud person is puffed up, but God’s righteousness, by which the ungodly person is justified. This indeed benefited many of them for good: pierced with compunction over their crime, they afterward believed in Christ. But the ears that are now made heavy and the eyes that are closed should not be understood as those of the outward person, but rather of the inward person. After the prophet was told, “Blind the heart of this people,” he added:

**VERSE 11.**—“And I said: How long, Lord? And he said: Until the cities are desolated without inhabitant, and the houses without a human being, and the land is left deserted.”

**VERSE 12.**—“And the Lord will remove human beings far away.”

For they persisted in blindness of heart until their cities were desolated by Vespasian and Titus, so that no inhabitant remained in them, their land was left deserted, and people [Col. 0094C] of the Jewish race were taken captive from it and led among all nations. But since the remnant of this people will be converted near the end of the age, let us see what follows: “And that which had been left in the midst of the land shall be multiplied.”

**VERSE 13.**—“And still there shall be a tenth in it, and it shall be converted, and it shall be for a display like a terebinth and like an oak which spreads out its branches: the holy seed shall be that which remains in it.”

The midst of the land is Jerusalem, as the Lord says through Ezekiel: “This is Jerusalem; I have placed her in the midst of the nations, with lands around her” (Ezek. 5:5). In this midst of the land the Lord left the Jewish people, saying: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate. For I say to you, you shall not [Col. 0094D] see me henceforth until you say: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 23:38). But this people, whom the Lord left while he was still dwelling in Judaea and which was afterward scattered throughout the whole world, will be multiplied as the end of the age approaches and will come to faith, as it is written: “Though your people be as the sand of the sea, a remnant from it shall be converted” (Isa. 10:22).

The “tenth” signifies the fulfillment of the Law on account of its Decalogue. Therefore there shall still be a tenth in it, because it will come to pass that it fulfills its law and is converted through the preaching of Elijah. And it shall be a display like a terebinth and an oak, because it will spread far and wide examples of its lofty manner of life and great holiness. For the terebinth and oak are very great trees. The holy seed shall be what then remains in it, as the Apostle says of that nation: “If the root is holy, so also are the branches” [Col. 0095A] (Rom. 11:16). For just as the root is holy in the patriarchs, so the branches will be holy in these children. Isaiah saw or prophesied these things during the reign of Jotham.

## CHAPTER VII

**VERSE 1.**—“And it came to pass in the days of Ahaz son of Jotham, son of Uzziah king of Judah, that Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel went up to Jerusalem to make war against it, but they could not overcome it.”

[Col. 0095B] **VERSE 2.**—“And they reported to the house of David, saying: Syria has rested upon Ephraim; and his heart and the heart of his people were shaken as the trees of the woods are shaken by the wind.”

We believe that these things truly happened according to history. But because “all these things happened to them figuratively” (1 Cor. 10:11), let us seek what was prefigured in them. Since Ahaz is interpreted “one who seizes,” what is signified by Ahaz except a type of the apostles and of the remaining faithful people of that time, who faithfully seized hold of Christ appearing in the flesh? Hence Simeon “received him into his arms” (Luke 2:28). And what is signified by Jotham, whose name is interpreted “his—and their brother,” except the prophets, [Col. 0095C] who clearly declared to whom Christ belongs: whether to the Jewish people or to Christians; he is, according to the flesh, brother to the Jews. Jotham is also called “the Lord’s perfection,” because the perfection which they possessed was given to the prophets by the Lord. What, then, is signified by Uzziah, who is called “strong,” except the manly host of the patriarchs? Ahaz, therefore, is born from Jotham, and Jotham from Uzziah, because the apostles are sons of the prophets and the prophets sons of the patriarchs. Ahaz is king of Judah because the apostles are rulers of the Church.

What is signified by Syria, which is called “lofty,” except proud Gentile society? What by Rezin, interpreted “things pleasing” or “entanglement,” except Gentile rulers entangled in errors? What by Israel except the faithless people of the Jews? What by [Col. 0095D] Pekah, king of Israel, whose name means “opening,” except teachers of the Jews, who ought to open the Scriptures by interpretation? But Remaliah is called “the Most High of the Lord,” and Pekah is son of Remaliah, because these carnal and faithless masters of the Jews were descended from ancient fathers who had been lofty before God in their life.

Therefore the king of Syria and the king of Israel came in the days of Ahaz to wage war against Jerusalem, because the leaders of the Gentiles and Jews began immediately, in the times of the apostles, to attack the Church. “And they could not overcome it,” because “the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Mark 16:18). And they reported to the house of David, that is, to the rulers of the Church: “Syria has rested upon Ephraim”—that is, the Gentiles agree with the Jewish people in persecuting the faithful. Thus we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “But the Jews who did not believe stirred up and provoked to anger the minds of the Gentiles against the brethren” [Col. 0096A] (Acts 14). And a little later: “When an attack by Gentiles and Jews with their rulers was made against the apostles in order to mistreat and stone them” (ibid., v. 5)—that is, Paul and Barnabas—“having learned of it, they fled to the cities of Lycaonia” (ibid., v. 6). Thus the king of Syria and the king of Israel went up against Jerusalem when the Gentiles and Jews, with their rulers, made an attack against the apostles. Thus Syria rested upon Ephraim when the Jews inflamed the minds of the Gentiles against the brethren. “And his heart and the heart of his people were shaken,” because both leaders and subjects wavered through fear of suffering. Against this wavering our Savior came to strengthen and console them. For it follows:

**VERSE 3.**—“And the Lord said to Isaiah: Go out to meet Ahaz, you and your son Shear-jashub, who was left behind, at the end of the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road of the fuller’s field.”

**VERSE 4.**—“And you shall say to him: See that you keep silence; do not fear, and let not your heart be dismayed at these two tails of smoking firebrands, in the anger of the wrath of Rezin king of Syria and the son of Remaliah.”

**VERSE 5.**—“Because Syria, Ephraim, and the son of Remaliah have formed an evil plan [Note: [Col. 0095D] Elsewhere: ‘for evil.’] against [Col. 0096C] you, saying:”

**VERSE 6.**—“Let us go up against Judah, arouse him to join us [Note: [Col. 0096D] Elsewhere: ‘and tear him away to us.’], and set in his midst a king, the son of Tabeel.”

**VERSE 7.**—“Thus says the Lord God: This shall not stand, and it shall not be.”

**VERSE 8.**—“But the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin.”

For Isaiah, whose name means “salvation of the Lord,” goes out to meet Ahaz because, in the distress of our tribulation, there comes to our mind how the Son of God was sent into the world for suffering. Hence the Apostle says: “Consider him who endured such contradiction from sinners against himself, lest you grow weary and faint in your minds” [Col. 0096D] (Heb. 12:3). Isaiah’s going out is for us a remembrance of the Lord’s coming. What, then, does his son Shear-jashub, “the one left behind,” signify except those of whom it was said: “Everyone left in Zion and remaining in Jerusalem shall be called holy” (Isa. 4:3)? Hence Shear-jashub means “returning,” because those of the circumcision who believed returned to him through the preaching of the apostles.

What is signified by the upper pool except the Gospel, set above the Law? What by the aqueduct except the Old Testament, from which the New proceeds? Isaiah therefore went out at the end [Col. 0097A] of the aqueduct of the upper pool because Christ was born at the end of the Law and still appears to us from it. What is signified by the fuller’s field, where the dirt and stains of garments were cleansed, except the Church of the Savior, in which we, who are Christ’s garments, receive remission of sins? What is signified by the road of the field except the activity of the Church? Isaiah therefore went out on the road of the fuller’s field, because Christ appears in the activity which the Church maintains, and says: “See that you keep silence”—that is, do not utter a voice of complaint. “Do not fear”—understand, “those who kill the body” (Matt. 10:28).

He calls the anger of Gentiles and Jews the two tails of smoking firebrands, because in their first part they burn with the fire of their own wickedness, and in their last they are to be burned with the fire of Gehenna. They burn in anger against the Church and smoke with the mist of error; they seek to tear Judah—that is, the Christian people—away from the Church to themselves, [Col. 0097B] and to involve it in their errors. Thus the Jews had begun to tear away the Galatians, when Paul recalled them to the Church through his Epistle. Thus the Gentiles tore away all who denied Christ in persecutions.

Tabeel, however, means “good God.” Gentiles and Jews, denying the goodness of our Redeemer, consider better the things which they themselves worship. They therefore seek to tear Judah away so as to set in its midst as king the son of Tabeel—that is, of the good God—those whom they would desire to establish among us as leaders and teachers, worshippers of their own error.

“But this shall not be, and shall not stand.” But the head of Syria is Damascus, which means “cup of blood,” because Gentile rulers thirst for the blood of the faithful [Note: [Col. 0097D] Codex Cruc.: “thirst.”] And the head of Damascus—that is, of the very cruelty of the Gentiles—is Rezin, that is, “course,” because their tyrannical domination shall pass away with swift course. Or, the entanglement of error shall be the head of their cruelty. For Rezin means “course,” “entanglement,” or “things pleasing.” It follows:

**VERSE 9.**—“And still sixty-five years, and Ephraim shall cease to be a people.”

“And the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is the son of Remaliah. If you do not believe, you shall not remain.”

From the Nativity of the Lord until the rebellion of the Jews against the Romans were sixty-five years. For in the sixty-sixth year they rebelled under the governor Fullo [Note: [Col. 0098D] Codex G: *Follo*.]. The obstinacy of that rebellion, increasing in the time that followed, grew so strong that they themselves were destroyed, along with their cities, and were led captive among all nations. Therefore it is rightly said: “Still sixty-five years, and Ephraim shall cease to be a people.” Perhaps another period of time is also mystically signified through the whole number of sixty-five years. For six times ten is sixty; and because under the Law one may work for six days, six signifies activity; ten signifies the Law because of the Decalogue; five, the five bodily senses. What, therefore, is expressed by the sixty-five years except the whole time [Col. 0098A] during which this faithless Jewish people maintains the carnal observance of the Law and serves the five bodily senses? After this period, with Elijah preaching, the unbelieving Jewish people will fail, so that the number of believers may be multiplied. “For blindness has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and so all Israel should be saved” (Rom. 11:25–26). Thus, as if after sixty-five years, apostate Ephraim will cease to be a people, almost no unbeliever remaining from its multitude; because after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, all Israel will be saved. Hence it adds:

“And the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is the son of Remaliah.” For Samaria means “watch” or “guard,” and Remaliah, “the Lord’s going beyond.” Therefore observance will be their head, because then they will truly submit themselves to the observance of God’s commandments. And the head of this observance will be the son of the Most High Lord, because they will have leaders of religion who are sons of the patriarch Abraham not only in flesh but also in faith and conduct. But to show that all these things have been said mystically, he adds in explanation, addressing those who fight against the Church: “If you do not believe”—namely, in Christ—“you shall not remain,” but shall quickly perish from the face of the earth while the Church grows: “For the upright shall dwell in the land, and the innocent shall remain in it; but the wicked shall be destroyed from the earth, and those who act unjustly shall be taken away from it” [Col. 0098B] (Prov. 2:21–22).

If anyone, however, wishes to refer these sixty-five years historically to the captivity of the ten tribes, let him observe that the prophet has placed three kings of Judah in this narrative, under whom he also prophesied. “[Col. 0098C] And it came to pass,” he says, “in the days of Ahaz, son of Jotham, son of Uzziah.” Therefore let him calculate, as the Hebrews wish, from the twenty-fifth year of Uzziah’s reign to the sixth year of Hezekiah’s reign, in which Shalmaneser captured Samaria and carried Israel away to the Assyrians. For when Uzziah, under whom this prophet also began to prophesy, entered the Temple and wished to burn incense, and was struck with leprosy, the Hebrews hold that it was the twenty-fifth year of his reign; twenty-seven years remained of it. For he reigned fifty-two years in all. After him his son Jotham reigned sixteen years, and this man’s son [Col. 0098D] Ahaz another sixteen. After him Hezekiah reigned, and in the sixth year of his rule Samaria was captured. Thus the years together make sixty-five. It follows:

**VERSE 10.**—“And the Lord continued to speak to Ahaz, saying:”

**VERSE 11.**—“Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, in the depth of hell,” etc.

**VERSE 12.**—“And Ahaz said: I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test.”

**VERSE 13.**—“And he said: Hear then, house of David: Is it too little for you to be troublesome to men, that you are troublesome also to my God?”

**VERSE 14.**—“Therefore the Lord himself will give you [Col. 0099A] a sign. Behold, a Virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel.”

**VERSE 15.**—“He shall eat butter and honey, that he may know how to reject evil and choose good.”

Even if this could not be understood here, it would nevertheless become known to us from the book of Matthew as spoken by the Lord: “Behold, a Virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Matt. 1:23). And the Lord who says this introduces it by saying: “Is it too little for you to be troublesome to men, that you are troublesome also to my God?” Who, then, is the Lord who says, “You are troublesome also to my God,” except he who elsewhere says: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John 20:17)? For because of the mystery of the future Incarnation, he already calls God the Father his God; and thus, speaking of himself as to be incarnate, he speaks as though of another: [Col. 0099B]

“Ask,” he says, “for yourself a sign in the depth of hell, or in the height above.” For the sign in the depth and in the height is Christ’s descent into hell and ascent into heaven. Was it not a wondrous sign when he broke and despoiled hell, and, ascending, opened the kingdoms of heaven? Ahaz is commanded to ask for the sign not simply, but for himself; for Christ descended to the depths of hell and ascended to the throne of the Father’s majesty, not for himself but for us. But Ahaz, a sinner ignorant of God’s mysteries, says: “I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test.” For he thought it would be a testing if he asked for such a sign. And the Lord, rebuking the entire offspring of unbelievers, says: [Col. 0099C]

Hear then, house of David, which does not wish to ask for the sign of your deliverance and salvation: “Is it too little for you to be troublesome to men, that you are troublesome also to my God?” They were troublesome to men—that is, to those endowed with reason—because they would not ask for what the reason of human salvation required. For the human race could not be saved unless hell, which received and held all souls, were broken, and heaven opened to the people of the saints. Yet they were troublesome also to God, because they did not wish to ask for what God wished to give. For whoever withdraws himself from salvation and does not present himself as one who can readily be saved is troublesome to God, who seeks human salvation. “Therefore,” he says, “because you are troublesome not only to men but also to God, unwilling to ask for the sign of Christ’s victory through which you might be saved, the Lord himself will give you, though you have not asked, the sign of his birth.” [Col. 0099D]

“The Lord will give you a sign.” And what sign? “Behold, a Virgin shall conceive and bear a Son.” Rightly is the Virgin’s conception and childbirth called a sign, since she became a mother in such a way as not to lose the seal of virginity. For a seal is customarily called a sign; and for this reason she herself is called in the Song of Songs the untouched seal of perpetual virginity: “A garden enclosed, a fountain sealed” (Song 4:12). Or her conception and childbirth are called a sign, that is, a miracle, because the whole world joyfully marvels that a virgin conceived, bore a child, and remained a virgin forever. And you, O house of David, shall call his name Emmanuel, [Col. 0100A] that is, “God with us.” He is called God with us because, although he is the Only-begotten of God, he was seen upon earth in the flesh, “and conversed with men” (Baruch 3:38); and when he was about to ascend bodily into heaven, he promised us: “Behold, I am with you always, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). For the house of David which calls his name Emmanuel is first Mary and Joseph, who are “of the house and family of David” (Luke 1:27), and then the whole Church.

“He shall eat butter and honey.” Butter comes from milk, and milk from flesh; honey, however, falls from the air. What, then, is expressed by butter except the knowledge of his humanity? And what by honey except the sweetness of his divine wisdom? He therefore eats butter and honey because he possessed both human and divine wisdom. And for that reason he knew how to reject evil and choose good: through the prudence of human and divine understanding, he wisely rejected everything evil and chose everything good. Hence it came about that he committed no sin, fulfilled all righteousness, and at the end of the age will judge the human race. [Col. 0100B]

But, to pursue the mystical understanding of these matters, Ahaz is commanded to ask for a sign in the depth and in the height, and he replies, “I will not ask”—as if the apostles had been told to desire the Savior’s death and ascension, while they instead dreaded it. For it is written that “Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem, suffer many things from the elders, scribes, and chief priests, be killed, and rise on the third day. And Peter took him aside and rebuked him, saying: Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen to you. But he turned and said to Peter: Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me” (Matt. 16:21–23). For the Lord’s foretelling his death and resurrection to the disciples, and Peter’s saying, “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen to you,” are, according to the mystery, what is meant by Ahaz’s being commanded to ask for a sign below and above and saying, “I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test.” And Peter’s hearing, “You are a stumbling block to me,” is what is said to the house of David, as to Christ’s disciples: “Is it too little for you to be troublesome to men, that you are troublesome also to my God?” The apostles were troublesome not only to holy men, that is, the prophets, but also to God, because they did not wish Christ to die and rise, as the prophets had foretold and God had ordained. [Col. 0100C–D]

“Therefore,” he says, “the Lord himself will give you a sign”: because, behold, the virgin Church shall conceive and bear a son, that is, a people of the elect endowed with manly virtue; and you shall call his name Emmanuel, that is, Christian. For Christ is with us also by participation in his name, since from him we are called Christians. “He shall eat butter and honey.” Butter denotes the richness of spiritual grace, as Solomon says: “He who presses the breasts hard to draw out milk produces butter” (Prov. 30:33). For we press the breasts hard when we weigh the breasts of sacred utterance with subtle understanding. While under this pressure we seek milk, we find butter; because, while we seek to be nourished even with slender understanding, we are anointed with the abundance of inward richness. Honey, however, denotes the sweetness of heavenly teaching, as the aforementioned Solomon says: “Eat honey, my son, because it is good, and the honeycomb is very sweet to your throat; so also is the teaching of wisdom to you” (Prov. 24:13). The people of the elect, whom the Church bears, are fed by such butter and honey; and through this it knows how to reject evil and choose good. For instruction in the Scriptures is not enough for us unless God’s anointing also teaches us concerning all things. It follows: [Col. 0101A]

**VERSE 16.**—“For before the child knows how to reject evil and choose good, the land which you detest shall be forsaken before the face of its two kings.”

Who these two kings are has been said above: namely, the king of Syria and the king of Israel, fighting against the people of God. And before the child Jesus, through the awareness belonging to humanity, knew how to distinguish good from evil, the land which Ahaz—that is, the ecclesiastical ruler—detests was forsaken, as the Magi and shepherds turned to him. For Syria is in the East; and the Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying: “Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? For we have seen his star,” etc. “But when King Herod heard it, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. And gathering together all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where Christ was to be born. They said to him: In Bethlehem of Judah” (Matt. 2:2 ff.). When it is said, “Herod was angry, and all Jerusalem with him,” it is clear that Syria had already begun to rest upon Ephraim against Judah. [Col. 0101B–C] For of these two kings we may understand one here as Herod, who was a Gentile, and the other as the chief priests and scribes of the people. Before their face the Magi forsook their land: “When they had heard the king, they went away and found the child with Mary his mother; and falling down, they worshiped him” (Matt. 2:9–10). The shepherds too forsook the detestable land and “came with haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the infant lying in a manger” (Luke 2:16). Although both groups changed places in coming to Christ, nevertheless the detestable land which they left is more properly understood as the perfidy of the Jews and the unbelief of the Gentiles. It follows: [Col. 0101D]

**VERSE 17.**—“The Lord shall bring upon you, upon your people, and upon your father’s house days such as have not come since the days of Ephraim’s separation from Judah—with the king of Assyria.”

According to what we have considered thus far, Ahaz bears the figure of the apostles and of the chief priests of the Church. He therefore says: The Lord shall bring upon you, upon your ecclesiastical people, and upon your father’s house—that is, upon the priestly order—good days, such as have not come since Ephraim was separated from Judah; that is, since the Jewish people was separated from the faithful people and joined with the king of Assyria, that is, with the prince of demons, the devil. For “Assyrians” means “those who convict” or “those who rebuke,” because evil spirits convict and rebuke before the tribunal of the eternal Judge those who now consent to them as they persuade them to iniquity. [Col. 0102A] Why he promised desirable days, he makes clear in what follows.

**VERSE 18.**—“And it shall be in that day: the Lord shall whistle for the fly which is at the extremity of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee which is in the land of Assyria.”

**VERSE 19.**—“And they shall all come and rest in the torrents of the valleys, in the caves of the rocks, in all thickets, and in every hollow.”

For what is prefigured by the whistle except either the sound of divine preaching or inward inspiration? The fly, moreover, is a most insolent, restless, unclean, and black creature. What else is expressed by it except every proud and restless sinner? And what are the rivers of Egypt except the flowing vices of the flesh? Yet there is a difference between being in the rivers of Egypt and being at the extremity of the rivers of Egypt. He is in the rivers of Egypt who dwells in vices and blindness of heart; but he is at their extremity who has arrived at the worst wickedness of every disgraceful deed. Therefore, who is denoted by the fly at the extremity of the rivers of Egypt except either the Gentile world or any soul held fast by every sin and error? [Col. 0102B]

But what is denoted by the bee in the land of Assyria except the philosophers and poets of the Gentiles, who bear sweet things in their mouths but sting secretly at the end and infuse hidden poison? Or it denotes all who at first sweeten their words, but in the end sting sharply. For what is the land of Assyria except unbelief, or the mind and will of the ungodly, where the ancient enemy reigns? This is the distant country in which the younger son squandered his goods “by living riotously” (Luke 15:13). Yet the Lord does not deny the whistle of his voice to this fly or bee.

Or the fly denotes the Jewish people, who flocked, like flies, to the blood of sacrifices. And this fly, because it had become exceedingly foul amid filth, was exiled at the extremity of the rivers of Egypt; because the more familiar this people had been with God, the more grievously, by disobedience, it flowed away beyond those “who sat in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Luke 1:79). [Col. 0102C–D]

But by the bee, naturally honey-producing, the Gentile world is expressed, because “when Gentiles who do not have the law do by nature the things of the law, these people, although they do not have the law, are a law to themselves; they show the work of the law written in their hearts” (Rom. 2:14). Thus, without a guide and without a teacher, the Gentiles naturally labored to produce honey when, without the Law, they did the things belonging to the Law. Or this bee was in the earth of which it was said: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:10): in unfruitful earth, in the land of Assyria, which is interpreted “captivity,” “exaltation,” or “devastation,” so that we understand the souls of the Gentiles as captive, puffed up, and devastated by the devil until the Lord’s coming.

What, then, is represented by the torrents of the valleys except the teaching of the humble? And what by the caves of the rocks except the wounds of martyrs? For we call torrents those streams which gather waters in winter and dry up in summer. Therefore the preaching of the saints is rightly called torrents of the valleys: while it flows into us in the present life, masses of water are, as it were, gathered in winter; but when the summer sun comes, they withdraw, because when the light of the eternal homeland shines forth, teachers will cease preaching. [Col. 0103A] Concerning the caves of the rocks, however, we have spoken above. The flies and bees therefore rest in the torrents of the valleys and in the caves of the rocks, because converted sinners delightfully drink the preaching of teachers and seek the protection of martyrs. What, then, is denoted by thickets except the prickly harshness of discipline? For bees commonly gather honey from thickets, because those who live under discipline shall receive eternal sweetness from it. And what is figured by hollows except the piercings and openings of mystical sayings? For just as a precious stone is pierced and carved in diverse ways, so the mystical word of God is opened through diverse interpretations. The flies and bees rest, therefore, in these hollows, because converted sinners delight in the spiritual understanding of the Scriptures. It follows: [Col. 0103B]

**VERSE 20.**—“In that day the Lord shall shave with a hired razor, by those beyond the river, by the king of Assyria, the head and the hair of the feet, and the whole beard.”

What is denoted by the head except the summit of the priesthood? What by shorn hair except the removal of the subtlety of the sacraments? What by the hair of the feet except the sacraments of the Levites? What by the beard except the strength of kingship? Thus the Lord shaved the head, by the king of Assyria, among those beyond the river, because he stripped the Jewish priesthood of the sacraments of his commandments—those who, refusing to pass through baptism to Christ, remain in the devil’s kingdom. He also shaved the hair of the feet, because he took spiritual sacraments away from the ministry of the Levites. He shaved the beard also, because, abandoning the Israelite kingdom, he cut off the splendor of its strength. He shaved these things with a hired razor, because by the sword of the Roman army he took their kingdom away from them, and also the Temple in which the offices of priests and Levites were performed. [Col. 0103C–D] It follows:

**VERSE 21.**—“And it shall be in that day: a man shall nourish a young cow of the herd and two sheep.”

**VERSE 22.**—“And because of the abundance of milk, he shall eat butter.”

Who is this man except the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus? And what is this young cow of the herd which he nourishes except the Church, daughter, as it were, of the apostles and doctors, who are oxen? We also read of this young cow in Abraham’s sacrifice (Gen. 15:19). What are the two sheep except the simple and gentle faithful from the two peoples, of whom he says: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 12:12), and: “I have other sheep which are not of this fold” (John 10:16). [Col. 0104A] Milk, moreover, is elementary discourse, by which those of lesser capacity are instructed, as the Apostle says: “As to little children in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3:2). But from the young cow and the two sheep, because of the abundance of milk, the man shall eat butter; because the Lord is fed with richness from the Church, in which are circumcision and uncircumcision, through the abundance of good discourse, while his members are fed. It follows:

“For butter and honey shall eat [Note: [Col. 0103D] Otherwise, ‘shall consume.’] everyone who is left in the midst of the land.” The midst of the land is Judea and Jerusalem. The one left in the midst of the land is he of whom he said above: “Everyone who is left in Zion and remains in Jerusalem shall be called holy.” [Col. 0104B] Honey falls from above, but butter is collected from animals’ milk. Honey, therefore, is from the air; butter from flesh. Yet the Only-begotten of the supreme Father, although he is God above all, became man among all. Since he fills us with the sweetness of his divinity and the mystery of the Incarnation, he satisfies us alike with honey and butter. Therefore, because the Spirit of Christ filled the minds of faithful Hebrews and made them glad both by the sweetness of his divinity and by faith in the Incarnation, it is rightly said that “butter and honey shall eat everyone who is left in the midst of the land.” It follows:

**VERSE 23.**—“And it shall be in that day: every place where there were a thousand vines and a thousand pieces of silver [Note: [Col. 0104D] Otherwise, ‘a thousand vines for a thousand pieces of silver,’ and in, etc.] shall become thorns and briers.” [Col. 0104C]

**VERSE 24.**—“They shall enter there with arrows and a bow.”

What are denoted by vines except saints bearing clusters of good works, to whom the Lord says: “I am the vine; you are the branches” (John 15:5)? What is figured by pieces of silver except good sayings? For “the tongue of the just is choice silver” (Prov. 10:20). What does the thousandfold number mean except fullness of number? Wherever there are a thousand vines, there will also be a thousand pieces of silver; because where there is an abundance of spiritual men, there will also be an abundance of preaching. For under the Old Testament scarcely anyone was found who possessed knowledge of preaching. But in the time of revealed grace, of which discourse is now being made, the mouths of the faithful everywhere overflow with the word of truth. “And they shall become thorns and briers,” because they are directed against the sins and vices of the Gentile world. For what do thorns and briers suggest except the pricks of sins, with which the Gentile world was full as though it were a desert? “They shall enter there with arrows and a bow,” because, assuredly, the holy apostles came with the sharp shafts of words to strike the hardness of the Gentiles’ life. For Holy Scripture is a bow, from which judgments come to human hearts like arrows that strike and terrify. It follows: “For briers and thorns shall be throughout the whole land.” [Col. 0104D]

**VERSE 25.**—“And all the mountains which shall be dug with the hoe—the terror of thorns and briers shall not come there; and it shall become pasture for the ox and a place to be trodden by cattle.” [Col. 0105A]

Briers and thorns denote either sins or sinners; mountains, however, those exalted by holy conduct. The hoe is a two-pronged digging implement of iron, signifying the word of teaching, sharp from both Testaments. Thus on the mountains which are hoed—that is, dug—the terror of thorns and briers shall not come; because those who are cleansed by the word of teaching will not fear sins and vices, since they root out the harmful weeds of vices with the hoe of the divine word. Nor will they fear “those who kill the body” (Matt. 10:28). And the land, understand, shall become pasture for the ox, because every holy preacher will find throughout the breadth of the world those whom he may incorporate into himself. And it shall become a place to be trodden by cattle, because the remaining multitude of the faithful merely treads earthly things underfoot and is not nourished by the conversion of sinners as the preacher is; for the ox is the teacher, while the cattle are the people of the faithful. [Col. 0105B] It follows:

## CHAPTER VIII

**VERSE 1.**—“And the Lord said to me: Take for yourself a great book, and write in it with a man’s stylus: Swiftly take away the spoils; quickly plunder.”

**VERSE 2.**—“And I summoned for myself faithful witnesses: Uriah the priest and Zechariah son of Berechiah.”

**VERSE 3.**—“And I approached the prophetess; and she conceived and bore a son. And the Lord said to me: Call his name: Hasten to take away the spoils; make haste to plunder.” [Col. 0105C]

**VERSE 4.**—“For before the child knows how to call his father and mother, the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria shall be taken away before the king of Assyria.”

What is signified now by Isaiah except Moses and the prophets? What by the great book except the Old Scripture? What by the stylus of a man except the knowledge of the rational mind? What by Uriah the priest except those who exercised the priesthood under the Law? For *Uriah* is interpreted “my light is God,” because they confessed that the light of truth and righteousness which was in them was God’s gift. What by Zechariah, whose name means “remembrance of the Lord,” except teachers who, meditating day and night upon the Lord’s law, always retained divine remembrance? *Berechiah*, moreover, is interpreted “blessing of the Lord.” And Berechiah is Zechariah’s father, because holy teachers are sons of the Lord’s blessing. [Col. 0105D] What, then, is figured by the prophetess except the Synagogue? What by her son except our Redeemer?

Thus Isaiah, taking a book for himself, writes in it with a man’s stylus, saying to the child Jesus: “Swiftly take away the spoils; quickly plunder.” For all writers of the Old Testament wrote in it with rational judgment that the Son of God, appearing in the flesh, was swiftly to invade the devil’s kingdom and rescue captive men from him. The prophet summoned Uriah and Zechariah as witnesses to this matter, because Moses and the others who wrote the books of the Old Testament handed down their hidden mysteries to priests and teachers. [Col. 0106A] With these brought in as witnesses, Isaiah approached the prophetess in order to make her pregnant, because the holy prophets, with priests and teachers as witnesses, instilled into the heart of the Synagogue faith in the Lord’s Incarnation. For the Synagogue conceived Christ when it began to believe that he would be born from its flesh; and it bore him when, through the Virgin’s childbirth, it brought him forth to us incarnate. The prophet called his name: “Hasten to take away the spoils; make haste to plunder,” because he foresaw that, soon at the time of his birth, he would draw shepherds and Magi to himself. And with eager desires he urged him to hasten to do these things. For, being about to overthrow the devil’s kingdom throughout the whole world, while still a child he took these first spoils from him: he turned the shepherds away from Jewish unbelief toward himself, and he turned the Magi, converted to worship him, away from the plague of that superstition. [Col. 0106B] At that time, because of infantile ignorance, he did not know how to call his father—that is, his foster-father Joseph—and his mother, the Virgin; just as he says in Jeremiah: “Behold, I do not know how to speak, because I am a child” (Jer. 1:6). For the Wisdom of God knows all things; but infancy, lacking knowledge, through human lack of understanding did not know what it had not yet learned. Hence “he advanced in wisdom and age and grace” (Luke 2:52). For in his divinity he did not need to advance. Yet he took away the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria.

For we have said that Syria signifies the Gentile world; Damascus, however, is interpreted “cup of blood” or “drinking blood.” Damascus is the head of Syria, because the Gentile world, subject to the worship of demons, pours out its soul, as though its own blood, to the devil as a drink offering. [Col. 0106C] What, then, do we suppose the strength of Damascus—of idolatry, the death of souls, and cruelty—to be except the Magi? For in magical art the power of all error and its propagation was strong. But what is signified by Samaria except the perfidy of the Jews? Therefore, when the Child turned the Magi and shepherds to himself, he took away the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria. And this was done before the king of Assyria, because the devil recognized the loss suffered by his Magi. Hence he inflamed Herod, so that, seeking to destroy the newborn King, he killed all children of the same age as he was (Matt. 2). It follows:

**VERSE 5.**—“And the Lord continued to speak to me, again saying:” [Col. 0106D]

**VERSE 6.**—“Because this people has rejected the waters of Shiloah, which go softly, and has preferred Rezin and the son of Remaliah.”

**VERSE 7.**—“Therefore behold, the Lord shall bring upon them the strong and many waters of the river—the king of Assyria and all his glory—and he shall rise over all its streams and flow over all its banks,”

**VERSE 8.**—“and he shall pass through Judah, overflowing and passing on; he shall reach to the neck; and the spreading of his wings shall fill the breadth of your land, O Emmanuel.”

Since *Shiloah* is interpreted “sent,” by Shiloah we understand Christ, who was sent to redeem the world, [Col. 0107A] and by the waters of Shiloah his preaching. For teaching is denoted by waters, as it is written: “He gave him to drink the water of saving wisdom” (Ecclus. 15:13). These waters go softly—that is, they gently enter the mind with spiritual power, without the noise and clamor of words—because, as Solomon says, “The words of the wise are heard in silence” (Ecclus. 9:17). What, then, did he intend by Rezin, king of Syria, except Caesar? What by Pekah, son of Remaliah, except the Pharisees and doctors of the Law? Thus the Jewish people rejected the waters of Shiloah because it rejected the Lord’s preaching. And it chose Rezin, that is, the king of the Gentiles, saying: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15). Hence *Rezin* is interpreted “pleasure,” because they said this in accordance with the pleasure and choice [Col. 0107B] of their own will; and they preferred the son of Remaliah—that is, the Pharisees and scribes, who derive their origin from the holy Fathers.

Therefore the Lord brought upon them the strong and many waters of the river—that is, the strong and numerous peoples of humankind, namely the king of Assyria, Vespasian, commander of the Romans. Since Assyrians are called “rebukers,” the Romans are rightly called Assyrians, because they avenged the Jews’ iniquity while rebuking it. And because he called the people of the Roman army the waters of a river, he speaks metaphorically of it as of a river rising excessively and filling all things. Or, by the waters of the river, let us understand the force of the tribulation which the Jews then endured. For waters here signify either peoples or tribulations. [Col. 0107C]

“And he shall rise over all its streams,” he says, etc. Perhaps he calls its individual tribes and families its streams, and the boundaries of tribes and families its banks. But this river of tribulations, overflowing all, encompassed every tribe and boundary; and, flooding and passing through Judah, it rose to the neck, so that it might drown all, as a river does when it has risen to the neck. And the spread of the wings of his army filled the breadth of Emmanuel’s land—that is, Judea and all Galilee. Then, seeing that all the Jews would gather in Jerusalem and be overcome by Titus, Vespasian’s son, the prophet says:

**VERSE 9.**—“Gather yourselves, peoples, and you shall be conquered [Note: [Col. 0107D] Otherwise, everywhere, ‘you shall be conquered’]; hear, all distant lands: strengthen yourselves, and you shall be conquered; gird yourselves, and you shall be conquered.” [Col. 0107D]

**VERSE 10.**—“Form a plan, and it shall be scattered; speak a word, and it shall not come to pass, because God is with us.”

These things were fulfilled at the time of that siege and captivity. For God was no longer with the Jews, but with Christians. For it follows:

**VERSE 11.**—“For thus the Lord says to me: As he instructed me with a strong hand, that I should not walk in the way of this people, saying:

**VERSE 12.**—“Do not say: A conspiracy. For everything which this people says is a conspiracy.”

“God is with us,” that is, Christ. For Christ the Lord himself says to me: “As God my Father instructed me with a strong hand”—that is, as one to whom he had given mighty power; for God does not give the Spirit by measure—“that I should not walk in the way of this people,” following its weak actions with a feeble mind and walking in the path of fools with an untrained heart, but that I should firmly and wisely maintain the path of my own uprightness. Hence, angry against him, they said among themselves: “He is burdensome to us even to behold, because his life is unlike that of others, and his ways are changed; we have been judged by him as trifles, and he abstains from our ways as from uncleannesses” (Wis. 2:15–16). Therefore he did not walk in the way of this people; but he who strengthened him with a mighty hand and wisely instructed him not to walk in this people’s way, said to him and his disciples: Do not say, “A conspiracy is being made against us”; for everything which this people says concerning us is a conspiracy. For they conspired against the Savior, and “agreed together that if anyone confessed him to be the Christ, he should be put out of the synagogue” (John 9:22); and, as if always forming a conspiracy, they never ceased plotting evil against him until they killed him. So too they continually maintained sworn hostilities against his disciples, always contriving evils against them. Hence it is added: “And do not fear their fear [Note: [Col. 0107D] Otherwise, ‘his’], nor be terrified.” [Col. 0108A]

**VERSE 13.**—“Sanctify the Lord of hosts himself; let him be your fear, and let him be your dread.” [Col. 0108C]

As if it were said: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. 10:28). As Peter also says: “Do not fear their fear, so that you are not troubled; but sanctify Christ the Lord in your hearts” (1 Pet. 2:14). It follows:

**VERSE 14.**—“He shall be for you a sanctification, but a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense to the two houses of Israel, a snare and ruin to the inhabitants of Jerusalem.”

**VERSE 15.**—“And many among them [Note: [Col. 0108D] Codex Cruc., ‘in them.’] shall stumble, fall, be broken, be ensnared, and be taken.” [Col. 0108D]

He was for the disciples a sanctification because he gave them the grace of his Spirit. But to the two houses of Israel—that is, Judah and the remaining ten tribes—he became a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense. For the Jews hoped that he would come. But because he came humble and hidden, they despised him and stumbled at him. For, wise in their own pride, they disdained to believe in him whom they saw as humble. He was therefore to them a stone of stumbling. And when they also saw him die, they suffered a more grievous offense concerning him, so that they could by no reasoning believe him to be God whom they had seen dying; and thus he became for them also a rock of offense. To the inhabitants of Jerusalem he was a snare and ruin, because in persecuting him particularly, they entangled themselves in the snare of their own deception and gained for themselves the ruin not only of their souls but of the entire city, so that the city itself was destroyed together with them. [Col. 0109A]

“And many among them,” he says, “stumbled.” Not all stumbled, but many, because among them were many who believed in Christ. “And they shall fall,” he says, “and be broken.” Those who fell were broken because, abandoning heavenly things, they sought earthly things. For what fall or breaking can be greater than to abandon the Creator and seek the creature, to forsake heavenly joys and yearn for the lowest things? They therefore suffered fall and breaking because, having lost heavenly desires, everything they know is earthly. [Col. 0109B] And they shall be ensnared by their sins and taken in the snare of everlasting death. Or they were ensnared in the siege of Jerusalem, when the city was captured and they were taken captive. Therefore, because the multitude of Jews that stumbled at the stone of stumbling was broken, while the election obtained true righteousness, it is fittingly added:

**VERSE 16.**—“Bind up the testimony; seal the law among my disciples.”

**VERSE 17.**—“And I shall wait for the Lord, who has hidden his face from the house of Jacob; and I shall look for him.”

For Christ’s voice is now addressed to the prophet. The prophet binds Christ’s testimony in us, [Col. 0109C] because prophetic speech attaches faith in him very firmly to the mind, when we are certain that what the prophets said could in no way have been fabricated. He also seals the Law in us, because he more firmly encloses its commandments within our heart. For we are gladly “mindful of his commandments, to do them” (Ps. 102:18), and we cannot doubt his power and promise. “Bind up,” he says, “the testimony of the Old Testament, and hand it over to my disciples”—that is, to the apostles and the faithful who have received the Gospel—“and seal the Law among them.” Therefore, because the disciples held the Savior’s faith and Law, which the Jews especially lost at the time of his Passion: “Bind up the testimony; seal the Law among my disciples; and I shall wait for the Lord to raise me up, because ‘my flesh rests in hope’” (Ps. 15:9), “who has hidden his face from the house of Jacob,” because from the time they denied me, they lost the Father as well. For “everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father either” (John 2:23). It follows: [Col. 0109D]

VERS. 18.—“Behold, I and the children whom the Lord has given me are for a sign and a portent to Israel from the Lord of hosts, who dwells on Mount Zion.”

Those are called children who serve the heavenly commandments; and by the name of children he now denotes his disciples, who especially kept his precepts. “Behold,” he says, “I and my children, whom the Lord has given me, [Col. 0110A] are for a sign and a portent to Israel”; that is, I and my disciples shall perform signs and portents among the people of Israel. He says that God the Father dwells on Mount Zion, that is, in heaven—not because the Son himself did not always remain in heaven with the Father, but because he was bodily conversant on earth. For Mount Zion is now understood to be that of which the Apostle says: “You have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to the assembly of many thousands of angels, and to the church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven” (Heb. 12:22). It follows:

VERS. 19.—“And when they say to you, ‘Seek those who have familiar spirits and diviners, who chirp in their incantations’: should not a people seek from its God on behalf of the living and the dead?”  
[Note: [Col. 0109D] Another reading: “seek a vision for the living from the dead.”]

[Col. 0110B] VERS. 20.—“Rather, to the law and to the testimony. But if they do not speak according to this word, they shall have no morning light.”

What divination by a pythoness accomplishes we find in the Book of Kings (1 Kings 28), where, at Saul’s request, the pythoness called up from the lower world either Samuel’s soul or, rather, an unclean spirit in his place. They say that this kind of magical illusion was discovered by Pythian Apollo and was so named from his surname. The interpretation of the name also agrees, since Python is called “the mouth of the abyss.” Let us therefore consider the meaning.

“I,” he says, “and my children shall perform signs and wonders in Israel; but you who await these things, beware lest you be deceived by the lying signs of false prophets. For when any deceivers say to you, [Col. 0110C] ‘Seek those who have familiar spirits and diviners,’ that is, consult magicians, so that through them you may learn truth from the dead, answer them: ‘Should not a people seek from its God on behalf of the living and the dead,’ etc.—on behalf of all [Note: [Col. 0110D] C. Garst.: that is, on behalf of all.]? For everything that is sought is sought either for the living, or for the dead, or perhaps for both. Why then should we consult demons, when all things ought to be sought from God?

Rather, let us attend to the law and to his testimony. But if the children of Israel do not speak according to this word—that is, if, rejecting sorcerers, they do not attend to God’s law, which forbids every sort of sorcery, and to the testimony of the lawgiver and prophets concerning the coming of the Savior—there shall be no morning light for them, that is, no beginning [Col. 0110D] of the new grace. “For if they do not listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe him even if someone rises from the dead” (Luke 16:31), that is, our Redeemer, who says: “If you believed Moses, perhaps you would believe me also; for he wrote of me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?” (John 5:46). Therefore, because they did not attend to the law and the testimony, they were not illumined by the morning light when the Lord preached; they will scarcely possess evening light when Elijah appears. It follows:

VERS. 21.—“And he shall pass through it, and fall, and hunger; and when he is hungry, he shall be angry and shall curse his king and his God.”

[Col. 0111A] The Jewish people shall pass through that light, that is, through the period in which Christ is to work wonders and teach wonderful things; and, stumbling like a blind man against the stone of stumbling, it shall fall from every state of uprightness. It shall hunger, because it shall no longer be fed with the bread of life and understanding. For just as bodily hunger is the withdrawal of bodily sustenance, so hunger of the mind is the silence of divine speech. And because, when heavenly teaching deserts the human mind, the temptation of the ancient enemy gains strength against it, after this people lost the understanding of the Scriptures and could not—or would not—understand the Savior’s words, it immediately blazed up in anger against him at the devil’s instigation and cursed him. This is what is now said: when it is hungry, it shall be angry and shall curse its king and its God [Col. 0111B]. For Christ is both King of Israel and God of Israel. When he said that there were many lepers in Israel in the days of Elisha the prophet and that none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian, all in the synagogue who heard these things were filled with anger; they cast him out of the city and led him to the brow of the mountain in order to throw him down headlong (Luke 4:27–29). At the time of his passion they were more fiercely enraged and cursed [Col. 0112A] him, “who, when he was reviled, did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten” (1 Pet. 2:23). After his passion, because Jerusalem was to be besieged and captured, it is rightly added: “And he shall look upward.”

VERS. 22.—“And he shall look upon the earth, and behold tribulation and darkness, dissolution and distress, and pursuing gloom; and he shall not be able to fly away from his distress.”

The Jewish people shall look upward for knowledge of God and help, and behold the tribulation of adversity and the darkness of ignorance, because God blinded their hearts and did not deliver them. And it shall look upon the earth—that is, upon those things which will happen around it on earth—and behold tribulation. “There shall be,” he says, “great distress upon the earth, [Col. 0112B] and wrath upon this people; and they shall fall by the edge of the sword and shall be led captive among all nations, and Jerusalem shall be trampled by the nations until the times of the nations are fulfilled” (Luke 21:23–24). This too is what is said here: “Dissolution and distress, and pursuing gloom; and he shall not be able to fly away from his distress.” Likewise we read in Daniel: “After the end of the war, desolation is decreed” (Dan. 9:26). It follows:

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0111]

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0111B]
