VERS. 1.—“In the former time the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali were lightened; but in the latter time the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations, was burdened.”

VERS. 2.—“The people who walked in darkness [Col. 0111C] saw a great light; for those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, a light has arisen.”

The discourse now concerns the time when the Lord, dwelling among human beings, deigned to preach the Gospel in person. For Matthew writes, after his baptism and fasting, that “he withdrew into Galilee; and leaving the city of Nazareth, he came and dwelt in maritime Capernaum, in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali, so that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations: the people who walk in darkness have seen a great light, and upon those seated in the region of the shadow of death a light has arisen.’ From that time Jesus began to preach and to say: [Col. 0111D] ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near’” (Matt. 4:12–17).

Therefore, in the first period of the Lord’s preaching, the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali were lightened from the burden of sins, because there the Savior, before choosing his disciples, began to preach the remission of sins and entrance into the kingdom of heaven, promising it to those who repented. But concerning the way of the sea, that is, the maritime region, which at the final period of his preaching was burdened by the weight of sins, he says later in the Gospel [Col. 0112B]: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty deeds done among you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. Yet it shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon in the judgment than for you. And you, Capernaum, exalted up to [Col. 0112C] heaven, shall be cast down to hell” (Matt. 11:21–23).

Therefore the way of the sea of Galilee of the nations, which lay beyond the Jordan, was at the last burdened with its iniquities because it despised the Lord’s preaching with an obstinate mind. But the people of the nations, formerly set in the darkness of ignorance and walking on the broad way of the world which leads to destruction, saw a great light when the Lord preached and shone with miracles. It saw a light not small, like that of the other prophets, but great, like that of him who says: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). And for the inhabitants of the region of the shadow of death—that is, of sins and unbelief—a new light of righteousness and faith arose. This [Col. 0112D] distinction may be made between death and the shadow of death: death is understood as belonging to those who descend to the lower world with dead works, because “the soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18:20); but the shadow of death belongs to those who, although they sin, have not yet departed from life, because, if they wish to repent, they can do so. Yet these things may also be understood otherwise. For he says:

“In the former time the land of Zebulun,” etc. Certainly, Zebulun is interpreted “his oath”; [Col. 0113A] Naphtali, “discernment.” And the Jewish people had received God’s oath, as is said through Zechariah: “He swore to Abraham our father that he would give himself to us” (Luke 1:73). It was also discerning, that is, set apart from all other peoples. Therefore in the former time the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali were lightened, because the Lord taught in the land of the Jews, to whom he had long ago sworn this and whom he had chosen from all peoples under heaven; and there he first sent disciples to preach. It follows:

“And in the latter time the way beyond the Jordan of Galilee of the nations was burdened.” What is signified by “way” except action? And what by “sea” except the world? What, indeed, by the Jordan except baptism? Hence Jordan is interpreted “their descent,” because those who are baptized descend from their self-exaltation to the depths of humility. Galilee, however, which is called “a migration accomplished,” is the passage from sins to righteousness. Therefore the way of the sea—that is, worldly action—which is beyond the Jordan, that is, after baptism, is of the accomplished migration of the nations, was in the latter time burdened by the weight of sins. For we too, who have been called from the nations to Christ, after we have passed through the sacraments of baptism, after we have migrated from vices to virtues, now near the end of the world, when the love of many has grown cold and iniquity has abounded, again enter upon the way of the world and become entangled in secular affairs, although we ought to serve God as soldiers. Thus we are weighed down exceedingly by the burden of sins, so that we can scarcely raise our heart toward heavenly desire.

[Col. 0113C] Or these things may also be expounded thus. When Christ came and his preaching first shone forth, the land of Zebulun and Naphtali was freed from the errors of the scribes and Pharisees and shook from its neck the very heavy yoke of Jewish traditions. But afterwards, through the Gospel of the apostle Paul, who was the last of all the apostles (1 Cor. 4:9), the preaching was “burdened,” that is, multiplied; and the Gospel of Christ shone into the boundaries of the nations and throughout the way of the whole sea, that is, the world. For the Gentile people, which formerly sat or walked in darkness and was held fast by the bonds of idolatry and death, beheld the bright light of the Gospel. Hence it is added:

“For those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, a light has arisen [Col. 0113D] for them.” For the region of the shadow of death is the land of the nations, since the shadow of death is understood as imitation of the ancient enemy. For he himself, because he brought in death, is called death, as John testifies when he says: “His name was Death” (Rev. 6:8). Therefore his imitation is signified by the shadow of death, because just as a shadow is cast alongside a body, so the deeds of the wicked are shaped in the likeness of his imitation. Thus the prophet, seeing the Gentile peoples perish in imitation of the ancient enemy and foreknowing that they would rise to the rising of the true sun, narrates as though past events those things which he certainly knew would occur, saying: “For those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, a light has arisen for them.” And concerning the multitude of those same Gentiles who had by no means [Col. 0114A] known the joys of that same light, he adds:

VERS. 3.—“You have multiplied the nation; you have not magnified its joy.”

For the nation had been multiplied throughout the breadth of the whole world. But its joy had not yet been magnified, while God was still known only in Judea; for this had not yet been fulfilled: “I proclaim to you great joy, which shall be for all the people” (Luke 2:10). But now there follows concerning its magnification:

“They shall rejoice before you, as those rejoice [Note: [Col. 0113D] Another reading: “who rejoice.”] at harvest,” etc.

For the apostles gathered an abundant harvest of the human race when they assembled not only Jews but also nations into the faith. [Col. 0114B] Hence it had been said to them: “Lift up your eyes and see the fields, for they are already white for harvest; and he who reaps receives wages and gathers fruit unto eternal life, so that both he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice together. I have sent you to reap that for which you have not labored. Others labored, and you entered into their labors” (John 4:35–38). Therefore in this harvest the holy preachers rejoiced before the Lord as they rejoiced at the conversion of the nations. Having received the Holy Spirit from above and overcome the ancient enemy and all his army—for “everything born of God conquers the world” (1 John 5:4)—they exulted as victors. And exulting, they divided the spoils, because they distributed the sacred utterances among all nations throughout the world. For divine utterances are signified by the name “spoils,” as it is written: “I shall rejoice over your utterances as one who finds abundant spoils” (Ps. 118:162).

Or: You have multiplied the nation of believers, O Christ, you who have established your Church throughout the whole world; but you have not magnified joy, because you have left us sorrow over the faithlessness of the Jews. But when you come and the whole nation of Christians has been gathered together, then the apostles shall rejoice before you like harvesters, because the fruit of the human harvest shall have been gathered into eternal life; and like victorious men who divide captured plunder, because then the devil shall be perfectly conquered and human beings shall be divided into those on the right and those on the left. But why these victors shall exult in the division of the spoils [Col. 0114D] is shown when, concerning the Gentile people, he adds:

VERS. 4.—“For you have overcome the yoke of his burden, and the rod upon his shoulder, and the scepter of his oppressor, as in the day of Midian.”

In rescuing the Gentile world, the Lord overcame the yoke of its burden when by his coming he freed it from the slavery of that demonic tyranny. He overcame the rod upon its shoulder when the Redeemer restrained, for the human race, the persecution by which that tyranny grievously oppressed it through perverse action. He overcame the scepter of its oppressor when he destroyed from the hearts of believers the kingdom of the devil, who by the pestilential practice of vices was accustomed to exact the debts of punishments. [Col. 0115A] But let us hear how these things were accomplished.

“As in the day of Midian”: that is, just as holy Gideon, with three hundred men, defeated the innumerable multitude of the Midianites. At this point it is pleasing to make a digression and show why Christ’s triumph is compared with Gideon’s victory. For it is written in the Book of Judges:

“All Midian and Amalek and the peoples of the east gathered together. Crossing the Jordan, they pitched camp in the valley of Jezreel. But the Spirit of the Lord clothed Gideon. Sounding the trumpet, he summoned the house of Abiezer to follow him. He sent messengers throughout all Manasseh, which also followed him, and others into Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, who came to meet him. Gideon said to the Lord: [Col. 0115B] ‘If you save Israel by my hand, as you have spoken, I shall place this fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If there is dew upon the fleece alone and dryness over all the land, I shall know that through my hand, as you have spoken, you will deliver Israel.’ And it happened so. Rising by night, he wrung out the fleece and filled a bowl with dew. And he said again to the Lord: ‘Let not your anger be kindled against me if I test once more, seeking a sign in the fleece. I pray that the fleece alone may be dry and all the land wet with dew.’ The Lord did that night as he had requested: there was dryness in the fleece alone and dew throughout all the land (Judg. 6:33), etc.

“Therefore Jerubbaal, who is also Gideon, rising by night, and all the people with him, came to the spring [Col. 0115C] called Arrath [Note: [Col. 0115D] Another reading: Harad.]. But the camp of Midian was in the valley, toward the northern side of the high hill. The Lord said to Gideon: ‘The people with you are too numerous, and Midian shall not be delivered into his hand, lest Israel boast against me and say: “I was delivered by my own strength.” Speak to the people and proclaim in the hearing of all: “Whoever is fearful and timid, let him return.”’ Twenty-two thousand men withdrew from Mount Gilead and returned from the people, and only ten thousand remained. The Lord said to Gideon: ‘The people are still too numerous. Lead them down to the waters, and there I shall test them. Of whom I say to you, “Let him go with you,” he shall proceed; but whoever I forbid, let him return.’ When the people had gone down to the waters, the Lord said to Gideon: ‘You shall set apart those who lap the waters with their tongue, as dogs are accustomed to lap; but those who drink with bent knees shall be on the other side.’ The number of those who had lapped water, bringing it to their mouth with the hand, was three hundred men; but all the remaining multitude had drunk with bent knee. And the Lord said to Gideon: ‘With the three hundred men who lapped the water I shall deliver you and give Midian into your hand; but let all the remaining multitude return to their homes.’

“Having taken provisions and trumpets according to their number, he dismissed all the remaining multitude to their tents, while he himself committed himself to the contest with three hundred men. The camp of Midian lay below in the valley. [Col. 0116A] That same night the Lord said to him: ‘Arise and descend into the camp, for I have given them into your hand. But if you fear to go alone, let Phara, your servant, descend with you. When you hear what they are saying, then your hands shall be strengthened and you shall descend more confidently to the camp of the enemy.’ Therefore he himself and Phara his servant descended to the part of the camp where the watches of armed men were. Midian, Amalek, and all the peoples of the east lay spread out in the valley like a multitude of locusts. Their camels also were innumerable, like the sand lying on the seashore. When Gideon arrived, someone was recounting a dream to his companion and told what he had seen in this manner: ‘I saw a dream, and it seemed to me that a barley cake baked under ashes was rolling down into the camp of Midian. [Col. 0116B] When it came to a tent, it struck it, overturned it, and leveled it completely with the ground.’ The one to whom he spoke replied: ‘This is nothing other than the sword of Gideon son of Joash, an Israelite man. God has given Midian and all its camp into his hand.’

“When Gideon heard the dream and its interpretation, he worshiped; and, returning to the camp of Israel, he said: ‘Arise, for God has given Midian into your hands.’ He divided the three hundred men into three groups and put trumpets in their hands, together with empty jars and lamps within the jars. He said to them: ‘What you see me do, do likewise. I shall enter into a part of the camp; follow what I do. [Col. 0116C] When the trumpet in my hand sounds, you also sound the trumpet around the camp and cry out: “For the Lord and for Gideon!”’ Gideon and the three hundred men who were with him entered a part of the camp at the beginning of the middle watch of the night, when the guards had been roused; they began to sound the trumpets and strike the jars against one another. And when they sounded in three places around the camp and had broken the jars, they held lamps in their left hands and sounding trumpets in their right, crying: ‘The sword of the Lord and of Gideon!’ Each stood in his own place around the enemy camp. Then the whole camp was thrown into confusion; shouting and howling, they fled. Yet the three hundred men continued sounding their trumpets. The Lord brought a sword throughout the whole camp, [Col. 0116D] and they cut one another down in mutual slaughter, fleeing as far as Bethsetta and the border of Abel-meholah at Tabbath. The men of Israel from Naphtali, Asher, and all Manasseh cried out and pursued Midian. Gideon sent messengers throughout all Mount Ephraim, saying: ‘Come down to meet Midian, and seize the waters as far as Bethbera and the Jordan.’ All Ephraim cried out and seized the waters as far as Bethbera; they captured two men of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb, and killed Oreb at the Rock of Oreb and Zeeb at the winepress of Zeeb. They pursued Midian, carrying the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon across the Jordan” (Judg. 7:1 ff.).

Thus far we have set forth the words of sacred history. But what profit is there in setting forth the words unless we at least briefly touch upon their mystical meaning?

Therefore Gideon, coming to battle, signifies the advent of our Redeemer, concerning whom it is written: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and the King of glory shall enter. Who is this King of glory? The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. 23:7). He prophesied our Redeemer not only by deed but also by name. For Gideon is interpreted “going about in the womb.” Our Lord, by the power of his majesty, encompasses all things, and yet by the grace of his dispensation came within the Virgin’s womb. For what is “going about in the womb” but almighty God redeeming us by his dispensation, [Col. 0117B] embracing all things by divinity and assuming humanity within the womb? He was incarnate in that womb and yet not enclosed there, because he was in the womb in the substance of weakness and outside the womb in the power of divinity.

Midian, however, is interpreted “from judgment.” For the repelling and destroying of its enemies came not from a defect in the one who repelled them, but from the judgment of one judging justly. They are therefore called “from judgment,” because, alienated from the Redeemer’s grace, they bear even in the meaning of their name the desert of just condemnation.

Amalek is interpreted “a people that laps.” What is signified by the lapping people except the minds of worldly persons, which, craving all earthly things, as it were lap them up, while delighting only in temporal things?

The peoples of the east are so called because, just as they were born, so they remain—neither circumcised nor baptized. “Therefore all Midian and Amalek and the peoples of the east gathered and crossed the Jordan,” because all of these, in one conspiracy, rushed upon those who have been baptized. For we have crossed baptism, as it were the Jordan, with Jesus as our leader, and now inhabit the Church, as it were the land of promise. Therefore, when unbelievers come against us, they hasten as though to lay waste those who are in the land beyond the Jordan.

And they camped in the valley of Jezreel, because in the pilgrimage of this present life they tyrannically oppressed and trampled upon the humility of the faithful. Jezreel [Col. 0117D] is called “the seed of God”; and “he who sows the good seed is the Son of Man, and the good seed are the children of the kingdom” (Matt. 13:37).

“But the Spirit of the Lord clothed Gideon,” because, “when Jesus had been baptized and was praying, the Holy Spirit descended upon him in bodily form like a dove” (Luke 3:22). “Sounding the trumpet, he summoned the house of Abiezer,” because Jesus began to preach and chose disciples. Abiezer is interpreted “my Father is a helper.” By this name, what is signified except the person of the prophets and ancient fathers, whose house was the company of the Lord’s disciples?

[Col. 0118A] “And he sent messengers throughout all Manasseh,” that is, apostles, saying: “Do not go into the way of the nations, but go to the sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 10:5–6). “Manasseh,” interpreted “necessity,” is a figure of that people which served God from necessity, that is, from fear. “And others into Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali,” because he sent Paul and Barnabas to the Gentile people, which became blessed in Christ, full of strength, and enlarged in love. For Asher is called “blessed,” Zebulun “dwelling-place of strength,” Naphtali “enlarged” or “he enlarged me.” The dew upon the fleece and dryness over all the earth signify faith among the whole Jewish people and unbelief among the nations.

“Rising by night, he wrung out the fleece and filled a bowl with dew,” because Christ, rising from death before dawn, took the grace of faith from the Jews and filled the minds of the disciples with it. Conversely, dryness in the fleece and dew over all the earth signify faithlessness among the Jews and faith throughout the whole world. Gideon means Christ. Jerubbaal [Note: [Col. 0117D] Codex G: Jeroboam.], that is, “having a judge,” refers to the reproach of the devil, who, although he has the reprobate, nevertheless cannot judge and avenge the destruction of idolatry. Rising by night, he came to the spring called Harad, because, rising from the tomb before dawn, he came to the immortal spring by ascending into heaven. For Harad is interpreted “the rising together of descent.” And all the people of believers, rising with him, came to this spring, because “God raised us together and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (Eph. 2:6).

[Col. 0118C] Midian was in the valley, that is, in the depth of vices, on the northern side, that is, in the left-hand, icy, and dark unbelief. The high hill is the Church, standing in Christ’s side opened by the lance, the mountain on the summit of the mountains.

Mount Gilead, interpreted “heap of testimony,” is the lofty and manifold testimony rendered by the martyrs in their sufferings. From that mountain twenty-two thousand fearful men returned, that is, the multitude of transgressors of both Testaments and apostates. For twenty-two is twice eleven, and the number eleven signifies transgression, whereas ten signifies observance of the commandments. For ten thousand remained with Gideon. But because not all who are believed to keep the law are able to preach or suffer for Christ, the people are still too numerous.

They were therefore led to the river to lap the water; and those who drew water with bent knees were removed from the purpose of war. For by the waters is signified the teaching of wisdom, and by knees standing upright, right action. Those who bent the knee while drinking the waters were recalled from the contest of wars, because Christ goes to battle against the enemies of faith with those who, while drawing from the streams of teaching, do not bend the uprightness of their works, so that they may excel both in the teaching of wisdom and in the virtue of works. For because slackness of works is signified in the very bending of the knees, Paul says: [Col. 0119A] “Raise up the slack hands and the feeble knees, and make straight paths for your feet” (Heb. 12:12).

“Therefore the number of those who had lapped the water, bringing it to their mouths with the hand, was three hundred men.” The hundredfold number is customarily understood as the fullness of perfection. Therefore, what is meant by a hundred taken three times except perfect knowledge of the Trinity? [Note: [Col. 0119D] Codex G: “is expressed.”] With these, indeed, the Lord destroys the adversaries of faith; with these he descends to the battles of preaching—those who know how to think perfectly concerning the Trinity, which is God.

On the same night on which he supped with the disciples, the Lord said to him: “Rise from supper and descend into the camp,” that is, into the place where Judas was to come with a crowd of Jews. “But if you fear to go alone, let Phara your servant descend with you.” This, unless I am mistaken, Mark expresses thus: “He took Peter, James, and John with him, and began to be afraid and distressed” (Mark 14:33). Phara, interpreted “little flask,” is a type of the apostles, who were filled with new grace as if with new wine. “Therefore he himself and Phara his servant descended to the part of the camp where the watches of armed men were,” because he came with his disciples into the garden, where he knew that he was to be seized by the servants of the Pharisees and a cohort of soldiers. In the camels is signified the crookedness of vices, and in the locusts the instability of minds. The one who recounted or interpreted the dream appears to signify diviners and worldly wise men, and also certain Gentile seers to whom many things concerning Christ were revealed, such as the Sibyls and Nebuchadnezzar.

[Col. 0119C] The barley cake baked under ashes signifies Christ, who is harsh, sharp, and piercing to sinners. For just as bread is baked beneath a mass of ashes, so Christ endured the fire of the passion beneath the multitude of the Jews and was hardened unto the power of the resurrection. He is rolled about by the tongues of preachers, in order that he may descend into human hearts. “It struck the tent, overturned it, and leveled it completely with the ground,” either when he reduced by death to dust the flesh of persecutors, in which their souls dwelt; or when, mercifully striking their fleshly vices with the sword of preaching, he destroyed them and made the persons themselves humble. Or rather, the Scripture of the Old Testament may be signified in the barley bread, whose most tenacious inner meaning [Col. 0119D] is covered by the chaff of the letter. This is also signified by the five barley loaves in the Gospel, with which the Lord fed the crowds (John 6). This bread is indeed baked under ashes, because the old Scripture, according to its carnal sense, lies in the dust of earthly thoughts.

“This is nothing other than the sword of Gideon son of Joash.” Joash, interpreted “hoping,” signifies the ancient people of God, which hoped that the Savior would be born from it. When our Gideon heard—that is, caused his own people to hear—the dream and its interpretation, he filled his members greatly with joy and stirred them to thanksgiving. He divided the three hundred men, [Col. 0120A] that is, the holy preachers, among the three parts of the world: Asia, Europe, and Africa. “And he gave them trumpets in their hands, empty jars, and lamps in the midst of the jars.” In the trumpets is signified the cry of preaching; in the lamps, the brightness of miracles; in the jars, the fragility of bodies.

“Gideon and the three hundred men with him entered a part of the camp.” This means that Jesus began, in his preachers, to attack a portion of the unbelievers in order to conquer them for their salvation and subject them to himself. At the beginning of the watches of midnight, that is, of profound error, and when the guards had been awakened, because the rulers of the world began to appoint more cunning keepers of ancient errors against the new preaching of the apostles. They began to sound the trumpets, [Col. 0120B] that is, they began to preach; and to strike the jars against one another, that is, to dash their own bodies in suffering. For they sounded the trumpets when they preached; they broke the jars when, in their passion, they exposed their bodies, which were to be dissolved, to hostile swords.

“But when the jars had been broken, the lamps shone forth,” and after the dissolution of their bodies, they shone with miracles. Immediately the enemies were turned to flight, because when they saw the bodies of dead martyrs shine with miracles, broken by the light of truth, they believed what they had opposed. Therefore they sounded the trumpets so that the jars might be broken; the jars were broken so that the lamps might appear; the lamps appeared so that the enemies might be put to flight. That is, the martyrs preached [Col. 0120C] until their bodies were dissolved; their bodies were dissolved in death so that they might shine with miracles; they shone with miracles so that they might cast down their enemies by divine light, so that they would no longer stand erect in resistance to God, but, subdued, might fear him.

And it should be noted that they stood firm before the jars but fled before the lamps. For indeed the persecutors of the faith resisted the preachers while they were still in the body, but after their bodies had been dissolved, when miracles appeared, they were turned to flight; terrified by fear, they ceased from persecuting believers. They feared the preaching of the trumpets when, after the jars of bodies had been broken, they saw the lamps of miracles.

[Col. 0120D] “And when they sounded in three places around the camp,” that is, when they preached in Asia, Europe, and Africa, “and had broken the jars, they held lamps in their left hands and sounding trumpets in their right.” We call that “right-hand” which we consider of great importance; “left-hand,” however, what we regard as of no account. Therefore they rightly held the trumpets in their right hands and the jars, or lamps, in their left; because Christ’s martyrs regard the grace of preaching as great, and regard the usefulness of bodies or the glory of miracles as of no account [Note: [Col. 0120D] Codex G: “as very small.”].

“And the Lord sent the sword” of the divine word “throughout the whole camp, and they cut one another down in mutual slaughter”; [Col. 0121A] that is, they killed in one another their former way of life, “fleeing as far as Bethsetta and the border of Abel-meholah at Tabbath.” Bethsetta is called “house of the thorn”; Abel-meholah, “mourning of a woman in childbirth”; Tabbath, “good reception.” What is the house of the thorn except a mind pierced by compunction for its sins? Who is this woman in childbirth except the Church, which never ceases to bring forth spiritual children for God? And what is the border of the mourning of this woman in childbirth except the wound in Christ’s side? For from it the Church takes the cause of its mourning. Therefore those who, pierced by compunction for their crimes, practice repentance fled as far as Bethsetta. And they fled as far as the border of the mourning woman in childbirth, that is, as far as faith in the Lord’s passion, from which the Church’s mourning began. And they fled into Tabbath, that is, into good reception.

[Col. 0121B] But the men of Israel—that is, the faithful who see God with the eyes of faith—crying aloud with the voice of preaching, pursued Midian, equipped with heavenly arms: from Naphtali, that is, from the breadth of charity or the expanse of the world; from Asher, that is, from the nation of the blessed; and from all Manasseh, that is, from those who forget the things behind. For Naphtali is called “breadth”; Asher, “blessed”; Manasseh, “forgetful” or “having forgotten.”

“Gideon sent messengers throughout all the hill country of Ephraim,” which means “fruitfulness”; that is, Christ sent preachers throughout the whole world. “Come down,” he says, “to meet Midian”: that is, take on humility, so that you may withstand the pride of your enemies. “And seize the waters of wisdom as far as Beth-barah,” that is, as far as the Church, [Col. 0121C] where there is a well of living waters. For Beth-barah is called “house.” And as far as the Jordan, that is, to their descent and humiliation. For Jordan is interpreted “their descent”; or baptism may be understood under the name Jordan.

“And having captured the two men of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb, he killed them.” Oreb is interpreted “raven,” Zeeb “wolf.” Both raven and wolf feed upon a corpse. Yet the wolf seizes and kills animals and feeds on their flesh, whereas the raven, though it eats flesh, is unable to kill. What, then, is denoted by the wolf except the insatiable rage of those who killed the martyrs and fed upon their deaths? What by the raven except those who, blackened by sins, [Col. 0121D] indeed delighted in the death and torments of the righteous, but were not able to destroy them? Oreb is also interpreted “hole.” And a serpent is accustomed to enter a hole. What, then, is denoted by the hole except those in whose heart the ancient serpent was accustomed to enter and dwell?

Ephraim, therefore, killed Oreb and Zeeb: because the converted Gentiles either brought to the faith, or overcame by suffering, both those in whom serpentine malice lay hidden, so that they rejoiced at the punishments of the righteous, and those who killed the martyrs themselves. And Oreb, indeed, that is, those in their hardness; Zeeb, however, that is, the plunderers and devourers of the saints, were killed “at the winepress of Zeeb,” that is, in the oppression by which they afflicted the righteous. For in the very fact that they were endured by the saints even to death, while they thought that they were killing the righteous, [Col. 0122A] they themselves were killed. Their heads—that is, victory over them—the martyrs brought back to Gideon, that is, to Christ, beyond the streams of the Jordan, that is, beyond the sacraments of baptism, through which passage is made to him. Thus it is well said to God concerning the Gentiles: “You have overcome the yoke of his burden, the rod of his shoulder, and the sceptre of his taskmaster, as in the day of Midian.” And that the sceptre of his taskmaster has now been overcome is proved when it is added:

**VERSE 5.—** “For every violent plunder with tumult, and every garment mingled with blood, shall be for burning, fuel for the fire.”

For that wicked taskmaster was accustomed to carry out violent plunder with tumult, because once he imposed upon the human race the coinage of deception, and from then on he did not cease daily to demand the debt of death. He carried out violent plunder with tumult because, rushing upon souls at the time of death with unrestrained assault and shouting, he violently snatched them away. But now this violent plunder—that is, the importunate cruelty of the ancient enemy—shall be for everlasting burning.

The garment, moreover, is our body, with which the soul is clothed; and blood signifies sins of the flesh, concerning which it is said: “Deliver me from bloodguiltiness” (Ps. 50:15). A garment is mingled with blood when the body is defiled by fleshly desires. “Therefore the garment mingled with blood shall be fuel for the fire,” because the flesh of the licentious shall be consigned to the fires of Gehenna. But why shall this violent plunder and the garment [Col. 0122C] polluted with blood be for burning? Because now, in the flesh, the King of peace and righteousness has appeared, who grants to all who believe in him purity not only of soul but also of body.

**VERSE 6.—** “A little child has been born to us, a son has been given to us, and dominion has been placed upon his shoulder.”

For this is that little child who “was made a little lower than the angels” (Heb. IX), who “came not to be served but to serve” (Matt. 20:28). The kings of this world, however, bear their royal insignia not on their shoulders but upon their heads. But our King alone raised the glory of his power upon his shoulders. Thus Isaac also, when he was led by his father to be sacrificed, himself carried the wood [Col. 0122D] (Gen. 22:6), signifying the extraordinary patience of Christ, who bore the cross of his Passion. Therefore his dominion is upon his shoulder: because, while he bore the cross upon his own shoulders, he conquered the prince of this world and acquired dominion over those whom he redeemed. It follows:

“And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace.” He is a wonderful counsellor in all that he is recorded to have taught in person in the Gospel. He was known as Mighty God in the resurrection, because by divine power he overthrew the ancient enemy and raised his own flesh. These names may also be read separately: Wonderful and Counsellor, likewise God and Mighty. For he is Wonderful because he is [Col. 0123A] “fairer in beauty than the children of men” (Ps. 44:3), “into whom angels desire to look” (1 Pet. 1:12). He is Counsellor because he says: “I, Wisdom, dwell in counsel, and counsel is mine” (Prov. 8:12). He is God from the substance of the Father. He is Mighty because he himself is the power of God. And, as Adam is the father of the present age and the prince of the discord that existed between us and God, so Christ is the Father of the age to come and the Prince of our peace with God. For “the first man is earthly, from the earth; the second man is heavenly, from heaven. As is the earthly man, such also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly man, such also are the heavenly” (1 Cor. 15:47 ff.). And: “As through the trespass of one man condemnation came upon all human beings, so also through the righteousness of one man justification of life came upon all human beings” (Rom. 5:18). It follows:

**VERSE 7.—** “His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace. He shall sit upon the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish it and strengthen it in judgment and righteousness from now until eternity.”

His dominion shall be multiplied, “so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2:10). And there shall be no end of peace, because through his death he has reconciled us to God forever. And where shall these things occur? Upon the throne of David and over his kingdom, because “the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he shall reign in the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end” (Luke 1:32).

The throne of David is the royal seat. The kingdom, however, according to Dionysius, is every end, the adornment of law, and the distribution of order. Or the throne of David and his kingdom are the people of God.

“To establish it,” he says, “and strengthen it”: because when that same throne and kingdom was renewed through evangelical grace and made spiritual from carnal, it was so established and strengthened as to endure without end. Moreover, he shall establish it in judgment and righteousness, because, as Solomon says of him: “A king who judges the poor in truth, his throne shall be established forever” (Prov. 29:14). And: “For the throne is established by righteousness” (Prov. 16:12). “From now,” that is, from the time dominion was placed upon his shoulder, and forever. It follows:

[Col. 0123D] “The zeal of the Lord of hosts shall accomplish this.” One is said to be jealous who guards the chastity of his wife with anguish of mind. How, then, does God become jealous or have zeal, since he is touched by no anguish of mind in guarding our chastity? Yet because he guards the chastity of each soul, he is called jealous in a human manner, though he is affected by no anguish of mind. Dionysius the Areopagite says: “The causal Good of all good things, through the excellence of loving goodness, comes to be in all existing things as one who provides for all, and cherishes them by goodness, affection, and love. Therefore those wise in divine things call him zealous, as showing an exceedingly good love toward existing things, as one who awakens it, and who is zealous for the things desired, and as causing the existing things for which he provides to be zealous through itself.” Such, therefore, is the zeal of the Lord which shall accomplish what has been said above concerning the incarnation of Christ and his kingdom. It follows:

**VERSE 8.—** “The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it fell upon Israel.”

Jacob is said to mean “supplanter,” Israel “a man seeing God.” What, then, is denoted by Jacob except the Jewish people, and what by Israel except the Gentiles? For the one whom Judaea sought to supplant by the death of the flesh, the Gentiles surely saw as God through the eyes of faith. Therefore the word sent to Jacob fell upon Israel: because the one whom the Jewish people rejected when he came to them, the Gentile people suddenly found by confessing him. [Col. 0124B] It follows:

**VERSE 9.—** “And all the people of Ephraim shall know, and the inhabitants of Samaria, speaking in pride and greatness of heart:

**VERSE 10.—** ‘The bricks have fallen, but we shall build with squared stones; the sycamores have been cut down, but we shall replace them with cedars.’”

The ten tribes, who had abandoned the temple of the Lord, worshipped Jeroboam’s calves, and whose land was called Samaria, were called Ephraim. What, then, is denoted by Ephraim and the inhabitants of Samaria except the Gentile people? Therefore all the people of Ephraim and the inhabitants of Samaria—that is, the entirety of the Gentiles—shall know that the word which had been sent to Jacob fell [Col. 0124C] upon Israel. “Pride” is sometimes used for the authority of exaltation, as the Lord says to the Church: “I will make you the pride of ages” (Isa. 60:15). And Wisdom says: “With me are riches and glory, the resources of pride and righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0123D] Elsewhere: “proud sheep and righteousness.”] (Prov. 8:18). Therefore, because the Gentile people, converted to the faith, was not thereafter to be bound by the necessity of fear, as the Jewish people once was, but was to be released by the grace of liberty, which gave it the authority of exaltation, it is rightly said to speak in pride, and not in faint-heartedness like the Jews, but in greatness of heart. And what shall it say?

“The bricks have fallen,” etc. What is expressed by bricks except the muddy Jewish people? And what do we understand by squared stones except saints whose life knows how to stand firm in prosperity and adversity? For a square stone stands equally firm whichever side it is turned upon. Whoever, therefore, is not raised up by prosperity, not broken by adversity, not drawn to evil by persuasions, and not recalled from good work by reproaches, is a square stone and, as it were, has stability on every side: in any change of circumstances, such a person does not fall. Therefore, seeing that the Jewish people had perished from the faith and that the apostles were rising in the Church, through whom many from the Gentiles were to be made firm in the strength of faith and life, the prophet spoke in great consolation with the voice of the Gentiles: “The bricks have fallen, but we shall build with squared stones.” [Col. 0125A] For, seeing apostles, martyrs, and teachers rise in the Church from the fall of the bricks—that is, from the destruction of the Jews—he grieved less, because he saw God’s building, that is, the holy Church, being built from squared stones.

The sycamore, a tree whose leaves resemble the mulberry’s but which surpasses it in height, is called the foolish fig. The cedar, however, has a remarkable fragrance, is naturally incorruptible, and of remarkable height. What, then, is expressed by sycamores except the folly of carnal Jews? And what by cedars except the lofty and sweet-smelling life of the saints, which can no longer be corrupted by any decay of earthly love? Therefore malignant spirits cut down the sycamores—that is, carnal Jews—and cast them down from the standing of faith. But the Church replaced them with cedars—that is, it substituted spiritual and fragrant men in their place. It follows:

**VERSE 11.—** “And the Lord shall raise up against him the enemies of Rezin, and shall turn his enemies into tumult.”

From the Book of Kings we have learned (1 Kings 16) that Tiglath-pileser, king of the Assyrians, yielding to Ahaz’s money and entreaties, came to Damascus and killed Rezin, king of Syria. It follows:

**VERSE 12.—** “Syria from the east and the Philistines from the west”—understand, “the Lord shall raise up”—“and they shall devour [Note: [Col. 0125D] Codex Cruc.: ‘he shall devour.’] Israel with their whole mouth.”

For in ancient times these two peoples greatly afflicted the people of Israel, especially shortly before the captivity of the ten tribes, in the days of Ahab and [Col. 0125C] the others of that time, and thereafter. It follows:

“In all these things his anger has not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out.” Since they have not turned from their wickedness on account of the evils they have suffered so far, neither has the Lord turned from his anger; rather, he will yet increase their tribulations by delivering them into captivity. For it is added:

**VERSE 13.—** “And the people did not return to the one striking them, and they did not seek the Lord of hosts.”

**VERSE 14.—** “And the Lord shall destroy from Israel head and tail, the one bending and the one restraining, in one day.”

That is, when they are led captive to the Medes. What “head” and “tail” mean, the prophet himself explains by adding:

**VERSE 15.—** “The elder and the honoured man is the head, and the prophet teaching falsehood is the tail.”

What, moreover, is expressed by “the one bending” except a teacher humbling those subject to him under discipline? And what by “the one restraining” except any teacher? Concerning the false prophets he further adds:

**VERSE 16.—** “And those who call this people blessed shall be deceiving them, and those who are called blessed shall be cast down.”

And because all were therefore delivered to death and captivity, since they believed false prophets, it follows:

**VERSE 17.—** “Therefore the Lord shall not rejoice over its young men, and shall not have pity on its orphans and widows, because everyone is a hypocrite and wicked, and every mouth has spoken folly.”

They were hypocrites because they pretended to be God’s people; and they spoke folly because they praised idols and mocked the holy prophets. There follows the verse frequently inserted:

“In all these things his anger has not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out.” But it should be understood that God has neither fury nor anger within himself. One is said to be angry when one is inflamed by passion of mind against a vice to be punished. How, then, does God become angry, since no disturbance of mind moves him when he avenges our vices? Yet he who strikes sins is said, in the manner of human speech, to be angry or to have fury, though he is moved by no disturbance of mind. For God can no more become angry than he can in any way change. His hand also is said to be stretched out, so that the posture of one striking may be described in him, although he is bounded by no bodily form. Why his fury has not turned away from them, the prophet shows by adding:

**VERSE 18.—** “For wickedness has been kindled like fire; it shall devour brier and thorn; it shall burn in the thicket of the forest, and the pride of smoke shall be rolled up.”

[Col. 0126C] The wickedness of idolatry and cruelty was kindled in the kings of Israel, and it shall devour brier and thorn, that is, those of whom it is said in David’s song: “But transgressors shall all be plucked out like thorns” (2 Sam. 23:6). The fire of wickedness shall burn in the thicket of the forest, so as to devour all Israel. But when wickedness is called fire, what is this smoke proceeding from this fire except the teaching of wickedness? And the pride of smoke is the pride of perverse teaching. Therefore the pride of smoke is rolled up in the thicket of the forest when the arrogance of idolatry becomes entangled among the multitude of Israel’s people, so that that people can no longer be released from it, being wholly enwrapped in it. It follows:

**VERSE 19.—** “In the anger of the Lord of hosts the land has been troubled, and the people shall be like fuel for fire.”

[Col. 0126D] The land of Israel has been troubled in the anger of the Lord. And because wickedness is fire, the people become like fuel for fire, since they are afflicted by the wickedness of evil rulers and each harms his neighbour. For it follows: “A man shall not spare his brother.”

**VERSE 20.—** “And he shall turn to the right and be hungry; he shall eat on the left and shall not be satisfied.”

He shall turn to the right in order to oppose the good; and to the left in order to harm the evil. It follows:

“Each shall devour the flesh of his own arm.” What is denoted by the arm except any close neighbour, in whom one has strength and through whom one carries out one’s [Col. 0127A] actions? [Note: [Col. 0127D] The manuscript here reads: “they have actions.”] Therefore one devours the flesh of one’s own arm who seizes the substance of one’s neighbour and friend. And because this was done not merely by man against man, but also by tribe against tribe, it follows:

**VERSE 21.—** “Manasseh [shall devour] Ephraim, and Ephraim Manasseh”—understand, “shall devour”—“and together they [shall be] against Judah.”

Thus the land was troubled in the anger of the Lord. After this, the text deals with those who promulgated unjust laws among the people of Israel, and captivity due to them is promised: “Woe,” he says, “to those who enact unjust laws,” etc. (Isa. 10:1). Finally many things are said concerning the king of the Assyrians, which we now omit to treat historically. But since the spirit of prophecy is accustomed to embrace different matters in the same words, let us see whether these things may be understood according to the higher sense.

“And the Lord shall raise up against him the enemies of Rezin.” Since Rezin was king of Syria, and since by Syria we understand the Gentile world, what is denoted by Rezin except the rulers of the remnant of the Gentiles who refused to believe? Their enemies are raised against them, as John says: “Woe to the earth and the sea, because the devil has come down to you, having great wrath” (Rev. 12:12). It follows:

“Syria from the east, and the Philistines from the west, and they shall devour Israel with their whole mouth.” Syria is interpreted “lofty”; Philistines, “a double fall” or “two have fallen.” What, then, is figured by Syria except the lofty nature of angels, created in the heights? What by the Philistines except the human race, driven from the happiness of paradise as if into the west—that is, into this valley of tears, where, as light fails, night and the boundless abyss of damnation are found? For the designation “Philistines,” “two have fallen,” is evident in the first-created humans themselves: the two who sinned and were expelled from paradise’s pleasantness [Note: [Col. 0128D] Codex G: “They fell from pleasantness.”], and suffered the ruin of body and soul.

“Therefore the Lord raises up Syria from the east and the Philistines from the west, that they may devour Israel with their whole mouth,” because, by divine judgment, both evil spirits, corrupted from their origin at the beginning, overcome the Jewish people, and human beings from this present age persecute him from the Passion and setting of the Saviour. Nor should it seem absurd that Rezin, Israel, Ephraim, and the other names are understood under different meanings. For readers must exercise great discernment, so that in sacred discourse, although a given word is one, it is not believed always to signify one and the same thing, but may be understood in different ways according to the diversity of contexts, as is fitting. It follows:

“In all these things his anger has not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out.” While Vespasian laid waste the regions of Judaea, the Lord was unwilling to be propitiated because they were unwilling to be converted. For it follows: “And the people did not return to the one striking them, and they did not seek the Lord of hosts,” that is, Christ.

[Col. 0128A] “And the Lord shall destroy from Israel head and tail, the one bending and the one restraining, in one day”: that is, Titus, when he captures Jerusalem. During that siege John and Simon and the other Jewish leaders ruinously deceived the people by their flatteries, asserting that nothing was more pleasing to God than to fight for liberty. Concerning them it is added: “And those who call this people blessed shall be deceiving them, and those who are called blessed shall be cast down.” And because every sex and every age perished, it is fittingly added:

“Therefore the Lord shall not rejoice over its young men, nor have pity on its orphans and widows.” And their cause is further added: “Because everyone is a hypocrite and wicked, and every mouth has spoken folly.” All the people were hypocritical, corrupted as they were by “the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy” (Matt. 16:6). “And every mouth of theirs spoke folly,” when they said: “Take this man away, and release Barabbas to us” (Luke 23:18); and, “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John 19:7); and, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25). It follows: “In all these things his anger has not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out.” And why his hand is still stretched out to strike is added:

“For wickedness has been kindled like fire; it shall devour brier and thorn.” The wickedness of the Jewish rulers was kindled like fire against the apostles, who steadfastly preached the Lord’s resurrection. It shall devour brier and thorn: that is, the same wickedness shall inflame the Jewish people against the apostles. Of such thorns and briers it is said: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters” (Song 2:2). “And it shall burn,” he says, “in the thicket of the forest”: that is, the same flame of envy shall blaze against Christians among the uncultivated people of the Gentiles. “And the pride of smoke shall be rolled up,” because all the rulers of the Gentiles conspired in this, to defend the old error of idolatry and unanimously attack the new preaching of Christian doctrine. And because the whole world was stirred against Christians, it is rightly added:

“In the anger of the Lord of hosts the land has been stirred, and the people shall be like fuel for fire.” For the fire of persecution shall devour the people of the saints. Thus the Lord says to them: “Then they will deliver you up to tribulation and kill you, and you will be hated by all nations for my name’s sake. And then many will be scandalized, and will betray one another and hate one another; and many false prophets will arise and deceive many” (Matt. 24:9–11). Likewise here it follows: “A man shall not spare his brother. And he shall turn to the right and be hungry; he shall eat on the left and shall not be satisfied,” etc. “A man shall not spare his brother”—for “brother shall deliver brother to death” (Matt. 10:21). He shall turn to the right against the righteous and hunger for their punishment; and he shall consume sinners on the left and not be satisfied with afflicting them. By “arm,” however, we have already understood a necessary friend, in whom one has strength and through whom one accomplishes one’s actions. Therefore one devours the flesh of one’s own arm who kills or tortures the body of a friend.

What, moreover, is denoted by Manasseh, which means “forgetful,” except the Gentile people, who forgot their Creator and worshipped the creature? What by Ephraim, interpreted “fruitfulness,” which, having abandoned God’s temple, served idols, except the multitude of heretics? And what by Judah except the people of Catholics? Therefore Manasseh shall devour Ephraim and Ephraim Manasseh, because the Gentiles persecuted heretics, thinking them Christians, and heretics converted to their own sect as though to religion those among the Gentiles whom they could; and again together—that is, Gentiles and heretics—they raged against Judah, that is, against the Church. But after these things were fulfilled, persecutions still did not cease; for it follows: “In all these things his anger has not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out.” For concerning impious rulers who then enacted unjust laws against Christians, it is added:

## CHAPTER X

**VERSE 1.—** “Woe to those who enact unjust laws, and who, writing, have written injustice!”

**VERSE 2.—** “That they may oppress the poor in judgment, do violence to the cause of the humble among my people, make widows their prey, and plunder orphans.”

For after they had condemned or killed martyrs by unjust judgment, they plundered their goods, leaving nothing to their wives and children. Wishing to terrify them concerning the day of the future judgment, in which each shall receive according to his work, the prophet adds:

**VERSE 3.—** “What will you do on the day of visitation and of calamity coming from afar?”

For that examination is often called “visitation” in the Scriptures: “I will visit,” he says, “the evils of the world, and the iniquity of the wicked” (Isa. 13:11); for “that day is a day of wrath, a day of calamity and misery” [Col. 0129D] (Zeph. 1:15). That calamity is said to come from afar, in accordance with: “Behold, the name of the Lord comes from far away; his wrath burns and is heavy to bear” (Isa. 30:27). Concerning the severity of that day it is further added:

“To whose help will you flee, and where will you leave your glory, lest you bend beneath the bond and fall with the slain?” For kings and tyrants shall then find neither help nor escape, but shall be bowed beneath the bond of perpetual death with the rest whom the Lord will kill by the spirit of his mouth, saying: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41). It follows:

[Col. 0130A] **VERSE 4.—** “In all these things his anger has not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out.”

For tribulations still remain; evils still multiply. Or his anger has not turned away from the wicked after he has delivered them to Gehenna, but his hand is still upon them, so that they may be punished without any end or limit. It follows:

**VERSE 5.—** “Woe to Assyria! The rod of my anger and the staff—my indignation is in their hand.”

Assyria, interpreted “rebuking” or “convincing,” is the ancient enemy, who in the examination of future judgment will convict and rebuke those who now consent to his suggestions. This Assyria is the rod or staff of God’s anger, because those with whom God is angry are struck by him. He is also in the hand of the rulers of this world, who do evil through [Col. 0130B] him, and he is the very indignation of God. For because Satan can do nothing by himself, he is rightly called God’s rod, whom the Lord in some manner puts or permits in the hands of those who effect God’s anger through him. It follows:

**VERSE 6.—** “I shall send him against a deceitful nation, and against the people of my wrath I shall command him, that he may take spoils, seize plunder, and make it a trampling-place like the mud of streets.”

**VERSE 7.—** “But he shall not think thus, nor shall his heart judge so” [Note: [Col. 0129D] Elsewhere: “suppose so.”]; “rather, his heart shall be bent upon crushing and upon the destruction of no few nations.”

What does he now call the deceitful nation or the people of his wrath except the Jewish populace? Against it he sent [Col. 0130C] this enemy, because he released him against it to take away from it the spoils of virtues, seize the plunder of souls, and make this people a trampling-place like the mud of streets, so that it might become altogether mud as once in Egypt and, lying broadly spread in works of the flesh, might be trampled by unclean spirits. Satan himself, however, did not suppose this: that the Lord had sent him to the Jews and restrained him from other nations. Rather, his heart and evil thought are still bent upon crushing many, because he still strives to destroy no few nations. Hence it follows:

**VERSE 8.—** “For he shall say: ‘Are not my princes all kings together?’

**VERSE 9.—** ‘Is not Calno like Carchemish, and Hamath like Arpad? Is not Samaria like Damascus?’

**VERSE 10.—** ‘As my hand found the kingdoms of the idol, so also their images from Jerusalem and Samaria.

**VERSE 11.—** Shall I not do to Jerusalem and her images as I have done to Samaria and her idols?’”

The ancient enemy speaks this after the times of the apostles. Paul says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood” (Eph. 6:12), that is, against any human being, “but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of [Col. 0131A] the darkness of this world” (ibid.), that is, of evil and unbelieving people. Satan therefore boasts that these his princes—that is, malignant spirits—are kings, because they are rulers of the darkness of this world.

Carchemish is a city beside the Euphrates, where Nebuchadnezzar defeated Pharaoh’s army (Jer. 46:2). Calno, however, is interpreted “all of us.” Thus the wicked enemy presumes that, as the king of Babylon prevailed at Carchemish, overcoming the multitude of Egyptians—a type of the same ancient enemy overcoming the multitude of worldly people—so he will prevail at Calno, that is, in all of us.

Arpad means “healed,” and Hamath “indignation.” A person is spiritually sick who neglects now to say: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak” (Ps. 6:3). “In much wisdom there is much indignation” (Eccl. 1:18). The shameless adversary therefore says that, as Arpad—that is, every negligent person who thinks himself sound—so shall Hamath be: that is, the mind of those who, indignant at transitory things, hasten to eternal things.

Damascus is interpreted either “drinking blood” or “people of blood”; Samaria, “their guard.” The enemy thinks that, as the cup of blood—that is, the sin of homicide—so shall be their guard: that is, whatever those appear to do according to observance of God’s commandments who are not held guilty of shedding blood.

“As my hand found the kingdoms of the idol,” he says—that is, all nations—“so also their images [Col. 0131C] from Jerusalem,” etc. We understand Jerusalem as the Church. And many are called children of the Church in whom we know there is avarice, “which is the service of idols” (Eph. 5:5). These are their images from Jerusalem, that is, of those from the Church. What now is denoted by Samaria except the impious church of heretics? Its images are all the inventions and teachings of heretics. Thus the ancient deceiver presumes that, as he subjected the Gentiles to himself, so he can overcome Catholics through avarice and heretics through false doctrines. And he adds again:

“Shall I not do to Samaria,” that is, to its doctrines, “as I shall do to Jerusalem,” that is, to the Church, “and to its images,” that is, to its avarice and false [Col. 0131D] inventions? Because as he separated heretics from God and joined them to his own condemnation, so he presumes that he can still deceive Christians. Such are the thoughts of our enemy, against which we must always think carefully, because he would by no means think such things unless he also sometimes carried them out in part. It follows:

**VERSE 12.—** “And it shall come to pass, when the Lord has completed all his works on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, that I will visit the fruit of the proud heart of the king of Assyria and the glory of the loftiness of his eyes.”

The Lord had completed all his works on Mount Zion when, crucified at the place of Calvary, he said: “It is finished” (John 19:30). And after supper he said to the Father: “I have glorified you upon [Col. 0132A] the earth; I have completed the work that you gave me to do” (John 17:4). Then he visited the fruit of the proud heart of the king of Assyria because through death he destroyed him who held the dominion of death, that is, the devil. His heart is called proud because he devises such things. The fruit of his heart is the work which proceeds from such thoughts. He also has loftiness of eyes because he looks upon all as though they were beneath him, while he proudly exalts himself above all. Or all the works of the Saviour shall then be fulfilled on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem—that is, in the Church—when, at the end of the age, the entire number of the elect has been completed and their works brought to completion. Then he will visit the fruit of the king of Assyria, because, punishing his malice, he will cast [Col. 0132B] him into eternal fire before the eyes of all. But what he conceived before the coming of the Redeemer is added:

**VERSE 13.—** “For he said: ‘By the strength of my hand I have done this, and by my wisdom I have understood; I have removed the boundaries of peoples, plundered their rulers, and cast down, as one mighty, those seated on high.’

**VERSE 14.—** ‘And my hand found the strength of peoples like a nest; and as abandoned eggs are gathered, so I gathered the whole earth, and there was none to move a wing, open its mouth, or chirp.’”

The ancient enemy said: “By the strength of my hand I have done this,” because no one was able to resist him; rather, he conquered all people everywhere after he had subjected the first man to himself. Indeed, no one overcomes him except through Christ’s grace. And when he deceived the first parents, he was cunning in evil, because “the serpent was more crafty than every animal of the earth” (Gen. 3:1). For he seduced the human race by crafty deceit.

What does he call the boundaries of peoples except the natural law? Let us consider these boundaries: “Do not do to another what you do not wish done to yourself. And as you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them” (Luke 6:31). These are the boundaries that reason naturally established for each person. But the ancient enemy removed them, so that the human race might wander indiscriminately along every path of wickedness. [Col. 0132D] He plundered their rulers and cast down those seated on the lofty citadel of holiness, such as Balaam, Solomon, and others of that kind.

“And his hand found the strength of peoples like a nest,” because his action found rest in those who fought in defence of idols or errors. He compares the whole earth—that is, all inhabitants of the earth—to abandoned eggs, because the Creator had abandoned all nations on account of their iniquities and the enemy had gathered them to himself into the unity of his malice. For the devil had seized the human race as eggs belonging to another: he had not created it, yet he possessed it under the false name of father; he had not begotten it, and he did not brood over this pitiable [Col. 0133A] offspring, but oppressed it and held it captive beneath the burden of slavery.

“And there was none to move a wing, or open the mouth, or cluck.” For he had not yet come who likened himself to a hen, saying to Jerusalem: “How often I wished to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling!” (Matt. 23:37). No other bird is so recognized as a mother as the hen, which becomes so weakened for her chicks that she keeps her wings lowered, her feathers bristling, her voice hoarse, and all her limbs drooping and abject; so that, even if the chicks themselves do not follow and you do not see the children, you nevertheless recognize the mother. Thus Jesus became weak for our sake, that he might warm, protect, and nourish us as eggs or chicks. Protecting [Col. 0133B] his disciples, still weak like chicks, he moved a wing, opened his mouth, and clucked, saying to the persecutors: “I am he. If therefore you seek me, let these go” (John 18:15). There the Evangelist added: “That the word which he had spoken might be fulfilled: ‘Of those whom you gave me I lost none’” (ibid., 9). Thus, while protecting his chicks, he fittingly moved a wing, opened his mouth, and chirped like a hen against the robber; for, lest he should lose any of them, he wished to be taken alone. He moved a wing, protecting his faithful beneath it as beneath wings; he opened his mouth, contradicting the ancient plunderer; he clucked, because he himself took our infirmities and bore our sicknesses. But before he came, the common adversary, reflecting upon the things said above, boasted. Therefore, against his folly the prophet adds:

**VERSE 15.**—“Shall the axe boast against him who cuts with it? Or shall the saw be lifted up [Note: [Col. 0133D] Elsewhere: “shall be exalted.”] against him by whom it is drawn? As though a rod should lift itself against the one lifting it, and a staff—which is certainly wood—exalt itself.”

For just as an axe, saw, or staff cannot of itself cut or strike anything, so the devil can do nothing by himself; rather, he is like a rod or axe in God’s hand. His pride against God, because he prevails against many, is as though an axe, saw, staff, or rod should boast against the one who strikes with it. It follows:

[Col. 0133D] **VERSE 16.**—“Therefore the Lord, the ruler of hosts, will send leanness among his fat ones; and beneath his glory a burning will be kindled, like the burning of fire.”

This is because he exalted himself against God, as though he could do anything without him. But who are his “fat ones” except priests of idols abounding in worldly wealth and honours, or any proud rich persons? Among these fat ones leanness will be sent, because priests of idols are now despised throughout the world; and the proud sometimes lose their riches so that they may be humbled.

[Col. 0134A] “And beneath his glory it shall burn like the burning of fire.” For he will be consumed inwardly by the fire of his own wickedness when he has lost those whom he possessed, although outwardly he boasts and styles himself prince of the world, as when he tempted the Lord, saying: “I will give you all this power and their glory, because they have been handed over to me, and I give them to whomever I wish” (Luke 4:6). Or: “Beneath his glory a burning like fire will burn,” because Satan, who boasts outwardly, and his angels, wherever they fly in the air, wander on earth or beneath the earth, or are held confined, always carry with them the torments of their own flames—like a feverish person who, though placed in ivory beds and sunny places, cannot escape the heat or cold of his innate illness. Thus demons, even if worshipped in gilded temples and roaming through the air, always burn with the fire of Gehenna; and from their own punishment they are warned. Yet, out of envy, they suggest to deceived human beings the fuel of vices by which those persons too may perish.

**VERSE 17.**—“And the light of Israel shall be in fire, and his Holy One in flame; and it shall be kindled and shall devour thorn and brier in one day.”

Saint Father Ambrose (*On the Holy Spirit*, book I, ch. 14) says: “Isaiah signifies that not only light but also the Holy Spirit is fire, saying: ‘And the light of Israel shall be in fire.’” And he adds: “Thus he prophesies also in burning fire, because in these three kinds we perceive more fully the majesty of divinity: for sanctifying belongs properly to divinity, illumination belongs to fire and light, and it is customary for the divine nature to be expressed or seen in the form of fire. For God is a consuming fire, as Moses said” (ibid.). Therefore the light of Israel was in fire, because the Spirit appeared in tongues of fire (Acts 2:3).

“And his Holy One [shall be] in flame,” because the Saviour endured the Passion. Or, he will be in flame because he will come “in a flame of fire” (2 Thess. 1:8) to render to each according to his works. And the fire of the Holy Spirit will be kindled in human hearts, and the thorn—that is, original sin—will be devoured; likewise the brier, that is, the harshness of vices, in one day: that is, in the time of grace, or on the day of Christ’s Passion. It follows:

[Col. 0134D] **VERSE 18.**—“And the glory of his forest and of his Carmel shall be consumed from soul even to flesh, and he shall be a fugitive in terror.”

**VERSE 19.**—“And the remnant of the trees of his forest shall be numbered because of their fewness, and a child shall write them down.”

What is signified by the forest except the Gentile world? And what by Carmel, which means “knowledge of circumcision,” except the Jewish people circumcised in the flesh? And what is Satan’s glory in this forest or Carmel except sin? But this glory is consumed from soul to flesh, because through Christ’s grace the sins of both soul and flesh are forgiven. And first the glory of the forest, then that of Carmel, is consumed, because the Gentile world received grace before Judaea, as it is written: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and so all Israel should be saved” (Rom. 11:25–26); while the enemy of human salvation is put to flight.

But the remnant of the trees of his forest is the remnant of the Gentiles who refused to receive the faith. Yet they can now be numbered because of their fewness, since one rarely finds anyone who is not a Christian. And who is the child who writes them down except he of whom it was said above: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us”? For he writes in the book of life those who believe, as he said to them: “Rejoice and exult, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20).

**VERSE 20.**—“And it shall come to pass in that day that the remnant of Israel, and those who escaped from the house of Jacob, shall no longer lean upon him who strikes them, but shall lean in truth upon the Lord, the Holy One of Israel.”

This was said of those Jews who believed when the apostles preached. For the remnant of Israel is that of which Paul says: “At this present time a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Rom. 11:5). And those escaped from the house of Jacob—that is, from the Synagogue—who at last understood that this was the Christ whom they had crucified, “were pierced in heart and said to the apostles, ‘What shall we do, brothers?’” (Acts 2:37). For they were already seeking escape. Nor did they any longer lean upon him who struck them—that is, the ancient enemy, who persecuted them and wounded their souls—but they leaned upon the foundation, which is Christ, persevering in the teaching of the apostles. This may also be understood of those who will believe at Elijah’s preaching. For “blindness in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and so all Israel should be saved” (Rom. 11:15). But whether it is understood of those who believed in the time of the apostles or of those who will believe at the end, what follows is evident:

**VERSE 21.**—“In truth the remnant shall return—the remnant, I say, of Jacob—to the mighty God.”

**VERSE 22.**—“For though your people Israel should be as the sand of the sea, a remnant of it shall return.”

[Col. 0135D] And because those who could not be justified under the Law followed perfect righteousness in Christ, it is fittingly added: “A shortened consummation shall overflow with righteousness.” For, as Paul says, “The whole Law is fulfilled in one saying: ‘You shall love your neighbour as yourself’” (Gal. 4:14). It follows:

**VERSE 23.**—“For the Lord God of hosts will make a consummation and a shortening in the midst of all the earth.”

When the Lord taught in person in the land of the Jews, which is the centre of the whole earth, he made a consummation and a shortening, saying: “All the good things whatsoever you want people to do to you, do likewise to them; for this is the Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 7:12). And again, after saying: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbour as yourself” (Matt. 22:37), he added: “On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets” (ibid.). This is the brief consummation which abundantly overflows with righteousness. Therefore, after prophesying the conversion of the Israelites, he adds consolation in the meantime. For it follows:

**VERSE 24.**—“Therefore thus says the Lord God of hosts: Do not fear, my people, inhabitant of Zion, because of Assyria.”

That is: do not fear the ancient enemy, you Hebrew people who await the Saviour’s coming. It follows: “He will strike you with a rod and lift up his staff over you in the way of Egypt.” So long as you remain in Zion—that is, in faith in the Lord’s coming—he will not touch you. But if you begin to go into Egypt—that is, into the darkness of unbelief—he will immediately strike you with a rod: that is, through perverse conduct he will stir up persecution against you. Why he said, “Do not fear because of Assyria,” he makes clear by adding:

**VERSE 25.**—“For yet a very little while, and my indignation and wrath against their crime shall be brought to an end.”

For, as is said of the time of grace through Jeremiah: “I shall be merciful to their iniquities, and I shall remember their sins no more” (Jer. 36:3). This is understood particularly of those who were pierced at Peter’s preaching, whose greatest crime had been the death of the Saviour. But even against this crime their indignation was brought to an end, because he forgave them this sin also. It follows:

**VERSE 26.**—“And the Lord of hosts shall raise up a scourge against him, according to the defeat of Midian at the rock of Oreb; and his rod over the sea, and he shall lift it up in the way of Egypt.”

There is no need now to speak of the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb, which occurred under Gideon. But how the Lord lifted his rod over the sea is known from where he said to Moses: “Lift up your rod, and stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it, so that the children of Israel may walk through the midst of the sea on dry ground. But I will harden the heart of the Egyptians, that they may pursue you; and I shall be glorified in Pharaoh and in all his army” (Exod. 14:16). And likewise: “Stretch out your hand over the sea, that the waters may return upon the Egyptians, upon their chariots and horsemen” (ibid., v. 26). The sea signifies baptism; the rod, the Lord’s cross or his teaching; the drowning of the Egyptians, the abolition of sins.

“And he shall lift it up in the way of Egypt.” Just as formerly, when Moses went into Egypt, “carrying the rod of God in his hand” (Exod. 4:20), so Christ also came through the apostles to the Gentiles, to whom it is sung: “The rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom” (Ps. 44:7). Or, because the devil lifts up his rod and staff against us in the way of Egypt, as formerly, in order to strike the virtues, Christ conversely extends the kindly rod of discipline in the way of Egypt, in order to correct vices. It follows:

[Col. 0137A] **VERSE 27.**—“And it shall come to pass in that day: his burden shall be removed from your shoulder, and his yoke from your neck; and the yoke shall rot away because of the oil.”

The Lord removed his burden and yoke from the neck of our mind, because he freed us from that slavery to demonic tyranny under which we were grievously oppressed, saying: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls. For my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. 11:28–30). For in place of the enemy’s harsh yoke he set within us a sweet yoke, and in place of the heavy burden he gave us a light burden.

[Col. 0137B] “And the yoke,” he says, “shall rot away because of the oil.” For, as has been said, we were held under the yoke of demonic slavery. But we have been anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit. And because the grace of freedom has anointed us, the yoke of demonic condemnation has rotted away, as Paul testifies when he says: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17). It follows:

**VERSE 28.**—“He shall come to Aiath; he shall pass through Magron; at Michmash he shall entrust his vessels.”

**VERSE 29.**—“They have passed swiftly; Gibeah [Note: [Col. 0137D] Elsewhere, *Gaba*.] is our dwelling; Ramah is astonished; Gibeah of Saul has fled.”

**VERSE 30.**—“Neigh with your voice, daughter of Gallim; attend, Laish; poor little Anathoth.”

**VERSE 31.**—“Medemena has migrated; inhabitants of Gebim, take courage.”

**VERSE 32.**—“It is still day, that he may stand at Nob; he shall shake his hand over the mountain of the daughter of Zion, the hill of Jerusalem.”

Aiath means “condemnation”; Magron, “throat.” He shall therefore come to Aiath—that is, to condemnation—because “the prince of this world has been judged” (John 16:11). He shall pass through Magron, that is, through the throat: meaning that, once his dominion is condemned, worshippers of idols, no longer daring publicly to preach their error, will teach their superstitions secretly. Michmash means “paltry tribute.” Satan’s vessels are reprobate human beings, of whom the Apostle says that “God endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction” (Rom. 9:22).

[Col. 0137D] Therefore he entrusts his vessels to paltry tribute, because the wicked always remain under the tribute of shameful conduct, which they do not cease to render to him.
