Yet those chief vessels of his passed swiftly, because death more quickly removed the remnant of unbelievers from the course of temporal life. When they had been removed, Gibeah—that is, the hills—became our dwelling: those hills, namely, of which Jacob said, “Until the desire of the eternal hills should come” (Gen. 49:26), that is, the prophets and apostles. In a dwelling, moreover, the authority of teaching is signified. The hills are therefore our dwelling, because the holy Church authoritatively preaches the teaching of the apostles and prophets. But because after the persecution of the Gentiles came the persecution of heretics, it is rightly added:

“Ramah is astonished,” that is, the Church of the saints, which says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). For Ramah means “Church.” And the Lord, foretelling the persecution of heretics and followers of Antichrist, says: “False Christs and false prophets shall arise and give signs and wonders to deceive, if possible, even the elect” (Mark 13:22). For these things Ramah—that is, the Church—is said to be astonished, and because of their impious teaching. After these things we await the conversion of the Israelites. Hence it follows:

“Gibeah of Saul has fled.” For Gibeah means “hill of the kinsman”; Saul, “desired.” And who is desired except the Redeemer of humankind, whom the prophets desired, saying: “Show us your mercy, Lord, and give us your salvation” (Ps. 84:7)? He is also David’s son, as Matthew says: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David” (Matt. 1:1), and so forth. We understand the other Jews who lived in David’s time as his brothers—that is, as the Lord’s paternal uncles—and their children are his cousins, that is, David’s descendants. After the destruction of Jerusalem, Domitian ordered all of David’s line to be killed, so that only the Lord’s cousins might remain after the killing of his brothers, that is, David’s sons. Therefore, when the Jewish stock that descends from David’s brothers—that is, from the ancient Fathers—has been cut down, the hill of Saul’s kinsman is called Christ’s hill. Thus Gibeah of Saul has fled, when the people of Israel, kin to Christ, flee from the wrath to come and receive faith. Accordingly it is added:

“Neigh with your voice, daughter of Gallim,” that is, daughter of those who migrate. For then, strengthened by Elijah’s coming, the Church—which, pressed by tribulations, had been silent in sorrow—will neigh, that is, exult and preach rejoicingly. But she will neigh not with the voice of Antichrist’s preachers, nor of unbelieving Jews, nor of heretics, nor of Gentiles, but with a sweet, native, and proper voice. Gallim—that is, “those who migrate”—are those who have not fixed the root of their heart in love for this world but hasten toward heaven, saying: “For we do not have here a continuing city, but seek the one to come” (Heb. 13:14). Their daughter is generated from the Church by their preaching and imitation. For her consolation, the extermination of Antichrist is then added.

“Attend, Laish; poor little Anathoth; Medemena has migrated.” Interpreted, this says: “Attend to the lion, poor little obedient one; he has migrated from his forest.” Attend to the lion; consider Christ, because in dying he migrated from his forest—that is, from the Gentiles, among whom he raged as a lion while reigning in the forest—O poor little obedient one, that is, the humble Church serving Christ.

Then he addresses those who, at the very end of this age, will do penance after Antichrist’s death: “O inhabitants of Gebim,” that is, “of pits,” who have until now remained hidden in the deep recesses of wickedness, “take courage and fight against Satan. For it is still day”: that is, a small space of this life still remains, “that one may stand at Nob,” that is, that one may stand against the barking of the devil’s suggestions. For Nob means “barking.” After Antichrist’s death, forty-five days will remain, as is gathered from the book of Daniel; and then many whom Antichrist had deceived will resort to remedies of repentance. And because Antichrist will rage especially in Jerusalem and in those places, perhaps the following is therefore added:

“He shall shake his hand over the mountain of the daughter of Zion, the hill of Jerusalem.” This may also be understood of the temptation with which the ancient enemy attacks everyone. For what is signified by his hand except temptation? He therefore shakes his hand over mountain and hill because he harasses all believers, both greater and lesser, with temptations. It follows:

**VERSE 33.**—“Behold, the Lord, the ruler of hosts, shall break the flask in terror; those lofty in stature shall be cut down, and the high shall be humbled.”

**VERSE 34.**—“The thickets of the forest shall be overthrown with iron, and Lebanon with its lofty ones shall fall.”

The Lord shall break the flask in terror, as happened formerly in Gideon’s battle (Judg. 7:20). Bodily frailty is signified by the flask. Therefore the Lord broke the flask in terror, because when Christ died, “darkness came, the veil of the temple was torn, the earth shook, rocks were split, tombs were opened, and many bodies of saints who had slept arose” (Matt. 27:45–52). But the centurion and those with him guarding Jesus, seeing the earthquake and the things that happened, feared greatly and said: “Truly this was the Son of God” (ibid., 54). Thus the flask of the Lord’s body was broken in terror.

And after this, those lofty in stature—that is, the leaders of the Jews—were partly cut down by the Romans, that is, killed, and partly humbled, that is, led into captivity. The thickets of the forest were overthrown with iron because Jerusalem was destroyed; and Lebanon with its lofty ones fell because the Temple was burned and its proud priests cast down.

[Col. 0139D] Or we may understand by those lofty in stature the kings and rulers of the world, or any persons placed in high position, or certainly the proud, whom Christ, through the flashing forth of the Gospel, either cut down by death or humbled by repentance. “And the thickets of the forest,” he says, “shall be overthrown with iron.” “For now the axe has been laid to the root of the trees. Therefore every tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. 3:10). What is Lebanon except worldly glory? For Lebanon means “whiteness,” and those who attain worldly rank are outwardly white-clad and adorned. Thus this Lebanon with its lofty ones fell, because Christ has now laid low the glory of the world and humbled the exalted. It follows:

## CHAPTER XI

**VERSE 1.**—“And a rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root.”

Jesse was the patriarch of the royal family. The root of Jesse is the royal family. The rod is Mary; the flower of Mary is Christ, who, about to spread the sweet fragrance of faith throughout the whole world, sprang from the virginal womb, as he himself said: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 2:1). A flower retains its fragrance even when cut, increases it when crushed, and does not lose it when plucked. Thus also the Lord Jesus, upon that scaffold of the cross, neither withered when crushed nor vanished when plucked; and, cut by the thrust of the lance, he blossomed more beautiful in the sacred colour of the blood poured out—he who knew not death and, though dead, breathed forth the gift of eternal life.

Perhaps the rod may also be understood as the Lord’s flesh, which, rising from an earthly root toward heavenly things, bore to the world the fragrant fruits of holy religion, pouring upon the heavenly altars the grace of the mystery of divine revelation. Christ himself may also be understood as both rod and flower: rod to one who is punished; rod to one who needs rebuke; rod to one who must be corrected. But flower to one already instructed; flower to one able to begin from the flower and advance to perfect fruit. It follows:

**VERSE 2.**—“And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety.”

**VERSE 3.**—“And the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him.”

So great gifts of the Spirit are proclaimed to rest upon Christ because the Holy Spirit does not dwell in him by measure [Note: [Col. 0139D] Codex G reads: “co-dwells.”] as in us; rather, the whole fullness of divinity and of graces is present in him. Since he descended from heaven to us, the prophet, in speaking of his descent, numbers these grades over him in descending order: wisdom, understanding, counsel, strength, knowledge, piety, fear. For, since it is written, “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:9), it is clear that one ascends from fear to wisdom, rather than returning from wisdom to fear; for wisdom has perfect love, and “perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18). Therefore, because the prophet spoke from heavenly things to things below, he began with wisdom and descended to fear. But we, who tend from earthly to heavenly things, number them in ascent, so that we may arrive from fear at wisdom.

For in our mind the first step of ascent is fear of the Lord; the second, piety; the third, knowledge; the fourth, strength; the fifth, counsel; the sixth, understanding; the seventh, wisdom. Fear of the Lord is indeed in the mind. But what kind of fear is it if piety is absent from it? Whoever does not know how to have mercy upon a neighbour, whoever feigns indifference toward another’s tribulations, has no fear before God’s eyes, because he is not raised to piety.

But piety often errs through disordered mercy if it does not correct with the lash of discipline sins that can be struck by the fires of Gehenna. Therefore, for piety to be true and ordered, it must be raised to another grade, namely knowledge, so that it knows what to punish through severity and what to pardon through mercy. But what if a person knows what ought to be done, yet lacks the power to do it? Let our knowledge therefore grow into strength, so that, when it sees what must be done, it can accomplish it through strength of mind. But strength, if it is imprudent and insufficiently watchful against vices, often falls through its very self-confidence. Therefore let it ascend to counsel, so that by foresight it may fortify beforehand everything that it can do courageously.

But counsel cannot exist if understanding is lacking; for one who does not understand the evil that weighs upon the agent cannot establish the good that helps him. Therefore let us ascend from counsel to understanding. But what if understanding is awake with great acuteness, yet does not know how to govern itself with maturity? From understanding, then, one must ascend to wisdom, so that wisdom may maturely order what acute understanding has discovered. Thus by fear we rise to piety; through piety we are led to knowledge; through knowledge we are strengthened to courage; through courage we tend to counsel; through counsel we advance to understanding; through understanding we mature into wisdom.

But in order that we might be able to ascend this ladder, the Creator himself deigned to descend even to us, to bring it to us, and to show it in himself. The other grades are plain enough. But someone may perhaps wonder whether the fear of God was present in him. Yet without doubt the spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him, because, in order to redeem proud humanity, he assumed, in opposition to our pride, a humble mind in which he feared God. But let us hear what he, who appeared thus in his first coming in order to form us after his own example, will do at his second coming. It follows: “He shall not judge according to the sight of his eyes, nor rebuke according to the hearing of his ears.”

**VERSE 4.**—“But he shall judge the poor in righteousness, and rebuke with equity on behalf of the meek of the earth.”

He who is witness of consciences will judge deeds not according to outward sight or hearing, as worldly judges do, who do not know hearts and need witnesses, but according to the intention of hearts. The poor are those of whom he says: “Blessed are the poor” (Matt. 5:3). He will judge them in righteousness because through just judgment he will free them, and on behalf of the meek of the earth he will rebuke those who afflicted them. It follows:

“And he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the spirit of his lips he shall kill the wicked.” Every sinner is earth, because after transgression it was said to man: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19). The rod of the Lord’s mouth is the sentence of judgment. Therefore “he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth” when he says to sinners: “Depart from me, you accursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41). “And with the spirit of his lips he shall kill the wicked,” that is, Antichrist, as Paul says: “Whom the Lord Jesus shall kill with the spirit of his mouth” (2 Thess. 2:8). And it should be noted that these words plainly declare the Holy Spirit coeternal with the Son and proceeding from him in such a way as always to remain in him, because it is the spirit of his lips and the spirit of his mouth. Then, looking back to his first coming, the prophet adds:

**VERSE 5.**—“And righteousness shall be the belt of his loins, and faith the girdle of his reins.”

In the loins other human beings are commonly subject to lust; but he alone brought in himself the health of virtues against the sicknesses of our vices, in order to pour it into us. Therefore righteousness is rightly said to be the belt of his loins, because he was especially girded with righteousness precisely where other people most commonly lose righteousness and are loosened to sin. If the mystery of his Incarnation should be understood in the loins, then the righteousness with which he is girded must be understood as ours: our righteousness is the belt of his loins while we cleave by good works to God incarnate for us. The same mystery of the Incarnation may be signified by the reins. Our faith, then, is the girdle of his reins while we believe most firmly in the truth of his Incarnation. Since the Church followed him, it is rightly added:

**VERSE 6.**—“The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; calf, lion, and sheep shall remain together, and a little child shall lead them.”

**VERSE 7.**—“The calf and bear shall feed together; their young shall rest, and the lion shall eat straw like an ox.”

“Those of us,” says blessed Gregory (*Homilies on Ezekiel*, book II, homily 4), “who seem to be clothed in a religious habit, have come together from differing conditions of the world, and, gathered from unlike iniquities into the concord of the holy Church, we now see plainly fulfilled what is said in the promise concerning the holy Church: ‘The wolf shall dwell with the lamb,’ and so forth. For through the bowels of holy charity the wolf dwells with the lamb, because those who had been plunderers in the world rest peacefully with the gentle and meek. And the leopard lies down with the kid, because one who was varied by the spots of his sins consents to be humbled with one who despises himself and confesses himself a sinner.

“Calf, lion, and sheep remain together, because one who through a contrite heart prepares himself as a daily sacrifice for God; another who raged cruelly like a lion; and another who endures like a sheep in the simplicity of his innocence, have come together in the folds of the holy Church.”

“And a little child shall lead them.” Who is this little child except he of whom it is written: “A child is born to us, a son is given to us”? He leads those dwelling together because, lest our hearts should cleave to earthly things, he daily kindles them by inward desire. And this very leading of his is continually to inflame us toward the highest love, lest, when we love one another in turn, our mind remain in this exile; lest the rest of this life please us in such a way as to bring us into forgetfulness of our homeland; lest the mind, delighted by prosperity, grow numb while it fears the Lord’s scourges for itself. Rather, may everything that delighted us in the world become bitter to us, and may that fire arise in the soul which always stirs us, restlessly [perhaps “in tranquillity”], toward heavenly desire, and which, so to speak, bites delightfully, tortures sweetly, and makes us sorrowful cheerfully. Therefore the little child leads us, because he who was made a little lower than the angels does not permit us, through the charity he bestowed upon us, to fix our minds in this world.

“The calf and the bear shall feed together,” because one who is a sacrifice to God and one who had been fierce and savage receive the same food of holy teaching. “And their young,” that is, those born through their imitation, now rest together in the same fold. But while the prophet spoke these things about the elect, seeing the lives of sinners devoured by the ancient and insatiable enemy, he says:

“And the lion shall eat straw like an ox.” What is signified by straw except the life of carnal persons? But why is this lion—that is, the devil—compared not with a horse but with an ox in eating straw? We understand this if we consider what difference there is between the foods of the two animals. Horses eat any kind of dirty hay, but drink only clean water. Oxen, however, drink any water, however dirty, but eat only clean hay or straw. What then does the comparison of this lion with an ox, which eats clean food, mean, except what is said of this ancient enemy through another prophet: “His food is choice” (Hab. 1:16)? For he does not delight in snatching those whom he sees voluntarily lying with him in the depths, entangled in perverse and filthy actions. Therefore he desires to eat straw like an ox because he seeks to crush beneath the tooth of his suggestion the clean life of spiritual persons.

But how is this lion, eating straw like an ox, said to consume the life of spiritual persons, if—as said above—the life of carnal persons is signified by straw? For his food will no longer be choice if, in eating straw, he seizes carnal persons. Yet some people are straw in God’s sight and are esteemed under the name of holiness in human sight, when their life displays one thing before human eyes and their conscience intends another before divine judgments. For the discourse now concerns those who, with a feigned heart, pursue a religious manner of life among those truly religious. Such persons are elect in human judgment, but straw under God’s subtle scrutiny. Therefore, because some pursue a clean life through diligence but do not desire to please God inwardly by it, it is rightly said both that his food is choice and that this lion eats straw like an ox.

For clean straw lies, as it were, before his mouth upon the ground and in low places when a life apparently innocent is lived through observance of the commandments, but the heart is nevertheless not raised during the apparently good action toward the desire for sublime things. What benefit, then, does someone gain who preserves purity of life in himself if, through a lowly intention, he leaves himself to be found in the earth in this lion’s mouth? It follows:

**VERSE 8.**—“And the infant at the breast shall delight himself over the hole of the asp, and he who has been weaned shall put his hand into the den of the basilisk.”

**VERSE 9.**—“He shall not harm [Vulgate: *they shall not harm*], and they shall not kill, on all my holy mountain.”

Whom does he call now the infant at the breast, or the one who has been weaned, except the Lord? And what does he signify by the hole of the asp or the dens of the basilisk except the hearts of the wicked? For when the ancient enemy has wholly given himself over to their consent, he has, like a twisting serpent in its own hole, coiled and gathered the folds of his cunning. He calls him an asp, because he rages secretly, and a basilisk, because he strikes openly. Therefore the Lord put his hand into the hole of the basilisk and asp when divine power took hold of the hearts of the wicked and drew forth from them the basilisk or asp—that is, the captive devil—so that neither he nor his angels might harm the elect faithful upon his holy mountain, which is the Church.

But the infant at the breast first delighted himself over the hole of the asp when, while still lying in the manger, he converted the eastern Magi to himself. Why the serpent was cast out of its dens, the prophet shows by adding:

[Col. 0144C] “For the earth has been filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters covering the sea.” For now the Gospel, as though a sea, has filled the whole world; now the knowledge of truth has covered the entire world like a flood, and has submerged every doctrine of falsehood. And just as the waters of the sea cover the depths of the sea—that is, the land which is covered by the waves—so the whole earth has been filled with the knowledge of the Lord. Sacred knowledge is fittingly compared with the sea, because we cross the sea by ships when we make for lands that we desire. But what do we desire except that land of which it is written: “My portion is in the land of the living” (Ps. 141:6)? And, as I said, one who crosses the sea is carried over by wood. Therefore, for us who are making for our homeland, the knowledge of divine preaching is a sea which proclaims the cross, because it bears us by wood to the land of the living. It follows:

VERSE 10.—“On that day the root of Jesse, which [Note: [Col. 0143D] Otherwise, who.] stands as a sign for the peoples—the nations shall entreat him, and his tomb shall be glorious.”

How the root of Jesse—that is, Christ, son of David—stands as a sign for the peoples, and how the nations entreat him, he himself explains, saying: “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:14). For just as those who had been struck by serpents, when they looked upon the bronze serpent which Moses had lifted up as a sign, were freed from temporal death and recovered health (Num. 21:9), so all those upon whom evil spirits have inflicted the wounds of sins, if they faithfully look upon Christ lifted up on the cross and entreat him, are freed from the danger of eternal death and attain everlasting life. Thus the root of Jesse, lifted up on the cross, stands as a sign for the peoples, so that all may entreat him and be saved through him. Hence in all basilicas a sacred image has been set up representing him hanging upon the cross. His tomb, moreover, is glorious, because, besides the reverence it possesses on account of his burial and resurrection, that place—radiant with miracles—draws the whole world to itself for the sake of his glory. It follows:

[Col. 0145B] VERSE 11.—“And it shall be on that day: the Lord shall stretch forth [Vulgate: may stretch forth] his hand a second time to possess the remnant of his people which shall be left from the Assyrians, from Egypt, from Pathros, from Ethiopia, from Elam, from Shinar, from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea.”

After the calling of the Jews, described above when it was said, “The wolf shall dwell with the lamb,” etc., “the Lord shall stretch forth his hand a second time to possess the remnant of his people,” as he himself says: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; these also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold and one shepherd” (John 10:16). This remnant of his people is left from the Assyrians because evil spirits will lose the Gentile world which they possessed.

For *Assyrians* is interpreted “those who convict”; and, as we have frequently said and must always retain in constant remembrance, demons are therefore called Assyrians because before the Judge’s tribunal they will convict of wickedness those whom they now persuade to commit wickedness.

Egypt, however, is called “darkness”; Pathros, “dissolving”; Ethiopia, “gloom”; Elam, “opponents” or “castaways”; Shinar, “their stench”; Hamath, “indignation”; and an island is so called because it is situated in salt water, that is, in the sea. The Gentile world which comes to Christ will therefore be left from Egypt—that is, from the darkness of unbelief and ignorance; from Pathros—that is, from dissolving negligence, sloth, and acedia; from Ethiopia—that is, from the gloom of errors; from Elam—that is, from unclean spirits, who have been cast out from the fellowship of the blessed angels and strive to set themselves between us and heaven lest we ascend to it, being opposed and hostile to all our good works; from Shinar—that is, from the stench of its former manner of life which it had spread from itself; from Hamath—that is, from the indignation of God which had remained upon it; and from the islands of the sea—that is, from remote extremities of the world situated far out in the sea, or from hostile nations, so that we understand the nations by the islands. It follows:

VERSE 12.—“And he shall raise a sign among the nations, and shall gather the exiles of Israel, and shall collect the scattered of Judah from the four quarters of the earth.”

The Lord will raise the sign of the cross among the nations, and from the four regions of the world he will gather into the Catholic Church all the elect, who had been scattered everywhere as exiles from paradise; and then they will flee from the wrath to come. But what does Israel signify, whose name is interpreted “seeing God,” except the faith by which God is now seen? Judah, moreover, means “confession.” Israel and Judah—faith and confession—rightly issue in salvation. Perhaps the raising of the sign and the gathering of the scattered may also be referred to the Day of Judgment, because “then the sign of the Son of Man shall appear in heaven; and he shall send his angels with trumpet and loud voice, and they shall gather his elect from the four winds, from the ends of the heavens to their extremities” (Matt. 24:30). It follows:

VERSE 13.—“And the jealousy of Ephraim shall be removed, and the enemies of Judah shall perish.”

[Col. 0146B] And what is expressed by Judah but the Church confessing Christ? What by Ephraim but the faithless people of the Jews? At first the Jewish people indeed exercised great jealousy against us; but as time passed, their jealousy, by which they persecuted our people, grew cold. The enemies of Judah—that is, the adversaries of the Catholic confession—have already perished from the world, and will perish still more. It follows:

“Ephraim shall not envy Judah, and Judah shall not fight against Ephraim.” This seems now to be the case between us and the Jews: they do not envy us so as to attempt to subject us to the observance of their servitude; nor do we frequently contend with them in disputations, because we see that their heart is blinded and hardened. It follows:

[Col. 0146C] VERSE 14.—“And they shall fly upon the shoulders of the Philistines across the sea; together they shall plunder the children of the east. Edom and Moab shall be the command of their hand, and the children of Ammon shall be obedient.”

*Philistines* is interpreted “those falling by a draught.” Falling, however, is sometimes used in a good sense. For I see that Saul fell well, so that, rising again, he could say: “Yet I live—no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20). There is also a certain draught, bitter indeed but health-giving, which is customarily offered to such persons. Hence the Lord says: “Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?” (Matt. 20:21). They fall by this draught when their body is cast down into death through martyrdom. What, then, should we understand here by the Philistines, “those falling by a draught,” except either martyrs [Col. 0146D] or any persons resembling Saul in falling and rising? Thus here we understand the Philistines as holy teachers.

The peoples therefore fly upon the shoulders of the Philistines when, running eagerly to the faith, they entrust themselves to holy teachers to be carried. And they fly across the sea—that is, through the waves of this age. For the sea signifies the shifting tumults and frenzies of this world, where wicked people, like most ravenous fish, pursue and devour one another. Amid these perils, those who desire to find the harbor of salvation fly to Christ and leap upon the shoulders of the saints to be carried.

Whom does he call the children of the east except those who, according to the manner in which they are descended from Adam, customarily remain as they are, having received neither circumcision nor baptism? [Col. 0147A] Holy preachers will plunder even these, take them away from the devil, and lead them to Christ. But what is signified by Edom, which is the land of Esau and is interpreted “earthly” or “red,” except the earthly Jewish people, stained with Christ’s blood, which lost its birthright? It is also signified by Moab and Ammon. For just as Lot’s daughters made him drunk in order that, lying with him, they might conceive (Gen. 19:35), so the house of Israel and the house of Judah put the spiritual sense of the Law to sleep in order to bear carnal children. Hence Moab is called “from the father,” because this people has been begotten from a carnal understanding of the Law, as though from a drunken and sleeping father. Ammon, too, is interpreted “son of my people,” because those whom we see as unbelieving Jews were born from the ancient people of God.

[Col. 0147B] Thus Edom and Moab are “the command of their hand,” that is, their works, because it is right for the apostles to work for this people’s salvation by preaching. Or this people received the command of their hand—that is, the example of the apostles’ conduct—because they did everything that they were going to command. And the children of Ammon—that is, those who will be born from this faithless Jewish people—will be obedient to Elijah’s preaching.

It should be noted that the prophet rarely maintains chronological order. For, having spoken a little earlier of the Savior’s Passion, he introduces an oracle concerning the Nativity, saying, “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse,” etc.; and afterwards he has up to this point variously prophesied, now of the calling of the Gentiles, now of that of the Jews, sometimes with a changed order. So, almost always in the books of the Prophets, what is first in chronological order is often last or middle in the narrative. It follows:

VERSE 15.—“And he shall lay waste the tongue of the Egyptian sea, and shall lift up his hand over the river in the strength of his spirit; and he shall strike it into seven streams, so that they may cross it shod.”

The tongue of the sea is the knowledge of secular teaching. It is rightly called the Egyptian sea because it is darkened by the obscurity of sin. The Lord therefore lays waste—that is, destroys—the tongue of the Egyptian sea, because by manifesting himself in the flesh he overthrew the false wisdom of this world. For where now is the error of the Academics, who certainly endeavor to establish that nothing is certain, yet with shameless boldness demand that their hearers believe their assertions, while testifying that nothing is true? Where is the superstition of astrologers, who, while watching the courses of the constellations, suspend human lives upon the moments of the stars? The birth of twins frequently and plainly destroys their doctrine: though twins emerge at one and the same moment and hour, they do not continue with one identical manner of life. Where are the many propositions of falsehood, too numerous to enumerate?

[Col. 0147D] The Lord therefore laid waste the tongue of the Egyptian sea, because, appearing in the flesh, he condemned every proposition of error. Once his truth was known, those doctrines of falsehood fell silent. Hence he is said to lift up his hand over the river of the aforesaid tongue of the sea in the strength of his Spirit, because through the working of evangelical grace and the power of his Spirit he made foolish the wisdom of this world. And he struck the same river of worldly teaching into seven streams, in which it stood opposed to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Once it had been struck, they crossed it shod, because a way was opened there for preachers, to whom it is said: “And your feet shod in readiness for the Gospel of peace” (Eph. 6:16). By those shod we here understand evangelists, that is, ministers of the divine word. The shod therefore crossed through the river because they found there a path for preaching, where the streams of secular teaching had customarily flowed in greater abundance. Then, when the following is added, the sacrament of baptism is plainly foretold by the oracle:

VERSE 16.—“And there shall be a way for the remnant of my people which shall be left from the Assyrians, as it was for Israel on the day when [Col. 0148B] he came up from the land of Egypt.”

For just as the people of Israel crossed the Red Sea to the promised inheritance, so now the people acquired by God cross through the sacrament of baptism to the heavenly kingdoms. Or, just as Israel walked through the midst of the sea, so the people of the faithful walk through the different river of secular teaching. Hence it follows.

CHAPTER XII

VERSE 1.—“And you shall say on that day: I shall confess to you, O Lord, because you were angry with me; your wrath has turned, and you have comforted me.”

VERSE 2.—“Behold, God is my savior; I shall act confidently and shall not fear, because the Lord is my strength and [Col. 0148C] my praise, and he has become salvation to me.”

For just as the Hebrew people of old, coming up from Egypt, sang a song to the Lord after crossing the Red Sea, so now, after the tongue of the Egyptian sea has been struck and its river dried up and divided, the Christian people glorify God, saying, “I shall confess to you, O Lord,” etc. The people of the faithful confess and give thanks to God because he has laid waste the tongue of the Egyptian sea and struck its river. For they endured God’s anger while that river was still flowing and obstructing their way; but when the river was dried up, the Lord’s wrath turned into mercy and he comforted his servants.

Or perhaps a confession of sins may be understood. For what does this people confess except that “we lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the will of our flesh and of our thoughts” (Eph. 2:3)? What does “You were angry with me” mean except that “we were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (ibid.)? But, “Your wrath has turned,” he says, “and you have comforted me,” because “God, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ” (ibid.).

Then, “Behold,” he says, “God is my Savior.”—“Long ago the Lord, angry with Israel, delivered them into the hands of Chushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, and they served him for eight years. And they cried to the Lord, who raised up for them a Savior and delivered them: namely Othniel, son of Kenaz [Note: [Col. 0149D] Codex G: Enez.], Caleb’s younger brother. Again the children of Israel added to do evil in the sight of the Lord, who strengthened Eglon, king of Moab, against them, and they served him for eighteen years. Afterwards they cried to the Lord, who raised up for them a Savior named Ahoth” (Judg. 3:8 ff.). We read that the people of Israel had many other saviors in ancient times, through whom they were delivered from their calamities. But from that captivity in which the ancient enemy held us, we could not be rescued unless God himself came to rescue us. Therefore the people of the faithful, now released from it through him, rightly exult and say: “Behold, God is my Savior.” For it was not a prophet, patriarch, angel, or archangel, but God’s only-begotten Son who was given to us as Savior.

[Col. 0149B] And because the Apostle says to us: “You have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, Abba, Father” (Rom. 8:15)—“I shall act confidently,” he says, “and shall not fear.” For the Savior has taken from us the fear of the old slavery and given us the grace of new freedom, so that we may do the good we do not from fear but from love.

“Because the Lord is my strength and [Note: [Col. 0150D] Codex Cruc.: ‘because the Lord is my lot and my praise,’ etc.] my praise,” so that I may say: “I can do all things in him who strengthens me” (Phil. 4:13), and, “My soul shall be praised in the Lord” (Ps. 33:3). For one does not judge the Lord to be his strength if he thinks that he can do any good by himself; and one neglects to have the Lord as his praise if he seeks human praise for the good things he does. “And he has become salvation to me”: not because he himself began to be something which he was not, but because, having turned to him, I began to possess in him the salvation which, when turned away, I had not possessed. It follows:

VERSE 3.—“You shall draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Savior.”

The fountains of the Savior are the hearts of the apostles of the Lord Jesus, from which streams of truth flow forth. Thirsting, we go to their teaching and bring back the little vessels of our hearts filled with truth. The river of the tongue of the sea is rightly struck first, and then the fountains of the Savior are opened: secular teaching is first despised, and then apostolic preaching is eagerly drunk. It follows:

[Col. 0149D] VERSE 4.—“And you shall say on that day: Confess to the Lord and call upon his name; make known among the peoples his devices; remember that his name is exalted.”

VERSE 5.—“Sing to the Lord, because he has done magnificently; proclaim this in all the earth.”

“Confess to the Lord,” he says, “and call upon his name” (Ps. 104:1). Do not call upon him before you confess. Confess, and call upon him. For the one whom you call upon, you call into yourself. What is it to call upon him except to call him into yourself? If he is called upon by you—that is, if he is called into you by you—to whom does he come? He does not come to the proud. Therefore confess and call upon him; for by confessing you cleanse the temple into which he comes when called.

“Make known his devices”—understand, the devices by which he outwitted the stratagems of the ancient enemy. For when the devil held us under his captivity, having tripped us up in that root of our first parent, he could not justly lose us unless the guilt were wiped out; and guilt could not be wiped out except through a sacrifice. But by what sacrifice? For it was not right that victims of brute animals should be slain for a human being. A human being had to be offered for human beings, so that a rational victim might be sacrificed for a rational sinner. But no sinless human being could be found who descended from the intercourse of sin; and how could the victim offered for us cleanse us from sin if that victim itself did not lack the contagion of sin? For what is defiled could not cleanse those who are defiled.

[Col. 0150B] Therefore, for our sake the Son of God came into the womb of a virgin; there he was made human for us. From her he took nature, not guilt; he made his body a sacrifice for us and presented, for sinners, a victim without sin—one able to die in its humanity and to cleanse in its righteousness. For since death had entered the world through a woman, the Savior, by a fitting dispensation, brought life back also through a woman; and he established our salvation on the wood of the cross, so that life might rise from that place whence death arose, and the enemy who conquered on the wood of transgression might be conquered on the wood of redemption. For from the very source from which he received outward power to kill the Lord’s flesh, his inward power, by which he held us, was slain. He was defeated inwardly while he seemed to conquer outwardly; and he who held us by right as debtors to death, by right lost in us the claim of death, because through his agents he sought the death of Christ’s flesh, in whom he found nothing owing on account of guilt. The faithful are therefore commanded to make these and similar devices of the Savior known among all peoples. After these, it is fittingly added:

“Remember that his name is exalted,” because “God exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name” (Phil. 2:9). And because at that time holy preachers sang his triumphs throughout the whole world, the following is aptly added: “Sing to the Lord, because he has done magnificently”—the Lord Jesus, destroying death, binding the enemy, freeing humankind, and rising from death. Though in his humanity he ascended into heaven, in his divinity he nevertheless always remains here with us. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0150D] VERSE 6.—“Exult and praise, O dwelling-place of Zion, because the Holy One of Israel is great in your midst.”

For the dwelling-place of Zion is the dwelling-place of the Church in the present age, which is commanded to exult and sing praises because the Holy One of Israel—that is, Christ—is great in its midst. For, as has been said, in the flesh he indeed ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father; yet he is also here. The presence of his majesty has not departed. For according to his majesty, providence, and ineffable invisible grace, what he said is fulfilled: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). We also hold him here through faith, through the teaching of the evangelists and apostles, through the sign of the cross, through the sacrament of baptism, and through the food and drink of the altar. Through all these, therefore, the Holy One of Israel is great and glorious in the midst of the Church, fills all with his spiritual joy, and kindles them to praise.

CHAPTER XIII

VERSE 1.—“The burden of Babylon, which Isaiah son of Amoz saw.”

Now he begins once more to prophesy in a new manner. For he describes ten burdens weighing down those who refuse, or have refused, to bear Christ’s light burden through observance of the ten commandments. For just as Egypt was formerly struck with ten plagues, against the salvation which the people of Israel were to receive through God’s ten commandments, so now those who refuse to bear Christ’s sweet yoke, which would lift them up, are described as weighed down by ten burdens. Of such burdens the Apostle also says: “Each one shall bear his own burden” (Gal. 6:5). Among these burdens, the burden of Babylon is set first, because it is principal, and because it contains the condemnation and punishment of its angel, who sinned first, and of the other princes of evil. [Note: [Col. 0151D] Codex G: “and contains the punishment.”] Babylon, indeed, which is interpreted “confusion,” is that great city of the wicked, opposed to our Jerusalem. Its citizens are all the apostate angels and all reprobate human beings. As the prophet begins to speak of its burden, he says:

[Col. 0151C] VERSE 2.—“Upon a dark mountain [Note: [Col. 0151D] Otherwise, ‘misty.’] raise the sign; lift up the voice; raise the hand; and let the leaders enter the gates.”

Blessed Gregory says (*Morals*, book 33, chapter 1) that by the mountain an apostate angel is signified, as under the figure of the king of Babylon it is said to the preachers concerning the ancient enemy: “Raise the sign upon a dark mountain.”—“For holy preachers raise the sign upon a dark mountain when, against Satan’s pride, which is often hidden beneath clouds of pretence, they exalt the power of the cross.” They are also commanded to raise against him both the voice of preaching and the hand of good action, so that they may assail him in word and deed. They forcefully enter the gates of Babylon and take it when, by the power of their preaching, they open the consciences of sinners and prepare dwellings for Christ within them. It follows:

VERSE 3.—“I have commanded my sanctified ones and have called my mighty ones in my wrath, those exulting in my glory.”

Those are sanctified who have obtained in Christ Jesus the grace of holiness. He himself commanded them to do what was stated above: namely, to “raise the sign upon the misty mountain and enter the gates of Babylon.” The mighty are those whom no adversity can break. [Col. 0152A] His wrath here means that by which the ancient enemy is subdued and the sinner rescued from his hand. Hence it is said of this wrath in the Psalm: “Arise, O Lord, in your wrath, and be exalted at the borders of your enemies” (Ps. 7:6). In this wrath, therefore, the Lord called his mighty ones, because, desiring to rescue the human race from the enemy’s power, he summoned to preach preachers whom no adversity could conquer. They exulted in his glory because they sought not their own glory but God’s. It follows:

VERSE 4.—“The voice of a multitude on the mountains, like that of many peoples; the voice of the noise of kings and nations assembled.”

The mountains are the apostles, on whom the voice of the multitude resounds when the Church’s confession is made according to their teaching.

The kings of the nations are the rulers of churches. The voice of the noise of kings is the voice of teachers’ preaching, because “their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Ps. 18:4). The nations are assembled because the Church has been gathered from all nations. It follows: “The Lord of hosts has commanded the army [Note: [Col. 0152D] Otherwise, ‘the army of war’; Codex G, ‘the army of heaven.’] of his warfare.”

VERSE 5.—“Those coming from a distant land, from the summit of heaven: the Lord and the instruments of his wrath, to destroy the whole earth.”

The army of war is the host of saints fighting in this age against evil spirits; of such an army the Apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Tim. 2:4). The Lord has commanded them because, like a good commander, he arranges how they are to fight in this battle. They come to him from a distant land—that is, from the Gentile world—and from the summit of heaven, that is, from east and west and north and south. The Lord comes with this army against Babylon because he kindles them with his zeal to pursue the confused life of sinners.

These warriors may also be understood as the angels who will be sent at the end of the world to burn bundles of tares. The whole earth is likewise destroyed when earthly works are overthrown. What, moreover, are the instruments of his wrath but evil spirits? For he brings not only holy preachers against Babylon to call sinners to repentance, [Col. 0152D] but also apostate angels, to weigh down still more heavily the hearts of the unrepentant. Hence he said above: “Woe to Assyria, the rod of my wrath, and the staff itself: my indignation is in their hand. I will send him against a deceitful nation, and against the people of my wrath I will command him.” Thus he sends the instruments of his wrath—that is, he releases evil spirits—to possess more grievously those who choose to persevere in evil. And with all these he comes “to destroy the whole earth,” because he brings this age to its end in such a way that some daily turn from their sins through holy preachers and pass to life, while others are compelled by wicked angels to remain in malice and perish. Hence he immediately frightens us with the last day, when sinners will be punished, and urges us to the lamentation of repentance, adding:

[Col. 0153A] VERSE 6.—“Howl, because the day of the Lord is near; it shall come as devastation from the Lord.”

“The day of the Lord is near”: the day on which he will judge the world, or each person departing from this life, and will reveal his power, because, as another prophet says, “The day of the Lord is near, near and exceedingly swift” (Zeph. 1:14). “It shall come as devastation from the Lord,” because then this world will be so laid waste that nothing will be left upon the earth. It follows:

VERSE 7.—“Therefore all hands shall be weakened, and every human heart shall melt and be crushed.”

VERSE 8.—“Tortures and pains shall seize them; they shall suffer as a woman in labor.”

At fear of the coming judgment, hands once strong in evil work will be weakened, and the heart of a human being—that is, of one who thinks rationally—will melt and be crushed by the pain of repentance. Pangs of the belly will seize them because each person will be tormented by his own conscience. A woman in labor painfully expels what she has long carried inwardly as a burden. Therefore the repentant “shall suffer as a woman in labor,” because they will painfully cast out in confession sins long hidden and weighing them down within. Or when the day of judgment or of death arrives, then all hands will be weakened, because no work worthy of God’s justice will be found, [Col. 0153C] and every heart will melt because of the consciousness of its sin. It follows:

“Each one shall be astonished at his neighbor; their faces shall be faces burned.” Each person will be astonished at his neighbor because of the greatness of terror and wonder when he begins to consider that exceedingly dreadful condemnation of the reprobate. Their countenances will be burned, because the beauty of their faces will be altered by the fire of fear and the squalor of repentance. Or they will have faces burned by that fire which they kindled for themselves. And “each one shall be astonished at his neighbor” as he sees the other in the same torments by which he himself is tortured. Why they will be so astonished and melt away is further indicated when it is said:

[Col. 0153D] VERSE 9.—“Behold, the day of the Lord shall come, cruel and full of indignation, wrath, and fury, to make the earth a desolation and to crush its sinners from it.”

One is called cruel who does not spare when striking with severity. The coming day will be cruel because it will strike sinners no longer with pardon but with strict judgment. It will also be full of indignation, wrath, and fury when it is said to the reprobate: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry and you did not give me food” (Matt. 25:41 ff.), etc. It will make the earth a desolation and crush its sinners from the earth, because then that consuming fire will consume the whole surface of the earth and everything in the world, and will carry the wicked off into the abyss of perdition. It follows:

VERSE 10.—“For the stars of heaven and their splendor shall not spread their light; the sun is darkened at its rising, and the moon shall not shine in its light.”

The Lord says this elsewhere as well: “The sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give its light, and the stars shall fall from heaven” (Matt. 24:29). When the cruel day of the Lord arrives and his fury has laid all things waste, then, because of the magnitude of their fear, everything will grow dark to mortals, and the heavenly lights will seem to withhold their brightness. Pressed by evils, people will perceive nothing except that which every tribulation compels them to see. Or Christ will darken all the stars by his own brightness. It follows:

[Col. 0154B] VERSE 11.—“And I shall punish the world for its evil, and the ungodly for their iniquity; I shall make the pride of the unbelieving cease, and I shall humble the arrogance of the strong.”

“I shall visit the evils of the world,” because he will hold a public examination and bring all the sins of the reprobate to light before all angels and human beings. Then he will show all their iniquity to the ungodly face to face, that they may be ashamed and perish. Their pride, moreover, will then be made to cease—that is, it will cease—because they will be so humbled that they will not add further pride. It should be noted how plainly the prophet shows in this passage that he is speaking in this vision not of that Babylon in which the Jewish people were captive, [Col. 0154C] but rather of that Babylon which exists throughout the whole world until the end of the age. For just as Jerusalem—that is, the Church—is the city of those who love heavenly things, so Babylon is the city of those who love the present age. Whoever loves temporal things from the heart is a citizen of this Babylon; and whoever is nourished by love of eternal things is a citizen of our Jerusalem. But because among the multitude of Babylon’s citizens who will then perish, scarcely anyone is found who is a citizen of Jerusalem and is taken away from their lot, perhaps, after much has been said concerning the reprobate—“I shall visit the evils of the world”—he now adds concerning the elect in the singular number:

VERSE 12.—“A man shall be more precious than gold, and a human being than pure, refined gold.”

A *vir* (“man”) is customarily called one who acts manfully and vigorously, as it is written: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord” (Ps. 30:25). A *homo* (“human being”) is called one who is distinguished from beastly behavior by rational understanding, as the Lord says: “But you, the sheep of my pasture, are human beings” (Ezek. 34:31). Foretelling the future glory of every such man or human being, he says: “A man shall be more precious than gold, and a human being than pure gold of Ophir.” For after Jesus has refashioned the body of our lowliness, making it conformed to the body of his glory, every vigorous man, although he may now appear lowly and despised, will be more precious than gold, because his body will possess an incorruptible, unfailing, and abundant brightness. [Col. 0155A] And every human being who now lives rationally amid the beastly conduct of the ungodly will then be more precious than pure, refined gold—that is, gold purified, fresh, new, and shining. For in the glory of resurrection and transformation the bodies of the saints will be renewed, so that they may retain an everlasting brightness of splendor [Note: [Col. 0155D] Codex G: “perpetual brightness.”] and never again grow old through age.

This appropriately pertains to the burden of Babylon, because on that day the multitude of the reprobate is greatly burdened by the fact that it not only blushes doubly at its own confusion, but, before falling into the abyss of perdition, also beholds the glory of those whom it had despised. Or, when the Antichrist performs such great signs and wonders that, if possible, even the elect are led into error, then “a man shall be more precious than gold, and [Col. 0155B] a human being than pure, refined gold.” Here “more precious” means “rarer.” For everything rare is also called precious. A man will therefore then be rare, because “when the Son of Man comes, do you suppose that he will find faith on earth?” (Luke 18:8). It follows:

VERSE 13.—“Because of this I shall trouble heaven, and the earth shall be moved from its place, because of the indignation of the Lord of hosts and because of the day of the fury of his wrath.”

“Because of this”—that is, because “I shall visit the evils of the world”—I shall trouble heaven and the earth shall be moved, because heaven and earth alike will be shaken at the coming of the Judge. Meanwhile, many [Note: [Col. 0155D] Codex G: “very many.”] Babylonians—that is, sinners—thoughtfully bring to mind the severity of that judgment, fear it, and seek to avoid it by fleeing to the remedy of repentance. Hence he immediately adds concerning Babylon:

VERSE 14.—“And it shall be like a fleeing doe, and like a sheep; and there shall be no one to gather them.”

A doe or a sheep is a timid and gentle animal. Babylon, therefore, will be like a fleeing doe and like a sheep, because sinners who have turned back, laying aside fierceness and pride, will flee in meekness and fear through repentance from the Judge’s wrath. “And there shall be no one to gather them”: again this concerns the citizens of Babylon, because the ancient deceiver will no longer be able to join them to sinners through works of wickedness; instead, through works of righteousness, they will be joined to the citizens of Jerusalem. Hence it follows:

“Each one shall return to his own people, and [Col. 0155D] each shall flee to his own land.” Very many people, predestined for the glory of God and destined through adoption to be co-heirs with Christ, are now held captive in this Babylon through sin. Yet they begin to leave it first in heart, through confession of iniquity and love of righteousness; then, at the end of the age, they will be separated from it also in body. For many secretly depart from this Babylon, which is confusion; and the feet of those departing are the affections of the heart. Those who were at first confused by like desires begin to be distinguished by charity. Once distinguished, they are no longer confused; and although they are still mingled bodily, they are nevertheless separated by holy desire. Because of their bodily intermingling they have not yet gone out, [Col. 0156A] but because of the affection of the heart they have begun to go out. For one begins to depart when one begins to love. “Therefore each one shall return to his own people, and each shall flee to his own land,” because whoever is predestined to life, whoever is to belong to the people of the saints, whoever is to inherit the land of the living, though he is still in Babylon through sin, shall by no means remain in it for its overthrow—that is, until his own death. It follows:

**VERSE 15.**—“Everyone who is found shall be slain, and everyone who comes upon it shall fall by the sword.”

He is found in Babylon and slain who, ending his present life in sins, is delivered over to eternal death. But he comes upon it and falls by the sword who has long lived religiously, as it appeared, yet toward the end [Col. 0156B] of life falls into some crime and thus at last, dying without repentance, is cast down into Tartarus by the sentence of divine judgment.

Or the devil, and every doctrine contrary to truth, shall flee like a doe; nor shall there be anyone to gather his disciples. For, delivered from evil teachers, they shall turn to the people of the Church, whence they had been led away, and shall flee to their own land, which is the Church. Each one of them shall be slain in that in which he is found, so that he may cease to be a heretic; and whoever comes upon it shall fall by the spiritual sword. It follows:

**VERSE 16.**—“Their little children shall be dashed to pieces before their eyes; their houses shall be plundered, and their wives violated.”

Who are denoted by the name of little children except still tender [Note: [Col. 0156D] Codex G: “earthly.”] [Col. 0156C] works? Therefore the little children of the Babylonians are dashed to pieces [Note: [Col. 0156D] Ibid.: “shall be dashed to pieces.”] before their eyes, because often the upright mind sees clearly, yet does not boldly rise against perversity; and, though resisting, is overcome, while it judges the very thing it does and is conquered by the pleasure of its flesh. For often upright action is outwardly lost, while the light of reason is still retained in the heart. Jeremiah indicates this when, in recounting Zedekiah’s captivity, he declares the order of inner captivity, saying: “The king of Babylon killed the sons of Zedekiah at Riblah before his eyes, and killed all the nobles of Judah; he also put out Zedekiah’s eyes” (Jer. 52:10).

The king of Babylon is the ancient enemy, possessor of inward confusion. He first slaughters the sons before the beholder’s [Col. 0156D] eyes, because he often destroys good works in such a way that the captive person himself sees with grief that he is losing them. For the soul commonly groans; yet, conquered by the pleasures of its flesh, it loses, though loving them, the good things for which it groans. It considers the losses it suffers, yet does not raise the arm of virtue against the king of Babylon. But while it is struck down in full awareness by committing wickedness, it is sometimes brought by habitual sin to be deprived even of the light of reason itself. Thus, after first killing Zedekiah’s sons, the king of Babylon puts out his eyes, because the malignant spirit, after first removing good works, afterwards takes away the light of understanding. Zedekiah rightly suffers this at Riblah. For *Riblah* is interpreted “many things.” [Col. 0157A] The light of reason is at times taken away from one who is weighed down by the multitude of his iniquity through a perverse habit. Rightly, therefore, it is said here of the Babylonians: “Their little children shall be dashed to pieces before their eyes.”

What, moreover, does he call their houses except their minds? Their houses are therefore plundered when all the good things of their minds are devoured by malignant spirits. For after they allow their children to be dashed to pieces before their own eyes, they subsequently come to such misery that they lose all the furnishings of virtues that were in the houses of their hearts.

Understand their wives, however, as their understandings, with which the rational mind begets good works as though legitimate children. Hence it is said by someone concerning wisdom: [Col. 0157B] “I loved her and sought her from my youth, and I sought to take her as my bride, and I became a lover of her beauty” (Wis. 8:2). Their wives, therefore, are violated when their understandings are corrupted. For the statement here that the wives of the Babylonians are violated is nearly the same as Jeremiah’s report that Zedekiah lost his eyes. Or the Medes are understood as teachers of the Church, who dash to pieces the little children of heretics—namely, those who have not yet reached the full maturity of error. They plunder their houses, that is, their churches. They violate their wives, that is, their perverse wisdom and corrupt teaching. It follows:

**VERSE 17.**—“Behold, I shall stir up against them the Medes, who do not seek silver and do not desire gold.”

[Col. 0157C] **VERSE 18.**—“But with arrows they shall kill the little ones; they shall not pity the infants of the womb, and their eye shall not spare their children.”

The Medes are interpreted “measured.” And what is expressed through the Medes except demons, who can do harm only according to the measure divinely permitted them, and who seek to snatch away not silver or gold but inward riches? What is denoted by the name of little ones except thoughts? What by the expression “infants of the womb” except tender works, which still need gentle admonition as though milk? And what by children except manly acts? Therefore the Medes kill little ones with arrows, because malignant spirits also strike good thoughts with the darts of temptations. “And they do not pity the [Col. 0157D] infants of the womb,” because they wickedly seek to extinguish good works as soon as they are born and before they are strengthened. “And their eye does not spare their children,” because wherever they see robust and manly deeds, they do not cease to attack them. For each person is commonly pressed by more grievous assaults of demons in proportion as he himself is stronger in good works.

Or may we, at least, desire neither the silver nor the gold of worldly eloquence and wisdom, but kill the children of heretics and of all who have been deceived with spiritual arrows—that is, with the testimonies of the Scriptures. And let those nourished on the milk of error be slain without any mercy, so that they may perish through the cruelty of their first principles; and let us spare no infancy, that we may be worthy of that blessedness: “Blessed is he who shall seize and dash your little ones against the rock” (Ps. 130:9). But after the loss of the children—that is, of good works—the eternal destruction of the city itself is also added. For it follows:

**VERSE 19.**—“And that Babylon, glorious among kingdoms, renowned in the pride of the Chaldeans, shall be as when the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.”

Babylon is glorious among kingdoms because the confused dignity of this age appears splendid to lovers of the world, and riches and pleasures are judged by carnal people to be the highest goods. The Chaldeans are interpreted “captors,” or “as demons.” For the wicked, who both commit iniquity themselves and draw others into iniquity by persuasion, are surely captors. They are also rightly interpreted “as demons,” because [Col. 0158B] those who draw others into iniquity by persuasion assume within themselves the ministries of demons for iniquity, although they are not demons by nature.

Therefore Babylon is exceedingly renowned in the proud mind of such persons, because “they rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Prov. 2:14). But this Babylon shall one day be like Sodom and Gomorrah, so that, overthrown, it may be consumed by everlasting fire. But meanwhile let us hear what it suffers. It follows:

**VERSE 20.**—“It shall not be inhabited unto the end, nor founded from generation to generation.”

Christ promised to remain in the Church unto the end of the age. In contrast, Babylon “shall not be inhabited unto the end,” because “wisdom shall not enter into an ill-disposed soul” (Wis. [Col. 0158C] 1:4), and wisdom is Christ; “nor shall it dwell in a body subject to sins” (ibid.). He says that it shall not be inhabited unto the end because it is known to all that, after the end of this present life, God in no way dwells in that mind in which he had in no way dwelt before it ended its temporal life. And it shall not be founded on the foundation which is Christ, from generation to generation: that is, neither in the generation of God’s ancient people, which preceded his coming, nor in that of the new people called Christian. It follows:

“Nor shall the Arab pitch his tents there, nor shall shepherds rest there.” *Arab* is interpreted “western” or “of the plain.” And he is rightly called western who, through the setting [Col. 0158D] of the true sun—that is, through Christ’s death—has died to sin. He is likewise of the plain who, enlarged by charity, bears abundant fruits of good work like a fertile field. This Arab, therefore, pitches no tent in Babylon, because he does not place his mind there. Nor do shepherds of souls rest there; rather, they labour, because they see their preaching despised. Thus the city of confusion shall be overthrown like Sodom, so that no trace of its former dwelling-place remains in it. But after there has been a new heaven and a new earth, and the fashion of this world has passed away, it shall not be inhabited forever, nor regain the same condition. The Arab, called western and evening-born, shall not pitch tents there, because he forgets things past and continually reaches forth to things ahead. Nor shall the shepherds rest there, [Col. 0159A] whether those who feed the Lord’s flock or the angels who preside over humankind. For at the end of the age, or at each person’s death, all present glory and pride shall fall, and this state of the world shall exist no more but shall perish forever. It follows:

**VERSE 21.**—“But wild beasts shall rest there, and their houses shall be filled with dragons; ostriches shall dwell there, and hairy creatures shall dance there.”

**VERSE 22.**—“And [Vulgate: ‘there’] owls shall answer in its buildings, and sirens in the shrines of pleasure.”

These same fierce demons rightly always rest in Babylon, which is confusion. The houses of the Babylonians are the minds of worldly people. What is denoted by dragons except malice, and what by ostriches except [Col. 0159B] hypocrisy? For the ostrich is a bird that indeed has feathers, yet does not fly. Thus the hypocrite seems indeed to have the feathers of good conduct, yet is never raised from earth by desire. “Therefore the houses of the Babylonians are filled with dragons, and ostriches dwell there,” because in minds confused by sins [Note: [Col. 0159D] Manuscripts: “beloved.”] hidden [Note: [Col. 0160D] Codex G: “hidden.”] malice is craftily concealed, while an outward appearance of goodness is displayed.

What, then, is denoted by the name of hairy creatures except the roughness of every sort of sinner? For hairy creatures begin above with a human appearance, but at their extremity end as beasts. Thus sin, although it commonly begins under the pretext of reason, nevertheless always leads to an irrational end. Therefore hairy creatures [Col. 0159C] dance in the houses of the Babylonians, because in confused minds hard and harsh sins frolic in harmony, as though gathered into a herd.

Owls are birds named from lamentation and mourning. For when they cry, they imitate either weeping or groaning. Sirens, however, are monsters, partly maidens and partly birds, as is reported; by their excessively delightful song they draw sailors to dangerous places. What, therefore, is represented by owls except demons, who suggest the sorrow of the world that works death? And what by sirens except deceiving spirits, who, by recommending empty joy, draw the unwary into the danger of eternal death? Thus there are owls and [Col. 0159D] sirens in the dwellings of Babylon, because most wicked spirits now produce sorrow and now joy in confused minds. The owls answer, therefore, in its buildings when, in troubled minds, sorrow meets sorrow and lamentation brings on lamentation.

And sirens answer one another in the shrines of pleasure because, in those who serve the pleasures of the flesh, deceptive joy answers empty joy, and a delight born from the opportunity of some pleasure meets a delight arising from the commission of some sin. Such sirens—that is, deceptive joys—are always in the sea, that is, in this world, and seek to drown those sailing toward the harbour of the heavenly homeland. [Col. 0160A] The shrines of pleasure are the bodies of the pleasure-loving, or their minds. Or all these beasts are understood as demons, to whom Babylon is delivered for punishment. It follows:

## CHAPTER XIV

**VERSE 1.**—“Its time is near to come, and its days shall not be prolonged.”

That is, the time and day of Babylon, when it shall perish, are now at hand, as Moses also sang: “The day of destruction is near, and the times hasten to be present” (Deut. 32:35). It follows:

“For the Lord shall have mercy on Jacob, and shall yet choose from Israel, and shall make them rest upon their own ground.”—“For the Lord shall have mercy on Jacob, [Col. 0160B] and shall yet choose from Israel,” because in truth a remnant shall be converted when Elijah preaches: the remnant, I say, of Jacob, to the mighty God—that is, to Christ—because “his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God” (above, 9:6).—“And he shall make them rest upon their own ground,” as he promises through Ezekiel, saying: “Behold, I shall open your tombs and bring you out of your graves, my people, and shall lead you into the land of Israel” (Ezek. 37:12).

Yet the statement, “Its time is near to come”—that is, Babylon’s time, when it is to be destroyed—can be referred to the coming of the Saviour, in which Babylon was overthrown throughout the whole world: that is, the confusion of ancient errors and vices, as the nations were converted to faith. “For the Lord shall have mercy on Jacob,” that [Col. 0160C] is, on the Jewish people, who sought to supplant him through the death of the flesh, when on the day of Pentecost three thousand of them believed at Peter’s preaching. “And he shall yet choose from Israel” (Acts 2:41), because afterwards many thousands were converted through the teaching of the apostles. “And he shall make them rest upon their own ground,” that is, in the Church, when, stripped of worldly desires, they left everything belonging to the world and, cleaving to apostolic teaching, all had one heart and one soul. It follows: “The stranger shall be joined to them and shall cleave to the house of Jacob.”

**VERSE 2.**—“And peoples shall take them and bring them to their own place; and the house of Israel shall possess them in the Lord’s land as male and female servants; and they shall take captive those who had taken them captive, and shall subject their oppressors.”

The stranger—that is, the Gentile people—shall be joined to those who believed from the circumcision, so that from both there may be one flock. And the Gentile peoples shall receive them, because they shall eagerly embrace their preaching. For one does not receive preachers who rejects their teaching. And they shall bring them—that is, the Gentiles—to their own place, that is, to the Church. And the house of Israel—that is, the apostles—shall possess them in the Lord’s land, that is, in the Church, as male and female servants, because they shall be obedient to their teaching. And they shall take captive those who had taken them captive: that is, they shall convert those who deceived them. And [Col. 0161A] they shall subject their oppressors, because they shall conquer malignant spirits. For oppressors are demons, who are accustomed daily to demand with interest the coin of evil persuasion once entrusted to human beings. It follows:

**VERSE 3.**—“And it shall be in that day: when God has given you rest from your labour, from your agitation, and from the hard servitude in which you formerly served, you shall take up this parable against the king of Babylon and say:

**VERSE 4.**—‘How the oppressor has ceased! The tribute has rested!’

**VERSE 5.**—‘The Lord has broken the staff of the wicked, the rod of rulers.’

**VERSE 6.**—‘He who struck peoples in indignation with an incurable wound, who subjected nations in fury, who persecuted cruelly.’”

[Col. 0161B] “When God has given you rest from your labour,” that is, when he has removed from you all desires and cherished you by his grace, according to that saying: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened,” etc. (Matt. 11:28). For what is more laborious in this life than to burn with earthly desires? Or what is more restful here than to desire nothing of this age? “And he has given you rest from your agitation,” so that you are no longer a little child tossed by waves and carried about by every wind of doctrine, but may say to him: “My protector; I shall not be moved forever” (Ps. 61:3). There is also a certain hard servitude, of which the Lord says: “Everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:34). And Peter says: “For by whom anyone has been overcome, by him he is also enslaved” (2 Pet. 2:19).

[Col. 0161C] But the Lord frees from this servitude, saying: “If the Son shall free you, you shall be truly free” (John 8:36).

“You shall take up a parable,” he says, “against the king of Babylon,” that is, against the devil, who is king of confusion. This importunate persuader is also an oppressor: once in paradise he lent to the human race the money of sin, but as iniquity increases, he daily exacts it with multiplied interest. Tribute, too, is what each person pays him while sinning. But through Christ “the oppressor has ceased and the tribute has rested,” because, as John says: “Everyone who has been born of God does not sin; but the begetting of God preserves him, and the evil one does not touch him” (1 John [Col. 0161D] 5:18). Hence there is added:

“The Lord has broken the staff of the wicked, the rod of rulers.” For malignant spirits were ungodly rulers in this world. Their staff and rod may be understood as the power to harm which they possessed. But Christ has now broken this staff and rod. For this rod struck peoples in indignation with an incurable wound, because demons grievously scourged the human race and inflicted deadly wounds of sin upon it; and they subjected nations in fury because, violently oppressing them, they subjected them to their tyranny, compelled them to serve sins, and persecuted them cruelly inwardly and outwardly, harming not only their souls but also distressing [Col. 0162A] and killing their bodies miserably. These things may also be understood of the end of the age.

“And it shall be,” he says, “when God has given you rest.” For then God shall give you rest from your labour, as it is written: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. From now on, says the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours” (Rev. 14:13). And from your agitation, “because the righteous shall not be moved forever” (Ps. 111:6). Elsewhere it is written: “He shall not give the righteous to be shaken forever” (Ps. 54:23). And from hard servitude, of which the Apostle says: “For I do not do the good that I will, but the evil that I hate, that I do” (Rom. 7:15). And shortly afterward: “Therefore I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin” (ibid., 25). We shall be free from this servitude when, already mocking death, we say: “Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death? For the sting of death is sin” (1 Cor. 15:55).

But the oppressor has not yet entirely ceased from us, nor has the tribute rested; for while we live here, the devil strives to incite us to sin, and we cannot wholly avoid sin. Rather, “we all stumble in many things. For there is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin” (Jas. 3:2). But after this mortal has put on immortality, the oppressor shall then cease and the tribute shall then rest, because the devil shall no longer persuade anyone to sin, nor shall anyone sin. Rightly, therefore, the people of the elect, triumphing in the kingdom, then rejoice and say: “How the oppressor has ceased! [Col. 0162C] The tribute has rested!” For there true freedom shall be. Then, indeed, what follows shall truly be fulfilled: “The Lord has broken the staff of the wicked,” etc. For when Christ, driving the devil and his angels out of this world, has shut them up forever in hell, then he shall utterly break their staff and rod, so that they may no longer thereafter strike us, while they themselves are subjected to the persecutions of eternal torments. But, returning to the higher sense, let us see what follows. For when the prince of this world was bound and the nations were converted to faith, that was fulfilled which is now added:

**VERSE 7.**—“The whole earth has rested and grown still; it has rejoiced and exulted.”

**VERSE 8.**—“The fir trees also rejoiced over you, and the cedars of Lebanon: Since you fell asleep, no one has come up to cut us down.”

**VERSE 9.**—“Hell beneath was troubled at your coming; it roused giants for you to meet you. All the princes of the earth arose from their thrones, all the princes of the nations.”

**VERSE 10.**—“All shall answer and say to you: You too have been wounded like us; you have become like us.”

For when the nations were converted to Christ, the whole earth rested, as he himself says: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me” (Matt. 11:29), etc. And it was still because the tumults of perverse action had been calmed. For, as we have said above, every iniquity has voices of outcry before the hidden [Col. 0163A] judgments of God. Hence it is written: “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied” (Gen. 18:20). The whole earth was therefore still because the whole world was filled with Christ’s grace and freed, in those who believed, from the tumults of malice. It rejoiced and exulted, as it is written: “The Lord has reigned; let the earth exult” (Ps. 96:1).

Lebanon, moreover, is called “whitening.” And what is signified by Lebanon except this world, which is beautiful and bright to its lovers?
