By the firs and cedars of Lebanon are meant the rulers of this world. Therefore the firs and cedars of Lebanon rejoiced over the king of Babylon, because the powerful and noble people of this world also rejoice at the binding of the ancient enemy. But first the earth was still and rejoiced, and then the firs and [Col. 0163B] cedars rejoiced, because first the peoples believed and afterwards the rulers. Thus the cedars rejoiced, saying: Since you fell asleep—that is, since your cruelty has been lulled, since your power has been removed, since you have been bound in the abyss by the triumph of Christ’s cross—none of the demons has come up from the abyss to cut us down, as you did: that is, to trip us up and make us fall from the state of uprightness. Once this strong man was conquered and his vessels plundered, his other attendants also ceased.

“No one has come up to cut us down.” How many did these tree-cutters cut down and make fall with their axes! The earth indeed rested and rejoiced after you lost the power to harm. But hell beneath was troubled by the greatness of its astonishment [Col. 0163C] and amazement when you were led captive there—though it had thought you could never be conquered. And it raised up giants to meet you: that is, powerful princes of the world, because they had already been condemned there and were mocking your fall. The giants it raised are then specified:

“All the princes of the earth,” he says, “arose from their thrones,” etc. What is denoted here by thrones—that is, seats—except places of punishment in which those princes were? They arose, therefore, from their thrones to meet the falling Satan, mocking him. Hence Ezekiel also says: “The mightiest of the strong shall speak to him from the midst of hell, who with his helpers went down and lay uncircumcised, slain by the sword” (Ezek. 32:21).

[Col. 0163D] All the princes of the nations shall answer him from hell after the day of judgment, once he is conquered. Likewise they answered after the Lord’s Passion, saying: “You too have been wounded like us; you have become like us.” As though they said: Now we grieve less that we have been slain by the sword of divine judgment, since you too have fallen, wounded by the same sword—you who caused us to be slain. Although the pain and sorrow of those tortured in these punishments is always immense, and is thought then to increase through Satan’s companionship, nevertheless they shall have some consolation when they see him endure the same torments which they suffer through having been deceived by him. For the rich man who burned in hell desired that his five brothers whom he had left should not come down into the same place of torments (Luke 16:30). It follows, therefore, that the place to which he did not wish his friends to come was one into which he wished his enemies to be plunged. Thus there is no doubt that those in hell desire the devil, by whom they were deceived, to be tortured there also, so that they may thus be avenged upon him, even though they are not freed from punishments. Therefore, mocking him, they say: “You too have been wounded like us; you have become like us,” and add:

**VERSE 11.**—“Your pride has been brought down to hell; your corpse has fallen. The moth shall be spread beneath you, and worms shall be your covering.”

He who exalted himself above all things has been brought down [Col. 0164B] to hell, that he may be beneath all things. His corpse means he himself, cast down from the heavenly seats. For *cadaver* (“corpse”) is so called from *cadere* (“to fall”). This corpse stood while Satan reigned in the world. But his corpse fell when he himself was cast down into the abyss.

The moth is called a worm of garments because it clings and sits upon them until it eats them away. The moth shall therefore be spread beneath the ancient enemy, because beneath him shall be biting torments in which, lying forever, he shall be gnawed away. What is denoted by worms except the unrest of punishments? For it is the nature of worms to move incessantly at every moment. Therefore worms shall be Satan’s covering, because every kind of most biting punishment shall be heaped upon him, [Col. 0164C] so that, endlessly decayed, he may without cessation be agitated and torn apart. This is the devil’s rest; this is his bed.

Decay, moth, and the covering of worms are eternal punishments, produced by one’s own conscience, or the matter of punishments that arises from one’s own sins. For just as, so long as there is material in a corpse and some moisture in it, worms arise from decay, so punishments arise from the very matter of sins. But amid these things the prophet recalls how great was this wretch’s former dignity and through how many stages of falling he fell from it. For he adds:

**VERSE 12.**—“How have you fallen from heaven, Lucifer, you who arose in the morning? You have fallen to earth, you who wounded the nations!”

[Col. 0164D] **VERSE 13.**—“What did you say in your heart [Note: [Col. 0163D] Otherwise: ‘from your heart.’]? ‘I shall ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I shall exalt my throne; I shall sit upon the mount of the Testament, on the sides of the north.’”

**VERSE 14.**—“I shall ascend above the height of the clouds; I shall be like the Most High.”

**VERSE 15.**—“Yet you shall be brought down to hell, into the depth of the pit.”

As Lucifer is brighter than all the other stars, so this angel was brighter and more splendid than all the remaining angels. He also arose in the morning because, at the beginning of the new light, he shone gloriously with the wonderful splendour of his created nature. But the prophet marvels how so happy a creature could [Col. 0165A] fall so unhappily.

For first he fell from heaven, losing blessedness and the rank of angelic dignity; and in the world he held the principality of iniquity over idolatrous nations. Hence he was called “the prince of this world” (John 12:31). But, when the apostles preached, he fell to earth—he who wounded the nations, that is, who wounded their minds with the sword-point of temptation—because he lost those whom he had possessed through idolatry, and now holds the Jews and a few unbelieving remnants of the nations. He fell to earth from the nations whom he wounded: that is, from the minds of those who came to faith into the hearts of those who remained in unbelief; not because he had not been in them before, but because, being driven out from the former, he began to rule the latter more fully.

The earth received his fall because he wholly invaded the minds of earthly-wise persons. Cast down from the heights, he had presumptuously said in his heart: “I shall ascend into heaven,” that is, I shall exalt my throne above God’s illustrious saints. Did Satan not ascend into heaven when he entered Solomon’s heart? Did he not set his throne above God’s stars when he subjected Saul, Solomon, Judas, and the seventh deacon to himself? But if he conceived these things at the beginning of his pride, before he was cast from heaven, then by the name of heaven are signified the minds of the elect angels, which this proud adversary wished to enter against God and occupy. And by the term stars are signified the individual persons [Col. 0165C] of blessed spirits whom he attempted to subjugate when he drew to destruction from among them those now called demons.

Then he says: “I shall sit upon the mount of the Testament, on the sides of the north.” For the evil spirit occupied the mount of the Testament because he subjected the Jewish people, who had received the law, to himself in unbelief. Whenever he holds the hearts of teachers, the devil possesses the mount of the Testament. He also sits on the sides of the north because, in his presumption, he inhabits the cold minds of human beings. This proud pretender further added:

“I shall ascend above the height of the clouds,” that is, of angels or preachers. “And I shall be like the Most High.” And as blessed Pope Gregory says (*Morals*, book [Col. 0165D] 23, chapter 6): “Whoever rejoices to possess a good uniquely, whoever seeks to appear higher than others, imitates him who, despising the good of fellowship with the angels, setting his throne in the north and proudly desiring likeness to the Most High, strove through an iniquitous desire to break forth, as it were, into a certain summit of singularity.” The person who seeks a singular pinnacle and despises the social life of the angels is likened to him who says: “I shall ascend above the height of the clouds; I shall be like the Most High.” Since he desired, in a perverse order—that is, through pride—to become like God, he deserved to possess the opposite unlikeness. For the one says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. 11); [Col. 0166A] and the other “is king over all the children of pride” (Job 41:25). The one, “being in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized” (Phil. 2:6); the other, desiring by seizure to usurp the likeness of God which he did not naturally possess, says: “I shall be like the Most High.” As the one is the head of all the righteous and all the righteous are his members, so the other is the head of all the wicked and all the wicked are his members. As the one is Most High above all things, so the other is cast down lowest beneath all things; and Satan and the Most High are in every respect wholly opposed.

After the Holy Spirit had indicated to us through the prophet these thoughts of Satan’s presumption, he says: “Yet you shall be brought down to hell.” Though you thought to ascend into heaven, you shall be plunged “into the depth of the pit,” you who desired to be exalted to the likeness of the Most High. Hell is called a pit because it swallows up those whom it has once seized, always wavering and terrified amid the encircling torments. It is not enough that this adversary be cast into it unless he is also plunged into its lowest depth, that he who wished to glory above all things may be tormented beneath all things. Since the elect, established in the kingdom, shall always see him consigned to everlasting ignominy, so that their joy may increase thereby, it is rightly added:

**VERSE 16.**—“Those who see you shall bend down toward you and gaze upon you: Is this the man who troubled the earth, who shook kingdoms?”

[Col. 0166C] **VERSE 17.**—“Who made the world a desert and destroyed its cities, who did not open the prison for his captives?”

Those who see you in the lowest abyss of the deep pit shall bend down toward you as though toward someone placed at the bottom of a well. And they shall gaze upon you because you shall be far away, and, marvelling at you in your punishments, they shall say: “Is this the man who troubled the earth?” The devil is figuratively called a man, as the Gospel also says of him: “An enemy, a man, did this” (Matt. 13:28). He troubled and shook kingdoms because he stirs up tribulations and wars in the world, together with every other evil.

“He made the world a desert” because he took away from the nations the worship [Col. 0166D] of the true God. “And he destroyed its cities” because he overthrew from human hearts the structures of true religion. Or, he troubled the earth—that is, those who hear with Adam: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19). And he shook the kingdoms of the Church by tempting them, but did not overthrow them. And he made the world a desert, so that it might have no virtue but lie subject to vices, with which the wilderness of the nations is full. He also destroyed its cities by making synagogues of Satan out of Christ’s churches, corrupting their faith with heretical plague.

He did not open the prison of his captives—that is, of those bound fast by the chains of sins—the prison of their heart, because he did not give them freedom to go forth through confession. For everyone who acts wickedly makes his own conscience a prison for himself, because, while he is left by God’s avenging [Col. 0167A] [Note: [Col. 0167D] Codex G: “judging.”] judgment in the darkness of his wickedness, he is, as it were, shut up within himself, lest he find a place of escape which he does not deserve to find. Satan does not open the prison for such captives, whom he strives always to keep enclosed within themselves. It follows:

VERSE 18.—“All the kings of the nations, all of them, have slept in glory, each in his own house.”

VERSE 19.—“But you have been cast forth from your tomb like a worthless shoot, defiled and wrapped up with those who were slain by the sword and went down to the foundations of the pit, like a rotting corpse.”

VERSE 20.—“You shall have no fellowship even with them in burial. For you have destroyed your land [Note: Col. 0167D: Alternatively, *your own land*]; you have slain your people.”

If these kings are now to be understood mystically, whom should we understand but the rulers of the Churches, who, having died, sleep in glory because they rest with God in honour? And each in his own house—that is, in his own dwelling—for “in my Father’s house are many dwelling-places” (John 14:2), where each receives a dwelling according to his merit.

“But you have been cast forth from your tomb,” that is, from the hearts of the Gentiles, where you lay rotting as in a tomb. For tombs cover the dead. And who else has undergone death except one who, despising his Creator, abandoned life? When human hearts receive this dead one by consenting to wickedness, they undoubtedly become his tombs. But he is cast out from his tomb when, through God’s grace, he is expelled from human hearts.

[Col. 0167C] A shoot, as I find it described, properly speaking is what grows among the roots of trees beside the trunk; and it is therefore called worthless because it takes strength away from the fruit-bearing tree yet produces no fruit itself. For if it were cut away, it would greatly help the tree to recover its strength and bear fruit. So too the ancient enemy, at the root of the human heart, beside that which is principal in it, commonly arises, grows, and gains strength like a shoot beside a tree-trunk, through the insertion of evil thoughts. Taking away the power of reason, he does not allow the fruit of good work to be produced. Yet he is sometimes cut away from there by the sword of God’s word, that he may be cast into the fire; and the human being recovers the power to bear good fruit.

Satan, therefore, is aptly said to have been cast out from his tomb like a worthless shoot. [Col. 0167D] And he has been cast out, defiled and wrapped up like a rotting corpse, which no one can touch or endure its most foul stench. For no one who reads can doubt that the devil’s rotting corpse is most foul with sins because of their magnitude, when the sinner himself says: “My wounds have putrefied and become corrupt,” etc. (Ps. 37:6). In contrast to this is the virtue of a good fragrance.

“He has been cast out, defiled,” because he who had seemed beautiful in the human mind while his wickedness still pleased there was at last, when he was cast out, recognized as being [Col. 0168A] of such ugliness and uncleanness. “And wrapped up,” because by the power of heavenly judgments he has at once been hemmed in and surrounded on every side. “He has been cast out, I say, with those who were slain by the sword of God and descended to the foundations of the pit,” because in the end he is hurled into Tartarus together with the other sinners.

He will have no fellowship in burial even with those who were slain by the sword of the Judge, because one punishment belongs to the author of a sin and another to one compelled by its author. And for them there will be, as it were, a certain rest, since they are tormented somewhat more tolerably by comparison with him. For he destroyed the whole earth, because he drew the human race after himself into ruin. It follows:

[Col. 0168B] “The seed of the wicked shall not be named for ever,” because there will never be any remembrance with God of those who, once condemned for this cause in hell, followed the footsteps of the demons’ wickedness as though of most evil fathers. Or because the time is near when every generation of the ungodly will be exterminated by the coming of the Judge. Hence it adds:

VERSE 21.—“Prepare his children for slaughter because of the iniquity of their fathers” [Note: Col. 0168D: Alternatively, *their own fathers*].

For then the angels will prepare for slaughter the children of this Satan, in the iniquity of their most wicked parentage which they had imitated—that is, of demons or perverse human beings—when “the Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all stumbling-blocks and those who commit iniquity, and will cast them [Col. 0168C] into the furnace of fire” (Matt. 13:41). For what is added here, “They shall not rise up, nor inherit the earth, nor fill the face of the world with cities,” is what we read elsewhere concerning Antichrist: “He shall have neither offspring nor posterity among his people, nor any remnant in his territories” (Job 18:19). For this head of evils, with his entire body, will perish at the coming of the Judge. Hence follows:

VERSE 22.—“And I will rise up against them, says the Lord of hosts, and I will destroy the name of Babylon, and remnant, and shoot, and offspring, says the Lord.”

VERSE 23.—“And I will make her a possession of the hedgehog, and pools of water; and I will sweep her away, grinding her with a broom, says the Lord of hosts.”

[Col. 0168D] For on the day of judgment, the day of vengeance, the Lord will rise against them, to destroy Babylon’s name and remnant, so that neither her memory nor anyone of her progeny may remain. Whoever commits sin is the devil’s seed. The children of this seed—that is, his most evil thoughts and actions, born from demons—must be slaughtered, lest they rise again, possess the land of our heart, and fill it with cities of vices. And because a human being’s victory is not perfect, the Lord himself rises against these most evil children and destroys from us the name and remnants of confusion, together with its shoot.

[Col. 0169A] “And he will make her a possession of the hedgehog, and pools of water.” Who is this hedgehog but the ancient enemy, whose entire body is surrounded by prickles and thorns? For he is the head of all evils; the whole multitude of evildoers is his body; and every perverse person who overshadows and protects weaker workers of iniquity, and who by wickedness pricks the good persons he touches, is a thorn in this body. For this hedgehog’s body has as many thorns by which it is covered and fortified as it has defenders of evil. Babylon, therefore, is made a possession of the hedgehog, because she is handed over to the most harsh devil to be possessed perpetually in torments, when she hears: “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41). [Col. 0169B] By pools of water understand the Tartarean lakes in which souls are suffocated and burn as though in boiling waters, concerning which it is written below: “Her torrents shall be turned into pitch” (Isa. 34:9).

“And I will sweep her away,” he says, “grinding her with a broom.” For just as no dirt or chaff can remain against a broom pressed down strongly, so none of the reprobate will withstand the stern sentence of the Judge. John too, foreseeing this broom, says concerning him: “His winnowing fan is in his hand, and he will cleanse his threshing-floor, and gather his wheat into his barn; but he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Matt. 3:12). For he calls the Judge’s sentence, which is here called a broom, a winnowing fan.

[Col. 0169C] Or, according to the saying of the Lord, who called the cares of this age and the deceitfulness of riches thorns (Mark 4:18), the hedgehog may be understood as one who delights in uncertain riches and is armed with the prickings of sins. Such inhabitants has Babylon, deserted by virtues: there is no field there to produce fruit, but unfruitful muddy and filthy pools—that is, unclean consciences—in which foul spirits crawl like animals delighting in mire. Therefore the most merciful Lord will sweep her away, grinding her down most forcefully, and will cleanse her, as it were, with a little scourer down to purity, in order to destroy Babylon’s seeds. It follows:

[Col. 0169D] VERSE 24.—“The Lord of hosts has sworn, saying: Surely as I have thought, so shall it be; and as I have purposed in my mind—”

VERSE 25.—“So shall it come to pass: that I will crush the Assyrian in my land and trample him on my mountains; and his yoke shall be taken from them, and his burden removed from their shoulder.”

Instructing us concerning God’s oaths, the Apostle says: “For when God made promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself, saying: Surely, blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you. And so, having patiently endured, he obtained the promise. For men swear by one greater than themselves, and an oath is the end of all their dispute for confirmation. Therefore, God, willing more abundantly to show to the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, interposed an oath, so that through two immutable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge to hold fast the hope set before us may have the strongest consolation” (Heb. 13:6 ff.).

When, therefore, God, who never lies, swears, he declares his counsel to be established with the utmost firmness, and he will doubtless fulfil it—since even human beings, who often lie, keep their oaths and possess nothing stronger than an oath. The unfinished form of the statement is likewise an indication of the strongest confirmation when he says: “Surely, as I have thought, so shall it be; and as I have purposed in my mind, so shall it come to pass.” Yet God does not, after our manner, merely suppose that something will happen in the future; rather, whatever he wills, he orders both that it be done and how and when it shall be done. But what is it that he affirms will happen so firmly? For God must not be thought to swear over some trifling matter.

“I will crush,” he says, “the Assyrian”—that is, the devil—“in my land,” that is, in the minds of my elect, or in the Church. Thus it was said to that same Assyrian in Genesis: “She shall crush your head” (Gen. 3:15). The head of the devil is the beginning of an evil suggestion. The Church crushes this head because she reduces the devil’s suggestion to nothing at its very beginning. Therefore the Lord swears that in his land, that is, in the minds of his own people, he will crush the Assyrian, so that he may conquer every temptation of his in [Col. 0170C] our heart. He also tramples him upon his mountains, that is, in the apostles and greater saints, as he says to them: “Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and nothing shall harm you” (Luke 10:19). “And his yoke shall be taken from them,” concerning which the Apostle says: “Do not bear the yoke with unbelievers” (2 Cor. 6:14). And his burden—that is, his tyrannical dominion—shall be removed from the shoulder of their heart. It follows:

VERSE 26.—“This is the counsel that I have devised over the whole earth, and this is the hand stretched out over all nations.”

He has devised to do throughout the whole world what was said above: that, as all nations come to the faith, he may everywhere crush the Assyrian, trample him in his elect, and remove the yoke of slavery by which he oppressed them. Again he shows that this will inevitably take place, adding:

VERSE 27.—“For the Lord of hosts has decreed, and who shall weaken it?” That is, who can weaken his decree? “And his hand is stretched out, and who shall turn it back?” His hand is stretched out to strike and crush the Assyrian; and no one will turn it back, because he is almighty. Thus far have been expounded the things Isaiah saw in the times of Ahaz; the rest, which follows to the end of the book, he prophesied under the glorious king Hezekiah.

## THIRD BOOK

[Col. 0171]

## CHAPTER XIV CONTINUES

[Col. 0171A]

VERSE 28.—“In the year in which King Ahaz died, this burden came to pass.”

VERSE 29.—“Do not rejoice, all Philistia, because the rod of him who struck you is broken. For from the root of the serpent shall come forth a basilisk, and its offspring a bird-devouring creature.”

The number two commonly signifies the work of uncleanness, because two of every unclean animal entered the ark (Gen. 7:2). Therefore the burden of Philistia, whose name is interpreted “two have fallen,” or “the fall of the cup,” is now placed in the second degree, so that we may observe that the subject concerns the unclean. For in the abomination of fornication lies the fall of two persons. And one falls through a cup who, intoxicated by earthly desires, loses the state of uprightness. What, then, does the sinful king Ahaz signify but either any ruler of the Church or all evil rulers of the Church? What does Philistia signify but the multitude of carnal subjects? What does the death of Ahaz signify but the grave sin of any superior? If a prelate commits something shameful, the unruly crowd of subjects immediately rejoices, like the Philistine nation, over the death of Ahaz. But “in the year in which King Ahaz died, this burden came to pass”—namely, what follows—because, while the prelate offends and the populace exults, it lays upon itself a heavy burden of sins. For all who hate discipline are greatly accustomed to rejoice if their superior falls so far that he no longer dares rebuke them freely. But it is said to them:

[Col. 0171C] “Do not rejoice, all Philistia, because the rod of him who struck you is broken.” That is, because the superior who was accustomed to strike you with the rod of discipline for your fault has lost the rod of just severity through shame or fear because of his own sins. While you rejoice to be stripped of discipline, you receive within yourself the yoke of Antichrist.

“For from the root of the serpent shall come forth a basilisk.” The serpent bites secretly and injects poison. So now the devil secretly wounds human hearts and infects them with the poison of his wickedness. But from the root of this serpent—that is, from Satan’s secret suggestions and hidden malice—will come forth the basilisk, that is, the pestilential perversity of Antichrist. For the basilisk does not kill by its bite but consumes by its breath. It also often draws in the air by its breath, and whatever it touches, even though placed far away, it causes to waste away by the breath of its nostrils alone. [Col. 0171D] Thus Antichrist, infecting the entire world with the smell of his pestilential exhalation, will introduce deadly poison into human minds.

For the *regulus* is the basilisk itself. It is called *regulus* because it is the king of serpents, so that those who see it flee, because it kills them with its breath. It kills human beings also if it merely looks at them; indeed, no flying bird passes its gaze unharmed, but, though far away, it is burned by its mouth and devoured. Yet it is conquered by weasels; people introduce these into the caverns in which it hides, and it is killed by them. Likewise Antichrist, who is king of the wicked, will corrupt everything by his breath, that is, by his teaching; by his gaze he will kill in soul those rational persons who are wise; and he will devour those who flew on high in contemplation. Yet he will be overcome, as by weasels, by nimble and lowly faithful persons whom his poisons cannot infect.

What the prophet adds, “and its offspring a bird-devouring creature,” may be understood of its offspring—that is, of the serpent’s offspring—as Antichrist himself, who will devour even contemplative persons like birds in flight. Or let us refer “its offspring” not to the serpent but to the basilisk, saying that the offspring of the basilisk are Antichrist’s disciples, who will also draw into their destruction those devoted to spiritual contemplation. These things are said for the sake of those who, while sinning, rejoice in their own impunity and in the fall of their superior, because they are slain either by this serpent’s poison, by the basilisk’s breath, or are drawn away by the mouth of its offspring. Yet though Ahaz has died—that is, though the pastor has fallen into sin—what follows will nevertheless occur:

VERSE 30.—“And the firstborn of the poor shall feed, and the poor shall rest securely.”

For God is able to nourish the understanding and virtues of his elect even if a preacher is lacking. For who are these poor people except those of whom it is said, “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5:3)? And who are their firstborn except the first good thoughts that prevenient grace generates in their hearts, and the first ardour for living rightly? Hence it was said in the law: “You shall give me the firstborn of your sons” (Exod. 22:29). Or understand their firstborn as whatever is chief and best in their works, concerning which the Lord says: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness” (Matt. 6:33). Such firstborn, therefore, will be fed by God’s grace. And although the persecution of Antichrist rages, the poor will rest so securely because it is written: “Whoever fears God shall not be alarmed or afraid, for he himself is his hope” (Ecclus. 34:16). It follows:

“And I will cause your root to perish by famine, and I will kill your remnant.” He had said concerning the elect that the firstborn of the poor would feed, even though Ahaz had died—that is, though the preacher had been spiritually extinguished. [Col. 0172D] Now, conversely, it is said to Philistia, that is, to the multitude of the unclean and undisciplined who rejoice in his death and their own impunity: “I will cause your root,” that is, the thought of your heart, “to perish through famine of God’s word, because you will not hear words of salvation from a human being, while I shall feed the minds of my elect inwardly. And I will kill your remnant,” that is, if any good things remained in you, I will extinguish them, because I shall entirely take my grace from you. Hence it adds:

[Col. 0173A] VERSE 31.—“Howl, O gate; cry out, O city; all Philistia has been cast down.”

For the gate is commanded to howl—that is, every faithful person or holy preacher is commanded to lament—and the city to cry out, that is, to mourn, because through Antichrist “all Philistia has been cast down” into unbelief, that is, the whole multitude of religious persons [Note: Col. 0173D, Codex G: that is, of irreligious persons]. What he had already stated as accomplished in the prophetic manner, he shows still to be future by adding:

“For smoke shall come from the north, and there is none who escapes his troop.” For the cold north wind is the evil spirit, to whom it is said in the Song: “Arise, north wind” (Song 4:16), that is, “Flee, devil”; and smoke is harmful to the eyes (Prov. 10:26). Therefore smoke will come from the north—that is, from the devil through Antichrist: the dark doctrine of errors, which will blind the eyes of human hearts. Even now the smoke of his exaltation and of his suggestion blinds the eyes of many. And there is none who will escape the troop of his army, which will fill the whole world and subject everyone to him. But because the people of the elect now seemed liable to be overcome by him, since it had been said, “There is none who escapes his troop,” it therefore adds:

VERSE 32.—“And what answer shall be given to the messengers of the nation? That the Lord has founded Zion, and in him the poor of his people shall hope.”

“What answer,” he says, “shall be given to the messengers of the nation?” That is, what will the faithful answer to Antichrist’s envoys? They will answer this: that the Lord has founded Zion—that is, the Church—upon a firm rock. “And in him [Col. 0173C] the poor of his people,” that is, the humble saints, “shall hope.” For this will be the confidence of the elect.

## CHAPTER XV

VERSE 1.—“The burden of Moab. Because Ar of Moab has been devastated by night, it is silent; because the wall of Moab has been devastated by night, it is silent.”

It offers little edification if we now speak historically about the people of the Moabites and recount its devastation and captivity, which, as is here foretold, occurred first through the Assyrians and then through the Chaldeans. Let us therefore see what is to be understood mystically by Moab, and let us examine mystically the prophet’s mystical words, as God unlocks them.

Moab, whose name is interpreted “from the father,” commonly signifies the Jewish people. For just as Lot’s daughter made him drunk, slept with him, conceived, and bore a son whom she therefore called Moab, that is, “from the father,” so too the Synagogue, making drunk and putting to sleep the spiritual understanding of the law by carnal tradition, thereby produced this carnal people, like Moab from an unaware father.

The metropolitan city of the Moabites was called Ar, which is interpreted “watchfulness,” “watchful,” or “rising.” The Jewish people once possessed Ar—that is, watchfulness—and, in its elect, a watchful understanding that rose to heavenly things, like a most strongly fortified city in which they dwelt safely. For, awaiting Christ in faith, it kept watch and raised its heart to the love of heavenly things. But because it did not wish to recognize and receive him when he came, Ar—that is, their watchfulness—was devastated in the night of unbelief, and all fell asleep. For sleep of the soul is forgetfulness of its God.

Therefore Ar, the watchfulness of faith, was devastated; all fell silent from the confession of Christ: “They had all agreed that, if anyone confessed him to be Christ, he should be put out of the Synagogue” (John 9:22). And because the wall of faith or discipline was devastated by evil spirits in the night of unbelief and negligence, this Moab fell silent from the confession of truth. But since we undoubtedly await the conversion of this people, as Jeremiah also says: “I will restore the captivity of Moab in the latter days, says the Lord” (Jer. 48:47), its repentance is now set forth:

VERSE 2.—“The house has gone up, and Dibon to the high places, to mourn; Moab shall howl over Nebo and Medeba.”

Dibon is interpreted “sufficiently understanding,” or “sufficient for understanding,” or “understanding abundantly”; Nebo, “a seat”; Medeba, “waters hanging above.” What is signified by the house but the Synagogue? What by Dibon but the teachers of the law, who were wise in their own eyes? What by Nebo but the authority of their teaching? For a teacher customarily teaches while seated. What by Medeba but the waters of their wisdom, which seem to them to be lofty? Therefore the house—that is, the Synagogue—and Dibon too—that is, the experts in the law—will go up in penitential mourning to the high places of faith, recognized truth, and virtues. They will mourn over Nebo, that is, over the seat and teaching office of the Pharisees. For “the scribes and Pharisees sat on Moses’ seat” (Matt. 23:2). And they will mourn over Medeba, that is, over the eminent waters of their wisdom and teachings. It follows: “On all its heads shall be baldness; every beard shall be shaved.”

VERSE 3.—“In its crossroads they are girded with sackcloth; upon its roofs and in its streets every howl shall descend into weeping.”

What is expressed by heads but minds? What by baldness but the shamefaced disclosure of the mind’s intention? For what is the forehead of the mind but its intention, where shame too is customarily held to have its seat as upon a forehead? Therefore there will be baldness upon all its heads, [Col. 0174D] because each person will uncover his conscience by humble confession and blush for his sins. And every beard will be shaved, because they will cast away all confidence in their own strength. For manly strength is denoted in the beard. The beard is shaved when confidence in one’s own strength is cut off and the frailty of one’s own weakness begins to be openly known.

Their crossroads consist in the fact that they divide all the canonical Scriptures into three parts: the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa. Therefore they are girded with sackcloth in their crossroads because, when they rejected Christ, they will repent of having erred in all the divine Scriptures. Those among them who had seemed to grow in holiness were as though upon the roofs of their bodies; but the rest of the people were in the streets of broad conduct. The howl, therefore, will rise from above the roofs and from the streets into weeping, because both the more eminent and the common people will raise a howl of mourning and humble themselves in tears of repentance. It follows:

VERSE 4.—“Heshbon cried out, and Elealeh; their voice has been heard as far as Jahaz.”

Heshbon is called “knowledge of sorrow,” or “a girdle of sorrow,” or even “a thought of sorrow.” Elealeh means “toward ascent”; Jahaz, “half,” or “the command fulfilled.” Therefore Heshbon—that is, knowledge of sorrow or a girdle of sorrow—cried out in lamentation; and Elealeh—that is, toward the ascent of the arduous way which leads to life—cried out. Their voice was heard as far as Jahaz, [Col. 0175B] that is, as far as the half or middle, because they knew only how to speak of the Old Testament, in which lies one half of God’s utterances, and did not receive the other half, which is in the New. Or their voice was heard as far as Jahaz, that is, as far as the command fulfilled, because they boast as though from works. It follows:

“Because of this, the unencumbered men of Moab shall howl; his soul shall howl for itself.” Those are commonly called unencumbered who have neither wives nor children and are suited for war, because an army or cavalry expedition is called an *expeditio*. Therefore “the unencumbered men of Moab shall howl” because of this, namely because “their voice was heard as far as Jahaz”: even those who seemed unencumbered for spiritual warfare will, in repentance, utter a howl of grief because they had boasted as though from works and had preached only the teaching of the ancient law. “His soul shall howl for itself,” because each person will mourn himself. The prophet, sympathizing with this grief, adds:

VERSE 5.—“My heart shall cry out for Moab.” And afterward he adds: “Its bars shall reach as far as Zoar, a heifer that casts itself down.”

Zoar is one of the five cities and is interpreted “small.” Because the law is contained in the number of five books, and the action of those under the law is small and often casts itself down into sin, its bars reach as far as Zoar, a wanton heifer casting itself down. Its bars are the teachers of the Synagogue, who are now carried captive as far as Zoar because they still miserably preach the carnal observance of the law, which resembles [Col. 0175D] a wanton heifer. It follows:

“For by the ascent of Luhith [Note: Col. 0175D, Codex G: Liuth] he shall go up weeping, and on the road of Horonaim they shall raise a cry of destruction.”

VERSE 6.—“For the waters of Nimrim shall be desolate, because the grass has withered, the shoot has failed, and every green thing has perished.”

We interpret Luhith as “cheeks” or “jaws.” In the Song, the bridegroom calls the holy preachers the cheeks of the Church, saying: “Your cheeks are beautiful as those of a turtledove” (Song 1:10). Again, Jeremiah calls these same preachers the jaws of the Church, speaking in the person of Judaea concerning her: “She weeps bitterly in the night, and her tears are on her cheeks” (Lam. 1:2), because in the Church’s adversity those grieve more deeply who know how by preaching to break the life of carnal persons. For through them the holy Church crushes the wicked out of their vices and, as it were swallowing them, converts them into its own members. Therefore by the ascent of Luhith—that is, of the jaws—he shall go up weeping, because, when it has repented, it will be led by preachers to the heights of virtues and in the progress of righteousness will imitate their daily ascent.

Horonaim means “the opening of sorrow.” And what is the opening of their sorrow but the wound in the Lord’s side? “They shall raise a cry of destruction on the way of Horonaim,” because, coming to faith in Christ’s Passion, they will weep intensely. “For the waters of Nimrim,” [Col. 0176B] that is, the teachings of the apostate Pharisees, who are mottled with the stains of their own sins, “shall be desolate, because the grass has withered”: the practice that they teach has lost the greenness of spiritual grace; the shoot of good thought has failed; and all the greenness of righteousness or faith has perished from them. For Nimrim is interpreted “of leopards” or “of apostates,” signifying the savagery and variability of the apostate Pharisees and scribes. It follows:

VERSE 7.—“According to the greatness of their work, so shall be their visitation.”

For as they sinned monstrously in killing the Author of life, so they will be visited with a great regard of mercy when Elijah comes, who, as the Lord says, “will restore all things” (Matt. 17:11). But the preachers of Antichrist will lead those of them whom they can deceive to the torrent of willows—that is, to the course of this age’s unfruitful lovers. For thus it follows: “They shall lead them to the torrent of willows.”

VERSE 8.—“For the cry has gone round the border of Moab.”

For by the torrent is expressed the course of the human race; by the willows, unfruitful human beings. Therefore whoever is enticed to the flux of worldly carnal conduct is led captive to the torrent of willows. “For the cry has gone round the border of Moab,” because repentance on the part of Israel will be heard everywhere. It follows: “Its howl is as far as Gallim, and its cry as far as the Well of Elim.”

[Col. 0176D] VERSE 9.—“For the waters of Dibon are full of blood.”

“Even to Gallim,” that is, “even to the emigrants, is its howl.” For through the mourning of repentance it will reach the fellowship of those who migrate from vices to virtues and from temporal things to eternal things. Elim, which means “Ram,” signifies Christ. The Well of Elim is the depth of Christ’s divinity and mysteries. Therefore “its cry is as far as the Well of Elim,” because, by confessing itself guilty when it repents, it will deserve to penetrate to the secrets of the Godhead and draw from there the draught of life. [Col. 0177A] “For the waters of Dibon,” that is, the teachings of the scribes and Pharisees, who seem wise to themselves, “are full of blood,” that is, of the deaths of souls. It follows: “For I will place additions upon Dibon: a lion upon those who flee from Moab,” that is, Antichrist. And upon whom will I place these things? “Upon those who flee from Moab,” that is, those who, from the Jewish people, flee Elijah’s preaching because they do not wish to be converted. “And upon the remnant of the land,” that is, upon all the other reprobate persons who will be in the world. The faith of the Church maintains that Antichrist’s persecution will last three and a half years; but lest its unexpected arrival indiscriminately overwhelm all those whom it finds unprepared, Enoch and Elijah will come into the world before his appearance, in order to convert the Israelite people to the grace of faith and render the elect among them invincible against the pressure of so great a tempest. When they have preached during the first three and a half years, that dreadful persecution, then inflamed, will first crown them with the virtue of martyrdom [Note: Col. 0177D: Another reading, *will crown others*], and afterward, seizing the other faithful, will make them either martyrs or apostates. Thus it is fittingly said that the lion Antichrist will be placed upon the Jews who flee Elijah’s preaching, and upon the other unbelievers among the nations. But meanwhile the prophet, considering that this people at first would refuse to receive Christ when he came, prays that he may pass from it to the Church. For he adds:

## CHAPTER XVI

VERSE 1.—“Send forth, O Lord, the Lamb, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion.”

For he calls him “the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). He also declares him ruler of the earth, according to the words: “He shall rule from sea to sea” (Ps. 71:8), etc. “Send forth,” he says, “O Lord, the Lamb,” that is, your Christ, “from the rock of the desert,” that is, from the hardness of this Jewish nation, which you have deserted because of its unbelief, “to the mountain of the daughter of Zion,” that is, to the height of the Church’s new manner of life. It follows:

VERSE 2.—“And it shall be as a fleeing bird and young birds flying from the nest: thus shall the daughters of Moab be at the crossing of Arnon.”

As a mother bird and her young fly from the nest and flee if they see a robber coming to their nest, so the teachers of the Jews and those whom they cherished will flee from the old nest when they see the day of judgment near at hand, and the devil eager to devour them if they are found in the nest of their former life. “For thus shall the daughters of Moab be at the crossing of Arnon.” Arnon is interpreted “their curse.” And their curse is that of those who said concerning Christ: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25). But they will cross beyond this curse when they pass over to Christ. It follows:

VERSE 3.—“Take counsel, summon an assembly; make your shadow like night at midday; hide the fugitives, and do not betray the wanderers.”

[Col. 0178A] VERSE 4.—“My fugitives shall dwell with you; be for them, O Moab, a hiding-place from the face of the devastator.”

In order, he says, that you may cross beyond the aforesaid curse and escape the enemy who comes to devour you, take counsel, O Jewish people, carefully consider what you ought to do, and, having taken counsel together, receive Christ’s preachers. Make your shadow like night, in which you may hide them from unbelievers at midday, that is, in the heat of persecution. For then all who are found to be Christians will be dragged to punishments. But hide those fleeing the fury of persecution, and do not betray the wanderers, who will not dare remain in one place but, hiding in various places, will be harassed. It follows: “For the dust is ended, the wretched one is consumed, he has failed who trampled the earth.”

[Col. 0178B] VERSE 5.—“And a throne shall be prepared in mercy, and one shall sit upon it in truth in the tabernacle of David, judging and seeking judgment, and swiftly rendering what is just.”

“The dust is ended,” that is, Antichrist is dead: he did not acknowledge that he was dust, but exalted himself above everything called God or worshipped, and trampled the whole earth under his tyranny. But after that divinely struck son of perdition has died, one must not suppose that the day of judgment will follow immediately. Otherwise people of that age could know the time of judgment, if it followed at once after the three and a half years of Antichrist’s persecution had begun. But now everyone may know that the day of judgment will not come before the time of that persecution is completed; yet no one at all is permitted to know how long after its completion it will come. Hence, after it has been said of Antichrist’s death, “He has failed who trampled the earth,” the day of judgment is indicated as still to come after a little while, when he adds in the future tense:

“And a throne shall be prepared in mercy.” For a throne of judgment will be prepared for Christ, so that he may sit upon the throne of his majesty, judging the world in equity. It will be prepared in mercy, as it is also said elsewhere of those who fear God and think upon his name: “They shall be mine, says the Lord of hosts, on the day when I act, as a special possession; and I will spare them as a man spares his son who serves him” (Mal. 3:17). Thus he will judge the elect in mercy and have mercy on his servants.

And he shall sit upon it in the truth of judgment, so as to render to each according to his work. And this shall take place “in the tabernacle of David,” that is, in the royal house which is the Church, and swiftly after the death of Antichrist. Or, while we live here, his throne is prepared in mercy, because through his mercy his sitting and dwelling are prepared in our hearts; for it cannot be prepared by our merits. Mercy is indeed now being prepared, but in the age to come he will sit upon it in truth, because “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV [XXV], 10). It is prepared in mercy [Col. 0179A], but he sits in truth, as it is written: “I will sing of mercy and judgment unto thee, O Lord” (Ps. I [CI]). Then the prophet returns to his description of Jewish perversity, saying:

**VERSE 6.**—“We have heard the pride of Moab: he is exceedingly proud; his pride, and his arrogance, and his indignation are greater than his strength.” And he adds:

**VERSE 7.**—“Therefore Moab shall howl unto Moab; all of it shall howl.”

“We prophets,” he says, “have heard in the Spirit the pride of Moab,” that is, of these apostate Jews. “He is exceedingly proud,” because, glorying singularly in the works of the Law, he despises the entire human race and boasts that he alone is the people of God. His pride [Col. 0179B] is that, “being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they are not subject to the righteousness of God” (Rom. X, 3). His arrogance likewise lies in his presumptuous boasting about righteous works. His indignation is that he disdains sinners and is angry with Christians; and these things exceed his strength, because he is proud and arrogates to himself more from works of righteousness than he is able himself to perform in righteousness. He is more indignant with others because they are not righteous than he himself is able to become righteous, and he desires to harm believers more than he can. Therefore one shall howl to another when the time of their conversion comes. It follows:

“Speak to those who rejoice upon walls of baked brick of their wounds.”

[Col. 0179C] **VERSE 8.**—“For the suburbs of Heshbon are desolate, and the vineyard [Note: [Col. 0179D] Recent edition: ‘the vineyard.’] of Sibmah; the lords of the nations have cut down its shoots; they have reached as far as Jazer; they have wandered in the wilderness; its branches are left behind; they have crossed the sea.”

“You apostles,” he says, “speak to those who rejoice upon walls of baked brick of their wounds,” that is, to those who trust in the carnal observance of the Law. For brick signifies a carnal and earthly work; indeed, this people made bricks for Pharaoh in Egypt. But brick is baked when a carnal work is done from fear. A wall, however, is the protection of righteous action, in which one remains safe from invisible adversaries. Therefore anyone rejoices upon walls of baked brick who takes delight in the fact that he has, as he supposes, been justified [Col. 0179D] by works of the Law and fortified against Satan. But the prophetic Spirit, who commanded preachers to speak of their wounds to those who rejoice upon such a wall, now himself begins, through his own words, to speak to and announce it to them.

“For the suburbs of Heshbon are desolate, and the vineyard of Sibmah.” Heshbon is said to mean “girdle of sorrow” or “thought of sorrow,” and it denotes the sorrow of repentance. Therefore Heshbon’s suburbs are desolate for the Jews, because whatever in them is outside repentance, though it may be near or adjoining it, is rejected by Christ. For God receives nothing from them except repentance first. From him “the vineyard of Sibmah” is also deserted [Col. 0180A], that is, the Jewish people itself, which used to exalt the Most High in praises. “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (above, V, 7), and Sibmah means “exalting the Most High.” The lords of the nations—that is, Vespasian and Titus—have cut down its shoots: that is, they killed and carried its children away captive.

Jazer is interpreted “help” or “strength.” And “they have reached as far as Jazer,” that is, as far as their help and strength—namely, as far as Jerusalem and the Temple, where the confidence of their power and help was—“the lords of the nations,” in order to destroy their strength. But the lords of the nations themselves “wandered in the wilderness” of paganism, because they did not acknowledge Christ, who gave them victory. “Its branches are left behind,” that is, some planting [Col. 0180B] of the Jewish people remained after Jerusalem’s destruction, in order that it might grow. These branches “crossed the sea,” because they passed beyond the wickedness of the world or of paganism. For the sea commonly denotes the world or paganism. Therefore these branches crossed the sea because the remnant of this people has surpassed the wickedness of the Gentiles or of other worldly people. It follows:

**VERSE 9.**—“Over this I shall weep with the weeping of Jazer for the vineyard of Sibmah; I shall make thee drunk with my tears, O Heshbon and Elealeh, because over thy vintage and over thy harvest the voice of tramplers has fallen.”

The prophet, grieving over the miseries and destruction of his people, says: “Over this,” that is, because of what has been said above [Col. 0180C], “I shall weep for the vineyard of Sibmah,” that is, for the Israelite people, “with the weeping of Jazer,” that is, of their help and strength, because they have thus been deprived of help and strength. “I shall make thee drunk with my tears,” that is, I shall lament thee, O Heshbon and Elealeh, with a continual flood of tears: “thought of sorrow unto ascent,” namely, that one here is afflicted with sorrow in order that one may ascend to the joys above. “Because over thy vintage and over thy harvest,” that is, over thy death, “the voice of tramplers,” that is, the cry of demons, has fallen. For vintage or harvest is the end of each of those who depart from the world. The voice of the tramplers of this vintage is now the accusation of malignant spirits, who strive to seize the soul. Therefore, because demons come to seize the soul [Col. 0180D] of every Jew who dies, “over their vintage and harvest the voice of tramplers has fallen.” Hence it follows:

**VERSE 10.**—“And joy and gladness shall be taken away from Carmel; and in the vineyards he shall not rejoice or shout for joy; he who was accustomed to tread shall not tread out wine in the winepress; I have taken away the voice of the tramplers.”

**VERSE 11.**—“Therefore my belly shall sound for Moab like a harp, and my inward parts for the wall of baked brick.”

For at the death of each individual, “joy shall be taken away from Carmel,” that is, from the knowledge of circumcision, because every Jew who dies is led not to joy but [Col. 0181A] to punishment. “And in the vineyards he shall not rejoice or shout for joy,” because, when he has died, he will not rejoice in his own deeds, nor break forth into a cry of gladness.

“He who was accustomed to tread shall not tread wine in the winepress,” because Christ, or a good angel, no longer receives, as he was accustomed to do before the Lord’s Passion, the souls of Jews departing from the body. For the winepress is called the pressure of death, as the Lord says: “I have trodden the winepress alone” (Isa. LXIII, 3). The soul may also be signified by the liquid of wine, because Job said: “As waters depart from the sea, and the river is emptied and dries up, so man, when he has fallen asleep” (Job XIV, 11). He compares the soul to the waters of the sea and to a river. Therefore the winepress is the crushing and distress of death [Col. 0181B], while the wine is the soul. For just as, when grapes are squeezed in the winepress, wine comes forth and the pomace remains, so through death’s distress the soul is drawn forth from the body. Thus he treads wine in the winepress who presses the soul to depart from the body in death and receives it as it departs.

“I have taken away the voice of the tramplers,” because the holy angels, who receive the souls of the righteous, will not speak in defense of Jewish souls against malignant spirits, but will leave their souls to them without opposition. Thereupon the compassionate prophet immediately adds: “Therefore,” that is, because of this—that, if he is left to demons—“my belly shall sound for Moab like a harp,” that is, my mind shall form manifold strains of grief in lamenting the Jewish people, and when thinking of it it will desire nothing but [Col. 0181C] weeping. “And my inward parts shall sound for the wall of baked brick,” because with all the inward parts of my heart and with the compassion of love I shall grieve for those who suppose that, through the works of the Law without Christ’s grace, they are safe from the death of the soul and from invisible enemies. It follows:

**VERSE 12.**—“And it shall be, when it appears what Moab has laboured for upon his high places, that he shall enter his sanctuaries to entreat, and shall not prevail.” Then is added:

**VERSE 13.**—“This is the word which the Lord spoke concerning Moab from that time.”

**VERSE 14.**—“And then the Lord spoke, saying: Within three years, as the years of a hired labourer, the glory of Moab shall be taken away amid all the great multitude of people; and there shall remain in him as it were a small and scanty cluster [Col. 0181D], by no means numerous.”

At the end of the ages, “when it appears what this Moab has laboured for upon his high places,” that is, what he has deserved for the labour of the carnal works of the Law, which he considered righteous and exceedingly lofty, “he shall enter his sanctuaries to entreat,” that is, he shall return to his heart and consider the intention for which he performed these carnal works of the Law, so that from it he may seek mercy from the Judge whose Law he thought he had kept. “And he shall not prevail” in entreating, because, recognizing that he did not perform these works by faith in Christ, he will not dare to ask pardon from him whose faith and grace he was unwilling to possess in his works. Thus far he has expounded in many ways the wounds of those who “rejoice upon walls of baked brick.”

[Col. 0182A] Then, he says, “this is the word which the Lord spoke concerning Moab,” that is, concerning the Jewish people, “from that time”: that is, from the time when he gave them the Law, through Moses having foretold to them all these wounds; and now also through me or the other prophets he has spoken, saying: “Within three years,” etc. The three years are three periods: from Moses to David, from David to the Babylonian captivity, and from the captivity to Christ. During these the Jewish people served God not as a son but as a hired labourer, because on account of the carnal observance of the Law it did not await an eternal inheritance but sought temporal wages. Therefore, while for their impieties they were frequently taken captive and slain by enemies throughout these three periods, so that often few remained out of many, [Col. 0182B] within three years their glory amid all their great multitude was taken away, like the glory of a hired labourer’s year. And after these three years had passed, following Jerusalem’s overthrow, there remained in it as after a vintage a small cluster and not a numerous one: small in size and not numerous in number. These are the wounds of those “who rejoice upon walls of baked brick.” But, now that the exposition of this vision is finished, I think it should be added that this burden has been placed third after the two preceding ones on account of these three years, or because of what was said above: “They are girded with sackcloth at its crossroads” (above, XV, 3), or because of some other hidden mystery whatsoever. It follows:

## CHAPTER XVII

**VERSE 1.**—“The burden of Damascus. Behold, Damascus [Col. 0182C] shall cease to be a city, and shall be like a heap of stones in ruin.”

Damascus is interpreted “cup of blood,” or “drinking blood,” or “offering blood.” What, then, is expressed by Damascus except the cruelty of persecutors? And fittingly the burden of persecutors is placed in the fourth rank, because the Church endures four kinds of persecutors. For it suffers persecutions from Jews, Gentiles, heretics, and false believers. Moreover, in the four quarters of the world the people of the elect are afflicted by those opposed to divine religion. Thus Daniel also comprehends all persecutors of the faithful under the form of four beasts, saying: “Four great beasts, different from one another, came up from the sea: the first like a lioness, the second resembling a bear, the third like a leopard, the fourth terrible, wonderful, and exceedingly strong” (Dan. VII, 3 ff.). And the angel in the Apocalypse: “He cried with a loud voice to the four angels to whom it was given to harm the earth and the sea, saying: Do not harm the earth, nor the sea, nor the trees, until we have sealed the servants of God upon their foreheads” (Rev. VII, 2). The burden of persecutors is appropriately in the fourth place, because the four angels whose office is to harm are restrained from injury, and in Daniel the power of the four beasts is taken away. Hence it is said here as well: “Behold, Damascus shall cease to be a city and shall be like a heap of stones in ruin.” For Damascus shall cease to be a city because wicked men, murderers, and persecutors of the servants of God, swiftly losing power [Col. 0183A] and dignity and kingdom, shall be reduced to nothing. And, when overthrown, it shall be like a heap of stones in the ruin of a city, when their bodies have been brought down to the earth by the sentence of death.

The calling of the Gentiles may also be understood by Damascus: they were previously fed by cruelty and blood, but after they have believed in Christ they will cease to be a city of their former manner of life. “And it shall be like a heap of stones in ruin.” For just as heaps of stones scattered throughout fields are carried together into one mound, so from all nations a heap of believers is to be gathered in the ruin of the Jews: they falling, and we rising. It follows:

**VERSE 2.**—“The deserted cities of Aroer shall be for flocks; they shall rest there, and there shall be none to terrify them.”

[Col. 0183B] We say that Aroer means tamarisks. Tamarisks are small, fruitless trees, always exceedingly green and very bitter, growing in deserts. And what is represented by tamarisks except men who are bitter and fruitless and cling to this world through desire? By flocks he means the assemblies of God’s sheep, of whom it is said through Zechariah that “the Lord visited his flock, the house of Judah” (Zech. X, 3). And Ezekiel says: “I will multiply them as a flock of men, as a holy flock, as the flock of Jerusalem” (Ezek. XXXVI, 37). Therefore “the cities of Aroer,” that is, of the tamarisks, “shall be deserted for these flocks,” because where fruitless and bitter unbelievers lived, there the people of believers shall remain. “And there shall be none to terrify them,” because persecutors shall fail, whether removed by death [Col. 0183C] or converted to God. It follows:

**VERSE 3.**—“And help shall cease from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus; and the remnant of Syria shall be like the glory of the children of Israel, saith the Lord of hosts.”

“Help shall cease from Ephraim,” that is, from the multitude of Gentile peoples. For Ephraim is called “fruitfulness.” “And the kingdom shall cease from Damascus,” because the persecutors of the saints shall lose all the power which they possessed in the world. Or sin shall no longer reign in them, but they shall serve righteousness, and worshippers of religion shall obtain kingdom and glory throughout the world. “And the remnant of Syria,” that is, those from paganism [Col. 0183D] who have been converted to God, shall be “like the glory of the children of Israel,” because they shall be equal to believers from the circumcision.

Or the faithless people of the Jews may be signified by Ephraim, and the rule and headship of the Gentiles by Damascus. For Damascus is the metropolis of Syria. “Help shall therefore cease from Ephraim,” because no one shall help the Jews against Titus. “And the kingdom [shall cease] from Damascus,” that is, from pagan emperors, because all the princes of the world shall be Christians, and the enemies of religion shall be exterminated. “And the remnant of Syria,” that is, those who among the Gentiles persisted in unbelief, shall be “like the glory of the children of Israel,” that is, like the shame of the Jews, because those who have not believed—Gentiles and Jews alike—shall come to the utmost shame and rejection. For he has used “glory” ironically for shame and disgrace. It follows.

**VERSE 4.**—“And it shall be in that day: the glory of Jacob shall be made thin, and his fat flesh shall waste away.”

**VERSE 5.**—“And it shall be as one gathering what remains in harvest, and his arm shall gather ears of grain; and it shall be as one seeking ears in the valley of Rephaim.”

**VERSE 6.**—“And there shall be left in him as it were a cluster, and as the shaking of an olive tree: two or three olives upon the top of a branch, or four or five of its fruit upon its highest boughs, saith the Lord God of Israel.”

On that day when the Gospel is preached, the glory of Jacob—that is, of the Jewish people which wished to supplant Christ through death—shall be diminished and become feeble [Col. 0184B], because the Jews shall be dishonoured throughout the whole world; and their fat flesh shall waste away. Having no prophets, no signs and miracles, no dignity of the Temple, the whole body of their people shall wither and be reduced to nothing.

And just as a few ears of grain and olives commonly remain in a field or on a tree, so few shall remain in Israel. And whereas it is said of the calling of the Gentiles, “The harvest indeed is great, but the labourers few” (Matt. IX, 37), those poor remnants of the harvest, saved through the apostles, shall gather the rarest ears not on mountains but in the valley of Rephaim—that is, in the valley of giants, who are the scribes and Pharisees; that is, in the lowliness of the letter. For Rephaim means “giants.”

The Jewish people heard: “The Lord called thee a fruitful olive tree” [Col. 0184C] (Jer. XI, 16); yet Christ, being hungry, scarcely found in it a few, that is, two. Now the two and three olives, and the four and five, may be understood as the twelve apostles—that is, the twelve whom the Gospel, together with Paul and Barnabas, records. Or understand the two and three olives as Peter, John, and James, who saw the Lord transfigured on the mountain and entered with him to raise the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue. The four and five, however, make up the other nine apostles, who, certainly according to a diversity of graces unknown to us, were divided into four and five olives in order to show in themselves the number of the Gospels and the books of the Law, as preachers of both Testaments.

Or, according to the historical sense: “And this Jacob shall be like one gathering what remains in harvest,” because while he is being destroyed by Vespasian, he will seek out and gather for resistance those who still survive. “And his arm shall gather ears of grain,” because with whatever strength he can he will gather individual Jews. “And he shall be as one seeking ears in the valley of Rephaim,” that is, of giants, because, Jerusalem having been captured by Titus, he will seek for some Jewish remnants in the humiliation of his proud leaders, who considered themselves strong like giants. For just as the rarest ears remain behind the backs of reapers, so the very fewest Jewish remnants shall remain after Jerusalem’s overthrow.

[Col. 0184D] “And its fruit shall remain in him,” that is, his posterity [Col. 0185A], “like one cluster” after the grape-gatherers, or “like the shaking of an olive tree, with two or three olives remaining upon the top of its branch, or four or five olives upon its highest bough.” For when olives are shaken from an olive tree, two or three, or four, commonly remain at its summit or upon the top of some branch. So too the Jewish remnant was small after Jerusalem’s destruction. But after the extermination of the Jews, the conversion of the Gentiles is added, when it says:

**VERSE 7.**—“On that day man shall incline toward his Maker, and his eyes shall look to the Holy One of Israel.”

**VERSE 8.**—“And he shall not incline toward the altars which his hands have made, nor toward what his fingers [Col. 0185B] have fashioned.”

This is plain. It follows: “He shall not look to groves and shrines.” Groves are called wooded and shady places in which, because of their pleasantness, people placed their idols and indulged every pleasure before their altars. Shrines, moreover, were temples so called from washing; either because they thought that there they were *delui* (“washed,” that is, purified) from their sins by a multitude of sacrifices [Note: [Col. 0185D] Cod. G.: *dilui*, “to be washed/cleansed”], or because streams were not far away, in which they washed themselves and washed the victims. Then he returns again to the Jewish people:

**VERSE 9.**—“On that day the cities of his strength shall be abandoned, like ploughlands and crops which were abandoned before the children of Israel.”

For just as formerly, before the children of Israel in the times of Joshua [Col. 0185C], the Canaanites abandoned their regions, so now the Jews shall abandon their cities before the Romans. And it adds: “And it shall be desolate.”

**VERSE 10.**—“Because thou hast forgotten God thy Saviour, and hast not remembered thy strong helper.”

For because this nation consigned to forgetfulness God, who had always been accustomed to help it with a mighty hand, it was abandoned by him into the hands of the Romans; and its spiritual powers were also abandoned into the hands of internal and invisible enemies. For it follows:

“Therefore thou shalt plant a faithful planting, and shalt sow a foreign shoot.” A faithful planting is when one plants a vineyard and himself gathers its fruit. But a planting is unfaithful, and a foreign shoot, when what one plants or sows [Col. 0185D] is not gathered by him, but enemies plunder it. Therefore, when it says, “Therefore thou shalt plant a faithful planting,” it should be understood ironically. And what is added, “And thou shalt sow a foreign shoot,” must be read affirmatively. Whatever virtue this people plants in the field of its heart, and whatever good work it sows, it shall obtain no fruit from it; rather, malignant spirits shall devour it.

Or: thou shalt plant a faithful planting, preaching one God, and thou shalt sow a foreign shoot, not receiving the Son, who is consubstantial with the Father, but sowing blasphemy against him. Therefore there shall be not a grape but a wild grape [Col. 0186A] of unbelief in thy planting. And although thy seed at first flourishes under the appearance of religion, thou shalt nevertheless receive no fruit from it on the day of inheritance. It follows:

**VERSE 11.**—“On the day of thy planting, a wild grape; and in the morning thy seed shall blossom: the harvest has been taken away on the day of inheritance, and thou shalt grieve bitterly.” [Note: [Col. 0185D] What follows from here, from the Crucensis codex, is lacking in the Garstensis codex [Col. 0186D] throughout, down to verse 7 of the following chapter.]

He plants who builds virtues in himself or in another. But Judaea produces a wild grape on the day of her planting, because while she supposes herself to be planting virtues, she performs or teaches the uncultivated works of paganism. For what is more pagan than slaughtering a goat and sacrificing an ox? Such indeed are the sacrifices of idols. Therefore, while Judaea teaches or performs actions of this kind as works of virtue, on the day of planting she has a wild grape [Col. 0186B].

Our seed likewise is the good work which we now do, so that in the future we may reap the fruit of its recompense. But the seed of Jews or hypocrites blossoms in the morning, because from the good things they do they seek human approval and passing rewards; of them the Judge says: “Amen I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI, 2). Hence it is added here: “The harvest has been taken away on the day of inheritance,” that is, thou shalt find no fruit on the day of recompense, because it now vanishes in the flower of the mist of human praise and lowly desire.

“And thou shalt grieve bitterly,” because elsewhere it is said: “When the master of the house has entered and shut the door, you will begin to stand outside and knock at the door, saying, ‘Lord, [Col. 0186C] Lord, open to us’; and he will answer and say to you, ‘I do not know whence you are; depart from me, workers of iniquity.’ There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Luke XIII, 25). Thus the seed of the five foolish virgins blossomed in the morning; and on the day of inheritance they grieved bitterly, their harvest having been taken away, because they did not keep “oil in their vessels” (Matt. XXV). When the bridegroom came, their lamps having gone out, they remained outside. After the rejection and calamity of the Jews, I think that the advent of Antichrist is added, whom his hosts await.

**VERSE 12.**—“Woe to the multitude of many peoples, like the roaring of the sea; and the tumult of crowds, like the sound of many waters!”

**VERSE 13.**—“The peoples shall roar like the sound [Col. 0186D] of flooding waters.”

For we read in Daniel that, like a tempest, “the king of the north shall come” (Dan. XI, 15), who is Antichrist, “against the king of the south” (ibid.), that is, Egypt, with chariots and horsemen and a great fleet; and he shall enter lands, crush them, and pass through them. Of his destruction it is added: “And he shall rebuke him, and he shall flee far away, and he shall be carried away like mountain dust before the wind, and like a whirlwind before the storm.”

**VERSE 14.**—“At eventide, and behold, trouble; by morning it shall not remain.”

For according to Daniel, “he shall set up his tent upon the glorious and holy mountain” (this is the Mount [Col. 0187A] of Olives), “and he shall come to its summit, and none shall help him” (Dan. XI, 45). As the Apostle says, “the Lord Jesus shall slay [him] with the Spirit of his mouth and destroy [him] by the brightness of his coming” (II Thess. II, 8). The Judge, when he comes, shall rebuke him, as holy Job also signifies, saying: “Who shall reprove his way before him, and who shall repay him for what he has done?” (Job XXI, 31). “And he shall flee far away” from the Judge’s face, “and shall be carried away like mountain dust before the wind, and like a whirlwind before the storm,” when, as it is written, “he shall drive him from light into darkness, and shall remove him from the world” (Job XVIII, 18). For “a fire is before him, and a mighty storm round about him” (Ps. XLIX [L], 4).

Therefore this son of perdition shall be carried away by the whirlwind of that storm [Col. 0187B] and cast down into Gehenna. At eventide—that is, at the end of the world—he will still seek to exercise tyranny; and behold, sudden trouble shall come upon him. By morning—that is, at the time of the resurrection of all—he shall be visited, and shall not remain.

Or it may have been said of pagans who persecuted the Church: “Woe to the multitude,” etc. “The peoples shall roar” in the displays of theatrical luxury, in the cruelty of the amphitheatre, and in the frenzies of the circus: “like the sound of flooding waters,” when with one voice of impiety they blaspheme and lead Christians to the lion, and do other things of this kind. But while they rage like the sea, the Lord shall rebuke the author of their sedition and drive him away from them. And just as dust stirred up [Col. 0187C] upon mountains is carried away more violently the higher it is, and just as a whirlwind which rises from the earth in a sudden storm is borne aloft, so he too shall be snatched away and separated from the people of believers, and shall flee lest he be bound in the abyss. And when the day of consummation, which is evening, arrives, then shall be his tribulation, as he recognizes his sins; and at the time of morning—that is, on the day of resurrection—he shall not remain:

“This is the portion of those who have laid us waste, and the lot of those who plunder us.” Church-destroyers acquire this portion and lot for themselves: that they may be punished with so terrible a destruction; but especially the followers of Antichrist, concerning whom he adds again:

## CHAPTER XVIII

**VERSE 1.**—“Woe to the land of the cymbal of wings, which is [Col. 0187D] beyond the rivers of Ethiopia!”

**VERSE 2.**—“Which sends envoys by sea and in vessels of papyrus upon the waters. Go, swift angels, to a nation torn away and rent in pieces, to a people terrible, after whom there is none other: a nation waiting and trampled down, whose land rivers have plundered.”

For just as incarnate Truth chose poor, unlearned, and simple persons in his preaching, so, conversely, that condemned man whom the apostate angel will assume at the end of the world will choose to preach falsehood those who are shrewd and double-minded and possess the wisdom of this world. Therefore it is rightly said now: “Woe to the land of the cymbal of wings,” etc. The land to which “Woe” is spoken is principally that condemned man [Col. 0188A] who is called the clatter of wings because those who soar aloft in the height of thought through pride make that perverse man resound by preaching him. This land is rightly said to be “beyond the rivers of Ethiopia.” For Ethiopia produces a black people. And because this world brings forth sinful human beings, it gives birth, like Ethiopia, to a black people. But the land to which “Woe” is spoken is said to be beyond Ethiopia’s rivers because that condemned man is wicked with such boundlessness that he surpasses the sins of all sinners. “Which sends envoys by sea,” because he scatters his preachers throughout the world. Their manner of being sent is fittingly added when it says:

“In vessels of papyrus upon the waters.” Paper is made from papyrus. What, then, is signified by papyrus except secular [Col. 0188B] learning? Therefore vessels of papyrus are the hearts of secular teachers. Thus, to send envoys in vessels of papyrus upon the waters is to place his preaching in the minds of the carnally wise and summon peoples flowing away into sin. He therefore sends envoys into the sea, saying: “Go, swift angels,” that is, my messengers, “to the Jewish nation torn away from its own soil and rent by enemies; to a people once terrible, which exercised God’s authority, after which there was none other,” that is, a people to whose power no other was comparable; “a nation awaiting” the Saviour’s coming, and again awaiting Antichrist after rejecting the Saviour, and meanwhile trampled down by enemies.

The rivers that plundered its land may be understood as Titus and Vespasian with their armies [Col. 0188C], because above he said: “The strong and many waters of the river are the king of the Assyrians and all his glory” (above, VIII, 7).
