After the persecution of this adversary, the day of judgment shall come, as the Lord says: “Immediately after the tribulation of those days, the sun shall be darkened, the moon shall not give its light, and the stars shall fall from heaven” (Matt. XXIV, 29). Hence it follows here:

**VERSE 3.**—“All inhabitants of the world, you who dwell upon the earth, when the sign has been raised upon the mountains.”

**VERSE 4.**—“You shall see, and you shall hear the blast of the trumpet.”

For all inhabitants of the world shall see the sign [Col. 0188D] of the cross and hear the trumpet’s blast, because “the powers of heaven shall be shaken, and then the sign of the Son of Man shall appear in heaven; and then all the tribes of the earth shall mourn, and they shall see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty. And he shall send his angels with a trumpet and a great voice, and they shall gather his elect from the four winds and from the farthest bounds of the heavens to their limits” (ibid.). Therefore he shall raise the sign upon the mountains—that is, in the heights—because it shall appear amid the hosts of heavenly powers in the clouds. And the trumpet’s blast shall be heard: “For the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall rise” (I Cor. XV, 52). But because the Judge observes each person’s works, the prophet adds:

“Because the Lord says this to me: I shall rest, etc. [Col. 0189A], and I shall consider in my place, as the clear light of noon, and as a cloud of dew on the day of harvest.” What indeed is God’s place but the heart of angels or of elect human beings? For the Apostle says, “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (I Cor. III, 17). When he calls the incorrigible to repentance, he may be said to labour. Thus he says: “I have laboured in bearing with them” (above, I, 14). But when, leaving sinners in their wickedness, he dwells among the elect alone—not now persuading the wicked to repentance but preserving them for future judgment—he finds rest, as it were, after labour. Therefore he now says: “I shall rest in my place,” that is, I shall dwell only in the heart of saints, where I have rest; nor shall I labour further in correcting the perverse, because I am wearied in vain among them. And thus I shall rest [Col. 0189B] “as a cloud of dew on the day of harvest.” For just as a cloud of dew is most welcome to weary reapers, so refreshing to me shall be the relief which I find in the minds of the elect, weary from the wickedness of the ungodly, whose minds are scorched by earthly desires. Nor without reason is the Lord compared to a reaper, because, as crops from a field, he daily cuts people off from this world by the sentence of death. “And I shall consider,” he says, each person’s actions as manifestly “as the clear light of noon.” For now the Judge, who is hidden, observes without interruption everything that we do, so that one day he may render what is just for these things. It follows:

**VERSE 5.**—“For before the harvest it has wholly blossomed, and unripe perfection has sprouted [Note: [Col. 0189D] Vulgate: ‘shall sprout.’]; and its little branches [Col. 0189C] shall be cut off with sickles, and whatever is left shall be cut off and shaken out.”

**VERSE 6.**—“And they shall be left together to the birds of the mountains and to the beasts of the earth; and the birds shall spend the whole summer upon it, and all the beasts of the earth shall winter upon it.”

Just as a crop or a tree which flowers sooner than it ought does not bear fruit at the proper time, so one who does what he does not for the expectation of heavenly recompense but for the desire of worldly things cannot bear the fruit of a good work, because he is emptied by flowering before the time. For the flower of a future work is the thought which precedes it. But one who, in the work which he intends to perform, seeks not eternal recompense but temporal reward, flowers before the harvest [Col. 0189D], because the flower of his thought does not sprout toward the harvest of the life to come. For the harvest is the consummation of the age. And his unripe perfection sprouts who, before the last day, considers the things he has done sufficient for himself, as though already perfect.

Therefore, as the end of the world approaches, it is said that it has wholly “blossomed before the harvest, and unripe perfection has sprouted,” because then especially the human race shall love present things and neglect to await those to come. Its little branch—that is, of the world or of the human race as of a certain tree—is each individual person; the sickles are the judgments of the heavenly Judge. And the little branches of this tree [Col. 0190A] are cut off with sickles when the Judge’s judgments sever individual persons from this life. And whatever remains shall be cut off when the entire world comes to an end together. And, once cut off, they shall be shaken out, because in judgment they shall be examined and tested.

After those who had flowered before the harvest have been condemned in judgment, “they shall be left to the birds of the mountains,” that is, to evil spirits dwelling in the hearts of the proud, “and to the beasts of the earth,” that is, to savage demons who trample sinners—or the earth. For the Lord indicates that birds are demons when He says of the seeds: “Another fell beside the way, and was trampled down, and the birds of heaven devoured it” (Luke 8:5). Explaining this below, He says: “Those beside the way are they who hear; then [Col. 0190B] the devil comes and takes the word from their heart” (ibid., v. 12).

The beasts likewise are those same demons who, at the time of death, rush with the violence of cruelty to seize the souls of sinners; against them it is said: “Do not deliver to the beasts the souls that trust in you” (Ps. 73 [LXX 74]:19). The mountains are all the proud, because “the mountains shall melt like wax before the Lord” (Ps. 96:5); while the earth is the sinner, who deserved to hear: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19). Thus the birds of the mountains and the beasts of the earth, to whom these shaken-off persons are left, are evil spirits; but the everlasting summer is the kingdom of God after judgment. For He compared it to summer, saying: “Look at the fig trees and all the trees: when they now put forth fruit of themselves, you know [Col. 0190C] that summer is near; so also you, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of heaven is near” (Mark 21:29).

Winter, however, is the condemnation of the reprobate, because “there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 8:12). For because of excessive cold teeth are accustomed to gnash. And Job says: “Let him pass from the waters of snow to excessive heat” (Job 24:19). For snow-water is extremely cold. “Therefore the birds shall be upon him in perpetual summer,” because, when the righteous shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father, then evil spirits will burn the bundles of tares.

“And all the beasts of the earth shall winter upon him.” For all the most savage demons, who feel absolutely no warmth of charity, will lie numb, constrained by the cold of everlasting [Col. 0190D] condemnation; contracted upon them, they will lie amid punishments and be punished together with them. After this follows the conversion of Israel, which will take place under Elijah:

**VERSE 7.**—“At that time a gift shall be brought to the Lord of hosts from a people torn apart and rent, from a terrible people, after whom there has been [Vulgate: was] no other, from a nation waiting and trampled underfoot, whose land rivers have plundered, to the place of the name of the Lord of hosts, Mount Zion.”

That is, to the Church. For then the Hebrew people will bring to Christ, in the Church where confession of His name dwells, the welcome gift of faith and good works.

Or thus: the branches which are useless shall be cut off with sickles, as the Lord says: “I am the true vine and my Father is the husbandman. Every branch in me not bearing fruit, He shall take it away” (John 15:1). And those which have been cut off shall be left to the birds and beasts of the earth, that is, to demons, so that whoever has been cut off and chosen by God, and separated from His body, which is the Church, may become in both summer and winter—that is, in prosperity and adversity—the dwelling-place of birds and beasts. And just as those who are unfruitful in the Church are cut off and cast away, lest a little leaven corrupt the whole mass, so conversely it may happen that those deceived [Col. 0191B] by heretical error, torn away from God and rent apart, dreadful because of blasphemy, vainly awaiting lies, trampled by demons and scattered in various directions by rivers, may come to the Church.

## CHAPTER XIX

**VERSE 1.**—“The burden of Egypt. Behold, the Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud and shall enter Egypt; and its images shall be moved at His presence, and the heart of Egypt shall melt in its midst.”

This burden is also in the fifth degree, and it is so called here because “there shall be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the language of Canaan” (below, v. 18), so that we may observe that the subject now is those who are devoted to the five bodily senses. For Egypt, interpreted as “tribulation” or “darkness,” signifies the world [Col. 0191C] full of tribulations and distresses, or the Gentile world covered in the darkness of errors. These things said concerning Egypt must be referred to the coming of the Savior, the reconciliation of the world, and the conversion of the Gentiles.

“For behold, the Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud.” We ought to understand the light cloud either literally as the Lord’s body, because it was light—that is, weighed down by no sin—or certainly as His Virgin Mother, burdened by no human seed. Therefore the Lord ascended upon a light cloud and came into Egypt when, assuming the flesh of our humanity, He appeared in the world without the weight of sin.

Or we may understand the light cloud to be the apostles, relieved of every earthly possession, of whom it is said: “Who are these that fly like clouds?” (Isa. 60:8). Seated upon them, the Lord entered Egypt, because through them He came to the Gentiles. And the images of Egypt were shaken at His presence, because, once truth had been known, errors were put to flight and idols were destroyed wherever God became known to the Gentiles. And the heart of Egypt—that is, the dark mind of those who persisted in unbelief—wasted away in excessive grief when they saw the worship of idols being abolished. It follows:

**VERSE 2.**—“And I shall set Egyptians against Egyptians, and a man shall fight against his brother, and a man against his friend; city against city, kingdom against kingdom.”

The preaching of the Lord Jesus did this throughout the whole world, [Col. 0192A] while some received faith and others attempted utterly to oppose it. Hence He Himself had foretold the same thing, saying: “Do not think that I have come to bring peace upon the earth. I have not come to bring peace but a sword. For I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man’s enemies shall be those of his own household” (Matt. 10:34). It follows:

**VERSE 3.**—“And the spirit of Egypt shall be broken in its inward parts, and I shall cast down its counsel.”

The spirit of Egypt, which before had been whole in evil—that is, the will of the Gentiles—was broken, being divided, some wishing to believe and others refusing. And the counsel of the wicked, by which they sought cunningly to attack the faith by stirring up persecutions, was cast down, because faith endures and they have been destroyed. It follows:

“And they shall consult their images, their diviners, python-spirits, and soothsayers.” The unbelievers anxiously inquired both of their gods and of their wise men why such things had now arisen in the world: that the human race, abandoning its old custom, should embrace the worship of a new religion. It follows:

**VERSE 4.**—“And I shall deliver Egypt into the hand of cruel masters, and a strong king shall rule over them, says the Lord God of hosts.”

He is called cruel who, striking strictly, does not spare. Therefore, if Egypt is here understood in those who are corrected, [Col. 0192C] what is signified by the title “cruel masters” except the pious severity of teachers of the Church, who, burning with zeal for God, do not soften the sins of those subject to them? Or let us understand as cruel in this place those who strike sins strictly and spare no one in punishing offences. For blessed Job himself, when afflicted, said to God: “You have been changed to cruelty toward me, and by the hardness of your hand you oppose me” (Job 30:21). If therefore a holy man did not fear to call God cruel because He did not spare him, why should we not call the leaders of holy Church benignly cruel, when they strike the faults of offenders with the severity of mercy? Egypt—that is, this world—is therefore delivered to such cruel masters in order that it may be disciplined under their correction.

[Col. 0192D] And the strong king is Christ, their ruler. But if we understand Egypt in the reprobate, Egypt is delivered into the hands of cruel masters, because those who will not be converted are handed over to be possessed more fiercely by evil spirits. Yet, lest the demons themselves rage beyond measure, the strong King, the Lord Jesus, rules them. After this he adds, concerning false teachings and how they were to be reduced to nothing:

**VERSE 5.**—“And water shall dry up from the sea, and the river shall be laid waste and dried up.”

**VERSE 6.**—“And the rivers shall fail; the streams of the embankments shall become thin and dry up. Reed and rush shall wither.”

**VERSE 7.**—“The channel of the stream shall be laid bare from its source, [Col. 0193A] and every irrigated seed-field shall dry up, wither, and be no more.”

For what is the water of the sea but knowledge of secular teaching? And what is the river of this water but the overflowing current of carnal wisdom? The water shall therefore dry up from the sea, because worldly teaching shall fail from the age. And the river of human wisdom shall be dried up, because God will make foolish the wisdom of this world.

And the rivers of diverse teachings, which flowed through the world, shall fail. “And the streams of the embankments shall be dried up,” that is, carnal forms of knowledge shall be dried up from human hearts. For one who endeavors to carry a stream over an embankment digs away earth in order to bring water to a place toward which its natural force did not direct it. Similarly, one who strives to pour the little stream of his knowledge into another’s heart digs deeply into that heart and casts out its thoughts, like earth that prevented the little stream from running. This is how Gentile teachers acted, so that they might set the knowledge of their error in the hearts of hearers without obstruction. But now, through evangelical preaching, such streams of embankments have become thin and dried up.

What, then, is signified by the reed, with which writing was formerly done, except the skill of writers? What by the rush except the freshness of hearers? Thus reed and rush shall wither: that is, teacher and disciple of earthly wisdom, when the faith of Christ begins to flourish.

The channel of the stream of secular knowledge shall be laid bare from its source—that is, from the devil’s suggestion—because that ancient deceiver will no longer pour into them the water of deceitful wisdom when it has been dried up by Christ’s grace. [Col. 0193C] Hence Jeremiah also said concerning Babylon or its king: “I shall make her sea a desert and dry up her spring” (Jer. 50:36). But the seed was irrigated while the teaching of error was moistened by the devil’s suggestions. Therefore every “irrigated seed shall dry up, wither, and be no more,” because the devil’s irrigating spring shall be stopped up and the teaching of the world which it watered shall fail. But meanwhile let us hear what shall happen to teachers of this kind. It follows:

**VERSE 8.**—“And fishermen shall mourn, and all who cast a hook into the river shall lament; and those who spread a net over the surface of the water shall wither [Vulgate: become bitter].”

**VERSE 9.**—“Those who worked flax, combing and weaving fine fabrics, shall be confounded.”

**VERSE 10.**—“And its irrigated places shall be languishing: all who made pools to catch fish.”

For what is signified by fishermen but philosophers and others of that sort, deceiving miserable human beings in this world as though they were fish in the sea? For concerning the catch to be made by evangelical preaching, it was said to the apostles: “Come after me, and I shall make you fishers of men” (Matt. 4:19). So here too we understand fishers of men, but in an evil sense. What is signified by the river but the human race, which flows from birth to its end and, like water, runs onward from the fluidity of flesh until it reaches its appointed limit? And what is signified by the hook but the deceptive teaching of philosophers and poets? For on a hook bait is shown and the barb hidden. So too in Gentile teaching the sweetness of words is displayed while the poison of deception is concealed. They therefore cast a hook into the river who offered the teaching of deception to the human race. What, indeed, is expressed by their net except false preaching? The intertwined words of preachers are like nets, which do not easily let go those whom they catch; hence nets are called, as it were, “holders” (*retinentia*). They spread nets upon the surface of the water who scattered the preaching of falsehood over the heart of the people. For the water is the people. Therefore these fishermen, who formerly rejoiced while catching many, mourned and grieved in the times of evangelical preaching, when they could no longer catch anyone.

[Col. 0194B] “And,” he says, “the philosophers who worked flax—that is, more subtle teaching—shall be confounded.” For they treated many subtle matters concerning virtues and vices, the more hidden natures and causes of things, and sometimes even concerning God; and all their teaching was more refined than that of the poets. They combed fine materials when they made divisions and drew out and discarded less subtle matters as though they were tow, as happens in dialectical divisions. They wove fine materials when they formed acute arguments, connected propositions to propositions, and filled books. But all these shall be confounded when the Savior’s teaching shines upon the Gentiles. And the irrigated places of this river—that is, human hearts, which were watered by secular teaching—shall become languishing and withered, [Col. 0194C] because they will lose the verdure of love for present things, that they may become verdant in love for things to come. They “made pools to catch fish” who dug and constructed teachings of error for the deception of human beings. It follows:

**VERSE 11.**—“The princes of Tanis are foolish; the wise counselors of Pharaoh have given foolish counsel. How will you say to Pharaoh: I am a son of the wise, a son of ancient kings?”

**VERSE 12.**—“Where now are your wise men? Let them announce to you and declare what the Lord of hosts has devised concerning Egypt.”

Tanis, said to mean “commanding low things” or “a low command,” is the teaching of the wise of this world. For teachers [Col. 0194D] of secular learning know how to command only low and base matters, which are to be observed for this present life. The precepts of heavenly teaching, on the other hand, are lofty and sublime, because they were given for the sake of the kingdoms of heaven. But the princes of Tanis—that is, of secular knowledge—were foolish, not knowing how to foresee future things. Pharaoh, however, is the devil, as Ezekiel indicates when he says: “Behold, I am against you, Pharaoh king of Egypt, great dragon, who lie in the midst of your rivers” (Dan. 29:3). Hence Pharaoh is interpreted “he stripped him” or “he scattered him,” because in the first man the devil stripped the human race of the garment of immortality and the clothing of righteousness; he scattered its mind from unity of thought and dispersed it among various desires.

And who are the counselors of this Pharaoh but demons, [Col. 0195A] who give foolish counsel when they suggest evil things to human beings, as though advising rationally? Or let us understand as his counselors philosophers, priests of idols, and heretics, who gave foolish counsel to the rulers of this age—namely, that they should persecute the Church and labor to extinguish the faith of God. Or they gave counsel to Pharaoh himself, because there are certain people so ready to devise evil that in their inventions they seem to outrun the devil’s cunning. Thus they gave counsel to the Evil One, that he might fill the world with doctrines of error, in order to hold everyone more firmly entangled; for they were so swift in sowing errors that they seem rather to suggest such things to the devil than to learn them from him. For when could even the devil [Col. 0195B] have devised the things Arius invented? When could he have fabricated what other inventors of errors discovered? They therefore gave counsel to Pharaoh, but their counsel was foolish, because errors have now been destroyed, the world has now been illuminated by knowledge of truth, and it has been freed from Pharaoh’s yoke.

“O wise men of the world,” he says, “how will each of you say to Pharaoh—that is, to the prince of this world—when the apostles preach: ‘I am a son of wise men and of ancient kings,’ that is, how will you, in helping Satan your father, boast that you are children of the ancient wise men who discovered these doctrines of error, which you are unable to defend against the preachers of the Gospel? Where [Col. 0195C] now, O Pharaoh, are your wise men? Let them tell you, if they can, what the Lord has devised concerning Egypt—that is, concerning the Gentile people: namely, to destroy all errors, make the light of truth known to all, and set all mortals free.”

Or thus: foolish shall be the princes of Tanis, which means “a low command.” For all heretics teach a height contrary to humility; they pull people down to the depths and are princes of a low and abased command. The counselors of Pharaoh also, who is king of Egypt and rightly “the scatterer,” being divided and separating into various parts, shall be convicted of having given foolish counsel when the Lord destroys and rejects the wisdom of the wise. Heretics, moreover, are accustomed to say to this their king—that is, to their swollen opinion—“We are sons of wise men, who from the beginning handed down to us apostolic doctrine. We are sons of ancient kings,” who are called kings among philosophers, “and we possess knowledge of the Scriptures joined to secular knowledge.” They ask this king where his wise men are, those who despised ecclesiastical simplicity. It follows:

**VERSE 13.**—“The princes of Tanis have become foolish; the princes of Memphis have withered; they have deceived Egypt, the corner of the peoples [Note: [Col. 0195D] Alternatively: ‘its peoples.’].”

**VERSE 14.**—“The Lord has mingled in its midst [Col. 0196A] a spirit of dizziness; and they have made Egypt err in all its work, as a drunken man staggers and vomits.”

**VERSE 15.**—“And Egypt shall have no work which head and tail, the one bending and the one restraining, might do.”

Since God made foolish the wisdom of this world, the princes of Tanis also—that is, of that same worldly wisdom, which commands low and earthly things—have become foolish; and the princes of Memphis, that is, teachers of vain speech, have withered. For Memphis is interpreted “from the mouth.” They have deceived Egypt—that is, the world, full of the duplicity of deceitful and impure minds—the corner of the peoples. For what is signified by a corner (since walls are always double at a corner) except impure hearts which, [Col. 0196B] fleeing the simplicity of truth, in some fashion turn back upon themselves through the perversity of duplicity? To them James openly says: “Purify your hearts, you double-minded” (Jas. 4:8). Therefore he fittingly calls the world or the Gentile world the corner of the peoples, because among all peoples and nations there was this duplicity and this corner of deceit.

“The Lord has mingled in its midst a spirit of dizziness,” that is, of error, because, in a just judgment, He hid the light of His knowledge and allowed a spirit of error to enter it. And the aforesaid princes—that is, teachers of perverse doctrines—made Egypt err in all its work, as a drunken man who vomits staggers, because, taking away its reason, they enslaved it to idolatry. For one who is drunk and vomits is so deprived of rational sense and so confused or alienated in mind that he does not know what he does or suffers. But it was carried away by dizziness, so that it did not understand the evils it worked; and it vomited forth the excessive surfeit of its drunkenness—that is, the filth of error with which it was filled—through its mouth, while it praised idols and polluted the ears of hearers and minds, like the surrounding air, with a most foul odor.

And when the preachers of grace have come, Egypt—that is, the part of those who remain in unbelief—will have no work [Col. 0196D] by which it can restrain them. The aforesaid princes made head and tail—that is, first and last—err: “the one bending,” that is, one holding others under discipline; and “the one restraining,” that is, one ruling subjects. It follows:

**VERSE 16.**—“On that day Egypt shall be like women; they shall be astonished and afraid at the presence of the shaking of the hand of the Lord of hosts, which He Himself shall shake over it.”

**VERSE 17.**—“And the land of Judah shall be to Egypt an occasion of festivity [Note: [Col. 0196D] Alternatively: ‘of terror.’]; everyone who remembers it shall be afraid at the presence of the counsel of the Lord of hosts, which He has devised against it.”

Egypt—that is, the Gentile world—will be fearful, that is, weak, like women. And the Egyptians—that is, the Gentiles—will be astonished and fear because of their iniquities at the shaking of the Lord’s hand; for He will shake all [Col. 0197A] hearts, and by terrifying and shaking them all He will arouse them to repentance. And after the disturbance and fear arising from consciousness of evil, the land of Judah—that is, the Catholic Church, outside which there is no confession of truth—will be to Egypt, that is, to the Gentile world, an occasion of festivity, that is, of joy and veneration.

Every Egyptian who remembers it—that is, the Church—will be afraid at the Lord’s counsel, who has devised to turn the Gentiles from vain images to the living God and to condemn more harshly those who refuse conversion. In comparison with Christians, all pagans are like women, having lowly opinions; and whatever they say turns to foolishness, as they are astonished at the conversion of so great a nation, marvel, [Col. 0197B] and understand the Lord’s hand. And whoever among them remembers the Christian name confesses, through fear, the weakness of idolatry; but if he is converted, the land of Judah becomes to him an occasion of festivity—that is, knowledge of the Scriptures: the Law and the Prophets, the Gospel, the Epistles of the Apostles. And everyone who remembers this land will be afraid—but with a fear [Note: [Col. 0197D] Both manuscripts: “and with fear.”] which leads to life. “For the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Prov. 1:17). It follows:

**VERSE 18.**—“On that day there shall be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the language of Canaan and swearing by the Lord of hosts; one shall be called the city of the sun.”

What is now signified by the five cities but the five bodily senses? For in order to indicate this the prophet added, by way of explanation, that one of them would be called the city of the sun. For what is the city of the sun in a human being except sight, which illuminates the whole body as the sun illuminates the world? Canaan is said to mean “changed.” Thus the five cities in the land of Egypt speak the language of Canaan—that is, a changed language—when the five bodily senses, changed from sin among the Gentiles, serve righteousness. Whoever does not restrain these five from perverse pleasures still speaks the Egyptian language. But whoever now occupies them with works of virtue speaks the language of Canaan in his five cities, because he has been changed from vices to virtues. For we speak to God not so much by words as by works.

Some have understood the five cities as either the law of the Lord, which was first translated at Alexandria, or the orders of the Church—bishops, presbyters, deacons, faithful, catechumens—or certainly the spiritual understanding of the law, concerning which the Apostle also says: “I would rather speak five words in the Church with my understanding than ten thousand in a tongue” (1 Cor. 14:19).

And one of the five cities is called the city of the sun of righteousness, which seems to me to refer to sight. For as a city needs sun and moon in order to be seen, so for our eyes to be enlightened we need the sun, which is Christ. The Law therefore speaks the language of Canaan—that is, a changed language—when it is translated into Greek or expounded spiritually. And it swears by the Lord of hosts, [Col. 0198A] because it confirms all its statements in Christ. But as regards ourselves, it must be asked why these cities speak not Hebrew but Canaanite. “Hebrew” signifies one who passes over, who passes from place to place. And although we are holy, so long as we are in Egypt—that is, while we live amid the darkness of this world—we cannot speak the Hebrew language, that is, the passing-over language, but the language of Canaan. For Canaan is interpreted “as it were, movement,” or “as it were, responding.” Therefore, when we wish to depart from Egypt and, desiring to leave Pharaoh’s power, to be wholly free of sin and dwell in the homeland of the saints where righteousness reigns, then we are moved and in a manner answer Christ who calls us. Yet because we are still held in this present age, we cannot yet [Col. 0198B] speak the Hebrew language until we pass from this life. It follows:

**VERSE 19.**—“On that day there shall be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt, and an inscription of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0198D] Alternatively: ‘an inscription of the Lord beside its border.’] beside its border.”

**VERSE 20.**—“And it shall be a sign and a testimony to the Lord of hosts in the land of Egypt.”

In Egypt—that is, among the Gentiles—there shall be an altar of the Lord, so that, from the rising of the sun to its setting, in every place, as Malachi says, a “pure offering” may be offered to His name (Mal. 1:1). But as the Church is one, so there is one altar throughout the whole world, because there is also one sacrifice. The inscription beside the altar is the Gospel and the teaching of the apostles.

Or the altar is faith, upon which we offer sacrifices, concerning which Peter says: “Be built up as spiritual houses, a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices” (1 Pet. 2:5). The inscription beside this altar is good action and imitation of the Lord’s Passion. And that altar or inscription shall be a sign and testimony of His resurrection. It follows: “For they shall cry to the Lord before the oppressor, and He shall send them a savior and defender who may deliver them.”

**VERSE 21.**—“And the Lord shall be known by Egypt, and the Egyptians shall know the Lord on that day; and they shall worship Him with sacrifices and gifts, shall vow vows to the Lord, and shall fulfill them.”

Pressed by the ancient enemy, who afflicts them in perverse works, they will finally cry to the Lord, like Cornelius, who “was always praying to God” (Acts [Col. 0198D] 10:2). And through the apostles He will send them Christ the Savior, who will free them.

Or martyrs and other faithful persons, pressed by afflictions, will cry to the Lord before the world that troubles and attacks them. And spiritually He will send them His Savior, because through Christ’s grace He will deliver them and fight against unbelievers on their behalf. For as often as we are afflicted by persecutors, by the assaults of demons, or by any adversity, and are freed and protected by God’s aid, God in some manner sends His Son to us as Savior and defender, who frees us. Thus He then sent Him to His faithful when, after the affliction of the martyrs, He granted peace.

“And the Lord,” he says, “shall be known by Egypt,” because after persecutions had ceased, the whole world believed. “And the Egyptians shall know the Lord on that day and worship Him with sacrifices and gifts”—the spiritual sacrifices and gifts of good works—and shall vow and fulfill for Him vows of pious conduct. For that person offers and fulfills a vow to the Lord who is holy in body and spirit. It follows:

**VERSE 22.**—“And the Lord shall strike Egypt with a plague and heal it; and they shall return to the Lord, and He shall be appeased toward them and heal them.”

God wounds in two ways those whom He seeks to restore to salvation. Sometimes He strikes the flesh and melts the hardness of the mind by His terror. Thus by wounding He calls back to salvation when He afflicts His elect outwardly so that they may live inwardly. Sometimes, even if outward scourges seem to cease, He inflicts wounds within, because He strikes the hardness of our mind with His desire. Yet by striking He heals, because He recalls us, pierced by the dart of His terror [Note: [Col. 0199D] Thus both manuscripts read *terrore sui jaculo* (“by the dart of His terror”) in place of *terroris sui jaculo* (“by the dart of His fear”)], to awareness of rectitude. For our hearts are unsound in a bad way when they are wounded by no love of God, when they do not feel the misery of their exile, when they do not languish with even the slightest affection at a neighbor’s weakness. But they shall be struck with a wound in order to be healed, because God pierces insensitive minds with the darts of love and immediately makes them sensitive through the burning of charity. Hence the bride says in the Song of Songs: “I am wounded by charity” [Col. 0199C] (Song 4).

For the soul, unsound in a bad way and blind in the condition of this exile, cast down by self-assurance, neither saw God nor sought to see Him. But the heart struck by the darts of His charity is wounded, because inwardly it burns, with the affection of devotion, with longing for contemplation; and in a wonderful way she who formerly lay dead in health is made alive from the wound. She burns, pants, and now desires to see Him whom she had fled.

Therefore she is brought back to salvation by a blow when, through the disturbance of His love, she is recalled to the security of inward rest. It was therefore well said: “The Lord shall strike Egypt with a plague and heal it.” And, he says, they shall return to the Lord, stimulated by charity, from whom they had withdrawn, enticed by desires. And He shall be appeased toward them when they repent, though He had been angry with them [Col. 0199D] when they sinned. And He shall heal them from the languor of sin and inward numbness. Or the Lord struck Egypt—that is, believers from among the Gentiles—because He delivered the martyrs to suffering. But He will heal them again in the resurrection. “For whom the Lord loves He rebukes; and He scourges every son whom He receives” (Prov. 3:12). It follows:

**VERSE 23.**—“On that day there shall be a way from Egypt to the Assyrians; and the Assyrian shall enter Egypt, and Egypt into Assyria; and the Egyptians shall serve Assur.”

There shall be a way from Egypt to Assyria—that is, from the Gentile world [Col. 0200A] into the Church of the saints, who guide themselves and others rightly. For “Assyrians” are interpreted “those guiding,” and Assur “one guiding.” And the Assyrian—that is, the preacher—shall enter Egypt, that is, the Gentile world; and Egypt into Assyria, that is, the Gentile into the Church. And the Egyptians shall serve Assur, because the Gentiles will obey Christ. For Assur, as has been said, is interpreted “one guiding.” And who is this guide but He to whom it is said: “Guide me in your truth and teach me, for you are God my Savior” (Ps. 24:5)?

The way from Egypt to Assyria was first opened when Cornelius was commanded to send to Simon Peter (Acts 10). And the Assyrian entered Egypt when Peter entered the house of Cornelius. Egypt entered Assyria—that is, the Gentile was incorporated into the Church [Col. 0200B] of the saints—when “the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard the word, and Peter commanded them to be baptized” (ibid., 10:44). And the Egyptians served Assur when Cornelius and those baptized with him observed what they had heard from Peter: “God is no respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to Him” (ibid., 10:34). It follows:

**VERSE 24.**—“On that day Israel shall be third with the Egyptian and Assyrian: a blessing in the midst of the earth.”

**VERSE 25.**—“Whom the Lord of hosts has blessed, saying: Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands; but Israel is my inheritance.”

Israel—that is, “the man seeing God”—shall be third with the Egyptian, [Col. 0200C] that is, the converted Gentile, and the Assyrian, that is, the preacher. Or Israel and the Egyptian are circumcision and uncircumcision; and when the preacher is among the Gentiles, Israel—that is, the Hebrew people—is added to them as third. The blessing is in the earth, that is, in the Church. “Whom the Lord has blessed, saying: Blessed be Egypt my people,” that is, the Gentile world; “and Assyria shall be the work of my hands,” because I shall cooperate with the preachers, as Mark says: “They preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word through the signs that followed” (Mark 10); and Paul says: “He who worked through Peter in the apostleship of the circumcision also worked through me among the Gentiles” (Gal. 2:8)—“but Israel is my inheritance,” which means “the man seeing God” or “a prince with God,” because those shall be God’s inheritance who [Col. 0200D] will see Him without end and reign with Him. These things indeed concern the elect; what follows concerns the reprobate, when it says:

## CHAPTER XX

**VERSE 1.**—“In the year in which Tharthan entered Ashdod, when Sargon king of the Assyrians had sent him, and he had fought against Ashdod and captured it.”

**VERSE 2.**—“At that time the Lord spoke through Isaiah son of Amoz, saying: Go, loosen the sackcloth from your loins and take your sandals from [Col. 0201A] your feet. And he did so, walking naked and barefoot.”

**VERSE 3.**—“And the Lord said: As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot, it shall be a sign and portent for three years over Egypt and Ethiopia.”

**VERSE 4.**—“So the king of the Assyrians shall threaten Egypt with captivity and Ethiopia with exile, young and old, naked and barefoot, with buttocks uncovered, to the shame of Egypt.”

**VERSE 5.**—“And they shall fear and be ashamed because of Ethiopia, their hope, and Egypt, their glory.”

**VERSE 6.**—“And the inhabitant of this island shall say on that day: Behold, this was our hope, to whom we fled for help, that they might deliver us from the king [Col. 0201B] of the Assyrians; and how shall we escape?”

But what does the time when Tharthan captured Ashdod have to do with the captivity of Egypt and Ethiopia? Yet the less the historical sense seems to fit, the more fitting is the logic of the spiritual interpretation. For what is expressed by Ashdod, which is said to mean “fire of generation,” except the inborn burning of lust? What is signified by Tharthan, interpreted “superfluous” or “one who removes afar,” except a superfluous thought that separates from God? “For perverse thoughts separate from God” (Wis. 1:3). And He Himself says: “I broke their heart, which was fornicating and turning away from me” (Ezek. 6:9). For the heart that loves fornication has departed from God.

What, then, is signified by Sargon, who is called “prince of the garden,” that is, [Col. 0201C] of pleasure and luxury, and who is king of the Assyrians, except the devil, prince of demons? Thus Sargon, king of the Assyrians, sends Tartan against Ashdod, to storm and capture it, because the ancient enemy plants vain and licentious thoughts in the heart, to stir up the native fire of lust, so that he may storm the city of chastity. And at the time when Tartan captured Ashdod—by which capture the flesh or mind, burning with native heat, is signified as overcome through the devil’s injection of thoughts—“the Lord spoke by the hand of Isaiah,” because from his action He fashioned His words. “Loose,” He says, “the sackcloth from your loins,” etc. What does it mean that the prophet loosed the sackcloth from his loins and the shoes from his feet, except that many were [Col. 0201D] going to loosen their loins from the girdle of chastity, with which they had previously bound themselves while clothed in the haircloth of penitence or discipline, and were going to strip the steps of their deeds of the protection afforded by paternal examples? And perhaps, because many who were thought to be members of Christ are so shamefully led captive by the devil into luxury and wickedness, Isaiah—whose name means “the salvation of the Lord,” and who commonly signifies Christ—goes naked and barefoot after loosening the haircloth from his loins. For this reason he walked naked for three days, as is made clear, prefiguring a captivity of three years, in order to indicate that some among those who confess faith in the Trinity would thus be taken captive. For when the Lord says, “Just as my servant Isaiah walked naked and barefoot, it shall be a sign and portent of three years over Egypt [Col. 0202A] and Ethiopia; so shall the king of the Assyrians threaten the captivity of Egypt,” it is understood that the prophet walked naked for three days, so that his shameful three-day walk might signify a captivity of three years. For in Scripture a day sometimes signifies a year, as Ezekiel was told: “A day for a year, I say, a day for a year I have given you” (Ezek. 4:6). And under Moses, when the scouts returned and disparaged the land which they had inspected, and the children of Israel grieved that they had left Egypt, the Lord says: “According to the number of forty days in which you considered the land, a year shall be reckoned for a day, and for forty years you shall bear your iniquities” (Num. 14:34). So also here the prophet, in order to represent three years, walked naked for three days; [Col. 0202B] indeed, even one walk could signify either three years or whatever length the Lord wished.

What, then, is expressed by this three-year captivity except the time of Christians from the Lord’s resurrection until the end of the world, during which those are thus taken captive who turn the Lord’s grace into luxury? “So shall the king of the Assyrians threaten the captivity of Egypt and the removal of Ethiopia,” and so forth. As we have already said, the king of the Assyrians is the devil. But what do Egypt, which is called “darkness,” and Ethiopia, interpreted as “gloom,” signify except the darkened consciences of certain people? For according to the Apostle, demons are “the rulers of this world of darkness” (Eph. 6:12). Therefore the king of the Assyrians threatens captivity for Egypt and removal for Ethiopia, [Col. 0202C] because the ancient enemy causes those whose minds are not illumined by knowledge of God’s teaching—or who, after illumination, have again been darkened by consenting to sin—to go captive from vice to vice according to his desire.

He threatens the young man, because he takes captive even one who was thought to flourish in spiritual vigor and mental soundness; and the old man, because he drives even one who seemed mature in conduct and perfect into the path of wickedness. The man who prayed, saying, “Let not the hand of the sinner move me” (Ps. 35:12), did not wish to be threatened in this way. He threatens her naked, that is, stripped of the garment of righteousness and barefoot of the examples of the fathers. For the feet of our deeds are protected from the bite of the ancient serpent as though by the skins of dead animals, [Col. 0202D] while they are kept within the rule of life established by the fathers. Therefore he goes barefoot who imitates in his deeds the example of none of the fathers who went before.

Egypt is also interpreted as “pursuing” or “troubling,” and Ethiopians as “humble and cast down,” because “everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke 14:11). They are to be led into captivity—the young and the old shall go into it—because they have become strong in malice and have reached the vices of full maturity; naked, so that all their crimes may be laid bare. “For nothing is hidden that shall not be revealed” (Luke 8:17). And barefoot, lest they be able to eat the Lord’s Passover, but instead be bitten by serpents. What, moreover, is signified by their exposed buttocks, through which excrement is discharged, except the uncovering of disgraceful and shameful [Col. 0203A] deeds, from which the report of a foul odor goes forth?

And this is the disgrace of Egypt, that is, of those who, through the blindness of their hearts, have been brought even to detestable deeds. For on account of these they are regarded as dishonorable and infamous. Therefore, when certain persons who were considered great in holiness have been so miserably taken captive, those lesser persons who followed them will fear before their fall lest they too fall in the same manner, “and they shall be ashamed because of Ethiopia, their hope, and because of Egypt, their glory,” because they will now blush for those in whom they had placed great hope of their salvation and in whom they gloried, since they judged them truly holy. This has often happened in our own days as well.

“And the inhabitant of this island shall say,” that is, the one who [Col. 0203B] remains steadfast in this religion: Behold, these are the men in whom we placed our hope, and to whose counsel and assistance we fled, so that by instructing and praying for us they might deliver us from the face of the king of the Assyrians—that is, from Satan’s assault—yet now they have been unable to deliver even themselves! How then shall we weak people be able to resist or escape, when these strong men have been so feebly defeated in the contest of temptations? It follows:

## CHAPTER XXI

**VERSE 1.**—“The burden of the desert of the sea.”

This burden is set in the sixth degree, because it belongs to those who attain neither the Sabbath-rest of souls after death nor the eighth day of blessed resurrection, but devote themselves wholly in an animal-like manner to the present life, which is represented by the six laborious days. This too is a burden of Babylon, and that one generally of all sinners—that is, both of the reprobate and of those who return to penitence. For the sea signifies those of whom this prophet says: “But the wicked are like a boiling sea, which cannot rest” (Isa. 57:20). The hearts of people who seek earthly things swell with diverse waves of thoughts; stirred by the elevation of pride, as they strike themselves in alternating impulses, they collide as waves opposing one another. Therefore the sea is the heart of the wicked; and that sea is a desert, because abandoned and rejected by God. But let us see what burden this sea bears. It follows: “As whirlwinds come from the southwest, [Col. 0203D] it comes from the desert, from a dreadful land.”

**VERSE 2.**—“A hard vision has been reported to me.”

What is designated by the desert or dreadful land except the mind of reprobate angels? What is expressed by the southwest wind, which is a warm wind, except the breath of the Holy Spirit? Hence Zechariah says: “The Lord God shall sound the trumpet and shall go in the whirlwind of the south wind” (Zech. 9:14). For the south wind and the southwest wind signify the same thing. God sounds the trumpet when Christ preaches either through His preachers or by Himself. And He goes in the whirlwind of the south wind because, when our mind is violently shaken by divine fear, God comes to it. For the whirlwind of the south wind is the fear which divine grace instills into the sinner, that he may be converted. But just as from the southwest wind of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0204A] there come divine terrors that overthrow the evil structure, so, contrariwise, from the desert of the multitude of demons comes a whirlwind of temptations, shaking and overthrowing the mind’s stability. This may also be understood otherwise.

For what is signified by the southwest wind except the warm breath of hostile suggestions? What by the desert except the deprivation of good? Hearts empty of the fear of God and dry from the sprinkling of heavenly grace are compared to the barrenness of a desolate wilderness. In this desert John saw “a woman sitting upon a scarlet beast full of names of blasphemy” (Rev. 17:3). The woman is Babylon; the beast is the devil. Therefore, just as whirlwinds—that is, disturbances of vices which overturn the heart—come from the southwest wind, that is, from the enemy’s heated suggestion, so also from the desert, that is, from one who has voluntarily abandoned [Col. 0204B] the good, comes the burden of this desert sea; for, according to another prophet, “its judgment and its burden shall proceed from itself” (Hab. 1:7).

“A hard vision,” he says, “has been divinely reported to me concerning a dreadful land,” concerning demons prevailing terribly over lovers of the world. Thus it is also said through John: “Woe to the earth and the sea, because the devil has come down to you in great wrath” (Rev. 12:12). This is the hard vision reported to the prophet; thus a vision, or burden, is seen against the sea of this world, and the prophet considers with how many temptations this world is filled. This very tempest of temptations comes from the desert, in which the Lord too was tempted and in which the Israelites perished from serpent bites. [Col. 0204C] Amid these temptations and distresses, a dreadful and hard vision is heard. Rightly, then, whirlwinds and storms come from the desert and from a dreadful land, where God is not an inhabitant and where all things are earthly.

And every unbeliever acts in a manner fitting his unbelief, and the plunderer plunders. For this follows:

“He who is unbelieving acts unfaithfully, and he who is a plunderer plunders.” Whoever does not believe the holy preachers performs works of unbelief. And whoever is a plunderer and destroyer lays waste the Church, as Saul did (Acts 8:3). Or the ancient enemy, who is the plunderer of good things, lays waste inwardly Babylon—that is, the heart of worldly people. It follows:

“Go up, Elam; besiege, Mede; I have made all her groaning cease.” Elam is interpreted as “the world,” or “before the doors,” or “outside the doors,” or “worldly things”; but Mede as “measured” or “measuring.” What then is signified by Elam except all these temporal things that stand before our doors, that is, before our eyes? And what by the Mede except Satan, who cannot harm except according to the measure divinely allowed him? Thus Elam goes up against one whose mind worldly and visible things strive to conquer through delight; and the Mede besieges when the devil surrounds and attacks the mind on every side with prolonged temptations. Yet amid all these things, he says, “I have caused her groaning,” that is, Babylon’s—the groaning of the confused mind—to cease, [Col. 0205A] because, intoxicated with worldly joy, it is unable to feel the spiritual losses it suffers within and therefore does not know why it should groan. But the compassionate prophet shows how greatly he grieves and marvels concerning such a soul, adding:

**VERSE 3.**—“Therefore my loins are filled with pain; anguish has seized me like the anguish of a woman in labor. I collapsed when I heard; I was troubled when I saw.”

**VERSE 4.**—“My heart withered; darkness stupefied me.”

The anguish of a woman in labor seized the prophet because, with extreme pain, he brought forth what he held within: namely, the sorrowful vision shown him concerning Babylon. On hearing it he could not remain standing, but [Col. 0205B] withered with pain and languished, lying on the ground; and the darkness of his confused heart and of his bodily eyes stupefied him, so that, absorbed in immeasurable sadness, he lay for a long time stunned and weak, without bodily sight and without sober understanding of mind. At last, scarcely able to say why he suffered such things, he adds:

“Babylon, my beloved, has been made a wonder to me.” In the affection of pity and compassion the holy man calls Babylon his beloved, because in all human beings he loves his own nature and kindly shares in the miseries of all. How full of charity, then, must we think him who thus loves even Babylon? And what is this Babylon except that part of humankind which loves this world alone? It was made a wonder to the prophet because he saw it flourishing at one moment [Col. 0205C] and shortly afterward destroyed. Present life seems long to those who do not think of eternity. But the prophet, intent upon heavenly and eternal things, considered how quickly this temporal glory comes to an end. He also added, saying to Babylon:

**VERSE 5.**—“Set the table; look out from the watchtower. You who eat and drink, arise, princes; seize the shield.”

“Set for yourself,” he says, “a table,” that is, worldly learning, upon which you may feed on the varied dishes of carnal knowledge. Or, set for yourself a table—that is, an array of pleasures. But while seated at this table, look out from the watchtower: from the height of your mind, look beforehand from afar at how great a destruction threatens you. And you princes of Babylon—that is, sages of the world—who eat and drink both obscure and manifest worldly knowledge: rise from this feast and seize the shield of protection, with which you may oppose the devil’s darts, so that you may protect yourselves from the threatening sword of death. “For Belshazzar king of Babylon gave a great feast to his nobles, and, already drunk, commanded that the vessels which had been in the temple of the Lord be brought; and the king and his nobles, his wives and his concubines drank from them. They drank wine in them and praised their gods, and that same night Belshazzar was slain” (Dan. 5:1 ff.).

So too the sages of this world and heretics feed and intoxicate their household members and subjects [Col. 0206A] with Babylonian food—that is, the teaching of confusion. Intoxicated by it, if they can draw any away from the Church, they drink in them the wine of confusion and madness and praise their own errors. But in the night of that same confusion and drunkenness they are slain by the devil, because they die without knowledge of the truth. “For those who sleep, sleep at night; and those who are drunk, are drunk at night” (1 Thess. 5:7).

Therefore, in this night of mind, drunkenness, and sleep, they are killed by the ancient enemy. Thus the Lord says to the rich man: “Fool, this night they demand your soul from you” (Luke 12:20). Against this drunkenness, sleep, and death Peter carefully warns us, saying: “Be sober and watchful, because your adversary [Col. 0206B] the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5:8). Considering this feast and the death threatening in the night, the prophet therefore says: “Set the table; look out from the watchtower; you who eat and drink, arise, princes; seize the shield.” Such revelers should know that their enemy Satan is preparing sudden death for them, and that they cannot protect themselves against him.

Or the prophet is commanded, as one feeding at the Lord’s table and filled with His food, diligently to contemplate what is to come upon the world; and through him all believers are told that, eating and drinking the body and blood of the Lord, they are to become princes of the Church, hear with the apostles, “Arise” (John [Col. 0206C] 14:31), and seize the shield of faith from the armor of the Apostle Paul, with which they may “quench the fiery darts of the devil” (Eph. 6:16). It follows: “For thus the Lord said to me.”

**VERSE 6.**—“Go and set a watchman, and let him announce whatever he sees.”

**VERSE 7.**—“And he saw a chariot of two horsemen, a rider on a camel, and he watched diligently with close attention.”

**VERSE 8.**—“And the lion cried: Upon the Lord’s watchtower I stand continually by day, and upon my guard I stand [Note: [Col. 0205D] Otherwise: ‘I stand,’ etc.] through all the nights.”

**VERSE 9.**—“Behold, this man comes, a rider of a chariot of horsemen; and he answered and said: Babylon has fallen, and [Col. 0206D] all her carved images are shattered upon the ground.”

“Set,” he says, “a watchman in your heart,” that is, the prudent vigilance of the mind, which from lofty consideration may foresee the coming conflicts of vices and demons, and through the prophetic spirit may foresee what shall occur in the world. For the understanding of prophets, filled with inward inspirations, is raised from below and ascends to things above; from there, as if from a summit overlooking events, it sees what is to come beneath it.

Therefore, the watchman appointed by the prophet may fittingly be understood as his own understanding. Set upon the watchtower of prophetic contemplation, he saw in this world a chariot of two horsemen: that is, [Col. 0207A] the proud pomp of the devil and Antichrist. He saw a rider on an ass, that is, the devil, and a rider on a camel, that is, Antichrist. For the ass is the foolish and irrational people of the Gentiles, possessed by the devil before the coming of the Redeemer; but the camel is the crooked multitude of utterly perverse people who will follow Antichrist.

“And he watched,” he says, “their cunning diligently with close attention.” And lest he be deceived by any artifice of theirs, he cried confidently and strongly, saying: “Upon the Lord’s watchtower I stand,” etc. For the one stands upon the Lord’s watchtower whose mind is fixed with firm steadfastness in the desire for the heavenly homeland. For, withdrawing his intention from all outward movements, he has sought a certain most hidden retreat, [Col. 0207B] and, adhering there immovably and transcending all changeable things, by the very tranquility of his repose he is already in the world yet outside the world.

He also stands upon his guard who, through the carefulness of discipline, does not yield to earthly desires but rises above them, so that, while always striving toward the standing eternity, everything that passes may lie beneath him. For the prudent discernment of the saints, while set on high and looking carefully in every direction, detects sin before it arrives and, the more watchfully it recognizes it in advance, the more strongly avoids it.

The watchtower by day may also be understood as the guarding of virtues; the guard in the nights as careful observation against the trials of vices. But he attributes the watchtower of day to the Lord and testifies that the guard of nights is his own, because whatever virtues we possess are from God and not from ourselves. And however this sentence is understood, in it the night is assigned to us and the day to the Lord.

One interpreter understood the rider on the ass, in accordance with the Gospel passage, to be Christ (Matt. 21), and, conversely, the rider on the camel to be the opposing power because of the ugliness of that crooked animal. Others refer the two riders, of letter and spirit, to the two Testaments.

“Behold,” he says, “behold, this watchman comes, this man,” that is, Antichrist, who will be a human being, not an angelic spirit, “a rider of a chariot of horsemen,” that is, possessor of the worldly glory of the powerful. And the watchman answered his wickedness [Col. 0207D] and said: “Babylon has fallen, has fallen.” For that pestilential man will rise in such perversity against the Lord of heaven that, because of his malice, the world will end, and he himself with all Babylon—that is, the whole assembly of the wicked—will be cast down into Tartarus, he who exalted himself above all that is called God or worshipped. Thus, rightly, after his coming it is now said: “Babylon has fallen, has fallen,” that is, both soul and body have been sent into outer darkness. “And all the carved images of her gods,” that is, all the fabrications of his false doctrines, are shattered upon the dark land covered by the gloom of death. As the watchman says these things in Isaiah, so John likewise saw an angel saying: “Babylon the great has fallen, has fallen, she who made all nations drink of the wine of the wrath [Col. 0208A] of her fornication” (Rev. 14:8). And another angel followed, saying: “If anyone worships the beast and his image and receives the mark upon his forehead, he shall drink of the wine of God’s wrath” (ibid., 9). These will then be the carved images of Babylon’s gods: namely, the beast, that is, Antichrist, and his image, his mark, and the number of his name. But these images will be shattered when Babylon falls, because when the wicked perish, Antichrist and his idols will be destroyed.

In another sense, the man riding the chariot of horsemen is understood as the incarnate Lord, seated upon the chariot of the Church, in which the horsemen are preachers and rulers. This rider of the chariot answered the prophet who desired and wished to hear His words, and said: “Babylon has fallen, has fallen”—the confusion of the whole world has fallen at my coming [Col. 0208B] and will utterly collapse at the end of the age—and her idols have been shattered. Thus far the prophet has related how Babylon was made a wonder and astonishment to him, and why he was affected by such sorrow in this vision. After this, turning to the people of the faithful, he adds:

**VERSE 10.**—“My threshing, and daughter of my threshing-floor: what I have heard from the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, I have announced to you.”

That is, the sudden ruin of unbelievers while they exalt themselves in their iniquities. The threshing, however, is the Church, which is beaten down by present evils so that through these the grains may be separated from the chaff—that is, the righteous, worthy of heavenly granaries, from the reprobate.

[Col. 0208C] **VERSE 11.**—“The burden of Dumah. One cries to me from Seir: Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?”

**VERSE 12.**—“The watchman said: Morning comes, and night. If you seek, seek; turn back, and come.”

This burden concerns Jews beginning to desire to believe near the end of the age, and it is in the seventh degree because of the Sabbath.

Dumah is interpreted as “silence” or “joy.” The Jews have remained silent concerning the confession of the Redeemer ever since “they agreed that if anyone confessed Him to be Christ, he should be put out of the synagogue” (John 9:22). They will then rightly rejoice when they begin again to confess Him. Therefore this present silence of the Jews, [Col. 0208D] and their joy still to come, bears this burden which the prophet now describes. “To me,” says the Savior, “everyone cries from Seir,” that is, from the thorny people of the Jews, designated by Seir, that is, Esau, who was born altogether hairy like a skin; for Seir means “hairy” or “goat”: “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” Understand: Have you come? For our Watchman came in the night, because the protector of the human race appeared manifestly in the flesh; nevertheless Judea, oppressed by the darkness of its unbelief, did not recognize Him. Yet in its folly, coming to its senses, it complains why He came in the night. To it the ever-watchful Watchman, who guards Israel, says: The morning of the Gentiles’ illumination has come, and the night of the Jews’ blindness. For by His presence a new light shone upon the world, and yet in the hearts of unbelievers the old blindness remained. Indeed, some were blinded at His coming. “If you now seek me,” He says, “by faith, seek me also by works; turn back from oldness and come to newness.” For this, as we have said before, is addressed to those who have already begun in some measure to believe.

Or the Church may say that the Lord cries out to her from Seir, that is, from earthly places, and calls her to salvation; and she speaks to Him: O Watchman, who, rising from the night, move about in darkness—who are without sin in sinful flesh—for what reason did You will to assume a human body? The Watchman replies, that is, the Samaritan who placed the wounded man upon His beast of burden (Luke 10:33 ff.): “Morning comes, and night”; that is, to the multitude of Gentiles the Sun of righteousness has arisen, and darkness has come to the Jews. And He says to the Gentiles: If you seek me, seek more earnestly; turn from errors and come to me.

**VERSE 13.**—“The burden in Arabia. In the forest at evening you shall sleep, on the paths of the Dodanim.” [Note: [Col. 0209D] Otherwise: *Dedanim*.]

**VERSE 14.**—“Bring water to meet the thirsty, you who inhabit the land of the south; with bread meet the fugitive.”

**VERSE 15.**—“For they have fled from the face of swords, from the face of the threatening sword, from the face of the drawn bow, from the face of grievous battle.”

**VERSE 16.**—“For thus says the Lord God [Note: [Col. 0209D] Otherwise: ‘For thus the Lord said to me,’ etc.]: Yet within one year, as in the year of a hired laborer, all the glory of Kedar shall be removed.”

[Col. 0209C] **VERSE 17.**—“And the remnant of the number of the mighty archers among the sons of Kedar shall be diminished; for the Lord God of Israel has spoken.”

This burden, unless I am mistaken, concerns penitents, and is therefore set in the eighth order on account of fear, namely, fear of the coming judgment. For no one does penance unless he fears the day of judgment. That day will be the eighth, because it will come after temporal worldly things, which are completed in seven days. This burden is said to be in Arabia because it pertains to those who are humbled by their sins and believe, or reflect, that the end of their life is drawing near.

For Arabia, interpreted as “low,” “western,” or “evening,” signifies the end of this life or old age. Therefore this burden is in Arabia—that is, in the humble [Col. 0209D] mind of the penitent, who considers the end of life to be near. “You,” he says, “O penitents, shall sleep,” that is, rest from the tumult of desires, “in the forest,” that is, in the harsh and dreadful conversion of penitence, “at evening,” that is, when the sun of carnal desires is setting, or near the end of the present life.

Or, “in the forest,” that is, in a remote and secluded way of life, you shall sleep from the tumult of the world, “on the paths of the Dodanim,” that is, in the ways of Christ, who deigned to become our kinsman. For *Dodanim* means “cousin,” and Christ is this especially to us who believe from among the Gentiles. For the Jewish people and the Gentile peoples are two brothers. Christ is indeed the son of the Jewish people; but we were born from the Gentile people. Christ, therefore, is our cousin, that is, the son of our uncle. Thus he sleeps on the paths of the Dodanim who, leaving the turbulent activities of the world, follows with a quiet heart the narrow ways of Christ. Jacob slept on these paths when in a dream he saw the ladder whose top reached heaven (Gen. 28:12 ff.).

Or thus: Arabia is called evening, which is the beginning of night and darkness; and everyone who has entered upon the beginnings of sins is in the evening. But one who comes to the height of evil stands in the middle of the night; and those who have begun to be in malice and enter the path of sins do not sleep or tarry in fields and grainlands, but in unfruitful forests. Rightly, then, since evening is the beginning of evils, they are said to dwell on the paths of Dodanim, which is interpreted as “judgments.” For as many kinds of sins as they have, so many sentences of judgment they deserve. *Dodanim* may also be interpreted “great judgment.”

The prophet now admonishes spiritual persons to offer the gift of human kindness to every penitent. “Bring,” he says, “water”—a draught of spiritual teaching, of divine preaching—to the thirsty, you who inhabit the land of the south, that is, who live spiritually in the Church. With the breads of sacred nourishment meet everyone fleeing the defilements of the world and the punishments of future condemnation. For water signifies the knowledge of Holy Scripture, [Col. 0210C] because it is written: “He shall give him to drink the water of saving wisdom” (Ecclus. 15:3); and, “Deep water is the word from a man’s mouth” (Prov. 18:4). They inhabit the land of the south who, established in the holy Church, are breathed upon by the wind of the Holy Spirit.

Bread likewise signifies instruction in heavenly teaching, as it is written: “He shall feed him with the bread of life and understanding” (Ecclus. 15:3). The one flees who desires to escape the evils of this world. Therefore, let the one who dwells in the land of the south meet fugitives with bread: that is, let one already filled with the Holy Spirit within the holy Church comfort by the speech of instruction the person striving to escape his evils. To meet the fugitive with bread is to offer the food of sacred teaching to one fearing eternal punishments, now to restrain fear by terror, now to sustain dread through exhortation.

This passage may properly be understood against those who give themselves over to leisure and idleness, content with their own salvation, and do not lend a hand to penitents and converts. “For,” he says, “the penitents have fled from the face of swords,” which the saints will hold in judgment, as it is written: “Two-edged swords in their hands, to execute vengeance” (Ps. 149:6); “from the face of the threatening sword,” of which Job says, “Flee from the face of the sword” (Job 19:29)—the threatening sword. What sword is so great? [Note: Both manuscripts read *tantum* (“so much” or “only”).] “And know that there is [Col. 0211A] judgment” (ibid.). “From the face of the drawn bow,” of which it is said: “You have given a sign to those who fear you, that they may flee from the face of the bow” (Ps. 59:5). For both sword and bow here signify the judicial sentence. “From the face of grievous battle,” namely, the future judgment, of which the Lord says: “What king, going to make war against another king, does not first sit down and consider whether he can meet with ten thousand him who comes against him with twenty thousand? Otherwise, while he is still far away, he sends an embassy and asks for terms of peace” (Luke 14:31). Every person who governs himself well is a king. He is going to make war against another king because at the end he is to be judged by the Lord. But he cannot meet with ten thousand Him who comes against [Col. 0211B] him with twenty thousand, because he is not sufficient to answer the Judge with perfection of works, since He will demand an account not only of deeds but also of thoughts. Therefore let him meanwhile send to Him an embassy of prayers and penitence, asking for terms of peace. Thus he calls the coming examination a grievous battle, because no one is so holy as to be able to bear that weight of strict examination if he is examined with mercy removed. Or they have fled the swords of heretics, the doctrine of Gentiles, and the blasphemies of Jews. Because they saw many slain by their darts and very many fallen in battle, they themselves desire to be delivered by your assistance.

He then shows what those who do penance with their whole heart obtain in this life: “Yet within one year,” he says, that is, within the remaining span of their life, [Col. 0211C] “all the glory of Kedar shall be removed from them,” that is, their sin, in which demons, the princes of darkness, gloried. For Kedar means “darkness.” But this year shall be like the year of a hired laborer, because they will judge themselves unworthy to be called children of God, being content with the name of hired laborers alone. Thus that penitent says in their person: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me as one of your hired laborers” (Luke 15:18).

Or this year is called like a hired laborer’s year because they shall deserve the reward of heavenly recompense from the Lord. Thus blessed Job speaks of such a servant: “Withdraw a little from him, that he may rest, until his desired day comes like that of a hired laborer” (Job 7:1). Therefore, in this hired laborer’s year, all the glory of Kedar—that is, of darkness—shall be removed from them, so that they may hear: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8); and: “What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6:21).—“And the remnant of the number of archers among the sons of Kedar shall be diminished,” because the sons of darkness, the demons, will gradually dare less and less each day to shoot the arrows of temptations into their hearts. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXII

**VERSE 1.**—“The burden of the valley of vision.”

This burden is set in the ninth degree to intimate to us that it belongs to those who appear to be contained within the sacrament of faith in the Church. For since three times three are nine, the number nine is rightly desired for the mystery of faith. Or this passage may call those who transgress faith. For since the Church is a mountain, why is it now called a valley, unless so that all the leaders of perverse doctrines, who have fallen from the height of their understanding of the Scriptures and descended to the depths, may be known to dwell in the valley of vision?

The valley of vision is also the Church, which, standing in the strength of humility, is accustomed to possess enlightened eyes of the heart. Yet it bears an exceedingly grievous burden, because it is oppressed by the multitude of the reprobate and weighed down in many ways by the burden of temptations, especially near the end of the age. Therefore it is now said to them: “What then has happened to you also, that you have all gone up upon the roofs?”

[Col. 0212B] **VERSE 2.**—“Full of shouting, crowded city, exultant town?”

It is as though he said: Concerning the others whom I have described up to this point, it is not at all surprising if they bear diverse burdens of evils. But what has happened even to you, that you too have all gone up onto the roofs—that is, onto the tops of houses—to look in every direction at the deaths of your children, full of lamenting cries, once crowded with a multitude of citizens and exultant in your children or in prosperity? What is signified by roofs except earthly bodies? Therefore those go up upon the roofs who transcend the desires of the body, as the Apostle says: “But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you” (Rom. 8:11). To them the Lord also says: “What you have heard in the ear, preach [Col. 0212C] upon the roofs” (Matt. 10:27).

Thus the Church, which once remained on the roofs in a time of peace, will in the onset of the final tribulation all go up upon the roofs. For she who lawfully used earthly things for the body’s convenience will then leave all worldly things and ascend the citadel of the mind; foreseeing and repelling on every side the temptations of enemies, she will mourn the spiritual death of her citizens. For then no Christian will be able to possess anything on earth when the followers of Antichrist know of it. It follows:

“Your slain were not slain by the sword, nor did your dead die in battle.” This is the cause of her intense sorrow: the citizens of the holy Church are not bodily killed by a material sword, but die spiritually, pierced by the invisible blade of temptations. And what do the shepherds do while the sheep are thus destroyed? It follows:

### Verse 3

> “All your princes have fled together; they are harshly bound. All who were found are bound alike; they fled far away.”

This passage accords with what the Lord says in the Gospel: “The hireling, who is not a shepherd and whose sheep are not his own, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees” (John 10:12). For the discourse now concerns useless rulers of the Church: when they see wrongdoing, they do not dare to oppose it, but hide themselves in silence. Such rulers flee not by changing place, but by withholding help; they flee because they see injustice and remain silent. Therefore, near the end of the age, almost all who seemed to be set over the Church [Col. 0213A] will conceal themselves in silence, since they do not presume to resist the injustice of the wicked. “All your princes,” he says, “have fled together,” not because every one of those throughout the whole world will then flee, but because all those who are in most regions, struck by fear, will give way. Thus they are harshly bound by the chains of their own sins—those to whom authority had been given in order that they might loose the chains of others. “All who were found are bound alike,” because all who are found in certain provinces will be overcome by Antichrist, just as even now many are overcome by various iniquities. “They fled far away,” he says, because, fearing for themselves, they withdrew far from justice.

Or thus: “What then is also the matter with you?” and so forth. That is, [Col. 0213B] when philosophers are swollen with pride, and all secular wisdom, disputing about lofty matters, despises the Church’s simplicity: why do you also pursue lofty things? “Full of shouting,” and so forth. The teaching of heretics consists not in sound understanding but in much speaking and clamour. Hence, because of the multitude of those deceived, it is called a populous city, and exultant because of pride. “Your slain,” and so forth. The greater part are overthrown by the deceits of heretics without any conflict or disputation; they are not wounded by the sword, but of their own accord pass over to the heretics. And all their rulers have migrated from the Church to the synagogue of Satan; discordant in unbelief, they have passed over together, yet united in their crossing over. Therefore they are harshly bound in their errors and have fled far from God. It follows:

[Col. 0213C]

### Verse 4

> “Therefore I said: Depart from me; I will weep bitterly. Do not press upon me, to comfort me over the devastation of the daughter of my people.”

In his customary manner, the compassionate man, seeing the sorrowful vision, fell down from excessive grief, I suppose; and when friends approached in order to raise or console him, he said: “Depart from me; I will weep bitterly.” For he was affected with such sorrow from the innermost marrow of his soul that he could receive no consolation by any means. And when those who wished to lessen his grief immediately bent over him as he lay there, he added: “Do not press upon me, to comfort me.” Why he rejects consolation he still shows, saying:

### Verse 5
