> “For a day of slaughter and trampling [Col. 0213D] and weeping, from the Lord God of hosts, is in the valley of vision—searching out the wall, and one magnificent upon the mountains.”

For in the time of the final persecution they will slay the works of the righteous, and those who consent to iniquity will be trampled by demons in the mire of vices.

Or, the souls of those who give assent to Antichrist will be slain; the rest, however, will be trampled down and afflicted by all, while amid these things all the pious will weep. And this is a day from the Lord, because it has long been divinely appointed that the time of that tribulation should come. “Searching out the wall,” because then, assailing the mind from every side, it will test how strongly each person’s conscience is fortified with virtues. “And magnificent upon the mountain” [Col. 0214A] of the Church, because it will attack the loftier saints with extraordinary temptations.

Or, the day of judgment and slaughter arises from the Lord in the valley of vision; and, in order to reveal the works of each person, it searches out the wall of the heretics, which they have built against the Church as a very strong rampart, and the magnificent and glorious one—that is, any one of their teachers who glories that he stands upon Christ the mountain. It follows:

### Verse 6

> “And Elam took up the quiver, the chariot of the horseman-man; and the shield will strip the wall bare.”

Elam is interpreted “world,” or “before the doors,” or “in front of the doors,” or certainly “worldly things”; and it signifies this world and all these visible things which are, as it were, before the doors of our eyes. Again, Elam is interpreted [Col. 0214B] “opponents,” signifying all who oppose us on the way of God. What is understood by the quiver except a design to harm? What by the chariot except the pompous glory of the world? What by the horseman-man, whose chariot this is, except Antichrist, who will rule over all others in secular glory?

Elam, therefore, besieging the valley of vision, takes up the quiver, because either this world or the ancient enemy, wishing to assail God’s servants, devises an evil plan from which he may suddenly shoot deadly missiles upon them as arrows from a quiver. And what is this quiver? The chariot of the horseman-man—that is, the glory which Antichrist will possess. For by this he will overcome many: that son of perdition will then obtain all the glory of the world [Col. 0214C].

Or, he will take up the quiver, the chariot of the horseman-man, because, in order to wound the hearts of believers, he will offer them the temporal glory which every powerful person possesses in the world. “And the shield will strip the wall bare,” because many believers who were devoted to the outward ministries of the Church, like the walls of the temple, will cast away the faith by which they could repel all the devil’s devices, and will remain naked before his quiver, loving the chariot of worldly glory. Hence John too was told: “But cast out the court which is outside the temple, and do not measure it, because it has been given to the Gentiles” (Rev. 11:2). For what is called a wall in Isaiah is called a court in John; and what is described as a wall stripped by a shield is shown as “the court cast out [Col. 0214D] and given to the Gentiles.” The shield, indeed, is faith, because Paul says: “In all things taking up the shield of faith, with which you may be able to extinguish all the fiery darts of the wicked one” (Eph. 6:16). Therefore the shield will strip the wall bare because those occupied with outward affairs will lose faith.

Or, Elam, which is interpreted “their ascent,” or the Elamites, who are called “despisers,” took up the quiver “to shoot in darkness at the upright in heart” (Ps. 10:2); they are men in chariots and horsemen, in order to strip bare with their shield and assault the wall of Zion and the stronghold of the Church. But the chosen valleys and humble doctrines will be full of the chariots of pride; and through ecclesiastical men God will uncover [Col. 0215A] the coverings of Judah, and all the secrets of those who are to stand in the confession of faith. It follows:

### Verse 7

> “And your chosen valleys will be full of chariots, and horsemen will set their stations at the gate.”

### Verse 8

> “And Judah’s covering will be uncovered, and on that day the armoury of the house of the forest will be seen.”

The chosen valleys—that is, those who, because of the humility they displayed, were thought chosen—will in that time be filled with chariots of empty glory. For the ruin of souls will then be so great that those who already seemed numbered among the elect because of the grace of exceeding humility will, alas, lifted up in pride, prefer the riches and honours of the world to Christ.

[Col. 0215B] And the horsemen—that is, evil spirits who ride upon the necks of the wicked—will set their stations at the gate of faith, because they will block for many the door of confession. “For confession is made with the mouth unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10). But because many then, from fear, will not confess themselves Christians, although they retain the truth of faith in their hearts, the horsemen are said to set “their stations at their gate,” because they will rule over their faith.

“And Judah’s covering will be uncovered,” because the conscience of those who confessed themselves Christians in a time of peace will be laid bare. For Judah means “confession.” An armoury is a place where weapons are kept. And what are the weapons of believers except virtues and the words of sacred speech? What is the armoury [Col. 0215C] of such weapons except the heart of the righteous? For what is the house of the forest except the conscience of the perfect, which, having driven away the noise of carnal desires, is free and sees that the Lord is God? “Therefore on that day the armoury of the house of the forest will be seen,” because the tribulation of temptation will reveal the mind of the elect, which had been removed from worldly disturbances and filled with heavenly weapons. Thereafter the perversity of heretics is described more clearly. For he adds:

### Verse 9

> “And you will see the breaches of the city of David, because they are multiplied.”

The city of David is the Church of God, which heretics strive to tear apart in the reprobate through various sects. To them also belongs what follows: “And you gathered the waters of the lower pool.”

[Col. 0215D]

### Verse 10

> “And you counted the houses of Jerusalem, and you destroyed the houses in order to fortify the wall.”

### Verse 11

> “And you made a reservoir between the two walls, and the water of the old pool; but you did not look to him who made it, nor did you see its maker from afar.”

For what is the lower pool except their teaching, always tending downwards? They also count the houses of Jerusalem because they rejoice not in spiritual progress but in the abundant number of disciples. And they destroy houses—that is, they overthrow the minds of believers whom they can seduce—in order to fortify their wall of protection against the Church. While they reject the Old [Col. 0216A] Testament, they have not followed the New, because the New is strengthened by the testimonies of the Old. Therefore between the two walls, the Old and the New, they made for themselves new waters, which they suppose to be more inward and to contain greater mysteries than those contained in the Old Testament. They made not a well that possessed living and everlasting waters, but a muddy reservoir unable to hold waters, between the two walls of the Old and New Testaments; and they made the water of the old pool—that is, the shadow of the ancient Law. And they did not look to God, who is the maker of the Old Testament. Nor were they willing to see him from afar, while he still delays his coming for judgment. Yet he would not have them perish, but turn back. For it follows:

### Verse 12

> “And the Lord God of hosts will call [Col. 0216B] on that day to weeping, and to mourning, and to baldness, and to the girding of sackcloth.”

For daily the Lord calls heretics and sinners to the weeping of repentance; to mourning for the evils which they have done; to baldness, that they may uncover the forehead, which is the seat of shame, and, confessing, lay bare the sins of which they are ashamed or ought to be ashamed; and to the girding of sackcloth, that they may gird themselves with the harshness of repentance. But they, on the contrary, have or have had joy and gladness instead of weeping and mourning; and, as though everything ended with death, killing calves and slaughtering rams, while eating flesh and drinking wine, they spoke the words of blasphemers: “While we are in the present world, let us abound in delights. For tomorrow—that is, the future time—will be without [Col. 0216C] consciousness.”

Or, on the day of death the person who before death refused to mourn the evils he had done will be called to weeping and mourning. Baldness and the girding of sackcloth likewise show the dress of mourners. The Lord fittingly declares in the Gospel that this day will come upon every such ruler, saying: “If that evil servant should say in his heart, ‘My master delays his coming,’ and should begin to strike his fellow servants, and eat and drink with drunkards, the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him, and at an hour which he does not know, and will divide him and assign his portion with the hypocrites; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 24:48; Luke 12:45). For those who above are described as having committed so many evils, as though striking [Col. 0216D] their fellow servants, and afterwards are said to be called to weeping, are now meanwhile declared to feast and drink with drunkards, when the text adds:

### Verse 13

> “Behold joy and gladness: killing calves and slaughtering rams, eating flesh and drinking wine. Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.”

For those who do not doubt that they will die, while they still have the opportunity, occupy themselves with empty joys, drinking, and luxuries, so that they may not be stung by any fear of the evils to come. Thus elsewhere they say: “Let us fill ourselves with costly wine and ointment, and let not the flower of time pass us by. Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither; let there be no meadow [Col. 0217A] through which our luxury does not pass; let none of us be without a share in our luxury; everywhere let us leave signs of joy, for this is our portion and this is our lot” (Wis. 2:7).

Thus the fact that they are said, in joy and gladness, to eat flesh and drink wine, saying, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die,” plainly shows that some of the reprobate abandon themselves to present pleasures because they think they will remain in this life for a long time; others, because they believe that they will sooner lose the ability to do so, serve these same pleasures more luxuriously, saying, as we have already noted: “For this is our portion, and this is our lot.” They love the delights of the present life so greatly that they have no hope of delight thereafter. Often too one and the same [Col. 0217B] person both thinks that he will live here a long time and fears that he will quickly lose through death the capacity to enjoy fleshly pleasures. Thus he promises himself at once a long life and the nearness of death, yet does not cease from iniquities. But concerning these the prophet announces the divine sentence. It follows:

### Verse 14

> “And it was revealed in my ears by the Lord of hosts.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0217] Elsewhere: “The voice of the Lord of hosts was revealed in my ears.”]

They are rightly declared to be about to die in their iniquities, because the nearer they suppose death to be, the more they increase their iniquity, saying: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.” Whereas, on the contrary, they ought to say: “Let us fast and pray, for tomorrow we shall die.” This iniquity will not be forgiven them until either they die in sin and vices, or they are dragged down [Col. 0217C] to hell with their offences. But when the Lord says, “If this iniquity shall be forgiven you,” the incompleteness of the expression indicates the feeling of one vehemently indignant and confirms the threat, just as in the Psalm he says: “As I swore in my wrath: If they shall enter into my rest” (Ps. 94:11). It follows:

### Verse 15

> “Thus says the Lord God of hosts: Go, enter in to him who dwells in the tabernacle—to Shebna, the overseer of the temple—and say to him:”

### Verse 16

> “What have you here, or as who are you here, that you have cut out for yourself a tomb here? You have cut out a memorial for yourself on high, carefully hewing out for yourself a dwelling in the rock.”

[Col. 0217D] The tabernacle, or temple, is the present Church, of which it is said: “Behold the tabernacle of God with men” (Rev. 21:3); and: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 3:17). The overseer of this temple is any proud and useless bishop, who in the Gospel is called a hireling (John 10:12). Hence Shebna is interpreted “returning,” because priests of this sort return to the things behind and do not stretch forward to those things before them. When, however, the Lord said, “Go, enter in to him who dwells in the tabernacle,” he showed that any perfect saint ought privately to rebuke such overseers, [Col. 0218A] as Samuel rebuked Eli, the chief priest.

But let us see what he says to such a ruler: “What,” he says, “are you doing here?” As if to say: You accomplish nothing here for those subject to you. “Or as who are you here?” That is: Who are you here, as though you were someone? For you hold the place of prelacy but do not fulfil the work of a prelate. “That you have cut out for yourself a tomb here”: that is, spiritually dead yourself, you have corrupted human hearts so that they might love you, and so that you might be buried, as it were, in the tomb of the minds of those who favour you. For when a useless priest obtains human favour, he makes their hearts into a tomb in which he, already spiritually dead, may rest.

“You have cut out your memorial on high,” because you sought to be exalted long after death through human [Col. 0218B] praise. “Carefully in the rock”: that is, you have cut out for yourself a dwelling in the hard mind of worldly people, in which to shelter yourself. It follows:

### Verse 17

> “Behold, the Lord will cause you to be carried away as a capon is carried away, and, like a garment, he will lift you up.”

### Verse 18

> “He will crown you with a crown of tribulation; like a ball he will throw you into a broad and spacious land. There you will die, and there will be the chariot of your glory—the disgrace of your master’s house.”

### Verse 19

> “And I will drive you from your station, and I will depose you from your ministry.”

A capon is a castrated cock; the useless ruler is compared with it. For just as this cock cannot make hens fertile, so such a ruler, having lost the manly vigour of his mind, cannot cast spiritual [Col. 0218C] seed into the hearts of those subject to him. But as a fox carries off cocks, so the demon more deceitfully carries off his soul. And as a robber lifts away a cloak—that is, a garment—so the ancient ravisher will take up his body at the resurrection. And he to whom the crown of life had been promised, if he acted rightly, will now be crowned—that is, surrounded—with everlasting tribulation.

A ball is a round mass of hair with which young men play. Therefore this man will be thrown like a ball into a broad and spacious land, because he will be tossed far and wide for the sport of demons, struck and shaken by all, and there he will die the eternal death. And there will be the chariot of his glory: that is, his pomp of boasting and self-exaltation [Col. 0218D] will be reduced to this. This chariot of his glory is called “the disgrace of your master’s house,” because the pompous exaltation of a priest is the disgrace of the whole Church. Therefore one such as this is often expelled from his office even before death, in order that someone better may be appointed in his place. Hence it adds:

### Verse 20

> “And it shall be on that day: I will call my servant Eliakim, son of Hilkiah.”

### Verse 21

> “And I will clothe him with your robe, strengthen him with your girdle, and give your authority into his hand; and he will be like a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah.”

### Verse 22

> “And I will give the key of the house of David upon [Col. 0219A] his shoulder; and he will open, and none will shut; and he will shut, and none will open.”

### Verse 23

> “And I will fasten him as a peg in a faithful place, and he will be a throne of glory to his father’s house.”

### Verse 24

> “And I will hang upon him all the glory of his father’s house: diverse kinds of vessels, every small vessel, from vessels of bowls to every vessel of musicians.”

### Verse 25

> “On that day, says the Lord God of hosts, the peg which had been fastened in a faithful place will be removed; it will be broken and fall, and that which hung upon it will perish, because the Lord has spoken.”

What, indeed, is to be understood by Eliakim, whose name means “God’s resurrection” or “God has raised up,” except the reviving of divine grace and the restoration of holy religion [Col. 0219B] and devout conduct, which God awakens through good shepherds? For under evil rulers the institutions of holy religion and sacred order often collapse. But after good shepherds have succeeded in the place of bad ones—shepherds who are sons of Hilkiah, whose name means “the Lord’s portion,” that is, sons of love—all that had fallen is restored.

Therefore, after Shebna is deposed, Eliakim son of Hilkiah succeeds, to be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. For when useless pastors of the Church die, or are deposed on account of their fault, gentle and devout shepherds are often substituted in their place; with fatherly affection they provide for all things and, with fatherly compassion, console each individual believer.

Jerusalem and the house of Judah are the Catholic Church. [Col. 0219C] And although worse pastors more often succeed better ones than better pastors worse ones, nevertheless the prophet, herald of divine grace, foretells what he knows will be done through God’s grace: “And I will give,” he says, “the key of the house of David,” that is, of the Church, “upon his shoulder,” because he will bear the burden of pastoral care and, in his deeds as upon his shoulders, bear the discernment and authority of opening and shutting—that is, of loosing and binding—so that by his works he may show that what he looses and binds ought indeed to be loosed or bound. That is, he himself does those things for which he looses others, and does not do those things for which he binds others.

“And he will open, and none will shut,” because “whatever he looses on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16:19). “And he will shut, and none [Col. 0219D] will open,” because “whatever he binds on earth will be bound also in heaven.”

Or thus: understand the key of David as discernment and knowledge in interpreting the Scriptures, because those things which are explained are opened, and those concealed from us are shut. It is borne on the shoulder so that the teacher may do what he understands or teaches.

“And I will fasten him as a peg in a faithful place,” that is, in the Church, so that the conduct of all may depend on his teaching and his firm rectitude may raise and sustain everyone. “And he will be a throne of glory to his father’s house,” because all the elect will rest and glory in him. For his father is Hilkiah, whose name means “the Lord’s portion.” The vessels hanging upon him are the people whom he causes to tend upward. The vessels of bowls are those who make the minds of believers drunk with the cup of holy preaching. The vessels of musicians are those who soothe the hearts of hearers with divine songs. Or certainly, a musical vessel is whoever truthfully says: “Your statutes were songs to me in the place of my pilgrimage” (Ps. 118:54). Therefore all these and the rest who are described will hang upon him because, attending to his examples and words, they will abandon low things and be raised to things above.

[Col. 0220A] “On that day the peg that had been fastened in a faithful place will be removed and broken,” because, as has been said, when a good overseer succeeds, the useless overseer is cast down.

But if you understand the name “valley of vision” to signify the Church in general, from the beginning of the age to the [Col. 0220B] end, you may understand by Shebna the priests of the Old Testament and their teaching, and by Eliakim the priesthood of Christ, which is in the New Testament, and its priests, the preachers of his resurrection. For who is the one who dwells in the tabernacle of the Jews and in the house once belonging to God, except Jewish discourse and reasoning occupied with the reading of the Old Testament? To this tradition and teaching, therefore, it is said: “What are you doing here?” Why do you wish to build yourself a house in the setting of the letter, and a tabernacle which has no foundation in the hardness of that same letter? Therefore I tell you that you ought not labour in cutting out a tomb in which to lay the dead, or in which you yourself may lie dead, because the Lord will transfer your priesthood as a feminized [Col. 0220C] cock is customarily removed—a cock which can neither beget nor sing.

For Shebna means “turning” or “conversion.” Therefore the ruler of the Jews is told to turn from the Law to the Gospel; abandoning the images of sacrifices, he is to pass over to the reality of the spiritual sacrifice. Eliakim, however, whose name means “God’s resurrection” or “God has raised up,” by the interpretation of his name signifies Christ raised from the dead. He is also the son of Hilkiah, that is, of the Father of the Lord. For God the Father sealed him and said to him: “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17). Thus, after the old priesthood in Shebna has been deposed, the new one arises in Eliakim according to the order of Melchizedek. “I will call,” he says, “my servant Eliakim, and clothe him with your robe,” and so forth. Christ is clothed with the priestly robe [Col. 0220D]—that is, with his own flesh or with the holy Church—and is strengthened with the priestly girdle, because “the Lord has clothed himself with strength and girded himself with power” (Ps. 92:1).

Or the priestly girdle is justice, because it is written: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. 131:9). The Lord was strengthened with this girdle because it had been foretold of him: “Righteousness will be the girdle of his loins” (above, 11:5). To him the key of the house of David was given, as he himself says: “Thus says the Holy and True One, who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens: I know your works” (Rev. 3:7). He has this key upon his shoulder because through the cross which [Col. 0221A] he bore on his shoulder he opened for us the kingdoms of heaven and disclosed all the mysteries of the Law and the Prophets. Yet he also gave it to the first shepherd, who bore the person of the others, saying: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 16:19).

“And I will fasten him as a peg in a faithful place,” because he himself upholds and strengthens his Church, so that the gates of hell may not prevail against it. “And he will be a throne of glory to his father’s house,” because “the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever” (Luke 1:32), “that he may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory” (1 Sam. 2:8).

“And I will hang upon him all the glory of his father’s house,” so that all may honour the Son [Col. 0221B] as they honour the Father—he “who, being the radiance of his glory and the image of his substance, and sustaining all things, sits at the right hand of majesty on high” (Heb. 1:3). Thus all the glory of his Father’s house is rightly said to hang upon him, who is said to sustain all things, “into whom angels desire to look” (1 Pet. 1:12), and who themselves hang upon him. For indeed no one is glorified in the house of his Father except through him, “because there is salvation in no one else” (Acts 4:12).

And diverse kinds of vessels—that is, people—hang upon him, as he himself says: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32). How these things also apply to other priests may readily be understood from what has preceded. On that day—that is, in the time of Antichrist—the peg that had been fastened in a faithful place will be removed and broken, because many rulers will be taken from the Church and broken and cast down by adversities; and, when the peg—that is, the righteous pastor—is broken, the people who depended upon him will fall from faith and perish. To show that all these things will inevitably come to pass, he added at the end: “Because the Lord has spoken.”

## Chapter 23

### Verse 1

> “The burden of Tyre. Wail, ships of the sea, because the house from which they used to come has been laid waste; it has been revealed to them from the land of Kittim.”

This burden, placed in the tenth degree, pertains to those who have promised by a special profession to keep the commandments of God, signified by the number ten. Tyre means “narrowness,” [Col. 0221D] signifying the manner of life of those to whom it is said: “Enter through the narrow gate, for broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter through it. How narrow is the gate and confined the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it!” (Matt. 7:13). Hence Tyre too is situated on an island, bearing the figure of holy monasteries, where dwell those who have escaped the storms and shipwrecks of the world and have attained the stability of a settled way of life. Some among them are compelled, in order to provide necessities for their subsistence, to undertake certain worldly occupations. Thus at one time, like ships, they travel over the sea of the world to bring provisions; at another, they retreat to the monastery as to the quiet shore.

[Col. 0222A] What else, then, could we call these persons but ships of the sea? But because religion has now greatly declined in most monasteries, he says: “Wail, ships of the sea.” Those who gloried and rejoiced in their monastery’s religious observance now blush and grieve over its irreligion. And he adds why he commanded them to wail and lament: “Because the house from which they used to come has been laid waste”—that is, invisible enemies have carried off the inward riches from their monastery and destroyed the defences of virtues.

“It has been revealed to them from the land of Kittim,” because they often perceive the destruction of their own religious life more clearly when they see the good life of laypeople or speak with them. For what is signified by the land of Kittim, which also signifies Greece, [Col. 0222B] except the conduct of laypeople? Since laymen sometimes live rightly and fear the future judgment, Kittim is interpreted “marked” and “fearful.” A person in whose conduct the likeness of divine goodness is visible is rightly called marked; but the fearful person is he of whom Solomon says: “Blessed is the man who is always afraid” (Prov. 28:14). Therefore the devastation of their house is rightly revealed to them from the land of such people, because through consideration of their religious conduct they recognize that they themselves have lost religion.

Or every soul occupied by vices and evil thoughts may be called Tyre, that is, narrowness. The ships of the sea are minds devoted to worldly desires and affairs; they are commanded to wail by practising repentance, because “the world passes away and its desire” [Col. 0222C] (1 John 2:17), and so do all worldly things. For this sea can no longer be sailed, but all things will freeze. This age is already growing numb and is, as it were, gripped by icy cold, so that its activities can scarcely be carried on. Hence it is evident that the world itself is near its end. It follows:

### Verse 2

> “Be silent, you who dwell on the island. The merchants of Sidon, crossing the sea, have filled you.”

### Verse 3

> “In many waters is the seed of the Nile, the harvest of the river, its produce; and it became the commerce of the nations.”

“Be silent,” he says, “be silent, you who dwell on the island,” that is, in the monastery, because from shame you will not dare any longer to open your mouth. We dwell on an island as long as [Col. 0222D] we are battered by the temptations of this world and our island and little boat are struck on every side by the waves of the sea. The merchants of this island are from Sidon, which means “huntress,” and in which hunters dwell, of whom it is written: “He delivered me from the snare of hunters” (Ps. 90:3). But all merchants of the nations are compared with crops which quickly wither, or with the harvests of a river which receive no rain from heaven but water from the earth, and which will perish with the nations.

But let us return to the former sense. Sidon means “useless hunting.” What, then, is the commerce of useless hunting except the occupation of certain professed religious who, pursuing earthly things with their whole heart, strive continually to devote themselves to worldly affairs and business? Crossing the sea—that is, moving through the world—they fill this commerce in the waters, that is, among many peoples, because running here and there through different places, they gather temporal riches.

[Col. 0223A] The seed of the Nile—that is, what is sown beside the Nile—and its produce, that is, Tyre’s produce; and the harvest [Col. 0223B] of the same river—that is, what grew through the inundations of the Nile—and its produce. In the literal sense, the land of the Canaanites, in which Tyre is located, is barren; Egypt, however, which the Nile waters, is most fertile. Therefore Tyre’s merchants brought grain from Egypt by ship. This is what the text means: what the Egyptians sowed, the Tyrians received, and the harvest of the Egyptians was the produce of the Tyrians. So too those professing holy religion, receiving from laypeople, or from Egyptians, the things necessary for sustenance, are accustomed to repay them with spiritual gifts. But if such commerce is conducted immoderately, it is exceedingly harmful to religious people. Therefore, under the figure of Tyre, which receives the produce of the Egyptians, the life of those is now rebuked who say that they have renounced the world yet, doing nothing with their own hands, always seek with every greed to receive the goods of laypeople.

[Col. 0223C]

And their life has become “the commerce of the nations,” because very many who give them carnal things receive spiritual things. Yet this commerce is not transacted according to the perversity of Simon, but according to the custom of God’s servants to pray for their benefactors and repay them with spiritual benefits, and according to the Apostle’s statement concerning the holy poor who were in Judaea: “If the Gentiles have become partakers of their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in carnal things” (Rom. 15:27). It follows:

### Verse 4

> “Be ashamed, Sidon, says the sea—the strength of the sea, saying: I have not been in labour, nor have I given birth; I have not nourished young men, nor brought up virgins to maturity.”

The sea of this world, in which are small creatures with great ones, and the dragon which God formed to play in it, seeing that those who had formerly been captured by demons have been hunted [Col. 0223D] and caught from every mountain and hill by Christ’s hunters, speaks to the contrary strength of the hunters, which is interpreted Sidon, and says to it: “Be ashamed, Sidon, says the sea.” For I have neither laboured nor given birth, nor nourished young men captured by you, nor raised virgins whose foolishness is condemned in the Gospel. For the evil labour, birth, nourishment, and upbringing of virgins have been destroyed by the labour of Christ’s apostles, one of whom said: “My little children, for whom I am again in labour” (Gal. 4:19); “I gave you milk to drink” (1 Cor. 3:2); and “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2).

Saint Pope Gregory, speaking of blessed Job, says [Col. 0224A] (*Morals*, Preface to Book I): “A Gentile, a man without the Law, is brought forward so that the perversity of those who are under the Law may be put to shame. This is well and briefly said through the prophet: ‘Be ashamed, Sidon, says the sea.’ In Sidon, indeed, is figured the steadfastness of those established in the Law; in the sea, the life of the Gentiles. Therefore, ‘Be ashamed, Sidon,’ says the sea, because the life of those established under the Law is reproved by the life of the Gentiles, and the conduct of religious persons is put to shame by the conduct of secular people: for the former do not keep, even when promising, what they hear in the commandments, whereas the latter keep in their lives those things by which they are in no way bound through legal commands.”

Likewise Gregory in the *Pastoral Rule* (Part III, chapter 28) says: Often the life of the continent is put to shame by the conduct of secular people [Col. 0224B], since the latter undertake works beyond their station, while the former do not stir their hearts in accordance with their own order. Hence the prophet rightly says: “Be ashamed, Sidon, says the sea.” For Sidon is, as it were, brought to shame by the voice of the sea when, by comparison with the lives of secular persons who are tossed about in this world, the life of one who appears fortified and, as it were, steadfast is condemned. But “the strength of the sea” is the virtue of the good conduct of secular people.

It says: “I have not travailed nor given birth,” because secular men do not strive to bear children through preaching. Wherever these two words occur together, *to travail* means to suffer before birth, while *to give birth* means to bring forth the child. Spiritually [Col. 0224C], then, those travail and give birth who endure the labours of holy conception and carry within the womb of charity the children to be brought forth for God, so that they may give them birth in holy conduct—as religious men do, who watch over the winning of souls, begetting children for God through conversion and nourishing them by forming them in good morals. By “young men and virgins,” perhaps, he means both sexes, because holy men nourish young men for God, and religious women likewise. Thus Sidon is shamed when “the sea and the strength of the sea say: ‘I have not travailed nor given birth, nor have I nourished young men or brought virgins to maturity.’” It is as though secular life reproached the religious order, saying: You, who used spiritually to bring forth others for God [Col. 0224D], to nourish them, and to form them by good morals unto perfection, do not observe that saying of the Apostle: “Lest perhaps, after I have preached to others, I myself should become reprobate” (1 Cor. 9:27). What you have been accustomed to preach to others, you do not do yourself; whereas I, who have never borne or nourished others through conversion, perform holy works. It would not be so surprising if I lived secularly as it is in your case, since you have renounced the world. It follows:

**VERSE 5.**—“When it is heard in Egypt, they shall grieve when they hear concerning Tyre.”

Because good secular people grieve when they hear of the fall of religious persons. Or, when Egypt—which means “afflicting” and “confining”—hears, it too will be terrified, understanding that it will suffer the same things that Tyre has suffered [Col. 0225A]. Although this applies to every vice, it may also be understood of the diversity of heresies: when one heresy has been captured, another fears, and in another’s confusion recognizes that it too is about to be captured. It follows:

**VERSE 6.**—“Cross over the seas; howl, you who dwell on the island.”

What is signified by the seas except the bitter waves of secular activities? Therefore, to religious persons who desire to pursue worldly activities, this divine and striking sentence is spoken: let them cross the seas, because they are permitted to surpass the life of secular persons in earthly business and turbulent actions. For Tyre crosses the seas when a religious person pursues the bitterness of earthly activities more than secular men do [Col. 0225B]. But while such persons cross the seas, those who dwell in the monastery as on an island, and who would still wish—if possible—to preserve the uprightness of their order, are commanded to howl; that is, to lament the fall of their religious life.

Or: having crossed in mind the seas—that is, secular matters—and hastening toward the harbour of the heavenly homeland, mourn your sins, you who dwell upon an island, exposed on every side to the waves of temptations. It follows:

**VERSE 7.**—“Is this not she who was yours, who gloried from ancient days in her antiquity? Her own feet shall lead her far away into exile.”

Tyre “gloried from ancient days in its antiquity,” because many monks and professed religious are accustomed to glory more in the long duration of their way of life than in the perfection of their morals. But “her own feet shall lead her far away into exile,” because, at the prompting of the hidden adversary, such people sometimes flee from the monastery.

Or, her feet—that is, the affections of her heart—will lead her far from righteousness and toward foreign actions, that is, toward iniquities which she did not know.

Or, she who gloried in ancient errors will now withdraw far from them and devoutly receive the Gospel, so that she may be a stranger and sojourner upon the earth. It follows:

**VERSE 8.**—“Who has devised this against Tyre, once crowned, whose merchants were princes, whose traders were the renowned of the earth?”

[Col. 0225D] **VERSE 9.**—“The Lord of hosts has devised it, to strip away the pride of all glory and to bring all the renowned of the earth to dishonour.”

“Who,” he says, “has devised this against Tyre?” That is: Who would have thought that this would come upon the Church of religious persons, so that it should fall in this manner? He calls Tyre “once crowned,” that is, adorned with disciples. For the disciples of teachers are their crown. Hence Paul said to those whom he had gained for the Lord: “For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Are not you before the Lord Jesus at his coming?” (1 Thess. 2:19). And again: “My joy and my crown, stand firm thus in the Lord, dearly beloved” (Phil. 4:1).

[Col. 0226A] Tyre, then, was once crowned because those who had renounced the world, converting others by word and example, were adorned by a multitude of disciples. “Her merchants were princes.” Preachers are merchants because they distribute the talent of the word and are enriched by the good conduct of their hearers. Hence the master of the household says to them: “Conduct business until I come” (Luke 19:13).

A *trader* (*institor*) is one who constantly attends to business. Therefore the spiritual trader is the one who does what the Apostle says: “Preach the word; persist in season” (2 Tim. 4:2). These merchants and traders of Tyre were princes and renowned persons of the earth because they were set over churches and were everywhere held in distinction. But because this Tyre began, as prosperity followed prosperity, to grow proud [Col. 0226B] and to boast abroad of its holiness, it was permitted by divine judgment to fall openly into sins, for which it would blush before men. Thus, humbled through outward disgrace, it might return to the grace from which it had departed through pride while seeking human praise.

For the Lord of hosts devised this, that he might take from her the pride of all her glory and bring all the renowned of the earth to dishonour: that is, that he might show as dishonoured all who, while still upon earth, boasted that they were renowned for holiness, or who were thought renowned because of their merits. Or, he might bring to dishonour and confusion the “renowned of her earth”—that is, the excellent virtues of her mind—because of pride. It follows:

[Col. 0226C] **VERSE 10.**—“Pass over your land like a river, daughter of the sea; there is no girdle for you any longer.”

**VERSE 11.**—“He will stretch out his hand over the sea; he will shake kingdoms. The Lord has commanded against Canaan, that he may crush its strong men.”

**VERSE 12.**—“And he said: You shall no longer continue to glory, O oppressed virgin, daughter of Sidon. Rising up, pass over to Kittim beyond the straits; even there you shall have no rest.”

Just as a river, when it has swollen violently, cannot hold its water within its bed, so a depraved soul is often filled to such a degree by the flood of unlawful thoughts that it can no longer contain within the secrecy of its heart the overflowing river of wickedness, but allows it to burst forth into outward action. Hence the rebuke now aptly follows: “Pass over your land like a river, daughter of the sea.” For one passes over the land of one’s body like a river extending beyond its banks when one expresses in bodily action the malice conceived in the heart. And this soul is rightly called not the daughter of Jerusalem, but the daughter of the sea—that is, of the world—because desires of this kind have been generated in its heart not from heavenly love but from the wickedness of the present world; and, receiving worldly malice within itself, it has become a daughter of the world.

Since after impure thoughts the integrity of the flesh perishes, he says: “There is no girdle for you any longer.” For restraint of lust is signified by the girdle. Hence the Lord also says: “Let your loins be girded” [Col. 0227A] (Luke 12:35). We gird our loins when through continence we restrain the lust of the flesh. Whoever therefore loosens the flesh unto lust is rightly said no longer to have a girdle. But because the perverse soul thinks in this way in prosperity and lays aside the girdle of continence, it is just that it should be struck by adversities, so that perhaps even amid adversity it may recover its senses.

Therefore the Lord will stretch out his hand over the sea, stirring the stormy tempests of the world against it, and he will shake the kingdoms of the world against it. What is said, as it were, concerning one soul is to be understood of many. Hence the sea—that is, the world—rises against any such soul, and kingdoms are shaken against it, because in all earthly kingdoms secular men detest religious persons [Col. 0227B], and, by God’s ordering, worldly adversities rise against them.

Now Canaan is interpreted as “their movement.” Their movement is that of which the Psalmist says: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps had nearly slipped” (Ps. 72:2); and of which he again says: “Let not the foot of pride come against me, and let not the hand of the sinner move me” (Ps. 35:12). Therefore, because those who love the world’s blandishments or grow proud of their virtues are moved from the state of perseverance by Satan’s impelling hand, “the Lord commanded against Canaan”—that is, he stirred up manifold scandals against their movement—so that through adversities he might crush its strong men: that is, the virtues in which they had begun to glory. And when the strong men, that is, the virtues, had been crushed [Col. 0227C], he said:

“You shall no longer continue to glory in your religious way of life, daughter of Sidon, once a virgin, but now enduring the accusation and reproach of dishonourable conduct.” For the Lord permits virtues from which the mind drew pride to be crushed, so that, taking from it the boasting of vain presumption, he may instil a sense of humility. She is called a virgin not because she is now a virgin, but because, after losing the state of salvation, she is called what she had been to increase the fullness of her shame. For this reason she is also called the daughter of Sidon, since in Sidon the steadfastness of life expresses continence. Then he says by way of rebuke:

“In Kittim, rising up, pass over beyond the straits.” That is: [Col. 0227D] Go into the world, O religious person; “even there you shall have no rest,” because there too you will suffer exceedingly grievous adversities. Every soul also that is set amid the waves of the world and carried about by every wind of doctrine should be called Canaan, which is interpreted as “wavering” or “commotion.” Thus it benefits Tyre and its afflictions that the strength of the Canaanites should perish, so that its inhabitants may be told that they can no longer inflict injuries or oppress by iniquity the virgin daughter of Sidon. Whoever has been captured by the devil amid the disturbance of various vices and given over to the insults of dishonour, so as to defile his body with pleasures and shamefulness, is a son or daughter of Sidon. Kittim, however, is called “the completed scourge.” And we often see in the world some people pass from one pursuit [Col. 0228A] to another: for example, those who have had an unhappy experience of military service become merchants, and advocates in turn take up arms. Yet those among them who are to be saved, by God’s dispensation, always find labour and miseries, so that they may learn to trust not in their own skill but in God. It follows:

**VERSE 13.**—“Behold the land of the Chaldeans: such a people did not exist. Asshur founded it; they led away its mighty men into captivity, undermined its houses, and reduced it to ruin.”

The Chaldeans are said to mean “as it were, words,” or “as it were, of iron.” Those men are “as it were, words” of whom Solomon says: “My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent to them” (Prov. 1:10). They are also “as it were, wild beasts,” that is, living after the manner of beasts, of whom the Lord said to his disciples: “Behold, I send you as lambs among wolves” [Col. 0228B] (Luke 10:3). Understand these Chaldeans, then, as those who overthrew Tyre. For perverse human beings, and even demons, try to deceive us in two ways: by flattering and by terrifying.

“Such a people did not exist,” because they are exceedingly cunning in deception. “Asshur”—that is, the devil—“founded their land,” that is, their pregnant mind, just as, on the contrary, the Lord founded Zion. For as Christ is the foundation of the assembly of religious persons, so the devil is the foundation of the assembly of the reprobate. Such men or malignant spirits led Tyre’s mighty men into captivity because by either pleasing persuasions or harsh terrors [Col. 0228C] they drew into sin religious persons who were thought strong in firmness of mind.

Their houses—that is, their minds—are undermined because, God abandoning them, their hearts do not seek the inward reward; and they are undermined because they are deceived into rejoicing in temporal rather than eternal glory. They are undermined because, while neglecting the future things of the heavenly homeland, they fall into their own pleasures. When the houses have been undermined, Tyre is reduced to ruin, because when the foundation of charity has been removed, the Church of religious persons falls. For if they remained firmly rooted and founded in charity, their city could in no way be reduced to ruin by the Chaldeans. When it has been overthrown, the prophet repeats the sentence set forth at the beginning, saying [Col. 0228D]:

**VERSE 14.**—“Howl, ships of the sea, because your strength has been laid waste.”

For when religious life has been scattered from the monasteries and their order has slipped away, those who used to go out for necessary provisions have lost their strength.

Or, all the good things of this world and the entire labour of mortals are compared to the uncertain course of ships, because they quickly perish and all the strength of those sailing is dissolved. It follows:

**VERSE 15.**—“And it shall be in that day: You, O Tyre, shall be forgotten for seventy years, as the days of one king. But after seventy years Tyre shall be like the song of a harlot.”

By Tyre, as has often been said, is understood the life of religious persons, or their Church, or any religious soul. But Tyre, brought to ruin, shall be forgotten because that which was celebrated everywhere by a famous reputation while it lived holily, having now fallen from its state, has been consigned to oblivion by all, made vile, and accounted as nothing both by God and by human beings for seventy years: that is, until the completion of seventy years, namely, until the perfection of good works. For the seventy years during which Israel also served signify the fullness of good works, which is given through the grace of the Holy Spirit according to the Decalogue of the Law. For seven times ten makes seventy: seven pertains to the sevenfold grace, and ten to the number of God’s commandments.

[Col. 0229B] “You shall be forgotten,” he says, “as the days of one king”: that is, as, when some king has died, the days during which he reigned are consigned to oblivion, so the days during which righteousness held dominion in you shall be forgotten, since the righteousness that reigned in you has died and another king has succeeded in its place—namely, sin. For it is written: “Even if I say to the righteous that he shall surely live, and, trusting in his righteousness, he does iniquity, all his righteous deeds shall be consigned to oblivion” (Ezek. 33:13).

“But after seventy years”—that is, after the time during which it served injustice—“Tyre shall be like the song of a harlot”: that is, the recollection of its evils, namely, the lament of repentance. For after a harlot has ceased to commit fornication, she is accustomed sorrowfully to remember [Col. 0229C] the things she did and to recall them in a mournful song. Similarly, the soul that long consented, as though subject to the lust of corruptors, to the suggestions of unclean spirits, at last recovering its senses, is ashamed of what it has done and laments the deeds it shamefully committed. For “song” here signifies not the voice of joy but that of sadness and lamentation. It follows:

**VERSE 16.**—“Take the harp; go around the city, harlot consigned to oblivion. Sing well; repeat the song often, that you may be remembered.”

What is figured by the harp except the chastisement of the flesh? For the harp gives its sound from the lower part; likewise bodily mortification and humble repentance make a sweet song rise up from below to the ears of the heavenly beholder. Therefore, he says, take the harp—that is, the mortification of the flesh—upon which you may sound sweet melody before God; and go around the city of the Church: that is, be among penitents, who customarily stand outside the house of prayer, or be among the least of the faithful. Some faithful persons are in the midst of this holy city; others are at its extremities. For the holiest are in its midst, while those who are least in the body of Christ dwell at its extremities. Therefore one goes around the city when, counting oneself humbly among these, one pursues works of righteousness.

“Sing well,” he says: that is, fittingly lament the evils you have done, and tune all the strings of the virtues [Col. 0230A] that were once slackened into praises. “Repeat the song often”: that is, lament frequently, so that you may be remembered by God, who had consigned you to oblivion because you too had forgotten his commandments. It follows:

**VERSE 17.**—“And it shall be after seventy years: the Lord will visit Tyre and restore her to her earnings, and she shall again commit fornication with all the kingdoms of the earth upon the face of the earth.”

**VERSE 18.**—“And her trade and her earnings shall be consecrated to the Lord; they shall not be stored up or laid away, because her trade shall be for those who dwell before the Lord, that they may eat unto fullness and be clothed unto old age.”

[Col. 0230B] After seventy years—that is, after repentance has been performed and the fullness of good works attained—the Lord will visit Tyre, restoring its former grace; and after this he will restore it to its earnings, that is, its gains, so that it may again acquire temporal goods in sufficient measure.

And again, as it used to do, it will commit fornication—that is, engage in trade. For fornication is used for trade or the acquisition of riches. For when it says, “She shall commit fornication, and her earnings shall be consecrated to the Lord, because her trade shall be for those who dwell before the Lord,” this agrees with the saying in which the Lord exhorts: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity” (Luke 19:9). *Mammon* is interpreted as riches; although acquired by just labour, they are nevertheless called riches of iniquity because it is unjust—that is, at variance with equity—that one should abound in riches while another is in need. The desire for them is called fornication because only that love is chaste by which God and one’s neighbour are loved. Whatever is loved below God, especially by those who have renounced the world, is not loved with chaste love; and therefore, as has been said, the desire for and acquisition of temporal goods is called fornication.

But the trade and earnings of one who thus commits fornication are consecrated to the Lord, and that person’s trade is for those who dwell before the Lord when he makes friends for himself from the mammon of iniquity; when [Col. 0230D] he acquires riches for no other purpose than to provide them for God’s servants. Thus he will again commit fornication with the kingdoms of the whole earth upon the face of the earth, because in all kingdoms and nations the righteous are compelled by the necessities of this life to acquire temporal goods.

“And her trade and her earnings,” which she obtains in those very transactions, “shall be consecrated to the Lord,” because they will spend them on works of almsgiving and mercy. For they will not be avariciously stored up or laid aside to be kept for private use. Her trade shall serve those who dwell before the Lord—that is, those who remain in monasteries—so that they may eat and be clothed from it: they may eat unto fullness, not unto luxury, but unto the satisfaction of nature [Col. 0231A]. But now that the ten burdens and their treatises have been completed, let us also bring this present little book to an end [Col. 0232A], in order that in other volumes we may explain what follows.

Here ends the third book.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0231]

## CHAPTER XXIV

[Col. 0231A]

**VERSE 1.**—“Behold, God will lay waste the earth and strip it bare; he will afflict its face and scatter its inhabitants.”

**VERSE 2.**—“And it shall be as with the people, so with the priest; as with the servant, so with his master; as with the maidservant, so with her mistress [Col. 0231B]; as with the buyer, so with the seller; as with the lender, so with the borrower; as with the creditor, so with the debtor.”

**VERSE 3.**—“The earth shall be utterly laid waste and utterly plundered.”

These and the following words can be understood in a particular sense of the captivity and destruction of the Jews, because the Lord himself also foretold it, saying: “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, then know that its desolation has drawn near. Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, and let those in its midst depart, and let those in the regions not enter into it; for these are days of vengeance, that all things which have been written may be fulfilled. But woe to the pregnant and nursing women in those days. For there shall be great distress [Col. 0231C] upon the earth and wrath against this people; and they shall fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive into all nations” (Luke 21:20).

Thus the prophetic discourse can be understood to concern the sense contained in these words of the Lord, from the place where it says, “Behold, the Lord will lay waste the earth,” up to that where it is said, “Terror and pit and snare are upon you, inhabitant of the earth.” For then, through Vespasian and Titus, the whole land of the Jews was laid waste and devastated in vengeance for the blood of the Lord, stripped of every good thing; and its inhabitants were scattered in captivity among all nations. People and priests, slaves and free persons, rich and poor alike perished in the same destruction [Col. 0231D] or were led into captivity. The remaining matters that follow, to be understood in this manner, we leave to diligent readers for the sake of brevity. But returning to the beginning of the discourse, let us apply these things generally to the day of judgment.

For then “the Lord will lay waste the earth,” because he will level mountains with valleys and consume with fire all things upon the earth; “and he will strip it bare” of all inhabitants, plants, trees, and every impurity. “And he will afflict its face,” because the whole surface of the earth will burn. “And he will scatter its inhabitants,” because all nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another as a shepherd separates sheep from goats (Matt. 25:32). He will also scatter the reprobate themselves into distinct groups: the proud with the proud [Col. 0232A], the avaricious with the avaricious, murderers with murderers, deceivers with deceivers, and all like persons with their like. What follows:

“And it shall be as with the people, so with the priest,” and so forth, through, “As with the creditor, so with the debtor,” must be understood in accordance with what the Lord said: “In the days of Lot they ate and drank, bought and sold, planted and built; but on the day Lot went out from Sodom, fire and sulphur rained from heaven and destroyed them all. So it shall be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed” (Luke 17:28). Thus, as in Sodom all who were intent upon different worldly activities perished together, so also at the end of the age all those of whom the prophet now speaks will perish together, because the world will end with its inhabitants. Then “the earth shall be utterly laid waste,” because it will be wholly changed from the form it now has. “And it shall be utterly plundered,” because all sinners will be snatched away from it. It follows: “For the Lord has spoken this word.”

[Col. 0232C] **VERSE 4.**—“The earth mourned and faded away; the height of the people of the earth was weakened.”

**VERSE 5.**—“And the earth was slain [Vulgate: defiled] by its inhabitants, because they transgressed the laws, changed justice, and broke the everlasting covenant.”

**VERSE 6.**—“Therefore a curse shall devour the earth, and its inhabitants shall sin; therefore its cultivators shall become mad, and few human beings shall be left.”

By these words the Lord announces the evils that were to come near the end of the age—that is, in our own times. “The earth mourned,” he says. As the earth rejoices in the virtues of its inhabitants, so it mourns over their vices and iniquities [Col. 0232D]. “And the world faded away,” because wickedness abounds everywhere. Wickedness (*nequitia*), so called from *nequidquam*, “to no purpose,” is a falling away from good, by which each person tends toward nothingness. Therefore the earth is said to fade away and be weakened because its inhabitants fade and fail through wickedness, and their minds are weakened away from good. The world faded away because throughout the whole world not only the goods of the heart but also those of the body have been greatly altered and almost reduced to nothing. “The height of the people of the earth was weakened,” because the pride of earthly people has been weakened. “And the earth was slain by its inhabitants,” which lost its customary fertility because of the malice of those who inhabit it.

Or “the earth was slain” is expressed figuratively when earthly people are said to have been killed by evil deeds [Col. 0233A]. For he explained in what way he called the earth slain when he showed carnal persons, like fools, submerged in utterly wicked conduct: because they transgressed God’s laws by following their own desires, changed justice into injury, and broke the everlasting covenant of mutual fellowship and friendship. Brotherly love and the covenant of fellowship are rightly called everlasting, because “charity never fails” (1 Cor. 13:8).

Therefore, because they acted thus, the curse shall devour the earth, because on account of human malice the heavenly curse consumes the earth so that it bears no fruit. Hence the first man heard after his sin: “Cursed is the earth in your work” (Gen. 3:17). For divine mercy does not yet wish to curse human beings, but turns upon the earth the curse which they themselves deserve, so that, afflicted by its barrenness, they may recover their senses.

But alas! Human perversity is no longer corrected by afflictions but becomes worse. This is what he says: “The curse shall devour the earth, and its inhabitants shall sin.” For the more the heavenly curse removes the earth’s fertility, the more greedily some of its inhabitants sin; and therefore, abandoned in their iniquities through the Lord’s wrath, its cultivators will become mad in still graver wickedness, losing reason and slaughtering one another like beasts. And few human beings shall be left, once the rest have been consumed by famine, sword, and manifold calamity [Col. 0233C].

Or, at the Judge’s coming, they shall become mad through fear of the punishments threatening them, through inward confusion, and through pain. When these have been cast out, few human beings shall remain, that is, only the elect; for “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20:16). They are few in comparison with the multitude of the reprobate, but many in their own number. Yet the coming calamity of the wicked is described in many ways, as follows:

**VERSE 7.**—“The vintage mourned, the vine was weakened, all who were glad in heart groaned.”

**VERSE 8.**—“The joy of tambourines ceased; the sound of those rejoicing was silent; the sweetness of the harp was hushed.”

**VERSE 9.**—“They shall not drink wine with song; the drink shall be bitter to those who drink it.”

[Col. 0233D] **VERSE 10.**—“The city of vanity has been crushed; every house has been closed, with no one entering.”

**VERSE 11.**—“There shall be a cry concerning wine in the streets; all joy has been deserted; the joy of the earth has been taken away.”

**VERSE 12.**—“Solitude has been left in the city, and calamity shall crush its gates.”

The vintage is when individual human beings are gathered from this world like grapes from a vineyard. But the vintage mourned because the end of sinners is sorrowful and lamentable. The vine is the human race, because “Israel is a luxuriant vine” (Hos. 10:1). But the vine was weakened because those now strong in committing evils will be weak in the resurrection. And then all who were glad in heart will groan. Though the righteous sometimes appear outwardly glad [Col. 0234A], their conscience is always inwardly sorrowful while they are pilgrims here; but the reprobate rejoice with their whole heart in worldly prosperity. Hence Solomon says: “The heart of fools is where there is joy, and the heart of the wise where there is sorrow” (Eccl. 7:5). Those, therefore, who now rejoice in heart in present things will groan at the end. Of this it is added:

For “the joy of tambourines has ceased, the sound of those rejoicing has been silent, the sweetness of the harp has been hushed.” All the things in which perverse human beings now rejoice will then have passed, and the Judge will appear, to render to each according to his work. Sinners will no longer drink wine with song, but the drink of the cup of God’s wrath will be bitter to them. Let those hear this who at banquets indulge not only their gluttony and drunkenness but also their ears [Col. 0234B], so that every sense and the strength of the soul are softened. Every drink and intoxication which now falsely promises them sweetness will be turned into bitterness.

“The city of vanity has been crushed”: that is, that great city Babylon, whose citizens are all the reprobate, and in whose figure the murderer Cain first built a city (Gen. 4:17). Hence also the Lord says to Israel through Hosea: “For I am God and not a man, the Holy One in your midst, and I will not enter the city” (Hos. 11:9). But this impious city, into which God does not enter and whose beginning was from the accursed fratricide, is the city of vanity. For all passing things are designated by the name of vanity, as Scripture says: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Ecclus. [Col. 0234C] 1:1). This city, therefore, will be crushed at the end. And what are the houses of this city except individual reprobate persons? Hence the most wicked demon says: “I will return to my house, from which I came out” (Luke 11:24). For these houses are now open because the minds of the perverse lie open to all suggestions of demons and gladly receive them. But then every house shall be shut, with no one entering, because then, too late, the reprobate will shut their consciences so that they no longer consent to the will of malignant spirits, once they have begun to be punished.

“There shall be a cry concerning wine in the streets,” because those who walk the broad way of the world and are intoxicated with wine or earthly cares will weep bitterly. For what is signified by wine except excessive drinking, worldly care, or whatever badly intoxicates the mind? And what do streets, named from breadth, express except the life of those who walk the broad road which leads to perdition? *Platos* (πλάτος), indeed, is called “breadth” in Greek, and from it the name *platea*, “street,” has been derived among us. Thus there shall be a cry concerning wine—that is, arising from wine—in the streets, because “then all the tribes of the earth shall mourn” (Matt. 24:3). Hence it is added that “all joy has been deserted; the joy of the earth has been taken away”—taken away, certainly, to heaven. And because, as was said, “the city of vanity has been crushed,” it fittingly follows that “solitude has been left in the city, and calamity shall crush its gates.” For what city is this except Babylon? And what are the gates of that city [Col. 0235A] except teachers of error, who lead those whom they have captured into confusion as into Babylon? But solitude is left in this city because Babylon, cast into outer darkness, will henceforth be visited by no human being. “And calamity shall crush its gates,” because the teachers of error will be subject to torments. Or the gates are sins, which will then be crushed by calamity because they will be punished eternally. It follows:

**VERSE 13.**—“For these things shall be in the midst of the earth, in the midst of the peoples.”

The things described above shall be in the midst of the earth because, as is said, the Lord will come for judgment in the air above the Mount of Olives. Or, because what is common is called “the middle,” these things will happen in the midst of the earth, because the Lord will be present to all alike, so that all may render an account and each may be judged without respect of persons [Col. 0235B]. Above he had said that “few human beings shall be left,” that is, the elect alone, all the rest perishing. He now supplies a comparison to show how they are to be left, adding:

“As if the few olives that remained were shaken from the olive tree, and the clusters after the vintage has been completed.” For just as a few olives remain on the tree after shaking, and a few clusters in the vineyard after the vintage, so few elect will remain on the day of judgment. The olive tree is the *olea*, the olive fruit the *oliva*, oil the juice (*oleum*), and *olivum* the liquid; yet they are customarily used interchangeably. The verse as expounded may also be read thus: “For these things shall be in the midst of the earth, in the midst of the peoples: as if the remaining olives that remain were shaken from the olive tree, and clusters after the vintage has been completed.” Thus also will be done the things said below concerning the elect: as if the remaining olives or clusters were gathered. For when the multitude of the reprobate has been gathered—of whom he said above, “For the vintage mourned”—and trodden in the winepress of the wine of God’s wrath, the few elect who remain shall be led to the joys of which it follows:

**VERSE 14.**—“These shall lift up their voice and give praise.”

They will indeed fulfil the Scripture which says: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; for ever and ever [Col. 0235D] they shall praise you” (Ps. 83:5). It follows:

“When the Lord has been glorified, they shall neigh from the sea.” On the day of judgment, according to the Apostle’s declaration, “the Lord will come to be glorified in his saints and to be made wonderful in all who have believed” (2 Thess. 1:3). Therefore, when he has been glorified, they shall neigh from the sea, because the saints, returning from this world to their homeland, shall utter a voice of exultation. For then those redeemed by the Lord “shall return and come to Zion with praise, and everlasting joy shall be upon their heads” (Isa. 35:10). It follows:

**VERSE 15.**—“Therefore glorify [Col. 0236A] the Lord in teachings, the name of the Lord God of Israel in the islands of the sea.”

Because the wicked shall be destroyed and the Lord shall be glorified in his saints, therefore, O preachers, glorify the Lord in your teachings; and preach the name of the Lord God of Israel not only throughout the whole world, but even in the remote islands of the sea—he who was once known in Judaea alone. Then the voice of the prophets is introduced, saying:

**VERSE 16.**—“From the ends of the earth we have heard praises: glory to the righteous one.”

For the prophets heard in the Spirit the praises of Christ resounding not only from the world, but even from the world’s farthest bounds. Hence they also say: “Sing to the Lord a new song; his praise from the ends of the earth” (Isa. 42:10). [Col. 0236B] Or let us understand “the ends of the earth” as the point at which earthly desires come to an end. Thus praises come from the ends of the earth, because only after earthly desires have come to an end within us are we able to praise God. “For praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15:9). Yet there the prophet saw Christ’s glory to be sung throughout the whole breadth of the world; considering that this glory would not be known by the Jewish people, he added:

“My secret is mine, my secret is mine.” [Note: [Col. 0235D] Another reading: “And I said: My secret,” etc.] As though he said: What I know, this Jewish people does not know; rather, it lies hidden in my heart and in that of the faithful. Again, seeing that, stirred by zeal for the Law, they persecuted the Lord for healing the sick on Sabbaths [Col. 0236C] and persecuted his disciples for preaching new things—although, on the contrary, they themselves thereby violated the Law more truly—he grieved over their blindness and wickedness, saying:

“Woe is me! Transgressors have transgressed, and by the transgression of transgressors they have transgressed.”

They transgressed the Law when they defended the Law against Christ and his disciples. Or, after contemplating the condemnation of the wicked and the recompense of the righteous, the prophet spoke to himself in the inward feeling of his heart: I cannot recount all that I see; my tongue clings in my throat, and grief shuts up my voice. Woe is me! How great are the punishments I behold! And I grieve most of all because all have transgressed God’s Law and are struck by the just Judge. But let us return to the former sense. For since persecutions [Col. 0236D] followed from this, he added:

**VERSE 17.**—“Terror and pit and snare are upon you, inhabitant of the earth.”

**VERSE 18.**—“And it shall be: whoever flees from the sound of terror shall fall into the pit; and whoever extricates himself from the pit shall be caught in the snare.”

In times of persecution, the Christian who was an inhabitant of earth—that is, whose way of life was not in heaven, who had planted the root of his heart in the love of earthly things—fearing temporal evils, said to himself: “If this persecution presses us, I shall deny that I am a Christian merely in words, and afterwards I shall do penance; otherwise I cannot escape.” While thinking such things [Col. 0237A] and fleeing from the sound of terror—that is, seeking to escape the persecutors’ threats—he fell into the pit of denial. And while he wished to extricate himself from the pit, that is, while he thought of doing penance, he was suddenly put to death by persecutors, or forestalled by death of whatever kind; and thus, bound with Satan in the snare of everlasting damnation, he was held fast.

The snare may also be understood as covetousness, by which one was held while trying to extricate himself from the pit; for often someone was prevented from doing penance in such circumstances because he feared losing the possessions he held in the world. The same will happen in the time of Antichrist; after the savagery of whose persecution, because the day of judgment will come, it is appropriately added:

“For the floodgates on high are opened, and the foundations of the [Col. 0237B] earth shall be shaken,” etc. Then the floodgates—that is, the windows—on high shall be opened, because the heavens will visibly stand open, both to receive the elect and to show the reprobate the source of their endless grief. “And the foundations of the earth shall be shaken,” because there will be an earthquake such as never was. Mystically, however, the earth is the sinner, because after his sin man heard: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19). But what this earth—that is, each individual sinner—will then suffer is shown when it says:

**VERSE 19.**—“With breaking the earth shall be broken; with crushing the earth shall be crushed; with shaking the earth shall be shaken.”

**VERSE 20.**—“With agitation the earth shall be agitated like a drunkard, and shall be removed like a one-night tent; [Col. 0237C] and its iniquity shall weigh upon it, and it shall fall and shall not add to rise again.”

For every reprobate person shall then be crushed and shaken; and, like a tent in which he stayed for one night of this present life, he shall be removed in the morning—that is, at the resurrection. The weight of his iniquity shall press upon him, so that he cannot be lifted from the earth when the saints are caught up “in the clouds to meet Christ in the air” (1 Thess. 4:16). He shall fall into the abyss of eternal damnation and shall not add to rise again, because he shall never afterwards come forth from it. It follows:

**VERSE 21.**—“And it shall be on that day: the Lord will visit upon the host of heaven on high, and upon the kings who are upon the earth.”

[Col. 0237D] By “the host of heaven” he means demons, who are in this air. For air is called heaven, as it is written: “The kite in heaven knew its time” (Jer. 8:7). Therefore, on that day the Lord will visit upon the host of heaven, because he will exact vengeance upon the powers of the air; and upon the kings of the earth—that is, the princes of this age, or the demons who are the rulers of this world’s darkness. It follows:

**VERSE 22.**—“And they shall be gathered into the gathering of one bundle in the pit; and they shall be shut up there in prison, and after many days they shall be visited.”

When the prophet had spoken of the last day, saying that “on that day the Lord will visit upon the host of heaven and earth,” he at once turned the eye of his mind to the things which occur daily at the death of the reprobate. For when they depart [Col. 0238A] from their bodies, they are gathered into the Tartarean pit; and just as those said to have laboured in the vineyard all received together the denarius of eternal life (Matt. 20:10), although “in the Father’s house are many dwelling-places” (John 14:2), and “star differs from star in glory” (1 Cor. 15:41), so all the reprobate are gathered into the one bundle of eternal damnation, although tares are burned in separate bundles. Although the kinds of punishments are various, they are all nevertheless bound together in one bundle. For, just as one sun touches all of us, yet we do not all burn under it in the same degree, because the weight of heat is felt according to the constitution of each body, so there is one Gehenna that afflicts the condemned, yet it does not burn all with the same intensity; for what bodily constitution accomplishes here, [Col. 0238B] the differing basis of merits accomplishes there.

Therefore, as each departs this life, he shall be gathered into the gathering of one bundle, into the pit, and shall be shut up there in prison. Hell, as was said above, is called a pit because it swallows up forever, amid encircling torments, all whom it has once seized, leaving them constantly tossed and terrified. It is also called a prison because whoever is captured by it is held fast permanently. “They shall be shut up in prison,” he says, after being brought forth from their bodies. And after many days—that is, at the end of the age—they shall be visited, so that they may come to resume their bodies and thereafter be punished doubly. It follows:

**VERSE 23.**—“And the moon shall blush, and the sun shall be confounded, when the Lord of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and is glorified in the presence of his elders [Col. 0238C].”

“The moon shall blush and the sun shall be confounded,” because “the sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give its light” (Matt. 24:29). Yet it is reported that the sun, moon, and stars will not then lose their light, but that all lights will seem darkened in comparison with the light that is Christ, just as a candle has no light in the sunbeam.

Or the moon shall blush and the sun shall be confounded when they see that people who enjoyed their light did nothing worthy of God’s goodness—he “who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil” (Matt. 5:45)—just as a steward or manager, upon his lord’s arrival, sees the household subjected to various punishments and sees that it has not fulfilled [Col. 0238D] his commands.

Mount Zion and Jerusalem are the Church. “For that Jerusalem which is above is free, which is our mother” (Gal. 4:26). The elders are those mature in the old age of character. “For the grey hairs of humanity are understanding, and a spotless life is old age” (Wis. 4:9). Therefore the Lord shall reign on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem—that is, in the Church—and shall be glorified in the presence of his elders, that is, of the faithful mature in character.

Or Mount Zion is the height of contemplation, because Zion means “watchtower”; Jerusalem is the vision of peace. Its elders are the apostles, patriarchs, and leaders of religion. Therefore, on this mountain and in this Jerusalem, the King of the ages will reveal himself and disclose his glory before these elders.
