Thus, having prophesied the condemnation of the reprobate [Col. 0239A] and the glory of the righteous, the prophet sings a hymn to God concerning all these things, adding:

## CHAPTER 25

**VERSE 1.**—“O Lord, you are my God; I shall exalt you and give thanks to your name, because you have done wonders: ancient counsels, faithful. Amen.”

“I shall give thanks,” he says, that is, I give thanks to your name, because you have done wonders by rendering to sinners what you had threatened and to the saints what you had promised. In these things you have fulfilled ancient counsels, saying to the elect: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34); and likewise to the reprobate: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid., 41). For you determined long ago [Col. 0239B] what you prepared from the foundation of the world. And these counsels were faithful, because you faithfully fulfilled what you had determined, just as in the Book of Joshua, by prophetic speech, the future kingdom of the righteous is spoken of as though past: “Not one word of what he had promised to bestow upon them proved void; rather, all things were fulfilled in deeds” (Josh. 21:43). Hence *Amen* is added, which means “truly” or “faithfully.” But what wonders he has performed, and what counsels he has fulfilled, is also made clear here when it follows:

**VERSE 2.**—“For you have made the city a heap, the strong city a ruin, the house of foreigners so that it is no city, and it shall never be built again.”

But what is this city except that of which he said above: “The city of vanity has been crushed”? When a city [Col. 0239C] is wholly destroyed, it is reduced to a heap. Therefore the Lord has made the city a heap, because in judgment he utterly overthrew that great Babylon. It is also the house of foreigners, that is, of those alien to the fellowship of the righteous. But it shall no longer be a city, nor shall it ever be built again, as was said above: “That glorious Babylon in the kingdoms, renowned in the pride of the Chaldeans, shall be as when the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah” (above, 13:19). It follows:

**VERSE 3.**—“Because of this a strong people shall praise you; a city of mighty nations shall fear you.”

**VERSE 4.**—“For you have become strength to the poor, strength to the needy in tribulation, hope from the storm, and shade from the heat.”

[Col. 0239D] Because of this—that is, because you have made the city an everlasting heap—a strong people, the elect in harmony with the judgments of your justice, shall praise you; and the city of mighty nations, that is, the Church of saints gathered from all nations, shall fear you.

For “the fear of the Lord is pure, enduring for ever and ever” (Ps. 18:10). With this fear the Church of the righteous will always fear God, even in that kingdom of blessedness, because it would not love perfectly unless it also feared God. But this people is called strong, and this city of mighty nations, because the saints are strong here in spiritual conflict and are strengthened there by the power of resurrection. Why they ought to praise and fear is then shown.

[Col. 0240A] “For you have become,” he says, “strength to the poor,” etc. Who is this poor one except him “who for our sake became poor when he was rich, so that by his poverty we might be made rich” (2 Cor. 8:9)? And who is this needy one except Christ the Lord, or any poor person in spirit? Therefore the Lord became strength to the poor in tribulation, because he gave power to his Christ in his Passion, that through suffering he might overcome Jewish savagery. He also became strength in tribulation to the needy, because he stood by anyone suffering for his sake. And he became hope to him against the storm of tribulations, because amid adversities he hoped in him. For “tribulation produces patience; patience, testing; and testing, hope” (Rom. 5:3). He became a shade from the heat of sufferings for that needy one, lest his mind be burned by the fire of excessive grief. It follows:

[Col. 0240B] “For the spirit of the mighty is like a storm driving against a wall.” Just as a storm strikes a wall in order to throw it down, so the spirit of the mighty—that is, the fierce determination of powerful persecutors—attacks our body in order to hurl it into death. But in so great a storm the Lord does not cease protecting his own. Or, just as a wind may strike a wall and pass on, so the storm of the blaspheming and raging Jews could not harm Christ. It follows:

**VERSE 5.**—“As heat in thirst, you shall humble the tumult of foreigners; and, like the heat beneath a cloud scorching fiercely, you shall cause the offshoot of the mighty to wither.”

As heat humbles the tumult of people when the very disturbers suffer thirst, because their voice fails them, [Col. 0240C] so you shall humble the tumult with which persecutors, alien to the lot of the elect, bark against the martyrs. For the heat of tribulations shall exhaust them when God repays tribulation to those who afflict the righteous; and they shall suffer thirst because they will be unable to have anything they desire.

Or they shall be humbled in heat and thirst when they are cast down with fire into Tartarus from the Judge’s presence. And just as vine-shoots wither when fiercely scorched by the heat of the sun hidden beneath a cloud, so you shall cause the offshoot of mighty persecutors to wither. For what is signified by the sun hidden beneath a cloud except the Judge, who does not yet appear? He is indeed “the Sun of righteousness” (Mal. 4:2). And what is signified by the sun’s heat except the Judge’s sentence? Thus the heat of the hidden sun dries the vine’s [Col. 0240D] offshoot, because the sentence of the still-hidden Judge makes the life of sinners wither in death. It follows:

**VERSE 6.**—“And the Lord of hosts shall make for all peoples on this mountain a banquet of rich things, a banquet of marrow-filled things, of clarified vintage.”

Above he had said that “the sun shall be confounded when the Lord reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem” (above, 24:23), and now, looking back to this, he adds: The Lord will make a banquet on this mountain, namely Mount Zion—that is, in the kingdom of heaven—because “the God of gods shall be seen in Zion” (Ps. 83:8). Let us understand this banquet as that of which it is written: “Blessed are those invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” [Col. 0241A] (Rev. 19:9). And again: “Let the righteous feast and exult before God, and delight in joy” (Ps. 67:4). And again: “A secure mind is like a continual banquet” (Prov. 15:15). For that banquet is the satisfaction of inward sweetness, which they will receive from the vision of their Creator, so that they may live eternally. The Lord will make it for all peoples on Mount Zion, because, as Luke says: “They shall come from east and west, north and south, and recline in the kingdom of God” (Luke 13:29).

This banquet will be of rich and marrow-filled things, because they are fattened with the fatness of inward abundance and filled with the marrow of love; or because those who are rich in good works and marrow-filled in the grace of right intention are gathered there. It will also be of clarified vintage, because the end of the human race is a vintage [Col. 0241B], and individual people are like clusters. But the vintage of the elect is clarified, because they do not die in the dregs of their sins, but strive to be purified before death. Therefore that banquet will be of clarified vintage, since those alone who end this life unstained shall be admitted to those feasts. It follows:

**VERSE 7.**—“And on this mountain he shall cast down the face of the bond binding all peoples, and the web which he has woven over all nations.”

**VERSE 8.**—“He shall cast down death [Vulgate: mountain] for ever.”

What is indicated by the term “bond” except this mortality? [Col. 0241C] Hence it is written: “You have torn apart my bonds; I shall sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 115:16). And what is figured by the web except the life of mortality? For Job says: “My days have passed more swiftly than the web is cut by the weaver” (Job 9:25). The bond is bound over all peoples because all human beings are held fast by the bonds of flesh. The face of the bond is the visible appearance of this mortality, seen in our bodies.

The Lord has also woven a web over all nations because, on account of Adam’s sin, after eternal life was taken away, he gave the human race temporal life for the present, until, through the intervention of death, immortality should be restored to it by resurrection. When the day of this resurrection comes, “the Lord shall cast down [Col. 0241D] on this mountain the face of the bond binding all peoples,” because he shall erase from the bodies of the righteous the appearance of mortality, apparent in the flesh of all, when “the dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (1 Cor. 15:51). For this reason the face of this bond is said to be cast down on this mountain, which is the Church, because in the rest of those who rise, who will not be changed, the appearance of mortality will by no means be abolished, since they will still be capable of suffering.

Likewise, he shall cast down the web, because he shall take this mortal and wretched life away from all, in order to grant blessed immortality to those who are worthy. Explaining what he had said about the casting down of the face of the bond and the universal web, the prophet says: “He shall cast down death [Col. 0242A] for ever.” For they shall no longer be able to die, but shall be equal to the angels, who are counted worthy of that age. It follows:

“And the Lord God shall wipe away every tear from every face, and shall remove the reproach of his people from the whole earth, because the Lord has spoken.” The elect now weep for various reasons, because this is now the time for weeping. One laments because he has done evil; another because he has not done good; another because he is attacked by vices; another because he is in exile from God’s kingdom. They also suffer reproach from the wicked and unbelieving. But on that day the Lord shall wipe the tear from every one of their faces, because “they shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and groaning shall flee away” (Isa. 35:10). Their reproach shall be removed from the whole earth because [Col. 0242B] nowhere shall anyone dare utter a word against them; rather, they shall be gathered by the angels with great honour from the four quarters of the earth and borne up into heaven. Or he shall remove the reproach of those who had been created in the image of their Creator and who shall then escape the slavery of the devil and death.

**VERSE 9.**—“And they shall say on that day: Behold, this is our God; we have awaited him, and he will save us. This is the Lord; we have endured for him; we shall exult and rejoice in his salvation.”

**VERSE 10.**—“For the hand of the Lord shall rest on this mountain.”

On Mount Zion “they shall say on that day: Behold, this is our God,” because, according to the Psalmist, “the God of gods shall be seen in Zion” (Ps. 83:8). “For blessed are the pure in heart, because they shall see God” [Col. 0242C] (Matt. 5:8). For “now we see through a mirror, in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12). God will thus be known and manifest to us: he will be seen in spirit by each of us in each of us; seen by one person in another; seen in himself; seen in the new heaven and the new earth; seen in every creature that shall then exist; and seen through bodies in every body to which spiritual eyes, directed in piercing vision, may reach.

Therefore, when the elect attain this vision after the darkness of this life, they shall exult with one another, saying: “Behold, this is our God; we awaited and endured for him” amid the adversities of temptations, as it is written: “Wait for the Lord; act courageously, let your heart be strengthened, and endure for the Lord” (Ps. 26:14). And because in this age we did not choose to rejoice, henceforth we shall exult and rejoice in his salvation—that is, in Jesus his Son—because on this mountain the hand, that is, the operation, of the Lord shall rest. Although Genesis records that on the Sabbath he rested from his works (Gen. 2:2), nevertheless his Truth says: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5:17). Therefore, after he has ceased at the end of the age from making the things which he creates daily, the operation of his hand shall rest in the mountain of the Church of the righteous, “so that they themselves may rest from their labours” (Rev. 14:13). What shall then happen to the reprobate is added:

“And Moab shall be threshed beneath him as straw is threshed [Col. 0243A] in a cart.” Moab, as Jerome says, means “from a father,” that is, one departing from God the Father. Therefore whoever by sin withdraws from God, who is the Father of all, is Moab. Under the name Moab he also indicates the devil and all hostile powers as destined to be humbled, led down into Tartarus, and ground like dust. But this Moab shall be threshed—that is, ground down by trampling—so that it may be separated from the elect and nothing whole remain, just as straw is threshed by a cart so that it may be separated from the grain. In certain regions, farmers gather the harvest into one place and drive carts with serrated wheels over it, so that the wheat may be shaken out and the stalks crushed into chaff to become fodder for animals. Therefore, so that the elect alone may remain like wheat, this Moab shall be threshed in that tempest which will occur at the coming of the Judge. For “fire shall blaze before him, and a mighty tempest round about him” (Ps. 49:2). In this tempest, then, this fugitive from goodness—that is, Moab departing from God—shall be threshed [Col. 0243B]. It follows:

**VERSE 11.**—“And he shall stretch out his hands beneath him, as a swimmer stretches them out in swimming.”

When someone slips downward from above to the depths, he falls with his arms outstretched, like one who is swimming. Therefore, when this Moab—that is, the people of the reprobate—is cast down into the abyss, he shall fall with arms spread like a swimmer, tossed by encircling waves of torments. And as a swimmer is accustomed to stretch out his whole body, so he too shall be dashed to the ground and, rushing down, shall make a sound.

[Col. 0243C] “And he shall humble his glory with the striking together of his hands,” so that, cast into the lowest part of the pit, he may endure everlasting reproach in exchange for temporal glory. And he shall humble him with the striking together of his hands, with which he worked iniquities, because, as it is written, “by that through which one sins, by that also one is tormented” (Wis. 11:17). Turning to him, the prophet adds:

**VERSE 12.**—“And the strongholds of his lofty walls [Note: [Col. 0243D] Another reading: ‘your lofty walls.’] shall fall, and be humbled, and be brought down to earth, even to dust.”

The lofty walls of Moab are utterly wicked and proud persons who, through worldly power, protect other wicked persons who are less powerful. But on that day the strongholds of these walls shall fall, because the defenders of evildoers [Col. 0243D] shall then fall into punishments, be humbled by the sentence of death, and be brought down to earth, even to dust, because their flesh shall become dust.

We may also understand this destruction of the walls otherwise, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “Though we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not fleshly, but powerful through God for the destruction of fortifications, destroying counsels and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing every understanding into captivity to the obedience of Christ” (2 Cor. 10:3). Therefore, while these things are accomplished through the apostles and the other holy preachers, what the prophet said is fulfilled [Col. 0244A]: “The strongholds of your lofty walls shall fall,” etc.

For he is brought down to earth, even to dust, who, having laid aside the arrogance of pride, knows himself to be earth and dust. The overthrow of Jerusalem by the Romans may also be foretold by these words. For we have shown above that the Jewish people are mystically called Moab. Thus the saying that Moab “shall be threshed beneath him” may be understood of that tribulation of the Jews. Likewise, the other statement a little above—“You have made the city a heap”—or the saying, “Desolation has been left in the city” (above, 24:12), may be referred to the same destruction of Jerusalem, which we passed over because of brevity. It follows:

## CHAPTER 26

[Col. 0244B] **VERSE 1.**—“On that day this song shall be sung in the land of Judah: Zion, the city of our strength; in it a wall and outer wall shall be set.”

**VERSE 2.**—“Open the gates, and let the righteous nation enter, keeping truth.”

**VERSE 3.**—“The old error has departed; you shall preserve peace—peace—because we have hoped in you,” etc.

On that day when the strongholds of Moab’s walls shall fall—that is, at the time when preachers destroy every height exalting itself against the knowledge of God—or on the day of judgment, when all defenders of evil shall perish, this song of exultation shall be sung in the land of Judah, that is, in the land of confession, which is the Church. For Judah means confession or [Col. 0244C] praise. Thus Christ’s confessors and praisers sing, saying: “Zion, the city of our strength,” etc. Zion is interpreted “watchtower,” and the watchtower is called the city of the righteous’ strength because their watchful mind, set on high while carefully looking about on every side, detects sin before it comes; and, insofar as it shrewdly foresees sin, it overcomes it courageously.

Or the Church is the city of our strength, because no one outside it can withstand the ancient adversary. In the building of this Church the Saviour is said to be established as a wall. For he is a wall to you, because he prevents the course of evil spirits from reaching our hearts. He has also set an outer wall for our faith because, before displaying himself in the flesh, he sent prophets, preachers [Col. 0244D] of his mystery. For they are rightly called by the name “outer wall,” because, while they preached the Lord who would follow, they stood as it were before the wall.

Or his divinity is our wall and his humanity the outer wall. After his coming, because all nations were admitted to the faith, he says: “Open the gates of Zion, O preachers, and let the righteous nation enter”—that is, the Gentile people justified by faith without works of the Law, henceforth keeping evangelical truth by its deeds. For the old error of idols has departed. Paul says: “Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, [Col. 0245A] through whom we have access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and boast in the hope of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. 5:1). Likewise here: “You shall preserve peace—peace—because we have hoped in you.” For those who trust and hope not in themselves but in the Lord are preserved in peace by divine grace, lest they lose his grace through some offence.

Or it may be said to the angels: “Open the gates of the kingdom of heaven, and let the righteous nation of Christians enter, keeping in works the truth of faith.” For the error of former ignorance has wholly departed, since “no one shall any longer teach his neighbour or his brother, saying, ‘Know God’; for all, he says, shall know me, from the least of them to the greatest” (Jer. 31:34). For teaching shall then cease, because all shall see God [Col. 0245B] as he is, and they shall say that the old error of former ignorance has departed. And because they shall most certainly know that they will never lose his grace—which they had always sought while living here—or suffer any adversity any longer, they shall rejoice together, saying: “You shall preserve peace—peace—because we have hoped in you.” Perhaps peace is doubled because of the tranquillity of soul and body. The prophet confirms and explains their statement, “Because we have hoped in you,” saying:

**VERSE 4.**—“You have hoped in the Lord for everlasting ages, in the Lord God, strong for ever.”

For the elect hope to receive from the Lord their reward not in transitory but in everlasting ages; he is strong for ever and can give everlasting punishments to his [Col. 0245C] enemies. For it follows:

**VERSE 5.**—“For he shall bow down the inhabitant [Note: [Col. 0245D] Another reading: ‘inhabitants.’] on high; he shall humble the lofty city; he shall humble it to the ground and bring it down to dust.”

**VERSE 6.**—“The foot of the poor shall trample it, the steps of the needy.”

At the time of death he shall bow down those dwelling on high, because, humbling the proud, he shall consign them to eternal punishments; and he shall humble their lofty city to the ground and bring it down to dust, because he shall make their proud flesh, in which they lived, return to earth and dust.

Or this city may be understood as that great Babylon [Col. 0245D]. Or again, the Lord bows down those dwelling on high when he bends the proud toward the grace of humility. He humbles the lofty city to earth and dust when he so humbles the proud mind that it knows itself to be earth and dust. The foot of the poor and the steps of the needy trample it, because it is pressed down by the example of the Lord’s humility and that of his disciples. For by the poor man here we understand him of whom Paul says: “For our sake he became needy when he was rich, so that by his poverty we might become rich” (2 Cor. 8:9).

Those too were needy to whom he said: “Do not possess gold or silver or money in your belts, nor a bag for the journey, nor two tunics, nor footwear, nor carry a staff” [Col. 0246A] (Matt. 10:9). Of their steps it was said there: “Go to the sheep that have perished of the house of Israel. And as you go, preach, saying: The kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (ibid.). Therefore the foot of the poor is the course of the Lord’s Incarnation, by which he went from place to place; and the steps of the needy are the movement of the apostles’ preaching. The foot of the poor and the steps of the needy thus trample him whose pride is crushed by the humility and conduct among human beings, and by the teaching, of the Saviour and his disciples.

Historically, he bowed down those dwelling on high because he subjected as captives to Titus the Jews who were in the citadel of Zion. And he humbled the city of Jerusalem [Col. 0246B] to dust because no stone was left in it upon stone. The foot of the poor and the steps of the needy had trampled it, because the Lord himself and his disciples had preached and walked there. Concerning his way of life it follows:

**VERSE 7.**—“The path of the righteous is straight; the track of the righteous is straight for walking.”

The path or track of the righteous is the action of the well-trodden way of life which Christ lived while he traversed the course of this present life. This path is straight for walking, so that all who desire to follow the way of upright conduct may not hesitate to walk upon it after him. To him it is added in the voice of the prophets:

**VERSE 8.**—“And in the path of your judgments, [Col. 0246C] O Lord, we have awaited you; your name and remembrance were the desire of our soul.”

For the prophets awaited the Lord because they long expected his coming. What is the path of his judgments except the uprightness of conduct proved in his judgments? In this the holy prophets awaited him. His name and remembrance were the desire of their soul, because their minds, wounded by love for him, delighted greatly if they heard even his name or mention from anyone’s mouth.

Sacred Scripture may also be called his remembrance, because his works are remembered there. It is the desire of the soul because the holy soul desires to hear divine readings. [Col. 0246D] Indeed, all who truly love the Saviour’s coming may sing this verse to him. For one who has the Lord’s name in his heart desires nothing else. Then the prophet discloses his own desire, saying:

**VERSE 9.**—“My soul desired you in the night; but also with my spirit, in my inmost heart, I shall watch for you in the morning.”

Night is this present life, in which, so long as we are here, while we gaze upon inward things, we are darkened beneath uncertain imagination. Therefore the prophet, now feeling himself pressed by a certain darkness as he seeks to see the Lord, says: “My soul desired you in the night.”

[Col. 0247A] As though he were saying: “In this darkness of the present life I seek to see you, but I am still hemmed in by the cloud of weakness.” But the person who keeps watch for the Lord in his inmost heart is one who, driving away from himself the darkness of sloth and negligence, keeps the eyes of his mind open for the vision of the true light. Morning, moreover, is early life. Or morning comes to be in us when the darkness of our error is illumined by the radiance of truth. Morning comes to be in us when the brightness of righteousness illumines our hearts, which the blindness of sin had oppressed like night. Therefore the prophet declares that from morning he keeps watch for God in his inmost heart, because either from early life, or from the time when he was illumined by the light of God’s knowledge, he always directs himself toward him and strives to obey his will. And he adds a sentence concerning those who neglect to keep watch, saying:

[Col. 0247B] “When you execute your judgments upon the earth, the inhabitants of the world will learn righteousness.”

“They will learn righteousness”—that is, the inhabitants of the world, those who inhabit the world in their mind, will begin to keep watch. But when will they learn righteousness? “When you execute your judgments upon the earth.” For when you come in judgment, each person is brought back to his own heart, so that, when he can no longer perform holy deeds, he recognizes them; and by the punishment for his crookedness he comes to know the right path which he ought to have followed. Hence it is well said through Jeremiah: “Gather them as a flock for sacrifice, and sanctify them on the day of slaughter” (Jer. 12:3). For on the day of slaughter the reprobate are sanctified, because then they recognize the holy deeds which they ought to have done, when they can no longer avoid the punishments deserved by their wickedness. It follows:

VERSE 10.—“Let us have mercy on the ungodly man, and he will not learn to do righteousness; in the land of the saints he has done wickedly, and he will not see the glory of the Lord.”

VERSE 11.—“Lord, let your hand be exalted, and let them not see; let those who are jealous of the people see and be put to shame, and let fire devour your enemies.”

This is the voice of those who said above: “In the path of your judgments, O Lord, we have awaited you.” “Let us have mercy,” they say, “on the ungodly man,” not immediately condemning him, but still waiting for him and proclaiming to him the divine mercy, in case he should repent. And indeed we shall have mercy upon him, but he will not learn to do righteousness—that is, to live rightly. Hence his subsequent conduct is perverse. And after he has received mercy, this is added: namely, that “in the land of the saints he has done wickedly”—that is, among good people he has lived wickedly, increasing his iniquity. For just as it is great praise to live well among the wicked, so it is great disgrace to act wickedly among the saints. Therefore, one so hardened in wickedness that he is not ashamed to live wickedly even among the righteous will not see the glory of the Lord, which the elect alone will see; but, condemned forever, he will endure everlasting darkness.

Or the Lord says: “Let us have mercy on the ungodly man”—that is, let the ungodly man rather obtain mercy and learn my clemency, while he himself is saved. To him the prophet answers, speaking in the person of human impatience: “And he will not learn to do righteousness.” The sense is: How will he be able to know your righteousness if he has experienced such great clemency? And he gives reasons why he wishes him to learn God’s righteousness: because “in the land of the saints he has done wickedly” [Col. 0248A] and has continually fought against your saints, he ought to suffer punishments. Again the Lord tempers the sentence: “And he will not,” he says, “see the glory of the Lord”—that is, it will suffice for his entire punishment that he will not see me reigning in my majesty with my saints. But how all the wicked are deceived is added:

“Lord, let your hand be exalted, and let them not see; let those who are jealous of the people see and be put to shame”—that is, those who envy the faithful. The merits of the reprobate now obscure their understanding, but then awareness of guilt illumines it, so that now they do not see the eternal realities which they ought to pursue, and then, after they have lost them, they behold them. For now they neglect to understand them, or despise to desire what they have understood; but then, understanding and undoubtedly desiring them, they behold them when they are in no way able to attain what they desire. Then they are put to shame when the witness convicts them in the sight of the Judge [the printed text has *addicit*; perhaps *adducit*, “brings forward”]. For then the Judge is seen outwardly and the accuser is endured inwardly. Then every sin is brought before the eyes, and the mind is more grievously tormented by its own fire than by the fires of Gehenna, and at last is handed over to the flames of hell. “Let them see,” he says, “and be put to shame, and let fire devour your enemies.” The hand of divine operation is exalted beyond the knowledge of the reprobate, because the day of judgment secretly draws near. Yet these things may be understood otherwise.

For who is ungodly except the people of the Jews, who wickedly killed the Savior? But “let us have mercy,” he says, “on the ungodly man,” because after the Lord’s passion that faithless people was waited for a long time in expectation of repentance. “And he will not learn to do righteousness,” because, even while waited for, he was unwilling to come to his senses and believe in him who justifies the ungodly. “In the land of the saints he has done wickedly,” because he filled Jerusalem and Judea, where the holy fathers had dwelt, with iniquities. “And he will not see the glory of the Lord,” but “they shall look upon him whom they pierced” (Zech. 12:10). For they will not see the glory of his divinity, but the form of a servant which they crucified. Or, at his first coming they saw his glory as we did, when “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory” (John 1:[Col. 0248D] 14).

“Lord,” he says, “let your hand be exalted, and let them not see,” etc. For the hand of the Lord is Christ, since “all things were made through him” (John 1:3).

Therefore the hand of the Lord was exalted, and the Jews did not see, because Christ ascended into heaven while they did not believe. But when he comes for judgment, those Jewish people who persecuted the apostles out of zeal for the Law will see and be put to shame, and the fire of Gehenna will devour his enemies. Then the voice of the elect is added:

VERSE 12.—“Lord, you will give us peace, for you have wrought all our works for us.”

For then he will give eternal peace to those who, while living here, fought daily against the devil. He wrought all their works for them, because, as the Apostle says, “There are varieties of operations, but it is the same God who works all things in all” (1 Cor. 12:6). Yet although God works all the works of the righteous in them, he nevertheless rewards them as though they had done all these things without him. And it should be noted that those for whom God has wrought all their works have no wicked work. Then the penitent speak, which may fittingly be referred to the remnant of Israel who will believe under Elijah.

VERSE 13.—“O Lord our God, masters other than you have possessed us; in you alone may we remember your name.”

These words are spoken by those who ought to have served the Lord but afterward, through their sins, came under the dominion of unclean spirits. But now they wish to remember [Col. 0249B] his name, so that, always mindful of him, they may take care no longer to offend him; and they seek to remember his name in him alone, because “no one can serve two masters” (Matt. 6:24). For the one who both thinks of God and sometimes does things outside his good pleasure remembers his name, but not in him alone. It follows:

VERSE 14.—“The dead shall not live; the giants shall not rise again; therefore you have visited and crushed them, and have destroyed all memory of them.”

There is no obstacle to understanding the giants as either apostate angels or any proud human beings, when the prophet says: “The dead shall not live; the giants shall not rise again.” For whom else does he call dead but sinners? And whom does he call giants but those who even take pride in sin? Thus the dead do not live because, by sinning, they have lost the way of righteousness. Nor can the giants rise after death, because, swollen with pride after their sin, they do not have recourse to the remedies of repentance. “Therefore you have visited and crushed them”—that is, without doubt, you will visit and crush them on the day of judgment. “And you have destroyed,” that is, you will destroy, all memory of them, so that there may no longer be any remembrance of them. It follows:

VERSE 15.—“You have shown favor to the nation, O Lord; you have shown favor to the nation. Have you been glorified? You have removed all the boundaries of the earth.”

The Lord often showed favor to the Jewish nation—that is, he forgave its sins—but he was not glorified by it; indeed, he was greatly dishonored. And he loved this [Col. 0249D] nation so much that he chose it alone and removed from himself all the boundaries of the earth—that is, all the surrounding nations—and regarded them as strangers. But because these too approached him in repentance after his resurrection, it fittingly follows:

VERSE 16.—“Lord, in their distress they sought you; in tribulation your instruction was to them in a murmuring.”

For all the boundaries of the earth—that is, all the nations of the world—sought him while afflicted by distress of heart. And his teaching was to them amid the murmur of tribulation, while, with a contrite spirit, they meditated upon his commandments. Here “murmur” signifies the groaning and prayer of penitents. And because many from the nations became martyrs throughout the world, their voice is added, saying:

VERSE 17.—“As a woman who conceives, when she draws near to giving birth, cries out in pain amid her sufferings, so have we become before your face, O Lord.”

VERSE 18.—“We have conceived, and as it were have been in labor, and have brought forth a spirit of salvation.”

For just as a woman who conceives cries out in her pains when childbirth is near, so holy martyrs, having conceived the word of God in their hearts, were as though in labor—that is, they were afflicted by the anguish of sufferings in their torments—and brought forth a spirit, that is, they yielded up the soul. For, as we have already said, to be in labor is to suffer before birth, but to give birth is to bring forth what has been conceived. Thus the blessed martyrs were in labor while they were oppressed by suffering in their passion, and they gave birth when they surrendered their souls. Perhaps their voice is still added:

“We have not brought about deliverances upon the earth; therefore the inhabitants of the earth have not fallen.”

For in heaven—that is, in the hearts of the elect—the martyrs wrought many kinds of deliverances; but upon earth—that is, in the minds of the reprobate—they wrought no deliverances. And therefore the inhabitants of the earth have not fallen but are still raised up in pride: those, namely, who love the present exile as though it were their native dwelling. Or this is the voice of those who lived in a time of peace after the martyrs: “We have not wrought deliverances upon the earth.” For when the mighty men of Israel inflicted great slaughter upon their enemies, they were said to have wrought deliverances among their people. Thus Samson, after killing a thousand Philistines with the jawbone of an ass, said to the [Col. 0250C] Lord: “You have given this great deliverance and victory into the hand of your servant” (Judg. 15:18). Likewise Jonathan, Saul’s son, struck down the Philistines, and it was said: “Because you have wrought a great deliverance in Israel” (1 Sam. 14:45); this was the customary expression. Therefore they say: “We have not wrought deliverances upon the earth; therefore the inhabitants have not fallen.” As though they said: “With the sword of preaching we have not powerfully exterminated the nation of vices while fighting for the people of virtues; and therefore the vices of our flesh have not been overthrown—that is, the inhabitants of the earth have not fallen.”

Or the inhabitants of the earth are lovers of the world, because their minds dwell in earthly things; they have not fallen from their exalted pride, because we have not wrought deliverances upon the earth—that is, with the sword of God’s word we have not powerfully slain their malice and inward sickness. The Church’s voice concerning the martyrs follows:

VERSE 19.—“Your dead shall live; my slain shall rise again.”

This is plain. For those who have undergone death for Christ will truly live. It follows:

“Awake and give praise, you who dwell in the dust, for your dew is the dew of light, and you will cast down the land of the giants into ruin.”

“Awake, you who dwell in the dust”—that is, wake up, you who sleep in tombs, because your dew, O Lord, by which they will be watered so as to rise again, is the dew of light. That is, the grace which you will pour into them illumines them, so that, when the mists of the heart have fled, they may now see your glory openly. For just as dew makes seeds cast into the earth gradually grow into plants and arrive at fruits of their own kind, so your dew will work in the elect. “And you will cast down the land of the giants into ruin”—that is, you will plunge the flesh of the proud into hell.

Or thus: “Awake, you who dwell in the dust”—that is, cast away sloth and negligence, you who always think earthly thoughts. For those whose minds linger in earthly thoughts dwell in the dust. But how such persons can awaken to the Creator’s praise is disclosed: because your dew, by which you wash them from this dust, is the dew of light—that is, your grace, through which you cleanse the heart from earthly thoughts, is illuminating. For the dust of carnal thoughts blinds the [Col. 0251B] mind, but the dew of grace coming upon it illumines it. “And you will cast down the land of the giants into ruin,” because you will weigh down the minds of the proud, that they may fall more grievously. It follows:

VERSE 20.—“Go, my people, enter into your chambers; close your doors behind you; hide yourself for a little while, for a moment, until indignation passes by.”

We go when we act; we enter chambers when we enter the hidden places of our mind; we close doors when we restrain unlawful desires. For the doors of our mind are its desires. Therefore, while acting, we are commanded to enter chambers, lest we remain outside in the favor of those who praise us, but, returning to the secret place of the heart, seek glory there. The doors must also be carefully closed, lest what Jeremiah laments happen in us: “Death has climbed in through our windows; it has entered our houses” (Jer. 9:21). For death enters through the windows or doors of a house when sin penetrates our minds through hearing and sight or through desires. We are commanded to hide ourselves briefly, for a moment, so that while we are in the present life we may not seek outward glory from our works. For the whole duration of human life is brief as a moment in comparison with eternity. The indignation of almighty God daily exercises the force of its severity in this: it plunges those living unworthily into punishments worthy of them. This indignation indeed passes now, but it will pass away at the end, because it is now enacted but is consummated at the end of the world. [Col. 0251D] Therefore, until it passes—that is, until the end of the age—the people of the Church are commanded to hide themselves, because in the night of this present life the Lord passes through the land of Egypt—that is, through this world—striking the firstborn of the Egyptians and all whom he finds outside. It follows:

VERSE 21.—“For behold, the Lord will go forth from his place to visit the iniquity of the inhabitant of the earth against him; and the earth will reveal its blood, and will no longer cover its slain.”

What is the Lord’s place but the heavenly dwelling above? Hence it is written: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place?” (Ps. 23:3). Therefore he will go forth from his holy place because he will come from heaven for judgment. “To visit the iniquity of the inhabitant of the earth against him”—that is, to examine the perversity of the people of the reprobate, who inhabit the world in their minds, and, opposing it, to avenge it.

“And the earth will reveal its blood,” which it drank when it was shed from human bodies, because then every blood which was shed will be revealed, and why it was shed will be declared and made known. “And it will no longer cover its slain,” because then all will rise again.

Or the Lord goes forth from his place when the merciful, compassionate, and gracious Father is compelled to strike his negligent children, and in a certain way to depart from his own disposition, in order to visit and bring his wrath upon the inhabitants of the earth. For just as those who are in [Col. 0252B] the flesh cannot please God, so neither can those who dwell upon the earth. Here earth signifies the soul that lives carnally. It will reveal its blood if it has scandalized anyone and extinguished him from the life of love. Or it will reveal our blood, which it had received, and will no longer cover us, but bring us forth. It follows:

CHAPTER 27.

VERSE 1.—“On that day the Lord will visit with his hard, great, and strong sword Leviathan, the bar-serpent, and Leviathan, the twisting serpent; and he will kill the sea-monster which is in the sea.”

The sword of the Lord is the sentence of the Judge, of which Job says: “Flee from before the sword, because the sword is the avenger of iniquities; and know that there is judgment” (Job 19:29). This sword is hard because it strikes harshly; great because it strikes with so great a blow that it inflicts eternal death; and strong because it cannot be broken or bent from its severity, by which it eternally punishes the ungodly.

With this sword, therefore, the Lord will visit Leviathan on that day, because he will consign the devil to everlasting torments. Leviathan, indeed, is said to mean “their addition,” that is, the addition to human beings. For this serpent is called Leviathan—that is, “their addition”—because he added sin to human beings whom God created. Or because, while he deceitfully promised that he would add divinity to them, he took away immortality, he is called Leviathan in mockery. But the prophet, who had just called him a serpent and then adds “twisting,” inserts “bar,” because in the twisting of a serpent there is yielding softness, while in a bar there is the hardness of rigidity. Therefore, to signify him as both hard and soft, he calls him both a bar and a serpent. He is hard through malice, soft through blandishments. He is called a bar because he strikes unto death, but a serpent because he insinuates himself softly through snares.

What is signified by the name of the sea except the hearts of carnal people, tossing with swelling thoughts? And what is expressed by the name of the sea-monster except the ancient enemy, who, as he penetrates and possesses the minds of worldly people, as it were swims in their slippery thoughts? Therefore the Lord will kill this sea-monster on that day, [Col. 0253A] because he will consign him to everlasting punishments. It follows:

VERSE 2.—“On that day the vineyard of wine will sing to him.”

The vineyard of wine is the Israelite people, which formerly possessed, in the holy Fathers, the wine of spiritual grace and good works, but at the Passion gave vinegar instead of wine to him when he thirsted. But when its remnant is converted at the end and says, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” then on that day “the vineyard of wine will sing to him” (Matt. 21:9). Since the Lord himself had formerly always been accustomed to guard it, yet was about to afflict it through the Romans, he adds:

VERSE 3.—“I, the Lord, who guard it, will suddenly give it drink.”

This is said of ancient and recent times. [Col. 0253B] “I guard it” in the times of Hezekiah, in the times of Zerubbabel, in the times of the Maccabees, in the times of the apostles. But now, through Vespasian and Titus, “I will suddenly give it drink” from the cup of my wrath. Again he speaks of the former time:

“Lest it be visited against it, I guard it night and day.” “Lest it be visited against it”—that is, lest evil be done to it by anyone. “Night and day”: in prosperity and adversity, or continually, I guard it. And because of the evils which under the New Testament it committed against him, he adds:

VERSE 4.—“There is no indignation in me.”

For the Lord was justly indignant, because “he came unto his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1:11). And he added:

[Col. 0253C] “Who will make me a thorn and a brier in battle?” That is, who will make me hard and harsh, so that through the Romans I may rise in battle against this people—I who have always been accustomed to be gentle and merciful? And he adds:

“I will march over it; I will burn it together.”

VERSE 5.—“Or rather, shall I hold [Note: [Col. 0253D] Elsewhere: *he will hold*.] my strength?”

“I will march over it,” trampling it down; “and I will burn it together,” that is, I will consume the whole nation at once with the fire of my wrath. Or rather, shall I restrain my strength by sparing it? Certainly I shall spare it, because it follows:

“It will make peace with me; it will make peace with me.” It will make peace under the apostles, and peace under Elijah.

[Col. 0253D] VERSE 6.—“Those who enter Jacob with force: Israel will blossom and bud, and they will fill the face of the world with seed.”

The apostles, who “where the impulse of the spirit was, thither they went” (Ezek. 1:12), entered Jacob—that is, the Jewish people—with the force of a vehement spirit, preaching the Gospel to them. Then Israel—that is, the Hebrew people—blossomed in faith and good thoughts, and budded in holy works. Then those preachers themselves, who entered Jacob with the force of the Spirit, filled the face of the whole world with the seed of preaching. When it is said, “Those who enter Jacob with force,” there is inserted: [Col. 0254A] “Israel will blossom and bud”; and concerning those who entered Jacob with force, it is added: “And they will fill the face of the world with seed.” It follows:

VERSE 7.—“Has he struck him according to the stroke of one striking him, or has he fallen [Note: [Col. 0254D] Elsewhere: *has killed*.] among his slain as he was killed?”

The Lord did not strike the Jewish people as he himself was struck by it; nor did he kill it as it killed his martyrs. For they crucified him without mercy and killed his preachers; but he mercifully granted them forty years’ space for repentance. But what is said of this people, unwilling to be converted?

[Col. 0254B] VERSE 8.—“By measure against measure, when it has been cast away, you will judge it.”

“When it has been cast away”—that is, abandoned by the apostles because it was unwilling to repent—“you will judge it by measure against measure,” so that it receives what corresponds to what it did. It killed the Savior: let it be killed by the Romans. It scattered the preachers throughout the world by expelling them from its borders: let it be scattered from its own soil throughout the whole world. It follows: “It devised in its hard spirit through the day of heat.”

VERSE 9.—“Therefore, on this account, the iniquity of the house of Jacob will be forgiven; and this is all its fruit: that its sin may be taken away.”

The day of heat is the time of tribulation. Judea, in the day of heat—that is, at the time when it persecuted Christ—devised in its hard spirit, because it trained itself in evil with an adamantine heart and contrived the evils it would inflict upon the Lord, according to the words: “They who devised iniquity in their heart, all day long prepared battles” (Ps. 139:3). For they always strove to persecute him. Therefore, because they persecuted him even unto death, on this account—that is, because they thus devised against him—the iniquity of the house of Jacob will be forgiven: of those who after his resurrection will believe through the apostles. To them he himself said: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he” (John 8:28). And afterward Peter said to those already pierced in heart and seeking counsel, because they knew that they had crucified Christ: [Col. 0254D] “Repent,” he said, “and let every one of you be baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ for the remission of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:38). Thus he says that therefore the iniquity of the house of Jacob will be forgiven, and this is all its fruit: that its sin may be taken away. For unless they had stumbled over the stone of stumbling, so that their faces might be filled with shame, they would not seek the name of the Lord Jesus, through whom remission of sins is given. Or the Lord, in his hard and vehement Spirit, devised against Judea in the day of heat—that is, in the time of persecution, when the day of indignation and punishments burns more fiercely. It follows:

[Col. 0255A] “When he has made all the stones of the altar like shattered stones of ash, sacred groves and shrines will not stand.”

What the Romans were going to do, he says that Judea would do, because it happened through its rebellious obstinacy. For the Romans made all the stones of God’s altar like shattered stones of ash because they burned the Temple, as had also been said in the Psalm: “They have burned your sanctuary with fire” (Ps. 73:7). But when the Temple of Jerusalem was destroyed, sacred groves and shrines did not stand, because then, while the apostles preached among the nations, the groves of idols were cut down and their temples overthrown, so that the Church might be built there. For concerning the destruction of Jerusalem he further adds:

VERSE 10.—“For the fortified city will be desolate; the beautiful city will be abandoned and left like a wilderness; [Col. 0255B] there the calf will graze, there it will lie down, and it will consume its highest parts.”

Jerusalem had been fortified with walls and beautiful in worldly glory; but at last, after the Romans had departed, it was left like a wilderness. He calls Titus, Vespasian’s son, a calf, because Jeremiah likewise says to the Chaldeans: “You rejoice and speak proudly, plundering my inheritance, because you have been poured out like calves upon the grass, and have bellowed like bulls” (Jer. 50:11). Therefore this calf grazed there and lay down there, because he devoured everything there; he besieged it there and consumed its heights, because he destroyed its towers. It follows:

VERSE 11.—“In drought its harvests will be crushed; women will come and teach it.”

Since “the harvest is the consummation of the age,” as the Lord says (Matt. [Col. 0255C] 13:39), the harvest of this people may be called the death which it endured in that siege, because nearly all were killed by famine, plague, and swords. But this harvest experienced drought because all these people died without the grace and faith of God. In contrast, he says of the people of the elect: “Dew will remain in my harvest” (Job 29:19). For dew, which falls from above, is grace descending from on high. And dew remains in the harvest of the righteous because they end their present life in the grace of God.

Therefore, in drought its harvests were crushed—women—because not only the male but also the female sex was consumed there in the sin of unbelief. “Women,” he says, “will come and teach it.” Perhaps, when the siege was impending, distinguished [perhaps *illustres*, “illustrious”] women had previously come to Jerusalem and taught the men how to resist their enemies. Or by the name “women” the remaining cities of the Jews may be signified, which gave assistance to the people of Jerusalem. But that women taught men may be believed also from what follows:

“For it is not a wise people.” Because it ignored the wisdom of God, which is Christ, it therefore also lost human resourcefulness. And concerning its ruin he adds: “Therefore he who made it will not have mercy upon it, and he who formed it will not spare it.” Or it is not wise because it lost the knowledge of the Scriptures, and therefore, when the Romans come, the Lord will not spare it. It follows:

[Col. 0256A] VERSE 12.—“And it will be on that day: the Lord will strike from the channel of the river as far as the torrent of Egypt, and you, children of Israel, will be gathered one by one.”

The Lord will strike and lay waste the land of the Jews from the Euphrates, or the Jordan, as far as the Nile, or the Ryconorum [reading uncertain]; and when the regions have been devastated, the few Jews who survive will be gathered, one by one, in different places so that they may still attempt rebellion. But after these statements concerning the extermination of the Jews, he adds concerning the calling of the Gentiles:

VERSE 13.—“And it will be on that day: a great trumpet will sound, and those who had been lost from the land of the Assyrians and those who had been cast out in the land of Egypt will come and worship the Lord on the holy mountain in Jerusalem.”

The great trumpet is the voice of apostolic preaching. The land of the Assyrians is the Gentile world. For the Assyrians are demons, who will convict sinners of their iniquities and rebuke them at the coming of the Judge. And the land of Egypt is also the Gentile world, because Egypt means “darkness,” and by the designation of darkness is expressed the obscurity of minds ignorant of the light of truth. The holy mountain in Jerusalem is Christ in the Church. It follows:

CHAPTER 28.

VERSE 1.—“Woe to the crown of pride, to the drunkards of Ephraim, and to the fading flower of the glory of his rejoicing, who were on the summit of the richest valley, wandering from wine!”

VERSE 2.—“Behold, the Lord is mighty and strong, like the onset of hail, a shattering whirlwind, like the onset of many flooding waters, sent forth over a broad land.”

VERSE 3.—“The crown of pride of Ephraim’s drunkards will be trampled underfoot.”

VERSE 4.—“And the fading flower of the glory of his rejoicing, which is upon the summit of the fertile valley, will be like an early fruit before autumn’s ripeness: when the beholder sees it, as soon as he has taken it in his hand, he will devour it.”

VERSE 5.—“On that day the Lord of hosts will be a crown of glory and a diadem of rejoicing to the remnant of his people.”

VERSE 6.—“And a spirit of judgment to him who sits in judgment, and strength to those returning from battle to the gate.”

[Col. 0256D] VERSE 7.—“But these also did not know because of wine, and through drunkenness they were swallowed up by wine; they wandered in drunkenness, did not recognize the seer, and did not understand judgment.”

VERSE 8.—“For all tables were filled with vomit and filth, so that there was no place left.”

We have set forth the literal text in order to arrive more truly at its meaning. The ten tribes were called Ephraim, either after Ephraim son of Joseph, whose tribe was more numerous and distinguished, or after Jeroboam son of Nebat, an Ephraimite, who was first established as king over them.

“Woe,” he says, “to the crown of pride!” That is, woe to the proud multitude, namely the drunkards of Ephraim—the idolatrous, wandering ten tribes—and woe to the flower of its glory, because it will quickly fade. In the times of David and Solomon they were upon the summit of the richest valley—that is, upon the Temple mount, which stands above the valley of Gethsemane. For they came to the Temple from the side of that valley and pitched their tents there.

Behold, the Lord is mighty and strong, to conquer them through the hands of the Assyrians, like a violent, shattering whirlwind of hail, overturning buildings. And just as the onset of strongly flooding waters readily carries away all light things across a full land, so the Lord, through the onset of the Assyrian multitude, will carry the ten tribes away into captivity. Then the crown of these people’s pride will be trampled beneath their enemies’ feet, because their kingdom will be destroyed.

[Col. 0257B] “And the flower of its glory will be like an early fruit before ripeness, which is immediately devoured.” This means: just as, if a cluster is found on a vine, or fruit upon a tree before autumn’s ripeness, someone sees it and, led by desire, immediately snatches it greedily and eats it, so Sennacherib and his army, seeing the glory of the ten tribes, will desire it, seize it, and take away all their goods.

On that day—that is, at the time when the ten tribes have been led into captivity—the Lord will be to the remnant of his people, namely Judah and Benjamin, a crown of glory, to protect and honor them. And he himself will be a spirit of judgment to Hezekiah sitting in judgment—that is, on the judicial throne—because he will inspire him how to judge. And he himself will be “strength to those returning from battle” (4 Kings 19:35), in which the Angel of the Lord struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians. For the Jews went to gather their spoils, and returned to Jerusalem, having strength from heaven.

But these also—that is, the two tribes—did not know their deliverer because of the wine of error; and through drunkenness, that is, through idolatry and through Manasseh, they wandered. Priest and prophet did not know because of the drunkenness of errors, because the priest sacrificed to idols and the prophet prophesied in Baal. For all tables were filled with vomit and filth, because on all their tables were meats that had been offered to idols and other sacrifices of demons, so that no place remained there without such filth for the Lord to have a dwelling-place in them.

[Col. 0257D] But these things may also be understood otherwise. For what is signified by the ten tribes, which deserted the Temple of the Lord and worshiped idols, except the multitude of heretics? For they are drunk with their errors—that is, alienated from rational understanding. The crown, however, consists of teachers’ disciples, as the Apostle says to those whom he had converted: “What is our hope, or joy, or crown? Is it not you before the Lord?” (1 Thess. 2:19). Likewise, heretics boast that those whom they have deceived will be, as it were, their crown. But woe to this crown! As blessed Job says concerning any heretic: “If his children are multiplied, they will be for the sword” (Job 27:14).

This prophet teaches what the flower of this crown is: [Col. 0258A] “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. 40:6). But this flower fades, since “the grass has dried up and the flower has fallen, because the Spirit of God has blown upon it” (ibid., v. 7). “Who were on the summit of the richest valley,” because they oppressed the Church. For they were, as it were, above her summit, whom they trampled by worldly power. Or because they did not follow the thinness of manna and ecclesiastical humility, but occupied the richly fertile mountain of pride, drunk with errors.

“Behold, the Lord is mighty and strong, like the onset of hail, a shattering whirlwind,” because, according to what follows in this book, coming for judgment, “he will strike them with a whirlwind and hailstone” (Isa. 30:30); “like the onset of many flooding waters,” because “his Spirit is like a flooding torrent up to the middle of the neck, to destroy the nations unto nothing” (ibid., v. 28).

“The crown of pride of Ephraim’s drunkards will be trampled underfoot,” as it is said to the righteous through Malachi: “You will go forth and leap like calves from the herd, and you will trample the wicked, when they are ashes beneath the soles of your feet on the day which I make, says the Lord” (Mal. 4:2).

“And the fading flower of its glory will be like an early fruit before autumn’s ripeness, which, as soon as morning comes, will be eaten,” because heretics, when they depart this life, do not wait for the day of judgment and its torments—which may be understood by the ripeness of autumn—but are immediately devoured by the ancient enemy, swallowed into the abyss of eternal destruction.

“In that day the Lord will be a crown of glory to the remnant of his people,” that is, to those who remain in the Church; for the perfect, when they depart from this world, immediately receive the crown of the kingdom. And the Lord himself will be a spirit of judgment for him who sits in judgment, because he will make known to our Savior how he should judge, who says: “I can do nothing of myself; but as I hear, I judge” (John 5:30).

And the Lord himself will be strength for those returning from battle, that is, from the contest of this life, to the gate, that is, to the entrance of the kingdom of heaven. For the ancient enemy, with his attendants, is accustomed to stir up severe battles before the gate of the kingdom, so that he may not allow the souls of the faithful, departed from their bodies [Col. 0258D], to enter heaven; and therefore the Lord is strength at the gate for his elect.

“But these also have not known because of wine,” because even those who are in the Church are made drunk by worldly cares and various desires. For there are many intoxications: we are intoxicated by anger, grief, love, lust, vain glory, and the other draughts of vices; and whatever so inebriates the mind may be denoted by the name of wine. For, just as we see the body of a drunkard move, his feet stagger, his head and temples grow heavy, his tongue become bound, and words cut off as his lips cling together, so also we may see how those drunk in mind are moved, how unsteady their steps are, how, with their mind weakened and their thought wavering, they hold nothing firmly, but are always driven by uncertain disturbances [Col. 0259A]. For whoever abandons the practice of continually thinking on God has his heart filled with agitation, disturbance, malice, and bitterness. Men indeed endure harsh things out of love for this present life; yet, bound by the affection of excessive desire, they regard the labor of such endurance as pleasure. Hence Jeremiah rightly, assuming in himself the figure of all human life, complains in lamentation: “He has made me drunk with wormwood” (Lam. 3:15). For a drunkard does not know what he suffers. But one made drunk with wormwood finds what he has taken bitter, and yet does not understand the very bitterness with which he is filled.

Thus the human race, by the just judgment of God left to itself in its pleasures and through those same pleasures handed over to voluntary afflictions [Col. 0259B], is drunk with wormwood: for the things it endures for love of this life are bitter, yet through the blindness of desire it does not recognize that same bitterness, as though through the insensibility of drunkenness. Thirsting for the glory of the world, while it finds many tribulations for its sake, it drinks what is bitter. But because it has taken this in with excessive eagerness, it is no longer able, through the very drunkenness, to discern the evil of that bitterness. Since therefore not only Gentiles and heretics, but also many who confess themselves faithful, and moreover very many professors of religious life, have, confused by intoxications of this kind, lost the faculty of reason, it is rightly now said: “But these also have not known because of wine, and have erred because of drunkenness.” For, drunk with the wine of desires, they do not know the rule of truth [Col. 0259C]. Yet what follows is more serious: that priest and prophet have not known because of drunkenness. For who is called a priest here except one who has indeed assumed the priestly office but does not fulfill its work? And who is called a prophet in this place except any preacher who foretells the coming joys of the righteous and torments of the wicked? Yet these too have not known because of drunkenness: while their minds are occupied with temporal things, they do not know how to provide eternal things for those subject to them; and while they devote themselves to outward matters, they have lost knowledge of inward things. For scarcely is a priest now found, or a prelate of the Church, who meditates upon the Scriptures of God; rather, “they have been swallowed up by wine; they have erred in drunkenness,” because, intent upon worldly cares, they are swallowed up by those cares to the extent that they have gone outside divine contemplation [Col. 0259D]. Their mind, hardened by the habit of temporal care, is hardened against heavenly desire; and, hardened through the very practice of worldly action, it can scarcely be softened toward those things that pertain to the love of God.

And because most of them do not carefully consider that God observes all things now done, and will render judgment concerning all things, they have not known God who sees all things; they have been ignorant of his coming judgment.

“For all tables are filled with vomit and filth.” What is signified by the name of tables except the Holy Scriptures, which feed us with spiritual banquets? Hence the Psalmist also says: “You have prepared a table before me” (Ps. 22:5). And what is meant by filth except sins? Hence Jeremiah says of the negligent soul: “Her filthiness was in her feet, and she did not remember her end” (Lam. 1:9) [Col. 0260A]. Filth in the feet means sins in works. And what is signified by vomit except sins cast out by confession and afterwards resumed? For “as a dog returns to his vomit, so the imprudent man repeats his folly” (Prov. 26:11).

Therefore, because these men have covered all the precepts of the Holy Scriptures with faults either committed once or repeated, all their tables are said to be filled with vomit and filth, so that no place now appears in them which they have not defiled with filth. Or their entire teaching and all their mysteries are full of vomit and filth, since they do not digest the foods of the Holy Scriptures but discharge them immature and fetid [Col. 0260B], so that God finds no place in them.

But having discussed these matters, we suggest to the diligent reader that Ephraim may still signify that faithless people of the Jews, and the remnant of God’s people the Christian people; or certainly Ephraim, which is interpreted “fruitfulness,” may signify the multitude of carnal persons who are in the Church, while the remnant of God’s people signifies professors of sacred religious life. But let us consider what follows according to the preceding interpretation. For the prophet cries out to the Jews, saying:

**Verse 9.**—“Whom will he teach knowledge, and whom will he make to understand what is heard? Those weaned from milk, those torn away from the breasts.”

**Verse 10.**—“For command, command again; command, command again; wait, wait again; wait, wait again: [Col. 0260C] a little there, a little there.”

**Verse 11.**—“For in the speech of the lip and in another tongue he will speak to this people.”

**Verse 12.**—“To whom he said: This is my rest; refresh the weary; and this is my refreshment; and they would not hear.”

**Verse 13.**—“And the word of the Lord shall be to them: Command, command again; command, command again; wait, wait again; wait, wait again; a little there, a little there; that they may go and fall backward, and be confounded, ensnared, and taken.”

Whom among the Jews, he says, will the Lord teach, so that he may understand and perform what he has heard? He will not teach those who always need milk, but Christians [Col. 0260D] weaned—that is, withdrawn from the milk of childish knowledge and torn from the breasts of infant teaching. For “everyone who partakes of milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, for he is a little child; but solid food belongs to the perfect, to those who by practice itself have their senses trained to distinguish good and evil” (Heb. 5:13). Therefore the Lord will no longer teach these in a childish way, but others who no longer need milk and can receive the word of righteousness. For these men are accustomed to say, “Command, command again,” and so forth. When the Lord rebuked them through one of the prophets, exhorted them to repentance, and threatened captivity and evils, they saw that the captivity and affliction foretold did not at once come; they did not believe the prophet, but mocked him, saying [Col. 0261A]: “Command, command again”—as though they said: Command, command what we ought to do, and threaten evils to us. What you threaten will not come upon us. Conversely the prophet replied: “Wait, wait again; a little there, a little there,” that is, in that threat which you heard through my mouth: for after a little while the evil which I have spoken will come upon you.

“For in the speech of the lip and in another tongue he will speak to this people,” that is, he will speak presently and he will speak otherwise: for he will soon bring upon them the evil that he has spoken, allowing no further place for repentance.

“This,” he says, “is my rest: refresh the weary,” that is, provide me rest and a banquet within yourselves by living well, for I have long been wearied in enduring your iniquities. For the person who, converted to repentance [Col. 0261B], devotes himself to good works refreshes the Lord, who says: “Let us eat and feast, for this my son was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15:23). But he who remains in sins makes him labor, who says: “You have given me labor in your iniquities” (Isa. 43:24). Yet the Jews would not hear this: that they should give him refreshment in themselves.

“And,” he says, “the word of the Lord shall be to them: Command, command again.” For when, as we have said, some prophet exhorted them to repentance and threatened adversities, they did not correct themselves; rather, they turned the prophet’s word into a song of mockery, saying: “Command, command again; command, command again; wait, wait again; wait, wait again; a little [Col. 0261C] there, a little there.” As though speaking foolishly, they said: Command and command what we should do; and command us repeatedly to wait in expectation of captivity for a little while. We shall depart this life before what you foretell comes. For they were accustomed to speak so and to increase their iniquities, until they were carried captive by their adversaries. Hence he appropriately says that “the word of the Lord shall be to them: Command, command again,” and so forth, “that they may go, fall backward, be confounded, ensnared, and taken.” For they went in their own inventions so that they might fall into the hands of enemies, be ensnared by them, and be confounded.

But let us apply these words also to those who are in the Church. For, the Jews having been rejected, whom will Christ teach [Col. 0261D] to endure coming tribulations for his name? Surely those weaned from milk—that is, the apostles and their followers. “Wait,” he says, and so forth. He speaks to the choir of apostles and all believers, that one may prepare oneself not for one but for many tribulations, so that when afflicted and pressed, one may hope and place one’s hope in God. And if the things promised are delayed a little, one should not be unbelieving. For in a little while, in a short time, the things promised will come. But the ungodly would not listen to the apostles; rather, they raged with swords and blasphemies. Hence what was said to God’s people—“Endure tribulation; wait in hope, wait in hope; still a little while, still a little while”—was turned into punishment for them, so that they might go and fall backward and fall into the peril [Col. 0262A] of eternal death, and be taken without any end to their miseries.

It should be noted, however, that the other manuscripts do not have *ablactatos* (“those weaned”) but *ablactatum* (“one weaned”), nor *avulsos ab uberibus* (“those torn from the breasts”) but *avulsum* (“one torn from the breasts”). Thus it is read: “Whom will he teach knowledge, and whom will he make to understand what is heard? One weaned from milk, torn away from the breasts.” The only-begotten Son of God, made man for us, deigned as a child to suck his mother’s breasts, so that we might not always need the milk of souls like little children; and, advancing in age, he was torn from the breasts in order to lead us forward to the solid food of eternal life. But scarcely is one found who, reflecting thus, transcends childish understanding and abandons infant manners through mature progress. Hence amid the multitudes of those who confess themselves Christians the prophet cries: “Whom will he teach [Col. 0262B] knowledge, and whom will he make to understand what is heard? One weaned from milk, torn away from the breasts.” For rarely does anyone offer himself as teachable; rarely does anyone receive the understanding of wisdom. Rather, the Apostle’s saying fits almost all: “I could not speak to you as spiritual persons, but as carnal; as little children in Christ I gave you milk to drink, not solid food. For you were not yet able, nor indeed are you yet able; for you are still carnal” (1 Cor. 3:1).

Hence, in the voice of those who persist in being such, it follows: “For command, command again.” For when at the beginning they promise obedience, they say to the preacher: “Command,” that is, order what we should do. But because they hear, and then the devil comes and takes the word from their hearts, they return to the preacher, saying: “Command us again [Col. 0262C] what you previously commanded.” And because, even after retaining the word, they do not hasten to fulfill it in work, they say: “Wait,” like those in Haggai who said: “The time has not yet come to build the house of the Lord” (Hag. 1:2). Still postponing from day to day and promising themselves long spans of life, they say: “Wait for us again, for much time remains; and there is a little there,” that is, in waiting, for after a little while we shall do what you command. Again, if they are rebuked for delay, they reply with shameless face that there is only a little in any postponement; and thus, continually weaving delays until the end of life, they defer doing the good things they have learned, and are suddenly snatched away to the tribunal of the eternal Judge to receive according to their [Col. 0262D] works.

“For in the speech of the lip he will speak to this people.” But the prophet’s repeated phrase—“For command, command again; command, command again; wait, wait again; wait, wait again; a little there, a little there”—makes clear to us that he himself is affected with great weariness at such words of theirs, and that the obstinacy of their perversity is exceedingly burdensome to him. Since they do not obey the words of God which they hear through preachers, he speaks to them in the speech of the lip and in another tongue. For now he speaks through the pages of Scripture and the tongues of teachers; but when he utters words with his own mouth, appearing in judgment, then he speaks in the speech of his own lip and in another tongue. For he who now speaks through the leaders of the Church will then [Col. 0263A] speak through himself and say to them: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was a stranger, and you did not take me in” (Matt. 25:42). For this reason he became poor and wearied with labor for us: that we might refresh him in the poor and weary, and that he might say to us: “As long as you did it to one of my least ones, you did it to me” (ibid., 40). This is indeed what he says here: “This is my rest: to refresh the weary; and this is my refreshment.” But those who always defer doing good will not hear this. Therefore “the word of the Lord shall be to them: Command, command again,” so that, always promising obedience and never obeying, but extending holy things into the distant future, they may go after their desires and at the end fall backward—that is, plunge into unknown punishments—and [Col. 0263B] then be confounded too late by their evils, when nothing can any longer benefit them; and in the hour of death be ensnared by evil spirits and afterwards captured by them to be led to torments.

In the words, “and they may fall backward,” it should be observed that the good are always said in the Holy Scriptures to fall upon their face, but the wicked backward. Why is this, except because one who falls upon his face falls where he sees, while one who falls backward does not see where he falls? The elect, humbling themselves here voluntarily, see why they are cast down; but the reprobate, when humbled unwillingly in death, do not know where they fall. For they are carried away to unknown punishments. Now let us see what follows. For the prophet speaks to the rulers [Col. 0263C] of the synagogue who say: “Command, command again; wait, wait again.”

**Verse 14.**—“Therefore hear the word of the Lord, you scoffing men, who rule over my people that is in Jerusalem.”

For those who mocked the prophets, saying “Command, command again,” were scoffers. And a more serious cause concerning them is further added when it is said:

**Verse 15.**—“For you have said: We have struck a covenant with death, and have made a pact with hell. When the overflowing scourge passes through, it will not come upon us, because we have made falsehood our hope and are protected by falsehood.”

For they thought, saying: We have labored in vain in observing the law of the Lord, because we shall descend into hell like the other nations [Col. 0263D]. Yet it will be lighter and more tolerable for them than for us, because those nations daily appease the princes of hell with sacrifices and gifts. It is therefore better for us, imitating the rites of the nations, to establish a pact with the devil and the princes of punishments and offer sacrifices to them. Thinking—or even saying—such things, they sacrificed to demons. This, therefore, is what they say: “We have struck a covenant with death and have made a pact with hell.”

And concerning the present life they add that, when the overflowing scourge—that is, any roaming tribulation—comes and passes through, “it will not come upon us, because,” they say, “we have made falsehood our hope” [Col. 0264A].
