One hopes in falsehood against the coming scourge who prepares to excuse himself with lies and defend his fault so that he may not feel the scourge of correction, as many now do; and they did so then as well. They were protected by falsehood because, under the pretext of religion, they preached their avarice. For God had commanded that children honor their parents by providing them with the necessities of life; but these men said that it was better for children to offer to their parents [Note: [Col. 0263D] The passage is corrupt in both manuscripts.] than in the temple of the Lord, and they themselves took the people’s offerings. Hence they were rebuked by the Savior himself in this way: “Why do you transgress the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition? For God said: Honor your father and your mother. But you say: Whoever says to his father or mother, ‘Whatever gift from me might benefit you,’ and does not honor his father and mother—you have made void the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition” (Matt. 15:3–6) [Col. 0264B]. Thus they protected themselves with falsehood. It follows:

**Verse 16.**—“Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will lay in the foundations of Zion a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, firmly founded in the foundation; whoever believes will not hasten.”

**Verse 17.**—“And he will set [Note: [Col. 0264D] Alternatively: ‘and I will set.’] judgment by weight and righteousness by measure; hail will overthrow the hope of falsehood, and waters will flood the protection.”

**Verse 18.**—“And your covenant with death shall be destroyed, and your pact with hell shall not stand. [Col. 0264C] When the overflowing scourge passes through, you shall be trampled by it.”

“Whenever it passes through, it will take you away; for early in the morning it will pass through by day and by night, and vexation alone will give understanding to hearing.”

Because you said, he says, “Command, command again”; because you said, “We have struck a covenant with death”; because you said, “The overflowing scourge will not come upon us,” therefore the Lord says: “Behold, I will lay in the foundations of Zion a tested stone,” and so forth. For a new foundation of the Church must be laid, because the old building of the synagogue has been destroyed. The Psalmist’s words are also fitting here: “It is time for you to act, O Lord: they have destroyed your law” (Ps. 118:126). For when the Lord, dwelling bodily among men, acted—that is, fulfilled the law—the Jews had destroyed it by their transgressions and traditions or false interpretations [Col. 0264D].

Therefore, because the people of the synagogue, saying “Command, command again,” made a pact with hell, along with the leaders of that people, God the Father builds another, firmer edifice: “He lays a stone in the foundations of Zion.” The foundations of Zion—that is, of the Church—are the apostles and prophets, as it is written: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. 86:1). And again: “But you are fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets [Col. 0265A], Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone, in whom all the building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord” (Eph. 2:19). In these foundations Christ the stone is laid through the mystery of the Incarnation, so that the entire structure of the sacred building may be built up; he has been tested by temptations. Hence he says: “Lord, you have tested me and known me” (Ps. 138:1).

He is called the cornerstone because he joins in himself two walls: circumcision and uncircumcision, or angels and men, or the contemplative and active life. He is called precious because his holiness and righteousness are so great that, in comparison with him, no human being is known to possess any holiness or righteousness. Hence he gave his precious blood [Col. 0265B] as a ransom for the world. And he is founded in the foundation of the sacred building because he alone supports the entire structure. For, as courses of stones in a wall are supported by others, so each of the faithful is supported in the Church by the righteous who have preceded them. They in turn support those who follow by teaching and endurance, down to the last righteous person, who, though supported by those before him, will have no successor whom he himself must support. But he who supports the whole building and is supported by no one is the Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, as we said above, he is called “founded in the foundation.”

“And whoever believes in him will not hasten,” but will patiently await his promises. For “an inheritance hastily acquired in the beginning will lack blessing in the end” (Prov. 20:20) [Col. 0265C]. Whoever believes in him will not hasten to seek at his first coming what he will render at his second. Or, one will not hasten, lest Christ’s coming seem slow. For “if he delays,” according to Habakkuk, let no one despair, “for he that comes will come” (Hab. 2:3) and fulfill his promises.

“And I will set,” he says, “judgment by weight” through him, so that, weighing all things in an equal balance, he may judge; “and righteousness by measure,” so that each may receive according to the measure of his action. “For with the same measure with which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you” (Matt. 7:2). Even now his judgment is accomplished in the balance of equity, even when he does not seem to repay people according to their own actions. For even that which we do not understand is brought forth from the not-unjust balance of hidden judgment; and though the things we suffer may appear less than right, they are nevertheless decreed by a just and hidden examination [Col. 0265D]. But those men did not judge with a just weight: comparing the devil with the Lord, or preferring him, they rejected God’s law, established a pact with hell, and protected themselves with falsehood against truth. Accordingly he says to them:

For hail—that is, the manifold blow of heavenly judgments—will overthrow the hope of falsehood; and waters—that is, the onset of tribulations—will flood, that is, submerge and destroy, the protection of falsehood that shielded you. “And your covenant with death shall be destroyed,” because eternal death will torment you more severely than the other nations—you who thought it would be lighter for you because you sacrificed to demons. When the overflowing scourge passes through your regions, whether through the Romans or through another means, it will trample and crush you [Col. 0266A].

“For early in the morning it will pass through.” *Diluculum* means, as it were, doubtful light. It is called *diluculum* when the nighttime is already changing into the brightness of light; morning, however, is called such after the sun has risen. Therefore, when it says “morning early,” it is as if it said “at first morning” or “very early morning.” And what is expressed by “very early morning” except preceding swiftness? Day is accustomed to signify prosperity and night adversity. Or continual recurrence may be understood by night and day. Therefore the overflowing scourge [Note: [Col. 0265D] Codex Cruc., Fl.: “but overflowing.”]—that is, the widely spread scourge—will pass through early in the morning, that is, with utmost speed, by day and by night, that is, in prosperity and adversity, or continually [Col. 0266B].

This scourge may be understood as the affliction that rushes upon every sinner in the hour of death. It will pass through early in the morning, that is, as the night begins to end—that is, at every time—or both upon those who are in prosperity and upon those who are in adversity. Then vexation from the torments of Gehenna alone will give understanding to your hearing: it will make you understand what you heard but refused to understand, namely, the good you ought to have done while saying, “Command, command again.” For guilt now closes the eyes of the wicked, but punishment opens them at the end. They do not know the evils they have done until they have already begun to be punished for those same evils. Well, therefore, is it said: “Vexation alone will give understanding to hearing,” because they understand what they heard when they grieve that they are now being tormented for contempt [Col. 0266C].

But the things we have interpreted concerning the leaders of the synagogue may perhaps also be understood of the worst leaders of the Church, or even of heretics. For he says: “Hear the word of the Lord, you scoffing men who rule over my people that is in Jerusalem.” Some prelates of the Church are indeed scoffers: they themselves often mock the good which they proclaim to others. They “rule over the people of Jerusalem,” that is, the Church, because they seem to sit, as it were, upon some pinnacle of eminence, looking down upon those over whom they preside as though they were below; and they scarcely deign to speak to them with care, but rather to lord it over them. For they seek not to benefit them but to dominate, because they pursue not Christ’s glory but their own. In a manner they say: “We have struck a covenant with death and made a pact with hell,” while they declare by their conduct that they are confident they will never be injured by the second death or punished by hell. They announce that the overflowing scourge will not come upon them because they have acquired and greatly secured for themselves the prosperity of this present life. “And they have made falsehood [Col. 0267A] their hope and have been protected by falsehood,” because they are accustomed always to deny and conceal their own faults and to speak well of themselves.

But in order that the hypocrisy of such persons may be dissipated, Christ the stone is laid in the foundations of Zion—that is, in the root of believers’ hearts—so that Christ’s teaching may be firmly held and their perversity rejected. For although this stone was laid long ago in the foundations of Zion, it is nevertheless laid daily in the foundation of those who are converted. “Whoever believes in him will not hasten” to be blessed with such persons in the present life. “And hail”—the hail of heavenly judgments—“will overthrow their hope of falsehood,” because what they always hope to conceal by falsehood will be uncovered in the judgment of the supreme Judge. “And waters will flood the protection,” because the flood of final tribulations will destroy the pretext by which they now protect their iniquities through excuses [Col. 0267B]. “And their covenant which they made with death shall be destroyed,” because death will no longer be at peace with them, but will oppose them eternally.

“And when the overflowing scourge passes through, it will trample them,” because they will be afflicted even in the present life by adversities, though they always thought themselves safe from adversity. For the scourge will trample them because they will be overcome by tribulation. But after saying that a stone is to be laid in the foundations of Zion, so that the pact which these leaders of God’s people made with hell might not stand, he fittingly adds:

**Verse 20.**—“For the bed is too narrow, so that one must fall out, and the short cloak cannot cover both [Col. 0267C].”

This is as though a husband said to a wife wishing to admit an adulterer beside him: O wife, this bed is narrow; it cannot hold both me and your seducer, and this cloak is short and cannot cover both me and the adulterer. For those who said that they served God and yet made a pact with hell—that is, with the princes of hell—wished to admit an adulterer beside the bridegroom in the bedchamber of their hearts. But the bed of the human heart is too narrow, so that one must fall out: either the lawful husband or the adulterer, that is, either Christ or the devil, because “no one can serve two masters” (Matt. 6:24). And the cloak of our action cannot cover both, because under the action of one person [Col. 0267D] Satan cannot rest together with Christ. Hence it is added:

**Verse 21.**—“For as on the mountain of divisions the Lord will stand, and as in the valley that is in the valley of Gibeon, he will be angry.”

As the Lord stood on the mountain of divisions between David and Saul his persecutor, so he will stand between the Christian and Jewish peoples, separating them. David and his men were fleeing along one side of the mountain, while Saul and his men pursued along the other. When Saul’s men surrounded David like a crown in order to seize him, a messenger came to Saul because the Philistines had invaded the land; thus he withdrew from David, and for that reason they called that place “the Rock of Division” (1 Sam. 23:28). What then is signified by the mountain except God’s covenant? Hence it is written: “The Lord will come from Lebanon, and the Holy One from the shady and thick mountain” (Hab. 3:3) [Col. 0268A]. For he is said to come from where he had been promised—that is, from his covenant, shady and thick with the obscurity of mysteries. What is represented by David except Christ, by Saul except the Jewish people, and by the Philistines except the Roman army? David and his men went along one side of the mountain, and Saul and his men along the other, the Lord separating them, because in the law of God Christ proceeds with his own in newness of spirit, while the Jewish people proceed in oldness of letter. Saul did not cease to pursue David until the Philistines poured over the land, because the Jewish people persecuted Christ and his faithful until the coming of the Romans. The prophet therefore says that, as on the mountain of divisions, he will stand—that is, as the grace of religion increases under the New Covenant, he will divide between those who, following the oldness of the letter, wish to serve God and the devil together, and those who in newness of spirit serve God alone [Col. 0268B].

Or the mountain of divisions may be understood as that mountain to which David, after consulting the Lord and at his command, ascended against the Philistines who had come against him. There he struck them and said: “The Lord has divided my enemies by my hand, as waters are divided.” Therefore the name of that place was called Baal-perazim, that is, “having divisions”; and there they abandoned their gods (2 Sam. 5:20). Therefore, as God struck and divided David’s adversaries by his hand so that they fled and left their idols behind them, so now he spiritually strikes and divides Christ’s adversaries by his hand, through the sword of his preachers: some, fleeing the preaching, are hardened still more in wickedness; others leave their gods—that is, the vices which they had served—and turn to Christ [Col. 0268C].

Thus the Lord stands among us as upon the mountain of divisions, secretly dividing and judging our actions, so that each person may belong either to Christ’s side or to the adversary’s side. “For now is the judgment of the world; now shall the prince of this world be cast out” (John 12:33). But the Lord will also be angry with the enemies of the Church, as he was angry with the Canaanites in the valley of Gibeon when Joshua fought. Of them it is written: “Joshua rushed upon them suddenly, and the Lord threw them into confusion before Israel, and crushed them with a great blow at Gibeon” (Josh. 10:9) [Col. 0268D]. Gibeon is interpreted “hill of sorrow.” And what is signified by the hill of sorrow except the present Church, which, standing upon the side of the highest mountain—that is, Christ—is now afflicted with sorrow and grief? What is represented by the Canaanites except unbelievers, and by the Israelites except believers? Therefore, when Joshua rushed upon them, the Lord threw the Canaanites into confusion before Israel, because Christ’s grace, in the presence of preachers, unsettles the minds of unbelievers toward repentance. And he will crush them with a great blow at Gibeon because he gives them a contrite and humbled heart in the Church and brings all their former perversity to nothing. Well, therefore, was it said [Col. 0269A]: “As in the valley that is in Gibeon, the Lord will be angry.” Of this it is fittingly added:

“That he may do his work—his work is alien; that he may perform his work—his work is strange to him.” For it is God’s work to gather the souls he has created and call them back to the eternal joys of light. But to be scourged, spat upon, crucified, die, and be buried is not, in his own substance, God’s work, but the work of sinful humanity, which deserved this through sin. Yet he himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree; and he who remains always incomprehensible in his own nature deigned, in our nature, to be comprehended and scourged. For unless he had taken on the things that belonged to our weakness, he would never have raised us to the power of his strength. Therefore, “that he may do his work, his work is alien”; and “that he may perform his work, his work is strange to him,” because God incarnate, in order to gather us to his own, deigned for us to be beaten like a sinful human being [Col. 0269B]. He did an alien work in order to do his proper work: because, through suffering our evils in weakness, he led us, who are his creatures, to the glory of his strength. Since the Pharisees were to mock him in his passion, the prophet carefully forewarned them, adding:

**Verse 22.**—“And now do not mock, lest perhaps your bonds be made tight.”

For they mocked him, saying: “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matt. 27:42) [Col. 0269C]. Therefore the bonds of their sins, which would have been loosed through his death if they themselves had believed, have been so tightened that they can never be loosened. It follows:

“For I have heard from the Lord God of hosts a consummation and a shortening over the whole earth.” That is, a consummation of righteousness and a shortening of the commandment. “For the end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 5). Therefore the Lord has wrought consummation and shortening over the whole earth, because to all people in the world he has given one commandment, in which the whole perfection of righteousness is contained. “Therefore love is the fulfilment of the law” (Rom. 13:10). Then, about to begin another discourse, he introduces it by saying:

[Col. 0269D] VERSE 23.—“Give ear and hear my voice; attend and hear [Note: [Col. 0269D] Otherwise: hear my utterance.] my speech.”

Perceive with the ears of the body, and hear my voice with the ears of the heart; attend carefully and understand my speech. By this preface he seeks attentive hearers and shows that what he is about to say is mystical. For he adds:

VERSE 24.—“Does the ploughman plough all day in order to sow, breaking up and harrowing his ground?”

VERSE 25.—“When he has levelled its surface, does he not sow gith, scatter cumin, set wheat in rows, and barley and millet and vetch at their boundaries?”

[Col. 0270A] VERSE 26.—“And his God will instruct him in judgment; he will teach him.”

VERSE 27.—“For gith is not threshed with saws, nor does the wheel of a cart pass over cumin; but gith is beaten out with a rod, and cumin with a staff.”

VERSE 28.—“But bread is crushed. Yet he will not go on threshing it for ever, nor vex it with the wheel of a cart, nor crush it with its hoofs.”

VERSE 29.—“This also has come forth from the Lord God of hosts, that he might make counsel wonderful and magnify righteousness.”

Analogies are always fittingly drawn from things known to things unknown, as now he has given a parable from things we see, in order to instruct us concerning invisible things. For the Lord teaches who this ploughman is mystically, saying: “My Father is the husbandman” (John 15:1). The field is the world, that is, the whole human race. In cultivating this field, he does not plough it all day—that is, throughout the whole lifetime of each person—without sowing. Rather, he first breaks up the rough field of the mind with the ploughshare of new preaching or knowledge, and again harrows it, pulling up or cutting away the harmful weeds of vices.

Or, he does not throughout the whole day of each person’s present life break it up by the teaching of beginnings and harrow it with the hoe of correction, without mystically scattering any seed. For when he has levelled its surface—that is, made the mind fit to receive the seed of teaching—he will sow gith and scatter cumin, and so forth. Gith resembles cumin; it has grains somewhat whiter and larger, and a better flavour. Cumin, I think, is *cuminum*. What, then, is signified by gith and cumin but the Gentiles, receiving from the Lord understanding and the natural law? “For he was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9). Nor is it surprising that the husbandman is said to break up and harrow the ground in order to sow gith and cumin, because no one can receive even the knowledge of the natural law unless the mind has first been exercised by meditations and purified.

And since by gith and cumin we understand the Gentiles, it is not absurd that the husbandman is said to sow gith and cumin, although he rather sows teaching, according to that saying from the Gospel: “The seed is the word of the Lord; but that which fell among thorns are those who heard, and, going their way, are choked by the cares, riches, and pleasures of life, and bring forth no fruit” (Luke 8:1). For he says that the seed is the word of God, and that the seed which fell among thorns denotes those who heard the word and are choked by cares, riches, and pleasures. In the same manner of speech our husbandman is now said to sow gith and cumin, to set wheat and barley in order, and to scatter millet and vetch.

What, moreover, are denoted by wheat and barley but the pastors of the Church, gentle and harsh: gentle through meekness, harsh through severity? And what are expressed by millet and vetch but two kinds of subjects? Some are white with righteousness like millet; others black with sin like vetch. Gith and cumin, indeed, are scattered and sown indiscriminately, because the manner of life of the Gentiles is scattered and unordered; but wheat and barley are set in order, to signify that the life of the rulers of the Church is regular and ordered. Millet and vetch are placed at the boundaries of the field, to show the humility of subjects, who count themselves among the last members of the Church.

“And God,” he says, “will instruct him,” namely the husbandman, “in judgment”: that is, he will teach him what to do at the time of harvest, as the Lord will act in judgment.

“For gith is not threshed with saws,” and so forth. A saw is a piece of wood having many teeth, which oxen draw. Here, according to the letter, he refers to the custom of certain regions in which farmers, because of a shortage of hay, as was said above, gather the crops together and drive carts with toothed wheels over them, so that the grains may be cleaned and the stalks reduced to chaff, to become fodder for animals. But gith and cumin are not threshed with saws and carts like other crops; rather, gith is beaten out with a rod and cumin with a staff. So also in judgment the Gentiles will not be examined, but will be punished without reconsideration. “For as many as have sinned without the law shall perish without the law” (Rom. 2:12).

What is represented by the rod or staff but Satan, of whom it is written: “Woe to Assyria, the rod and staff of my wrath!” (above, 10:5). Thus gith is beaten out with a rod and cumin with a staff, because the devil shakes the souls of the Gentiles from their bodies with torments.

But what does the cart signify except the Lord himself, who says through Amos: “Behold, I will creak beneath you as a cart creaks that is laden with hay” (Amos 2:13)? And what do the cart’s wheels signify except the rolling course of the Judge’s words? For he will say to the reprobate: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry and you did not give me food; I was thirsty and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger and you did not receive me; naked and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison and you did not visit me” (Matt. 25:41). [Col. 0271D] This circuit of words, therefore, is understood through the wheels.

What are the saws but the Judge’s harsh sentences, which crush the reprobate like chaff and separate the elect like grains? But “gith will never be threshed with saws, nor will the wheel of a cart pass over cumin,” because unbelievers will not be worthy even to hear the Judge’s words, so as to be examined and condemned; rather, they will perish without inquiry.

But bread—that is, wheat and barley, from which bread is made—will be crushed by saws and by the wheel of the cart, because the prelates of the Church will be examined in judgment. Of millet and vetch, however, he does not say whether they are threshed, because subjects are judged daily for their weak actions by their prelates; and if they patiently accept the present judgment and thereafter amend their conduct, they will not be judged further. Otherwise, they too will be judged. “But bread will be crushed,” because the Lord himself will examine the deeds of the rulers.

“Yet he will not go on threshing it for ever,” because after this life he afflicts some persons so that they may be purified from certain lighter sins, but he will not punish them for ever. Hence the Apostle says: “If anyone’s work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss; but he himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire” (1 Cor. 3:14). For many endure a purgatorial fire after death and at last attain rest. Blessed Augustine, too, in the twentieth book of *The City of God*, understands from the sayings of the prophets that in the fire which will be spread abroad at the coming of the Judge, certain of the elect will be purified from some lighter offences. Bede agrees with him in his book *On Time*.

Therefore he will not go on threshing it for ever—that is, trampling and crushing it; nor will the wheel of the cart—that is, the Judge’s reproachful words—vex it for ever; nor will he crush it with its hoofs for ever, that is, in the final divisions. For the hoof is sharp and is itself the end of the toe.

Again, lest we should think little of these matters, he adds at the end of the discourse that what has now been said about seeds and threshing “has come forth from the Lord God of hosts, that he might make counsel wonderful and magnify righteousness.” For in this diversity of seeds he makes counsel wonderful, and in their beating out and threshing he magnifies righteousness, wisely and justly ordering everything in the disposition of the human race. It follows:

## Chapter 29

VERSE 1.—“Woe to Ariel, Ariel, the city which David conquered: year is added to year; the solemn feasts have passed away.”

We understand this historically of the destruction of Jerusalem which occurred through the Romans and of the captivity of the Jews. For Ariel is called “lion of God,” and Jerusalem was called the lion of God because of the strength it once possessed under the Lord’s protection. David conquered it by driving out the remaining rebel Jebusites. But now it has “Woe,” because it has been miserably overthrown. Therefore, with an expression of grief, he repeats: “Woe, Ariel, Ariel!” For she who had been unconquerable was so destroyed that not one stone was left upon another; and, after the Temple was burned and the Jews taken captive, year of captivity was added to year, and year to year, because this city remains captive through every age until the coming of Elijah. And the solemnities of Passover, Pentecost, and Tabernacles, and the other feasts, have passed away, because they are no longer kept, but have been reduced to nothing. Yet what he related as though past, though it was still future, he plainly reveals by what means it would be fulfilled, saying:

[Col. 0273A] VERSE 2.—“And I will besiege Ariel, and she shall be sad and mourning, and she shall be to me as Ariel.”

“I will besiege Ariel” by the Roman siege. “And she shall be sad and mourning,” when she is tortured by famine and no one can enter or leave. “And she shall be to me as Ariel,” because she will retain only her former name, having lost dignity, power, and religion. But what he had said, “I will besiege Ariel,” he carefully explains, adding:

VERSE 3.—“And I will encircle you round about as with a sphere, and I will cast up a mound against you, and set fortifications in siege against you, and you shall be humbled.” Thus it was done by the Romans. It follows:

[Col. 0273B] VERSE 4.—“You shall speak from the earth, and your speech shall be heard from the dust; your voice shall be like that of a python from the earth, and your speech shall mutter from the ground.”

“You shall speak from the earth,” though you were accustomed to speak of heavenly things. “And your speech shall be heard from the dust,” though you had set your mouth in heaven. “And your voice shall be like that of a python from the earth,” because many of your inhabitants will hide in caves and underground places, either from the faces of plunderers while you are besieged, or from the Romans when you have been captured. But because the Romans themselves were also soon to perish and be brought to nothing, since they did not know Christ, it is added:

[Col. 0273C] VERSE 5.—“And the multitude of those who winnow you shall be like fine dust, and the multitude of those who prevailed against you like passing ash.”

For they perished like dust scattered by a whirlwind. Again, what follows may be understood of their coming:

VERSE 6.—“And it shall be suddenly, at once. She shall be visited by the Lord of hosts with thunder, earthquake, a great voice of whirlwind and tempest, and a flame of devouring fire.”

For all these things took place in that tribulation. But because the Romans did not possess the life which is Christ, the prophet shows how empty they are, adding:

[Col. 0273D] VERSE 7.—“And the multitude of all the nations which fought against Ariel, and all who fought, besieged, and prevailed against her, shall be like a dream of a night vision.”

VERSE 8.—“And as one who is hungry dreams that he eats, but when he awakens his soul is empty; and as one who is thirsty dreams that he drinks, but after he awakens he is still weary with thirst and his soul is empty: so shall be the multitude of all the nations that fought against Mount Zion.”

These things fit those armies which were then against Jerusalem. But, returning to the preceding matters, let us see whether all these things can also be understood otherwise.

[Col. 0274A] “Woe,” he says, “to Ariel, Ariel,” and so forth. What is signified by Ariel but the Church? David conquered her—David meaning “beloved” or “strong of hand”—because Christ expelled from her the race of vices. Yet she is said to have woe because she endures temporal tribulations. For “woe” does not always signify eternal bitterness, but sometimes temporary affliction. Thus in the Apocalypse of John it is said: “The first woe has gone” (Rev. 9:12), and again: “The second woe has gone” (Rev. 11:13). Therefore, “Woe to Ariel” should be understood of the Church’s tribulations and temptations.

“He says, ‘Year has been added to year; the solemn feasts have passed away,’” that is, they have gone by, because in the time of persecution Christians did not dare for many years to celebrate feasts publicly.

“And I will besiege”—understand, with temptations and adversities—“Ariel,” that is, the Church, or any faithful and steadfast person. “And she shall be sad and mourning,” because she will fear that she has offended God and therefore suffers such things; and so she will grieve in repentance. “And then she shall be to me as Ariel,” that is, strong in my sight, though she appears weak in the eyes of men. Then he repeats the same points by way of emphasis, because the Church does not suffer such things only once.

“I will encircle you,” he says, “round about as with a sphere.” As if to say: I will surround you with temptations, so that you may feel adversity on every side. “And I will cast up a mound against you,” that is, a mass of temptations; “and I will set fortifications in siege against you,” that is, I will hem you in everywhere with the engines of visible or invisible enemies; “and you shall be humbled,” that is, pressed down by adversities, or humbled by practicing repentance.

“You shall speak from the earth, and your speech shall be heard from the dust,” because you will say: “For our soul has been humbled into the dust; our belly clings to the earth” (Ps. 43:25); and: “My soul clings to the pavement; give me life according to your word” (Ps. 118:25). “And your voice shall be like that of a python from the earth,” because you speak as one rescued from the abyss of perdition. For by the art of divination associated with the python, souls are summoned from the lower world. Whose voice, then, is like that of a python from the earth? It is the voice of one delivered from the depth of wickedness, who says that he has been drawn out of hell, singing with the Psalmist: “For your mercy is great over me, and you have delivered my soul from the lowest hell” (Ps. 85:13).

“And your speech,” he says, “shall mutter from the dust,” as Jeremiah too says of a devout man: “He shall put his mouth in the dust, if perhaps there may be hope” (Lam. 8:29). For one puts his mouth in the dust who humbly confesses himself to be dust. But what is to be done at the time of judgment concerning the persecutors of the Church, which is now so distressed and humbled, is added:

“And the multitude of those who winnow you,” that is, afflict you, “shall be like fine dust”: that is, they shall be dry, empty, wandering, and light, as it is written: “Not so the ungodly, not so; but like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth” (Ps. 1:5). “And the multitude of those who prevailed against you shall be like passing ash,” because, as holy Job says: “They shall be like chaff before the wind, and like ash scattered by the whirlwind” (Job 21:18).

“And it shall be suddenly, at once. She shall be visited by the Lord,” because he is near and exceedingly swift, and so unforeseen that it is unknown whether he will come in the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow, or in the morning. Therefore, at once—that is, very swiftly—the action of each person will be visited by the Lord God of hosts “with thunder, earthquake, a great voice of whirlwind and tempest, and a flame of devouring fire”; for then all the elements will be shaken and disturbed, and the Lord will come in fire, and all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come forth.

“And the multitude of all the nations which fought against Ariel, and all who fought, besieged, and prevailed against her, shall be like a dream of a night vision,” because the power and glory of the Church’s persecutors will pass away like a phantom. For all worldly power is a dream, not reality.

“And as one who is hungry dreams that he eats, but when he awakens his soul is empty; and as one who is thirsty dreams that he drinks, but after he awakens he is still weary with thirst and his soul is empty: so shall be the multitude of all the nations that fought against Mount Zion.” That is, those who fought against the religion of the Church with swords, tongues, or depraved conduct. Those who delight in prosperity in this world are like one who eats and drinks in dreams. While asleep, he seems to be filled with food or drink; but when he wakes, he begins to hunger more, and then understands how empty was that food and drink of his dreaming. So a person who sleeps in this world and does not open his eyes to the divine mysteries, as long as he is weighed down by the slumber of torpor, thinks that this worldly power is of some consequence, as though seeing it in a dream. When he wakes, he discovers how empty the pleasure of this world is.

Hence the Apostle says, by contrast, of the elect who labour and are afflicted here: “As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing” (2 Cor. 6:10). For the sorrow of the righteous is as though it exists; but their joy is not as though it exists, because their hope is sure. Why does the sorrow of the righteous exist only “as though”? Because it passes like a dream. If someone recounts a dream, he adds “as though”: “I was, as though, sitting; I was, as though, speaking; I was, as though, dining; I was, as though, riding; I was, as though, disputing.” It is all “as though,” because when he wakes he does not find what he saw. “I had found, as though, a treasure,” says the beggar. If it were not merely “as though,” he would not be a beggar. But because it was only “as though,” he is a beggar.

Thus those who now open their eyes to worldly delights and close their hearts have an “as though” which passes away, while their reality comes: their worldly happiness is their “as though”; their punishment is their reality. But our sorrow is “as though”; our joy is not “as though.” For the Apostle does not say, “As though rejoicing,” but says: “As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing.” Therefore lovers of present pleasures are rightly compared to one who eats and drinks in dreams. They act in dreams while they are in this life. They eat and drink while they satisfy their pleasures. But at the time of death or resurrection they will awake, and their soul will be empty, because all their pleasure will then have passed away and punishment will remain. Their soul will be empty because no food can satisfy the soul so that it does not hunger except him who says: “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst” (John 6:35). It follows:

[Col. 0276B] VERSE 9.—“Be astonished and marvel; waver and stagger.”

Be astonished and marvel, O faithless Jews, seeing the Saviour’s miracles; and, hearing his teaching, waver in mind and stagger, saying: “How long do you hold our soul in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly” (John 10:24). But because the Jews were then answered, “I speak to you, and you do not believe” (ibid., 25), and afterwards took up stones to stone him, it fittingly follows: “Be drunk, but not with wine; be moved, but not with drunkenness.” For they were drunk then not with wine but, what is worse, with unbelief; and they were moved against him not by drunkenness but by faithlessness. It follows:

[Col. 0276C] VERSE 10.—“For the Lord has mixed for you a spirit of sleep.”

The sleep of the soul is to forget one’s God. Whatever soul has forgotten its God sleeps. Therefore, because the Jews had forgotten Christ who was present—whose remembrance they had always had while he was yet to come—and because he himself had now, by just judgment, deprived them of knowledge of himself, it is rightly said to them: “For the Lord has mixed for you a spirit of sleep.” For their minds were stupefied by sleep, since they did not recognize him when present. He himself causes to wake the souls he enlightens. But if he withdraws his light, they fall asleep; or, if they turn away from him and sleep, the light is present to them but they cannot see because they sleep. Just as a person sleeping bodily may find that the sun has risen and the day is already warm, yet he is as though in night because he does not wake to see that day has already dawned: so these, because the sleep of the soul had grievously overcome them, did not know the present Sun of righteousness. Accordingly it is said to them:

“He shall shut your eyes and cover your prophets and your princes, who see visions.” The Lord, abandoning the eyes of the proud Jews, shut them. Thus it is said through the Psalmist: “You have made darkness, and it is night” (Ps. 103:20). For the Lord made darkness because, rendering judgments for sins, he withdrew from the Jews the light of his understanding. And it became night because their mind was blinded by the errors of its ignorance. For preceding sins cause people to be enveloped in the darkness that follows, so that they are no longer able to see the light of righteousness or right understanding, because they refused to be enlightened when they could.

Moreover, the Lord is said to shut their eyes and cover their prophets and princes with the darkness of the mind, not because he himself brings in darkness, but because he mercifully does not enlighten the dark hearts of sinners and the proud. Thus, for the Lord to have shut or covered their eyes is simply not to have been willing to free them from the darkness of blindness. But after their eyes are shut and their princes—that is, their teachers and prophets—are covered, he adds:

VERSE 11.—“And for you the vision of all things shall be like the words of a sealed book; when they give it to one who knows letters, they will say: Read this; and he will answer: I cannot, for it is sealed.”

VERSE 12.—“And the book shall be given to one who does not know letters, and they will say to him: Read; and he will answer: I do not know letters.”

The vision of all the prophets will be closed and wrapped up for you like the words of a sealed book, because you who rejected him of whom all the prophets spoke will be entirely unable to understand the prophetic Scriptures. For Christ alone opened the prophets by his coming, passion, and resurrection. Hence whoever does not believe that he came and suffered and rose again is unable by any means to understand the sayings of the prophets. This is the book which John saw in the right hand of him sitting upon the throne, “sealed with seven seals” (Rev. 5:1), and afterwards the Lamb opened “its seven seals” (ibid., 5). For all divine Scripture, because it was written by the one Spirit of God, is called one book.

Therefore, because the Jews do not possess this Lamb, the seals of this book—that is, of divine Scripture—have not yet been opened to them; rather, “until this day, when Moses is read, a veil is placed over their heart. But when they shall have turned to God, the veil shall be removed” (2 Cor. 3:15). Thus neither learned nor unlearned persons among them will ever be able to know the sense of this book until they come to him “who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens” (Rev. 3:7). For they have been so blinded that the learned err among them as much as, or even more than, the ignorant. It follows:

VERSE 13.—“And the Lord said: Because this people approaches me with its mouth and glorifies me with its lips, while their heart is far from me, and they feared me according to the commandment and teachings of men.”

VERSE 14.—“Therefore, behold, I will add that I may work wonder upon this people, a great and astounding miracle.”

We read in Mark: “The Pharisees and some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem gathered around Jesus, and when they saw some of his disciples eating with common—that is, unwashed—hands, they rebuked them. For the Pharisees and all the Jews do not eat unless they wash their hands frequently, holding to the traditions of the elders; and when they come from the market, they do not eat unless they wash themselves; and there are many other things handed down to them to observe: washings of cups, jars, bronze vessels, and beds. And the Pharisees and scribes asked him: Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat bread with common hands? But he answered and said to them: Isaiah prophesied well concerning you hypocrites, as it is written: This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. Yet in vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines and commandments of men, washings of jars and cups; and you do many other things like these” (Mark 7:1 ff.).

These words of the Gospel, therefore, explain the prophetic statement. For this people approached the Lord with its mouth and withdrew farther away in heart, as the Saviour himself rebukes it, saying: “Generation of vipers, how can you speak good things when you are evil?” (Matt. 3:7). They drew near to God with their mouths because they boasted that they observed the worship of one God and rejected idols; but their heart was far from him because they did not believe in his Christ and feared him according to human commandment and teaching, as has been shown. Therefore he declares that he will perform for them a wonder, a great and astounding miracle. What that wonder is becomes clear when he adds:

“For wisdom shall perish from its wise men, and the understanding of its prudent men shall be hidden.” Because, he says, “this people glorifies me with its lips, but its heart is far from me, and they feared me according to the commandment and teachings of men, therefore wisdom shall perish from its wise men.” Thus it happened. They abandoned God’s commandments in observing human traditions, and for this reason the teachers themselves came to such blindness that they lost all wisdom and every understanding was hidden from them. For if they had kept God’s commandments, they would surely have received his Son, who is his wisdom. Because they did not receive him, they were blinded so as not to receive him who is contained in the letter.

While he was yet to come and they believed that he would come, they understood rightly. But from the time he came, because they did not believe that he had come but still thought him to be coming, they lost understanding. And as, after rising, he opened the understanding of his disciples so that they understood the Scriptures, so conversely he shut their understanding, so that they lost what they had understood.

This is the wonder which he declared that he would perform for them, because it is exceedingly remarkable how all alike have been blinded. In this sense, too, what he said above to them may fittingly be understood: “Be astonished and marvel; waver and stagger,” and so forth. For they can be astonished and marvel because they have lost all understanding and remained in darkness. It follows:

VERSE 15.—“Woe to those who are deep in heart, that they may hide counsel from the Lord; whose works are in darkness, and who say: Who sees us, and who knows us?”

The chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees were deep in heart in order to hide their counsel from the Lord, when they sent spies who pretended to be righteous, so that they might catch him in his words and hand him over to the authority and power of the governor. They questioned him, saying: “Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly and do not regard persons, but teach the way of God in truth. Is it lawful for us to give tribute to Caesar or not?” (Matt. 22:16). This and things like it was the depth of their heart directed against God’s wisdom, and their works were in darkness. For it is shameful even to speak of the things done secretly by them. Thus the Lord rebuked them, saying: “Outwardly you appear righteous to men, but within you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity” (Matt. 23:28). For while committing many evils in secret, they said: Who sees us, and who knows what we do here? Being blind, they thought themselves unseen by God; and the prophet rebukes them, adding:

VERSE 16.—“This thought of yours is perverse: as though clay should think against the potter and say to its maker: You did not make me; and the thing formed should say to its former: You do not understand.”

Clay indeed thought against the potter while the Jews formed a plan against Christ. And the work said to its maker, “You did not make me,” while they denied that he was their Creator. For Christ is the potter, while the Jews are his clay and formation, as they say repentantly at the end: “And now, O Lord, you are our Father; we are clay, and you are our potter, and we all are the work of your hands” (Isa. 64:6).

[Col. 0279C] Therefore it is fittingly said to those who were forming counsel against him: “This thought of yours is perverse: as though clay should think against the potter and say to its maker: You did not make me.” And the formed thing said to its maker, “You do not understand,” while they perpetrated evils in darkness and thought that they had escaped the sight of the Godhead, saying: “Who sees us, and who knows us?” It follows:

VERSE 17.—“Will not Lebanon, yet in a little while and a short time, be turned into Carmel, and Carmel be reckoned a forest?”

The time from the Lord’s preaching to the calling of the Gentiles was little and short. Then Lebanon was turned into Carmel. For Lebanon is interpreted “whitening” or “being made white,” and Carmel “knowledge of circumcision.” What is signified by Lebanon but the Gentile people, washed in baptism, cleansed from former defilements, and made white? What is signified by Carmel but the Jewish people circumcised in the flesh? Lebanon was therefore turned into Carmel, because “the wild olive was grafted in and made a partaker of the root and richness of the olive tree” (Rom. 11:17). For the Gentile people attained the grace and faith possessed by the Hebrew people.

But Carmel has been reckoned a forest, because the Jewish people, having lost faith, has been turned into the twisted forest of Gentilism, as it says: “We have become as at the beginning, when you did not rule over us and your name was not invoked over us” (Isa. 63:19). For the Hebrews are now such as they were in the times of Terah, and worse. It follows:

VERSE 18.—“And in that day the deaf shall hear the words of the book, and out of darkness and gloom the eyes of the blind shall see.”

On that day, when Lebanon is turned into Carmel and Carmel into a forest, the deaf—that is, the Gentiles—shall hear the words of the book, which remains sealed among the Jews and cannot be opened, that is, the sacred Scripture. And the inner eyes of the blind Gentiles shall see, out of the darkness and gloom of their old ignorance, the mysteries of the book which the Lion of the tribe of Judah has opened for us. It follows:

VERSE 19.—“And the meek shall add joy in the Lord, and poor people shall rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.”

The Apostles, who first rejoiced in converting thousands of Jews, will add to their joy in the Lord when they convert the Gentiles. And poor people—that is, the multitude of believers who had sold possessions and goods and laid their proceeds at the feet of the Apostles (Acts 4:34)—shall rejoice in the Holy One of Israel, that is, in Christ. But the following statement proves that the deaf can hear the words of the book and that the poor in spirit can rejoice in the Lord:

VERSE 20.—“For he that prevailed has failed; the mocker has been brought to an end.”

For the ancient enemy prevailed by oppressing the human race under his yoke, mocked it by suggesting deceptive pleasures, and made it serve sins. But now he has failed and been brought to an end—that is, consumed—because through Christ he has been conquered, bound, and made nothing. It follows: “And those who watched over iniquity have been cut off.”

VERSE 21.—“Those who made people sin in word, who tripped up him who rebuked at the gate, and turned aside in vain from the just one.”

The Jews who watched over iniquity—that is, who strove to persecute the Saviour—were cut off by the sword of the Romans. They made people sin in word, that is, they caused people to blaspheme, because “they had agreed that if anyone confessed him to be Christ, he should be put out of the synagogue” (John 9:22). And they tripped up him who rebuked them at the gate—that is, in the place of judgment—because while, during the five days before his passion, he rebuked them more sharply in the Temple, they were always devising snares to bring about his death.

“And they turned aside in vain from the just one,” that is, from the same Lord, because it did not benefit them to say: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 12:15). The ancients, moreover, used to conduct judgments at the gate. Hence it is said through the prophet: “Establish judgment in the gate” (Amos 5:15). Thus he calls the Lord one who rebuked them at the gate because, judging their malice, he reproved them. But if a material gate is sought, he rebuked them in Solomon’s porch, saying: “You do not believe because you are not of my sheep” (John 10:26). But they tripped him up, because “they took up stones to throw at him” (ibid., 31).

[Col. 0281A] Or the demons were cut off, who watched over iniquity and made the whole human race sin in the word of blasphemy, so that they might deny the Word of God and preach doctrines of error. And, so far as lay in them, they tripped up him who rebuked at the gate and in judgment; they made people turn away from righteousness—he who was exalted in the gates of the daughter of Zion from the gates of death, and who rebuked those who hated him that rebuked in the gates. It follows:

### Verse 22

“Therefore thus says the Lord to the house of Jacob, he who redeemed Abraham: *His face shall no longer blush.*”

### Verse 23

“But when he sees his children, the work of my hands, sanctifying my name in his midst, they shall sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and proclaim the God of Israel.” [Col. 0281B]

### Verse 24

“And those who err in spirit shall know understanding, and murmurers shall learn the law.”

Because the poor shall rejoice in the Holy One of Israel, and those who watched for iniquity shall be cut off, therefore thus says the Lord, who redeemed Abraham. An ancient tradition holds that the Chaldeans threw Abraham and Aram into fire, which in their language is called *Ur*, because they would not worship it; for the Chaldeans worshipped fire. Aram died there in Ur of the Chaldeans, but Abraham came forth unharmed. Hence God is reported to have said to him: “I am he who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans” (Gen. XV, 7), that is, out of the fire of the Chaldeans. For it is plainly read in the book of Ezra that the Lord himself delivered Abraham “from the fire of the Chaldeans” (II Esdr. IX, 7). [Col. 0281C] This, therefore, is said to be recalled here when it is written: “Thus says the Lord to the house of Jacob, he who redeemed Abraham.” But why does he repeat this ancient event when he is about to speak of new preachers, unless because, just as he then rescued Abraham and confounded his enemies, so now he will rescue his faithful people, who have despised the commands of the sacrilegious, and will confound their persecutors? Very often the martyrs overcame literal fire, and all overcame the fire of tribulation or desire.

“Jacob,” he says, “shall no longer be put to shame”: that is, at the time when the prophet spoke these words, the Jewish people would endure disgrace, and his face would blush; but when he sees his children—that is, the apostles [Col. 0281D] and believers, whom my hands will create in good works—sanctifying my name in the midst of Jerusalem by living well and preaching. For, when the Holy Spirit had been poured out and the apostles were speaking the mighty works of God, the unbelieving Jews were greatly confounded: some wasted away in their iniquities and were tormented with envy against the believers. When he adds that “they shall sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and proclaim the God of Israel,” he plainly declares that the apostles will preach no one other than the God worshipped by Israel and the Holy One awaited by Jacob. For Jacob said as he was dying: “I will await your salvation, O Lord” (Gen. [Col. 0282A] XLIX, 18).

When the new preachers proclaim this salvation, that is, the Lord Jesus, those erring in spirit shall know understanding: that is, the Jews, who always wandered in heart, though in their deeds they seemed to walk rightly. And the murmurers—that is, these same Jews, who, like stammering infants, mumbled the teaching of the law—shall learn the law which previously they had been unable, by any effort, to expound. For the grace of Christ will teach what man could not teach. It follows:

## Chapter XXX

### Verse 1

“Woe to the apostate children, says the Lord, who make a plan, but not from me; and weave a web, but not by my Spirit, so as to add sin upon sin.”

### Verse 2

“You who go to descend into [Col. 0282B] Egypt, and have not asked my mouth, hoping for help in the strength of Pharaoh and placing confidence in the shadow of Egypt.”

### Verse 3

“And the strength of Pharaoh shall be to you for shame, and confidence in the shadow of Egypt for disgrace.”

### Verse 4

“For your princes were in Tanis, and your messengers reached Tanes [Note: [Col. 0281] Alternatively: ‘For your princes were in Tani, and your messengers reached as far as Hanes.’].”

### Verse 5

“All were put to shame because of a people who will not be able to benefit them: they were not for help or any advantage, but for shame and reproach.”

This prophecy was fulfilled historically under Jeremiah, when, after the overthrow of Jerusalem, the remnant, in defiance of God, fled into Egypt [Col. 0282C] from the face of the Chaldeans, and there perished together with the Egyptians.

But what is signified by the remnant of Judah except certain faithful persons who will be found lax in the time of the final persecution, when others have already been taken captive? For now that spiritual captivity of the people of God is taking place which holy Jeremiah so grievously laments, and which has already been fulfilled in great part. What, then, does the remnant of Judah signify except ourselves, who still survive, and those yet to come who will be like us? Let us hear, then, what is said to such people, and take warning.

“Woe to the apostate children, says the Lord.” They are children because they are Christians; apostates because they abandon their Father. They forsake God’s commandments in order to cling to sins. They make a plan, but not from God, because [Col. 0282D] they think that they prudently provide for themselves when they resolve to seek worldly prosperity and fulfill their own pleasures. They weave a web, but not through the Spirit of the Lord, because they propose or begin to do what is not lawful; and thus the sin of action is added to the sin of their thought.

They go—that is, they act—in order to descend into Egypt, that is, into the world. For what is going except acting? And what is represented by Egypt except this world and the life of secular persons or unbelievers? What is represented by the mouth of the Lord except Holy Scripture or any preacher of righteousness? [Col. 0283A] And what is represented by the king of Egypt except the powerful men of the age? For those go down into Egypt who carry out those actions by which they descend from the height of religious life into secular conduct.

And in doing these things they have not asked the mouth of the Lord, because they have not sought in the Scriptures, or from any saint, whether they might lawfully do such things. They desire to descend into Egypt—that is, to lead a secular life—because they hope for help against persecutors in the strength of Pharaoh, that is, in the power of worldly rulers, if they attach themselves familiarly to them. And against the heat of tribulation they place their trust in the shadow of Egypt, that is, in worldly protection. To such persons, the strength of Pharaoh—that is, of worldly powers—shall be not help but shame; and their hope in Egypt’s shadow shall be disgrace. [Col. 0283B] For perhaps even worldly rulers will not be able to protect them under Antichrist from punishment; and they shall bear everlasting reproach, because, fearing to suffer tribulation, they abandoned righteousness or faith and yet did not escape tribulation. For we believe that this will happen to many in that final persecution: even on account of the Christian name alone which they once bore, they will be tortured or suddenly killed while still thought to be believers. Even now, many religious persons become too intimate with wicked rich men and serve them, hoping always to be protected from adversity by their defense or to gain the prosperity of this life. But when the storm of tribulation rises, they are not helped by them; rather, they are more deeply put to shame.

“For your princes were in Tanis,” etc. The princes and leaders of the Church go to Tanis—that is, “a low command,” namely an earthly one—when they obey the commands of secular rulers against their own canon. And they reach as far as Tanes, interpreted “has he been changed?”, when they become like any apostate, concerning whom it is not evident that he has changed from unbelief to righteousness. Thus they will act in the time of Antichrist, and some have already acted thus. [Col. 0283C]

But what is added? “All were put to shame because of a people who will not be able to benefit them.” For the Egyptian people—that is, secular people or unbelievers—will not benefit them against Nebuchadnezzar, that is, the devil; but they shall be punished by him temporally or eternally, or indeed both temporally and eternally. For just as the remnant of Judah perished with the Egyptians to whom they had fled to escape tribulation, so these too shall perish with the wicked with whom they associated themselves out of fear of persecution. It follows:

### Verse 6

“The burden of the beasts of the south. In a land of tribulation and distress: lioness and lion; from them viper and flying basilisk, carrying their riches upon the shoulders of beasts and their treasures upon the humps of camels, to a people who will not be able to benefit them.”

### Verse 7

“For Egypt will help in vain and to no purpose; therefore I cried concerning this: ‘It is mere pride; be still.’”

[Col. 0284A] Above we described ten burdens, and now he adds an eleventh, to show that he speaks of transgressors. For the number ten expresses the perfection of the law, and eleven its transgression. Here he also predicts the history that occurred in the days of Jeremiah, when, after the murder of Gedaliah, Johanan son of Kareah and the other leaders led the remnant of Judah into Egypt against the Lord’s command, given through Jeremiah, that they should remain in the land of Judah. This remnant is called beasts because it was senseless and brutish, still worshipping idols; beasts of the south because the tribe of Judah occupied the southern region.

“The land of tribulation and distress” is the expanse of the wilderness through which they fled into Egypt for fear of the Chaldeans. [Col. 0284B] The lioness is the people of the remnant; Johanan is the lion, together with the other leaders. The viper and basilisk arising from them—that is, the sons of the lioness and lion—were venomous because they sprang from cruel parents. Fleeing to the Egyptian people, which could not help them, they carried their riches, though slight, on the shoulders of beasts and the humps of camels. For, taking away all that they could possess, they fled there. But when Nebuchadnezzar came, they perished by famine and sword together with the Egyptians in whom they trusted. Egypt indeed helped them in vain—that is, to no effect—and uselessly, because its help failed and vanished. Therefore the prophet cries to the people of the remnant, hastening into Egypt: “There is only pride in Egypt, not strength; remain still in the [Col. 0284C] land of Judah.” When they did not remain still, the Lord commanded Jeremiah, saying:

### Verse 8

“Now go in, write it for them upon boxwood, and carefully engrave it in a book; and it shall be for them, in the last day, a testimony forever.”

Having entered Egypt with them, write for them upon boxwood, an incorruptible wood, so that it may endure forever; and engrave it in a book, that all may know that the Lord forbade them to go into Egypt, yet they went. It shall be for them a testimony of condemnation on the last day. It follows:

### Verse 9

“For it is a people provoking wrath, lying children, children unwilling to hear [Col. 0284D] the law of the Lord.”

The same is also read in Jeremiah. When they sent him to consult the Lord, they said: “May the Lord be a true and faithful witness between us, if we do not act according to every word with which the Lord your God shall send you to us” (Jer. XLII, 5). Yet when the Lord had answered them, “Johanan son of Kareah, all the leaders of the warriors, and all the people did not obey the voice of the Lord, to remain in the land of Judah” (Jer. XLIII, 4). It follows:

### Verse 10

“Who say to those who see: ‘Do not see’; and to those who behold: ‘Do not behold for us what is right. Speak pleasant things to us; see errors for us.’”

[Col. 0285A]

### Verse 11

“Take the way away from me; turn the path away from me; let the Holy One of Israel cease from before our face.”

This is what they said to Jeremiah already in Egypt: “We will not listen to you concerning the word which you spoke to us in the name of the Lord; rather, we will certainly do every word that proceeds from our own mouth, so that we may sacrifice to the queen of heaven—that is, the moon” (Jer. XLIV, 16). They often spoke such things. They said to those who saw—that is, to Jeremiah and Baruch—“Do not see for us what is right.” They said, “Let the Holy One of Israel cease from before our face,” because they could neither speak of God nor hear of him, nor allow the memory of him to come before the face of their mind. It follows:

### Verse 12

“Therefore thus says the Holy One of Israel: Because you have rejected this word [Col. 0285B] and have hoped in calumny and tumult, and have leaned upon it.”

### Verse 13

“Therefore this iniquity shall be to you like a falling breach, sought out in a high wall, whose ruin shall come suddenly, when it is not expected.”

### Verse 14

“And it shall be broken as a potter’s vessel is broken with a mighty breaking; and among its fragments no shard shall be found with which a little fire may be carried from the hearth or a little water drawn from a pit.”

“I commanded you,” he says, “to remain in the land of Judah; but you rejected this word from the mouth of Jeremiah, and you hoped in the calumny of words and in tumult, saying, ‘The Lord has not sent you; rather, Baruch son of [Col. 0285C] Neriah incites you against us’” (Jer. XLIII, 3). Therefore your iniquity of unbelief and contradiction shall be like a breach in a wall, sought by enemies and found without the knowledge of those within. For while you think you are hiding safely from the Chaldeans in Egypt, you are opening a way to them; you shall be captured unexpectedly and shattered like a potter’s vessel. Thus it was also said concerning Jerusalem through Jeremiah: “So I will break this people and this city, as a potter’s vessel is broken, which cannot be restored again” (Jer. XIX, 11). Thus the people of the remnant in Egypt was shattered so that it could not be restored. And just as among the fragments of a broken vessel no little shard is found with which a small amount of fire or water may be carried, so none of them survived [Col. 0285D] who would thereafter be fit for any good work. It follows:

### Verse 15

“For thus says the Lord God, the Holy One of Israel: If you return and rest, you shall be saved; in quietness and hope shall be your strength.”

This is evident. If you return to the land of Judah and remain there, you shall be saved from the Chaldeans whom you feared. It follows:

### Verse 16

“But you were unwilling, and said: ‘No; rather, we shall flee upon horses.’ Therefore you shall flee. ‘We shall mount swift ones’; therefore those who pursue you shall be swift [Note: [Col. 0285D] Alternatively, *swifter*.].”

[Col. 0286A] This too is plain. Because they fled to horses, it therefore happened that they fled from the Chaldeans; and because they mounted swift horses, as they said, the Chaldeans pursuing them were swift, so that they did not escape. It follows:

### Verse 17

“A thousand men shall flee at the terror of one; and at the terror of five you shall flee, until you are left like a ship’s mast on a mountain summit, and like a signal upon a hill.”

A thousand Egyptians, in whom you trust, shall flee at the terror of one Chaldean; and all you Jews shall flee at the terror of five Chaldeans, until you are left like a ship’s mast or a signal on a hill. For just as, when after a shipwreck a mast has been placed on a mountain summit or upon a hill as a signal, all [Col. 0286B] who see it understand that the ship has been wrecked, so the few Jews who remained made it evident to all who saw them that Jerusalem had been destroyed. Because they were afflicted for a long time among their enemies in captivity and misery, the prophet consoles them, adding:

### Verse 18

“Therefore the Lord waits to have mercy upon you, and therefore he shall be exalted in sparing you, for the Lord is a God of judgment. Blessed are all who wait for him.”

### Verse 19

“For the people of Zion shall dwell in Jerusalem; weeping, you shall by no means weep; in pity he shall pity you.”

“The Lord,” he says, “has not forgotten you in the hand of your enemies, as you suppose. Rather, he waits to free you in order to have mercy upon you, forgiving sin and delivering you. Therefore, by crushing your enemies, he shall be exalted above them; and he shall spare you from this affliction which you endure, because the Lord is a God of judgment—that is, doing all things by righteous judgment, whether when he afflicts you or when he spares you. Blessed shall be those who wait to be delivered through his mercy, because the people of Zion, held captive in Persia, shall again dwell freely in Jerusalem and abound in good things. Then you, O Israel, shall by no means weep, [Col. 0286C] but shall rejoice, because the Lord will have mercy upon you, delivering you from every tribulation.

Now, returning to the beginning of the passage, let us see whether it can also be expounded differently, since prophetic speech often comprises many things in one statement.

“The burden,” he says, “of the beasts of the south.” What the south is, we learn in Ezekiel, to whom the Lord says: “Son of man, set your face against the way of the south, and pour out speech toward Africa, and prophesy against the forest of the southern field; and you shall say to the southern forest: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will kindle a fire in you and burn in you every green tree and every dry tree” (Ezek. XX, 46). Repeating the same matter, he expounded it thus: “Son of man, set your face against Jerusalem, and pour out speech toward the sanctuaries, and prophesy against the land of Israel; and say to the land of Israel: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I am against you, and I shall draw [Col. 0287A] my sword from its sheath and kill in you the righteous and the wicked” (Ezek. XXI, 2). What he had said, “Set your face against the way of the south, and pour out speech toward Africa,” he interpreted by saying, “Set your face toward Jerusalem, and pour out speech toward the sanctuaries.”

The southern way, therefore, is Jerusalem—that is, the Church—and Africa or the south is the sanctuary. What, then, are the beasts of the south or of the sanctuary except men who profess the Christian religion but live like beasts? “Man, though he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. XLVIII, 13). Beasts lack reason and carry without distinction whatever burden is placed upon them. So too, a man who does not, by the reason of his mind, discerningly distinguish good from evil—rejecting evil and choosing good—but agrees to bear any load of sins imposed upon him, is a beast.

The burden here signifies the weight of sins and afflictions.

“In a land of tribulation and distress: lioness and lion; from them viper and flying basilisk, carrying their riches on the shoulders of beasts and their treasures upon the humps of camels, to a people who cannot benefit them.” What is the land of tribulation and distress except that in which the faithful are afflicted? For in it are the lioness and lion, that is, Babylon and the devil. As lioness and lion customarily signify Christ and the Church whenever they are understood in a good sense, so they signify the devil and Babylon whenever they are read in an evil sense. [Col. 0287C]

From this lion and lioness arises the flying basilisk, that is, the deadly Antichrist, who through pride flies above all things in the height of his thought; and the viper, that is, the venomous throng of his preachers. Taking the beasts of the sanctuary—that is, Christians and professors of religion—they place upon the shoulders of their hearts their riches, that is, sins; and upon the humps of camels—that is, upon the pride of their twisted minds—their treasures, that is, iniquities. For these are those “who enter houses and lead captive little women burdened with sins, who are led away by various desires” (II Tim. V, 6).

Therefore, although the devil, Antichrist, and their followers even now lay their riches upon the shoulders of the beasts of the south, they will do so especially in that final deception: seducing the faithful away from the Church through false promises, they will burden them with sins and afflictions. For “those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and into the snare of the devil, and into many useless desires which plunge people into destruction and perdition. For covetousness is the root of all evils; desiring it, some have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows” (I Tim. VI, 9). [Col. 0287D] Through avarice, then, these beasts of the south are deceived so as to take upon themselves so great a burden of iniquities and misery. Through it they fall into the devil’s snare and into desires that draw people into perdition. And when, overcome by covetousness, they consent to Antichrist, they wander from the faith and pierce themselves with many sorrows.

The lioness and lion, the viper and basilisk, lead them, burdened with sins, into Egypt—that is, into the darkness of unbelief—to the people of the gentiles and unbelievers, who will be unable to benefit them on the last day, just as the Egyptians did not benefit the remnant of Judah when the Chaldeans came. Egypt—that is, the dark multitude of secular persons and unbelievers—will help them in vain, because it will not profit them, and uselessly, because it vanishes and passes away. [Col. 0288A]

Or the people of unbelievers will be unable to benefit the lion, lioness, viper, and basilisk by punishing the martyrs, because through torments the martyrs shall pass to rest and glory and shall all the more strengthen the Church against Antichrist. Since Egypt will help in vain, therefore I cried concerning this: the beasts of the south descend to it with their loads. It is mere pride, not benefit, that you descend into the Egypt of unbelief, whoever you are that abandon the land of Judah—that is, the Church, in which is the confession of truth. Cease from this perverse journey by remaining in the Church.

But because they refuse to remain still: “O Elijah, now enter among them and write for them upon boxwood”—that is, in your abstinent manner of life, figured by the pallor of boxwood, set forth for them what they ought to do—“and carefully engrave it in a book,” that is, labor by preaching to impress it memorably upon their hearts. For each person’s book is the memory of his own conscience, and we write in a book when we impress something upon a neighbor’s conscience. [Col. 0288B]

“And this writing,” he says, “shall be for them, on the last day, a testimony of just condemnation,” because they did not fail to know the good which they should have done, but despised it. “For it is a people provoking wrath,” because one provokes God to wrath by knowingly transgressing his commandments. This people, then, provokes wrath, and is made up of lying children—that is, children who do not fulfill what they promised God—children now unwilling to hear the law of God but following the law of their own will. They say to those who see—that is, to teachers of religion—“Do not see whether we walk in order”; and to those who behold—that is, those who continuously observe whether the life of their subjects is upright—“Do not behold for us what is right, but speak [Col. 0288C] pleasant things to us,” that is, things conducive to vain delight. “See errors for us, which we may follow.”

“Take away from me the way of righteousness, that I may walk through byways; turn from me the path of narrow conduct, and I shall walk by the broad way of destruction. Let the Holy One of Israel”—that is, God—“cease from before our face,” so that he may no longer come before the face of our heart. To speak or think in this way is to descend into Egypt. For those who abandon the Christian religion and join themselves to Antichrist already say these things, and will say them still more. “For there will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their own desires they will heap up teachers for themselves, with itching ears; and some will turn their hearing away from the truth and turn instead to fables” (II Tim. IV, 3). “For in the last times some shall depart from the faith, attending to spirits of error” (I Tim. IV, 1), that is, to doctrines of demons, speaking falsehood in hypocrisy and “having their own conscience seared” (ibid.). [Col. 0289A] These, then, will say: “Take away from me the way; let the Holy One of Israel cease from before our face.”

To them the divine judgment answers: “Because you rejected this word by which I commanded you to remain still and not go into the Egypt of unbelief”; or, “because you rejected this—that those who behold should behold for you what is right—and hoped in calumny and tumult,” raising calumny against sound doctrine, making tumult, and insolently leaning upon the tumult of contradiction and disobedience: “therefore this iniquity shall be to you like a falling breach in a wall,” a hole sought out by enemies seeking an entrance. For while in Egypt—that is, in the company of unbelievers—you suppose yourselves secure as within the circuit of a wall, you shall be unexpectedly taken and perish, though you would have been secure in the Church.

And the wall of your protection shall be shattered like a potter’s vessel, because the bodies of the carnal men who protected you shall be destroyed in death. “And among its fragments no shard shall be found with which a little fire may be carried from the hearth or a little water drawn from a pit,” because, after the reprobate have been shattered in death, none of them will be found able any longer to take even a small spark of charity from the fire by which the minds of the elect burn, or to draw a little water of compunction from the pit [Col. 0289B] of humility. For every sinner is a shard, to whom it is said: “Woe to him who contends with his maker, a shard among the shards of earth!” (Isa. XLV, 9). But after shattering, this shard cannot carry a spark from the hearth, because on the sabbath day, as the law says, “You shall not kindle fire in any of your dwellings” (Exod. XXXV, 3). The sabbath is when, after death, it is no longer permitted to do anything. No one kindles fire in his dwelling on the sabbath day, because whoever does not now kindle the fire of charity in his heart will be unable to kindle it after death. Nor can he draw water of compunction, because, although there is weeping and gnashing of teeth in hell, cleansing water is by no means found there. We speak, indeed, of those tears which wash the one who weeps. [Col. 0289C]

Having shown what awaits those who descend into Egypt—that is, into the world and unbelief—he again shows what they will gain if they return to the Church as to the land of Judah, adding:
