“If you return and rest, you shall be saved; in quietness and hope”—not in calumny and tumult—“shall be your strength,” because you will resist your invisible enemies. But these, blinded by pride and covetousness, answer: “No; rather, we shall flee upon horses.” Yet the prophet, eager to correct the sinful, strives to recall sinners by rebuke: he restrains the rush of passions, imposes the reins of reason, recalls them from fault, and corrects error, while urging them to return and rest and not descend upon horses into Egypt. For a horse cannot stand still: swift to rush forward, it raises its neck and neighs toward lust. What is more like sin? Fault first seethes in its rush and outruns every right thought; in immature movement it leaps forth, so that reason can scarcely call it back. It is borne headlong and casts its rider into this sea of the present age, lifting its swollen neck and refusing the yoke of correction. There is also a particular form of lust that changes a person’s voice, corrupts the words of the lover, and reveals itself in its speech. [Col. 0290A] Those who say to the prophet recalling them, “No; we shall not return, but shall flee upon horses,” hasten, he says, to such riding. Their senses decline and flow away, they have cast off the discipline of the mind, and therefore are scattered outwardly in action and rush into sin.

“We shall flee upon horses,” they say, lest we suffer the adversities of the world. To them the prophet answers: “Therefore you shall flee from invisible adversaries in the time of necessity, because you now flee discipline.” They add: “And we shall mount swift ones,” that is, we shall be exalted in sins that swiftly carry us toward the things we wickedly contemplate. And the divine word says: “Therefore evil spirits, who will pursue you in the hour of death, shall be swift.”

“A thousand men shall flee at the terror of one, and at the terror of five you shall flee.” For at the time of death Satan rushes in with his attendants to seize the soul. Thus Solomon, after saying, “Keep the law [Col. 0290B] and counsel, and it shall be life to your soul” (Prov. XXXI, 21), shortly afterward added concerning the hour of death: “Do not fear sudden terror or the forces of the wicked rushing upon you” (ibid., 25)—understand: therefore keep the law and counsel. Those who refuse to keep law and counsel, saying, “No; we shall flee upon horses,” shall be afraid when the moment of death comes stealthily upon them and shall flee from the demons. They will flee indeed, but will not escape, just as the remnant of Judah fled from the Chaldeans into Egypt but did not escape. For the soul flees from its persecutors at the time of its departure because it seeks to flee, and in its trembling runs through the limbs.

Concerning Babylon it is also written: “For in one day her plagues shall come: death, mourning, and famine; and she shall be burned with fire. And the kings of the earth who committed fornication with her and lived in luxury shall weep and mourn over her when they see the smoke of her burning; standing far off for fear of her torments, they shall say: Woe, woe, that great city Babylon, that mighty city!” (Apoc. XVIII, 8–10). Yet these kings shall stand far off not in place but in affection, not in body but in will, since they shall be burned together with her. Therefore, just as those in the same condemnation are said to stand far off because they would wish to be far away, so these persons are now said to flee their adversaries in death because they desire to flee them. Thus it is said to the reprobate regarding their end: “A thousand men shall flee at the terror of one, and at the terror of five you shall flee,” etc. [Col. 0290C]

Who, then, is this one who pursues sinners in their last moments except the devil? And who are these five persecutors except the evil spirits who enticed their five bodily senses to sin? What is signified by the number one thousand except totality? He therefore says to those who neglect to make provision for the last things: “A thousand men”—that is, all of you—“shall flee at the time of your summons from the terror of one,” Satan; “and at the terror of five,” that is, of the demons who caused you to sin through the five senses of the body. You shall flee, I say, “until you are left like a ship’s mast on a mountain summit”: that is, until your lifeless body is left behind and it is evident to all that you have suffered shipwreck on the sea of this age. And you shall be left “like a signal upon a hill,” which shows travelers the way up the mountain, because the fear inspired by your punishment will persuade others not to stray, as you did, from the way of uprightness, but to strive upward by a straight path. Thus Lot’s wife, because she looked back, was changed into a pillar of salt, becoming a seasoning for everyone’s mind, lest they look back again. The judgment upon those now said to be left like a ship’s mast on a mountain summit or like a signal upon a hill is the same as upon the woman who remained, changed into a pillar of salt. [Col. 0291A]

Then the prophet strengthens the long-suffering of the elect, adding:

“Therefore the Lord waits to have mercy upon you, and therefore he shall be exalted in sparing you, for the Lord is a God of judgment. Blessed are all who wait for him.”

Peter, in his Epistle, agrees with the preceding words by which the prophet rebukes those who will turn aside into errors near the end of the age: “In the last days mockers shall come in deception, walking according to their own desires and saying: ‘Where is his promise or coming? For since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of creation’” (II Pet. III, 3). And what the prophet now says—“Therefore the Lord waits to have mercy upon you, and therefore he shall be exalted in sparing you”—Peter writes thus: “The Lord does not delay his promise, but is patient on your account, not wishing any to perish but all to return to repentance” (ibid., 9). And where this text continues, “For the Lord is a God of judgment. Blessed are all who wait for him,” Peter adds: “But the day of the Lord shall come as a thief, on which the heavens shall pass away with a great rushing sound and the elements shall be dissolved by heat” (ibid., 10). Since, therefore, all these things are to be dissolved, what kind of persons ought we to be in holy conduct and pieties, waiting for and hastening toward the coming of the day through which the burning heavens shall be dissolved and the elements melt from the heat of fire? But according to his promises, we await new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells. To the apostle’s words also accords what is added here: [Col. 0291B]

“For the people of Zion shall dwell in Jerusalem.” Zion means “watchtower” or “command,” while Jerusalem means “vision of peace.” The people of the faithful now remain in the command and in the watchtower because, keeping God’s law, they look watchfully in every direction from the citadel of the mind, detect the assaults of vices before they come, and bravely overcome them when they do come. This people, then, shall dwell in Jerusalem because, in place of temporal wars, it shall live in eternal peace.

Or Zion is to be understood as the present Church, and Jerusalem as the future one. The people of Zion shall dwell in Jerusalem because those who do not turn aside into errors but persevere faithfully and righteously in this Church shall without doubt reign in that one; and those who now mourn for various reasons shall then rejoice without end. For it follows: “Weeping, you shall by no means weep.” And because they shall then find mercy in timely help, “In pity,” he says, “he shall pity you” (Ps. CXXXIV, 14), because “the Lord shall judge his people and have mercy on his servants, because his mercy is forever” (Ps. CXXXV, 1). [Col. 0292A–B]

After this, the text speaks of the grace of the New Testament:

“Immediately, at the sound of your cry, when he hears it, he will answer you.” The Lord answers our petition at once when he hears the cry of our request, by doing what we ask—if it is just and beneficial, if the time has come when it ought to be done, and if we are worthy that he should do it for us. We said “if it is just and beneficial,” because Paul asked that the angel of Satan, who by the Lord’s judgment was buffeting him, be taken away from him; and he did not obtain this, but only received in answer the words: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9). We said “if the time has already come,” because when we say, “May your kingdom come” (Matt. 6:10), we are indeed heard, [Col. 0292C] but we do not at once receive that kingdom itself. The cry of those who are unworthy is truly not heard, because “he who turns away his ear so as not to hear the law, even his prayer shall be an abomination” (Prov. 28:9). For this has not been promised except either to the people of the elect or to any righteous person. And it should be noted that he does not say, “He will do whatever you ask,” but “He will answer you,” namely, according to what is fitting and just. Thus, as in Paul’s case, he did not do what was asked, but answered with what was beneficial.

**VERSE 20.**—“And the Lord will give you narrow bread and scant water.”

What is denoted by bread and water except the teaching of wisdom? For it is written: “He fed him [Col. 0292D] with the bread of life and understanding, and gave him to drink the water of saving wisdom” (Ecclus. 15:3). Therefore, in the New Testament the Lord gave us narrow bread and scant water. “For every law,” as the Apostle teaches, “is fulfilled in one saying: You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Gal. 5:14). What could be briefer than this saying, in which the whole breadth of the commandments is comprehended? It follows: “And he will no longer cause your teacher to fly away.” This is what the Teacher himself says: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). It follows: “And your eyes shall see your instructor.”

**VERSE 21.**—“And your ears shall hear a word of one warning behind your back.”

In Holy Scripture, what has passed is sometimes stated as though it were future. Thus we read of Hagar that, seeing herself to have conceived, she despised her mistress. When Sarai afflicted her, therefore, she fled. And when the angel of the Lord found her in the wilderness, he said to her: “Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son” (Gen. 16:11). Such is what the prophet now says: filled with the spirit of eternity, he beholds past and future alike with the enlarged eye of his mind, and pronounces judgment concerning ancient and final things as though they were future, saying to humankind: “And your eyes shall see your instructor,” and so forth. For in Paradise human beings saw their instructor, because, as we read: “He established with them an everlasting covenant, and showed them his righteousness and his judgments; and their eye saw the greatness of his honor, and [Col. 0293B] their ears heard the glory of his voice” (Ecclus. 17:10). Thus God admonished the human race face to face when, after creating man in Paradise and placing him in free choice, he commanded what he ought to do and what he ought not to do. But man turned his back upon the face of God when, in pride, he despised his commands. Yet God did not abandon him in his pride, for he gave the Law in order to renew humanity, sent angels to exhort it, and appeared in the flesh of our mortality. Therefore, standing behind our back, he admonished us, because he called us back to grace after our rejection of him. Rightly, then, it is said to the human race: “And your eyes shall see your instructor, and your ears shall hear a word of one warning behind your back.”

But what is understood generally of all must necessarily be understood particularly of each individual. For each person receives the words of God’s admonition as though standing before God when, before committing sins, he knows the commandments of God’s will. For to stand still before his face is not yet to despise him by sinning. But when one abandons the good of innocence and, choosing iniquity, longs for it, one has already turned one’s back upon his face. But behold, even behind the back God follows and warns, because even after guilt he persuades us to return to him. He calls back the one who has turned away when that person looks back upon what has been committed; to one returning he opens the bosom of his mercy. Therefore, we hear the voice of one warning behind our back if at least after our sins we return to the Lord who invites us. We ought therefore to be ashamed before the mercy of him who calls [Col. 0293D] us, if we wish to fear justice, because he is despised with all the graver wickedness in proportion as, though despised, he does not disdain still to call us back. Concerning this admonition the prophet adds:

“This is the way; walk in it, neither to the right nor to the left.” This admonition of the Savior is the way of righteousness in which we ought to walk, without turning aside from it in any direction. For the person who is proud of righteousness, or practices what is just without moderation, strays to the right. Hence Solomon warns: “Do not be excessively righteous” (Eccl. 7:17). But the one who turns aside to an evil work declines to the left. Let us therefore not stray in either direction, but walk with straight step through the teaching of the Savior. Since, after his coming, the nations were to receive his faith, the prophet adds, speaking to the Gentile people:

**VERSE 22.**—“And you shall defile the plates of your silver graven images and the covering of your molten gold; you shall scatter them like the uncleanness of a menstruous woman. ‘Get out!’ you shall say to it.”

For the Gentile world, coming to Christ, defiled all the ornaments of idols along with the idols themselves and cast them away. Hence it is subsequently said to the order of preachers:

**VERSE 23.**—“And rain shall be given to your seed wherever you sow it in the earth, and the bread of the produce of the earth shall be most abundant and rich.”

The seed is the word of preaching; the rain that falls from above and causes the seed to germinate is the watering of grace that comes upon it. Therefore, wherever the teacher casts seeds, rain will be given, because in every people and nation grace follows the word of preaching, as in the house of Cornelius: while Peter was speaking, “the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard the word” (Acts 10:44). Thus rain was given to his seed.

What, then, is denoted by the bread of the produce of the earth except the refreshment of good works? Of such bread the Lord says: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4:34). Therefore the bread of the produce of the earth will be most abundant, because the faithful will be abundantly refreshed by good works. It will also be rich, that is, filled with spiritual richness. It follows: “On that day the lamb shall graze spaciously in your possession.”

[Col. 0294C] **VERSE 24.**—“And your oxen and the young asses that till the ground shall eat mixed fodder, as it has been winnowed on the threshing floor.”

What is the possession of the faithful except the field of good conduct and the riches of virtues? In this possession the Lamb of Christ grazes, as it were, upon the grass of good works, in the spacious breadth of love. Oxen, moreover, lead herds. And what is signified by oxen except rulers of churches? What, then, is expressed by asses except Gentiles? For the Gentile people is called an ass where it is said: “The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger” (above, 1:3). What then shall we understand by the young of asses except the children of Gentiles, who, abandoning their paternal error, came to Christ? They till the earth—that is, by meditations and disciplines they plough up their own conscience. *Migma* is barley mixed with chaff. And what is denoted by chaff except the outer surface of the letter? What by barley except inward understanding? Thus oxen and young asses—that is, prelates and subjects in the Church—eat mixed *migma*, as though in a stable, because they receive both the historical and the mystical sense, are nourished by both, and eat it as it has been winnowed on the threshing floor—that is, purified and examined in the Church. For they are not nourished either by allegorical or historical understanding unless it has first been cleansed from error and approved by ecclesiastical authority. It follows:

[Col. 0295A] **VERSE 25.**—“And upon every high mountain and upon every elevated hill there shall be streams of running waters in the day of the slaughter of many, when the towers fall.”

What is figured by mountains and hills except the more eminent saints? What by streams of water except the rivers of holy teachings? “Therefore, upon every high mountain and every elevated hill there shall be streams of running waters,” because those who draw near to heavenly things through the merit of their life pour forth flowing streams of teaching. And when? In the day of the slaughter of many: that is, at the time of revealed grace, when many are slain by the sword of God’s word from their former manner of life, mortifying their members which are upon earth—fornication, uncleanness, lust, and things like these.

The towers also fall, because those who had generally hardened themselves against God—that is, had raised themselves up in pride—are humbled when preachers destroy strongholds and every height exalting itself against the knowledge of God.

Or understand by streams of water the outpourings of spiritual graces. “Therefore, upon mountains and hills there shall be streams of running waters,” because the Holy Spirit will overflow the elect in seven streams of graces. And this shall happen in the day of the slaughter of many—that is, on the day of judgment, when the whole multitude of the reprobate shall perish. And the towers shall fall: that is, all the proud and powerful of the world shall be cast down. It follows:

**VERSE 26.**—“And the light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun, and [Col. 0295C] sevenfold, like the light of seven days, on the day when the Lord binds up the wound of his people and heals the bruise of their blow.”

Our elders understood this literally: when judgment has ended and there is a new heaven and a new earth, the moon shall receive the splendor which the sun now possesses, and the sun shall shine seven times more brightly than it now does. But if it must be understood mystically, the sun and moon are Christ and the Church; Christ’s face shone like the sun in the Transfiguration. Therefore the light of the moon shall be like that of the sun, because “then the righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13:43). “His face shone like the sun,” and the righteous shall shine like the sun (Matt. 17:12). “Therefore the light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun. For we know that, when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

“And the light of the sun shall be like the light of seven days,” according to what is sung in the Apocalypse of John: “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and divinity and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing” (Rev. 5:12). These are the seven days, whose light the Sun of righteousness received in his resurrection: namely power and divinity, wisdom and strength, honor and glory and blessing.

The wound and bruise of the people lie in this: through the sin of the first parent we lost immortality and likeness to him. But in the resurrection the Lord will bind up the wound of his people, because he will make the bodies of the righteous [Col. 0296A] immortal, incorruptible, and incapable of suffering.

“And he will heal the bruise of their blow,” because he will restore to their minds, now scattered by diverse thoughts, an unshakable tranquility, so that, abiding always in the same state, it may never become unlike itself. Concerning that day, when the Judge comes, he fittingly adds:

**VERSE 27.**—“Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar, his wrath burning and heavy to bear; his lips are full of indignation, and his tongue like a devouring fire.”

The name of the Lord is the Only-begotten, because when the Son is heard, the Father is understood, just as a person is known by his proper name. But the name of the Lord comes from afar, because the Only-begotten of the Father descends to destroy sinners. “For salvation is far from sinners” (Ps. 118:155). Therefore he comes from afar when the Judge approaches from the region of the living to those who are far from salvation. Or he comes from afar because, in order to fulfill his purpose, after a long period of time he descends to punish sinners.

His wrath is burning and heavy to bear, because to the reprobate he will appear inflamed with excessive wrath when he begins to strike them without pardon, although he is moved by no disturbance of mind; and no one will be able to bear the weight of his anger. His lips are filled with indignation when he reproaches those on the left, saying: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger, and you did not take me in” [Col. 0296C] (Matt. 25:42). And his tongue is like a devouring fire when he says to them: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire,” and so forth (ibid., 41).

It follows:

**VERSE 28.**—“His spirit is like an overflowing torrent, reaching to the middle of the neck, to reduce the nations to nothing; and there shall be a bridle of error in the jaws of the peoples.”

Just as a swift torrent, when by swelling it reaches to a person’s neck, throws that person down and submerges him, so the spirit of the Judge’s wrath will choke and destroy the unbelieving and reprobate; and it will destroy the bridle of error—that is, the devil, who ruled unbelievers along the path of error and bent them at the pleasure of his own will, just as a horse is ruled by a bridle. Having said these things against the reprobate, he adds concerning the joy of the elect:

[Col. 0296D] **VERSE 29.**—“You shall have a song like the voice [Vulgate: night] of a sanctified solemnity, and joy of heart like one who goes with a flute, to enter the mountain of the Lord, to the Mighty One of Israel.”

Just as at some chief solemnity the people of God customarily do nothing but sing solemn praises, so after the judgment the elect shall fulfill the Scripture which says: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; for ages upon ages they shall praise you” (Ps. 83:5).

And just as the people of Israel, when they carried their first fruits and tithes to the temple of the Lord, went with flute and exultant voice because they abounded in the fruits of the earth, so on the day of judgment the saints shall enter, singing with every joy, that temple and sanctuary of the heavenly country. “For they shall indeed come with exultation, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. 125:8).

We may also refer this to the time of evangelical preaching, by punctuating it thus: “And the bridle of error, which was in the jaws of the peoples, shall be a song to you like the voice of a sanctified solemnity.” For the bridle of error restrained the jaws of the peoples when the Gentile world, bound by the error of idols, did not know how to offer God the true praises of confession. But this very bridle of error has now been turned for us into song, when we say: “For all the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Ps. 95:5).

It is well said, moreover, “like the voice of a sanctified solemnity,” [Col. 0297B] because when we render to God the praise of confession, we rejoice in a sanctified solemnity. And it is joy of heart for us when we enter into faith, just as it was for the children of Israel as they ascended to the temple of the Lord with flutes and songs. But according to the higher sense, let us consider what follows. It follows:

**VERSE 30.**—“And the Lord will make heard the glory of his voice, and will show the terror of his arm in the threat of wrath and the flame of devouring fire.”

He will make heard the glory of his voice, because all who are in the tombs shall hear the voice of the Son of God and shall come forth. And he will show the terror of his arm, that is, of his power, in the threat of wrath and the flame of devouring fire, when, as was said above, he shall say to the reprobate: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire” [Col. 0297C] (Matt. 25:41), and so forth. It follows:

“He will strike in whirlwind and hailstone.” He will strike the reprobate in a whirlwind, because then all the elements shall be shaken, and with hailstone, because “a mighty tempest is round about him” (Ps. 49:2). Hence it is also said in the Book of Wisdom: “Hailstones full of anger shall be hurled from rocky wrath. The water of the sea shall rage against them, and rivers shall rush together fiercely. Against them shall stand the spirit of power, and like a stormy wind it shall divide them” (Wis. 5:23). It follows:

**VERSE 31.**—“For Assyria shall be terrified by the voice of the Lord, struck with the rod.”

**VERSE 32.**—“And the passage of the appointed rod shall be established, for the Lord shall make it rest upon him.”

Assyria is the devil; the rod is the scourge with which the Judge shall strike him. Struck, he shall be terrified before the Lord, because he too shall dread the Judge’s sentence when he begins to be punished. The passage of this rod is the descent from judgment to hell. For, having received their sentence, all the reprobate will immediately begin to be tortured and, together with their torments, shall fall headlong into the abyss from the Judge’s presence. This, therefore, is the passage of this [Note: [Col. 0297D] The codex has “this” (*istae*) instead of “of this” (*istius*).] rod. But that passage is established—that is, firm—because the punishments that descend with them into hell are never bent or softened. Hence it is added that the Lord will make this rod rest upon Assyria, because torments shall remain without end upon the ancient enemy. It follows:

[Col. 0298A] “With timbrels and harps, and in chief battles, he will overcome them.” What is denoted by timbrels and harps except the applause and joy of the saints? And what by chief battles except the issuing of sentences against the ungodly, by which they are struck as by swords? Therefore, with timbrels and harps and in chief battles the Lord will overcome them, because they shall flee from the joy of the saints and be driven out by sentence. It follows:

**VERSE 33.**—“For Topheth has been prepared from yesterday; it has been prepared by the king, deep and wide. Its fuel is fire and much wood; the breath of the Lord, like a torrent of sulfur, kindles it.”

Topheth is interpreted as “the Gehenna of life.” For *Toph* is called Gehenna, and *Phet*, life. Therefore hell is called “the Gehenna of life,” because there is living [Col. 0298B] fire there and a worm that does not die. The king is Christ; “yesterday” is past time. Thus Topheth—that is, Gehenna—has been prepared from yesterday by the King for all the reprobate: that is, long ago, from the beginning of the world. It is exceedingly deep, so as to swallow up, and wide enough to contain all the ungodly. Its fuel—that is, Gehenna’s—is fire, because that fire always sustains punishment; and much wood, that is, the bodies of the reprobate, feed it, multiplying and kindling the affliction of the reprobate themselves.

But the breath of the Lord also kindles it. When we breathe, we draw air inward from outside and return outward what has been drawn within; this is how breath comes about. Thus God is said to breathe forth the requital of vengeance, because from external causes he conceives inwardly the plan of judgment, and from his inward counsel he sends forth the sentence outwardly. For, as though God were breathing, something is drawn from outside to within when he conceives evils outwardly and disposes them inwardly; and again, as though God were breathing, breath is sent outward from within when, from inwardly conceived counsel, he brings outward the judgment of condemnation.

This, then, is the breath of the Lord kindling Gehenna, compared to a torrent of sulfur because, overflowing in a strong rush, it descends upon the ungodly, bringing stench with burning. For what is sulfur but fuel for fire? Yet it so nourishes the fire that it exhales a most grievous stench. Therefore the breath of the Lord, which sets Gehenna ablaze, is like a torrent of sulfur, because the issuing of the Judge’s sentence, which punishes sinners, [Col. 0298D] gives stench in return for stench and burning in return for burning. For those who burned with the heat of lusts and other vices shall burn in everlasting fire; and those who delighted in the stench of sins shall be tormented by everlasting stench. But after the prophet has shown the future joy of the righteous and the damnation of the wicked, he returns to those who descend into Egypt—that is, into the darkness of worldly life and unbelief—adding:

## CHAPTER 31

**VERSE 1.**—“Woe to those who go down into Egypt, hoping for help in horses, and trusting in chariots because they are many, and in horsemen [Col. 0299A] because they are exceedingly strong; and they have not trusted in the Holy One of Israel, nor sought the Lord.”

**VERSE 2.**—“Yet he is wise: he has brought evil, and has not withdrawn his words; and he shall rise against the house of the wicked and against the help of those who work iniquity.”

Above, indeed, he sternly rebuked those who go down into Egypt, threatened them with woe, and nevertheless calls them back. But now he no longer calls them back, but declares their condemnation certain. What the horse signifies we said above: namely, sin; and we gave the reason for it—or rather, we cited the words of Ambrose. Therefore the horseman who mounts this horse is the sinner who, through evil actions, becomes exalted in this [Col. 0299B] world. What, then, does the chariot denote except the pomp of worldly glory? Hence it was said above to the proud bishop: “There shall be the chariot of your glory” (above, 22:18).

Therefore those who, abandoning discipline or faith, turn aside into Egypt—that is, into the darkness of worldly vices or unbelief—hope in horses, that is, in sins, while they expect to fulfill their pleasures or desires; and they trust in chariots, that is, in the pomp of worldly glories because they are many, to be exalted in this world; and in horsemen, that is, in powerful worldly sinners, because they are very strong for evil and support others in iniquity.

But woe to believers who prefer such things to sacred religion, trusting in such things and hastening toward them, and who do not trust in the Holy One of Israel, who is Christ, nor seek the Lord with devout zeal. Or, “they do not seek” means that they do not ask him whether they ought to do these things. Yet by his wise counsel he has brought upon them the evil they did not fear, and has not withdrawn his words, by which he had threatened them with destruction—that is, he has not rendered them void, but fulfilled them.

And in judgment he shall rise against the house of the wicked—that is, against the generation of those who, casting off religion, descend into the Egypt of worldly life—and against the help which Egyptians—that is, worldly and unbelieving persons who work iniquity—provide for them in evil. For the Lord shall destroy all alike: both those who aid evil and those thus aided. It follows:

[Col. 0299D] **VERSE 3.**—“Egypt is human, and not God; and their horses are flesh, and not spirit.”

Egypt is human—that is, Egyptians are human beings. “Egypt is human and not God.” “Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm, and whose heart withdraws from the Lord” (Jer. 17:5). Woe to those who go down into Egypt. “And their horses are flesh and not spirit.” Again: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26:41). And again: “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6:64). Such horses, therefore, are weak and useless. Egypt is human and not God, because the darkness of worldly errors comes from humanity and not from God. And their horses are flesh and not spirit, [Col. 0300A] because their sins come from the flesh and not from the spirit. It follows:

“And the Lord shall stretch out his hand, and the helper shall fall, and he to whom help is given shall fall, and all together shall be consumed.” The Lord shall stretch out his hand, by which he sustained them, and the people of worldly and unbelieving persons who helped those turning aside to iniquity shall fall; and everyone who descends into Egypt in heart, to whom Egyptians provide help for wickedness, shall fall. Together all shall be consumed in everlasting torments—deceivers and deceived alike.

Having spoken of the final destruction of the reprobate, when they shall find no helper, he immediately adds an oracle concerning the Savior’s first coming, in which he fought against the devil for the elect and, redeeming us by his blood, saved us from eternal damnation. As though he said: Truly, all who abandon religion and sink into error shall perish and shall find no deliverer, because those who remain in ecclesiastical religion shall be saved under the Lord’s protection. Thus he adds:

**VERSE 4.**—“For thus says the Lord to me: As when a lion roars, and a lion’s whelp over its prey, and a multitude of shepherds comes against it, it will not fear their voice nor be alarmed by their multitude, so shall the Lord of hosts descend to fight upon Mount Zion and upon its hill.”

**VERSE 5.**—“As flying birds, so shall the Lord of hosts protect [Col. 0300C] Jerusalem: protecting and delivering, passing over and saving.”

For our Savior is the lion of whom Solomon says: “The lion, strongest among beasts, shall fear no encounter” (Prov. 30:30). And he is the lion’s whelp, as Jacob says: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hand shall be on the necks of your enemies; the sons of your father shall worship you: Judah, a lion’s whelp” (Gen. 49:8). For these words can be understood only of Christ, who roared over the prey he had seized, because he revealed the terrible power of his divinity, saying of his sheep: “No one shall snatch them from my hand. My Father, who gave them to me, is greater than all; and no one can snatch them from the hand of my Father. I and the Father are one” (John 10:28).

A multitude of shepherds from the synagogue came against him when Judas betrayed him so that they might seize him. For a multitude of shepherds came to seize him, as Luke indicates, writing: “Jesus said to those who had come to him—the chief priests, officers of the temple, and elders—‘Have you come out with swords and clubs as against a robber?’” (Mark 14:48). But he did not fear their voice or dread their multitude because, according to John: “He came forward and said to them, ‘Whom do you seek?’ And they answered him, ‘Jesus of Nazareth.’ Jesus said to them, ‘I am he.’ When therefore he said to them, ‘I am he,’ they went backward and fell to the ground” (John 18:5–7).

He also fought against the devil on Mount Zion and on its hill—that is, in the house of the shepherds. [Col. 0301A] Hence it is said here: “So shall the Lord of hosts descend to fight upon Mount Zion and upon its hill.” For this purpose he descended into the world: that he might thus fight for us. But because he fought alone in the Passion, after the Resurrection he was no longer alone. For in the Ascension he is compared not to a bird but to birds, because he himself first flew to heaven and daily causes the souls of the elect, which are his members, to fly after him when they leave their bodies. “For wherever the body may be, there also the eagles shall be gathered” (Luke 17:37), because where our Redeemer is according to the substance of flesh, there the souls of the righteous are gathered.

But these birds—that is, the Lord and his saints who have already flown to heaven—protect Jerusalem, that is, the Church, often descending to us and invisibly hovering over us. Rightly, therefore, he says: “As flying birds, so shall the Lord of hosts protect Jerusalem.” Hence Moses also says of him: “Like an eagle provoking its young to fly and hovering over them, it spread its wings and took them up” (Deut. 32:11). For because, while protecting us as little ones, he nourishes us and cherishes us not with a harsh and burdensome protection but with one that is light and gentle, while extending his mercies toward us, he stretches out wings over us in the manner of birds. He both protects the Church against temptations and delivers it from adversities; and, passing from judgment to the kingdom, he saves it with everlasting and true salvation. It follows:

**VERSE 6.**—“Return, O children of Israel, as deeply as you had withdrawn.”

[Col. 0302A] Everyone who abandons the way of life and casts himself into the darkness of sins plunges himself, as it were, into a pit. Thus Jeremiah, seeing that Judaea had been buried in iniquities by long habit, laments himself under her figure, saying: “My life has fallen into the pit, and they have laid a stone upon me” (Lam. 3:53). For life falls into a pit when it is defiled by the stain of iniquity. A stone is placed upon it when the mind is also swallowed up in sin by hardened habit, so that, even if it wishes to rise, it can scarcely do so, because it is grievously weighed down from above by the mass of habit.

But because it was subject to divine power [Note: [Col. 0301B] The codex reads “is subject” (*subjacet*).] and could be called back after the constriction of evil habit to the breadth of good action, the prophet, proclaiming the grace of God, rightly exhorts his people to repentance, saying: “Return, O children of Israel, as deeply as you had withdrawn.” For one who, after the yoke of iniquity, is brought back through repentance to the freedom of good work, aided by the hand of grace that lifts him up, so that he rises to as great a freedom of righteousness as the abyss of sins into which he had sunk, returns as deeply as he had withdrawn, according to that saying of the Apostle: “As you presented your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification” (Rom. 6:19). For even those among the children of Israel who had crucified the Savior and afterward believed in him through the apostles were converted as deeply as they had withdrawn. Then follows the conversion of the Gentiles, when he adds:

## BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0301]

## CHAPTER 31 CONTINUED

[Col. 0301C]

**VERSE 7.**—“For on that day each man shall cast away the idols of his silver and the idols of his gold, which your hands made for you as a sin.”

This needs no exposition. But he adds how it could come about that the Gentiles, whom the devil held captive in his own snare, would abandon idols:

**VERSE 8.**—“And Assyria shall fall by a sword not of man, and a sword not of a human being shall devour him; and he shall flee, not before a sword, and his young men shall become tributary.”

**VERSE 9.**—“And his strength shall pass away in terror, and his princes shall flee in fear.”

Assyria is Satan, who falls by a sword not of man but of God, because it belongs to divine, not human, power alone to cast down the adversary. For the Lord [Col. 0301D] Jesus through death destroyed him who had the empire of death, that is, the devil. But when the prophet says that “Assyria shall fall by a sword not of man, and a sword not of a human being shall devour him,” he by no means denies that our Redeemer, who is also God, is human; rather, he agrees with the Apostle who says: “Paul, an apostle, not from men nor through a human being, [Col. 0302C] but through Jesus Christ” (Gal. 1:1). Thus Assyria shall fall not by the sword of a man but by Christ’s triumph, and he shall flee not before a sword but before the Lord’s cross.

And his young men—that is, those who were eager and strong for sinning—shall become tributary: that is, submitting themselves to Christ’s yoke, they shall humbly serve him. And his strength, by which he oppressed the nations, shall pass away, fleeing from place to place, and afterward out of the world before the terror of Christ’s preachers. And his princes, that is, the demons, shall flee in fear. Therefore, after the devil and his attendants have been driven out from Christ’s kingdom and the apostles’ rule, it is added:

“The Lord has said, whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem.”

## CHAPTER 32

[Col. 0302D] **VERSE 1.**—“Behold, a king shall reign in righteousness, and princes shall rule in judgment.”

Now Zion, which is called a watchtower, denotes the present Church, which watches from the citadel of the mind against the snares of demons and contemplates heavenly joys, though as through an image. Jerusalem, however, interpreted “vision of peace,” is the glory of the blessed in [Col. 0303A] heaven, where peace and security reign. The fire and furnace of God are the burning of his love. But it must be considered that fire can be small in comparison with a furnace. A furnace is accustomed always to overflow with immense heat. Therefore, because the hearts of the elect now conceive the fire of divine love, but in that kingdom of blessedness are filled much more abundantly with the same fire, his fire is in Zion and his furnace in Jerusalem. For the difference between that fire of love which the elect have here and that which, united to God, they will have in the kingdom of heaven is as great—and much greater—as the difference between a tiny spark and a vast furnace. He mentioned fire beforehand when he was about to speak of Christ’s kingdom because Christ reigns only in those hearts in which this fire of love exists. “For if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:9). “Behold,” he says, “King Christ shall reign in righteousness,” after Satan, who exercised tyranny in iniquity, has been expelled. And the apostles, as princes, shall rule in judgment, because the princes of Assyria have been put to flight, those who sought to rule without judgment. It follows:

**VERSE 2.**—“And a man shall be like one hidden from the wind and concealing himself from the storm, like streams of water in thirst and the shade of a projecting rock in a desert land.”

Every man—that is, one acting manfully in faith—shall be in the Church like one hidden from the wind and concealing himself from the storm, because under divine protection he shall be safe [Col. 0303C] from the wind, the blast of demons, and from the storm of tribulation, so that he may say of the Lord: “For he has hidden me in his tabernacle in the day of evil; he has protected me in the secret place of his tabernacle” (Ps. 26:5).

And he shall be like streams of water in a thirsty land, because “out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (John 7:38), which he will give to his thirsty neighbours to drink. He shall also be like the shadow of a projecting rock in a desert land, so that those wearied by the heat of tribulations may flee to him. We may understand the land of this world as a wilderness: “And the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). By the shadow of the rock is signified the imitation of Christ, because, as a shadow is cast according to the form of the body, so the life of the righteous is fashioned after the pattern of his imitation. [Col. 0303D] Therefore a man shall be like the shadow of a projecting rock in a desert land, because every holy person shall become lofty and strong in likeness to his Redeemer, and conspicuous amid a crooked and perverse nation. Again, concerning those who were to see and hear Christ in the flesh, it continues:

### VERSE 3.—“The eyes of those who see shall not be dim, and the ears of those who hear shall listen attentively.”

For those are here called seeing and hearing, to whom it was said: “But blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear. For amen I say to you, that many prophets and righteous persons desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Matt. 13:16). But their eyes were not dim, and their ears listened attentively [Col. 0304A], as it was said to them: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but to the rest it is in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand” (Luke 8:10). For the Lord explained to them privately all that he spoke to the crowds in parables; concerning them it also continues:

### VERSE 4.—“And the heart of fools shall understand knowledge, and the tongue of stammerers shall speak quickly and plainly.”

For what does he designate by the appellation of fools and stammerers except the simple and unlettered fishermen whom the Lord chose as apostles? For “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1:27). But their heart understood knowledge, and [Col. 0304B] their tongue spoke quickly and plainly, because the Lord “opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45), and, having received the Holy Spirit, “they spoke in various tongues the mighty works of God” (Acts 2:11). But when these men had been raised to such authority, the teachers of the Synagogue were refuted and cast down. For it follows:

### VERSE 5.—“He who is foolish shall no longer be called a prince, nor shall the deceitful man be called great.”

For who is foolish and deceitful except the scribes and Pharisees and the chief priests, who, rejecting the wisdom of God, which is Christ, continually devised frauds and snares against him? Yet these are no longer called princes and great men among the people of God, because [Col. 0304C] they refused to serve Christ the King. Their perversity is further described:

### VERSE 6.—“For the fool shall speak folly, and his heart shall work iniquity, to accomplish hypocrisy and to speak deceitfully to the Lord, to make empty the soul of the hungry and to take away drink from the thirsty.”

For, as we have said, the assembly of those to whom the Lord said is called foolish: “Woe to you, blind guides, who say: Whoever swears by the temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the temple is bound. Fools and blind! For which is greater, the gold or the temple that sanctifies the gold?” (Matt. 23:16). This fool therefore spoke folly concerning the Lord, [Col. 0304D] saying: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” (John 9:16); and: “How can a sinful man perform these signs?” (ibid.).

And his heart worked iniquity, because, when he had said to the paralytic, “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you” (Matt. 9:2), behold, certain scribes said within themselves: “This man blasphemes” (ibid. 3); and immediately they heard: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (ibid. 4). The heart of this fool worked iniquity in order to accomplish hypocrisy and speak deceitfully to the Lord, when the chief priests and scribes sent spies who pretended to be righteous, so that they might catch him in his speech and hand him over to the authority and power of the governor; and they questioned him, saying: “Teacher, we know that [Col. 0305A] you speak and teach rightly, and do not show partiality, but teach the way of God in truth: is it lawful for us to pay tribute to Caesar or not?” (Matt. 22:16). But perceiving their deceit, he said to them: “Why do you test me?” (ibid. 18).

But this fool also strove to make empty the soul of the hungry people and to take away from the thirsty people the drink of the Lord’s preaching. For all the people hung upon his words as they heard him; but the Pharisees and scribes said: “He has a demon and is mad; why do you listen to him?” (John 20:20). Hence it was also said to them: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who shut the kingdom of heaven before men: you yourselves do not enter, nor do you allow those entering to enter” (Matt. 23:13). Concerning them it also continues:

[Col. 0305B]

### VERSES 7–8.—“The vessels of the deceitful are evil. For he has devised schemes to destroy the meek by a lying word, while the poor man was speaking judgment.

“But the prince has devised things worthy of a prince, and he himself shall stand above rulers.”

For the deceitful assembly is that of the scribes, Pharisees, and priests; their vessels are the hearts of the people into which they poured their malice. This deceitful one therefore devised—that is, prepared—schemes to destroy the meek, that is, to seduce the simple through his vessels by a lying word, when the chief priests, assembled with the elders, took counsel and gave a large sum of money [Col. 0305C] to the soldiers, saying: “Say that his disciples came by night and stole him while you were sleeping” (Matt. 28:13).

“But the poor man, who, though he was rich, became needy for our sake, spoke judgment” (2 Cor. 8:9), saying: “If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do them, then, even if you do not wish to believe me, believe the works” (John 10:37); and concerning the adulteress: “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her” (John 8:7); and the like. But while the deceitful one was devising destruction, our Prince Christ devised things worthy of a prince, because, having risen after conquering death, he said to his disciples: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Therefore go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you” (Matt. 28:18). And he himself stands above the rulers of the Churches, as he added there: “Behold, I am with you all days, even unto the consummation of the age” (ibid. 20). It follows:

### VERSE 9.—“Rise up, wealthy women, and hear my voice; confident daughters, receive my speech with your ears.”

### VERSE 10.—“After days and a year, you confident ones shall be troubled. For the vintage is finished; the gathering shall come no more.”

[Col. 0306A]

### VERSE 11.—“Be astonished, wealthy women; be troubled, confident ones; strip yourselves and be ashamed; gird your loins above your breasts [Note: [Col. 0305] Elsewhere: ‘your loins.’ ‘Mourn over the breasts,’ etc.].”

### VERSE 12.—“Mourn over the desirable land, over the fertile vineyard.”

In sacred discourse, “woman” is used either for sex or for weakness. For sex, as there: “God sent his Son, made of a woman” (Gal. 4:4). For weakness, as a certain wise man says: “The iniquity of a man is better than a beneficent woman” (Ecclus. 42:14). For any strong and discerning person is called a man; but a woman is understood as a weak or undiscerning mind. And it often happens that even a discerning person suddenly falls into fault, while another, undiscerning and weak, performs a good work. But the person [Col. 0306B] who is undiscerning and weak is sometimes raised up all the more by what he has done well, and falls more grievously into fault; whereas every discerning person, even from realizing that he has acted badly, is brought back more strictly to the rule of discernment, and advances thence more highly toward righteousness, from the very point at which for a time he seemed to have fallen from righteousness. Therefore it is rightly said: “The iniquity of a man is better than a beneficent woman,” because even the fault of the strong sometimes becomes an occasion of virtue, and the virtue of the weak an occasion of sin.

Accordingly, what is figured here by the name of women except weakness of mind? The prophetic discourse is therefore directed to these women, that is, to weak souls. Hence it calls them wealthy and confident, because they think themselves filled with works of virtue and as though [Col. 0306C] they relied upon their own righteousness. For there are many professed religious persons, whom the divine discourse now denotes under the designation of women, who judge themselves holy because they have changed their outward dress, while they exercise themselves in no virtues. Desiring to rouse them from the sloth of their torpor, it says: “Rise up and hear my voice.” For the person who rises to hear the prophet’s voice is one who, leaving negligence and idleness, hears the sacred utterances with an attentive heart, ready to act.

“After days,” it says, “and a year, you shall be troubled.” What is expressed by “days,” which it states indefinitely, except the time of the present life, whose number of days is uncertain? And what is signified by “a year” except that interval extending from each person’s death until the resurrection of all, concerning which sort of year the Psalmist says: “You shall bless the crown of the year of your goodness” (Ps. 64:12)? Therefore, after days and a year—that is, on the day of judgment—you who now seem confident because of the merit of righteousness shall be troubled. For then the vintage is finished: that is, on that day the human race is utterly cut off from the world. The gathering shall come no more: that is, no more human beings will be born upon earth to be gathered from it by death. Therefore, while it is permitted to do penance, be astonished now at the future condemnation of the wicked—you who think yourselves spiritually wealthy—considering [Col. 0307A] that “it is terrible to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10:31). And be troubled, shaken by a saving fear toward repentance, you who are confident as though in holiness. Strip yourselves and be ashamed: that is, do not attend in yourselves to the outward manner of life, visible to men and seemingly religious; rather, look at what you are beneath its covering, and blush at the deformity of the inward person.

“Gird your loins above your breasts”: that is, restrain and repress the lust of the flesh in the thoughts of your breast, so that you may preserve chastity not only in the flesh but also in the heart. For lust is in the loins, while thoughts are signified by the breasts. One therefore girds the loins above the breasts who constrains lust in thoughts through continence, so that the breast may not be scattered by [Col. 0307B] unclean thoughts.

Then, he says, “Mourn over the land,” and so forth. What is signified by the desirable land except the multitude of religious persons or their manner of life? Hence the Lord promises his people through Malachi, saying: “For you shall be a desirable land” (Mal. 3:12). And what is expressed by the fertile vineyard except the people of the faithful, or their conduct, bearing clusters of spiritual fruits? “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5:7). He therefore commands mourning over the desirable land and the fertile vineyard because the life of many religious persons is now losing the grace of religion; and those who were accustomed to produce the spiritual fruits of devout conduct now bring forth lamentable deeds, and, as thorns of vices spring up, their life becomes like a wilderness. Hence it follows:

### VERSE 13.—“Thorns and briers rise up upon the ground of my people; how much more upon all the houses of joy of the exultant city?”

The Lord calls the ground of his people the mind of all the elect, upon which he declares that thorns and briers rise up because he sees that even it is not without the prickings of vices. But the houses of joy of the exultant city are the minds of the wicked, which, because they neglect to contemplate future punishments, abandon themselves to the pleasure of the flesh and rejoice vainly. He therefore says: “Thorns and briers rise up upon the ground of my people; how much more upon all the houses of joy of the exultant city?” As though he said plainly: If [Col. 0307D] vices oppress even the minds of those who afflict themselves for heavenly desires, beneath what sins lie those who, without any fear, abandon themselves to the pleasure of the flesh? It follows:

### VERSE 14.—“For the house has been deserted; the multitude of the city has been abandoned.”

The house—that is, the mind of the wicked—has been deserted by him who says: “I dismissed them according to the desires of their heart” (Ps. 80:13). He also abandoned the multitude of the city, because he rejected from the lot of his kingdom that portion of the human race which enters by the broad way, which is numerous through an abundance of iniquity, and left it among unclean spirits. Hence it adds: “Darkness and groping have come upon the caves [Col. 0308A] for ever; the joy of wild asses, the pastures of flocks.”

### VERSE 15.—“Until the Spirit be poured out upon us from on high.”

For what are signified by the caves except the deep and dreadful minds of the wicked in the wilderness of this world, of whom he said above: “Woe to you who are deep in heart, so as to hide counsel from the Lord” (above, 29:15)? Now an *onager* is a wild ass. And what are expressed by wild asses except the strong and proud leaders or teachers of unbelievers, who wandered like wild asses in solitude while among unbelievers they followed the judgment of their own will? And what are signified by flocks of beasts except a multitude of vices and demons? Therefore the house and the multitude of the city, abandoned, were turned into a wilderness; and darkness came upon the caves of this wilderness—that is, upon the deep minds of sinners—because through sin they lost the light of truth.

But groping also occurred there: that is, the blind activity of unbelief. For just as a person set in darkness gropes this way and that, so unbelievers and wanderers did not know where they should turn or what they should do. And this came upon the minds of those who died without end, for ever.

And there was joy of wild asses there, because in those whom God had abandoned the proud teachers of error and followers of their own hearts rejoiced. The flocks of wild beasts also—that is, of demons and vices—had pastures there, until the Holy Spirit [Col. 0308C] should be poured out upon the apostles and the people of believers, who would recall the nations to the Lord. Hence it is fittingly added: “And the wilderness shall become Carmel, and Carmel shall be reckoned as a forest.”

### VERSE 16.—“And judgment shall dwell in the wilderness, and righteousness shall sit in Carmel.”

He calls the abandoned multitude of the city—that is, the Gentile world, in which there had been darkness and groping—a wilderness. But Carmel means “soft” or “tender,” or “knowledge of circumcision,” and denotes the Jewish people, whose heart had been softened by faith and who knew circumcision of the flesh. Therefore, when the Holy Spirit was poured out, the wilderness became Carmel, because the Gentile was cut from the natural wild olive and, contrary to nature, grafted into the good olive of the patriarchs. [Col. 0308D] The wilderness was changed into Carmel because the heart of the abandoned Gentile world was softened toward faith and spiritually circumcised. And Carmel was reckoned as a forest because the Jewish people were turned into the wilderness of unbelief. But judgment of right discernment dwells in the wilderness of the Gentile world, because believers from the nations now examine beforehand, by the judgment of equity, all that they are to do; and in the Carmel of that same converted Gentile world righteousness of righteous conduct sits and reigns. It follows:

### VERSE 17.—“And the work of righteousness shall be peace, and the cultivation of righteousness silence and security for ever.”

In ancient times the work of righteousness was that the saints should repay their enemies. [Col. 0309A] But now the work of righteousness is peace, because the person who harms no one, but loves all as himself, and does for others in like manner the good things that he wishes people to do for him, practises righteousness.

And the cultivation of righteousness is silence, because one who desires to cultivate righteousness must set a guard upon his mouth. For the righteousness of the mind is laid waste when one does not spare oneself from immoderate speech. He too is silent who makes no noise through the cries of wicked action. And this silence is the cultivation of righteousness, because by keeping oneself from sin one also cultivates righteousness.

Or, “the peace which surpasses all understanding” (Phil. 4:7) shall be the work of the righteousness of the saints; and the cultivation of righteousness shall be silence, so that they may worship the Lord not in the verbosity of the Jews, [Col. 0309B] but in the brevity of faith. Moreover, it is a wonderful security to possess a good conscience of heart. From this security, indeed, perennial rest is born, because one passes from good and tranquil thought to eternal joys. It follows:

### VERSE 18.—“And my people shall sit in the beauty of peace, and in the tabernacle of confidence, and in abundant rest.”

The people of God sit in the beauty of peace because he “makes those of one manner of life dwell in a house” (Ps. 67:7), so that “the multitude of believers may be of one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32). For the beauty of peace is that all say the same thing and that there be no schisms among them, but that they be perfected in the same understanding and in the same knowledge.

[Col. 0309C] The tabernacle of confidence, or dwelling places, are the monasteries of religious persons, or their assemblies and orders, who place their confidence in Christ. They sit in abundant rest when they seek nothing of this world and are inwardly enriched with an abundance of virtues. Although these things are venerably fulfilled even today in those who live under a rule in monasteries, they were accomplished most fully in the primitive Church. Hence a sentence concerning those Jews who refused to believe is immediately added:

### VERSE 19.—“But hail shall fall in the descent of the forest, and the city shall be humbled with humiliation.”

The Jewish people are called a forest because Carmel was reckoned as a forest. But what is the descent of this forest except the casting down of its exaltation? [Col. 0309D] Upon its descent fell the hail of a most violent storm through the Romans; and the city of Jerusalem was humbled and destroyed to its very foundations. But because the holy preachers then scattered the word of life throughout the whole world, it follows:

### VERSE 20.—“Blessed are you who sow upon all waters, sending forth the foot of ox and ass.”

The angel in the Apocalypse of John teaches that waters are peoples; but the ox and ass are the Jewish and Gentile peoples, because “the ox knew its owner, and the ass the manger of its lord” (above, 1:3). Therefore, to sow upon all waters is to preach fruitful words of life to all peoples; but to send forth the foot of ox and ass is to bind the ways of the Israelite and Gentile people by the bonds of heavenly [Col. 0310A] precepts. But because some unbelievers persecuted preaching while others despised it, it fittingly continues:

## CHAPTER XXXIII

### VERSE 1.—“Woe to you who plunder: shall you not yourself also be plundered? And you who despise: shall you not yourself also be despised? When you have completed your plundering, you shall be plundered; when, wearied, you cease to despise, you shall be despised.”

For those who dragged martyrs to punishments and plundered their goods were plundering. But those who are to say of them at the end were despising: “These are they whom we once held in derision and as a likeness of reproach. We fools thought their life madness and their end without [Col. 0310B] honour” (Wis. 5:3). But woe to them, because evil spirits have now plundered them, and they endure a reproach that shall never be erased. And it is altogether just that whoever plunders should himself become plunder, and whoever despises should himself be despised. “For with the same measure with which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you” (Matt. 7:2).

This sentence may also be understood of modern robbers and despisers. For whoever seizes what belongs to another shall himself be seized at his end; and whoever despises good things shall fall without honour and remain in disgrace among the dead for ever. It follows:

### VERSE 2.—“Lord, have mercy on us. For we have waited for you: be our arm in the morning, and our salvation in the time of tribulation.”

This is the voice of faithful Hebrews receiving Christ [Col. 0310C] at his first coming. For, meeting him, they say: “Lord, have mercy on us,” and so forth. Morning comes to be in us when we begin to be irradiated by the knowledge of truth and illumined by the brightness of righteousness, though we had been oppressed, as it were in night, by the darkness of error and fault. But when we are stripped of the darknesses of error, it is now necessary for us to struggle against the suggestions of the devil. Yet we cannot overcome them except by God’s help. If Satan cannot subject our minds to himself through consent, he immediately seeks to stir up adversities against us outwardly. Hence these people, having now received Christ, say: “Be our arm in the morning,” that is, our strength against Satan’s inward assaults, in the beginning [Col. 0310D] of our conversion; “and our salvation in the time of tribulation,” which we shall suffer outwardly where we have not been able to be conquered inwardly. Thus it happened to the apostles. For when they did not comply with the chief priests commanding them “not to speak in the name of Jesus” (Acts 4:18), they suffered most grievous tribulations. The same commonly happens to the rest of the faithful. It follows:

### VERSE 3.—“At the voice of the angel the peoples fled, and at your exaltation the nations were scattered.”

What is expressed by this angel except the choir of the apostles? At its voice the peoples fled (Acts 3:41), because, when the Holy Spirit had been sent, three thousand of those who had gathered for the feast believed through their preaching, and thereafter many thousands more from among those same Jews [Col. 0311A]. For the Hebrews who believed fled because they sought to escape the eternal punishments which they had incurred through the killing of the Saviour. But the nations also were scattered at his exaltation, because from the time of his ascension some from the nations began to come to faith, while others persisted more obstinately in unbelief. Concerning the Jews who refused to believe it continues:

### VERSE 4.—“And your spoils shall be gathered as the locust is gathered, as when pits are filled with it.”

For what does he call their spoils except their bodies? For flesh is the garment of the soul. People are accustomed to gather a multitude of locusts from the fields, because it devours crops, and to fill pits with them, [Col. 0310B] throwing earth over them and killing them. Thus, in the siege of Jerusalem, the bodies of those who died by famine, sword, and pestilence were gathered together. Or understand “spoils” as their possessions, which the Romans gathered without number like a multitude of locusts. It follows:

### VERSE 5.—“The Lord is magnified, because he has dwelt on high; he has filled Zion with judgment and righteousness.”

### VERSE 6.—“And faith shall be in its times.”

After his ascension the Lord was magnified in the world through the apostles because he dwelt in the high dwelling-place of heaven, though he had dwelt with men on earth. He filled Zion—that is, the Church—with judgment and righteousness, so that it may prove all things by examination and hold fast what is good and just.

The times of faith are those of which the Apostle says: [Col. 0311C] “Before faith came, we were kept under the law, shut up unto that faith which was to be revealed. Therefore the law was our pedagogue in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by faith. But when faith came, we are no longer under a pedagogue” (Gal. 3:23). Therefore these are now the times of faith, because God now justifies the nations by faith without works of the law, and faith bears fruit throughout the whole world. It is therefore well said: “For faith shall be in its times.” It follows:

“Wisdom and knowledge are the riches of salvation; the fear of the Lord is his treasure.”

Action, which makes good use of temporal things, differs from the contemplation of eternal things; the latter is assigned to wisdom, the former to knowledge. For it is written in the book of Job: “Behold, piety is wisdom; but to abstain [Col. 0311D] from evils is knowledge” (Job 28:28). This distinction should be understood to mean that wisdom pertains to contemplation and knowledge to action. Therefore wisdom and knowledge are riches of salvation, because the Church comes to eternal salvation through being in some measure nourished by contemplation of heavenly things and making good use of temporal and earthly things. Of works of this kind the Apostle also says to his disciples: “I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God which has been given to you in Christ Jesus, because in all things you have been made rich in him, in every word and in all knowledge” (1 Cor. 1:4).

But the fear of the Lord—chaste fear, sober fear, secure fear—is itself his treasure: not that servile fear which charity casts out, [Col. 0312A] but that holy fear which remains for ever and ever, that is, which charity produces. For a loving wife fears her husband in one way, and a sinful maidservant fears her master in another. Thus the Church, Christ’s bride, having cast off the fear of the law, is filled with joyful fear, so that loving Christ she may fear him, and fearing him may love him.

And that fear is a rich treasure, so that whoever has it may regard all the riches of the world as of little value. With these saving riches—that is, knowledge, wisdom, and fear—our King came to enrich his soldiers, “who became poor for our sake although he was rich, so that by his poverty we might become rich” (2 Cor. 8:9). But because the Jews refused to receive these riches, he gave them to the nations. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0312B]

### VERSE 7.—“Behold, those who see shall cry outside; the angels of peace shall weep bitterly.”

For those are “seeing” to whom it was said: “Blessed are the eyes which see what you see” (Matt. 13:16). And these are the angels of peace, announcing reconciliation to the world, because it is written of them: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things” (Rom. 10:15). Therefore those who see cried outside—that is, outside Judaea—because the apostles preached to the nations unto the ends of the earth.

And the angels of peace wept bitterly because the apostles themselves, who announced peace to the nations, grieved that the wrath of God remained upon the Jews. Hence one of them says: “I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart. For I myself wished to be anathema from Christ for my brethren, who are my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites” (Rom. 9:3) [Col. 0312C]. Concerning the destruction of these Israelites it continues:

### VERSES 8–9.—“The ways have been scattered; one passing through the path has ceased; the covenant has been made void; he has cast down cities; he has regarded men as nothing.

“[Col. 0311C] The land has mourned and languished; Lebanon has been confounded and has become foul; Sharon has become like a wilderness, and Bashan and Carmel have been shaken.”

The ways were scattered through the land of the Jews when every region was laid waste by the Romans. Even one passing through the path of the wilderness ceased there, because the land was left without an inhabitant. For the covenant which the Lord had promised was made void, when he said: “I will appoint a place for my people Israel, and I will plant him, and he shall dwell in it and shall be disturbed no more; nor shall the children of iniquity continue to afflict him as before, from the day when I appointed judges over my people Israel” (2 Kings 7:10). Therefore this covenant was made void for the Jews because the Lord cast down their cities and regarded them almost as nothing. And amid these things their land mourned and languished.

But what should be understood by Lebanon except the Temple that was in Jerusalem? Hence it was said through Zechariah: “Open your gates, O Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars” (Zech. 11:1). Therefore Lebanon was confounded and became foul because the Temple of the Jews was polluted and dishonoured by foreigners—indeed, destroyed. Sharon, however, is a province between [Col. 0313A] Joppa and Lydda, which was made like a wilderness by the Romans. Bashan also, beyond the Jordan, was shaken by them, and Carmel was in the territory of Judah. But because the Jews were to suffer all these things because of the killing of the Saviour, while he himself was to destroy death by his death, rise again immediately, and thereafter reign for ever, it fittingly follows:

### VERSE 10.—“Now I shall rise, says the Lord; now I shall be exalted, and now I shall be lifted up.”

Now I shall rise from the dead; now I shall be exalted in heaven; now I shall be lifted up in the kingdom. And because the leaders of the Jews were to be inflamed with the fire of envy against the preachers of his resurrection, it rightly continues:

### VERSE 11.—“You shall conceive burning heat and bring forth stubble; [Col. 0312A] your spirit shall devour you like fire.”

You shall conceive the burning heat of envy against the apostles, O chief priests, Pharisees, and elders. You shall bring forth stubble, that is, a work worthy of avenging flames. For stubble is a work which will be burned on the day of judgment, as the Apostle says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus. But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold and silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble, each person’s work shall be manifest; for the day of the Lord shall declare it, because it shall be revealed in fire, and the fire shall test what sort each person’s work is. If anyone’s work which he has built upon it remains, he shall receive a reward; if anyone’s work is burned, he shall suffer loss” (1 Cor. 3:11–16). Therefore, he says, you shall bring forth stubble: that is, a work which will be burned on that day. Your spirit shall devour you like fire because you shall be laid waste inwardly by the burning of your malice, just as later you are to be laid waste outwardly by the fire of Gehenna. But because those subject to them also were to be burned by this fire of envy, which first burned in the hearts of their leaders, it follows:

### VERSE 12.—“And the peoples shall be like ashes from a conflagration.”

For all were burned by the fire of malice, persecuting the apostles, preachers of grace, as though out of zeal for the law. And because they were likewise to perish when the Romans besieged Jerusalem, it fittingly continues:

“Gathered thorns shall be burned with fire.”

For the thorns are those of whom David speaks in the book of Kings: “But transgressors shall all be plucked out like thorns, which are not taken up by hands; and if anyone wishes to touch them, he shall arm himself with iron and with a spear-shaft, and, set on fire, they shall be burned to nothing” (2 Kings 23:6). But the Lord teaches in Ezekiel what the fire is when, having said to Jerusalem, “Behold, I will kindle a fire in you, and I will burn in you every green tree and every dry tree” (Ezek. 26:47), he thus explains what he had said: “Behold, I am against you, and I will draw my sword out of its sheath and kill in you the righteous and the wicked” (Ezek. 21:3). The transgressing Jews, therefore, are thorns, while the fire is the sword of God. Thus the gathered thorns were burned by fire because the Jews [Col. 0312B] who had flocked to Jerusalem for the feast of Passover perished by the sword of heavenly vengeance. After their extermination, the Lord added:

### VERSES 13–14.—“Hear, you who are far off, what I have done; and you who are near, know my strength.

“Sinners in Zion have been terrified; trembling has seized the hypocrites.”

“You,” he says, “who are far from Jerusalem”—that is, near the ends of the world—“hear what I have done to the unbelieving Jews; and you who are near”—that is, the Moabites, Palestinians, and the other neighbouring peoples—“know my strength by which I defeated them.” For sinners in Zion—that is, on the Temple mount—were terrified, those who, “if I had not come and spoken to them, would not have had sin” (John 15:22). And when Jerusalem was taken, trembling seized there the hypocritical Pharisees and scribes, who relied in vain upon divine help.

But these things can also be understood otherwise. For he says: “The ways have been scattered,” and so forth. And what does he call ways except actions? But here we understand “path” as that of which the Lord says: “Narrow is the way which leads to life, and few are those who find it” (Matt. 7:14). Therefore, as the end of the world approaches, ways are scattered—that is, the actions of people who do not keep the rule of righteousness. One passing through the path has ceased, because there is now lacking one who travels the course of this present life by the way of narrow conduct; rather, all strive to walk the broad way of the world. And on this account the covenant—that is, the promise of the kingdom of heaven—has been made void. For a crown is promised to those who begin, but it is given to those who finish; for those who do not persevere, the covenant of this promise becomes void.

And the Lord has cast down cities—that is, the multitudes of those who follow the broad paths of destruction. Nor has he regarded them as men: that is, he reckoned them as though they did not exist. Or he did not reckon as men those who through their own fault wished to be beasts. For whoever does not have charity is nothing before God, as the Apostle says: “If I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so that I move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13:2). But amid this abundance of iniquity the land—that is, the Church—mourns and languishes with grief of heart.

[Col. 0314D] Lebanon, however, is said to mean “whitening” or “making white.” And what is represented by Lebanon except the whitened way of life of hypocrites? Thus Paul says to one of them: “God will strike you, you whitewashed wall” (Acts 23:3). Lebanon, therefore, has been put to shame and has become foul, because the outward whiteness of those who maintain a religious manner of life externally without a religious intention of heart commonly bears the disgrace of shame through the manifest commission of wickedness, and at the end is stained by evident blemishes of sins.

Sharon, moreover, is interpreted as “prince of sorrow,” or “singing sadness.” And what is denoted by Sharon except any religious person devoted to sorrow, who, in the manner of one lamenting, has groaning instead of song? [Col. 0315A] Sharon therefore has become like a wilderness, because, as wickedness has now grown excessively, every holy person is regarded as worthless, is little frequented and deserted, since he rejects worldly glory and rejoices in tears.
