Bashan means “fatness,” while Carmel means “soft.” Here we understand fatness as that of which the Psalmist says: “My soul is filled as with fat and richness” (Ps. 62:6). The mind of holy Job was soft when he said: “God has softened my heart, and the Almighty has troubled me” (Job 23:16). Bashan, therefore, is understood as the richness of spiritual grace; Carmel as a mind made soft toward charity and compassion. Carmel is also interpreted as “knowledge of circumcision.” And he knows circumcision well [Col. 0315B] who is circumcised in heart, deed, and tongue.

“But Bashan and Carmel have been shaken,” because even the minds of the righteous will be shaken in that final trial. “For false prophets and false Christs will arise, and will give great signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error” (Mark 13:12).

But because, after the tribulation of those days, they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty, the following is appropriately added here:

“Now I shall arise, says the Lord,” etc. Now I shall arise from my excessive patience—I who until now lay, as it were, while I was despised and trampled underfoot, and did not avenge myself. Now I shall arise, as it is written: “Arise, [Col. 0315C] O God, judge your cause; remember your reproaches” (Ps. 73:22). Now I shall be exalted, because the Lord alone will be exalted on that day, and because then “all the tribes of the earth will mourn” (Matt. 24:30). “You will conceive,” he says, “the burning of inward grief; you will bring forth the straw of futile words, saying: ‘We have grown weary in the way of wickedness and destruction, and we have walked difficult paths; but we have not known the way of the Lord. What has pride profited us, or what has the boasting of riches brought us? All those things passed away like a shadow.’” For such words will be spoken in hell by those who sinned, since “the hope of the wicked is like down carried away by the wind” (Wis. 5:7 ff.).

“You will conceive,” he says, “the burning of late repentance on [Col. 0315D] that day, and you will bring forth the straw of words of vain lamentation. Your spirit, like fire, will devour you,” because then every former fault will be brought before one’s eyes, and the mind will be tortured by its own fire more grievously than by the fires of Gehenna. And the peoples of the reprobate will be like ashes from a conflagration, as Malachi says to the elect: “Go forth and leap like calves from the herd, and you shall tread down the wicked when they are ashes beneath the soles of your feet” (Mal. 4:2). Then thorns—that is, sinners—will be burned by unquenchable fire; and they will be burned when gathered together, because “they will be gathered together into the gathering of one bundle in the pit” (above, 24:22).

Having thus spoken of the condemnation of the reprobate, and wishing to deter those who still live from wickedness, he adds: [Col. 0316A] “Hear, you who are far off, what I have done,” etc. You who are far from righteousness, hear what I have done—that is, what I shall do to the reprobate on that day; and you righteous, who by the merit of your lives are near to me, know my strength against them. For sinners in Zion—that is, in the Church—are crushed, or rather will be crushed: those who presumed upon the saying, “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16:16). But they will be crushed when they hear: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire; for I was hungry and you did not give me food” (Matt. 25:42), etc. And then trembling will possess the hypocrites, because those who now boast of holiness before human eyes will then be ashamed when the Judge of hearts appears. Since all the reprobate are then [Col. 0316B] to be cast into the furnace of unquenchable fire, the text appropriately adds further for the terror of the living:

“Who among you will be able to dwell with devouring fire? Who among you will dwell with everlasting burnings?” For the severity of the fires of Gehenna is so great that it cannot be endured, and then the wicked will be tortured in it without end. But after again saying to everyone who will dwell in hell, “Who among you will dwell with everlasting burnings?” he immediately adds, conversely, concerning every future inhabitant of the kingdom of heaven:

VERSE 15.—“He who walks in righteousnesses and speaks truth; who rejects gain from oppression, and shakes his hands free from every gift; who stops his ears lest he hear of blood, and closes [Col. 0316C] his eyes lest he see evil,”

VERSE 16.—“This man shall dwell on high; the strongholds of rocks shall be his lofty refuge; bread is given to him; his waters are sure.”

VERSE 17.—“His eyes shall see the king in his beauty; they shall behold a land afar off.”

VERSE 18.—“Your heart shall meditate on fear.”

He walks in righteousnesses who conducts his life in good deeds. He speaks truth if he simply declares without deceit what he knows; and he rejects gain from oppression if he refuses to take from others through false accusation what he may acquire for himself. There are three kinds of receiving gifts: from the heart, from the mouth, and from the hand. A gift from the heart is favor sought by inward thought; [Col. 0316D] a gift from the mouth is favor obtained through fear; a gift from the hand is a reward received by payment. But every righteous person shakes his hands free from every gift, because in doing what is right he seeks to receive neither empty glory from a human heart, nor praise from the mouth, nor a payment from the hand.

What is it to stop one’s ears lest one hear of blood, except not to consent to sins that urge us and arise from flesh and blood? And what is it to close one’s eyes lest one see evil, except not to approve anything contrary to righteousness? But, having spoken of the active life, the prophet at once shows to what heights of contemplation one ascends through these things: “This man,” he says, “shall dwell on high,” [Col. 0317A] etc. This man shall dwell on high, because, although the flesh holds him in lower things, he has already fixed his mind upon higher things.

“The strongholds of rocks shall be his lofty refuge,” because, while he avoids the base desires of earthly life, he raises himself toward the heavenly homeland by the examples of the fathers who went before; and because he is nourished by spiritual grace through the gift of contemplation, “bread is given to him”: that is, he has received the refreshment of spiritual grace, because in hope of heavenly things he has detached himself from lower goods. To dwell on high is to set one’s heart upon heavenly things; and the strongholds of rocks are our lofty refuge when we behold the precepts and examples of the mighty Fathers and separate ourselves from lowly thought. The strongholds of rocks are our lofty refuge when in mind we are joined to the choirs and camps [Col. 0317B] of heaven, and, standing upon the citadel of the heart, we overcome the malicious spirits that lie in wait below us.

Then bread is also given to us when an intention raised toward heavenly things is refreshed by contemplation of eternity. Our waters are sure because the teaching of God gives there in fulfillment what it promises here through hope. But the wisdom of this world is unreliable, because it does not endure after death. Our waters, however, are sure because the words of life show even after death what they suggest before death.

Our eyes behold the King in his beauty, because our Redeemer will be seen as a man in judgment even by the reprobate; but only those who are elect will be raised up to behold the sublimity [Col. 0317C] of his divinity. For to see, as it were, a certain ugliness of the King is to behold only the form of a servant in which he was despised by the wicked. But the King is seen in his beauty by the elect, because, caught up beyond themselves, they fix the eyes of their hearts upon the very splendor of his deity. While they remain in this life, however, they cannot see that homeland of the living as it is; hence it is fittingly added:

“They shall behold a land afar off.” The higher the human mind is raised to contemplate eternal things, the more gravely it is shaken with fear at temporal deeds, because it sees itself to be truly guilty in proportion as it perceives how far it has departed from the very light that shines down from above. Thus it comes about that, when enlightened, it fears more, because it sees more clearly how greatly it disagrees with the rule of truth. For when our uprightness is brought before the inward rule and finds strict judgment, it strikes against inward rectitude with the many bends of its own crookedness. Therefore the prophet now turns his speech toward him of whom he was speaking and adds: “Your heart shall meditate on fear.” But if anyone had formerly wished to live in this way, he was greatly hindered—on one side by the carnal teaching of the Jews, on the other by the empty talk of the Gentiles. Now, however, both have been annulled, and the righteous person finds many helpers. For it follows: “Where is the learned man? Where is he who weighs the words of the law? Where is the teacher of little children?”

VERSE 19.—“You shall not see a foolish [Vulgate: shameless] people, a people of lofty speech, [Col. 0318A] such that you cannot understand the eloquence of its tongue, a people in whom there is no wisdom.”

For the Pharisee was learned in letters, because he pursued only the surface of the letter; and he weighed not the meaning but the words of the law as though in a balance, showing which things were weightier. And he was a teacher of little children because he taught the Jewish populace, who, like little children, always need milk.

The foolish people, however, are the Gentiles, who did not know true wisdom. Their speech was lofty—that is, profound—so that the simplicity of the faithful could scarcely understand its eloquence, that is, the fluency of its language. Yet there was no wisdom in it, because it uttered words with excessive polish and eloquence, but had no meaning of wisdom in those words. For just as [Col. 0318B] heavenly teaching attends not to words but to meaning, so worldly teaching glories not in meaning but in the arrangement of words and the boastfulness of eloquence. But teachers of this kind and their teachings have now vanished, so that evangelical preaching may remain, as the Apostle also says: “Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the inquirer of this age? Has not the Lord made foolish the wisdom of this world? For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the folly of preaching to save those who believe” (1 Cor. 1:20). Therefore, as the preachers of vain teachings fail and the Church rises, the prophet adds:

VERSE 20.—“Look upon Zion, the city of our solemnity; your eyes shall see Jerusalem, a rich habitation, [Col. 0318C] a tent that cannot be moved; its pegs shall never be removed, and none of its cords shall be broken.”

VERSE 21.—“For only there is our mighty God.”

Zion, indeed, or Jerusalem, is the Church. It is the city of our solemnity, because there we sing the praises of the Creator. For no one can rightly praise God outside the Church, because it is written: “How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land?” (Ps. 136:4). And again: “Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion, and a vow shall be fulfilled to you in Jerusalem” (Ps. 64:2). It is itself the rich habitation, because there are the riches of salvation—wisdom and knowledge—[Col. 0318D] and the fear of the Lord is its treasure, by which the inhabitants of this city are enriched. Or it may be said thus: Your eyes shall behold the vision of eternal peace and the unexpected riches which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor the human heart conceived.

The Church is also called a tent because, on the journey of this pilgrimage, it is God’s lodging or dwelling-place. This tent cannot be moved, because the Church remains in that which it believes. Nor shall its pegs ever be removed, because the words of its preaching shall not be taken away, as John says: “Let what you heard from the beginning remain in you” (1 John 2:24). And in his Apocalypse “the eternal Gospel” is mentioned (Rev. 14:6).

[Col. 0319A] And none of its cords shall be broken, because its commandments shall never be destroyed. For the ancient tent was often moved—from the wilderness to Shiloh, to Nob, and thence to Jerusalem—because the Synagogue was always to be advanced through certain stages until it came into the Church. But the new tent is never moved, because there is no further religion into which one may advance from that which the Church holds, the Lord saying: “Only hold fast what you have until I come” (Rev. 3:11).

That its words are signified by the name “pegs” is shown by Solomon, who says: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like pegs driven deeply” (Eccl. 12:11). The subtle character of its spiritual commandments is expressed by the designation “cords,” when Jeremiah is read to have been drawn from the pit by cords (Jer. 38:11). For he signifies the sinner who is brought up from the depth of wickedness through observance of spiritual commandments. Pegs, therefore, are words, and cords are commandments. And just as a tent is fastened by pegs and stretched out by ropes, so the Church is strengthened by the powerful utterances of Holy Scripture and enlarged in action by its commandments. These pegs and cords will never be removed or broken, as the pegs and cords of the old tent were removed and broken. For the words that spoke of the future were removed: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (above, 7:14). And it is said that “when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made of a woman” (Gal. 4:[Col. 0319C] 4), that is, of a female. And the commandments concerning the offering of victims, Sabbath rest, and other such observances were broken. But the words and commandments of the Church’s new preaching will never be changed or destroyed, because only there is our mighty God. For our God does nothing great among unbelievers, however many temporal benefits he may perform for them; but he performs great things only in the Church, because he bestows on his own the remission of sins and the grace of holiness, and leads them to eternal life.

Or the heavenly Jerusalem is the eternal tent of God, where he himself dwells forever. Therefore this tent can never be moved, because it will never again change its place but will remain perpetually in that kingdom of blessedness. Thus it is metaphorically added: “Its pegs shall never be removed, nor its cords broken,” in order to show that it remains with stable firmness in one place without end, “because only there is the mighty Lord,” since he is seen there and grants eternal joys to those who behold him. It follows:

“A place of rivers, broad and open streams.” The Church is the place of rivers because it abounds with prophetic and apostolic rivers, and within it are very broad streams of exposition. For the clear statements of interpreters make the meanings of the ancient Fathers apparent to us; and what the Fathers said briefly, these interpreters make plain by explaining it more fully. Isaiah, therefore, beholding the plain [Col. 0320A] words of the holy Church’s exposition, not obscured by the darkness of allegories, says: “A place of rivers, broad and open streams.” The sayings of the Old Testament had been like narrow and enclosed streams, compressing all the meanings of their knowledge in a most obscure compactness. In contrast, the streams of holy Church’s teaching are open, because its sayings are abundant for those who find them and plain for those who seek them. It follows: “No ship of oarsmen shall pass through it, nor shall a great trireme cross it.”

VERSE 22.—“For the Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our king; he himself will save us.”

No ship of oarsmen shall pass through it—that is, through the aforesaid place of rivers. What is denoted by a ship of oarsmen except the mind [Col. 0320B] of the reprobate, which is driven through the sea of this world by malicious spirits as by oarsmen? Thus this prophet says later that the Chaldeans glory in their ships, because most wicked demons glory in their hearts, whom they drive according to their will, by varied desires, through the stormy bitterness of the world.

A trireme is a ship having three ranks of oars. And what is expressed by the great trireme except the aforesaid mind of the wicked, or Babylon? It has three ranks of oars because it is governed by malicious spirits in thought, word, and deed. “Therefore no ship of oarsmen shall pass through it, nor shall a great trireme cross it,” because the mind of the wicked will be unable to set the foot of its wickedness among [Col. 0320C] the assembly of the righteous. It would pass through it if it could fulfill its will within it. But it shall not pass through, because it cannot accomplish the evil it attempts against the good. For the Lord will save us—that is, will guard us lest the wickedness of the ungodly pass through us. The Lord our judge will save us now, because he has given the new law through himself: “For there is one lawgiver and judge, who can destroy and deliver,” as James says (ch. 4:12). And he is our king, who now rules us and will reign in us eternally. Therefore he who will judge us, who gave us in the Gospel the rule for living, and who invisibly rules us, himself saves us amid the dangers of temptations, lest, overcome, we perish.

Or eternal Jerusalem is a place of rivers because there the rivers of spiritual graces always flow forth in the seven abundant courses of the Holy Spirit, spreading broadly and openly through all things. No ship of oarsmen shall pass through it, because no assailant or tempter will disturb those who dwell there. For the Lord, when judgment has been completed, will save them forever from every evil. But because the prophet had spoken of the mind of the reprobate as though of a ship, and of the Church of the righteous as though of a river which that ship could not cross, he further shows the attempt of this ship against that river, adding:

VERSE 23.—“Your cords are slackened, but they shall not prevail.”

O ship, your cords are slackened, so that, with the ropes of your sails loosened, you may be driven more strongly by the blast of demons [Col. 0321A] to attack the Church. But they shall not prevail, because “the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. 16:18). What are the cords of this ship except sins, of which it is said: “Woe to you who draw wickedness with cords of vanity!” (above, 5:18). This ship loosens these ropes so as to cross the river, because the mind of the ungodly gives full rein to all its wickedness while it strives to attack the Church. It follows:

“Thus shall your mast be, that you cannot spread the banner,” that is, the sail. What is expressed by the mast of this ship, which stands upright on high, except the pride of mind of the wicked? Hence it is written: “The pride of those who hate you rises continually” (Ps. 73:23). This is the mast extended upward. [Col. 0321B] And what is signified by the banner—that is, by the sail suspended from this mast—except the veil of error, which, descending from proud self-exaltation, darkens the conscience of the wicked and drives it on by the gusts of temptations? He says, therefore: “Thus shall your mast be,” that is, your pride, “that you cannot spread the banner,” that is, spread the sail of error throughout the world. For error will everywhere be confined and destroyed, while evangelical preaching will be extended among all nations. Hence it follows: “Then the spoils of many plunderings shall be divided; the lame shall seize the prey.”

VERSE 24.—“And no neighbor shall say: ‘I am weak.’”

The spoils of many plunderings are people taken from the ancient enemy, as it is written: “When a strong man armed guards his courtyard, the things he possesses are in peace. But if one stronger than he comes upon him and conquers him, he takes away all his weapons in which he trusted and distributes his spoils” (Luke 11:21). For the devil, armed, guarded this world as his courtyard and possessed it without opposition. But our Savior, coming down from above, conquered him, took from him his weapons—that is, his power to harm—and distributed in his Church his spoils—that is, the people whom he wickedly possessed. For “he gave some indeed to be apostles, some prophets, others evangelists, others pastors and teachers” (Eph. 4:11). Then, therefore, the spoils of many plunderings were divided, when God placed in the Church “first apostles, second prophets, [Col. 0321D] third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, kinds of tongues” (1 Cor. 2:28).

The lame are those whose foot of worldly love has withered. Thus Jacob (Gen. 32), who held the angel, limped on one foot, because one who truly loves and looks toward heavenly things no longer knows how to walk in this world with twofold desires. He rests upon one foot who is strengthened by the love of God alone, supports himself with all his strength upon the one foot of God’s love, and stands upon it, because he now carries raised from the earth the foot of worldly love which he had been accustomed to set upon the earth. Such lame persons seize the prey when they convert to Christ those whom the devil possessed.

And no neighbor shall say, “I am weak,” because their neighbors are willingly stirred by their example to a similar seizure of prey. It follows:

“The iniquity of the people who dwell in it shall be taken away.” The people of the faithful who persevere in the Church as they ought will alone obtain remission of their sins. It follows:

CHAPTER XXXIV.

VERSE 1.—“Draw near, nations, and hear; peoples, attend. Let the earth hear, and its fullness; the world and all its offspring.”

VERSE 2.—“For the indignation of the Lord is upon all nations, and wrath upon all their wickedness.”

Now, intending to speak of the universal judgment and the condemnation of the wicked, he summons every race of human beings together [Col. 0322B] to hear what he is about to say concerning all the reprobate. “Draw near,” he says, “nations, in mind, and hear with attentive heart what I say. Let the whole earth hear the general judgment, and its fullness—that is, all who are in it; and let the entire world, with all its offspring—that is, all who are born in it—fear.” And why are all thus commanded to hear? Because on the last day the indignation of the Lord will come upon all nations, and his wrath upon all their wickedness. For if those who did not give food to the hungry are to go into eternal fire, what will robbers and murderers suffer? Even now his indignation rests upon all unbelievers. “For he who does not believe the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him” (John 3:36), as John the Baptist says. [Col. 0322C] For in this world we are all born under God’s wrath, as the Apostle says: “We were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:3). But the wrath of God is removed from us by the grace of Christ alone. It is therefore rightly said that the indignation of the Lord is upon all nations that do not believe. It follows: “He has slain them and given them over to slaughter.” This is what the Lord himself says: “Fear him who, after he has killed, has power to cast into Gehenna” (Luke 12:5). It follows:

VERSE 3.—“Their slain shall be cast out, and from their corpses a stench shall rise.”

Their slain shall be cast out from the face of the Lord when they hear: “Depart from me, you cursed, into [Col. 0322D] eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41). And from their corpses a stench shall rise, because an unbearable stench will issue from the bodies of fornicators. It follows: “The mountains shall melt away with their blood.”

VERSE 4.—“And all the host of heaven shall melt away.”

What are the mountains in this place except the powerful people of this world, who swell high with earthly possessions, of whom the Psalmist says: “Touch the mountains, and they shall smoke” (Ps. 143:5)? And what is signified by blood except the sin of cruelty? Hence it was said above to some: “Your hands are full of blood” (above, 1:15), that is, your actions abound in cruelty. The mountains, therefore, shall melt away with their blood, because rulers will perish eternally in torments on account of the cruelty exercised under their rule by those over whom they presided. For whatever offense their subjects committed through their leadership will recoil upon them.

By the host of heaven he means the demons of this air, concerning whom Paul says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood” (Eph. 6:12), that is, against human beings, “but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the world of this darkness” (ibid.), that is, of wicked and unbelieving people, “against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (ibid.). Here, however, we do not understand ethereal heavens, but aerial ones. Thus we also call birds “birds of heaven,” though we see them flying in the air. Therefore all their host shall melt away, because all demons wandering through this air and daily fighting against [Col. 0323B] us will, on the last day, fall down into hell; there they shall melt away and perish without end. It follows:

“And the heavens shall be folded together like a book, and all their host shall fall away as a leaf falls from the vine and from the fig tree.”

VERSE 5.—“For my sword has been made drunk in heaven.”

It should be considered that he does not say that the heavens perish, but that they are folded like a book, so that, once all sins have been opened and left behind, the heavens that were previously open may be folded together, and the offenses of many may no longer be written in them.

Or the heavens are now spread out like a book so that the names of those who live well may be written in them daily. Thus the Lord says to his chosen disciples: “Rejoice, because your names [Col. 0323C] are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). But on that day they shall be folded like a book, so that thereafter no one’s name may be written in them.

“And all their host shall fall away as a leaf from a fig tree,” because just as the leaf of a tree, after it has withered and fallen, never becomes green again or returns to the tree, but rots in the earth, so those spirits fallen from heavenly places shall not be restored to their former state or grow green again through repentance, but shall rot eternally in the punishments of Gehenna.

Or their host shall fall like leaves because “the stars shall fall from heaven” (Matt. 24:29). “For my sword,” he says, “has been made drunk in heaven,” as though he said: Since I strike down the proud in wrath, then consider whether I have spared even those whom I created near myself in heaven from being struck for the fault of pride. Or, in heaven—that is, in the air—my sword has been made drunk by striking the powers of the air. It follows:

“Behold, it shall descend upon Idumea, and upon the people of my slaughter for judgment.”

Idumea is called “earthly” or “red.” Therefore, he says, the sword of my vengeance shall descend upon Idumea—that is, upon that part of the human race which is earthly and red with the blood of sins—and upon the people of my slaughter: that is, upon the whole multitude of those whom I shall slay in the judgment of condemnation, of which it is said: “Those who have done evil, unto the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:29). It follows:

[Col. 0324A] VERSE 6.—“For the sword of the Lord is filled with blood; it is made fat with fatness, with the blood of lambs and goats, with the blood of rams full of marrow.”

To show that this sword has killed many, it is said to be filled with blood and made fat with fatness. Since lambs, rams, and goats used to be sacrificed, he says that the great victim of all the reprobate, which he now sacrifices, consists of lambs, rams, and goats. Thus he says through Jeremiah: “I shall lead them down like lambs for slaughter, like rams with goats” (Jer. 51:40). Those predestined as occasions for eternal death are called by such names, just as these animals are destined for sacrifice. Or certainly by blood we understand the sin of the flesh, because it is written: “Deliver me from bloods” (Ps. 50:15); [Col. 0324B] and by fatness, pride, of which it is said: “Their wickedness came forth as if from fatness” (Ps. 72:7).

What is denoted by lambs except those who appear gentle and innocent, yet did not strive to make themselves such for God’s sake? What by goats except leaders of unbelievers, horned by worldly power and foul through lust? And what by rams except leaders of peoples, wrapped in abundance of riches as in wool? What, moreover, by the marrow of rams except the pride of their hearts? The sword of the Lord, therefore, is filled with blood and made fat with fatness, because it especially strikes lust and pride: with the blood of lambs, that is, the sin of those who seemed simple and innocent but were not so for God’s sake; and of goats, that is, lustful rulers; and of rams full of marrow, that is, proud leaders. It follows:

“For the Lord has a sacrifice in Bozrah, and a great slaughter in the land of Edom.”

This sacrifice is the general slaughter of the reprobate. Bozrah means “tribulation,” while Edom means “earthly.” And who is earthly is evident. For “the first man is from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly. As is the earthly, so are those who are earthly; and as is the heavenly, so are those who are heavenly” (1 Cor. 15:47). The Lord’s sacrifice is therefore offered in Bozrah, because sinners are slain in tribulation. And a great slaughter takes place in the land of Edom—that is, in the land of the earthly—because all who are like Adam perish: those who, as [Col. 0324D] they bore the image of the earthly, did not bear the image of the heavenly. It follows:

VERSE 7.—“And unicorns shall descend with them, and bulls with the mighty.”

With those mentioned above—that is, lambs, goats, and rams—unicorns shall descend. What does he call unicorns except those emperors who held monarchy over the whole world, such as Alexander, Caesar, Augustus, and Antichrist? What are bulls except the remaining kings who attacked their adversaries with the horns of kingship? And what are the mighty except the other rulers of the world? Unicorns, therefore, descend into hell with them because even the highest emperors will fall with other sinners into the abyss of that condemnation; and bulls with the mighty because kings will be shamefully cast down with their nobles. Hence it is written: “A most severe judgment shall befall those who rule. For mercy is granted to the lowly; but the mighty shall suffer mighty torments” (Wis. 6:6). It follows:

“Their land shall be made drunk with blood, and their soil with the fatness of the fat ones.”

What is denoted by their land or soil except the dwelling-place of hell, concerning which it is written: “A land of darkness, covered with the gloom of death, a land of misery and darkness” (Job 10:21), and again: “This is the place of him who does not know God” (Job 18:21)? How then shall this land be made drunk with their blood and fatness, when after the resurrection [Col. 0325B] their bodies are immortal and incorruptible, though then still possessing the sense of pain, and when there is no necessity that those now fat should rise with the same fatness? Blood and fatness, therefore, must be understood differently. For elsewhere too it is written: “Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed” (Gen. 9:6). This statement cannot stand according to the letter. For many have shed human blood whose blood was not shed in this life; and it would seem absurd for anyone to say that their blood will be shed at the resurrection of the dead. A person’s blood, therefore, must be understood as the vital principle by which he is animated, sustained, and lives. Whoever sheds this, whether by scandal or by perversity of teaching, shall have it shed from him on the day of judgment, when he will be compelled to lose even that vital principle which he possessed, so as to die perpetually.

Therefore, when “the life of the flesh,” as Moses says, “is in the blood” (Lev. 17:14), the shedding of blood signifies the loss of life—that is, the eternal death of the reprobate. Fatness, however, is the pride of the heart in the inward person, which dulls and weighs down the mind. Hence it is written: “The heart of this people has grown fat” (Acts 28:27). For just as bodily fat is commonly produced from an abundance of food, so pride of heart arises from abundance of riches. What then is figured by the fatness of the fat except the pride of the rich? Yet fat commonly melts by the heat of fire, and, when added, more quickly kindles and feeds the fire. What, therefore, should be understood by fat dissolved in fire except the pride of the reprobate [Col. 0325D] wasting away and burning without end in the fires of Gehenna? Thus their land shall be made drunk with blood, and their soil with the fatness of the fat ones, because Tartarus will be immoderately filled with their death, signified by the loss of blood, and with burning, indicated by melted fatness. It follows:

VERSE 8.—“For it is the day of the Lord’s vengeance, the year of recompense for Zion [Note: [Col. 0325D] Alternatively: ‘the year of the recompenses of Zion’s judgment.’].”

Then there will be the day of the Lord’s vengeance, which he will exact from his enemies; and then there will be the year in which Zion—that is, the Church, having received the power of judgment—will repay her persecutors what they deserve. “Then the righteous will stand in great steadfastness against those who afflicted them” [Col. 0326A] (Wisdom 5:1). Hence in the Apocalypse it is said to them concerning wicked Babylon: “In the cup in which she mixed for you, mix for her double” (Rev. 18:6). Day and year signify either the time of judgment or that boundless duration which will follow the end of the age. It follows:

**VERSE 9.**—“And her streams shall be turned into pitch, and her soil into sulphur; and her land shall become burning pitch.”

**VERSE 10.**—“It shall not be quenched night or day; its smoke shall rise for ever. From generation to generation it shall lie waste, unto ages of ages.”

He had previously stated that their land—that is, hell—would be made drunk with blood; and now, speaking more fully of that same land, he adds that its streams shall be turned into pitch [Col. 0326B]. Blessed Gregory relates in the *Dialogues* that a certain person who returned here saw a river in places of punishment, in which many were tormented, and from which a stench-laden mist rose. Other orthodox Fathers likewise often wrote similar things. Thus it is credible that there are streams in hell in which the souls of the damned are boiled. These streams will be turned into pitch because they will resemble boiling pitch: whatever they touch, they will burn and hold fast. And its soil will be turned into sulphur because it too will burn and exhale a most grievous stench. Its land shall become burning pitch because the ground there will burn like pitch.

[Col. 0326C] What, then, is denoted by night and day—for there is perpetual night there—except the changing variety of punishments? For the wretched pass continually through diverse torments. The land will be burning pitch by night and day because, amid every variety of punishment, the earth will burn like pitch; nor will it be extinguished for ever, but, burning eternally, it will torment the ungodly, so that in those ages they may never be without punishment who in this life were never willing to be without sin.

Or the wicked will be tormented in the day when in hell they think of the glory of the saints, and in the night when they consider the enormity of their own condemnation. But the smoke of this burning land will rise from generation to generation, because during the generation of the faithful Hebrews which preceded the Saviour’s coming [Col. 0326D], and during the generation of Christians which follows it, the smoke of this fire endures; and, judgment having been completed, it will lay waste unto ages of ages all whom it has held, because it will remove every remedy from them. It follows: “There shall be none passing through it,” because there will be no righteous person to visit them.

**VERSE 11.**—“The pelican and the hedgehog shall possess it; the ibis and the raven shall dwell in it.”

The *onocrotalus* is a bird so called because it makes a sound in the water with its beak like a cymbal. For in Greek κρόταλον (*krotalon*) means “cymbal.” Since the knowledge of Sacred Scripture can be understood by water, what is denoted by the *onocrotalus* except those preachers [Col. 0327A] who, lacking charity, have become “like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal” (1 Cor. 13:1)? The hedgehog, however, is an animal covered with spines and bristles in place of hair, wounding whatever it touches. What, then, is signified by the hedgehog except every sinner surrounded by the prickings of vices, who wounds the heart of anyone attempting to touch him by correction with an evil reply? The ibis—that is, the stork—is a sluggish bird that lives near waters but does not swim in them. What is denoted by the ibis except those who often hear the Scriptures but are slow to act and do not swim in their understanding, since they do not attain to them? The raven represents the blackness of sinners or unbelievers.

These, therefore, shall possess that land which will burn like pitch [Col. 0327B], and they shall dwell in it, because this is the proper abode of the wicked, prepared for them from the foundation of the world. Or, certainly, let us understand all these things of that great Babylon, although its name is not mentioned here. For now the *onocrotalus* and the hedgehog possess it, and the ibis and raven dwell in it, because those who have deserved to be called by such names are its citizens through their pursuit of wicked conduct. It follows:

“And the measuring-line shall be stretched over it, that it may be reduced to nothing, and the plumb-line unto desolation.”

A measuring-line will be stretched over the burning land, that it may be reduced to nothing, because sinners will there perish eternally according to the measure by which God in just judgment disposes their punishments. “And the plumb-line [Col. 0327C] unto desolation,” that is, unto demolition, because the damned there will be scattered and torn apart by punishments according to the decision of the justice of the supreme Creator. For a *plumb-line* is what masons use to bring a wall to straightness, or to curve arches in equal roundness. But *desolation* here is not derived from *desolor, desolaris*; it is from *desolo, desolas*, signifying the laying waste of a land. Or a measuring-line will be stretched over Babylon, that it may be reduced to nothing, and a plumb-line unto desolation, because it will be destroyed according to the manner of God’s just ordinance and exterminated according to the rule of his judgment. It follows:

**VERSE 12.**—“Her nobles shall not be there; rather, they shall call upon the king.”

Her nobles are the elect who are born or live among the reprobate [Col. 0327D] in this age. They will not be there—that is, in that everlasting condemnation—but while they live they will call upon Christ the King, and he will save them. It follows:

“And all her princes shall be reduced to nothing.” Her princes are the powerful and wise persons of this world, who on the day of vengeance will be reduced to nothing, because neither their power, nor wisdom, nor strength will avail them. But before the day of that condemnation, let us hear what meanwhile takes place in this Babylon. It follows:

**VERSE 13.**—“Thorns and nettles shall spring up in her houses, and the paliurus in her strongholds.”

What do we understand by nettles except the irritations of thoughts, and by thorns except the prickings of vices? Thus nettles and thorns spring up in Babylon’s houses [Col. 0328A], because in the confused minds of the wicked arise both desires of thoughts that irritate and sinful deeds that pierce. Yet those who do these things also have still worse defenders. Hence it is added: “And the paliurus in her strongholds.” The *paliurus* is so densely surrounded by thorns that, because of its harshness, it can scarcely be touched. Such indeed are perverse people: surrounded by the hard spines of sins, they do not allow themselves to be touched by one who corrects them. Nettle and thorn grow within, while the *paliurus* is outside in the fortress: lesser wicked persons commit every sort of evil, but the more wicked and greater persons defend them. It follows: “And it shall be a lair of dragons and a pasture for ostriches.”

[Col. 0328B] **VERSE 14.**—“Demons shall meet with onocentaurs, and the hairy one shall cry to another.”

What is denoted by dragons except malice, and what by the name of ostriches except hypocrisy? For the ostrich possesses the capacity for flight but not the use of flight, just as hypocrisy presents to all beholders an image of holiness, yet neglects to possess the virtue of holiness. Thus in a perverse mind the dragon lies down and the ostrich feeds, because hidden malice is craftily covered and a pretence of goodness is displayed before the eyes of onlookers.

What is denoted by the name of onocentaurs except those who are both lustful and proud? In Greek, ὄνος (*onos*) means “ass,” and by the designation “ass” lust is signified, as the prophet testifies when he says: “Their flesh is the flesh of asses” [Col. 0328C] (Ezek. 23:20). By the term “bull,” however, the neck of pride is shown, as the Lord says concerning the proud Jews through the Psalmist: “Fat bulls have surrounded me” (Ps. 21[22]:13). Onocentaurs, therefore, are those who, subject to the vices of lust, lift up their neck from that very source from which they ought to have been humbled. Serving the pleasures of their flesh, with shame cast far away, they not only do not grieve at losing uprightness but even rejoice in their shameful action. Demons therefore meet onocentaurs because evil spirits gladly serve those whom they see rejoicing in things over which they ought to weep. Hence it is fittingly added:

“And the hairy one shall cry to another.” Who are denoted by the designation “hairy ones” except those whom [Col. 0328D] the Greeks call πάνας (*panas*), and the Latins *incubi*? Their form begins with a human appearance but ends in an animal extremity. By the name “hairy one,” then, is signified the roughness of any sin: though it sometimes begins under the pretext of reason, it nevertheless always tends toward irrational impulses. It is as though a human being ends in a beast when guilt, beginning under the image of reason, drags one to irrational effects. For the pleasure of eating often serves gluttony and pretends to serve the necessity of nature; but when greed has swollen the belly, it raises the limbs to lust. Thus one hairy one cries to another when committed wickedness provokes the committing of wickedness, and, as it were by a voice of thought, a sin already committed invites still further sin that accompanies it. One hairy one [Col. 0329A] cries to another when, under some appearance of reasoning, a subsequent fault ensnares a perverse mind through the occasion of a preceding fault; and, as harsh and rough sins crush it, hairy ones, as though summoned together, rule within it in concord. It follows:

“There the lamia lay down and found rest for herself.”

**VERSE 15.**—“There the hedgehog had its den, and nourished its young, and dug around it, and warmed them in its shadow.”

By the *lamia* hypocrites are denoted; by the hedgehog, all malicious persons who cover themselves with diverse defenses. For the *lamia* is said to have a human face but an animal body. So too all hypocrites: in the outward face that they display there seems to be something proceeding from the reason of holiness; but an animal body follows, because what they contrive under the appearance of good is exceedingly wicked [Col. 0329B]. Therefore the *lamia* lay down there and found rest for herself, because the pretense of hypocrites is nourished among lovers of the world.

By the name of the hedgehog, moreover, is signified the self-defense of malicious minds. When a hedgehog is caught, its head, feet, and whole body are visible; but as soon as it is seized, it draws itself into a ball, retracts its feet inward, hides its head, and all at once disappears within the hands of the one holding it—that whole which had previously been visible all at once. Such, indeed, are malicious minds when they are apprehended in their transgressions. The hedgehog’s head is seen because the beginning by which a sinner approached wrongdoing is visible [Col. 0329C]; its feet are seen because the steps by which wickedness was committed are known. Yet, when excuses are suddenly brought forward, the malicious mind draws its feet inward, because it hides every trace of its wickedness. It withdraws its head because, by astonishing defenses, it makes it appear that it did not even begin anything perverse. It remains like a ball in the hand of its holder because the reprover, suddenly losing all that he had known, holds the sinner wrapped up within his conscience; and he who had perceived everything by discovery, deceived by the evasiveness of perverse defense, is altogether ignorant of it. Thus the hedgehog has a den among the reprobate because the malicious mind, gathering itself within itself, hides in the darkness of self-defense.

But because it is not enough for such people [Col. 0329D] to hide themselves in such dark concealments unless they also train others in the perversity of the same cunning, the hedgehog is said to have nourished its young. It also digs around, because such persons constantly search in every direction and seek grounds for excuses. And it warms its young in the shadow of its pretence and defense, because lesser persons progress in wickedness and are strengthened under the protection of their superiors. It follows:

“There kites are gathered, one to another.” Kites are gathered because the greedy and rapacious associate with one another and jointly crave plunder. It follows:

**VERSE 16.**—“Seek diligently in the book of the Lord and read: not one of these was lacking; one did not seek another [Col. 0330A], because what proceeded from my mouth, he commanded, and his Spirit gathered them.”

Perhaps we should understand by the book of the Lord this book, written at the Lord’s command, in which he directs us diligently to seek what these birds and beasts, which he has now set forth, signify: namely lambs and goats, bulls and rams, and the *onocrotalus*, hedgehog, ibis, raven, and other such things. Each has a definite significance among the reprobate, and not one of them remained absent; rather, all these are found in them. One among the rams, ibises, hairy ones, or kites did not seek another, because they found one another equally without the labor of searching. So great is the multitude of the wicked that there is no need for one to seek another. And lest it weary us to investigate these matters diligently [Col. 0330B], the prophet did not speak them from himself: rather, the Lord commanded him to speak what proceeded from his mouth, and his Spirit gathered all these things in the prophet’s heart.

Or certainly we may understand the book of the Lord as the remembrance of all things which is in his wisdom, concerning which Malachi says: “The Lord gave heed and heard, and a book of remembrance was written before him” (Mal. 3:10). In this book, we are commanded to seek diligently and to read these things, because not one of them was lacking. We must carefully investigate them in the knowledge of God’s wisdom and consider how those things are contained there which are described to us under the metaphor of unclean birds and beasts [Col. 0330C], and of a land turned into everlasting desolations. It follows:

**VERSE 17.**—“And he himself cast the lot for them, and his hand divided it to them by measure; they shall possess it for ever; from generation to generation they shall dwell in it.”

He “made us worthy to share in the lot of the saints in light” (Col. 1:12); he himself cast for sinners the lot of reprobation, so that all might be held in one lot of condemnation. And his hand divided it to them by measure, so that the measure of vengeance may correspond to the measure of guilt: murderers with murderers, fornicators with fornicators, deceivers with deceivers, the avaricious with the avaricious, and all such persons [Col. 0330D] with their like may be punished. They will possess that lot of condemnation for ever, so that those who, while living here, set no end to their wickedness may burn without end. And meanwhile, even before the day of judgment, from their departure from their bodies they will dwell in the same lot of punishments, or in the burning land during the time of the generation of the Synagogue and the generation of the Church.

Having thus described the present conduct of the reprobate and their future condemnation under the figure of unclean birds and beasts and of a region turned into eternal desolation and burning, the prophet now turns to the portion of the elect. Under the type of a wilderness transformed into every kind of beauty, he describes their conduct, life, and glorification. For he adds concerning the Gentiles:

## CHAPTER XXXV

**VERSE 1.**—“The desert and trackless land shall rejoice; the wilderness shall exult and blossom like a lily.”

**VERSE 2.**—“It shall bud and blossom, and shall exult rejoicing and praising; the glory of Lebanon has been given to it, the beauty of Carmel and Sharon.”

For Gentile humanity was a desert, in which there was no patriarch, no prophet. There was no one there who used reason to understand God; there was no human being there. This Gentile world was also trackless, for the way of the Lord had not been opened to it by the word. When our Redeemer came, it received the calling of grace in such a way [Col. 0331B] that the way of prophecy had not previously existed in it. But, converted to Christ, it rejoiced and exulted, hearing from the Apostle: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. 4:4). And it blossomed like a lily, because the bright and fragrant life of the righteous spread itself there.

Budding in the heart, it blossomed in action; and it exulted rejoicing and praising because it delighted in the praises of God. Lebanon, as we have said, is interpreted “whitening” or “being made white”; Carmel, “knowledge of circumcision”; Sharon, “singing sorrow.” Therefore the glory of Lebanon—that is, of whitening—was given to it, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “You will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. 50[51]:9). The beauty of Carmel was given to it, that it might know how to circumcise itself in heart [Col. 0331C], tongue, hands, eyes, and ears. And the beauty of Sharon was given to it because, through the gift of heavenly grace, it delights in tears and loves sorrow in place of song. Thus Gentile humanity, converted, was made white with the brightness of righteousness, spiritually circumcised from all vices, and, devoted to compunction of heart, sings sorrow. But after these things, what remains except that, so cleansed, it should be brought into the vision of the heavenly majesty, and eternal joy should succeed temporary sorrow? Hence it follows:

“They shall see the glory of the Lord and the beauty of our God.” None of the reprobate will see the Lord’s glory; but these will behold the glory of majesty and beauty, because “they shall see the King in his beauty” [Col. 0331D] (above, 33:17). But whoever hopes to attain this vision must exercise himself more and more each day in good deeds. Hence it follows:

**VERSE 3.**—“Strengthen hands that are slack.”

For “he who is lax and slack in his work is brother to one who destroys his works” (Prov. 18:9).—“And strengthen weak knees,” that is, weak actions, so that they may no longer bend toward evil deeds or curve toward sin through weakness of heart. It follows:

**VERSE 4.**—“Say to the fainthearted: Take courage; do not fear. Behold, your God will bring the vengeance of recompense; he himself will come and save you.”

You, he says, O teachers, say to those who are fainthearted: “Be strengthened, act courageously, and let your hearts be strengthened. ‘Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul’” (Matt. 10:28). For behold, your God, for whose sake you suffer, will repay affliction to those who afflict you, and to you who are afflicted, rest at the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ from heaven. Behold, your God will bring upon them the vengeance of just recompense. God himself will come in person and save you. In the same spirit the Apostle says to the Philippians: “May I hear of you that you stand in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the Gospel, and are in no way frightened by your adversaries; this is for them a cause of destruction, but for you of salvation” (Phil. 1:27–28). For what the prophet says to those who are fainthearted—“Be strengthened” [Col. 0332B]—is what the Apostle exhorts his disciples to do: stand in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the Gospel. And what Isaiah adds—“Do not fear”—is what Paul appends: “And be in no way frightened by your adversaries.” What follows here—“Behold, your God will bring the vengeance of recompense”—is there added as: “This is for them a cause of destruction.” And what is added here—“God himself will come and save you”—is there supplied as: “But for you, of salvation.” But let us hear with full desire what will occur at that coming of the Saviour. It follows:

**VERSE 5.**—“Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unsealed.”

**VERSE 6.**—“Then the lame shall leap like a stag, and the tongue of the mute shall be opened.”

[Col. 0332C] In this life we are blind because, expelled from the light of paradise, we endure the darkness of our condemnation. Hence Moses was told: “You cannot see my face, for no human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 33:20). We are also now deaf because we cannot hear the hymns of inward praise sung by the angels. We are likewise lame while we live here because, although the mind keeps the path of uprightness, the body nevertheless totters through weakness. Hence the Apostle says: “I delight in the law of God according to the inner person; but I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. 7:22–23). And again: “Thus [Col. 0332D] I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but the law of sin with my flesh” (ibid., 25). The one who serves the law of God with the mind but the law of sin with the flesh is therefore lame.

We are also mute because we cannot speak heavenly praises as we ought. Thus, when David said, “Praise the Lord, O my soul” (Ps. 145:1), because he knew that he was mute while he was still alive, he immediately added: “I will praise God in my life” (ibid.), that is, after the resurrection of bodies. Before the eloquence of God he saw himself wholly mute and irrational, saying: “I became like a beast before you” (Ps. 72[73]:22). Therefore we are blind and deaf, lame and mute. But when the Lord comes, the eyes of the blind will be opened, because when the darkness of our minds has been driven away, the power to see him will be granted us, as he himself says: “Father, I desire that those whom you have given me may be with me where I am, that they may see my glory” [Col. 0333A] (John 17:24).—“We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (John 3:2).

And the ears of the deaf will be unsealed because, when the ears of the heart have been opened, we shall hear not only angelic harmonies but also clearly the unique Word of God himself, as he promises when he says: “I will openly announce the Father to you” (John 16:25).

And then the lame will leap like a stag because the bodies of the saints will be changed: every sense of discomfort, all corruptibility and slowness, and every earthly frailty and blemish will be removed; they will be transformed and changed into heavenly purity and stability [Col. 0333B]. Thus they will leap like a stag because no frailty or slowness will impede them. Hence Malachi promises them that agility: “You shall go forth and leap like calves from the herd” (Mal. 4:2).

And the tongue of the mute will be opened because then the breath of the righteous will be unsealed in praise of God, when they hear: “Give praise to our God, all his saints” (Rev. 19:5). Then they will be able to speak those secret words once heard by Paul in paradise, “which it is not now permitted for a human being to speak” (2 Cor. 12:4).

At his first coming, these things were fulfilled not only bodily but spiritually as well, and are fulfilled every day: those whom unbelief had blinded open the eyes of their minds to the light of truth; those who could not hear the words of Scripture with deaf ears afterward rejoice in God’s commandments; those formerly lame and not keeping the straight way leap forward in the progress of righteousness like stags, imitating agile and spiritual people; and the tongue of the mute is opened when Satan had shut their mouths so that they could not confess the true God. It follows:

“For waters have burst forth in the desert, and streams in the wilderness.”

**VERSE 7.**—“And what was dry shall become a pool, and the thirsty land springs of water.”

What should be understood by waters and streams, Solomon indicates when he says: “Deep water is the words from a person’s mouth, and an overflowing stream is a fountain of wisdom” (Prov. [Col. 0333D] 18:4). These waters—that is, the words of heavenly teaching, or also the waters of baptism—have burst forth, that is, flowed out, in the desert of the Gentile world; and streams of wisdom overflowed in the wilderness of the nations as the apostles preached. Gentile humanity itself, formerly dry—that is, without every moisture of wisdom—became a pool, that is, an immense depth of spiritual understanding; and what was thirsty now sends forth springs of heavenly teachings. It follows:

“In the dens in which dragons formerly dwelt, there shall spring up the green growth of reed and rush.”

What is denoted by the reed except writers? What by the rush, which always grows in moisture near water, except little and tender hearers of the sacred word? Therefore, in the dens of dragons the green growth of reeds and rushes springs up [Col. 0334A], because among those peoples whom the malice of the ancient enemy possessed, both the knowledge of teachers and the obedience of hearers are gathered in abundance. But because both rush and reed usually grow in the moisture of water and both prosper from one and the same water—although the reed is used for writing, whereas one cannot write with the rush—what ought we to understand by rush and reed except that there is one teaching of truth which irrigates many hearers? Of those thus irrigated, some advance so far in the word of God as to become writers like reeds; others hear the word of life and retain the freshness of good hope and upright deeds, yet cannot advance to writing. It follows:

**VERSE 8.**—“And there shall be there a path and a way, and it shall be called the holy way; the unclean shall not pass through it.”

There will be a path in the martyrs, a way in the confessors. Or a path in those who abandon all that belongs to the world, and a way in those who make lawful use of worldly things. This way—that is, the conduct of the faithful by which they make for their homeland—will be called holy, so that no one defiled by sins can pass along it. For according to Dionysius (*On the Divine Names*, ch. 12): “Holiness is purity free from every defilement, most perfect and utterly unstained.” No one, therefore, who is defiled by the filth of vices shall pass along the way of holiness; rather, “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. 118[119]:1). It follows:

[Col. 0334C] “And this shall be for you a straight way, so that fools may not go astray upon it.”

**VERSE 9.**—“No lion shall be there, and no evil beast shall go up by it, nor shall it be found there.”

The way of the elect, by which they hasten to their homeland through observance of God’s commandments, is straight. “Fools” are those who, having abandoned harmful wisdom, have learned praiseworthy foolishness, as the Apostle says: “If anyone among you thinks himself wise in this age, let him become foolish, that he may be wise” (1 Cor. 3:18). These fools do not go astray on the way of righteousness; rather, they walk on it more cautiously insofar as they know themselves more humbly to be fools. “For God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise” (ibid., 27). Since the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God, the more a person tries to appear wise outwardly, the more foolish he becomes inwardly [Col. 0334D].

The lion, however, is the devil, who will not be there—that is, on the way of the righteous—because it is said of evil spirits: “You have set a stumbling-block for me beside the way” (Ps. 139[140]:6). The evil beast is the ancient enemy, who lies in wait for this world’s plunder and daily satisfies himself with human death, raging with the violence of cruelty to seize, at the time of death, the souls of sinners. He shall not ascend by that way on which the elect walk, because, condemned without pardon, he will return to the heavenly homeland through no amendment. Nor shall he be found there—that is, on the way of righteousness—because he always walks by the way of wickedness.

[Col. 0335A] Or, according to Gregory (*Morals*, book 27, ch. 26), let us say: “The evil beast shall not pass through it,” that is, through the Church. For the beast, as we have said, is that enemy who savagely assailed the first human being by deception and tore apart the integrity of that person’s life by persuading evil. Against him it is now said concerning the holy Church of the elect, to be restored to its ancient state: “And the evil beast shall not pass through it”; and it is added: “Nor shall it be found there”—understand, as the serpent was formerly found in paradise—because through Christ’s grace we are to obtain better things than we lost through Adam. For in that life the enemy is nowhere; no assailant will be found or feared. Therefore, after a way has been made in the Gentile world, which was formerly desert and trackless, it is added:

“And those who have been delivered shall walk.”

[Col. 0335B] **VERSE 10.**—“And those redeemed by the Lord shall return and come to Zion with praise, and everlasting joy shall be upon their heads; they shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and groaning shall flee away.”

Those who have been delivered and redeemed through Christ from the captivity of Babylon—that is, “from their vain manner of life handed down from their fathers” (1 Pet. 1:18)—shall walk by the way of righteousness which God prepared for them in this wilderness. They shall return to the ancient dwelling-place of paradise and come to Zion, that is, to the heavenly Jerusalem, with praise of the Saviour. Joy without end will be upon their head—that is, upon their mind. For the mind is called the head because, just as the head governs the members, so thoughts are ordered by the mind. A further addition is made to the abundant sum of their happiness: they shall obtain and possess joy and gladness [Col. 0335C]. For what could they do in that blessedness except always rejoice and delight in the vision of the Creator? Hence the Psalmist says: “Let the righteous feast and exult before God, and delight in gladness” (Ps. 67[68]:4). Sorrow and groaning shall flee away because they will experience no further affliction, and there will no longer be anything able to make them sad; all things will be calm and pleasant for them. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXVI

**VERSE 1.**—“And it came to pass in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah that Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and took them [Col. 0335D].”

In Sacred Scripture, even those matters that may be understood according to history must often be understood spiritually as well, so that faith may be retained in the truth of the history and spiritual understanding drawn from the mysteries of allegory. Thus we believe that the things now related concerning the king of Assyria and Hezekiah truly occurred at that time according to history, but also that they prefigured other things that were to be accomplished in the New Testament.

For what is denoted by Hezekiah, king of Judah—whose name is interpreted “strength of the Lord” or “the Lord is strong”—except our King Christ, who is the power of God? What is expressed by the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah except the period in which Christ, living bodily among human beings [Col. 0336A], fulfilled both Testaments? For the number four commonly signifies the New Testament because of the four books of the Gospels, and ten the Law because of its Decalogue. What is understood by the king of Assyria except the devil? He is called Sennacherib, that is, “lifting up deserts,” because, stirring up the hearts of unbelievers against the faithful, he raises them up into persecution. What is denoted by fortified cities except the minds of the Jews, who had fortified themselves against divine preaching? Thus, in Hezekiah’s fourteenth year, the king of Assyria took all the fortified cities because, when the Lord appeared in the flesh, the devil brought the Jewish people under his own rule. It follows:

**VERSE 2.**—“And the king of Assyria sent Rabshakeh [Col. 0336B] from Lachish to Jerusalem, to King Hezekiah, with a heavy hand; and he stood by the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road of the fuller’s field.”

Rabshakeh is interpreted “a prince who kisses” or “many by a kiss.” What, then, is signified by Rabshakeh except the feigned friendliness of the scribes and Pharisees when they say: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth” (Matt. 22:16), and other things of this kind? Lachish is called “it is situated between” or “a man unto himself.” What is denoted by Lachish except the Hebrew people, which alone received the Law among those peoples and acted manfully for itself alone? What, however, is denoted by Jerusalem except the Church? Thus, after the cities of Judah had been taken, the king of Assyria sent Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem [Col. 0336C] to Hezekiah, because, after the Jews had been brought into subjection in unbelief, the ancient enemy stirred up the chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees from the same Jewish people against Christ and against his faithful; and he sent them with a heavy hand, that is, with the strength of the people of the Synagogue.

What is the upper pool except the preeminent teaching of the Gospel? And who is the aqueduct of this pool except the hidden knowledge of the Old Testament, in which the overflowing fountain of Gospel preaching is concealed and from which it eventually proceeds? Rabshakeh therefore stood, because the hypocritical scribes and Pharisees, persisting in the oldness of the letter, did not come to the newness of the Spirit. Malachi says of Christ: “For he is like a refining fire and like the herb of fullers” [Col. 0336D] (Mal. 3:2). If Christ is like the herb of fullers, what is the field in which this herb grew except the Jewish people? The fuller’s field, therefore, is the Jewish people. The road of the fuller’s field is the conduct of the Synagogue, on which road Rabshakeh stood because the Pharisees and scribes did not abandon carnal observances.

Yet we should understand Rabshakeh as signifying the Pharisees, the scribes, and the high priests in such a way that we do not deny that, secondarily, the other leaders of the Church’s adversaries may be understood through him—namely, the patrons of heretics and pagans. Hence in the Book of Kings (4 Kings 18:17) two other leaders are reported to have come with him, namely Tartan and Rabsaris. For Hezekiah may perhaps also signify the holy rulers of the Church, who are members of Christ; and the fourteenth year of Hezekiah [Col. 0337A], their time in which they keep both Testaments; the king of the Assyrians, the swollen opinion of perverse doctrines; the fortified cities of Judah, the minds of those who profess themselves Christians and shut their hearts against the word of preaching. Thus the king of the Assyrians captured Judah’s fortified cities, because, in time of persecution, Christians who did not receive the Church’s doctrine obediently readily assented to the error of pagans or heretics. Lachish, which is said to mean “it lies between,” can express the people of heretics, who are, as it were, intermediate between us and the pagans. But the fact that Lachish is interpreted “a man for himself” also shows that heretics are lovers of themselves: “For charity does not seek its own” (1 Cor. 13:5). Yet all heretics seek what is their own, not what is Jesus [Col. 0337B] Christ’s. From Lachish, therefore—that is, from the people of heretics—comes Rabshakeh, that is, each heresiarch, into Jerusalem, that is, against the Church.

But the fuller’s field, in which filth is washed away, is the people of believers, in whom Christ the fuller removes the stains of hearts. The way of the fuller’s field is the activity of the Christian people; the upper pool is divine Scripture. This pool is indeed on the way of the fuller’s field, since the commandments of heavenly Scripture are present in the activity of the faithful people. The aqueduct of this pool is the secret preaching of heretics, as though stealthily drawn forth from sacred Scripture. Hence the harlot in Solomon, who bears the type of heresy, says: “Stolen waters are sweeter” (Prov. 9:17). Rabshakeh therefore stood at this aqueduct against Jerusalem, because heresiarchs took their stand against [Col. 0337C] the Church in their stolen preaching. Yet this Rabshakeh can also represent the leaders of pagan error. But let us pass on to the rest. It follows:

**VERSE 3.**—“And Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, went out to him, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph, keeper of the records.”

Eliakim is interpreted “God has raised up”; Hilkiah, “the Lord’s portion”; Shebna, “sitting”; Joah, “the Lord’s brother” or “the making of a brother”; Asaph, “gathering.” And what is signified by Eliakim, the steward of the Lord’s house, except the pre-eminent summit of the apostles? He is rightly called “God has raised up,” because he took especial care to affirm the Savior’s resurrection. For it is written that “with great power the apostles gave testimony to the resurrection [Col. 0337D] of Jesus Christ our Lord” (Acts 4:33). They are sons of the Lord’s portion, that is, of election, as he himself says: “Of those whom thou gavest me I lost none” (John 18:9).

A scribe, however, is a writer, as Jeremiah makes clear when he says concerning some: “Truly the deceitful pen of the scribes has wrought falsehood” (Jer. 8:8). And what is signified by this scribe except the Fathers who composed the canonical Scriptures? Hence he is called Shebna, that is, “sitting,” because authority of teaching is signified by sitting, as the Lord indicated when he said: “The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat. Therefore keep and do all whatsoever they tell you” (Matt. 23:2).

[Col. 0338A] By *commentaries* we customarily mean expositions of books. What then is signified by Joah, who went out from his commentaries with the other two to Rabshakeh, except interpreters of the sacred Scriptures? Hence Joah is called “the Lord’s brother,” because holy teachers, through the merit of their life, have become close to the Savior, who says: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. 12:50). And the interpretation of Joah as “the making of a brother” is understood in the same sense: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared that we should walk in them” (Eph. 2:10). For Christ himself deigned to become our brother. Thus Joah is the son of Asaph, that is, the son of the Gatherer [Col. 0338B]. For God is called the Gatherer because he gathers the Church of the elect from all peoples and nations, as it is written: “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples, says the Lord, who gathers the dispersed of Israel” (Isa. 56:7). Those who expound the sacred utterance imitate this by striving to unite the flock of the faithful; therefore they are rightly called sons of the Gatherer.

We may also understand holy preachers by Shebna the scribe. For “scribe” denotes not always a writer, but often a wise man, as the Lord shows where he says: “Every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure things new and old” (Matt. 13:52). By Joah the recorder, however, we may understand those who wrote the deeds [Col. 0338C] of successive ages after the apostles. A *commentariensis*, that is, a chancellor, is one who records events; and *commentarii* are called the little books of documents which he writes.

Therefore Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph, keeper of the records, went out to Rabshakeh, because the apostles and authors of the holy Scriptures—or the Church’s rulers, wise men, and interpreters of the sacred utterance, or writers of sacred deeds—have often given an account of our faith to Jews, pagans, and heretics. For we go out from ourselves to him when, by speaking, we bring forth the hidden things of our mind. It follows:

**VERSE 4.**—“And Rabshakeh said to them: Say to Hezekiah: Thus says the great king of the Assyrians: What is this confidence in which you trust?”

**VERSE 5.**—“Or by what counsel or strength do you plan to rebel? In whom do you trust, that you have withdrawn from me?”

Because Rabshakeh bears the type of Jews, heretics, and pagans, he speaks in the voice of them all. First he begins to speak in the voice of Jews and pagans: “Say,” he says, “you rulers, say to Hezekiah,” that is, to the Church, which is Christ’s body. For Christ and the Church are one person; and thus what is said of Christ must sometimes be referred to the head, sometimes to the body. “Thus says the great king, the king [Col. 0339A] of the Assyrians,” that is, the mighty conception of our doctrine: “What is this confidence in which you trust, O Christian people?” For Jews and pagans think that we trust in Christ in vain, and they prefer the conception of their doctrines to the Gospel. The meaning of their error, moreover, is understood as the devil, whom the king of the Assyrians signifies. So too, when it is said that “Satan entered into Judas” (Luke 22:3), we understand that Satan’s thought and malice entered him, not Satan himself essentially.

“What,” he says, “is this confidence which you have recently adopted, so that you do not fear those who kill the body? Or by what counsel or strength do you plan to rebel against me?” For we rebel against the thought of Jews and pagans because, converted to the Gospel, we no longer receive but oppose the carnal [Col. 0339B] interpretation of the Law and the error of idolatry. We do this by the counsel of which it is written: “I, Wisdom, dwell in counsel, and am present with learned thoughts” (Prov. 8:12); and by the strength of which it is said: “I can do all things in him who strengthens me” (Phil. 4:13). But the blind enemy did not know our counsel or strength. Repeating himself, he says: “In whom do you trust, that you have withdrawn from me?” For we have withdrawn from idolatry and from the carnal doctrine of the Pharisees, placing our confidence in Christ. Then Rabshakeh adds, in the voice of Jews and heretics, something which must be referred to our very head.

**VERSE 6.**—“Behold, you trust in this broken staff of reed, in Egypt: if a man leans upon it, it will enter his hand and pierce it. So is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him.”

The Pharisees and heretics, who glory as though in their own religion, derisively call Egypt—that is, paganism—a broken staff of reed, because it shone outwardly but was empty within, and its mental strength, yielding to sins, was broken. If anyone wishing to lean upon it, by use of reason, for good action, were to place the hand of his own activity upon it for support, his action would at once be torn by it and covered with sin as with blood. So Pharaoh king of Egypt acted—that is, such were the pagan sages toward all who committed themselves to them, desiring to live well [Col. 0339D] in their teaching. Yet the Lord also trusted in these, because he made those converted to his faith into preachers. After this Rabshakeh adds in the voice of the pagans:

**VERSE 7.**—“But if you answer me, ‘We trust in the Lord our God’: is he not the one whose high places and altars Hezekiah removed, and who said to Judah and Jerusalem, ‘Before this altar you shall worship’?”

**VERSE 8.**—“And now yield yourself to my lord, the king of the Assyrians, and I will give you two thousand horses; nor will you be able to provide riders for them from among yourselves.”

**VERSE 9.**—“And how will you withstand the face of one judge among the least of my lord’s servants?”

These things are spoken to the people. By high places and altars we understand the teachings and sects of heretics [Col. 0340A], which he calls the Lord’s, because pagans think that heretical preachers are from God. But Hezekiah—that is, Christ—removed these and said to Judah and Jerusalem, that is, to his Church: “Before this altar you shall worship,” that is, in one Catholic faith you shall worship God. By the term horses, however, secular dignities are signified, Solomon saying: “I saw servants on horses, and princes walking on the ground like servants” (Ecclus. 10:7)—that is, sinners elevated in dignities, and the righteous cheapened and despised as though sinners.

In the number one thousand is the complete perfection of numbers. He therefore offers two thousand horses, being ready to give or promise to those who agree with him all worldly glory outwardly and all pride inwardly, [Col. 0340B] just as the king of the Assyrians himself presumptuously said to our King when, blind, he tempted him: “I will give thee all this power and their glory, for they have been delivered to me, and I give them to whom I will. Therefore, if thou wilt worship me, all shall be thine” (Luke 4:6). So in this passage too, the people of the pagans, or any one of their leaders, says to the people of the faithful: “Yield yourself to my lord, the king of the Assyrians”—that is, consent to the worship of idols—“and I will give you two thousand horses,” that is, I will exalt you with every worldly dignity; “nor will you be able to provide riders for them from among yourselves,” that is, you will not find among your own people persons to receive as many honors as I am willing to give.
