But after the blandishments of seduction he adds terror: [Col. 0340C] “How,” he says, “will you withstand the face of one judge,” that is, of any ruler of the pagans, if he comes against you in anger? Thus the powerful of the world formerly spoke to our martyrs. Again Rabshakeh adds, in the voice of Pharisees and heretics, speaking to Christ:

“But if you trust in Egypt, in chariots and horsemen:

**VERSE 10.**—“And now, have I come up against this land without the Lord, to destroy it? The Lord said to me: Go up against this land and destroy it.”

In Egypt, that is, in paganism, Christ trusts; Christ trusts in chariots and horsemen, concerning whom it had been said to him: “Thou shalt ride upon thy horses, and thy chariots are salvation” (Hab. 3:8). His horses are holy preachers; his horsemen are the souls of preachers. The Lord rides upon his horses, as it is written: “Glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 6:20). His chariots are Gospel preachings. Yet the Pharisees say that they have not gone up without the Lord to destroy the land of the Church, because they suppose that they serve the divine will while persecuting preachers of the new faith, as the Lord himself foretold: “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he offers service to God” (John 16:2). Hence the Apostle also bears witness concerning them that “they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. 10:2). This is what he now says: “The Lord said to me: [Col. 0341A] Go up against this land,” that is, against the Church, “and destroy it.” Likewise heretics, because they think themselves to speak for God, assert that they have been sent by God against the Church. It follows:

**VERSE 11.**—“And Eliakim and Shebna and Joah said to Rabshakeh: Speak to thy servants in the Syrian language, for we understand it. Do not speak to us in Jewish in the ears of the people who are upon the wall.”

In the words, “Speak to thy servants,” the humility of the faithful is shown. The Syrian language is the voice of unbelievers; the Jewish language is the voice of believers. Jews and heretics often speak Jewish—that is, they utter the voice of right confession—when they are heard by Catholics, in order that they may deceive more easily. Hence Rabshakeh is told by Shebna on behalf of their nation: “Speak Syrian [Col. 0341B] language,” that is, speak as an unbeliever, speak as a barbarian. “Do not speak Jewish to us,” that is, as though you were a Catholic or one who knew God, lest by this pretence you draw the faithful to yourself. For these are those sitting upon the wall—that is, founded upon Christ, who is a wall to us—as it is written: “Sion, the Savior, is the city of our strength; a wall shall be set in her” (above, 26:1). It follows:

**VERSE 12.**—“And Rabshakeh said to them: Has my lord sent me to your lord and to you, to speak all these words, and not rather to the men who sit upon the wall, that they may eat their own dung and drink the urine of their own feet with you?”

[Col. 0341C] He was by no means sent to your Lord, that is, to Christ, and to these three men, that is, to the rulers of the Church, to speak in the way he speaks; rather, he was sent to the men who sit upon the wall, that is, to the common people in the Church. For deceivers do not seek to address the strong and learned, whose minds can no longer be drawn away, but the weak and unlearned, whom they may easily deceive. But the Apostle (Rom. 10), who had been circumcised on the eighth day, of the race of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; according to the law, a Pharisee; according to zeal, persecuting the Church of God; according to the righteousness which is in the law, living without reproach—because of Christ counted all these things loss and judged them as dung, that he might gain Christ and be found in him, not [Col. 0341D] having his own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through faith in Jesus Christ. These are the dung, and this is the urine trampled under the feet of the faithful, which this Rabshakeh wants them to eat and drink again. For thus it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “Certain men who came down from Judaea taught the brethren that, unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved” (Acts 15:1). And again: “Some of the sect of the Pharisees who had believed rose up, saying that they ought to circumcise them and command them also to keep the law of Moses” (ibid., 5). Hence it is added here:

**VERSE 13.**—“And Rabshakeh stood and cried with a loud voice in Jewish, and said: Hear the words of the great king, the king of the Assyrians.”

[Col. 0342A] **VERSE 14.**—“Thus says the king: Let not Hezekiah deceive you concerning the Lord, for he will not be able to deliver you.”

**VERSE 15.**—“And let not Hezekiah give you confidence in the Lord, saying: The Lord will surely deliver us; this city shall not be given into the hand of the king of the Assyrians.”

Rabshakeh cried in Jewish because certain men of the sect of the Pharisees who had believed taught error. For what is called “in Jewish” here is called “who had believed” there. For those cry in Jewish who pronounce what they say, as though under Christ’s name. Here also this should be noted: Pharisees and heretics are the same, when it is said: “Some of the sect of the Pharisees rose up.” “Hear,” they say, “the words of the great king,” that is, the doctrine of our ample conception. “Let not Hezekiah deceive you, for he will not be able to deliver you”: this is to say, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.” “And let not Hezekiah,” that is, Christ, “give you confidence in the Lord, saying, ‘The Lord will deliver you,’” that is, you will be saved by God’s grace without observance of the Law. “And this city,” that is, the Church, “shall not be given into the hand of the king of the Assyrians,” that is, into the operation of the Pharisees’ carnal understanding. Or the people of the Church will not be given into the hand of the ancient enemy when it departs from this life. It follows:

**VERSE 16.**—“Do not listen to Hezekiah; for thus says the king of the Assyrians: Make a blessing with me, [Col. 0342C] and come out to me; and let every one eat his own fig and every one drink his own vine and the water of his own cistern.”

**VERSE 17.**—“Until I come and take you away to a land which is like your land, a land of grain and wine, a land of bread and vineyards.”

“Make a blessing with me,” he says, that is, communicate with heretics; “and come out to me from the Church, and let every one eat his own vine,” that is, let each perform his own work, which he was accustomed to perform. For our vines are the actions in which we sweat with daily labor. “And let everyone eat his own fig,” that is, let him take up whatever seems good and sweet to himself. “And drink each the water of his own cistern,” that is, his own knowledge, which each of you has stored away among us [Col. 0342D]. “And meanwhile do these things, until I come and, completely separating you from the Church, take you away to a land like your land,” that is, to the congregation of heretics, which is in some way like the Church, where there appears to be grain of inward refreshment, wine of spiritual intoxication, bread of understanding, and a vineyard of right action. For heretics boast that they possess all these things. It follows:

**VERSE 18.**—“Let not Hezekiah trouble you, saying: ‘The Lord will deliver you.’ Have the gods of the nations each delivered its own land from the hand of the king of the Assyrians?”

**VERSE 19.**—“Where is the god of Hamath and Arphad? Where is the god of Sepharvaim? Have they delivered Samaria from my hand?”

[Col. 0343A] **VERSE 20.**—“Which of all the gods of these lands has delivered its land from my hand, that the Lord should deliver Jerusalem from my hand?”

It is the voice of the king of the Assyrians through Rabshakeh, that is, of the ancient enemy through heretics. “Do not,” he says, “let Hezekiah,” that is, Christ, “trouble you by saying, ‘The Lord has delivered you from the wrath to come or from the ancient enemy.’” Equating the Savior’s teaching with that of pagans, he blasphemes with a dog-like mouth: because they were unable to be saved through those teachings, so we too shall be unable to be saved through this one. For what does he call the gods of the pagans except the spiritual conceptions of their individual sects? Whatever each person worships particularly is his god. To the wise of this world, their particular wisdom is god. But the gods of the nations—that is, each pagan’s sect—did not deliver its own [Col. 0343B] land, that is, its own people, from the hand of the king of the Assyrians, that is, the devil, because no one was saved through their teachings.

“Where,” he says, “is the god of Hamath?” and so forth. Hamath is “indignation”; Arphad, “healed” or “healing”; Sepharvaim, “books” or “letters.” There were certain philosophers who, thinking themselves righteous, were indignant with others who acted wrongly and sharply rebuked them; and, while believing themselves healed from the sickness of sins, they claimed also to heal others. They were also devoted to the reading of books and to literary studies. Their conception by which they were indignant with sinners is therefore called the god Hamath, that is, the god of indignation; the conception by which they thought themselves healed and promised salvation to others, the god Arphad, that is, the god of one healed or healing; the understanding [Col. 0343C] which they possessed in secular books, the god Sepharvaim, that is, the god of books and letters. “But where,” he says, “is this conception of indignation and healing, and this conception of letters?”

“Have they delivered Samaria,” that is, the nation of idolaters, “from my hand?” By no means. For pagans cannot be saved through the empty religions of philosophers. Samaria is used for idolaters because there the people of Israel turned to the worship of idols.

“Which,” he says, “of all the gods of these lands has delivered its land from my hand?” Which of all pagan teachings has delivered its followers from eternal death? “That the Lord,” that is, the Lord’s teaching, “should deliver Jerusalem,” that is, the Church, from [Col. 0343D] my hand? For the wicked enemy presumes that, just as he did not cease to seize unbelievers because of the things they worshipped, so he still does not cease to seize believers because of God’s teaching, which they serve. But, with the Lord protecting us, he will not do to us as he did to unbelievers. The proud conception of heretics can also speak these things and presume that, just as it has drawn pagans to itself by turning them as though from religion, so it will seize Catholics too. But after the madness of this Rabshakeh the prophet adds concerning the men sitting upon the wall:

**VERSE 21.**—“And they were silent and did not answer him a word; for the king had commanded, saying: Do not answer him.”

King Christ had commanded the inhabitants of Jerusalem, that is, those who are in the Church, not to answer him, saying through Solomon: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him” (Prov. 26:4). The people are forbidden to answer him because wise persons should answer heretics—those who know how to expose their deceits—not the simple and unlearned, who can be led astray. It follows:

**VERSE 22.**—“And Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph, keeper of the records, went in to Hezekiah with their garments torn, and reported to him the words of Rabshakeh.”

They went in to Hezekiah because in the secrecy of their minds they heard Christ. They reported to him the words of Rabshakeh because, in prayer, they complained to him of the blasphemies of heretics and unbelievers. The garments of preachers, however, are their hearers, who cleave to them in harmonious unity on every side. Thus, in the torn garments of faithful teachers, it is signified that a schism had been made in the people of the faithful through the word of heretics. It follows:

## CHAPTER 37

**VERSE 1.**—“And it came to pass, when King Hezekiah heard it, that he tore his garments, covered himself with sackcloth, and entered the house of the Lord.”

**VERSE 2.**—“And he sent Eliakim, who was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests, covered with sackcloth, to Isaiah son of the prophet Amos.”

King Hezekiah heard the words of his rulers when Christ mercifully heard the prayers of the Church’s rulers [Col. 0344C], which they poured out because of the blasphemies of heretics. Let us therefore see what he did after the prayers were heard. He tore his garments: that is, by a just judgment he allowed those whom he knew would perish to be drawn away from the Church by heretics, and retained those whom he had predestined to life. For the Lord’s garments are his faithful. “For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27). He therefore tore the garments because he separated the elect from the reprobate. The remaining deeds now attributed to Hezekiah must be referred to the people of the elect, who are Christ’s body.

Sackcloth is the garb of penitents. The people of the faithful therefore covered themselves with sackcloth because, amid adversities, they turned to repentance. And it entered the house [Col. 0344D] of the Lord because it entered heaven in mind; pressed by tribulation, it sent Eliakim and Shebna and the elders of the priests—that is, its teachers and rulers—to Isaiah the prophet, that is, to examine the prophetic utterance, in order to inquire what the prophets had thought concerning these afflictions. For Isaiah is shown to signify prophetic Scripture where we read that the Ethiopian eunuch (Acts 8:27 ff.) had come to worship in Jerusalem and was returning, seated in his chariot and reading Isaiah, that is, the book of Isaiah the prophet. Hence Isaiah is interpreted “the salvation of the Lord,” so that he is shown to signify the saving teaching of sacred Scripture. Amos, his father, is called in our language “strong,” “stout,” or “powerful,” if indeed it begins with the letter Aleph and ends in Tsade. But if it begins with *Am* and ends in Nun, it is interpreted “separating a people.” What is signified by this strong and powerful people except the power of the Holy Spirit, who is also rightly called “separating a people,” because he separates the people of possession from the world? Amos is therefore Isaiah’s father because the Holy Spirit is the author of sacred Scripture. It follows:

**VERSE 3.**—“And they said to him: Thus says Hezekiah: This day is a day of tribulation and rebuke and blasphemy; for the children have come to birth, and there was no strength in the woman giving birth.  
[Note: [Col. 0345D] Alternatively: ‘and there is no strength for giving birth.’]”

**VERSE 4.**—“If perhaps the Lord thy God may hear the words of Rabshakeh, whom the king of the Assyrians [Col. 0345B] his lord has sent to blaspheme the living God and to reproach him with words which thy lord has heard: therefore lift up prayer for the remnant which has been found.”

They spoke thus to Isaiah—that is, to the prophetic utterance—not with their words but in their hearts, because they thought this in their hearts while anxiously consulting the sacred Scriptures. “Thus,” they say, “says Hezekiah,” that is, the people of the faithful: “This day is a day of tribulation,” that is, this time is a time of tribulation, because we are now grievously afflicted; “and of rebuke,” because we are rebuked by the Lord; “and of blasphemy,” because God is blasphemed by the wicked; “for the children have come to birth, and there is no strength in the Church that gives birth.” For when the holy Church, through its teachers, considers the conversion or progress of hearers, it carries conception in the womb, as it were. But while, through the obstacles of adverse circumstances, it is not yet permitted to convert those whom it strives to convert or to bring to progress those whom it desires, it is like a woman carrying offspring in her womb, laboring in pain to bring it forth yet unable. Thus it is aptly said: “This day is a day of tribulation and blasphemy and rebuke, for the children have come to birth, and there is no strength in the woman giving birth.” For when enemies of the Church are permitted, by divine judgment, to rage against it with words or swords, then it is less often allowed to give birth by converting anyone, or to strengthen one already converted. Thus the anxious people aptly add:

“If somehow the Lord thy God may hear,” that is, show that he hears, [Col. 0345D] “the words of Rabshakeh,” that is, of Pharisees, heretics, and pagans, whom the king of the Assyrians, their lord—that is, Satan, who rules them—or the proud conception of perverse doctrines, has sent to blaspheme the living God: that is, the Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, who, “having risen from the dead, dies no more” (Rom. 6:9). For this was especially how pagans and Jews formerly mocked us: because we believe in the Crucified One, they call us wretches, confessing the death of our Redeemer but denying his resurrection—and thereby they blaspheme the living God. For they mocked him who was God in the beginning and, near the end of the world, assumed our humanity, in which, having risen, he now lives forever. Or certainly, they blaspheme the living God when they chatter that the Son is less than the Father or speak wrongly about that Trinity which is God.

“Therefore lift up prayer to the Lord for the remnant which has been found”: that is, for those found remaining in the Church, whom heretics have not carried off. But if Isaiah signifies the prophetic utterance, how will the prophetic utterance pray for the remnant of God’s people? This, however, is very easy to discover. For the prophetic Spirit was for God’s people against the blasphemies of enemies who, like this Rabshakeh, thought our God similar to idols, saying: “O God, who shall be like thee? Do not be silent or restrained, O God; for behold, thy enemies have made a noise, and those who hate thee have lifted up their head. They have devised a malicious plan against thy people and plotted against thy holy ones” (Ps. 82:1). Thus the prophetic utterance lifts up prayer for the remnant of the faithful. It follows:

**VERSE 5.**—“And the servants of King Hezekiah came to Isaiah.”

By an artificial order, he recounts below what happened earlier. For they came first and afterwards spoke the words which he has set above. It follows:

**VERSE 6.**—“And Isaiah said to them.”

That is, the utterance of prophecy: “Thus shall you say to your lord,” that is, to the people of the faithful, which is Christ’s body: “Thus says the Lord: Do not fear because of the words [Col. 0346C] which you have heard, by which the servants of the king of the Assyrians have blasphemed me.” This means: “Do not fear the reproaches of men, nor be afraid of their blasphemies.” It follows:

**VERSE 7.**—“Behold, I will give him a spirit, and he will hear a report and return to his own land, and I will make him fall by the sword in his own land.”

This verse will become clear in what follows. It follows:

**VERSE 8.**—“But Rabshakeh returned and found the king of the Assyrians fighting against Libnah; for he had heard that he had departed from Lachish.”

Rabshakeh returned from Jerusalem because Jews, pagans, and heretics will at last cease persecuting the Church; and they will find in Antichrist the devil, their king, fighting against Libnah, that is, against the people of the remnant of Israel. Libnah, which means “white” or “bright,” signifies the life of those faithful Hebrews flourishing in the brightness of righteousness, against whom the devil will fight fiercely. He departed from Lachish because he formerly ceased attacking the Jews once he had subjected them to himself in unbelief. Lachish, which is said to mean “it lies between,” expresses that ancient people of the Jews who, placed in the midst of the nations, cultivated the promised land.

But since by Jerusalem we understand the Church; by Lachish, the people of the Hebrews who preceded the Redeemer’s [Col. 0347A] coming; and by Libnah, those Jews who will believe at the end of the world, it seems necessary to ask why the king of the Assyrians, who is the devil, fights in person against Lachish and Libnah, yet does not himself come to Jerusalem but sends his own agents. The answer is that the ancient enemy, who formerly ruled in the world, is now bound through the victory of the Lord’s cross; but in the times of Antichrist he will again be summoned to more open conflict and will be wholly released against us in his own powers. For John says: “I saw an angel descending from heaven, having the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand; and he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and cast him into the abyss” (Rev. 20:1). And again: “When the thousand years are completed, Satan shall be loosed” (ibid., 7). Therefore he is now held chained, but then he will be loosed. Thus it is clear why he did not come to Jerusalem, though he fought in person against Lachish and Libnah. It follows:

**VERSE 9.**—“And he heard concerning Tirhakah king of Ethiopia, as they said: ‘He has gone out to fight against thee.’”

Tirhakah means “withdrawn”; Ethiopia, “darkness” or “gloom.” What then is expressed by Ethiopia except the error of paganism? For the Apostle says to converted pagans: “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8). What is signified by the king of those [Col. 0347C] shadows, who is called “withdrawn,” except their leaders—that is, philosophers, poets, and powerful men of the world who taught and defended idolatry, and who had withdrawn farther from their Creator? Yet at last they went out from the gloom of their old ignorance to the light of truth, so that, fighting well in the arena of the present life against the king of the Assyrians, who is the devil, they might deserve to receive the eternal crown. Satan, bound in the abyss, heard malignant spirits saying to him concerning these men: “They have gone out to fight against thee.” It follows:

When he heard this, he sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying:

**VERSE 10.**—“Thus shall you say to Hezekiah king of Judah: Let not thy God, in whom thou [Col. 0347D] trustest, deceive thee by saying, ‘Jerusalem shall not be given into the hands of the king of the Assyrians.’”

**VERSE 11.**—“Behold, thou hast heard all that the kings of the Assyrians have done to all lands which they have overthrown; and shalt thou be delivered?”

**VERSE 12.**—“Have the gods of the nations delivered those whom my fathers overthrew—Gozan and Haran and Rezeph, and the sons of Eden who were in Telassar?”

**VERSE 13.**—“Where is the king of Hamath, and the king of Arphad, and the king of the city of Sepharvaim, Ana, and Ava?”

After Satan learned that our religion had increased so greatly that it converted even the leaders and philosophers of the pagans, he added further blasphemers to be sent against the Church, such as Arius and others of that kind. “Thus,” he says, “you shall say [Col. 0348A] to Hezekiah,” that is, to the people of the faithful, who are Christ’s members: “Let not thy God deceive thee,” that is, do not err by believing of God as you believe, in whom you trust—that is, in whose faith you hope to be saved—when you say: “Jerusalem,” that is, the Church, “shall not be given into the hand of the king of the Assyrians,” that is, to the ancient enemy for punishment when it departs from the present world. For heretics attempted to say that it could not be saved in the faith which the Church holds. Or: “Jerusalem shall not be given into the hand of the king of the Assyrians,” that is, the Church will not be subjected to the thought of heretics. Hence they add:

You have heard what the kings of Assyria—that is, the founders of heresies—have done to all lands, that is, to the peoples of all lands whom they overthrew. And can you remain safe from them or be delivered?

[Col. 0348B] Have the gods of the nations—that is, the things the nations worship—delivered those whom my fathers, the heresiarchs, overthrew? And what are these gods of the nations? Gozam, that is, “their strength”; Haram, that is, “splendour”; and Reseph, that is, “swiftness.” For the nations held their strength, beauty, and speed as gods, because they served these things and trusted in them. For whatever each person in error worships is spiritually that person’s god, as is said of the enemies of Christ’s cross: “Their end is destruction; their god is their belly” (Phil. III, 10). Thus too “covetousness is called the service of idols” (Gal. V, 20); for one who sees a woman and lusts after her, lust is that person’s god; for those who trust in their own strength, their strength is their god. For each such person, [Col. 0348C] that which he desires and venerates is his god. Thus Gozam, Haram, and Reseph—that is, their strength, splendour, and swiftness—were gods to the nations, because they gloried in them. Yet these gods did not rescue them from the kings of Assyria, since they were overcome by the heresiarchs and led into their sects as though into religions.

Eden, moreover, means “pleasure,” “delights,” or “adornment”; Thalassar means “a suspended prince” or “suspending a prince.” And who is the suspended prince except the devil, who was suspended on that cross on which he caused the Lord to be hung, as Haman was upon the gallows which he had prepared for Mordecai? (Esth. VII, 10.) Hence the Apostle testifies that Christ “blotted out the handwriting of the decree which was against us, which was contrary to us; and he took it out of the way, fastening it to the cross; stripping principalities and powers, he made a public display of them, triumphing over them in himself” (Col. II, 14).

But if we say that Thalassar means “suspending a prince,” who was it that suspended the Prince except the Gentile people, who, in Pilate’s soldiers, suspended Christ upon the cross? For the soldiers who crucified him were Gentiles. Thalassar, therefore, not inappropriately signifies either the devil or the Gentile people. Whom, then, does he call the sons of Eden—that is, sons of pleasure and delights—who were in Thalassar, except those among the nations who abounded in carnal pleasures and delights? Yet neither did their gods deliver them—that is, the pleasures which they served—because they were overthrown [Col. 0349A] by the heresiarchs, or by the kings of Assyria; that is, they were led into their sects.

Or these matters may be understood thus: You have heard all that the kings of Assyria—that is, evil spirits—did to all lands, that is, to all nations whom they overthrew at the time of death; and can you be delivered from them at the hour of death? It is as though the heretic said: “Just as you have heard that all nations, when they depart from their bodies, are snatched away by unclean spirits to torments, so you too will be snatched away at your departure, because you disdain to follow our sect.” And when he adds, “Have the gods of the nations delivered those whom my fathers overthrew?”—that is, those whom demons plunged into Tartarus—the heretic confesses, not in speech but in deeds, that demons are his fathers. [Note: [Col. 0349] The words from “In this…” through “he says therefore…” are absent in the Garst. codex.] In [Col. 0349B] what he does, he declares himself to be a son of the wicked spirits whom he always imitates. He therefore says: “Have the gods of the nations delivered those whom, at their departure from their bodies, my fathers—namely, the demons—overthrew, that is, cast down into death?”

And who are the gods that did not deliver them? Their spiritual strength, which they thought they possessed in the soul against the softness of vices; the beauty of the religious way of life which they appeared to lead; and the course of upright conduct. Those Gentiles who did not know Christ often seemed to possess all these things. Yet through them they could not be delivered, because “whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. XIV, 23), and “salvation is far from sinners” (Ps. CXVIII, 155). [Col. 0349C] Nor did their gods deliver the sons of Eden—that is, those who appeared to live so religiously that, adorned with virtues, they were thought to be like a paradise of pleasure and a garden of delights. They were in Thalassar, that is, in the Gentile people who suspended Jesus, the Prince of life, upon the cross. For no one could be saved without Christ, because “there is salvation in no one else” (Acts IV, 12).

“Where,” he says, “is the king of Hamath”—that is, the faculty of indignation by which philosophers were indignant at sinners? “And the king of Arphad”—that is, the faculty of healing by which each philosopher wished to heal those held in the sickness of sin? “And the king of the city of Sepharvaim”—that is, the faculty of the strong defence of letters? Ana—that is, [Col. 0349D] “Has this faculty been changed from the wickedness of the world?” It has not been changed from it; rather, Ava means “iniquity,” because the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God. For Ana is interpreted “Has it been changed?” and Ava, “iniquity,” because the understanding of the wise men of the world has not been changed from worldly wickedness, but is iniquity. Yet all these kings or gods of the nations described thus far were unable to deliver their worshippers; and the messengers of the king of Assyria—that is, the heretics—try to establish that likewise our God, that is, the faith which we hold concerning God, will not be able to save us. It follows:

**VERSE 14.**—“And Hezekiah took the letters from the hand of the messengers, [Col. 0350A] and read them; and he went up into the house of the Lord and spread them out before the Lord.”

What Hezekiah is now said to have done must be referred to the pastors of the Church, who are members of Christ. Hezekiah took the letters from the hand of the messengers and read them, because Catholic teachers frequently read books of heretics in order to refute them from their own statements. And he went up into the house of the Lord, because good teachers return from conflict with heretics into the Church. And he spread the letters out before the Lord, because teachers lay bare and make known to God’s people the deceits contained in the books of heretics. It follows:

**VERSE 15.**—“And he prayed to the Lord, saying:”

**VERSE 16.**—“O Lord of hosts, God of Israel, who dwellest above the cherubim, thou alone art God of all the [Col. 0350B] kingdoms of the earth; thou hast made heaven and earth.”

**VERSE 17.**—“Incline, O Lord, thine ear and hear; open thine eyes and see; and hear all the words of Sennacherib, which he has sent to blaspheme the living God.”

**VERSE 18.**—“For truly, O Lord, the kings of Assyria have laid waste the lands and their regions.”

**VERSE 19.**—“And they have given their gods to the fire. For they were not gods, but works of human hands, wood and stone; and they have crushed them.”

**VERSE 20.**—“And now, O Lord our God, save us from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that thou alone art the Lord.”

This prayer belongs principally to the rulers [Col. 0350C] of the Church, but secondarily also to the whole people of the faithful. God is called the Lord of hosts because the armies of angels, fighting for our defence against evil spirits, serve his will, as it is written: “Michael and his angels fought with the dragon” (Apoc. XII, 7). They carry out these battles not by labour but by command.

The order of blessed spirits in which the Lord especially sits is called the throne. Yet because, in the very distinctions of the angelic ranks, the order of the holy cherubim is joined to the order of thrones, he is also said to sit above the cherubim, by virtue of the equality of the neighbouring rank. Cherubim means “fulness of knowledge.” [Col. 0350D] Those higher ranks are called cherubim because they are filled with knowledge more perfectly in proportion as they contemplate God’s brightness more closely, so that, according to the capacity of a creature, they know all things more fully in proportion as by the merit of their dignity they draw near to the vision of their Creator. Or he is said to sit above the cherubim—that is, above the fulness of knowledge—because no knowledge can ever comprehend his sublimity.

He is the God of all kingdoms of the earth, because there is no God besides him, nor is there more than one faith. He is said to incline his ear when, from the immeasurable height of eternity, he lowers his hearing in a certain gracious condescension, so that, mercifully hearing, he fulfils the prayers of his own people—for he hears minds more than tongues. Thus, “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor; thy ear has heard the preparation of their heart” (Ps. X, 16). [Col. 0351A]

He also opens his eyes and sees when, showing the assistance of his grace to his servants, he drives away the evils they suffer, as it is written: “A king sitting on the throne of judgment scatters every evil with his glance” (Prov. XX, 8). For by looking upon the tribulations of the faithful, he scatters them and bestows great benefits of peace and grace. For he is, as it were, not seeing when he permits his own people to be afflicted here.

The kings of Assyria have laid waste lands because the heresiarchs destroyed the vain religions of the nations in order to turn them to their deadly sects as though to a path [Col. 0351B] of truth.

And they gave their gods to the fire because they declared that those who worship such things are worthy of everlasting fire. They were not gods but works of human hands, because the evil which each person especially practised was worshipped by that person as his own god; indeed, as many sins as one was subject to, so many gods one served. By wood may be understood a robust work of sin; by stone, the hardened commission of iniquity. Or when one sins in one’s will, one worships, as it were, a stone. The kings of Assyria gave gods of this kind to the fire, because heretics too affirm that such works deserve the flames of Gehenna.

“And now, O Lord, save us from the hand of this king,” who is the understanding of heretics, lest we be captured by him. “And let all the kingdoms of the earth know that thou alone art [Col. 0351C] Lord”: that is, let the Catholic faith be held throughout the whole world, not the inventions of heretics.

Or the kings of Assyria have laid waste lands because demons have taken piety and the worship of God away from all nations throughout the world. And they gave their gods to the fire because they sent the Gentiles, together with their false religions, into eternal fire. “And now, O Lord, save us from his hand,” that is, from the hand of the ancient enemy, lest he deceive us by surrounding us in temptations, or snatch us away at the time of death. “And let all the kingdoms of the earth know that thou alone art Lord,” whom the Church proclaims, not the one whom heretics devise according to their own judgment. It follows:

**VERSE 21.**—“And Isaiah son of Amoz sent to Hezekiah, saying: Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Concerning [Col. 0351D] the things for which thou hast prayed to me regarding Sennacherib king of the Assyrians.”

**VERSE 22.**—“This is the word which the Lord has spoken concerning him: The virgin daughter of Zion has despised thee and mocked thee; the daughter of Jerusalem has shaken her head after thee.”

Isaiah—that is, the prophetic word—sent teachers to Hezekiah, that is, to the people of the Church, which is Christ’s body, saying: “Thus says the Lord God: Because of your prayers, in which you have asked me concerning the king of Assyria—that is, the devil, or the proud understanding of heretics—hear what I have spoken concerning him.” This king is called Sennacherib, meaning “raising up desolate places,” because, as has already been said, he raises the hearts of unbelievers against us.

[Col. 0352A] In the Lord’s addition, “This is the word which the Lord has spoken concerning him,” it is declared that the Father is one person, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. The Lord spoke concerning him, saying to him: “O king of iniquity, king of Assyria, the daughter of Zion—that is, the Church, whom you thought you would overcome—has despised you.” For Zion, or Jerusalem, is that Church of the blessed which already reigns in heaven; this Church which journeys on earth is her daughter. “For that Jerusalem which is above is free, and she is our mother” (Gal. IV, 26). The daughter of Zion is called [Note: [Col. 0351D] Codex Cruc. has “called.”] a virgin because the faith of the Church cannot be corrupted. For the discourse now concerns the Church of the elect, not the multitude of the reprobate, of whom he said above: “How has the faithful city become a harlot?” (Above, I, 21.)

[Col. 0352B] Therefore the daughter of Zion—that is, the Church of the saints—has despised you, O king of Assyria, as she herself says: “The Lord is my helper, and I shall look in disdain upon my enemies” (Ps. CXVII, 7). She has therefore despised you when raging, mocked you when flattering, and, as you withdrew, shaken her head after you in wonder. For when, after the enemy’s temptation has been overcome, we reflect and say, “Oh, what would I have done if I had yielded to this deceiver’s persuasions?” do we not shake our head after this departing king? To him it is also said:

**VERSE 23.**—“Whom hast thou reproached and blasphemed? Against whom hast thou raised thy voice and lifted up the height of thine eyes? Is it not against the Holy One of Israel?”

**VERSE 24.**—“By the hand of thy servants thou hast reproached [Col. 0352C] the Lord.”

By these words the madness of the ancient enemy is plainly rebuked. But let us hear what he thought when he was violently oppressing the Church. It follows: “And thou hast said: ‘With the multitude of my chariots I have climbed the height of the mountains, the ridges of Lebanon; and I will cut down its lofty cedars and its choice fir trees, and I will enter the height of its summit, its forest of Carmel.

**VERSE 25.**—“I have dug and drunk water, and with the sole of my foot I have dried up all the streams of embankments.”

Just as the Lord’s chariots commonly signify evangelical preachings, so the chariots of the king of Assyria may signify the preachings of heretics. What is expressed by the mountains except those whose manner of life appeared exalted? And what is signified by Lebanon except the holy Church? Lebanon is a mountain of remarkable size, whose trees are fragrant and incorruptible. It signifies the loftiness of the Church which says: “But our citizenship [Col. 0352D] is in heaven” (Phil. III, 20). Its elect give off the fragrance of virtue and are not corrupted by the rot of vices. Thus Lebanon is interpreted “whitening,” to signify the sanctification of the Church which says: “Thou shalt wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. L, 9).

What then is signified by the ridges of Lebanon except the yokes of the Church’s sacred disciplines, beneath which are held the lives [Col. 0353A] of monks and hermits, nuns, and other religious persons? The ancient enemy of the good therefore says: “With the multitude of my chariots I have climbed the height of the mountains and the ridges of Lebanon,” because through the many preachings of heretics he subjected to himself many who stood forth like mountains of God among the faithful people and who appeared to lead a religious life.

Or we may take chariots to mean the pomp and boasting of the world. He therefore ascends the heights of the mountains and the ridges of Lebanon amid the multitude of his chariots because by pride, vain glory, arrogance, self-display, and exaltation, he frequently overcomes some who have already attained the heights [Col. 0353B] of virtue or who live beneath the yoke of discipline.

Cedars surpass the height of all other trees by their tallness; they are of marvellous fragrance and naturally incorruptible. Fir trees too are very lofty, so that by their height they approach the clouds. What, then, are the cedars of Lebanon except those in the Church who are most eminent, whom no decay of earthly love corrupts, who can say: “We are the sweet savour of Christ to God” (II Cor. II, 15)? And what are its choice fir trees except those among them who are outstanding: though they still touch the earth bodily, yet, making great progress in the power of contemplation, they already raise the summit of their mind near the heavens?

Our adversary therefore boasts that he will cut down from [Col. 0353C] the Church the cedars of Lebanon and its choice fir trees, because he presumes that he can cast down the Church’s highest and chosen men, especially in times of persecution, of which the present passage speaks. He also says that he will enter the height of Lebanon’s summit because he strives to enter the pure mind of the elect within the Church, or whatever most excels among the saints.

Carmel, as has been said above, means “knowledge of circumcision.” The faithful know what the Church’s knowledge of circumcision is: “For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter; whose praise is not from men but from God” (Rom. II, 28). The forest of this Carmel—that is, of the knowledge [Col. 0353D] of circumcision—is the way of life of the saints, quiet from every tumult of carnal desires and free from every disturbance of evil action. The ancient enemy boasts that he will enter the forest of the Church’s Carmel—that is, the secret and free manner of life of the elect, who know always to circumcise themselves spiritually from every vicious excess—seeking some entrance by which to enter and defile it.

He especially attempted to do all these things when, through heretics, he fiercely attacked the Church. Hence he added: “I have dug and drunk water.” One digs for water who seeks knowledge by profound investigation; and having found it, drinks it when one satisfies oneself with the draught of the knowledge discovered. Satan therefore dug in order to find water because, searching out the teachings of heretics, he found them; and he drank what he found because he fulfilled the desire of his malice with their doctrines, causing many through them to err according to his own will.

The streams of embankments are those which are artificially conducted through ditches [Col. 0354A] to places where they did not naturally go. What is signified by the streams of embankments except spiritual gifts flowing in those hearts from which earthly thoughts have been expelled? The devil therefore says, “With the sole of my foot I dried up all the streams of embankments,” because, while through heretics he impressed the footprint of iniquity upon human hearts, he excluded from them every gift of spiritual grace. For wherever he fixes his foot, he immediately diverts from there the course of the spiritual stream. These things, as we have said, the ancient enemy spoke in his heart while fiercely oppressing the Church, boasting that he had already prevailed. The Lord responds to him, adding:

**VERSE 26.**—“Hast thou not heard what I have done to it of old?”

Understand “to Lebanon” or “to the daughter of Zion,” that is, to the Church. He explains and adds: “From ancient days”—that is, from the beginning of creatures—“I formed,” that is, by predestining I fashioned and ordained, “that [Col. 0354B] thing” which I was to do for the testing of the Church; “and now,” through your savagery, “I have brought it” into action. For it has been determined how much either the whole Church or each individual elect person is to be worn down by present evils. Hence Paul says: “I shall fulfil in my flesh those things which are lacking of the sufferings of Christ” (Col. I, 24). It follows:

“And it has come to pass for the uprooting of embattled hills and fortified cities.”

**VERSE 27.**—“Their inhabitants, with shortened hand, trembled and were confounded; they became like the grass of the field, and the herbage of the pasture, and the vegetation of the roofs, which withered before it ripened.”

The evil of adversity which I brought has resulted in the uprooting of embattled hills and fortified cities, because the king of Assyria went up against all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them. For the embattled hills—that is, the proud leaders of the Jews persecuting the Lord—were uprooted from the land of the living; as were the fortified cities, that is, the minds of the other Jews [Col. 0354C] closed against his teaching.

Or, to speak of those who appeared to be ours: embattled hills were uprooted because some who had already grown in virtues, but were not “eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. IV, 3), were drawn away from the Church by heretics or Gentiles in the time of persecution. And fortified cities—that is, the defences and heights of hearts lifting themselves up against the knowledge of God—were likewise torn from the Church. For those who had fortified their hearts against the word of preaching were easily uprooted by persecutors.

The inhabitants of such cities, while they walked along the broad way of the world, stretched out their hands far to do [Col. 0355A] whatever they wished. But when the straitness of persecution came, their hand was shortened, because they were able only slightly to fulfil their will; and with shortened hand they trembled, because they feared to suffer adversities. For they would not heed that command: “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matt. X, 28). Thus, fearing torments, they lost the faith, and having lost faith, they were confounded.

And they became like the grass of the field—that is, wholly carnal—because “all flesh is grass, and like the herbage of the pasture” (Isa. XL, 6); because they were given as fodder to herds of every animal, that is, to the crowds of vices. And they became like vegetation on roofs which withered before it ripened, because they lost the verdure of righteousness before the end of their present life. For roof vegetation grows high up, but is not established by a rich root; so the vain Christian is sometimes seen to undertake lofty things, yet is not strengthened in them by purity of heart. That vegetation indeed withers even before it ripens, because the pseudo-religious person, even before reaching the end of this life, already loses works of holiness, as it were the appearance of greenness. It follows:

**VERSE 28.**—“I have known thy dwelling-place, thy going out and thy coming in, and thy madness against me.”

I have known your dwelling-place in your land, O king of Assyria—that is, in the minds of unbelievers; and your departure from there, when you who lay hidden proceeded to works of wickedness; [Col. 0355C] and your entry here with your followers for the persecution of the saints; and your madness, when through the mouths of blaspheming heretics and Gentiles you raged against me. Hence it is added:

**VERSE 29.**—“When thou didst rage against me, thy pride ascended into my ears.”

This is clear. It follows:

“I will therefore put a ring in thy nostrils and a bridle in thy lips, and I will lead thee back by the way through which thou camest.”

Just as nostrils signify snares, so the ring signifies the omnipotence of divine power. When this prevents us from being seized by temptations, it holds the snares of the ancient enemy enclosed in wonderful arrangements. A ring is thus put in his nostrils when the strength of heavenly protection, drawn round him, restrains his craftiness, lest he prevail against human weakness to the full extent [Col. 0355D] that he secretly explores devices of destruction.

The name “ring” may also signify the assistance of hidden judgment, which is placed in this enemy’s nostrils when he is restrained from his cunning cruelty. Therefore, because he is now prevented from harming the faithful, it is well said to him, “I will put a ring in thy nostrils,” as though he openly said: “You breathe out schemes as you devise snares, but because you cannot carry out what you desire, you bear the ring of my omnipotence in your nostrils; so that, when you pant more fiercely for the death of the good, you return empty-handed from their life.”

A bridle is likewise put in his lips when he is so restrained by the power of divine might that he can rage only insofar as he is permitted. Restrained by that power, he was led back by the way through which he had come, because he had come from the hearts of unbelievers against the Church, and was forced to return from persecution of the Church to the hearts of unbelievers and wicked persons, there to lie hidden until the coming of Antichrist. Thus the Lord answered the ancient adversary, who had boasted that he had already climbed the ridges of Lebanon and would cut down its lofty cedars. After this he speaks to Hezekiah—that is, to the Lord Jesus—saying:

**VERSE 30.**—“And this shall be a sign to thee: [Col. 0356B] Eat this year what grows of itself; and in the second year eat fruits; but in the third year sow and reap, plant vineyards, and eat their fruit.”

The designation of three years commonly signifies three periods: the first before the Law, the second under the Law, and the third under grace. Hence in the Gospel the master of the house says: “Behold, for three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none” (Luke XIII, 7). For the master of the house came to his fig tree seeking fruit in the third year because the Lord came to the Jewish people seeking in it the fruit of righteousness through the patriarchs, the prophets, and himself, but did not find it.

[Col. 0356C] Thus of these three years it is here said: “Eat this year”—that is, before the Law—“what grows of itself,” that is, good works which each person does voluntarily without the compulsion of the Law; “and in the second year”—that is, under the Law—“eat fruits,” that is, the sweet fruits of trees, namely the good deeds of righteous people.

Yet it especially belongs to domestic trees to bear fruit. And what are domestic trees except the Jews, once citizens and members of God’s household? Therefore, in the second year the Lord made use of fruits because in the time of the Law he delighted in the good works of the Hebrews. Nor is this interpretation contradicted by the fact that no fruit was found on the fig tree, because here the Lord speaks only of the elect, whereas there he complains of the fruitless reprobate.

“But in the third year”—that is, in the time of grace—the apostles are commanded to sow and reap, that is, to preach the words of life and gather those who believe; and to plant vineyards and eat their fruit, that is, to found churches and be satisfied with their good manner of life.

Thus a sign is given to Hezekiah that Jerusalem shall not be captured by the king of Assyria: namely, that in the first year he eats what grows of itself, in the second he eats fruits, and in the third they sow and reap. For the Church’s salvation is made sure in our Redeemer through this: that he is fed by the good fruits of the elect before the Law, under the time of the Law, and under [Col. 0357A] grace. For that person makes his salvation sure before God who perseveringly devotes himself to good works. It follows:

**VERSE 31.**—“And that which has been saved of the house of Judah, and that which remains, shall send down roots and bear fruit upward,”

**VERSE 32.**—“For a remnant shall go forth from Jerusalem, and salvation from Mount Zion.”

That which has been saved from Assyria out of the house of Judah—that is, from the people of confessors—and that which remains, namely the remnant in the Church which heretics or Gentiles have not taken away, shall send the root of good thought downward and bear the fruit of works upward. To send a root downward is to multiply good thought in hidden places; to bear fruit upward is to display in the effectiveness of upright action what has been thought. Thought is rightly signified by a hidden root, because from what is not seen within springs forth what is seen outside. Thus he says: “It shall send down roots and bear fruit upward.” As though he openly said: “Thought shall arise in the depths, so that recompense may be granted on high.”

For a remnant shall go forth from Jerusalem: that is, the Church shall not now be destroyed, as the enemy supposed; rather, the children who shall be born and arise shall recount the Lord’s praises to their children. And salvation shall go forth from Mount Zion—that is, from the Church’s loftiness—to all the nations of the world, so that in proportion as the Church of the righteous is now constrained, it may then be enlarged. It follows:

“The zeal of the Lord of hosts shall accomplish this.” The zeal [Col. 0357C] of the Lord is the affection of his loving goodness, by which he guards the chastity of our souls, lest our minds be corrupted either by the deceits of heretics or by the craftiness of the ancient serpent, and fall away from the simplicity that is in Christ Jesus. This zeal therefore shall accomplish what has been said: that what has been saved from the house of Judah shall send down root and bear fruit, and that a remnant shall go forth from Jerusalem and salvation from Mount Zion. It follows:

**VERSE 33.**—“Therefore thus says the Lord concerning the king of Assyria: He shall not enter this city, nor cast an arrow there; nor shall he take it with a shield, nor cast up an embankment around it.”

**VERSE 34.**—“By the way by which he came, by that way shall he return; and he shall not enter this city, says the Lord.”

**VERSE 35.**—“And I will protect this city, to save it for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant.”

The king of Assyria, who seeks to corrupt the minds of the faithful, shall not enter the city of the Church—that is, the heart of the elect—because the Lord’s zeal guards it. Nor shall he cast an arrow there, because, as soon as vices strike at the minds of the righteous, they rebound rejected and do not penetrate within. For each elect person fears the darts of the ancient enemy less in proportion as he strongly arms his breast against their onset. Nor shall the shield of the attacking enemy take it, because the ancient persecutor of the Church will not be able so to protect himself against the arms of the faithful as to conquer her; rather, struck, he will fall backward.

[Col. 0358A] Nor shall he cast up an embankment around it, because the minds of those whose citizenship is in heaven are not enclosed by a heap of earth—that is, they are not held entangled in earthly things. For the enemy casts up an embankment around the person whose mind, seized in love of the world, he constricts, afflicts, and tempts on every side through earthly things, so that one thus besieged can no longer find a way of escape into freedom. Therefore he does not cast up an embankment around our city; but, driven back by God, he returns by the way through which he came, because he returns to the hiding places in the minds of the wicked, from which he bursts out against us.

And he shall not enter this city because his malice is not received in the hearts of the saints. And amid the dangers of temptations the Lord protects this city—that is, the Church—so that he may save it forever for his own sake and for the sake of David his servant, that is, for Christ’s sake, “who, taking the form of a servant, became obedient unto death” (Phil. II, 7). Christ is called David and servant of the Lord, as the Lord himself says elsewhere: “I have found David my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 21). And a little later he adds: “He shall call upon me: Thou art my Father, my God, and the defender of my salvation. And I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth” (ibid., 27). Christ, therefore, as we have said, is called David. Hence David means “beloved” [Col. 0358C] or “strong of hand.” For Christ is the Beloved One, of whom Haggai says: “The Desired One of all nations shall come” (Hag. II, 8). And he is strong of hand, he who bound the strong adversary, as it is written: “When a strong man armed guards his courtyard, all that he possesses is in peace; but when one stronger than he comes upon him and overcomes him, he takes away all his weapons in which he trusted and distributes his spoils” (Luke XI, 21). After the Lord’s words, the prophetic narrative adds:

**VERSE 36.**—“And the Angel of the Lord went forth and struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians. And they rose in the morning, and behold, all were dead bodies.”

[Col. 0358D] But, to investigate the mystery: what is signified by the thousand except the totality of all the reprobate? For no number proceeds beyond a thousand. And what is understood by the hundred except the completion of the present life? Hence it is written: “The child shall die a hundred years old, and the sinner a hundred years old shall be accursed” (Isa. LXV, 20). What, then, is figured by eighty except the day of judgment, which is frequently called the eighth in Scripture? And what is expressed by five except the carnality of those who are devoted to the five bodily senses? What is signified by the Angel who struck them except the sentence of the Judge? They were struck at night because “the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night” (I Thess. V, 2).

[Col. 0359A] The Angel of the Lord therefore went forth and struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians, because the divinely sent sentence strikes, at the completion of this life and on the day of judgment, the multitude of all the reprobate who served the devil and lived according to the five bodily senses—that is, carnally. Morning signifies the time of resurrection, as the Church of the elect says to the Lord: “In the morning I shall stand before thee and see” (Ps. V, 5).

What, then, is expressed by the dead bodies except the bodies of the reprobate, which will in no way be changed to incorruptibility and impassibility like those of the elect? Hence this prophet says concerning the righteous: “They shall see the dead bodies of those who have transgressed against me” (Isa. LXVI, 24), that is, the bodies of those who sinned. Thus those who had been struck rose in the morning, because on that day all the reprobate are awakened from the sleep of their death. And behold, all were found to be dead bodies, because they will again possess flesh that is burdened and capable of suffering, though immortal. It follows:

**VERSE 37.**—“And the king of Assyria departed, went away, returned, and dwelt in Nineveh.”

The king of Assyria—that is, Satan—departed from the regions of the faithful, returned to the unbelievers, and dwelt in Nineveh—that is, in the minds of the reprobate, which rejoice in present things and seem beautiful to themselves in their pleasures. For Nineveh means “festive,” “beautiful,” or “shoot of beauty.” It follows:

[Col. 0359C] **VERSE 38.**—“And it came to pass, when he was worshipping in the temple of Nesroch his god, that Adrammelech and Sarasar, his sons, struck him with the sword; and they fled into the land of Ararat, and Asarhaddon his son reigned in his place.”

Just as it is said to the elect: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. 3:17), so all the reprobate are the temple of Satan. Nesroch, moreover, means “tender temptation” or “soft temptation.” The evil to which anyone is spiritually enslaved is, as we have said, as it were his own god. Therefore the devil worships tender temptation as a god, because he takes great delight in having his suggestion accepted as soon as it strikes the mind. Thus the ancient enemy worships his god, called tender temptation, in his temple—that is, in the heart of the reprobate [Col. 0359D]—because, as soon as his soft and tender temptation arises in the minds of the wicked, those perverse persons prostrate themselves before it, ready to obey it. For what is done in the hearts of the reprobate at Satan’s instigation is said to be done by Satan himself; just as, conversely, it is written of the Holy Spirit: “He intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings” (Rom. 8:26), because he makes those whom he has filled both pray and groan. Whether, then, the devil himself, the head of evils, or those who are his members, are said to worship tender temptation, this is because Satan highly venerates it and the reprobate willingly subject themselves to it. In contrast, it was said to that same enemy concerning the Church of the elect that “she shall crush your head” (Gen. 3:15). For the head of the ancient serpent [Col. 0360A]—that is, tender temptation—is crushed by the one who tramples down and brings to nothing the beginning of a wicked suggestion.

Adramelech means “the king’s robe” or “the king’s adornment,” and Sarasar means “prince of tribulation.” He is the robe or adornment of the king of the Assyrians who presents himself to Satan as clothing or glory. The prince of tribulation is one who, endowed with worldly power, inflicts evils upon the saints. Such persons are sons of the king of the Assyrians, worthy to hear: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8:44). Yet very often such persons are converted to God and even become preachers of the truth; and they pursue the ancient enemy all the more strongly and fiercely because they had formerly been accustomed to cling to him more intimately, not now as servants, but as sons. Hence they are now described as having struck him with the sword of preaching [Col. 0360B], just as it was said to him through Ezekiel under the designation of the prince of Tyre: “Behold, I will bring upon you foreigners, the most powerful of the nations; and they shall draw their swords against the beauty of your wisdom and defile your splendor. They shall kill you and cast you down, and you shall die the death of the uncircumcised in the heart of the sea” (Ezek. 28:7). For what the same prophet says a little earlier to the same prince is plainly said of the devil: “You are the seal of likeness,” and so forth.

Those, therefore, whom Isaiah calls Adramelech and Sarasar—that is, the king’s adornment and the prince of tribulation, sons of the king of the Assyrians—Ezekiel calls foreigners, the most powerful of the nations. For those who are sons of the king of the Assyrians, that is, of the devil, must necessarily be strangers to God [Col. 0360C]. And what Isaiah relates mystically, that they struck him with a sword, is foretold through Ezekiel: “They shall draw their swords against the beauty of your wisdom, and they shall defile your splendor, kill you, and cast you down.” The Apostle teaches what sword it is by which this king dies, saying: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. 6:17). Gentiles of this kind drew swords against the beauty of the devil’s wisdom because, by preaching the truth, they destroyed ancient errors. They defiled his splendor because they showed how defiled he is. They killed him because they extinguished his malice from the hearts of those who were converted. Moreover, what Isaiah narrates, that he was struck in his temple [Col. 0360D], is what Ezekiel foretold: “You shall die the death of the uncircumcised in the heart of the sea” (Ezek. 28:8). For the heart of the sea—that is, the mind of worldly people—is his temple, where he is in a sense slain in the death of the uncircumcised when sinners are converted. The death of the uncircumcised is indeed the conversion of sinners. Thus, while the king of the Assyrians was causing his god, tender temptation, to be worshipped in the temple of Nesroch—that is, while he was causing his tender suggestion to be worshipped in the hearts of the perverse throughout the world—many of those formerly close to him were converted; becoming preachers of truth, they struck his wickedness in the hearts of their neighbors with the sword of God’s word.

[Col. 0361A] “And they fled into the land of Ararat.” Ararat is Armenia itself. Its name is interpreted “a plucked mountain” or “a bound mountain.” What is signified by the mountain except that same proud enemy, to whom it is said through Jeremiah: “Behold, I am against you, pestiferous mountain, you who corrupt the whole earth” (Jer. 51:25)? He has been plucked from the place where he stood—that is, drawn out of human hearts—as the Lord himself foretold: “Now the ruler of this world shall be cast out” (John 12:31); and he has been bound, as the Lord again says: “How can anyone enter the house of a strong man and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man?” (Matt. 12:29).

What, then, is the land of the plucked or bound mountain, except the converted Gentile world, which the ancient enemy formerly possessed [Col. 0361B], but from which he has now been torn away and bound through Christ? Thus those who struck this king, fearing eternal punishments, fled into the land of Ararat—that is, into the Church converted from the Gentiles—in order that they might be saved there. For one flees who desires to escape the evils of this world, so as to be secure from the wrath to come. The death of this king is the extinction of unbelief and error throughout the world, and the fullness of faith.

Yet although this king is dead—that is, although paganism with its errors has been extinguished and Christianity has succeeded everywhere—the son of this king nevertheless still reigns in his place, because every tyrant has not ceased to exercise power in this world. For he is a son of the king of the Assyrians who imitates the devil’s tyranny. This son [Col. 0361C], therefore, who reigns in his father’s place, signifies tyrants who still rule in the world. Hence he is given the name Asarhaddon, which means “conquering” or “sharpened,” because one who is sharper in cruelty, so as to cut down everything like a sword, and who has conquered others, will be able to obtain dominion in the world, which lies wholly in the power of evil. It follows:

## Chapter XXXVIII

**Verse 1.**—“In those days Hezekiah was sick unto death.”

Hezekiah—that is, our Redeemer—was sick, because it is written: “He took our infirmities and bore our sicknesses” (Matt. 8:17). For him, to be sick was to assume the weakness of flesh [Col. 0361D], in which he hungered, labored, and grew weary. And he was sick unto death because he bore mortal flesh until, through death and resurrection, he came to immortality. It follows:

“And Isaiah the prophet, son of Amos, came to him and said: Thus says the Lord: Set your house in order, for you shall die, and not live.” We have already said what Isaiah, son of Amos, signifies: the prophetic word. This word remained outside while it was understood carnally and had not yet been fulfilled in Christ. But it entered into him when it began to be fulfilled in him and understood spiritually concerning him. Having entered, it says: “Set your house in order, for you shall die.” But what prophetic word said such things to the Lord? Surely that history which relates that Joshua [Col. 0362A] (ch. 23:2), when about to die, summoned the elders of the children of Israel and earnestly exhorted and instructed them concerning what they ought to do after his death: namely, that they should love the Lord their God, cling to him, and diligently keep his law. For then it was prefigured that Jesus, about to pass from this world to the Father, would carefully instruct the apostles and arrange each matter for his house, which is the assembly of disciples. Therefore, being about to die, he set his house in order in that notable discourse which he spoke to the disciples after supper, or during supper. But when it says, “For you shall die and not live,” it does not at all deny the glory of the resurrection, soon to come; rather, it means that the Savior would no longer live as a mortal, but, having conquered death, would attain the glory of immortality [Col. 0362B]. It follows:

**Verse 2.**—“And Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall and prayed to the Lord.”

By the face is expressed the mind’s intention; by the wall, the barrier of sin which separates us from God, as it is written: “Your iniquities have divided between you and your God” (Isa. 59:2). Thus Ezekiel says concerning the sinner whose evil works flatterers praise: “He was building a wall, but they were plastering it” (Ezek. 13:10). He builds a wall who sins; and those plaster the wall once built who, praising an evil already committed, turn it into a good. Thus Hezekiah, given over to death, turned his face toward the wall because our Savior, in his passion, turned his attention toward our sin, he who suffered for the sin of the world [Col. 0362C]. And he prayed to the Lord because, as Luke says: “Kneeling down, he prayed, saying: Father, if you will, remove this cup from me. And being in agony, he prayed more earnestly” (Luke 22:41). It follows:

**Verse 3.**—“And he said: I beseech you, Lord, remember, I pray, how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done what is good in your sight.”

As if he said: “I have glorified you upon earth; I have finished the work which you gave me to do; and now, Father, glorify me with yourself” (John 17:4). It follows: “And Hezekiah wept with a great weeping,” because the Savior “began to be sorrowful and distressed [Col. 0362D] and said: My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Mark 14:34). It follows:

**Verse 4.**—“And the word of the Lord came to Isaiah, saying:

**Verse 5.**—‘Go and say to Hezekiah: Thus says the Lord God of David your father: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears.’”

The word of the Lord came to Isaiah—that is, the Lord commanded the prophetic word, saying, “Go and say to Hezekiah”; that is, he caused it to be understood as speaking of Christ in what follows. For what is it to say “Go” to the prophetic word except to advance prophecies toward a spiritual understanding? Therefore he said to the prophet that he should go and tell our Hezekiah that the Lord says: “I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears,” when I caused it to be understood of Christ that which is written concerning Solomon: when he had prayed at the dedication of the temple, it was divinely said to him [Col. 0363A]: “I have heard your prayer and your supplication which you have made before me. I have sanctified this house which you built, to put my name there forever; and my eyes and my heart shall be there always” (1 Kings 9:3). For Solomon is Christ, and Solomon’s house is the Church, for which the Lord prayed, saying to his disciples: “Holy Father, keep those whom you have given me” (John 17:11); and again: “I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from evil” (ibid., v. 15); and again: “I ask not for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that they may all be one” [Col. 0363B] (ibid., v. 20).

Therefore, for the reason stated, the Lord commanded the prophet to say to Christ praying for us: “Thus says the Lord God of David your father: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears.” Since this Christ was made from David’s seed according to the flesh, he is called the son of David, as the Evangelist says: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David” (Matt. 1:1). The Lord heard his prayer and saw his tears, as the Apostle also says of him: “In the days of his flesh, offering prayers and supplications with loud cries and tears to him who was able to save him from death, he was heard because of his reverence” (Heb. 5:7). Whether, therefore, the Lord Jesus prayed for himself or for the Church [Col. 0363C], the Father heard his prayer and saw his tears. It follows:

“Behold, I will add fifteen years to your days.”

**Verse 6.**—“And I will deliver you and this city from the hand of the king of the Assyrians, and I will protect it.”

According to the historical sense, it must first be noted that it is fixed for every human being how long he is to live temporally in this mortal life. For even though almighty God here added fifteen years to King Hezekiah’s life when he allowed him to die, he then foreknew that he would die. This raises the question: how can it be said to him through the prophet, “Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live,” when, as soon as the sentence of death was pronounced, life was added in response to his tears? But he says through the prophet at the time when Hezekiah deserved to die; through the bounty of mercy, however, he postponed his death until that time which he himself had foreknown before the ages. The prophet, therefore, is not deceptive, because he made known the time of death at which the man deserved to die; nor were the divine decrees overturned, because the increase in his years of life by God’s bounty was likewise fixed before the ages, and the span of life unexpectedly added outwardly was inwardly established without any increase in foreknowledge [Col. 0363D].

But having said this briefly according to the historical sense, let us seek the mystery. The number fifteen, because it consists of seven and eight, contains some heavenly or spiritual mystery: either the life which now is and that which is to come; or the Old and New Testaments; or the Sabbath-rest of souls in the future and the resurrection of the flesh; or certainly something else. Therefore fifteen years are added to the Lord after his passion because from his death arises the life of the Church, which both has the hope of rest after death and, at the end, of resurrection; and therefore now keeps in its life the commandments of both Testaments. Fifteen years are added to the Lord because from his temporal death have been given to us the present life of souls and the future life of bodies, while the knowledge of both Testaments has been revealed and every rule for living and hoping shown.

The Lord, too, is delivered from the hand of the king of the Assyrians—that is, the ancient enemy—as he prays in the Psalm, saying [Col. 0364B]: “Save me from the lion’s mouth” (Ps. 21:22). And his city, that is, the Church, is delivered together with him, because Satan’s power is driven from the human race through the Savior’s death. Amid the dangers of temptations, moreover, this city is always protected by the Lord. Thereafter, wishing to confirm his promise, God says:

**Verse 7.**—“And this shall be the sign to you from the Lord that the Lord will perform this word which he has spoken.

**Verse 8.**—‘Behold, I will cause the shadow of the lines, by which it had gone down on the sundial of Ahaz, to go backward ten lines in the sun.’”

To the Lord’s words the prophet adds: “And the sun returned ten lines by the steps which it had gone down.”

[Col. 0364C] Here it must be considered, according to the truth of the history, that since a day normally has twelve hours, this day, on which the sun returned ten lines, is proved to have had thirty-two hours. For the sun had already completed ten hours when it began to return; it completed another ten as it returned to the east; then, coming again from the east as far as the point from which it had begun to return, it spent ten more hours; and after completing the day as far as sunset, it added two further hours. Thus, as we have said, it became a day of thirty-two hours—that is, four hours short of completing the duration customarily filled by three days.

[Col. 0364D] At this point it may trouble the mind that holy Scripture elsewhere reports that, at Joshua’s word, the sun stood in the midst of heaven and did not hasten to set for the space of one day; and immediately adds: “For there was no day so long before or afterward, when the Lord obeyed the voice of a man and fought for Israel” (Josh. 10:14). For when it is said that the sun did not hasten to set for the space of one day, it is made clear that that day lasted the span of two days, as Jesus son of Sirach also plainly declares: “By his wrath the sun was held back, and one day was made as though two” (Ecclus. 46:5).

Therefore, since this day under Hezekiah had eight more hours than the one on which holy Joshua caused the sun to stand still, why is it said there that “there was no day so long before or afterward” [Col. 0365A]? For this one was much longer. But he who wrote the book of Joshua is understood to have lived before Hezekiah and to have borne witness concerning events which he knew as past. Thus when he says, “There was no day so long before or afterward,” we understand this of the time from the world’s beginning to Joshua’s time, and from Joshua’s time to the writer of that history, or to the time at which it was written. Therefore he does not contradict Isaiah, who introduces a longer day later, because when he said, “There was no day so long before or afterward,” he did not add, “nor will there be.” Had he added that, he would indeed appear wholly contrary to Isaiah.

Having thus completed the historical exposition, let us endeavor, with the Lord opening the way, to discern the spiritual meaning. “Behold,” he says, “I will cause the shadow of the lines to go backward,” and so forth. What is expressed by the ten lines of the sundial, that is, the ten hours, except the Decalogue of the Law? Hence, in order that our Redeemer might be shown to be a teacher of the Law, John’s disciples said to him at about the tenth hour: “Rabbi,” which is interpreted “teacher” (John 1:38). What is signified by the shadow of the lines except the overshadowing and veiling of the Old Testament? What is signified by the sundial, on which there are twelve lines, except the Old Testament, in which are the most upright precepts of life and which speaks of all times as of individual hours, either by weaving history or by prophesying? And what is signified by Ahaz, the maker of the sundial, except the writers of that Testament? Hence Ahaz is interpreted “continent,” to signify the religious continence of the prophets [Col. 0365C]. What is signified by the sun except understanding? Hence the ungodly are reported as saying: “The sun of understanding has not risen upon us” (Wis. 5:6).

The sun therefore returned ten lines in the sundial by the steps which it had gone down, because the understanding of the divine Law, which through Pharisaic traditions had already been approaching its end, was brought back to the intention which Moses and the prophets had at the beginning. For the sun to return where it had come from is for the understanding of the Scriptures to return to its original state, so that they may be understood by us as they were understood by Moses and the prophets, not according to the carnal interpretation of the Pharisees, for whom the sun of understanding had already set and the night of ignorance had covered their minds [Col. 0365D]. For the sun had gone down through the ten lines of the sundial and had left its shadow upon them, because the understanding of the Decalogue had declined through the Jews and the shadow of the letter had covered the Decalogue itself for them. But now the shadow has been driven back ten lines by the sun, because the obscuring of the Decalogue—that is, of the Old Testament—has been repelled through spiritual understanding.
