Thus, the fact that the shadow of the lines returns backward ten lines in the sundial, by which it had descended while following the sun, is a sign to Hezekiah that the Lord will add fifteen years to his days and deliver him and his city from the hand of the king of the Assyrians. For, in the fact that the mysteries of the Law are revealed in the Lord’s passion [Col. 0366A], it is clearly indicated that the Church will rise again from his death and that the ruler of this world has nothing in him, but that through him all who believe will be saved. For this is an evident sign of our salvation: that the spiritual understanding of the Law is opened to us, so that we may fulfill spiritually what the Jews could not fulfill carnally. And Jesus is declared to be the Son of God because, in his death, the Law’s obscurity is removed. Hence the veil of the temple is described as having been torn (Matt. 27:51), and the centurion as having said that this man truly was the Son of God (ibid., v. 54). It follows:

**Verse 9.**—“The writing of Hezekiah king of Judah, when he had been sick and had recovered from his sickness.”

**Verse 10.**—“I said: In the middle of my days [Col. 0366B] I shall go to the gates of hell; I sought the remainder of my years.”

**Verse 11.**—“I said: I shall not see the Lord God in the land of the living; I shall see man no more, nor the inhabitant of rest,” and so forth.

Hezekiah is king of Judah—that is, our Savior is king of confession—because “if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you shall be saved” (Rom. 10:9). He is king of Judah, that is, of confession, “so that every tongue may confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:11). For, that he might openly be shown to be king of Judah, they placed above his head on the cross the written charge: “This is Jesus of Nazareth, king of the Jews” (Matt. 27:38). For him, to be sick [Col. 0366C] was to assume the weakness of our mortality; and to recover from his sickness was to attain the glory of resurrection.

The writing which Hezekiah gave when he had been sick and had recovered signifies the Scripture which the Lord established through the Evangelists and apostles after his resurrection. Since he is the head of the Church, he begins to speak in the voice of his body, saying: “I formerly, before grace came, said: In the middle of my days I shall go to the gates of hell”—that is, from the beginning of the world until the passion of the Redeemer, when I depart from this life, I shall descend into hell. For then all descended there.

It should be noted that he does not say, “I shall go to the depths of hell,” but “I shall go to the gates of hell,” because the righteous who descended there were held in the upper regions without torment, whereas sinners were punished in the lower regions [Col. 0366D]. But because the Church was to remain from the Lord’s passion until the end of the age, he adds:

“I sought the remainder of my years”—that is, I asked that the span of my time remaining until the end of the world should be granted to me. This is what is elsewhere said in the voice of the Church: “Do not call me back in the middle of my days” (Ps. 101:25), that is, do not bring me to an end until I have completed all my days in the consummation of the age. And because the Lord assumed the nature of our humanity, he says in the voice of the human race descending into hell without hope: “I said: I shall not see the Lord God in the land of the living” [Col. 0367A], that is, in the heavenly homeland, because “I shall go and not return to a land of darkness and covered with the gloom of death” (Job 10:21).

“I shall see man no more,” when I have been sent into outer darkness, because I shall be blinded by the night of eternal damnation. Nor shall I any longer see an inhabitant of rest; rather, I shall be held among those who remain in torments. For this is what humanity deserved through sin. Therefore the Lord, made a participant in our humanity, took upon himself the voice of those who were perishing because of sin, so that, obtaining the remission of sin, he might save sinners from death. Hence, taking up our cause in the Psalm, he says: “Lord God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me? The words of my sins are far from my salvation” (Ps. 21:2). Since he lost the Jewish people from whom he had assumed flesh, he rightly adds:

**Verse 12.**—“My generation has been taken away and rolled up from me like a shepherds’ tent.”

For his generation was taken away from him because he lost Judea. And as shepherds’ tents are rolled up in one bundle and carried away to the fire when their occupants depart, so, when the Lord departed, that people was rolled up into the gathering of a single bundle [Note: [Col. 0367D] Both codices: *bundle* (*fasci*).] and cast into the pit, to be burned there eternally. In the voice of this people he adds:

“My life has been cut off as by a weaver: while I was still beginning, he cut me down.”

For the Lord speaks in the voice of the Jewish people because, through the mystery of assumed humanity, he became one with it [Col. 0367C]. Since “the righteous lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17), but this people lost at the Lord’s coming the faith by which it lived, he says: “My life, that is, my faith, has been cut off and severed.” This life is compared to woven cloth because the faith of that unformed people was advancing by certain stages, as cloth advances when it is woven. And just as cloth is stretched and woven by being fastened to two beams above and below, so the faith of that people was held and advanced in the humanity and divinity of the Redeemer.

Therefore its life was cut off as though cloth were cut by the weaver, because the Lord, who used to increase its faith, cut it off by a just judgment. While this people was still beginning the warp, it was cut off, because when it lost the life of faith it was still at a beginning [Col. 0367D]. Hence the Apostle reproaches them, saying: “Though by this time you ought to be teachers, you again need to be taught what are the elementary beginnings of God’s words; and you have become such as need milk, not solid food. For everyone who partakes of milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, for he is an infant” (Heb. 5:12). That people, therefore, was still beginning—that is, it was still only starting—when it was cut down. “For the Law brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. 7:19).

Again, in the voice of the chosen part of the same people, he adds: “From morning until evening you will make an end of me.” And “I said” is to be understood from what precedes. For the phrase “I said,” which occurs twice above, can frequently be understood in what follows. What, then, does he call morning except the time when that people began to know God, either through Abraham or through Moses? And what does he call evening except the setting of the sun of righteousness—that is, the Lord’s passion? Thus the Hebrew people said that “from morning until evening you will make an end of me,” because it prophesied that it would live religiously from the giving of the Law at the beginning until the Lord’s passion [Col. 0368A]. For one is brought to an end daily who, for love of the heavenly homeland, increasingly ceases to love present things and extinguishes the desires of the flesh, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Always carrying about in your body the dying of Jesus, that the life also of Jesus Christ may be manifested in your body. For we who live are always being handed over to death for Christ, that the life of Jesus may be manifested in our mortal flesh” (2 Cor. 4:10). For even under the Old Testament some lived in this manner. Then the Lord adds in his own voice:

**Verse 13.**—“I hoped until morning.”

That is, I awaited the resurrection, according to the words: “My flesh shall rest in hope” (Ps. 15:9). For he calls morning the hour of the resurrection. Of the evening mentioned before and of this morning it is elsewhere written: “Weeping shall linger at evening, and joy at morning” (Ps. 29:6). For the disciples wept when the Lord died, but rejoiced when he rose again. After this manifold variation of voices, frequently changing the persons speaking up to this point, the voice of the Church now continues at greater length in what follows [Col. 0368C]. For it adds:

“He has crushed all my bones like a lion,” and so forth. The strength of the body is in its bones. And what are the bones of this sacred body, that is, of the Church, except the apostles? Therefore, just as a lion crushes the bones of someone whom it devours, Satan, at the time of the Lord’s passion, crushed the bones of the Church: for then he broke the minds of all the apostles and shattered their steadfastness. But this danger soon passed, so that the religion of the Church might endure until the consummation of the age. For it continues: “From morning until evening you will make an end of me.” Morning, as above, means the hour of the Lord’s resurrection; evening means the end of the world. And from morning until evening it is brought to an end, because from the time of the Lord’s resurrection until the end of the world, by crucifying its flesh with its vices and desires, it imitates the Apostle, who says: “I die daily” (1 Cor. 15:31) [Col. 0368D]. And it adds:

**Verse 14.**—“Like the young of a swallow I shall cry; I shall meditate like a dove.”

“I shall cry,” he says, “like the young of a swallow,” which is born with its eyes closed until the eighth day and cries because of blindness and hunger. Thus a human being, born into the blindness of this life, dwelling in darkness and want until the day of the final resurrection, ought continually to cry to God for these things and, cultivating compunction, meditate like the dove, which continually moans instead of singing. But after the Church of the righteous, or any holy soul, has thus cried and meditated for a long time, it follows, saying:

“My eyes have grown thin as they look upward.” For the eyes of the heart are dulled by a kind of thickness arising from worldly cares and lowly thoughts, as it is said of some: “The heart of this people has grown fat” (Matt. 13:15). But whoever transcends all earthly things in mind and, subtly cleansing his thoughts, is nourished by contemplation and desire of heavenly things—his eyes, looking upward, grow thin. Thus holy Job wished his eyes to grow thin when he said: “My spirit shall be made thin” (Job 17:1). The Church, therefore, rightly says, intent upon the contemplation of things above [Col. 0369B], “My eyes have grown thin as they look upward.” But, returning from the height of contemplation to consider the evils that it suffers below, it adds in supplication: “Lord, I suffer violence; answer for me.” And, reflecting within itself, it adds:

**Verse 15.**—“What shall I say, or what will he answer me, when he himself has done it?”

“Lord,” it says, “I suffer the force of tribulation; answer you on my behalf, because I cannot answer you, since it is written: ‘O man, who are you to answer God?’” (Rom. 9:20). Answer for me, that is, mercifully defend my cause against the severity of your justice, so that by the reason of justice you may remove the violence of affliction which I suffer justly. “For what,” it says, “shall I say to my God?” As if it said: “If I would justify myself, my own mouth shall condemn me; if I show myself innocent, it shall prove me perverse” (Job 9:20). “Or what will he answer me, when he himself has done it?” That is, what explanation will he give me concerning the things I suffer, when he is my Creator, who either afflicts me or permits me to be afflicted? For he who graciously created me does not permit me to be unjustly tormented [Col. 0369C]. But amid these things there is one wholesome course I may take: “I shall recount all my years in the bitterness of my soul”—that is, I shall call to mind the whole time of my past life and weep for everything which I recognize that I have done wrongly.

**Verse 16.**—“Lord, if this is how one lives, then in such things is the life of my spirit.”

In this present life one lives as he said above of himself, that is, by suffering pains and afflictions. For all of us who live are oppressed by affliction, and we cannot answer him who afflicts us. And in such pains is the life of my spirit—that is, the life which the spirit gives to these limbs.

Or, true life is lived in this way: by recalling past years with the bitterness of repentance. And in such bitterness and recollections is the life of my spirit, because through repentance the soul, which had been dead in sins, comes alive again. Or the life of my spirit is nourished in such afflictions, because the spirit of the mind lives more truly the more strongly the flesh is crushed. Hence it is added:

[Col. 0370A] “You will correct me and give me life.” You will correct me outwardly by scourging, and thereby give me life inwardly, so that I may say: “The Lord has severely chastened me, but he has not delivered me over to death” (Ps. 117:18). The Church, or any righteous person with Paul, speaks these words, glorying in tribulations. But let us see what one who desires to be corrected in this way does when outward correction has ceased. It adds:

**Verse 17.**—“Behold, in peace my bitterness is most bitter.”

For the bitterness of the elect is most bitter in peace, because those who are always in bitterness of heart are then filled with bitterness more intensely when they suffer no outward adversity. But what they have merited through this correction and bitterness follows: “But you have delivered my soul, that it should not perish”—that is, you have saved it from the impending danger of eternal damnation. And how did you deliver it from the danger of death? It follows: “You have cast all my sins behind your back,” that is, removing them from your sight, you left them among the things behind, so that they may no longer be seen among the things before—that is, in the ages to come. It follows:

**Verse 18.**—“For hell will not confess you, nor will death praise you; those who go down into the pit will not await your truth.”

**Verse 19.**—“The living, the living, he shall confess you, as I do today; a father will make known your truth to his children.”

That you delivered my soul from death by forgiving sins is proved by this: hell will not confess you—that is, to those who are in hell remission will no longer be given through confession of sins; nor will death praise you—that is, those who are in that death. And those who once descend into the pit of that perdition will no longer await the knowledge of the truth of your teaching, because, consumed in their folly, they will be punished without remedy.

Or certainly, they will not await the truth of your promise, which the elect await. Hell and death will not confess you; but “the living, the living, he himself will confess you,” that is, while each person lives in the present age, he has power to confess his sins, just as I too confess while I am still alive today. And those who descend into the pit will not await your truth. But every spiritual father will make your truth known to his children, whom he has begotten in Christ Jesus through the Gospel. For this life is the place for learning, not hell; and here is the place for confessing and purging sins. Thus far the Lord has spoken in the voice of your body. But after this he speaks to the Father in his own voice, saying:

**VERSE 20.**—“Lord, save me.”

That is, raise me up. And again he adds in the voice of his members: “And we shall sing our psalms all the days of our life in the house of the Lord,” that is, we shall remain in the Church, singing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, and making melody to the Lord in our hearts. For this is what the faithful do everywhere from the resurrection of the Lord onward. And this is the prayer of the Church in supplication in the Psalm: “Lord, save the king, and hear us on the day when we call upon you” (Ps. XIX [20]:10). For what is said there, “Lord, save the king,” is what the king himself says here: “Lord, save me”; and what follows there, “And hear us on the day when we call upon you,” is added here: “And we shall sing our psalms all the days of our life in the house of the Lord.” The prayer of King Hezekiah being finished, the prophetic narrative continues:

**VERSE 21.**—“And Isaiah commanded that they should take a mass of figs and apply it as a poultice upon the wound, and he would be healed.”

But in Hosea the Lord says: “Like grapes in the wilderness I found Israel, like the first fruits of a fig tree” (Hos. IX:10). And Jeremiah, recounting a certain vision, says among other things: “One basket had exceedingly good figs, such as are usually the figs of the first season” (Jer. XXIV). And he adds that the Lord said: “Like these good figs, so shall I acknowledge for good the exile of Judah, whom I sent away from this place into the land of the Chaldeans; and I shall set my eyes upon them for favour” (ibid., v. 5).

What, then, is signified by the mass of figs except a multitude of elect persons, sweet and pleasant? What then does it mean that a mass of figs is laid upon Hezekiah’s wound, except that, while our Redeemer hangs upon the cross and is wounded by the lance, he purchases the Church with his own blood? Hence Paul says: “To govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood” (Acts XX:28). Therefore, being wounded, he acquired the Church: this is the mass of figs laid upon the wound.

And this mass of figs is applied as a poultice to the wound because the Church of the righteous adheres, by the bond of charity, to the Lord’s Passion. But when this mass is applied as a poultice to the wound, the king is healed; because after Christ, by suffering, had joined to himself the multitude of the elect—who are all one—he rose again, death having been trampled down, no longer to return to corruption. For he was healed because he was clothed in the glory of resurrection. It follows:

**VERSE 22.**—“And Hezekiah said: What shall be the sign that I shall go up to the house of the Lord?”

[Col. 0371D] When the king had said this, Isaiah answered him with what had been set forth above in the Lord’s voice: “This shall be a sign to you from the Lord that the Lord performs this word which he has spoken: Behold, I shall cause the shadow of the lines to return” (Apoc. III:7), etc. Hezekiah was to go up to the house of the Lord because Christ, rising from the dead, ascended into that house of eternity, where he now sits at the right hand of God the Father. But the sign of this ascension was that the sun went back ten lines; for, when the mysteries of the Law were laid open in his death and resurrection, an evident indication was given that he was also to unlock the kingdoms of heaven. For no one could open either the Law or heaven except the holy and true one, “who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens” (Apoc. III:7). Since, after his ascension, the nations came to faith, it is fittingly added:

## CHAPTER XXXIX

“At that time Merodach-Baladan, son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and gifts to Hezekiah; for he had heard that he had been ill and had recovered.”

For what is denoted by Merodach, which is interpreted “bitter arrogance” or “one who instils bitterness,” except the teachers of secular wisdom, who because of that same wisdom had assumed excessive arrogance and instilled into their followers the bitterness of their arrogance or wisdom? He is also surnamed Baladan, which means, “He comes judging for himself,” because the wise men of the age came to judge for themselves, preferring their own things to those belonging to others; of them the Lord rightly says: “All who came were thieves and robbers” (John X:8). And this Merodach is the son of Baladan, because those who believed from among the wise men of the world were the first-born from the teaching of the ancient wise men. Merodach is also said to have been king of Babylon—that is, of confusion—because the wise men of the age were princes of error.

Therefore this Merodach sent to Hezekiah—that is, to Christ—books of sound doctrine and gifts of good works. For many among the wise men of the Gentiles, having been converted, wrote excellent books and offered the gifts of their devotion to Christ, such as Justin the philosopher, Dionysius the Areopagite, and Augustine Aurelius. For through the apostles this Merodach had heard that [Col. 0372C] Hezekiah had been ill and had recovered; that is, that Christ had assumed the weakness of our mortality and had attained the glory of immortality. It follows:

**VERSE 2.**—“Hezekiah rejoiced over them, and showed them the storehouse of spices, and of silver and gold, and perfumes, and the best ointment, and all the storehouses of his equipment, and everything that was found in his treasures.”

Christ rejoiced over the converted Gentiles and showed them the storehouse of spices: that is, he brought them into the Church, which is filled with the fragrances of virtues. This storehouse is also of silver—that is, of the divine word—and of gold—that is, of heavenly wisdom; and of perfumes, which are the prayers of the saints; and of the best ointment—that is, the anointing of the Holy Spirit. For the best ointment is the Holy Spirit, because he preached “Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit” (Acts X:38).

Ἀποθήκη (*apothēkē*) is Greek; in Latin it is called a *repositorium* or *reconditorium*, “storehouse” or “place of keeping.” But what does Hezekiah’s equipment signify except the adornments of virtues and the various instruments of good works? What, then, ought we to understand by the storehouses of his equipment except the congregations of the faithful, or their minds, where a manifold equipment of virtues is stored? Then, having described these things individually, he adds generally, “everything that was found in his treasures,” calling them all good things; and Christ showed all these things to the converted Gentiles. It follows:

[Col. 0373A] “There was not a word which Hezekiah did not show them in his house and throughout all his power.”

His house is the Church. His power is that of which he says: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII:18). Therefore, there was not a word which he did not show them in his house and throughout all his power, because he made known to them all things which are in the Church, or in heaven and on earth, insofar as the piety of Christian religion ought now to know them; as he says: “But I have called you friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John XV:15). It follows:

**VERSE 3.**—“But Isaiah the prophet entered in to King Hezekiah and said to him: What did these men say, and from where did they come to you?”

When the Gentiles were called to faith, Isaiah—that is, the prophetic word—entered in to Hezekiah, that is, to Christ, in order to speak about them; because then that which the prophets had long ago spoken concerning their conversion began to be fulfilled in their conduct. He asks about them as though they were unknown, because the prophets regarded the Gentiles as unknown persons, to whom they did not speak in their own presence. It follows:

“And Hezekiah said: They came to me from a far country, from Babylon.” The Gentiles were far from God in Babylon—that is, while they remained in the confusion of the error of idolatry. Thus the younger of two brothers is said, having received his share of the property, to have gone “into a far country” (Luke XV:12), and there to have squandered that same property in riotous living; but at last, at some point rising up, to have returned to his father. Therefore the Gentiles who were converted from ancient errors to Christ came from a far country, from Babylon. It follows:

**VERSE 4.**—“And he said: What have they seen in your house? And Hezekiah said: They have seen everything that is in my house; there was no thing which I did not show them among my treasures.”

The converted Gentiles saw and recognized everything that is in the house of the Lord—that is, in the Church—and were carefully instructed in all things. There was no thing among his treasures that he did not show them, because he disclosed to them all the riches of the soul and the resources of virtues. But now we see, and lament, that what follows is being fulfilled in great measure.

**VERSE 5.**—“And Isaiah said to Hezekiah: Hear the word of the Lord of hosts.”

**VERSE 6.**—“Behold, days shall come, and all things which are in your house, and which your fathers have stored up until this day, shall be carried away into Babylon; nothing shall be left, says the Lord.”

The days are coming—and have already begun—of which the Apostle says: “In the last days perilous times shall come, and people shall be lovers of themselves, covetous, proud, arrogant, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, without peace, slanderers, incontinent, cruel, without kindness, traitors, reckless, swollen with pride, lovers of pleasures more than of God, having indeed the appearance of godliness but denying its power” (II Tim. III:1–5). Therefore, as regards the multitude of such pseudo-Christians, in those days all things which are in the Lord’s house will spiritually be carried away into Babylon. For the Apostle is not speaking of unbelievers in all these matters, but rather of those called Christians, concerning whom the Lord also says: “Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, do you think that he will find faith on earth?” (Luke XVIII:8). What wonder, then, if all the things in the Lord’s house are said to be carried away into Babylon, when the Lord himself will scarcely find faith upon earth at his coming?

Yet in saying this we do not deny that at that time some righteous persons will be most valiant; but we speak of the multitude concerning whom it is written: “Because iniquity will abound, the charity of many will grow cold” (Matt. XXIV:12). Leaving aside the few righteous, the statement concerns the abundant multitude of the reprobate, which will then prevail, when it is said that all things in Hezekiah’s house—that is, among this Christian people—will be carried away into Babylon: namely, the spices of virtues, the fragrance of an excellent reputation, the silver of the divine word, the gold of heavenly wisdom, the perfumes of prayers, and the other things described above.

But the fathers of the Lord are called the prophets and patriarchs, who until this day stored up in his house treasures of good conduct and wisdom; because through their deeds and words the Church is filled with spiritual riches. Yet all these treasures will shortly be carried away into Babylon—that is, into confusion—because through Antichrist all the goods of the inner person will be led captive. “Nothing shall be left,” says the Lord, because that pestilent one will corrupt and destroy everything. But after these statements concerning the ruin of conduct, he adds concerning the captivity of the faithful:

**VERSE 7.**—“And they shall take of your sons, who shall come forth from you, whom you shall have begotten; and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.”

He does not say, “They shall take all your sons,” but, “They shall take of your sons.” Here it clearly appears that not all the faithful will then be deceived. For all Christians are his sons, as he himself shows when he says: “Can the sons of the bridegroom fast while the bridegroom is with them?” (Mark II:19). And it is rightly said, “Who shall come forth from you,” because according to the Apostle we are “of his flesh and of his bones” (Eph. V:30).

Therefore the preachers of Antichrist will take some of these sons and make them eunuchs—that is, devoid of manly vigour of mind—in the palace of the king of Babylon, that is, in the court of the prince of this world, who is Satan. For he is a eunuch who has lost the manly strength of mind by which he ought to beget spiritual children through preaching. Hence Moses says: “A eunuch whose testicles are crushed or cut away, and whose member is severed, shall not enter the Church of the Lord” (Deut. XXIII:2). For the testicles of one whose inward manliness is crushed by adversities are crushed; but the testicles of one whose spiritual manly powers, by which he might beget children through the Gospel, are taken away along with his member, are cut off. But whoever is such a person cannot enter the heavenly Church of the Lord, into which the elect alone enter. Therefore it is rightly said: “They shall take of your sons, who shall come forth from you, whom you have begotten, and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon,” because under Antichrist many Christians will be deceived and will attach themselves, enervated, to the service of the king of inward confusion. It follows:

**VERSE 8.**—“And Hezekiah said to Isaiah: Good is the word of the Lord which he has spoken.”

It is good that the multitude of the reprobate, which now burdens the Church, should be wholly separated from the elect through Antichrist. It follows:

“And he said: Let there only be peace and truth in my days.”

[Col. 0375B] By “days” the conduct of the elect is customarily signified, as Solomon says: “But the path of the righteous is as a shining light: it goes forth and increases unto the perfect day” (Prov. IV:18). Who, then, are Hezekiah’s days—that is, Christ’s—except his elect, to whom the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. V:8)? Let there therefore be peace in these days, so that there may be “peace on earth to people of good will” (Luke II:14), lest they be spiritually assailed and made captive by the king of Babylon. Let there also be truth in them, lest they belong to those to whom God, through Antichrist, will send an operation of error so that they may believe a lie, as the Apostle says: “Because they did not receive the love of the truth, that they might be saved” (II Thess. II:10). Although the righteous suffer persecution outwardly, nevertheless peace is always in them, because they deserve to hear within themselves: “May the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (Phil. IV:7). For in those whose hearts and minds the peace of God guards in Christ, peace is rightly said to come about, because no hostile assault separates them from the peace of God. And peace comes about only in these, because “there is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord” (Isa. XLVIII:22). Truth likewise comes about in them when, doing the truth in charity, they grow in every respect into him who is the head, Christ. But because sorrowful things have been foretold concerning the spiritual captivity of the faithful, the consolation of the elect is fittingly added:

## CHAPTER XL

[Col. 0375D] **VERSE 1.**—“Comfort, comfort my people, says your God.

**VERSE 2.**—“Speak to the heart of Jerusalem, and call her away [Note: [Col. 0375D] Elsewhere: ‘summon her.’], because her term of service is completed, her iniquity is forgiven; she has received double from the hand of the Lord for all her sins.”

For the Lord, considering the abomination of that final desolation which will occur through Antichrist, graciously consoles his own amid adversities, saying: “Comfort, comfort my people.” And, so that those who have already received consolation may strive to console others, he adds:

[Col. 0376A] “Speak to the heart of Jerusalem, and call her away.” To speak to the heart is to address one who is sorrowful by gently consoling her. Hence Ruth is said to have told Boaz: “You have comforted me and spoken to the heart of your handmaid” (Ruth II:13). The Apostle agrees with this passage when he says: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our tribulation, so that we too may be able to console those who are in every tribulation through the exhortation by which we ourselves are exhorted by God; because, as Christ’s sufferings abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds” (II Cor. I:3–5).

For where the Lord says, “Comfort, comfort my people,” the Apostle says, “Who consoles us in all our tribulation.” And where the Lord adds, “Speak to the heart of Jerusalem,” the Apostle adds, “So that we too may be able to console those who are in every tribulation,” etc. “Speak,” therefore, he says, “to the heart of Jerusalem,” that is, to the Church, or to the soul of any faithful person placed amid adversities, speaking the things that her heart desires to hear; and call her away, so that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord may depart from iniquity, and thus, abandoning the depraved pursuits of human conduct, may not imitate the ruined ways of earthly people, who are many because of the abundance of iniquity.

For in that final tribulation her *malitia*—that is, her affliction or hardship—will be completed, namely the hardship of which it is written: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own hardship” (Matt. VI:34). For then every faithful person will be compelled to leave behind all concern for bodily necessity, which is now called *malitia*, and to reckon himself a sheep for slaughter. Therefore her hardship will then be ended, because she will cast off all worldly care; and because she suffers persecution for righteousness, her iniquity, which perhaps she had previously committed, is forgiven. For she has received double from the hand of the Lord for all her sins, because she is most grievously tormented both in body and soul for all the former pleasures of sins. “For there will be great tribulation such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor will be” (Matt. XIII:21).

These words can, however, suitably be understood concerning the coming of the Lord. For the principal consolation of God’s people was Christ’s coming, because, from the time he began to be promised to the fathers, it had been desired with many tears by the saints. Hence that old man Simeon was “awaiting the consolation of Israel, and had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death unless he saw the Christ of the Lord” (Luke II:25). Therefore the prophet now offers to that same people the consolation of Israel which was to come through Christ’s advent, saying: “Comfort, comfort my people, says the Lord your God”; and he adds, speaking to the apostles: “Speak to the heart of Jerusalem,” that is, to the heart of the Jewish people, gently and rationally exhorting it to repentance for the killing of the Lord. And call her away from unbelief to faith, from oldness to newness, because her wickedness was completed in killing the Saviour, and afterwards her iniquity was forgiven through believing in him.

But, that we may understand what follows—“She has received double from the hand of the Lord for all her sins”—let us remember that in this corruptible body, which weighs down the soul, we live a wretched life. Yet because we have now been redeemed through the Mediator and have received the Holy Spirit as a pledge, we possess the blessed life in hope, although we do not yet possess the reality itself. “But hope that is seen is not hope. For what a person sees, why does he hope for it? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it through patience” (Rom. VIII:24). In the evils which each person suffers, not in the goods which he enjoys, patience is necessary.

Therefore a person is compelled to endure this life, of which it is written, “Is not human life upon earth a temptation?” (Job VII:1), in which we cry daily to the Lord, “Deliver us from evil” (Matt. VI:13), even when sins have been forgiven—although sin was originally the cause of one’s coming into that misery. For the punishment lasts longer than the fault, lest the fault be regarded as small if the punishment ended with it. And so, whether to demonstrate the misery deserved, to correct a changeable life, or to exercise necessary patience, punishment holds a person for a time even when guilt no longer holds him liable to eternal condemnation. Thus, after it had been said, “Her iniquity is forgiven,” it was rightly added: “Because she has received double from the hand of the Lord for all her sins,” because both while she was sinning and after she ceased to sin, she endured the affliction of the present life. It follows:

**VERSE 3.**—“The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight in the desert the paths of our God.”

When John the Baptist was asked who he was, he answered: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Make straight the way of the Lord, as Isaiah the prophet said” (John I:23). [Col. 0377D] John is therefore called a voice because he precedes the Word. For, as we know from the practice of our speech, the voice sounds first so that the word may afterwards be heard. Thus John, going before the Lord’s advent, is called a voice because through his ministry the Word of the Father is heard. A word is the thought itself, still retained within the secret places of conscience; but a voice is the sound that indicates thought. For that which we conceive in the mind within the silence of the soul is called a word; voice, however, is that through which we utter the word. The word is also reason, which is heard through the voice. Therefore, just as when we conceive a word in the heart, a voice is necessary as a kind of vehicle for the word, and although by the sound of the mouth we convey the word itself to another, it nevertheless remains whole within us—thus it is transferred from the speaker while remaining in its own seat—so the almighty Father, wishing to make known to us the Wisdom and Word which in the beginning was God with God, as he himself says, “My heart has poured forth a good word” (Ps. XLVI [45]:2), took up blessed John as a kind of voice through which to utter his Word to us. That Word descended to us from that heavenly seat in such a way that it nevertheless remained in the depth of the Father’s bosom, visiting earthly things without leaving heavenly things. John is therefore rightly called a voice: when his proclamation began, human mortality, long deaf, began to hear the mystery of human redemption. He also cries in the wilderness or desert because he announces the consolation of salvation to Judaea, abandoned and forsaken.

[Col. 0378B] Or the wilderness and desert may signify the deprivation of good. For hearts empty of the fear of God are compared to the barrenness of a desolate wilderness. John therefore cries in the wilderness, saying: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God” (Luke III:4), because “he turned many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God, going before him to prepare for the Lord a perfect people” (Luke I:16). And he still commands us, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation—that is, among the wicked people with whom we live—to prepare a way for the Lord within ourselves by living well; he says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV:23).

By “way” action may be signified, and by “paths” thoughts. He therefore commands us to prepare the Lord’s way and make his paths straight, so that we may prepare both our outward conduct and the inward thoughts of our mind for his spiritual coming.

Or he also commands preachers to prepare the Lord’s way. The person who preaches his glory to the minds of hearers prepares the Lord’s way, so that when he himself subsequently comes he may enlighten them by the presence of his love. Every upright preacher prepares the Lord’s way, because words of exhortation go beforehand, and thereby truth is received in the mind. It follows:

**VERSE 4.**—“Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be humbled; crooked things shall become straight, and rough places smooth ways.”

What is denoted here by valleys except humble persons, and by mountains and hills except proud persons? Therefore, at the coming of the Redeemer valleys were exalted, but mountains and hills humbled, because according to his saying, “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke XIV:11).

Crooked things become straight when hearts twisted by the injustice of evil people are directed to the rule of justice. And rough things are changed into smooth ways when harsh and irascible minds return, through the infusion of heavenly grace, to the gentleness of meekness. When the word of truth is not received by an angry mind, the roughness of the road, as it were, repels the step of one travelling on it. But when an angry mind, through received grace of meekness, receives the word of correction or exhortation, there the preacher finds a smooth way where formerly he could not proceed because of the roughness of the road—that is, could not set down the step of preaching. Having spoken these things concerning the first coming of the Saviour, he immediately adds concerning the second:

**VERSE 5.**—“And the glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh together shall see that the mouth of the Lord has spoken.”

For then the glory of the Lord will be revealed, because “they shall see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty” (Matt. XXIV:30). Since all flesh means every human being, then, when the Lord’s glory has been revealed, all flesh together will see what the mouth of the Lord has spoken, when, the heavens being opened, angels ministering, and apostles sitting down, Christ appears upon the throne of his majesty. All the elect together with the reprobate will see him, so that the righteous may rejoice without end in the gift of recompense and the unrighteous may groan forever in the vengeance of punishment. Therefore all flesh—that is, every human being—will together see what the mouth of the Lord has spoken concerning the glory of the saints and the condemnation of the wicked. It follows:

**VERSE 6.**—“The voice of one saying: Cry out. And I said: What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field.”

**VERSE 7.**—“The grass has dried up and the flower has fallen, because the Spirit of the Lord has breathed upon it. Truly the people are grass.”

[Col. 0379C] **VERSE 8.**—“The grass has dried up and the flower has fallen; but the word of the Lord remains forever.”

A voice of the Lord saying to me, “Cry out,” he says, was heard. And I said, “What shall I cry?” And he said, “All flesh is grass.” The prophet’s faith is proved by the oracle. “Cry out,” says the Lord; and the prophet asks, “What shall I cry?” Then the Lord answers: “All flesh is grass.” Observe the command of the one commanding, the obedience of the one complying, the desire of the one asking, and the oracle of the one obeying. For the person who asks what he should cry out believes, and prophesies what he has believed. Before Christ came, who made known to us the glory of another life, the glory of this age—the life of mortal flesh—was thought to be something; but in him we have learned how frail and fleeting it is. Hence now, after announcing his advent, the prophet is commanded to cry out that all flesh is grass and all its glory like the flower of the field.

And flesh is rightly called grass because it is swiftly cut down from this life and withers; and just as grass has greenness when it springs up and beauty when it grows, but when cut dries up and is reduced to dust, so mortal flesh flourishes in childhood and shines in youth, but when it has been cut down by death it becomes dust.

Its temporal glory is also shown to be brief when it is added that all its glory is like the flower of the field. For the glory of the wicked is compared with the flower of grass or of the field because the glory of the flesh, while it shines, falls; while it exalts itself in its own estimation, it is ended by a sudden, intervening end. For the flower of grass delights both the smell and the sight, but very swiftly loses the glory of its beauty and sweetness; and therefore present carnal prosperity, which can in no way be lasting, is most rightly compared to it.

The grass has dried up and the flower has fallen because the temporal beauty of carnal persons is consumed at the end. “Because the Spirit of God has breathed upon it,” that is, because the sentence of the strict Judge dries up the life of the flesh as the greenness of grass. “Truly the people are grass, because they shall wither swiftly as grass” (Ps. XXXVI [37]:2). But “the word of the Lord”—that is, Christ—“remains forever” (I Pet. I:25) in the flesh which he raised up. But let us hear what his preachers ought to do among those who are grass. It follows:

**VERSE 9.**—“Go up upon a high mountain, you who proclaim good news to Zion; lift up your voice with strength, you who proclaim good news to Jerusalem; lift it up; do not fear. Say to the cities of Judah: Behold your God.”

Go up upon a high mountain—that is, transcend far above the common conduct of other human beings—so that, ascending from low thoughts to heavenly desires and from earthly deeds to the exercises of virtues, you may offer others an example of seeking lofty things: you who proclaim good news to Zion, that is, to the watchtower of prudent watchfulness against the approach of each vice. Raise in the strength of robust action the voice of your preaching, you who proclaim good news to Jerusalem—that is, the vision of that perpetual peace. Raise your voice freely; do not fear adversaries, because the peace which you announce will soon come. Say to the cities of Judah—that is, to the Churches of catholic confession—“Behold, your God will very soon come to give you the vision of everlasting peace, you who now fight for righteousness in time.” Hence it is added:

**VERSE 10.**—“Behold, the Lord God shall come in strength, and his arm shall rule; behold, his reward is with him, and his work before him.”

The Lord will come in great strength, and his arm—that is, his power—will rule, because “when the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all his angels with him, then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty, and all nations will be gathered before him” (Matt. XXV:31). “Behold, his reward is with him,” because then he will say to those at his right hand: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid., 34).

And his work—that is, the work deserving reward—will be before him, because he will weigh and examine the work to which he will render so great a reward, adding: “For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat” (ibid., 35), etc. Or his work—that is, the human race which he himself created—will be before him, when, as was said, “all nations will be gathered before him.” For “we must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to the things done in the body, whether good or evil” (II Cor. V:10). It follows:

**VERSE 11.**—“Like a shepherd he shall feed his flock; in his arm he shall gather the lambs, and in his bosom he shall lift them up; he himself shall carry the ewes with young.”

Living bodily among human beings, the Lord fed the flock of his sheep like a shepherd, saying: “I am the good shepherd; I know my own, and my own know me” (John X:14). He fed his flock by his preaching, and he still does not cease to feed it with his body and blood. He gathered and gathers the lambs—that is, the meek, innocent, and simple—in the arm of his power; he carries them in his embrace, and lifting them up in the bosom of his mercy, cherishing and protecting them. And he gently carries the ewes with young, weakened by their offspring: that is, the holy teachers, who say to those whom they have spiritually begotten, “We became little ones in the midst of you, as though a nurse should cherish her children” (I Thess. II:7). They are designated by the feminine gender both because of maternal affection and the inward bowels of charity, and because of merciful weakness. Therefore he carries those with young, because with more abundant mercy he sustains, lifts, and advances those who mercifully become weak in order to gain the weak.

For then is truly fulfilled what is written: “Strength is made perfect in weakness” (II Cor. XII:9). But now let us bring this little book to an end, so that we may treat what follows in other works.

## BOOK SIX

[Col. 0381]

## CHAPTER XL CONTINUES

[Col. 0381B]

**VERSE 12.**—“Who has measured the waters in his fist and weighed the heavens with his palm? Who has suspended the mass of the earth with three fingers, and weighed the mountains in a balance and the hills in scales?”

The prophet, intending in many ways to disprove the error of idolatry, first teaches that God is unbounded, immeasurable, omnipotent, and all-wise, so that it may become more plainly evident how great a madness it is to believe a stone or metal image to be God.

“Who,” he says, “has measured the waters in his fist?” Understand: except God, who, enclosing them all in his fist, has measured them. And who has weighed the heavens with his palm except that same Creator, who, supporting their breadth with his palm, has weighed them so that their eastern and western parts should be of equal weight, and the northern should not outweigh the southern or be lighter? And who has suspended the mass of the earth with three fingers, balancing it amid the waters, except the supreme Craftsman? And who has weighed the mountains in a balance, so that they should not weigh down the earth more on one side than on another, and suspended the hills in scales, so that they might be of equal weight, except their Creator?

How great, then, is he who, holding all the waters in his fist, has measured them; who, sustaining the heavens by the breadth of his hand, has weighed them; and who has suspended the earth above the waters with three fingers? He who could do these things is unquestionably immeasurable—not because he must be believed to possess bodily limbs, but because through these [Col. 0381D] comparisons the greatness of his divine power is intimated. He measured the waters in his fist because by the power of his action he enclosed them and caused them to overflow or diminish by whatever amount he willed. He weighed the heavens with his palm because by the abundant power of his working he disposed them in equilibrium. And he suspended the mass of the earth with three fingers because he founded it by threefold power. Likewise he established mountains and hills by the threefold power of his operation—that is, by the power through which the Trinity works.

[Col. 0382B] But if these things ought to be understood morally, by the waters are customarily signified the minds of good people who follow the teachings of faith, as he says above: “Blessed are you who sow beside all waters” (Isa. 32:20). And the Psalmist says: “The voice of the Lord is over the waters” (Ps. 28:3). Therefore, in this place, what is signified by the name “waters” but the hearts of the elect, which through the understanding of wisdom have now received the hearing of the heavenly voice? Of these it is rightly said: Who has measured the waters in his fist?—that is, except God alone? For the saints, who, lifted up by the Spirit, are carried to the heights, are nevertheless, as long as they remain in this mortal life, restrained by certain temptations through the disposing hand of the Lord, lest they grow proud through some exaltation and lest they be able to advance as far as they wish. For they are confined in measure by God’s fist. The Lord measures them in his fist because he moderates them so that none of them, negligently falling short, fails even in the least things; nor, proudly stretching beyond measure, reaches after the greatest; nor attempts to fulfil less than is sufficient; nor seizes more than he has undertaken—lest he either fail to reach the measure he ought to attain, or, abandoning that measure, fall outside the boundary. Hence the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “We do not boast beyond measure, but according to the measure which God has apportioned to us, a measure extending even to you” (2 Cor. 10:13). Rightly, therefore, is it said that God measured the waters in his fist.

But what is expressed by the name “heavens” except the minds of the righteous, lifted by inward love above every earthly contamination, in whom the Lord now reigns as though in [Col. 0382D] heavenly places? Therefore he weighed the heavens with his palm, because, while giving the saints an abundance of virtues with a generous hand, by which they are lifted up, he does not remove the weight of weakness by which they are still pressed down. For the flesh draws them downward lest the spirit exalt them; the spirit draws them upward lest the flesh cast them down. Thus, through the Lord’s hand lifting and depressing them in a sure moderation, while each of them is indeed inwardly carried to the heights but is still outwardly tempted, he incurs neither the fall of despair [Col. 0383A] nor that of pride: outward temptation does not bring sin to completion because inward intention draws upward; nor, again, does inward intention raise him into pride, because outward temptation, while burdening him, humbles him. Thus, while the spirit draws and the flesh pulls back, the soul is balanced, by the most subtle moderation of inward judgment, beneath the heights and above the depths, in a kind of middle state. Therefore the Lord weighed the heavens with his palm, as Solomon testifies: “The Lord is the weigher of spirits” (Prov. 16:2).

What, indeed, is figured by the earth except the Church, which receives the seed of preaching and yields the fruit of good works? Therefore the Lord suspended the mass of the earth with three fingers, because he upheld the weight of the Church in the grace of faith, so that it might seek the things above, not those upon the [Col. 0383B] earth. For on account of the divine Trinity faith is signified by three fingers, although the gifts of the Holy Spirit may also be understood under the name of fingers, as the Psalmist says: “For I shall behold your heavens, the works of your fingers” (Ps. 8:4)—that is, the saints, wrought by the grace of your spiritual gifts. By these fingers, then—that is, by the grace of faith—the mass of our soul is suspended, so that, transcending earthly things, it may be held aloft in love and contemplation of heavenly things.

And what are mountains and hills except the saints, who by the merit of their life draw near to heavenly things? Solomon indeed says that “weight and scales are the judgments of the Lord” (Prov. 16:11). Therefore he balanced mountains in a weight and hills in scales, because, in the just moderation of his judgments, as was said above, he suspends the saints on high.

**VERSE 13.**—“Who has assisted the Spirit of the Lord? Or who was his counsellor and showed him?”

**VERSE 14.**—“With whom did he take counsel, and who instructed him, taught him the path of justice, trained him in knowledge, and showed him the way of prudence?”

Who has assisted the Spirit of the Lord? Understand: no one, because he is almighty. Or who was his counsellor and showed him what he ought to do? Understand: no one, because he knows all things, received knowledge from no other source, and is himself the fountain of wisdom, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. With whom did he take counsel, that he might be instructed by that person? Understand: with no one, since he eternally knows all things. “In him also [Col. 0383D] we have been called by lot, predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will” (Eph. 1:11). And who taught him the path of justice—that is, by what way he should exercise the subtlety of his justice, showing mercy to those to whom it was just to show mercy, and becoming angry with those with whom it was just to be angry? The implied answer is no one, because, according to the Apostle, “He has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills” (Rom. 9:18). And who trained him in knowledge? No one, because without beginning he knows all things. And who showed him the way of prudence by which he should proceed, choosing good things, rejecting evil things, and acting prudently in all matters? No one suggested any of these things to him, because through himself he can do all things and knows all things. But since God has been shown to be of such greatness, power, and wisdom, let us see what those who think falsely concerning him are judged to be in his sight.

**VERSE 15.**—“Behold, the nations are like a drop from a bucket and are reckoned to him as the slightest movement of a balance; behold, the islands are like fine dust.”

**VERSE 16.**—“Lebanon will not suffice for kindling, nor its animals suffice for a burnt offering.”

**VERSE 17.**—“All nations are as though they were not; before him they are reckoned as nothing and emptiness.”

The nations that serve idols are reckoned by him as a drop from a bucket—that is, as nothing—for a drop of water falling from a bucket is considered very small by the one carrying it, because, as it were, they have fallen from the vessel, the Church of the faithful, into idolatry. A *momentum* is so called from motion: it is the slightest inclination of a balance, and its swiftest movement toward either side, caused by a small weight. Therefore the nations are reckoned by God as the slight movement of a balance, which is bent in whatever direction by a light motion, because they are unstable in mind and always depart from equity. This is also said in the Book of Wisdom: “For before you the whole world is like the slightest movement of a balance, like a drop of dew falling upon the earth before daylight” (Wis. 11:23). Thus all who follow wickedness in the world are judged very small in God’s sight. Even the islands of the sea, with their inhabitants, are reckoned as fine dust seen in a ray of sunlight, when compared with God’s greatness.

[Col. 0384C] Lebanon is a mountain of remarkable height, rich in trees and most fertile pastures. But Lebanon, with its timber and animals, does not suffice for a burnt offering to the Lord, because even if all the animals feeding in Lebanon were sacrificed to him, and all the timber there were cut down to burn the burnt offerings, these could not be enough to appease such great majesty. He says this in order to destroy the error of the gentiles, who thought that they could appease God in their images by the blood of cattle.

What he had first said—that the nations are reckoned as a drop from a bucket—he further indicates by adding that all nations are before him as though they were not. For because they have withdrawn from him who alone truly said, [Col. 0384D] “I am who I am” (Exod. 3:14), they are deservedly said to be as though they were not, since through wickedness they tend toward non-being, though they cannot become absolutely nothing. Having therefore shown that God is immeasurable and almighty, knows all things, and that all nations are reckoned as nothing in comparison with his greatness, he rebukes the folly of the gentiles by adding:

**VERSE 18.**—“To whom, then, have you made God like? Or what image will you set before him?”

**VERSE 19.**—“Has a craftsman cast an image? Or has a goldsmith fashioned it in gold, and has a silversmith made it with silver plates?”

Since God is unbounded and incorporeal, to whom have you made him like by fashioning a god for yourselves out of material? Or what image will you set before him, who is spirit? Has a craftsman cast any carved image like him who measured the waters in his fist and weighed the heavens with his palm? Or has a goldsmith fashioned in gold an idol that might be like him who balanced mountains in a weight and hills in scales? Or will a silversmith make with silver plates an image of him of whom it was said: “Who has assisted the Spirit of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor?” Certainly not, because, as follows:

**VERSE 20.**—“Perhaps a skilled craftsman has chosen wood that will not rot and seeks how to set up an image that will not move.”

The order of the prophetic argument must be carefully observed. First, he teaches that God embraces and sustains all things; then he declares him almighty and his wisdom incomprehensible, and that compared with his immensity all nations are reckoned as nothing. Then he refutes by open reasoning the opinion held concerning idols: that the Lord of all, who is both unbounded and immeasurable, cannot be enclosed in stone temples or represented by any image; that the giver of every benefit does not need, or is not appeased by, the blood of victims; that finally the Creator and Governor of all things cannot be made by a human hand; and that God, in whose image human beings were made, ought not to be conceived as existing in metals and images. For the Apostle similarly reasoned among the Athenians, saying: “God, who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not dwell in temples made by hands, nor is he served by human hands as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all life, breath, and all things [Note: [Col. 0385D] Elsewhere: ‘bones.’]” (Acts 17:24). And shortly afterward: “Since, therefore, we are God’s offspring, we ought not to think the divine being like gold or silver or stone—the sculpture of human art and thought” (ibid., 29).

According to the tropological sense, we may say that the leaders of heretics are rebuked for fashioning various idols out of their own heart: idols made attractive either by elegance of speech—signified by silver—or by the brilliance of gold, which refers to intellect; or by incorruptible wood, which denotes doctrines that are more worthless yet are thought by their inventors to be perpetual, and are strengthened by dialectical art so that they may not be moved and collapse, but may stand with a firm root.

[Col. 0385D] **VERSE 21.**—“Do you not know? Have you not heard? Has it not been announced to you from the beginning? Have you not understood the foundations of the earth?”

Do you not know by natural reason that no creature can be made like the Creator? And if you cannot know this naturally, have you at least not heard it from preachers? And has this not been announced to you from the beginning? Whenever you heard that “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1), you could there understand who the Creator was. “For from the greatness and beauty of created things their Creator may be known by analogy” (Wis. 13:5). Have you not also understood the foundations of the earth, which were established by him, so that through this you might understand the power of his might?

**VERSE 22.**—“He who sits above the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like locusts.”

He does not say, “He who sits above the earth,” but “above the circle of the earth,” that is, the globe of the world. For he sits above the whole earth equally, who is said to sit above the circumference of the earth, since he himself fills the world. By this, therefore, his greatness is declared, and the fact that no image like him can be made, in comparison with whose greatness all inhabitants of the world are like locusts—that is, exceedingly small. Yet he must not be thought to sit above the circle of the earth in bodily mass, since [Col. 0386B] he is Spirit; rather, he is wholly present everywhere on earth and reigns everywhere. For he remains inward and above the seat over which he presides—that is, the circle of the earth: inward by subtlety, and above by power; inward because he fills it, above because he reigns. Thus it is rightly said: “He who sits above the circle of the earth.”

“He who stretches out the heavens as though they were nothing, and spreads them out like a tent to dwell in.”

He stretches out the heavens as though they were nothing—that is, extremely subtle and thin, like smoke.

And he spreads them out like a tent for habitation, so that human beings and the other animals might dwell beneath their rounded covering as in a tent.

[Col. 0386C] **VERSE 23.**—“He reduces investigators of hidden things to nothing; he has made the judges of the earth like emptiness.”

By “investigators” are meant philosophers and the wise of this age, whom the Lord has reduced to nothing, as the Apostle says: “Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the inquirer of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?” (1 Cor. 1:20). He also made the judges of the earth, who unjustly condemned Christians, like emptiness, removing their power. These two classes of people—the wise of this age and judges—greatly resisted evangelical preaching; and therefore a divine sentence had to be pronounced especially against them. Of them it is added:

[Col. 0386D] **VERSE 24.**—“Indeed, neither planted nor sown nor rooted in the earth is their stock.”

For their body was not established in the earth with any strength such that it could not easily be overthrown.

“Suddenly he blew upon them, and they perished; and a whirlwind shall carry them away like stubble.” The Lord suddenly blew upon them—that is, the sentence of the Judge came upon them unexpectedly—and through death they withered from the freshness of the present life. The whirlwind of the Lord’s judgment swept them from this life like stubble: dry, empty, and fit for burning. After the Lord had declared the works [Col. 0387A] of his power and his own greatness, he again rebukes those who thought that he could be represented in some image, saying:

**VERSE 25.**—“To whom have you likened me and made me equal, says the Holy One?”

That is: To what image have you made me like and equal, I who am so great?

**VERSE 26.**—“Lift up your eyes to heaven and see who created these things.”

That is, look up to heaven and understand who it is that created the things found there. For all people are vain in whom knowledge of God is absent; and from the things that appear good they could not understand him who is, nor, attending to the works, recognize who the craftsman was. “For his invisible things, from the [Col. 0387B] creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that have been made—his eternal power and divinity as well—so that they are without excuse” (Rom. 1:20).

“He who brings forth in number the host of heaven [Note: [Col. 0387D] Elsewhere: ‘their host.’], and calls them all by name.” He calls the stars “the host of heaven,” as Moses shows when he says of certain people “that they transgress the covenant of the Lord by going and serving foreign gods and worshipping them—the sun, the moon, and all the host of heaven” (Deut. 17:2). Therefore he brings forth the host of heaven in number because he causes the stars to appear at fixed times so that they may shine, and he holds their number in his wisdom. And he calls all the stars by name because he alone knows their [Col. 0387C] names. This is also said by the Psalmist: “He counts the multitude of the stars and calls them all by names” (Ps. 146:4). Or we may understand the host of heaven as the angels and all the heavenly armies.

“Because of the abundance of his strength, his might, and his power, not one was left behind.” Not one of these stars was left behind—that is, not one was lacking—because of the abundance of the strength of him who created them. For manifold is that power which made all these things such that not one should be missing; and the greatness of his strength causes all things always to obey their own order.

**VERSE 27.**—“Why do you say, Jacob, and speak, Israel: ‘My way is hidden from the Lord, and my judgment has passed from my God’?”

The ten tribes, which were already held captive among the Assyrians when Isaiah spoke these things, had, because of the enormity of the evils they suffered, reached the point of thinking that God did not know what happens here, since they believed themselves afflicted more than was just. For that people said: “My way is hidden from the Lord,” that is, the Lord does not see my action; “and my judgment has passed from my God,” that is, God has omitted to judge me, because I suffer so many evils undeservedly. It was as though they said: Earthly things do not concern God, because, seated in heaven, he does not consider what each of us does; and therefore we are afflicted here not unjustly, because we have no ruler or defender. Hence they are now divinely rebuked when it is said: “Why do you say, Jacob, and speak, Israel: ‘My way is hidden from the Lord, and my judgment has passed from my God’?”

In our own times too, a great part of this people called Christian says similar things, when it supposes either that God does not see the many wrongs done here, or that he permits them to occur by a just judgment. For one says, “My way is hidden from the Lord,” when he thinks that his manner of life is not seen by God; and he says that his judgment has passed from God when he does not think himself now justly judged by him in what he suffers. He too is rebuked by the words that follow:

**VERSE 28.**—“Do you not know, or have you not heard? The everlasting God, the Lord who created the ends of the earth, will not fail or grow weary, and there is no searching out of his wisdom.”

You who say that your way is hidden from the Lord and your judgment has passed from God: do you say this of yourself, or have you not heard from another that God, the everlasting Lord, who created not only the things you see but also the farthest ends of the world—so that he is understood to have created everything within its boundaries—will not fail, since he is eternal, nor grow weary, since he is impassible, and that his wisdom cannot be searched out? For if you say that your judgment has passed from him, you will think that he who created all things, rules all things by eternal power, governs and orders all things, has failed in his customary governance of everything—as though he toiled in governing and ordering, though he created all things without toil and rules all things without disturbance. And if you think your way hidden from him, you will judge the wisdom of him who eternally knows all things to be scant. That he himself cannot fail is demonstrated by what follows:

**VERSE 29.**—“He gives strength to the weary, and multiplies strength and power to those who are not.”

For how can he fail or grow weary when he strengthens the weary? By “those who are not,” he means, I think, those of whom the Apostle says: “God chose the lowborn and despised things of the world, and the things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are” (1 Cor. 1:28). [Col. 0388D] To them the Lord multiplies strength for good works and strength of mind. Their strength is then shown in what follows:

**VERSE 30.**—“Boys shall fail and grow weary, and young men shall fall in weakness.”

**VERSE 31.**—“But those who hope in the Lord shall change their strength; they shall take up wings like eagles; they shall run and not grow weary; they shall walk and not fail.”

Boys—that is, youths—will fail through toil, and young men will become weak. That is, those who flourish among worldly people in great health, who are most strong and swift, will become weary in their labours and weak, [Col. 0389A] because even a flourishing age quickly collapses and robust bodies wither. But those who hope not in their own powers but in the Lord will be stronger than all worldly people.

They shall change their strength, because those formerly strong in the flesh will become stronger in spiritual work. For the strength of the righteous is one thing and that of the reprobate another. The strength of the righteous is to overcome the flesh, oppose their own pleasures, extinguish delight in the present life, love this world’s hardships for the sake of eternal rewards, and conquer the opposing enemy in the heart. But the strength of the reprobate is to love transitory things without cessation; to persist without feeling against the Creator’s chastisements; to attain empty glory even at the cost of life; to attack the life of the good not only by words and conduct but also by swords; to place hope in themselves; and to perpetrate iniquity every day without any decline in desire. How well the prophet has now embraced both kinds of strength by saying: “But those who hope in the Lord shall change their strength!” For when he said not that they would receive strength, but that they would change it, he plainly made known that one strength is laid aside and another begins.

They take up wings like eagles because they fly in contemplation. They run and do not grow weary because with great swiftness they preach to the swift. They walk and do not fail because they retain the swiftness of their understanding in order to accommodate themselves to those who are slower.

Or, those who now have strength in good works will change their strength in the resurrection, because “the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (1 Cor. 15:52)—“For the body is sown in weakness, but rises in power” (ibid., 43).

They shall take up wings—that is, the flight of eagles—when they are caught up in clouds to meet Christ in the air. They shall run and not grow weary because “then the lame shall leap like a deer” (above, 35:6). Hence Malachi also promises them, as we have often said: “You shall go out and leap like calves from the herd” (Mal. 4:2).

They shall walk and not fail when “they shall follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Rev. 14:4). For by that transformation every corruption, [Col. 0389D] slowness, sense of suffering, and frailty will be removed from their bodies, so that wherever they wish to go, they may go without delay or difficulty, and do whatever pleases them. Since, therefore, God grants such strength to those who hope in him, it is evident that he himself neither fails nor grows weary.

## CHAPTER XLI

**VERSE 1.**—“Let the islands be silent before me, and let the nations change their strength.”

Let the islands that are far out at sea be silent in order to hear me, so that they no longer utter their old errors but listen to my teaching. And let the nations change their strength by hoping in the Lord, so that those who were strong in the flesh may become strong in spirit, and those who served [Col. 0390A] sin may now serve righteousness.

“Let them draw near, and then speak; together let us approach judgment.”

Let them draw near to me through faith, and then speak, as it is written: “I believed, and therefore I spoke” (Ps. 115:10). For one who is far from God in error does not know how to speak rightly. Let us approach judgment together, so that, seeing in their hearts both the good things they received from me, who gives life, breath, and all things to everyone, and the evil things they rendered in return for my benefits by living perversely, they may justify me and correct their perversities.

**VERSE 2.**—“Who raised up the righteous one from the east, called him to follow himself? He will give nations before him, and he will subdue kings; he will make them like dust to his sword and like stubble driven by the wind to his bow.”

**VERSE 3.**—“He shall pursue them, pass on in peace; the path beneath his feet shall not appear.”

The Jewish people is called the east because from its flesh was born he who is called the Sun of righteousness. The righteous one is the same as our Saviour, “who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22). Therefore the Father says: Who raised up the righteous one from the east—that is, Christ from the Jewish people—except myself? The same Father called him to follow himself to the peoples of the nations, because “the Son cannot do anything of himself except what he sees the Father doing. For whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does; for the Father loves the Son and shows him all that he himself does” (John 5:19). Thus the Father is rightly said to call the Son, so that in undifferentiated and inseparable operation he may follow him, because the Son is from the Father. This Father will give nations before him, according to what the ambassadors of the peoples are reported to have said to Holofernes: “Behold, we are servants of King Nebuchadnezzar the Great before you; use us as is pleasing before your face” (Judith 3:1–7). Therefore he will give nations before him, for him to use them in all things as he pleases. And he himself will subdue kings—that is, overcome and capture them spiritually—so that they may serve him and all nations may worship him.

He calls his sword “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. 6:17), and his bow Holy Scripture, from which, as arrows striking human hearts, sentences come to terrify them, because “he has bent his bow and made it ready” (Ps. 7:13). Dust and stubble, light and dry, which the wind easily drives, signify the fickleness of sinners, who are shaken by the wind of temptation; for the sinner deserved to hear: “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3:19). Again, it is said of the sinner: “You pursue dry stubble” (Job 13:25).

Therefore the Father gave them as dust to his sword and as stubble driven by the wind to his bow, because his preaching found all pagan sinners dry, empty, and wandering, unable to stand before him with any weight of reason or truth, but fleeing because of their own lightness. Pursuing them as they fled from place to place with the sword of his preaching, he passed on in peace through the teachers, once faith had grown so that no one dared wage war upon his saints. And the path beneath his feet did not appear because wherever he went he trod upon the necks of his enemies and, as it were, did not touch the earth.

Or, kings and nations will bow their necks before his face, and hostile powers will be subjected to his sword and arrows like stubble and dust. He will pursue them—that is, the kings and rulers of each individual nation—and pass through in peace, calling all to peace, that they may be reconciled to God. The path beneath his feet shall not appear: that is, he will feel no weariness of the road nor any exhaustion belonging to human weakness, but “he shall drink from the torrent on the way; therefore he shall lift up his head” (Ps. 109:7).

**VERSE 4.**—“Who has wrought and done these things, calling the generations from the beginning? I, the Lord, am the first, and I am the last.”

Who has wrought the things stated above except I, God the Father, who have called each generation from the beginning of the world to know me? I, the Lord, have done it. For I am the first and the last; therefore, as the everlasting Lord, I called the human race both in ancient and in latter times. I called through angels, through Noah, through Abraham and the other patriarchs, through the lawgiver, through prophets, and through teachers in ancient times; and in latter times through the heralds of new grace.

[Col. 0391C] **VERSE 5.**—“The islands saw and feared; the ends of the earth were astonished; they drew near and came.”
