The islands—that is, the more remote regions of the ocean—saw the nations of the world given like dust to the sword of my Righteous One, and they feared, because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. 1:16). The ends of the earth—that is, the boundaries of the world—were astonished when they heard the preaching of the Gospel, recoiled at the enormity of their sins, and dreaded the condemnation impending over such people. And after fear they drew near in faith to this Righteous One, who slays all with the sword of his preaching so that they may be wounded unto salvation; and they came near through action.

**VERSE 6.**—“Each shall help his neighbour and say to his brother: ‘Be strong.’”

**VERSE 7.**—“The bronze-worker who struck with the hammer strengthened him; the one who forged at that time said the solder was good, and he strengthened it with nails, that it might not move.”

Each person coming to Christ will help his neighbour, so that “he who hears may say, ‘Come’” (Rev. 22:17). For that is true charity which hastens to God in such a way as not to leave one’s neighbour behind. And every stronger person will say to his weaker brother: “Be strong in the Lord, for the idols you thought were gods are nothing.” For the bronze-worker who struck it with a hammer strengthened the idol; the forger, while idols were being made, said to the solder of iron or bronze, “It is good”—that is, it is well made. After completing the idol, he set it in its place and fastened it with nails, lest it move or fall through some impact. Thus spoke one who wished to strengthen in the faith a gentile newly converted. Therefore, after the conversion of the nations, he addresses the Church itself from among the nations and fortifies it against persecution by unbelievers, saying:

**VERSE 8.**—“But you, Israel, are my servant; Jacob, whom I chose; the seed of Abraham, my friend.”

**VERSE 9.**—“In whom I took hold of you from the ends of the earth, and called you from its distant regions, and said to you: ‘You are my servant; I chose you and did not cast you away,’” etc.

For the spiritual Israel, or Jacob, is the one now under discussion, concerning whom the Apostle also says: “As many as shall follow this rule, peace be upon them and mercy, and upon the Israel of God” (Gal. 6:16). This is the Israel of God—that is, the people of believers—because those who are of faith are children of Abraham, who is father of us all, as it is written: “I have made you the father of many nations before God, whom you believed” (Rom. 4:17). Therefore the people gathered from the nations into faith is called Abraham’s seed, as the Apostle also says: “But if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise” (Gal. 3:29). This people of believers was taken hold of in Abraham, as the Apostle shows when he says: “Scripture, foreseeing [Col. 0392C] that God justifies the nations by faith, announced beforehand to Abraham: ‘In you all nations shall be blessed’” (ibid., 8–9).

This people, therefore, the children of Abraham, has been summoned from the whole world. To it, as it enters the faith, the Lord says: “You are my servant,” because he found it especially obedient. For it is a great privilege of election when the Lord deigns to call someone his own in preference to others. “I chose you,” he says, “that you might be mine, and I did not cast you away,” although you have fallen into various temptations. Or we may here understand Israel as the primitive Church, which he called from the ends and distant regions of the earth, gathering from all nations first the people of the Jews.

**VERSE 10.**—“Do not fear, for I am with you; [Col. 0392D] do not turn aside, for I am your God.”

Do not fear the savagery of persecutors, for I am with you to protect you and direct your works. Do not turn aside from the way of truth, deceived by the enticement of unbelievers, for I am your God, who enlightens you.

“I have strengthened you and helped you, and the right hand of my Righteous One”—that is, Christ—“has upheld you.” This is clear.

**VERSE 11.**—“Behold, all who fight against you shall be confounded and ashamed.”

The enemies of the Church were ashamed when faith prevailed and unbelief gradually failed together with its supporters. Hence it is also plainly added:

“They shall be as though they were not, and the men who oppose you shall perish.”

[Col. 0393A] **VERSE 12.**—“You shall seek them and not find your rebellious men; they shall be as though they were not, and like the destruction of a man fighting against you.”

That is, as if any insignificant man should attempt to fight against you and, while fighting against you, be consumed and come to nothing. Here a most evident oracle has been uttered concerning the destruction of the Church’s enemies.

**VERSE 13.**—“For I, the Lord your God, take hold of your hand and say to you: ‘Do not fear; I have helped you.’”

I am God, who take hold of your hand in order to lead you while sustaining you, so that you may say to me: “You have held my right hand; in your will you have guided [Col. 0393B] me, and with glory you have received me” (Ps. 72:24). I am the one who says to you: “Do not fear any adversary or labour, for I have helped you.”

**VERSE 14.**—“Do not fear, worm Jacob, you who are dead from Israel.”

The worm Jacob is called the Church, imitating him who said: “I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. 21:7). For a worm is produced without seed, and those were begotten without corruptible seed “who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God” (John 1:13). A worm is trodden underfoot, just as the Church was then trodden underfoot by the ungodly and cast aside. A worm pierces the earth with its mouth; so too the speech of the Church wore away the hearts of the faithful. Therefore the Lord commands the worm—that is, [Col. 0393C] the Church—not to fear its adversaries. Its elect are spiritually dead to this world, that they may live to God, as the Apostle says to them: “For you are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3:3). They too are commanded not to fear. It follows:

“I have helped you, says the Lord, and your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel.”

“I have helped you,” says the Lord, so that through patience you might overcome all your enemies. And my Christ has helped you: he who redeemed you by his own blood, and who is the Holy One of the saints, whom Israel awaited, saying: “I will await your salvation, O Lord” (Gen. 49:18). It follows:

[Col. 0393D] VERSE 15.—“I have made you like a new threshing-sledge having serrated teeth.”

Just as in threshing a new sledge with serrated teeth is drawn over the crops, in order to crush the chaff and bring out the grain, so the Church, made new through Christ and endowed with most keen tongues, advances over the human race, in order to reveal the elect through cleansing and crush the reprobate by trampling them down. And the Church is aptly compared with a sledge. The sledge, like the Church, is borne by the four books of the Gospels, and is drawn along the way of righteousness by the laborious striving of holy preachers. It follows:

“You shall thresh the mountains and crush them, and make the hills like dust.”

VERSE 16.—“You shall winnow them, and the wind shall carry them away, and [Col. 0394A] the whirlwind shall scatter them; and you shall exult in the Lord and rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.”

What are meant here by mountains and hills except those who swell with worldly power? “You shall thresh the mountains,” therefore, he says: that is, by preaching you shall crush the hearts of the proud powers of this world; and you shall make the hills—that is, exalted rulers—like dust: you shall cause them to recognize that they are dust.

“You shall winnow them,” that is, you shall agitate them by your teaching; “and the wind shall carry them away,” that is, the present life, which passes swiftly like the wind, shall take them away through death; and the whirlwind of the Lord’s judgment shall scatter them. Life is called wind, as Job says: “Remember that my life is wind” (Job 7:7). The judge’s sentence is also denoted by the name of a whirlwind, as was said above: [Col. 0394B] “the whirlwind shall carry them away like chaff.” Therefore, once the enemies of faith have been removed and peace granted, you shall exult in the Lord, because he has subjected the whole world to you.

Or this signifies that evangelical preaching crushes hostile powers and spiritual wickedness that exalts itself against the knowledge of God; these are called mountains and hills according to the varieties of their pride. When they have been removed and scattered like a whirlwind, Israel exults in the Lord. Again he begins to speak of the conversion of the Gentiles, saying:

VERSE 17.—“The needy and poor seek waters, and there are none; their tongue has dried up with thirst. I, the Lord, will hear them; the God of Israel will not forsake them.”

[Col. 0394C] The needy and poor are the Gentiles, who lacked inward riches. They sought the waters of true knowledge, like that Ethiopian who had come to worship in Jerusalem and was returning, seated in his chariot and reading the prophet Isaiah. Yet there were no waters for them, just as the Ethiopian could not find the water of understanding. When Philip said to him, “Do you think you understand what you are reading?” he answered, “And how can I understand unless someone shows me?” (Acts 8:30). Their tongue dried up with thirst, because the word of truth had departed from their mouth through ignorance. Or they sought wholesome waters through different teachers and the various doctrines of philosophers, but did not find them, because they were not there. Their tongue dried up with thirst, lacking the Law and the prophets.

[Col. 0394D] Yet the God of Israel did not wholly forsake them: “I, the Lord, will hear them,” as he heard Cornelius, who was “devout and fearing God with all his household, giving many alms to the people and praying to God continually” (Acts 10:2).

“I, the God of Israel, will not forsake them,” because “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and there shall be one fold and one shepherd” (John 10:10). It follows:

VERSE 18.—“I will open rivers upon the sloping hills, and fountains in the midst of the plains; I will make the desert into pools of water, and the pathless land into streams of water.”

What is denoted by sloping hills except those to whom [Col. 0395A] the Apostle says: “If you have risen again with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God” (Col. 3:1)? For since Christ is a mountain, those who cling to him and are raised up with him are rightly called hills; and they are sloping, that is, looking upward, while they seek the things above. Therefore God opened rivers of preaching among the Gentiles upon these hills. For behold: in holy preachers, even those not descended from Judea, streams of heavenly commandments flow abundantly from Gentile mouths throughout the Church spread over the whole world. And in the midst of the plains—that is, in the midst of peoples—he opened fountains of new knowledge, so that all who thirst might go to them and carry back vessels of their hearts full of truth.

[Col. 0395B] He also made the desert—that is, the Gentile people, formerly dry and unfruitful—into pools of water, that is, into the abundance and depth of the knowledge of truth; and the pathless land, that is, that same Gentile world through which no preacher had walked, into streams of water, that is, of heavenly teaching. It follows:

VERSE 19.—“I will give in the wilderness cedar and thorn, myrtle and olive tree; I will set in the desert fir, elm, and box tree together.”

VERSE 20.—“That they may see, and know, and consider, and understand together that the hand of the Lord has done this, and the Holy One of Israel has created it.”

[Col. 0395C] The divine discourse now promises rational trees, of which it now says: “That they may see, know, and understand together.” Let us therefore strive to understand them rationally. Since cedar has a great fragrance and an incorruptible nature, the name cedar signifies those who work virtues and signs, who can say: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Cor. 2:15). Their hearts are so strengthened by inward love that no decay of earthly love can now corrupt them.

The thorn signifies teachers who, while discoursing on sins and virtues and now threatening eternal punishments, now promising the joys of the heavenly kingdom, pierce the minds of their hearers with the pain of compunction, so that tears—the very blood, as it were, of the soul—flow from their eyes.

[Col. 0395D] Myrtle possesses a moderating power, so that it restrains and gathers together loosened limbs by tempering them. The myrtle signifies those who know how to sympathize with the afflictions of their neighbors and temper their tribulation through compassion. When they bring to afflicted neighbors a word or aid of consolation, they restore them to a state of uprightness, lest excessive tribulation dissolve them into despair.

The olive, indeed, represents the merciful, because in Greek *eleos* means “mercy,” and the fruit of mercy shines before God’s eyes like the liquid of an olive.

The fir, because in growing it rises very high, signifies the saints who, though still placed bodily on earth, already contemplate heavenly things in mind; and although by birth they have sprung from earth, yet in contemplation [Col. 0396A] they already raise the summit of the mind close to the heavens.

The elm, however, because it has no fruit of its own but nevertheless commonly bears the fruit-bearing vine, represents those who, while occupied with earthly cares, bear no fruit of spiritual virtues, yet sustain by their generosity saints who are full of spiritual gifts.

The box tree, which does not grow high and, although it bears no fruit, remains green, signifies those in the Church who, because of the weakness of their age, are not yet able to bear good works, but retain through imitation of the Fathers the faith of unfading greenness.

[Col. 0396B] After all this it is aptly added: “That they may see, and know, and consider, and understand.” For this purpose the cedar is placed in the Church: that whoever draws the fragrance of virtues from a neighbor may himself be kindled with desire for heavenly gifts. For this purpose the thorn is placed there: that one who has been pierced by the word of its preaching may himself learn to pierce the hearts of others with the word of preaching. For this purpose the myrtle is placed there: that one who, in the heat of tribulation, receives from the word or deed of a compassionate neighbor the moderation of consolation may himself learn how to offer the moderation of consolation to afflicted neighbors. For this purpose the olive is placed there: that one who recognizes works of another’s mercy may himself learn to show mercy to those in need. For this purpose the fir is placed there: that one who recognizes its power of contemplation may be kindled to contemplate eternal rewards. For this purpose the elm is placed there: that one who sees a man unable to possess the fruit of virtues yet sustaining spiritual men may himself strive to minister to the saints. For this purpose the box tree is placed there: that one who sees children flourishing in faith may be ashamed to be unbelieving.

[Col. 0396C] “Together” is well added, because, although the dispositions of people and their orders in the Church are diverse, all must learn at once when they see at once men of different spiritual quality, age, and rank set before them for imitation. For what they ought to see and understand is then added, namely: that the hand of the Lord of hosts has done this, causing the aforesaid trees to grow in the wilderness of the Gentiles—that is, the above-mentioned varieties of saints—so that every person may find in them what [Col. 0396D] he ought to imitate. “And the Holy One of Israel created it,” namely, what was said concerning the trees. For this is the new creation (2 Cor. 5:17) praised by the Apostle. After this the discourse turns to those Gentiles who refused to believe, commanding them to give an account of the unbelief in which they chose rather to remain.

VERSE 21.—“Bring forward,” he says, “your case, says the Lord; produce, if perhaps you have anything, says the King of Jacob.”

VERSE 22.—“Let them come near and declare to you whatever things are to come.”

Bring forward your case, by which you judge it good to remain in idolatry; that is, bring it here before me, and let us see whether you refuse to believe by a just [Col. 0397A] judgment. Bring here, if perhaps you have any just cause why you are unwilling to see, know, consider, and understand that I have placed the aforesaid trees in your wilderness, so that they might sprinkle it all with their fragrance and renew it.

Or, “if perhaps you have anything,” that is, if you possess any valid ground of honorable defense, bring it forward.

Let the gods whom you preferred to serve come here and declare to you the things to come. For if they are gods, they can foretell future things without falsehood; but if they cannot, it is evident that they are not gods. No one can truthfully foretell future things except God, since even prophets cannot know beforehand except through his Spirit. For he alone who orders all things knows how he will order each thing; and he alone who does [Col. 0397B] whatever he wills knows what he will do, unless he chooses to reveal something to someone. Then, turning his speech toward those themselves who are called gods of the Gentiles, he adds:

“Declare the former things that have been, and we will set our heart upon them and know their final outcome; and make known to us the things that are to come.”

VERSE 23.—“Declare what is to come in the future, and we shall know that you are gods.”

Declare to us, O gods of the Gentiles, if you can, the former things that existed before the world; and we will set our heart upon them, that is, we will think upon them. We shall know their final outcome, because one who knows the former things can also know their final outcome. And declare what is to come after the end of the age, and we shall know that you are gods. For [Col. 0397C] this knowledge belongs to Divinity alone. What creature can know what existed in the eternity of things before this world was created? Or who can know what will happen after the consummation of the age? Hence the seraphim, who by the merit of their dignity stand immediately before God, are said to “cover his face and feet” (above, 6:2), signifying that former things and final things are hidden from every creature. Thus it is rightly said to those called gods of the Gentiles that, if they declare these things, it will be known that they are gods, because knowledge of these matters belongs to divine knowledge alone. Therefore whoever cannot declare them is plainly not God.

This statement also signifies that after Christ’s advent all idols fell silent. [Col. 0397D] For where now is Delphic Apollo, and the other demons who promised knowledge of the future and deceived the most powerful kings? Why could they foretell nothing concerning Christ, when they were able to announce things belonging to others, whether evil or good? But if someone says that many things were foretold by idols, he should know that they always joined falsehood to truth and so framed their oracles that, whether good or evil happened, either outcome could be understood. Moreover, in what the supreme Divinity says, “We will set our heart,” it should be noted that one heart—that is, one will and one wisdom—is shown to belong to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. It follows:

“Do good or evil, if you can, and let us speak and see together.”

[Col. 0398A] The gods of the Gentiles are so useless that they can not only not declare former and final things, but can do neither good nor evil, because “they have hands and shall not feel; they have feet and shall not walk” (Ps. 113:7). Nor can they speak or see, because “they have mouths and shall not speak; they have eyes and shall not see” (ibid., 5). It follows:

VERSE 24.—“Behold, you are from nothing, and your work is from that which does not exist; an abomination is he who chose you.”

Idols are from nothing, because one wishing to make an idol fashions in his heart what never was and never will be, and makes an image according to the likeness of his conceived thought. Thus it is rightly said to them: “You are from [Col. 0398B] nothing, and your work”—that is, that by which you have been fashioned into gods—“is from that which does not exist,” because no god was ever like these images. Therefore whoever chooses to worship you is an abomination, that is, an object of rejection and detestation. It follows:

VERSE 25.—“I have raised one up from the north, and he shall come from the rising of the sun; he shall call upon my name and shall bring rulers as mud, and as a potter trampling clay.”

What is signified by the north except the Gentile world, constrained by the cold of unbelief? Hence the ancient enemy planned to place his seat in the north (above, 14:13). And what is expressed by the rising of the sun except the Jewish people, in whom the sun of righteousness, born according to the flesh, first began to shine and afterward illumined the whole world? “I have raised up the Gentiles from the north,” he says, “to faith,” that is, from unbelief; and through the apostles the Savior shall come to them from the rising of the sun—that is, from the Jewish people, first illumined by the splendor of faith. Cornelius was raised from the north when he persevered in continual prayers and almsgiving, and at last the true sun came to him through Peter (Acts 10). The Ethiopian eunuch likewise, raised from the north, came to worship in Jerusalem and was divinely enlightened through Philip (Acts 8). “He shall call upon my name,” he says, because he will do all things in the name of his Father.

And he shall make rulers like mud: that is, he shall reduce the powers of this world to mud, casting down [Col. 0398D] all worldly glory. And as a maker—that is, a potter—trampling clay makes new vessels as he wills, so Christ will trample down all worldly pride, that he may fashion vessels of mercy according to his pleasure, he who says through Jeremiah: “Behold, as clay in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand, house of Israel” (Jer. 18:6). It follows:

VERSE 26.—“Who declared it from the beginning, that we might know, and from the first, that we might say: You are righteous? There is none declaring, nor foretelling, nor hearing your words.”

Which of all the gods of the Gentiles declared these things from the beginning, as I did when I said to Abraham that “your seed shall possess the gates of its enemies, and in your seed all nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:17)? And which of them declared these things from the first, so that, when he had done them as he foretold, we might say to him: “You are righteous, for you have fulfilled all things as you foretold”? None of your gods can do these things; I alone do them, for I alone am God. For none of them declares or foretells future things, nor can any hear your words if you say to him, “You are righteous,” because a senseless statue can neither hear nor speak. By many modes of reasoning the Lord deigns to show that idols cannot possess divinity. It follows:

VERSE 27.—“The First said to Zion: Behold, I am here; and I will give Jerusalem an evangelist.”

He is the First of whom we read: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). He said to Zion—that is, [Col. 0399B] to the Jewish people—“Behold, I am here,” because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father” (ibid., 14). For he said, “Behold, I am here,” when he made known that he was present, he whose coming was awaited. And because he preached the Gospel in Judea, the Father rightly adds concerning him: “I will give Jerusalem an evangelist,” that is, a preacher of the Gospel, who says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he anointed me and sent me to preach good news to the poor” (Luke 4:18). For an evangelist is called a bringer of good news, and Christ is the bringer of good news, of whom we read: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of one announcing and preaching peace, announcing good, preaching salvation” (Isa. 52:7). Having sent this Evangelist [Col. 0399C] into Jerusalem, the Father adds concerning his contemporaries:

VERSE 28.—“And I looked, and there was no one—not one among these—who would enter into counsel and, when questioned, answer a word.”

“I looked,” that is, I considered all people who were then on earth, and among them there was no one who would enter into counsel concerning how he might attain salvation, or who, when questioned, would answer a word about his manner of life. “Not one among these”—that is, among the Jerusalemites, among the Jews—did this. For the Jews had also lost knowledge of the Scriptures, and were unwilling to form a resolution to believe in Christ or to act rightly; when questioned about what they did, [Col. 0399D] they could not answer. It follows:

VERSE 29.—“Behold, all are unrighteous, and their works are vain; their idols are wind and emptiness.”

Behold, all are unrighteous, as the Apostle says: “We have charged both Jews and Greeks, all of them, with being under sin, as it is written: There is no righteous person, not even one; there is none who understands, none who seeks God. All have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Rom. 3:9). All were such when the Savior appeared in the flesh. And their works were vain, because they did everything for temporal life. “Their idols are wind and emptiness.” For “we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is no God but one” (1 Cor. 8:4). [Col. 0400A] But among such people, let us hear what kind of person our Redeemer was found to be. It follows:

## CHAPTER XLII

VERSE 1.—“Behold my servant: I will uphold him; my chosen one, in whom my soul has taken pleasure. I have put my Spirit upon him; he shall bring forth judgment to the Gentiles.”

VERSE 2.—“He shall not cry out, nor show partiality, nor shall his voice be heard outside.”

VERSE 3.—“He shall not break the bruised reed, and he shall not quench the smoking flax; in truth he shall bring forth judgment.”

VERSE 4.—“He shall not be sad nor troubled, until he has established judgment on earth; and the islands shall await his law.”

[Col. 0400B] “Behold my servant,” whom above I gave to Jerusalem as an evangelist. He is called servant, for he “though he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6). And he is chosen from among all: “For God the Father has sealed him” (John 6:27). In him the soul—that is, the will—of the Father rightly took pleasure, because in all things he saw him. When he adds, “I will uphold him,” he speaks of the glory of his assumption. For he upheld him, “setting him at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality and power and might and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come, [Col. 0400C] and subjected all things beneath his feet” (Eph. 1:20).

“I have put my Spirit upon him,” he says. John likewise bore testimony, saying: “I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and it remained upon him” (John 1:32). He rightly says “upon him,” because he speaks of the Son of Man, whom he also called his servant. For according to divinity the Spirit is not upon Christ but in Christ; for as the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, so the Holy Spirit is in the Father and the Son. Thus according to divinity he is not upon Christ, because the Trinity is not above itself but above all things; it is not above itself, but within itself.

The Savior brought forth to the Gentiles the judgment of just discernment, concerning which it is said that “there is no judgment [Col. 0400D] in their paths” (Isa. 59:8). For paths are called the actions on which they rely. But there is no judgment in their paths because they neglect to examine their actions, so as to avoid evil and perform good in doing all things with judgment. The Lord therefore issued such judgment to the Gentiles through his apostles, granting them the word of knowledge, though they were held fast by errors.

The words that follow, “He shall not cry out, nor show partiality, nor shall his voice be heard outside,” are read thus in Matthew: “He shall not contend or cry out, nor shall anyone hear his voice in the streets” (Matt. 12:19). This must therefore be understood of the gentleness of his character, because he did not speak in a loud or contentious voice. Here too his truth [Col. 0401A] is evident, because he showed partiality to no person in order to flatter anyone, but rebuked all as was fitting. His modesty is also shown by the fact that no one “heard his voice outside in the streets.” For he never uttered an idle or frivolous word, as do those who cry out in the streets and reveal the vanity of their hearts. Or his voice was not heard outside because he did not preach the Gospel beyond Galilee, Judea, and Samaria.

What is designated by the reed except the temporal kingdom of the Jewish people [Note: [Col. 0401] Everything is missing in the Garsten manuscript down to: “his foreign-born [one].”], outwardly indeed standing erect but inwardly empty? And because in that people the royal line had already failed and a foreigner possessed its kingdom, that kingdom is aptly called a bruised reed. What, moreover, is expressed by flax except [Col. 0401B] its priesthood, which used linen garments? Since at the Lord’s advent it had lost the ardor of charity, it was, as though the fire of faith had now been lost, not burning but smoking. Therefore the incarnate Lord did not break the bruised reed or quench the smoking flax, because he did not strike by the power of judgment the kingdom of Judea, already almost destroyed, nor its priesthood, which did not retain the fire of faith; rather, he endured them with the long-suffering of patience.

Or, “he shall not break the bruised reed,” because he will be gracious to sinners and grant pardon to sinners. And “he shall not quench the smoking flax,” because those who were near to extinction will be saved by his mercy. For at the second advent he will bring forth judgment in truth, when he renders to each according to [Col. 0401C] his works. Or even at the first advent he brought forth judgment in truth, as he says: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39).

He was not sad or troubled, but always performed his actions cheerfully and gently, until he established judgment on earth—that is, until he formed all people for imitation of himself, so that they might do everything with judgment, as was said above. It is evident that he was not afterward sad or troubled; but the prophet bore testimony concerning the period about which doubt could arise, just as the evangelist, speaking of his virgin mother, declared that Joseph did not know her “until she bore a son” (Matt. [Col. 0401D] 1:25), though certainly he did not know her afterward either. For the divine Scriptures frequently use this manner of speaking. After the Lord established judgment on earth—that is, in the breadth of the world—by which those who believe in him discern all that they intend to do, even the islands, that is, the more remote regions of the Ocean, received the law of his preaching, which they awaited. Turning his speech toward him, the Father adds:

VERSE 5.—“Thus says the Lord God, creating the heavens and stretching them out, establishing the earth and what springs from it, giving breath to the people who are upon it and spirit to those who tread upon it.”

VERSE 6.—“I, the Lord, have called you in righteousness, [Col. 0402A] and have taken hold of your hand, and preserved you, and given you as a covenant of the people, as a light of the Gentiles.”

VERSE 7.—“That you might open the eyes of the blind, and lead the bound person out of confinement, those sitting in darkness out of the prison-house.”

The Lord indeed creates the heavens and stretches them out like a tent for habitation; and he himself establishes the earth by its lofty mass, that it may not incline for ever and ever. He also establishes what springs from it, such as trees, so that they may stand upright upon their trunks. He gives breath—that is, the breath of life—to the people upon it, that they may live as animate beings; and the Holy Spirit to those who tread it underfoot, that is, who despise earthly things.

But this Lord, who does such things, addresses Christ, saying: “I have called you in righteousness,” so that, being righteous, [Col. 0402B] you might proceed to justify the world. “And I have taken hold of your hand,” so that, strengthening you, I might lead you in my will, because whatever the Son does, the Father also does. “And I have preserved you,” he says, from sin; “and given you as a covenant of the people,” that is, into the fellowship of friendship of the multitude of believing Hebrews, whose heart and soul were one. “And I have given you as a light of the Gentiles,” that you might illumine those sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death; that you might open the inward eyes of the blind Gentiles, that they might behold the light of truth. For the Gentiles were blind because, not having received the Law, they did not see where they ought to go.

“And you might lead out,” he says, “from the confinement of the heart the Gentile people bound by the cords of their sins, and from the prison-house of the heart those sitting in the darkness of error [Col. 0402C] and ignorance.” For what else does every person make for himself by acting wickedly except a prison of his own conscience? For when, under God’s judgment, he is left in the blindness of his wickedness, he is as though shut up within himself, lest he find a place of escape which he does not deserve to find. Often some wish to depart from evil deeds, but they are pressed down by the weight of those same deeds, so that, enclosed in the prison of evil habit, they cannot escape from themselves. Indeed, when they desire to punish their own faults, they turn what they think they are doing rightly into graver sins; and in a wondrous way, what they regard as an exit becomes for them imprisonment. Thus the reprobate Judas, when he brought death upon himself after his sin, came to the punishments of eternal death, [Col. 0402D] and repented of his sin worse than he had sinned. From such confinement the Savior came to lead out the bound; he was sent to free those sitting in such a prison-house, in outer darkness. It follows:

VERSE 8.—“I am the Lord: this is my name. I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to carved images.”

He wished to be called Lord in order to show that all things serve him, as it is said to him through the Psalmist: “For all things serve you” (Ps. 118:91). He did not give the glory of this lordship to another, because “there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. 4:5). For just as there cannot be two or more faiths, or two [Col. 0403A] baptisms, so neither can there be two, three, or more lords. For the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one Lord. He will not give his glory to another—that is, to any idol—as those thought who imposed the undefiled Name upon stones and wood. “They changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds and quadrupeds and serpents” (Rom. 1:23). The Lord will not give his glory to such an image, as those wished who “exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator” (ibid., 25). But lest the Father seem by this statement to exclude the Son from his glory, while excluding idols, he added: “nor my praise to carved images” [Col. 0403B]—understand, “will I give.” For the Son is not separated from the Father’s glory, he who says: “All things that the Father has are mine” (John 16:15), and: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). It follows:

VERSE 9.—“The former things, behold, have come to pass; and I announce new things; before they spring forth, I shall make them heard by you.”

The things said above concerning the coming of the Savior, by which our salvation was to begin, were formerly future. “But these,” he says, “have now come to pass. I also announce to you new things that will follow”: that is, the preaching of the apostles and the calling of the Gentiles. “Before they spring forth, I shall make them heard by you,” so that you may not doubt that they will come to pass, just as you now see that these have come to pass. What these new things [Col. 0403C] are which I announce to you is made clear when he adds:

VERSE 10.—“Sing to the Lord a new song, his praise from the ends of the earth: you who go down into the sea and its fullness, islands and their inhabitants.”

A new song is the proclamation of evangelical preaching, in which a new thing is heard: Christ’s incarnation, death, ascension after his resurrection, the sending of the Holy Spirit, and the calling of the whole world. The Church sings this song everywhere, because it continually recalls and proclaims that Christ accomplished these things for it; having put off the old human being through the grace of baptism, it has itself faithfully been renewed and walks in newness of life. Whoever still maintains the old manner of life [Col. 0403D]—that is, loves earthly things—sounds the old song; but whoever loves eternal things sings the new song. For the new human being sings a new song, not the old one, who, not yet laying aside Adam’s sins, persists in the transgression of the old human being. It is new because nothing like it has ever been seen or heard; new because it is not defiled by any age, but always endures in the grace of its own dignity.

Therefore the whole world is commanded to sing this song to God, so that “his praise may resound from the ends of the earth,” according to what the Church says also in the Psalm: “From the ends of the earth I cried to you” (Ps. 60:3). Or we may understand differently the words, “His praise [Col. 0404A] from the ends of the earth.” There are some who are first on earth and others who are last. Who are first? The wise of this world, the noble, the rich, the great. Who are last? “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God chose the ignoble and despised things of the world, and things that are not, to destroy the things that are” (1 Cor. 1:27). From these last ones of the earth, therefore, the praise of God always resounds.

The sea is this bitter and turbulent world. Into this sea fishers of men descended to cast the net of evangelical preaching, of which it is said: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind; when it was full, they drew it out and, sitting beside the shore, selected the good into their vessels, but cast the bad [Col. 0404B] outside” (Matt. 13:47). The fullness of this sea is the multitude of worldly people or Gentiles; the islands are the various nations or regions. All of these are commanded to sing to the Lord the song of new praise. It follows:

VERSE 11.—“Let the wilderness be raised up, and its cities; and Cedar shall dwell in houses.”

Let the wilderness be raised up: that is, let the heart of the Gentiles be lifted toward love of the heavenly homeland, and let their cities lift up their minds in hope of eternal salvation. Cedar was a son of Ishmael, from whom the province also took its name. Those from his stock are accustomed to dwell not in houses but in tents, wandering through deserts. Its name is interpreted “darkness,” and it signifies the Gentile people, who wandered through the wilderness of this age [Col. 0404C] in the darkness of errors; but, converted to faith through the apostles, it began to dwell in houses—that is, in churches—as a member of the household. It follows:

“Praise, inhabitants of the Rock; from the summit of the mountains they shall cry out.” Who are the inhabitants of the Rock except those who remain in the hardness of their hearts? Yet these too are stirred to praise through the visitation of new grace. Preachers cry out from the summit of the mountains when, standing on the height of virtues and despising earthly things, they summon those who dwell low in spirit to seek the things above. It follows:

VERSE 12.—“They shall give glory to the Lord and declare his praise in the islands.”

Preachers set the Lord’s glory in the hearts of their hearers [Col. 0404D], and proclaim his praise not only throughout the whole world, but even in the distant islands of the sea. And because after these things the Judge will come, to render to each according to his work, it is fittingly added:

**VERSE 13.**—“The Lord will go forth as a mighty man, and like a man of war he will stir up zeal.”

For he who first went forth as weak will go forth a second time as mighty, when they shall see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and glory. And like a man of war he will stir up zeal to avenge himself upon his enemies, when, as the Book of Wisdom also says: “Zeal will take up his armour, and the world will fight with him against the foolish” (Wis. V, 18). For a warrior, when he is about to fight [Col. 0405A] against his enemies, is accustomed to stir up zeal and anger in his own mind, lest in a spirit of gentleness he spare his adversaries. The Lord, therefore, is said to be about to stir up zeal like a man of war, because he will come with such a disposition that he will not spare his enemies. It follows:

“He will cry aloud and shout, and will prevail over his enemies.”

**VERSE 14.**—“I have kept silence; I have always been silent; I have been patient; like a woman in labour I will speak: I will lay waste and swallow up together.”

**VERSE 15.**—“I will make mountains and hills desolate, and I will dry up all their grass.”

He who once, like a lamb before one shearing him, was silent and did not open his mouth, will now cry aloud and shout; and he who so strengthened his enemies against himself [Col. 0405B] that he could be bound, scourged, and crucified by them, will then be strengthened over them in order to punish his enemies, saying: “I have kept silence; I have always been silent,” and so forth. But how was he always silent, when through the Law and the prophets, through the Gospel and the apostles, he never ceased to cry out? He was silent in judgment, certainly, but not silent in commandment. He is patient now also, because he long endures sinners so that they may repent.

A woman in labour brings forth with pain what she has long carried within with a burden. Therefore, after long silence, the Lord speaks like a woman in labour, because what he now silently endures in himself, he will one day reveal in the vengeance of judgment, as if with pain. He who had always been silent speaks like a woman in labour, because he who long endured human deeds without vengeance will at some time, with the heat of examination [Col. 0405C], show as if with pain of mind how severe a sentence of punishment he had kept within. In his wrath he then lays waste all the reprobate and swallows them up—that is, plunges them into the depth of the abyss of his judgments.

Likewise, he then makes mountains and hills desolate, so that no inhabitant remains in them. For what is understood by mountains and hills but the proud rulers of this age? And what is represented by the inhabitants of the mountains but the people whom their rulers bear by governing? For just as mountains support their cultivators, so rulers bear the burden of those whom they govern. Therefore, in judgment the Lord will make mountains and hills desolate, because he will remove from proud rulers every power [Col. 0405D] of pre-eminence. He will also dry up their grass, because he will make the oldness of their carnal action wither, so that it may be burned up. The Lord has spoken these things concerning his second coming; and he adds concerning those things which he was to do at the first [Note: [Col. 0405D] The manuscripts read *in the first place* or *at the first*.]:

“And I will set rivers among the islands and dry up pools.”

**VERSE 16.**—“And I will lead the blind by a way they did not know; I will make them walk in paths they had not known. I will turn darkness before them into light, and crooked things into straight.”

He has indeed turned rivers into islands, because he causes the streams of the Gospel to flow even to the remote places of Ocean; [Col. 0406A] or to overflow among all nations, so that the nations are represented by islands. And he dries up pools, because he dried up the depth of the knowledge of the Jews, which lay stagnant in one people as in one place. For the wisdom of the scribes and Pharisees was dried up.

Now the Way is he who says: “I am the way” (John XIV, 6). The paths, however, are the prophets. Hence it is also said through Jeremiah: “Ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is, and walk in it, and you shall find refreshment for your souls” (Jer. VI, 16). He calls the prophets ancient paths, for they all point in a singular way to the one good Way through which we attain refreshment of soul, that is, Christ. By this Way, therefore—that is, by paths of this kind—the Lord leads the blind nations, their hearts having been enlightened [Col. 0406B]. Or he makes them walk by the way of the knowledge of God and by the prophetic paths. For he has made the darkness of their former ignorance into the light of true knowledge before them, and has straightened their hearts, distorted through iniquity. It follows:

“These things I have done for them, and I have not forsaken them.”

**VERSE 17.**—“They have turned backward.”

The Lord has fulfilled for us the things that have been said, and does not forsake us, but is with us all days until the consummation of the age (Matt. XXVIII, 20). Yet we, ungrateful for his benefits, have turned back to the vices of the world from which he had freed us. Or perhaps the words, “They have turned backward,” may be understood of the dwelling-place of Paradise which we had abandoned by sinning. After this he adds concerning the remnants [Col. 0406C] of the Gentiles who preferred to remain in idolatry:

“Let those be put to shame with shame who trust in a graven image, who say to a molten image: ‘You are our gods.’” He does not say that they say to the molten image, “You are our God,” but, “You are our gods,” just as they said concerning the calf: “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exod. XXXII, 4). For one who worships an idol has forsaken the one true God and made himself a servant to many false gods. But when the Gentiles have everywhere been enlightened and made straight, and idolaters put to shame, the Lord rebukes the hardness of the Jews, adding:

**VERSE 18.**—“You deaf, hear; and you blind, look [Col. 0406D] so as to see.” And concerning the same people he adds:

**VERSE 19.**—“Who is blind but my servant? and deaf, but he to whom I sent my messengers?”

For that people is blind, because it always served God from fear and does not know the light of charity; and deaf, because it does not hear the prophets crying to it. Of it there is also added: “Who is blind but he who has been sold? Who is blind but the servant of the Lord?” For who is so blind as one who has been sold by sinning and yet considers himself free? Its still-blind sight and deaf hearing are rebuked when there follows:

**VERSE 20.**—“You who see many things, will you not keep them? You who have open ears, will you not hear?”

[Col. 0407A] For they saw many things in the Scriptures but did not keep them. They had the ears of the heart open to understand many things, but they were unwilling to hear so as to do them. Hence the Apostle also said to it: “You who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege? You who glory in the Law, do you dishonour God through transgression of the Law?” (Rom. II, 21).

But these things may also be understood of the carnal people who are in the Church. For those are deaf who do not receive the words of God in the ear of the heart; and among such deaf persons he himself cries: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. XI, 15). Those are blind who, occupied with earthly gains, do not [Col. 0407B] see the losses they suffer within. Therefore such deaf persons are now commanded to hear with the ears of the heart, and the blind to look so as to see—though they are not accustomed to look so as to see. For to look so as to see is to think upon those things which enlighten the mind. But one looks so as not to see when he exercises his mind upon earthly things. Concerning such a one it is rightly added:

“Who is blind but my servant? and deaf but he to whom I sent my messengers?” This is the servant who “does not remain in the house forever” (John VIII, 35). He is blind because he does not see with spiritual eyes, and deaf because he does not hear holy preachers with the ears of the heart. To him also applies what is added: “Who is blind but he who has been sold? Who is blind but the servant of the Lord?” For this carnal man has been sold [Col. 0407C] under sin and does not understand that, by sinning, he has sold himself to the devil. And he, though useless, is a blind servant of the Lord, because “the servant does not know what his lord does” (John XV, 15).

But when it is added, “You who see many things, will you not keep them?” this servant is shown to be both blind and seeing: blind in that he does not see, but seeing in that he does not understand. Similarly, when it is joined, “You who have open ears, will you not hear?” he is declared to be both deaf and hearing. For he is plainly deaf with respect to doing, yet he has open ears, not for understanding. Whoever understands the Scriptures but does not do them—that is, every person like myself—is rebuked in this place when it is said: “You who see many things, will you not keep them? You who have open ears, will you not hear?” [Col. 0407D] It follows:

**VERSE 21.**—“And the Lord willed to sanctify him, and to magnify and exalt the Law.”

**VERSE 22.**—“But that people has been plundered and laid waste; all the young men are a snare, and they are hidden in prison-houses.”

The Lord willed to sanctify this servant, that is, the Jewish people or even carnal Christians, but the servant was unwilling to be sanctified by him. Or certainly, the Lord willed that this servant should sanctify him in himself, according to what is written: “Sanctify the Lord of hosts” (above, VIII, 13). Or: “Sanctify [Col. 0408A] the Lord Christ in your hearts” (I Pet. III, 15).

And he willed that he should sanctify [Note: [Col. 0407D] Thus both manuscripts.] the Law by doing it and exalt it by understanding it. For whoever so advances in keeping the heavenly commandments that his mind also is raised to the higher things of spiritual understanding, magnifies and exalts the Law. But the slothful servant neglects to magnify and exalt the Law, because the people of the Jews understand or observe it carnally, while this people of vain Christians does nothing great, but always crawls in weakness of heart. Therefore each people has been plundered and laid waste by its enemies: the former indeed by the Romans, but the latter, which is more serious, by evil spirits.

For all these are a snare for the young, that is, for those who burn with the heat of the flesh, because, in Peter’s words, “they entice through the desires of the flesh those who have only just escaped” (II Pet. II, 18). All these worldly persons are a snare for the young, because by their conversations they entice into sin those who are heated by the warmth of temptations. For “evil conversations corrupt good morals” (I Cor. XV, 33).

They are also hidden in prison-houses because, in the dark hiding-places of their consciences, where they are held captive by the devil, they conceal the deceit of their wickedness. For they are not truly such as they show themselves outwardly to be, but rather such as they lie hidden inwardly. To such persons the Lord said: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to men, [Col. 0408C] but within are full of dead men’s bones and every uncleanness. So you also outwardly appear righteous to men, but within you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity” (Matt. XXIII, 27).

This, then, is what is meant by their being said to be hidden in prison-houses—prisons of the sort concerning which we have spoken above. It follows:

“They have become a spoil, and there is none to rescue them; a plundering, and there is none to say: ‘Restore.’”

The Jews became spoil and plunder for the Roman people, and there is none to rescue them or to say, “Restore,” because they are still held captive. Some also of those who are reckoned by the Christian name have become spoil for demons, so that whatever good they seemed to possess might be plundered by invisible adversaries; [Col. 0408D] and there is none to rescue them, because by the just judgment of God they have been abandoned in their wickedness. Then the prophet cries out amid the multitude of the people and says:

**VERSE 23.**—“Who among you will hear [Note: [Col. 0408D] Another reading: *give heed to*.] this, hear and listen for things to come?”

Who among you, O Jews, will hear this which I have declared by a verb in the past tense as undoubtedly to happen concerning you: “They have become a spoil, and there is none to rescue”? Whoever hears this will fear to sin, lest he become spoil. The same is said to us: “Who among you will hear this?” For among the Christian people a hearer of this discourse is seldom found. Rare indeed [Col. 0409A] is anyone who reflects on the captivity of the soul, fears to lose the goods of the heart as invisible adversaries plunder them, and carefully attends to—or strives to hear—the things awaiting him in the age to come. It follows:

**VERSE 24.**—“Who gave Jacob over to plundering [Vulgate: *to guidance*] and Israel to those who laid waste? Was it not the Lord himself, against whom we sinned?”

The Lord Jesus himself gave the Jewish people over to the Romans who laid them waste, because they had sinned by killing him. We too, on account of sins of which we are conscious, will be handed over to hidden adversaries to torture us sensibly, unless we repent. It follows:

“And they were unwilling to walk in his ways, and they did not hear [Col. 0409B] his Law.”

That is, Jews or pseudo-Christians were unwilling to walk in his ways or to hear the Law so as to do it. He does not say, “They did not know” or “They were unable to walk in his ways,” but “They were unwilling,” so as to show that they sinned not from ignorance or weakness but from pride: they knowingly despised God’s commandments or refused to know them. Such persons deservedly were given over to plunder. It follows:

**VERSE 25.**—“And he poured out upon him the indignation of his wrath, and mighty war.”

The Lord poured out his indignation upon the Jewish people through the Romans, and mighty war, as it is also said in the Psalm: “Pour out your wrath upon them, and let the fury of your anger overtake them. Let their habitation become desolate, and let there be none to dwell in their tents” (Ps. LXVIII, 26). [Col. 0409C] Hence it is added:

“And he burned him round about, and he did not know; and he set him on fire, and he did not understand.”

He burned him all around, setting all Judaea aflame; and he set him on fire, consuming Jerusalem by fire. But this people, thus burned, did not know why it suffered these things, nor did it understand that it was being set on fire in this way because of the murder of the Saviour.

But if we understand these things spiritually in accordance with the preceding sense, we should know that the indignation or wrath of God is said to be the abandonment of good actions, as it is written: “Lest the Lord become angry, and you perish from the righteous way” (Ps. II, 12). If, therefore, the Lord is said to become angry when men lose the way of righteousness, he more extensively pours out upon that person the indignation of his wrath [Col. 0409D] who, unwilling to walk in his ways, knowingly abandons the path of uprightness.

He also suffers war who is assailed by the temptations of his flesh. Yet this war is in some sense still weak. But the Lord pours down mighty war when he strikes the proud heart and terribly destroys, by the swords of his judgments, works that appeared good. He pours down mighty war when, by just judgment, he releases the ancient enemy into his powers. This adversary burns him round about, and he does not know; he sets him on fire, and he does not understand. For Satan himself does what the Lord is now said to do, because the devil can do nothing unless he has received authority from the Lord. “There is no authority except from the Lord” (Rom. XIII, 1).

Therefore the ancient deceiver, having received power from God, burns round about the one whom, by tempting him on every side, he kindles with the fires of vices on every side. He goes around each of us and suggests vices from every direction. He presents alluring forms and easy pleasures to the eyes, so as to destroy chastity through sight; he tempts the ears with excessively musical music, so as to relax hearing by the force of sweeter sound and soften Christian firmness; he provokes the tongue to abuse; he incites the hand, when injuries provoke it, to the insolence of killing; he adds unjust gains, that he may make a man a cheat; he promises earthly honours in order to take away heavenly ones; he displays falsehoods in order to steal away truths. [Col. 0410B] Therefore it is rightly said of one whom the devil, tempting him from every side, kindles with vices: “He burned him round about, and he did not know; and he set him on fire, and he did not understand.” For one so burned does not know that he is being burned, because, blinded by worldly pleasures, he does not understand the spiritual sufferings he endures.

But the addition, “And he set him on fire,” without the words “round about,” may be referred to the inner person, so that “And he burned him round about” is understood of the outer person. Thus one is set on fire both outside and within who has lost the goods of flesh and spirit through the fire of vices. For unless the flame of lust is extinguished by purity of heart, virtues of whatever kind arise in vain, as it is said through Moses: “A fire has been kindled by my wrath, and it shall burn down to the lowest hell; [Col. 0410C] it shall devour the earth and its produce” (Deut. XXXII, 22).

For fire devours the earth and its produce when lust consumes the flesh and, through it, all good deeds. Whatever comes forth from the fruit of uprightness, that the flame of corruption certainly burns up. Therefore, by the fire of lust alone, the whole person is burned, both within and without, even if the other conflagrations of vices were absent.

But after these things have been said concerning the reprobate who appear to hold the faith, the following discourse is directed to the elect. Or rather, he next addresses the faithful Jews of the circumcision who were laid waste by the Romans and whom he sent forth to preach throughout the world, like lambs among wolves, [Col. 0410D] saying:

## CHAPTER XLIII

**VERSE 1.**—“And now thus says the Lord who created you, Jacob, and formed you, Israel: Do not fear, for I have redeemed you and called you by your name: you are mine.”

Whenever Jacob or Israel is used with an addition of honour, it must be understood of the spiritual Jacob. But where it is said without an addition indicating election, it should be understood of carnal Jacob or Israel—that is, of the Jewish people or of carnal persons in the Church. Thus, when it is now said, “Thus says the Lord who created you, Jacob, and formed you, Israel,” the Lord undoubtedly addresses the elect worshippers of the New Testament. For he created them not only that they might exist, but also that they might be righteous. “For we are,” they say, [Col. 0411A] “his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Eph. II, 10). And he formed them in his own image and likeness, so that the form of his goodness might be seen in them. To them, because of Catholic unity, he speaks as though to one person, saying: Do not fear to suffer adversities for my name, because I redeemed you at the price of my blood and called you: you are mine, for you I gave so great a price.

But perhaps someone may ask why almighty God allowed the adversaries of his elect temporarily to grow powerful. It was, of course, so that the life of the good might be purified by the cruelty of the wicked. For God would never allow there to be adversaries of the good unless he saw how much they also benefited them. For while the unjust rage, the just are purified; and the life of the wicked serves the benefit of innocence, while by pressing upon it they humble it, and by humbling it continually form it for the better. Hence Solomon says: “The fool shall serve the wise” (Prov. II, 29), because, when the foolish person who is pre-eminent exercises the terror of power against the wise person’s life, wearies him with labours, and tears him with insults, he thereby cleanses him through use from every rust of vices. Thus the fool serves the wise even by ruling, since he advances to a better state the one whom he improves by oppression. The Lord, therefore, permits his own people to be afflicted temporarily, but amid adversities always grants them the consolation of his mercy. Hence he now adds:

**VERSE 2.**—“When you pass through waters, I will be with you; rivers shall not cover you. When you walk in fire, you shall not be burned, and flame shall not burn [Col. 0411C] in you.”

**VERSE 3.**—“For I am the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Saviour.”

Holy martyrs frequently experienced this promise to be true even according to the letter. For many of them, cast into waters and rivers while God was present with them, could not be drowned or harmed; many walking in fire could not be burned, nor did the flame touch even a hair of their heads by burning it. But because some of them were consumed in waters or fires, we ought rather to understand this promise spiritually, lest it seem false in any respect.

By the designation of waters or rivers, tribulations are signified, as Solomon says: “Many waters could not quench charity, nor shall rivers overwhelm it” (Cant. VIII, 7). Fire or flame, however, expresses the heat of suffering, as the Apostle teaches: “The bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest for sin are burned outside the camp. Therefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate” (Heb. XIII, 11). Since that burning of the bodies of animals prefigured the Lord’s passion, it is clear what fire mystically signifies.

Therefore he says: When you pass through waters—that is, through [Col. 0412A] the waves of tribulations—I will be with you, to guard you; and rivers—that is, the rapid assaults of tribulations—shall not cover you, that is, shall not overwhelm you, because they shall not prevail. When you walk in fire—that is, amid the heat of raging sufferings—you shall not be burned in soul, because I shall inwardly give spiritual refreshment [Note: [Col. 0411D] Both manuscripts read *giving*.]; and flame—that is, the fury of persecutors—shall not burn in you, since it shall not reach your soul, though it rage against the body. For I am the Lord your God, whom you confess in suffering against worshippers of false gods; and I am the Holy One of holy ones, whom Israel awaited. I am also your Saviour, because by delivering you from present evils I shall bring you to eternal salvation.

Or waters and rivers are the activities of this world. Rivers cover those whom the activities of this world do not throw into mental confusion. For those who are held fast in mind by the grace of the Holy Spirit pass through the waters and yet are not covered by rivers, because even amid the crowds of peoples they so make the steps of their journey that they do not lower the head of the mind to worldly activities. It follows:

“I have given Egypt as your propitiation, Ethiopia and Saba for you.” Egypt means “darkness” or “tribulation.” Ethiopia denotes black peoples and is interpreted “gloom.” Saba, moreover, is called “captivity” or “net.” What, then, are represented by Egypt, Ethiopia, and Saba but the Gentile world, which the ancient enemy afflicted while it was set in the gloom of errors and held captive in his net? The Lord says to the order of preachers [Col. 0412C]: “I have given Egypt, Ethiopia, and Saba as your propitiation for you.” As though he said: I have given you this mercy and propitiation, that I might save the Gentile people for you. It follows:

**VERSE 4.**—“Since you became honourable in my eyes and glorious, I have loved you.”

This Israel became honourable and glorious before God from the time when it began to preach throughout the whole world, shine with signs wherever it went, and convert all nations. And from that time the Lord especially loved it, although he had loved it before as well; but perhaps he did not then appear to love the one whom he had sent among persecutors. It follows:

[Col. 0412D] “And I will give men for you, and peoples for your life.” This is, unless I am mistaken, what Solomon says: “The wicked shall be given for the righteous, and the unjust for the upright” (Prov. XXI, 18). And again: “The righteous is delivered from distress, and the wicked shall be given in his place” (Prov. XI, 8). Hence he still strengthens this elect Israel against persecutors by adding:

**VERSE 5.**—“Do not fear, for I am with you.”

And he promises it a fruitful offspring of believers when he adds: “From the east I will bring your seed, and from the west I will gather you.

[Col. 0413A] **VERSE 6.**—“I will say to the north: Give; and to the south: Do not withhold.”

For he plainly showed in this place that the Church was to be gathered from the four quarters of the world. Hence it is declared that at the end even the faithful will come from the furthest bounds of the world, when it is added:

“Bring my sons from afar and my daughters from the ends of the earth.”

But if these things are to be understood spiritually, what is meant by the east but the Jewish people, which first possessed the light of divine knowledge and brought forth to the world the Sun of righteousness? And what by the west but the Gentile people, which lay in the setting of the sun through love of transitory things and, near the end of the world as at the end of the day, received Christ, the Sun of righteousness? The seed of the Church is thus brought from east and west, because believers come both from circumcision and from uncircumcision.

The Gentile world is also signified by the north, because it was set, as it were, in a leftward, frozen, and dark region in unbelief. Judaea, however, is represented by the south, which grew warm as though under the noonday sun, because when the Redeemer appeared in flesh it was the first to receive the warmth of faith. Therefore it is said to the north, “Give,” when the Gentile world is commanded to offer God the gifts of its faith. The south is commanded not to withhold, because Hebrews established in the faith are instructed not to despise the lives of Gentiles by rejecting them. For at first they wished to reject the Gentiles, as the Acts of the Apostles sufficiently makes clear.

[Col. 0413C] The Lord commands his sons to be brought from afar, so that the son who went into a far country, where in prodigal living he dissipated his goods, may return to his father (Luke XV). He also commands his daughters—that is, weak and despised persons—to be brought from the lowest extremities of the earth’s lowliness, because “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong; and he chose the ignoble and despised things of the world, and things that are not, to destroy those which are” (I Cor. I, 27). These, indeed, are the daughters coming from the ends of the earth. It follows:

**VERSE 7.**—“And everyone who calls upon my name, I created him for my glory; I formed [Col. 0413D] him and made him.”

The Lord created for his glory everyone who calls upon his name. For “everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Rom. X, 13). But he calls upon his name who cleanses his heart and with entire devotion prays for his coming into himself. Whoever acts in this way, God has created anew in righteousness and holiness of truth for his glory, renewing him in the spirit of his mind.

He formed him in his likeness, because he expressed in him the form of his goodness. And he made him righteous. “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared that we should walk in [Col. 0414A] them” (Eph. II, 10). But because “blindness has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter” (Rom. XI, 25), it is rightly added:

**VERSE 8.**—“Bring forth the blind people, though they have eyes; and the deaf, though they have ears.”

This blind and deaf Jewish people was sent out, and the Gentiles entered into faith in its place. Hence it is added:

**VERSE 9.**—“All nations are gathered together, and the tribes are assembled.”

For the whole body of the nations has been gathered into one faith, and a multitude of believers has been assembled from all the tribes of Israel. Having foretold these things, the Lord rebukes the error of the Gentiles, who thought to be gods those who could foretell none of these things, when he adds:

[Col. 0414B] “Who among you shall declare this, and make us hear the former things? Let them produce their witnesses and be justified; let them hear and say [Note: [Col. 0413D] Another reading: *say: Vercelli manuscript*.].” Which of your gods, he says, O Gentiles, will declare among you the unified fellowship of Gentiles and Jews? And which of your gods will make you hear the former things—that is, the things which the Saviour was to accomplish in the flesh? The answer understood is: none. Let your gods produce witnesses of the former things, if they proclaim them, just as I give prophets and apostles as witnesses of the things I proclaim. Let them be justified in their words when they are known to foretell true things, just as I am justified in my utterances. Let them hear the charges made against them and speak—that is, answer. For if they truly are gods, they ought to do all these things.

But after refuting the unbelievers who worshipped such gods, the Lord addresses believers, showing that he has done all these things as befitted God. For it follows:

**VERSE 10.**—“Truly you are my witnesses, says the Lord, and my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know, believe me, and understand that I myself am.”

You, he says, O apostles and believers, are witnesses of my words and of my divinity; and he “who, being in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 6), is my witness. I chose him above all others for this very purpose: that through him you might know what mortals must know concerning me, [Col. 0414D] believe me in all things without doubt, and understand that I myself am, remaining eternally immutable. It follows:

“Before me no God was formed, nor shall there be after me.”

Before me none of those whom the Gentiles fashion for themselves as gods was formed, because I am before any idol came to be; nor shall any one of them exist after me, but I shall remain after them all, because, when idols have been destroyed, I shall remain without end. This is a certain moderation of divine speech: while it says less concerning itself, it intends a greater meaning; and by speaking in this way it shows that none of such gods can be like itself. It follows:

**VERSE 11.**—“I am the Lord, and apart from me there is no saviour.”

I alone am the Lord, whom it is fitting that all things should serve, because I not only preside over those subject to me but possess every good. And apart from me there is no saviour, because apart from me there is none who can save. For the gods of the Gentiles do not save their worshippers but destroy them. The Father does not deny that the Son is Saviour when he says that apart from himself there is no Saviour, because the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, is not apart from the Father; rather, the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father. Thus Father and Son are not two saviours, but one Saviour, just as they are not two lords but one Lord. [Col. 0415B] It follows:

**VERSE 12.**—“I announced and saved; I made it heard, and there was no strange god among you.”

I announced through the prophets, saved through Christ, and made it heard through the apostles; and there was no strange God among you, but I was in all of you, both under the Law and under grace. It follows:

“Truly you are my witnesses, says the Lord, and I am God,” because I alone am God. It follows:

**VERSE 13.**—“And from the beginning I myself am, and there is none who can rescue from my hand.”

As though the Lord said: No one is older than I, and no one stronger than I. Hence he adds: “I shall act, and who shall turn it back?” For no one can turn aside his work, he who has resolved to accomplish the salvation of the world. For [Col. 0415C] it follows:

**VERSE 14.**—“Thus says the Lord, your redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: For your sake I sent into Babylon and removed all the bars, and the Chaldeans glorying in their ships.”

**VERSE 15.**—“I am the Lord, your Holy One, creator of Israel, your king.”

Properly and customarily, the Son of Man is called Redeemer, since he gave his life as a redemption for many. Yet because the works of Father and Son are inseparable, the Father too can be called Redeemer—not because he himself suffered for us, but because he redeemed us by the blood of his Son. For *redemption* is customarily used to mean rescue or liberation.

[Col. 0415D] Moreover, according to Dionysius (*On the Divine Names*, ch. 8), the Lord is called redemption insofar as he does not allow true beings to fall into non-being [Note: [Col. 0415D] Garst. manuscript: *without*.]; and insofar as, if anything has been led astray into sin or disorder and suffers some diminution of the perfection of its proper goods, he redeems it from suffering and inertia, filling its need, compassionately regarding its weakness, restoring it from evil—or rather, establishing it in good—ordering and adorning what is disordered and unadorned, perfecting its integrity, and removing all its stains. According to this sense, therefore, not only the Son but also the Father and the Holy Spirit are Redeemer or redemption [Col. 0416A], because the whole Trinity accomplishes all these things.

In the same way, “the Holy One of Israel” is a name not only of the Son, but also of the Father and the Holy Spirit, as the first powers bear witness when they cry: “Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts” (above, 6:3). For this Lord is holy by nature and holy through himself, sanctifying all things; and therefore he is called the Holy One of Israel, as it were, the Holy One of holy ones. Therefore the Father too is called the Holy One of Israel: for our sake he sent forth his Only-Begotten into Babylon—that is, into this world confused by vices and errors—and removed all the bars of Babylon’s gates, so that, the bars having been taken away, the gates might stand open and those held captive in this Babylon might go forth free.

[Col. 0416B] What is signified by the name “bars,” Solomon indicates when he says: “Judgments are like the bars of cities” (Prov. 18:19). For while the Gentiles still judged that idols ought rather to be served than God, services of this sort held Babylon’s gates fastened against them like bars, so that they could not enter them or admit the preachers of truth. While we judged it better to serve sin than righteousness, the judgments of our own will, like bars, fastened against us the gates of this confused Babylon. Therefore the Lord removed the bars of such perverse judgments, so that, the bars and fastenings of evil will having been removed, we who were held captive within ourselves as though in Babylon might go forth from ourselves.

The Chaldeans likewise gloried in their ships, [Col. 0416C] because the malignant spirits exulted excessively in the minds of human beings, whom they were leading about as wanderers across the bitter sea of this age. But the Lord also removed these, because he cast them out of the hearts of those whom they thus possessed. He is our Holy One, because he himself is holy by nature and sanctifies us through the gift of his grace; therefore he alone is rightly holy, because “no one is good except God alone” (Matt. 19:17). He also creates spiritual Israel in good works, because “in Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything nor uncircumcision, but a new creation” (Gal. 5:6). And he himself is our king, who rules us and reigns in us. It follows:

VERSE 16.—“Thus says the Lord, who made a way in the sea and a path in the rushing waters.”

[Col. 0416D] VERSE 17.—“Who brought forth chariot and horse, army and strong man: together they slept, and shall not rise; they were crushed like flax and extinguished.”

The Lord made a way in the sea because, as Exodus relates: “The water was divided, and the children of Israel entered through the midst of the dry sea” (Exod. 21:29). He also provided a path in the torrents of the Arnon. Hence it was said in the book of the wars of the Lord: “As he did in the Red Sea, so he will do in the torrents of the Arnon” (Num. 21:14). Israel also crossed the Jordan “through its dry bed” (Josh. 3:17), when the Lord dried up its waters.

[Col. 0417A] He brought forth after the children of Israel Pharaoh’s chariot, his horse, the army of the Egyptians, and their strong commander. “For the heart of Pharaoh and his servants was changed concerning the people of Israel, and they said: What have we wished to do, that we should let Israel go and no longer have them serve us? Therefore he harnessed his chariot and took his people with him; he took six hundred chosen chariots, whatever chariots there were in Egypt, and commanders of the whole army. And the Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and he pursued the children of Israel” (Exod. 14:5).

The Lord recalls that he did these things so that we may understand that, just as he led the children of Israel from Egypt through the sea, so now he leads believers from the darkness of unbelief through baptism.
