Just as he gave them a path in the rushing waters so that [Col. 0417B] they might freely cross into the land of the promised inheritance, so now, through tribulations, he opens for believers the way to the kingdom of heaven. Just as he drowned Pharaoh with his army, pursuing the children of Israel, in the sea, so now he destroys in baptism the devil with his angels and the multitude of vices as they pursue the faithful. Hence he says that they slept together and shall not rise. For their power, by which they formerly held and afflicted us in sins, has been put to sleep. They were crushed like flax, when through repentance we crushed their suggestions in our heart; and they were extinguished if their malice has now been extinguished in us. It follows:

VERSE 18.—“Do not remember former things, nor look upon things of old.”

You apostles, he says, do not now remember former things, [Col. 0417C] because I shall now do greater things than I once did through Moses, when I made a way in the sea and a path in the rushing waters. For the reason why they ought no longer to remember the things formerly done follows.

VERSE 19.—“Behold,” he says, “I make new things, and now they shall spring forth; surely you shall know them.”

And he adds what those new things are: “I shall make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the pathless place.” In the wilderness of the Gentiles I shall give a way of going to God; and among the heathen people, through whom no preacher of truth had passed, I shall set the streams of the Gospel. It follows:

VERSE 20.—“The beasts of the field shall glorify me, the dragons and ostriches, because I gave waters in the wilderness, rivers in the pathless place, that I might give drink to my people, [Col. 0417D] my chosen people.”

Since the field is the world, every person living beastially in this world is called a beast of the field. And what this beast is is made clear: namely, dragons and ostriches. What is designated by the name of dragons except the life of malicious people, of whom elsewhere it is said: “They drew in the wind like dragons” (Jer. 14:6)? For all perverse persons draw in the wind like dragons when they swell with malicious pride.

But what are commonly understood by the name of ostriches except pretenders? The ostrich has feathers but has no flight, because pretenders possess the appearance of holiness but not the power of holiness. The appearance of good action adorns them, but the wing of virtue does not raise them from the earth. Such are those [Col. 0418A] who seem to observe religion yet are not Christians. Thus the beast glorifies God when the Gentile world exalts his faith; it is marked by the name of dragons because of malice, and by that of ostriches because of hypocrisy. For the Gentile world, as it were, received feathers but could not fly: it had the nature of reason, yet did not know the practice of reason. Such dragons and ostriches at last glorified God because he gave, in the wilderness of the nations, the waters of wisdom and, in the pathless region of Gentile life, the rivers of the teachings of the elect, in order to give the drink of heavenly preaching to the people of believers drawn from the nations. It follows:

VERSE 21.—“This people I formed for myself; it shall declare my praise.”

As it is also said through Peter: “But you are a chosen race, [Col. 0418B] a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession, that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you from darkness into his marvelous light” (1 Pet. 2:9). Having spoken these things about the chosen people from among the nations, he immediately rebukes the people of the Jews, or carnal persons who are in the Church, when he adds:

VERSE 22.—“You did not call upon me, Jacob, nor did you labor in me, Israel.”

One calls upon God who, with a purified heart, humbly prays that he may come within him; and one labors in him who sweats in good works in his faith. For each person ought so to act as both to persevere in devout prayers and to exercise himself in holy labors. But the Jew, or the carnally minded Christian, is rebuked for not having done these things. It follows:

VERSE 23.—“You did not offer me the ram of your [Col. 0418C] burnt offering, nor did you glorify me with your sacrifices.”

Because the ram leads the flock, whatever is chief in our thoughts is appropriately expressed by the ram; for thoughts themselves can be signified by the flock. A burnt offering, however, is said to be wholly burned. Therefore one offers to God the ram of one’s burnt offering who wholly kindles with the fire of charity that which is greatest and foremost in one’s desires and thoughts, just as Abraham prefigured for us by his example when he offered his only-begotten son, whom he loved uniquely, as a burnt offering—or rather, the ram in his place (Gen. 22). One sacrifices this ram of the burnt offering who loves God above all things, so that love of God may be greater in him than any other love. But every carnal person has not offered such a ram, because “people loved darkness rather than light” (John 3:19).

What is signified by the name of sacrifices except the slaying of the fleshly vices? The Apostle commands that these sacrifices be offered when he says: “Put to death your members which are upon the earth: fornication, impurity, lust, evil desire, and covetousness, which is the service of idols” (Col. 3:5). Whoever slays them glorifies God, as the same Apostle says: “Glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 6:20). But the Jew or the empty Christian neglects to do this. Since the Lord did not seek carnal gifts from such a person, he rightly adds:

[Col. 0419A] “I did not make you serve me with offerings, nor did I burden you with labor for incense.”

For he does not receive outward gifts when he does not approve the giver himself inwardly. It follows:

VERSE 24.—“You did not buy me cane with silver, nor did you make me drunk with the fat of your sacrifices.”

“The words of the Lord are chaste words, silver tried by fire” (Ps. 11:7). Cane (*calamus*) is said to be a shoot of an aromatic tree. John, however, explains in his Apocalypse that fragrances are the prayers of the saints (Rev. 5:8). What then is signified by cane except those who, through the power of prayer, smell sweetly to God, saying with Paul that “we are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Cor. 2:15)? Therefore one buys cane for God with silver who acquires such persons by preaching. But the Jew did not do this, because he taught not purity of heart but a merely apparent respectability of conduct. Nor could the carnal Christian do it, because one who does not possess good within oneself cannot perfectly build up the minds of others by speech.

[Col. 0419B] Sacrifices, as we have said, are the extinguishing of vices, or also good actions. There are some who sacrifice by extinguishing vices and doing good, yet are not at all contrite in the good things they do; and because they do not kindle themselves from love unto tears, their sacrifices are without fat. Hence it is said: “May your burnt offering become fat” (Ps. 19:4). For a dry burnt offering is a good work upon which the tears of prayer are not poured; but a fat burnt offering is when that which is done well is watered even by tears from a humble heart. Hence again it is said through the Psalmist: “I shall offer you burnt offerings full of marrow” (Ps. 65:15). For one who does good works, already longs for the vision of his Creator, hastens to attain the joys of eternal contemplation, and sacrifices himself in tears from the love by which he is kindled, has offered the Lord burnt offerings full of marrow.

[Col. 0419C] The Lord is made drunk with the fat of sacrifices and burnt offerings of this kind, because, delighted by the devout tears of the humble, he forgets all the things they had formerly done wrongly. For one who is drunk consigns to forgetfulness those things formerly retained in the heart’s memory. Therefore, because every Jew or feigned Christian does not appease God with such offerings, so that he may consign that person’s sins [Col. 0419D] to forgetfulness, “You did not make me drunk,” he says, “with the fat of your sacrifices.” It follows:

“Yet you made me serve in your sins; you gave me labor in your iniquities.”

In a certain sense, one makes God serve in one’s sins and gives him labor in one’s iniquities when, through divine patience, one is awaited in long-lasting wickedness so that one may at some point come to one’s senses. Therefore, mercifully prepared to forgive, he adds:

VERSE 25.—“I am, I am he who blot out your iniquities for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins.”

And he adds the condition on which he will blot out that person’s iniquities and forget those sins:

[Col. 0420A] VERSE 26.—“Recall me to remembrance, and let us be judged together; declare what you have, that you may be justified.”

“I blot out your iniquities,” he says, “O people of the Jews, by the blood of Christ for the sake of my goodness. Only recall me to remembrance, whom you have forgotten exceedingly, and let us be judged together in your heart, so that you yourself may judge which of us has acted more justly toward the other, I toward you or you toward me. And if you have any injustice, declare it—that is, confess it—that you may be justified. For lest you think yourself righteous, I make known to you the fault of those whom you believed to be greatest among the righteous.” For it follows:

VERSE 27.—“Your first father sinned, and your interpreters transgressed against me.”

VERSE 28.—“I defiled the holy princes.”

[Col. 0420B] Some before us understood the statement, “your first father sinned,” to refer to blessed Abraham. For when God had said to him: “I am he who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldeans, to give you this land and that you might possess it” (Gen. 15:7), he answered as though unbelieving: “Lord God, how can I know that I shall possess it?” (ibid., v. 8). Although he did not then sin, we know that he could not pass through this present life without sin. “For there is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin” (Eccl. 7:21).

The interpreters in this place are called Moses and Aaron, who reported the Lord’s words to the people and the people’s words to God. They transgressed, as it was divinely said to them: “You transgressed [Col. 0420C] against me among the children of Israel at the waters of contradiction” (Deut. 32:51). He also calls them holy princes, but because of the fault of their transgression he defiled them, so that they might not enter even the land of promise itself. It follows:

“I gave Jacob over to utter destruction, and Israel to blasphemy.”

A war in which all perish is commonly called *internecio* or *internecium*, “utter destruction.” Jacob was then given over to utter destruction, although not in battle, because all but the two who had come out of Egypt died in the wilderness. He was also given over to blasphemy, so that his unbelief might be accused.

Again, to each of us who remains in sins the Lord says: “I blot out your iniquities; [Col. 0420D] only recall me to remembrance, that we may be judged together”: that you may conceive me in your heart and, through diligent inquiry under my presence, discern your actions; and if you have any iniquity, declare it in confession, that you may be able to be justified. For each person’s mind ought, by diligent inquiry, to examine both its own case before God and the Lord’s case against itself. It ought carefully to weigh both what good things it has received from him and what evils it has perversely returned for his benefits by its manner of life. It ought to approach the Judge’s inner chamber and, within the bosom of the heart, consider how strictly he will one day strike, though he has long waited patiently; and, while it is permitted, it ought to punish with weeping whatever wrong it recognizes itself to have done.

For, lest one think oneself without sin, the fault of one’s generation is recalled to one’s memory, so that one may remember oneself conceived in iniquities and not doubt that one is a sinner. “Your first father,” he says, that is, he who begot you according to the flesh, sinned in the very act of intercourse while begetting you. The second father, however, is he who is the author of the second birth.

[Col. 0421A] “And your interpreters,” that is, the priests and others who ought to have made my words clear to you by interpreting them, “transgressed against me,” because they did not do this as they ought, but sought what was yours rather than what was mine. “And therefore I defiled the holy princes,” because, through the fault of evil priests, even good rulers were brought into disrepute.

“And I gave Jacob over to utter destruction,” because I destroyed the multitude of wicked Christians. “And Israel,” that is, those who live spiritually, “I gave over to blasphemy,” that is, to disgrace because of the examples of the perverse among whom they live. Hence the discourse is subsequently turned toward those spiritual persons, to console them as they dwell among the wicked. Or certainly, having thus far rebuked the hardness of the Jews, he now begins gently to address the primitive Church, saying:

CHAPTER 44.

VERSE 1.—“And now hear, Jacob my servant, and Israel, whom I have chosen.”

VERSE 2.—“Thus says the Lord who made and formed you, your helper from the womb: Do not fear, Jacob my servant, and *rectissime* [‘most upright one’], whom I have chosen.”

The Lord made this Jacob because he created him in good works, and formed him in this pattern of righteous living, so that he might say to us: “Be imitators of me, brethren, and observe those who walk thus, as you have our pattern” (Phil. 3:17). He was also this Jacob’s helper from the womb of mother Church in every battle of spiritual conflict. Hence he commanded him not to fear those who kill the body.

[Col. 0421C] Now *Israel*, according to the proper sense of the Hebrew language, is translated “most upright.” The customary statement that it means “a man seeing God” does not lie in the written form of the letters but in the sound of the word. What the Lord now says, “and most upright, whom I have chosen,” is as though he said, “and Israel, whom I have chosen.” The translator also preferred to render it “most upright,” in order to show that the discourse now concerns spiritual Israel. The reason why this Israel ought not to fear follows:

[Col. 0421D] VERSE 3.—“For I shall pour waters upon the thirsty one, and streams upon the dry land.”

I shall pour the waters of wisdom or spiritual grace upon the thirsting Gentile world, and the streams of heavenly preaching upon the dry mind of the Gentiles. Therefore do not fear them, because they gladly receive your teaching. It follows:

“I shall pour out my Spirit upon your seed, and my blessing upon your offspring.”

I shall pour out my Spirit upon your seed—that is, upon those whom you shall have begotten in Christ Jesus through the Gospel—and the blessing of my grace upon the offspring of these same spiritual children of yours. For the children of the Church, being reborn from water and Spirit, receive [Col. 0422A] the gift of the Holy Spirit and the heavenly blessing.

VERSE 4.—“And they shall spring up among the grass like willows beside flowing waters.”

Willow trees are indeed unfruitful, but they possess such greenness that even when dried up, cut off at the root, and cast away, they can scarcely wither. Hence, because they express the life of the elect through the constancy of their greenness, it is rightly said of the children of the Church that they shall spring up among the grass like willows beside flowing waters. For the children of holy Church spring up among the grass like willows when, amid the withering life of carnal persons, they endure in both great number and perpetual greenness of mind. They are rightly said to spring up beside flowing waters because each receives abundance for fruitfulness from the teaching of Sacred Scripture, which passes by in time. It follows:

VERSE 3.—“This one shall say, ‘I am the Lord’s’; that one shall call in the name of Jacob; and this one shall write with his hand, ‘For the Lord,’ and shall be likened in the name of Israel.”

This one shall say, “I am the Lord’s,” that is, he shall confess himself a Christian. That one, made Jacob—that is, a supplanter of vices—shall call upon the Lord’s name for help, in this name: namely, in that he is called Jacob by the merit of his action, that is, “supplanter” and “wrestler.” And this one shall write with his hand, “For the Lord,” because, assigning his merit in the book of divine remembrance through his own action, he directs it toward heaven. And he shall be likened in the name of Israel, so that he may be “most upright,” which is the interpretation of Israel. For he is likened in the name of Israel when he is such as the name Israel signifies. It follows:

[Col. 0422C] VERSE 6.—“Thus says the Lord, the King of Israel and his Redeemer, the Lord of hosts: I am the first and the last, and apart from me there is no God.”

These words suit the Son. For he is the King of Israel, of whom it is sung: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel” (John 12:13). He is its Redeemer, “who visited and wrought redemption for his people” (Luke 1:66). He is the Lord of the heavenly hosts, because “angels came and ministered to him” (Matt. 4:11). He is the first, because “in the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). He is the last, because “the Word was made flesh” [Col. 0422D] (ibid., v. 14) at the end of the ages. Hence he was also called the “last Adam” by the Apostle (1 Cor. 15:45). He is the first, through whom all things were made in the beginning; he is the last, through whom all things were restored at the end.

“And apart from me there is no God,” he says, as though saying: Because the Father is in me and I in the Father; or: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). For when he says that apart from him there is no God, he teaches that he alone, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is God, whereas idols are not gods. And because he says that he alone is God, he adds:

VERSE 7.—“Who is like me?”

That is, what god is like me? It follows:

[Col. 0423A] “Let him call and announce, and set forth to me the order of things, from the time when I established the ancient people.”

If anyone, he says, is like me, let him call me and announce to me, and set forth the order of the individual things which have happened since I established the Jewish people; or let him call into being things which are not as though they were, and set forth the order of my creation, by which I have disposed all things according to reason, since I made humanity upon the earth. Or let him call the human race to himself and announce future things to it, if he is truly God like me. Hence he also adds concerning those false beings who were thought to be gods: “Let them announce to them the things which are coming and which shall be.” For if they are gods, they ought to announce future things to their worshipers. And immediately the Lord strengthens his own against those who defended the worship of gods of this kind, saying:

[Col. 0423B] VERSE 8.—“Do not fear, nor be troubled.”

Do not fear their cruelty, nor be disturbed by their threats. And he continues, saying to the people of these same faithful persons: “From that time I caused you to hear, and I announced it; you are my witnesses.” From that time—that is, from the time when I established the ancient people—I caused you to hear from the beginning of the book of Genesis that none is like me and that there is no God besides me. And you are from that time my witnesses against those who chatter that there are many gods. Again, as though reasoning, he adds:

“Is there a God besides me, and a maker whom I do not know?”

He who knows all things would certainly know if there were another God besides himself, another maker, and another world; for our God made this world, as Genesis teaches. But because the Lord denied that there is a maker besides himself, someone might perhaps answer: “Are not those who make idols makers apart from you?” To this he adds:

VERSE 9.—“All the makers of an idol are nothing.”

For, as the Apostle says: “We know that an idol is nothing” (1 Cor. 8:4). And it is said of idols: “May those who make them become like them” (Ps. 113:8). Therefore, if an idol is nothing and those who make them become like them, surely all *plastae*, that is, makers or fashioners of idols, are nothing. Of them it is further said: “And their most beloved things shall not profit them; they themselves are their witnesses, because they do not see [Col. 0423D] nor understand.” Their own conscience bears witness that they made these things out of insensible material; and therefore those who do this and call them gods shall be confounded. Hence, reproaching their folly, he says:

VERSE 10.—“Who formed a god, and cast a graven image useful for nothing?”

And concerning just retribution he adds:

VERSE 11.—“Behold, all its associates [Note: [Col. 0423D] Elsewhere: its associates omitted.] shall be confounded.”

That is, those who make it and those who worship it. It follows:

“For the craftsmen are from among human beings; [Col. 0424A] they shall all gather together and stand; they shall fear and be confounded together.”

On the day of judgment, all makers and worshipers of the idol shall gather together; they shall stand fearful and confounded before the tribunal of the eternal Judge. Then, in order to show more plainly that idols cannot be gods, he recounts how mean their origin is.

VERSE 12.—“The smith,” he says, “has worked with a file; in coals and with hammers he formed it, and he worked with the strength of his arm.” And of the same craftsman he adds: “He shall hunger and fail; he has no water [Note: [Col. 0424D] Elsewhere: ‘he shall drink water.’], and he shall grow weary.”

For it is evident that an idol has no divinity, since it is made by human art and labor, and its maker, while making it, would fail unless he were sustained by outward food. These things have been said concerning iron idols; and concerning wooden ones he adds:

[Col. 0424B] VERSE 13.—“The carpenter stretches out a rule,” that is, a line; “he shapes it with a plane; he makes it with angles,” that is, square; “and turns it with a compass.”

A plane is a slender, curved carpenter’s tool, by which boards of a house are hollowed so that one may be fitted into another. A compass is so called because, by turning, it makes a circle; it is a double-pointed instrument with which painters make circles. But concerning the maker of the idol it is added: “And he made the image of a man, like a handsome human being dwelling in a house.” This is evident. It follows:

[Col. 0424C] VERSE 14.—“He cuts down cedars; he takes holm-oak and oak, which stood among the trees of the forest; and he plants a pine, which the rain nourished.”

VERSE 15.—“And it became fuel for people: he took from them and warmed himself; he kindled it and baked bread; but from the remainder he made a god and worshiped it: he made a graven image and bowed down before it.”

The Gentiles served gods of this sort, concerning whom he further adds:

VERSE 16.—“Half of it he burned with fire; from half of it he ate flesh; he cooked a dish and was satisfied; he warmed himself and said: ‘Ah! I am warm; I have seen the fire.’”

[Col. 0424D] VERSE 17.—“But from its remainder he made himself a god, a graven image; he bows down before it and worships it, and entreats it, saying: ‘Deliver me, for you are my god.’”

Nowhere more clearly than in this passage is the error of idolaters declared. Of them he further adds:

VERSE 18.—“They did not know, nor did they understand; for their eyes have been obscured so that they may not see, and their hearts so that they may not understand.”

VERSE 19.—“They do not reflect in their mind, nor know nor perceive, so as to say: ‘I burned half of it in the fire, and upon its coals [Col. 0425A] I baked bread, cooked flesh and ate; and from its remainder shall I make an idol? Shall I fall down before a trunk of wood?’”

VERSE 20.—“Part of it is ashes.”

We pass over these words thus because they need no exposition. But concerning the idol he further adds:

“His foolish heart worshiped it, and he did not deliver [Note: [Col. 0425D] Elsewhere: ‘he shall deliver.’] his soul, nor say: ‘Perhaps—that is, possibly—there is a lie in my right hand.’”

Thus far the Lord, laying bare the folly of the Gentiles, has proved quite plainly what he said above: “For apart from me there is no God.” Then he addresses the Jewish people, saying:

VERSE 21.—“Remember these things, Jacob and Israel, because you are my servant.”

Remember what we have said concerning idols, lest you wish [Col. 0425B] to serve them, because you are my servant. It follows:

“I formed you; you are my servant, Israel: do not forget me.” I formed you in your mother’s womb that you might be my servant; you did not form me, as worshipers of idols form gods for themselves in order to serve them. Therefore do not consign me to forgetfulness by following such gods. And concerning the time of grace he adds:

VERSE 22.—“I have blotted out your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like a mist.”

For a cloud or mist is dissolved and blotted out by the heat of the sun, though it did not permit the sun itself to be seen. So also the sins which overshadowed the heart of the Jews were at last driven away and blotted out in the light of the true sun, which is Christ, from the time when they were converted to faith. [Col. 0425C] For “to this day, when Moses is read, a veil is placed over the hearts of those among them who do not believe. But when one turns to God, the veil shall be removed” (2 Cor. 3:15). Hence, admonishing the same people, he adds: “Return to me, because I have redeemed you.” And because, after his resurrection, the whole world sang his triumphs, it fittingly follows:

VERSE 23.—“Praise, O heavens, because the Lord has acted [Note: [Col. 0425D] Elsewhere: ‘because he has shown mercy.’]; rejoice, O ends of the earth; resound with praise, O mountains, forests and every tree in them, because the Lord has redeemed Jacob, and Israel shall glory.”

The words “Praise, O heavens, because the Lord has acted” mean that this was fulfilled when the angels announced his resurrection. Or the apostles can be signified by the name “heavens,” of whom it is said: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18:2). They praised because the Lord acted, because they preached everywhere the triumph of his resurrection. Hence also the ends of the earth rejoiced in his praise.

[Col. 0425D] *Jubilus* (“jubilation”) is the term for when ineffable joy is conceived in the mind, so that it can neither be concealed nor unfolded in words, yet is expressed by certain movements, although it is articulated by no determinate expressions. Thus holy David, seeing the souls of the elect conceive such great joy as speech cannot disclose, says: “Blessed is the people [Col. 0426A] that knows jubilation” (Ps. 88:16). He does not say, “that speaks,” but “that knows,” because jubilation can indeed be known by the understanding, but cannot be expressed in speech [Note: [Col. 0426D] Codex Cruc.: *dictum*, “in utterance.”]. For through it that which is beyond sense is felt. And when scarcely the conscience of the one feeling can suffice to contemplate this, when will even the tongue of the one speaking suffice to express it?

Therefore, because, as the apostles preached, “their sound went forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:4), the light of truth, revealing itself to the hearts of the elect throughout the nations, filled their minds with inexpressible joy, the ends of the earth—that is, the ends of the world—are fittingly also commanded to rejoice. And so that the whole earth might rejoice, the mountains—that is, the saints approaching heavenly things by the merit of their lives—[Col. 0426B] resounded with praise; that is, after the apostles, they preached the Gospel.

The forests too—that is, the Gentile world—and every tree in them—that is, every Gentile person—are commanded to resound, because the Lord redeemed Jacob, that is, his people, with his blood; and Israel, that is, the same people of the elect, shall glory in the Lord their Redeemer. After these things the omnipotent Father, wishing to make known to us the greatness of his works, says:

VERSE 24.—“Thus says the Lord, your Redeemer and your former from the womb: I am the Lord who makes all things.”

For by the blood of his Only-Begotten he redeemed us before we were created, and then formed us in our mother’s womb. It follows:

[Col. 0426C] “Stretching out the heavens alone, establishing the earth, and no one is with me.” By his power the Creator stretched out the breadth of the heavens to cover all things, and established the earth so that it might stand immovable.

The saints can be signified by the heavens, and the Church by the earth. Therefore the Lord stretches out the heavens because he causes the righteous, forgetting those things which are behind, to stretch forth to those which are before. He stretches out the heavens when, opening to his saints the way of preaching, he scatters them throughout the breadth of the world. He also establishes the earth because he founded the Church in Christ.

Or the sacred books may be expressed by the heavens, from which the stars of examples and virtues in the Fathers shine upon us. The Lord stretches them out because, by unfolding them through the words of teachers, he spreads them before our eyes. When the heavens have been stretched out, the earth is established, because when the sacred volumes are expounded our mind is confirmed, “so that we may no longer be children, tossed to and fro and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the wickedness of people, by craftiness and the deceits of error” (Eph. 4:14).

[Col. 0426D] When the Father testifies that he alone does all these things, he does not exclude the Son from his work, but idols. “For whatever the Father does, these things the Son also does in like manner” (John 5:19). For the operation of the Trinity is inseparable. It follows:

VERSE 25.—“Making void the signs of diviners, and turning soothsayers into madness.”

[Col. 0427A] Diviners observed certain signs from which they derived grounds for divination. But the Lord made these void, so that nothing true might be known through them. He also turned soothsayers, who prophesied beside the altars of demons, into madness, so that they could do nothing but rave and act in bacchic frenzy through a demonic spirit. It follows:

“Turning the wise backward, and making their knowledge foolish.”

He turns the wise of this world backward—that is, into folly—and makes their vain knowledge foolish. For it is written: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the prudence of the prudent. Where is the wise person? Where is the scribe? Where is the inquirer of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe” (1 Cor. 1:19–21). Hence he adds:

[Col. 0427B] VERSE 26.—“Raising up the word of his servant and fulfilling the counsel of his messengers.”

For the Lord Jesus is here called “servant” because of the form of a servant which he himself assumed. His word—that is, whatever he himself spoke in the Gospel—the Father raised up so that it might come to pass. His messengers are called the apostles; their counsel was that, dispersed through the four quarters of the world, they should harmoniously preach one Gospel and convert the whole human race to faith. And the Lord fulfilled this counsel as they had determined it. It follows:

[Col. 0427C] “Who says to Jerusalem: You shall be inhabited; and to the cities of Judah: You shall be built, and I shall raise up the desolate places.”

Now, in the historical sense, he signifies the return of the Israelite people from Persia into Judaea. Mystically, however, Jerusalem is the Church, which the Lord promises shall be inhabited by believers. The cities of Judah—that is, the cities of confession—are the various churches of the faithful, which nevertheless make one. The deserts of the Church or of confession are persons predestined for life but still remaining in unbelief; or persons who already possess faith but lack good works and are filled with vices. They are raised from the sleep of their former sloth when divine grace touches and awakens their minds, so that they may be converted. It follows:

[Col. 0427D] **VERSE 27.—**“Who say to the deep: Be desolate; and I will dry up your rivers.”

The rivers of Babylon are reported to have been dried up by the enterprise of the Medes when Belshazzar was killed, so that the city might be captured by way of the dry riverbeds. But according to the spiritual understanding, what is the deep—that is, the sea—except the present age? It is made desolate when the glory and power of the world are destroyed, and when what is written is fulfilled: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world” (1 John 2:15). And its rivers dry up when the doctrines of worldly learning are brought to nothing.

Or certainly the Lord abolished the deep when, as our Saviour descended into hell, he broke its gates and drew his chosen ones out from there. He dried up the rivers of this deep [Col. 0428A] when he drained from our hearts the slippery promptings of demons. It follows:

**VERSE 28.—**“Who say to Cyrus: You are my shepherd, and you shall fulfil all my will.”

Cyrus, king of the Persians, was God’s shepherd because he guarded the flock of the people Israel and fulfilled the divine will in releasing them from captivity. His name is interpreted “heir,” and he signifies him to whom the Father said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession” (Ps. 2:8). Therefore the Lord says to Cyrus: “You are my shepherd,” because our Saviour is the good shepherd, who laid down his life for his sheep, as he had received commandment from the Father; and he truly fulfilled in all things the whole will of the Father [Col. 0428B]. It follows:

“Who say to Jerusalem: You shall be built; and to the temple: You shall be founded.”

Here also he signifies the restoration both of the temple and of Jerusalem, which was to be carried out through Nehemiah and Zerubbabel (1 Esdras 3:2; 2 Esdras 2). Our Jerusalem also, which is above, is built through Christ with living stones. The temple likewise is founded when the mind of believers is established in faith. “For the temple of the Lord is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 3:17), says the Apostle, “and no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, namely, Christ Jesus” (ibid. 11).

## CHAPTER XLV

**VERSE 1.—**“Thus says the Lord to my anointed [Col. 0428C], Cyrus, whose right hand I have taken hold of, that I may subdue nations before his face, turn the backs of kings, open doors before him, and the gates shall not be shut.”

**VERSE 2.—**“I will go before you, and humble the glorious ones of the earth,” and the rest.

Kings among the people Israel were anointed with holy oil and were therefore called christs, that is, anointed ones; but this anointing was not performed among the Gentiles. Why, then, is Cyrus called christ, when he was not anointed with the oil of blessing? Because imperial dignity is reckoned to him in place of anointing. What he says, “Thus says the Lord to my anointed Cyrus,” is as though he said: “I, the Lord, say these things to my anointed Cyrus.” Or the Father calls Cyrus his king [Col. 0428D]. And what the Holy Spirit says to him is made known: “Whose right hand,” he says, “I have taken hold of”—that is, I have given him power, so that no one might be able to resist his strength—“that I may subdue nations before him,” that is, Babylonians, Medes, Egyptians, and the other nations; “and turn the backs of their kings before his face,” so that they may flee. For what nation could resist him? Which king did not turn his back to him? “And I will open doors before him, and the gates shall not be shut.” What city was not opened to him?

“I,” he says, “will go before you,” that is, I shall instil my terror into those to whom you are to come; “and I will humble the glorious ones of the earth under your hand; I will break bronze gates and shatter iron bars.” And this was so accomplished. For what walls, previously impregnable, were not overthrown when Cyrus besieged them [Col. 0429A]? The rest can easily be understood in the same manner. For he adds:

**VERSE 3.—**“And I will give you hidden treasures and the secret things of mysteries, that you may know that I am the Lord, who call you by your name, the God of Israel.”

**VERSE 4.—**“For the sake of my servant Jacob and Israel my chosen one.”

Long before he was born, Cyrus was called by his own name by the Lord for the sake of the people Israel, whom he was to release from captivity. It follows:

“And I have called you by your name; I have likened you, and you have not known me.”

I called you by name before you existed, just as long ago I called Isaac and Josiah beforehand. I likened you to my Son in title, so that you too might be called Christ, that is, anointed [Col. 0429B], and Cyrus, that is, heir, because you received the inheritance of your uncle Darius—namely, his kingdom. And you have not known me, because you remained in the error of idols. For if you had known me with a pure mind, you would know what follows:

**VERSE 5.—**“I am the Lord, and there is no other; apart from me there is no God.”

Therefore you have not known me, because you believed that there were foreign gods besides me. It follows:

“I have girded you, and you have not known me.”

**VERSE 6.—**“That they may know, from the rising of the sun and from the west, that apart from me there is no God.”

I have girded you with power so that you might dismiss my people, in order that, through their release, many from east and west might know that I alone am God, who thus delivered them when I willed.

But now let us see whether these things can also be understood otherwise. For it is known to all who the Christ of the Lord is: namely, he whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and power, who is also Cyrus, that is, heir, according as the Apostle says that we are “indeed heirs of God, but co-heirs with Christ” (Rom. 8:17). “Whose right hand,” he says, “I have taken hold of,” so that he might say to me: “You have held my right hand, and guided me according to your will” (Ps. 72:32). “That I may subdue nations before his face,” so that “at the name of Jesus every knee may bend” (Phil. 2:10). “And I will turn the backs of their kings,” because I shall put demons to flight [Col. 0429D]. “And I will open before him the doors of human hearts,” and the gates of minds shall not be shut against him but shall stand open to receive him joyfully.

What follows—“I will go before you, and humble the glorious ones of the earth”—must be understood in accordance with what he said above: “Who raised up the righteous man from the east, calling him to follow himself? He shall give nations before him, and shall rule kings” (above 41:2). “I will break,” he says, “bronze gates and shatter iron bars.” Since bronze is not consumed by rust, it is highly durable. And what is expressed by bronze gates except the entrances of human minds, long kept shut? What is figured by iron bars except the hard obstinacy of an evil will, which does not permit the door of the heart to be opened to Christ? Therefore, by the power of my [Col. 0430A] Spirit, I shall break the gates of minds, resembling bronze in their long-standing hardness, and the bars of inward obstinacy, hard as iron, so that even the hardest hearts may be opened to the coming of your grace.

“And I will give you hidden treasures and the secret things of mysteries,” so that “in you are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2:3). Or, the hidden treasures are persons predestined to life but still covered by sins. Saul was a hidden treasure while he persecuted the Church. Therefore I shall give you treasures of this kind, and I shall disclose to you secret things of mysteries, so that concerning each person you may know who will persevere in wickedness or holiness, and who will not. “And that you may know”—that is, cause your members to know—“that I am the Lord, who call you by your name, Cyrus,” that is, heir, “for the sake of my servant Jacob,” that is, for the sake of those who struggle with vices and deserve to be called not yet friends but still servants; “and for the sake of Israel my chosen one,” that is, for the sake of those intent upon contemplating heavenly things. For the sake of my faithful ones I called you my heir, because they are my inheritance, which I gave to you.

“And I have called you by your name,” Jesus, that is, Saviour. For you shall save your people from their sins. Or, “by your name,” as has been said, I called you heir, because “I will give you the nations for your inheritance” (Ps. 2:8). “And I made you like other human beings,” because you were “made in the likeness of men and found in outward form as a man” (Phil. 2:7). All these things were done for the sake of my servant Jacob and Israel my chosen one [Col. 0430C].

But what is added, “And you have not known me,” may by no means rightly be referred to the person of our Redeemer. Yet because the same Lord, taking flesh from the Jews, became one with them in lineage, it can, as it seems to me, be referred to the unbelieving people of the Jews: “And you have not known me.” For those who for so long a time worshipped Baal and also offered sacrifices to the Lord did not know him. Therefore he adds:

“I am the Lord, and there is no other; apart from me there is no God.”

For those who supposed other gods to exist did not know him who alone is God and Lord. Then, he says: “I have girded you, O Christ, with wondrous power, and you, people of the Jews, have not known me” [Col. 0430D]. Therefore I have girded you, my Christ, so that through you those who are from the rising of the sun and from the west may know that apart from me there is no God, so that “from the rising of the sun unto its setting the name of the Lord may be praised, and the Lord be exalted above all nations” (Ps. 112:3). Hence he repeats: “I am the Lord, and there is no other.” And he adds:

**VERSE 7.—**“Forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evil: I, the Lord, make all these things.”

The Lord forms in us the light of true knowledge, and outwardly creates the darkness of affliction. He makes inward peace of mind and outwardly creates the evils of adversity. Of these evils it is also said through blessed Job: [Col. 0431A] “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?” (Job 2:10). For evils that have no existence by their own nature are not created by the Lord; but the Lord declares that he creates evils when he fashions things well made into a scourge for us who act badly, so that those same things may be evils to sinners through the pain by which they strike, and goods through the nature in which they exist. Thus poison is death to a human being, but life to a serpent. Through love of present things we withdrew from the love of our Creator; and the perverse mind, while subjecting itself to love of the creature, separated itself from fellowship with the Creator. We had to be struck by those things which, in going astray, we had preferred to the Creator, so that where human beings had not feared proudly to incur guilt, there they might find punishment for their correction; and so that they might return all the sooner to their senses and to the things they had lost, the more full of pain they saw to be the things they had sought [Col. 0431B]. Therefore it is well said: “Forming light and creating darkness,” because when outward darkness is created through scourges, inwardly the light of the mind is kindled through instruction. “Making peace and creating evils,” because peace with God is restored to us when those things, well made but not rightly desired, are turned into scourges that are evils to us. For through sin we became estranged from God. It is fitting, therefore, that we should return to his peace through scourges, so that, while every thing well made is turned into pain for us, the corrected mind may humbly be re-formed for the Creator’s peace. Thus the Lord calls these scourges evils because, by disturbing the good of health and tranquillity, they strike. But [Col. 0431C] because up to this point he has set forth what he was to do through Christ, or to do for him, he now adds concerning his birth:

**VERSE 8.—**“Drop down dew from above, O heavens, and let the clouds rain the Just One; let the earth be opened, and let it bring forth the Saviour, and let righteousness arise at the same time: I, the Lord, created him.”

That is: let the angel come and proclaim the word; let the earth be opened, let Mary hear; and let it bring forth the Saviour and bear Jesus; and let righteousness arise at the same time, so that he may not be justified afterward, but may be born together with righteousness. For he was born righteous and holy, as the Angel testified when he said to his mother: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you; therefore also that holy thing which shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). Hence he adds: “For I, the Lord, created him” [Col. 0431D]. That is to say: by the operation of my Spirit he was created in the womb of a virgin, not begotten through intercourse with a man. But because every Jew asserts that he is not the son of a virgin but the son of Joseph, it rightly follows:

**VERSE 9.—**“Woe to him who contradicts his maker, a potsherd from earthen Samian vessels!”

For one contradicts his maker—that is, his fashioner—when the carnal Jew says that Jesus, whom God the creator of all things testifies that he himself uniquely created, was created from a man’s seed like the rest. Samos is an island or city in which the art of pottery is said to have been invented; and therefore earthenware vessels are called Samian. Thus what he says, “a potsherd among earthen Samians,” is as though he said: “a potsherd among earthen potsherds,” a clay vessel among clay vessels of the earth. Every person generated from man and woman is an earthen Samian potsherd. And does this potsherd dare contradict its maker if he wishes, out of the same clay, to make a marvellous vessel, uniquely sanctified for honour and prepared for every good work [Col. 0432A]? Hence it follows:

“Will the clay say to its potter: What are you making? And your work is without hands?”

The clay says to its potter, “What are you making?” when a human being made of clay dares to dispute against the action of his maker, by which he creates Christ from a Virgin, and says to him: “Your work is without your hands”—that is, your hands are not in this work—when he denies that God made what he made, namely, created Christ from a Virgin. Hence he further adds:

**VERSE 10.—**“Woe to him who says to a father: What are you begetting? and to a woman: What are you bringing forth?”

He says to the Father, “What are you begetting?” either when he rashly attempts to investigate the hidden causes of the eternal generation of the Son of God, or when in any respect he contradicts that generation. And he says to the woman—that is, to the chosen woman who bore him as a virgin—“What are you bringing forth?” either when he tries rashly and presumptuously to examine her childbirth, or when he censures that same childbirth. “Woman” is used here for sex, as also in: “God sent his Son, made of a woman” (Gal. 4:4). Or he says to the Father, “What are you begetting?” when he reproves a preacher because through the Gospel he begets children of adoption for God [Col. 0432C]. And he says to the woman, “What are you bringing forth?” when he is indignant with the Church because she bears spiritual children. It follows:

**VERSE 11.—**“Thus says the Lord God [Note: [Col. 0431] Elsewhere: God, Holy One of Israel], Israel’s maker: Ask me concerning things to come.”

He is Israel’s maker who says elsewhere: “Behold, as clay is in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel” (Jer. 18:6). Or this refers to Christ, whom God fashioned through the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin. He now says also to that people Israel: Do not contradict me in those things which I foretell concerning Christ’s incarnation, but rather ask me about things to come concerning him or concerning his Church. And in rebuke he adds: “Command me concerning my sons and my daughters [Col. 0432D], and concerning the work of my hands [Note: [Col. 0431] Elsewhere: “my sons and concerning the work of my hands,” etc.].” As though he said: It is not necessary that you should prescribe to me how I am to do the things which I shall do concerning Christ and the Church. Therefore, displaying the power of his action, he adds:

**VERSE 12.—**“I made the earth, and I created humankind upon it; my hands stretched out the heavens, and I commanded all their host.”

It is so: he made the earth and humankind, stretched out the heavens, and commanded all their host—that is, the angels, to fulfil their ministries and offices; and the stars, to accomplish their courses and appear in their own places and times. The Church may also be understood by “earth,” [Col. 0433A] and by “human being,” the man Christ Jesus, mediator between God and humankind.

But what is designated by the heavens except the minds of the elect, raised by inward love above every contagion of earthly things? The Lord’s hands stretch out these heavens because the bosom of the mind is enlarged by the light of inward vision; it is so expanded in God that it stands above the world, and, when it is caught up in God’s light, it is enlarged even beyond itself in its inward depths. While it sees itself beneath itself, it grasps in exaltation how brief is that which, when humbled, it could not grasp. Thus the Lord stretches out the heavens, because whatever small portion of the Creator’s delight a mind sees, everything created becomes narrow to it. And what is the host of such heavens except the conduct of the righteous? For “the life of man upon earth is warfare” [Col. 0433B] (Job 7:1). The Lord has commanded this host because he has given the saints’ lives precepts for acting in this way. Concerning his Christ, of whom he has often spoken, he adds:

**VERSE 13.—**“I have raised him up for righteousness, and I will direct all his ways.”

“I have raised him up,” that is, I caused him to be born to perform righteousness, as it is also said elsewhere: “For I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and he shall execute judgment and righteousness in the earth” (Jer. 23:5). “And I will direct all his ways,” because “the will of the Lord shall be directed in his hand, and all things whatsoever he does shall prosper” (Isa. 53:16).

“He shall build my city, and shall release my captivity [Col. 0433C] neither for a price nor for gifts, says the Lord God of hosts.”

He shall build the heavenly Jerusalem with living stones, and shall freely deliver us from the captivity of this Babylon, that is, of this confused age. For when our first parent sinned, he was taken captive by the devil and, cast out from his homeland, sent into the exile of this pilgrimage. Hence all his children are held captive in this world as though in Babylon, until they are delivered through him who says: “If the Son sets you free, you shall be truly free” (John 8:36). Therefore he releases this captivity when he leads us back to the homeland of our former blessedness, not for a price which he receives from us, nor for gifts, but through free mercy. “For you have been saved freely,” says the Apostle (Eph. 2:8) [Col. 0433D]. To this our deliverer, accordingly, it is said by the Father’s promise:

**VERSE 14.—**“Thus says the Lord: The labour of Egypt, the merchandise of Ethiopia, and the tall men of the Sabaeans shall pass over to you and shall be yours; they shall walk after you; they shall go with hands bound [Note: [Col. 0433] Elsewhere: “bound in manacles.” Codex G.: “with hands bound in manacles.” Crucensis below: “bound in manacles.”], and shall worship you and make supplication to you: Only God is in you, and there is no God apart from you.”

**VERSE 15.—**“Truly you are a hidden God, the God of Israel, the Saviour.”

**VERSE 16.—**“They are confounded and ashamed; all together the makers of errors have gone into captivity.”

[Col. 0434A] **VERSE 17.—**“Israel is saved in the Lord with eternal salvation.”

Egypt, as was said above, is interpreted “darkness”; Ethiopia, “gloom”; and the Sabaeans are called “captives.” What, then, are expressed by Egypt and Ethiopia except the nations, whose understanding is darkened by darkness, alienated from the way of God through the ignorance that is in them because of the blindness of their hearts? And who are the tall men of the Sabaeans—that is, proud captive men—except those concerning whom we pray that God may give them repentance for the knowledge of truth, and that they may come to their senses from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive according to his will?

Egypt laboured and Ethiopia traded because the blind Gentiles devoted themselves to earthly labour [Col. 0434B] and became entangled in worldly business. But the labour of Egypt and the merchandise of Ethiopia shall pass over to you, who release captivity not for a price, so that Gentiles who laboured in the darkness of unbelief for temporal life may labour in your faith for everlasting life; and those who pursued carnal business may become spiritual merchants acquiring inward riches. For this reason: “The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking good pearls; when he found one precious pearl, he went away, sold all that he had, and bought it” (Matt. 13:45–46).

The tall captive men also—that is, heretics, or the powerful of this age, or any stubborn persons who are converted—shall now faithfully pass over to you, leaping across the wall of sin that stood between you and them, or deserting the camp of the ancient enemy and passing to your side. They shall be yours and shall walk after you, following your footsteps. “For whoever says that he abides in Christ ought himself also to walk as he walked” (1 John 2:6) [Col. 0434C].

“They shall go bound in manacles,” because they shall follow the way of righteousness in such a manner that their hands are restrained from evil work by the bonds of your commandments. And they shall worship you supplicantly and make entreaty to you, saying: “Only God is in you, and there is no God apart from you.” For God is not in the dwelling-place of a nature opposed and foreign to himself; rather, God remains in God, the Father in the Son, in that which is his own and begotten from himself. For he says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 10:38). And, they say, “there is no God apart from you, O Christ.” For it is proper to the Son of God that no God should exist apart from him. The Father is not apart from the Son, who says: “I and the Father are one” (ibid. 30); and: “The Father is in me, and I am in the Father.” For the Father and Son are not two gods, but one God. The same is to be understood concerning the Holy Spirit.

Then the tall men say: “Truly you are a hidden God,” whom this wretched world does not know, the God who saves Israel, who alone can save. For the gods of the nations cannot save their worshippers. Or, you are a hidden God because “the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, is rightly called a hidden God [Col. 0435A]. Or he is called a hidden God on account of the mystery of the body assumed. But where this hidden God became known to the world, the Gentile and heretical makers of errors were confounded and ashamed, all together drinking the reproach of their folly; and they went into the captivity of everlasting damnation, where, bound perpetually with the devil, they shall be kept in the prison of hell.

But Israel—that is, the people of the elect—is saved in the Lord with eternal salvation. “We know that if our earthly house of this dwelling should be dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Cor. 5:5). But because the godly are accustomed to be mocked by the ungodly [Note: [Col. 0435D] Codex G.: “to be derided.”], a consoling promise is fittingly added to them [Col. 0435B]: “You shall not be confounded or ashamed for ever and ever.” You shall not be confounded by the blasphemies of unbelievers in the present age, until the age of ages comes—that is, the age which shall succeed this one—in which you shall glory perpetually. And why you have no reason to be confounded or ashamed follows [Note: [Col. 0435D] In the Garst. codex, these words, “and why,” etc., down to “because these things,” etc., are lacking.]:

**VERSE 18.—**“For thus says the Lord, who creates the heavens, he himself God, who forms the earth and makes it, he himself its maker: he did not create it in vain [Note: [Col. 0435D] Elsewhere: “in emptiness.”]; he formed it to be inhabited: I am the Lord, and there is no other.”

Therefore, he says, you shall not be ashamed, because the Lord Jesus, who by the power of his divinity created the heavens and made and formed the earth to be inhabited by human beings, now proclaims to all its inhabitants that he alone is Lord and that apart from him there is no Lord [Col. 0435C]. It follows:

**VERSE 19.—**“I have not spoken in secret, in a dark place of the earth.”

This is, unless I am mistaken, what he says in the Gospel: “I have spoken openly to the world; I have always taught in synagogue and in the temple, where all the Jews assemble, and in secret I have spoken nothing” (John 18:20). For how could he speak in secret who proclaimed common salvation to all who came together to him generally? Heresy, on the contrary, speaks in secret, in a dark place of the earth, because it is said in Proverbs: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasant” (Prov. 9:17) [Note: [Col. 0436D] Both codices read “which.”; Col. 0435D]. Or he did not speak in secret when he declared himself alone to be God, he who cried from the summit of Mount Sinai: “You shall have no foreign gods apart from me, nor shall you make for yourself an idol” (Deut. 5:7). But it is better understood of apostolic preaching. The Lord further adds:

“I did not say to the seed of Jacob: Seek me in vain.”

As though he said: I did not make them await my coming to no purpose, because I came to them as I had promised. And concerning his teaching he adds: “I, the Lord [Col. 0436A], speak righteousness, declaring things that are right.” As though he said: Everything that proceeds from my mouth is just and right. And truly it is so. For what is more right than what he commands or says in the Gospel? By this righteousness believers are justified, who could not be justified in the law. As he says there, “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened” (Matt. 11:28), so here too he adds:

**VERSE 20.—**“Gather yourselves and come; draw near together, you who have been saved from among the nations.”

Gather yourselves into the folds of the Church; come in the merit of good action; and draw near together, all you who have been saved in hope from among the nations. “For we were saved in hope” (Rom. 8:24). And why you ought to hasten to draw near to me follows:

[Col. 0436B] “Those who lift up the sign of their carved image and pray to a god that cannot save have not known.” For those who carve an idol for themselves and worship it do not know what they are doing, because their foolish heart has been darkened. Then the preachers of the Gospel are commanded:

**VERSE 21.—**“Declare and come, and take counsel together.”

For holy preachers, after they had made their proclamation, came and took counsel together when the Jews maintained that Gentiles coming to faith ought to be circumcised, and Paul with Barnabas went up to Jerusalem to hear (Acts 15) what the earlier apostles thought about this matter. Even now the leaders of churches take counsel together, often meeting in synods and councils. But to the converted Gentiles the Lord adds:

[Col. 0436C] “Who made it known from the beginning [Note: [Col. 0436D] Elsewhere: “made this from the beginning.”]? Did I foretell it from that time?” [Note: [Col. 0436D] Elsewhere: “he foretold.”]

For from that time—that is, from the beginning—he foretold it, announcing the conversion of the nations to Abraham: “Because in your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). Again he testifies that he alone is God, saying: “Am not I the Lord, and is there no God besides me? There is no just and saving God apart from me.” This is evident. For all those called gods among the nations are unjust and do not save their worshippers but destroy them. It follows:

**VERSE 22.—**“Turn to me and you shall be saved, all ends of the earth, because I am God and there is no other.”

[Col. 0436D] This too is evident. For there is no God besides Christ, who saves the whole world when it turns to him. It follows:

**VERSE 23.—**“I have sworn by myself; the word of righteousness shall go out from my mouth and shall not return: for every knee shall bend to me [Note: [Col. 0436D] Elsewhere: “every knee shall bend.”], and every tongue shall swear.”

“I have sworn by myself,” he says, because, having none greater by whom he might swear, he swore by himself. For human beings swear by one greater than themselves, and the oath is the end, for confirmation, of all their disputes. “Wherein God, willing more abundantly to show the heirs of the promise the immovability of his counsel, interposed an oath, so that through two immutable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we might have the strongest consolation” (Heb. 6:13 ff.) [Col. 0437A].

But let us hear what he swore. “The word of righteousness shall go out from my mouth”: that is, the judgment whereby all who have believed are to be judged through faith. “And it shall not return,” because the righteousness given through faith to the elect shall remain for ever, nor shall I repent of having uttered this word. For “every knee shall bend to me,” “so that at the name of Jesus every knee may bend” (Phil. 2:10). “And every tongue shall swear to me,” “so that every tongue may confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (ibid. 11) [Col. 0437B]. Every tongue shall swear to me because the diversity of all tongues shall agree in this: to swear devoted service to me.

Or let us understand the statement, “Every knee shall bend to me, and every tongue shall swear,” as the Apostle explained it, saying: “We shall all stand before the judgment-seat of Christ. For it is written: As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bend to me, and every tongue shall confess to God. Therefore each of us shall render an account of himself to God” (Rom. 14:10–12). In this sense, to bend the knee to God is to stand before the judgment-seat of Christ; and to confess or swear to God is to render to him an account of oneself. It follows:

**VERSE 24.—**“Therefore in the Lord one shall say: Righteousnesses and dominion are mine.”

Because the word of righteousness shall go out from my mouth and every tongue, with bent knee, shall swear to me, therefore every tongue swearing to me shall say “in the Lord,” that is, in my Father: “Righteousnesses are mine, because I have been justified through the word of Christ; and dominion is mine, because in Christ I have been made a queen.” These things the Church says, which exists among all tongues and nations [Col. 0437C]. She also calls dominion hers because she rules throughout the whole world. But concerning those who did not receive the Gospel of God, it follows:

“To him they shall come, and all who resist him shall be confounded.”

For they come to the Lord either now by believing, and are confounded concerning their evils by doing penance; or afterward, in order to stand before his tribunal and bear the reproach of eternal confusion. But concerning the elect he adds:

**VERSE 25.—**“In the Lord all the seed of Israel shall be justified and praised.”

In the Lord Jesus Christ it shall be justified, just as Paul says to the Jews: “Be it known to you, brethren, that through him forgiveness of sins is announced to you, from all things from which you were not able to be justified in the law of Moses. In him everyone who believes is justified” (Acts 13:38). And it shall be praised in him, because “all who swear by him shall be praised” (Ps. 62:12) [Col. 0438A]. All the seed of Israel—not carnal but spiritual—shall be justified in this life and praised in the other. “For not all who are from Israel are Israelites; neither are all who are Abraham’s seed children; but in Isaac your seed shall be called: that is, not the children of the flesh are children of God, but the children of promise are reckoned as seed” (Rom. 9:6–8). After believers have been justified in Christ and all tongues have sworn to him, it fittingly follows:

## CHAPTER XLVI

**VERSE 1.—**“Bel is melted down [Note: [Col. 0437D] Elsewhere: “broken.”], Nabo is crushed; their images have become for beasts and cattle.”

For believers have melted down and crushed all idols. Bel and Nabo were idols. Bel is interpreted “ancient,” and Nabo, “seat.” And who is this ancient one except the ancient enemy? Or what is this seat except that which he desired when he thought to set his throne in the north? This seat is his kingdom among unbelievers. Therefore Bel is melted down and Nabo crushed because the devil has been consigned to Tartarean fires, and his kingdom has been crushed by repentance out of the hearts of those who have believed [Col. 0438B].

Their images—that is, the images of the devil and of his dominion—were idols, and these became for beasts and cattle because people who raged with beastly ferocity, and who carried without resistance whatever burdens demons laid upon them, worshipped them. Of these it is then said:

[Col. 0438C] “Your burdens, of heavy weight, unto weariness.”

**VERSE 2.—**“They have wasted away and been crushed together; they could not save the one carrying them.”

For the idols, which wearied with heavy weight those carrying them, were afterward broken and decayed, nor could they save their bearers. For it follows:

“And their soul shall go into captivity.” That is, it shall be led, bound with everlasting chains, into the prison of perpetual condemnation.

Or this should be said: the exceedingly heavy burden among the Gentiles was the error of idolatry, which pressed its worshippers down to earth. The gods of the nations are made by their worshippers and carried by them; they cannot save those who carry them. But our God himself made us, and himself bears and saves us. It follows:

**VERSE 3.—**“Hear me, house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel, you who are carried from my womb, who are borne from my belly.”

**VERSE 4.—**“Even to old age I am he, and even to grey hairs I will bear you; I have made, and I will carry; I will bear and save.”

For the house of Jacob is the Church holding the faith of the patriarchs, because Christ “shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever” (Luke 1:33). And what is the remnant of the house of Israel except that of which it is said: “Everyone who is left in Zion and remains in Jerusalem shall be called holy” (above 4:3) [Col. 0439A]? The house of Jacob and the remnant of the house of Israel may also, in the historical sense, be understood as the ancient people of God.

In the womb offspring is conceived, which is brought forth into this life. What, therefore, ought we to understand by the womb or belly of God except his counsel, in which before the ages we were received through predestination, so that, created within the ages, we might be brought forth? Ambrose, however, speaking of the Only-begotten, says: “Just as the bosom of the Father is understood spiritually as a certain innermost secret of paternal love and nature, in which the Son always is, so also the Father’s womb is the spiritual mystery of his interior being, from which the Son proceeded as from a generative belly.” But since we speak of adopted children, we understand the womb [Col. 0439B] or belly of God, as we have said, to mean his counsel. We are borne from that womb, namely because God, in the counsel of wisdom, patiently bears us, knowing who are his.

And what is his old age except everlasting infinity? Thus he himself is unto old age, who remains forever without change or variation, of whom it is said: “But thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail” (Ps. CI. 28). He indeed remains unto his own old age, which is perpetual immortality and infinity; but he bears us unto the gray hairs of our old age—that is, he long-sufferingly endures us until the end of the present life, and then will render to each what they have deserved. Or, he bears us unto old age not his own [Col. 0439C] but ours, enduring and advancing us; and through just compassion he will save us forever. And in all these works he is utterly contrary to the gods of the nations. Therefore he again rebukes idolaters, saying:

**VERSE 5.**—“To whom have you likened and equated me, and made me similar?”

**VERSE 6.**—“You who pour gold from a bag and weigh silver in scales, hiring a craftsman to make a god.”

For in their estimation they made him like a material idol—him who, as the Apostle says, “they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, and four-footed beasts, and creeping things” (Rom. I. 23). Of them it is further said: “And they fall down and worship.”

**VERSE 7.**—“They carry it upon their shoulders, bearing it and setting it in its place; and it will stand and shall not move from its place. But when they cry to it, it will not answer [Note: [Col. 0439D] Alternatively, it will not hear, etc.], nor will it save them from tribulation.” All this is plain. It follows:

**VERSE 8.**—“Remember this, and be established [Note: [Col. 0440D] Alternatively, be confounded.]; return, transgressors, to your heart.”

**VERSE 9.**—“Remember the former age, because I am God, and there is no other God, nor is any like me.”

O worshippers of the idol, he says, remember—that is, reconsider—this: your god was manufactured in this fashion; and, once placed [Col. 0440A] in its location, it could not move itself, nor can it hear or help its worshippers. Be established in the truth, lest your mind be tossed about by varying errors.

Return to your heart from the image which you behold outside yourselves, because in such things you have lost the capacity for right thought. What is nearer to us than our heart? Yet when it is scattered through evil thoughts, our heart wanders far from us. He therefore sends far away those whom he commands to return to their own heart, because the more they have poured themselves outward, the more scarcely do they discover whence they may return to themselves. For minds scattered abroad find it difficult to return to themselves, because those entangled in earthly desires, once caught, are held by evil paths with so much delight as they are permitted in them to do whatever they please [Col. 0440B]. For no wall of discipline confronts them to restrain them; no punishment of recompense is foreseen to frighten them. Instead, with the eyes of the heart shut, the soul is hurled headlong into low things in proportion as it is darkened from the highest; and it commits temporal evils all the more securely as it despairs more harshly of eternal goods.

Such were those “who, when they had known God, did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. For, professing themselves to be wise, they became fools, and, as has been said before, changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, and four-footed beasts, and creeping things. Therefore God gave [Col. 0440C] them up to the desires of their heart, to uncleanness, so that they dishonoured their bodies among themselves” (Rom. I. 21–24). Therefore, when it pleases divine goodness that such persons repent, he fittingly says to them: “Return, transgressors, to your heart.” For transgressors are those who, having known the Lord, did not glorify him as God. In knowing God, they in a certain manner received a law requiring them to give him glory; but they transgressed it in the worship of idols. Or, they transgressed the natural law by acting wickedly.

After commanding those whom idolatry had scattered outward in vanity to return to their heart, he says: “Remember the former age,” because then an idol had not even been named. For if idols were gods, they would surely have made the world. But they did not exist in the former age, and therefore they cannot be gods. For I, who created the world, am God, and there is no other God, just as there is no other world; nor is anyone like me. To what he had said, that there is none like him, he aptly adds:

**VERSE 10.**—“Declaring the last things from the beginning, and from the outset things not yet done, saying: My counsel shall stand, and all my will shall be accomplished.”

For God declared the last things from the beginning, saying in Adam that “a man shall leave his father” (Gen. II. 24): that is, Christ will descend from the throne of his majesty [Col. 0441A]; “and his mother” (Gen. II. 4): that is, he will leave the Synagogue; “and shall cleave to his wife” (ibid.): that is, to the Church; “and the two shall be one flesh” (ibid.). His counsel shall stand, and all his will shall be accomplished, since not even those things which appear to occur contrary to his will can oppose his will. For he sometimes permits to happen what he has not commanded, so that by this means what he commands may be fulfilled more certainly. The apostate angel has a perverse will; nevertheless, it is wonderfully ordered by God, so that even his snares serve the benefit of the good, whom they purify while tempting them. Thus his counsel stands: from that very source from which someone strives to oppose the counsel of his will, he fulfills his will the more.

But when he declares the last things from the beginning, and from the outset things [Col. 0441B] not yet done, saying, “My counsel shall stand, and all my will shall be accomplished,” he sufficiently shows that he speaks of the counsel by which he determined that, as the end of the world approached, the devil should lose the human race through the Passion of the Saviour. For he announced this from the beginning, saying to the serpent: “I will put enmities between thee and the woman, and thy seed and her seed” (Gen. III. 15). And his will is the salvation of the world—he “who wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (I Tim. II. 4). He announced this will of his from the beginning to Abraham, promising him that “in thy seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII. 18). But these things had not yet happened: that is, his will in the salvation of the world had not yet been fulfilled when he spoke these things through the prophet. Since he raised Christ from the dead and placed him at his right hand in the heavenly places, he fittingly adds concerning him, after proclaiming the counsel of that Passion:

**VERSE 11.**—“Calling a bird from the east, and from a distant land the man of my will.”

For he calls him a bird who, by ascending into the heavens, lifted up the fleshly body which he had assumed. And he calls the same one “the man of his will,” of whom he elsewhere testifies: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III. 17). We have already said that the people of the Jews is for this reason called “the east”: because from its flesh was born that same Saviour who is called the sun of righteousness. This region of ours, in which we live as exiles and strangers, is called a distant land [Col. 0441D]. Thus God called the bird from the east and the man of his will from a distant land when he raised Christ from Bethany into heaven.

Or the Gentiles may be called the distant land, because they were far from God while serving idols. He called the bird from the east when, through the apostles, he sent Christ from the Jews to the Gentiles. And again he called the man of his will from a distant land when through Elijah’s preaching he will bring him back from the Gentiles to the Hebrews. And in all these things what he said will be fulfilled: “My counsel shall stand, and all my will shall be accomplished.” Concerning this he also adds:

[Col. 0442A] “I have spoken, and I shall bring it to pass; I have created it, and I shall do it.” I have spoken my counsel through the prophets, and I shall bring it to pass in its own time; I created it by predestining it, and I shall perform it by working it. Therefore it follows:

**VERSE 12.**—“Hear me, you hard of heart, who are far from righteousness.”

**VERSE 13.**—“I have brought my righteousness near; it shall not be far off; and my salvation shall not delay. I shall give salvation in Zion, and my glory in Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0441D] Alternatively, and my glory in Israel.].”

For the Jews were always hard of heart and far from righteousness. “For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God and seeking to establish their own, they have not submitted themselves to the righteousness of God” (Rom. X. 3). To them he says: “I have brought my righteousness near; it shall not be far off, and my salvation shall not delay”—[Col. 0442B] that is, the time has drawn near for the righteousness of faith to be revealed [Note: [Col. 0442D] Both codices: “lifted up.”] through Christ. It shall not be deferred any longer, and eternal salvation, which is to be given through him to believers, shall delay no longer.

I shall give eternal salvation in Zion to those among you who have believed, and in Jerusalem I shall give my glory to those who have received the faith of my Christ, so that, filled with the Holy Spirit, they may speak in every language, prophesy, and shine with signs and miracles. This occurred in that “multitude of believers, who were of one heart and one soul” (Acts IV. 32). It follows:

## CHAPTER XLVII

**VERSE 1.**—“Come down; sit in the dust, virgin [Col. 0442C] daughter of Babylon; sit on the ground.”

In the reprobate, even when an opportunity to commit sin is lacking, thoughts of desire are by no means absent from their hearts; and although they do not always follow the devil in action, they bind themselves strongly to him in thought. Therefore it is now rightly said: “Come down; sit in the dust, virgin daughter of Babylon; sit on the ground.” Although dust is always earth, earth is not always dust. What then ought we to understand by dust except thoughts, which, as they fly about importunately and silently in the mind, blind its eyes? And what is signified by earth except earthly action?
