Since the mind of the reprobate is first led to think evil and afterwards to do it, the daughter of Babylon, who has descended from the judgment of inward rectitude, is rightly told in a striking sentence first to sit in dust and afterwards on the ground: for unless she had prostrated herself in thought, she would not have clung to evil action. Here the human mind is called a virgin, I think, not because it is uncorrupted, but because it is barren.

And because Babylon is interpreted “confusion,” a barren mind is rightly called Babylon’s daughter: since it produces no good works and is not ordered by any rule of right living, it is, as it were, begotten by confusion as its mother. But if “virgin” means not barren but uncorrupted, then, after it has lost its state of salvation, it is called what it once was as an addition to the fullness of its confusion. To it it is fittingly said in rebuke: “Come down.” [Col. 0443A] For the human mind stands on high when it longs for heavenly recompense; but it descends from this state when, shamefully conquered, it subjects itself to the flowing desires of the world. To it is rightly added at once: “Sit in the dust.” For one who descends sits in the dust when, abandoning heavenly things, he is besprinkled with earthly thoughts and becomes vile among low things. It is further repeated: “Sit on the ground.” It is as though he said reproachfully: Since you refused to raise yourself by heavenly conduct, humble yourself beneath yourself in earthly actions. Therefore it is necessarily added immediately:

“There is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans.”

For the Chaldeans are fierce, because, following their own wills, they do not know how even to spare their own deaths. Earthly desires are fierce: they render the mind hard and unfeeling not only against the Creator’s commandments, but often even against the blows of punishments. But the daughter of the fierce has no throne, because the mind which is born into love of the world from evil desires, and hardened by those same desires, loses the seat of judgment in subjecting itself to earthly lusts. No one presides over a throne within himself who lacks the judgment of discernment. He is, as it were, expelled from the seat of his own judgment when he wanders through outward desires. It is plain that the mind which has lost within the seat of counsel scatters itself outward through innumerable desires; and because it neglects to act upon what it understands, it is rightly blinded so that it does not even know what it does. Often, by just judgment, it is left to its own will and released beneath the burdensome services of the world which it anxiously seeks [Col. 0443C]. Therefore it fittingly adds:

“Because thou shalt no longer be called soft and tender.”

**VERSE 2.**—“Take the millstone and grind flour.”

“It is certainly established (St Gregory the Great, *Morals*, book VI, chapter 16) that parents spare tender daughters and do not afflict them with hard and servile labours. Therefore almighty God calls the beloved soul of each person a tender daughter when he recalls it from the burdensome services of this world, lest, while it is occupied with outward actions, it become hardened against inward desires. But the daughter of the Chaldeans is not called soft and tender, because a mind given over to evil desires is left in the toil of this age which it anxiously seeks, so that it may serve the world outwardly like a slave-girl, since inwardly it does not love God as a daughter [Col. 0443D]. Therefore she is commanded to take up the millstone and grind flour.

“The millstone is turned in a circle and produces flour. Every action of this world is therefore a millstone: while it heaps up many cares, it turns human minds as if in a circle; and it casts forth from itself, as it were, flour, because it continually generates very minute thoughts in the deceived heart. Sometimes, moreover, one who is believed to possess some merit in tranquillity is exposed when placed in some activity. Hence it immediately adds:

“‘Strip thy shame naked; uncover thy shoulder; reveal thy legs; cross the rivers.’

“For in the management of work shame is uncovered, when a vile and abject mind becomes known in the display of its work, though it was previously thought great while at rest. The mind uncovers its shoulder when it shows the work which had been unknown. It reveals its leg because it discloses by what steps of desire it longs after worldly gain. It also crosses rivers because it incessantly seeks the actions of this age, which daily flow toward their end. And while it leaves some behind and pursues others, it is as though it always comes from river to river.” Blessed Gregory says these things, showing how low the mind lies when cast down from the throne of holy intention: if it ceases to long for the things above it, it also falls continually beneath itself. Since its hidden shame is now uncovered, as has been said, by the reprobation of its work, or is later openly shown to all in the final judgment, it is rightly added:

[Col. 0444B] **VERSE 3.**—“Therefore thy shame shall be revealed, and thy reproach shall be seen.”

Concerning the vengeance which will occur at that judgment, or at the death of any reprobate person, it plainly adds: “I shall take vengeance, and no man shall resist me.” For then no one will any longer resist him. Formerly, however, Moses resisted his wrath for the people, saying: “Forgive them this sin; otherwise blot me out of thy book which thou hast written” (Exod. XXXII. 32). So too Aaron resisted him, when he took the censer between the living and the dead and tempered the fire of punishment with the smoke of incense (Num. XVI. 46). David also resisted his wrath (II Kings XXIV. 16): offering himself to the smiting angel, he obtained the grace of appeasement before the appointed time. All the saints likewise who withstand his wrath receive from him the power to oppose the onset of his punishment. Thus, so to speak, they rise with him against him; divine power sets them in opposition to itself together with itself, because, while they restrain outwardly the wrath of one raging against them, inwardly the grace of the angry one cherishes them, and raises inwardly those whom he outwardly endures as if they were opponents [Col. 0444C].

Therefore he bears the contradiction of those who pray—a contradiction which he inspires—and that which he himself commands to be done is imposed upon him as though he were unwilling. This is apparent in his words when he says to Moses: “Let me alone, that my fury may be angry against them and that I may destroy them” (Exod. XXXII. 10). What is it to say to a servant, “Let me alone,” except to grant boldness to one who intercedes? But when heavenly indignation, so to speak, is stirred from the very marrow, human opposition does not restrain it, nor does anyone’s prayer usefully interpose itself when God has once determined something in inward wrath. Hence it is said through blessed Job: “God, whose wrath no one can resist” (Job IX. 13). For divine wrath is restrained by no intervention when it is stirred up implacably.

Therefore, moved by this inexorable indignation against the daughter of Babylon, he says: “I shall take vengeance, and no man shall resist me.” For man is altogether unable to resist him when he rouses himself to take vengeance and does not inspire the prayer poured out to him. Hence Solomon also says: “He will not spare in the day of vengeance, nor yield to anyone’s prayers, nor receive abundant gifts as ransom” (Prov. VI. [Col. 0445A] 34). Those who celebrate masses or offer prayers or alms for utterly wicked persons who have died ought to take heed of this judgment. Yet often such a soul, having acquired power in this world, afflicts God’s servants, as the Chaldean people of old afflicted the children of Judah in Babylon. But when a ruler of this kind is led to vengeance on the day of his death, the people of God, whom he had oppressed in slavery, are redeemed from his hand. Hence he immediately adds in the voice of that same people:

**VERSE 4.**—“Our Redeemer—the Lord of hosts is his name—the Holy One of Israel.”

For he who redeems us from the hand of the oppressor—that is, frees us—is called the Lord of hosts, because the hosts of angels serve him in avenging evils. His name is the Holy One of Israel, who was unwilling to tolerate further the irreligion of Babylon’s daughter. Hence he adds:

**VERSE 5.**—“Sit; be silent [Note: [Col. 0445D] Alternatively, sit silently, etc.]; enter into darkness, daughter of the Chaldeans, because thou shalt no longer be called mistress of kingdoms.”

For she who stood sits when she is cast down and becomes vile, though she gloried while upright. She is silent when, finding no excuse for her perversity, she wastes away in grief. And she enters into darkness when she is sent into the night of perpetual damnation, as the Lord says: “Bind him hand and foot and cast him into the outer darkness” (Matt. XXII. 13). Nor is she now called mistress of kingdoms, because with life she loses the glory of singular power. It follows:

[Col. 0445C] **VERSE 6.**—“I was angry with my people; I defiled my inheritance, and gave them into thy hand.”

This is plain. For the Lord, angered with his people, often gives them a harsh or cruel ruler, because it is written: “He makes a hypocritical man reign because of the sins of the people” (Job XXXIV. 30). It follows:

“Thou didst not show them mercies; upon the old man thou didst heavily lay thy yoke.”

**VERSE 7.**—“And thou saidst: I shall be mistress forever.”

This too is clear. A wicked ruler mercilessly afflicts God’s people and treats them inhumanely; he does not spare even the aged from the affliction of slavery, and says, as though he would rule forever, while, believing that he will exercise power for a long time, he neglects to think of the last day. Hence it adds:

“Thou hast not laid these things upon thy heart, nor remembered thy latter end.” Thou hast not laid it upon thy heart—that is, thou hast not considered—that I, being angry with my people, gave them into thy hands. Nor hast thou remembered thy end, when I shall take vengeance upon thee with no one resisting. It follows:

**VERSE 8.**—“And now hear these things, thou voluptuous one, who dwellest confidently, who sayest in thy heart: I am, [Col. 0446A] and there is none besides me; I shall not sit as a widow, nor know barrenness.”

**VERSE 9.**—“These two things shall come upon thee suddenly in one day: barrenness and widowhood.”

The soul is voluptuous which enjoys its own pleasures in the present and abounds in delights; it dwells confidently when it is compelled by no fear of death, but judges the pilgrimage of the present exile to be the dwelling-place of its homeland. And when it sees itself surpassing others in the power of rank, it despises all as nothing and exalts itself in its thoughts: “I am, and there is none besides me.”

It also says that it will not sit as a widow because it considers that it will always possess understanding wisely. For understanding is often called the husband of the soul. Thus the Lord says to the Samaritan woman, who did not understand his words: “Call thy husband” (John IV. 16)—that is, employ thy understanding and come here; that is, draw near to the things I say. For as a husband rules a wife, so understanding rules the soul. And as a woman conceives by her husband, so the soul conceives from understanding what it brings forth in action. Therefore it says: “I shall not sit as a widow”—that is, I shall not be despised after losing understanding, because I shall never lose it, but shall always understand prudently. “And I shall not know barrenness”—that is, I shall not be unfruitful, but shall continually bear works pleasing to me as though they were children. But she who speaks thus ought to hear what is divinely answered her: “These two things shall come upon thee,” namely barrenness and widowhood, “suddenly in one day”—that is, in the hour of death—so that [Col. 0446C] thou mayest no longer be able to work anything, and mayest lose understanding. And as though these things had already befallen her, he adds:

“All things have come upon thee because of the multitude of thy wicked deeds, and because of the great hardness of thy enchanters.” All that I threatened thee above has come upon thee because of the multitude of evils which thou didst commit. What is expressed by her enchanters except the other powerful persons who serve her, and who through the vanity of worldly power or their own deceit, like the illusion of magical art, deceive the eyes of onlookers in their fraudulent acts, so that their works may be thought good or honourable? They possess great hardness because, ignorant of the bowels of compassion, they injure the innocent and plunder their goods. Therefore their ruler is punished also because of their hardness, since she ought to have restrained their impiety. She is further told:

**VERSE 10.**—“And thou hast trusted in thy wickedness, and hast said: There is none who sees me.”

She trusted in wickedness because through evil cunning she was confident that she would surpass others and always prosper. She also supposed that she was not seen by God in the evils which she committed. But it follows:

“Thy wisdom and thy knowledge have deceived thee.”

This wisdom, by which thou trustedst in thy wickedness and thoughtest that thou wast not seen by me, deceived thee because it constantly entangled thee in thy evil deeds [Col. 0447A]. Or let “thy wisdom and thy knowledge” be pronounced first, and then let “this has deceived thee” be added, so that it may be understood not only of that wisdom, but of all her wisdom and knowledge: for “the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God” (Rom. VIII. 7). Wisdom and knowledge are aptly said to have deceived her. For “the prudence of the flesh is death” (ibid. 6), and “knowledge puffeth up” (I Cor. VIII. 1). Hence that arrogance of hers, by which she exalts herself through temporal glory and despises others, is repeated when it adds:

“And thou hast said in thy heart: I am, and there is none other besides me.” For she is exalted so singularly that she glories in being the only one, because she sees no one equal to herself. A sudden death due to her pride is promised as about to come upon her, when it immediately adds:

**VERSE 11.**—“Evil shall come upon thee, and thou shalt not know its rising; calamity shall rush upon thee, which thou shalt not be able to expiate; misery shall come upon thee suddenly, which thou dost not know.”

For all these things shall occur at the time of death. Against its coming, the daughter of Babylon who gloried singularly in power is immediately addressed in reproach:

**VERSE 12.**—“Stand with thy enchanters and with the multitude of thy wicked deeds, in which thou hast laboured from thy youth; perhaps something may profit thee, or perhaps thou mayest become stronger.”

For if she is truly powerful, let her now stand against death [Col. 0447C] and strongly resist it. Let her also bring with her for aid all her enchanters—that is, the powerful and wise persons subject to her, who deceive human eyes by the vanity of deceitful action, and by their artful speech alter the minds of men as if through certain incantations.

Let her also set against the divine judgment which comes upon her the multitude of evils in which she has exercised herself from youth, because she trusted in her wickedness. Therefore, after standing with all these—that is, after resisting heavenly wrath—let us see whether this may perhaps benefit her, or whether she can become stronger against God. And because the aforesaid enchanters offer manifold counsels but their counsels avail nothing against God, it is rightly added:

[Col. 0447D] **VERSE 13.**—“Thou hast failed in the multitude of thy counsels.”

Again it adds reproachfully:

“Let the diviners of heaven stand and save thee, those who observed the stars and counted the months, that from them they might announce things to come upon thee.”

What is meant by the diviners of heaven, who observed the stars and counted the months in order to announce future events from them, except superstitious people who attempt to discover the future from the elements of time? To such persons the Lord says: “When you see a cloud rising from the west, you immediately say, ‘A shower is coming,’ and so it happens. And when the south wind blows, you say that there will be heat, and it happens. Hypocrites, you know how to discern the face of heaven and earth” [Col. 0448A] (Luke XII. 54–56). And Paul says: “You observe days and months and seasons and years. I fear lest perhaps I have laboured among you in vain” (Gal. IV. 10). Since, therefore, the aforesaid daughter of Babylon—that is, the mind of a superstitious and perverse ruler—has hoped more in such things than in God, she is rightly told in rebuke as death approaches: “Let the diviners of heaven, who observed the stars and counted the months in order to announce things to come upon thee from them, stand and save thee.” But how will those who cannot stand for themselves stand for others? Or how will those who cannot save themselves save another? For it follows:

**VERSE 14.**—“Behold, they have become like stubble, and fire has burned them; they shall not deliver their soul from the hand of the flame. They are not coals by which they may warm themselves [Col. 0448B], nor a hearth by which they may sit.”

At death they became dry and empty like stubble; hell-fire burned them, and they will no longer be able to deliver their souls from the hand of that flame, but there they shall be held and burn without end. For there are no coals in that fire by which they may be pleasantly warmed, as in all fires here; nor is that fire a hearth beside which those who are there may sit. Rather, that fire fills the whole of hell, tormenting all the reprobate whom it contains within itself; it has no coals because it is not fed by wood, but burns unquenchably. Or, in this life they have no coals by which they may be warmed, nor a hearth by which they may sit: that is, they have no knowledge that gives warmth nor understanding that gives light, which could shake off their darkness and drive away the cold of error. It follows:

**VERSE 15.**—“Thus have they become to thee, all those in whom thou hadst laboured.”

That is, all thy works have been consumed by that fire. For, as the Apostle says: “The work of each shall be made manifest. For the day of the Lord shall declare it, because it shall be revealed in fire; and fire shall test the quality of each person’s work. If anyone’s work remains, he shall receive a reward; if anyone’s work is burned, he shall suffer loss” (I Cor. III. 13). It follows:

“Thy merchants from thy youth have wandered, each in his own way, and there is none to save thee.”

This unrighteous rich man was eager from his youth to have merchants [Col. 0448D] and accumulators of money. All of them wandered in the way of their trade, because, just as “no one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular business” (II Tim. II. 4), so one entangled in secular business cannot serve as a soldier of God. And because all who wished to assist him are bound by their own guilt, there is none to save him from perpetual death. These things have been said against any proud powerful person who afflicts the people of God. And immediately afterward, fittingly, he speaks to the same people who were handed over because of their sins:

## CHAPTER XLVIII

**VERSE 1.**—“Hear this, house of Jacob, who are called by the name of Israel and have come forth from the waters of Judah [Col. 0449A], who swear by the name of the Lord and remember the God of Israel, not in truth nor in righteousness.”

For divine speech now speaks to the carnal persons who are in the Church. For they too are the house of Jacob, because they follow the faith of the patriarchs, although they avoid their morals. “You, O house of Jacob,” he says, “hear this which I have spoken to the ruler who oppresses you, or which I have spoken to you: you who are called by the name of Israel”—that is, who are designated by the name of Christianity—“and have come forth from the waters of Judah,” that is, from the waters of confession, which are the waters of baptism; or, who have sprung from Christian peoples; “who swear by the name of the Lord,” that is, who affirm that you are Christians; “and remember the God of Israel,” that is, think upon Christ, “not in truth,” because you do not truly love him, “nor in righteousness,” because you do not do what he commands [Col. 0449B]. The Lord speaks to Christians of this sort, whom he handed over to a wicked ruler to be chastised because of their irreligion. Of them it adds:

**VERSE 2.**—“For they are called from the holy city and established upon the God of Israel; the Lord of hosts is his name.”

They ought therefore to hear words of consolation, because they have been called by God from the holy city. For the Lord who dwells in the heavenly Jerusalem himself called them. And they have been established upon the God of Israel—that is, founded upon Christ—who is called the Lord of hosts because the hosts of the heavenly army serve him. The Lord next says to that people of carnal Christians:

[Col. 0449C] **VERSE 3.**—“I announced former things from then onward; they went out from my mouth, and I caused them to be heard. Suddenly I acted, and they came to pass.”

What are the former things except those which, according to the Apocalypse of John, “must shortly come to pass” (Apoc. I. 1): that is, the temptations and evils which the faithful endure in this life? “For all who desire to live godly in Christ Jesus suffer persecution” (II Tim. III. 12). The things awaiting us in the age to come are later things. Hear what the former things are: “My son, when thou comest to the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare thy soul for temptation” (Ecclus. II. 1). Hear the former things: “Whoever seeks to save his life shall lose it” (Luke XVII. 33). Thus I announced these former things and caused thee to hear them from then onward: that is, from the time when thou didst come forth from the waters of Judah and wast established upon the God of Israel. And just as I had announced to thee from the beginning, so then I acted suddenly, and all things came to pass. I foretold all the things which thou wast to suffer, lest, finding thee ignorant, they should overwhelm thee; and thou didst hear from my mouth what thou oughtest to do, so that thou mightest have no excuse from ignorance. It follows:

**VERSE 4.**—“For I knew that thou art hard, and thy neck is an iron sinew, and thy brow is bronze.”

Thou art hard because thou canst not be softened to love God. The neck of thy heart is an iron sinew because it cannot be bent beneath my yoke. Thy brow is bronze because thou persist long in thy shamelessness, refusing to blush for thy evil actions [Col. 0450A]. For the brow is the seat of shame, while bronze is exceedingly durable. Therefore one has a bronze brow who stubbornly persists against modesty. It follows:

**VERSE 5.**—“I foretold it to thee from then onward; before it came to pass I made it known to thee, lest perhaps thou shouldst say: My idols did these things, and my carved images and molten images commanded them.”

**VERSE 6.**—“What thou hast heard, behold all of it; but you have not announced it [Note: [Col. 0449D] Alternatively, have you not announced it?].”

What are now signified by idols, molten images, and carved images except false thoughts? For the mind makes itself an idol when it forms within itself a thought of error; it carves it, as it were, when it cuts into form the things that seem right to it and fashions it according to its own pleasure; and it casts it, as it were, because it inwardly melts it down in the spirit of its mind before making it.

What, therefore, are expressed in idols, carved images, and molten images except the opinions of errors which the mind forms for itself according to its own thought? He says, then, that I foretold to thee from then onward things to come—that is, from the time when thou wast established upon the Lord above—and before they came I made them known to thee, lest, when they came, thou shouldst say that my idols, that is, my false opinions, had done these things, and that my carved and molten images—that is, the errors which I formed for myself—had commanded them. For this carnal people is full of many errors and attributes many events not so much to God as to its own superstitions and opinions. Therefore, he says, I foretold all things to thee through my Scriptures [Col. 0450C] and through the mouths of teachers; and now behold all the things which thou then heardest, because everything happens to thee just as I foretold. But you have not announced to others what I announced to you, because you neglected to speak of such matters. It follows:

“Anew have I made known to you things heard from this time onward, and things kept in store which you do not know.”

VERSE 7.—“Now they have been created, and not from the beginning, nor before this day; and you did not hear them, lest perhaps you should say: Behold, I knew them.”

VERSE 8.—“You neither heard, nor knew, nor from that time was your ear opened.”

I have made known to you, from the time when you came forth from the waters of Judah, the new things of a new manner of life—that is, from the time when you were reborn [Col. 0450D] from water and the Spirit—and the rewards of the righteous kept in heaven, which you do not know. And the things concerning spiritual conduct or temptation which you had heard have now been created: that is, it has now been granted you by me that, if you will, you may do them—not from the beginning or before the day, but in their proper time. For a child cannot at once undertake the difficult things of a new way of life; but at mature age he can endure temptations and train himself in spiritual disciplines. And the Lord orders each thing in its proper season, since “all things have their season, and all things under heaven pass through their allotted intervals” (Eccles. III, 1). Therefore, when he grants a person at a fitting time the grace to live well, unless that person is slothful, [Col. 0451A] he rightly declares to him that new things have now been created, and not from the beginning or before the day.

But when he has said, “I have made new things heard by you from that time,” he seems to add something contrary when he says that you did not hear them. Yet you heard with the ear of the body, but not with the ear of the heart. “You did not hear them,” he says—that is, you did not understand them—lest, puffed up with knowledge, you should perhaps say, “Behold, I knew them.” But you neither heard them—that is, understood them—nor knew them, nor from that time was your ear opened: that is, the ear of your heart. For because you heard good things indeed, yet neglected to do them, what you heard you did not hear. And as no one knows what charity is unless charity is in him, so no one truly understands heavenly commands except one who performs them. Rightly, therefore, it is said to one who scorns to put into practice the good things he has heard: “You neither heard, [Col. 0451B] nor knew, nor from that time”—that is, from the time when you were made steadfast upon the Lord—“was your ear opened.” It follows:

“For I know that you will deal most treacherously, and from the womb I called you a transgressor.”

I know that you have not yet abandoned your wickedness, but will still trample upon my commands by transgressing them. You are of the children of Adam, through whom sin entered into this world, and through sin death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned. Therefore I called you a transgressor from your mother’s womb.

Thus far the Lord has rebuked the hardness of each of those whom he reproves elsewhere, saying: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do the things which I say?” (Luke VI, 46). But now, in accordance with that [Col. 0451C] which he said to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I have mercy” (Rom. IX, 15), he shows in what merciful manner he acts toward one to whom he wills to show mercy, adding:

VERSE 9.—“For my name’s sake I will defer my wrath, and for my praise I will restrain you, lest you perish.”

“Not for your sake,” he says, “but for the sake of my name, which has been invoked over you, I will keep far from you my wrath, by which I had delivered you to the daughter of Babylon to be afflicted. For you are still worthy of my wrath; but now, having had mercy on you, I shall spare you. And lest you should henceforth freely go whither you will by following your evil desires, I shall restrain you by my praise, lest you incur eternal death, but [Col. 0451D] joyfully sing: ‘I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall continually be in my mouth. In the Lord my soul shall be praised’” (Ps. XXXIII, 2). It follows:

VERSE 10.—“Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have chosen you in the furnace of poverty.”

I have refined you in the fire of tribulation, under the hand of the daughter of Babylon—that is, of any powerful person exercising tyranny—but not as silver, because you have not been cleansed from your filth. Silver is purified by fire; but you were not purified in tribulation, because even amid adversities you did not cease to sin. But, refining you in the furnace of poverty, I chose you. Concerning this statement we need now say nothing else than what blessed Gregory admonishes in a homily (Hom. [Col. 0452A] 40 on the Gospels):

“Whoever among you possess good things in this world, when you see any poor persons committing certain blameworthy acts, do not despise them; do not despair of them. For perhaps those whom the excess of a very slight fault defiles are purified by the furnace of poverty. Be altogether afraid for yourselves, because a prosperous life has followed even some evil deeds; but carefully consider their case, because poverty, their teacher, afflicts them until it leads them to uprightness.”

And below:

“When you see any persons cast down in this world, even if they appear to have certain blameworthy traits, do not despise them; for perhaps those whom weakness of character wounds are healed by the medicine of poverty.”

It follows:

VERSE 11.—“For my own sake, for my own sake, I will act, that [Col. 0452B] I may not be blasphemed; and I will not give my glory to another.”

For my own goodness’ sake I will cause you to live, so that my name may not be blasphemed on your account; and I will not give to another—that is, to Satan—the glory in which I ought to glory through you, for he glories in those whom he draws into perdition. After this, the divine discourse returns to the earlier times of the Church. For it continues:

VERSE 12.—“Hear me, Jacob and Israel, whom I call: I am he; I am the first, I am the last.”

Jacob or Israel, whom the Lord calls, are believers from the circumcision, whom he draws to his Christ by inward inspiration. To them he says: “I am he,” not another, because I do not change. “I am the first and the last,” because I am before all things and after [Col. 0452C] all things. For God’s being is wholly simultaneous and always is: it neither ever began nor will ever cease—an inseparable and endless ocean of being, bounded by no terms or limits, surpassing every understanding and all time and nature. He then declares the power of his action, saying:

VERSE 13.—“My hand also founded the earth, and my right hand measured out the heavens; I will call them, and they shall stand together.”

For he himself made earth and heaven, and all the heavens obey his command. Yet, as we have often said, the Church may be signified by the earth, for it receives the seed of preaching and produces the fruit of good work; and holy preachers by the heavens, who, like rains, send forth the utterances of their wisdom. Therefore the Lord’s hand founded the earth, because he established the Church upon the foundation which is Christ. And his right hand measured out the heavens—that is, the preachers—as the Apostle says to the disciples: “We do not glory beyond measure, but according to the measure of the rule which God has measured out to us, a measure reaching even unto you” (II Cor. X, 13). And again: “To each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. IV, 7). But when he says, “I will call them, and they shall stand together,” he shows that all of them are ready for service. For those who stand when called stand ready; they are prepared to do what has been commanded them. Having set forth the example of the Church’s foundation and [Col. 0453A] the obedience of the saints, he says to Israel, to whom he was speaking:

VERSE 14.—“Gather yourselves together, all of you, and hear.”

Gather yourselves all into one and the same will, so that all of you may have one heart and one soul; and hear me as the heavens hear me. It follows: “Who among them has declared these things? The Lord loved him; he will do his will in Babylon, and his arm among the Chaldeans.”

Who among the heavens—that is, the preachers—has declared these things which have been said concerning their obedience and the other matters just set forth? Understand: Christ. For he deigned to become one of them. “The Lord loved him,” saying: “This is my beloved Son” (II Pet. I, 17). [Col. 0453B] And he will accomplish his will in Babylon—that is, in this confused world, or among the Gentiles—he “who wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (I Tim. II, 4). And he will exercise the arm of his power among the Chaldeans, because, stripping principalities and powers, he will display them openly, triumphing over them in himself. For the Chaldeans are evil spirits. It follows:

VERSE 15.—“I have spoken, and I have called him, and I have brought him, and his way has been made straight.”

I, the Father, spoke of him through the prophets, and called him into this world, and brought him; and the way of his conduct was made straight, because he did no iniquity, nor was deceit found in his mouth. His voice is immediately introduced, saying:

[Col. 0453C] VERSE 16.—“Draw near to me, and hear this: From the beginning I have not spoken in secret; from the time before they were made, I was there; and now God has sent me, and his Spirit.”

“Draw near to me in faith, my people, and do not think that I am Joseph’s son, or that I took my beginning from the conception of the Virgin; but rather hear what I say. For I did not speak secretly from the beginning; rather, it is manifest that I spoke from the origin of the world to the most renowned fathers. For from the time—that is, from the beginning of time—I was there, namely with the Father, because ‘in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God’” (John I, 1). And lest you should think that I began with time: before creatures [Col. 0453D] were made, I was there. Then indeed I was with God, and now he himself and his Spirit have sent me, that the Word might become flesh and dwell among us. For the Father sent the Son because he appointed him to become incarnate. But the Holy Spirit also sent him because he was the author of his incarnation. For when the Holy Spirit came upon her, the Virgin conceived him. The Spirit sent him so that, when you read that the same Son sends the Spirit, you may not believe the Spirit to be of inferior power. For the Son also sends him, as he says: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father” (John XV, 26). If, therefore, the Son and the Spirit send one another, this is not the indignity of subjection but a sharing of power. It follows:

[Col. 0454A] VERSE 17.—“Thus says the Lord God, your redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: I am the Lord your God, teaching you profitable things and guiding you in the way in which you walk.”

Our Redeemer says to his people: “I am the Lord your God.” For he himself is Lord and God, just as the Father is. For he says: “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30); and: “All things that the Father has are mine” (John XVI, 15). Therefore he testifies that he is Lord and God, so that all may honour the Son as they honour the Father. He always teaches us sufficiently profitable commands, both in the Old and the New Testament, and governs and directs us in the path of righteousness in which we walk. How profitable are the things he has taught us, and how greatly he has desired our salvation, he shows when he adds:

[Col. 0454B] VERSE 18.—“Would that you had attended to my commandments! Your peace would have become like a river, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea.”

VERSE 19.—“Your seed would have been like sand, and the offspring of your womb like its pebbles; its name would not have perished, nor have been destroyed from before my face.”

VERSE 20.—“Go forth from Babylon; flee from the Chaldeans.”

“Would that you, O human being, had attended to the commands of life which I gave you in Paradise! For as the water of a river continually flows in unfailing abundance, so your enduring peace would always have flowed abundantly. And as the waves of the sea abound in the manifold mass of their waters, so your righteousness would have increased without measure in manifold heaps of virtues. And as sand is innumerable, [Col. 0454C] so would have been the multitude of children whom you would have begotten in Paradise. Your seed would not have perished, because none of your children would have died. And its name would not have been destroyed from before my face, because it would not suffer punishment, cast away from my presence into everlasting oblivion. For if the first human being had not sinned, he would never have begotten children for Gehenna; rather, he was to beget in Paradise only as many children as the elect who shall be placed at the Judge’s right hand on the day of resurrection. When their number was complete, they would have come, without any death or affliction, to the everlasting life and fellowship of the angels.”

“All these things,” he says, “would have been so, if you had been willing to attend to my commands. But since matters have fallen into the contrary [Col. 0454D] condition, now at least, children of Adam, go forth from Babylon—that is, from the confusion of desires, in which you have hitherto been held captive—so that, set free, you may return to the homeland of the eternal inheritance. Flee from the Chaldeans—that is, depart as swiftly as possible and far away from the evil spirits who hold you captive in this confusion of passionate vices. For ‘Chaldeans’ is interpreted ‘captors.’ The Saviour came to call us back from exile to our homeland, from the world to Paradise, from captivity to the kingdom. Therefore, also [Note: [Col. 0453D] Both manuscripts: “also” from the preceding text.], commanding his heralds, he adds:

With a voice of exultation announce to all their departure from Babylon, and make this known to all who are in the world: that now, by my grace, they have been granted the ability to return to Paradise.

And carry this also to the ends of the earth, so that no one in the world may fail to hear it. It follows:

“Say: The Lord has redeemed his servant Jacob.”

VERSE 21.—“They did not thirst in the wilderness when he led them forth; he brought them water from the rock, and he split the rock, and waters flowed.”

Say that the Lord redeemed his servant by the blood of his Son, and that his faithful did not thirst in the wilderness of this world when he led them out from the darkness of ignorance and unbelief, as though from Egypt. For from the rock, which is Christ, he brought forth for them the water of saving wisdom to sustain them; and he split the rock—[Col. 0455B] that is, wounded Christ upon the cross—and the waters of life-giving drink flowed. Having said these things, the prophet adds:

VERSE 22.—“There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord.”

That is, Christ my Lord. Above it was said [Col. 0456A] to the human being: “If you had attended to my commandments, your peace would have become like a river.”

And now, conversely, peace is denied to the wicked because they refuse to attend to God’s commands. For as, when the Saviour was born, “peace was announced to people of good will” (Luke II, 14), so now, when he comes, peace is consequently denied to the wicked, because “righteousness and peace have kissed each other” (Ps. LXXXIV, 11). For the wicked can have peace neither with God, nor with angels, nor with another human being, nor with themselves. Peace is the virtue joining all things both to themselves and to one another, harmonizing all things with itself through their undivided unity, by which the one and indissoluble interweaving of all things is established according to its divine harmony and bound together in perfect concord [Col. 0456B]. But the minds of the wicked, which are always at strife even with themselves, are far from this. But now, bringing this little book to an end, let us take a brief rest, so that we may set ourselves more vigorously to what follows.

## BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 0455]

## CHAPTER XLIX

[Col. 0455B]

[Col. 0455C] VERSE 1.—“Hear, islands, and give heed, peoples from afar: the Lord called me from the womb; from my mother’s belly he remembered my name.”

VERSE 2.—“And he made my mouth like a sharp sword.”

Christ now speaks these things, he who alone was worthy to be called by the Lord from the womb of his virgin mother. For just as, when he was born, the angel appearing to the shepherds said: “Behold, I bring you good news of great joy, which shall be for all the people, because today a Saviour has been born to you, who is Christ the Lord” (Luke II, 10–11), so now the same Saviour announces to all peoples who are far away that he was called by the Lord from his mother’s womb. The Lord calls us from baptism, because then for the first time we are named children of God and receive the name of Christianity, which [Col. 0455D] he deigns to name. But he called this one from the womb because he was born both Holy One and Son of God, as the angel had said to his mother: “That holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke I, 33). Therefore all peoples are commanded to attend to this, so that they may know that he alone was born without sin, in order to blot out the sins of all. He alone came righteous, in order to justify all who believe.

“Hear,” he says, “O islands of the nations; give heed, all you who dwell far away, or who have departed far from God. Know, all you who were conceived in iniquities, that the Lord called me from the womb by my name, as one born from a Virgin. For as soon as he was born, through the angel he called him by his own name, saying to the shepherds: ‘Today a Saviour has been born to you, who is Christ the Lord’” (Luke II, 11). And thus, from his mother’s womb, he remembered [Col. 0456B] his [Col. 0456C] name, because he called his name Saviour—that is, Jesus—“which was called by the angel before he was conceived in the womb” (ibid. 21). He caused him to be born in this manner so that, free from sin, he might freely rebuke sinners and turn them to repentance. Hence he made his mouth like a sharp sword, so that by his words, as by a sword, he might strike transgressors forcefully, saying: “Serpents, brood of vipers, how shall you escape the judgment of Gehenna?” (Matt. XXIII, 33); and: “Every tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. III, 10). Since the Jews, whom he thus struck, often wished to seize and kill him, but could never do so except at the hour appointed by the Father, he rightly adds:

“He protected me in the shadow of his hand.”

[Col. 0456D] And because, protected by the hand of the Lord, he pierced their hearts most powerfully by his word, he adds:

“And he made me like a chosen arrow.” For he penetrates their minds like a most sharp arrow. “For the word of God is living and effective, and more piercing than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, and of joints and marrow” (Heb. IV, 12). When he says “a chosen arrow,” he shows that God has many arrows, but not chosen ones. These arrows are the prophets and apostles, who range throughout the whole world, of whom it is elsewhere said: “Your arrows are sharp” (Ps. XLIV, 6). But Christ, among many arrows and many sons, is the one chosen arrow and the only-begotten Son. It follows:

“He hid me in his quiver.”

VERSE 3.—“And he said to me: You are my servant, Israel, because in you I shall be glorified.”

[Col. 0457A] By God’s quiver is signified his hidden judgment. Therefore the Saviour was hidden in God’s quiver because, by the ordering of his hidden counsel, he came hidden in his first advent. Or, while he was a child, he was hidden in God’s quiver, because he lay concealed under the covering of God’s deep counsel, like an arrow in a quiver. And as an arrow springs suddenly from the quiver, so he sprang suddenly from his concealment in order to pierce the nations of humankind by preaching. While he still lay hidden in this quiver, he heard from the Father: “You are my servant, Israel, because in you I shall be glorified.” He was called servant because, “taking the form of a servant, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Phil. II, 7). In him the Father was glorified, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. XVII, 5). He is also [Col. 0457B] called Israel—that is, “ruler with God”—because he reigns always with the Father. For Israel is interpreted “ruler with God.” Or he was called Israel because he was born from the seed of the Jews. It follows:

VERSE 4.—“And I said: I have laboured in vain; without cause and vainly I have spent my strength. Therefore my judgment is with the Lord, and my work with my God.”

This statement is, I think, very profound. We shall say what it seems to us to mean in such a way that, if someone can explain it better, we shall be more ready to follow that person’s interpretation. Thus our Redeemer, while living bodily on earth, says: “I have laboured in vain.” For human beings are accustomed to exert themselves in labour for temporal advantages. But he both endured labours in the flesh and received no reward for those labours in this world. Therefore, because he did not seek transient gain by his actions, he regarded his labour as empty in relation to the world’s advantages.

He also says that he spent his strength without cause and vainly. For because of the fault of the first transgression, every human being is subject to mortality and is so wearied in this life by so many pains that, unable long to endure the evils he suffers, he fails and dies. But although Christ assumed flesh from Adam’s flesh, he did not derive sinfulness from that flesh. Nor did he commit sin while living here; and thus, so far as he himself was concerned, he spent his strength without cause in enduring the penalties of our mortality. Had he not spent his strength [Col. 0457D] when “wearied from the journey, he sat by the fountain” (John IV, 6)? And he spent it vainly insofar as, sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, he could not convert that people. Therefore, with respect to those who heard his teaching and saw his miracles but did not believe, he spent his strength vainly—that is, to no purpose—when they did not receive the remedies for the salvation of their souls, for whose sake he was bodily weakened and laboured even unto death. Accordingly he aptly adds:

“Therefore,” he says, “my judgment is with the Lord”—“For I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and judges” (John VIII, 50)—“and my work [Col. 0458A] is with my God.” Because “the Son cannot do anything of himself, except what he sees the Father doing; for whatever he does, the Son likewise does” (John V, 19).

Yet these words may be understood otherwise. For when our Lord heard from the Father: “You are my servant, Israel, because in you I shall be glorified,” he said: “I have laboured in vain; without cause and vainly I have spent my strength.” Perhaps, then, because he was called by the name Israel, he immediately spoke in the person of the people of Israel what follows. Thus the people of the circumcision, finally understanding that a human being is not justified by works of the law except through faith in Jesus Christ, now speaks in Christ, saying: “I have laboured in vain; without cause and vainly I have spent my strength.” For “Israel,” says the Apostle, [Col. 0458B] “pursuing a law of righteousness, did not attain to the law of righteousness. Why? Because not by faith but as though by works” (Rom. IX, 31). Therefore he laboured in vain, without cause, and spent his strength vainly, who thought that he could be justified by his own strength through the carnal observance of the law. “But that no one is justified before God by the law is evident, because the righteous person lives by faith. But the law is not of faith; rather, the one who does these things shall live in them” (Gal. III, 11). Therefore this Apostle laments that he had laboured vainly and without cause when he laboured to be justified without faith by works of the law. So also the Apostle, “circumcised on the eighth day, of the race of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; according to the law, a Pharisee; according to zeal, persecuting the Church of God; according to the righteousness which is in God’s law, living without blame,” judged all the things that had been gains to him to be losses for Christ’s sake, for whom he made all things loss and judged them as dung, that he might gain Christ and be found in him, not having his own righteousness which is from the law, but that which is through faith in Jesus Christ (Phil. III, 5).

According to this sense, therefore, that part of Israel which received faith speaks with the voice of its head: “I have laboured in vain; without cause and vainly I have spent my strength.” And it adds: “Therefore my judgment is with the Lord”—that is, I shall now judge as the Lord judges: namely, that it is best not to be justified by the law, [Col. 0458D] but to await by the Spirit, from faith, the hope of righteousness. “And my work is with my God,” because, with God cooperating, I shall do my work, and with grace helping shall fulfil the law.

Still, these things may, unless I am mistaken, be understood in yet another way. For because it was said to the Lord’s human nature, “You are my servant, Israel,” perhaps he immediately spoke in the voice of the servant—that is, in the voice of the human race: “I have laboured in vain.” For because of the mystery of assumed humanity he takes upon himself the voice of other human beings, now indeed of those who repent. For rightly in this place the voice of the human race is understood to be the voice of those who, after the darkness of their ignorance, turn to the love of righteousness and, illuminated by the rays [Col. 0459A] of truth, atone with tears for their former error. For every enlightened person looks back and sees how shameful it was to labour for love of the present life. Thus, in those in whom the human race returns to life, it says, counting its past labour as nothing: “I have laboured in vain.” For it sees how emptily one labours for this life. To suffer adversities for love of the world is both empty and laborious, because the mind is distressed by adversity and is not filled by the reward of recompense. Therefore whoever endures the world’s evils for the world labours in vain, because he spends the time of his life without recompense. And he spends his strength in such labours without cause and vainly, because no ensuing reward remunerates his life, while present tribulation exhausts him. Solomon’s testimony is sufficient to confirm all this fittingly: “I saw all things which are done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and affliction of spirit” (Eccles. I, 14). And again: “When I turned to all the works which my hands had made, and to the labours in which I had sweated vainly, I saw vanity and affliction of spirit in all things, and that nothing endures under the sun” (Eccles. II, 11).

Therefore, after the darkness of ignorance, the soul illuminated by the light of truth grieves that it laboured without cause for temporal advantages; and, struck with terror at the future judgment, adds: “Therefore my judgment is with the Lord.” As though saying: Until now I was ignorant of the coming judgment, but now I know that my judgment shall be [Col. 0459C] with the Lord, because at my end I shall be judged with him, when in that dreadful examination there shall be scrutiny concerning each of my acts and, conversely, concerning the benefits bestowed upon me. “And my work is with my God,” because whatever I do here is kept with him to be judged on the last day, as he says: “Behold, it is written before me” (Isa. LXV, 6). And, as Malachi says: “The Lord gave heed and heard, and a book of remembrance was written before him” (Mal. III, 16). Or, “my work is with my God,” because I shall now do holy and righteous things with God, by his help. Let one who can interpret these things better do so; but let us consider what follows. For our Redeemer adds:

VERSE 5.—“And now the Lord says, who formed me [Col. 0459D] from the womb as his servant, that I might bring Jacob back to him; and Israel shall not be gathered.”

He rightly says: “From the womb.” For he was formed from a virgin womb through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, not begotten from the wombs of two parents. He was formed a servant because, according to the form of a servant which he received from the Virgin, he was created. For this reason also the Lord is said to have formed him from the womb as his servant: because he came to do God’s will, and was born God’s servant, whereas we, conversely, are born servants of the devil. For after baptism we become servants of God. “The Lord,” he says, “who formed me from the womb as his servant now says, that I might bring Jacob back to him.” As though he said: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. X, 6). But because not all will believe, [Col. 0460A] all Israel shall not be gathered into the Church, but shall rather be dispersed captive throughout the whole world. It follows:

“And I have been glorified in the eyes of the Lord.” When I said to him, “Father, glorify your Son” (John XVI, 1), he answered from heaven: “I have glorified him, and I will glorify him again” (John XII, 18). “And my God” in the Passion “has become my strength,” because the Father is with me. And because “it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke XXIV, 46), it is rightly added:

VERSE 6.—“And he said: It is too little that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to convert the dregs of Israel. I have given you as a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation unto the end of the earth.”

Indeed, it would have been too little for the Son of God to take the form of a servant for the conversion to faith of the tribes of Israel and the dregs of Israel—that is, the carnal remnant of the Jewish people—unless he also enlightened all nations throughout the world and saved all who are in the whole breadth of the world, if they believed. But Paul and Barnabas, rejected by the Jews, said: “Behold, we turn to the nations. For thus the Lord commanded us: ‘I have set you as a light to the nations, that you may be for salvation unto the end of the earth’” (Acts XIII, 46). It is clear that this was said especially of Christ the Lord. Yet the apostles considered that it had also been said to themselves, remembering that they were his members, just as he himself, because of the unity of the same body, said: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts IX, 4). Thus the apostles also interpreted as said to themselves what had been said to Christ, because Christ preached to the nations not by himself alone but through the apostles. It follows:

VERSE 7.—“Thus says the Lord, the Redeemer of Israel, his Holy One, to the despised soul, to the abhorred nation, to the servant of rulers: Kings shall see and rise; princes also shall rise up and worship, because of the Lord, for he is faithful, and because of the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you.”

To the despised soul of the Gentiles, to the abhorred nation of pagans, to the Gentile people [Col. 0460D] enslaved to many rulers—that is, idols—the Redeemer and Holy One of Israel now says that kings shall see in you my salvation unto the end of the earth, and princes shall rise from the sleep of their former unbelief and worship your God, not because of you but because of the Lord, because he is faithful in the promise by which he said to Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII, 18); and because of the Holy One of Israel, who has now chosen you through his immeasurable mercy. For kings and princes finally believed because they saw nations everywhere receiving the faith. It follows:

VERSE 8.—“Thus says the Lord: In an acceptable time I have heard you, and in a day of salvation I have helped you.”

[Col. 0461A] The acceptable time is from the Saviour’s resurrection until the end of the age, in which God hears the despised soul, as he heard Cornelius. The day of salvation likewise extends daily from that resurrection, because “everyone who truly asks receives, and whoever seeks finds” (Matt. VII, 8). For every day we are told concerning this day: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Ps. XCIV, 8). Paul shows that these things are so, saying to the Corinthians: “We exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain. For he says: ‘In an acceptable time I heard you, and in a day of salvation I helped you.’ Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI, 1). Peter likewise said that “all the prophets, from Samuel onward, announced these days” (Acts III, 24). Therefore, in this acceptable time—that is, in this time of reconciliation—and on this day of salvation, God hears and helps the Gentile world, because “everyone whoever calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Rom. X, 13). It follows:

“And I have preserved you and given you as a covenant of the people, that you may raise up the earth and possess the scattered inheritances.”

VERSE 9.—“That you may say to those who are bound: Go forth; to those who are in darkness: Be revealed.”

“I have preserved you from evil, O Church from among the nations, and given you as a covenant of the people, that you may raise up the earth”: that is, that you may bind the whole people together in covenant, so that all may be one in Christ, clothed with “the new human being, who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created [Col. 0461C] him, where there is neither Jew nor Gentile, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free, but Christ is all things in all” (Col. III, 10). “That you may raise up the earth,” he says: that is, awakening the minds of earthly people from the sleep of their former torpor to good action, making them watchful, or raising them now from inward death; and that you may possess in Christ the scattered inheritances—that is, the nations which evil spirits had scattered through different errors—so that you may say to those bound in the prison of their own heart by the cords of sins: “Go forth, confessing the evils which you conceal within”; and that you may say to those who, darkened in understanding, are alienated from the way of God through the ignorance which is in them because of the blindness of their hearts [Col. 0461D]: “Be revealed”—that is, cast away the veil of ignorance by which your mind is covered, so that, the veil cast away, you may be illumined by the light of truth. It follows:

“They shall feed upon the ways, and their pastures shall be in all the plains.”

What is signified by the ways except the apostles, who lead us back by a straight course to our homeland? For when “way” is read in the singular, it usually signifies Christ; but when “ways” are put in the plural, they generally signify the apostles. Therefore, upon the ways—that is, upon the apostles, namely in their teaching—the faithful shall feed; and their pastures shall be in all the plains, because their minds are refreshed with spiritual food in the open and broad utterances of the interpreters. Formerly, however, the pastures of the faithful were not in the open and broad sayings of interpreters, but in steep, [Col. 0462A] mountainous, and rugged places, when they were fed upon the strict and intricate teaching of the law; but now they are refreshed with sweet nourishment in the open and broad sayings of teachers. It follows:

VERSE 10.—“They shall not hunger or thirst, nor shall heat and sun strike them; because he who has mercy on them shall guide them, and shall give them drink at fountains of waters.”

They shall not hunger, nor shall they thirst, as the Lord says: “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst” (John 6:35). Nor shall heat and sun strike them—that is, the burning of tribulation shall not weary or injure their minds, because they shall be protected by God, as it is written: “You have overshadowed my head in the day of battle” (Psalm 139:8). And again: “In the shadow of him whom [Col. 0462B] I desired I sat” (Song of Songs 2:3). Because their merciful one shall rule them, so that they may say: “The Lord rules me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture he has set me” (Psalm 22:2). And he shall give them drink from springs of water, of which it was said: “You shall draw waters with joy from the springs of the Savior” (above, 12:3). For the springs of water are the apostles, from whom streams of truth flow forth. It follows:

**VERSE 11.—**“And I shall make all my mountains into a way, and my paths shall be raised up.”

Those signified by the ways and springs are also expressed by the mountains: that is, the apostles, who by the merit of their lives draw near to heavenly things, to whom it was said: “You shine wondrously from the everlasting mountains” (Psalm 75:5). All are made into a way [Col. 0462C] when they are sent forth to preach, so that they may lead the whole world to the heavenly kingdom. Notice that they are not made into *ways*, but into *a way*, because all become the one way, which is Christ, and all preach one Gospel in harmony. The paths, however, are the prophets, who are raised up when their sayings are elevated to a spiritual understanding.

Or the divine commandments may be denoted by the paths, which are raised up in the New Testament, as the Lord says: “You have heard that it was said to those of old: You shall not commit adultery. But I say to you that everyone who looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:27). Again: “You have heard that it was said to those of old: An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth. But I say to you [Col. 0462D] not to resist evil; but if anyone strikes you on one cheek, offer him the other also” (ibid., 38). And likewise: “You have heard that it was said to those of old: You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy. But I say to you: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (ibid., 43). Thus the paths of God—that is, his commandments—have been raised up and exalted to a heavenly manner of life, whereas formerly they lay in low places.

Or he makes the mountains into a way and raises the paths, because every obstacle that could impede the steps of believers he turns into level ground, humbling what is high and raising what is low, so that they may have a level [Col. 0463A] and open road. Since the whole world was to come to him by these ways and paths, he fittingly adds:

**VERSE 21.—**“Behold, these shall come from afar; and behold, those from the north and from the sea, and these from the southern land.”

For some came to Christ through faith from the northern quarter, some from the southern, and others from the remaining distant regions. Yet these places may also be understood spiritually. “Behold,” he says, “these shall come from afar,” that is, from a sinful way of life; “and those from the north and from the sea,” that is, from cold, bitter, and turbulent Gentile life; “and these from the southern land,” that is, from the Jewish people, once made warm by the heat of the age as though by the noonday sun, and borne along by the breath of the Spirit as by a warm wind. Because of this calling together of all peoples, [Col. 0463B] which occurred after Christ’s resurrection, all creation is commanded to rejoice, as follows:

**VERSE 13.—**“Praise, O heavens; exult, O earth; mountains, ring out praise, because the Lord has comforted his people and will have mercy on his poor.”

By the heavens the angelic powers may be denoted; by the earth, the Church; and by the mountains, holy preachers. Thus the heavens—that is, the angels who inhabit heaven—are commanded to praise; the earth—that is, the Church—to rejoice; and the mountains to ring out praise—that is, the apostles to proclaim the glory of God—because the Lord Jesus himself has comforted, visited, and redeemed his people, and after the tribulation of this life will have mercy upon his poor, who now endure voluntary poverty for love of him, saying: “Because of the words of your lips, I have kept hard ways” [Col. 0463C] (Psalm 16:4). Such poor persons shall receive complete mercy when the times of refreshment come. Since, therefore, they are meanwhile oppressed by harsh afflictions and none of them become faint-hearted amid adversities, it is fittingly added:

**VERSE 14.—**“And Zion said: The Lord has forsaken me, and the Lord has forgotten me.”

For Zion—that is, a Christian soul not yet fully perfected, or even the Church in its weaker members—thinks itself forsaken by the Lord amid adversities because it is not immediately delivered from tribulations; and it thinks itself given over to his forgetfulness because it is permitted to be worn down for a longer time by present evils. But God’s remembrance is neither broken by forgetfulness nor supplemented by recollection. Rather, when he leaves something aside, he is said to forget it in the manner of human minds; and when after a long time he visits what he wills, he is called mindful according to the custom arising from our mutability. [Col. 0463D] Thus in times of persecution the Church sometimes judged itself to have been given over to divine forgetfulness because it suffered so many and such great evils from adversaries over many years that it was compelled to despair of itself. But the Lord replies to this judgment of hers:

**VERSE 15.—**“Can a woman forget her infant, so as not to have compassion upon the son of her womb? And even if she should forget, yet I will not forget you.”

Nothing can be found in this world which anyone loves with so great [Col. 0464A] an affection as a mother loves her child. Yet God loves his children with more abundant bowels of charity and a more persevering affection. Therefore no one, when suffering anything grievous, should judge himself forsaken by God or given over to forgetfulness: “For whom the Lord loves, he corrects; and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Proverbs 3:12). He then adds, saying to Zion:

**VERSE 16.—**“Behold, I have delineated you upon my hands; your walls are always before my eyes.”

**VERSE 17.—**“Your builders have come; those who destroyed and laid you waste shall depart from you.”

“I have delineated you upon my hands”: I have represented what you were to be when built, just as was shown to Ezekiel in the final vision of his book, where he carefully determined [Col. 0464B] the measurements of every virtue. For all the descriptions and measurements of that house portray the building of the Church and the conduct of the righteous. Thus the same prophet was told: “Son of man, show the house of Israel the temple, that they may be ashamed of their iniquities, and measure its plan and blush because of all that they have done: the form of the house and its construction, its exits and entrances, and its entire description, all its commandments, its whole arrangement, and all its laws, that they may keep all its descriptions and its commandments and perform them” (Ezekiel 43:10). So too I have delineated you upon my hands, painted you in beautiful variety, and always hold you in my hands, as I said concerning my sheep: “No one shall snatch them [Col. 0464C] from my hands” (John 10:28).

Moreover, the walls of your virtues are always before my eyes, because I watch over them without interruption, lest they be broken at any point and admit enemies into their interior. Therefore I have not, as you thought, forsaken or forgotten you, for you have always been so dear to me. I indeed delineated you as you were to be built; and now your builders have come, who shall build you as I delineated you—that is, the holy preachers, one of whom says: “As a wise architect I laid the foundation” (1 Corinthians 1:3). But those who destroyed and laid you waste—that is, the Gentiles, who compelled your children to sacrifice to idols, or heretics, who deceived them—shall now depart from you; that is, they shall be driven far away [Col. 0464D] from your borders. It follows:

**VERSE 18.—**“Lift up your eyes round about and see: all these have gathered together and come to you. As I live, says the Lord, you shall be clothed with all these as with an ornament, and bind them about yourself as a bride.”

Lift up your eyes round about—that is, look upon every region of the world—because all those who are around you, in east and west, north and south, have assembled in one will of faith and have come to help you with the steps of their hearts.

The words, “As I live, says the Lord,” are God’s oath. He therefore swears, saying: You shall be clothed with all [Col. 0465A] these who have gathered as with a precious ornament, and bind them about yourself as a bride in great beauty. For just as the whole Church is generally called Christ’s garment, so the individual souls that turn from error are the Church’s garment, surrounding that same Church by believing and faithfully cleaving to it. Blessed is the person of such merit and virtue as to be called an ornament of the Church! It follows:

**VERSE 49.—**“For your deserted places, your solitudes, and your ruined land shall now be too narrow because of their inhabitants, and those who swallowed you up shall be driven far away.”

Your deserted places and solitudes—that is, places in which scarcely any of the faithful had dwelt—and your ruined land [Col. 0465B]—that is, where your children had fallen into idolatry through fear of punishments—shall now all be too narrow for the faithful dwelling in them. And the Gentiles who swallowed up your children into the abyss of idolatry, or the heretics who swallowed up and incorporated into themselves these same children born to you, shall be driven far away from your territories. It follows:

**VERSE 20.—**“The children of your barrenness shall still say in your ears: The place is too narrow for me; make room for me, that I may dwell.”

For a long time you were as though barren in the times of the martyrs, because you could scarcely generate anyone through the Gospel. But now you are to have so many children that you must build very spacious basilicas. Or your children will say: “The place [Col. 0465C] is too narrow for me in the synagogues; make room for me in the churches, that I may dwell more freely; that I may not be cramped by the blasphemies of the Jews; that your breadth may contain the whole world together with me.” It follows:

**VERSE 21.—**“And you shall say in your heart: Who has begotten these for me? I was barren and did not bear, exiled and captive; and who has raised these? I was forsaken and desolate [Note: [Col. 0465D] Elsewhere the text reads: ‘and alone, and these’]; and where were these?”

When peace was at last granted to the Church and the whole world flocked to the faith, the Church herself marveled at the multitude of her children: that she, who had formerly been as though barren, should be granted such fruitfulness. She had been accustomed to flee from place to place because of adversaries [Col. 0465D] according to the saying: “When they persecute you in this city, flee into another” (Matthew 10:23); and she was held captive in the land of her enemies, as though in Chaldea, and enslaved to servile tasks. Thus she appeared deprived of all assistance and desolate in the hands of enemies. Therefore she herself wondered whence so great a fruitfulness had so suddenly come to her. But how it could come about that her abundant multitude of children should say, “The place is too narrow for me; make room for me, that I may dwell,” the Lord indicates in what follows:

**VERSE 22.—**“Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I lift up my hand to the Gentiles, and to the peoples I shall raise [Col. 0466A] my standard; and they shall bring your sons in their arms and carry your daughters upon their shoulders.”

“I lift up my hand,” says the Lord Jesus, “to the Gentiles,” calling them as it were by a gesture and saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I shall refresh you” (Matthew 2:28 [probably an OCR error for 11:28]); “and to all peoples beneath heaven I shall raise my royal standard,” that is, the power of my cross, so that all may gather to it. “And they shall bring your sons in their arms”: that is, through the power of the examples of their good conduct, as though supporting them, they shall lead them to live well. “And they shall carry your daughters”—that is, weak souls—“upon the shoulders of their hearts,” bearing them patiently so as faithfully to offer them to you. It follows:

[Col. 0466B] **VERSE 23.—**“And kings shall be your foster-fathers, and queens your nurses.”

Holy men are called kings because, set over all movements of the flesh, they now restrain the appetite of lust, now temper the heat of avarice, now humble the glory of self-exaltation, now suppress the suggestions of envy, and now extinguish the fire of wrath. They are kings, therefore, because they know not to yield by consenting to the movements of their temptations, but to preside by ruling them. Likewise queens are either holy women or chosen souls of lesser strength. Such kings are foster-fathers of the Church, and such queens her nurses. Let us hear these foster-fathers themselves. Paul, Silas, and Timothy say to their disciples: “We became little ones in your midst, as though a nurse [Col. 0466C] cherished her children” (1 Thessalonians 2:7). And Paul also says: “As to little children in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Corinthians 3:2). Peter likewise says: “Like newborn infants, desire the rational milk without deceit, that by it you may grow into salvation” (1 Peter 2:2). The other holy teachers, too, nourish her as kings even to the present day. Holy women do the same among the communities of handmaids of God. Therefore it was rightly said to the Church that kings shall be your foster-fathers and queens your nurses. It follows:

“They shall worship you with faces lowered to the ground, and they shall lick the dust of your feet.”

This was fulfilled when pagans coming to the Church cast themselves at the feet of the saints [Col. 0466D] and kissed them, that they might obtain forgiveness of their sins and the grace of baptism. Or because Christ is the head of the Church, the head is worshiped in the body. And the dust of its feet is licked because the aforesaid kings, by their teaching, wipe away and lick up whatever earthly work clings to the feet of the Church. It follows:

“And you shall know that I am the Lord, upon whom those who wait for him shall not be confounded.”

When all these things had come to pass, then the Church, which previously had thought itself forsaken and given over to forgetfulness, certainly knew that whoever waits for the Lord [Col. 0467A] Jesus amid tribulations and temptations shall not be confounded, because he will be present with timely aid to deliver and glorify them. “Those who wait for him shall not be confounded.” Why they shall not be confounded he also shows in the following words:

**VERSE 24.—**“Can prey be taken from the strong, or can that which has been captured by the mighty be saved?” [Note: [Col. 0467D] Elsewhere: “can be preserved safe.”]

Among human beings, indeed, it seems impossible that prey seized by a most powerful tyrant could be snatched from him, or that what a very strong robber has captured could be saved from his hand. But since nothing is difficult for God, the Lord Jesus overthrew not a human being but the ancient enemy who held all human beings captive; and thereafter he took captivity from him [Col. 0467B]—that is, every nation whom he compelled to serve him as captives in sins—and what that strong one had violently taken away, he saved by omnipotent mercy. This captivity was especially liberated when the Gentile world, which served this mighty tyrant in idols, was converted to faith. And because, after it began to live devoutly in Christ, it endured persecutions from unbelievers, it is fittingly added:

**VERSE 25.—**[Note: [Col. 0467D] Supplied from a recent edition: “For thus says the Lord: Even captivity shall be taken from the strong, and what has been carried away by the mighty shall be saved. But those who,” etc.] “But I shall judge those who have judged you, and I shall save your children.”

**VERSE 26.—**“And I shall feed your enemies with their own flesh; they shall be drunk with their own blood as with new wine; and all flesh shall know that I am the Lord who saves you, and your redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob.”

For those who judged the martyrs the Lord shall judge [Col. 0467C] on the last day according to the torments which they inflicted on them; and the children of the Church, whom unbelievers once condemned, he himself shall save in the heavenly kingdom. Then he shall feed their enemies with their own flesh, because he shall cause them, in excessive pain, to devour their own carnality with the teeth of the inner person, lamenting without end and quarreling with themselves because they lived carnally. He shall feed them with their own flesh, so that they may be filled not by another’s death but by their own; and because they are carnal and do not have the Spirit of God, they shall feed upon their own flesh.

“And they shall be drunk with their own blood as with new wine”: that is, with sin, which is from flesh and blood. When, as it is written, “the earth shall be shaken with shaking” [Col. 0467D] (Isaiah 24:9), each sinner shall be agitated in thought like one drunk. For the recollection of the evils they have done shall disturb and intoxicate their minds, so that with calm and sober hearts they cannot share in the joy of the righteous. Then all flesh—that is, every human being, good and evil alike—shall know without doubt that the Lord saves the Church of the elect, and that the Mighty One of Jacob—that is, he who wrestled with Jacob (Genesis 32:24)—has redeemed it from all evils.
