For “they shall see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty, and he shall send his angels with trumpet and loud voice, [Col. 0468A] and they shall gather his elect from the four winds, from the heights of the heavens to their ends” [Note: [Col. 0468D] Elsewhere: “to their boundaries”] (Matthew 24:30). Thus far the Lord Jesus has promised many good things to his elect. Now he begins to address the unbelieving Jews. For it follows:

## CHAPTER 50

**VERSE 1.—**“Thus says the Lord: Where is this bill of divorce for your mother, by which I dismissed her? Or who is my creditor, to whom I sold you? Behold, you were sold because of your iniquities, and because of your crimes I dismissed your mother.”

**VERSE 2.—**“Because I came, and there was no man; I called, and there was no one who heard.”

A husband gave a bill of divorce to a hated wife when he dismissed her; and a needy man [Col. 0468B] sometimes sold his children to his creditor. But the Lord Jesus does not acknowledge that he gave the mother of the Jews—that is, the synagogue—a bill of divorce as to a hated spouse, because she rather abandoned him than he her. Nor did he sell them to a creditor, because he had not borrowed an alien debt—that is, he had committed no sin—so that, compelled by necessity, he should hand them over to the greedy creditor, that is, the devil. For he received nothing from this creditor: “For,” he says, “the ruler of this world comes, and he has nothing in me” (John 14:30). The Lord, therefore, did not himself sell the Jews; rather, they sold themselves in their iniquities to the devil, taking his money. For murder is the devil’s money: “For he was a murderer from the beginning” (John 8:14). Have you committed [Col. 0468C] murder? You have received the devil’s money. Adultery is the devil’s money, for in it are the devil’s image and inscription. Have you committed adultery? You have received a coin from the devil. Theft, false witness, rapacity, violence, envy, pride: all these are the devil’s tribute and treasure. Such money proceeds from his mint. With this money he buys those whom he buys, and makes slaves of all who have received however much of such tribute.

The Jews, therefore, were not sold by the Lord but by themselves in their iniquities, because each person freely sells himself to the devil when he sins voluntarily. Hence it is said of Ahab that “he was sold to do evil” (3 Kings 21:25). [Col. 0468D] Therefore those who killed the author of life, who brought false witness against him who is truth, who betrayed him through envy, are rightly said to have been sold in their iniquities.

Their mother was dismissed because of their crimes, because they committed such great evils against the Lord and his disciples that the whole synagogue, agreeing with itself, went together into perdition: from the time when the chief priests and elders persuaded the people to demand Barabbas and destroy Jesus; from the time when all that people said: “His blood be upon our children” [Col. 0469A] (Matthew 27:25). For the Savior came to them, being born of the Virgin, and there was no man among them—that is, no one acting manfully—but “all turned aside; together they became useless” (Psalm 13:3). He called them to grace by the preaching of newness, and there was none among them willing to hear him. There was no man or human being among them; for, abandoning the image of the true God, all took the image of beasts and serpents. The Lord did not give a bill of divorce to their mother, nor sell them to a creditor; rather, their crimes and sins sold them to demons, entangled in the pleasures of this present age [Note: [Col. 0469D] Thus both manuscripts], so that he left her who was a parent to them and a spouse to him, whom he could no longer retain as though adulterous, but allowed to depart willingly. Therefore they were dismissed by him [Col. 0469B] so as to be overwhelmed by innumerable calamities with no one to help them. To them he adds:

“Has my hand become shortened and small, so that I cannot redeem? Or is there not strength in me to deliver?”

For his great hand—that is, his power, by which he formerly used to rescue their fathers from every tribulation—has not become shortened, so that he could not likewise redeem these from the captivity in which they are held scattered throughout the whole world, if they deserved to be redeemed. Nor does he lack strength to free them from this most prolonged slavery, if they were worthy of deliverance like their fathers. To show that his power has not been diminished, he adds:

“Behold, by my rebuke I shall make the sea a desert; I shall make rivers dry land; the fish shall rot [Col. 0469C] without water and shall die of thirst.”

**VERSE 3.—**“I shall clothe the heavens with darkness, and make sackcloth their covering.”

He who formerly rebuked the Red Sea and dried it up shall now, by his rebuke, make the sea of this world a desert: that is, turbulent and bitter idolatry, or worldly wickedness. And he who dried the waters of the Jordan so that the people of Israel might cross shall now dry up the rivers of worldly doctrines, so that the people of the elect may pass without hindrance by the way of uprightness to the kingdoms of the poles. When rivers of this sort have been dried, their fish shall rot: that is, either the demons that swam in them, or unbelieving people who, generated from them in wickedness, always lived in them [Col. 0469D] blind in evil, left under the depth of errors to their own wills in harmful freedom. The fish shall rot without the water of worldly wisdom, because when all the teachings of errors have been condemned, the stench of their impiety shall appear. And they shall die of thirst: when those doctrines of falsehood have fallen silent after truth is known, the life of their perversity, which was sustained from such waters of doctrine, shall fail.

The heavens also—that is, the teachers of the synagogue, who appeared to savor things above—shall be clothed, that is, covered, with the darkness of ignorance, so that the light of truth or understanding may not appear in them. Sackcloth, the garb of mourners or penitents, shall become their covering [Col. 0470A] so that under the apostles or under Elijah they may repent. Or, if sackcloth denotes harshness and the piercing awareness of sins, the teachers of the Jews are covered with sackcloth because they are surrounded by sinful conduct, so that nothing but sin appears in them. Then the Savior turns his speech to the time when he lived among them, adding:

**VERSE 4.—**“The Lord gave me a learned tongue, that I may know how to sustain with a word him who has fallen [Vulgate: ‘is weary’].”

For according to the dispensation of the body assumed, he was instructed and received the tongue of discipline, so that he might know when he ought to speak and when to be silent. The Father gave him a learned tongue for preaching, so that he might wisely sustain by his word one who had fallen into sin [Col. 0470B] and prevent him from falling worse, but rather raise him to good. He had a learned tongue, since both enemies and friends confessed that “never has a man spoken as this man speaks” (John 7:46). He sustained by a word one who had fallen when he said to the paralytic: “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you” (Matthew 9:2); and to another: “Behold, you have been made whole; do not sin any longer, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14); and to the woman: “Neither do I condemn you; go, and sin no more” (John 8:10); and at the same time to all: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew 4:17). Thus the Lord sustained by his word those who had fallen. It follows:

[Col. 0470C] “He raises in the morning; morning by morning he raises my ear, that I may hear as a teacher.”

What is expressed by morning except the heavenly coming of divine contemplation, when the mind is wholly suffused with divine light? Therefore in the morning the Lord raised the ear of the Son of Man, so that he might hear him as a teacher; for, surrounding his mind with the light of his contemplation, he raised it to things above, and in that inaccessible light taught him whatever he was to teach human beings. Hence he says: “For I have not spoken from myself; but the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment, what I should say and what I should speak; and I know that his commandment is eternal [Col. 0470D] life. Therefore what I speak, I speak as the Father said to me” (John 12:49). And when he had completed his preaching, he said to his disciples: “Everything that I heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:16). It follows:

**VERSE 5.—**“The Lord God opened my ear; but I do not resist; I did not go backward.”

The Lord God opened the ear of his heart, so that he might understand his words and hear his commandments. But he did not resist what he heard; instead, he was obedient in all things. Nor did he turn back from what had been commanded, but persevered in it to the end, “becoming obedient unto death” (Philippians 2:8). By contrast, after the Lord has opened our ears [Col. 0471A], we resist him because we are unwilling to do the good things that we understand; and if we have begun anything good, it often happens that we turn back from it. But “whoever says that he abides in Christ ought himself also to walk as he walked” (John 2:6), so that he may not resist the commandments of God which he has heard, but may obey in all things; that he may not turn backward from that obedience, but may persevere to the end in the good things he has begun. Our Redeemer, however, received this command especially from his Father—that he should give up his life, in which he preserved obedience—as he immediately begins to relate, saying:

**VERSE 6.—**“I gave my body to those striking me, and my cheeks to those plucking them; I did not turn my face away from those reproaching and spitting upon me.”

[Col. 0471B] For these things occurred when the Jews condemned him as guilty of death and began to spit upon him, veil his face, strike him with fists, and say, “Prophesy” (Luke 22:64); when the attendants struck him with slaps; and when Pilate handed him over after scourging to be crucified. The soldiers led him into the courtyard of the praetorium, summoned the whole cohort, clothed him in purple, plaited and placed upon him a crown of thorns, and began to salute him: “Hail, King of the Jews” (Matthew 27:24). They struck his head with a reed and spat upon him. It follows:

**VERSE 7.—**“The Lord God is my helper; therefore I am not confounded. Therefore I have set my face like the hardest stone, and I know that I shall not be confounded.”

[Col. 0471C] **VERSE 8.—**“Near is he who justifies me.”

In this contest of passion, the Lord is my helper. “For I am not alone, but the Father is with me” (John 16:32). Therefore amid so many insults, mockeries, and reproaches I am not confounded; rather, with joy set before me, I endure the cross, despising shame. Therefore I have set my face like the hardest stone amid every mockery and injury, so that I may in no way be ashamed. And I know that for all I endure I shall not be confounded, but rather glorified; for though I now refuse to descend from the cross while the Jews insult me, afterward I shall rise from the tomb when the soldiers are terrified. “Near is he who justifies me,” because “he who sent me is with [Col. 0471D] me and has not left me alone, because I always do what pleases him” (John 8:29). It follows:

“Who will contradict me? Let us stand together. Who is my adversary? Let him come near to me.”

“If anyone,” he says, “contradicts me, let him come and let us stand together before Pilate’s tribunal, that he may accuse me as much as he can. And if anyone is my adversary, let him approach me, that he may fulfill his unjust will in my punishments.” Notice in these words how greatly the Savior desired to suffer for us. It follows:

**VERSE 9.—**“Behold, the Lord God is my helper: who is there who shall condemn me?”

The Lord God is my helper, because “you shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of God’s power and coming in the clouds of heaven” (Matthew 26:64). [Col. 0472A] Who, then, would dare condemn me? Yet when the Lord had said this, immediately the high priest tore his garments and said: “You have heard the blasphemy. What seems right to you?” And they answered: “He is guilty of death” (Mark 14:64). But lest their atrocity be feared, their weakness is shown when it follows:

“Behold, all shall be worn out like a garment; the moth shall eat them.”

As if it were said: They shall quickly die from old age and be eaten by worms. Or indeed they shall be worn out like a garment of the soul in eternal torments. Or because none of them can be justified while the Lord is present, all shall grow old like a garment. “But that which grows old is near to destruction” (Hebrews [Col. 0472B] 8:12). And the moth that eats them is, namely, the consciousness of sins and jealousy at the Gentiles’ salvation. Again the Lord cries out to them:

**VERSE 10.—**“Who among you fears God, hearing the voice of his servant?”

As if he said: If any of you fears God, let him hear my voice. For “I have not come of myself, but he sent me” (John 7:28). “Why do you not understand my speech?” (John 8:43). “If I speak truth, why do you not believe me? He who is of God hears the words of God; therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God” (ibid., 46). It follows:

“Who has walked in darkness and has no light? Let him hope in the name of the Lord and lean upon his God.”

[Col. 0472C] “Who,” he says, “has until now conducted his life in the darkness of ignorance and has not yet been illumined by the light of truth? Let him hope in the name of the Lord, because henceforth ‘everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved’” (Romans 10:13), whether Jew or Gentile. And let him lean upon his God: that is, let him not seek to be justified by works of the law, but believe in him who justifies the ungodly, so that his faith may be counted to him as righteousness according to the purpose of God’s grace. “For if Abraham,” says the Apostle, “was justified by works, he has glory, but not before God” (Romans 4:2). Therefore the person who seeks justification not by faith but by his own works leans not upon God but upon himself. But he leans upon his [Col. 0472D] God who believes in Christ Jesus, so as to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law. Again the Lord says to his persecutors:

**VERSE 11.—**“Behold, all of you who kindle fire, girded with flames.” And he adds: “Walk in the light of your fire and in the flames which you have kindled; this has been done to you by my hand: you shall sleep in sorrows.”

For they kindled for him the fire of passion and were girded with flames—that is, armed against him with fury. But from this fire light shone forth, because through the Savior’s passion and resurrection the whole world was illumined. Thus when he says, “Behold, all of you who kindle fire, girded with flames,” he mercifully admonishes them, adding:

“Walk in the light of your fire”: that is, set the step of your conduct in the light of faith, which answers you through the glory of the resurrection arising from my passion, of which you were the authors. “And walk in the flames which you have kindled”: that is, willingly endure now as friends for my name the burning tribulations which you, as enemies, stirred up against me, as Saul afterward suffered the evils which he had inflicted upon the saints. “This has been done to you by my hand,” because it has been granted to you not only to believe in me but also to suffer for me. “You shall sleep in sorrows” [Col. 0473A]: that is, you shall delight in sufferings for my name and regard them as rest.

[Col. 0473B] But if this speech is addressed to those who remained in unbelief, it is spoken to them as a judgment of just recompense: “Walk in the light of your fire and in the flames which you have kindled.” As if he said: Endure the fire of passion which you kindled for me, and pass through the flames which you set ablaze for me, so that whatever I or my disciples suffered from you, you may suffer from the Romans. “This has been done to you by my hand,” so that you might suffer all these evils, because I caused the Romans to come against you and granted them victory over you. But when led into captivity, you shall sleep in sorrows, because until Elijah’s coming you shall lie in the miseries of this captivity and be weighed down by the sleep of unbelief. Or, after all this tribulation, you shall sleep in sorrows, because when the body has been laid to sleep in death, your soul shall endure the pains of hellish torments.

Or they all kindled a fire for themselves and strengthened the flames, because they had within themselves wood, hay, stubble, thorns, briars, and tares. And because they are girded with flames, surrounded by them, and have strengthened a conflagration for themselves, they are summoned to salvation and are told: “Walk in the light of your own fire and amid the flames which you have kindled,” so that amid punishments and sufferings they may learn God’s power and return to salvation. This signifies, as has been said, their captivity. Having spoken of the overthrow brought about by the Jews’ unbelief, he proceeds to speak of the building up of the Church, addressing those who received the faith from the same people:

## CHAPTER LI

**VERSE 1.**—“Hear me, you who pursue what is just and seek the Lord: consider the rock from which you were cut, and the hollow of the pit from which you were hewn.”

**VERSE 2.**—“Consider Abraham your father, and Sarah who bore you; for I called him alone, blessed him, and multiplied him.”

**VERSE 3.**—“The Lord will comfort Zion; he will comfort all her ruins; he will make her wilderness like delights, and her deserts like the garden of the Lord: joy and gladness, thanksgiving and the voice of praise, shall be found in her.”

“Hear me,” he says, “you who follow the righteousness which is from faith, and who seek not gold or silver but the Lord the Father, hastening to attain the vision of him. Consider the rock from which you were cut,” that is, consider the hardness of heart of the unbelievers, from which you were cut away by the iron of my preaching through my grace, so that you might be placed as living stones in the building of the Church. “And consider the hollow of the pit from which you were hewn,” that is, reflect upon the jaws of the abyss from which you were mercifully delivered. For that faithless people has, in large part, already been condemned in hell, and is daily condemned in those who die from it. But although you stood in the same unbelief and were about to fall into that same Tartarean place, you were cut away from its mouth before you were wholly swallowed up—that is, before the end of this present life.

Consider these things, he says, and then consider Abraham your father. This is like what the Apostle says to the Ephesians: “Remember that you were once Gentiles in the flesh, called the uncircumcision by that which is called circumcision in the flesh made by hands; at that time you were without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants, having no hope of promise and without God in this world; but now in Christ Jesus you who were once far off have been made near by the blood of Christ” (Eph. II, 11). Likewise Christ adds in this place: “Consider Abraham your father, whose children you have become by faith. For not all who are of Israel are Israelites; nor are all who are Abraham’s seed children; but ‘in Isaac,’ he says, ‘shall your seed be called’: that is, it is not the children of the flesh who are children of God, but the children of the promise are reckoned as the seed” (Rom. IX, 6).

[Col. 0474C] “And consider Sarah, who bore you,” because you are not children of a slave woman but of the free woman. For Jews, begotten into the slavery of the Law, are children of Hagar; Christians, however, begotten as children of Sarah, are born into the freedom of grace. “For I called him alone,” he says, “and blessed him and multiplied him,” “that he might be the father of all believers—not only of those who are of the circumcision, but also of those among the Gentiles who follow the steps of his faith” (Rom. IV, 11); for those who are of faith, whether Jews or Gentiles, are Abraham’s children.

Therefore the Lord—that is, my Father—will comfort Zion, that is, the Church. Or, if perhaps the Father is speaking these words, when he says that the Lord will comfort Zion and her ruins, he must be understood to speak of the Son or of the Holy Spirit. Therefore the Lord will comfort Zion, giving her peace after affliction, joy after sorrow, and fruitfulness after barrenness. He will comfort all her ruins, raising what has been cast down and restoring what has been destroyed, because “the Lord lifts up all who fall and raises all who are bowed down” (Ps. CXLIV, 14). And he adds how this consolation comes about:

“Because he will make her wilderness like delights,” etc.

What else is signified in this passage by the Church’s wilderness or desert than a lack of good? Thus, under the figure of Judaea, Jeremiah laments the soul of the sinner, saying: “How does the city once full of people sit solitary?” (Lam. I, 1). Hearts empty of the fear of God and parched for lack of the moisture of heavenly grace are compared to the desolation of a barren wilderness. This world had become a wilderness [Col. 0475A] when the Redeemer appeared in the flesh. For it was deserted of every cultivation of faith and fear of God, overgrown with the thorns of sins. It was bleak like an uncultivated field, utterly lacking the fruitfulness of good works and receiving no rain of spiritual grace. But through apostolic preaching the untilled field is broken up and cultivated, made fruitful with the seed of the divine word, and adorned with flowers of virtues, like a flourishing paradise of delights. Rightly, then, when the complete reconciliation of the world is promised, it is said that God will make Zion’s wilderness like delights and her desert like the garden of the Lord, so that “where sin abounded, grace might abound still more” (Rom. V, 20), and their soul may be, according to Jeremiah, “like a watered garden” (Jer. XXXI, 12). The addition, “For joy and gladness, thanksgiving and the voice of praise shall be found in her,” is to be understood of the rejoicing of the faithful and the public solemnities of the Church which, after persecutions ceased, are held everywhere. After this the omnipotent Father addresses his people concerning the coming of the new grace, saying:

**VERSE 4.**—“Attend to me, my people, and hear me, my tribe; for a law shall go out from me, and my judgment shall rest as a light for the peoples.”

For he calls the ten tribes his people, and the tribe of Judah his tribe: Judah worshipped God for a long time even while Israel served idols, and the Savior was to be born from Judah. So that this people might always await his coming with anxious expectation, he commands it to attend to him, saying: “For a law shall go out from me”—namely, the new law, since the old had long ago been given—“and my judgment,” by which I shall judge between those who will believe in me and those who will reject me, “shall rest as a light for the peoples,” that is, in the illumination of the Gentiles. Of this judgment the Son of God says: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John IX, 39): that is, that humble Gentiles may see and proud Jews incur blindness of heart. Then concerning the presence of the same Only-begotten Son he adds:

**VERSE 5.**—“My righteous one is near; my Savior has gone forth.”

[Col. 0475D] He is near because he walks among you and you do not know him. For he has gone forth from that hidden dwelling-place of his eternity, because “his going forth is from the height of heaven” (Ps. XVIII, 7). Or he “went forth as a bridegroom coming out of his chamber” from the Virgin’s womb (ibid., 6). Here he adds concerning the rulers of the Churches:

“And my arms shall judge the peoples.”

What are the Lord’s arms but the apostles, through whom he works mighty deeds powerfully? For, just as Christ is the one foundation of the Church and the apostles and prophets its foundations, so Christ is the arm of the Lord and the apostles are his arms. They shall judge the peoples, as it was said to them: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John XX, 23). They shall also judge the peoples when they sit “upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX, 28). It follows:

“The islands shall wait for me, and shall sustain my arm.”

“Not only,” he says, “shall regions spread over the broad expanse of the world wait for me, but even the islands of the sea shall wait for me; they shall sustain my arm,” that is, await my Son, because “he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX, 10). These islands may also be understood as the souls of the saints, made firm in faith in God amid the persecution of this world, or as the multitude of Churches from among the Gentiles. For the Father comes in the Son, because “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (II Cor. V, 19). But the Father is named first and then the Son, that is, the Father’s arm, because the Son is from the Father, not the Father from the Son. For the Son is the arm of God, not because God the Father is bounded by the form of human flesh and the Son is joined to him as a bodily member, but because “all things were made through him” (John I, 3), and therefore he is called the arm of the Lord. For just as your arm is that by which you work, so God’s arm is said to be his Word, because he made the world through the Word. Why does a human being extend an arm to do something, except because what he says does not immediately come to pass? But if one possessed such power that what one said came to pass without any movement of the body, one’s arm would be one’s word. Thus the Only-begotten Son [Col. 0476C] is not a member of the Father’s body; rather, because the Father works all things through him, he is the Father’s arm, and also the Father’s Word. Such an arm is neither stretched out when extended nor contracted when drawn in. Therefore, proclaiming that he himself and his Son would come to the Gentiles through the apostles, the Father says that the Gentiles would then first attain salvation: “The islands shall wait for me, and shall sustain my arm.”

But if this is said concerning the day of judgment—“The islands shall wait”—then even those who are in the islands, all the reprobate, will fear him coming in the Son, and will bear the weight of his arm when he strikes them with an incurable wound, saying: “Depart from me, you accursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV, 41). For the following words show that this sentence is to be understood more in this sense, since it is immediately added:

**VERSE 6.**—“Lift up your eyes to heaven, and look beneath the earth below; for the heavens shall melt away like smoke, the earth shall be worn out like a garment, and its inhabitants shall perish likewise; but my salvation shall be forever, and my righteousness shall not fail.”

“Lift up your eyes to heaven,” he says, that is, look upon this heaven, for “the heavens shall melt away like smoke” on the last day. Then, as Peter says, “the heavens, being on fire, shall be dissolved, and the elements shall melt with the heat of fire” (II Pet. III, 22); not the ethereal heavens, however, but the aerial ones. For that fire shall occupy only as much of the region of this air [Col. 0477A] as the waters of the flood rose, and shall burn the same heavens that the water then covered. Above we read concerning the Lord, “who stretches out the heavens as nothing” (above, XL, 22), and now it is said: “The heavens shall melt away like smoke.” From this it is sufficiently apparent what sort of nature the heavens have: namely, one like the nature of clouds—light, not solid or hard.

“And look,” he says, that is, consider the things beneath the earth below, namely the punishments of hell. For the earth, which the wicked now love, shall be worn out like a garment by the harshness of that fire and levelled, so as to be changed into a better form; and its inhabitants, who would have wished always to dwell in it, shall perish like it. For the saints “shall be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air” (I Thess. IV, 17); but the reprobate shall be left upon the earth, so that they may burn with it and fall with the devil into the abyss of perdition.

Or: just as the earth shall be worn out in order to be changed for the better, so its inhabitants also shall perish—not to their own destruction, but to the abolishing of the evil baseness of the old state and the renewal of future glory—when the righteous shall shine as the sun and, with former things passed away, all things shall have become new. But the salvation which the elect shall then obtain shall be eternal, and the righteousness given to them shall not fail, because in the reward of recompense they shall receive this also: that they can never again sin, they who now avoid sins as far as they are able. Then he strengthens his elect against worldly adversities, saying:

**VERSE 7.**—“Hear me, you who know what is just, my people in whose heart is my law: do not fear the reproaches of men, nor be afraid of their blasphemies.”

For the Lord speaks these words to those of whom the Apostle also says: “Do all things without murmurings and doubts, that you may be blameless and innocent, children of God without reproach in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine as lights in the world, holding fast the word of life” (Phil. II, 14). Those who are such certainly know what is just, and the divine law is in their heart as they meditate upon God’s commandments. Formerly they suffered reproaches from unbelievers as believers in the Crucified One, when it was a grave charge to be a Christian, and they were blasphemed as deceivers and evildoers. Even now all who are good live among the wicked, suffer mockery and reproaches from false Christians, and are blasphemed. But to all such the Lord says that they should not fear the reproach of scorn and accusation which they suffer from depraved people, nor the blasphemies falsely alleged against them. He adds why they ought not to fear their slanders:

**VERSE 8.**—“For as a garment, so the worm shall consume them; and as wool, so the moth shall devour them; [Col. 0478A] but my salvation shall be forever, and my righteousness unto generations of generations.”

Just as a worm is born from a garment, or a moth from wool, and consumes the same garment or wool, so after these people have died, a worm shall arise from their flesh to consume it; and therefore they are not to be feared, since in a little while they will be such.

Or, because the flesh is like the soul’s garment, the worm that consumes it is carnal temptation, since it arises from the flesh itself and tears that same flesh. Thus the sinner, like a garment, is consumed by a worm when his flesh comes to destruction through the corruptible temptation which it produces. The same thought is repeated concerning wool and moth which was stated concerning garment and worm. A person [Note: [Col. 0477D] C. Garst., “By a worm.” “For not by temptation,” etc.] is consumed by temptation just as wool is usually devoured [Col. 0478B] by the moth which arises from it, so that it may be torn apart and destroyed. Such are the persecutors of the saints; therefore they are not to be feared.

Or, in the punishments of eternal condemnation, “as a garment, so the worm shall consume them, and as wool, so the moth shall devour them,” because “their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. LXVI, 24). But the Lord’s salvation, which he will give to his saints, shall be eternal, because “the righteous shall live forever, and their reward is with the Lord” (Wis. V, 16). His righteousness, which he shall give them, shall remain unto generations of generations, because those who have attained that perfected righteousness will never again be able to lose it; but they will happily persevere as righteous throughout every generation of ages upon ages, [Col. 0478C] because they now pursue righteousness as far as they are able.

Therefore the righteous ought not to fear the reproach they suffer from unbelieving and depraved persons, knowing that Christ their head endured more grievous things from them. “If they called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more his household?” (Matt. X, 25). For all that reproach which is commonly cast upon the saints is written preeminently concerning the Savior’s passion. Thus the Apostle, after saying that Jesus suffered outside the gate, added this exhortation: “Therefore let us go forth to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach” (Heb. XIII, 13). Hence the prophet, now recalling the same passion whose reproach his elect bear, addresses him as though laid in the tomb and exhorts him to rise, saying:

**VERSE 9.**—“Arise, put on strength, O arm of the Lord.”

Arise from the tomb; put on strength, that is, the power of immortality. It follows:

“Arise as in the days of old, in the generations of ages.”

Arise as in the days of old: just as of old through Moses you delivered the children of Israel from Pharaoh’s hand and led them through the midst of the sea into the wilderness, so now, through yourself, lead by the water of baptism into a new manner of life those who have been foreordained to life [Col. 0479A] and still serve the ruler of this world in the mire of carnal pleasures. Just as through Joshua you gave them the land which you promised, so now may those called to the eternal inheritance receive the promise anew. Just as through Gideon you delivered them from the hand of Midian, so now through yourself deliver believers from the hand of unbelievers. Just as through David you conquered their enemies and slew or subjected them, so now through yourself, waging war against all destroyers of the Church, either convert or destroy them. Therefore arise, now doing mighty deeds as you did in the days of old, in the generations of ages that have passed. It follows:

“Was it not you who struck down the proud one and wounded the dragon?”

In the Passion, having been struck, you struck the ancient enemy, who boasted that he had conquered all human beings; and, wounded by the lance, you wounded the venomous dragon who had killed all people by the poison of his wickedness. It follows:

**VERSE 10.**—“Was it not you who dried up the sea, the water of the mighty abyss?”

What is signified by the sea but the world? And what by the water of the abyss but the dark learning of Gentile errors? Because it could not be completely comprehended, but always plunged its followers into deeper errors and veiled its falsehoods in certain figurative expressions, it was like a vast abyss which could not be penetrated by any practice [Note: [Col. 0479D] Both manuscripts: “could not be penetrated by any practice.”]. Therefore the Lord dried up the sea, namely the water of the mighty abyss: that is, he cleansed the world by annulling the teaching of ancient errors, because he “made foolish the wisdom of this world” (I Cor. II, 20). It follows:

“You made the depths of the sea a way, that the redeemed might pass through.”

If the sea should be understood as the world, nothing prevents us from taking the depths of the sea to mean the confines of hell. The Lord entered these depths of the sea when he entered the lowest parts of hell to snatch away the souls of his elect. Therefore it is rightly said: “You made the depths of the sea a way, that the redeemed might pass through.” For before the Redeemer’s coming, these depths of the sea were not a way but a prison, because they enclosed within themselves even the souls of the good, although [Col. 0479D] not in places of punishment. Yet the Lord made those depths a way because, coming there, he enabled his elect to pass from the prisons of hell to the heavenly realms. Thus it is rightly added: “That the redeemed might pass through.” It follows:

**VERSE 11.**—“And now those redeemed by the Lord shall return and come to Zion with praise; everlasting joy shall be upon their heads; they shall possess joy and gladness; sorrow and groaning shall flee away.”

Those redeemed by the Lord from the hand of death shall now return to paradise, from which they had been expelled, and shall come to the Jerusalem above [Col. 0480A] in a voice of exultation, praising their Redeemer. Everlasting joy shall rest upon their heads, that is, upon their minds, which they shall receive from the Creator whom they behold above themselves. They shall possess joy and gladness without interruption in that blessedness; sorrow shall flee from them, because by that happy transformation they shall become incapable of suffering; and groaning shall depart from them, because there shall then be nothing from which they can groan. It follows:

**VERSE 12.**—“Behold, I myself shall comfort you.”

The Lord himself shall comfort them, because when he reveals himself, he will make them regard all past afflictions as nothing. The Apostle had this consolation in mind when he said: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18). It follows:

“Who are you, that you should fear a mortal human being and a son of man who shall wither like grass?”

**VERSE 13.**—“And you have forgotten the Lord your maker, who stretched out the heavens and founded the earth; and you have continually feared all day long because of the fury of him who afflicted you and was prepared to destroy you. Where now is the fury of the afflicter?”

**VERSE 14.**—“He who walks shall come quickly to open up; he shall not kill unto utter destruction, nor shall his bread fail.”

Moving from the plural to the singular number, he suddenly turns to the person of each individual weak one, perhaps because whatever is heard in the singular is more readily recognized by individuals, so that each may return to his own heart and rebuke in himself what is said of each. He therefore maintains the singular number, saying: “Who are you, that you should fear a mortal human being and a son of man who shall wither like grass? And have you forgotten the Lord your maker?” For whoever is broken by the tribulation of adversities does not remember by whom he was made. For he who made what did not exist does not abandon what he made without governance; and he who graciously created a human being does not permit him to be unjustly afflicted, nor does he allow to perish through neglect that which exists—he who created even what did not exist in order that it might exist.

When, therefore, we seek the cause of our tribulation and perhaps find it too slowly, this is the consideration: that we suffer nothing unjustly. For if, though we did not exist, we exist through God as author, then, now that we exist, we are not unjustly afflicted under God’s governance. For this reason we should not fear the adversities inflicted on us by another human being, because the very person who persecutes us, being mortal, flourishes today and tomorrow withers into grass. But our Creator, who governs and protects us by the greatness of his power, made heaven and earth and therefore orders most excellently whatever happens in heaven and on earth. Because every weak person, when oppressed, is wearied by excessive faintheartedness away from the hope of joy, and while enduring—or fearing to endure—outward adversities, inwardly forgets what he rejoiced in, he is rightly rebuked [Col. 0481A] here: “Who are you, that you should fear a mortal human being and a son of man who shall wither like grass? And have you forgotten the Lord your maker, who stretched out the heavens and founded the earth? And you have continually feared all day long”—that is, throughout the whole time of this present life—“because of the face,” that is, the presence, “of the fury of him who afflicted you for the Redeemer’s name and was prepared to destroy you,” that is, to draw you into eternal destruction, if you did what he urged. These words are spoken as if to one already delivered from the evils of the present life and brought into the joys of everlasting peace. Hence it is aptly said: “Where now is the fury of the afflicter?”

Again, to one still striving in the present contest it is said: Your Lord and maker, walking upon the waves of this tribulation, will quickly come to open for you [Col. 0481B] the gate of the kingdom of heaven; and the fury of the afflicter shall not kill you unto utter destruction, that is, it shall not destroy you wholly at once, because although it may “kill the body, it cannot kill the soul” (Matt. X, 25). Or it shall not kill the whole Church unto utter destruction, but shall glorify by martyrdom certain persons to whom this has been granted. Or again, the Lord is said not to kill unto utter destruction because he always preserves the souls of his own unharmed from death, although he afflicts their bodies temporarily or even puts them to death. “Nor shall his bread fail,” that is, the Lord’s bread by which he will always feed you inwardly while you suffer hunger and torments outwardly; for as much as your outward person is destroyed, so much more your inward person shall be renewed. It follows:

**VERSE 15.**—“But I am the Lord [Col. 0481C] your God, who trouble the sea and its waves swell; the Lord of hosts is my name.”

The sea is this world; the sea’s waves are the tribulations of the world. Often the storm of the sea rises against us: that is, the rulers and powers of the world are stirred up, foam in swelling anger, and seek to strike and overwhelm us. But we must not fear this storm. The Lord our God is he “who troubles the sea and its waves swell.” For while we sail in this little ship of the Church across this billowing world, he himself, wishing to exercise our patience as he knows is expedient for us, stirs up the bitter and swelling waves of this world. Nor can the waves rage except as far as the shore where he has set their limit. For there is no temptation that does not receive its measure from the Lord. Let there be temptations; let there be the tribulations of the sea: you will not be consumed by them. But see whether temptations themselves are not beneficial. Consider the Apostle: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation will also provide the way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (I Cor. X, 13). He does not say: He will not allow you to be tempted at all. For if you reject temptations, you reject restoration. Therefore you are being restored; and if you are being restored, you are in the hands of the craftsman. He removes something from you, corrects something, levels something, cleanses something; he works upon you with certain of his tools—the scandals of this world themselves. Only do not fall from the craftsman’s hand; no temptation shall come upon you beyond your strength. “I,” he says, [Col. 0482A] “am the Lord your God, who trouble the sea and its waves swell.” Therefore do not fear the waves of the world, which the Lord your God causes to swell in his gracious providence for your testing; rather, be confident in the Lord your God. He does not allow them to rage beyond the measure which he knows will benefit your progress. For God does, or permits to be done, that from which you may make progress, for your benefit.

He also recalls that he calls himself the Lord of hosts, because hosts serve him: not only the hosts of good angels, who guard and assist the elect amid the perils of this life, but also those of evil angels, who test them by temptation and destroy the reprobate human beings who afflict the good. After this the discourse returns to our head, saying:

**VERSE 16.**—“I have put my words in your mouth, and protected you in the shadow of my hand, that you may plant the heavens and found the earth, and say to Zion: You are my people.”

For the Father speaks these words to the Savior while he dwells among human beings. He placed his words in his mouth, as John says of him: “For he whom God has sent speaks the words of God” (John III, 34). And he himself said: “I have not spoken from myself, but the Father who sent me himself gave me a commandment what I should say and what I should speak” (John XII, 49). God also protected him in the shadow of his hand from the heat of tribulations among his adversaries, so that they could never touch him except when he willed it. He was protected so that, preaching freely, he might plant the heavens in faith—that is, the apostles—[Col. 0482C] and found the earth—that is, the Church—and say to Zion, that is, to the faithful Hebrews: “You are my people.” “Has God cast away his people whom he foreknew?” (Rom. XI, 1). Thus he said, “You are my people,” when, making himself known to her as her God, he chose her by his grace. Here an appropriate exhortation follows:

**VERSE 17.**—“Lift yourself up, lift yourself up; arise, Jerusalem, who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his wrath.”

Lift yourself up to spiritual understanding; lift yourself up to the heavenly kingdoms; arise to a spiritual manner of life. O Jerusalem, that is, the Hebrew people, who drank from the Lord’s hand the cup of his wrath—that is, you experienced the bitterness of affliction as God was angry at your sins. For the cup signifies suffering, as the Lord indicates when he says to Peter: “The cup which the Father has given me, do you not wish that I should drink it?” (John XVIII, 11). Jerusalem therefore had drunk the cup of God’s wrath when he came who said to her: “You are my people,” because while awaiting the Redeemer’s coming, she had meanwhile been afflicted with many evils. Or this exhortation is addressed to that Jewish people which did not receive him but denied him, and it is urged to repent because, on account of the Savior’s death, it has endured the affliction of captivity until this day. It follows:

“You drank to the bottom of the cup of stupor, and drank even to the dregs.”

The cup of stupor is an excess of affliction which causes the mind to sleep in its inward watchfulness while, in considering the evils it suffers outwardly, it keeps watch more than is necessary. The bottom of the cup is the deepest extremity of suffering from evils. The dregs of the cup are the sin it contracts from the depths of affliction, because when one oppressed by many tribulations is not corrected but made worse. Jerusalem therefore drank to the bottom of the cup of stupor when it was afflicted by such great evils that, made drunk and sleepy by them, it forgot its own mind and did not remember heavenly goods, but continually thought of the outward evils it endured. And it drank even to the dregs because, reaching the uttermost misery, it was not inwardly cleansed of sins through tribulation, but was filled far more abundantly with defilements. It follows:

**VERSE 18.**—“There is none to sustain her among all the sons whom she bore, and none to take her by the hand among all the sons whom she nourished.”

When the Lord came, there was none among all her sons to sustain her, or to take her hand, support her weakness, and lead her in the way of righteousness, because, as it is written, “All have turned aside; together they have become worthless” (Ps. XIII, 3). Yet much more after the Passion was she left bereft of every consolation, because there was then no prophet or apostle in her to comfort her, take her by the hand, and raise her as she lay fallen. It follows:

**VERSE 19.**—“Two things have happened to you; who shall grieve for you? Desolation and destruction, [Col. 0483C] famine and sword.”

“Two evils,” he says, “have happened to you, O Jerusalem. And who will grieve for you who suffer such things? But what are the things that happened to you while awaiting the Savior’s coming? Desolation and destruction, famine and sword.” He said that two things had happened, and then stated that four had happened. But perhaps he explained the same two things twice—as if we asked what those two things were, and he replied, “Desolation and destruction,” and then, wishing again to interpret the same things, said that famine and sword are those two things. For he often speaks in this way, repeating his own words with a certain elegance, as an eloquent man does. It follows:

“Who shall comfort you?”

**VERSE 20.**—“Your children have been cast down; they have lain asleep [Col. 0483D] at the head of every road like a trapped beast [Note: [Col. 0483D] Elsewhere: “like an oryx,” etc.], full of the Lord’s indignation and the rebuke of your God.”

“Who,” he says, “can comfort you amid such great evils? For your children were cast down in your bosom; exiled from you, they lay helpless on different roads, afflicted with the bonds of their enemies, like a trapped beast, when they were led captive, filled with God’s wrath and his rebuke, broken by scourges and subjected to reproaches and insults.” Jerusalem endured these and similar things under Nebuchadnezzar and Antiochus, but more harshly under Titus. It follows:

**VERSE 21.**—“Therefore hear this, poor little one, drunken but not with wine.”

[Col. 0484A] **VERSE 22.**—“Thus says your ruler, the Lord and your God, who fought for his people: Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of stupor, the bottom of the cup of my indignation.”

He calls her “poor little one” because she endured miseries. She was drunk not with wine, but with affliction. Her ruler is Christ, who fought against the devil for his people. She held the cup of stupor in her hand while, because of her perverse conduct, she suffered by divine judgment such great affliction that she lost the inward wakefulness of her mind. She also bore the bottom of the cup of divine indignation with its dregs, suffering the extremity of evils while the Lord was angry, and thus contracting the dregs of sins. But after her ruler fought for his people, he took from her hand the cup [Col. 0484B] of stupor and the bottom of the cup of his indignation, because, rising from the dead, he converted her to himself and removed the evils by which, deservedly because of her wickedness, she was spiritually put to sleep; and he took away the depths of miseries in which, having lost patience, she was filled with the defilements of sins through murmuring. Therefore it is aptly added:

“You shall not continue to drink it any longer.”

For that people, once it was converted to the newness of grace, no longer drank this cup: although it suffered much for Christ, it did not take the dregs of sin into the cup of suffering. Rather, if it had any dregs in that cup, it was cleansed from them; nor was it put to sleep in afflictions, but became more watchful. Yet the part of that people which has not yet believed still does not cease to drink this cup and to remain amid its dregs. But if it repents and rises up, having lifted itself, let it know that the cup of stupor and ruin will be taken from its hand and that it shall no longer drink it. It follows:

**VERSE 23.**—“And I shall put it into the hand of those who humbled you and said to your soul: ‘Bend down, that we may pass over.’” And it is added: “And you made your body like the ground, and like a road for those passing over.”

Unclean spirits humbled this people because they bent its mind toward earthly desires; and they said to its soul: “Bend down, that we may pass over.” For the soul stands upright when it desires what is above and does not bend down to what is below. But when evil spirits see it in this uprightness, they cannot pass through it. For their passing through is to scatter unclean desires within it. Therefore they say: “Bend down, that we may pass over.” For unless the soul itself casts itself down to seek what is below, their perversity has no power at all against it; nor can they pass through a soul which they fear as standing firm against them in an intention toward things above.

Therefore the souls of Jerusalem said: “Bow down, that we may pass over.” For, so that they might be able to fill her with unclean desires, they persuaded her to bend herself down toward the desire for the lowest things. Yet she not only bent her soul at their persuasion, but also made her body like the earth [Col. 0485A] and like a road for them as they passed through it, so that they might not only pass through her soul by scattering desires, but might also trample her body, by the uncleanness of a most wicked act, as though it were earth; and, passing through it like a road in continual acts of sin, might imprint the traces of their iniquity. But at last she is raised up through the grace of the Redeemer, and the cup of drowsiness which she had drunk is placed in the hand of those who had humbled her, so that, drinking in their punishments the bitterness of eternal pain, they may, as Jeremiah says, “sleep an everlasting sleep” (Jer. 51:39). Therefore it is added:

## CHAPTER LII

**VERSE 1.**—“Arise, arise; put on your strength, [Col. 0485B] O Zion; put on the garments of your glory, O Jerusalem, city of the Holy One; for the uncircumcised and the unclean shall no longer pass through you.”

Because, he says, you bent your soul down to demons and made your body earth for them to trample, now arise in soul from the onslaught of earthly things; arise in body from the mire of vices. And because they will undertake to attack you once you refuse to be subject to them, put on—that is, surround yourself with—your strength, that you may vigorously resist their temptations on every side. Put on the garments of your glory—that is, cover yourself with the adornments of virtues, you city of the Holy One, that is, of God, who says: “Be holy, for I am holy” (Lev. 11:44), so that you may strive to imitate the holiness of your King. [Col. 0485C] For the uncircumcised and the unclean shall no longer pass through you: that is, none of the demons will now be able utterly to trample you down in consent to wickedness, as he formerly did when you lay subject to him.

He will indeed pass, but will not pass through, because he will often introduce fleeting thoughts into you; yet he will no longer be able wholly to accomplish his will in you. For he passes through the person whom he finds consenting to him, because he does not cease to trample that person down all the way to the accomplishment of a wicked deed. It follows:

**VERSE 2.**—“Shake yourself from the dust; arise, sit down, O Jerusalem; loose the bonds of your neck, captive daughter of Zion.”

**VERSE 3.**—“For thus says the Lord: You were sold for nothing, [Col. 0485D] and you shall be redeemed without silver.”

Shake yourself from the dust of earthly and empty thoughts, in which you have lain until now. Arise from it and sit down—that is, at last lift up your heart from low thoughts; mourn the evils which you have perpetrated; and, by doing penance, loosen the bonds of your sins and of evil thoughts from the neck of your mind, by which you are held captive by the devil. For you were sold to Satan for nothing in your iniquities, and you shall be redeemed without silver, because that deceiver paid no price for you, nor will he receive silver or gold for your redemption; rather, you shall be redeemed by my blood. It follows:

**VERSE 4.**—“For thus says the Lord God: My people went down into Egypt at the beginning, that [Col. 0486A] they might dwell there as sojourners, and Assyria oppressed them without any cause.”

At the beginning God’s people went down into Egypt to dwell there as sojourners, because the human race, cast out from paradise, came into the darkness of this age to live here as a stranger, until, when the time of its sojourning was completed, it should receive permission to return to its homeland. And Assyria—that is, the ancient enemy—wrongfully laid claim to it without any cause, as though it were his own; for he even strove to claim the righteous because of the guilt of the first parent. Yet it was not just that those who could not be condemned for the merit of their own iniquity should perish because of the fault of another’s iniquity, since it is written: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father” (Ezek. 18:20).

Yet we say this only concerning those who are counted [Col. 0486B] among God’s people, not concerning miscarried children and others of that sort, who belong to the multitude of the lost, although they have done nothing. But all who, pursuing righteousness, fled from iniquity—these Assyria falsely accused without cause on account of Adam’s sin, because, as the divine law decreed, “Fathers shall not be put to death for sons, nor sons for fathers; but each shall die for his own iniquity” (Deut. 24:16). Thus this wicked accuser falsely accused God’s elect, though without cause, so that they were compelled on account of this accusation to descend into hell, where they were detained in places of rest, until, through the grace of redemption, the accusation having entirely ended, they might pass free into the kingdoms of heaven. It follows:

[Col. 0486C] **VERSE 5.**—“And now, what have I here, says the Lord, since my people have been taken away for nothing?”

“What have I here?”—that is, what have I in this world, what have I on earth, since my people have been taken from me for nothing: that is, not because of their own fault, but another’s fault, namely, the sin of the first human being. It follows:

“His rulers act unjustly, says the Lord, and continually all day long my name is blasphemed.”

His rulers—that is, the demons—act unjustly in claiming dominion over him; and continually, throughout the whole world, my name is blasphemed all day long—that is, throughout all time—while idols are everywhere proclaimed. It follows:

[Col. 0486D] **VERSE 6.**—“Therefore my people shall know my name in that day, because I myself who spoke, behold, am present.”

Because the rulers of my people act unjustly and cause my name continually to be blasphemed, therefore my people, whom I have predestined to life, shall know my name, which they still blaspheme in ignorance, in that day when you shall be redeemed without silver—that is, at the time of my resurrection, when this Gospel of the kingdom shall be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations. For I myself, who was speaking these things to you through the prophets, behold, am present in the flesh, in order to redeem you as I have spoken.

Then the prophet, considering this Redeemer’s manner of life among human beings, says:

[Col. 0487A] **VERSE 7.**—“How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of one announcing and preaching peace, announcing good things, preaching salvation, saying to Zion: Your God shall reign!”

“How beautiful,” he says, that is, wonderfully beautiful, “upon the mountains”—that is, upon the most eminent mountains, upon the prophets and apostles—are the feet of the one announcing peace: that is, the steps of Christ’s deeds, who, on coming, preached “peace to you who were far off, and peace to those who are near” (Isa. 57:19). For the things he himself did, while he preached our reconciliation to God, announced by promising the good of the heavenly homeland, and preached by promising everlasting salvation, are so illustrious and wonderful that they so transcend all the summits of the saints [Col. 0487B] that those who make great progress in God can scarcely touch the traces of his works, gazing in wonder from the height of contemplation.

The prophet therefore rightly marvels at his beautiful feet upon the mountains. And he said to Zion, “Your God shall reign,” when he began to preach and say: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 4:17). He said, “O Zion, your God shall reign,” whenever he spoke to believers about the kingdom of God, whenever he announced that the devil’s kingdom was to be overthrown and God’s kingdom would come. He also sent the apostles to preach the kingdom. Hence, with the address now turned toward him, it is added:

**VERSE 8.**—“The voice of your watchmen: they have lifted up their voice.”

For his watchmen are those whom he himself set over [Col. 0487C] the churches, who, established on the summit of a higher rank, foresee coming good and evil, and, when spiritual enemies approach, rouse the peoples subject to them to battle with the trumpet of preaching. Therefore the voice of these watchmen—that is, of the apostles and teachers—was heard. For they lifted up their voice in preaching, so that they might be heard by many.

After the prophet had spoken these matters as though past, considering them still to be future, he added:

“They shall praise together, because they shall see eye to eye, when the Lord restores Zion.”

For the watchmen—that is, the apostles—praised together because they preached one Gospel harmoniously throughout the whole world. For they saw eye to eye [Col. 0487D] and face to face when the Lord converted the people of Zion to the newness of grace; for then it was said to them: “Blessed are the eyes which see what you see. For I say to you that many prophets and kings wished to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Matt. 13:16). It follows:

**VERSE 9.**—“Rejoice and praise together, desolate places of Jerusalem, for the Lord has comforted his people; he has redeemed Jerusalem.”

While the watchmen praise, you too praise and rejoice together, O desolate Jerusalem: that is, you people who were deprived of good among the Jewish people, yet ordained to life. For the Lord Jesus, by his visitation, comforted his Israelite people [Col. 0488A] and redeemed Jerusalem—that is, the Hebrew people or the Church—at the price of his blood. Then the Gospel was preached to every creature throughout the whole world. For it follows:

**VERSE 10.**—“The Lord has prepared his holy arm in the sight of all nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.”

The Lord—that is, God the Father—has prepared his arm, namely his Only-Begotten Son, for the inward eyes of all nations, that they may behold him with the gaze of faith. And he will cause not only the nations who are in the breadth of the world, but also those who are at its edges, to see and recognize his salvation, namely the Lord Jesus. Therefore the prophet accordingly admonishes believers to withdraw from the contagion of the life of unbelievers, when he adds:

[Col. 0488B] **VERSE 11.**—“Withdraw, withdraw; go out from there; do not touch what is unclean. Go out from its midst; be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord.”

Withdraw more in heart and deed than in place from the defilement of the conduct of unbelievers, and let everyone who names the Lord’s name depart from iniquity. Withdraw, then, by a change of action more than of place. Go out from there—that is, from your former way of life. Do not touch what is unclean—that is, do not consent to anyone’s sins. For what is it to touch what is unclean except to consent to sins? Go out from its midst—that is, from the midst of evil, from the midst of defilement, from the midst of your former manner of life, from the midst of worldly allurements.

It is one thing to be in an evil way of life and another [Col. 0488C] to be in its midst. It can happen that someone is in it, but, because he remains at its outer limits, he seems in a sense to be outside it. But one who remains in its midst is so surrounded by evil that its extent is equal to him from every side. Therefore sinners are now commanded to go out from its midst, as though from its heart. For one deeply immersed in vices dwells in the midst of the old way of life; but one who gradually abandons evil and turns toward better things, who has not so much begun to possess virtues as to desire them—even if this person has departed from the midst of the old life, he has not yet gone out from it.

This also is commanded to us while we remain in the Church, which was said to those believers who began to believe among the nations: “Withdraw, withdraw; go out from there; do not touch what is unclean.” Withdraw not bodily but spiritually, not in place but in mind. Go out from there—that is, rebuke the wicked, lest you too, if you keep silent, become entangled in their sins. Do not touch what is defiled by vices—that is, do not give it your assent, lest you share in their offenses. For what is it to withdraw from there except to separate one’s heart from evil? What is it to go out from there except to do what pertains to the correction of the wicked, insofar as it can be done, with peace preserved, according to each person’s rank or position? What is it not to touch what is unclean except not to consent to another’s sins? By abandoning sin you have withdrawn from there; by rebuking it in others you have gone out from there, free in heart and before God; and thereafter, by restraining yourself [Col. 0489A] from consent, you have not touched what is unclean.

Or the apostles, preachers, and believers are commanded to withdraw from Jerusalem and preach the Gospel throughout the world, and not to touch the uncleannesses of the law’s carnal observance.

What follows—“Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord”—Gregory explains thus (*Pastoral Rule*, book 2): “Let the ruler,” he says, “always be pure in thought, so that no uncleanness may pollute the one who has undertaken the office of wiping away the stains of defilement even in the hearts of others. For the hand which seeks to wash the filth of others must strive to be clean, lest it make whatever it touches more unclean if its attendant heart contains mud. Hence it is said through the prophet: ‘Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels [Col. 0489B] of the Lord.’”—“For they bear the vessels of the Lord who undertake, within their own manner of life in faith, to lead their neighbors’ souls into the inner sanctuaries. Let those, therefore, who carry living vessels to the temple of eternity in the bosom of their own conduct consider how greatly they ought to be cleansed within themselves.” It follows:

**VERSE 12.**—“For you shall not go out in tumult, nor shall you hasten in flight. For the Lord shall go before you, and the God of Israel shall gather you together.”

You shall not go out from your old manner of life in tumult, but silently and secretly, for the feet of those going out will be the affections of the heart. For you will first begin to go out from it in heart, through confession of iniquity and love of righteousness; afterward, at the end of the age, you will also be separated in body from those who remain in wickedness. Nor shall you hasten in [Col. 0489C] flight, because, with Christ as your leader, you will not fear the devil and the adversities he will bring against you. For, as it is written: “He who fears the Lord trembles at nothing and shall not be afraid, because he himself is his hope” (Ecclus. 34:16). For Christ the Lord shall go before you, leaving you an example that you may follow his footsteps, and he shall gather you together in his Church.

Or you shall not depart from this life in tumult, because at your death you will not hear the unrestrained cries of the ancient enemy, with which, at the time of death, he accuses the souls of sinners. Nor shall you hasten in flight, because, with Christ as your leader, you will not fear the devil, who will attempt to pursue and hold you. For the Lord Jesus shall go before you [Col. 0489D] and gather you together in the kingdom of heaven, because “wherever the body is, there the eagles shall be gathered” (Luke 17:37): that is, where the Redeemer is in body, there the souls of the saints shall be gathered.

Or this saying may be understood of the Apostles, who withdrew from Jerusalem not as defeated men but as victors, so that they who, daily preaching the Gospel of God in the temple, had subjected thousands of Jews to Christ’s faith might also subject the world to his Gospel. For they had the Lord going before them, who would gather them together—that is, would make one flock from the whole world—of which it is added:

**VERSE 13.**—“Behold, my servant shall understand; he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be exceedingly high.”

For he is called servant, “who, though he was in the form [Col. 0490A] of God, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6). Going before his own to the glory of the resurrection, he understood—that is, he caused them to understand and gave them understanding—because then “he opened their minds that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45). Seeing this time, Hannah said: “Let old things depart from your mouth, because the Lord is a God of knowledge” (1 Sam. 2:3).

Or he himself also understood, not as the Word of God but as servant, because “he advanced in age and wisdom” (Luke 2:52). And he says in the Psalm: “I will bless the Lord who has given me understanding” (Ps. 15:7). He was afterward exalted above all heavens, lifted above all ranks of angels, and is exceedingly high, because he sits at the right hand of the throne of majesty on high. For “God [Col. 0490B] raised him from the dead and set him at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality, power, might, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come; and he subjected all things under his feet” (Eph. 1:20). Concerning his humility also, by which he was to be despised, it is added:

**VERSE 14.**—“As many were astonished at you, so inglorious shall his appearance be among men, and his form among the children of men.”

The discourse is directed to Jerusalem, unless I am mistaken. When she was formerly pressed at times by great calamities, many who admired her in the time of prosperity were astonished at her when they saw the magnitude of her afflictions. But the Redeemer willed to become, by his compassionate manner of life, the leader in these afflictions of his people, so that those who saw his sufferings might likewise be astonished at him. Therefore he says: “As many were astonished at you,” O Jerusalem, seeing your misery and affliction, “so inglorious shall his appearance be among men, and his form among the children of men,” who will despise him when they see him subject to suffering and humble.

Or it can be said to him himself that many were astonished at you when they saw your signs. Yet a greater miracle resulted from this: he who had shown his glory by so many mighty works appeared inglorious at the time of his Passion. For his appearance was inglorious among men when “Herod, with his army, despised him and mocked him” (Luke 23:11); and his form [Col. 0490D] had no glory among the children of men when Pilate’s soldiers put a scarlet cloak around him, placed a crown of thorns upon his head and a reed in his right hand, and, bending the knee before him, mocked him, saying: “Hail, King of the Jews” (Matt. 27:24). It follows:

**VERSE 15.**—“This one shall sprinkle many nations.”

It was said in the Law (Num. 19:13) that a clean person should sprinkle with water of expiation those who were unclean, in order that they might be cleansed. They were cleansed in no other way. But things which were to be sanctified were also sprinkled with the blood of sacrifices. Therefore this one, who alone is free from every stain of sins, this high priest who is to cleanse the nations, sprinkles them either with the water of expiation—that is, the washing of baptism—or with the grace of [Col. 0491A] his Spirit, concerning which he promised: “I will pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements” (Ezek. 36:25); or with the blood of his sacrifice, that is, his own blood, of which Peter says: “For obedience and sprinkling with the blood of Jesus Christ” (1 Pet. 1:2). It follows:

“Kings shall keep their mouths closed before him.”

Kings who promulgated most cruel laws against Christians and blasphemed him at last kept their mouths closed after the nations had been sprinkled with the water of baptism. It follows:

“For those to whom no report of him had been given have seen, and those who had not heard have contemplated him.” But Israel, which had always heard the words of the prophets about him, did not recognize him. Therefore it is added:

## CHAPTER LIII

[Col. 0491B]

**VERSE 1.**—“Who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?”

Who, understand, among the Jews has believed our report, which we prophets received from the Lord concerning his Christ, or the preaching which this people heard from us? And to which Jew has the arm of the Lord, which is Christ himself, been revealed? For although he performed such great signs before them, as John says: “They did not believe in him, that the saying of Isaiah might be fulfilled, who said: ‘Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?’” (John 12:38).

**VERSE 2.**—“And he shall rise up like a shoot [Col. 0491C] before him, and like a root from thirsty ground.”

The arm of the Lord rose up like a shoot before him, because, like a shrub from the earth, he sprang up in the Virgin’s womb, and the splendor of new light, sent forth from his mother’s womb, rose up. He rose up like a shoot before him because he was made for him from David’s seed according to the flesh (Rom. 1:3), and appeared worthy for the Lord always willingly to look upon him with a friendly countenance; and, through the increase of his years, he advanced as a true human being. And he rose up like a root from thirsty ground—that is, from dry ground—because he was created from the flesh of the Virgin, which had not been watered by human seed. It follows:

“He has neither form nor beauty; and we saw him, and there was no appearance, and we desired him.”

[Col. 0491D] **VERSE 3.**—“Despised and the lowest of men, a man of sorrows and knowing infirmity; and his face was as though hidden and despised. Therefore we did not esteem him.”

In these words the faithlessness of the Jews is indicated. Christ was long desired by them beforehand, yet when he came in person, because he came humble, he seemed to them to have neither form nor beauty. To us, however, he seems “beautiful in form beyond the children of men” (Ps. 44:3). “We saw him,” they say, “and there was no appearance,” because the arm of the Lord was hidden in weakness. “We saw him despised,” as he says: “I honor my Father, and you have dishonored me” (John 8:49); “and the lowest of men,” because he came not to be served but to serve; “a man of sorrows,” for he endured many in the flesh; and “knowing”—that is, experiencing in himself—the infirmity of this body.

“And his face was as though hidden and despised,” because, although his face sometimes shone to the elect, unbelievers, not understanding his majesty, regarded as despised his face which they saw humble and weak, because divine power was concealed in a human body. Therefore, they say, because he appeared such, we did not esteem him to be what he was; that is, we did not judge him to be the arm of the Lord. And to which of us was the arm of the Lord revealed? The arm of the Lord is the Son, coeternal and consubstantial with the Father, who is also his power. Concerning him, now in the voice not of those in error but of those rightly confessing, it is added:

**VERSE 4.**—“Truly he bore our infirmities [Col. 0492B] and pains.” He mercifully carried the pains of our mortality in his flesh for a time, that he might grant us the everlasting health of souls and bodies.

And he bore them not fictitiously or phantasmatically, but truly, as one truly human, weak, and suffering. Seeing him so weakened, the Jews did not recognize him. For their voice again plainly appears when it is added: “And we considered him as though leprous, struck by God, and humbled.” Yet, now recognizing him, they immediately add:

**VERSE 5.**—“But he was wounded for our iniquities; he was crushed for our crimes.”

“We,” they say, “considered him as though leprous”—that is, inwardly defiled by the leprosy of the soul—when we said: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath. And how can a sinful man perform these signs?” (John 9:16). Or: “By Beelzebub, prince of the demons, he casts out demons” (Matt. 9:34). We considered him struck by God in his Passion and humbled when we insulted him, saying: “He saved others; he cannot save himself. If he is King of Israel, let him come down from the cross, and we will believe him. He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he wishes. For he said: ‘I am the Son of God’” (Luke 23:35; Matt. 27:42). By saying these things, they say, we considered him struck by God for his own sins. But he was wounded by nails and a lance for our iniquities, and crushed by scourges for our crimes. Therefore it is added:

[Col. 0492D] “The chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we have been healed.”

For *disciplina* is customarily used when someone is beaten with rods or scourges. And Pilate, wishing as it were to correct him through chastisement (Luke 23:16), seized and scourged him. But this chastisement was for our peace, because through it we obtained peace with God. In that scourging his back was marked by bruises. And when the Jews struck him with blows and slapped his face, his cheeks became bruised and his neck livid from the blows. But through these bruises and blows the health which we had lost in the first parent was restored to us.

It is therefore rightly said that the chastisement of our peace was [Col. 0493A] upon him and that by his bruise we have been healed, because through the scourges which he endured for us our sins were forgiven, we were reconciled to God, received into friendship with him, and through the bruising of the blows he suffered eternal health was given to us. For what we ought to have suffered for our crimes, he suffered for us, “making peace through the blood of his cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven” (Col. 1:20).

In this he set before us an example of his compassion: although he could have aided us without dying, he nevertheless preferred to assist human beings by dying. For he would have loved less had he not also taken up our wounds, nor would he have shown us the force of his love unless he himself endured for a time what he removed from us. He found us subject to suffering and death; and he who made us from nothing could indeed have recalled us from suffering even without his own death. But, in order to show how great was the power of fellow-suffering, he deigned to become for us what he did not will us to be, so that he might take death upon himself for a time and banish it from us forever. It follows:

**VERSE 6.**—“All we like sheep have gone astray; each one has turned aside into his own way, and the Lord laid upon him the iniquity of us all.”

Before this good shepherd came, we wandered like sheep without a shepherd through the wilderness of this age, full of savage beasts—that is, demons: all of us, namely all human beings; and each one of us turned aside from the straight path into his own way, that is, into the pursuit [Col. 0493C] of his own business, while following the perverse will of his own heart.
