Hence the Apostle says: “We have charged that Jews and Greeks are all under sin, as it is written: ‘There is no one righteous, no one understanding, no one seeking God; all have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one’” (Rom. 3:9). And a little later: “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus, whom God put forward as propitiation through faith in his blood” (ibid. 23).

Likewise, here it is added that the Lord laid upon him the iniquity of us all, so that he alone might bear and erase it [Col. 0493D] and justify us all. It follows:

**VERSE 7.**—“He was offered because he himself willed it, and he did not open his mouth.”

He was offered as a lamb in sacrifice for the sin of the world. And he was offered not unwillingly but voluntarily, because he himself willed it. For he says: “Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my life and take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself” (John 10:17). And he did not open his mouth, because he answered Pilate and the chief priests little, but Herod not at all.

The prophetic discourse has related these matters as though completed. But considering again that these same things had then not yet been done but were still to be done, it added:

“Like a sheep he shall be led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he shall be silent, and shall not open [Col. 0494A] his mouth.” As a sheep, when it is led to sacrifice, does not resist, so he, when he was led to his Passion, did not resist, but patiently endured without struggle whatever pleased his adversaries. And as a lamb, when it is shorn, is stripped in order to clothe others, so he was stripped in order to clothe us, and was divested of flesh in order to surround us with the garment of righteousness and the robe of immortality. For he not only redeemed us by his blood, but also opened his side in order to warm with his garment those who were chilled by their unbelief, and that we might hear from the Apostle: “All of you who have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27).

But while this lamb was thus being stripped, he was silent and did not open his mouth. Hence the Evangelist writes: “When he was accused by the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing. Then Pilate says to him: ‘Do you not hear how many testimonies they give against you?’ And he did not answer him a single word, so that the governor marveled greatly” (Matt. 27:12). And throughout the Passion he sought silence, lest he be recognized by his persecutors. “For if they had recognized him, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). He is also said to have kept silent like a lamb so that he might seem to have kept silent like one guilty. It follows:

**VERSE 8.**—“From anguish and judgment he was taken away; who shall declare his generation? For he was cut off from the land of the living.”

From the anguish of death and an unjust judgment he was taken up by the power of resurrection. And why? Because he was without fault—he whom the Virgin bore ineffably and who, as God, was born of the Father before the ages. For who shall declare [Col. 0494C] his generation? It is impossible to know the mysteries of his divine birth, concerning which the Father says: “Before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. 109:3). For inasmuch as he is the power and wisdom of God, he was born from the Father before time; or rather, because he neither began to be born nor ceased, we should more truly say: he is always born. Yet we cannot say, “he is always being born,” lest he seem imperfect. Rather, in order that he may be designated both eternal and perfect, we say both “always” and “born”: “born,” as belonging to perfection, and “always,” to eternity, so that in whatever way possible that timeless essence may be designated by temporal speech. For the begetter did not precede the one begotten, nor did the one begotten follow the begetter. For we also say that the Father is eternally born [sic]. But in contemplating this generation weak sight trembles and cannot gaze upon the ineffable brightness of eternal light. And since no mind can conceive it as it is, who shall declare it?

Or this statement should be understood of the Virgin’s childbirth, because it can scarcely be explained; when Mary sought its reason from the angel, she was told: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you” (Luke 1:35). Thus so great a sacrament of his birth is spoken of only by the angel or by the evangelist, whose narrator is most rare, lest, if it were spoken of by many, the devil might understand it and not bring about his crucifixion. But because the wicked enemy did not know his blameless generation, in blindness he sought the penalty of death from him. [Col. 0495A] For he was cut off from the land of the living—that is, by the Passion of death he was removed from this world in which we live a mortal life, in order to live immortally in heaven.

The Father discloses the cause of his Passion in what follows: “For the crime of my people I struck him.” This is clear. It follows:

**VERSE 7.**—“And he shall give the wicked for his burial, and the rich man for his death, because he did no iniquity, nor was there deceit in his mouth.”

He shall give the wicked Jews who crucified him for his burial, because from the time he was buried by them, he cast them away so that they are no longer his. Thus the angel had said to Daniel: “Christ shall be killed, and the people who will deny him shall not be his” (Dan. 9:29), namely [Col. 0495B] the Jewish people. Or he shall give the wicked Gentiles, who did not possess the devotion of faith, and the rich man—that is, the Jewish people, who abounded in the riches of the Scriptures—for life through his burial and death, because he suffered for the salvation of both peoples.

Or he shall give the wicked demons for his burial, so that they themselves may be buried and shut up in hell, perpetually dead, because they pursued him as far as his burial. And he shall give the rich man for his death, because the prince of this world, who caused him to be killed, was judged and handed over to eternal perdition. And why shall he give his murderers for his burial and death? Because he was unjustly killed by them. For he did no iniquity, but lived among sinners without sin; nor was there deceitful dissimulation in his mouth, but always simple [Col. 0495C] and pure truth. It follows:

**VERSE 10.**—“And the Lord willed to crush him in infirmity.”

For the Lord willed to crush him through the Passion in the weakness of assumed mortality, because his adversaries could do nothing to him unless the Lord willed it. It follows:

“If he gives his life for sin, he shall see long-lived offspring, and the will of the Lord shall be directed in his hand.” If he gives his life for the sin of the world—that is, undergoes death—he shall see long-lived offspring: that is, his children possessing the long duration of everlasting immortality. Or he himself shall see the seed which he sowed in good ground to be long-lived, because he shall rejoice [Col. 0495D] that his teaching endures until the end of the age. “And the will of the Lord, who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, shall be directed in his hand” (1 Tim. 2:4)—that is, in his work—when he sends his apostles everywhere to preach, so that the whole world may believe in him and be saved. It follows:

**VERSE 11.**—“Because his soul has labored, he shall see and be satisfied.”

His soul labored when he said: “Now my soul is troubled” (John 12:27); “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26:38); and “My soul is filled with evils” (Ps. 87:4), that is, with pains. But because it labored, it shall therefore see that for which it labored—that is, the salvation of the human race—and shall be satisfied, because it shall save all, as it desired. His soul labored for a long time, finding no rest among the Jews. But now it shall see churches arise throughout the world and shall be satisfied by their faith. Or that blessed soul shall see the face of the Father and be satisfied, as he says: “You will fill me with joy with your countenance” (Ps. 15:11). For he did not enter a handmade sanctuary, a copy of the true things, but heaven itself, that he may now appear before the face of God for us. It follows:

“In his knowledge the righteous one himself shall justify many of my servants, and he himself shall bear their iniquities.”

[Col. 0496B] He alone, righteous among sinners, shall justify many through his knowledge—that is, through recognition of his name, faith, and teaching. Hence he also says to the apostles: “Already you are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you” (John 15:3). For he had justified them in his own knowledge. And Paul declares that “a human being is not justified by works of the law except through faith in Jesus Christ” (Gal. 2:16), and that “for one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith will be reckoned as righteousness” (Rom. 4:5). But in order to justify sinners, he bore in his body upon the wood their iniquities, which they could not bear and beneath whose weight they were crushed, so that, dead to sins, they might live to righteousness. It follows:

[Col. 0496C] VERSE 12.—“Therefore I shall distribute to him very many.”  
[Note: [Col. 0495D] Elsewhere: “I shall distribute.”]  
“And he shall divide the spoils of the mighty, because he delivered his soul to death and was reckoned with criminals.”

Because he shall justify my servants and bear their iniquities, therefore I shall distribute very many to him. Or: he shall divide among his apostles the spoils of the mighty—that is, the people whom he has taken from them—so that Peter, James, and John become leaders of the circumcised people, while Paul and Barnabas are sent to the Gentiles; separated in place, not in spirit, they stand under one Lord in different battle-lines, dividing his churches among themselves throughout the whole world. And why shall he divide these spoils? Because he delivered his soul to death. “For he came not to be served but to serve, and [Col. 0496D] to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matt. 20:28).

“And he was reckoned with criminals.”

That is, he was crucified among thieves. For Mark writes: “They crucified with him two thieves, one on the right and the other on the left, and the Scripture was fulfilled which says: He was numbered with the wicked” (Mark 15:25). It follows:

“And he himself bore the sin”  
[Note: [Col. 0496D] Elsewhere: “sins.”]  
“of many, and prayed for transgressors.”

He bore the sin of many, because he is the Lamb who, having been sacrificed, bore the sin of the world; and he prayed for transgressors, because while he was being crucified he said: [Col. 0497A] “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). It follows.

## CHAPTER LIV

VERSE 1.—“Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; sing praise and neigh aloud, you who did not give birth, because the children of the forsaken woman are more numerous than those of her who had a husband, says the Lord.”

After speaking of the head, he addresses the body. For up to this point he has set forth the oracle concerning the Lord’s humility and passion; now he shows how, from the one who died for all, a multitude of believers was to arise throughout the breadth of the world. “Rejoice,” he says, “O barren Church, you who do not bear; sing praise,” that is, preach; “neigh aloud,” that is, rejoice exultantly, “you who did not give birth, because now the children of the Church [Col. 0497B] once forsaken will be far more numerous than those of the Synagogue, which was joined to a husband.” For many years the Church that was to exist among all nations did not appear in her children—that is, in her saints. But now the children of the forsaken woman are said to be more numerous than those of her who had a husband.

By the name “husband” is signified the Law or the king received by the first people, Israel. The Gentiles had received no Law when the prophet spoke, nor had the king of Christians yet appeared; yet from these nations comes a far more fruitful and more numerous multitude of saints. Therefore the Church, spread among the nations, once barren but now more fruitful in many children than the Synagogue which had received the Law or king as a husband, rejoices. Hence it is added:

[Col. 0497C] VERSE 2.—“Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out the skins of your tabernacles; spare not; make your cords long and strengthen your pegs.”

For the Church enlarges the place of its tent, occupying all nations and languages, so that it may extend farther than the boundaries of the Roman empire and stretch its cords even to Persians, Indians, and other barbarian peoples. The Church’s tent may be understood as the present Church on the journey of this life; its tabernacles are the many churches which together make the one Catholic Church. For one who is in a tent does not possess a fixed and permanent dwelling, but continually changes [Col. 0497D] places and hastens toward others, forgetting what lies behind, until reaching the prize of the heavenly calling. The end of the tabernacles is possession of the eternal dwelling. The skins of the tabernacles are the saints, who mortify the vices within themselves in the churches. These skins are spread out without restraint when the elect are dispersed in every direction throughout the whole breadth of the world to preach. Its cords are its commandments, which are made long when extended to distant barbarian nations. Its pegs are its words, strengthened when its preaching is firmly established by authority or made steadfast by the assertion of truth.

Or it should be said that God called all nations in the sons of Noah, but afterward chose Abraham and left the multitude of the Gentiles. Thus Gentile peoples, [Col. 0498A] long remaining widowed and bearing the shame of having been abandoned by their lawful husband, are brought back to their former husband by the apostles’ preaching. They receive such great grace that they consign all their former shame to oblivion and no longer remember the reproach of their widowhood, because they have cast off the dominion of demons and render devout service to their Creator. It follows.

VERSE 3.—“For you shall break forth to the right and to the left, and your seed shall inherit nations and inhabit deserted cities.”

As the multitude of Gentiles enters, the holy Church breaks forth into the regions of unbelievers, to the right and to the left, because it gradually spreads in every direction through the whole world among unbelievers. Or it breaks forth to the right when it reaches those who are to be justified. It also breaks forth [Col. 0498B] to the left when it admits to itself some who will remain in wickedness. Thus it extends to the right through true Christians and to the left through false Christians among so many peoples; its seed inherits nations and inhabits cities deserted from the true worship of God and true religion. Since, scattered everywhere throughout the world among unbelievers, it endured many persecutions and reproaches, the following is fittingly added:

VERSE 4.—“Do not fear, for you shall not be confounded, nor be ashamed.”

For it did not fear human threats and rage when it was clothed, as it were, in the purple adornment of martyrs’ blood, prevailing over so many, such vehement, and such powerful persecutors. And [Col. 0498C] now it is neither put to shame nor confounded, because it is now glorified by all peoples, though formerly mocked by all, when becoming or being a Christian was considered a great crime. It follows:

“For you shall not be ashamed, because you shall forget the shame of your youth and shall remember no longer the reproach of your widowhood.”

It is not now ashamed that it was once detestable. At the time when the Lord lived upon earth, it was little, because newly born, and because of its weakness it could not yet preach the word. But it became a young woman in the time of the apostles, when, united to God’s word through the ministry of preaching, it began to conceive children. A young woman, certainly—not made old by sin, but renewed by grace; not barren through age, but suited by the age of its mind for spiritual fruitfulness. Since it is spiritually united to Christ, it is called a widow when he died. In this youth [Col. 0498D] it endured shame, because in its earliest times, as has been said, it was mocked everywhere, and it bore the reproach of its widowhood while unbelievers reproached it with Christ’s death. But now it has forgotten the shame of its youth and no longer remembers the reproach of its widowhood, because, though briefly forsaken and subjected to reproaches, it blooms anew in surpassing glory. It follows:

VERSE 5.—“For he who made you shall rule over you; the Lord of hosts is his name.”

[Col. 0499A] For a long time now persecutors and unbelievers have ceased to rule over the Church; its Creator alone rules it. It follows:

“And your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel, shall be called the God of the whole earth.” The Redeemer of the Church, once called the Holy One of Israel, known and worshipped only in Judaea, is now called the God of the whole earth, because “he has been exalted above all the heavens, and his glory above all the earth” (Ps. 56:12; 107:6). It follows:

VERSE 6.—“For as a woman forsaken and grieved in spirit the Lord has called you, and as a wife rejected from youth, says your God.”

The Church has been left bodily by Christ as a woman by her husband, [Col. 0499B] and therefore is afflicted with grief of mind, as he himself foretold, saying: “Can the sons of the bridegroom fast while the bridegroom is with them? But days will come when the bridegroom is taken from them, and then they will fast” (Matt. 9:15). The apostles could neither fast nor mourn while Christ was with them, because they rejoiced that God dwelt bodily among them. But after Christ went to heaven, the saints began to fast and weep, and remain in this affliction until he returns. This, then, is why he calls the Church a woman forsaken and grieved in spirit.

It is also compared to a wife rejected from youth, because when Christ, its bridegroom and husband, ascended to heaven, it remained among the miseries of the world from its earliest [Col. 0499C] times. Or: through the apostles the Lord called Gentile peoples to himself as a forsaken woman and a wife rejected from youth, because he has now reconciled to himself the people he had abandoned in Abraham’s time. It follows:

VERSE 7.—“For a moment, for a little while, I forsook you; but with great mercies I shall gather you.”

A point is raised as soon as the stylus is placed upon it, and no delay occurs as a line is drawn out. The tribulation of the elect is therefore like a point, because it appears for a moment but disappears forever. And just as the stylus is raised when it is set down as a point, so each elect person, when he encounters the affliction of this present life, loses it. For the entire length [Col. 0499D] of this present life is known to be a point when it is bounded by its end. For when anyone comes to the end, he possesses nothing any longer from the past, because all times have passed away; he possesses nothing from the future, because not even the moments of one hour remain. Therefore life, which can be narrowed in this way, is a point.

Because almighty God permits either the Church or any one of the elect to be afflicted in the shortness of this life, he rightly says to it: “For a moment, for a little while, I forsook you.” For those whom he loves eternally he is accustomed to leave for a time. Thus the Psalmist prays: “Do not forsake me utterly” (Ps. 118:8). He knew that he could beneficially be forsaken for a little while, and therefore prayed that he might not be forsaken utterly. The Lord aids [Col. 0500A] his saints by coming, tests them by leaving them, strengthens them by gifts, and examines them by tribulations.

Whether, then, any elect person or the Church is subject to tribulations for a long or short time, it is fittingly said: “For a moment, for a little while, I forsook you.” And because afterward it will be gathered into the fellowship of the blessed, so that for temporal labor it may find everlasting rest, he beautifully adds: “But with great mercies I shall gather you.” Yet the words, “For a moment, for a little while, I forsook you,” should be understood particularly of the period when the Church formerly endured persecutions; and the addition, “But with great mercies I shall gather you,” of the time of peace, when the saints whom unbelievers had scattered were gathered, and gathered all the remnants of the nations into the faith, so that no one remained to stir up persecution against the Church. This interpretation is immediately confirmed by what follows:

VERSE 8.—“In a moment of my indignation I hid my face from you briefly, but in everlasting mercy I have had compassion on you, says the Lord, your Redeemer.”

He calls that period of persecutions a moment of his indignation. During it he briefly hid his face—that is, the regard of his favor, help, and grace—from the Church, when he left it for a time to be tested by tribulations. But afterward he had compassion on it in everlasting mercy, because he granted it peace until [Col. 0500C] the end of the age; when that age is completed, it will receive everlasting tranquility.

But if you understand the moment of divine indignation as either the entire span of this present life or every period in which each person is tempted, the Lord hides his face in this moment from each of the elect, because in providential ordering he leaves that person for a time in tribulations. But afterward the Lord, his Redeemer, has compassion upon him in everlasting mercy, because “when he has been tested, he shall receive the crown of life” (Jas. 1:12). Or the Lord left the multitude of Gentiles for a moment, for a little while—that is, from Abraham until the Savior’s advent—because all time is little and like a point in comparison with eternity. [Col. 0500D] But through the apostles the whole world was gathered into faith. For the period in which God, in just judgment, hid his face from the nations was a moment; afterward he bestowed everlasting mercy upon them. It follows:

VERSE 9.—“This is to me as in the days of Noah, when I swore that I would no longer bring waters upon the earth; so I have sworn that I shall not be angry with you or rebuke you.”

Just as after the flood the Lord swore to Noah that he would no longer bring the waters of the flood upon the earth (Gen. 9:11), so after the afflictions of this life he swears to each of the righteous that he will no longer be angry with or rebuke that person. For now he mercifully rebukes his own, saying: “Those whom I love I rebuke and chastise” [Col. 0501A] (Rev. 3:19). But after this life he will neither be angry with them nor rebuke them. For he says: “Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life” (John 5:24). This, therefore, is what he now says: “I have sworn that I shall not be angry with you or rebuke you.”

Or, just as the Lord swore to his servant Noah that he would no longer bring flood-waters upon the earth, so after the times of the martyrs he swore to the Church that he would no longer be angry with it—that is, he would no longer cause it to feel the anger of persecutors—and would not rebuke it—that is, would not allow it to be rebuked by enemies. This statement makes sufficiently clear that the ark signified the Church and the flood the Church’s tribulations. Therefore, as there will no longer be a flood [Col. 0501B] devastating the earth, so there will be no general persecution of the saints until the time of Antichrist, when the world also will end. For the following words declare that enduring peace will be with it:

VERSE 10.—“For mountains shall be moved and hills shall tremble; but my mercy shall not depart, and the covenant of my peace shall not be moved, says the Lord who has compassion on you.”

VERSE 11.—“Poor little one, shaken by the storm, without any consolation.”

“It is easier,” he says, “for mountains and hills to be moved than for my decree to be changed.” The Church from the Gentiles is called “poor little one,” because it did not possess the Law, [Col. 0501C] prophets, or the word of the Lord. It was shaken by a storm because it had endured many worldly tempests, wavered amid the various errors of idols, and had no consolation. Or mountains and hills signify kings and rulers, who, finally discovering the truth, were moved in heart to repentance and trembled before God’s judgment.

God’s divine mercy, because it spares it tribulations, does not depart from it, and the covenant of peace is not moved, but endures with it until the kingdom of Antichrist. For this poor little one—that is, the humble and poor Church—was tossed by the storm of tribulations and shaken from its places, fleeing its persecutors as an exile and wanderer; it found no consolation in the world. Paul says to the Corinthians concerning the sort of storm that tossed this poor little one [Col. 0501D] without consolation: “We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of our tribulation which occurred in Asia: we were burdened beyond measure, beyond our strength, so that we even despaired of life. But we had within ourselves the answer of death, so that we might not trust in ourselves but in God, who raises the dead, who delivered us from such great dangers” (2 Cor. 1:8). This poor little one afterward endured many such and still harsher storms, until it pleased God to moderate the waves of this world and calm its tempests, so that by a now tranquil voyage our poor little one might reach the harbor of everlasting salvation. Therefore, with the coming of peace, he adds:

[Col. 0502A] “Behold, I shall lay your stones in order and found you upon sapphires.”

VERSE 12.—“And I shall make your battlements of jasper, your gates of carved stones, and all your boundaries of precious stones.”

VERSE 13.—“All your children taught by the Lord, and an abundance of peace for your children.”

VERSE 14.—“And you shall be founded in righteousness.”

For the Lord has laid stones in order in the Church, because he distinguished holy souls within it by the diversity of their merits. He founded it upon sapphires, stones which bear in themselves the likeness of an airy-blue color, because the Church’s strength is made firm in souls seeking heavenly things. And since jasper is green in color, he made its battlements jasper, because those placed as a defense [Col. 0502B] of the holy Church against adversaries flourish in inward desires and do not wither through any aridity of reprobate lukewarmness.

He made its gates carved stones. These indeed are the Church’s gates, through whose life and teaching a multitude of nations enters it. Because they are strong in great works and demonstrate in life what they affirm in speech, they are called not plain but carved stones. For in the life of those whose upright action is seen, what they have done is, as it were, impressed upon them. Then, embracing the whole number of saints in a general collection, he adds: “All your boundaries [shall be] precious stones.” And as though we who hear this were asking him to identify the stones of which he spoke, [Col. 0502C] he adds: “All your children taught by the Lord.” For the Church’s children, whom the inward anointing of the Holy Spirit teaches concerning all things, are the precious stones which angels desire to place in the building of the heavenly city. To them he promises that he will give an abundance of peace, and he declares that the Church itself is founded in righteousness, so that it may stand firm in righteousness. Almost all these things indeed existed in the Church during the time of persecution, but much more abundantly and honorably in the time of peace; and therefore these too are promised among the promises of peace. It follows:

“Withdraw far from calumny, for you shall not fear; and from terror, for it shall not come near you.”

Withdraw from the calumny which unbelievers inflicted upon you, and from fear of their rage. Or, if you do not wish to fear enemies, [Col. 0502D] withdraw from calumny, so that you may bring calumny against no one and may not desire unjustly to take anyone’s property; for then you will be safe and without fear. For if you wish to cast off terror, it shall not approach you, because the Lord will protect you and make you secure. It follows:

VERSE 15.—“Behold, a sojourner shall come, one who was not with me; your former stranger shall be joined to you.”

Peace having been granted, a sojourner comes to me through faith—that is, every Gentile, who lived as a stranger in the regions of the faithful and was not with me but with the devil. And one who was formerly your stranger shall now be joined to you, O Church, and shall become your citizen and native inhabitant. This is said of the remnants of unbelievers [Col. 0503A] who, after peace was established everywhere, were converted.

VERSE 16.—“Behold, I created the smith who blows coals in the fire and brings forth an implement for his work. And I created the destroyer to destroy.”

VERSE 17.—“No instrument fashioned against you shall prosper, and every tongue resisting you in judgment you shall judge.”

Who is this smith except Satan, who does not cease, insofar as he can, to fashion evils against the good? God created him in his essential being. He blows coals in the fire because he incites human minds with the burning heat of perverse desires. Hence elsewhere the Lord says concerning him: “His breath makes coals burn” (Job 41:17). What does he call coals except [Col. 0503B] the kindled inward thoughts or desires of reprobate minds? A coal is called *pruna* while it burns, but once extinguished it is called *carbo*. *Pruna* is so called from burning through; *carbo*, because it lacks flame. Understand, therefore, the coals as minds burned by their own desires, and the breath or blowing of the ancient enemy as his hidden instigation. Thus his breath makes coals burn because his persuasion inflames much more intensely with worldly desires the minds of the wicked, already kindled in themselves. For they burn when they desire any temporal thing, because they are consumed by desires which do not allow the mind to remain calm and whole. Therefore he blows coals in the fire, because by his suggestion [Col. 0503C] he touches reprobate minds and fiercely kindles them with the fire of desires. Or he kindles them also against the good; and thus, by blowing, fashions and brings forth an instrument of iniquity for his work, because he does not cease to breathe his instigation into the heart of one whom he deceives until he makes that person an instrument of his malice and brings him to the practice of perversity. Thus this smith fashioned and brought forth for the work of his iniquity the instruments of which the Apostle speaks, saying that God “endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction” (Rom. 9:22).

Against this smith the destroyer was created, to destroy the instruments of iniquity. And who is this except our Lord, who “will slay the wicked one with the spirit of his lips” (2 Thess. 2:8)? He was created according to his humanity, [Col. 0503D] and was created to destroy every instrument of the most evil smith, because “the Lord preserves all who love him, and will destroy all sinners” (Ps. 144:20). God created him to destroy the wicked because “he gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5:27).—“For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (ibid., 22). Therefore he says: “Behold, I created the smith who blows coals in the fire and brings forth an instrument for his work; and I created the destroyer to destroy.” That is: I created the first angel, who, after beginning to work iniquity, does not cease to incite human minds until he accomplishes the evils which he suggests; and against him I caused my Son to assume flesh, so that by dying [Col. 0504A] he might destroy him and undo his works. The following statement shows that this is so.

“Every instrument,” he says, “which has been fashioned against you shall not prosper”—that is, every person made against you; thus the evil smith fashioned his instruments against the Church. “And every tongue,” he says, “which resists you by contradicting your teaching, you shall judge in judgment,” because from the remnants of the nations which have not believed you shall judge as you will. You shall condemn heretics by anathematizing them. Or in the future judgment you shall judge all who contradict you. Hence it is added:

“This is the inheritance of the servants of the Lord, and their righteousness is from me, says the Lord.”

For this is the inheritance and righteousness of the Lord’s servants: that in the future judgment [Col. 0504B] they shall judge every tongue now resisting them. Finally, he calls all nations to the streams of sacred utterance, saying:

## CHAPTER LV

VERSE 1.—“All who thirst, come to the waters; and you who have no silver, hasten, buy, and eat.”

The Gentiles thirsted, desiring the drink of heavenly preaching. By the name of waters is signified the knowledge of sacred Scripture, which is accustomed both to wash its hearers from the filth of sins and to give them drink from the fountain of divine knowledge. Hence it is written: “He gave him to drink of the water of saving wisdom” (Ecclus. 15:3). By the designation of silver are signified the divine utterances, as the Psalmist testifies, saying: “The words [Col. 0504C] of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire” (Ps. 11:7). Therefore those who have no silver are called to the waters, because the Gentiles, who had not received the precepts of sacred Scripture, are satisfied by the flood of sacred speech. They drink it now with so much greater eagerness because they had thirsted for it, dry, for so long. Nor do they merely drink it; they also eat it. For sacred Scripture is drink in its clearer passages, since it is absorbed as it is found; but it is food in its more obscure passages, because it is, as it were, broken by exposition and swallowed by chewing. It is bought without price by believers, who, when they willingly do the good things they know, are led to inward understanding. Thus the Psalmist had bought it by living well when he said: “From your commandments I have gained understanding” [Col. 0504D] (Ps. 118:104).

Or let us understand by those who thirst those “who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matt. 5:6), and by waters the infusion of spiritual graces. What, then, does he say: “All who thirst, come to the waters”? This is what he cries in the Gospel: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7:38). Thereupon the Evangelist immediately adds: “But he said this concerning the Spirit, which those who believed in him were going to receive” (ibid., 39). Therefore, when he says, “All who thirst, come to the waters,” he calls believers to spiritual gifts. And those who have no silver are ordered to hasten to them, because those who have wealth can enter the kingdom of God only with difficulty; and “Blessed are the poor in spirit, [Col. 0505A] for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). He calls them poor because “whoever has not renounced all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33). It follows:

“Come, buy wine and milk without silver and without any exchange.”

What does wine signify except the spiritual sense of divine Scripture, which gladdens believers’ minds and changes them through inebriation? Hence Proverbs says: “Give strong drink to those who mourn, and wine to those bitter of heart; let them drink and forget their need, and remember their pain no more” (Prov. 31:6). And what does the designation of milk signify except sweet and plain statements, by which the simple and little ones are nourished? Hence Peter says to them: [Col. 0505B] “Like newborn infants, desire rational, unadulterated milk, so that by it you may grow into salvation” (1 Pet. 2:2). Therefore he commands us to buy wine and milk without silver and without any exchange of price, yet nevertheless to buy them, because we acquire neither the strong nor the simple sense of Scripture with money, but by living well; we do not purchase it for a price, but attain it by the merit of a good life. Since he calls all to the newness of spiritual gifts, he consequently rebukes the Jews, who are unwilling to come to spiritual understanding, adding:

VERSE 2.—“Why do you weigh out silver for what is not bread, and your labor for what does not satisfy?”

For breads suitably signify the refreshment of sacred Scripture, because it is written: “He fed [Col. 0505C] him with the bread of life and understanding” (Ecclus. 15:3). Therefore he says to Jews who preserve the letter alone: “Why do you weigh out silver for what is not bread?” As though he said: You weigh sacred utterances, but not for refreshment; because, while preserving only the outward appearance of the letter, you lose the richness of inward refreshment found in spiritual understanding. Hence he fittingly adds: “And your labor for what does not satisfy?” For the knowledge which they labor to learn will never satisfy their minds, because “they are always learning and never able to come to the knowledge of truth” (2 Tim. 3:7). Likewise rebuked are those who follow worldly wisdom, the feigned teachings of heretics, and every falsely named knowledge; they weigh out silver of great price [Col. 0505D] and continuous labor for a discipline in which there is no bread, and sweat for foods in which there is no satisfaction. It is therefore clear that the wisdom to be pursued is not in the leaves and blossom of words, but in the marrow and fruits of meanings—not that which merely passes over the ear, but that which refreshes the mind. It follows:

“Hear me, you who hear, and eat what is good, and your soul shall delight in richness.”

“You,” he says, “O Jews, who hear me with the ear of the body, hear me with the ears of the heart; eat the good of spiritual meaning, and your soul shall delight in richness. For, abandoning the thinness of the letter, you shall grow rich through the grace of spiritual understanding, and be raised from earthly desires to the heights of heavenly love.” To preserve only the surface of the letter, or to set one’s thought upon what is low, is nothing other than a certain thinness of heart. But one who is fed by the food of inward delight through spiritual understanding or love of heavenly things grows fat, as it were, on more abundant nourishment. [Col. 0506A] The Psalmist desired to be filled with this richness when he said: “May my soul be filled as with fat and richness” (Ps. 62:6). He therefore rightly promises that the soul of those who eat the good of spiritual grace will delight in richness. In this richness delighted the soul of that holy multitude “of believers, whose heart was one and whose soul was one” (Acts 4:32). It follows.

VERSE 3.—“Incline your proud ear to my word, and come to me through him who says: ‘I am the way, the truth, and the life, and no one comes to the Father except through me’” (John 14:6). Hear him, obey him, and your soul shall live.

For he says: “Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life” (John 5:24). Or: hear me in all the commandments which I have now given you concerning the reception of the new order, and you shall live. It follows:

“And I shall make with you an everlasting covenant, the faithful mercies of David.”

“I shall make with you an everlasting covenant”—that is, I shall establish between myself and you the New Testament, which shall be eternal. And what covenant? “The faithful mercies of David”: that is, what I mercifully promised David, I, the most faithful guarantor, [Col. 0506C] shall most certainly fulfill for you—namely, that Christ should be born from his lineage. For I promised that I would faithfully perform these mercies for him, and I shall perform them also for you, if you hear me. This is the everlasting covenant or Testament which I shall make with you: I shall bring it about that through Christ the mediator you are reconciled to me and obtain eternal peace with me. For this is the New Testament, the evangelical Testament—namely, concerning Christ’s coming.

Paul, however, referred this to his resurrection, saying of the Father: “But that he raised him from the dead, no longer to return to corruption, he spoke thus: ‘I shall give you the holy and faithful things of David’” (Acts 13:34). He interpreted the holy things of David as the Savior’s resurrection, and called these holy things faithful because Christ would not return again to corruption. Likewise we call the mercies of David, as we read in the new translation, the Lord’s resurrection, and call them faithful because “Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more” (Rom. 6:9). And this is the everlasting testament concerning his death and resurrection, “because he is the mediator of the New Testament, so that, death intervening for the redemption of those transgressions which were under the former testament, those who are called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance. For where there is a testament, the death of the testator must intervene. For a testament is confirmed in the dead” (Heb. 9:15). Thus it is fittingly said concerning Christ’s incarnation or resurrection: [Col. 0507A] “I shall make with you an everlasting covenant,” or testament, “the faithful mercies of David.” Or, as the old translation reads: “I shall establish for you an eternal testament, the faithful holy things of David.” It follows:

VERSE 4.—“Behold, I have given him as a witness to peoples, a leader and teacher to nations.”

I have given my Christ as a witness to peoples, that he may bear witness to them concerning me and be witness and guarantor of all that I have promised, showing that I am faithful in my words. Or, I have given him as a witness to peoples, that he may see all that human beings now do or think and be witness and judge of all on the last day. I have given him as leader and teacher to nations, to lead them into the way and set before them the teaching of truth. Since this was to be done through [Col. 0507B] the ministry of the Church’s preaching, the address is rightly turned to it in what follows:

VERSE 5.—“Behold, you shall call a nation which you did not know, and nations which did not know you shall run to you because of the Lord your God and the Holy One of Israel, because he has glorified you.”

For she indeed called to the faith the foreign nation which you formerly did not know; and the nations that had not known her all ran to her, because they saw her so glorified by God that the whole world venerated her. But perhaps this utterance will seem rather to be addressed to Christ. For he too, through the apostles, called a nation which he did not know—that is, did not approve—of which he says through the Psalmist: “A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” [Col. 0507C] (Ps. XVII, 45). And all the nations which had not known him gathered to him from the whole world on account of his Lord, who is also the Holy One of Israel—that is, on account of his Father, who according to his humanity is his Lord and God—because he glorified him, “exalting him and giving him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II, 9). Therefore the prophet accordingly admonishes all mortals concerning this time of reconciliation and grace, saying:

VERSE 6.—“Seek the Lord while he can be found; call upon him while he is near.”

For the Lord has not yet appeared in judgment, and if he is sought, he is found. For, in a wondrous way, when he comes in judgment, he can both be seen and not be found. Now he is not seen, and he is near; then he will be seen, and he will not be near. Hence he says through Solomon concerning the reprobate: “Then they will call upon me, and I will not hear; they will rise early, and they will not find me” [Col. 0507D] (Prov. I, 28). Therefore he must now be sought while he is found, now called upon while he hears, since he is near. The prophet shows how he is to be sought and called upon, adding:

VERSE 7.—“Let the ungodly man forsake his way, and the unjust man his thoughts; and let him return to the Lord, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he is abundant in forgiveness.”

Let us all therefore follow the prophet’s counsel or admonition [Col. 0508A], so that whoever is ungodly may swiftly forsake his way—that is, the practice of his ungodliness—and whoever is unjust may as quickly as possible abandon not only deeds but also thoughts of iniquity, and return to the Lord with his whole heart. He will undoubtedly find mercy, because our God is abundant in forgiving those who repent. For he does not think as a human being does, so as to seek vengeance in remembrance of his injuries, even if those who wronged him should repent. For the text continues:

VERSE 8.—“For my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are my ways your ways, says the Lord.”

For divine thoughts are not like ours, because God thinks one way and man another. Nor are his ways—that is, his actions—your ways, because his goodness acts otherwise than the perversity of human hardness: he mercifully wipes away all the sins of those who repent. It follows:

VERSE 9.—“For as the heavens are exalted above the earth, so my ways are exalted above your ways, and my thoughts above your thoughts.”

As much as the heavens rise above the earth, so much, and more, do divine thoughts surpass human thoughts, and divine actions human actions. For human beings think and do transient, earthly things; God, however, eternal and heavenly things, whose thoughts and actions surpass every understanding. Thus the Apostle cries out in wonder: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways!” [Col. 0508C] (Rom. XI, 33). Let no one, therefore, attempt to examine why he forgives some and does not forgive others, because in his secret judgment he does all things: “He has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens” (Rom. IX, 18); and his thoughts are exalted above ours as the heavens above the earth. He also repeats the promise concerning the coming of his Only-begotten, adding:

VERSE 10.—“And just as rain and snow descend from heaven and do not return thither, but soak the earth and water it and cause it to sprout, and give seed to the sower and bread to the eater,”

VERSE 11.—“so shall my word be, which goes forth” [Col. 0508D] “from my mouth.”

The Son of God is the Word. He is called Word because, if a human word, conveyed into the ears of many, is not divided among individuals—so that one part belongs to one person and another part to another—but is possessed whole and complete by all who hear it, so that the whole is in each one: how much more is the Only-begotten Word of God wholly everywhere, in heaven and on earth, and not divided or made into parts, but wholly contains all things, fills all things, illumines all things, and possesses all things?

For the Word did not become flesh in such a way as to cease to be God, just as the word which we hold in the heart becomes a voice when we utter it with the mouth; yet the word is not converted into the voice. Rather, while it remains whole, that in which it may proceed is taken up, so that [Col. 0509A] what is understood remains within, while what is heard sounds without. Yet it brings forth in sound the same thing that before the sound was in silence. Thus, although a word becomes a voice, it is not changed into voice; rather, though it is a voice, it is not changed into a voice, but, remaining in the light of the mind and taking up the voice of flesh, it proceeds to the hearer and does not leave the thinker.

For when the very voice is thought in silence—whether it belongs to Greek, Latin, or any other language—the reality itself which was to be spoken is, before all diversity of languages, still in some manner bare to the understanding in the chamber of the heart; and, in order to proceed from there, it is clothed in the speaker’s voice. So too the Word of God went forth from his mouth when, taking flesh, he came to us; yet he remained in his heart, and was not changed into flesh, but remained the Word.

[Col. 0509B] He descended like rain and snow from heaven because he was sent not by human activity but by divine goodness. And just as rain does not return to heaven, but soaks, waters, and makes the earth fruitful, so the Son of God did not return empty to the Father. Rather, he accomplished on earth all things for which he had been sent, or still accomplishes them, remaining here with us in his divinity, as he promised: “Behold, I am with you always, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20).

For he drenches the earth—that is, the Church—with the flood of his knowledge, changing its heart so that it forgets temporal things and thinks on eternal things. He pours in the grace of his Spirit and makes it sprout—that is, produce good works. To the sower [Col. 0509C]—that is, the preacher—he also gives the seed of preaching; and to the eater—that is, the doer—he grants bread, that is, the good work by which he is fed. For to sow is to preach, and to eat is to do. Thus blessed Job says: “If my eye has followed my heart, and a stain has clung to my hands, let me sow and another eat” (Job XXXI, 7): that is, let me speak what is good, and another do it.

Therefore the supreme Father fittingly promised: “It shall not return to me empty.” For the Son did not return to him empty or void, but fulfilled all his will and prospered in those things for which he had been sent, as the Psalmist had foretold concerning him: “For whatever he does shall prosper” (Ps. I, 3). What those things are which the Father willed and for which he sent him, he himself declares [Col. 0509D] by adding:

VERSE 12.—“For you shall go forth in joy and be led forth in peace; the mountains and all the hills shall sing praise before you, and all the trees shall clap their hands.”

Christ came to us for this purpose: that, having bound the prince of this world, he might plunder the vessels of captivity and bring forth the bound from confinement, those sitting in darkness from the prison-house. “For how can anyone enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? Then he will plunder his house” (Matt. XII, 29). Christ was sent for these things and prospered in them, because he bound this strong man—that is, the devil—and, entering his house, that is, the Gentile world, he plundered his vessels: human beings who had become vessels of his wickedness, and converted them to his own worship.

Freed by Christ from this house of the strong man, this prison-house, we went forth in joy, because we were filled with great gladness when we understood that through Christ we had been freed from Satan’s bonds. And we were led forth in peace, our adversary who held us captive having been bound; and unless he had been bound, he would not have allowed us to be led forth in peace. So that we may not turn aside from the way of righteousness along which we are thus led, the mountains—that is, the apostles—and the hills—that is, the other teachers—sing before us the praise of preaching; and all the trees—that is, all the people of the land—clap their hands at the sound of the song: that is, they rejoice by doing good works. For those clap their hands at the sound of melody who willingly and eagerly do what they hear in sacred preaching.

[Col. 0510A] This may also have been promised to the saints who were held in hell: “You shall go forth in joy and be led forth in peace,” namely, into the kingdoms of heaven. It can also fittingly be said concerning those righteous persons who still live as pilgrims in the body, at their departure: “You shall go forth in joy from this life, and be led forth in peace by angels to the place of blessed dwelling.” And what follows suits both groups: namely, that the mountains and hills—that is, the angelic powers—will sing praise before you, and all the trees of the land—that is, all the inhabitants of that country—will clap their hands when they see you rejoicing in your fellowship.

For the sake of all these whom Christ thus causes to go forth and leads in peace, the Father had said concerning his Word: “It shall not return to me [Col. 0510C] empty, but shall do whatever I have willed and prosper in those things to which I sent it.” For he who brings so many with him to life and acts successfully in all these things does not return empty to the Father. The promise continues:

VERSE 13.—“In place of the saltwort the fir-tree shall rise, and in place of the nettle the myrtle shall grow.”

For in the Church the fir rises in place of the saltwort when, in the hearts of the saints, the height of heavenly contemplation springs up in place of the lowliness of earthly thought. The nettle is wholly of a fiery nature; the myrtle, however, is said to possess a moderating power. The myrtle grows in place of the nettle when the minds of the righteous pass from the itching and burning of vices to the moderation and tranquility [Col. 0510D] of their thoughts: when they no longer desire earthly things, when they quench the flames of the flesh by heavenly desires. It follows:

“And the Lord shall be named as an everlasting sign, which shall not be taken away.” The Lord who shall be named as an everlasting sign is the same as “the root of Jesse, who stands as a sign to the peoples” (above, XI, 10). For the sign that shall not be taken away is the sign of the Lord’s passion and cross, because the mark of the cross will appear forever in those redeemed through the cross; and the Redeemer himself willed that this same sign should appear in himself without end, because when he rose from the dead, he did not wish to erase the scars of his wounds. Therefore the Lord shall be named as an everlasting sign, because the saints will praise him endlessly for having endured the sufferings of the cross [Col. 0511A], when they see in his flesh the traces of his wounds. Concerning his first coming, the Father again makes a promise and commands the Jews to be ready to meet him. For it follows:

## CHAPTER LVI

VERSE 1.—“Thus says the Lord: Keep judgment and do righteousness, for my salvation is near to come, and my righteousness to be revealed.”

VERSE 2.—“Blessed is the man who does this, and the son of man who holds fast to it: keeping the Sabbath so as not to profane it, keeping his hands from doing every evil.”

“Keep judgment,” he says, “and do righteousness.” If anyone, before beginning any work, examines whether it will please God or not, [Col. 0511B] and, whenever he does not know that what he is about to do will be pleasing to God, immediately abandons it, that person keeps judgment and does righteousness. He therefore wishes the Hebrews to act thus while they await Christ. For he is the salvation and righteousness of God, who, according to the Apostle, “became for us wisdom from God, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption” (I Cor. I, 30). Or he calls “salvation” that which was to be given through Christ, and “righteousness” the righteousness of his faith which was to be revealed.

To what he had said, “Keep judgment and do righteousness,” he added: “Blessed is the man who does this, and the son of man who holds fast to it,” so that a person may not only do what is right but hold it firmly with a tight hand. He confirms this statement through the Psalmist: “Blessed are those who keep judgment and do righteousness [Col. 0511C] at all times” (Ps. CV, 3).

He keeps the Sabbath who, resting from the desire for worldly things, keeps his heart with all vigilance. For what is more laborious in this life than to burn with earthly desires? Or what here is more restful than to desire nothing of this world? Therefore, whoever awaits Christ should observe the Sabbath—that is, rest of mind—so that he may not be wearied in this life by any craving of carnal desires. For he profanes the Sabbath if, consenting to temptations, he defiles his mind with unclean desires. Therefore, let one who desires to be blessed keep the Sabbath so as not to profane it, because “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8). It follows:

[Col. 0511D] VERSE 3.—“And let not the son of the stranger who joins himself to the Lord say: ‘The Lord will surely separate me from his people.’ Nor let the eunuch say: ‘Behold, I am a dry tree.’”

The Gentile people was a stranger. “The son of the stranger who joins himself to the Lord” is the people who came to Christ from among the Gentiles, whom the Lord did not separate from his Israelite people but joined to them: “For he himself is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II, 14). The eunuch here is understood to be such as those of whom we read in the Gospel: “There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX, 12). Such eunuchs are forbidden to say, “Behold, I am a dry tree,” that is, an unfruitful man, because he ought to think not of carnal but spiritual fruitfulness. It follows:

VERSE 4.—“For thus says the Lord to the eunuchs: ‘Those who keep my Sabbaths and choose the things that I have willed and hold fast my covenant,’”

VERSE 5.—“‘I shall give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters; I shall give them an everlasting name which shall not perish.’”

Eunuchs are those who, suppressing the motions of the flesh, cut off within themselves the result of a wicked deed. They keep the divine Sabbaths who do not violate sacred rest, but rest from evil action and from the toil of carnal desires. Yet because it is not enough to abstain from evils unless one also strives to do good, the things which the Lord has willed must be chosen. He also makes a covenant with the one who, agreeing with his will, promises him obedience [Col. 0512B]. This covenant must therefore be held perseveringly until the end.

Or such a eunuch keeps the Sabbaths by never performing the works of marriage; and he chooses what the Lord willed in order to offer more than is commanded, considering not the Apostle’s concession but the will of his Lord. And he holds his eternal covenant, so as not to devote himself to prayer merely for a time and then return again to the same thing. Therefore let eunuchs who keep God’s Sabbaths, have chosen what he willed, and hold his everlasting covenant hear the rewards they deserve, that they may gladly tread underfoot the labors of temptation which they endure. For if the happiness attained without passing away is considered, every hardship endured in passing through becomes light.

“I shall give them,” he says, “in my house and within my walls”—namely, in that heavenly royal court of mine—a place of chosen dwelling and a name better than my sons and daughters, because they shall have greater glory than the other saints. The place such eunuchs—that is, virgins—hold with the Father is thus shown, because in the Father’s house, that is, in the eternal dwelling, they are preferred even to sons. Likewise the book of Wisdom says: “The eunuch who has not wrought iniquity with his hands, nor thought most wicked things against God, shall be given a chosen gift of faith and a most acceptable portion in the temple of the Lord” [Col. 0512C] (Wis. III, 14). And because “incorruption makes one near to God” (Wis. VI, 20), virgins are far preferred to the other saints, since they draw nearer to God than others and follow the Lamb wherever he goes. To them an everlasting name is given which shall not perish, so that they may possess in that kingdom the name of eternal praise and shine forth, distinguished and illustrious above the rest. It follows:

VERSE 6.—“And the sons of the stranger who join themselves to the Lord, to worship him and love his name, to be his servants; everyone who keeps the Sabbath so as not to profane it and holds fast my covenant,”

VERSE 7.—“I shall bring them to my holy mountain and make them joyful in my house of prayer.”

By “sons of the stranger who join themselves to the Lord” he means those who have been converted to the faith from the Gentile people. For they worship him, love his name, and are [Col. 0513A] his servants, because they serve him with complete devotion. They too keep the Sabbath so as not to profane it. For servile work is forbidden on the Sabbath, and sin is servile work: “Everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John VIII, 34). Therefore the Sabbath must always be kept, because one must always cease from the action of sin and take care that it is not profaned. For he profanes the Sabbath who, after renouncing evil works, again commits the evil from which he ought always to rest. We keep the Sabbath when we rest in mind from the desire for temporal things.

The covenant which we have made with God must likewise be kept, lest we be separated from agreement with him and begin by wicked works to rebel against him with whom, by consenting to him, we made peace and covenant. Therefore, these sons of the stranger, who join themselves to the Lord, keep the spiritual Sabbath, and hold his covenant, he himself brought to his holy mountain—that is, into the Church—so that those who were far off might become near in the blood of Christ. Or he will bring them to his holy mountain, that is, into the kingdom of heaven. And he makes them joyful in his house of prayer, saying through the Apostle: “Rejoice always; pray without ceasing” [Col. 0513B] (I Thess. V, 16).

For the Church will be called a house of prayer, not a house of frivolity; therefore whoever is in the Church should abandon tales and idle words. Wherever a Christian may be present in body, he should always strive to pray—if not always with the mouth, yet with the heart. It follows:

“Their burnt offerings and their sacrifices shall be pleasing [Col. 0513C] to me upon my altar.”

Since a burnt offering is called an offering wholly burned, what is signified by the burnt offering of the sons of the stranger except the burning of heart in converted Gentiles? They were so wholly inflamed with the most vehement fire of love that they left nothing of themselves for themselves, but offered themselves wholly and entirely to God. And what is signified by their sacrifices except the mortification of their flesh? “For those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. V, 24). And what is expressed by the altar except faith? Therefore, according to this sense, it is rightly said: “Their burnt offerings and their sacrifices shall be pleasing to me upon my altar.”

Eunuchs offer burnt offerings, because they consecrate themselves wholly [Col. 0513D] to God; the rest offer sacrifices, because they devote themselves to prayer for a time. These are offered upon the altar which is in heaven, after the likeness of which Moses made the altar of the tabernacle. It follows:

“For my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples,”

VERSE 8.—“says the Lord, who gathers the scattered of Israel.”

The house of God is the Catholic Church, because according to the Apostle, “Christ is as a son over his own house, whose house we are” (Heb. III, 6). And this house is called a house of prayer for all peoples: all nations are to come to it from afar and, bringing gifts, worship the Lord within it. For the Lord gathers to it the scattered of Israel—that is [Col. 0514A], the scattered members of his people, namely all whom he predestined to life, who are scattered throughout the world or amid various errors. It follows:

“I shall yet gather to him his gathered ones.”

The Lord will yet gather to his people those who are already gathered in the unity of faith and love, as each departs from this life; for “many shall come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VIII, 2). And because “the children of the kingdom,” that is, the Jews, “shall be cast into outer darkness” (ibid., 12), the following is fittingly added here:

VERSE 9.—“All beasts of the field, come to devour; all beasts of the forest.”

For after he has joined the sons of the stranger—that is, believers from among the Gentiles—to his people, and brought them to his holy mountain, making them joyful in his house of prayer, he consequently hands unbelieving Jews over to demons to be devoured. “Come to devour,” he says, “all beasts of the field,” that is, all cruel demons who wander with savage fury through the expanse of this world, seeking whom you may devour; for the field is the world. “And all beasts of the forest,” that is, all evil spirits who are accustomed to dwell among the pagan people. And why this flock of the Jewish people was especially to be devoured by beasts of this kind is shown when he immediately adds:

VERSE 10.—“His watchmen are all blind; all are dumb dogs, unable to bark.”

[Col. 0514C] Priests are called watchmen, because, set in a more elevated place, they ought with vigilant care to see clearly and foresee from afar the coming of spiritual enemies, and warn those subject to them. But all the watchmen of Judaea are blind guides of the blind. They all lack knowledge, because they have lost the understanding of the Scriptures and have not known Christ. Preachers are also called dogs, because they have charge of the Lord’s sheep and, as they keep watch day and night for their Lord, they give, so to speak, the barks of preaching. But all the dogs of the Jewish nation are mute and unable to bark, because they cannot withstand the invisible beasts devouring their flock, nor raise the voice of preaching against their snares. Of them it is further said:

“Seeing vain things, sleeping and loving dreams.”

They see vain things because they consider a carnal meaning in the Scriptures and look in them at things which profit nothing, such as Sabbath rest, circumcision made by hand in the flesh, and other things of this kind which are shadows of things to come. They also sleep in negligence and in the night of their heart, and love dreams, never wishing to shake off their torpor so as to awaken to the light of truth, but always seeking to behold the phantasms of the opinions of their own interpretation as though they were nocturnal dream-visions. They also delight in the visions of demons in sleep. It follows:

[Col. 0515A] VERSE 11.—“And the most shameless dogs have known no satiety.”

As greedy dogs are always ready to eat without any shame, so those whom he describes under the figure of dogs do not keep watch against the assaults of beasts for their flock, but shamelessly seek to feed the hunger of their covetousness upon temporal profits. Yet they cannot satisfy it and are never sated with their error. But what he spoke under the metaphor of watchmen and dogs, he now begins to explain, adding:

“They themselves are shepherds who have not known understanding; they have all turned aside to their own way, every one to his own greed, from the highest even to the last.”

VERSE 12.—“Come, let us take wine and be filled [Col. 0515B] with drunkenness; and as today, so tomorrow shall be, and much more besides.”

What he had said, “His watchmen are blind,” he now explains by saying, “They themselves are shepherds who have not known understanding.” And what he had asserted—that the most shameless dogs had known no satiety—he interprets by saying that all have turned aside to their own way, each to his own greed. For shepherds are those who have undertaken the office of feeding human minds by the word of preaching. Thus the Lord promised us through Jeremiah: “I shall give you shepherds according to my heart, who shall feed you with knowledge and teaching” (Jer. III, 15).

But the shepherds of the Jews did not know the understanding of sacred speech, [Col. 0515C] because they did not come to him who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens; who, rising after trampling down death, opened the understanding of his disciples so that they might understand the Scriptures. They all turned aside to their own way, each seeking his own advantage; and everyone, from the first to the last among them, turned aside to his own greed. Thus having turned aside, they said to one another:

“Come, let us take wine and be filled with drunkenness; and as well as things are with us today, so they shall be tomorrow, and much more besides.”

For they knew no satiety: they are not satisfied with past pleasure but prepare delights to come, much greater than those which they had enjoyed before. For such things delighted the priests of the Jews, and in such things they wish to occupy themselves: “For they love the first places at feasts and the chief seats in synagogues” [Col. 0515D] (Matt. XXIII, 16). Hence they intoxicate themselves not only with bodily wine but with spiritual wine, that is, worldly covetousness and the desire for empty glory. For a person is spiritually drunk when he is alienated from rational understanding.

Such people therefore urge one another to drink this wine day after day and to be filled with drunkenness, while they corrupt in themselves and in one another the sense of righteousness, and mutually hand down this example: that they wish to walk in robes, love greetings in the marketplace, and devour widows’ houses while making a pretense of long prayer (Matt. VII, 14). For what else is desiring such things but drunkenness of mind? It follows:

## CHAPTER LVII

[Col. 0516A]

VERSE 1.—“The righteous person perishes, and there is no one who lays it to heart; men of mercy are gathered away, because there is no one who understands: the righteous person has been taken away from before evil.”

VERSE 2.—“Let peace come; let him rest in his bed, he who walked in his uprightness.”

The Lord Jesus, indicating the place of his passion, says that “it cannot be that a prophet should perish outside Jerusalem” (Luke XIII, 33). Likewise, what is said here, that the righteous person perishes, is as though it said that Christ dies. Therefore the righteous one perishes among the other watchmen because Christ dies among scribes and priests; and none of them lays it to heart, because they did not repent even afterward. And men of mercy—that is, believers who had obtained mercy in Judaea—are gathered away from there and brought together into the kingdoms of heaven, because among the Jews there is no one who understands that they were placed among them for the purpose that the Jews might imitate their faith and manner of life.

For the righteous one was taken away from before evil: that is, Christ was removed lest he should see the evils of the age; or, on account of the wickedness of men, whose sins he bore, he ascended in victory. Let peace therefore come after the persecutions which this righteous one unjustly endured from them; let the righteous one rest in his bed, that is, in the dwelling of eternal rest—he who walked in his uprightness, that is, who conducted his life in rectitude.

These things may also be understood of certain persons who are called by the Christian name. “All beasts of the field, come to devour; all beasts of the forest” [Col. 0516C] (above, LVI, 9). By the beasts of the field are expressed the vices of the age; by the beasts of the forest, the iniquities of pagans. Therefore the Lord calls all beasts of the field and all beasts of the forest to devour all those against whom he is vehemently angry, because in his just judgment he permits all worldly vices and all pagan crimes to rush upon certain people who are called Christians, so that they may live after the manner of secular persons and Gentiles. This is what he says: “Now I will show you what I shall do to my vineyard: I shall take away its hedge, and it shall be trampled down; I shall tear down its wall, and it shall be plundered” (above, V, 5).

This people or flock is easily devoured because “all its watchmen are blind and lack knowledge, and all its dogs are mute, unable to bark” [Col. 0516D] (above, LVI, 10). This is said only of unfit and reprobate priests, who are also called hirelings. Thus the watchmen of the Lord’s vineyard or house are blind and ignorant, because priests indeed abound among God’s people, but scarcely can anyone among them all be found who knows how to foresee coming temptations and announce them to those subject to him. They are mute dogs, unable to bark, because those who ought to keep the flock, drive away wolves, and bark for the Lord have fallen silent because they lack the knowledge of preaching. Yet even if one of them is learned in the Scriptures, the perversity of his own conduct prevents him from being able freely to speak [Col. 0517A] the good things that he knows and to bark against the coming of the beasts, that is, against the assaults of vices.

They are those “seeing vain things, sleeping and loving dreams” (ibid.). For all temporal things are vain, since they swiftly vanish and tend toward nothingness. Hence it is written: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccl. I, 2). Thus evil watchmen and lazy dogs see vain things. Therefore they sleep in this world and do not open their eyes to divine mysteries or to guarding the flock. But loving dreams—that is, the things possessed in the present life as though in dreams—they cannot satisfy their hungry gluttony. For concerning such sleepers, who do not know satiety, it was said above: “As a hungry man dreams and eats, but when he has awakened [Col. 0517B] his soul is empty; and as a thirsty man dreams and drinks, but after he has awakened he is still weary and thirsty, and his soul is empty: so shall be the multitude of all who fought against Mount Zion” (above, XXIX, 8).

For useless priests fight against Mount Zion because they attack the Church’s religion by their character and deeds, and persecute the good. Therefore they love dreams, that is, the honors and riches of this age. For all the power and glory of this world is a dream, not reality. And they eat because they delight in temporal goods. Yet they know no satiety because worldly wealth can never fill the poverty of the human mind.

Or they are said not to know satiety in order to show their insatiable greed, because, like “the most shameless dogs,” they always seek to devour whatever goods are given to them. And the flock of Christian people is so unlearned that the shepherds themselves lack understanding. For scarcely can a shepherd of the Church now be found who had understanding of the holy Scriptures; instead, “they have all turned aside to their own way, every one to his own greed” [Col. 0517C] (above, LVI, 11). “For all seek their own things, not those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. II, 21). Because they have turned aside from the way of God and followed their own paths, they burn with greed. And they do this from the chief pontiff down to the lowest overseer of the Church.

They also urge one another to drink the wine of worldly covetousness and become intoxicated with outward concerns, so that they may not think of spiritual and inward matters. Against this it is said in Proverbs: “Do not give wine to kings, because there is no secret where drunkenness rules” [Col. 0517D] (Prov. XXXI, 4). For kings are rulers of the Church, who ought not to drink such wine, lest, intoxicated by worldly cares, they lose the inward secret of the mind.

Or this passage censures the immoderate and frequent banquets of priests, who strike their fellow-servants and eat and drink with drunkards. But while these drink and become ever more intoxicated from day to day, any righteous person perishes—that is, dies in affliction—and there is none among them who lays this to heart, pondering his glory in mind and wishing to imitate his ways. Peter to Gregory (*Dialogues*, book III, ch. 37) [Col. 0518A]: “What, I ask, do you suppose yourself to be, when good people are taken away, and those who could live for the edification of many either cannot be found at all or certainly become altogether scarce?” Gregory replies: “The wickedness of those who remain deserves that those who could be of benefit should swiftly be taken away. And as the end of the world approaches, the elect are removed so that they may not see worse things. Hence it is written: ‘Open the way, that those who trample it may go out; remove the stones from the way’ (Jer. L, 26). Therefore, as the end of the world presses on, it is necessary that living stones be gathered for the heavenly building, so that our Jerusalem may grow to the full measure of all its construction. Yet we do not believe that the elect are taken away in such a fashion that only the wicked remain, because sinners would never return to the lament of repentance [Col. 0518B] if there were no examples of the good to draw their minds.”

But where there is no one to imitate them, there is good reason to believe that they are more swiftly removed from the midst of evils. For the prophet indicates this reason for their removal when he says: “The righteous person perishes, and there is no one who lays it to heart; men of mercy are gathered away, because there is no one who understands.” Thus, while the wicked desire only temporal things and disdain to know what eternal goods await the elect; while they see the affliction of the righteous and do not recognize what recompense belongs to affliction, they extend the foot of their conduct into the abyss, because they voluntarily close their eyes to the light of understanding.

For the righteous person has been taken away from before evil, because he has been snatched away lest wickedness should alter his understanding [Col. 0518C] or deceit deceive his soul. Let peace therefore come swiftly to the righteous person drawn out from the midst of iniquities, so that he may rest in his bed—that is, in the dwelling prepared for him by God—he who did not follow the crookedness of human perversity, but walked in his uprightness.

VERS. 3. — “But you,” who are unwilling to reflect upon him, “come here” for judgment, that you may receive what is just, “O sons of a sorceress, offspring of an adulterer and a prostitute.”

For that people was a sorceress to whom Paul said: “How is it that you turn again to the weak and beggarly elements, to which you wish once more to be enslaved? You observe days and months and seasons and years” (Gal. 4:9). [Col. 0518D] It was also a prostitute, having turned aside into errors after the faith. By its perverse doctrines it bore most wicked children, that is, heretics, from an adulterous father, namely the devil. To them it is fittingly said:

VERS. 4. — “At whom have you mocked? At whom have you opened your mouth wide and thrust out your tongue?”

For the heretics mocked the Lord whom they did not know; they opened their mouths wide and thrust out their tongues when they blasphemed him in many ways and raved against him in their utterances. What follows also applies to them:

“Are you not wicked children, a deceitful offspring?”
