VERS. 5. — “You who find comfort in gods beneath every leafy tree, sacrificing little children in the torrents beneath towering rocks?”

For those are transgressors who daily bring about the deaths of souls. They are a deceitful offspring who profess themselves Christians, yet fall away from all Christianity. But who are their gods except the errors which they serve? One kind of tree is fertile by richness of fruit; another merely abounds in leafy foliage. In groves and sacred woods no one plants a fig tree, a vine, or fruitful trees, but only leafy trees for pleasure. Such are heresiarchs, who compose their speech with verbal elegance, not in order to turn their hearers from vices, but to delight them. Those, therefore, who have subjected themselves to heresiarchs in order to worship their errors find comfort in gods beneath every leafy tree. They also sacrifice little children to those same gods when they spiritually destroy the simple and weak, so that they may be attached to their errors.

What is signified by the name of torrents except the swift current of their eloquence? And what by towering rocks except either the powers of this world or the aforesaid heresiarchs? Therefore, in the channels of the torrent they sacrifice little children beneath overhanging rocks when they kill the souls of the foolish by their eloquence, drawing them into error, while worldly powers protect them, or while the inventors of errors lend them authority. Then the following is said to that wicked people:

VERS. 6. — “Your portion is in the channels of the torrent; this is your lot.”

For since the torrent is understood as the impetuous course of heretical eloquence, its portion is in the channels of the torrent because it has chosen to remain in the teaching of heretics. And this is its lot, because it has now been separated from the lot of Catholics and anathematized. It also pours out a libation to its gods and offers sacrifice when it celebrates Masses sacrilegiously, or when it does in secret those things which it is shameful even to mention. Heretics do not offer sacrifice to God, but to their own errors. Therefore, speaking in anger, he says: “Shall I not be indignant at these things?” Understand: at all the things which I have recounted that you have done.

VERS. 7. — This prostitute has placed her bed upon a high and lofty mountain [Col. 0519D] when she has delightfully set her mind upon some exalted leader of heresy, in order to rest in him. These things are said against those who turn aside into heresies. Then what follows applies to the utterly wicked multitude of perverse persons who are within the Church, or to every such soul. For the Lord says:

VERS. 8. — “Behind the door and behind the doorpost you have placed your memorial, because beside me you have uncovered yourself and received an adulterer.”

Behind the door of the heart, and behind the doorpost of that inner door, the soul places a memorial of its iniquity when, although outwardly it has abandoned perverse actions, it nevertheless keeps hidden malice within, in a corner of the heart. [Col. 0520A] And, uncovering herself beside her husband, she receives an adulterer: though lawfully joined to Christ, she opens the entrance of her mind to the devil. Hence Paul says: “Do not give place to the devil” (Eph. 4:27). It follows:

“You have enlarged your bed; you have made a covenant with them.” The soul enlarges the bed of its heart when it wishes to receive Christ and the devil together in its mind. But this can in no way happen. “For the bed is too narrow, so that one must fall off” (above, 28:20). It makes a covenant with demons when it determines always to consent to their suggestions. It follows:

“You have loved their bed with an open hand.”

The soul loves their bed with an open hand when, desiring to commit adultery with them, [Col. 0520B] it reveals its conduct to them so that they may enter more willingly—not waiting for them first to suggest evils to it, but anticipating every suggestion of theirs by evil deeds. Thus it is ready to receive their suggestions, no longer ashamed of its sin or concealing the shamefulness of its prostitution, but sinning with complete freedom. It follows:

VERS. 9. — “You have adorned yourself with royal ointment and multiplied your perfumes.”

She adorns herself with royal ointment in order to please her lovers, because, from the very fact that she is anointed with holy chrism, she is more eagerly corrupted by malignant spirits. And she multiplies her perfumes when she indulges in diverse scents and manifold pleasures. It follows:

[Col. 0520C] “You sent your messengers far away, and you humbled yourself even to hell.”

She sends messengers far away to her lovers when, spreading the report of her perversity afar, she invites malignant spirits to herself. And she is humbled even to hell when her mind is so utterly bowed down that it becomes equal to demons in evil will. Or indeed, she is humbled to hell through sin when she perseveres in evil to the end of the present life. Hence Job says: “His sin reaches even to hell” (Job 24:19). For his sin reaches to hell who does not cease sinning until he descends into hell—that is, until he ends this life most wickedly. Or this prostitute was humbled even to hell, not with that humility which is praiseworthy, but with that by which Amnon humbled his sister Tamar [Col. 0520D] (2 Kings 13). Truly, it is a great humiliation—indeed, a plunge even to hell—to be cast down from the light and summit of chastity into the darkness of a brothel, indeed into the abyss of lusts. It follows:

VERS. 10. — “You have labored in the multitude of your ways; you did not say, ‘I will rest.’”

She labors in the multitude of her ways while she endures heavy labors in the various actions she performs. Hence it is said through Solomon that “God gave the sinner affliction and superfluous care” (Eccl. 2:26). Yet while she labors in many ways, she does not say, “I will rest,” because no labors can break her so as to make her willing to rest from worldly actions. It follows: [Col. 0521A] “You have found the way [Note: [Col. 0521D] Elsewhere: “your life.”] of your hand; therefore you did not pray.”

VERS. 11. — “For whom did you anxiously fear, that you lied and did not remember me, nor consider in your heart that I, being silent and as though not seeing, have been forgotten by you?”

She finds the way of her hand—that is, the way of her activity—when she is able to do the things she wishes to do. And therefore, while she has confidence in riches from full granaries, she neglects to pray to God, and consequently fears many people anxiously. For she cannot say: “The Lord is my helper; I shall look down upon my enemies” (Ps. 117[118]:7). Or she does not pray regarding that for which she anxiously fears; for though she dreads the punishment of eternal death, she nevertheless does not pray from her heart to escape it, while refusing to turn away from her perversities. [Col. 0521B] For how will she be able to raise her face to the Lord in prayer unless she has first cast aside those things of which she may be ashamed before him? She lies if she pretends to pour out prayer to him, because she does not even remember him so long as she does not cease to persevere in such things. Nor does she consider that he is now silent while we act wickedly, and is thought not to see because he does not immediately show that he has seen by striking us, but still defers judgment so that in the meantime we may be converted to repentance. Concerning that judgment there follows:

VERS. 12. — “I shall declare your righteousness, and your works will not profit you.”

VERS. 13. — “When you cry out, let your gathered company deliver you; the wind will carry them all away, the breeze will take them.”

“I shall declare,” he says, “your righteousness which you have followed—that is, I shall reveal your unrighteousness to all on that day. Then your works, in which you now labor, will profit you nothing. For when you cry before the door of the bridal chamber with the foolish virgins, saying, ‘Lord, Lord, open to us’ (Matt. 25:11), let your lovers deliver you, if they can—those who gathered from every side to commit fornication with you. But then the wind of the tempest will carry them all away [Col. 0521C] and cast them into the abyss.” Thus far he has reproached the multitude of wicked Catholics, or each soul of this kind, for the evils it performs. Now he adds concerning the people of the elect:

[Col. 0521D] “But whoever has confidence in me shall inherit the land and possess my holy mountain.”

The prostitute people, which has trusted in its lovers, that is, unclean spirits, will perish. But whoever has confidence in God will be saved. One trusts in God when the consciousness of good works establishes one in the confidence of hope. Hence John says: “If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God” (1 John 3:21). Whoever therefore has this confidence will inherit the land of perpetual stability and secure rest, and will possess the mountain of blessed exaltation. It follows:

VERS. 14. — “And I shall say: Make a way; prepare the road; turn aside from the path; remove stumbling-blocks from the way of my people.”

VERS. 15. — “For thus says the Lord, high and exalted, who inhabits eternity, whose name is holy: dwelling in the high and holy place, and with the contrite and humble in spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble and to revive the heart of the contrite.”

VERS. 16. — “For I shall not contend forever, nor will I be angry unto the end.”

“I shall say,” he says, “make a way for my elect, O preachers. Prepare the road for them, O unbelievers, who wished to obstruct their way. Turn aside from their path, O demons; do not oppose them upon the path of uprightness by which they walk. Or thus: Make a way for them, O angels; prepare a passage for them to cross, O demons—that is, flee from their way. Turn aside from the path, O crowds of vices, who were accustomed to meet their merits as those went before and rebuked the blind man. And you, preachers or angels, ‘remove stumbling-blocks from the way of my people’ (Luke 18:39), so that they may travel the way of uprightness without the snare of offense; and so that what is written may come to pass: ‘The way of the righteous is without stumbling’ (Prov. 15:19). Paul took every precaution lest he give the brethren any example from which a scandal of offense might be taken (1 Cor. 9:12). Likewise, the other good stewards of the Church did and do this.

And, so that the Lord might be believed to honor his people in this way, he adds: “For I shall not contend forever, nor will I be angry unto the end.” Formerly, indeed, he often contended through the prophets with the people of the Jews, rebuking their iniquities, and was angry with them, handing them over into the hands of their enemies. But he will not contend forever, nor was he angry until the end of the age, because through the gift of the Mediator’s grace that anger and contention have now ended.

God is called high and exalted because he surpasses every sense and understanding. For the superessential divinity carries both word and understanding beyond all things into obscurity, because his essence is neither a name nor a word; rather, he is exalted beyond measure. Rightly, therefore, God is called high and exalted. Eternity, however, is defined as the whole, simultaneous, and perfect possession of interminable life. This will become clearer by comparison with temporal things. Whatever lives in time—that is, in the present—passes from past things into future ones; and nothing established in time can embrace the whole extent of its life. It has not yet grasped tomorrow; it has already lost yesterday; and even in today’s life it lives no more than a moment. Therefore, whatever suffers the condition of time, even if it lives without end like the human soul, is nevertheless not yet such that it should be believed eternal. It does not comprehend and embrace at once the whole extent of its life, however infinite: it has not yet had future things, and no longer has what has passed. But that which at once comprehends and possesses the whole fullness [Col. 0523A] of interminable life, from which nothing future is absent and nothing past has flowed away, is rightly said to be eternal or to inhabit eternity. Thus God inhabits eternity, because his being is whole and always is; it knows no mutability, since it has never begun and will never cease: an unconquerable and endless ocean of being, bounded by no limits or borders, surpassing every sense, all time, and every nature.

His name also is holy. Holiness is, so far as it can be spoken of according to our capacity, purity free from every defilement, most perfect and utterly uncontaminated. Therefore his name is called holy because in him there is a purity of supernatural cleanness far surpassing anything any mind can understand, so that he purifies and sanctifies all who believe in this his name. “He dwells also in the high and holy place, because in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). For the Father is the high and holy dwelling-place of the Son, just as the Son is the dwelling-place of the Father. For he says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 10:38). Likewise the Holy Spirit is in the Father and the Son. Thus we should understand that God is said to dwell in the high and holy place because he himself is to himself a high and holy dwelling-place, just as he himself is the eternity which he inhabits.

This high and holy dwelling-place may also be understood as the heart of angelic spirits, in which he dwells. [Col. 0523C] Hence it is written: “Look down from your sanctuary, from the lofty dwelling-place of heaven” (Deut. 26:15). But he, so exalted and so immense, not only dwells on high, but mercifully deigns to dwell also with the contrite and humble spirit; and “he is near to those who are troubled in heart” (Ps. 33[34]:19). Therefore he dwells with the contrite and humble spirit in a human being, so that by the grace of his Spirit he may revive the spirit of the humble and the heart of the contrite. For he gives grace to the humble, makes the repentant and compunctious—who had been inwardly dead through sin—to live, and kindles them more and more toward his love. Therefore he, so great, so exalted, and so gracious, will not contend forever as he once contended with the Synagogue; but when Christ has risen and returned to heaven, he will pour out his Spirit upon all flesh, so that he may no longer contend or be angry, but accomplish all things through grace. Hence he adds:

“Because the Spirit will go forth from before me, and I shall make breath.”

For the Spirit went forth from before the Lord when the Paraclete came—the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, whom Christ sent from the Father to the disciples. And the Lord made breath when he gave spiritual gifts to human beings. “For grace has been given to each one of us according to the measure of his gift” (Eph. [Col. 0524A] 4:7). Having said that he would graciously revive the spirit of the humble, he adds:

VERS. 17. — “Because of the iniquity of his covetousness I was angry and struck him; I hid [Note: [Col. 0523D] Elsewhere: “I hid my face from you,” etc.] myself from him and was indignant, and he went wandering in the way of his heart.”

VERS. 18. — “I saw his ways [Note: [Col. 0523D] Elsewhere: “I saw his ways and healed him, and led him back, and restored,” etc.] and dismissed him; and I restored consolations to him and to his mourners.”

VERS. 19. — “I created the fruit [Note: [Col. 0524D] Elsewhere: “Peace, peace, the fruit of the lips, to him,” etc.] of the lips: peace to him who is far off and to him who is near, says the Lord, and I healed him.”

The iniquity of the covetousness of the human spirit was that in paradise it proudly desired the glory of exaltation when it heard from the serpent: “You shall be like gods” (Gen. 3:5). Its covetousness was iniquitous because it sought for itself a divinity not granted to it. Because of this iniquity the Lord was angry, struck it, hid himself from it, was indignant with it, and allowed it to go wandering in the way of its heart. Formerly the human spirit enjoyed the tranquil stability of the mind, intent upon heavenly contemplation; but afterward it was subjected to instability, flowing through countless motions. For when the mind strives to remain within itself, it is somehow led away from itself even without knowing it; and from every object upon which it fixes its attention it is driven away by weariness. But while it becomes weary of things vainly to be thought upon, it shows that it depends upon another, since wherever it is placed it does not rest. It is suspended upon him from whom it was created. Because it was created to desire God alone, and everything it desires below him is less, whatever is not God rightly does not suffice it. Therefore it was grievously struck, because it lost the one whom it could possess sufficiently, and is scattered here and there among many things.

As has been said, the Lord struck it by taking away its inward health and hid from it his radiant face, withdrawing from it the beauty of his vision. Cast out from inward things, it went outward, wandering in the way of its heart and following its desires. The Lord saw the ways of its thoughts, because it abandoned invisible things and sought visible ones; and by just judgment he dismissed it according to the desires of its heart. It went wandering in the way of its heart because it was carried along by the light mobility of its thoughts. But weighty counsel of heart expels every instability of wandering, so that it no longer lightly falls away from attention to God, but stands fixed in him with the weight of steadfastness. [Col. 0524D] Since there are souls which, by a light movement, now desire this and now that, almighty God, because he does not weigh those light fluctuations lightly, judges the wandering of the heart by abandoning it. But when he looks upon it through grace, he fixes the wandering mind in the stability of counsel. Hence he adds:

“And I led him back,” because when he mercifully deigns to look upon the light movements of the soul, he immediately forms it into the maturity of steadfastness. Thus, in the beginning, God struck the human spirit because of pride and allowed it to wander [Col. 0525A] in the way of its heart, so that, having lost the stability of mind, it might go outward far from him through wandering motions and varied desires. For it went out from him because it was proud and followed visible things. But it will return if, humbled, it flees inward to his protection and seeks the things that are within. For to enter within is to desire inward things; to go out is to desire outward things.

“I led him back,” he says, “and restored consolations to him,” so that by humility he might return to that sweet consolation or inner secret of the mind, which is free from the bitterness of evil thoughts. This was accomplished by the gift of grace in those who received the Holy Spirit. The merciful Lord called his servant back to himself, brought back the fugitive, forgave the penitent for his error, and consoled the sorrowing man by giving him the Paraclete, the consoling Spirit. His mourners are those who mourned or mourn for their spirit struck by God. To them the Lord restored consolations, renewing in them health of mind through the healing medicine of the Holy Spirit. For he created peace as the fruit of the lips—that is, he instituted that “confession might be made with the mouth unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10). The fruit of the lips is fruitful confession of the mouth. That fruit is peace, because when we confess our sins, or Christ before human beings, we obtain peace with God.

And this peace “was created for him who is far off and for him who is near” (Eph. 2:17), that is, for the Jewish and Gentile peoples. For Paul says of Christ to the Gentiles: “Coming, he preached peace to you who were far off, and peace to those who were near” (ibid.), that is, to the Jews. [Col. 0525C] Where he created peace, the fruit of the lips, he also healed the human spirit which he had struck while it was discordant, because through the confession of our sins [Col. 0526A] we cast out inward maladies and receive the health of the inner person. These things have been done, and are done, throughout the whole world by Christ’s grace. But now that the elect have obtained peace, let us see what is said concerning the reprobate. It follows:

VERS. 20. — “But the wicked are like a boiling sea, which cannot rest; its waves overflow into trampling and mire.”

VERS. 21. — “There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord.”

The wicked are like a boiling sea because they are turbulent with rage, bitter in quarrels, swollen with the pride of arrogance, dark with deceit and malice. Boiling with the fury of cruelty, they rage against the good and overflow with the waves of perverse works into trampling and mire. [Col. 0526B] The waves of tribulations which they stir up are trampled down by the elect; and mire is the uncleanness of the carnal works which they perform. Rightly is the bitter unrest of the minds of the wicked called, or compared with, a sea, because while they attack one another in mutual hostilities, they clash against each other as enemies. Rightly is the life of the perverse compared with a sea that is continually boiling, because, stirred by stormy actions, it is separated from the way of wisdom, rest, and stability. Therefore peace is denied them, because they are always turbulent and restless in their hearts, and often quarrel even with themselves. For the Savior came so that there might be “peace on earth to men of good will” (Luke 2:14), but not to the ill-disposed. Therefore he created peace, the fruit of the lips, for the repentant. But there is no peace [Col. 0526C] for the wicked, because they lack good will. It is sufficient to have extended the measure of this volume thus far, so that we may reach the end of this work in another.

# BOOK EIGHT

[Col. 0525]

## CHAPTER 58

[Col. 0525C]

VERS. 1. — “Cry out; do not cease; lift up your voice like a trumpet, and declare to my people their transgressions and to the house of Jacob their sins.”

[Col. 0525D] In this the Lord speaks to every priest, showing that no one ought in any way to become a ruler of the Church unless he is able unceasingly to proclaim the teaching of truth. For whoever approaches the priesthood undertakes the office of a herald, so that before the coming of the Judge, who follows terribly, he himself may go forward crying aloud. If a priest is ignorant of preaching, what cry of proclamation is a mute herald to give? Even if he preaches continually, he will scarcely be able to render as much as he ought. For the Lord does not say, “Cry out after many days,” but: “Cry out; do not cease,” so that he may persist without interruption in preaching. Paul also says to the disciples: “For three years, night and day, I did not cease admonishing every one of you with tears” (Acts 20:31). And if the Apostle, in order to clear himself before God, did not cease day and night from preaching the word of the Lord, what will become of those who scarcely provide spiritual pastures for the flock entrusted to them even after many days?

The preacher must also lift up his voice like a trumpet, so that he may be heard by many and stir the minds of all to spiritual warfare. He must lift up his voice like a trumpet, so that just as at the end of the age the resurrection of the dead will occur at the trumpet’s voice, so the hearers of the preacher may be raised from the death of the soul. He must declare to the people their transgressions and to the house of Jacob their sins—that is, he must make known to them and rebuke the evils which they do in the Church. Hence elsewhere the Lord threatens them, saying: “If you do not declare his iniquity to the wicked man, I shall require his blood from your hand” (Ezek. 3:18). The house of Jacob is the Church, because Christ, as it is written, “will reign over the house of Jacob forever” (Luke 1:32). Why the sins of the faithful people must be declared to them is then added:

[Col. 0527A] VERS. 2. — “For day after day they seek me and desire to know my ways, as though they were a nation that had done righteousness [Note: [Col. 0527D] Elsewhere: “had done righteousness and had not forsaken the judgment of their God.”].”

“Day after day,” as though he said, “daily.” Or “day after day,” that is, from light to light, from understanding to understanding, they seek me. They desire to know the ways of righteousness by which they may come to me, as though they were a nation that had done righteousness. For whoever has already begun to do righteousness ought to inquire more diligently into the ways of God; and whoever has fulfilled in deed the lesser things which he could know ought to learn the greater things in which he may advance. It follows: “They ask of me judgments of righteousness”—that is, they ask me to make known to them the judgments of my righteousness, by which I approve the actions of some and disapprove those of others. And they desire to draw near to God through the merit of good conduct, saying:

VERS. 3. — “Why have we fasted,” etc. God is said not to see and not to know what he does not accept and what is not pleasing to him. He explains why he has not seen their fasting and humiliation, replying to them: “Behold, on the day of your fast your own will is found, and you exact all your debts.”

VERS. 4. — “Behold, you fast for strife and contention, and strike wickedly with the fist.”

“This,” he says, “is found blameworthy in your fasting: while you fast, you do not cease to follow your perverse will, though you ought to do not your own will but God’s. And you exact all your debts.” One who demands from his debtor what he has given does nothing unjust. Yet it is fitting that whoever chastens himself in repentance should deny himself even that which is justly due to him. For when we are afflicted and repentant, God forgives what we have done unjustly if, for his love, we remit even what is justly due to us. Those who abstain should always carefully watch lest, while fleeing the vice of gluttony, more grievous vices arise in them as though from virtue; lest, while they mortify the flesh, they break out into impatience. For there is no virtue when the flesh is conquered but the spirit is overcome by anger. Sometimes, while the mind of abstinent persons restrains itself from anger, joy arrives like a stranger and corrupts it; and the house of abstinence is ruined insofar as it does not guard itself against spiritual vices. Hence it is rightly said: “On the days of your fasts your own wills are found.” And again: “Behold, you fast for strife and contention, and strike wickedly with the fist.” Will pertains to joy; strife and the fist pertain to anger. Therefore the body is vainly worn down through abstinence if the mind, abandoned to disordered impulses, is dissipated by vices; if the soul is not restrained from its perverse pleasures; if quarrels are not stilled. Hence it is added:

“Do not fast as you have done until this day, so that your cry may be heard on high.”

Our cry is heard on high when the perversity of our actions accuses us before God. Of such a cry it was said: “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied” [Col. 0528A] (Gen. 18:20). Or our cry is heard on high when angels carry to God the cry of sin concerning us. But we are afflicted by fasts in vain so long as a cry concerning us is heard above. Again, those who abstain must be admonished both always to preserve their abstinence without change and never to regard it, before the hidden Judge, as a virtue of outstanding worth, lest perhaps, if it is judged to be of great merit, the heart be lifted up in pride. Hence it is added:

VERS. 5. — “Is this the fast that I have chosen: for a person to afflict his soul for one day?”

But that fasting may be acceptable, it is said below: “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the needy and wandering into your house” (below, v. 7). Here we should consider how small the virtue of abstinence is seen to be when it is not commended by other virtues. To what he had said, “Is this the fast that I have chosen?” he adds:

“Is it to bend his head like a circle and spread sackcloth and ashes?”

To bend the head like a circle, he says, is to bow it excessively. For one who lowers the head too much bends himself as it were into the shape of a circle. But bowing the head in this way and lying in sackcloth and ashes do not commend the fasting person unless he also performs works of mercy. For God does not seek affliction alone and humiliation through injury to the body: that someone should bend his head like a circle, bow down body and neck, put on sackcloth, and sleep in ashes. Hence it is added:

[Col. 0528C] “Would you call this a fast and a day acceptable to the Lord?” After the Lord has shown the fast which he does not approve, he makes known which fast pleases him, saying:

VERS. 6. — “Is not this rather the fast that I have chosen? Loosen the bonds of impiety; untie the oppressive bundles; set free those who are broken, and break every burden.”

If you have bound any captives in prison, release them, because these are bonds of impiety; and untie the bundles by which you burden your captives with certain weights. Or these bonds and bundles are bundles of documents in which the exactions of moneylenders are contained and the poor are oppressed by debt. [Col. 0528D] If a priest has unjustly excommunicated someone, I see there a bond of impiety. If he has imposed upon someone the unbearable burden of excessive penance, I see there an oppressive bundle. If impiety has bound someone’s mind, I discern there a bond of impiety. Therefore all such bonds and bundles ought to be untied, that the fast may become acceptable. Let servants also, who are bent with old age, now be set free, and let every burden be broken from them. Whoever seeks that the bonds of his conscience be divinely loosened ought mercifully to release all these things. And in order to receive heavenly benefits, he should perform what follows:

VERS. 7. — “Break your bread for the hungry, and [Col. 0529A] bring the needy and wandering into your house; when you see one naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh.”

That is, the flesh of your needy neighbor, because it is your own.

VERS. 8. — “Then your light shall break forth like the morning, and your health shall rise quickly; your righteousness shall go before your face, and the glory of the Lord shall gather you.”

VERS. 9. — “Then you shall call, and the Lord will hear; you shall cry out, and he will say: ‘Behold, I am here.’”

“Then,” he says, “when you have done these things, your light shall break forth like the morning, because the fault that darkened your heart will immediately depart, and the brightness of righteousness will illumine it. Then your light shall break forth like the morning, because the darkness of sins will leave you and you will shine with the light of righteousness. The health of your soul, which had languished in sins, will come quickly. Your righteousness shall go before your face, because you will send your good works before you to God, storing up treasures for yourself in heaven; and then the glory of the Lord will gather you, when you hear: ‘Enter into the joy of your Lord’ (Matt. 25:23), or: ‘Receive the kingdom’ (ibid., 34). When you have performed the aforesaid works of mercy, then you will call and the Lord will hear, because prayer is heard more quickly when the merit of good works supports it. For how will God hear one who prays, if that person refuses to hear God commanding? For he says: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do the things I say?” (Luke 6:46). Whoever therefore willingly hears—that is, does—the Lord’s commandments, God gladly accepts that person’s prayers and answers one crying in prayer: [Col. 0529C] ‘Behold, I am here.’ It follows:

“If you remove from your midst the chain, and cease extending the finger and speaking what does not profit.”

VERS. 10. — “When you pour out your soul to the hungry and satisfy the afflicted soul, your light shall arise in darkness, and your darkness shall be as noon.”

First you must remove the chain from your midst—that is, from your heart—so that you cast away every bond of sin that constrains your mind. Therefore loosen from your heart the bonds of impiety; then, with the bond of conscience loosed, cease extending the finger and speaking what does not profit, and abandon undisciplined movements and useless words. In the extending [Col. 0529D] of the finger and in speech which does not profit is denoted the wandering and undisciplined dissipation of hands and tongue. For outward movement shows that no root of good counsel stands firm within. Or the soul extends the finger and speaks what does not profit it when it disparages others, pointing them out one by one as with a finger. But once the chain of the heart has been removed and the movements of the outward members set in order, you must now devote yourself to virtues: namely, mercifully pour out your soul to the hungry, so that with compassionate feeling you may pour yourself out in pious works, helping him in whatever ways you can, from your heart and with good will; and fill the afflicted soul of the needy with the benefits of almsgiving.

And then your light shall arise in the darkness of the present life, [Col. 0530A] and your darkness shall be as noon, because the Lord “will bring forth your righteousness as the light, and your judgment as the noonday” (Ps. 36[37]:6). Your light shall arise in darkness because in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation you will shine as a light in the world. And your darkness shall be as noon: “For once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8).

Or the future life may be denoted by the name of darkness, because the reprobate will be cast into outer darkness. Hence the Lord says: “I must work the works of him who sent me while it is day. Night is coming, when no one can work” (John 4:4). He calls the present life—or even himself in this life—day; but night, the time which succeeds this life [Col. 0530B], because then no one is able to work. Therefore your light shall rise in darkness, because in that age you will see the light when sinners are wrapped in darkness. And your darkness shall be as noon, because you will be surrounded by the brightest radiance.

VERS. 11.—“And the Lord your God will always give you rest.”

He will bring you into his rest, so that you may rest with him; and when your soul has departed from the body, he will fill it with the splendors of eternal light, and at the end of the age, when he raises your body, he will free your bones from destruction and everlasting fire, “and the humbled bones shall rejoice” (Ps. 50:10). But what you will meanwhile attain through divine grace is then added:

“And you shall be like a watered garden, and like a fountain [Col. 0530C] of waters whose waters shall not fail.” You shall be like a watered garden because, drenched with the streams of heavenly grace, you will always have the flowers of virtues and flourishing works. And like a fountain of unfailing waters, as the Lord says: “Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; rather, it shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4:13). It follows:

VERS. 12.—“And the ancient waste places shall be built up in you; you shall raise up the foundations of generation after generation.”

The ancient waste places are the sayings and examples of the fathers of old, long ago abandoned by worldly people. But they shall be built up in you when you set the words and deeds of the holy Fathers in the structure of your manner of life [Col. 0530D]. The foundations of generation after generation are the prophets and apostles. Hence believers are told: “You are now fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph. 2:19). These foundations, indeed, in a sense lie low among those who neglect them and do not exalt their precepts and practices in their own deeds. But you shall raise them up in yourself when you erect them in the building of your life. It follows:

“And you shall be called a builder of hedges, turning paths toward rest.”

You shall be called a builder of hedges because you will build a hedge around your life when, restraining the desires of the flesh, you block their unlawful paths. You will set a hedge about the vineyard [Col. 0531A] of God, which is your soul or the Church, so that every beast is prevented from entering it. And you will turn paths toward rest when, abandoning worldly occupations, you serve God alone with a tranquil mind. You will turn paths toward rest so that God’s wrath may by no means rage, but the Lord may be appeased toward you and all the paths of his indignation may be quieted. Or you will build hedges and turn paths toward rest if, out of love for religion, you block off every avenue of access for yourself, so that you may cease to wander abroad in various directions and, remaining in your own place, do what is written: “Be still, and see that I am God” (Ps. 45:11). Therefore it adds:

VERS. 13.—“If you turn back your foot from the sabbath, from doing your own will on my holy day, and call the sabbath delightful, the holy day of the Lord glorious, [Col. 0531B] and glorify him, while you do not go your own ways, nor find your own will, nor speak a word.”

VERS. 14.—“Then you shall delight yourself in the Lord, and I will lift you up above the heights of the earth, and feed you with the inheritance of Jacob your father.”

The sabbath of the elect consists in fleeing worldly occupations, lest they be entangled in sin through them, and thus being free to devote themselves to God. This sabbath is the Lord’s holy day, because the tranquil life of religious persons is holy and bright before God. Therefore turn back your foot from this sabbath, from doing your own will on this holy day of God: do not go out to worldly occupations in order to do your own will, you who have chosen to devote yourself inwardly to God; rather, “turn away from your own desires” (Ecclus. [Col. 0531C] 18:30), lest you violate the sabbath of holy rest. Call the sabbath delightful and the Holy One of the Lord glorious, and glorify him by not going your own ways.

For you must call it delightful—that is, subtle or refined—lest you speak of it in a Jewish sense, supposing that one must cease not only from every unlawful work, but also from every desire for worldly things. For the sabbath is delightful when the mind rests from every labor of desire. Indeed, it is a great rest of mind to possess no worldly covetousness. For if the heart longs after earthly things, it cannot possibly be tranquil: either it desires what it does not possess in order to possess it, or it fears lest it lose what it has acquired. But if the mind is firmly fixed once for all in the desire for heavenly things, it is less troubled by the disturbance of temporal things [Col. 0531D], because it rests, as it were, in a certain secret place and does not feel the tumult of the world. Thus you must celebrate the sabbath as delightful; and call the holy God—that is, his Christ—glorious, singing his name; and glorify him by not going your own ways, that is, your own occupations. Having abandoned the ways of your activities for love of him, you must not be idle, but strive to glorify him in yourself, so that according to the Law you may sanctify the sabbath day. For he sanctifies the sabbath day who rests from unlawful things and performs those things that are holy.

And glorify him—that is, the sabbath day—by not going your own ways, so that, resting from your own occupations and works of private advantage for the sake of religion, you may glorify the sabbath of this holy rest by worthy works [Col. 0532A] of righteousness and holiness. “And let not your own will be found, so as to speak a word”; rather, in this break your own will, so that you do not speak at its bidding; and keep silence for love of religion, lest perhaps you sin with your tongue. And when you have lived in this way, then you shall delight yourself in the Lord, because by these advances in holy conduct you will reach perfect charity, which casts out fear, so that you observe all these things no longer from necessity but from love, and rest in the love of God.

“And I will lift you up above the heights of the earth,” so that you may transcend everything that is lofty in the estimation of human beings. For losses, insults, poverty, and abasement are, as it were, the low places of earth; even lovers of the world, while they walk along the level expanse of the broad way, never cease to trample them down in avoiding them [Col. 0532B]. But the heights of earth are gain in possessions, the flatteries of dependents, abundance of riches, honor, and the exaltation of offices. Whoever still walks in lowly desires esteems these things lofty precisely because he judges them great. But once the heart is fixed in heaven, it immediately perceives how base are the things that seemed lofty. For just as, when one climbs a mountain, one looks down upon the things lying below all the more as one directs one’s step higher, so one who strives to fix his intention upon the highest things, discovering through that very striving that no glory of the present life has any reality, is raised above the heights of earth; and what he formerly, placed among lowly desires, thought was above himself, he comes to recognize, as he makes progress in ascent, as lying beneath him.

[Col. 0532C] “And I will feed you,” he says, “with the inheritance of Jacob your father,” because you shall be satisfied by heavenly contemplation. Just as one who has faith is called a son of Abraham, so one who supplants vices and sins is called a son of Jacob; and whoever imitates a person’s virtue is also called that person’s son. The inheritance of Jacob is that homeland of blessed dwelling concerning which the Lord promises through Ezekiel to the elect who have died: “I will open your tombs and bring you out from your graves, my people, and bring you into the land of Israel” (Ezek. 37:12). Thus he is fed with Jacob’s inheritance who enters that homeland in mind and feeds upon its contemplation. But then all the righteous shall be fed fully in that inheritance, when “they shall come and recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” [Col. 0532D] (Matt. 8:11). To establish all these things with firm authority, as a man filled with God, he added: “For the mouth of the Lord has spoken.” For the prophet did not speak from himself, but uttered all these things while God spoke in him. Thus far he has shown each of the faithful how great an advance in virtue he will attain if, wholly converted to religion, he strives with his whole heart to pursue righteousness. After this he addresses this people of carnal persons, who through their wickedness have withdrawn far from God, saying:

## CHAPTER LIX

VERS. 1.—“Behold, the hand of the Lord is not shortened, that it cannot save; nor is his ear made heavy, that it cannot hear.”

[Col. 0533A] VERS. 2.—“But your iniquities have divided between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you, so that he will not hear.”

For some people think that God is now of a different will or power from what he formerly was, when they hear that our fathers were heard more quickly in prayer, while they see themselves not heard; that the fathers were speedily saved from their tribulations or led to eternal salvation, while they themselves are not saved from their prolonged calamities and cannot attain everlasting salvation. They are fittingly answered that the hand of the Lord is not shortened so that he cannot save, as he formerly saved the fathers, if anyone is worthy to be saved; nor is his ear made heavy so that he cannot now hear, as formerly, if there is someone who deserves to be heard.

“But your iniquities have divided between you and your God.” Remove, therefore, iniquities from the midst, and you yourselves will make God near to you. For this is why God was so swiftly present to the prayers of the holy Fathers: there was no intervening barrier separating them from God. “And your sins have hidden his face from you, so that he will not hear.” For your heart has been darkened by the darkness of sins, so that it cannot see the serene countenance of his goodness and grace or obtain from him what it asks. It follows:

VERS. 3.—“For your hands are defiled with blood, and your fingers with iniquity; your lips have spoken falsehood, and your tongue utters iniquity.”

[Col. 0533C] For this reason you are unworthy to be heard: your hands are defiled with human blood which you have shed. Or your hands are polluted with blood—that is, with sin—and your fingers with whatever iniquity you have committed; and your lips have uttered not merely idle speech but also falsehood, which is worse, because “the mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11). How then can the petition of a mouth accustomed to speak such things be heard, unless it first does penance? Yet concerning such persons it is further added:

VERS. 4.—“There is none who calls upon righteousness, nor any who judges truly; but they trust in nothing and speak vanities.”

[Col. 0533D] There is no one in this multitude of wicked people who calls upon righteousness—that is, who prays to be made righteous in his heart. For he calls righteousness, that is, calls it into himself, who prepares his heart as a fitting dwelling-place for righteousness and asks righteousness from God. But among these there is no one who does this. Nor is there anyone who judges truly, because by the false judgment of their minds they prefer temporal things to eternal ones. But they trust in nothing—that is, in the present life, in their own strength, in horses, arms, and riches. For all these are nothing in comparison with heavenly and eternal things. And they speak vanities because they praise temporal things or utter idle and empty words. It follows:

“They conceived toil and gave birth to iniquity.”

[Col. 0534A] They conceived toil because they labored grievously in their hearts, devising how they might acquire temporal things by right or wrong and surpass others. And they gave birth to iniquity by bringing into action what they had conceived within. It follows:

VERS. 5.—“They have broken the eggs of asps and woven spiders’ webs; whoever eats of their eggs shall die, and what has been warmed shall hatch into a basilisk.”

The eggs of asps are broken when the counsels of evil spirits, hidden in the hearts of the wicked, are exposed through perverse works. They also weave spiders’ webs because, for the desire of this world, they perform whatever temporal works they can. Since these are founded on no stability, they undoubtedly perish in the breath of passing life. It is well said: “Whoever eats [Col. 0534B] of their eggs shall die,” because whoever receives the counsels of unclean spirits kills the soul’s life within himself. “And what has been warmed shall hatch into a basilisk,” because the counsel of an evil spirit, concealed in the heart, is nourished unto the punishment of iniquities. For the basilisk is called king of serpents; Antichrist is the head of the reprobate. Therefore, what has been warmed hatches into a basilisk because whoever receives within himself the counsels of asps to be nourished, becoming a member of the wicked head, grows into the body of Antichrist. It follows:

VERS. 6.—“Their webs shall not become clothing, nor shall they be covered by their works; their works are useless, and the work of iniquity is in their hands.”

Their webs shall not become clothing because from what they do [Col. 0534C] no garment for the soul will be made. Nor shall they be covered by their works; rather, they shall remain naked and full of shame. For because they do not seek eternal things, they lose temporal goods along with time; and they come naked before the Judge because they refused to weave for themselves the garment of good works. For if our works did not cover us before God as a garment, it would not be said in an angelic voice: “Blessed is he who watches and keeps his garments, lest he walk naked and they see his shame” (Rev. 16:15). For our shame is then seen when a blameworthy life is not veiled before the eyes of the righteous at judgment by the covering of a good work. Therefore the wicked shall not be covered by their works, since their works are useless, because they do everything for temporal life [Col. 0534D]. It follows:

VERS. 7.—“Their feet run to evil and hasten to shed innocent blood; their thoughts are useless thoughts; devastation and destruction are in their paths.”

VERS. 8.—“They have not known the way of peace, and there is no judgment in their steps; their paths are crooked for them: everyone who walks in them knows not peace.”

Their feet run and hasten to evil because they hurry to seize the possessions of others. And they shed innocent blood because they unjustly kill those whose goods they seize. Their thoughts are useless because they constantly think not of eternal goods but of transitory things, and devise evil against their neighbors in their hearts [Col. 0535A]. Devastation and destruction are in their paths because, having assembled armies, they ravage and destroy the regions through which they pass.

They have not known the way of peace because wherever they go, they invade others’ resources. And there is no judgment in their steps because they rush indiscriminately upon the good and innocent just as upon the wicked or those opposed to them. Or certainly devastation and destruction are in their paths because, while they unceasingly pursue turbulent occupations, all their rest, inward and outward alike, is devastated and shattered. They have not known the way of peace because they do not know how to be in accord with God in their actions. For that person follows the way of peace who is not diverted from the path of truth into the way of stumbling. Hence it is said through Zechariah: “To guide our feet into the way [Col. 0535B] of peace” (Luke 1:79). For then we direct our steps into the way of peace when we proceed by that course of action in which we do not depart from the grace of our Creator. But the reprobate do not know the way of peace because, blinded by voluntary perversity, they are ignorant of the path of uprightness which accords with the divine will. And there is no judgment in their steps because in what they do they have no test of discernment. Their steps are the actions upon which they rely and by which they advance, as though by paces. But there is no judgment in their steps because they neglect to examine their actions; following the pleasure of their own will, they do what pleases them, whether good or evil. Their paths are crooked for them because in the actions by which they walk they always pursue earthly and low things. [Col. 0535C] Everyone who walks in them knows not peace. For “whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is made an enemy of God” (Jas. 4:4). It follows:

VERS. 9.—“Therefore the judgment of right discernment has been removed far from you.”

“For the natural person does not receive the things that are of the Spirit of God, but the spiritual person judges all things” (1 Cor. 2:14).—“And righteousness shall not overtake you,” so long as you act thus, because iniquity must first be abandoned in order that righteousness may afterward be granted you. After this, the Jewish people, about to do penance, is introduced, as it immediately adds:

“We have waited for light, and behold darkness; for brightness, [Col. 0535D] and we have walked in darkness.”

VERS. 10.—“We groped for the wall like the blind, and as though without eyes we felt our way; we stumbled at noon as in darkness, and among dark things as dead men.”

VERS. 11.—“We shall all roar like bears, and, meditating like doves, we shall moan.”

For because they waited long for the coming of the Redeemer but, at his coming, fell into the darkness of unbelief, they rightly say now as they come to their senses: “We have waited for light, and behold darkness; for brightness, and we have walked in darkness.” For Christ is the light of the world and the splendor of the Father’s glory. They awaited his coming in prophecy, but did not recognize him when he came; they opened the eyes of their minds unto hope, but closed them to the presence of light, and, rejecting light, chose darkness. They add: “We groped for the wall like the blind.” For they had seen manifest miracles, and yet were still seeking him as though groping, when they said: “How long do you hold our soul in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly” (John 10:24). Behold, the light of miracles was before their eyes, yet, encountering darkness in their hearts, they still groped in inquiry. For unwilling to enter the now-open door of light through faith, they groped outside like blind men, testing the wall. Hence they add:

“We stumbled at noon as in darkness.” For while they saw the miracles of divine power and yet doubted his divinity, they suffered darkness at noon [Col. 0536B], because they lost sight in the very light of truth. Moreover, they stumbled among dark things like dead men when, having lost the sight of the heart, they struck against the stone of stumbling. Or, they awaited brightness and walked in darkness, groping the sacred Scriptures like a wall, blind—seeking only their words and leaves, not the fruit or sense contained in the letters. For while the splendor of the sun of righteousness shines throughout the whole world, they remain in darkness and the error of unbelief. But for these misdeeds they add concerning the mourning of their repentance:

“We shall all roar like bears, and, meditating like doves, we shall moan.” For the bear roars most vehemently when it laments; whereas the dove customarily moans always instead of singing. So too these act at Elijah’s preaching; and concerning their vain expectation they consequently add: “We have waited for judgment, and it is not there; for salvation, and it is far from us.” For in this captivity they waited a very long time for God, judging their cause, to set them free, but in vain; and they awaited the salvation of their deliverance, but it was far from them. And why they did not find judgment and salvation they show by adding:

VERS. 12.—“For our iniquities have multiplied before you, and our sins have answered against us.”

For from the time when they lost Christ, they have always added iniquities to iniquities. And their sins answered them, because they received what they deserved. It follows:

“For our crimes are with us, and we have known our iniquities.”

VERS. 13.—“To sin and to lie against the Lord.”

Therefore their iniquities have multiplied, because their crimes are with them. Their crimes are with them because they lost Christ, who alone washed away sins by his blood. “For it is impossible for sins to be taken away by the blood of goats and bulls” (Heb. 13:4). They sinned and lied against the Lord when they accused him with false charges and caused him to be killed. It follows:

[Col. 0537A] “And we turned away, so as not to go after the back of our God, that we might speak calumny and transgression.”

They turned away so as not to go after the back of their God because they refused to follow Christ in the grace of evangelical newness, but spoke calumny and transgression, saying: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the sabbath” (John 9:16). Or: “Behold, a glutton and a drinker of wine, a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (Matt. 11:19), and similar things. But those too turned away so as not to go after the back of their God, of whom John relates that “many of his disciples went back and no longer walked with him” (John 6:67). They spoke calumny and transgression because, when they heard of eating and drinking his body and blood, they said: “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” (ibid.). It follows:

“We conceived and spoke words of falsehood from our heart.”

While seeking to accuse the Savior, they conceived and spoke many words of falsehood, and did this from their heart. “For from the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries” (Matt. 15:19). Or, they conceived from their heart and spoke falsehoods, despising God’s law and following traditions which they devised in their own heart. It follows:

VERS. 14.—“And judgment has been turned backward, and righteousness stands far off, because truth has fallen in the street [Col. 0537C] and equity could not enter.”

VERS. 15.—“And truth has been reduced to forgetfulness, and whoever withdrew from evil was exposed to plunder.”

Judgment has been turned backward because the chief priests, scribes, and elders, who ought to judge justly, condemned Christ as deserving death without judgment. And all righteousness then stood far from them when they handed him over through envy. For truth fell in the street which was before Pilate’s praetorium. Therefore truth fell in this street, where the Jews’ perversity alone reigned. Equity could not enter there because the Jews’ faithlessness sought to have not the innocent man but the guilty one released. And from that time truth was reduced to forgetfulness among the Jews, and the people of believers, who withdrew from the evil of their faithlessness [Col. 0537D], were exposed to the plunder of violent men. Hence they deserved praise from the Apostle, who says: “You accepted with joy the plundering of your possessions, knowing that you have a better and enduring possession” (Heb. 10:34). It follows:

“And the Lord saw, and it appeared evil in his eyes, because there is no judgment.”

It displeased him because there is no judgment among the Jews, while they unjustly condemn the Savior, or in the other things they afterward do. It follows:

VERS. 16.—“And God saw that there was no man; and he was distressed because there was no one to meet him.”

There is no man among the Jews—that is, none upright and acting manfully; rather, all are common and senseless, because [Col. 0538A] “all have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13:3). Hence there is no one to meet God, because among them there is no righteous person worthy to turn divine wrath away from that people by the resistance of his intercession. To be *aporiate* means to labor, or to be straitened or afflicted, because we call the pores the openings of the skin through which sweat comes out. Therefore God saw that there was no man among the Jews; and he was *aporiatus*, that is, he labored, because there was no one to meet him. For it is, as it were, a great labor and affliction to God when no one, through prayer, opposes his punishment. Or, as has been said before us, *aporia* is contempt or deprivation. Hence the Apostle says: “We are *aporiamur* (‘treated with contempt’), but not destitute” (2 Cor. 4:8), that is, we are despised [Col. 0538B] and deprived, as it were, of our own gains. For *porion* in Greek is called “gain” in Latin. Thus we say *aporiari*, to be despised and deprived of one’s own gains; God was *aporiatus*, that is, he lost the gains of souls among the Jews, because there was no one to meet his wrath, and he is despised by them. It follows:

“And his arm saved for himself, and his righteousness itself strengthened him.”

He saved his arm for himself—that is, he raised up his Christ for himself; and his righteousness, which he has against the Jews, itself strengthened him against them. Or his righteousness—that is, Christ’s righteousness—itself strengthened him in the kingdom. Hence he says to the Father: “But because of my innocence you have upheld me and strengthened me in your presence forever” (Ps. 40:13).

[Col. 0538C] But it is pleasing to consider these things concerning evil Catholics. For they say:

“We have waited for light, and behold darkness; for brightness, and we have walked in darkness.” For wicked people often, while through unlawful actions they seek to attain the brightness of prosperity and honor, find the darkness of tribulation and confusion. They add: “We groped for the wall like the blind.” For the perverse grope at the wall like blind men because, when they see good works in their neighbors, they often investigate whether any evils may be hidden; and they labor in anxious searches to discover, perhaps, something they can accuse. They see sound limbs, but, with the eyes of the heart closed, seek a wound by groping. And [Col. 0538D] they stumble at noon as in darkness because the day of a good work shines outwardly, but those who bear within themselves the darkness of their envy stumble in light as though in night: since they cannot accuse the good they see, they seek for accusation an evil they do not see; and because they cannot find it, they stumble and fall at the noon of a good work. And they wander among dark things like dead men because, surrounded by their own darkness, they do not know where they ought rather to turn themselves, since they have lost the life of love. “For whoever hates his brother walks in darkness and does not know where he is going, because darkness has blinded his eyes” (1 John 2:11).—“And whoever does not love remains in death” (1 John 3:14). But because divine mercy sometimes looks upon these also so that they may lament their evils, it is rightly added:

[Col. 0539A] “We shall all roar like bears, and, meditating like doves, we shall moan.”

Again, because they are often oppressed by prolonged afflictions on account of their iniquities, he says: “We have waited for judgment, and it is not there; for salvation, and it is far from us. For our iniquities have multiplied before you, and our sins have answered against us.” For they await the judgment of their deliverance, and it is not there; salvation of liberation, and it shall be far from them, because their sins have answered them by promising and rendering these afflictions. They still confess, saying: “For our crimes are with us, and we have known our iniquities: to sin and lie against the Lord.” For their crimes are with them because they do not deserve pardon. For they sin continually [Col. 0539B] and frequently lie against the Lord by swearing falsely in the Lord’s name. It follows:

“And we turned away, so as not to go after the back of our God, that we might speak calumny and transgression.”—“Whoever says that he abides in Christ ought himself also to walk as he walked” (1 John 2:6). But false Christians turn away from following behind the Lord, because they do not follow his footsteps to the end, but return to the world’s desires. For they speak calumny and transgression when they slander their superiors as transgressing divine commands. Hence they add: “We conceived and spoke words of falsehood from our heart.” For they often conceive and speak from their heart words of falsehood even against the good.

[Col. 0539C] Next: Judgment has been turned backward because now very many people judge carnal things to be better than spiritual, earthly things than heavenly. And righteousness stands far off because they have driven it far from their actions. The street takes its name from breadth, because *πλάτος* (*platos*) means “breadth” in Greek. And what is denoted by the street except those who walk the broad way of the world? Therefore truth has fallen in the streets because lovers of the world trample truth and exalt falsehood. And equity cannot enter this street, which iniquity has occupied. And truth has been reduced to forgetfulness because there is almost no one who remembers truth; instead, all lie to one another, so that no one knows whom he can trust. And whoever withdraws from evil is exposed [Col. 0539D] to plunder, because there is now no one who defends the innocent against the violence of robbers, who plunder their goods so that they spare neither monks nor hermits. “And the Lord saw, and it appeared evil in his eyes, because there is no judgment,” since no one is willing to judge his own actions, but each follows his own will.

And God, who alone knows hearts, saw that there was no man in this people of carnal persons; and he was *aporiatus*, that is, he labored or suffered losses, because there was no one to meet him by praying for this people. And he saved his arm for himself because his power—that is, the power of God—without ceasing saved for himself those whom he willed. And his righteousness itself strengthened him against the rest, so that he would not be bent by any mercy [Col. 0540A] into sparing them, but would exact just vengeance from them. It follows:

VERS. 17.—“He put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation upon his head; he put on garments of vengeance and was covered, as with a cloak, in zeal.”

VERS. 18.—“As for vengeance, as for a recompense of indignation to his enemies, and requital to his foes.”

If the preceding statement concerned the Son, so that it was said that his arm—that is, the Son—saved for himself those whom he willed, it is consequently now said that the Son himself, coming for judgment, has put on righteousness as a breastplate in order to overthrow his adversaries. For he appears surrounded and fortified on every side by righteousness, since he cannot be shown unjust in any respect, so that he can be struck in any point by anyone’s complaints [Col. 0540B]. For he would be exposed to the blows of the complaints of those who perish if he appeared unjust in any respect and struck sinners because of injustice. But he appears righteous on every side when he says: “What more ought I to have done for my vineyard that I did not do for it?” (above, 5:4). Therefore he has put on righteousness because he has done everything that he ought to do. And he has put on this righteousness as a breastplate because his own righteousness defends him as a breastplate does a warrior. For this is why no one can then harm him: no one can show him unjust in anything. And the helmet of salvation is upon his head because he is protected from above by God. He has put on garments of vengeance and is covered as with a cloak of zeal because he is outwardly displayed in such attire as to show all that he possesses zeal of indignation and has come to exact vengeance from his enemies and render recompense for evil to his foes [Col. 0540C]. It follows:

“He will render recompense to the islands.”

VERS. 19.—“And those from the west shall fear the name of the Lord, and those from the east his glory, when he comes like a violent river driven by the Spirit of the Lord.”

VERS. 20.—“And the Redeemer shall come to Zion, and to those in Jacob who turn from iniquity, says the Lord.”

He will render the recompense of just retribution not only to the Jewish people and others who are near, but also to the islands of the Gentiles that are far off. “And those who are from the west shall fear the name of the Lord, and those from the rising of the sun his glory,” because “as lightning comes forth from the east and appears even to the west, so shall the coming of the Son of Man be” (Matt. 24:27). For the Lord will come like a violent river driven by the Spirit of the Lord. For just as a swift torrent carries away whatever it seizes, so the force of his judgment will swiftly sweep all the reprobate together down into Gehenna. And he will come as Redeemer to Zion—that is, to the Church—and to those who turn from iniquity in Jacob, that is, who do penance among the people of God. It follows:

VERS. 21.—“This is my covenant with them, says the Lord.”

This is my covenant with those who turn from iniquity: that they may not perish with the reprobate, but that the Redeemer may come to them, as to the righteous, on the day of judgment. But to Zion, that is, to the Church, it is added:

“My Spirit who is in you, and my words which I have put in your mouth, shall not depart from your mouth nor from the mouth of your seed [Note: [Col. 0541D] Vulgate: ‘from your mouth and from the mouth of your seed.’], says the Lord, from now and forever.”

For the Holy Spirit who is in the Church of the righteous shall never depart from them. Thus the Savior promised his disciples: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may remain with you forever” (John 14:16). And the words of truth which the Lord has put in her mouth shall not depart from her mouth or from the mouth of her seed—that is, those whom she has begotten in Christ Jesus through the Gospel—because the Church’s preaching shall not fail until [Col. 0541B] the end of the age. From now on—that is, from the time when the Spirit was given and God’s words were placed in the mouth of the Church—they shall not fail forever.

Or it is said to Isaiah: “My Spirit who is in you, and my words which I have put in your mouth, shall not fail from your mouth,” nor from the mouth of your children and grandchildren, so that every generation in succession may be indicated: namely, that the grace of the prophets may come to the apostles and to the rest who have believed from Israel. And what follows, “from now and forever,” accords with that saying: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matt. 24:35). It follows:

## CHAPTER LX
[Col. 0541C] **VERSE 1.—** “Arise, be enlightened [Note: [Col. 0542D] Elsewhere: ‘Be enlightened, Jerusalem,’ etc.], because your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you.”

“Arise,” he says, “you Zion, that is, the Church, because ‘it is now the hour for us to rise from sleep’ (Rom. XIII, 11). And be enlightened, because the darkness has passed away and the true light now shines. Therefore be enlightened, because the light has come, the Lord Jesus, who says: ‘I came as light into the world, that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness’ (John XII, 46). And the glory of the Lord has risen upon you, because ‘the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father’ (John I, 14). It follows:

**VERSE 2.—** “For behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gloom the peoples.”

[Col. 0541D] On the day of judgment darkness shall cover the earth—that is, earthly people—and gloom the peoples of the reprobate, because the day of the Lord shall come, because the day of cloud and tempest is near. “But upon you the Lord shall arise,” that is, the Lord shall appear in his splendor, as he promised through Malachi: “The sun of righteousness shall arise,” he says, “for those who fear my name” (Mal. IV, 2). And his glory shall be seen in you, “when he comes,” according to the Apostle, “to be glorified in his saints and to be made marvelous in all who have believed” (II Thess. I, 10). But at the beginning, what was to be done is added:

[Col. 0542A] **VERSE 3.—** “And nations shall walk in your light, and kings in the splendor of your rising.”

The nations shall walk in the way of uprightness and in the light of the Gospel by which you are enlightened. And kings shall walk in the splendor of your rising—that is, the apostles, who saw from the beginning the radiance of the Savior’s miracles and the beginning of the nascent Church. For the apostles are kings, having been established as rulers of peoples. It follows:

**VERSE 4.—** “Lift up your eyes round about and see: all these have gathered together; they have come to you.”

Turn your eyes, he says, toward every part of the world, because all these who are around you have gathered into the sheepfold of the faithful and have come to you for help. Or this could have been said to the primitive Church on the day of Pentecost, because those who had gathered from the whole world for the feast day [Col. 0542B] (Acts II, 5) came to you, because they receive the apostles’ preaching. It follows:

“Your sons shall come from afar, and your daughters shall rise from beside you.” From afar—that is, from great iniquities—as Jeremiah admonishes: “You who have fled the sword, come; do not stand still; remember God from afar, and let Jerusalem rise upon your heart” (Jer. LI, 50). For to flee the sword is, by repentance, to forestall the impending sentence of future judgment. But whoever flees this sword must not stand still; rather, by the merit of good action he must hasten to draw near to Christ.

“And your daughters shall rise from beside you.”

From the side of the Redeemer, wounded on the cross for us, because the weak derive more benefit from his humanity and passion [Col. 0542C] than from his divinity and the other mysteries. Hence the Apostle says to such persons: “I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (I Cor. II, 2). Or, “from beside you,” that is, from nearby: your daughters shall rise from lesser sins.

And it should be noted that sons—that is, the robust—are said to come from afar, while daughters—that is, weak souls—are said to rise from beside you. For according to the evangelical saying, that debtor “loves the creditor more to whom more is forgiven by him; but he to whom less is forgiven loves less” (Luke VII, 47). Or sons are said to come from afar—that is, from distant lands—and daughters to rise from beside you—that is, from neighboring regions.

**VERSE 5.—** “Then you shall see and overflow; your heart shall marvel and be enlarged, when the multitude of the sea has been converted to you and the strength of the nations has come to you.”

When the multitude of the sea, or of the world, has been converted to you, and the strength of the nations has come to you, so that everything in the age or in the world may be yours, then you shall see what I promised you by their conversion; and you shall overflow with spiritual delights like an inundating river; and your heart shall marvel at so great a change of affairs; and it shall be enlarged when you see them converted to the love of truth. It follows:

**VERSE 6.—** “A flood of camels shall cover you, dromedaries of Midian and Ephah.”

[Col. 0543A] What is signified by camels except the crooked minds of the Gentiles? Dromedaries too are swift camels. For there is a breed of camels smaller in stature but swifter, from which it takes its name. For δρόμος (*dromos*) in Greek is called a course or swiftness. They can travel one hundred miles and more in a single day. Midian means “iniquity.” And what is figured by the dromedaries of Midian except Gentiles crooked and swift in the course of perverse action? Ephah likewise is interpreted “unrestrained.” And who was unrestrained except the Gentile people, bound by no law but badly left to itself? The dromedaries of Ephah, therefore, are called Gentiles who, among that people unrestrained by harmful liberty, wandered everywhere toward all the evils they desired. Thus the flood of camels covered the Church, and the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah, because now among this people of believers nothing is seen except converted Gentiles. For so great is the multitude of nations who have believed in comparison with those who came from the circumcision. Of these he further adds:

“All shall come from Sheba, bringing gold and incense and proclaiming praise to the Lord.”

Sheba is called captivity or a net. By Sheba, Gentile life or unbelief is signified, where the human race was held captive in the net of the ancient enemy. Therefore all came from Sheba because all nations have been converted by Christ. Gold belongs to the tribute of a king, incense to sacrifice offered to God. Thus the Gentiles bring gold and incense to Christ when they confess in him royal divinity and divine majesty. Yet by gold may be expressed [Col. 0543C] the splendor of religion and the brightness of innocence, changed into the blackness of guilt, over which Jeremiah grieved when he said: “How the gold has grown dim!” (Lam. IV, 1). But by incense, which is burned for God, the power of prayer is signified, as the Psalmist says: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight, O Lord” (Ps. CXL, 2). Thus the Gentiles bring gold when, living precious lives, they hasten to Christ in order that they may see him in his kingdom. They also bring incense when they burn the thoughts of the flesh through holy practices of prayer upon the altar of the heart, so that by heavenly desire they may exhale something sweet to God. And they proclaim God with praise because they preach his glory with others. It follows:

**VERSE 7.—** “All the flocks of Kedar shall be gathered to you; the rams of Nebaioth shall minister to you; they shall be offered upon my pleasing altar, and I shall glorify the house of my majesty.”

Kedar indeed means “darkness,” while Nebaioth means “prophecy.” And what is figured by the flocks of darkness except Gentiles, who, born in the darkness of their ignorance, were like brute animals while they did not use reason to know God? And what is signified by the rams of prophecy except the Hebrews, who, being like clean and domestic animals familiar with God, knew beforehand through prophecy that Christ would come? Therefore all the flocks of Kedar are gathered to the Church [Col. 0544A] when the whole Gentile world is brought to faith; and the apostles minister to her the rams of Nebaioth when they convert Jews to her. These flocks of Kedar and rams of Nebaioth are offered to God in grateful service—that is, as sacrifice—upon the altar of faith. For God’s pleasing altar is faith in Jesus Christ, whom, according to the Apostle, “God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood” (Rom. III, 25). Upon this altar the whole people of the elect is offered to God when they “present their bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God” (Rom. XII, 1). And when the whole world is converted by Christ, he himself glorifies the house of his majesty, that is, his Church. For Christ “is as a son in his house, whose house we are” (Heb. III, 3).

[Col. 0544B] We may, however, understand the rams of Nebaioth—that is, of prophecy—especially as the apostles, of whom the Prophet had long ago said: “Bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. XXVIII, 1); and: “I shall offer to you fat burnt offerings with the incense of rams” (Ps. LXV, 15). They minister to the Church according to the Lord’s saying: “Whoever is greater among you shall be your minister” (Matt. XXIII, 11). Of these he adds in admiration:

**VERSE 8.—** “Who are these who fly like clouds and like doves to their windows?”

The preachers of the New Testament are rightly compared to clouds, because they rain by words and flash by miracles. They are said to fly like clouds because, while living on earth, everything they did was outside the earth. Hence it is said through a certain cloud: “Though walking in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh” (II Cor. X, 3). The earlier fathers used marriage, begot children, possessed property, and attended to household concerns. But when the prophet saw these men despising earthly things, drawing near in mind to heavenly things, raining by words, and flashing by miracles—men whom both holy thought and an exalted life suspended above earthly contagions—he surely calls them both flying and clouds.
