Our windows are the eyes, because through them the soul looks upon what it desires outwardly. The dove is a simple creature, free from the malice of gall. Thus they are like doves at their windows who desire nothing in this world, look upon everything simply, and are not drawn by a desire of rapacity toward the things they see. But, by contrast, he is a kite, not a dove, at his windows who pants with a desire of rapacity for the things he considers with his eyes. And because through these men the whole world was to know God, he fittingly adds at once:

**VERSE 9.—** “For the islands await me, and the ships of the sea from the beginning, that I may bring your sons from afar, their silver and gold with them, for the name of the Lord your God and for the Holy One of Israel, who [Note: [Col. 0543D] Elsewhere: ‘because.’] has glorified you.”

The sea signifies the turbulent, swelling waves of this world, in which all the wicked who delight unjustly are like fish given over to the depths and do not direct their minds toward heavenly joys. The islands may be understood as the various nations and provinces. The ships of the sea are Churches, which through the waves of this age make for the harbor of salvation and stability, that is, for the land of the living. Therefore the islands and ships of the sea awaited the Lord from the beginning, because before regions and Churches that are in this world could receive his faith, he first had to come to them through his preachers. He therefore came to them first, in order to bring to the name of the Lord the sons of mother Church from afar—that is, from Gentile life—and their silver and gold—that is, their eloquence and natural wisdom—with them, so that their eloquence and understanding, joined to the gifts of heavenly inspiration, might serve God. Of these he adds:

[Col. 0545B] **VERSE 10.—** “And the sons of foreigners shall build your walls, and their kings shall minister to you.”

The sons of foreigners are the sons of unbelievers converted to faith. They build the walls of the Church because in word and deed they construct the bulwarks of her defenses, disciplines, and virtues. And their kings minister to her because scarcely any king can be found under the whole heaven who does not rejoice to serve the Church. It follows:

“In my indignation I struck you, and in my reconciliation I had mercy on you.”

I struck you in the time of tribulation, and afterward, having had mercy, I gave you grace. Or: I reconciled you to myself, formerly afflicted and handed over to captivity among the Jewish people, in the calling of the nations. It follows:

[Col. 0545C] **VERSE 11.—** “And your gates shall be continually open; by day and by night they shall not be shut, that the strength of nations may be brought to you and their kings led in.”

The gates of the Church remain open by day and by night because the Church is always ready to receive those who wish to enter the faith. For her gates are not shut either in the day, that is, in prosperity, or in the night, that is, in adversity; rather, without interruption they stand open to all who flee to her. And their kings also shall be led together to Christ, that all kings may worship him and all nations serve him, and that the strength of nations flocking to faith may be brought to her. It follows:

**VERSE 12.—** “For the nation and kingdom that shall not serve you shall perish, and the nations shall be laid waste in desolation.”

Whatever nation or kingdom does not wish to serve the Church by obeying her commands shall undoubtedly perish forever. But even in the present, unbelief and disobedience cause many to perish from the earth. And the nations that persist in unbelief are devastated, so that they are reduced to desolation. It follows:

**VERSE 13.—** “The glory of Lebanon shall come to you: fir tree and box tree and pine together, to adorn the place of my sanctification; and I shall glorify the place of my feet.”

Lebanon frequently signifies the temple of the Jews in the Scriptures. Hence Zechariah, when he foretold the burning of that temple, said: “Open your gates, O Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars” (Zech. XI, 1). For Lebanon is very renowned and beautiful above the other mountains, fittingly figuring that temple once noble above all others. But it has now long been since that temple was burned and its glory passed to the Church. The fir tree, because it grows very high, signifies the saints, who, imitating Paul, rise in mind above themselves toward God. The box tree, which does not grow tall but retains its greenness at every season, expresses the humble, whose greenness never withers because their goodness never fails. The pine abounds in resin, bears fruit at every season, and is always seen as green; it signifies the elect, overflowing with spiritual grace, possessing the unfading vigor of righteousness, and always displaying in themselves the fruits of good works.

The Lord therefore promises these precious trees to adorn the place of his sanctification, which is the Church. For outside the Catholic Church there is no place of divine sanctification. The place of his feet is also this same Church, in which he is accustomed spiritually to stand and walk. Elsewhere it has been said of this place of sanctification and of his feet: “We shall enter into his tabernacle” (Ps. CXXXI, 7); “God stood in the synagogue of gods” (Ps. LXXXI, 1); and “He walks in the midst of the seven golden lampstands” (Apoc. II, 2). He therefore promises to adorn and glorify this place, as we now see has happened. It follows:

[Col. 0546C] **VERSE 14.—** “And the bent sons of those who humbled you shall come to you, and all who spoke against you shall worship the footsteps of your feet.”

The bent—that is, humbled—came penitently to the Church: the sons of the persecutors, who, while afflicting her, had humbled her. And all who had spoken against her during the time of persecution, once peace had been granted, fell at her feet asking forgiveness. It follows:

“And they shall call you the city of the Lord, Zion of the Holy One of Israel.”

**VERSE 15.—** “Because you were forsaken, hated, and there was no one passing through you.”

Those who had formerly abandoned her, separated her from their fellowship, and held her in hatred called her Zion, the city of the supreme King—that is, the holy city of the God of Israel. None of them passed through her, because no one deigned to look upon her or to walk according to her ways. Their way of life was far from the Church. It follows:

“I shall make you the exaltation of ages, joy from generation to generation.”

Here “exaltation” (*superbia*) signifies not the swelling of pride but the freedom of deliverance. For Wisdom also says of this kind of exaltation: “With me are riches and glory, splendid wealth and righteousness” (Prov. VIII, 18). He therefore says: “I shall make you the exaltation of ages,” that is, a status of elevation that will endure through all ages; and I shall make you joy in the generation of this world and in the generation to come. It follows:

[Col. 0547A] **VERSE 16.—** “And you shall suck the milk of nations, and you shall be nursed at the breast of kings; and you shall know that I, the Lord, am saving you, and that your Redeemer is the Mighty One of Jacob.”

You shall suck the milk of nations when you receive from the mouths of Gentiles converted to faith the word of sacred admonition. And you shall be nursed at the breast of kings because from kings also you shall draw the sweet drink of the word, by which you may advance and be nourished. For pious kings too are accustomed to offer the people of God words of sacred admonition.

And when faith has advanced so far that you receive the milk of divine preaching from nations and kings, then indeed you shall know that I am the Lord saving you, and your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob, who redeemed you from all tribulations and made the kings who persecuted you your nourisher. Perhaps someone will understand these kings as the apostles and preachers. But the promise here seems greater to me if we understand it of the kings of the earth, especially since the discussion now concerns the time when persecutions had ceased and peace had been granted to the Church everywhere. It follows:

**VERSE 17.—** “Instead of bronze I shall bring gold; instead of iron I shall bring silver; instead of wood, bronze; and instead of stones, iron.”

When it is said, “Instead of bronze I shall bring gold, and instead of iron I shall bring silver,” bronze and iron are rejected. Again, when it is added, “Instead of wood I shall bring bronze, and instead of stones, iron,” bronze and iron, which were rejected, are promised in another sense, because what is rejected or removed pertains to the old life, while what is promised pertains to the new.

By bronze, which is very resonant, the speech of preachers who lack love is signified. Hence the Apostle says: “If I speak with the tongues of human beings and of angels” (I Cor. XIII, 1), and so forth. And because charity, which is more precious than all virtues, is signified by gold, the name of gold expresses the precious manner of life of the saints, in whom charity shines. Of such people Jeremiah says: “The illustrious sons of Zion, clothed in finest gold” (Lam. IV, 2). The Lord brings gold instead of bronze when, in place of those who preached without charity, he gives the Church teachers adorned with charity.

[Col. 0547C] What is signified by iron if not those who always use iron to strike others? And what is signified by silver if not those who shine with the brightness of heavenly eloquence? For Solomon says: “The lips of the righteous are choice silver” (Prov. X, 20). Therefore the Lord brings silver instead of iron when, in place of those who used iron and weapons, he grants the Church those who shine among their neighbors through sacred utterances.

Wood is easily shaken by the wind and is often overturned. By it the carnal and weak are signified, those who are quickly moved by adversities and broken by them. Bronze, which remains unharmed by rust for a longer time, demonstrates the strongest long-suffering of the patient. Therefore bronze is promised instead of wood—that is, the strong and long-suffering instead of the weak and impatient.

What, however, do stones signify if not the hardness and insensibility of the hearts of those who have become hardened in iniquity? Iron signifies strong men, who pierce the hearts of sinners with the sharpest swords of their tongues. Hence Job says: “Iron is taken from the earth, and stone, loosened by heat, is turned into bronze” (Job XXVIII, 2).

Iron is taken from the earth when a strong defender of the Church is separated from the earthly conduct he previously followed. And stone, loosened by heat, is turned into bronze when a hard and cold heart is melted by the fire of divine love and changed into true strength, so that the sinner who had previously been insensible may afterward become strong through authority and resonant through preaching. Therefore the Lord brings iron instead of stones when, in place of those who are hard and cold in wickedness, he gives the Church strong and penetrating preachers. It follows:

“And I shall make your visitation peace, and your overseers righteousness.”

Previously the Lord had visited the Church through scourges of correction, as it is written: “I shall visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with stripes” (Ps. LXXXIII, 33). But now he promises to visit her through peace, granting her enduring peace and kindling her more fervently toward his love through the benefits of tranquility.

Yet because, in the time of peace, all who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution (II Tim. III, 12), the Lord will more fully make the visitation of his Church peace on the last day, when through his coming and visitation she will receive everlasting peace.

He promises that the future overseers of the Church will be so righteous that they will themselves be righteousness, as we see that iron becomes fire when it is intensely inflamed. But then her overseers will more truly be righteousness when, beholding the very fountain of righteousness, they become like him, because they will then retain in themselves no remnants of injustice, however slight. Hence he adds:

[Col. 0548C] **VERSE 18.—** “Iniquity shall no longer be heard in your land, nor devastation and destruction within your borders.”

For in that land of the living, where the Church will then dwell, iniquity shall never be heard, because none of her children will any longer sin. Nor shall devastation or destruction be heard within her borders, because no hostile attack will be present to lay waste or destroy that blessed region from any side. It follows:

“And salvation shall occupy your walls, and praise your gates.”

The walls of the Church, which are now frequently assaulted by enemies, are the defenses of virtues. Her gates, at which lamentation is now often heard, are the holy preachers who bring into her those who come to faith and mourn those who perish. But then salvation shall occupy her walls and praise her gates, when there will no longer be any attacker and no one among the number of the righteous will be able to perish; rather, each will sing endless thanks and praises to the Creator for his salvation. It follows:

**VERSE 19.—** “You shall no longer have the sun for light by day, nor shall the brightness of the moon enlighten you; but the Lord shall be your everlasting light, and your God your glory.”

**VERSE 20.—** “Your sun shall no longer set, and your moon shall not wane, because the Lord shall be your everlasting light, and the days of your mourning shall be completed.”

[Col. 0549A] The sun and moon will no longer illuminate the Church, but the splendor of the Creator’s countenance, which will then be seen as it is. “For that city has no need of sun or moon to shine in it. For the glory of God shall enlighten it, and its lamp is the Lamb” (Apoc. XXI, 23). God will be glory to that city, because “when he appears, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is” (I John III, 2). For all who see his glory will receive the likeness of his glory. Hence Paul says: “We all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same glory” (II Cor. III, 18).

It has also been said concerning us that neither the sun nor the moon will henceforth seek their setting, but will remain forever in the places in which they were created, lest, if they came to their setting, they perhaps offer some brightness to those who have been condemned in hell. For since night will no longer exist but perpetual day, it follows that the sun will no longer set and the moon will not wane, because then “the light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun sevenfold, like the light of seven days” (above, XXX, 26).

But this is said to the Church because her sun shall no longer set and her moon shall not wane: she will no longer be beneath the sun or need the sunlight, but God shall be her everlasting light, so that she may enjoy the splendor of her Creator forever and not be subject to created light. And when she has attained this blessedness, the days of her mourning shall be completed—that is, ended—because, according to John, “there shall no longer be mourning, nor crying, nor pain” (Apoc. XXI, 4). It follows:

[Col. 0549C] **VERSE 21.—** “But your people shall all be righteous; they shall inherit the land forever: the shoot of my planting, the work of my hand, for glorification.”

The people of the Church shall be righteous, and all who are in that people shall be righteous; they shall all inherit forever the land of everlasting stability and rest. For the heavenly planting of the right hand caused them to sprout in the Church. In contrast, it was said of the Pharisees: “Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted shall be uprooted” (Matt. XV, 13).

Therefore this planting of the righteous, which the Father planted, can in no way be uprooted from the land of the living but shall possess it perpetually. They are also the work of his hand, because “he made us, and not we ourselves” (Ps. IX, 3). “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Eph. II, 10). And this work was made for glorification, because he prepared vessels of mercy for glory. Or he made this work—that is, the righteous—for his own glorification. It follows:

**VERSE 22.—** “The least shall become a thousand, and the smallest a most mighty nation.”

The least of the righteous shall become a thousand, because each, according to his measure, shall possess complete perfection—that is, the perfect number of spiritual men. For completion is represented by the number one thousand. And the smallest shall become a most mighty nation, because he shall bring forth a nation of virtues prevailing over the nation of vices. Or then the one who proved faithful in little shall be set over much.

“I, the Lord, shall do this suddenly in its time.”

Everything that I have now promised I shall do suddenly and without difficulty when the time arrives in which it ought to be done. For whatever he promised concerning the calling of the Gentiles and the temporal glorification of the Church, he quickly fulfilled when the time came. Thus there is no doubt that he will also faithfully fulfill what he has added concerning the future blessedness of the saints, as soon as the time arrives in which he promised to do it. It follows.

## CHAPTER LXI

**VERSE 1.—** “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me; he sent me to announce good news to the meek, to heal the brokenhearted, and to proclaim release to captives and opening to those shut up.”

**VERSE 2.—** “To proclaim a year pleasing to the Lord and a day of vengeance to our God, to console all who mourn.”

**VERSE 3.—** “And to give strength [Note: [Col. 0549] Our edition: ‘that I might appoint for the mourners of Zion, and give them,’ etc.] to the mourners of Zion, and to give them a crown instead of ashes, the oil of joy instead of mourning, and a garment of praise instead of a spirit of sorrow.”

Having overcome the devil’s threefold temptation, as Luke relates: “Jesus went out in the power of the Spirit into Galilee, and a report about him went out through the whole region. And he taught in their synagogues and was glorified by all. And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, and entered the synagogue according to his custom on the Sabbath day, and rose to read. And the book of Isaiah the prophet was handed to him. And when he had unrolled the book, he found the place where it was written: ‘The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me,’ etc. And when he had folded the book, he gave it back to the attendant and sat down, and the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him. Then he began to say to them: ‘Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.’ And they all bore witness to him and marveled at the words of grace that proceeded from his mouth” (Luke IV, 4).

It is therefore clear who is speaking: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me.” It is plainly he who went out in the power of the Spirit into Galilee. For earlier in the Gospel it is also read that “the Spirit descended upon him in bodily form like a dove” (Luke III, 22). By this Spirit he himself was anointed, because, according to John, God anointed him with his Spirit (Luke IV, 18). He “sent him to evangelize the poor, or to announce good news to the meek” (ibid.) and humble, because “he came into Galilee preaching the Gospel of the kingdom of God and saying: ‘The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has drawn near. Repent and believe the Gospel’” (Mark I, 14).

He heals the broken and crushed in heart when he gives hope to the despairing and promises kingdoms to the penitent, so that they may come to the kingdom of God. He sends the broken forth in remission when he forgives the sins of the afflicted; and to the one who was held captive by the devil and exiled from paradise, he proclaims release from captivity when he commands him to repent, so that he may return to the kingdom of God, which has drawn near. He announces sight to the blind when he illumines by the light of his preaching those who did not have the light of the heart. Or he proclaims opening to those shut up in the prison of the heart when he commands them to confess their sins.

[Col. 0551A] The acceptable and pleasing year of the Lord is this time of reconciliation and grace, in which God graciously receives all who turn to repentance. Therefore let no one allow this pleasing year to pass by empty, because afterward there will come the day of recompense and vengeance for iniquities, when each person will be repaid according to his work.

Moreover, by “year” he understands the multitude of the redeemed. For just as a year is named from a multitude of days, so that innumerable totality of the elect is completed from the gathering of all good things. Therefore, proclaiming this year of perfect multitude, the Savior says: “To proclaim a year pleasing to the Lord.” For the year of the Lord’s reconciliation is proclaimed when a people of believers is announced as destined to be illumined by the light of truth.

The Lord was also sent to console all who mourn, because he graciously deigned to relieve the tears of the humble through the promise of future joy, saying: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V, 5). These indeed are the mourners of Zion—that is, of the people of God—because they mourned the people of God, expelled from paradise and miserably possessed by the devil in the captivity of this present exile. To them the Lord gave strength so that they might powerfully overcome the devil and free the people of God, saying: “Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over every power of the enemy” (Luke X, 19).

“And he gave them a crown instead of ashes.” Because, after humbling themselves and mournfully lamenting Zion, they rejoiced in her deliverance. Those who mourn are customarily sprinkled with ashes, and those who rejoice are adorned with crowns. The multitude of disciples is called the joy and crown of the teacher, as Paul says to those whom he had won for Christ: “My joy and my crown: stand firm thus in the Lord, beloved” (Phil. IV, 1).

Therefore, “I gave them a crown instead of ashes,” because I made them rejoice over the salvation of converts, when they had previously mourned over the perdition of sinners. And instead of mourning he gave them the oil of joy, that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit, which anoints and gladdens the minds it fills. He also gave them the garment of praise, that is, gladness of mind, instead of a spirit of sorrow. For the garment of praise is the disposition of a heart that joyfully renders praises to God. It follows:

“And they shall be called in her the strong ones of righteousness, the planting of the Lord for glorification.” In her—that is, in Zion—those shall be called strong, not those who are strong in sin, but those who are strong to perform righteousness. These are the Lord’s planting, rooted and founded by the Lord in charity. And this planting was made for glorification. It follows:

[Col. 0552A] **VERSE 4.—** “And the deserts of old shall be built up; they shall raise up the ancient ruins and restore the deserted and ruined cities from generation to generation.”

The men strong in righteousness in Zion shall build up the deserts—that is, they shall place within the building of the Church the nations whom God had abandoned from the beginning—and they shall raise up the ancient ruins, that is, what fell long ago through Adam they shall now raise again through Christ.

And they shall restore for the better the cities which, in the ancient and new generation—that is, before the Savior’s coming—had been deserted by the Lord and ruined by perverse actions, so that they may recognize their Creator, serve him faithfully with reformed conduct, and be inhabited by him. We may understand these cities figuratively as either gatherings of nations or human minds.

But the Lord, turning his address toward the aforesaid strong ones of righteousness—that is, the holy preachers coming from the circumcision—adds:

**VERSE 5.—** “And foreigners shall stand and feed your flocks, and the sons of foreigners shall be your farmers and vinedressers.”

**VERSE 7.—** “But you shall be called priests of the Lord; you shall be called ministers of our God. You shall consume the strength of the nations, and you shall exult in their glory.”

The Gentiles were formerly strangers both to God and to the way of life of Israel. After they stood firm in faith, many of them were placed over Churches and fed the flocks of these strong ones of righteousness—that is, the peoples whom the apostles had converted to faith.

The sons of foreigners were likewise those who, carnally begotten by unbelieving parents, abandoned their errors and came to Christ. They became farmers and vinedressers because they cultivated with the hoes of holy preaching the field of God, which is the people of believers, and the vineyard, which is the human being.

The apostles, however, were called priests of the Lord—that is, those who offer sacred things to him—with a great privilege of honor. They were also called his ministers, because authority was entrusted to them, and through their giving and ministry the Church received whatever she possesses. Hence they say: “Let a man regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God” (I Cor. IV, 1).

[Col. 0552D] They also consumed the strength of the nations, because they incorporated the whole Gentile world into themselves, transferring it into the inner parts of the Church. More particularly, however, the strength of the nations is the triumph of the martyrs. And they took pride in their glory; that is, they received grounds for exultation and confidence, saying: “For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory, if not you before the Lord?” (1 Thess. 2:19). Then, unless I am mistaken, the discourse turns to the faithless priests of the Jews, who persecuted the apostles, that is, the true priests, when it adds:

VERSE 7.—“For your double confusion and shame they shall praise their portion; therefore in their land they shall possess double things; everlasting joy shall be theirs.”

[Col. 0553A] VERSE 8.—“For I, the Lord, love judgment and hate robbery in the burnt offering.”

For when the righteous Judge appears, examining the thoughts and deeds of every individual, then the chief priests, who commanded the apostles not to speak in the name of Jesus, and all the hypocritical Pharisees, being reprobate together, will be doubly confounded and ashamed: inwardly and outwardly, both before the eyes of those standing by and in their own consciences. Conversely, all will praise the portion of the apostles and believers, so that from the confusion of the hostile party the glory of the elect party may appear greater.

Or this is still said to the apostles: because you had a twofold shame, both over the Jewish people, who had departed from God, and over the nations, [Col. 0553B] who served idols, you shall see them, converted to the fear of God, praise their portion—that is, God, whom they alone chose. And as the reprobate shall be doubly confounded, so the righteous in their own land—that is, in the kingdom of heaven—shall possess double things, because they shall enjoy perpetual blessedness not only of their souls but also of their bodies; and in place of temporal sorrow they shall have everlasting joy. They shall possess double things in their own land, so that they may rejoice also in that very flesh in which they endured pains and torments for the Lord.

Nor is it surprising if this exchange occurs on both sides: that the reprobate, who now rejoice and boast, should then be held in double confusion, while the elect, now sorrowful and despised, possess double goods. For our Lord loves [Col. 0553C] judgment and will render to each what is just. And he detests robbery in a burnt offering, so that he rejects the sacrifices of the Jews, which they brought from plunder and fraudulent gain, and condemns all alms and offerings made from what has been stolen; for “he who offers sacrifice from the substance of the poor is like one who sacrifices a son in the sight of his father” (Ecclus. 34:24).

Concerning the aforesaid worthy ministers of the New Testament, he added:

“And I will give their work in truth, and I will make an everlasting covenant with them.”

For he gave their work in truth, so that, unlike under the Law, there might no longer be a shadow of truth, but truth itself. And he made with [Col. 0553D] them an everlasting covenant or compact—not such a covenant as he had given to Moses, which passed away, but the covenant of the Gospel, of which he says: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matt. 24:35). Of them he further adds:

VERSE 9.—“And their seed shall be known among the nations, and their offspring in the midst of the peoples. For all who see them shall recognize them, because these are the seed which the Lord has blessed.”

For we plainly see this. In every people and nation the race of Christians is recognized, the race disseminated from the apostles; and it is known that God’s blessing rests upon them all. Whoever sees them will recognize at first glance that they are the seed blessed by the Lord. For who, from their manner of life, gentleness, self-restraint, hospitality, and other [Col. 0554A] virtues, would not recognize the people of God? The Savior still speaks, saying:

VERSE 10.—“Rejoicing, I will rejoice in the Lord, and my soul shall exult in my God, because he has clothed me with the garment of salvation and surrounded me with the robe of joy, like a bridegroom adorned with a crown and like a bride bedecked with her jewels.”

He says that he will rejoice in the Lord and that his blessed soul will exult in his God, because he will rejoice eternally in the Father, sitting at the right hand of Majesty on high. And why will he rejoice in him? “Because he has clothed me with the garment of salvation”: that is, he sent him in the likeness of sinful flesh, so that, fortified against every sickness of vice by the garment of salvation—that is, by his most holy flesh—diabolical temptation might not penetrate to his inward parts.

[Col. 0554B] He is clothed with the garment of salvation and health, because in the flesh he assumed he endured no contradiction and no tempting vice; and he is surrounded with the robe of righteousness, because he possessed all righteousness and holiness in the flesh with which he clothed himself. And he is surrounded with this robe as the Bridegroom of the Church, adorned with the crown of the everlasting kingdom. Yet because he and the Church are one person, he is also surrounded as a bride. For the head and the body, as is clearly shown here, are one Christ. The one and same person, as we see here, says: “He has surrounded me with the robe of righteousness, like a bridegroom adorned with a crown and like a bride bedecked with her jewels.” This is not because he is incomplete without the body, but because he deigned to be complete with us, though he is always complete without us.

[Col. 0554C] For how are we his body unless Christ is one also with us? Thus he calls himself bridegroom according to the head, bride according to the body. Two are seen, and yet he is one. Therefore what was said, “Rejoicing, I will rejoice in the Lord,” and so forth, must also apply to the body. For every elect person who refused to rejoice in the world will rejoice wholly, in soul and flesh, in the Lord, when this mortal nature has put on immortality. For while living here, one is clothed in the garment of salvation in the mind and surrounded by the robe of righteousness in action. When we are clothed with a garment, we are encompassed on every side.

Therefore whoever is guarded on every side from the sickness of sin through God’s grace is clothed with the garment of salvation; [Col. 0554D] and whoever is protected on every side by good work is surrounded with the robe of righteousness, so as to leave no part of his conduct exposed naked to sin. For one who is righteous in some actions and unrighteous in others has, as it were, covered one side and left the other bare. Therefore whoever is righteous on every side in all his works is surrounded with this robe of righteousness. And with such a garment the Church of the elect, or bride of the eternal King, is clothed—adorned with precious virtues as with jewels, and adorned upon her head, which is Christ, with a royal diadem. It is fittingly added:

VERSE 11.—“For as the earth brings forth its shoot, and as a garden causes its seed to germinate, so the Lord God shall cause righteousness and praise to germinate before all nations.”

[Col. 0555A] For as the earth brings forth its shoot, so the faithful soul brings the shoot of good thought into action. And as a garden makes its seed germinate, so the mind of the elect brings the seed of the divine word that it has received into the fruit of action. Yet God is said to do this, because he himself grants his elect that they may do it. Thus the elect proclaim to all nations beneath heaven the righteousness of upright living and the praise of preaching. After this Isaiah, bearing the person of all the prophets, speaks.

## CHAPTER LXII

VERSE 1.—“For Zion’s sake I shall not be silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I shall not rest, until her righteous one goes forth like splendor and her Savior is kindled like a lamp.”

For Zion and Jerusalem signify the faithful people. For their instruction Isaiah was not silent, nor did he cease from prophesying, until her righteous one—that is, Christ—went forth like splendor. For “all the prophets and the Law prophesied until John, and from then on the kingdom of God is proclaimed” (Luke 16:16). The prophets began to fall silent in John’s time, when Gospel preaching took its beginning. At that time the righteous one whom Zion awaited went forth like splendor from the Virgin’s womb: immediately an angel, appearing to the shepherds with great brightness, announced his birth, and the magi saw a star in the East. And he was kindled as a lamp, because, radiant with the light of miracles and teaching, he shone upon the world and, driving away the darkness of sin, brought to humankind the light of his grace.

[Col. 0555B] Therefore the prophet did not cease speaking for Zion’s sake until her righteous one went forth like splendor, because it was necessary for believers of that time to possess the prophetic word, to which, by doing good, they might give heed as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day of the Savior’s coming dawned and the sun of righteousness illuminated the world. After speaking of such future splendor, the prophet fittingly adds, saying to Zion:

VERSE 2.—“And the nations shall see your righteous one, and all kings your illustrious one.”

For the nations and kings of the whole world shall see him, because he will be kindled like a lamp in order to shine upon all. It follows:

“And you shall be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord [Col. 0555D] shall name.”

You shall receive a new name, because you shall be called Christian. It follows:

VERSE 3.—“And you shall be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord, and a royal diadem in the hand of your God.”

For Christ will possess you, that he may be crowned from you in his glory, namely with a royal diadem. For the choir of all the saints will be Christ’s crown in that kingdom of blessedness. It follows:

VERSE 4.—“You shall no longer be called Forsaken, and your land shall no more be called Desolate; but you shall be called My delight is in her, and your land shall be inhabited, because the Lord has delighted in you. [Note: [Col. 0555D] Thus both manuscripts.]”

[Col. 0556A] Formerly Zion was called forsaken, because it was said that, on account of Adam’s sin, God had forsaken his people, whom he expelled from Paradise and deprived of the light of his vision. Its land can be understood as its mind, according to the words: “My soul is like land without water before you” (Ps. 142:6). This land was called desolate because it said that it had no consolation when it did not find redemption. But when it finds the Redeemer, it shall not be called forsaken, because it shall never be forsaken by him who says: “I am with you always, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

But from that time its name has been called My delight is in her, because God declares that his will is in his people, since by Christ’s grace it has become accustomed to fulfill [Col. 0556B] his commands, which it had been unable to fulfill while deprived of grace’s help. And the land of its heart shall no longer be called desolate, but shall be called inhabited, because it shall have the consolation of the Holy Spirit and shall be inhabited by him who says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23). And this shall happen because the Lord has delighted in her. According to the good pleasure of his grace, he shall inhabit the land, as it were, of her soul. It follows:

VERSE 5.—“For the young man shall dwell with the virgin, and your children shall dwell in you; and the bridegroom shall rejoice over the bride, and your God shall rejoice over you.”

The young man shall dwell with the virgin: that is, John the apostle with the Lord’s mother. And Zion’s children dwelt in her—that is, in the Church; namely, that multitude “of believers [whose] heart and soul were one” (Acts 4:32). And the bridegroom, Christ, rejoiced over the bride, the Church, when he saw her everywhere growing and advancing in religion. And her God rejoiced over Zion, that is, over the faithful people. Since after this rulers of the Church were established in individual places throughout the world, it fittingly follows:

VERSE 6.—“Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen; all day and all night they shall never be silent.”

[Col. 0556D] The walls of Jerusalem are the defenses of Church discipline. Upon these walls the Lord appointed watchmen all day and all night, because in congregations of religious persons he ordained superiors who might guard the observance of discipline day and night, lest those subject to them transgress the walls of sacred institution. They are never silent, because by continual exhortations they admonish the citizens dwelling within the walls of this city to guard themselves, and diligently make them cautious against the snares of spiritual enemies.

Or day may signify prosperity, and night the time of adversity. Thus the Lord set watchmen over Jerusalem’s walls by day and night, because he gave the Church prelates who watch vigilantly over the walls of religion both in prosperity and adversity, lest the enemy break into [Col. 0557A] the holy city from any quarter. Here it is fittingly added: “You who remember the Lord, do not be silent.”

VERSE 7.—“And give him no silence, until he establishes and until he makes Jerusalem a praise in the earth.”

For those remember the Lord who frequently bring him before the eyes of their heart in devout meditation. Before the holy Church attained such authority everywhere, it suffered much from unbelievers. Therefore the prophet now admonished those who remembered the Lord—that is, spiritual men—not to cease from the cry of prayer, because “one ought always to pray and not grow weary” (Luke 18:1), nor to give him silence; rather, they were to send forth persistently the voices of their prayers into his ears, until he established [Col. 0557B] Jerusalem—that is, granted a firm condition to the wavering Church—and made her a praise in the earth, that is, in this world, where she had been an object of reproach and mockery.

But we too are still commanded, if we remember the Lord with devout longing, not to be silent in crying to him with unwearied prayers, until he himself establishes our Jerusalem, which is tossed upon the sea of this age, in the land of blessed solitude, and makes her there praise and glory. But because the Lord speaks to those who lead a new life, let us hear what he promises also concerning those who stubbornly remain in their old state. It follows:

VERSE 8.—“The Lord has sworn by his right hand and by the arm of his strength: If I ever again give your grain as food to your enemies, or if strangers drink [Col. 0557C] your wine, for which you have labored.”

VERSE 9.—“For those who gather it shall eat it and praise the Lord; and those who carry it together [Note: [Col. 0557D] Elsewhere: ‘carry together and gather.’] shall drink it in my holy courts.”

For God’s oath is his unchangeable affirmation. His right hand and the arm of his strength are his Christ; Zion’s grain is the nourishment of holy understanding; Zion’s enemies are the Jews persecuting the Church; its wine is spiritual knowledge, which gladdens and intoxicates the minds of believers. The Jews too are strangers, for they forsook the Lord, blasphemed the Holy One of Israel, and were estranged backward.

Therefore the Lord swore by his right hand and by the arm of his strength—that is, he established immutably in Christ, who is his power—saying: “If I ever again give your grain as food to your enemies”: that is, I shall no longer give sacred understanding to the Jews as food for the soul, because they shall no longer understand the Scriptures after rejecting Christ, who alone opens their understanding. “Or if strangers drink your wine”: that is, the Jews shall no longer drink your spiritual meaning, by which you are divinely intoxicated so as to transcend yourself in mind toward God. For those who gather your grain—that is, the harvest of sacred understanding—from the broad field of divine utterances, shall eat it with the mouth of the heart and praise the Lord, saying: “I will bless the Lord who has given me understanding” (Ps. 15:7). Those who bring together the wine of spiritual meaning from the vineyard of [Col. 0558A] Holy Scripture, gathering the clusters of interpretations, shall drink it in my holy courts—that is, in the assemblies of the Church and among the ordered ranks of believers.

Or the enemies and strangers are demons, who ate and drank the grain and wine of the Jews—that is, devoured all the fruits of their labor—while they wavered between God and idols. But enemies do not seize the Church’s grain and wine, because she, seeking to please God alone, shall eat from good works the labor of her hands, exalt God with everlasting praise, and drink in the courts of eternal dwellings with the Father. For because we labor in field and vineyard in order to gather grain and wine, grain and wine rightly signify the fruit of heavenly recompense [Col. 0558B] that we attain for the labor we undertake in the body. Then the faithful Hebrews are commanded:

VERSE 10.—“Pass through, pass through the gates; prepare the way for the people; make the road level; and choose the stones; and raise a standard for the peoples.”

“Pass through the gates,” he says—that is, at the command of the apostles, who are the gates—go forth to preach to the nations. Or it may be said to those who are outside that they should pass through the gates, that is, enter the Church through the teaching of the apostles. Prepare the way for the people who are coming: that is, point out beforehand to the Gentile people the way of faith by which one comes into the Church. Make the road level: that is, remove from the believers’ way the stumbling-blocks of dissension and the scruples of doubts, and everything that can impede [Col. 0558C] their steps as they hasten toward the heavenly dwelling. And choose precious and living stones, so that whoever renounces the world may not remain among worldly persons but may avoid their crowds and flee their companionships.

Or, “choose the stones” means: soften every hardness in the hearts of believers; and raise the sign of the cross before all peoples, so that the whole army of Christ’s soldiers may see it and follow.

VERSE 11.—“Behold, the Lord has made his name heard” even by those nations “at the ends of the earth.” It follows:

“Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your Savior comes; behold, his reward is with him, and his work is before him.”

You preachers, he says, tell the daughter of Zion—that is, the Church drawn from the nations, which is the daughter of the primitive Church—Do not fear; do not fail, for behold, your Savior is coming to judgment. Delivering you from every tribulation, he shall grant you everlasting salvation. And behold, the reward which he shall render you is with him; his work is before him—that is, the human being whom he created will stand [Col. 0558D] before his tribunal to be judged. It follows:

VERSE 12.—“And they shall call them: A holy people, redeemed by the Lord. But you shall be called a sought-out city, and not forsaken.”

We call the Hebrews who have believed thus, saying: This is a holy people, nurtured in holiness, who have also been redeemed by the Lord. The Church from the nations, though she too may be called a holy people, is nevertheless not customarily so called, because she formerly lived in the squalor of paganism. Rather, she is especially called a sought-out and not-forsaken city, because the Savior sought her as lost and, having found her, did not forsake her. It follows:

## CHAPTER LXIII

VERSE 1.—“Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah? This one, beautiful in his robe, advancing in the abundance of his strength?”

This is spoken in the person of the first angels, marveling at Christ’s ascension. For seeing him return from this world to the heights, they marvel among themselves, or inwardly, saying: Who is this who comes from Edom? That is, who has ascended here to us from this earthly age? For Edom is interpreted “earthly.” With dyed garments—that is, with flesh made bloody by the blood of his passion. Bozrah means “tribulation,” and the Lord’s garment is his body, which he took from the Virgin; yet his garment is not one thing and he another. For our flesh too is called a garment; nevertheless, we ourselves are the flesh with which we are clothed.

[Col. 0559B] “This one, beautiful in his robe”: that is, possessing absolutely no deformity of sin in the humanity he assumed, he shines in it with the wondrous beauty of holiness. “Advancing in the abundance of his strength”: that is, powerfully carrying forward the course of his activity by his manifold power.

Or, “this one, beautiful in his robe” means beautiful in the flesh glorified through the resurrection; “advancing in the abundance of his strength” means making for heaven by his own power. Thus the heavenly powers first deliberate among themselves, showing that they learn and seek divine knowledge. Therefore, because they had said, “Who is this?”, Jesus himself immediately approaches, answers them, and teaches them, saying:

“I am he who speak righteousness and am a defender unto salvation.”

“I am he who speak righteousness”: that is, who teach on earth what is just—namely, that all should reject the persuasions of the deceiver and do the Creator’s will. “And I am a defender unto salvation,” because in the passion I fight against the ancient enemy for the salvation of humankind. Having heard this, the angelic powers, [Col. 0559D] as though granted permission to speak with him, ask:

VERSE 2.—“Why then is your garment red, and your clothing like that of those treading in the winepress?”

Since you possess such power and righteousness, they say, why then is your garment red—that is, why is your flesh bloodied? And why is your clothing like that of those treading in the winepress—that is, why is your body like the bodies of other dying persons? To them he answers:

VERSE 3.—“I have trodden the winepress alone, and there was no man with me from the nations; I have trodden them in my fury and trampled them in my wrath, and their blood has been sprinkled upon my garments, and I have defiled all my clothing.”

[Col. 0560A] “I have trodden the winepress alone”: that is, I alone, by rising again, have trodden down death, which crushes others. For he alone trod the winepress in which he was trodden, because by his own power he overcame the passion that he endured. For he who suffered even unto death on the cross rose gloriously from death. It is rightly added: “And there was no man with me from the nations.” For those for whom he came to suffer ought to have shared in his passion. Because at that time they had not yet believed, he complains in the passion concerning those whose life was being sought by that passion.

But because he condemned without mercy in the underworld all the nations who departed this world before this saving passion of his, with very few escaping, such as Melchizedek and Job, he says: “I have trodden them in my fury and trampled them [Col. 0560B] in my wrath.” He trod in his fury those whom, in anger, he plunged into hell. And his discourse here concerns the nations. Yet because he himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree, that, dead to sin, we might live to righteousness, he adds: “And their blood has been sprinkled upon my garments”: that is, the stains of their sins upon my flesh; “I have defiled all my clothing”: that is, I have defiled my whole body with the filth of others’ sins. This is not because he himself was contaminated by our iniquities, but because he alone received the sins of us all in order to wipe them out and endured the sufferings, insults, and rejection due to them.

The opposing powers may, however, be signified by the nations, whom he himself trampled and crushed. [Col. 0560C] And their blood is said to have been sprinkled upon his garments, not because demons have blood, but because such language shows that he fought against them, conquered them, and killed them. He further adds:

VERSE 4.—“For the day of vengeance is in my heart; the year of my recompense has come.”

When the Savior suffered, he foresaw in his heart the day of vengeance on which he would avenge himself through Titus and Vespasian upon the Jews, his persecutors; and he saw the year coming in which he would repay them. Thus, with this same passion impending, he foretold to his disciples: “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, then know that its desolation has drawn near. [Col. 0560D] Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains; let those who are in its midst depart; and let those in the surrounding regions not enter into it, because these are days of vengeance, that all things written may be fulfilled” (Luke 21:20).

The day of judgment may also be understood as the day of vengeance, and the year of recompense as that span of eternity which will be after the end of the age, in which each person will experience the just recompense of his own merits. Therefore the day of vengeance is in his heart because he knows when the day of judgment will come. But to this statement one may object that elsewhere it is written: “But of that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, but the Father” (Mark 13:32). The answer to this objection is that, in the customary language of Scripture, the Son is said not to know that day because he causes it to be unknown [Col. 0561A] to all. For the Father knows nothing that the Son does not know, because the Son is the Father’s wisdom. It follows:

VERSE 5.—“I looked around, and there was no helper; I sought, and there was no one to aid.”

Placed among his persecutors, the Lord looked around and saw no helper, because “all the disciples left him and fled” (Matt. 26:56), although they could not have brought him aid even had they stood firm. Or he looked around throughout the whole expanse of the world, and there was no helper, because there was no one who could assist him by suffering in seeking humankind’s salvation. It follows:

“And my arm saved for me, and my indignation itself helped me.”

“I indeed,” he says, “found no helper; but my arm—that is, my power—not only delivered me, but also saved all whom I wished. And it saved them not for themselves but for me, so that they might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose again for them.” Whoever has received forgiveness of sins or escaped some danger but still lives for himself has not yet been saved by Christ for Christ, but for himself. Whoever, having obtained pardon for sins, dedicates the remaining span of life to God, has been saved not for himself but for God. And Christ has saved for himself the one who, delivered from adversities endured on account of sins, henceforth lives religiously.

[Col. 0561C] But what does he mean when he adds, “My indignation itself helped me,” except what the Apostle says concerning the Jews: “Their transgression is the riches of the world, and their diminution the riches of the nations” (Rom. 11:12)? For if their loss is the reconciliation of the world, certainly God’s wrath upon them helped bring about our salvation. Therefore his indignation helped him, because by being angry with the Jews he worked all the more toward the salvation of the world. Concerning them he further adds:

VERSE 6.—“And I trampled the peoples in my fury, and made them drunk in my indignation, and cast down their strength to the earth.”

Through Vespasian and Titus he trampled the Jewish peoples in his fury, made them drunk with the bitterness of tribulations, and cast down their entire strength to the earth, breaking it beneath the Romans, so that from this humiliation they might be unable to rise again until Elijah’s coming. Or his indignation against the demons helped our salvation: he trampled them in his fury and cast down their strength to the earth in order to free us.

After this, the prophet speaks in his own person and that of the people, recounting in himself God’s benefits and the people’s hardness of heart, on account of which Jerusalem was delivered to fire and Israel to captivity. For it follows:

VERSE 7.—“I will remember the Lord’s mercies and the Lord’s praise, for all that the Lord has rendered to us, and for the multitude of good things of the house [Col. 0562A] [Note: [Col. 0561D] Elsewhere, ‘to the house.’] of Israel, which he has bestowed upon them according to his forgiveness and according to the multitude of his mercies.”

“Pressed,” he says, “by the weight of evils, I have hope in nothing other than God’s mercy—he who shows mercy to thousands who love him and extends kindness to those who know him.” But no one can say this except one who understands that he justly endures what he suffers. It follows:

VERSE 8.—“And he said: Surely they are my people, children who do not deny; and he became their Savior.”

God, who by a just judgment delivered this people to captivity, tempering the severity of justice with mercy, said: “I have begotten children and exalted them, but they have despised me” (above, 1:12). Yet because they are my people and have once been called children, they shall not perish forever, if they cease to despise and deny me; rather, if they believe in him, they shall experience my Savior Christ, who was made from David’s seed according to the flesh. It follows concerning the Lord:

VERSE 9.—“In all their tribulation he was not afflicted, and the angel of his face saved them.”

This can aptly be understood in accordance with what Job says: “If he scourges, let him kill at once, and not laugh at the punishments of the innocent” (Job 9:23). For God scourged, because he afflicted humankind for their sins. But at last he killed once, because, in order to destroy our twofold death—that of soul and flesh—he caused Christ to die only in the flesh. “For in that he died to sin, he died once” (Rom. 6:10).

[Col. 0562C] Nor did he any longer laugh at the punishments of the innocent, because he made his beloved Son a participant in their tribulations. For he seemed, as it were, to laugh at their punishments when, in the affliction preceding their redemption, he showed them no feeling of his compassion. Likewise here it is said that “in all their tribulation he was not afflicted,” when he saw their affliction and had not yet sent the Redeemer. For what Job said—that he was said to laugh at the punishments of the innocent—the prophet now says in these words: “In all their tribulation he was not afflicted.” But at last the angel of his face—that is, the Son coming from him—saved them, because he who scourged killed once. It follows:

[Col. 0562D] “In his love and his mercy he redeemed them, and he bore them and lifted them up all the days of the age.” In love and mercy he redeemed them by the blood of his Son. For “God commends his love toward us, because while we were still sinners Christ died for us” (Rom. 5:8)—“in whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins according to the riches of his grace” (Eph. 1:7).

“And he bore and lifted them up all the days of the age,” that is, of the present life, “because his mercy is forever” (Ps. 105:1). Or, he redeemed them from Egypt—that is, freed them—and patiently bore [Col. 0563A] their conduct, sustaining and lifting them up through all days from the beginning of the age. It follows:

VERSE 10.—“But they provoked him to anger and afflicted the Spirit of his Holy One; and he turned into an enemy to them, and he himself fought against them.”

They afflicted the Spirit of his Holy One—that is, the soul of his Christ—and he fought against them through Titus and Vespasian. But because in Elijah’s time he will restore to it its former grace, it plainly adds:

VERSE 11.—“And he remembered the days of old, of Moses and his people.”

That is, he remembered his covenant, which he made with them through Moses when he led them from the land of Egypt, that he might be their God. But because for the present he does not look upon [Col. 0563B] them, and permits them, scattered throughout the whole world, to be afflicted by most prolonged calamities, the prophet fittingly adds:

“Where is he who brought them up from the sea with the shepherds of his flock?” That is, with Moses and Aaron. He who cast Pharaoh with his army into the sea now does not exact vengeance upon their oppressors. It follows:

“Where is he who put in their midst the Spirit of his Holy One?” He who once placed the Spirit of his Holy One—that is, of his Christ—in this people now gives it no grace of that same Spirit. It follows:

VERSE 12.—“Who led Moses at his right hand by the arm of his majesty, who divided the waters before them, that he might make for himself an everlasting name.”

[Col. 0563C] Supply, “Where is he?” For he now works nothing like this for them, but has departed from them and hidden his face. “Who led Moses at his right hand”: because he held Moses’ spiritual right hand when he led him from Egypt under the guidance of his power. And he divided the waters of the sea before them, so that the memory of his wondrous works might be celebrated forever. It follows:

VERSE 13.—“Who led them through the depths like a horse in the wilderness, not stumbling.”

VERSE 14.—“Like an animal descending into the plain.”

As a horse proceeds freely without obstacle through the level places of the wilderness, and any animal through the breadth of a plain, so this people passed through the depths of the sea with the Lord as its guide. It follows:

[Col. 0563D] “The Spirit of the Lord was their guide.” The Spirit of the Lord was their guide through sea and wilderness, but now he grants them no guidance. That this Spirit may return to them, the penitent add and say to Christ:

“Thus you led your people, that you might make for yourself a name of glory.” For by so many miracles he led them from Egypt to the land of promise, that his name might become widely known and glorified. They further add in prayer:

VERSE 15.—“Look down from heaven and see from your holy dwelling and your glory.”

For now they confess in supplication that the Son of Man is in heaven and in the dwelling-place of his glory. It follows:

[Col. 0564A] “Where are your zeal and your strength, the multitude of your tender affections and mercies? They have withheld themselves from me.” Where is your zeal, by which you loved me as a bride, and the strength by which you freed me from the hand of adversaries? For now, for a very long time, you have withheld from me the abundance of your loving tenderness and mercies, because no feeling of pity and compassion for me has moved you to free me from such prolonged captivity. It follows:

VERSE 16.—“For you, Lord, are our Father, and Abraham has not known us, and Israel has not recognized us; you, Lord, are our Father, our Redeemer; your name is from everlasting.”

You are our Father, because Abraham or Jacob—whose sons we boasted that we were—did not know us, nor did he deem us worthy to acknowledge as sons, because we offended you. You are our Father, because you created us and deigned to say: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Jer. XXXI, 9). You are our Redeemer, because you shed your blood for us. Your name is from everlasting. For Moses relates that in the beginning God made every single thing through his Word, which you are, when he said: “Let there be light, and there was light” (Gen. I, 3), and likewise created the rest by his word. It follows:

VERSE 17.—“Why, O Lord, have you made us stray from your ways? You have hardened our heart, so that we would not fear you?”

The Lord made them stray because, in just judgment, he abandoned them to their pride and took from them the light of understanding. And he hardened their heart because he justly withdrew his grace, by which they might have been softened. For the Lord’s having hardened their heart means that he was unwilling to free it from hardness, but allowed that same hardness to grow. Therefore the fault of their wandering and hardening is attributed not to God but to them, because they deserved to be thus blinded and hardened. For, because they swelled not from faith but as though from works, by that very swelling they went astray and were hardened, so that, “being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own, they were not subject to God’s righteousness” (Rom. X, 3). This, indeed, is to stray and not to fear him. For whoever think so proudly as to believe that so much must be attributed to the powers of their own will that they deny their need of divine help for living well, certainly stray from the ways of the Lord’s commandments and, with hardened heart, do not fear him. It follows:

“Return for the sake of your servants, the tribes of your inheritance.”

The Lord will return to them when he begins once more to give them his grace. It follows:

VERSE 18.—“They possessed your holy people as though they were nothing; our enemies trampled down your sanctuary.”

After Jerusalem was taken, the Romans trampled down the holiness of the Temple; and, scattering this worthless people through all kingdoms, killing and dishonouring them in captivity, they possessed them as though they were nothing. It follows:

VERSE 19.—“We have become as at the beginning, when you did not rule over us and your name was not invoked over us.”

Since this people denied Christ the King and chose the dominion of an earthly and foreign emperor, saying, “We have no king but Caesar” (John XIX, 15), it has become as at the beginning, when it served Pharaoh and the Egyptians. From then on it ceased to have God as king and served no longer God but human beings. Yet at last, through the humility and lamentation of this devout confession, it returns to the grace of its king. Hence it now confidently longs for his final coming, saying:

## CHAPTER LXIV

VERSE 1.—“Would that you would rend the heavens and come down; that the mountains might melt away before your face.”

[Col. 0565B] VERSE 2.—“As when the burning of fire melts things away, and they burn with fire, so that your name might be made known to your enemies, and the nations might be troubled before your face.”

For at his descent there will be, as it were, a rending of the heavens: the heavens will be opened, angels will minister, apostles will sit with him, and the King of kings himself will come upon the throne of his majesty, so that he may then be seen by all, elect and reprobate alike. And because fire will burn before him, they say: “Would that the mountains might melt away before your face, and, as when fire burns things up, might melt away and burn with fire.” For that fire, consuming every mountain, will level them with the valleys and make all the earth smooth.

Before the Lord comes, however, Antichrist will reign. He will pour such darkness of his wickedness over the human race that scarcely anyone will behold the light of truth; even Christ’s name will turn to ignorance among them, and they will remember it only in order to blaspheme the Lord. But Christ himself will come like a flash of lightning to drive away this dreadful gloom. Therefore they fittingly add: “So that your name might be made known to your enemies, and the nations might be troubled before your face.” For then his name will become known even to his enemies, and they will suddenly be troubled before his face, because then, as it is written, “All the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven” (Matt. XXIV, 30). In the greatness of such terror, all the elect who are found still living in the flesh will also be greatly afraid. Hence they add:

[Col. 0565D] VERSE 3.—“When you perform wonders, we shall not be able to endure them.”

For then he will perform wonders which scarcely any human being can endure. For “the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light, the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken” (ibid., 29). What mind, then, when these things begin to happen, will not be terrified? But because the fear of the elect will be turned into security, rejoicing now in the Judge’s presence they add:

“You came down, and the mountains melted away before your face.”

VERSE 4.—“From everlasting they have not heard, nor perceived with the ears; no eye has seen, O God, apart from you, what you have prepared for those who wait for you.”

[Col. 0566A] VERSE 5.—“You met him who rejoices and works righteousness.”

You came down for judgment, and the fire running before your face consumed the mountains, so as to renew the earth by making it level. By mountains let us understand the proud, who will then melt away when their pride wastes away, so that “as wax melts before fire, so may sinners perish before the face of God” (Ps. LXVII, 3).

Those living in the flesh have not heard—that is, have not understood—from everlasting, that is, from the origin of the world up to the present; neither have they heard with bodily ears, nor has any person’s eye seen, apart from you—that is, except you alone—what rewards you have prepared for those who wait for you, who bear your promises patiently. Or, “apart from you” means that if anyone was able to see those things, that person also saw you together with them. For no one is now able to see, hear, or think how great that reward of the righteous is; only those who possess it could know it. It surpasses every sight, hearing, and thought. But on that day he will reveal himself to the worthy; and then God will joyfully meet everyone who now gladly works righteousness, in order to receive that person.

The discussion returns to the Jews:

“In your ways they will remember you.” And they themselves immediately add: “Behold, you were angry, and we sinned; and we have always been in them, and we shall be saved.”

For they will remember him in the Lord’s ways when they recognize that “a human being is not justified by works of the law except through faith in Jesus Christ” (Gal. II, 16). At present they have forgotten him in his ways, because they seek to be justified not by faith but by works. But when they learn that they cannot fulfil the commandments of the law by their own powers and begin to implore the help of grace, then they will remember him in his ways. Yet because they consigned him to oblivion, he was angry with them and abandoned them; and, after forgetting him, they did not cease to sin. This is what they lament when they say: “Behold, you were angry, and we sinned.”

But again, boasting of their observance of God’s ways, they say: “We have always been in them.” This is what the same people boast elsewhere, saying: “Behold, for so many years I have served you, and I have never transgressed your commandment” (Luke XV, 29). “We have always been in them,” they say, “and in them we shall be saved,” because “the one who does them shall live in them” (Rom. X, 3). But immediately coming to their senses, they add in lament:

[Col. 0566D] VERSE 6.—“We have all become as an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are like the cloth of a menstruating woman.”

We have become like an unclean thing because they were cast out of the Church of the faithful as an unclean person is cast out of the camp, unwilling to do what the Apostle warned them concerning Christ: “Let us draw near to him,” he says, “with a true heart, in fullness of faith, our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our body washed with pure water” (Heb. X, 22). For this reason all their righteousnesses became like the cloth of a menstruating woman: they were defiled by the impurity of their carnality, so that everyone who touches them is defiled. Hence the Apostle judged those carnal ceremonies to be “as dung, that he might gain Christ and be found in him, not having his own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through faith in Jesus Christ” (Phil. III, 8). Now, approaching this righteousness, they compare their own righteousnesses, in which they formerly gloried, to a menstruous cloth. Here it must be observed that righteousness which is in the law is called uncleanness in comparison with evangelical purity. It follows:

“And we have all fallen like a leaf, and our iniquities, like the wind, have carried us away.”

All fell like a leaf from the tree of patriarchal stock, because, according to the Apostle, “the branches of the olive tree were broken off and fell” (Rom. XI, 17), and the wild olive was grafted in their place. And their iniquities carried them away like the wind carries a leaf from a tree, because, while they falsely gloried in righteousness and were truly filled with iniquities, they were separated from the faith of their fathers, so that they did not receive the Saviour when he came, though their fathers had awaited his coming.

This saying, however, may be understood not only of the Jews but also of the whole human race. For what is a human being but a leaf that fell from the tree in paradise? What is he but a leaf, carried away by the wind of temptation and lifted up by the gusts of desires? For the human mind suffers as many temptations as it is moved by gusts. Anger often disturbs it; when anger withdraws, foolish joy succeeds. It is pressed by the goads of lust and stretched far and wide by the heat of avarice in pursuing earthly things. At one time pride lifts it up; at another, disordered fear casts it down into low things. Since, then, human hearts are lifted up and cast down by so many gusts of temptation, it is fittingly said: “We have all fallen like a leaf, and our iniquities, like the wind, have carried us away.” For iniquity carried us away like a wind because, fastening us by no weight of virtue, it raised us into empty exaltation. A human being is aptly called a leaf, because one who was a tree in creation became a leaf through temptation by his own doing. For one who has fallen from on high is a leaf.

But let us return to the Jews, for they add in lament:

VERSE 7.—“There is no one who calls upon your name, who rises up and holds fast to you.”

For there is no one among them who, calling on the Lord’s name in prayer, rises up against the movement of his indignation and holds him back lest he strike. All are unjust, and none is found among them who can meet divine wrath with prayer, deriving the authority to resist from the consciousness of good deserts and restraining the heavenly punishment that rages against this people. It follows:

“You have hidden your face from us and crushed us in the hand of our iniquity.” He hid from them the face of his divinity or knowledge, saying: “You will not see me from now on until you say, Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. XXIII, 39). And he crushed them in the hand—that is, in the action—of their iniquity, they who on account of their wickedness suffered such grievous things. But now, wholly repentant, they fall down in every humility and say in supplication:

[Col. 0568A] VERSE 8.—“And now, O Lord, you are our Father; we indeed are clay, and you are our potter, and we are all the work of your hands.”

For Christ himself is their Father, that is, their Creator; they are clay, and he is their potter and maker, who fashioned them from the mud of the earth and said: “As clay is in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand, house of Israel” (Jer. XVIII, 6). In prayer they add:

VERSE 9.—“Do not be angry, O Lord, beyond measure, and do not remember our iniquity any longer. Behold, look upon us: we are all your people.”

[Col. 0568B] And concerning the destruction of Jerusalem carried out by Titus, they add:

VERSE 10.—“Your holy city [Note: [Col. 0567D] Otherwise, ‘the city of your Holy One,’ etc.] has become a wilderness; Zion has become a wilderness; Jerusalem is desolate.”

VERSE 11.—“The house of our sanctification and our glory, where our fathers praised you, has been given over to the burning of fire, and all our desirable things have been turned into ruins.”

Then they add:

VERSE 12.—“Will you restrain yourself over these things, O Lord? Will you remain silent and afflict us exceedingly?”

To these words the Lord Jesus immediately replies.

## CHAPTER LXV

VERSE 1.—“Those who did not previously inquire after me sought me; those who did not seek me found me”—that is, the Gentiles. “I said, ‘Behold me, behold me,’ to a nation that did not call upon my name.”

For after his resurrection the Gentiles began to seek him; and after he had been rejected by the Jews, he voluntarily offered himself even to those who did not seek him. Concerning them it follows:

VERSE 2.—“I spread out my hands all day to an unbelieving people who walk in a way that is not good, after their own thoughts.”

VERSE 3.—“A people [Note: [Col. 0568D] Otherwise, ‘the people.’] who continually provoke me to anger before my face.”

If we understand, in the words “I spread out my hands,” the cross’s instrument of execution, how are we to understand “all day”? Did he hang upon the wood throughout the whole day? But if we wish to take “day” as “time”—especially since he used the word in the feminine gender, which in Latin speech commonly signifies only time—we may suitably understand by the hands extended all day the continuance of good works, from the pursuit of which he never ceased. Since that faithless people saw—or rather, experienced—these works, the Lord spread out his hands to the unbelieving people.

We may also understand by the outstretched hands the generosity of the giver: he denied them nothing when they asked, but immediately restored health to the leper who asked (Mark I, 40) and opened the eyes of the man blind from birth (John IX, 1). The outstretched hands also signify a father’s tenderness, eager to receive his children into his embrace. He showed these things to the Jewish people, who walk in the way of evil action, following their perverse thoughts and continually provoke God to anger by proudly scorning to do his will. They continually provoke him before his face because the Lord placed them, as it were, before his face when he chose them from among all peoples. Yet from the beginning they have not ceased perversely to act, sinning in the sight of the Lord, before whose eyes all things are open, or sacrificing to idols in the Temple. For concerning those who once, among this same people, turned to idols, it follows:

“They sacrifice in gardens and offer sacrifice upon bricks.”

[Col. 0569B] VERSE 4.—“They dwell in tombs and sleep in the shrines of idols; they eat swine’s flesh, and unclean broth is in their vessels.”

VERSE 5.—“They say: ‘Keep away from me; do not come near me, because you are unclean.’ These will be smoke in my anger, a fire burning all day.”

For ancient Jews who worshipped idols did these and similar things. Joining luxury to idolatry, they sacrificed in gardens; and instead of the single altar that the law had ordered to be built from unhewn stones, they stained bricks with the blood of victims. They also lived in tombs and slept in idol shrines, where they customarily lay upon the spread skins of victims in order to learn the future from dreams; and whoever was not led by a similar error they deemed unclean and avoided that person’s touch.

Or they said to God: “Keep away from me and do not come near me,” when they endeavoured to reject him from themselves so that they might be allowed to live in the manner of the Gentiles; and they said to him, “You are unclean,” when they blasphemed him. But all these will be smoke in his anger, because like smoke they will vanish before the Judge. And they will be a fire burning all day, because they will burn without interruption unto eternity. For they will burn throughout the whole day of eternity. It follows:

VERSE 6.—“Behold, it is written before me: I will not be silent, but I will repay and requite in their bosom your iniquities and the iniquities of your fathers together, says the Lord.”

VERSE 7.—“They who sacrificed upon mountains and reproached me upon hills—I will measure out their first work again into their bosom.”

Every evil that they did is written before me—that is, it remains recorded, as though in a book, before the gaze of my memory. When the day of judgment comes, I shall not keep silent concerning what those sons of yours did; rather, I shall repay into the bosom—that is, into their minds—so that their own conscience may torment them, your iniquities, O most wicked fathers, and the iniquities of your fathers together. That is, I shall repay to your sons, who imitated your perversity and that of their fathers, the evils which you and your fathers committed; and I shall first measure out again their first work, so that they may be punished for their own iniquities and for those of you and your parents. Hence it is written elsewhere: “I, the Lord your God, am a strong and jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of those who hate me” (Exod. XX, 5).

These idolaters, who will also receive recompense on the last day, were especially exterminated and killed under Nebuchadnezzar. But because not all that people was then to be destroyed at once, even though for the most part it was to perish, the prophet fittingly adds:

VERSE 8.—“Thus says the Lord: As when a grain is found in a cluster and it is said, ‘Do not destroy it, for a blessing is in it,’ so will I do for the sake of my servants, that I may not destroy the whole.”
