[Col. 0570B] For just as a grain is selected from a cluster to be preserved while the cluster is crushed, so that people then perished because of its impieties. Yet a remnant was left from it, to be preserved like a blessing. Hence it follows:

VERSE 9.—“And I will bring forth from Jacob a seed, and from Judah one who will possess my mountains; my elect will inherit it, and my servants will dwell there.”

VERSE 10.—“The plains will become sheepfolds for flocks, and the valley of Achor a resting-place for herds, for my people who have sought me.”

For the Lord brought forth from Jacob—that is, from the ten tribes which were in captivity—children who would return to their own land; and from Judah, held captive in Babylon, a people who would once more possess his mountains. His elect, returning from captivity, inhabited his land. Flocks of sheep remained in the plains, and in the valley where Achan—who had sinned by stealing what had been devoted to destruction—was once stoned [Note: [Col. 0569D] The codex reads: Achor.], herds of cattle lay down; that is, the people who sought the Lord in the distress of captivity (Josh. VII, 25).

But after promising these good things to those who were to return to repentance, he again threatens the idolaters who were to perish in this affliction, saying:

VERSE 11.—“But you who have forsaken the Lord, who have forgotten my holy mountain, who set a table for Fortune and pour libations upon it—”

VERSE 12.—“I will number you for the sword, and you will all fall in slaughter, because I called and you did not answer; I spoke and you did not hear; you did evil in my eyes and chose what I did not will.”

For they forsook the Lord and clung to idols; they forgot Mount Zion, where his Temple stood, not coming there to worship or sacrifice, but they set a table for Fortune and sacrificed upon it. For in many cities, and especially in Egypt and Alexandria, there was an ancient custom of idolatry: on the final day of the year they would set out a table laden with food of every kind and a cup mixed with honey, considering either the past year’s fertility or that of the year to come. The Jews also did this, worshipping the monstrosities of every image; and instead of pouring libations upon the altar for victims, they poured libations upon a table of this sort.

For this reason they were numbered for the sword—that is, for punishment. Whatever punishes, strikes, torments, or afflicts is called a sword in Holy Scripture. Not all that people was slaughtered by iron; rather, it was handed over to punishments, tortures, captivity, and slavery.

The Lord had called the Jews because, by giving gifts—as though sending out a voice—he had endeavoured to draw them to himself; but they did not answer because they scorned to render works worthy of his gifts. The Lord calls us when he anticipates us with gifts; we answer his calling when we render worthy service according to his commands. Therefore, because he had anticipated the Jews—and also certain Christians—with so many gifts, he says: “I called.” But because they scorned so many of his gifts, he adds: “And you did not answer.” He had also called them to repentance through the prophets, and they did not answer; he spoke, and they refused to hear, but instead provoked him more greatly.

But perhaps these words should be referred to the time of the apostles. For he says: “As when a grain is found in a cluster and it is said, ‘Do not destroy it, for a blessing is in it,’ so will I do for the sake of my servants, that I may not destroy the whole.” For a grain was found as it were in a cluster when the portion that had received the Church’s teaching was found among the Jewish people. As a grain is to a cluster, so few Jews who believed were in comparison with the remaining multitude, which perished because it refused to believe. And concerning this smallest chosen portion it was said, “Do not destroy it, for a blessing is in it,” when he prayed to the Father for his disciples. Therefore the Lord did not wholly destroy that people, because he saved from destruction those who received faith and delivered them from their devastation and captivity. Concerning them he adds:

“For I will bring forth from Jacob a seed.” That is, the seed of which the same Apostle says that “unless the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed, we should have become as Sodom” (Rom. IX, 29). “I will bring forth from Jacob”—that is, from the ten tribes—the children of election; and from the tribe of Judah a multitude of believers possessing my mountains, that is, the prophets and apostles, because “his foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXXVI, 1). “My elect will inherit it,” that is, the Church; “and my servants will dwell there,” because there is now no place in which they may dwell outside the Catholic Church.

“And the plains will become sheepfolds for flocks,” because the common multitude of the faithful will be content with a level and less exalted manner of life. For what are the plains but this broad and lowly way of life of the weak? Yet there we have sheepfolds for flocks, because they too are kept within the folds of the Lord’s sheep. Achor, however, means “trouble.” What is the valley of Achor but the humiliation of repentance, troubling the sinner’s mind? And what is expressed by the name “herds” but a multitude of great and strong believers? Thus the valley of Achor will be a resting-place for herds because great and strong saints lie in the humility of repentance, are gravely troubled by the slightest offences, and afflict themselves.

In this valley lay that great ox who said: “I am the least of the apostles, not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (I Cor. XV, 9); and he who said: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (I John I, 8); and another who said: “For in many things we all offend” (James III, 2). The Lord promised these things to the people who, whether coming to faith from the Jews or from the Gentiles, sought him.

“But you,” he says, “O faithless Jews, who have forsaken the Lord, saying, ‘We have no king but Caesar’” (John XIX, 15), “hear what has befallen you. You who have forgotten my holy mountain”—that is, the height of spiritual conduct or the loftiness of the heavenly homeland—“who set a table for Fortune,” that is, an altar for riches, “and pour libations upon it,” that is, who make your sacrifices for the sole reward of this present life: “I will number you for the sword” of the Romans or of final vengeance. “And you will all fall in slaughter,” either by the Romans or through the punishment of the final stroke, because I called you to faith and grace but you did not answer me by coming to me; I spoke to you, proclaiming the will of my Father, and you refused to hear. You did evil in my eyes even while I dwelt bodily among you, and you chose the Pharisees’ traditional commandments, which I did not will. It follows:

[Col. 0572C] VERSE 13.—“Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, my servants will eat, but you will be hungry; behold, my servants will drink, but you will thirst.”

VERSE 14.—“Behold, my servants will rejoice, but you will be put to shame; behold, my servants will praise because of exultation of heart, but you will cry out because of sorrow of heart, and you will howl because of the breaking of spirit.”

My servants will eat and drink because “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst” (John V, 35). But you, O Jews, will hunger and thirst, because “I will send a famine upon the land—not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but for hearing the word of the Lord” (Amos VIII, 11). For you will no longer find anyone to feed or give you drink with the knowledge of the Scriptures. My servants, having received the Holy Spirit, will rejoice; but you who crucified me will be ashamed when you see the glory of my resurrection becoming known everywhere. My servants will rejoice in the churches because of the exultation of spiritual joy; but you will howl because of sorrow of heart amid the miseries that you will endure. We see that all these things have thus come to pass.

If these words are to be referred to the future life, God’s servants will then eat because “he will make them recline, and, passing by, will serve them” (Luke XII, 37). His servants will drink because they will be intoxicated by the abundance of his house, and he will give them drink from the torrent of his delight. Dionysius explained these banquets of the saints (*Epistle* XIX to Titus), saying:

> These things signify a certain common and equally invisible fellowship of the saints in divine goods; the Church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven; and the spirits of the righteous made perfect in every good thing and filled first with the good things. By reclining I understand rest: a life unharmed by many pains; divine fellowship in light and in the land of the living, filled with every sacred sense; and the abundant bestowal of the most generous and blessed goods, through which they are filled with every joy—Jesus causing them to rejoice and recline, ministering to them, granting eternal rest, and at once distributing and pouring in the fullness of good things.

It is therefore rightly said that his servants will eat and drink, since they will share in such a banquet. Hence, conversely, it is plain enough that then the Jews and all the reprobate will hunger and thirst, because they will not be admitted to such feasts. Of them the angry master of the house says: “None of those men who were invited shall taste my supper” (Luke XIV, 24). Then God’s servants will rejoice in that joy of perpetual blessedness, but the Jews and other reprobate will be ashamed and blush in everlasting disgrace. Then indeed the saints will praise because of exultation of heart, while the ungodly will howl and bellow because of the breaking of spirit. What follows is still said to the carnal Jews.

VERSE 15.—“And you will leave your name as an oath for my elect.”

Their name, indeed, is “Jew” or “Israelite.” “Jew” is interpreted as “confessing,” “glorifying,” or “praising”; “Israel,” however, as “seeing God.” Thus carnal Jews left their name as an oath for God’s elect because they have now lost that very name, and all the elect swear by it—that is, they firmly resolve to confess with the mouth unto salvation, to praise and glorify Christ, so that they may be worthy to attain the vision of him. For whoever confesses God, or confesses to God, and praises him possesses the force of the Jewish name; and whoever sees God now in a mirror and in the future age face to face possesses the reality of the name Israel. This faithless Jewish people, as has been said, lost the force of this name together with faith, and left it to God’s elect, who would attain it by the oath of their profession.

Or their name will be an oath for God’s elect, so that they may hold them as an example of evils, abhor suffering such things, and swear: “If I do otherwise, may what befell the Jews slain by the Romans happen to me.” To this is added as a threat:

“And the Lord will kill you.” Then it is added: “And he will call his servants by another name.”

VERSE 16.—“In which he who is blessed upon the earth will be blessed in the Lord, Amen; and he who swears in the earth will swear by the God of Amen, because the former distresses have been consigned to oblivion and because they have been hidden from our eyes.”

For the Lord will kill this people with his sword when he comes for judgment.

The Lord, who is the true God and eternal life, killed it when he withdrew himself from it. He no longer calls his servants by the name by which he formerly called them, but by another, nobler title, one that signifies newness and grace. Although his servants possess the reality of the ancient name, they are not called by that name; instead, they are reverently named by the designation of Christianity. “For no other name is given under heaven among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts IV, 12). Hence none of God’s servants is now called, as stated, a Jew or Israelite, but all are Christians.

In this name of Christianity, one who is blessed upon the earth—that is, one who in this life has received the blessing given in baptism—will be blessed in the Lord, if by living well he preserves the blessing he has received, when he hears: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom” (Matt. XXV, 34). And those who, while they remain on this earth, swear in him with the Psalmist saying to the Lord, “I have sworn and established to keep the judgments of your righteousness” (Ps. CXVIII, 106), will swear in him “Amen”; that is, in that kingdom of blessedness they will truly affirm: “The former distresses have been consigned to oblivion”—that is, all the afflictions and necessities by which we were constrained in the world—“and they have all been hidden from our eyes,” that is, we neither remember nor see them any longer. This is what that joyful people of the blessed will then proclaim.

For confirmation of the most certain truth, *Amen* is inserted here; it means “truly” or “faithfully,” so that the things promised may be shown to be truly to be fulfilled and faithfully rendered to the worthy. It follows:

VERSE 17.—“For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth; the former things will not be remembered, nor will they rise upon the heart.”

[Col. 0574C] VERSE 18.—“But you will rejoice and exult for ever in the things that I create.”

The Lord will make new heavens and a new earth on the last day. Thus John, in the Apocalypse, after the judgment had been determined, added: “And I saw a new heaven and a new earth. For the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea is no more” (Rev. XXI, 1). Yet neither of these—that is, heaven and earth—is to be created as something other; rather, these very things are renewed. They pass away in the form which they now possess, but persist without end in their essence. For “the form of this world passes away” (I Cor. VII, 31). Thus heaven and earth both pass away and will remain, because they are purified by fire from the appearance which they now have, yet are always preserved in their own nature. Hence the Psalmist says: “You will change them, and they will be changed” (Ps. CI, 28). Therefore he will create new heavens and a new earth when, cleansing these by the fire of judgment, he renews them. Nor will the former things rise upon the heart, because the beauty of those things which then will be will be so great that no one will deign to remember the things which now exist. Everyone will regard these as nothing and delight in the things which they will see. For all the elect will then rejoice without end in the things created by the Lord. It follows:

“For behold, I create Jerusalem as exultation, and her people as joy.” Jerusalem—that is, the Church—will not merely exult, but will itself be exultation. Its people will not merely rejoice, but will themselves be joy. For we see iron changed into fire when, placed in fire, it becomes intensely heated. So too the people of the saints, when they enter into the joy of their Lord, will be changed into joy. It follows:

VERSE 19.—“And I will exult in Jerusalem and rejoice in my people.”

Then the Lord will rejoice in his people, when there is no longer any sin in them and he has made all of them immortal and blessed. So long as we sin and are mortal and wretched, he cannot rejoice in us. For he does not rejoice in us while we are still such as he made us in the beginning. When, therefore, he has restored us to the former state, then he will have joy in us. It follows:

[Col. 0575B] “And the voice of weeping and the voice of crying will no longer be heard in it.” It is clear that among the people of the saints there will no longer be mourning, crying, or pain. It follows:

VERSE 20.—“There will no longer be for you an infant of days, nor an old person who does not fill up his days.”

An “infant of days” is one who has lived long but is still little in mind. Wisdom rebukes such infants, saying: “How long, little ones, will you love infancy?” (Prov. I, 22). An old person who does not fill up his days is one who has indeed lived long but has spent the years of life in vanity. That person fills his days with works who does not neglect daily to weigh himself watchfully in this life, and who is not numbed by any sloth from everything that he is able rightly to do. In the present Church, indeed, there are many such children and old persons. But in that future Church of the elect there will be no infant of days and no old person who does not fill up his days, because whoever persists always in being an infant in character will not attain it; nor will an old person who has refused to fill the days of life with good works. Hence it follows:

“**For a boy of a hundred years shall die, and the sinner of a hundred years shall be accursed.**” A hundred is a perfect number, and therefore by the designation “a hundred years” either the whole span of the present life or a long duration of time is expressed. Whoever, then, has completed a hundred years and is still a boy—that is, has lived a long time and yet [Col. 0575D] has not been corrected from childish deeds—shall die the eternal death. And the sinner of a hundred years—that is, one whom not even length of time has been able to restrain from committing sin—shall be accursed on the last day, when he hears: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41). But concerning the elect still dwelling in this life, it continues:

VERS. 21.—“And they shall build houses and inhabit them; and they shall plant vineyards and eat their fruit.”

VERS. 22.—“They shall not build and another inhabit; they shall not plant and another eat.”

For they shall build houses of their hearts, and shall dwell [Col. 0576A] in them by not wandering outward in thought through the desires of the world. For one who abandons the inward places of his own mind and pursues external things—that is, thinks upon visible things—does not remain in the house of his breast. And they shall plant vineyards: that is, they shall establish good actions for themselves, in which they may be exercised by daily labor. And they shall eat their fruit: that is, in the future they shall be satisfied by the reward of their good works. “They shall not build and another inhabit,” because the ancient enemy will not be able to inhabit the house of their conscience, which they build with heavenly disciplines and stones of virtues, as he inhabits the negligent person’s mind, of which he says: “I will return to my house, from which I came out” (Matt. 12:44). They shall not plant and another eat, because the devil shall not devour the fruit of their action. For another eats [Col. 0576B] the fruit of their vineyards when people do not obtain, by their deeds, the fruit of good recompense which they expected; instead Satan feeds on their punishment. But this cannot happen to the elect.

Or these houses are the various dwelling places with the Father, which the person who has built them will possess continually; and the vineyards are the many Churches, whose fruits are eaten and drunk, gladden the heart of man, intoxicate the Bridegroom’s friends, are daily drunk in the kingdom; and the dwelling and planting of the righteous shall be eternal, nor shall they be overthrown by the deceits of the devil and his attendants. It follows:

“For as the days of a tree shall be the days of my people, and the works of their hands shall grow old for my elect. [Note: [Col. 0575] Elsewhere: ‘shall grow old.’ ‘My elect shall not labor,’ etc.]”

[Col. 0576C] “As the days of a tree shall be the days of my people,” because, as a tree bears its fruit in its season, so the people of the elect, as long as the condition of this present life lasts for them, shall not cease to produce the fruit of good work. “And the works of their hands shall grow old for my elect,” because they shall hold fast to the end and complete the good works which they have begun. For “the one who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10:22). It follows:

VERS. 23.—“They shall not labor in vain, nor bear children in turmoil; for they are the seed of those blessed by the Lord, and their descendants are with them.”

They shall not labor in vain, because whatever good they labor to do they shall accomplish by the help of my grace, and they shall eat the labors [Col. 0576D] of their hands. Nor shall they bear children in turmoil, because, in order that they may be able by the word of truth to beget spiritual children, they shall remove from their hearts every disturbance of vices and every tumult of worldly desires, so that, with the eye of their mind purified, they may freely see and speak what is just. For they are the seed of those blessed by the Lord: that is, these are the children of Christ’s apostles; and their descendants, that is, the children of their children, are with them. For those whom we have spiritually begotten are our children; but those whom our spiritual children have themselves spiritually begotten are our grandchildren. Therefore, because such propagation takes place manifoldly in the Church, it is fittingly said of the holy [Col. 0577A] fathers: “Their descendants are with them.” It follows:

VERS. 24.—“And it shall be: before they call, I will answer.”

As it is written: “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor; your ear has heard the preparation of their heart” (Ps. 9:10). And again: “For your Father knows what you need before you ask him” (Luke 12:30). While they are still speaking in prayer, I shall hear. I shall always hear them for their salvation, though not always according to their will; just as I heard Paul so that my grace might remain in him, not so that “the thorn of the flesh,” as he had asked three times, “might depart from him” (2 Cor. 12:8). By this promise the Lord shows how greatly he loves the elect of the New Testament, [Col. 0577B] whose petitions he shows himself always ready and swift to grant. It follows:

VERS. 25.—“The wolf and the lamb shall feed together; the lion and the ox shall eat straw; and dust shall be the serpent’s bread. They shall neither harm nor kill on all my holy mountain, says the Lord.”

The wolf—that is, one who had formerly belonged to the world—and the lamb—that is, one who has always been gentle and innocent—shall feed together in the Church upon the one pasture of heavenly doctrine. And the lion and the ox shall eat straw, because the worldly ruler and the common person shall feed upon the same divine utterances. Straw signifies the simple words of Scripture, whereas wheat signifies the inward meaning. It often happens that people of the world, ignorant of mysteries, feed upon a simple reading of the Scriptures.

In another sense, [Col. 0577C] the lion is Satan, because “your adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5:8). The ox signifies the preacher, as it is written: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain” (1 Cor. 9:9). The straw is sinners, of whom John says: “But he shall burn up the straw with unquenchable fire” (Luke 3:17). Thus both the lion and the ox eat straw: the ancient enemy devours some sinners, while any preacher converts others and incorporates them into himself, sending them into the inner parts of the Church.

The serpent likewise is the same enemy, as we read: “The ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan” (Rev. 12:9). Dust also is the sinner, because after his sin the first man heard: “You are dust, [Col. 0577D] and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3:19). Therefore dust is the serpent’s bread, because the devil feeds upon the devouring of sinners. But on God’s holy mountain—that is, in the exalted conduct of the righteous—such lions and serpents shall not harm those righteous persons, though they afflict them; nor shall they kill any one of them, that is, they shall not pour into him the poison of their malice. “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 15:4), but the soul of the elect is immune from this death. And lest such beasts should harm them, they heard from the Lord: “Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon beasts” (Luke 10:19), namely serpents and scorpions, “and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall harm you” (ibid.). Since he named a mountain, lest you should understand, in a Jewish sense, the mountain [Col. 0578A] on which the Jews’ temple stood, he shows by a higher reasoning that he who fills all things is not locally in a part of things, nor in material buildings, but dwells in the hearts of believers. For it follows:

CHAPTER LXVI

VERS. 1.—Thus says the Lord: “Heaven is my throne, and the earth the footstool of my feet. What is this house that you will build for me, and what is this place of my rest?”

VERS. 2.—“My hand has made all these things, and all these things have come to be, says the Lord. But to whom shall I look, except to the poor and contrite in spirit, and to one trembling at my words?”

For when he calls heaven his throne and earth the footstool of his feet, he shows that he is inward to all things [Col. 0578B] and above all things, because he is everywhere, from the highest to the lowest and most inferior. Heaven indeed excels among material things; beneath it is the air, then fire and water, while earth is last. For earth is found to be the fourth and final part among the distinct members of this world: beginning with heaven, you count air second, water third, and earth fourth. Therefore, when he says, “Heaven is my throne, and earth the footstool of my feet,” he declares that he is in all the elements, according to what he says through Jeremiah: “Do I not fill heaven and earth?” (Jer. 23:23). And since in this whole body of the world heaven has the greatest form and earth the least, as though the divine power were more present to surpassing beauty and arranged the least things at the extremes and lowest places, God is fittingly said to sit in heaven and tread upon the earth, because “heaven is above and earth below,” as Scripture says (Prov. 25:3). But because God is of such greatness that he fills and surpasses all things, he fittingly rebukes the Jews, saying:

“What is this house that you will build for me?” For I do not dwell in a house made by hands. “And what is this place of my rest?” For I cannot rest locally anywhere, as though you thought that I dwell or rest in Solomon’s temple. For all these things that you see my hands have made, and all these things have come to be. But I have no dwelling in things made by hands and material things, because, being Spirit, I seek a spiritual house. For to whom shall I look, [Col. 0578D] so as to turn aside to him and remain in him, except to the poor—that is, the humble—and contrite in spirit, that is, one who by weeping has crushed his spirit, namely the hardness of his heart; and one who does not despise but trembles at my words? Whoever is such a person, I shall look upon him with a serene countenance; and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him, in a temple not made by hands. Therefore, once the material temple was rejected, it followed that the fleshly victims offered in it should also be rejected. Hence it continues:

VERS. 3.—“He who sacrifices an ox is as one who kills a man; he who slaughters a sheep, as one who breaks a dog’s brain; he who offers an oblation, as one who offers swine’s blood; he who remembers incense, as one who blesses an idol.”

[Col. 0579A] For after the true Lamb of God was sacrificed and the prophetic mystery of these victims ceased, God is not propitiated by them but is gravely offended, especially now that the temple—where alone it was lawful to offer them—has been destroyed. Thus it is fittingly said: “He who sacrifices an ox is as one who kills a man.” For Moses had said: “Any man of the house of Israel, if he kills an ox, sheep, or goat in the camp or outside the camp and does not present an offering to the Lord at the entrance of the tabernacle, shall be guilty of blood, as though he had shed human blood; thus he shall perish from the midst of his people” (Lev. 17:3). Therefore, since there is now nowhere a tabernacle or temple in which such an offering ought to be presented, the person who still sacrifices an ox is rightly compared with one who kills a man, since he can no longer present his offering at the entrance of the tabernacle. Each is deserving of the same penalty, both the one sacrificing an ox and the one killing a man.

Likewise, one who slaughters a beast—that is, a goat or sheep—commits an abomination equal to pouring the brain of a dog upon God’s altar. One who offers any such oblation commits a crime as great as if he offered the blood of pigs, which is an abomination. One who still remembers incense in order to place it in sacrifice commits sacrilege equal to blessing an idol. For these sacrifices are equivalent to the sacrifices of idols. To serve fleshly observances and seek salvation through them is as destructive as [perhaps: “as much as”] worshipping idols. For to place hope of salvation and justification where it is not is idolatry.

[Col. 0579C] Therefore, if anyone thinks that holiness and righteousness lie in these things, he is an idolater, seeking salvation where it is not; and still to observe the shadow is to deny that the truth has come. For if they are still observed, either it is signified that Christ was not promised, or he is still promised as one who is to come, and it is denied that he has come. It is plain that such ceremonies are now destructive and deadly, so that whoever observes them has without doubt been cast down into the devil’s abyss. For it is written: “The law and the prophets were until John” (Luke 16:16). Therefore, whoever seeks to extend the law beyond the limit God set for it now serves not God but the devil. “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” [Col. 0579D] (Rom. 10:4). But concerning those faithless Jews who still wish to maintain it, it adds:

“They chose all these things in their ways, and their soul delighted in their abominations.”

For rejecting the precepts of life which they heard from the Savior, they chose in their ways—that is, in their actions—all these execrable things that have now been mentioned; and they delighted in such abominations, not in the grace of the New Testament which was offered to them. Hence they said to the man who had been blind: “You be his disciple; but we are disciples of Moses” (John 9:28). It follows:

VERS. 4.—“Therefore I also will choose their mockeries, and I will bring upon them the things they feared” (John 11:45).

They devised against the Lord, saying: “If [Col. 0580A] we let him go on thus, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John 11:48). But in what they craftily devised against the Lord, the Lord mocked them; for because they did not let him go on thus, it came about that everyone believed in him. And he brought upon them the things they feared, for he caused the Romans to come and take away their place and nation. This happened because of the abominable fleshly observances which they had chosen, because they were exterminated by the Romans precisely because they refused to pay tribute, saying that it was unjust for a people who rendered tithes, firstfruits, and sacrifices to God also to pay tribute to men—although the Savior had commanded them to render “to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22:21). It follows:

“Because I called and there was no one to answer; I spoke and they did not hear; and they did evil in my sight, and chose the things that I did not will.”

The Lord who afterwards called us through the apostles first called the Jews. But they did not answer his call, because they did not return good works for the good words which they heard from him, nor did they come to him through faith. He spoke to them the things written in the Gospel, but they did not hear—that is, they did not obey—but unceasingly did evil in his sight; and they chose the fleshly precepts of the letter, which displeased him, together with the vain traditions of the Pharisees. Then the Savior addresses the multitude of saints who [Col. 0580C] were then in Judaea and Jerusalem, saying:

VERS. 5.—“Hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his word: your brothers who hate you and reject you for my name’s sake said, ‘Let the Lord be glorified, and we shall see in your joy’; but they themselves shall be put to shame.”

For that unanimous multitude of the first believers did not hear the word of divine preaching with a hard and unfeeling heart, as we do; rather, they received it with trembling and reverence. Their worst brothers were the remaining Jews who persisted in unbelief, who hated the believers and cast them out from the synagogue or from their territories for Christ’s name. And they said to them: “Let the Lord be glorified, so that we may see [Col. 0580D] him and you may rejoice. Why do you introduce to us a humble God? Why a crucified one? We wish, as you say, to behold him reigning in his majesty, so that you too may rejoice in his presence.” They spoke this in unbelieving mockery, thinking that these people hoped in Christ in vain. But when they see the glory of the righteous, they shall be ashamed, saying: “These are those whom we once held in derision and made a byword of reproach. We fools considered their life madness and their end dishonorable. How then were they counted among the children of God, and why is their lot among the saints? Therefore we strayed from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness did not shine for us, and the sun of understanding did not rise upon us” (Wis. 5:3). Thus they shall speak in grief and shame when the Lord is glorified [Col. 0581A] in the joy of those whom they hated and rejected for his name. Yet even in the present life they were ashamed when they saw all people flocking to faith in him whom they had crucified, every tongue confessing that Christ is in the glory of God the Father, and the guilt of his death charged against them by all. Hence it follows:

VERS. 6.—“The voice of a people from the city, a voice from the temple, the voice of the Lord rendering recompense to his enemies.”

The voice of the people from the city resounded with God’s praises, and the voice from the temple; for, as is written: “Many signs and wonders were done through the apostles in Jerusalem, and great fear was upon all. And daily, persevering unanimously in the temple and breaking bread from house to house, they received food with exultation and simplicity of heart, praising God” (Acts 2:43). But afterward came the voice of the Lord, rendering recompense through the Romans to his Jewish enemies. Thus he himself had earlier said: “There shall be great distress upon the earth and wrath against this people. They shall fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive into all nations” (Luke 21:23).

Or certainly the sound of shouting, sedition, and weeping resounded from the temple and city when they were surrounded by the Roman army and divided into three factions by seditions: when one faction occupied the temple and possessed all the formerly sacred things, fighting outside against enemies and within against fellow citizens; and in the city and temple the wailing was heard [Col. 0581C] of priests, Levites, the lowly populace, women, and children, as the Lord rendered them just recompense. But because the Church was then easily begetting people everywhere into faith, it fittingly adds:

VERS. 7.—“Before she travailed, she gave birth; before her labor came, she brought forth a male.”

To travail is to suffer before birth, whereas to give birth is to bring forth what has been conceived. And the Church gave birth before she travailed, because before she suffered the straits of persecution she brought forth a numerous offspring of spiritual children. Before her labor came, she brought forth a male: that is, a strong and manly people; for, after the Holy Spirit was received on the day of Pentecost, immediately [Col. 0581D] at Peter’s voice about “three thousand” from the people believed (Acts 2:41), and on another day “five thousand” believed (Acts 4:4). Before she travailed, she gave birth, because, as ecclesiastical History recounts, in those first beginnings the gospel message ran everywhere without any hindrance. Thus it happened that suddenly, as if a heavenly light had been displayed or a ray of the sun had burst forth, it illuminated the whole world with the brightness of heavenly light [Note: [Col. 0581D] Both manuscripts: “may illuminate”]; and thereafter, in every city and village, immense multitudes gathered to the Churches as grain gathers to threshing floors at harvest time [Note: [Col. 0582D] Both: “as though”]. Therefore the prophetic utterance adds in wonder:

[Col. 0582A] VERS. 8.—“Who has ever heard such a thing, or who has seen anything like this?”

For never did anything such occur upon the earth; never was anything like it heard or seen: that all nations should believe within a short time, that one nation of Christians should be made from all peoples, and that the Apostle’s saying should be fulfilled: “The old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new” (2 Cor. 5:17). It adds:

“Will the earth give birth in one day, or will a nation be born all at once, because Zion has travailed and brought forth her children?”

For when, as was said, three thousand believed in one day at Peter’s preaching, and many thousands were later added, then one could see a nation born together in one day by the word of God, illuminated by [Col. 0582B] the sun of righteousness; and the barren woman suddenly giving birth, to whom it was said: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; sing praise and cry aloud, you who did not give birth, for the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (above, 54:1). For the Church was forsaken by God, while the Synagogue, which had a husband, had the law and God. But afterwards the barren and forsaken woman became much more fruitful than she who had been joined to a husband. For she travailed and brought forth her children: she travailed by exhorting them, and brought them forth by converting them.

Or, she who at the beginning gave birth before travailing afterwards travailed in order to give birth, because, in order to be able to bear children to God, she labored with many efforts and was tormented with many pains while preaching God’s word; and she gave birth in faith or good conduct to those whom [Col. 0582C] she bore within the womb of love. But because the Lord himself was to preach on earth in person and beget children of this kind, it fittingly adds:

VERS. 9.—“Shall I, who make others give birth, not myself give birth, says the Lord? Shall I, who grant generation to others, be barren, says the Lord your God?”

For he makes others give birth, as he did the one who said: “My little children, for whom I am again in travail” (Gal. 4:19). But he himself also gave birth, because by his preaching he begot the apostles into faith. Hence he calls them his children when he says: “Can the children of the Bridegroom fast while the Bridegroom is with them?” (Matt. 9:15). He himself grants generation to others, as to the one who says: “In Christ Jesus through the Gospel I begot you” (1 Cor. 4:15). But neither is he barren, because “he willingly begot us by the word of truth” (Jas. 1:18). Since after this, as faith and religion increased throughout the world, the Church was to possess prosperity and glory, it fittingly continues:

VERS. 10.—“Rejoice with Jerusalem and exult in her, all you who love her; rejoice with her in joy, all you who mourn over her.”

VERS. 11.—“That you may suck and be filled from the breasts of her consolation; that you may milk and overflow with delights from all her glory.”

[Col. 0583A] “All you,” he says, “who love Jerusalem—that is, the Church—rejoice with her over the blessings which she is now to possess, and exult in her. And you who mourn over her because of the tribulations and evils which she suffers, now rejoice with great joy with her in the blessings with which she shall now be filled, so that you too, made sharers in her blessings, may delightfully suck, drink, and be filled from the breast of her consolation: that is, from the cup of mercy, sweetness, and beneficence by which God will now comfort her, because ‘as you have been companions in sufferings, so you shall be also in consolation’” (2 Cor. 1:7). “And you shall milk from all her glory,” which she is now to have everywhere, “and overflow from it with delights,” both bodily and spiritual. It follows:

[Col. 0583B] VERS. 12.—“For thus says the Lord: Behold, I will turn upon her, as a river of peace, and as an overflowing torrent, the glory of the nations; and you shall suck.”

“I will turn,” he says, “that is, I will cause to descend upon her like a river of peace”—that is, a full and lasting abundance of peace—“and I will bring down upon you, as it were, a great torrent which shall bring in overflowing measure the glory of all nations, so that you may suck it”—that is, drink it like milk—because, once peace has been given, all the remnant of the nations shall flock to faith.

Or the apostles and apostolic men, mourning for Jerusalem which had fallen among the Jews and awaiting the new Jerusalem which was to arise, are commanded to rejoice in it and with it, because it is now to be built [Col. 0583C] with living stones. Those who are little children among them and need the milk of consolation should suck from the breast of its consoling preaching; but those who, after the milk of consolation, have advanced to solid food should abound in the delights of truth and in the knowledge of all glory. Then the Lord shall turn upon her like the river of peace, of which it is said: “The rush of the river gladdens the city of God” (Ps. 45:5), so that, as peace possesses all things and the wars of nations cease, the torrent of God’s teachings waters the path of believers. It follows:

“You shall be carried at the breasts, and they shall caress you upon the knees.” At the breasts the Apostle gave drink to those to whom he said: “As to little children in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3:2). And upon the knees—that is, upon the examples of his good works—he caressed those to whom he said: “Whatever things are true, whatever modest, whatever just, whatever lovely, whatever of good report—if there is any virtue, if there is any praise of discipline—think on these things; and what you have learned, received, seen in me, and heard, do these things, and the God of peace shall be with you” (Phil. 4:8). Likewise the other holy teachers gave, and give, drink to their little children at the breasts of doctrine in the manner of mothers; supporting and cherishing them upon the examples of their good works as though upon knees, they caress them so that they may make progress. For that knees signify works we learn from the history of Gideon, where the three hundred men who drank water with the knee bent upright [Col. 0584A] are reported to have conquered in battle (Judg. 7:5). For water is sacred knowledge. It follows:

VERS. 13.—“As when a mother caresses someone, so I shall comfort you, and in Jerusalem you shall be comforted.”

VERS. 14.—“You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice, and your bones shall spring up like grass.”

As a mother caresses her crying little child so that it may cease weeping, so shall I do for you: while you are still faint-hearted because of the evils which you suffer for correction, and give voice to complaint, I shall caress you with manifold consolation and sweetly soothe you. But after passing from this present life you shall find a far sweeter consolation, because immediately you shall be led into the heavenly Jerusalem, where you may rejoice perpetually, and shall not [Col. 0584B] descend into hell as the ancient fathers did. And in that Jerusalem—which is not without reason interpreted “vision of peace”—you shall see, as he is, the glory of the Creator, and your heart shall rejoice from its inmost marrow at his sight. When the day of resurrection comes, your bones shall spring up from the dust like grass, because they shall live again, flourish, and bloom in unfading glory. That these things must be understood thus is shown by what follows immediately:

“And the hand of the Lord shall be known to his servants, and he shall be angry with his enemies.”

VERS. 15.—“For behold, the Lord shall come in fire, and his chariots like a whirlwind, to render his fury in indignation and his rebuke in a flame of fire.”

[Col. 0584C] VERS. 16.—“For the Lord shall judge in fire, and with his sword, all flesh.”

Then the mighty hand of the Lord shall be known to his servants, because in the arm of his power he shall deliver them; and he shall be angry with his enemies—that is, all who did not love him from the heart. For he shall come surrounded by fire, and his chariots—that is, the angelic powers in which he sits—shall come like a whirlwind, to overthrow all the reprobate and, driving them with torments, carry them away from the world like straw. The Lord, I say, shall come to render his fury with great indignation to the wicked, and to rebuke in flame of fire those deserving rebuke. For “fire shall test what sort of work each person has. If anyone’s work remains, he shall receive a reward; if anyone’s work is burned, he shall suffer loss” (1 Cor. 3:14–15). Especially the reprobate shall then be in the fire to be rebuked, because the saints shall immediately be caught up in clouds to meet Christ in the air and placed at his right hand, while sinners shall remain on earth, be set at the left, and, surrounded by fire which shall burn all the lower regions of this air, shall await the Judge’s sentence while tasting beforehand the severity of hellish torments. For that fire is to occupy as much of this air as the floodwater occupied when it was fifteen cubits higher than the mountains which it covered beneath the whole heaven.

Therefore, when the righteous have been lifted on high and sinners left below in the midst of that fire, the Lord shall render [Col. 0585A] his rebuke to those same sinners set in flame, saying: “I was hungry and you did not give me food; I was naked and you did not clothe me” (Matt. 25:42). For in that fire and by the sword of his mouth he shall judge all flesh—that is, against all who are fleshly—because then it shall be demonstrated how justly, indeed how mercifully, he always acted toward them in every respect, and conversely how unjustly they always acted toward him. Therefore they shall be struck by his sword when they hear: “Depart from me, you accursed, into eternal fire” (ibid., 41). By “all flesh” he means all who have not attained the glory of incorruption through that transformation which shall be given to the saints. Of this flesh the Apostle says: “For flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 15:50). [Col. 0585B] This flesh, therefore, which does not enter God’s kingdom is handed over outside to fire and sword. But after this a sentence most fearful is added:

“And the slain of the Lord,” he says, “shall be multiplied.”

VERS. 17.—“Those who sanctified themselves and thought themselves clean in gardens behind the inner door.”

For what is signified by the inner door but entry into a more religious and secret manner of life, such as belongs to those who renounce the world, approach the service of the altar, or perform some act more sacred than others? And what is signified by the name of gardens but the manner of life of such persons, adorned with the flowers of life and flourishing in the strength of good works? In these gardens they bear fruit, because they perform deeds of holiness; and they think themselves clean because they judge that they have already been cleansed from the filth of sins and arrogate to themselves the purity of holiness. Since they presume upon their merits, they are killed when he comes who strikes all pride. Hence elsewhere it is said to each such person: “The more beautiful you are, descend, and sleep with the uncircumcised” (Ezek. 32:19). For everyone who neglects to consider the foulness of his own weakness, but in the haughtiness of pride regards the glory of his own virtue, descends precisely by being more beautiful: exalting himself on account of his merits, he inwardly falls into the depths from that very point at which he judged himself glorious. Descending, he sleeps with the uncircumcised because he perishes in eternal [Col. 0585D] death with the other sinners.

It is therefore rightly said that “the slain of the Lord shall be multiplied, those who sanctified themselves and thought themselves clean in gardens”—that is, in cultivated plantations of virtues—“behind the inner door,” that is, after entering a holier life; for many who seem more religious and closer to God shall be slain on that day by the sword of his judgment. For who does not think himself to approach God when he recognizes that he is growing in heavenly virtues or gifts, whether he receives the gift of prophecy, the office of teaching, or strength to exercise the grace of healing? Yet often, while the mind relaxes through confidence in its virtue, the adversary lies in wait and it is pierced by the dart of an unexpected fault; and it becomes eternally far from God at the very point where [Col. 0586A] for a time it had drawn near to him without the safeguard of vigilance.

Therefore it is rightly said of all these and such persons that “the slain of the Lord shall be multiplied, those who sanctified themselves and thought themselves clean in gardens behind the inner door.” Nor are we ignorant that, according to the historical sense, the Jews are denoted by these words—indeed, the scribes and Pharisees—who, according to the Lord’s judgment, cleansed what was outside the cup and dish while inwardly they were full of impurity (Matt. 23:25). For through Moses God had commanded that, if anyone had been overtaken in sin, he should return to the temple after being sprinkled with the ashes of a red heifer and through other modes of expiation by sacrifices and victims (Num. 19:2). Neglecting this, in places of pleasure and delight—that is, in most pleasant gardens—they built either baptisteries or pools [Col. 0586B] for watering garden beds, imagining that by simple washings of water they cleansed adultery and every filthiness of lust. For while they clung to prostitutes like dogs and males practiced shamefulness with males, they sanctified themselves in gardens—that is, they washed themselves—and believed themselves clean; but at the coming of the inward Judge they shall be killed. Those ancient Jews also are rebuked by these words, who secretly worshipped idols in gardens and there sanctified themselves—that is, were praised—and thought themselves clean; but when the Lord comes, they shall be slain. For they shall be confounded by the idols to which they sacrificed and ashamed of the gardens which they chose.

We may also understand idolaters to mean heretics, who, separating themselves from the unity of the Church, worship in their conventicles, as in gardens, the inventions of their errors as though they were certain images. There, according to their own judgment, they sanctify themselves by fasts, vigils, and diverse abstinences, and judge themselves clean because they do not communicate with the luxurious, drunkards, perjurers, and other criminals who are in the Church. They suppose that we are contaminated by sins because we preferred to dwell among such people rather than divide ourselves from the unity of the Church. But there is no doubt that all this multitude, which sanctifies itself through impiety and glories in its purity, shall perish when the Judge comes. This, then, is what is said: “The slain of the Lord shall be multiplied, those who sanctified themselves and thought themselves clean in gardens behind the inner door.” It follows:

[Col. 0586D] “Those who were eating swine’s flesh, and abomination, and mouse, shall be consumed together, says the Lord.”

But the Law says: “The pig, because it divides the hoof and does not chew the cud, shall be unclean” (Deut. 14:8). It also counts the mouse among unclean animals (Lev. 11:29). And what is it to divide the hoof and not chew the cud, except to possess discernment indeed, but not to reconsider and ponder the food of life—that is, the words of righteousness—but carelessly to hand them over to forgetfulness? What, then, is pork, except the embodiment of the weak way of life of those who have the sharpness of discernment but neglect to chew over God’s commandments in their hearts so as to perform them? Thus he eats pork who receives [Col. 0587A] and imitates the example of the unclean conduct of such supposedly wiser persons. An abomination, however, is any detestable sin.

The mouse is always at work because of its voracity, signifying those who follow the gluttony of their belly, “whose god is their belly” (Phil. 3:19). And he eats a mouse who adopts from someone an example of excessive eating. He eats an abomination who admits into himself a detestable deed. Therefore, whoever eat pork and abomination and mouse, unless they are cleansed as quickly as possible through repentance, will all be consumed together on that day. Or they will be consumed together with the impurities which they eat, so that both those who provide an example of wickedness and those who receive it may perish together. Or together with those who consider themselves clean in their gardens. It follows:

[Col. 0587B] VERSE 18.—“But I come to gather their works and their thoughts with all nations and tongues.”

The Lord will then conduct a public examination, and in the sight of the whole human race he will gather and reveal not only the deeds of each individual, but also their thoughts from the beginning to the end of their lives—except those erased through repentance; and each will receive according to what he has thought and done. But concerning the elect he adds: “And they shall come and see my glory.” For, when judgment has been completed and the reprobate have fallen into punishment, he will bring the righteous into his kingdom, and there reveal himself to them, so that they may see eternally, as it is, the glory of his divinity, and rejoice without end in the sight of him. [Col. 0587C] It follows:

VERSE 19.—“And I will set a sign among them.”

He will set a sign among them because, according to John’s Apocalypse, “they shall have his name written on their foreheads” (Rev. 14:1). Or the words may be understood as having suddenly turned to the times of the present life, because now he sets the sign of the holy cross upon all who come to the faith. Hence he adds: “And I will send from among them those who have been saved, to the nations—to the sea, to Africa, to Libya [Note: [Col. 0587D] Alternatively, Lydia, ‘drawing an arrow.’], holding an arrow; to Italy and Greece; to the distant islands, to those who have not heard of me and have not seen my glory. And they shall proclaim my glory among the nations.”

VERSE 20.—“And they shall bring all your brethren [Col. 0587D] from all nations as an offering to the Lord, on horses and in chariots and in litters and on mules and in carts, to my holy mountain Jerusalem, says the Lord, just as the children of Israel bring an offering in a clean vessel into the house of the Lord.”

VERSE 21.—“And from among them I will take priests and Levites, says the Lord.”

For, as Paul writes concerning this: “Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration” (Titus 3:5), that is, through baptism. And again: “For in hope we were saved” (Rom. 8:24). From those who had been saved by baptism and hope, [Col. 0588A] Christ sent to the nations Paul himself, Barnabas, and others such as these. He sent them to the sea, that is, to the islands which are in the sea. Divine speech has expressly named Africa, which is the southern part of the world, and Libya, which is above it, as well as Italy, which lies to the west, and Greece, which is situated toward the north, as though it had named south and east, west and north, because these are the principal regions of the world. The word of preaching is called an arrow because, by striking the life of those who live badly, it pierces their hearts. Heralds of truth were also sent to islands far away in the Ocean and to all who had previously heard nothing from God and had not seen the glory of the wonders which he performed in the flesh.

[Col. 0588B] The brethren of believers are all who come to the faith and begin to have God as their Father with them. They are brought from all nations to the Lord on horses and chariots and litters, on mules and carts. For what does he call horses except God-bearing preachers? And what are chariots except their preachings, borne, as it were, on the four wheels of the four books of the Gospel, or resting as upon four wheels upon the Law and the Prophets, the Gospel and the Apostles? Hence elsewhere it is said to him: “You shall ride upon your horses, and your chariots are salvation” (Hab. 3:8).

A litter is so called from its resemblance to a bed; it is a conveyance in which the daughters of nobles, covered by a canopy above, were customarily carried, as it were in a carriage, upon four horses. Similar to this conveyance was the vessel [Col. 0588C] sent down from heaven to Peter. For Peter saw in a trance “a certain vessel descending, like a great linen cloth, lowered from heaven to earth by its four corners, in which were all the four-footed creatures and creeping things of the earth and birds of heaven; and a voice came to him: ‘Rise, Peter; kill and eat’” (Acts 10:11). The litter, therefore, is believed to signify the same thing as that vessel: namely, the vehicle of evangelical preaching, in which the delicate souls of believers are gently carried, find rest, and are nourished, and are concealed from the tumult of worldly affairs. He used the plural “litters,” because every prudent and devout teacher composes from the words and skill of his preaching such a conveyance for nourishing in secret and advancing [Col. 0588D] the souls of believers, like daughters of noble rank.

But what is signified by mules, male or female, which are always sterile, except the perpetual chastity of the elect priests? For that the mule signifies virginity or continence we recognize when we read that Solomon was placed upon “David’s mule” in order to be made king over Israel (3 Kings 1:38). For what is designated by Solomon except Christ, and by “David’s mule” except the primitive Church, chaste in mind and body? Upon her the Savior was placed as king over all Israel—that is, appointed over the whole people of believers. Therefore let us understand by mules [Col. 0589A] the ever-chaste prelates of the Church.

Carts too are noble vehicles, taking their name from *carrus*, “wagon.” And what is expressed by carts except the preachings already mentioned, which carry us on God’s way and convey us upward to heavenly things? Thus on horses and in chariots and little beds and on mules and in carts your brethren are brought from all nations to the Lord’s holy mountain, Jerusalem, while believers are brought from every side to the Church through holy preachers and through the ministry of their teaching and conduct. And they are brought as an offering, which the children of Israel were accustomed to bring in a clean vessel into the house of the Lord, because they too are an acceptable offering and are brought by teachers into the Church in the holy vessel of preaching.

[Col. 0589B] Or, those who are swift in faith ride upon horses; those manifold in grace, in chariots; those needing consolation, in covered beds and shelters, so that they may deserve to hear: “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night” (Ps. 120:6). The continent and sterile are brought on mules. Carts, however, are to be understood as those to whom the Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Gal. 6:2). And your brethren are brought to the Lord in the clean vessel of a chaste body. And from among them the Lord takes priests and Levites, because priests and Levites worthy of God are now chosen not from the tribe of Levi alone but from all nations. Since those whom holy preachers bring to the Church please God eternally and reign with him, he fittingly adds:

[Col. 0589C] VERSE 22.—“For as the new heavens and the new earth, which I cause to stand before me, says the Lord, so shall your seed and your name stand.”

For just as the new heavens and new earth, which the Lord will cause to stand before him after the day of judgment, shall stand for ever, so the seed of the preachers—that is, the children whom they have begotten through the Gospel—shall stand eternally before him; and their name shall remain in the Book of Life before God’s eyes. Hence the blessed Apostle wrote to the faithful concerning him: “He is able to preserve you without sin and to set you spotless before the presence of his glory at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Jude 24). Therefore the elect shall stand without end before his face, where they will raise themselves from themselves to behold him; and, carried away by the attention of their hearts and the sweetness of contemplation, [Col. 0589D] they will continually behold the beauty of his countenance. It follows:

VERSE 23.—“And there shall be month after month, and Sabbath after Sabbath.”

The month is used for perfection. For what is a month except the perfection of days? And what is the Sabbath except rest, in which no servile work may be done? There shall therefore be month after month, because those who have lived perfectly here will there be brought to the perfection of glory. And there shall be Sabbath after Sabbath, because those who have ceased here from perverse work will there rest in heavenly recompense. And because on the day of resurrection the Lord will also bring the bodies of the righteous into that homeland of the living, it is fittingly added:

[Col. 0590A] “And all flesh shall come to worship before my face, says the Lord.”

For, having received their bodies, all the elect will enter the court of the everlasting kingdom, and, coming before the throne of his majesty, they will fall upon their faces, rejoicing and giving thanks, and will worship him, as we clearly learn from John’s Apocalypse (Rev. 4:10). As soon as they behold his immeasurable light, they will perceive how narrow are all created things, and will easily see what occurs in every creature. Hence it is added:

VERSE 24.—“And they shall go out and see the corpses of the men who have transgressed against me.”

We do not, however, believe that they will go bodily out from that region of the blessed; rather, they will go out by the greatness of their vision, because the vastness of heaven will not contain the breadth [Col. 0590B] of their minds. Their sight will exceed the boundaries of the heavenly homeland, so that they may see clearly not only what is within but also what is outside. For by the light of inward vision the bosom of the mind is enlarged. And when it is carried above itself in God’s light, it is expanded inwardly and enlarged so greatly in God that every creature appears narrow to it. Therefore they are said to go out not by a change of place, but by receiving a broader and purer sight, in order to see the corpses of transgressors—that is, the bodies of sinners burning in punishments. For, while they behold the immeasurable light of the Creator, it is too little for them to see everything which is in that kingdom of blessedness unless they also behold with the sight [Col. 0590C] of a free mind everything that takes place in the whole creation.

Thus the righteous always behold the unrighteous in torments, so that their joy may increase from this: they see the evil which they have mercifully escaped; and they give greater thanks to their deliverer in proportion as they see in others what they themselves could have suffered had they been abandoned.

Nor does the sight of the punishment of the reprobate darken in the mind of the righteous the brightness of so great a blessedness; for where compassion of mercy will no longer exist, it will certainly be unable to diminish the joy of the blessed. What wonder is it, then, if, when the righteous behold the torments of the unrighteous, this contributes to the service of their joys, when even in a painting black color is laid underneath so that white or red may appear brighter? And [Col. 0590D] although their own joys fully suffice for their enjoyment, they nevertheless always behold the evils of the reprobate as an increase of joy, without doubt, because, as was said, those who see the brightness of their Creator cannot be unable to see anything done in creation.

He calls the bodies of the reprobate “corpses,” because they are foul-smelling and fail in everlasting death. Concerning them it is added:

“Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished.” For that Gehenna-fire will never be extinguished, as John also affirms, saying of the Lord: “But he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Matt. 3:12). In it the worms too must be believed immortal, eating the flesh of the impious without end, so that they may be tormented perpetually not only by fire [Col. 0591A] but also devoured by worms. Hence Judith says in her song: “He will give fire and worms to their flesh, that they may burn and feel evils for ever” (Judith 14:21). And elsewhere it is written: “The vengeance upon the flesh of the ungodly is fire and worms” (Ecclus. 7:19). Therefore, just as that fire is corporeal, so too the worms are corporeal, because the fire burns the bodies of the reprobate and the worms tear them apart. Or, by the worm is signified the putrefaction of Gehenna, and by fire its burning. Or the worm is called the late repentance for sins, which will never cease to bite the conscience of the afflicted in torments, so that fire is punishment raging outwardly, while the worm is inward pain accusing them. Concerning them it is further added:

“And they shall be unto the satiety of vision for all [Col. 0591B] flesh.”

They shall be unto the satiety of vision because all the righteous will be satisfied by the sight of them, whom they will see without interruption consigned before their eyes to everlasting disgrace. By “all flesh” he now means all the elect, clothed after the resurrection of their bodies in the glory of incorruption.

With these words the prophetic book reaches its end. And blessed Isaiah fittingly ends his book at this point: having spoken hitherto chiefly of those things which occur in the present life, he now makes an end of speaking with those things which will be fulfilled in the future.

We too, desiring to attain the glory of the resurrection which is displayed at the end of this book and is frequently signified by the number eight, have treated his sayings briefly in eight volumes, so far as heavenly inspiration opened them to us, and according to the sense of Catholic truth, which is found in all the books [Col. 0592A] of the orthodox Fathers, and according to the rule of faith which the Church maintains. We do not prejudge the understanding of others who perhaps have thought or will think differently on these matters; we merely set forth simply what has seemed to us.

For it does no harm that Holy Scripture should be understood in different ways, provided Catholic truth is maintained, that what is understood nourishes piety, and that it cannot be disproved by other statements of Scripture. Therefore, whoever can interpret these things better should diligently make known what he knows to be useful to many, lest at the last he be accused of having hidden his master’s money. But whoever has not explained these things better, or has no better explanation of this book, should not disparage this which [Col. 0592B] our small ability has published. For, since there was need of an interpreter if this prophetic book, so useful and necessary—a book which the Church uses more frequently than the other prophetic books—was to be understood, and since nowhere in our regions could we find a complete exposition of it, I was moved to undertake this work, that I might give whatever small measure of understanding I could to those who read or heard the prophet’s words and did not understand them.

Therefore, whoever does not understand this prophet and has not, or cannot find, another exposition of him should not disdain to receive this one, unless he wishes always to remain ignorant of Isaiah. But if anyone perhaps judges this work pleasing to himself or derives any fruit [Col. 0592C] from it, let him give thanks for it to the Author of all good things, and pray to him that he may restore to me in the world to come the reward for so great a labor. He, God, lives and reigns unto all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0591]

# COMMENTARIES OF HERVEY, MONK OF BOURG-DIEU, ON THE EPISTLES OF SAINT PAUL

(Edition of the Works of St Anselm, published at Cologne in 1573 by Maternus Cholinus, folio, vol. II.)

## PREFACE

[Col. 0591D] As, with the Lord’s help, we are about to speak concerning the epistles of the Apostle Paul, let us first see what the very name *epistle* [Col. 0592D] signifies. The Greek *epistola* is called *supermissa* in Latin, just as an *epigram* is an inscription upon a letter and an *epitaph* an inscription upon a tomb. For Greek *epi* means Latin *super*, “upon”; while *stola* means “sent.” Hence epistles are called *supermissae*, “things sent in addition,” because they were sent to the faithful in addition to what they had received. For they had received the Gospel, and the Epistles were subsequently added to them and sent for various reasons.

For just as the prophets, after the Law of Moses had been promulgated, in which all God’s commandments were read, continually restrained by their teaching the recurring sins of the people and transmitted them in books, by way of example, even to our remembrance, so too the Apostle, after the Gospel—which is the supplement to the Law and in which examples and precepts for living are most fully arranged for us—wished to send these epistles to the individual churches: namely, so that, in the beginning of the Church’s growth, when new occasions arose, he might cut off present and emerging vices and exclude future questions. Therefore, just as prophecies were necessary after the Law, so epistles are necessary after the Gospel. For just as what had been said most obscurely in the Law was somewhat made manifest through the prophets, and its transgressors were corrected through them, so what had been said obscurely and generally in the Gospel was elucidated in detail by apostolic instruction; transgressors of evangelical precepts were corrected and urged to observe them.

The epistles of this Apostle Paul which the Church reads are fourteen, though he undoubtedly also wrote a fifteenth to the Laodiceans. And when in the first epistle which we have to the Corinthians he says, “I wrote to you in the Epistle not to associate with fornicators” (1 Cor. 5), he appears to indicate that he had already written another epistle to them. Therefore, although he wrote many epistles, the Fathers did not without a definite mystical reason wish that only fourteen should be read in church: namely, ten sent to churches and four to disciples. Moreover, from the very number of the epistles they wished to show that this outstanding teacher had searched out the mysteries of Law and Gospel. For the number ten signifies the Law because of its Decalogue; the number four signifies the Gospel because of its four books.

Thus ten epistles which he wrote to churches are retained, to demonstrate that the New Testament does not disagree with the Old and that the Apostle did nothing in any respect against the Law of Moses. His epistles are arranged according to the number of the first commandments of the Decalogue of that Law; and as many precepts as Moses used to instruct the children of Israel, freed from Pharaoh’s yoke, so by the same number of epistles this Apostle instructs those rescued from the slavery of the devil and idolatry. By the four written to disciples, however, the New Testament is signified. Accordingly, these same disciples were of greater perfection than the churches to which the ten were sent, so that the imperfection of those under the Law and the perfection of those who keep the Gospel might be signified.

That the Fathers placed the four written to disciples after the nine addressed to churches, and placed the one to the Hebrews last, makes it most certainly understood that the New Testament is contained in the Old [Col. 0594A] and that one is of no benefit without the other. For as four joined to ten completes this total, namely fourteen, so the New and Old Testaments accomplish one thing and aim to impress upon the hearts of their hearers the truth of faith and uprightness of conduct.

Thus the doctrine of Paul is contained in fourteen epistles, through which both greater and lesser persons are instructed how they ought to live and believe, since the holy Church, keeping both Testaments according to his teaching and living both according to the catalogue of the Law and according to the four books of the Gospel, advances to the summit of perfection.

Having set this forth, we must see why, by the counsel of the Holy Spirit, the holy Fathers collected these epistles in one volume in an order different from that in which the Apostle composed them. They have also been left to us for our correction and exhortation, so that all of us, whenever we fall wounded, may find there how we are able to rise again and recover what we have lost. Thus we can discern in them a certain ascending progression: the epistles to churches governed more by faith and uprightness of conduct than by the exposition of those matters are placed first, so that, as epistles sent to less perfect churches precede and those addressed to more perfect ones follow, a certain ascending scale from lesser to greater things may be found. No one becomes eminent suddenly; everyone begins with the least things in order to arrive at greater.

[Col. 0594C] Therefore the Epistle to the Romans is first, because faith is the first virtue and the foundation of the other virtues, and without it it is impossible to please God (Heb. 11). It was fitting that the epistle dealing with the first virtue should be placed at the head of the others, and that all who resemble the Romans in imperfect faith should be corrected and recalled therein to the perfection of faith. The Epistle to the Corinthians is rightly placed beneath it, because it instructs in good works those who have already received faith. For first the foundation—that is, faith—must be laid, and then good works must be built upon it. Therefore the Epistle to the Romans gives instruction to all believers concerning faith; this Epistle to the Corinthians gives instruction concerning conduct. Thus the rest too are subsequently arranged in a fitting order.

Some, however, have said that the Epistle to the Romans was placed first because the Romans were so ignorant that they believed themselves saved not by God’s grace but by their own merits. But the entire text of that epistle, which is deeper in meaning than all the others, does not establish this. It is therefore more credible that those who gathered the members of the epistles into one body judged that epistle worthy to sit at the head because it was directed to the city which at that time was the head of the whole world, and because to this day the Roman Church holds primacy over all churches.

The subject matter of all the epistles is faith [Col. 0595A] and good morals. Their purpose is to commend that faith and those morals and to urge people toward them: by commending good things, discouraging evil things, threatening evildoers with evils, and promising good things to those who do good. And for what final cause? Without doubt, for the attainment of true blessedness. To this single general purpose all the particular purposes are reduced; and throughout all the various discussions nothing is inserted that does not contribute, principally or secondarily, to the instruction of faith and morals. Therefore the treatment of these epistles belongs to ethics.

The Epistle to the Romans, as far as may be understood from its text, raises this question: did Christ’s Gospel come to the Jews because of the merits of works of the Law, or, with no merits of works preceding, did the justification of faith which is in Christ Jesus come to all nations, so that people should believe not because they were righteous, but, having been justified through believing, should thereafter begin to live righteously?

In this epistle, therefore, the Apostle intends to teach that the grace of Christ’s Gospel came to all. He shows why it is called grace: because it was not rendered as a debt of justice but freely given. For certain persons who had believed from among the Jews had begun to raise a disturbance against the Gentiles, and especially against Paul himself, because he admitted uncircumcised persons and persons free from the bonds of the old Law to the grace of the Gospel, preaching that they should believe in Christ without imposing upon them the yoke of bodily circumcision. But with such moderation does the Apostle reconcile both parties that he permits neither the Jews to be proud as though on account of the merits of works of the Law, nor the Gentiles to be puffed up against the Jews on the merit of faith, because they had received the Christ whom the Jews crucified (2 Cor. 5).

For, acting as an ambassador for Christ, as he says elsewhere, that is, for the cornerstone, he joins in Christ through the bond of grace both peoples, from Jews and Gentiles alike. He removes from both all pride in merits and unites both, who are to be justified through the discipline of humility. If anyone asks how the Jews converted at Rome could murmur against Paul, whom they had not yet seen, let him know that Paul was not unknown to them, because the report of his preaching was heard everywhere. Certain of his disciples and of Peter’s disciples had already come to Rome and converted many there to the faith, both Jews and Gentiles. But among these recent converts there was, as we said, schism and contention. The Jews gloried in their merits and nobility of lineage, failing to understand that they had come to faith through God’s grace and believing that they had received this through their own merits and those of their fathers. The Gentiles, however, although no merits had preceded by which they could glory in order to prefer themselves to the Jews, nevertheless despised the Jews as killers of Christ and transgressors of the Law, and asserted that ignorance alone had held them back from believing earlier—thus relying on the powers of their own reason and free choice, and not considering the work of divine grace necessary.

The Apostle corrects both groups as they lived in this contentious manner.
