He shows the Jews that faith [Col. 0596B] and the other spiritual goods had come to them with no preceding merits, but from grace alone, since the Law justified no one, giving only knowledge of sin. In the same way he proves that the Gentiles offended God not through ignorance but knowingly, deliberately, and very seriously. For although they did not have the written Law, they did have the natural law; and, though they ought to have honored as God the Creator known through creation, they changed his glory into handmade images. He demonstrates by the truest reasoning that both, having obtained forgiveness alike, are equal—especially since it was foretold in the Law that both Jews and Gentiles were to be called to faith in Christ. Therefore, humbling them each in turn, he exhorts them to peace and concord.

[Col. 0596C] The occasion for this epistle, then, was their contention, around which the whole matter revolves. In this discussion the Apostle intends to restrain the pride and arrogance of both parties by which they disagreed with each other, so that they may glory in neither any right nor any merit of their own, but rather be recalled to humility, attribute to God’s grace whatever good they possess, and thus return through humility to concord and peace.

The subject matter of this epistle is the Church of Jews and Gentiles, divided for the reasons stated above. But now that these matters have been completed, let us approach the book. Before the Apostle begins to expound his intention, he gives a prologue by which he makes his hearers attentive, teachable, and well disposed; and he greets them, saying:

# EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0595D]

“Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called as an Apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the Holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined Son of God [Col. 0596D] in power according to the Spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord; through whom we received grace and apostleship for obedience to the faith among all nations for his name, among whom you also are called of Jesus Christ; to all who are at Rome, beloved of God, called [Col. 0597A] saints: grace to you and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Let us first see why he who was formerly called Saul is now called Paul. King Saul was proud and unrestrained, a persecutor of holy David, and born from the tribe of Benjamin. This Saul too was from that tribe and received from Saul, as by inheritance, both his name and his cruelty. Saul, therefore, is the name of a proud persecutor. Moreover, Saul and Saulus are the same name. What we call *Saulus* is due to Greek and Latin usage, which declined Hebrew names according to the pattern of their own cases; just as Joseph became *Josephus* and Jacob *Jacobus*, so Saul too is called *Saulus* in our language.

When he had subjected the proconsul Paul to Christ, he too wished to be called Paul instead of Saul, in commemoration of so glorious an emblem of a beautiful victory. For an enemy is conquered more fully in that by which he holds more firmly, and by which he holds more people [Note: [Col. 0597D] An obscure passage.]. The proud, moreover, are held more firmly by a noble name, and more of them by a name of authority. Therefore, just as Scipio, who subdued Africa, was called Africanus, so this Apostle, after Paul’s subjugation, was always called Paul, though he had formerly been accustomed to be called Saul. Nor without reason: for *Saulus* or *Saul* is interpreted “asked for,” because he had been requested from the devil for the purpose of waging war upon the Church. But Paul is called “wonderful,” and was fittingly sent to preach to the Gentiles. He is named Paul—that is, “wonderful”—so that he might wonderfully gain the reward of faith. For he is a most wonderful leader who glories not in wisdom of speech, riches, eloquence, or empty worldly glory, but in Christ’s sufferings.

Another explanation of this matter may also be offered: perhaps he had two names, that is, was called both Saul and Paul. This indeed appears more probable, because no such custom is found in the divine Scriptures as the claim we made that he was called Paul after the proconsul Paul whom he subjected to Christ. But in those same Scriptures we find some using two names and others even three: for example, Zedekiah, who was also Jehoiakim; Uzziah, who was also Azariah; Solomon, who was also Jedidiah or Ecclesiastes; and very many others. Nor was this custom lacking among Christ’s apostles. One of them was called [Col. 0597D] Matthew and Levi; another, Lebbaeus and Judas Thaddaeus.

Since it was customary for Hebrews to use two or three names, this Apostle too appears to have used a double appellation. While he ministered especially to his own people, he was called Saul, because that seemed a more native name of his homeland (Acts 13); but Paul when he gave laws and precepts among Greeks and Gentiles. For the very words of Scripture, “Saul, who is also Paul,” plainly seem to show not that the name Paul was then first imposed upon him but that it was an old appellation. Whether this explanation or the former is truer, one thing is certain: from the time when this Apostle was sent with Barnabas to preach [Col. 0598A] to the Gentiles, he preferred to be called Paul rather than Saul. He places this celebrated and universally known name of his own at the beginning of this epistle so that, upon hearing the name of so great a man, the Romans may attend to what he wishes to persuade them, what he deigns to command—namely, that they may be eager to hear and ready to obey.

“Paul,” he says, as if saying: You Romans ought to have peace among yourselves, because he who writes to you is Paul—that is, not a persecutor of Christians but a teacher; not a destroyer of the Church but a builder; not a persuader of dissension but of unity and concord. Nor ought you to be lifted up in pride, because he who teaches you is a servant—that is, humble and not without the Lord’s yoke. For “servant” is a name of humility, intended to invite them to it. But since the Lord says to his chosen disciples, “I will no longer call you servants” (John 15), how is this man a servant?

There are two kinds of servitude: one of fear, the other of love; one belonging to servants who fear, the other to sons who love and please. Therefore the chosen disciples are not servants according to the servitude of fear, which perfect love casts out (1 John 4), but according to the servitude of chaste fear, which perfect charity produces. Paul, therefore, is a servant, serving God not out of slavish fear but out of chaste love. He first commends his person and office so that the Romans may more readily yield to his words and corrections, and may take from him an example of humility and concord.

For Paul, as we have said, means “wonderful.” And he truly was wonderful, since God had made him marvelous through so great a prerogative of merits. Yet in all things he humbled himself and humbly confessed himself a servant, in order to give everyone an example of humility, lest anyone should glory in personal merits or powers, but that all should attribute whatever good they had to the Lord’s grace and recognize themselves not proudly as free but humbly as servants. As for what others say, that Paul means “small” in Latin and “quiet” in Greek, we do not greatly approve it, because this name is neither Greek nor Latin but Hebrew, and therefore must be understood according to the Hebrew sense.

Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ. As though he said: “I do not make myself free, nor do I make myself equal to my Lord; rather, I account myself [Col. 0598D] his servant and subject, and I ascribe wholly to his grace whatever good I possess. But you make yourselves not his servants but free persons, and, diminishing the gift of his grace which is in you, you have ascribed it to your merits and the powers of your intellect.” “I am,” he says, “a servant of Jesus Christ.” This contributes to the commendation of his person, because both the servant is honorable and the Lord incomparably more honorable. Therefore such an honorable servant of so great a Lord ought gladly to be received. He does not yet call himself an apostle, but only a servant, whereas in his other epistles he at once puts forward the name of authority; for he had not yet preached to the Romans, nor did he yet appear to be an apostle to them. Therefore he sets before them [Col. 0599A] the name of humility, since he was inviting them to humility—something he would not have done had he constrained them to obedience by the name of authority.

A servant of Jesus Christ. Jesus has one meaning and Christ another, although Jesus Christ, our Savior, is one. [Note: [Col. 0599D] A rather obscure passage.] For Jesus is his proper name, just as Moses was called by his proper name, as Aaron was, and as Elijah was. Christ, however, is the name of a mystery, as when one says “lawgiver,” “priest,” or “prophet.” Thus Christ too is commended as the one in whom there would be redemption for the whole people of Israel. The Jews awaited his coming; but because he came in humility, they did not recognize him.

Called an apostle for the Gospel of God. He was called [Col. 0599B] from unbelief to faith when Christ spoke to him from heaven as he was on his way to Damascus (Acts 9). And he was appointed an Apostle—which in Latin means “one sent”—when, afterward, while he was praying in the temple, the Lord appeared to him and said: “Hurry and leave Jerusalem quickly, because they will not receive your testimony concerning me. Go, for I shall send you far away to the nations” (Acts 22). He was also set apart for the Gospel of God when, afterward at Antioch, the Holy Spirit said: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work to which I have appointed them” (Acts 13).

Paul could boast in all these things, since he obtained them all while the Lord appeared and spoke to him. For he is shown to be great whom God deigns thus to advance by himself. Yet, though he has the greatest [Col. 0599C] grounds for boasting, he humbles himself in everything, in order to draw all men to humility by his example. Therefore he calls himself a servant at the very outset.

The calling by which he was called is not that of which it is said, “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20), but rather that of which he himself speaks: “Those whom he predestined, them he also called; and those whom he called, them he also justified” (Rom. 8). He is also an Apostle—that is, one sent by Christ—so that, acting as Christ’s ambassador, he might call all to life. He was not sent as the other apostles were, but was set apart for the Gospel of God. For when a particular province had been assigned to each apostle for preaching, Paul and Barnabas were entrusted with the office of preaching among all nations. [Col. 0599D] Thus these two were set apart—that is, sent to evangelize separately from the company of the other preachers. Or they were set apart for the Gospel because, from the company of the other preachers residing at Antioch, they were chosen by the Holy Spirit for the work of preaching.

“Gospel” means “good news,” because it announces human salvation through Christ’s incarnation, death, and resurrection. This Gospel is not of men but of God: it was not instituted or devised by men, but by God.

Which he had promised beforehand through his prophets. For the commendation of the preacher, he adds the commendation of the Gospel. Hence the preacher himself could sufficiently [Col. 0600A] boast, as though he said: “I have been set apart for the Gospel, which is not sudden or unforeseen, because before its fulfillment God promised it, so that it might be awaited with longing and, when it came, received devoutly and without any scruple.” It is neither frivolous nor recent: God the Father promised it freely, and not newly but beforehand—that is, through many preceding ages. He promised it beforehand through prophets, not through foreign prophets but his own. For prophets who were not his also foretold some things about Christ, such as the Sibyl and Virgil. But the Apostle speaks of prophets who were his own, such as Isaiah and Jeremiah.

He promised it, I say, through the prophets, not merely in words but in Scriptures—not secular writings, but holy, that is, divine Scriptures. [Col. 0600B] For testimonies to the truth are found in the books of the Gentiles, as the Apostle himself showed in speaking to the Athenians. But because errors too are proclaimed in those books, they are not holy, although something relating to Christ may be found in them. Rather, those Scriptures are holy which were divinely entrusted to the Hebrew people, and in them are read the promises that the Gospel would be given, promises made from ancient times through his true prophets.

In those Scriptures the promises were left in writing, lest they be consigned to oblivion and fail to come to the knowledge of later generations. I say, “Scriptures concerning his Son,” because all those promises were made concerning the only-begotten Son of God; all proclaim his divinity, through which all things were made, and foretell that all things would be restored through his humanity.

[Col. 0600C] Who was made—that is, while remaining what he was, he assumed what he was not. I say that he was made not according to divinity, but according to the flesh. For according to divinity he was begotten of the Father, not made; but according to the flesh he was made for him—that is, for the Father’s honor—so that the Father might be glorified through the humility of his incarnation and obedience. He was made not from just any stock, but from the seed of David, because his incorrupt mother, from whose sanctified virginal womb he assumed flesh, sprang from David’s line. God had promised David that an eternal king would be raised up from his seed. For he is read to have said:

> “When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, [Col. 0600D] I shall raise up your seed after you, which shall come forth from your womb, and I shall establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I shall establish the throne of his kingdom for ever. I shall be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me” (1 Chron. 17).

According to this promise, the Son of God was made man from David’s seed, in order to build the house which is the Church and to reign for ever.

Who was predestined Son of God in power. “Predestined,” that is, preordained by God the Father according to his humanity: chosen beforehand by grace alone, so that he who was to be David’s son according to the flesh [Col. 0601A] might nevertheless be the Son of God in the power of divinity. That is, his humanity was assumed by the Word of God into unity of person in such a way that this same man was the Son of God by reason of the union with the Word. He was Son of God according to the Spirit of sanctification—that is, because the Holy Spirit sanctified the virgin’s womb from which he was to be born, as the angel also said: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you; therefore also the Holy One who shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1).

He was predestined also from the resurrection of the dead—that is, so as to go before the resurrection of the dead. Of which dead? Of the same Lord Jesus Christ. It is as though it said: of his dead, those who belong to him and are his members. He went before these, who will follow him into the heavenly [Col. 0601B] kingdom into which he went before them, and into blessed incorruption. But he was not predestined from the resurrection of the other dead, whom he was not to precede but to condemn. For he did not go before those who would not follow him to the glory of eternal life—that is, the reprobate, who will rise for punishments.

Or thus: He was predestined according to the flesh, because God from eternity predestined that his Word should become flesh, which, when raising it, he would also glorify. He was predestined to be Son of God in the power of immortality and might, of which after the resurrection he said: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28). For since he himself says of the elect that they are children of God because they are children of the resurrection, why should not he all the more—who according to divinity is naturally and always Son of God—be said, in the resurrection according to humanity, to have become the Son of God?

This is what the same Paul teaches when, in the Acts of the Apostles, he says of the Father: “Raising Jesus Christ, as it is written in the second Psalm: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’” (Acts 13). [Col. 0601C] Therefore the Father, in raising Christ, said to him, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you,” so that, in Paul’s meaning, that resurrection may be understood as a kind of generation. Our resurrection too is called regeneration, as the Lord says: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit upon the throne of his majesty” (Matt. 19).

Thus Christ according to humanity, who while mortal was Son of Man, became Son of God in the resurrection by clothing himself with immortality. Yet he did not cease to be Son of Man, because he remained truly human; rather, he received the glory which he had not possessed in his humanity. This is what is now said: he was predestined to be Son of God in power from the resurrection. It is not said “from his resurrection,” but, what indicates greater power, “from the resurrection of the dead,” because he caused many dead persons to rise with him. Lest we understand the general resurrection of good and evil, which is to occur on the last day, “of the dead [Col. 0601D] of Jesus Christ” means only the elect who belong to Christ, because then only the saints rose with him. Therefore he calls him our Lord: he who, in his death, destroyed our death and the ancient enemy, received in his resurrection the dominion owed over us. As we said before, he then declared: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28).

“He was predestined,” he says, “to be Son of God in power from the resurrection,” and this according to the Spirit of sanctification—that is, because the Holy Spirit sanctified him from the very beginning of his conception. For by the Spirit through whom he had thus been sanctified, he was raised from death, so that he might be, in the manner described, Son of God. For it is also said to us: “He who raised Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies on account of his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. 48 [sic]).

Or, as we said, he was predestined according to humanity to be Son of God in power—that is, in the same power as the Father through the union of the Word, to whom that man was personally united—according to the Spirit of sanctification, that is, because the Holy Spirit effected his conception in the virgin’s womb. This Spirit is the Spirit of sanctification because he sanctifies all who are sanctified. And this sanctification is from the resurrection of the dead—that is, it begins with the remission of sins. For those who are dead in soul first rise from the death of sin, and then are sanctified by the Holy Spirit. Such dead persons, returning in this manner to life, belong to Jesus Christ our Lord. For they have been preordained to life, to be members of Christ; therefore they do not remain in the death of sin, but rise through repentance.

Accordingly, when we hear “Son of God in the power of Jesus Christ,” or “Son of God according to the Spirit of sanctification [Col. 0602C] of Jesus Christ,” or “Son of God from the resurrection of the dead of Jesus Christ,” though it could customarily have been said “in his power,” “according to his Spirit of sanctification,” “from the resurrection of his dead,” or “of his own dead,” we are not compelled to understand another person, but one and the same person: namely, the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we received grace.

For the commendation of his own person Paul had commended the Gospel which he preaches, and for the commendation of the Gospel he commended Christ, its author. Now he states what he himself obtained through Christ. As though he said: “Christ is such and so great, through whom I, Barnabas, and the other apostles received from the Father grace and apostleship through the Mediator: [Col. 0602D] grace, along with all believers; but apostleship, not along with all.” If he had said only that he received apostleship, he would have been ungrateful for the grace by which his sins were forgiven, and he would have seemed to have received apostleship as the reward of prior works. Therefore he observes the causal order most fittingly, so that no one may dare to say that he was brought to the Gospel by the merits of his former life. For not even the apostles themselves could properly receive apostleship unless they had first received, together with the rest, the grace that heals and justifies sinners.

First, therefore, they received grace, by which they might be cleansed from sins and sanctified; then apostleship—that is, the commission to go everywhere preaching the very grace of the Gospel, for obedience to faith, that is, so that faith may be obeyed, [Col. 0603A] for Christ’s name: so that all may believe in Christ and be marked in his name if they desire salvation. This is to take place not among Jews alone, but among all nations, wherever nations are spread throughout the whole breadth of the world.

Or, faith is to be obeyed so that believers may do whatever faith requires, not only by believing but also by acting; and this is for Christ’s name—that is, for his glory, not their own—so that in the good which they do, they may seek not their own glory but Christ’s, and desire to magnify not their own name but Christ’s name. “I received,” he says, “apostleship among all nations, in order to make very many in them obey faith for the glorification of Christ’s name.” Among these nations—over which, that is, apostleship was given to me—you also are included. He says this in order to admonish them more familiarly.

You too, O Romans, are among those obeying the faith, called through the grace of preaching to faith; and you belong not to those who called you, but to Christ, to whom they called you.

For you are called to belong to Jesus Christ: that is, you have been called to faith in order that you may belong to Jesus Christ, not Peter or another. Up to this point it has been said who is writing the letter. The writer is Paul, servant of Christ Jesus, called an Apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God. But since the question arose, “What Gospel?”, he answered: “Which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son.” Again, since the question arose, “Concerning what Son?”, he answered: “Who was made for him from David’s seed according to the flesh, who was predestined Son of God in power, according to the Spirit of sanctification, [Col. 0603C] from the resurrection of the dead of Jesus Christ our Lord.” And if it were asked, “How do you belong to him?”, he answered: “Through whom we received grace and apostleship for obedience to faith among all nations for his name.” Again, if it were asked, “What reason then have you for writing to us?”, he answered: “Among whom you too are called to belong to Jesus Christ.”

Then, following the custom of letters, he adds to whom he writes: “To all,” he says, “who are at Rome, beloved of God, called to be saints.” He does not say, “saints, loving God,” but “beloved,” in order to signify God’s goodness rather than their merit (1 John 4). For he first loved us before any merits existed, so that, being beloved, we might love him. Those whom he loved he also called through his gratuitous gift by means of preachers and sanctified through baptism. Therefore every good is to be ascribed to divine grace, not human merits. For those who were hateful, distant, and foul, he loved, called, and sanctified. Or, to state it more briefly: he loved them in order to call them to holiness.

After this, to complete the customary opening of a letter, he greets them, saying: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and from the Lord,” and so forth. Let grace and peace be yours from God; for not every grace and not every peace is God’s or from God. Evil judges also show favor when receiving persons, enticed by some desire or terrified by fear; and there is an evil peace by which one agrees with vices or the devil. But that grace is from the Father and Christ by which our sins are forgiven, through which we were hostile to God; and that peace is by which we are reconciled to him. [Col. 0604A] For when, by grace, sins have been forgiven and enmities removed, it remains for us through peace to cleave to him from whom sins alone separated us.

It is called grace because it is not returned as a reward for merit but granted by the Giver. “May such grace and peace,” he says, “be yours from God our Father, who adopted us as sons and wishes to be loved and honored by us as a father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ,” that is, from the Son who redeemed us from the hand of the enemy, made us his own possession under his lordship, and is our Savior and King. He wishes grace and peace from Father and Son, and does not add the Holy Spirit, because the Holy Spirit himself is God’s gift, and God’s gift is grace and peace. Therefore the whole Trinity is set forth in this greeting: the Father and Christ are named, while the Holy Spirit is signified by grace and peace. [Col. 0604B] For in no way can grace, by which we are freed from sins, and peace, by which we are reconciled to God, be given to human beings except in the Holy Spirit.

> “First indeed I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world.”

Having commended his person in many ways and offered the greeting, as is customary in letters, he again makes them well disposed by showing that he has an exceeding love for them. Since he was going to rebuke them very sharply, he begins gently and seeks their goodwill, lest, if he began at once to reproach them severely, their impatience should receive those rebukes with resentment. As though he said: “I have much to say to you. But first, before I say those things, [Col. 0604C] I disclose this to you from my heart: I give thanks to my God for all of you, rejoicing with you over your good beginning.”

“I give thanks,” I say, “to my God,” who, although by nature and power he is God of all, is by merit and will the God of few. Therefore he said, “my God.” For this voice can belong only to the saints, whose God he is called—the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. It cannot be the voice of those whose god is their belly, or who have made some other vice their god.

“I give thanks to God”—that is, I offer him a sacrifice of praise—not through myself but through the great high priest, Jesus Christ. Whoever wishes to offer a sacrifice to God ought to offer it through the hands of the high priest. And I offer such a sacrifice through this priest for [Col. 0604D] all of you, so that you may likewise do the same, always giving thanks to God for the benefits he has bestowed upon you. To give thanks to God is to recognize that all good things have been given by him and to praise him for them in heart, speech, and deed. You too should give thanks to God through Jesus the Mediator, through whom God gave you whatever good you possess and through whom you receive whatever good you offer.

Or thus: “I give thanks for all believers; and first indeed for all of you”—namely, because you are first, since the Roman Church holds primacy among all churches. Here too it is evident that this letter ought to have been placed first. “I give thanks to God, whom I make mine by worshiping him worthily, not through the Law but through Christ. I give thanks, first indeed for you, and then for the rest.” First [Col. 0605A] for you, from whom great benefit comes to all, because your faith, although not yet perfect, is nevertheless already proclaimed throughout the whole world.

Rome was then the head of the world. People from the whole world gathered there and spread everywhere the report that the Romans had embraced the faith of the Christian religion; thus the other nations throughout the world now received the same faith with greater confidence. This is the praise of the faithful Romans: such an example concerning them was being spread everywhere. They therefore had to take care lest, just as the fame of their faith had been heard far and wide, so too a report of their dissension might be heard and harm many. They are urged toward progress by the fact that their faith is proclaimed everywhere.

Faith is the confession of divinity and the firm foundation of religion, because we truly believe what we cannot see. [Col. 0605B] More precisely, the name “faith” is derived from the fact that what has been said or promised is done. For faith is so called because what has been agreed between the two parties is fulfilled—between God and the human being—that is, that the human being performs in deed what he says with his mouth, and God grants him the blessedness he promised.

> “For God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit in the Gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I always make remembrance of you in my prayers, asking whether somehow at last I may at some time have a prosperous journey, in the will of God, to come to you. For I desire to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual grace for your strengthening—that is, that I may be mutually comforted among you through the faith which is shared between you and me.”

[Col. 0605C] I said that I give thanks for you, and I did not say this deceitfully; for God is my witness that I always remember you in my prayers. God, whose knowledge is not deceived—he who knows secrets and considers truth—he himself is my witness that what I say is true. I serve him in my spirit, that is, in the affection of my mind, because I do not render him service by pretense. Whatever good I do outwardly in his service, I likewise do inwardly in the intention of my heart.

I serve him in the Gospel of his Son—that is, in the preaching of his only-begotten Son, through whose incarnation, death, and resurrection I proclaim that salvation has been given to the world. The Father himself is my witness that in my prayers [Col. 0605D] I always make remembrance of you: whenever I pray for myself, I pray also for you. I do not forget you in my prayers, but remember you continually, and this without ceasing.

See how the Apostle himself first does what he commands others: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. 5). Yet when he says, “I make remembrance of you without ceasing,” this is not to be understood as though he did this at every moment, since human frailty cannot fulfill that; rather, it means that no day passed on which he did not pray for them. He says this also so that they may love and desire to hear one whom they know to be praying for them with such earnestness.

“I remember you in my prayers, asking”—that is, pleading by the sacred things which you have received, praying to God—“whether somehow,” that is, whether by some means, prosperous or adverse, [Col. 0606A] “at last,” after many desires, “at some time,” at least once if I cannot do so more often; or “at some time,” at some season, whether summer or winter, I may have a prosperous journey—that is, one effective for attaining my desires—a journey, I say, to come to you. And this is in God’s will, because only then will my arrival be beneficial.

May I have a prosperous journey in God’s will, because otherwise I do not have a prosperous journey unless God’s will, which knows all things and anticipates and sustains us with every good, directs me to where I may obtain some fruit. Or: “May I have a prosperous journey in God’s will,” because the success of a journey is not always accomplished in God’s will, as is the case with those who, in successful undertakings, rush toward evil.

Therefore I ask to come to you, because I desire to see you, namely, in order that I may impart to you [Col. 0606B] something—that is, make you participants in some spiritual grace—who now contend with one another in a carnal spirit. I want to impart to you some spiritual grace which is in me, that is, the gratuitous benefit of God, namely preaching or miracles, for your strengthening: that I may strengthen you. You already have something, but you are still weak and wavering and therefore need spiritual grace for confirmation, by which you may become firm.

“I wish,” I say, “to impart to you some spiritual grace to strengthen you in faith”—that is, I wish to be mutually comforted among you through the faith shared between us, so that through our common faith we may comfort one another and rejoice with one another in the grace of the Holy Spirit. At present I am desolate, and you likewise, though you do not perceive it. But you and I shall receive consolation if I see my work among you firm and stable, and if you become participants in apostolic grace. Thus together—that is, reciprocally, I in you and you in me—we shall have consolation through that faith which is mutual, that is, common; which in Greek is *Catholic*: I mean your faith and mine. If I see your faith to be mine and mine to be yours, so that one and the same faith is both yours and mine, then we shall be comforted together.

> “For I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that I have often intended to come to you, and have been prevented until now, in order that I may have some fruit among you as also among the other nations, Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish. I am debtor to them, so that, as far as lies within me, I am ready to evangelize also you who are at Rome.”

What I said—that I have the desire to come to you—must be believed. For, O my brothers, that is, children of the same mother Church, I do not want you to be unaware that I not only wished but intended to come to you. I intended this often, but have not yet been able to accomplish it, because I have been prevented until now—that is, up to this time—either by the Holy Spirit or by the members of the devil, who, by God’s dispensation, have brought many obstacles against me.

I intended so often to come to you in order that I might have among you some fruit of eternal reward, as also among the other nations: that for the labor of preaching which I expend upon you, I might have the fruit of heavenly recompense, as I shall have for the other nations [Col. 0607A] to whom I have preached thus far, from Jerusalem and round about through all Asia as far as Illyricum, where Europe begins. By the example of these nations he urges the Romans on.

Or, “that I may have fruit among you,” that is, that, having received the seed of preaching, you may bear the fruit of virtues and good works, because I count that fruit as mine. “I wish,” he says, “to acquire fruit among you in this manner, as also among the others, because I am debtor to all. God has made me debtor to all: Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish.”

The Greeks divided the entire human race under two names, calling every person either Greek or barbarian. Because the Greeks themselves used laws, they called all the rest barbarians, as though living without laws. The Apostle is debtor not only to Greeks but also [Col. 0607B] to barbarians, and not only to the wise but also to the foolish, because he was sent to preach to all. He calls Greeks wise, among whom all philosophy existed; barbarians he calls foolish, as unlearned people.

But how is he debtor to all these, from whom he received nothing? Because through the grace of the Holy Spirit he was granted the ability to speak in all their languages. Since no one receives knowledge of languages for himself but for those to whom he must preach, he becomes debtor to all those whose language he receives knowledge of from God. He is debtor to the wise because he received wisdom hidden in mystery, which he might speak to the perfect and wise. He became debtor also to the foolish because he received the grace of patience and long-suffering. For it is a mark of the highest patience to endure the outbursts of foolish people.

Therefore the Apostle is debtor to the wise, in order to advance them to greater mysteries of wisdom; and to the foolish, in order to instruct them, patiently bearing with them until he removes their foolishness. The righteous may also be denoted by the name “wise,” and sinners by the designation “foolish.” The Apostle is debtor to wise and foolish alike, because it is the preacher’s obligation to watch over the righteous lest they fall, and over sinners that they may rise; to admonish the righteous to keep the way of righteousness, and to rebuke sinners so that they abandon the way of iniquity.

“I am debtor to Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish. So also I am debtor to evangelize you who are at Rome,” because, as I owe preaching to others, so [Col. 0607C] I owe it to you, since I am sent to all. He is silent about the Jews because he is the teacher of the Gentiles. It is ready within me, that is, I am prepared and eager to evangelize.

> “For I am not ashamed of the Gospel. For it is the power of God unto salvation for everyone who believes, for the Jew first and also for the Greek. For the righteousness of God is revealed in it from faith unto faith, as it is written: ‘But the righteous lives by faith’” (Hab. 2; Heb. 10).

Therefore I am ready to evangelize because I am not ashamed of the Gospel. That is, I feel no shame at preaching the Gospel, as some were ashamed to preach Christ crucified, not understanding that nothing is more worthy of God than what advances human salvation. For it is an outstanding mark of power and mercy [Col. 0608A] that the Lord deigned, for the salvation of his image, to humble himself even to the passion of the cross. Considering this, the Apostle says: “I am not ashamed of the Gospel.”

And why are you not ashamed? Because the Gospel itself is the power of God. That is, what is preached in the Gospel—the cross, death, and resurrection of the Savior—is God’s power, although it seems foolishness to unbelievers. For there is no greater power than to conquer death and restore to humanity the life it had lost. The Gospel is such power, because it announces the power of Christ’s victory. It is power also because it supplies grace, by whose help we are able to do what it commands. Since the Law did not do this, it was weak.

It is a power effective for salvation to every believer, first to the Jew and then to the Greek—that is, the Gentile. [Col. 0608B] The Gospel is effective for eternal salvation to every believer, whether from circumcision or uncircumcision. The Jew is placed before the Gentile because of the fathers and because he first knew God, though he is no longer more worthy on that account, because the Lord said: “Israel is my firstborn son.” The Gospel is truly God’s power, for in it the righteousness of God is revealed, which had been veiled in the Old Testament.

Or thus: the Gospel truly avails for salvation to every believer, for in it the righteousness of God is revealed—that is, the righteousness of faith which was concealed in the Law. For the righteousness of God is that by which he freely justifies the ungodly person through faith without works of the Law. The Gospel reveals it by giving faith to a person, through which one is justified who believes God to be just and true in his promises, so that he rewards those who seek him and [Col. 0608C] condemns those who neglect him.

I mean a righteousness moving from faith to faith: from the faith of the Old Testament to the faith of the New. For the people of Israel were in faith, because they believed God and Moses his servant. From that faith they now pass to evangelical faith. The righteousness belongs to one who passes from faith to faith, so that the Jew and anyone else may willingly pass from the faith of the Old to the faith of the New Testament.

Righteousness is revealed from the faith of the Law, in which one God is proclaimed, to the faith of the Gospel, in which the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are manifested; from faith in the Lord’s first coming to faith in his second; from faith in the first resurrection to faith in the second; from the faith of preachers to the faith of peoples; from faith in Christ’s humanity to faith in his divinity. Thus righteousness is revealed in the Gospel from faith—[Col. 0608D] the righteousness through which we are saved—as it is written in Habakkuk: “But the righteous shall live by faith,” that is, the one justified by faith obtains eternal life. Thus righteousness comes from faith, and life from righteousness.

Or the righteous person lives meanwhile by faith while in this pilgrimage, until, arriving in the homeland, he lives by sight. The soul, dead through unbelief, begins to live through faith. But the faith by which one lives is that which works through love, because faith, if it does not have works, is dead in itself (James 2). This, however, is to be understood of those who have time to work. If anyone, immediately after being justified by faith in baptism, departs from this life, that person will attain life by faith alone, without any works. But whoever [Col. 0609A] has time to do good and neglects to act vainly presumes upon faith.

The Apostle said, “The righteous lives by faith.” In the prophet we read: “But the righteous shall live in his faith.” Yet the Apostle used the translation of the Seventy Interpreters instead because he was writing to Romans who did not know the Hebrew Scriptures. Nor was he concerned with words when the sense was secure and the present discussion suffered no loss; for Hebrews who had learned Greek letters also read the edition of the Seventy Interpreters. For this reason, this testimony and many others which he adduces appear to differ from the translation of the Hebrew truth which we now use: sometimes he draws from the Seventy Interpreters; sometimes, speaking in the same Spirit as the prophets, he takes only the sense, using his own words and arrangement.

> “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of those human beings who hold down the truth of God in unrighteousness, because what is known of God is manifest in them [Gal. 3]. For God has made it manifest to them. For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are understood through the things that have been made and are seen—his everlasting power also and divinity—so that they are without excuse.”

Now he addresses the Gentiles in their former condition, who boasted of a good nature and excused their shameful acts on the ground of ignorance. He shows that they had once possessed knowledge, that they afterwards lost it through fault, and that the good nature left to them by God they had themselves hurled into every kind of evil. As if he said: In the Gospel the righteousness of God is revealed, not only that by which he justifies the penitent through faith, but also that by which he condemns those who persist in wickedness. For the wrath of God which he will justly inflict upon sinners—that is, the vengeance by which he will strike them—is revealed in the same Gospel as coming from heaven upon them. Or thus: righteousness comes from faith, and thence salvation, because unrighteousness comes from impiety, and thence wrath—that is, punishment. For the wrath of God is revealed, etc. He did not say “is inflicted,” but “is revealed.” Where it is revealed, it is not inflicted; it does not strike, but is revealed in order to frighten, so that it may not be inflicted upon those who have been frightened. It is revealed through the Gospel, though it was formerly hidden from human beings. The wrath of God is revealed—that is, the visitation of the strict Judge. It is revealed from heaven, so that human beings may know that they are to expect from heaven not only benefits but also punishments. Or “from heaven,” that is, the wrath of the future judgment is revealed from the Church, since through the Church the wrath of the Judge who will come from heaven at the end of the age is made known to sinners, against all the impiety and unrighteousness of human beings—that is, in order to trample under punishments the perversity of those who deny God the worship due to him and who live wickedly in luxury and other vices. For impiety signifies unbelief, while unrighteousness signifies criminal conduct. The impiety of human beings—of those human beings, I say, who hold down the truth of God in unrighteousness.

Everything that can change is not truth. The truth of God is his invisible and unchangeable substance. They hold it down in unrighteousness, whoever, through visible and changeable creatures, have shown people that the worship of idols ought to be observed. They hold down the truth of God—that he himself is the true God—in unrighteousness, because, although they truly know that the worship of highest veneration ought to be rendered to the one Creator God, they unjustly render it to a creature. They hold down the truth of God—that is, true knowledge concerning God—in unrighteousness, that is, in an evil deed: preferring unjustly to remain in their pleasures, unwilling to depart from their wickedness for the truth of God, which freely offers itself to them, but wishing, if possible, to hold the truth itself fast with them in wickedness. I said that they hold down the truth of God and do not allow it to come to the knowledge of others, while they teach that images should be worshipped as God. For they know the truth itself which they conceal from others, because what is known of God—that is, what can be known concerning God by natural intelligence—is manifest to them.

For there are many things which cannot be known concerning God through nature, such as the mystery of the Incarnation and Passion, which was hidden from the wise of this world. But this can naturally be known concerning God: that he is God. For every creature shows that it is not God, but that there is another who made it and whose service must be obeyed. Thus what is known concerning God is manifest to them. Or, it is manifest in them—that is, in their hearts—although outwardly it does not appear in their conduct. For they possess within themselves the means of knowing him, namely natural reason. It is truly manifest in them, or to them, because God has manifested it to them through his work: since his hidden power is made manifest from things openly visible. The Lord has made it manifest; that is, not only did natural reason avail, but God also helped daily, lest nature alone seem sufficient. God manifested it to them by the display of creatures, because by natural intelligence they understood that the creature is not the Creator.

For his invisible things—that is, eternity, power, divinity, and omnipotence—are perceived from the creation of the world, that is, from the human being, in whom all creatures exist by a certain affinity: because he shares being with stones, life with trees, sensation with animals, and understanding with angels. From this creation of the world—that is, from the human being—the invisible things of God are perceived, being understood through the things that have been made, that is, through creatures. For if we watchfully consider outward things, through those same things we are recalled to inward things. The footsteps of the Creator are the wondrous works of the invisible creation; for through those things which are from him, we go to him. For God does not yet thus make himself inwardly known to our mind, scattered outwardly through its sin; but when he sets before us outwardly the beauty of his creation, he gives us, as it were, certain signals, indicates what we should pursue inwardly, and in a wondrous way leads us through these outward forms themselves to inward things.

For the considered works of creation are paths to the Creator: when we see the things made, we marvel at the power of the Maker. For wherever the soul turns, if it attends watchfully, it finds the Lord in those very things through which it left him; and by considering again the things through love of which it deserted him, it recognizes his power. Through the things by which it fell into adverse circumstances, it is recalled when turned back. For where we fell, there we apply ourselves in order to rise. And, as we rise there, we fix the hand of consideration where, falling through the foot of slippery love, we lay through neglect. Since we fell from invisible things through visible things, it is fitting that we should again lean upon these visible things in order to reach invisible things; and by the same descent through which the soul came to the lowest things, it should return by degrees to the highest.

Therefore it is rightly said that the invisible things of God are perceived from the creation of the world—that is, from the human being—being understood through the things that have been made, since the invisible Maker is understood through visible things made. Thus the Gentiles too, although they did not have the Law or the prophets, knew God, reaching an understanding of the invisible Creator through visible creation. “His invisible things from the creation of the world,” that is, from the human being, who surpasses every creature in the world; or, “from the creation,” that is, from the constitution of the world, are perceived, understood through the things made by him, together with his eternal power and divinity, which are likewise recognized as eternal from inferences drawn from creation.

> [Note: Col. 0611D: An obscure passage.]

Power is that which governs all things; divinity is that which fills the universe. His eternal power may also be understood as his Son, through whom all things were made, and who never began to exist but is everlasting—that is, always eternal—with him; while divinity is the Holy Spirit. Thus, through visible creatures, the invisible Father is understood, together with his eternal power, which is the Son, and divinity—that is, the Holy Spirit, to whom sanctification chiefly belongs. Thus even the Gentiles, who did not possess the divine Scriptures, are without excuse, because they were not ignorant of the truth, but proved ungrateful toward the very truth which had revealed itself to them.

> “Because when they had known God, they did not glorify him as God, nor give thanks; but they became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. For, professing themselves to be wise, they became fools [Eph. IV]. And they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds and four-footed beasts and serpents. Therefore God gave them over to the desires of their hearts unto uncleanness, so that they might dishonour their bodies in themselves—those who changed the truth of God into a lie, and worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen.”

They cannot excuse themselves by ignorance, as they wished to maintain. They truly knew God through natural reason. And when they had known him, they did not glorify him as God by living and worshipping rightly; nor did they give him thanks for the knowledge of him which they had received through his gift. For they ought to have glorified him by worshipping and proclaiming him worthily, by doing his will, and by always giving him thanks because he had deigned to pour the knowledge of himself into their hearts. To give thanks is to be grateful in devout reverence, so that they might acknowledge that they had wisdom and every good thing from him. But they did not glorify him or render thanks to him; rather, attributing to themselves wisdom which they did not have from themselves, and thinking themselves something when they were nothing, they became vain in their thoughts, which they had conceived from themselves rather than from God. Their heart was gradually darkened, until it became wholly foolish.

They became vain because they were vain and false in their thoughts, and the reasoning of their minds was darkened by the smoke of pride while they gloried in themselves. And indeed they became vain, for, professing themselves to be wise—that is, boasting as though they had discovered wisdom by their own understanding—they became fools; that is, their foolish heart was darkened. For although some of them turned the keen edge of their minds not only to the invention of highly useful arts and the teaching of liberal disciplines, but also to the inquiry after the highest good, and perceived the invisible things of God, understood through the things that have been made, nevertheless, because they did not give thanks to God nor confess him to be the author for them of this capacity, but professed themselves to be wise—that is, gloried not in God but in themselves, as though through their own studies and reasoning they had drawn near to the vision of truth—they became vain in their thoughts. What they had found through the illuminating grace of God, they lost through blinding pride, falling back from the heavenly light into their own darkness—that is, from the unchangeable and eternal good to mutable and corruptible nature.

And they changed, not only in understanding but also in deed; so far as lay within them, they changed the glory of the incorruptible God, fashioning, that is, such a God as he is not, and presenting him to people not as they had known him, but judging that images should be worshipped as God. While, through the vanity of their thoughts, they sought forms and images in God, they lost the image of God; and they fell into such darkness of folly that they turned the glory of God toward the bodily and corruptible likeness of human form, and lowered the eminence of divine majesty to the shapes of brute animals.

They changed the glory of God, who is incorruptible and eternal, into the likeness of the image of corruptible man, as though making the glory of God—that is, the glorious God—like the image of a human being, and worshipping the image itself as God. Nor did they change the glory of God only into the likeness of a human being, but also into the likeness of birds, four-footed beasts, and serpents. He descends step by step from more worthy creatures to less worthy, in order to show that they had fallen into deeper darkness of folly. From ancient times it was Roman custom to worship images of human beings, such as Romulus, Jupiter, and others, especially from the arrival of Aeneas in Italy; but to worship birds, four-footed beasts, and serpents dates from the time when Alexandria was conquered by Augustus and subjected to Rome. For they had been accustomed to worship the gods of all the nations they had overcome. Into such vile forms, as stated, they changed the glory of God.

Therefore God gave them over—that is, abandoned them—to the desires of their hearts. For God is said to “give over” when, because of the freedom of the will which is most ready for evil, he does not restrain sinners. It is also manifest that God works in human hearts to incline their wills wherever he wishes: toward good through his mercy, or toward evil according to their merits, by his judgment, sometimes open and sometimes hidden, but always just. For following sins are multiplied because of preceding sins. And God, who waits long for the sinner to return, gives the one who does not return and despises him a place in which to strike more grievously.

For a sin which is not promptly destroyed by repentance is either sin and the cause of sin, or sin and the punishment of sin, or at once sin, the cause of sin, and the punishment of sin. Everything first committed wickedly is sin. But if it is not promptly wiped away by repentance, almighty God, in his just judgment, permits a mind bound by sins to fall even into another fault. Therefore a sin not washed away by the lament of repentance is both sin and the cause of sin, because from it arises that by which the sinner’s mind is bound still more deeply. But a sin which follows from sin—that is, from the second sin—is at once sin and the punishment of sin, because, as blindness grows, it is produced as a requital for the earlier fault, so that the very increase of vices may already be, as it were, punishments in the sinner.

It also sometimes happens that one and the same sin is at once sin, the punishment of sin, and the cause of sin. The Apostle rightly demonstrates this here when he says concerning unbelievers and those given to impurity: “When they had known God, they did not glorify him as God, nor give thanks; but they became vain in their thoughts.” Behold sin and the cause of sin. What follows from this cause, he adds: “And their foolish heart was darkened. For, professing themselves to be wise, they became fools. And they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds and four-footed beasts and serpents.” Behold sin alone. And it would be the punishment of sin if another sin did not yet follow from it. For after their unbelief he adds: “Therefore God gave them over,” etc.

Thus those who, knowing God, did not glorify him as God, were brought from that sin and its cause also to this: that they fell into the worship of serpents and birds. But because through this blindness they also fell into the uncleanness and dishonours of the flesh, this very blindness of their unbelief is, with regard to the preceding knowledge, both sin and punishment of sin; but with regard to the ensuing uncleanness, it became sin and the cause of sin. By the merit of the earlier sin, therefore, the pit of subsequent sins is covered over, so that one who knowingly commits evil may thereafter justly fall, even unknowingly, into other evils. For this is brought about: sins are punished by sins, so that the very growth of vices becomes the punishment of sinners.

It is therefore rightly added after the fault of idolatry: “Therefore God gave them over,” and the rest, because God justly deserted those who had preferred idols to him and gave them over to their own wills; as Scripture says: “The beginning of fornication is the seeking out of idols, and their invention is the corruption of life” [Wisdom XIV]. Therefore, because of idolatry, he gave them over—that is, by withdrawing his grace, he permitted them to fall into the desires of their hearts, namely into those things which their hearts desired according to the burning of the flesh; desires, I say, tending toward uncleanness, that is, the defilement of the flesh, to such a degree that they might dishonour their bodies—that is, that they themselves might give up their bodies to dishonours, that is, shameful acts.

A dishonour is something inflicted upon someone contrary to the dignity of that person. And these people inflicted great dishonour upon their bodies and their nature by subjecting themselves to such shameful acts. They dishonoured their bodies, and this among themselves—that is, defiling themselves alone, without others. Those dishonour their bodies in this way who changed the truth of God into a lie: that is, they gave to an idol what is true of God, when, as Scripture says, “they imposed the incommunicable name upon wood and stones” [Wisdom XIV]. For the name of deity cannot be shared with creatures, since the Creator alone is properly and truly called God. But the Gentiles imposed this name upon wood and stones when they established that wooden and stone idols should be called God. This is what they are now said to have changed: the truth of God into a lie. For the truth of God is that he is truly God. Whoever says or thinks that an idol is God turns this truth into a lie. For this is false.

Nor did they change truth into falsehood only in this way, by judging idols to be gods—which is false—but they also worshipped the idols themselves, lest they should say, “I do not worship images, but the things represented by them,” such as the sun and other things of this kind. They worshipped not the Creator but the creature—that is, not God but idols—carefully adorning the very images of demons with golden crowns and worshipping them with bent knees; and they served the creature rather than the Creator by offering incense and sacrifices, as though it were better to serve the creature—that is, idols and demons—than God, who is blessed for ever—that is, eternally. Amen, that is, truly. Those who cleave to him will themselves truly be blessed with him for ever. But the Gentiles became accursed and temporal, having forsaken him who is blessed for ever.

> “For this reason God gave them over unto passions of dishonour. For their women changed the natural use into that use which is contrary to nature. Likewise also the men, having abandoned the natural use of the woman, burned in their desires toward one another, men committing shamefulness with men, and receiving in themselves the recompense which was fitting for their error.”

I said that they served the creature; for this reason God gave them over—that is, he permitted them to go into passions, that is, pleasures which, even if they delight, are passions of nature. Behold again vengeance. For the preceding fault, by which they served the creature, is a punishment for the ensuing passions of shameful acts. Above they were said to have changed the glory of God into the likeness of the image of birds and serpents, but he did not yet say that they worshipped those things. And therefore, through God’s vengeance, they fell into uncleanness of the flesh, because they had changed his glory into idols. Then, as their error increased, they worshipped as God the idols which they had made and served them, as the Apostle says; and for this reason they are punished with still more detestable uncleannesses.

God gave them over unto passions of dishonour—that is, to burnings of pleasures not fit to be named. *Ignominia* (“dishonour”) is so called as though it were “without a name.” For a person caught in some crime is said to be in dishonour because he ceases to retain the name of dignity. And they were indeed given over to dishonourable passions: “For their women changed the natural use.” He did not say “the marital use,” but “the natural,” intending that use which takes place in the members created for this purpose, so that through them either sex may unite for generation. Thus, even when anyone has intercourse with a prostitute by means of those same members, the use is natural, though not praiseworthy but blameworthy. But if anyone uses, even with a spouse, that part of the body which was not established for generation, it is contrary to nature and shameful.

Thus their women changed the natural use into that which is contrary to nature, because women themselves committed shameful acts with women. Nor did women alone commit fornication against nature, but men also: likewise abandoning women, with whom they could naturally unite, they burned through unlawful pleasure in their desires—that is, desires produced by themselves. They burned toward one another with the spirit of fornication, fulfilled most wicked desires through most shameful acts, and received in themselves the recompense fitting for the error of their error—that is, they experienced God’s vengeance in their own nature. For this reason the Apostle expressly described the crimes themselves: that we may recognize that those who became so mad as to pervert everything in perversity toward God had lost nature’s reason. For they could not preserve the order of nature when they had forsaken the Author of nature. Therefore women committed shameful acts with women and men with men; in these there was equal guilt, both of women and of men.

> “And just as they did not approve having God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do things which are not fitting: filled with all unrighteousness, wickedness, fornication, avarice, malice; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, malignity; whisperers, slanderers, hateful to God, abusive, proud, haughty, inventors of evils, disobedient to parents, foolish, disorderly, without affection, without covenant, without mercy. Though they had known the righteousness of God, they did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death; not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them.”

The Gentiles committed the evils already mentioned. And because they still would not look back, they fell yet further into others. For they committed the abominations which we have described, and they did not approve that the Lord had knowledge of these things; that is, although by many arguments they could have proved that God had knowledge of these crimes, they nevertheless thought that God was ignorant of them and neglected them. And just as they thought this through their own fault, so it came about through that same fault that God gave them over to a reprobate mind, so that they might suppose that all things which deserve reprobation ought to be done; and while they performed such shameful acts, they might not know that they were doing evil.

Or thus: they not only committed the abominations mentioned above, but they also did not approve—that is, did not choose—to have God in their knowledge, that is, to know him. The one who approves—that is, judges it good and praiseworthy—to have God in his knowledge is the one who, in devout reverence, strives always to have him in mind, fears and reveres him as present, and does not dare to sin. But the Gentiles did not do this. And just as they did not approve having God in their knowledge—that is, having him in their awareness, or knowing that he knew the evils they committed—God gave them over, that is, abandoned them, to a reprobate mind, so that they might understand nothing except what is remote from uprightness and do what is not fitting to do: namely, perform those acts which the divine laws detest.

I mean those who had not merely a little unrighteousness, but were filled with all unrighteousness. Its parts are enumerated when he adds: “Wickedness, fornication,” etc. For the genus is first set forth and the species follow, so that the Gentiles may be more openly accused and frightened. Wickedness pertains to the mind; fornication to the flesh. For wickedness is that by which a person plots to harm another in whatever way. Fornication is so called from *fornices*, that is, arches, in which prostitutes offered themselves. But here fornication is understood to mean whatever is committed outside lawful marriage. Avarice is an insatiable love of possessing. Malice (*nequitia*) is rashness or presumption, when someone dares what he cannot accomplish. Or *nequitia* is said to derive from *nequidquam* (“in vain”); it is a falling away from good, when someone falls away from love of heavenly things and burns toward love of earthly things. For thus he tends toward *nequidquam*, that is, vanity and non-being, departing from the true being of God.

Envy is that which is tormented by another’s happiness, and it is divided into a double passion: when someone either does not want another to have what he himself has, or, seeing another to be better, grieves that he is not like him. Homicide is composed from *homo* (“human being”) and *caedes* (“killing”). The Apostle fittingly joined homicide to envy, because envy is the first source of this crime. For the first homicide both of the devil and of Cain arose from envy, and even now homicides sometimes result from envy. Strife is where something is defended not by reason but by obstinacy of mind, and where truth is not sought but contentiousness is wearied out. Deceit is a cleverness of mind, from its deceiving. For it does one thing and pretends another. Deceit, I say, is hidden wickedness adorned with flattering words, when one thing sounds in the mouth and another lies hidden in the heart.

Malignity is an evil will, kindled by an evil fire, which wishes to love no one and to do nothing by which it ought to be loved. The distinction between wickedness (*malitia*) and malignity (*malignitas*) is this: the depraved thought of the mind is called wickedness, but the intention or deed of wickedness is called malignity. Whisperers are those who speak evil of one person into another’s ears. Slanderers are those who by their words take away or diminish another’s virtues. A whisperer is so called from the sound of speech, because he does not speak to someone’s face but secretly in the ear while disparaging. Slander is either to twist the well-done acts of others viciously into evil or deceitfully to diminish them through envy, when either things that are good are called evil, or great goods are called small. For to slander is to drag another’s goods downward—that is, to lower and press them down—or to take something away from those goods, so that they appear fewer or less than they are.

Lest whisperers and slanderers seem to sin only slightly, he immediately added: “Hateful to God.” For those who maliciously whisper about their neighbours or slander them are hateful to God. Or those are called hateful to God who sow discord among friends. Hence Solomon testifies [Prov. VI] that there are six things which God hates, and a seventh which his soul detests; and this seventh is the person who sows discord among brothers. Those are called abusive who are quick to inflict injuries by word or deed. For an insult is a deed or word unworthy and unfitting for the person upon whom it is unjustly and insolently inflicted.

The proud are those who judge themselves to be above what they ought to be. For pride is the desire for perverse exaltation. Perverse exaltation is this: when the soul forsakes him to whom it ought to cleave as its principle and in some manner makes itself its own principle. This happens when it is too much pleased with itself—that is, when it falls away from that unchangeable good which ought to please it more than it pleases itself. The haughty are likewise those who raise themselves above their measure, or who do not submit to the institutions of their elders, because they are unwilling to endure a superior or an equal. Inventors of evils are those who devise new kinds of sin, new tortures with which to torment others, new unjust laws, or who are the first to devise any other evils. For persons with evil pursuits are accustomed to discover things to be done which do not suffice for them merely to commit the evils their predecessors committed or which they still observe their contemporaries committing.

Those who are disobedient to parents are more untamable than wild beasts, because wild beasts are subject and compliant to their parents. The foolish are those who have departed from God himself, the fountain of wisdom. And therefore they are disorderly, because every fool is disordered. They are disorderly in dress, gait, and movement. For the disorderliness of the body indicates the quality of the mind. Those without affection are without the inward feelings of love by which they may be moved toward another, but carry a hard and unfeeling heart toward love of their neighbour. Those without covenant shun all fellowship and are unwilling to have a covenant of concord and companionship with anyone. Those without mercy do not sympathize with the miseries of others.

All these evils were among the Gentiles. Although they had known the righteousness of God, they did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death. By the fact that evil naturally displeases them, they knew God’s righteousness. And although they had known it in this way, they did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of everlasting death. For if they had understood, they would have feared; if they had feared, they would never have committed such things. They lost the light of understanding when they forsook the fountain of heavenly wisdom. Therefore, although they did not understand, they cannot be excused, because through their preceding faults they had deserved to be so blinded.

Lest they should be thought to be afflicted only by those punishments in which they delighted—that is, by the shameful acts of the crimes mentioned above—the Apostle adds the final, eternal death: “Those who do such things,” he says, “are worthy of death.” Here it should be observed with great fear that he has included among these things, by which eternal death is incurred, certain matters thought to be slight, such as the acts of whisperers, slanderers, the disorderly, and the contentious. “They are worthy of death,” he says, “not only those who do these things, but also those who consent to those who do them,” so that no one may excuse himself. For there are some who do not think themselves guilty if they do not perform evil acts but consent to those who perform them. To consent is for someone, although able to rebuke, to remain silent or to flatter. But those who act and those who consent merit eternal death.

Thus far the Apostle has made known, in detesting them, the vices of the Gentiles, so that they might no longer excuse themselves concerning their former acts, but might humbly acknowledge what they had formerly been; lest they should proudly prefer themselves to the Jews, but should love God all the more and become indebted to his grace in proportion as they considered that more and greater sins had been forgiven them by him.

## Chapter II

> “Therefore thou art inexcusable, O every man that judgest [Matt. VII]. For in that wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself. For thou doest the same things which thou judgest. For we know that the judgment of God is according to truth against those who do such things.”

“All,” he says, “both those who do them and those who assent to them, are worthy of death.” Therefore—that is, for this reason—you are inexcusable, O every human being who judges others. I say “human being,” not merely a Gentile, but every person, whether Gentile or Jew, great or small. For when he says “every,” he begins now to show that he means not only the Gentile but also the Jew who wished, according to the Law, to judge the Gentiles. He therefore now treats Jews and Gentiles together: for the Jew judged the Gentile according to his former way of life, and the Gentile judged the Jew. Yet each is a human being. If a Jew judges a Gentile for idolatry, many Jews also worshipped idols. If a Gentile judges a Jew for transgression of the Law, he himself is a transgressor of the natural law.

“You are inexcusable,” he says, “O every human being who judges.” Here he shows that every person naturally knows, even if he does not notice that he knows it, namely that he is to be judged by God according to his own acts. For how could he himself condemn another sinner by his own judgment unless he perceived by natural sense that God would do likewise? For all people know through natural law and reason both that innocence deserves reward and that wickedness deserves punishment. You are inexcusable because you yourself are the witness of your own condemnation. For in the judgment by which you condemn another, you condemn yourself, because you yourself do the same things which you judge to be condemnable in another. And just as you judge another, so you can know that God will judge you yourself.

And you will indeed be judged by God as you judge others who do the things which you too do, because we know that God’s judgment against those who do such things is according to truth. For he will not show partiality in judgment; but whether anyone is great or small, Jew or Gentile, God will judge him in true judgment according as he deserves. It should also be noted that this saying shows that any judge of our own time, whether ecclesiastical or secular, who does the things he judges in others, is likewise to be condemned.

> “But dost thou think this, O man, who judgest those who do such things and doest them thyself, that thou wilt escape the judgment of God? Or dost thou despise the riches of his goodness and patience and long-suffering, not knowing that the kindness of God leads thee to repentance? But according to thy hardness and impenitent heart thou treasurest up wrath for thyself in the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will render to every person according to his works [Matt. XVI]: to those indeed who, by perseverance in good work, seek glory and honour and incorruption, eternal life; but to those who are contentious and do not submit to the truth but believe unrighteousness, wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress upon every soul of a human being that does evil, of the Jew first and also of the Greek. But glory and honour and peace to everyone who works good, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.”

We know that God’s judgment is against those who do such things. But when you do the same things, do you suppose that you will escape that judgment? This is the reproach implied in the words: “Do you suppose this, O man, you who judge”—that is, condemn by your judgment those who do such things—“and do them yourself, that you will escape the judgment of God?” Although you now possess authority over others, and no one in this world judges you in this matter, you ought not suppose that God will spare you if you act wickedly. For an uninstructed person might think that he may sin the more freely in proportion as he restrains others from sin more diligently. Do you suppose that you will escape his judgment—that is, do you flatter yourself with impunity because God does not exact payment in the present?

Or do you despise the riches of his goodness—that is, his rich and abundant goodness—because this is now the time of mercy; and the riches of his patience, by which he patiently endures sinners; and of his long-suffering, by which he waits longer for them to repent? The Apostle speaks severely, because an evil and hard mind is not recalled except by fear. The riches of God’s goodness are made manifest in this: people daily commit so many evils upon the earth, yet God causes his sun to rise for them, supplies rains, and grants many other goods (Matt. VII), gently drawing them, so that he may summon them to repentance through benefits. His patience too is shown to be rich, since he patiently endures those who commit so many and such great evils. His long-suffering is likewise rich, because he does not punish them at once, but waits through much time for repentance.

But the person who does not use these riches of goodness, patience, and long-suffering for repentance as God intends, but turns them into vain security, despises them, supposing either that God does not care for human affairs or that he remits what he postpones. “Do you despise,” he says, “these riches, not knowing”—that is, not considering—“that the kindness,” namely the merciful compassion, “of God leads you,” so far as it lies in itself, “to repentance,” while he still grants you an interval of time? That very kindness urges you to repent.

Thus, according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself, because you are hard and stubborn in your wickedness, of which you do not repent even in heart.
