For there are some to whom the evils they do are displeasing. But you do not repent even in heart, because your heart is too hardened in wickedness. According to this hardness you store up wrath for yourself—that is, you accumulate and lay up for yourself vengeance to be carried out on the day of wrath, that is, on the day of final retribution. You store up wrath—that is, you multiply it for yourself secretly [Col. 0620C], sinning more grievously through the interval of time granted to you. For if you do not wish to be converted, even when time has been given, you increase your evils into guilt by that very means through which you could have washed them away, had you wished to be converted.

For the reprobate stores up wrath for himself out of the goodness of God, because, while he receives time for repentance and spends it in sinning, he turns the very remedy of grace into an increase of guilt. Therefore almighty God, seeing that the remedies he has bestowed are being drawn into evidence of guilt, turns the very kindness which he bestowed into the dispensation of judgment [Note: [Col. 0619D] “Otherwise, into severity.”], so that he strikes more severely from that source from which he now waits longer; and because a person is unwilling to abandon evil in order to live, he increases that by which he may die.

“You store up,” he says, “wrath for yourself” [Col. 0620D] “to come on the day of wrath,” that is, the day of judgment, on which God will appear to be angry with the reprobate, although he is moved by no disturbance of mind; “and on the day of the revelation of the righteous judgment,” that is, on which the righteous judgment of God, now hidden, will be revealed—God who will judge so justly as to render to each according to his works. And indeed he will render thus to every person: good things to the good and evil things to the evil.

This means: to those who are of good work according to patience—that is, who do good works, making good use of God’s patience; or who work well in accordance with patience, that is, await through patience the reward of their good work, persevering to the end in goodness and patience, so that they do good and endure evil—he will render glory, so that they shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father; honor, so that they may be like him, as John says: “Because when he appears, we shall be like him” (1 John III); and incorruption, that is, immortality. God will render these things to those who are of good work according to patience, and who seek eternal life—namely, only to those who seek nothing other than eternal life from their patience and good action. For even if they display patient good work, they will not receive glory and incorruption if they do not seek eternal life in the intention of their heart. To these, then, glory will be given.

But to those who are contentious, such as you who now contend with one another—to those who are contentious, that is, who attack the truth, where what is asserted is defended not by reason but by obstinacy of mind; and who do not yield to evangelical truth when it is announced to them, so as to do what truth commands, but believe in the iniquity which they love, promising themselves impunity for the evils they do—to these will be rendered wrath, that is, God’s just vengeance, and indignation, that is, his severity; tribulation from the guilt of conscience, and distress from vain repentance, when they will repent among themselves and groan from anguish of spirit.

Or, wrath means punishment, and indignation that by which they will be indignant with themselves because, acting wickedly, they deserved God’s wrath. Such wrath and indignation will be given to their bodies and souls in the future. Before their souls are reunited to their bodies, meanwhile, tribulation will come as external torment, and distress [Col. 0621C] as to conscience, which will inwardly torture the souls themselves. Or, after the resurrection, tribulation will be in the bodies and distress in the souls. This punishment will come upon every soul of one doing evil, because the soul sins first and therefore principally feels punishment.

Above it was also said that the reprobate stores up wrath for himself on the day of judgment. Now, lest anyone suppose that the reprobate will remain without punishment until that day, it is added that punishment is to be given to every soul of a person doing evil. It is as though he said: The wicked person will suffer wrath not only on that day and thereafter, but before it as well: upon every soul doing evil, “of the Jew first and then of the Greek,” that is, the Gentile. The Jew is set above the Gentile in guilt, because besides the natural law he had Moses’ written law and transgressed it. The Jew is always placed first because he first knew God; if believing, he is more honorable because of Abraham, but if unbelieving, he is to be treated more severely because he rejected the promises made to the fathers.

Having shown that evildoers from both peoples are to be punished, he shows conversely that those doing good from circumcision and uncircumcision are to be glorified; and therefore he repeats the foregoing sentence: punishment will be for the evildoer. But glory—that is, the splendor of the glorified body—honor—that is, a place at the Judge’s right hand—and peace—that is, every good which is in the kingdom—will be for everyone doing good. I do not say everyone who appears to do good, but one who truly does what God judges good. “To the Jew first” [Col. 0622A]: first in time of believing, not in dignity. For the Jews first believed and did good, and afterward the Greeks, by whom the Gentiles are signified; but now both have an equal place of blessedness in the kingdom.

> “For with God there is no respect of persons. For all who sinned without the law will also perish without the law; and all who sinned in the law will be judged through the law. For not the hearers of the law are righteous before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified.”

The Jew and the Gentile are rightly made equal in punishment and glory, because God judges not according to persons but according to merits. For with God there is no respect of persons, but acceptance of good works. [Col. 0622B] Whether Jew or Gentile, each is judged by God according to his works. And truly God does not respect persons. For all who sinned without the law, such as the Gentiles who did not receive the written law, will perish without the law—that is, no legal judgment will take place concerning them, because they will be cast into Gehenna without judgment. And all who sinned in the law, such as the Jews who did not keep the law of Moses, will be judged through the law—that is, condemned—because they themselves will hear the Judge’s words, in order that they may perish on account of the law which they received and violated.

Or this statement may be understood to show that whoever sins less will be punished less, and whoever sins more will be condemned more severely. For all who sinned without the law—that is, without transgression of the law—such as the nations, namely [Col. 0622C] those who sinned less, will perish without the law, that is, will be punished less; for they will be condemned only for their sins, not for transgression of the Mosaic law, which they did not have. Conversely, all who sinned in the law—that is, sinned more grievously by transgressing the law—will be judged through the law, that is, condemned more harshly, because they will be punished both for violation of the law and for their sins.

And they will truly be judged through the law so as to perish, because they will not be saved on account of the knowledge of the law alone; for they are not justified by hearing the law alone, and without righteousness no one is saved. For those who are merely hearers of the law are not righteous before God, although they may be considered righteous before human beings; rather, the doers of the law [Col. 0622D] shall be justified—that is, the righteous shall be justified. For the doers of the law are certainly righteous. Thus it amounts to the same as if it were said, “The doers of the law shall be made,” not because they already were, but so that they may be; so that even the Jewish hearers of the law might understand that they need the grace of the one who justifies, in order to become doers.

Or “shall be justified” means “shall be reckoned righteous.” For the doers of the law are those who believe in Christ, whom the law promised and of whom Moses said: “You shall hear him as myself” (Deut. XXIV). But no one can believe in him and hear him—that is, obey him—unless his grace grants it.

> “For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, naturally do the things of the law, these people, not having the law, are a law to themselves. They show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing them witness, and their thoughts accusing or even defending one another, on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings according to my Gospel, through Jesus Christ.”

The doers of the law are justified, because this is so even among the Gentiles. This is what he adds: “For when the Gentiles,” and so forth. Or he had said that the Gentile is condemned if he acts wickedly and saved if he acts well. But since he does not have the law and seemingly does not know what is good and what is evil, it might appear that neither ought to be imputed to him. The Apostle answers: even though he does not have the written law, he has the natural law, through which he understands and is conscious of what is good or evil; and [Col. 0623B] therefore he must be understood to act well or wickedly, and deservedly to be saved or condemned.

But this is only through grace and faith, which renews the natural image of God written in the human being; without that renewal he acts wickedly and is condemned, his conscience accusing him. This is what he says: the Gentiles, who do not have the Mosaic law, naturally—that is, by the prompting of natural reason—do the things belonging to the law, namely, those things which the law commands to be done. Though they do not have such a law—that is, the written law—they are a law to themselves: natural reason is their law. By praising good things and condemning evil things, they show that the work of the law is written in their hearts, that is, firmly impressed upon their reason.

For no one wrongs another unless he would not wish the same to be done to himself. In this he transgresses the law of nature, which he is not permitted to ignore, since he does not wish to suffer what he does. For the work of the law is not to kill, not to commit adultery, not to steal, not to covet, not to bear false witness, to honor father and mother, to do similar things, and to believe in the one God, Creator of all things (Exod. XX). Natural reason wrote all these things in the hearts of the Gentiles. Thus they knew what ought to be done and what avoided, their own conscience bearing witness to them on the day of judgment concerning what they have done, because they themselves will be witnesses to the good and evil they have performed, knowing that they deservedly are saved or condemned thereby.

Nor will there be only the conscience of works, but also that of evil or good thoughts [Col. 0623D]—thoughts, I say, accusing or even defending one another—because the thoughts themselves will in turn accuse or defend one another in the presence of the Judge. Thus all our thoughts, gathered together at one time, will prove the Judge just, while our conscience either accuses or excuses us, according as sins or good works are more numerous; and according as they are old or new, blotted out by repentance or renewed by fresh crimes. Thus our thoughts will accuse or defend us—not, certainly, those which will then exist, but those which now exist in us.

For when we think either good or evil things, as it were uncertainly, certain marks and seals of both good and evil thoughts remain in [Col. 0624A] our heart. Though now placed in the hidden recesses of the breast, they will be revealed on that day by him who alone can know the hidden things of human beings. Our conscience too will attest that the causes of these marks are not hidden from God. And because in that judgment not only works but thoughts too will be examined with such subtlety, every believer ought now to examine himself inwardly and scrutinize himself vigorously before judgment, so that, when the strict Judge comes to examine his accused person, he may come already tranquil, seeing that he has already been punished for his fault.

“Conscience,” he says, “bearing them witness,” because one’s own conscience is sufficient testimony for each person. [Note: [Col. 0623D] A rather obscure passage.] “Conscience” is understood as the conscience of works, and of thoughts accusing or even defending one another. He does not say that the same thoughts accuse and defend, but that some accuse in turn and some defend against the accusation of malicious spirits. Conscience bears witness “on the day when God will judge,” or “in the day,” that is, in the light, when God will judge the hidden things of human beings—that is, secrets of the heart or hidden sins not made manifest through confession. God will judge according to “my Gospel,” that is, the Gospel which I preach; and he will judge not by himself but through Jesus Christ, because “the Father judges no one by himself, but through the Son, because he has given all judgment to the Son” (John V).

> “But if you are called a Jew, and rest upon the law, and glory in God, and know his will, and approve the things that are more excellent, being instructed through the law; if you are confident that you yourself are a guide of the blind, a light of those who are in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of infants, having in the law the form of knowledge and truth.”

After addressing the Gentile party, or after speaking generally concerning Jews and Gentiles, he now directs his discourse to the Jews alone. He wishes to humble them because they were proud on account of the law they had received and despised the Gentiles as sinners. For he accuses them more severely of sinning by transgressing the law. [Col. 0624D] It is as if he said: the Gentile has only the natural law; but you, if you are called a Jew and possess the written law, have received greater divine gifts and ought to do greater good.

“If you are called a Jew”: that is, if you derive from your kindred the name Jew, without possessing what the name signifies—being not a Jew in the reality of the thing, but in name alone—a name which you claim for yourself as an honor from Judah, who was more distinguished among Jacob’s sons. “And rest upon the law”: that is, you take delight in the scriptural law, because you need not labor to seek out truth, as Gentiles must, since they do not have the law. “And glory in God,” not in the manner required by grace, which is given freely and not by the merits of works, but as one who alone deserved to receive his law. “And know his will”: that is, what he himself wills human beings to do; or his will concerning the redemption of the human race. “And approve the things more excellent”: that is, among useful things you know how to choose the more useful, having been instructed through the law; for many useful things are approved through nature, more useful ones through the law, and more perfect ones through grace.

If you are such a person, you are confident that you are a guide of the blind—that is, that you can lead by the way of righteousness those who do not understand what they ought to do—and a light of those in darkness, able, namely, to enlighten them. By the blind set in darkness, understand the Gentiles, who are deprived even of the light of reason; and even if they know something, they nevertheless remain in darkness. Or let us understand any persons blinded in mind and placed in the darkness of ignorance, over whom the Jew glories not merely to be a guide but an illuminator because of his knowledge of the law.

“And an instructor of the foolish”: that is, one capable of raising unlearned Jews out of their rudimentariness—those who know the law in some manner, but are uncertain how they ought to understand it, and therefore discuss it among themselves. “And a teacher of infants”: of those Jews who do not even know how to speak about the ambiguities of the law, “having in the law the form of knowledge and truth,” so as to be for others an example of knowledge of the law and of truth.

For some have knowledge and understanding of a book and thus think as its author himself thought, yet do not thereby possess truth, because they do not know how it is true, nor even know that it is true. But the Jew boasts that he has both the meaning of the law and knowledge that this meaning of the law is true, so as to be an example to others desiring to possess it, as one who has received from the letter of the law a form of knowledge and truth. And because he professes all these things but does not truly possess them, the following is added:

> “Therefore, you who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege? You who glory in the law, do you dishonor God through transgression of the law? For through you the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles, [Col. 0625D] as it is written” (Isa. LII; XXXVI).

Since you thus glory in the law and boast that you teach others, you who teach another—why do you not teach yourself? That is: you who are a guide of the blind, how do you fail to see the straight way? For if you saw it, you would surely walk in it. You who are a light to those in darkness, how do you not cast off works of darkness? Instructor of the foolish, why have you also abandoned the fear of the Lord, which is the beginning of wisdom? (Eccles. I.) Teacher of infants, why are you childish in understanding? You who have in the law the form of knowledge and truth, why do you neither follow it yourself nor allow others to follow it, through your evil example? Why does your life not accord with your teaching, and why does your action destroy your faith?

“You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? You who say” [Col. 0626A] “that one must not commit adultery”—that is, one must not adulterate—“do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege?” That is, you yourself do what you preach ought not to be done, when by a bad interpretation you steal Christ’s faith from the law and adulterate the law, placing falsehood where truth has been removed; and you are sacrilegious when you deny Christ, whom the prophetic utterance signifies.

Why do you do this? Why do you steal the meaning concerning Christ from the law? And why do you commit adultery—that is, adulterate—making your mind corrupted by falsehood, despising the truth of Christian faith as a lawful husband and choosing falsehood as an adulterer? For adultery is not only one thing: whatever you owe wholly to God, if you render it to someone other than God—whether love, fear, service, obedience, or hope—you commit adultery. Therefore one from whom perfection is preached sins more gravely.

And you who detest idols, why do you commit sacrilege? That is, why do you remove Christ from what is sacred, namely from the law, by denying that he is signified there? For sacrilege is called the theft of a sacred thing, because *legere* or *sublegere* is called “to steal.” Sacrilege indeed is either to remove a sacred thing from a sacred place, such as relics from a church; or a sacred thing from a non-sacred place, such as a cross from a layperson’s house; or a non-sacred thing from a sacred place, such as a layperson’s cloak from a church. And he commits sacrilege who takes Christ’s sacred meaning from the sacred law. In this place, sacrilege properly means what is committed against God, as a violation of the sacred, or transgression of the commandments.

Therefore it is added: [Col. 0626C] “You who glory in the law”—that is, who boast that you alone, of all peoples under heaven, have received the law—why do you dishonor God through transgression of that same law, by committing thefts, adulteries, and sacrileges? For, according to the letter, many Jews are found to have done these things: thefts, adulteries, and sacrileges.

But in the person whom the Apostle now rebukes in this way is represented every teacher of the Church who preaches good things and does evil, destroying by his conduct what he establishes by his words. Such a person is rightly told: “You who teach another, do you not teach yourself?” and so forth. Then he proves that the Jews dishonored God by transgressing the law. You and persons like you truly dishonor God. For the name of God—that is, the glory and renown of God’s name—is blasphemed, that is, reviled, among the Gentiles through you, that is, through your evil conduct.

For just as the good life of believers gives those who see it cause to glorify God, so, when those who have received God’s law live wickedly, their depraved conduct gives cause for God to be blasphemed, as it is written. He did not add where or in what words this was written, because he was speaking to Jews who possessed the law and prophets and knew well enough where it was written: namely, in Ezekiel, through whom God complained concerning those held captive in Chaldea, saying: “They entered among the nations and polluted my holy name, when it was said of them, ‘This is the people of the Lord, and they have gone out from his land’” (Ezek. [Col. 0627A] XXXVI).

Thus the name of the Lord was then blasphemed through them, since they had polluted it in the eyes of the Gentiles by their evil deeds. For the Gentiles thought that what the Jews did pleased their God, and therefore reviled him. Likewise, through the wickedness of those who, at the time Paul wrote this, were scattered among the Gentiles, God was blasphemed by the Gentiles. So too now God is often blasphemed by the unlearned and worldly through certain professed adherents of religion, when they show examples of depravity in themselves.

> “Circumcision indeed is of use if you keep the law. But if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision. Therefore if uncircumcision keeps the righteous requirements of the law, will not his uncircumcision [Col. 0627B] be reckoned as circumcision? And will not that uncircumcision which is by nature, fulfilling the law, judge you, who through letter and circumcision are a transgressor of the law? For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is that circumcision which is outwardly in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart in spirit, not letter, whose praise is not from human beings but from God.”

He had shown that the law did not avail the Jews, and now shows that circumcision does not benefit them either. He had proved that they could not glory in the law because they transgressed it—that is, its moral commandments. They might answer: “Although the law itself does not profit us, because we have transgressed it, as you say, still we can glory in circumcision, because through it we excel the uncircumcised Gentiles.” And the Apostle replies: “Circumcision indeed is of use if you keep the law,” that is, together with the observance in faith of the moral commandments. But if you are a transgressor of the law, as you are, as we have proved—that is, if you do not fulfill what circumcision requires—then your fleshly circumcision, in which you greatly glory, has become uncircumcision: it benefits you no more than if you were not circumcised.

Circumcision, he says, is useful in its own time because it causes the Jew to live and not be cut off. Circumcision is useful because it causes one to be within the law. It is useful because, by obeying God, it makes a sign of future truth, while an unformed people are kept under fear; for circumcision of the flesh prefigures true circumcision of the heart. [Col. 0627D] Therefore, before the Savior’s advent, fleshly circumcision is useful if you keep the law—that is, if you are circumcised also in conduct. For true circumcision is understood to be nothing other than purification of the soul and casting away of vices. Thus circumcision of the flesh is useful if the mind too has been circumcised through observance of the law’s moral commandments. The sign is useful if the reality is present; otherwise, a sign without the reality will be superfluous.

This is what follows: if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision, because, although circumcised in flesh, you are uncircumcised in deed. In like manner one may say to a Christian: baptism is useful if you keep the Gospel; but if you are a transgressor of the law, that is, of the Gospel, your baptism will not benefit you. Likewise, a monk’s hood is useful [Col. 0628A] if he keeps the rule; but if he transgresses the rule, his hood has become useless.

Then the conclusion is drawn by opposites as follows. Since, if you are a transgressor of the law, circumcision benefits you no more than uncircumcision, therefore, if uncircumcision keeps the law, it benefits equally for salvation as circumcision together with observance of the law. This is the meaning: if uncircumcision—that is, a Gentile, who comes in the uncircumcision of the flesh to faith in Christ—keeps the righteous requirements of the law, namely the moral commandments by which a person is justified, such as: “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not covet; honor father and mother; and, you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Exod. XX), will not his uncircumcision be reckoned as circumcision? That is, will not he who has uncircumcision be made equal to a Jew possessing circumcision [Col. 0628B] together with observance of the law? His possessing uncircumcision will not harm him if he keeps the law spiritually; rather, he will be reckoned among Abraham’s children. And what circumcision does for the Jew who keeps the law, uncircumcision will do for him once, with faith, he keeps the commandments of the law.

Nor will he merely be equal to the Jew: he will also judge the Jew, not by judicial authority but by comparison with the better deed. Uncircumcision—that is, the uncircumcised person—fulfilling, that is, completing, the law, will judge you, O Jew, who through letter and circumcision are a transgressor of the law. I mean the uncircumcision which is by nature—that is, which remains as nature ordained and has not, through circumcising, cut away what nature gave it—that uncircumcision, by keeping the natural law which you transgress [Col. 0628C] in the letter, will judge you: that is, by comparison with itself, it will show you liable to judgment.

Thus a layman, if he lives religiously, will condemn in comparison with himself one who possesses the habit and profession of religion but does not live religiously. I said that your circumcision has become uncircumcision and the Gentile’s uncircumcision will be reckoned as circumcision—and rightly so. For the true Jew is not the one who is outwardly a Jew, that is, in designation, nation, and fleshly observance of the law; nor is true circumcision that which is outward, that is, visible to bodily eyes in the flesh, namely in the cutting away of the skin. Rather, the true Jew is one who is a Jew inwardly, confessing and praising God in the secret of the heart; and true circumcision is circumcision of the heart.

The ancient fathers had circumcision of the flesh because it was a seal of faith, and circumcision of the heart because of faith itself. Thus there are Jews in circumcision of the flesh, and Jews in circumcision of the heart. Those who have degenerated from these fathers, glorying in the name and having lost their deeds, remained Jews in the flesh and pagans in heart.

They were especially called Jews because Judah was one of Jacob’s twelve sons, and the kingdom came to the Jews from his tribe, as Jacob himself prophesied, saying: “The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a ruler from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent” (Gen. XLIX). Thus after David the Jews never had a king except from the tribe of Judah, until Christ came, who himself deigned to be born of Judah’s tribe as the true king. Herod, [Col. 0629A] under whom the Lord was born, was the first foreigner to reign in Judaea. Therefore, when the Lord himself had now come, the Jews’ kingdom was overthrown and taken from them. They now possess no kingdom because they were unwilling to recognize the true king.

Therefore, those who were called Jews from Judah, from whose line they had their king—let us see whether they should now be called by this name. For by their own utterance they renounced themselves from this name, so that they deserve to be called Jews only according to the flesh. When they raged against Christ, the king given to them from Judah and David, Pilate said to them: “Shall I crucify your king?” (John XIX). But they said: “We have no king but Caesar” (ibid.). If they had no king but Caesar, the scepter had been taken away from Judah. And if the scepter had been taken away from Judah, the one who was to be sent had already come, and they had lost the force of the Jewish name.

But those who became Christians from among the Jews are truly Jews. The other Jews, who did not believe in Christ, deserved to lose even the name itself. Therefore the true Judaea is Christ’s Church, believing in that king who came from Judah’s tribe through the Virgin Mary. The Apostle rightly says that the true Jew is not one outwardly a Jew, nor true circumcision that which is outwardly in the flesh, but the one inwardly a Jew, and circumcision which is of the heart in spirit, not in letter: that is, the law is to be understood according to the spirit, not according to the letter.

Circumcision of heart is a will pure from every unlawful desire. This circumcision is not accomplished by the letter teaching and threatening, but by the Spirit helping and healing. The praise of this circumcision or Jew is not from human beings but from God, because he is praised not by people for an empty designation but by God for inward truth—God who by his grace has granted him what enables him to be praised and to say: “My soul shall be praised in the Lord” (Ps. XXXIII). For even if human beings praise such a Jew or such circumcision, that praise is not from human beings but from God: that is, it comes not from human merits but from God’s grace. For no one can rightly be praised on merits alone if heavenly grace is lacking; but whoever possesses that grace, it truly makes praiseworthy.

So too some glory before people in an outward religious habit while lacking inwardly what they display outwardly; whereas others are religious in conduct without wearing the garment of religion. They are not praised by human beings as religious, but by God, who knows what they are.

## Chapter III

> “What then is the advantage of the Jew? Or what is the usefulness of circumcision? Much in every way. First indeed, because the utterances of God were entrusted to them. For what if some of them did not believe? Has their unbelief nullified the faithfulness of God? Far be it! But God is true, while every human being is a liar (Ps. CXV), as it is written: ‘That you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.’”

The Apostle had said that circumcision is useful if it keeps the law, [Col. 0630A] but, if it transgresses it, it is turned into uncircumcision; and conversely, if uncircumcision fulfills the law, it is reckoned as circumcision. But now, because he sees that the Jews might object to him: “Then we have no advantage over the Gentiles, and God made us be circumcised in vain,” he himself raises this objection, showing what advantage they have over the Gentiles. Since circumcision which transgresses the law becomes uncircumcision, and uncircumcision which fulfills the law is reckoned as circumcision—that is, the Jew becomes a Gentile and the Gentile a Jew—what advantage then has the Jew, who is called God’s peculiar people, over the Gentile, who is called an unclean dog? Or what is the usefulness of circumcision—that is, what has he obtained from circumcision? To this question or objection [Col. 0630B] the answer is that, in former times, the Jew had a great advantage, and this in every respect, that is, both corporally and spiritually. For in both respects God did many things for the Jews that he did not do for the Gentiles; and thus, according to their former condition, they were more worthy, though now they are not more excellent in faith. Corporally, he rained manna upon them in the wilderness, brought them into the land of promise, and enriched them with great resources. Spiritually too he dealt well with them, giving them knowledge of himself, opening his will to them, and justifying them through faith in the Redeemer who was to come.

“First indeed.” As if to say: Passing over the other, lesser temporal matters, I set down this first and chief point: that the oracles of God—that is, the law and the prophets—were entrusted to them as friends, so that through them they might understand the future [Col. 0630C] incarnation of God’s wisdom and the redemption of humankind. Or, they were entrusted by them, because we believe the Scriptures to be true which they handed down to us, and from no other nation have we received books of divine authority. Or, they were entrusted by them—that is, they themselves believed those things which the prophets and the law foretold concerning Christ; and so they received Christ more readily, since they understood him to have been promised in those oracles. And indeed they were entrusted to them; that is, they believed them. For what harm is it if some of them did not believe?

Or thus: Truly they had the greater privilege in that God entrusted his oracles to them, because on account of these Christ came to them and brought them first to faith. For what harm was there if some of them did not believe? [Col. 0630D] Did their unbelief make void the faith of God—that is, make empty the faith by which people believe in God? Far be it that it should make it void! For believers did not receive any less because others were unwilling to believe; nor did faith remain empty on their account, but it was fulfilled in believers.

Or “the faith of God” is the faithfulness of the promise which he made to Abraham concerning Christ and the multitude of spiritual children. And if some Jews did not believe, did their unbelief make void the faith of God? That is, did it make God’s promise empty and unfulfilled? Far be this from human hearts: that they should think the divine promise made void! For although some were unbelieving, others nevertheless believed, and in them the truth of the promise was fulfilled. The faithfulness [Col. 0631A] of God’s promises was not made void; rather, God is true in his promises, because he truly fulfills them.

God indeed is true in all that he says, but every human being is a liar. He adds this so that it may appear that God’s promise was made and fulfilled, not because of any human worthiness, but because of misery, so that grace might be given to the unworthy and grace might be more highly commended. God is called true, that is, unchangeable, both in his essence and in his promises. But a human being is a liar, not possessing true being, because he slips away through sins. For every human being is a liar: human nature has been so corrupted from the primal fall and infected by the serpent’s poison that it does not exist in this world without the falsehood of sins. For a person is a liar not only in words but also in deeds. Yet some who [Col. 0631B] through God’s grace rise above ordinary human beings are also made true by that same grace.

For these reasons God did not permit his faithfulness to be made void: both because of his own immutable truth and because of the pardonable condition of human frailty, which, after falling away from truth, cannot exist without the falsehood of sins. Thus God is true and humanity false, as it is written in the Psalm: “That you may be justified in your words” (Ps. 50). As though the Psalmist said: “O Lord, you have declared that you will punish sinners without respect of persons; yet, when you now forgive me, they judge your mercy to be falsehood. But you prevail when you are judged unjust for forgiving my sins, because, while the human being himself pursues his guilt by lamenting it, [Col. 0631C] the indulgence of your mercy is shown not to be unjust. While you accuse my guilt through the prophet, you prove that you care about our deeds, and you overcome those who judged you indifferent to human actions.” And thus you are proved true, while human beings are false.

“I sinned and did evil before you, so that you, by sending your Son from my stock, as you promised, may be justified in the words of your promise”—that is, may be proved just and true, not allowing my iniquity to prevent you from causing your Son, as you declared, to assume flesh from my seed, in order to redeem the world; and may prevail by fulfilling your promises when you are judged not to be bound to fulfill them because of my sins. “That you may be justified in your words,” by fulfilling them. For the justice [Col. 0631D] of words is truth; and you overcome your false accusers when they judge you unjust because you spare me and make me worthy of your promise.

The Apostle now follows this line of thought, as though saying: Or, the transgressing Jews indeed caused the Lord’s name to be blasphemed, so that it was said: “Was this that holy nation and chosen people, which has now entangled itself in transgression, inexpiable sacrilege, and the crime of impiety? Behold, through their wickedness God’s promises have been made void.” But it is not so. For if transgressors have fallen from grace, the obedience of believers obtains the Lord’s truthful promise. Thus, when those who boasted that the divine oracles had been brought to nothing are confounded, God is justified in his words and prevails when he is judged, [Col. 0632A] because he grants to believers the grace rejected by unbelievers.

> “But if our unrighteousness commends the righteousness of God, what shall we say? Is God unrighteous who inflicts wrath? I speak according to human fashion. Far be it! Otherwise, how will God judge this world? For if the truth of God has abounded through my falsehood to his glory, why am I still judged as a sinner? And why not, as we are slanderously reported, and as some claim that we say, ‘Let us do evil that good may come’? Their condemnation is just.”

He said that the Lord is true and every human being false, and that he gives good things to the unworthy, whereby his justice and grace appear more commendable. Hence some perverse person, saying that God uses evils as an instrument [Col. 0632B] for his glory, draws the conclusion that God is unjust when he punishes sins which benefit him. The Apostle rejects this. For here the argument turns upon two persons: that is, any ignorant person who interprets badly, and the Apostle who refutes him.

For, because of the statement, “that you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged,” the opposing party seemed to reply: “O Apostle, you have given great comfort to our sins by saying that God is justified by forgiving countless offences; therefore our sins are unjustly punished, though they serve to display God’s patience and benevolence.” And the Apostle replies: God indeed is justified in his words. But if our unrighteousness, [Col. 0632C] as you suppose, commends God’s righteousness—that is, makes it greater by displaying it when he forgives or judges—what shall we say, understand, of the incongruity that follows from this? Namely: Is God unrighteous when he inflicts wrath—that is, punishment—for sins? That is, he would then be unjust if he punishes us for our sins, which increase his glory. “I speak according to human fashion,” that is, according to your carnal understanding, who think so ignorantly about the foregoing statement. By what justice could he condemn unrighteousness if, according to your opinion, he himself became more unrighteous through human wickedness? But far be it that he should be thought unjust when he punishes sinners. Therefore our unrighteousness does not commend his righteousness; sins do not glorify him, but the deeds of the good do. Therefore he justly takes vengeance upon sins, since he delights mercifully in holy works.

[Col. 0632D] Truly he is not unrighteous in striking sinners. For otherwise—that is, if it is otherwise, if it is not the case that he is not unjust—how will God judge this world? For it is contradictory that he should be unjust and become a judge, since every judge is equitable. Therefore he cannot be Judge if he is unjust in inflicting wrath upon sinners. It follows, then, that he is just and equitable in punishing sins, and thus will judge justly when he renders good things to the good and evil things to the evil; for our unrighteousness, as you said, did not help to commend his righteousness, nor was he glorified through it.

The Apostle further replies to the objection just stated, proving that our unrighteousness does not glorify God’s justice and that he is not unjust if he punishes. Truly it is so. For if the truth—that is, the righteousness—[Col. 0633A] of God has abounded through my falsehood—that is, through my sin—to his glory; that is, if the falsehood of my sin has caused the truth of God’s justice to increase, so that his glory might be more widely displayed thereby, according to your opinion: why, after I have thus sinned and, according to you, glorified God, am I still judged by him as a sinner, not merely in the future, when I would not be a sinner if my sins glorified God?

Unrighteousness is a genus or whole; falsehood is a species or part of unrighteousness. Similarly, righteousness is a genus or whole; truth is a species or part of righteousness. Hence “truth” is put for “righteousness,” since every truth is righteousness; and “falsehood” for unrighteousness or sin, since every falsehood is unrighteousness or sin. “Why,” he says, [Col. 0633B] “am I still judged, if the falsehood of my unrighteousness, according to what you suppose, glorified God?” And why—that is, why do we not do evil so that good may come? Why do we not sin continually, so that God may continually forgive and become more praiseworthy? “As we are slandered,” that is, as perverse people charge us with holding; and “as some wicked people say that we say”—that is, preach—“Let us do evil that good may come.”

The Apostles did not say this; rather, they said that “where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” (Rom. 5). But perverse people, seizing upon words of this kind, maintained that they said, “Let us do evil that good may come,” so as to cherish and defend their sins under the authority of apostolic preaching. Their condemnation is just, because they will justly be condemned [Col. 0633C] who flatter themselves in their sins with a security hostile to them and are confirmed in their evils from the Apostles’ words.

The statement may also be understood differently, once the argument has been examined. Truly God, if he inflicts wrath upon evil people, is not unrighteous. For if it were otherwise, why am I, even after conversion, I who am now so great an Apostle, still judged by you as a sinner—that is, as one who sinned in persecuting the faithful? That is: if God does not justly inflict wrath upon the wicked, why do you judge the greatness of my unrighteousness to deserve punishment? I say that I am judged—and deservedly—if the truth of God has abounded in my falsehood; that is, if the falsehood of my unbelief and denial was so great before God that the truth of the divine promise and faith thereby became more commendable to his glory. This [Col. 0633D] means: I am deservedly judged as a sinner, because I denied the truth of the Christian faith and strove, by persecuting believers, to make void the truth of the heavenly promise; and yet that very truth of faith or promise became clearer in those whom I made martyrs, as in Stephen, through my cruelty. And since I am deservedly judged for these things, it is evident that God is not unjust when he condemns sinners at the judgment.

And it is not true of us, as we are blasphemed—that is, unjustly and falsely reproached—and as certain unnamed persons say that we tell others: “Let us do evil,” that is, let us sin, “so that good things may come to us from God,” that is, so that God may grant us the remedies of his mercy by forgiving sins. The condemnation of those who babble such things about us is just [Col. 0634A]: by God’s just judgment such people are condemned; nor is God unjust when he inflicts wrath upon them.

> “What then? Do we excel them? Not at all. For we have charged both Jews and Greeks with all being under sin, as it is written: ‘There is no one righteous, not even one; there is none who understands, none who seeks God. All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; there is none who does good, not even one. Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they acted deceitfully; the poison of asps is under their lips’ (Ps. 11). ‘Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood’ (Isa. 69). ‘Destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace; there is no fear of God [Col. 0634B] before their eyes.’”

Because he had said that in every respect the Jew had formerly had a great advantage over the Greek, the Jews now wished to prefer themselves to the Gentiles, as though they had deserved to be called to grace through their previous works of righteousness. But he, suppressing their arrogance, shows that they had been sinners like the Gentiles. Granted that, in their former condition, God did much more for the Jew than for the Greek in every respect, what then seems to follow from this? It would seem to follow that we excel them—that is, the Greeks—in the new grace which we have now received. But it does not follow that we Jews excel them and are worthier than they, because we too, like them, have sinned. For we have charged—that is, by many grounds and [Col. 0634C] arguments have already shown—both Jews and Greeks all to be under sin before this grace. Therefore no one precedes another.

Above, he showed the Gentiles to be under sin when he said: “God gave them over to the desires of their hearts,” and so forth. He showed the Jews to be under sin where he said: “You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery?” and so forth. Thus we have said that they are under sin, as it is written concerning the Jews, of whom this seemed less likely: there is no one righteous among them, because no one is justified by works of the law without grace; there is no one who understands, because none of them understands the holy Scriptures or recognizes Christ as God, whether through his words or through his miracles. There is none who seeks God, although Christ God [Col. 0634D] came to seek them in order to lead them back to their eternal homeland; nevertheless none of them seeks him, though he has already sought them. This was said of those who had not yet come to Christ.

There is none, either Jew or Gentile, who seeks God in the sense of seeking and searching how he may fulfill his will so as to deserve to attain the finding of his vision; rather, all have turned aside—that is, drawn themselves downward away from seeking him—setting their hearts on low things and occupying themselves with bodily concerns. Together all have become useless, that is, acquiring no benefit for themselves, because not only the Gentiles, but also the Jews who wished to be saved through the law without Christ, laboured in vain. There is none who does good, since the Jews are condemned by transgression of the commandments [Col. 0635A] and the Gentiles by their violation of the law of nature. And therefore there is none among them who does good, because whatever is done without faith in Christ is by no means good, however good it may seem. “Not even one”: that is, not one of them does good, because if someone went through them one by one, counting and searching down to the last, he would not find anyone who did good.

Or, there is none among all who does good “until one comes”—that is, until one comes to him who is one and unique, namely Christ, with whom no one can be compared. Christ alone does good, both in himself and in his own. He is not one of them who does good; rather, all of them do many evils. For “their throat is an open tomb” (Ps. 13), because just as an overpowering stench of a decomposing corpse comes forth from an open tomb, [Col. 0635B] so from their opened throat there proceeds, through evil speech, the stench of their rotten conscience, to infect and corrupt the morals of their hearers. Their throat would be a closed tomb if shame still restrained them from bringing the inward stench of their dead soul out into public through speech. But their throat is an open tomb because, in the worst degree of evil, they have lost shame, so that they are no longer ashamed publicly to speak of their crimes, but brazenly open their throat and bring forth to those around them the stench of their dead soul.

And even while humbly uttering sweet and flattering words with their tongues, they acted deceitfully, because they brought forth one thing with their mouth and meditated another in [Col. 0635C] their heart, in accordance with the saying: “They speak peace with their neighbour, but evils are in their hearts” (Ps. 27). They had good things in their words, but beneath their lips was the poison of asps—that is, incurable hatred lay hidden beneath their utterances. The poison of asps is more deadly than that of other serpents, and therefore it signifies the worst malice. The poison of asps is concealed beneath the lips of those who speak smoothly but fraudulently kill the hearer’s soul with the bite of a poisoned word: detractors, poets, and every sort of seducer. For they are enemies of souls, although they pretend to be friends; and therefore, through the malice of deceit, they infect souls with their poison in order to kill them.

Their mouth also is full of cursing and bitterness, because they not only flatter some with feigned words, but also curse others with full mouth and speak bitter things. These are the arts of the worst people: to flatter some, curse others, be smooth with some, and speak bitterly to others. Nor are they merely said to have cursing and bitterness in their mouth; rather, their mouth is reported to be full of cursing and bitterness, so as to show the abundance of cursing and bitterness in their mouth.

[Col. 0635D] Their feet too are swift to shed blood, because they run quickly to commit murder. Or their feet—that is, their affections—are swift, that is, ready and eager, to shed blood, because they commit murders deliberately. Destruction and misery are in their ways, because both they and all who walk in the paths of their actions will be crushed by the punishments of Gehenna and [Col. 0636A] deprived of the happiness of heavenly blessedness. And this is because they have not known the way of peace—that is, the way of righteous action by which they might reach the rest of perpetual peace. Nor is it surprising that they do not know the way by which they ought to tend toward eternal peace, because the fear of God, “which is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. 1), is not before the eyes of their heart. For because they rejected the beginning of wisdom, they did not attain its progress. Thus pride, by which they removed the fear of God from their mind’s gaze, caused them to be ignorant of the way of peace and to walk the way of death.

The Apostle said these things concerning the wickedness of unbelieving Jews and Gentiles on prophetic authority, especially in order to convict the Jews, who boasted in works of the law, of being entangled in many sins. But one must not suppose [Col. 0636B] that he took these passages from the thirteenth Psalm alone. They are not found together in this order in the Hebrew; rather, he joined them from different Psalms and from the book of Isaiah. For the words, “There is no one righteous, none who understands, none who seeks God; all have turned aside, together they have become worthless; there is none who does good, not even one,” he took from the thirteenth Psalm. What he then added, “Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they acted deceitfully,” is read in the fifth Psalm. And what he immediately added, “The poison of asps is under their lips,” belongs to the one hundred and thirty-ninth Psalm. Again, “Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness” is taken from the ninth Psalm, where it is said in the singular: “Whose mouth is full of cursing [Col. 0636C] and bitterness.” The following words, “Their feet are swift to shed blood; destruction and misery are in their ways; and they have not known the way of peace,” are found in Isaiah. And again, what is said at the end, “There is no fear of God before their eyes,” occurs thus at the beginning of the thirty-fifth Psalm: “The unjust person said, that he might sin within himself: there is no fear of God before his eyes.”

Nor should anyone think there is any discrepancy in this, if what is said in the singular in its original places is put by the Apostle in the plural, since he was writing to many and gathering many examples into one meaning. Thus it is clear not so much that the Apostle took from the thirteenth Psalm what is not found in the Hebrew or in the Septuagint translators, but is found in the Vulgate edition [Col. 0636D], as that those who did not know the Apostle’s art of weaving the Scriptures together sought a suitable place in which to put the testimony he cited, since they did not think that it had been placed in the Epistle without Scriptural authority.

> “But we know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may become subject to God, because by works of the law no flesh will be justified before him. For through the law comes knowledge of sin. But now, apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been manifested, being attested by the law and the prophets: the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ unto all and upon all who believe in him.”

Lest the Jews should say, “These things which you have brought forward were not [Col. 0637A] said of us, but of the Gentiles,” the Apostle shows that the things written in the law were said to those held under the law. Here he calls the book of Psalms “the law,” as does the Lord when he says: “Is it not written in your law, ‘I said, You are gods’?” (Ps. 81). Or he now calls the whole Old Testament “the law.” As though he said: “You indeed wish to twist these words toward others, but we know that not only these things, but whatever the law says, it says to those who are under the law—that is, to the Jews—whether good or evil. Although all these evils which the Apostle has now described in prophetic words were also found among the Gentiles, yet they were all said properly concerning the Jews; for there was no need to establish the crimes of the Gentiles, about which no one doubted, by prophetic [Col. 0637B] testimonies, but rather those of the Jews, who wished to boast in their past works of righteousness.

“Whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law,” because everything which the law says about Gentiles says this very thing also about Jews, since they are its principal concern. Everything the law says, even when it describes the worst crimes, it undoubtedly says to those established under the law; and whatever the law says pertains to them, so that every mouth—not only that of Gentiles, but also of Jews—may be stopped, that is, silenced, since they have no ground for boasting but are shown all to be under sin. Or, the law says all these things to those under the law so that every mouth, even that of Jews, may be stopped, finding nothing of which to boast in its merits, when the law says: “All have turned aside; together they have become worthless” (Ps. 3).

[Col. 0637C] And so that the whole world may become subject to God: so that it may know that it cannot be saved without God’s grace; or at least, recognizing itself to be in sins, may hope for mercy in confession of sin. Let the whole world—that is, all people in the world, not Gentiles alone but Jews also—be made subject to God. They ought humbly to do this, because by works of the law no flesh—that is, no one living in the flesh—will be justified before God, who sees the secrets of the heart, although before human beings one may seem to be justified.

Here the Apostle begins to argue, in a great and prolonged contest, against those who boasted in the law and believed that they were justified through the law rather than [Col. 0637D] grace. He teaches in sequence that the law could not take away sin, but rather increased it; grace takes it away. For the law knows how to command, and human weakness succumbs to it; grace knows how to help, and through it love is poured in. It should be noted that he now calls the five books of Moses “the law.” No one will be justified before God by the works of this law, because the law brought nothing to perfection: it instilled fear of punishment but did not infuse love of righteousness. For one who kept the law from fear of punishment rather than love of holiness would certainly prefer that the thing he feared did not exist, so that he might be allowed to transgress the law with impunity. Further, even if he fulfilled the law itself in outward acts and appeared righteous in human eyes, he was nevertheless unrighteous in the eyes of the inward Inspector, because what he displayed outwardly in action he did not possess inwardly in his will. [Col. 0638A]

We do not say that those obedient to the law were not justified; rather, we say that, unless they had been justified by grace, they would not have been truly obedient. Truly no one is genuinely justified by works of the law, because through the law there is knowledge of sin only, not its removal. For the law forbids sin; it does not take it away; and by forbidding it, it shows that what it forbids is evil. Through the law came knowledge of sin, and through it no one was justified without grace. But now, in this time of grace, God’s grace—hidden during the time of the law—has been manifested. Apart from the law—that is, without the law’s assistance—the righteousness not of a human being, nor of one’s own will, but of God, has been manifested. And it is God’s righteousness not by which God himself is righteous, but by which he clothes a human being when he justifies the ungodly.

[Col. 0638B] And so that this righteousness may be held more certainly, it has been attested by the law and the prophets; that is, the law and the prophets have borne testimony to it. For the law, in commanding and threatening and justifying no one, sufficiently indicated that a human being is justified by God’s gift through the help of the Spirit. The prophets likewise bore witness because Christ’s coming fulfilled what they foretold. This righteousness is apart from the law, because God grants it to the believer through the Spirit of grace without the law’s assistance—that is, without help from the law—although through the law he showed a human being his weakness, so that, fleeing through faith to God’s mercy, the person might be healed.

I said that the righteousness of God has been manifested. But this righteousness of God is through faith in Jesus Christ—that is, through the faith by which one believes in Christ. For this is called the faith of Christ, by which we believe in Christ, just as that is called the righteousness [Col. 0638C] of God by which we are justified by God. Both are ours; but they are called God’s and Christ’s because they are given through his generosity. This righteousness, which is conferred through faith, and faith itself, are infused by God’s hidden inspiration and the gift of grace; they are not acquired by human labour or by the work of the Old Testament, because it is his gift that we believe. Therefore this righteousness, bestowed from heaven, is upon all who believe, surpassing the merits of all, Jews and Gentiles alike. Thus righteousness is also upon them through faith, which could not come through the law, because faith obtains what the law commands.

> “For there is no distinction: for all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace through the redemption which is in [Col. 0638D] Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood, to display his righteousness because of the remission of former sins, in God’s forbearance, to display his righteousness at this present time, so that he may be just and the justifier of the one who is of faith in Jesus Christ.”

Therefore I said that righteousness through faith is equally available to all, because there is no distinction in receiving that righteousness: whether Jew or Gentile has faith, he will be justified. Truly there is no distinction between the two, because all—both Jews and Gentiles—have sinned, whether in themselves or in Adam. For the law, whether given in Paradise, implanted naturally, or promulgated in written form, has been transgressed by them. Therefore all have sinned and still daily need the glory of God: that is, that [Col. 0639A] God may be glorified in them ever more and more, by bestowing the benefits of his grace through the forgiveness of daily offences and the multiplication of virtues. They do not need their own glory, so as to boast as though from their own merits; rather, they need God’s glory—that is, it is altogether necessary for them that God’s glory should be enlarged in them. For if righteousness were obtained from works of the law, that righteousness itself would no longer be God’s glory, but rather the glory of human beings who observe the law. But since righteousness is obtained through grace, not through the law, that righteousness is God’s glory, not human glory, so that whatever a person has, he may ascribe not to himself but to God.

They still need God’s glory, although they have already been justified freely—that is, without any merits at all. And they are justified not through the law or their own will, but through grace. This does not happen without our will [Col. 0639B]; rather, our will is shown by the law to be weak, so that grace may heal the will, and the healed will may fulfil the law—not placed under the law, nor needing the law. The Apostle says all this lest faith itself begin to grow proud and say: “If it is from faith, how is it free? For what faith merits, why is it not repaid rather than given?” But if someone says, “In order that I may merit justification, I have faith,” the answer is given him: “For what have you that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4). Therefore, since faith obtains justification, and since God has apportioned even its measure of faith to each person, no human merit precedes God’s grace; rather, grace itself merits to be increased, so that, having been increased, it may merit to be perfected—with the will accompanying as a handmaid, not leading or going before.

“Justified,” he says, “through grace” [Col. 0639C] which is not repaid for merits but freely given, and is therefore called grace. This grace comes through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus, not in anyone else. For the redemption of the human race was found in him—that is, in his blood—and could be found in nothing else. Christ did not make us his because we had always been his by nature; rather, he redeemed us because we were held captive by sin. For one who redeems someone shows that the person he redeems was his own. Thus Christ redeemed us because we were his.

God the Father set forth this Christ—that is, he long beforehand ordained him to be the future propitiation, that is, the expiation of our sins: namely, that through him the Father himself might expiate us from sins and become propitious toward us. [Col. 0639D] Or, “he set forth” means that he openly presented him to all as propitiation in his blood: that he might be not only the propitiator but also the propitiation, and that we might have that propitiation in his blood, which was shed for the forgiveness of sins. For without the shedding of blood, as this Apostle says, forgiveness of sins does not take place, since propitiation and forgiveness of sins can be given only through Christ’s blood. As often as sins are said to be forgiven in the law, the blood of a victim is offered as its type.

God set Christ forth as propitiation through faith, so that those who believed in him might possess this propitiation. Or, he set him forth as propitiation through faith in his blood, because he will otherwise be propitiation for no one unless that person [Col. 0640A] believes that he shed his blood for the redemption of humankind and, so far as he can, joins good works to that faith. “He set him forth,” he says—that is, he publicly declared through the preaching of the apostles that this one is propitiation for our sins. He did this for the manifestation of his righteousness: that through him he might reveal to human beings his true righteousness, formerly hidden while people supposed that they could be justified by works of the law. Therefore he revealed true righteousness in those believing in Christ, and showed it to be his own, not human: bestowed by himself upon people, not originating from them or obtained from works of the law.

He revealed this righteousness for the forgiveness of former offences: that is, in order to forgive offences which had preceded, not only among Gentiles but also among [Col. 0640B] Jews who had not yet known true righteousness. For all have sinned. But through the manifestation of his righteousness it pleased God to forgive them their preceding faults and justify them, so that thereafter they might live righteously. The Apostle specified “preceding” offences in order that no one should suppose that those sins are forgiven which one commits after receiving grace. The offences came first; and this happened in God’s forbearance, for he did not immediately strike offenders, but patiently endured them for a long time in order to turn them to repentance.

I say that this forbearance was granted beforehand for the manifestation of his righteousness: he endured them long-sufferingly in order finally to show his righteousness to those who had been converted, in this time of grace—a righteousness which he had not manifested in earlier times, while [Col. 0640C] people supposed that they could justify themselves. For this purpose, I say, he endured them and showed his righteousness, by which people could be justified: so that he himself might be righteous—that is, acting justly in all things. For it was just that he who will judge each person in the age to come according to that person’s works should patiently endure them in this age and show them what they ought to do. Therefore he is righteous in this forbearance and manifestation of righteousness, because he has done everything that he ought to have done.

And through these things he is also the justifier of the one who is of the faith of Jesus Christ: for while he endures and displays his righteousness, he pours that righteousness into the believing heart. He does not justify the one who is of the law, but the one who is of Christ’s faith—that is, of the faith by which one believes in Christ. For justification is given from this faith, and not from works [Col. 0640D] of law or nature.

> “Where then is your boasting? It has been excluded. By what law? Of works? No, but by the law of faith. For we judge that a human being is justified by faith without works of the law. Is God the God of Jews only? Is he not also of Gentiles? Yes, of Gentiles also, since God is one, who justifies circumcision from faith and uncircumcision through faith. Do we then destroy the law through faith? Far from it; rather, we establish the law.”

Since righteousness is God’s, not humanity’s, and comes from faith, not from law, where then is your boasting, O Jew? That is, where is your exaltation, in which you boasted that you were justified through works of the law? You have no matter for boasting in the law, because it has been excluded—that is, the ground of your boasting has been cast out [Col. 0641A] and taken away from you; the boasting which you held in your heart has been eliminated. And observe by what means. By what law do you suppose it was excluded? Do you suppose it was by the law of deeds—that is, works? It was not excluded by the law of works, but by the law of faith: not through the labour of works, but through the ease of faith.

For the law of faith is that by which we believe in Christ and ask the aid of his grace in order to do good. The law of faith is in the assisting Spirit; the law of works is in the commanding letter. What the law of works commands by threatening, the law of faith obtains by believing. The law of works says: “You shall not covet” (Exod. 20); the law of faith says: “When I knew that no one can be continent unless God gives it, and that it was wisdom itself to know whose gift this was, I approached the Lord and entreated him” (Wisdom [Col. 0641B] 8). This is that wisdom called piety, by which the Father of lights is worshipped, “from whom is every good gift and every perfect donation” (Jas. 1). He is worshipped by a sacrifice of praise and acts of thanksgiving, so that his worshipper may boast not in himself but in him.

Accordingly, by the law of works God says, “Do what I command”; by the law of faith God is told, “Give what you command.” Therefore the boasting of those who, when they seem to themselves to live righteously, boast as though they had not received it, is not excluded by the law of works, but by the law of faith. For through it each person recognizes that, if he lives well in any respect, he possesses this through God’s grace; and that he will obtain perfection in the love of righteousness from no other source. Thus in the law of deeds there is the righteousness of God who commands; but in the law of faith there is the mercy of God who helps. For this is the law [Col. 0641C] of faith: that we believe and pray that through grace we may be given the ability to do what we cannot fulfil by ourselves, lest, ignorant of God’s righteousness and desiring to establish our own, we should not be subject to God’s righteousness.

Truly, he says, your boasting—by which you were swollen with pride over observance of the law—has been excluded through the law of faith, because we apostles judge, that is, are certain, that any person is justified through faith without preceding works of the law. The Apostle does not say this in order that, if someone believes, good works should not concern him; rather, he says it so that no one may think himself to have attained the gift of justification, which is in faith, through the merits of earlier good works. For in this the Jews wished to prefer themselves to Gentiles believing in Christ: they said that through the merits of good works under the law they had attained evangelical grace. Therefore many Jews who had believed were scandalized [Col. 0641D] that Christ’s grace should be bestowed on uncircumcised Gentiles. Hence the Apostle now says that a person can be justified by faith without works—namely, works that precede.

For once justified by faith, how can one thereafter fail to work righteously, even though one had previously done nothing righteous in attaining faith’s justification? It is attained not by the merit of good works, but by God’s grace, which cannot be idle in that person when he now works well through love. But if, having believed, he immediately departs from this life, justification by faith remains with him: neither preceding good works [Col. 0642A] are present, because he arrived at it not by merit but by grace, nor subsequent works, because he is not permitted to remain in this life. Hence it is plain that when the Apostle says a person is justified by faith without works, he must not be understood to mean that, after faith has been received, a person who lives on may be called righteous even if he lives wickedly; rather, each person should know that he is justified through faith even if works of the law have not preceded. For works follow one who has been justified; they do not precede one who is to be justified.

But James testifies concerning those who, after receiving faith, are unwilling to work well: “Faith, if it does not have works, is dead in itself” (Jas. 2). After this, in order to show that Gentiles too ought to be admitted to this grace just as Jews are, the Apostle says: “Is God the God of Jews only?” It is as though he said: “You suppose that God belongs only to you and that you alone ought to receive his grace. But is this true? Is he God only of Jews? Is he not also of Gentiles, just as he is of Jews?” “Yes”—that is, I choose rather to say that he is God both of Gentiles and of Jews: he made all people, and he has equal care for all. Christ came not only to you but also to Gentiles: promised to you from the law, but sent to them.

For this reason he is much more the God of Gentiles, because before the law holy persons in uncircumcision pleased God. Therefore he said, “Yes, of Gentiles also,” in order to show the priority of the Gentiles: for holy uncircumcised persons existed before circumcised ones, and Abraham was justified by faith before circumcision. But the Jews say proudly: “The Gentiles abandoned God by worshipping idols.” They are answered: “And [Col. 0642C] so did you.” “But,” they say, “we are converted.” And the others say: “Christ came to us as promised.”

[Note: [Col. 0641D] An obscure passage.]

And to them: “Therefore he does not appear to be God only, since we are born from Adam and it was foretold through the prophets that the Gentiles would believe in Christ.” Truly he is God of Gentiles as of Jews. Though this can be proved in other ways, I offer this one point: God is one, not many gods. And that he is one God of all is evident because he justifies all by the same means. For he justifies circumcision—that is, the circumcised—by faith; and uncircumcision—that is, the uncircumcised—through faith. For “by faith” is the same as “through faith.” Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision is justified without faith.

And since a person is justified through faith without works of the law, do we then destroy the law through faith? No; rather, we establish it. The Apostle himself presents, in the form of a question, the inference a Jew might make, in order to remove it. Since, he says, we declare that any person is justified through faith without a work of the law, do we destroy the law through faith? Far be it from us to destroy it! Rather, we establish it—that is, we make the law firm and stable. For through the law comes knowledge of sin; through faith, the obtaining of grace against sin; through grace, the healing of the soul from the defect of sin; through the soul’s health, freedom of choice; through free choice, love of righteousness; and through love of righteousness, the practice of the law. Thus the law is not destroyed but established through faith: faith obtains the grace through which the law may be fulfilled; grace [Col. 0643A] heals the will, through which righteousness may be freely loved.

Or thus: “Do we then [establish] the law,” and so forth. Since the Apostle said that a person is justified by faith without observance of the law, lest the Jews should say, “Then you destroy the law, under which all who believed were righteous and circumcised,” he says: “I do not abolish or destroy it; I confirm it, while I preach the circumcision which it foretold: ‘In the last days the Lord your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your seed’” (Deut. 30). I would destroy the law if I said that it had lied—that is, if I said it would not cease when it had promised that it would cease. As Jeremiah says:

> “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall complete a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah—not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers [Col. 0643B] on the day when I took their hands to lead them out of the land of Egypt; but this is the covenant which I shall establish with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: giving my laws in their hearts, and I shall write them upon their minds” (Jer. 31; Heb. 8).

The law is not destroyed when it ceases because it has been fulfilled. We do not destroy it; rather, we establish it—that is, we cause it to stand—when we prove true what it said concerning the righteous of old, the Gentiles who would believe, and the coming spiritual circumcision, while faith accomplishes what the law commands.

## Chapter IV

> “What then shall we say that Abraham, our father according to the flesh, has found? For if Abraham is justified by works, he has glory—but not [Col. 0643C] before God. For what does Scripture say? ‘Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness’” (Gen. 15).

He brings them back to the source of circumcision, so that what was established at the beginning may hold throughout. Since a person is justified by faith without works and no one can be justified without faith, what then, he says, shall we say that Abraham our father—whom we must imitate—found according to the flesh, that is, according to circumcision of the flesh or the fleshly works of the law? It is as though he said: We can say that he found nothing of justification according to the flesh, but rather according to the mind. For circumcision is in the flesh, but faith in the mind. And he himself is read to have found justification not through circumcision but through faith [Col. 0643D], as was said generally: that every person can be justified through faith without works.

Or, he is our father according to the flesh because we derive our fleshly origin from him, and we Jews have circumcision of the flesh from him. According to faith, however, he is father of believers from among the Gentiles. And what shall we say he found, through which he was righteous? Works of the law? No. For if we say that he was justified from works of the law, we incur the absurdity that he has glory from his own works but not before God—which is altogether false, because we all know that he has glory before God. Therefore he was justified not by works but by faith.

For just as faith without subsequent [Col. 0644A] good works is empty, so are any good works before faith. They have glory in one’s own eyes or before people, but not before God. Many boast of their works, and many pagans refuse to become Christians for this reason: they consider their good life sufficient for themselves. Such a person says: “One must live well. What will Christ command me except that I live well? I already live well. What need have I of Christ? I commit no murder, no theft, no robbery; I do not covet another’s possessions; I am defiled by no adultery.
