Nothing blameworthy is found in my life; and whoever finds fault with me, let him make me a Christian.” Such a person has glory, but not before God.

But our father Abraham did not boast in this way. For he found righteousness not from [Col. 0644B] works of the law—since he lived before the law—but rather from faith, because he believed God’s promises. Truly, he was not justified by works. For what does Scripture say in Genesis? That is, from what does Scripture say that Abraham was justified? From faith. For it testifies that Abraham believed God when he promised that his seed would be as numerous and as illustrious as the heavens; and because he believed so firmly, it was reckoned to him by God as righteousness. That is, by this belief he was not only freed from every original and actual sin, but was also reckoned righteous by God. Therefore Abraham was justified by faith.

Yet although works did not precede faith, they followed it. For he who was first justified by faith in God’s sight was afterward justified by works also in the sight [Col. 0644C] of people. Hence the Apostle James, in his epistle against those who did not wish to work well but presumed upon faith alone, commended Abraham’s works, saying: “Do you wish to know, empty man, that faith without works is idle? Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered his son Isaac upon the altar?” James is not opposed in this judgment to Paul, who says: “If Abraham is justified by works, he has glory, but not before God,” and who therefore maintains that he was not justified by works. Both speak truly.

Paul, indeed, commending the righteousness which comes from faith against those who neglected faith and boasted of the righteousness which comes from works, said that Abraham was not justified by works which preceded faith. James, as stated, against those who became sluggish in idleness after receiving faith and supposed that, since they were justified by that same faith, they could be saved even without good works, said that Abraham was justified by works—but works which followed faith. Therefore, to show that he did not disagree with Paul but rather agreed with him, James immediately added: “You see that faith cooperated with his works, so that faith was perfected by works, and Scripture was fulfilled, which says: ‘Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness’” (Gen. 15), “and he was called the friend of God.” He then further added: “You see that a person is justified by works and not [Col. 0645A] by faith only.” It is evident that he speaks of works which follow faith, because Paul said that a person can be justified by faith alone without preceding works. For no one can possess faith through preceding merits of his own.

Therefore the person who is justified by faith freely given to him boasts not in himself but in the Lord, because, having confidence not from works, he understands in every respect that he is indebted to God, finding nothing which he can arrogate to himself from merits.

> “But to the one who works, the reward is not reckoned according to grace, but according to debt. Yet to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, faith is reckoned as righteousness according to the purpose of God’s grace; as David also [Col. 0645B] declares the blessedness of the person to whom God reckons righteousness without works: ‘Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not reckoned sin’” (Ps. 31).

I said that Abraham is righteous by faith. But for one who performs works of the law—which Abraham did not perform—or any good works in order to merit grace, as the Jew claimed to have done: if there is a reward for him, it is not from grace but due to his own merit. But should anyone wish to ask what he merited before grace in order to receive it, he will find his evils, not goods. For grace is given freely, whence it is also so called. If it is grace, therefore, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace.

[Col. 0645C] Therefore the Jew—or anyone else—errs when he thinks he has attained God’s grace through the merit of preceding works. “For who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid him?” He supposes that he first gave to God and received evangelical grace as the recompense for his work; but this is not so. For to one who works beforehand, not grace but a debt is paid. Yet to one who does not perform works of the law but comes to faith without a preceding work, faith itself suffices for righteousness. Thus the Apostle attributes to others what he said of Abraham: namely, that if he is righteous by works, he has glory, but not before God, and therefore he is righteous by faith.

Or faith in this manner justifies at the outset without works. But one justified in this way ought not thereafter to be idle in good works. For to the one who, after faith freely received, [Col. 0645D] performs good works, the reward—that is, eternal recompense—is not reckoned according to grace, that is, according to faith alone, but according to the debt owed for his work. This is what happens to the person who lives and works well after receiving faith; for he receives no reward otherwise from the Lord. But to the one who does not work—that is, who after baptism has no time to work, or cannot work because of infirmity although he wishes to do so, but is taken from this life without works while possessing faith and good will—to this person, who does nothing but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, that is, in God, his faith is reckoned as righteousness. That is, faith alone suffices for his righteousness and thus for salvation, according to the purpose of God’s grace: according to what God had long beforehand purposed through [Col. 0646A] his grace, or according to God’s grace set forth for all who are willing to believe.

“Believes in him who justifies the ungodly,” he says. It is one thing to believe that he exists (*credere eum*), another to believe him (*credere ei*), another to believe in him (*credere in eum*). To believe that he exists is to believe that he is; to believe him is to believe that what he says is true; to believe in him is, in believing, to love, in believing to go into him, and to be incorporated into his members. Therefore faith by which one believes in him is the only faith that he approves.

The ungodly person is one who does not believe rightly, even if he takes nothing from anyone, gives to the poor, does not covet another’s wife, wrongs no one, and restores a deposit: because he does all these things without the intention with which he ought to do them. Therefore they are not good, because they do not proceed from [Col. 0646B] a good root. Whoever wishes to perform good works without faith is certainly ungodly. But let him believe in him who justifies the ungodly, so that he too may become godly from ungodly; and, justified by faith, may thereafter be able to perform works of piety and righteousness.

For one who thus believes, faith is reckoned as righteousness according to the purpose of God’s grace, who so purposed and decreed by his grace that, when the law has ceased, faith should justify. And I say that this happens by grace, just as David says here (Ps. 31) that blessedness belongs in the future to that person to whom God, having received him—that is, admitted him to grace—reckons righteousness without preceding works. For it is a great blessedness for a person, without the labour of law or penance, to obtain faith through grace alone according [Col. 0646C] to God’s purpose, by which he purposed freely to forgive sins.

God reckons righteousness without works to the one whom he has received, who by the faith through which he first believed God is both absolved from the past, justified in the present, and prepared for future works of faith. The Apostle wishes to prove that righteousness without works is proclaimed as beneficial in the law itself, and that he is not maintaining this from his own resources, but confirms it by prophetic testimony. “Blessed,” he says, “are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered from God’s sight.”

Iniquity is acting against the law or outside the law. Hence in Greek it is called *anomia* (ἀνομία), that is, “without law,” because law is *nomos* (νόμος). Iniquity, therefore, is deviating from the law or acting against the law. Sin, however, can also mean committing an offence contrary to what nature teaches and conscience reproves. [Col. 0646D] According to this sense, iniquity appears to concern Jews, but sin Gentiles. Yet if they believe, the Lord washes away the faults of both through his grace. For what is forgiven is no more; what is covered does not appear, and is therefore not reckoned.

Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven in baptism, or later melted and consumed by the fire of love, as in the case of that sinful woman whose many sins were forgiven because she loved much (Luke 7); and whose sins are covered by good works superimposed upon them. For everything that is covered is placed within, while that by which it is covered is drawn over it from above. Therefore, when we reject the evils that we have done and choose the goods that we do, we draw over the thing of which we are ashamed a kind of covering [the text reads: “we Jews”]. Thus sins are covered before God’s eyes [Col. 0647A] when good deeds are laid over them.

Or iniquity, called *anomia*, “without law,” may more properly concern Gentiles, because Gentiles were without the law. We may also understand the whole thing as occurring in baptism: iniquities are forgiven—that is, erased—and sins covered, so that they are no longer seen for punishment. Blessed also is that man to whom, when he believes, the Lord on account of his faith has not reckoned original sin or any other sin for punishment. For just as faith was reckoned to Abraham as righteousness, so also for every believer: when faith is reckoned as righteousness in baptism, sin is certainly not reckoned.

> “Does this blessedness, then, remain in circumcision only, or also in uncircumcision? For we say that faith was reckoned to Abraham as righteousness. How then was it reckoned? [Col. 0647B] In circumcision or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision. And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of faith which is in uncircumcision, that he might be the father of all who believe through uncircumcision, so that it might be reckoned to them also as righteousness; and that he might be the father of circumcision—not only of those who are of circumcision, but of those who follow the footsteps of the faith which is in the uncircumcision of our father Abraham.”

Since David says universally that the person whose iniquities or sins God freely forgives is blessed, does this blessedness of the promise of forgiveness of sins remain only in circumcision—that is, among Jews—or also in uncircumcision—that is, among Gentiles? That is, [Col. 0647C] since it is established that this blessedness is by faith through grace, the question now is in whom it resides: in Jews only, or in Gentiles also? I ask this because it is established concerning Abraham that he is righteous through faith. Since this is established, I ask in what state he was justified: after he was circumcised, or before. And as it is seen in him, so it may be believed concerning others.

This is the point: we ask whether this blessedness is also in uncircumcision because we say and all confess that Abraham’s faith was reckoned as righteousness—that is, he was justified by faith. How, then, was it reckoned as righteousness? In circumcision or in uncircumcision? That is, since all confess that he was justified through faith, let us see whether he was righteous because he was circumcised, or circumcised because he was found righteous. [Col. 0647D] His faith was not reckoned as righteousness in circumcision, but in uncircumcision. That is, he was justified through faith before he was circumcised. Therefore he was not justified on account of circumcision.

How, he says, was his faith reckoned? When he was in circumcision, or when he was in uncircumcision? If he had then been in circumcision, uncircumcision would indeed seem excluded from the grace of this faith. But at that time he was still in uncircumcision. And because, while in uncircumcision, he was justified through faith, he is rightly called the leader and father of all believers in uncircumcision.

He was justified in uncircumcision. Why then was he circumcised afterward? This was not done superfluously; rather, he received the sign of circumcision, not by which he became righteous, but by which he was shown to be righteous. He was justified through faith in uncircumcision, and afterward received [Col. 0648A] the sign of circumcision—that is, the outward circumcision which would be a sign of the inward. A sign is so called when, through what is seen, something else is indicated. Circumcision is therefore rightly called a sign in Abraham, because one thing was seen in it and another understood: for that fleshly circumcision was already then a sign of spiritual circumcision, which is received not in the flesh but in the heart. It was also such a sign as to be a seal: that is, it had a likeness to the thing sealed, so that, as the flesh of lust is stripped off, so one may be stripped of all the defilements of one’s first birth.

And because he had not yet said of what it was the sign, he adds: “of the righteousness of faith”—that is, which comes from faith. I mean faith “which is in uncircumcision”: that which Abraham himself possessed while he was in uncircumcision. Or *signaculum*, “seal,” means concealing a certain mystery. [Col. 0648B] A seal is spoken of when a safeguard is placed upon something to be preserved for a time, which no one except the one who affixed it ought to unseal. Thus, in Abraham’s circumcision a certain mystery was for a time enclosed, to be hidden from enemies and preserved for friends, after the pattern of a seal: namely, that just as a person from Abraham’s seed was commanded to be circumcised on the eighth day, so on the eighth day after the end of the seven days of the age all oldness and corruption would be removed from God’s elect.

Or this mystery was sealed in the fact that Abraham was first justified and afterward received circumcision, which was to be the seal of the righteousness of his faith: so that he might be father of believers through uncircumcision—that is, in uncircumcision—and father [Col. 0648C] of circumcision. For he became the father of both kinds: of those who are in uncircumcision through faith, and of those who are in circumcision through the flesh. We believe that this seal of Abraham will then be unsealed—that is, opened—when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered and all Israel is saved. For then it will be openly known that Abraham is father not only of Gentiles but also of circumcision through faith.

For this reason he was first justified in faith while still uncircumcised, and afterward commanded to be circumcised: so that he might be shown first to be the future father of many Gentiles, and afterward of those who would believe from among the circumcised. For those born from Abraham according to the flesh are not to be called Abraham’s children unless they possess Abraham’s faith and works. [Col. 0648D] This, therefore, was sealed in Abraham’s circumcision: that he might be father, that is, exemplar, of all who believe through uncircumcision—that is, in uncircumcision. For “through uncircumcision” is said in place of “in uncircumcision,” just as we commonly say “through that time” in place of “at that time”; or he may be father “through uncircumcision,” that is, through what was given him during the time of uncircumcision.

For if it had been given after circumcision, he would be said to have received this from circumcision. Through what he received in uncircumcision—that is, through faith—he is father of believers from the Gentiles, so that their belief too may be reckoned as righteousness: just as Abraham was justified by faith in uncircumcision, so they too may be justified by believing, although they have not put off uncircumcision. And he received circumcision in order to be father of circumcision—that is, of the Hebrews. For he was righteous first in uncircumcision so that he might be father of righteous uncircumcised persons [Col. 0649A]; and he remained righteous when circumcised so that he might become father of righteous circumcised persons.

He became father, I say, not only of those who are of fleshly circumcision—that is, Jews—but also of those circumcised in heart, not flesh—that is, Gentiles who follow the footsteps of Abraham’s faith: who imitate him in faith, believing as fully as he did. This faith “is in the uncircumcision of our father Abraham”: that is, it appears in our father Abraham while he is still in uncircumcision. He repeats “uncircumcision” so often in order to show that Gentiles are justified through faith in the same way as Jews.

> “For the promise to Abraham or to his seed—that he should be heir of the world—was not through the law, but through the righteousness of faith. For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith has been emptied [Col. 0649B] and the promise abolished. For the law works wrath; for where there is no law, neither is there transgression. Therefore it is from faith, so that the promise may be firm according to grace for all the seed: not only for the one who is of the law, but also for the one who is of Abraham’s faith, who is father of us all, as it is written: ‘I have made you father of many nations,’ before God whom you believed, who gives life to the dead and calls the things that are not as though they are” (Gen. 17).

Truly Abraham is the father of all believing Jews and Gentiles, because he attained this fatherhood through faith, not through the Law. For the promise was not made to him through the Law, since the Law did not yet exist. It was not through the Law, but through the righteousness of faith—that is, the righteousness which [Col. 0649C] he had obtained through faith—that the promise was made to Abraham and to his seed, that is, to Christ. This was the promise: that he himself should be heir of the world, that is, possessor of some persons from the whole world who would imitate him; and that in Christ, who was to be born from him, he should possess all things. Abraham is heir of the world, that is, he possesses the whole world through faith, because he is an example of faith to all, and all the saints are his children through faith. His seed also, that is, Christ, is heir—that is, Lord of the world according to royal authority—through whom blessing comes to Abraham’s children, and to whom the Father said: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. II), etc.

And these things were promised to Abraham and his seed, not through the Law, which did not yet exist [Col. 0649D], but through the faith by which he had believed God. And rightly so. For observance of the Law merely escapes punishment, whereas the merit of faith awaits the hope of the promised recompense. A command is imposed upon servants; faith is sought from friends.

Truly Abraham is heir of the world not through the Law but through faith, because if those who are of the Law—that is, carnal Jews—are heirs, that is, possessors of the inheritance which God promised to Abraham, then faith has been emptied, that is, rendered void and useless, since the Gentiles cannot through it inherit the heavenly homeland; and the promise of God has been abolished, that is, erased and made ineffective, by which it was said to Abraham: “In your seed,” that is, in Christ, “all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII), that is, they shall possess blessing as an inheritance. For if heirs were made only through the Law [Col. 0650A], as the Jews wished to maintain, the Gentiles, who lack the Law, would remain without the blessing of inheritance.

Therefore Abraham is not heir of the world through the Law, because neither are his children heirs through the Law, that is, possessors of the eternal inheritance. For if this were so, absurd consequences would follow: namely, that the faith through which he was justified and through which others are justified would be superfluous, since eternal inheritance could not be acquired through it; and that the divine promise, which promised that all nations would be blessed, would remain unfulfilled, because no Gentile would be blessed, and thus no one would be an heir.

And indeed inheritance does not come through the Law. For the Law rather works wrath, because it commands one who sins against it to be put to death at once, whether by stoning, by burning with fire, or by some other kind of punishment. The Law works wrath and [Col. 0650B] transgression. For transgression arises from it; without it, there is no transgression. For where there is no Law, neither is there transgression, that is, violation. Those, therefore, who have not received the Law may be called wicked, but they cannot be called transgressors. Both are judged according to their merits; yet God’s wrath is greater against transgressors, who know sin through the Law and nevertheless commit it. Thus inheritance cannot be had through the Law, but rather wrath.

Therefore heirs are heirs through faith. Through faith, which is a gift of mercy and justifies believers, inheritance is obtained, so that according to God’s grace—not according to human merits—the promise that God made to Abraham concerning the multiplication of children who would possess perpetual inheritance may be firm, that is, true and certain. For it would not be firm, but rather weak [Col. 0650C] and void, unless he himself fulfilled it through his grace. Therefore he promised it not by the power of our will but by his own predestination. For he promised what he himself was to do, not what human beings were to do. For although people do good things pertaining to the worship of God, he causes them to do what he commanded; they do not cause him to do what he promised. Otherwise, the fulfillment of God’s promises would lie not in God’s power but in human beings’; and what the Lord promised would be rendered to Abraham by them. But this cannot be so. Therefore his promises are fulfilled through God’s grace, freely bestowed upon us, while through the gift of his grace he causes us to believe and to work well, and thus to become heirs.

May the promise be firm for all [Col. 0650D] Abraham’s seed—that is, not for part of the seed but for all the seed. For the Jews wished it to be firm insofar as concerned themselves, and void insofar as concerned the Gentiles. But God did not promise in this way when he said: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed.” Let it be firm for all the seed, that is, for every people of believers who imitate Abraham—not only for the one who is of the Law, that is, who comes from the Old Testament to the New, but also for the one who is of Abraham’s faith, that is, who, without following a law promised to himself, follows the faith of Abraham, who is remembered as having been justified through faith without the Law.

He is father not of all human beings, but of all of us—that is, not only of those who descend from the Law, but also of those who succeed the Law through faith. He is father, that is, founder and example, both of believing circumcised persons and of believing uncircumcised persons. He is thus father [Col. 0651A] of believers, as it is written in Genesis, with the Lord saying: “I have made you a father,” that is, an author according to faith, not, I say, of Jews, but “of many nations” (Gen. XVII). And of many—not merely of some, but of all. If, therefore, he is promised that he will be father of many nations, he is rightly called father not only of those who come from circumcision, but also of those who believe from among the Gentiles.

For in his being called father of many nations, the pride of the Jews is confounded: he is father of Jews by flesh, but of Gentiles by faith. Here the Apostle rightly added, by his own interpretation, “before God in whom you believed,” signifying that faith in the inward person is before the sight of God, not displayed before human beings like carnal circumcision; and that through the same faith, not through [Col. 0651B] flesh, he is father of the nations whom he begot in faith before God’s eyes.

This God, as the Apostle adds, “makes the dead alive,” that is, through baptism raises Jews from the death of the soul; and “calls” to faith “things that are not,” that is, the Gentiles, concerning whom it is written: “All nations are as though they were not before him.” For he truly is the one who says: “I am who I am” (Exod. III). Whoever departs from him loses even being, so that he is rightly said not to be. Such were the nations while serving idols. But he calls things that are not as though they were—that is, he brings the Gentiles to faith, just as he does the Jews, who, because of their worship of the one God, are said to be.

Or let us understand all sinners, whether Gentiles or not, as the dead. For God also makes these alive through his grace, so that they may live by faith. And he calls things that are not [Col. 0651C] as though they were. For with him that which is to come about by his ordering has already been done, because it is said of him through the prophet: “He who made the things that are to come.” Those to whom the promise would be made did not yet exist when he spoke to Abraham, lest anyone should glory in merits. And those to whom it was promised were themselves also promised, so that the whole body of Christ may say: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (I Cor. XV).

For when God is said to call things that are not, only the grace of the caller appears, not any merit of those who did not yet even have being when they were called. “He chose us,” he says, “before the foundation of the world” (Eph. I). We were made in the world, and the world did not exist when we were chosen. Who is sufficient to explain this? Those who [Col. 0651D] are not are chosen; he who chose did not exist; nor did he choose in vain. Yet he chose, and he has those chosen whom he will create, to be chosen. He has them, however, with himself, not in his own nature but in his foreknowledge. Therefore it is rightly said that he calls things that are not as though they were.

But concerning Abraham it is added:

> “Who, against hope, believed in hope, that he might become the father of many nations, according to what was said to him: So shall your seed be” (Gen. XV), “as the stars of heaven and as the sand of the sea. And he was not weakened in faith, nor did he consider his own body as dead, when he was nearly a hundred years old, nor Sarah’s womb as dead. Nor did he hesitate in unbelief at God’s promise; rather, he was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, fully knowing that whatever he promised he is able [Col. 0652A] also to do. Therefore it was reckoned to him as righteousness; but also for our sake, to whom it shall be reckoned, if we believe in him who raised Jesus Christ our Lord from the dead, who was delivered up for our offenses and rose again for our justification.”

He begins to commend Abraham’s faith so that we may imitate it. For he had often already said that Abraham believed, and therefore now proceeds to show how and how firmly he believed. He believed in the hope of having a son by God’s promise, and this against the hope of his flesh, which was by nature already failing and cold—against hope, that is, against what he had previously hoped, namely that he would no longer beget a son—he believed, proceeding into hope, that is, so as to hope that he could beget a son because God promised it [Col. 0652B].

For while they were in vigorous age, he hoped according to nature to have offspring by his young wife, and he could not. But now he hoped the opposite: namely, that an old man by an old and barren woman would beget through God’s power. Thus, against the old hope, he believed in a new hope. For it is greater to hope contrary to something despaired of than simply to hope.

Abraham believed so that he might become father of many nations; that is, he believed so strongly that, as the reward of faith, he would receive a son by his wife, from whom the Hebrew people would descend, and from that people Christ would take flesh, in whom all nations would believe. For in this order Abraham became father of many nations. And this was in accordance with what was divinely said to him: “So shall your seed be, as the stars of heaven and as the sand [Col. 0652C] of the sea.” Not because as many persons were to proceed from him, either carnally or spiritually, as there are stars or grains of uncountable sand, but because those who were to be born from him, whether carnally or spiritually, would be as innumerable to human beings as the stars and the sand.

Mystically, however, the stars signify spiritual children who cleave to heaven and shine from above with the splendor of virtues; the sand signifies carnal Jews or Christians, lying low in heart and bearing no fruit of good work.

Abraham believed. And since he might have believed for a time and afterward failed, it is added that “he was not weakened in faith.” For he believed God who promised, and was not weakened, that is, debilitated, in that faith, although according to human reasoning he had many grounds for weakening [Col. 0652D]—namely, that neither he nor his wife was now fit for begetting children. Thus, in what he believed, he did not consider his body as dead—and truly dead, since he was nearly a hundred years old. And though he had lived so long, he did not attend to this; nor did he even consider Sarah’s womb as dead.

For Sarah was barren and had already ceased to have menstrual blood; on that account she could no longer bear, even if she had not been barren. Moreover, if a woman is of such advanced age that her customary monthly flow still occurs, she can bear by a young man, but not by an old man; although that old man may still be able to beget by a young woman, as Abraham could after Sarah’s death by Keturah, because he found her in the vigor of youth. This, therefore, is the remarkable thing the Apostle commends [Col. 0653A], and for this purpose he says that Abraham’s body was already dead: because at that age he could no longer beget by every woman who still retained some final capacity for childbearing. We must understand his body to have been dead in one respect, not in every respect. For if it were dead in every respect, it would be not the living body of an old man but the corpse of a dead man.

Sarah likewise was still more deprived of all powers of begetting. Yet Abraham considered none of these things when he heard God promising him offspring; but, attending to the power of the one who promised, he believed that nothing was difficult in the things which the Almighty promised. Thus he was trusting in the promise by which it was said to him: “He who shall come forth from your womb, him you shall have as heir”; or when he heard: “From Sarah I will give you a son, whom I will bless.”

Even at God’s repeated promise [Col. 0653B]—that is, when God promised him again, “Returning, I will come to you at this time, life accompanying me, and Sarah your wife shall have a son”—he did not hesitate in unbelief, that is, he did not doubt so as to distrust the fulfillment of the promises. Rather, he was strengthened in faith, that is, he was made altogether strong and steadfast in faith, giving glory to God. That is, he glorified God, who by the gift of his grace was to give him both a son contrary to nature from an old barren woman, and through that son, in Christ, a people of believers; fully, that is, with great perception of God’s truth and power, knowing that whatever he promised he is also able to do.

Therefore God makes those whom he has promised to be good such that they themselves do good. For he did not promise them to Abraham because he foreknew that they would be good by themselves. For if that [Col. 0653C] were so, what he promised would be theirs, not his. But Abraham did not believe in this way. Rather, he gave glory not to human merits but to God, fully believing that he was able also to do what he had promised. He does not say: “He is able to promise what he foreknew,” or “to show what he foretold,” or “to foreknow what he promised”; but: “He is able also to do what he promised.”

Therefore he himself makes good those who become good, and he himself causes those who persevere to persevere in goodness. For this is what God promises: what he himself does. He does not promise and then do something else. That is no longer promising, but predicting. We must beware, therefore, lest a human being exalt himself against God by saying that he does what God promised. For he who is able [Col. 0653D] to do what he promised brings about the faith of the Gentiles, as he had promised Abraham, and works every good thing in the saints.

Abraham believed these things in this way, and therefore it was reckoned to him as righteousness. Someone might say: What does it matter to us that Abraham believed and was justified through faith? This was his glory. And the Apostle says: He indeed was thus magnified through faith. Yet it was not written only for his sake—that is, for his praise and commendation—that his good faith was reckoned to him as righteousness; it was written also for our instruction, that we might gain growth in faith from that Scripture, understanding that if we believe God as he believed, faith will also be reckoned to us as righteousness, if we believe in him who raised Jesus from the dead—that is, separated him perpetually from the number of the dead, raising [Col. 0654A] him so that he would no longer return to corruption. This the Jews do not believe.

He raised him from the dead so that he might make us rise from the filth of vices. Jesus was delivered up to death so that we might be able to die to our offenses; and he rose again so that we might rise as righteous persons to the honorable life of virtues. For his death signifies the destruction of our old life, while his resurrection signifies the grace of a new manner of life. He was delivered into the hands of persecutors because our offenses were to be removed, lest we be delivered because of them into the hands of demons for torment. And, having destroyed the devil’s legal claim through death, he rose for our justification—that is, so that by justifying us he might raise us from the death of the soul, in order that we might live righteously, which otherwise we could not do.

He was delivered up for our offenses and rose again [Col. 0654B] for our justification. In his being delivered up, offense resounds; in his resurrection, righteousness resounds. Therefore let offense die, and righteousness rise.

## CHAPTER V

> “Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace toward God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we also have access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and glory in hope of the glory of the children of God. And not only this, but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces patience” (Jas. I), “and patience testing, and testing hope. But hope does not confound, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given [Col. 0654C] to us.”

Since it has hitherto been proved in many ways that a human being is justified not by works of the Law nor by the powers of free choice, but by faith, therefore we have been justified by faith, not by the Law nor by ourselves. And, being thus justified, let us have peace toward God—a peace which you do not have while you arrogate to one another a false justification, some through the Law and others through the powers of free choice.

It is as though he said: This disagreement, by which you glory in your merits as though you were justified through yourselves, is against God. But justification which comes through faith makes peace with God, because it drives out the hostile presumptions of human merits and humbly subjects the mind to God, while it recognizes that it is saved by grace alone. We have been justified by faith, yet freely; for faith itself is a gift of heavenly grace. And when faith obtains justification, no human merit precedes God’s grace; rather, grace itself merits increase, so that, having increased, it may also merit to be perfected—will following as an attendant, not leading as a guide, and not going before.

Thus, being justified, from now on let us have peace toward God, because we have been reconciled to him through the mediator Jesus. Let us no longer disagree with the divine will, but endeavor to have peace toward God through the Lord Jesus—that is, not through ourselves but through the help and grace of our reconciler. Through him we have not only the washing away of our oldness in his blood, so that we may thus rise to the clothing of righteousness and newness, but also access through him into this [Col. 0655A] grace—that is, into this freely given height of virtues—and this not through the Law but through faith.

That is to say: faith bestowed on us by grace obtains with God both forgiveness of offenses and perfection in every virtue. Through Christ, who is the door, we have gained access by faith into this grace—that is, into the observance of a good life—in which we stand; that is, we possess a state of uprightness, though we had fallen in Adam. For one who remains in vices does not stand, but lies cast down. Elijah, however, stood when he said: “The Lord lives, in whose presence I stand” (III Kings XVII; IV Kings IV). “We stand,” he says, “in this grace,” neither falling away from it nor departing from it; “and we glory in hope of the glory of the children of God,” that is, in our hope for the glory possessed by God’s children.

For what we hope for is so great that no one would dare presume it of himself, because it lies in God’s power alone for a human being to rise to the number of God’s children. And it is exceedingly great glory to be admitted, through faith and hope, into the number of God’s children. This is so great that, because of its very magnitude, it seems unbelievable to many: that we hope to attain the glory of God’s children.

And not only do we glory in the hope of this glory, but through Christ’s grace we also glory in tribulations, through which “we must enter the kingdom of heaven” (Acts XIV). We glory without danger of vanity in enduring tribulations, because we know how great a reward follows from them. This is what he proceeds to set forth by ascending step by step. We glory in tribulations because we know that tribulation produces in us [Col. 0655C] patience, that is, makes us patient. For no one can be patient except in adversity.

But patience produces testing, because one whose patience cannot be overcome is proved perfect. For many, before they experience tribulation, think themselves strong, yet fail in the actual trial and are shown to be weak; and many first think themselves weak, yet at the very moment of suffering appear most strong, while they overcome everything by enduring courageously. Thus patience produces testing, while it clearly reveals each person both to himself and to others, though before he began to suffer he was unknown both to himself and to others.

Testing, moreover, produces hope, because each person, from having been proved unconquerable through tribulations, begins to have hope—that is, certainty—of future glory. This appears vain to human reasoning but is confirmed by the testimony of virtue. For if someone who has not yet been proved hopes for a reward, he does not hope but presumes.

Now by the tribulations through which the patience of believers is tested we should understand not only those which happen externally—losses, illnesses, or any bodily torment—but also those which people inflict upon or endure within themselves, when, while at rest, they afflict and wear themselves down by resisting their pleasures and restraining desire, and by doing such things as pertain to the good of continence or abstinence. From these patience undoubtedly arises; when it has been made proven, it produces hope.

Hope is the expectation of future goods. It expresses the disposition of humility and the obedience of diligent service. It is not empty, because it does not confound—that is, it does not generate confusion for one who hopes in this way—because he obtains whatever he hoped for. For one is confounded in his hope who says: “I did not find what I hoped for.” But the person who has been proved through patience in temptations is not confounded in his hope, because the greatness of the reward he finds surpasses the greatness of his hope.

Hope does not confound because it is placed in God, who cannot deceive because he is true, not in a human being, who would deceive because he is false. It is placed in God, and therefore it follows: “because the love of God,” etc. Or thus: hope does not make one ashamed because it is fulfilled. And it is certain that it will be fulfilled because we already have the Holy Spirit as a pledge, through whom we also love abundantly [Col. 0656B].

And this is what is meant: because the love of God—that is, the love we have from God after we love God and our neighbor—has been poured out, that is, generously and abundantly bestowed, in our hearts. For where love is, how can there be narrowness? Narrowness is immediately excluded, and the heart is enlarged so that it may contain within itself so great an inhabitant, namely the Holy Spirit. For we cannot have love from ourselves, but from the Holy Spirit.

For when he had said, “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts,” lest anyone think that his love of God came from himself, he immediately added: “through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.” Therefore, in order that you may love God, let God dwell in you and love himself from you—that is, move you toward love of himself, kindle you, enlighten you, and stir you. “Through the Holy Spirit,” he says, “who has been given to us,” because he is both God and God’s gift.

And because of this rich inhabitant the Apostle did what he said above: “We glory in tribulations.” For how could he glory in them if he suffered poverty within? Outwardly there seemed to be constraints, but inwardly there was spaciousness. But what does an evil person do when he begins to suffer tribulation? He has nothing outside; all things have been taken away; in his conscience there is no consolation. There is no place to go out, because external things are harsh; there is no place to go in, because inward things are evil. He must be miserably tormented within himself, because he himself is his own torment. He is his own punishment, whom his conscience tortures.

But good people easily overcome whatever they suffer outwardly through inward consolation. And if in this life, where there are such great torments, good and righteous persons can, while suffering such things, not only endure with equanimity [Col. 0656D] but even glory in God’s love, what must be thought concerning that life promised to us, where we shall feel no bodily suffering at all?

> “For why did Christ, when we were still weak, die at the appointed time for the ungodly? For scarcely does anyone die for a righteous person. Yet perhaps someone may dare to die for a good person” (I Pet. III). “But God commends his love in us, because while we were still sinners, Christ died for us at the appointed time. Much more, therefore, now justified in his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him.”

Since God loves us—or since we love him through the Holy Spirit—our hope will be fulfilled. For unless this is so, Christ suffered in vain. And this is the meaning: Why did Christ die for the ungodly, that is, because of love for the ungodly, unless hope might be fulfilled?

Or thus: wishing more fully to show the virtues of the love which he had said was poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, the Apostle explains for what reasons it has been poured out in us, asserting that Christ died for the ungodly. For we were ungodly before we were converted to God through Christ. And Christ certainly accepted death for us before we believed. He undoubtedly would not have done this unless he had had an immense and most abundant love toward us—either Christ himself, by dying for the ungodly, or God the Father, by delivering up his only-begotten Son for the redemption of the ungodly [Col. 0657B].

Truly the love of God has been poured out in our hearts. For why did Christ die for us, except that God’s love might be poured out in us, so that we might love him who first loved us? “For why,” that is, for what other reason, did Christ die for us while we were still weak—that is, in need of a physician? For we were so gravely ill that we could not be healed except by the death of the physician.

He died “at the appointed time,” that is, not as others are held in death, but he endured death for us for a time, rising on the third day, lest we despair of his power, whose benevolence is apparent in his death. “He died,” he says, and this not for just anyone, but for the ungodly—that is, the foul, execrable, and wholly separated from God. He did something so great as to deem it worthy to die temporarily for such persons, in order to turn eternal death away from them.

From this the magnitude of his benefits appears: since we were loved so greatly by him without deserving it, we should consider how greatly we ought to love him, or whether we ought to prefer anything to him, since he, for us ungodly people, neither preferred his own life nor refused death. For we ought to love the merciful Lord even unto death, whom we know accepted the torment of death for ungodly servants. Here, too, human presumption is restrained, lest it attribute anything to its own merits.

And truly his goodness is wondrous, since he deigned to die for the ungodly. For scarcely does anyone die for a righteous person—that is, it is rare for anyone to die for a righteous person, much less for an ungodly one—because everyone hesitates to undergo death even when the cause of death is just. I say “rarely,” for perhaps one may be found who dares to die for a good person—that is, for a good thing or for a good man. It is as though he said: this is difficult to find, since the fear of death terrifies all things.

Or “righteous” may be understood as the righteousness of the Law, and “good” as the goodness of evangelical grace. Thus scarcely does anyone die for the righteous, because under the old Law, in which righteousness is found, scarcely a few were found who poured out their own blood in martyrdom. Yet perhaps someone may dare to die for the good, because in the New Testament, in which there is goodness and mercy, innumerable people arose who courageously surrendered their lives to death. Nevertheless, in comparison with carnal people and those who tremble to die for the Lord, they were so few that, because of their rarity, it is said of them [Col. 0658A], “perhaps someone may dare to die.” “Perhaps” is said because of those who do not yet dare to die; “someone,” because of the rarity of those who dare, although they are innumerable.

Some, however, interpret it thus: If he died for us while we were ungodly and sinners, how much more ought we, without any doubt, to die for the righteous and good? But we should not suppose that “righteous” and “good” are different, or that either properly signifies a person; rather, they signify absolutely a righteous and good cause, for which, though with difficulty, someone may sometimes be found to shed his blood. Scarcely does anyone die for the righteous and good.

But our Lord died for the ungodly and sinners, in which a more praiseworthy love shines forth. For our merits had not preceded, on account of which the Son of God would die; rather, because there were no merits, mercy was great.

Someone might say: Since God is omnipotent and could have delivered us in other ways, why did he wish his Son to die for us? To this the Apostle replies: God did not do this without reason, but in this manner commends his love in us. When something is repaid though undeserved, love is commended. And what is so undeserved as that the merciful Lord, without sin, should die for sinful, ungodly servants? And the Father’s love is commended to us in this, that he so loved us.

Why then should Christ’s death not have happened? Indeed, why, passing over countless other means by which the Almighty could have used to deliver us, should he not especially have chosen this means, in which nothing in his divinity was changed and such a benefit was bestowed on human beings through the humanity he assumed: that the undeserved temporal death should be rendered by the Son of God, because he would free them from the deserved eternal death?

For the devil held our sins, and through them he justly held us in death. He released them to one who had none of his own, and he unjustly brought him to death. For that blood had such power that one clothed with Christ ought not to be held in the deserved eternal death by one who killed Christ, though only for a time, by an undeserved death.

Therefore God the Father commends his immense love in us, because while we were still sinners, and nothing but punishment was due to us, Christ accepted the penalty of death for us in order to save us from the torment of perpetual death. Therefore, what does he reserve for the righteous but his life, who gave his death to sinners? For it is more incredible that the eternal one died than that the mortal should live eternally. We already hold what is more incredible. If God died for a human being, will not a human being live with God? Will not the mortal live eternally, for whose sake he who lives eternally died?

Yet he died only in the flesh. He died for us sinners. Therefore much more will he save those who have been justified. For he who has done what is greater and more difficult will much more easily do what is lesser and easier. For it is harder to die for sinners and take away sins than to save the righteous who cooperate. Therefore much more shall we who have been justified—that is, freed from all sins—now, that is, in this time of grace, in his blood shed without guilt for our sins [Col. 0659A], be saved from wrath, that is, from the punishment of eternal condemnation, through him, the mediator and reconciler.

> “For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved in his life. And not only this, but we also glory in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.”

Truly, we shall be saved from wrath through him. For if, while we were enemies—that is, opposed to God through love of wickedness—we were reconciled, that is, brought back into peace with God through the death of his Son, then much more, now that we have been reconciled, shall we be saved in his life; because the life which he now possesses according to his humanity [Col. 0659B], we too shall possess. We who were reconciled through death shall be saved in life. For he gave his death for us, and we were reconciled, having been made estranged and enemies through transgression. For no one is reconciled except from enmity. The transgression of our first parent made us enemies of God. Those whom he had above called sinners he now calls enemies of God; those whom he had above called justified in Christ’s blood he now calls reconciled to God through the death of his Son; and those whom he had above called saved from wrath through him he now calls saved in his life. Therefore, before this grace, we were not sinners in merely some fashion, but were in such sins that we were enemies of God. Yet we were reconciled to him through the death of his Son [Col. 0659C]. How through death? When he was angry with us, did he see the death of his Son for us and become appeased toward us? Was his Son then already so far appeased toward us that he deigned even to die for us, while the Father was still so angry that, unless the Son died for us, he would not be appeased? No. For it was said above: “But God commends his love toward us, in that, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” Therefore the Father had love toward us even when, exercising hostility against him, we served sins. And later in this epistle it is said: “If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare even his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8). Would he [Col. 0659D], then, if he were not appeased toward us, deliver up his Son for us? For it was truly said to him that “you hate nothing that you have made” (Wisdom 11 [the source cites ch. 2]). Yet it was nevertheless truly said to him: “You hate all who work iniquity” (Ps. 5). Accordingly, in a wondrous way he both loved us and hated us. He loved us as he himself had made us; he hated us as we had made ourselves through the working of iniquity. And by a certain justice of God, the human race had been delivered into the power of the devil: the sin of the first man passing originally to all born through the union of both sexes, and the debt of the first parents binding all their descendants. If, therefore, the commission of sins subjected man to the devil through God’s just wrath, then surely the remission of sins, through God’s gracious reconciliation [Col. 0660A], rescues man from the devil.

For God’s wrath is not a disturbance of mind, as it is in man; rather, his wrath is called just vengeance. And although just divine vengeance has received such a name, so too is there a reconciliation of God—which cannot be rightly understood except when such wrath comes to an end. Nor were we enemies of God otherwise than sins are enemies of justice. When these sins are forgiven, such enmities end, and those whom he justifies are reconciled to the Just One. Yet he certainly loved them even as enemies, since he delivered up his Son for them while they were still enemies. Therefore, that we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son must not be understood as though the Son reconciled us to him in order that he might begin to love those whom he hated—just as one enemy is reconciled to another so that afterward they become friends and mutually love [Col. 0660B] one another, though they had mutually hated one another. Rather, we were reconciled to one who already loved us, although on account of sin we were at enmity with him.

And through this reconciliation we were rescued from the devil, who had to be overcome not by God’s power but by justice. For what is more powerful than omnipotence, or what creature’s power can be compared with his? But since, through the fault of his own perversity, the devil has become a lover of power and a deserter and assailant of justice—and human beings imitate him especially in this—God was pleased that the devil should be conquered not by power but by justice, so that human beings too, imitating Christ, might seek to conquer the devil by justice rather than by power.

What, then, is the justice by which the devil was conquered [Col. 0660C] by Christ? It is this: although he found in Christ nothing deserving death, he nevertheless killed him. And surely it is just that the debtors whom he held should be released when they believe in him whom he killed though he had no debt at all. This is what is meant when we are said to be justified in Christ’s blood. For that innocent blood was shed for the remission of our sins. This is what is meant when we are said to be reconciled to God through the death of his Son. For when our sins are forgiven, enmities end, and we attain peace with God, from whom sins alone separated us. Thus, reconciled through his death, we shall much more be saved in his life—we who had perished in our own life. For if his death had such power as to accomplish what was more difficult, then his life, that is, his resurrection and glory, will be able to accomplish that in which [Col. 0660D] there is less difficulty. And not only shall we be saved in the future, but we also glory in hope in God—that is, in considering that we shall be with God in that glory. Or, we glory not in ourselves but in God, and not through ourselves but through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now, already in the present life, received reconciliation, according to what has been discussed above.

> “Therefore, just as through one man sin entered into this world, and death through sin, and thus passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned. For until the law sin was in the world. But sin was not imputed when there was no law. Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not [Col. 0661A] sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is a figure of the one to come.”

He now begins to argue at greater length concerning two men: the first, Adam, through whose sin and death we and his descendants have been bound, as it were, by hereditary evils; and the second Adam, who is not only man but also God. Since he paid for us what he did not owe, we have been freed from both ancestral and personal debts. Accordingly, because the devil held all who were begotten through the corrupted flesh of that one man in concupiscence, it is just that, on account of this one man, he should release all who are spiritually regenerated through his spotless grace. For since the Apostle had said that we are reconciled to God through Christ, he proceeds to show how fittingly [Col. 0661B] we are reconciled through one obedient man, having been separated from God through one disobedient man. We received reconciliation through Christ; therefore—that is, because we are reconciled through him—just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, so, understand, righteousness has been restored through one redeemer, and life through righteousness.

Through the one man who first sinned, original sin entered this miserable world—that is, the entire human race—because, by sinning, he corrupted all his offspring in himself as in a root. Thus whatever offspring should be born from the wife, jointly condemned with him, through whom he had sinned, would draw original sin through carnal concupiscence, in which a corresponding punishment was repaid to the disobedient. For just as Christ, in whom all shall be made alive, besides offering himself as an example of righteousness to those who imitate him, also gives to believers the most hidden grace of his Spirit—which he secretly infuses even into baptized infants—so Adam, in whom all die, besides being an example for imitation to those who voluntarily transgress the Lord’s command, also corrupted within himself all who would come from his stock by the hidden contagion of his carnal concupiscence [Col. 0661C]. For the sin understood here is that of generation, not imitation. For just as the beginning of sin came from the woman, so the beginning of generation is from the man. The man first sows, in order that the woman may give birth. Therefore sin entered the world through one man because it entered through the seed of generation, which the woman receives from the man and conceives. This work, chaste within marriage, entails no fault; but the origin of sin carries with it its due punishment. For a husband is not immortal because he is a husband, nor is he mortal for any reason other than sin. Thus through one man sin entered into the world, and death through sin, because, if man had not sinned, he would never have died. And thus sin, or death, passed into all human beings, so that no one born of man and woman was free from sin and death.

For the word “passed” must be noted. This is why an infant is guilty: he has not yet committed sin, but he has contracted it. For that sin did not remain in its fountainhead, but passed into all who were born through corrupted flesh. “In whom,” that is, in the first man, all sinned [Col. 0662A], because when he sinned, all were in him, and the whole mass of the human race was infected in him with the poison of sin. Likewise, in Christ all who believe in him are justified through the hidden communion and inspiration of spiritual grace, because whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit with him. And just as through the sin of the first man, which passed into all, we lost life, so through the righteousness of the second man, which is poured out upon all who become his members, we shall recover life.

I said that sin passed into all, and I spoke truly. For from Adam until the law, original sin was in all. I do not prove concerning the Jews that they were under original sin, because they had the law and could recognize through the law that they were under it; but I speak of [Col. 0662B] those who lived before the law and did not know original sin. For until the law of Moses, that sin was throughout the whole world. It was indeed present, but it was not imputed; that is, no such sin was thought to exist within the soul when there was no law to disclose the fall of the first man, from whom that sin had been propagated. Therefore that sin passed into all, because it existed even before the law, when it was not so perceived, since the law did not teach it.

Or thus: since the Jews might wish to say that righteousness and life were restored through the law rather than through Christ, as the Apostle taught, the Apostle shows that righteousness could not be restored through the law, which was unable to remove sin. For until the law—that is, as long as the law remained—original sin was in the world; that is, it was not erased by the law. This “until” is not restrictive but inclusive, as when it is said: “and life for evermore” (Ps. 133 [the source cites Ps. 132]). Sin was until the law because not even the law could remove it; the law entered in so that sin might abound still more—whether the natural law, in which each person, once capable of reason, begins to add personal sins to original sin; or the law itself, written and given to the people through Moses [Col. 0662C].

Therefore, when he says that sin was in the world until the law, it is not said because sin did not exist afterward, but because what could be removed only by the Spirit of grace could not be removed through the letter of the law. Therefore, lest anyone, trusting in the powers not, I say, of his will, but rather of his vanity, should suppose that the law could suffice for free choice and should ridicule Christ’s grace, the Apostle says that sin was in the world until the law. And he added: “But sin was not imputed when there was no law.” He did not say, “It was not,” but, “It was not imputed”; that is, it was unknown and was not considered to be sin. For it was not regarded by the Lord God as though it did not exist; rather, it was unknown to blind human beings because there was no law to demonstrate and convict it—whether the law of reason in infants or the written law among the people.

Before the law, sin was not imputed; but death reigned, the devil securely possessing human beings because they believed themselves unpunished, until Moses, through whom knowledge of the one God returned. For previously people either did not know God or did not think that he cared what they had done [Col. 0663A]. But when the law was given, they knew that God cared for human affairs and judged them. “Death,” he says, “reigned from Adam to Moses”; that is, from the first man even to the law itself, divinely promulgated, because not even it could remove death’s reign, and death certainly reigns only through sin. By “the reign of death” he means the condition in which the guilt of sin so rules human beings that it does not permit them to attain eternal life, which is true life, but draws them even to the second death, which is eternally penal. In any person this reign of death is destroyed only by the Savior’s grace, which also worked in the ancient saints—whoever, before Christ came in the flesh, nevertheless belonged to his aiding grace and not to the letter of the law, which could only command and could not help.

But when he says “until Moses,” that is, until the end of the law and the beginning of grace, that death reigned, he speaks in the same manner in which we say, for example, “the Huns lasted until Attila.” We do not designate the beginning of his reign but its end. Thus “until Moses” means until the end of the law and the beginning of grace: the plague, widely spread through the world, reigned because the physician was absent. But when the physician came from heaven, death lost its power. Therefore death reigned in all from Adam until Moses who were not aided by Christ’s grace; in them death’s reign was not destroyed. Truly, it reigned in all, even in those who had not sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression—that is, those who had not yet sinned by their own [Col. 0663B] and personal will as he did, but had contracted original sin from him. Since they had not yet been born and did not yet use the reason which he used when he sinned, nor had received the command that he transgressed, they were held bound by original corruption alone, through which death’s reign drew them to condemnation, which is to be slain in Gehenna.

It can also be understood thus. Having said, “Death reigned even over those who did not sin,” as though warning us why it reigned over those who had not sinned, he adds, “in the likeness of Adam’s transgression”; that is, because in the members of these persons there was a likeness of Adam’s transgression. “Who is a figure of the one to come,” because he imposed upon his descendants the pattern of death. For in him was established the pattern of condemnation for future descendants [Col. 0663C] who would be created from his progeny: that they should be born from one man into condemnation, from which only the Savior’s grace frees them.

Or Adam is a figure of the one to come, that is, of Christ, partly by similarity and partly by contrast. By similarity: just as Adam was made by God without a father from virgin earth, so Christ was created by God from the virgin Mary without seed. Just as Adam is father of all according to the flesh, so Christ is father according to faith. Adam slept so that Eve might be made; Christ died so that the Church might be made. Eve was made for sleeping Adam from his side; when Christ was dead, his side was pierced with a lance so that the sacraments by which the Church might be formed should flow forth. Adam is also a figure of Christ by contrast: just as through Adam’s disobedience many were made sinners, so through Christ’s obedience [Col. 0664A] many may be made righteous. And as all die in Adam, so all shall be made alive in Christ. For just as Adam ate at the devil’s urging, and all born from him are consigned to death, so Christ fasted, and all reborn through him are restored to eternal life. Just as Adam could communicate sin and death to his children, so Christ communicates his righteousness and life to his own. Just as Adam is father of the present age and prince of discord, so Christ is Father of the age to come and Prince of Peace (Isa. 9). But the gift is not like the trespass.

> “For if many died through one man’s trespass, much more did the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abound for many. And the gift is not like that which came through one sin. For judgment indeed came from one trespass to condemnation; but grace, from many trespasses, to justification. For if death reigned through one by the trespass of one, much more shall those who receive abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one, Jesus Christ. Therefore, as through one man’s trespass came condemnation to all human beings, so through one man’s righteousness comes justification of life to all human beings. For as through one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one many shall be made righteous.”

By these words the Apostle explains how Adam is a figure of Christ by contrast, and how the same figure [Col. 0664C] is not alike in every respect. For they are indeed similar by contrast; yet they differ in this, that Adam’s trespass is not like Christ’s gift, because Christ confers more good than Adam inflicted evil. Christ and Adam are similar, but the trespass is not like the gift; that is, Adam’s sin is not as effective for condemnation as Christ’s grace is for salvation. Although trespass and gift are alike in this: just as trespass works discord between us and God, and finally death in us, so the gift works reconciliation and eternal blessedness; and just as sin entered all through one man, and death through sin, so the gift comes to all through one and life through the gift. Yet they differ in this: trespass [Col. 0664D] works temporal death in all, while the gift works everlasting life. Thus Christ bestows more upon those regenerated than Adam harmed those generated.

And truly the gift is greater and more powerful than the trespass. For if one man’s trespass had such power and efficacy as to lead many into death, much more did the grace of God abound—that is, the remission of sins which God freely gives without any preceding human merit—and the gift, that is, the bestowal of virtues. This grace and gift, I say, abounded in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ—that is, in the perfection of virtues which is in the man Christ—and it abounded for many, that is, it came abundantly to all his own. Grace does not pass to more people than trespass, for more are not justified than condemned, since the wicked are far more numerous. But “for many” is said as if one said, “not for a few.” For those upon whom this grace overflows are not few, but many. And it abounds much more than trespass, because all who are freed through Christ die temporally on account of Adam, but on account of Christ himself they will live without end.

Moreover, when he said, “If many died through the trespass of one,” in saying “many” and not “all,” he indicated that he was speaking of those in whom Adam’s trespass effected death of the soul. But the grace of God abounded much more, because the first parent transmitted one trespass to all, whereas Christ by his grace removed not only that original sin in which people are born but also those trespasses which they added by their own will, and gave justification and eternal life. And the gift of grace, granted after one [Col. 0665A] sinner, is not like the condemnation that came through one sinner, because the gift is greater than the trespass.

He had shown that trespass and gift differ in effect, because trespass produced death whereas the gift produced life. Now again he shows that they differ in another manner: the gift of grace through the one Christ who gives is not merely as great, but more abundant, as was the trespass through the one Adam who sinned. “The figure,” he says, “is unequal not only in this, that Adam harmed temporally those whom Christ redeemed eternally, but also because, unless they are redeemed by Christ, Adam’s descendants are delivered to condemnation through his one trespass; whereas Christ’s redemption also dissolves many trespasses that have been added to the original sin.” And this is indeed so. For judgment—that is, the sentence [Col. 0665B] of the divine judgment—leads from Adam’s one trespass to condemnation; but grace, that is, God’s freely given gift, freeing from many trespasses in baptism, leads to justification, because it not only forgives but also justifies.

Therefore he said, “Judgment from one trespass to condemnation,” because it would suffice for condemnation even if human beings had no sin except original sin. For although the condemnation of those who have added personal sins to original trespass is more severe, and is more severe for each person in proportion as that person has sinned more grievously, nevertheless even that which alone has been contracted originally not only separates from God’s kingdom but also makes persons strangers to salvation and eternal life. Nor can there be any other salvation and eternal life outside the kingdom of God, into which only fellowship with Christ brings one. Thus, from Adam, in whom we all sinned, we contracted not all our sins but only original sin; but from Christ, in whom we are all justified, we obtain forgiveness not only of that original sin but also of the other sins that we ourselves add [Col. 0665C].

Therefore the gift is not like one sin. For judgment from one unremitted trespass—that is, original sin—can already lead to condemnation; but grace, after many trespasses have been forgiven, that is, not only original sin but also all the rest, leads to justification. For all those who were to become many in themselves from that one man were nevertheless one in him. Accordingly, that sin would have belonged to him alone if no one had come forth from him. But because common nature was in him, no one is free from its corruption. Yet Christ’s grace alone frees from it, and this grace is given not according to human merits but freely, because God is merciful. It is not given to all, because God is judge; and by his just judgment, in some people is shown what grace bestows upon those to whom it is given. Let us therefore not be ungrateful to him who, according to the good pleasure of his will, frees so many from so deserved a ruin that, if he freed no one from it, he would not be unjust. Rather, let those who are freed love grace, and let those who are not freed acknowledge their due. If goodness appears in remitting a debt and equity in exacting it, let those who are freed praise mercy; let those who are punished not blame judgment [Col. 0665D].

He had said that grace, cleansing us from many trespasses, justified us; and now he accordingly adds that through the remission of those trespasses and the attainment of righteousness we shall not only live but also reign, and this through Jesus Christ. But he first presents, as it were, a proof of this: if we were dying in Adam’s sin, much more shall we live in Christ’s grace. And this is the meaning: God’s grace, freeing us from many trespasses and justifying us, saves us from the condemnation of the rest; through this grace we shall reign. For death, passing from one into the rest, reigned by trespass—that is, on account of the trespass of one—meaning that it powerfully obtained the kingdom of killing all. Or it reigned through one, because it acquired its rule in all in such a way that it had the beginning of its kingdom in the one who first sinned. Or through one, as we have said, it came into the rest, because it exercised upon all descendants the power which it had in him [Col. 0666A].

And if death so reigned through one in the trespass of one, then much more shall those reign through the one Christ who receive—that is, who possess not from themselves but from God—the abundance of grace, namely abundant remission of sins, because not only original but also actual sins are forgiven; and the abundance of the gift, that is, spiritual charisms; and righteousness, that is, good action. These persons, I say, who receive these things from God, shall reign through the one Jesus Christ. They shall reign much more than death reigned in them, because they shall reign eternally whereas death reigned temporarily. Thus, because of one man’s trespass, death reigned through one: all were held in the bond of death in that one in whom all sinned, even if they added no personal sins. Otherwise death would not reign through one because of one trespass, but through each person who sinned because of the trespasses of many.

But they receive abundance of grace, gift, and righteousness because the grace of forgiveness destroys not only the sin in which all sinned, but also the sins which they have added; and so great a righteousness is bestowed on them that, when Adam yielded to the one persuading him to sin, they do not yield even to one compelling them. They shall reign much more in life, because in eternal life they shall reign without end, more than death reigned in them temporarily and with an end [Col. 0666B].

“Therefore, as through one man’s trespass,” and so forth. Since he had inserted much pertaining to the proposed proof, showing that the gift is more efficacious and more abundant than trespass, he repeats the antecedent in order fittingly to infer the consequent itself. This is the sense: since, through the trespass of one passing into all human beings, human beings came to condemnation, therefore through the righteousness of one passing into all human beings, they come to justification, which is the cause of everlasting life. And just as the former happened, so the latter happens; that is, as fittingly as the former, so fittingly the latter.

Or thus: since Adam is a figure of Christ, and since Christ’s gift is greater and confers more, therefore just as through the trespass of one passing into all human beings, persons justly came to condemnation of body and soul, so by a just judgment through the righteousness of one coming into all the elect, persons come to justification, so that they may be justified through participation in Christ’s righteousness [Col. 0666C]. This justification is the cause of life, just as condemnation is the cause of eternal death. Just as trespass alone, without actual sin, cast all into condemnation and thus into death, so, without any preceding work of ours, Christ’s grace brought us to justification and thus to eternal life.

For he means that justification by which Christ justifies the ungodly. This justification passes into all human beings, not because all human beings come to the grace of Christ’s justification, since so many who are alienated from it die eternally, but because all who are reborn into justification are reborn only through Christ, just as all who are born into condemnation are born only through Adam. For no one is in that generation apart from Adam, and no one is in this regeneration apart from Christ. Therefore “all” and “all” are said. For if some could be generated in the flesh otherwise than through Adam, and others spiritually regenerated otherwise than through Christ, they would not plainly be called “all” in either case. The same “all,” however, he afterward calls “many.” For in some respect all may be few. But carnal generation has many, and spiritual generation also has many, although this spiritual generation has not as many as carnal generation [Col. 0666D]. Yet just as the former contains all human beings, so the latter contains all righteous human beings; for as no one is a human being apart from the former, so no one is a righteous human being apart from the latter, and in each there are many.

Concerning these he adds: “For as through disobedience,” and so forth. The Apostle specifies the trespass of one and the righteousness of one, so that just as Adam destroyed many by the merit of sin, so Christ may be seen to have freed them by the merit of righteousness. Truly, just as the trespass of one condemned all, so the righteousness of one justifies all.
