For as through the disobedience of the one first man, which is his trespass, many—that is, all who were born from him—were made sinners, having contracted original sin from him, so through the obedience of the one man Christ many shall be made righteous; that is, they shall be justified by faith in his incarnation and passion, in which he was obedient unto death. Therefore he here calls Christ man, though he is also God, lest anyone suppose that even the ancient righteous could have been justified by Christ only as God—that is, through the Word which was in the beginning—and not also through faith in his incarnation, by which he is also man.

Here ends the discussion concerning the two men, Adam and Christ: the one brought us sin and death; the other restored righteousness and life [Col. 0667A]. It follows:

> “But the law entered in, so that trespass might abound. But where trespass abounded, grace superabounded, so that, as sin reigned in death, so grace might reign through righteousness unto eternal life, through Jesus Christ our Lord.
>
> **CHAPTER VI.**
>
> What, then, shall we say? Shall we remain in sin so that grace may abound? By no means! For how shall we who have died to sin still live in it?”

Previously he had said that until the Law sin was in the world; by this he meant not only original sin but every sin. And therefore it was until the Law [Col. 0668B], because not even the Law could remove it. “Until the Law” is said so that this statement may include the Law itself, just as it is said in the Gospel: “All the generations from Abraham until David are fourteen generations” (Matt. I). The number is not completed by excluding David, but by counting him as well. Thus the Law is not outside the continuance of sin, which was said to have existed until the Law itself. Indeed, as is now said, “the Law entered in, that the offence might abound.” For sin or offence had entered the world from the beginning, but the Law entered in—that is, it entered at a subsequent time—not in order that the offence might be ended through it, but that it might abound through transgression. For the Law, whether we understand the natural law, which appears in the ages of those who are already able to use reason [Col. 0668C], or the written law given through Moses, could not give life or free men from the law of sin and death derived from Adam; rather, it added an increase of transgression. For where there is no law, neither is there transgression. Therefore, after the law given in Paradise was transgressed, man is born from Adam with the law of sin and death, of which it is said: “I see another law in my members” (Rom. VII), etc. Yet unless this is afterward strengthened by evil habit, it is more easily overcome, though not without God’s grace.

But when the other law is transgressed—the law operative in the exercise of the rational soul’s reason, at the age when a human being already uses reason—all sinners on earth become transgressors. And when the Law also given through Moses is transgressed, the offence abounds much more. Therefore the Law entered in that the offence might abound, whether people neglect what God commands, or whether, presuming upon their own strength, they do not seek the help of grace and add pride to weakness. Those who are such do not know the dispensation according to which the Law was given. For the Law was not given which could give life, since grace gives life through faith. Rather, the Law was given to show by how many bonds of sins they were bound, since they presumed upon their own strength to fulfill righteousness. Thus it did not lessen sins but added to them. Yet it was not given for this effect; rather, this happened through human perversity. For sin thus abounded not through a fault in the Law, but through their fault: concupiscence was made more ardent by prohibition, and to those sinning against the Law was added [Col. 0669A] the crime of transgression.

Therefore let not the Jews glory in the Law, since they were not justified by it, but burdened with a more abundant offence; and so let them humble themselves the more and flee to implore Christ’s grace, through which they may be freed and healed from the sin of transgression. For the offence abounded through the Law. But the Jews who came to Christ are not therefore to be despised; for where—that is, in those in whom—the offence abounded, because, having received the Law, they sinned not ignorantly but knowingly, there—that is, in them—the grace of God superabounded. That is, it abounded and multiplied its gifts so greatly as altogether to erase the offence and to be superior and greater than the offence had been. It superabounded because it perfects even those whom the devil could not conquer; and the offence was for a time, whereas grace is forever.

Thus grace superabounded, so that, just as sin reigned unto death—including sin which people did not derive from Adam but added by their own will—so grace also might reign through righteousness unto eternal life. Yet there is no righteousness apart from Christ, just as there are some sins apart from Adam. Therefore, when he had said, “As sin reigned unto death,” he did not add here, “through one,” or “through Adam,” because above he had also spoken of that sin which abounded when the Law entered in, and this surely is not from origin, but already from one’s own will. But when he had said, “So grace may reign through righteousness unto eternal life,” he added, “through Jesus Christ our Lord,” because by carnal generation only that which is original sin is transmitted; but by spiritual regeneration [Col. 0669C] there is remission not only of original sin but also of voluntary sins.

Thus grace superabounded, so that, just as sin reigned unto death—that is, just as actual sin prevailed and was effective in leading people into death—so grace, that is, the remission of sins and the accumulation of virtues, may reign, that is, prevail and powerfully accomplish its entire will in us, through righteousness—that is, through our subsequent good action—leading us into eternal life, not through ourselves nor through the Law, but through Jesus Christ. After this he puts to himself a question that another might have raised, and removes what might be objected. As though he said: Since I said above that where sin abounded, grace superabounded, what then shall we say from this? “Shall we remain in sin, that grace may abound in us,” that is, that we may obtain an abundance of grace? God forbid that we should now remain in it! For we who are already dead to sin—that is, who through baptism have already been extinguished to sin—how shall we still live in it? To obey the desires of sin is to live to sin. But when grace has granted that we should die to sin, what else do we do, if we live in it, but show ourselves ungrateful to grace? For one who praises the benefit of medicine does not commend the diseases and wounds from which it heals a person; rather, the more medicine is extolled, the more wounds and diseases are condemned. So the praise and proclamation of grace is the reproach and condemnation of offences.

[Col. 0670A] “Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness.”

We are dead to sin through baptism, which we received into Christ’s death (Eph. IV; Col. III)—and do you not know this? Do you not know that all of us, whether slaves or free, little children or adults, who were baptized—that is, immersed and washed—into Christ Jesus, that is, in Christ’s name, were baptized into his death? It is as if he said: Do you not know the sacrament of baptism itself? For we are baptized into Christ’s death so that, believing in and imitating his death, we may live as though dead [Col. 0670B]. Since we are dead to sin through baptism, we ought not to live to it again, so that it would be necessary to die to it again. For we have been baptized into Christ’s death—that is, into the likeness of Christ’s death—so that, just as he died once and lives forever, we too, having died once to evil, may live forever to good.

For just as a dead person cannot sin, so we too have died together with Christ and ought not to be entangled in deadly sins. For one who has been crucified does nothing but await the hour of death and commend his spirit to God; he desires nothing further in this world. For just as Christ’s feet and hands were fastened to the cross so that they could not move in any direction, so our hands and feet ought to be bound by imitation of his death, so that they cannot move toward sin. And thus we should understand Christ’s baptism as nothing other than a likeness of Christ’s death; and Christ’s death upon the cross as nothing other than a likeness of the remission of sin: so that, as in him there was a true death, so in us there may be a true remission of sins; and as in him there is a true resurrection, so in us there may be a true justification.

And if we are shown to be dead to sin because we have been baptized into Christ’s death, then surely little children baptized into Christ die to sin, because they are baptized into his death. For without exception it has been said: “All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death.” And this was said to prove that we are dead to sin. But to what sin do little children die in being born again, except that which they contracted in being born? Or we are baptized into Christ’s death because his death is the cause of this purification. Truly we are baptized into Christ’s death—that is, in baptism we are made like his death—because we are also buried with him through baptism.

For as no living person can be buried with a dead person, so no one who still lives in sin can be buried together with Christ in baptism. We are buried with him through baptism so that, as he was buried in body, our sin may lie hidden and be buried in the tomb of water. As he lay in the tomb for three days, so we are immersed three times in the tomb of baptism. For in being immersed a third time we signify the mysteries of the three-day burial; and in being brought out of the waters a third time, the resurrection of the three-day period is represented [Col. 0671A]. We are buried in that element of water so that, renewed through the Holy Spirit, we may rise again. For in water there is an image of death; in the Spirit, a pledge of life. Thus through water the body of sin dies, water enclosing the body as in a kind of tomb, so that through the power of the Spirit we may be renewed from the death of sin.

We are buried with him through baptism, and this “into death,” that is, into the destruction of vices, so that vices may be dead in us after the example of his death. For this purpose we have died together and been buried, so that, as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too, rising from vices to good works, may advance from good to better in newness of life. That is, as the Father is glorified through the resurrection of the Son, so he may be glorified through the newness of our conduct. Newness [Col. 0671B] of life is where we put off the old man with his deeds and put on the new man, who was created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth.

“For if we have been made planted together with the likeness of his death, we shall likewise be of his resurrection, knowing this: that our old man was crucified together with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that we might no longer serve sin (Eph. IV; Col. III). For he who has died has been justified from sin. But if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live together with him.”

We ought to walk in newness of life after the example of Christ’s resurrection, so that we may lead a new and incorruptible manner of life and no longer be corrupted by the rot of vices. For if we have been made “planted together,” that is, torn away from the old manner of life and transferred into a new way of living, adhering to the likeness of his death—that is, imitating his death to the extent of our ability, that we may abstain from the sin which he wholly lacked—we are at the same time planted together with the likeness of his resurrection.

A tree that is planted dies before it grows; once dead, it is made alive; and once made alive, it bears fruit. So also Christ, who according to Solomon is the tree of life (Prov. II), was torn away from the present age, died, and, made alive through resurrection, grew over the whole breadth of the world, in which he bears much fruit. But it should be noted that the Apostle did not say, “If we have been planted together with his death,” but “with the likeness of his death.” For Christ died once [Col. 0671D] to sin—that is, to the flesh—in such a way that he committed no sin at all. But because he died that death, we cannot die to sin so as to know sin altogether no more; nevertheless, we can have its likeness, so that by imitating him we abstain from sin. For human nature can receive this: that it may be made in the likeness of his death when, by imitating him, it does not sin.

Therefore we ought to be planted together with the likeness—that is, with the likeness of his death—so that, imitating the innocence of his death, we may be extinguished to vices and bear fruit in good works. Then we shall also be planted together with the likeness of his resurrection. For every planting, after the death of winter, puts forth a resurrection in spring. If therefore we too have been planted together in Christ’s death through the winter of this age, in the spring of the age to come [Col. 0672A] we shall bring forth from that very root the fruits of righteousness. We shall be planted together in the likeness of his resurrection when he reforms the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory.

“We are planted together,” he says, “with the likeness of his death,” knowing this: that our old man was crucified together with him, because in that death of the Lord the figure of our sin hung. For the crucifixion of the old man is understood as the pain of repentance and the salutary suffering of self-restraint. Christ, who had lived as an old man according to punishment—that is, according to hunger, thirst, and the like—ended and laid aside in this way oldness, that is, the weakness of our mortality: by enduring the pain of the cross, he had his limbs stretched out and nailed fast so that they could not be moved to their former actions. Then, being buried, he rested, withdrawn from human sight. He requires from us that we lay aside the oldness of sins with the pain of repentance, and that our limbs be nailed fast through self-restraint lest we return to former things; and that we rest from them so perfectly that even their sight and remembrance may be absent.

If we have already fulfilled these things, then indeed our old man has been crucified together with Christ. For the old man is the old manner of life, the tinder and habit of sin, and whatever of the vices took its beginning from the first parent. Yet it is ours because it is from us, not from God. And this old man was so weakened by Christ’s crucifixion that, with reason ruling, the body of sin may be destroyed—that is, the whole mass of sins—so that we may no longer serve sin. The body of sin, that is, sin [Col. 0672C], must be destroyed in all its members. For one vice is a member of sin; but its body is the totality of offences, whose beginning is original sin. But Christ was crucified not partially but whole, so that we may die wholly to sin and live to God.

For the grace of God through Christ’s baptism—Christ who came in the likeness of sinful flesh—works so that the body of sin may be destroyed. It is destroyed, however, not so that in this living flesh the mingled and innate concupiscence is suddenly consumed and ceases to exist, but so that what was present in one born may not harm one dead. It is destroyed not so that it does not exist for the present, but so that we are not compelled to serve it. This is what he says: “That we might no longer serve sin.” And indeed we shall not be compelled to serve sin because we have been justified; and truly justified because we have died. For one who has died with Christ has been justified—that is, made free from sin and separated from it—and can no longer sin, because, as John also says: “Everyone born of God does not sin” (1 John III).

For one who has been crucified, all whose limbs are occupied by pain, cannot sin, but opposes concupiscences and passions. “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and concupiscences” (Gal. V). He is justified who has died—that is, who has mortified himself to vices for Christ, or has endured martyrdom. But if we have died with Christ—that is, if we have been mortified to vices by imitating his death, so that we may no longer live to them—we believe and confidently hope that we shall also [Col. 0673A] live with him, so that we may be where he is; and as he lives forever and blessedly, so we too may live.

“Knowing that Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him. For in that he died, he died to sin once; but in that he lives, he lives to God. So also reckon yourselves indeed dead to sin, but living to God in Christ Jesus.”

We shall live with Christ, who lives without end—I mean, we who already know that Christ, having risen from the dead, does not die any longer, that is, is not dissolved, as Lazarus and the widow’s son, whom he himself raised, died again. For his resurrection was not like theirs, but such that he cannot die again; and such a resurrection has also been promised to us. Christ dies no more, and death shall no longer have dominion over him. For a time it had dominion over him on the cross through his own merciful will. This was said against the Manichees, who deny that Christ had true flesh. For he took humanity in order that temporal death might have dominion over him in the Passion—that is, might truly afflict him as a true human being and kill him—so that eternal death might lose dominion over us.

But death will no longer have dominion over him through any suffering, because he will endure no further affliction. The impious, however, though after the general resurrection they no longer die, will nevertheless be under death’s dominion without end, because, as it is written: “Death shall feed upon them” (Ps. XLVIII). In distinction from such immortality [Col. 0673C], Christ is now said to be immortal after his resurrection in such a way that death can no longer exercise dominion over him through the suffering of any affliction. For a like incorruption and impassibility shall also be bestowed upon his elect.

Truly Christ dies no more because he died once—that is, in such a manner that he does not repeat death. Once, because one death is sufficient to endure for taking away sin, and therefore repetition is unnecessary. This is the meaning of: “For in that he died, he died to sin once.” Or, he died to sin—that is, to the flesh, in which there was not sin but the likeness of sin. For he died to sin because he died to the likeness of sinful flesh, when by dying he put off the flesh, so that by this mystery he might signify that those baptized into his death die to sin in order to live to God.

For sin was not in him. Yet in a certain sense he died to sin when he died to the flesh in which was the likeness of sin, so that, although he had never lived according to the oldness of sin, he might by his resurrection signify our new life revived from the old death in which we had died in sin. Therefore he died once in order to free us from double death. For because we have both departed from God in mind and return to dust in body, we are bound by the punishment of a twofold death. But he died for us in body alone, so that he might join his single death to our double death and free us from each death. Therefore, in that he died to sin—that is, to the likeness of sin—he died once, that is, in body alone. But in that he lives after the resurrection [Col. 0674A], he lives to God—that is, in the eternal blessedness of the Father—because, just as the Father’s life, so Christ’s life admits no disturbance.

So also you: as Christ’s death to sin happened once, and his life to God remains forever, so die once to sin, that you may no longer live to sin and need not die again to sin; and live always to God in good works. This is the meaning of: “So also reckon yourselves,” that by imitation of Christ you are indeed dead to sin—that is, separated from sin at the time of baptism—but living to God in virtues and newness of life, which is the first resurrection, so that you may cleave to God and become one spirit with him. And this is not by the powers of your own will, but in Christ Jesus—that is, in his grace and power—because, as Peter says: “There is salvation in no one else” (Acts IV).

Nor is it without reason that it is said, “Reckon,” that is, consider yourselves dead to sin. For whoever considers or reckons within himself that sin is dead does not sin. For example, if desire for a woman draws me, or desire for silver, gold, or an estate assails me, and I set in my heart that I have died with Christ and reflect upon death, concupiscence is immediately extinguished and sin put to flight. All these things look back to that question, lest the Apostle seem to have given room for sinning when he said: “Where sin abounded, grace shall superabound.”

“Therefore let not sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its concupiscences. Neither present your members as weapons of unrighteousness to sin, but present yourselves to God as alive from the dead, and your members as weapons of righteousness to God. For sin shall not have dominion over you. For you are not under the Law but under grace.”

Because he said that they are dead to sin and ought not to live again in it, since no one is without sin he defines those things especially to be avoided, as though concluding the question he raised above: “Shall we remain in sin?” Because, he says, you are dead to sin, and yet cannot in this life be without sin, at least do not let sin reign in your mortal body. He did not say, “Let it not be,” but, “Let it not reign.” For he did not forbid sin from being in the mortal body, but from reigning, because in corruptible flesh it cannot fail to be present, though it need not reign [Col. 0674D].

This very fact of being tempted by sin is sin; and while we live, we are not altogether and perfectly free from it in every respect. Since the Apostle could not utterly expel it, he took its kingdom from our hearts, so that unlawful desire, even if it often secretly enters into our good thoughts like a thief, may not rule if it enters. For when any fault assaults the heart of the wicked and finds no resistance, but subdues it to its own master, it undoubtedly reigns in that person, because as soon as it knocks, it bends him toward vices. But let it not be so in you.

Even though sin—that is, the tinder and pleasure of sin—is in your body, that is, in your body now under your control, a mortal body and therefore not without sin, nevertheless let sin not reign in it—that is, let it not do what it unlawfully desires [Col. 0675A]. “In the mortal body” is said because there will be no sin in the immortal body. Sin is now present when you take pleasure in it; it reigns if you consent. Therefore sin is in the body, but let it not reign, so that you obey its concupiscences, which arise from the weakness of the flesh. For if you do not obey, even though sin is in the flesh, suggesting and enticing evil, by not obeying you ensure that what exists does not reign; and afterward it will come about that what once existed will not exist, when death is swallowed up in victory.

And not only let it not reign in you through consent, but neither through action. This is the meaning: Do not obey unlawful concupiscences by consent; nor present—that is, give—your members to sin, that is, to the tinder of sin, as weapons, that is, instruments, of unrighteousness [Col. 0675B], namely of wrongful action, by which virtues are attacked as though with weapons. The members are called weapons because by them we serve in the ranks either of righteousness or of sin. And each member, if it turns its function to evil uses, becomes a weapon of unrighteousness for assaulting righteousness: if the hand is occupied with theft, the tongue with lying, the eye serves concupiscence in assaulting chastity, and the other members are occupied with similar vices.

For the sin which is in our body is a kind of tyrant fighting against us and seeking to have our members as weapons for defeating us. Therefore let us not allow it to fight against us with our members. Does anger arise? Let us not give anger the tongue for cursing, or hand or foot for striking. This irrational anger would not arise unless sin were in the members. But let us take its kingdom away: let it have no weapons with which to fight against us. It will learn not to arise when it begins not to find weapons.

Do not, I say, present your members to sin as weapons of unrighteousness, that is, as means by which unrighteousness is accomplished; but present yourselves to God as alive from the dead, that is, as though already raised from death. For after the resurrection one does not live carnally or sin, but attends to divine and spiritual matters. And you who have risen from the death of the soul ought now to live spiritually, holily, and for God, and to present your members to God as weapons of righteousness, so that through them God may fight for righteousness against the kingdom of sin. For it is God who works in you: namely, so that the hand [Col. 0675D] which formerly snatched what belonged to another may now give what is its own; the eye which formerly looked in order to sin may now look to serve a good work. Thus let the other members also serve righteousness.

If you wish, you can properly fulfill this. For sin—that is, the tinder of sin and the delight in unrighteousness that is in the flesh—shall not have dominion, that is, shall not prevail over you as it formerly did. It shall not have dominion because you are now not under a Law that commands but does not help, but under grace that frees and helps. For sin has dominion over those who are under the Law and not under grace; a person is not made free from it by the Law but by grace. Not because the Law is evil, but because it does not free those whom it makes guilty by commanding without helping. Grace indeed helps each person to be a doer of the Law; without this grace, one under the Law was only a hearer of the Law [Col. 0676A].

“What then? Shall we sin because we are not under the Law but under grace? God forbid! Do you not know that when you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one whom you obey: either of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness? But thanks be to God that, though you were slaves of sin, you obeyed from the heart that form of teaching into which you were delivered. And, having been freed from sin, you became slaves of righteousness.”

Since we are under grace, what then shall we do? Shall we sin because we are not under the Law but under grace? That is, with the Law’s punishment removed, shall we sin with impunity? God forbid that we should sin! For the Law commanded that sinners be immediately put to death [Col. 0676B], whereas grace waits even after guilt for repentance. And therefore these people wished to twist the Apostle’s statement to mean that they were permitted to sin, since they had been stripped of fear of the Law. But he himself removes this. “God forbid,” he says, “that we should therefore sin more freely,” that is, commit criminal and deadly sins such as the Law was accustomed to condemn—for this life cannot be lived without lesser sins.

Truly you ought not to sin, but rather to act rightly, because if you sin, you will be slaves of sin; conversely, if you do good, you will become slaves of righteousness. And it is the more shameful that, after God’s grace has freed us from sin, you should again serve sin on the occasion of that grace. Or do you not know—that is, are you ignorant—that the one to whom you present, that is, prepare and offer, yourselves as slaves, that is, as ready [Col. 0676C] to obey, you are that one’s slaves? That is, you must serve that one’s will whom you obey, that is, to whose obedience you have subjected your necks. Once you have obeyed that one, you are that one’s slaves, even if you were not so before, when you first presented yourselves to that one by consenting. Whomever you obey, you are that one’s slaves: whether of sin, which leads to eternal death, or of holy obedience, which leads you to righteousness, that is, to the completion of righteousness. For you who were first justified through faith will now ascend to the highest perfection of righteousness if you obey the divine commands.

You are the slave of the one whom you obey. But I give thanks to God because, although you were formerly slaves of sin, you are so no longer. I render thanks not to you nor to your free will, but to God, through whom it came about that you escaped the slavery of sin. “Thanks,” he says, “be to God, because you were slaves of sin; but, he freeing and helping you, you are so no longer, because you obeyed God not from fear of the Law but from the heart,” that is, from the good will of the heart; or not merely outwardly, not by pretence, but from purity of heart.

You obeyed, I say, directing yourselves to that form—that is, rule—of evangelical teaching into which you were delivered. That is, into the teaching which forms and admonishes your conduct, into which you were delivered by God’s grace: you did not come to it through yourselves; or you were delivered into it by teachers. This teaching is a form because it restores the image of God that had been disfigured. And you not only obeyed, but were also freed from sin through the Holy Spirit whom you received in baptism, because “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. III) [Col. 0677A]. And, freed from the slavery of sin, you became by consent and action slaves of righteousness, which is the highest freedom. You are slaves of the righteousness which you obey, that is, of Christ, who was made for us wisdom from God, righteousness, and sanctification.

“I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you presented your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification.”

Up to this point he has said that one must not sin; now he says what must hereafter be done, concerning which no one can excuse himself, since there is no one who cannot do good, at least by will—which likewise is through grace. “I speak in human terms,” he says—that is, I speak what you can bear, what does not exceed the powers of your humanity and frailty [Col. 0677B], but what you can sufficiently fulfill. And I do this because of the weakness—that is, the feebleness and frailty—of your flesh, that is, of your carnality, because I see that you are still weak according to the flesh; therefore I instruct you in human terms.

Truly what I say is human—that is, easy and not harsh—because I command this: Just as you presented—that is, prepared—your members to serve uncleanness by acting, that is, lust which defiles the flesh, and iniquity, that is, wrongful action which, even if it does not defile your body, nevertheless seeks to injure your neighbor; iniquity, I say, leading to another and greater iniquity, so that by increases of evils you continually advanced toward worse things—so now, after conversion, since you have been freed, present—that is, prepare—your members, which are under your control [Col. 0677C], to serve righteousness by acting, righteousness which leads to sanctification, that is, the completion of good. Thus righteousness must be served, from which so great usefulness and honor arise.

This means: just as then no fear compelled you, but the pleasure of sin led you, so now let a mature, though not yet perfect, delight in righteousness lead you. If you can do no more, at least be as fruitful in good deeds as you once were active in vicious deeds, lest holy freedom find you weak where the practice of earthly pleasure found you strong in the flesh. Thus let each one of you serve virtues as he formerly served vices. For righteousness must be served much more and much more earnestly than uncleanness. But I, he says, act in human terms. I ask for the same things; I require comparable things: that each member adapt to virtues the service it gave to vices, and that the action it gave to uncleanness now turn to chastity and sanctification.

If you cannot do more, at least now do as much as you then did, lest you flee our faith and teaching as harsh and unbearable. But what does “Do this just as you did that” mean, except that, as no fear compelled you to sin but the desire and pleasure of sin itself, so in living rightly let not fear of punishment urge you, but let delight and love of righteousness lead you; and perform these things now as strongly and persistently as you performed those. Yet this is not perfect righteousness. Is righteousness worthy only as much as iniquity was worthy [Col. 0678A]? Is this to be loved as that is loved? God forbid that it should be so—or that life should be so. Therefore it must be loved more.

For in iniquity you pursued pleasure, but for righteousness you ought to endure pain. Consider some unchaste young man who casts his eyes upon another man’s wife, falls in love, and desires to attain her, yet seeks to remain hidden. For he loves pleasure in such a way that he fears pain more. The sweetness of that pleasure is not so great that it overcomes even the pain of punishments. But the beauty and delight of righteousness are so great that, when they have perfectly inspired their love in anyone, they make that person despise not only whatever pleased him in this world, but also everything that terrifies and tortures.

The Apostle wished now to exhort his hearers to this perfect delight in righteousness, but he saw that they were less capable of it. Therefore he condescended to their weakness and moderated the command he gave them. “I speak in human terms,” he says, etc., down to “unto sanctification.” Here he has named righteousness for all virtues together, just as conversely he set iniquity for all vices together. Then he adds sanctification to righteousness, in order to commend the element of chastity both generally along with the rest and specially in itself. And he admonishes his hearers that, if they are not yet able to despise punishments, pains, and death for righteousness, at least they should prefer the delight of righteousness to the pleasures of their body, so that they may gradually advance to greater merits of righteousness and serve holiness more strongly and devotedly than they formerly served luxury; nor should they any longer refuse to suffer anything for righteousness [Col. 0678C].

For as that person is most unrighteous whom not even bodily punishments deter from the unclean deeds of sordid pleasure, so that person is most righteous whom not even the terror of bodily punishments calls back from the holy works of most radiant love.

“For when you were slaves of sin, you were free with respect to righteousness (John VIII). What fruit, then, did you have at that time in those things of which you are now ashamed? For their end is death” (Isa. I; Ezek. XXXV).

Therefore you ought to serve righteousness, not impurity, because when you were slaves of sin—that is, when sin ruled you and reigned in your mortal body—you were free from righteousness; that is, you lacked the dominion of righteousness, because “no one can serve two masters” [Col. 0678D] (Matt. 6; Luke 16). For as long as anyone serves sin, he is free from righteousness, that is, estranged from righteousness. And it should be noted that there is both a culpable freedom and a praiseworthy servitude. For to be free from righteousness is a crime, whereas to be its slave is praiseworthy.

Free choice has not perished from human hearts to such an extent that all those who sin with pleasure and love of sin chiefly sin through it. For when the Apostle says, “When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness,” he shows that they could not have served sin except through another freedom. Thus people are free from righteousness only through freedom of choice; but they are not made free from sin except through the grace of the Savior. For this reason the admirable teacher even distinguished the very words: he called them *free* from righteousness, not *freed*; but with regard to sin he did not say “free,” lest they attribute this to themselves, but a little earlier most carefully chose to say “freed,” referring to that saying of the Lord: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8).

But this will, which is free in evil because it delights in evil, is not free in good because it has not been set free. It is badly free when it delights in sinning. For he serves freely who willingly does his master’s will. Accordingly, the one who is a slave of sin is free to sin. Hence he will not be free to act justly unless, having been freed from sin, he begins to be a slave of righteousness. This is true freedom, because of the joy of right action, and at the same time devout servitude, because of obedience to the commandment.

And since you served sin, what fruit—that is, what benefit—did you then have [Col. 0679A] in those sinful actions [Col. 0679B] of which you now, when of sound mind, are ashamed because of their greater shamefulness? It is as though he said: You then had no fruit there; or, if you think that you had some fruit of pleasure, it was of such a kind that you now rightly blush for it. This recompense makes them abhor their former deeds and become more indebted to grace. You rightly now blush for the past, for their end—that is, the outcome of life—is death. Or thus: I ask about the fruit, for the end is obvious: their end is death—not the death common to all, but that death which no one can escape unless he turns to righteousness and blushes for his former evil conduct.

> “But now, having been freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit unto sanctification, [Col. 0679C] and the end, eternal life. For the wages of sin is death; but the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

From the slavery of sin you had the fruit of shame, and in the end you would have had eternal death; but from the service of God you now have the fruit of sanctification, and in the end you will have everlasting life. And this was indeed so then. But now that you have been converted through Christ’s grace, freed from the sin which you served—not only rescued from the service of sin, but also made servants of God, though formerly free from righteousness—you may now freely perform good works. And you have your fruit, that is, fruit beneficial and fitting for you; this fruit is undoubtedly charity and its works, which we can in no way possess through ourselves [Col. 0679D], but through the Holy Spirit who has been given.

You have this fruit through the gift of the Holy Spirit, being led into sanctification—that is, into the perfection of virtues. Nor will you have this alone: you will also receive the end of the labor which you endure in God’s service, namely eternal life of body and soul. I said that the end of the things which you formerly did is death, and I said it rightly. For the wages—that is, the recompense—of sin is death. But conversely I added that, for the things you now do on our behalf, you will receive eternal life in the end, because the grace of God, which mercifully rewards those who do good, is eternal life.

“Wages” (*stipendium*) is so called from *stips* (“a payment”) and *pendo* (“I pay”). What wages are to a laborer, pay is to a soldier. Therefore death is rightly called the pay of sin, because eternal death is rendered as a debt, as it were, for the devil’s military service [Col. 0680A]. Although the Apostle could have said—and said rightly—“But the wages of righteousness are eternal life,” he preferred to say, “But the grace of God is eternal life,” so that we might understand from this that God brings us to eternal life not by our merits but by his mercy.

For after he had said, “The wages of sin are death,” who would not judge it entirely fitting and consequent if he added, “But the wages of righteousness are eternal life”? And it is true: as death is rendered as wages by the desert of sin, so eternal life is rendered as wages by the desert of righteousness. But, carefully contending against pride, he says, “The wages of sin are death.” Correctly, “wages,” because they are owed, because they are deservedly repaid, because they are rendered by merit. Then, lest righteousness [Col. 0680B] pride itself on a human good by merit—as human evil merit is undoubtedly sin—he did not set the opposite in correspondence, saying, “The wages of righteousness are eternal life”; rather, he says, “But the grace of God is eternal life.”

And lest some other path beyond the Mediator be sought for this, he added, “in Christ Jesus our Lord.” It is as though he said: Having heard that the wages of sin are death, what are you preparing to boast of, O human being—not righteousness, but clearly pride bearing the name of righteousness? What are you preparing to boast of, and to demand eternal life, the opposite of death, as wages owed to you? True righteousness is that to which eternal life is owed. But if it is true righteousness, it is not from yourself. “It is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (James 1); in order that you might possess it, you surely received it. “For what good do you have [Col. 0680C] that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4).

Therefore, if he is to receive eternal life, it is indeed the wages of righteousness, but for you it is grace, since righteousness itself is grace to you. For it would be rendered to you as a debt if you possessed from yourself the righteousness to which it was owed. But now from his fullness we have received not only grace (John 1), by which we may now live justly amid labors to the end, but also grace for this grace, so that afterward in rest we may live without end. For unless grace were gratuitous, it would not be grace. Therefore, as we have said, it must be understood that even a human being’s good merits are gifts of God. When eternal life is rendered for these, grace is rendered for grace.

## Chapter VII

[Col. 0680D]

> “Or do you not know, brothers—for I speak to those who know the law—that the law has dominion over a person for as long as he lives? For a woman who is under a husband is bound by the law to her husband while he lives (1 Cor. 7). But if her husband has died, she is released from the law of her husband. Therefore, while her husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she is with another man. But if her husband has died, she is freed from the law of her husband, so that she is not an adulteress if she is with another man. Therefore, my brothers, you too have been put to death to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who rose from the dead, in order that we might bear fruit for God.”

The Jews might say: Why do you say that eternal life is in Christ Jesus, and not rather in observance of the law? [Col. 0681A] And the Apostle replies: Because it has now reached its end and does not give life, but increases sin. Thus far he has spoken about the power of grace; now he begins to show the difficulty of the law and that it is no longer to be retained, in order to exhort them to live without fear under grace.

So that they might not be surprised at his statement, “You are not under law, but under grace,” he begins by arguments to demonstrate that the law has come to an end, and that even previously it had not justified those subject to it but rather had made them sinners. For it was given until Christ, and therefore, after grace has been received, it is not to be retained. This is shown in these statements: “Do you not know, brothers,” and so forth.

The order is: Do you not know this, that the law has dominion over a person, so that he obeys it, for as long as it lives—that is, as long as the law itself has standing? You ought not to be ignorant of this, because [Col. 0681B] you know the law, and I speak to those who know the law, in which what I say is made clear. By “those who know the law,” let us understand the Hebrews, whom the Apostle instructs according to the law concerning the end of the law. Or even the Gentile Romans knew the law, because they were not barbarians but had grasped natural justice partly from the Greeks, just as the Greeks had from the Hebrews.

The law has dominion over a person for as long as the law itself lives; therefore, when it has died, it will no longer rule him, but will leave him free. The Lord teaches that it is now dead—that is, that it has ceased according to its carnal understanding or observance—when he says: “The law and the prophets were until John; from then on the kingdom of God is proclaimed” (Matt. 11). This was fittingly prefigured when Moses died and Joshua assumed leadership [Col. 0681C] of the people of Israel. For Moses signified the law, and Joshua [*Jesus*] the Lord Christ and evangelical grace. Therefore, when Moses died, Joshua succeeded to leadership, because when the law has died according to carnal observances, evangelical grace succeeds.

And this is what the Apostle had said: “You are not under law, but under grace”; that is, you are not under Moses but under Jesus, because Moses has died and Jesus rules. It was therefore right that Moses—that is, the law—should rule in every person subject to it as long as it lived, and should lose its dominion after its death, so that those who in the time of the law were compelled to observe it slavishly might, after the Liberator’s coming, be able freely to enter evangelical freedom.

The Apostle proves this by an analogy. For a woman who is under a husband is, while the husband lives, bound by the law [Col. 0681D] of her husband, so that she cannot leave him. But if her husband has died, she is released from the law of her husband. Likewise, as long as the law had standing, it ought to be observed; but if the law loses its standing, a person is released from it. And because, while the husband lives, she is bound by the law, therefore while the husband lives she will be called an adulteress if she is with another husband. Likewise, when the law has ended and been set aside, a person is freed through grace so that he does not transgress if, leaving behind the figures, he passes over to Christ.

By this example the Apostle teaches that the Christian has been stripped of the law of works, not of every law, just as the woman is stripped of the law of her husband, not of the law of nature; nor ought he any longer to be under the law. For if the law still lives for him, he is an adulterer, and it does him no good to be called a Christian. For if he observes the law, he is an adulterer in faith and in the law, and Christ does him no good. [Col. 0682A]

This entire analogy must also be understood mystically: the husband is Moses, that is, the law; the woman is the soul or the people. For the woman who is under a husband—that is, the Jewish people or soul, which is under Moses—is, while the husband lives, that is, while Moses lives, namely while the law has standing, bound by the law, so that she cannot depart from its carnal observance. But if her husband has died—that is, Moses, as we explained above—the woman is released from the law of her husband; that is, the Hebrew people are released from the yoke of the law, so that they may not be hindered from being joined to Christ.

And because she is released only now, therefore, while the husband lives—that is, while Moses lives and the law remains in force—she will be called an adulteress if she is with another husband; that is, she incurs the crime of adultery if, abandoning the carnal observance of the law, she wishes to hold only to the spiritual [Col. 0682B] teaching of Christ. For that carnal observance of the law was not to be abandoned in its own time, just as it is not now to be assumed. But if her husband Moses has died—that is, if the law, its operation having ceased, has fallen asleep—the Hebrew people themselves are freed from the law of their husband, that is, from the crushing burden of the Mosaic institution, so that they may not be adulterous but chaste if they are with another husband, that is, with Christ; so that they may cling to him alone in the embraces of love and keep only the spiritual teaching.

Then the Apostle applies the analogy. Since, he says, while the husband lives the woman is bound, and when he dies she is released, according to the interpretation already discussed, therefore you too, my brothers, like us apostles, have been put to death to the law, so that you may no longer live in it. He ought to have said, “The law has been put to death [Col. 0682C] for you,” but to say this among the Jews still seemed unmanageable, and therefore he left it rather to be understood. It amounts to the same thing as what he said: the law is dead when its carnal practice has wholly ceased; and the person who has ceased from such practice is dead to the law.

The Apostle therefore spoke cautiously, lest he offend the Jews, choosing rather to say, “You have been put to death to the law,” than “The law has been put to death for you,” although both mean the same thing. You owe nothing, he says, to the law which was given until Christ; rather, you have been put to death to it through the body of Christ—that is, through Christ’s assumption of flesh. For from the time when he put on a body, the law began to die in the practice of believers, because “the law and the prophets were until John,” as he himself says [Col. 0682D] (ibid.).

Therefore, sins having been dismissed through the newness of grace, and the law’s practice in you having ceased, you have been put to death to the law through the body of Christ—that is, through the mystery of his incarnation. Or, you have been put to death to the law, that is, to its figurative shadows, through the body of Christ, that is, through the fulfillment of the solid reality which is in Christ. For as great as the difference between shadow and body is, so great is the difference between the things done in the Old Testament and those done in the New. Thus a person has died to the law through the body of Christ because, through evangelical truth, he has ceased from the shadowy practice of the law.

You have been put to death to the law—that is, released from the law—Moses having died for you, so that you may be the bride of another husband, one to whom it is not shameful to belong because he rose from the dead and, death having been overcome, lives eternally. Or, you ought rightly to belong to him because he redeemed you by his blood [Col. 0683A] and, trampling death underfoot, rose again in order to possess you, whom he acquired by dying. He rose in order also to make us rise from the death of the soul, so that we might bear fruit—that is, perform the fruit of good work—for God, whereas formerly we bore fruit for death.

> “For when we were in the flesh, the passions of sins which were through the law worked in our members, so that they might bear fruit for death. But now we have been released from the law of death, in which we were held, so that we may serve in the newness of the spirit and not in the oldness of the letter.”

Truly we ought now to bear fruit for God, since we have been put to death to the law, because formerly we bore fruit for death. For when we were in the flesh, working the things of the flesh—which is to be under the law—the passions of sins [Col. 0683B] which were through the law worked in our members. “When we were in the flesh,” he says: that is, when we were held bound by carnal desires. “When we were in the flesh”: that is, when we presumed upon the flesh.

For the Apostle who was speaking had not yet left this flesh, nor was he speaking to people who had already left this flesh; rather, both he who spoke and those to whom he spoke were still in the flesh. What, then, does “when we were in the flesh” mean, except “when we presumed upon the flesh,” that is, trusted in ourselves? For it is said of humankind: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3), that is, every human being. Therefore, when we were in the flesh—that is, when we lived amid carnal desires and placed our whole hope there, as though in ourselves—the passions of sins, that is, incitements to vices [Col. 0683C], which were through the law because they had increased through the law (for where the Liberator’s grace was absent, the prohibition of sins increased the desire to sin), worked in our members; that is, they led our members into evil works. And this was so because we were in the flesh.

For these passions of sins—that is, violent desires—are called passions because inwardly they afflict the mind. They conquered us because they found us in a bad place, namely in the flesh. We must therefore depart from the flesh even while we still live in the flesh, so that we may not be in the flesh but in the spirit; that is, so that we may place our hope not in ourselves but in God, and delight not in carnal but in spiritual things. For one who is in the flesh—that is, who remains in himself and does not transcend himself in order to lift his heart to God—does not have God as helper [Col. 0683D], and therefore is overcome and becomes not a fulfiller of the law but a transgressor.

Thus the passions of sins—that is, violent cravings and immoderate desires—work in the members of those who are in the flesh; that is, they bring to the effect of action the evil things they desire: hands do evil, the mouth speaks falsehood, the eyes look upon unlawful things, and the ears take pleasure in hearing wickedness. These passions are through the law, because the law’s prohibition itself was the cause that the appetite of the flesh became so violent. For desire was less when, before the law, a person sinned without concern. But it became much greater when he began to transgress God’s law. And these passions, as was said, worked in our members [Col. 0684A] so that they might bear fruit for death; that is, so that they might produce works deserving eternal death. For the fruit of sin is death. And if the sinner was to be condemned, what hope does the transgressor have?

At that time, being under the law, we bore fruit for death. But now, since we have been put to death to the law through the body of Christ, we have been released from the law through the freedom of new grace. It is called the law of death because, through an intermediary—that is, through sin—it was the cause of death, since it did not await sinners’ repentance but commanded that they be killed immediately. It is also the law of death because “the wages of sin is death,” while “the sting of death is sin” and “the power of sin is the law.” For by sinning we fall into the death of the soul, and we sin more violently when the law forbids than we would if no law prohibited us.

But now, sins having been forgiven, we have been released from [Col. 0684B] this law in which we were held; that is, by a certain force of necessity we were compelled to keep its carnal commands and were not permitted to rise to spiritual freedom, because we could never be released except through Christ’s grace. We have been released, I say, so that we may serve God in the newness of the spirit and not in the oldness of the letter; that is, so that we may obey the commands of spiritual grace, not following the letter of the law, which has now grown old and ought to die, that is, to cease. For what is becoming obsolete and growing old is near destruction.

And what is the law but mere letter to those who know how to read it but cannot fulfill it? It is not unknown to those for whom it was written. But because it is known only insofar as it is read as written, not insofar as it is fulfilled in love, to such persons it is nothing other than letter [Col. 0684C]. This letter is not a helper of those who read it, but a witness against those who sin. Therefore those who are renewed through the Holy Spirit are freed from its condemnation, so that they are no longer bound to the letter for punishment but joined to understanding through righteousness.

Therefore let us serve in the newness of the spirit, that is, in the newness which the Holy Spirit gives by pouring in charity and renewing the inner person. And let us serve in this newness so as to add nothing from the works of the law, which are old and are more fit to be committed to burial.

> “What then shall we say? Is the law sin? By no means! But I did not know sin except through the law. For I did not know covetousness unless the law said, ‘You shall not covet’ (Exod. 20; Deut. 5). But sin, taking occasion, worked in me through the commandment [Col. 0684D] every covetousness.”

By the foregoing words the Apostle seemed to have blamed the law. Therefore, perceiving human thoughts stirred against the obscurity of his sayings, he himself first chose to state and remove what someone could object to him: Because, he says, I stated that the passions of sins are through the law; because I stated that we have been released from the law of death in which we were held; because I stated that we should serve in the newness of the spirit and not in the oldness of the letter—what then shall we say on the basis of these words of mine? Shall we say that it follows from them that the law is sin? By no means that we should say this; by no means that the law should be sin!

The law is not sin, because it is not evil but good in itself. Yet though good, it is not sufficient for salvation [Col. 0685A] without grace. The Apostle now begins to show this, speaking in the voice of the human race: the law, he says, is not sin but the indicator of sin, because “I did not know sin except through the law.” Thus we understand that the law was given not in order that sin might be introduced, nor that it might be uprooted, but only that it might be displayed, so that by this very display of sin it might make the human soul, formerly secure as though innocent, guilty; and so that, because sin could not be overcome without grace, the anxiety of this guilt might turn it toward receiving grace.

For this reason he did not say, “I did not commit sin except through the law,” but “I did not know sin except through the law.” From this it is clear that sin was not implanted through the law but displayed by it. And just as medicine is not the cause of death if it shows deadly poisons [Col. 0685B], though evil people misuse these to death, either killing themselves or plotting against enemies, so the law was given in order to show the poisons of sins and to restrain by the bridle of the law a person misusing his freedom, who previously rushed heedlessly onward and fell over precipices, and to teach him to walk with ordered steps.

The law taught a person what sin was, because previously some things were not known either to be sins, or to be so grave, or to be punishable. Truly, I did not know sin except through the law. For I did not know that covetousness was sin unless the law said, “You shall not covet.” The Apostle chose this general expression because it embraces everything, as though this were the law’s voice forbidding every sin: “You shall not covet.” For no sin [Col. 0685C] is committed except by coveting. He did not say, “I did not have covetousness,” but “I did not know it to be sin.” I did indeed have it, but I believed it to be a natural good. But after the law said, “You shall not covet,” I learned that covetousness was not a natural good but an evil incidentally arising through sin.

Through these and the following words the Apostle treats a universal case in himself alone and describes, under his own person, the frailty of the human condition. “I did not know,” he says, “that covetousness was evil until I heard it forbidden in the law. But sin,” that is, the tinder of sin, “having taken an occasion to spur me on, worked in me through the commandment of the law every covetousness.” By “sin” is here understood either the tinder of sin [Col. 0685D] or the devil, the author of sin.

Such is our carnality that it desires forbidden things more ardently, whereas without mention of them it would lie, as it were, dormant. Moreover, the devil, seeing that the law had been given to help human beings, burned more fiercely and pressed harder to turn it into their ruin, whereas before, possessing them almost securely, he tempted them less. Thus, taking occasion through the commandment, he produced in me every covetousness. For desire was less when, before the law, I sinned without concern. It was less when it stirred my lust. It is total when it transgresses the law. Therefore, when I thought that by my own strength, with the law commanding me, I could conquer lustful desire, I was pressed by its greater goads, and as it weakened me, its craving increased.

For where the Holy Spirit does not help, inspiring in place of evil covetousness good covetousness—that is, pouring charity into hearts—the law, though good, increases evil desire by forbidding it. It is like the rush of water: if it does not cease flowing toward a particular side, it becomes more violent when a barrier is set against it; and when it has overcome the mass of that barrier, it plunges downward in a greater flood and rolls all the more violently over the slopes. So too the river of covetousness, checked by the barriers of the law set against it, was restrained but not dried up; afterward, when those same barriers were broken, it burst forth more violently.

I do not know how, but the very thing coveted becomes more pleasant when it is forbidden. Thus it is rightly said that sin, taking occasion to spur on through the commandment of the law, worked in me every covetousness [Col. 0686B], because where the Liberator’s grace is absent, the prohibition of sins increases the desire to sin; and while the law forbids covetousness, it in some way inflames it.

> “For without the law sin was dead. But I was once alive without the law. Yet when the commandment came, sin revived, but I died; and the commandment which was for life was found to be for death to me. For sin, taking occasion, deceived me through the commandment and killed me through it.”

Truly, I came to know sin through the law. For without the law sin was dead; that is, it lay hidden, did not appear, and was wholly unknown as though buried. Or thus: I rightly said, “through the commandment.” For when the law was not present [Col. 0686C], sin was dead, that is, weak and as though dormant, since it was not stirred by the law’s prohibition. Sin was indeed dead before the law. But I was once alive without the law, that is, before the law was given. I was alive without the law, that is, no death from sin frightened me, because it did not appear when there was no law.

It is clear that the Apostle does not speak strictly in his own person, but generally in the person of humanity. “I was alive,” that is, I thought myself alive because I did not know that my soul was dead through sin, while I imagined that I was without sin. But when the commandment came—that is, when the law was given—at once sin revived: it appeared, began to make itself felt, began to rebel against me. Sin revived because it had once lived. For nothing can revive unless it formerly lived. Sin had indeed once lived in paradise, when it was plainly committed against the commandment that had been given.

But when it is inherited by those being born, it lies hidden as though dead, so that its evil, which opposes righteousness, is not felt through prohibition. For when one thing is commanded and approved, and another pleases and is condemned, then sin in some manner revives in the awareness of the person born, although it had once already lived in the awareness of the first-created person. Thus, upon the arrival of the commandment of the law, sin revived—which had been dead, that is, hidden—when mortal persons born without the commandment of the law lived, following their desires without any restraint.

Sin indeed revived, but I died [Col. 0687A]; that is, through the manifestation of sin I learned that I was dead. For one also sins by transgression who sees through the law what he ought not to do and nevertheless does it. I died in soul because I became a transgressor, and thereby perceived that I was dead. Or I saw that I was dead because the guilt of transgression threatened a certain punishment of death. And the commandment which had been given for attaining life was found for me to be for incurring death. For what, if it were kept, advanced one toward life, when neglected led one to death. For if the commandment is obeyed, it is surely life. But it was found to be for death when action is contrary to the commandment, so that not only is sin committed—as it was committed even before the commandment—but it is committed more abundantly and more ruinously, since one now sins knowingly and by transgression.

“It was found to be for me,” that is, God did not give the commandment for death; rather, it seemed to me as though deadly because I could not fulfill it by my own power, while I died, struck by death not through a defect in the commandment but through the goad of covetousness. For sin is the sting of death. Therefore the same commandment which, according to the giver’s intention, had been given for life because it was good for the obedient, was found—that is, proved—to be for death to me when I sinned. And truly it was for death. For sin, that is, the tinder and pleasure of sin, taking occasion through the commandment—which was against it—deceived me by false sweetness; that is, it led me away from good and drew me into evil, and through it killed me, that is, led me through transgression of the commandment to eternal condemnation [Col. 0687C].

For the enemy killed me with the sword that I carried—that is, the commandment of the law—because I presumed upon my own strength and therefore was conquered. For sin deceived me, taking occasion through the commandment, either because the persuasion of pleasure toward sinning is more forceful when prohibition is present, or because even if a person does something according to the commands of the law, if he does not yet have the faith that is in grace, he wishes to attribute it to himself rather than to God and sins more by pride. Thus sin, not using the law lawfully, became sweeter because desire was increased by prohibition, and thus deceived or misled. For sweetness is deceptive when it is followed by more numerous and greater bitter punishments.

Therefore, because what is forbidden is more sweetly embraced by people who have not yet received spiritual grace, sin deceives by false sweetness; and because the guilt of transgression is also added, it kills. We have said these things with reference to the law given through Moses. But there is also a natural law, written in the heart, which encompasses all nations; and no human being, except one who is still without the use of reason, is ignorant of this law. Hence the whole world is under sin, and all human beings are transgressors of the law. Accordingly, the judgment of God, who writes in the heart of the human race, is just: “What you would not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” (Tob. 4; Matt. 7). For who does not know murder, adultery, theft, and every covetousness to be evil from the fact that he does not wish them done to himself? For if he did not know them to be evil, he would never grieve when they were inflicted upon him.

Childhood does not know this law [Col. 0688A]; infancy is ignorant of it. One who sins without a commandment is not bound by the law of sin. A child curses his father and beats his parents; and because he has not yet received the law of wisdom, sin is dead in him. But when the commandment comes—that is, when the time of understanding arrives, seeking good and avoiding evil—then sin begins to revive in him, and he begins to die and to be guilty of sin. Thus the time of understanding, by which we know God’s commandments in order to attain life, brings about death in us if we act too negligently, and the occasion of wisdom deceives and trips us up and leads us to death. Not that understanding is sin: the law of understanding is holy, just, and good. But through understanding sins and virtues, sin arises in me, which before I understood I did not know to be sin. Thus what was given to me for good is, through my fault, changed into evil.

> “Therefore the law is indeed holy, and the commandment holy and just and good” (1 Tim. 1). “Then has what is good become death to me? By no means! But sin, in order that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good, so that through the commandment sin might become sinful beyond measure.”

Since the law says, “You shall not covet” (Exod. 20), and the commandment of the law was given for life, the law, therefore, is holy—that is, without fault, since it forbids what ought to be forbidden. And the commandment—that is, whatever I am commanded to do—is holy, that is, beyond reproach; and just, that is, equitable, because [Col. 0688C] it commands nothing to be done except what is equitable when it says: “You shall exact eye for eye, foot for foot, tooth for tooth,” and similar things. For this is exceedingly just. And the commandment is good (Exod. 21), that is, useful and fruitful.

The law itself is holy, that is, pure from the stain of every fault, because it contains no defilement but teaches without fault when it says: “You shall not covet; you shall not commit adultery” (Deut. 5), and similar things—although through it depraved people are more inflamed to covet and to commit adultery. And the commandment—that is, what is commanded through it—is holy in itself and just, that is, making the sinner righteous; and good, that is, useful, obtaining life.

For “law” is used here insofar as it prohibits evil, [Col. 0688D] as when it says: “You shall not covet; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness.” But “commandment” is used insofar as it prescribes the doing of good, as in: “Honor your father and mother,” and, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Note how openly the Apostle now praises the law. A little earlier, with the word by which he had said, “By no means!” he defended it from accusation; he had not yet praised it. For it is one thing to defend something from an accusation brought against it, another to proclaim it with the praise due to it. The accusation brought was: “What then shall we say? Is the law sin?” The defense: “By no means!” But now: “Therefore the law is holy,” and so forth.

The law is indeed holy, but those who misuse the law are not holy. For the fault lies in the person who misuses it, not in the commandment itself, which is good. For the law is good if anyone uses it lawfully. [Col. 0689A] But that person misuses the law who does not submit himself to God with devout humility, so that through grace the law may be fulfilled. For the law does not command transgression, so that, when it entered in, transgression might abound; rather, it made even the proud into additional transgressors, so that, humbled in this way, they might learn that they belong to grace through faith, and might no longer be subject to the law through guilt but joined to it through righteousness.

The law, indeed, is holy, and the commandment good. And since it is established that the law itself is holy and its commandment good, and yet that same commandment which was for life has been found to be death to me, then has the commandment that is good become death to me? That is, has the good commandment, given against the works of death, been changed into death for me? By no means! Plainly, when I die, [Col. 0689B] I do not die through a fault in the good commandment; rather, I transgressed the good commandment through my own fault and thus deserved death. The commandment itself was not the cause of death to me; rather, I made it so for myself by sinning and committing deeds worthy of death.

The commandment is not the efficient cause of death to me; rather, sin—that is, the fuel of sin—which turns a good thing into evil, is the efficient cause of death. For sin—that is, the fuel of sin, the incentives of vices, and evil pleasure, or the devil, author of sin—worked death in me; that is, it made me perform works worthy of death through transgression of the good commandment. Thus it worked the death of my soul in me, so that sin itself, which had previously lain hidden in my heart, might appear outwardly as sin in manifest action. Thus, that [Col. 0689C] same sin—that is, the fuel of sin and concupiscence—might become sinning beyond measure: more than before, through the commandment, without which it did not burn so greatly, and through which transgression increased.

Or it should be understood thus: that through the law sin might appear, though it was hidden through ignorance. For he had already said, “Without the law sin was dead,” that is, it was hidden and unknown, as though buried in certain darknesses of ignorance. Now let us see how truly he says, “that sin might appear as sin.” He does not say “that it might be,” because it already was sin even when it did not appear. What does “that sin might appear as sin” mean? “I did not know covetousness unless the law said, ‘You shall not covet.’” He does not say, “I did not have covetousness,” but “I did not know covetousness.” So also here he does not say, “that there might be sin,” but “that sin might appear as sin”: through the good it worked death in me.

What death? “That sin might become beyond measure sinful through the commandment.” Beyond measure, because transgression was added. For when I sinned without a commandment, it was less. But when I sin in relation to a commandment, I exceed the measure. For the law had set limits for everything, but I transgress the law’s limit, driven by the impulse of concupiscence. Or “beyond measure,” because sin grew very much more immoderate through the law, while it was more inflamed by the law’s prohibition and knowingly transgressed it. This was useful for the purpose that the soul might feel that it was not sufficient in itself to draw itself out of slavery to sin; and in this way, [Col. 0690A] when all swelling pride had been extinguished, it might submit itself to its Deliverer and implore the help of his grace.

> “For we know that the law is spiritual; but I am carnal, sold under sin. For I do not understand what I do. For I do not do the good that I will; but the evil that I hate, that I do.”

Above I said that the law is holy. And it truly is holy, because we know that it is spiritual—that is, given by the Holy Spirit, commanding spiritual things, and nourishing the human spirit and instructing it concerning divine and heavenly things. But I am carnal—that is, I consent to the flesh—and sold under sin, that is, sinning for the price of temporal pleasures. For the sweetness of deadly [Col. 0690B] pleasure is the price by which each person sells himself to the devil, placing himself under sin—that is, making himself sin’s slave.

Truly I sold my soul to the devil, receiving the price of pleasure and subjecting myself to sin. For I do not understand what I do, because I see myself doing one thing and know another through the law. “I do not understand what I do,” that is, I do not recognize it in the precepts of truth, where true knowledge is found. In this manner of speaking the Lord says to sinners: “I never knew you” (Matt. 7). Nothing, of course, is hidden from him. But because sins are not found in the standards of the precepts possessed by Truth, Truth itself says to sinners: “I never knew you.” For just as darkness is perceived by the eyes through not seeing, so sins are perceived by the mind through not knowing.

Truly, I do not understand that what I do [Col. 0690C] ought to be done according to the law. For the good which I will according to reason, I do not do; but the evil which I hate according to reason’s judgment, that I do according to the appetite of the flesh. For reason naturally wills the good, but this will always lacks effective affection unless it is aided by grace.

These words indeed fit in this way the carnal person placed under the law; but they are better understood also of the spiritual person, already established under grace, or of the Apostle himself. “We know,” he says, “that the law is spiritual,” that is, it commands spiritual things. Up to this point he had excused the law, showing that blame ought not to be cast upon it. Here he begins to show that blame ought not to be cast upon the ruling nature either, and thus not upon the Creator, but upon human beings who are corrupted from themselves and therefore cannot resist depraved [Col. 0690D] movements.

The law is spiritual, but I am carnal—that is, I still bear a carnal body, in which I feel carnal movements. For so it is as long as one lives here. Thus the Apostle said, “But I am carnal,” because he did not yet have a spiritual body; just as he might say, “But I am mortal,” which would surely be understood as said only according to the body, because it had not yet been clothed with immortality.

Likewise, lest anyone suppose from the addition, “sold under sin,” that he had not yet been redeemed by Christ’s blood, this too can be understood according to what he says: “We ourselves also groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption as sons, the redemption of our body.” For if he calls himself sold under sin in the sense that [Col. 0691A] his body has not yet been redeemed from corruption—or sold at one time in the first transgression of the commandment, so as to have a corruptible body which weighs down the soul—what prevents the Apostle from saying this of himself here? He says it in such a way that it may be understood also in him, even if, speaking in his own person, he intends to include not himself alone but all who know themselves to struggle, with spiritual love, against the affection of the flesh without consenting to it (Wis. 9).

“I am sold,” he says, because what I do through the movement of concupiscence itself—not through an affection that consents to and performs it—I do not recognize in the standards of heavenly precepts. Or, “I do not understand” means “I do not approve.” And truly I do not approve what I do. For I do not do the good that I will; but the evil that I hate, that I do.

Let us not understand this [Col. 0691B] as though the Apostle wished to be chaste and yet were adulterous; or wished to be merciful and yet were cruel; or wished to be devout and yet were impious. Rather, in what sense? I will not to covet, and I covet. Even if I do not consent to concupiscence and do not follow my concupiscences, nevertheless I still covet.
