And this is what it means that I do not do the good that I will—that is, not to covet—but do the evil that I hate—that is, I covet—namely, I covet from the flesh.

For as long as the flesh is mortal, it cannot be entirely free from concupiscences. Concupiscences can indeed be diminished daily, but they cannot be wholly removed as long as one lives here. Therefore I do not do the good that I will—that is, that I should not covet—but I do the evil [Col. 0691C] that I hate—that is, I covet—although I do not yield, although I do not consent, so as to obey the desire for sin.

> “But if I do what I do not will, I agree with the law that it is good. But now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me. For I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh. For willing is present to me, but I do not find the accomplishing of the good. For I do not do the good that I will, but I do the evil that I do not will. But if I do what I do not will, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me.”

I said that I do not do what I will, but rather what I do not will. But if I do what I do not will—that is, if through the weakness of the flesh I covet what I would not wish to do—[Col. 0691D] I agree with the law, because I do not will what the law does not will. While I do what I do not will—that is, while I do not will to covet and yet covet—I agree with the law that it is good, because I myself do not will what the law does not will. For I do not will to covet, and the law says: “You shall not covet.” In this, then, that I will what the law also wills, I undoubtedly agree with the law; yet I covet, because I am not without sin.

My weakness does not fulfill the law, but my will praises the law. Therefore, if I do what I do not will, I agree with the law because I do not will it, not because I do it. What I do, however, is to covet, not to consent to concupiscence. The law says: “You shall not covet” (Exod. 20; Deut. 5), and I do not will to covet, but nevertheless I covet, although I do not give assent to my concupiscence and do not follow it. [Col. 0692A] For I resist; I turn my mind away; I withhold weapons; I keep my members under control; and nevertheless what I do not will happens in me. What the law does not will, I do not will along with the law; therefore I agree with the law.

“But now it is no longer I who do it.” “Now,” that is, now redeemed—I who formerly was sold under sin—now under grace, which has freed the delight of my will from consenting to desire: the mind is free, the flesh captive. “I do not do it,” because I do not consent, but sin that dwells in me—that is, the fuel of sin and concupiscence which is in my flesh—does it.

For when the sin that dwells in us works in us, then we do not perform it, provided that our will does not at all consent to it and also restrains the bodily members so that they do not obey its desires. For what does sin work in us against our will, except illicit desires alone? [Col. 0692B] If the assent of the will is not applied to these, there is indeed a movement, but no effect is allowed it. Therefore sin works these desires in us. If we obey them, we too perform them. But if we do not obey them, it is not we who perform that deed, but the sin dwelling in us.

But if we had no illicit desires, neither we nor sin would work anything evil in us. Moreover, we are said to perform the movement of illicit desire—when, by not obeying it, we do not perform it—because it is not an alien power of nature but the weakness of our own nature. We shall be wholly healed of this weakness when we have become immortal in both soul and body.

The entire guilt of this weakness and infirmity, from which illicit desires are stirred, which [Col. 0692C] the Apostle calls sin, was absolved by the sacrament of baptism, together with all the things which, while obeying it, we did, said, and thought. Nor would this weakness thereafter harm us if we never gave obedience to its illicit desires, whether by deed, speech, or silent assent, until it too should be healed.

But whereas every other sin is voluntary, so that it cannot occur at all apart from the will, this one alone, of which we are now speaking, happens even apart from the will, in the way we have explained. Yet it is called sin because it came about through sin and is the punishment of sin.

“It is not I,” he says, “who do it, but sin that dwells in me.” Yet the person is greatly mistaken who, while consenting to the concupiscence of his flesh, thinks that he can still say, “It is not I [Col. 0692D] who do it,” even if he hates it, because he consents. For if he covets, consents, and acts, how does he not himself do it, even if he grieves that he does it and groans heavily at being conquered?

I said that sin dwells in me. I said this because I know that good does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh. Perhaps what he said, “in me,” might otherwise have been understood; and therefore he explained it, adding, “That is, in my flesh,” and thereby showed most plainly what he was speaking about. It is as though he said: I am certain that this concupiscence, which opposes my striving in my body, is not good. The defect of the flesh in a good thing is not good. When it ceases to exist, there will still be flesh, but it will no longer be flesh that has been corrupted or is defective.

I do not say, “My flesh is not good”; rather, “Good does not dwell in my flesh,” which the habit of sin weighs down [Col. 0693A] and which I cannot conquer. Truly good does not dwell in my flesh, for this is why I cannot accomplish the good that I will. For willing is present to me—that is, good will is ready at hand for me—but I do not find the accomplishment of the good; that is, the perfection of the good is so far from me that I cannot find it.

This is to accomplish the good: that a person should not covet. But good is imperfect when he covets, even if he has not consented to concupiscence for evil. For good is then perfected when there are no evil desires; just as evil is then perfected when evil desires are obeyed. But when they are indeed present and are not obeyed, neither evil is perfected, because they are not obeyed, nor good, because they are present; rather, good is accomplished in some respect, because evil concupiscence is not consented to, [Col. 0693B] and evil remains in some respect because there is coveting. [Note: [Col. 0693D] An obscure passage.]

Therefore the Apostle did not say, “I do not find doing the good,” but “I do not find accomplishing it.” For he does much good, because he does what is written: “Do not follow your concupiscences” (Ecclus. 18); but he does not accomplish it, because he does not fulfill what is likewise written: “You shall not covet” (Exod. 20; Deut. 5).

But at some time there will be perfection of good and consummation of evil: the former will be supreme; the latter will be nonexistent. If we think this is to be hoped for in this mortal state, we are mistaken. For then it will be, when death no longer exists; and it will be there, where eternal life will be. Therefore the law said, “You shall not covet,” so that, finding ourselves lying in this sickness, we might seek the medicine of grace and, in that [Col. 0693C] commandment, know both what we ought always to strive for through progress toward the better in this mortal state, and what we may attain in that most blessed immortality, where concupiscence will not exist.

For if it were never to be accomplished that we should not covet and should have no evil desire whatever, it would never have been commanded. Until this is fulfilled in us, we must always acknowledge ourselves sinners and imperfect in goodness, fight against sin, and make progress in goodness. I do not find the perfection of the good as long as I live in this mortal state, because I cannot be wholly without concupiscence.

“For I do not do the good that I will,” and so forth. For I will not to have concupiscence, and yet I have it. He repeats what he said above, impressing it upon them and showing it, as it were, to the very slow, [Col. 0693D] awakening them from sleep. “For I do not do the good that I will, but I do the evil that I do not will.” For, as I said, I will to be entirely free from concupiscence, but I am unable. And I do not will to covet, but nevertheless I covet from the flesh, not from the mind. I do what I do not will; but if I do what I do not will—that is, if I covet unwillingly—it is not I who do it, because I do not consent in my mind; rather, the sin dwelling in me does it—that is, the fuel of sin and concupiscence dwelling in my flesh. This concupiscence, namely, and the lust or pleasure of sin, was transmitted to me from corrupted nature through the transgression of the first parent.

> “Therefore I find the law, when I wish to do good, [Col. 0694A] that evil is present with me. For I delight in the law of God according to the inward man, but I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin which is in my members. Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. Therefore I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin.”

Since I do not perform evil but wish to perform good, therefore I find the law good for me when I wish to do what it commands, because evil is present with me. I find the law good. The law is good. How do I prove it? Because I wish to fulfill it. Therefore, when I wish to do good, I find the law good—that is, [Col. 0694B] I find it useful, since it teaches what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.

The law is truly something good, because evil is present not with it but with me, arising from concupiscence, to which nevertheless I do not consent. The evil of depraved pleasure is present with me—that is, it is a defect in me and presses upon me, and does not permit me to accomplish the good I will. Evil is present with me—that is, the sin dwelling in my flesh, namely carnal concupiscence, which is called by the name of sin because every sin arises from it.

For whatever sins there are in words, deeds, or thoughts arise only from evil desire, only from illicit pleasure. Thus this illicit pleasure, which I nevertheless resist, is the evil present with me—that is, with my flesh. For my flesh is not flesh of another substance, nor flesh from [Col. 0694C] another principle, nor is the soul from God while the flesh is from a race of darkness; rather, sickness resists health, because it lies half-dead upon the road.

Truly evil is present with me, because while I delight in the law of God according to the inward man, I nevertheless see another law in my members resisting the law of my mind. Or thus: I truly agree with the law and find it something good and useful, although evil is present with me. For I delight in the law of God—that is, I delight along with the law which God gave, because whatever pleases it also pleases me, according to the affection of spirit and reason, that is, according to the inward man.

I indeed delight in it according to the affection of good will, but I cannot fulfill it, [Col. 0694D] because I see—that is, observe—another law, different from God’s law: a depraved prompting in my members. It is rightly called a law, because it was established in justice that the flesh of the person who refused to obey his Lord should not serve him. For God is above the human being, and the flesh below the human being. Because the human being despised what was above, he is tormented by what is below.

This law was born when the first law was despised and transgressed by humanity in Paradise. For when he ate the forbidden food, he immediately began to feel an illicit movement of the flesh (Gen. 2). I see another law—that is, the itching of sin—in my members: in the ears, to hear [Col. 0695A] illicit things; and in the eyes, to covet. I see such a law—the fuel of sin, which rules badly—in my members, resisting the law of my mind—that is, reason, which is a law naturally written in the heart of all—and taking me captive, that is, attempting to take me captive: compelling me to consent and fulfill the law of sin, that is, carnal concupiscence, which is in my members and there stirs illicit desires. It is more dangerous in proportion as it is nearer.

The Apostle shows four laws fighting one another: the law of God and the law of the mind, which agree together in good—that is, the law of Moses and the law of nature or of faith; likewise the law of prompting and the law of sin, which agree with each other in evil. In the opposition and conflict of these laws [Col. 0695B] lies the labor and struggle of all Christ’s soldiers, as they resist lest they agree with depraved laws.

We may also understand this “other law” and the “law of sin” not as two laws but as one: namely, the burden of mortality, through which it often comes about that even what is unlawful gives unjust pleasure. And “taking me captive” means taking my flesh captive to the law of sin—that is, to itself. For he said, “taking me captive,” because even in the flesh itself there is not an alien nature but our own. Unless carnal concupiscence, which he calls the law of sin, held it, it would certainly stir up in it no illicit desire to which the mind ought not to obey.

For in one respect a person is taken captive and in another is already free. The mind, which inwardly has its own other delights, does not consent but resists [Col. 0695C] the pleasures of the flesh. “I delight,” he says, “in the law of God”: the law delights me; what the law commands delights me; justice itself delights me according to the inward man. Here is freedom on the higher side. For freedom delights. The one who still does what is just out of fear is not yet delighted by God, and therefore is a slave. But when one no longer fears punishment but loves righteousness, in that very love and delight in righteousness one will be free.

“But I see,” he says, “another law in my members.” This is the weakness which remains. In this respect a person experiences captivity, where righteousness is not fulfilled. For where one delights in the law of God, one is not a captive but a friend of the law. Therefore it delights, because one is its friend. But freedom is not yet whole, not yet pure, [Col. 0695D] not yet complete, because eternity has not yet come. There is something dead in me and something living. Death contends; the mind does not consent. What, then, should be hoped for? “Wretched man that I am!” Though not wretched in mind, yet wretched as a human being in flesh. For one is not a human being in mind and not a human being in flesh; rather, one is a human being in mind and a human being in flesh. “Wretched man that I am!”

Thus the person who cries out that he is wretched implores, in mourning, the help of the Consoler. Nor is recognition of one’s own wretchedness a small approach to blessedness. “Wretched man that I am!” And since I cannot be freed from this wretchedness by myself, who will deliver me? Who can do this, unless someone great delivers me from this body of death—that is, from this corruptible body in which death is present?

This is the voice of a soldier fighting and groaning [Col. 0696A] in the labor of battle. To the one groaning and imploring the Deliverer’s help, the answer is given: “The grace of God will deliver you from this body of death through Jesus Christ our Lord,” when you have an immortal body in which no concupiscence remains.

For not all who end this life are delivered from this body of death. To depart from the body is one thing, to which the final day of this life compels all people; to be delivered from this body of death is another, which neither law nor one’s own powers, but God’s grace alone through Jesus Christ grants to his holy and faithful people. To be delivered from this body of death is, when every weakness of carnal concupiscence has been healed, not to receive the body for punishment but for glory.

For the ungodly certainly are not delivered from this body of death, [Col. 0696B] since the same bodies are restored to them for eternal torments. Then this body of death returns to the ungodly person and will never thereafter be released from it. Then there will not be eternal life for that person, but eternal death, because there is eternal punishment. But the righteous person will be delivered from this body of death, not so as not to have this body, but so as not to have it mortal and burdensome. He will indeed have the same body, but immortal, light, and without affliction.

In these words, as was said above, the Apostle is rightly understood to have signified not only himself in his own person but also others established under grace. Since I delight in the law of God according to the inward man and see another law in my members, therefore I myself serve the law of God with my mind, loving righteousness and resisting concupiscence, [Col. 0696C] but with my flesh I serve the law of sin by coveting. I myself do these things. For there is not one person in the mind and another in the flesh; rather, I myself am in the mind and I in the flesh—not two, but one composed of both.

With my mind I serve the law of God in Christ’s freedom, but with my flesh the law of sin through Adam’s oldness. I am raised up by the joy of newness; I am weighed down by the burden of oldness. I have war against myself. But in the respect in which I displease myself, I am joined to God. And in the respect in which I am joined to God, I shall be fit to conquer myself, because he who overcomes all things is with me.

With my mind I serve the law of God, willing what it wills and not willing what it does not will; but with my flesh I serve the law of sin, not indeed by giving my members over to committing iniquities, but only by coveting, although I do not give my hands to illicit concupiscence [Col. 0696D].

## CHAPTER VIII

> “Therefore there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free from the law of sin and death. For what was impossible for the law, in that it was weak through the flesh, God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and concerning sin, condemned sin in the flesh, so that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.”

Accordingly, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but the law of sin with my flesh. And indeed I—the one in whom I signify any righteous person established under grace—serve the law of God with my mind [Col. 0697A]. Therefore there is now no condemnation, though there was before, for those who are in Christ Jesus, in whom all things have been forgiven them through baptism. While they were not in Christ and consented to concupiscence, condemnation was theirs. But now, since they are in Christ and resist concupiscence, there is no condemnation for them, although they experience concupiscence through the flesh; for it is not combatants but the defeated who are condemned. Nor is it condemnable that fleshly desires arise, but that they are obeyed unto sin. There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ. And lest you suppose that this would happen only later, “now” has therefore been added. Later expect this: that there will not even be concupiscence within you against which you struggle, because it itself will no longer exist. Therefore there is now no condemnation for them, although another law in their members still resists the law of their mind [Col. 0697B].

There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ—I mean those who do not walk according to the flesh, that is, who do not act according to fleshly desire. For some are called Christians and yet walk according to the desires of their heart. To distinguish them, it is said that there is now no condemnation for those Christians who do not walk according to the flesh, that is, who do not live carnally. Truly there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ; for not the law of the letter on Mount Sinai, but the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death, through which law there was condemnation. That law of sin is still present in my members, but it no longer makes me guilty, because I have been freed from it; and therefore, being free, I fight against it.

The law of Moses is spiritual, but [Col. 0697C] not a law of life, because it does not give life by forgiving sins. But the law established by the Holy Spirit is a law of life, because it gives life by remitting sins. The law of Moses is God’s law, but a law of deeds: the law of works, the law which commands but does not help; the law which reveals sin but does not remove it. But the law of the Spirit is the law of faith, the law of grace, the law of mercy, the law which removes sin and frees from the law of the members—which is not God’s law but the law of sin and death, because it makes persons guilty and produces death. This, then, is the meaning: “For the law of the Spirit of life has freed [me] from the law of sin and death.” That good law has freed me from this evil law. And this is in Christ Jesus, that is, in the blood and grace of Jesus Christ. It has freed me—that is, any righteous person established under grace—in Christ, so that I do not [Col. 0697D] consent to the law of sin and death, that is, to concupiscence.

And the manner in which I have been set free and escaped condemnation is subsequently explained: for what was impossible for the law, God accomplished in Christ, namely, condemning sin and giving righteousness. It was impossible for the natural or written law to free from the law of sin and death, because it could neither remove sin nor conquer death, nor could it make anyone obedient to itself or perfect. What was impossible for the law God did—an impossibility in which the law itself was weakened through the flesh [Col. 0698A], that is, because it could not be fulfilled by the weak through the flesh, for it is fulfilled through the Spirit. For the law is understood to be weakened because it is not fulfilled, not because it is itself weak, but because it makes people weak by threatening punishment and not helping through grace. It is said to have been weakened through the flesh because the flesh does not fulfill what is fulfilled through the Spirit, that is, through spiritual grace. For, where grace was absent, the flesh resisted with the utmost force.

And the law was weakened through the flesh—that is, through fleshly desires and through the tinder of vices which is in the flesh—because the flesh rebelled excessively and, upon hearing the law, stirred concupiscence more strongly. Thus the law of the letter was weakened through the flesh: it did not make righteous those given over to the flesh, since the flesh powerfully opposed the fulfillment of the law, and the law had no strength by which to break the assault of the flesh. Or the law was weakened through the flesh, that is, through a fleshly understanding and a fleshly observance; it was weak in this respect, not in itself. But what the weak law could not do, God did: sending his Son [Col. 0698B] in the likeness of sinful flesh, he also condemned sin in the flesh through sin.

God sent his Son—that is, one proper to himself, consubstantial and coeternal with him—meaning that he ordained him to become incarnate, so that, remaining what he was, he might assume what he was not. He sent him in the likeness of sinful flesh, not because his flesh was unreal, but in the likeness of sinful flesh because it was flesh, though not flesh of sin. For our flesh is flesh of sin because it was generated through the exercise of lust. His flesh alone, however, was not flesh of sin, because his mother conceived him not through concupiscence but through grace. Yet it was the likeness of sinful flesh: that is, it was capable of suffering and death; it could be nourished, hunger, thirst, sleep, grow weary, and die [Col. 0698C]. For death and weakness exist only because of sin. And certainly that body was mortal and weak, like other bodies.

Sinful flesh has death and sin; but the likeness of sinful flesh had death without sin. If it had sin, it would be sinful flesh. If it did not have death, it would not be the likeness of sinful flesh. Such was the Savior’s coming. “And through sin he condemned sin in the flesh”: that is, by assuming the flesh of sinful humankind and teaching how we ought to live, he condemned sin in that very flesh, so that our spirit, aflame with love of eternal things, might not be led captive into consent to lust. For Adam did not incur death except by sinning, and Christ assumed mortal flesh. Therefore death is called “sin,” since it came about through sin—just as one speaks of the Greek language or Latin language, meaning not the bodily organ itself but what is done through that bodily organ. Greek language means Greek words, not because the words are a tongue, but because words are spoken through the tongue.

Thus the Lord’s “sin” was made “from sin,” because he assumed flesh from that very mass which had deserved death through sin [Col. 0698D]. Or, to say it more briefly: Mary, descended from Adam, was dead because of sin, unless she had been divinely exempted; and the Lord’s flesh, from Mary, was dead for the destruction of sins. Therefore, “through sin”—that is, through the death which befell humanity through sin—he condemned sin in the flesh. [Col. 0699A] Or “through sin” means through the sacrifice offered for sins. For in the Law, a sacrifice for sin was called “sin.” And the Lord’s flesh was such a “sin.” Therefore, through sin—that is, through the sacrifice which he became for sins—he condemned sin, so that the righteousness of the law, that is, the righteousness which it commanded or promised, might be fulfilled in us through the Spirit who helps. This is to say: the law of the letter might be fulfilled in us through the Spirit of life.

I mean in us who do not walk—that is, act—according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. Flesh was made from earth, but spirit was given by God. Each therefore desires that from which it comes: flesh, earthly things; spirit, heavenly things. If, then, spirit overcomes flesh, heavenly things operate in it. But if it consents to flesh, earthly things prevail over it. Therefore those do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit who attend not to earthly and fleshly things but to heavenly and spiritual things, and who observe the law not carnally but spiritually [Col. 0699B]. For what is it to walk according to the flesh? To consent to fleshly concupiscences. And what is it to walk according to the Spirit? To be helped by the Spirit in the mind and not to obey the flesh’s concupiscences. Thus the righteousness of the law is fulfilled in us through Christ: not yet that righteousness which says, “You shall not covet” (Exod. 20), but meanwhile that which commands, “Do not go after your concupiscences” (Ecclus. 18).

> “For those who are according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh; but those who are according to the Spirit, on the things of the Spirit. For the prudence of the flesh is death, but the prudence of the Spirit is life and peace. For the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God; for it is not subject to God’s law, nor indeed can it be. But those who are in the flesh cannot please God.” [Col. 0699C]

Righteousness is truly fulfilled in those who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. For those who are according to the flesh—that is, those who consent to flesh and conduct their lives by following its appetite—set their minds on the things of the flesh: they know fleshly things, are inquisitive about fleshly matters, and seem to find a pleasing savor in temporal and earthly things which belong to, or pertain to, the flesh. Therefore such persons are not justified. But those who are according to the Spirit—that is, who consent to the Holy Spirit and are in harmony with him, so as to live spiritually—perceive the things of the Spirit: they inwardly perceive divine and spiritual goods and are filled with spiritual sweetness. Therefore the righteousness of the law is fulfilled in them through charity. [Col. 0699D]

Truly, those who set their minds on the things of the flesh are not justified; rather, those who perceive the things of the Spirit are. For the end of things demonstrates this, since the wisdom of the flesh produces death, while the wisdom of the Spirit produces life. Punishment or reward plainly shows both that those who die were not justified and that those who attained life fulfilled righteousness. For the prudence of the flesh is eternal death, but the prudence of the Spirit is life and peace.

The prudence of the flesh is to conceal one’s heart by schemes, to veil one’s thought with words, to represent false things as true, and true things as deceptive. This prudence, indeed, young people learn by practice; children learn it at a price [Col. 0700A]. Those who know it grow proud by despising others; those who do not know it, submissive and fearful, admire it in others, because they love that same duplicity when it is veiled under the name of fairness, while perversity of mind is called polish. It commands its adherents to seek the heights of honors, to rejoice in the emptiness of acquired temporal glory, and to repay wrongs inflicted by others with multiplied wrongs. When strength is available, it commands yielding to none who resist; when the possibility of force is lacking, whatever it cannot accomplish through malice it counterfeits by a peaceless kindness. Rightly, then, such prudence is called the death of the soul.

But the prudence of the Spirit—that is, the wisdom of the righteous—is to feign nothing by appearances, to disclose one’s thought by one’s words, to love true things as they are, to avoid false things, to bestow good things [Col. 0700B] freely, to endure evils more willingly than to inflict them, to seek no revenge for an injury, and to count it gain to endure reproaches for truth. This prudence is the life and peace of the soul, not only in the age to come but also in the present. The definition of prudence, moreover, is commonly explained in terms of seeking goods and avoiding evils. For the same nature of the soul has the prudence of the flesh when it pursues lower things, and the prudence of the Spirit when it chooses higher things, just as the nature of water freezes through cold and melts through heat.

Through the prudence of the flesh the Jews worshipped God in order that matters might go well for them in the flesh; and therefore they were dead in soul. But through the prudence of the Spirit the righteous worship God freely—that is, because he himself is good, not because he gives other goods, which he gives even to those who are not good [Col. 0700C]. Therefore through this spiritual prudence they already live in soul and have peace, being in accord with the divine will, loving their neighbors, and not avenging themselves when injured. Much more, however, in the future they will have eternal life and the peace of everlasting tranquility. Conversely, those prudent in a fleshly way—that is, those who desire temporal goods, fear temporal evils, shrewdly avenge their own injuries, and trust natural reasonings more than divine pronouncements—will suffer the eternal death of soul and body.

And truly through such prudence soul and body die. For the wisdom of the flesh—that is, wisdom attentive to fleshly things and zealously engaged in them—is hostile to God, whom it does not establish [Col. 0700D] as its end. “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world will be made an enemy of God” (Jas. 4). It is hostile to God when it thinks that the Lord can do nothing beyond what appears in the natures of things; it is hostile to God because it does not obey his will. For it is not subject to God’s law. And acting against the law is being hostile to God. Not that one can harm God in any way, but whoever resists God’s will harms himself. Therefore, when it says that the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God, we should not understand this as though such hostility could injure God. It is hostile by resisting, not by harming. Rather, it harms the person in whom the wisdom of the flesh exists, because it is a vice. It harms the nature in which it exists. Let the vice be driven out, and nature will be healed.

This fleshly wisdom is not subject to God’s law; indeed, it cannot be subject to it [Col. 0701A]. I did not say that a human being cannot; I did not say that the soul cannot; I did not say that flesh cannot. Rather, I said that the wisdom of the flesh cannot—that is, the vice cannot, not nature. It is as if one said: “Lameness is not subject to straight walking; indeed, it cannot be.” The foot can do so, but lameness cannot. Remove lameness, and you will see straight walking. But so long as lameness exists, it cannot do so. Let there be no wisdom of the flesh, and there is the human being. Thus it is said, “It is not subject to God’s law, nor indeed can it be,” as though one were to say, “Snow does not warm, nor indeed can it.” For so long as it is snow, it does not warm. But it can melt and boil, so as to warm. Yet when it does this, it is no longer snow.

[Col. 0701B] Likewise, prudence or wisdom of the flesh is so called when the soul desires temporal goods as great goods. For so long as this desire remains in the soul, it cannot be subject to God’s law, that is, it cannot fulfill what the law commands. But if it begins to desire spiritual goods and to despise temporal ones, it will cease to be fleshly prudence, and the spirit will not resist the law. The wisdom of the flesh is not subject to the divine law. Nor do I say only this, but also that those who are in the flesh—that is, who yield to the pleasures of the flesh—cannot please God. For those are in the flesh who put their trust in the flesh, follow their own concupiscences, dwell in them, delight in their pleasures, and place a blessed and happy life in their enjoyments. Therefore, as long as they are such, they can do nothing pleasing to God.

> [Col. 0701C] “But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person does not belong to him. But if Christ is in you, the body indeed is dead because of sin, but the Spirit lives because of righteousness. And if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies, because of his Spirit dwelling in you.”

Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh, and therefore you please God. You still live in this age, indeed, but you are not in the flesh because you do not lie immersed in fleshly pleasure; rather, you have transcended fleshly desires. For lest anyone suppose that the preceding statement—“those who are in the flesh cannot please God”—was said of people who had not yet departed from this life, he most aptly added: “But you are not in the flesh.” He was certainly speaking to persons still situated in this life, and yet he said that they were not in the flesh. He wrote indeed to the Romans, but he spoke to the whole Church of the elect: he spoke to the wheat, not the chaff; to the hidden mass, not the visible straw [Col. 0701D].

You are not in the flesh because you do not perform the works of the flesh by consenting to fleshly concupiscence. But you are in the Spirit because, according to the inner person, you delight in the law of God. And this is what is meant by “if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you.” For if you rely on your own spirit, you are still in the flesh. Thus [Col. 0702A] you are not in the flesh so as to be in the Spirit of God. For if God’s Spirit departs, the human spirit, by its own weight, rolls back into the flesh. It returns to fleshly deeds; it returns to worldly concupiscences. Therefore hold free will in such a way that you implore help. You are not in the flesh. And is this by your own strength? Far be it. Whence, then? “If indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you.” Then you are not in the flesh, but have God’s Spirit as an indweller.

But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person does not belong to him: that is, he is not possessed by Christ, nor is he a member of Christ. He had said “the Spirit of God” and then added “the Spirit of Christ,” because there are not two Holy Spirits belonging separately to each, one of the Father and another of the Son; rather, there is one Spirit of the Father and the Son. Just as my soul—that is, my spirit—gives life to all the members of my body, so Christ’s Spirit gives life to all the members of Christ’s body, that is, to all his elect [Col. 0702B].

But if anyone does not have Christ’s Spirit—that is, if anyone is not animated by Christ’s Spirit, if anyone does not live by Christ’s Spirit—that person is not a member or possession of Christ, but of the devil. Charity, moreover, is evidence that Christ’s Spirit is in the heart which it has filled. Does the person have Christ’s Spirit whose mind is scattered by hatreds, swollen by pride, embittered by anger even to the breaking apart of the mind, tormented by greed, or enervated by lust? Certainly not. For where Christ’s Spirit dwells, it causes friends and enemies to be loved, earthly things to be despised, heavenly things to be ardently desired, the flesh to be worn down because of vices, and the mind to be restrained from concupiscences. This Spirit is, as it were, [Col. 0702C] a mark of divine possession. Whoever entirely lacks it does not belong to Christ.

But if Christ is in you—who dwells in the same place as his Spirit, and nowhere else—the body indeed is dead, not because of earthly frailty, because it was made from the dust of earth, but because of sin. I do not say “mortal,” but “dead.” For before it was changed into that incorruption which is promised in the resurrection of the saints, it could have been mortal without being destined to die, just as this body of ours could be liable to sickness without ever being destined to fall sick. For whose flesh is incapable of becoming sick, even if it should perish from some other cause before becoming sick? So too the first human being’s body was already mortal before he sinned [Col. 0702D]. That mortality would have undergone transformation into eternal incorruption if righteousness—that is, obedience—had remained in the human being. But the mortal body itself was not made dead except because of sin: for as soon as the human being transgressed the command, death itself, like a fatal disease, was conceived in his members. He passes on this sickness of death to all of us; and through it we necessarily die.

Therefore our body is not merely destined to die because of the coming departure of the soul; it is also already dead because of the weakness of flesh and blood. It still indeed has life, but compared with that body which will exist in the resurrection it is found to be dead, though it still has a soul. Thus the body is still dead because of sin, but the spirit now lives because of righteousness [Col. 0703A]. This life comes about through faith, because “the righteous person lives by faith” (Hab. 2; Rom. 1; Heb. 12). For the soul, now devout though formerly impious, is said to have revived from death and to live because of the righteousness of faith.

Meanwhile, the Savior’s grace has granted us this: that the soul now lives through righteousness, just as it had been dead through sin. This was said so that people would not suppose they receive either no benefit or only a small benefit from Christ’s grace because they must necessarily die bodily. They should attend to the fact that the body indeed still bears the desert of sin, being bound by the condition of death, but that the spirit has already begun to live through the righteousness of faith, though it too had been extinguished by a kind of death of unbelief. [Col. 0703B] Therefore, he says, do not consider the gift bestowed upon you to be small: because Christ is in you, while the body is dead because of sin, your spirit now lives because of righteousness.

Nor should you despair concerning the life of the body itself; rather, believe that, if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies. Or the connection may be understood thus: your spirit indeed already lives; but if God’s Spirit dwells in you, your body too will live, just as Christ’s body, already raised, lives. He had said, “But if Christ is in you”; he added, “And if the Spirit of peace dwells in you.” The Spirit whom he had called Christ’s Spirit he then called the Spirit of peace, because where Christ is, there the Holy Spirit undoubtedly dwells; and the Spirit of Christ and of God is one [Col. 0703C].

Since, moreover, the future transformation in that resurrection will possess not only no death—which came about through sin—but not even mortality, which the animate body had before sin, he now says: “He who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies,” so that they may no longer merely not be dead, but may not even be mortal, when the animate body rises as spiritual, this mortal puts on immortality, and mortality is swallowed up by life. For when, defining the grace of the present time, he said that the body was dead because of sin—since the desert of sin, namely the necessity of death, remains while it has not yet been renewed by resurrection—he said that the spirit lives because of righteousness. Although we are still burdened by the body of this death, through the renewal begun in the righteousness of faith we already breathe freely according to the inner person.

Yet, lest human ignorance should have no hope for the resurrection of the body, he says that this very body which in the present age he called dead because of the desert of sin will in the future be made alive because of the desert of righteousness—not only so that it becomes living from being dead, but also immortal from being mortal [Col. 0703D]. For by God’s gift bestowed upon the soul, that is, by the Holy Spirit, not only does the soul receiving it become saved, peaceful, and holy, but the body itself also will be made alive and will be most pure in its own nature. “He will give life,” he says, “to your mortal bodies,” not because of your merits but because of his gifts, that is, because of his Spirit dwelling in you.

[Col. 0704A] When the human being has been perfected by these stages, no substance is found to be evil. Nor is the law evil, which shows a human being in what chains of sins he lies, so that by faith, after imploring the Liberator’s help, he may deserve both to be released and raised up and firmly established. Thus, in the first state, which is before the law, there is no struggle against the pleasures of this age. In the second, which is under the law, we struggle but are defeated. In the third, which is under grace, we struggle and conquer. In the fourth, which is in the resurrection, we do not struggle, but rest in perfect and eternal peace, because then nothing resists us when we do not resist God. That which is lower than we are is made subject to us—a subjection which did not occur because we had abandoned God, who is above us [Col. 0704B].

> “Therefore, brothers, we are debtors—not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live.”

I have said that you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed God’s Spirit dwells in you; that Christ is in you; and that God will give life even to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit dwelling in you. Therefore, brothers, having received help—divine aid extended to us from above, the arm of the Lord, help extended to us by the Holy Spirit—we are debtors: that is, we ought, as a matter of obligation, to serve not the flesh but the divine Spirit dwelling in us and bestowing such great goods. We are debtors, I say, but not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh—that is, to conduct our life according to fleshly pleasures and allurements [Col. 0704C].

For in this way your mortal bodies too will be given life because of God’s indwelling Spirit: that is, life will transform death in itself by putting death to death, if you strive to live not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. Immortality of the flesh has been promised us because of God’s Spirit, whom we have within us. Therefore, brothers, if we wish to attain this immortality, we are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to its allurements, for it draws us to death; but rather to the Holy Spirit, striving to direct our life according to him, because he has prepared eternal life for us. And we shall reach it if we now follow his will.

[Col. 0704D] And the outcome of each course is indeed so. For if you live according to the flesh, you will die: that is, if you live according to death, the whole person will die. If you live according to the flesh’s concupiscences, you will die perpetually in both body and soul. But if by the Holy Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh—that is, by living according to God, extinguishing the flesh’s pleasures and desires—you will live blessedly forever. This is our task in this life: daily, by the Spirit, to put to death the deeds of the flesh, to afflict, lessen, restrain, and destroy them. For how many things no longer delight those who are making progress which formerly delighted them! When something did delight, yet was not consented to, it was being put to death. If it no longer delights, it has been put to death.

> “For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. For you have not again received a spirit of slavery in fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’ For the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God. And if children, then heirs: indeed heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ, provided that we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified with him.” [Col. 0705A]

Truly, you shall live, if by the Holy Spirit you put to death the works of the flesh. For now you are children of God, and with him you shall reign for ever. And this is what these words of the Apostle show: You shall live, because you are children of God. For all who are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.

When the Apostle had said, “But if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you shall live,” that is, those desires of the flesh—to which not consenting is a great praise, and not having them is perfection—it was to be feared that someone might presume upon the Holy Spirit for putting to death the deeds of the flesh. Therefore, lest the human spirit here exalt itself and boast that it is capable and strong for this work, he added and said: “For all who are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.” Not those who live according to their flesh, not those who are led by the pleasure of the flesh, not those who are led by their own spirit, not those who are led by the Law; but all who are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.

The Spirit of God by whom they are led is himself the Spirit by whom the deeds of the flesh are put to death, because he gives the self-restraint by which desire is checked, subdued, and conquered. They are led by the Spirit of God so that they themselves may do what must be done, and, when they have done it, may give thanks to him by whom they are led. For the Spirit of God who leads them is the helper and guide of those who act. Thus they are led so that they may act; and for this purpose they are shown what they ought to do, so that they may do it as it ought to be done—namely, with delight, and with delight in righteousness. For those who are led by the Spirit of God are led and stirred by charity.

Therefore they are led not by the letter but by the Spirit; not by a Law commanding, threatening, and promising, but by a Spirit exhorting, enlightening, and helping. This is not because they themselves do nothing, but lest they do no good, they are led by the Good One so that they may act. For the better a person becomes as a son, the more abundantly the good Spirit is given to him by the Father.

But to be led is more than to be governed. For one who is governed does something, and is therefore governed in order that he may act rightly. But one who is led is scarcely understood to be doing anything himself. Thus what the Holy Spirit does is what God works, “all in all.” Nor can free will do anything better in us than commend itself to him who cannot act wrongly.

I said that you are children of God if you are led by the Spirit of God. And you are truly children. For you have not received a spirit of slavery, but of sonship. “You have not received again the spirit of slavery,” that is, as once under the Law. This spirit of slavery is not again yours, but rather the spirit of freedom. For the Spirit of the Law and of the Gospel is the same, but because of the different works, it is differently named. To the Jews it was a spirit of slavery, but to Christians it is a spirit of freedom.

For by the same Spirit—that is, the finger of God—by whom the Law was written upon tablets of stone, fear was instilled into those who did not yet understand grace, so that through the Law they might be convicted of their weakness and sins, and the Law might become for them a pedagogue by which they would be brought to the grace that is in faith in Christ. That fear was servile, because through it righteousness was loved less than punishment was feared.

Therefore the Spirit is now given to you not for fear but for love, so that we may be not servants but children. Whoever still does good merely because he fears punishment and does not love God is not yet among the children. For if God’s command is performed from fear of punishment, not from love of righteousness, it is performed slavishly, not freely—and therefore it is not performed at all. For no fruit is good which does not proceed from the root of charity.

In the New Testament you have not again received a spirit of slavery in fear, as formerly in the Old; but you have received “the Spirit of adoption as sons,” [Col. 0706B] that is, the Spirit who has adopted you as God’s sons, in whom we cry out—that is, say with the whole affection of the mind—“Abba, Father.” The Spirit himself makes us call God our Father. And if he is our Father, then we are his children.

Children cry, “Abba, Father.” *Abba* means the same as “Father.” For *Abba* is Hebrew, while *pater* (“father”) is Greek or Latin. But because of both peoples, namely those of circumcision and of uncircumcision, who have come to the cornerstone—that is, to Christ—these two names of identical meaning have been placed together. For faithful Hebrews cry, “Abba!” while the Gentiles cry, “Father!”

This cry is of the heart, not of the throat or lips. It sounds inwardly in God’s ears. When they cry, moreover, they ask for something. And what do they ask except what was said of them: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5)? [Col. 0706C] What is this petition except hunger and thirst for righteousness?

Let those who are under the Law therefore pass over to this, so that from servants they may become children; yet not so that they cease to be servants, but so that, as children, they may freely serve the Lord and Father. We have received the Spirit of adoption, through whom we call God our Father; for the divine Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit—that is, makes our spirit recognize and understand—that we are children of God.

For it belongs to him that we become one body of the only-begotten Son of God. And through the fact that the Holy Spirit himself pours charity into us, which makes us imitators of the divine goodness, so that we may love our enemies and do good to those who hate us (Luke 6), just as the heavenly Father “makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5), [Col. 0706D] he clearly testifies to our mind that we are children of God, whose goodness we follow according to our measure. For it belongs to children to imitate their father. The Spirit of God, by making us act well, bears witness that we are children of God.

But if we are children, we shall also be heirs—that is, sharers in the same glory. We are not children in vain, but shall gain a great benefit from this, because we shall be heirs of our Father; indeed, he himself will be our inheritance, as we sing in the Psalm: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. 15).

We shall indeed become heirs of God. But if this seems too little, let us hear further cause for greater rejoicing: we shall be co-heirs with Christ—that is, heirs together with Christ, possessing with him the inheritance of blessedness which he himself possesses. We become heirs of God when we begin to possess what belongs to God: the glory of incorruption and immortality, and “the hidden treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2). [Col. 0707A] We become co-heirs with Christ when he himself reforms the body of our lowliness so that it is conformed to the body of his glory (Phil. 3).

We shall be heirs of God, but we shall not obtain this inheritance through his death, since he cannot die; rather, he himself is the inheritance which we shall receive from him. Yet because, when we are called, we are still little children and less capable of contemplating spiritual things, divine mercy has lowered itself to the level of our thought, so that we might strive somehow to perceive what we do not perceive plainly and clearly. What we see in a riddle dies when we begin to see face to face (1 Cor. 13).

It is therefore fittingly said that what is taken away will die. But “when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part will be taken away” (ibid.). Thus in some manner the Father dies for us in the riddle, and the same one becomes our inheritance when he is possessed face to face—not because he dies, but because our imperfect vision of him reaches perfect vision. Yet unless that former vision had nourished us, we would not become fit for the other, most full and most clear vision.

We shall also be co-heirs of Christ when, at the end of the age, death has been swallowed up in victory (1 Cor. 15). He did not fear to have co-heirs, because his inheritance does not become narrow if many possess it. [Col. 0707C] For if a man has an only son, he rejoices the more in him because he alone will possess everything, and will not have brothers to divide the inheritance with him, leaving him poor. But God sent into this world his Only-begotten, whom he had begotten and through whom he had created all things, so that he might not remain alone but might have adopted brothers who would possess with him the inheritance of eternal life.

That inheritance, I say, in which we shall be his co-heirs, is not diminished by the multitude of children, nor made narrower by the number of co-heirs; rather, it is as great for many as for few, as great for each as for all. We shall be his co-heirs, provided that we suffer with him: that is, if we now become participants in his sufferings; [Col. 0707D] if we do not refuse to suffer for his name what he suffered for us; if we endure adversity not for human favor or temporal advantage, but for love of him, in order that we may also be glorified with him—that is, glorified with him as his co-heirs and participants in his glory.

For we shall be glorified with him, if his grace grants this to us, because “when he appears, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3).

> “For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us.”

Lest anyone think burdensome what he had said—that we must suffer with Christ—the Apostle immediately adds that the sufferings of this temporal life are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that is to be revealed [Col. 0708A] in us. By this he shows that one who looks to things unseen—that is, to the joys of everlasting blessedness—accounts every tribulation that happens to him, however cruel and however long-lasting it may seem, light and momentary, even if he is subjected to tortures, racks, and claws.

For at the time when his body is worn down by punishments, if he looks to the future glory and considers how through these torments the body of his lowliness will be transformed, so as to become conformed to the body of the glory of God’s Only-begotten, he will regard present tribulation as very small, but will judge the reward of future blessedness to be immeasurably great. And the more he sees tribulation and punishments multiplied for himself, the more he understands the weight and greatness of glory to be accumulated for himself.

In saying now, “I consider,” the Apostle does not himself doubt, but rebukes doubters, just as elsewhere, speaking to certain persons who despised him, he says: “But I think that I too have the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 7). [Col. 0708B] One who says “I think” or “I consider” appears to doubt. But he rebukes; he does not doubt. So also the Lord himself, who knows all things, rebuking the future unbelief of humankind, says: “When the Son of Man comes, do you suppose that he will find faith on earth?” (Luke 18).

For even people sometimes cast doubt reproachfully concerning matters they know with certainty: that is, they use the language of doubt while not doubting in their heart. Thus someone might be indignant with his servant and say: “Do you despise me? I think that I am your master.” So too the Apostle, in saying “I consider,” rebukes those who did not consider—or do not consider—this.

For some people, because they give too little attention to future joys, think unbearable the present evils that they endure. The Apostle therefore rebukes their faint-heartedness or unbelief: “If we suffer with him,” he says, “we shall also be glorified with him.” And truly we shall attain glorification through suffering. For I consider—what you do not consider—that is, I know without doubt—that the sufferings of this present time, which is so brief, are not worthy: that is, even taken all together they are not worthy to merit the future glory which will be revealed in us, [Col. 0708C] that is, will be manifested in such a way as to be in us, because it will remain in each one of us and appear outwardly.

That is, even if someone suffered every harsh punishment that can be endured during the present life, all those sufferings would not be a merit worthy of attaining the future glory which, with every veil removed, will be revealed in us, when we receive that “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2).

> “For the expectation of the creation awaits the revelation of the children of God. For the creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope, because the creation itself also shall be freed from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.”

Truly glory shall be revealed in us who now endure troubles for God, because this glory is that we may appear as children of God. This, indeed, is what we await. For “the expectation of the creation awaits the revelation of the children of God.”

This means: for even that which suffers in us when we put to death the deeds of the flesh; when we hunger or thirst through abstinence; when by chastity we restrain the delight of desire; when by patience we bear the wounds of injuries and the stings of insults; when, neglecting and rejecting our own pleasures, we labor for the fruit of Mother Church—whatever suffers in us in this and similar affliction, is creation. [Col. 0709A] For body and soul suffer, and they are certainly creation; and they await the revelation of the children of God, that is, they await the time when what has been called to glory will appear in the glory to which it has been called.

Because the only-begotten Son of God cannot be called a creature, since through him all things were made which God made, we too are distinctly called “creation” before that manifestation of glory, and distinctly called children of God, although we receive this by adoption. For he is Son by nature, not by adoption.

Therefore the expectation of the creation—that is, our expectation—awaits the revelation of the children of God: namely, when what has been promised appears; when what we now are in hope becomes manifest in reality. “For we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3). This is the revelation of the children of God which the expectation of the creation now awaits.

This does not mean that creation awaits the revelation of another nature which is not creation; rather, it itself, being now what it is, awaits the time when it shall be what it is to become. [Col. 0709C] It is as though one said: while a painter is at work and colors are laid before him and made ready for his work, the expectation of the colors awaits the manifestation of the image—not because then they will be other colors or cease to be colors, but because they will possess another dignity.

I said that the expectation of the creation awaits the revelation of the children of God. I said this rightly. For creation itself is still subjected to vanity—that is, to temporal things, which are vanity because they cannot fulfill what they promise and vanish away, that is, fail and pass away. For Solomon says: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity. What profit has a man in all his labor which he labors under the sun?” (Eccl. 1).

Thus the human creature, to whom the Lord said, “In toil you shall eat bread” (Gen. 3), is subjected to vanity. And it is subjected not willingly, because a human being sinned voluntarily, but was not condemned voluntarily. For sin was voluntary—that is, acting against the command of truth—but the penalty of sin, namely being subjected to deception, was not voluntary.

This creation, as I said, sinned voluntarily and became an enemy to truth; but it was not voluntarily subjected to vanity in order to be punished according to merit. A human being willingly loves vanity when, abandoning the solidity of truth, he follows things based on opinion, that is, changeable things. [Col. 0709D] For vanities are things that change and pass away. But when he pays the penalties he has deserved, he is unwillingly subjected to vanity, as it was subjected in the human being who sinned.

For creation is unwillingly subjected to vanity because the human being who willingly abandoned the state of inborn constancy, pressed under the weight of just mortality, unwillingly serves the corruption of his own changeableness. Therefore creation was not voluntarily subjected to vanity, but because of him who subjected it in hope: that is, because of his justice and mercy, who neither left sin unpunished nor wished the sinner to be incurable.

It was subjected to vanity in hope because of the mercy of the one who frees through the remission of sins and the adoption of grace. Therefore, in the hope by which it hopes to cling to the truth which is to be contemplated, it is meanwhile subjected to vanity.

For this creation—that is, the human being himself—although he lost, because of sin, the seal of the image, yet with the image not altogether entirely erased, remained merely a creature. And this creature itself, [Col. 0710B] that is, even that which is not yet called the perfect form of children but merely creation, “shall be freed from the bondage of corruption.”

Accordingly, when he says, “It too shall be freed,” he makes us understand: it too, like us. That is, we must not despair even of those who are not yet called children of God because they have not yet believed, but are merely creation; for they too will believe and will be freed from the bondage of corruption, just as we who are already children of God, although it has not yet appeared what we shall be.

Therefore it shall be freed from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God: that is, they too will become free from servants, and from corruptible beings incorruptible in the perfect life possessed by the children of God. For then creation will be rescued from the bondage of corruption when, rising again, it is raised to the incorruptible glory of the children of God.

For the penalty of corruption now weighs upon the elect, but then the glory of incorruption exalts them. And as regards the burdens of present necessity, no freedom is now apparent in God’s children; just so, in the glory of the freedom to come, no slavery will then appear in them. [Col. 0710C]

Thus creation, stripped of the slavery of corruption and attaining the dignity of freedom, is transformed into the glory of the children of God, because, united to God through the Spirit, it is shown to have passed beyond and overcome, as it were, the very fact of being creation. Then it clings to him so fully that nothing from the corruption conquered by resurrection opposes him any longer in its love; rather, it becomes united to the glory of its Redeemer.

With reference to this Redeemer one may understand the statement, “It too shall be freed,” namely that the Lord himself has already been freed from corruption.

> “For we know that every creature groans and labors in childbirth even until now. And not only it, but we ourselves also, having the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves as we await adoption as sons, the redemption of our body.”

Truly creation was subjected to vanity unwillingly. For it groans because of this: “For we know that every creature groans.” Or, it will be freed from the bondage of corruption; for it groans for this reason, that it has not yet been freed from it.

In each human being, “every creature” can be understood not universally, as heaven and earth and all that is in them exist, but in a certain generic sense. For in a human being there is the rational nature, which angels too are believed to possess; the sentient nature, which even beasts do not lack, for they use senses and sentient impulses to seek what is useful and avoid what is contrary; and the living nature without sensation, such as may be observed in trees. [Col. 0711A] For even within us, without our awareness, bodily growth takes place; hair does not feel even when it is cut, and yet it grows.

Moreover, bodily creation is more plainly apparent in us. Though it is made and fashioned from earth, there are nevertheless within it particles from all the elements of this corporeal world, for the balance of health. The limbs are strengthened by heat, which comes from fire, and whose light also shines forth through the eyes. The passages of the veins called arteries and the respiratory channels of the lungs are filled with air. And unless moisture were present, no channels would flow, and dryness would take over life. The blood itself, filling other veins in a moist flow, is spread through all things like streams and rivers.

Thus there is no kind of creature which cannot be recognized in the human being. It is as if every creature still groaned together in him. For this reason the Lord commanded that the Gospel be preached to every creature (Mark 16), because in every human being, as we have explained, there is every creature.

Therefore every creature groans in the human being—not the whole creation, but every kind of creation. It is as though one said that all healthy people see the sun, but do not see it with their whole selves, because they see it only with their eyes. So too, every creature is in the human being, because he understands, senses, lives, and has a body; but the whole of creation is not in him, because apart from him there are angels who understand, animals that sense, [Col. 0711C] trees that live, and stones that merely exist.

Thus we know that every creature—that is, the faithful human being—groans: that is, he groans inwardly and has an ever-fresh groan as long as he is subjected to vanity. He also labors in childbirth: that is, he performs a good work with the greatest difficulty and burden. For just as a woman brings forth a child with great pains and efforts, so the faithful person produces the fruit of a good work with great exertions and labors. He labors and afflicts himself with vigils, fasts, and other holy practices. And he does this even until now.

For although there are some already in Abraham’s bosom, and although that thief, placed with the Lord in paradise on the day he believed, ceased to groan, nevertheless every creature groans and labors in childbirth even until now in those saints who still labor in the present life.

“And not only it groans, but we ourselves also”: that is, not only do body, soul, and spirit together suffer from bodily difficulties in the human being, but we ourselves too, apart from our bodies, groan within ourselves—we, I say, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit; that is, whose spirits have already been offered to God as a sacrifice and seized by the divine fire of charity.

For these are the human being’s firstfruits, because truth first takes possession of our spirit, in order that through it the rest may be taken possession of. Therefore he already has firstfruits offered to God who says: “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin” (Rom. 7), and of whom it is said: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Mark 14). [Col. 0712A]

“Not only,” he says, “does every creature”—that is, body, soul, and spirit together—“groan, but we ourselves also, having the firstfruits of the Spirit”: that is, we souls who have already offered our minds, our firstfruits, to God. “We groan within ourselves,” that is, apart from the body, “awaiting adoption as sons, the redemption of our body”: namely, that the body itself too, receiving the benefit of the adoption as sons by which we are called, may show that we have been wholly set free, all troubles having passed, and are in every respect children of God.

“Not only it groans, but we ourselves also, having the firstfruits of the Spirit”: that is, those who now serve in spirit because we now believe God with our mind, and in that very faith have given certain firstfruits, so that we may follow our own firstfruits.

“And we ourselves, having the firstfruits of the Spirit”: that is, those who are not yet subjected wholly, in all that we are, to God rather than vanity, but are subjected to God in that part by which we are better than sinners. This is what it means that, through the firstfruits of the Spirit, we ourselves too groan within ourselves.

The Apostle also seems specifically to designate apostolic dignity in saying, “We ourselves, having the firstfruits of the Spirit”: that is, we who first received the Holy Spirit and have his more worthy gifts. “Not only,” he says, “does every creature”—that is, the whole Church created in good works, which is subject to us—“groan, but we ourselves, having the firstfruits of the Spirit”: that is, we apostles, who were chosen for this purpose, to receive the firstfruits of the Spirit.

We are greater through having his firstfruits, either because he first came to us, or because he manifests his gifts in us more worthily and evidently: through kinds of tongues, through the healing of the sick, through the raising of the dead, [Col. 0712C] and through similar works. And we ourselves, who are so great, who already rejoice at receiving the firstfruits of the Holy Spirit, nevertheless still groan, having miseries like others. We groan within ourselves because in us there is that on account of which we groan.

Or, although not before people, we groan within ourselves—that is, in our inner being. Nor is our groaning feigned; it resounds in the secrets of the mind. And we groan while awaiting adoption as sons, because neither delay nor adversity breaks us, but we await adoption as sons with endurance and courage: namely, that according to the body we may receive the glory of adoption, so that wholly, in soul and body, we may be immortal and blessed, and may appear in all our substance as children of God by adoption.

We await this adoption, namely “the redemption of our body”: that is, that even what is still corruptible may become incorruptible and immortal. For this is the redemption of our body: that it may be redeemed, that is, freed, from every trouble and attain true health.

For it does not yet have health. Hunger and thirst kill it if no help is given. Food is the remedy of hunger, drink the remedy of thirst, and sleep the remedy of fatigue. If, after these things are set aside, there are no illnesses, there is health. But if you have something that can kill you unless you eat, do not boast of health; rather, groaning, await the redemption of your body. Rejoice that you are redeemed, but not yet in reality. You are secure in hope. For if you do not groan in hope, you will not attain the reality.

[Col. 0713A]

> “For in hope we were saved. But hope which is seen is not hope; for what a person sees, why does he hope for it? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it through patience.”

It is as though someone said to the Apostle: “What benefit did Christ bring you if you still groan? And how has the Savior saved you? For one who still groans is sick.” He therefore adds and says: “For in hope,” and so forth.

We groan because we were saved in hope. We therefore hope that we shall be saved; and what we hope for we already await, but do not yet possess. Until we possess it, we sigh in time, because we desire what we do not yet possess. We have not yet been saved in reality, but still only in hope, because the fullness of our joy has not yet come. We do not yet have a heavenly and spiritual body—that is, an angelic body in fellowship with angels—but we hope.

Yet already we possess this salvation, this glory—but as hope. Hope which is seen is not hope. Therefore we do not yet see in reality the salvation which we possess in hope. Certainty seen as present is not hope. For “what a person sees, why does he hope for it?” For why is what is seen hoped for? It is not hoped for, but known.

But if we hope for what we do not see—that is, the redemption of our body and fellowship with angels—we await it through patience. For hope produces in us, for the increase of merit, an expectation of future salvation, and also patience in that expectation, because, strengthened by hope, we await invisible salvation by enduring present evils with patience. Therefore we are compelled to groan. [Col. 0713C] For patience is needed when one suffers amid evils, not amid the goods which one enjoys.

> “Likewise also the Spirit helps our weakness. For we do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with unutterable groanings. And he who searches hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he intercedes for the saints according to God.”

Hope helps us so that we may be able to wait patiently; and likewise does the Spirit. Therefore we attribute nothing of our expectation or patience to ourselves, but all to God, by whose benefits we are able to do these things.

For not only does hope help us, but the Holy Spirit likewise helps our weakness, because he pours charity into us, through which our weakness is strengthened, so that it may be able patiently to await the salvation it hopes for. Just as hope helps us, so charity—that is, the Holy Spirit—helps us, not only in enduring adversities but also in prayers, because without him we cannot even pray well.

For because we groan and ask to be delivered, the Spirit helps us lest we seek to be delivered before the proper time, or ask for things contrary to our good. He helps our weakness by teaching and enabling us to pray. For we do not know what we ought to pray for, but he himself intercedes for us.

We do not know, as we ought, what we should pray for, because temporal troubles and tribulations often benefit us: either by healing the swelling of pride; by proving and exercising patience, for which a clearer and greater reward is reserved when it has been tested and exercised; or by scourging and removing whatever sins need to be scourged and removed. Yet, not knowing how such things benefit us, we wish to be delivered from every tribulation.

For we do not sufficiently know what is beneficial to us. Sometimes what we think harmful is beneficial, and what we think beneficial is harmful. We are weak; the physician knows what remedies are useful for us, but we do not. In these tribulations, therefore, which can both benefit and harm, we do not know what we ought to pray for; yet, because they are harsh, troublesome, and contrary to the sense of our weakness, with the universal human will we pray that they may be removed from us.

But we owe this devotion to the Lord our God: if he does not remove them, we should not for that reason think ourselves neglected by him; [Col. 0714B] rather, with devout patience in evils we should hope for greater goods. “For strength is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12).

Or again, while we seek the blessed life in which we are immortal and incorruptible in body and spirit—however great the peace itself may be, which surpasses all understanding—even in asking for it in prayer, we do not know what we ought to pray for. But whatever occurs to our thoughts, we reject, repudiate, and disapprove; we know that it is not what we seek, although we do not yet know what that reality is like.

There is, then, in us a certain, so to speak, learned ignorance—learned from the Spirit of God, who helps our weakness. We do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us: that is, he makes us persons who pray, with unutterable groanings. [Col. 0714C]

For he makes us pray by inspiring in us desire for so great a thing, still unknown, which we await through patience. And he causes us to pray with unutterable groanings. For how can what is unknown be described when it is desired? Yet if it were wholly unknown, it would not be desired. And again, if it were seen, it would not be desired, nor sought with groanings.

But one who makes petition is lesser than the one to whom petition is made. How then is the Spirit said to make petition, since he is not lesser? For petitioning with groanings is the surest sign of one in need. But it is right to believe that the Holy Spirit is in need of nothing.

Yet, as we said above, he himself intercedes because he inflames those whom he has filled to make petition. And he himself is said to groan because he makes us groan in desire for future blessedness. Thus he is said to “intercede” because he makes us intercede and inspires in us the affection of petitioning and groaning, just as in the Gospel: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10).
