Nor does this happen in us as though we ourselves did nothing. The help of the Holy Spirit is thus expressed: he is said himself to do what he causes us to do. Such ways of speaking are common when an effect is signified through that which produces it; thus we call cold “sluggish” because it makes people sluggish, and a day “sad” or “cheerful” because it makes people sad or cheerful.

Thus too the Lord said to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear God” (Gen. 22), [Col. 0715A] that is, “Now I have caused you to know.” In accordance with this manner of speaking, he who is God’s Wisdom himself said that he did not know the day or hour of the end of the age (Matt. 25). For what could there be that he himself did not know? But because he usefully concealed this from the disciples, he said that he did not know it, because by concealing it he made them not know.

According to this figure he also said that the Father alone knew that day, because he caused the same Son to know it. In the same manner of speech the Holy Spirit is said to intercede or groan because he makes those in whom he dwells intercede and groan.

Or, by the designation “Holy Spirit” charity is meant, which has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit. Therefore the Holy Spirit intercedes and groans for us: that is, charity intercedes, charity petitions, charity groans, charity prays. He who gave it does not know how to close his ears against it.

But he who searches hearts—that is, God, who sees in the hidden realm of his thought all the secrets of hearts—knows what the Spirit desires: that is, he approves and fulfills what the Spirit causes us to desire, because he makes the saints petition for themselves according to God, that is, according to God’s will. Or the Spirit—that is, charity—intercedes according to God for the saints because charity asks for nothing except what is pleasing to God; and therefore he knows, that is, approves, its desire or petition. [Col. 0715B]

> “And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called saints according to his purpose. For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, [Col. 0715C] so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined, these he also called; and those whom he called, these he also justified; and those whom he justified, these he also glorified.”

While we suffer adversity, we do not know, as we ought, what we should pray for. But this we know with certainty: that for those who love God, so as to prove that love by their works, all things—whether adverse or prosperous—work together, that is, jointly result, for good. For the expression “work together” here has a passive sense. And for lovers of God all things work together, that is, all things jointly result in good, because everything that happens to them is turned to their good, not only those things which are regarded as troublesome. [Col. 0715D] Indeed, so completely are all things included that, even if any of them stray and go astray, even this itself profits them for good: they return more humble and better instructed, and afterward persevere more firmly and cautiously in good works.

Or: God himself, or the Holy Spirit—of whom it was said above, and who is God—works together for good for those who love God. For God works together, that is, he works with his elect while they act, and he acts with them. And he works with them in such a way that he turns all things to their good and advantage. But because some love God and yet do not remain until the end in the good which they have begun, he immediately adds by way of qualification: “those who are called saints according to his purpose.” For these remain to the end in their love of God; and those who depart from it for a time return, [Col. 0716A] so that they may carry through to the end what they began in goodness.

For according to the purpose of his most hidden justice and goodness, God calls, justifies, and glorifies those whom he predestined. For God purposed that they should come to life, and his purpose cannot be changed. According to this purpose, not according to their own merit, they were called by God through preachers in order that they might be saints. And truly according to God’s purpose: “for those whom he foreknew,” etc.

The order is this: “For those whom he foreknew would be conformed to the image of the Son,” that is, would become imitators of Christ, he also predestined to be so, “so that he might be the firstborn among many brethren,” that is, holding the pre-eminence in the company of saints, rightfully receiving the Father’s inheritance and distributing it among his other brethren.

[Col. 0716B] They are called “according to purpose,” that is, their calling arises from nothing other than God’s prior ordering. For those whom God foreknew from eternity would be conformed to his Son, he also predestined—that is, by added grace he prepared them to believe the word of preaching. Predestination is the preparation of grace; it cannot exist without foreknowledge, though foreknowledge can exist without predestination. For by predestination God foreknew those things which he himself was going to do. Hence it is said: “He made the things that were to be.” Yet he can foreknow even things which he himself does not do, such as all sins. Therefore God’s predestination, which concerns good, is, as I have said, the preparation of grace. Grace, however, is the effect of predestination itself.

This is the predestination of the saints: namely, the foreknowledge and preparation [Col. 0716C] of God’s benefits, by which all who are delivered are most certainly delivered. For from among those who are predestined, none perishes with the devil; none remains under the devil’s power until death. If any one of these perished, God would be deceived. But none of them perishes, because he who predestined them cannot be deceived.

What he says—“predestined to be conformed to the image of the Son of God”—may be understood with reference to the inner person, so that we may be conformed to him in mind. It may also be understood thus: just as he became conformed to us in mortality, so we may become conformed to him in immortality. According to this image of the Son, to which we are conformed in body through immortality, we also do what the Apostle likewise says: “As we have borne the image [Col. 0716D] of the earthly man, let us bear also the image of him who is from heaven” (1 Cor. 15), so that we who were mortal according to Adam may hold, with true faith and sure and steadfast hope, that we shall be immortal according to Christ.

For in this way we can now bear that same image: not yet in sight, but in faith; not yet in possession, but in hope. For the Apostle was then speaking of the resurrection of the body when he said these things. Then, he says, “that he may be the firstborn among many brethren.” According to that in which he is the only-begotten, he has no brethren; but according to that in which he is the firstborn, he deigned to call brethren all who, after and through his primacy, are reborn into God’s grace through adoption as sons. For he is called firstborn in relation to the brethren who follow him into that which he himself entered first. [Col. 0717A]

Thus elsewhere he also calls him “the firstborn from the dead,” so that he may hold the pre-eminence; for before him there was no resurrection of the dead such that they should die no more, but after him there is that resurrection of many saints.

I have said that those whom he foreknew and predestined—“those whom he predestined, these he also called.” Here we must understand: “according to purpose.” For others also are called, but not chosen; and consequently they are not called according to purpose. “Those whom he called,” that is, according to purpose, “these he also justified.”

It is as though an emperor intended to raise some lowly person to the consulship, supplied him with the resources by which he might make himself fit, and adorned him so that he could worthily be advanced to so great an honor. Thus God gives those whom he predestined to life degrees of virtues and good works [Col. 0717B] by which they may be raised to so great an exaltation. For he calls them, justifies them, and magnifies them. And whatever persons he has granted these gifts, he undoubtedly foreknew that he would grant them and prepared them in his foreknowledge.

Those, therefore, whom he predestined, he also called by that calling of which it is said: “The gifts and calling of God are without repentance.” For to arrange his works in his foreknowledge—which cannot be deceived or changed—is, in the Lord, nothing other than to predestine. Therefore he called not others, but those whom he predestined; he justified not others, but those whom he so called; and he magnified, or glorified, not others, but those whom he predestined, called, and justified.

Our predestination was accomplished in us, but hidden with him in his foreknowledge. The three [Col. 0717C] remaining things, however, occur in us: calling, justification, and magnification. We are called by the predestination of repentance; we are justified by the renewal of mercy and fear of judgment; we are magnified by progress in virtues, or glorified by eternal blessedness.

All these things have already been done: he predestined, foreknew, called, justified, and magnified; because all have already been foreknown and predestined, and many have already been called, justified, and magnified, although many still remain to be called, justified, and magnified until the end of the age. Nevertheless, the verbs are put in the past tense even concerning future things, as though God had already done what he disposed from eternity to be done—he who made the things that were to be.

Therefore, whatever Jews have been foreknown, predestined, called, justified, and magnified or glorified by the most provident ordering [Col. 0717D] are already children of God, even though they are not yet reborn and indeed not yet born; and they cannot perish at all. For such persons God himself works all things together for good.

> “What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare even his own Son, but delivered him up for us all—how did he not also give us all things with him?”

Since God has bestowed upon us so many and such great benefits, not on account of our merits but by grace, what shall we say in response to these such great gifts? Shall we perhaps further say that we possess anything from ourselves? No: rather, we shall ascribe everything to God’s grace. And if God bestows such great things upon us by his free gift, [Col. 0718A] who can take any of them from us? Or who can resist his will, by which he has predetermined to bring us to glory?

“If God is for us, who will be against us?” God is for us in predestining us; God is for us in magnifying or glorifying us. If God is for us, who is against us? If in all these things God is for us, whoever wishes to oppose us should prepare himself, if he can, to wage war against God. For no one harms us unless he conquers God. And who conquers the Almighty? Whoever wishes to resist him harms himself.

“If God is for us, who is against us?” Even if the whole world should rise against us and rage against us with every kind of torment, what is the whole world when he through whom the world was made is for us? What is anyone who strives to resist God [Col. 0718B] as he prepares to bring us into the kingdom? He “did not spare his own Son,” that is, not an adopted son but one natural and consubstantial; “but delivered him up for us all,” that is, for the salvation of us all, exposing him to death.

And he who gave us the greater thing, namely his Son, will also give us the lesser thing, namely his kingdom. For how could he who gave his Son deny anything? How did he not also give us all things with him? For where he gave us him in whom all good things are, there with him he gave us all things useful to us: faith, forgiveness of sins, perfection of virtues, the diverse gifts of the Holy Spirit, and, in the age to come, everlasting blessedness.

[Col. 0718C] And then what will the human spirit be like—having no defect at all, none beneath which it lies, none to which it yields, none against which it must struggle even praiseworthily; perfected in utterly peaceful virtue? How great, how splendid, how certain will be its knowledge of all things, without any error or toil, where God’s wisdom itself will be drunk from its own fountain with highest happiness and without difficulty? What will the body be like, wholly subject to the spirit and sufficiently enlivened by it, needing no nourishment? For it will not be animal but spiritual, indeed possessing the substance of flesh, but without any fleshly corruption.

When we have attained that blessedness, then we shall possess all things. For the things above us will be ours for life; equals will be ours for fellowship; inferiors will be ours for judgment. Thus all things are possessed there: each thing belongs to all, and all things belong to each. [Col. 0718D]

> “Who shall bring an accusation against God’s elect? God is the one who justifies. Who is he that condemns? Christ Jesus, who died—indeed, who also rose again—who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us.”

Truly God has given us salvation and every good thing with Christ, and we shall have them. For who will accuse us in order to cause us to be deprived of them? Who will accuse God’s elect—those whom he has called according to his unchangeable purpose? Or who will bring an accusation against God’s elect? No accusation can harm them.

The devil indeed strives to accuse them. But who is [Col. 0719A] the devil, or what is his accusation, against those whom God chooses? His accusation against them has no force. Who, then, will accuse them? God? No, because he himself justifies them. And it is inconsistent that he should accuse those whom he justifies. God does not wish to accuse them; no one else can. And when no one accuses them, who is there to condemn them? No one.

Will Jesus Christ condemn them? By no means: the saving King will not condemn those for whom he died that they might live. I say that he died so that we might die to sin; indeed, to signify the greater benefit, I say that he also rose again so that we might rise with him and share in the first resurrection. He was also raised into heaven to the right hand of God, that he might lift us up after himself and cause us to possess the right-hand portion, which signifies perpetual blessedness (1 John 2). [Col. 0719B]

He is able to help his own because he is at the right hand of God, that is, set above every creature and placed in the honor in which the Father is, because he also intercedes for us; for we have him as advocate and intercessor with the Father. For the only-begotten Son’s interceding for human beings is his showing himself as man before the coeternal Father; and his having asked on behalf of human nature is his having assumed that same nature into the height of his divinity. Therefore the Lord intercedes for us, not by voice but by compassion, because by assuming what he did not will to be condemned in the elect, he set it free.

> “Who, then, shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written [Col. 0719C]: ‘For your sake we are being put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter’ [Ps. 43]. But in all these things we overcome through him who loved us.”

Since Christ suffered death for us and still intercedes for us, who then will separate us from the love of Christ? That is, who can separate us from the love by which we love Christ? No one can do this. Will tribulation, that is, bodily affliction, do it? By no means. Or will distress, that is, anxiety of mind, make us cease to love Christ? Not at all. Will persecution, that is, expulsion from place to place, separate us from Christ’s love? No.

Even if we endure tribulation of every kind, [Col. 0719D] even if we are tormented by mental anguish, even if opponents pursue us through different places, we can never be torn away from Christ’s love. Will famine separate us from him, that is, the desire for food without abundance of food? Far from it. Or will nakedness, that is, lack of clothing, do this? By no means. Will danger, that is, the approach of death, divide us from Christ? Or will the sword—that is, death itself inflicted by the sword—be able to do so? By no means.

By these seven are signified all things which can afflict us in this age, because the number seven commonly expresses totality. Yet none of them can separate us from Christ’s love, if we are elect. And I say this as it is written concerning us, where our voice is expressed, speaking to Christ: “For your sake we are being put to death,” because we cannot be separated from you. [Col. 0720A]

We are put to death not because of a crime, nor for human favor, but for your sake. This is the cause of the martyrs. For your sake, from whom we do not wish to be separated, we are put to death—that is, afflicted by various punishments—“all day,” that is, throughout the entire time of our enlightenment, from when we came from darkness into light. For our adversaries have regarded us as sheep for slaughter: that is, they judge that we ought to be killed without any regard for mercy, since we do not resist them but are ready to die innocently in our simplicity and gentleness.

We suffer all these things for Christ, and are not overcome by them; rather, in all these things we overcome, that is, we are made superior and victorious, not through our own powers but through him who loved us. For while we cling to his love, we do not receive the sensation of pain. For his love, by which he loved us and drew our affection to himself, does not allow us to feel bodily torment and pain. [Col. 0720B]

> “For I am certain that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities nor powers, neither things present nor things to come, neither strength nor height nor depth nor any other creature shall be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

Truly nothing will separate us from God’s love; for of this I am certain. I do not merely suppose it, but am certain—that is, I firmly hold it as certain and settled—that no death, no promised temporal life, nor anything that follows, can separate us from Christ’s love.

No one separates us from it by threatening [Col. 0720C] death, because that very one whom we love, God, cannot die. No one separates us from it by promising life, for no one separates us from the fountain itself by promising water. The person who threatens death does not separate us from it, because whoever believes in Christ, even though he dies, lives. Nor does the person who promises life, because Christ gives eternal life. Therefore the promise of temporal life ought to be despised in comparison with eternal life.

Nor do angels separate us from it, whether good or evil. Even if good angels should tell us not to love Christ—which they never teach—we would not obey them. “Even if an angel from heaven should preach to you something besides what you have received, let him be anathema” (Gal. 1). Therefore no angel separates us from it, because, when we cling to God, there is no angel more powerful than our mind. Nor do principalities, that is, those angels who hold dominion over others, whether good or evil; for in both groups some are pre-eminent over others. And the Lord stripped the hostile principalities, triumphing over them in himself. Good principalities, however, will never wish to separate us from him, since their greatest concern is to bring those subject to them back to him.

Nor do powers separate us from it, that is, the still more exalted angelic strengths: if they are good, they favor our union with God; if evil, they are restrained by him. Having enumerated all the adversities that are on earth, he ascends to heaven; and, wishing to show that it is a small thing to despise earthly punishments for Christ, he also adds this: neither angels, nor principalities, nor powers, [Col. 0721A] etc.

What he says, however, is this: Not only can human beings not draw me away from Christ’s love, but not even angels, nor all the powers of heaven together if they should assemble as one; not even if I must depart from the kingdom or be cast into hell for Christ. For by “height and depth,” and “life and death,” he seems to signify the kingdom of heaven and hell. He says this, not because angels could ever desire to separate him from Christ, but because he says that even impossible things could happen more readily than that he should be separated from Christ’s love, so as to show by these things how great was the power of God’s love in him.

Nor do present adversities separate us from it, for we feel them the lighter the more closely we cling to him from whom they attempt to separate us. [Col. 0721B] Nor does “things to come,” that is, the promise of future things, separate us from it, because God promises more surely whatever good is to come; and nothing is better than God himself, who is certainly already present to those who rightly cling to him.

[Col. 0721C] Neither things present—that is, anything presently impending, adverse or prosperous—nor future good or evil things separate us from Christ; that is, neither present nor future temporal things that either delight, oppress, give hope, or inspire fear. Nor does the strength of someone violently inflicting force upon us separate us from it, because he to whom we cling is stronger than all. Nor does height—that is, if someone lifts us on high in order to cast us down more harshly. Nor does depth—that is, if someone plunges us into the depths of the sea or places us in the lowest part of a prison.

Or “height” means the promise of lofty worldly honor, and “depth” the final abasement of the extreme calamity which can be endured in this world. Or height and depth mean the elevation of secular eloquence and the deep investigation of natural things. Or again, height and depth mean vain curiosity about those things which are, or are thought to be, in heaven or in the abyss. But in whatever way height and depth are understood, they cannot separate us from Christ’s love.

Nor does “any other creature,” that is, visible creation—for we too are indeed creatures, but visible ones. Therefore another creature, that is, one different from our inner person by which we love Christ, will not divide us from his love, because the love [Col. 0721D] of bodies, expressed by “another creature,” will not accomplish this. Or “another creature” is better understood as referring to things which do not exist. Thus he mentions even things which are not, to show that even if the things which are not did exist, they still could not move him from his purpose or change him.

“I am certain,” he says, “that none of the things I have enumerated can separate us from the love of God, who is better than all things and has bestowed upon us such numerous and great benefits”—the love which is for us in Christ Jesus our Lord. For the Father showed us his love in Christ, whom he delivered up for us; and no one can love the Father unless he has loved Christ.

## Chapter IX

> “I speak the truth in Christ Jesus; I do not lie, [Col. 0722A] my conscience bearing witness to me in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart. For I wished that I myself might be anathema from Christ for my brethren, who are my kinsmen according to the flesh: who are Israelites, whose is the adoption as sons, and the glory, and the covenant, and the giving of the law, and the worship, and the promises; whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen.”

Now nothing can separate me and the other elect from Christ; but formerly I was separated from him and continually wished to remain estranged, a fact from which I now grieve, and so evils are turned into good. For “I speak the truth,” etc.

Or the connection is thus: I am certain that nothing can [Col. 0722B] separate us from Christ’s love, both from the benefits mentioned above—because he foreknew, predestined, called, and justified us—and from this fact: when I was a persecutor of God’s Church, I was wholly unable, however much I labored, to tear believers from his love. Thus I now grieve greatly that I exercised such cruelty against them.

For I, existing in Christ, that is, in Christ’s body, speak to you a truth so pure that I do not lie like certain persons who, while they speak true things, mingle falsehoods with them. And because some appear to speak truth who do not hold it in their heart, I add that I utter truth with my mouth, my conscience bearing witness to me; for, even if you do not believe, my conscience is nevertheless witness to me that I speak the truth. And it bears this witness not on its own authority [Col. 0722C] but in the Holy Spirit, who causes it to bear this testimony.

I speak this most certain truth: that I have sorrow not slight but great, and pain not for an hour but continual, in my heart. Why then do I now have such great sorrow and such prolonged anguish of mind? Namely because I myself, who am now so great an apostle, before faith not only wished but desired to be anathema—that is, to be the estrangement of others from Christ, so as to make them estranged, divided, or separated from Christ. And I desired this for my brethren, that is, for the Jews, who are my brethren in the law, whose law I wished to defend, who are my kinsmen according to the flesh; and therefore they ought especially to have been helped, because we ought to seek the welfare of all, but especially that of blood-relations. [Col. 0722D] But I helped them wrongly, because I hindered them from believing in Christ, who are Israelites, that is, descended from the stock of Israel.

Or otherwise: the Apostle displays his affection toward the Jews, saying—and confirming with an oath—that he grieves exceedingly on their account because they refused to believe in Christ, who had been promised to them and came sent to them. “I have sorrow,” he says, “not slight but great, and continual pain in my heart”: not a pain which pricks for an hour and passes away, but one which remains constantly. I grieve that my nation is deprived of Christ’s benefit.

“For I wished,” that is, I began long ago to wish, “that I myself might be anathema,” that is, estranged from Christ, for my Jewish brethren, so that they themselves might cling to Christ. I wished to perish so that they might be saved. In this sense blessed Micah also, when he prophesied many evils to come upon the Jews, said: “Would that I were not a man possessing the Spirit, and that I might rather speak falsehood” (Mic. 2). [Col. 0723A] For love of his nation he wished to be estranged from the Holy Spirit and to be a speaker of falsehood, provided that the Jewish people might escape those scourges, captivities, and destructions which he had predicted in his prophecy.

Therefore, just as Micah wished to become estranged from the Holy Spirit because of his love for his people, so Paul wished to become anathema—that is, estranged—because of the excess of his love for his brethren. For to be estranged from the Holy Spirit and to be estranged from Christ are equivalent. Moses also interceded wonderfully for the same people, offering himself on their behalf and saying: “If you forgive them their sin, forgive it; but if you do not wish to, blot me out of your book which you have written” (Exod. 32). [Col. 0723B]

Here it is shown how much the intercession of saints avails with God for those persons. For Moses, secure in God’s justice, which could not blot him out, obtained mercy so that God would not blot out those whom he could justly have blotted out. Therefore he interceded, more ready to be blotted out for them than to have them blotted out, knowing that he dealt with mercy, which, because it would by no means blot out Moses himself, would spare them also for his sake.

But if we consider Moses’ voice as he intercedes, we shall perceive that Moses and Paul had the same affection for the flock entrusted to them. “For the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10). And this very thing is to say: “I wished to be anathema from Christ,” and, “Blot me out of the book which you have written.” For one who is blotted out of God’s book becomes anathema [Col. 0723C] from God.

At the same time, let us observe how great is the Apostle’s love in Christ: he desires to die for him and to perish alone, provided that the whole human race may believe in him. Yet he wishes to perish not eternally but for the present. He wishes to perish in the flesh so that others may be saved in spirit; to pour out his own blood so that the souls of many may be preserved. For *anathema* sometimes signifies being killed, as it does here.

Therefore he wishes for the salvation of his brethren to be anathema, desiring to imitate the Lord, who, though he was not a curse, was made a curse for us. For it was written concerning him: “Cursed by God is he who hangs on a tree” (Deut. 21; Gal. 3). And just as Christ was cursed by God, so the Apostle was anathema from Christ. [Col. 0723D] What “anathema” means here is what “cursed” means there; and what “from Christ” means here is what “from God” means there.

For Christ hanging on the cross was cursed—that is, consigned to death—by the Father; and Paul in the passion of martyrdom was anathema from Christ—that is, estranged and deprived of life—by Christ’s will. “For I wished to be anathema from Christ for my brethren,” so that they might not be estranged from Christ, who are my kinsmen not according to the spirit but according to the flesh, because in spirit they are estranged from me.

As we have said, he displays his affection for them and enumerates many of their distinctions, in order to instil grief in everyone for them, since they are thereby even worse than the Gentiles. “Whose,” he says, “is the adoption as sons”: of whom the Lord formerly said, “Israel is my firstborn son” [Col. 0724A] (Exod. 2); and, “I have nourished and exalted children” (Isa. 1). “And whose is the glory”: that they were chosen from among all nations as God’s special people. “And whose are the covenants”: one in the letter, the other in the spirit, so that those who formerly served in the flesh under the ceremonies of the law, once those ceremonies were abolished, might afterward serve in spirit under the commands of the everlasting Gospel.

For the covenants belong particularly to them, because the Old Covenant was given to them, and the New was prefigured in the Old. “And whose is the giving of the law,” that is, the giving of the Old and New Covenants, because in the Old the New was given to them. Or “the giving of the law” means the giving of the Mosaic law. “And whose is the worship,” that is, the carrying out of heavenly commands and the worship of God. “And whose are the divine promises,” so that whatever was promised to their fathers might be fulfilled in their children, unless their fault stood in the way. [Col. 0724B]

For many promises concerning Christ were made to their fathers, whose fathers are those most renowned men whom the Old Scripture praises. And, what is greater than all, “from whom is Christ according to the flesh,” born of the Virgin Mary. “Whose are the fathers”: behold their honor from those who went before. “And from whom is Christ”: behold their honor from those who came after. From them—that is, from their stock—is Christ according to the flesh, who was made from David’s seed according to the flesh; but according to the nature of his divinity, in which he is equal to the Father, he himself is “God over all, blessed for ever. Amen.”

For by saying “God over all,” he shows that Christ is God by nature. “God” is sometimes said by designation, and sometimes essentially. It is said by designation, as was said to Moses: “Behold, I have made you a god to [Col. 0724C] Pharaoh” (Exod. 7). It is said essentially, as he says: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. 3). One who is called god by designation is among all things; but one who is called God essentially is above all things.

Therefore, in order to show that Christ is God by nature, Paul called him not merely God, but God over all. For, as we said before, any elect person, or one set as a model to be imitated, may be called god, but among all things, insofar as the designation is concerned; Christ, however, is God over all because he is God by nature. And this “Amen” means: truly.

[Col. 0724D] For this reason the Apostle has pain in his heart: because this holy and such great one is not received by the Jews, from whose stock he was born. And, where so many good things had been, he grieves that so many evils are now present. Yet he nonetheless praises the truth of the judgment, lest God’s sentence against his own relatives and brethren seem displeasing, or harsh, or excessive. For he adds:

> “But it is not as though the word of God had failed. For not all who are from Israel are Israelites; nor, because they are Abraham’s seed, are they all children. But: ‘In Isaac shall your seed be called.’ That is, it is not the children of the flesh who are God’s children, but the children of the promise are reckoned as seed. For this is the word of promise: ‘At this time I shall come, and Sarah shall have a son.’”

“I grieve,” he says, “over the destruction of these persons, but not because the word of God has failed,” that is, not because God’s promise, who promised Abraham’s seed [Col. 0725A] salvation, has vanished. Yet I do not grieve because God’s word has failed, for it has not failed: it has not been rendered void, but remains valid and firm, even though some of them have not believed, because the word of promise was made not to Jews alone, but to the elect.

For not all who are from Israel—that is, from Jacob’s fleshly stock—are Israelites, that is, persons to be counted in Israel’s inheritance by the merit of faith and righteousness. Nor are all children merely because they are seed according to the flesh. For many were physically begotten from him who are not reckoned as his children, such as all whom Keturah bore or the son of Hagar.

Thus the word of God would fail if the promises were not fulfilled. But the Apostle, wishing to show that the word of the divine promise has not failed, says: “For not all who are from Israel are Israelites; nor, because they are Abraham’s seed, are they all children, but ‘In Isaac shall your seed be called.’” [Col. 0725B] For here he declares that those who did not believe are neither Israelites nor Abraham’s children, and that God neither promised nor decreed that they would be saved.

He therefore begins to reason why, by God’s deep and just judgment, the Gentiles were admitted after those persons had been rejected. Not all of them are children, and consequently not all will possess the inheritance or salvation; but, he says, “In Isaac shall your seed be called”: “It is not the children of the flesh who are God’s children, but the children of the promise are reckoned as seed.”

For in Isaac, the son promised to Abraham, were prefigured not those who make themselves righteous, but those whom God himself was going to make. Therefore they are called children of promise; and accordingly, in order to be Abraham’s seed, [Col. 0725C] these children of promise are called in Isaac, that is, gathered into Christ by calling grace.

For children of the flesh belong to the earthly Jerusalem, which is in bondage with her children; but children of promise belong to her who is above, our free and eternal mother in heaven. These, then, are truly Abraham’s children, who, like Isaac, are promised by God’s free gift and are made good by his free gift. For just as Isaac did not merit being promised before his birth, so neither do they.

And indeed a son was promised to Abraham. For this is the word of promise, that is, in these words God promised: “At this time I shall come,” that is, when the year has revolved, I shall show myself present to you in the effecting of power, “and Sarah shall then have a son in her womb.” [Col. 0725D] “At this time,” he says, “I shall come,” as, for example, if it was spring or autumn then, he would come in the following year in spring or autumn.

In this statement the Apostle strives to show how Isaac was not a son of flesh but a son of God, returning to what is written concerning him in Genesis. “The word of promise,” he says, etc. Therefore Isaac was not born by the order of fleshly generation, since Abraham’s body was already regarded as dead and Sarah’s womb was dead, as was shown above; but by the power of him who said: “At this time I shall come, and Sarah shall have a son,” that is, Sarah will have a son. Rightly, then, he is called a son not of flesh but of God, since he is born by God’s coming and word; and for this reason he most fittingly prefigures the spiritual children of the Church.

[Col. 0726A]

> “And not only so, but Rebekah also, having conceived by one intercourse with Isaac our father (Gen. 25). For when they had not yet been born or done anything good or evil, in order that the purpose of God according to election might remain—not by works, but by him who calls—it was said to her: ‘The greater shall serve the lesser’; as it is written: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated’” (Mal. 1).

Isaac, who was promised, had certainly earned by no works that he should be promised as one who was to be born, so that Abraham’s seed might be called in Isaac; that is, that those should belong to the lot of the saints which is in Christ, who understood themselves to be children of promise, not vaunting themselves over their merits, but reckoning it to the grace of the calling that they were co-heirs with Christ. For when it was promised that they should exist [Col. 0726B], those who did not yet exist had certainly earned nothing. Isaac, I say, was promised. But not only was he promised, who, Ishmael having been rejected, should alone possess his father’s inheritance; Rebecca too received a similar promise from God, having twins in her womb from one intercourse with Isaac, our father, whom we have as a father to imitate.

Rebecca had them from one intercourse, so that Jacob might not boast that his lot had been altered for the better not only through his own merits or those of his parents, but not even through a change in the disposition of the one father, saying that he was loved by the Creator because his father, when he begot him, had been of better and more praiseworthy character. “From one intercourse,” he says. The father had one and the same merit when begetting them; the mother, one and the same merit when conceiving them. For both were conceived together [Col. 0726C] at one time.

The promise made to Sarah or Abraham shows that no one is saved because of lineage; that made to Rebecca, that no one is chosen for any merit of his own or of his parents, but by grace alone. Or lest anyone say that Ishmael, born from a slave concubine, ought not to have become heir, while Isaac, born of a free wife, did become heir—namely, that the former was deprived of inheritance because of his mother’s unworthiness, while the latter became heir not through God’s grace but through his mother’s merit and dignity—the Apostle sets forth the example of two others, Esau and Jacob. In them the father’s and mother’s merit was one and the same; yet one was rejected and the other chosen by grace alone. And these two, like Abraham’s two sons, bore the figure [Col. 0726D] of those rejected and those saved.

We have said that Rebecca, carrying twins in her womb, received from God the promise in which it was declared that one of them would be rejected and the other chosen. For it was said to her: “The elder shall serve the younger.” And this promise was made when the sons had as yet done neither good nor evil. For when they had not yet been born, nor had done anything good or evil—since even in the womb they might have seemed to earn something by struggling—it was said to her, that is, to the mother: “The elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. 25).

It was said then so that God’s purpose—that is, his predetermination or preordination—might remain, that is, might be fulfilled and stand firm according to election, that is, according to the grace by which he chooses whom he chooses. And it was said not because of the works of father or mother [Col. 0727A], nor because of the future works of the sons, but because of him who calls—that is, because of God, who was calling Jacob by grace. For if the Apostle had wished future works to be understood, whether this man’s good works or that man’s evil works, which God certainly foreknew, he would never have said, “not from works,” but would have said, “from future works.” It was said to her, he says, “the elder”—that is, Esau, who was firstborn—“shall serve the younger,” that is, Jacob.

Here the servitude of one and the freedom of the other were already foretold. And in this place servitude certainly signifies the practice of iniquity, while freedom signifies the practice of righteousness. For if we look to bodily servitude, Jacob will seem rather to have served Esau than Esau Jacob. For Jacob, returning from Mesopotamia, offered him many gifts, called him lord, and humbly bowed down before him. How then did Esau serve him, except by afflicting [Col. 0727B], oppressing, and persecuting him? Hence Solomon says: “The fool shall serve the wise” (Prov. 11). For when a preeminent fool exercises the terror of power against the life of the wise man, wearies him with labours, and rends him with insults, he surely purges him by burning away every rust of vice. Thus the fool serves the wise man even by ruling over him, since by oppression he advances him to a better state. In this way Esau served his brother.

According to the letter, Esau—that is, the people of the Idumaeans, descended from Esau—served the younger: that is, they were subject to the Jewish people. Allegorically, however, Esau—that is, the Jewish people, who were firstborn—served the younger, that is, the Christian people who followed.

In this connection the blessed Apostle also employed the testimony [Col. 0727C] of the much later Malachi, so that we might understand that what was afterward made manifest through the prophet—that the Jews were so by predestination through grace—had been so before those men were born. Thus, he says, it was said, “the elder shall serve the younger,” as it is written—that is, as is read in Genesis—and as Malachi (Mal. 1) much later disclosed God’s ancient counsel in this matter, saying: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” For the phrase “as it is written” refers both to the book of Genesis and to Malachi’s writing.

But what did God love in Jacob before he had done anything good, except the gratuitous gift of his mercy? And what did he hate in Esau before he had been born and done anything evil, except original sin? [Col. 0727D] For he would not have loved in the former a righteousness which he had not performed; nor would he have hated in the latter a nature which he himself had made good. For before they were born, they had done neither good nor evil.

This statement makes clear that they neither sinned nor performed righteousness in the womb, nor had their souls dwelt in heaven before their union with their bodies, according to the fables of the Gentiles. For if their souls had been in heaven before being joined to bodies, they would certainly have done something good or evil there. But they had done nothing. Hence it is evident that their souls had never been in heaven before their birth. They had done nothing; and as regards original sin, both were equal, while as regards anything personal to either of them, there was none. Yet one of them is chosen and the other rejected; one succeeds [Col. 0728A] to the inheritance, the other is disinherited. God does not make his people from Esau, but makes them from Jacob. One seed; those conceived are different. One womb; those born are different.

While they were in the womb, it was said to their mother: “The elder shall serve the younger”; and it was said not from works but from him who calls, that is, from him who, by calling to faith, freely justifies the ungodly, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain, and human merit might not come first. For he does not speak of an election of human will or nature, since the condition of death and condemnation would be alike in both; rather, without doubt, he speaks of the election of grace, which does not find persons to choose but makes them such.

The purpose of justification remains according to the election not of what is due, but of grace, by which God makes those whom he chooses rather than finds them such; for [Col. 0728B] he certainly does not find good works in human beings to choose, but makes them perform works which he can choose. Yet no one is chosen unless already distinct from the one who is rejected. Therefore justification precedes election. And yet, of these two, before they had done anything, one was chosen and the other repulsed, so that Jacob might understand that, from that mass of original iniquity—in which he saw his brother, whose case was common to both, deservedly condemned by justice—he could have been distinguished only by grace.

> “What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? By no means! For he says to Moses: ‘I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will show mercy to whom I will show mercy’ (Exod. 33). Therefore it depends not on one who wills nor on one who runs [Col. 0728C], but on God who shows mercy. For Scripture says to Pharaoh: ‘For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth’ (Exod. 9). Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills.”

Having set forth the astonishing matter of how it could rightly be said of persons not yet born and doing neither good nor evil that God loved one and hated the other, the Apostle, by raising an objection against himself, expresses the disturbance of the hearer. “What then shall we say,” he says, “Is there injustice with God? By no means!” For he saw that, upon hearing this, human weakness or ignorance might think such a thing; and he puts the same question to himself.

“If,” he says, “Esau and Jacob had not yet been born and had done neither good nor evil [Col. 0728D], so as either to deserve or offend God, and if their election and rejection displayed not the merits of individuals but the will of him who chooses and rejects, what then shall we say? Shall we infer that there is injustice with God, who chooses one and rejects the other when each has equal merit—or rather, no merit at all? Far be it that there should be injustice with him!”

And why is it far from him? Because he chooses the one through mercy and rejects the other through justice; and in neither is there injustice. He chooses this one through mercy, because he says to Moses: “I will have mercy, so that he may believe, on whom I will have mercy, so that I may call him; and I will show mercy, so that he may work well, to him on whom I have had mercy so that he may believe.” Or: “I will have mercy by calling, on whom I will have mercy by predestining; and I will show mercy by giving eternal life, to him on whom I have had mercy by granting good [Col. 0729A] works.” Or: “I will have mercy by inspiring a good will, on whom I will have mercy according to predestination; and I will show mercy, in accordance with the carrying out of good will, by giving grace for the accomplishment of every good work, to him on whom I have had mercy by forgiving sins.”

In these words we are taught that, from that mass of the first human being, to whom death is deservedly due, the deliverance of each person belongs not to human merits but to God’s mercy. Thus there is no injustice with God, because he is unjust neither when remitting nor when exacting what is due. For pardon is gratuitous where vengeance could be just; and thus it may appear more clearly how great a benefit is bestowed on one freed from a punishment due and justified freely, when the other, equally guilty, is punished without injustice on the part of the punisher [Col. 0729B]. For God is not unjust whether he imposes penal judgment on one who deserves it or extends mercy to one who does not deserve it.

Both twins, therefore, were born by nature children of wrath, bound by the same bond of condemnation—not indeed by any works of their own, but originally. But he who said, “I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy,” loved Jacob by gratuitous mercy and hated Esau by deserved judgment. Since this was due to both, the one recognized in the other that he had no cause to boast of his own differing merits because he did not incur punishment in the same case, but only of the abundance of divine grace.

Likewise, everyone who receives mercy is forbidden to boast of the merits of his own virtues, for the Lord says: “I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy.” He does not say [Col. 0729C], “I will have mercy on such and such persons,” but, “on whom I will have mercy,” so as to show that no one, by prior good works, has merited the mercy of so great a calling.

Moreover, in adding, “and I will show mercy to whom I will have mercy,” perhaps it should be understood either that by this repetition God demonstrated the firmness of his own mercy—as in “Amen, amen,” “Let it be, let it be,” the repetition of Pharaoh’s dream, and many similar instances—or that he foretold in this manner that he would show mercy to both peoples, that is, Gentiles and Hebrews.

And since God chooses Jacob by mercy without any preceding merit, and likewise the rest, therefore it depends not on one who wills nor on one who runs—that is, one who works—to attain life, but on God who shows mercy, who grants mercy to that person. “If,” he says [Col. 0729D], “we admit that God does whatever he wills, and that, without merit or works, he chooses or condemns someone, then it depends not on a human being who wills or runs, but on God who shows mercy.” Therefore God did not have mercy because Jacob willed and ran; rather, Jacob willed and ran because God had mercy. For the will is prepared by the Lord; and a person’s steps will be directed by the Lord, and he will desire that person’s way (Ps. 36).

Then, because this general statement, “it depends not on one who wills nor on one who runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Ps. 98), was made concerning Jacob, an example is also given concerning Pharaoh, on account of the statement, “Esau I hated”; and there follows: “For Scripture says,” and so forth. God rejected Esau by justice, because Scripture says this, introducing [Col. 0730A] God as speaking to Pharaoh through Moses: “For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you.” “I did not make you evil, but I raised you up. For you were evil, but as though asleep. Yet I, by showing you signs and commanding you to let my people go, raised you up into the same wickedness, that you might become worse. For it is just that ‘the one who is filthy should become still more filthy’ (Rev. 22).”

Nor was your being raised up useless, but it was so that in you—hardened and resisting—I might show my power by multiplying my signs and finally drowning you while powerfully delivering my people. “And that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth”: that is, that the fame and glory of my name might resound everywhere, and that all nations might learn knowledge of me, when the report of the mighty deeds I have worked has been spread everywhere [Col. 0730B]—namely, how by a strong hand I brought my people out from among their enemies, and drowned in the Red Sea those who pursued them from behind, so that not one survived.

After this, a conclusion is drawn from both matters: from what was said concerning Jacob and from what was said concerning Esau or Pharaoh. Since, he says, God chose Jacob by mercy alone, but justly rejected Esau or raised Pharaoh up for his own destruction, because he so willed in both cases, therefore “he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills.” He has mercy by a gratuitous gift; he hardens by altogether just desert. He has mercy according to grace, which is freely given and not repaid to merits; he hardens according to judgment, which is repaid according to merits. He has mercy in great goodness; he hardens with no injustice, so that neither the delivered person may boast of his own merits [Col. 0730C], nor the condemned person complain except of his own merits.

For the grace of the Redeemer alone distinguishes from the lost those whom the cause of a shared origin had compacted into one mass of perdition. Therefore, although the whole world could most justly be condemned, God has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills: that is, he does not show mercy to that person nor soften that person’s heart. Yet his will, by which he wills to have mercy on one and does not will it for another, is not unjust. For who would say that someone powerful acts unjustly if, of two guilty persons, he rightly wills to put one to death and mercifully free the other? So too God can be blamed in no respect, whether he condemns or has mercy. For there is no merit for mercy; but the merit for hardening is the sin [Col. 0730D] of the whole condemned mass. God does not harden by imparting hardness, but by not imparting mercy, since they are not worthy of it. He does this by a hidden equity, remote from human understanding.

> “You will say to me, then: ‘Why does he still find fault? For who resists his will?’ O human being, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’ (Isa. 45; Jer. 18). Or does not the potter have power over the clay, from the same mass to make one vessel for honour and another for dishonour?”

From the preceding statement the Apostle foresaw that the rash weakness of those would be stirred who try, by the conjectures of the human heart, to consider the unsearchable height of God’s judgments, seek to excuse themselves from their sins [Col. 0731A], and oppose this objection to him. He says: “Since I have said that God has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills, you therefore—that is, consequently—say, that is, object, to me: ‘Why does God still complain of us? For who resists his will?’”

This means: Why is there a complaint against us because we offend God by living wickedly, when no one can resist his will—he who hardened us by not granting mercy? For God often complains of human beings, as is evident from innumerable passages of Scripture: they do not wish to believe and live rightly (Luke 1). Hence believers who do his will are said to conduct themselves blamelessly, because Scripture does not complain of them. Yet he complains of various others.

But they ask: Why does he complain and accuse us because we have not done good [Col. 0731B] or have done evil, when it is in his power and will, without good or evil works, either to choose someone or reject someone—especially when human frailty cannot resist his will? Why should he complain of human sins when a person cannot avoid what he himself wills?

Those who live carnally in pleasures are accustomed thus to murmur against God, attributing their wickedness to his will rather than to their own fault, and preparing a forceful accusation against him in such words. The Apostle rebukes them for this presumption and resolves their question in a brief saying: “O human being, who are you to answer back to God?” The sense is: in wanting to answer, you bring an accusation against God; and because you investigate Scripture so deeply as to speak against God and inquire into the justice of his will [Col. 0731C], you show that you possess free choice and can act rightly if you wish.

Some foolish people have thought that here the Apostle failed to give an answer, and restrained the audacity of his opponent because he lacked an explanation. But great weight lies in the words, “O human being, who are you,” and so forth. In questions of this kind, to call a human being back to consideration of his own capacity is indeed a brief verbal answer, but in reality a great one. For if someone does not grasp these matters, who is that person to answer back? If someone does grasp them, he finds all the more that he has no answer.

If one understands, then, one sees that the whole human race was condemned in the apostate root by so just a divine judgment that, even if no one were delivered from it, no one could rightly blame God’s justice [Col. 0731D]. And those who are delivered ought to have been delivered in such a way that, from the many not delivered and left in most just condemnation, it might be shown what the whole mass had deserved, and whither God’s due judgment would have led even these, had unmerited mercy not come to their aid. Thus every mouth of those wishing to boast in their own merits is stopped, and “the one who boasts, let him boast in the Lord.”

“O human being, who are you to answer back to God?” Consider who he is; consider who you are. He is God; you are a human being. Yet you seem to speak justice: has that fountain of justice run dry? Let it for the present suffice you, still living by faith and not yet seeing what is perfect, but knowing only in part, to know or believe that God delivers no one except by gratuitous mercy and condemns no one except by most equitable justice. But why he delivers [Col. 0732A] one rather than another, or does not deliver one rather than another, let one investigate who can fathom so great a depth of his judgments—but let him beware the precipice.

For you, a human being, who are you to answer back to God? One who is called a human being is shown unable to answer God, because, being taken from the earth, he is not worthy to examine heavenly judgments. O human being: that is, fleshly, belonging to Adam; you who are made of clay, who are you—that is, of what strength—who answer back to God, who argue against God that he chooses and rejects unjustly, or inquire into the causes of his judgments, why he chooses this one and rejects that one?

God in some sense questions you through his works; and if you understood the causes and reasons of his works, you would answer him, because you would understand the counsel of his will. But you, a human being—who are you [Col. 0732B] to do this? Go beyond humanity; go beyond carnality; go beyond human habits and perceptions, if you wish to attain this. First become one of those of whom it is said: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Cor. 2); and then at last you will rightly, and not prematurely, hear whatever may be said concerning the merits of souls and the hidden grace or justice of almighty God.

For sinners are commanded to believe, so that by believing they may be cleansed from sins. They do not know what they will see by living rightly. Therefore, since they cannot see unless they live rightly, and cannot live rightly unless they believe, it is clear that one must begin with faith, so that the commandments by which believers are turned away from this world may make the heart clean, where God may be seen.

Therefore it is rightly said to persons [Col. 0732C] remaining in the oldness of life and consequently bearing a darkened eye of the mind: “O human being, who are you,” and so forth. For here the Apostle did not forbid the saints to inquire, of whom he says: “The spiritual person judges all things” (ibid.); rather, he forbade persons of clay and earth, who still bear the image of the one first made earthly from the earth, and who, because he was unwilling to obey the one by whom he was made, fell into that from which he had been made.

Such persons, therefore, are told: “O human being, who are you to answer back to God?” And he adds: “Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’” Here he shows, as it were by an analogy—and indeed from the lesser case—that God does nothing unjustly if he has mercy on one and withholds mercy from another. “If,” he says, “a thing formed for an unclean use cannot accuse its maker of injustice [Col. 0732D], although the formed object is a work far more worthy in relation to the potter than you, a human being, are in relation to God, then he who is the true potter—that is, our creator, craftsman, and maker—has the power, without prejudice to justice, to have mercy on whom he wills and to harden whom he wills.”

But as long as you are a thing formed, you are not yet a perfected son, because you have not yet received the fullness of grace. For power has been given to us to become children of God (John 1), so that you may be able to hear: “I shall no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15). Yet you already wish to answer back to God and know his counsel. If you wished to know the counsel of a human being equal to yourself, you would act shamelessly unless you had first been received into friendship. Therefore, if you wish to know God’s counsel, first strive to become his friend through the merit of holiness, so that you may not be a clay formation but [Col. 0733A] a spiritual person.

For, to make clear that these words are directed not to one sanctified by the Spirit but to carnal clay, he immediately adds: “Does not the potter have power over the clay, from the same mass to make one vessel for honour and another for dishonour?” Since our nature sinned in Paradise, we are now formed by God’s providence not according to heaven but according to earth: that is, not according to spirit but according to mortal generation. All of us have been made from one mass of clay, which is the mass of sin.

Therefore, since by sinning we have lost merit, and with God’s mercy removed nothing but eternal condemnation is due to sinners, what does a human being from this mass want, that he should answer back to God and say: “Why have you made me thus?” If this mass were indeed neutral, deserving neither good nor evil, it would not seem without reason to be unjust that vessels for dishonour should be made from it. But since through the free choice of the first human being all have flowed into condemnation [Col. 0733B], undoubtedly the fact that vessels for honour are made from it is to be attributed not to its own righteousness—which did not precede grace at all—but to God’s mercy; whereas the fact that vessels for dishonour are made from it is to be ascribed not to God’s injustice, which does not exist, but to judgment.

He is a potter when he makes persons fragile, weak, and earthly. And from the same mass, which wholly perished in Adam, he makes according to his will some vessels for honour through mercy, others for dishonour through judgment.

> “But if God, willing to show wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience [Col. 0733C] vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, in order that he might show the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory—us also, whom he called not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles—as he says in Hosea: ‘I will call not-my-people, my people; and her who had not obtained mercy, one who has obtained mercy. And it shall be, in the place where it was said to them, “You are not my people,” there they shall be called sons of the living God.’”

It has been shown above that even if God gives no good thing, he is nevertheless not unjust, and a human being cannot answer him. But what is this? He himself has also given good things to some. What answer will you make to him? What will you say if God bestowed good things upon them—namely, when they were fitted for destruction, endured them with much patience, and meanwhile [Col. 0733D], while waiting, showed by many indications, either by sometimes punishing them or others before their eyes, the coming wrath, so that they might beware? And in that he endured them and showed wrath, he made his power known, because through evil persons he purges the good.

It is as if he said: You can say that he justly withdraws grace and condemns those who, though thus waited for, did not wish to repent but abused that grace. If God, willing to show wrath in the lost by inflicting vengeance upon them and to make known his power by making good use of evil persons—because his goodness is so powerful that he makes good use even of evil persons—endured with much patience, that is, tolerated for a very long time, vessels of wrath, namely people full of his wrath; vessels, I say, fitted for destruction, that is, suited to eternal death: if God did this, his patience is not to be blamed, but their [Col. 0734A] obstinacy, since though long awaited they did not wish to be converted.

For he endured them, although he knew they would not be converted, so that they might become inexcusable and that through their wickedness the good might be purified. Therefore he endured them, so that in the world to come he might show the riches of his glory—that is, the abundant wealth of eternal blessedness—which would come to vessels of mercy, that is, to chosen people filled with his mercy. These chosen vessels he himself prepared for glory, whereas, conversely, vessels of wrath are fitted to fall into destruction. For what the justice of the punisher exacts from vessels of wrath, the compassion of the deliverer remits for vessels of mercy; and beyond that, the grace of the Saviour bestows his glory upon them.

It should be noted that in what he said above—that the potter has power from the same mass to make one vessel for honour and another for dishonour—he mystically showed [Col. 0734B] that the Creator cannot be censured if, from the same mass of human nature, he creates some for the honour of holiness, while he creates others in such a way as to allow them to go into the dishonour of utterly wicked action and just condemnation.

But in what you now say, “But if God, willing,” and so forth, he declares that he cannot be accused if he patiently tolerates evil persons living long in the flesh, in order later to punish them more severely as they persist in wickedness; and if he permits good people to be harassed by their perversity, in order to repay them with a greater crown of glory as the reward of patience. If he patiently endures those whom he hardens, in order more justly to condemn them after enduring them for a long time, it is not his patience and boundless clemency that should be blamed, but their hardness, since they abuse his goodness to their destruction.

Otherwise, the sun’s heat is one, yet according to the substances subjected to it, it hardens some things, melts others, dissolves others, and binds others. Wax melts, clay hardens, yet the nature of the heat is not different. So too God’s goodness and clemency harden vessels of wrath—that is, the Jewish people and the other reprobate—while melting vessels of mercy, that is, the elect. The formed thing cannot say to its maker, “Why have you made me thus?” because the maker himself has authority to make, from the same clay, according to his will, some vessels for honourable uses and others for dishonourable uses [Col. 0734C].

“But if God, willing to show wrath, endured with much patience vessels of wrath,” who are you to answer back to God? God wished to show his wrath—not an emotional disturbance such as is named among human beings, but just vengeance—and to make known his power, to which it belongs to condemn the wicked. His power is also shown in this, that he who is supremely good can make good use even of evil persons.

Therefore he wished to show this power, by which he makes good use even of evil persons, granting them many natural and temporal goods and applying their wickedness and their comparison for the exercise and admonition of the good, so that in them the good may learn to give thanks to God because they were distinguished from them, not by their own merits, which were equal in the same mass, but by his mercy.

For if only those who would be redeemed by grace were created from Adam, and, apart from those adopted as children like Jews, no other people were born, the benefit bestowed on the undeserving would remain hidden, because [Col. 0735A] no one coming from the same condemnable stock would receive the punishment due. Therefore God, willing to show wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction—that is, reprobate people, in whom his wrath lies hidden and who are fitted for perdition. He bore them long-sufferingly, so that he might order them suitably and use them for the instruction in salvation of those on whom he has mercy; and for this reason these are called vessels of mercy.

This is not because either angelic or human sins were necessary to him, to whom not even the righteousness of any creature is necessary, but so that he might show the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, lest they exalt themselves in good works as though by their own powers. Rather, they might humbly understand that, unless God’s grace—not owed but freely bestowed—came to their aid, what was repaid to others in the same mass would have had to be repaid to their own merits [Col. 0735B].

For those justified freely thus recognize what is bestowed upon them, when they are distinguished from the condemned not by their own merit but by the glory of God’s most abundant mercy, although they too would have been condemned with the same justice. The remaining people, who do not belong to this grace—though God’s goodness made both their soul and body, and whatever nature itself possesses apart from the vice implanted in it by the audacity of a proud will—were created by God, who without doubt foreknew that they would sin in such a manner as to be condemned to eternal fire, in order that in them he might show what the free choice of one who abandons him can accomplish without his grace. And in their just and deserved punishments, the vessels of mercy, distinguished [Col. 0735C] from that common creation not by merits of their own works but by God’s gratuitous grace, might learn what had been bestowed upon them: “that every mouth may be stopped” (Rom. 3), and so forth; “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1).

“So that he might show,” he says, “the riches of his glory,” by which he is glorified in the saints, causing them to act well, “upon vessels of mercy,” that is, upon people whom he fills with his mercy; “which,” that is, whom—the elect people—he prepared, that is, preordained, for eternal glory. “Whom he also called”—namely, us—not only from the Jews, as the Jews themselves wished, but also from the Gentiles, so that from both there might be one people of believers. From this it is shown that not Gentiles or Jews are chosen, but human wills divinely illuminated.

“Whom he also called us” is put as though he had said: “Just as he called us [Col. 0735D], not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles.” For above he seems, as it were, to be discussing Pharaoh and the Egyptians, who were vessels of wrath, and the children of Israel, who were vessels of mercy. But now, lest only those ancient Israelites be understood as vessels of mercy, he shows that we also, called to the new grace not only from that people of the Hebrews but also from Gentile stock, are called vessels of the same mercy.

God also called us from the Gentiles, as he himself says in Hosea: “Not-my-people”—that is, the Gentile world, which was not my people—“I will call my people”: that is, I will give it the designation of my special people through the grace of the Christian name. And “her who had not obtained mercy”—that is, the same Gentile world, which had not obtained mercy [Col. 0736A] but had been left without mercy to destruction—“I will call one who has obtained mercy”: that is, I will give it this designation, that it may be called one having obtained mercy, so that the name indicates the benefit.

And this will take place in the time of grace, “in the place,” that is, in the land of the Gentiles, where it was divinely said to them: “You are not my people.” There, that is, in the same Gentile region, those who are there will be called “sons of the living God.” Because God did not call the Gentiles to his worship but left them in error, he said to them: “You are not my people.” But in the Gentile place where this had formerly been said, there afterward, when the grace of the Gospel was preached through the apostles, those who believed there were called sons not of a dead god but of the living God.

For formerly they worshipped many dead gods—that is, dead human beings whom they had made their gods—such as [Col. 0736B] Jupiter, Apollo, and Hercules. Therefore, lest anyone understand one of such beings to be the God now named by the prophet when he speaks of the Gentiles, he calls him “the living God.”

> “But Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: ‘Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, the remnant shall be saved’ (Isa. 10). ‘For he is bringing the matter to completion and cutting it short in righteousness, because the Lord will perform a shortened matter upon the earth.’ And as Isaiah foretold: ‘Unless the Lord of Sabaoth had left us seed, we would have become like Sodom, and would have been made like Gomorrah’ (Isa. 1).”

Because he had said that these were called not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles, and had established by prophetic testimony the calling of the Gentiles, concerning whom there seemed to be less evidence [Col. 0736C], he wishes likewise to show by prophetic authority the calling of the Jews. Hosea speaks of the conversion of the Gentiles, but Isaiah cries out—that is, testifies openly and publicly—for Israel, that is, for the conversion of the Jews. “Though the number,” etc.: that is, even if the multitude does not believe, nevertheless a few will believe. And indeed, if we read Josephus, how great was the multitude of persons in Jerusalem and Judaea when the Lord suffered, we shall understand that scarcely a few Jews were saved in the apostles and apostolic men. But because the unbelieving and proud—and therefore fruitless—branches were broken off so that the wild olive of the Gentiles might be grafted in, the root of the patriarchs and prophets could not therefore perish. For, he says, “though the number of the children [Col. 0736D] of Israel be as the sand of the sea,” that is, though there be so many Jews that they cannot be comprehended by number, and their multitude surpasses every calculation, like sand which cannot be numbered, “the remnant shall be saved”: that is, those whom the Lord reserves for himself, when he rejects the others, shall be saved. Or, if their number is barren and heavy like the sand of the sea, the remnant, which will be shining and cleaving to heaven like the stars, shall be saved. For both were promised to Abraham: “Your seed,” he says, “shall be as the stars of heaven and as the sand upon the shore of the sea” (Gen. XXVIII).

They shall truly be saved, for the word will be completing and shortening in righteousness. Therefore they shall be saved, because the word of the Gospel delivered to them will complete a person in righteousness—that is, grant the perfection of righteousness [Col. 0737A]—and complete and perfect those things which the law could not. And it is “shortening,” that is, it comprehends in the one precept of twofold love all that the law had established by many commandments. And it will be shortening in righteousness, according to the saying: “What you do not wish another to do to you, do not do to another” (Tob. IV); and, “As you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them” (Matt. VII). Or it abbreviates all legal ordinances in the one Christ; and this in righteousness, because it is fitting for this word to be shortened, so that nothing may be lacking to righteousness from all that had been prefigured. Or, “in righteousness,” because it retains what is just, such as moral precepts, and removes what is right to remove, such as figures.

The word will truly be new and shortening, because “the Lord Jesus will make a shortened word upon the earth”: that is, by the concise faith of grace he will save believers [Col. 0737B], not by innumerable observances, under which the Jewish people were oppressed by a servile burden. The Lord made this word while dwelling upon earth among human beings. It was said that a remnant was to be saved from the multitude that perishes. And as Isaiah again foretold: “Unless the Lord Sabaoth”—that is, the Lord of hosts, whom the hosts of angels and human beings serve—“had left us Jews a seed,” that is, chosen children to be scattered throughout the world, “we should have become as Sodom, and should have been made like Gomorrah.” That is, just as in Sodom and Gomorrah, after Lot’s departure, only reprobates remained to perish together, so we too in Jerusalem, after Christ’s resurrection, would have remained solely reprobate and destined to perish. For those who believed from the circumcision [Col. 0737C] are called “seed,” because, scattered through the lands, they multiplied and, like grains of seed, produced an abundant harvest of believers. Because of these, the Jews were not like Sodom and Gomorrah: not all were reprobate, nor did all perish, since these were chosen and saved from their multitude.

> “What then shall we say? That the Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, attained righteousness—indeed, the righteousness which is from faith; but Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness, did not attain the law of righteousness. Why? Because not from faith, but as though from works. For they stumbled over the stone of stumbling, as it is written: ‘Behold, I place in Zion a stone [Col. 0737D] of stumbling and a rock of scandal; and everyone who believes in him shall not be put to shame’” (Isa. VIII).

From the authority of both prophets he concludes: Since, he says, Hosea says of the Gentiles, “I will call not-my-people, my people” (Hos. II), and Isaiah cries out concerning the children of Israel that their remnant shall be saved—that is, a few from the multitude—what then shall we say? That is, what shall we determine from these prophetic sayings concerning Gentiles and Jews? From the preceding oracles we can infer and affirm this: the Gentiles, who pursued God’s righteousness neither through sacrifices nor through their own will, attained righteousness—not any sort of righteousness, nor that which is from the law, but the righteousness which is from faith, that is, through grace, because they did not become proud but believed in Christ. [Col. 0738A] But Israel—that is, the carnal people of the Jews—while pursuing through carnal observances the law of righteousness, that is, the law which, rightly understood, is righteousness, did not attain the law of righteousness. They came indeed somewhat into the law of righteousness, but did not attain it; for although they performed works of the law, they did not perform them from love of righteousness but from fear of punishment, and thus could not possess innocence of heart.
