Here the truth of the aforementioned statement is proved: “It is not of the one who wills nor of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy.” For the Gentiles, as was said, who did not seek righteousness found righteousness; and Israel, which pursued the law of righteousness, could not attain it. “God is terrible in his counsels over the children of men” (Ps. LXV), and his judgments are hidden [Col. 0738B], not unjust. The Gentiles, who did not pursue the righteousness which is from the law, attained as their own righteousness the righteousness which is from faith. But Israel, pursuing through works the law of righteousness, did not attain the law of righteousness in heart.

And why? Let us carefully consider why it could not attain it. Because it was not from faith: that is, because it did not hope in God, did not seek it from God, and did not believe in him who justifies the ungodly. “Not from faith, but as though from works”: that is, as though producing righteousness through itself, not believing that God worked in it. For God is the one who works in us both to will and to work according to good will. But Israel did not seek to be justified by faith, but as though by works, because it did not regard faith as the cause and beginning of righteousness; rather, it believed that the works of carnal observances were the beginning of righteousness [Col. 0738C], and, glorying as though in works, excluded grace from itself; and, presuming upon health, rejected medicine.

The people of the Jews truly did not seek justification from faith, but as though from works; for they stumbled over the stone of stumbling—that is, Christ. Wishing in their pride to trample upon the humble Christ, they injured the step of their upright conduct and, shaken, fell. As though through their very righteousness they stumbled over Christ, because they feared as though for the sake of righteousness and despised Christ’s faith. Like a small stone against which one does not guard, he was apt for them to stumble over, hidden in humility. Christ too is a stone of stumbling to all evil persons, because whatever he says is bitter to them, and they are disturbed by his words.

Thus they stumbled over this stone, as it is written in Isaiah, the Father saying: “Behold, I place in Zion a stone of stumbling”—that is, through the mystery of the incarnation I place Christ in Zion, namely in the Church, as a foundation; he will be a stone of stumbling to the Jews, because through the blindness of their minds they will not guard themselves against him who is humble and small, but will stumble over him and fall. And I place there “a rock of scandal,” that is, the same Christ, who in his passion will be to them a rock of scandal—that is, ugly, rough, and hard—over which they will take offense in anger and indignation when he declares himself the Son of God. A stone is called polished and slippery, when, if stepped upon, the foot quickly slips; but it is called a rock when it is unworked and rough. Therefore Christ, in his birth, manner of life [Col. 0739A], and preaching, was a stone of stumbling to the Jews; and in his passion, a rock of scandal. For he who had first appeared contemptible and fit to be trodden underfoot in his origin and human life afterwards appeared to them in his passion exceedingly ugly and rough.

But scandal is greater than stumbling, because *scandal* is said to derive from the Greek *skandalizō*, and properly means a striking of the feet. Thus the Jews stumbled over Christ so as wholly to strike their foot there and break it. For they not only despised him but also crucified him. I place this stone of stumbling with respect to the reprobate; and with respect to the elect I add: every person—Jew or Gentile, slave or free—who believes in him shall not be put to shame, that is, shall not blush in the future when he comes for judgment. [Col. 0739B] For whoever believes in him will not possess his own righteousness, which is from the law, even though the law is good; rather, that person will fulfill the law itself, not by personal righteousness but by righteousness given from God. Thus that person will not be put to shame. For one who glories in oneself will be put to shame, since one will not be found without sins. But that person alone will not be put to shame who glories in the Lord.

All who await him in faith will rejoice when he comes. Those who are without faith, when that which they do not now see comes, will blush, as people are ordinarily put to shame when they are found guilty of some fault and are mocked by everyone; yet that shame will not pass away or be erased. It should be noted that the Apostle combined this testimony from two places in the book of Isaiah. For there it reads: “Behold, I will lay in the foundations of Zion a tested stone [Col. 0739C], a precious cornerstone, firmly founded in the foundation. Whoever believes shall not hasten” (Isa. XXVIII). And elsewhere in the same book: “He shall be for your sanctification; but a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal to the two houses of Israel” (Isa. VIII). Hence it is plain that in interpreting the Old Scriptures the apostles sought the sense, not the words, and did not greatly concern themselves with order or wording when the meaning was clear.

## Chapter X

> “Brothers, indeed the desire of my heart and my supplication to the Lord for them is for salvation. For I bear them witness that they have zeal [Col. 0739D] for God, but not according to knowledge. For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they are not subject to God’s righteousness; for Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.”

Here he now begins to speak of hope for the Jews, lest the Gentiles too dare to become proud against them. For just as Jewish pride had to be refuted, as the pride of those who glory in works, so the Gentiles must be met, lest they grow proud as though preferred to the Jews. I said that they did not attain the law of righteousness but stumbled over the stone of stumbling, not because I hate them or wholly despair of them. For know, brothers, that the innermost desire of my heart is for their salvation: that is, I desire their salvation from the heart. [Col. 0740A] The desire of my heart wishes for them to receive salvation, although their own will still resists. For God is able to turn their hearts.

Not only desire, but also supplication—that is, prayer with adjuration by sacred things—is made by me to God for them unto salvation: that is, in order that my prayer for them may be more effective, I make it with an adjuration by sacred things, directing my intention toward their salvation, namely that they may believe and through faith attain salvation. For otherwise they cannot be saved. Although the Apostle preached the Gospel to them urgently, he nevertheless judged it insufficient unless he also prayed for them to believe, because the will, in order to be moved to believe true things, is not sufficient for itself unless God helps it by grace; nor can conversion itself occur without God’s assistance.

“I make supplication for them,” he says, “and it is right that I should do so, for they have zeal for God.” For I, who was once like them, and therefore know the intention of their hearts, bear them witness that they have zeal for God: that is, they are moved by good zeal to defend the law, but not according to knowledge, because they act imprudently when they persecute us as transgressors of the law. For they do not know that we, rather than they, fulfill the law by observing it spiritually; and therefore, although with good intention they wish to defend the law against transgressors, they do so not according to knowledge, because they do not know who those are against whom they are stirred. The Lord also foretold this: “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God” [Col. 0740C] (John XVI). For they thought they pleased God by killing Christians as though in defense of the law, because they had zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.

Truly, it was not according to knowledge. For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness—that is, the righteousness given by God through faith in Christ—and seeking to establish their own righteousness—that which they think they make by their own powers through observance of the law—they were not subject to God’s righteousness, that is, to Christ. Presuming upon themselves, they rejected grace and therefore did not believe in Christ, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own. “God’s righteousness” here means not the righteousness by which God himself is righteous, but that which he gives a human being, so that the human being may be righteous through God. Their righteousness, however, was that they presumed upon their own [Col. 0740D] powers and called themselves fulfillers of the law by their own strength.

They were therefore ignorant of God’s righteousness—that which God gives a human being, God who alone is righteous and makes righteous—and wished to establish their own, as though prepared by themselves for themselves, not bestowed by him. Therefore they were not subject to God’s righteousness, because they were proud, thinking that they could please God through what was their own, not through what was God’s. They were truly ignorant of God’s righteousness, for Christ, whom the blind rejected, is the end—that is, the completion—of the law, because in him the law is completed and perfected. Christ is the end, that is, the perfection, of the law for the fulfillment of righteousness in everyone who believes in him; because everyone who believes in Christ has Christ himself as the completion of the law, so as to perform righteousness through him.

For there are works which appear good without faith in Christ and are not good, because they are not referred to the end from which they are good. Such were the works of those who sought to establish their own righteousness; for the command, “You shall not covet” (Exod. XX), and other holy and good commandments of this kind, were given to them. In order that a human being may perform them, God works in the human being through faith in Christ, who is the end for righteousness to everyone who believes. Incorporated through the Spirit and made his member, each person can perform righteousness while he inwardly supplies growth; concerning these works he himself also said: “Without me you can do nothing” [Col. 0741A] (John XV).

Christ himself is called the end because whatever we do, we refer to him; and when we reach him, we shall have nothing further to seek, but shall remain there. For our intention is directed toward him. When we have reached him, there will be no further goal toward which we must strive, because there is the fullness of all good things.

> “For Moses wrote that the person who does the righteousness which is from the law shall live in it” (Lev. XVIII). “But the righteousness which is from faith speaks thus: ‘Do not say in your heart, Who shall ascend into heaven?’” (Deut. XXX), “that is, to bring Christ down; or, ‘Who shall descend into the abyss?’ that is, to bring Christ back from the dead. But what does Scripture say? ‘The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart.’ This is the word of faith which we preach: because if you confess the Lord Jesus with your mouth, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, [Col. 0741C] you shall be saved.”

Christ is truly the end of the law unto true righteousness, for in the law itself, before one comes to Christ, there is a certain shadowy righteousness. For Moses wrote thus. The Apostle proves from Moses’ authority that there are two righteousnesses, because he had said that the Jews were ignorant of God’s righteousness and sought to establish their own. There are truly two: one through the law, the other through Christ. Moses wrote that the person who performs the righteousness which is from the law shall live in it, using “law” here for the works themselves. Those, however, who lived in these works certainly feared that, if they did not perform them, they might suffer stoning, burning, or something similar. Therefore, “the person who performs them,” he says, “shall live in them”: that is, shall have the reward of not being punished by this death; not, therefore, [shall he live] with God; for if anyone lives in this present life by faith in him, then, when that person departs from here, that person will have the more immediate reward.

Thus whoever desires or fears the visible present things does not live by faith, because faith in God pertains to invisible things which will be given afterwards. Yet there is also a certain righteousness in works, when it is not left without its own reward, so that the one who performs it may live in it. Hence it was also said above that even if Abraham was justified by works, he has glory, but not before God. Therefore, not being justified before God is one thing; not being justified at all is another. Whoever is not justified at all observes neither those things which have a temporal reward nor those which have an eternal reward; but one who is justified in works of the law [Col. 0742A] is not justified before God, because that person expects from them a temporal and visible recompense. Yet even this, as I said, is a certain earthly and carnal righteousness. This is what Moses says of the righteousness of the law.

But the righteousness which is from faith speaks thus, either Moses himself says it, or righteousness itself speaks in the human heart: “Do not say in your heart,” etc. Or, if the righteousness of the law, in which one lives, is to be understood as true righteousness that confers eternal life, then the righteousness of the law is set forth—“the person who performs it shall live in it”—so that, when a person has recognized personal weakness, that person may attain it, perform it, and live in it, not by personal powers nor by the letter of the law itself, which is impossible, but by faith conciliating the justifier. For the work which, when someone performs it, that person lives in, is not done except by one who has been justified. Justification is obtained from faith; and thus, through the righteousness of faith [Col. 0742B], the true righteousness of the law is fulfilled.

Concerning the righteousness of this faith Moses speaks thus—or righteousness itself speaks in the human heart: “Do not say in your heart,” that is, do not even think, “Who shall ascend into heaven?” That is, no human being will ascend, because this is, as far as you are concerned, to bring Christ down: if you think this, you will deny that Christ ascended. Or do not say in your heart, “Who shall descend into the abyss?” That is, no one shall descend into hell because of a despised law, because this is, as far as you are concerned, to bring Christ back from the dead. To think this is not to believe that Christ died for us and descended into hell for the liberation of the righteous who were held there.

Or thus: when after the resurrection you hear Christ preached as having ascended into heaven, do not say in your heart, “It is a lie; for who shall ascend?” For this unbelief, as far as you are concerned, brings Christ down from heaven to earth. Or when you hear it preached that he descended into hell, do not doubt or judge this unbelievable; for this unbelief, as far as you are concerned, brings Christ back from the dead, that is, denies that Christ was dead. For if it is doubted that he descended into the abyss, neither is it believed that he was dead; because as he died in order to destroy death, so he descended into the abyss in order to draw his own out from there. This is the righteousness of faith, distinct from the righteousness of the law’s mortality: that one should not doubt God’s hope, which is in Christ; that one should not distrust that Christ despoiled hell and ascended into heaven with the souls of the saints. For one who believes this is thereby made righteous.

It can also be understood thus: “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who shall ascend into heaven?’” That is, who will ascend there in order to bring Christ down to us? Or, “Who shall descend into the abyss?” That is, who will descend into hell in order to bring Christ back from the dead? Christ did not wait for any human being to ascend into heaven to bring him down, which was impossible; but he himself freely descended, coming from his Father’s seat to seek and save that which had perished. Nor was it necessary or possible for anyone to descend into the abyss in order to bring Christ back from the dead, because by his own power, having bound the strong adversary and despoiled hell, he rose from the dead [Col. 0742D] (Luke XIX).

“Do not say,” he says, “Who shall ascend into heaven to bring Christ down?”—as though Christ were not also on earth, he who by divinity is everywhere; [Col. 0743A] or, “Who shall descend into the abyss to bring Christ back from the dead?”—as though Christ could be contained in the abyss, he who is contained by no place but contains all things; or as though he could remain among the dead, he who is life. Do not say this. But what does Scripture through Moses (Deut. XXX) say concerning Christ? “The word is near”: that is, Christ, who is the Word and Wisdom of God (1 Cor. I), is near, that is, not far from the nature of minds and the faculty of speech. He is near in your mouth for confession and in your heart for faith. Therefore do not seek him by places, he who, as Word, Truth, and Wisdom, is everywhere and remains in the heart and mouth of the righteous; rather, believe that the Word personally united to humanity is near us, because he is not remote from our speech or our understanding. [Col. 0743B]

This word, which Moses says is so near, is the word of faith which we preach: that is, Christ, in whom our faith rests and whom we proclaim. We preach this concerning him: that if you confess, etc. Or the reason is given why this word ought to be in the mouth and heart: because if you confess the Lord Jesus with your mouth and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you shall be saved. The praise of Christians’ faith is not that they believe Christ died, but that they believe Christ rose again. For even a pagan believes that he died. This is the praise of faith: that we believe he rose and hope that we too shall rise through him. For he did not say, “If you confess that God delivered him up to be killed”; but, “If you confess that God raised him [Col. 0743C] from the dead, then you shall be saved.” You are saved to the extent that you are righteous.

Why, then, do we also believe that he died? Because we cannot believe that he rose unless we first believe that he had died. This confession pertains especially to martyrs, who confessed Christ before tyrants and died for his confession. For in our time it is easy for anyone to confess Christ with the voice; and therefore the voice alone is not sufficient without works.

> “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. For Scripture says: ‘Everyone who believes in him shall not be put to shame’” (Isa. XXVIII). “For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek. For the same Lord of all is rich toward all who [Col. 0743D] call upon him. For everyone, whoever calls upon the name of the Lord, shall be saved” (Joel II).

Truly, if you believe Christ’s resurrection in your heart and confess it with your mouth, you shall be saved; for with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. That is, one who believes in the heart possesses righteousness in the present, because “the righteous shall live by faith” (Hab. II); and one who confesses with the mouth possesses salvation in the future. Therefore we must remember both righteousness and salvation, since, although we shall reign in everlasting righteousness, we cannot be saved from the present evil age unless, striving also for the salvation of our neighbors, we profess with our mouths what we carry in our hearts.

For believing gives salvation, because it produces righteousness, which is the cause of salvation, provided that the mouth confesses what the heart believes. For this is to confess: to say what one has in one’s heart. But if you have one thing in your heart and say another, you speak; you do not confess. Do not be ashamed of your hope before people. As Christ lives in your heart, so let him dwell in your mouth; for not without reason did Christ will his sign to be marked on our forehead, as though on the seat of shame, lest a Christian be ashamed of Christ’s reproaches. Therefore it is too little to have Christ in the heart and refuse confession when reproach is feared. For whoever desires to have salvation ought to utter faith with the mouth, because confession is made with the mouth unto salvation. Otherwise faith of the heart does not give salvation, although with the heart one believes unto righteousness.

Faith truly uttered with the mouth leads to salvation, for Scripture says in Isaiah: Everyone—not only a Jew but also a Gentile—who believes in him, that is, in Christ, [Col. 0744B] shall not be put to shame, that is, shall not blush on the day of judgment, because that person shall attain the salvation believed in. And truly, everyone. For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek: that is, the prophet named neither Jew nor Gentile, but in saying “everyone” showed both peoples, because whoever, with sincere faith and upright works, groans to God may be saved. Truly there is no distinction. For the same Lord is Lord of all, both Jews and Gentiles, rich toward all: that is, sufficient to enrich all who call upon him, that is, who by devout dedication call him into themselves, preparing themselves as worthy of such an indweller.

He is rich toward those who call upon him, not merely those who believe; because belief gives forgiveness of sins, while calling upon him obtains God’s promises. One who prays calls upon him, but cannot do so without first believing. Rightly, I said that he is rich toward all, not toward certain or few who call upon him; for as Joel testifies when foretelling the time of grace, everyone whoever calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. No one is excepted; this grace is denied to no one. Rather, every Jew and Gentile, of whatever rank or condition, whoever calls upon the name of the Lord in devout prayers, preparing oneself as worthy to receive God, the indweller, in the temple of one’s heart, shall be saved with eternal salvation. [Col. 0744C]

> “How then shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how shall they believe him of whom they have not heard? But how shall they hear without a preacher? And how indeed shall they preach unless they are sent, as it is written: ‘How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things’” (Isa. LII; Nahum I).

Having proved that those who are to be saved are taken from both peoples, he shows that they are taken through the mission made to both; whoever does not receive it is without excuse. “Whoever calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Joel II). Therefore one must believe. For how shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Calling upon him, he says, saves; but no one calls upon him without belief. Unless they believe, they will not call upon him; and unless they call upon him, they will not be saved. This is said especially concerning the Gentiles, lest anyone suppose that only Jews are called to faith.

How shall they call upon Christ in whom they have not believed? They must first believe. Or how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? For it is first necessary that they hear him from someone’s mouth. For belief is from hearing. But how shall they hear him without someone preaching? It is necessary that someone preach, from whom the rest may hear what they ought to believe. For they will not hear unless it has been preached. But how shall teachers preach unless they are sent? They cannot preach unless they have been sent, because they are not true apostles unless sent. Human effort is empty unless God helps those whom he has sent; nor does any power of proclamation endure for them unless he who sent them is present with them. [Col. 0745A]

By these words the Apostle refutes those who denied that Christ’s heralds ought to be sent to uncircumcised nations, and shows that salvation has come to all through God’s grace. Salvation, he says, is from calling upon God; calling upon God, from faith; faith, from hearing; hearing, from preaching; preaching, from mission—so that everything descends from the fountain of grace. Therefore all things are ours not from ourselves but from God’s grace, by which heralds of our salvation were sent beforehand, as it is written in Isaiah: “How beautiful,” that is, how wonderfully lovely, “are the feet,” that is, the steps, “of the apostles enlightening the world,” whereby it appears that they were sent by God, since otherwise they could not do this. They are beautiful—that is, adorned with the beauty of virtues and the brightness of miracles and preaching—the feet, that is, the progress, of the apostles who evangelize, that is, who announce to human beings peace, namely reconciliation and concord with the Lord, and proclaim the good things of the kingdom of heaven. [Col. 0745B]

> “But not all obey the Gospel. For Isaiah [Col. 0745C] says: ‘Lord, who has believed our report?’” (Isa. LIII; John XII.) “Therefore faith is from hearing, but hearing through the word of Christ.”

The apostles indeed proclaim peace to all, but not all obey the Gospel, so as to repent of what has gone before and henceforth endeavor to have peace with God by living uprightly. For, since hearing is from grace, another grace that moves the heart is necessary; for the teacher’s outward speech profits nothing if God has not inwardly touched the hearer’s heart. And truly, not all obey the Gospel, but few do. For Isaiah, speaking in the voice of preachers, laments the scarcity of hearers: “Lord, who”—that is, how rare is the person—“has believed our report,” that is, the report of preaching which we heard from you and announced to them? Out of many, one who believes is rarely found. And it is clear that those who do not believe do not obey. Few from the multitude believed the report of preaching; therefore faith is from hearing, because from what we have heard from teachers we begin to believe. But hearing is not through our merits; it is through Christ’s word of preaching, which teachers have received from his grace. [Col. 0745D]

> “But I say: Have they not heard? Indeed, their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII).

Isaiah says that few believed, but I say: “Have they not heard?” Certainly they have heard, and therefore those who did not believe are without excuse. Indeed, not only those nearby but those most remote were able to hear. For their sound—that is, their fame, the fame of the apostles—has gone into all the earth; and their very words have gone forth to the ends of the world, that is, to every boundary of the world round about, so that truth might be heard not only by report but also known through the actual words of the preachers. Yet this had not been fulfilled entirely when the Apostle wrote; but he spoke in the past tense, as did the prophet concerning what was future and already fulfilled in large part. [Col. 0746A]

> “But I say: Did Israel not know? Moses first says: ‘I will provoke you to jealousy by that which is not a nation; by a foolish nation I will provoke you to anger’” (Deut. XXXII). “But Isaiah ventures and [Col. 0746B] says: ‘I was found by those who did not seek me; I appeared openly to those who did not ask for me.’ But to Israel he says: ‘All day long I stretched out my hands to a people not believing, but contradicting me’” (Isa. LXV).

The renown of the Christian name has gone forth among all nations, even to the limits of the world. But I say: Did Israel not know what the whole world has heard? Israel did not fail to know this salvation, but knew that it could have heard and known it. It knew, because it could not contradict it. Yet it did not truly know it, so that it might be firmly established in its mind. It knew it as testimony to its condemnation, not as aid toward its salvation. It truly knew it, because Moses, their first teacher, says this, and all the prophets after him speak similar things [Col. 0746C]. For this is implied when Moses is now called “first,” whom others followed in the same sense.

Moses, speaking with God’s voice, says to the Jews in the Song, while foretelling their unbelief: “I will provoke you to jealousy by a non-nation,” that is, I will do such a thing for the nation of pagans—which ought not even to be called a nation because of the folly of idolatry—that you will feel jealousy, that is, envy. For the Jews waste away with envy when the nations call their God their own and say that the Law and the prophets belong to them. And so they were led into envy against a non-nation, that is, against the Gentile people, concerning whom it was said: “All nations are as though they were not before God” (Isa. XL). [Col. 0746D]

Or, “by a non-nation”: it was a nation, but by believing it laid aside its gentile character; and it became a non-nation, that is, the Christian people through baptism. For so long as it was unbelieving, it was a nation; but in the Church it is called “a people for possession” (I Pet. II). “Thus,” he says, “I will provoke you to jealousy against a non-nation,” that is, against Gentiles converted to the faith, who will embrace the faith which you reject; “against a foolish nation,” that is, against those same Gentiles, who had been ignorant of God’s wisdom and had proclaimed the folly of idolatry; “and I will provoke you to anger,” that is, to indignation—I shall permit you to be angry and indignant. That is, I shall grant such great benefits to the Gentiles that you will be angered by them.

Moses said this, and the Jews read and have read this Scripture; therefore they know that the preaching of Christ is throughout the nations over the world [Col. 0747A]. This was Moses; but Isaiah “dares and says,” that is, he speaks more boldly concerning the salvation of the Gentiles, since, although he knew danger threatened him, he nevertheless boldly preached God’s word. For King Manasseh, as the Hebrews attest, afterward sawed him with a wooden saw. Isaiah therefore knew that he would be despised by the ungodly and killed; yet, casting fear aside, he preached the grace of God and said in Christ’s person: “I was found by those who did not seek me,” that is, I freely offered myself to the Gentiles, and by faith made myself to be found by those who did not know how to seek me, nor searched out my coming in the Scriptures as the Jews did, who even now seek and await the Messiah’s coming in their books.

“I appeared openly”—not through riddles and figures [Col. 0747B], as in the Law, but in manifest knowledge of the truth—“to those Gentiles who did not ask about me from others,” because they had not learned to inquire. Thus he speaks to the nations; but to carnal Israel he says: “All day long,” that is, throughout the entire time when I lived among them on earth, enlightening the world, “I stretched out my hands,” that is, I enlarged the benefits of my works, “to the Jewish people who did not believe me and, what is worse, contradicted me.”

For by hands stretched out all day, the continual performance of good works is fittingly understood, from which the Savior never ceased; he always offered them to the unbelieving people, and, like a nurse, stood ready to receive a little child with outstretched arms. Outstretched hands signify also the gentleness of a parent eager to receive his children into his bosom [Col. 0747C]. They can also express the generosity of a giver: he denied nothing to those who asked him, but immediately restored health to the leper who asked (Matt. VIII), at once opened the eyes of blind men who asked (Luke XVIII), and so gave other things to those requesting them.

## Chapter XI

> “I say, then: Has God rejected his people? By no means! For I too am an Israelite, of Abraham’s seed, from the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.”

Since he has refuted the Jews by so many authorities, lest the Gentiles insult them and say that they had been rejected altogether, he begins again to speak of their salvation, showing that not all have been reprobated. For he had recalled the prophet’s testimony concerning the foretold future unbelief of the people of Israel: “All day long I stretched out my hands,” and so forth. And lest anyone, misunderstanding, should think that the whole people had been condemned for the crime of unbelief and contradiction, he immediately added: “I say, then,” and so forth.

Here he shows which people he meant: certainly the Israelite people. If God had altogether rejected and condemned it, he himself would certainly not be Christ’s apostle, being of Abraham’s seed and of the tribe of Benjamin [Col. 0747D]. “Because,” he says, “I called the people unbelieving and contradicting, I therefore also say and raise this question: Has God, because of the multitude of unbelievers and contradictors, rejected his people, so as to nullify the promises which he made to their fathers? Far be it that he should reject the people from whom he chose so many thousands of believers!”

Truly he did not reject that whole people. For I too, who speak these things, am an Israelite; that is, I am a Jew from that same people, not a proselyte; “of Abraham’s seed,” that is, descended from Abraham; “from the tribe of Benjamin,” that is, through Benjamin’s line. God did not reject me, who am thus from that nation. Likewise, he has not rejected his people from Israel, whom he foreknew, that is, predestined. For predestination is here denoted by the term foreknowledge. “God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew,” that is, whom he predestined to life [Col. 0748A].

And, in order to show that the remnant of the Israelite nation had been preserved by God’s grace, not by the merit of their works, he next added a most necessary testimony, saying:

> “Or do you not know what Scripture says in Elijah, how he pleads with God against Israel? ‘Lord, they have killed your prophets; they have dug down your altars; and I alone am left, and they seek my life’ (III Kings XIX). But what does the divine answer say to him? ‘I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal.’ So therefore, at this present time also, a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace. But if by grace, then no longer by works; otherwise grace is no longer grace.”

From this, he says, it can be seen that God has preserved many by his grace, whom he did not reject. For in Elijah’s time there were so few that to Elijah himself there seemed to be none whom God had not rejected; and yet, amid such overwhelming oppression of the good, there were many whom God preserved for himself in grace [Col. 0748B].

This is what he says by way of a question, in rebuke of those who thought that the entire Israelite people had been rejected by God: “Do you not know what the Scripture of the Third Book of Kings says in Elijah,” that is, in the deeds of Elijah—namely, how he himself pleads with God against Israel, that is, calls upon him as judge between himself and them and appeals against the faithless: “Lord,” he says, “at the command of the most wicked Queen Jezebel, they have killed your prophets; they have dug down your altars,” that is, overthrown them from their foundations; “and I alone am left of your own people, and they seek my life,” that is, to kill me. It is as if he were saying: You ought not spare them, because they have done such great evils. He pleaded thus and thought himself alone.

“But what does the divine answer say to him?” that is, what does the Lord answer him? “I have left for myself seven thousand men.” He does not say, “There have been left for me,” or “They left themselves for me,” but “I have left for myself.” Here not human work but divine grace is plainly shown [Col. 0748D]. In the seven thousand men is expressed the perfect number of those who act manfully. “I have left for myself,” he says, that is, I have preserved by grace, seven thousand men. For there were then many whom God had reserved for himself, although Elijah did not know it, because the grains lay hidden beneath a heap of chaff. “Who have not bent the knee before Baal,” that is, who have not worshipped the demon whom the people of Israel worshipped under King Ahab. Where the prophet had thought the whole people rejected at once, seven thousand men were found who remained in God’s covenant.

“So therefore, at this present time also, a remnant has more readily been saved by grace.” That is: since, before the time of grace, God preserved so many thousands by his grace, contrary to the judgment of so great a prophet, therefore, in the same way, even in this present time of grace and Gospel preaching, we must believe that there are many whom God foreknew and predestined to be his own; and this is not according to human merit, but according to the election of grace, which no merits of works preceded [Col. 0749A]. Thus, in this election and in these remnants is that people whom God did not reject precisely because he foreknew it. For he foreknew the remnant which he himself would make according to the election of grace; that is, he predestined it.

I said that they have been saved according to the election of grace. But if they were saved by grace, then that salvation did not proceed from their works. Otherwise, that is, if it is otherwise, grace—that is, God’s free gift—is no longer grace, that is, a free gift, but something owed. For if grace is given for any good merits, it is no longer given freely, but rendered as a debt. Accordingly, it is not rightly called by that name where recompense is reckoned not according to grace but according to debt. But if grace is true grace, that is, freely given, it finds nothing in a human being to which it is due as a merit. This is well understood in the saying: “You will save them for nothing” (Ps. LV). For grace itself gives merits; it is not given for merits. It even precedes faith, from which all good works begin.

> “What then? Israel did not attain what it sought; but the election attained it. The rest [Col. 0749C] were blinded, as it is written: ‘God gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes that they might not see, and ears that they might not hear, down to this present day.’ And David says: ‘Let their table be made before them into a snare, and into a trap, and into a stumbling block, and into a recompense to them’ (Ps. LXVIII). ‘Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see; and bow down their back always.’”

Since the remnant from the multitude of Israelites was saved not by works but by God’s grace alone, what then is to be said? This: what Israel sought—that is, the righteousness or salvation which the Jewish people sought in the Law—it did not attain by works of the Law; but the election, that is, the part elected from that same people, attained righteousness and salvation by grace [Col. 0749D]. The election attained it; but the rest, who do not belong to the lot of election, were blinded by God’s just judgment, as it is written: “God gave them,” that is, justly permitted them to have, “a spirit of compunction,” that is, an evil spirit by which they were pricked and goaded toward evil.

For “compunction” here means something bad, because often something good is burdensome to a person—as Christ’s teaching was to the Pharisees. And by a just judgment he gave them eyes so that they might not see, and ears so that they might not hear, down to the present day. Here we must understand the eyes and ears of the inner person, by which those became blind and deaf who, seeing Christ in the body and hearing his teaching, refused either to believe the works which they saw or to obey the word which they heard [Col. 0750A]. For whoever, after understanding, refuses to believe what is true ought to receive what he wants: that from then on he cannot believe. Thus they were aided in their own will, so that because they knowingly called truth false, they would no longer understand.

Therefore the eyes of their heart are blind, so that they cannot see the light of Christ’s truth; and their ears are deaf, so that they cannot hear the spiritual senses of the Scriptures. Where this sentence is written is not sufficiently clear. Yet blessed Jerome says that it is written in Isaiah, where we read: “The Lord has mingled for you a spirit of slumber; he will close your eyes, and cover your prophets and your rulers who see visions” (Isa. XXIX). [Col. 0750B] But if I dared to say something other than so great a teacher, I would think it more likely to be found in Deuteronomy, where Moses says: “The Lord has not given you an understanding heart, seeing eyes, and ears able to hear, down to the present day” (Deut. XXIX).

Isaiah or Moses speaks thus of their blindness and deafness. And David says of it (Ps. LXVIII): “Let their table,” that is, the Scripture which is accustomed to feed them with the various courses of its meanings, “be made into a snare,” that is, be turned into a snare for them, so that it entangles them, “before them,” that is, while they see it, so that they acknowledge their iniquity and most obstinately persist in it. So great may be the presumption of their minds that the snare is before their eyes and they fall into it.

These are words not of one wishing this, but of one prophesying [Col. 0750C]; not of one imprecating that this should happen, but of one declaring that it will happen. “Let it be,” therefore, because it cannot be otherwise than that these things should happen to such people. Let their table become a snare, so that Scripture wrongly understood may entangle them and make them cling to the letter, lest they come to Christ and to the Gospel; and let it become a trap to them, so that it captures and holds them, lest they be able to withdraw from antiquity; and let it become a stumbling block to them, so that through it they are scandalized at Christ’s working miracles on the Sabbaths; and let it become a recompense to them, so that through it they receive the return for their evils, that is, eternal condemnation.

“Let the eyes of their heart be darkened, that they may not see,” so that, because they saw without cause, it may come about for them that they do not see. And after the darkening of their eyes, “bow down their back always” [Col. 0750D], so that after they have ceased to know things above, they may always think of things below. For those who attend to things above do not have a bent back, because they stand upright while awaiting the hope laid up for them in heaven. But those who do not understand the hope of the future life, now blinded, think of earthly and low things; and this is to have a bent back, because one who is bent always looks at the ground. Such now are all the Jews: like brute animals, whose face is inclined toward the earth and attentive to the belly.

> “I say, then: Have they stumbled so as to fall? By no means. But by their transgression salvation has come to the Gentiles, in order that they may emulate them. Now if their transgression is the riches of the world, and their diminution the riches of the Gentiles, how much more their fullness?”

[Col. 0751A] Since he taught by the authority of the prophets that the Jews had been blinded and had suffered a stumbling block—that is, an obstacle and a striking of the feet—lest the Gentiles take occasion from these words to despise them, he again undertakes to speak of their salvation. “Because,” he says, “I have spoken harshly about their blindness and stumbling, therefore, lest anyone despair of their salvation, I say: Have they stumbled,” that is, struck their feet, “so as to fall?” that is, merely to fall, as though only for their own punishment? By no means.

It is as though he said: They have not fallen, because not all have fallen; and some of those who fell—the Jews—have always stood by predestination; and through the fall of the rest the world has been raised. For they did not fall irreparably and without benefit; their fall is beneficial, and they themselves can be restored [Col. 0751B]. Far be it that they should have fallen altogether. They did not fall in that way, but salvation came to the Gentiles through their transgression. He says that their very fall is such, not in order that they should fall, but in order that through their transgression they might give salvation to the Gentiles.

From this point he begins to commend the Jewish people, even from the very fall of their unbelief, so that the Gentiles may not be proud. For even the fall of the Jews proved so precious for the salvation of the Gentiles; rather, they should beware lest, while they are proud, they too fall in the same way. “Far be it,” he says, “that they should fall; but salvation came to the Gentiles through their transgression.” He did not say that they did not fall, but that their fall was not empty, because it advanced the salvation of the Gentiles when they repelled from themselves the preachers of the Gospel and caused them to go over to the Gentiles.

Salvation came to the Gentiles through their transgression, because, dispersed on account of the Savior’s death [Col. 0751C], they carry the holy Scriptures among all nations and are witnesses to us that we have not invented the prophecies concerning Christ; and they strengthen the faith of the Gentiles. Salvation came to the Gentiles through their transgression, in order that the Jews might emulate them, that is, imitate them. This has often happened, and will happen more fully [variant: indeed] at the end of the age, when the Jews will follow Christians in faith in Christ. For just as their fall has now given salvation to the Gentiles, so now the faith and conduct of the Gentiles confer upon the Jews an emulation leading to conversion and salvation.

It can also be understood as meaning that the Gentiles emulate the Jews, that is, believe as they too had believed, so that they are stirred by zeal for God against the Jews’ evil deeds. I said that their transgression is beneficial. “Now if,” that is, but if [Col. 0751D] their transgression—namely, that they killed Christ or rejected the word of preaching—is the riches of the world, that is, enriched the world with faith, religious works, and conduct; and their diminution, that is, the small number converted to faith—namely, the few of them who were converted—is the riches of the Gentiles, that is, enriched the Gentiles with faith, perfection of virtues, and charisms of the Holy Spirit: how much more will their fullness, which will be converted at the end of the world, enrich the world?

That is, if God turned their evil into good, namely into the riches of the world, much more will their good, when their multitude or fullness has been converted at the end, enrich the Gentiles by teaching and example. In this he shows that their fall is neither useless nor irreparable. For God’s wisdom wonderfully orders all things; with it neither transgressions nor falls themselves turn out uselessly [Col. 0752A]. For although each person sins through the freedom of his own purpose, the dispensation of divine wisdom makes others rich through the very thing in which sinners become poor by the loss resulting from their negligence. Thus the transgression of the Jews has now enriched the Gentiles, so that without the labor of the Law they might become fellow-heirs and one body with them.

It may also be understood thus, when he says: “If their diminution is the riches of the Gentiles, how much more their fullness?” That is, if the few of them who believed benefited the Gentiles so greatly that they filled them with spiritual riches, how much more, had most or all believed, could they have benefited them by teaching? For their diminution was turned into the riches of the Gentiles in two ways: either because the Gentiles took from those few the example of believing, or because, when only a few Jews had believed [Col. 0752B], the preaching came to the Gentiles, so that the number of believers might become greater.

> “For I speak to you Gentiles: insofar as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I will honor my ministry, if somehow I may provoke my flesh to emulation and save some of them.”

I said that their fullness will be converted. Indeed, they can be converted, for I too labor for their conversion. “For I speak to you Gentiles,” who are specially entrusted to me. “Insofar as I am the apostle of the Gentiles”—which I am always, as long as I live—“I will honor my ministry.” I am the apostle of the Gentiles, not of the Jews, yet I am minister to these also. And as long as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, to whom I was specially sent [Col. 0752C], I will honor—that is, make honorable—my ministry through the conversion of the Jews. For though I have been appointed to preach to the Gentiles, I shall not preach only to them, but shall also labor that the Jews may be converted. In this I make my ministry honorable, by adding more than I owe.

The person who makes his ministry honorable is one who does all that has been commanded him and more. But one who works less and more slackly than he ought makes his ministry blameworthy. “I will honor,” I say, “my ministry,” trying whether somehow—that is, in some manner—I may provoke “my flesh,” that is, the Jews, from whose stock I come, “to emulation,” that is, to imitate me; if by any means I may show myself such that they emulate me and desire to be such themselves [Col. 0752D]. If I cannot do it by this path, I shall take another: now teaching, now exhorting, now writing, now displaying good examples, now praying, now performing miracles. I shall try whether in some way I may provoke to emulation those who are my flesh, so that they may become my brothers in the Spirit and that I may thus save at least some of them.

> “For if their rejection is the reconciliation of the world, what will their reception be but life from the dead? And if the first portion is holy, so also is the lump; and if the root is holy, so also are the branches.”

I labor to convert someone from among them to faith because their conversion will be beneficial. For if their rejection—that is, God’s losing them because of unbelief [Col. 0753A] and leaving them in the hand of the ancient enemy—is the reconciliation of the world, that is, the cause by which the Gentiles from the whole world were reconciled to their Creator, what will their reception be—that is, God’s receiving them at the end of the age, those who shall then exist—except life from the dead?

If the rejection of this nation brought reconciliation to the world, and such was the grace in this nation that, removed from it, it was sufficient to reconcile the whole world to God, how greatly should we suppose that God will then have mercy on the world when this nation has merited reconciliation with God? And what the world will gain from Israel’s reconciliation is briefly shown: life from the dead. For Israel’s reception will occur when the dead already receive life, the world is changed from corruptible to incorruptible, and mortals are granted immortality. For it would seem absurd if their offense gave reconciliation to the world, but their reception did not bestow upon the world something greater and more excellent [Col. 0753B]. Their reception will be life from the dead.

“But if their first portion is holy, so also is the lump.” Do not say, he says, that it cannot happen that their multitude should be received, as though the whole race had been rejected. For if the first portion—that is, a few taken from among them, such as the apostles and other disciples—is holy, then the lump, that is, the whole nation, can also be sanctified. He shows by a comparison that, as those few who were converted in the time of the apostles were sweet, so the multitude that will be converted at the end will also be.

For as a taste of some bread is sweet and good, likewise the lump which remains ought to be believed sweet and good [Col. 0753C]. A first portion is a small quantity taken from some thing in order to test the whole mass, as from food or drink. But if the first portion is holy, so also is the lump, because the savor of holiness found in the first few will be found also in the multitude of the last; and if the root is holy, that is, the patriarchs, from whom they draw the moisture of faith, then the branches too are holy—the persons who grew out of their lineage.

> “But if some of the branches were broken off, while you, though you were a wild olive, were grafted among them and became a partner in the root and richness of the olive tree, do not boast against the branches. But if you boast, you do not support the root, but the root supports you.”

The branches too are holy; but if some of the branches [Col. 0753D] have been broken off—that is, cut off from the tree of God’s holy people through pride and unbelief—do not boast. The olive tree was pruned, not cut down; and from it proud branches were broken off: this is the blasphemous and ungodly Jewish people. Yet good and useful branches remained, for from it came the apostles and many others.

And when useful branches had remained there through God’s mercy, you too, a Gentile, were grafted in while you were a wild olive, that is, naturally uncultivated and barren. You were grafted among them, that is, by another’s working joined to the root in their place. For they lost the root; you hold it. The root of this tree is Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, from whom the people of God blossomed; and these are now at rest with God in great honor.

Let us therefore see how the Lord himself foretells both the grafting of the wild olive and the breaking of the branches. “Many,” he says, “will come from east and west” (Matt. VIII). The wild olive, a bitter and barren forest, had occupied the earth so widely. But those who come have already been cut out of the forest. Where are they to be grafted so that they may not wither? “And they shall recline,” he says, “with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.” And what will become of those who came from Abraham’s stock? What will happen to the branches with which the tree was full? What but that they will be cut off and wither, so that these may be grafted in? “The children,” he says, “of the kingdom shall be cast into outer darkness” (ibid.) [Col. 0754A].

The Apostle therefore recalls as accomplished what the Lord foretold would be done. “If some branches,” he says, “have been broken off,” that is, some children cut off from the holiness and promise of the fathers, so that they may wither and be burned; “but you, though you were a wild olive, were grafted among them,” that is, through the operation of divine mercy planted in their place; “and you became a partner in the root,” that is, in the patriarchs’ faith and conduct, “and in the richness of the olive,” that is, the spiritual grace of the fruitful Hebrew people before the Lord’s coming. You have now become a sharer and participant. Do not boast against the broken branches, that is, do not insult the misfortunes of others.

For the Gentiles who had now believed in Christ exalted themselves against the Jews because they had crucified Christ, although from the Jews too another wall came to the cornerstone; and therefore the Apostle restrains them: “Do not boast,” he says, “against the branches.” But if you boast against them, know that you do not bear and support the root—which is in the patriarchs and prophets—but the root bears you [Col. 0754C]. That nation has no faith from you; you have faith from it. You are not stable, yet you destroy those through whom you stand.

> “You will say, then: ‘Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.’ Well. They were broken off because of unbelief, but you stand by faith. Do not think highly, but fear. For if God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps neither will he spare you.”

Since I said that some branches were broken off, but you, though you were a wild olive, were grafted in in their place, you therefore say to me because of my words: “Branches were broken off for this purpose, that I might be grafted into the place of their breaking.” And I answer you reprovingly: “Well.” That is to say: You do not speak well, because you speak boastfully and falsely [Col. 0754D]. For they were broken off because of their unbelief, not because of your grafting; but you stand in the root from which they were cut off by faith. You were grafted freely, by no merits of your faith [variant: faith]. Do not think that God has favored your person and cast them away without cause. For it is God’s benefit, not your merit.

For you stand by faith, that is, not by your own merit but by God’s grace. The branches were not broken off because of your righteousness or merit, but because of their unbelief. Through their own fault they were broken off, and from this came to you the opportunity of salvation—not because of you, but because of God’s mercy. Therefore do not think highly, that is, do not be proud because you have been grafted in; rather, fear lest you be broken off through unbelief or pride, as they were broken off because they refused to believe in Christ [Col. 0755A], who was always preached in that root and in that tree. Therefore they were broken off from it because they did not believe in him when he came; and you were grafted in there because you believed in him.

Therefore do not think highly, that is, do not exalt yourself, but fear lest you lose the grace you have received. Fear, not with the slavish fear which love casts out (I John IV), but with the chaste fear which endures for age upon age (Ps. XVIII). By the former one fears falling into the torment of punishment; by the latter, lest the grace of benefaction be withdrawn. By the former the mind is frightened by punishment, not delighted by righteousness; by the latter the soul fears lest it lose the grace through which it has come to delight in not sinning, fearing lest God abandon it, even if no one inflicts the torments of pains upon it. This fear is chaste, and love does not cast it out but adopts it.

Therefore do not think highly, but fear with this fear, because one who thinks highly and therefore does not fear certainly fails to fear destructively. Fear is the guardian of virtues; security readily leads to a fall [Col. 0755B]. Fear giving offense; fear being uprooted. For if God did not spare the natural branches—that is, those who, according to the institutions of their fathers, had been planted in this root of faith and naturally derived their origin from the stock of the patriarchs—it must be feared that perhaps he will not spare you either. Do you suppose that he will spare you, an outsider, if you offend him, when he did not spare the natural branches? If he struck and broke them because of the fault of unbelief, beware lest he strike and crush you as well.

> “See, then, the goodness and severity of God: severity indeed toward those who fell, but God’s goodness toward you, if you remain in goodness; otherwise you too will be cut off. And they also, if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in. For God is able to graft them in again.”

Since the branches were rightly broken off by God’s judgment, while you were grafted into their place by God’s grace alone, therefore see—that is, consider and attend to—on the one hand the goodness of divine mercy, by which sins are forgiven to those converted; and on the other, God’s severity [Col. 0755C], that is, the strict justice by which the unbelieving pride of the natural branches is broken. For it is salutary to behold not only God’s goodness but also his severity, because God is both usefully loved and feared.

The Apostle admonishes the Gentile people by precept and frightens it by example, so that it may remain stable and firm in faith. “See,” he says, “God’s merciful goodness and righteous severity: while he mercifully elects some and justly rejects others, learn humility from both. Toward the branches that fell after being broken off, see the severity of just punishment; but toward you, who were mercifully grafted in in their place, acknowledge the goodness of God’s grace—provided that you remain in goodness, persevering humbly in good works to the end. Otherwise,” that is, unless you remain and persevere in good and religious conduct, “you too will be cut off” from the tree of the holy nation into which you have been grafted.

It should be noted that those who fall from their own olive tree are called “broken off”; but those grafted in from the wild olive, if they sin again, are not said to be broken off—which would certainly be milder—but [Col. 0756A] to be cut off. In this God’s severity is shown to be sharper indeed if one who was a wild olive, gathered from the forest of sinners and brought to the root of faith and holiness, thereafter again produces the bitter sap of wickedness. “If,” he says, “you cease to be good, you too will be cut off from the good root.”

And not only will you suffer cutting off if you return to wickedness; they also will be grafted in, just as you have already been grafted in, if they do not remain in unbelief. This can readily happen. For God is able to call them back again to their own root through faith and graft them in.

> “For if you were cut off from the wild olive tree, natural to you, and contrary to nature grafted into a good olive tree, how much more will these, according to nature, be grafted into their own olive tree?”

[Col. 0756B] God truly can graft them in again, since he was able to graft you in. For if you were cut off by the sword of God’s word from the natural wild olive tree—that is, from the uncultivated Gentile state in which you were born—and contrary to nature grafted into the good olive tree, that is, into the fruitful people of God, how much more will these, born under the Law and taught God’s worship through the Law, be grafted according to nature into their own olive tree, that is, united to their own people?

You were grafted contrary to nature into the olive tree, because the olive is usually grafted into the wild olive, not the wild olive into the olive. For whoever does this will find no fruit but that of the wild olive. Whatever is grafted grows, along with the fruit of that thing. But by his omnipotence God brought it about that the wild olive should be grafted into the root of the olive tree and bear not wild berries but olive fruit. By “contrary to nature” he means contrary to the customary course of nature, as human knowledge comprehends it: that a wild olive grafted into an olive tree should bear not wild-olive berries but the richness of the olive [Col. 0756C].

God, however, the creator and maker of all natures, does nothing contrary to nature. We appropriately say that God does something contrary to nature when he does something contrary to what we know in nature. For this is what we call the course of nature known to us. When God does something contrary to it, such acts are called mighty deeds or miracles. But against that highest law of nature, removed from our knowledge, God no more acts—whether in the case of the ungodly or the weak—than he acts against himself.

Thus the Gentile people was cut off from the wild olive, that is, from the rites of barren nations [Col. 0756D], and was grafted into the good olive, that is, united through faith to the patriarchs, so that it might bear the olive’s fruit contrary to nature, that is, contrary to the institutions of its forefathers; for idolatry and works of that kind are customary, and thus natural, among the Gentiles. The designation “olive” is taken from the book of Jeremiah, where it is said to the Israelite people: “The Lord called your name a luxuriant, beautiful, fruitful, fair olive tree” (Jer. II).

> “For I do not want you, brothers, to be ignorant of this mystery, lest you be wise in your own eyes: that blindness has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter; and thus all Israel might be saved, as it is written: ‘From Zion will come one who delivers and turns away ungodliness from Jacob’ (Isa. LIX). And this is my covenant with them [Col. 0757A], when I take away their sins.”

I said that the broken branches will be grafted into their own olive tree. And this is true: for meanwhile some of them, and at the end their full number, will be grafted in. This is what I want you to know, so that you may rejoice in hope for their salvation. For I do not want you, brethren, to be ignorant of this mystery—that is, the secret sacrament of the divine judgment—so that you may not be wise in yourselves; that is, lest you suppose that you can investigate this by your own judgment and ingenuity, or lest you grow proud because of your election and their rejection. For one who thinks according to God does not exult over the rejected in God’s benefits, but with fear gives thanks to the mercy that bestows them. Be wise not for yourselves but for God, so that your wisdom may serve not yourselves but God.

I do not want you to be ignorant of this mystery of the divine counsel: that blindness has happened [Col. 0757B] in Israel, not wholly but in part. That is, not all Israelites but some have been blinded: namely, defenders of the Law, expounders of the Law, teachers of the Law, interpreters of the Law, who did not recognize and crucified the author of the Law. This is the blindness which happened in part to Israel, so that Christ might be crucified. The Jews did not recognize him and crucified him. Thus blindness happened to them, remaining in them until the full number of the Gentiles should enter into faith; and thus—that is, after the complete multitude of the Gentiles had been converted—all Israel might be saved by emulating the Gentiles and believing in Christ through Elijah’s preaching.

For the end of Israel’s blindness will come when the full multitude from all nations has entered; because then those Jews who are found will believe and will receive the light of the mind’s eyes through the preaching [Col. 0757C] of Elijah and Enoch. Israel will be saved by receiving Christ’s grace, as it is written in Isaiah, chapter 59: “There will come from Zion”—that is, Christ will be born from the Jewish people, who watches from afar for the future salvation and redemption of the human race. For Zion means “watching.” There will come, I say, he who with a certain force rescues impiety from Jacob—that is, unbelief from those from whose stock he will be born. This happens for the present, because scarcely anyone among them is converted; and at the end he will turn it away, because then it will be easy.

The Jewish cult has been impiety since the Lord’s Passion. Christ has with a certain difficulty rescued this impiety from those among them who have believed from Jacob: namely, through many preachings and signs, through many heralds of the new grace. Christ [Col. 0757D] did this among those who believed in his own time or in the time of the apostles and afterwards; and he still does it daily among those from the same people who receive faith and are converted with great labor. And he will more fully turn impiety away from those who are turned from unbelief and idolatry through Elijah and Enoch, lest they receive Antichrist as God, like the Gentiles.

And this covenant—that is, the firm and stable promise—the Lord says, will be fulfilled for them by me: namely, that impiety will be turned away from them through Christ, when I have taken away their sins in baptism. That is: then, through the grace of my Christ, iniquity will be turned away from them, when through the blood of that same Christ I have blotted out their sins.

This passage is read thus in Isaiah: “And a redeemer will come to Zion, and to those who return from iniquity in Jacob [Col. 0758A] (Isa. 59),” says the Lord; “This is my covenant with them” (ibid.), says the Lord. For where our translation says, “A redeemer will come to Zion,” the Apostle says, “There will come from Zion one who rescues.” And where it adds, “and to those who return from iniquity in Jacob,” he has put, “and he will turn impiety away from Jacob.” And where it continues, “This is my covenant with them,” he has interpreted it, “This is my covenant with them from me,” and by apostolic authority has added, “when I have taken away their sins.”

> “According to the Gospel, indeed, they are enemies for your sake; but according to election they are most dearly loved for the sake of the fathers. For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance.”

They will be converted at the end, but now they are enemies. For above [Col. 0758B], when it was said that blindness had happened in part to Israel, it was apparent that one part of that people had been blinded and another enlightened by the light of faith. This occurred because some among them became enemies of Christ and others most dearly loved. According to the Gospel they are enemies; that is, insofar as the new preaching of the Gospel appears to abolish circumcision, the Sabbath, and the carnal ceremonies of the Law. And they are enemies for your sake—you who have been received into faith—because they are deeply angered that you have been brought to the worship of God. Or, “for your sake” means that they were allowed to burst into hostility in order that room for your entry might be made.

According to the Gospel, then, they are enemies for your sake, because their hostility, by which they killed Christ, has undoubtedly advanced the Gospel, as we see [Col. 0758C]. And this comes from God’s dispensation, who knows how to use even evils well—not so that vessels of wrath may benefit him, but so that, while he uses them well, he may benefit vessels of mercy. Therefore it lies within the power of evil persons to sin. But that this or that good should result from their malice when they sin does not lie within their power, but in the power of him who divides and orders the darkness, so that even what they do against God’s will is not fulfilled except by God’s will.

For the hand and counsel of God predestined so great an assault from the hostile Jews against Jesus as was necessary for the Gospel for your sake. Thus, according to the Gospel they are enemies for your sake; but according to election others among them are most dearly loved—not on account of their own merits, because [Col. 0758D] they have been chosen freely, but for the sake of the fathers to whom these things were promised. According to election, which was made from among them according to grace and not according to debt, that is, according to the fact that God chose them from eternity, they are most dearly loved for the sake of the fathers: namely, in order to fulfill the promises made to the fathers, so that God might fulfill in the children what he had promised their fathers.

I rightly say, “according to election,” not according to their work, because God’s spiritual gifts, which he grants to his faithful, and the calling by which he calls them to faith, are without their repentance, since God’s mercy precedes every good will or action of theirs. Nor does divine grace in baptism require their groaning, lamentation, or any work, but faith alone; rather, it forgives all things freely. He says this lest they suppose [Col. 0759A] that they cannot receive mercy because they do not see them grieving.

Or rather thus: according to election they are chosen for the sake of the fathers, because the gifts of virtues which God bestows on the elect, and the calling by which he called them from eternity, are without his repentance—that is, they are fixed firmly without change and remain without a change of his counsel. For since all who repent ordinarily change that concerning which they repent, “repentance” is customarily used for “change,” as cause for effect. Hence Scripture testifies that the Lord repented of having made Saul king (1 Sam. 15), and said concerning those whom he was about to destroy in the flood: “I repent that I made them” (Gen. 6).

Therefore the gifts—that is, God’s promises freely made—and the calling from eternity are without repentance, because [Col. 0759B] God will not change the determination of his calling or bounty. Rather, those whom he chose in his predestination before the foundation of the world (Eph. 1), he will make to bear the fruit of good works in their due season (Ps. 1); and their fruit will remain. The end of this life will find it only abiding, because they will have perseverance in good deeds. For they were not called by that calling of which it was said, “Many are called, few are chosen” (Matt. 20); but by that through which the elect alone are called, who hear inwardly from the Father, learn, and come to the Son (John 18). None of these perishes, because of all that the Father gave him he loses nothing. Whoever, therefore, is of that number does not perish at all; nor was one who perishes of that number. Hence it was said: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been [Col. 0759C] of us, they would surely have remained with us” (1 John 2).

> “For as you also once did not believe God, but now have obtained mercy through their unbelief, so these also now have not believed in your mercy, that they too may obtain mercy. For God has shut up all in unbelief, that he may have mercy on all.”

Truly, when the full number of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved, although they are now enemies. For just as—that is, for the reason that you might not have a cause for pride—you once, that is, for a long time, longer than they, did not believe God, which served the purpose that you might now believe humbly; but now [Col. 0759D], that is, recently or in the time of grace, you have obtained mercy through their unbelief, which is in some way a cause of your mercy: so likewise, by the same reasoning, these also, lest when later converted they have matter for glorying in the Law, now in the time of grace have not believed, coming into your mercy, so that they too, humbled at the end, may obtain mercy.

That is, just as you Gentiles formerly did not believe God, yet God did not therefore wholly abandon you—especially since in the period of Israel’s calling you were never excluded, but the door of return always stood open to you through proselytes—and at last you obtained full mercy; yet the unbelief [Col. 0760A] of the people became the occasion for mercy being bestowed on you. So also these, who now have not believed from the people of Israel and have been abandoned because of their unbelief, so that God’s mercy might turn toward us, will not be abandoned altogether in their unbelief. Rather, after the dispensation of the full number of the Gentiles has been fulfilled, they too will obtain mercy; and the door of mercy stands open to them daily, if they wish to be converted.

For when merciful God drew the Gentiles, he rejected Judea in anger. And it came about that, just as formerly the Gentile world had been hardened against receiving faith, so afterwards, when the Gentile world had received faith, Judea became hardened in the torpor of unbelief. This statement of the Apostle, therefore, was first uttered subtly concerning the calling of the Jews and the rejection of the Gentiles. Thus it was done concerning [Col. 0760B] both, because God shut up—that is, permitted all, namely Jews and Gentiles, to be shut up—in unbelief, so that unbelief might enclose and hold them, since otherwise they would fall through pride; in order that he might have mercy on all—that is, on Jews and Gentiles—not that he will condemn none, as some have falsely thought.

Therefore he has mercy on all vessels of mercy. What does “all” mean? Both those whom he predestined, called, justified, and glorified from among the Gentiles, and those whom he predestined, called, justified, and glorified from among the Jews. For when faith had failed on both sides, unless divine power deferred its judgment, the whole human race would incur the sentence of condemnation. But wrath was changed into mercy especially at that point when no one could glory in his own merits.

The Apostle, therefore, considering [Col. 0760C] such riches of God’s goodness and so great a work of his wisdom toward rational creatures—he who is so rich in mercy, whose goodness, patience, and forbearance are so great—while he contemplates their immensity with the eyes of his heart, suddenly struck by both astonishment and awe, cries out, adding:

> “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? (Wis. 9; Isa. 40; 1 Cor. 2). Or who has been his counselor? Or who first gave to him, and it shall be repaid to him? For from him and through him and in him are all things. To him be glory for ages of ages. Amen.”

[Col. 0760D] For since above he had set forth many matters from which these questions might arise—why he chose Jacob but rejected Esau; why he hardens some and has mercy on others; why he chose the Jews before the Gentiles; why, after the Savior’s coming, he rejected the Jews, his people, and received the Gentiles; and again, near the end of the age, why he will save all Israel and permit the multitude of the Gentiles to perish—lest anyone seek a solution from which one could never arrive at an end, he bursts into admiration, showing by it that these matters are not intelligible to human understanding.

For lest anyone ask why they are saved in this way when there are many other modes of salvation, the Apostle indicates by his amazement that this cannot be known: “O,” he says, [Col. 0761A] “the depth,” and so forth—as though he said: Here one must stop; here human reason fails and does not penetrate the secrets of divine wisdom, so as to understand why God acts thus in respect of individuals: why these are chosen and those rejected, and why now Jews, now Gentiles, enter into faith.

For O how great is the depth of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge, who by his secret counsel so orders all things that, while preserving the freedom of choice for each person, he turns the evil of some to the good of others, and works the salvation of some through the unbelief of others. This depth is so great that it surpasses every understanding, because it leads every intellect and every reasoning beyond all things into darkness. And this depth is that of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge; for his wisdom and knowledge possess great riches: it knows [Col. 0761B] all things and orders all things wisely (Wis. 8).

“Wisdom” is spoken of divine and spiritual things; “knowledge” of human and bodily things. For in God there is wisdom concerning himself, the angels, and all the supercelestial creatures, because no one besides God perfectly knows these. For not even the angels themselves perfectly know themselves to the full extent in which God perfectly understands them. Likewise, in him there is perfect knowledge of all human and worldly things.
