By this wisdom and knowledge he wisely governs and orders all heavenly and earthly things, although we do not know the hidden causes of his works.

According to blessed Gregory, the public works of supreme wisdom are these: when almighty God governs those whom he creates, brings to completion the good things that he begins, [Col. 0761C] and by breathing upon them aids those whom he illumines with the light of his visitation. For it is clear to all that he completes what he himself began by the gift of his kindness. But the secret works of supreme wisdom are these: when God abandons those whom he created; when he does not bring to completion, by following it through, the good which he had begun by preceding grace; when he illumines us with the brightness of his illumination and yet, permitting temptations of the flesh, assails us with the darkness of blindness; when he does not preserve the gifts which he bestowed; when he both awakens the desires of our mind toward himself and yet, by hidden judgment, constricts the weakness of our frailty with difficulty.

Few indeed can investigate these secrets of his wisdom, but none can discover them. For what immortal wisdom orders concerning us above us is not unjustly ordered; and it is certainly right that we, still mortal, should not know it. Yet to behold somehow these very secrets of his wisdom is already to see the power of its incomprehensibility; because, while we fail in the very investigation of his counsels, we learn more truly by failing whom we ought to fear. The Apostle therefore, reaching toward these secrets of that wisdom, says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!”

For marvelous is the height of such riches of divine wisdom and knowledge, from which nothing can be hidden or escape; rather, it beholds all things in a single glance and holds the universe together by the power of its omnipotence. O how incomprehensible are his judgments—that is, his dispositions concerning all things—and unsearchable his ways, by which he proceeds [Col. 0762A] in all his works. For no one is sufficient to penetrate his judgments, by which he administers each soul and every rational nature; nor can anyone investigate the ways by which he proceeds providentially—not man, nor angel.

We therefore have a very limited understanding for examining the justice of his judgments, for examining grace freely given with no preceding merits: grace which is not unjust, and which does not so much disturb us when given to the undeserving as when withheld from others equally undeserving. But his unsearchable ways are those of which the Psalm sings: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24). Therefore his mercy and truth are unsearchable, because he has mercy on whom he wills, not by the claim of justice but by the grace of mercy; [Col. 0762B] and he hardens whom he wills, not by injustice but by the truth of retribution. By these ways he comes to all, and it cannot be investigated why he comes to this one by the way of mercy but to that one by the way of truth or justice. For no creature can scrutinize why he has mercy on this person rather than that.

Truly his wisdom and knowledge are wonderful, and his judgments incomprehensible. For who has known the Lord’s mind in wisdom and knowledge? That is, who has perfectly known the secrets of that mind? Who has been aware of the mysteries of his thought? No one. Or who has been his counselor in the ordering of things, by whose counsel he might act, or who might know his counsel? No one. This verse is taken from the book of Isaiah, by whose authority the Apostle proves that human beings ought not to investigate such things, since even the prophet shows that he does not know them.

If someone knows another’s counsel, he knows it either because he himself has given advice when consulted—that is, asked—or because the other has revealed to him what he discovered. Therefore no one is given knowledge of God’s hidden counsel, since he neither consulted anyone nor revealed his discovery to anyone. For as his mind cannot be known, so his counsel cannot be known. Who was his counselor? Or who first gave him anything, and thereby will be repaid by him? No one, because he precedes all.

This proves that his ways are unsearchable: because, since he is the beginning of every good, it cannot be investigated why he freely bestows his grace upon some and does not bestow it upon others, as we see in Jacob and Esau. “Who first gave to him, and it shall be repaid to him?” That is, who [Col. 0762D] first did any good thing without God, whose goodness is even the cause that we are and live? For no one precedes God by merits so as to hold him, as it were, a debtor; rather, as stated, he himself precedes all by his grace, so that their good works may follow.

“For from him and through him and in him are all things.” Therefore even the beginning of our faith is from him; for with no exception all other things are from him. All things are from him: that is, good will, good action, and all natures. Sins, however, are not from him; they have no natural subsistence, but corrupt a substance that was well made. “From him,” however, does not mean “of him.” What is of him can be called from him; but not everything that is from [Col. 0763A] him is rightly said to be of him. Heaven and earth are from him, because he made them; but they are not of him, because they are not from his substance. Just as if a man begets a son and builds a house, both the son and the house are from him, but the son is of him, while the house is of earth and wood. This is so because a human being cannot make anything even from nothing. But God, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things, does not need some material which he himself had not made to assist his power; and therefore he made all things from nothing.

“From him” can be understood as “from the Father are all things”; “through him,” as “through the Son are all things”; and “in him,” as “in the Holy Spirit are all things.” Through these prepositions—*from*, *through*, *in*—the distinction of persons is shown; through the same pronoun, *him*, the identity of substance is indicated, when it says, “from him [Col. 0763B] and through him and in him.” And in this not only is the same substance of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit demonstrated, but also equality; and it is declared that the whole Trinity created and sustains all things. Therefore, to him be glory for ages of ages. Amen. By saying “him” three times, he distinguished, as we have said, the persons; by adding “to him be glory,” he did not divide the substance.

These words may also be understood of the same one who is Trinity, without a distinction of persons. Ambrose explains them thus. What is “from him”? That by his will the nature of all things exists, and that he is the author of all things that began to be. What is “through him”? That through him establishment and continuance are seen to have been imparted to all things. What is “in him”? That all things, by a certain wonderful desire and ineffable love, look upon the author of life and dispenser of their grace [Col. 0763C] and gift, according to what is written: “The eyes of all hope in you, and you will open your hand and fill every soul with good will” (Ps. 144). And because all things are thus from him, through him, and in him, therefore to him be glory for ages.

But those do not wish glory to be his in the gratuitous grace by which the ungodly are justified who, ignorant of his righteousness, wish to establish their own, so that something of their own merit may precede—as though they first wished to give, in order that he might repay them—and who think that their merits go before him from whom are all things.

## Chapter XII

> “I beseech you therefore, brethren, through the mercy of God, that you present your bodies as a living sacrifice, [Col. 0763D] holy, pleasing to God: your rational service.”

From this point begins the moral exhortation after the discussion of the Law and faith, and of the nature of the Jewish and Gentile peoples. For throughout the preceding course of this epistle the Apostle had taught how the sum of religion was transferred from Jews to Gentiles, from circumcision to faith, from letter to spirit, from shadow to truth, and from carnal to spiritual observance; and he had shown through prophetic utterances that these things had been foretold. Now he begins to establish the morals and ordinances of this spiritual observance, to which he taught that the rite of God’s worship had been transferred, and to exhort both peoples together to a good life.

For until now it has been shown that neither should grow proud against the other; [Col. 0764A] now it is shown that each should labor for the other’s benefit—as though he said: “Up to this point I have uprooted vices; now, therefore, I have resolved to plant virtues.” Therefore, “I beseech you, brethren,” and so forth. Or it may be connected thus with what immediately precedes: Since all things are from God and through his grace we possess whatever good we possess, therefore I beseech you, brethren—that is, what I ask is required by brotherhood. I do not command by force, for the command of the Law profits nothing; rather, as one who has undertaken the office of reconciling you to God, I beseech you through God’s mercy—that is, through the mercy God has shown you.

For since all have been shut up under sin, human salvation now rests not upon human merits but upon God’s mercy. This mercy includes the sacrifice by which each person offers himself to God through extinguishing vices, because he also shows mercy to himself, as it is written: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Sir. 30). Therefore, through mercy the Apostle asks that bodies be presented as a sacrifice. “I beseech you,” he says, “that you present”—that is, offer—“your bodies as a living sacrifice.” For a sacrifice is both slain and living when a person does not depart from this life and yet kills himself to carnal desires.

A sacrifice is slain in order to be offered. But the living sacrifice is the body afflicted for the Lord. It is both called a sacrifice and living because it lives in virtues and is slain to vices: a sacrifice, indeed, because it is now dead to this world in its wicked actions; living, because it performs every good work within its power. Under the Law the bodies of brute animals were a dead sacrifice; [Col. 0764C] under the Gospel human bodies are offered as a living sacrifice. Then the sacrifice was slain, so that people, subject to death because of sin, might be shown to be so; now, because they are free from sin, a living sacrifice is offered as a sign of eternal life.

For those who mortify their members against the incitement of lust and make the actions of their bodies pleasing to God offer a living sacrifice and spiritually fulfill the law of sacrifices laid down in Leviticus. Present your bodies thus, a living sacrifice, holy—that is, clean from the contagion of sin—and pleasing to God—that is, acceptable through the merits of virtues. And present your service in the worship of God as rational, so that you may do all things rationally and there may be nothing in the acts of service which you render to God for which you cannot give an account. [Col. 0764D] Or “rationally” means: do everything with discernment, lest you do anything excessively or imprudently, but do all things moderately and wisely (Eph. 5; 1 Thess. 4).

> “And do not be conformed to this age, but be re-formed in the newness of your mind, that you may prove what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.”

Thus make yourselves a sacrifice. And do not be conformed to this age—that is, do not imprint upon yourselves the form of this age, so that you become like this wicked age—but be re-formed: that is, be formed again according to the image of God, which was deformed in you through sin, so that that image may begin to be formed again [Col. 0765A] by him by whom it was formed. For it cannot reform itself in reality, as it was able to deform itself.

From that deformity, by which through worldly desires you are conformed to this age, be re-formed now in the newness of your mind, so that the understanding of your mind may always be renewed, like gold, by the fire of love. Just as the Law has the general prohibition, “You shall not covet” (Exod. 20), and the general command, “You shall love,” so now in the Apostle the prohibition is, “Do not be conformed to this age,” while the command is, “Be re-formed in the newness of your mind.” The former pertains to not coveting; the latter, to loving. The former pertains to continence; the latter, to justice. The former concerns turning away from evil; the latter, doing good. For by not coveting we are stripped of oldness; by loving we are clothed with newness.

Our understanding is re-formed through the exercises of wisdom, the cleansing of God’s word, and spiritual understanding of his Law. The more someone daily progresses through reading the Scriptures, the higher that person’s understanding ascends; and that person becomes ever more new, daily, and according to this beauty is re-formed in the image of God. For justice in us, or any virtue through which one lives rightly and wisely, is the beauty of the inner person. And the soul which refers itself to God, so that, kindled with the fire of his love, it loses the form of worldly desire, is re-formed by being subjected to him as the unchangeable form; and it pleases him through what it has received from his beauty.

“Be re-formed,” he says, “in the newness of your mind, that you may prove what is the will of God.” Unless [Col. 0765C] our understanding is renewed by the Lord and illumined by God’s wisdom, it cannot prove what God’s will is. For in many things people suppose that God’s will is present when it is not; therein those who do not have an understanding divinely re-formed err and are deceived. You may prove what is the good will of God in those who begin good things; pleasing in those who persevere; and perfect in those who bring them to completion. Or: good with respect to married persons; pleasing with respect to the continent; perfect with respect to virgins.

> “For I say, through the grace given to me, to everyone who is among you: do not think more highly than one ought to think, but think unto sobriety, and to each one as God has apportioned a measure of faith. For as in one body we have many members, [Col. 0765D] but all members do not have the same action, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another.”

Prove the will of God which is in his commandments, so that you may live rightly according to it. For I say to you—that is, I command you—not to presume to examine his inscrutable mysteries. “For I say through the grace given to me”—that is, through the apostleship freely given me—“to everyone among you, not to think more highly,” that is, not to investigate mysteries more than one ought to think. It is suggested that some among them concerned themselves with the questions he had censured above and tried to search out those secrets of God. He now corrects them by apostolic authority, [Col. 0766A] saying, “Do not think more highly”: that is, do not inquire into God’s hidden things beyond what is fitting—that is, beyond what pertains to faith and religious conduct—but think unto sobriety, so that their minds may not become intoxicated and lose understanding through an excess of wisdom, by plunging into matters beyond the powers of human reason, but may be sober from a moderate cup of understanding.

This command must be greatly obeyed. For if an infant is fed according to its strength, it will grow able to receive more; but if it exceeds the strength of its capacity, it will fail before it grows. Therefore wisdom should not be sought beyond measure; rather, moderation must be maintained in inquiries of this kind. Or what he says, “not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think unto sobriety,” is what he said above: “Do not think lofty thoughts, but fear” (Rom. 11). For he still sees the proud branches of the wild olive insulting the branches broken from the good olive; and therefore he commands them not to think more highly than they ought—that is, not to think more of themselves than is expedient, not to glory more in themselves because of the fall of others.

For pride always seems wise to itself; therefore to think more highly than one ought means to be proud. “I say,” he says, “to everyone among you, not to think beyond measure, but unto sobriety”; and I say that each should think as God has apportioned to each a measure of faith, because God has given each a measure of faith, so that one may have less and another more, and each person’s proper measure may be filled according to the degree of that person’s perfection. Or let each think as God has apportioned a measure of faith—that is, let each understand [Col. 0766C] what measure of God’s grace is in him, which he has merited to receive through faith.

For sometimes someone receives from God understanding in the office of visiting the sick, or in mercies toward the poor, or in the defense of widows and orphans, or in concern for hospitality. God has apportioned each of these things to each person according to a measure of faith. But unless the person who has received grace to exercise understanding in some one of these matters recognizes the measure of grace given to him, and instead wishes to presume upon God’s wisdom, upon the word of teaching, or upon the subject of deeper knowledge—in which he has received no grace—and to teach rather than learn what he does not know, then, though he understands less, he wishes to think more highly than he ought. For he does not think unto sobriety, so as to observe how God has apportioned to each a measure [Col. 0766D] of faith.

But in order that the Apostle may make this point still clearer, he introduces an example and says: “For as in one body we have many members, but all members do not have the same action, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another.” With the greatest order he arranges the whole body of the Church by such an example. “Just as,” he says, “each of the members of the body has its own proper actions and each member serves by its own office, yet it is impossible that they should not mutually yield to one another by common agreement, so in the Church, which is Christ’s body, we each have different actions.”

For example, one applies himself to wisdom and the word of teaching, and is an eye in this body. Another is devoted to the ministry of brethren and the care of the needy, and is a hand of this body. Another is a diligent hearer of God’s word and is an ear of this body. Another is tireless in visiting the bedridden, seeking out the afflicted, and rescuing those placed in need, and is a foot of the body of the Church. Thus each person is found to devote special effort to one particular office.

Yet one thing alone ought not to suffice. Rather, according to the form of the proposed example: just as, for example, the eye has the special office of seeing, nevertheless it is one with all and in all the members, and acts all things with each, while every individual member acts all things with it; so too, one who has merited through the grace of faith one particular special gift principally administers that gift, [Col. 0767B] yet shares in all the acts of others and participates in them. This is what he says: truly a measure of faith has been apportioned to each, and the gifts of faith are diverse; for so it is also in the other gifts of grace. “For as in one,” and so forth.

Or God apportioned the gift of faith in measure because we, though many, are one body. Therefore all necessary things must be given, but not to one member alone, so that the Church may not be in need and there may be occasion for service, and thus mutual love may exist while one person needs another. For just as our body is one and in it we have many members, so the body of Christ, which is the Church, is one, and in it there are many faithful persons like diverse members, because we, though many, are one body in Christ. No one, greater or lesser, is rejected.

And just as in the human body not all members have the same action, but different members have different actions, and not all possess all actions in themselves but are supplied through others, so in the Church each of us is a member of another, so that we may serve one another. Just as the hand serves the eye and the eye the foot, so in the Church the service of all ought to be common. We, though many, through diverse gifts or works, are one body through the unity of love and concord in Christ; but individually we are members of one another—that is, serving others and needing others—so that in this manner we may be joined among ourselves by the bond of love, because each of us needs the others, and what is lacking to one in himself is supplied through another.

> “But having gifts that differ according to the grace [Col. 0767D] given to us.”

Each of us is a member of the other—not indeed in one and the same way, but possessing different gifts, differing from one another in the number of spiritual endowments, according to the grace given to us by God. In accordance with what God has freely given to each, one has this gift and another that.

> “Whether prophecy, according to the proportion of faith; or ministry, in ministering; or he who teaches, in teaching.”

He now begins to explain the distinction among gifts and, as it were, to enumerate the functions of different members. Just as he assigns sight to the eyes, so he assigns the mystery of prophecy to the mind, which is the inner eye. To another, as to a hand, he ascribes ministry [otherwise, service]; and [Col. 0768A] to another, as to a tongue, he grants teaching. In like manner he distributes the rest.

We are members of one another, having different gifts for this purpose. Whether we have prophecy—that is, the disclosure of future things or of any hidden matters—we are members for the sake of others, so that we may prophesy to them; so that, just as the eye serves the other members, we too may serve other believers through prophecy, foreseeing future events for them and making them more cautious in order to avoid impending evils. I mean us who have this grace of prophesying according to the proportion of faith: so that we say or think nothing outside the rule of faith. Or, “according to the proportion of faith” because the grace of prophecy is given in accordance with the faith, capacity, or salvation of believers or hearers.

He begins the enumeration of spiritual gifts with prophecy [Col. 0768B], because believers, on receiving the Holy Spirit, immediately prophesied. Or, having ministry, as deacons do, so that we minister at the sacred altars: in ministering we are members of those for whose benefit we minister. Or ministry may mean providing earthly food for the saints; in serving them we are their members. Or he who teaches the ignorant becomes their member in teaching, that is, in the imparting of instruction.

> “He who exhorts, in exhorting; he who gives, in simplicity; he who presides, in diligence; he who shows mercy, in cheerfulness (Amos V). Let love be without pretence (I Pet. II).”

He who exhorts others to do the good which they themselves do not do, though they know it and neglect it, becomes their member through exhorting them [Col. 0768C]. He who gives what is his to others becomes their member in simplicity; that is, if he seeks nothing back from those to whom he gave, but only from God, who rewards every good deed. Or, he who gives to the needy should do so with simplicity of heart—that is, he should not seem with his hands to do good to the needy while in his heart he seeks praise from human beings. Simplicity excludes hypocrisy.

He who gives alms should do so with the singleness of a heavenly intention, not with a double intention of present and future glory. He who presides over brothers or over the Church should preside with diligence: he should vigilantly watch over the care of the flock entrusted to him, not with concern for human lawsuits or secular affairs. This latter concern [Col. 0768D] must be cast off by those who preside over the Church; rather, theirs should be the kind of concern which the Apostle had in bearing anxiety for all the Churches. Therefore, one who presides over the Church ought to have such concern, and ought entirely not to have worldly concern.

He who shows mercy should do so cheerfully. That is, one who piously sympathizes with a miserable person and bestows upon him the benefit of mercy should act with cheerfulness of mind, because “God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. IX). For one who distributes his possessions, if he is unbelieving and despairs of receiving anything in return, grieves as though he had lost them. But one who does this with faith and hope acts with cheerfulness and joy, certain that he will receive great things in return for small ones and, besides, will obtain eternal life.

For works of mercy are performed for no other reason than that we may be delivered from misery [Col. 0769A], according to the saying: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. V). In contrast James says: “Judgment without mercy to him who does not show mercy” (Jas. II). For since we all offend in many things, the work of mercy is urged upon us as a daily remedy for daily, though lighter, wounds. Mercy is manifold: namely, forgiving one who sins, helping one who is oppressed, feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, and doing similar things. Therefore, he who shows mercy should do so cheerfully, so that by the cheerfulness of his face and mind his benefit may be made more pleasing both to God and to human beings.

He had already said, “He who gives, in simplicity,” and now says, “He who shows mercy, in cheerfulness.” Perhaps the two statements seem to concern one work [Col. 0769B], yet the disposition involved is not one and the same. For it is one thing to give to a needy person; it is another to share the feeling of mercy with the needy person. And simplicity is one thing, cheerfulness another: simplicity excludes a double intention, whereas cheerfulness shows a mind relying upon the hope of heavenly rewards.

Let love also be without pretence among you. Every love which is not according to God is pretended and not genuine, because God, the Creator of the soul, has implanted in it, together with the other virtues, the disposition of love, so that it may love God and the things God wills. Therefore, when God has given this work of love to the soul, whoever loves something other than God and what pleases God must be said to possess feigned and pretended charity. Moreover, if someone loves his neighbour, yet, when he sees him erring, does not admonish or correct him [Col. 0769C], that charity too must be called pretended. Thus charity ought to contain nothing flattering and nothing artificial.

> “Hating evil, clinging to good; loving one another with brotherly charity; outdoing one another in honour; not slothful in diligence; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord; rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; persistent in prayer; sharing in the needs of the saints; pursuing hospitality” (Heb. XIII).

Be hating every evil and clinging to good. He hates evil who not only is not overcome by pleasure, but also hates deeds of pleasure. And he clings to good whom no temptation and no adversity can separate from good [Col. 0769D]. You ought thus to advance in order: first, hate every evil both in yourselves and in others; then cling firmly to good, lest you ever be torn away from it.

Be loving toward one another with brotherly charity; that is, love among yourselves brotherly charity itself. Love and strive to possess that love which binds you together as brothers. Let this man love toward that one, and that one toward this man, this brotherly charity, and strive to preserve it. And be outdoing one another in honour: let each hasten to honour the other more than to be honoured by him, show him greater reverence, prefer him to himself, and let the other do the same in return.

Be also not slothful in diligence: that is, be both concerned in heart and energetic in deed, being concerned for your own salvation and that of others, and not sluggish in doing what pertains to salvation [Col. 0770A]. Be also fervent in spirit, so that, even if you cannot always fulfil in deed what you piously desire, the spirit may nevertheless burn within you with the fire of charity, so that there may be nothing slack and nothing lukewarm in you.

Be also serving the Lord, so that you serve none of the vices, but the Lord; for a slave of vices cannot serve the Lord. Serve the Lord so that whatever good you do, you may refer it to the Lord’s glory; and whatever you do for neighbours out of love for him, you may believe that you do to him. Be rejoicing in the hope of heavenly goods, so that you look not at the things seen but await those unseen. Be patient also in tribulation, so that for the sake of a heavenly reward you patiently endure every affliction and are neither disturbed by anger or hatred against the persecutor [Col. 0770B] nor murmur against God.

And, in order that you may be able patiently to bear adversities, be persistent in prayer, lest you fail in tribulation. Where human frailty is insufficient, God’s help must be implored through prayers. Be sharing your goods with the needs of the saints; that is, provide for the needy honourably and fittingly, not as though giving alms, but having, as it were, your own feeling in common with them. Be also pursuing hospitality: do not merely receive guests who come to your house, but pursue and seek them out everywhere, lest perhaps they sit somewhere in the streets or lie outside without shelter.

> “Bless those who persecute you; bless, and do not curse. Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep [Col. 0770C] with those who weep. Be of the same mind toward one another, not thinking lofty things, but consenting to the humble.”

Bless those who persecute you; that is, pray good things for those who have done evil to you. Bless them and do not curse: that is, do not even have the will to curse in your heart. He removes them from common custom when he forbids them to curse their adversaries. And because this command—to bless persecutors—was hard and seemingly intolerable to them, he repeats it in order to impress it more deeply upon their minds and so that their blessing may contain no admixture of cursing, saying: “Bless, and do not curse.”

Holy Scripture, however, speaks of cursing in two ways: one which it approves, and another which it condemns. A curse is uttered in one way by the judgment of justice, in another by the spite of vengeance [Col. 0770D]. A curse is uttered by the judgment of justice, as it is said to Abraham: “I will curse those who curse you” (Gen. XII). Again, because a curse is uttered from the spite of vengeance, the Apostle now admonishes: “Bless,” he says, “and do not curse.” Thus God is said to curse, and yet a human being is forbidden to curse, because what a human being does through the malice of vengeance, God does only by the examination and power of justice.

You ought, as is understood, to rejoice with those who rejoice in spiritual progress, and to weep with those who weep over spiritual loss. For our joy is not to be joined to every sort of rejoicing, nor our tears to every sort of weeping. We have not been commanded to rejoice with those who rejoice over the acquisition of money or things of that kind [Col. 0771A]; rather, we are to rejoice with those who rejoice in the hope of heavenly goods, or delight in received forgiveness of sins and in the grace of the Holy Spirit, and in similar goods. Likewise, we are not commanded to weep with those made to weep by worldly sorrow, which produces death, but rather with those who weep over their own sins or those of others, or who shed tears through desire for eternal life or for any such causes.

Be of the same mind toward one another: that is, what this person thinks, let that person think also; and what that person thinks, let this person likewise think, so that there may be no disagreement among you but a harmonious unanimity. I mean you who are not thinking lofty things—that is, not swollen in heart or proud—but consenting to the humble; that is, assenting to the will of the humble, so that you yourselves also may be humble [Col. 0771B]. Consent to them in a way that is not done with the mouth but with the heart, for humility is true only when it is not on the tongue alone.

> “Do not be wise in your own sight.”

That is, do not arrogate wisdom to yourselves. One who seems wise to himself is foolish through arrogance. Nor can he know the true wisdom of God who cultivates his own folly as though it were wisdom (Prov. III). Therefore, one who is wise in his own sight cannot be wise in God’s sight, because “knowledge puffs up” (I Cor. VIII).

> “Repaying evil to no one for evil.”

For one who repays evil for evil commits either a similar sin or a graver one. The person who first inflicted evil may perhaps not have realized that what he did was evil [Col. 0771C]. But the person who repays evil, by the very fact that he is moved to vengeance, is proved to have understood that the thing he repaid was evil. Therefore let no one avenge himself, lest he sin worse than his enemy.

> “Providing things good not only before God, but also before all human beings.”

Be providing things good: that is, consider with prudent discernment so that the things you do may be good not only before God, who sees the conscience, but also before all human beings, believers and unbelievers, who see the action, lest they be able to criticize it. Good things must indeed be provided before all people, not in order that we may please each person’s vices or manners—lest we contradict the saying, “If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be Christ’s servant” [Col. 0771D] (Gal. I)—but so that one keeps the balance of one’s life, character, and actions in such a way that no human being can criticize it. Such a person provides things good before all people, whether the good things please them or not. Therefore we must take care lest our good works become a stumbling block to human beings rather than a good example. For there are some who do not care what is said about them, provided only that they themselves have a good intention. But one who neglects the salvation of his neighbour is cruel.

> “If possible, so far as it depends on you, having peace with all human beings” (Heb. XII).

Have peace with all human beings, if possible, because it is difficult for this to happen; yet do what depends upon you [Col. 0772A], that is, let the failure to have peace with all not come from your side, because you violate peace with no one. Or, if the good which is on your side—namely, the observance of justice—can be done without being hindered by those people, have peace with all people.

According to blessed Gregory, however, the Apostle directed this command to rulers of the Church. For, when he was about to exhort them to have peace with all, he prefaced it by saying, “If possible,” and added, “so far as it depends on you.” For it was difficult, if they corrected evil deeds, for them to be able to have peace with all. But when temporal peace is disturbed in the hearts of the wicked by our rebuke, it is necessary that peace remain inviolate in our own heart. He therefore rightly says, “so far as it depends on you.” It is as though he said: Since peace subsists by the agreement of two parties [Col. 0772B], if it is driven away by those who are corrected, nevertheless let it be kept whole in the mind of you who correct them.

> “Do not defend yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath. For it is written: ‘Vengeance is mine, and I will repay,’ says the Lord” (Deut. XXXII).

I say: have peace, if possible, with all, not defending yourselves, beloved, if someone attacks you; that is, do not strike one who has struck you. But give place to wrath: that is, allow the persecutor’s wrath to be fulfilled against you. For one gives place to wrath who permits his adversary to do what he wishes. Or one gives place to wrath who humbly avoids the anger of the proud by flight, not raising himself against insults received but withdrawing from the place with pious humility [Col. 0772C]. Or, “give place to wrath” means: give place to God’s judgment.

He does not command that they should be unwilling to be avenged, but that, by not avenging ourselves, we should give place to God’s wrath, who said: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Deut. III; Heb. X). The saints do not desire vengeance in order to satisfy hatred, which is far from their perfection. For every righteous person would rather have his enemy corrected than punished. And when he sees the Lord taking vengeance upon him, he takes no delight in the enemy’s punishment (Ps. LVII; Ps. CXXXIX), because he does not hate him; rather, because he loves God, he delights in divine justice. Thus an enemy is loved in such a way that God’s justice, by which he is punished, is not displeasing. And the justice by which he is punished pleases in such a way that one rejoices not in his evil but in the goodness of the judge (Luke XVIII).

He therefore says: “Do not defend yourselves, beloved, but give place [Col. 0772D] to wrath.” As though he said: What need is there for you yourselves to avenge your injuries, when you are unable either to know human hearts or calmly to judge their recognized crimes? Rather, forgive from the heart what is sinned against you, as against brothers and neighbours, so that God too may forgive your sins (Matt. VI), knowing that, if they are willing to be corrected, you will have them as companions in good; but if otherwise, they will more rightly be condemned by the divine judgment—which can neither err nor become angry—than by yours.

And indeed you ought to await his judgment, for it is written in Ezekiel (ch. IX). For where we read according to the Hebrew truth, “The visitations of the city have drawn near,” the Seventy Interpreters translated: “Vengeance is mine, and I [Col. 0773A] will repay,” says the Lord. Thus it is clear that the Hebrews who believed at Rome held the translation of the Seventy Interpreters as authoritative, according to which the Apostle adduces testimony to them; for he would not have brought them testimony from a Scripture they did not accept.

“For this reason,” he says, “await the Lord, because he himself, as it is written, said: ‘I will repay vengeance to myself.’” That is, all evils inflicted upon you are inflicted upon me, though I am impassible; but I will repay vengeance to myself for these things, eternally punishing those who afflict you temporarily.

> “But if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he thirsts, give him drink” (Prov. XXV). “For by doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head. Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.”

[Col. 0773B] Do not defend yourself against an adversary by striking him back and repaying him evil for evil; rather, repay him good for evil. Thus, according to Solomon’s command, if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he thirsts, give him drink. Why? Because by doing this you will heap upon his head—that is, accumulate upon his mind—coals of fire: the burning and scorching pains of repentance. Overcome by your benefits, he will grieve that he inflicted injuries upon you, from whom he receives good things, and will turn to repentance; thus you will gain him for Christ.

Or “coals of fire” means charity burning with the fire of the Holy Spirit, which you heap upon his heart. This is to say: just as burning coals set on fire the body upon which they are heaped, so your good deeds will kindle to love the heart of one who persecuted you; and thus by your example you will provoke him to the fervour of the Holy Spirit, so that he may do good [Col. 0773C].

Far be it from us to believe that Solomon or the Apostle intended to teach that we should do good to our enemies with the purpose that they, by persisting in ingratitude, might endure greater fires of torments forever. That is not doing good to those who hate us (Matt. V), but doing them evil. Rather, this saying commands us, in showing mercy to needy enemies, to soften the hardness of their hearts with the soothing applications of benefits and to strive to kindle them to redeem us in the Lord, applying the fire of love, so that, admiring the power of our gentleness and patience, they may begin to imitate it and, rejecting vices, turn to works of virtue.

Therefore, lest anyone should wish to understand Solomon’s words in a Jewish sense, the Apostle immediately added: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” [Col. 0773D]. For how can one overcome evil with good if one is good on the surface but evil in secret—if one spares in deed yet rages in heart, gentle in disposition but cruel in will? Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good. Contend with evil, but through goodness. This alone is true conflict, or salutary contest: that good may oppose evil, not that there may be two evil persons. If you are no longer evil, resist evil so that you may be good. If an evil person displeases you, do not become evil yourself. For if you strike back, you wish to overcome evil with evil.

In the dispositions or movements of minds, that person is said to have conquered who has drawn the other to his own side, as with a heretic or pagan. Therefore, if that person receives from you a return of evil, he has conquered you [Col. 0774A] and, by making you share his passion, has subjected you to his vice. But if through your patience you cause him to desist from anger or injury, you have conquered, and have triumphed by winning your neighbour from sin to salvation.

## Chapter XIII

> “Let every soul be subject to the higher powers. For there is no power except from God” (Wis. VI). “And those which exist have been ordained by God. Therefore, whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance; and those who resist acquire condemnation for themselves.”

Just as above he rebuked those who gloried in their merits, so now he proceeds to rebuke those who, after being converted to the faith, were unwilling to be subject to any authority. For it seemed that unbelievers ought not to rule over God’s faithful people [Col. 0774B], although believers ought to be equals. He removes this pride by saying: “Let every soul,” that is, every human being, “be humbly subject to authorities higher than itself,” whether secular or ecclesiastical. That is, let every human being be subject to authorities set over him.

For the whole human being is signified by the greater part, just as again the whole human being is signified by the lower part where the prophet says: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isa. XL). He rightly warns lest anyone, because he has been called to freedom and made a Christian, exalt himself in pride and suppose that, in the course of this life, he need not maintain his proper order or be subject to authorities to whom, for the time being, the administration of temporal affairs has been entrusted.

Since we consist of soul and body, and as long as we are in this temporal life use temporal things to sustain this life, we must, in that respect which belongs to this life, be subject to authorities—that is, to those who administer human affairs with a certain honour. But in that respect in which we believe in God and are called into his kingdom, we must not be subject to any human being who wishes to overthrow in us the very thing which God has deigned to grant for eternal life [Col. 0774C].

Therefore, if anyone thinks that, because he is a Christian, he need not pay tax or tribute, or need not show due honour to the authorities who manage these matters, he is in great error. Likewise, if anyone thinks himself so subject that he supposes a person distinguished by some higher rank in the administration of temporal affairs has authority even over his faith, he falls into a greater error. Rather, the rule must be observed which the Lord himself commanded: that we render “to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. XXII; Luke XX).

Although we have been called to that kingdom where no such authority will exist, we must nevertheless endure our condition in this journey, for the sake of the order of human affairs, doing nothing hypocritically and obeying in this matter not so much human beings as God, who commands it. Therefore let every soul be subject to higher powers: that is, let every human being be subject first to divine power and then to worldly power. For if worldly power commands what you ought not to do, disregard that authority out of fear of the higher authority [Col. 0775A].

Consider the very ranks of human affairs. If a procurator commands something, should it not be done? Yet if he commands something contrary to the proconsul, you do not thereby despise authority; rather, you choose to serve the greater authority. The lesser ought not be angry because the greater has been preferred. Again, if a proconsul commands one thing and an emperor another, is there any doubt that, disregarding the former, one must serve the latter? Therefore, if the emperor commands one thing and God another, what shall we do? Must not God be preferred to the emperor? Thus let the soul—that is, the human being—be subject to higher powers.

Or “soul” is used for a human being because by it one discerns to whom one ought and ought not be subject. Or a person raised up by the advancement of virtues is called “soul” from the nobler part. Or, not only let the body be subject, but also the soul—that is, the will: serve not only in body but also in will.

You ought to be subject because there is no authority except from God. It could never happen except through the operation of God alone that so many persons should serve one person whom they see shares their own frailty and nature. But because God inspires subjects with fear and a willingness to obey, it comes about thus. Nor can anyone possess any power unless it has been given him by God. “All authority is from God” (John XIX). But the things that are from God are ordained; therefore authority is ordained—that is, rationally disposed by God.

Thus one who resists authority by refusing to pay taxes, show honour, and do similar things resists God’s ordinance, who ordained that we should be subject to such authorities [Col. 0775C]. This is said against those who thought they ought to use Christian freedom in such a way as to show honour to no one or pay taxes to no one, from which great scandal against the Christian religion could arise among worldly rulers.

In the case of good authority, it is evident that God has established it rationally. This can also be seen in bad authority: through it the good are purified, the evil are condemned, and authority itself is cast down more grievously. One who resists authority, when God has ordained it, resists God’s ordinance. But this sin is so grave that those who resist acquire for themselves, by their obstinacy and perversity, the condemnation of eternal death. Therefore no one ought to resist, but rather be subject.

> “For rulers are not a terror to good work, but to evil. Do you wish not to fear authority? Do good, and you will have praise from it. For it is God’s minister to you for good. But if you do evil, fear; for it does not bear the sword without cause. For it is God’s minister, an avenger unto wrath against one who does evil. Therefore be subject by necessity, not only because of wrath but also because of conscience. For this reason you also pay tributes. For they are God’s ministers, attending continually to this very thing. Render therefore to all their dues” (Matt. XXII): “to whom tribute, tribute; to whom tax, tax; to whom fear, fear; to whom honour, honour.”

Those who resist authority rightly acquire condemnation for themselves, because rulers are not a terror to those who do good work but to those who are wicked—that is, not to those acting well [Col. 0776A], but to evil-doers. He calls “rulers” those established to correct life and prevent harms, bearing God’s image, so that the other human beings may be under one person. They are not a terror to the good but to the evil, because they are instituted not to punish the good but the bad. For everyone naturally knows that innocence deserves reward and wickedness punishment.

If a ruler is good, he does not punish one who acts well but loves him. If he is bad, he does not harm the good person, but purifies him. Therefore one who acts well has nothing to fear. But one who does evil ought to fear, since rulers are established for the purpose of punishing evil. Let that person fear. But if you wish not to fear authority, I give you this counsel: do a good work, and you will have praise from it.

The apostles and martyrs did good works, yet authorities did not praise them but rather killed them. The Apostle therefore wished to say, “Do good, and authority will praise you”; but he moderated his words and said, “Do good, and you will have praise from it” [Col. 0776B]. For if authority is just, you will have praise from it when it itself praises you. But if it is unjust, when you die for faith, justice, or truth, you will have praise from it while it rages against you. You will have it “from it,” not because it praises you, but because it provides you an occasion for praise. This is Augustine’s interpretation.

Holy Gregory, however, says this: when Paul considered that his weak hearer might still wish either to commit wicked deeds or to delight in the reward of human praise for right action, he said: “Do you wish not to fear authority? Do good, and you will have praise from it.” Good things must not be done merely so that the authority of this world may not be feared, or that through them the glory of transient praise may be sought. But, since he considered that a weak mind could not rise to such strength as at once both to avoid wickedness and reject praise, the outstanding preacher, even while admonishing, offered something and took something away. By conceding lesser things, he removed more serious ones, so that, since the mind could not rise to abandon everything at once, it might, while being familiarly left in one of its attachments, be drawn away with less pain from another end of its own [Col. 0776C].

You will have praise from authority because that ruler, whether good or bad, is God’s minister, working for your good. For if you are good, he is your nourisher; if you are evil, he is your tempter. Receive nourishment gladly, and in temptation prove yourself as gold. If you do well, you will not fear the ruler. If you do evil, then fear him. And he is to be feared, because he does not bear the sword without cause, but in order to punish evil-doers. He has a material sword, or “sword” means judicial power, by which he strikes the guilty.

Nor is this surprising, because he is God’s minister, an avenger unto wrath against one who does evil, so that he may take vengeance upon evil-doers in God’s place. He is an avenger “against him,” that is, for the harm of one who does evil. He is an avenger “unto wrath,” that is, in vindication of God’s wrath, or an avenger showing God’s wrath. This punishment indicates that those persisting in evil will be punished more severely. For if a human judge punishes the sins of subjects out of love for justice, we must consider with what severity God the judge—who is without sin and possesses pure justice—will punish the sins of the perverse [Col. 0777A].

Therefore a worldly ruler is God’s minister, so that for the present he may exercise vengeance in God’s stead and prefigure God’s judgment. For God has willed that grave crimes which he wishes punished should be punished not through bishops and rulers of Churches, but through worldly judges. Knowing this, the Apostle rightly calls him God’s minister and an avenger against the one who does evil.

He is God’s minister. Therefore be subject to him by necessity, because it is necessary, for the sake of this life, that you be subject to him and not resist if he wishes to take something from possessions necessary for this temporal life, over which he has been given authority. Be subject not only because of wrath, so that you may avoid offending human beings, but also because of conscience: so that you do not do these things hypocritically, as before human eyes, but with the pure conscience of love for God [Col. 0777B], “who wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (I Tim. II).

Do not be subject to them merely to avoid the wrath of rulers, which can also be done hypocritically, but also because of conscience, so that in your conscience you may be certain that you do this out of love for those to whom God has willed you to be subject. And you ought to be subject because, for this reason also—that is, because of obedient subjection—you pay them tribute, as though rendering what is due while they fight for their country and administer judgments.

You pay tribute, and rightly, because they are God’s ministers, and God has appointed them for you. For by the command of him by whose command human beings are born, kings are also appointed, fitted to those governed by them at that time. Some rulers are given for the correction and benefit of subjects and the preservation of justice [Col. 0777C]; others for fear, punishment, and rebuke; and still others for mockery, contempt, and pride. They are God’s ministers, serving him in this very thing: demanding tribute from you and exercising authority for the benefit of the good and the detriment of the evil.

Or you pay them tribute, in this very thing serving God, because they are God’s ministers. Or certainly, those who exact tribute from you are serving you in this very thing, because, in return for what they receive from you, they serve your benefit by defending the country and guarding your possessions. Since they are God’s ministers, and he has subjected you to them, render to all of them what is due, just as the Lord paid the tax for himself and Peter, signifying that spiritual authority does not deprive secular authority of its right.

Render to all what is due, so that ecclesiastical teaching may thus be commended. To whom you owe tribute, render tribute; and to whom tax, render tax. *Tributum* is a revenue or payment. It is called *tributum* because formerly it was levied by individual tribes, as later by individual territories. For the Roman people were divided into three parts, and those presiding over the individual parts were called tribunes. Hence they called the contributions which peoples gave *tributa* [Col. 0777D].

*Vectigal* also is a revenue, payment, or fiscal tax; yet *vectigal* is said to derive from *vehendo*, “carrying.” *Tributum* denotes the assessments paid from lands and those paid by persons on their heads; *vectigal*, that which is brought in from distant regions [Col. 0778A]. *Tributum* is what is given by those present; *vectigal*, what is sent from remote provinces. *Tributum* is what regions pay; *vectigal*, the payment given to lords when they travel through territories. *Tributum* is what is paid at home at fixed times; *vectigal*, what passers-by and those transporting merchandise pay so that their goods may be protected.

To whom you owe fear, render fear: revere and fear masters. And to whom honour is due—whether a king, parent, elder, or person of that sort—render honour. By these commands the Apostle orders God’s Church so that, undertaking nothing against the rulers of the world, it may practise works of justice and piety in the peace and tranquillity of life.

For if, by way of example, we supposed that believers in Christ were not subject to worldly authorities, did not pay tribute or taxes, and showed fear or honour to no one, would not kings and rulers rightly turn their arms against them? They would make their persecutors excusable and themselves blameworthy [Col. 0778B]. For they would appear to be attacked not on account of faith but on account of obstinacy; the cause of their death would indeed be deserving, though the merit of death would be undeserving. Thus the Jews deserved to perish by the sword of the Romans.

“**Owe no one anything, except to love one another. For whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law. For: You shall not commit adultery; You shall not kill; You shall not steal; You shall not bear false witness; You shall not covet; and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in [Col. 0778C] this saying: You shall love your neighbor as yourself**” (Matt. XXII; Gal. V; Jas. II). “**Love does no harm to a neighbor. Love, therefore, is the fulfilment of the law.**”

Thus render to all what is due, although you ought to owe no one anything except mutual love. For all other things, once rendered, are no longer owed; but love is owed all the more as it is bestowed more abundantly. For it itself demands this debt: that, serving brotherly charity, we should help, insofar as we can, one who rightly wishes to be helped, always remaining debtors to charity. For it is that which is always rendered and always owed. It is owed even when it has been rendered, because there is no time when it should not be bestowed [Col. 0778D]. Nor is it lost when it is rendered; rather, it is multiplied by being rendered, because it is rendered by possessing it, not by being deprived of it. For when money is received, it comes to the one to whom it is given, but departs from the one by whom it is given. Charity, however, not only grows in the one who requires it from the person whom he loves, even if he has not received it; but also the one from whom it is received then begins to possess it when he renders it. Therefore render other things in such a way that you no longer owe them; but render charity in such a way that you always possess and owe it. And rightly it must always be possessed, because whoever loves his neighbor fulfils the law.

For charity alone fulfils the righteousness of the law, which fear could not fulfil. In this place love of neighbor alone seems to be commanded unto perfection, while love of God is passed over, although the law [Col. 0779A] and the prophets hang upon both commandments. But it follows that one who loves his neighbor chiefly loves love itself. For he can neither truly love his neighbor without God nor truly love God without his neighbor. But why did the Apostle prefer to mention love of neighbor alone, when he said that the law is fulfilled, unless because people can lie about their love of God, since fewer trials test it; whereas in love of neighbor they are more readily convicted of not possessing it, when they act unjustly toward all people or toward some? Therefore, since one commandment of love cannot be kept without the other, it is often enough, when works of righteousness are under discussion, to mention even one of them—yet preferably that one by which each person is more readily convicted.

Thus the law is fulfilled by love of neighbor. And [Col. 0779B] this is proved point by point. For all these commandments are fulfilled through love of neighbor. “You shall not commit adultery.” For who commits adultery with the wife of one whom he loves? “You shall not kill.” Who kills one whom he loves? “You shall not steal.” Who steals the possessions of one whom he loves as himself? “You shall not bear false witness.” Who gives false testimony against one whom he loves as himself? Therefore all these commandments, and any other commandment like them in the law, are summed up—that is, fulfilled and perfected—in this saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” that is, with the upright love with which you love yourself. For one who loves himself as he ought, and then his neighbor as himself, must necessarily keep all these commandments. For these commandments prohibit evil. Love of neighbor does no evil.

[Col. 0779C] Therefore one who loves human beings ought to love them either because they are righteous or in order that they may become righteous. For so he ought to love himself: either because he is righteous or in order that he may become righteous. Thus he loves his neighbor as himself without any danger. For one who loves himself otherwise loves himself unjustly, since he loves himself in order that he may be unjust—in order, therefore, that he may be evil—and thereby he no longer loves himself. “For whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. X). True love, therefore, must be maintained, by which every evil work is avoided and every good work fulfilled. And since one who loves his neighbor fulfils every individual commandment of the law, because he neither does evil nor fails to do good, love is therefore the fulfilment of the law—that is, the complete fulfilment of the law [Col. 0779D]—because it fulfils the law completely, both by abstaining from what the law forbids and by doing what the law commands.

“**And do this, knowing the time: that it is now the hour for us to arise from sleep. For now our salvation is nearer than when we believed.**”

I said that you should owe no one anything except love, because through it you can fulfil the whole law; and now I say that you should know—that is, recognize and understand—this time of grace, in which the Holy Spirit is given to believers, through whom they are filled with charity, by which they fulfil the law and so worthily receive eternal life. Know this time in which, through the coming of the Saviour, the grace of God has shone upon the world: that it is the hour—that is, an opportune but brief space of time—for us now to arise from sleep; that is [Col. 0780A], let us rise to do good from the torpor of negligence or ignorance.

It is the hour—that is, a brief span—for we who have the present hour do not know whether we shall have life tomorrow. And therefore now, that is, with a certain haste and without delay, we must arise from the sleep of sloth, so that we may be watchful in mind and occupied with good works. We rested sluggishly in our vices, held as though by a kind of sleep; but now we ought to know what this time in which we are is: that it is the hour now to rise from that sleep of the mind and henceforth to labor in good works. Truly we must no longer lie in sleep; rather, we must rise, because our eternal salvation is now nearer than it was when we believed—that is, when we began to believe—since we are now nearer to death, in which [Col. 0780B] we shall receive recompense.

And as we draw nearer and nearer to our salvation, and all things hasten toward their setting, let every torpor in doing good now be shaken off from us, and let us hasten eagerly toward the salvation that is now imminent, since this present life is coming to an end. For it is more shameful if we do not arise when we are already approaching the salvation that will be ours if we arise; otherwise we shall be deprived of salvation. Or, “now,” that is, when we arise, our salvation is nearer—that is, nearer to us; that is, it pertains to us more and is more within our possession than it was when we first believed. For if we had died then, salvation and life would have been near us; but now it pertains to us more, because then forgiveness was from mercy alone, whereas now the crown comes from grace and from the working [Col. 0780C] of our merits. For one who works well is nearer to eternal life. Baptism belongs to forgiveness, but a good life to the crown.

“**The night has passed; but the day has drawn near. Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the weapons of light, so that we may walk honorably as in the day.**”

Truly our salvation is nearer than before. For the night of unbelief and iniquity has passed, but the day of faith and righteousness has drawn near. We are weighed down by the darkness of night when we are obscured by the commission of iniquity. But night is turned into light when the darkness of our error is illuminated by the knowledge of truth. Night is turned into light when the darkness of our error is illuminated by the knowledge of truth. Night is turned into light [Col. 0780D] when the radiance of righteousness illuminates our hearts, which the blindness of sin had oppressed.

The Apostle saw this dawn now rising in the minds of the disciples when he said: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near.” For in indicating, after the departure of night, not that the day had already come but that it had drawn near, he undoubtedly shows that after darkness there is still dawn before the sun. For Christ, the sun of righteousness, has not yet appeared in the splendor of his brightness, but his coming is already near at hand. Therefore we do not yet possess the perfect day, but still dawn and sunrise. The life of believers, lived in this flesh and in this age, is not unreasonably called light and day in comparison with the life of unbelief and impiety; yet, compared with that day in which, made equal to angels [Col. 0781A], we shall see God as he is (1 John III), it is still night. It is both night and day: day in comparison with unbelievers, night in comparison with angels. For angels possess the day which we do not yet possess; yet we already possess the day which unbelievers do not possess.

Therefore, rightly passing over the day which the life of believers now has, it is said that the night of unbelief has passed and the day of eternity has drawn near. The day of eternal blessedness has drawn near because sins have now been forgiven and believers have now been justified. And because night has passed and day has drawn near, let us therefore cast off the works of darkness—that is, those deeds which we used to do while oppressed by the darkness of ignorance—and put on the weapons of light, that is, the virtues required by the light of divine knowledge, through which we may fight against the works of darkness [Col. 0781B] and the rulers of such works, that is, demons. For it is less fitting, in the time of new light, to perform the works of former darkness—that is, evil works which arose in the darkness of ignorance, or which love darkness and lead to darkness.

The works of light are called not so much works as weapons, because when we act rightly, when we follow the light of faith by good works, we overcome our enemies with such weapons. Let us put on as an ornament the works of light—that is, the works which faith requires; and, having received such weapons, let us walk honorably as in the day—that is, let us proceed commendably along the way of God’s commandments, as is fitting in the day of faith. For, as we have said, the life of believers is day in comparison with the life of unbelievers. Therefore we who are already in the day ought to walk honorably as [Col. 0781C] in the day, so that the beauty of virtues may adorn us on every side in the course of our conduct—us whom the day of faith and knowledge of truth illuminates, in which we see what is honorable and what dishonorable.

What works of darkness must be cast off is then shown, when it is said:

“**Not in revelries and drunkenness, not in beds and indecencies, not in strife and jealousy**” (Gal. V; 1 Pet. II).

And concerning the weapons of light which must be put on, it is added:

“**But put on our Lord Jesus Christ.**”

And afterward there is appended:

“**And make no provision for the flesh in its desires.**”

Let us walk honorably as in the day—I mean, while being [Col. 0781D] not in revelries, that is, excessive eating, and drunkenness, that is, excessive gulping of wine; not in beds, that is, slothful sleeping, and indecencies, that is, lusts nourished by excessive feasting, drinking, and beds. Revelries are dishonorable and luxurious banquets, whose necessary companion is most shameful drunkenness. And what else follows except beds and indecencies? “Beds” are so called from filthy lying together, practices fitting not so much for rational human beings as for wild beasts and animals. For those act in beds and indecencies who share their couches and unlawfully couple there in the manner of beasts.

It should be noted [Col. 0782A] that the Romans were involved in these things and therefore had no right to boast. These are four vices of the flesh. Two others belonging to the mind follow when it is said: “Not in strife and jealousy.” The Romans acted in strife and jealousy because they contended with one another and preferred some above others, in which the greater envied the lesser. The mother of these diseases—namely, strife and jealousy—is pride and the craving for human praise; nor can anyone yet be healed unless he has trampled down pride and despised human praises.

Do not be found in these things, because they are works of darkness; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, because this is to put on the weapons of light. For Christ is wisdom and righteousness and sanctification and [Col. 0782B] truth and all virtues together (1 Cor. II). Whoever has assumed these is said to have put on Christ. Put on Christ—that is, take the form of Christ as a garment—so that his bearing and form may shine forth on every side and be represented in us. When we put on a garment, we are covered from every side. Thus he has put on Christ who is protected on every side by good work, so that he leaves no part of his conduct naked to sin. For one who is righteous in some actions and unjust in others has, as it were, covered this side and left that side bare. Nor are works good any longer when they are defiled by other wicked works that arise alongside them. Therefore whoever appears a Christian on every side in all his works is to be said to have put on Christ.

Put on Christ, and make no provision for the flesh [Col. 0782C]—I do not say in necessities, but in desires. Provision may be made in necessities, for “no one ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. V); but it is forbidden in desires (1 Pet. II), because fleshly desires wage war against the soul. For those still living in mortal flesh are not required utterly to cut off care for the flesh; rather, it must be regulated so that it serves in due measure. It must be restrained by the discernment of great moderation, so that it may serve and not rule; so that it may not overcome the mind as though it were mistress, but, subdued under the mind’s dominion, may serve like a handmaid; and so that provision may be made for the need of health, not for the desires of pleasure. For what is forbidden in desires is undoubtedly permitted in necessity. The mind, indeed, must be kept from being overcome by fleshly delight [Col. 0782D], but it must not be separated from necessary care for the flesh.

## Chapter XIV

“**Receive one who is weak in faith, but not for disputes over thoughts. For one person believes that he may eat all things; but one who is weak should eat vegetables. Let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat; and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats. For God has received him. Who are you to judge another’s servant?**” (Jas. IV.) “**He stands or falls to his own master. Yet he shall stand; for God is able to make him stand.**”

Again, because another kind of contention existed among the Romans, he rebukes them for it and calls them back to concord [Col. 0783A]. For they disputed over distinctions of foods, because some of them, with sound faith, ate all foods, while others believed that certain foods ought to be abstained from; thus they disagreed with one another. Those who had believed from among the Gentiles exalted themselves in the freedom of faith, believing that nothing was common or unclean, against those coming from circumcision, who still observed the distinction of foods by the tradition of the law. The Apostle therefore restrains them and warns them not to insult those in whom long custom in observing food distinctions still produced some hesitation and uncertainty.

He calls every such person weak in faith because he does not believe that all things may be eaten. For perfect faith believes that no food should be rejected in a Jewish [Col. 0783B] sense, because every creature of God is good and nothing is to be rejected when received with thanksgiving. But whoever does not so believe is still weak in faith, if he already has faith. Yet the Apostle commands that such a person not be rejected but received, and not judged as though he were an unbeliever. For it is one thing to be an unbeliever and another to be weak in faith: the unbeliever does not possess faith, but the weak person already has it, though he still doubts in part. Therefore he is not to be driven away but received.

This is what he says: “Receive one who is weak,” and so forth. The sense continues thus: Do among yourselves the things I said above, in the manner in which I taught you—that is, put on Christ and do similar things; but do toward your neighbors what I now say: receive one who is weak in faith [Col. 0783C], so that you may heal him, just as Christ the physician received sinners—that is, the sick—in order to heal them. Receive him not for disputes over his thoughts—that is, do not judge him concerning the hidden matter of his thoughts. Perhaps his newness causes him to doubt something. Love the doubter more abundantly. By your love heal the doubt from the weak person’s heart. And if it is unknown to us in what spirit he does this, let us not dispute about it. Let us not arrogate to ourselves the judgment of others’ thoughts, but let us prove our own thoughts before God even on behalf of those about whom we perhaps entertain some doubt.

Truly the weak person must be received by one who is strong. For one person believes that it is lawful to eat every kind of food; this person is strong and ought to receive the weak. Another does not believe that it is so lawful and is weak [Col. 0783D] and needs to be received. This seems to be what he ought to have said. But he offers advice about that person from which this is sufficiently understood, saying: “But one who is weak should eat vegetables”; that is, let him be left to his own choice, lest he eat with scruple—so that, if he wishes, he may abstain not only from all meat but also from other foods and eat vegetables only.

“One person believes that he may eat all things,” that is, any Gentile converted to the faith judges that all foods may be eaten without distinction. But “one who is weak,” that is, any Hebrew still faint-hearted and wavering in faith, who judges some meats clean and others unclean, “should eat vegetables,” in which there is no suspicion of uncleanness, but which are eaten indiscriminately by all [Col. 0784A]. It is better that he be permitted to eat only those things which the rite of the law in which he was nourished did not prohibit, and that he be retained in the faith despite his faint-heartedness, so that by gradual growth he may advance to higher things, than that he be uprooted from the faith because of faint-heartedness and depart from it entirely.

Therefore the one who eats all things—that is, the Gentile who believes no food unclean—must not despise, that is, regard as worthless, the one who does not eat—that is, the Hebrew who, because of the custom of the law, still rejects certain foods. And the one who does not eat—that is, the Jew who abstains from certain things lest he violate the rite of the law—must not judge, that is, condemn, the one who eats—that is, the Gentile who consumes all foods without distinction.

For the Gentiles, whom the carnal [Col. 0784B] understanding of the law did not draw back from faith, firmly believed that nothing received with thanksgiving should be rejected; and therefore they despised the Jews, weaker in faith, whom they still saw distinguishing foods because of the ancient observance of the law. Conversely, when Jews saw them partake of the foods which they themselves thought unclean, they judged them severely for this. Therefore the Apostle commands the former not to despise the latter as weak and dull, and the latter not to judge the former as gluttonous and unclean.

There were also some among them who abstained from meat and wine not for the law’s sake but for sobriety’s sake; and they were despised by the others as persons rejecting God’s creatures. They themselves, however, judged the others as ravenous and gluttonous. Therefore the Apostle commands [Col. 0784C] that one who eats every food and does not fast should not despise the one who does not eat—that is, one who fasts and abstains from meat—since it lies within each person’s will whether to eat or not to eat. Conversely, one who does not eat but abstains and fasts must not judge, that is, think ill of, one who eats twice a day and consumes meat or foods of that kind, since all human foods may be eaten indiscriminately with a good intention and a simple heart, without the fault of concupiscence.

Concerning such matters, which may be done with a good intention although they may also be done without a good intention, those people, being human, wished to pass judgment upon the secret of the heart, although God alone judges it. Human beings can judge matters that are manifest; but concerning things done with an uncertain intention [Col. 0784D], since they may be done with either a good or an evil intention, judgment must be left to God, so that no one may dare to judge another’s conscience, which he does not see. For one whose thought is not open, and concerning whom it is unknown what he will later become, is not to be condemned.

The faster must not judge the one who eats—that is, must not believe him to sin—when he does not know in what intention he eats. And why? Because God has received him, that he might be his own. And since he has been received by God so as to belong to God and serve God, who are you—that is, what is your standing—that judge, that declare condemnable, another’s servant? Since he is not your servant but another’s, in judging him you especially offend his master, because [Col. 0785A] you presume to judge his servant despite the master’s prohibition. For the Lord is judge of the intention in which each person eats or does not eat. Therefore he is not to be judged by a human being, because he stands or falls not for a human being but for his own Lord: he stands for the honor of his own Lord, if he stands; and his fall also belongs to his Lord, if he falls, because the Lord can either raise him up or judge him.

I say, “He stands or falls,” because the matter is uncertain: perhaps the person thought to fall stands, or the person thought to stand falls. “Yet he shall stand.” Here it is suggested that we should interpret uncertainties in the better sense, desire a person’s salvation more than his death, and have hope for his good in the future even if he is otherwise in the present. He shall stand because God is able to make him stand [Col. 0785B]. It is not he himself but God who is able to do this. For one who falls falls by his own will; but one who stands stands by God’s will, and one who rises rises by God’s will. By himself a person can fall, but through God he can rise again.

Although the Apostle was speaking of all who have been regenerated and live piously when he said, “Who are you to judge another’s servant?
