He stands or falls to his own master,” he nevertheless immediately looked to the predestined and said: “Yet he shall stand.” And lest they should attribute this to themselves, he says: “For God is able to make him stand.” He, therefore, gives perseverance, who is able to establish those who stand so that they may stand most perseveringly, or to restore those who have fallen.

Perhaps these words may also be understood thus concerning spiritual eating or fasting. Receive one weak in faith, so that you may gradually heal his weakness, not for disputes over thoughts [Col. 0785C]—that is, not so that you may dispute and argue about his thoughts, but leave them to God for judgment, for he is able to correct whatever there seems displeasing to him. For one person—that is, one different from this weak person and strong—believes that he ought, according to his ability, both to understand and to practise in works all that is said in the Scriptures. But one who is weak—that is, one still held by weakness of heart and deed—should eat vegetables: let him consume such sayings of Scripture as suit his weakness, by which he may be filled against the vices of the flesh and the sickness of the mind.

The one who eats—that is, who understands the mysteries of Scripture—must not despise the one who does not eat, that is, one unable to understand these things [Col. 0785D]. And one who does not eat—that is, who does not understand—must not judge the one who eats, that is, one who understands. For those who seem to make some small advance in knowledge commonly despise and count as nothing those less capable of higher understanding; and, conversely, the inexperienced and unlearned judge—that is, accuse and condemn—those who inquire into higher and deeper things which they themselves cannot grasp or attain. Therefore, wishing to cut away the fault arising on both sides, the Apostle commands the former not to despise and scorn their inferiors, and the latter not to judge their superiors, since they lack competence to judge.

The one who does not eat must not presume, with the mouth of the heart, to judge the one who eats—that is, the person who understands—because God has received as his own servant the one who eats in this manner [Col. 0786A]. And you, unlearned person, who are you to judge another’s servant—that is, to think God’s servant deserving of condemnation? He stands in good work or falls in wicked action for his own Lord, because, if he stands in good, he will perish for his Lord, or through his Lord he will rise again. He stands or falls. But he will stand even if he now lies fallen, because God is able to raise him up. This is said against the unlearned, who rebuke the learned or pass judgment on them concerning some of their weak actions.

“**For one person judges one day above another; but another judges every day. Let each be fully assured in his own judgment. The one who regards the day, regards it for the Lord. And the one who eats, eats for the Lord, for he gives thanks to God. And the one who does not eat, does not eat for the Lord, and gives thanks to God.**”

[Col. 0786B] I rightly said that the one who eats, or the one who abstains, will stand, because what he does, he does by judgment. For one of them judges one day to be spent in abstinence rather than another—that is, to be assigned to abstinence—while another judges every day to be spent in abstinence: that is, one judges that abstinence is to be observed on fixed days, another on every day. For some determine and appoint in their hearts to spend a day in abstinence—that is, to abstain on one day and not on another, as those who fast on the fourth and sixth days and eat on the other days. Others, however, because they consider this life brief, judge that every day—that is, the continuous course of their lives—should be spent in abstinence.

Let each person—that is, both the person who judges that abstinence is required on certain days and the person who judges it required every day—abound in good works according to his own judgment [Col. 0786C]; that is, let him do what he judges ought to be done, because both are acceptable before God. “Let him abound in his own judgment,” that is, let him be left to his own counsel, lest, encountering scandal, he depart from charity, which is the mother of all things. And he should be permitted to abound, because the one who judges that a day—whether every day or some day—should be devoted to abstinence, regards it for the Lord; that is, he thinks he pleases God for the Lord’s honor.

And the one who eats—that is, who does not abstain—eats for the Lord, that is, to the praise of the Lord, whose creatures he believes all clean and from whom he who is to serve is sustained by them. Truly, he gives thanks to God for benefits bestowed upon him. The result shows that he eats for the Lord, since he gives thanks to him. And the one who does not eat—that is, who fasts and abstains—does not eat for the Lord [Col. 0786D], that is, he fasts for the honor of the Lord and gives thanks to God, who has given him endurance in abstinence. For “and gives thanks to God” is added to show what it means to do something “for the Lord,” namely, to do it for his praise. For then an action is rightly, justly, and piously done when a good work is done for the praise of him by whose grace it is granted to be done. Advancing in this disposition, whatever good a person does, he does for the Lord: that is, for the praise of him by whose grace he receives the ability to do it.

Therefore thanks are given to God by both: by the former for freedom to eat, by the latter for the fruit of abstinence. Thus neither is to be reproved.

Otherwise: I said that the one who eats with the mouth of the heart the food of holy teaching will stand. Nor is it surprising if he is raised up to stand. For one among those who eat in this way judges one day above another, while another judges [Col. 0787A] every day. This means: one understands some things, but another recognizes, seeing them as they are, all things capable of being understood. For if the darkness of ignorance is the night of the heart, understanding is deservedly called day.

Or let this statement be understood not of two human beings but of a human being and God. For one is he who judges one day among days; another, he who judges every day. A human being judges one day among days—that is, the present, which is between past and future; but God judges every day—that is, past, present, and future. Therefore the one who did not seem to stand will stand, because God, who judges every day, is able to make him stand and knows whether one who lies fallen today will stand tomorrow.

The one who judges one day among days is a human being, because he may judge one thing today and [Col. 0787B] another tomorrow: that is, the person whom today he condemns as evil, having been convicted or having confessed, tomorrow he may find good after he has corrected himself; and the person whom today he praises as righteous, tomorrow he may find condemned. But the one who judges every day is God, because he knows not only what each person is now, but also what he was and what he will be on every future day. And therefore he judges according to foreknowledge, by which he knows those whom he predestined before the foundation of the world. Many who openly appear evil are better than many good persons. For we see what they are today, but we do not know what they will be tomorrow. With God, indeed, for whom future things are present, even what they will be already is; but we can judge each person only according to what exists in the present. Therefore let each person abound in his own judgment [Col. 0787C]: that is, let him dare to judge only as much as human understanding, or as much as is granted to each person, permits; let him not rashly investigate the more exalted hidden mysteries, but take care to abound in good works according to the judgment which he has. Let him not usurp God’s judgment so as to judge the future, but be content with his own judgment, by which he can judge only the present.

[Col. 0787D] The one who regards the day regards it for the Lord: that is, one content to judge only present things usurps nothing against God, because this very act of judging the present day rightly is for the Lord, that is, for the Lord’s honor. To judge the day rightly means to know that one whose manifest fault you have judged in the present must not be despaired of as to his correction in the future.

And the one who eats, understanding the foods of wisdom, eats for the Lord—that is, for the Lord’s honor—because he gives thanks, saying: “I will bless the Lord who has given me understanding” (Ps. XV). And the one who does not eat—that is, who does not grasp the stronger meanings of Scripture—does not eat for the Lord, because he thereby becomes more humble. And this is to give thanks: to presume nothing of oneself, but to cast oneself down before God in humility.

“**For none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself. For whether we live, we live for the Lord; whether we die, we die for the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s. For to this end Christ died and rose again, that he might rule both over the dead and the living.**”

I said that the one who eats eats for the Lord’s honor [Col. 0788A], and the one who does not eat does not eat for the Lord’s honor. I said this rightly. For all of us, whether we eat or do not eat, are the Lord’s. None of us lives for himself but for the Lord, and none of us dies for himself but for the Lord. No one lives for himself because one restrained by law lives not for himself but for God who gave the law. If there were no law, each person would then live for himself. But now he obeys the command given to him from heaven and lives for him who gave it. Nor does anyone die for himself, but for God, by whose judgment he is either crowned or condemned.

For whether we live—that is, live for the honor of the Lord whom we serve—or whether we die—that is, bring the present life to an end by the separation of body and soul—we die for the Lord, that is, for his glory and according to his will, because in both living and dying we seek not our own glory but his [Col. 0788B]. And because we do both for the Lord, whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s, so that we may be possessed by him both living and dead. And if we are always his, both in life and death, whatever is done by us or concerning us is always done for his praise.

Whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s, because Christ by his death and resurrection acquired lordship over all believers, whether they live or are dead. For Christ died and rose again for this purpose, that he might rule over both the dead and the living. We are the Lord’s also after death, because by the price of his blood he redeemed us even while dead. For how can death’s kingdom lose dead servants when his death is their price? The kingdom of death will not hold those for whom he, free among the dead, died.

He rules over living and dead, lest anyone suppose that he judges only the dead, as though judgment over people while they live were entrusted to humans, but after death to Christ. For both now and then he himself rules and judges; and the saints reign with him both now and then, because even now their commonwealth is in heaven, and afterward they themselves will be in heaven. Nor are the souls of the pious dead separated from the Church, which even now is the kingdom of Christ and reigns with him already in both living and dead.

Or thus: both the one who eats and the one who does not eat do this to the glory of the Lord, because none of us lives for himself in virtues: he seeks not his own glory but Christ’s, from whom he has the ability to live in this way [Col. 0788C]. And no one dies for himself to sins, because by this he seeks to glorify not himself but Christ, who has granted him the ability to mortify himself to sins. For whether we live—that is, walk in newness of life—we live for the Lord: our life is attributed to the Lord, because it comes not from us but from him and is lived for his praise. Or whether we die—that is, are mortified to the world and to sin—we die for the Lord: we die to vices for the honor of the Lord, so that, dead to sins, we may live to righteousness.

Therefore, whether we die to sin or live to righteousness, we are the Lord’s, so that both the extinction of evil and the quickening of good may occur in us for his glory. For Christ died and rose again for this purpose, that he might rule over the dead and the living: namely, over those dead persons who mortify their members which are upon the earth and bear about in their body the mortification of Christ [Col. 0789A], and also over those living persons who, by the example of his resurrection, live on earth a new and heavenly life (Col. III; 2 Cor. IV). Christ rules over these, because such persons are worthy of his lordship.

“But why do you judge your brother?” (Jas. IV.) “**Or why do you despise your brother? For we shall all stand before the judgment-seat of Christ**” (2 Cor. V). “**For it is written: As I live, says the Lord**” (Isa. XLV), “**every knee shall bend to me, and every tongue shall confess to God**” (Phil. II). “**Therefore each of us shall render an account of himself to God. Let us therefore no longer judge one another; but judge this rather: that you do not place a stumbling-block or an offense before a brother.**”

[Col. 0789B] Thus Christ rules over all. But why do you—that is, for what reason do you—judge your brother who eats, when you do not know under what necessity he eats, or with what intention? Or why do you who eat despise your brother who does not eat, when you do not know with what devout dedication he observes abstinence? You ought neither to judge nor to despise, because you yourself are to be judged. For all of us, abstainers and eaters alike, shall stand to be judged before the tribunal, that is, before the judicial seat, of Christ. It belongs to the judge to sit, but to those being judged to stand before the judge. We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ. Therefore whoever judges his brother incurs so great a crime of pride that he seems to arrogate Christ’s tribunal to himself and to anticipate His judgment. The form of that judgment, in order that it might become more familiar to human beings, has been taken from the manner of judging practiced among men, so that we might recognize that, just as an earthly judge is higher and ascends a certain place called a tribunal, so as to be higher and more eminent from it than the rest who are to be judged, lest either the punishments of the accused or the pleadings of the innocent escape his sight; so too Christ, the judge of all, superior to all by nature and majesty, looks into the hearts and consciences of each person and will reveal hidden things, in order to grant praise to the good and that the wicked may receive the punishment they deserve. We shall all stand before Christ the judge.

For it is written in Isaiah concerning Christ, in His own person: “As I live, says the Lord” (Isa. XLV)—Christ—“to me every knee shall bend”; that is, I who was dead live perpetually, so that I can die no more. And the reason why I thus live is that every knee shall bend to me: that is, all stiffness and strength shall be humbled beneath my power, so that by the bending of knees the subjection of all may be understood; and every tongue, that is, every conscience, shall confess to God whatever it has done, whether good or evil. This will occur at the judgment. And since, according to the testimony of Scripture, every tongue will confess to God, therefore each of us shall render an account of himself to God the judge; that is, he shall answer God for the things he did and why he did them. For to render an account to God is to confess to God. And because each person shall answer for himself to God the judge, let us therefore no longer judge one another by conjecture, as we have done hitherto.

For there are two cases in which we must avoid rash judgment: when it is uncertain with what intention something was done, or when it is uncertain what sort of person he will become who now appears either good or evil. If, then, someone—for example—complaining of his stomach, did not wish to fast, and you, not believing him, attributed this to the vice of gluttony, you would judge rashly. Likewise, if you recognized manifest gluttony and drunkenness and reproved them as though they could never be corrected and changed, you would nevertheless judge rashly. Therefore let us not condemn things whose intention we do not know; nor let us condemn manifest things in such a way as to despair of healing. But those judge rashly concerning uncertain matters and readily find fault above all who love blaming and condemning more than amending and correcting. This vice is either pride [Col. 0790B] or envy.

Let us no longer judge one another: neither the abstainer the eater, nor the eater the abstainer. But judge this rather—that is, decide and determine this in your hearts—that you do not place before a brother a stumbling-block or an occasion of scandal; that is, that through your food and fasting you do not give your brother grounds for stumbling or falling into scandal. Determine this instead: that through observances concerning food you do not produce offenses or scandal for your brothers. He warns those from the Gentiles who ate not to scandalize the Hebrews by their food, who were still weaker in faith and distinguished foods. For the Gentiles, who were stronger in faith, believed that all foods could be taken without distinction; but the Jews were scandalized when they saw them eating common foods in their presence.

There were also some among them who, knowing that an idol is nothing and that every creature of God is good, ate things sacrificed to idols. Others, seeing this and supposing that there was some sanctity in that meat because it had been offered to idols, ate it and perished; while the rest were angered by it. This is what he says: “Do not place before a brother a stumbling-block or scandal”; that is, do not do before your brother something through which, following your example, he may perish by doing the same thing, or may be grieved. For it would be a stumbling-block if, through such an example, he fell away from Christian faith; but it would be scandal if he were provoked to sorrow or anger. If he saw an idol-sacrifice eaten by a Christian, he would stumble—that is, be moved away from the faith—because he would think that an idol was something. But if he saw him eating food which he regarded as unclean, he would be scandalized—that is, compelled to indignation and anger.

> “I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is common through him, except to the one who thinks something to be common: to that person it is common. For if because of food your brother is grieved, you no longer walk according to love. Do not destroy by your food the one for whom Christ died.”

I do not call it a stumbling-block or scandal because food is unclean, or because I recommend, in the Jewish manner, observing distinctions of foods. For I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is common; that is, I know that nothing is common because I have confidence in the Lord Jesus, since after He came He released us from the Law [Col. 0791A].

The Jewish people, boasting that they were God’s portion, call “common” those foods eaten by all people: pork, oysters, hares, and animals of that sort, which neither divide the hoof nor chew the cud, nor, among fishes, have scales (Lev. XI). Thus what is open to other human beings and is, as it were, not God’s portion, is called unclean. And just as vessels set apart for the services of the Temple were called not common but holy, in distinction from which the other vessels devoted to human uses were called common; so, in distinction from those foods which Scripture set apart as, supposedly, clean and to be eaten according to the Law, all the rest were called common.

But the Apostle, now freed from the letter of the Law, says that nothing is common “through itself,” that is, by its own nature. For nothing among God’s creatures is unclean by its nature. Since all were created by the good God, they are plainly good and clean. Yet he does not thereby condemn the Law’s distinction, as though he were absolutely saying that none of those things which the Law declared unclean is common. For he gives beforehand the reason why, through itself—that is, by its own nature—nothing is common: “I know,” he says, “and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus.” For it is plain that, by the Savior’s benefit, all things are clean, since He rescued humanity from beneath the yoke of the Law and restored its former condition of freedom (Matt. VII). Therefore, whether on account of God’s creation or on account of the Savior’s coming, nothing among creatures is naturally unclean. Hence He Himself says: “What enters the mouth does not defile a human being” (Matt. XV).

Nothing is common except to the person who thinks something common; for to him it is common because of the judgment by which he thinks it common, that is, unclean. For the mind’s thought makes food polluted which by its own nature is neither common nor defiled. Conversely, simplicity of mind, having no anxious scruple of thought, frees from every suspicion of contamination food that is truly defiled—for it is truly defiled when it has been offered to idols. Again, even if food is clean, if someone nevertheless has a suspicion that it has been offered to idols, it is called defiled because of the scruple of conscience.

I said, “Do not place before a brother a stumbling-block or scandal,” precisely because, if your brother is even grieved because of your food, you no longer walk according to love; that is, the course of this action of yours no longer keeps to the path of brotherhood. And therefore you sin gravely, because you have abandoned love, without which nothing pleases God. Do not destroy him by your food. You ought not even to grieve him by your food; much more, beware lest you destroy him in this way. Do not, for your food—for so cheap and quickly perishing a thing—destroy something of such great value and dignity, for which Christ endured death.

Although the Apostle had established by apostolic teaching that through the Lord Jesus nothing is to be regarded as common or unclean by its own nature, and had granted complete freedom to all believers in the use of foods, he again recalls the liberty of freedom in order to build up the authority of brotherly love, saying: Even though nothing is common [Col. 0792A] and every use of food is freely permitted, yet if because of food which you consider lawful you scandalize a brother who is not yet capable of this knowledge, you no longer act according to love and do not show in yourself the affection of brotherly love. Therefore, so that you may neither harm nor grieve him, you ought even to abstain from lawful things. For your abstaining from lawful things is no crime; but for him, among foods which he distinguishes and considers unlawful, their use is defiling. “For the one who distinguishes, if he eats, is condemned.” If you do this, you surely despise and destroy your brother, for whom Christ died, and you incur for him a cause of destruction.

> “Therefore let not our good be blasphemed. For the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and [Col. 0792B] peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. For whoever serves Christ in this pleases God and is approved by human beings. Therefore let us pursue the things of peace, and let us keep between ourselves the things of edification.”

Since our brother is grieved or destroyed by our food, let us therefore take care that our good is not blasphemed. For our good is blasphemed if quarrels arise because of foods, since eating, good in itself, becomes liable to blasphemy when it harms others. And because it harms, abstain. One must abstain because the kingdom of God is not food and drink; that is, the kingdom of God, for which we labor and run, does not consist in food or drink. These things are alien to the kingdom of God and to that future manner of life of the saints. There will not be carnal banquets there, but righteousness, peace, and joy. And because people are accustomed greatly to rejoice in bodily foods, he added, “in the Holy Spirit.”

Therefore let us exercise ourselves in those virtues which can pass with us into the kingdom of heaven: righteousness, peace, and spiritual joy. He set forth these three virtues because he saw that they particularly served his purpose and the correction of the Romans: righteousness, so that no one does to another what he would not wish done to himself, and does to another what he rightly desires done to himself; peace, so that there may be rest and concord among them, not boasting and discord; joy, so that each person rejoices in his brother’s goods as in his own. These virtues are the kingdom of God, because the kingdom of heavenly blessedness consists in virtues of this kind [alternate reading: is established]. Or they are the kingdom of God because, even in the present life, God reigns in those in whom these virtues are found. Truly these are, in the Holy Spirit, the kingdom of God. For whoever serves Christ in this—that is, in the Holy Spirit—by striving, after receiving the grace of the Holy Spirit, to obey Christ’s commands, pleases God the Father, who said of Christ: “Hear him” (Matt. XVII; Luke IX; II Pet. I). And he is approved by human beings, who, seeing his good works, glorify his Father who is in heaven (Matt. V).

He pleases God according to the joy which is in the Holy Spirit; he appears approved by human beings according to righteousness and peace. And because peace and joy are the kingdom of God, and through these each person can please both God and human beings, therefore let us always pursue what belongs to peace and concord, not what belongs to war and discord; and let us keep what belongs to edification—that is, observe what pertains to building up—toward one another: Jew toward Gentile and Gentile toward Jew, so that we may always be built up more and more by one another, or others through us.

> “Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food. All things indeed are clean, but it is evil for the person who eats through offense [Tit. I; I Cor. VIII]. It is good not to eat meat or drink wine, nor anything in which your brother stumbles, is scandalized, or is weakened. Do you have faith? Have it before God within yourself. Blessed is the one who does not judge himself in what he approves. But the one who distinguishes, if he eats, is condemned, because it is not from faith. But everything which is not from faith is sin.”

We ought to keep the things of edification; therefore do not, through your food, destroy in others the work of God—that is, overthrow the faith and love which God has worked in them. For one dissolves God’s work and destroys the edifice of love who, through intemperance in foods, places scandal before brothers. All kinds of foods are indeed clean, but nevertheless some must be foregone lest through them God’s work be destroyed; for it is evil for the person who eats through the offense of others—that is, who eats in such a way that others fall through his eating and depart from the faith. What is good by its own nature therefore becomes evil through offense, because your brother takes offense while you use foods in which he suffers scandal.

All things are naturally clean, although the Law of Moses signified some things as clean and some as unclean, so that the people reckoned under the Law might seem distinguished from other nations by observances of this sort. And while that people was regarded as holy and set apart from other nations, an equitable distinction between clean and unclean things seemed necessary, by which that people might be separated from nations made unclean by ignorance of God and idolatrous worship. But now, when all the Gentiles have entered the faith, it is not necessary to observe distinctions of this sort; rather, every creature of God is to be regarded as good, as indeed it is. Therefore all things are clean and good, but they are turned to evil for those who eat them through offense to brothers. And therefore, lest a brother be offended, one must abstain from them.

For it is good not to eat meat or drink wine through offense to a brother, nor anything else in which your brother stumbles, is scandalized, or is weakened. Otherwise, eating meat or not eating it, drinking wine or not drinking it, is neither evil nor good, but intermediate and indifferent. For even an evil person, alien from faith, may refrain from eating meat and drinking wine—as it sometimes happens that some do this even for the sake of idols. But not eating meat and not drinking wine in order that a brother may neither be offended nor give offense is no longer intermediate or indifferent, but truly good [Col. 0794A]. For it is good to abstain from meat and wine if a brother takes offense at them.

For all things must be done in order that God’s work may not be destroyed. Therefore one must eat if by this a brother is built up; and one must not eat if through it God’s work is diminished. One must drink if through it a brother advances in faith; and one must not drink if through it either a brother suffers loss of faith or you incur harm to love. There are also other reasons why many religious persons abstain from such foods, but the Apostle now passes over them in silence because he speaks to beginners. For this one reason alone he now recommends abstinence: lest a brother be offended, scandalized, or weakened.

A person stumbles if, offended by eating or drinking, he withdraws from the faith; or he gives offense, troubled and not knowing what to hold. He is scandalized if he is grieved. He is weakened in faith if, though he does not withdraw, he begins to doubt. And lest your brother suffer these things because of your food, you ought to abstain. You can rightly do this, because you lose nothing of your good. For you have within yourself—that is, in your heart, whence no one can take it away—faith: you believe that it is lawful to eat all things. Have that faith before God; that is, preserve it within your conscience and do not parade it before others, lest what you believe become more a matter of display than of virtue. It is enough for you to have such faith before God. Yet another person who does not yet have such faith, so as to believe all things may be eaten, is not therefore to be compelled to eat everything. Do not then boast of this faith before people by despising those who do not yet believe thus, but retain it in the sight of the inward Judge.

For blessed is the one who does not judge himself: that is, who does not make himself condemnable by harming others in what he approves, namely in that act which he praises and judges good. Blessed is the person who does nothing other than what he judges beneficial. For that person judges himself—that is, condemns himself by his own judgment—who does what he says he ought not to do. Faith by which we believe all things clean is good, and we rightly approve it in ourselves as good. But if we misuse this good of faith by eating to the offense of weak brothers, we judge ourselves, because we knowingly do what our mind judges ought not to be done. Blessed indeed is the one who does not judge himself in this way.

But the one who distinguishes—that is, who makes distinctions among foods, thinking some clean and others unclean—if he eats with such a conscience, is condemned because he does not eat from faith. Therefore we ought neither to compel him to eat nor provoke him to eat by our example, but rather abstain from such foods for his sake. If he eats, he is already condemned while his conscience accuses him, because he does not eat from faith: he does not at all believe the food clean, and yet eats it. For he rightly lies under condemnation, because he believes one thing ought to be done and does another. He does not eat from faith. But every work which is not from faith is sin. Therefore, because his eating is sin, he is rightly condemned. Everything which is not from faith [Col. 0795A] is sin, because even what is good, if it is thought evil and then done, is sin. For example, if someone believed chastity to be evil and lived chastely, he would certainly sin. Therefore the whole life of unbelievers is sin, and nothing is good apart from the highest good. For where knowledge of eternal and immutable truth is absent, virtue is false even in the best morals.

## CHAPTER XV

> “But we who are stronger ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not please ourselves. Let each of us please his neighbor in what is good, for edification. For Christ also did not please himself, but as it is written: ‘The reproaches of those who reproached you fell upon me’” (Ps. LXVIII).

[Col. 0795B] If the weak person eats, he is condemned; but we who are stronger ought to bear the weaknesses of such persons. Or thus: we ought not to place a stumbling-block or scandal before a brother, but rather we who are stronger ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, so that we who are more robust may patiently endure those things in which others sin through weakness. We must not immediately despise, reject, and abhor them if perhaps they are overcome in some fault of weakness; nor, under the pretext of a purer life, drive them away from the gathering of brothers and the fellowship of the Church. Since they cannot raise themselves to us, we ought patiently to bear—that is, carry and raise—their weaknesses, not reject and despise them.

For if a weak person is borne, either he is ashamed to be borne for long and corrects his habitual sinning; or, if he refuses to correct himself, the one who bears him will have the reward of patience, while the other will perish more grievously. We ought, I say, to bear their weaknesses lest those who stagger fall, and not please ourselves; that is, not love with private love, so that, loving ourselves, we take no care for others and, seeking our own advantages, neglect their benefit. Let no one do this. Rather, let each of us please his neighbor, not by assenting to his wickedness or to any other evil, but instead in good work and speech, for his edification.

We ought not please a neighbor in the good we do for the sake of human favor, but for his edification, so that we may build him up by words and examples. Let us not please ourselves, but our neighbor in good things for his benefit. For Christ, who is our head and leader, did this: He did not please Himself, because “though he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God to be robbery” (Phil. II). But wishing to please human beings, in order to give them an example of right conduct and restore them to salvation, He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant; and, as it is written, He endured reproaches: “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell upon me” (Ps. LXVIII), O Father.

For while they reproached me, they reproached you; because just as “whoever receives me receives him who sent me” (Luke IX), and “whoever despises me despises him who sent me” (John XIII), so whoever reproaches me reproaches Him who sent me. Thus the reproaches of the Jews, reproaching you in this way, fell upon me—that is, they overwhelmed me with the burden of death. For they said that I blasphemed you, and for this reason they killed me (Matt. IX; Mark II; John X). Thus the sins of those sinning against you fell upon me, because I, innocent, was killed by sinners as a blasphemer; and you who sent me are dishonored.

> “For whatever things were written were written for our instruction, so that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope.”

I said that Christ, whom we ought to follow, endured reproaches for the salvation of human beings, as it is written, and did not please Himself but others, that they might be saved. And truly by this scriptural passage from the Psalm we are taught by His example to seek not our own advantages but those of others [Col. 0796B]. For whatever things were written in the Old Testament were written for our instruction—that is, in order that we might be taught through them. The Apostle shows the usefulness of reading the ancient Scriptures. Because the Jews did not understand them, whereas we understand them when Christ opens them, what is read there was written not for their instruction but for ours. For things that are written are undoubtedly written for those who will understand and draw benefit from them. Therefore everything read in the Law and the Prophets was written for our sake, so that we, who were to understand it, might be taught by it what we ought to believe, do, and hope.

Thus, through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures, we may have hope. Through patience we have hope because patience produces testing, and testing hope (Rom. XV; Jas. I). And through the consolation of the Scriptures we have hope because, while the Scriptures console us in adversities, they raise our minds to hope in heavenly blessedness. In the Scriptures themselves we are taught patience, so that we may share Christ’s sufferings and willingly endure for the salvation of our neighbors, as He endured for us. There too we receive consolation—that is, relief of sorrow and affliction—lest we be swallowed up by excessive grief. For consolation does not signify the removal of pain but restraint and a certain mitigation of it.

We have this consolation from the Scriptures, and through it hope; because when God lightens our present sorrow by the sayings of His Scriptures and turns it into joy, He gives hope that we shall attain that joy with which no sorrow will be mingled. Consolation is given to us in the refreshing remembrance of Christ’s sufferings, because when we read or hear how many and how great things He endured without fault, we understand that we, being sinners, ought willingly to endure all things. Then hope follows, because through these afflictions we hope to attain that blessedness to which Christ attained by the merit of His passion.

> “May the God of patience and consolation grant you to think the same thing toward one another according to Jesus Christ, so that, being of one mind, with one mouth you may glorify God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore receive one another, as Christ also received you, unto the honor of God.”

[Col. 0797A] The Scriptures teach us, but may God grant you that you can do what the Scriptures teach. May God strengthen your weakness by the light and power of His grace, so that you may will and be able to do what you hear in the Scriptures. I say, the God of patience and consolation—that is, the one from whom patience and consolation come, as do the other virtues. When He is called the God of patience, this indicates that God is with those who possess in themselves the virtue of patience; just as, when He is called the God of righteousness, it is shown that God is in those who keep righteousness. Likewise, when He is called the God of consolation, it is shown that He is with those who through spiritual understanding receive consolation from the divine Scriptures.

“May the God of patience and consolation grant you to think the same thing toward one another.” Following the custom of patriarchs and prophets, the Apostle now gives the Romans a blessing. Great indeed is this blessing, by which he prays that they may be granted by God to think the same thing toward one another; that is, that there may now be no dissension among them, but that all may think and feel one and the same thing, and each may will for his neighbor as for himself. He rightly adds, “according to Jesus Christ.” For people can also think and agree with one another in wickedness. But those who think according to Christ undoubtedly think only what is good.

May He grant you, he says, to think the same thing toward one another: may He grant you such mutual concord that what one thinks, another may think, and that the understanding of wisdom may pass to and fro, from this person to that and from that person to this. And this according to Christ: that is, in every good thing by which we follow our King, not in evil by which we oppose Him. Think in this manner, so that, being of one mind—that is, all having one mind—you may with one mouth glorify God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. “With one mouth” is said when one and the same thought and speech proceeds through the mouths of different people. Think the same thing so that, being of one mind, you may honor God with one mouth, because otherwise you cannot honor Him. For He is honored only by those who think the same thing in Christ, so as to praise Him with unanimous will and the same confession of mouth. According to Christ’s humanity, God is His God; according to His divinity, He is His Father. You ought to honor Him with one understanding and a concordant life.

Therefore—that is, in order that you may honor Him concordantly—receive one another, each receiving the other, lest one now reject another because he disagrees with him over clean or unclean foods. Where he first offers prayer for them, he shows that salvation comes not from human strength and merits but from God’s grace. Yet where he adds the exhortation that they receive one another, he shows free choice in them, and indicates that through their own choice, strengthened by God’s preceding grace, they can work out their salvation. For if they could do nothing by their own powers, he would not admonish them; and if their choice alone sufficed, he would not pray to God for them but merely exhort them.

Receive one another as Christ also received you: He abhorred no one’s uncleanness and charged no one with his sins. Therefore do not judge anything concerning the uncleanness of animals, just as He did not impute to believers their uncleannesses. He received you unto the honor of God, because He received you for this purpose: that, according to His command, people might see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven (Matt. V).

> “For I say that Christ Jesus was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, in order to confirm the promises to the fathers; but that the Gentiles glorify God for mercy, as it is written: ‘Therefore I will confess you among the Gentiles, and I will sing to your name’ [II Sam. XXII; Ps. XVII]. And again he says: ‘Rejoice, Gentiles, with his people’ [Deut. XXXII]. And again: ‘Praise the Lord, all Gentiles, and magnify him, all peoples’ [Ps. CXVI]. And again Isaiah says: ‘There shall be a root of Jesse, and one who shall arise to rule [Col. 0798B] the Gentiles; in him the Gentiles shall hope’ [Isa. XI].”

Truly Christ received you: the Jews because of truth, the Gentiles because of mercy. For I say that Jesus Christ was a minister of circumcision—that is, I, who must be believed without doubt; I, who learned not from a human being but from Christ Himself; I, who am so great an apostle—I say that Christ was minister of circumcision, that is, apostle and preacher to those who are of the circumcision, as He says: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. XV). And this was in order to fulfill God’s truth: He had spoken to Abraham and David that Christ would come from their seed (Gen. XXII; Ps. CXXXI), to confirm the promises to the fathers—that is, to make firm and sure the promises concerning His coming which were made to the fathers and are read in the Scriptures. For He ought to come to those whose fathers had been promised Him.

But God did not close the fountain of His goodness even to the foreign Gentile nations; rather, through the same Redeemer He mercifully saved them. Or Christ is called a minister of circumcision because He received circumcision in His flesh, in order openly to declare that, coming from Abraham’s seed, to whom God had promised that all nations would be blessed in his seed, He fulfilled in Himself what had been promised to the fathers. Thus the Gentiles might understand that those who remain in observances of the Law are not wholly to be condemned, since Christ Himself also became in His flesh a minister of circumcision—that is, an observer.

I say that Christ was minister of circumcision because of God’s truth; but I say that the Gentiles glorify God—that is, I say that Gentiles converted to faith glorify God by good works and religious conduct—for mercy: that is, on account of, or in return for, the mercy bestowed on them by Him. For truth is among the Jews, mercy among the Gentiles: truth there, where God’s oracles were; mercy among those who had forsaken God and turned themselves to the worship of the devil, had received no divine promise, and possessed no merit of righteousness. Thus God called the Gentiles solely by mercy to honor and glorify Him, as it is written in the Psalm in Christ’s person [Col. 0799A] (Ps. XVII): “Therefore”—that is, because of my resurrection and ascension, since you will exalt me from those rising against me and rescue me from the unrighteous man—“I will confess you among the Gentiles,” that is, the Gentiles will confess you through me; “and I will sing to your name,” that is, I shall cause them to sing.

He shows that greater thanks must be rendered to God by the Gentiles. “To whom more is forgiven, he loves more” (Luke VII). He also removes arrogance from the Jews by teaching that the salvation of the Gentiles too was similarly foretold. When the Lord says, “I will confess you among the Gentiles,” He makes clear that He Himself confesses in them, just as He speaks in them, being in His members. Confession is not only confession of sins, but also praise of God. And when He says, “I will sing,” this is that new song of which another Psalm says: “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth” (Ps. XCV). For He sings in us, by whose grace singing occurs in us. There is inward joy where the voice of praise is both sung and heard: by that voice is praised the One who ought freely to be loved with all the heart, all the soul, and all the mind, and who by the grace of the Holy Spirit kindles His lover in Himself.

These things David says in the Psalm concerning the salvation of the Gentiles (Ps. XVII). And again Moses, in the song of Deuteronomy, where we have, “Praise, O Gentiles, his people” (Deut. XXXII), says according to the Seventy Interpreters: “Rejoice, Gentiles, with his people”; that is, rejoice with the Jews, having become one flock in Christ. Again David says (Ps. CXVI): “Praise the Lord, all Gentiles,” because He has increased the number of His people by associating all of us with them; “and magnify him,” that is, show Him great and glorious by your works, “all peoples of the Jews,” that is, the twelve tribes and all the families of Israel.

And Isaiah again says (Isa. XI), to the same effect: “There shall be a root of Jesse,” that is, the origin of the royal family, and from this root Christ shall come, who shall rise from the dead to rule the Gentiles—that is, to rule them through faith and good works. Therefore the Gentiles shall hope in Him as coming to judgment, in order to receive from Him the crown of glory. Or, because Christ Himself says in the Apocalypse of John, “I am the root and offspring of David” (Rev. XXII), He Himself should rather be understood as the root of Jesse: that is, deriving the origin of His flesh from Jesse through David and Mary. “There shall be a root of Jesse,” that is, there shall be a son of Jesse, there shall be one leading forth Jesse’s line; and He shall be the one who rises from death to rule the Gentiles. And in Him, as we have said, the Gentiles shall hope, that when He returns they may receive the kingdom from Him (Matt. XXV).

> “May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that you may abound in hope and in the power of the Holy Spirit.”

Beautifully, having said that it is written in Isaiah that the Gentiles will hope in him, he adds: “Now may the God of hope …,” as though it had been written that the Gentiles would believe in him and then had added, “Now may the God of hope ….” He invokes the God of hope upon those who hope in him, from whom he prays that the gift of blessing may be increased for them [Col. 0800A]. As though he said: By the testimonies of Scripture I have shown that both you Gentiles and Jews belong to the faith through Christ; but may God, who is able to fulfill all that I have said—the God of hope, that is, he who gives hope, or he in whom we hope—fill you with every spiritual joy, so that none of you may now be distressed, as you were accustomed mutually to distress one another in contention [Note: [Col. 0799D] Another reading omits “in contention.”], but may rejoice in your progress and hope; and may he fill you with peace, that is, concord in believing, lest there be any discord in your faith, but peace among yourselves, so that you may abound in good works in the hope of future recompense and in the power of the Holy Spirit, by which you are now strengthened. Or: may you abound through good works, that is, may you more certainly hope for eternal blessedness, and abound in the unity and power of the Holy Spirit, that is, be more abundantly filled [Col. 0800B] with the strength of that same Spirit, so that you may be robust for all things.

> “But I myself am convinced concerning you, my brothers, that you yourselves also are full of charity, filled with all knowledge, so that you are able to admonish one another.”

Lest he seem to understand all of them to be discordant and foolish in need of correction, he removes that impression. He begins thus in order to admonish the more perfect concerning the correction of the lesser, and then sets himself forth as an example, since he labored for others. And it is necessary that they do this, since he, being hindered by other matters, cannot yet come to them.

“I admonish you,” he says, “to receive one another and live concordantly—not all of you, however; but I myself am convinced concerning you who are greater, O my brothers, who speak in this way, that not I alone, but you yourselves also are full of charity [Col. 0800C], by which you desire to benefit others, and filled with all knowledge, by which you are able to fulfill what you desire concerning the progress of others.” Filled with all knowledge of the Old and New Law—not indeed completely, but in part—so that you may be able to admonish one another: that is, you have learned the whole knowledge of Scripture sufficiently to be able through it mutually to admonish one another to act well, unless you remain in your own fault.

> “But I have written to you rather boldly, brothers, in part, as though recalling you to remembrance, because of the grace given to me by God, that I may be a minister of Jesus Christ among the Gentiles, sanctifying the Gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may become acceptable and sanctified in the Holy Spirit.”

[Col. 0800D] I am convinced concerning you, and I know that you too are filled with knowledge; yet I have written to you, O brothers, more boldly than perhaps you would have supposed, and I have written in part. Since now the Apostle, from whom the word of knowledge has been poured out to us, says that he has written in part, we must believe that, although elsewhere he says, “We know in part and prophesy in part” (1 Cor. 13), nevertheless he knew more, and far more, than he wrote. For, as one who knew much yet did not dare to set forth much, he says that he acted more boldly, in order to direct some saving instruction to them through writing.

But when he says, “as though recalling you to remembrance,” he indicates that he had indeed already spoken with them on such matters, and had often [Col. 0801A] discoursed on the mysteries; but because forgetfulness can easily carry away what is spoken only orally, by these few things which he wrote he recalls them to remembrance of what he had often discussed more fully. Or: “I have written to you more boldly,” rebuking more boldly certain of you who are behaving wrongly. I have written, I say, not as though thinking you ignorant, but as though recalling you to remembrance—that is, making you mindful of what you ought to do. By praise he recalls them to better things, in the manner of one exhorting. Hence he does not say that he teaches them, but admonishes them, as though the matter is known but has escaped the mind. Yet he covertly rebukes them as though forgetful of what they ought to have retained with diligent attention.

“I have written to you,” he says, “and this because of the grace of apostleship given me by God,” as though he said: “I could not omit this because of my office [Col. 0801B].” For this purpose grace was given to me: that I might be a minister of Christ among the Gentiles—that is, that I might minister and serve Christ by preaching him to the Gentiles. He does not write rashly; rather, having been appointed Apostle of the Gentiles, he dares to write to all Gentiles. “I am a minister of Christ,” appointed by him himself, not by another; I say, “sanctifying the Gospel of God,” that is, showing it holy by my example, which I minister with such great reverence, so that the offering of the Gentiles may become acceptable—that is, so that all may be offered to the Lord as an acceptable sacrifice, when, believing in Christ, they are sanctified through the Gospel. Or: “that the offering of the Gentiles may become acceptable,” that is, that the Gentiles whom I offer may be accepted by God through perfection of faith and sanctified by good works in the Holy Spirit—that is, in the grace of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0801C]

> “Therefore I have glory in Christ Jesus toward God. For I do not dare to speak of any of those things which Christ does not accomplish through me for the obedience of the Gentiles, by word and deed, in the power of signs and wonders, in the power of the Holy Spirit, so that from Jerusalem and round about as far as Illyricum I have filled all with the Gospel of Christ.”

I said that I am a minister of Jesus Christ, sanctifying the Gospel of God. Therefore I have glory in Christ Jesus, whom I serve, toward God, whose Gospel I sanctify. I have this glory in Christ, because no one can have glory before God except in Christ. For Christ is truth, wisdom, and righteousness; and without these no one has glory before God.

[Col. 0801D] I have glory in Christ, and rightly so, because I do not dare, like the pseudo-apostles, to speak of anything which Christ does not accomplish through me. That is, I should regard it as great disgrace if I were to speak of something which Christ did not work through me, for the obedience of the Gentiles—that the Gentiles may obey him through the word of my preaching and the deeds of my activity—in the power of signs and wonders, that is, the power of mystical and ordinary miracles, performed in the power of the Holy Spirit.

“What I speak,” he says, “is not the language of another’s work; nor do I become a praiser of deeds performed by others. Rather, I write to you those things which I know Christ has done through me, which he has accomplished through the obedience of the Gentiles by word and work: by the word of teaching, and by works of signs and wonders.” Signs are called those things in which, although something marvelous occurs, something future is also indicated [Col. 0802A]. Wonders, however, are those in which only something marvelous is displayed. Yet he called signs and wonders as though they contain both. Divine Scripture sometimes maintains these distinctions, and sometimes uses the terms loosely, putting wonders for signs and signs for wonders.

The Apostle says that these things were done through himself in order to prove that he could do nothing less than the earlier apostles who had been with Christ. In “the power of the Holy Spirit” may be understood that power by which he laid hands upon believers and they received the Holy Spirit, or upon the sick and they were healed.

“Christ works in me thus,” he says, “that from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum I have filled with the Gospel of Christ all the peoples round about”; or, “I have filled the Gospel of Christ,” that is, I have preached it fully [Col. 0802B] as far as Illyricum, which is a great region, beginning from the beginning of Europe and containing nineteen provinces, among which are Dalmatia, both Pannonias, Epirus and Achaia, Macedonia and Thessaly.

> “And thus I preached this Gospel, not where Christ had been named, lest I should build upon another’s foundation; but as it is written: ‘Those to whom no announcement has been made concerning him shall see, and those who have not heard shall understand.’ For this reason I was very greatly hindered from coming to you. But now, having no longer a place in these regions, and having for many preceding years already had a desire to come to you, whenever I begin to journey into Spain, I hope that, as I pass by, I shall see you [Col. 0802C] and be escorted thither by you, if first I have in part enjoyed you.”

I have filled everything with the Gospel through such extensive spaces of land, and I did not do it after others, but preached this Gospel in such a way as to anticipate everyone, because I preached it not where Christ had been named—that is, not in places where he had already been preached by others—lest I should build upon another’s foundation: that is, lest I add the structure of my preaching upon the foundation of faith laid by another and seem to steal the glory of another’s work.

Rather, I did as it is written in Isaiah (Isa. 52), where we read: “For those to whom no announcement has been made concerning him,” that is, concerning Christ, “shall see him with the eyes of the heart; and those who had not previously heard the preaching [Col. 0802D] concerning him shall understand what is said about him.” In accordance with this testimony of prophecy, the Apostle carefully observed that he should announce Christ to those to whom no one had announced him, and that those should understand concerning him who had learned from no one before.

For since he knew that pseudo-apostles spoke falsehoods under Christ’s name, which afterward required the greatest labor to correct, he was careful to anticipate them and hand on the truth intact where Christ had not yet been announced. And so that there might be a true understanding of him, he hastened to imbue the Gentiles with truth, in order to make all cautious against the inventions of pseudo-apostles.

“I have preached Christ,” he says, “to so many Gentiles who did not know him. For this reason”—that is, because I was detained by the task of founding churches, and of founding them in places where no foundation of faith had preceded—“while I traveled round about and anticipated false teachers, I was very greatly hindered from coming to you,” whom, as I said at the beginning of the epistle, I desire to see.

“But now, having no longer a place [Col. 0803A],” that is, no reason for remaining in these regions, because I have filled all with knowledge of God; “but having had for many preceding years the desire to come to you, when I begin to journey into Spain,” to which it is difficult for pseudo-apostles to go, and therefore delay was permissible, “I hope that as I pass by I shall see you.”

He seems to say these things while situated in Achaia, at Corinth. Achaia is indeed neighboring and contiguous to Macedonia. While dwelling in these places, having traversed every part and preached the Gospel only in territories where Christ had not previously been preached, and having filled all things with the knowledge of God [Col. 0803B], he says that he has no further place in these regions: that is, nothing remains for him empty of Christ’s preaching, and the time is now at hand when he should fulfill his desire to see the Romans, which he had cherished for many years but postponed because others continually needed conversion.

Nor does he speak falsely in promising that he will go to Spain. For he did go, as Jerome, Bede, and the other teachers testify. Thus, passing through Narbonne, he is said to have left there as bishop a certain disciple of his named Paul. He therefore reached Spain and ran in preaching from the Red Sea to the Ocean, imitating the course of the sun from east to west, so that the earth would fail him before his zeal for preaching.

Because, therefore, he was also hastening to anticipate pseudo-apostles in Spain, “when I begin to journey into Spain,” he says, “I hope that I shall see you,” as though he said: “Of myself I can do nothing, but I hope that God will grant that I see you—and that while passing through, because you do not require a long stay, whereas others altogether need my arrival. I hope that I shall see you and be escorted thither by you, if meanwhile you prepare yourselves, lest you delay me from the rest; namely, if first I have enjoyed you [Col. 0803C] in part,” that is, if first I receive fruit from you, if first I rejoice in your fruit, and this from a portion of you—that is, from those who do not yet bear such fruit as they ought.

When he says, “I hope that as I pass by I shall see you,” this must not be understood as though he were bound to the Romans by such slight love that he judged them to be visited only in passing while going somewhere else. Hence he adds, “if first I have in part enjoyed you.” In this he seems to place within their power how long he ought to relax his purpose of going elsewhere for their sake; and in some measure he invites and nourishes their love for himself, so that they may be held by an insatiable affection toward the Apostle and may know that he too has this purpose: not to depart from them, nor to enjoy any benefit other than their love—though that love will not be satisfied completely but only in part.

For he forewarns them that the necessity of evangelizing the many must take precedence over them. And rightly, to those whom he had not yet seen according to the flesh and to whom he had not yet come in the body, he promises his presence and delay more moderately [Col. 0804A]. For we receive more eagerly goods which we fear will soon be taken away; but we more securely neglect those which we believe will satisfy us for a longer time.

> “But now I shall depart for Jerusalem, ministering to the saints. For Macedonia and Achaia have approved making some contribution for the poor among the saints who are in Jerusalem. For it pleased them, and they are their debtors. For if the Gentiles have become partakers of their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in material things [1 Cor. 9]. Therefore, when I have completed this and have delivered to them this fruit, I shall go by way of you into Spain. And I know that, when I come to you, I shall come in the abundance of the blessing of Christ.”

[Col. 0804B] Since I have no further place here and desire you, therefore I shall depart without delay for Jerusalem, that from there I may come to you. I shall go to minister to the saints who laid the prices of their sold possessions at the feet of the apostles (Acts 4). And I have something to minister to them, because Macedonia and Achaia—that is, the Macedonians and Achaeans—have approved, that is, have judged good, making some contribution. Therefore I did not compel them; rather, they themselves approved making some monetary contribution for the poor among the saints—that is, for those saints who are poor in Jerusalem. For not all are poor, but those who sold everything and, as we said, laid the price at the apostles’ feet.

Here, subtly and tactfully, while praising the Greeks, he exhorts the Romans; for devout minds are more easily invited to good action by examples than by words [Col. 0804C]. And those who live through God’s mercy ought to be merciful to their fellow brothers. They approved, I say, making a contribution from their possessions, which they might send to needy saints, because it pleased them to do this; and rightly did it please them, because they are their debtors. Likewise, the Romans are their debtors.

The Apostle so greatly desires them to be merciful that he says even this is owed by one who expects mercy. They are debtors. For if the Gentiles have become partakers of their spiritual things—that is, of the spiritual goods possessed by the Hebrews, who sent them preachers—then these Gentiles ought to minister to them in material goods. The latter had given themselves wholly to divine service, taking no care for worldly things, and gave believers an example of good conduct [Col. 0804D]. Therefore the Apostle appointed the Gentiles, who could not leave all worldly things, as it were their tributaries and providers, to supply them from their possessions with sustenance.

And because this pleased them, therefore, when I have completed this ministry and have delivered—that is, handed over under the mark of each individual church or region—this fruit born from a good tree, I shall go by way of you into Spain. Therefore, meanwhile correct yourselves: I shall pass through you, and not uselessly, but I know—that is, I am certain—that when I come to you, I shall come in the abundance of Christ’s blessing, that is, I shall benefit you greatly. He promises this only through the spirit of prophecy. For it is beyond human capacity to know concerning future events [Col. 0805A] that he will come to them not merely with Christ’s blessing, but with an abundance of blessing, in which both the grace of the visitor and the merits of those receiving him are alike indicated.

> “Therefore I beseech you, brothers, through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the charity of the Holy Spirit, that you assist me in your prayers to God, that I may be delivered from the unbelievers who are in Judea, and that the offering of my service may become acceptable to the saints in Jerusalem, so that I may come to you with joy through the will of God, and be refreshed with you.”

Since I am going to Jerusalem and afterward intending to travel to you, therefore I beseech you, brothers: if you wish to see me, obtain by prayer that, having been delivered, I may be able to come to you. I beseech you through our Lord [Col. 0805B] Jesus Christ and through the charity of the Holy Spirit—that is, the charity which the Holy Spirit gives—that, if you love the Lord Jesus and if the charity produced by the Holy Spirit is in you, you assist me in your prayers to God, so that what I alone cannot obtain, I may obtain with the help of your prayers. For when many gather together with one mind, they become great, and it is impossible that the prayers of many should not obtain their request.

Assist me, that I may be delivered from the unbelievers who are in Judea, lest they detain me longer and delay your salvation and that of others, or take away the provision which I bring to the saints. Pray that I may be delivered from these unbelievers, so that the offering of my service—that is, the service imposed upon me—may become acceptable, that is, sufficient and not diminished, to the saints in Jerusalem. Or “acceptable”: pleasing and agreeable to them, so that, understanding my charity toward them [Col. 0805C], they may with one mind give thanks with me. For it will be a great benefit to me if, made glad by my ministry, they praise God.

Pray that I may accomplish these things thus and so be able to come to you with joy at your future progress, through God’s will, and be refreshed with you—that is, rest in your peace and concord. For I have no refreshment among you if you are divided. Although above he had said through prophecy, “When I come to you, I shall come in the abundance of Christ’s blessing,” nevertheless he knew that prayer was necessary even in matters which he had manifestly known would occur. Unless prayer had been applied, what had been prophesied would undoubtedly not have been fulfilled.

Who, then, reading or hearing this—that Paul asks those in Rome to pray for him—will disdain to request the prayers of the Church, even if those whose prayer is requested seem inferior in merits? For behold, Paul, endowed with apostolic merits, humbly exhorts his disciples to pray for him. It should also be noted that there are some who say: “Why should we labor by good works to attain life? For if we are predestined, we shall undoubtedly attain it.” Their error is refuted when he exhorts the Romans to pray for the fulfillment of those things which he himself had foretold as future through the spirit of prophecy. For God has predestined many things to come about in such a way that the saints obtain them through labor; therefore, whoever neglects to labor will not attain them.

Let us see by what powerful and religious sacraments [Col. 0806A] he always binds them. “I beseech you,” he says, “through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the charity of the Holy Spirit, that you assist me in your prayers to God, that I may be delivered from the unbelievers who are in Judea.” Yet he did not deserve to suffer from unbelievers, for Christ’s sake, those things which pertain to the glory of his apostleship; rather, he fears being hindered, lest, detained longer by obstacles, he either render less pleasing service to the saints or his desire to visit the Romans be delayed longer.

For if he accomplishes these things thus, then rejoicing in affairs well conducted, he will quickly come to them through God’s will and be refreshed with them—that is, rest in their charity and good works. For the Apostle has refreshment where the Holy Spirit rests.

[Col. 0806B]

> “Now may the God of peace be with you all. Amen.”

“I desire,” he says, “to come quickly. But whether I come quickly or late, may the God of peace be with you all. Amen”—may he preserve you all in peace, that is, Christ, who promised that he would be with his own until the end of the age. He fittingly ends with peace, having recalled the two peoples to concord, showing that the God of peace dwells only among the peaceful.

From this point he begins to set before them many persons whom the Romans ought to trust. For he adds:

## Chapter XVI

> “I commend to you our sister Phoebe, who is in the ministry of the church at Cenchreae, that you may receive her worthily in the Lord, as saints ought, [Col. 0806C] and assist her in whatever matter she may need from you. For she herself has also assisted many, including me.”

Cenchreae is said to be a place near Corinth, namely, the port of Corinth. Phoebe was a woman both very noble and very wealthy, who supported the church at Cenchreae from her own resources. At that time she had gone to Rome on some business, and therefore the Apostle commends her to the Romans, that they may receive her worthily as saints ought to be received. Perhaps he also sent this epistle through her.

This passage also teaches, by apostolic authority, that women are appointed to ministry in the Church. The Apostle now commends Phoebe, who held this position, with great praise, enumerating [Col. 0806D] her distinguished deeds and saying that she assisted everyone and was present in their needs to such an extent that she also attended upon me myself in my apostolic necessities with devotion of mind. He also shows that those who devote themselves to good work in the churches ought to receive from the brethren recompense and honor, so that in whatever need there may be—whether spiritual or material services—they may be helped and held in honor.

> “Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ, who laid down their own necks for my life, to whom not I alone give thanks, but also all the churches of the Gentiles, and greet their household church.”

Prisca, who in the Acts of the Apostles is called Priscilla [Col. 0807A], was the wife of Aquila. For Luke says of them: “Paul, having departed from Athens, came to Corinth” (Acts 18). And he found a certain Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently come from Italy, and Priscilla his wife, because Claudius had ordered all Jews to leave Rome; and he came to them. And because he was of the same trade, he stayed with them and worked. For they were of the trade of tent-making, that is, makers of tents, namely leatherworkers.

It is believed that, because at that time the Jews had come to Corinth after being expelled from the city by Caesar’s decree, they had returned to Rome when the ruler’s severity was again softened, at the time when Paul sent this epistle. Thus they were his fellow workers in Christ—that is, in Christ’s preaching—because they believed rightly and made themselves companions in apostolic labor, so that they too might exhort others to the right faith. Indeed, although Apollos was trained in the Scriptures, he was nevertheless more diligently instructed by them in the way of the Lord.

It is also apparent that, when Paul was in danger from Jewish plots, they exposed themselves so that he might escape freely. He himself does not pass over this praise of them in silence, but commends it as worthy of admiration to all the churches. “They laid down their own necks for my life,” he says, “to whom not I alone give thanks, but also all the churches of the Gentiles.” Rightly did the churches of the Gentiles give thanks to those who offered themselves to death so that the teacher of the Gentiles might escape freely and go forth to the work of preaching. Therefore the Romans ought to obey them, because they returned to Rome [Col. 0807C] to exhort and strengthen them. “Greet these,” he says, “and their household church,” that is, their family, because it imitates their holiness.

> “Greet Epaenetus, beloved to me, who is the firstfruits of the church of Asia in Christ Jesus.”

This man is understood to have been the first of all from Asia to believe and to have come to Rome for the strengthening of the Romans. Thus the others also whom the Apostle greets are understood to have come there for the edification of the brethren.

> “Greet Mary, who labored much among you.”

She too undertook no small but a great and considerable labor for the benefit of the Church.

> “Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and fellow captives [Col. 0807D], who are distinguished among the apostles, and who were in Christ Jesus before me.”

These were Paul’s kinsfolk according to the flesh and endured imprisonment with him on account of the faith. It may perhaps also be understood of them that they were among the seventy-two disciples of the Lord, who are rightly called apostles. Therefore they are called distinguished among the apostles—that is, among those seventy-two—who were also in Christ before Paul, that is, in faith in Christ. Or the two themselves were in Christ before him because they followed the earlier apostles; and therefore they are called distinguished among the apostles, that is, among the preachers who were disciples of the apostles.

> “Greet Ampliatus, most beloved to me in the Lord.”

[Col. 0808A] Although nothing outstanding beyond the others appears to be ascribed to this man, nevertheless the very fact that he is most beloved to the Apostle shows him to be praiseworthy and worthy of greeting.

> “Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ Jesus, and Stachys, my beloved.”

He joins these too with the others as worthy of greeting, but gives Urbanus precedence in praise. For he calls the former a fellow worker of the apostles in Christ, that is, a participant in apostolic work; but Stachys his beloved, that is, his particular friend, though not a fellow worker.

> “Greet Apelles, approved in Christ.”

Although this man was neither a particular friend of the Apostle nor a participant in apostolic work, he was nevertheless found faithful in Christ through trials. For he is understood to have passed through many tribulations patiently and courageously endured, and therefore to be pronounced approved by the Apostle, in accordance with what he said above: “Tribulation produces patience, and patience testing” (Rom. 5; Jas. 1).

> “Greet those who are from the household of Aristobulus.”

[Col. 0808B] Aristobulus is understood to have been a gatherer of brethren in Christ. The Apostle approves his deed in such a way that he marks those whom he gathered as worthy of his greeting.

> “Greet Herodion, my kinsman.”

This man is called only the Apostle’s kinsman. No merit of his is clearly shown, except that he is declared to have been devout in Christ because the Apostle greets him.

> “Greet those from the household of Narcissus who are in Christ.”

[Col. 0808C] Narcissus is said to have been a presbyter who, while traveling, strengthened the brethren by exhortations. Since he was not present then, the Apostle greets his people. But because he did not know the merits of all of them, he distinguishes those who are in the Lord: that is, those worthy of my greeting because of the merit which they have in the Lord.

> “Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who labor in the Lord.”

Their labor was not undertaken for this world or present life, but for the hope which they had in the Lord. They are understood to have labored in the ministry of the saints.

> “Greet Persis, beloved, who has labored much in the Lord.”

[Col. 0808D] She is greatly preferred to those two, because she is called beloved and is affirmed not only to have labored, but to have labored much in the Lord.

> “Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine.”

I believe that the Apostle knew this man to be among the number—not of the many who are called, but of the few who are chosen (Matt. 20). Or “chosen” means advanced to administer ecclesiastical affairs, so that he presided in some rank of honor. His mother too had such merit that the Apostle even called her his own mother and shared with him [Col. 0809A] a mother’s affection, as John did with Christ (John 19). For the same woman was Rufus’s mother according to the flesh and Paul’s according to charity and beneficence. Or perhaps the Apostle’s natural mother was then living in Rome with this woman.

> “Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes, and the brothers who are with them.”

Those whom he names are understood to have lived together, been of one mind in Christian friendship, and been renowned in religion; and to have had with them other brethren who were not of such great merit or renown. I think that this Hermas was the author of that little book called *The Shepherd*.

> “Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister [Col. 0809B], and Olympias, and all the saints who are with them.”

These too were united together, and those mentioned by name are indicated to have been the greater persons. All those whom he has greeted thus far are understood to have been distinguished in faith and merits, so that the Romans ought rightly to honor them and trust their words.

> “Greet one another with a holy kiss.”

Greet one another with a kiss that is not feigned, deceitful, or lustful, but holy, devout, and chaste. “With a holy kiss,” that is, greet one another in Christ’s peace, so that your kisses may not be pretended or carnal but devout. From this command and others like it, the Church’s custom has been handed down that after prayer the brethren receive one another with a kiss.

[Col. 0809C]

> “All the churches of Christ greet you.”
