By this statement it is understood that churches may be called churches which are not Christ’s. Hence the Psalmist says: “I have hated the assembly of evildoers” (Ps. 25). He says that the churches in all those places greet the Romans, that they may grow in faith and devotion.

> “But I urge you, brothers, to watch those who cause dissensions and stumbling-blocks contrary to the teaching which you have learned, and turn away from them. For such people do not serve Christ the Lord, but their own belly [Phil. 3], and through smooth words and blessings deceive the hearts of the innocent.”

Now the Apostle warns them above all things to beware of pseudo-apostles. As though he said: “Greet and imitate those whom I have mentioned; but mark and avoid these. I commanded you to greet the former, but I ask you to beware of the latter.”

“I urge you,” O brothers, children of the mother Church, “to watch”—that is, distinguish and mark—“those who cause dissensions,” that is, discords of minds and judgments, “and stumbling-blocks,” that is, occasions by which brethren offend one another, so that one may offend another. Or “stumbling-blocks” means precipices of sins prepared to make the unwary fall into works of wickedness.

[Col. 0809D] They do these things contrary to the teaching which you learned from good preachers, because such works are transgressions of the holy teaching you have received. Therefore watch them and turn away from them. Why? Because people of this kind, in the deceitful preaching they conduct, do not serve Christ but their own belly, since they preach not from love for their hearers [Col. 0810A], but with the aim of receiving food from them; and by smooth words, with which they sweetly pour in the poison of their wickedness, and by deceitful blessings, they deceive the hearts of the innocent.

For it is characteristic of heretics and of those who deceive hearers to speak sweetly to them. Flattery is always treacherous, crafty, and pleasing; and philosophers aptly define the flatterer as a pleasing enemy. Their smooth words may also be understood as minimizations of sins, when they say that these things are not serious, give foolish people assurance in sinning, promise them impunity from God’s mercy, and frequently bless them in order to appear holy to them. Thus they deceive—that is, lead away from the path of uprightness—the hearts of the innocent, that is, of the simple who do not know how to beware [Col. 0810B].

For the Apostle commands not only the Romans then living in the flesh, but still more all believers everywhere until the end of the age, diligently to consider and discern who generate dissensions and stumbling-blocks in the churches. For he says that stirring up dissensions and stumbling-blocks is contrary to Christ’s teaching which we have learned. Therefore whoever provokes conflicts, whoever serves quarrels, whoever excites disputes and pursues contentious strife, should be alien to us and not received among us at all. For those who are such do not serve Christ the Lord, who is our peace, but rather serve their belly.

Why are quarrels and disputes raised in churches? The Holy Spirit now indicates it through the Apostle: “For the sake of the belly,” he says—that is, for gain and greed [Col. 0810C]. Hence some also go about houses, speaking ingratiatingly with every deceit of flattery, not in order to build souls up to virtues through God’s word, but to destroy them through flatteries and smooth words, even exhorting them to advance in vices by praising and blessing things worthy of correction.

> “For your obedience has been made known in every place. Therefore I rejoice in you, but I want you to be wise in what is good and simple in what is evil” (Matt. 10).

Therefore, he says, I warn you to avoid deceivers, because not only your faith but also your obedience has been heard of everywhere, since you are at the head of the world; and thus [Col. 0810D] by your example others might already be corrupted, if you were led astray. Or: I ask you to avoid them because you obey readily, as has already been spread abroad everywhere. He subtly does not praise their undiscriminating and easy obedience in every respect, but says that it is widely known. And lest he should make them disobedient again by correcting this more openly, he added: “Therefore I rejoice in you,” as though to say: You obey readily, and this is good; and I rejoice in this, because you obey in this way. Yet I want you to be wise in good and simple in evil—that is, I want you to be wise in discerning good, and to be without any share in evil, so that you may wisely discern to whom you ought to offer the good of obedience, lest, if you heedlessly obey perverse persons, the evil of duplicity mingle itself with your good. For what you do will not be simple but double [Col. 0811A], if it is good on account of obedience and evil on account of indiscretion. Be simple in evil, that is, be without any folding—without any admixture or association—lest some evil join itself to your good. Be wise also in good, so that you may do good wisely and cautiously. For you ought to join prudence to simplicity, so that you may possess the security of simplicity without neglecting the circumspection of prudence. For simplicity also signifies a certain ignorance: “be simple in evil,” that is, unknowing—namely, not knowing evil by doing it.

> “But may the God of peace crush Satan under your feet swiftly.”

I want you to be wise in guarding against evil. [Col. 0811B] But may the God of peace, its giver and lover, swiftly crush Satan—that is, everyone who opposes you on God’s way. For *Satan* is interpreted “adversary.” By this name the ancient enemy is denoted, or any perverse person who devises opposition against the saints as they press on toward God. But may the God of peace swiftly crush him beneath their feet, so that the suggestion of the ancient adversary, as soon as it assails their minds, may be trampled down, crushed, and reduced to nothing; and so that every false preacher, or anyone who destroys peace, may swiftly be crushed or removed from the world. The God of peace crushed Satan beneath the feet of the Church because, converting to faith his members through whom he persecuted the Church, he subjected them to the Church itself.

> “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. [Col. 0811C] Amen.”

That Satan may be crushed, may Christ’s grace be with you, guarding and helping you.

> “Timothy, my fellow worker, greets you, and Lucius and Jason and Sosipater, my kinsmen. I, Tertius, who wrote this letter in the Lord, greet you.”

Timothy was a companion in the Apostle’s labors. For a long time he went with him to preach, and at length, having been made bishop by him, he governed the Church with great diligence. But it is written concerning Lucius that in the church at Antioch there were prophets and teachers, among whom were Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, and Lucius of Cyrene. [Col. 0811D] Jason, however, is the Thessalonian mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts XIII, XX, XXIV), and Sosipater the Berean. “These,” he says, “greet you”—as though to say: You are their concern. And I who wrote the letter greet you in the Lord.

*Tertius* is a name, not a number, so that Timothy, who is designated as the special helper, may be understood as first; then Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, taken as though one, as second; and thus the writer of the letter as third. Or he is third after Jason and Sosipater—that is, either the writer or the Apostle himself is to be understood; or, as others have thought, the Apostle’s secretary. Yet it is better that *Tertius* be understood as a proper name, because *Tertius* means “one who joins,” that is, one who attaches himself.

> “Gaius, my host, and the whole [Col. 0812A] Church greet you. Erastus, the city treasurer, greets you, and Quartus the brother.”

From these words it appears that the letter was written from Corinth. For concerning this Gaius he says to the Corinthians: “I give thanks to my God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius” (1 Cor. I). And concerning Erastus he writes to Timothy: “Erastus remained at Corinth” (2 Tim. IV). Gaius appears to be indicated as hospitable, in that he received not only Paul and each individual arriving in Corinth into his lodging, but also provided his house as a meeting-place for the whole Church. [Col. 0812B] For this is plainly what the Apostle seems to imply when, after saying, “Gaius my host greets you,” he immediately adds, “and the whole Church”: namely, that Corinthian Church which met at Gaius’s house. John also writes to a certain Gaius (3 John I), perhaps this very man, praising him because he ministered to the brethren.

Erastus, however, is called *arcarius*, “treasurer,” from the treasury, because he was a city administrator, as it were a curator, governing the city at justice’s direction, especially in regulating prices. It is written to the Romans, to the praise of the Corinthian Church, concerning this man, that he who was the city’s chief was not ashamed to believe in Christ crucified and to send greetings to those who believed in him. The Apostle names all these men individually in his greeting to the Romans, so that they might know what kind of—and how great—men rejoiced with them in their good beginning.

> “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.”

[Col. 0812C] So many and such great persons send you greetings; but may Christ’s grace remain with you. He said this a little earlier, but through the excess of ardent love he repeats what he earnestly desires.

> “Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my Gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery kept silent through eternal ages, but now disclosed through the writings of the prophets, according to the command of the eternal God, made known among all nations for the obedience of faith—to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.”

I have thus instructed and warned you in this letter; but [Col. 0812D] to him who is able to strengthen you—to the only wise God—be honor and glory for ages of ages. He gives glory to God, from whom are all things, that he may deign, because he is able, to complete the Romans’ undertaking by strengthening their souls in faith and charity; in this the summary of the letter is indicated.

And glory be to him who is able to strengthen you according to my Gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ: that is, who can bring you to as great a perfection as I proclaim in the Gospel, and as Christ preached and established by preaching. This Gospel and preaching occur according to the revelation of the mystery—that is, according to the disclosure from God’s hidden counsel of the very mystery of Christ’s incarnation; the mystery, I say, kept silent through eternal ages, that is, through the periods before [Col. 0813A] the foundation of the world, because God alone knew that the Father’s only-begotten Son would assume humanity for human salvation.

Yet after the world had already been made, this mystery of Christ’s incarnation and humanity’s restoration remained silent; for, although it was in some measure known to the ancient fathers, it was not fully known to any of them. It has now been disclosed through the writings of the prophets—that is, it was revealed by Christ’s coming, after he had opened the prophetic writings, which bear testimony to this preaching. It was disclosed according to the command of the eternal God, that is, according to what God commanded, who had ordained this from eternity. And it was disclosed for the obedience of faith among all nations—that is, it is now manifest among all peoples so that all may obey [Col. 0813B] faith by doing good works.

I mean the mystery formerly kept silent from others but known to the only wise God. For, even if it has now been revealed to human beings, it is nevertheless known to God alone, who alone knows why it was done in this way. In this the Apostle rebukes those inquisitors who ask why God delayed so long and why he permitted so many nations to perish. Now God alone is wise—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—because the Trinity is one God. He is rightly called alone wise because he alone is wise according to his own wisdom and substance, not according to an accidental or supervening participation in wisdom, as every rational creature is wise. The Trinity, I say, is the only wise God, who neither ever could have been unwise nor can be, not a participant in wisdom through grace [Col. 0813C] but wise by the immutability of nature.

Therefore to the only wise God be glory through Christ Jesus—that is, clear knowledge with praise—because God the Trinity has become known to the nations. This is through Jesus Christ because, [Col. 0814A] to say nothing of other things, he himself commanded all nations to be baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. XXVIII; Mark XVI), where the glory of this indivisible Trinity is especially commended.

The addition of “to whom,” so that it is said “to whom be glory,” when it would have sufficed to say “to him be glory,” indicates an unusual construction in our language; it does not suggest a meaning for us to seek or about which to be uncertain. What is lost in sense if we say, “and glory to whom through Jesus Christ be glory”? For “to him, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory” is the same as “to whom, through Jesus Christ, be glory.” But one order of words is unusual and the other customary. Or it was said, “To him be glory, to whom through Jesus Christ be glory,” or, “To him be glory through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory,” so that we might understand that he who is always glorious [Col. 0814B] in himself is glorified among human beings through Christ’s incarnation and resurrection.

Or: “to him who is able to strengthen you,” that is, to the Trinity, be glory through Jesus Christ; and to Jesus Christ himself, even according to his humanity, belong honor and glory, as is sung in the Psalm: “You crowned him with glory and honor” (Ps. VIII). The phrase appended, “for ages of ages,” is the custom of divine Scripture, by which it signifies immeasurable duration. Or “for ages of ages” means “into eternal ages,” which are more excellent than passing ages, just as the Holy of Holies and the Song of Songs are more excellent than other holy things and songs; or as the King of kings and Lord of lords is more excellent than other kings and lords.

But *Amen*, which is interpreted [Col. 0814C] “truly” or “faithfully,” he placed at the end as a confirmation of all that has been written above, signifying in the native speech of the Hebrews that what is written is true and trustworthy.

# ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 0813]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0813D]

Corinth is a metropolitan city, the capital of Achaia and the glory of Greece. When Paul came to it, he converted many of its citizens to the faith. There too the Lord said to him by a vision at night: “Do not fear, but speak and do not be silent. For I am with you, and no one shall attack you to harm you, because I have a great people in this city.” He therefore remained a year and six months, teaching among them the word of the Lord.

After his departure, some of them were subverted by false apostles, some also by followers of worldly eloquence, while others were corrupted by Jewish traditions. Some of them also, considering the rank of persons in baptism, thought that they had received more grace and remission of sins if they had been baptized by worthier and holier men. By this they wished to prefer themselves to others who had not had such worthy baptizers. And there were among them many [Col. 0814D] grave schisms and vices. From all these the Apostle intends to correct them and to teach them the rule of Christian conduct, writing from Ephesus.

This letter is rightly placed after that to the Romans, although it was written before it, because whoever has already been instructed in faith—the subject treated with the Romans—ought afterward to be corrected from creeping vices and more fully formed in virtues, just as the Corinthians are now corrected and instructed. It is also placed after that letter because it has a certain affinity with it in subject matter. For just as the Romans gloried in the merits of their ancestors and attributed their salvation not to grace but, in some cases, to observances of the law and, in others, to ability of intellect and freedom of choice, so these people gloried in the holiness of their baptizers and attributed to them whatever good they possessed, wishing to prefer some persons over others. But let us come to the text.

# CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0815A]

> “Paul, called an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and Sosthenes the brother, to the Church of God which is at Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called saints, together with all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place, theirs and ours: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

*Paul* means “wonderful.” And indeed he was a wonderful teacher, with whom none can be compared in knowledge; a wonderful worker, who labored more than all others. By this name, therefore, he already renders his hearers astonished and restrains them by the authority of so great a name, lest they dare to contradict the words that follow or resist in disobedience. He also says that he was called, so that he may appear to possess greater [Col. 0815B] authority, because, unlike the others, he was called to faith not by human beings but by Christ himself from heaven (Acts IX). He is also an apostle—that is, one sent—of Jesus Christ, from whom he heard: “Go; I will send you far away to the Gentiles” (Acts XXII).

Paul is an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God—that is, sent by Christ to the Gentiles through the Father’s will. By this he also touches those whom neither Christ had sent nor who preached by God’s will. Paul, such and so great a man, writes to the Corinthians, along with Sosthenes the brother. He joins this man also to confirm all that he writes, because he held great authority among them, having been ruler of the synagogue there and, after conversion to faith, having bravely endured many persecutions from the Jews before the tribunal [Col. 0815C] of Gallio the proconsul (Acts XVIII).

Paul and Sosthenes write to the Church, not of baptizers, but of God, which is at Corinth. He writes to the Church because rulers had not yet been appointed for the individual churches. Paul writes to God’s Church, namely to those sanctified—that is, regenerated in baptism—in Christ Jesus, that is, in the representation of the death and resurrection of Christ Jesus. Sanctified in Christ, not in Peter or Paul or any other baptizer, because Christ works this sanctification equally through all his ministers; therefore no one should glory in the merits of his baptizer. He said that he wrote to the Church and added “sanctified in Christ,” to show that the whole Church had been sanctified in Christ, though some of them afterward began to live badly.

[Col. 0815D] He also writes to those called by evangelical preaching and made holy by their good conduct. Or “called saints” means called in order to be saints: that is, so that they may not depart from the rule of holiness by falling into some error or evil action. Or it may mean divinely called from eternity—that is, predestined before the foundation of the world—and holy in the time of their conduct.

Paul writes to these together with all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place, theirs and ours: that is, he joins Gentiles to Jews converted to the faith, because salvation is from the Jews (John IV), so that in every place, both where Gentiles call upon the Lord’s name and where such Jews are found, all alike may be one. Or rather, he writes to the Corinthians together with all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0816A] in every place belonging to the Corinthians—that is, subject to them: with all the suffragans of Corinth, with all who are subject to Corinth as a metropolitan city. He writes with all who call upon God in every place belonging to the Corinthians—that is, serving them—and ours, that is, belonging equally to us as to them. For those in places subject to Corinth belong to our apostolate, and therefore we write to them as to the Corinthians.

Now one calls upon God who seeks from him in prayer nothing other than God himself. For whoever calls upon God in order to become rich does not call upon God, but upon that thing which he wants [Col. 0816B] to come to himself. For what you want to come to you, that is what you invoke. If, however, you invoked God, he himself would come to you, and you would possess him as your riches. Therefore those who call upon God for worldly advantages or earthly prosperity do not call upon God. But those call upon God, those call upon the Lord’s name, who seek from him nothing except himself, who devoutly ask him to deign to come into them, dwell in them, and make them the temple of his glory. Such persons, wherever they may dwell, are rightly joined with those to whom the Apostle writes.

He greets them all together, saying: May grace be to you, by which your sins may be forgiven and your virtues preserved—grace for those who have fallen, that they may rise; grace for those standing, that they may remain. And may peace be to you, by which those made God’s enemies through sins may be reconciled to him [Col. 0816C], and by which those who have not departed from his love may cling steadfastly to him. This grace and peace be to you, not from your baptizers or other people, but from God our Father, who deigned to adopt us as sons, and from the Lord Jesus Christ—that is, Savior, King, and our Lord, who snatched us from Satan’s power and made us servants under his own dominion. For we are his servants, although his Father has adopted us as sons, because he is Son by nature and we by grace; he is Creator and we creatures; he is without sin and we have been freed from sin.

> “I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God which was given to you in Christ Jesus, because in everything you have been enriched in him, in every word and in all knowledge, just as the testimony of Christ [Col. 0816D] was confirmed among you, so that you lack no grace, while awaiting the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ, who will also confirm you blameless to the end, on the day of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. God is faithful [1 Thess. V], through whom you were called into fellowship with his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.”

Although this letter is written to the people of one city, because of the diversity among its inhabitants—saints and sinners—it now praises them, now corrects them, now teaches, now rebukes, so that each person may understand what is said for or against himself: when it praises them, the good may know that the words are directed to them; and when it rebukes, those who have acted badly may know that these things are said to them. See how he begins with the perfect, whom he follows with abundant [Col. 0817A] praise, so that afterward he may come to the weak, whom he is going to rebuke.

He first addresses the perfect, showing them worthy of commendation, so that those who have remained good until now may strive to become better, and the rest who have fallen into some error may be ashamed and endeavor to become like them. “I give thanks,” he says, “to my God always for you”: to God, who belongs to all, but who is mine by the privilege of holiness that he has granted me. I always give thanks for you because I know that whatever good you have was given to you by him, not by people. I give thanks for the grace of God given to you—that is, because of the grace which God granted you in Christ Jesus, not in Peter or Paul. Grace was given in Christ because God ordained that whoever believes in [Col. 0817B] Christ should be saved without works, through faith alone, and should freely receive remission of sins.

Nor had they received this only; many spiritual gifts had also been divinely granted to them. Truly great grace was given to you in Christ, because you were enriched in him in every spiritual gift, so that you abound in all spiritual riches. And he supplies certain parts of these riches: in every word, that is, in every kind of language, so that you can speak Greek, Latin, Hebrew, and every other language. Or “in every word” means in every manner of preaching: gently to the little ones, moderately to the intermediate, and perfectly to the perfect; and “in all knowledge” means understanding of the Scriptures according to the historical, mystical, and moral senses.

You were enriched in every word for preaching and in knowledge for understanding, just as the testimony of Christ—that is, what Christ testified concerning himself by dying and rising—was confirmed in you, that is, in your life and conduct. You are so enriched with every gift that you lack no grace of the Holy Spirit, because you possess prophecy, kinds of languages, the power of healings, and the other gifts of charisms. You lack nothing that it is necessary to possess; for although you do not have everything that the apostles have, you nevertheless have everything necessary for you to have. You are so filled that you lack nothing—you, I say, who await, that is, eagerly expect and worthily prepare to receive, the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ, [Col. 0817D] when he will be revealed coming in flaming fire for judgment and will appear to all.

The ungodly fear this revelation and do not want it to come. But the godly, who on account of the merit of their good conduct hope to reign with Christ, desire with all their longing that he may be revealed, because they hope, at his revelation, to attain the vision of his glory. And therefore, persevering tirelessly in good works, they await it; and they keep watch with cautious circumspection lest, when he comes, they be found blameworthy in any respect. Thus you await the revelation of the Lord, in which he will make himself manifest in judgment to good and evil alike. By the help of his grace he will also ensure that you do not fail in this expectation, because he will strengthen you in virtues and good works until the end—that is, until the death of each [Col. 0818A] of you.

He will strengthen you, I say, in good things, without blame—that is, without any grave sin of mind or flesh. For some await the Lord’s revelation as though secure concerning their righteousness, and yet remain in grave sins: envy, detraction, hatred, dissension, and things like these. But you will be preserved by God’s grace free from these and such things on the day of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, so that on that day you may be found liable to no crime. For as each person dies, so he is found on that day. And the day of death is also for each person the day of the Lord’s coming, as he himself declares when he says: “Watch, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come” (Matt. XXIV).

The Apostle, confidently encouraged by hope concerning these people, is certain that they will remain unviolated until [Col. 0818B] the last day. For those who could not be changed amid so many dangers to their convictions and disturbances from conflicting influences undoubtedly show that they will remain in their goodness. While the Apostle praises them, he invites the others who had been corrupted by the error of false apostles. For while he proclaims these persons’ faith and holiness, he calls the others to repentance.

I said that he will confirm you to the end. And he truly will confirm you, because God is faithful, that is, true in his promises, and will faithfully render whatever he has promised. He promised eternal salvation and blessed life with the angels without end; an unfading inheritance, everlasting glory, the sweetness of his countenance, the house of his sanctification in heaven, and resurrection from the dead, where thereafter there will be no fear of dying (1 Pet. I). He has promised such things, and in giving them he will be faithful, because without deceit he will give them to those to whom he promised them. God is faithful, through whom you were called, because he who called you when you had turned away will now more readily strengthen you.

You were called into fellowship not only with the apostles or angels, but also with his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, so that you may share in the inheritance and glory possessed by his Son. For this is what he granted you to be when you believed: because you believed Christ to be the Son of God, you too might become sons of God, remaining in the same dignity in which Christ remains. For fellowship is a fellowship of brotherhood. You have become his brothers and companions, whom you have firmly believed to be God’s Son.

Thus far the preface with praise. [Col. 0818D] From here he proceeds to the cause of dissension, adding:

> “But I beseech you, brothers, through the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing, and that there be no schisms among you, but that you be perfected in the same mind and in the same knowledge. For it has been reported to me about you, my brothers, by those of Chloe, that there are contentions among you. What I mean is that each of you says: ‘I indeed am of Paul’; ‘but I am of Apollos’; ‘but I am of Cephas’; ‘but I am of Christ.’ Is Christ divided?”

If one does not carefully consider how something is said and to whom it is said, there is great danger. Modest minds, if perhaps they have committed faults, ought to be rebuked gently; for if they are [Col. 0819A] reproved too harshly, they are broken rather than instructed. This the Apostle now shows well. Knowing that the Corinthians were divided into schism through love of persons, and having regard for their modesty, he began his address to them with thanksgiving and praise. Those whom he had praised for every word and all knowledge, and of whom he had said that they lacked no grace, he gradually addresses and gently comes to rebuke, reproving them for being divided against themselves. And after first recounting their health, he afterward exposed their wounds.

For a skilled physician, seeing that a wound must be cut but perceiving that the patient is fearful, feels it for a long time and then strikes suddenly. First he lays on the gentle hand of praise, and afterward drives in the iron of rebuke. Unless modest minds are reproved by such gentling—[Col. 0819B] so that from other matters they hear something from which to take consolation—they immediately fall into despair through rebuke. The Apostle was not lying when he first said that they lacked nothing in every grace, although he would afterward say that they lacked unity. For there were among them some filled with every grace, and some divided in partisan favoritism. Therefore, as has been said, he began with the praises of the perfect so that by a restrained attack he might come to the rebuke of the weak.

In this too he derived a practice for healing the heart from bodily medicine. For when a physician sees that a wound must be struck, he first feels the healthy limbs around it, so that afterward he may gently come by touch to the wounded parts. Thus, when Paul praised the perfect among the Corinthians [Col. 0819C], he touched the healthy limbs near the wound; but when he reproved the weak for division, he struck the wound in the body. But let us now consider his words.

He seems to say: For the perfect who have remained in good, I give thanks; but you, brothers, who have been led astray and glory in human merits, I beseech through the name of our Lord Jesus Christ—who alone redeemed you and in whose name you were baptized—that you all say the same thing. Namely, that all of you may say with one mouth the same thing said by those whom I praised; and that there be no schisms among you—that is, among you or in your hearts—no divisions. These schisms are understood as divisions in the faith of certain persons, while they held differing opinions. For whereas all ought to [Col. 0819D] say that they belong to Christ, one said, “I am of Paul,” another, “I am of Peter.”

Let there be no schisms among you, but be perfected in the same mind—that is, in the same will in which are those whose praise I previously set forth—and in the same knowledge, that is, in the same understanding of the Scriptures in which they are. Or, “say the same thing” means: let all alike profess the one catholic faith; and let there be no schisms among us, that is, divisions of minds or words, but be perfected in the same mind which I handed down to you concerning Christ, so that you may all think perfectly that glory is to be given to him alone, not to human beings; and in the same knowledge which I handed down to you concerning Christ, so that you may know perfectly that you were redeemed by his blood and sanctified through baptism in his name.

*Mind* may refer to Christ’s [Col. 0820A] divinity and *knowledge* to his humanity, so that you may all firmly hold the same mind and understanding concerning his divinity and the same knowledge concerning his humanity, and thus all together believe the same concerning his divinity and humanity. I say these things because it was reported to me about you by letter, O my brothers, by those of Chloe—that is, those in the place so called—that there are contentions among you. Although they had turned away, the Apostle nevertheless calls them brothers, so that by this they might not dissent from him, to whom the assembly of brothers dwelling at Chloe’s had reported that there were contentions among them, by which the diversity of their thinking concerning the Lord’s teaching was made manifest.

Those brothers reported your contentions to me. Nor do I know those alone; I also know the very words [Col. 0820B] that you say. This, then, is what I mean: each of you says—that is, there is none of you who does not say one of the things which I set below. For one indeed says, “I am of Paul”; another, “I am of Apollos,” that is, a son of a most learned teacher; another, “I am of Cephas,” that is, Peter; and another, who alone is wise, says, “I am of Christ.” Thus you are divided into parties, as though some of you were Paulinians, others Apollonians, others Petrinians, and others Christians. And thus, according to you, Christ is divided. As if it were said: You make many Christs—that is, many givers of graces.

Or, he who works the same in all is divided when he is believed to work more grace in one person and less in another. Or Christ is divided—that is, cut off and separated from you, though he was your head—because you withdrew yourselves from him when you began to ascribe the cause of your salvation to human [Col. 0820C] merits. The Apostle showed the error, but did not disclose the names of its authors. For they did not remain in one place but traveled about to overthrow the simple. Those whom he named were undoubtedly good teachers; but under their appearance he attacks false apostles. For if he forbids glorying in these men, how much more in evil teachers, whose perverse doctrine he indicates in what follows?

Nevertheless, among them he identifies those who persevered, who said that they belonged to Christ and not to a human being—the persons he praised above—and invites the others to imitate them. He called Christ divided because human beings apportioned his glory to themselves, as heretics did who did not shrink from calling themselves Photinians, Arians, or [Col. 0820D] Manichaeans. The Corinthians too had begun to submit to the different names of heretics, appearing to venerate human beings in Christ’s place. Those who receive divergent beliefs concerning Christ divide Christ. One accepts Christ as merely a human being; another professes him as pure God without a body. One says that Christ was foretold through the prophets; another denies that the prophets spoke of Christ. Therefore, since Christ is one, God and human being, these persons divide Christ when one claims one thing about him and another something else.

> “Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul? I give thanks to my God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, lest anyone should say that you were baptized in my name. But I also baptized the household of Stephanas. [Col. 0821A] Beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.”

You ought not to say, “I belong to Paul,” for was Paul crucified for you, so as to redeem you by his blood and be the author of salvation? Or were you baptized in Paul’s name, so that the invocation of Paul’s name might cleanse you from sins in baptism? By no means: Christ, the just, bore the cross for you, the unjust; and you received baptism not in Paul’s name but in Christ’s. The holy Apostle, modestly and humbly zealous for the Church, yet for the bridegroom rather than himself, and abhorring those who wished to say, “I belong to Paul,” “I to Apollos,” “I to Cephas,” took up his own person rather than trample upon and despise others, so that he might glorify Christ. He repels them from himself only in order to send them to Christ. [Col. 0821B] He does not wish the bride to love him instead of the bridegroom. For this reason he preferred to disparage himself in commending Christ, lest, if he disparaged others by name, he might seem to reject their persons in order to commend his own.

If Christ died for you and you received the sanctification of baptism in his name, how do you now, to his injury, ascribe his grace and benefit to any human being? Since you glory in those who baptize, I give thanks to my God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, who are not party to your contention—not because baptizing is evil, but lest anyone say that you were baptized in my name, and glory in this all the more. Not only were you not baptized in my name, but not even through my ministry; and [Col. 0821C] for this I give thanks to my God, who did not will that I should be an occasion of this error. I baptized only Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, and Gaius, who were persons of standing and among the first to believe. They ascribed the grace of baptism to no human being, but to Christ alone; and they are understood to be among those praised above. Nor did I baptize only these: I also baptized the household of Stephanas—that is, the family of that noble matron—of whom it is said near the end of this epistle that they are the firstfruits of Achaia and devoted themselves to the service of the saints. Of these, he says, I am certain that I baptized them; but apart from this, I do not know whether I baptized any other among you. By this he shows that he is not the Savior. For if he saved some by justifying them himself, he would not be unaware of them.

[Col. 0821D] He says that he baptized certain people, but not in the manner in which he is accustomed to baptize, of whom it was said: “This is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John 1). Paul baptized as a minister, not as the power itself. Christ, however, baptized as power. He could have given this power to a servant, but he did not will to do so. For if he had given this power to servants—that is, if what belonged to the Lord had belonged to them—there would be as many baptisms as servants. Just as one says “the baptism of John,” so one would say “the baptism of Peter,” “the baptism of Paul,” “the baptism of James,” and of the others. Therefore, lest there be said to be as many baptisms as there were servants baptizing with power received from the Lord, the Lord retained for himself the power of baptizing and gave the ministry to servants, so that the hope of those baptized might rest in him [Col. 0822A] by whom they knew themselves to have been baptized.

Therefore he did not wish a servant to place hope in a servant. And so he retained this power for himself alone. If he had wished, he could have given it either to one or to each of his servants, so that the baptism of a servant might have as great an efficacy as the baptism given by the Lord; but he did not will this. Accordingly, it makes no difference whether the one entrusted with the ministry of baptizing is good or bad: whoever the minister may be, Christ is the Lord who baptizes. For this reason baptism administered through a contemptible man has as much efficacy as baptism administered through an apostle.

> “For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the Gospel—not in wisdom of speech, lest the cross of Christ be emptied. For the word of the cross is indeed foolishness to those who are perishing, but to those who are being saved—that is, to us—it is the power of God. For it is written: ‘I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the prudence of the prudent’ (Isa. 29; above, ch. 8). Where is the wise man? Where the scribe? Where the investigator of this age? (Isa. 33). Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe.”

For this reason I baptized so few: I was not sent for this. Christ, whose minister I am, did not send me to baptize, but to preach the Gospel—that is, to proclaim. For preaching the Gospel is greater than baptizing, since not everyone who baptizes is capable of preaching the Gospel. Since even lesser persons can baptize, [Col. 0822C] though they do not possess the wisdom and power of preaching, I was not sent to baptize, lest I be hindered from preaching; rather, I was sent to scatter the seeds of the Gospel. By this statement those are humbled to whom the Corinthians attributed great importance because they had been baptized by them, since it becomes known that baptizing is not a great matter.

I was sent to preach the Gospel, and this not in wisdom of speech, because Christian preaching does not require the pomp and ornament of eloquence. Therefore fishermen, unlearned men, were chosen to preach the Gospel, so that the truth of the doctrine itself might commend itself through attested power, lest it seem acceptable through human cunning and the craft of human wisdom rather than through truth—as are disciplines devised by men, in which not reason, not power, but [Col. 0822D] arrangement of words is sought. Thus, whoever endeavors to adorn Christ’s faith with words seeks his own glory, because he obscures it with the brilliance of words, so that not it but he may be praised.

Likewise the false apostles, lest they appear foolish to the wise of the world, preached Christ in human wisdom, avoiding those things which the world judges foolish in us. Thus they taught neither that the Son of God was incarnate and born of a virgin nor that men are saved by his death; nor did they proclaim the future resurrection of our flesh, because worldly wisdom judges these things foolish. For physical wisdom maintains that God cannot become human; that the invisible cannot become visible; that the immortal cannot become mortal; that a virgin cannot conceive and give birth; that the author of life cannot die; [Col. 0823A] that the death of one cannot give life to many; that one dead cannot rise when the tomb has been opened; and that a true human body cannot enter a house through closed doors. Yet we preach all these things concerning Christ.

Therefore the Apostle does not preach in the wisdom of men, which is wisdom of speech—that is, ornate discourse according to dialectic and rhetoric. “I was not sent,” he says, “to preach the Gospel in wisdom of speech,” that is, to compel hearers to faith by argument through human cleverness and artfully arranged words, but to announce the truth simply to all. Therefore I do not preach in human wisdom of speech, lest the cross of Christ be emptied—that is, lest Christ’s passion be thought empty and idle, rather than full of humanity’s redemption and salvation. For if natural capacity through free will suffices for itself, as the wise men of the age say, both to know how one ought to live and to live well, then Christ died gratuitously and his cross is devoid of all benefit. But it is impossible that his cross should be empty and superfluous, because human salvation could come about only through that cross. Therefore worldly wisdom of speech, which did not know this, is foolish.

The cross would truly be emptied by wisdom of speech, because the word of the cross—that is, the preaching of Christ crucified—seems to be foolishness to those who are perishing, that is, to the wise of the world, whose wisdom perishes and is shown to be false. They themselves are thereby to be condemned, because they do not establish the hope of their salvation in the cross of Christ. For it seems foolish to them to say that the Son of God was crucified; [Col. 0823C] and therefore they are in perdition, because they have not been rescued from the death of hell. To unbelievers and those who perish it is foolishness; but to those who are being saved—that is, to us who believe—the cross itself is the power of God. For we believe that Christ’s cross is not weakness but power, understanding that death was conquered on the cross. Those who bear its sign are strong and are saved, because death cannot hold them.

Nothing is said in the word of Christ’s cross in which Christ’s power and strength do not appear, because by dying he conquered death, the devil, hell, and sin; he set humanity free; he quenched with his blood, for believers, the fire at the gate of paradise; he overcame all the kingdoms of the world; and he opened the kingdom of heaven. Therefore there is no power so great as the power [Col. 0823D] in all that is said concerning Christ crucified. I do not preach in wisdom of speech lest the cross be emptied in this way; for it would be emptied if it were said that people could attain righteousness and eternal life in some manner apart from its mystery. For it is written in Isaiah that God would destroy worldly wisdom.

For this reason the Lord did not send me to preach the Gospel in worldly wisdom: he himself, as Scripture testifies, had foretold that he would not admit it into Gospel preaching, but would destroy it and reject it from the company of his preachers. Hence he says: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the prudence of the prudent.” God does not destroy and reject in them the wisdom which he himself gave, but the wisdom which they arrogate to themselves, who do not possess his own wisdom.

[Col. 0824A] It should be noted that wisdom consists in the subtle devising of things, whereas prudence consists in the polished exposition of those same things. Or wisdom is that by which they dispute about God through human reasoning and despise his incarnation and death as foolish; prudence is what they possess in their conduct, or by which they devise something to be proved. God destroyed—that is, rendered vain and overthrew—the wisdom of the wise and rejected the prudence of the prudent when he did those things which they deny can be done and sent fishermen to preach. Where he caused the Son of God to be incarnate of a virgin and crucified for human salvation, he opposed and destroyed the wisdom of the wise. And where he made unlettered and unlearned men preachers, so that through them, by simple words, he converted dialecticians and rhetoricians to faith, [Col. 0824B] he rejected the prudence of the prudent from his preaching and cast aside their shrewdness and habits.

It should be known, however, that in Isaiah this statement, according to the Hebrew, is said thus concerning the Jewish people: “Wisdom shall perish from its wise men, and the understanding of its prudent men shall be hidden” (Isa. 29). This was fulfilled after the Lord’s advent, when at one and the same time Jerusalem was burned, the Temple destroyed, and all the learning of their ancestors taken away. For because the wise men of that people did not receive Christ, who is the wisdom of God, all their wisdom perished from them. And because the prudent men strove by crafty devices to oppose that same wisdom of God, living bodily among human beings, all understanding which they possessed in the Scriptures was hidden from the eyes of their hearts, lest they find Christ who is contained in the letter.

This also accords very closely with the present passage of the epistle, because the false apostles against whom Paul is now arguing belonged to those foolish doctors of the Jews. They had scattered through the world, speaking in worldly wisdom to overthrow those who had recently come to faith. After the prophetic testimony the Apostle adds: “Where is the wise man?” and so forth. It is as though he said: Thus it was prophesied long ago, and in our own time we see it fulfilled. For where is the wise man? That is, in what Church, among Jews or Gentiles, has any rhetorician or dialectician been appointed a preacher of the Gospel? If one wished to be a preacher in the Church, [Col. 0824D] he had to cast aside the wisdom of the age. And where is the scribe chosen to preach? That is, one who gives precepts or composes books concerning morals or arts. And where is the investigator of this age chosen to teach in the Church? That is, one who searches out the secrets of nature.

Scribes are authors of books on natural and moral matters and writers on secular arts—that is, those who give precepts concerning those arts. Investigators of the age, however, are those who believe that the world is governed by constellations and determine that risings and settings occur through the twelve signs, thinking that nothing at all can happen without their movement; by their wisdom they inquire, examine, and investigate hidden things and the natures of individual beings. “Wise man” is the general term for both. The Apostle declares that these have been rejected and reduced to nothing—not because he wholly disapproves their teaching, for in many matters they agree with the sacred writings, but because they thought and wrote certain things contrary to the Christian religion, especially regarding the worship of a plurality of gods. God did not receive such persons, but made them foolish.

Therefore the Apostle mocks wisdom and cunning, proved false and rejected, when he says: “Where is the wise man? Where the scribe? Where the investigator of this age?” It is as though he said: The cleverness of such men avails nothing. This is an invective against Jews and Gentiles. For the scribes and doctors of the Law among the Jews think it foolish to believe that God has a Son. In the same manner, Gentiles daily make this a subject of laughter. But the Jews distrust it because it is not signified so openly in the Law; [Col. 0825A] the Gentiles, because the reasoning of the world does not admit it, judge it foolish, since they say that nothing can be begotten without the union of two.

“But where,” he says, “are such dogmatizers?” That is, they have been confounded and driven backward, or reduced to nothing. “Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this”—that is, the wisdom according to the reasoning of this world? Certainly he made it foolish by doing those things which it said could not be done. And so that which thought itself wise was found foolish. What it judged impossible has been shown possible. God made such wisdom foolish because through foolishness he gave salvation to believers.

For since, in the wisdom of God—that is, in the light of the divinity of the Son of God—the world, meaning any lover of the world or follower of worldly wisdom, did not know God through the proud wisdom of the age, since by manifold disputations [Col. 0825C] and most skillful inquiry it could not discover the Creator, though it attained investigation of the creature, it therefore pleased God to save believers through the foolishness of preaching: that is, through the thing preached which appears foolish, namely the incarnation and humility of his Son. For the Word of God is wisdom; but the flesh of the Word has been called the foolishness of this wisdom. Or, since carnal people could not by the prudence of their flesh reach wisdom, they might be healed through the foolishness of preaching—that is, through the proclaimed flesh of the Word.

This is what is meant by “in the wisdom of God the world did not know,” and so forth. It is as though one said: Since the world could by no means discover God, who is wisdom, through its own wisdom, it pleased God that it should know God made human through the foolish things of humanity, so that his wisdom might descend to our foolishness and our blindness might see, illumined by the mud of his flesh, the light of heavenly prudence, as that blind man was illuminated when mud was placed upon his eyes (John 9).

> “For Jews demand signs, and Greeks seek wisdom; but we preach Christ crucified: a stumbling block to Jews, and foolishness to Gentiles; but to those who are called, Jews as well as Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. For what is foolish in God is wiser than human beings, and what is weak in God is stronger than human beings.”

Therefore the world did not know God through wisdom because the Jews, accustomed from ancient times, seek signs of power, [Col. 0826A] while the Greeks inquire whether what is preached can occur by nature. We, on the contrary, preach Christ crucified. This is not for the Jews a sign of power but a stumbling block, because they rage against the preachers from shame at their crime; and for Gentiles it is foolishness, because according to worldly reasoning it is unfitting that God should die for human beings.

This is the meaning of “Jews demand signs”: they require not physical or argumentative reasons, but miracles. They do not doubt that something contrary to nature can happen, but ask whether it has happened. They know that Aaron’s dry rod sprouted and bore fruit (Num. 17); they know that Jonah came forth alive from the belly of the fish after three days (Jonah 2); they know that many other things have been divinely done, and thus they have become accustomed to demand signs (Matt. 12). But Greeks seek wisdom [Col. 0826B] because they do not wish to hear things which are impossible according to worldly reasoning. They think that nothing contrary to nature can happen and therefore investigate diligently according to physical principles whether what they hear can happen; they wish to discover that which appears wisdom to human intellect.

Jews and Gentiles act thus, but we on the contrary preach Christ crucified: to Jews indeed a stumbling block, but to Gentiles foolishness. The Jews are troubled, indignant, and enraged when they hear proclaimed as the Son of God the one whom they themselves crucified. The Gentiles, however, think it foolish that the immortal could die, and that he who had the power to cast down his persecutors by one word endured being scourged, spat upon, seized, crowned with thorns, [Col. 0826C] and crucified by them. For it seems foolish to Gentiles that the author of life should die for human beings, because this does not accord with worldly wisdom.

We preach Christ crucified for the redemption of the world. As we have said, this is a stumbling block to unbelieving Jews and foolishness to Greeks. But to those Jews and Greeks who previously considered it a stumbling block and foolishness, once they are called—that is, after they have been called or converted to faith, or called to life not by the common calling but by that whereby only those predestined before the beginning of the world are called—we preach Christ as the power of God, because by dying he conquered, and as the wisdom of God, by which he wisely deceived the devil. Here the Apostle refers “power” to signs because of the Jews, and “wisdom” to doctrine because of the Greeks, that is, the Gentiles.

For this power suffices for Jews who seek signs, if they believe; and this wisdom suffices for Greeks who seek wisdom. Believers will understand these signs of power in Christ: that his death destroyed our death and that, though himself dead, he gave us eternal life. Greeks too, if they believe, will see in him great evidences of wisdom and understand their secular wisdom to be foolishness. They will see by what provident and wise counsel he raised us by his humility, we who had fallen through pride. For this reason Christ is also called the power of God, because through him God made all things; and the wisdom of God, because through him God is known. From this it is clear that the same Son is coeternal and coequal with the Father. For since the Son himself is God’s power and God’s wisdom, if there was ever a time when God was [Col. 0827A] without the Son, he was without power and wisdom—that is, he was weak and foolish. Likewise, anyone who says that God’s power or wisdom is less than he is inflicts a great insult upon God, since not even an ordinary powerful human being would bear such a statement calmly.

Nor is it surprising that Christ crucified is, for believers, God’s power and God’s wisdom; for what is foolish in God—that is, humility and passion—is wiser than human beings, beyond what human beings can see or be; and what is weak in God—that is, the incarnation—is stronger than human beings, because, though conquered, he conquered death, from which no giant escaped. When we come to divine wisdom, we act wisely; when it came to us, proud people judged it to have acted foolishly. And when we come to it, we are strengthened; when it came to us, it was judged weak. We were deceived by the wisdom of the serpent; we are freed by the foolishness of God (Gen. 3).

But just as that which is called wisdom was in fact foolishness for those who despise God, so this which is called foolishness is wisdom for those who conquer the devil. It is not truly foolishness; rather, because it does not accord with worldly reasoning, people judge it foolishness, though it is spiritual reasoning. This foolishness surpasses all wise persons because it wisely restores salvation to the human race, a salvation which none of the wise knew how to find. This foolishness, I say, exceeds all human wisdom, because those who could not be freed through their own wisdom are saved through the mystery of the cross. Nor is what is weak in God weak, because Christ’s weakness is a great victory. He conquered [Col. 0827C] the strong man armed, who had conquered all (Luke 11); and therefore this weakness of God is stronger than all human beings, because it overcame him who had overcome all, and the weakness of the Crucified conquered death, from which not even giants could escape.

> “For consider your calling, brothers: not many are wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble. But God chose what is foolish in the world to confound the wise; and God chose what is weak in the world to confound the strong; and God chose what is ignoble and despised in the world, and things that are not, to destroy things that are, so that no flesh may glory in his presence (Jer. 9). But you are in Christ Jesus from him, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption, so that, as it is written: ‘Let the one who glories glory in the Lord’ (2 Cor. 10).”

Truly, what is foolish and weak in God is wiser and stronger than human beings, because you can experience this in yourselves: for you were called foolish and weak. Consider your calling, brothers—that is, consider by whom you were called—for not many among them are wise according to the flesh, that is, according to human wisdom; not many powerful according to worldly power; not many noble according to nobility of the flesh. At first, none among those called were such. Perhaps he says “not many” on his own account, since he alone among the Apostles was skilled in secular literature, rich in earthly wealth, and conspicuous through kinship of Roman rank; yet he counted these things as nothing and did not make use of them.

[Col. 0828A] There were already also some other holy preachers among those who had been wise according to the flesh, powerful, and noble, such as Dionysius the Areopagite and others. Or thus: “Consider your calling”—that is, prove in yourselves what I say: not many of you wise according to the flesh were called to faith; rather, few wise persons believed. For through the pride of secular wisdom many despised being subject to God’s wisdom. Persons of this kind can scarcely be brought to faith. Nor were many powerful or noble persons in this world called to Christ among you. For powerful, noble, and rich persons—and much more difficult than these, eloquent persons—find it difficult to believe God. Their minds are blinded by riches, wealth, luxury, or pride; surrounded by vices, they cannot see virtues. They judge the simplicity of Holy Scripture not by the majesty of its meanings but by the lowliness of its words.

Not many such persons were called; rather, God chose what is foolish in the world—that is, people unacquainted with worldly wisdom—in order through their teaching to confound, that is, make ashamed and reduce to foolishness, the wise of the age. For the wise are confounded when they see many confessing things which they deny: the childbirth of a virgin, the cross of the Son of God, resurrection from the dead, and other such matters. God chose what is foolish in the world—that is, people untrained in the liberal disciplines and wholly uncultivated, so far as secular learning is concerned, skilled neither in grammar nor armed with dialectic. He made fishermen his preachers so that he might show plainly in them all that it was not eloquence but the cause that persuaded believing peoples to life.

[Col. 0828C] And God chose what is weak in the world—that is, the poor and powerless—in order through their power to confound the strong, that is, to overcome them and make the powerful ashamed. For when proud rich people saw new virtues in humble sinners, they afterwards stood amazed at the miracles of those whose life they had first despised. Thus, soon returning in fear to their own hearts, they revered in miracles the holiness which they had despised in precepts. The strong, therefore, were confounded by the weak: as reverence for the life of the humble arose, the pride of the proud fell.

And God chose the ignoble and despised of the world—that is, people who are common and abject in this world—and things that are not, that is, those not counted, namely people who seemed to be nothing, in order to destroy, that is, humble by conquering, things that are, namely things considered great. Therefore he chose the unlearned, weak, ignoble, and poor—not because he abandoned the wise, strong, noble, and rich, but because, if he had chosen these first, they would seem to have been chosen because of the merit of their wisdom, power, birth, or riches; puffed up by these things, they would not receive the salvation of humility. If he had chosen wise people first, it would be thought that he had chosen them for the merit of their learning; their knowledge would thus be praised and the praise of Christ’s grace diminished. If he had chosen the powerful, he would seem to have chosen them for the merit of their rank; similarly, the rich, for the merit of their [Col. 0828D] wealth.

Therefore he neither omitted nor despised these who could glory in themselves, from themselves; but he delayed them for a while and preferred first to choose those who had nothing in themselves from which they could glory. For such people had to come to preach who possessed nothing for their own praise, so that what they did might be known all the more to be the work of truth alone, insofar as it was plainly seen that they would not have been fitted for that work by themselves. Therefore he first chose such people, so that through them he might humble the rest and bring them to faith, “so that no flesh may glory in his presence”—that is, no human being before him; or, “so that no flesh may glory in his presence,” that is, no one may glory in himself while looking upon him. Certainly no one should glory in personal merits.

For the unjust do not glory, since they have nothing from which to glory; nor do the just, because they have from God that in which they ought to glory. They have no glory but him to whom they say: “My glory and the lifter up of my head” (Ps. 3). [Col. 0829B] Accordingly, what has now been said concerns every human being, whether just or unjust: “so that no flesh may glory in his presence.” That is, no one should glory in merits, wisdom, power, nobility, riches, or any other possession of one’s own. No one can glory from oneself; but glory in God, because you are in Christ Jesus from God himself—that is, by his gift—not from yourselves. [Col. 0829C] It arose from his grace that you are in Christ, not from your merits, because it was his purpose that you should be members of Christ.

Therefore, if you are from him, do not admire those whom he did not choose. You are in Christ, who became for you wisdom, so that through participation in him we might be made wise, receiving from him the understanding of prudence; and he became righteousness for us, so that through participation in him we might be justified by works of virtue; and sanctification, so that he might sanctify us in baptism, making us free from sin; and redemption, so that he might redeem us by giving himself for us.

Therefore he became wisdom for us, that is, enlightening us toward truth and knowledge of God; righteousness, because he first justifies by good action; sanctification, because he first cleanses in baptism; and redemption, because he first redeemed by his passion. He who is in himself eternal and unchangeable wisdom also becomes wisdom for us when, through participation in him, we become in some measure wise for right understanding. So too, though he is in himself righteousness itself, which lives in itself and lives unchangeably, he becomes righteousness for us when, cleaving to him, we live righteously; and we are more or less righteous according as we cleave to him more or less. Likewise, since he himself is eternal holiness in himself, he also becomes sanctification for us when he sanctifies us through participation in himself.

Therefore he was made for us by God wisdom, righteousness, and sanctification, because we turn to him in time—that is, from some point in time onward—in order to remain with him eternally; and he, from some point in time, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). [Col. 0829D] He was made all these things for us by God so that whoever glories may glory not in self but in the Lord, as it is written in Jeremiah: “Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom; let not the strong man glory in his strength; let not the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this: that he knows and understands me, that I am the Lord, that I perform mercy, judgment, and righteousness on earth” (Jer. 9).

See how he took glory from us in order to give glory: he took ours in order to give his; he took away the empty in order to give the full; he took away the unstable in order to give the firm. How much stronger and steadier is our glory in God than glory in ourselves! Therefore no one should glory in personal wisdom, strength, riches, or things of this kind. But if one wishes to glory, let one glory in the Lord, who performs mercy, judgment, and righteousness. For the person who glories in the Lord alone recognizes that it is not his own, but the Lord’s—not only that he exists, but also that he fares well only through him from whom he has existence—and in all that he does seeks not his own glory but the Lord’s glory.

Therefore one ought to glory in the Lord, because one who glories in him cannot be confounded; but one who glories in this age or in oneself will be confounded.

## Chapter II

> “And when I came to you, brothers, I came not in loftiness of speech or wisdom, declaring to you the testimony of Christ. For I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified. And I was with you in weakness and fear and much trembling; and my speech and [Col. 0830C] my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in a manifestation of Spirit and power, so that your faith might not be in human wisdom but in God’s power.”

I said above that God chose weak and foolish preachers. I too appeared such to you, because when I came to you I came not in loftiness of speech—that is, not with rhetorical and dialectical disputations, so as to preach to you artfully and elaborately according to logic—nor in loftiness of wisdom—that is, of human reasonings according to natural philosophy—which you praise in the false apostles. By their eloquence they commend their perverse teaching, and by worldly wisdom they empty the cross of Christ. [Col. 0830D] I came not in loftiness of speech or wisdom, but rather in humility; for one who speaks loftier matters to those of lesser capacity seeks not their benefit but his own display. I came proclaiming to you the testimony of Christ: that is, what the prophets testified concerning his incarnation, passion, and resurrection; or what he himself testified concerning himself by dying and rising again; or what we apostles testify concerning him. I came, I say, not in the loftiness of secular eloquence or wisdom, because neither did I come in the loftiness of that wisdom which concerns God. And I did this deliberately: for I did not judge that I knew anything among you, whom I saw to be of lesser capacity, except Jesus Christ, and him crucified—that is, except the saviour-king, and that through crucifixion. This is to say: because I considered that you could not grasp the mysteries of his divinity, [Col. 0831A] I spoke to you only of the weaknesses of his humanity. For the Apostle did not “know” among them what they could not know through him; and he said that he knew only what it was necessary for them to know through him. By this mode of expression, someone is said not to know what he conceals, just as a pit is called “blind” when it is hidden.

Yet in Christ crucified there is no small measure of knowledge, but much is learned in him; above all, that our old self was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be made void and we might no longer serve sin (Rom. IV). For this belongs to his cross: that we too are crucified to the world in his body; by this is understood every restraint of evil desires. Therefore it cannot happen that thefts, adulteries, or other crimes are permitted to those who are formed by the cross of Christ. [Col. 0831B] For the cross of Christ puts to death every vice of flesh and spirit, in order to make us live in virtues; because he himself was crucified for our sins, that he might redeem us from all iniquity and save us from eternal torments. These and many other things are learned in Christ crucified.

Thus I preached humble and weak things to you. And I myself was humble and weak, because I was among you in weakness—that is, as though I possessed no strength or power—or in weakness, that is, in tribulation; and in fear, that is, anxiety of mind; and in bodily trembling because of the afflictions of punishments. For by preaching Christ amid the foolishness, as it seemed, of human wisdom, I provoked against myself the hatred and persecutions of Jews and Gentiles, [Col. 0831C] as though I proclaimed an empty thing and preached a dead God. And while I lived among you in this way, my discourse concerning morals and my preaching concerning Christ—or, my discourse privately before a few and my preaching publicly before all—was not in persuasive words of human wisdom: that is, words which through human wisdom would induce belief in what I said. Rather, it was in a demonstration of Spirit and power: that is, I showed that I possessed the Holy Spirit by living devoutly and prophesying, and by obtaining that same Spirit for others through the laying on of hands; and I showed that I possessed power by performing miracles. I did this so that your faith might not be founded upon human wisdom, but upon the power of God: that is, so that, following human wisdom, it might not seek reasons [Col. 0831D] for what it ought to believe, but might attribute all things to divine power as possible, knowing that nothing is impossible to God.

> “Yet we speak wisdom among the perfect; but wisdom not of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are being brought to nothing. Rather, we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, the hidden wisdom which God predestined before the ages for our glory, which none of the rulers of this age knew. For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. But, as it is written: What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, the things which God has prepared for those who love him (Isa. LXIV). But God has revealed them to us through his Spirit.”

[Col. 0832A] Since above he had said, “I came not in loftiness of speech or wisdom,” lest anyone think him foolish and suppose that his preaching contained no wisdom, he shows that he who spoke simply to these people pours forth the depths of wisdom to others. “Among you,” he says, “we spoke simply; but among the perfect”—not persons who know, who have no need for us to speak, but hearers not capable—“we speak wisdom,” that is, concerning God’s secrets. It is as if he said: We too possess wisdom, but you cannot grasp it, because you are still nourished with milk and are found small in understanding. But we speak it among the perfect: that is, among those who acknowledge the cross of Christ, by the testimony of its power, to be wisdom.

For all perfected persons understand that the highest wisdom is what you regard as abasement: namely, [Col. 0832B] that God became man, that he hungered, that he was weary, that he was crucified. All these things, when preached among the blinded, appear to be foolishness; but among the perfect, who possess the light of the heart, they are the highest wisdom. We speak wisdom, but wisdom not of this age: that is, not wisdom established by human arguments; not of this age but of the age to come; nor the wisdom of the rulers of this age, that is, kings and philosophers who seemed in this age to hold the preeminence in wisdom. These rulers are being brought to nothing: that is, their wisdom is scattered, because Christianity cuts away the errors which they implanted—namely idolatry, avarice, and the other vices.

We do not speak their wisdom, but rather God’s wisdom [Col. 0832C] concerning the redemption of humankind through the incarnation and passion of his Only-Begotten Son. We speak it in mystery: that is, we disclose it in the hidden meaning of prophetic sayings or deeds, as in Isaac’s sacrifice (Gen. XXII), or David’s victory over the Philistine (I Kings XVII). This wisdom is hidden from the wise and prudent of the age and is therefore thought foolish by them, because they do not know it. It is hidden because it is not in words but in power; it is not possible by human reasoning but credible by spiritual efficacy.

Or, we speak it in mystery, that is, in the hidden reality of the sacraments, which the eye of our reason cannot behold without the labour of inquiry and the illumination of the Holy Spirit. It was hidden in the Father’s heart, because “the Word was with God” (John I). This wisdom, which is the Word of the Father, [Col. 0832D] God predestined according to his future humanity—that is, he ordained before the ages, before the world existed, that his Only-Begotten should become man in the fullness of time (Gal. IV), be crucified, and rise again—for our glory, who believe; as also for the confusion of those who do not believe and account his cross foolishness.

[Col. 0833A] No ruler of this age knew this wisdom of his divinity to be hidden by God: that is, none of the proud philosophers, teachers of the Law, or powers of the age had known it when the Apostle spoke these words. Or, God predestined the wisdom of the Lord’s incarnation and passion for our glory, so that his humanity and death might become everlasting glory to us. No ruler of this age—that is, none of the evil spirits—knew this wisdom, because none of them understood that through his passion the human race would be redeemed. That they did not know is evident from this: if the demons had known that wisdom of his passion to avail for the redemption of humankind, they would never have crucified him—that is, they would never have caused the Lord of glory to be crucified; the devil would never have suggested that he be crucified, through whom he would lose his own right.

Nor would human beings have crucified him, if they had known that he was the God of glory. Though crucified in the form of a servant, he was nevertheless the Lord of glory crucified. For such was that assumption [of humanity] as to make God man and man God. In what respect and for what reason this is said, [Col. 0833B] the prudent, diligent, and devout reader understands with the Lord’s help. For it is rightly said that God was crucified—not by the power of divinity, but through the weakness of flesh—for God and man are one person. Those who crucified him did not know him; the faithful, however, knew him.

They did not know him; but from this it follows, as is written in Isaiah, that “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared” (Isa. LXIV) for those who love him; but he has revealed these things to us through his Spirit. For just as these things remain hidden from carnal people according to the prophecy, but have nevertheless been revealed to us who are spiritual through God’s Spirit, so the wisdom of the divine incarnation and of our redemption through his death was hidden from unbelievers [Col. 0833C] but made manifest to believers.

The things which God has prepared in the kingdom of heaven for those who love him with a pure heart are so great, so splendid, and so spiritual that eye has not seen how great or what kind they are; nor has ear heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man. The eye has not seen them, because they are not colour; the ear has not heard them, because they are not sound; they have not entered into the heart of man, because they are not an earthly thought. For what enters into a person’s heart was below that heart. It enters into the heart because the heart into which it enters is above it. But the reward kept in heaven for the elect does not enter into a person’s heart; rather, it ascends to that person’s heart. Eye has not seen it with bodily sight, nor ear heard it with bodily hearing, nor has it entered into the heart of man: that is, it could not be known by the reasoning [Col. 0833D] of one who is carnal rather than spiritual.

For in the statement, “it has not entered into the heart of man,” it may be understood that it is not human, but above humanity, and ascends into the human heart. A thing is said to ascend into the heart when it enters so as to be intelligently understood and, once understood, to please. It should be noted that this sentence is read in the prophet not in the same words but with the same truth of meaning. For it is written there: “From of old they have not heard, nor perceived with their ears; eye has not seen, O God, apart from you, what you have prepared for those who wait for you” (ibid.).
