Yet prophet and Apostle alike say, “eye has not seen.” But where the Apostle says, “nor has ear heard,” the prophet says, “nor perceived with their ears.” Where the Apostle says, “nor has it entered into the heart of man,” the prophet says, “they have not heard,” that is, they have not understood. And where the Apostle has, “for those who love him,” the prophet said, “for those who wait for you.” But, as we said before, the meaning in the Apostle is the same as in the prophet.

[Col. 0834A] For from of old people have not heard—that is, they have not understood—the rewards of the righteous, because their greatness has not entered into the heart of man: that is, human thought does not comprehend them. Nor have they perceived them with their ears, because human hearing has not heard anyone speaking of them; and eye has not seen them, because what is promised in the future is not seen in the present. For hope that is seen is not hope, but already a sure promise. Thus these things were unknown to people from of old; but to us, who are above human beings, God has revealed them—not through the industry of our own intellect (Rom. VIII), but through [Col. 0834B] his Spirit, by which he illuminated our minds so that we might understand those ineffable goods which he has prepared for those who love him. They will possess them when God is all in all (I Cor. XV). Therefore God is all those goods which he has prepared for those who love or await him.

> “For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. For who among human beings knows the things of a human being, except the spirit of that person which is within him? So also no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God.”

These things have been revealed to us through the Spirit, and this is no wonder, because the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God: that is, the things hidden in God, far removed from the knowledge of creatures. [Col. 0834C] He searches, not indeed in order to find what he does not know, but because he leaves nothing whatever unknown; he searches the depths of God because he knows his secrets and hidden things. Thus he is shown to be God, since he is shown to know all God’s hidden things. He is said to search all things because, dwelling in us, he causes us to search them. What we do by his gift, he himself is said to do, because without him we cannot do it.

Truly the Spirit of God investigates hidden things, just as the spirit of a human being investigates the hidden things of that human being. For what human being knows the hidden things of a person, except that person’s own spirit which is within? Every person has a spirit proper to himself. For each person’s mind is that person’s own spirit. And no one knows the things of a person except that person’s spirit. For I do not know what you are thinking, nor do you know what I am thinking. What we think in the mind is our own peculiar possession; and a person’s own spirit bears witness to that person’s thoughts. Another does not know what is happening in that person, but that person’s spirit knows it. [Col. 0834D] So too no one has known the hidden things of God except the Spirit of God.

Yet God’s wisdom, which is the Son, is not excluded from this knowledge of secrets, since the Spirit receives all things from the Son, as he himself says to the disciples: “All things whatsoever the Father has are mine” (John XVI). “Therefore I said that he will receive from what is mine and declare it to you.” And, having received God’s Spirit, we too learn what occurs in God; for when we know through his Spirit, even so no one knows except the Spirit of God. Thus he himself knows in us, just as he speaks in those to whom it is said: “For it is not you who speak, [Col. 0835A] but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X).

> “But we have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we may know the things given to us by God. These things also we speak, not in words taught by human wisdom, but in the teaching of the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual. But the natural person does not receive the things which are of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are examined spiritually. But the spiritual person judges all things, while he himself is judged by no one, as it is written: For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has instructed him? (Isa. XL; Rom. XI). But we have the mind of Christ.”

[Col. 0835B] The Spirit of God alone knows the things which are God’s. But we have received, not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit of God, that we might be taught not worldly things but the things of God; for the spirit of the world cannot know the things which this Spirit has made known to us. The spirit of the world is what they call the *python*; through it fanatics, who are without God, are seized. It is accustomed to divine worldly matters by conjectures, and is deceived and deceives through what seems probable. It also spoke through the Sibyl, following our own understanding and wishing to have a place among heavenly beings; it was also in the false apostles and made them pursue worldly wisdom.

But we have received not the spirit of this world, by which we might be taught the wisdom of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, [Col. 0835C] by whom we are taught the things which are from God. We have received the Spirit who is from God: that is, a certain divine ray illuminating us, so that through him we may know the benefits granted to us by God. For the Spirit of God enlightens the mind which he fills, whereas the spirit of the world blinds it. Those who possess the latter do not understand God’s gifts which they have received, nor from whom they received them. But through his Spirit we know both that we possess his gifts and that we have received them from him.

For every good thing is granted by him. He himself gave us his Christ, and in him redemption and remission of sins, the multiplication of virtues, the hope of eternal blessedness, and whatever we have or are. We understand that we possess these things and have received them from him. We also speak these things, so that it may thereby appear that we know them, because [Col. 0835D] we speak them so that others may learn them. We speak not in words taught by human wisdom through reasoning or ornament, but in the teaching of the Spirit, because, while we speak, the minds of the hearers are taught by the Holy Spirit. For humanly wise words do not grasp this meaning, nor is it apprehended by learned literary study; rather, it is conceived through faith by spiritual reasoning. Therefore the Spirit of God spiritually teaches human hearts through the Gospel, stirring them to the knowledge of their Creator.

I say that we speak, and do this by comparing spiritual words with spiritual persons: that is, by moderating what we say so that it suits each person’s capacity, because we distinguish what we say according to the differing understanding of our hearers and adapt it to each person’s intelligence, considering what should be said to whom. [Col. 0836A] We do this for spiritual persons—which you are not—and therefore the fault is yours, not ours, that we have not spoken greater things to you. We know the things of God and speak them to spiritual persons.

But the natural person, such as the false apostles are, does not receive the things of God’s Spirit—for example, the virgin’s childbirth or the resurrection of the dead. A person is called natural who lives in the manner of animals and thinks that there is nothing after death. Such a person is rightly called natural because he is carried away by the unrestrained wantonness of his own soul, which the spirit neither governs nor restrains within the bounds of the natural order, because he himself does not submit to God’s governance. For *animalis* (“natural”) is derived from *anima* (“soul”), just as *carnalis* (“carnal”) is derived from *caro* (“flesh”).

Such a person does not receive the things of God’s Spirit: that is, what grace Christ’s cross bestows upon believers; and he hears whatever he hears [Col. 0836B] about God’s nature in such a way that he cannot think of anything other than a body—however vast, supreme, or immeasurable, however luminous and beautiful, yet still a body. He is also said not to receive, that is, not to understand the things of God’s Spirit, because he thinks about and desires only the carnal goods of the present life, while he does not understand spiritual and eternal things. For whatever he hears concerning such things is foolishness to him, and he cannot understand it. Like cattle, he presses his understanding down toward the earth, and therefore reaches only what he sees; nor does he think anything can be done other than what he himself knows. Hence whatever he hears otherwise than he knows, he judges foolish.

Therefore he cannot understand these things because he is examined spiritually: that is, he is invisibly judged by God, [Col. 0836C] so that, by God’s just judgment, he is not allowed to understand spiritual things. Or, he is examined spiritually: that is, he is proved to be natural only by spiritual things, because he rejects these things when he hears them, and they are set before him for no other purpose. Or, he cannot understand because the thing which he regards as foolishness is examined spiritually: that is, it is discerned and understood through the Holy Spirit.

The natural person cannot understand; but the spiritual person—that is, the one whose mind is illuminated by the light of the Holy Spirit and taught to live spiritually—judges, that is, discerns and distinguishes, all things. For such a person judges and approves what is right, but disapproves whatever is found wrong in the deeds and morals of believers. He judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one: that is, by no human being, but only by the very law according to which he judges [Col. 0836D] all things, since it has most truly been said: “We must all be presented before the judgment-seat of Christ” (II Cor. V). Therefore he judges all things, because he is above all things when he is with God. And he is judged by no one, because he himself is above the rest, and inferiors cannot judge a superior.

And truly he is judged by no one as to whether he understands or acts well or badly. For what natural person has known the mind of the Lord which the spiritual man possesses? No one. Therefore such a person cannot judge it, because no one judges rightly concerning things unknown. And who has instructed him? That is, who has taught the Lord what he ought to have done? No one. For people who do not have God’s Spirit wish to instruct the Lord when they say to themselves: God ought never to have died in order to free his creature from the devil’s power; rather, being omnipotent, [Col. 0837A] he ought to have saved his own merely by command. And because they wish to instruct him thus, it follows that they do not know his mind. For they do not know that a just God ought not in this matter to have used the power of might, but the principle of justice.

Or the text can be read in this manner according to other manuscripts: “For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has instructed him?” The mind of the Lord is that by which he performed these things through which the wisdom of the world is proved foolish, since it denies that the things accomplished could be accomplished. There is no one who has known this mind so as, if it displeased him, to wish to correct God’s counsel. For whoever has known it praises the wisdom and power of God. Who has known the mind of our Lord Jesus Christ? But we spiritual persons have the mind of Christ: that is, by receiving the Holy Spirit we have become participants in Christ’s knowledge. [Col. 0837B] Therefore natural persons or false apostles cannot judge us, who possess the Lord’s mind which they do not know.

## Chapter III

> “And I, brethren, could not speak to you as to spiritual persons, but as to carnal persons. As to little children in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food. For you were not yet able; indeed, even now you are not able, for you are still carnal. For when jealousy and contention are among you, are you not carnal and walking according to man? For when one says, ‘I am of Paul,’ and another, ‘I am of Apollos,’ are you not human beings? What then is Apollos? And what is Paul? Ministers of him whom you believed. [Col. 0837C] And each as the Lord gave. I planted; Apollos watered; but God gave the growth. Therefore neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth. The one who plants and the one who waters, however, are one. Each will receive his own reward according to his own labour” (Ps. LXI; Gal. VI; Matt. XX).

We compare spiritual things with spiritual persons, because we have the mind of Christ. Yet, brethren, I could not speak to you as to spiritual persons, but as to carnal persons, because I saw that you could not grasp spiritual things owing to the weakness of your understanding. Therefore I spoke to you as you were able to hear; and I kept the mysteries of God silent from you not because of your ignorance, but because of your weakness. For hearers’ minds are not to be instructed beyond their strength; rather, lofty and elevated matters should be veiled from many hearers and opened only with difficulty to a few. To beginners or weak persons, then, one should preach not lofty and mystical matters but certain things which they can grasp; whereas to the perfect one should speak profound and mystical things.

But we must fear and take care lest, under this pretext, the utterances of false apostles or of any heretics, as though they were things carnal persons cannot grasp, should seem not merely to be whitewashed with excuse but even to be praised. Therefore it must be known that Christ himself crucified, by whom the Apostle says he has nourished little children as it were with milk—that is, the very true flesh in which his death truly took place, and the true wounds of the nailed and blood-stricken body—[Col. 0838A] is not thought of by carnal persons in the same way as by spiritual persons. To the former he is milk; to the latter, food. For although they hear no more, they understand more. For even what both alike receive in faith is not received equally by the mind.

Once this is first understood—that the very things which spiritual and carnal persons hear together are grasped by each according to his own mode, the former as little children and the latter as adults, the former as the nourishment of milk and the latter as strengthening food—there seems no necessity for certain secret teachings to be withheld and hidden from little believers, to be spoken separately to the older, that is, the more intelligent. There is only this: solid food, which suits the perfect, does not profit little children when they cannot grasp it, and things that raise up the strong weigh down the weak. For the very fact that the Apostle judged that he knew among them nothing except Jesus Christ and him crucified, he could not speak to them as to spiritual persons but as to carnal persons, because they could not grasp it as spiritual persons do. [Col. 0838B] But whatever spiritual persons were among them heard the same thing as those who were carnal, yet they grasped it in a spiritual understanding. Thus his statement, “I could not speak as to spiritual persons, but as to carnal persons,” should be understood as if he said: You could not grasp what I spoke as spiritual persons, but as carnal persons.

“I spoke to you as to carnal persons.” And I did this so carefully that, as to little children in knowledge in Christ, I gave you milk to drink: that is, easy teaching, sweet and nourishing; not food, that is, not robust teaching concerning spiritual [Col. 0838C] matters. Yet, as we said above, it can happen that what is called milk for little children is food for grown persons; just as “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I), which little children drink and grown persons eat. Nevertheless, milk was especially expressed for little children through the Saviour’s flesh. For just as a mother eats food so that, passing it through her flesh, she may give it to her infant as milk, so the Lord, the food of angels, the Word made flesh, became milk. For Christ in humility is our milk; the same Christ, equal to the Father, is our food. He nourishes with milk in order that he may feed with bread.

The little child suckles from the breasts of the Church the milk of all the sacraments performed in time for our eternal salvation, so that, nourished and strengthened, he may arrive [Col. 0838D] at eating the food of eternal divinity. To such people it is now said: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food.” And why? Because you were not yet able to receive solid food while I was with you; indeed, even now you are not able, because you are still carnal: that is, you follow the mind of the flesh rather than that of the spirit. They were carnal because they still served the pleasures of the age, although they had already been baptized and had received the Holy Spirit. For because after baptism they had relapsed into their old life, they are called carnal. But where “not yet” or “not still” is said, there is certainly no despair, provided one strives toward the time when that which is not yet will be.

“For you are still carnal,” he says; and showing why they are carnal: “For when jealousy”—that is, envy—“and contention”—that is, quarrelling over words—[Col. 0839A] “are among you, are you not carnal,” trusting in flesh, that is, in man, “and walking according to man?” That is, progressing toward worse things. It is as if he said: Since you harbour discordant minds, do you not still sin from blameworthy human weakness? For “man” is here named in a culpable sense.

When he had called them carnal, he did not say, “You walk according to flesh,” but “according to man,” because he wished this also to be understood: “according to flesh.” For certainly, if walking according to flesh were culpable but walking according to man—that is, living—were praiseworthy, he would not reproach them by saying, “You walk according to man.” For to walk according to man is to be carnal. But one who does not walk according to man, but according to God, assuredly does not walk according to himself, since he too is a human being. Those, however, who walk not according to themselves but according to God are called not human beings but gods (Ps. LXXXI; John X).

And truly, he says, jealousy and contention are among you, and you walk according to flesh. For when one of you says, “I am of Paul,” and another says, “I am of Apollos,” are you not human beings? Just as those who glory in God and expect every grace from him are called gods, as adopted by God, so those who glory in man are called human beings. For the Apostle wishes those whom he rebukes because they are human beings to be gods or angels: that is, in these disputes they savour not the things of God but those of man. [Col. 0839B] He begins from his own person, lest perhaps he seem through envy rather to be attacking the persons of others. [Col. 0839C] He shows that it is a great error and an insult to God when, though God is preached, glory is given to human beings, and hope which ought to be placed in God is placed in human beings. For Scripture says: “Cursed is the man who puts his hope in man” (Jer. XVII).

What is less unlike Gentilism than when the glory which ought to be given to the Creator is given to a creature, that is, to a human being? And since one of you says, “I am of Paul,” and another, “I am of Apollos,” and you glory in these teachers by a vain error, then answer me: What is Apollos, and what is Paul, who is still greater? If you do not know how to answer, I answer that they are not God, who gives, but those through whom God gives, because they are ministers of him in whom you believed. Since they are ministers, hope is not to be placed in them but [Col. 0839D] in God, whose ministers they are. For thanksgiving must be rendered to him whose gift it is, not to servants, who must administer it even against their will.

They are ministers, and not in one manner only, but as the Lord gave to each: that is, as he willed and as he apportioned to individuals the offices of ministry. For I, by his own giving, planted: that is, by evangelizing I converted you to faith; and Apollos watered: that is, as your bishop, after you were founded in faith, he watered your hearts with the rain of his speech. Yet it was not we, but God, who gave you growth in progress. For we who speak outwardly to your ears are like labourers applying cultivation from outside to a tree; but we cannot give growth or form fruit. But he who created, redeemed, and called you through faith and the Holy [Col. 0840A] Spirit, dwelling in you—unless he speaks to you within, we make noise in vain.

Therefore it is the inward teacher who teaches. Christ teaches; his inspiration teaches. Where his inspiration and anointing are absent, words make an empty noise outside. For a farmer can plant a tree, apply water from without, and give cultivation’s care; but he cannot form leaves and fruit. This exceeds human lowliness, exceeds angelic sublimity, and belongs wholly to the Creator alone. Since God alone gives growth, therefore neither the one who plants—that is, who establishes in faith—is anything by giving anything of himself, nor the one who waters—that is, who either baptizes or subsequently instructs morals. Rather, God, who gives growth, is effective for salvation: that is, his anointing which teaches you inwardly.

[Col. 0840B] For the labourer would work all things outwardly in vain unless the Creator secretly worked within. Neither planter nor waterer is anything for the salvation of those watered or planted, because planted things often die, and watered things fail to reach the effect of fruitfulness, unless God grants enlivening grace. Therefore, as regards the honour due to God, a human being is nothing. But as regards ministry, he is necessary, to be honoured as a servant, not so that anything may be hoped for from him to God’s injury. God alone is he in whom one should glory, because he gives growth.

But the one who plants and the one who waters are one: that is, both are ministers. Though their offices differ, they are one: that is, both are [Col. 0840C] human beings and think the same thing concerning God in harmony. They are one: that is, undifferentiated. For it might seem that although they give nothing from themselves, God nevertheless gives more through one than through the other. Therefore it is said that they are one: that is, one does not confer more grace than another, because God alone gives through them. They do not differ in giving, but in labour and reward, because each of them will receive his own reward from the Lord according to his labour: that is, the one who laboured more will have a greater reward, and the one who endured less labour will receive a lesser recompense. For God will render to each according to his work (Rom. II). Hence it is clear that neither of them is the author of salvation, and therefore one should not glory in them.

[Col. 0840D]

> “For we are God’s fellow-workers; you are God’s cultivated field, God’s building. According to the grace of God given to me, I laid a foundation as a wise architect. But another builds upon it. Let each take care how he builds upon it. For no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus. But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, each person’s work will become manifest. For the Day of the Lord will declare it, because it will be revealed in fire, and the fire will test what sort each person’s work is. If anyone’s work which he built upon it remains, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss. But he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire.”

[Col. 0841A] We shall receive a reward, because we are God’s fellow workers in cultivating his field. For the one upon whom he himself pours inward grace, we assist with the voice of exhortation; what he accomplishes inwardly through the Spirit, we assist outwardly by the ministry of speech. And our exhortation is brought to completion only when God is present in the heart to help. We are God’s fellow workers, and you are the cultivation of God’s field and the building of God’s temple. We assist him when, while he cultivates the field of your heart through inward grace, we cultivate it with the plough of preaching; and while he builds for his own dwelling the edifice of your mind, we too labour to build it. For God’s field is cultivated when vices are uprooted from the people of the faithful and virtues are planted, so that they may grow [Col. 0841B] and bear fruit. His building is erected when the Church is built up by those who are set upon the foundation of faith, so that it may rise on high as some support others; or when the minds of the faithful are constructed through the imposition of virtues, so that they may become a dwelling worthy of God.

I said that you are God’s building, and that I laid the foundation of this building; and I did not do this from myself, but according to the grace of God given to me, that I might be worthy to preach God’s Gospel and to lay the foundation of faith in human hearts. Hence it is evident that what I did belongs to God, not to man. “According to the grace of God,” that is, according to the apostleship freely given to me by God. In the building of your mind I laid the foundation—that is, faith in Christ—and I did so with discernment, as a wise architect, that is, the master-builder [Col. 0841C] who lays the foundation of a house to be built in a firm place, using strong, squared stones. A wise architect is one who sets the foundation according to the instruction of its author: that is, one who preaches the faith according to the tradition of the Saviour.

But another builds upon it. Whoever, whether a good or evil teacher, comes after the preaching of the apostles and preaches, builds upon it. Yet let each one see how he builds upon it: that is, let the superimposed building accord with the foundation, lest, if it be crooked and flimsy, it cause ruin while the foundation remains unharmed. For even if he teaches badly, Christ’s name, which is the foundation, remains; but bad teaching perishes. Let him see, I say, how he builds upon it, not how [Col. 0841D] he lays the foundation. For no one can lay another foundation besides that which was laid by me, which is Christ Jesus—that is, faith in Christ Jesus. Therefore no one can lay another foundation, because not even heretics can teach except under Christ’s name. Otherwise they cannot commend the inventions of their errors unless they preach while interposing the Saviour’s name, so that the dignity of the name may render acceptable things contrary and absurd.

The foundation remains; but what is built upon it, if it is useless, will not stand. Only what is useful, if it is added above, will remain. For if anyone builds upon this foundation of Christ’s name gold, silver, precious stones—by which three excellent teaching is denoted—or wood, hay, stubble—by which various, [Col. 0842A] frivolous, and corrupt teaching is signified—each person’s work will be made manifest on the last day; that is, each person’s teaching will be manifest to all at judgment, whether it was good or bad. For the day of the Lord will declare this. The day of judgment is called the day of the Lord, not because all days are not his, but because it is so called by way of eminence and in contrast with the human day. The day of the present time is the day of man, because in it a human being does what he wishes; but that day will be the Lord’s, because on it the Lord will do what is just, rendering to each according to his work (Matt. 16). Therefore that day will disclose the quality of each person’s work, because it will be revealed in fire: that is, the same day, which is now hidden from all, will be made manifest and then known to all. When all see that fire [Col. 0842B] spread throughout the whole world before the Judge’s face, they will know that the day of judgment has arrived. Or the Lord will be revealed in that fire: that is, he will appear to all, good and evil alike. Hence the Thessalonians are told: “At the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven with the angels of his power, in a flame of fire” (2 Thess. 1).

And that fire will test what sort each person’s work is: that is, whether it is firm or perishable. The fire will test the work, that is, each person’s teaching. Since the examination will take place through fire, if it finds in someone nothing to burn up, it will show that person to have been a good teacher. But evil and adulterated teaching is for this reason signified by wood, hay, and stubble: to show that it will be fuel for the fire. Truly, the fire will test each person’s works. For [Col. 0842C] if someone’s work, which he has built upon it, remains, he will receive a reward. For just as gold, silver, and stones which the fire has not consumed endure, so too the good teacher will remain incorruptible. And when no defilement or perverse teaching is found in him, he will receive, with glory, the reward of everlasting recompense.

But if someone’s work is burned—that is, if someone’s perverse teaching fails in the fire—such a worker will suffer loss: that is, he will be cast down into punishments. Yet he himself will be saved, because the substance of which he consists will not perish, just as his bad teaching, which is an accident, will perish. This, however, must not be understood of a heretical teacher, but of a Catholic who has not taught rightly. For even in the books of holy teachers which the Church reads as authoritative, certain [Col. 0842D] perverse or heretical things are sometimes found; nevertheless, neither the books nor their authors are condemned on their account. Let the prudent reader read through their books, and he will find what I say to be true.

“And he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire”: so that this salvation is not without punishment. He will indeed be saved, but he will nevertheless suffer the punishment of fire, so that, purified through fire, he may be saved and may not, like the lost, be tormented forever in everlasting fire, since it will benefit him in some measure to have believed unto eternity.

It may also be understood otherwise, and more truly: “I,” he says, “laid the foundation, but another builds upon it.” As though he said: Once the foundation has been laid—that is, once faith has been founded in you—it no longer belongs to me to build upon it; rather, it belongs to another to build upon it, namely, to the one who has faith to build good works upon it. It belongs to the believer to build upon it. But let each one see how [Col. 0843A] he builds upon it: that is, what kind of works he adds. Namely, whether he prefers to adhere to the contemplative life and to live continently without the yoke of a wife—which is indeed the better and more praiseworthy counsel—or rather seeks the active life and the bond of a wife, which is weaker and less praiseworthy. With respect to building upon the foundation by good action, one need only consider what kind each person wishes to choose, since there are many kinds of acting well. But no one is granted the power to choose the foundation, because there is only one foundation, that is, one faith, which no one can alter, as the pseudo-apostles attempt to do.

The faith of Christ is Christ in us, who dwells in our hearts through faith (Eph. 3). And this is the foundation from which the whole structure of good living rises. [Col. 0843B] This faith must not be understood as idle (Jas. 2), but it will work through love whatever good it can do (Gal. 5). For the faith of demons, who also believe and tremble, and confess Jesus as the Son of God (Matt. 8; Mark 5; Luke 8), cannot be accepted as a foundation, because it is not faith that works through love, but faith expressed through fear. Therefore faith in Christ—the faith of Christian grace, that is, the faith which works through love—once laid as a foundation, permits no one to perish.

“But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble, each person’s work will be made manifest.” Whoever lives well and honours and praises God, not clinging in love to earthly things but desiring the eternal homeland, [Col. 0843C] and either sells all that he has and distributes it to the poor (Luke 18), or possesses as though he did not possess and uses this world as though he did not use it (1 Cor. 7), builds upon it gold, silver, and precious stones. By gold an inward meaning is denoted; by silver, teaching speech; by precious stones, works pleasing to God. Such a person builds upon it the gold of wisdom, which shines by God’s true light in his inward understanding and the secret place of his heart; and silver, that is, the brilliance of holy eloquence by which he teaches others; and precious stones, that is, examples of virtues and good works, with which he adorns what he says or thinks.

But whoever still loves worldly things, is entangled in earthly business, and is devoted to certain bonds and affections [Col. 0843D] of the flesh—to his house, wife, and property (ibid.)—yet is nevertheless a Christian, so that his heart does not depart from Christ and nothing is preferred to the foundation, builds upon it wood, hay, and stubble. These may reasonably be understood as such desires for lawfully permitted worldly things that they cannot be lost without pain: wood, namely, for desires that are hard and weighty; hay and stubble for those that are small and light.

But each person’s work will be made manifest in the heat of temptation. For the day of the Lord will declare it—the day, of course, of tribulation (Zeph. 1). For the tribulation of the present time torments the elect by God’s ordering judgment, because “it is time for judgment to begin from the house of the Lord” (1 Pet. 4). Therefore the day of tribulation is called the day of the Lord, that is, the day of judgment. “Because,” he says, [Col. 0844A] “it will be revealed in fire.” He calls the same tribulation fire, as is read elsewhere: “The furnace tests a potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclus. 27). And the fire of tribulation will test what sort each person’s work is.

This fire must be understood in such a way that both pass through it: both the one who builds upon this foundation gold, silver, and precious stones, and the one who builds wood, hay, and stubble. For, in this present life, the fire of tribulation tests the work of both, if it befalls two faithful persons: one, that is, thinking of the things of God, how he may please God—that is, building upon Christ’s foundation gold, silver, and precious stones; the other thinking of the things of the world, how he may please his wife (1 Cor. 7)—that is, building upon the foundation [Col. 0844B] wood, hay, and stubble. The former’s work is not burned, because he did not love the things whose loss would torment him. But the latter’s is burned, because the things possessed with love do not perish without pain.

And this is what is said: “If someone’s work remains.” The work remains when someone thinks of the things of the Lord, how he may please God. “What he built upon it will receive a reward”: that is, he will receive that upon which he set his thought. Nor only after death; even in this life the soul of one who despises all things has its rest. “If someone’s work is burned,” that is, consumed by the fire of tribulation, “he will suffer loss,” because he will not have what he loved. “But he himself will be saved,” because no tribulation has moved him from the firmness of that foundation. “Yet so as through fire,” because what he did not possess without enticing [Col. 0844C] love, he will not lose without burning pain.

For the one who builds love for earthly things upon the foundation of the kingdom of heaven—that is, upon Christ—will have the love of temporal things burned away; and he himself will be saved, if he remains firm in the foundation, that is, if he has loved Christ before all things in such a way that he cannot be separated from Christ’s love. In the loss of temporal possessions he will suffer loss, and through a certain fire of pain he will arrive at salvation. Each person is safer from that pain and loss in proportion as he has loved temporal things less, or possessed them as though not possessing them.

Nor is it unbelievable that something of this kind may take place after this life: namely, that certain faithful persons may be saved through a certain purgatorial fire more swiftly or slowly according as they loved temporal goods less or more. For it must be believed that before the resurrection of bodies there is a purgatorial fire for certain light faults, because Truth says that if anyone speaks blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, it will be forgiven him neither in this age nor in the age to come (Matt. 12). In this statement it is given to understand that certain faults may be forgiven in this age and others in the age to come. For when it is denied of one, the consequent sense is clear: it is granted concerning some.

Yet this should be believed possible only in the case of small and very minor sins, such as habitual idle speech, excessive laughter, or the sin involved in concern for household affairs—a concern which can scarcely be conducted without fault even by those who know how fault ought to be avoided—or an error of ignorance in matters that are not serious. All these things weigh upon a person even after death if they have not been remitted while that person still lives [Col. 0845A] in this life.

For it must be considered carefully that the Apostle said that one can be saved through fire not when he builds upon this foundation iron, bronze, or lead—that is, greater and therefore harder sins, then incapable of being dissolved—but wood, hay, and stubble: that is, the smallest and lighter sins, which the fire easily consumes. Yet this must be known: there, at least, no one will obtain purification even from the smallest sins unless, while still in this life, he has merited by good deeds to obtain it there. It must also be known that that fire is more severe than anything a human being can suffer in this life. For all the torments which are here are far lighter [Col. 0845B] than it. Yet, in order not to suffer them, people do whatever they are commanded by another human being. How much better it is to do what God commands, lest they suffer those more severe things!

> “Do you not know that you are God’s temple, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? (2 Cor. 6.) But if anyone violates God’s temple, God will destroy him. For God’s temple is holy, and that temple is you.”

I said that you are God’s building, and that I laid the foundation of this building; whence it is evident that you are God’s temple. And do you not know this? Do you not know that you are God’s temple? You are God’s temple according to faith; at some time you will be God’s temple according to the Spirit. You are God’s temple so that he may dwell in you through faith and place in you the perfection of wisdom and the knowledge [Col. 0845C] of his mysteries. You are God’s temple, and the Spirit of God dwells in you. He did not say, “And the Spirit of God sanctifies and purifies you, so that God may dwell in you”; rather, he said, “The Spirit of God dwells in you.” Surely God dwells in his own temple. For what is God’s temple except God’s dwelling-place? Therefore the Holy Spirit is God, whose temple and dwelling-place we are. For he would not have a temple unless he were God.

“Do you not know,” he says, “that you are God’s temple, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” Above he had said of them that “the natural person does not receive the things of the Spirit of God” (above, ch. 2). Therefore they did not apprehend the knowledge of God’s Spirit dwelling in them; and, although the Holy Spirit dwelt in them, they were still natural, not yet [Col. 0845D] spiritual, because they were not yet able to apprehend their indwelling Spirit by knowledge. The Spirit is said to dwell even in such persons because he works secretly in them so that they may be his temple. And he accomplishes this in those who make progress and persevere in progressing.

Nor should it seem strange that someone has something and yet does not know what he has. To say nothing of the divinity of the Almighty: who readily grasps by knowledge what the soul is? Yet who does not have a soul? Finally, so that we may know most certainly that little ones in Christ, who do not apprehend the things of the Spirit of God—that is, who do not understand—nevertheless have the Spirit of God: he now rebukes as little ones those very persons whom, as we have said, he had above called natural, saying, “Do you not know that you are God’s temple, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” They ought not [Col. 0846A] to have been ignorant of this.

For you are God’s temple. But beware lest you violate his temple, because if anyone violates God’s temple—that is, either by corrupting his own or another’s body, or by dividing the people of the Church—God will destroy him: that is, he will destroy him with various punishments, both body and soul. Therefore beware of bodily sins, lest you offend him whose temple you are, lest he depart from you and you be turned into ruin. Beware also of the perverse teaching of the pseudo-apostles, lest your mind be violated through it. And rightly will God destroy the violator of his temple, because God’s temple is holy from the time it began to be God’s temple—that is, from baptism—which temple you are. He repeated this to pierce those who, living shamefully, had fallen by violating their own bodies.

[Col. 0846B]

> “Let no one deceive himself” (Col. 2). “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish that he may be wise” (Rom. 1). “For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written: ‘I shall catch the wise in their craftiness’” (Job 5); “and again: ‘The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain’” (Ps. 93).

Therefore let no one glory in human beings. You are God’s temple, and therefore let no one deceive himself: that is, let no one, deceived by his own vanity, flatter himself by promising himself future impunity for violating God’s temple, as though God disregarded sins of the flesh. Or, “let no one deceive himself” means: let no one lead himself away from Catholic truth into empty errors by turning after the pseudo-apostles, as though loving their wisdom. [Col. 0846C] Let no one do this.

But if anyone among you seems to be wise in this age—that is, if anyone among you is considered wise by the foolish wisdom of the age, which is a human invention—let him become foolish in his own eyes: let him cast aside empty wisdom and seem to himself to know nothing, so that he may be truly wise in God. For one deceived by confidence in his false wisdom cannot attain true wisdom, as were the pseudo-apostles, who, wishing to seem wise in the world, preached that God does not have a Son, that the incarnation is not real, and that the flesh cannot rise again. Thus the excellent teacher rightly now urges those Corinthians whom he had found wise in a carnal way first to become foolish, so that they may be able to grasp true wisdom.

And he adds why: because the wisdom of this world is foolishness with [Col. 0846D] God; that is, what the world judges wisdom, God judges foolishness. And while God does what the world denies can be done, he shows its wisdom to be foolishness—and truly foolishness. For it is written in the book of Job: “I shall catch,” that is, hem in on every side and, as it were, confine beside the net of my strict judgments, “the wise of the world in their craftiness,” so that their craftiness may avail them nothing either to escape my hand, or to accomplish what they devise against me, or to hinder what I have resolved to do against their wisdom.

Eliphaz expressed this saying thus: “He catches the wise in their craftiness” (Job 5). Yet divine wisdom rebukes Job’s friends for their speech, saying: “You have not spoken rightly before me, as my servant Job has” [Col. 0847A] (Job 42). Why, then, does Paul employ their sayings with such authority, if their sayings are shaken by the Lord’s rebuke? Or how do we reject their words as though evil when Paul establishes them on authority? Or how shall we judge right, on Paul’s testimony, what the Lord himself declared not right?

But we quickly recognize that these two things are not opposed if we weigh more closely the words of the same divine pronouncement. When he said, “You have not spoken rightly before me,” he immediately added, “as my servant Job has.” It is therefore clear that some things in their sayings are right, but are surpassed by comparison with what is better. For among some things which they say irrationally to blessed Job, they utter many forceful statements; but when compared with more forceful sayings, these lose the force of their strength.

And again, concerning the same matter, it is written in the Psalm: “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain”—namely, the thoughts of human beings, because those wise men themselves judged that they alone were human, while all others were like brute animals. The wise of the age do not know God’s thoughts, because they are just; but the Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, because they are vain. Their craftiness has no power against God, because he knows their thoughts. They are vain, that is, empty and false, because they think true what is false and false what is true. The thoughts of the wise are vain—of those who, with astonishing vanity, wished to be happy here and to make themselves happy by themselves.

And since human thoughts are vain, and the counsels of the wise are improvident and [Col. 0847C] weak—those who think that they can benefit themselves or others without God—therefore let no one glory in human beings, as though one might receive better things from one person than from another. For human beings understand nothing rightly and can do nothing by themselves; therefore one should not glory in them, but in him through whom they understand and are able.

> “Let no one glory in human beings. For all things are yours: whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come—for all things are yours. But you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.”

Let no one glory in human beings—teachers or baptizers. You ought not to glory in particular teachers or each defend his own, since you use them all. For not only these men, but all things are yours: that is, given to serve you; and one ought to glory only in things more excellent. Therefore you must glory in Christ alone, who is above you and has subjected all things to you, not in the things subjected to you. For all things are yours, to serve your advantage, including those things more dignified among human beings. Whether Paul be chosen or Apollos, they are yours, to minister to you; and so too is Cephas, that is, Peter, who is first among all the apostles. Thus it is evident that all the apostles are yours, since their chief is yours. For all apostles and preachers were sent for this purpose: to minister the word of salvation to you or to your brothers throughout the world. And what they do for your brothers [Col. 0848A] they must be believed to do for you also, because they benefit you too.

All things are yours: whether preachers, or even the world, if you think about it according to God’s will and place its ordained courses within God’s will; or life: your present life is yours if you pass it moderately and for God’s glory; or death is yours, that is, the dissolution of body and soul serves you, because for you it is a passage from this misery to eternal blessedness; or things present, if you use them so as not to offend; or things future, if, believing them, you desire them more, since they are better and eternal.

Or, the world is yours: that is, the four elements of the world serve you, for they were created for this purpose; and your present life serves you if in it you are corrected and earn eternal salvation; and death serves you if you are willingly prepared to die for Christ in hope of the future [Col. 0848B] promise; and present good things serve you, by which you may be sustained in serving God; and future things, in whose hope you serve. These are yours; for all things whatsoever are yours to possess.

But you are Christ’s possession, not a human being’s, so that just as all things have been granted to your judgment and subjected to you, so you too may be subjected to Christ, because through him you began to be, both in your first origin and in regeneration. Why, then, do you hope in human beings to Christ’s dishonour, when he himself has subjected both human beings and all things to you, so that you may be subject to him and place all your hope in him? But Christ is God’s, as his proper Son doing his will, so that you too may do Christ’s will. You are Christ’s, but Christ is God’s; and thus, through Christ as mediator, you are God’s. Christ is subject to God not [Col. 0848C] as unlike him or of another nature, but, as has been said, as Son to Father.

Thus far the Apostle has spoken concerning the glorying of the pseudo-apostles; here he begins to speak of his own being despised, because some Corinthians thought less highly of him. Therefore he warns that one should think of him as God who chose him thinks of him, and says:

## CHAPTER IV

(1 Cor. 4.) “Let a person so regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of God’s ministries. Here, moreover, it is required among stewards that a person be found faithful.”

Thus, he says, it has been divinely ordained that all things should be yours—whether Paul, Apollos, or Cephas—while you are Christ’s. And since this is so, no one should think more or less highly of us than God has appointed. Rather, let him regard us as ministers of Christ: that is, neither despise us as worthless nor glory in us as though we could accomplish anything through ourselves, but honour in us him whose ministers we are in the Gospel which we offer to you. And let him regard us not as masters, but as stewards of God’s ministries, because we distribute his ministries among you according to each person’s capacity.

Since the Apostle relied neither upon a clatter of words nor upon human wisdom, it ought to have been understood that he dispensed Christ’s ministries, in which not words but power shone forth, and through which not a human being but God appeared glorious. As a companion of fishermen, he preached Christ no differently from them. [Col. 0849A] Therefore, when he proves himself a minister of Christ and steward of God’s ministries, he marks out the pseudo-apostles and denies that what they hand down belongs to Christ, because they dissent from apostolic tradition.

“I and my fellow servants,” he says, “are stewards of the ministries of eternal salvation, by teaching and distributing the other sacraments.” There are indeed many stewards through whose ministry one comes to eternal salvation. But now, among those who administer baptism, impose hands, and give the Eucharist, it is required that someone be found faithful, so that he may be trusted to dispense rightly. For not all do this faithfully; rather, many act deceitfully, seeking what is their own, not what is Jesus Christ’s (Phil. 2), and turning heavenly ministry to the use of earthly profit. They seek not the salvation of those subject to them, [Col. 0849B] but their own advantages. Some who do not appear thus to seek earthly things alone nevertheless, from shame, fear, or concern for their own reputation, hesitate to rebuke offenders steadfastly.

Therefore it is required which among them may be found to perform faithfully the office of his stewardship, so that without deceit he may seek only the gains of his Lord. Or, those subject to them are rebuked by this passage because they now seek from them what is to be sought from the Lord in the age to come: namely, they inquire and investigate among them so as to find someone faithful among the stewards—that is, fit and worthy to dispense God’s sacred ministries to others. Such investigators are rightly rebuked, because they wish already here to do what God will do in the other life; they presume to judge the lives of their superiors, by whom they themselves ought to be judged; and they think that more worthy sacraments are dispensed to them by more worthy persons, whereas the sacrament of the saints is more or less beneficial not according to the holiness of the dispenser, but according to the devotion of the recipient.

> “But to me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by a human day; indeed, I do not even judge myself. For I am conscious of nothing, but I am not justified by this. Yet the one who judges me is the Lord.”

“You,” he says, “judge some stewards to be faithful and others unfaithful; but to me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you to be faithful or unfaithful.” For the righteous look not to human judgments, but to the examination of the eternal Judge, [Col. 0849D] and therefore despise the words of detractors. Hence the Apostle now says to the Corinthians who disparaged him: “To me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you.” Since he rebuked them for such great vices, he regarded it as a small thing to be judged by them, because, as they were not righteous, so they could not judge rightly. Or “by a human day” means by human light and reason: that is, he considered it a very small thing to be judged according to human laws. For, transcending human justice, he devoted himself to heavenly justice.

Or “by a human day” means by human understanding, which does not see hidden things and can be deceived. Or “by a human day” means by human beings while they are in their own day and the Lord’s day has not yet come. For the human day is called that on which human beings judge, because the Lord’s day also will come, on which the Lord will judge. It is a small thing for me to be judged by you or by [Col. 0850A] a human day; but neither do I judge myself, though I know myself better than you do. Therefore it is dangerous for you to judge concerning unknown things. For how can you discern my conscience? Or how can you examine with what intention I do whatever I do? As much as human beings can judge another, surely a person can judge himself more; but God judges a person more than that person judges himself. For there is such depth in a human being that the human being himself is hidden from himself, but he cannot be hidden from the Lord.

Therefore, rightly making little of human praises or reproaches, the excellent teacher says: “To me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by a human day.” Finding nothing even in his own heart for which he could reproach himself, he adds: “But I do not even judge myself. I am conscious of nothing.” He was conscious of no sin in himself. But because he had read, “Who understands transgressions?” (Ps. 18), he moderated his assertion, lest perhaps he had sinned through ignorance, and added: “But I am not justified by this.” Seeing that even his own judgment would not suffice for him unto perfection of holiness, he said that he was not justified by this.

Why, indeed, he did not trust even himself concerning himself, he explained when he added: “But the one who judges me is the Lord.” As though he said openly: I do not think even my own judgment about myself should be trusted, because he judges me whose judgment I do not comprehend. For I know that I am examined minutely by him who judges me. I recall that I have acted rightly, yet I do not presume upon my merits, because our life is brought before his examination, under which even our virtues tremble (Isa. 64). Neither I nor [Col. 0850C] you judge me; but the one who judges me is the Lord, who knows all things without hesitation.

> “Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes, who will also illuminate the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts; and then each one will have praise from God.”

Since, therefore, I do not even judge myself but reserve myself for judgment by the Lord, you too, restrained from judging by my example, should not judge before the time, because it is not yet time for judging. You cannot now form true judgments about people’s actions, because you are human beings and suspect things concerning them otherwise than they are. And if, because you are human beings, you cannot restrain suspicions, nevertheless restrain judgments—that is, definite and firm decisions—so that you may judge nothing [Col. 0850D] before the time, that is, before the day. For it is still night, and what will be seen in the day cannot be seen now. Do not judge before that time, but wait until the Lord comes to judgment and illumines all things in his day. He will also illuminate—that is, make clear—the hidden things of darkness: that is, hidden sins [variant: “of sinners”] which darken the mind; and he will reveal the counsels of hearts: that is, good thoughts which were considered in the heart with more mature deliberation and rational reflection.

Then, when all are set in the light, no one will be hidden from another; rather, all things will lie open to all. Nothing of what has been done and known can be concealed. There simplicity and hypocrisy alike will appear, so that one who was thought contemptible [Col. 0851A] may perhaps appear worthy, and one thought to be something may be found reprobate. Then, therefore, will be the time to judge without error. But now whoever departs from uprightness in thought sins in darkness. Hence we ought to rebuke others’ hearts boldly all the less because we know that our sight cannot illumine the darkness of another’s thought. But then all things will be open.

And then each one who acts or thinks well will have praise from God. For now human beings do not know who is worthy of praise. Then the praise will be from God, because that which will be praised and loved by one’s neighbour in another will be illuminated in that person by God so that it may not remain hidden. This is said only of the elect, whom God will praise and show to be worthy of praise (Matt. 25). Conversely, each of the reprobate will then have reproach.

> “But these things, brothers, I have transferred figuratively to myself and Apollos for your sake, so that in us you may learn not to go beyond what is written, that no one may be puffed up on behalf of one against another.”

I said that we must not glory in ourselves. But these things, brothers, I have transferred figuratively to myself and Apollos, so that you may not glory in us, for your sake—that is, for your benefit—so that in us, who are greater, you may learn not, by acting beyond what is written, where we read: “Let him who glories, glory in the Lord” (above, ch. I); or, “Cursed is the man who trusts in man” (Jer. XVII)—that one may be puffed up against another on behalf of another, that is, on behalf of a teacher or baptizer, or on his own behalf. “I,” he says, “and Apollos I have set forward as a figure for all, so that you may shrink from all others as from us” [Col. 0851C]. For he transferred these matters to himself and Apollos when, under the persons of himself and Apollos, he invalidated the boasts and perverse traditions of the false apostles, indicating them generally rather than individually, lest perhaps greater discord should arise among the people. For no one, upon hearing his own name, or that of one whom he favors, marked out, is willing to keep silence. But if the name is left unspoken, should anyone hear something, even if he understands that it is said of himself, he nevertheless pretends otherwise. Under this formulation, therefore, he invalidated their persons when he said: “I planted, Apollos watered” (above, ch. III), and so forth, so that in these things they might learn that nothing is to be ascribed to human beings.

> “For who distinguishes you? And what do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you glory [Col. 0851D] as though you had not received it? You are already filled; you have already become rich; without us you reign. And would that you did reign, so that we also might reign with you!”

One ought not to be puffed up against another for the sake of another teacher or baptizer. For what teacher or baptizer distinguishes you? That is, for example, if you were baptized by Peter, how are you distinguished from one baptized by Paul? There is no distinction, from whomever you have received sound teaching or baptism. But through the tradition of the false apostles you suppose yourself to be distinguished from the rest as though holier. Yet what have you from them that you did not receive from me? For whatever does not descend from apostolic tradition is corrupt. But if you received from me whatever good you possess, why do you glory in yourself or in them against me, as though you had not received this same thing from me [Col. 0852A]?

This is said against those who, hearing from false apostles the very things they had received from the Apostle, gloried in their teaching; for the false apostles, commending themselves by eloquence, turned glory toward themselves, whereas the Apostle had made himself appear contemptible, in order to render glory to God.

Or thus: the Apostle commands that no one should glory in a human being, but in the Lord. Yet the false apostles, and those whom they had deceived, thinking that they made themselves righteous by themselves, as though God had not given this to them but they themselves had done so, gloried not in the Lord but in themselves. Hence the Apostle now says to each such person: “For who distinguishes you?” He says this because, from that mass of perdition which came about through Adam, no one distinguishes a human being, so as to make him a vessel unto honor [Col. 0852B] or unto dishonor, except God (Rom. IX). But since a carnal and vainly puffed-up person, upon hearing, “Who distinguishes you?” might answer either aloud or in thought and say, “My faith distinguishes me; my prayer distinguishes me; my righteousness distinguishes me,” the Apostle immediately meets his thoughts and says: “For what do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?” For those who suppose themselves to be justified by themselves glory as though they had not received it; and therefore they glory in themselves, not in the Lord. Nothing is so contrary to this statement as for someone to glory in his own merits as though he himself, rather than God’s grace, had produced them for himself.

Or, as we have said, you ought not to be puffed up on behalf of any of the teachers whose disciple you profess yourself especially to be. [Col. 0852C] For which of them distinguishes you from those who perish? None: only the grace of God does so; yet you suppose that you are distinguished through your own merits. But what good do you possess which you have not received from God? Did God make you to exist, and did you make yourself good? Far be it. For if God gave you existence, and another could give you goodness, the one who gave you goodness would be better than the one who gave you existence. But none is better than God. Therefore you received from God both existence and goodness. But if you received them from him, why do you glory as though you had not received them—that is, as though you possessed them from yourself?

“You are already filled.” This must be read ironically, not affirmatively. “Already,” that is, before you are fit to receive solid food, you are already filled with the spiritual food of doctrine; that is, you seem to yourselves sufficiently strong, filled with the food of wisdom [Col. 0852D]. And before you have been stripped of poverty, you have already, as you suppose, become spiritually rich—that is, filled abundantly with the riches of the soul, which are virtues. And “without us,” that is, without our help, “you reign”: you rightly order the governance of your lives, as you imagine, glorying in what you have received from false preachers. According to your own estimation, you reign. “And would that you did reign, so that we also might reign with you”—that is, that we might follow you, although you disdain to follow us. It is as though he said: Would that you were not deceived by false boasting; perhaps then we might reign together. For the saints’ reigning now consists in being secure concerning Christ’s hope and promises, and rejoicing in adversities which befall them for Christ’s name.

> “For I think that God has displayed us, the apostles, as the last [Col. 0853A] of all, as men appointed to death; because we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings.”

We truly reign, and I fear that we do so without you. For “I think,” that is, I am thought to suppose, “that God has displayed us apostles as the last,” that is, as the most despised of all, as though reserved for no use but for death. This “I think” is according to your estimate—as something which ought by no means to be thought. For when he now says, “I think,” he indicates the rebuke of those to whom he speaks, not his own opinion.

Therefore we reign without you, because through the evils we suffer God displays us apostles to the eyes of the proud as the last—that is, as the most rejected, persons for whom he has no concern—as though appointed to death, that is, led away to death. This seems evident [Col. 0853B] because we have become a spectacle to this world, that is, to lovers of this world, who gather as if for a show to watch our punishments. Yet through all these things we are proved rather to be dear to God, who thus glorifies us through sufferings. Therefore I do not—as you supposed—think that God has made us most vile, because I humble myself in order to exalt God.

Or: you ought for this reason to reign with us, because I think, and know with certainty, that God has displayed us apostles as the last, after whom no apostles will succeed so perfect or so necessary for human salvation as Elijah and Enoch, who will appear at the end of time, and whom God preserves in order to free the children of Israel from the seduction of Antichrist. Thus he sent us also, to free you from the seduction of the false apostles, and to endure death for your life [Col. 0853C], just as they too will suffer. He has displayed us as the last, that is, as like those last heralds in the suffering of adversities, as persons appointed to bodily death for the deliverance of others, because we have become a spectacle to this world, whose injuries all publicly await in the sight of the whole people. For just as everyone runs together where a play is being performed, or wrestlers contend, or some monster is exhibited, so all alike, good and evil, gather to watch our punishments.

We are a spectacle both to angels and to human beings, whether good or evil. For among angels there are holy angels, whom we please by living well; and among human beings there are holy persons to whom our life is pleasing. There are also exceedingly wicked [Col. 0853D] human beings who mock our good life. These are the weapons of the right hand and of the left by which we overcome our enemy, if we are neither corrupted by prosperity nor broken by adversity (II Cor. VI). Good angels gather to behold the spectacle of our suffering, so that they may strengthen us by their presence and encourage others by the example of our contest; evil angels, so that they may rejoice when they see us, their adversaries, tortured, and turn others away from faith by the shock of punishments. Good people come to praise; evil people, to mock. The good, that they may be strengthened by our example; the evil, that they may delight in our punishments.

> “We are fools for Christ’s sake, but you are prudent in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are honorable, but we are dishonored. To this [Col. 0854A] very hour we both hunger and thirst, are naked, are struck with fists, are unsettled, and labor, working with our own hands (Acts XX; I Thess. II; II Thess. III). We are cursed, and we bless; we suffer persecution, and endure it; we are slandered, and we entreat. We have become like the refuse of this world, the offscouring of all things, even until now.”

He now shows how they reign without the true apostles, and how the apostles appear most despised to fools. This is a rebuke expressed with irony. “We,” he says, “are considered fools by Gentiles and Jews for Christ’s sake, whom we preach as crucified for the salvation of the human race. But you are prudent in Christ because you wish neither to preach nor say anything concerning him which might seem foolish to human wisdom [Col. 0854B]; and you wish to be Christians in such a way as not to lose the wisdom of the age.” This is like wishing to serve two masters, in the manner of the ancient Samaritans, who worshiped both God and idols (Matt. VI; Luke VI; IV Kings XVII).

“We are weak,” because we do not return injury to those who harm us and do not resist; “but you are strong,” because you powerfully resist opponents and suppress them by worldly strength. “You are honorable,” that is, revered and glorious; “but we are dishonored,” that is, despised and vile. All the things which he seems to deny, he affirms; and those which he appears to affirm, he denies. For these are the words of one who is angry, who confesses by denying and denies by confessing.

Then he speaks affirmatively, setting forth point by point his weakness, so that the power of his kingdom may shine out more fully. “To this very hour,” that is, from the first day of our conversion or preaching until now, we have endured want of food, drink, and clothing, and also blows from fists; because, freely and according to the true faith, preaching Christ without flattery and rebuking the deeds of the wicked, we have found no favor with people, but have suffered blows from them [Col. 0854C]. We are unsettled because they always drive and persecute us, lest, remaining long in one place, we teach more people. And we labor, working with our hands, that we may have something by which to live when no one gives to us; for not only, as was said, do we lack favor with people, but it is also unworthy to receive from those devoted to error. We preferred to do this because whoever receives from one who gives in order not to be corrected loses the freedom to rebuke and sins [Col. 0854D].

We are cursed by wicked people, and, on the contrary, we bless them by urging them toward good. We suffer persecution from them, and though persecution itself is severe, nevertheless we endure it and neither flee nor resist. We are slandered by them because they call us deceivers and evildoers; and we entreat God for them, or we entreat them not to blaspheme but to allow an explanation to be given them. And we have become “like the refuse of this world,” that is, persons by whom the world is defiled and, when they are cast out, cleansed—just as a house is cleansed of filth cast out from it. That is, we are so blasphemed by the impious and judged so vile that, in their estimation, we have become such persons as though we were sinners and so filthy that, once we were removed, the whole world would be cleansed of every sort of dirt. And we are reckoned “the offscouring of all,” that is, so superfluous, unclean, and useless for human purposes as the filings of iron or the peel of an apple, which is removed from every side so that the apple itself may be fitter and sweeter to eat [Col. 0855A]. For *peripsema* means the scraping or filing of any thing, or the refuse of fruits; and we are judged to be of so little value and utility as shavings of wood, iron, or tin, or an apple peel. We have endured these things from the beginning of our preaching until now—that is, down to the present.

Through all these things the Apostle and those like him are proved prudent in Christ, strong, and honorable, by the very means through which he appeared foolish, weak, and dishonored [Col. 0855B]. For he was rendered contemptible and despised even among the Corinthians, for whom he endured the evils mentioned thus far. And because he saw that his humility accomplished nothing among them, he complains, moved by grief, that so great a submission and such injuries could bear no fruit, but, what is worse, had advanced toward something worse. He adds:

> “I write these things not to put you to shame, but I admonish you as my dearest children. For though you may have ten thousand pedagogues in Christ, yet you do not have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, I begot you. Therefore I beseech you, be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ (Eph. V; Phil. III). Therefore [Col. 0855C] I sent Timothy to you, who is my dearest and faithful son in the Lord, that he may remind you of my ways which are in Christ Jesus, just as I teach everywhere and in every Church.”

Like a healing physician, he softens harsh things with gentle ones. For because in all these matters he had, as it were, sharply bitten them in secret, lest they, provoked to anger, should reject his admonitions, he shows that in everything he said he had held toward them a fatherly affection of love, so that they might obey him more willingly. The Corinthians would indeed have been hard if they had not been softened by this admonition, in which, as beloved children, they are so humanely entreated by their father.

“I do not write these things,” he says, “in order to put you to shame,” that is, to bring such shame upon you, but rather I admonish you so that you may be corrected—that is, through these things I exhort you toward better things—as my dearest children, namely spiritual children, for whom I have endured so many labors and so many stripes, and than whom I have none dearer. You are truly my children because I am your father. For even if you have ten thousand pedagogues in Christ—that is, as many perfect instructors as you might need, which is signified by “a thousand,” a number perfect in knowledge and in the observance of the ten commandments of the Law, signified by the number ten—or if you have ten thousand pedagogues, that is, however great a multitude of teachers in the observance of commandments, which is found not in Judaism but in Christ: even if, I say, you have pedagogues, that is, teachers, still you do not have many fathers [Col. 0855D], but rather one; for I alone begot you, because I alone preached to you. For I was chosen for this purpose: to proclaim to the Gentiles salvation through Jesus Christ (Acts XIII, XXII), through the Gospel—that is, through the preaching of evangelical doctrine—not in myself but in Christ Jesus, that is, in faith in Jesus Christ and in Christian newness; for when I first preached, you came into a new life.

Having said this, he shows that no one can love them with the affection with which he himself loves them. For who would love others’ children as he loves his own? Therefore they ought not to reject the admonitions of one who has suffered so much for them. Yet God is the one true Father, not in order to take this name away from others, but lest the grace of God by which we are begotten unto eternal life should be attributed to the nature, power, or even holiness of any person.

“Because,” he says, “I begot you, I therefore rightly beseech you, as children, to be imitators of me [Col. 0856A] in the things I do and endure, just as I am an imitator of Christ in the things he did and endured; for it belongs to children to imitate their father.” He wants them to imitate him, so that just as he suffered many destructions while proclaiming Jesus Christ for their salvation, at the hands of unbelievers and other faithless people, and did not yield or fall away from the faith but preached steadfastly, provided only that he might proclaim to them day and night the gift of God’s grace, so they too, remaining in his faith and teaching, might not receive the corrupt doctrines or inventions of the false apostles—that is, false apostles—but might resist them, despising reproaches and calumnies, in order to preserve for their spiritual father an affection inviolate and unstained.

“Therefore,” he says, “that you may imitate me as good disciples and faithful children obeying their father, I sent Timothy to you [Col. 0856B], through whom this letter is believed to have been sent. He is my dearest son in the faith through good conduct, and faithful in the preaching of the Gospel, which he faithfully ministers openly to all, in the Lord, not for earthly gain.” Or, “in the Lord he is my son,” that is, one whom I begot not in the flesh. “That he may remind you,” that is, admonish you by his conduct; or, “that he may remind you,” that is, instruct you by admonition in my ways, my ordinances, precepts, and teachings, which are in Christ Jesus—that is, according to his will and teaching, for in nothing do I depart from him, and for that reason they must be observed—as I teach everywhere in the world and, that is, in every Church; therefore they are authoritative.

Through him he wished to bring them back to the rule of truth handed down by himself [Col. 0856C], so that, reminded by his words and examples of conduct, they might reflect and recognize that they had not been wrongly instructed by the Apostle Paul, when they learned that all the churches maintain the same things which had been commanded to them.

> “Some have become puffed up, as though I were not going to come to you. But I shall come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I shall ascertain not the speech of those who are puffed up, but their power. For the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power. What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?”

It was necessary to send Timothy because certain persons among you have become so fearlessly puffed up with the doctrine of philosophers and the eloquence of orators, as though I were not going to come to you again [Col. 0857A]. They were puffed up and glorying one against another because they thought that the Apostle Paul would not come to them any more. For disciples are very often drawn back from evil by fear of their teacher’s arrival. For this reason some Corinthians were also indignant that he did not come to them, not from longing but from pride, as though he considered them unworthy of his visitation, whereas the Apostle’s aim was rather to make worthy persons out of the unworthy. He therefore had the intention of going, but the matters he was undertaking were more important.

“You suppose,” he says, “that I shall not come, or you are indignant because I do not come; but I shall come to you soon, if the Lord wills,” whose will must always be added to our plans, according to James: “You should say, ‘If the Lord wills, and if we live, we shall do this or that’” (Jas.
