IV) [Col. 0857B]. Or, “if the Lord wills,” that is, unless my own fault hinders it, so that we may know that all things depend not upon ourselves but upon God’s judgment.

“I shall come to you soon, if the Lord wills.” He who said, “I shall come to you,” shows that he wills it; he makes known his desire and promises a near arrival. But in order to speak more cautiously, he adds, “if the Lord wills,” so that, if he did not come, the Lord might be shown to have detained him for a just reason—namely, because of their unworthiness and unbelief. “I shall come,” he says, “and ascertain,” that is, test, not the worldly or human wisdom in the speech of those puffed up with this world’s wisdom, but their power in good works or in the performance of miracles. For the Lord himself did not say concerning Pharisees or deceitful people, “You will know them from their words” or from the sheep’s clothing [Col. 0857C] with which they are very often clothed (Matt. VII), but “from their fruits,” that is, from their works.

Therefore, as we have said, I shall ascertain and approve not the speech of human eloquence but the power of a good life, because the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power. That is, no one acquires or merits the kingdom of God through worldly eloquence or fluency, but through the power of good works; nor is the kingdom of God commended by brilliance of speech, but by the power of signs, just as good wine is not commended by ivy.

Indeed I shall come as quickly as I can; but which of these do you wish? Do you wish me to come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness? Above he had said that they needed a pedagogue and thereby signified that they were children [Col. 0857D]; then he said that they were loved by him as dearest children; now, as a wise father, he sets before them a rod, not death; a spirit of gentleness and love, not anger or hatred. For the rod signifies severity and correction. Now the Apostle adds words of terror, so that those who were puffed up, having undergone shame, might humble and correct themselves; for if he found them uncorrected, he would need to employ the rod against them—excommunicating some, that is, depriving them of communion and fellowship with believers; severely rebuking others; and physically chastising others, as befits a father.

If they truly prepared themselves as worthy to receive him, so that they might be found free from offense, then, when he came to them, he would have joy as a father with his dearest children. This is what he says: “Do you wish me to come to you with a rod [Col. 0858A],” that is, with the rigor of justice and correction, in which, although love is present, it does not appear to be present; “or in love,” that is, not in a hidden affection of love, but in manifest and open love, so that I may supply good things, “and in a spirit of gentleness?” It is more desirable to seek the former than to lack the arrival of a loving good father, even though stern; for, as Solomon testifies, the wounds of one who loves are better than the kisses of one who flatters (Prov. XXVII). “In a spirit of gentleness,” that is, with a gentle and indulgent disposition, so that I may spare your sins and show you the gentleness of my spirit through a cheerful countenance and sweet words.

## Chapter V

It is altogether reported among you that there is fornication, and such

> “fornication as is not even among the Gentiles: that one of you has his father’s [Col. 0858B] wife. And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that he who committed this deed might be removed from your midst.”

It is necessary that I come to you with a rod, not in love or a spirit of gentleness, unless you correct yourselves; because it is altogether—that is, by everyone or in every way—heard, known, reported, and perceived by me and by others that there is among you notorious fornication, which is lawful for no one; and such fornication as is not even among the Gentiles—that is, fornication so shameful and wicked that not even such occurs among the Gentiles—namely, that someone has his father’s wife: that is, one of you commits fornication also with his stepmother. The matter needs no witnesses, because it was committed publicly.

And in order to heighten this crime excessively, he says that not even those who do not know God commit such a thing, thereby showing what punishment should be inflicted upon the man who, standing under terrible divine justice, had admitted the guilt of so great a crime; and he shows that those who adhere to him are not free from the same crime. Such fornication is reported among you. And you, though such a crime is among you, are puffed up with pride and have not rather done what should have been done—that is, you have not mourned; you have not grieved over your brother’s sin or sympathized with him—so that he who did this deed might be removed, that is, cast out, from your midst [Col. 0858C], so that you might all by one counsel expel him from your community, that, put to shame, he might do penance, and the rest might not be infected: that is, that others might neither commit a like or the same crime because of indulgence. For you all appear participants in the crime so long as you allow one guilty of so great an offense to assemble with you unrebuked. Since you all know his crime and it cannot be concealed by any evasion, he must be expelled from the gathering of the brethren.

> “For I indeed, though absent in body yet present in spirit (Col. II), have already judged, as though present, him who has done such a thing: when you are gathered together in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and with my spirit, with the power of the Lord Jesus, to deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

You, among whom he is bodily present, have neither rebuked nor expelled him; but I indeed, though absent in body, am present in spirit—that is, absent in face, but present through the authority of the Spirit, which fills the world by power (Wis. I), not by bulk, and is absent nowhere. I have already judged him who has acted thus, so that you may not suppose that, though present through the same Spirit, I pronounce judgment from report alone. Without delay I have already judged him “in the name,” that is, in the place, of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose embassy I fulfill; “when you are gathered together,” that is, when you all assemble as one without dissension and expel him from the communion of believers.

“When you are gathered together as one, and with my spirit,” that is, by my authority, which I possess through the Holy Spirit given to me, “with the power,” that is, authority, “of the Lord Jesus,” who is the Savior of humankind, I have judged that such a man should be delivered to Satan [Col. 0859A]—that is, that you should deliver him to Satan by expelling him from the Church, since my authority and Christ’s power will cooperate with you in this. I have judged that such an offender should be delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that Satan may afflict him bodily and thus he may come to his senses.

For by a great art of teaching he was handed over in punishment to the one from whom he had voluntarily withdrawn in guilt, so that he who had been the author of the wicked vice might himself become the scourge of discipline. The Apostle is said to have possessed this power: if he excommunicated anyone, that person was immediately rebuked and afflicted by the devil, as much and for as long as the Apostle wished. For when he says, “to deliver to Satan for the destruction of the flesh,” the destruction of the flesh signifies a severe bodily affliction wrought through the devil. Or, “for the destruction of the flesh” means that carnal pleasure might perish in him; he was delivered to Satan for this end.

And this was done “that his spirit may be saved in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” [Col. 0859B], that is, that his soul may be saved on the day of judgment. For Satan did not receive power over his spirit when he afflicted him bodily, and therefore it is reserved safe for the Lord’s final judgment. Or, “that the spirit may be saved,” that is, that his soul may be made safe in the Lord’s day—that is, if at some time the Lord should visit his heart, if at some time the Lord should shine in his heart.

> “Your glorying is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump?” (Gal. V)

Your glorying is not good. You are proud, when instead you ought to have mourned for a brother sinning so grievously and removed him from among you, lest, by assenting to him, you should be defiled by his contagion. Or do you not know that “a little leaven,” that is, a little of the old dough—namely, fermented dough—“corrupts the whole lump”? That is, it changes all the sweetness of newness into the bitterness of oldness. So also the sin of one person, if known and not rebuked, contaminates many—indeed, all who know it and do not avoid it, or who, though able to rebuke it, conceal it. For a person does not seem to himself to be sinning when no one rebukes or avoids him. But if someone lacks the authority to cast out or convict a person whom he knows guilty, he is free from blame.

“A little leaven corrupts the whole lump,” because sometimes one vice or any incentive to wickedness infects a multitude of virtues with its poison.

> **Note:** [Col. 0859D] These words appear to be spurious.

Observe, diligent reader: according to Jerome, in the Epistle to the Galatians (ch. V), the wording should be: “A little leaven leavens the whole mixture.” In the same chapter he criticizes the old translator, saying that he translated his own sense rather than Paul’s words; and he prefers *mixture* (*conspersio*) to *lump* (*massa*). They define *conspersio* as flour moistened with water [Col. 0860A].

> “Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new mixture, as you are unleavened.”

Purge out from yourselves the old leaven—that is, cast out from yourselves and from your midst the foment of old wickedness which is in the fornicator, who is a member of the old human being and corrupts the whole multitude of people consenting to him. Therefore purge out this leaven, that is, cast it outside yourselves, cleansing yourselves from it, lest through consent to his wickedness it corrupt the sweetness of virtues in you [Col. 0860B]. Purify yourselves from this leaven in order that you may be a new mixture—that is, a new union joined together in unity—as you are unleavened; that is, as through baptism you have been made pure from corruption.

For a *conspersio* is flour joined together by water, commonly called dough. But a new mixture is one into which leaven has not yet been put. Therefore it is called *azyma*, that is, unleavened. For ζύμη (*zymē*) is the Greek word for “leaven.” Therefore, he says, be a new mixture, as you are unleavened: that is, let all of you be one thing through love, pure from the corruption of sin, having put on the new human being, as you were made unleavened in baptism.

> “For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed. [Col. 0860C] Therefore let us feast, not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.”

You ought to be a new mixture, because Christ, “our Passover,” that is, our paschal sacrifice, has been sacrificed. For the lamb which the Jews sacrificed at Passover was called “Passover,” as Luke plainly declares when he says: “The day of unleavened bread came, on which the Passover had to be killed” (Luke XXII). In accordance with this manner of speaking, Christ is called our Passover. The Jews’ Passover was a lamb sacrificed; our Passover is Christ sacrificed.

For just as the Jews, through the sacrifice of the lamb, were freed from the power of Pharaoh and his attendants [Col. 0860D], crossed the sea, and came into the wilderness (Exod. XII), and, after an interval of time, entered the land of promise, so we, through Christ’s sacrifice, have been freed from the power of the devil and malignant spirits; and, having crossed through baptism, have come to this conversion, in which we are now as though in a wilderness, awaiting entry into the heavenly inheritance. The Jews, freed from Egyptian slavery after the lamb was sacrificed, ate unleavened bread for seven days; and we, freed from demonic slavery after Christ was sacrificed, should eat unleavened bread throughout the whole course of this present life, which is measured by seven days—that is, we should be filled with good works without an admixture of the corruption of vices [Col. 0861A].

For we eat unleavened bread—that is, bread without leaven—if we perform upright works without the corruption of vainglory, and if we fulfill God’s commandments without an admixture of sin. Passover is also interpreted as “passage”; and Christ, sacrificed for our redemption, is our Passover—that is, our passage—because through him we pass from the devil to himself, and from this unstable age to his most firmly established kingdom. We pass to him who remains, lest we pass away with the world. Christ is for us the passage from vices to virtues and from present exile to the heavenly homeland, because he was sacrificed for us in order that, freeing us, he might cause us so to pass.

Therefore we ought to be a new mixture—that is, all renewed and, through the infusion of the Holy Spirit, made one through love [Col. 0861B]—so that we may be fit to eat the Passover; for Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed, and we are invited to his meal. For this reason also we ought to be such a mixture, because Christ himself is our passage, so that, if he finds us worthy, he may transfer us to the homeland of life. And because he is our Passover, that is, our paschal sacrifice, therefore let us feast—that is, let us eat this Passover—if we wish to be free from Pharaoh’s dominion, that is, from the ruler of this world, the devil.

Or, because Christ is our Passover, that is, our passage, therefore let us feast—that is, let us eat his body sacrificed for us—so that through this we may be able to pass to life, because otherwise we cannot pass to God (John XII, XIV, XVI). For when we desire to pass to life and glory, it is not sufficient for us to be a new mixture and unleavened, unless our spirit is aided by spiritual food and its singular provision for the journey, and our weakness is strengthened [Col. 0861C]. Therefore let us feast: that is, let us be refreshed by the feasts of his body and blood, so that we may not be in the old leaven, that is, in the corruption of our former manner of life. For whoever wishes lawfully to eat the Passover must cast off the leaven of oldness. For one who is still subject through lack of self-control to the old corruption has not known what the festival of new incorruption is. Therefore let us feast, not with old leaven, so that, receiving the sacrament of resurrection and incorruption, we may no longer be subject to corruption through any vices.

Let us feast, I say, not with old leaven, that is, not with the once customary heat of carnal desires [Col. 0861D], nor with the leaven of malice, by which we burn to injure others, and wickedness, by which we fail in goodness within ourselves; but rather let us feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. That is, let sincerity make life pure, and truth exclude every deceit. With the unleavened bread of sincerity, that we may be without decay—that is, without the leaven of vices corrupting us—and of truth, that the truth of good works may be in us.

> “I wrote to you in the letter: Do not associate with fornicators. Not at all with the fornicators of this world, or the greedy, or robbers, or idolaters; otherwise you would have had to go out of this world. But now I wrote to you not to associate: if anyone called a brother among you is a fornicator, or [Col. 0862A] greedy, or an idolater, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or a robber, not even to take food with such a person. For what is it to me to judge those outside? Do you not judge those within? But God will judge those outside. Remove the evil one from among yourselves.”

I now admonish you to purge yourselves of this. Yet even without this admonition you ought to have done so, because in another letter I already wrote to you not to associate with fornicators. He had sent them a certain letter which is not now extant, in which he had commanded them not to join themselves to fornicators and to the others of whom he now speaks. But because he had not distinguished which fornicators and criminals he meant—whether Christians or Gentiles—the Corinthians supposed that he had spoken of Gentile fornicators. [Col. 0862B] He now corrects their erroneous understanding and explains what he had said, declaring: Not at all with the fornicators of this world, that is, with Gentiles; rather, I wrote that you must withdraw from brethren of such a kind. You did not understand this correctly, and therefore did not take grievously the presence among you of the man who had his father's wife. But certainly—that is, in truth—I say that I commanded you not to associate with the fornicators of this world: those who wholly belong to this world, who have nothing in common with the heavenly world, but who, because of their unbelief and earthly desires, are children of this age. For a believer, even if he commits fornication or is avaricious, does not wholly belong to this world, because he believes and hopes.

This I did not command; rather, in that letter I wrote to you what you must also observe now: [Col. 0862C] that you should not associate with believing fornicators, or believing covetous persons, or extortioners—that is, those who commit acts of robbery—or even with those who, after baptism, serve idols: those who, through fear of punishments or for any other reason, after coming to the faith served idols and offered sacrifices to them. Do not associate with brethren who are such apostates. Otherwise—that is, if you associate with them—you ought to have departed from this world; that is, it would be better for you to die. It is an advantage to evildoers if they die sooner rather than continue longer in sins.

Or: I did not write that you should not associate with unbelieving fornicators and the rest who do not yet possess faith and are criminal; otherwise, that is, if I had commanded you not to associate with Gentiles, [Col. 0862D] you would have had to depart from this world—that is, you would necessarily have had to withdraw from worldly intercourse, since such people are everywhere. For people living in this world cannot avoid living among such persons, nor can they win them for Christ if they avoid their conversation and table fellowship. Hence the Lord also, eating with publicans and sinners, said: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill do” (Matt. X). And: “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners” (Luke V).

At that time I wrote that you should avoid fornicators and the rest, which you did not understand correctly because I did not specify whom I meant. But now, in this present letter, I have expressly written to you not to associate with those who do such things after baptism. Behold, I say this to you without ambiguity: if anyone who is called a brother among you—that is, one who bears the name of Christianity—[Col. 0863A] is a fornicator, that is, proved guilty of the crime of fornication; or covetous, that is, one who heaps up money beyond measure, trusting in it more than in God’s bounty; or an idolater, that is, one who returns to idols he had renounced, or eats idol-offerings; or a reviler, that is, one accustomed to curse others and speak ill of them; or a drunkard, that is, one who becomes drunk not once only but habitually; or an extortioner, that is, one accustomed violently to take other people’s goods—with such a criminal believer, that is, not only with the one found guilty of any of these crimes, but also with others held in similar vices, I command you not even to take food.

The Apostle does not forbid taking food with unbelievers; rather, later in this letter [Col. 0863B] he says: “If any unbeliever invites you to dinner, and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you” (below, X). For often through sharing meals and conversation with a faithful man, an unbeliever, while coming to love the believer, is converted to the faith. But with a believer in whom the aforementioned crimes or similar ones are found, he permits not only no sharing of the sacraments, but not even a common meal, so that, being shunned by all, he may be ashamed and correct himself.

Yet such a person is not to be avoided in this manner unless he has either voluntarily confessed his crime, or is publicly known to be such, or has been accused and convicted in some secular or ecclesiastical court. Many good Christians, however, remain silent and bear the sins of others [Col. 0863C] which they know, because they are often without proofs, and cannot demonstrate to ecclesiastical judges what they themselves know. For although certain things are true, they should not readily be believed by a judge unless shown by definite indications. Therefore the wicked are not to be removed from communion with the Church rashly or in whatever manner, but through judgment. If they cannot be removed through judgment, they should rather be tolerated, lest anyone, avoiding evil persons on his own authority and thereby himself departing from the Church, send to Gehenna those whom he seems to be fleeing.

Therefore, he says, I wrote expressly: if a brother is proved to be such, do not even eat with him, much less pray with him; for what concern is it of mine to judge those—that is, unbelievers—who are outside, that I should judge them to be avoided by you, as you supposed? Such persons [Col. 0863D] must be treated gently, so that through love and kindness they may be won for Christ. But do you not judge those who are within—that is, believers—and cut away from them, by ecclesiastical censure, the putrefaction of vices, so that they may be punished in this life for their sins and afterwards come cleansed to God’s judgment?

He also judges those who are within who discerns to which brother he should cleave, whom he should rebuke, and whom he should avoid. You judge only those who are within, lest they be condemned in the future judgment. But God has not entrusted those who are outside to your judgment; rather, he himself will judge them in the future according to the strictness of his justice, rendering them punishments worthy of them. Above, concerning unknown and doubtful matters, and especially concerning a superior, it was said: “Do not judge before the time” (above, IV). Here, however, [Col. 0864A] it is shown that churchmen ought to judge their brethren concerning manifest and certain faults. And because it belongs both to me and to you to judge only those who are within, therefore remove the evil man from among yourselves: cast out from your assembly the fornicator, by whose fellowship you are defiled.

The words, “Remove the evil from among yourselves,” are not to be understood as though each person should remove evil from himself, but rather that the evil man should be removed from among good people. That this is done by ecclesiastical discipline is sufficiently indicated by the Greek language, where it is written without ambiguity so as to mean “this evil man,” not “this evil thing.”

## Chapter VI

> “Does any one of you, having a case against another, dare to be judged before the unrighteous and not before the saints? Do you not know that the saints shall judge this world? And if the world shall be judged by you, are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters? Do you not know that we shall judge angels? How much more, then, secular matters? Therefore, if you have secular lawsuits, appoint as judges those who are held in contempt in the church. I say this to your shame. Is there then not a single wise person among you who can judge between his brother and his brother, but brother goes to law with brother, and that before unbelievers?”

On the occasion of this judgment, he begins to discuss judgments. In these they sinned in many ways: they disregarded believers and resorted to unbelieving judges; they appointed foolish judges; they litigated and defrauded one another; and they did other such things. Not only, he says, are you blameworthy because you do not judge a brother who is to be judged, although you ought to judge those who are within; you are also blameworthy because you transfer your cases to pagan judges to be decided. For one of you—that is, one from among you—having a dispute, that is, a matter of contention, against another believer among you, dares—that is, so boldly tramples upon the reverence due to Christianity—to seek judgment before the unrighteous and not before [Col. 0864B] the saints: that is, before unbelieving judges, who are not lovers of equity, rather than before Christians, who would judge you holy and justly.

It is as if he said: In this you despise sacred religion too boldly: you bring before unrighteous judges disputes which you ought to judge [Col. 0864C] among yourselves. He calls unbelievers “unrighteous” because they often despised the laws granted by God to humankind, or by false interpretation attributed their authority to idols. Therefore he rather urges that the case be conducted before God’s ministers, because they more readily pronounce the true judgment of the law out of fear of God. You sin in not bringing your disputes for judgment before the saints. For they ought to judge even such matters, because they will also judge the world. Surely those who are to judge the world itself are not unworthy to judge matters belonging to the world.

And this is what is meant: “Do you not know that the saints shall judge this world?” Namely, this world which is in errors and wickedness; for there is another, higher world. The saints shall judge this world—that is, people who belong to this lower [Col. 0865A] world—because they will come with Christ to judgment (Matt. XIX), and will wholly agree with his equity when he condemns worldly perversity. And if the world is then judged in you—that is, the wicked conduct of the world—are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters, that is, these earthly affairs? The world shall be judged in you if there is not then found in you the work of those who love only the world, if you do not appear like worldly and faithless people in conduct. And if this is so, you are unworthy now to judge the smallest matters. Therefore beware lest you perform the works of unbelievers and wicked persons by resorting to pagan judges, like the rest who do not know the Lord.

I prove further that the saints can judge earthly matters. Do you not know that we shall judge apostate angels? [Col. 0865B] How much more can we judge secular matters, which are inferior? We who, above our nature, have by God’s help preserved obedience shall judge those angels who sinned against their nature, because we shall agree with the justice of God in condemning them, and they will appear more condemnable by comparison with us. For since they themselves were of a loftier and worthier nature, and no frailty drew them away from that highest and unchangeable good, yet fell voluntarily through pride; while we, weak as we were, drawn toward sin and pressed down toward lower things by the infirmity of the flesh, have by humility and justice strained with all our might toward things above: they will deservedly be condemned more severely in comparison with us [Col. 0865C], and our consolation will torment them more harshly (Wisdom V).

And since it has been shown sufficiently reasonably that we can judge these secular matters, therefore, if you have secular lawsuits—that is, matters concerning worldly affairs—appoint as judges those in the church who are held in contempt. This means: let those of lesser merit in the church, who do not excel in the powers of great gifts, judge earthly affairs, so that lesser matters may be supplied through those who cannot perform great goods, and those unable to penetrate inward things may at least perform necessary outward services. Thus those whom spiritual gifts do not adorn should serve in earthly administrations. You ought to appoint such persons from among yourselves as judges, rather than carry your cases to unbelievers.

And I say this to your shame: [Col. 0865D] you have cause for shame from what I say, namely, that there is not among you anyone wise enough to judge between his brother and his brother; rather, brother litigates with brother—which is evil—and does so before unbelievers—which is worse. The Apostle wishes a wise believer to be chosen as judge because he knew the Corinthians to be so inconsiderate that they might perhaps choose unskilled brethren as judges. For he knew how lukewarm and unprovident they had been found in other matters. Although he called those whom he commanded to be appointed judges “contemptible,” he nevertheless now calls them wise.

What follows from this except that those should examine earthly cases who have acquired wisdom concerning external affairs? But those enriched with spiritual gifts certainly ought not to be entangled in earthly [Col. 0866A] business, so that, being not compelled to administer lower goods, they may serve higher goods more actively. Yet they ought not wholly to abandon the affairs of weak neighbours, but should entrust them to others fit to handle them. Hence Moses also appointed seventy men over the people in his place (Num. XI), so that the more he withdrew himself from external affairs, the more ardently he might penetrate inward things. Thus both the foremost men make greater progress in spiritual gifts, because base matters do not trample down their minds; and, conversely, the least in the Church do not live without good work, because they find right things to do in outward affairs.

> “Indeed, it is already altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another. Why do you not rather [Col. 0866B] accept wrong? Why do you not rather endure being defrauded? But you yourselves do wrong and defraud—and this to brothers.”

Because of the foregoing, one might have thought that having a lawsuit against another was not a sin, but only seeking to have it decided outside the Church, unless he had now immediately added: “Indeed, it is already altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another.” For the Lord also said: “If anyone wishes to take your tunic and contend with you in court, let him have your cloak also” (Matt. V). Therefore he forbade his own to litigate with others about worldly matters. For this reason the Apostle now says that it is a fault.

Still, since he permits such cases to be settled in the Church by brethren judging brethren, while [Col. 0866C] sternly forbidding them outside the Church, it is plain that this is granted by concession to the weak. Although a Christian ought not to litigate, nevertheless, if a matter is grave and cannot be disregarded, he should bring the case before the Church, lest he incur both present loss and perhaps offence. “Indeed,” he says—that is, so soon after the sanctification of baptism—it is altogether a fault among you, from this fact alone, that you have lawsuits among yourselves concerning perishable matters, whereas you ought to despise all outward things in order to preserve the inward goods of your minds.

And lest anyone excuse this by saying that he has a just case, but wishes by a judicial decision to remove from himself an injustice he suffers, he immediately meets [Col. 0866D] such thoughts or excuses and says: Why do you not rather—that is, more willingly—accept, that is, hold as welcome and pleasing, an injury—that is, an open violence unjustly inflicted upon you—rather than destroy peace with a brother by litigation? And why do you not rather endure hidden fraud committed against your possessions than lose tranquillity of heart by contending with one another in court?

Here “injury” denotes unjust harm violently inflicted, such as robbery, assault, a wound, shameful abuse, and similar things. Fraud, however, is perpetrated craftily, deceitfully, and treacherously against one whom a person intends to deceive. Why do you not endure both patiently? But you commit injury, though you ought to have endured it when committed; and you defraud, rather than enduring fraud. And you are not afraid to do this to brethren, although you ought not to do such a thing even to [Col. 0867A] enemies. You commit injury when, through your injustice, a dispute arises before judges; and you defraud when you corrupt the judges themselves by gifts. And you do this to brethren, whom you ought to help; and one who spares not his own people—what will he do to others?

> “Do you not know that the unrighteous shall not possess the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived. Neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners shall possess the kingdom of God. And such indeed were you; but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (Gal. VI; Eph. V; 1 Tim. I).

[Col. 0867B] You inflict injury and fraud upon brethren, yet flatter yourselves on account of the Christian name, as though by it you would be saved while doing such things. But do you not know that the unrighteous—that is, those who transgress equity by committing injuries, frauds, and similar acts—shall not possess the kingdom of God, which God promised to the righteous and holy? Therefore take care not to be unrighteous, lest you lose God’s kingdom. For no unrighteous person shall possess it, even if he possesses the sacraments of Christianity; and apart from that kingdom there is no salvation, because everyone will be either in that kingdom or in hell.

Therefore do not be deceived, thinking that there is a place of salvation outside the kingdom, or that God, through his mercy, will bring you into it solely because of Christian faith if he finds you unrighteous. For neither fornicators, who sleep with women to whom they are not married, [Col. 0867C] nor idolaters shall possess the kingdom of God, but shall perish in the kingdom of the devil; nor adulterers, who violate other men’s wives; nor the effeminate, who defile themselves by themselves; nor men who lie with males, after the manner of the Sodomites; nor thieves, who secretly take others’ goods; nor covetous persons, who, fearing that God will cease to provide them with necessities, gather superfluities beyond measure; nor drunkards, who pursue the vice of drunkenness; nor revilers—that is, detractors, who strive to speak evil of brethren, or who are not ashamed to curse them; nor extortioners, who are accustomed openly to plunder other people’s goods: none of those who are such shall possess the kingdom of God, because any single one of these crimes [Col. 0867D] takes away that kingdom.

And such indeed were you—that is, you were such persons, because all these evils were in you. Yet do not despair of receiving the kingdom, because you were washed from these things in baptism; and therefore it is more shameful if you return to them. Nor were you only washed for the remission of sins, but you were also sanctified in baptism through the Holy Spirit. Nor merely sanctified, but justified through faith. And you received these great gifts of grace in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose name was invoked over you in baptism, and in the Spirit of our God, who filled the water of baptism. For both the invocation of Christ’s name and the infusion of the Holy Spirit granted these things to you. Therefore do not return again to your former evils, lest you lose all these goods [Col. 0868A].

Or: you were washed by tears, and sanctified by amendment of life; for an improved life sanctifies those whom the affliction of tears, washing them through repentance, cleanses. And you were justified by persevering in righteous works. Therefore beware of committing crimes again, lest you come to lose the kingdom.

> “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial” (below, X; Sirach XXXVII). “All things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any. Food is for the belly, and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them. The body, however, is not for fornication, but for the Lord; and the Lord for the body. And God indeed raised the Lord, and will raise us also by his power.”

Because above he had said that loss should rather be endured than cases wrongly pursued, lest anyone suppose that one’s property [Col. 0868B] should never under any circumstances be reclaimed, he adds: “All things are lawful for me,” that is, all my goods may lawfully be reclaimed by me; yet I shall not reclaim them through a lawsuit, because this is not beneficial for my course, but hinders it. All things are lawful for me to reclaim by legal right through a judgment; but I, being free, will not be brought under the power of anyone—that is, I do not wish to be made subject to the authority of any judge or witnesses by entreating them to favour me more. Therefore they are not to be reclaimed. [Note: [Col. 0867D] An obscure passage.]

Nevertheless, food is due to the belly, for which it was created; and the belly to foods, because it cannot otherwise be sustained. But God will destroy both it and them, so that neither the belly will require food nor food provide any sustenance for the belly. When it is said, “Food is for the belly and the belly for food,” these things relating to food are shown to be necessities of nature, and therefore it is lawful to reclaim them. [Col. 0868C] Yet one should not labour greatly for them, because they will be destroyed; and therefore a lawsuit concerning them may either be pursued or omitted.

Food is due to the belly, but the body is not due to fornication; and thus judgment concerning this cannot be omitted, as you are accustomed to do, since you did not judge fornication. But let us return to what was said: “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial.” For only those do not fall into unlawful things who sometimes restrain themselves even from lawful things. Bound by this restraint, the Apostle fittingly indicates himself to be so bound, saying: “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial.” Yet, to show in how great liberty of mind he expanded himself by his self-restraint, he added: “All things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any.”

For when the mind follows conceived desires [Col. 0868D], it is proved to be enslaved to the things by whose love it is overcome. But Paul, for whom all things are lawful, brings himself under the power of none, because by restraining himself even from lawful things, he transcends with contempt those things which, if enjoyed, would oppress him. “All things,” he says, “are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial.” As he shows lawful those things forbidden by no command of the Lord, so it is more beneficial that they be governed not by the prescription of law but by the counsel of charity. These are the things additionally spent upon the wounded man who was brought, through the mercy of that Samaritan, to the inn to be healed (Luke X); and therefore they are said not to be commanded by the Lord, although it is urged that they be offered to the Lord, so that they may be understood to be more pleasing insofar as they are shown to be not owed.

Therefore something may be lawful [Col. 0869A] and yet not beneficial; but what is not lawful cannot be beneficial. Hence not all lawful things are beneficial, while all unlawful things are not beneficial. Those things seem to me lawful but not beneficial which are permitted by the justice that is before God, but are to be avoided because they might cause offence to people and thereby impede them from salvation. But those things are not lawful, and therefore not beneficial, which justice itself forbids in such a way that they are not to be done, even if praised by those to whose knowledge they are brought. If this is so, the Lord forbids only unlawful things in order that lawful things which are not beneficial may be avoided not by the bond of law but by the free beneficence of love.

It should also be noted that, while the Apostle preached these things to them, he received nothing from them, but lived by the labour of his hands. [Col. 0869B] Hence some of them thought that he had refused support because he knew that he was not an apostle. Against them he now says: “All things are lawful for me”: all worldly things lawful to the other apostles are lawful to me also, because, like them, I may receive maintenance from disciples. Yet not all lawful things are beneficial, because if I received lawful support, I would give pseudo-apostles an occasion for receiving it. All these things are lawful for me, but for the sake of this support I will not be brought under anyone’s power, so as to lower my authority because of their gifts.

For if the Apostle received from those whom he rebuked for such great vices, he would weaken the authority of teaching granted him by the Lord. One cannot rebuke firmly a person from whom one receives, especially since an ill-disposed person is ready to give precisely in order to humble [Col. 0869C] the preacher. Therefore he says: “But I will not be brought under the power of any.” Pseudo-apostles, however, who preached for the sake of gain, did not wish to be disliked by sinners.

“All things,” he says, “are lawful for me, as for the others: I may receive support as they do, because food is due to the belly and the belly to food.” Yet these things are not to be greatly cared for, because they are transitory: God will destroy both the belly and foods. For in the future we shall not eat and drink, but shall feed on that bread which came down from heaven, so that what is written may be perfectly fulfilled: “Man ate the bread of angels” (John VI; Psalm LXXVII). God will destroy foods and the belly when he destroys need by wondrous satiety and clothes this corruptible body with everlasting incorruption, so that salvation in this body may be perfect [Col. 0869D], with no corruption remaining and no decay succeeding, and so that it may need no support from bodily food. I said that the belly is due to foods by which it is sustained temporarily. But the body is not due to fornication; it is due to the Lord.

The holy Apostle, arguing against excess of food, consequently comes to fornication. For excess of food is the mother of lust: pleasure in sexual organs follows a belly stretched by food and drenched with draughts of wine. The order of the vices corresponds to the order of the members. The body is not due to fornication as the belly is to moderated foods, because the body can always subsist without fornication, whereas the belly cannot subsist without food. Therefore fornication is [Col. 0870A] superfluous, but the restoration of food is necessary. Hence, although for a time the belly is due to moderate foods, the body is never due to fornication but always to the Lord Christ, in order to serve him. And the Lord Christ is due to the body, that he may himself be its reward, granting it a share in his immortality.

For the body dedicated to Christ will be rewarded with a spiritual gift on account of the merit of its leader—that is, the soul. And the glory of Christ’s body will be given to the body which now continually serves his commands. Thus the Lord Christ is the reward due to our body if our body has been subject to him in all things. But God the Father raised the Lord Christ and will likewise raise us. This means: just as God the Father raised him who is Lord, because he found him obedient in all things, [Col. 0870B] so he will raise our body, if it has been altogether subject to the same Lord, and make it a participant in the Lord’s glory—and this by his power, which is Christ, to whom nothing is impossible.

For the Lord also raised Christ by the power which is Christ himself—that is, by the power of Christ’s own divinity—and he will raise us by that same power, so that we may follow our head into incorruption and glory, if we are worthy members. Therefore we must withdraw from every fornication and impurity and devote ourselves to the pursuits of holiness, so that we may be worthy to attain such great glory.

> “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Far be it. Or do you not know that [Col. 0870C] he who cleaves to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, he says, ‘The two shall be one flesh’” (Gen. II; Eph. V; Matt. XIX; Mark X). “But he who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit.”

Truly, the body ought not to be enslaved to fornication but to the Lord. For do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ, who is your head because he became man for our sake? If he had assumed only a human soul, our souls alone would be his members. But because he also assumed a body, through which he is also head to us, who consist of soul and body, certainly our bodies too are his members. Our bodies, I say, are his members because of the body which he himself assumed from the stock of our body. And since this is so, shall I take [Col. 0870D] Christ’s members and make them members of a prostitute through fornication? Far be it that I should do this. For I ought not take Christ’s members away from him and give them to a prostitute.

They cannot at the same time be members of Christ and members of a prostitute; rather, they cease to be Christ’s members when they cleave to a prostitute. For as long as our body perseveres in the purity of holiness, it is a member of Christ. But if it embraces a prostitute, it is separated from Christ and becomes a member of a prostitute. Therefore, if anyone desiring fornication has become vile to himself and despises himself in himself, let him not despise Christ in himself; rather, out of reverence for Christ, whose member his body is, let him restrain himself from this shamefulness. For he will inflict great injury and great [Col. 0871A] contempt upon Christ if he prefers a prostitute to him, separating himself from Christ and cleaving to a harlot.

Those who cleave to her truly become members of a prostitute. For do you not know that one who cleaves—that is, mingles—with a prostitute becomes one body with her? Fornication makes both one, so that, as they are one in nature, they are also one in stain, while through that attachment of utterly wicked pleasure the two become one body: that is, they are united in the same crime. Truly one body, because one flesh. For the book of Genesis says, “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II). This was also said concerning those lawfully joined. And just as in lawful union the two become one body and one flesh through attachment, so that the members of one become those of the other through consent and fleshly pleasure [Col. 0871B], so it is also in unlawful attachment.

One who cleaves to a prostitute is one body with her; but one who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit with him. The spirit of a human being and the Spirit of God are indeed different in nature, but by cleaving there is made one spirit from two distinct spirits. Thus God’s Spirit is blessed and perfect without the human spirit, whereas the human spirit cannot be blessed except with God’s Spirit. Yet this human mind, which is the image of God, is so capable that it can cleave to him whose image it is, because it is ordered in the order of natures, not places, so that none is above it except him. When it has wholly cleaved to him, it will be one spirit, itself indeed coming to share in his nature, truth, and blessedness, but he not increasing in his own nature, truth, and blessedness [Col. 0871C]. When it cleaves happily to him, it will see as unchangeable everything that it sees, and then its desire will be satisfied with good things (Psalm CII).

> “Flee fornication. For every sin whatsoever a person commits is outside the body; but he who commits fornication sins against his own body.”

Do not become one body with a prostitute, but one spirit with the Lord: flee fornication. I do not say, “Fight against it,” but, “Flee from it,” because conflict may be awaited with other vices, whereas this one must be fled, since it can be conquered best in no other way. Therefore men ought to keep far away from women, and not even approach this vice in mind, if they wish to become victors. And rightly you ought to flee this evil, because no sin harms and defiles the body as fornication does. [Col. 0871D] For every sin whatever a human being commits—that is, one inclined to sin from his own frailty, since he was made from earth—is outside the body, that is, outside the defilement of the body: plainly, from all other sins no deformity or disgrace is brought upon the body. But one who fornicates sins against his own body, that is, against the honor of his body. For fornication pollutes the body itself so greatly and inflames the heat of lust so greatly, insofar as the poison of unlawful pleasure spreads itself through the whole body. In other sins too, not all the members desire the same thing in the way they do in fornication. Therefore by this sin a person is more deformed, because this more than another sin ranges about in the heart, [Col. 0872A] and all the members are enslaved to this work.

Or: “Every sin whatever a human being commits is outside the body,” that is, in every sinful desire the soul remains outside the nature of the body, because it remains in its own awareness, understanding that the things it does are evil. But one who fornicates sins against his own body, because in the desire and act of fornication the soul sins in such a way that it is reduced to the nature of its body: then it thinks of nothing, relishes nothing, attends to nothing except things of the flesh. For the whole person is so swallowed up by and in the body itself that it can no longer be said that his very mind is his own; rather, the whole person together may be called flesh, “a spirit that goes and does not return” (Ps. 77). Therefore the Apostle seems to heighten the evil of fornication above all other sins. Although these are committed through [Col. 0872B] the body, they do not make the human mind so bound and enslaved to fleshly desire as, in the act of bodily fornication alone, the mind is mingled and glued together with it—so utterly conquered that at that moment, in the experience of so great a shameful act, a person is permitted to think or attend to nothing else except what he gives himself over to.

Hence he is rightly said to sin against his own body, because nowhere is the whole person so fastened to the pleasure of the body itself that, in comparison with this great evil, other sins seem to be outside the body, even though they are exercised through the body. For the force of fornication alone is so great that the fornicator subjects himself to the condition of imperious lust and makes himself the most wretched slave of his own body during that most unclean [Col. 0872C] act. Thus, as has been said, the human mind is not free to think or attend to anything other than what it does in the body itself; and so it sins against its own body—that is, in the very commission of sin it is miserably submerged wholly in the pleasure of its body.

These things have been said concerning the particular fornication of this body. But there is also a general fornication of the human soul, by which anyone who does not cling to God clings to the world. James rebukes such people thus: “Adulterers, do you not know that friendship with this world is enmity with God? Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of this age is made an enemy of God” (Jas. 4). And concerning this general fornication of the mind, which contains every evil within itself—by which one does not cling to God while clinging to the world—the present statement may rightly be understood: “Every sin whatever a human being commits is outside the body, but one who fornicates sins against his own body.” For if the human soul does not fornicate by clinging to the world, but remains chaste by clinging to God, whatever other sins it may incur through ignorance, negligence, forgetfulness, or failure to understand, owing to the frailty of mortality, will be outside the body—that is, outside the evil of bodily and temporal desire. But if, by clinging to the world, it makes itself far from God, it sins against its own body, because the human mind is drawn out and stretched toward every temporal and fleshly thing by bodily desire and by fleshly perception and prudence, “serving the creature rather than the Creator” (Rom. 1).

[Col. 0873A] “Or do you not know that your members are a temple of the Holy Spirit (2 Cor. 6; above, ch. 3), who is in you, whom you have from God, and that you are not [your own], having been bought at a great price (below, ch. 4; 1 Pet. 1)? Glorify and bear God in your body.”

Again, fornication must be fled because your bodily members are a temple of the Holy Spirit; and do you who wished to fornicate not know this? Therefore do not suppose that God is unconcerned about sins of the flesh. You grievously offend him if you corrupt his temple, that is, the members of your body. Just as you do not want your own houses to be defiled, so neither does God want his house, that is, your body, defiled. If you do not spare yourselves for your own sakes, spare yourselves for God’s sake, who made you his temple. For you sin grievously if you corrupt his temple, which is in you. [Col. 0873B]

Your members are a temple of the Holy Spirit. Indeed, the same Spirit is most plainly declared to be God, because, unless he were God, he certainly would not have a temple. Nor is he less than Christ, whose temple your bodies are, since they are members of Christ. The members of your body are a temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you as God in his temple, whom you have from God the Father. Therefore take care not to offend the Holy Spirit who dwells in you, nor God, who gave you this Spirit. You are a temple of the Holy Spirit so that, remaining in you, he may govern all your members and move them to act well. And you are not your own, so that you may be free to do what you wish; rather, you belong to him who bought you with his own blood, [Col. 0873C] so that you may do his will.

For it is plain that one who has been bought is not at his own disposal, but at the disposal of him by whom he was bought, so that he does not do his own will but that of the other. Therefore serve the Lord more earnestly, who bought you out of the enemy’s hand, lest, offended by you, he hand you back to that same destroyer. Truly, you are not your own to do whatever pleases you, because you were bought for God’s service at a great price, that is, with the blood of the Lord himself. That blood is a great price, not by bodily quantity but by spiritual power and holiness, because there was no sin in him but all righteousness. Therefore take care not to join your members—which are a temple of the Holy Spirit and have been redeemed at the price of the Lord’s blood—to a prostitute, to the dishonor of the Redeemer and the Holy Spirit. Rather, “glorify and bear God in your body,” [Col. 0873D] that is, the Holy Spirit in his temple.

To glorify God is to live according to his law. To bear God is to show his image in good deeds. Glorify God by acting well, and bear God by taking his yoke upon yourselves (Matt. 2), and do this in your body—that is, in the governance of your body—so that nothing may be observed in your body that pertains to God’s dishonor rather than commends his glory.

## Chapter VII

“Now concerning the matters about which you wrote to me: it is good for a man not to touch a woman. But because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, [Col. 0874A] and let each woman have her own husband (1 Pet. 3). Let the husband render the due to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. A woman does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; and likewise a husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does. Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, so that you may be free for prayer; and return together again, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control. But I say this by way of concession, not command. Yet I wish all people to be as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God: one indeed in this way, another in that way. Now I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they remain as I am. But if they do not exercise self-control, let them marry. For it is better [Col. 0874B] to marry than to burn.”

The Corinthians, stirred up by the perverse opinions of pseudo-apostles, who said hypocritically—so as to seem purer than others—that marriage ought to be despised, sent the Apostle a letter concerning these matters in order to learn what he himself thought. Because they were not pleased with that opinion, they passed over other matters and asked only about marriage and matters that seemed to pertain to it. Among other things, they asked by letter whether, after coming to faith in Christ, they ought to remain celibate and dismiss the wives they had for the sake of continence; or, if virgins had come to faith, whether they should enter into marriages. They also asked whether, when one of two pagans had believed in Christ, the believer should leave the unbeliever; and, if wives were to be taken, whether he commanded that only Christian women be taken [Col. 0874C] or pagan women too. Let us therefore see what the Apostle wrote back in reply.

But the text is connected thus: I urge you to glorify and bear God in your body, which is clean and holy. But concerning the matters about which you wrote to me, I want you to know that it is good for a man not to touch a woman. From this it is clear that touching is evil. For nothing is contrary to good except evil. But if it is evil and yet forgiven, it is granted so that something worse may not result from evil.

At the same time the Apostle’s prudence must be noticed. He did not say, “It is good not to have a wife,” but, “It is good not to touch a woman,” as though there were danger even in touching, as though one who touched her could not escape. For just as one who touches fire is immediately burned, so a man, by touching a woman, becomes aware of his nature [Col. 0874D] and understands the difference of sex. It is good not to touch. But in order to avoid fornication, let each have his own lawful wife, not a concubine, and let each woman have her own husband. Fear of fornication alone causes these things to be permitted.

It is as if someone were to determine: “It is good to eat wheaten bread and to consume the purest fine flour; yet, lest anyone compelled by hunger eat cow dung, I permit him to eat barley also.” Wheat does not thereby lose its purity if barley is preferred to dung, just as marriage is now preferred to fornication. Nor did he say, “Because of fornication let each man take a wife.” Otherwise, under this excuse he would loosen the reins of lust, so that whenever a wife died another would have to be taken lest we [Col. 0875A] fornicate; and those who had promised continence, or who by divine authorities cannot have a wife, would seem to be released to take one. But he says, “Let each have his own wife”—his own, namely, the one whom he had before believing. How good it was not to touch a wife and, after faith in Christ, to know her only as a sister and not as a spouse, unless fornication made touch excusable.

Let the husband render the due to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. Once spouses have been joined together, it is not permitted for one to practice continence without the other’s consent; rather, one is compelled to render the due to one’s spouse, lest the incontinent person fall into the condemnable crime of adultery. Yet God accepts the intention of continence alone in the person who would wish to preserve continence but renders the due so that the spouse [Col. 0875B] may not perish.

A woman does not have authority over her own body, either to give it to another man or to practice continence, but her body is under her husband’s authority. Likewise a husband does not have authority over his own body, either for another woman or for continence, but the woman has it in her power. Here lordship is not taken away from the man, but vice is. For in this matter both are equal, so that neither may do what he wishes with his own body—that is, with that part of the body by which the two sexes are distinguished by the fleshly lot—though in other matters the husband has precedence. And because neither has authority over his or her own body, therefore do not defraud one another—that is, withhold the marital due from one another—lest disagreement produce adultery.

That spouses have intercourse apart from the intention of procreation [Col. 0875C] is not an evil of marriage, but is pardonable because of the good of marriage, which is threefold: fidelity, offspring, sacrament. Fidelity: that one does not have intercourse with another man or woman. Offspring: that it may be reared religiously. Sacrament: that the marriage may not be separated.

Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by agreement—that is, by mutual arrangement—for a time, that is, for some interval of more sacred time, so that you may be free for prayer. For your weakness cannot accomplish what is commanded elsewhere: that you pray without ceasing (1 Thess. 5), because whenever you render the due to one another, you cannot pray. Therefore, if prayer must always be offered, marriage would never have to be served. But because you are not equal to this, at least abstain at intervals, so that you may be able to persevere in prayer, because you need the aid of prayer.

[Col. 0875D] For lest such married life be condemned, simple prayer to God must be offered. And although marriages are pure, one must nevertheless abstain even from lawful things so that prayer may more readily be brought to its effect. For even under the law, those wishing to be sanctified abstained from marital intercourse so that they might become holier. When someone does not touch even what is permitted, he shows that he desires to receive what he prays for.

I said that, for the sake of prayer, you should mutually agree to observe continence for a time; and, once the time for that prayer is completed, return again to the same marital act. For though it is a fault, it is pardonable because of marriage, and by it fornication is avoided (Ps. 5). The least fault must indeed be allowed if the greatest cannot otherwise be avoided. Return to the same natural use, [Col. 0876A] lest Satan—that is, the devil, adversary of your salvation—tempt you toward fornication because of your lack of self-control, that is, because you cannot contain yourselves. For if both of you could observe continence, Satan’s temptation would not be to be feared, because he would prevail against neither of you.

I say that you should return together, but I say this by way of concession, not command, because this is granted to you, not commanded. Therefore one who acts otherwise does not sin; indeed, one who acts thus sins, but more lightly. For what is forgiven, and not commanded, is not without fault. But when we are constrained amid uncertainties, it is useful to submit in lesser matters lest we sin in greater ones. For that is found to be a fault which is said to be granted; yet it is the more readily remitted insofar as, through it, no unlawful thing is done, provided that what is lawful is not kept without moderation. [Col. 0876B]

For spouses are free from fault in intercourse only when they come together not to satisfy lust but to receive offspring. Yet other intercourse, done for pleasure alone, receives pardon because of marriage. “This,” he says, “I permit you weak persons by concession; nevertheless, I wish, if possible, that all people should be as I myself am,” that is, abstaining from all intercourse, as I abstain. But every believer has his own gift from God: one in this way, so as to be wholly continent; another in that way, so that, joined to a wife, he has intercourse with no one else. Here it clearly appears that not only continence is a gift of God, [Col. 0876C] but also the chastity of married people. Since these are shown to be God’s gifts, we learn from whom they must be sought if they are not possessed, and to whom thanks must be given if they are possessed.

Let those who are joined render the due. But to the unmarried—that is, virgins—and to widows I say that it is good for them if they remain thus, as I am, that is, chaste. After granting married persons the use of marriage and showing what he himself wished and what he permitted, he turns to unmarried women and widows, sets himself forward as an example, and calls them blessed if they remain thus. How could he say, “It is good for the unmarried if they remain as I am,” unless he were physically intact? Or how could he say, “I wish all people to be as I myself am”? For if the one who said this had a wife, then he wished all people to be married [Col. 0876D] and no one to be a virgin. But far be it from us to suppose that he had a spouse. From childhood he was so fervent in spirit that he took no thought for this matter; while still a young man, he had been anticipated by God’s grace. Therefore he wishes all people to be virgins as he is, and unmarried women to remain such as he is.

“But,” that is, “if they do not exercise self-control”—if they see that they cannot restrain the incitements of the flesh—“let them marry.” They are unable to exercise self-control because they do not desire it with their whole heart, and therefore do not deserve divine help. For God helps the person whom he sees striving with all strength, and does not allow that person to be tempted beyond his own powers (below, ch. 10). Therefore women who, because of weakness of mind, cannot restrain the impulse of the flesh should marry, lest through fornication they fall into the abyss of the devil. [Col. 0877A] For it is better to marry than to burn with the heat of fleshly desires. They come to marriage without fault, provided they have not yet vowed better things. It is better to marry because it is worse to burn. “Better” looks to comparison with what is worse, not to the simple nature of an incomparable good in itself—as if one were to say, “It is better to have one eye than none.” To burn is to be inflamed with desires of the flesh. For when the mind consents to the heat of the flesh, it burns. But to suffer desires and not be conquered is the mark of an illustrious and perfect person.

“To those who are joined in marriage I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not depart from her husband. But if she does depart, she should remain unmarried or [Col. 0877B] be reconciled to her husband. And a husband should not dismiss his wife” (Matt. 9; Mark 10; Luke 16).

I advise the unmarried and widows to remain thus; but to those who are joined in marriage—that is, to men and women already united in matrimony—I do not command, but the Lord himself commands through the Gospel, that a wife should not depart from her husband. But if she departs from him for the reason permitted by the Lord, that is, because of the husband’s fornication, the Lord commands her to remain unmarried while her husband lives; or, if she cannot exercise self-control, to be reconciled rather to her husband—whether corrected or endured—than to marry another. Yet if he is not corrected, she will become a participant in the sin of her husband.

And a husband should not dismiss his wife, because, if she has fornicated, she is not a lawful wife and therefore may be dismissed. It must be understood [Col. 0877C] that the same is said of the husband as was previously stated of the wife: if a husband dismisses his wife because of her fornication, he should remain unmarried; or, if he cannot exercise self-control, he should be reconciled to his wife, whether she has been corrected or must be endured. Yet if she has not been corrected, the husband who keeps her will become a participant in her sin. “For one who joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body” (above, ch. 6); and, as Solomon says, “He who keeps an adulteress is foolish and senseless” (Prov. 18).

These things have been said concerning those who entered marriage after receiving Christianity. But concerning those whom faith found already in marriage, he adds:

“But to the rest I speak, not the Lord: if any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, he should not dismiss her. And if any [Col. 0877D] believing woman has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to live with her, she should not dismiss her husband. For the unbelieving husband has been sanctified through the believing wife, and the unbelieving wife has been sanctified through the believing husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean; but now they are holy.”

Where both are believers, the Lord commands that they not be separated. But to the rest—that is, to those who are not both believers, but one has believed while the other remains in unbelief—I speak, not the Lord. “If any brother,” and so forth. Since the Lord neither forbids nor commands departure from an unbeliever, the Apostle says—not the Lord—that one should not depart; yet he certainly has the Holy Spirit, by whom he could give useful and faithful counsel.

[Col. 0878A] This was to be urged, not commanded, because people should not be prohibited with the same weight from doing lawful things which are not advantageous as they are prohibited from unlawful things. Therefore, when he says, “I speak, not the Lord,” he sufficiently shows that the Lord did not prohibit what he himself prohibited. Accordingly, it was lawful by justice, but it was also not to be done out of free goodwill: namely, that a believer should leave an unbeliever, because perhaps he or she would be converted to the faith. The Lord would have forbidden it if it had been unlawful.

If any brother—that is, any Christian—has an unbelieving wife whom he married before coming to faith, and she consents to live with him—that is, she does not abhor him on account of faith in Christ and does not detest the fact that he is a Christian—he should not dismiss her, because perhaps she too will afterward [Col. 0878B] become a Christian if she remains continually with him. For she has already in some measure become a member of the household, since she endures a Christian husband. Likewise, if a Christian woman has an unbelieving husband whom she married before believing, and he consents to live with her, knowing her to be a Christian and not abhorring her for that reason, she should not dismiss her husband, because he has already been subdued in some respect.

This is not a command but the Apostle’s counsel and admonition. If anyone does otherwise, he will not be a transgressor of a command, but will not follow the Apostle’s counsel. But since a spouse may be dismissed because of unbelief, while according to the Lord’s ruling a spouse may not be dismissed except for the cause of fornication, it is clear that unbelief also is fornication. For idolatry, which unbelievers follow, [Col. 0878C] and every harmful superstition, is fornication; and the Lord permitted a spouse to be dismissed because of fornication (Matt. 5, 19). But because he permitted it and did not command it, he gave the Apostle room to advise that anyone who wishes should not dismiss an unbeliever, because in this way that person may perhaps become a believer. For this can be an occasion for gaining many, if believing spouses do not make use of the permitted liberty of leaving unbelievers.

For the husband who was unbelieving “has been sanctified,” that is, has been made holy, through the believing wife; and the wife who was formerly unbelieving has been sanctified through the believing husband. It is to be believed that it had already happened that some men came to faith through believing wives, and women through believing husbands. And although he did not name them, he nevertheless encouraged them by examples [Col. 0878D] in order to confirm his counsel. Then he added: “Otherwise,” that is, if your marriage were dissolved, “your children would be unclean,” that is, illegitimate, not born from a lawful union. “But now they are holy,” that is, clean, because you remain in your marriage. For there were already little Christian children who had been sanctified by baptism through the agency of one parent, or with both parents’ consent. This would not happen if, when one believed, the marriage were dissolved and the unbelief of the spouse were not endured until an opportunity for belief.

Or, in the statement, “The unbelieving husband has been sanctified,” and so forth, the Apostle may have used a past-tense word for the future through the Spirit of prophecy, because it often afterward occurred that one spouse was converted to faith through the other. Otherwise, if one [Col. 0879A] did not consent to the other, your children would be unclean. But now they are holy, because they were begotten from lawful marriage and, for the most part, born under reverence for the Creator, since one of you was a Christian and the other consented to that one. For just as everything done through dedication to idols is unclean, so whatever is done under profession of God the Creator is holy.

But what the Apostle’s words now seem to say more strongly and, in some fashion, compel us to understand is some sanctification by which an unbelieving husband or wife was sanctified in a believing spouse, and by which children of believers were born holy. [Note: [Col. 0879D] An obscure passage.] This may have been because any husband or wife who had learned it in the law abstained from intercourse during a woman’s menstrual blood—for Ezekiel places this among precepts that are not to be understood figuratively [Col. 0879B]—or because of some other sprinkling of holiness, not openly set forth there, arising from the very necessity of marriages and children.

Nevertheless, this must be maintained without doubt: whatever that sanctification may be, it has no power to make Christians or to remit sins unless people are made believers by Christian and ecclesiastical instruction and sacraments. For unbelieving spouses, however closely they cling to holy and righteous spouses, are not cleansed from the iniquity which, separating them from God’s kingdom, compels them to come into condemnation; nor are little children begotten from any holy and righteous persons released from the guilt of original sin unless they have been baptized in Christ.

“But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart. For a brother or sister is not [Col. 0879C] subject to bondage in such cases. But God has called us in peace. For how do you know, woman, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife, except that each should live as the Lord has apportioned?”

A believer should not depart from an unbeliever. But if an unbelieving husband or wife departs out of hatred of the faith, let that person depart; let departure be allowed. Therefore I say that he or she should be given freedom to go, because a brother or sister—that is, a Christian man or woman—is not subject to bondage to such a spouse, so as to be compelled to abandon the faith in order not to lose an unbelieving spouse.

But so long as they can remain together in peace, they should not be separated, because God called us, who had been turned away from him, in peace—that is, while we were in harmony with one another. Therefore we ought not, because of his calling, [Col. 0879D] to break the peace in which his calling found us; rather, if possible, to remain in it. Indeed, marital peace ought to be maintained, and it is not advantageous to separate even though it is permitted. For how do you know, woman, whether you will save your husband by converting him to faith, just as an unbelieving husband has often already been sanctified through a believing wife? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife by converting her to Christ through your shared dwelling, conversation, and friendship, just as an unbelieving wife has often been sanctified through a believing husband? What has already happened in others may perhaps happen in you also; for perhaps those who do not abhor Christ’s name will believe.

Therefore, I say, how do you know [Col. 0880A] whether you will save your spouse, unless you relate to that person as the Lord has apportioned to each—that is, for the husband to govern and the wife to be subject? Or: how do you know whether you will save him or her, unless you await, as the Lord has apportioned to each person when he or she is to be saved—that is, unless you recognize that he predetermined when that person would believe and endures him until the appointed hour of faith arrives? So you too wait patiently for belief.

“Let each live as God has called him, and as I teach in all the churches. Was anyone called while circumcised? Let him not draw on a foreskin. Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but keeping the commandments of God is what matters (Gal. 5, 6). Let each remain [Col. 0880B] in the calling in which he was called (Eph. 4). Were you called as a slave? Let it not concern you; but even if you can become free, make use of it rather. For the slave called in the Lord is the Lord’s freedman. Likewise, the free person who was called is Christ’s slave. You were bought at a price (above, ch. 6; 1 Pet. 1). Do not become slaves of human beings. Therefore, brothers, let each remain with God in the condition in which he was called.”

“Do not, I say, separate from one another. But as God has called each person, so let the one who has been called walk; that is, if at the time when he believed he was married, circumcised, or uncircumcised, let him remain such after baptism, just as I teach not only among you but also in all the churches. Therefore you must hold what all the churches hold, [Col. 0880C] unless you prefer to observe a rite different from that of all the churches.

Truly, each person ought to walk as he was called. For has someone been called while circumcised? That is, if he was already circumcised when he was called to faith, let him not restore the foreskin; that is, let him not live as though he had restored the foreskin—namely, as though he had again drawn a covering of flesh over the part he had uncovered and had ceased, as it were, to be a Jew—so that, once made a Christian, he should not think himself deficient because he lacks a foreskin, giving glory to the foreskin as though it were of any value. But if someone was called to faith while uncircumcised, let him not be circumcised, supposing circumcision to be of some benefit. For circumcision is nothing—that is, it neither benefits nor harms salvation—and uncircumcision is nothing; [Col. 0880D] it neither hinders nor advances it.
