Rather, the keeping of God’s commandments avails for salvation. For whether anyone is circumcised or uncircumcised, if he keeps God’s commandments he will be saved; otherwise he cannot be saved.

The Apostle nowhere abolishes a custom whose observance causes no hindrance; nevertheless, he warns that hope of salvation should not be placed in such things. Hence he calls them nothing, and then adds, repeating the preceding statement: “Let each person remain in the calling in which he was called,” that is, in whatever condition does not conflict with his calling. He referred this to those customs or stations of life that do no harm to faith and good morals. For a person is not to remain in robbery merely because he was a robber when [Col. 0881A] he was called.

I say that he should remain in the same condition. For if you were called as a slave, remain in the same slavery. Do not be concerned that you are a slave; do not grieve over it or be anxious about it, desiring thereby to be released. But even if you can become free, make the more use of slavery, as of something good and useful. For slavery is useful for preserving humility and exercising patience; and one who serves well in these earthly circumstances, with the intention of maintaining righteousness and humility, lays up great merit for himself with God, who looks not at human conditions but at minds and actions.

Therefore embrace slavery as though it were a good thing, and do not think that you cannot please God if you serve a human being. For the slave called in the Lord is the Lord’s freedman: that is, the Lord Jesus has freed him from the slavery of sin, [Col. 0881B] which is worse. For if sins make people slaves, then the one whose sins are forgiven becomes free. Likewise, one who was called to faith free according to the condition of this age is Christ’s slave, that he may serve him by working righteousness; and thus each is a slave.

The Apostle cuts off pride and establishes unity, so that neither the slave should think himself despised because of the shame of his condition, nor the free person, puffed up in mind, exalt himself above the slave. Truly, everyone who comes to faith is Christ’s slave, even if he is judged free among human beings; for you have all been bought with a price—that is, with Christ’s blood, which he shed for you on the cross—in order to buy you as his slaves, though you had been wrongly free. For it is the greatest crime to be free from God, and the greatest advancement to become, from being free, a slave of God.

And because he bought you as his slaves, therefore serve [Col. 0881C] him alone, and do not become slaves of human beings, so as to set God’s service aside for the sake of people, or act against his commandment. For these are slaves of people: those who subject themselves to human superstitions, who desire only to please people and neglect to serve God.

Just as he had previously warned believing spouses not to depart from unbelievers, so he exhorted slaves whom faith found in slavery not to be concerned to leave their slavery. But now he warns those who have already received faith and have always been free not to become slaves of people any longer, lest perhaps they be hindered from God’s service if they subject themselves to human obedience. Hence he repeats the foregoing statement, saying: “Therefore, each brother, in whatever”—with “station” understood—“he was called, [Col. 0881D] let him remain in that station with God,” that is, in the house of God, which is the Church. That is: if he was free when called, let him remain free; or if a slave, let him remain so. For the divine calling changes not one’s condition but one’s morals.

But blessed Jerome interprets these words differently. He says that, in relation to the preceding discussion—where the Apostle had taught that a believer ought not to depart from unbelievers, but should remain in marriage as faith found them, and that each person, whether celibate or married, should continue as he was found by Christ’s baptism—the Apostle introduces the comparisons of the circumcised and the Gentile, the slave and the free, and under their metaphor discusses married and unmarried persons.

“Was someone called while circumcised? Let him not restore the foreskin.” At the time, he says, when you were called and believed [Col. 0882A] in Christ, if you were called circumcised—separated from a wife and celibate—do not take one; that is, do not restore the foreskin, lest you burden the freedom of circumcision and chastity with the load of marriage.

Conversely, was someone called while uncircumcised? Let him not be circumcised. Did you have a wife when you believed? he says. Do not regard faith in Christ as a ground for separation, because God has called us in peace. “Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of God’s commandments.” For celibacy and marriage avail nothing without works, since even the faith that belongs to Christians is said to be dead if it has no works (James 2); and by this principle even the virgins of Vesta could be counted in the order of the holy.

“Let each person remain in the calling in which he was called.” When he believed, he says, whether he had [Col. 0882B] a wife or did not have one, let him remain in the condition in which he was called. Thus he prohibits not so much the marriage of virgins as repudiation; and just as he removes from those who have wives the freedom to dismiss them, so he cuts off from virgins the opportunity to marry.

“Were you called as a slave? Do not be concerned. But even if you can become free, make the more use of it.” Even if you have a wife, he says, and are bound to her, and pay the marital due, and do not have authority over your own body—and, to speak more plainly, are your wife’s slave—do not grieve because of this, nor sigh over lost virginity. But even if you can find some grounds for separation, so as to enjoy the freedom of chastity, do not seek your own salvation at another’s destruction. Keep your wife for a little while; do not outrun one who delays, but wait until she follows. [Col. 0882C] If you act patiently, your wife will be changed into a sister.

“For the slave called in the Lord is the Lord’s freedman. Likewise, the free person called is Christ’s slave.” He gives reasons why he does not wish wives to be abandoned. Therefore, he says, I command those who believe in Christ from among the Gentiles not to leave marriages entered into before faith; because, if one with a wife has believed, he is not bound to God’s service to as great an extent as virgins and unmarried women are, but is in some sense freer and the reins of slavery are loosened for him. And while he belongs to a wife, he is, so to speak, the Lord’s freedman. On the other hand, one who believed while having no wife, and was called free by the Lord from the slavery of marriage—this person is truly Christ’s slave, not in the flesh but in the Holy Spirit. “For the one who is joined to the Lord [Col. 0882D] is one spirit.”

And lest, perhaps, in what he had said above—“Were you called as a slave? Do not be concerned; but even if you can become free, make the more use of it”—he should seem to have disparaged continence, he introduces a statement that cuts off every quibble: “You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of human beings.” We were redeemed by Christ’s most precious blood; the Lamb was sacrificed for us, and, sprinkled with the burning dew of hyssop, we have boiled away every onset of harmful pleasure. Since Pharaoh and all his army were drowned for us in baptism, why do we seek Egypt again? And after manna, the food of angels, why do we long for garlic, onions, melons, and various meats?

Thus Jerome. Having set forth the discussion of married persons and those living continently, [Col. 0883A] the Apostle finally comes to virgins and says:

> “Now concerning virgins, I have no commandment from the Lord; but I give counsel, as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord to be faithful. For I think that this is good because of the present necessity: that it is good for a person to be so.”

Concerning married persons I gave the Lord’s commandment, which I had received from the Gospel, and I added my own counsel. But concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord to lay before you, because the Lord did not compel virgins by the necessity of a command to remain thus; rather, he placed it in the discretion of their will, so that, if they wished, they might marry or remain virgins. For what is not compelled but offered is worthy of greater [Col. 0883B] reward. For if virginity had been commanded, marriage would seem to have been taken away; and it would have been exceedingly harsh to compel people contrary to nature, to exact an angelic life from human beings, and in some sense to condemn what he had created.

For if the Lord had commanded virginity, he would seem to have condemned marriage and taken away the seedbed of humankind, from which virginity itself is born. If virginity had been commanded, whoever failed to keep it would be condemned. “I have no commandment from the Lord concerning virgins, but I give counsel.” For where there is a command, there is the necessity of servitude; but where counsel is given, there is the freedom of one making an offering. There one may not do otherwise; here one may. Therefore Christ loves virgins more, because they freely give what had not been commanded them. It is a greater [Col. 0883C] grace to give up what you do not owe than to render what is demanded of you.

I give counsel as one who, after my past errors, has obtained mercy from the Lord, so that henceforth I may be faithful. Or: I have obtained this mercy, that I may be faithful, because through God’s mercy it was granted to me that, delivered from unbelief, I should be faithful; and therefore the counsel I give is faithful and comes from the Lord, through whose mercy I am faithful.

Truly I give counsel, because I think this good—that is, the keeping of virginity. Or, because I can give faithful counsel, I therefore think this good: that whoever is able should remain a virgin. I say that I think this good because of the present necessity, which presses upon those entering marriage; because thereafter they must always be concerned with temporal things. [Col. 0883D] Then women’s wombs swell, they give birth with the greatest pain, and raise their children with great labor; and then it frequently happens that they are deprived of children and husbands, and spend the rest of their lives in poverty and distress.

But the observance of virginity is good not only because of the heavenly reward, but also because of such present necessity. Or, “because of the present necessity,” because necessity presses upon everyone to prepare for the Judge’s coming, which married persons can do less easily while occupied with worldly cares. Because of such necessity, I think it good to remain in virginity, “for it is good for a person to be so,” that is, in virginity; because virginity possesses not only glory in the future age, [Col. 0884A] but also rest and freedom in the present.

> “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife.”

I have said that it is good for a person to be so; nevertheless, if you are bound to a wife, do not seek release in order to live continently, because it is not lawful to dismiss a wife except on account of fornication (Matt. 5:19). But if you are released from a wife, then accept my counsel not to seek a wife. Each of us has his own limits: give me mine, and you keep yours. If you are bound to a wife, do not give her a divorce; if you are released, do not seek a bond. Just as I do not dissolve marriages once they have been bound, so you should not bind what has been released.

[Col. 0884B]

> “But if you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned. Yet such persons will have tribulation in the flesh; but I spare you.”

I said, “Do not seek a wife.” Yet if you take a wife, you have not sinned. Not sinning is one thing; doing well is another. For one who takes a wife does not act wrongly, but fortifies himself against the evil act of fornication. And if a virgin marries, she has not sinned—not a virgin who has once dedicated herself to God’s service. For if one of these marries, she will incur condemnation, because she has made void her first faith. Virgins who marry after consecration are not so much adulteresses as unjust women (1 Tim. 5).

But lest the Apostle, by saying, “And if a virgin marries, she has not sinned,” should seem [Col. 0884C] again to summon unmarried persons to marriage, he immediately restrained himself and, by adding another consideration, weakened what he had conceded and deterred them from marriage, saying: “Yet such persons will have tribulation in the flesh [Col. 0884D].” That is, although those who enter marriage do not sin, they can live more easily without marriage, because those who are such will have tribulation in the flesh. Yet we, ignorant of realities, imagined that marriage at least possessed the joys of the flesh. But if even those who marry have tribulation in the flesh—the very sphere in which they seemed to have pleasures—what remains for which they should marry, when there is tribulation in spirit, soul, and flesh itself? For those who delight in fleshly pleasures frequently receive the greater tribulations from the flesh.

But in counseling you to avoid this, I spare you—that is, I do not want you to experience it, but to be free from it. Or, “I spare you” means: I present the tribulation of the flesh as though there were not greater reasons why you should not marry.

> “But this I say, brothers: the time is short. What remains is that those who have wives should be as though they had none; those who weep, as though they did not weep; those who rejoice, as though they did not rejoice; those who buy, as though they did not possess; and those who use this world, as though they did not use it. For the form of this world is passing away.”

Since I spare you tribulation, so that you may not be compelled to bear it through the entanglements of marriage, therefore, brothers, I tell you this: the time [Col. 0885A] of the present life is short. God’s people are no longer to be propagated by carnal generation, but are now to be gathered again by spiritual regeneration, since all things will shortly come to an end.

“What remains” means that this alone remains to be done: that those who have wives, and so forth, should be as though they had none. For one has a wife but is as though not having one if he knows how to render the dues of the flesh in such a way that he is not compelled through them to cling to the world with his whole mind. For when this Apostle says again, “The one who has a wife is concerned with the things of the world, how he may please his wife,” that person has a wife as though not having one who so endeavors to please his spouse that he nevertheless does not displease his Creator.

He also weeps, but as though he did not weep, who is so afflicted by temporal losses that he nevertheless always consoles his mind with eternal gains. He rejoices, but as though [Col. 0885B] he did not rejoice, who is so made cheerful by temporal things that he nevertheless always considers everlasting punishments; and, when joy lifts his mind, immediately presses it down with the weight of provident fear.

I say that he has a wife as though not having one who uses her for bodily consolation in such a way that he is never bent by love of her from the rectitude of a better intention toward wicked works. He has a wife as though not having one who, seeing these things to be transitory, endures the care of the flesh from necessity but awaits eternal joys from the desire of the spirit.

To weep while not weeping is to lament outward adversities in such a way that one nevertheless knows how to rejoice in the consolation of inward hope. Again, to rejoice while not rejoicing is to lift the mind by lower things in such a way that it never ceases to fear the highest things. One buys [Col. 0885C], but as though not possessing, who procures earthly things for use while foreseeing with a lofty thought that he will leave them soon. One also uses the world, but as though not using it, who brings all necessary things outwardly into the service of his life, yet does not allow them to dominate his mind, so that they may serve as subjects outwardly and never break the purpose of a mind tending toward other things.

Therefore, all who are such have all earthly things at hand not for desire but for use. They use necessities, indeed, but desire to possess nothing in common with sin. From the things they possess they daily seek rewards, and rejoice more in a good work than in a good possession. Thus, he says, you ought to act, “for the form of this world is passing away.” [Col. 0885D] It is as though he openly said: Do not steadfastly love the world, when the very thing you love cannot endure (1 John 2). You fix your heart vainly as though permanently, while that which you love itself flees away.

And if the world passes away, within which all things are enclosed—indeed, if this form and course of the world passes like clouds—then among the other works of the world marriages too will pass away (Matt. 22; Mark 12; Luke 20). For there will be no marriages after the resurrection. If death is the end of marriage, why do we not turn necessity into a voluntary act, and offer to God, in hope of rewards, what must be exacted from us against our will?

The form of the world passes away, not its nature, so that the world may be changed into another appearance and, out of this old heaven and earth, there may come a new heaven and a new earth (Isa. 25, 66; 2 Pet. 3; Rev. 21). Then [Col. 0886A] the form of the daily aging world will pass away completely, when, in the worldly conflagration, the qualities of the corruptible elements, which suited our corruptible bodies, are utterly destroyed by burning; and the very substance of the world begins to possess qualities suited, by a wondrous transformation, to immortal bodies, so that the world, renewed for the better, may fittingly be adapted to human beings likewise renewed for the better even in the flesh.

> “But I wish you to be without anxiety. The one without a wife is concerned for the things of the Lord, how he may please God. But the one with a wife is concerned for the things of the world, how he may please his wife, and he is divided. The unmarried woman and the virgin are concerned for the things of the Lord, that she may be holy in body and [Col. 0886B] spirit. But she who is married is concerned for the things of the world, how she may please her husband. Now I say this for your benefit, not to cast a snare upon you, but for what is honorable and what affords the opportunity to entreat the Lord without hindrance.”

The form of the world and all these things are passing and temporal. But I wish you to be without the temporal anxiety that married persons have, so that you may freely direct your minds to divine things. For the man without a wife is concerned with the Lord’s things: that is, he devotes himself to fasts and prayers, humility and mercy, and the other virtues, considering how he may please God by doing what is pleasing to him.

But the man with a wife is concerned with the things of the world, that he may have the means to feed [Col. 0886C] his wife and children: that is, he endeavors to increase riches, possess broad and fertile vineyards and fields, and own varied household goods, attending to how by these things he may please his wife; and he is divided, that is, drawn in many directions by anxieties and miseries. Or, he is divided because he does not serve the Lord alone, but partly the Lord and partly the age.

For earthly anxieties proceed from marriage; and therefore each person ought rather to choose the celibate life, lest marriage compel him to be occupied with worldly cares. Marriage is good, but evil are the things that grow around it from this world’s care. Thus, when the Apostle was instructing people toward the grace of celibacy, he did not reject marriage, [Col. 0886D] but drove away the worldly cares that arise from marriage.

And what has been said concerning the man likewise holds concerning the woman, because “the unmarried woman and the virgin are concerned with the things of the Lord.” Not every unmarried woman is a virgin, but every virgin is certainly unmarried. For this reason the Apostle now placed “virgin” after “unmarried woman,” in order to signify that the woman was not a virgin. Although, for elegance of expression, he may have repeated the same thing in another word: “the unmarried woman and the virgin.” Or perhaps he wished to define what an unmarried woman and virgin were, lest we should think prostitutes—who are joined to no fixed marriage—were unmarried women.

The unmarried woman and virgin thinks of the things of the Lord. She no longer thinks of temporal matters, nor does she think how she may avoid being punished by God, but how she may please God by inward beauty, the adornment [Col. 0887A] of the mind, the loveliness of the inward person. Even if there were nothing else and no greater reward followed the virgin, this distinction alone would suffice for her: to think of the Lord’s things and adorn herself for the heavenly bridegroom.

“She thinks that she may be holy in body and spirit,” that is, in flesh and mind. For some are virgins in flesh but not in spirit: their bodies are intact, but their souls corrupt. But that virginity is Christ’s offering whose mind is stained by no thought and whose flesh is stained by no desire. Such a woman is holy in body and spirit.

This does not mean that a married woman who is faithful, chaste, and, according to Scripture, subject to her husband, is holy only in spirit and not in body. For it cannot be that the body used by a sanctified spirit should not also be holy. Rather, by these words the Apostle intended a greater sanctification, both in body [Col. 0887B] and spirit, for unmarried women; he did not deprive married women of all sanctification. For divine holiness is lessened in that measure of cares in which worldly pleasure is considered.

The unmarried woman—that is, the widow—and the virgin think of God’s things. But she who is married, by contrast, thinks of the world’s things, studying how to please her husband. For, constrained by the marital law, she is concerned how to fulfill the right of the marital office, subject to worldly necessities. Therefore, whatever intention of mind is expended even upon those matters in which the husband must be pleased, the unmarried woman ought in some way to gather and direct into the intention by which God is to be pleased.

Yet we see virgins thinking of the age and [Col. 0887C] women joined in marriage devoting themselves to the Lord’s works. Holiness will not be credited by God to those virgins, and those married women will have reward with God. The same must be thought concerning men. But the Apostle speaks to those who, with wondrous devotion, desire to obey heavenly commands, showing by what shortcut one runs more swiftly to God: namely, if one lives a celibate life and devotes oneself solely to divine things.

And lest he should perhaps seem to impose at once upon unwilling persons the exceedingly heavy burden of chastity, he immediately adds the reasons for his counsel and says: “Now I say this”—I counsel continence—“for your benefit,” that is, so that you may acquire a greater reward with God and live more easily in this age; “not to cast a snare upon you,” that is, not to constrain you unwillingly to this, and so that this snare may become an occasion of fornication for you [Col. 0887D] if you are incontinent; but I counsel you toward what is honorable and becoming, that is, holy and pure, so that the person may be chaste in body and mind. This is not because marriage is dishonorable or shameful, but because this is more honorable; and I counsel toward that which affords the opportunity to entreat the Lord without hindrance—something not found in marriage—or to entreat the Lord without hindrance from marital intercourse.

> “But if anyone thinks that he is behaving improperly toward his virgin, because she is past her prime, and it ought to be so, let him do what he wishes: he does not sin if she marries. But the one who has resolved in his heart, being steadfast and under no necessity, but having authority over his own will, and has determined this in his heart, to keep his virgin, does well. Therefore both the one who gives [Col. 0888A] his virgin in marriage does well, and the one who does not give her does better.”

As he determined concerning virgins, so he determines concerning fathers of virgins. I invite you, he says, to celibacy, because it is more honorable and freer from hindrance. But if someone who has a virgin daughter thinks—that is, fears—that he may at some time appear disgraceful, that is, dishonored, with respect to his virgin, because she is past her prime, that is, beyond puberty and long ripe for marriage; and if it must be so—that is, if she must be given in marriage because she does not wish to restrain herself and wantonness is noticed in her words and actions—then, to avoid the reproach of fornication, let the father do what she wishes: let him give her to a husband. For he does not sin if she marries, since she is now past her prime and desires marriage. [Col. 0888B]

Therefore I say: if it must be so, he does not sin if he gives her to a husband; for the one who does not give her but preserves her in holiness does well. But not sinning is one thing, doing well another. “Turn away,” he says, “from evil, and do good” (Ps. 30:6). We turn away from the former and pursue the latter; in one is vice, in the other perfection.

And this is the meaning: the aforementioned man does not sin—that is, he does not do evil. But the person of whom I now speak does good: the one who, steadfast, that is, constant and unchanging, has resolved in his heart, that is, has proposed in the counsel of his reason, to keep his virgin in the perseverance of virginity; who is under no necessity to give her to a husband, since she herself does not desire it; but has authority to fulfill his own will, [Col. 0888C] since the virgin does not oppose but assents to this paternal will that she should remain intact; and who has determined this in his heart, that is, has decided by judgment of mind that it is good and established through rational deliberation to preserve his virgin untouched—such a man has not merely not sinned in this, but does well, because he does what is pleasing to God.

Or by “virgin” let the flesh be understood. If anyone, he says, sees his virgin—that is, his flesh—growing wanton and boiling over into lust, and is unable to restrain himself, and a twofold necessity presses upon him, either to take a wife or to fall, let him do what he wishes: he does not sin if he takes a wife. Let him do what he wishes, not what he ought. He does not sin if he takes a wife; yet he does not do well if he takes a wife. For the one who has steadfastly resolved in his heart to keep [Col. 0888D] his virgin—that is, his flesh—in virginity, does well.

Then the Apostle draws a conclusion from both interpretations: Since the one who gives her to a husband whom she ought to be given does not sin, and the one who keeps her whom he can preserve does well, therefore the one who gives his virgin in marriage does well, because what he does is lawful; but the one who does not give her, while having authority over his own will, does better, because he lays up merit with God and frees her from the anxiety of the age.

Had he not intended to add, “does better,” he would never have first said, “does well.” But where one good is better than another, the reward of the good and the better is not one and the same. And where the reward is not one, there are certainly different gifts. Thus, the difference between marriage and virginity is as great as that between not sinning and doing well; or, to put it more mildly, as great as that between [Col. 0889A] good and better.

Having completed his discussion of marriages and virginity, and having employed a careful moderation of precepts between the two, so that he might turn neither to the right nor to the left but walk the royal road (1 Sam. 6; 2 Sam. 14; 4 Kgs. 22), and fulfill the saying, “Do not be overly righteous” (Eccl. 7), he again compares monogamy with second marriage; and just as he had made marriage subordinate to virginity, so he makes second marriage subordinate to first marriage, and says:

> “A woman is bound by the law for as long as her husband lives. But if her husband falls asleep, she is freed from the law [Rom. 7]. But let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. Yet she will be happier if she remains thus, according to my counsel. And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.”

[Col. 0889B] It is not a sin if a virgin marries. But let the woman who wishes to marry hear the law to which she wishes to submit herself. A woman is bound by the law for as long as her husband lives, and she cannot be released from the law of her husband in order to marry another while he lives. For this bond is not dissolved even if an adulterous wife is separated by divorce from her chaste husband; nor does she have permission to marry another as long as her husband lives, whether he be chaste or adulterous.

But if he “falls asleep,” that is, if her husband tastes the sleep of death, from which he will be awakened in the resurrection, she is freed from his law, so that she may marry another if she cannot contain herself. “If he falls asleep, she is freed.” He did not say first, second, third, or any number whatsoever; nor is it for us to determine what the Apostle did not determine. Therefore we ought neither to condemn such marriages [Col. 0889C] nor shame them for their number.

For neither did the Lord, by any implication of his judgment in the Gospel, condemn the woman said to have had seven husbands (Matt. 22), nor did he say that such persons could not be among the elect in the resurrection. Therefore, Augustine says, I dare not say, contrary to the sense of human modesty, that a woman may marry, whenever she wishes, after her husbands have died; nor do I dare, from my own heart and apart from the authority of Holy Scripture, to condemn any number of marriages.

“Let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord.” That is, let her marry both without suspicion of impropriety and to a husband of her own religion. For neither virgin nor widow is permitted to marry a Gentile husband. I say that she may marry. Yet she will be happier if, after her husband’s death, she remains unmarried according to [Col. 0889D] my counsel. She will be happier if she remains a widow, since, even if she marries again, she can be blessed by observing righteousness.

“She will be happier,” he says, “if she remains thus.” Immediately he adds apostolic authority: “according to my counsel.” And lest the Apostle’s authority should appear lighter, as though merely human, he adds: “And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.” Where he urges continence, there is counsel not of a human being but of the Spirit of God; but where he permits marriage, he does not name the Spirit of God, but weighs counsel by prudence, thus relaxing matters according to what each individual can bear.

I give counsel. But do not despise this as human, because I think that I, like the other apostles, have the Spirit of God. That is, [Col. 0890A] do not suppose that this comes from myself. In what I say, the Spirit of God speaks in me, and it is not advantageous to despise him.

When the Apostle said, “I think,” he seems to doubt; but he rebukes, he does not doubt. He rebukes his despisers, who did not think that he spoke these things through the Spirit of God. For people sometimes express an apparently doubtful question rebukingly about matters they know to be certain: that is, they use a word of doubt though their hearts do not doubt. For example, someone may become indignant and say to his servant: “Do you despise me? Consider—perhaps I am your master.” So too the Savior does not doubt but rebukes when he says to the Jews: “If you believed Moses, perhaps you would also believe me” (John 5). He said “perhaps” not doubtingly but rebukingly.

## Chapter VIII

[Col. 0890B]

> “Now concerning things sacrificed to idols: we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. But if anyone thinks that he knows anything, he does not yet know as he ought to know. But if anyone loves God, this one is known by him.”

He begins to correct those who were eating meats sacrificed to idols, saying: “Every creature of God is good, but an idol is nothing”; and they erred more through this appearance than through sound reasoning. For the others, who were simple and unlearned, when they saw these persons eating food sacrificed to idols, supposed that there was some holiness in those meats, and thus were weakened in faith (1 Tim. IV). “Concerning marriage,” he says, “and the other matters treated thus far, you asked, and I taught you; but concerning things sacrificed to idols, there was no need to ask, because you know about them as I do, since we all possess this knowledge.” He speaks to the more perfect, whose knowledge was a scandal to others—that is, to the unlearned—because they knew well that an idol was nothing and that there was no God except Christ; therefore, so far as they themselves were concerned, it was lawful for them to eat God’s creature. Yet they ought to abstain, lest they become a cause of offense to the weak. For what they ate by virtue of such knowledge, others, in ignorance, ate in veneration of the idol.

“We have knowledge,” both you and I, concerning what may be done with sacrificed meats. But this knowledge is of no avail, because it puffs up—that is, it makes you proud over the ignorant. But charity builds up the weak, since it gives up what may harm them; and therefore it is better to possess charity than vain knowledge. For knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up: since, where charity does not raise up by building, knowledge overturns by puffing up. Knowledge is useless in itself when it stands alone without charity; but it is useful through charity, when charity is joined to it. For it is tempered by charity, so that it may not be too pure and intoxicate the knower, causing him not to exalt himself. Just as wine untempered by a mixture of water unsettles the mind, so knowledge makes a person proud unless it has been tempered by charity.

Those were puffed up with such knowledge who, because they knew that an idol was nothing, ate sacrificial meats against the salvation of their unlearned brethren, having no charity before their eyes; for they ought to have despised the meats, lest they cause scandal to the weak. Their knowledge indeed was destroying the minds of unlearned brethren, who supposed that some grace existed there at the idol, when they saw more learned brethren present there and not recoiling from it. Therefore he says: “Charity builds up,” so that, striving for the salvation of their brethren, they would not use there the prerogatives of knowledge and would not cause them scandal. For knowledge without charity puffs up; but where charity has filled by building up, knowledge finds there nothing empty to inflate.

“Knowledge,” he says, “puffs you up, so that you despise others; and thus it is neither useful nor perfect knowledge. For if any of you supposes that he knows something in this matter, he has not yet known how he ought to know”; and thus he does not know sufficiently, though he boasts of knowledge. And even if he knows that he may eat meats, he does not know that he himself ought to use that knowledge in such a way as not to harm others. For each person ought so to know that his knowledge benefits both himself and others, not harms them. For whoever eats food sacrificed to idols through such knowledge—his knowledge and eating contribute to the overthrow of weak brethren and to the confirmation of unbelievers; and therefore he does not know as he ought.

“But if anyone loves God,” to whose love he cannot attain unless he loves his neighbor, “he is known”—that is, approved and chosen—by Him. For love of God is demonstrated in love of one’s neighbor (Rom. XIV), because one who strives to benefit the brother for whom Christ died shows that he loves Christ; and therefore he is worthy that God should deign to know him—God who says to the reprobate: “I do not know you” (Matt. VII, 25).

> “Concerning foods sacrificed to idols, we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is no God except one. For although there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many gods and many lords—yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we unto Him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through Him” (Exod. XX; Ps. LXXXI; John X).

Because, on account of the intervening passage, he could not explain what they knew concerning sacrificed foods, he now returns to the matter after making that digression and showing that knowledge without charity is neither sufficient nor useful, but harmful. He explains what they knew about sacrificial meats, on account of which they judged it lawful to eat them.

He who boasts in knowledge does not know how he ought to know. But concerning foods sacrificed to idols, he and we know that they are lawful for those who understand to eat. Or: “Concerning foods sacrificed to idols, we know”—that is, we have this knowledge—that an idol is nothing; and therefore it is lawful to eat the foods, because they are not defiled by idols, since the idol is nothing.

An idol is an image made and consecrated in human, animal, or bird-like form, according to the interpretation of its name. For εἷδος (*eidos*) in Greek is translated in Latin as *forma* or *species*, “form” or “appearance”; and from it, by diminution, comes εἴδωλον (*eidōlon*), that is, “a little form.” Since, as the Apostle now says, an idol is nothing, the maker of an idol makes that which is not. But what is that which is not? A form which the eye does not see, but which the mind itself invents: for example, if someone fashions a dog’s or ram’s head upon human limbs; or again invents two faces in one human figure; or joins the hind parts of a horse or fish to a human breast. Whoever makes these and similar things makes not a likeness, but an idol. For he makes what is not and has nothing like it; and therefore the Apostle says that “an idol is nothing in the world,” that is, among the creatures of the world. If we consider all creatures which God made, we shall never find an idol created thus by God. He indeed created the material, but human folly gave it this form; therefore, insofar as it was not made by God, it is nothing, since God made all things.

Evil too is nothing for the same reason, because God did not make it. Or an idol is nothing with respect to salvation, as foolish persons think who worship it in order that it may confer some salvation upon them. And in respect to divinity an idol is nothing—that is, it has no divinity in itself, so that it ought to be worshiped.

We know this, and that there is no God except one, who is the immutable Trinity and truly one alone (John X). “For although there are those who are called gods”—that is, those who are called gods by title, not essentially, because God has given them a participation in himself by grace—whether in heaven, such as the blessed angels, or on earth, such as the prophets and apostles: indeed there are many such gods, such as angelic spirits and priests. And there are many lords: those spirits called Dominions, and preachers, who are sometimes called lords in the Scriptures; or even secular rulers, who exercise lordship over others. Yet, although there are such gods and lords, for us, as regards worship, there is only one God and Lord. For we do not worship angels or holy human beings, though they are called gods, as gods or lords.

Yet for us there is one God to be worshiped: the Father, from whom are all things—that is, from whose goodness and counsel all things have proceeded—and we believers look toward Him. Brute animals and unbelieving persons bend toward the earth and seek earthly things; but we, through faith and longing, tend toward Him from whom we have descended. And for us there is one Lord to be worshiped, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, since, as John also affirms, “All things were made through him” (John I); and through him we are not merely human beings, as others are, but also good and wise. Here the Spirit of the Father and the Son is likewise understood to be worshiped by us. But because the Apostle was speaking of gods and lords, he said that for us there is one God, the Father, and one Lord, the Son—although the Son is also God and the Father also Lord. For he set these two things in correspondence with those two, namely gods and lords; therefore he did not add the third, that is, the Holy Spirit.

> “But not in all is there knowledge. For some, with a consciousness of the idol even until now, eat as though it were food sacrificed to an idol; and their conscience, being weak, is defiled.”

We indeed know that an idol is nothing, and that there is no god except the one Trinity, Creator of all things, whom we worship. But this knowledge is not in everyone—that is, not everyone knows this; rather, some suppose that some divinity exists in idols. Not all know this, but there are among you certain people who, even now, with a consciousness of the idol—that is, even now as before conversion, supposing the idol to be something—eat food sacrificed to the idol as though it were *idolothytum*, that is, as though it had been made holy by consecration to the idol and transformed into a spiritual power. For *idolothytum* means, as it were, “given to an idol.”

Their conscience is “of the idol,” that is, possessed by the idol, even until now—that is, even after they have come to faith—because they have not yet entirely withdrawn their minds from the error of the idol. And they eat that food as *idolothytum*, that is, as consecrated to the idol, with reverence for the idol; and thus their conscience is defiled by the pollution of the idol, not because of the food, but because of their own weakness. For it is weak in faith, while the ignorant are endangered by your knowledge, when they eat, following your example or authority, the foods which they see you eating.

Mystically, however, the Corinthians, because they were zealous students of Greek letters and lovers of philosophy, ate the doctrines of philosophers as though sacrificed to idols (below, X). These perhaps could not harm those who had received full knowledge of the truth. But those less instructed in Christ, if they imitated them by reading such things and still devoting themselves to those studies, could be wounded and entangled in the various errors of diverse doctrines. Thus the unlearned could be harmed by that from which those who possessed perfect knowledge could not be harmed. But because charity does not seek what is useful to itself, but what is useful to the many so that they may be saved, we must abstain from such food of doctrine, which builds up and delights us alone but offends and harms our neighbors. For just as discourse which teaches piety, justice, and truth is sacrificed to God—that is, consecrated to God—so discourse directed toward impiety, injustice, and error is sacrificed to idols. Whoever receives it eats, as it were, things sacrificed to idols. But according to the earlier sense, let us consider what follows.

> “Food, however, does not commend us to God. For neither, if we eat, shall we abound; nor, if we do not eat, shall we lack.”

The weak are harmed by our eating. But that food does not commend us to God, because we do not please God by eating food sacrificed to idols on the ground that we know it to be lawful for us; and therefore such food ought to be rejected. For if it is despised, there will certainly not be lacking something to eat. But if it is taken, there will not be such abundance that nothing further is required. Therefore, as we have said, it ought to be cast aside, since it is a scandal to brethren and we can live without it. Or it does not commend us to God by making us more acceptable to him: for if we eat it, we shall not thereby abound in good so as to suffice for salvation; nor, if we do not eat it, shall we therefore lack—that is, our merit before God will not be diminished.

> [Col. 0894A] “But take heed lest perhaps this liberty of yours become a stumbling-block to the weak. For if anyone sees one who has knowledge reclining in an idol-temple, will not his conscience, being weak, be built up to eat things sacrificed to idols? And the weak brother, for whom Christ died, will perish through your knowledge. Thus, sinning against the brethren and striking their weak conscience, you sin against Christ. Therefore, if food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat flesh, lest I cause my brother to stumble” (Rom. XIV).

It is indeed lawful for you to eat sacrificial meats, because you know them to be God’s creatures and the idol to be nothing. But see lest perhaps this liberty of yours become an offense to the weak in faith—that is, lest it produce offense in brethren who do not yet know that an idol is nothing. By saying “lest perhaps,” he shows that a stumbling-block may, or may not, come to weak brethren from their liberty. By this he suggests that where there is no stumbling-block to anyone, they may use lawful things; but where there is a stumbling-block, he shows that they must altogether abstain.

For when a mistaken judgment, insofar as it can exist without sin, is not removed from the mind of those who observe, fault is offered through example to all who believe evil. Thus it frequently happens that those who carelessly permit others to think ill of them may themselves do nothing wrong, yet offend more abundantly through those who imitate them. Therefore these persons, who could eat unclean foods without defiling themselves, are rightly now warned not to stir up a scandal of temptation for weak brethren by this eating of theirs. For they can cause scandal to brethren by it.

If any weak person, not yet knowing that an idol is nothing, sees someone who possesses correct knowledge—by which he knows the idol to be nothing—reclining in an idol-temple, that is, eating sacrificial meats with unbelievers in the idol’s presence, will not the conscience of the ignorant person, being weak, be built up by the example of the knowledgeable person—that is, raised up to eat *idolothyta*, as though sanctified by the idol—supposing that some grace exists there because he saw a learned brother eat them without recoiling? For how do you suppose people can be deceived by images which they think are honored by Christians? The pagans say in their hearts: “Why should we abandon the gods whom Christians worship there together with us?” And weak brethren are prompted to desire not only to eat there, but even to sacrifice.

An *idolium* is a place in which sacrifice is made to idols. If a weak person sees any learned man eating there with unbelievers, he will think that the latter understands those foods to have received some sanctification from the idol; he will begin to eat them with such a mind, and thus the weak brother will perish through your knowledge, when he sees him reclining in such a fashion. The weak person will perish if, contrary to faith in the one God, he eats of the sacrificed things. He will perish through your knowledge—that is, your expertise will kill him, while he sees you doing what he understands otherwise. You will be the occasion of his death, though Christ died to redeem him.

Through your knowledge, which you say that you possess—knowing that an idol is nothing, while you have God in mind and thus recline in an idol-temple—the weak person perishes in this knowledge. And lest you despise the weak person because of the defect in which he is weak, hear that he is a brother. If you are strong, tend to your brother’s weakness; and lest you even despise a brother, I add: “for whom Christ died.” If you wish to despise him, consider his price. Consider who died for him, and do not neglect Christ on account of the weak person, when you ought to love the weak person on account of Christ.

“You,” he says, “lead the weak into error by your example; this is no light sin. For thus, sinning against brethren and by the example of your conduct striking—that is, harming—their weak conscience, you sin against Christ, who died for them and whose members they are. Therefore do not despise this sin, if you do not wish to be blotted out of the book of life. Do not suppose that you sin only against human beings and that the offense is therefore slight, because in this way you sin against God, whose members you destroy.”

Or, according to other manuscripts: “you sin in Christ.” For by not being imitators of that charity by which Christ set you free, you sin in Christ, not against Christ. According to this sense, to sin against Christ is to deny Christ; but to sin in Christ is to sin in those things which are Christ’s. For just as one who is under the Law is said to sin in the Law (Rom. II), so those who are under Christ are said to sin in Christ.

And because, by the aforesaid eating, in sinning against brethren you sin against Christ or in Christ, therefore, “if my food causes my brother to stumble”—that is, offends him and disturbs him from a good purpose—“I will never eat flesh,” that is, I shall never eat any flesh, but shall always abstain from eating meat; not because food is evil, but lest I cause my brother to stumble by such eating. You too ought to act thus. For just as it is lawful to have a wife, but, if she has committed adultery, she must be put away, so it is lawful to eat meat, but, if it has been offered to idols, it must be rejected. Charity must be pursued to such an extent that even lawful things are to be rejected as though unlawful, lest they harm a brother.

Typologically, moreover, in the passage: “Take heed lest perhaps this liberty of yours,” and so forth, down to “for whom Christ died,” the Apostle seems to say in other words: “Do not read philosophers, poets, or orators, nor repose in their reading, lest in this way you destroy a weak brother. Nor should we flatter ourselves if we do not believe what is written in these works, when another’s conscience is wounded in this way, and we are thought to approve what, by reading it, we do not condemn.” Otherwise, what would it mean for us to suppose that the Apostle approved the conscience of one who ate in an idol-temple and called perfect one whom he knew to eat things sacrificed to idols? Far be it that “Jupiter almighty,” “by my Hercules,” “by my Castor,” and other things more monstrous than divine should sound from a Christian mouth.

## CHAPTER IX

> “Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Christ Jesus our Lord? Are you not my work in the Lord? Even if I am not an apostle to others, yet I am to you. For you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.”

He begins to set himself forward as an example, so that, just as he abstains from lawful things because of scandal to brethren, they too may do so; as though he said: “Abstain from this lawful thing for the benefit of your brethren, because I have freedom to receive support, yet do not receive it for the salvation of others.” And this is what he says reproachfully by means of questions: “Am I not free?” That is, have I not been given liberty, like the other apostles, to receive support from your goods? “And am I not”—that is, am I not an apostle, so that what is lawful for apostles may also be lawful for me? Certainly I am an apostle. For “have I not seen Christ Jesus our Lord” on the road or in the Temple? As though he said: “I am free to receive, because I am an apostle. I am an apostle because I have seen Christ.”

He proves himself to be an apostle because, due to the occasion given by false preachers, they held a lesser opinion of him. To prove this, he says that he saw Christ, because some said that he was not an apostle because he had never seen Christ. Or he calls himself free because he coveted nothing belonging to anyone and did not teach by flattery. But he is an apostle—that is, one sent by Christ, who said to him: “I will send you to the Gentiles” (Acts XXII). For he saw Christ no longer mortal, but already glorified, when he was appointed apostle by him, so that the dignity of his apostleship might thereby become manifest.

“Truly,” he says, “I am an apostle, because you are the work of my apostleship. For are you not my work in the Lord?” That is, have I not, as an apostle, accomplished this: that you should be in the Lord? “Even if I am not an apostle to others”—that is, to the Jews—“yet I am to you,” who believed through me. Those who had believed from among the Jews and still observed the Law carnally denied that he was an apostle, because he openly preached that the Law ought no longer to be observed carnally. While the other apostles, because of scandal, dissembled about this matter, he seemed to teach otherwise, and was therefore not received by those Jews.

“To you,” he says, “I am an apostle. For you are the seal”—that is, the sign and proof—“of my apostleship in the Lord,” believing through me. That is, the form of my apostleship, like the impression of a seal, appears in you, since you possess the things which other believers possess through other apostles.

> [Col. 0896D] “This is my defense before those who question me.”

That is, the defense which I have stated is mine before those who ask whether I am an apostle: I show them your faith and your devout manner of life, which you attained through my teaching; and thus I am defended by works as an apostle against those who denied this of me. Thus I am proved to be an apostle before those who doubted it; therefore it is not fitting that you too should doubt it.

> “Do we not have power to eat and drink? Do we not have power to take about with us a woman, a sister, as also the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas? Or do only I and Barnabas not have power to do this?”

I said above that I am free because, do not I and my companions have power to eat and drink what is ours? Certainly we have this power, like the other apostles. We have power from Christ, not a command concerning this matter; for the Lord permitted preachers to receive support, but did not command them to do so, so that one who did not receive it might thereby acquire a greater reward (Matt. X; Luke IX, 10). Likewise, he praised virginity but did not command it, for the increase of the glory of those who preserve it (Matt. XIX).

And do we not have power to take with us “a woman, a sister” in preaching—that is, a Christian and holy woman—to minister to us from her means? Cannot we do this if we wish, as the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas did? That is, James of Alphaeus and Thaddaeus, who were relatives of the Savior—namely, from the sister of the Virgin Mary—and Peter, who is chief of the apostles. For Peter himself did not refuse support offered by women, just as the Lord had not refused it (Matt. XIII; Mark VI). Women, in longing for heavenly teaching, supplied them with provisions and services so that they might not lack things necessary for this life. Therefore taking women about was more than receiving food from hearers, because women provided clothing and every necessity (Luke VIII). Nor was this judged at all blameworthy, especially among the Jews.

“And was not this power granted to us too, as to the other apostles? Or do only I and Barnabas, because we are pleased to live by the labor of our hands, lack power to do this?” That is, to receive support and take women about with us? Are we two alone unable to do what everyone does? He does not blame the others, but by their practice proves that what was lawful for them was lawful for him. For some Corinthians supposed that it was not lawful for him to receive support as the others did, because he lived by his own labor; consequently, they thought him of lesser dignity and did not believe him to be an apostle, saying to themselves: “If he were an apostle, he would receive support, as all the apostles do.” Against them he now speaks, showing that he is an apostle and has power to receive support, but does not wish to receive it. And lest he seem to blame his fellow apostles because he abstains, he adds:

> “Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who tends a flock and does not eat of the flock’s milk?”

By these comparisons from human custom he reasonably shows that it is lawful for himself and other preachers to receive support. For they themselves served Christ the King as soldiers in spiritual warfare, and therefore received support from Christian peoples as from provinces. They planted the Church as a vineyard and therefore deservedly ate of its fruit. They fed Christ’s flock of sheep with the teaching of truth and therefore rightly received from the flock’s milk—that is, from its temporal provisions.

Paul, however, who says these things, served as a soldier at his own expense; he did not eat from the fruit of the vineyard that he planted, nor drink from the milk of the flock that he fed. For he wished to receive no recompense in the present life, so that in the age to come he might receive a full reward for everything. Having set forth these comparisons, he adds:

> “Do I say these things according to man? Or does not the Law also say these things? For it is written in the Law of Moses: ‘You shall not muzzle an ox treading grain’ (Deut. XXV; 1 Tim. V). Is God concerned about oxen? Or does he certainly say this for our sake? For these things were certainly written for our sake: because the one who plows ought to plow in hope, and the one who threshes, in hope of receiving fruit.”

I say that a soldier ought to obtain support from his king, and a farmer ought to take fruit from the vineyard. Yet, though I employ human comparisons, do I say these things “according to man”? That is, do I follow merely a human analogy in these things? Or does not God’s Law also say what I say? Certainly it says the same things. For it is written in the Law of Moses (Deut. XXV): “You shall not muzzle an ox treading grain,” that is, you shall not prohibit a preacher from living by preaching.

He shows that the aforesaid arguments agree with the divine judgment, so that we may understand that he did not reject receiving support without cause, though he showed by so many proofs that it ought both to be given and received. But lest this statement be taken literally, he adds: “Is God concerned about oxen?” This is not to be understood as though he himself does not feed brute animals and birds, which neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns; rather, it means that he is not concerned, in giving a command, to instruct a human being how to provide for his ox. Is God concerned about oxen, then, so that he commanded this in the Law concerning them? Or does he certainly say it for our sake, who are his oxen?

For we thresh—that is, on the threshing-floor of the world we crush with the saws of our preaching the chaff of unbelief and vices, and separate from it the grains of faith and the other virtues; or we distinguish believers from unbelievers as grain from chaff. Therefore it is just that we should not be prohibited from taking food from the threshing-floor which we thresh. For these things were certainly written for our sake in the Law, and truly for us spiritual oxen.

For the one who plows—that is, who opens the hearts of subjects to faith with the plowshare of preaching—ought to plow in hope, that is, hoping to gain the fruit of his labor. This is not that his intention should be to preach for the sake of that expectation, namely temporal food, but that he should be certain that he will not lack sustenance if he labors in preaching. Likewise, the one who threshes—that is, who distinguishes grain from chaff, namely virtues from vices—ought to do this in hope of receiving the fruit of support.

Historically, threshing is done when oxen or horses are sent over harvested crops gathered and laid upon a threshing-floor, in order to crush them and shake out the grain, as is customary in some regions. But when preachers break open the hearts of unbelievers, cultivate them with the plowshare of preaching, and plow them for receiving the seed of faith, then they prepare the ground to receive the seed of grace and separate it from uncultivated wilderness—that is, from the multitude of unbelievers. Those who first plow in conversion afterward thresh in instruction, because by continual correction and teaching they separate good persons from evil, not locally but morally.

Yet threshing also occurs before faith, when someone is separated from unbelievers by receiving faith; and after faith, when within the Church a certain moral distinction is made between good and evil persons through the instruction of preachers. The Apostle now speaks of this Church, in which some are rejected, others corrected, and others grow worse.

> [Col. 0899B] “If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things? (Rom. XV.) If others share in your power, why not we more? But we have not used this power; rather, we endure all things, lest we give any hindrance to the Gospel of God.”

He still proves by arguments that it is lawful to receive support. “If we,” he says, “have sown for you”—that is, first begun to scatter spiritual things in your minds, things given by the Holy Spirit and enlivening your spirit, so that they may bear fruit in you as in good soil—is it a great matter if, for the support of our bodies, we reap your carnal provisions? As though he said: It is not great, but very small, if, while giving you eternal things, we receive temporal things from you.

Again, he proves this same point from the lesser to the greater. “If others,” he says, “share in your power”—that is, use your goods as powerfully as you yourselves do—why should not we do so even more, who were the cause of your salvation? What are the spiritual things which he sowed except the word and ministry of the sacrament of the kingdom of heaven? And what are the carnal things which he says he may lawfully reap except those temporal things granted for the life and need of the flesh? Others too received these from them with authority, although they had not first proclaimed the Gospel to them, but came later to their church preaching the same thing.

Hence he adds: “If others share in your power,” that is, the authority granted to preachers over you, to make use of your goods, why not we more? Or let us understand these “others” as false apostles, who devoured their goods while contributing nothing useful to them. “Behold,” he says, “it has been proved that we have power to receive support. Yet we have not used this power”—that is, we have not taken support as we could have done. For one uses one’s power when one receives whatever pertains to oneself and refuses to abstain from any due of one’s authority.

“But we have not acted thus; rather, we endure all things”—that is, we most willingly bear hunger, thirst, and nakedness—“lest we give any hindrance to the Gospel of Christ,” that is, lest the Gospel be impeded from running through us. For it would run less readily to your hearts if you suspected that we preached it for earthly profit. Or, if you had given us something, perhaps you would have thought that you had purchased freedom to preach, and our freedom to rebuke would have been diminished. Or, if we received the support due to us, false apostles would then freely receive it by our example and would persist in preaching. Or, if we took a woman about with us, an unfavorable suspicion might arise from it. In such ways the course of evangelical preaching would be impeded.

> “Do you not know that those who work in the sanctuary eat the things from the sanctuary? And that those who serve at the altar share with the altar? So also the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel” (Matt. X; Luke IX, X).

Again he returns to the proof, and in every possible way repeatedly establishes what is lawful for him, though he does not do it. “It is lawful for me,” he says, “to receive support from preaching, just as those who minister among the Jews in the sanctuary may live from the things of the sanctuary; for natural reason itself holds that everyone should live from the work at which he labors.

“Do you not know that those who work in the sanctuary”—that is, in the tabernacle or Temple, such as ministers and craftsmen—“eat the things from the sanctuary,” that is, certain offerings presented there which belong to them? And do you not know that those who serve at the altar, such as priests and Levites, share with the altar? That is, they receive a part of what is offered upon the altar. And just as these things were done according to ancient custom among the ancient Hebrews, so the Lord Jesus ordained in the New Testament—that is, reasonably arranged—that those who proclaim the Gospel, that is, preach it, should live from the Gospel, that is, have sustenance, so that they may be more unencumbered when they are not anxious about bodily food.

The Lord ordained this—that is, arranged it in this order—that those who give spiritual things should receive carnal things, when he said: “Remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they have; for the worker is worthy of his wages” (Luke X). Not that anyone ought to evangelize in order to eat, but that he ought to eat in order to evangelize. For whoever evangelizes in order to eat values the Gospel less highly than food.

After the Apostle has shown by many comparisons, examples, arguments, and authorities that it is lawful for him to receive necessities, he adds:

> [Col. 0900D] “But I have used none of these things. Yet I have not written these things in order that they may be done so in my case. For it is better for me to die than that anyone should make my glory void. For even if I preach the Gospel, it is no glory to me; for necessity is laid upon me. Woe is me if I do not preach the Gospel. For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, a stewardship has been entrusted to me. What, then, is my reward? That, in preaching the Gospel, I may present the Gospel without cost, so that I may not misuse my power in the Gospel.”

So many examples and authorities, he says, establish that I may lawfully receive support. Yet I have made use of none of these examples, authorities, or arguments, in order to do what I have shown that I may do—namely, to receive expenses and sustenance from preaching. I have made use of none of these. Nor do I wish to use them, since I did not write that these things are lawful for me in order that they should now be done in my case—that is, that from now on all necessities should be supplied to me by those subject to me. And if, for the salvation of others, I have abstained and do abstain from the support due to me and from every necessity, at least you, moved by so great an example, should abstain from meat sacrificed to idols, lest you cast many brethren into destruction.

For this reason also the Apostle did not wish to accept support: lest he should become a model for hirelings and false apostles. For already there were many who desired to have an opportunity of gaining earthly things [variant: support] and of selling the Gospel; and, wishing to charge this against them, he earned his living with his own hands. He also did not wish to receive support or anything else from his disciples, lest through this they should take confidence in sinning and the force of evangelical authority in him should grow weak. In this too he spared them, lest he should burden them by living from their goods. “I do not wish,” he says, “that these things should be done in my case.” For it is better for me to die—that is, I would rather die than endure that someone, by giving, should make void my glory, which I wish to possess in Christ before God for this abstinence, while I sympathize with the weak by taking nothing from them. Truly it would thus be made void and empty.

For if I should preach the Gospel in order that these things might be done in my case—that is, if I should preach in order to attain them, and should place the end of the Gospel in food, drink, and clothing—then I have no glory before God, but belong to the number of those of whom it was said: “For they have received their reward” (Matt. VI). And why have I no glory? Because the necessity of sustaining this life lies upon me, so that I preach for this reason: because I have nothing by which to live, in order that I may gain temporal profit from the preaching of eternal things. Thus there would already be necessity in the Gospel, not free choice. And necessity truly lies upon me, because woe is to me if I do not preach the Gospel—that is, if I do not preach, it will be to my own harm, because I shall be tormented by hunger and shall have nothing from which to live.

Truly, to preach for bodily necessity is not glory. For if I do this willingly—that is, without any necessity of supporting this life—I have from God the reward of everlasting glory. But if unwillingly—that is, compelled by necessity—I do it, a stewardship is entrusted to me, so that I may distribute the Gospel to others for their benefit, while I myself do not have that glorious reward before God. For in this place such a steward is understood as one who administers what belongs to another, from which he himself receives nothing. A stewardship is entrusted to me as to an unwilling servant, so that I may distribute it as though it were another’s possession and receive nothing from it except provisions—given outwardly not as a share in the kingdom, but as support for wretched servitude.

And since, if I preach willingly, I have a reward before God, what then is my reward, which I desire to obtain from preaching, since I do not wish to receive any earthly reward from it? This indeed is my reward: that I, preaching the Gospel without charge, may set the Gospel in the hearts of people—that is, that the Gospel may not be burdensome in cost to believers, lest they suppose that it is preached to them in order that evangelists may seem to sell it. This reward I choose for myself: to place the Gospel freely in the minds of my hearers, so that I may not abuse, in the Gospel, the authority given me by the Lord to receive support, and so create an obstacle to the Gospel. For if I took support, so that the Gospel would thereby be hindered and proceed more slowly, it would become an abuse of my authority; for in taking it I would act contrary to the purpose for which that authority itself was granted to me.

Thus far he has shown in many ways that he was permitted to receive support, though he did not receive it. But that, sympathizing with human weakness, he abstained from support due to him is shown by what follows, when he says:

> “For though I was free from all, I made myself the servant of all, that I might gain the more. And I became to the Jews as a Jew, that I might gain the Jews; to those who are under the law, as though I were under the law, though I myself was not under the law, that I might gain those who were under the law; to those who were without law, as though I were without law, though I was not without the law of God but was under the law of Christ, that I might gain those who were without law. I became weak to the weak, that I might gain the weak. I became all things to all men, that I might save all. But I do all things for the sake of the Gospel, that I may become a participant in it.”

“This alone,” he says, “do I seek as a reward in this life: that I may minister the Gospel freely to all. For although I was free from all—that is, although I was so separate from all that I owed them nothing, and no merits of theirs could bring me to minister the word of life to them—I voluntarily humbled myself in order that I might be exalted by the Lord, and made myself the servant of all, as the Lord himself said: ‘Whoever wishes to be first among you shall be the servant of all’ (Matt. XX; Mark IX). I was free from all—that is, owing nothing to anyone, since I had received nothing from anyone by which I would be bound to render service to him. Yet for Christ’s sake I made myself the servant of all, that I might serve the advantage of all; and this I did in order that, by converting more people to faith, I might gain them—that is, make them the gain of my preaching. Therefore I adapted myself to all.

For I became to the Jews as a Jew—that is, I so sympathized with their blindness and misery as though I myself were a Jew and held together with them in the same blindness and misery. This means: Whatever grief and concern I would have over my own unbelief, ignorance, and death, if I could perceive the matter as it really is, that much I had for the Jews, so that I might gain the Jews—that is, bring them to faith by assisting them as I should wish to be assisted myself. And to those under the law—that is, to Samaritans or to the Jews just mentioned—I became as though I were under the law: that is, I sorrowed with them mercifully and laboured to rescue them from the yoke of slavery, just as I should rightly wish to be pitied and rescued if I were one of them.

Thus through the compassion of mercy I became to them as though I were under the law, although I myself was not under the law in a servile manner—that is, although I did not observe it carnally—in order that by so devout a condescension I might gain, that is, acquire for Christ, those who were under the law. The outstanding teacher did not, in becoming as a Jew, break out into unbelief; nor did he return to carnal sacrifice in becoming as though under the law. Rather, by condescension he drew near to unbelievers, not by falling. Thus, receiving each person into himself and transforming himself into each through sympathy, he gathered them and supplied to them what he would rightly have wished others to supply to himself. He ran to meet each person in error to the degree that he had learned, from considering himself, the measure of that person’s salvation.

He did not return to carnal sacrifice in order to suppose that by offering it he could obtain any justification or salvation from it. Otherwise, in order to avoid scandal, he observed at Jerusalem the ancient custom of sacrifices (Acts XXI). Nor did he do this by pretence, as some have thought, but according to his own free judgment when he says: “Was anyone called circumcised?” (above, VII): “Let him not draw on foreskin”—that is, let him not live as though he had drawn on foreskin, as he says elsewhere: “Your circumcision has become uncircumcision” (Rom. II).

According to this judgment he did those things which, to those who did not understand and paid little attention, he seemed to have feigned. For he was a Jew and was called while circumcised; he did not wish to draw on foreskin—that is, he did not wish to live as though he were uncircumcised. For this was now within his power; and although he was not under the law as were those who kept it slavishly, he was nevertheless in the law of Christ—which is also the law that the Jews held—in order that he might fulfil it freely. While celebrating its ancient sacraments among the Jews, he thereby commended them as having been commanded by God until the dispensation of a definite time, and distinguished them from the sacrilegious rites of the Gentiles.

For in this also he became to the Jews as a Jew, and to those placed under the law as though he were under the law: because he did this at Jerusalem; elsewhere he circumcised Timothy (Acts XVI); among Jews he abstained from foods prohibited by the law; and he always disputed among them from the law and the prophets, affirming Christ’s coming by their testimonies. He did all these things and similar things in order to gain for Christ those who were of the law, not because he still regarded those ceremonies as possessing any justification.

And he adds: “To those who were without law”—that is, the Gentiles—“I became as though I were without law, though I was not without the law of God but was in the law of Christ, that I might gain those who were without law.” He became to Gentiles as a Gentile in that he accepted uncircumcision; in that he allowed without distinction the eating of foods condemned by Jews; in that he agreed with them, according to physical reasoning, that the world was made by God; and in similar condescensions.

It should be noted that he calls the Jews “under the law,” himself “in the law,” and pagans “without law.” To be under the law is one thing; to be in the law is another. The person under the law is acted upon according to the law; the person in the law acts according to the law. The former is a servant, but the latter free. But the person without law is estranged from every divine servitude, so that, like a wild ass in the wilderness (Job XXIV; Jer. II), he may live with a wicked freedom in the present age.

To both groups—that is, to those under the law and to those without law—the Apostle testifies that he adapted himself through mercy and compassion, not through deceitful pretence. That is, he assisted a carnal Jew or a pagan in the way in which he himself, if he were such a person, would secretly have wished to be assisted: bearing their weakness in a likeness of compassion, not deceiving through the fabrication of a lie. This follows immediately when he says: “I became weak to the weak, that I might gain the weak.” For it was from this source that he spoke, so as to say all the preceding things as well. Therefore, just as his becoming weak to the weak was not a lie, so neither were the other things which he had set forth.

For what weakness does he say that he had toward the weak, unless it was sympathy with them to such an extent that, lest he should appear to be a seller of the Gospel and hinder the course of God’s word by allowing it to fall into evil suspicion among the unlearned, he did not wish to receive what was due to him by the Lord’s law? For he became weak precisely in that he did not wish to use his authority. He was clothed with so merciful an affection that he considered how he himself would wish to be treated if he too were weak in such a way that, from those through whom the Gospel was preached to him, he might suspect a kind of commercial market if he saw them taking support.

Thus to those weak in heart he became weak through compassionate mercy, not through deceptive pretence. For one who ministers to a sick person becomes as though sick, not by pretending that he has fevers, but by considering with the mind of one who sympathizes how he would wish to be served if he himself were sick. In this sense he adds universally:

> “I became all things to all men, that I might save all.”
