As though he said: Why should I enumerate each matter separately at greater length? I state it briefly: I became all things to all—that is, as though I belonged to every group. He became all things to all not by the act of one lying, but by the affection of one sympathizing: that is, not by deceitfully doing all the evils of everyone, but by diligently providing the remedy of mercy for all the evils of all others as though they were his own. For as a human being he would consider that he too might have been in the vices from which he wished to free others; and so he helped them as he would wish to be helped if he himself were in the same vices. Piously transforming in himself the persons of all, he learned from himself how he should have mercy upon each one, so as to supply to every individual what he himself would rightly have wished supplied to him if he were in that condition.

Thus, he says, I accommodate myself to all, not because their errors and vices please me, but because I do all the things mentioned above, conforming myself to each person for the sake of the Gospel, that I may become a participant in it—that is, that I may share in the good intention which the Gospel has toward human salvation. Or: I do all the things I have said toward each person for the sake of the Gospel, that I may gently bring it to them and myself become a participant in its reward.

> “Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all indeed run, but one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain it. For everyone who competes in the contest abstains from all things. And they indeed do so that they may receive a corruptible crown, but we an incorruptible one.”

For this reason I do all things for the Gospel, because otherwise I shall not be a participant in it. For it is necessary for me to do everything that must be done and to abstain from everything from which one must abstain, because otherwise I cannot possess the Gospel’s crown and reward. This is plainly apparent in the comparison which I now offer. No one receives the prize in the stadium unless he has done everything that must be done; and you can all know this from worldly custom. For do you not know that those who run in the stadium all indeed run, but one receives the prize? Although all are alike in running and labour there, nevertheless all run in vain except that one person who receives the prize, which is the reward of the race.

A stadium consists of one hundred and twenty-five paces. But here, whether it has less or greater length, the stadium is called that stretch of road over which a race was customarily run up to a certain goal, so that upon reaching the goal one had to stand. Hence the stadium received its name from standing. The *bravium* is a kind of palm, or the prize proposed for runners. All run, but the one who by running defeats the rest receives the prize, because he has done everything belonging to the race and abstained from everything that hinders it.

Likewise, then, I cannot attain the prize of heavenly reward unless I do everything that must be done by runners and abstain from everything contrary to it. Let each of you similarly judge concerning himself and run lawfully. For all indeed run, but one receives the prize. Jews run; heretics run; some Christians who are not predestined to life run; for all these hope that in the end they will gain a reward, and they stretch toward it through the stadium of the present life. But the one people of predestined Christians, who run lawfully, receive the prize, because only the unity of those who are Christ’s body attains the palm.

And because not all who run receive the prize, therefore run in such a way—doing what pertains to running and avoiding what hinders it—that you may obtain it. You ought to be cautious and unencumbered in running, lest perhaps it happen that you fail to obtain the reward toward which you run. For not all obtain it. Run by believing, hoping, desiring, doing good works, afflicting the body, praying, loving, and applying yourselves to every good pursuit.

Such is the case with runners. But let us hear of those who box. Every runner hastens toward the prize, but everyone who contends in the contest abstains from all things—that is, every boxer who fights in the contest abstains from foods and other things which impede the contest. Likewise every Christian who wrestles against the devil in the arena of this world ought to abstain from everything that entangles a Christian with the earth. For we have been anointed with chrism because we have become wrestlers; and just as those who wrestle in the arena are naked, so we ought to be stripped of worldly things, so that by loving we may possess nothing in this age, since the malignant spirits against whom we wrestle possess nothing proper to themselves in it.

Therefore we must wrestle naked with the naked—that is, possessing nothing with those who possess nothing—if we do not wish to yield to them. Yet let us strive to be clothed with the arms of virtues, by which we may both be protected and strike our adversaries. Thus let us imitate boxers and wrestlers, who abstain so completely from every harm to their contest that they diligently endeavour to avoid even nocturnal pollution, which is accustomed to occur in sleep, lest through it they become weaker in the contest.

They indeed abstain and fight in order to receive, with praise and reward, a corruptible crown woven from flowers and quickly perishing; but we abstain and fight in order to receive an incorruptible—that is, an eternal—crown. Therefore we ought to be more diligent, for whom there is reserved not a crown of earthly and fading flowers, but a spiritual crown set with eternal gems in the fashion of a royal diadem.

> “Therefore I so run, not as toward uncertainty; I so fight, not as one striking the air. But I chastise my body and reduce it to slavery, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate.”

The Apostle sets himself before the rest as an example. Since, he says, our present life is a stadium in which we run and contend, and an incorruptible and eternal crown is proposed to the victor, therefore I—who, as was said above, do all things for the Gospel—so run, that is, so lawfully, eagerly, and unencumberedly perform the course of good work that I do not run as toward uncertainty, because I am certain of the crown. One runs toward uncertainty who does such things that from some he may hope and from others despair.

But I, holding from all that I have done after conversion the certainty of a good hope, do not run as toward uncertainty, like those who run for a worldly prize and are not certain whether they can receive it. I so fight against the devil that I am not as one striking the air—that is, I do not fight vainly like one who throws blows to no effect and strikes the air instead of an enemy. Certainly I contend not in words but in deeds, because I am not among those preachers who say and do not do (Matt. XXIII).

For however abundantly a preacher pours forth words, the sword of his mouth does not reach to wound the enemy, but his voice is judged empty and idle if he himself stands contrary to his own preaching. For one who acts otherwise than he preaches makes his hearers suspicious, so that they doubt the promises; and therefore he cannot expel evil from their hearts or wound the enemy dwelling in them. But I do not hurl empty verbal blows against the adversary. Rather, in order that I may wound him, I chastise my body with fasts and afflictions, so that I may also give others an example of abstinence. Therefore I do not fight as one striking the air: because while I restrain the flesh, with the very blows of my abstinence I strike not the air but the devil; and while I subject what is within me, I strike the adversary who is outside.

To chastise the body is to restrain it by fasts and to give it what benefits life, not luxury. I chastise my body through abstinence, lest it become insolent through wantonness; and I reduce it to slavery, so that it may fulfil not its own will but the will of the spirit, and in all things serve the spirit rather than resist it. I therefore so restrain the body lest, if I act otherwise, there should happen what can still happen while I am in this changeable life: namely, lest, after I have preached to others and brought them by my teaching into the part of the elect, I myself, by living wickedly, should become reprobate—that is, rejected by God and alienated from the heavenly joys which I preach.

Certainly it had already been said concerning this Apostle by the Lord’s voice: “He is a vessel of election to me” (Acts IX); and yet he still, while chastising his body, fears lest he be rejected, although above he said: “I so run, not as toward uncertainty.” Thus he is certain of the reward in such a way that he fears to lose it; and he fears to lose it while being certain of it. And if this man, whom God testifies to be a vessel of election, thus fears becoming reprobate, what will become of us wretches, who have not yet heard any voice of God concerning our election and already grow torpid in leisure as though secure?

For everything that he has now said concerning himself he said in order to teach us by his example to act likewise: namely, that we should so vigorously pursue the course of upright work that we may have a sure hope of receiving the future reward; and that we should so fight with the ancient enemy, chastising our bodies, that we strike not the air but the enemy himself with the sure blows of our abstinence—lest perhaps through creeping vices we should still become reprobate. That rejection can still happen, he proves by the example of the Jews, adding:

## Chapter X

> “For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink (Num. IX; Exod. XIII, XIV, XVI, XVII). But they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them (Num. XX), and the rock was Christ. Yet God was not well pleased with most of them, for they were struck down in the wilderness” (Num. XIV).

He presents this example from the former people so that no one among the Christian people, relying merely on the fact that he has been baptized and received the food and drink of the Lord’s body and blood, may suppose that God will spare him if he sins. Rather, he should know that all these things will benefit him only if he perseveres in humbly obeying God.

As though he said: Every Christian ought to run and fight as I do while he remains in the stadium of mortal life, and to fear lest, after all the good things divinely received, he should still become reprobate and fail to reach the prize for which he runs. For we see that the Hebrews, who prefigured us, after the crossing of the sea and heavenly food, could not reach the land of promise, as it were the proposed prize, because they offended God by their sins.

“For I do not want you to be ignorant”—that is, I do not wish you to be ignorant—“brothers, that our fathers,” that is, the ancient Hebrews, founders of our faith and moral instruction, “were all,” both good and bad, when they left Egypt, “under the cloud” (Num. IX; Exod. XIII), which did not allow the Egyptian army to approach them and signified the protection of heavenly guardianship; “and all alike passed through the sea” (Exod. XIV), in which their persecutors perished; “and all were baptized into Moses”—that is, under Moses’ leadership—“in the cloud and in the sea,” because, when their enemies were submerged, they were delivered from death, which baptism accomplishes for us. They were cleansed from their former sins so that these might no longer be imputed to them, and cleansed from ignorance of God, which oppressed all nations, so that they might be fit to receive the divine law.

They were baptized because they received the sign of baptism, which availed believers among them as much as baptism itself avails us. Then all alike, good and bad, “ate the same spiritual food” (Exod. XVI), that is, manna prepared by spiritual power. They ate the same food because those to be saved did not eat one food and those to perish another, but all ate the same. Likewise all “drank the same,” not a different, “spiritual drink” (Exod. XVII), that is, water brought forth from the rock by spiritual grace.

That manna and water are now called spiritual food and drink because they were created temporarily not by the law of the world but by the power of God, without a mixture of elements, and bore within themselves the figure of the Lord’s body and blood. Hence manna was called the bread of angels, because it was created by the power through which angels subsist, signifying him who says: “I am the living bread who came down from heaven” (Ps. LXXVII; John VI).

Or: they ate the same food, Christ’s body, which we eat in bread, in manna; and they drank the same drink, Christ’s blood, which we drink from the cup, from the rock. Therefore they ate the same food spiritually as we do, but another food bodily. For they understood visible food spiritually, hungered spiritually, tasted spiritually, in order to be satisfied spiritually. We too have received visible food, but the sacrament is one thing and the power of the sacrament another. Similarly, they received the same spiritual drink as we do, though bodily a different one.

But they did not drink this spiritual drink from just anywhere, but from the spiritual rock—that is, from Christ. For as that food and drink were spiritual, so by the same reasoning the rock was spiritual, which poured forth spiritual drink. “They drank from the rock that followed them,” that is, satisfied their desires; for the abundance of its bounty followed them, exhausted by thirst and crying to Moses, and satisfied them in such a way that they no longer then sought drink. Or the spiritual rock followed them through the desert, because where human assistance failed them Christ was present. It followed for this reason: that where a human being failed, he might aid them. For it was not the rock but Christ who gave water. He likewise does not now cease, after baptism—as it were after the passage through the sea—to accompany his own by following grace.

“They drank from the rock, but the rock was Christ.” It was not said, “The rock signified Christ,” but “The rock was Christ,” because Scripture is accustomed to speak in this way, calling things which signify by the names of the things signified. For all signs seem in some manner to bear the persons of the things which they signify; and therefore it was said, as though it were truly so, “the rock was Christ.” Certainly it was not so in substance, but in signification.

Christ is called a rock because of firmness. Fastened to the two beams of the cross, he poured forth from his side the sacraments of our salvation, by which our inward thirst might be given drink; just as that rock, struck twice, gave water by which that people was satisfied. For the twofold striking signifies the two beams of the cross.

Behold, all alike received all these benefits of God, but not all alike arrived at salvation. For “God was not well pleased with most of them”—that is, most did not please God after all these things, but gravely displeased him. This is clear from the fact that “they were struck down in the wilderness” (Num. XI, XIV), and did not reach the land of their promised inheritance. Let us therefore take care lest the same happen to us. For all the benefits which they received from God are spiritually the same as those which we have received.

We know that Egypt is interpreted as “affliction,” “one who afflicts,” “one who oppresses,” or “darkness”; and it is often used as an image of this world, from which one must depart spiritually, lest we be yoked together with unbelievers (II Cor. VI). This occurs through the first warmth of faith. For a person first becomes fit to be a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem when he has renounced this world, just as that people could not be brought into the land of promise unless it first departed from Egypt.

But just as that people did not depart from Egypt except by divine protection, so no one turns his heart away from this world unless he is anticipated and aided by the gift of the Lord’s mercy. The protecting cloud accompanies such a person, driving far away the army of pursuing Egyptians, because through the faith which a catechumen receives he has God’s grace overshadowing him like a cloud. It does not allow the former habit of vices, which follows him at the devil’s instigation, to approach him; rather, it is extinguished in the water of baptism as in the Red Sea.

For baptism, consecrated by Christ’s blood, is fittingly signified by the Red Sea. The death of the Egyptians in the sea signifies the abolition of sins in baptism. The Israelites crossing over prefigure those now baptized. By such a mystery all those fathers, leaving Egypt, were under the cloud; all passed through the sea; and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea. Moses signifies Christ, the cloud the Holy Spirit, and the sea the water of baptism. Thus they are said to have been baptized into Moses in the cloud and sea, as though they were said to have been baptized into Christ in the Holy Spirit and water.

Afterward they were led through the desert. Similarly, all who are baptized now do not yet enjoy the promised homeland of the kingdom of heaven; but hoping for what they do not see and awaiting it through patience, they are as though in the desert. There they are fed with manna and given drink from the rock—that is, with Christ’s body and blood. For just as that people could not eat manna before crossing the sea, so no one can receive the Redeemer’s body before baptism.

Then, as the law was given to the Hebrews, so to believers is shown the sublimity of the knowledge of Christ’s love. But those who sin criminally after all these things will not reach the heavenly homeland unless they perform fitting repentance; just as the Jews, because of their sins, did not reach the land of promise but perished in the desert. Although God was well pleased with some, he was not well pleased with most of them.

The sacraments were common to them all, but grace was not common. So now baptism is common to us all, but the power of baptism is not; the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood is common to us, but the power of the sacrament is not common. Therefore let us not trust in sacraments alone, since by them alone we shall not reach the kingdom of heaven if we neglect to do good works or do not fear to offend the Saviour after the manner of the ancients.

> “Now these things were done as a figure of us, that we should not be desirers of evil things as they also desired them (Num. XI); nor become idolaters, as some of them did, as it is written: ‘The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play’” (Exod. XXXII).

After the crossing of the sea, after angelic food and spiritual drink, the Jews, because they grievously offended God, did not reach the promised inheritance but perished in the wilderness. Yet these things narrated concerning them were then done as a figure of us, who were to come after; for in them was prefigured that, if after baptism and after the food and drink of the Lord’s body and blood we likewise sin, we shall not reach the heavenly homeland. Instead, dying in this evil age, we shall be led to the punishments of hell, which the punishments of those people prefigured.

Let us therefore take care not to offend in the same way, lest we suffer in reality such things as they endured in figure. For these things, as has been said, were done as a figure of us, so that we might be corrected by fear of the punishments which befell them, lest we be desirers of evil things—that is, desirers of vices—as they desired them. For through desire they longed for the foods of Egypt, which they had left behind while being fed with manna sent from heaven; and, weeping for the eating of meat, they murmured.

Let us likewise beware the enticements of gluttony and the greediness of the belly, lest we perish through like desires for feasts. “Nor become idolaters,” by eating in an idol’s temple, as some of them did by eating before the calf. Do not become idolaters—that is, do not build up toward idolatry, by your example, the weak conscience of brethren, who, seeing you reclining in an idol’s temple, think that you eat there in honour of the idol.

Do not become idolaters, as not all the Jews but some of them became idolaters, worshipping the golden calf while Moses remained on the mountain with the Lord for forty days. As it is written in Exodus (Exod. XXXII): “The people sat down before the calf to eat and drink; and when they had become cheerful through food and drink, they rose up to play”—that is, to perform games in veneration of the calf. “They rose up to play,” that is, to dance before the calf. Or “to play,” that is, to worship the calf. For what is more like childish play than worshipping idols? Therefore take care lest you too now sit down before an idol to eat and drink, and stir up the weak to the play of idolatry.

> “Nor let us commit fornication, as some of them committed fornication (Num. XXV), and in one day twenty-three thousand fell. Nor let us tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him and perished by serpents (Num. XXI). Nor murmur, as some of them murmured and perished by the destroyer” (Judith VIII).

Nor let us turn aside into idolatry after we have been brought out of the darkness of unbelief, as they turned aside after they had been brought out of Egypt, where they had served idols. Nor let us commit fornication with pagan women, lest through them we be led astray into the worship of idols, as some of them committed fornication (Num. 25) with the daughters of Midian, ate of their sacrifices, and worshipped their gods; and this was done [Col. 0911C] by Balaam’s counsel. See that you likewise are not deceived by the counsels of false apostles, who plot your destruction, just as Balaam contrived the ruin of the children of Israel. For because of this fornication twenty-three thousand fell by the sword in one day, since Moses immediately commanded the judges of Israel that each should kill his neighbours who had been initiated into Baal-peor; and so great a multitude of them was slain.

Here was prefigured that even men perfect in love, in observance of the Decalogue, and in faith in the Trinity, if they commit fornication, will be slain at the future judgment, as it were in one day, by the judges of Israel (Matt. 19; Luke 22), that is, the Apostles. For the Decalogue of the Law is understood through ten; through twenty—that is, the doubling of the number ten—is expressed the twofold [Col. 0911D] love which fulfils the Law; through three, faith in the Trinity; and through a thousand, perfection. Thus, as we have said, by the twenty-three thousand are denoted those who are perfect in love, in observance of the divine commandments, and in faith. Yet let them beware of fornication, since because of this alone they can fall into hell on the day of judgment.

Nor let us test Christ, distrusting his help and loathing his spiritual food, lest we be handed over to be destroyed by evil spirits, as some of them tested him and perished by serpents. For, as Scripture relates, the people began to be weary of the journey and labour; and they spoke against the Lord and Moses, saying: “Why have you brought us out of Egypt, that we should die in the wilderness? Bread fails; there is no [Col. 0912A] water. Our empty soul now loathes this very light food. Therefore the Lord sent fiery serpents among the people” (Num. 21).

For in this way they tested Christ: by speaking against the Lord, who is Christ himself, and against Moses his servant, because they were weary of the long journey and labour and lacked more substantial food, while they regarded manna as though it were worthless. Thus Christ is shown to be God, since he was already tested by them. To signify the sins by whose poison they were invisibly dying, he sent them visible serpents as a warning; and by a corrective plague he made bodily deaths signify the deaths of souls.

Let us too beware lest we test Christ in a similar way, speaking against him and against the superior whom he [Col. 0912B] has given us: asking why he brought us out of Egypt—that is, out of the dark pleasures of the world—while we are afflicted in the wilderness of this mode of life and endure scarcity of bodily sustenance, though spiritual sustenance abounds; and weary of journey and labour because through patience we are unwilling to wait long for what we do not see, but desire to reach the kingdom quickly, without enduring any labour. For since we must enter the kingdom of heaven through many tribulations (Acts 14), if we refuse to bear tribulations on the way with long-suffering, by God’s just judgment we shall be handed over to fiery serpents (Judith 8), that is, to evil spirits, who inflame us with the fire of vices and infect and destroy our souls with the poison of sins.

It should also be noted that, just as the Jews had despised Christ in Moses, [Col. 0912C] so the Corinthians despised him in the Apostle, speaking ill of their leader, the Apostle, as the Jews did of Moses (Exod. 15, 16, 17; Num. 14, 17, 19); and now by such an example he wishes to restrain them. He adds: “Nor murmur.” For they murmured against their elders, whose better charisms they envied, or even against the Apostle himself. “Do not murmur,” he says, “as some of them murmured,” that is, they unjustly complained of their rulers, “and therefore perished by the destroyer” (Judith 8): that is, by the angel who struck them outside the borders of the promised land, or cast them outside the bounds of the inheritance of the elect.

For Korah and his companions murmured against Moses and [Col. 0912D] Aaron (Num. 16), alleging that they had been set over the people not by divine election but, as it were, by themselves. Therefore they were so destroyed that, when the earth beneath their feet was split open, they went down alive into hell. On the following day, because of this, the multitude of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron, saying: “You have killed the people of God” (ibid.). For this reason the wrath of the Lord went forth against them, and they were devastated by fire; fourteen thousand persons were struck down, apart from those who had perished in Korah’s rebellion.

Thus, because of their murmurings, by which they falsely complained against their rulers, they perished and were exterminated from the midst of the multitude by the angel administering their punishments. See, therefore, that you too, if you murmur in like fashion against me or against [Col. 0913A] any who are set over or placed above you, do not perish likewise—indeed, more grievously. For it is beyond doubt that those who sin are to be subjected to greater torments when the punishments of sinners have been recounted to them precisely so that they might not sin.

> “Now all these things happened to them in a figure. But they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come. Therefore let him who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.”

Thus, after the crossing of the sea and heavenly food, they perished in different ways because of their various offences. But all these things happened to them in a figure, because then it was prefigured that after baptism and the sacrament of Christ’s body we too can perish through like offences. For the fact that God was not well pleased with many of them [Col. 0913B] and that they were overthrown in the wilderness prefigured that among the Christian people now “many indeed are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20). “For broad is the way which leads to destruction, and many are they that go in by it” (Matt. 7), and God is not well pleased with them either.

That they desired evil things and returned in heart to Egypt signified that carnal Christians would desire evil things and would return in mind to the vices of the world which they had left. That some of them became idolaters, some committed fornication, some tested Christ, and some murmured, signified that some Christians would fall into idolatry, some commit fornication, some test Christ, and some [Col. 0913C] murmur, and would invisibly suffer their punishments. Therefore it is said that not all of them but some of them committed these evils, because not all Christians, but some, do like things now; and those who now imitate their ancient sins must also suffer their punishments.

Therefore all these things happened to them in a figure. But they were written for our correction: that, on hearing their sins and punishments, we may be corrected, and beware of belonging to those who do and suffer similar things. Everything under the Old Testament happened in a figure; and therefore, now that we enact manifest realities, it is no longer necessary to observe the celebration of foreshadowing figures—that is, to keep Sabbaths, distinctions of foods, and the like. Yet these things were written on our account, and therefore they must be read and understood by us with great care [Col. 0913D] and held in great authority, since they were written for our benefit.

The vices and punishments of the ancients were also written for our correction, upon whom—that is, upon us—the ends of the ages have come, that is, have turned aside, because we are in the last age and ought to be corrected all the more by so many examples of those who came before us. Otherwise their punishment will be doubled in us, because greater knowledge of the Law makes more guilty the person who does not keep it. The ends of the ages are signified by the sixth age, as the old age of the old man, if we conceive of the whole human race as one man; in that age the Lord came. For there are also six ages in one human being: infancy, childhood, adolescence, youth, maturity, and old age.

The first age of the human race [Col. 0914A] is from Adam to Noah; the second, from Noah to Abraham; the third, from Abraham to David; the fourth, from David to the Babylonian deportation; and from there the fifth extends to the coming of the Lord. The sixth, however, runs from the coming of the Lord to the end of the age, because the outward human being decays, as it were, through old age—he is also called the old man—while the inward human being is renewed day by day. Thereafter is everlasting rest, signified by the Sabbath.

Since, therefore, the ends of the ages have thus come upon us—that is, worldliness in us has diminished and begun to end—it will be more shameful if we should now sin any further. After this there follows a salutary warning: because the Israelites, after receiving benefits from God, fell into various offences through which they deserved to perish; because the falls of the Israelites [Col. 0914B] prefigured the falls of Christ-worshippers; and because everything that happened to them then was written for our correction, therefore whoever thinks himself to stand—that is, to possess a settled state of uprightness—should take heed, that is, be watchful lest he fall, that is, slip into grave sin. For “the righteous falls seven times” into a slight sin “and rises again” (Prov. 24). Let him take heed lest he fall while he thinks himself to stand.

This was especially said to those Corinthians who, presuming upon their knowledge that all foods could lawfully be eaten, were a scandal to weak brethren. They thought they had gained something from the teaching of the false apostles, by which they had become worse, and they judged the Apostle while they themselves were guilty. He therefore cuts off their pride, lest through it they fall into various sins like the Jews; for by speaking proudly against the Apostle [Col. 0914C] they were testing Christ. He also restrains many others who were yet to come from destructive exaltation, when he exhorts the one who stands to watch lest he fall—that is, lest he consent to sin or cause another to sin (Hosea 13). For one who falls falls by his own will; but the one who stands, or rises again, does so by God’s will.

> “Let no temptation seize you except what is human. But God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but will also provide, with the temptation, an outcome, so that you may be able to endure.”

Let the one who stands take heed lest he fall—not that he can persevere altogether without a fall. But at least see to this: that temptation, that is, the delight of sin, does not seize you, [Col. 0914D] that is, draw your reason into consent, except what is human—that is, except in those slight sins without which human life cannot be lived; or, let no demonic but only human temptation seize you. For it is human indeed to suffer temptation in the heart; but it is demonic to be overcome in the contest of temptation and in action.

Again, to think otherwise than the matter is, is a human temptation. But to love the opinion of this person, that person, or oneself; or to envy those who are better, until one reaches the sacrilege of cutting off communion and establishing schism or heresy—this is diabolical presumption. But in no respect to think otherwise than the matter is, is angelic perfection. Therefore, because we are human beings, but are to be equal to angels in the resurrection (Matt. 22; [Col. 0915A] Mark 12; Luke 20), so long as we do not possess angelic perfection, let us beware of diabolical presumption.

For it is human to form an untrue judgment concerning another’s hidden matters: so that a person believes someone good whose evil he does not know; and again, on uncertain opinion, believes evil of someone whom he has not proved evil, and judges before the time what he does not know. Human temptations also occur when someone with good intention, yet according to human frailty, errs in some counsel; or is stirred up against a brother from zeal to correct him, though a little more than Christian tranquillity requires. In these and similar cases there is human, not demonic, temptation. For it belongs to the devil knowingly and voluntarily to sin when no frailty draws him to it; but it belongs to a human being to sin through ignorance [Col. 0915B] or weakness.

And because you must be tested by temptations, I do not say or pray that you should not be tempted, but that no temptation may seize you except what is human—that is, that you may be tempted as human beings, not as demons, so that you may make progress through temptations rather than succumb to them. I indeed say this, but God will fulfil what I say, because he faithfully fulfils what he promised when he said: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). God is faithful—that is, true in this promise—that he may always be with you in every temptation and not allow you to be tempted beyond your strength, but make the temptation lighter so that you may overcome.

We say in one sense concerning someone, “He did not have faith in me”; in another, “He did not keep faith with me.” The former means: he did not believe what I said; the latter: he did not do what he said. According to that faith by which we believe, we are faithful to God; according to that by which what is promised is done, God himself is faithful to us. [Col. 0915C] God is faithful in promising to help his own and to give them a crown of glory after temptations (James 1); therefore he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear—that is, he will not allow the burden of any temptation to grow beyond the measure of your powers.

For unless merciful God moderates temptations according to our powers, certainly no one can bear without falling the temptations [or: snares] of evil spirits. If the Judge does not set a measure to temptations, he immediately casts down the person who stands by laying burdens upon him beyond his strength. Therefore, in a merciful ordering, he permits and restrains our enemy, loosens and checks him: that we may be tempted for our progress, yet not overcome to the enemy’s desire. For he is faithful, and therefore causes either temptation to cease quickly or, if it lasts long, himself gives strength to endure it.

He will not allow you to be tempted beyond your strength, but with the temptation itself he will also provide the means of endurance, so that you may bear the burden of temptation. For he comes to aid in order to fulfil what he promised, because he is faithful; and he brings about that which human frailty can endure. He knows when to permit the storm of temptation to arise and when to restrain it when arisen. He knows, for our preservation, how to limit what he permits to go forth [Col. 0916A] against us for our exercise, so that the raging storm may wash over us, not drown us.

Therefore he provides an outcome in temptation, because he both allows temptation to come as he knows to be expedient, and swiftly causes the work of consolation to come to meet us; he mitigates the rising stings of temptation and calms with inward peace the hostile movements of thoughts. Then the soul perceives an immense joy from heavenly hope when it sees the evil overcome which it endured.

> “Therefore, my beloved, flee from the worship of idols.”

I have said that all these things happened in a figure to the Israelites, who, after heavenly food, turned to idols and sinned in many ways; and that you [Col. 0916B] have God as a faithful helper in every temptation. Therefore, O beloved, to whom I give counsel because of great love, flee—that is, quickly remove yourselves, not only in mind but also in body—from the worship of idols, lest, like the Jews, you become idolaters again. For whoever is continually in an idol-temple hopes for something from it; and to hope in it is to doubt God. Thus Saul returned to the idolatry which he had exterminated, hoping for something from it (1 Sam. 28).

Flee, therefore, from the worship of idols, lest through it temptation against God arise in you. Flee as from plague, poison, and death; for unless you flee quickly, you will not escape. Flee the idol-temple, so that you may not eat there to the stumbling of simple brethren, because you have already become idolaters in their weak conscience when they suppose that you eat there in honour of idols. [Col. 0916C]

> “I speak as to prudent people; judge for yourselves what I say. The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not a communion in the blood of Christ? And the bread which we break, is it not a participation in the body of the Lord? Because we, though many, are one bread and one body, and all partake of the one bread.”

Flee idolatry; and in order that you may flee from it, I speak to you of a profound matter, not as to unlearned people but as to prudent people capable of reason. Therefore you yourselves, as prudent people, judge what I say: that is, whether, because of the reason which I now add, you ought to flee far [Col. 0916D] from idols and utterly abstain from their sacrifices.

“The cup of blessing,” etc. He speaks first of the cup because afterwards he was to say more about the bread. “The cup of blessing which we bless,” that is, the cup over which Christ gave blessing at supper, and over which we priests give blessing in the Mass; or, the cup of blessing, that is, the cup by whose draught blessing is poured into believers, over which we priests give blessing in the consecration of the sacraments—“is it not a communion in the blood of Christ?” That is, does it not make those who drink it worthily participants in Christ’s life, which is signified by blood, since, as Moses says, “the life of the flesh is in the blood” (Lev. 17)?

That is, does it not make us participants in that blessedness and glory in which your soul becomes one thing with his [Col. 0917A] soul through participation in the same glory? Here it is implied that, similarly, the cursed cup of idols makes those who drink it participants in the death of demons. And the bread which we priests break upon the altar, dividing one bread into many parts to signify the union in love of those who receive it, is it not a participation in the body of the Lord? That is, does it not effect in us that our bodies may at last receive a share in the immortality and glory of our body? This means: participation in the Lord’s cup and bread makes our soul and body at last conformed to the soul and body of Christ by receiving the same blessedness.

But this will then be so if what is visibly received in the sacrament is spiritually eaten and spiritually drunk in the reality [Col. 0917B] itself. For just as, in order that there may be a visible form of bread, many grains are mixed into one—as though there is brought about that which Scripture says concerning the faithful: “They had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4)—and just as in making wine the liquid of the grapes is blended into unity, so the Lord Jesus signified that we belong to him through unity of love and consecrated at his table the mystery of peace and of our unity. Therefore the person who receives the mystery of unity but does not hold the bond of peace receives the mystery not for himself but as testimony against himself.

The bread which we break is participation in the body of the Lord, because the very bread which we divide among many is the true body of the Lord; those who receive from it receive from the body of the Lord [Col. 0917C] and themselves become what they receive. “For we, though many, are one bread and one body.” For as one bread is composed of many grains and one body of many members, so the Church of Christ is joined together from many faithful persons by uniting love.

Therefore we are one bread. For we began to be ground by fasts and exorcisms; then in baptism we were moistened; and through receiving the Holy Spirit we were baked; and thus we became the Lord’s bread, if we have persevered in being one. For this reason, as has been said (Matt. 26; Mark 14; Luke 22), the Lord commended his body and blood in things which are reduced into one thing from many: for one thing is made into one from many grains, and another flows into one [Col. 0917D] from many grapes. Accordingly, communion in Christ’s body and blood signifies and effects the eternal fellowship of the saints, where peace and unity will be full and perfect.

For all these reasons we are rightly called one bread and one body, because we all partake of the one bread of Christ’s body. The fact that each person receives his own portion from this bread signifies that each becomes a participant in this grace according to his measure. But if the one bread of the Lord’s sacrament makes one body of Christ in the Church, then the bread of idolatry is communion with demons; and just as all of us who partake of the one bread and one cup of the Lord become one body, so if we eat and drink [Col. 0918A] with idolaters from their sacrifice, we surely become one body with them. For whoever eats idol-sacrifice (*idolothytum*) becomes one with the demon, just as one who eats Christ’s body becomes one with Christ.

> “See Israel according to the flesh. Are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar?”

I have said that those who eat Christ’s flesh and drink his blood are participants in Christ, and I show you this by an analogy. For see—that is, consider—Israel, which is Israel not according to the spirit as we are, but according to flesh alone: that is, the Jewish people, who are children of Jacob in flesh alone and who understand and keep the commandments of the Law carnally. Are not those among them [Col. 0918B] who eat sacrifices, carnally offered, participants in the altar? That is, do they not receive a portion of the altar’s sacrifice for food? Certainly. For one part was burned upon the altar and another part was eaten. And just as the Jews became participants in the altar by eating the sacrifices, so we become participants in Christ by eating his flesh, because the true substance of the flesh which is in Christ passes into us, just as that sacrifice which was on the altar passed into those who ate it. Similarly, those who eat sacrifices offered to idols become companions of demons, just as carnal Israel, eating the sacrifices, was companion to the altar in the Temple.

> “What then? Do I say that what is sacrificed to idols is [Col. 0918C] anything? Or that an idol is anything? But the things which the nations sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God” (Deut. 32). “And I do not want you to become companions of demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot be participants in the table of the Lord and in the table of demons.”

Because the Apostle warned them to flee the worship of idols so that they might not be defiled by such foods, he perceived the movement of their hearts, and therefore forestalled anyone saying to him: “Then you say that an idol has some power or can defile.” “No,” he says, “the insensible idol does not defile; rather, the demons who preside over the temples, to corrupt people and enslave them to their own service.” He condemned not what was offered, [Col. 0918D] but the fact that it was offered to them.

As though he said: Since I said, “Flee from the worship of idols,” lest anyone be disturbed by this, I ask: what do I say in those preceding words? Do I mean to say that something sacrificed to idols is something—that is, that it is changed into some dignity? Or do I mean that an idol is something—that is, that it can benefit or harm in any respect? I do not say this. Rather, I assert this: that the sacrifices which the nations offer, they offer not to idols but to demons, which are hidden in idols, and not to God. For they are more devoted to demons, and this is more dangerous. For if they worshipped idols only, then, as idols would give them no help, so neither would they harm them. For an image truly is nothing, but beneath the covering of the image the devil is worshipped.

The nations [Col. 0919A] sacrifice to demons. But I do not wish you, who have been incorporated into Christ, to become companions of demons through the sacrifices of the nations. For not everything that is seen is in the idol; beneath the covering of the idol is the hidden mystery of iniquity. Therefore one must abstain from eating such sacrifices. Yet the Lord says: “What enters the mouth does not defile a human being” (Matt. 15; Mark 7). Here it should be known that the foods themselves, and indeed every creature of God, are clean in themselves (1 Tim. 4), but invocation of idols and demons makes them unclean.

You ought, therefore, to reject sacrifices to idols, because you cannot drink the cup of the Lord, in which is his blood, and the cup of demons, in which is the wine of sacrilegious superstition; nor can you be participants in the table—that is, the altar—of the Lord, on which is his body, and the table—that is, altar—of demons. You will endure so great a loss that you are separated from the body and blood of the Lord, without which you cannot have life, because no one can eat both Christ’s sacrifice and the devil’s sacrifice (John 6). “For what fellowship has Christ with Belial? Or what share has a believer with an unbeliever? Or what agreement has the temple of God with idols?” (2 Cor. 6). There is no fellowship between these, because death and life do not agree together. It follows:

> “Or do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?”

We ought not eat sacrifices to idols to the ruin of brethren. [Col. 0919C] For do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? That is, do we envy the Lord so as to diminish his kingdom by eating idol-sacrifices to the destruction of brethren? We ought not provoke him to jealousy by trying to take away his members. For are we stronger than he, so that we can prevail against him and draw to destruction those whom he wishes to preserve for life, or defend ourselves against his blow? We act to our own harm if we act against Christ.

Or thus: “Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy?” That is, do we imitate Christ, who ate with tax collectors and sinners (Matt. 9; Mark 2; Luke 5), when we eat with idolaters? We do not at all imitate him in this act, because he did not take food with idolaters but with those who worshipped one God, though they were sinners, in order to draw them to repentance by the sweetness of his familiarity. Do we imitate the Lord? Not at all. “And are we stronger than he?” That is, do we perform deeds greater than his, by the knowledge through which we know an idol to be nothing, taking idol-sacrifice though he did not do so? For to do what he did not do is to be stronger than he—yet this is not strength but weakness.

> “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient” (Ezek. 37; above, ch. 6). “All things are lawful for me, but not all things build up. Let no one seek what is his own, but what belongs to another.”

We must abstain from things offered in sacrifice. All kinds of food are indeed lawful for me, since I can take them with a pure heart; but not all are expedient for me, that is, [Col. 0920A] some do not assist but impede my course. They are lawful according to the law of nature, because all things are naturally clean; and therefore they are lawful—that is, prohibited to me by no commandment. All kinds of food are lawful for me, both by the law of nature and by the power of free choice; but not all build up neighbours, because things offered to idols destroy them and overthrow them from the faith. Therefore we must abstain even from lawful things lest brethren be scandalized.

For no one should seek what is his own, that is, his own private advantage, but another’s advantage. The person who truly understands that an idol is nothing and every creature of God good (1 Tim. 4), and nevertheless eats sacrifices to idols without fearing to scandalize brethren for the sake of his food, seeks what is his own, [Col. 0920B] not what belongs to others. But the person who abstains from lawful things lest he injure brethren seeks not what is his own but what belongs to others, because, compelled by love, he seeks others’ advantage even through his own losses. What we have said concerning food should be understood concerning every matter: the person who disregards his own advantages for the advantages of neighbours is righteous.

> “Eat whatever is sold in the market, asking no questions for conscience’ sake. ‘The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness’” (Ps. 23).

Since these things are lawful, yet ought not always be used, he determines how and for what reason they may be eaten: namely, if they are found for sale in the market. “Eat,” he says, “whatever is sold in the market,” [Col. 0920C] that is, whatever is sold where meats are sold, “asking no questions”—that is, not asking whether it has been offered in sacrifice or not. Do this for conscience’ sake—that is, so that your conscience may be free; for even if something has been offered to an idol, if the buyer does not know this, he suffers no scruple and is guiltless before God.

Or this is for the preservation of the seller’s conscience: because if, after he had said it had been offered in sacrifice, you ate it, he, if an unbeliever, would be confirmed in unbelief; or, if a believer, would be drawn back from faith. Ask no questions, because if you ask unbelievers, who know that you are Christians, they will answer in mockery that everything has been sacrificed. I said that you should eat without inquiry because the earth, which nourishes [Col. 0920D] and sustains all things, is the Lord’s, and its fullness, that is, all things with which the earth is filled. What belongs to the Lord cannot be unclean. Therefore, if something is offered to idols, or is not known to be so offered, it may be taken for necessary use without any scruple of conscience. But if it is certainly known to have been offered, it is better rejected through Christian virtue.

> “If one of the unbelievers invites you to supper and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no questions for conscience’ sake. But if anyone should say, ‘This has been sacrificed to idols,’ do not eat, because of the one who informed you and because of conscience. Now I mean conscience, not your own but that of the other. For why is my liberty judged by another’s conscience? If I partake with thanksgiving [Col. 0921A], why am I reviled for that for which I give thanks? Therefore, whether you eat or drink, or do anything else, do everything for the glory of God.”

I explained how what you buy may be eaten; I shall also explain how what is given without charge may be eaten (Col. III). Thus, namely: “If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner,” etc. A dinner is so called from the fellowship of those eating; for the Greeks call “common” κοινόν (*koinon*). Hence also “those who communicate,” because they come together jointly, that is, alike. Among the ancients it was customary to eat in public view and feast together, lest isolation breed extravagance.

If an unbeliever invites you to dinner, I do not command you to go, but leave it to your own choice. A Christian ought to go to an unbeliever’s dinner if he has some gain to make there, [Col. 0921B] that is, if he knows he can win that person over; just as Christ ate with sinners in order to turn them to repentance (Matt. IX). If you wish to go to such a dinner, eat simply everything set before you, without asking where it came from, for the sake of the conscience of those reclining with you, lest you confirm unbelievers in their error if you knowingly eat before them foods connected with idolatry. This, however, is said to the perfect, who, despising the idol because it is nothing, can eat from the sacrifice, being certain that what is eaten under the name of God the Creator cannot defile.

Eat without inquiry what is set before you. But if anyone says of what is set before you, “This has been sacrificed to idols,” no longer eat, for the sake of the person who pointed it out, lest he suppose that you eat it in veneration of idols, and [Col. 0921C] for the sake of others’ conscience. For one who serves idols will boast if he sees you eating from sacrifices, will be confirmed in error, and you will give your brethren a bad example. It is clear that flesh is not in itself unclean. For if the very nature of sacrificial flesh were unclean, it would certainly defile even one unaware of it; for it would not be any less itself because it was taken by someone unaware. But abstain for conscience’ sake, lest you appear to have shared fellowship with demons.

By “conscience,” however, I mean not yours, which is firm in knowledge of the truth, but that of another, who is still weak in faith or has not yet come to faith. For every unbeliever will rejoice within his own conscience if he sees you eagerly desiring what has been sacrificed to idols, and will say: “How is it that [Col. 0921D] Christians forbid us to sacrifice, as though it were evil, while they themselves eat those things as though they were holy and clean?” Therefore one must abstain, lest a bad opinion of us arise in others’ minds. For why is my liberty judged by another’s conscience? That is: when my conscience is free from veneration of an idol, why need I give a bad impression of myself and cause people to suppose that I eat things sacrificed to idols for the sake of veneration? For I would be judged not to differ from idolaters if I did not recoil from what has been offered to idols.

And if I partake with thanksgiving—that is, if I share in God’s grace, because I eat in his name—why am I reviled for that for which I give thanks? That is, why need I incur the blasphemy of the ignorant? Why is it necessary for me to make people suppose that I am devoted [Col. 0922A] to an idol, because I do not shun things offered to it? For I am reviled and reproached on this account, because I seem to think something great of the idol; unbelievers rejoice in idolatry, since they suppose me to be a participant and so have an occasion to remain in error; and the faithful are given a bad example. Since these evils would result from it, therefore beware of things offered to idols, so that you may eat to the praise of God.

Although through the purity of your conscience it is lawful for you to consume such things, knowingly eating them is nevertheless hostile to God, because they are dedicated to the devil in reproach of the one God. Therefore do not cause God to be blasphemed by your food or your act; rather, “whether you eat or drink, or do anything else, do all things to the glory of God”—that is, do everything in such a manner that [Col. 0922B] God is glorified and praised by it. By eating and drinking modestly, sparingly, and temperately, glorify God.

For if you take what you eat and drink for the refreshment of the body and the restoration of its members, giving thanks to him who has afforded you, mortal and frail as you are, these consolations of sustenance, then both your food and your drink praise God. But if you exceed nature’s due measure through the excess of gluttony, and gorge yourself with wine, you blaspheme God in eating and drinking. If after food and drink you rest in order to sleep, and do nothing shameful in bed, nor exceed the permission granted in God’s law, you praise him. And when you sleep, if an evil conscience does not rouse you from rest, the innocence of your sleep praises God; and when you are awake and act well, and God is praised for your good work, you praise God by your work [Col. 0922C]. Thus everything must be done for his praise.

> “Give no offense to Jews, to Gentiles, or to the Church of God, just as I too please all people in all things, not seeking what is useful to myself but what is useful to the many, so that they may be saved.”

So order your conduct that no one suffers scandal from it. Be, that is, without offense to Jews, Gentiles, and the Church of God. Jews are offended if they see a Christian—who says that he accepts the Law and the Prophets—not abhorring idols, which they themselves abhor. Gentiles, however, are offended if, in the matter in which they stand, they are not merely unrebuked but are made readier still, since the offerings [Col. 0922D] to their idols are not avoided. The Church of God is offended when it sees some of its own number clinging to things hostile to God. Take care, therefore, not to offend all alike by one food of yours, just as I not only offend no one, but also please everyone in all that I do.

The Apostle did not indeed please everyone in such a way as to please even his many persecutors; rather, he pleased every class of persons whom Christ’s Church gathered, whether those already within it or those to be brought into it. Good rulers ought to desire to please people, but for this purpose: that by the sweetness of their good repute they may draw their neighbors into love of the truth. They should not desire to be loved for themselves; rather, they should make their own being loved, as it were, a road by which they lead the hearts of their hearers [Col. 0923A] into love of the Creator. For it is difficult for a preacher, however rightly he may proclaim, to be heard willingly if he is not loved.

Therefore one who presides ought to strive to be loved, so that he may be heard; yet he must not seek that love for his own sake, lest he be found, while he is seen to serve through his office, to rebel against the one whom he serves through the hidden tyranny of his thought. Rightly, therefore, the Apostle now says, “I please all people in all things,” although elsewhere he denies that he pleases human beings (Gal. I). For he adds, “not seeking what is useful to myself, but what is useful to the many, so that they may be saved.” It is not useful for salvation to anyone if a person pleases him for that person’s own sake, because one does not rightly please except when one pleases for God’s sake—that is, so that God may please and be glorified, when his gifts are observed in a person [Col. 0923B] or received through a person’s ministry. But when a person pleases in this way, it is no longer the person but God who pleases. Paul therefore both pleases and does not please, because, in seeking to please, he seeks not to please people with himself but, through himself, with the truth.

## CHAPTER XI

> “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ.”

“I,” he says, “please all people, seeking to benefit everyone; and you too be imitators of me, so that you may offend no one, but may seek to please people through a praiseworthy life with this intention.” Be imitators of me as I am an imitator of Christ, because in imitating me you will imitate Christ, who offended no one but came to save all. “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ.”

In the Church this is the order: some go before and others follow; those who go before offer themselves as an example to those who follow, and those who follow imitate those going before (I Tim. II). Yet those who offer themselves as an example to their followers themselves follow Christ. For since they have surpassed all others in making progress, and no human being remains whom they may imitate, Christ himself remains for them to follow to the end [Col. 0923C].

> “Now I praise you, brethren, because in all things you remember me and keep my ordinances as I delivered them to you. But I want you to know that Christ is the head of every man; the man is the head of the woman (Eph. V); and God is the head of Christ. Every man praying or prophesying with his head covered dishonors his head; but every woman praying or prophesying [Col. 0923D] with her head uncovered dishonors her head. For it is one and the same as if she were shaved. For if a woman is not veiled, let her also be shorn. But if it is shameful for a woman to be shorn or shaved, let her veil her head.”

Having rebuked their morals and conduct, he now wishes to correct their traditions. Therefore he begins speaking not by approval, but ironically. “I commanded,” he says, “that you imitate me, and I cannot rebuke you for disobedience; rather, I praise you because in all things you remember me and keep the instructions I delivered to you.” By these words he strikes them more sharply than if he openly rebuked them. For although he was their apostle, they were forgetful of his traditions; nor did they follow, from the tradition of other churches, what they had not yet learned. Therefore he delivered this to them as though newly, [Col. 0924A] saying, “But I want you to know,” etc.

It is as though he said: “You have forgotten me and do not keep my traditions; but I want you to know the matters I now add.” I want you to know that Christ is the head of every man, because man was indeed made by God, but through Christ (Gen. II); but man is the head of woman, because although woman too was made through Christ, she was nevertheless made from man and therefore is subject to man. And just as a man ought to follow Christ, so a woman ought to follow the man and, after his example, do good works. Thus, secondarily, she is subject to Christ through the man. For the man is subject to no one but Christ, while the woman must be subject both to man and to Christ.

Christ is the head of the man, who is governed by wisdom; but man is the head of the woman, who is governed by the man. By man the rational spirit is signified; by woman, the soul. For the spirit of a human being is in a manner the soul’s husband, because it governs the animal affection as though its spouse [Col. 0924B]. Christ, therefore, is the head of man; that is, the governing wisdom of God is the head of that spirit which is in a human being, by which a person can understand spiritual things, if that spirit devoutly subjects itself to God. For nothing is higher than that spirit except wisdom, which is God. But man is the head of woman because the spirit governs the soul.

For there is one thing in a human being that is rational and governs, and another that is animal and is governed, so that the flesh may not desire against the spirit (Gal. V), but may be subjected to the spirit; that is, so that carnal desire may not oppose reason but, by obeying, cease to be carnal, and so that the inner mind, as a masculine reason, may hold subject the soul’s appetite by which we pursue bodily pleasures [Col. 0924C]. Thus Christ is the head of man, and man the head of woman.

But God is the head of Christ, according to the sense in which the Father is greater than he (John XIII): thus God himself, who is one with the Father, is the head of Christ the mediator, who is man. This mediator is he alone. For if we rightly call the mind the ruling principle of a human being, that is, as it were the head of human substance—although the human being is human together with the mind—why should not, much more fittingly, indeed much more truly, the Word together with the Father be God, the head of Christ, although Christ cannot be understood as man except together with the Word which was made flesh (John I)?

“Every man praying,” etc. He comes to the issue, because among the Corinthians men wore their hair long, while women came into church with uncovered heads, glorying in their hair [Col. 0924D]. This was not only indecent but also supplied fuel for lust. Since Christ is the head of man, therefore every man, rich as well as poor, who in church prays to God or prophesies to others—that is, declares things future and hidden—with his physical head covered, dishonors, that is, disgraces, his spiritual head, Christ, or also his bodily head.

Conversely, every woman, because she is inferior and subject to man, if she prays or prophesies in church with her head uncovered, dishonors and renders shameful her own head, which she displays so bare to all. Since Christ, whose service is supreme freedom, is the head of man, it is therefore not right for him to pray or teach in church with his head covered, because there is no intermediary between him and Christ [Col. 0925A]. Therefore he ought not to display in himself a sign of servitude, but of freedom. For since Christ is his head without another intermediary, and God through Christ, he wears no veil as a sign of freedom, since a veil is a sign of subjection.

For he would dishonor his head if he prayed or prophesied with his head covered, because he would seem to regard it as disgraceful to be under Christ as under his head, and to regard as shame what ought to appear to him as supreme freedom and glory. But a woman standing in church with her head uncovered—that is, without the sign of the subjection she owes to man—dishonors her head, that is, disgraces the man, as though she had no intermediary between herself and Christ; or she dishonors her bodily head by laying it bare. For it is the same as if she were shaven—that is, it is equally shameful as if she were shaved.

Indeed, it amounts to the same. For if a woman is not veiled, let her also be shorn. She ought to be shorn if she is not veiled. But if it is shameful for a woman to be shorn or shaved, let her veil her head. For when she stands in church with braided hair upon her back and her forehead bare, this is as shameful as if her hair had been removed by shaving or shearing [Col. 0925B].

Let us now briefly touch on the spiritual meaning. In man, as stated above, rational perception is understood; in woman, the human soul, governed by rational perception as a woman by a man. The human soul itself, which becomes one with both, is, whenever it thinks of the things of God, as it were a man. It ought not to restrain itself from such spiritual contemplation by a veil—that is, by carnal thoughts—but with unveiled face, that is, with a pure heart, it ought to stretch itself out to contemplate heavenly and spiritual things.

But whenever it thinks of the things of the world, it is as it were a woman. Yet lest it become occupied in earthly affairs beyond what is necessary, it must be restrained by the veil of discernment, lest, while wishing to procure things lawful and necessary, it be drawn into thoughts of things unlawful and superfluous. This is the spiritual meaning of the fact that a man ought not to veil his head, but a woman ought to do so.

For man—that is, the manly faculty of reason—praying, that is, desiring things above, or prophesying, that is, considering beforehand future things, with his head veiled, that is, with his keenness overshadowed by clouds of earthly thoughts, dishonors his head: he darkens for himself, by the ugliness of his thoughts, the beauty of heavenly wisdom [Col. 0925C]. But woman—that is, the lower part of the mind intent upon temporal matters—praying, that is, seeking what is necessary for the body, or prophesying, that is, foreseeing future things which she must do, without her head veiled, that is, without having her keenness restrained by the moderation of discernment, dishonors her head: she defiles the higher faculty of the mind, which ought to long only for heavenly things, by the ugliness of inward desires [Col. 0925D].

For it comes to the same thing when, without the veil of modest restraint, she gives herself free rein in the desire for temporal things, as if she were shaved—that is, as though her perverse intention, of which she ought to be ashamed, were laid bare and visible to all. This is signified by the forehead, which is the seat of shame and is prominent. For woman—that is, the part of reason intent on the administration of temporal affairs—if she is not veiled, that is, if she is not modestly restrained from superfluous thoughts, let her also be shorn: that is, let her remove from herself all thoughts of worldly cares [Col. 0926A]. For it is better to cast off every worldly care than, while providing necessities, to be scattered among every worldly desire.

But if it is shameful for the woman to be shorn or shaved—that is, if this lower part of the soul, which is of little use for anything else, considers it unsuitable to cut away from itself, as though hair, all worldly cares, or to expose to all the shamelessness of its intention toward temporal things—let her veil her head: that is, let her modestly restrain her keenness from superfluous thoughts.

> “A man indeed ought not to veil his head, because he is the image and glory of God. But woman is the glory of man [Col. 0926B]. For man is not from woman, but woman from man (Gen. II). Indeed, man was not created for woman, but woman for man. Therefore a woman ought to have a covering upon her head, also because of the angels. Nevertheless, neither is man without woman nor woman without man in the Lord. For as woman is from man, so also man is through woman. But all things are from God.”

A man indeed ought not to veil his head; that is, he ought not to bear over himself a sign of servitude or authority, but of freedom, because he has nothing over him except God. For he is the image and glory of God. The image—that is, the impress of likeness—and glory of God are seen in man, because the one God made one human being [Col. 0926C], so that, just as all things are from one God, all human beings might be from one human being, and so that the one visible human being might bear on earth the image of the one invisible God. Thus the one God was seen, in one human being, to preserve the authority of a single principle, to the confusion of the devil, who, abandoning the one God, wished to usurp lordship and divinity for himself.

Therefore man is the image and glory of God: as God rules all things through omnipotence, so man rules earthly things through understanding. Woman, however, is the glory of man, because she was made as his helper, so that the man might have glory from her when he led her toward God and offered himself to her for imitation in holiness, just as he himself was the glory of God when he followed God’s wisdom. Woman is the glory of man when he governs and she obeys: he is governed by wisdom [Col. 0926D], she by man. Woman is the glory of man because she is from him and subject to him. For man is not from woman but woman from man; that is, Adam was not from Eve, but Eve from Adam.

And I demonstrate by yet another reason why woman is man’s glory: because man was not created for woman, but woman for man; that is, Adam was not created to assist Eve, but Eve to assist Adam. This confirms what we said, that the one God made one human being, because man and woman are one in nature, since the origin of woman is man. Therefore, to show that she is subject, a woman ought to have a veil over her head—that is, authority, signifying the authority of man over her. She should not have her head free in church, but covered by a veil.

And this is also because of the angels—that is, the priests, messengers of the divine will—lest they be stirred to lust by seeing her face; and because a priest bears the person of Christ, a woman ought, on account of the origin of guilt, to appear subject before the priest, who is Christ’s vicar, as before a judge [Col. 0927A]. Or it is because of the angels assigned to guard us, lest the wanton exposure of a woman displease them when they see the fuel of sin stirred up by her.

I said that woman is the glory of man, both because she exists for man and because at the beginning she was created from man. Yet in subsequent generation this is not so, because neither man without woman nor woman without man is created in the Lord—that is, through the working of the Lord, who at first made both from one and made them one. For they are one flesh and one body in the Lord, that is, according to God, who created them.

Or thus: although a woman bears the sign of subjection on account of the origin of guilt, she is nevertheless not excluded from salvation; for neither man without woman—that is, with woman excluded—nor woman without man—that is, with man excluded—is in the Lord, that is, in the Lord’s grace and eternal salvation. Neither is excluded; both are admitted. And why is this? Because, as woman was first made from man, so man is afterward born through woman. Woman is from man; man through woman. But all things are from God. What “all things,” except those of which the discussion is now concerned? That is, the man from whom woman comes, the woman who is from man, and the man who is through woman.

After the Apostle has explained each matter step by step, in order to subject all things to God while preserving one principle, he says, “All things are from God,” so that [Col. 0927C] neither woman might grieve over subjection nor man grow proud, as though over exaltation.

But it is fitting to return to the spiritual meaning. For man ought not to veil his head because he is the image and glory of God. Genesis teaches that man and woman were made in the image of God: “God,” it says, “made the human being; in the image of God he made him; male and female he made them” (Gen. II). For it calls human nature itself, completed in both sexes, made in God’s image; nor does it separate woman from the image of God that must be understood.

How then does the Apostle say that man is the image of God, and for this reason is forbidden to veil his head, whereas woman is not, and therefore is commanded to veil her head? Only if we understand, in the nature of the human mind, woman together with her man to be the image of God, so that that entire substance is one image [Col. 0927D]. But when it is apportioned to a service which pertains to it alone, it is not the image of God. What pertains to man alone, however, is the image of God as full and whole as it is when woman is joined with him in one.

For man was created principally in God’s image, and in him reason naturally has greater force, as though he himself were reason, which is God’s glory. Woman, however, is sensation itself, which by serving is the glory of reason, because this naturally prevails in woman. Therefore the nature of the human mind is the image of God only in the respect in which it cleaves to the consideration of eternal reasons. For even if it contemplates the whole truth, it is the image of God; and when something is apportioned from it and directed by a certain intention to the conduct of temporal affairs, nevertheless, in the respect in which it consults the truth it has beheld, it is the image of God; but in the respect in which it is intent on lower actions, it is not the image of God [Col. 0928A].

And because, the more fully it extends itself toward what is eternal, the more it is thereby formed to the image of God, it must not be restrained from that, so as to contain itself and turn away from it. For this reason man ought not to veil his head. But because excessive descent into lower things is dangerous to that rational activity which deals with temporal and bodily matters, it ought to have authority over its head; this is indicated by the veil, by which it is signified that it must be restrained.

Man is not from woman but woman from man: that is, the truth of eternal contemplation does not come from the administration of temporal things, to be governed by it; nor does reason come from sensation, but the reverse. For man was not created for woman—that is, rational perception does not serve sensation, nor is contemplation of eternal things subject to temporal action—but the reverse. Therefore woman—that is, sensation and that part of reason which turns aside to govern temporal things—should have authority, that is, the yoke of higher governance, over her head, so that by discipline she may be pressed back from the harmful freedom of wandering thoughts, because of God’s angels, who always see us, lest they be offended by the unrestrained wantonness of our thoughts [Col. 0928B].

Nevertheless, neither is man—that is, rational perception—without woman, that is, without sensation or the management of temporal things; nor is woman—that is, sensation or temporal action—without man, that is, without higher perception, in the Lord, that is, in the Lord’s work. Rather, the Lord made both that which has the power of governing in a human being and that lower thing which is to be governed. For as woman is from man—that is, as good action has its origin from knowledge of truth—so also man is through woman: that is, in like manner knowledge of truth is afterward sharpened through good action. But all things are from God: that is, both contemplation of truth and good action, or the higher and lower part of the soul.

Alternatively, by man are signified the spiritual rulers of the Church’s people, in whom there ought not to be the veil of ignorance. By woman, however, are represented weak souls, which cannot grasp anything spiritual or anything concerning invisible things. Yet the veil of ignorance does them no harm if, concerning matters they do not understand, they presume nothing from their own judgment, but, giving honor to their priests as to angels, ask them about what they do not know [Col. 0928C]. But if any weak person, still thinking carnally, presumes to compare herself with spiritual men, she dishonors her head—that is, she dishonors the Church’s priests. But leaving these points aside, let us consider what follows; for he adds:

> “Judge for yourselves: is it fitting for a woman to pray to God unveiled? Does not nature itself teach you that, if a man wears his hair long, it is a disgrace to him, but if a woman wears her hair long, it is her glory, because her hair has been given to her for a covering?”
