I said that a woman ought to have her head veiled in church; judge for yourselves whether I have said this reasonably [Col. 0929A]. Judge whether it is fitting for a woman to pray to God unveiled. It is not fitting, because nature itself teaches you that this is proper, since it multiplies a woman’s hair so abundantly.

Although this was the rationale of apostolic tradition, that women should be veiled in church, they, on the contrary, allowed them to be unveiled in church (Ezek. XLIX). Therefore he now strives to persuade them of the truth not through the authority of the tradition they had neglected, but through nature itself. “Does not nature itself,” he says, “teach you this?” And nature teaches that if a man wears his hair long—although the Law also forbids this—it is a disgrace, that is, a great reproach to him; but if a woman wears her hair long, it is her glory, because her hair grows and multiplies so long and beautifully that it appears her highest glory and beauty.

Therefore it is her glory because, by nature’s ordinance, hair has been given her as a covering—that is, it has been given her to indicate that another covering should be added, as is implied by the growth of the hair [Col. 0929B]. For hair is a sign of a veil, so that nature’s intention may be supplemented. Therefore a man is not naturally long-haired because he is not to be veiled.

But according to the preceding exposition of spiritual meaning, nature itself does not teach a woman to pray to God without a veil, because the upright stance of a human being indicates that the part of reason which manages temporal matters ought not to ask such things of the Lord without the veil of discernment, lest, like God’s animals, it cast itself wholly down into desire for earthly things. It ought to be restrained by a veil from excessive thought and desire for lower things.

A man—that is, the higher faculty of the mind, which ought serenely to think heavenly things—if he grows hair, that is, a dense mass of superfluous thoughts, incurs disgrace. But woman—that is, that part of the mind which administers temporal matters—if she grows hair, that is, a multitude of useful thoughts through which she wisely carries out the necessary administration of bodily things, it is her glory, because she thereby has a reward with God [Col. 0929C]. Because hair has been given to her for a covering—that is, manifold thought concerning necessary matters has been given to her, so that beneath it she may be covered and hidden from the unrestrained wandering of useless and harmful thoughts.

> “But if anyone seems to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the Church [Col. 0929D] of God. But in commanding this, I do not praise you, because you come together not for the better but for the worse.”

I said that men ought not to wear their hair long, but that women ought to grow their hair and veil their heads, and I have shown many reasons for this. But if anyone seems contentious, wishing still to dispute about this matter, at least he ought to yield to authority, because we Jews—from whose instruction the religious practice of the Church proceeded, and who have always been God’s people—have no such custom, namely, that men should wear long hair and women uncover their heads; nor does the Church of God, constituted from Jews and Gentiles.

After reasons he adduces authority in order to overcome the contentious, because neither Judaism nor the Church of God possessed this practice [Col. 0930A], showing that neither Moses nor the Savior handed it down in this way. Then he no longer wishes to dispute further about men’s tonsure or women’s veiling, but gives a command concerning it, saying: “But in commanding this”—that is, so that the ingenuity of one who argues is not sought, but the authority of one who commands is regarded. It is as though he said: “Perhaps someone still wishes to argue that this should not be done; but I command it to be done in this way and establish it by my authority. I speak, not praising but rather censuring, because you come together in church to receive the body and blood of the Lord not for the better, as would be proper, but for the worse.” That is, your assembly for the Lord’s supper is not for your improvement but for your deterioration, because you sin there in many ways.

> [Col. 0930B] “First of all, when you come together in the church, I hear that there are divisions among you, and in part I believe it. For there must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you.”

“First of all,” that is, the greatest of all evils among you is that schisms occur in your assembly. For you come together not for the better but for the worse, because when you come together in church—where there ought to be the bond of charity, one will, and perfect concord, to which the one place invites and exhorts you—I hear that there are divisions, that is, dissensions, among you; and I believe that these exist “in part,” that is, among some of you.

There were divisions among them because those who possessed the higher gifts of the Spirit despised the rest, who had not received such great gifts, and separated themselves from them [Col. 0930C]. The lesser members themselves also, in a kind of despair, withdrew from them, when they marveled at those persons’ great excellence in spiritual gifts, which they could not attain. I believe that divisions of schism exist among you. Nor is this surprising, because heresies must exist—that is, it is useful for the faithful that they exist against them for their exercise—so that through these, the good, those already approved and known by God, may become manifest to human beings among you, that is, in your midst.

Some of these people were heretics, such as those who denied the resurrection (Matt. XXII; Acts XXIII). But through them those who firmly held the apostolic faith became manifest to the rest, saying, “I am Christ’s,” when [Col. 0930D] others said, “I am Paul’s,” and “I am Apollos’s” (above, I). Heresies always benefit the faithful. For heretics arise from those people who, even if they remained in the Church, would nevertheless err.

When they are outside, however, they are of great benefit, not by teaching truth, which they do not know, but by stirring up carnal Catholics to seek the truth and spiritual Catholics to disclose it. There are indeed countless men in the holy Church approved by God, but they do not become manifest among us so long as, delighting in the darkness of our ignorance, we prefer to sleep rather than behold the light of truth. Therefore many are awakened from sleep by heretics, so that they may see and rejoice in God’s truth.

Let us therefore make use of heretics, not so as to approve their errors, but so that, in defending Catholic teaching against their snares, we may be more watchful and cautious, even if we cannot bring them back to salvation. Therefore heresies must exist, so that those who are approved may become manifest among us [Col. 0931A]. For those are approved by God who can teach well. Yet they cannot become known to human beings unless they teach. But they do not wish to teach except those who seek to be taught.

Many, however, are too sluggish to seek unless they are awakened, as though from sleep, by the troubles and assaults of heretics; unless they are ashamed of themselves in their ignorance and feel themselves endangered by it. Therefore divine providence permits many heretics of diverse error to exist, so that when they assail and question us concerning matters we do not know, we may at least shake off sluggishness and desire to know the divine Scriptures. A heretic is one who, for the sake of some temporal advantage, and especially for the sake of the glory and primacy of his own rule, either generates or follows false and novel opinions [Col. 0931B].

> “Therefore, when you come together in one place, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s supper; for each one takes his own supper beforehand to eat. And one indeed is hungry, while another is drunk. Do you not have houses in which to eat and drink? Or do you despise the Church of God and shame those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I praise you? In this I do not praise you.”

Since there are divisions among you, therefore when you come together in one place, it is no longer possible to eat the Lord’s supper—that is, to eat what you do there—for you do it discordantly; it is no longer [Col. 0931C] to eat the Lord’s supper. For each of you presumes to eat separately in the church his own supper, that is, his own offering, whereas the Lord’s supper ought to be common to all Christians, just as Christ supped in common with his disciples. He touches upon their custom: for frequently in the year, on certain appointed days, all used to assemble in the church to receive the body and blood of the Lord, and to hold a meal in the church from their offerings, after the example of the supper which the Lord held with his disciples. But very many of them had perverted this custom. According as one arrived before another, bringing his own food, he ate and became drunk, without waiting for his poor [Col. 0931D] brother; and afterward he received the body of the Lord, or mixed it with the food of his own table, failing to judge that it differed from other foods.

For when they offered their gifts upon the arrival of the presbyters—because rulers had not yet been appointed to churches in every place—they claimed for themselves all that they had offered, because of schism. For pseudo-apostles had sown dissensions among them, so that they jealously guarded their offerings, although the offerings of all were blessed by one and the same prayer; and thus those who, as often happens, had offered nothing or had nothing from which to offer, were put to shame and embarrassed, receiving no share. They acted so quickly that those arriving later found nothing to eat. Therefore the Apostle reproves them. “If,” he says, “you assemble in such a manner that each takes his own food, these things must be done at home [Col. 0932A], not in church, where people assemble for the sake of unity and mystery, not of dissension and the belly. For the gift that is offered becomes that of the whole people, because all are signified in the one bread. Since all are one through this, all ought to receive from the one bread.”

Thus it is said: “When you come together in one place, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s supper”; that is, you can no longer receive the sacraments of the Redeemer, nor do you any longer hold there a meal in likeness of the Lord’s supper. Why? Because each of you presumes his own supper—that is, what he has brought with him—namely, he takes it before the Lord’s supper and before the others assemble, in order to eat, not to distribute to the poor. And one person, who has brought nothing to eat or has come late, goes hungry; another, who has hastened to consume [Col. 0932B] his own food, is drunk. Thus you are no longer fit to eat the Lord’s supper—that is, to receive the sacred Eucharist, which must be received by those who are fasting and in concord—although the apostles at first received it without fasting.

For it pleased the Holy Spirit that, in honor of so great a sacrament, the Lord’s body should enter the Christian’s mouth before other foods. Thus this custom is observed throughout the whole world. Nor did the Lord give it after food for this reason: brethren who have already dined or supped ought to assemble to receive it, or else, as those whom the Apostle now rebukes and corrects did, they would mix it with their own tables. For the Savior, in order to commend more forcefully the profundity of that mystery, wished to impress this last act upon the hearts and memory of the disciples, [Col. 0932C] from whom he was soon to depart for his passion. Therefore he did not prescribe the order in which it was thereafter to be received, reserving this matter for the apostles through whom he was to order the Church.

“You,” he says, “eat in such a way, each his own offerings, and do not make them, as you ought, common to all. But why do you come to church for such eating? Do you not have homes in which to eat and drink, so that you may hold meals of this kind there? Or do you despise the Church of God—that is, the house of prayer (Isa. LVI; Matt. XXI), consecrated for praying to God in it and for receiving his sacraments? You certainly despise it when you irreverently consume bodily foods in it. And you also put to shame those who do not have [Col. 0932D] anything to eat there, while you overflow with luxuries before their eyes and they either remain fasting or eat only their own bread. You also shame the poor who have nothing to eat because you eat before they arrive and leave them nothing; thus when they come, they find nothing to eat and are ashamed. For in this way you shame both those who are present and receive nothing, whether they consume their poverty alongside your excessive wealth, and those who arrive afterward and find nothing.

“And what am I to say to you who do such things? I do not find what I might say to you worthy of the commission of such deeds. Do I praise you? In this, in which you act so badly, I do not praise you, but greatly rebuke you. Or, I praise [Col. 0933A] you in certain other matters, but in this I find nothing praiseworthy.”

> “For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you: that the Lord Jesus, on the night in which he was betrayed, took bread; and, giving thanks, broke it and said: ‘Take and eat: this is my body, which will be handed over for you. Do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup, after he had supped, saying: ‘This cup is the New Testament in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me’” (Matt. XXVI; Mark XIV; Luke XXII).

Rightly I do not praise you but censure you for assembling for the Lord’s supper in so perverse and irreverent a manner, because you have not properly [Col. 0933B] kept my tradition concerning this matter. Yet you ought diligently to have kept it, because I did not devise it myself, nor did I learn it from Peter or Andrew, but received it from the Lord; and I handed it on to you concerning so great a matter. Therefore you must hold reverently and inviolably what the Lord handed on to me and I to you. This I handed on to you: “that the Lord Jesus,” and so forth.

The Apostle shows that the mystery of the Eucharist, celebrated during a supper, is not itself a supper. For it is a spiritual medicine which, tasted reverently, purifies the devout recipient; and it is a memorial of our redemption, so that, mindful of the Redeemer, we may deserve to receive greater things from him. He was handed over by night to his passion, but from thence he came to the light of the resurrection.

The Lord Jesus—that is, the Savior [Col. 0933C] of believers—on the night in which he was handed over, when the moment of his passion was already at hand, took bread and, giving thanks, broke it. He took bread to signify that he had taken the body by which he would feed us. He gives thanks to the Father for the restoration of humankind to be accomplished through his passion and through the sacrament of his body and blood. He broke the bread to show that the breaking of his body—that is, his passion—would come not without his own will and purpose, but that he himself would bring it about, as he says: “For I lay down my life, that I may take it up again; and no one shall take it from me, but I lay it down of myself” (John X).

He broke the bread in order to give from it to all his own and make them all one, and he said to them: “Receive this spiritual food and eat this sacrament”: that is, receive with your mind [Col. 0933D] and eat with your mouth, namely so that you may not eat my flesh merely sacramentally, as many other wicked people do, but eat unto participation in the Spirit, so that you may remain in my body as members and be quickened by my Spirit. “For he who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me and I in him” (John VI). The sign that one has eaten and drunk is this: if he abides and is abided in, if he dwells and is dwelt in, if he clings so as not to be abandoned. Thus I give you my flesh to eat: namely, that by eating it you may not abandon my unity.

“Eat what I give, for this is my body.” To the outward senses it appears to be bread, but recognize with the senses of the mind that this is my body: not another, but that same body substantially [Col. 0934A] which will be given over to death and crucified for your redemption. What he said—“Do this”—means: receive and eat my body, through the succession of time until the end of the age, in remembrance of me; that is, in memory of my passion. Ponder and consider what worthy, holy, and efficacious medicine for human salvation you receive, so that, from consideration of such holiness, you may receive the sacred Eucharist with greater veneration and desire to imitate my passion, being ready, if necessary, to die for the salvation of your brethren. For in receiving my body you ought to be mindful of me, carefully reflecting who I am, what I did while living among human beings, and what I endured, so that you may follow as I went before.

Or: you priests, do this—that is, consecrate my body from bread through mystical words—in remembrance of my passion, so that you may recall it while offering this sacrifice. Likewise, as he had taken bread and made from it his true body, he also took the cup and made his blood from wine, after he had supped—that is, after the old Passover which he had then eaten with his disciples had been completed. [Col. 0934B] For he passed from the old to the new Passover, which he handed over to the Church for celebration, in order to substitute the sacrament of his own body and blood for the flesh and blood of the legal lamb. He also did this after the end of supper, so that what he did with them last might be impressed more deeply on their minds. For what was more useful for their salvation ought to have been reserved for them until last and most strongly commended to their hearts.

He took the cup and said: “This cup”—that is, this drink—“is the New Testament”: that is, the new promise of the heavenly inheritance in my blood, with which this same cup is filled. That is, the drink of this cup is my blood, which promises not old but new goods—not earthly but heavenly goods (Heb. IX). For Moses’ cup was the Old Testament, because it promised an earthly inheritance in the blood of calves and goats, concerning which Moses himself says: “This is the blood of the covenant which God commanded to you” (Exod. XIV). For an inheritance is given through a testament; and in Christ’s blood we have received the New Testament—that is, the new law which gives to those obedient to it the inheritance [Col. 0934D] of the kingdom of heaven.

We have obtained the New Testament in Christ’s blood, through which we may come to a new inheritance, because the blood of the divine benefaction is its witness. Hence we receive his sacraments for the protection of our body and soul: because his flesh was offered for the salvation of our body, while his blood was shed for our soul, so that both substances of our being might be able to receive the inheritance of everlasting life. Nor is it surprising that he made his flesh and blood from bread and wine. For in every human being he makes flesh and blood from bread and wine: bread eaten is changed into flesh, and wine drunk is turned into blood through the working of the Creator.

The cup of Christ which we drink in the mystery is therefore also called a testament in his blood [Col. 0935A], which he shed once upon the cross for us, because it fortifies and defends us against the accusations of the ancient enemy, lest he be able to take away our heavenly inheritance. It is like those documents called a testament, which protect the heir against an accuser lest he take away the inheritance. “Do this,” he says—that is, drink this cup in remembrance of me, as often as you drink it—so that you may never drink it without memory of my passion, but may have it in mind that I endured death for you. Or rather, you who are priests, do what I have now done: consecrate the cup of wine so that it may become my blood; do this in remembrance of me, so that in this act you may be mindful of me and of the things I suffered for you.

The Lord said this as though someone, dying, left to one whom he loves some pledge; when that person looks upon it after his death, he cannot restrain tears if he loved him perfectly. [Col. 0935B]

> “For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you will proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.”

He explains in what remembrance of Christ we ought to celebrate or receive the sacrament of his body and blood: namely, in remembrance of his death. Therefore, he says, the Lord said that this should be done in remembrance of him, because whenever you eat this bread of life and drink this cup of eternal salvation, you proclaim—that is, represent—the death of the Lord accomplished for us, until he himself comes for judgment. For this sacrament will not [Col. 0935C] be changed as the sacraments of the Jews will be changed. He signifies the end of the age, when there will be rest for the saints, no longer in the sacrament of hope by which the Church is joined together in this time, while that which flowed from Christ’s side is drunk, but already in the very perfection of eternal salvation, when the kingdom is delivered to God and the Father (below, XV), so that in that clear contemplation of unchangeable truth we shall need no bodily mysteries.

> “Therefore whoever eats this bread and drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a person examine himself, and thus eat of that bread and drink of the cup. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment [Col. 0935D] upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord.”

Since we have proved by the authority of the Lord Jesus that this bread is his body and this wine his blood, and that this mystery is to be celebrated or received in remembrance of his death, therefore any person—whether rich, of moderate means, or poor; cleric or layman—who eats this bread of the Lord and drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. He eats and drinks unworthily who celebrates or receives this mystery otherwise than Christ handed it on. Therefore he becomes guilty of the body and blood of the Lord—that is, he will pay the penalty for the Lord’s death. For he was slain on account of those who make his benefit void.

He eats [Col. 0936A] and drinks unworthily who receives the sacred Eucharist without due reverence. He eats and drinks unworthily who approaches this sacrament without first being cleansed through repentance. For this is to receive unworthily: to receive it at a time when one ought to be doing penance. Thus he becomes guilty of the body and blood of the Lord—that is, from wrongly receiving the good sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, he draws not cleansing but the stain of guilt by which he perishes. Nor, if he approaches unworthily, should he congratulate himself because he has not immediately been condemned; for the punishment of the sinner is often deferred, but the hidden judgment is deferred.

Let no one presume to approach unworthily; rather, let a person—that is, one acting rationally—examine, that is, investigate and test himself first. Indeed, from the very fact that he is human, he is not without sin. Let him first examine himself—that is, inspect and consider his life, whether he can approach worthily or not. For scarcely can anyone be found so great and righteous that, upon examination, nothing is found in him which ought to delay him from the body and blood of the Lord, unless he has confessed it and blotted it out through repentance. Let him examine himself, and thus—that is, after he has examined himself—let him eat from that bread and drink from the cup, because then it will benefit him. Therefore let him first investigate and cleanse himself, because whoever eats and drinks unworthily—that is, without examining himself—eats and drinks judgment upon himself.

He eats and drinks unworthily who has committed either some grave sin or many slight sins and does not confess them before approaching communion. We must also eat and drink this sacrament in two ways [Col. 0936C], namely with the mouth of the heart and with the mouth of the body. For one who eats with the mouth of the body alone eats unworthily; but one who receives with both the mouth of the body and the mouth of the heart eats worthily. Whoever eats unworthily eats judgment upon himself—that is, final condemnation, which is here denoted by the term “judgment,” just as when the Lord says: “Those who have done evil [shall rise] to the resurrection of judgment” (John V).

He eats judgment upon himself, not upon another, because communion with wicked persons does not defile anyone through participation in the sacraments, but through sharing in their deeds. For if one does not consent to them in evil deeds, the wicked person bears his own cause and his own person; therefore the good ought to tolerate the wicked. He eats judgment [Col. 0936D] upon himself, not because the thing he receives is evil, but because, being wicked and receiving wickedly, he receives for judgment the good thing which he receives. For Judas, to whom the Lord gave the morsel (John XIII), made room within himself for the devil not by receiving something evil but by receiving wrongly. So whoever receives the Lord’s sacrament unworthily does not make it evil because he himself is evil; nor, because he does not receive it unto salvation, does he receive nothing. It is nevertheless the body of the Lord and the blood of the Lord; but he receives it not for life but for judgment, because he does not discern the body of the Lord—that is, he does not distinguish how much more worthy than all creatures is this body which appears to be bread.

For if he considered that this body is personally united with the Word of God and is the life and salvation of those [Col. 0937A] who receive it worthily, he would not presume to receive unworthily, but would prepare himself to be worthy. One must approach it with a devout mind and with fear, so that the mind knows that it owes reverence to him whose body it approaches to receive, and discerns within itself the dignity of that body. Therefore the Apostle now calls it unworthily received by the Corinthians, because they did not distinguish it from other foods with the singular veneration due to it. For immediately after saying, “he eats and drinks judgment upon himself,” he added, “not discerning the body of the Lord.” They did not discern it, but received it indiscriminately and negligently as though it were any other food. It follows:

> “Therefore among you are many sick and weak, and many sleep.”

[Col. 0937B] Because you eat this body and drink this blood unworthily, therefore among you are many sick, languishing under severe illness; and weak, numbed by prolonged infirmity; and many also sleep—that is, are overtaken by the sleep of death. To prove true that there will be an examination of those receiving the Lord’s body, he already shows here in some persons an image of the judgment: they had received that body heedlessly and were afflicted by illnesses and long infirmities, while many died. Thus the others might learn from them that they do not receive the Lord’s body negligently with impunity; frightened by the example of the few, the rest might amend themselves, knowing that they would suffer more serious punishments in the age to come for this fault if they were not corrected. For even now, for such a reason, [Col. 0937C] many people after Easter are seized by various illnesses because they received the body of the Redeemer unworthily.

> “But if we judged ourselves, we certainly would not be judged. Yet when we are judged by the Lord, we are corrected, so that we may not be condemned with this world.”

We suffer these evils by divine judgment because of contempt for the Lord’s body. But if we judged ourselves—that is, if we turned the eyes of our mind over the different parts of our deeds and thoughts, and judged ourselves sternly in repentance for each thing we had done or thought wrongly—we certainly would not be judged by the Lord. Let a person therefore set up against himself the tribunal of his own mind; let him place himself before his own face. Then, when judgment has been established in the heart, let thought be the accuser, conscience the witness, and fear the executioner. Then let a certain blood of the confessing soul flow through tears. Finally, from the mind itself let such a sentence be pronounced: that a person judge himself unworthy to participate in the Lord’s body and blood if he finds such faults in himself.

Let the image of the future judgment be before his eyes; and whatever he sees in himself that could be reproved and punished by the Judge who is to come, let him now himself reprove and punish in himself. For sins, whether small or great, cannot remain unpunished: they are punished either by the person or by God’s judgment. But divine vengeance ceases if human conversion comes first. Because [Col. 0938A] if we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged by the Lord—that is, punished—whether in the age to come or in this present age. But when, in the present life, we are judged by the Lord—that is, punished for our sins by infirmity, adversity, or bodily death—we are mercifully corrected and amended by him, so that we may not be eternally condemned in the future life with this world—that is, with unbelievers and lovers of this world. Therefore he does not spare us now, in order to spare us forever. But he spares now those whom he has determined to punish eternally.

> “Therefore, my brethren, when you come together to eat, wait for one another. If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that you may not come together for judgment. The remaining matters I shall arrange when I come.”

[Col. 0938B] Since whoever receives the Lord’s body unworthily receives judgment upon himself, and many are even punished in the present age with various diseases or deaths because of this offense, therefore, my brethren, take care no longer to receive it unworthily. Take care not to assemble for it in schism; rather, when you assemble to eat it, wait for one another in brotherly love, so that the offering of many may be celebrated together and distributed to all. But if anyone is hungry and cannot wait until all have assembled because of sharper hunger, let him eat his bodily food at home; and then, when he comes to church, let him not receive the Eucharist. Thus wait for one another for these reasons, so that you may not assemble for judgment—that is, so that you may not conduct the sacred mystery blameworthily and with [Col. 0938C] offense, thereby incurring the judgment of condemnation.

Observe these things for the present. But I shall arrange for you the remaining matters that must be done when I come. He first showed how a man and how a woman ought to comport the head; then how persons of both sexes ought to assemble in church. Error in these matters is no slight sin. But he promised that he would order in person the remaining matters pertaining to the edification of the Church, because it would have been too much to set before them in his letter the entire order of practice observed by the Church throughout the world.

## Chapter XII

> “Now concerning spiritual things, brethren, I do not wish you to be ignorant. You know that when you were Gentiles, you were going to dumb idols, as you were led. Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Anathema to Jesus’; and no one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (Mark IX).

As faith increased, the grace of tongues was diminishing, which they had received on account of unbelievers. Hence very many, distressed by this, began to envy those who still possessed this grace, thinking it greater than all the other charisms. Therefore the Apostle now corrects them, because, as though through a certain uniformity, they sought knowledge of tongues more keenly, and he shows what ought especially to be sought. “The remaining matters,” he says, “I permit you not to know until I come. But concerning spiritual things”—that is, the gifts [Col. 0939A] of the Holy Spirit, because of which the greater members grow proud and the lesser envy or despair—“I do not wish you to be ignorant of what the truth is, so that there may not be schism among you, but peace and concord.”

I show this by comparison. For you know that when you were Gentiles—that is, Gentiles devoted to diverse errors—you were going to dumb idols, as you were led by one evil spirit. And if then one diabolical spirit led you, some to one idol and others to another, why should not one divine Spirit now lead you, some to one good work and others to another, or give one gift to some and another to others? For there is now one good Spirit in all of you, although he has bestowed different gifts upon different persons, just as there was then one evil spirit in all of you, although he led you into diverse errors of idols. Those [Col. 0939B] idols were mute, though you sought answers from them.

Since the Apostle is about to say that all good things are from the Holy Spirit, he first introduces an analogy from the contrary: namely, that all evils are from the evil spirit. For, as was said, he shows by likeness that all possess the same Spirit of God, reproving those who, because they had received greater charisms, broke away from those below them who had lesser charisms. For while they were in the unbelief of idolatry, all alike, greater and lesser, participated communally in one evil spirit. Then they were many nations; but now they are one nation, because there is one faith, one hope, one love, one expectation, and one heavenly homeland.

“You know,” he says, “from experience, that when you were diverse nations—that is, living as Gentiles amid various errors—you were going continually, as it were, to mute and irrational idols, as you were led to these by a deceiving spirit. Therefore, because you know that the evil spirit, drawing you away from good, led you into so irrational an evil—that is, idolatry—I make known to you easily from this that through the Spirit of God one abstains from evil and does good. This is what it means: no one speaking in the Spirit of God—in thought, speech, and action—says in the same three ways, ‘Anathema to Jesus,’ that is, alienation from Christ. That is, [Col. 0939C] no one commits any sin through which he becomes alienated from the Savior, because by the Holy Spirit one abstains from evil. And no one, however great he may be, can say in heart, tongue, and work that Jesus is Lord, to whom all things ought to serve, except in the Holy Spirit, from whom comes every truth. That is, through the Holy Spirit good is done.

Or: no one speaking in the Spirit of God—that is, no one whose mind and mouth are moved by the Spirit of God—says, “Anathema to Jesus,” that is, speaks alienation concerning the Savior, by saying that he is alien from the substance of the Father, as Arius said, who spoke in the spirit of the devil. And no one can say—that is, utter this confession of truth—that Jesus is Lord, except while speaking in the Holy Spirit. For he is not called Lord through human flattery, as idols are called gods by people though they are not gods. Therefore that Jesus is called Lord is not human favor but the gift of God, who has revealed his mystery to human beings. Nor does one who says this confer a benefit on religion [Col. 0940A], but receives one, as Gentiles call idols gods through the favor of princes or high priests, though they are not gods.

But how can no one say, “Jesus is Lord,” except in the Holy Spirit, when Jesus himself declares that not everyone who says to him, “Lord, Lord,” will enter the kingdom of heaven (Matt. VII)? The saying itself which the Apostle has given must be weighed not according to spoken words but according to the disposition of the heart. For he used precisely the word “says,” to signify the will and understanding of the speaker. But the Lord spoke generally only of utterance by the mouth. For even a person who neither wills nor understands what he says seems to speak. But the person properly speaks who announces his will and mind by the sound of his voice; and the one who says, “Jesus is Lord,” is the one who loves him, if he says it in the manner the Apostle intended [Col. 0940B]. For many say it with their voice but deny it in heart and deeds.

Again, no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, “Anathema to Jesus”—that is, alienation from the Savior, namely any word by which he himself or another becomes alienated from the Savior. For just as the evil spirit that presides over idols says nothing in anyone by which a person might be separated from idols, so the Spirit of God, who presides over the Church, says nothing in anyone by which a person might be separated from Christ or from Christ’s members. For there are some who think that they speak in the Spirit of God—that is, think themselves to speak rightly—when they say things that separate either themselves or those who hear them from Christ, as did the lesser Corinthians, who through foolish humility severed themselves from union with the greater members and made themselves strangers to the fellowship of Christ’s members because they did not resemble the greater members in charisms.

But detractors also, and all who sow dissensions among brethren under the appearance of correct speech, or who corrupt the faith of hearers or good morals by their address, colored with some paint of holiness [Col. 0940C] (I Cor. XV), appear to speak as though in the Spirit of God, while they say, “Anathema to Jesus.” For under an image of truth and rectitude they speak things through which they make their hearers strangers to the Savior. But the Holy Spirit has never taught words of this kind.

And no one can say, “Jesus is Lord”—that is, no one can devoutly proclaim the glory of the Lord Jesus Christ, so as to announce or confess that he is the Lord to whom the universe ought to render service—except in the Holy Spirit: that is, unless the Holy Spirit has enlightened his mind and kindled it with love of truth. For as that evil spirit teaches no one to speak in a way by which he may be separated from Christ, so this Spirit teaches every word by which human beings are drawn to Christ. Therefore whoever preaches God’s glory in order to draw hearers to him should not ascribe this to himself, because he does not have it from himself but from the Holy Spirit, who breathes where he wills (John III). The greater Corinthians arrogantly gloried in spiritual goods as though they had them from themselves, and despised those who could not possess them, as though the Holy Spirit could not have given these same gifts to those they despised, and not given them to themselves. Therefore they did not rightly exalt themselves above others because of God’s benefits, whereas they certainly ought [Col. 0941A] to have become more humble through them and given thanks to God.

> “Now there are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit; and there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of operations, but the same God, who works all things in all.”

It is common to all the elect to be partakers of the Holy Spirit, but the graces they receive from him are various. For there are divisions of graces—that is, gifts freely given by the Holy Spirit—but one and the same Spirit divides these graces among human beings. The divisions of graces are assigned to the offices of the Church, not to human merits. For just as whoever he may be, the person who says “Jesus is Lord” says it in the Holy Spirit, so also, whoever he may be, one placed in the rank of an ecclesiastical office possesses grace—not indeed grace proper to himself, but that of the office, through the working of the Spirit.

There are divisions of ministries, through which believers minister to God in various ways while, for love of him, they serve his servants and provide necessities for them. Yet the Lord Jesus, to whom service is rendered in various ways and who bestows various ministries, is one and not various. There are divisions of operations, performed by the elect; but God the Father is one, who works all good things in all believers. He does not work all things in one person, lest one become proud; but in all, so that what one does not have in himself, he may have in another, and thus love may endure.

Because Arians, wishing to establish ranks in the Trinity, argue from the fact that the Father is named first, the Son second, and the Holy Spirit third, [Col. 0941C] the Apostle changed this order, placing the Spirit first, then the Lord—that is, the Son—and thirdly God—that is, the Father. And when he says “the same Spirit,” “the same Lord,” “the same God,” he shows altogether the same substance of the three persons.

Or, against Macedonius and the other heretics who denied that the Holy Spirit is God, the whole passage may be understood of the Spirit alone, so that the Apostle calls him both Lord and God. He is not divided when he divides his gifts; and what he works, the whole Trinity works. For God, being incorporeal by nature, can be wholly present to all things and wholly present to each individual, because he remains immutably one in himself with eternal stability; although those in whom he dwells possess him according to the measure and diversity of their capacity—some more, others less—whom he builds up by the grace of his goodness as a temple most beloved to himself.

And the divisions of graces are like the parts, or members, of one human being. Thereby we are all at once one temple and individual temples, because God is not greater in all than in each one. It often happens that many receive him less, and one more. This was also the case among the Corinthians: a few spiritual persons received him more, while the multitude of carnal persons received him less. Thus various gifts are variously distributed among Christ’s members, so that all the members may be bound to one another by a certain necessity, love one another, and serve one another.

For the eye alone sees in the body. But does it see for itself alone? It sees for the hand, the foot, and the other members. Again, the hand alone works in the body. But does it work for itself alone? Thus the foot, by walking, serves all the members. The other members are silent, and the tongue speaks for all. Thus the members are harmoniously distributed among diverse offices. So the Holy Spirit deals with the members of Christ, so that all may be mutually fitted and joined together by necessity. For if you love unity, whoever possesses anything in it possesses it also for you. Remove envy, and what he has is yours. Remove envy, and what you have is mine. Envy separates; unity joins. Therefore unity must be maintained, because each person possesses the Holy Spirit to the degree that he loves Christ’s members; and he possesses in them what he is unable to possess in himself.

> “But to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit [Col. 0942B] for profit. To one indeed, through the Spirit, is given the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another the grace of healings in the one Spirit; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discernment of spirits; to another kinds of tongues; to another interpretation of utterances. But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each individually as he wills (Rom. XII; Eph. IV).”

The Holy Spirit is in all Christ’s members; but to each of them, both greater and lesser, is given a manifestation of that same Spirit—that is, the gift of grace—through which the Holy Spirit who is in that person is made manifest to others, and is made manifest for the benefit of that person and of others. For by the gift received he benefits both himself and others [Col. 0942C], when, governing his own life well, he offers an example of good conduct, or also preaches aloud. And he shows in detail that the manifestation of the Spirit is given to each in different ways.

For to one is given, not through human ability nor through literary study, but through the Holy Spirit, not only wisdom but also the word of wisdom, so that he may be able to speak to others that very wisdom which he understands. To another, according to the same Spirit, is given not merely knowledge but also the word of knowledge, through which he may teach others. The very Spirit who gives one person the word of wisdom gives this person the word of knowledge; yet he is not diverse in himself, but remains the same.

Wisdom belongs to the contemplation of eternal things, knowledge to the action of temporal things. The word of wisdom is given through the Spirit so that [Col. 0942D] someone, speaking of the eternal and unchangeable good and of everlasting joys, may raise others to love of the heavenly homeland. But the word of knowledge is bestowed so that someone may teach others by speaking about things that were done in time, historically; and about things to be done or avoided morally—that is, about virtues and vices.

Or otherwise: there are some who, through the gift of grace, understand even things which they have not heard explained by teachers; these, clearly, have received the word of wisdom. And there are some who cannot understand for themselves what they hear, but retain what they have read in expositors and knowingly set forth what they have learned by reading; these are full of the word of knowledge. Yet this may also be understood otherwise: for wisdom [Col. 0943A] belongs to life, while knowledge belongs to teaching. Therefore, one who lives well and preaches wisely has received wisdom and knowledge from God.

To another is given faith—that is, steadfastness in faith—in the same Holy Spirit, so that, although he may not know how to instruct others by preaching, he nevertheless believes rightly and firmly, and does not fail, through fear or shame, to confess his faith with his mouth. To another is given the grace of healings, that he may heal the sick, in one Spirit—that is, in the one Holy Spirit, who is one, that is, unchangeable and undivided in himself. To another, through the same Spirit, is given the working of miracles, that he may perform miraculous deeds contrary to nature, such as raising the dead or miracles in the expulsion of demons. To another is given prophecy, that, filled with the Spirit, he may foretell the future. To another, discernment [Col. 0943B] of spirits, that he may know how to distinguish evil spirits from good while hearing them speak.

For discernment is most difficult, since even a malignant spirit acts as though peaceful and, having assumed a human spirit without any bodily affliction, says whatever it can. It even speaks truths and preaches useful things, so that, once it has been believed in evident good things, it may lead people astray to its own ends. This spirit cannot be discerned except by the gift of the Holy Spirit. For it is no great matter to recognize it when it has arrived at, or led others to, things contrary to good morals or the rule of faith; then it is discerned by many. But by the gift of the Holy Spirit, at its very beginning—when it still appears good to many—it is immediately judged whether it is evil.

Moreover, human spirits—that is, wills—are through this gift [Col. 0943C] distinguished as good or evil. To others are given kinds of tongues, so that they may speak many languages, such as Greek, Latin, and Hebrew. To another is given the interpretation of utterances, so that in one language he may know how to interpret obscure sayings of the Scriptures. Thus the manifestation of the Spirit is given to each for profit, when each receives from God his own gift, through which he benefits others who do not possess it.

For it may happen in one and the same Spirit that this person excels in the word of wisdom, yet is not supported by the word of knowledge—that is, by teaching—because it is enough for him to discern and discover even what he has not apprehended through the effort of learning. That person shines through the word of knowledge, yet does not grow strong through the word of wisdom, because he is capable of fulfilling what he has learned, but does not rise of himself to some subtle act of understanding [Col. 0943D].

This person commands even the elements through faith, yet does not cure bodily illnesses through the grace of healings. That person removes diseases by the help of prayer, yet does not restore rain to parched ground by his word. This person, through the working of miracles, recalls even the dead to this present life, and yet, lacking the grace of prophecy, does not know what is to come to him. That person beholds all future things as though present, yet does not exercise himself in any working of signs. This person, through discernment of spirits, subtly perceives minds in their actions, yet does not know languages of different kinds. That person examines languages of different kinds, yet does not weigh dissimilar hearts by comparable powers. Another, in the one language he knows, prudently evaluates the force of sayings by interpreting them [Col. 0944A], and yet patiently lacks the other gifts which he does not possess.

Thus our Creator and disposer governs all things, so that one who could be exalted because of the gift he possesses may be humbled by the virtue he lacks. Thus he governs all things: while he lifts each person up through grace bestowed, he also places one beneath another through an unequal gift; and each may regard as superior in another gift the person placed beneath him, and, although he recognizes himself as preceding that person in some matters, may nevertheless place himself after the one whom he surpasses in other matters. Thus he governs all things, so that, while each individual gift belongs to all, through a certain intervening bond of charity all things may become the possession of each individual; so that each person may possess in another what he himself has not received, while he humbly bestows upon the other, for that other’s possession, what he has received [Col. 0944B].

For this reason spiritual gifts are distributed among the elect in a most beautiful diversity. But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit. Above, we understood the statement concerning the Father, that the same God works all things in all; and now we read that the Spirit works all things, so that the operation of the Trinity may be understood as inseparable. Thus, when the operation of the Father is spoken of, we must not understand it to be performed without the Son and the Holy Spirit; when the operation of the Son is spoken of, not without the Father and the Holy Spirit; and when the operation of the Holy Spirit is spoken of, not without the Father and the Son.

Therefore, when it is said of the Spirit that he works all these things, it is not said because the Father and the Son do not work with him; rather, it is said because one and the same Spirit works these things, since in these works there are not many spirits but one, and in his different [Col. 0944C] operations he is not different from himself. The Spirit works all these things, certainly as God. For who can work these things except God? He works all these things, distributing them to individuals while himself undivided; and he does and distributes all these things as he wills—that is, as Lord of all, as God, as subject to none.

For he works not as one sent, but voluntarily, because it belongs to God alone to do his own will. He distributes his gifts not as human beings wish, but as he himself wills, for he alone knows what he ought to will and what is expedient for each person. Hence neither should this person grieve nor that person become proud. For when you are sorrowful that you have received a lesser grace, you envy another as though he had seized the greater share, although this lies not in our power but in the power of the giver. For, as was said above, the lesser Corinthians envied the greater ones [Col. 0944D], as though the latter were claiming the greater charisms for themselves, not understanding that these are dispensed by the will of God alone.

> “For just as the body is one and has many members, while all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Gentiles, whether slaves or free; and we were all given to drink of one Spirit.”

Therefore the Holy Spirit grants different gifts to different persons, because, just as a human body is one and has many members devoted to various functions, yet all the body’s members, though many, are one body, so also Christ has one body [Col. 0945A] made up of various members. For the body of Christ is one: the Church, consisting in a diversity of members—that is, a variety of persons—having different offices and different graces.

And therefore it was fitting that the one Spirit of Christ should carry out various actions through the different members of the one body of Christ, since the one human spirit also works differently in the eyes, differently in the ears, differently in the nostrils, and differently in the hands. So too the Spirit of Christ works in different ways in Christ’s members. For if charisms were not bestowed differently upon individuals but were the same, then the different members would possess the same gift, and the many would not become one through charity, because one would not need another’s office through sharing the same gift.

He uses the comparison of the human body in order [Col. 0945B] to show that offices, not the nature of the members, are different; and that no one ought to ask what office he has, since all are animated by one Spirit and fitted together in one body. By this he also teaches that the person of no one, as though contemptible, should be despised; nor should that of anyone, as though perfect, be preferred; nor should the glory due to God alone be given to human beings, since in all there is one and the same glorious God.

For, speaking of Christ’s members—that is, his faithful—he did not say, “so also are Christ’s members,” but called this whole reality “Christ.” Therefore all the faithful together with their head are Christ; and for that reason the head cried from heaven: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts IX). For Christ is head and body; and the same Christ is the Word of God, the only-begotten Son, equal to the Father. From this we see how great is the grace by which we belong to God: he who is one with the Father willed to be one with us. “I and the Father,” he says, “are one” (John X). Yet he is one with us because he does not say “and to seeds,” as though to many, but “as to one, ‘and to your seed,’ who is Christ” (Gal. III).

Truly, all of us together with our head are Christ, because in one Spirit—that is, in the grace and operation of the Holy Spirit, who is always one and the same—we all, whether Jews or Gentiles, slaves or free, that is, those who were formerly unequal and diverse both in nation and social condition, were baptized into one body. That is, by the washing of baptism through faith we were brought into the one body of Christ, so that from now on we are all [Col. 0945D] one, like those whose heart and soul were one (Acts IV). And we were all given to drink of one Spirit: that is, according to the capacity of each of us, we all received the Holy Spirit, by whom we might be made drunk and who, though one, might work in us in different ways, just as the one human soul sees in the eye, hears in the ear, speaks in the mouth, walks in the foot, and does other things in the other members.

> “For the body is not one member, but many. If the foot should say, ‘Because I am not a hand, I am not of the body,’ is it therefore not of the body? And if the ear should say, ‘Because I am not an eye, I am not of the body,’ is it therefore not of the body? If the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the sense of smell be? But now [Col. 0946A] God has placed the members, each one of them, in the body as he willed. And if all were one member, where would the body be? But now there are indeed many members, yet one body.”

And we are rightly all called one. For the human body, to which the Church is like, is not one member but many. So too we, of whom the Church consists, do not all have one office or gift, but many. Therefore the lesser person should not grieve because he has less, nor should the greater become proud because he has received a greater gift or office. There are truly many members in Christ’s body.

For if the foot—that is, a believer who has an inferior gift and proceeds through earthly activities—should say, “Because [Col. 0946B] I am not a hand, because I do not have the higher and pure activity of spiritual works, I am not of Christ’s body,” is it therefore not of the body? That is, does it follow that he is not of Christ’s body because he may be something other than a hand and yet remain in this body?

And likewise if the ear—that is, one who hears teaching from masters—should say, “Because I am not an eye, because I do not contemplate the splendid light of wisdom so that I may provide for myself and others, I am not of Christ’s body,” is it therefore not of the body? That is, does it follow that he is not of this body because it contains many members besides eyes?

This is said because of the lesser Corinthians, who, despairing, said [Col. 0946C] that they did not belong to Christ’s body because they could not possess those great charisms which they observed in spiritual men. Concerning the same weak persons it was said above that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says “Anathema to Jesus.” For they said “Anathema to Jesus,” which means alienation from the Savior, when they declared themselves alien to the Savior’s body because they were not among its higher members.

But diverse members must be in the body. For if the whole body were an eye—that is, if the whole Church had only the office of beholding spiritual things—where would hearing be? That is, where would there be disciples who hear from teachers the voice of preaching? Or if the whole body were hearing—that is, if the whole Church were a people of subordinates obediently hearing the commands [Col. 0946D] of teachers—where would smelling be? That is, where would be those who, like nostrils, subtly distinguish and perceive from afar the good fragrance of virtues and the bad odor of vices?

It is as if one said: if all had one office or function, how would the remaining needs of the body be supplied, when the body’s governance plainly requires many offices? For the Church is the body of its heavenly head. In it, one person is the eye by seeing lofty things; another, the hand by doing what is right; another, the foot by running to duties imposed; another, the ear by understanding the voice of commands; another, the nostril by distinguishing the stench of evils and the fragrance of goods. While, in the manner of bodily members, they render their received offices to one another in turn, they make one body out of themselves all; and while they perform diverse things in charity [Col. 0947A], they prevent diversity among those whom the body contains. But if all did one thing, they would certainly not be a body composed of many members, because it would not exist as a manifoldly joined whole if it did not maintain this harmonious diversity of members.

But now, to avoid these inconveniences, God has placed the members in the body of Christ, each one of them—that is, greater and lesser—as he himself willed. Therefore neither should the greater be proud and despise the lesser, nor should the lesser grieve or envy the greater. For God has so arranged them, and his arrangement is not to be changed by human beings; he willed them to be so, and his will is never unjust.

And if all were one member—that is, if all the faithful had one office—where would the body of the Church be [Col. 0947B], which is governed only by the various offices of its members? For if all were of one rank, the orderly composition of diverse parts would already have perished. But now—that the body may not perish, since it can consist only of diverse members—there are indeed many members, but one body from them all. Since the many need one another, they do not differ in unity of nature, though they are diverse, because this diversity converges into one so that the body’s welfare may be fulfilled.

> “But the eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I have no need of your works’; nor again the head to the feet, ‘You are not necessary to me.’ Rather, those members of the body which seem to be weaker are much more necessary; and those members of the body which we consider less honorable, upon these we bestow more abundant honor; and our unseemly members have more abundant comeliness. But our comely members have no need.”

The members are indeed many, but none of them is superfluous; rather, all are necessary to one another. For the eye—that is, one who foresees for the rest the path of right action—cannot say to the hand, that is, the worker, “I do not need your work,” that is, the diligence of your action. For just as the hand needs the eye in order to be able to work—that is, the disciple needs the teacher’s foresight in order to accomplish a good work—so the eye needs the hand’s action. That is, the teacher, who cannot himself do what he foresees must be done, [Col. 0947D] needs a disciple through whom what he foresees as necessary may be done. For he would foresee in vain if there were no one to do what follows.

Or again, the head—that is, one placed in the highest rank—cannot say to the feet, that is, the lowest members of the Church, “You are not necessary to me.” Those subject to him are altogether necessary, because the humble person can do what the exalted person cannot, just as iron can do what gold cannot. And although someone may be high in rank, if there is no subordinate who makes him glorious through services rendered, that very rank will be contemptible.

This is said especially now because those who excelled among the Corinthians in the highest charisms despised and rejected the lesser members as superfluous and useless. Yet such members of the Church, though inferior, are not useless. Rather, those members of the Church’s body which seem weaker—that is, more lacking in spiritual charity—are much more necessary, because the lesser persons in the Church, though they may appear weak and contemptible, are sometimes more useful. And those whom we consider the less honorable members of the Church’s body—that is, those who degenerate through baseness of conduct—we surround with more abundant honor. That is, we sometimes cover their degraded conduct with our words.

For people who are despised need the exhortation of good speech, by which some honor may be added to them so that they may become useful; otherwise, through the very fact of being despised, they will become more negligent regarding themselves and worse. And our members which are unseemly through some sin [Col. 0948B]—that is, the carnal children of the Church—receive from us more abundant comeliness, while we conceal their foulness. But our comely members—that is, members of the Church who have sufficient honor through the beauty of their holiness—need no adorning through the covering of ugliness.

We show this better if we set forth the things which commonly occur. Whenever some powerful and arrogant person is known to have committed an injustice, an appropriate time is sought in which he may be reproved for the evil he has done. For unless the preacher waits until that person can fittingly bear correction, the evil which follows in him is increased. Often, indeed, it happens that such a person will bear no words of rebuke. What, then, ought the preacher to do concerning such a person’s fault, except, in a sermon of admonition which he delivers for the common salvation of all his hearers [Col. 0948C], to bring before them faults of the kind which he sees that person has committed? The person is present, yet cannot as yet be accused of himself alone, lest he become worse; and when an attack is made generally against the fault, the word of correction is willingly brought to mind, because the powerful wicked person does not know that it is spoken especially of him.

Thus it often happens that he mourns his committed fault all the more keenly because, while he feels his guilt struck, he thinks it is unknown. Therefore the great art of preaching must be exercised so that those made worse by open correction may return to salvation through a certain moderation of correction. Hence it is now plainly said: “Those members of the body which we consider less honorable, upon these we bestow more abundant honor; and our unseemly members have more abundant comeliness. But our comely members have no need.”

For just as there are unseemly members in the body, so there are certain powerful and wicked people within the holy Church. Since they cannot be struck by open reproof, they are, as it were, covered by the honor of a veil. But we speak of hidden offenses of the powerful. For when they sin with others also knowing, they must be reproved with others also knowing, lest, if the preacher is silent, he seem to have approved the fault and it grow into an example, because the shepherd’s tongue does not cut it off.

Or, if these words are understood of the bodily members of each of us, it is evident that our private parts, which seem shameful because they avoid public view, [Col. 0949A] are covered with comeliness so that they may not be regarded with horror through irreverence. Far be it from us to say or believe that there is any shamefulness in the members of the saints, even their generative members. They are called unseemly because they lack that appearance of beauty which belongs to members placed openly in view. Or certainly—and this is more plausibly said—it is because of the law in the members resisting the law of the mind, which arose from sin and not from the nature of our original creation. Therefore the illicit use of those members, not subject to the laws of temperance, is shameful—not the members themselves.

> “If God has tempered the body, giving more abundant honor to that which lacked it, so that there may not be schism in the body, but the members may be mutually solicitous for one another; and if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; or if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it (Heb. VI; Rom. I, 8).”

Those things which appear unseemly in the members of the Church are not unseemly. But God has tempered the body itself by the variety of its members, which preserve diverse offices within the binding unity, by giving through worthy members more abundant honor to the member who lacked it in himself, as we showed in the case of the arrogant powerful person. Or by giving, through good life, more abundant honor to the member who lacked it through knowledge of preaching. Or to the person who appeared contemptible to human beings God gave a more generous honor through the immeasurable grace of miracles or other charisms [Col. 0949C].

God so tempered the body of the Church that none of its members is superfluous, but all are necessary; so that there may be no schism in the body of the Church, where there ought to be unity and concord—that is, so that one may not reject another as useless or superfluous. Rather, the members should be solicitous for one another: the greater for the lesser and the lesser for the greater, since they cannot exist without one another. I mean members tending toward the same thing—that is, unity—so that all may strive to have one heart and one soul. Thus, if one member suffers some adversity, all members suffer with it, as if that adversity belonged to all; or if one member is glorified through some good, all the members rejoice with it, as if that good belonged to all.

For we see all these things also in the members of the human body, from whose unity and joined structure charity is now commended to the members of the Church, since each does its own office not for itself alone but also for the others [Col. 0949D]. For the eye sees but does not hear; the ear hears but does not see; the hand works but neither hears nor sees; the foot walks but neither hears nor sees nor does what the hand does. But if there is health in the one body and the members do not contend against one another, the ear sees in the eye and the eye hears in the ear.

Nor can it be objected to the ear that it does not see, with the words: “You are nothing; you are inferior. Can you see and distinguish colors, as the eye does?” For the ear answers from the peace of the body and says: “I am there where the eye is; I am in that body. I do not see in myself; in the one with whom I am, I see.” Thus, when the ear says, “The eye sees for me,” the eye says, “The ear hears for me”; eyes and ears say, “The hands work for us”; the hands say, “The feet walk for us.” When all work in one body, if there is health there and the members agree, they rejoice and rejoice together; and if there is some distress in one member, they do not abandon one another but suffer with one another [Col. 0950A].

So also the children of the Church—that is, Christ’s members—ought altogether to act. Nor should they think that they do not belong to God if they have not worked miracles. But whoever in the body cannot raise a dead person should not seek that power, lest he create discord in the body; just as the ear, if it seeks to see, may create discord, because it cannot do what it has not received. But if it is objected to him and said, “If you were righteous, you would raise the dead as Peter did,” let him answer: “Peter did it for me too, because I am in the body in which Peter did it. In the one who can do it, I can do it, since I am not separated from him. He sympathizes with me in what I can do less; and I rejoice with him in what he can do more.”

Therefore, if each person does justly what he can do, endeavors to benefit others through the good he has received, and does not envy another’s greater ability but rejoices with him as one established with him in a single body, that which the bodily members of any human being mutually preserve will be preserved in Christ’s members [Col. 0950B].

> “But you are Christ’s body, and members from a member. And God has placed some in the Church: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers; then miracles; then graces of healing, helps, governments, kinds [Col. 0950C] of tongues, interpretations of utterances (Eph. IV). Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles? Do all have the grace of healings? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret?”

The Apostle shows that he had treated our case through the analogy of bodily members, because we cannot all do the same things, but each according to the measure of faith and grace received. “This harmony,” he says, “of acting differently and of rejoicing or suffering together is found in the members of the human body. But you are Christ’s body”: that is, you are joined and united in Christian faith and truth. And you are also Christ’s members, so that each of you may serve the others through charity from the gift or office which he has.

You are members dependent upon a member—that is, upon me, who am a greater member of Christ—and I have made you adhere to myself in his body as fingers adhere to a hand. For a member of the body is one thing, a member of a member another. A member of the body is a part in relation to the whole; a member of a member is a small part in relation to a part. A finger is a member of the hand, and a hand a member of the arm; but all these together are a member of the body in relation to the whole body. Thus, in the Lord’s spiritual body, those who are governed by others in his Church are called members from a member.

Here the Apostle explains the diversity among the faithful which he had mentioned in the members, and determines which gifts of God are higher and which lower [Col. 0951A]. The Corinthians considered what was lesser to be greater, and what was greater to be lesser. “You,” he says, “are Christ’s members; and though you are members, you are not equal, because God has placed in the Church believers of various ranks: first, in dignity and time, apostles preaching in Christ’s stead; second in rank of dignity, prophets foretelling future things, who existed after the Lord’s coming, such as Agabus and blessed Benedict (Acts XI, 12); third in rank of dignity, teachers—that is, preachers—who instructed the Church in the teaching of truth.

“Then [he placed] miracles”: that is, those who work mighty signs, such as expelling demons and changing the elements—for example, changing the serenity of the air into rain, or walking on water with dry feet. “Then he placed graces of healings”: that is, those who heal the sick through prayer; and helps: that is, those who assist greater persons, as Titus assisted the Apostle or an archdeacon a bishop; and governments: that is, offices of oversight over lesser persons, such as presbyters; and kinds of tongues: that is, knowledge, through the gift of grace, of speaking various languages.

Because the Corinthians especially desired this gift, considering it the greatest, the Apostle placed it last, indicating that it was lower and less worthy than the other gifts set before it. God distributes such gifts among his faithful in various ways, giving grace to each according to the measure of his gift. For one person has one gift, another another; and what this person has, that person does not have. A measure is a certain division of gifts [Col. 0951C].

For not all are apostles, but only those whom Christ sent; nor do all possess the spirit of prophecy, but those to whom this grace has been granted by God; nor do all possess the knowledge of teaching others; nor do all work miraculous signs; nor do all possess the grace of healing illnesses; nor do all speak various languages; nor do all interpret the Scriptures or languages. For if all had all these things, there would no longer be persons to whom these offices might render service. Therefore it is beautiful and necessary that some have what others do not, and others in turn other things, so that each may minister to the rest what he himself possesses and they lack.

> “But earnestly desire the better charisms. And [Col. 0951D] I show you a still more excellent way.”

Up to this point he has recalled them from schism to concord and unity, so that no one may glory in a superior charism and no one grieve over an inferior one. From here he directs them toward charity, showing that without it all other things are worth nothing. “God,” he says, “is accustomed to bestow diverse gifts upon his faithful. But earnestly desire the better charisms”: that is, among those which I have shown above, desire the more useful ones, not tongues, as you used to do.

“And beyond these things already shown, I show you a more excellent way”: that is, charity, which holds the preeminent place among the other virtues and is the way by which those who strive toward the kingdom of heaven advance. For even those who descend to lower things can walk by the ways of the other virtues. But [Col. 0952A] whoever follow the way of charity tend toward the heavenly homeland.

For just as oil is not pressed down by any liquid but, bursting through all things, springs upward and rises above them, so charity is. It cannot be pressed down into the depths, but must shine forth toward things above. Therefore whoever wishes to arrive at the heavenly kingdoms above should endeavor to walk by the way of charity. Why the Apostle called charity a more excellent way he himself explains when he immediately adds:

## Chapter XIII

> “If I speak with the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have charity, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. And if I have all prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge; and if I have all faith [Col. 0952B], so as to remove mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing. And if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I give up my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing (Matt. XXI; Mark XI).”

Because the Corinthians especially desired to speak in different languages, the Apostle therefore shows first of all that this gift is of no benefit without charity. “Though I speak,” he says, “with the tongues of all human beings and of angels,” that is, though it were granted me by grace to know how to speak as all people on earth speak, and as the angels in heaven speak, “but have not charity”—which one who speaks with every tongue may lack—“I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal.” [Col. 0952C] For speaking in various languages, or doing similar things, is not always given for merit, but in order to display God’s glory to the nations; nor can those who do such things thereby attain eternal life. Charity, however, always increases merit and bestows eternal life.

The angels too have their own languages, by which the greater communicate to the lesser what they have perceived concerning God’s will, or which they employ when sent to human beings. For the first rank of angels receive illuminations of knowledge from God himself and then transmit them to the spirits subject to them. The languages by which some thus speak to others are understood to be certain signs or inward movements through which they communicate to one another what they wish. For the lesser angels do not know everything that is known to the greater, [Col. 0952D] but only those things communicated to them by their superiors.

“But if,” he says, “such knowledge of languages were given me that I spoke with the tongues both of angels and of human beings, and I had no charity, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal.” For just as bronze or a cymbal does not resound of itself, but at some external stroke, so one speaking in tongues utters, not of himself—for he does not know—but by the prompting of the Spirit, things by which he delights his hearers. By bronze or cymbal are signified the insensible and dead minds of people who lack the life of charity. For just as a body without spirit—that is, without a soul—is dead, so a soul without the Holy Spirit—that is, without charity—is judged dead.

Those who hear the sound of bronze or a cymbal are delighted, or derive some benefit; but it profits the instrument [Col. 0953A] nothing, and indeed it produces benefit for others to its own loss. So too, the preacher who does not possess the meaning of charity in what he says delights others without knowing it, while he himself suffers loss from that by which his hearers profit. For as the sound of bronze is sweet to others but entails labor and diminution to itself, so it is with the speech of a preacher empty of charity.

Nor must this be understood only of the preacher.
