For bronze and cymbal aptly signify the hearts of any insensible people: they often receive heavenly blows, yet are softened by no stroke of discipline. When bronze is struck, a very musical sound is produced by the blow. Such people, although in no way differing from bronze in their metallic nature, when they receive the lashes of heavenly chastisement emit the sound [Col. 0953B] of a devout confession; but because they do not utter words of humility from the heart, once restored to a state of safety they do not know what they promised. Thus they in no way escape the likeness of bronze: under the blow, they speak good things which they do not feel. Whoever speaks good things but does not follow those same goods in love gives forth a sound like bronze or cymbal, because he does not himself feel the words that he himself makes.

“And if I have,” he says, “prophecy,” so that by God’s Spirit I foretell future things, as Balaam did (Num. XXII, XXIII, XXIV) and Caiaphas (John XI); “and know all mysteries,” that is, the hidden things of the Old and New Testaments, as Solomon did; “and know all knowledge” concerning things that have been, are, and will be, or concerning divine and human matters, as that same Solomon did; “and if I have all faith,” [Col. 0953C] that is, faith concerning every matter in which it ought to be possessed, so perfect that by its power I move mountains from place to place—yet, possessing all these things, if I do not have charity, I am nothing, even though these things are great.

The Savior had said that faith like a grain of mustard seed could move mountains (Matt. XVII); and now the Apostle says that all faith is that which moves mountains. From this it is understood that the faith compared with a grain of mustard seed is perfect faith, and that this was said not because of its smallness but because of its completeness. But faith without charity is of no value for salvation (Jas. II), since demons too possess faith of this sort.

“And if I distribute,” he says, “my possessions,” that is, if I divide everything that I can possess, in order to benefit many, giving [Col. 0953D] everything as food not to the rich who may repay, but to the poor who have no means to repay (Luke XIV); “and”—what is greater—“if, in time of persecution, I surrender my body for the faith to most cruel torments, so that I may be burned, but do not have charity,” that is, if I do this not from charity but from self-display, or retain hatred in my heart against someone, “all of this profits me nothing.”

Great, therefore, and wonderful is charity. Without it, neither speech in diverse languages, nor prophecy, nor knowledge of mysteries and sciences, nor faith, nor distribution of possessions, nor the suffering of martyrdom profits anything. Since these greater things profit nothing without charity, it is evident that the other good things too cannot profit without this charity. For the reprobate may possess other goods, but charity [Col. 0954A] is possessed only by the elect. The Apostle subsequently describes its members and forms, saying:

> “Charity is patient; it is kind. Charity does not envy; it does not act perversely; it is not puffed up; it is not ambitious; it does not seek its own things (Phil. II); it is not provoked; it does not think evil; it does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices together with truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Charity never fails.”

All good things without charity are cheap and useless; with charity they are precious and useful. This charity contains in itself the virtues now enumerated. For it is patient, that is, it keeps patience. To keep patience is to endure calmly the evils inflicted by others, and not to be stung by any resentment even against the person who inflicts them. For one who bears a neighbor’s evils in such a way as silently to grieve and seek the time of fitting retribution does not keep patience but feigns it.

But charity is patient because it tolerates others’ evils with an even mind; and it is kind because it loves even those from whom it suffers evil. It is patient because it calmly bears the evils inflicted by neighbors; it is kind because it generously supplies good things in return for evils. It is patient because it preserves a tranquil mind amid adversities; it is kind because it mercifully expends its own goods upon needy neighbors. It is patient because, fixed upon God against the temptations or storms of the world, it stands immovable; it is kind because it delights in the progress of neighbors.

“Charity does not envy,” that is, it is not envious, because where envy exists, brotherly love [Col. 0954C] cannot exist. It does not envy because, by desiring nothing in the present world, it does not know how to envy earthly success. It does not envy because it loves another’s good as its own. “It does not act perversely,” that is, wrongly, because, in extending itself wholly into the love of God and neighbor, it does not know anything that departs from rectitude. “It is not puffed up,” that is, it does not swell with temporal prosperity, noble birth of the flesh, knowledge, merit, or any other thing; because, anxiously desiring the reward of inward recompense, it does not exalt itself over external or passing goods.

“It is not ambitious,” that is, desirous of worldly honors, because it does not seek to be greater than others, to rule over the rest, or to appropriate things belonging to another’s right. It is therefore not ambitious because, while it ardently labors inwardly toward its own goods, [Col. 0954D] it in no way covets what belongs to others outwardly. “It does not seek its own things,” because it disregards as alien everything that it possesses here only temporarily, recognizing that nothing is properly its own except what remains with it. It does not seek its own things because it abandons its own advantages for the benefit of others and strives to exalt not itself but others.

“It is not provoked,” that is, it is not stirred to anger, because even when assailed by injuries it rouses itself to no movements of revenge, while it awaits greater rewards after great labors. “It does not think evil,” that is, it does not consider how to repay the person who injures it. It does not think evil because, establishing the mind in love of purity and rooting out all hatred, it does not know how to entertain in the soul that which defiles it.

“It does not rejoice over iniquity,” because it pursues love for all alone [Col. 0955A] and does not exult in the destruction of opponents. Some people neither do evil nor contemplate doing it to those from whom they suffer adversity; yet, if evil is done to those people by others, they rejoice. Therefore, after saying that charity is not provoked and does not think evil, it is added that it does not rejoice over iniquity: that is, it is not pleased if any evil is suffered by the very person who opposes it.

“But rejoicing together with truth,” it delights in words of truth or works of genuine holiness. For, loving others as itself, when it sees what is right in others it rejoices as though at an increase in its own progress. “It bears all things,” because in hope of eternal rest it refuses to suffer no adversity. It was said above that it is patient, that is, that it does not murmur in adversities but bears everything with a silent heart; [Col. 0955B] and now it is said that it bears all things and in action endures whatever adversity occurs. There the tranquility of the heart was praised; here, the strength of suffering. It therefore bears all things in the present life because it believes all things concerning the future life. And it endures all burdens imposed here because it hopes for all sweet things promised to it. Therefore it never fails, that is, it never falls, but persists without falling.

Nor should we understand “it believes all things” in such a way as to detract from anyone’s charity if that person does not immediately believe evil reported concerning a brother (1 John IV). For charity itself, which believes all things, does not believe every spirit. Accordingly, it indeed believes all things—but believes God, for it was not said, “It believes everyone.” It therefore believes all things [Col. 0955C] which the saints ought to believe, and hopes for all things divinely promised to it; and it endures all things, that is, it patiently and long-sufferingly awaits those same goods for which it hopes, or meanwhile endures adversities in hope of those goods.

Charity has also this above the other virtues, wherein again it is more worthy than they: it never fails, that is, it never wholly falls. Although its works fall—that is, fail and cease—in the future age, charity itself will never fall from its state, but will stand stronger and endure in another age than in this one. For if, while it believes, hopes, and waits, it loves what is not yet seen, how much more will it love when it sees and possesses it?

> “Whether prophecies shall be made void, whether tongues shall cease, [Col. 0955D] whether knowledge shall be destroyed. For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part shall be made void.”

Charity indeed never fails: neither now nor in the other life does it fall from its state, so as to be diminished or fail; but the other gifts fall away and fail. For whether prophecies are understood—which are now necessary during the time of our blindness—they will be made void in the light of the future age, that is, they will become empty of all usefulness and therefore will cease. For when all things are present, how could anything future be foretold? Or whether tongues are understood, that is, utterances in various languages, they will cease in that age. For when all things are manifest, why would anything be said to anyone? [Col. 0956A]

The saints may indeed speak with one another if they wish, but it will not be necessary, where knowledge will precede speech. And if they then speak among themselves, they will not do so in the manner in which we now speak, but rather in the manner in which angelic spirits speak among themselves in heaven. Or whether knowledge is now understood, by which something is known of God and his secrets, it will be destroyed in the future age, because whatever knowledge of God we now possess, we possess it not in the nature of divinity itself but through likeness and external natures.

For however intensely the human mind may stretch itself, even if it has already restrained from thought the phantasms of bodily images, even if it has already removed from the eyes of the heart all circumscribed spirits, nevertheless, while placed in mortal flesh, it is not able to see or know [Col. 0956B] the glory of God as it is; and that which shines in the mind concerning it is a likeness, not the thing itself. Therefore such knowledge of ours will be destroyed when truth itself is purely revealed.

This knowledge, prophecy, or speech will be destroyed because they cannot grasp or recount the fullness of truth, since they are partial. For we know truth in part, not wholly: whatever we yet know of God, we know imperfectly. And we prophesy in part concerning future things, because through prophecy we announce certain future things, but are ignorant of very many. But everything partial will be destroyed. For when that which is perfect comes, that is, when knowledge of God is given which is not partial but arises from perfection, because [Col. 0956C] we shall see him as he is (John XIII), then that which is in part will be made void: every imperfection will come to nothing. Our imperfection will be destroyed; not that which is true will be made void. The destruction of imperfection will occur when that which is perfect is fulfilled by the perfection of truth.

Then, in order to show by some comparison how far this life is from that which is to come—not merely the life of ordinary persons but even of those endowed with exceptional holiness—the Apostle adds:

> “When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child. But when I became a man, I made void the things of a child.”

Applying some example from familiar things to those ineffable realities, he compared childhood to the age of a man. [Col. 0956D] Therefore, in this life, the prophecy or knowledge of even remarkable people is to be compared with that life as the knowledge of a child with that of a man. For as this life is imperfect, so also is its knowledge. But then we shall attain manly perfection, when by vigorous understanding we arrive at equality with angels.

It is as though he said: Prophecy and knowledge, which are in part, will be made void when that perfect knowledge of truth comes, just as the understanding and speech of a child are made void when he reaches perfect knowledge. The reason why the Apostle said this he indicates by adding:

> “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I shall know as I also am known.”

[Col. 0957A] From this it may be seen that, when perfection comes, imperfection will be made void: now, that is, amid the darkness of the present life, we see through a mirror—that is, we know God through his image; but then, that is, in the future age, we shall see manifestly. For an image is seen in a mirror. And we, who are the image of God, endeavor somehow to see him through this image of himself, as through a mirror.

The rational soul is the mirror, in the contemplation of which we somehow see God, though obscurely. For we see through a mirror in an enigma. An enigma is not every allegory, but an obscure allegory. For just as every horse is an animal but not every animal a horse, so every enigma is an allegory but not every allegory an enigma. Allegory is when one thing is signified through another, [Col. 0957B] that is, one thing is said and another understood; as in: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain” (Deut. XXV; above, IX), that is, you shall not forbid a preacher to live by preaching. But allegory is an enigma only where the meaning is difficult to perceive; where it is easily understood, it is not an enigma.

When, therefore, it is said, “We now see through a mirror in an enigma,” as an image is indicated by the term “mirror,” so by the term “enigma” is indicated an obscure likeness, difficult to distinguish. Let no one, therefore, wonder that even in this mode of seeing granted to this life—through a mirror—we labor in an enigma, so as somehow to see. For the word “enigma” would not be used here if vision were easy.

“We now see through a mirror in an enigma,” but then, when that perfection comes, we shall see face to face: that is, manifestly, after the likeness of two persons who look directly upon one another’s countenances without anything interposed. The face of God is to be understood as his manifestation; our face is the intention of our heart. We shall therefore see face to face: that is, with God’s manifestation set before the intention of our mind, so that nothing stands between us and him. For in no member is anyone known so well as in the face. And when one person’s face is directed toward another’s face, they know each other without any ambiguity. Thus we shall see him manifestly in himself. Now indeed we do not see him in his face, but in an alien likeness of creatures, very different from him.

And I, [Col. 0957D] even I who have been endowed with such great knowledge beyond others, now know God in part; but then I shall know him as I am known by him. For our own weakness is a great barrier before our heart in contemplating God’s sublimity. But then we shall behold him in purity, whom we now behold subtly, when, laying aside this weakness, we have come to the grace of inward contemplation. “Then I shall know him as I am known by him”: that is, I shall know him purely, just as he himself knows me; for then we shall not see him through something else but shall plainly contemplate in him himself that which he is, just as he perfectly knows that which we are. Or: then I shall know him without ambiguity in manifest [Col. 0958A] vision, as formerly, before I existed, I was known by him in predestination.

> “But now remain faith, hope, charity: these three. But the greater of these is charity.”

We shall attain such knowledge of God. But that we may be able to attain it, faith, hope, and charity now remain with us during this pilgrimage and prepare us for that vision: faith, by which we believe whatever Holy Scripture declares that we must believe; hope, by which we hope for the rewards divinely promised to us; and charity, by which we love God and neighbor, and those rewards themselves. These three virtues are so joined together during this life that none of them advances without the other two.

Faith, hope, and charity—these three—now remain in the saints: few indeed, but very useful, because without them no one becomes worthy to ascend to that vision. These three goods are great; but greater than these is charity: that is, charity, which is one of these three, is the greater, having greater merit than faith and hope. It should be known that, when a comparison is made among several things of the same kind—as here of charity with faith and hope, which are likewise virtues—the comparison can and ought to be made with the genitive: “greater **of these** is charity,” where *horum* is used because “three” preceded. Faith and hope cannot be absent from charity, but faith and hope can exist without charity.

Or charity is greater because faith will cease when the future things believed have come, and hope will reach its end when one receives the blessedness [Col. 0958C] for which one waits; but charity alone will endure eternally and will rejoice without end in the vision of the Creator and in the blessedness of the saints.

## Chapter XIV

> “Pursue charity; desire spiritual things, but especially that you may prophesy. For one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to human beings but to God. For no one hears. Yet the Spirit speaks mysteries. But one who prophesies speaks to human beings for edification, exhortation, and consolation.”

Since charity is so great, alone leads to life, and remains eternally, therefore pursue charity with your whole desire. Desire also spiritual things, that is, the gifts [Col. 0958D] of the Spirit, such as kinds of tongues and so forth; but after charity desire more to prophesy than to speak in tongues or perform miraculous powers. After charity, he urges that zeal for prophecy be held more highly, because, although the ranks of spiritual gifts which he listed above are great, this gift is nevertheless greater, since it advances the benefit of the Church. For whatever one directs one’s mind toward, in that very thing one receives a gift. Therefore the grace of prophecy is to be desired, so that it may be received through desire for the edification of many, rather than variety of tongues, which does not benefit hearers.

For one who speaks in an unknown tongue does not speak to human beings—that is, to human understanding—but to God, whose praises he declares and who knows what that person says. Human beings do not know; [Col. 0959A] thus no one gains anything from this speech. “For no one hears,” that is, understands what that person says. Yet he himself speaks mysteries, that is, God’s secrets, by the Holy Spirit, though people do not know what he says. Or the Holy Spirit, not he himself, speaks mysteries of God’s secrets through him.

You ought therefore especially to desire prophecy, because one who prophesies—that is, who makes future or hidden things manifest—speaks to human beings for the edification of their mind, which is built up to be God’s temple; for exhortation to good action; and for consolation, lest they despair because of the greatness of their former sins, or for consolation amid the sorrow of present tribulations through the promise of future rewards.

Teachers who expound the Scriptures to others can also be designated by the name of prophets, according to the saying of the Wise Man: “I shall yet pour forth teaching as prophecy” (Ecclus. XXIV). For just as a prophet foretells future things which are unknown, so a teacher is said to prophesy when he reveals the meaning of Scripture, hidden from many. Such a teacher prophesies for the benefit of many, and the meaning of his words is from the Holy Spirit, not from a human being.

> “One who speaks in a tongue edifies himself; but one who prophesies edifies the Church of God. I wish all of you to speak in tongues, but rather that you prophesy. For one who prophesies is greater than one who speaks in tongues, unless perhaps he interprets, so that the Church may receive edification.”

[Col. 0959C] Again, you ought to desire prophecy rather than a tongue because one who speaks in a foreign tongue some mystery and does not interpret what he says edifies only himself, by what perhaps he alone knows that he says. But one who prophesies—that is, who announces future things to others, or in charity reveals to the brethren the good things he understands in the hidden depths of Scripture—edifies God’s Church because all understand what he says. One who speaks an unknown tongue edifies himself, not others.

But I wish—that is, it is my desire, nor does it displease me—that you all speak in tongues, that is, that all of you possess the gift of speaking in various tongues, because no one would have material for boasting over or envying another, since you would all be equal in this. I do not forbid all of you, if you can, [Col. 0959D] to speak in different tongues, because it is a gift of the Holy Spirit; but I rather wish you to prophesy, because that is more useful. For one who prophesies—that is, who foretells the future or opens the Scriptures—is of greater dignity in the Church than one who speaks in tongues, that is, who utters mysteries in unknown expressions, because he benefits himself alone. For that is greater which benefits more people.

One who speaks in tongues is lesser, unless perhaps he interprets, that is, explains to others what he himself speaks to God. For if he can interpret his own words so that the Church receives edification from them, he will not be lesser. He says “perhaps” in order to suggest that it rarely happens that both gifts are granted to one person.

> “But now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, what shall I benefit you, unless I speak to you either [Col. 0960A] in revelation, or in knowledge, or in prophecy, or in teaching?”

I said that one who prophesies is greater, on account of the edification he gives to the Church, than one who speaks in a tongue and edifies himself alone. But you can see this in myself as well. For if I come to you, brothers, speaking in unknown tongues, what shall I benefit you, since you will not know what I have said? I shall benefit you in no way unless I speak to you either in revelation—that is, in an exposition of a revelation in which mysteries of Christ have been shown to me through certain figures, as things shown to John in his Revelation are read—or unless I speak to you in knowledge, which I have acquired through my study and instruction, so as to make you know how you ought to use these temporal things and what you ought to think of them; or in prophecy, [Col. 0960B] so as to foretell future things to you or reveal hidden things; or in teaching, so as to instruct you concerning faith and morals.

And since I would not benefit you now, when you are already brothers—that is, Christians—if I spoke in unknown tongues, it is evident that I would benefit you much less then, when you were still unbelievers. And since I, such a great Apostle, could not benefit you by speaking in tongues, it is clear that you can benefit your hearers much less by such speech.

“Tongue” is understood here as speaking obscure and mystical significations. If the understanding of the mind is removed from these, no one is edified by hearing what one does not understand. Hence he said above: “One who speaks in a tongue speaks not to human beings but to God. For no one hears. Yet the Spirit [Col. 0960C] speaks mysteries.” There he sufficiently indicated that he calls that a tongue in which there are significations like images and likenesses of things, which require the gaze of the mind in order to be understood. When they are not understood, he says that they are in the spirit, not in the mind.

One who speaks in a tongue—that is, in the spirit, not yet understanding the significations which the tongue of the spirit intended—edifies himself more. For it happened that those who thus spoke God’s mysteries, even though they did not understand their depth, were nevertheless moved by the utterance itself to compunction of heart and often to good work. Therefore, since even by the tongue—that is, the bodily member which we move in the mouth when speaking—signs of things are certainly given and not the things themselves uttered, the Apostle has transferred the term “tongue” [Col. 0960D] to any expression of signs before they are understood. When understanding, which properly belongs to the mind, is added to it, it becomes revelation, knowledge, prophecy, or teaching.

Therefore he says: “If I come to you speaking in tongues, what shall I benefit you unless I speak to you in revelation, or in knowledge, or in prophecy, or in teaching?” That is, unless understanding is added to signs—that is, to the tongue—so that what is done is done not only in the spirit but also in the mind. Accordingly, one to whom signs were shown in the spirit through certain likenesses of bodily things was not yet a prophet unless the work of the mind were added so that they might also be understood. One who interpreted what another had seen was more of a prophet than the person who saw it. From this it appears that prophecy belongs more to the mind [Col. 0961A] than to this spirit, which in a certain special sense is called “spirit”: a power of the soul inferior to the mind, in which likenesses of bodily things are represented.

Thus formerly Joseph was more a prophet, because he understood what the seven ears of grain and the seven cattle signified, than Pharaoh, who saw them in a dream (Gen. XLI). Pharaoh’s spirit was formed so as to see; Joseph’s mind was illuminated so as to understand. Accordingly, in the former there was a tongue; in the latter, prophecy: in the former, an imagining of things; in the latter, an interpretation of images. Thus less of a prophet is one who sees in the spirit only the signs themselves, in bodily images, of the things signified; more of a prophet is one endowed solely with their understanding. But greatest of all is the prophet who excels in both: who both sees in the spirit the significant likenesses of bodily [Col. 0961B] things and understands them by the liveliness of his mind, as Daniel’s excellence was tested and proved, when he told the king the dream he had seen and disclosed what it signified (Dan. II). For the bodily images themselves were represented in his spirit, and their meaning was revealed in his mind. But let us pass on to what follows in the epistle.

> “Nevertheless, things without life that give sound—whether pipe or lyre—unless they give distinction to their sounds, how will what is played on the pipe or lyre be known? For if the trumpet gives an uncertain sound, who will prepare himself for battle? So also you: unless through the tongue you give intelligible speech, how will what is said be known? For you will be speaking into the air. There are, as it were, so many kinds of tongues in this world, and nothing is without a voice.”

I have shown above through myself, though I am rational, that tongues are of no use without an interpreter; and the same point is clear even from inanimate things. For things without life that give sound, whether a pipe or a lyre, unless they give a distinction of sounds—that is, distinct, intelligible sounds—how will what is played on the pipe or what is played on the lyre, that is, sounded on the lyre, be known? So too your speech, whose spiritual sweetness ought not to delight the ears but the mind, will be empty if it is not understood.

What is unknown of the pipe and lyre is likewise unknown of the trumpet. This is another comparison concerning the same matter. For if the trumpet gives an uncertain sound, that is, one that does not clearly signify battle, who will prepare himself for battle? The Jews used the trumpet in festivals and in war, with different sounds. This is the meaning: if the trumpet’s sound is uncertain, no one will distinguish whether it belongs to a solemnity or to war, and no one will arm himself for battle.

So also you, who ought, as a trumpet, to raise your voice (Isa. LVIII) in order to prepare Christ’s soldiers for spiritual battle against demons: if, while speaking in a foreign tongue, you do not give clear speech by interpreting it—speech which openly holds the hearers’ attention—how will others know what is said by you in a foreign tongue? The meaning of your speech will not be known to its hearers. For you will be speaking into the air: that is, saying things which profit no one but dissipate into the air, because, finding no receptive place in the ears of hearers to be understood, they will be scattered [Col. 0962A] into the air; for people will not even deem such things worthy of hearing. You will not speak to human hearts but into the air: that is, your words will not be useful, but you will speak idly and vainly.

“There are, as it were, so many kinds of tongues,” that is, even if you speak as many as there are kinds of languages throughout this whole world, what will your speech benefit, when no one understands? There are many kinds of languages, and nothing is without a voice, because no thing lacks its own name and designation in each language. For although there are very many kinds of languages, they nevertheless have their own significant vocal expressions so that they may be understood; nor can anything be found that has no voice signifying itself. Therefore speech that is not understood is empty.

> “If, therefore, I do not know the force of a voice, I shall be a barbarian to the one to whom I speak, [Col. 0962B] and the speaker a barbarian to me. So also you, since you are zealous for spirits, seek to abound for the edification of the Church. Therefore let one who speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret. For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is without fruit. What then? I shall pray with the spirit; I shall pray also with the mind. I shall sing psalms with the spirit; I shall sing psalms also with the mind.”

For since others will not understand without an interpreter—or rather, since there are so many languages, and each has its own proper distinction—if I do not know the force of the utterance, that is, if I am ignorant of the proper meaning of the word I pronounce, as are those who have only the gifts of tongues, I shall be not understood but a barbarian to the person to whom I speak, [Col. 0962C] whom I ought to instruct, because I shall be unable to explain to him the sense of my words; and he in turn who speaks to me will be a barbarian to me, since I do not know the meanings of the words that he utters, nor can he expound them to me. Thus you too will be barbarians to one another if one speaks to another in an unknown language, and so there will be dissension among you. Therefore you ought not to seek the discordance of unknown languages, through which discord is generated, but the unity of understanding, through which you may glory in common joy.

And because you are emulous of spirits, that is, desirous of spiritual gifts, seek to abound in them for the edification of the Church: that is, do not merely speak in tongues, but also interpret, so that the Church may receive edification, since you are seekers after [Col. 0962D] spiritual charisms. And therefore, that is, so that the Church may be edified, let the one who speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret: that is, let him pray to receive the gift of interpretation, so that his effort may benefit others. Let him pray not with his lips alone, but with the affection of his heart, that he may deserve to be heard.

For if even I, great as I am, pray in a tongue, that is, with voice alone, my spirit, that is, the breath of my mouth, prays while I speak in prayer; but my mind is without fruit, that is, it receives no fruit from the prayer itself, to which it is not attentive. This often happens to us when we utter a psalm or prayer with our lips but do not consider in our minds what the mouth utters. And since the mind which does not inwardly pray with devout affection, while the mouth outwardly petitions in speech, has no fruit of prayer, what then must I do? What is useful to me? [Col. 0963A] This, namely: “I will pray with the spirit” expressed through the mouth, that is, I will pray by speaking; “I will pray also with the mind,” that is, with the affection of the mind; “I will sing psalms,” that is, I will recite psalms, “with the spirit,” that is, with the utterance of the mouth; “I will sing psalms also with the mind,” that is, with the mind’s attention.

Or thus: the one who speaks in a tongue should pray in such a way, that is, speak in such a way, as to interpret what he says. For I offer myself to you as an example: if I pray, that is, if I speak in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is without fruit, that is, without understanding of the things I say. For if I say in a language what I do not understand, as though inspired by the Spirit I speak in church, and the mind is without fruit. For the soul does not know, if it speaks in a language it does not know, just as Latin people commonly sing in Greek, delighted by the sound of the words, yet not knowing what they say.

As was said above, “spirit” is called a certain power of the soul [Col. 0963B] inferior to the mind, in which likenesses of bodily things are represented. But the mind is that higher part of the soul in which understanding and reason properly have their seat. “Tongue,” too, as was said above, can denote any utterance of signs before they are understood. Thus it is said: “If I pray in a tongue,” that is, if I speak by uttering signs not yet understood, “my spirit prays,” that is, only that part of my soul speaks in which images of bodily things are represented; but “my mind,” that is, the higher subtlety of my soul, “is without fruit,” because it has there no refreshment of understanding.

For when the spirit, the inferior nature of the soul, speaks by uttering signs which it does not understand, the mind, to which understanding belongs, receives no fruit from this. [Col. 0963C] What, then, is to be done? This indeed: what I say that I shall do. For “I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray also with the mind”; that is, I will speak with spirit and mind, so that the signs of things may be formed for me in the spirit and their understanding may shine forth in the mind, just as Daniel saw the king’s dream in the spirit (Dan. 2:4), and understood its interpretation in the mind. Thus I too shall act, because I shall speak the signs with the spirit and understand their meaning with the mind. With the spirit I shall speak the expressions; with the mind, the meanings. Likewise, “I will sing psalms with the spirit,” that is, I will make the harmony of the psalmody’s sounds resound in the spirit; “I will sing psalms also with the mind,” that is, I will modulate the harmony of the meanings with the attention of the mind, delighting myself in the understanding of spiritual senses.

Or, “I will sing psalms with the spirit, and I will sing psalms [Col. 0963D] with the mind,” that is, I will compose concord among the members of the Church, so that they may agree also in mind and, from their own concord, beautifully express a sweet and richly varied melody. Thus you too ought to speak with spirit and mind, so that you may both see the signs and understand the meaning and expound it to others. And this is to sing psalms with spirit and mind: that the meanings of the psalms which you sing with your mouths may resound in your hearts.

> “Otherwise, if you bless with the spirit, how will one who fills the place of the uninstructed person say ‘Amen’ at your blessing? For he does not know what you are saying. For you indeed give thanks well, but the other is not edified.”

You ought to pray with mind and spirit, so that you may both utter the words of the history or letter and expound the mystical sense [Col. 0964A] for the instruction of the hearers. Otherwise—that is, if you bless with the spirit, if you say something, if you utter praises of God, or pronounce some blessing in an unknown language which you cannot interpret to the hearers—who fills the place of the uninstructed person?

The person who does not understand the good things he says blesses in the spirit, not in the mind; for when the signs of things are not understood, they are in the spirit and not in the mind. An *idiota*, moreover, is an uneducated person, who knows nothing except what the property of nature has given him; for Greek *idiōma* (ἰδίωμα) is called *proprietas*, “property,” in Latin. The place of the uninstructed person is to say at the end of the blessing, “Amen,” which means “true”; by this he both indicates his assent and confirms the blessing.

But if you bless with the spirit, that is, if you give a blessing [Col. 0964B] in an unknown language, so that neither you understand the sense of your words nor explain it to others, who fills the uninstructed person’s place? That is, who answers “Amen” in place of the uninstructed person at the end of the discourse? Not even a wise person knows how to do this, much less an uninstructed one. For how will he say “Amen” at your blessing, when he does not know what you say? One who is unskilled and without letters, hearing what he does not understand, does not know the end of the prayer and does not answer “Amen,” that is, “true,” so that the blessing may be confirmed. For the confirmation of the prayer is completed by the one who answers “Amen,” so that all that has been said may be confirmed in the minds of the hearers by the testimony of truth.

The uninstructed person will not be able to answer your blessing which he does not understand. For you indeed give thanks well to God [Col. 0964C] in that blessing, and what you say is good; but the other is not edified by your words, which he does not understand. Therefore, when you assemble in church for edification, those things ought to be said in the Church which are understood by people and provide edification for the hearers. Therefore the one who speaks an unknown language ought to be silent in church, so that those may speak who benefit the hearers.

> “I give thanks to my God that I speak in the tongue of all of you. But in church I wish to speak five words with my understanding, so that I may instruct others also, rather than ten thousand words in a tongue.”

He sets himself forward as an example that they ought not publicly to speak in languages in which there is no edification of those who receive them, just as he himself does not use tongues in church, although [Col. 0964D] he knows all their languages. “I do not criticize,” he says, “your speaking in tongues because I cannot possess this gift,” as some are accustomed to do, envying what they themselves cannot attain. “For I speak in the tongue of all of you”: that is, none of you speaks any language in which I also do not speak whenever I wish. And for this I give thanks to my God, who through the gift of his grace has granted me to be able to speak the languages which you all have among you.

But although so great a knowledge of languages has been divinely given to me, in the Church, where I ought to be useful, I wish to speak five—that is, a few—words with my own understanding, that is, words which I understand and expound so as to instruct others also, rather than ten thousand—that is, a very excessive multitude—of words in a tongue, that is, so as neither to understand nor to teach others. [Col. 0965A] His use of “five words” and “ten thousand” is ordinary idiom.

Or, as has seemed good to some, by “five words” he designated the five books of Moses. “I wish,” he says, “to speak in church five words with my own understanding,” that is, the five volumes of the Law with spiritual understanding, “rather than ten thousand words,” that is, rather than the perfection of the Law “in a tongue,” that is, in the utterance of signs not understood. For ten signifies the Law on account of the Decalogue, and a thousand signifies perfection. The Apostle used *quam* (“rather than”) without *magis* (“more”), to indicate that the part joined to *quam* is in no way to be embraced. For where *quam* is used thus, it shows that one part can stand, but the other cannot.

> “Brothers, do not become children in understanding; but be little children in malice, while in understanding be perfect. For it is written in the Law: ‘In other tongues and with other lips I will speak to this people’ (Isa. 28), ‘and not even so will they hear me,’ says the Lord. Therefore tongues are for a sign, not to believers but to unbelievers; whereas prophecies are not for unbelievers but for believers.”

Therefore you ought not to desire merely to speak in tongues, because in this way you would have the understanding of children, who do not consider what is useful to others but what childishly delights themselves. But do not become children in understanding, so as to have childish notions in your desire for tongues, attending to them like children’s games and not considering what serves the welfare of your neighbours. Do not be children in understanding, but be adults. [Col. 0965B] For those who do not persevere in attaining to the perfect man, whether through weakness of strength or levity of mind, are to be compared with women and little children. Do not be children in understanding, that is, do not be foolish.

But because the Lord says, “Unless you are converted and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18), be children in malice. If you delight in imitating children, let it not be their lack of knowledge that delights you, but their innocence and humility. Be little children in malice. In what malice especially, if not that of pride? For pride, presuming on empty greatness, does not allow a person to walk by the narrow way and enter through the narrow gate; but a child easily enters through a narrow opening. Therefore no one enters the kingdom of heaven except as a child.

Be, then, little children in malice: that is, lay aside every kind of greatness [Col. 0965C] which the malice of pride produces, so that, like children, you may be removed from all malice, striving for what promotes the good of the brethren; this is perfection in understanding. Therefore, do not become children in understanding through ignorance, so as, like children, not to understand what you say; but be little children in malice, so that you may be free from every malice like children; while in understanding be advanced, so that you may fully understand what you say and know what is necessary for the instruction of the Church.

Nor should you childishly desire to speak languages which you do not understand, because tongues are given as a sign to unbelievers—which you are no longer—and not for the edification that is now necessary for you as believers. This is the meaning: do not seek tongues, because it is written in the Law, that is, in the book of Isaiah (Isa. 28), “In other tongues,” [Col. 0966A] that is, in diverse kinds of languages, “and with other lips,” that is, with spiritual words, “I will speak through the apostles to this Jewish people; and not even so will they hear me,” they who never wished to hear me through the Law and the prophets, says the Lord.

Or, “I will speak in other tongues,” that is, I will preach the New Testament; “and with other lips,” that is, I will expound the Old Testament spiritually, which they expounded carnally. For this is to speak to them otherwise than the words of the old Law present themselves: when they hear the Sabbath annulled, new moons abolished, circumcision cease, sacrifices changed, foods formerly prohibited permitted to be eaten, and Christ—God from God—proclaimed. This is to speak in other tongues and with other lips, because of that variety of tongues which sounded through the apostles on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2).

But [Col. 0966B] even so the unbelieving Jews would not hear God, so as to obey him by faith and devout conduct. Take care, therefore, lest God too speak to you in various tongues and you fail to heed the words of his commands by doing them. And since the Lord spoke in other tongues to those who did not hear him so as to be converted at last, therefore tongues are for a sign, not to believers, who believe that God can do all things, but to unbelievers, who do not believe this. For outward miracles are performed in order to lead human minds to inward realities, so that, through what is visibly shown to be wonderful, things invisible and more wonderful may be believed.

Tongues, therefore, have been given as a sign, that is, to be a sign of the invisible presence of God, because through the miracle of tongues unbelievers understand that the power of God who is preached to them is present. [Col. 0966C] But prophecies are not a sign for unbelievers, because unbelievers do not believe future things which they cannot yet see, if these are foretold to them by prophecy. Therefore prophecies have not been given to unbelievers, who refuse to believe prophets proclaiming coming events, but to believers, who wisely assent to the prediction of future things. Consequently believers ought not to seek tongues, but prophecies.

Or, by the name “prophecies” interpretations of the Scriptures may be denoted. Prophecies, then, are not a sign for unbelievers but for believers, because unbelievers do not come to know God through the exposition of Scriptures to which they give no faith, whereas believers understand there his hidden [Col. 0966D] mysteries. Prophecy, that is, the interpretation of the prophets, which benefits believers and is always needed, is greater and more useful than speaking in tongues, which was given temporarily for the sake of unbelievers.

> “If, therefore, the whole Church should come together in one place and all should speak in tongues, and uninstructed persons or unbelievers should enter, will they not say that you are mad? But if all prophesy, and some unbeliever or uninstructed person enters, he is convicted by all; he is judged by all. For the hidden things of his heart are made manifest; and thus, falling on his face, he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among you.”

This is another reason why you should not speak in tongues but rather prophesy. Since tongues are a sign for unbelievers rather than an edification for believers, whereas prophecies always edify believers, if the whole Church comes together in one place—that is, if the entire assembly of the faithful gathers into one—and all there speak in tongues without an interpreter, but uninstructed or unskilled persons or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are mad, like persons possessed, since no one understands another? [Col. 0967A] They will surely say that you are mad when they see that your speech benefits no one, but produces a certain unknown tumult, as though you suffered frenzy. Thus you make yourselves an object of derision to those whom you ought to convert by your example.

But if all in the Church prophesy, that is, make future or hidden things manifest by prophecy, and some unbeliever or uninstructed person enters among them, he is convicted by all concerning his error, which he cannot deny against those who behold his heart through the spirit [Col. 0967B] of prophecy; and he is judged by all, that is, he is shown to be worthy of condemnation while each declares how guilty he is. The hidden things of his heart become manifest, or his thoughts are uncovered by those who prophesy; and thus, when he sees that the secrets of his mind have been laid bare by the Holy Spirit who speaks in you, falling on his face, that is, humbling himself, overcome by so evident a presence of God he will turn to repentance and worship God—that is, the Holy Spirit, who was able through you to reveal the hidden things of his heart as God—declaring by confession of the mouth what he understands in his heart: namely, that God is truly in you, who searches out through you the secrets of other hearts.

It should be noted that prophecy is properly so called because it predicts the future. Yet prophecy has three times: past, present, and future. Prophecy concerning the past occurs where the fall of the first angel is described: “How have you fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, who rose in the morning?” (Isa. 14). [Col. 0967C] Prophecy concerning the future is: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people” (Isa. 3). Prophecy concerning the present is displayed in the Apostle’s present words. For when it is said, “The hidden things of his heart are made manifest,” it is plainly shown that by this mode of prophecy the spirit does not predict what will be, but reveals what is. But in what sense is it called a spirit of prophecy when it indicates nothing future but recounts the present? It is rightly called prophecy not because it foretells future events, but because it discloses hidden things. For just as time conceals from our eyes any thing whatsoever in the future, so in the present its cause conceals it from our eyes. A future event is hidden in future time; a present thought is hidden in a concealed heart. [Col. 0967D]

> “What then is it, brothers? When you come together, each of you has a psalm, has teaching, has a revelation, has a tongue, has an interpretation. Let all things be done for edification.”

He now begins to determine how tongues are to be used. Since the things we have stated follow from speaking in tongues, what then, brothers, is to be done? They are to be exercised for edification, like the other gifts. For when you come together in church, where you ought to work for the edification of the hearers, each of you [Col. 0968A] has something by which he can benefit others. Therefore let no one excuse himself. One has a psalm, that is, praise of God through song; another has teaching, that is, an exposition of meanings through spiritual wisdom, by which he can instruct both himself and others in morals; another has a revelation, that is, a disclosure of hidden things which the Holy Spirit has shown him; another has a tongue.

He said this so as not to grieve those who could speak in tongues. For he allowed them to speak in tongues, provided, however, that interpretation followed. Therefore he added, “has an interpretation.” He said this so that, if an interpreter were present, opportunity might be given to the one speaking in tongues. He did not say that each person had all these things, but showed that there was no one among them who had none of them. For the sense of this mode of speech [Col. 0968B] is that the person who understands a psalm should speak on the psalm; the person who has knowledge to teach should teach; the person who has an apocalypse, that is, some revelation of mysteries, should declare what has been revealed to him; and likewise with the rest, so that there may be nothing among them which does not edify another. “Let all things,” he says, “be done for edification.” This is the conclusion: that nothing should be done uselessly in the Church, but that they should labour instead so that even the unskilled may advance. Therefore he wishes all to assemble prepared with diverse spiritual gifts, so that, watchful through this eagerness of mind, they may encourage one another and emulate better gifts for the illumination of the brethren.

> “Whether anyone speaks in a tongue, let it be by two, or at most three; and in turns; and let one interpret. [Col. 0968C] But if there is no interpreter, let him be silent in church; but let him speak to himself and to God.”

He begins to show how all these things may be done for edification. “Let all things,” he says, “whether speaking in tongues or the other gifts, be done for advancement.” This is the meaning: if anyone speaks in a tongue, let speaking be done by two, or, at most, by three; that is, let two or three speak in tongues, and no more, lest they occupy the day and leave no opportunity for the prophets to speak, who are most useful. Let them speak in turns, that is, not all at once, lest they seem mad, but one by one—that is, one after another—or in different parts of the church. And let one interpret: that is, let someone explain to the people the words of the speaker.

The custom at that time was that, [Col. 0968D] when they gathered in church or somewhere else for teaching, those who had received knowledge of languages would speak and others would expound; and this was done in the Church in groups. In one part of the church was one gathering and in another part another; and each section had its own speaker and its own interpreter. This is what the Apostle said: that in one church no more than two or three should speak, and in turns, so that where one speaks another does not speak; or that one speak after another, and one person interpret for each.

But if there is no interpreter, that is, one to interpret, let the person speaking in tongues be silent in church, where no speech should be heard except what edifies; but let him speak to himself, that is, pray silently within himself, and speak to God, who hears all mute things. He speaks to himself who is pierced with compunction by what he says; and he speaks to God because he prays to or praises God. [Col. 0969A]

> “Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others judge. But if something is revealed to another who is sitting by, let the first be silent. For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all may be exhorted; and the spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets. For God is not of dissension but of peace, as I teach in all the churches of the saints.”

As I spoke concerning those who speak in tongues, so I speak concerning prophets: let two or three prophets speak, that is, address the people in different parts of the Church. Let two or three speak, because the discourse of so many persons is sufficient and every word stands in the mouth of two or three [Col. 0969B] (Deut. 18; Matt. 17; John 8; 2 Cor. 13). But let the remaining prophets judge their words, distinguishing better things from good and best things from better.

But if in the meantime something better is revealed through the Holy Spirit to another person sitting and listening, let the first, who was speaking, be silent, so that the latter too may speak what has been divinely revealed to him. For the Lord often reveals to one younger what is better; therefore the first should allow him to speak. Nor should he think himself wronged if he is silent so that an inferior may speak, because what is not granted to the superior is often granted to the inferior. That one to whom it has been revealed ought to speak, because you can all prophesy: both the one who first received the revelation and the one who had begun speaking first.

I say that all [Col. 0969C] can prophesy, not indeed at the same time, lest there be confusion, but one by one, each after another; so that even all the elders may learn what they do not know, and all may be exhorted, that is, admonished concerning matters which, though they understand them, they neglect. The speaker ought to yield to the seated person so that he may speak, because the spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets: that is, it fulfils the prophets’ will in this respect, allowing the prophet to be silent when he wishes, and again allowing him to speak when he wishes.

Lest anyone say that he cannot be silent because the spirit ministering to him compels him, it is said that the spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets, so that they have it in their own power when to be silent and when to speak. The spirit is subject to the prophets so that, when they wish, they can be silent, and when they wish, speak; [Col. 0969D] nor does it compel them, like a Pythonic spirit, to cry out or to keep silent. Hence, if the first prophet does not yield to another, the Spirit of God seems not to be in him. Truly, the spirit is subject to them, so that according to their own will they may reasonably be silent or speak, because God is not a God of dissension but of peace. That is, the Holy Spirit, who is God and fills the prophets, is not the author of dissension and discord, but of peace and concord.

For he would be the author of dissension rather than peace if he neither allowed the person who had first begun speaking to be silent, nor compelled the one who in the meantime had been filled with sudden revelation to speak. From this discord and dissension would arise. But this Spirit produces peace, not discord, so that one prophet reasonably yields to another and the two do not speak at once. God, I say, is a God of peace, not of discord, so that all who [Col. 0970A] desire to cleave to God may pursue peace and flee dissension, as I teach in all the churches of the saints. Therefore, if you wish to share communion with the churches of the saints throughout the world, keep peace with one another in God as they do.

Or, those who have received knowledge of tongues and those who have the grace of prophecy should speak in church as I have now taught, and as I teach in all the churches of the saints. As though he said: what I have now said is neither peculiar nor new; therefore hold firmly what all the churches hold.

> “Let women be silent in the churches. For they are not permitted to speak, but to be subject, as the Law also says (Gen. 3). But if they wish to learn anything, let them ask their own husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church. Did the word of God go forth from you? [Col. 0970B] Or did it come to you alone?”

Although I have said that you can all prophesy, nevertheless let women be silent in the churches. The Apostle now returns to what he had previously passed over. For above he commanded women to be veiled in church; now he shows that they should be quiet and modest, because it is contrary to the order of nature or law for women to speak in an assembly of men. For they are not permitted by any authority to speak in church, but are commanded to be subject, as the Law says in Genesis: “You shall be under the power of your husband, and he shall rule over you” (Gen. 3).

This law is imposed especially upon women; and for this reason Sarah was subject to Abraham, calling him lord (Gen. 18; 1 Pet. 3). A woman is commanded to be subject for two reasons: because she is from the man, and because sin entered through her (Gen. 2). She rightly keeps silent among men, she who, when she spoke to her husband, persuaded him to sin (2 Cor. 2; Gen. 3). [Col. 0970C] Let them not speak in church; but if they wish to learn anything, let them ask their own husbands at home with discipline and submission.

For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church. It is shameful because it is contrary to discipline that, in the house of God—who has commanded them to be subject to men—they should presume to speak about the Law, when they know that men hold primacy there and that it more properly befits them in God’s house to devote themselves to prayers and, keeping their tongues, to open their ears, so that they may hear how God’s mercy conquered death through Christ, which had reigned through them. For if they dare to speak in church, it is disgraceful, because they are veiled for this reason: that they may appear in humility. But if [Col. 0970D] they show themselves irreverently, it is a reproach to men, because husbands too are censured in the insolence of their wives.

You ought to keep these things which I hand down to you, not preferring your own institutions to my traditions and wishing to hand them on to the other faithful as though you were a fountain of religion. For did the word of God’s preaching go forth from you? Certainly not; it came from us to you, because evangelical preaching began from us who are of the circumcision, not from you. Nor did you confer the benefit, but received it. Nor ought you to glory as though uniquely chosen, or be puffed up over singular knowledge. For did the word of God come to you alone? Certainly not; it likewise came to others throughout the world. Therefore do not wish to become teachers by establishing your own new traditions, [Col. 0971A] but hold what the other churches among the nations hold everywhere.

> “If anyone thinks himself to be a prophet or spiritual, let him acknowledge that the things I write to you are commandments of the Lord. But if anyone is ignorant, he shall be ignored.”

I indeed write such things to you. And if there is anyone among you who seems to be a prophet, that is, one who foreknows future things, or spiritual, that is, living spiritually though not possessing knowledge of future things, let him recognize that these things which I write to you are not from me but are commandments of the Lord. The Apostle said this because he knew that what he wrote could be understood one way by the immature and another way by the more capable. For he wished the knowledge of spiritual things to be solid, where faith was not merely accommodated but certain knowledge was held. Thus [Col. 0971B] the immature believed what the spiritual additionally knew.

By these words he also restrains and recalls to peaceful order the restless, who were all the more prone to sedition because they seemed to excel in spirit while by their pride they threw everything into disorder. “If anyone,” he says, “seems to be a prophet or spiritual, let him recognize that the things I write to you are commandments of the Lord.” If he merely seems to be so, he certainly is not. For the person who truly is so recognizes without doubt. He needs neither admonition nor restraint, because he judges all things and is judged by no one. Therefore they caused seditions and disturbances in the Church because they seemed to be what they were not. And he teaches them to recognize that what he writes are the Lord’s commandments.

Yet in this statement he especially strikes at the false apostles [Col. 0971C] by whom they had been corrupted. They taught not divine things but earthly things, according to human desires. Therefore here he says that he hands down nothing of his own but the Lord’s, so that those whom he persuades may appear to have been won for God, not for human beings. “Let him recognize,” he says, “that the things I write to you concerning tongues, prophets, women, and the other spiritual matters are commandments of the Lord.”

But if anyone is ignorant of these things, he will be ignored by the Lord: that is, he will be rejected with those to whom it will be said, “I never knew you” (Matt. 7), that is, “I did not know you to be mine,” or “I did not know you among the predestined.” For this is not said against the little ones who glory in Christ’s cross and yet do not understand the most subtle discussions of divine mysteries. For not one of the little ones [Col. 0971D] for whom Christ died perishes (Matt. 10; Luke 12). But, as what precedes and follows makes clear, the Apostle spoke about matters which would build up the faith and conduct of many: that one ignorant of them will be ignored—that prophecy should be preferred to tongues; that these things should not be done in disorder, as though the spirit of prophecy compelled even unwilling persons to speak; that women should be silent in church; and that everything should be done honourably and in order. Whoever is ignorant of these and similar matters will be ignored—not the hidden mysteries which scarcely belong to the understanding of a few.

> “Therefore, brothers, desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. But let all things be done among you honourably and according to order.”

Since prophecy is so useful, as we have shown above, therefore, brothers, desire [Col. 0972A] to prophesy for the edification of many. And although tongues profit little, do not forbid speaking in tongues, lest dissension arise. But let all things, both these and the rest, be done among you honourably, that is, with peace and discipline, and according to order, so that some things are done first and others later, and prophecy is preferred to tongues (Gal. 1).

## Chapter XV

> “Now I make known to you, brothers, the Gospel which I preached to you, which you also received, in which you also stand, through which you are also saved, by what reasoning I preached it to you—if you hold it fast—unless you believed in vain.”

Here the Apostle begins to rebuke the Corinthians, who, deceived by false apostles, doubted the general resurrection, thinking that no one would rise again because they saw the bodies of the dead buried and decaying. The Apostle destroys this error, proving that the dead will rise at the end of the age; and he does this through Christ’s resurrection, concerning which they were most certain.

“Up to this point,” he says, “I have discussed spiritual gifts. But now I make known to you the Gospel,” that is, the good news that the righteous are announced to be about to rise to glory. It is not new, but was preached to you long ago by me; and you received it, that is, judged it worthy of acceptance and devoutly embraced it, and in it you also stand, that is, you persevere firmly. By saying “in which you also stand,” he speaks to those who were firm in faith in the resurrection. For he speaks to a mixed body, so that those who are in the faith may rejoice and those who waver [Col. 0972B] may grieve at being rebuked and be corrected.

“You stand,” he says, “in the Gospel of the resurrection, you who are steadfast in faith; through it you are also saved,” that is, you attain eternal salvation when you depart this life, or are already saved through the certainty of hope by it. You are saved, I say, if you retain in memory and faith the reasoning by which I preached to you: that is, how, on the basis on which Christ is believed to have risen, I taught the resurrection of the dead. You retain or hold this fast, unless you have believed in vain. That is, either you hold the resurrection of the dead, or you received the faith uselessly, for faith is not received except in hope of resurrection. For all the hope of believers consists in this: that the dead will rise. Whoever does not hope for this has received even the other [Col. 0972C] parts of faith in vain.

> “For I delivered to you first of all what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures (Isa. 53), and that he was buried, and that he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures (John 2; Hos. 6).”

Now first he sets forth what was most certain, in order by it subsequently to prove what was held doubtful. “Truly,” he says, “I make known to you the Gospel concerning the resurrection, which I preached to you long ago, and I show on what grounds I preached it. For I handed on first of all—that is, among the chief mysteries of faith, or at the beginnings of faith—that which I too received from the Lord himself by hidden inspiration; I did not discover it by myself: that Christ died, not from his own [Col. 0973A] necessity, but for our sins, and this according to the prophetic Scriptures which foretold it; and I handed on to you that after his death he was buried, as the Scriptures had foretold; and that he rose on the third day—that is, so swiftly that he is believed, by that power, to have been able not to raise [the object is uncertain in the supplied reading].

“He died and was buried for our sins,” as the Father says of him through Isaiah: “Because of the wickedness of my people I struck him, and he will give the wicked for his burial, and the rich man for his death” (Isa. 53). “And he rose on the third day,” as Hosea foretold: “He will give us life after two days; on the third day he will raise us up” (Hos. 6). For in his resurrection we have been made alive and raised up, as this Apostle says elsewhere: “He made us alive together with Christ, and raised us together, and made us sit together in the heavenly places” (Eph. 2). Therefore, if one who died [Col. 0973B] and was buried rose again, on the same grounds we ought to believe that those who die and are buried will rise again.

> “And that he was seen by Cephas, and after this by the eleven. Then he was seen by more than five hundred brethren at once, of whom many remain until now, but some have fallen asleep. Then he was seen by James; then by all the apostles” (John 20; Luke 24).

I handed on to you, according to the testimonies of the prophets, that Christ truly rose again. And, as an argument for surer faith, I also handed on to you that he was seen by Cephas, that is, Peter, before he appeared to other men on the day of the resurrection; and after this by the eleven apostles in the evening, who had shut themselves in for fear of the Jews. But since Judas was dead, and, according to John, Thomas was absent, [Col. 0973C] how was the Lord then seen by the eleven, unless this is understood by synecdoche? Where the larger or more important part is present, it is customary for that name to include also what does not properly belong to it. How much more, then, could Thomas, who was one of those eleven, be included in their number of eleven, although he was absent when the Lord came?

Then he was seen by more than five hundred brethren assembled together, concerning whom the Gospel is silent. Many of these remain, still abiding in Jesus’ testimony as witnesses for those who inquire; but some of them have fallen asleep in the sleep of death, because they are to awaken again. Then he was seen by James, the Lord’s brother, in a distinct and individual manifestation. The four Evangelists are silent about this matter. But in the Gospel called *According to the Hebrews*, which was also held in authority among the ancients, it is related that after the resurrection the Lord came to James the Just and appeared to him. For James had sworn that he would not eat bread from the hour in which he drank the Lord’s cup until he saw him risen from the dead. And again, a little later: “Bring,” says the Lord, “a table and bread.” And immediately it is added: “He took bread, blessed and broke it, and gave it to James the Just, and said to him: ‘My brother, eat your bread, because the Son of Man has risen from those who sleep’” (Luke 24; Acts 1). Then he was seen by all the apostles on the mountain in Galilee, or at the place of the ascension.

> “But last of all, as to one untimely born, he was seen also by me” (Acts 9). “For I am the least [Col. 0974A] of the apostles, not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace in me was not empty; rather, I labored more abundantly than all of them” (Eph. 3). “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me. Therefore, whether I or they, so we preached, and so you believed.”

Thus, as I have said, he was seen by the others. But last of all he was seen also by me, calling me from heaven after his ascension, or while I was praying in the Temple. By me, I mean, as by one untimely born—*abortivus*, like an aborted birth. For just as one untimely born is compelled by a kind of violence of nature to be born before the proper time, so I, through the terrifying vision of the Lord and the loss of my bodily sight through light, was compelled, before I wished, to come forth from the blind womb of the synagogue [Col. 0974B] and to emerge into the light and freedom of faith.

He was seen by me last after all the others, so that you may understand that my vision was more recent and may thereby have greater certainty. Nor is it surprising that he was seen by me last. For I am the least of the apostles: least in time, not in dignity; least in humility, not in activity; least in myself, great in the Lord. I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because from my former life I possess nothing good, but remember that I committed many evils, for which I deserved punishment, not apostolic grace, because I persecuted the Church of God.

This Apostle, when by laboring more vigorously in preaching he surpassed the care of the other saints, pressed himself down against exaltation and nourished his strength in the bosom of humility. Not forgetting his former cruelty, he considered the innocence of the other apostles: “I,” he says, “am the least of the apostles, because I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God.” For, as we have said, he considered the apostles’ innocence; and because of his preceding wickedness, all the care he showed in the Church became insignificant in his own eyes. He did not attend to how greatly he surpassed many through the understanding he had received; for, weighing their innocence, he grieved that he had once been a persecutor.

What else is accused in these words but the hardness of our mind? He wept over what he had committed before baptism; but we have committed many things even after baptism and yet refuse to weep. “I am not,” he says, [Col. 0974D] “worthy to be called an apostle; but by the grace of God I am what I am.” That is: through my merits I obtained no good thing; rather, by grace—that is, by God’s free gift—it was given me to be what I am in holiness, knowledge, and apostleship. And after this grace was given to me, it was not empty in me, that is, idle, but full of good works, because in preaching I labored more abundantly than all those apostles who preceded me.

For they preached to Jews, who had been instructed through the Law and the Prophets and were persuaded by the authority of the Scriptures to turn to the new grace. But I, with heavier labor, converted to faith Gentiles who had heard nothing about God and yielded to no authority of the divine books. They received support from those [Col. 0975A] to whom they preached; but I received nothing from my hearers, and lived by the labor of my own hands. Finally, none of them preached in so many places, nor did all of them write so many letters. Therefore I labored more abundantly in apostleship than they did.

But I did not do this from myself; rather, the grace of God, working with me, did it. It should be noted that heavenly mercy first works something in us without us, so that, when our free choice follows, it may work with us in doing the good which we already desire. Yet at the final judgment it so rewards this in us through bestowed grace as though it had proceeded from us alone. Since divine goodness goes before us in order to make us innocent, the Apostle fittingly now says: “By the grace of God I am what I am.” And since that same grace follows our free choice, he adds: “And his grace in me was not empty; rather, I labored more abundantly than all of them.”

When he saw that he was nothing of himself, he said: “Yet not I.” Nevertheless, because he found that he was something with grace, he added: “But the grace of God with me.” For he would not say “with me” if subsequent free choice did not exist alongside prevenient grace. Thus, to show that without grace he is nothing, he says: “Not I, therefore.” But to show that he worked with grace through free choice, he adds: “But the grace of God with me.”

Therefore our good things are both God’s and ours: his, because by inspiring he goes before us that we may will; ours, because by helping he follows so that we may not will in vain, but may be able to fulfill what we will. Thus, when grace goes before and good will follows, what is God’s [Col. 0975B] gift becomes our merit. The Apostle fittingly explains this now when he says: “I labored more abundantly than all of them.” Lest he should seem to attribute to his own power what he had done, he added: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me.” Since he was anticipated by the heavenly gift, he acknowledged himself as in a sense alien to his own good work, saying: “Yet not I.” But since prevenient grace had made his free choice good, and by that free choice he followed the same grace in work, he added: “But the grace of God with me.” As though he said: “In the good work I labored—not I, yet also I. In that I was anticipated by God’s gift alone, not I; but in that I followed the gift by my will, also I.”

“I labored,” he says, “more than all of them.” From this it is evident that both I and they labored in preaching. For whether I or they, we preached as I mentioned above: namely, that Christ died for our sins, rose on the third day, and appeared often to many. Whether I or they, we preached Christ’s death and resurrection according to the testimonies of the prophets, because they and I preach the same thing in agreement; there is no discord in our preaching, but the peace of concord and the fellowship of love. Therefore, whether I or they, we preached that Christ rose, and you so believed. Hence it is even clearer how foolishly you act: although this belief is manifest in all the churches, and although you too received it, you have now departed from it because of false apostles.

[Col. 0976A]

> “But if Christ is preached as risen from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? But if there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ risen. But if Christ has not risen, our preaching is empty, and your faith also is empty.”

Now he comes to the matter for which he spoke about the Lord’s resurrection. Having proved by many arguments that Christ rose, he proceeds by Christ’s resurrection to prove the resurrection of the other dead. “I,” he says, “and the other apostles preach that Christ rose, and you firmly believed this. But if Christ is preached as risen from the dead, how—that is, for what reason—do some among you say that there will be no resurrection of the dead?”

For if Christ rose, it must necessarily be granted that the dead too will rise. But those corrupted by false prophets denied this. For the wise of this world also judge it foolish when they hear of the resurrection of the dead. Therefore some Corinthians, lest they should be judged foolish by them, said that the resurrection of the dead would not occur. But if the resurrection of the dead will not occur, neither has Christ risen. For he too truly died, being a true human being. And if the others will not rise, neither did he rise; for his resurrection brings about the resurrection of the others.

Just as he could not die without purpose, [Col. 0976B] neither could he rise without purpose. As he died to destroy our death, so he rose to raise us. Therefore, since he could not rise in vain, if he does not raise us, neither did he rise. If, then, there is no general resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ risen. Whoever denies that the dead will rise also denies that Christ rose.

But if Christ has not risen, then hear how many absurdities follow. If he has not risen, then our preaching—that we who preach proclaim him risen—is empty, that is, useless and without the weight of truth. Your faith also is empty—you who, when we preached, believed that he rose so that his members too might rise at the end.
