The Corinthians had believed this at the Apostle’s teaching: that as Christ rose, so the dead would rise; and by this hope they had been drawn to faith. He now asserts that this would surely turn to their loss if they believed something that will not happen.

It is shameful for someone to profess that he has believed what is false. Therefore he brings shame upon them and says that their labors are fruitless, if what they heard from the false apostles is true—namely, that the dead will not rise. No one can bear to hear this; thus, seeing that it is against them, they might return to their first faith. “Empty,” he says, “is not only our preaching, [Col. 0976C] but also your faith”: that is, we preached the resurrection in vain and without the fruit of recompense, and you believed in vain and without such fruit, if the dead do not rise. Yet they must rise if Christ rose; for he did not rise if they too will not rise.

> “Moreover, we are found to be false witnesses of God, because we gave testimony against God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise if the dead do not rise. For if the dead do not rise, neither has Christ risen. But if Christ has not risen, your faith is vain. You are still in your sins. Therefore those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. If we have hoped in Christ only in this life, we are more pitiable than all human beings.”

Not only are our preaching and your faith empty—that is, void, false, and fruitless—if Christ has not risen in order that others might rise through him; [Col. 0977B] we apostles also, whom everyone believes, are found to be false witnesses of God in this matter. Indeed, falsehood in relation to God is praised with no lesser, and perhaps with even greater, wickedness than truth is blamed.

We are proved false witnesses, if this is so, because we have testified against God—that is, contrary to God, to whom all falsehood is contrary—asserting that he raised Christ. This is not true at all if the dead do not rise. Thus this lie will bring us condemnation (Prov. 19), because a false witness shall not go unpunished. And you who believed this will also share in the condemnation. Whoever asserts that God raised Christ is a false witness if it did not happen. Yet he proclaims God’s power, not as an enemy, when he attributes so wonderful a deed to that power; still, he will not escape punishment.

But if it is true that God raised Christ, what will those suffer who have both become witnesses against God and declare his work to be folly? I rightly said that it is false that Christ was raised by the Father if the dead do not rise. For if they do not rise, neither did he rise. But if Christ has not risen, then your faith is vain—that faith by which you believed that through Christ’s death and resurrection you had been freed from sins. For after baptism you are still in your sins, which you believed forgiven, if Christ has not risen.

The Apostle terrifies them so that they may grieve at having begun, through seducers, to believe something against themselves. For who wishes to hear that his sins have not been forgiven? Yet these connections in the Apostle’s reasoning are true connections, though they contain false propositions, which follow from the error of those against whom he argues. The Apostle introduces them so that those whose error entails them may blush and abandon that error; for if they wish to remain in it, they must also be compelled to maintain what they themselves condemn.

For he does not infer truths when he says, “Neither has Christ risen,” and, “Our preaching is empty, and your faith also is empty,” and the rest—all of which are entirely false, since Christ has risen, the preaching of those who announced this was not empty, and neither was the faith of those who believed it. But these false things are most truly connected with the proposition of those in error, which said that there is no resurrection [Col. 0978A] of the dead. When these false conclusions are rejected, the resurrection of the dead follows.

But let us return to the order of the passage. “You are still in your sins,” he says, “if Christ has not risen.” And because you still remain in sins, those also who have fallen asleep in Christ—that is, died in faith in Christ—were likewise in sins and therefore have perished. He adds this to frighten them, since they surely do not wish to regard the departure of their dear ones as perdition. Those who left the world under this hope, or did not fear to be killed because they believed they would rise by Christ’s example, have perished if it is not true. He tells them what, out of love for their deceased, they do not wish to hear, in order to cut away what they had first wrongly begun to believe through error.

He adds another absurdity: if we hope in Christ only in this life—that is, if after death we hope to receive no good from Christ, but worship him only for the goods of the present life—then we are more pitiable than all other human beings, since we constantly endure so many adversities. Unbelievers at least enjoy the present world. But we are wearied in this life by self-restraint, fasts, vigils, and various afflictions. If we expect no reward in the age to come for these things, we are the most foolish of all. But it is evident that we hope in Christ both in the present life and in the future: he gives grace to his own now and everlasting glory in the future.

> “But now Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep” (Col. 1), “since indeed through a human being came death, and through a human being the resurrection of the dead” (1 Thess. 4). “And as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive. But each in his own order.”

It was said above that if the dead do not rise, it follows that Christ also did not rise. And if it be granted that Christ did not rise, many great and serious absurdities follow, as was argued. But now—that those aforesaid absurdities may not follow—it is evident that Christ rose. “Now,” that is, from these absurdities and the previously mentioned prophetic Scriptures and appearances which took place to the disciples, it is clear that Christ rose from the dead. He himself, I say, is the firstfruits of those who sleep: the first to rise from the dead and the cause who raises the dead, who will rise whole as easily as sleepers awaken.

He is the firstfruits of those who sleep, the first in time and dignity to awaken from those who sleep, so as to awaken the multitude from the sleep of death. Just as the firstfruits of anything, offered to God, consecrate the whole mass which follows, so, because through the first human being’s sin the death of all was found, Christ’s righteousness has obtained the resurrection of the dead. And it was fitting that they could rise through the human being Christ, since death came through a human being much lesser—namely Adam—and therefore the resurrection of the dead fittingly comes through the human being Christ. As death entered through Adam, because he was the first to die, so resurrection comes through [Col. 0979A] Christ, because he was the first to rise. As the former is the pattern of those who die, so the latter is the pattern of those who rise.

And as all die in Adam because they are his children, so all will be made alive in Christ because they are his children. No one comes to death except through Adam; no one to eternal life except through Christ. This is what “all” and “all” means: as all human beings belong to Adam through the first—that is, carnal—generation, so all human beings come to Christ through the second—that is, spiritual—regeneration, whoever come to him. Therefore “all” is said here and “all” there, because as all who die die only in Adam, so all who will be made alive will be made alive only in Christ.

This making alive properly belongs to the elect. Nevertheless Christ will effect a general resurrection, so that, as all die in Adam, whether righteous or unrighteous, so all will rise in Christ, whether believers or unbelievers. Yet unbelievers will not be made alive in Christ in such a way as to be members of Christ, just as the righteous do not die in Adam in such a way as to belong to the mass perishing through Adam. Rather, unbelievers will be made alive in Christ—that is, by Christ’s power or command—so that they may live without end for punishment. But the elect will be made alive in Christ—that is, in Christ’s righteousness, which they have kept—so that they may live forever in Christ’s body, which is the Church. For as no one is in the kingdom of death without Adam, so no one is in Christ’s kingdom without Christ.

“All,” he says, [Col. 0979B] “will be made alive”; this will be common to all, yet they will differ from one another, because each will rise in his own order: the martyr in the order of martyrs, the virgin in the order of virgins, the married person in the order of married persons, the priest in the order of priests. Or, “in his own order” means according to the dignity of his own merits: so that the outstanding Vincent may be set before very many martyrs, and the great Martin before very many priests.

> “Christ the firstfruits. Then those who belong to Christ, who believed in his coming. Then the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God and the Father, when he abolishes every rule and authority and power.”

[Col. 0979D] All will rise because Christ is their firstfruits, he who first rose so as to become the cause, pattern, and sign of the future resurrection of all. Just as the first sheaves gathered are called firstfruits and signify that the whole harvest will be gathered, so he himself has already risen, as the firstfruits are first gathered and offered. But afterwards, as the multitude of the harvest is gathered, those who belong to Christ will rise—not now, indeed, but at his final coming. For if the head has risen, the members must follow.

As we have said, Christ is the firstfruits: the first, greatest, preceding, and consecrating the rest. Then—that is, after him—come the others, as less worthy: those who are Christ’s members, who believed in his coming; and they too will awaken at his coming to meet him. Then will come the end—that is, completion and the full perfection of the sufficient goods of body and soul—when the mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, delivers the kingdom to God and the Father. That is, he will lead the righteous, in whom he now reigns as they live by faith, to the contemplation of God, who created him according to his humanity, and of the Father, who begot him according to his divinity.

For his kingdom in this place is called the Church of believers. His kingdom is called one thing according to the power of divinity, because every creature is subject to him; and another according to the property of faith, namely the Church which is in him. Nor should we suppose that he will deliver this kingdom to God and the Father so as to take it away from himself, [Col. 0980A] since he himself, together with the Father, is one God. He will therefore deliver the kingdom to God and the Father, not separated from it himself, nor the Holy Spirit, because he will lead believers to the kingdom and contemplation of God. There are the end of all goods, everlasting rest, and joy which shall not be taken away. For we shall seek nothing else when we have reached that contemplation, because there will be nothing further to seek.

“End” is said in one way with reference to completion, and in another with reference to consumption. Cloth is ended by weaving it; food is ended by eating it. Thus the end that pertains to the most perfect completion of all goods will be when Christ has delivered the kingdom to the Father. Not because the Father does not now possess the kingdom, but because Christ is said to be about to deliver the kingdom to the Father since he will show the Father reigning: through visible appearance and manifestation, what is now believed by the faithful and not thought by unbelievers will become clear.

For Christ’s kingdom now properly belongs to his humanity, because he now reigns in us through the dispensation of his sacrament, by his incarnation and passion. But insofar as he is the Word of God, his kingdom, like the Father’s, is without end, defect, or interruption. Yet insofar as “the Word became flesh” (John 1), he began to reign in believers through faith in his incarnation. But he will deliver the kingdom to the Father: he will lead those nourished by faith in his incarnation to sight, because he is equal to the Father. He will deliver the kingdom to the Father when, through that in which he is equal to the Father, he reigns in those who contemplate truth and makes them see the Father through the only-begotten himself by sight.

He will deliver the kingdom to the Father, I say, leading those who now believe in him from faith in his incarnation to the sight of deity—not so that he himself loses it, but so that both jointly offer themselves as one to those who contemplate them for enjoyment. He will deliver the kingdom to the Father when he abolishes every rule, authority, and power. By what will he abolish them, if not by humility, patience, and weakness? What rule is not abolished when the Son of God reigns precisely because the rulers of this world judged him? What authority is not abolished when he through whom all things were made reigns in believers precisely because he was so subject to authorities that he said to a human being: “You would have no authority over me unless it had been given you from above” [Col. 0981A] (John 19)? What power is not abolished when he through whom the heavens were made firm reigns in believers precisely because he was made weak even to the cross and death (Phil. 2)?

Thus, while Christ reigns through faith in those who believe, every rule, authority, and power of creatures is abolished. When this has been fully accomplished, then, as we have said, he will deliver the kingdom to the Father: he will advance believers to the vision of the Father so that through the sight in which he is equal to the Father, he may reign with the Father in them.

Or he will then abolish every rule, authority, and power by manifesting the Father’s kingdom, so that it may be known to all that no ruler and no authority or power, whether heavenly or earthly, has possessed any rule, authority, or power of itself, but only from him from whom all things come—not only that they may exist, but also that they may exist in order. In that manifestation no hope will remain in any ruler or any human being. The Prophet also sings: “It is good to hope in the Lord rather than to hope in princes” (Ps. 117), so that by this meditation the soul may already rise into the Father’s kingdom, magnifying no power except his and never ruinously flattering itself.

He will therefore abolish every rule, authority, and power, so that none who looks upon the Father through the Son will need or wish to rest in the power of any creature or in his own. So long as the manner of this present life endures, we have need of angelic principalities, authorities, and powers, through whose administration we may be governed, do good, overcome evil, and be illuminated with virtues. We must also have human superiors, such as bishops, presbyters, and deacons, and kings, consuls, and other rulers. But in the age to come all such prelations will be abolished, where none of them will any longer be necessary to us.

> “For he must reign until he puts all enemies under his feet” (Ps. 109). “But the last enemy to be destroyed is death. For he has subjected all things under his feet. But when he says, ‘All things are subjected to him,’ it is without doubt excepting him who subjected all things to him” (Ps. 8). “But when all things have been subjected [Col. 0981D] to him, then the Son himself also will be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all” (Heb. 2).

I said that he will deliver the kingdom to the Father, that is, lead believers to the open vision of himself and the Father. But meanwhile he must reign through faith in his own until he places all his enemies under his feet. That is to say: so long as it is necessary, for all persons able to behold with the clear light of the mind the equality of Father and Son, Christ must reign through what such persons can grasp and what he especially assumed for them—namely, the humility of the incarnation—until he subjects all his enemies beneath his feet, that is, until all worldly pride is subjected to the humility of his incarnation. This happens daily, and at the end of the age it will be wholly completed; then he will deliver the kingdom to the Father, as we explained above.

Or thus: he himself will deliver the kingdom to the Father, and then it will be clear to all that he reigns eternally with the Father. But meanwhile he must reign until he places all his enemies beneath his feet; that is, his kingdom must be manifested so fully that all his enemies acknowledge that he reigns. This is what is meant by enemies being under his feet. If we understand this of the righteous, they are called enemies because they are made righteous from being unrighteous and are subjected to him by believing. But regarding the unrighteous, who will not share in the future blessedness of the righteous, it must be understood that, confounded by the very manifestation of his kingdom, they too will acknowledge that he reigns.

Therefore he must reign until he places all his enemies under his feet. This is not said as though, when he has placed them there, he will no longer reign; rather, he must bring his kingdom to such evident manifestation that his enemies no longer dare deny that he reigns. “Until” is used here in the sense of “no further.” For to what further—that is, to what greater—manifestation can his kingdom be made manifest than that all enemies acknowledge him to reign? When will his kingdom be more manifest than when it has shone forth to all enemies? And from that point it will remain forever (Ps. 60).

All enemies will be placed beneath his feet. But last, death, the enemy, will be destroyed through the resurrection of the dead. “Last,” that is, after everything else, death will be destroyed, so that those who have risen may no longer be dissolved: “For there will be nothing to be destroyed after this mortal has put on immortality.” Then death, our enemy because it begrudges us life, will be destroyed.

Truly enemies will be placed under Christ’s feet and death will be destroyed by him, because, as Scripture says, the Father “subjected all things under his feet” (Ps. 3), so that he might destroy death also. For among the other things subject to him, it is clear that he possesses authority over the dead. The Father subjected under his feet—that is, beneath the humility of his humanity—all things whatsoever in the whole creation. We see that this is not yet fully completed, since unbelievers still disdain to be subjected beneath his feet; but at the end, willing or unwilling, they will be subjected.

But both the Apostle and the prophet use the past for the future to give greater certainty. When the prophetic saying declares that all things have been subjected to him, it undoubtedly means not only the good but also the evil, and everything except the Father who subjected all things to him. This statement must be understood so broadly that nothing is excluded from subjection to him except the one who subjected all things to him. God alone is excepted from this subjection. For God is not subject to him; rather, he is subject to God, according to his humanity.

Since all things will have been subjected to him, as the Scripture of the Psalm foretold, then the Son himself also, in that very preeminence, will be subject to him who subjected all things to him. He will be subject according to his humanity, lest anyone suppose that the human nature which he assumed is to be changed into the nature of divinity so as to become equal to the Father and not subject.

Nor is it unreasonable to understand the statement, “he himself also will be subject to him who subjected all things to him,” so that “he himself” means not only the head of the Church but also all the saints with him, who are one in Christ, one seed of Abraham: namely, the whole Church, which is Christ’s body and his fullness. Thus, when all things have been subjected to Christ—both head and body—they will without doubt be subjected. For insofar as he was born God outside time, nothing could ever fail to be subject to him.

We therefore understand, as has been said, that the head with the body will be subject to God: subject through the contemplation of eternal truth, for the obtaining of blessedness, with no movement of the soul and no part of the body resisting, so that in that life, when no one loves a power of his own, God may be all in all. But now, while certain members still resist, even the head appears not to be subject. When all the members, in flesh and spirit, have been devoutly subjected to God and joined together, then the Son himself, who is their head, will plainly be known as subject to God in all.

Then God will be all in all: whatever human beings rightly desire—life, salvation, sustenance, abundance, glory, honor, peace, and every good. He will be the end of our desires, because then nothing will be lacking for the satisfaction of righteous desires. Here the Apostle mentioned the end above, when he first wished briefly to conclude the whole matter, and then, as it were, to unfold and explain it part by part. He arrives at this, to say at the end that God will be all in all. For we shall seek nothing further after we have reached this fullness of all goods. Toward this we must direct our faith through everything we now do. It follows:

> “Otherwise, what will those do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise at all? Why then are they baptized for them?”

It has been said above that each person will rise in his own order. Otherwise—that is, if they are not to rise—what will those do, or what benefit will they obtain, who are baptized on behalf of their dead friends, if the dead do not rise at all? That is, what benefit will they confer on them through baptism [Col. 0983D], if they are in no way going to rise? Why, too, are they baptized on their behalf, if they are not to rise, since sins are not remitted by baptism except with a view to the future resurrection?

There were certain ignorant persons who were baptized for their friends who had died without baptism, thinking that this would benefit them. The Apostle does not approve their practice, but displays their fixed faith in the resurrection. For he wishes to show the resurrection to be so certain and firm that he gives the example of those who were so sure of it that they were even baptized for the dead, if someone had perhaps been overtaken by death. They feared that one who had not been baptized might either rise badly or not rise at all; and one was immersed under the name of the dead person, supposing that by this means remission of sins would be conferred on that person [Col. 0984A], so that he might rise in the lot of the righteous. It is as though the Apostle said: “If fools are so certain about the resurrection, you ought not to doubt.”

> “Why too do we endanger ourselves every hour? I die daily, by [alternative reading: through] your glory, brothers, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord. If, according to man, I fought with beasts at Ephesus (Acts 19), what does it profit me if the dead do not rise? Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. Do not be deceived. Evil conversations corrupt good morals. Awake, righteous ones, and do not sin. For some have ignorance of God. I speak this to your shame.”

Foolish people, as has been said, are baptized for the dead [Col. 0984B] in hope of the resurrection. For why would they do this unless they hoped that the dead would rise? And why—that is, for what reason—do we too, who appear wise, endanger ourselves, that is, incur dangers on account of Gospel preaching, every hour, that is, continually, unless because we hope for the coming resurrection? In saying, “Why too do we endanger ourselves?” he distinguishes himself from those mentioned above, showing that those baptized for the dead are not Catholics.

I said that we preachers are endangered every hour. And I not only suffer dangers but also die daily: that is, I endure such harsh [variant: dreadful] afflictions as though I were breathing out my spirit. And I swear this by your glory, brothers, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord—that is, by the glory of recompense which I have with God for the labor expended among you [Col. 0984C]. For the words “by your glory” are an oath: “By your glory which I have in Christ,” that is, by the glory which, through the gaining of your salvation, I am so certain that I shall have in Christ as though I already possessed it.

By this glory I swear that I die daily in hope of the resurrection, lest you hesitate to believe me. Indeed, this is more than “Yes, yes; no, no” (Matt. 5; Jas. 5), and therefore it is from evil—but from your weakness and unbelief, since you are not otherwise moved to faith.

And again I say: if according to man—that is, rationally—I fought with beasts at Ephesus (Acts 19), that is, against Demetrius and the other beastlike men who, with him, stirred up a popular riot against me on account of the image of Diana, whose worship I was destroying [Col. 0984D], what profit is it to me to have fought in this way, if the dead do not rise? For it was because of hope in the resurrection that I fought them: that is, I overcame their errors, offering myself to their beastly fury without fear of death.

For they were beasts, that is, beastlike, because they were given over in brutish understanding to the belly and bent toward earthly things, believing that there would be no life after this one, and raging against me with bestial fury in defense of their idol. But I fought bravely as a soldier of Christ, destroying their errors. And I did this according to man: that is, speaking and acting as a human being, as a rational creature, when I showed that it was not reasonable, despising the Creator, to worship the creature, or, despising everlasting life, to love temporal life.

Thus I fought [Col. 0985A] according to man: that is, I disputed, and I offered myself by reason to those who raged like beasts. And what does it avail me to have fought amid such dangers if I shall not rise, so as to rejoice in the flesh in which I suffered troubles for God? If, then, the dead do not rise, why should we further afflict the flesh in the present life? Let us no longer strive after abstinence, but let us be devoted only to luxury and the belly, like brute animals, saying: “Let us eat and drink” (Isa. 22)—that is, let us nourish the flesh with delights—“for tomorrow,” that is, soon, “we die,” and are reduced to nothing.

The false apostles advised such things to the Corinthians, namely, so that by distrust of the resurrection they might draw them into satisfying the flesh, and thus themselves might freely indulge with them. Therefore they wished them to think that this alone was life [Col. 0985B], which we share with cattle; that after death the whole human being comes to an end; and that there is no further hope of a better life.

Hence the Apostle adds: “Do not be deceived,” that is, do not be diverted from the straight path by the words of fools, who, through despair of the resurrection, desire to enslave you to fleshly pleasures. Therefore avoid their conversations, since evil conversations corrupt good morals. For continual bad conversation corrupts the mind and must therefore be avoided, especially by the weak. We take into our minds the words of those near us every day, just as by breathing we draw air into the body. And as bad air, continually drawn in, infects the body, so perverse speech continually heard infects the minds of the weak, so that they waste away through delight in evil action [Col. 0985C] and through the persistence of wicked speech.

In this way the false apostles corrupted the minds of the weak Corinthians with their discussions, saying that human beings would die like beasts and would not rise thereafter; therefore they urged them to eat and drink and satisfy fleshly pleasures. For while they denied that another life exists, they also denied that punishment would be given to the wicked and glory to the good. And while they denied the punishments of the wicked and the joys of the good, they drove people toward every vice pleasing to this life and overthrew every good purpose of the mind. In these and countless other ways evil conversations corrupt good morals.

For this reason association with the wicked must be avoided by the weak, lest, while they are unable to correct them, they be drawn into imitation; and lest those who are not changed from their own wickedness [Col. 0985D] pervert those joined to them. It should be noted that the Apostle took this iambic verse from a comedy of Menander:

> Evil conversations corrupt good morals.

“Do not,” he says, “be deceived by those who strive to corrupt good morals by their discussions. Rather awake: shake off the sleep of torpor and negligence, and open the eyes of the mind to the sight of the true light, so that you may be watchful in mind; lest, captured by the deceitfulness of perverse thought and led away from the faith, you be corrupted by not believing in the resurrection. Awake against the seducers who lie in wait for you.

“Awake, righteous ones”: that is, you who have been justified by faith and have fallen asleep in it for a little while, when you began to doubt the resurrection [Col. 0986A]. Recover steadfastness and vigilance in faith, lest you lose righteousness altogether. You righteous ones, awake, lest you be deceived by sinners. Awake in faith in the resurrection and in the caution of prudent watchfulness; and do not sin—that is, do not serve the belly and pleasures, after the manner of beasts, as though you did not hope for another life after this one, as the corrupters of minds urge when they say, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”

And you ought to awake lest the words of fools entice you to sin. For some have ignorance of God: that is, they do not know God’s purpose concerning the resurrection of the dead, and therefore urge you to live in the present life after the manner of pigs, hoping for nothing beyond. And I say this—that they themselves do not know God and his purpose—to you for shame: that is, to instill shame in you [Col. 0986B], who are so imprudent that you believed those who, through ignorance of God, teach foolish things. I say this to your shame, so that henceforth you may be ashamed to comply with them and may blush to believe the ignorant.

> “But someone will say: How do the dead rise? And with what kind of body do they come? Fool, what you sow is not made alive unless it first dies. And what you sow, you do not sow the body that is to be, but a bare grain—perhaps of wheat or of some of the others. But God gives it a body as he wills, and to each of the seeds its own body.”

Up to this point the Apostle proved the resurrection by arguments; now he shows, through the very nature of things, that it can occur [Col. 0986C]. It is as though he says: “It is certain from the arguments stated above that there will be a resurrection of the dead. Yet perhaps someone will say to me: ‘How do the dead rise?’”—as though it could not occur by nature. “How do they rise?” that is, “How can it happen that they rise?” Or, “How do they rise?” means, “What will be the mode of those who rise?” But if they do rise, with what kind of body will they come to life: a heavy or a light one, mortal or immortal? It is as though he says: “It cannot be anything other than it is now, namely passible and mortal.”

In answering this question, the Apostle adduces the example of seeds and says: “You fool, who do not know the wisdom of this mystery: what you sow in a field is not made alive—that is, does not grow—unless it first dies [Col. 0986D], that is, decays.” Plants and trees live, not by a soul, but by greenness. With the merely animate person he does not argue from the authority of the law—which, if such a person accepted it, would prevent error—but by physical reasoning, in which the person prides himself so as not to believe that bodies, dissolved and dead, can rise.

For he shows that dead things are restored again to life in a more abundant state, so that human error may be confounded. “You,” he says, “who think yourself wise while, by the wisdom of the world, you assert that the dead cannot rise: hear from worldly things that the wisdom on which you rely may be proved foolish. For the seed which you sow in the cultivation of a field is not made alive unless it first dies. So also the human body does not become immortally alive unless it first dies and returns to the earth, like a seed that is sown.”

For if the sown grain must first decay and dissolve in the earth [Col. 0987A], so that afterward it may be made alive and grow, then likewise the human body, after it has died and decayed, will be made alive. Behold, you have how the dead will rise; now hear with what kind of body they will come. For what you sow, you do not sow the body which is to be: that is, you do not sow herb or stalk and the many coverings of the grains in their husks, but a bare grain, which afterward grows with stalk and leaves and produces an ear with many growing grains. You sow a grain bare of husk, perhaps of wheat or of some other seed.

But afterward God gives that grain a body as he wills: that is, he brings it forth into a great ear and into many grains, not bare but clothed with husks and awns. And he does not give the same body to all grains, but gives to each seed its own body: wheat to wheat and millet to millet. Therefore, if God can bring forth what was not present in the bare seed, much more can he restore what was present in the human body. For if a bare grain is sown and, by God’s ordinance and in some manner through the service of the elements, rises clothed and bearing with it many increases useful to human beings, why should it not be believed that by God’s power a dead human being can rise with an improved substance, not multiplied in number?

For just as God gives to the grain of each seed its own new body, so he will give each human being his or her own body, renewed. Therefore those who rise will come with such a body: that is, each will receive his or her body of the same substance, but improved and renewed [Col. 0987C]. What the Apostle now adds concerns the distinction among those who rise, because of the differing glories of believers and saints.

> “Not all flesh is the same flesh: but one is that of human beings, another that of cattle, another that of birds, and another of fish. There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies. But the glory of the heavenly is one thing, and that of the earthly another. One is the brightness of the sun, another the brightness of the moon, and another the brightness of the stars. For star differs from star in brightness; so also is the resurrection of the dead.”

The sense throughout all this is as follows. The kinds of flesh, though all mortal, nevertheless differ among themselves according to the differences of living creatures. And bodies, though all visible, nevertheless differ according to the differences of places [Col. 0987D]; hence the glory of the heavenly is one thing, and that of the earthly another. And if, in the lofty regions, though all things are heavenly, the brightnesses of the lights differ among themselves, it is no wonder that, in the resurrection of the dead, the glory of merits will differ.

Just as, therefore, from one common material the flesh of diverse living creatures is one, so human beings of one flesh will differ in dignity when they rise, so that each will appear such as he or she has deserved to be. Nor does the flesh of different living creatures alone differ among itself; earthly bodies also differ from the heavenly bodies of the stars. And he who made the bodies of the elements so bright—why should he not make the bodies of the righteous splendid?

By figurative meaning, heavenly bodies are those of persons who rise, while earthly bodies are those before they die [Col. 0988A] or rise. And because Christ is heavenly, bodies are called heavenly from him; but from Adam, because he is earthly, bodies are called earthly. But just as sun, moon, and star, though of one nature, nevertheless differ in brightness, so human beings, though of one kind, will differ in glory according to merit.

The discourse here is only about the elect, whom virtues, not sins, will make diverse. Virginity will shine there in one way, marital chastity in another, holy widowhood in another. They will shine differently, but all will be there: diverse splendor, a common heaven. Even if one of the elect is stronger than another, another wiser, another more righteous, another holier, “in my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14); each will receive a dwelling place according to his or her merit [Col. 0988B].

For the saints, like stars, receive in the kingdom various dwelling places of varying brightness, as though in heaven; but because of the one denarius no one is excluded from the kingdom. Thus God will be all in all, because God is love: through love, what individuals possess becomes common to all. For each even possesses what he or she does not possess personally when he or she loves it in another. Therefore there will be no envy because of unequal brightness, since the unity of love will reign in all.

The Apostle now comes to that which all flesh rising to eternal life has in common, and says:

> “It is sown in corruption; it will rise in incorruption. It is sown in dishonor; it will rise in glory. [Col. 0988C] It is sown in weakness; it will rise in power. It is sown an animate body; it will rise a spiritual body.”

To sow is to bury; for just as wheat is covered in a field in order to rise renewed, so the body of the dead is placed in a tomb in order to rise from it improved. It is therefore sown in corruption: that is, a corruptible human body is buried; but it will rise in incorruption: that is, it will rise incorruptible, because it will no longer be able to decay.

Or this sowing may be understood in creation. “It is sown in corruption; it will rise in incorruption”: that is, although a human being, from conception until dissolution, is in corruption, nevertheless that person will rise in incorruption. It is sown in dishonor [Col. 0988D], that is, buried in baseness and abjection, so as to stink and teem with worms; but it will rise in glory, that is, glorious and radiant. For what is more dishonorable than dead flesh? Or what meanwhile is more glorious than that flesh when it rises and receives incorruptibility?

It is sown in weakness: that is, as a seed-grain is committed to the earth weak and feeble, but it will rise in the power of angelic strength. And why should I describe each point separately? It is sown an animate body: that is, one sustained by food and finally dissolved from its soul, like the bodies of other animals; but it will rise a spiritual body: that is, needing no nourishment and now incapable of being separated from the soul.

The bodies of the saints, therefore, will rise without any defect, deformity, corruption, burden, or difficulty. In them there will be as much ease as there will be blessedness [Col. 0989A]. For this reason they are called spiritual, though beyond doubt they will be bodies, not spirits. But just as a body is now called animate, though it is not itself an animal, so then it will be a spiritual body—yet still a body, not a spirit.

For this reason it is said that an animate body is sown but a spiritual body rises: because there will then be such harmony of flesh and spirit, the spirit giving life to flesh subject to it without need of any support, that nothing in ourselves will resist us. As we will suffer no enemies outside ourselves, so neither will we suffer ourselves as enemies within. For just as a spirit serving the flesh is not improperly called fleshly, so flesh serving the spirit is rightly called spiritual—not because it will be changed into spirit, but because it will be subjected to the spirit with the highest and marvelous ease of obedience [Col. 0989B], until the utterly secure will of indissoluble immortality is fulfilled. Every sensation of trouble, every corruptibility and slowness, every earthly frailty and stain will be removed; it will be transformed and converted into heavenly purity and stability, suitable for a heavenly dwelling.

> “If there is an animate body, there is also a spiritual body, as it is written: The first man Adam became a living soul; the last Adam, a life-giving spirit (Gen. 2). But what is spiritual is not first, but what is animate; afterward, what is spiritual. The first human being is from the earth, earthly; the second human being is from heaven, heavenly. As is the earthly one, so also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly one, so also are the heavenly. Therefore, just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us bear [Col. 0989C] also the image of the heavenly. But this I say, brothers: flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, nor will corruption possess incorruption.”

“Truly,” he says, “a spiritual body will rise. For if a body is now animate, there is also a spiritual one”—that is, it is certain that it will at some time be spiritual. For as we are animate because our fleshly father Adam became a living soul, so at the resurrection we shall be spiritual because our spiritual Father Christ became, in his resurrection, a life-giving spirit.

He explains this as follows: it is written in Genesis that we are animate, descending from an animate father. “The first man Adam became a living soul”: that is, a soul able to live only through the support of food, not itself life-giving [Col. 0989D]. To these words of Moses the Apostle adds: “The last Adam became a life-giving spirit”: that is, Christ became a spirit which gave life to the body in such a way that it no longer needed any support from food and could not be dissolved.

Or he proves the existence of a spiritual body, as it were, from correlated terms. “If there is,” he says, “an animate body, there is also a spiritual one.” When “body” is said, “animate” is added in vain unless there is another body, spiritual, in contrast with which it is called animate. And he proves from Genesis that there is an animate body, because the first human being became a living soul. It was also said of animals: “Let the earth bring forth a living soul” (Gen. 1).

Thus an animate body is understood to be one like other animals, on account of death’s dissolution [Col. 0990A] and corruption: it is restored daily by food, and afterward the organism of the living creature, once separated, is dissolved. But the spiritual body is that which, together with the spirit, is now immortal. “The first Adam became a living soul; the last Adam a life-giving spirit.”

Whether the first Adam is understood as the one formed earlier from dust and the last Adam as the one begotten from a virgin; or whether both are fulfilled in each human being, so that the first Adam is the human being in a mortal body and the last Adam that same person in an immortal body: nevertheless, he intended this difference between a living soul and a life-giving spirit, that there the body is animate, here spiritual.

For the soul indeed lives in the animate body, but does not give life so as to remove corruption. But in the spiritual body [Col. 0990B], because, perfectly cleaving to the Lord, it is one spirit, it gives life in such a way as to make a spiritual body, consuming all corruption and fearing no separation. Accordingly follows: “But what is spiritual is not first, but what is animate; afterward, what is spiritual.”

For the animate body comes first, such as the first Adam had—though it would not have died if he had not sinned; such as we now have, its nature having since been changed and corrupted; such as Adam’s became after he sinned, and thus now has the necessity of dying; and such as Christ also first deigned to have for our sake, not by necessity but by power. But the spiritual body comes afterward: such as has already gone before in Christ, as in our head, and will follow in his members in the final resurrection of the dead [Col. 0990C].

“For the first human being is earthly, from the earth,” and so forth. Yet it is rightly asked why Christ is called the second human being after so many human beings, or why Adam is called the last, when so many generations followed him; since the second cannot be after many, and the last ought not to be called such when many come after him. Here the reasoning must be sought not from flesh but from operation.

The Apostle explains this not by human concepts, since he refers and brings both old Adam and the Lord Christ back to the first beginnings of good and evil things, placing two patterns of life in two persons. Thus anyone who follows in the tracks of Adam’s error is regarded as the first Adam; but the latter is the one who has imitated the Lord.

Meanwhile, the Lord is called last in relation to the first because death, discovered by that first one, descended from him until Christ; death held the power of the old human being until the Lord’s cross [Col. 0990D]. The last Lord, by destroying it through death, blots it out. Therefore he is last in relation to death, not salvation: he alone, by dying, discharged and so erased the bond-document which had come from the first-formed human being through all generations by hereditary right.

The first human being, made from earth—that is, from the mud of earth—was earthly. Yet he is called earthly not because of flesh but because of sin: because, when he had already become guilty and been assigned to death’s punishment, he heard: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3). The second human being is heavenly, from heaven, because the Son of God came to flesh; by taking it up, he became human outwardly while remaining God inwardly [Col. 0991A].

For he did not fall for his own sake, but descended for ours. And he assumed flesh without sin, in which he might show the resurrection of our flesh. For “as is the earthly one, so also are the earthly” means nothing other than “mortals from a mortal”; and “as is the heavenly one, so also are the heavenly” means nothing other than “immortals through the immortal.” The former is through Adam, the latter through Christ.

For the Lord became earthly for this purpose, though he was heavenly: that he might make heavenly those who were earthly. That is, he who was immortal became mortal by assuming the form of a servant, not by changing the nature of the Lord; by imparting the Lord’s grace, not by suffering a servant’s injury. “As is the earthly one, so also are the earthly”: that is, all destined to die. “And as is the heavenly one, so also are the heavenly”: that is, all destined to rise. For the heavenly one has already risen.

And since the earthly are like the earthly one and the heavenly like the heavenly one, therefore, “just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us bear also the image of the heavenly”: that is, just as we have imitated the earthly one, let us imitate the heavenly. We put on the image of the earthly human being through the propagation of transgression and death, which generation brought upon us [Col. 0991B]; but we put on the image of the heavenly human being through the grace of forgiveness and everlasting life, which regeneration grants us through Christ. One generates into death, the other into salvation.

Through Christ, I say, we are renewed. He is called the heavenly human being because he came from heaven to earth in order to be clothed with a body of earthly mortality, which he would clothe with heavenly immortality. Others, however, are called heavenly because by grace they become his members, so that with them Christ is one, as head and body.

Let us therefore bear the image of this heavenly human being now in heart, conduct, and worthy action; afterward, in the resurrection of the dead, also in body. I do not exhort this without reason, but say it for this purpose, brothers—namely, that we may bear the image of the heavenly one—because flesh and blood, that is, the corruption of vices and mortality, cannot possess the kingdom of God.

“Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God,” because there will be no corruption and mortality of flesh and blood there. For according to these qualities flesh and blood are so named in this place. Flesh according to the substance of which it was said, “A spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have” [Col. 0991D] (Luke 24), will possess the kingdom of God; but flesh understood according to corruption will not possess it.

For this is made clear when he immediately adds, “Nor will corruption possess incorruption.” This repetition explains the preceding words: we are to understand “flesh and blood” as corruption, not the substance of flesh; and “kingdom of God” as the incorruptibility of the heavenly homeland. Thus we should think that “flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God” says nothing other than “corruption cannot possess incorruption”: that is, the corruption of flesh and blood will not exist in the incorruptibility of that kingdom, because of the transformation into incorruption.

Therefore he does not contradict the resurrection of the flesh when he says, “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God,” because by “flesh and blood” he signifies the belly and lust—that is, works of the flesh—which will not be there at all [Col. 0992A]. He did not wish them to build upon this statement the belief that they would do in the kingdom of heaven the things done in this life amid the corruptions of eating and drinking, taking wives, and begetting children.

But he did not say that flesh itself would be abolished. For when the resurrection of the body has occurred, freed from all sufferings, we shall enjoy eternal life with ineffable brightness and stability, without corruption. Therefore, in the glory of that heavenly kingdom flesh will exist according to nature, but not according to the desires of passion; for, with death’s sting conquered, it will reign in eternal incorruption. Accordingly, whoever desires to attain this glory of incorruption should now hasten to put off works of corruption and bear the image of the heavenly human being by holy living [Col. 0992B].

> “Behold, I tell you a mystery: indeed, we shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For this corruptible thing must put on incorruption, and this mortal thing put on immortality.”

I said that flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God, though I preach the resurrection of the flesh. And behold, I tell you therein a mystery—that is, a certain secret hidden from many—in which you may understand how flesh will not be flesh, and yet flesh will be flesh that shall possess the kingdom of God. For *mystērion* (μυστήριον) is called thus in Greek because it has a secret and hidden meaning. What I say is a mystery—that is, obscure and concealed—because unbelievers do not know it. This, then, is the mystery I declare: that all of us, both good and evil, shall indeed rise again, or—as is read in the Greek manuscripts—shall sleep, that is, die; but not all shall be changed unto glory, because only the good shall be changed. And therefore the nature of our flesh will then become fit to possess the kingdom of God, because from the time of that angelic change it will no longer be flesh and blood, but only a luminous and spiritual body.

We shall all sleep in the sleep of death and rise again. For one is properly said to rise again who first fell asleep. But how shall all sleep or rise again, if so many whom Christ will find in the body shall neither sleep nor rise again? Therefore, if we believe that the saints who are found alive at Christ’s coming and caught up to meet him will, in that same catching-up, depart from their mortal bodies and immediately return to them immortal, we shall suffer no difficulty in these words, where it is now said, “We shall all rise again,” or “We shall all sleep,” or where it was said, “What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies”; for neither will they be made alive unto immortality unless they first die, however briefly. Thus they will not be excluded from the resurrection, because they will precede it by sleep, though most brief, yet not nonexistent.

Therefore all of us who have human nature shall rise again; yet not all shall be changed, because resurrection is indeed common to all, but transformation unto glory and incapacity for suffering belongs properly to the righteous. We shall all rise, and this will happen “in a moment,” or “in an atom,” that is, at a point of time incapable of division; “in the twinkling of an eye,” that is, with the utmost swiftness; “at the last trumpet,” that is, at the final sign given for these things to be accomplished.

This is said to display God’s omnipotence against those to whom it seemed impossible that the bodies of the dead should be restored from ancient ashes and live again. For the resurrection will occur with such speed that the living, whom the time of the end finds in their bodies, will not be able to outstrip those rising dead from the dust; nor will some rise first and others last, but all together in a moment, so that the resurrection may be more wonderful. And because even a moment contains some delay, however slight, it is added, “in the twinkling of an eye,” because it passes with such speed that it almost escapes the perception of one looking.

For the twinkling of the eye is not that by which, moving the eyelid, we close or open the eye, but the emission of rays in order to see something. It is called a “stroke” because sight strikes swiftly. For as soon as you open your eye, your ray is emitted—not merely to a nearby wall, but to a mountain far away; and not merely to a mountain, which seems near because it is upon the earth, but to the sun, the moon, and the stars, which are separated from the earth by so great an interval. For if, with your eyes closed, you set your face toward the sun, then as soon as you open them, would you not think that you found your gaze there rather than brought it there—so that the eyes themselves do not seem to have been opened before arriving at that upon which they were fixed? Therefore, just as the ray of your eyes reaches nearer things no more swiftly and farther things no more slowly, but joins both distances with equal speed, so the resurrection of the dead occurs in the twinkling of an eye. To the omnipotence and ineffable command of God it is as easy to raise bodies recently dead as bodies that have decayed over a long period.

By the name “trumpet,” moreover, the Apostle intends some most manifest and illustrious sign. Elsewhere he calls it “the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God” (1 Thess. 4), and in the Gospel it is called the voice of the Son of God [Col. 0993D] (John 5), which all who are in the tombs shall hear and shall come forth. Thus the trumpet-blast or voice signifies either greatness, as it is written: “Lift up your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58), or the open manifestation of the resurrection of all, according to the saying: “When you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you” (Matt. 6), that is, perform mercy secretly and in private, lest you seem to glory in another’s misery.

But it must be asked why the dead are said to rise at the last trumpet. For it would not be called the last unless previous ones were envisaged. In the Apocalypse of John (Rev. 8, 9, 10, 11), seven angels with trumpets are described; and what was accomplished at the sounding of the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth is indicated. But when the last—that is, the seventh—angel sounds the trumpet, the dead are raised. Very many teachers have understood these angels to be preachers in the seven stages of the Church, and the last angel to be those preachers found in the flesh when the Lord comes. For this reason the dead are raised at their voice, which is understood as the last trumpet, because after it the voice of preachers will no longer be heard.

Truly, the resurrection shall take place at the last trumpet. “For the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed.” The dead shall rise, that is, all the departed. Or, by the name of the dead sinners are understood, and “we,” who belong to glory, shall be changed. When he says “we,” he indicates that he and those with him are distinct from the dead. The dead shall rise [Col. 0994B] incorruptible, and Paul and his companions shall be changed. For the reprobate will not be changed into that incorruptibility which cannot undergo even the corruption of pain. That belongs to the faithful and the saints. But these “shall be tormented in perpetual corruption, because their fire shall not be quenched and their worm shall not die” (Isa. 66; Mark 9).

What, then, does this distinction mean—“The dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed”—unless it means that all shall rise incorruptible, but among them the righteous shall also be changed into that incorruptibility which no corruption whatsoever can harm? Consequently, those who are not changed into it shall indeed rise incorruptible in the integrity of their limbs, yet liable to be corrupted by the pain of punishments. They will have an incorruptibility of flesh in which they may suffer, not one in which they may die; otherwise even those pains would end. For this purpose they shall rise incorruptible: that they may be able to endure eternal punishments. Incorruptibility, therefore, is common to all because in it sinners shall be more wretched, so as to be perpetual for torments and punished in an immortal and incorruptible body.

But after speaking of the transformation of the righteous, saying, “and we shall be changed,” as though we asked how this happens or what that transformation will be, he adds: “For this corruptible must put on,” and so forth. Here he plainly teaches that the very body which was buried rises again, but changes its glory, not its nature. For when he says “this,” he seems, as it were, to point out the body held between two fingers: this body in which we are born; this in which we die; this which those to be punished fear to receive. “We,” he says, “shall be changed,” because it is necessary—that is, it must happen—both because we have served well and because God has promised. This corruptible body must put on incorruption as an adornment, so that it may no longer hunger or suffer injury in any respect; and this mortal body must put on immortality, so that it may no longer be dissolved.

Or, with reference to what he had said, “The dead shall rise incorruptible,” he added, “This corruptible must put on incorruption”; but with reference to what he had added, “and we shall be changed,” he appended, “And this mortal must put on immortality.” For immortality is one thing and incorruption another, just as mortality is one thing and corruptibility another. Everything mortal is corruptible; but not everything corruptible is immediately mortal. Bodies lacking a soul are corruptible, yet not mortal, because they never had the life that properly belongs to living creatures. Hence the Apostle now deliberately sets incorruption against corruption, and immortality against mortality. Therefore all, righteous and unrighteous, shall be incorruptible; but the righteous shall also become immortal, so that they may in no way experience the death of Gehenna’s punishments.

> “But when this mortal has put on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying which is written: ‘Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death?’ (Hos. 13). Now the sting of death is sin, and the strength of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who gave us the victory [Col. 0995B] through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Heb. 2).

Where we, following Jerome, read in Hosea, “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O hell,” the Septuagint translated: “Where is your cause, O death? Where is your sting, O hell?” In place of this, the Apostle now has: “Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death?” This mortal body of ours, as we have said, shall put on immortality. But when that has occurred, then the saying of Scripture shall come to pass—that is, be fulfilled—which could never otherwise be fulfilled: “Death has been swallowed up,” that is, it appears nowhere, as water when it has been swallowed up. When this mortal has put on immortality, then the death [Col. 0995C] of the body shall be swallowed up—that is, reduced to nothing—in the victory of those rising again. Then it will be mocked and told: “Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death?”

This will be said to the death of the body. For victorious immortality shall swallow it up when this mortal puts on immortality. To the death of the body, I say, this will be said: Where is your victory, by which you conquered all so that even the Son of God had to contend with you and overcame you, not by avoiding you but by undergoing you? You conquered among those dying; you have been conquered among those rising. Your victory, by which you swallowed up the bodies of the dying, was temporary; our victory, by which you have been swallowed up in the bodies of the risen, shall stand eternally. Where is your sting—that is, the sin by which we were pierced and poisoned, so that you might come even into our bodies [Col. 0995D] and possess them for so long a time?

It shall be said to death: “Where is your sting?” But the sting, or goad, of death is sin. The sting of death is called that by which death came about, not that which death made. For we die because of sin; we do not sin because of death. The sting of death is original sin, through whose wound death entered. The sin that pierced and killed us is the sting of death; but the power and strength of sin is the law of Moses. For all of us sinned in one man, so that all of us might die in one man. We received the law not so that sin might be ended through correction, but so that it might be increased through transgression. For the law is the strength of sin because prohibition increases the desire for an unlawful deed when righteousness is not loved in such a way that the desire to sin is overcome by delight in righteousness; and deeds forbidden by the law are committed much more wickedly and shamefully than if no law prohibited them.

I say that the sting of death is sin and the strength of sin is the law. But we give thanks to God, who gave us victory over death and its sting: victory over death through the immortal resurrection, and over its sting, sin, through gratuitous justification. Indeed, the victory by which sin is conquered is nothing other than God’s gift, helping us in this contest. He gave victory, not through the law nor through our own powers, but through Jesus Christ our Lord, through whom, as mediator, all the good things we have are given to us by the Father.

But if, according to other manuscripts, we read, “Death has been swallowed up in contention. Where is your contention, O death? Where is your sting, O death?” we shall understand death as the carnal habit that resists good will by the pleasure of enjoying temporal things. For while we are in this life, this death contends against us and we against it, because “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5). But when we rise, death shall be swallowed up in contention—that is, annulled in the conflict which it had against us—because the flesh shall wholly agree with the spirit, and there shall be no pleasure of sin resisting good will. Since the war shall then be finished and peace shall hold the victory, we shall mock death itself—that is, the desire and habit of temporal pleasures—saying: “Where is your contention, O death?” You have been defeated and can contend no longer.

It should also be noted that the Septuagint translated: “I shall redeem them from death. Where is your cause, O death? Where is your sting, O hell? For the cause of death and the sting of hell is sin.” But in the resurrection of those whom Christ redeemed, it will not be found; therefore they shall mock death and hell. Yet above all the Savior, when he had poured out his own blood for the redemption of humankind and had destroyed the sin of the world, for which we were dying and being led to hell, mocked death and hell, saying: “Where is your cause, O death? Where is your sting, O hell?” And according to the new translation he said: “I shall redeem them from death. I shall be your death, O death! I shall be your bite”—that is, biting you—“O hell.”

For what we kill, we cause to cease entirely; but by what we bite, we take away one part and leave another. Therefore, because the Lord utterly kills death in his elect, he became death to death. But because he took one part from hell and left another, he did not utterly kill hell, but bit it. For he did not draw from hell all unbelievers and those handed over to eternal punishments for their crimes, but only those whom he recognized by faith and deeds. It follows:

> “Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labor is not in vain in the Lord.”

[Col. 0997A] Since I have made you certain concerning the future resurrection and have carefully instructed you in the remaining matters, therefore, O my beloved brothers—that is, those whom I greatly love—be steadfast in faith in the resurrection or in your good resolve, and immovable, so that no one may henceforth move you from the state of hope for the future. I mean you who always abound in the work of the Lord’s commandments, knowing certainly that your labor is not in vain—that is, not empty—in the Lord, that is, in the Lord’s service, because even in the very flesh that now labors you shall rejoice.

Having thus far explained everything necessary for establishing ecclesiastical teaching, and having shown what should be avoided and what followed, he now exhorts them to be firm in goodness and always ready [Col. 0997B] and abundant in works that bear fruit before God. For through the matters he has explained, they are certain that henceforth they shall receive from the Lord the reward of good work, lest they be perverted by wicked conversations.

## CHAPTER XVI

> “Now concerning the collections which are made for the saints: as I directed the churches of Galatia, so you also must do. On the first day of the week, let each of you put something aside at home, storing up whatever is pleasing to him, so that collections may not be made when I come.” But “when I am present, I shall send those whom you approve by letters to carry your gift to Jerusalem. And if it is fitting that I also go, they shall go with me.”

Thus far, he says, I have instructed you concerning other matters. But now I instruct you [Col. 0997C] concerning the collections made for the saints—that is, concerning the resources gathered through the individual churches to be sent to the saints at Jerusalem, who are in great need among the unbelieving Jews, as though they had deserted their ancestral laws and believed in a crucified man. I instruct you that, just as I arranged for the churches of Galatia, each of you should put aside at home, on the first day of the week—that is, Sunday—what he is to send them. Let him put it aside at home, lest he suspect fraud if he stores it with another. Let him, I say, store it away, lest he take it back again; and let him store whatever is pleasing to him—that is, whatever he wishes to offer with a devout heart, not what burdens his mind.

I give this prior instruction so that collections may not then be made when I come, because it would be burdensome if everything were suddenly done all at once, and I am devoted to more important tasks. Gather on the Lord’s Day, so that the holy poor may have relief, and that on the day on which Christ rose, you may rise to works of mercy. Gather, I say, because what is collected little by little from many people is neither burdensome nor insignificant. Meanwhile, let each of you collect and place in store among yourselves, as in a treasury, whatever he wishes.

But when I am present, I shall send to Jerusalem those whom you approve—that is, judge upright—to carry your gift, that is, your free offering; and I shall send them with letters, because letters give testimony to those sent, so that they may be received graciously. I place both matters in your judgment: both that you give what pleases you and that you choose those whom I shall send to carry it. But if it is fitting that I also go—that is, that I ought to travel—if the collection of resources is abundant, then they shall go with me.

> “But I shall come to you when I have passed through Macedonia, for I shall pass through Macedonia. Perhaps I shall remain with you, or even spend the winter, so that you may send me onward wherever I go. For I do not wish to see you now merely in passing. For I hope to remain with you for some time, if the Lord permits. But I shall remain at Ephesus until Pentecost. For a great and manifest door has been opened to me, and there are many adversaries.”

After all his instruction, in order to make them glad, he promises them his coming. By this he also makes all his admonitions, by which he corrects them, firmer; for one who hears that he is coming from whom he received the law becomes more careful lest, when that person arrives, he be ashamed. Prepare the collections before I come, he says. But I shall come to you when I have passed through Macedonia, visiting each church there and strengthening the minds of the brothers. For I shall pass through Macedonia because there is no need to remain long there, since there are few things among them needing correction. But perhaps I shall stay with you, or even winter with you—that is, remain throughout the winter season—because there are many things in you requiring correction.

But among the Ephesians, with whom I remain while writing this letter, I shall stay until Pentecost. Nor is it surprising that I wish to remain there so long, for a great [Col. 0998C] and manifest door has been opened to me there—that is, a door open to my preaching, through which I may enter by preaching into the hearts of hearers and introduce the Christian faith. And many adversaries oppose me, attempting to hinder my work; and therefore I must still contend with them.

For the number fifty is customarily referred to repentance or remission and contains many mysteries. Hence the Apostle now says that he shall remain among the Ephesians, to whom he had unfolded mystical matters, until Pentecost—that is, until the fiftieth day—until they are perfectly converted to God and made worthy by the coming of the Holy Spirit. For he had found there hearts thirsting for God’s grace, into which he might readily pour the mystery [Col. 0998D] of Christ; and he had found many adversaries. For the more fit they were found for faith, the more those arose who were jealous, contradicting and resisting the Lord’s teaching.

For when he says, “A great and manifest door has been opened to me, and there are many adversaries,” what else can be understood except that, after the Gospel had first been preached there by him, many believed, and many opponents of that same faith arose, according to the Lord’s saying: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given” (Matt. 13; Mark 4; Luke 8). Therefore the door is opened in those to whom it has been given; the adversaries are among those to whom it has not been given. A great door has been opened—that is, many hearts have been opened to hearing.

> “But if Timothy comes, see that he may be with you without fear. For he works the work of the Lord, as I also do. Therefore let no one despise him. But send him onward in peace, that he may come to me. For I am expecting him with the brothers.”

[Col. 0999A] Although Timothy preached what he had received from the Apostle, yet because he did not possess the same authority, the Apostle commends him, lest perhaps he should not be received as worthily as he deserved by those dissenting among the people, and lest their noisy opposition produce fear in him and his coming accomplish nothing for their salvation. For the Gentiles too might be stirred to sedition by the people’s discord, taking an opportunity to rush upon Timothy. Therefore, he says, let no one despise him, because he works the work of God as I do, so that he may be received with the same authority as the Apostle; for he too was a bishop.

He declares Timothy to be of such great merit that he commands not only that he be honored among them, but also that, when he prepared to depart, he be escorted with due service as an apostle of the Lord. For he shows him to be so necessary that he himself awaits him with the brothers for the sake of Christ’s Gospel.

> “Now concerning brother Apollos, I make known to you that I strongly urged him to come to you with the brothers; and certainly it was not his will to come now, but he will come when he has leisure.”

This Apollos was a Jew, Alexandrian by birth, learned in the law and most eloquent, and bishop of the Corinthians [Col. 0999C] (Acts 18); but because of their dissensions he had withdrawn from Corinth. The Apostle says that he refused to return, thereby indicating their fault, so that, hearing this, they might reject the false apostles and pursue peace, and thus deserve to have their own bishop return to them. Therefore he had said concerning Timothy, “See that he may be with you without fear,” because certain emissaries had not been well received; and consequently Apollos would not come unless they became harmonious.

“It was not his will,” he says, “or God’s will, that he should come now while you are such as you are; but he shall come when he has leisure”—that is, when he finds you so free from pseudo-apostles and dissensions that you wish to devote yourselves to hearing his preaching, or when he himself has been freed from the things he is now doing.

> “Keep watch; stand firm in the faith; act manfully [otherwise, *viritim*, ‘individually’] and be strengthened. Let all that you do be done in charity.”

[Col. 0999D] So that Apollos may gladly come to you, keep watch—that is, open the eyes of your mind to guard against the devil’s cunning, lest you be deceived either by unclean spirits or by false preachers. Stand firm in the faith—that is, do not yield either to pseudo-teachers or to Gentiles who strive to assail your faith and drive you from its citadel. Act manfully: do not become weak, do not lose vigor, do not become effeminate; rather, do good manfully and endure evil, and be strengthened—that is, continually become more robust, so that there may be progress in your strength.

And let everything you do be done not in dissension, anger, or desire for worldly [Col. 1000A] glory, but in charity. For whatever is done without charity is nothing, however very good it may seem. When he says “everything,” he sufficiently shows that even reproofs, which those reproved experience as harsh and bitter, must be administered with charity.

> “Now I beseech you, brothers: you know the household of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, that they are the firstfruits of Achaia and have devoted themselves to the service of the saints, that you also may be subject to such persons and to everyone who works and labors with them. I rejoice at the presence of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, because they have supplied what was lacking from you. For they have refreshed both my spirit and yours. Therefore acknowledge those who are such.”

I have urged you to let all your works be done in charity. But now I beseech you to be subject to those who are such as the household of Stephanas and Fortunatus. For you know the household of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, because they are the firstfruits of Achaia—that is, they were the first among those in Achaia to believe; for the Corinthians too are Achaeans. And they devoted themselves to the service of the saints, that is, by trampling down avarice, to supply the saints from their labors with necessities, especially the preachers. I beseech you to be subject to workers of this kind and to everyone working and laboring with such persons. Be subject to such people.

But I rejoice at the presence of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus [Col. 1000C], either because they are present among you and you may gain great benefit through them, or because they came to me to minister on your behalf. For they supplied what was lacking from you—that is, they supplied for me what you had not done. For they refreshed my spirit by supplying me with necessities, and yours by preserving the Apostle for you. They refreshed my spirit for my joy; they refreshed yours through the charity shown on your behalf. Therefore acknowledge—that is, love and honor—those who are such.

> “All the churches of Asia greet you. Aquila and Prisca, with the church in their house, among whom I also lodge, greet you warmly in the Lord. All the brothers greet you. Greet one another with a holy kiss. This greeting is in the hand of Paul.”

[Col. 1000D] “All the churches of Asia greet you,” he says. As though he said: What I write, all desire. By this he also exhorts them to strive to become like those from whom they receive greeting. Aquila and Prisca are husband and wife, who are read of in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 8 [materially uncertain reference as printed]). Their household church is the fellowship of brothers dwelling with them. For they were hospitable. The holy kiss is a sign of peace. He exhorts them to give chaste and peaceful kisses in the churches, without pretense, so that they may cling to one another after discord has been removed.

Then he shows that he has signed this letter, saying, “This greeting is in the hand of Paul,” so that they may know without doubt that it is his letter. It follows:

> “If anyone does not love our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema, maranatha.”

[Col. 1001A] I greet those who love Christ, he says. But if anyone does not love our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema—that is, estranged from God. For *anathema* is interpreted as estrangement or one estranged. According to Augustine, *anathema* means “condemned”; *maranatha* means “until the Lord returns.” Therefore the Apostle excommunicates one who does not love Christ until the Day of Judgment, when he himself will render to each person what it is just to render (Matt. 16; Rom. 2), so that then, if it pleases Christ, one who had been anathematized may receive communion.
