Jerome, however, says this: *Maranatha* is more Syriac than Hebrew, although from the borderland of both languages it has something of a Hebrew sound; and it is interpreted, “Our Lord comes.” Thus the sense is: “If anyone does not love our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema.” And, once that has been stated, let “Our Lord comes” be added thereafter. For it is superfluous to wish to contend with persistent hatred against one whom it is certain has already come. “If anyone does not love,” and so forth, is as though it were said: If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus, let his coming, already [Col. 1002A] accomplished, be of no benefit to him; and so let his second coming, still future, be for his condemnation.

> “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. My charity be with all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen.”

May Christ’s grace always be with you, without whose aid you cannot stand nor do anything good (John 15). Because of those who, pursuing dissension, did not love Christ, it was said: “If anyone does not love our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema.” For those who said, “I am Paul’s,” “I am Apollos’s,” or “I am Cephas’s,” did not love Christ, because they gave glory not to Christ but to human beings. Therefore, because all hope must be placed not in human beings but in Christ: “The grace,” he says, “of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.” And he adds: “My charity [Col. 1002B] be with all of you in Christ,” that is, love one another in Christ with that charity with which I love you. Love one another in Christ Jesus after my example, not in worldly love. Then he adds, “Amen,” which means that these words are confirmed as true and faithful. For *Amen* is the confirmation of all that precedes.

## ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 1001]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 1001C]

Knowing that the letter he had sent to the Corinthians had been effective, the Apostle writes to them again, exhorting their obedience and touching upon the obstinacy of certain persons who had refused amendment. Yet, encouraged by the report that the matters pertaining to ecclesiastical order had been corrected, he was henceforth certain that their vices too would gradually be corrected, especially because a large part of them had begun to be obedient. For those who had corrected what concerned faith and ecclesiastical order gave certain hope concerning themselves that they would also amend their morals and conduct.

For this reason the Apostle wrote to them promptly, so that, having been saddened by the rebuke of the former letter, they might receive consolation in this one [Col. 1001D], and the fruit of repentance might increase in them; so that, seeing that they had now become pleasing to him to whom they had been displeasing, they might become more ready for good deeds. This is the principal reason for this letter.

Some of them, however, as has been said, were unwilling to be corrected. Entangled by the pleasure of sins and corrupted by false apostles, they set aside the Apostle of truth and obeyed those false apostles. Therefore the excellent teacher, in order to call them back from following those pseudo-preachers, shows in many ways the error and deceit of their fraud, so that they may place no further confidence in them or give faith to their deceitful preaching, since they see that they are tending toward the destruction of souls. For this reason he also commends himself in many ways [Col. 1002C], so that, recognizing the authority and dignity he possesses, they may gladly receive his teaching and thus attain the salvation of their souls.

He also commands that the corrected fornicator be received back. He likewise notes that they are sparing in almsgiving. But because, in the preceding letter, he had especially rebuked their teachers for certain persons’ sins, and they had been greatly saddened, he now consoles them, setting before them his own example and teaching that they ought not impatiently to bear rebuke administered for the salvation of others, since he himself was daily exposed to dangers and death for another’s salvation. He also consoles them concerning the tribulations they suffered by the example of his own tribulations, which were much more severe. Always, whether principally or secondarily, he seems to aim at recalling from the pseudo-apostles that portion of the people still following them.

## CHAPTER ONE

> “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and Timothy the brother, to the Church of God which is at Corinth, with all the saints who are in all Achaia: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

It is as though he says: You Corinthians ought to obey me and reject the false apostles because I am Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ—that is, the distinguished envoy of the Savior-King. That King, who alone saves eternally, sent me to lead you to himself, that he might reign in you and save you. Therefore you ought gladly to obey me. I am Christ’s apostle, not by usurpation but through the will of God the Father—that is, I was appointed an apostle by Christ through the will of the Father, as Christ himself says: “For I always do the things that please him” (John 8). It is evident that God’s will is just and reasonable. Accordingly, I am reasonably and justly called an apostle, since the Son sent me to you through the will of the Father. But the pseudo-apostles were neither sent by Christ nor came through God’s will, nor do they seek the salvation of their hearers. Therefore they must be rejected.

Paul addresses you, and Timothy the brother, who carried that first letter to you and reported your correction to you. It should be noted that he does not say, “Paul and Timothy,” but “Paul and Timothy the brother,” because they are not both apostles. To the Philippians, however, where such great authority was not necessary, both are described as servants, because both are servants, not both apostles. Paul and Timothy write to the Church of God that is at Corinth, together with all the saints throughout Achaia. For Corinth is the metropolis of Achaia; therefore what is written to the Corinthians is written to all the faithful of the province of Achaia.

May grace, through which your sins are forgiven, and peace, through which you are reconciled to God, be with you to whom we write. May grace and peace be with you from God our Father, who adopted you as sons, and from the Lord Jesus Christ, who graciously made you subject to his lordship. He names only the Father and the Son because at that time no one erred concerning the Holy Spirit; rather, whoever erred in faith in the Trinity erred either concerning the Father or concerning the Son. For the Holy Spirit, concerning whom he is now silent, was sufficiently manifested through his works: that is, through diverse languages, prophecies, the word of wisdom or of knowledge, and so forth.

> “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who comforts us in all our tribulation, so that we ourselves may be able to comfort those who are in every affliction through the encouragement by which we ourselves are encouraged by God. For just as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so also through Christ our consolation abounds. But whether we are afflicted, it is for your encouragement and salvation; whether we are comforted, it is for your consolation; whether we are encouraged, [Col. 1003D] it is for your encouragement and salvation, which produces endurance of the same sufferings that we also endure, so that our hope may be firm concerning you, knowing that, just as you are companions in sufferings, so you will also be companions in consolation.”

He first speaks to those who are perfect concerning tribulation, setting himself before them as an example of patience and of consolation received from God. In this very matter he shows himself worthy of commendation, whereas the false apostles and their followers regarded him as worthless and contemptible, because he was treated so shamefully by all those among whom he preached, and was so hated by all that he was continually subjected to insults and tribulations. His detractors said these things about him, wishing to diminish his glory; but [Col. 1004A] he himself glories in all these things and blesses God on their account, because he suffers them for Christ and is never abandoned without consolation in them.

“Blessed,” he says, “be God, who created Christ according to his humanity and begot him according to his divinity, and thus is his God and Father.” Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ for his so many and such great benefits toward us. He is, I say, the Father of mercies, because his mercies flow toward us from his very inmost being: by them he both forgives the multitude of our sins and tests us, like gold, in the fire of tribulations; and he is the God of all—that is, of complete—consolation, because he gives perfect consolation to those who suffer adversity for his name, or who are afflicted in the mourning of repentance.

This is also said on account of the Corinthians, who had been made sorrowful by correction. For it gives them much refreshment to hear that God is the Father of mercies, because they understand that they were corrected in order to turn to a merciful Father, who would blot out their many sins through many mercies and give them the grace of virtues. For why is he called the Father of mercies, unless because through the inward tenderness of paternal mercies he receives the children of repentance and restores them to their former grace, so that there may be not forgiveness alone but also restoration to their previous state? And he is the God of all consolation, who gives perfect consolation to those made sorrowful in repentance, granting them hope not only of escaping punishments but also of attaining rewards.

He comforts us, the preachers of Christ, in every tribulation of ours, both [Col. 1004C] of body and of soul. He comforts us not in some tribulation, but in every tribulation, lest we fail. He comforts us either by appearing to us himself, or by warning us through an angel, or through the Scriptures, or through other saints, or through hidden inspiration, or by the alleviation of tribulation, or by delivering us from tribulation.

Thus he comforts us so that we ourselves may also comfort those who are under every oppressive tribulation for the name of Christ, or who are under every pressure of sins—that is, those whom the burden of crimes weighs down. For we offer them consolation when we give repentant persons hope of pardon. God comforts us so that we may comfort others; and thus he leaves none of his own desolate, and [Col. 1004D] much more abundantly rewards in the future those whom he does not abandon even in the present.

We are able to comfort those who are in the pressure of adversities by exhorting them to repentance and endurance, through the encouragement by which we ourselves are inwardly encouraged by God to steadfastness in sufferings. Truly we receive consolation and encouragement from God so that we too may minister consolations to others. For just as the sufferings of Christ, which he himself first endured and left for us to endure, abound in us who are his members, so also—that is, no less—does our consolation abound, which God inwardly supplies to us through Christ. For just as Christ is the cause of sufferings, so he himself is also the cause of consolations. Therefore we must be judged not more worthless but more glorious because we share in [Col. 1005A] Christ’s sufferings—those whom God so continually comforts amid every adversity that we are able also to comfort others.

Indeed, we endure sufferings from wicked people and receive consolations or encouragements from God; but all these things happen for your sake. For whether we are afflicted—that is, tested by the fire of tribulation—this is for your encouragement and your salvation, because by our example God exhorts you to endure tribulations through which you will come to eternal salvation. Or whether we are inwardly comforted by God, this is for your consolation—that is, so that you may especially be comforted by it. Or whether we are encouraged by God, after evils have ended or strength has been given us to bear more grievous things, this again is for your encouragement and salvation, because God likewise encourages you to remain in the faith and to suffer for it greater things than you have suffered.

This encouragement, namely, produces—that is, intends to produce in you—endurance of the same sufferings that we also endure. Or, it “produces endurance,” that is, it works toward your maintaining endurance of the same sufferings. Or we may read, in one part, “intolerance,” that is, severe endurance. For just as *impotens* [“powerless”] is sometimes called “very powerful,” so here *intolerantia* [“intolerance”] may mean great endurance. Therefore the encouragement which you receive from God through us produces in you “intolerance,” that is, strong endurance of the same sufferings that we also endure; and this happens so that our hope concerning you—that is, by which we hope for your salvation—may be firm and secure.

We endure adversities and have good hope concerning you, knowing [Col. 1005C] certainly that, just as you are companions with us in sufferings, so in the age to come you will be companions also in the eternal consolation which we are to receive. By these words the Apostle greatly encourages them to endure adversities for Christ. He also added:

> “For we do not wish you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning our tribulation which occurred in Asia: that we were burdened beyond measure, beyond our strength, so that we were even weary of living. But we ourselves had within ourselves the answer of death, so that we might not trust in ourselves but in God, who raises the dead; who delivered us and delivers us from such great dangers, in whom we hope that he will yet also deliver us, while you too help by prayer for us, so that, from the faces of many persons, thanks may be given by many on our behalf for the gift [Col. 1005D] which is in us.”

He describes the greater adversities which he suffered for Christ and for the salvation of others, so that, since he himself suffered such great things, his disciples and others, who are lesser, may not refuse to suffer whatever tribulations may come; and so that disciples may be ashamed, by comparison with their master, to grieve over their own injury when they recognize that their master endured much greater things.

“I said,” he declares, “that we suffer tribulations so that you too may imitate us. And we truly do suffer. For we do not wish you, brothers, to be ignorant—that is, we do not wish you to be ignorant—of our tribulation, lest perhaps you grieve over your own. For it benefits you to know it, because then you will recognize that you suffer small things. The false apostles recount their glories, but we recount [Col. 1006A] our sufferings. We do not wish you to be ignorant of our tribulation which happened to us in Lesser Asia, which is part of Greater Asia, because beyond measure—that is, beyond the extent of all preceding tribulations—we were weighed down by the burden of that tribulation beyond human strength.”

For no human strength could sustain so great a weight of affliction while remaining alive, unless divine grace had supplied strength to human frailty. And so we were overwhelmed by the magnitude of tribulations, so that we were weary not only of enduring, but even of living. Nor were we merely weary of living: we ourselves also had the answer of death. That is, when some people asked others concerning our life, no answer was given them concerning life, but only concerning death, because no one promised us life.

We had, I say, the answer [Col. 1006B] of death not only in others, but also within ourselves: when we consulted our own reasoning, it promised us no remedy except death. We had within ourselves the answer—that is, the certainty—of death, because our inmost thoughts answered us that death was at hand. Or, we had the answer of death, that is, death itself answered us and taught us that every human help had failed and that remedy must be hoped for from him alone for whom it is possible even to raise the dead, so that we might not trust in ourselves but in God, who raises the dead and who delivered us from such great dangers.

Such an extraordinary violence of wickedness rose up against the preachers of the faith that they had death before their eyes. Finally, having been delivered from such pressure, they say that they were raised to life. For they had been so afflicted that they despaired of their present life. But because God does not deny his protections to those placed in necessity, especially to his own, he brought out those who despaired of themselves but trusted in God. For they confessed that they were failing under excessive pressure unless God was present; and this is what is meant by, “that we might not trust in ourselves but in God, who raises the dead,” and who, as though raising us from death, raised us from the pressure of tribulation.

He delivered us from such great dangers and daily delivers us from adversities. In him we hope that he will also still deliver us, while you too assist our deliverance by prayer made for us. That is, not only will the other faithful help us before God so that we may be delivered from evils, but you too, praying for us, will do so. Therefore he will deliver us while you and others pray, so that, from the persons of many faces—those converted to God through [Col. 1006D] our preaching—thanks may be given by many faithful to God on our behalf: thanks, I say, for the gift bestowed upon us, that is, for deliverance from the dangers in which we are.

Because the grace of God delivers us for the sake of many, for whom we also suffer, many should therefore give thanks to God for us when we are delivered, or pray when we suffer. “Persons of many faces” are people of many ages and various conditions: children, adolescents, young people, old people, and veterans, of both sexes. And these persons belong to the gift bestowed upon us—that is, through our teaching they have been made participants in the faith that God granted to us. Therefore, from these persons converted to God through us and made participants in his gift—that is, in the faith which is in us—[Col. 1007A] thanks should be given to God by many believers for us who have been delivered from adversity.

Or the saints are called “persons,” because they are honorable and acceptable before God. And they are “of many faces,” because each one of them has, in his inner person, his own face by which he is known by God—that is, an intention to do good. For one intends to instruct others by preaching; another, to give alms; another, to pray frequently; another, to minister bodily assistance to those who pray. Thus each has his own face—that is, his own good intention—and these persons of many faces belong to his gift, that is, to his grace divinely bestowed on us, which is in us. Therefore, through many, thanks should be given to God from these persons on our behalf, [Col. 1007B] since we made them participants in our gift.

> “For this is our glory: the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity of heart and sincerity of God, and not in carnal wisdom but in the grace of God, we have conducted ourselves in this world, and more abundantly toward you. For we write no other things to you than those which you have read and recognized. And I hope that you will recognize us to the end, just as you have recognized us in part: that you are our glory, just as we also are yours in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Therefore, he says, we do not distrust God’s help but hope that he will deliver us, because our conscience is pure and we glory in it before his eyes. For this is our glory: namely, the good testimony which our conscience bears to us, testifying [Col. 1007C] that we did whatever we did with a good and simple mind. Just as conscience is a great punishment to the impious, so conscience is a great joy to the devout. For even if the devil or a perverse person tries to bring false accusations against them, they nevertheless inwardly glory before God in the testimony of a good conscience.

Therefore the Apostle now calls the testimony of his conscience his glory, because, not seeking the favor of another’s mouth, he does not know how to place the joys of his life outside himself. It is as though he were saying: “I glory in tribulations because my conscience does not reproach me for having preached for the sake of profit or temporal glory, but bears witness for me that I sought your salvation with devout zeal.”

For this is our glory, the testimony of our conscience: namely, that we have conducted ourselves in this world in simplicity of heart and sincerity [Col. 1007D] of God. This is the glory of our conscience: simplicity and sincerity. Simplicity, because we did nothing by duplicity, having one thing in our heart and another on our lips, but everything with straightforward purity. Sincerity [Note: This etymology is not accepted by scholars.], because, without decay—that is, without corruption—we possessed a sound conscience. And this sincerity and simplicity were “of God,” because in all that we did we sincerely and simply sought to please God, and in this we were simple and sincere.

But the false apostles do not walk simply but doubly, because by hypocrisy they do whatever good they seem to do; and they mingle carnal observances of the law with the grace of the Gospel. [Col. 1008A] Nor do they do anything sincerely—that is, with a conscience free from the decay of being bored through and corrupted. But we have conducted ourselves in simplicity of heart and sincerity of God, and not in carnal wisdom, which is to love pleasures, avoid labors, seek bodily advantages, and please people; or to preach according to the natures of things and not contrary to them. Rather, we have conducted ourselves in the grace of God—that is, in the grace of evangelical preaching and holiness—in this world, where so many evils occur; but we did this more abundantly toward you, because we never received anything from you, although we could have taken support from our own goods.

The false apostles, however, preached according to the wisdom of the world, lest they offend people, and they preached for gain. Therefore the Apostle never wished to receive expenses from the Corinthians, lest he provide them an occasion to receive such things. This is why he says that he conducted himself more abundantly among them—that is, with them—in the grace of God: although he sometimes received from others, he never wished to take anything from them, lest he diminish his authority to rebuke them.

Truly, among you we conducted ourselves in grace more abundantly than among others—that is, we ministered everything to you freely—because now we write to you no things other than those which you read in the earlier letter and recognized in experience of our works. That is, neither do we now demand anything from you through this letter, nor did we demand anything through the preceding letter, nor, when we were present, did we receive anything from you, as you acknowledge. And you do not merely acknowledge this now; [Col. 1008C] I also hope that you will recognize the same concerning us to the end of our life: namely, that we remain in the same course and take nothing from you, just as you recognized us in part, not wholly. For you know that we abstained, but you do not know with how great love we did so.

Therefore you will recognize that we persevere in this, because we are your glory just as you are ours: that is, through us you ought to attain eternal glory, and we through you when you have been well instructed. This would not be so if we received from you with offense. And this glory will be ours not in the night of the present age but in the day and manifestation of our Lord Jesus Christ, because he himself will reveal all things and no one will resist his will. Then you too will be glorified because you obeyed us well, and we because we taught you well. [Col. 1008D] Therefore you must persevere in the good things you have begun and always improve.

> “And with this confidence I wished first to come to you, that you might have a second grace, and through you to pass into Macedonia, and again from Macedonia to come to you, and by you to be sent on to Judea. Therefore, when I wished this, did I use fickleness? Or do I plan the things that I plan according to the flesh, so that with me there should be ‘Yes’ and ‘No’?”

After showing himself commendable through his tribulations, on account of which he could be judged worthless and rejected by some, he also clears himself of a matter on account of which he could be considered a liar and fickle by some. For in the earlier letter he had promised that he would come to them as he passed through Macedonia and remain with them for some time; yet he did not come. Accordingly, in the estimation of some who understood things simply, he could seem a liar and unstable, and thus he was already losing among them the firmness of his authority.

Therefore he excuses himself and shows by many arguments that he should not be judged a liar because he did not come to them, since he did not say without qualification that he would do this, but said: “If the Lord permits” (1 Cor. 16). Nor should someone be judged a liar who says what is false while thinking it true, because, so far as he himself is concerned, he does not deceive but is deceived. Conversely, the person who says what is true while thinking it false lies; nor is a person free from lying who unknowingly speaks what is true with his mouth but knowingly lies in his will.

“You are our glory,” he says, “and we are yours. And with this confidence—because I trust that we are each other’s glory, that is, because your life has now been corrected so that it is worthy to glorify us—I wished, before going into Macedonia, to come to you, so that by my arrival you might have a second grace, having long ago received the first when I converted you to the faith: that is, so that you might have confirmation, which comes after faith.

“Therefore it is not without purpose that I wished to come and did not come. For you ought to understand that there are some among you on whose account I did not fulfill my intention; they must first correct themselves, so that they may receive me with joy. I wished to come to you, whom I desired to see corrected, and through you—that is, under your guidance—[Col. 1009C] to pass into Macedonia. For although I could have gone there more directly by another way, I resolved, out of love for you, to pass through you; and again to come to you from Macedonia, so that I might confirm you repeatedly; and to be sent on by you into Judea, so that I might carry alms.

“And because I wished this and did not fulfill it, when I wished this, did I use fickleness, so that I wished it not by established reasoning but by levity of mind, and abandoned it with the same levity? This must by no means be thought. For I do not yield to the fault of fickleness, and therefore I am not moved by the wind of changeableness. Since I acted not from fickleness but from deliberation in not fulfilling what I had intended, I did nothing other than what had to be done, because usefulness must be preferred to will, not [Col. 1009D] will to usefulness.

“Or do I plan what I plan according to the flesh—that is, in the manner of carnal people, who easily change their intention for earthly advantage? Do I think carnally, so that I resolved to come for a carnal advantage and abandoned the plan because that advantage was not present? No. For the person who thinks according to the flesh fails to fulfill what he planned when he either defers to more important persons or is overcome by profit or display. But a spiritual person fails to fulfill what he planned when, more providently, he considers something for the salvation of the soul. Thus I too did not fulfill what I had wished so that by this very fact you might become better, knowing that I postponed it because some among you had not yet purified themselves from sins.

“Do I think according to the flesh so that there should be with [Col. 1010A] me ‘Yes’ and ‘No’—that is, affirmation and denial concerning the same thing through inconstancy of mind, so that there may be duplicity in me and contradiction in my words? By no means.”

> “But God is faithful, because our word which was among you is not in it ‘Yes’ and ‘No,’ but ‘Yes’ is in it. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you through us—through me and Silvanus and Timothy—was not in him ‘Yes’ and ‘No,’ but ‘Yes’ was in him. For however many promises of God there are, in him is ‘Yes.’ Therefore through him we also say: ‘Amen’ to God for our glory.”

There is no contradiction in my word, such that I deny what I affirmed by saying “Yes” and “No.” But God is faithful—that is, true—who speaks through my mouth, because our word which was among you, that is, which we speak [Col. 1010B] to you; or which was among you, that is, which we spoke to you at your conversion while we remained with you, is not unstable and mixed with lies but steadfast and true. For “Yes” and “No” are not in it—that is, ambiguity and variation are not in it—but “Yes” is in it: namely, the certain assertion of pure truth.

For when I said that I would come to you, I postponed it because you had not yet been well corrected so that you could rejoice at my arrival. Therefore the reason I did not come remained not in me but in you. Yet I always had the intention of coming; there was never in me a willing and an unwilling, but willing is always in me. And thus my word does not vary but remains in its affirmation.

“Yes” and “No” are not in my word. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you through us—[Col. 1010C] through me and Silvanus, that is, Silas, and Timothy—whom I, Silvanus, and Timothy preached to you, does not have in his preaching “Yes” and “No,” that is, duplicity, so that something is now affirmed in it and now denied. Nor was “Yes” and “No” ever in him; rather, “Yes” was in him, that is, the certain affirmation of consummate truth.

If we were liars, then he himself would be a liar, because we preach only what he taught. But he did not teach that concerning the same thing one should say, “It is” and “It is not,” because “It is” and “It is not” were not in him, and consequently neither are they in us. “Yes” and “No”—that is, duplicity or falsehood—are not in him; but “Yes” was in him, that is, truth and immutability, as he said to Moses: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3). For he truly is who is always the same and remains immutable.

Or, “Yes was in him,” that is, the assured affirmation of those things which he accomplished temporally in humanity. “Yes” and “No” were not in him, but “Yes” was in him, because he never willed anything other than what is useful. For his will is always joined to usefulness; he was not changed so as unwillingly to do, like a human being, what is useful, nor did he doubt about certain matters and change his will.

Truly this variation is not in him but immutable firmness is, because however many promises of God there are—that is, however many promises God the Father made through the Law and the Prophets—in him they are “Yes,” that is, they have their reality in him, because all have been fulfilled or are fulfilled in him. All God’s promises have been established and displayed in him, because in him has been fulfilled whatever was prophesied [Col. 1011A] for our salvation. Thus it is clear that he was not a liar in his words, whether through himself or through others, through whom the Father was shown to be true.

And because the promises of God have being in him—that is, stand in him and are fulfilled—therefore through him is “Amen,” that is, truth, to God the Father, for our glory, through whom this is made known. It is evident that truth is always in God: this is “Amen,” made manifest through Christ and afterward preached through the apostles, while the powers of signs bear witness that the things God promised through Christ are true. The meaning is: all the truth of the promises is in Christ, and it is announced through us. Hence we too have glory, because we are shown to speak the truth. For the glory of the apostles [Col. 1011B] was to preach a truthful master in whom the promises of God had been fulfilled, and to establish their sayings by miracles.

> “But he who confirms us with you in Christ, and who anointed us, is God; and he who sealed us and gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts. But I call God as witness upon my soul that, sparing you, I did not come again to Corinth. Not that we lord it over your faith, but we are helpers of your joy. For you stand by faith.”

I said that you are our glory; yet I do not ascribe it to ourselves, but God is the one who confirms us. Or thus: through Christ we say “Amen” to God, that is, we praise him as true; but God [Col. 1011C] is the one who confirms us in Christ. And therefore everything is from him. Moreover, we are more truthful for this reason: he himself confirms us in the truth which is Christ.

God is the one who confirms us in Christ, that is, in the true preaching of Christ, so that we may be stable and firm in him and never turn aside to a word of falsehood. He confirms us, and this with you. This seems to be said ironically, as though he were saying: “If you are certain of your confirmation, then be certain also of ours, since we are confirmed in Christ’s truth no less than you.” For the confirmation of teachers is more certain than that of disciples, who are confirmed through teachers.

Or, “he confirms us with you,” that is, he establishes Jews together with Gentiles in the faith of Christ. And he anointed us—that is, he made us Christs [anointed ones] by the anointing of the Holy Spirit in baptism. He anointed us as kings [Col. 1011D] and priests, because kings and priests were anointed when they were appointed. And he sealed us: that is, he distinguished us from unbelievers by the sign of the cross, which he placed upon our foreheads. And he gave in our hearts the pledge of the Spirit, when through the laying on of hands we received the Holy Spirit as a pledge of future blessedness.

For there is no doubt that he who has already given his Spirit to mortals will add glory to them when immortal. For this reason we receive the pledge: that we may hold certainty concerning the promise made to us. Therefore the gift of the Holy Spirit is called a pledge because through it our soul is strengthened unto certainty of inward hope. Whoever burns with the fire of love has the gift of the Holy Spirit; therefore, if he perseveres, he should not doubt that he will attain eternal blessedness.

[Col. 1012A] But whoever has not yet tasted that the Lord is sweet (Ps. 33), and has not yet felt the love of charity, is still without a pledge and has no certainty of future blessedness [variant: salvation].

I said that God confirms us in Christ, who is truth, so that we may remain firmly in truth and may not lie in any respect concerning his teaching. But when I did not come again to Corinth, I did not act deceitfully; rather, I spared you—that is, I did not wish to strike you, who had not yet been corrected. And on this point I call God as witness upon my soul, so that he himself may examine whether I speak the truth and be my witness; but if I lie, may he punish me.

He now reveals why, though he had wished to go to them, he postponed it: namely, in order to go when he would find almost all of them already corrected. For he now speaks to those who seemed willing [Col. 1012B] to correct themselves but did not take care to fulfill this. Therefore, because it was necessary to correct them, he turned his journey away from them, lest he make many sorrowful or drive some into rebellion. Thus he spared them, so that they might correct themselves of their own accord before he came. To commend this to their minds, he offers God as witness, lest they think themselves despised by him. Once they recognize this, let them correct themselves so as to deserve his presence.

And this is the meaning: “Sparing you, I did not come again to Corinth after the first occasion”; that is, after the first occasion I did not come to you, lest I should be compelled to strike you. And lest they become indignant as though he were claiming lordship, he added: “I said, ‘sparing you,’ not because we lord it over your faith, but because we are helpers of your joy. For you stand by faith.”

It is as though he said: “For this reason we do not lord it over your faith: because you stand by faith. We are not superiors but equals to you in that by which we know you stand.” In this place the Apostle does not regard himself as their superior. But above, when he had learned of the grave fault of the fornicator, he immediately remembered that he was their teacher, saying: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod?” (1 Cor. 4). For the highest position is well governed when the one who presides rules vices rather than brothers.

Therefore, because faith is a matter not of necessity but of will, “we do not lord it over your faith,” he says. For lordship is a cause of necessity. We do not lord it over your faith, which cannot endure compulsion; rather, we are helpers of the joy which you will have in correction. For as you wish to correct yourselves, we provide admonition so that you may fulfill what you have begun [Col. 1012D] to will; and, when I come, you may have joy as persons well corrected, and finally rejoice in the heavenly kingdom. Therefore we do not lord it over your faith, because you stand by faith, which works through love (Gal. 5) and is not compelled through domination.

## Chapter II

> “But I determined this with myself: not to come to you again in sorrow. For if I make you sorrowful, who is there to make me glad except the one who is made sorrowful by me? And I wrote this very thing to you, so that when I come I may not have sorrow upon sorrow from those concerning whom I ought to have rejoiced, having confidence in all of you that my joy is the joy of you all. For out of much tribulation and anguish of heart I wrote to you through many tears, not [Col. 1013A] so that you might be made sorrowful, but so that you might know the abundant love that I have for you.”

I said that I spared you in not coming, lest it be necessary for me to treat you harshly. Nor did I merely delay my journey while sparing you, but I determined this with myself—that is, decreed in my heart—not to come to you again in sorrow. That is, I deferred my arrival until you should be corrected, lest when I came I should again be grieved by your lack of correction, since I am now grieved by your sins.

Or, having once come to you when I converted you to the faith, I determined not to come to you again in sorrow: that is, not to make you sorrowful by rebuking some when I came again. Therefore I determined not to come, lest I have sorrow again, or lest by my repeated coming I make you sorrowful. [Col. 1013B] For if I now make you sorrowful by letter, you in turn make me sorrowful by your sins. And who is there to make me glad when I come except the one who is now made sorrowful unto repentance because I have been made sorrowful by him—that is, because he made me sorrowful by his sins—or “by me,” that is, by my words?

Therefore, if now in my absence I move you to the sorrow and tears of repentance, I am certain that when I come I shall rejoice. For who is there then to make me glad except the one who now turns to the sorrow of repentance because of me whom he made sorrowful? For you ought to be sorrowful not only because you sinned and offended God, but also because by sinning you made me, your teacher, sorrowful.

And I wrote this very thing to you—that no one makes me glad except the one who is made sorrowful by me—so that, knowing this, you may now weep for [Col. 1013C] your sins, lest when I come I may have sorrow upon sorrow, that is, be sorrowful again over you, rather than rejoice. Or I wrote this very thing to you in sorrow—that I spare you by not coming and that I determined not to come—so that meanwhile you may quickly turn to the mourning of repentance, lest when I come I have sorrow over your lack of correction in addition to the sorrow that I have over your sins.

Let not sorrow concerning you be added to me—concerning you, over whom I ought to have rejoiced not only now but long ago, when you made me sorrowful and sinned so grievously. I wrote to you and did this, trusting concerning all of you that I would no longer have sorrow concerning you. See that I have not trusted in vain, because my joy is the joy of all of you: that is, my joy is your purification and your progress, which makes you yourselves rejoice in the Lord.

I said, lest I should have sorrow over you added to my former sorrow. For I suffered severe sorrow because of the ugliness which you incurred by sinning, because I wrote my first letter to you out of much tribulation and anguish of heart—that is, out of much pain and great anxiety of mind over your fall. I wrote through many tears, which outwardly displayed the inward pain of my soul. And I wrote rebuking you harshly, not so that you might be made sorrowful by my words, but so that you might know how abundant is the love I have for you: that is, with how great an affection of love I seek your salvation, desiring to rescue you from sins and restore you to Christ.

Whoever rebukes someone with this disposition, so that he grieves more over that person’s sin than that person does himself, does not rebuke in order to make him sorrowful, but in order to show him with what love he loves him. But the person who does not rebuke with this disposition makes his brother sorrowful. For the one who does not grieve with his brother mocks him.

> “But if anyone has made me sorrowful, he has not made me sorrowful, except in part, so that I may not burden all of you. Sufficient for such a person is this rebuke which is made by the many, so that, on the contrary, you should rather forgive and comfort him, lest perhaps the one who is such should be swallowed up by excessive sorrow. Therefore I beseech you (John 4) to confirm love toward him. For this reason also I wrote to you, that I might know the proof of you—whether you are obedient in all things. But to whom you forgive anything, I also forgive. For I too, what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, I have forgiven for your sake in the person of Christ, so that we may not be outwitted by Satan. For we are not ignorant of his designs.”

I had sorrow. But if anyone, by sinning, has caused me sorrow, he has caused sorrow not to me alone but also, in some measure—that is, to certain among you, namely the good and corrected persons who grieved over a brother’s sin—to you yourselves. I say that you were grieved in part, so as not to burden all of you; that is, so that I may not lay the burden of sorrow upon all of you, since not all of you love justice sincerely enough to be willing to grieve over sin. Here he rebukes those who did not grieve over the exceedingly grave death of their brother’s soul.

It may also be understood thus: He did not grieve me wholly, but only in part, so that I may not burden all of you with the magnitude of my sorrow, if I should say that I was wholly grieved. He has grieved me, and nevertheless—[Col. 1014C] spare him. For the rebuke administered by the many is sufficient for one such as he is; that is, for one who has sinned so gravely. Great indeed is the pain suffered by one who sees his offence abhorred and censured by many. And because such a person might easily despair, the rebuke of the many is sufficient for him: the rebuke with which you rebuked him is itself a sufficient remedy for the removal of his guilt. It is sufficient in such a way that you should not further embitter him, but rather—indeed, conversely—should forgive him; for the more persons have rebuked him, the more he ought to be forgiven.

He now recalls the man whom he had handed over to Satan and reunites him with the members of the Church (1 Cor. 5). He certainly would not have done this unless, with the passage of time, he had foreseen in him fruits of repentance worthy of the name; and unless [Col. 1014D] his flesh had already undergone its prescribed destruction—namely, had died to sin and vices—so that in this way it might live to God.

Forgive him; console him. That is, be now as ready to pardon and console as you then were to rebuke and expel, lest perhaps one such as he is—that is, one thus rebuked and cast out—be swallowed up by excessive sorrow: lest he be overwhelmed by the waves of immoderate grief, if he sees himself for too long rejected by everyone and, despairing of himself, gives his mind over to enjoyment of the world, as though he had no longer any place with God. For this is to be swallowed up by greater sorrow: one who despairs of himself turns to committing sins, and, weighed down by them, is swallowed up by the second death.

Therefore console him after the rebuke, because repentance, if it proceeds from a true disposition [Col. 1015A]—that is, if the person rebuked immediately grieves inwardly—at once bears fruit. And true repentance is now to cease from sin. Thus he shows that he is turning back, and that he grieves, if henceforth he ceases.

For this reason—that he may not, through an excessively harsh correction, be swallowed up by the surge of more violent sorrow and fall into the abyss of despair—I, who could command, beseech you: receive him into communion and confirm your love toward him, so that the love with which you love him may become firm, and the affection of your love may be shown to pass steadfastly into him through the sweetness of devout consolation. Or: by your exhortations confirm his love in him, which is now weak and wavering because of this sadness.

And you ought to do this. For this is why I also wrote to you [Col. 1015B]—that is, I endeavoured by writing to persuade you—in order that in this matter I might know the proof of you; that is, might discover what was the character of the obedience which I had experienced in you when you obeyed me in his excommunication. I might test and know whether you expelled him with a good or an evil disposition. For I experienced that you were obedient in rejecting him; but wishing to ascertain that proof, I wrote to you concerning the confirmation of love. For if you now appear loving toward him in reconciliation, then I shall know that you cast him out willingly not from hatred but from love.

I wished to know the proof of you, testing whether you are obedient in all things: whether you will now obey in receiving and consoling him, as you obeyed in expelling and rebuking him, and also as you obeyed in correcting those matters which concern [Col. 1015C] ecclesiastical order.

I exhort you to become merciful toward him; but you have already forgiven him in your hearts, because you saw that he had undertaken severe repentance. And to whom you have forgiven anything, I too have forgiven it. And truly I have done this as you have. For what I forgave him—that is, pardoned him—if I forgave him anything, I did for your sake, since I recognized that you were moved compassionately on his behalf. This, however, is to be understood of the holier persons, not of the multitude of the carnal, who did not yet possess the bowels of compassion and therefore are moved to mercy. For your sake—you who are spiritual and compassionately grieved for him—I forgave him.

And lest a forgiveness of this kind, granted for friends’ sake, seem ineffectual, I did it in the person of Christ; that is, as though Christ himself [Col. 1015D] forgave him. I did this so that we might not be outwitted by Satan; that is, lest we be deceived by the adversary, who, through the severe penance we imposed upon him, may cause him to despair. We ought to guard against the enemy’s devices, because we are not ignorant of his wiles, by which he intends to destroy both us and him.

For consolation ought to follow a brother who weeps over his sin, lest, saddened for long and despised by the Church’s love, he begin to despair of himself. The subtle devil, who is always lying in wait, sees his mind rendered base and approaches, suggesting to him that he should at least enjoy present things, since he has been cast down from hope of future reward; and thus he perishes, possessed by the devil, though penance had been given to him so that, converted, he might restore himself.

It should be observed how diligently the Apostle preserves unity with his disciples. For when he had learned that they had already been moved mercifully toward this brother because he had performed penance well, he says: “To whom you forgive anything, I also forgive.” It is as though he said: “I do not dissent from your good; whatever you have done for him is mine.” And immediately he added: “And if I have forgiven anything, I did it for your sake.” It is as though he said: “Whatever I have done mercifully for your sake, I have added as good to your actions.” Therefore my goodness is your benefit, and your goodness is my benefit.

Then, joining the very bond of hearts by which they are thus held together, he added: [Col. 1016A] “In the person of Christ.” If we should venture, as it were, to ask him: “Why do you so carefully bind yourself to your disciples? Why, with such attentive concern, do you bring either yourself into conformity with their actions or them with yours?”—he immediately added: “So that we may not be outwitted by Satan.” For this reason [Col. 1016B] he joins himself with such humility to their will in pardoning: because, with the watchful eye of providence, he observes that often, while one person forgives, another becomes angry. And what kind of sacrifice of mercy is that which is offered amid discord with one’s neighbour?

Thus it is rightly said: “So that we may not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs.” For he is accustomed to introduce the evil of strife into one person’s heart precisely from the circumstance in which he sees another performing an act of piety. A good is imperfect when it is done in such a way that one does not attend to whether evil may creep in from another direction—unless perhaps the thing which cannot be done without causing someone scandal is a fault not to have done. Therefore the Apostle rightly guards against the evil of discord in his good action when he says, “So that we may not be outwitted by Satan,” who is accustomed to generate evils from good things [Col. 1016C] and to draw into discord that which is done through love.

This may also be understood in another way. I said that you should confirm love in the aforesaid penitent; but you ought willingly to do this for my sake, because I have done similar things for your sake. For if you forgave someone guilty—that is, remitted some part of his fault—I have done the like for you. Therefore it is just that you too forgive this man for my sake. For what I forgave—if I forgave anyone any sin—I did for your sake, assenting to your prayers.

By saying this he presses them. For if the master, at his disciples’ request, forgave the sin of the person whom they chose, how much more ought disciples to obey their master, so as to forgive the one for whom he himself asks? And in order to show that what he forgave that person was ratified before God, he says that he forgave it in the person of Christ; that is, in the place of Christ, who says: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them” (John 20). If, therefore, he himself forgave for Christ’s sake the man for whom they asked the Apostle, how much more ought the man to be forgiven whom he himself urges them to forgive?

“Forgive,” he says, “as I forgave, lest through discord we be outwitted by Satan. For if I did not forgive for your sake, and you did not forgive for mine, discord would now arise between us, mutual love would perish, and thus our adversary would rejoice in victory. For we are not ignorant how cunningly he continually seeks evils against us.”

> “But when I had come to Troas for the Gospel of Christ, and a door had been opened to me in the Lord, [Col. 1017A] I had no rest for my spirit because I did not find Titus my brother; but, taking leave of them, I departed for Macedonia. But thanks be to God, who always triumphs over us in Christ Jesus and manifests through us in every place the fragrance of his knowledge; for we are the sweet fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to some indeed a fragrance of death unto death, but to others a fragrance of life unto life. And who is so fit for these things? For we are not, like the many, adulterating the word of God; but from sincerity, as from God, before God, in Christ we speak.”

He now recounts to the Corinthians what he suffered and how in all things he gives thanks to God, in order to encourage them by his own example to strive. “In Asia,” he says, [Col. 1017B] “I endured, as I said above, a most severe tribulation. But when I came to Troas, I did not rest.”

Or thus: I did not come merely for the reasons stated above—namely, that by not coming I might spare you, and that I might not have sorrow upon sorrow—but also because, when I came to Troas, I did not find Titus, whom I had sent to you so that he might report to me whether you had been corrected, as I had arranged there. Therefore, knowing nothing of your correction, I could not come to you. Moreover, your failure to amend caused serious loss to others, because I was able to make little progress among the Trojans without Titus, whom your failure to amend detained. For as it was your fault that I did not come to Corinth, so it was that I made no progress in Troas while Titus was delayed among you; without him I could not make progress there.

And this is the meaning: “I came,” he says, “to Troas, formerly called Troy, in order to preach the Gospel of Christ in Asia. And when a door had been opened to me in the Lord”—that is, when many had believed, or when, through the signs and powers which God worked in me, there was hope of a faith being born and growing in the Lord—“I had no rest for my spirit”; that is, I could not find the hoped-for consolation, because I did not find Titus as we had previously agreed.

For a “door” means an access or opportunity for preaching; or it is so called because God opened the hearts of those to whom he preached. And, as blessed Jerome says, although the Apostle possessed knowledge of the holy Scriptures and had the grace of speech and of various languages, he could not express the majesty of divine meanings in Greek discourse worthy of them. [Note: [Col. 1017D] An obscure passage.]

He therefore had Titus as an interpreter, just as blessed Peter had Mark. And for this reason he was grieved, because he did not find present the pipe and instrument of his preaching, through which he sang to Christ.

There is also another, perhaps more probable, reason why he was distressed by Titus’s absence: alone he could not both instruct the faithful and withstand the clamorous unbelievers. For although some of them had opened their hearts to receive God’s word, the insolence of the unbelievers nevertheless rose up no little against the Apostle because of zeal for the believers. One person could not accomplish both tasks: both instruct the believers and [Col. 1018A] resist the unbelievers. Therefore the labour was intolerable when Titus’s assistance was lacking.

For this reason he departed from there, taking leave of those who had believed, in whose hearts, that is, a door had been opened to the evangelist. And this is what “I had no rest for my spirit” means: I could not fulfil my purpose, because I did not find Titus there as I had hoped. He was necessary there, perhaps because he could use their language more expressly. But, taking leave of those who had been converted, I departed for Macedonia, in the hope that I might find Titus even there and have the assistance of interpretation and of the Gospel. Therefore I went there, and there too endured many things.

But I give thanks to God, who does not permit us to fail, but always triumphs over us in Christ; that is, makes us triumph. Or, he triumphs over us, or conducts his triumph through us, and everywhere spreads through us the fragrance—that is, the good report—of his knowledge.

The Apostle, having endured many adversities, gives thanks to God in Christ Jesus, whom he preached to the nations, because God chose him worthy of the triumph of his Son. God’s triumph is the suffering of martyrs: the shedding of blood for Christ’s name and joy amid torments. For when someone sees martyrs stand with such endurance, suffer torture, and glory in their own sufferings, the fragrance of the knowledge of God is spread among the nations; and a silent thought speaks within him: unless the Gospel were true, it would never be defended by blood.

This too is for God to triumph over the apostles in Christ: to make them victors in faith in Christ, so that, unbelief having been trampled down, faith may possess its trophy, while unbelievers become believers and malicious persons do not succeed in persecuting the faithful.

The fragrance of God’s knowledge is manifested through signs and wonders, when preaching is proved true by the testimony of divine power. This preaching is designated by fragrance because, although God is not seen, he is understood to be present in the apostles through the things he visibly works, so that the truth of doctrine may be made manifest. For just as certain things, though unseen, are nevertheless recognized by their scent, so God, who is invisible, willed to be known through Gospel preaching, which comes invisibly to the ears as fragrance comes to the nostrils.

It should be observed that up to this point he has spoken of his tribulations and why he did not come to Corinth. From here he begins to commend himself and humble the false apostles. [Col. 1018D] Whatever he now says about himself must be excluded from them.

“The fragrance,” he says—that is, the sweet report of his knowledge—“he manifests through us in every place,” that is, wherever we preach, because we are the good and sweet fragrance of Christ to God, even if we are not thus the fragrance of Christ to you. That is, the purity of our conduct breathes forth Christ, and the fragrance of our preaching spreads far and wide.

And we are a good fragrance among those who are saved and among those who perish. For human beings have been left to their own choice: they do not do good by necessity but by will, so that believers may receive a crown and unbelievers be consigned to punishments. Therefore our fragrance, good in itself, passes into life or death through the virtue or fault of those who receive [Col. 1019A] or do not receive it: so that those who believe may be saved, while those who do not believe may perish.

Nor is this surprising, since the rays of the sun fall alike upon clean and unclean places, shining both upon flowers and upon dung, and yet the sun’s rays are not polluted thereby. Thus also the good fragrance of Christ, which can never be changed or lose its own nature, is life to believers and death to unbelievers.

The good fragrance of Christ is the preaching of truth. The person who receives that fragrance unto life is one who serves and accords with the Gospel by good conduct. He incurs death whose life disagrees with the good things he says. This condition also binds hearers: sound preaching, heard by some through unbelief, is unto death; received by others through faith, it is unto salvation.

“We are,” he says, [Col. 1019B] “a good fragrance,” both in relation to those who are saved by it and in relation to those who perish by despising it, because we act with good intention. Whether you consider those saved by our preaching or those lost through contempt of it, we nevertheless always appear a good fragrance to God, because he sees our intention—what we intend in speaking: namely, that we intend all hearers to be saved, not that some of them should perish. Therefore we are a good fragrance to God.

But to human beings we appear, to some, a fragrance of death because we preach the cross—that is, we are judged ministers of death; to others we are believed to be a fragrance of life, a fragrance breathing life through the Saviour’s preaching. And each experiences what he judges. For those by whom we are judged a fragrance of death, [Col. 1019C] that judgment turns for them into eternal death; and those to whom we seem a fragrance of life, their faith leads them into eternal life.

God works these things through us. And who is so fit for these things as to understand how God works in wondrous ways, so that by a good fragrance the good live and the evil die?

Paul the Apostle, acting well, living well, preaching righteousness by word and demonstrating it by deed, a wonderful teacher and faithful steward, was made famous everywhere. Some loved him; others envied him. Those who loved lived by the good fragrance; those who envied perished by the good fragrance. Therefore for those who perish the fragrance was not evil but good. Indeed, they envied all the more because such good grace prevailed. No one envies a miserable person.

For he was glorious in [Col. 1019D] preaching God’s word and in living according to the rule of God’s commands. Those loved him who loved in him the good fragrance—that is, the good which they followed. Others, however, the more they envied him for the glory of his preaching and his blameless life, the more they were tortured and killed by the good fragrance of envy. Whoever envies the glorious reputation of Christ or of any saint dies by a good fragrance; but whoever loves it lives by a good fragrance.

Therefore, because it is difficult to understand by what reasoning anyone perishes through a good fragrance—or because by God’s hidden judgments, which cannot be comprehended by human beings in this life, it comes about that by the same good fragrance some live and others die—it is rightly said: “And who is so fit for these things?” As though it were said: We are fit to observe that these things occur, but we are not fit [Col. 1020A] to investigate why they occur. Who is so fit to examine these matters that he may discover why they occur thus? Or who is so fit to understand them that he may know how a good fragrance invigorates some and kills others?

That is, who is fit to understand how justly the Lord’s saying comes about: “I came so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9)? For this is the depth of the riches of God’s wisdom, by which he makes from the same lump one vessel for honour and another for dishonour (Rom. 9).

“Truly,” he says, “we are a good fragrance to God, because we are not adulterating the word of God”; that is, mingling falsehood with it and pouring out the seed of the word for pleasure rather than for producing offspring.

Or he speaks against false apostles and hirelings: “And who is so fit for these things?” That is, for [Col. 1020B] those things which God works through you, who is as fit as you? For it is difficult to find a worthy herald of Christ’s virtues, one who in proclaiming them seeks not his own glory but Christ’s, and considers not his own gain but the Lord’s.

And truly no one besides us is so fit for these things. For we are not, like the many—that is, false apostles and hirelings—adulterating the word of God, either by corrupting the sense of divine preaching through a mixture of falsehood or by seeking from it the pleasure of carnal profit. Rather, we speak from sincerity—that is, from a sincere intention, not for gain—and as from God, possessing from him whatever we say; before God, seeking by our speech to please him alone and not human beings; and in Christ, never going beyond him, as the false apostles did, who mingled legal observance and worldly philosophy with [Col. 1020C] Christ’s Gospel.

An adulterer in carnal intercourse seeks not offspring but pleasure. Thus every perverse person serving vain glory is rightly said to adulterate the word of God, because through sacred speech he desires not to beget children for God but to display his own knowledge. For the person whom desire for glory draws into speech gives his labour more to pleasure than to generation.

To adulterate the word of God is either to think of it otherwise than it is, or to seek from it not spiritual fruits but adulterous offspring—the praise of human beings. But to speak from sincerity is to seek in speech nothing beyond what ought to be sought. He speaks as from God who knows that he does not possess from himself what he says, but has received it from [Col. 1020D] God. He speaks before God who, in everything he says, seeks not human favour but attends to the presence of almighty God, seeking not his own glory but that of his Author. And he speaks in Christ whose discourse wholly persists in Christ’s truth, so that he is neither false nor preaches anything other than Christ.

But one who knows indeed that he has received from God what he says, yet seeks his own glory in speaking, speaks as from God but not before God. For when he preaches, he considers as absent the one whom he does not set before his own heart. Holy men, however, speak both as from God and before God, because they know that they possess from him what they say, and they regard him as present—the judge and hearer of their words.

[Col. 1021A] The mystery of the Trinity may also be shown at the end of this chapter: “From God,” that is, from the Holy Spirit; “before God” the Father; “in Christ,” we speak.

## Chapter III

> “Are we beginning again to commend ourselves? Or do we need, like some persons, letters of recommendation to you or from you? You are our letter, written in our hearts, known and read by all people; made manifest that you are Christ’s letter, administered by us and written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshly hearts.”

Because he knew that they had taken his self-commendation in the first letter unfavourably, as though he sought his own glory, he begins to speak against their opinion. [Col. 1021B] For the false apostles reproached him precisely because he commended himself and declared to others the good things God had placed in him; on that basis they alleged that he was proud and a seeker of empty glory.

Therefore he now shows that his commendation does not aim at commending himself but only him whose worthy minister he is. This is what he says reproachfully by interrogation, or ironically: “Are we beginning again, as in the first letter, to commend ourselves rather than God? Are we beginning, as though this were always something new for us, again to commend ourselves, when we say that we are Christ’s good fragrance,” and so forth?

It is as though he said: We do indeed commend ourselves in this letter as in the first, but not ourselves; for in our commendation we chiefly commend him [Col. 1021C] to whose glory we refer all things. Therefore we commend ourselves not carnally but spiritually, for the advancement of your salvation, so that you may believe concerning us what is true. For one who thinks ill of good commits sin. It is also expedient for you to know us, because then you will receive our words gladly and thus attain salvation. Consequently, the commendation benefits you rather.

For we do not commend ourselves for our own sake, as the false apostles do, who commend themselves while seeking their own glory and gain. Or do we need letters of recommendation, sent by other believers to you or from you to others, as some persons do—that is, as the false apostles, whom no virtue or wisdom of their own commends? They need to be commended by letters, [Col. 1021D] since they travel through churches for the sake of their own honour and profit, not to bestow salvation but to take it away. But we, whom God commends wherever we go by the power of wondrous works and the light of wisdom, have no need to be commended somewhere by human letters.

For you are our letter and recommendation among people: that is, your faith, love, and every good that is in you make us commendable, because we are praised for the fact that through us God gave you all these things. For a letter is a sign of salvation. You are our letter, in whom our knowledge and life are displayed to others.

I say, our letter written in our hearts, that is, placed in the memory of our mind, because we always retain you in our heart [Col. 1022A] and always have concern for your salvation, desiring correction of your sins and always wishing for you progress toward better things and perseverance in good. This letter, indeed, is known and read by all people. It is known by all people—that is, everyone knows that you were instructed by us; and it is read—that is, in you they learn to imitate us. Thus, through knowledge and reading of this letter—that is, through acquaintance with and consideration of your good conduct—we become commendable to all.

I said that you are our letter. I mean you who are made manifest to all as being Christ’s letter, administered by us. For it is evident to everyone that through our ministry you have believed in Christ, who confirms our doctrine [Col. 1022B] through miracles. Thus you are principally Christ’s letter and secondarily ours, because he principally wrote you and we secondarily: that is, through our ministry he wrote in you faith, hope, love, and the remaining goods.

You are a letter written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God; that is, the fact that you are a representation of Christ and of us is firmly written in our hearts, not so as to be erased, like what is written with ink. It is not written with ink—that is, not in such a way as may be erased, like things written with ink—but with the Spirit of the living God, so that it may remain eternally and livingly in our or your hearts, just as he who wrote it lives and is eternal. Because the things promised to us are eternal, this letter is said to be written [Col. 1022C] with God’s Spirit, who abides forever. Temporal things, however, are written with ink and are effaced and lose remembrance.

Or: it is not written with ink—that is, not with dark marks, as the false apostles write, inserting heresies—but with the light of the Holy Spirit; not on tablets of stone, as was the ancient law, but on tablets of fleshly hearts. There, on tablets of stone, the finger of God (Exod. 8; Exod. 31)—that is, the Holy Spirit—worked; here he works in human hearts. There the law was set externally, so that the unjust might be frightened; here it was given inwardly, so that they might be justified. The former is written outside the human being, to terrify from without; the latter is within the human being, to justify from within.

By “fleshly tablets of the heart” I mean not carnal wisdom, but something like that which lives [Col. 1022D] and possesses understanding, in contrast with stone, which lacks understanding. For he looked to what God promised through the prophet: “I shall remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezek. 11). He intended the fleshly heart to be distinguished from the stony heart by sentient life, and by “sentient life” he signified intelligence.

It was not therefore said, “on tablets of fleshly hearts,” so that you might live carnally; you ought to live spiritually. But because stone is without sense—and the hard heart is compared to it—to what should the intelligent heart be compared, if not to sentient flesh? Since the heart of stone itself signifies nothing but a will most hard and wholly inflexible against God.

The Jews received the law on stone tablets to signify the hardness of their hearts [Col. 1023A] toward love of God and understanding; for they would neither love God nor understand the law itself. The stone tablets signify their hard and insensible hearts. The tablets of the heart, however, signify minds expanded by the breadth of love. Thus they are called fleshly—that is, soft and sensitive, possessing affection for love or good action. For animate flesh feels and has affection toward what it touches; so that through the heart we possess understanding and through the flesh the affection of love. Therefore the Holy Spirit wrote our letter on tablets of fleshly hearts: that is, he so placed his commands in you as to give you capacity for understanding and an affection of love for fulfilling them.

> “And such confidence we have through Christ toward God (Heb. 4), not because we are sufficient to think anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God.”

After showing why he does not need letters of recommendation, he responds to what he had said earlier: namely, that he does not commend himself but God, from whom he has all things. It is as though he said: We said that God always triumphs through us and everywhere manifests through us the fragrance of his knowledge, and that we are Christ’s good fragrance to God. When we speak these things and similar things with such confidence, we do not do so for our own commendation, as though glorying in our own powers and referring these things to ourselves; rather, we have such great confidence—that is, we refer it to God, from whom whatever good we possess has been given to us.

Or this is connected with the preceding passage: You are Christ’s letter and ours. But we refer the confidence to say such things [Col. 1023C] not to ourselves but to God. For from purity of conscience we have such confidence toward God: that is, we trust that it pleases him that we speak thus. We have it through Christ the mediator, through whom this power has been given to us.

But we ascribe nothing to our own powers. For through Christ the mediator we have great confidence before God, yet not in such a sense that we are sufficient even to think any good thing from ourselves—that is, arising on our side, as though having its beginning from ourselves. Rather, all our sufficiency for thinking and doing good is from God. From this we know that we are nothing unless we are governed by God’s mercy and [Col. 1023D] grace.

Let those who think that the beginning of faith is from us and its completion from God attend to these words. For who does not see that thinking comes before believing? No one believes anything unless he has first thought that it is to be believed. If, therefore, we are not sufficient of ourselves to think any good thing, certainly neither are we sufficient to believe, which we cannot do without thought. Rather, our sufficiency, by which we begin even to believe, is from God.

Thinking, we believe; thinking, we speak; thinking, we do whatever we do. But with respect to the way of piety and true worship of God, we are not sufficient even to think anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves; rather, our sufficiency is from God. For our heart and our thoughts are not in our own power.

The Apostle says this [Col. 1024A] in order to show that neither he nor his companions does anything by his own power or wisdom, since so few persons, and unlearned ones, could never have converted the whole world to faith without God’s cooperating grace. He also said this beforehand so that he might not seem to claim anything for himself when he was about to say that he had undertaken a ministry greater than Moses’s by as much as the New Testament is greater than the Old. For he adds:

> “Who also made us fit ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.”

And now he begins to commend himself in a different manner from above, so as also to expose the false apostles, suggesting that they are ministers of the Old Testament while showing himself to be a minister of the New. Our sufficiency [Col. 1024B] is from God. He has exalted us so greatly as to make us fit ministers of the New Testament—that is, so that through us, adorned with perfection of knowledge and life, he might administer the New Testament to others. For new wine was to be put into new vessels (Matt. IX; Mark II; Luke V), so that it might be served without sourness.

I say, of a Testament existing not in the letter that merely teaches, but in the Spirit who assists and is bestowed by God through us. By “letter” nothing other than the Decalogue itself, written on those two tablets, is now meant. The “Spirit,” however, may be understood as the law of faith, which is not written down but is held in the mind. Therefore the New Testament is administered through us not in the letter but in the Spirit, because the letter kills, whereas the Spirit gives life. The letter kills by making one sin knowingly, adding transgression [Col. 1024C] and provoking all the more; but the Spirit gives life by causing what has been commanded to be fulfilled. For the letter, while prohibiting sin, does not give a human being life, but rather kills by increasing desire and accumulating iniquity through transgression, unless grace sets one free through the law of faith which is in Christ Jesus, when love is poured into the heart through the Holy Spirit.

For when grace does not help, the law makes transgressors and remains merely in the letter. Let the Spirit, then, be joined to the letter: the letter does not kill when the Spirit gives life. Let us not, therefore, suppose that the letter is condemned or censured because it was said, “The letter kills.” This means: the letter makes persons guilty. For in the same manner it was said, “Knowledge puffs up” (1 Cor. [Col. 1024D] VIII). What does “knowledge puffs up” mean? Has knowledge been condemned? Far from it. But because he added, “Love, however, builds up” (ibid.), just as he now adds, “But the Spirit gives life,” he makes it understood that the letter without the Spirit kills, while the Spirit gives life and causes the letter to be fulfilled. If knowledge without love puffs up, love with knowledge builds up.

Thus the letter by itself, prohibiting evil and commanding good, kills the souls of those who transgress it. But the Spirit, who is in the hearts of believers through the grace of the New Testament, gives life in the present to their souls by justifying them; and in the future he will cause their bodies also, together with their souls, to live perpetually.

Or again, the letter understood carnally kills the soul. We must beware lest a figurative expression be taken literally. For when something figuratively spoken is so received as though it had been spoken in a proper sense, one thinks carnally. No death of the soul is more fittingly named than when that which makes it superior to beasts—namely, intelligence—is subjected to the flesh by following the letter. For one who follows the letter takes transferred words as though they were proper; nor does he relate what is signified by the literal word to its intended meaning. Thus, when he hears “Sabbath,” for example, he understands nothing but one day out of seven, recurring in an unbroken cycle; and when he hears “sacrifice,” his thought does not go beyond that which is customarily made from animal victims or earthly fruits.
