This, indeed, is the miserable slavery of the soul: to take signs for things, and to be unable to raise the eye of the mind above bodily creation in order to drink in the eternal [Col. 1025B] light. But the Spirit gives life and frees the soul, teaching it inwardly how it ought to understand what it hears.

> “But if the ministry of death, engraved in letters on stones, came in glory, so that the children of Israel could not gaze upon the face of Moses because of the glory of his countenance (Exod. XXXIV), which is being abolished, how shall not the ministry of the Spirit be much more in glory? For if the ministry of condemnation is in glory, much more does the ministry of righteousness abound in glory.”

“We,” he says, “are ministers of the New Testament, and this ministry will be in everlasting glory.” He proves this from the lesser—that is, from the Old Testament, which formerly existed in glory. It is as if he said: We administer the New in Spirit, not letter, where worshippers are given life through the Spirit. But if the ministry of death—that is, the law whose letter kills—was in glory through Moses, its minister, how shall the ministry of the Spirit—that is, the New Testament, which is administered in the Spirit and in which the Spirit is given—not be much more in glory for you?

“The law indeed is holy, and the commandment just and holy and good” (Rom. VII). Yet, because the disobedient soul is put to death by that very good thing where God’s grace does not assist, the law in the Old Testament became a ministry of death because of the killing letter; and grace in the New became a ministry of life because of the life-giving Spirit. The law is therefore distinguished from grace in that [Col. 1025D] under the former the proud are crushed, while under the latter the crushed are raised up; and in that the former is good enough to command good things, whereas the latter is good enough to confer them: the former makes one a hearer of righteousness, the latter a doer of it.

Thus, under the former, the sinner—indeed, a transgressor besides—lies convicted, his excuse of ignorance taken away. Under the latter, which both spares and assists, even the one who has done evil is not extinguished; rather, he is kindled to do good. What wonder, then, that the former was called a ministry of death, where the letter kills by prohibiting evil that is done and commanding good that is not done; while the latter was called the ministry of the Spirit, certainly the life-giving Spirit, except so that we may rise from the death of transgression and possess righteousness not as guilty persons reading it on tablets, but as free persons possessing it in our hearts and conduct?

For the law was called a ministry of death with reference to the Jews, to whom it was also written on stones, to signify their hardness—not with reference to those who fulfil the law through love. For it was inscribed in letters—that is, plainly set down—so that it could be clearly read on the stones of the two tablets, both openly recognized and used to convict the hardness of their hearts. And although this ministry was one of death—that is, administered through Moses, and although it was a cause of death for transgressors—nevertheless it was attended for its minister Moses with such glory that the children of Israel could not direct the gaze of their eyes upon his face because of the glory of his countenance, which he had received from his converse with the Lord.

They could not look upon the splendour of his face when he came down from the mountain bearing the law on tablets received from the Lord, because the guilt of the calf [Col. 1026B] blunted their sight, so that they could not openly behold the glorious face of the righteous man (Exod. XXXIV). This also signified that they would not see the spiritual meaning of the law. For the shining face of Moses was a figure of truth; and that figure is abolished through the manifestation of truth—that is, the visible glory of the law is abolished by the glory of the Gospel.

It is abolished in such a way as to be brought to fulfilment, just as childhood is abolished in youth, and seed in fruit. Moses’ glory is therefore abolished because all signifying shadows are abolished when the thing signified has come. For just as the knowledge that now exists will be abolished when that comes which will be face to face (1 Cor. XIII), so too those things given to the Jews in the Old Testament under shadows had necessarily to be abolished by the revelation [Col. 1026C] of the New Testament.

The glory Moses had is now abolished in the ministers of that law, lest the false apostles, who still preach its carnal observances, should share in Moses’ glory. For as long as those carnal observances retained their standing, their ministers derived a certain glory and reverence from them. But after spiritual observance succeeded carnal observance, the glory of carnal ministers vanished. Even in Moses himself this glory did not remain forever.

Therefore, if the ministry of death belonged to Moses in such great glory, how much more shall the ministry of the Spirit—that is, the New Testament which we administer, in which faith obtains the life-giving Spirit—be in glory for us? It shall indeed be in glory for us much more than the Old Testament was for Moses. The splendour on Moses’ face, being upon a carnal and mortal face, could not be lasting or eternal, since it was removed even by death. But the splendour of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, in which we shall share, is everlasting.

For just as the promises of the Old Testament were temporal—that is, promising temporal goods—so also Moses’ glory was temporal. And just as the promises of the New Testament, which is administered through us, are eternal, so the glory which we are to receive in Christ for this ministry is eternal. Truly the ministry of the Spirit shall be for us in the greatest and enduring glory. For if the ministry of condemnation—that is, the law which condemns transgressors so that they are immediately destroyed, not reserving them for repentance—was for Moses in [Col. 1027A] glory, then the ministry of righteousness—that is, the New Testament administered through us, in which true righteousness is given through faith and the Holy Spirit—abounds much more in glory: it gives far more abundant glory to us, its ministers. That glory, as we have said, is temporal; this is eternal. That is earthly; this heavenly.

Or the New Testament has greater glory in itself than the Old, because it is a greater glory to justify a sinner than to condemn one. For although it condemns justly, it contributes more to praise if it pardons, so that the guilty person may correct himself and rise again to righteousness.

> “For what was glorified has not been glorified in this respect, because of the surpassing glory. For if that which is abolished is through glory, much more that which remains is in glory.”

Truly the New Testament has greater glory. For in comparison with it Moses’ glory is not even glory. This is the meaning: what shone—that is, Moses’ face, which emitted a ray of brightness so that it seemed horned—has not been glorified in this respect; that is, it had no glory when considered beside the New Testament, because of the surpassing glory found there. It has not been glorified because it did not bear the fruit of glory. For since the glory of his countenance benefited no one, but rather harmed them—though this was not its own fault, but the fault of those who sinned—there is in this respect no glory there.

But that glory is greater which abounds in grace, so that human beings purified by God’s gift, the darkness of their minds wiped away, may be able to see Christ’s glory. The glory [Col. 1027C] of the New Testament is more excellent, for in it grace and mercy prevail. In comparison with the glory of the Gospel, the glory of the law is overshadowed so that it seems not to exist, just as at sunrise the light of a lamp is obscured, though it had previously appeared to shine greatly.

Truly the glory of the New surpasses. For if the Old Testament, which is abolished in respect of carnal observances, was administered and received through the glory of Moses’ face—without which it would not have been commended—much more is the New, which remains, that is, to which no other succeeds, in glory. The former is through Moses’ glory; that is, it existed as authoritative in its own time. Yet it is abolished in respect of its figures at the coming of abiding truth. Therefore the glory of the New is greater [Col. 1027D] than that of the Old, because as great as the difference between figure and truth, so great is the distance between the glory of Moses’ face and the glory of Christ. For as stars are glorious at evening, but their brightness is abolished when the sun rises, so Moses’ glory, which formerly shone, is abolished when Christ’s glory appears.

Or the glory of the New Testament should be referred to its ministers. Truly it abounds in glory for us. For what shone—that is, Moses’ face, which shone at the giving of the law—has not been glorified; that is, it does not even appear to have had glory in this respect, namely in comparison with our portion, because of the surpassing glory which we have and shall have from the New Testament. Or, “what shone in the respect mentioned above” means Moses, who appeared bright and glorious in face, yet has not been glorified as regards us because of the surpassing glory to be given to us. This is not said of Moses’ future glory, but of that which he appeared to have when he came down from the mountain (Exod. XXXIV).

Truly we shall attain surpassing glory from this ministry, because it remains and will endure without change. For if that which is abolished—that is, what ceases according to the shadows of carnal interpretation or observance—was in its own time through Moses’ glory, or, as is found in ancient codices, “was in glory,” much more is this ministry of the New Testament, which remains without change, in glory for its ministers.

> “Therefore, having such hope, we use great boldness; and not as Moses put a veil over [Col. 1028B] his face, so that the children of Israel might not gaze upon his face, which is being abolished (ibid.). But their minds were dulled. For until this very day the same veil remains unrevealed in the reading of the Old Testament, because it is abolished in Christ. But until this very day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart. But when one has turned to the Lord, the veil shall be removed. Now the Lord is the Spirit (John IV); and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.”

Since the ministry of the New Testament will be for us in abiding glory, we therefore, having such hope—that is, hoping that through our preaching we shall receive eternal and immeasurable glory—use great [Col. 1028C] boldness in preaching. That is, we preach so steadfastly that neither threats nor beatings nor any tortures make us keep silence concerning the proclamation of truth. And we do not preach as Moses did when he put his veil over his face: we do not conceal our meaning as Moses did, but speak openly, because we preach not carnal observances but rather truth itself and the meaning of the Old Testament.

For one who preaches carnal observances puts a veil over his own face and covers his inward meaning with the veil of the letter. But we do not veil our face, because we do not withhold from you the sight of inward splendour, as Moses put the veil of carnal figures over [Col. 1028D] his face—that is, over the clear spiritual understanding of his words—so that the children of Israel should not gaze upon his face, that is, should not examine its spiritual meaning, because they could not bear it due to their weakness and irreligion.

For the brightness of Moses’ countenance signified the truth of the new law, which was designated through carnal observances. And just as the Jews could not endure that great brightness unless it was moderated for them by the interposition of a veil, so likewise the weakness of their minds could not endure the perfection of life or understanding signified there, if the very truth of the New Testament had been shown to them unveiled. Therefore the face of truth, which was to be revealed in the time of grace, was shaded by the veil of carnal observances and promises.

For if they had understood Moses’ words spiritually, their weakness would not have ascended to such perfection, nor would their bleary eye have endured so great a brightness of wisdom. And if truth itself without a veil had been shown to them, they would have been the more blameworthy in proportion as they had known a greater perfection of righteousness while retaining nothing of perfection in their conduct. For this reason Moses covered for them, with the veil of the letter, the face of spiritual understanding, so that they might not gaze upon this splendour of his countenance. That veil is now abolished in the time of grace, so that the inward beauty of truth which had lain hidden may be revealed.

But the false apostles, who still preach carnal observances, do not wish the veil to be abolished. Instead, they wish truth always to be shadowed in figures and never made manifest. Thus [Col. 1029B] they lead their hearers into shadow and do not show them the light of truth.

The veil is indeed now abolished and removed through our expositions; but the minds of the Jews are dulled—that is, blunted—and cannot behold with the eyes of the heart the splendour of naked truth. This dullness comes from unbelief. Therefore, when they are converted to faith, the mental gaze is sharpened so that they may see the brightness of the divine light. The eyes of their minds have been blunted so that they may not see the spiritual light.

For until this very day, although truth now revealed shines everywhere, the same veil of carnal understanding remains in the reading of the Old Testament. When they hear that Scripture read, they understand nothing except what the letter outwardly sounds in a carnal way, and thus the inward meaning is concealed from them. Hence Moses, when speaking to them, veiled his face, signifying that this people would indeed know the words of the law, but would not at all see the brightness of that law.

For Moses’ shining face, as has been said, was a figure of truth; Moses’ face signified Christ. Moses’ voice sounded through the veil, and Moses’ face did not appear. So now Christ’s voice sounds to the Jews through the voice of the ancient Scriptures. They hear the speaker’s voice but do not see his face. Moses bore his person, and for that reason put a veil before himself when speaking to the people.

Thus the same veil remains to this day in the reading of the Old Testament because, as long as they understand carnal joys, pleasures, and earthly goods to be promised in the law, a veil lies [Col. 1029D] over the face of their heart, so that they do not see Christ in the Scriptures. The same veil that Moses put on remains in that reading, because now too, as before the Saviour’s coming, the surface of the letter carnally understood conceals from them the spiritual meaning.

By “veil” I mean a veil unrevealed to them, because they do not even know that it is a veil; that is, they do not even perceive that this literal surface is the covering of some hidden meaning enclosed within it. For they think that nothing there ought to be understood except what the letter carnally sounds. Nor is it surprising that the veil still remains for them, so that they do not even understand it to be a veil of hidden beauty, because it is abolished only in Christ—that is, only in faith in Christ.

For in Christ not the Old [Col. 1030A] Testament, but its veil is abolished, so that through Christ what is obscure and covered without Christ may be understood and, as it were, unveiled. The veil is indeed abolished for those who are in Christ. But over the heart of those who persist in unbelief a veil remains placed to this day—that is, a blindness oppressing their reason whenever Moses is read—because they understand everything carnally and cannot look toward the spiritual meaning because of the mist of blindness which they bear in their hearts. Thus two things hinder them from understanding: the veil of the reading and the veil of the heart.

But when one of them has been converted to the Lord Jesus, the veil is immediately removed. The veil is removed when, after the covering of likeness and allegory has been taken away, truth is laid bare [Col. 1030B] so that it may be seen. For the veil to be removed is for the carnal knowledge of the law to be abolished. The intention of the converted person is changed from the Old to the New Testament, so that he no longer aims to receive carnal happiness but spiritual happiness: that is, he turns from the expectation of shadowy and carnal blessedness in an earthly kingdom to the expectation of most true and spiritual blessedness in the heavenly kingdom.

Thus the veil is removed which covered the beneficial mysteries of the law, when folly and the mist of ignorance are taken away from one who comes to Christ. But what wonder? For the Lord is Spirit (John IV): that is, the Holy Spirit is Lord, possessing authority of his own and able to accomplish what he wills. Accordingly, he enlightens whom he wills and leaves whom he wills in the darkness of ignorance.

The Son seems, in a proper sense, to be called Lord. But in this passage the Holy Spirit is also called Lord when the Apostle says, “Now the Lord is the Spirit.” Lest anyone should suppose that the Son is signified and that he was called Spirit on account of his incorporeal substance, he continued: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.” Therefore the Holy Spirit is Lord—that is, he possesses nothing of servitude, but rules all things by sovereign power. Therefore, just as the Lord removes from the converted the veil of ancient servitude, the Spirit himself is Lord.

But wherever the Spirit of the Lord is—that is, the same Holy Spirit who is the Spirit of the Son—there is freedom of the mind, so that, with the servile veil removed, the mind may freely behold truth. Since this Spirit [Col. 1030D] is Lord and is the Spirit of the Lord, through him the Lord Jesus gave the law of freedom, not written in letters but inwardly communicated to minds through faith—not a law teaching visible things, but one persuading us to believe invisible things, which the mind apprehends spiritually rather than the bodily eye sees.

Thus, through this Spirit, the veil of carnal understanding, which is of servitude, is removed; and by the gift of spiritual understanding, the grace of freedom is bestowed. Moreover, freedom is always present in conduct wherever this Spirit dwells, because he causes good to be done not from fear of punishment but from love of righteousness. For the mind does not know the grace of freedom when it is bound by the slavery of fear. Whoever does good merely because he fears the evils of torments wants that which he fears not to exist, so that he may boldly commit unlawful acts.

[Col. 1031A] But since this Spirit, wherever he remains, pours out love, and love casts out servile fear, it is evident that wherever the Spirit of life is in a mind, freedom immediately obtains the sovereignty there.

Origen: Because the Apostle’s discourse now calls his hearers to a more subtle and spiritual understanding and wishes them to perceive nothing carnal in the law, he says: Whoever wishes the veil to be taken from his heart should turn to the Lord, not to the Lord as flesh—though this too is true, that the Word became flesh—but to the Lord as Spirit. For if he turns to the Lord as Spirit, he will come from carnal things to spiritual ones and pass from slavery to freedom; for where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. Therefore to those who are summoned from carnal to spiritual understanding it is said: “Now the Lord is Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.”

It may also be understood thus: when any one of them is converted to the Lord, who is Father and Son and Holy Spirit, the veil of carnal understanding will be removed from him. He will turn from carnality to the Lord, who, as we have said, is the indivisible Trinity. But the Lord to whom he turns is Spirit—that is, incorporeal—as the Gospel says of this whole Trinity: “God is Spirit” (John IV), and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.

Likewise here it is said that the Lord is Spirit, so that we may observe that whoever turns the intention of his mind toward him in order to understand him must understand in spirit and truth, not in flesh and shadow, as those wish to do who are held [Col. 1031C] under the law. The Lord is Spirit and must be understood spiritually; and he gives spiritual understanding. But wherever the Spirit of the Lord is—that is, the spiritual grace of love—there is freedom both to understand rightly and to act rightly.

> “But we all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.”

Those people, indeed, because they have not turned to the Lord, who is Spirit, have a veil over their heart. But all of us who have obtained freedom through the Spirit of the Lord, with the face of our heart unveiled—that is, with the intention of the mind uncovered from every veil of error—behold the glory of the Lord; that is, [Col. 1031D] we see through a mirror. For “beholding” is said in the sense of seeing through a mirror, not looking out from a watchtower. This is unambiguous in Greek. Yet in a mirror nothing is seen except an image.

And we, who are the image of God, behold—that is, through the mirror, through this image of him, we see the glory of the Lord. For when we carefully consider ourselves with the sharpness of reason, we somehow penetrate to the vision of the glory of him whose image we are; and we are transformed into that same image of God through which we behold—that is, we are changed so as to become perfectly the image of God. We are transformed: changed from form to form, passing from an obscure form to a bright form. For even the obscure form is the image of God.

When human nature, the image of its Creator, is justified from impiety, it is transformed from an unattractive form into a beautiful form. It is transformed from the brightness of creation into the brightness of justification. And we are transformed as by the Spirit of the Lord—that is, as persons whom the Spirit of the Lord transforms and changes for the better through his grace. When this image has been renewed to perfection through that transformation, we shall be like God, because we shall see him not through a mirror but as he is (1 John III).

Or, because *speculatio* commonly means contemplation, this may also be understood thus: all of us, with the face of the heart unveiled from the veil of the law, which is a shadow of things to come (Heb. X), beholding [Col. 1032B] the glory of the Lord—that is, contemplating through faith—are transformed, that is, changed through daily progress, into that same image, that is, into the same likeness of the Lord’s glory which we contemplate, so that after the darkness of this mortality we may be found fully like his glory. “For we know that when he appears, we shall be like him” (1 John III).

We are transformed from glory to glory; that is, proceeding from one clear knowledge to another: from the brightness of faith to the brightness of sight; from the brightness by which we are children of God to the brightness by which we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (ibid.). And thus we are led from glory to glory as by the Spirit of the Lord, because such great brightness is given us as accords with the sublimity of the giver. For as much brightness or glory will be given us [Col. 1032C] as it is worthy for the Lord to give through his Spirit.

## CHAPTER IV

> “Therefore, having this ministry, according as we have received mercy, we do not lose heart; but we renounce the hidden things of shame, not walking in craftiness, nor adulterating the word of God, but by the manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every human conscience before God.”

From this, therefore, we ought to infer how much greater are the gifts which the heavenly clemency of grace has bestowed upon us than upon the Jews. For the Jews, although the glory of Moses’ face was lesser, could not behold it; but we believe that we shall see not Moses’ inferior glory, but the surpassing [Col. 1032D] glory of the Saviour. The Jews did not deserve to see the glory of a servant; but we shall see the glory of the Lord of all.

Therefore, having this ministry of the Lord, which advances us to such great glory, and having it according to the mercy we have received—that is, possessing it not from merits but from God’s mercy, which washed and justified us and made us his ministers—we do not lose heart in afflictions because of the hope of glory we await. Nor is the strength of our spirit diminished; rather, amid adversities we steadfastly fulfil the office of our ministry.

We do not lose heart because of any adversities, but renounce—that is, deny and put far away from ourselves—the hidden things of shame [Col. 1033A]: hidden acts of wickedness that produce disgrace and reproach, and are therefore done in secret, lest in public they bring shame upon those who practise them. “For everyone who does evil hates the light” (John II). And: “It is shameful even to speak of the things done by them in secret” (Eph. V). These are the hidden things of shame which we wholly renounce.

Or the hidden things of shame are thoughts of some shameful deed, or things devised by a person of perverse intention for preaching, in order to deceive hearers. For it contributes to the shame and disfigurement of one who craftily invents teaching with the intention of deceiving simple hearts. These words are directed against the false apostles, who did not have unveiled faces or the ministry of the New Testament; and if tribulation came upon them, they immediately lost heart. Though outwardly they displayed the appearance of religion, inwardly they did not renounce hidden shameful things; rather, they turned shameful matters over in their thoughts and committed them in secret places.

“We are not,” he says, “walking in craftiness”—that is, hypocrisy—like the false apostles mentioned above, who seem humble and religious before people. For they walk in craftiness when they do not reveal their hidden practices but display an image of holiness: although they receive nothing themselves, they allow everything to be given to their servants, through whom they know that all things will return to their own use. Nor are we adulterating God’s word as they do: that is, we do not preach for the pleasure of human praise or earthly gain, nor do we corrupt truth by an admixture of falsehood.

We do not do these perverse things, but commend ourselves [Col. 1033C] in the manifestation of truth, because we make manifest the truth that had been covered by Moses’ veil, and thus render ourselves worthy of commendation without comparison with our opponents. That is to say: the truth which we make manifest renders us ourselves commendable. And this is done before every human conscience, so that the conscience of those who understand reasonably may know that we, who so plainly hope in the truth, ought gladly to be received by all.

This commendation takes place before God, for his praise and good pleasure, since we commend ourselves to people for this purpose: that they may see our good works and glorify not us but our Father who is in heaven (Matt. V). Or we act before God because he himself is witness that we make manifest the pure truth, [Col. 1033D] from whose eyes nothing is hidden.

> “But if our Gospel is indeed veiled, it is veiled among those who perish, in whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that the illumination of the Gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, may not shine.”

Provenance: draft routed to GPT-5.6 Sol; actual draft-model identity is unverified. Independently reviewed against the supplied canonical source by GPT-5.6 Terra.  
Coverage: This supplied source chunk; the volume remains in progress.

Source preparation: supplied local source; recovery count 2.

We indeed preach with unveiled face and make the truth manifest. But if our Gospel is also veiled, it is veiled in those who are perishing, not in those who are being saved. For unbelievers or false apostles do not understand our preaching, but the faithful, through God’s revelation, know and understand it. The unbelieving, however, who are tending toward perdition, cannot see the things we say, because a veil of error and ignorance lies over their heart. In [Col. 1034A] those who are perishing—that is, in their heart—the Gospel of our preaching is covered by the veil of their own blindness.

In these perishing people God has blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this age. God has blinded the minds of unbelievers, he who also sent his Son saying: “I came for judgment, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9). He blinded them not through malice but through wisdom. For there is no injustice in him to whom it is said: “I will sing mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Psalm 100). Thus he illumines through mercy and blinds through judgment, which is wholly just even though wholly hidden. Something hidden comes first among hidden things, where he carries out the most just examination of his judgment, so that the minds of some are blinded and those of others illumined; to him it was said with complete truth: “Your judgments [Col. 1034B] are a great abyss” (Psalm 35).

The just God, therefore, blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this age, that is, made them wholly blind. In Adam they had already been blinded in a certain measure, but not so completely that they could not have looked upon their Creator if they had wished. Because they refused, God blinded them when he withdrew from them the present light of the Holy Spirit and hid the splendor of his vision. In this way he blinded their minds because of their unbelief, as though saying to them: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah 9, according to the Septuagint). They belonged to this age, that is, they did not belong to that other age where perpetual light and happiness exist.

Alternatively: “the God of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers.” The God whom the apostles preach is called the God of this age so that no one might suppose that some [Col. 1034C] other god exists in this age, where so many evils occur. For our God governs not only invisible creatures but also this visible age, and there is no God besides him, who even uses the malice of the wicked well. He blinded the minds of unbelievers so that the illumination of the Gospel might not shine upon them—that is, so that they might not see the radiance of the Gospel, which illumines the minds of believers, nor perceive that the Gospel is the light by which the faithful are enlightened.

I mean the Gospel of Christ’s glory, because in it are preached the excellence of his divinity and the glory of his resurrection, which unbelievers refuse to hear. They willingly hear the preaching of the shame of his Passion, but they do not believe that the preaching of the glory of his resurrection and divinity is true. This is what it means that the illumination of the Gospel of Christ’s glory does not [Col. 1034D] shine upon them. Christ is the image of God, that is, altogether and in every respect most like the Father, as he himself says: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14). For as the Son is, so is the Father; as great as the Father is, so great is the Son. As the Father has no beginning, neither does the Son. As the Father is eternal and unchangeable, so is the Son. As the Father is God, so is the Son. As the Father is Creator, so is the Son. As the Father knows and can do all things, so does the Son. What the Father is, the Son is also. Because the Son is from the Father and is consubstantial, coeternal, and coequal with him, and like him in every respect, he is rightly called his image.

The Gospel preaches this glory of Christ. Its illumination shines upon the minds of believers, but by God’s just judgment it is [Col. 1035A] hidden from unbelievers. For it is just that light should be hidden from those who close their eyes to it.

“For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord, and ourselves as your servants through Jesus. For God, who commanded light to shine out of darkness” (Genesis 1), “has shone in our hearts to give the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Christ Jesus. But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the sublimity of the power may be God’s and not from us.”

We neither adulterate the Gospel nor commend ourselves in the manifestation of the truth, because we do not preach ourselves but Jesus Christ. That is, our preaching does not aim at our glory or profit, but at the glory of Christ, who is the Savior [Col. 1035B] and King of his people and to whose dominion we willingly submit. We do not proclaim our own glory, as false apostles are accustomed to do, lest anyone say that we evangelize for our own sake, in order to appear glorious and to make a profit for ourselves from your possessions. One who seeks his own advantages does not preach Christ but himself, like those who serve their own belly.

We preach that Jesus is our Lord, but we say that we are servants—that is, your ministers through Jesus, who commanded us to serve you in the ministry of preaching. Although we are ministers, in humility we call ourselves servants, so that it may be apparent that we preach the Gospel not for our own glory but for Christ’s splendor. We obey him when we serve you in [Col. 1035C] the ministry of the word, not because of your merit but because of the Lord’s command. We do this through Jesus, I say, serving you in the ministry of preaching, because God also did greater things for us through him.

The God who at the creation of the world commanded—that is, by his Word, who is his Son, caused—light to shine out of darkness, when he said, “Let there be light, and light was made” (ibid.), is himself the one who has shone in our hearts. He who then made bodily light in the world through his Word has now given spiritual light within us through the same Word. Darkness did not always exist without a beginning. It began to exist when the confused mass of heaven and earth began to be, before this light was made to illuminate what had been dark without light. What inconsistency is there [Col. 1035D] if the beginnings of the world’s matter were dark, so that when light approached, what had been made might be seen better, and in this way the disposition of the one who would later make progress might be signified? Just as visible light took its beginning from darkness, so afterwards did invisible light, to which it was said: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5). Who did this except the one who, when darkness was over the abyss, said: “Let there be light, and light was made” (Genesis 1)?

God, therefore, who in separating the elements commanded—that is, by his Word caused—light to shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts. That is, he caused the light which he himself is to shine in our hearts, for the illumination of the knowledge of God’s glory: namely, so that we may illumine others through [Col. 1036A] the knowledge we possess of God’s glory. This is the knowledge of his glory by which we know that he is the light through whom our darkness is illumined, so that we who were once unbelieving in ignorance—that is, in darkness—may now present light to others.

By making light from darkness he signified that he would illumine those who had departed through ignorance into the region of unlikeness and had been placed in darkness; that he would entrust the word of preaching to them; and that in this way he would cause light to shine from darkness. He has therefore shone in our hearts so that we too may shine for you, in order that you may receive the illumination of the knowledge of God’s glory in the face—that is, in the recognition—of Christ Jesus, because each person is recognized by the face. He has shone upon our minds.

But we possess this treasure of the riches of eternal [Col. 1036B] wisdom in earthen vessels, that is, in earthly and fragile bodies. This treasure is the mystery of God in Christ, which is dispensed to believers but hidden from unbelievers. We possess in earthen vessels this treasure by which we enrich others and through which we frequently work signs—that is, in earthly bodies through which we ourselves are weakened, although we often confer health upon others—so that the sublimity of our miraculous works and preaching may belong to God’s power and not come from us. In other words, it may be evident that this comes from God’s power and not from our strength.

This would not be so evident if this treasure had been entrusted to angels to dispense. It was therefore entrusted to weak human beings to dispense to others, so that the sublimity of this treasure—[Col. 1036C] such wisdom, such eloquence, such a display of miracles, such constancy amid tribulations—might be understood to belong to God’s power and not to us. Earthen vessels signify the weakness of human nature, which can do nothing unless it receives power from God. Thus, to his own praise, God preaches himself through weak vessels, so that glory may be given to him rather than to the human being formed from clay (Genesis 2).

“In every way we suffer tribulation, but we are not distressed. We are at a loss, but we are not abandoned. We suffer persecution, but we are not forsaken. We are humbled, but we are not confounded. We are cast down, but we do not perish.”

From this it is proved that we are fit to enlighten others and to dispense the divine treasure: in [Col. 1036D] every place, or under every form, we suffer tribulation, yet we are not distressed in mind—that is, we are not so crushed that we become fainthearted and give way. We are afflicted under every form of tribulation, since in our bodies we endure chains, prisons, beatings, and the other kinds of tribulation. Yet we are not distressed; rather, we are enlarged with a greater breadth of heart, so that charity may reign within and the soul’s freedom may range widely, possessing in itself the riches of the heavenly treasure with which it may enrich the poverty of others as well.

We are *at a loss* (*aporiamur*), that is, we suffer want. For πορία in Greek means means or abundance, while ἀ is privative. We are *at a loss*, that is, we are left without gain, for *aporia* is the stripping away of all goods. We are therefore at a loss—that is, deprived of bodily goods—but we are not [Col. 1037A] abandoned, because God supplies what we need.

Or, *aporiamur* means that we sweat in our labor. For we call the openings through which sweat comes out *poroi*, and hence one who is *aporiatus* is so called as one who sweats. Thus we are at a loss—that is, we sweat amid the labor of tribulations—but we are not abandoned by God, who strengthens us lest we fail. Or again, we are *aporiamur*, as though we were made without pores, that is, without sweat, when the constraint of poverty makes us contract as if with cold. Yet we are not cut off from the heavenly treasure that we have in earthen vessels.

We suffer persecution—that is, we are driven in flight from place to place—but we are not forsaken into the hands of our enemies, so that they may satisfy themselves upon us [Note: [Col. 1037D] Something appears to be missing here.]. We are cast down—that is, knocked to the ground by blows—but we do not perish, that is, we are not put to death. Or, *we do not perish* means that we do not cease from [Col. 1037B] confessing and preaching the truth. For our perishing would occur if, just as they exercise dominion over our flesh, they were also to exercise dominion over our preaching.

“Always carrying about in our body the dying of Jesus Christ, so that the life of Jesus too may be manifested in our bodies. For we who live are always being handed over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus too may be manifested in our mortal flesh. Therefore death works in us, but life in you.”

Why should we enumerate one by one the things we suffer? We are always *carrying about*—that is, bearing outwardly and openly, and displaying to others as an example—in our body the dying of Jesus, namely [Col. 1037C] the death that Jesus endured for us and left for us to endure. We always carry this about in our body because, in imitation of him, we continually mortify the flesh, so that we may also furnish others an example of abstinence. We do this so that the life of Jesus, just like his dying now—that is, the glorious immortality of the resurrection—may be manifested in our bodies to everyone, even to our enemies.

See how we carry about the dying of Jesus: we who live inwardly through the observance of righteousness are always handed over to death—that is, to dangers of death—for the sake of Jesus, whom we preach. Or, *we who live are always handed over to death* means that, although we possess this present life and could go on living, we never refuse to be handed over to death for the sake of [Col. 1037D] our Lord Jesus. This is so that the life of Jesus—the life that he himself has possessed ever since he rose—may be manifested to all in our flesh, which is now mortal.

And because we carry his dying about in our outward man and do not refuse to be handed over to death for his name, in order that we may also share in his life, the death by which we die daily for the Savior is therefore not useless. Rather, it works something great in us: the life of everlasting felicity. Conversely, however, the life in which you take delight among earthly things works eternal death in you. This is said as a rebuke. We die daily to this world so that we may live to God; you live to the world so that you may die to God. Death works—that is, exercises dominion—in [Col. 1038A] us; you strive after the pleasures of life.

“But possessing the same spirit of faith, as it is written, ‘I believed, and therefore I spoke’ (Ps. 115), we too believe, and therefore we also speak, knowing that he who raised Jesus will also raise us with Jesus and will set us with you. For all things are for your sake, so that grace, abounding through many, may abound in thanksgiving to the glory of God.”

Death is indeed always at work in us, but we do not cease to speak the faith of Christ for which we die. This is what it means that we possess the same spirit of faith that the prophets possessed, as it is written in the words of David: “I believed, and therefore I spoke.” In the same way, we too believe, and therefore we also speak, [Col. 1038B] that is, we bring forth our faith in the confession of our mouth.

We possess the same spirit of faith. He does not say “the knowledge of faith,” but “the spirit of faith.” He said this so that we might understand that even faith is granted before it is asked for, so that through it other things may be granted to the one who asks: “For how shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed?” (Rom. 10). Thus the Spirit of grace causes us to possess faith, so that through faith we may obtain by prayer the power to do what we are commanded.

This same faith held the hearts of those who came before and filled the hearts of those who followed. Those spiritual fathers believed that almighty God is the Trinity just as the new fathers spoke openly of that same Trinity. The same faith in Christ’s incarnation also saved them by which we too are saved. For just as we believe that he came, suffered, [Col. 1038C] and rose again, so they believed that he would come, would suffer, and would rise again. The times changed, not the faith.

For we possess the same spirit of faith that they possessed, as it is written in their books: “I believed, and therefore I spoke”—that is, I believed perfectly. Those who are unwilling to speak what they believe do not believe perfectly. Indeed, it belongs to that very faith to believe also what was said: “Whoever acknowledges me before men, I too shall acknowledge him before my Father; but whoever denies me before men, I shall deny him before the angels of God” (Matt. 10). Rightly, therefore, he does not say, “I believed and I spoke,” but says that he spoke *because* he believed. For at the same time he both believed in what he should first hope for by speaking and believed that he ought not to fear the punishment incurred by keeping silent. [Col. 1038D]

They believed, and therefore they spoke. We too believe, and therefore we also speak. This is preeminently the voice of the martyrs. For if they had merely believed and had not spoken, they would not have been sought out. By believing they laid hold of life, and by speaking they found death—but a death in which the corruptible body would be sown and incorruption reaped.

No fear of torments makes us omit speaking the things we believe, because we know with certainty that he who raised Jesus will also raise us after we have died for confessing faith in him, placing us in the same glory, and will set us in that land of the living, so that we may die no more. And he will set us there with you, [Col. 1039A] so that those who possess one faith may be in one kingdom. He will set *us with you*, not you with us, so that, if you are willing, you may be not below us but our equals.

And rightly do we assert this concerning you. For everything we do is for your instruction: whatever we say and whatever we suffer, we do entirely for your salvation, so that by our example we may spur you to undergo the like and lead you to the banquet of God. Thus all the things about which we keep silent also look toward your good, so that God’s grace, abounding in us, may abound through many—that is, through you—and be multiplied far and wide through others in thanksgiving, so that in adversity and prosperity alike you may always give thanks to God, or may return thanks to him for us, since through us he pours his grace into you. And may this grace abound to the glory of God, so that he may be glorified by all.

For this reason [Col. 1039B] we do everything: so that the abounding, that is, copious, gift of God—which he is prepared to give to all, though not all are worthy to receive it—may not be diminished by being confined to a few but may abound through many in thanksgiving to the glory of God. For it is God’s glory that many should return thanks to him for the magnitude of the lavish gift of his grace.

“For this reason we do not fail. But although our outward man is corrupted, nevertheless the inward man is renewed from day to day. For that which is momentary and light in our present tribulation works in us, beyond measure and on high, an eternal weight of glory, while we contemplate not the things that are seen but the things that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things [Col. 1039C] that are not seen are eternal.”

We possess the hope of the blessed resurrection, and we strive to spread God’s abundant grace through many to his glory. For this reason we do not fail amid adversities, but steadfastly fulfill our office. We do not fail, however grave the things we suffer.

Although that man of ours who is outwardly exposed to evils—namely, the body—is corrupted by hardships, blows, hunger, thirst, cold, and nakedness, nevertheless the one who is inward, namely the protected soul, which human fury cannot reach, is renewed in the knowledge of God from day to day; that is, it is continually made purer by the fire of tribulation. Or *from day to day* means advancing from brightness to brightness. The inward man signifies the spirit of the mind, [Col. 1039D] while the outward signifies the body and mortal life.

Yet the Apostle is never found to have called these two together two men, but one man whom God made whole—that is, both what is inward and what is outward. But this whole man, in both his inward and outward parts, grew old because of sin and was condemned to the penalty of mortality. He is now renewed according to the inward man, where he is reformed according to the image of his Creator. In the resurrection, however, the outward man too will receive the dignity of a heavenly condition.

The renewal of the inward man begins with faith, is increased by good conduct, and is strengthened from day to day. For the renewal of one’s manner of life does not take place in a single moment as the remission of sins takes place in a single moment in baptism. Indeed, not even one sin, however slight, [Col. 1040A] remains unforgiven. But just as it is one thing to be free of fevers and another to recover from the weakness caused by the fevers; and again, it is one thing to remove a lodged weapon from the body and another, by a second treatment, to heal the wound it caused: so the first cure is to remove the cause of the sickness, which occurs through the forgiveness of all sins; the second is to heal the sickness itself, which occurs by gradually advancing in the renewal of this image.

These two cures are shown in the psalm where it is sung: “Who forgives all your iniquities” (Ps. 102), which takes place in baptism. And it adds: “Who heals all your infirmities” (ibid.), which takes place through daily advances as this image is renewed more and more. For it has not yet been wholly renewed. It is renewed [Col. 1040B] each day by advancing in holiness, when it transfers its love from temporal to eternal things, from visible to intelligible things, and from carnal to spiritual things, and diligently persists both in curbing and restraining its desire for the former and in binding itself to the latter through charity.

The body, as the outward man, is increasingly corrupted the longer it remains in this life, whether by age, disease, or various afflictions, until it comes to the last affliction, which all call death. Because, therefore, the more the saints fail outwardly, the more they advance inwardly, and the more adversities they endure outwardly, the more truly they shine inwardly with light, they rightly say that although our outward man is corrupted, nevertheless the inward man is renewed from day to day.

And so, they say, we do not fail under hardships, because this amount of our tribulation—that is, the little tribulation that we now suffer, which belongs to the present, namely to the time of this life in which no one is without afflictions—is momentary, that is, lasts a short while, and is light to endure; it works in us, that is, in our outward man, eternal glory, and this beyond measure, that is, beyond the whole extent of our tribulation. [Col. 1040C] For through small labors a great reward is acquired, so that for the humiliation of a light tribulation the height of eternal glory is repaid beyond measure. Compared with eternity, everything we suffer in the present life is momentary, although it may seem long-lasting.

The greatness of the reward is beyond the measure of tribulation because, if we judge rightly, eternal rest would have had to be purchased by eternal labor; yet in his mercy God gives eternal rest for the briefest labor, and everlasting glory for brief contempt. [Col. 1040D] Thus it is beyond measure. Or *beyond measure* means beyond the measure and comprehension of human reason, “because what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, will be given” (Isa. 64; 1 Cor. 2).

It works for us *unto height*, that is, so that we may be raised as high as the elevation of the angels; or *on high*, that is, in the height of heaven. And in contrast to the momentary and light character of tribulation, it works an eternal weight of glory in return for tribulation, so that for the momentary we may receive the eternal, for the light a weight, and for tribulation glory. This glory will be without end; this rest will be without end; this joy will be without end; this reward and incorruption will be without end. [Col. 1041A]

Therefore we reckon as nothing every hardship we endure in the present age, while we do not contemplate—that is, do not desire or attend to—the things that are seen, namely those subject to bodily eyes, but rather those that cannot be seen bodily. For these visible things quickly pass away with time, while invisible things remain without end. These visible things stand in relation to invisible things as a figure does to the truth. The figure passes away; the truth remains. For this reason the righteous rejoice to depart from this age.

CHAPTER V

“For we know that if our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved, we have a building [Col. 1041B] from God, a house not made by hands but eternal in the heavens. For in this too we groan, longing to be clothed over with our habitation that is from heaven, provided, however, that we are found clothed and not naked. For we who are in this tent also groan under our burden, because we do not wish to be stripped but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. But he who fashions us for this very thing is God, who has given us the pledge of the Spirit.”

We do not fail amid momentary and light tribulations because of the eternal weight of glory that we await. For we know that if our earthly house—that is, the flesh that comes from the earth, inclines toward earthly things, and is the dwelling of the soul during this present habitation [Col. 1041C] in which we dwell as long as we live—is dissolved, that is, destroyed for Christ’s sake, we know that we immediately have a building from God, namely a blessed dwelling: an eternal house in the heavens, not constructed by hand but prepared by God. Or, once driven from our temporal and earthly house, we are received into an eternal and heavenly house.

For after the preachers of the Church pass from their bodies, their reception of the heavenly homeland is by no means deferred through an interval of delay as it was for the ancient fathers; rather, as soon as they depart from the bond of the flesh, they rest in a heavenly dwelling, as this sentence demonstrates. For it does not say, “We *shall have* an eternal house in the heavens,” but “We *have* one,” because that house is indeed possessed [Col. 1041D] as soon as this one is dissolved.

Before our Redeemer by his death discharged the penalty of the human race, however, the confines of hell held even those who had followed the paths to the heavenly homeland after their departure from the flesh. This was not so that punishment might afflict them as sinners, but so that, because the Mediator’s intercession had not yet come, the guilt of the first fault might bar from entry into the kingdom those resting in more remote places. Now, however, all the perfect are received immediately into the kingdom.

The eternal house is a heavenly dwelling among the angels, where the changes of the seasons are not found. For it surpasses every distinction and the entire mutable span of time, and for it the good is always to cling to God (Ps. 72). This house is called a building because it is now being built by our good works, [Col. 1042A] so that it may be found ready at the end.

Or understand this eternal house in the heavens as the immortal body in which, once raised, we shall remain forever, and whose form has already been revealed in heaven in the Lord’s body. I call it a house not made by hand because an animal body comes into being through the activity of man and woman, but the spiritual body will come into being through the Spirit without human activity. For we shall not need the union of parents in order to rise as we needed it in order to be born.

This house will be built by divine power when that which was foreshown to Ezekiel comes to pass: “The bones,” he says, “came to the bones, each one to its joint; and sinews and flesh came upon them, and skin was stretched over them from above” (Ezek. 37). Thus the house of our soul will be built without hand when our body [Col. 1042B] is restored whole from the dust at the divine command. And we shall have an eternal house in the heavens.

For the sake of possessing it, we groan—that is, we always have a fresh groaning within: desiring that house, we sigh, and in our prayers we groan over the delay of such rest and glory. I mean that we long to be clothed over with our habitation that is in heaven, namely the glory of immortality. For death is from the earth; resurrection is from heaven.

Yet we long to be clothed over with it on this condition: that when we are clothed by receiving back the body, we may not be found naked, that is, strangers to the promised glory. For the soul must be clothed with the body and must also be clothed over with glory, which is transformation into brightness. In this—that is, in the contemplation and desire of such glory—we groan because of the delay and persevere in prayer, [Col. 1042C] because we long, over and above the renewal of the soul that we have already received, to be clothed with our habitation. That is, we long for the soul to be given a garment not from earth and therefore corruptible, but from heaven and therefore incorruptible and incapable of suffering, after the likeness of heavenly beings. This is provided that in that resurrection we are found clothed with the body, not naked of Christ but clothed with Christ. For immortality will benefit only those who, when clothed with the body, are found clothed with Christ, that is, surrounded with the garment of righteousness.

Nor is it surprising that we groan because we cannot yet reach the beatitude we desire. For we groan even over this lesser matter: that we must be stripped of the body in order to be able to arrive there. This is what he means by saying, [Col. 1042D] “For we who are in this tent”—that is, in this body, which is the soul’s tent so that in it the soul may serve God for a time along the road of the present life—“groan under the burden” of the flesh. And we groan because we do not wish to be stripped of the body, but to be clothed over with the robe of immortality, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life; that is, so that the body itself may be transferred from weakness to immortality without death.

If it could be done, we would wish to become immortal in such a way that immortality itself would come now and change us just as we are, so that this mortal part of ours might be swallowed up by life, and so that the body would not be laid aside through death only to be taken up again at the end. Therefore, although we pass from evils to good things, the passage itself is somewhat bitter because of the union of soul and [Col. 1043A] body and a certain familiar bond and joining together of the two. For this reason, even those who believe that they will live more blessedly after death try to defer the day of death. So powerful is the sweet companionship of flesh and soul. “For no one ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. 5). Therefore the soul is unwilling to depart even for a time from the flesh’s weakness, although it trusts that it will receive the flesh back without weakness for eternity.

Thus we are weighed down by the corruptible body; and knowing that the cause of this burden is not the body’s nature and substance but its corruption, we do not wish to be stripped of the body but to be clothed with its immortality. It will then be the very same body, but because it will not be corruptible, it will not weigh us down. Beneath the earthly tunic we groan; toward the heavenly one [Col. 1043B] we hasten. We wish to receive the latter and do not wish to lay aside the former.

Will this wrong, then, be done to so great a heavenly garment: that it should come upon us over these rags of mortality and corruption, with the latter underneath and the former above, the latter within and the former outside? By no means! We do not wish to be clothed over in such a way that corruption remains beneath incorruption, but so that the mortal may be swallowed up by life—that is, so that life may destroy mortality in us without any injury, and no mortal thing may be anywhere in us: not below, not above, not within, but cast outside.

We groan because we do not wish to be stripped of the body but to possess an immortal body. Yet the one who fashions—that is, who wholly makes and forms—us for this very purpose, so that we groan with desire for an incorruptible body, is [Col. 1043C] not man but God, who has given us the pledge that this will be fulfilled, namely the gift of the Holy Spirit. He has given us the pledge of the Spirit: he has given us the Holy Spirit, who is for us the pledge and certainty of future immortality. For through the Spirit whom he has given us, he causes us to sigh with desire for incorruptible life and makes us certain that we shall attain that life, whose pledge we already possess.

“Therefore we are always confident and know that, while we are in this body, we are away from the Lord. For we walk by faith and not by sight. Yet we are confident and possess the good will rather to be away from the body and to be present with the Lord. And therefore we strive, whether absent or present, to please him.”

[Col. 1043D] Since God causes us to groan in longing for immortal bodies, and has given us the Holy Spirit as the pledge of this, therefore we are always confident; that is, we always dare to wish to lay aside the body, so that we may attain heavenly glory. The will to lay aside the body is called boldness because the matter is difficult and feared by all. Therefore we are bold in putting off the body, because we know that, so long as we are in the mortal body, we are away from home—that is, removed from the Lord—because we do not see him, although he himself is everywhere. For in this respect we are exiles and pilgrims from him: cast far from the face of his contemplation, we suffer the darkness of our blindness in this valley of tears. For the ancient night still weighs upon us, and [Col. 1044A] the just Judge restrains from beholding the brightness of his inner splendor the eyes of this corruptible flesh, which the crafty enemy opened to desire.

For whoever supposes that a person still bearing this mortal life can attain the utterly serene, unchangeable light of truth—when every cloud of bodily and carnal imaginings has been removed and dispelled—and can cleave to it firmly and unwaveringly with a mind wholly detached from, and a manner of life alien to, this life, does not at all understand what he is seeking. Rightly, therefore, are we bold in laying aside the body, so that we may come to the manifest vision of eternal light; for we know that while we are in this corruptible body we are away from home, from the Lord—that is, strangers to that country of the blessed in which God is always seen as he is.

[Col. 1044B] For we walk by faith in things unseen; that is, we make our way toward the country of the living, in which God appears, and not by sight—that is, not by a manifest contemplation of his divinity. Contemplation, indeed, is the reward of faith; through faith hearts are purified for this reward, as it is written: “Purifying their hearts by faith” (Acts 15). Merit is gathered by the believer; the reward is rendered to the one who sees. Therefore one who is away from home and walks by faith is not yet in the country, but is already on the way. But one who does not believe is neither in the country nor on the way. For we walk by faith, and not by sight. Faith is the beginning, so that sight may be attained.

At present we are in the body, away from home, from the Lord and from our native country. But when we reflect upon this, we dare—[Col. 1044C] that is, with boldness we choose this rather—to be separated from the body and presented to the Lord, so that we may see him in the visible manifestation of his divinity and remain with him. For, if it were possible, we would not wish to be unclothed, but to become immortal and be presented to the Lord. But since this cannot occur without being unclothed, we dare to desire to be unclothed, so that we may reach the Lord; and we have good will—that is, we do not murmur at this, but desire it willingly.

We dare, I say, and gladly wish to be away from home—that is, to be removed from the body rather than remain here—so that we may be present with God and cleave to him. For nothing satisfies the soul except the true and certain eternity of incorruptible joy. And because we desire to stand before the Lord, therefore we strive—that is, by every [Col. 1044D] means we can, in heart, word, and deed, we endeavor to please him—whether absent, that is, pilgrims in this present life, or present, that is, dwelling in our native country. This means that we labor to do those things by which we may please him now and in the future. Now we strive, because there is a battle. But when death has been swallowed up in victory (1 Cor. 15), there will no longer be any battle or fall, because there will be no corruption. Therefore we shall no longer strive to please, but shall altogether please the Lord in the land of the living.

> “For we must all be manifested before the judgment-seat of Christ, so that each may bring back the things proper to the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil.”

And I rightly spoke of being present, because we shall all be presented [Col. 1045A] to Christ the Judge; or rather, we rightly strive to please him always, lest by displeasing him at judgment we be condemned. For all of us, whatever our sex, age, or condition, must—that is, necessarily will—have each person’s thoughts, words, and deeds made manifest. There it will be seen what each person is; for now this is only dimly discerned. Everything belonging to us will lie open before the tribunal—that is, before the judicial seat—of Christ, when we stand before God the Judge.

The greatness of the tribunal and judgment must be estimated according to the greatness of the Judge and his authority. For the greater the Judge’s authority, the greater necessarily is the terror of judgment. All without exception will be made manifest before the tribunal of so great a Judge, so that each person, whether just or unjust, may, after the likeness of harvesters, bring back—that is, carry there—[Col. 1045B] the deeds proper to the body, according as he has done them: as he himself performed each deed, whether good or evil. In the same manner and in the same measure in which each person has performed any work, he will recite it for judgment before the tribunal of the eternal Judge.

Each will bring back the things proper to the body; that is, what he did or thought while he was in the body. For if someone blasphemes with a malicious mind and impious thought, and does not perform this by any bodily members, he is not therefore free from guilt because he did not do it by bodily movement, since he did it during the time in which he bore the body. According as each has acted with mind, tongue, or hand while in the body, each will render account—even little children, who acted not by themselves but through others. For if they die at that early age, they are certainly judged according to the deeds proper to the body: that is, according to what they did while in the body, when through the hearts and mouths of those acting for them they believed or did not believe; when they were baptized or not baptized; when they ate or did not eat Christ’s flesh; when they drank or did not drink his blood.

[Col. 1045C] Therefore they are judged according to the things they did in the body, not according to what they would have done had they lived here for a long time. Nor do the benefits which we perform in commending the departed conflict with this apostolic statement, because each person acquired this very merit while living in the body: that such acts might be able to benefit him. For they do not benefit everyone. And why do they not benefit everyone, except because of the difference in the life which each lived in the body? [Col. 1045D] Those whom they do benefit are benefited either so that there may be full remission, or at least so that the condemnation itself may become more tolerable.

> “Knowing therefore the fear of the Lord, we persuade people; but we are manifest to God, and I hope that we are manifest also in your consciences. We do not again commend ourselves to you, but give you an occasion to glory on our behalf, so that you may have an answer for those who glory in appearance and not in heart.”

And because we must all be made manifest before Christ the Judge, so that each may receive according to what he has done, therefore, knowing this, we persuade people concerning the fear of the Lord: that is, we urge them, in every [Col. 1046A] thing they now do, to fear the Lord’s future judgment and to desist from wicked works, lest they begin to fear when they can no longer escape condemnation. Or, since all must be manifested before the tribunal of Christ the Judge, knowing the fear of the Lord—that is, knowing how greatly the Lord is to be feared in his judgment, since he will examine minutely the deeds and thoughts of each person—we urge people to fear and provide for themselves, lest they incur the judgment of condemnation.

We indeed urge this upon people, but we are manifest to God if we act otherwise than we teach: that is, God knows whether what we urge upon others is in us, and with what intention we make this exhortation. We know that we are manifest to God, who sees our hidden things; but I hope also that we are not manifest in your consciences. Their purity was evident to the Corinthians, because they had never been detected in flattery; their preaching had not displeased the saints; nor had they attempted, as is customary, secretly to extract anything from any of them, so as to appear outwardly simple before crowds while inwardly being deceitful. Therefore he appeals to their consciences, so that they might bear witness to themselves concerning the truth.

[Col. 1046B] It is as though he said openly in other words: “Although destructive persons may have spoken evil of us to you, I nevertheless think that your conscience does not admit suspicions about us other than what it knows, nor can you give more credence to others than to yourselves.” And because he appeared at that point to be praising himself, he adds: “We do not again commend ourselves to you.” That is, just as we did not commend ourselves to you in the first letter, as you supposed, [Col. 1046C] so neither do we now commend ourselves in this one; for by these things we say we do not seek praise for ourselves from you. Rather, for your benefit, by these words we give you an occasion—that is, matter—for glorying on our behalf against the false apostles: so that you may glory because you received from us the sound teaching of pure truth and rejected the deceptive preaching of the false apostles.

Or: glory on our behalf, because you know that we please God, so that you may have an occasion of glorying against those who glory in appearance and not in heart—that is, against the false apostles, who through hypocrisy glory in an appearance of piety and not in purity of heart. Or “in appearance” means in outward matters, that is, they glory in carnal observances, and not in heart—that is, in spiritual things done in the inward person. [Col. 1046D] The false apostles seemed to stir the Corinthians’ minds to hatred of the Apostle, so that apostolic faith might more easily slip away from their hearts; and many boasted that they had learned from other apostles who had always been with the Lord. Therefore he now says that he gives them an occasion—that is, a reason—by which they might glory against such people: because he was an apostle, from whom these others also had learned, just as those men boasted that they had been taught by the apostles from whom they claimed instruction. Such glorying was in appearance, not in heart, because they gloried in persons rather than truth.

> “For whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober-minded, it is for you. For the love of Christ urges us, [Col. 1047A] judging this: that if one died for all, then all died. And Christ died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose again for them.”

You may, he says, glory concerning us, because whatever we do is either for God’s honor or for our neighbor’s benefit. For if we are beside ourselves, going beyond all temporal things so as to contemplate eternal things, we do this for God; if we are sober-minded—that is, if we come down from that intoxication of mind to common understanding—this is for you, that is, for your benefit. The mind’s excess is its attention to things above, so that lower things somehow slip from memory. All the saints were in this excess of mind when God’s mysteries, transcending this world, were revealed to them. Of this [Col. 1047B] excess it is now said: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God.” For in being beside himself, the Apostle was beside himself for God.

For, surpassing in mind every human frailty, every temporal condition of the age, and all passing things that vanish by being born and dying, he dwelt in heart, insofar as he could, in a certain ineffable contemplation. Of this he says that he heard ineffable words which it is not permitted for a human being to speak (below, ch. 12). Therefore, if he had always wished to remain in what he had seen and could not speak, he would not raise up others so that they too might be able to see it. He therefore descended for their lifting up. This is what is added: “Or whether we are sober-minded, it is for you.” What does “we are sober-minded” mean? “We speak in such a way that you are able to grasp it.”

[Col. 1047C] The Apostle did these things, and good pastors ought to do them, because love then rises wonderfully to lofty things when it mercifully draws the lowly condition of neighbors to itself; and the more graciously it descends to the lowest things, the more powerfully it returns to the highest. “We are sober-minded,” he says, “for you. For the love of Christ urges us to act in this way.” For Christ’s love, which raises the minds of the saints to things above, also, by devout governance for the sake of brotherly love, forms them to the humility of condescension.

Thus it is said: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; whether we are sober-minded, it is for you. For the love of Christ urges us.” This means: If we wished only to do and contemplate the things which we behold in the mind’s excess, we would not be with you, but would remain in heavenly things as though despising you. And when would you, with feeble step, follow us to those higher and inward things, unless, as Christ’s love again urges us, we considered him “who, being in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2)? We should consider that we are servants and, not being ungrateful to him from whom we have received higher things, should not despise lower things on account of those who are weak, but should accommodate ourselves to those who cannot see sublime things with us.

[Col. 1047D] This, then, is “whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God.” For he sees what we see in the mind’s excess; he alone reveals his secrets. But it benefits you when we are sober-minded: that is, when we descend from that excess of mind which intoxicates the mind itself and changes it from the awareness of temporal things to common understanding, so that we may be understood by you. The love of Christ [Col. 1048A] urges us to incline toward you, judging this: that if one Christ died for all who were predestined to life, then all died by participation in his death with respect to what they previously were—that is, insofar as they had been members of the old man. Therefore we ought willingly to incline toward those who have already died with Christ through baptism.

Or: if one Christ died for all, that is, so that all might live, then it necessarily follows that all were dead in soul through sin, since their enlivening was sought by the death of the one who alone lacked sin and could not share in the soul’s death. Therefore we ought to humble ourselves in instructing those for whose enlivening the Savior deigned to bow down even to death. Thus [Col. 1048B] all were dead in sins, with absolutely no one excepted, apart from the Mother of God, whether by original sins or also by those voluntarily added, whether through ignorance or knowingly, and by not doing what is right. And for all who were dead, the one Christ died: he who had no sin at all and who alone was a sufficient offering for the sins of all, so that those who live through the remission of sins might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them all because of our sins and rose again because of our justification; so that, believing in him who justifies the ungodly (Rom. 4), justified from ungodliness and as though made alive from death, we may belong to the first resurrection, which is now.

Therefore let no one live for himself, but for Christ, doing not his own will but Christ’s, so that he may say: “Now it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me,” and “my soul shall live for him.” For him, certainly, not for itself. Human life ought to fail in itself and advance in Christ, who died so that we might die to sins and rose again so that we might rise to works of righteousness. And what else does it mean that they live not for themselves but for him, except that they should live not according to the flesh in hope of earthly and corruptible goods, but according to the Spirit in hope of the resurrection, which has already been accomplished for them in Christ? (Gal. 2; Ps. 21.)

> “Therefore from now on we know no one according to the flesh. And even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him thus.”

In his customary manner, the Apostle so meditates upon our future life—which has already been completed in Christ, our risen Head, [Col. 1048D]—with certain hope as though it were already present and held in hand. That life, indeed, will not be according to the flesh, just as Christ’s is not according to the flesh. Here he wishes “flesh” to be understood not as the substance of our body itself, but as the corruption and mortality of flesh, which then will not be in us, just as it is no longer in Christ.

“Because,” he says, “Christ’s resurrection has caused us to rise, therefore from this time of resurrection we know no one of those for whom Christ died and rose again, and who now live no longer for themselves but for him, according to the flesh”—that is, according to the corruption of flesh—because of the hope of future immortality in expectation of which they live, a hope which in Christ is no longer hope but reality. And even if we have known [Col. 1049A] Christ according to the flesh—that is, according to the mortality of flesh, when he was still to die—yet now we no longer know him thus, because that mortal element in him has now put on immortality.
