Therefore we knew Christ according to the flesh, that is, according to the mortality of flesh, before he rose; but now we no longer know him thus, because “having risen from the dead, he dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6).

For if, according to the heretics, Christ did not have flesh because the Apostle says that he now no longer knows Christ according to the flesh, then neither did those persons have flesh of whom he said beforehand: “Therefore from now on we know no one according to the flesh.” But because, as we said, he meditated with them upon the future life as though present—the life in which they, when risen, will be changed—he says: “From now on we know no one according to the flesh”; that is, we hold so certain a hope of our future incorruption and immortality that we already rejoice in this knowledge itself.

> “Therefore, if anyone is a new creation in Christ, the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (Rev. 21). “But all things are from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation. For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, not reckoning their trespasses against them, and he placed in us the word of reconciliation. Therefore we act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us. We beseech you for Christ: be reconciled to God. Him who knew no sin, he made sin for us, so that we might [Col. 1049C] become the righteousness of God in him.”

And because Christ is now no longer according to the flesh, nor is anyone who lives for him, therefore if any new creation—that is, if anyone renewed—can be in Christ, it is now clear that the old things of corruption have passed away, and behold, all things of immortality have become new. Since all of us in Christ, though not yet in reality, are nevertheless immortal already in hope, old things have passed away and all things have become new.

Therefore every new creation—that is, the people renewed through faith—so that it may meanwhile possess in reality what will later be completed in hope, already has in Christ what it hopes for in itself. Thus old things have now passed away according to hope, because this is no longer the time of the Old Testament, when a temporal and carnal kingdom is expected from God; [Col. 1049D] and all things have become new according to the same hope, so that we hold fast the promised kingdom of heaven, where there shall be no death or corruption.

But in the resurrection of the dead this will be not according to hope but according to reality: old things will pass away when death, the last enemy, is destroyed; and all things will become new when this corruptible thing puts on incorruption and this mortal thing immortality. This has already happened in Christ, whom the Apostle already knew in reality, not according to the flesh. But of those for whom he died and rose again, he knew no one according to the flesh—not yet in reality, but in hope.

[Col. 1050A] Yet morally also, the old things—that is, the vices of the old man—have passed away, and all things have become new—that is, the works of the new man. To the old man belong seeking the present world, loving transitory things through desire, raising the mind in pride, lacking patience, out of malicious grief plotting a neighbor’s injury, not giving one’s goods to the needy, seeking another’s possessions in order to increase one’s own, loving no one purely for God’s sake, repaying enmities to enemies, and rejoicing at a neighbor’s affliction. All these belong to the old man, which we draw from the root of corruption. But of one who already overcomes these things and changes his mind in kindness toward the Lord’s commandments, it is rightly said: “Old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new.” For new things then come about in our minds when the vices of the old man have passed away from us.

I said that there is a new creation in Christ and that all things have become new. Yet all these new things, whether they consist in conduct, hope, or reality, are from God the Father. All things which we have through Christ or in Christ are from the Father, because Christ himself is from the Father. There is no newness from ourselves; all things are from God, who reconciled us, formerly enemies, to himself through Christ the Mediator.

[Col. 1050B] Since human nature had sinned against God and was not repenting in order to return to him, God, unwilling that his work should perish, sent his Son. Through him, by the preaching of forgiveness of sins, he reconciled humanity to himself through the very one through whom he had created it. Through Christ he reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of reconciliation: that is, he entrusted to us an embassy, so that, traveling throughout the world, we might minister everywhere the teaching of the Gospel, by observance of which all might be reconciled to God and restored to friendship.

Truly, through him and through us he gave reconciliation to human beings. For God himself was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, and he placed in us the word of reconciliation. God was in Christ, who said: “The Father abiding in me, he himself does the works” (John 14). For the Father is in the Son because their substance is one. Therefore God was in Christ as he moved among human beings, reconciling the world to himself—that is, people from the world—for whom Christ himself said: “That the world may believe that you sent me” (John 17).

[Col. 1050C] Here “world” does not mean the world which lies wholly in the evil one, but the world for which God sent his Son (1 John 5), [Col. 1050D] so that the world might be saved through him (John 3): that is, the Church established throughout the world’s breadth. God reconciled this world to himself in this way: by not reckoning their trespasses against them in order to punish them for these, but by forgiving in baptism all sins, both original and actual. He was in Christ by nature, but in us by grace, because he placed in us—that is, in our inner being—the word, that is, the preaching, of reconciliation. This is: through the Holy Spirit he enlightened our hearts and taught us the means by which we might reconcile people to him, converting them to faith, repentance, and good works.

And since after Christ he placed us as reconcilers, therefore we act as ambassadors for Christ—that is, in Christ’s place we discharge God’s embassy. Christ himself was properly the Father’s ambassador, but we act as ambassadors in his stead, so that in his place we may preach reconciliation to the nations. We discharge God’s embassy to you, as though God were exhorting you through us to reconciliation. For he himself speaks in us, and the words which have proceeded from our mouth are his words; therefore you ought willingly to obey us.

[Col. 1051A] And because we are sent in Christ’s place, we beseech you for Christ—that is, as though Christ himself were beseeching you—be reconciled to God. We beseech you—that is, we adjure you by all holy things—to be reconciled to God through repentance, since by sin you are his enemies. For no one is reconciled except from enmity, and nothing produces enmity between God and human beings except sin.

Often a person who is angry with another person desires reconciliation with the one who is at variance with him, but is ashamed to go first and make satisfaction. Let us consider the deeds of truth, so that we may see where the perversity of our conduct lies. Behold, by sinning we made discord between ourselves and God; yet God first sent his ambassadors to us, so that we ourselves who sinned might come, when invited, to God’s peace. Let human pride therefore be ashamed. Let each person be confounded if he does not make satisfaction to his neighbor, when, after our fault, God himself—the offended party—by the intervention of ambassadors beseeches us to be reconciled to him.

But how could we be reconciled to him unless the sin which stood between us and him and separated us from him were blotted out? Accordingly, when the Apostle had said, “We beseech you for Christ: be reconciled [Col. 1051C] to God,” as if we were to ask, “How can we be reconciled to God?”, he added: “Him who knew no sin”—that is, Christ, who did not know sin by experience, although he knew it by wisdom—“God the Father made sin for us,” that is, a sacrifice for sin. Therefore we can fittingly be reconciled to him who blots out all our sin by the blood of his Christ, if we condemn that sin by repentance.

Christ indeed did not know sin because he never experienced the delight of sin. Yet by the wisdom through which he condemns sin, he knows sin: that is, he knows it to be evil. Therefore he did not commit sin, but God made him sin for us—that is, as I said, a sacrifice for sin. For in the Law the sacrifices offered for sins were called “sins.” In the same manner of speech Christ is now called “sin,” because he was offered for sin. The likeness of sinful flesh in which he came was also called “sin”: “God,” he says, “sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and through sin condemned sin in the flesh” (Rom. 8), that is, through the likeness of sinful flesh, which was his own, he condemned sin in the flesh of sin, which is ours.

[Col. 1051D] Therefore God made him who knew no sin—that is, Christ—sin for us, to whom we must be reconciled: that is, a sacrifice for sins, through which we might be able to be reconciled. He made him sin so that we might become the righteousness of God in him. Thus he became sin, [Col. 1052A] so that we might become righteousness—not our own, but God’s; not in ourselves, but in him—just as he became sin, not his own sin but ours; not constituted in himself but in us, by the likeness of sinful flesh in which he was crucified. This is that righteousness of God, not the righteousness by which he himself is righteous, but that by which we have been justified by him. “That we might become,” he says, not only righteous, but also righteousness: that is, so that through us others might become righteous. “That we might become the righteousness of God in him,” that is, in his body, which is the Church, of which he is the head (Col. 1).

## Chapter VI

> “And as fellow workers we exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain. For he says: ‘At an accepted time I heard you, and on a day of salvation I helped you’ [Col. 1052B] (Isa. 49). Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.”

God reconciles you to himself through Christ, sacrificed for our sins. But we assist in this work of reconciliation. For we are God’s fellow workers. Assisting the benefit of divine operation by the ministry of our preaching, we exhort you not to receive in vain the grace of God which he offers you. The grace of God is forgiveness of sins. Whoever does not afterward exercise himself in good works receives it in vain. The grace of God is the ability divinely granted to a human being to do good, of which it is said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15). Whoever does not labor with God’s grace or add his own effort, so as to be able with God’s help to fulfill God’s commandments, receives it in vain.

He receives this grace “in vain”—that is, so that it may be an empty thing to him—who does not strive to fulfill it with good works. But, as fellow workers, we exhort you to act well with the help of grace, lest through your negligence you be found to have received it in vain. And, as was said, we do this in assisting the work of heavenly grace and reconciliation; or in assisting you yourselves by our merits, prayers, and words.

Or thus: assisting you by the foregoing causes and arguments—that is, calling you to reconciliation—we exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain; that is, lest, believing false apostles, you receive and understand baptism and the faith which you have accepted in such a way that it becomes vain for you, passing into a thing empty and deprived of every fullness of benefit. For those who think that faith in Christ alone, without carnal observance of the Law, is insufficient for righteousness and eternal salvation understand the grace of God—that is, faith itself—as an empty thing, not filled with innocence and the perfection of all virtues. And as they suppose this grace of faith to be empty, so it becomes empty to them, because through it they obtain neither forgiveness of sins nor any grace.

[Col. 1052D] But you must not receive it in that way; you must not think of it in such a way that it becomes vain to you—that is, empty of every benefit for you. Truly you ought neither to think it empty nor make it empty to yourselves, for it is not empty but full of good works. For God himself, who offers this grace [Col. 1053A] to the human race, says in Isaiah (ch. 49): “At an accepted time”—that is, at a time acceptable to me or to human beings—“I heard you praying for your sins.” Therefore this grace is not empty, since in its time God hears those who pray.

This is a time pleasing to human beings and welcomed with the whole embrace of the heart. For *acceptum* (“accepted”) is more than *acceptabile* (“acceptable”): *acceptabile* denotes what is capable of being received, but *acceptum* what has already been received by the devotion of the mind. And after this time has been accepted by you—that is, after you have embraced it—God hears your prayers, which he did not hear in the time of the Law. “At an accepted time,” he says—that is, in the time of grace, which you accepted when you came to faith—“I heard you pleading for the forgiveness of [Col. 1053B] your sins; and on the day of salvation,” that is, in this same time of grace, in which true salvation came from heaven to human beings and the light of faith and righteousness put to flight the darkness of unbelief and sins, “I helped you in attaining virtues.”

The Law did not help but only commanded. But under grace, he says, God helps us so that we may be able to do the good things which he commands. For he helped us because he himself restored free choice in us; we labor by our free choice, and through the help of divine grace are made able, without which we could do nothing. God spoke this through the prophet to the Church from the nations: “At an accepted time I heard you, and on a day of salvation I helped you.” The Apostle now repeats this to the same Church converted from the nations and adds by way of exposition: “Behold”—that is, that time is deferred no longer, but now, in the present, is the acceptable time, which all ought gratefully to receive, so that they themselves may become acceptable to God; and behold, now, in the present, is the day of salvation, that is, the bright time of grace, in which people can merit eternal salvation through good works.

[Col. 1053C] For since the Savior appeared in flesh, the acceptable time and day of salvation continue until the end of the age. Yet for each person this time ends at the hour of death. For the day of salvation through Christ’s grace is the present life, since it is suited to doing good works; and it will be closed by the night of judgment, in which no one can work. Therefore the Apostle says that the time is at hand in which sinners may advance toward pardon; he says that the day is at hand in which the medicine of salvation may be applied to the mortal diseases of souls. [Col. 1053D] It follows:

> “Giving no offense to anyone, so that our ministry may not be blamed” (1 Cor. 4). “But let us show ourselves in all things as God’s ministers: in much patience, in tribulations, in necessities, in distresses, in beatings, in prisons, in tumults, in labors, in watchings, in fastings, in chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned love, in the word of truth, in the power of God.”

We exhorted you not to receive the grace of God in vain [Col. 1054A], and we exhort you to give offence to no one. Take care that by your evil example or corrupt speech you give any of the brethren occasion for offence; that is, do not cause him to stumble, so that through you he falls into sin. Do not become a stumbling-block to him, so that, offended by the example of your depravity, he falls into wickedness; nor offend him—that is, do not trouble him and provoke him to anger. Therefore see that by evil living or speaking you do not prepare an occasion of offence for any of your neighbours, lest because of you the ministry of our preaching be blamed—we who taught you how you ought to act. For those who see you behaving badly will suppose that we taught you so, and will begin to disparage our teaching. Give offence to no one, I say; rather, let us display ourselves in [Col. 1054B] all things—and you likewise—as ministers of God.

In order to exhort them more effectively, he joins himself to them and, as it were, admonishes himself, because he regards their weakness as his own; and if they make progress, their progress will be his. “Let us display ourselves,” he says; that is, let us offer to God ourselves—myself and you. Therefore, that each person may display himself, let us display—that is, offer and show—ourselves in all things as ministers of God. It is as though he said: I do not exhort you all to be apostles or to undertake the ministry of preaching, but to be as ministers of God; that is, in all things imitate the ministers of divine preaching, so that the likeness of their religious manner of life may be expressed in you. And although we are not all ministers, nevertheless let all of us display ourselves [Col. 1054C] as ministers of God, so that, as they live, we too may live.

Let us do this with patience that is great—that is, enduring many things, neither murmuring against God nor resenting the person who has brought evils upon us. These words are thus spoken generally to all Christians. More particularly, however, they may be addressed to ministers of evangelical preaching in this way: We who exhort others not to receive the grace of God in vain should guard our conduct with careful vigilance, so that we give offence to no one; that is, we ourselves should do what we urge others to do, and should not do what we forbid. Otherwise, if we appear to teach one thing and do another, we shall by our example cause others [Col. 1054D] to stumble. For every weak person pays more attention to the deeds of his superior than to his words, and thinks himself permitted to do whatever he sees him doing. Thus a superior who lives badly, even if he teaches well, provides an occasion of offence to his subjects.

Therefore let us give offence to no one, so that our ministry may not be blamed. For it will be blamed and torn apart by the tongues of detractors, not only if we do the evils that we condemn, but also if we fail to do the goods that we teach. Let us offend no one; rather, in all our words and actions let us display ourselves as becomes ministers of God: so that through our works people may glorify God, and we ourselves may please God inwardly. Let us do this with much patience, by which we may gradually correct the unruly behaviour of the brethren [Col. 1055A] through enduring it, and bravely withstand the persecutions of unbelievers. For what great extent this patience must have is subsequently shown in detail. These commands are given not only to ministers—that is, to the prelates of the Church—but also, as we have said, to those subject to them, who ought in their conduct to resemble good ministers.

“Let us have,” he says, “much patience in tribulations,” that is, in pressures and vexations inflicted upon us by wicked people; “in necessities,” that is, in shortages of food, drink, or clothing; “in distresses,” that is, in anxieties and cares of mind, and fear of punishments, by which the mind is constrained; “in beatings,” that is, in blows such as scourging with rods; “in prisons,” that is, when shut up in dark and foul-smelling places; “in tumults,” that is, in [Col. 1055B] uprisings of the people against us. If the people rise against us and, with some tumult, try to turn us away from good work, let us endure it patiently and not depart from what is good.

But let us also have patience “in labours”: if wicked people compel us to toil through long journeys or burdensome work, or if we seek our livelihood by the labour of our own hands; “in watchings”: if necessity requires us to keep awake so as to work through the night for our living, or in vigils for psalmody and prayer; and “in fastings,” whether we undertake them voluntarily, or are compelled to them by want or by any necessity whatsoever. In all these things let us retain patience and display ourselves as ministers of God. For all who work well are ministers, because they minister to God—that is, serve him.

Therefore, apart from the office of preaching and ministry at the altar, let all of us acknowledge that we are ministers of God, so that, as servants of so great a Lord, we may show ourselves worthy in chastity of mind and body, and in knowledge, lest, like the foolish virgins, we lose through imprudence the merit of chastity [Col. 1055C] (Matt. 25). Let us therefore possess knowledge of the Scriptures, or the knowledge by which we may know how prudently to do good and reject evil. Let us also display ourselves as ministers of God “in long-suffering,” that is, in the long expectation of the mind by which we persevere patiently to the end, bearing the adversities of this present life and hoping for the joys of the life to come.

And let us do so “in kindness,” lest through bitterness of spirit we become harsh toward those whose evils we endure long-sufferingly; rather, through sweetness of mind let us be kind and gentle to them, so that by neither word nor deed do we generate in them or in others the harshness of bitterness. And let us do so “in the Holy Spirit,” so that we do all things benevolently and sincerely, as the Holy Spirit teaches. And let us do so “in unfeigned charity,” so that we may have the affection of love not only in face and speech but also in heart, lest we be among those “who speak peace with their neighbour, while evils are in their hearts” [Col. 1055D] (Ps. 27).

And let us do so “in the word of truth,” in preaching or speaking, so that both our preaching and our speech may possess pure truth without any admixture of falsehood. And let us do so “in the power of God,” believing that whatever good we are able to do is possible not by our own strength but by the gift of divine power. All these things shone most eminently in the Apostle and guided his manner of life [Col. 1056A]; he now exhorts with himself the ministers of the Gospel and all Christ’s servants to endeavour to live in this way. For fervent love of God easily endures every adversity and attains every virtue. The Apostle further adds in his admonition:

> “Through the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left; through glory and dishonour, through ill repute and good repute; as deceivers, yet truthful; as unknown, yet known; as dying, and behold, we live; as chastised, yet not put to death; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as needy, yet enriching many; as having nothing, and possessing all things.”

“Let us display ourselves,” he says, “as ministers of God through the weapons of righteousness,” by which we may subdue the kingdom of sin; that is, through virtues opposed to vices: humility [Col. 1056B] casting down pride, generosity uprooting avarice, goodwill uprooting envy, and in the same way the other virtues destroying their corresponding vices. For virtues are weapons of righteousness, with which we ought to be armed on the right and on the left—that is, on the side of prosperity and on the side of adversity—so that, always fortified with the weapons of virtue against prosperity and adversity, we may neither be raised up by prosperity nor disturbed by adversity; neither softened into pleasure by flattering things nor pressed into despair by harsh things.

Hear what are the right and left—that is, prosperity and adversity: “through glory and dishonour,” and so on through “as having nothing, and possessing all things.” For the right hand of the righteous consists in glory, good reputation, being truthful, being known, living, not being put to death, rejoicing, enriching many, and possessing all things [Col. 1056C]. The left hand, however, consists in being regarded as dishonourable and infamous, being thought deceivers, being unknown, dying, being chastised, being made sorrowful, being needy, and seeming to possess nothing. But soldiers of Christ, armed through the weapons of righteousness on the right and the left, ought to proceed so that, defeating the devil on both sides, they fear amid prosperity and have confidence amid adversity.

Therefore let us display ourselves as ministers of God “through glory and dishonour”: when we are held in glory and veneration among people, let us not be exalted by it; and when they judge us dishonourable and contemptible, let us not be crushed by it. In the same way let us act “through ill repute and good repute”: whether we are falsely defamed for some crime [Col. 1056D] or have a good reputation for religious conduct, let us bear both with equanimity through patience, so that detractors may not cast us down nor praisers raise us up—for sometimes both lie.

Likewise, let us display ourselves “as deceivers, yet truthful”; that is, let us lead those who err to the way of truth, so that the rest, who persist in error, may judge us to be deceivers when we are truthful. For if to deceive is to lead someone by persuasion from one place to another, one must ask from where and to where. If from evil to good, he is a good deceiver; hence Jeremiah says: “You deceived me, Lord, and I was deceived” (Jer. 20). But if someone leads another by deception from good to evil, he is an evil deceiver. Would that all of us might be called and be deceivers in this sense, by which [Col. 1057A] people are led from evil to good. Yet unbelievers, or any who are in error, will call us evil deceivers if we draw any of their companions whom we can to faith and religious conduct. For we shall be truthful and teach what is true, but they will think us false and deceiving others by falsehood.

I say that we are, in the view of some, as persons unknown by God—that is, rejected—and, in the view of others, known by God—that is, approved. Or we are like those who are unknown because unbelievers and the proud do not deign to look upon or acknowledge us, or reject us after acknowledging us; and yet believers and religious persons acknowledge us. Under tortures we are “as dying,” because the impious torment us until we are believed to be dead; and behold, through God’s deliverance, we live, because we are rescued [Col. 1057B] from death and restored to life.

We are “as chastised,” because unbelievers think that with harsh beatings and threats they have chastised us so that we shall no longer preach the new religion; yet we are not put to death, because we have suffered death neither in body nor in soul. For our body still lives; and our soul too has not lost life, because it has not yielded to unbelievers by keeping silence concerning the preaching or confession of the truth. Even if many martyrs are killed, the Church nevertheless does not die. Moreover, when God’s elect fix their minds, snatched upward, on what is above them, they view whatever they suffer in this life as foreign to themselves and falling far beneath them; and, so to speak, while they strive to become in mind outside the flesh, they almost do not know the very things that they endure.

The Apostle speaks thus of himself and those like him [Col. 1057C] in order to exhort all the faithful to endure or do such things. It is as though he said to his disciples: We who are teachers live in this way; you, who ought to imitate us, follow the example of our conduct. He also adds: “as sorrowful”—understand, outwardly we appear sorrowful because of the troubles of tribulations that we endure, but inwardly we are always rejoicing because of hope for future reward. For not only are we not grieved amid adversities, but we even rejoice, and this always.

And we are “as needy,” because we appear to possess nothing in the present age; yet we enrich many, because we bestow spiritual riches upon believers. We are “as having absolutely nothing,” because carnally we have nothing of our own; yet we possess all things [Col. 1057D], that is, not merely money but even the owners of money themselves, who give themselves to us and lay their possessions at our feet. Likewise, even if you appear sorrowful in adversity, nevertheless always rejoice inwardly through hope. And if you have riches, be as needy, though you are not needy; that is, be poor in spirit, but take care to enrich many through the benefits of your alms. Be as having nothing—that is, regarding all that you possess as nothing through contempt of mind—and with such a disposition possess all your things; for then your mind will not be held down in low things by them.

Any holy poor also possess all things, even temporal things, because nothing is lacking to those who fear God. But when the Apostles seemed to have nothing, they possessed all things in this respect: being leaders of the Churches, they had authority to take from the goods of those subject to them whatever was necessary to them [Col. 1058A] (Matt. 10; Mark 6; Luke 9).

It should be noted, however, that in the expressions concerning adversity, the words *as*, *like*, and *as though* are used, whereas in those concerning prosperity they are not. For he says, “as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing,” and so forth. Our sorrow has an “as”; our joy does not have an “as,” because the hope in which we rejoice is certain. But our sorrow has “as,” because it passes away in dreams. One who reports a dream adds “as”: “I seemed to be sitting, I seemed to be speaking, I seemed to be dining, I seemed to be riding, I seemed to be disputing.” It is all “seemed,” because when he awakes he does not find what he saw. “I seemed to have found a treasure,” says the beggar [Col. 1058B]. If it had not been merely seeming, he would not be a beggar. But because it was only seeming, he is a beggar.

Thus, for those who now open their eyes to worldly pleasures and close their hearts, their “as” passes away and their reality comes: the happiness of this age is their seeming; punishment is their reality. Our sorrow, however, is seeming; our joy is not seeming. For the Apostle does not say, “as rejoicing, yet always sorrowful,” nor “as sorrowful and as rejoicing”; rather, he says, “as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing.” And likewise: “as needy”—there is *as* or *as though* there—“yet enriching many”: here there is no *as* or *like*.

The Apostle had nothing: he had left all that was his and possessed no riches. Yet he added, “as having nothing,” for even the Apostles’ having nothing was only a seeming kind of having nothing [Col. 1058C]. But “possessing all things”—there he did not say *as*. For he was seemingly needy, but he did not merely seem to enrich many: he truly enriched them. Indeed, he supplied provisions to the saints who were in Jerusalem. He seemed to have nothing; but he did not merely seem—he truly possessed all things.

Accordingly, in matters regarded as adverse, which he had above indicated by dishonour and ill repute and described as belonging to the left, he added *as*, *like*, or *as though*. But in matters considered prosperous, called the right-hand side and foreshadowed by the terms glory and good repute, he did not add *as* or anything similar. For in prosperity, or on the right hand, there is reality; but in adversity and on the left, there is shadow or likeness, not the thing itself. The things he described on the right are the right-hand weapons of the righteous. The things [Col. 1058D] he designated on the left are likewise their left-hand weapons.

For these things become weapons of righteousness to a perfect man if he bears what is inflicted upon him with greatness of soul. In fighting through them, and using as weapons those very adversities by which he is thought to be attacked—as though they were bow, sword, and strongest shield against those who inflict them—he will gain the increase of his patience and virtue, and a glorious triumph of constancy: neither cast down by adversities nor raised up by prosperity, neither driven to the left by sorrows nor moved to the right by joys, but walking undeviatingly in the middle by the straight way.

> “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged. You are not constrained in us, but you are constrained in your own affections. Now having the same recompense—as to children I speak—be enlarged yourselves also. Do not bear the yoke with unbelievers. For what participation has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement, moreover, has Christ with Belial? Or what share has the believer with the unbeliever? What consent, moreover, has the temple of God with idols?”

Even the righteous often praise the good things that they say, not because they thirst for their own praise, but because they wish to kindle their hearers’ eagerness to listen, so that, while these things are set before them in the speakers’ voice, they may be carried away from their hearts with a more ardent affection. Therefore, when the Apostle had said many wonderful things to the Corinthians, he added: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart [Col. 1059B] is enlarged.” He also said this because of his freedom and pure conscience. For a mind conscious of evil trembles to speak, loses its meaning, and goes astray in words.

The sense is: We have been so stirred by your progress that we cannot keep silent. For the progress of disciples opens the teacher’s mouth. “Our mouth is open to you,” because we have said and are saying many things to correct and instruct you, all of which you ought to receive gladly. And our mouth is open to you because our heart has been enlarged by charity. The broad love of our heart, which embraces all of you, does not allow us to be silent concerning what benefits you. For the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart; and where charity is, there are no narrow confines (Matt. 12).

“Our heart is enlarged.” The enlargement of the heart is delight in righteousness [Col. 1059C]. It is God’s gift that in his commandments we may not be constrained by fear of punishment, but enlarged by love and delight in righteousness. “Our heart is enlarged.” Although our flesh is constrained by tribulations and pressures, the heart inwardly rejoices, free in its spaciousness, amid outward punishments. For charity is not constrained. If anyone wishes not to be constrained on earth, let him dwell in the breadth of charity. Whatever a person does to him does not constrain him, because he loves that which cannot harm him.

Since our heart is thus enlarged and our mouth open, therefore you are not constrained in us: do not suppose that in our teaching or in the example of our conduct there is any narrowness or lack of knowledge or good work. For we say and do everything that we ought to say and do toward you. Rather, you are constrained in your own affections; that is, understand that the narrowness and scantiness of knowledge and good work which you possess is in your own hearts, which are hard toward understanding and doing. For you who prefer pseudo-apostles to us suppose that the narrowness and scantiness of your understanding or holiness is in us—that is, due to our fault—when it is rather in your own hearts [Col. 1059D], due to the fault of the hardness of your minds, because they are not enlarged as our heart is.

But now I speak to you as to children—that is, as to those who, since I am your father, ought to follow my example: “Be enlarged yourselves also,” as I am enlarged; that is, be enlarged in understanding by the help of God’s grace, so that you may receive his greater gifts [Col. 1060A]. Be enlarged through love of righteousness, so that you may receive an abundance of virtues in the spaciousness of your minds. I say this to you who will have in the future the same recompense as I, if you are now enlarged as I am. Be enlarged in the breadth of charity, so that you may love all people devoutly; and do good not through the narrowness of fear but through the breadth of love. Be enlarged also in good works through the freedom of love. Do not bear, with unbelievers—that is, with pseudo-apostles who strive to weaken the faith of Christ and establish the carnal observances of the Law—the yoke of the ancient servitude which is in the Law.

For they themselves are under the yoke of servitude, where everything is done through fear; they endeavour to persuade you, after you have cast aside the law of freedom—that is, the freedom of charity—to submit your necks with them to the yoke of the Law [Col. 1060B]. But do not become participants in their servitude, because you are righteous through faith, whereas they are unrighteous through transgression of the Law. And what participation is there between righteousness and unrighteousness? None. For righteousness is immediately annulled if it has participation with unrighteousness; and therefore, lest your righteousness perish, beware of having participation in their unrighteousness.

Let no communion in food or drink, or in any sacrament, join you to them, since because of the unrighteousness of their unbelief they are separated from the Church. Or what fellowship has light with darkness? That is, in what can those who are light, sufficient for the illumination of others, have communion with those who are darkness—that is, blind and blinding others? There is no fellowship between light and darkness, because the light of this world [Col. 1060C] is darkened if it joins itself to darkness. With such persons there is no fellowship.

But what agreement can Christ have with Belial—that is, the devil? In what can those in whom Christ dwells and who are members of Christ agree with those in whom the devil dwells and who are members of the devil? In nothing. For Christ immediately leaves them if they join themselves to the members of Satan. *Belial* is interpreted “without a yoke” (Judg. 19), and signifies the angel who refused to be subject even to God. All who refuse to submit to God’s commandments are his members. Or what share has the believer—that is, the Christian—with the unbeliever, that is, with the pseudo-apostle destroying the Catholic faith? They have no share in common. But what consent can the temple of God—that is, those [Col. 1060D] in whom God dwells—have with idols, that is, with the sacrifices of carnal observances? These are now offered not to God but to the devil, and are reckoned as idolatry. There is no mutual consent between them. In so many ways it has been shown that communion with pseudo-apostles must be avoided.

These words may perhaps also be treated otherwise. “Do not bear the yoke of unrighteousness with unbelievers,” that is, with Gentiles: do not be subject to the yoke of sin as they are, when you ought in the freedom of charity to serve righteousness. For what participation is there between righteousness and unrighteousness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? There is no participation between righteousness and unrighteousness—not only that which is outside, but also that which is within the Church. “For the Lord knows those who are his; and let everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord depart from unrighteousness” [Col. 1061A] (2 Tim. 2). Likewise, there is no fellowship between light and darkness, not only those outside but also those within. “For God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all” (1 John 1).—“But whoever hates his brother is in darkness and walks in darkness” (1 John 2). If we say that we have fellowship with God and walk in darkness, we lie (1 John 1).

Therefore there is no fellowship between light and darkness. What then shall we do? We must have fellowship with God; there is no other hope of eternal life. “God indeed is light, and in him there is no darkness at all” (ibid.). But iniquities and sins are darkness. We are burdened by iniquities and sins, so that we cannot have fellowship with God. What hope, then, is there? If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just, so as to forgive [Col. 1061B] us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness. When this has been done, we shall have fellowship with him, because we shall be light in him.

But what agreement has Christ with Belial? As we have said, *Belial* is interpreted “without a yoke” (Judg. 9). Therefore all who follow not God’s will but their own can be designated by this name, because they are without the yoke of the fear of God and without the yoke of spiritual discipline. Such people often call themselves Christians. But what agreement has Christ with Belial? “Christ humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Phil. 2), whereas these exalt themselves, refusing to submit to the yoke of obedience. What agreement, then, do such persons have with Christ? Therefore no one who wishes to agree with Christ should be without God’s yoke.

Or what share has the believer with the unbeliever [Col. 1061C]? Or what consent has the temple of God with idols? This was rightly said to those Corinthians who ate sacrificial offerings of idols with unbelievers. It can also be understood otherwise. “For the Lord is faithful in all his words” (Ps. 144), because he faithfully fulfils, or will fulfil, whatever he has spoken. But the unfaithful person is one who neglects to fulfil his own words, by doing the good that he promised to do. What share, then, has the faithful God with an unfaithful person? For one who refuses faithfully to fulfil God’s commandments—what share can he have with God?

And what consent has the temple of God with idols? “For the temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3), and “avarice is the service of idols” (Col. 3). Why then do those who are, or ought to be, the temple of God consent to the avaricious and not rebuke them [Col. 1061D]? Why do they not fear that through this consent God, who is accustomed to dwell in them, will leave them, and that they too will become a dwelling-place of Satan?

> “For you are the temple of the living God” (1 Cor. 3, 6), “as God says: ‘For I shall dwell in them and walk among them; and I shall be their God, and they shall be my people’” (Lev. 26). “Therefore, go out from their midst and be separated, says the Lord, and do not touch what is unclean; and I shall receive you, and I shall be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty” (Jer. 31; Isa. 52).

I rightly said that the temple of God has no consent [Col. 1062A] with idols. For you are that very temple—not of dead gods, but of the living God; that is, you are those in whose hearts God dwells and reigns, God who lives in himself and gives eternal life to his own. By contrast, idols are dead to their worshippers, because they cause them eternal death. You are thus the temple of God, as God himself said through the Scripture of the Old Testament: “I shall dwell in them” (Lev. 26), that is, in their minds. Although God is everywhere, he nevertheless dwells in those who experience his benefit and do his will.

“I shall dwell in them,” he says, “and walk among them”; that is, I shall advance them in the progress of virtues. For God walks in us through the presence of his majesty if he finds the spaciousness of charity. How spacious is the place in which God walks [Col. 1062B]! “And I shall be their God,” he says; that is, they will worship me alone as God, because they will not be among those whose god is their belly (Phil. 5), or among those who worship any vice as God. And I shall protect them from the assault of vices and grant them success in virtues. “And they shall be my people”; that is, they shall be so devoted and given over to me in the unity of concord that they shall not be of this world.

“Therefore”—that is, because I promise to dwell and walk in you—“go out from their midst,” that is, from the midst of the pseudo-apostles, “and be separated from them.” For so long as you permit them to remain among you and tolerate their preaching, you remain in their midst—that is, within their fellowship and entangled in their error. Go out from their midst, lest you be in the midst of their communion, enclosed under the same [Col. 1062C] guilt. Go out in such a way that you are separated; that is, set apart for doing good, withdrawn from communion with them. The Lord says and commands this, not I.

“And do not touch what is unclean,” that is, the carnal observances which they commend to you. Since the Lord’s resurrection, these have power not to cleanse but to defile those who touch—that is, observe—them. If in this way you separate yourselves from fellowship in their perversity and live holy and righteous lives, “I shall receive you” into the heavenly kingdom, though I had cast you from Paradise.

Or, “go out from the midst” of the perverse who are in the Church—not bodily, but spiritually. That is, do whatever belongs to their correction, so far as it can be done, consistently with peace, according to each person’s rank and circumstances [Col. 1062D]. Whoever acts in this manner goes out free from the midst of their wickedness and condemnation. For in rebuking criminals, he goes out free from their midst in God’s sight: God imputes to him neither his own sins, because he did not commit them; nor others’ sins, because he did not approve them; nor sins of negligence, because he did not keep silent; nor sins of pride, because he remained in unity.

Thus go out spiritually from their midst, not tearing apart the unity of the Church, but rebuking the perversity of wickedness, lest by separating the good you commit a greater evil than the one you flee in association with the wicked. Be separated from them not bodily, but spiritually from fellowship in their perversity. “And do not touch what is unclean,” that is, do not consent to their sin.

For neighbours are to be endured everywhere, because no one can become Abel whom Cain’s wickedness does not afflict [Col. 1063A]. Yet there is one reason why fellowship with the wicked ought to be avoided: lest, if perhaps they cannot be corrected, they draw others into imitation; and while they themselves are not changed from their wickedness, they corrupt those joined to them. “For evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15). Thus, perfect persons ought not to flee perverse neighbours, because they often draw them to uprightness and are themselves never drawn to perversity. But any who are weak ought to avoid fellowship with the wicked, lest they take delight in imitating evils which they frequently see and are unable to correct. Thus it is fittingly said to them now: “Go out from their midst and be separated.”

This must be done not in the manner of schismatics, but in the manner of those who seek the desert or a more remote place for religious reasons [Col. 1063B]. “And do not touch what is unclean,” that is, the defilement of their contamination, since they themselves refuse to touch your holy purity by participating in it. And I, as has been said, shall now receive you, once rejected, into heavenly glory. Having received you into that glory of the kingdom, I shall be a Father to you—that is, I shall be your Father, loving you as a Father, because I shall give myself to you forever. “And you shall be sons and daughters to me”; that is, you shall be sons and daughters to me—you shall be like me—as it is written: “We shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3).

Not only shall you be sons to me—that is, [you shall receive] my glory—but also daughters. This is said either because of both sexes, or because of the strong and the weak, or because greater diligent care and guardianship is usually given to daughters than to sons [Col. 1063C]. Perhaps by “daughters” he wished to show that he will treat faithful souls as a father treats daughters: adorning them with the garment of gladness and removing every desire for baseness, so that they may always please their heavenly bridegroom in the ornament of beauty and the love of purity.

Do not doubt this, he says, because the Lord Almighty says these things—that is, the one who promises you them is able to do all things. It should be noted that the Apostle has set down these words from diverse places in Scripture, either according to the sense or according to the letter. For where he says, “I shall dwell in them and walk among them, and I shall be their God, and they shall be my people,” we read thus in Ezekiel: “I shall place [Col. 1063D] my sanctification in their midst forever, and my tabernacle shall be among them, and I shall be their God, and they shall be my people” (Ezek. 37). For in place of “I shall place my sanctification in their midst,” the Apostle has written, “I shall dwell in them”; and in place of “my tabernacle shall be among them,” he added, “I shall walk among them.” For a tabernacle is on a journey.

This saying is also found in Leviticus, except that there it is in the second person. For it is said: “I shall place my tabernacle in your midst, I shall walk among you, and I shall be your God, and you shall be my people” (Lev. 26). But what the Apostle next added—“Therefore, go out from their midst and be separated, says the Lord; and do not touch [Col. 1064A] what is unclean, and I shall receive you”—is read thus in Isaiah: “Depart, depart, go out from there; do not touch what is polluted. Go out from its midst; be cleansed; and the God of Israel will gather you” (Isa. 52).

But the following words, “I shall be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me,” do not readily appear in our books, so far as I think, as having been taken from any particular place—unless perhaps from what he said through Jeremiah, “I became a Father to Israel” (Jer. 31), and through Isaiah, “Bring my sons from afar, and my daughters from the ends of the earth” (Isa. 43), or from some similar passage. It follows:

## Chapter VII

> “Therefore, having these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and [Col. 1064B] spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.”

Since the Lord commanded that we should go out from the midst of the defilement of sinners, and promised us such great blessings as a result, therefore, beloved, we who have such promises—that is, to whom such things have been promised if we separate ourselves from the contamination of evil people—let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, and bring to completion the sanctification of both. Defilement of the flesh is what is committed through the flesh, such as sexual immorality, homicide, and the like. Defilement of the spirit occurs when one sins by thought alone, as through pride of mind, envy, or hatred. Let us therefore cleanse ourselves not merely from defilement, but altogether [Col. 1064C] from every defilement of the flesh, so that we may flee all fleshly vices; and from every defilement of the spirit, so that we may expel from our hearts consent to sin and everything else that defiles the spirit.

We truly bring the sanctification of flesh and spirit to completion if we keep both clean and labor diligently in good deeds. For this sanctification of both was accomplished divinely in baptism. Yet we bring it to completion if, through the members of the body, we persist in good works, and inwardly adorn the mind more and more with holy virtues. It must be completed in the fear of the Lord, so that we may always fear to offend the Lord, without whose grace we can do no good. For one who wishes to do any good without the fear of the Lord is proud, and loses whatever he does.

Or: let us cleanse ourselves from [Col. 1064D] every defilement of the flesh, that is, from every contamination of fleshly observance; and let us be completing the sanctification of the spirit, that is, the spiritual observance which we have begun to practice, so that we may fulfill the Law spiritually, not carnally—and this in the fear of the Lord, who gave the Law not so that it should always be observed carnally, but only until the time of reformation.

> “Receive us. We have wronged no one; we have corrupted no one; we have defrauded no one. I do not say this to condemn you. For we have already said that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together.”

We thus admonish you. And you, receive us—that is, receive what we say; receive the spiritual food [Col. 1065A] which we offer you. Or, “receive us, not the false apostles”: that is, receive our example for imitation in all things, not theirs. Or, “receive us”: consider what sort of persons we are.

And you ought to make room for us, because we have wronged none of you by reproaching him with past crimes, as the false apostles do, who reproach you with your former idolatry. We have corrupted none of you—that is, we have violated the integrity of no one’s soul—as the false apostles have corrupted many among you by spoiling the chastity of faith and the integrity of innocence. We have defrauded none of you—that is, we have not deceitfully misled anyone by crafty circumvention in order to deprive him, through ourselves or our dependents, of his possessions—as the false apostles, who cleverly and smoothly entrap you by flattery and artfully take away your goods.

[Col. 1065B] “I do not say this to condemn you”: that is, I do not reject you, but admonish you so that you may be corrected. For one who condemns someone does not spare him. The sense is clearer thus: I do not condemn you by excusing myself, as though you were such people. I do not mention these things in order craftily to say that you have done what I deny that I have done. For I cannot think this of you, whom I love so greatly, as I said above, because your love gives me such confidence.

“For I have already said that you are in our hearts”—as an epistle. “I have already said that you are in our hearts”: that is, care and concern for your salvation remain in our hearts, for dying together and living together; that is, so that you may die with us for Christ, if necessary, and live with us forever in Christ’s kingdom.

[Col. 1065C] From what he has said, he wishes them to understand with what disposition he now speaks to them. For those whom he wishes to have as partners both in present sufferings for Christ and in the future life, he certainly does not reject; rather, he exhorts them so that he may make them worthy of participation.

Or, “you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together”: that is, so that we may die and live with you. That is, if you endure the death of sin in the soul, we should regard that death as our own; and if you live in the observance of righteousness, we should believe that we ourselves then live. For perfect love considers the progress or loss of others to be its own.

> “Great is my confidence toward you; great is my boasting on your behalf. I am filled with consolation; I overflow with joy in all our tribulation.”

Therefore you are in our hearts, because I have great confidence toward you—that is, I place great confidence in your correction and salvation when I consider what is present among you—and I have great boasting on your behalf, that is, I boast greatly to others concerning your religious devotion. See to it that I do not trust in you in vain; see to it that I do not boast about you in vain.

I was also filled with consolation when I heard of your correction, and I overflow with joy in all our tribulation: that is, the joy which I have from your amendment surpasses all the sorrow of our tribulations, which we endure in spirit partly on account of your sins.

“Great,” he says, “is my confidence toward you.” This confidence arose from your response to the first epistle: because you did not receive it harshly, you gave confidence that you could be admonished. For you seemed willing to correct yourselves. Hence he boasts concerning them, and declares that his mind is consoled in this respect, so much so that he says he overflows with joy in every affliction.

[Col. 1066A] For, seeing hope in those for whom he suffers distress, he rejoices while he is afflicted, certain that he will receive from God the reward for having won their salvation.

> “For even when we came into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest; rather, we endured every tribulation. Outwardly, conflicts; inwardly, fears.”

He recalls what he suffered for the sake of believers in order to provoke them to love and compassion. I said, “I overflow with joy in our tribulation.” For we endured tribulation not only in Asia, but also when we came to the Macedonians to show them the way of life. Our flesh had no rest, but was continually harassed by constant tribulations.

“The flesh had no rest.” It is as though he openly said: the spirit had rest, while the flesh endured the punishments of persecutions through the soul’s progress. For the spirit rested in the hope of future recompense while the flesh labored in the pain of present affliction. We were not permitted to breathe, but endured every tribulation, because we were both scourged in body and afraid in spirit for those whom we had converted to the faith. For outwardly—that is, in [Col. 1066B] our body—there were struggles of punishments; inwardly—that is, in our heart—there were fears, lest those recently converted should fail.

We would now understand the Apostle to be recalling the riot, the beatings, and the imprisonment which he is read to have suffered at Philippi with Silas, and again the riots and persecutions at Thessalonica and Beroea (Acts XVI, XVII), unless we knew that the Apostle had by no means yet come to Corinth when he endured those things. But these matters which he now recalls he suffered after the conversion of the Corinthians, when he went for a second time into Macedonia; they are not related in the Acts of the Apostles.

Outwardly there were conflicts for the body while they were being beaten, and inwardly fears for the mind. For fear exists where understanding also exists. But this fear was, as has been said, on account of those who had believed, lest they be scandalized by his suffering. What, indeed, could one who was suffering still fear for himself?

Or, outwardly they had conflicts because they were attacked by unbelievers who are outside the Church; inwardly—that is, in the Church—there were fears, because they feared that the devil might work something there. Outwardly, conflicts from open enemies; inwardly, fears from false brothers. Thus the Church always has enemies: some whom she bears outside, and some whom she mourns within. Those outside are easier to avoid; those within harder to endure.

[Col. 1066D] For there are false brothers and evil children, yet still children, who do not blaspheme Christ against us but worship Christ with us, and persecute Christ in us, as Absalom persecuted his father (II Kings XV). The Church fears concerning these, lest they draw the rest into imitation of themselves. For it is very dangerous for the weak to dwell with such persons.

> “But God, who consoles the humble, consoled us by the coming of Titus. And not only by his coming, but also by the consolation with which he was consoled among you, reporting to us your longing, your mourning, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced the more.”

We endured severe tribulation. But God, who consoles the humble—that is, those humbled by sufferings for his name—consoled us by the arrival of Titus returning from you, so that he might be a comfort to us. Since God is not forgetful of his own, but always gives them consolation in adversity, he hastened Titus’s arrival so that he might bring refreshment to us while we stood in the heat [Col. 1067B] of tribulation. For it is a great consolation to one who suffers if he has with him someone who suffers with him. And it was a great consolation to us when we saw present the helper of our preaching.

But God consoled us not only by his coming, but also by the consolation with which Titus himself, who had been grieved by your disobedience, was consoled among you—that is, received consolation from your repentance. For because I saw Titus consoled among you, I too was consoled by your amendment.

For he was consoled by your readiness of will for conversion, reporting to us your longing for amendment, your mourning for what you had committed, and your zeal—that is, indignation against the false apostles—for me, that is, in my defense; so that I rejoiced more over your correction [Col. 1067C] than I grieved over our tribulation.

Titus reported that they had a desire to amend themselves, that they wept for the things they had done wrongly, and that they had zeal for the Apostle. For, learning what had been promised to those who live well, they were stirred by a desire to act well, so that they might deserve to obtain eternal rewards. And, when rebuked, they did not strive to excuse themselves, but wept in grief because they had sinned. Understanding the Apostle’s love toward them, they began to defend him against his opponents. Hence he rejoiced the more, because they had not merely corrected themselves but had advanced further. For their progress increased his joy.

Or, they desired to see the Apostle and wept from longing for him, and one rivaled another [Col. 1067D] in longing to see the Apostle.

> “For although I made you sorrowful by the letter, I do not regret it. Even if I did regret it, seeing that that letter, though only for a time, made you sorrowful, I now rejoice—not because you were made sorrowful, but because you were made sorrowful unto repentance. For you were made sorrowful according to God, so that you might suffer no loss from us in anything (I Peter II). For godly sorrow produces a repentance leading to steadfast salvation; but the sorrow of the world produces death.”

Truly, I received great joy from Titus’s report of what had occurred among you. For although I made you sorrowful—that is, although I rebuked your errors rather severely in the first [Col. 1068A] epistle—I do not regret having written harshly, because the cause demanded this and a good result followed. I do not now regret that, by rebuking you sternly, I made you sorrowful, because your progress causes me not to regret it.

Even if I had regretted it out of love because I made you sorrowful, I now rejoice because it was beneficial that I made you sorrowful. I rejoice, seeing that that very harsh letter made you sorrowful, though only for a time—that is, although for a short time. For I weigh the benefit that proceeded from that very brief sorrow.

For I rejoice not because you were made sorrowful, but because you were made sorrowful unto repentance. That is, your sorrow does not bring me joy, but your repentance does; and that repentance could not exist without sorrow. I rejoice because you were grieved with shame, not with anger. For one who, when rebuked, feels shame promises to correct himself; but one who becomes angry shows that he will become worse.

I rejoice in this sorrow because you were made sorrowful according to God—that is, according to God’s will and inspiration—so that you might suffer no loss from us in anything, not even in your sorrow, but that all things might result in progress. For a hearer suffers loss from the teacher’s preaching when he is disobedient to the teacher’s commands and adds the sin of disobedience to his former sin. Because you were made sorrowful according to God, you will therefore suffer no loss, but will obtain benefit.

For the sorrow which is according to God—that is, by which a person grieves that he has done what God hates—produces repentance leading to a salvation not temporary but steadfast and eternal. [Col. 1068C] For one who is sorrowful because what displeases God displeases him in himself labors through repentance to erase it and make satisfaction to God, so that he may attain the salvation which he had lost by sinning. For he does penance and hopes for God’s mercy.

But, conversely, worldly sorrow—that is, the sorrow by which a sinner who does not wish to correct himself is grieved, distressed, and ashamed that he has been exposed in this world, where he wishes to feel no shame for his wickedness—produces eternal death. Therefore beware that sorrow. For worldly sorrow consists either in shame at a reproved fault, or in grief for present things lost, or for another’s possessions not seized, or for another’s prosperity, or in being distressed about something of that sort. While someone is held by such sorrow, his heart is possessed by the devil, prince of death; and this sorrow works death in him.

Sorrow truly according to God is to mourn either one’s own sins or those of another. Therefore it produces repentance, which leads to salvation.

> “For behold, this very being made sorrowful according to God—what earnestness it has produced in you! Indeed, what defense, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what punishment!”

Truly, the sorrow which is according to God and affects the heart produces repentance unto salvation, for it produces the things that are beneficial. For behold, this is apparent in you yourselves; you have experienced this in yourselves. For this very being made sorrowful according to God—that is, this very fact [Col. 1069A] that you were made sorrowful according to God, although it may seem a small thing—produces in you how great an earnestness to amend what you have sinned, or not to sin further.

And not only earnestness not to sin again, but also defense against the assaults of demons, because you no longer allow yourselves to be overcome by them, but vigorously defend yourselves. And not only defense against enemies, but indignation against yourselves for the evil things you have done. And not only indignation, but fear lest you be condemned for the sins you have committed, or lest henceforth you fall into faults, since “Blessed is the man who is always afraid” (Prov. XXVIII).

And not only fear, but longing, by which you desire to advance to what is better. And not only longing, but [Col. 1069B] zeal, that is, zeal and fervor in imitating me or other good people. And not merely zeal for doing good after the example of the saints, but also punishment, because you punish in yourselves the evils you have done.

This fact—that you were made sorrowful according to God—produces all these things in you. Therefore it is clear that sorrow according to God produces repentance unto salvation, because it generates all these virtues which lead to eternal salvation.

Or, “earnestness” means vigilance of mind against the deceptions of the false apostles; “defense,” that you may defend me or yourselves against them; “indignation,” that you may be indignant with them or with others who act wickedly; “fear,” fear of the punishment of Gehenna; and “longing,” longing for heavenly glory. Or, “fear” means suspicion of your own frailty, lest it cause you to fall; “longing,” the desire always to live rightly; “zeal,” that zeal for the house of God may consume you (Ps. LXVIII), and that you may burn inwardly with fervor for correcting what is done wickedly in the Church—that is, among the Christian people; and “punishment,” that with the same zeal for God you may punish sinners (John II), as Church discipline requires.

All these good things proceed from sorrow according to God; therefore I said above that I do not regret having made you sorrowful in this way.

> “In every respect you have shown yourselves to be undefiled in the matter. Therefore, although I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of him who committed the wrong, nor for the sake of him who suffered it, but in order that our concern for you before God might be made manifest. For this reason also we were consoled.”

To state universally what sorrow according to God has contributed to you: in every respect you have shown yourselves to be undefiled in the matter—that is, undefiled in conducting the Christian business, so that you may freely be able to punish the sins of others; for one who is defiled has no authority to exact punishment from others.

Or, you have shown yourselves to be undefiled—that is, you proved yourselves free from the matter, that is, from the sin of the man who had his father’s wife. Since you acted against him according to discipline, you showed that you were no longer defiled by the matter of that iniquity, to which you had formerly been defiled by consenting.

And because you are undefiled, it is therefore clear that I wrote principally not for their sake, but rather for that of the Church. This is the meaning: therefore, although I wrote to you concerning them, I did not write for the sake of him who wronged his father by taking his wife, nor for the sake of him who suffered it—that is, for the father whose wife was taken from him. For he too sinned grievously, neglecting the salvation of his wife or son, knowingly tolerating and silently allowing so great a disgrace. Rather, I wrote for all of you, in order that our concern [Col. 1070A] which we have for you before God might be made manifest: that is, so that we might make known to you how concerned and diligent we are regarding your salvation before God, who sees the hidden things of your intention.

We wished to make this known to you, so that you too might know the concern which we have under the divine gaze. For by correcting the unrighteous, sanctifying the defiled, and reconciling them to the Church, I demonstrate that I have concern for the whole people. For in one person acting wickedly many are disgraced, and in one person suffering insult many are indignant. And because I wrote concerning them for the salvation and amendment of all of you, and what I intended came to pass, we were therefore consoled when we heard that you had been corrected.

Or, you showed yourselves to be undefiled from secular litigation, by which you were previously defiled when I said to you: “Does any one of you, having a case against another, dare to be judged before the unrighteous and not before the saints?” (I Cor. VI). For you were defiled by this litigation when I said: “It is altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another” (ibid.). And because you have now shown yourselves undefiled by it, [Col. 1070C] therefore, although I wrote to you, I did not write principally for the sake of him who committed the wrong or who suffered it—that is, for the sake of any of those who perpetrated injuries and frauds against brothers, or suffered them from brothers—but rather for all of you, so that you might all beware of doing such things. And I wrote for this purpose: that I might make known to you that I was concerned for you before God. And because you are now undefiled from such a matter, we therefore have consolation in you.

> “But in our consolation we rejoiced still more abundantly at the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by all of you. And if in anything I boasted to him about you, I have not been put to shame. But as we spoke all things to you in truth, so also our boasting to Titus proved true. And his affections are more abundant toward you, as he remembers the obedience of you all, how you received him with fear and trembling. I rejoice because in all things I have confidence in you.”

We were indeed consoled in this, that you showed yourselves undefiled in the matter; but we rejoiced still more at the joy Titus has in you. When the Apostle heard that those rebuked through the first epistle wished to correct themselves, he received consolation. Learning also from Titus that they suffered grief over their error, he increased in consolation and was filled with joy, because their will had begun to be proved in action, as Titus reported this with gladness.

This is what he says: we were consoled by your improvement. But in our consolation [Col. 1071A] we rejoiced still more abundantly at—that is, over—the joy of Titus. For we rejoiced more abundantly over both things, namely your correction and Titus’s joy, than we grieved over our tribulation; but especially over Titus’s joy, because his spirit, which had failed through sorrow over your downfall, was refreshed by all of you—not because all of you had already been corrected, but because he now had some hope concerning the rest.

His spirit, which had failed through hunger for your good works, was refreshed by you with that food of which the Lord says: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John IV). And if I boasted to him of anything concerning you—that is, if I affirmed something good of you—I was not put to shame, that is, I was not ashamed of this boasting.

Before Titus went to them, he heard from the Apostle that they were of good will in correcting their vices. Thus, when Titus returned and reported the same thing, the Apostle was not ashamed but became cheerful, because Titus had found them no differently than he had heard from him.

“I have not,” he says, “been put to shame on your account; but just as all the things you heard from us, we spoke to you in truth without any admixture of falsehood, so also our boasting about you to Titus became not merely true, but, to say more, truth itself”: that is, the truth appeared to him when he saw that matters stood as I had said.

For the effectiveness of your correction became as true as our preaching. The truthfulness of one who rebukes is apparent if those who are rebuked begin to amend themselves, because, when those corrected are changed, they bear testimony to the one rebuking them.

You, I say, refreshed his spirit and proved that I had spoken truthfully to him about you. Therefore his affections—that is, his loving feelings—are more abundant toward you than toward others, because he saw your progress. For the mind of a holy person is occupied with every good. The affections of his heart are toward you, as he remembers the obedience of you all: how—that is, how carefully—you received him with all fear of heart and trembling of body.

[Col. 1071D] Knowing that Titus had been sent by the Apostle, and that they had been reproved by the Apostle for many vices, the Corinthians were frightened at his arrival. Since they had begun to amend their lives, they were careful to obey his commands, so that Titus’s return might soften the Apostle’s mind toward them. For this reason Titus praised them, because in him they had reverenced the Apostle.

Therefore he adds: “I rejoice that you have advanced so far, because I have confidence in you in all things”—that is, I trust that henceforth you will act well in all things. For he rejoiced not only in their good will, but also in the good works by which they amended what they had sinned. And therefore, like a wise physician, he treated their nearly healed wounds with the gentlest remedies, so that the burning caused by the former rebuke might be healed.

## CHAPTER VIII

> “Now, brothers, we make known to you the grace of God which has been given in the churches of Macedonia: that amid much testing by tribulation, the abundance of their joy and their very deep poverty overflowed into the riches of their simplicity. For, according to their ability—I bear them witness—and beyond their ability, they gave willingly, with much urging begging us for the grace and participation in the ministry which is carried out for the saints. And not as we had hoped, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and then to us through the will of God; so that we urged Titus that, just as he began, so he should also complete among you this grace.”

After they had been corrected, he exhorts them to act well, and by the example of the churches of Macedonia provokes them to mercy, so that they may not think burdensome what they see the Philippians or others have already done.

And because he had said above, “When we came into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest” (above, VII), lest anyone think that he had produced no fruit there but had merely endured punishments—which would not greatly contribute to his commendation—he shows that many were converted there and suddenly brought to the height of perfection.

It is as though he says: until now we have made known to you the consolation which we had from your correction amid the tribulation we endured among the Macedonians. But now we make known to you the grace of God—that is, the freely bestowed gift of spiritual goods—which was divinely given in the churches of Macedonia. For we did not fail in tribulation, but persevered courageously until many churches were built there.

And such great grace was given them that, amid much testing by tribulation—that is, while they experienced many tribulations—the abundance of their joy always overflowed. Because they received the word of God with a devout mind, grace was divinely given them so that, in the tribulation of Paul and Silas mentioned above, they might not be scandalized but might rejoice in the promised hope and show themselves proved through their sufferings.

[Col. 1072C] This is what “amid much testing by our, or even their own, tribulation” means: the abundance of their inward joy, which they had conceived from the hope of heavenly rewards, was not diminished but overflowed. And their very deep poverty overflowed into riches. It is as though he says: in the tribulations which they experienced by suffering, they also gave generously from their goods to Christ’s poor.

Their “very deep” poverty means most profound and lowly; or “very high” means most noble and worthy of praise. Their poverty overflowed into riches—that is, it became greater as it strove to give riches. Or, it overflowed into riches to be given: that is, although their poverty was great, they nevertheless distributed riches abundantly to the saints. For though their resources were slender in material wealth, their spirit was found rich in service to the saints.

I mean riches of their simplicity, because from what they had they distributed with a simple intention, in order to please not human beings but God alone. For they gave not with a double but with a simple heart: they did not seek recompense from both human beings and God, but only from God.

Truly their poverty overflowed into riches, because I bear them witness concerning their ability—that is, I affirm that they gave according to what their strength could bear—and that they willingly gave even beyond their ability, since [Col. 1073A] they wished to give more than their resources allowed. For they were not compelled; rather, they were willing in this matter even beyond the capacity of their resources, because they offered, with no one compelling them, even from their necessary possessions without which their life could not subsist.

They were, I say, begging us—that is, beseeching us with an adjuration by sacred things—that they might make from their possessions a grace, that is, a free gift, and a participation: that is, that they might not retain their goods as though they were their own, but might distribute them to the saints as common goods. This participation was to be a ministry performed for the saints: that is, their goods would become common goods so that they might be used to provide sustenance for the saints who were in Jerusalem.
