So simply and devoutly they offered what was beyond their means that, weeping and begging, they offered it in order thus to compel us to receive from them what did not seem fit to be received, because it exceeded the capacity of their substance—lest perhaps later need should persuade them to regret their good work. But because they showed themselves to be such persons as, with a pure mind now setting present things below future promises, strengthened themselves by confidence in God, it seemed right to accept from them, lest the grace of their good heart lose its fruit.

And they did not act as we had hoped: they did not give as though to redeem their faults, so that we might spare their vices; rather, they gave to the Lord not only their possessions but themselves also, as an unblemished sacrifice. First, they devoted themselves to the Lord, that they might serve him alone; then they gave themselves to us, that they might be ready to obey us in all things. And this was through the will of God, who wills human beings to be subject to his representatives, so that, instructed by us, they may carry out each command of the Lord according to the measure of our direction.

[Col. 1073C] Therefore we ought to accept what they offered, because, having first corrected their former errors and the vices of their life and character, they devoted themselves to God beyond what we had hoped. For they seemed to do this simply, so that the recipient need not fear to receive it, because they certainly did not offer with the intention that, by buying off their superiors with gifts, they might soothe them so that their vices would not be reproved; for gifts blind the eyes of the wise and pervert the words of the just.

Thus, giving themselves first to God by correcting their vices, and then to us by offering supplies to the saints, they ought not to have been grieved—those who, almost before they had begun, wished to be perfect.

By their example, therefore, you Corinthians ought willingly to complete what you have begun in the ministry to the saints. For they applied themselves so earnestly, and we were so moved by their generosity, that we urged Titus to encourage you to a like work: so that, just as he began to instruct you, after you had been corrected, in doing good, he might also complete this grace among you, by stirring you to give.

Because the Apostle knew Titus’s sincere affection toward these people, and also that they obeyed him, he indicates that Titus could more easily exhort them also to this work: so that, just as in other matters he had the fruit of his exhortation among them, he might have it also in this grace, making them ready for the ministry of the saints, so that, since [Col. 1074A] they were already correcting their vices, they might produce the fruit of this generosity.

> “But just as you abound in everything—in faith, speech, knowledge, every earnestness, and also your love for us—so abound also in this grace. I say this not as a command, but, through the earnestness of others, also demonstrating the noble disposition of your love. For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: though he was rich, for your sake he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich. And I give counsel in this matter. For this is beneficial to you, since you began not only to do but also to will it from the previous year. But now complete it also in deed, so that, just as the readiness of your will is present, so there may be completion from what you possess. [Col. 1074B] For if readiness of will is present according to what one has, it is acceptable, not according to what one does not have.”

Titus, we asked, should exhort you to the grace of generosity. But I too exhort you to this, that you may abound in it as you abound in all things: in faith, because sound faith now abounds in you in every respect; and in speech, that is, you abound in the grace of speaking, whether in one language or in several; and in knowledge of the Scriptures, or in skill in whatever matters God has granted. For some abound sufficiently in speech but have little knowledge; others abound in knowledge but lack eloquence of speech. But God has granted you abundantly both, namely speech and knowledge [Col. 1074C]; and you abound in every diligence, because you are sufficiently diligent in all matters in which you ought to be diligent. Moreover, you abound also in love for us; that is, your love extends abundantly to us, because you love us greatly. And as you already abound in these virtues, so I urge that you also abound in this grace of generosity, so that from your possessions you may bestow abundantly upon the saints according to the measure of your means.

I say this not as a command, lest I seem to compel you unwillingly to do this, since I want you always to be spontaneous in doing good, and lest you become transgressors of my command. I speak not as commanding but as advising you to send necessities to the saints, and as wishing to demonstrate to God and men [Col. 1074D] the good disposition of your love through your concern for others—that is, because you will be concerned for others, namely the saints, relieving their need—so that you may seem not to have learned mercy and generosity, but to possess them naturally. Thus I wish to demonstrate that your love is ingenious and prudent when, without my command, it takes upon itself concern for Christ’s poor, sending them means by which they may relieve their want.

Or “through the concern of others” means through that of the Macedonians, whom I report to you as concerned for the support of the poor saints. I wish also to demonstrate the good disposition of your love: to show that your love has a good disposition when, without my instruction, it begins of its own accord to do what it hears that the Macedonians have done.

And [Col. 1075A] it is right that you should abound in this grace and generously minister temporal goods to the poor, because you yourselves know how great a grace the Son of God has bestowed on you, how mercifully he acted toward you: he was willing to become temporally poor for your sake, that he might make you sharers in enduring riches. You know this grace of his: although rich in his majesty, he became needy in the world for your sake, that by his poverty you might be filled with spiritual riches. If, therefore, he who is Creator and Lord of all endured poverty for you, why should you not, for love of him, give a portion of your riches to his needy members?

He was rich. For by what are people rich? By gold, silver, household dependants, land. But all things were made through him (John 1). What then is richer than he through whom riches were made, even those which are not true riches? Through him too are those riches: intelligence, memory, life, the health of the body itself, the senses, and the strength of the limbs [Col. 1075B]. For when these are intact, even poor people are rich. Through him also are those greater riches: faith, godliness, righteousness, love, good character. No one possesses these either except through him who justifies the ungodly. See how rich he is. For who is rich: one who has what he wants because another has made it, or one who makes what he wants and has another possessing it? I think richer is he who made what you have, because what he has, you do not have. He is rich, being in the form of God and wholly equal to the Father. Yet he became needy for our sake when he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2).

But it was not said, “He became needy, though he had been rich”; rather, “He became needy while he was rich” [Col. 1075C]. For he assumed poverty and did not lose riches: rich within, poor without; God hidden in riches, man appearing in poverty. By his poverty we have been enriched, because in his blood the sackcloth of our sins was torn apart. Through that blood we cast off the rags of iniquity so that we might be clothed with the robe of immortality. Therefore, lest we should fear riches and not dare to approach him in our beggary, he showed himself poor: that is, God deigned to be born as a human being, humbling the power of his might so as to procure for human beings the riches of his divinity and make them partakers of the divine nature.

Yet, remaining invisible to us amid the riches of his divinity [Col. 1075D], he could have enriched us by wonderful powers. But so that humanity might return to inward riches, God deigned to appear outwardly poor. For indeed he would have loved us less, unless he had also taken up our poverty; nor would he have shown us the force of his love unless he himself endured for a time that which he removed from us. This is what the Apostle now says, in order to kindle the depths of our compassion toward the grace of generosity: “For your sake he became needy while he was rich.” By these words he exhorts his hearers to become, as it were, poor by giving, so that their poverty may benefit others as Christ’s poverty has benefited us.

“And in this,” he says—that is, in consideration of so great a benefit of God—“I give you counsel,” namely, that in imitation of Christ you should not refuse to undergo poverty [Col. 1076A], so that you may escape poverty through the saints.

For this is useful to you: that through imitation of Christ’s poverty you may strive toward his riches. It is useful to you because it benefits those who give more than those who receive. It is useful to you, who began not only to do this but also to will it from the preceding year—that is, last year, or from the earlier year of your conversion until now. For it is easy for even an unwilling person to obey in a good work; but this was a great virtue in you, that you had already willed the good which I now urge upon you. But now also complete in deed that which you have already done in will, so that you may not only will in your heart but also fulfill it in action. Thus carry out in deed what you long ago began to do in will [Col. 1076B], so that, just as the mind is ready in willing, so the mind may be ready in accomplishing—namely, according to what you have, whether more or less—so that each may give as much as he can. For a will that retains what it could give is fruitless.

Therefore I urge you to give from what you possess, because if the will is ready and prepared to give according to what it has, it is acceptable to God according to what it gives in this way, not according to what it does not have. It is as if he said openly: “Do not suppose that I demand from anyone beyond his strength, or require as much from a poor person as from a rich one.” For all give equally if each gives, out of what he possesses, as much as he has. Because the Corinthians are being urged to this work of ministry, they are instructed not to give more than they can, lest perhaps by offering more they might appear compelled rather than voluntary, and therefore to act without reward; for one who does something under compulsion has no reward.

Thus it is said to them that, if the will is ready in giving according to what it has, it is acceptable to God, not according to what it does not have. For the person gives from what he has when he retains what is necessary for himself and bestows upon the poor the rest, which he can do without. But one who gives from things necessary for his own use gives according to what he does not have—that is, beyond his strength—because the things he needs are, as it were, not his to give, since he cannot do without them; and therefore he does not have them for giving [Col. 1076C].

For this reason it is now said to the Corinthians, who are tight-fisted, that a will which gives freely according to what it has—retaining, that is, what is necessary for itself—is pleasing to God, not one which gives under compulsion according to what it does not have, that is, what it cannot endure to lack without complaining. This must not be understood to mean that it is unacceptable to God if anyone with a devout heart offers even beyond his means, since the Macedonians are greatly praised precisely because they voluntarily gave beyond their strength. They did not need exhortation, as the Corinthians did; rather, they voluntarily offered, with entreaties, to prove that they did this with their whole will, offering more than they could afford. Therefore it was acceptable. For the more they offered, the more they will receive. But the Corinthians, as still weak, are spared; hence it follows:

> “For it is not that others should have relief while you have affliction, but that by equality, at the present time, your abundance may supply their want, so that their abundance also may be a supply for your want, that there may be equality, as it is written: ‘He who had much did not abound, and he who had little did not lack’” (Exod. 16).

I rightly said that the will is acceptable if it is ready to give according to what it has. For I do not urge you to give so much that those to whom you give have relief—that is, an alleviation and easing of want—while you have affliction, that is, excessive poverty. Undoubtedly the Apostle added this, as we said before, in accommodation to the weak [Col. 1077B], because for some who cannot bear poverty it is more tolerable to give less than, after their generosity, to complain under the pressure of want. For when the mind of a giver does not know how to bear poverty, if it deprives itself of much, it seeks an occasion for impatience against itself.

Therefore the mind must first be prepared for patience; then either much or all should be given, lest, while poverty descending upon it is borne with too little equanimity, the reward of preceding generosity perish and subsequent complaint destroy the mind still more grievously. “I do not urge this,” he says, “so that others may live idly on your goods while you are tormented by the affliction of hunger; but that by equality you may aid them at the present time.” That is, each person should for a time share with the saints as much as he has [Col. 1077C], because no more is required than he ought to retain for himself. Scripture says, “You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (Lev. 19), and so forth: “He who has two tunics, let him give to one who has none” (Luke 3).

Or: during the present time of this brief life, share your riches with them, so that they too may share their own with you in eternal life. This is what follows: may your abundance of bodily goods supply, even if it does not wholly fill, the bodily want of those who have abandoned all worldly things, so that their spiritual abundance may supply your spiritual want. This is what the Apostle commands: because the saints were suffering want for a time, having left all worldly things and devoted themselves solely to divine works, in order that they might persist in prayer or teaching for the benefit of many, the other faithful—those occupied in commerce or crafts, or possessing inherited resources—should minister to their need. Then, again, where the saints are rich and these others poor—that is, in spiritual and eternal things—the saints may share with them, as though repaying in return their ministry [Col. 1077D].

For since few receive spiritual gifts while many abound in temporal possessions, the rich join themselves to the virtues of the poor by supplying comforts from their own riches to these poor saints. “Let your abundance,” he says, “supply their want, so that their abundance may supply your want,” so that we may carefully consider that those whom we now see as poor we shall one day see as abounding, while those whom we see as abounding will one day be poor if we neglect generosity.

Therefore, whoever now gives aid to the poor will later receive what is everlasting from him; he cultivates, so to speak, a field for harvest, which returns more abundantly what it receives [Col. 1078A]. It remains, therefore, that pride should never arise from a gift, since the rich person, by giving to the poor, acts so that he may not be poor forever. For those who live in the world do not have merits sufficient for eternal life (Matt. 5). But because they have made Christ’s poor—whose is the kingdom of heaven—friends and debtors to themselves through alms, they will obtain through the merits of those poor what they do not merit by themselves. Then equality of both groups will come about—not because they will not differ, but because all will possess the same kingdom, and what each has will suffice for each.

Or equality means this: because these persons minister to the saints in this present time, recompense will be made to them by the saints in the future, because they make the saints their debtors. This equality itself is the peace of our Jerusalem: bodily works of mercy are joined to spiritual works of preaching, and peace comes about through giving and receiving. Let equality come about in the kingdom, as is written figuratively in Exodus 16. He who had gathered much manna—that is, more than a *gomor*—did not abound, that is, did not have more than a *gomor*; and he who had gathered little—that is, less than a *gomor*—did not lack, that is, did not have less than a *gomor*. For when it came time for the meal, all had equally. By this God signified that his people, who travel through the wilderness of this life toward the land of eternal promise, will have equality at the banquet of heavenly refreshment [Col. 1078B], because all will see God.

And one who has laboured much here and accumulated very many merits will not possess more, as regards eternal life, than one who has done little good work. Thus the Gospel says that those who came at different hours to cultivate the vineyard all received a denarius alike in the evening (Matt. 20). Equality will therefore come about then, because all will have equality in eternal life. All will be in equality because all will be in eternity. For the life of poor saints will not be longer than that of elect persons living in the world. Nevertheless, poor saints will have greater glory and blessedness in body and soul.

Thus the rich are made equal to the poor saints in receiving the denarius of everlasting life, because they now make themselves equal to them in their own riches—not by exact parity, but so that the saints are sustained from their possessions as they themselves are. For the king, from his whole kingdom, has no more than food and clothing, without which the present life cannot exist. Thus a rich person makes a poor person equal to himself if he provides food and clothing, even though he retains more than he gives. “He who had much,” he says, “did not abound,” because he gave to the needy what he had beyond his needs; “and he who had little did not lack,” because he received from one who abounded [Col. 1078D].

He wishes us to possess all things in common, so that the perfect do not conceal their teaching and those who possess resources do not deny food to them. The saints have more also in the hope of the coming age than those who seem rich in this present time; nevertheless both groups, as has been said, will be made equal in that age, so that just as the saints’ want is now sustained by the benefit of these others, so these others may then become rich by the benefit of the saints. For they did not give themselves wholly to God so as to be poor here and rich there; therefore they seem poor there. But they will be enriched through the intercession of the saints, to whose virtues they joined themselves when they supported them in good works by ministering necessities to them, because “he who receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward” (Matt. 10).

> “But thanks be to God, who gave the same concern for you in Titus’s heart. For he indeed accepted the exhortation; but being more concerned, he went to you of his own accord. We also sent with him our brother whose praise in the Gospel is throughout all the churches [Col. 1079B]. And not only this, but he was also appointed by the churches as companion of our journey in this grace which is ministered by us for the glory of the Lord and for our declared purpose, avoiding this, lest anyone should blame us in this abundance which is ministered by us. For we provide things honourable not only before God but also before human beings” (Rom. 12). “But we sent with them also our brother whom we have often proved diligent in many things, but now much more diligent because of his great confidence in you—whether concerning Titus, who is my partner and helper among you; or our brothers, apostles of the churches, the glory of Christ. Therefore, before the churches of God, show toward them the demonstration of your love and of our boasting concerning you” [Col. 1079C].

Because God is just, knowing that the Corinthians wished to make progress, he kindled Titus’s affection for them, so that by his exhortation he might fulfil their willingness in a good work. Seeing their progress, Titus rejoiced in them. This is the meaning: “I indeed,” he says, “earnestly urge you toward the work of mercy; but I give thanks to God, who through the Holy Spirit gave Titus’s heart the same concern which I have for you, so that you may not fail but may advance in good work. For he did not resist but accepted our exhortation, by which we urged him to go and encourage you.”

He accepted our exhortation, but did not receive his willingness from us, because he already possessed it. He was concerned for you by his own will [Col. 1079D], but through our exhortation became more concerned. And once he had become more concerned, he went to you of his own accord, a will which God had inspired in him.

Or “he accepted the exhortation” means that he undertook this burden of labour: to exhort you to the generosity by which the saints are supported. But since he had become more concerned because of your progress, he went to you voluntarily. That is, seeing you making progress in good actions, he became more concerned for the care of your salvation, so that he went voluntarily to you, though before, even when asked, he had excused himself from going because of your faults.

He himself went freely. But we also sent with him that distinguished brother whose praise in the Gospel is throughout all the churches. This is understood of Luke, who possesses praise in the Gospel above the rest, because wherever the Gospel is read, Luke is praised, who was worthy to write it so elegantly [Col. 1080A]. But he is not only praised everywhere for composing the Gospel: he was also appointed by the churches as companion of our journey, to travel with me wherever I go as a pilgrim preaching, and to be my companion and helper everywhere in this grace, which is ministered by you—that is, in this distribution of alms, of which we are ministers—for the glory of the Lord, so that our Lord Jesus Christ may thereby be glorified; and for our purpose, by which we wish you to give well, a purpose directed toward such zeal, proper, and divinely preordained.

Or this refers to the spiritual grace of the New Testament, which is ministered by us to the Gentiles through the Gospel for the Lord’s glory and for fulfilling our purpose, by which we desire that the Gentiles may be saved—a purpose directed to this end. The Apostle commends Luke because the Corinthians did not know him, so that they might know in how good a reputation they already stood, to whom such men were sent, that they might rejoice with them and increase them in faith in God’s working, for whose glory they diligently did this, so that he might be acknowledged in these matters.

Some, however, have thought that this may be understood of Barnabas as well, because he too was appointed Paul’s companion in travel (Acts 13), when he was sent with him to the Gentiles, although he did not persevere with him. Luke, however, persevered. He was appointed Paul’s companion in this grace of alms because the apostles decreed that he and Barnabas should preach to the Gentiles (Acts 15), provided only that they remembered the poor saints in Judaea and, while that famine lasted, sent them provisions [Col. 1080C]. Barnabas’s praise was in the Gospel because he had preached vigorously throughout all the churches in which he had been with Paul.

But this seems discordant: that Paul should call this man “brother,” rather than “apostle” or “partner”; that he should say that he sent him with Titus as though he were Titus’s inferior, rather than Titus with him; or that he should commend him to the Corinthians as though unknown to them, when in the earlier epistle he had stated that Barnabas was not unknown to them, saying, “Or do Barnabas and I alone not have authority to do this?” (1 Cor. 9), that is, to receive support. With Luke, however, everything is fitting: although Luke is now greater than Titus among us, he was lesser in the estimation of the Corinthians, and therefore is appropriately said to have been sent with him. The Corinthians knew Titus’s distinction because he himself was a Corinthian.

“We sent with Titus,” he says, “the companion of our journey, who is praised in the Gospel throughout all the churches, avoiding this, lest anyone blame”—that is, reproach—“us in this abundance of alms which is ministered by us,” that is, which is carried out through our ministry. Unless the Apostle had with him suitable witnesses of good reputation, the weak or unbelieving, on seeing so great and abundant a contribution, might entertain some evil suspicion against him. They might think that he was receiving for himself and diverting to his own uses what was received to supply the saints’ necessities—funds to be offered or distributed to the needy by himself [Col. 1081A]. But in order to remove every perverse suspicion from himself, he employed many suitable witnesses in this grace, which was to be administered fully to the poor.

“Therefore,” he says, “we avoid reproach because we provide things honourable”: that is, we take care that what we do should be honourable not only before God but also before human beings. Before God a good conscience suffices for us; before human beings a good reputation is necessary. For our own sake our conscience suffices for us, but for the sake of others our reputation ought not to be sullied but to have force among them. One who, trusting in his conscience, neglects his reputation is cruel, because he disregards the salvation of neighbours.

Or the Apostle said that he avoided blame in this abundance of teaching and miracles because he might be judged negligent concerning the care of the saints if he provided their necessities too sluggishly [Col. 1081B], since the earlier apostles had enjoined on him and Barnabas that they remember the poor, as we have already said (Acts 15). Therefore, lest people should say of him, “He preaches well indeed and lives devoutly, but is not mindful of the poor saints, as had been enjoined on him,” although he himself was blameless in all things, he was unwilling to be judged negligent in this respect also. Instead, he urged Gentile believers to make contributions for the saints, so that, with this work completed, his diligence and foresight might appear in all things.

“For we provide things honourable not only before God but also before human beings.” He provided things honourable before God by teaching what God commands to be done concerning the ministry to the saints. He provided things honourable before human beings by sending to urge this work persons who would not cause them scandal but would, by their integrity, encourage them, lest the soundness of his teaching fall into reproach through imprudent ministers [Col. 1081C].

“And not only,” he says, “did we send these two, but also another brother with them,” whom some say was Apollos, but this is uncertain. We have often proved him diligent in many things concerning your salvation; but now we have found him much more diligent concerning you, when he heard that you had been corrected, being confident that you would obey in doing good. He became more diligent, I say, in seeing you and exhorting you to ministry for the saints because of this confidence in your change for the better; or because of Titus, who had reported many things about you to him, and who would not lie. Titus is my partner, travelling with me everywhere to preach, and is my helper among you—that is, in your conversion and correction.

He is my helper among you; or so are our other brothers whom I sent to you, who are apostles—that is, founders of churches—and the glory of Christ, because in those places they preached Christ where he had never been preached, and, to his glory, built churches from those whom they converted to the faith. Or our brothers, the earlier apostles who were with the Lord in the flesh, are my helpers among you: either because they sometimes passed through your city and contributed something to your improvement, or because the renown of their preaching and life benefited you [Col. 1082A].

And since we have sent such men to you, receive them with due honour and love. That is, now show toward them a demonstration of your love: show the love which you have customarily displayed by honourably receiving other brothers, now by receiving these men more attentively, so that they may prove true the good things they have heard about you. And show toward them the demonstration of our boasting concerning you: that is, the works of love which you likewise customarily show in receiving brothers, and for which we boast about you among other churches. Receive them now with greater reverence and devotion. Do this before and in the sight of the churches, so that the other churches may know the good reports they have heard about you are true and may receive a good example from you [Col. 1082B].

## Chapter IX

> “For concerning the ministry which is performed for the saints, it is superfluous for me to write to you. For I know your ready mind, for which I boast about you to the Macedonians: that Achaia has been prepared since last year, and your zeal has stirred up very many. But we sent the brothers so that our boasting about you in this matter might not prove empty, that, as I said, you may be prepared; lest, when Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we—not to say you—should be ashamed in this confidence. Therefore I considered it necessary to ask the brothers to go before me to you and prepare this promised blessing beforehand, so that it may be ready as a blessing and not as avarice” [Col. 1082C].

I exhort you concerning the reception of the righteous; for concerning the ministry performed for the saints, there is no need for me to exhort you. Concerning that ministry it is superfluous—that is, more than necessary—for me to write to you. For it is superfluous to remind someone whom you know will act. Yet, to show my diligence and make you readier, it is not idle for me to write, so that you may know you ought to carry out with great diligence what is frequently made known to you.

It seems superfluous for me to write to you about this because I know that your mind is ready for making this contribution. Because of your mind’s devotion to this grace [Col. 1082D], I boast of you among the Macedonians; see that it is not in vain. For a person of whom another thinks well commonly presents himself as better. I boast of you because not only Corinth, the metropolitan city, but all Achaia, a large region, has been ready since the preceding year to give what may be sent to the saints; and your emulation—that is, your fervour in being imitated—has stirred up many toward this work of piety.

For when other churches hear that the Corinthians had formerly been entangled in many errors but were afterward corrected and devoted to works of mercy, they have been stirred by emulation toward a good work, as though thinking and saying to themselves: “If these people, who had lived badly after receiving the faith, have begun to possess this willingness, why should not those do so all the more in whom such faults have not been found?”

“I indeed,” he says, “boast in the splendour of your mind, which is ready to give generously. But we sent the brothers not to exhort you to that for which you are already prepared in mind, but to remind you, lest you prove negligent concerning your vow and promise.” This is the meaning: your mind is ready, but we sent the aforementioned brothers to you so that you may be ready to produce what you have promised to give, lest, if you are unprepared, all that we boast about you should prove empty in this matter [Col. 1083A].

“We sent them,” he says, “so that, as I told them you were prepared, you may be prepared”; or, “as I told you, you may be prepared”; or, “as I told the Macedonians.” Otherwise, if Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we who boasted of you may be ashamed in this substance—that is, in this possession, this wealth which ought to have sustained the poor. I said, “lest we be ashamed,” not to say that you should be ashamed, that is, to leave your shame unmentioned. For your disgrace will be greatest in our embarrassment if your lack of preparation is found. If what I testified about you is not found, I too shall be ashamed because you have not rendered the resources promised to the saints; and you will be still more confounded because you did not even take pains, on account of my being your witness, to act in such a way as to prove that I spoke truthfully about you.

Therefore, lest both you and we should be deeply ashamed, I considered it necessary to ask the aforementioned brothers to go ahead of me to you and meanwhile prepare the blessing—that is, the generous and charitable gift [Col. 1083C]. I call it a blessing because you have already promised and pledged it. By preparing it, let them make it ready at our arrival as a blessing—that is, as a work of love—not as avarice, that is, not as a constrained gift which causes sorrow to its giver. For a gift made with a grasping, miserly, and sorrowful mind is called avarice; but a blessing is made with a generous and cheerful mind.

This expression is drawn from the patriarchs, who by their blessing filled their children with the fruitfulness of every good thing: Isaac blessing Jacob and Esau, and Jacob blessing Ephraim and Manasseh (Gen. 27; 48).

> “But this I say: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows in blessings will also reap from blessings” [Col. 1083D].

At this point the Apostle kindles his hearers’ minds toward great eagerness in giving, lest someone able to give much should give little. “Brothers,” he says, “have gone before me to prepare your gift; but I prescribe why you should give generously. For I say to you that whoever sows sparingly—that is, gives miserly—will also reap sparingly, that is, will receive little in the future age. For the miser is sparing: what he gives is extorted from him when he is compelled to give, whether through shame or through the lengthy exhortation of many. His harvest is small because he gave with a sparing mind, although he may seem to have given greatly.

“On the other hand, the widow who put two small coins into the treasury was praised for giving more than all the rich” (Mark 12; Luke 21) [Col. 1084A], because with a generous mind she gave all that she possessed, whereas the others gave with a sparing mind and retained for themselves things far greater than what they gave. They therefore sowed sparingly, although they seemed to sow much, because they were unwilling to sow as much as they could. For giving is not losing but sowing: doing without for a time in order to possess more abundantly afterward.

But whoever sows sparingly—that is, whoever is unwilling to give generously when able—will also reap sparingly, that is, will gather a small reward, because just as he is now sparing in giving, so God will be sparing in rewarding. And whoever sows in blessings—that is, gives with a good will in hope of future recompense—will reap from blessings, when he hears with the other givers of alms: “Come, blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom, because I was hungry and you gave me food” (Matt. 25). For one sows in blessings where disposition is weighed more than wealth: that is, one who generously gives good things according to his ability, with kindly dispositions, will therefore reap from God’s blessings the fruit of everlasting life [Col. 1084B].

> “Let each person give as he has determined in his heart, not from sorrow or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver” (Ecclus. 35).

And because one who now sows in blessings of good will—that is, gives with a joyful and generous mind, whether what is given is little or much—will reap from heavenly blessings, therefore each should give as he has determined in his heart: as he has deliberated and preordained in the counsel of his reason and will. Whatever a person has disposed in his heart to give, let him give, and let him give with the devotion he proposed [Col. 1084C]: namely, not from sorrow or compulsion, that is, not unwillingly or under coercion.

For almsgiving is often done by sad and complaining persons in order to be rid of the annoyance of a petitioner, not to refresh the need of the person in want; but such giving is not acceptable to God. Therefore what is given must be given not from sorrow but from joy of heart. For from among those who give, God chooses for recompense the person who gives with a devoted mind, as though storing treasure with God.

There are some who, when repeatedly asked by others, are compelled to give by weariness at the petition made to them through the persistent importunity of asking; and so they give sadly and unwillingly, not from love or devout compassion (Luke 18). There are also some who, although not sad or grieved through coercion, nevertheless give from necessity: either because everyone else gives, or because many urge them to give, and because they cannot, without damage to their honour, refrain from giving, they are driven to give by a kind of necessity [Col. 1084D]. But whoever wishes his gift to be pleasing to God should give not from sorrow or compulsion, but from joy and willing intention; for God loves a cheerful giver—that is, one who, through love, gives joyfully, cheerfully, and serenely in hope of heavenly recompense.

> “And God is able to make every grace abound in you, so that, always having all sufficiency in all things, you may abound in every good work, as it is written: ‘He scattered abroad; he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains for age upon age’” (Ps. 111) [Col. 1085A].

I indeed exhort you to this grace of generosity, but God is able to bring about in you what I exhort. For I can utter words of exhortation, but he can advance your minds toward what is better; for I can plant and water, but he alone is sufficient to give the increase (1 Cor. 3). And therefore I pray that his power may be present with you, so that, as he has touched your hearts in the correction of vices and in the truth of doctrine, so also he may favour your undertaking in the grace of generosity. For he is able to make abound abundantly in you not only this grace but every grace, [Col. 1085B] so that, always possessing every sufficiency in all things—that is, never lacking what is necessary for salvation—you may abound in every good work, that is, in giving as in other matters.

For if you choose only sufficiency for yourselves, you will be able to abound in God’s work; because, retaining for yourselves what suffices, you will expend the rest for the uses of the poor, and this will be to abound in a good work. For although the gift of a person of little means is small, it nevertheless abounds because it is made with a good disposition. Our outward possessions, however small, suffice for the Lord. For he weighs the heart, not the substance; nor does he consider how much is in his sacrifice, but from how much it is brought forth. For whoever has more ought to offer more.

Thus God can make every grace abound in you, [Col. 1085C] so that, without loss to yourselves, while generously bestowing benefits on others, you may abound, through generosity, in every good work, as it is written: that neither avarice nor prodigality may be in you, but that you may distribute your goods generously and reasonably, with a good intention—not for temporal advantage, but for eternal recompense—as Scripture says that the righteous man did (Ps. 3): “He scattered abroad,” that is, he did not give everything to one person, but scattered it in different ways among this person and that, so that more might benefit, and each might receive according to what was fitting. By this avarice is removed. “And he gave,” not indiscriminately to everyone, nor to the rich or to actors, but with reason and discernment to the poor alone, who could not repay him in this world. By this is removed [Col. 1085D] the vice contrary to avarice, namely prodigality, and also the desire for temporal repayment.

And therefore “his righteousness,” that is, his righteous work of mercy, “remains for ever and ever,” that is, eternally; for from acting justly in time he possesses eternal righteousness and life. For that person is righteous who regards the goods of the world as common property; who, knowing that God gives all things commonly to all—for he causes his sun to rise upon all, sends rain upon all, and gave the earth to all (Matt. 5)—therefore shares with those who do not possess an abundance of land, lest they seem deprived of God’s benefits. And because he does not keep for himself alone what he knows has been given by God to all, but believes it right that the one who has should give to the one who does not have, therefore his righteousness remains eternally, because in the world to come he will possess it with him for ever.

[Col. 1086A] And if the righteousness of one who gave to the poor remains for ever, how much more that of one who ministered to the saints? For those who are publicly needy may be called poor. But the saints are distinguished from these, because they are God’s servants, devoted to prayers and fasts and leading a pure life.

> “Now he who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will also provide and multiply your seed and increase the growth of the fruits of your righteousness, so that, enriched in all things, you may abound in every simplicity, which through us produces thanksgiving to God.”

You ought eagerly to minister to the saints because of the hope of heavenly recompense. Yet do not fear want in this life, because God, who supplies seed to the sower, [Col. 1086B] will also provide him meantime with bread for food, until he gathers a crop from that seed; and he will multiply your seed, which you have cast into the ground, so that an abundant harvest may spring up from it, enabling you to give more alms. Everything belongs to God—both seeds and growing things—and by God’s direction they grow and multiply for human use. Therefore God, who gives these things, also commands that from them provision be made for those in need. Accordingly, whoever gives according to God’s will is divinely increased, so that he may have the means to give yet more abundantly.

For God wills that believers who possess the substance of this world should minister to the necessities of the saints, so that nothing may be lacking to those who chose to hold a higher degree of holiness in the Church, to leave behind every bond of worldly hope, and to dedicate a free mind to the divine warfare. [Col. 1086C] And whoever ministers well to them, may there always be increased for him the means by which he can minister more generously. God, therefore, who supplies seed to the sower, by which he may live in the coming year and give alms, will meanwhile also provide bread—that is, the support of the present life—not for superfluity, but for food, that is, for necessary use.

And do not be anxious about the future, because he, on account of the present provisions which he will bestow upon you, will not fail to multiply your seed and cause the crops to grow, so that you may always be sufficient to give more and more. And he “will increase the growth of the fruits of your righteousness,” that is, he will grant far more abundant increase to the crops which your righteousness deserves. For it is righteousness that, because God gives, [Col. 1086D] a human being should in turn give from it to one who lacks. And because you have preserved such righteousness—that, as God gave to you when you lacked, so you also give to others who lack—therefore the increase of your crops is divinely enlarged, so that, enriched with everything necessary, you may abound in every simplicity; that is, in every act of generosity done not with a double but with a single intention.

For one who ministers well and simply to the saints is enlarged by divine direction, so that he may always have the means to give, being enriched both in the present and in the world to come. For sowing once, he will reap twice: that is, from one good work he will receive recompense here and in the future. Yet he ought not to perform good with a double intention, seeking recompense both in this world and in the other, lest he be numbered [Col. 1087A] among those of whom it was said: “They have received their reward” (Matt. 5). Rather, with a single heart he should seek recompense only in heavenly things, although God repays him also in this world.

Seed may be understood as whatever is given for God’s sake. And he who supplies seed to the sower—that is, who gives the almsgiver something to distribute to the poor—will also provide bread for food, that is, he will furnish him with the means of living. And he will multiply your seed, that is, he will cause your property, which you sow by giving to the poor, to abound in manifold ways, so that you may have both what to sow more generously and what to live on. And he will increase the growth of the fruits of your righteousness, that is, he will increase your alms, for which your righteousness will receive the fruit of eternal recompense.

For righteousness is the observance of God’s commandments, [Col. 1087B] and from it arise crops—that is, the fruits of eternal reward. The increases of this crop are alms, through the merit of which virtues are increased here and glory grows in the future. Or the increase of your heavenly fruits consists in dispositions to give more generously and to assist those in need; for the greater the affection of pious compassion with which someone relieves a neighbour’s need, the greater a fruit of eternal refreshment he acquires for himself.

And God will so increase your seed and fruit that, enriched in all bodily and spiritual things, you may abound—that is, inwardly in good will and outwardly in good action. I say that you may abound, tending toward every simplicity: that is, that you may do all things with a pure and single heart, seeking recompense for all things from God alone; [Col. 1087C] that you may desire neither subjection from the poor nor praise from human beings, nor any recompense in this life. This simplicity of your intention in good work produces through us thanksgiving to God: that is, it causes us to give thanks to God, who inspired you with this will, so that with such single intention you may make a contribution to the saints, and do the other things pertaining to the salvation of your souls. Or, through us preachers and exhorters, it produces thanksgiving: that is, it causes those who receive the benefits to give thanks to God.

> “For the ministry of this service not only supplies what is lacking to the saints, but also abounds through many thanksgivings in the Lord, through [Col. 1087D] the proof of this ministry, as they glorify God for the obedience of your confession in the Gospel of Christ, and for the simplicity of your sharing with them and with all others; and in their entreaty for you, as they long for you because of the surpassing grace of God in you. Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift.”

Therefore, because of your simplicity—that is, because of generosity performed with a single intention—thanks are given to God, since many good things are contained in it. For “the ministry of this service,” that is, the ministration which is rendered by you to the saints through our office, not only supplies what the saints lack—that is, it does not merely drive away the need of the saints, who do not labour but devote themselves to prayer and divine contemplation—[Col. 1088A] but produces still more: namely, it abounds in thanksgiving offered by many in the Lord. That is, it is a cause and incentive for many to give thanks for you in the Lord’s work which shines forth in you.

This is to say: our ministration, effected through the administration of our office, not only provides the saints with necessary expenses, but also has this further abundance: not only those sustained by your benefit, but many others also freely give thanks to God for you, commending your deed to the Lord; so that, while you give to a few, you may be commended to God by the prayers of many. Let thanks be given for you by many, and this through the proof of the ministry—that is, through their experience or approval of this ministration of yours.

I call them many, glorifying God for the obedience of your confession [Col. 1088B] in the Gospel of Christ. For, testing your mind in this work, they glorify in you God, in whose hope you have been established, and whose Gospel you have obeyed; and what you confess with your mouth you demonstrate in action. They therefore glorify God because you obeyed by doing the works demanded by the confession of Christian faith—and this in the Gospel, that is, in the precepts of Christ’s Gospel. They also glorify him for the simplicity of your sharing: that is, because with not a double but a single hope you make your goods common to those saints who are at Jerusalem and to all others whom you see in need.

They also glorify God in their entreaty for you: that is, because those whom you support pray for you. I mean those who desire to see you in the heavenly [Col. 1088C] kingdom, or even in the present world, that they may rejoice at seeing you. For who would not wish to see with his own eyes persons subjected to their own needs for God’s name’s sake? They desire to see you, and this because of the surpassing grace of God in you: that is, because God has heaped up his grace in you so excellently that, from the affection of pious love, you share with needy saints.

And because so many good things proceed on both sides from this ministry, therefore “I give thanks to God for his inexpressible gift”: that is, for the gift of love which he has placed in you and in those saints—a gift whose greatness and manifold character, or whose nobility, justice, and usefulness, no one can clearly describe. The Apostle was so filled [Col. 1088D] with the richness of holy joy while speaking of the reciprocal need and reciprocal relief of the Christians of the provinces and of Christ’s soldiers—on this side, material things flowing to them; on that side, spiritual things flowing to these—that now, at the end of his discourse, he cries out and, as it were, erupts with the fullness of holy joys, saying: “Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift.” For God’s gift is inexpressible, which urges people to do good when they perform good works in hope of those things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor the human heart conceived (1 Cor. 2).

## Chapter X

> “But I myself, Paul, entreat you by the gentleness and modesty of Christ—I who am humble among you in person, but bold toward you when absent. Yet I ask you, lest when present I should be bold with that confidence by which I am thought to dare against some who suppose that we walk according to the flesh.”

He speaks to those who were uncorrected, who followed the false apostles and considered him harsh because in the former letter he sharply rebuked the vicious. It is as though he said: “I invited those who had been corrected to almsgiving, but I entreat you others—I myself, the same person toward you as toward them, although you are different people. I, Paul, that is, ‘humble’ or ‘marvellous,’ humbly entreat you to reform your conduct.”

Or: the brethren previously sent had exhorted to service of the saints those among you who had been corrected; but now I, Paul himself, not another, earnestly entreat you who ought to have been corrected but delayed, [Col. 1089B] that you delay no longer. I entreat you by Christ’s gentleness: that gentleness by which Christ, though able to avenge himself, endured wrongdoers in order to correct them; and by his modesty, by which he wiped away their faults through the restrained scourge of penitence in baptism, Peter saying to them: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized” (Acts 2), etc.

Christ was gentle toward us when, without any vengeance, he forgave us our sins through baptism. He was modest when, even if not without vengeance, he nevertheless restored us to everlasting life by a punishment of tribulations not excessive but bearable and restrained. Christ is gentle in mercifully sparing and enduring; he is modest in punishing with measured vengeance. And the gentleness and modesty of Christ, whose imitator [Col. 1089C] I am, is why I speak to you not commanding but entreating: because I too am gentle, after Christ’s example, in sparing, and stern with moderation in inflicting measured punishment.

I, who in person—that is, in bodily presence and appearance—am among you humble and almost contemptible, am bold when absent toward you: that is, I confidently rebuke you by letter. Yet you think that I possess confidence of severity only when absent, that is, in a letter, and not when personally present. But I ask you not to make me bold when present: that is, I ask you to correct yourselves, lest, when I come, I punish you boldly with that confidence which I am thought to possess only while absent.

The Apostle’s confidence is trust in the authority given him by Christ, whose vicar he is, to punish those who act under Christ’s name but refuse, when rebuked, to obey and correct themselves. [Col. 1089D] And now, while absent, he entreats them not to make him presently dare to punish them through this confidence: that is, lest, when he is present, he be compelled to be angry because of their vices. Those who had not yet amended themselves should compose themselves and thereby soften for themselves his severity, so that, finding them moderate, he may restrain severity and rejoice in them.

“I ask,” he says, “lest when present I should dare”: that is, lest, when I am present, I should boldly strike you for your vices, as the law of ecclesiastical correction requires, with that confidence which is regarded as arrogance, by which I am thought by some to dare against certain unreproved persons while punishing sinners, such as the man who had committed fornication. Hence some of you think me excessively bold through a confidence of arrogance and domination, because [Col. 1090A] I dare punish even such persons. They suppose that we walk according to the flesh: that is, that we act according to the manner of carnal people.

Or, they suppose that we walk according to the flesh because they do not receive the spiritual things which we say; they judge us as though we uttered carnal things which ought not to be accepted. For they suppose that we walk according to the flesh—that is, preach with a carnal understanding—because whoever despises spiritual things considers them carnal.

> “For though we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful for God for the destruction of strongholds: destroying counsels and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing every understanding into captivity [Col. 1090B] to the obedience of Christ; and having readiness to avenge every disobedience, when your obedience has been fulfilled.”

They themselves, as I have said, suppose that we walk according to the flesh. And I rightly said “as though,” because we do not in fact walk according to the flesh, as they think. For, though walking in the flesh—that is, living the present life in the body—we do not wage war according to the flesh: that is, we do not exercise the warfare given us by God for carnal advantage. We wage war not carnally but spiritually, though we dwell in a frail body.

For one wages spiritual warfare who lives spiritually, because he fights against spiritual wickednesses. But one wages war according to the flesh who obeys the desires of the flesh. It may also be understood thus: those are said to wage war according to the flesh [Col. 1090C] who understand the Old Testament carnally; but those who follow the spiritual understanding, although indeed in the flesh because they possess the same letter as the Jews, do not wage war according to the flesh, having passed from flesh to spirit.

We do not wage war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but spiritual and powerful for God our king, whom we serve in warfare. We do not carry a material spear or sword; rather, by the word we cast down our enemies more powerfully than others do by carnal arms. Our weapons are the word of preaching, wisdom, miracles, charity, and other virtues. They are weapons because they oppose vices and overthrow the devil’s kingdom. They are powerful for God, so that through them we may forcefully conquer his enemies and subject the whole world to him.

[Col. 1090D] For as an earthly emperor vindicates his kingdom through his soldiers, so Christ through us defends the confession and discipline of the one God. And our weapons are powerful for him “for the destruction of strongholds”: that is, of worldly teachings and arguments or artifices with which perverse persons fortify and surround their hearts, lest the word of truth be able to reach them. For the battering ram of apostolic preaching forcefully penetrates and overthrows such strongholds by the power of spiritual grace.

And we, as has been said, serve Christ in warfare, “destroying counsels”: that is, the premeditated cunning devices of ungodly people or demons. For counsel is a mental plan devised for doing or not doing something. Counsel is also that which a perverse person gives to someone whom he deceives under the appearance of advice, while he seemingly shows by reasoning that what he urges is useful. Hence it is said: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly” (Ps. 1). But we destroy such counsels when we do not allow them to reach their effect.

And we destroy every proud height of heart, whether of tyrants or of the wise of the world, that exalts itself against the knowledge of God—that is, against the sense of evangelical truth. [Col. 1091A] For both those established in the elevation of worldly rank and those who had attained the loftiness of worldly wisdom exalted themselves with proud arrogance, resisting the humble knowledge of divine preaching. But the exaltation of such persons has now been cast down, and the knowledge of truth has subjected the world to itself.

The demons also exalted themselves when they were worshipped in idols, against the knowledge of the one God; likewise heretics exalted themselves against the knowledge of Catholic truth, but they have been destroyed by apostolic engines of war. And we also are “bringing every understanding into captivity”: that is, we bind by our reasoning every understanding of perverse doctrine and lead it captive into Christ’s obedience. For one takes an understanding captive when he overcomes its contradiction by reason and leads it, humble and gentle, to faith in Christ, which it had formerly resisted.

And we also have readiness—that is, an open and swift capacity for action, since nothing holds us back from daring—[Col. 1091B] “to avenge every disobedience”: that is, to punish the faults of those who refused to obey us by correcting themselves. This we shall do when your obedience has been fulfilled: that is, when all the rest of you have become obedient in all things out of love.

> “Look at the things that are before your eyes. If anyone is confident in himself that he belongs to Christ, let him again consider this within himself: that as he belongs to Christ, so do we. For even if I should boast somewhat more concerning our authority, which the Lord gave us for your building up and not for your destruction, I shall not be ashamed. But lest I be thought to terrify you by letters—for they say, ‘His letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible’—let such a person consider that what we are in word [Col. 1091D] through letters when absent, such also we are in deed when present.”

Now he wishes them to consider the things that are evident: that is, to judge openly the things he is about to say. It is as though he said: “If the things I have said, for which you ought to follow me rather than the false apostles, do not suffice for you—because perhaps you have not understood them plainly enough—look at the things I add, which are as evident as objects set before the eyes.” Namely: “If anyone is confident,” etc.

Or thus: “Look at the things that are before your eyes,” that is, examine carefully the deeds of those who strive to do good only before human eyes, lest perhaps they deceive you by them. See—that is, understand—these things which I now set before you, because they are before the eyes, [Col. 1092A] that is, plain to all: namely, “If anyone is confident in himself that he belongs to Christ.” That is, if anyone is certain, by the merit of a good life, that he himself belongs to Christ, that is, is among Christ’s elect, who are his possession, let him again consider this within himself—that is, in the subtlety of his reason—so as not to exceed the force of reason, whether on account of his own honour or hatred of us: that as he belongs to Christ through whatever good things are Christ’s, so we also belong to Christ through the same goods.

He speaks to those whose pride he touches: those who, presuming upon themselves and swelling with pride of mind, thought less worthily than they should about the Apostle, as though they did not need his precepts. He warns them that, if they trusted in themselves because they were servants of Christ, they certainly ought not to doubt concerning the Apostle, but should think similarly concerning him—indeed, they ought rather to prefer their teacher to themselves.

But he now teaches them humility in himself, making himself equal to them although he was a vessel of election and teacher of the Gentiles. Therefore he wants them to consider what is plainly visible: since no believer judged the Apostle more highly than himself, how much more should no one judge him less highly than himself. [Col. 1092B] He therefore calls these persons to witness and instructs them not to lose the merit of a good life through exaltation of mind; for one who knows himself to be something humbles himself in order to become greater.

I rightly said that we belong to Christ, just as that person who prefers himself to us is said to belong to Christ. For we belong to Christ even more eminently through an authority which that presumptuous person does not possess. And this is what follows: “For even if I should boast somewhat more,” etc. That is, if I say that I have received authority from God, proclaiming myself a true apostle, I shall not be ashamed, because I shall speak truth—not puffed up by glory, but compelled by the cause of your edification.

But the false apostles wish to exercise authority which they have usurped for your destruction. I shall not be ashamed if I boast somewhat more than they do concerning the authority of our apostleship, which the Lord gave to us, not to them, for building up and not for destroying you: that is, so that we may build you up in virtues, not destroy you by exercising tyranny, or overthrow you by evil example or false teaching, as the false apostles do.

In saying this, he indicates that above he humbled himself by comparing himself with them; yet if he raises himself, he need not be ashamed, because he received from Christ authority to preach and to absolve, that he might save, not destroy, those who obey, [Col. 1092C] and that he might build up their religious conduct, not demolish it. Thus every prelate of the Church has received authority from God in order to benefit those subject to him, not to injure them.

If, then, this man who was sent by the Lord lowers himself to and compares himself with inferiors, how much more ought those who possessed no testimony whatever not to compare themselves—much less, I do not say, prefer themselves—to their superiors? “We,” he says, “have authority to build you up and to punish the perverse. But lest I be thought to terrify you by letters, while writing in absence that I shall not spare the uncorrected when I am present, as though I did not dare fulfil what I threatened, let the person who is such”—that is, who holds such an opinion of me—“consider this,” that is, know this: “that what we are in word through letters while absent, such [Col. 1093A] shall we be also in deed when present,” that is, in administering correction to sinners.

He says this because of the preceding statement, in which he had said that he was ready to avenge every disobedience. “Lest,” he says, “I be thought,” etc. A person may seem to terrify by letters if he possesses no authority and has no confidence to rebuke when present; he dares when absent because he fears when present. “Lest I be thought to terrify you by letters”—an impression that may arise because some say: “His letters are weighty,” that is, weighty to understand, “and strong,” that is, formidable; “but his bodily presence is weak,” unable to exercise severity, “and his speech contemptible,” that is, unpolished and rustic.

Whoever disparages me with words of this sort should know [Col. 1093B] that what we threaten in letters we shall fulfil in deeds, since we have received authority from the Lord; and therefore what we threaten while absent we shall carry out when present. But one to whom authority has not been given may dare while absent, whereas when present he feels shame and fear. But I neither blush nor fear when I rebuke, because I act with confidence in my authority.

It should be known that, just as we ought not through our own activity provoke the tongues of detractors, lest they perish, so we ought patiently to endure them when their own malice has provoked them, so that our merit may increase. Yet sometimes we ought also to restrain them, lest, while they spread evils about us, they corrupt the innocent hearts of those who might listen to us for good. Therefore the Apostle now restrains with arguments the Corinthians who disparaged him, lest, spreading a bad report about him, they harm others who could listen to his teaching.

It should also be noted that, because they say, “the letters are weighty and strong,” and do not say, “the letter is weighty and strong,” they show that they had already received two letters from the Apostle besides this one, which they had not yet seen. It follows:

> “For we do not dare to number or compare ourselves with certain persons who commend themselves; but they, measuring ourselves among ourselves and comparing ourselves with ourselves. But we do not boast beyond measure, but according to the measure of the rule which God has apportioned to us as a measure, to reach even as far as you. For we do not overextend ourselves as though not reaching you; [Col. 1093D] for we came even as far as you in the Gospel of Christ, not boasting beyond measure in the labours of others. Yet we have hope, as your faith increases, to be magnified among you according to our rule in abundance, so as to evangelize also the regions beyond you—not to boast in another’s rule concerning things already prepared.”

Truly, he says, we are such in deed as we are in word, because we do not make ourselves like the false apostles, who usurp authority and flatter vices. And this is what is meant: “For we do not dare to insert or compare ourselves with certain persons who commend themselves,” that is, we cannot boast greater things of ourselves than we are, nor dare so to despise God as to be like certain persons who [Col. 1094A] prefer to commend themselves by their own praises rather than by God’s grace. For the false apostles commended themselves: having received no authority, they wished to rule, claiming authority for their own name. But one who is sent claims authority not for himself, but for him by whom he is sent. We do not dare to insert ourselves among those who preach without having been sent; that is, we do not dare to place ourselves in their number, seeking our own glory as they seek theirs, because we return to the Lord by whom we were sent, so that we may presume nothing beyond what has been granted. For whatever is done against God is audacity.

Nor do we dare to compare ourselves with them, that is, to make ourselves like or equal to them, lest, like them, we perish. That is, from fear of God we do not dare—as they do—to flatter you and indulge your vices. We do not do these things; rather, we ourselves, [Col. 1094B] within ourselves and not outside ourselves, measure ourselves, usurping nothing other than what has been enjoined; and we compare ourselves with ourselves, because we act as our office requires, saying or admonishing neither more nor anything other than we can or ought to do. This is what those now being opposed do not do, namely, the false apostles who seek to magnify themselves beyond what is fitting.

“But we shall not boast without measure,” that is, we shall not assume authority beyond measure, but according to measure. He says that he uses only as much authority as the author of it has granted, and that he does not go beyond its bounds. Therefore the boasting will not be proud, since it does not exceed the limit of the authority given. By “boasting” he means authority, [Col. 1094C] which he exercised in rebukes in order to make them safe. Yet he says that he boasts not in an exaltation of authority, but for their edification. For, in firmly rebuking the vicious, he boasted in their amendment; and the authority given him advanced their salvation, not his own self-exaltation.

Thus in two ways he did not boast without measure: both according to the authority granted him and because he claimed authority for himself no further than the reach of his preaching. For he claimed authority by right over those whom he himself had converted to faith through the Gospel. But he did not speak with such confidence to others, because they were under another’s rule, that is, in the portion of another evangelist.

“We shall not boast,” that is, we shall not exercise authority without measure, beyond the limit of our own measure, but “according to the measure of the rule which God has apportioned to us, a measure reaching even unto you” [Col. 1094D]; that is, according to the measure of governance which God gave us, so that our authority might extend to governing you. For, at Christ’s prompting, we preached the Gospel to you, and thus he caused us to reach even to you.

“For we do not overextend ourselves as though we did not reach unto you”; that is, when we claim the right of authority over you, we do not stretch ourselves over another’s province, as though the right of our authority did not reach to you. We do not do this by usurpation but by command; nor did we arrive among you in preaching as though not sent, but were appointed and sent to you by God. To overextend oneself is to stretch further than is permitted, or to extend oneself too high above one’s episcopate.

But we do not extend ourselves beyond what is fitting, nor [Col. 1095A] over other persons’ provinces, because we do not arrogate to ourselves the right of due authority over those whom other preachers established in faith before us. “For we reached even unto you”: that is, as we pressed onward preaching to diverse nations, we reached as far as you in the Gospel, that is, in the preaching of Christ; and we were the first to announce his name to you. We were not boasting without measure, that is, beyond measure, in others’ labours—where another had laid the foundation of faith. We therefore speak to you with such confidence because you were not brought to faith by another’s labour. We do not, then, boast beyond measure, since we boast in our own labour.

But the false apostles boasted without measure in others’ labours, because they always went to believers who did not require signs, [Col. 1095B] which they themselves could not perform. Thus they overextended themselves: that is, they extended themselves over those whom others had brought to faith, and wished to exercise dominion over them. For God had allotted that province to the former preachers when he distributed the several regions among holy preachers. Therefore these wanderers ran everywhere, sowing tares over the sowing of wheat.

“But we do not boast without measure,” that is, beyond what God has apportioned to us, because we do not seek glory in places where other preachers laboured before us. Rather, we have “hope in your growing faith”: that is, we hope to be magnified before God in you through your faith as it grows and advances. For the more your faith—which you learned through us—advances in virtues, the greater [Col. 1095C] is our merit before God. We hope, I say, to be magnified in you according to our rule, that is, according to the standard of right living and believing which we handed down to you; and we are prepared to preach the Gospel also in those places beyond you.

It is not enough for us to have reached as far as you. Rather, when your faith has increased, we shall pass onward, in the abundance of God’s grace and miracles, to preach the Gospel also to those nations beyond you. The progress of your faith encourages us not to be sluggish in calling still others to faith, who may advance in it by your example. Or again, we hope to be magnified among human beings through you, so that, when they see you making such progress, they may recognize us as true apostles and themselves readily receive [Col. 1095D] our teaching as well. And we hope to be magnified according to our rule, that is, the governance under which you make good progress.

“For we do not have hope of boasting in another’s rule,” that is, in those who are under the rule of any other apostle. “Also in abundance in preaching the Gospel”: we hope to preach not in a few places, but to pass also into those regions beyond you. “In abundance” may mean either that this preaching will surpass the preaching which we had among you, or that it will possess an abundance of heavenly gifts. And we shall preach there, not under another’s rule, that is, not under another’s governance, because those beyond you are not under another’s governance either. We hope, he says, to preach there; and we do not hope to boast under another’s rule in those increases of virtues which have been prepared [Col. 1096A] by other preachers. It is clear that a prudent man does not trust in, nor hope for glory from, things established by others’ labours. Therefore the Apostle does not dare to act among those who believed through others’ preaching, lest he seem to boast in others’ labours; rather, he strives to preach to those to whom the message had not been announced, that he may gain glory by his own labour.

> “But he who boasts, let him boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1; Jer. 9). “For it is not he who commends himself who is approved, but he whom God commends.”

The Apostle indicates that the confidence and glory of evangelizing itself must be given to the Lord, by whose grace it exists; thus, whoever trusts in evangelical authority should trust in God as its author, so that all gain from the divine work [Col. 1096B] may accrue to the Lord’s profit. But whoever has not received authority from the Lord cannot boast in the Lord, because he seeks his own glory.

“I,” he says, “will not boast under another’s rule.” Likewise, whoever boasts—that is, wishes to exercise authority—should boast in the Lord, that is, within the measure given him by the Lord. Or thus: I have hope of boasting, yet not in myself but in the Lord. For no one ought to boast in himself. Whoever boasts of any good should boast in the Lord: that is, he should turn back and attribute all glory, not to himself, but to the Lord. For whatever good we have or do, we have it not from ourselves but solely from the Lord, by whose power we act.

Therefore each person ought to boast not in himself but in the Lord, because he who commends himself—that is, who seeks his own glory in preaching, who [Col. 1096C] boasts apart from the Lord—is not approved by God or by human beings; but he is approved whom God commends by miracles and by the grace of holy conduct. God commends him, and he is approved whom God judges worthy and sends to preach his gift. But whom he does not send, him he does not commend. He commends himself who preaches without being sent. Accordingly he is not fit, but presumptuous and reprobate.

## Chapter XI

> “Would that you might bear with a little of my folly; indeed, bear with me. For I am jealous of you with God’s jealousy. For I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ. But I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning” (Gen. 3), [Col. 1096D] “so your minds may be corrupted and fall away from the simplicity which is in Christ Jesus.”

As he begins to speak about himself, he calls himself foolish, because what he is about to say seems to tend toward his own praise; and through God’s wisdom Solomon had said: “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips” (Prov. 27). But grief compels him to break out into self-praise for the salvation of those who, though they ought to have thought rightly concerning his commands, thought unworthily. This harmed not the Apostle but themselves. Therefore he seeks their advancement even in what seems to be boastful speech: “I boast,” he says, “of my governance,” which appears to be folly.

“But would that you might bear with me”: that is, I wish that you would bear without indignation a little of my folly, [Col. 1097A] that is, some small portion of my boasting, which appears to be folly. Bear with this small portion of my boasting, for I could boast much more. I desire that you should bear even a little of this folly of mine; but I also command and, as though by right, require that you bear with me in this folly of boasting. “Bear with me,” I say, as subjects, because “I am jealous of you”: that is, I am inflamed with chaste love for preserving the chastity of our mind. And I do this not with my own jealousy but with God’s jealousy, because I am jealous over you not for myself but for God.

He shows that he will say what follows out of love for them, so that it may contribute not chiefly to his own praise but to their progress. It is as though he said: I am not inflamed by the spur of human envy, but, like a father, I guard you with divine jealousy so that I may join you undefiled [Col. 1097B] to the heavenly bridegroom.

“For I have betrothed you”: that is, I betrothed you with the ring of faith, not to many, but to one; not to an adulterer, but to a husband, “to present a chaste virgin to Christ”: that is, that I may present all of you as one undefiled virgin to Christ the Judge.
