For the whole Church is a virgin in mind. The virginity of the mind is integral faith, firm hope, and sincere charity. Thus the Church, imitating the mother of her Lord, is both mother and virgin in mind, though she could not be so in body.

Christ, then, in no way took away his mother’s virginity by being born; he made his Church a virgin by redeeming her from the fornication of demons. The Church is now betrothed and is a virgin when she keeps herself from worldly corruption; but she will then be married when her Bridegroom comes in glory and brings her with him to remain for ever in the bridal chamber of the kingdom [Col. 1097C]. “I,” he says, “betrothed you to this husband, so worthy, that I might present you to him undefiled on the day of judgment. But I fear that virginity may be violated in you and that you may not attain the Bridegroom’s embrace.”

Just as virginity of the body is violated at some point in its members, so the seduction of speech violates virginity of heart. “I fear lest, as the ancient serpent deceived Eve by its cunning” (Gen. 3), so your thoughts—that is, your minds—may be corrupted by that same serpent. For that serpent, namely the devil, seeks to corrupt not virginity of flesh but virginity of heart. And just as an adulterous man delights in his wickedness when he corrupts flesh, so the devil delights when he corrupts the mind.

For truly the mind and faith of those who prefer falsehood to truth are corrupted. Those who build up falsehood in human beings—what do they expel from them except truth? They admit the devil and exclude Christ; they admit the adulterer and exclude the Bridegroom. When falsehood possesses the mind, then the serpent possesses it. “I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning”: that is, lest, as the devil, hidden in the serpent and speaking through its mouth, deceived Eve, so your minds may be corrupted by the same deceitful deceiver, hidden in false apostles and speaking through their mouths, and may fall away from the simplicity which is in Christ Jesus: that is, may fall from the paradise of simple Christian faith, which receives nothing alien but retains simple truth without any mixture of falsehood.

For the serpent deceived Eve by lying about God, [Col. 1098A] saying that God had threatened them with death merely to frighten them and would not inflict it if they sinned. Thus also the false apostles said that the precepts of the Gospel had been added so that the Law might at least be kept in this way, and that keeping the Law alone was sufficient. Even now the serpent similarly deceives, asserting that Gehenna is named merely for terror, and maintaining that it either does not exist at all or is not eternal. That serpent still mutters and is not silent. By a certain promise of knowledge, he seeks to cast down from the paradise of the Church the one whom he does not permit to return to that paradise from which he himself was first cast out.

What occurred in that paradise is occurring in the Church. Let no one seduce us away from this paradise. Let it suffice that we have fallen from it; or, having experienced this, let us be corrected. This is the serpent who always suggests [Col. 1098B] wickedness; he sometimes promises impunity, as there he promised, saying: “You shall by no means die” (ibid.). He suggests such things in order that Christians may now live wickedly. “Will God,” he says, “destroy everyone? Will God condemn everyone?” Thus he corrupts many persons’ minds and causes them to sin, so that they are expelled from these seats.

> “For if he who comes preaches another Christ whom we have not preached, or you receive another Spirit whom you have not received, or another Gospel which you have not received, you would rightly bear with it. For I think that I have done nothing less than the great apostles. For although I am unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge. But in all things I am manifest to you.”

[Col. 1098C] Therefore I said that I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, these persons likewise corrupt you. They preach the same faith as we do, but through their cunning and deceit mix the poison of falsehood with truth. For if they preached a different faith, something altogether different from what we preach, they could not deceive you so greatly.

And this is what is meant: “For if the preacher who comes and is sent by God preaches”—that is, were to preach to you—“another Christ whom we have not preached,” that is, a better Christ; or if through his teaching you “receive”—that is, were to receive—another, holier Spirit whom you had not received through us; or if you received from him another Gospel which you had not received from us, you would rightly endure his authority. For you could say: This man’s preaching is better than Paul’s. But now, since he preaches the same [Col. 1098D] Christ and adds, on his own part, more things that ought to be rejected, you ought not to endure him.

Or thus: There is truly simplicity in Christ, not duplicity, because there is one Christ, not two Christs; one Spirit of Christ; and one Gospel. “For if that teacher who came to you after us,” and so forth. This is now to be understood of any true preacher. He had spoken of the false apostles who corrupted the faith, and now adds something concerning true preachers, because the Corinthian people were tossed by various errors: some favoured the false apostles; others favoured those from whom, in polished language, they heard the same things they had heard from the Apostle; while others favoured the apostles who had been with the Lord and disparaged Paul because he had not followed the Lord in the flesh. Therefore he now speaks in this sense.

[Col. 1099A] If the same Christ is preached by these men as is announced by us, and the same Gospel, why should we be considered inferior, when they say nothing beyond what we say? For even if the preacher who comes to you were to preach a more excellent Christ than we have preached—which cannot happen—or if through him you were to receive another, better Spirit which you had not received through us, or another Gospel which you had not received from us—that is, another preaching concerning human redemption, which cannot exist—you would rightly endure such a teacher, to our disparagement. But because this is not so, you do not rightly endure him to our humiliation.

But why does he say, “you would rightly endure,” if another Christ had been preached to them, or another Spirit, or another Gospel delivered to them, when he says to the Galatians: “If anyone preaches to you a gospel other than that which you have received, let him be anathema” (Gal. 1)? For if it was perverse for the Galatians to receive something other than what had been handed down by the apostles, how could it be right for the Corinthians if another Christ had been preached to them?

But the Apostle, knowing that no Christ other than this crucified Christ could ever be preached, says that they would rightly endure it if a different, superior Christ were preached to them by those who come. To the Galatians, however, he pronounced anathema if they heard something else—not something greater, certainly, but something contrary. Since it might be said that, even if the others preached the same things as he did, they nevertheless preached them better, he removes this objection.

“You do not rightly endure it,” he says. [Col. 1099C] “For I think”—that is, I know with certainty, but by the word *think* I rebuke your uncertainty—“that I have done nothing less for you than the great apostles,” that is, than the great apostles would have done, lest you think that you have received anything less than the other churches to which the others preached. Therefore my works make me equal to them.

He does not wish grace to appear inferior in himself, because he taught likewise and did the same things as the apostles did—apostles who seemed more distinguished because they began teaching earlier and had been with the Lord, and were consequently thought to possess greater authority. Yet this Apostle’s election is attested, he laboured more than the others, saw the Lord on the road and in the temple, and heard his words. “I have done nothing less,” he says.

“For although I am unskilled in speech”—because I do not adorn my words, or have an impeded tongue—“yet I am not unskilled in knowledge,” since I know everything that is great. This does not refer to the apostles, for they were not eloquent, being unlettered, though filled with the Holy Spirit (Acts 9); rather, it strikes at the false apostles, whom they preferred to the Apostle because of their polished speech, although in religion the power of speech is necessary, not sweetness of sound.

Yet he humbles himself greatly when he confesses that he is unskilled in speech—he to whom Festus, because of the greatness of his eloquence and wisdom, said: “You are mad, Paul, you are mad; much learning drives you mad” (Acts 26). Thus in saying this he did not mean that he was unable to speak, but spoke on account of those who wished to be commended not by faith but by eloquence.

Nevertheless, he called himself unskilled only in what [Col. 1100A] is not blameworthy. In what cannot be lacking without guilt and, when present, gains salvation, he did not pronounce himself unskilled. Whoever is unskilled in speech is not guilty before God; but whoever lacks knowledge of God is guilty of an ignorance which he is not permitted to have, especially concerning salvation.

Therefore, setting aside eloquence, the Apostle sought that faith might be acceptable through the witness of power: that eloquence might not commend faith, but power, to which eloquence yields. “Although I am unskilled in speech,” he says—that is, although I do not cultivate that worldly skill of speech, the harmonious arrangement of finely placed words—yet you cannot call me unskilled in knowledge, for I know the truth of the matter so well and can speak of God as deeply as the others, or more subtly. I am not unskilled in the knowledge of divine things.

“But you too know this, for I am manifest to you in all things”: that is, in knowledge, miracles, holiness, power, and the like. You therefore know that I also possess skill in speaking. Hence it is worse that, favouring others for their skill in speech—a skill in which you know that I am not inferior—you rank me below them, when you see that through me not only is preaching fulfilled but apostolic signs and wonders are performed.

> “Or have I committed a sin by humbling myself, that you might be exalted, because I preached the Gospel of God to you without charge? I despoiled other churches, receiving wages for ministering to you. And when I was with you and was in need, I was burdensome to no one. [Col. 1100C] For what was lacking to me the brethren who came from Macedonia supplied. And in all things I have kept myself free from burden to you and will keep myself so. The truth of Christ is in me: this boasting shall not be hindered in me in the regions of Achaia. Why? Because I do not love you? God knows. But what I do, I will also do, in order to cut off the opportunity of those who desire an opportunity, so that in that in which they boast they may be found like us.”

“I have not done less,” he says, “than the others; rather, I could say that I have done more, because I preached without charge. I have done nothing less. Or, if less, have I sinned in this? Have I committed a sin by humbling myself, working with my hands to seek and obtain my livelihood, so that you might be exalted”—that is, might advance to the heights of virtue, [Col. 1100D] having cast off the yoke of false apostles by which you are oppressed?

Truly I humbled myself, because I preached the Gospel of God to you freely: that is, demanding nothing from you. Because they were puffed up because he refused to receive support from them, and for this reason preferred others to him, he says: Have I sinned because I humbled myself and judged myself unworthy to receive, so that you are angry with me for this, although it is not a matter of sin but of glory?

He humbled himself when he did not demand the wages due to him. He did not wish to receive them for two reasons: lest he be found like the false apostles, who preached not for God’s glory but for their own profit, and lest they have an opportunity to ask for money—for when one person does not receive it, another cannot demand much; and lest the vigour of evangelical authority grow slack, since one who receives from sinners loses authority to rebuke them.

Thus they are exalted when he receives nothing from them in order that they may be rescued from the false apostles who oppressed them, rebuked and corrected, raised from death to life and from vices to virtues.

“I preached the Gospel to you without charge,” he says, “but meanwhile received my livelihood from others. For I despoiled other churches”: that is, I took much from them to expend upon you, receiving wages for ministering to you—that is, receiving means of livelihood while ministering the Gospel to you. It was necessary that I receive from others the bread of the body. And when I was with you and lacked things necessary for the body, I was burdensome to none of you by receiving any bodily support from him.

While he was among the Corinthians, the Apostle never wished to say this, lest what they had not done toward him from good will should be done under command, and, once their mercy was made known, should remain unknown. But later, when far away, he wrote this to them, lest they remain altogether unrebuked [variant: uncorrected], and behave toward other brethren as they had behaved toward their teacher in stinginess.

Truly, as teacher of the nations, neglecting his own interests and caring for others’, he fulfilled what he said: “Let no one seek what is his own, but what is another’s” (1 Cor. 10). He endured such want there that he suffered severe need for sustenance, even while preaching the bread of heaven. He laboured in the word for the life of his hearers; he laboured with his hands for the life of [Col. 1101C] his body. Support was also sent to him by disciples from other lands, that he might be able to preach to the Corinthians.

“When I was with you and in need,” he says, “I was burdensome to none of you by receiving anything,” lest you should suppose that I preached the Gospel for earthly gain. “For what I lacked, after the resources of the churches and the labour of my hands, the brethren who came from Macedonia supplied.” He always received from the Macedonians because they had not been subverted by false apostles. And just as it was not fitting to receive from the Corinthians, lest this become a stumbling block to them, so it was fitting in turn to receive from the Macedonians, lest those who sowed well should lose their fruit. For they did not give because they wished to have their vices flattered. “The Macedonians supplied what I lacked.”

[Col. 1101D] And not only in respect to wages, but in every word and deed I kept myself free from burden to you: for I did not boast of my lineage against you, nor did anything of that sort. And I shall always keep myself so toward you, lest I give false apostles an example of rapacity or falsehood. “The truth of Christ is in me”: that is, the truthful Christ speaks in me. “This boasting”—that is, this ground of boasting, that I preach without charge and abstain from lawful things for your salvation—“shall not be hindered in me,” but shall remain whole in me throughout all the regions of Achaia. For it is glorious to abstain from lawful things, especially for others’ salvation. This glory shall not be hindered in me in your regions.

And why do you think I do this? Do you suppose I do so because I do not love you? That is, do you think that I refrain from your goods out of hatred for you, as the false apostles say? God, who knows the secrets of the heart, knows that I do not reject your gifts because I do not love you; rather, I do so precisely because I love you, so that the very fact that I receive nothing from you may benefit you.

I do not refuse your gifts because of hatred for you, but in order to remove from the false apostles the opportunity to receive your money; for if they do not receive it, they will not preach for long. I do not do this because I do not love you. Rather, what I do in this matter I shall continue to do: I shall always abstain from your gifts, so that by my example I may cut off the opportunity to take your goods—the opportunity, I mean, of those who wish through me to find an opportunity to receive what is yours.

I shall therefore remove this opportunity from them, so that, in that in which they boast, they may be found [Col. 1102B] like us: that is, similar to us. The false apostles’ boasting consisted in receiving money, and therefore the Apostle rejected this, lest he appear like them. For unless the Apostle had avoided it, they would have been given greater opportunity to receive, or even to extort, when they could point to the Apostle’s example in this matter.

There were also certain false apostles who, imitating the Apostle, wished to receive nothing for worldly glory; nevertheless, they would gladly receive if they first saw the Apostle receiving. Thus he now says that he wishes to receive nothing in order to cut off from them the opportunity of receiving, so that they may remain like him in that of which they boast greatly—namely, that they should always remain non-receivers.

> “For such false apostles are deceitful workers, transforming themselves into apostles of Christ. And no wonder: for Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light. Therefore it is no great thing if his ministers transform themselves as ministers of righteousness, whose end shall be according to their works.”

I wish to remove from them the opportunity of receiving your goods, for they greatly desire to find an occasion by which they may receive them, although they pretend to wish to take nothing. For such false apostles are deceitful workers: that is, they work under the deceit of pretence, because they cleverly deceive under the appearance of religion. They are deceitful because they preach Christ not from love of eternal life but from love of money, usurping the apostolic name when they have by no means [Col. 1102D] been sent.

For a deceitful worker feigns one thing and does another. Thus these persons conceal bestial rapacity beneath the appearance of Christ’s simple preaching. To please and, by pleasing, to receive, they must flatter; and by flattering, deceive—saying what pleases rather than what it is expedient to hear. They are therefore deceitful workers, working in this way; and by such arts they transform themselves into apostles of Christ: that is, they change the appearance of their falsity by assuming the form of true apostles, so that, while wickedness is cleverly concealed and the appearance of holiness is seen, they may deceive the unwary.

And because they wish to appear like true apostles, I do not receive your goods, so that, since I do not receive, neither may they transform themselves into apostles of truth and deceive in this way. Nor is it surprising [Col. 1103A] that Satan’s ministers do this. For Satan himself, whom they serve, transforms himself into an angel of light: that is, he assumes a splendid appearance and appears to human beings as though he were believed to be a holy angel, and thus deceives.

When he transforms himself in this way, we must judge and discern, lest he lead us by deception into things destructive. For when the bodily sense deceives but does not move the mind from the true and right judgment by which one lives faithfully, there is no danger in religion. Or when, pretending to be good, he does or says things fitting for good angels, even if he is believed to be good, this is not a dangerous or pernicious error of Christian faith. But when through these alien things he begins to draw a person to his own ends, then great and necessary vigilance is required, to discern him and not follow him.

Yet no one can escape all his deadly deceits unless God governs and protects him. The very difficulty of this matter is useful in this respect: that no one should place hope in himself or in another human being, but in God alone. And since Satan—whose name means “adversary,” because he opposes human salvation—so transforms himself, and by promising good things feigns himself an angel of light to human sight, it is no great thing if his ministers transform themselves so as to appear like ministers of righteousness: that is, if false apostles falsely claim to be companions of Christ’s apostles and thereby deceive their hearers.

The end of these ministers of Satan will be according to their works, because at the end they will be judged according to their pretended actions: they preached not for the Lord but for their own belly, while pretending to be God’s ministers. [Col. 1103C] Their end will be according to their works, because, just as care for the belly and the works done for the belly perish, so they too will perish.

> “Again I say: Let no one think me foolish. Otherwise, receive me as foolish, so that I too may boast a little. What I speak, I do not speak according to God, but as it were in folly, in this matter of boasting. Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast.”

Already above he said, “Would that you might bear with a little of my folly,” and now he repeats this, because he always sets forth beforehand what he will pursue after laying many things aside. Therefore, what he proposed above he now begins to recount. “I said,” he says, “that you should bear with some of my folly,” [Col. 1103D] that is, with my boasting; “and now I say again that no one should think me foolish in this boasting, because I do not boast with the intention with which they do, but for your benefit. Otherwise,” that is, if you are unwilling not to consider me foolish, receive me not as truly foolish but as though foolish, while I seem to praise myself, so that I too, like them, may boast a little according to the flesh. A little, because my boasting is directed toward you, not toward my own mind. For the Apostle does not truly say these things for his own glory; but, grieving because they glorified false apostles while despising him, he is unwillingly compelled to disclose his good qualities. Nor is he blameworthy for this, but rather praiseworthy. For every righteous person, if remaining in humble thought he should, when necessity or grief requires it, speak truthfully of his own good qualities, has departed [Col. 1104A] from righteousness only to the extent that he has in any way departed from truth. Therefore the Apostle recounts many strong things about himself for the edification of his disciples; but in recounting them he does not sin, because he does not depart from the path of truth and sure testimony, with a humble heart.

“I said,” he says, “that I am as though foolish, because what I speak in this matter of glory—that is, in bodily glory, which they regard as a substance—I do not speak according to God, but as though in folly.” He does not now speak according to God, because these matters pertain to the swelling of the flesh; nor does glory arise before the Lord from fleshly inflation, before whom humility alone is glorious, but it is as though folly. He did not call it complete folly, but as though folly, for it is true. But because self-exaltation is a vicious thing, therefore, although what is [Col. 1104B] said is true, for anyone to praise himself is nevertheless as though folly, since Wisdom says: “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips” (Prov. XXVII). Complete folly, however, occurs if someone lifts himself up with false praises. The former is proud on account of what is true; the latter foolish on account of what is false. The substance of boasting in this matter is merely fleshly, because this glory passes away like the flower of hay (Isa. XL; Jas. I).

“I speak as though in folly. For since many boast according to the flesh,” that is, because the false apostles claim for themselves nobility of flesh and thereby defend for themselves the prerogative of lineage, since they are called sons of Abraham, “I too will boast,” because I too am a son of Abraham. Yet it is of no benefit before the Lord to be Abraham’s son if Abraham’s righteousness or faith is lacking, [Col. 1104C] because it is faith that saves, not descent from Abraham’s stock. He says that he boasts according to the flesh, but counts this as folly, in order to empty this glory of its value and show that he has been compelled to break out into praise of flesh. For this reason he boasts: to show that he possesses more eminently, even in carnal terms, everything in which the false apostles boasted; and thus that he rather—the one who preaches Christ without falsehood—should be received, and that those who receive him may be saved.

> “For you gladly bear with the foolish, being yourselves wise. For you endure it if someone reduces you to slavery, if someone devours you, if someone takes from you, if someone exalts himself, if someone strikes you in the face. I speak according to dishonour, as though we had been weak [Col. 1104D] in this respect.”

“I said that you should receive me as though foolish, so that I too may boast a little according to the flesh. For you gladly bear with the foolish,” that is, you endure voluntarily, not under compulsion, the false apostles who boast in nobility of lineage and circumcision of the flesh, and who try to draw us ourselves into their folly. And because you endure with no good patience those who boast in this manner, it is right that you should rather bear with me in my boasting, because I shall boast not for my own exaltation but for your benefit. You gladly bear with those foolish persons—that is, those who boast according to the flesh and are wise according to the flesh—which is remarkable, since you yourselves are wise, that is, instructed in heavenly wisdom through my teaching. For this reason you are the more blameworthy, [Col. 1105A] because, although you have been instructed through me in evangelical wisdom, you now gladly bear with these deceivers, who wish to lead you into the folly of fleshly understanding and observance of the Law.

For you endure it if any one of them reduces you from Christ’s freedom into the slavery of the Law, which is observed out of servile fear. Or: you bear with the foolish while you yourselves are wise—not indeed all of you, but some wise in the understanding of divine things. Or: you bear with the foolish while you are wise; that is, this proves that you are not wise, because you gladly bear with the foolish. For a friend of fools will become like them; and truly, in wishing to endure their perversity, you are not wise, because you are so dull that you endure this injury: if any one of them reduces you from the freedom of the Gospel [Col. 1105B] into slavery to the Law.

Or, I show point by point how you bear with the foolish. For you endure their yoke if any one of them wishes to reduce you into slavery to the Law; and if any one devours you—that is, consumes your goods by eating them up with great greed; and if anyone takes your possessions in the manner of a hawk, whereas I, sparing you, do not wish to take them; and if any such person exalts himself by boasting of nobility of lineage, you bear with him also; and if any one of them strikes you in the face—that is, standing before you, he casts the insult of reproach upon you, despising you because you are not circumcised in the flesh and because you worshipped idols—you bear with him as well. For he is struck in the face upon whose mouth an injury is inflicted. Therefore he strikes you in the face who, striking your countenance with blows of abuse, makes you blush.

“I speak according to dishonour”: I say that you are so struck with the dishonour which the false apostles cast up to you, because you are of idolatrous stock; for the very reproach of dishonour is a blow in the face. And while they disparage you because you are uncircumcised, and boast of themselves because they are of Abraham’s seed—preferring themselves and humbling us—you endure them thus and prefer them to us, as though we had been weak in this matter, [Col. 1105C] that is, unable to boast of carnal nobility. This is: you allow yourselves to be struck by them, and not by us, as though we could not similarly hurl contemptuous words at you, exalting ourselves on account of lineage and despising you. For we are not weak in this matter of glory; indeed, those who had been joined to Abraham’s lineage from other nations would be judged weak. But we are strong in this respect, because we descend from Abraham’s stock. Why then do you prefer false apostles to us in this glory of flesh, in which we are not inferior?

> “In whatever anyone dares, I speak in folly, I dare also. Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they Abraham’s seed? So am I. Are they ministers of Christ? So am I.”

We are not weak in this matter of boasting, because in whatever any one of them dares to boast, I too dare similarly; and I say this in folly, because it is rash for anyone to boast or praise himself, since, as we have stated before, Wisdom says: “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips” (Prov. XXVII). [Col. 1106A] Therefore I say in folly that I dare in that in which these people dare, who boast that they are sons of Abraham, in order to show that they are foolish and to annihilate their glory. Truly, I am inferior to them in nothing. For they are Hebrews—that is, from the stock of the patriarch Heber—and I likewise am a Hebrew by lineage and language.

These verses must be read by question and answer: one asks, “Are they Hebrews?” and the answer is, “So am I a Hebrew.” “Are they Israelites?” that is, of the stock of Jacob, who was also divinely called Israel; and I too am no less an Israelite, that is, a son of the same distinguished father. “Are they Abraham’s seed?” that is, not proselytes but natural sons of Abraham; and I likewise am seed of the same patriarch. Why then are they preferred to me in things [Col. 1106B] in which I am not inferior to them? And are they ministers of Christ, as they say? I truly am a minister of Christ. For they call themselves Christ’s ministers in order to deceive by this means; but I am his minister without falsehood, that I may draw to him all whom I can.

> “I speak as one less wise: I am more.” In far more labours, more abundantly in imprisonments, beyond measure in beatings, frequently in deaths. From the Jews five times I received forty lashes less one. Three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned; three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I was in the deep of the sea.”

It should be understood that the righteous and perfect sometimes proclaim their virtues and recount the good things which they have received from God, [Col. 1106C] not in order that they themselves may advance in the estimation of people through displaying themselves, but in order to draw by their example to life those to whom they preach. Thus the Apostle now tells the Corinthians how often he was beaten with sticks, how often stoned, how often he endured shipwreck, how greatly he suffered for the truth, that he was caught up to the third heaven, and that he was brought into paradise, so that he might turn their minds away from false preachers; so that, when it became known what sort of person he was, those whom he had learned were unjustly revered by them might become cheap in their eyes.

When the perfect do this—that is, when they speak of their own virtues—in this too they imitate the almighty Lord, who speaks his praises to people so that he may be known by people. For since in Scripture he commands, saying, “Let another’s mouth praise you, and not your own,” how does he himself do what he forbids (Prov. XXVII)? But if the almighty Lord were silent about his virtues, no one would know him; if no one knew him, no one would love him; if no one loved him, no one would return to life. Therefore it is said through the Psalmist: “He will declare to his people the power of his works, that he may give them the inheritance of the nations” (Ps. CX). [Col. 1106D] He declares his virtues, not so that he himself may increase through his praises, but so that those who have learned these things from his self-praise may attain the everlasting inheritance.

Therefore, even when the righteous and perfect speak to the weak of the virtues they possess, they are not blameworthy, because by recounting their own life they seek to bring other souls to life. Paul therefore rightly recounts his own virtues to the Corinthians, [Col. 1107A] so that his merit before the Lord may become known to them; so that, knowing his merit, they may gladly receive the teaching through which they are saved, and reject the false apostles by whom they were being led astray. “They,” he says, “boast that they are ministers of Christ, though in truth they are not his ministers; but I truly am what they pretend to be. And I am even more a minister of Christ than they are,” or more than the other preachers of Christ. “And I say this as one less wise,” because it is not proper for a person to praise himself. In speaking truthfully about himself, he calls himself less wise, that it may be understood that he was compelled to burst forth into his own praise. For one who voluntarily recounts things that contribute to his praise does not acknowledge himself foolish.

[Col. 1107B] He thus shows what makes him more a minister of Christ than the other preachers. Having found an occasion, he touches on the persons of all, even the apostles, grieving because God’s grace was judged less in him, although he performed the same things as the other apostles and endured greater disasters for the faith. “I am more a minister of Christ than other preachers, proved in far more labours,” because I laboured more than all of them in the ministry of evangelical preaching. For they too laboured, but I more harshly and more repeatedly, because I endured more adversities, preached to more nations, wrote more, and took no stipend. “And I have been proved a minister of Christ more abundantly in imprisonments” than those whom you prefer to me, because, if [Col. 1107C] they were imprisoned for the ministry of preaching, I was nevertheless imprisoned more often and for longer. “And in beatings beyond measure”—either beyond their measure or beyond the measure of human strength—because, if they were beaten, I was nevertheless beaten more severely and more repeatedly. “And frequently in deaths,” because I was often tortured unto death.

“I received from the Jews five times forty lashes less one,” that is, I was five times scourged by the Jews according to the Law of Moses, as a transgressor of the Law because I preached the new grace, receiving thirty-nine strokes on each occasion (Deut. XXV). For the Law commanded that, when judges beat an offender, they should temper the measure of punishment so that the number of blows did not exceed forty. Accordingly, [Col. 1107D] on each of those five occasions when they beat me, they remitted one blow to me as though out of mercy. “Three times I was beaten with rods by the Gentiles,” as at Philippi; “once I was stoned by the Jews,” at Lystra (Acts XVI). “Three times I was shipwrecked,” that is, I endured the danger of a wrecked vessel while crossing seas in order to evangelize many nations.

Perhaps these shipwrecks might be understood to have occurred on the voyage by which the Apostle came to Rome; but when he wrote this epistle, he had not yet gone up to Jerusalem, where he was seized by the Jews and afterwards sent to Rome by Festus the governor (Acts XXVII). For earlier in this epistle he spoke at length to the Corinthians concerning the collection of alms which he was to carry to Jerusalem. Therefore all the tribulations and dangers [Col. 1108A] mentioned in this epistle occurred before he went to Jerusalem. Yet not everything is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles, because there too many things are found which are nowhere openly mentioned in these epistles.

For it is unknown when what he adds next occurred: “A night and a day I was in the deep of the sea.” This must nevertheless be understood according to the letter: namely, that the Apostle, by some accident, came into the depth of the sea and remained there through both day and night, then, under God’s guidance, returned safely to land. Thus it is reckoned among the other divine miracles that a man held for so long beneath the waves could neither be suffocated by the surrounding waters nor devoured by sea creatures. For what is more marvelous: that Peter walked upon the waters [Col. 1108B] (Matt. XIV), or that Paul lived beneath the waters day and night?

But if we seek something mystical in the very different miracles of the two apostles, Paul, not only shipwrecked for the third time, but also placed night and day in the deep sea, everywhere protected and delivered by the Lord, signifies that the righteous are to be divinely rescued from every danger: not only saved from temptations pressing upon them from without, but also, even if they seem to have been sunk in the whirlpool of death itself and hidden from human affairs, nevertheless restored to life by the power of their Creator. Peter, however, walking over waves stirred by the wind, but beginning to sink through fear and raised by Christ’s right hand, signifies that the same righteous overcome and trample underfoot, by unconquered faith, all the temptations and persecutions of the ungodly brought against them [Col. 1108C] at the devil’s instigation; nor can those who continually behold the help of God present be wholly submerged by the waves of the world. And if, as human beings, they sometimes stagger, they are promptly raised and strengthened by divine power.

After this the Apostle mentions other dangers and various labours, in order to show that he was afflicted in the flesh on land and sea for Christ, and to teach that in every place, or in every kind of affliction, he laboured for the Gospel. For he says:

> “Often in journeys; in dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my own people, dangers from the Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers among false brethren; [Col. 1108D] in labour and hardship, in many sleepless nights, in hunger and thirst, in many fasts, in cold and nakedness. Apart from those things which are outward, my daily pressure: concern for all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is caused to stumble, and I do not burn?”

“I have often been proved a minister of Christ in journeys,” he says, “by the dangers from rivers which I endured; because, as I continually went from place to place to make Christ’s name known everywhere, I frequently found rivers which I could not cross without danger. And by dangers from robbers, because the devil, envying my journey, stirred up robbers against me, though I carried nothing that robbers would desire. And by dangers from my own people,” that is, from the Jews, who envied me more than the other apostles [Col. 1109A] and continually sought to kill me, because more forcefully and plainly than the others I preached the new grace and the abolition of the old observance, although I had formerly been a zealot for the Law and a persecutor of the followers of grace. “And by dangers from the Gentiles,” because the Gentiles also sought to kill me on account of the overthrow of idolatry and the preaching of the one God.

“And by dangers in the city,” as at Ephesus, where, in defense of Diana, they rushed with one accord into the theatre (Acts XIX); and when I wished to enter the enraged crowd in order to suffer martyrdom, the disciples did not permit me. “And by dangers in the wilderness,” because while I travelled I suffered in the desert danger either from beasts, from people, from lack of drink, or from lack of food. “And by dangers at sea,” because there too I suffered dangers from [Col. 1109B] people, from want, or from storms. For when I was in Greece, the Jews laid plots against me while I was about to sail for Syria (Acts XX). “And by dangers among false brethren,” that is, those who had embraced Christianity but had not abandoned Judaism, who observed the Law carnally and persecuted me because, having preached Christ, I said that the Law had now ceased.

There were also other false brethren, such as Demas and Hermogenes, who loved this age [an apparent OCR corruption or uncertain reference] (II Tim. IV; II Tim. I); and the Church is even now full of such people. The other dangers may cease, but dangers from false brethren do not know how to cease until the end of the age.

Again, I have been proved a minister of Christ more than the others in labour of my hands, by which I sought my livelihood, and in hardship, [Col. 1109C] that is, the distress of pain or poverty; and in many sleepless nights, because I preached not only by day but also by night, often kept watch for the sake of prayer, and sometimes worked with my hands through the night at some task from which I might have a living. “And in hunger and thirst,” because, while I received nothing from my disciples, I necessarily endured hunger and thirst through want. I also laboured in hunger and thirst when I frequently fled my persecutors from place to place. “And in many fasts,” because I often fasted because I had nothing to eat. I also often voluntarily wore myself down with fasts, chastising my body and bringing it into slavery (I Cor. IX). I laboured also in cold and nakedness, when my clothing was scanty and torn in winter. And I endured all these things for Christ, [Col. 1109D] whose minister I am.

But apart from those things which are outward—that is, apart from the evils which I endure externally in my body—my daily pressure, which does not cease for even an hour, distresses me. And what is it? Concern for all the churches, because every day I devote myself to concern for the salvation of all who are in all the churches. Truly I always bear great concern for them. For who among the faithful is weak in faith, conscience, or conduct, and I am not weak? That is, do I not sympathize and condescend to him, so that I may apply a remedy to his weakness, which I grieve over as though it were my own? And who is caused to stumble—that is, who stumbles in the steps of conduct, so that the course of his good work is delayed, or even falls into fault, or whose faith is troubled by some [Col. 1110A] error—and I do not burn? That is, am I not inflamed with zeal for God?

For my mind is greatly tormented by the fire of spiritual zeal when it sees any of the weak abandoning eternal things and delighting in temporal things. I burn as gold is burned for purification, with the fire of devout grief, because this affection purifies the more, since it comes from charity. For the greater the charity, the greater the wounds caused by the sins of others. I do not burn as one angry with sinners, but as one grieving for them. Hence it is written: “He who adds knowledge adds sorrow” (Eccl. I).

Thus, as has been read, the Apostle enumerates the wars which he endures outwardly, saying: “Dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my own people, dangers from the Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers among [Col. 1110B] false brethren.” But he adds how many darts he hurls against the adversary in this warfare: “In labour and hardship, in many sleepless nights, in hunger and thirst, in many fasts, in cold and nakedness.” But, beset amid so many contests, he says by what protection of watchfulness he also guards the camp. For after recounting these outward matters, he immediately began to speak of the inward, adding: “Apart from those things which are outward, my daily pressure: concern for all the churches.” Behold: he courageously undertakes wars in himself, and mercifully expends himself in protecting his neighbours. He recounts the evils he suffers and adds the good he imparts.

Let us therefore consider what charity it is to care more for the benefit of one’s neighbours than for one’s own affliction. Let us consider what labour it is, at one and the same time, to endure adversities outwardly [Col. 1110C] and protect the weak inwardly. In himself he disregards wounds of the body, and in others he heals wounds of the heart. It is much less laborious either to teach while enduring nothing, or to endure while teaching nothing. But the Apostle diligently stretches himself to both, because he so undertakes outward wars that he carefully considers lest the inward parts of his neighbours be torn. Therefore he does not without reason confess that he has laboured more than all.

Who, then, would dare to prefer anyone to him in honour, who surpasses all in labour? And he adds:

> “If I must boast, I will boast of the things that belong to my weakness. The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ knows—he who is blessed for ever—that I do not lie. At Damascus, the governor of the nation under King Aretas guarded the city of the Damascenes in order [Col. 1110D] to seize me (Acts IX). And through a window I was lowered in a basket through the wall, and thus I escaped his hands.”

“If I must boast”: indeed it is not expedient. “If I must boast,” he says, as I must boast for your sake, I shall boast not in power or lineage, but in the things belonging to my weakness—that is, in the sufferings which I endure for Christ, although this appears contemptible. For if a Christian must boast, he must boast in humility, by which he grows before God. But the false apostles, because they have no merits of sufferings in which they can boast, boast in the loftiness of lineage.

But lest you think that I say anything false, I call God as witness to you of the truth. For God, [Col. 1111A] who knows all things, himself knows that I do not lie. God, who according to Christ’s humanity is his God, and according to his divinity is his Father—he who is blessed through all ages—knows, that is, bears witness to me that I do not lie in all the things stated above, or in what I add. For even after my conversion, when I was in Damascus, the governor of the nation under King Aretas guarded that city itself—that is, its gates—in order to seize me, so that he might thereby please the Jews who lay in wait for me, and might seem diligent in the office entrusted to him, if he killed, for the sake of public tranquillity, the man whom he heard called a disturber.

He guarded the gates because he knew that I was in the city but could not find me; or because he did not wish to seize me within, lest he violate the city’s law. [Col. 1111B] Meanwhile, I was lowered by the brethren through a window in a basket over the wall, and thus escaped his hands. Paul did not flee as a hired hand usually flees, leaving the sheep when the wolf comes (John X), because that wolf sought not the sheep but the shepherd himself; and therefore the shepherd, by fleeing, preserved himself for their benefit. Nor, when he departed, was the Church there left without necessary ministry; rather, through other brethren established in that same place, what was necessary was fulfilled. The Apostle did this at their desire, in order to preserve for the Church himself, whom that persecutor particularly sought.

Whenever any ruler of the Church is individually sought by persecutors, then he ought to flee, provided that [Col. 1111C] the Church is not deserted by others who are not sought in the same way, but that they provide the food of the word to their fellow-servants whom they know cannot live otherwise. But when a common danger presses upon all together, then either all—the rulers and the subjects alike—should pass together to other places, or all should remain there together. It is also necessary in everything we do to weigh on the balance of the mind, on one side the burden of labour and on the other the fruit of reward. When the burden of labour outweighs the fruit of recompense, each person may innocently avoid the labour, provided that he exercises himself in other works in which the gain of fruit outweighs the burden of labour. But when the measure of labour is equalled or exceeded by the ensuing quantity of fruit, then labour is not avoided without grave fault.

Therefore, when the outstanding teacher saw at Damascus the very obstinate minds of the persecutors, [Col. 1111D] he did not wish to contend against their hostility, because he saw that he could preserve himself, whom he knew would benefit many, while he would benefit there either no one or only a few. He therefore withdrew from the conflict and kept himself for happier fighting in other battles. For it was not courage that lacked a place, but a place that lacked courage. Accordingly, the bravest soldier sought a battlefield out of the straits of siege, where something mystical was also foreshadowed.

For this mode of escape is preserved in the Church to this day, when someone surrounded by the snares of the ancient enemy or the traps of this world is saved by the defense of hope and faith. The wall of Damascus, whose name means “drinking blood,” is the adversity of the world. The governor of Damascus is some persecutor [Col. 1112A] powerful in this world. King Aretas, whose name means “descent,” is understood as the devil. The basket, which is customarily made of rushes and palms, signifies the union of hope and faith. For the rush signifies the greenness of faith, while the palm signifies hope of eternal life. Whoever, therefore, sees himself encircled by the wall of adversity should hasten to climb into the basket of virtue by which he may escape.

But after recounting this escape, the Apostle immediately added:

## CHAPTER XII

> “If I must boast, indeed it is not expedient.”

“If I must boast,” that is, if I must boast because I escaped, since I kept the hands [Col. 1112B] of those lying in wait free from committing murder, “indeed it is not expedient to boast,” because one who boasts of having escaped death inflicted for the faith indicates that suffering for Christ appears vain. Or, if because of the false apostles I must boast in this boasting of mine and in the things stated above, nevertheless it is not expedient on account of pride, because we grow through humility and God’s help prospers the meek, not the proud. It is indeed not expedient; yet for your benefit it is necessary to boast.

> “But I will come to visions and revelations of the Lord. I know a man in Christ fourteen years ago—whether in the body or outside the body I do not know; God knows—such a one caught up to the third heaven. And I know such a man—whether in the body or outside the body I do not know; God [Col. 1112C] knows—that he was caught up into paradise and heard secret words which a human being is not permitted to speak.”

Hitherto, he says, I have related the tribulations and dangers from which the Lord delivered me; and now, continuing my account, I shall come to the visions and revelations of the Lord—that is, to the mysteries which I saw concerning the Lord and openly understood. I was not like Pharaoh, who saw the vision of the seven ears of grain and did not understand, because it had not been revealed what they signified (Gen. 41). For I beheld mystical visions and, as the Lord revealed what wisdom they contained, I understood. And hear the visions: “I know a man,” etc. He shows to what height he was lifted, so that the greatness and character of the things shown and spoken to him might be understood, lest he be thought, as seemed to some, younger than the other apostles.

For he speaks of himself [Col. 1112D] as though of another, in order to avoid boasting, because he reports something that pertains to the highest praise. And what is lost to truth when both the fact itself is stated and, by a certain manner of speaking, boasting is avoided? “I know,” he says, “a man in Christ, fourteen years ago, caught up to the third heaven.” From the time when the Apostle was thus caught up until the time when he wrote this epistle, fourteen years had elapsed. He noted this so that it might be understood that, when writing these things, he possessed much greater merit than when he saw them; and because he was speaking not from boastfulness, but from necessity, of things he had kept silent about for so many years.

“I know,” he says, “a man caught up—whether in the body I do not know, or outside the body”; that is, I know that that man was caught up, but I do not know whether with the body or without the body. “I do not know this; God knows”: that is, I confirm this to you by my customary oath. For an oath is what is meant by the saying, “God knows.” “I know such a man caught up to the third heaven. And I know such a man caught up into paradise.” For that man was caught up twice: that is, into the third heaven and again into paradise, concerning which the Lord promised the thief: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23).

But he did not know whether, when he was thus caught up, he was in the body—as the soul is in the body when the body is said to live—whether awake, asleep, or in ecstasy, withdrawn from the bodily senses; or whether he had wholly departed from the body, so that he made the body dead until, after that manifestation was completed, the soul was restored to the dead limbs, and he did not awaken as from sleep [Col. 1113A] or return anew to the senses after being removed in ecstasy, but was altogether brought back to life from death.

Many things may be said concerning the third heaven. For there are nine orders of angels, which, according to Dionysius, are distributed in three triads. Their first triple arrangement—that is, the one nearest the earth—consists of angels, archangels, and principalities; the middle one of powers, virtues, and dominions; and the highest of thrones, cherubim, and seraphim. The first arrangement, therefore, may rightly be understood as the first heaven; the second as the second heaven; and the third as the third heaven. Thus the Apostle, caught up into the third heaven, is understood to have been among the highest choirs of angels—that is, to have seen the secrets of God among the hosts [Col. 1113B] of seraphim or cherubim.

He was also caught up into paradise, whether earthly or heavenly, and there heard secret words—that is, an intimation concerning God’s hidden essence—which it is not lawful for a human being to speak: that is, which it is not lawful for him to disclose to any mortal, or which no human being can utter in this life.

Or let us understand the three heavens as three kinds of vision: the first corporeal, the second spiritual, and the third intellectual. For in this one commandment, when one reads, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Lev. 19), three kinds of vision occur. One is through the eyes, by which the letters themselves are seen; another through the human spirit, by which one thinks of one’s neighbor even when absent; the third heaven is through the mind’s apprehension, by which love itself is understood.

By corporeal vision heaven, earth, and all things visible to bodily eyes are seen. By spiritual vision bodily images are perceived in the spirit, as when we form in the mind likenesses of bodily things according to our knowledge. By intellectual vision those things are perceived which have no likenesses resembling themselves, such as charity, joy, peace, patience, and the like. Spiritual vision is superior to corporeal vision, and intellectual vision is superior in turn. For what is seen not imaginatively but properly, and not through the body, is seen by that vision which surpasses all the others.

By corporeal vision Belshazzar saw the fingers of a hand writing on the wall (Dan. 5). By spiritual vision Peter saw a vessel full of various [Col. 1113C] animals (Acts 10). By intellectual vision wisdom, truth, charity, and God himself are seen.

Therefore, if the Apostle called “the third heaven” this third kind of vision, which is above not only every corporeal kind by which bodies are perceived through bodily senses, but also above every spiritual kind by which likenesses of bodies are perceived by the spirit rather than the mind, then in it the brightness of God is seen not through some bodily or spiritually formed signification, as “through a mirror in an enigma,” but face to face, that is, by direct sight; because God—whatever and however little the mind, which is not itself what he is, can grasp—is apprehended by a mind cleansed from every earthly stain [Note: [Col. 1113D] An obscure passage.], separated and withdrawn from every body and bodily likeness.

Why, then, should we not believe that God wished to show to so great an apostle, the teacher of the Gentiles, caught up to this most excellent vision, the life in which he is to be seen eternally after this life? And why should this not be called paradise, apart from that paradise in which Adam lived bodily? For if paradise properly means a wooded place, but by transferred usage means every spiritual region, as it were, in which the soul fares well, then it may deservedly be called paradise—not only the third heaven, whatever that may be, which is certainly great and sublimely glorious, but even within a human being a certain joy of a good conscience is paradise.

If, therefore, we rightly understand the first heaven in the general sense as all this corporeal realm, whatever lies above the waters and the earth; the second [Col. 1114A] as that which is perceived in bodily likeness by the spirit, such as the sheet full of animals that was lowered to Peter in ecstasy (ibid.); and the third as that which is perceived by the mind, so hidden, remote, and altogether withdrawn from the senses of the flesh and purified that it can ineffably see and hear the things in that heaven, God’s very substance, and the Word of the Lord through whom all things were made (Ps. 32), in the charity of the Holy Spirit—then we do not think it incongruous that the Apostle was caught up there, and that there perhaps is a paradise better than all others, indeed, if it may be said, a paradise of paradises.

Nor is this understanding contrary to what the Lord said to Moses: “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 33). For the mind must be withdrawn from this life when it is taken up into the ineffability of that vision, just as the Apostle’s mind was divinely caught up from this life into the angelic life before, through the common death, he was released from the flesh. And there, enjoying God’s address, he heard ineffable words which it is not lawful for a human being to utter. Therefore, when he preached, he spoke what could be said to human beings and kept to himself what could not be said. Let what we can comprehend in mind, then, be heard; and let what we cannot comprehend be believed. If we said to him, “We ask you: explain to us its greatness,” would he not perhaps answer, “What I saw is not very great, if it can be explained by me”?

> “For such a one I will boast; but for myself I will boast of nothing [Col. 1115A] except my weaknesses. For even if I should wish to boast, I shall not be foolish, for I shall speak the truth. But I refrain, lest anyone think of me beyond what he sees in me or hears something from me.”

“For such a man,” or for such a vision, “I will boast”: that is, I will commend myself. But for myself as a son of Abraham or as circumcised, I will boast of nothing except my weaknesses—that is, the tribulations I suffer. He says that he will boast for such a man, namely one so worthy of God as to be raised to this excellence of visions; yet he does not wish openly to say that he speaks of himself, lest he appear to praise himself. Thus he does not boast for himself, because he does not openly declare that it is of himself.

But he boasts in weaknesses because recounting the pressures of sufferings and the weaknesses of distress seems not glorious but lamentable. Therefore he safely confesses that he boasts in these, knowing that they lead to the perfection of heavenly rewards. For what could be more glorious in the future for a Christian than to recount the destructions inflicted for Christ?

“For this man I will boast, not for myself. For even if I should wish to boast for myself”—that is, to declare the merit I possess before God—“I shall not be foolish” in this boasting, although I may seem so to some. For I shall not speak falsehoods, but shall tell the truth about myself; and therefore I shall boast humbly and truthfully, not in myself but in truth itself, which is above me.

I could indeed still boast of many things, but “I refrain”: that is, I speak sparingly, lest anyone think of me beyond what he sees in me—lest anyone suppose that I am of a more excellent nature than he can comprehend with his own eyes and begin to err concerning me, believing that I possess a divine or angelic nature, like those who said of me and Barnabas: “Gods in the likeness of human beings have come down to us” (Acts 14). For they thought us beyond what they saw in us because, although they saw in us an earthly and mortal body, they thought us heavenly and immortal. Therefore I refrain from boasting, lest, if I report more things, anyone think that I am beyond what he sees in me: that is, beyond the nature of humanity which he sees in me; or beyond [Col. 1115B] what he hears reported about me by others.

Or: lest anyone think of me beyond what he sees in me or hears concerning me; that is, lest anyone judge me to extend beyond my glory, beyond what the boundary of merits permits. All saints not only do not at all seek glory beyond their measure, but they also shrink from being thought to be what they have deserved to be.

Hence the outstanding preacher now speaks against the false apostles. While he was recounting the extraordinary powers of his ministry for the instruction of his disciples, while he was describing how he had endured so many dangers amid accumulated persecution, and while after these things he recalled that he had been caught up to the third heaven and again into paradise, where he could know such great things as he could not possibly speak, perhaps he was about to say still more wonderful things about himself. But, restraining himself from human praise by lofty reflection, he adds: “But I refrain, lest anyone think of me beyond what he sees in me or hears something from me”; that is, lest, if I say the rest, someone think me beyond the nature of human weakness, when nothing but weakness is visible in me or heard from others who see me.

He therefore still had something to say about himself which he refrains from saying. But the outstanding teacher did both: by speaking of what he had done, he instructed his disciples; and by being silent, he preserved himself within the bounds of humility. He would have been exceedingly ungrateful if he had kept such things about himself silent from his disciples; and perhaps exceedingly imprudent if he had disclosed everything about himself to them. But, as was said, he did both wonderfully: by speaking, he instructed the lives of his hearers; by silence, he guarded his own.

> “And lest the greatness of the revelations exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan, to strike me with blows. For this I begged the Lord three times [Col. 1116A] that it might depart from me; and he said to me: My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness. Therefore I shall most gladly boast in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me.”

“I,” he says, “saw such great and lofty things by divine revelation; and lest the greatness of such immense revelations exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh.” I was not exalted, but lest I should be exalted, God provided me with a remedy to set against the pride that might occur. For pride arising from an abundance of graces is greatly to be feared, lest anyone grow proud of God’s gift. Rather, one should preserve humility, and “the greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. 3).

This Apostle, though made a preacher from a persecutor, received in every apostolic labor more abundant grace than the other apostles, so that God might more clearly show that what he gives belongs to him, not to a human being—just as physicians are accustomed to display the power of their art in desperate cases. Since he possessed great grace and had received great gifts from God, and since pride could creep in upon him through the abundance of grace and revelations, God, who knows all things before they occur, set beside him a certain reminder of human weakness, in the likeness of triumphal processions, in which a companion stood behind the victor in the chariot, saying at every acclamation of the citizens, “Remember that you are human.”

“Lest I be exalted,” he says, “by the greatness of the revelations, there was given to me by God”—that is, for my benefit, to keep me in humility—“a thorn in the flesh,” that is, something pricking my flesh. And what is this thorn? “An angel of Satan”: that is, an evil angel, sent by Satan, “to strike me with blows,” that is, to smite me, restraining every movement of pride by constantly stirring up tribulations, bodily weaknesses, or, as some say, temptations through lust. Yet temptation to which one does not consent is not sin, but material for the exercise of virtue.

For this thorn was perhaps the concupiscence of the flesh. Considering these evils in the body of his death, in which he waged an inward war with an invisible enemy, the Apostle tells the Romans that he found absolutely no remedy for his salvation except the grace of God alone, delivering him in Christ Jesus (Rom. 7). But he is also said to have been violently afflicted by some bodily pain. Bodily pains are often inflicted by angels of Satan, but they cannot do this unless permitted. Thus Job too was tested (Job 2): Satan was permitted to test him and struck him with an ulcer, so that he decayed with worms.

Likewise, the angel of Satan was, as it were, willingly sent to strike the Apostle with blows, yet the Apostle was being healed. He therefore received this remedy from God so that, continually pressed by injuries and temptations through an unjust angel, he might not be exalted by revelations, since an idle heart could swell with the things it had seen. For by a hidden order of providence, the very source from which the devil’s wickedness is permitted to rage is also the source by which God’s goodness is mercifully brought to perfection. God would lose men made proud by holiness unless he tested them. [Col. 1116B] For saints who grew proud of the glory of holiness would not be saints; and the more they elevated themselves in their own virtues, the more they would fall under his dominion.

But by a wondrous order of providence, while they are tested they are humbled; while they are humbled, they cease to be his. Yet before the Apostle incurred the disease of pride, the heavenly physician, in his foresight, gave him the medicine of humility. Because the medicine prescribed by the physician was painful to him, he asked that it be removed.

“For this,” he says, “I begged the Lord”—God, who is threefold—“three times, that that thorn might depart from me”; and I begged the Lord to take from me the sharp medicine he had administered. He did not do what I asked, but what was expedient for me. For it is not a great thing to be heard according to one’s will; it is a great thing to be heard according to one’s benefit.

For he said to me: “My grace is sufficient for you”; that is, it is enough for you to possess my grace. Therefore do not seek superfluous bodily health, because I burn you not in anger but in grace. I know what I have applied; I know from what you are ill; I know from what you are healed. For I know better than you what is useful for you.

“For power is perfected in weakness”: that is, power is led to perfection through the opposing weakness with which it lawfully struggles, so that afterward it may be crowned. Power is perfected in weakness because the operation of weakness becomes the perfection of power: in the presence of weakness and temptation, pride in one’s strength is restrained, so that even awareness of one’s imperfection in truth and confession of it in humility belong to the perfection of that strength.

And because weakness thus benefits strength, “therefore I will gladly”—that is, not merely with resignation but willingly—“boast in my weaknesses,” given for this purpose, “so that the power of Christ may dwell in me.” That is, I shall count it the highest glory that I am weak in myself, so that Christ’s power may make me strong.

The Apostle then boasts when he is humbled by injuries and Christ supplies him the power to endure; so that injuries which formerly seemed harsh and intolerable may afterward be gladly received, because they are softened by Christ’s help. He therefore willingly suffers himself to be struck, provided that he is healed by Christ, after learning that what he thought harmful was beneficial. For he knows that God’s medicine adds more to salvation than weakness here takes away from health.

> “Therefore I take pleasure in my weaknesses, in insults, in necessities, in persecutions, [Col. 1118A] in distresses for Christ. For when I am weaker, then I am powerful.”

As has been said, power is perfected in weakness. “Therefore I take pleasure in myself”: that is, I delight greatly in my weaknesses. In this passage the Apostle has designated all the sufferings mentioned above and below by the name “weaknesses,” because these things prevail against human weakness. Thus, to instruct his disciples, he reported great things about himself; but to preserve himself in humility, he fixed the eye of his consideration not upon his strengths but upon his weaknesses.

“I take pleasure,” he says, “in my weaknesses, and in insults,” not in worldly honors; “and in necessities,” not in feasts or leisure, like the false apostles who preached for the sake of their bellies; “and in persecutions” (Matt. 5; 1 Pet. 3), not in greetings and flattering welcome; “and in distresses,” not in the boastfulness of pride or the abundance of riches. And this is for Christ, not for some crime, because blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake. For not all who suffer persecution and adversity are blessed, but those who suffer for the cause of righteousness.

Or: I take pleasure in bodily weaknesses, in the insults of words, in necessities—that is, lack of necessary things—in persecutions from place to place, and in distresses—that is, anxieties of mind inflicted for Christ. And I rightly take pleasure in such things, because when I am weakened outwardly by them, then I am powerful inwardly: that is, when I am afflicted by any of the tribulations mentioned above, God gives me power to overcome. For then [Col. 1118B] the Christian conquers when he is thought to perish; and then faithlessness perishes when it rejoices that it has conquered.

> “I have become foolish; you compelled me. For I ought to have been commended by you.”

After all his self-commendation, he shows that he did not report these things for his own boasting. “In the things,” he says, “which I have related thus far for my own commendation, I have become foolish,” according to the sound of the outward words, because I seem to have proclaimed my merits. But I did this not boastfully, but compelled by necessity for your benefit, because you forced me to speak in this way: you who did not think rightly about me and preferred false apostles to me. Therefore it is not my fault but yours that I have spoken such things about myself.

[Col. 1118C] He says that he was compelled in order to show what he was. Certainly one is not foolish who has spoken truthfully about himself, for above he said: “If I should wish to boast, I shall not be foolish, for I shall speak the truth.” But now he lowers himself and, through excessive humility or pain of heart, confesses himself foolish, so that it may be shown that he did not disclose his merits voluntarily. For it is the mark of a fool to recount his own labors and vaunt his own virtues.

But a righteous person never reveals his good deeds unless either the benefit of neighbors or overwhelming necessity compels him, as the Apostle, after enumerating his virtues, says that he was compelled to do this. For if he had kept his virtues silent, the disciples would not have known him. If they had not known him, they would not have ceased to prefer false apostles to him and their words to his. Thus ignorance of the Apostle’s dignity would cause the disciples always to remain in error. Therefore, in order to recall them from error, he was compelled to point out who he was.

“You compelled me,” he says, because, although you ought to have defended me against others, now again it is necessary that I myself commend myself to you. “For I ought to have been commended by you”; that is, you ought to have borne witness to me against detractors—you among whom I established the Church and worked the prodigy of signs—so that you might defend me when I was silent, since you have me as your father in Christ.

> “For I was in no way inferior to those who are apostles beyond measure. Although I am nothing, yet the signs of my apostleship were performed among you in all patience, in signs and wonders and powers. For in what were you inferior to the other churches, except that I myself did not burden you? Forgive me this wrong.”

Indeed, I ought to have been commended by you to others. For I was in no way inferior among you, whether in preaching or miracles, to those—that is, to the apostles who are beyond my measure, as some suppose because they followed the Lord in the flesh. I was not inferior to you in action to Peter, John, or James, who are apostles beyond my measure—not in dignity, but in time, although I labored more than they.

For if you think a prior date may be objected against me, John began to preach before Christ, and Christ did not baptize John, but John baptized Christ (Matt. 3; John 1). Andrew also followed Christ before Peter, yet Andrew did not receive the primacy but Peter did. Why, then, do some not think me an apostle, when through God’s grace I can do the same things as the other apostles?

Those who rejected his preaching out of zeal for the Law did not think him an apostle, as though he were an enemy of Moses’ tradition because he said that the Law had ceased. They favored the other apostles, humbling him below them because those apostles did not assert anything against the Law so steadfastly. Therefore he grieves to appear inferior and, compelled, shows how great his dignity is.

“I was not inferior among you in work to my predecessors, because although I am nothing, yet the signs of apostleship,” etc. Thus he humbles himself in order to raise himself. Yet he mentions patience first, because he bore them for a long time like impatient sick people, so that, by applying the medicine of signs and powers, he might heal the wounds of their error.

“I indeed,” he says, “am nothing, because I am human; but the apostleship which Christ himself gave me displayed signs among you: that is, power, mighty works, and wonders. ‘Although’—that is, although I am nothing insofar as I am human, or insofar as I seemed nothing to some who judge me to be nothing—yet the things I did mark me as an apostle, because the signs of my apostleship were performed among you.” That which descends upon you from above, from the Father of lights, through my teaching—so that you believed, were converted, and lived religiously—is a sign and demonstration of my apostleship.

And this was done in all my patience, because I patiently endured every evil inflicted upon me by you or for your sake. For among you I bore contempt, poverty, and other troubles; and I endured your conduct with patience in order gradually to correct it. Nor did I bring you to faith and improvement of conduct by patience alone, but also by signs, wonders, and powers.

There is a distinction between a sign, a wonder, and a power. A sign is a kind of wonder, whereas power is a kind embracing both. Every miracle can be called a power; but a sign is only that which signifies something in any time, whereas a wonder signifies only something future. A *prodigium* is so called as though it were a “foretelling” (*porro dictum*), because it speaks and signifies beforehand and portends that something is to come; for instance, the bodily healings performed through the apostles portended healings of souls.

“I did nothing less for you,” he says, “than the earlier apostles did—indeed, more. For in what were you inferior to the other churches?” That is, what less did you receive through me than the other churches through other apostles, except that I myself did not burden you—that is, I did not receive support from you, as other preachers receive it from their own people. For I preached the Gospel to you without charge, a concession granted to no other churches. “Forgive me this wrong”: that is, if you are so imprudent or malicious as to regard this as a wrong, pardon me. Grant me forgiveness for this action, for which I deserve praise rather than reproach. For this is not an injury, but mercy and friendship.

> “Behold, for this third time I am ready to come to you, and I will not be a burden to you. [Col. 1120C] For I seek not what is yours but you. Nor ought children to lay up treasure for their parents, but parents for their children. And I will most gladly spend and be spent myself for your souls, although, loving you more, I am loved less.”

Lest it perhaps be thought that at first he had abstained from accepting support in order to commend himself, but afterward wished to receive payment for Gospel preaching, he shows that he persists in the same resolve, lest he seem afterward to have changed his holy purpose and give detractors cause for reproach.

“I did not burden you,” he says, “nor shall I burden you. For behold, for this third time”—that is, on this third occasion—“I am ready to come to you, and I will not be a burden to you by receiving anything from what is yours, just as I took nothing from you.” He did not come to them a third time, but was ready to come a third time.

“I will not be a burden to you by receiving your gifts, because I seek not what is yours but yourselves”: that is, I do not seek your money; I desire to gain you yourselves by my preaching, so that I may have you with me in Christ’s eternal kingdom. “I do not seek what is yours; for children ought not to lay up treasure for parents”—that is, gather riches, as you do for the false apostles—“but parents for children,” as the false apostles do not do for you.

Here he speaks according to ordinary practice. It is customary for fleshly parents to lay up treasure for their children. Spiritual fathers, however, may rightly receive support from their children. But the Apostle so strongly proves that he does not wish to receive anything that he transfers the role of a fleshly father to a spiritual one, so that he not only receives nothing from them but, if possible, may himself give to them.
