By this saying he touches them, so that it may be understood how great he is and what those deserve who neglect the care of so great an apostle. “Parents,” he says, “ought to prepare treasures for their children; but I am ready to spend not only treasures but myself as well.” For I am moved toward you by such affection of charity that I shall spend upon you, not reluctantly but most gladly, either bodily or spiritual goods; and, after all else, if need be, I myself shall be spent for your souls—that is, I shall die for the salvation of your souls—although, loving you more, I am loved less by you.

For the charity of one who is ready even to die for the brethren is perfect (John 15). And since I am ready to meet death for you, I am shown to love you perfectly. For I love you more by not accepting your possessions than if I accepted them; but you love me less than you ought, or less than the false apostles, though you ought to love me more, especially since through me you learned the way of life.

> “But let it be so. I did not burden you; but, being crafty, I caught you by deceit. Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you? I urged Titus, and I sent with him a brother. Did Titus take advantage of you? Did we not walk in the same spirit? Did we not in the same steps?”

He leaves unspoken none of the things that could be objected against him, so that he may clear himself in every respect. For he did nothing among them by deceit, but simply provided for himself with pure virtue and for them in a twofold way: he sought for himself nothing except the future recompense of heavenly blessedness, and he made provision for them before the Lord while declining to receive their resources.

For perhaps they suspected that he had despised their gifts because what was offered was small, in order that he might obtain greater things; and that, surveying his own merits, he rejected not money but an amount he regarded as unworthy of himself. “I,” he says, “did not receive what is yours, but am ready to spend what is mine for you; and for this I am loved less by you, because you do not understand with what charitable intention I did this.”

“But let it be so”: that is, let it stand; let us now grant this—that I did not burden you personally by accepting your possessions; “but, being crafty, I caught you by deceit”: that is, by a cunning artifice of pretense, I deceived you, extracting your goods through others. He says this ironically [Col. 1121D], for the false apostles alleged that he acted in this way.

Or he says: You suspect such things of me, but the result itself proves that what you think is false. “Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you, deceiving you artfully, so that through them I might cunningly extort your goods?” This is what he means: those whom he sent did not tell them that, if they wished to have the Apostle favorable to them, they should offer an amount worthy of his person, because the reason he had refused to receive was that less than what was worthy was being offered. They were to understand this as a contrivance of the Apostle’s craftiness, so that he might be thought to have acted not from contempt but from greed.

“Truly,” he says, “I did not take advantage of you through any of my envoys, because I did not do this through Titus, through whom I could more easily have accomplished it. For I urged Titus to go to you, because you more readily obeyed him, and I sent with him the brother whose praise is in the Gospel, understood to be Luke. Did Titus, whose words you readily accepted, take advantage of you by cunningly persuading you to send something to me? By no means.

“Did we not walk”—that is, continue—“in the same spirit,” that is, with the same intention with which we began, so that, as we were unwilling at the beginning to receive anything from you, so we remained afterward? “And did we not walk in the same steps in which we began,” that is, always with the same course of conduct, so that we persisted in not receiving?

For our judgment is proved to be one in good things, every suspicion of greed excluded, when nothing of this sort was said or done by those I sent which could reveal greed. Or thus: Titus did not take advantage of you, just as I had not taken advantage of you. For did not he and I walk in the same spirit—that is, with the same good will? And did not he and I walk in the same steps—that is, with the same actions by which the will is made evident? “For every tree is known by its fruit” (Matt. 12).

> “Have you long thought that we are defending ourselves before you? Before God in Christ we speak; but all things, beloved, are for your edification.”

“Have you long thought”—that is, have you long judged—“that we are defending ourselves before you”: that is, that I speak as though pleading a defense, like one accused, because I did not burden you? For a long time you have doubted us, supposing that we do not deal simply with you because you believe the false apostles, who say that we reject your gifts by a certain evasiveness in order that we may receive larger ones. And do you think that we offer before you an excuse for such a feigned intention?

But “before God in Christ we speak.” As was said above, one speaks before God who, in everything he says, does not seek human favor but attends to the presence of almighty God, and seeks not his own glory but that of his Creator. He speaks in Christ when his whole speech abides in Christ’s truth, so that he neither lies nor preaches anything except Christ. And thus we speak before God in Christ.

But we speak and do all these things for your edification: that you may think well of us, reject the false apostles, and be built through our teaching into Christ’s temple. For your edification is advanced by everything we have said above concerning our tribulations [Col. 1122D] and revelations; by removing from your hearts evil suspicion concerning us; and by our not accepting your resources, so that we might not weaken the authority by which we rebuke the vicious.

For it undoubtedly benefits one who is reproved for amendment if his superior rejects what is offered for the very purpose of being able to rebuke him freely.

> “For I fear lest perhaps, when I come, I may not find you as I wish; and I may be found by you such as you do not wish: lest perhaps there be among you quarrels, jealousies, outbursts of anger, dissensions, detractions, whisperings, swellings of pride, seditions; lest, when I come again, God humble me among you and I mourn many of those who sinned before and have not repented of the uncleanness and fornication [Col. 1123A] and indecency which they committed” (1 Cor. 5).

Everything, as I have said, I say or do for your edification. For I fear that when I come I may find you uncorrected—such as I do not wish to find you—which may perhaps happen, since the matter can go either way, and either outcome may follow from your freedom of choice. Therefore prepare yourselves, lest I find you persisting in vices, such as I do not wish to find; and lest I in turn be found—that is, judged by you—to be severe and harsh, justly punishing your sins, such as you do not wish to find me. For someone finds another such as he does not wish when he makes himself such that he is at variance with him. Therefore present yourselves in such a way that you are not at variance with my holiness, so that when I come we may rejoice together.

That is, I fear lest there be among you quarrels and the other things which I reproved in the former epistle [Col. 1123B] (1 Cor. 1), when, showing partiality to persons and preferring one to another, you were divided from one another. A quarrel exists where something is defended not by reason but by the stubbornness of the mind. Rivalry here means envy. Irritability is a great and agitated persistence of mind against another, such as existed among those who had lawsuits against one another, which they brought before unbelievers for decision, and therefore were angry with one another. Dissension exists where not all agree in one will and one understanding, but desire different things and form factions. Detraction is when someone drags down another’s good qualities (1 Cor. 6), that is, belittles and suppresses them in speech, or takes something away even from those good qualities, in order to show them to be fewer or less than they are. Whispering is when [Col. 1123C] someone murmurs and does not speak to a person’s face, but speaks ill of him to others. Conceit is when someone inwardly swells with the pride of his heart. Sedition is an uprising of citizens against one another.

“And I fear,” he says, “lest these vices be found among you when I come”: lest there be among you quarrels concerning the merits of leaders, as there were when you said, “I am of Paul,” “I of Apollos,” “I of Cephas” (1 Cor. 1); and rivalries, that is, envies, on account of better charisms, through which lesser persons are accustomed to envy greater ones; and irritabilities in the rehearsal of grievances and retaliation, because of which you used to contend in court before unbelievers; and dissensions, that is, differences of mind or divisions of will; and detractions, by which one person, in speaking, diminishes and takes away whatever [Col. 1123D] he can from another’s good deeds (1 Cor. 6); and whisperings, through which discords are secretly sown; and conceits, through which some swell as though because of more excellent merits, and despise others; and seditions, that is, the tumults of angry and contentious people among the populace, even to blows.

I fear, I say, lest I find such things in you; lest, namely, when I come, God again humble me among you—that is, lest, as I grieved over your sins, so I should again grieve over your lack of repentance, and mourn there many of those who sinned before the first epistle and, still persisting in their wickedness, have not repented. He says that he is humbled and mourns while they persist in sin, because, like an affectionate father, he begins [Col. 1124A] to weep over his children’s faults and afflict himself for them in prayers and fasts. For what father does not rejoice when his children act well? So likewise he must grieve if they live wickedly. Therefore he warns them that, if any have not repented—as he signifies that others have done—they should not do so, so that when he comes he may be with them without sorrow. For when he says, “and I mourn many of those who sinned before and did not repent,” he proves that some of them repented, while others did not.

But repentance must be undertaken by all who have sinned, because it is not enough to change one’s conduct for the better and withdraw from evil deeds, unless one also makes satisfaction to the Lord for what has been done: through the sorrow of repentance, the groaning of humility, the sacrifice of a contrite heart, with alms cooperating. “They did not repent,” he says, “of uncleanness”—that is, of the most unclean commission of lust occurring between males, or by one person alone; “and fornication,” which occurs with public prostitutes, who offer themselves in arches (*fornices*), whence it is also called *fornicatio*; “and shamelessness,” which occurs with women of one’s own kin, as with a sister, niece, or brother’s wife, and is called incest. And since the Apostle urges repentance for these so detestable acts of lust, it is clear that there is no stain of crimes so dreadful that it cannot be wiped away through repentance.

## Chapter XIII

> “Behold, this is the third time that I am coming to you. By the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Deut. 17; [Col. 1124C] Matt. 18; Heb. 10; 1 John 8). “For I have foretold and now foretell, as present with you and now absent, to those who sinned before, and to all the rest, that if I come again, I will not spare.”

“I fear,” he says, “lest I find you such as I do not wish, and that I shall be found harsh by you when I come. Therefore do not delay repentance, because I will not delay coming. For behold, let it be certain to you that I am shortly coming to you with this third preparation.” He did not say that he had come twice and would come on this third occasion, but that he had twice prepared himself and had been unable to come, while on this third preparation he would come. “The third time,” he says, “I am coming. By the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Deut. 17). This was said in the Law, so that someone might either be acquitted or condemned by two or three witnesses.

Thus, at the Apostle’s second or third coming, these persons will either be found cleansed or liable to condemnation. Or, in the Apostle’s presence, every word of accusation or defense will stand in the mouth of two or three witnesses—that is, it will be firm and valid on the testimony of two or three suitable persons. Here it is implied that a ruler of the Church, even if he himself knows a subordinate’s guilt with certainty, nevertheless cannot condemn him unless that very guilt has been proved by two or three witnesses. “He who wishes to excuse himself before me,” he says, “will need witnesses.” For I foretold, while I was among you, and I still foretell, both as then present and now absent, to those who sinned before the epistle and to all the rest who sinned afterward, [Col. 1125A] that if I come again I will not spare them, but punish them; or: if I come, I will not spare them again, as I formerly spared them. He indicates that long ago, while present, he told them to correct themselves lest they be corrected with shame; and now, absent, he declares that he says the same again, so that after this second correction, if they do not amend themselves, they ought not to be spared.

> “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me, who is not weak among you but is powerful in you? For although he was crucified from weakness, yet he lives by the power of God. For we too are weak in him, but we shall live with him by the power of God in you.”

I said that I would not spare those who remain unreproved, but would punish them. And do you seek proof of him who [Col. 1125B] says these things in me, who is Christ? That is, do you wish to test whether Christ dares to punish—not to say whether I dare, but Christ, who remains and speaks in me? They seek proof of Christ speaking in the Apostle when they do not obey his commands, wishing to test whether he dares to exact vengeance, so that in this way he may be understood to possess firm authority and thereafter be feared. For whoever despises his teacher does not seek to amend himself. It should be noted that his teaching is proved to be not that of a human being but of Christ; whoever rejects it is found obstinate. For Christ speaks within him all that he himself speaks outwardly; and the person who wishes to test whether Christ himself dares to strike sinners tests Christ in him.

Therefore, threatening them not concerning himself but concerning Christ, he says: “Do you seek proof,” that is, a test, “of Christ who speaks in me?” And he adds: “Who is not weak in you,” that is, among you, “but is powerful in you.” He appeared among them not weak but powerful when, through the Apostle, he performed signs and wonders and bestowed various charisms of grace. Since they have experienced this, they should know that he is also powerful to punish them if they provoke him. Truly he is powerful to punish sinners. For although he was crucified from the weakness of the flesh, by which he appeared powerless against his enemies, yet—that is, nevertheless—he lives eternally by God’s power, that is, because he himself is God. Slain through our weakness, he rose by his own power and that of the Father. Truly he now lives perpetually, even in the flesh, though previously he had been weak in it.

“For we too,” [Col. 1125D] he says, “are weak in him”: that is, we apostles endure the wounds of weakness in preaching him, while we are beaten for his name and afflicted with various injuries. “But we shall live with him,” that is, raised in like blessedness to eternal life, by God’s power. For by God’s power we shall rise so that we may live always with Christ. And this is “in you,” because the death of martyrs flourishes in the faith of peoples. “In you,” that is, in your hearts, we shall live with Christ, because you will understand that we live with him. Therefore it is not remarkable if Christ lives by the power of divinity, when we too, who are far lesser, shall live by that same power.

> “Test yourselves whether you are in the faith; prove yourselves. Do you not know yourselves, that [Col. 1126A] Christ Jesus is in you—unless perhaps you are reprobate?”

I said that we shall live in you, for you received the faith from us. Therefore test—that is, examine and prove—yourselves, whether you are in the faith; and, if you see that you are in the faith, then know that we live in you. While you hear that we suffer so many tribulations for the faith, test—that is, prove—yourselves; and, if you are in the faith, prove yourselves. As if he said: Recall to mind the struggles of persecutions, and weighing the innermost and hidden things of your hearts, discover what sort of persons you are able to be amid sufferings.

“Do you not know yourselves?” That is, do you not know what you are inwardly: namely, that through the faith which you received from us, Christ Jesus is in you? Whoever has the understanding of faith in his heart knows that Christ Jesus is in him. And you likewise know that he is in you, unless perhaps you are reprobate. For this is what it is to be reprobate: not to know the faith one professes. For a reprobate person—that is, one turned back and estranged from uprightness—is one who does not know or has abandoned the uprightness of faith and good conduct that he received in baptism. And you know that Christ is in you through the understanding of faith, the affection of love, and the vigor of right action—unless perhaps you are reprobate, that is, turned back from what you first began and rejected by God.

> “But I hope that you will know that we are not reprobate. Yet we pray God that you may do no evil, not in order that we may appear approved, but that you may do what is good, though we should [Col. 1126C] appear reprobate. For we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth. For we rejoice that we are weak while you are strong. This also we pray: your perfection. Therefore I write these things while absent, so that when present I may not act more harshly, according to the authority which the Lord gave me for edification and not for destruction.”

He summons them to knowledge of faith and right life. For when they begin to know that their apostle has certain authority and merit before God, they too will be able to be concerned about themselves. “You know,” he says, “that Christ dwells in you, unless perhaps you are reprobate. But whatever may be the case concerning you, concerning us I hope that from now on you will know that we are not reprobate, but God’s elect.” For while you preferred false apostles to us, you thought them divinely chosen and us reprobate. But I hope that through the teaching of this epistle you will know that not we but they are reprobate; and therefore, abandoning them, you will follow our admonitions.

Or: you who tested Christ in us, wishing to find out whether we could punish sinners, I hope that you will know that we are not reprobate—that is, deprived of our authority through some fault—when you see us powerfully rebuking the guilty among you. But we pray God that this may not occur; we pray God that you may do no evil for which it would be necessary for you to be rebuked by us. He could have said, “We warn you to do no evil.” Had he said this, he would have said something certain, [Col. 1127A] because our own will also accomplishes something, though it is not sufficient by itself. Yet he preferred to say, “We pray,” in order to commend grace, so that they might understand that whenever they do no evil, they do not avoid evil by their will alone, but accomplish what is commanded by God’s help.

“We pray God,” he says, “without whom the choice of human will avails nothing, that you may do no evil—not that we may appear approved,” that is, not that we may seem authoritative over you when you sin; “but rather that you may do what is good, though we should appear as reprobate,” that is, as though without authority. He does not pray that he himself may be reprobate, but that, when they act well and he therefore does not dare to rebuke them, he may seem to be humbled, and, humbled, may appear reprobate. For they seem approved by God when, through their granted authority, they judge sinners. Therefore, if there are no persons for them to judge, their authority ceasing in this regard, they appear as though reprobate.

And lest they be thought capable of condemning unjustly, he aptly adds: “For we can do nothing,” and so forth. “May we be,” he says, “that is, may we appear reprobate, having nothing upon which to exact punishment. For we can do nothing against the truth”: that is, authority has not been given us against truth, to rebuke those who walk in truth—that is, who live rightly—but for the defense of truth, to punish those who are enemies of the law. Therefore our authority will cease if they do what is good. Thus it was said to the Romans: “Do you not wish to fear authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it” (Rom. 13). Whoever does not fear authority by doing good has rendered authority inoperative in his own case. This is to be as though reprobate, because that by which authority is proved ceases in him.

For this reason we pray God that you may do no evil: because we rejoice that we are weak, that is, that it is not necessary for our power to appear in punishing sinners. For this is to be weak: not to exercise authority. We rejoice if we are weak in this manner; but you are strong, that is, if by acting well you overcome vices, so that you keep from yourselves punishment or rebuke. For then you are strong, when, firmly prevailing over vices, you do not fear our authority. This also we pray to effect: your perfection; that is, we ask that you be made perfect in this, that you do not sin, perfected in the virtue of a good life and incorrupt faith.

And because this is what I desire and pray for, I write these things which I have said for your correction while absent, so that when I am present I may not [Col. 1127D] deal with you more harshly than I wish: namely, so that I may find you more corrected, and may not rebuke you shamefully before people, lest those who have sinned blush in the assembly of the brethren. I write these things lest I should deal more harshly than you wish, according to the authority of rebuking and punishing offenders which the Lord gave me for edification and not for destruction—that is, so that by it I may build up my subjects and not destroy them. For if I leave their sins unpunished, I destroy and do not build up; likewise, if I punish those who act well, I destroy and do not build up. But this authority must be exercised with such discernment for edification and not destruction that we encourage those who act well toward better things, and rebuke those who act badly, so that, corrected, they may be built up. For those who are rebuked in order to correct themselves are not destroyed [Col. 1128A] but rather built up. Authority must be exercised thus: we must absolve the penitent and bind the impenitent with the bond of anathema. Whoever acts otherwise uses this authority perversely and deprives himself of it in God’s sight.

> “Finally, brethren, rejoice; be made perfect; be exhorted; be of the same mind; have peace; and the God of peace and love will be with you.”

Up to this point I have admonished you toward love and correction, so that you may correct what you have hitherto done wrongly. But henceforth, that is, throughout the remainder of your lives, rejoice—that is, have joy from the consciousness of good merits—and avoid sins over which it would again be necessary to grieve. And so that you may be able to rejoice, be perfect in good works. And so that you may be perfect, exhort one another, so that each may advance ever more in the perfection of virtues. And in that perfection all be of the same mind, so that there may be no dissension among you, but that you may think one thing.

Or indeed, you who are perfect, exhort those who are lesser toward the same perfection; and you who are lesser, think the same thing as those who are greater, so that you may no longer dissent from them. And all alike, both greater and lesser, have peace together, so that your former discord may no longer be among you, but, like members of one body, you may all be harmonious with one another. And if you do these things, then the God of peace and love—that is, Christ—will be with you as helper and guide in all things. For Christ is the God of peace and love (1 Cor. 1), because he said to his own: “My peace I give you” (John 14), and so forth. “This is my commandment, that you love [Col. 1128C] one another” (John 15). He is with those whom he addresses, as he says: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). It follows:

> “Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the saints greet you. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all. Amen.”

So that peace may be among you, greet one another with a kiss that is not deceitful or lustful, but holy—that is, in Christ—full of true peace and chaste. And you ought gladly to do this because all the saints wish this for you. For they greet you so that you may profit from their greeting’s good wish and imitate their holiness. They greet you, and I more affectionately, saying: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ,” through which sins are freely forgiven and salvation bestowed; “and the love of God the Father,” by which he so loved us that he gave his Only-Begotten for us to death (John 3); “and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit,” who in each matter—that is, in the aforementioned grace and love—shared with Christ and God, jointly and equally working human salvation with them, be with you all, greater, lesser, and intermediate alike.

Here there is a compendium of the Trinity and unity of power, which is the perfection of all our salvation. For love sent us Jesus the Savior, by whose grace we have been saved; and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit enables us to possess this grace of salvation. For it preserves those beloved by God and saved by Christ’s grace, so that the perfection of the three may be the completion of the human person in salvation.

## On the Epistle to the Galatians

[Col. 1129]

## Argument

[Col. 1129A]

Galatia is a region in Asia, whose inhabitants Paul converted to the faith and formed in good morals. When he had departed from them, in order, according to his custom, to preach to other Gentiles also, false apostles came; and, preaching to them the carnal observance of the Law, they so thoroughly subverted them that they assented to the false apostles’ opinions in word and favor—though not yet in practice—in such a way that they wished to observe circumcision, the Sabbath, new moons, and other things of that kind.

For the aforesaid deceivers urged carnal observances upon them in many ways, saying that faith in Christ could not suffice for complete justification and salvation unless the ancient customs were observed. And they could persuade them more easily because Peter and the other apostles who had been with the Lord permitted the primitive Church for a time to Judaize, lest they cause offense to the Jews. For they could not immediately destroy Judaism, but gradually brought the Jews to the purity of truth; for if at their first approach they had begun to destroy all their rites, the Jews would have recoiled from our faith rather than accepted it.

But Paul, because he preached to Gentiles who possessed no rite of the Mosaic Law, in no way allowed his disciples to Judaize; rather, he instructed them in the observance of evangelical truth. Therefore the false teachers said that circumcision was necessary, since the great apostles, who had been instructed by the Lord Jesus, preached it. This, however, they did not do; but with a good intention, to avoid offense [Col. 1129C], they permitted it still to be observed. Consequently these most wicked deceivers, taking occasion from this, said that the apostles had preached circumcision and carnal observances. And because Paul destroyed those same observances, they disparaged him as much as they could, saying that he had not seen Christ and that he preached a Gospel different from that of the other apostles who had seen the Lord; therefore, they said, he was in no way to be believed.

Accordingly, the Apostle now writes from Ephesus with the aim of rebuking the Galatians because they had received false apostles and assented to their preaching, desiring circumcision and the strict observance of the Law. First he insists at length upon commending his own authority, so that his words may afterward carry greater weight. Having commended himself, he proceeds by disputation in many ways and arguments to destroy carnal observances.

This epistle is suitably placed after the Second Epistle to the Corinthians because it bears a certain affinity with that one in its manner of rebuke. In both, those who received false apostles and, setting aside the Apostle of truth, yielded to their preaching are rebuked. It also follows that epistle because in it the Corinthians are reproved not only for receiving false apostles, but also because they were ensnared in many and various vices. The Galatians are rebuked in this epistle for no other reason than that they were entangling their minds in the falsehood of false apostles without any reason. Therefore this follows that epistle because, whereas in that one the Apostle strove to destroy carnal observances, in this one he moves more strongly toward their annihilation. In the former he denounces false apostles in many ways; in this he anathematizes them. Thus he begins:

## Chapter I

> “Paul, an apostle not from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead; and all the brethren who are with me, to the churches of Galatia. Grace to you [Col. 1130B] and peace from God our Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins, that he might deliver us from the present evil age, according to the will of God and our Father, to whom be glory for ages of ages. Amen.”

So that they may recognize the one who sends him, he places first his own name, Paul, and adds the name of his office or dignity: apostle. For he wishes to bind them by his authority to listen to him. As was said, he had first preached to them and was their apostle. As though he said: “You Galatians, cast away falsehood and the deceit of pretenders, and the venom poured upon your simplicity under the appearance of truth; attend to your apostle, who is the teacher of truth. For Paul—whose name means ‘chosen’ or ‘wonderful,’ and whose name is received with authority throughout many churches—writes to you. This is not true of the false apostles, because they are neither divinely chosen, nor wonderful in the working of signs, nor possess any authority among the faithful.”

And he is “apostle,” that is, truly sent, not usurping another’s office, because he is a true apostle. But false apostles invade others’ offices; they are not sent, but shamelessly thrust themselves in and deceive innocent hearts under the appearance of truth. Of them the Lord says through Jeremiah: “I did not send them, nor command them, nor speak to them” (Jer. 14). And again: “I was not sending them, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied” (Jer. 13). Therefore they must in no way be obeyed.

But Paul, as has been said, is an apostle—that is, one sent—not from human beings, but from God. The election of apostles, that is, of those sent, takes place in four ways: by God and not by human beings; by God and by human beings; by human beings and not by God; or neither by human beings nor by God, but by the devil or by oneself. By God and not by human beings, as Moses and Aaron [Col. 1131A] were divinely sent to Pharaoh (Exod. 4, 10). By God and by human beings, as Joshua and Caleb were sent to explore the land (Num. 13; Deut. 1). By human beings and not by God, as occurred when “the Pharisees took counsel that they might entrap Jesus in speech, and sent their disciples to him with the Herodians, saying, ‘Teacher, we know that you are truthful,’” and so forth (Matt. 22; Mark 12; Luke 20). Neither by human beings nor by God, but by the devil or themselves, are false apostles, who, at Satan’s prompting, thrust themselves in without election and presume to put the sickle into another’s harvest (1 John 2).

Paul, therefore, is found in the first kind of election, because he was chosen as an apostle not from human beings, as from the apostles, nor through a human being, as through Ananias, who baptized him (Acts 9), but through Jesus Christ and God the Father. Nor was he chosen through Christ as mortal, as were Peter and Andrew (John 1), but through him as immortal, because the Father raised him from the dead. By placing Christ first and adding the Father afterward, he implies that Christ is equal to the Father, and that no one reaches the Father’s grace except through him, as he himself said: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14).

The earlier apostles were chosen through Christ still partly human—that is, mortal—but Paul, the last apostle, through Christ now wholly God—that is, wholly immortal. For this is what he says: “not from men, nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father,” as though Christ Jesus were not human. For he immediately adds, “who raised him [Col. 1131C] from the dead,” so that it may thereby appear why he said, “nor through a man.” Accordingly, because of his immortality Christ is now God, not human; but because of the substance of human nature in which he ascended into heaven, he is “the mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2).

This implies that, although Paul differed from the first apostles in that he had not seen the Lord in the flesh nor clung to him on earth with the others, what he lacked in time was supplied to him from Christ’s own dignity, because he was chosen by the immortal and impassible One; and thereby he is made equal to the earlier apostles. For they, following Christ for so long a time, could scarcely learn the Gospel; but he, within a short span, caught up into the third heaven [Col. 1131D] and into paradise, not only learned among angels what he was to teach among human beings, but also heard secret words which it is not lawful for a human being to speak (2 Cor. 12). For his apostleship was consecrated in heaven, whereas that of the others was consecrated on earth.

Since, therefore, he was chosen not from human beings nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ—not mortal, as were the preceding apostles, but raised—and through God the Father, his sayings must be accepted without hesitation, rather than the falsehood of false apostles. As though he said: “Paul, such a person and so chosen, writes to the churches of Galatia,” that is, to the assemblies of believers located in that province called Galatia; morally, however, to those in migration, because from the freedom of grace they had begun to migrate into the slavery of the Law. For *Galatia* means “migrated” or “migration.” And its region is aptly so named for those who migrated from faith to unbelief, so that even the land they inhabit bears witness by its name to their instability.

I, Paul, write to them, and all the brethren who are with me—men known to be great before God and the churches, who are grievously distressed at their subversion. His mention of “all the brethren” greatly draws them back from error because it shows that their conduct displeases not only him but also the multitude of preachers whom the Galatians loved so much that they did not wish to offend them. Perhaps they would have cared little about the Apostle, because the false apostles, speaking evil of him, had created great suspicion of him in them. Therefore he mentions all who were with him, so that the Galatians might recover their senses even for their sake; for one recovers more quickly who understands that his error displeases many, and especially friends.

Having commended himself, he shows his desire for their salvation, adding: “Grace and peace be to you from God our Father and from our Lord Jesus Christ.” As though he said: “What I say or am about to say to you does not come from ill will, but from abundant love and concern for your correction.” This is evident because I wish that not wrath and discord but grace and peace may be yours from the Father and the Son. For you deserved wrath because you cast away grace, and you lost God’s peace because you made discord. But now I pray that, with God’s wrath which has returned upon you and the discord through which you began to rebel brought to an end, reconciled as you are, God’s grace may be yours, through which your sins may be forgiven and the intimate love of God bestowed; and peace, through which you may always agree with his will in mind and works.

And may this grace and peace be given to you not from the carnal observance of the Law but from God the Father and from his Christ, who is our Lord Christ because he acquired lordship over us when he snatched us from the deceiver’s hand. For he gave himself as a sacrifice for the blotting out of our sins, seeking no offerings of the Law, so that by his righteous blood he might powerfully conquer the prince of iniquity and, freeing us from his yoke, deliver us from the present evil age, where that deceiver still spreads so many snares.

This age is called evil both because it is an age that invites us to follow it and generates evils from its desires in the hearts of its followers, and because it is present to our five senses, offering itself to us through its enticements to see what should not be seen and hear what should not be heard, and so concerning the other senses. Or it is called evil because of the utterly wicked people who are in it, just as a house is called bad when it has bad inhabitants. The Lord, I say, gave himself to deliver us; and this according to the merciful will of God and our Father, because the Father’s will was fulfilled not by legal sacrifices but by the offering of Christ’s body. In this deliverance of ours he declares himself to be our God and Father. For he who created us through his Only-Begotten, after the fall into sin restores us through that same One to our former or a higher dignity, and in the affection of paternal love adopts us as sons.

To him, for this deliverance of ours, be glory with the same Son and Holy [Col. 1133A] Spirit, enduring for ages of ages—that is, throughout all eternity. Amen: that is, truly.

> “I marvel that you are so quickly transferred from him who called you into Christ’s grace to another gospel—which is not another—except that there are some who trouble you and wish to distort the Gospel of Christ.”

He who in other epistles is accustomed to begin with thanksgiving and praise, in this one begins with rebuke. For hard minds, unless struck by an open reproof, would by no means recognize the evil they had done. Often, indeed, those who are shameless perceive that they have sinned only to the extent that they are rebuked for sins they have committed: they judge their faults smaller when a milder denunciation corrects them, and discover those faults to be greater which they see reproved more vehemently. Hence the preacher’s discourse must always be fashioned according to the character of the hearers, lest he speak harshly to the modest or lightly to the shameless. Paul, therefore, showing this, begins to address some gently; but the Galatians, whom he had learned to have departed from the faith, he rebukes by denunciation from the very opening of the epistle, after the greeting. And since all were overthrown, or already in the very movement toward overthrow, he had none for whom he might give thanks; therefore, as though in a certain agitation of mind over their ruin, he begins in such a way as to call them back more quickly, and he begins, as it were, abruptly. For we are accustomed to marvel at something great and unusual. Therefore, in order to show that they had gravely offended God, he suddenly introduces, as if abruptly, the beginning, saying:

“I marvel that you, formerly established in faith and good works, are now so—that is, so heedlessly and rashly—being transferred from new liberty to old slavery; so quickly,” that is, within so short an interval of time. For if you were being seduced through the persistence of a long period, it would not be so marvelous; but now it is very astonishing. He does not say, “You have been transferred,” but “You are being transferred,” showing that they had not yet come so far as to adopt the Jewish rite, but were already in the very movement of arriving at it. “You are being transferred,” he says, and this not from evil to good, but from good to evil, since from him—the Father—who called you by his free goodness into the grace of Christ, that is, into the remission of sins and justification given in Christ to believers, you are being transferred into [Col. 1133D] “another Gospel”: that is, another doctrine preached by pseudo-apostles, which seems to you to be Gospel, that is, good news. Yet it is not another Gospel, because there cannot be another besides that which I preach. What the pseudo-apostles preach is a proclamation in advance of Antichrist, not the Gospel of Christ.

“It is not,” I say, “another Gospel besides that which I preach” (1 John 2), unless there are some who trouble you—that is, unless one considers the estimation of those persons, who, after the manner of muddying clear water, render your mind turbulent. Or: your being transferred is nothing other than the fact that there are some who trouble you, that is, who by an admixture of falsehood make the sincere understanding of your faith foul and muddy, and who even wish to alter [Col. 1134A] the Gospel of Christ. For whereas the carnal observances were rightly changed into the Gospel of Christ—that is, shadow into truth—they wish, in the contrary order, to turn truth back into shadow, so that the Gospel may be nullified and carnal observances retained.

Or again: “You are being transferred into another Gospel,” namely, into observance of the Old Testament; yet it is not another, that is, it is not different from the New. For if the Old is understood spiritually, it differs in nothing from the New. “It is not another,” I say, unless there are some who trouble you; that is, if those who expound it carnally and perversely were absent, you would understand that the Old is, in meaning, nothing other than the New. For they trouble your mind as water is troubled, lest you possess the purity of that water which flows from Jesus’ belly for believers; and they wish to turn the Gospel [Col. 1134B] to another meaning—which cannot be done (John 7)—when John says: “What you heard from the beginning, let it remain in you” (1 John 2). Hence through the Holy Scriptures the Gospel is called eternal and the Testament eternal, because it will never be changed, as the Old Testament has been changed; rather, as it was given by Christ, it will remain.

“But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel besides that which we have preached to you, let him be anathema. As we have said before, so now again I say: if anyone should preach to you a gospel besides that which you received, let him be anathema.”

They themselves, as we have said, wish to alter the Gospel. But whoever they may be, let them all be anathematized. [Col. 1134C] I say this not merely concerning any persons whatever, but even concerning myself and my companions, even concerning a heavenly angel: for if we should preach another Gospel to you, we ought to be anathematized. Even if we ourselves should wish to alter what we preached to you, we should not be believed; or even if an angel from heaven should visibly come and preach—as may be supposed—anything besides that which we preached to you, let him be anathema, that is, condemned.

He set forward not only himself but also an angel, lest, had he named those seducers, he might appear to have done so out of envy. By this he shows that if he himself or the highest angel must be anathematized for proclaiming false doctrine, then much more the pseudo-apostles. Hence he repeats and confirms the sentence more strongly, saying of anyone whatsoever what he had said of himself and an angel: [Col. 1134D] “As we have said before,” he says, “I and all who are with me, so now I again repeat and say: if anyone, whether human or angel, whoever he may be, should preach to you besides that which you received”—that is, should preach anything other than what we handed down to you, so as in his preaching to exceed the rule of faith which you learned and to depart from the path of truth which you received from us—“let that person be anathema,” that is, condemned; or anathema, that is, alienated from the Church of God. For *anathema* is interpreted “condemned,” or “alienated,” or “alienation.”

In saying “even if we, or an angel,” and so forth, he saw that it could happen that some who are thought to possess apostolic perfection might still turn aside into the proclamation of falsehood. He saw that the deceitful mediator could transform himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. 2) and proclaim something false.

“For am I now persuading men, or God? Or do I seek to please men? If I were still pleasing men, I would not be Christ’s servant.”

As though someone said: “Paul, why do you speak so harshly?” He therefore says this, as though replying: “I rightly speak so. For am I now persuading men, or God?” That is: is my present persuasion, exhortation, and preaching directed toward human will and honor, or toward God’s will and glory? What I now urge upon you is directed not to human honor but to God’s glory. Formerly, however, my persuasion served the will of men, when for the favor of the high priests I dragged away Christians and [Col. 1135B] urged them to depart from Christ.

But the Apostle speaks reprovingly by means of a question. Accordingly he adds: “Or do I seek to please men?”—understand: as formerly I sought to please the Jews, when I had received letters from the chief priest and was travelling to Damascus (Acts 9). I do not at all now seek to please them; for if, after baptism, I were still pleasing men by preaching carnal observances, then I would not be Christ’s servant—that is, I would not be keeping Christ’s spiritual commands.

In all this Paul is opposed to the pseudo-apostles, because their persuasion was directed to the honor of men, not to God’s glory, while they urged people to believe that a human being could be justified by works of the law, not by faith in Christ. And they themselves sought to please men, that is, the faithless Jews, for whose favor [Col. 1135C] they had dispersed themselves through the world to overthrow the faithful.

It can also be understood in another way that the Apostle did not seek to please men, because in his works he did not intend that he himself should be praised by men, but that through what he did God should be glorified. Whoever boasts among men and displays his good works in such a way that he places their end in human praise, and counts that human praise as the reward of his works, is not yet Christ’s servant. But whoever desires that the good things he does or says should please people in order to draw them to imitate a good manner of life, or to kindle their hearts to praise God, does not seek to please men but God (1 Cor. 10). In this manner Paul did please [Col. 1135D] men, since elsewhere he testifies that in all things he pleased all people. But because he did not wish to please men in the manner of hypocrites, who seek transitory praises from their works rather than the salvation of those who see them, he now denies that he pleases them.

“For I make known to you, brothers, that the Gospel which was preached by me (1 Cor. 15) is not according to man. For neither did I receive it from man, nor did I learn it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ.”

Above he had said that he was an apostle not from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ; and now he proves this and commends his own person, so that they may receive what he is about to say [Col. 1136A] as authoritative. For his authority had been greatly diminished among the Galatians through the pseudo-apostles. “I,” he says, “was not sent by man, but by Christ; nor does my persuasion serve human will but God’s, because I did not receive from man the doctrine which I preach, as you supposed.

“For now, brothers, I make known to you what you did not know: namely, how great is the authority of the Gospel which was preached—that is, proclaimed—by me both to you and to others, because it is not according to the authority of any human being, but rather according to the authority of Christ himself. For neither did I receive it from man,” that is, it was not imposed upon me by a man. But since it could be that it had not been imposed upon him by a man, he adds: “nor did I even learn it from man.” I did not learn it from [Col. 1136B] man, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ. He himself taught me; he himself imposed it upon me.

Here he shows that, just as the ancient prophets were taught by the spirit of prophecy concerning Christ’s future incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension, so he himself came to know all these things concerning Christ, now already past, through that same spirit of prophecy, with Christ himself teaching him. For the spirit of prophecy touches the prophet’s mind not only through the future but also through the past, as it is now shown to have touched Paul’s mind. Moses too prophesied about things past when he wrote what happened at the beginning of the world, before humankind was created.

“For you have heard of my former manner of life in Judaism, that beyond measure I persecuted [Col. 1136C] the Church of God and laid it waste; and I advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries among my own people, being more abundantly zealous for the traditions of my fathers.”

For the commendation of himself, he more openly proves that he did not learn the Gospel from man. “I did not learn,” he says, “from man: neither before my conversion nor after it. Before my conversion I did not learn it, but rather persecuted the Church. For it is evident from this that I did not then learn the Gospel of which I was an enemy. For you yourselves have heard of my former manner of life in Judaism,” that is, in the religion of the Jews, “that beyond the measure of the other Jews I persecuted the Church of God,” inflamed with zeal for the law, driving the saints away, dragging the bound to punishment, and laying it waste—that is, devastating it, desiring entirely to destroy it.

Or, “beyond measure” means beyond what the faithful could endure; and in doing these things I advanced according to the carnal knowledge and observance of the law in Judaism, that is, in the Jewish rite, because I understood the Scriptures carnally and observed them more and more. And this advancement was not beyond the elders—such as Gamaliel, my teacher, and others like him, which would seem remarkable (Acts 22)—but beyond many of my contemporaries, not beyond all who were of my age; and not beyond proselytes, but “among my own people,” that is, among the children of Israel. And because I advanced further in understanding and fulfilling, I was also more abundantly zealous for the traditions [Col. 1137A] of my fathers—that is, with a more fervent zeal I strove to take vengeance upon those who, having been converted to the Gospel, violated the traditions of the elders that I had received from my parents.

Or all the carnal commandments of the law are called ancestral traditions, because they were formerly commands of God; but now they are traditions of men, after truth appeared and drove away the shadow.

“But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace to reveal his Son in me, that I might preach him among the Gentiles, immediately I did not yield to flesh and blood; nor did I go up to Jerusalem to the apostles who were before me, but I went away into Arabia and returned again to Damascus. Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Peter, and [Col. 1137B] remained with him fifteen days. But I saw no other of the apostles except James, the Lord’s brother. Now, concerning what I write to you, behold, before God, I am not lying. Then I came into the regions of Syria and Cilicia.”

He has proved that before conversion he did not at all learn the Gospel, and he begins to prove that after conversion he did not learn it from man. “This,” he says, “was my condition before conversion, from which it is clear that I did not then learn the Gospel; but after it pleased God to illuminate and convert my heart, I lived in another way, in which again it appears that I did not learn from man either then or afterward. And this is the point: ‘But when it pleased him,’ the gracious Father, and so forth.”

This pleased God—that is, it was not my merit, but God’s pleasure alone—who set me apart, that is, separated me from the mass of the lost, “from my mother’s womb,” that is, already choosing me by the hidden counsel of his mercy. Here the free mercy of God is noted (Rom. 9). It is as though he said: Before I had done anything good, by his grace he predestined me for life, and afterward called me through his grace. Here it was necessary to mention grace, because after birth he might have done something good through which he deserved to be called by God. But, just as his separation, so also his calling was effected freely.

Or “from my mother’s womb” means from the blindness of the Synagogue, where I was held shut in. He set me apart, that is, separated me from the multitude of the rest whom he left in that blindness. For just as the womb holds an infant shut within itself [Col. 1137D] and permits it neither to see anything nor to move about in any direction, so the blind destruction of discipline which exists in the Synagogue does not allow those whom it contains to behold the light of truth or to move freely in the liberty of charity. Rather, it miserably constrains them on every side, so that they advance neither toward light nor toward liberty.

But God set me apart from this womb of the Synagogue when he separated me from the blind custom of the people, so that I might freely behold Christ’s light and be enlarged in his charity. And he called me for this purpose: that “in me,” that is, in my heart, where true knowledge exists, he might reveal the Son—that is, uncover the knowledge of his only-begotten Son—which had been veiled to me while I had the veil of the law upon my heart. And he revealed him to me in order that I might preach him among the Gentiles, that is, proclaim him among the nations.

[Col. 1138A] After it pleased him thus to call me and reveal his Son to me, “immediately I did not yield to flesh and blood,” that is, I at once ceased to give assent to the Jews and my carnal relatives, who, in a carnal understanding, urged me to remain in the carnal observance of the law. I did not yield to them because they were flesh and blood—that is, they thought carnally and taught carnally. Nor did I come to spiritual teachers, that is, to the apostles who had preceded me in Christ and remained at Jerusalem, to seek doctrine from them. Rather, leaving Damascus, I went into Arabia to preach, where none of the apostles was present; and from there I returned to Damascus.

When the three years from the time of my conversion had been completed, during which I remained in Arabia and Damascus, I came to Jerusalem, not to learn the Gospel [Col. 1138B] but to visit Peter, that I might rejoice with him spiritually. Nor did I then learn the Gospel from him, because I did not remain with him more than fifteen days—a period within which I could not learn the breadth of such great knowledge. Nor did I learn from the other apostles, because, besides Peter, I saw no other apostle there except James, the Lord’s brother—that is, the Savior’s kinsman. For Mary the virgin, the Lord’s mother, and Mary, the mother of this James, were sisters; and therefore he was called the Lord’s brother. He was also the first bishop in Jerusalem. The other apostles had already scattered throughout the world to preach.

Therefore, because John was absent there, we believe that the Lord’s mother had by then been assumed into heaven; her tomb is shown in the valley of Jehoshaphat. I indeed relate such things to you concerning myself and the apostles, and perhaps they seem incredible to you; but these things that I write to you—behold, before God—I am not lying. And that this is so is “before God,” that is, manifest in the presence of the divine sight, from which nothing can be hidden.

At this point the Apostle swears, yet does not sin, because he saw that some of the Galatians would not otherwise believe him. For this oath did not arise from evil in the one swearing, but from the evil of those whose unbelief compelled him to swear (Matt. 5). Then, departing from Jerusalem, I came into the regions of Syria and Cilicia in order to preach there also. He mentions this journey so that the Galatians may know that, often moving from place to place, he did not learn the Gospel from man, and may assent without doubt to his doctrine.

[Col. 1138D] “But I was unknown by face to the churches of Judea which were in Christ. They had only heard that he who once persecuted us now preaches the faith which once he was destroying, and they glorified God in me.”

Not only did I not learn from the apostles, but neither from the other faithful who were in Judea, to whom I was wholly unknown by face. For they had not yet seen me after my conversion. Therefore it is plainly evident that they did not teach me the Gospel. They had not yet seen or known me by face; yet, as the report circulated from other Christians, they had heard that he who once persecuted us Christians now preached to many the Christian faith which he had once attacked. And in me—that is, in considering [Col. 1139A] my conversion and manner of life—they glorified God, that is, proclaimed as glorious the God who had thus converted me and made one so cruel so devout. That is, I was for them material for glorifying God, since I had been converted so well.

Or: in me, that is, in considering my preaching, they glorified God by their own preaching also; for, hearing that I steadfastly preached the faith which I had been accustomed to attack, they too, inflamed by my example, were encouraged to preach Christ.

## Chapter II

“Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus also with me. But I went up according to a revelation. And I laid before them the Gospel which I preach among the Gentiles, but privately before those who seemed to be something, lest perhaps I might be running, or had run, in vain.”

I had preached in Syria and Cilicia. Then I went up again to Jerusalem, which is in the hill country and cannot be approached except by going up. I went up, I say, after fourteen years from the time when I first came to see Peter. He reckons the time and number of years—that is, the earlier three and the subsequent fourteen, which together make seventeen—so that it may thereby be known that he preached for so long before he compared his Gospel with theirs. And when he received nothing from the apostles, it is evident that he received or learned it from no one.

I went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas, whom I brought as a witness, taking with us also Titus, who was a Gentile [Col. 1139C] and uncircumcised. I brought him as a witness to confirm my preaching: namely, so that the other Gentiles, seeing him believe while uncircumcised, might themselves believe without scruple. But if Titus himself had been circumcised there, the matter would have appeared otherwise, and all would have thought that I had not taught correctly because I had not taught him to be circumcised but had brought him as an uncircumcised companion.

I went up, and not rashly, but according to a revelation—that is, with the Holy Spirit revealing and admonishing me—so that by my presence carnal observances might be more effectually annulled. I went up and laid before those Jerusalem believers, who had previously doubted the truth of my preaching, the Gospel which I preach in converting the Gentiles. For I stated my Gospel and [Col. 1139D] they stated theirs, and no disagreement was found in our judgments. He began the whole discussion for this purpose: to draw the Galatians away from circumcision and carnal ceremonies, since his preaching did not differ from the teaching of the apostles themselves, and Titus, who was present, was not circumcised although he was a Gentile.

Then these people too ought no longer to doubt, since not even the churches of the Jews could contribute anything to him. He made this comparison because, though called from heaven after the Lord’s ascension, if he did not find apostles in the flesh with whom he could communicate and compare the Gospel, so as to appear a member of the same fellowship, the Church would not have believed him at all. Therefore it was now necessary to recount this comparison to the doubting Galatians.

[Col. 1140A] “I laid it before those Jerusalem believers,” not before everyone, because truth cannot be well discussed in a crowd. For if in the presence of all I had said that circumcision and carnal observances ought not to be performed, the uneducated multitude would immediately have cried out against me. Therefore, not before all, but only before those “who seemed to be something,” that is, of greater authority and knowledge; and this privately, that is, apart from the crowd.

Not that I had said false things to the many so as to say true things privately to the few; but because I had kept silent about certain matters which the little ones could not bear, and it was necessary that I should speak wisdom among the perfect, so that the other apostles and elders might recognize my perfection. The Apostle also compared his Gospel with theirs in order to remove suspicion from the churches of the Jews, who thought that he had preached, and still preached, a wholly different Gospel, because he had neither associated with the Lord, from whom he might have been instructed, nor been with any of the apostles who had seen the Lord in the flesh, so that he might preach to the Gentiles according to the example of their teaching.

Therefore, in order to remove this suspicion from the Hebrew churches and from the other faithful throughout the world, he made the comparison, as has been said above—made it, I say, lest he might now be running, or formerly have run, in vain, that is, without the fruit of reward. For through this it would be evident that those to whom he preached, or had preached, would not receive a reward if he himself were not to obtain a reward from his preaching. Or the statement, “lest perhaps I might be running or had run in vain,” may be understood as spoken in the form of a question, rebuking those who suspected this, so that it may thereby appear that he was not running, nor had run, in vain, since he was now proved by the testimony of the others to differ in nothing from the truth of the Gospel.

“But not even Titus, who was with me, though he was a Gentile, was compelled to be circumcised; but because of false brothers secretly brought in, who slipped in to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, in order to reduce us to slavery. To them we did not yield in subjection even for an hour, that the truth of the Gospel might remain with you.”

Not only did they add nothing to my Gospel, but [Col. 1140D] they did not even have Titus circumcised. For while he was with me in that conference and was a Gentile—that is, remaining as he had been born, in uncircumcision—he was not compelled to be circumcised. That is, no consideration of truth could there have been advanced by anyone on account of which he or any other person should be compelled to undergo circumcision.

And lest you suppose that the apostles wished to compel him to be circumcised and that he remained uncircumcised contrary to their will, know that I said “compelled” not because of the apostles or elders, but because of the false brothers secretly brought in. They slipped in where I was presenting my Gospel, to spy upon our liberty: that liberty by which through Christ we have been freed from every slavery of the law, or by which from free choice we voluntarily serve God rather than from fear of punishment. They slipped in, I say, for this purpose: by their words and disputations to compel us, before all who were present, to carnal observances, and thus to reduce us from the liberty of grace to the slavery of the law.

[Col. 1141A] To them we were unwilling to yield, not even for an hour, so as to be subjected to legal slavery. Rather, we resisted them manfully, so that the truth of the Gospel—which teaches that every person can be saved through faith and works of charity without works of the law—might remain with you as I preached it to you.

These false brothers lay in wait for the Apostle, seeking to see whether he would yield in anything either to circumcision or to the other carnal observances, in order to reduce him to slavery—that is, so that by Paul’s own example or testimony they might preach circumcision as necessary for salvation and thus cause them to return to circumcision. Therefore he refused to circumcise Titus, lest he give an opportunity to those who said that believers could not be saved without any circumcision and who, to deceive the Gentiles, boasted that Paul himself held this view.

Elsewhere, however, he circumcised Timothy for this reason (Acts 16): lest he should seem, to the Jews—and especially to Timothy’s maternal kindred, who had believed in Christ from among the Gentiles—to detest circumcision in the same manner in which idolatry ought to be detested—although God commanded the former to be performed, whereas Satan persuaded people to the latter. Therefore the Apostle possessed this liberty in Christ, both to perform circumcision and not to perform it, in order to show that those sacraments ought neither to be condemned as sacrilegious nor sought as necessary. The aforesaid slanderers slipped in to spy out this liberty, wishing to know [Col. 1141C] whether he would do in Titus what he had done in Timothy, so that they might then preach circumcision as necessarily to be performed by all on the basis of his example.

“But from those who seemed to be something—whatever they were formerly makes no difference to me; for God does not accept the person of a man [Rom. 2; Eph. 6; Col. 3; Acts 10; Jas. 2; 1 Pet. 1]. For those who seemed to be something added nothing to me. But, on the contrary, when they saw that the Gospel of the uncircumcision had been entrusted to me, as that of the circumcision to Peter—for he who worked in Peter in the apostleship of the circumcision also worked in me among the Gentiles—and when James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, recognized the grace given to me, they gave to me [Col. 1141D] and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship: that we should go to the Gentiles, but they to the circumcision; only that we should remember the poor. This also I was zealous to do.”

I did indeed lay the Gospel before the apostles and the other elders who were at Jerusalem. Yet those Jerusalem believers “who seemed to be something,” that is, to possess some great dignity, added nothing to me. This appears to be what he ought immediately to have said, but he makes an insertion, as if someone said to him: “You say that they seemed to be something; indeed they were nothing, since they had been fishermen and unlearned men.” He replies to this as follows: They truly were something then. For whatever they had formerly been, before Christ called them—whether fishermen, tax collectors, or illiterate men—makes no difference to my truth or my judgment, because I speak not according to what they had been before, but according to what they then were.

The foregoing statement was: “that the truth of the Gospel may remain with you”; and the present expression, “it makes no difference to me,” seems to refer to this truth—that is, whatever they once were makes no difference to my truth. The two expressions *refert* and *interest* are customarily construed with genitives and with ablatives of possessive pronouns.

Or it may be read without the insertion: “Those who seemed to be something”—namely Peter, John, and James—whatever they had been makes no difference to my truth or my judgment; that is, according to my judgment it makes no difference what they had formerly been in rank and learning, whether noble or ignoble. He does not disparage the other apostles; but because the Galatians magnified the other apostles beyond measure, preferring them to him and therefore holding his authority cheaper, he shows that he is their equal and that he did not receive doctrine from them.

It makes no difference what they formerly were, because God does not accept a person’s standing (Lev. 19; Deut. 1, 16; 2 Chr. 19; Job 34; Prov. 24; Wis. 6; Ecclus. 35 and 42), that is, he does not choose the rank or nobility of any person. For he did not despise me or judge me inferior because I came last; indeed, he showed me altogether equal to them. For those earlier ones, who seemed to be something great, added nothing to me in knowledge of preaching. On the contrary, I added to them, because they had formerly been certain that they preached rightly and that carnal observances ought to be abolished; but now, hearing me preach the same things, they became more certain that I had been taught not by any mortal but by Christ himself.

[Col. 1142C] They added nothing to me; but, on the contrary, when they saw that the Gospel of uncircumcision had been entrusted to me, just as the Gospel of circumcision had been entrusted to Peter—that is, that the Lord had entrusted evangelical doctrine to me as to a faithful steward, so that I might preach to the uncircumcised Gentiles, just as he had appointed Peter to preach to the people of the circumcision—they gave me the right hands of fellowship.

And truly the Gospel has been entrusted to me as to Peter, because he who made Peter an apostle of the circumcised made me also an apostle of the Gentiles. This is the meaning: “For he who worked in Peter,” that is, for Peter’s honor and assistance, raising [Col. 1142D] him to the apostleship of the circumcision—that is, of the Jewish people—both by preaching and by the working of miracles, also worked in me through miraculous powers, diverse graces, and the eloquence of powerful preaching among the Gentiles.

Here these two chief apostles are shown to have been chosen for the salvation of two peoples: Peter for that of the Jews, Paul for that of the Gentiles. And when James, Peter, and John, who seemed to be pillars—that is, upright, strong, and immovable, strengthening and sustaining the multitude of others—had certainly recognized the grace of apostleship and wisdom given me by Christ, they gave right hands to me and Barnabas. James is placed here before Peter and John [Col. 1143A] because of the primacy he possessed at Jerusalem, where he was bishop.

They gave us right hands of fellowship, that is, a sign of social friendship and apostolic dignity, showing that we differed in no respect from what they themselves had learned. Just as kissing one another is a sign of peace and love, so also is joining right hands. I say that this fellowship was agreed upon in such a way that we should go to the Gentiles to preach, but they to the circumcision; and that they should share in the benefit which we would accomplish in converting the Gentiles, while we in like manner should share in their reward for the conversion of the Jews.

Although Paul says that Barnabas was received with him into the fellowship of the apostles, he nevertheless does not say that Barnabas was equal to him in preaching. For he himself is the teacher of the Gentiles, who converted the greater part of them from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum by preaching in a circuit, and then not only as far as Rome but even as far as Spain (Rom. 15). All these points serve to commend his authority and also his purpose of recalling them from circumcision and slavery to the law.

They added nothing, but only imposed this requirement: that we should remember the poor who were in Jerusalem and had laid the prices of their possessions at the apostles’ feet for Christ’s sake (Acts 2). This too—that is, remembering them and sending them support—I was zealous to do, diligently carrying out that very thing.

Paul rightly recalled the foregoing comparison of his Gospel in order to draw the Galatians away from observance of the law, because he had gone up to Jerusalem on that occasion in order to hear what the earlier apostles thought about observing the law. Thus Luke relates concerning Paul and Barnabas that they remained at Antioch for no small time with the disciples (Acts 15), and that certain persons coming down from Judea taught the brothers: “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.” Therefore, after no small dissension had arisen between Paul and Barnabas and them, it was decided that Paul and Barnabas, with some others from among the rest, should go down to the apostles and elders at Jerusalem concerning this question.

When they came to Jerusalem, they were received by the Church and the apostles, reporting how great things God had done with them. But some from the sect of the Pharisees who had believed arose and said that it was necessary to circumcise them and also to command them [Col. 1143D] to keep the law of Moses. Then the apostles and elders assembled to consider this matter, and so forth. In this assembly the aforesaid comparison of Paul’s Gospel took place.

“But when Cephas came to Antioch, I resisted him to his face, because he was blameworthy. For before some came from James, he ate with the Gentiles; but when they came, he drew back and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision. And the other Jews joined in his dissimulation, so that even Barnabas was led away by them into that dissimulation.”

And this took place after Paul and Barnabas had returned to Antioch from the council mentioned above, together with Judas and Silas, carrying the apostles’ letter, in which [Col. 1144A] it had been decreed that the Gentiles should not be compelled to be circumcised or to live as Jews (Acts 15). For it is then written: “But Paul and Barnabas remained at Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord with many others also” (ibid.). And Peter is understood to have arrived at that time and to have done what Paul now recounts.

“Peter and the others contributed nothing to me in Jerusalem,” he says, “but when Cephas—that is, Peter—came to Antioch, I conferred with him.” Or thus: Not only in Jerusalem did I confer with Peter, but also in Antioch. For I resisted him to his face; that is, I did not disparage him in his absence, but confronted him openly, contradicted him publicly, and rebuked him freely, because he was blameworthy—that is, deserving of rebuke.

For before certain Jews came from James, from Jerusalem to Antioch [Col. 1144B], he ate with the converted Gentiles without any distinction of foods, so that he did not even reject pork. But afterward, when the Jews had come, he withdrew himself from their table, lest Jews newly come to faith, who still observed the Law, should be offended by foods which the Law had judged unclean. Nor did he withdraw from Gentile fellowship in such a way as to be with them sometimes and with the Jews at other times; rather, he separated himself altogether—that is, severed from the Gentile flock, he made his own flock among the Jews.

Thus, by a kind of pretence, he gave the impression that this distinction of foods and the other carnal observances were necessary for justification, and that Gentiles converted to Christ could not be joined to believing Jews. [Col. 1144C] This was indeed worse than offending the brethren, since it is worse to abandon truth than to allow an offense to arise. Thus he separated and withdrew himself from the Gentile flock and their food, making two flocks out of one, although Christ had made one out of two; for he feared not Gentile foods, but the Jews who were of the circumcision, lest they withdraw from the faith.

The other Jews consented to his pretence, by which he feigned to distinguish foods and to shrink from Gentile intercourse. They had previously been with him, but they also withdrew from table fellowship and association with the Gentiles. So even Barnabas—who was the teacher of the Gentiles and ought sincerely to have instructed them, being sent with me to the Gentiles—was led by them into that pretence [Col. 1144D] of Jewish eating and association.

Yet Peter had said in the aforementioned assembly of apostles and elders: “Why do you test God by placing a yoke upon the neck of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But through the grace of the Lord Jesus we believe that we shall be saved, just as they will” (Acts 15). He therefore rightly held that the Law had been abolished; but, out of fear of the Jews, he pretended otherwise, lest they should depart from the faith on account of the Gentiles and he thus lose his flock.

Paul too acted by pretence from a similar fear, when he circumcised Timothy (Acts 16), when he let his hair grow in the manner of a Nazirite and cut it at Cenchreae (Acts 21), or when, after purification in the Temple, he offered a sacrifice (Acts 18). Peter, therefore, as apostle of the Jews, was providing for the salvation of the Jews [Col. 1145A] in this pretence. He feared that if he ate common foods with the Gentiles before the Jews, they would reject his preaching and fall away from the faith. He therefore still allowed them to practise circumcision and observe the other rites of the Law, while himself observing them in part with them, so that he might gradually draw them toward faith and the purity of the Gospel. Thus, if any Gentile wished to be circumcised, he would not forbid it in the Jews’ presence.

Paul, however, aflame with great zeal for faith, did not wish the commandments of the Law to be kept carnally; and, being the apostle of the Gentiles, he prohibited circumcision among the Gentiles. Because Peter wished the customary observance of the Law still to be maintained even among the people of the circumcision, so that Gentile converts might be judged unequal to the Jews, Paul resisted him to his face and says that he was blameworthy [Col. 1145B] in this matter. He calls this conduct not merely a fault, but—what is worse—hypocrisy, that is, pretence.
