In that pretence Peter, as has been said, provided for the salvation of the Jews, but neglected the salvation of the Gentiles. Therefore Paul, apostle of the Gentiles and concerned for their salvation, resisted him to his face. Peter, however, received what Paul did usefully, with the freedom of holy and kindly love, in the humility of piety. Thus he gave later generations a rare and holy example: that those who are greater should not disdain to be corrected even by their inferiors, if perhaps they have departed from the path of right.

Nor did he merely endure this rebuke patiently at that time: afterward, when writing his second Epistle, he praised the letters of Paul, in which he had read this rebuke [Col. 1145C] (2 Pet. 3). Certainly, unless he had read Paul’s letters, he would not have praised them. But if he read them, he found there that he himself was called blameworthy. Therefore, as a friend of truth, he praised even that for which he had been rebuked; and this too pleased him: that he had not pleased in those matters in which he had thought otherwise than he ought.

He yielded assent also to his younger brother—for Paul was still the younger then, though now he is equal—and in this matter he became the follower of his inferior, so that he might lead also in this: that he who was first in the summit of the apostolate might be first also in humility. Thus in this matter Paul is praised for righteous freedom, Peter for holy humility.

There are, however, some who understand not Peter, the chief of the apostles, but another man of the same name [Col. 1145D], as the one rebuked by Paul. Had they read Paul’s words more attentively, they would not say this. For when he was about to say, “When Peter came to Antioch, I resisted him to his face,” he had already indicated in the narrative which Peter he meant, saying: “For he who worked through Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision also worked through me among the Gentiles.” It is therefore clear which Peter Paul speaks of: the one whom he calls an apostle and says presided over the Gospel for the circumcision.

And lest anyone, clinging still to the letter, say that the man rebuked by Paul is called not Peter but Cephas—although both names are identical—let him reconsider what was stated there before: “James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave to me their right hands.” [Col. 1146A] Clearly this Cephas, placed between James and John, was not less than John or James. And if no Cephas besides the apostle Peter can be found who is comparable to James and John, it must necessarily be confessed that this is the Cephas to whom Christ said: “You shall be called Cephas,” which is interpreted “Peter” (John 1).

> “But when I saw that they were not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel, I said to Cephas before them all: If you, though you are a Jew, live as a Gentile and not as a Jew, how do you compel the Gentiles to live as Jews? We are Jews by nature, and not sinners from among the Gentiles. Yet knowing that a human being is not justified by works of the Law, except through faith in Jesus Christ, we too have believed in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by faith in Christ [Col. 1146B] and not by works of the Law. For by works of the Law no flesh shall be justified” (Rom. 3). “But if, while seeking to be justified in Christ, we ourselves too have been found sinners, is Christ then a minister of sin?” Far be it! For if I build again the things which I destroyed, I make myself a transgressor. For through the Law I died to the Law, that I might live to God. I have been crucified with Christ. Yet I live—no longer I, but Christ lives in me. And the life which I now live in the flesh, I live in faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me. I do not reject the grace of God. For if righteousness is through the Law, then Christ died gratuitously.”

Peter and Barnabas were indeed pretending, but I [Col. 1146C], alone preserving sincerity, publicly rebuked their pretence. For I saw that they were not walking rightly; that is, they did not proceed equally with both feet, because they limped on one side with respect to the Gentiles, whose salvation they neglected. Yet with respect to their good intention concerning the salvation of the Jews, they walked rightly.

With respect to the Gentiles, they did not walk rightly toward maintaining and preaching the truth of the Gospel; for truth would perish if the Gentiles adopted Jewish observances. For the truth of the Gospel is that a person is justified by faith alone without works of the Law; that all foods are believed naturally clean; and that teachers of the Church neglect neither the salvation of Jews nor that of Gentiles. They acted otherwise.

But when I saw that they were walking not rightly but crookedly [Col. 1146D] toward preserving and teaching the truth of the Gospel, aflame with divine zeal, I said to Cephas before them all what follows. Had Paul said these things secretly to Peter alone, they would have benefited neither Jews nor Gentiles. Therefore he spoke while all heard, that all might benefit. For this reason he chose not timidly to conceal, but confidently to assert, what he already knew Peter to think with him: whether because he had conferred the Gospel with him (Acts 15), or because he knew that Peter had been divinely instructed about this matter at the calling of Cornelius (Acts 10), or because, before those whom he feared had come to Antioch, he had seen Peter reclining at table with the Gentiles.

Paul was not then teaching him what was true in this matter; rather, he was rebuking his pretence, by which Peter compelled the Gentiles by his example to adopt Jewish observances. “If you,” he says, “although you are a Jew, live [Col. 1147A] as a Gentile—that is, use all foods without distinction, counting no person unclean—and not as a Jew, that is, not by the Jews’ distinction of foods, how—by what reason or with what benefit—do you compel the Gentiles by your example to adopt Jewish observances? That is, to follow the Jewish rite in distinguishing foods and receiving carnal observances, when you separate yourself from them because they believe every creature of God to be good and seek to be justified through the Gospel without observance of the Law?

“You, who are a Jew by birth, have abandoned Jewish observance, and do you compel the Gentiles to adopt it? You who were a Jew have left Judaism, and will those who were never Jews take it up? You do not live as a Jew—that is, you do not observe Jewish custom in your eating—because you know there is no benefit in it. How, then, do you now compel [Col. 1147B] the Gentiles to adopt Jewish observances, when they think all that they see in you necessary for salvation?”

Truly the Gentiles ought not to adopt Jewish observances, because they could never be justified thereby. And truly they could never be justified by adopting Jewish observances, because not even we, Jews by nature, were ever able to be justified thereby. Therefore we abandoned the Law and fled to faith. And this is the meaning: “We are Jews by nature”—that is, not proselytes but Jews by descent, sprung from the seed of Abraham and possessing the Law of God—“and not sinners from among the Gentiles”; that is, not sinners in the way that all Gentiles were idolaters and unclean.

For the Jews had long, through a kind of ancient pride, applied the name “sinners” to the Gentiles, as if they themselves were righteous: they saw the speck in another’s eye but not the beam in their own. We are not, I say [Col. 1147C], sinners from among the Gentiles—utterly removed from the worship of God and given over to sins—but Jews by nature, that is, nurtured under the divine Law.

Yet we know that no human being, whether Jew or Gentile, is ever justified by works of the Law, except through faith in Christ, which removes carnal observances and causes the Law to be fulfilled spiritually, as we believe. Works are from grace, but grace is not from works; for grace itself comes first, and from it the rest are obtained. Therefore no one can in any way be justified by works except through faith, which proceeds from grace.

Knowing this, we too, Jews no less than Gentiles, believing in Christ Jesus, believe in him so that we may be justified by faith in Christ, through divine grace, and not by works of the Law through our own powers. Therefore—that is, because we Jews cannot be justified from works of the Law, though we would have been justified from them if anyone could be justified thereby—by carnal works of the Law no flesh [Col. 1147D], that is, no one living in the flesh, shall attain righteousness.

Above he had said that Jews were not sinners from among the Gentiles, and afterward added that even they are justified by faith in Christ. But everyone who is justified was unrighteous—that is, a sinner. Hence someone who misunderstands may perhaps suppose that Christ first supplied sins to Jews coming to him, so that afterward he might justify them through his faith and grace. This is what is said: “We are not sinners from among the Gentiles. But if, seeking to be justified in Christ, we ourselves too have been found sinners” [Col. 1148A]—that is, if, approaching the light of Christ, we saw in it the darkness of our sins, which previously, being blind, we could not see; and if, drawing near to the fine rule of Christ’s righteousness so that we might be directed by it, we noticed the ugly crookedness of our injustice, though earlier we had considered ourselves straight—“is Christ therefore a minister of sin?” That is, does it consequently follow that Christ, who takes away the sins of the world (John 1), supplies us with sin? Far be this from the hearts of believers: that they should think Christ supplies anyone with sin, he who offered himself as a sacrifice for the abolition of our sins.

Something ugly may lie hidden in darkness, but appear plainly in a ray of sunlight; yet the sun does not produce that ugliness. Thus Jews who had formerly thought themselves righteous, illuminated by Christ’s light, saw the uglinesses of their faults. Christ had not supplied these faults for them to commit, but had shown them so that they might recognize and correct them.

Or thus: As has been said, no one is justified by works of the Law. But if we Jews, passing over to Christ and seeking justification in him—since in the Law we could not attain righteousness—were found also to be sinners like the Gentiles, because it became known that we had always transgressed the Law in our hearts, though we observed it outwardly, is Christ, who instructed us to leave the Law and pass over to himself, a minister of sin? That is, does he supply us with sin in commanding us to depart from the rigor of the Law and come to grace? Far be it that he should in this supply us with sin [Col. 1148C].

For it is not sin to leave or destroy the Law in this manner; rather, it is sin to return to it again or rebuild it. For if I rebuild the things which I destroyed—such as the carnal works of the Law, which I have already overthrown in myself and others—that is, if I establish them again, either by pretence like Peter or by preaching like the false apostles, I make myself a transgressor. That is, I act against the Law itself, which foretold that it was to be brought to an end.

For by the authority of the Law I abandoned the Law, as though dead to it and having no perception of it. This is the meaning: “For through the Law I died to the Law, that I might live to God.” Truly I destroyed in myself the works of the Law, because I am dead to the Law; that is, I no longer live in works of the Law or in its carnal meaning. And I am dead through the Law because the Law itself preached Christ to me and warned me of its own ending and the reception of Gospel doctrine, saying through Moses: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren, like me; him you shall hear” (Deut. 18). That is, after Christ has come, the Law will no longer endure, but you will hear Christ’s new teaching.

Or: through the Law spiritually understood, I died to my Law, lest I should live carnally in it—not for myself, that is, so that throughout my life I may do God’s will rather than my own. This I can now do because I have been crucified with Christ—that is, fixed to the cross with Christ, a companion in Christ’s passion. This means that Christ’s cross extinguishes in me the ardor of sin [Col. 1149A], so that it no longer prevails in me; it binds my hands, so that they may not be stretched out to unlawful work, and my feet, so that they may not walk toward evil.

I have indeed been crucified with Christ, yet I live in virtues—that is, I now have the strength to act rightly—not I, the man who was formerly a sinner, but Christ lives in me; that is, Christ’s newness thrives and reigns in me. I have been crucified, but I live—yet no longer as I lived before. It is not I who live, but Christ lives in me.

That is to say: I have indeed been extinguished from myself, since I do not live carnally; nevertheless, I have not been extinguished essentially, since in Christ I live spiritually. This means: There is no longer in me my own righteousness, which is from the Law and in which I became a transgressor, but the righteousness of God—that is, that which is from God to me, not from myself. For in this way it is not I but Christ who lives in me, [Col. 1149B] “who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and sanctification” (1 Cor. 1).

“I no longer live, but Christ lives in me”; that is, I do not do my own will but the will of him who dwells in me. Yet “the life which I now live in the flesh”—that is, my not being extinguished by the fire of the flesh, and my being able to act rightly while placed in the body—“I live in faith,” not through the laborious works of the Law, but through faith in the Son of God, whose faith has power. “For the righteous lives by faith” (Hab. 2; Rom. 1), so long as he is in the body.

Christ’s faith is effective in me because he loved me and, through that love, gave himself over to death for me, redeeming me by giving himself, who is so great, not some other animal. Therefore I do not reject the grace of God, who through the passion of his Son freed me [Col. 1149C] from sins and gave true righteousness—something the Law could not do. That is, I do not seek justification through the Law, for that would be to reject grace.

Nor ought I to reject it. For if righteousness is through the Law, then Christ died *gratis*, that is, vainly, without cause or benefit, since observers of the Law would be justified through the Law without his death. But he did not die in vain, because righteousness leading to salvation could be obtained neither through the Law nor through any other thing except Christ’s death. It follows:

## Chapter III

> “O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you so that you do not believe the truth, before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly set forth and crucified among you? This alone I wish to learn from you: did you receive the Spirit by works of the Law or by hearing with faith? Are you so foolish that, having begun with the Spirit, you are now being brought to completion by the flesh? Have you suffered so many things in vain—if indeed it was in vain? He therefore who gives you the Spirit and works miracles among you, does he do so by works of the Law or by hearing with faith, just as Abraham believed God and it was reckoned to him as righteousness? (Gen. 15; Rom. 4; Jas. 2.) Know therefore that those who are of faith are sons of Abraham.”

Having finished the narrative in which he taught that he had not learned the Gospel from a human being, that he had compared his own Gospel with the apostles, and that he had afterward rebuked Peter for the pretence of adopting Jewish observances, he turns to rebuke the Galatians. He vigorously censures their madness [Col. 1150A], because they had abandoned his teaching, fortified by such great authorities, and believed the falsehood of the pseudo-apostles.

Observing their overthrow, he suddenly bursts into an exclamation, so that by emphasizing the magnitude of their guilt he might more easily call them back. This seems to be done in the manner of rhetoricians. “O foolish Galatians,” he says—that is, devoid of all rational sense, like brute animals—“who has bewitched you,” that is, harmed you with an envious glance, “so that you do not believe” evangelical truth?

You are truly foolish, because you accept the deadly persuasion of some pseudo-apostle, a man of no name or authority, who hides among the people and whose very name I do not know; while you set aside my teaching, which I received from God alone, not from a human being, and to which the apostles contributed nothing new in the comparison of the Gospel, but were themselves made more certain by me.

“Who has bewitched you?” That is, who injured you in your weakness by an envious look, and, grieving at the advance of your perfection and faith, harmed you through envy alone, like someone who is said to be able, by a glance alone, to diminish another’s possessions? Thus he wasted you away by his envious gaze, so that you should not believe the truth of my preaching but the falsehood of his perverse doctrine. Or, as enchanters bewitch and deceive people so that they believe falsehood to be truth, so some unknown person has so bewitched you by the spell of his deception and altered you by his words that you hold falsehood to be truth. Hence it is written: “The bewitching of folly obscures good things” (Wis. 4).

You do not believe the truth, like fools, although before your inward eyes Jesus Christ was set forth [Col. 1150C]—that is, displayed beforehand and marked out by us—not on tablets of stone as was the Law, but crucified also in you, that is, in your hearts, because his cross and passion, by which you were redeemed, ought above all to have been impressed upon you.

You are therefore all the more mad because you denied Christ, who was shown to you as crucified for your sins, by not believing that you could be justified through faith but rather through works of the Law. Or, you were once such people that Jesus Christ crucified was publicly depicted before your eyes, because, in order to stir compunction of mind, you painted him crucified in places where you could always see and remember him.

Or, you are so foolish because Jesus Christ has been *proscriptus*—that is, dispossessed—before your eyes, and you do not notice it. Those were called *proscripti* who, driven into exile for some deed, were deprived of inheritance and homeland. When the Galatians believed, through the apostle’s preaching, that they could be justified through Christ’s death, they became Christ’s inheritance, which he had rescued from the devil’s possession by his death. But after withdrawing from this faith and seeking justification in works of the Law, they were, so far as they themselves could do so, disinheriting Christ by withdrawing themselves from him.

Jesus Christ has been *proscriptus* [Col. 1150D], that is, condemned and disinherited by your withdrawal from him—he, I say, who was crucified. This must be read with emphasis, as concerning one who acquired you as his inheritance at so dear a price, suffering for you the harshness of the cross. Or, while you abandon Christ through the Law, Christ has been *proscriptus* by you, that is, condemned as by Pilate. And while you believe him insufficient, you differ in no respect from those who crucified him. Or, the sentence of condemnation pronounced on him by Pilate was as well known to you as though it had taken place before you, and his crucifixion was within you—that is, in your understandings—so that you knew how it happened and what it achieved.

By the foregoing rebuke he had moved them, and now accordingly proves to them that the Law is not to be observed, because all good things come not from it but from faith. As if he said: Although you are foolish and bewitched, nevertheless I wish to learn from you this one thing which I am about to say, because it is so evident that even fools can teach it; and if nothing else existed, this alone would suffice to prove that the Law ought not to be kept.

Since it is agreed that you received the Spirit [Col. 1151B], tell me whether you received him from works of the Law, which you had not yet performed, or from the faith which you heard from me. Or thus: I could use many profound arguments, but I wish to learn from you this one plain matter—that is, I wish you to answer me—because even from this alone it will sufficiently appear that justification is not from the Law but from faith.

Did you receive the Spirit—that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, such as speaking in diverse tongues, prophesying, healing the sick, and the like—divinely through works of the Law, or through hearing with faith? That is, did you receive the Spirit from the carnal observance of the Law, or from faith, which you received by the hearing of preaching alone? I do not think you will say that you received these spiritual gifts from works of the Law, since you know that at that time you had performed no works of the Law at all [Col. 1151C]. It remains, therefore, that you received them solely from faith.

You first received the gifts of grace through faith, and now you seek righteousness through the Law? Are you therefore so foolish that, having begun with the Spirit—that is, having made a spiritual beginning by receiving gifts of grace through faith—you are now brought to completion by the flesh? That is, are you reduced to nothing by carnal conduct, when through observance of the Law you nullify your spiritual goods? Having begun with the Holy Spirit, or by living spiritually, or by understanding the Law spiritually, are you now completed by the flesh—that is, by carnal life or by the Law carnally understood—being reduced to nothing and losing whatever you had?

And therefore you have suffered in vain—that is, without benefit to yourselves—so many, so great, and so numerous adversities in defense of the faith [Col. 1151D] which you now willingly abandon. Yet I do not say this as an assertion, lest you fall into despair and plunge still more deeply into the abyss of destruction. Rather, because both outcomes lie within your choice, I state conditionally that you have suffered so many adversities for Christ in vain, if indeed you have suffered them in vain. For you have suffered them in vain if you persist in this error; not in vain if you come to your senses.

And since you can thus lose all good things through observance of the Law, does God, who even now gives you the Spirit of prophecy, wisdom, and other graces, and works the powers of miracles among you, give you these through works of the Law or through the faith which you heard? He asks the same question as above [Col. 1152A], but now in the present tense, whereas above he used the past.

For they might have answered the first question: “We had not yet performed the works of the Law when we received the Holy Spirit; but had we done them, we would then have received through them a greater grace of that same Spirit.” Therefore he chose to question them a second time, because even now they cannot answer that they receive the Spirit from works. It is as if he says: Neither in the beginning nor now have you received the Holy Spirit from the Law, but from faith.

And you received the Spirit by faith just as Abraham received righteousness by faith: he believed God who promised, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness; that is, he was justified by faith, apart from works of the Law, because believing is a sufficient cause of justification. Since Abraham was justified by faith, know therefore that those who are of faith—that is, whose being is from faith—are sons of Abraham, that is, righteous after Abraham’s example.

> “But Scripture, foreseeing that God justifies the Gentiles by faith, announced beforehand to Abraham: ‘In you all the nations shall be blessed’ (Gen. 22; Ecclus. 44). Therefore those who are of faith shall be blessed with faithful Abraham. For all who are of works of the Law are under a curse. For it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all things that are written in the book of the Law, to do them’ (Deut. 27). But that no one is justified before God by the Law is evident, because ‘the righteous lives by faith’ (Hab. 2; Rom. 1). The Law [Col. 1152C], however, is not of faith; but ‘he who does these things shall live in them’ (Lev. 18).”

Not only righteousness but also blessing is given through faith, because Scripture said to Abraham that “the nations shall be blessed in you,” that is, in conformity with your faith. Or thus: I said that those who are of faith are sons of Abraham, and this is not new but has long been known in Scripture. For Scripture—that is, the Holy Spirit, or Moses, the compiler of Scripture—foreseeing, that is, showing that it had been foreseen long before it occurred, that God justifies the Gentiles through faith and not through works of the Law, announced beforehand—or reported that it had been announced beforehand—to Abraham that not Jews only, but all nations, should be blessed in you; that is, in your faith and in Christ, who was to be born from you.

Here we understand the blessing as the consecration of baptism, justification in good works, and the attainment of everlasting life. Since Scripture announced this beforehand, therefore those who are of faith—that is, who have begun spiritually to be through faith—shall be blessed with faithful Abraham. That is, they shall receive blessing through faith as Abraham was blessed through faith, and shall be joined with so great a patriarch.

And truly those who are of faith shall be blessed, for those who are of works of the Law shall be cursed. All who are of works of the Law—that is, who seek to be justified by carnal observances—are under a curse and cannot escape except through Christ’s deliverance. That is, they are liable on account of their transgression and prepared for the everlasting curse [Col. 1153A] of condemnation.

For thus it is written in Deuteronomy (chapter 27): “Cursed”—that is, condemned with an eternal curse—“shall be everyone who does not remain continually,” not merely in some things but in all things written in the book of the Law; nor do I mean merely that he understands them and wishes to perform them, but that he does them, that is, completes them in action. No one is able to fulfil this. For this is the “yoke which,” as Peter says, “neither we nor our fathers were able to bear” (Acts 15).

Therefore no one who has placed his neck under the yoke of the Law and has not sought the aid of grace is free from this curse. For no one has ever been able to fulfil all the commandments of the Law. Cursed shall be the one who has not done all of them; yet even if someone has done them, he will not thereby be justified. This is the meaning: Since no one is justified by the Law before God [Col. 1153B], who looks upon truth, even though he may seem righteous before deceived human beings, this is plain from the words of Habakkuk, who says that the righteous lives by faith (Hab. 2) in the soul; that is, is justified by faith, not by the Law.

For the life of the soul for the present is righteousness, until it comes to the vision of the Creator, by which it may live eternally; and this righteousness is from faith. The righteous lives by faith, that is, by believing those things which he does not see. But the Law is not from faith; that is, it commands nothing to be believed, but compels action by fear, saying that whoever does the things written there shall not be punished because he has not transgressed, but shall live temporally in the things which he has performed carnally; otherwise he would be punished.

> [Col. 1153C] “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us, because it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree’ (Deut. 21), so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.”

Previously, when he said, “Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all the things written in the book of the law, to do them,” he seemed to be arguing against himself. For by this he appeared to be preaching circumcision and the carnal observances, so that those who kept them might not be condemned by the eternal curse. He now answers this, as it were: We Jews, so long as we were enslaved to the law, were under a curse; but Christ, by his death blotting out our sins and giving us justification, [Col. 1153D] redeemed us from the curse of the law. Therefore there is no need for us now to remain in the shadow of that law, after the truth has shone upon us.

Or thus: From the law comes a curse, not righteousness; but Christ redeemed us Jews, who were under the curse, from the curse of the law. Why, then, are you pressing toward that? He redeemed us from the curse, having been made a curse for us; that is, reckoned not merely cursed, but even the curse itself. Or: in his death he was made a curse, that is, an offering for our curse—namely, mortal flesh, which is called a curse because it was made mortal through the evil word, that is, the sin, of the first parent. For it is written in Deuteronomy (chapter 21): “Cursed,” that is, consigned to death, “is everyone who hangs upon the wood of the cross.” Absolutely everyone who hangs upon the wood, [Col. 1154A] even the Son of God. For he said “everyone” against the heretics who were going to deny the true death of our Redeemer and, in their folly, separate him in honor from death.

For he who is always blessed in his righteousness deigned, for the sake of our offenses, to become cursed for an hour in the death which he took upon himself from our punishment. Yet he was cursed not by just anyone, but by God, as the law says. For unless God hated sin and our death, he would not send his Son to undergo and destroy it. What wonder, then, if that which God hates is cursed by God? For he gives us immortality, which is to come when Christ comes, all the more gladly inasmuch as he mercifully hates our death, which hung upon the wood. For death itself comes from the curse, [Col. 1154B] and every sin is a curse: either the very thing by which punishment follows, or punishment itself, which is also called sin because it comes about from sin.

Jesus, however, took our punishment upon himself without guilt, in order thereby to discharge our guilt and also bring our punishment to an end. Therefore, because his death was real, when he was crucified our curse hung upon the wood. For he took the curse upon himself for us because he died for us. The punishment for our sin which he endured, by the justice of the divine sentence, came from the curse. Thus he was made cursed for us, in order to free us from the curse and confer blessing: namely, so that the blessing promised to Abraham, in which it was said, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” [Col. 1154C] (Gen. 22), might be fulfilled in the justification of the nations through faith in Jesus Christ, who is Abraham’s seed.

Thus he redeemed us Jews from the curse, so that in the nations also—who had not been under the curse of the law—the blessing of Abraham might come through the nations’ faith in Christ Jesus; so that at last both groups might receive through faith, and not through works of the law, the promise of the Spirit, that is, blessedness, which the Holy Spirit, given as a pledge, promises; or the promise of the Spirit, that is, the Holy Spirit promised to believers; or the promise of the spirit, that is, gifts of grace promised by the Holy Spirit.

> “Brothers, I speak according to human custom: yet no one rejects or adds provisions to a confirmed human testament [Heb. 9]. The promises were spoken to Abraham [Col. 1154D] and to his seed [Gen. 12; 22]. He does not say, ‘and to seeds,’ as though to many, but as though to one: ‘and to your seed,’ which is Christ.”

Above I have spoken on the basis of arguments and the authority of the Scriptures: that the Holy Spirit, righteousness, and blessedness are given through faith, not through the law. And now, brothers, I say the same thing according to human custom. In that custom, although firmness is often lacking, nevertheless a human testament—that is, one made by a person for his heirs—is binding. So too the divine testament of promises given to Abraham cannot be invalidated by the subsequent law.

Although I speak according to human custom, nevertheless no one rejects or adds provisions to any person’s testament—that is, the written instrument in which he appoints who [Col. 1155A] shall possess his inheritance after him—once it has been confirmed by his death [Heb. 9]. For the death of the testator is the confirmation of the testament. No one thereafter rejects it, treating it as void and wishing entirely to destroy it by removing all the heirs and putting others in their place; nor does anyone add provisions to it, partly destroying it and partly leaving it as it is, retaining some heirs, removing others, and putting others in their place. If a testament of a man already dead and returned to dust is not altered, but remains as he established it while still living, how much more does the testament of the living and eternal God remain without alteration?

For just as no one rejects or adds provisions to a confirmed human testament, so the testament of God made to Abraham and his seed—in which [Col. 1155B] God appointed that Abraham with his seed should be heir of the heavenly homeland—is not made void by the subsequent law, nor altered even in part. For promises were spoken to Abraham; that is, an inheritance was frequently promised to him and to his seed by God. For example, when the land of the living was promised to him under the figure of the land of Canaan, the Lord said: “All the land that you see I will give to you and to your seed” (Gen. 12).

He does not say, “I will give this land to you and to your seeds,” as though it were to be possessed in many seeds, that is, in many sons; but as though it were to be obtained in one seed, that is, in one son. “And to your seed,” he says, “I will give it,” which is Christ. He used *who*, not *which*, because the relative pronoun *which*, when placed between a proper and a common noun, ought to refer to the proper noun—as here [Col. 1155C] to Christ—although Christ is not purely a proper name.

The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. Christ is Abraham’s seed, because the people of Israel came forth from Abraham; and from the people of Israel was born the Virgin Mary, who bore Christ (Luke 2). And because we too belong to that which is Christ, being incorporated together with them and alike joined to the head, there is one Christ. For Christ is one with all his members, as a head with its body, which is the Church. Therefore the Apostle used one seed to show that the Galatians and the other nations are not inferior to the Jews in faith, nor the Jews superior to them, but that all are seed in faith, as one body of Christ (Eph. 2). [Col. 1155D]

Yet, lest they themselves after receiving this should grow sluggish in good works, but each should strive to outstrip his brother in holy actions, so that he might also precede him in reward—for “each shall receive his own reward according to his own labor” (1 Cor. 3), and “in my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14)—he used *promises* in the plural, so that through the merits of a worthier life they might hasten toward the prize of greater glory, because “star differs from star in brightness” (1 Cor. 15). Nevertheless, as we have said, the seed to whom these promises were made is one, because all will receive one denarius of recompense (Matt. 20), and all are one in Christ.

For God does not say to Abraham, “To you and to your seeds I will give the inheritance or blessing,” as though he intended this to be understood of many seeds or sons; but as though of one, that is, Christ, since he truly intended it to be understood of the one seed, Christ. “And to your seed,” he says, “I will give the inheritance or everlasting blessing”; and that seed is Christ with his body.

[Col. 1156A]

> “But this I say: the law, which was made four hundred and thirty years afterward, does not invalidate a testament confirmed by God, so as to annul the promise. For if the inheritance is from the law, it is no longer from promise. But God granted it to Abraham through a promise renewed.”

Promises were spoken to Abraham. But the law given afterward did not destroy them. God made with Abraham a testament of promises of inheritance; but I, Paul, say that the law made at Sinai four hundred [Col. 1156B] and thirty years after the time of the promises does not make void—that is, false—this testament of divine promises, confirmed not by a human being but by God. It does not make it void so as to annul God’s promise, made in it concerning the eternal inheritance. It would do so if the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven were given through it.

For this is the meaning of the words of this verse: the law given to holy Moses could not annul or invalidate those promises which God had spoken to Abraham long beforehand (Gen. 12, 15, 22). After the Lord deigned to pledge those promises to blessed Abraham, the children of Israel went down into Egypt and lived there for four hundred and thirty years (Gen. 46). When these years were completed, they departed [Col. 1156C] from there, and so the Lord also gave the law to Moses on Mount Sinai (Exod. 12, 13, 14, 19). It was therefore not fitting that the law given after so long a time should make void—that is, empty and false—this holy testament previously confirmed by almighty God.

For the false apostles wanted the law to invalidate it, when they tried to maintain that justification and the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven are given not through grace, as God had promised Abraham, but through works of the law. Thus the divine promise would be annulled and God made a liar. But the law does not invalidate it by annulling the promise, as though it gave its observers the inheritance of salvation. For if the inheritance—that is, eternal blessedness—were from the law, that is, from works of the law, it would no longer be [Col. 1156D] from promise, that is, from God’s gift; and thus the promise would be deceptive. That is: if the heavenly inheritance came through the law of Moses, the promise made to Abraham would not be true, since the inheritance would not be given through it.

If the inheritance is from the law, it is no longer from promise. But it is from promise; therefore it is not from the law. And that it is from promise the Apostle adds, saying: “But God granted it to Abraham through a promise renewed.” That is, God granted the inheritance to Abraham, not through the law, which he did not possess because it did not yet exist, but through the grace which he promised anew. It is evident to all that Abraham has the inheritance, since no one can deny it. Since he has it, he has it either through observance of the law or through the grace of promise. But he does not have it through observance of the law, because the law had not yet [Col. 1157A] been given; therefore he has it through the grace of the divine promise.

And if blessed Abraham obtained the inheritance through faith by the grace of the heavenly promise, it follows that we too, who are his seed, obtain the same inheritance through faith by the grace of the divine promise. He said “a promise renewed” because God did not promise these things to Abraham only once (Gen. 12, 15, 22).

> “What then is the law? It was imposed because of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom he had promised, ordered through angels by the hand of a mediator. But a mediator is not of one; yet God is one.”

Someone could ask: If the law could not give the inheritance of the heavenly homeland, why then was it given after the promises to Abraham? Therefore the Apostle [Col. 1157B] himself puts the question to himself and himself resolves it. As if he said: Since righteousness and inheritance are not from the law, because it neither justified its observers nor opened the kingdom of heaven to them, what benefit, then, did the law bring? We must ask why it was given by God: with what usefulness, with what necessity it was given; what advantage it bestowed; and why it intervened between those two things, namely, the promise and the thing promised.

He now shows why it was given. It was imposed, he says, between the promise and the promised inheritance, because of those who transgressed the natural law: so that through fear they might at least cease to transgress, and might gradually be trained to do good out of love. But let us consider the order of the construction. The law, ordered through angels by the hand of a mediator, was imposed upon the Jewish people [Col. 1157C] because of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom God had promised.

The law was ordered through angels because God did not speak with Moses directly, but through angels, and arranged the precepts of the law (Acts 7). And because Christ, who is the mediator of God and human beings, was in those angels and arranged the law through them, it is said to have been ordered through angels by the hand of a mediator. It was ordered, therefore, that is, placed in good order between the promise and the fulfilment of the promise; it was ordered between the time of the natural law, to which human beings had been bound and which could not help, and the time of grace, before whose coming they had to be convicted by the written law. Therefore whoever now restores the law after the coming of grace acts against the order divinely arranged through angels.

It was ordered [Col. 1157D] so that it should always be in the hand of the mediator, that is, in Christ’s power: that it might remain as long as he wished and cease when he wished. And it was thus imposed upon the Jewish people to restrain their transgressions: namely, so that, hearing, “If anyone does this or that, let him surely die,” or “let him suffer such a punishment,” they might at least through fear of death or punishment cease from sinning.

For it was not imposed on account of the righteous and the prophets, who served God not from fear of punishment but from love of righteousness. Having full faith in Christ, they already belonged to the grace of the New Testament and already lived in the freedom of children. Nevertheless, for various reasons they themselves carried out the works of the same law carnally: both because they understood them to be signs of things to come, [Col. 1158A] and because they wished to give an example of keeping the law to the others for whom the law itself had been given. For if those who were wiser and holier had seemed to disregard the law’s carnal observances, that less-instructed people would have thought the law useless and would not have kept it.

But those who observed the law itself carnally through fear of punishment, awaited the redemption of the human race, and had some kind of faith in the coming of the Redeemer—though not as full as the prophets’—were saved through that same Redeemer, even if they do not possess the greatness of the higher glory attained by the prophets.

Because Christ was to be born from Abraham’s seed—in whom the blessing of all nations had been promised anew, through whom the heavenly homeland was to be given—[Col. 1158B] and because many ages were to pass from Abraham to Christ, God, foreseeing that the offspring of his beloved Abraham might mingle with other nations and that his family might gradually become unrecognizable, marked the Israelite flock with a certain cautery of circumcision. Thus, living among Egyptians, Canaanites, and Assyrians, they might be distinguished by this sign. For as long as they were in Egypt, they were circumcised among idolaters and the impure, so that they might always recognize themselves as God’s people, unlike those others, and might never do their works (Josh. 5).

But after they came into the wilderness, in the presence of the lawgiver himself they discontinued circumcision, because all were Jews worshipping one God and they saw no nations with whom they might mingle in idolatry. But as soon as [Col. 1158C] they crossed the bank of the Jordan, they resumed the circumcision which they had interrupted (ibid.). For this reason it too was called the second circumcision: because, being about to live among the nations, they feared that they might turn aside into idolatry through the nations’ example, and therefore wished to show themselves unlike them.

From this we may see that circumcision and the carnal observances of the law were in no way necessary for prophets and other righteous persons who belonged to the New Testament, since they served God not through fear of punishment but through love of righteousness, and without the law recognized themselves as unlike all idolaters. Nor now is there any need for the sign of circumcision, by which God’s people might be recognized, because God’s people are no longer one nation but one assembly from all nations, since Christ, the expectation of the nations, has now come [Col. 1158D] (Gen. 49).

Accordingly, the law was not imposed on account of the righteous, as we have said, but to restrain the transgressions of the rest, whether they had preceded or pressed upon their desires. And it was imposed until Abraham’s seed should come, to whom God had promised: that is, it was imposed to last until Christ came, to whom the Father had promised the heavenly inheritance, that with his body—which is the Church—he might possess it forever. Whoever, therefore, still wishes to prolong the law either denies that Christ has come, or denies that God imposed the law only until his coming.

But because the Apostle had mentioned the mediator, he wishes to show whom he meant and how mercifully that mediator always [Col. 1159A] cares for our salvation. For he says: “But a mediator is not of one.” The law is in the hand of a mediator, but the mediator is not of one. This is well known, because a mediator is not of one thing or one party, but of two. That is to say: a mediator—that is, a reconciler or advocate—is not needed for one thing or one party, but for two. For between two persons to be reconciled, a mediator is necessary who is a friend to both; that is, between two parties in discord a mediator, a reconciler, must intervene, one able to recall them to the harmony of peace. Thus Christ, through his humanity our friend and through his divinity the Father’s friend, made peace between us and God by his blood.

A mediator is not of one, but God is one. Therefore the mediator is not of God alone, but of God and human beings. [Col. 1159B] For Christ is mediator between us and God; and so, while through his humanity he reconciles us to God, he reconciles us to the Father, to himself, and to the Holy Spirit, because the Trinity is one God.

Or thus: A mediator is not of one but of two, because Christ made peace between two discordant peoples, Jewish and Gentile, making one Christian people out of both. Christ is mediator of two, but God is one, because Father and Son are not two gods but one God. For although the Father is God and Christ is God, both are one, not two gods. But the former interpretation is better and truer.

> “Is the law, then, against the promises of God? By no means! For if a law had been given which could give life, righteousness would truly be from the law. But Scripture shut up all things [Col. 1159C] under sin [Rom. 3], so that the promise from faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe.”

Because it was said above that, if the inheritance is from the law, it is no longer from promise, someone might suppose that the law was contrary to the promise. The Apostle now raises this objection against himself, as it were in the role of an opponent, and refutes it. “Since,” he says, “the inheritance cannot be from promise if it is from the law, the law is therefore against the promises of God,” that is, contrary to the preceding promises which God had given to Abraham. Far be it that God’s law should oppose God’s promises! It cannot be that God gave a law opposed to his own promises, since in that case God would be contrary to himself.

The subsequent law never opposed the earlier promises; rather, it continually admonished human beings [Col. 1159D] to prepare themselves worthily to receive them. Or thus: Since the law was imposed because of transgressions, is it therefore against God’s promises, so that they may be fulfilled through it otherwise than God promised? Far be this! It is not contrary to them, so as to hinder them in any respect or divert them in another direction, because the heavenly inheritance cannot be obtained otherwise than as it was promised to Abraham.

For the law cannot give that inheritance, because it cannot confer true righteousness, without which no one can reach the heavenly inheritance. And it truly cannot justify, because it cannot give life to the soul from the death of sin. If a law had been given which could give life, righteousness would truly be from the law. If through Moses [Col. 1160A] a law had been given which could give human beings life from the inward death into which they had fallen through the transgression of the first parent and through their own wickedness, then without doubt the law itself could confer true righteousness, by which human beings would be made fit for the kingdom of heaven.

But a law was not given that could give life; rather, one that could kill. “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3). For the letter of the law, prohibiting sin, does not give life to a person; rather, it kills, increasing desire and adding transgression to iniquity, unless grace through the law of faith, which is in Christ Jesus, sets one free, when love is poured into the heart through the Holy Spirit (Rom. 5). Therefore the law of Moses could not give life, because this was reserved for evangelical grace.

This was beautifully prefigured [Col. 1160B] when Gehazi, running ahead with the staff, could not raise the dead person; but Elisha, coming afterward, raised him (4 Kgs. 4). The dead child is the human race, lying in the death of sin. Gehazi with the staff is Moses with the terror of the law. Elisha following afterward is Christ coming later. But Gehazi, sent ahead with the staff, did not raise the dead person, because Moses, preceding Christ with the terror of the law, could not raise the human race from the death of the soul; for, according to the Apostle, no law was given that could give life. But Elisha, coming afterward, raised the child, because Christ, appearing incarnate at the end of the law, raised the human race from inward death.

The law, therefore, could not give life; had it been able to do so, it could also have justified. Hence it is plainly evident that evangelical [Col. 1160C] grace, which gives the mind life from the death of sin, provides true righteousness, making people fit for the inheritance of heaven.

A law was not given that could give life; but rather Scripture—that is, the law itself remaining and written, or that which does not give the Spirit but is merely Scripture—shut up all classes of human beings under sin. That is, it enclosed all Jews and held them under sin’s dominion, so that while they were held in the law they could not escape the yoke of sin in any direction; or because it was so difficult that, since no one could fulfill it, it made all transgressors and rendered them liable to accusation.

That the law shut up everything it contained under sin was aptly signified by that pool in Jerusalem which had five porticoes, in which [Col. 1160D] lay a great multitude of the sick (John 5). For the water of the pool represented either the people of the synagogue or the teaching of the law; the five porticoes enclosing the pool represented the five books of the law enclosing the synagogue. In those porticoes lay a great multitude of the sick because, as is now said, the Scripture of the law shut up all things under sin, and all who were enclosed within the bounds of the law lay in the weakness of sin, awaiting Christ the physician, through whom they might be healed. Scripture thus shut up all under sin so that people, conscious of themselves and of the law’s weakness, might hasten to grace; and thus the promise of blessing and Abraham’s inheritance might be given to believers, not from works of the law but from faith in Jesus Christ.

[Col. 1161A]

> “But before faith came, we were kept under the law, shut up unto the faith which was to be revealed. Therefore the law was our pedagogue unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith. But when faith came, we are no longer under a pedagogue.”

Now faith frees us and makes us attain the promise; but before it came with Christ, we were kept under the law. For the law shut up all under sin, yet it was useful, because before faith came of its own accord, not called forth by any merits of ours, we were kept under the law, shut up—that is, constrained like slaves by fear—so that it might enclose us under the burden of carnal observances, lest through arrogance and wantonness we should stray into idolatry.

Therefore we were kept shut up, so that, restrained by the discipline [Col. 1161B] of the law, we might be led into the faith that was to be revealed in Christ’s time, when many things were disclosed which had formerly been closed and veiled. We were kept shut up as though compelled to serve in prisons, so that we might pass into the faith which was to be revealed; that is, into the most manifest and complete faith which was to be unveiled in the time of grace, because in the saints of old it was veiled.

And because the law kept us for faith, therefore the same law was our pedagogue: restraining us, children in understanding, from unlawful things and directing us toward what is right through fear of punishments. Since it kept us until we could come to faith as adults, it was our pedagogue—that is, a temporary guardianship, not something that was always to remain, but something which, like a pedagogue, would cease.

For as a pedagogue whips a child in order to make him fit [Col. 1161C] to govern the household and possess his father’s inheritance when he has reached mature age, so the law was imposed upon us as a guardianship, so that the heavy burdens of the law, observed at least through fear of punishment, might restrain us and make us fit heirs of the highest Father. The law was our pedagogue unto Christ, that is, in expectation of Christ, so that by coming to faith, as children come to maturity, we might now be justified by faith and, justified, attain the inheritance.

Before faith we were under a pedagogue, that is, under the strictness and burden of the law. But after faith came, we are no longer under the pedagogue of the law’s servitude, but in the freedom of love, since we are no longer children in understanding but adults.

> “For you are all children of God through faith, which is [Col. 1161D]  
> [Note: [Col. 1161D] Anselm does not read these two words, *which is*.]  
> in Christ Jesus. For all of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ [Rom. 6]. There is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free, neither male nor female. For you are all one in Christ Jesus. And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise.”

The Galatians might say: The Jews had the law as a pedagogue which kept them, and therefore they can now be children by grace, to receive the inheritance of the heavenly homeland; but we, who did not have a pedagogue, are not children. Therefore a pedagogue—that is, the law—is necessary for us in order that we may be children. The Apostle appears to answer: This is not true. For [Col. 1162A] all of you, through the faith which you received without a pedagogue, have become children of God; that is, fit to possess the heavenly inheritance.

Or rather, it continues thus: We Jews abandon the pedagogue in the time of faith, because all of you Gentiles who did not have a pedagogue are children of God through faith. We abandon the pedagogue following your example, while you take it up; yet you are children through faith, being in Christ Jesus—that is, made members of Christ and participants in his innocence and holiness—and thus worthy to possess the inheritance of children.

And truly you are in Christ through the faith which you received in baptism. For all of you—of whatever condition, sex, or age—who have been baptized into Christ, that is, in Christ’s name, or into Christ, that is, in Christ’s baptism, which he ordained to be performed with water and the Spirit and in the name of the Trinity [Col. 1162B] (John 3; Matt. 28), have put on Christ. That is, you have received Christ as a garment, so that, clothed with the garment of his righteousness (Isa. 61), you may no longer show in any part of your works and conduct anything other than the holiness of Christianity.

You have received Christ as a garment, which is both an honor for you and a protection against the heat of temptations. In this putting on of Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek; that is, in this conformity to Christ neither does being Jewish benefit nor being Greek harm, because neither is the Jew superior there on account of Judaism nor the Greek inferior on account of Greekness. Nor is the slave more lowly there, because without distinction of nation, condition, or sex you are all in Christ. You are not different there, [Col. 1162C] because all of you—Jews or Greeks, slaves or free, males or females—are one in Christ Jesus through the unity of faith and love.

And if faith, through which one walks rightly in this life, gives us life in this way, how much more perfectly and happily will that very sight make us, by which we shall see as it is the thing toward which we are striving? For you are all one in Christ, that is, in Christ’s body, and thus have become his members. But if you are Christ’s members—that is, united to Christ—then you are Abraham’s seed, future heirs of the kingdom of heaven not according to the flesh but according to the promise which God made to Abraham. For through God’s grace you have become heirs according to Abraham’s promise. God did not make them Abraham’s co-heirs [Col. 1162D] on the basis of Abraham’s flesh. For by imitating Abraham’s faith you have become Abraham’s children.

## Chapter IV

> “Now I say: So long as an heir is a child, he differs in no respect from a slave, though he is lord of all; but he is under guardians and managers until the time appointed by the father. So also we, when we were children, were enslaved under the elements of the world. But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, in order that he might redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive the adoption of children.”

From the point at which he had said, “we are no longer under a pedagogue,” he has made an intervening digression until now on account of the Galatians [Col. 1163A]. Now, however, he explains in what comparison he had called the Law a pedagogue; he applies the comparison and shows that we ought not to have remained under the Law after faith came. It is as though he said: Above I stated plainly that, before faith came, we were kept under the Law as under a pedagogue; but once faith came, we were no longer under a pedagogue. Now I state the same thing by means of a comparison: namely, that a child who will become his father’s heir, for as long as he is a little one in age and understanding, differs in no respect from a slave—that is, he is compelled to obey another’s will and has no authority—although by nature he is already lord of all that his father possesses. He is not indeed a slave, yet he differs in no respect from a slave because he is not splendidly clothed [Col. 1163B] and is not under his own free control, but under a guardian who keeps him and leads him wherever he must be led; for *pais* (παῖς) means “boy,” and *agō* (ἄγω), “I lead.” He differs in no respect from a slave, but is under guardians, who protect him from injuries, and under agents, who act for him in matters which he is not yet able or knows how to perform himself.

Or, he is under agents, that is, instructors and formers of character, whose authority and dignity he is to follow, and who, by their authority, conduct his causes for him. He remains under them until the time appointed by his father—that is, until his fifth year, or until some other span of time which his father has ordained beforehand—so that thereafter he may be released to his own free will.

The same must be understood of the Jewish people, who through Christ’s grace were to become heirs of the kingdom of heaven. So long as they were little in knowledge and conduct, crushed by slavish fear under the discipline of the Law as under the strictness of a pedagogue, and compelled to serve the divine commandments, they were nevertheless to become through Christ masters of all the goods of the heavenly homeland—that is, possessors of heavenly riches. While they were little in the knowledge of God and in strength to resist sin, they differed in no respect from a slave, because the Law ruled them and frightened them with threats lest they dare to sin. For they were under guardians and agents—that is, under the words of the Law—which, like guardians, defended them against the assaults of evil spirits and against the Gentiles’ persuasions toward idolatry, by admonishing, rebuking, and punishing them; and which, like agents, formed their character [Col. 1163C] and pleaded their cause before God [Col. 1163D], since through sacrifices and expiations they rendered God favourable to them.

They remained under these until the time appointed by the Father—that is, until Christ’s coming—in which God determined that this people should become perfect and free and obtain its inheritance. But if, while they were little, they had disdained to be subject to the aforementioned guardians or agents, they could not have become fit, at the proper time, to receive their fatherly inheritance.

The Apostle himself declares that these things must be understood in this way, when he subsequently applies the comparison, saying: “So,” that is, similarly to the aforementioned child, “we Jews, when we were little,” not in age but in understanding, discernment, strength of mind, and activity in works, “were enslaved,” that is, living in bondage to the Law, “under the elements of the world,” that is, under the carnal observances by which we were restrained, lest we be allowed freely to indulge ourselves [Col. 1164A]. For just as children learn the letters and the joining of letters, yet cannot understand the depth of meanings until they are under their own free control, and later apply themselves to the liberal arts—yet cannot attain knowledge of these except through the elements—so the Jews were instructed through the Law’s carnal observances.

These observances were for them like elements, that is, beginnings through which they came to faith and to a fuller knowledge of God, namely to the spiritual understanding of those very carnal observances. They are called elements “of the world” because they were given to lovers of this world, who did not know how to desire eternal and invisible things but temporal and visible things; and therefore they had to be compelled to worship God in a childish or slavish fashion by terrors of bodily punishments and promises of temporal goods in the Law [Col. 1164B].

By “the elements of the world,” then, are understood the Law of Moses and the entire Old Testament, through which we too still learn God as through elements and first beginnings of religion. Thus letters are called elements, through which we join syllables into words and, by long meditation, proceed to weave a discourse. The art of music likewise has its elements, and geometry begins from the elements of lines. In this way, by the elements of the Old Testament, the infancy of holy men is instructed so that it may come to evangelical fullness. Hence also the one hundred and nineteenth Psalm, and all the others marked by letters, lead us through ethics to theology, and cause us to pass from the elements of the killing letter [Col. 1164C], which is destroyed, to the life-giving Spirit.

For this reason elements are also called, as it were, “liftings up,” because they raise us from visible things to the understanding of invisible things. Under these elements—that is, under the Law and Prophets understood carnally—the Jews were held in servitude while they were little and did not know how to govern themselves; accordingly, they needed the strictness and instruction of a pedagogue. “So,” he says, “while we were little in understanding, we were enslaved under the elements of the world until the time appointed by the Father.”

“But after the fullness of time came”—that is, after the whole period had been completed during which the heavenly Father had ordained that we should remain, like children, under the Law’s strictness as under a pedagogue [Col. 1164D], and after we had advanced to the strength of a mature mind and no longer needed a pedagogue’s guardianship—then God the Father, in order to free us from the bond of former servitude, sent not an angel or archangel but his only-begotten Son. He sent him, that is, caused him to become incarnate so that he might be visible to human beings: him, I say, who according to the flesh was “made of a woman,” that is, of a female mother, though according to divinity he was not made but begotten of the Father.

And he was “made under the Law,” that is, created according to the flesh under the observance of the Law, so that he might receive circumcision and be carried to the Temple with offerings according to Jewish custom, as truly the son of Abraham to whom he had been promised. Thus God brought forth before human eyes as a true human being him who was made of a woman—that is, conceived from the substance of maternal flesh without a man’s involvement [Col. 1165A]—who, remaining in divine power and substance wholly what he was, put on the true weakness of mortal nature, which he did not possess.

For the usage of the divine Scriptures, and especially of the Hebrew Scriptures, customarily calls not corrupted women but females “women,” as we read: “The Lord God built the rib which he had taken from Adam into a woman, and brought her to Adam” (Gen. II). Moreover, so that the Son of God might commend to us by a supreme example the necessary virtue of obedience, he was made under the Law, that is, he was made subject to the Law. This was not because he himself owed anything to the Law, he who alone is lawgiver and judge, but so that he might help by his compassion those placed under the Law, who had been unable to bear the burdens of the Law, and might generously bring them, rescued from the slavish condition that existed under the Law [Col. 1165B], into the adoption of sons which comes through grace.

He was made under the Law in order to redeem those who were under the Law, that is, to free them from the Law’s bondage, just as he also deigned to undergo death in order to redeem from death those unable to escape the lord of death. He was made under the Law not in order to be expiated by it, but in order to free those who were oppressed and guilty beneath it, so that all of us, Jews and Gentiles alike, might receive the adoption of sons, because he shared our nature and adopted us into his own. Therefore he willed to be made under the Law and to fulfil the Law: that he might redeem from the yoke of the Law those crushed beneath its burden, and that we all, Jews as well as Gentiles, might through the grace of new freedom receive the adoption of sons which we had lost in Adam [Col. 1165C]—that is, become adopted sons and attain the inheritance of the eternal Father.

> “And because you are sons of God, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father.’ Therefore he is no longer a slave, but a son; and if a son, then also an heir through God.”

Now he repeats what he had said above, that the Galatians are sons of God, in order to show that they too are adopted sons in the same manner as the Jews. It is as though he said: I said that you are sons of God through faith; and you are not so in vain. But because you Galatians are adopted sons of God, just as we Hebrews are, God has sent the Spirit of his natural Son into our hearts—that is, the Holy Spirit, who proceeds both from the Father and from the Son (John XV). For the mission by which he is sent by the Father is itself the procession by which he proceeds from the Father [Col. 1165D]. Therefore the Apostle says that he is sent by the Father and the Son, in order to show that he proceeds from both.

God the Father sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, that is, into the hearts of all of us who believe, Jews and Gentiles alike. For the sake of both peoples he sent him crying, “Abba, Father.” For he cries in our hearts to God—that is, by the great devotion of a pious mind he causes us inwardly to cry, “O Abba, Father.” Now *Abba* and “Father” are the same. But he cries “Abba” on account of the Jews, and “Father” on account of the Gentiles, in order to show that both have God as one Father. For *Abba* means “father” in Hebrew. Thus the effect proves both groups to be sons of God, since in the hearts of both the Holy Spirit cries to God, “Abba, Father” [Col. 1166A].

And what is that spiritual cry but the devout affection of the elect toward God and the pious petition of a mind hungering and thirsting for righteousness? Since he had said above that an heir, as long as he is little, differs in no respect from a slave—something which he wished to be understood mystically of the people who had been under the Law’s bondage—and had added how that same people was freed through the coming of the Son of God, he consequently infers that it is no longer a slave. As though he said: That people which was formerly little in understanding and conduct, and was slavishly oppressed under the Law, was later brought into freedom through the grace of God’s only-begotten Son and adopted as a son. Therefore it is no longer a slave as formerly under the Law, but a son, because it has received the adoption of sons through the gift of grace.

Or thus: the Spirit of Christ cries in the hearts of both peoples, “Abba, Father.” Therefore after receiving the Holy Spirit neither is a slave, but is a son through grace. “And if,” that is, if he is now, “a son,” then he will also be an heir in the future through God, that is, through God’s working and God’s grace. Or, “through God” means: I swear by God that it will be so. This sonship and inheritance have been granted to both peoples. But since the Apostle is addressing the Galatians, the following words concern them:

> “But then indeed, when you did not know God, you served those who by nature are not gods. But now, when you have known God—or rather, have been known by God—how do you turn again to weak and needy elements, to which you wish again to be enslaved? You observe days and months and seasons and years. I fear for you [Col. 1166C], lest perhaps I have laboured among you in vain.”

Now, he says, you are sons; but previously you were slaves, not in the bondage of the Law’s carnal ceremonies, as the Jews were, but of idols. For then, when you did not know God, you served those who are not gods by nature but only in the opinion of irrational people—that is, they are not natural but false gods. Here he shows that service ought to be rendered only to him who is God by nature. You then did not know the true God, whom alone one ought to serve; and therefore you had some excuse for serving false gods. But now that you have known God, no excuse remains for you if you go astray; rather, you will sin far more grievously than before.

There is now no place for error when the truth has been made manifest, when you have known God through faith—or rather [Col. 1166D], I can put it better, when you have been known by God, that is, approved by good works. Or, God is said to have known them because he caused himself to be known by those by whom he had been unknown. For it is not permissible for us to believe that God first knew the Galatians then, since he had foreknown them before the foundation of the world; but he is said to have known them then because he then caused himself to be known.

Since they had known him at that time by his gift, not through their own merit or capacity, he preferred to speak figuratively, saying that they were known by him at the time when he enabled them to know him; and he corrected the expression which he had properly used as though it had been less properly said, rather than allow them to claim for themselves the ability which he had granted them. For when it is said that God knows us [Col. 1167A], he bestows his knowledge upon us, so that we may understand from this that even our knowing God must not be attributed to ourselves, but that this knowledge too must be ascribed to his mercy.

“Formerly,” he says, “through ignorance of God you served idols; but now, when you have known God—or rather have been known by God, that is, have received knowledge of him from himself—how,” that is, for what cause or reason, “do you turn again,” as before knowing God, “to the bondage of error?” How, after truth has shone upon you, do you turn again as before, while becoming proselytes under the Jews? How, I say, do you turn to the elements, that is, to the Law’s carnal commands, which are beginnings of divine worship for the Jews and are weak, because in themselves they cannot help their worshippers [Col. 1167B], and needy, because they need the help of grace? How do you turn to these, to which you wish to be enslaved anew, that is, again, as the Jews once served them but have now been freed from their bondage? They ceased to serve them; for what reason do you wish again to serve them?

These elements, that is, the Law’s carnal precepts, had formerly stood as strong and as giving a certain firmness, while they still restrained the Jews, encouraged them toward the righteousness of faith, and gradually advanced them to fuller knowledge of God. They were also rich while they enriched them by giving them a certain righteousness before human beings, so that they might not be punished and might suffer no evil. For these were a kind of riches for them, preparing them for true riches—namely faith and righteousness—and also for receiving the inheritance above [Col. 1167C].

But now these elements are weak and needy, because, before truth came, they no longer prepared anyone for receiving it; they bind no one any longer to God’s worship; they prefigure nothing; they benefit their worshippers in nothing; they confer no good. And you wish again to serve these elements, so destitute and empty, as the Jews once served them before truth’s coming—although no one ought now to serve them, but all ought to remain in the freedom which Christ gave, and no longer live under a pedagogue now that the time appointed by the Father has been fulfilled. Truly you wish again to serve these elements and, after the period of infancy has ended, miserably to put your necks again beneath the yoke of a pedagogue.

For you observe—or plan to observe—days, such as Sabbaths; months, such as the first and seventh month; or “months,” meaning beginnings of months, that is, new moons; seasons, such as the occasions when all Jews came to the Temple three times a year and kept festivals; and years, such as the seventh and fiftieth year [Col. 1167D]. The Galatians, having been only recently led astray, had not yet observed this year. Therefore, as we said above, “you observe days and months and seasons and years” must be understood not as meaning that they already observed them, but that they wished to observe them. For they had not so much performed as planned to perform the Law’s carnal works.

And because, he says, you did not refuse to submit to such things, I fear for you, lest you cause me loss through yourselves—namely, lest I have laboured among you in converting and instructing you without cause [Col. 1168A], that is, without benefit to you. He does not fear this because he thinks that by their apostasy they can take from him the reward for the labour he bore in instructing them, but because he fears that, by withdrawing themselves from faith, they may make his apostolic labour of no benefit to them. He fears not the loss of his reward but their loss. “Perhaps” means that it can occur by their own choice. Either outcome is possible: his labour among them may be without result so far as they are concerned if they persist in error, or not without result if they repent.

Let us state what some have held: namely, that the Galatians had come to faith partly from Jews and partly from Gentiles; but after the Apostle’s departure they were being compelled to Judaize again by false preachers who had been converted from Judaism, while those who had believed from among the Gentiles were returning to observe the elements. The saying aptly applies to them: “But then indeed, when you did not know God, you served those who by nature are not gods. But now, when you have known God, how do you turn again,” as before you knew God, “to the elements”—that is, to the impious observance of sun, moon, stars, heaven, and earth? These are indeed weak in relation to you, because they cannot help you; and needy in themselves, because they possess nothing except by God’s ordinance. Yet after our conversion you wish again to serve them as before [Col. 1168B].

For you observe days, saying: “I shall not set out today because tomorrow is such a day,” or “because the moon is situated thus”; or, “I shall set out so that things may go well, because the position of the stars is such.” And you observe months, saying: “I shall undertake this business in this month because that star governs the month for me,” or “I shall undertake it because it has assumed the month.” You foresee seasons by auguries—what kind of season, whether dear, hot, or pestilential, is to occur—and years, as those do who say: “I shall not plant a vineyard this year because it is leap-year.”

Whether in these or other perverse ways, some Galatians observed days, months, seasons, and years. The Apostle therefore reproves them and all who still devote themselves to such observances; and he shows how grave the danger of observing such things is, when he fears that he has laboured in vain among those who observe them. For who would judge how great a sin it is to observe such things—as do those who, as stated, are willing or unwilling to begin something on certain days, months, seasons, or years because according to empty human teachings they judge the times fortunate or unfortunate—unless we weighed its greatness by the Apostle’s fear, when he now says to such people: “I fear lest perhaps I have laboured among you in vain” [Col. 1168D].

> “Be as I am, because I also am as you are. Brothers, I beseech you: you have injured me in nothing. But you know that through weakness of the flesh I preached the Gospel to you formerly; and you did not despise your temptation in my flesh, but received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.
