Where then is your blessedness? For I bear you witness [Col. 1169A] that, if it had been possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me. Have I therefore become your enemy by telling you the truth?”

Lest my labour among you be vain, be as I am: free from bondage to the elements, that is, from the Law’s carnal observance, because I too, who was subject to the Law and know its observance, am now as you are, without the Law. For because I, who had the Law, left it by the counsel of reason once I knew Christ, you may know that I found nothing useful for Christians in it, since I abandoned it completely. If, therefore, I who possessed it relinquished it, you who do not possess it ought not to take it up.

Or: be as I am in the love of faith, because I too am, as you are, a person corrected from error. For even now you may be withdrawn by my example from observance of the Law, as formerly you were recalled from the worship of idols. And you ought to be as I am because, brothers, I beseech you to be as I am—that is, I ask you by the sweetness of brotherly love. I beseech you in brotherly love because I do not seek to deceive you as an enemy, as the false apostles assert about me to you. For while I was among you, you injured me in nothing; rather, you held me in great honour [Col. 1169B].

Having rebuked them sharply above, he now soothes and recalls them by flattering entreaty and by recalling their good conduct. You did not injure me; rather, you yourselves know that through weakness of the flesh—that is, at the time when I was sick in my flesh—I formerly preached Christ’s Gospel to you. Yet you did not despise your temptation in my sick flesh by judging me worthless. For my bodily weakness was so great that you could have been tested by it and thought that I had no spiritual power, since I was bodily so weak, or that I was not an apostle of Christ, whom he permitted to be so tormented by the pains of weakness.

Or, this weakness was the suffering of various tribulations. “I formerly preached the Gospel to you through weakness of the flesh,” that is, through endurance of adversities by which my flesh was severely afflicted; and “you did not despise your temptation which occurred in my flesh,” that is, you did not regard as worthless the suffering of my tribulations by which you were tested, whether you would abandon me out of fear or embrace me in love. And I knew from this that you were steadfast: you did not turn aside from love because of the adversities which befell me in the flesh [Col. 1169C].

For when you saw me treated so shamefully by unbelievers on account of proclaiming the Gospel, you could also believe that you yourselves would likewise be ill-treated by them upon receiving the same Gospel. Therefore, in view of so great a persecution and punishment, some fell away from faith or feared to approach it. Thus all were tested; some were proved, and others were shown reprobate by the fire of tribulation.

You did not despise that weakness which was in my flesh and was your temptation, so as not to care about me as one so cast down and afflicted. Nor did you reject it altogether, so as wholly to refuse conversion on its account; rather, you received me as though I suffered nothing, as though I were immortal and incapable of suffering. You received me, that is, with such great reverence as you would receive an angel of God coming from heaven [Col. 1170A]; and, to say more, you received me as you would Christ himself, if he had descended again to earth and come to preach to you. You accorded me such authority as though an angel coming from the heights were speaking to you, or Christ himself, Lord of angels.

And since you then held me in such honour, whereas now you despise and reject me without cause, where is your blessedness? That is, where is that affection and humble devotion which you had toward me, which was the cause of your future blessedness? He appropriately recalls them by calling that affection “blessedness,” because if they lose the cause, they will lose the effect; if they lose that devoted affection, they will undoubtedly lose future blessedness.

Truly, he says, you received me as an angel or as Christ Jesus [Col. 1170B], and thereby merited blessedness, because, if it could rightly have been done and been to my benefit, you would have taken from yourselves those members which are dearest to a person and given them to me. For I bear witness to you that, if it could have been done for the Church’s benefit, if it could have been done consistently with your welfare and my advantage, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me—that is, for the benefit of my preaching. He speaks in the customary manner, as we are accustomed to say: “I would wish to give of my own flesh for your advancement, if I could.” He says such things to heighten their exceedingly great love for him.

But when such love and honour had been shown to him, did he spare them in their error because of the honour shown him and their affection, lest he perhaps be denied or be less praised or loved when he rebuked them? Certainly not. For he rejoiced not in the honour paid him but in their salvation. Therefore, for that same salvation, he did not fear to be reproached by them or hated by them, provided that he preached what was true and useful. Hence he immediately adds: “Have I therefore become your enemy by telling you the truth?” Since, he says, you loved me so greatly, do you regard me as having become your enemy because of the truth which I proclaimed? [Col. 1170C]

For the false apostles persuaded them that, out of hostility, he had been unwilling to teach them circumcision, although he preached it to others; and on that account they thought him their enemy. Therefore he now says in rebuke: “Have I therefore become your enemy by telling you the truth?” As though he said: You ought not to think that I am your enemy; rather, you ought to recognize me as your friend precisely because I preached to you the pure truth—namely, that you should seek salvation without observance of the Law, through observance of the Gospel alone. Or, because no one wishes to be rebuked, he now seems an enemy to them in rebuking them [Col. 1170D].

> “They are zealous for you, but not honourably; rather, they want to exclude you, so that you may be zealous for them. But be zealous for what is good always, and not only when I am present with you, my little children, whom I am again in labour to bear until Christ is formed in you. I would, however, be present with you now and change my tone, because I am perplexed about you.”

[Col. 1171A] I who speak the truth seem an enemy; but if I deceived you by flatteries, then I would be thought a friend. Yet I am not your enemy; rather, those whom you consider friends are your enemies. For they are zealous for you, but not honourably—that is, not with good will—because they are jealous of you not for the lawful bridegroom.

Holy men are jealous with God’s zeal for the souls of the faithful, lest the chastity of mind which they ought to preserve unstained for Christ their bridegroom be violated by some stealthy inroad of faithlessness or by the commission of sin. The false apostles pretended to be jealous for these people as with God’s zeal, judging that through transgression of the Law they were departing from spiritual chastity. But they did this dishonourably, because once Christ the bridegroom himself determined that you should be justified through faith, the soul which seeks justification through the Law’s carnal works is no longer chaste, since it has turned away from love of the bridegroom.

And this is what is meant: “They are not honourably zealous for you,” that is, they do not honourably strive to preserve chastity in you; but they want to exclude you from the bridegroom’s chamber, that is, from the Catholic Church, so that you may be zealous outside with them in fornication, that is, in their heresy [Col. 1171B]—that is, so that with a certain fervour of mind you may strive to imitate them. They want you to be zealous for them, that is, to imitate them. But you, do not imitate them; rather, be zealous for any good person—that is, strive to imitate with ardent love—not for an hour but always, and not in works which are either evil or neither good nor evil, but only in what is good.

For Peter was good, yet in that dissimulation by which, from fear of the Jews, he separated himself from believing Gentiles, he is not to be imitated, but only in the good which he did. Or, do not imitate the evil in the false apostles; but wherever good is found, be zealous for it, that is, imitate it with fervent mind “in what is good,” that is, in that which itself is good, not for some other reason. For some are zealous for good, but not for the good: seeing righteous people praised by others for a good work, they strive to do the same work in order to receive human praise.

Therefore good is to be sought only in what is good, not in evil—that is, you ought to imitate it solely because it is good, so that good itself may delight you and you may follow it out of love. Do this not only while I am bodily present with you but also while I am absent, my little children, whom I am now again in labour to bear until Christ is formed in you [Col. 1171C]. While he was absent, they had not been zealous for good as they had been when he was with them; therefore he warns them not to resemble a slave serving only under the eye, but to strive to do good in his absence as in his presence.

He calls them little children because their hearts had been diminished and they still remained in the darkness of their mother’s womb, not yet brought into the light through correction. He calls them his own because of his good will and the hope which he has concerning their correction. In motherly fashion, through God he had first conceived them by good will and love; he had laboured in childbirth through preaching; and he had borne them through their conversion. But afterwards they had been extinguished from the life of faith through the false apostles. Therefore he has now conceived them again through good will [Col. 1172A] and labours again in preaching, in order to bring them to light.

He suffers and labours in bearing them for as long as Christ, who had been deformed in them, is formed in them. This is a stronger expression than if he had said that they were formed in Christ. “Until Christ is formed in you,” he says: that is, until Christ’s likeness is expressed in you, so that in your faith and works nothing may appear except the form of the new human being. He says that he bears them in labour—which belongs to a mother, not a father—in order to show the maternal labour and affection which he has for them and toward them, because a mother alone feels the pains of childbirth and loves more affectionately than a father.

“Now,” he says, “while absent I call you little children, but I would now wish to be present with you and change my tone,” that is, deny that you are sons. “I would wish to be present, so that I might say to you things fitting for you which I do not wish to write lest they remain.” For while I am absent I address you gently, lest, if I exasperated you, you might think that I acted with ill will; but I would now wish to be present with you and change the tone of gentleness and mildness which I employ when absent into a tone of harshness and severity [Col. 1172B].

For neither a letter nor any writing moves human hearts as much as the living voice of one speaking in person. Bodily movement, bearing, expression, and manner of speech also greatly move hearers. Therefore I would wish sharply to rebuke you, because I am ashamed concerning you—that is, I blush before others because you have so departed from my teaching.

Or otherwise: I now speak many things to you in comparisons while absent, seeking to correct you; but I would wish now to be present with you so that by another manner of speaking I might open the matter more deeply and subtly, and set forth the truth not parabolically but openly. For if he were to speak deeper things to them now, they would have no one to explain them. But if he himself were present, wherever they doubted, he would explain. He wished to be present in order to expound the matter more plainly and profoundly by speaking otherwise. “I would wish to be present, because while absent I am perplexed about them,” that is, the teaching of one absent suffers confusion in the hearts of those who confusedly understand his subtle words [Col. 1172C]. But the earlier interpretation is truer and better. It follows:

> “Tell me, you who wish to be under the Law: have you not read the Law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman [Col. 1172D]. But the one by the slave woman was born according to the flesh (Gen. XVI), whereas the one by the free woman was born through the promise (Gen. XXI). These things are spoken allegorically. For these are the two covenants. One indeed is from Mount Sinai, bearing children into slavery, which is Hagar. For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, which is joined to the Jerusalem that now is, and is in slavery with her children.”

The Apostle again begins to show from the Law itself that it ought not to be retained. “Tell me,” he says—that is, answer me—you who carnally wish to be under the Law: have you not read the Law? Whichever alternative they choose, they are proved foolish. If they have not read it, they ought not to accept what they do not know. If they have read it, it itself proves that it must be abandoned. And if they do not understand it, they are foolish. The Law had been translated into Greek by the Septuagint interpreters, and therefore could be read by the Galatians. I ask whether you have read the Law because it is written there that Abraham had two sons; if you had attended to this, you would never have resorted to it, for there it is intimated that those who are under the Law are, through grace, in freedom.

For although that father had several sons, Scripture deals spiritually with two, indicating that something outstanding is prefigured in them. Thus one father had two sons, one by Hagar the slave-woman and one by Sarah the free woman. Although their father was one, the condition and birth of each were not alike. He who was begotten of the slave-woman was born according to the flesh—that is, according to the nature or customary course of the flesh—for a young woman, such as Hagar was, can normally conceive by an old man. But he who was born of the free woman was born not through sexual intercourse, but through God’s promise. For this reason he was born of Sarah: because God promised—indeed, promised beforehand—not because flesh could accomplish it. Sarah was barren and old; even if she had never been barren, she could no longer, as an old woman, conceive by her aged husband (Gen. XVIII). But God, by a miraculous operation, gave Abraham a son by her through the grace of his promise.

“These things are spoken allegorically,” that is, in another mode of speech, so that one thing is sounded outwardly and another understood inwardly. For these—that is, these two mothers—are, that is, signify, the two Testaments. He explains only the two, namely the slave-woman and the free woman, so that through them we may understand the rest. Abraham, therefore, is understood as God the Father; the two sons are the two peoples, namely Jews and Christians; the slave-woman is the fleshly teaching of the Old Testament, which bore children beneath the yoke of slavery while they were compelled by fear to serve God; and the free woman is the preaching or grace of the New Testament, which bears free children, who serve God through love.

For in each Testament God begot children to serve him; but in the Old Testament, Jewish slaves, who obeyed him slavishly through fear of punishment and promises of temporal things—and this is “according to the flesh,” which dreads punishments and loves pleasant things. In the grace of the New Testament, however, he begot free children, who serve out of love, not by the force of flesh but by God’s work. For who would believe things impossible according to nature, despise what is pleasant in the present life, and hope for what is unseen, unless God’s power worked this within him?

The two mothers, as has been said, are the two Testaments. One, indeed, proceeding from Mount Sinai—or given on Mount Sinai—that is, the Old Testament, begets children for God into slavery, so that they may be under the strictness of fear and serve God from fear. This thing—that is, this slavish Testament—is Hagar, that is, it is signified by Hagar. Here we must understand that Sarah the free woman signifies grace or evangelical preaching.

Then the reason is given why that Old Testament, which has been abolished, is signified by Hagar. For Sinai, where that Testament was given, is a mountain in Arabia, a province of foreign nations, not in the land of promise, which is the inheritance of sons. Thus we may understand that those who observe that Testament carnally do not belong at all to the inheritance of sons, but are strangers to the land of the living and aliens from the homeland of the saints. This mountain is joined to Jerusalem, because what was commanded carnally and slavishly on that mountain was observed in Jerusalem, where the Temple stood. That mountain is joined and associated not with the future Jerusalem, but with the Jerusalem which now is—not the heavenly, but the earthly—and it is not free but serves with its children, who follow its teaching and do everything from fear.

Or, because a mountain denotes the swelling of pride, and Sinai is interpreted “commandment,” the Jews possessed a slavish testament from Mount Sinai—that is, from the pride of commandment—because they deserved to receive such a law, which would restrain their stiff-neckedness, since they would glory beyond measure over the other nations because of the commandment of that Law. This Testament begets them into slavery to the Law or to sin, because it both compels them through the terror of threats to serve the Law carnally and makes all of them transgressors, since they cannot fulfil the Law itself. This slavery of the Testament is Hagar—that is, it is denoted by Hagar the slave-woman—whose name is interpreted “sojourner” or “alienation,” because she is a stranger with her children and alienates them from the heavenly inheritance.

Arabia, however, is interpreted “lowly,” signifying the weak, earth-crawling manner of life of those who serve the Law, just as Mount Sinai denotes the swelling of their pride, by which they are exalted because of the commandment of that same Law. For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia: that is, the commandment of the Law is a swelling of pride in the lowly—that is, earth-crawling—manner of life of the Jews, while, glorying that they possess God’s Law, they think themselves righteous and despise all people as sinners, though they themselves are never raised from the earth either in understanding or in action.

This mountain—that is, this proud swelling—is joined to and always clings to that Jerusalem which now is: that is, to that part of the Jews which, persisting in unbelief, seeks temporal things alone. Jerusalem, indeed, is called “vision of peace.” By this name that people is rightly denoted which now always desires to see temporal peace, so that it may serve the pleasures of its flesh without disturbance or fear. It is therefore called “now,” as though it were not to exist in another age, because now it enjoys present goods as much as it can and has its heart wholly fixed upon love of this age. But in the other life it will lack every good, and, failing eternally under punishments, will be reduced, as it were, to nothing. It is the Jerusalem which now is, as we have explained, and it still serves miserably beneath the yoke of the Law with its children, as Hagar with Ishmael, because it refused to receive the freedom brought by Christ. From all this it is plainly shown that after Christ’s coming the Law is no longer to be retained, but that the slavery which is under it must be fled by all people.

> “But that Jerusalem which is above is free, and she is our mother. For it is written: ‘Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail; for the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband’ [Isa. LIV]. But we, brethren, like Isaac, are children of promise.”  
> [Col. 1175A]

Thus, indeed, earthly Jerusalem serves with her children, because she is a slave-woman and, like Hagar, begets into slavery. But that Jerusalem which is above in mind with God is free, like Sarah, and is our mother, begetting us into freedom as Isaac was begotten. For above is the city of the saints, although here it bears citizens, among whom it lives as a pilgrim until the time of its kingdom arrives. The holy angels too, who dwell happily in heaven, are its citizens. That Jerusalem whose commonwealth is in heaven, whose heart is above, which seeks the things above, and which Sarah prefigured, is free: that is, out of the freedom of love it eagerly seeks with a good will to please God, rather than seeking to escape punishment from the slavery of fear.

[Col. 1175B] It is free through the Spirit of love which it received from Christ. “For where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (II Cor. VI). In its freedom, following Sarah’s example, it bore us, so that we may serve our Father who is in heaven not as slaves but as sons. It is truly our mother, although it had long been barren like Sarah. Hence it is written in Isaiah: “Rejoice, barren woman” (Isa. LIV), and so forth.

Isaiah, foretelling by the Holy Spirit the Church’s future fruitfulness, says: Rejoice, you heavenly Jerusalem—that is, the Church which would exist after Christ’s coming—now barren, indeed, as Sarah formerly was. You who in the time of the prophets do not bear children in faith, break forth into the voice of preaching, so that you who have long been silent may utter your voice with great force through the power of the Holy Spirit; and cry out, so that you may be heard by many—you who now, before the coming of the Bridegroom, do not give birth, that is, do not strive to give birth and do not suffer in order to give birth.

I exhort you to do these things because your children, you desolate and forsaken woman, will be more numerous than those of that synagogue which now has a husband, God or the word of the Law. Although more children are promised to the Church, the Synagogue is not altogether excluded from bearing children; rather, the multitude of Gentiles is preferred to it. For it too first bore a people from the Jews in the apostles and through the apostles.

Just as Abraham first joined Sarah to himself in marriage, but because of her barrenness knew the slave-woman so that he might beget offspring even by her, and finally begot a son from Sarah through the gift of God’s grace, so God from the beginning of the world joined the Church to himself in a few chosen persons. But because at that time it did not bear children through preaching, the Synagogue was meanwhile brought into his embrace as a slave-woman; it received the seed of preaching, by which it might bear a fleshly people in the slavery of the Law, until near the end of the age the Church, by divine grace, should be endowed with many children—indeed, should bear the Christian people as Isaac.

Therefore the Apostle adds by way of explanation: “But we, brethren, like Isaac, are children of promise.” As though he said: “The Jews indeed—according to the pattern which came first in Isaac—we are children of promise” [the source’s wording is syntactically irregular]. Or thus: God promised children to the Church, just as he had promised Isaac to Sarah; but we, brothers, are children of promise according to the pattern of Isaac. Here he shows the earlier promise concerning the calling of the Gentiles in Isaac—that is, in the son of promise.

[Col. 1176A] For just as Sarah bore Isaac because God had promised, so the Church bore the Gentile people in faith because God had foretold this through the prophets. Sarah’s barrenness, while prefiguring the Church, and her lack of hope of bearing offspring, signify that human nature, corrupted by sin and therefore justly condemned, deserved no true blessedness hereafter. But afterwards made fruitful by God’s free gift, the Church bore a multitude of free children, following the example of Sarah, who had borne Isaac by the grace of the divine promise.

Isaac, moreover, is interpreted “laughter” or “joy,” and signifies those who serve God in gladness, not from sorrow or compulsion, and rejoice if they have brought forth anything for righteousness or are deemed worthy to hear from their teachers: “You are our glory and joy.” Thus, from what the Apostle has said up to this point in the passage, it should be noted that Hagar signifies the Law and the Synagogue, whereas her son Ishmael signifies the Jewish people and individual Jews. When Hagar signifies the Law, Ishmael signifies the people; but when Hagar figures the Synagogue or community, Ishmael signifies individual Jews, or all of them.

For when the Apostle said that one Testament comes from Mount Sinai and begets into slavery like Hagar, he clearly showed that Hagar signifies the Law and Ishmael the people. In the following verse he likewise showed that Hagar signifies Jerusalem—that is, the Synagogue—and Ishmael its children, namely individual Jews. Similarly, Sarah denotes the new Law and the Church, while Isaac denotes the Christian people and individual Christians. When Sarah denotes the new Law, Isaac prefigures the new people; but when Sarah denotes the Church, Isaac denotes the Church’s children.

[Col. 1176C] For where the Apostle said that the two mothers denote the two Testaments and that Hagar figures the Old, he necessarily showed that Sarah represents the new Law and Isaac the Christian people. In what follows, moreover, when he says under Sarah’s likeness, “Rejoice, barren woman,” and so forth, he indicates that Sarah denotes the Church and Isaac each individual believer. For he who is born through promise fittingly denotes the children of grace, who are born from the Church not through fleshly generation but through spiritual rebirth.

> “But just as at that time he who had been born according to the flesh persecuted him who was according to the Spirit, so also now. But what does Scripture say? ‘Cast out the slave-woman and her son’ [Gen. XII; Rom. IX]. ‘For the son of the slave-woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman.’”  
> [Col. 1176D]

We, as has been said, are children of promise—that is, begotten through grace—according to the pattern which came first in Isaac. But just as at that time Ishmael, who had been born according to the flesh, persecuted him who had been born according to the Spirit—that is, Isaac, who was begotten from a barren old woman through the spiritual operation of divine grace—so we see this occurring now, when any Jew, born according to the flesh from the slave-woman Synagogue, persecutes a Christian born through spiritual grace from the free woman Church, either by inflicting bodily punishments or, what better pertains to the present matter, by recommending fleshly observances.

For those who understand the Law according to the flesh oppose those who think according to the Spirit, and persecute or attempt to seduce them. No persecution of Ishmael against Isaac, however, is reported except a certain childish play. For Ishmael was playing with the boy Isaac (Gen. XXI), and the Apostle now calls that play persecution. That play displeased Sarah because she understood that it contained something of seduction. For that playing was mockery; and if it was mockery, it was seduction and deception.

Every children’s game is an image of some more serious affair. When an older person plays with one younger, he plays in order somehow to deceive him, knowing that he has other business in view; while playing with the child—that is, the weak person—he pretends certain things. Ishmael was older and strengthened in malice. But, while playing with the boy Isaac, he deceived him and practised certain fraudulent games upon the weak one. The mother perceived that the play was persecution.

[Col. 1177B] Thus the Church also now, through the Apostle, understood that the sport by which false preachers mocked the Galatians and seduced them by malicious fraud was spiritual persecution. For those who seduce by mockery persecute more severely. The Jewish people, signified in Ishmael, was therefore persecuting in Galatia through false apostles the Christian people signified in Isaac, wishing to become, as it were, superior and more worthy, like the firstborn, in order to possess the inheritance with him.

But it shall not be so. For what does Scripture say of him? “Cast out from your house the slave-woman,” the Synagogue, “and her son,” the Jewish people, lest he become a sharer in the inheritance of Christians. And it is necessary that this happen. “For the son of the slave-woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman”: that is, the Jewish people, born from the slave-woman Synagogue, shall not possess the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven together with the Christian people born from the free woman Church.

We see this fulfilled in this way, seeing the slave-woman Synagogue, or the fleshly Law, cast out with her son and driven back from the heavenly inheritance. For just as Hagar the slave-woman remained in Abraham’s house with her son Ishmael before Isaac’s birth, but was expelled after his birth, so the Law according to fleshly observance, or the Synagogue with the Jewish people, remained with God before the Christian people began to be born from baptism; but afterwards it was cast out from the Church and separated from the embrace, household fellowship, and inheritance of the highest Father.

> “Therefore, brethren, we are not children of the slave-woman, but of the free woman, by the freedom with which Christ set us free.”  
> [Col. 1177D]

Since we are children of promise according to Isaac, and the Jews, children of the slave-woman, persecute us by urging fleshly observance of the Law, it is therefore clear, brothers, that we are not children of the slave-woman, to be subjected slavishly to the Law. Rather, we are children of the free woman—the Church or grace—that we may live by the freedom of love.

For if we were children of the slave-woman, her children the Jews would preserve peace toward us. But because they see that we have been born from another mother, namely the free woman, they envy our freedom and attempt to take it away. Lest anyone should think that we are free by nature in the same way as Isaac—that is, as if no slavery had preceded—the text adds that Christ set us free by this freedom: namely, from the yoke of the devil, beneath which we were previously held as slaves. Thus we came to the freedom of innocence, holiness, and righteousness, by which we are called sons, not through our own free choice but through Christ, the liberator from slavery to sin.

But some matters in this passage may be examined more subtly. For it is written that Abraham had two sons, and so forth. Abraham, the old man, as was said above, signifies God the Father, whom Daniel calls the Ancient of Days (Dan. VII). He had two sons, that is, two peoples: one loving earthly things, the other seeking heavenly things; and therefore one was born of a slave-woman and the other of a free woman.

[Col. 1178B] For even now, whoever in the Church seek earthly prosperity from God in return for their good deeds are still children of the slave-woman—that is, of the old slavery. All who love God carnally, that is, for temporal recompense, are in Ishmael; the Old Testament belongs to them, and they are still in slavery. Those who undertake or keep God’s Law for earthly goods are heirs of the Old Testament. Similarly, whoever have served or serve God, whether in the Old or the New Testament, for the sole reward of heaven are signified by Isaac and are heirs of the New Testament.

For the ancient righteous, though they fittingly kept the Old Testament, divinely given to the old people in accordance with the distribution of times, nevertheless became children of promise through God’s grace and were counted heirs of the New Testament in God’s hidden counsel. Indeed, in those times there were spiritual people whom the letter commanding did not kill, but the assisting Spirit made alive. And now also there are very many fleshly people who either produce heresies by not understanding the Scriptures, or, even within the Catholic faith, are still little ones nourished on milk, or persist like chaff [variant: *perseverans*, “persisting”] prepared for future fires.

Thus those who love temporal things and love this age belong to the Old Testament as children of the slave-woman, whatever time they may live or have lived in; and those who love eternal life belong to the New Testament as children of the free woman. Therefore all who come through faith to the knowledge of God may be called children of Abraham. But among them are some who serve God for temporal goods and others who cleave to God out of love. These are the two sons, one from the slave-woman and the other from the free woman.

But he who is from the slave-woman was born according to the flesh—that is, according to fleshly desire or covetousness—and entered upon this manner of life so that he might live honorably for temporal rewards. He who was born from the free woman entered upon spiritual life and the intention of heavenly recompense through the promise by which God promised Abraham children like stars, that is, splendid and heavenly children.

> “For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, joined to that Jerusalem which now is, and it serves with its children.”

As said above, Sinai means “commandment,” Arabia “lowly,” and Jerusalem “vision of peace.” Arabia signifies the lowly condition—that is, one clinging to earth and not raising oneself to heavenly things—in the temptation of those who seek only earthly things for the good they do. Jerusalem signifies the peace and prosperity which they delight to see in the present, so that they may enjoy the goods of this age without disturbance or fear.

[Col. 1179A] Sinai, then, is a mountain in Arabia: that is, God’s commandment is a swelling of pride in a mind cast down by an earthward intention. For whoever seeks low things from deeds which he seems to do well swells with pride because of his observance of the divine commandment and glories before people as though righteous. This swelling of arrogance is joined to that Jerusalem, namely the prosperity which now is, and it serves sins, pleasures, or desires with its children, because pride usually accompanies prosperity and riches, especially among those who love present things alone.

“But that Jerusalem which is above is free,” and so forth. This Jerusalem—that is, this vision of peace, this worldly prosperity, this city of fleshly people which now exists and for a moment flourishes—serves: that is, it performs the slavish works of sin forbidden by the Law and yields to the slavish desires of the world. But that Jerusalem—that is, that vision of peace, that prosperity, that city of the saints—which is above, is free from every slavery to sin and every desire of the world, because it neither sins nor desires worldly things. It is our mother if we too, following its example, refuse to serve sin and reject the desires of the world.

It was signified by aged Sarah because it too began from the origin of the world. It is called barren either because it does not bear according to the flesh or because for a long time it did not bear children on earth. Yet it is commanded to rejoice over the multitude of its future children: for if there is joy before God’s angels over one sinner doing penance (Luke XV), how much more over many converted to righteousness? It does not travail because it does not suffer pains, but bears spiritually without suffering, crying aloud in joy. It was also deserted by people who had abandoned a life of heavenly righteousness and pursued earthly gain. But at last it was made fruitful with an innumerable multitude of children.

But just as he who had been born according to the flesh then persecuted him who had been born according to the Spirit, so now those born according to the flesh persecute those born according to the Spirit. Those born according to the flesh are lovers of the world and lovers of this age. Those born according to the Spirit are lovers of the kingdom of heaven, lovers of Christ, desiring eternal life, and worshipping God freely. Thus spiritual people suffer persecution from fleshly people, because the play of fleshly people is persecution and affliction for spiritual people.

[Col. 1179D] Ishmael plays and, in playing, seeks to deceive his brother whenever fleshly people commend unlawful things with sweet words, speak vanities, provoke to pleasures, occasion laughter, arouse lust, and corrupt good morals by evil conversations (I Cor. XV). By such games they persecute spiritual people more severely than if they attacked them with swords. In every way, therefore, the flesh opposes the spirit. Whether the people of fleshly persons oppose the people of spiritual persons, or whether in each of us the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, these oppose one another; and the law in our members resists the law of our mind and takes us captive under the law of sin.

If, therefore, the flesh—whose role is borne by Ishmael, who was born according to the flesh—flatters the spirit, which is Isaac, and acts with alluring deceptions; if it entices by pleasures and softens by delights: such games of the flesh offend the spirit, especially Sarah, who is virtue; and Paul judges such flatteries to be a most bitter persecution. You therefore, whoever hear these things, should not suppose that the persecution now described is only when, through the fury of pagans, you are forced to sacrifice to idols. If perhaps fleshly pleasure entices you, if the allure of lust plays upon you, flee these as the greatest persecution if you are a child of virtue. Therefore it is said: “Flee fornication” (I Cor. VI).

If injustice also flatters you, so that you show partiality to a powerful person and, bent by his favor, render judgment unjustly, you must understand that under the appearance of play you suffer a flattering persecution from injustice. Indeed, through every form of wickedness, even if soft, delicate, and game-like, call them forms of persecution, because virtue is offended in all of them. Thus the son of the slave-woman persecutes the son of the free woman by playing.

But what does Scripture say? Hear the voice of the free woman herself: “Cast out the slave-woman and her son, for the son of the slave-woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman.” Cast out the slavery of the Law, by which God is served for temporal recompense, and the fleshly people, even though bearing the name of Christianity; for the son of the old slavery will not be an heir of the kingdom of heaven with the son of the new freedom.

[Col. 1180C] Whoever still retains the habits of the old person is a child of the slave-woman—that is, of old slavery—although called a Christian. He will therefore at the end be cast out from the Church of the righteous, so that he may not be an heir with those who walk in newness of life. Again, cast out heresy and the people it has begotten; for the son of heresy will not be an heir with the son of Catholic truth. For the slave-woman also signifies heresy.

Therefore, brothers, we are not children of the slave-woman, to serve sin, the desires of this age, or errors; but children of the free woman, so that, stripped of worldly desire, we may fulfil our own will or God’s will in the freedom of love. Christ set us free by this freedom through his grace, so that now, by the free choice of our good will, we may be able to render grateful service to God.

## Chapter V

> “Stand firm, and do not be held again under a yoke of slavery. Behold, I, Paul, say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing [Acts XV]. And I testify again to every person who has himself circumcised that he is bound to perform the whole Law.”

Now, as I said, you are free through Christ; therefore stand in the freedom you have received—that is, do not depart from it, but remain in it always until death—and do not again be held under a yoke of slavery. For previously the yoke of slavery to idols held you; and now you wish again to submit your necks under the yoke of slavery to legal observances.

From this admonition and many other statements in this Epistle, it is evident that they had not yet subjected themselves by performing the slavery of the Law, but wished to subject themselves. Do not again be held under the yoke of slavery—not even under the yoke of circumcision alone. For behold—that is, let it be known to you—that I, Paul, whose authority is recognized, who received this Gospel not from a human being but from Christ, who also speaks in me, tell you truly that if you are circumcised as you wish to be, so as to have any hope of salvation in circumcision, you will incur so great a loss that Christ will profit you nothing.

[Col. 1181B] Circumcision now not only does no good, but also does harm. A person could be circumcised with such an intention that the removal of that piece of skin would neither harm nor benefit him any more than trimming his nails or hair. But these people had been persuaded that they could not be saved without works of the Law; therefore they wished to be circumcised and to keep the Law’s severity, as though they could be justified and saved through these things.

Since, therefore, they supposed that their hope and salvation lay in such works of the Law, and especially in circumcision, they are warned as against certain destruction. For if, after the Savior’s coming, Gentiles were to observe those prophetic sacraments of the Law, either Christ would appear still to be promised as yet to come through them, or to have never been promised in them. Whoever therefore still observes that shadow denies that the truth, which is Christ, has come; and for that reason Christ will profit him nothing.

For, as has been said, they wished to be circumcised because they thought that they could not otherwise be saved in Christ. If they were circumcised with this disposition, Christ would profit them nothing at all. “For if righteousness is through the Law, then Christ died for nothing” (above, II).

Nor, he says, do I say only that, if you are circumcised, you will receive no benefit from Christ. I also testify again to every person, whether Jew or Gentile, who has himself circumcised in order to obtain righteousness, that he is bound to perform—that is, to fulfil in deeds—the entire Law, just as one who has received baptism is bound to fulfil the precepts of the Gospel. It is as though he said: You will not only suffer this loss through circumcision, that faith in Christ and baptism will profit you nothing; you will also necessarily have to undergo the labor of such great slavery that you continually perform all the Law’s commands. Circumcision must therefore all the more be abandoned.

> “You have been emptied of Christ. You who are justified in the Law have fallen from grace. For we, by the Spirit, through faith await the hope of righteousness. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love.”

If you are circumcised, you will have to observe the whole Law even if you do not wish it. And as soon as you begin to observe those harsh precepts of the letter, you are emptied of Christ, with whom you were filled, so that he no longer remains in you. For through faith you were vessels filled with Christ, and while Christ remained in you, you were filled with innocence, forgiveness of sins, the grace of the Holy Spirit, justification in good works, and hope of future glory. But if you submit yourselves to the Law’s slavery, then, with Christ departing, you are emptied of all that rich treasure.

[Col. 1182A] And you who “are justified in the Law”—that is, think that you are justified—have fallen, indeed fallen utterly, from the grace of the Gospel in which you formerly stood while striving to live spiritually in Christ. Grace came for this purpose: that, once the burden of the Law had ceased, grace alone might justify. Therefore whoever restores the Law’s slavery loses the freedom of grace.

The Apostle speaks as though they had already done or undergone all these things, so as to deter them more strongly from doing them when they see how great the losses that follow from them are. We may also understand that some of them had already fallen away into works of the Law, and that the Apostle now directs these words especially to them when he says: “You have been emptied of Christ; you who are justified in the Law have fallen from grace.”

You, he says, are justified—that is, you believe that you are justified—in the Law; but you are mistaken, because only we shall be justified who seek justification from faith. For we, by the Spirit—that is, through the Holy Spirit, who does not deceive, whom we have from faith—confidently await the hope of righteousness: that is, righteousness itself which is hoped for. Although we have been justified through faith, we nevertheless hope to make progress day by day in that same righteousness; and our mind, hungering and thirsting for righteousness, will not be fully satisfied except in the age to come. We await this hope through the Spirit of grace, not from works of the Law, for no one will be justified by these.

Or: you who are carnally justified in the Law have fallen from the grace of future blessedness into the desire for earthly prosperity, because we alone shall obtain the grace of that recompense for righteousness which we believe comes through faith. For we, through the Spirit received from faith, await with patience the hope of righteousness—that is, the hope which righteousness hopes for, namely the grace of eternal blessedness. Faith came first, and from it we received the Holy Spirit by God’s gift; he makes us await the grace of heavenly recompense for our labor.

[Col. 1182C] I rightly call it grace, because no one can justly earn eternal rest by temporal labor. I said “through faith” because faith itself is what avails before God. But the circumcision you wish to undertake profits nothing there. For in Christ Jesus—that is, in Christ’s members, in Christ’s religion—neither circumcision nor uncircumcision avails anything, but whole faith.

Lest the Galatians say that they wanted to undertake the circumcision performed by Abraham, who did not possess the Law, because—even if they were not justified by it—they would nevertheless have greater dignity in the Christian religion through it, the Apostle says that in Christ Jesus—that is, in Christ’s body, which is the Church—circumcision has no value: it confers no benefit or dignity. And lest they begin in turn to glory in uncircumcision, thinking it has some value elsewhere because he calls circumcision useless, he adds that uncircumcision also avails nothing there. For whether anyone is circumcised or uncircumcised, he is neither more worthy nor more contemptible for this reason in the Christian religion.

Rather, faith alone is of great worth there: faith which works through love, that is, not dead but living faith. For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead. Nor is this the faith of the Old Testament, serving from fear, but evangelical faith, performing good works from love and not awaiting temporal recompense but longing eternally to behold the Creator’s face. This is the faith of the elect which leads to salvation. Even demons believe and tremble, yet they do not love or act rightly. Therefore faith without love and good works is the faith of demons, not of Christians. The only faith which avails in Christ Jesus is that which both burns with love and labors diligently in good works.

> [Col. 1183B] “You were running well. Who bewitched you so that you do not obey the truth? Consent to no one. This persuasion is not from him who calls you. A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (I Cor. V).

The faith described above is the way to the vision of divine contemplation. In this faith you were running well, by working and by desiring, toward the prize of eternal reward. For there are some who run badly. But you were running well while, through works of faith joined with charity, you hastened toward the heavenly homeland. But now who has bewitched you—that is, who has harmed you with an envious glance—so that you do not obey, that is, so that you would not obey, the truth which freely presents itself to you? Who is he—that is, what learning and what authority does he possess—who by the enchantment of his speech has prevented you from obeying the truth which I handed down to you, namely, that you might [Col. 1183C] run toward life without works of the Law, by observance of the Gospel? For he must have seemed to possess extraordinary wisdom and authority, since you judged that he should be believed rather than I. But do not assent to anyone urging such things upon you; indeed, resist him manfully, because this persuasion is not from him who calls you to the heavenly homeland, but rather from the devil, who calls you back from it. Do not assent to any of those who urge upon you the works of the Law, because “a little leaven corrupts the whole lump”: that is, a few who err often corrupt the whole multitude of the Church by the sourness of their zeal for perverse teaching. Or, “a little leaven corrupts the whole lump”: that is, a slight persuasion toward error, if it is assented to and received into [Col. 1183D] the heart, renders the entire multitude of all virtues bitter and useless. For wherever even a little faithlessness has been admitted, there immediately every good thing perishes. This may also be understood of circumcision alone, because they greatly doubted concerning it, seeing that it had once been part of our faith. “Although circumcision,” he says, “is a little thing,” that is, a small part of the Law, “nevertheless it must by no means be performed by you who have been renewed, because a little leaven,” that is, a small portion of the old teaching, as is found in circumcision, “corrupts the whole lump”: it turns the whole new and sweet people into the bitterness and swelling of the old Jewish people.

> “I am confident in you in the Lord, that you will think nothing [Col. 1184A] else. But whoever he may be, the one who disturbs you will bear the judgment.”

A little perverse teaching corrupts the entire purity of Catholic truth. But I am confident—that is, I have confidence and certainty concerning you, whom I foresee will be corrected while the Lord works your salvation—that you will hold no view except that contained in the sincerity of the Catholic faith. Thus you indeed will come safely through by the Lord’s mercy. But he who disturbs you will bear the judgment of his own condemnation: that is, he who makes the pure spring of your understanding and the clarity of your faith muddy by pouring in the filth of his heresy, or who throws into confusion the straight course of your steps, by which you came from slavery to freedom. For the false apostles wish to reverse this order [Col. 1184B], seeking to bring you back from freedom into slavery—which is a perverse order. But whoever attempts this will bear judgment, that is, will endure the weight of his condemnation, whoever he may be: even if he is a son of Abraham, eloquent, or powerful. By the same Spirit through which the Apostle foresaw the correction of the Galatians, he also foresaw the stubbornness and condemnation of the false apostles who had deceived them. And he adds:

> “But I, brothers, if I still preach circumcision, why am I still suffering persecution? Then the scandal of the cross has been emptied of force.”

It should be understood that, when the false teachers wished to persuade the Galatians into slavery under the Law and saw [Col. 1184C] them recalled by the authority of the Apostle Paul, they said that Paul himself also held this view, but had not wished to disclose his opinion to them. He therefore added most appropriately: “But I, brothers,” and so forth. For he was suffering persecution from those very people who were attempting to persuade them of such things, although they seemed already to have accepted the Gospel. He also alludes to them elsewhere when he says: “In dangers among false brothers” (I Cor. XI). For because, in order to avoid offending the Jews whom he sought to bring to faith, he had circumcised Timothy (Acts XVI), they said that he preached circumcision among others. This he now rejects.

“They disturb you,” he says, “by urging circumcision and slavery to the Law upon you, and by saying [Col. 1184D] that I too still preach circumcision to others. But I, brothers, if after faith I still preach circumcision as I once did, as they say I do, why—that is, for what reason—do I still suffer persecution from them and from the Jews?” From this it is clear that I do not preach circumcision, because I suffer persecution from the Jews; for there is no other reason why they persecute me except that I do not acquiesce in circumcision. For if I preached it, they would never persecute me. And if, as they maintain, I do preach it, then the scandal of the cross has been emptied of force: that is, the Jews would not be angered concerning Christ’s cross if I maintained that human beings are justified by circumcision. If I preach it as necessary for justification or salvation, the scandal of the Lord’s [Col. 1185A] cross—by which the Jews are scandalized and enraged against me while I maintain that believers are justified by the cross and passion of Christ alone—has been emptied, that is, rendered void of usefulness. But both cannot occur: I cannot preach that righteousness or salvation comes both from circumcision and from the cross. For if I preach salvation from circumcision, my evangelical preaching, in which I proclaim the restoration of human salvation through the Lord’s cross, is destroyed; and it is precisely because salvation is preached from the cross that the Jews are indignant. Therefore there is no reason for me to suffer persecution if I preach circumcision, because by preaching it I destroy the preaching of the cross, which is the cause of my persecution. Thus the scandal of the cross, which troubles the Jews, has been emptied—that is, made superfluous and useless. In other words, Christ [Col. 1185B] died in vain if those who seek justification and salvation must still observe circumcision and the Law carnally.

> “Would that those who disturb you would even cut themselves off! For you, brothers, have been called to freedom; only do not make freedom an occasion for the flesh, but through the charity of the Spirit serve one another. For the whole Law is fulfilled in one saying: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself’ (Matt. XXII; Lev. XIX). But if you bite and devour one another, see that you are not consumed by one another.”

The scandal of the cross is emptied if I preach circumcision, as the false apostles say that I do. But would that they too, who wish to empty Christ’s cross of its saving power for us, might be emptied by their own [Col. 1185C] error. Would that they too might be cut off—that is, castrated; for there are eunuchs who have cut themselves off for the kingdom of heaven (Matt. XIX). Would that they might be cut off not carnally but spiritually: that they might lose the power of begetting, so that they may be unable to corrupt anyone; that they may cease to sow carnal things in you and in others; and that they may have no power at all to beget, these men who now trouble you by spreading the carnal seed of legal observances and begetting children of error. The Apostle wishes them good: namely, that that from which they burn spiritually for the corruption of other people’s minds may be cut away from them by a spiritual blade.

But if this is understood as having been said in cursing, it should be known that when holy men pronounce a sentence of cursing, they do not break forth into it from a desire for vengeance but from the judgment of justice. For inwardly they behold God’s subtle judgment, and recognize outwardly with what curse they ought to strike those who rise up;” and they do not sin by that curse by which they do not disagree with the inward judgment. Thus Peter pronounced a sentence of cursing against Simon, who offered him money, saying: “May your money be with you unto perdition” (Acts VIII). For he did not say “is,” but “may it be,” and thus indicated that he spoke these words not in the indicative but the optative mood. Thus Elijah said to two companies of fifty coming to him: “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you” (IV Kings I). The outcome of the case [Col. 1186A] showed how firmly both their sentences rested upon truth. For Simon perished in eternal destruction, and a flame coming down from above consumed the two companies of fifty. The power which follows, therefore, bears witness to the spirit in which a sentence of cursing is uttered. When the innocence of the one cursing remains intact, and yet the curse swallows up the cursed person even to destruction, the outcome on both sides shows that the sentence is launched against the guilty person by the Judge who is most lowly and inward.

Thus Paul too could curse in the same way the false apostles whom he foresaw would persist in error, saying, “Would that those who disturb you would be cut off!” For if every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and cast into the fire (Matt. III), how much more one which bears bad fruit? It is therefore better that the few who are going to perish [Col. 1186B] should perish, rather than that they should keep others, who can be saved, in error for a long time; better that they should perish than, living a long time, drag many with them into perdition. Accordingly, for the salvation of many, he could wish that these few—whom he foresaw by a prophetic spirit would perish—might be cut off from this life sooner, so that they might not add sins to sins any longer and acquire for themselves a more grievous destruction. For this curse arose not from the malice of one who sins, but from the rectitude of a judge. The one who uttered so upright a curse did not succumb to the fault of disturbance, but agreed with God’s judgment.

Or this cutting-off may be understood as the Lord commanded in the Gospel that members which cause us to stumble be cut off and cast away from us (Matt. V): because these men generate a stumbling-block among [Col. 1186C] them, they should be wholly separated and alienated from them. “It is advantageous,” he says, “that those who disturb you and throw into confusion the straight order of your journey—calling you back from freedom into slavery—be cut off from you, because you, brothers, who have begun to have one Father, God, and one mother, the Church, were divinely called from the slavery of sin into the freedom of faith.” You were called into freedom so that you might do good not from fear but from love. For whoever burns with true charity is so free that he is pleased to do whatever he wishes, because he wishes only what is good. Thus charity and the affection of good will are themselves the freedom to which you were called.

You are free, then; only do not misuse freedom by doing whatever [Col. 1186D] the flesh may please. For then you would lose freedom if you considered yourselves free to satisfy the flesh, because “whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John VIII). Since, therefore, you are in the freedom of grace and not in slavery to the Law, in the freedom of good will and not in slavery to sin, you must observe only this: do not give your spiritual freedom as an occasion for the flesh—do not, because you are free and the fear of the Law does not press upon you, follow fleshly desires as though you had unrestricted power to do whatever the flesh wishes. Do not allow the flesh to derive from freedom an occasion for a life of pleasure; rather, through the charity of the Spirit, which is the strength of the mind, serve one another. Since he had called them free, they might think that they ought [Col. 1187A] now to serve no one, but that each, on the basis of his own freedom, might presume against another. He removes this notion also. It is as though he said: “You ought not to pervert your freedom, but rather serve one another through the charity of the Spirit”—that is, one another, not with slavish fear but with the freedom of charity. This cannot happen unless each person regards another’s weakness as his own, so that he bears it patiently until the one whose salvation he seeks is freed from it. And you ought willingly to embrace this free service, because the whole Law which you wish to fulfill is fulfilled in one saying—that is, in the one command which says: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Lev. XIX). In love of neighbor you can fulfill all the commandments of the Law which concern good conduct. For rightly [Col. 1187B] the person who loves his neighbor as himself is said to fulfill the Law, because whatever he does not wish another to do to him, he strives to avoid doing to another; and whatever he rightly wishes another to do to him, he himself does to another as far as he can. Thus whatever the Law forbids is avoided, and whatever it commands morally is fulfilled.

For the one who loves his neighbor as himself must also love God, because the one who does not love God does not love himself but hates himself. For the one who does not love God loves iniquity; and “the one who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. X). Therefore, in the perfect love of neighbor all that is commanded in the Law is fulfilled. If, then, you serve one another through charity, you will fulfill the whole [Col. 1187C] Law through brotherly love. But if you bite one another hatefully, you violate all the Law’s commands. If you bite one another—that is, slander one another in some respect—and devour one another—that is, consume everything within you—see that you are not consumed by one another, that is, reduced to nothing.

By occasion of charity he rebukes this fault in them. If you bite one another with a dog’s tooth, secretly slandering one another and mutually tearing apart your manner of life, and openly contending in words, you devour one another: that is, in raging litigation you consume your whole mutual life, accusing one another and, by picking apart one another’s every good work, blaspheming them or inflicting injuries. Take care that, while you live like dogs, you are not consumed by alternating bites like dogs: that is, that all the goods of virtue [Col. 1187D] which were in you are not devoured by one another. For the person who detracts from another’s virtues diminishes or loses his own virtues. The one who tears apart another’s good things corrodes and annuls his own good things. And the one who injures another acquires a just condemnation for himself. Those, therefore, who bite and devour one another by slanders, injuries, or accusations mutually consume and lose their own good things. They are consumed by one another because the person receiving an injury consumes the one inflicting it—that is, he is the cause of that person’s consumption; and the other likewise, when he himself suffers injury, accusation, or slander from the former, consumes him—that is, becomes the cause of the consumption of his virtues and good things.

> “But I say: Walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires [Col. 1188A] of the flesh. For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. For these are opposed to one another, so that you do not do whatever you wish. But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the Law.”

“Above,” he says, “I said that you should not give freedom as an occasion for the flesh, but through charity serve one another; but now I say how you should do these things. Namely, walk in the Spirit—that is, advance from virtue to virtue (Ps. LXXXIII) in good works under the guidance of the Holy Spirit. This is to serve one another through charity, and then you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh—that is, you will not complete, by deed or assent, the pleasures which the flesh desires. This is what it means not to give your freedom as an occasion for the flesh.”

You must always walk—that is, [Col. 1188B] make progress—by the Spirit, so that in mind and deed you always strive toward inward things while you are on the way of this present life; and conversely, you must take care not to fulfill the desires of the flesh which wage war against the soul. I do not say that you must not have them, since in this age you cannot be without them; but that you must not fulfill them—that is, by the assent of pleasure carry out their works. For evil desires are not fulfilled when the assent of our will does not join them; yet they occur in the very fact that they are within us, because it cannot be that we do not desire. And you must resist altogether, lest you fulfill the desires of the flesh—that is, fleshly lusts—because the flesh desires against your spirit, or against the Spirit of God which is in you. For in evil people [Col. 1188C] it has no spirit against which to desire. There the flesh desires against the spirit where the spirit is present. But in the wicked the Spirit of God is not present. Nor does the flesh desire against their spirit, because it finds no spirit rebellious against its fleshly desires, but one that desires together with it.

But in the good, where both the Spirit of God is present and the human spirit resists the desires of the flesh, the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. This is a grievous and inward war. It would never have existed in you if human nature had remained, by free choice, in the uprightness in which it was made. But now, having unhappily refused to have blessed peace with God, it fights unhappily against itself. And although this evil is miserable, [Col. 1188D] it is nevertheless better than to serve vices without any conflict. For war with hope of eternal salvation is better than captivity without any thought of liberation.

Therefore the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. The flesh desires nothing except through the soul. But the flesh is said to desire against the spirit when the soul, through fleshly desire, resists the spirit. The cause of fleshly desire, however, is not in the soul alone but in both soul and flesh. For it arises from both: from the soul, because without it no pleasure is felt; and from the flesh, because without it fleshly pleasure is not felt. The flesh therefore desiring against the spirit is the fleshly pleasure which the spirit experiences from and with the flesh, opposed to the pleasure which it experiences [Col. 1189A] alone. For it alone experiences, unless I am mistaken, that pleasure not mixed with bodily pleasure or with desire for fleshly things, concerning which it is said: “Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the petitions of your heart” (Ps. XXXVI).

The desires of the flesh, therefore, are contrary to the desires of the spirit, and the desires of the spirit to the desires of the flesh. These two, namely flesh and spirit, oppose one another so much that you do not do whatever you wish, whether good or bad—that is, you are not allowed to do those things. For what do you wish except that there be absolutely no desires for evil and unlawful pleasures? What saint does not wish this? But he does not accomplish it. They do not allow you to fulfill what you wish. Do not allow them to fulfill what they wish, and then neither you nor they will do [Col. 1189B] what you wish. For while this conflict is in us, we do not do what we will.

For what do we will to do, when we will to be perfected in the end of the highest good, except that the flesh should not desire against the spirit and that we should not have this vice against which the spirit desires? Although we will this in the present life, because we cannot accomplish it, we at least do this through God’s help: we do not yield, overcome, to the flesh desiring against the spirit, [Col. 1189D] nor are we drawn by our consent to commit sin. Thus the desires of the flesh are not fulfilled, though they occur; nor are our good works fulfilled, though they occur. For just as the desire of the flesh is then fulfilled when the spirit consents to evil deeds, so that it does not [Col. 1189C] desire against it but together with it, so too our good works will then be fulfilled when the flesh consents to the spirit, so that it too no longer desires against it. This is what we will when we desire perfection of righteousness. But this will of ours is not fulfilled as long as the movements of fleshly desires to which we do not consent remain.

And in this disagreement of flesh and spirit we should not suppose that either is the other’s enemy, but rather that the enemy is the vice by which the flesh desires against the spirit. Once this vice has been healed, it too will no longer exist; both substances will remain safe, and there will be no conflict between them. After the Apostle said that flesh and spirit oppose one another, so that we cannot do what we wish, lest he make us idle through the conflict itself and seem, by this statement, to have given license for sinning, he added: “But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the Law.” It is as if he said: “When the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, the Law rightly rules those who are led by fleshly desires, in order to restrain them by fear. But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the Law.” For the person is under the Law who abstains from the act of sin not through love of righteousness but through fear of the punishment threatened by the Law: guilty in the will by which he would prefer that the thing he fears did not exist, so that he might freely do what he secretly desires. Such a person, therefore, does not yet have the Holy Spirit by whom he may be led. For whoever is led by the Spirit of God in his works is not under the Law, which instills fear, but in charity, which is poured into the hearts of the elect not through the letter of the Law but through that same Spirit. [Col. 1190A] But those are condemnably under the Law whom the Law makes guilty because they do not fulfill the Law, while, ignorant of grace’s benefit for performing God’s commands, they presume as though upon their own powers, because they do not have the Holy Spirit as ruler to lead and help them.

From this point the Apostle begins to show that one ought to walk by the Spirit, as he had advised, and not fulfill the desires of the flesh, by setting forth here the dishonorable and useless works of the flesh and there the honorable and useful works of the Spirit. For he adds:

> “Now the works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, impurity, lust, service of idols, sorceries, enmities, strife, jealousies, anger, quarrels, dissensions, sects, envies, murders, drunkenness, revelries, [Col. 1190B] and things like these; concerning which I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.”

“You ought to walk by the Spirit,” he says, “because, as has been said, if you are led by the Holy Spirit, you already have this advantage from it: you are not under the burden or slavery of the Law, but in the freedom of charity. Conversely, you must take care not to fulfill the desires of the flesh, because from their fulfillment proceed works which appear evil to everyone. For the works of the flesh are not doubtful but manifest: that is, they appear wicked and detestable to learned and unlearned alike, and therefore must be avoided. They are as follows.

Fornication is commonly committed with prostitutes, who were prostituted [Col. 1190C] beneath arched structures, and those places were called *fornices*, from which fornication received its name. Fornication is placed first among the works of the flesh because no sin reduces the soul to carnality so much as fornication; for the wretched soul can think of nothing except what belongs to the flesh as long as it is occupied with the most shameful act of fornication. Uncleanness is what males commit with one another, or what someone performs alone. Impurity is what relatives commit with one another, otherwise called incest, as we noted above. Lust is committed with women who are neither public prostitutes nor lawful wives. The service of idols also is numbered among works of the flesh because it is sometimes committed for love of women, as by Solomon on account of [Col. 1190D] foreign wives (III Kings XI), or by the children of Israel at Shittim on account of the daughters of Midian (Num. XXXI). Sorceries—that is, herbal potions and the preparation of poisons—are also often practiced because of fornication and lustful love. In all these things it appears how great and chief a vice fornication is, from which so many deadly plagues proceed.

Enmities occur when persons hate one another and mutually devise or do whatever evil they can. They commonly arise from disputes, when people first contend in words and then come to enmities. For contention is understood as litigation. Contention exists where a position is defended not by reason but by obstinacy of mind, and where truth is not sought but contentiousness is exhausted. Or contention concerns precedence, when one [Col. 1191A] person wishes to be preferred over another. Jealousy follows it aptly; jealousy is said to be a pain of mind when another attains the honor desired by two or more, and the rest are tormented by envy because they could not attain it. Anger is a sudden storm of mind, often accustomed to commit many evils, because it attends neither to reason nor to justice but irrationally rushes to do what the stirred-up mind urges. A quarrel occurs where two persons strike one another or fight among themselves. Dissension occurs where not everyone agrees in one will or one understanding, but they will different things and form parties. Hence a sect—that is, heresy—is also often produced. Envy is that which is tormented by another’s prosperity and is divided into a twofold passion: either one does not wish another to be what he himself is, or, seeing another to be better, he grieves that he is not like him. Murder is the killing of a human being; and murders are rightly joined to envies, because envy often generates murder, as the devil killed the first human being through the malignity of envy, and Cain killed his brother Abel (Gen. IV), and the chief priests killed Christ. Drunkenness is excessive drinking of wine which changes the state of mind. It makes the soul weak along with the body. In the sickness of drunkenness both body and soul are corrupted; spirit is corrupted together with flesh. All the limbs become weak: the feet, hands, and loosened tongue. Darkness covers the eyes, forgetfulness veils the mind, so that a person neither knows nor feels that he is human. Revelries are shameful and luxurious [Col. 1191C] banquets.

The Apostle calls all these things works of the flesh. For fornications, uncleannesses, impurities, lusts, drunkenness, and revelries belong to pleasure of the flesh. But service of idols, sorceries, enmities, and the rest which follow belong rather to the life of the mind than of the flesh, since it can happen that someone abstains from fleshly pleasures because of idolatry or heresy. Yet even then, although such a person seems to restrain the lusts of the flesh, he is convicted by this apostolic authority of living according to the flesh; and by the very fact that he abstains from fleshly pleasures, he is shown to perform condemnable works of the flesh. For the teacher of the Gentiles calls all these things and such like works of the flesh because, by the manner of speech in which the whole is signified by a part, he wishes the human being himself to be understood by the name “flesh.” Whoever does not live according to the spirit—that is, according to God—but according to the flesh—that is, according to the human being, namely according to himself—is rightly called flesh.

“These,” he says, “and things like them are works of the flesh, which I now, though absent, preach and foretell to you through a letter, just as I foretold while I was present that they are deadly. I preach and warn you now, while you may still take care, while you may still repent, before judgment and condemnation, what these works will do: namely, take away the kingdom of heaven. For even any one of them will take away that kingdom, because those who do such works will not obtain the kingdom of God.” He does not mean those who struggle against such things, but those who do them. For it is one thing to commit wicked works and another [Col. 1192A] to struggle against them. Thus far the useless and accursed works of the flesh have in part been described; after these, the useful and sacred works of the Spirit are set forth, when it is said:

> “But the fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, gentleness, faith, moderation, continence, chastity. Against such things there is no law.”

The character of the works of the flesh has been stated. But the works of the Holy Spirit dwelling in a human being are those which follow. They should rather be called fruits, because, as the best fruits come forth from a good tree to provide the elect with the refreshment of perpetual fullness, they are to be sought for their own sake. [Col. 1192B] For *fructus* (“fruit”) is named from *frui* (“to enjoy”), and we are properly said to enjoy only those things in which we place the end of our joy: namely, the eternal goods which we prepare at some time to possess in God.

Among these fruits charity comes first, by which the Lord and neighbor are loved, because it is greater than all the other virtues and all the others flourish from its root. For from it arises joy: the not proud but kindly elevation of a mind exulting in good. Whoever loves the Lord rejoices in God with a pure conscience; and whoever loves a neighbor rejoices in that neighbor’s good. The person who loves God also keeps peace with God, because as far as possible he avoids offending him and strives to please him. He also keeps peace with his neighbor, not troubling the neighbor if he loves him. Yet he does not violate [Col. 1192C] peace if, with pious concern, he rebukes a neighbor who is in error, or even, if necessary, strikes him.

Since there are many things in human life that can disturb peace, patience is necessarily added, by which injuries and adversities are endured with an even mind so that brotherly peace may be preserved. For patience is to bear evils calmly and not to be stung by any resentment even against the one who inflicts them.
