And because this patience must be kept not for an hour, but as long as the Lord wills, long-suffering is added, through which all things are endured perseveringly to the end. Long-suffering is the length of a mind patiently enduring adversities and waiting long for eternal rewards.

But lest a person, among those whom he endures over a long time, fail to love them, goodness follows: sweetness of mind and pious affection, so that we may bear not bitterness of mind but sweetness toward those who trouble us, and through it bestow upon them whatever good things we can. Lest this goodness be empty, another related and similar virtue is added, namely kindness: itself a good disposition of mind, freely giving what is its own and cheerfully bestowing for God’s sake whatever it can. And because there are some who, while bestowing good things on their neighbors, speak harshly to them and display severity, gentleness is fittingly added, so that the person who gives kindly may not be intractable or harsh, but gentle and mild—that is, meek, approachable, and friendly. For *mansuetus* (“gentle”) is said to be, as it were, *manu assuetus* (“accustomed to the hand”).

Faith is that by which [Col. 1193A] we truly believe what we cannot see. Its name is derived from the fact that what has been said or promised is wholly done. For faith is so called because that which has been agreed between the two parties—that is, between God and man—is done, when a human being does in deed what he said with his mouth, and the Lord renders what he promised. Therefore faith without works is not true faith, because it does not do what it says. Thus faith is also kept between two people when they faithfully preserve and do what they have said and mutually determined.

Moderation is when measure stands—that is, is maintained and observed—in words and deeds. Continence is where one abstains from unlawful acts of the flesh; chastity, however, is when the flesh has already been calmed. Continence is in struggle, but chastity in [Col. 1193B] peace. For where the opposition of pleasure still resists, it is called not chastity but continence. The perfection of true chastity is that which does not contend against the movement of fleshly desire, but detests it with utter horror, preserves its own purity continually and inviolate, and can be nothing other than holiness.

These, then, are the fruits of the Spirit which the Apostle, wishing to commend them in contrast to the works of the flesh, began—as was said—from the head, saying: “But the fruit of the Spirit is charity.” He then wove together the rest as though arising from and joined to this head: joy, peace, and so forth. For all these flow from the fountain of charity. Who rejoices well except one who loves the good in which he rejoices? Who can have true peace except with one whom he truly loves? Who is truly patient unless he has love? Who is long-suffering in persevering in good unless he burns with love? Who is good unless made so by love? Who is kind unless he loves the person whom he helps? Who is usefully gentle unless governed by love? Who is beneficially faithful except by the faith which works through love? Who is well-moderated unless love sets a measure in all things? Who abstains from what disturbs him unless he loves that by which he is made honorable? Who attains the holiness of chastity unless charity rules in his mind? Charity, therefore, cannot be possessed without the other goods, and the other goods cannot profit without charity. Against such spiritual fruits, which necessarily follow the Spirit of grace, [Col. 1193D] there is no law, because the Law contradicts them in no respect but favors them in all things. But the Law has been laid down against the works of the flesh previously set forth.

> “But those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires.”

Having set forth the two battle-lines, namely those of vices and of virtues, he shows who they are that fight against vices. For not all resist vices, but only those who belong to Christ’s side, who are Christ’s possession, who are Christ’s members: those who follow the footsteps of his Passion have crucified—that is, tortured—their flesh, nailing it down with its vices and lusts. Let us understand vices in terms of action, and lusts in terms of consent. For Christ’s servants labor neither to perform the works of vices nor to consent, even in their hearts, to fleshly lusts. And by repressing the pleasures of the flesh, they make a cross for themselves and, as though with certain nails, fasten themselves to the precepts of righteousness, so that they may restrain within themselves depraved action and perverse will.

This statement may also be understood especially of those who afflict their flesh with fasts in hope of heavenly reward. For we crucify the flesh with vices and lusts if we so restrain gluttony that we seek nothing further from worldly glory. For one who mortifies the body but pants after honors has indeed laid a cross upon the flesh, but lives all the worse for the world through lust.

> “If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit. Let us not become desirous of empty glory, provoking one another, envying one another.”

[Col. 1194B] Since he had said generally that those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and lusts, he turns his discourse toward those to whom he was writing and numbers himself among them, as though saying: “I do not tell you what I myself would not also desire.” Those who belong to Christ act as I have said; and we, because we belong to Christ, should walk by the Spirit, because by the Spirit we have come to this life. For all of us who have been put to death to vices in the flesh now live by virtues in the Spirit.

If we live by the Spirit—that is, if through God’s Spirit we live spiritually—let us also walk under the Spirit’s guidance; that is, let us not remain slothful in that to which we have attained, but always advance toward better things. For no one is so holy in this life that he cannot still make progress daily. But because some, after growing in virtues, [Col. 1194C] begin to wish to be praised as holier persons, he fittingly adds: Let us not become desirous of empty glory. That is, if we live spiritually and walk spiritually, advancing from virtue to virtue, let us not on that account desire the vain glory of passing praise, lest we resemble the foolish virgins, who displayed lamps shining outwardly but neglected to store oil within their vessels; and so, when the bridegroom came, their lamps failed (Matt. 25).

For this reason we must also beware the desire for empty glory: because from it we would become persons provoking one another to contention, anger, or worse things, and envying one another’s better qualities. Thus the appetite for vain glory would produce such overthrow in us that those thought better than others would now become worse than others.

## CHAPTER VI

> “Brothers, even if a person should be overtaken in some transgression, you who are spiritual should instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you too be tempted.”

Up to this point the Apostle has addressed the whole Church, rejecting the Law and commending grace; now he addresses its rulers. As I have taught, all must indeed live spiritually. Yet, my brothers, you who have undertaken the care of others: even if some person—that is, someone weak and fragile by reason of human frailty itself—has been overtaken, that is, has suddenly fallen into some transgression, he must be treated humanely.

A transgression [Col. 1195A] is a forsaking of good. For what else does *delictum* sound like than “something abandoned” (*derelictum*)? And what does one who transgresses forsake except the good? The Greeks also gave two names to this evil. For among them a transgression is called both πλημμέλεια (*plēmméleia*) and παράπτωμα (*paráptōma*). And πλημμέλεια is a name akin to negligence, since negligence in Greek is called ἀμέλεια (*améleia*), because that which is neglected is not an object of care. In this place, however, the Greek has παράπτωμα. In *paraptoma*, one who transgresses is understood, as it were, to fall down. Hence a corpse, which the Latins call *cadaver* from falling (*cadendo*), is called πτῶμα (*ptōma*) in Greek. Therefore, one who commits evil by sinning first falls from the good by transgressing. For transgression is turning aside from good, whereas sin is doing evil. It may also be that transgression is what is done in ignorance, whereas sin is what is done knowingly. Yet they are often used interchangeably.

An overtaking occurs in which one transgresses when either, for the moment, one does not see what ought to be done, or, though one sees it, one is overcome—so that sin takes place either because truth is hidden or because weakness compels. And when transgression arises not from malice but from weakness or ignorance alone, the correction of the transgression itself must necessarily be moderated with great restraint. This, then, is what is now commanded: If a person has been overtaken in some transgression, you rulers who are spiritual—that is, who live spiritually—must neither despise nor embitter such a person, who does not fall away through the daily practice of individual vices or willingly do evil, but has suddenly fallen into some fault through imprudence or weakness. Do not embitter him, [Col. 1195C] but reasonably instruct such a one toward repentance as a brother, in a spirit not of excessive fervor but of gentleness and meekness.

Correct him, I say, sweetly; admonish him to rise, you who are set over him, considering yourself—that is, your own frailty—lest you too perhaps be tempted by it. When what you see in another’s weakness displeases you, weigh what you are, so that the spirit may restrain itself in zeal for correction while it fears in itself the very thing it reproves. For as long as we exist in this mortal flesh, we are all subject to the weaknesses of our corruption. Therefore each person ought to infer from himself how he should have pity on another’s weakness, lest, if he is swept too fervently into reproof of a neighbor’s weakness, he seem to have forgotten himself.

After this the Apostle returns to general instruction, saying:

> “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfil the law of Christ. For if anyone thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself. But let each one test his own work; and then he will have glory in himself alone, and not in another. For each one shall bear his own burden” (1 Cor. 3).

You rulers, as was said, should gently restore a subject if he has transgressed. And you subjects should bear one another’s burdens. For example: you will bear a brother’s anger when you do not grow angry against him while he is angry with you, so that, in turn, when you are overtaken by anger, he may support you by gentleness and calmness. Thus, at different times, the same weakness may be borne reciprocally by each person.

A different kind of weakness may, however, be borne by both at the same time. For instance, if someone has conquered talkativeness in himself but has not yet conquered obstinacy, while another is still talkative but is no longer obstinate: the former should bear the latter’s talkativeness, and the latter the former’s obstinacy, in charity, until that fault in the one and this fault in the other are healed. The same must be done with the other weaknesses.

And this is what is said: Bear one another’s burdens—that is, bear mutually the weights of your weaknesses—and so fulfil the law of Christ, namely charity, concerning which he himself said: “This I command you, that you love one another” (John 15). For it is the office of this love to bear one another’s burdens. And it is just that one should suffer with another on account of the burden of his weakness.

[Col. 1196B] For if anyone has exalted himself above others, despising them because of their various moral weaknesses and refusing to bear their burdens sympathetically, while magnifying himself in his own eyes as though he alone were righteous, he is his own enemy. If anyone thinks in his heart that he is something great in comparison with another person who sins, though he is nothing from himself, he deceives himself away from truth, believing what cannot be true. For one who arrogates holiness to himself is said to be nothing, since in comparison with the spiritual person who knows that he is what he is by God’s grace, whoever vainly presumes is nothing.

For every elect person attends not to the good things already received, but to those which he has not yet been able to receive; therefore he is humbled the more as he considers his poverty, and thus merits to receive further good things. But the reprobate does not attend to what he lacks in order to be humbled; rather, considering what he has, he is exalted. And, judging himself to be of some consequence, he becomes nothing by losing the good things he had received. For his own conscience, which suggests the thought of pride that he is something great in virtues, deceives him—that is, leads him apart from the way of humility and from charity toward the neighbor whom he despises as fallen.

Such a person is said to be nothing because every creature that does not cling to him who always has being is nothing. Or again, the person who believes those praising him and judges true what they say of him when it is false, thus considering himself great and holy, is not deceived by flatterers but by himself, while he trusts others more than his own conscience.

No one should vainly think great things of himself [Col. 1196D] or believe flatterers; rather, each should test and examine his own work, not another’s sin—as did the Pharisee, who was righteous not in reality but deceitfully (Luke 18). And when he has tested his work and found it truly good, then he shall have glory in himself alone, that is, in his own conscience, and not in another, that is, in another’s mouth. To possess glory inwardly and not depend on another’s praise is to keep oil in one’s vessel with those prudent virgins (Matt. 25).

But what glory does the righteous person have within himself except him to whom it is said: “My glory, and the lifter of my head” (Ps. 3)? Thus, as must often be said: “Let the one who glories glory in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1; 2 Cor. 10; Jer. 9). Let no one who stands think himself something in comparison with someone who falls; rather, let each test his own work and look about and examine carefully, not another’s fall. Thus—that is, by testing his own work, not another’s—he will have glory in himself, that is, in his own good action, and not in another, that is, in another’s downfall.

That is, he will not seek glory outside himself, so as to prefer himself when others lie fallen; rather, remaining in consideration of himself alone, when he has proved that he acts well, he will glory with a pure heart in God, from whom he received the ability to do good. For each person should now examine his own work rather than another’s because, at God’s judgment, each shall bear his own burden: that is, he shall be weighed down by the particular load of his own sins.

The Apostle is not contradicting himself when he commanded above that we bear one another’s burdens and now says that each will bear his own burden. For the burdens of shared weakness are one thing; the obligation of rendering account to God for our deeds is another. The former are shared and sustained with brothers; the latter is borne individually by each person. One person does not bear this latter burden with another, nor cast it upon another; each is compelled alone to endure his own burden, so that he may be weighed down in judgment according as he has sinned more or less.

> “Let the one who is instructed in the word share all good things with the one who instructs him. Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, that will he also reap. For the one who sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh; but the one who sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit.”

[Col. 1197C] Keep what I have said, each of you mutually and in yourselves; but toward your teachers, as I now exhort you, be generous. That is, let the person catechized—that is, instructed in the word of sacred doctrine by another—share all his material goods with the one instructing him: let him make all earthly goods which he possesses common to himself and his teacher, supplying his teacher from his own resources with food, clothing, and every other necessity.

And do not be deceived in this matter by excusing yourselves greedily and saying, “I can give little or nothing to my teacher.” For God, who sees what or how much you are able to give, is not mocked, so that an unjust or deceitful person might pass his judgment with laughter; rather, each receives from him what he has deserved. For those things which a person now sows—that is, the works he stores up for himself as seed, whether good or evil, many or few—he will reap: that is, he will reap their fruit at God’s judgment. The works of this present life are the seed of the future harvest.

Or thus: Let the one instructed by a teacher’s word share with the one instructing him; that is, let him make himself his teacher’s sharer and participant in all good things, by receiving his teaching and imitating his virtues and good conduct. For the disciple shares in all his teacher’s good things when he becomes a participant and imitator of everything which the teacher does and says well. And in this sharing do not be deceived by acting hypocritically; rather, show purity of heart in it. For God is not mocked—that is, he is not deceived as a human being may be, so as to be ignorant of anything—but sees [Col. 1198A] the inner things of the heart.

Or again: Let the one instructed, even if only by the word and not by the preacher’s example, share with him—not in evil things, if he commits them, but in all the good things he teaches—that is, let him show himself a participant, receiving the teacher’s word and fulfilling it in everything. And do not be deceived by imitating his evil conduct if he lives badly while speaking well, because God is not mocked: no one, whether teacher or disciple, can mock God’s judgment; there each receives according to what he has done. For whatever a person sows—that is, whatever he has done—that he will reap: that is, he will receive its reward when God judges.

And truly he will reap whatever he sows, whether good or evil. For the one who now sows in his flesh—that is, performs works of the flesh in the flesh—will also reap corruption from the flesh, so that he may be continually corrupted, that is, worn away by torments, and may have within himself an unceasing stench. But, on the contrary, the one who sows in the Spirit—that is, performs spiritual works in the Holy Spirit—will reap eternal life from that Spirit; that is, he will receive in the future, as it were, a harvest that is contrary to the corruption just described.

Perhaps the human spirit may also be understood, in which one sows and from which life will be reaped, in accordance with Solomon’s saying: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, because life proceeds from it” (Prov. 4). For what Solomon says about life proceeding from the heart appears to be what the Apostle says about life being reaped from the spirit. For as is the root of the heart, so, before the inward Judge, is every fruit of action. But whoever desires in the future age to gather a harvest of unending life ought, throughout the time he lives in this world, always to sow good works. Hence he adds:

> “And in doing good, let us not grow weary; for in its own time we shall reap, if we do not grow weary” (2 Thess. 3). “Therefore, while we have time, let us do good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith.”

Whatever a person sows, that he will reap. Therefore we must sow—that is, do—no evil, but good. And in doing good, that is, sowing good, let us never cease while the time of sowing remains, lest we grow weary through being fatigued by some labor; for there will also be a time of harvest and rest. For in its appointed time we shall reap—that is, gather the reward of our works—without failing, that is, continually and without end. For just as we do not cease from sowing, so we shall not cease from reaping.

[Col. 1198D] And because then we shall not cease from reaping the fruit of good work, that is, of our seed, therefore, while we have the time of sowing and working—which we do not know how long we shall possess—let us now constantly do good, such as alms and other benefits, to all whom we can, but especially to those of the household of faith, that is, to the righteous, because “the righteous lives by faith” (Hab. 2; Rom. 1). One is of the household of faith when joined to you by the same religion and not separated from the fellowship of brotherhood by sins. For *domesticus* is so called as though “standing in the house.”

Therefore we ought especially to confer benefits upon the righteous and holy. Yet we must not close the bowels of mercy against other persons, even sinners, nor even if they bear a hostile mind against us, as the Lord himself commands: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5; Luke 6).

> “See with what letters I have written to you with my own hand.”

Up to this point I have recalled and instructed you by the letter. That you may know it has been sent by me, see with what letters—that is, with how well-formed letters—I have written to you, not with a secretary’s hand but with my own. So that they should not suspect that this letter had not been sent to them by the Apostle but deceitfully by someone else in his name, and thus hesitate to obey his admonitions, he now gives them a sure sign by which to recognize it. It is as though he said: “I wrote this letter with my own hand.” Recognize this from the forms and qualities of the letters themselves, through which you can recognize [Col. 1199B] my hand.

By this too he strongly invites them to heed him, since he shows how great a concern he had for them, writing to them with his own hand. Or, when he says, “See with what letters I have written to you,” he admonishes them to consider and understand how profound are the mysteries, and how reasonable and useful the admonitions, contained in the writing of this letter. For the term “letters” often denotes an epistle. “See,” he says, “with what letters”—that is, with what an epistle, how spiritual, how true, how reasonable—I have written correction to you with my own hand.

> “For all who wish to please in the flesh compel you to be circumcised, only so that they may not suffer persecution for the cross of Christ. For those who are circumcised do not themselves keep the Law; but they want you to be circumcised so that they may glory in your flesh.”

It was necessary for me to write to you because false preachers are pressing for you to be circumcised. For all teachers of this kind who wish to please unbelieving Jews in the flesh—that is, in fleshly observance—compel you through importunity, rather than lead you by reason, to be circumcised, not in order that you may fulfil the Law, but solely so that they themselves may not suffer persecution for Christ’s cross, that is, the persecution brought upon us because of preaching the cross of Christ.

The Roman rulers had commanded that Jews should be permitted, without disturbance or hindrance, to observe their rites and Law wherever they were; and if any Gentile wished to agree with them, he could take up circumcision, their Law, and their rites, and live with them in security. But Jews accused Christians before the rulers of the Gentiles because they saw them destroying their Law, circumcision, and fleshly observances. And because Christians observed neither Gentile rite nor Jewish Law, the Jews took an opportunity to accuse them. Stirred by envy, they did this to this Apostle in almost every city of the Gentiles.

But the false apostles, so that they might preach Christ and the cross without persecution, also taught circumcision and observance of the Law. They preached Christ in order to obtain gain from believers; but the Law in order to please the Jews. This is what is said: all who wish to please in the flesh, preaching the Law carnally, compel you [Col. 1200A] to be circumcised solely in order not to suffer persecution for Christ’s cross.

And indeed it is only in order not to suffer adversity that they compel you to be circumcised; for they do not do so in order that the Law may be fulfilled. For those who are circumcised do not keep the Law; rather, they violate it, because it can be kept not carnally by the circumcised but spiritually by the baptized. They wish you to be circumcised not so that you may keep the Law, but rather that they may glory among the Jews in your flesh—that is, in the pain of your circumcised flesh—so as to please them, lest perhaps they accuse them before Gentile rulers for their new preaching and cause them to suffer some adversity.

> “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.”

They glory in circumcised flesh and fear to preach the cross; but far be it from me to glory in Christ’s power, majesty, or authority, save in the cross—at which the wise of the world will blush, and in which lay every reproach suffered by Christians and every persecution they endured. Therefore he gloried in the cross for which the ungodly mocked them, because he knew that our life rests in Christ’s death, our exaltation in his humility, and our strength in his weakness.

For on the forehead of believers, where the seat of shame is, the cross is affixed so that they may not be ashamed of his name. Circumcision, in hidden flesh, is the sign of the Old Testament. The cross, on the uncovered forehead, is the sign of the New Testament. There is concealment; here is revelation. That is under a veil; this is upon the face. When anyone passes from that to Christ, the veil is removed from him, so that one who had circumcision in secret may bear the cross upon his forehead.

The false apostles, then, remaining as it were in darkness and shadow, gloried in circumcision, that is, the old and covered sign. But Paul, having emerged into the light, transferred the sign to the forehead and gloried in the cross, that is, the sign of newness, as one made new. “I do not glory,” he says, “except in the cross alone of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me,” so that neither threats nor flatteries can stretch out a hand against me—that is, touch my soul [Col. 1200D] so as to call me back from the purity of faith; “and I too have been crucified to the world through Christ,” that is, put to death, so that I cannot desire it in any way.

For if the world has been crucified to me, I know it is dead. I do not love it, because I know it passes away. I do not lust after it, because I know it will be consumed by corruption. I avoid it as foul, shun it as mud, and leave it as harmful. I too, as though dead and foul-smelling, am despised by it. The world has been crucified to me so that it may not hold me; and I to the world so that I may not hold it, because neither does the world recognize anything of its own in me, nor do I desire anything in the world.

For it often happens that a person no longer holds the world in his mind, but the world still binds him with occupations. He himself is already dead to the world, but the world is not yet dead to him. For the world still sees him as living while it strives, by its own affairs, to draw elsewhere one who is intent upon other matters. But when the Apostle both perfectly despised the age and saw himself become such a person that he could no longer at all be desired by this age, he declared himself free, the bonds of this life broken: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.”

For the world had been crucified to him because he no longer loved it in his heart as dead. And he had crucified himself to the world because he had labored to show himself such that, as one dead, he could not be desired by it. Therefore, since he neither sought the world’s glory nor was himself sought by worldly glory, he glories that both he to the world and the world to him had been crucified.

We too, insofar as we spiritually understand God’s wisdom, through which all things were made, die to fleshly affections, so that, reckoning this world dead to us, we ourselves may die to this world and say: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.” For no one can see the face—that is, the manifestation—of divine Wisdom itself and live (Exod. 33). For that very form draws every rational soul by desire for itself: the more ardently, the purer it is; the purer, the more it rises to spiritual things; and the more it rises to spiritual things, the more it dies to fleshly things.

> “For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but a new creation.”

For this reason I glory only in the cross and not in circumcision: because in Christ Jesus—that is, in the Christian religion—neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision profits anything, but a new creation, that is, renewal of conduct. For it is not of great merit if something is done externally to us; rather, what is done in the mind must be weighed with great care.

To despise the present world; not to love transitory things; to bow the mind from its depths in humility before God and neighbor; to keep patience amid injuries inflicted; once patience is preserved, to repel from the heart the pain of malice; to give one’s own goods to the needy; not to covet another’s goods; to love a friend in God; for God’s sake also to love those who are enemies; to mourn at a neighbor’s affliction; not to rejoice at an enemy’s death—this is the new creation.

> [Col. 1201D] “And as many as follow this rule, peace be upon them and mercy, and upon the Israel of God.”

I have taught you what must be done. And all of you Gentiles who follow this rule—that is, the rectitude of my teaching and of glorying in the cross—[Col. 1202A] so as to direct your faith and works according to what I have taught in this letter: may peace, that is, reconciliation with God, be upon them, and mercy, that is, forgiveness of the sin which they committed in departing from the faith; and may these be upon the Israel of God, that is, those Jews who through faith and works are God’s possession.

> “Henceforth let no one trouble me, for I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus in my body. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.”

By these reasons and arguments I have shown you that justification or salvation is not in the oldness of the Law. Henceforth, let none of you trouble me with a kind of disputation by which he might wish to weary me further, demanding that I prove the same thing still further by other and more profound arguments, when it has already been sufficiently proved and shown.

Or: for the rest of your life, let none of you trouble me; but from now on preserve faith and works in such a way that you give me no further trouble, for I am sufficiently burdened by other troubles. For I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus—that is, I bear throughout my body the scars of wounds suffered for Christ and am afflicted by various injuries, as though I were a slave recaptured after flight and branded with servile marks. For *stigmata* properly denotes slaves’ brands, by which slaves convicted of flight or another fault were marked by burning.

Or thus: let none of you trouble me by asking anything further, because my words must be believed without hesitation. For I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus in my body—that is, I belong to Christ’s household; I am enrolled in the army of the eternal King, as is indicated by the many wounds displayed in scars upon my body. Therefore let no one take my words lightly, but let all yield to the authority of my sayings.

For *stigmata* were certain marks made on soldiers’ hands, by which they were recognized as belonging to the Roman emperor’s army. In the same way Paul bore not merely one bodily mark but marks and signs on many and various parts of his body, wounds endured for Christ, by which he was shown to be the most courageous soldier of the highest King.

At the end he writes: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ”—that is, the grace which the Lord has given—“be with your spirit, brothers,” that is, with your rational faculty, so that with the help of grace it may rightly order all thoughts and actions and may not seek to be justified through the Law by itself. For confirmation of the firm truth of all that has been said, there is added: “Amen,” which is interpreted “truly,” “faithfully,” or “let it be.”

## ON THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS

[Col. 1201]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 1201D]

Ephesus is a metropolitan city of Asia, where Paul remained for three years preaching the Gospel, so that all who lived in Asia, Jews and Gentiles alike, heard the word [Col. 1203A] of the Lord. For he was the first to found the Church there, and he nobly instructed the Ephesians in faith and morals and wonderfully enriched them with the treasure of divine knowledge.

But, as the Holy Spirit revealed to him, he foresaw that certain false preachers would later arise in their Church and promulgate impious doctrines. Among these were Ebion and Cerinthus, whom John calls antichrists (1 John 2; 2 John 1). Hence he said to them at last:

> “You know how I held back nothing useful, so as not to proclaim it to you and teach you publicly and from house to house” (Acts 20).

And again:

> “Therefore I testify to you this day that I am clean from the blood of all. For I did not shrink from proclaiming to you the whole counsel of God. [Col. 1203B] I know that after my departure ravenous wolves will enter among you, not sparing the flock; and from among yourselves men will arise, speaking perverse things, to draw disciples after themselves. Therefore keep watch, remembering that for three years I did not cease, night and day, to admonish every one of you with tears” (ibid.).

With such great labor and care, over so long a time and so perfectly, the blessed Apostle instructed the Ephesians; and he foresaw that such wolves would arise among them, wishing namely to introduce the ceremonies of the Law and to subject those made so free by grace slavishly to fleshly observances. Some of them, indeed, would affirm that Christ was simply God and not human; others would teach that he was human and not God.

He therefore thought it fitting prudently to fortify the Ephesians beforehand by this letter, lest heretics should be able, through any artifice of persuasion, to enter among them or cut their throats with wolfish teeth. In this letter he first intends to confirm them in the faith by which Catholics believe Christ to be almighty God and true man, and repeatedly to commend the excellence of God’s grace, so that they might attribute no good thing to their own free will, but everything to grace. Then he teaches that they ought not to accept the yoke of legal observance.

For he does not openly rebuke them for any fault, which shows that they had faithfully kept his commands; but there was danger that they might fall. And because he was accustomed to speak wisdom among the perfect (1 Cor. 2), he unfolds for them in this letter, written from prison at Rome, very profound meanings and hidden mysteries altogether unknown to the age before that time.

This letter is rightly placed after that to the Galatians: there the Galatians are recalled to the faith; here the Ephesians are confirmed in faith. There fleshly observances are removed from those who had begun to take them up; here they are condemned beforehand lest they be taken up. Yet because no one is so perfect that he cannot still grow, he exhorts them to advance toward better things and not to yield because of his tribulations, but to remain rooted and grounded in charity; he treats nobly of moral instruction. And lest perfection raise them into pride, he also shows from what condition and to what dignity they were called.

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 1204A]

> “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, to all the saints who are at Ephesus and faithful in Christ Jesus: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

Paul writes—whose writings are authoritative—because he is an apostle of Jesus Christ, that is, an envoy of the Savior and King of the faithful. And he is an apostle not through his own merit or through human election, but through God’s will, since the will of God the Father alone made him an apostle of Christ. By calling himself an apostle of Christ, that is, one sent by Christ through God’s will, he commends himself in the authority of his apostleship, so that they may obey his admonition more readily, and so that he may suggest that all who should wish to dissent from his teaching are opposing Christ’s command [Col. 1204B] and resisting the Father’s will. He says “through the will of God,” rather than “through God,” in order to suggest that the establishment of all things comes about by the mere nod of the divine will. “For he has done whatever he willed” (Ps. 113).

Paul, of such great authority, writes to all the saints, that is, to those perfected in holy religion, and to the faithful in Christ Jesus, that is, to those less advanced who have already received faith. That is, he writes to all, perfected and imperfect, who are at Ephesus, that is, in that city which is the capital of Asia Minor. But if we seek a mystical sense, *Ephesus* is interpreted as “his will,” that is, God’s will. Therefore the apostle now writes, wherever they may be bodily situated, to all who are so holy and faithful that they remain in God’s will, not transgressing his wills.

*Ephesus* is also interpreted as “my counsel,” so that Paul says: I write to the saints and faithful who are at Ephesus, that is, in my counsel, who do not depart from the stronghold of my counsel. And they are saints and faithful in Christ Jesus, because holiness or faithfulness is of no benefit unless it is in Christ. For some philosophers seemed to possess holiness through fasting, chaste living, and contempt for the world, but not in Christ. Likewise, some are faithful, but not in Christ. If someone restores a deposit, if someone does not deny what was entrusted to him, he shows himself faithful. Such a person is faithful, but not in Christ. Therefore, in distinction from such people, the apostle says that he writes to the saints and faithful in Christ Jesus, who possess [Col. 1204C] holiness and faith in Christ, that is, in the Christian religion.

He also greets them, saying: May grace and peace be to you. Grace, by which your sins may be forgiven and virtues bestowed upon you; peace, by which through good will and action you may always be in harmony with God and the holy angels. And may this grace and peace be to you from God our Father, that is, the Creator who adopted us as sons; and from the Lord Jesus Christ, that is, the Redeemer who mercifully rescued us from the enemy and subjected us to his own lordship.

He is Jesus, which is interpreted “Savior,” because he saves his people from their sins (Matt. 1); and Christ, who is “anointed,” that is, king or priest (Heb. 7), reigning in us and interceding for us, because kings and priests were consecrated by anointing (1 John 2).

[Col. 1205A] “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, in Christ, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we might be holy and blameless before him in love.”

First of all, he blessed God, considering him to be the beginning and source of all goods. For, having shown that the Lord Jesus is equal to the Father—when he showed that grace and peace are given equally by the Father and the Son—he shows that God is to be blessed by us because of the gratuitous benefits which he has bestowed upon us, so many and so great. We ought not, indeed, to be ungrateful to him by ascribing to ourselves what we have received from him; rather, recognizing from whom they have been [Col. 1205B] given to us, we ought always to bless him and render to him the thanks due to him.

And since these same benefits are similarly given to us by the Son, it is plain that he too is to be extolled with equal blessing together with the Father, so that all may honor the Son as they honor the Father (John 5). Thus he is declared to be of equal power and equal to the Father. Blessed be God by us, so that we all may bless him and offer him thanks and praise for the benefits received from him, not supposing that we possess any good thing from ourselves.

Let us bless him because he is God, that is, our Creator; and the creature ought to bless its Creator. And he is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, that is, Father of him who, having rescued us from the tyranny of the devil, [Col. 1205C] mercifully subjected us to his own dominion, saved us from our sins, and reigns in our good actions. When he says, “Blessed be God,” he plainly shows that he too is God. I mean, he shows the Father’s Son to be worthy of praise with the Father’s blessing when he says, “Blessed be God,” that is, Creator of all things, because the Son also is Creator. “For whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does” (ibid.); and thus it is established that he is equal to the Father, of equal power and coeternal.

But when it is said, “Blessed be the Father of Christ,” it is clearly shown that Christ himself must likewise be blessed by us, because “whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him” (ibid.). For one cannot rightly bless the Father who does not equally [Col. 1205D] bless the Son, since Father is not said except in relation to Son. Hence it is clear that the Son is coeternal and coequal with the Father; for if the Father had at any time been without the Son, he would not have been Father. Consequently, he would not then have possessed as great a dignity as he now possesses; and thus he would have begun to increase—something it is impious even to suppose. Therefore the Father was never prior to the Son; rather, the Son is eternally begotten without beginning.

Or, in the statement, “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” Christ is shown to be both man and God. For he is man, whose God is the one who is blessed; and he is God, whose Father is that same one whom we bless. God is Christ’s God according to his humanity, and Christ’s Father according to his divinity. He is deservedly blessed by us because he [Col. 1206A] first blessed us.

Thus the apostle begins to enumerate the benefits granted to the human race by God through Christ. “Blessed,” he says, “be he who blessed us.” God blesses us when he grants us virtues or advances us in those very virtues. But we bless God when, for the benefits he has bestowed upon us, we praise him.

He blessed us not with some blessing, but with every blessing; not bodily but spiritual, that is, in the word of God, wisdom, truth, and all the other virtues; and not with earthly things but with heavenly things, so that, although we are still held here in the body, we may nevertheless already be in heavenly places in mind and manner of life. And this so abundant blessing of virtues and spiritual goods was given to us by the Father in Christ, that is, after we began to remain in him, the Mediator and Reconciler, incorporated into the members of the Church, which is his body. For this blessing is given to no one outside Christ.

Or the past tense is used for the future, so that we may believe without doubt, as though already done, what we hope will be done. “He blessed,” that is, he will bless us: he will enrich us on the day of judgment with every spiritual blessing, not a bodily one, because he will give spiritual rather than carnal riches. For then he will not provide carnal food, wives, gold, and the other delights possessed by the ungodly, but those spiritual delights which the angels possess above. Hence our body also, so that it may share in those delights, will be spiritual: “a natural body is sown, and a spiritual body will rise,” in power, to be sure, not in nature [Col. 1206C] (1 Cor. 15). For it will possess as much lightness and brightness as a spirit. Therefore whatever good that glorified body possesses will be spiritual.

Accordingly, let us expect nothing carnal but everything spiritual in that blessing, because it will be spiritual; and it will be not partial but universal. For he will make us blessed with every spiritual blessing, filling us with every good, so that no spiritual good at all may be lacking to us, when Christ says: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25); receive the kingdom. And he will place us locally in the heavenly places among the ranks of holy angels, virtues, and dominions, so that we may possess the same blessedness, glory, and knowledge as they do, being their equals even in the loftiness of our place.

And this is that glorious blessedness which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor the human heart been able to conceive (1 Cor. 2), which the Father has given us if he finds us in Christ, that is, true members of Christ. Otherwise no one can ascend to this blessedness, because “no one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3).

The apostle’s use of the past tense signifies, as has been said, that what God will bless us with in the future is as stable and unchangeable as something already past, which cannot be changed for any reason. For what has happened cannot not have happened. And by saying “he blessed,” rather than “he gave,” and “blessing,” rather than “blessedness,” [Col. 1207A] he wished to indicate to us the power of the Father and the Son. For to bless is proper to him as to do good. And what else will doing good then be but bestowing participation in blessedness? Hence the Psalmist says: “Return, my soul, to your rest, because the Lord has done good to you” (Ps. 114).

That he himself will bless us with that great blessing is as firm and certain as the fact that, before the world was made, he chose us by predestining us to life. Or, when he blesses us, he will not do so without foresight, but just as he chose us from the mass of those to be lost before the beginning of the world. For he will bless as he predestined, since he will give each person a blessing according to the measure he ordained for that person beforehand.

He chose us—that is, he selected and drew us out from the mass of sins—and he did this in him, that is, in Christ, so that we might be members of Christ. This election was made before the foundation of the world, that is, before every creature. He chose us for this end: that we might be holy and blameless.

There is this difference between “holy” and “blameless”: one who is holy may also be understood as blameless, but one who is blameless is not immediately holy. For infants too are blameless, because, with their bodies intact, they cannot commit any sin; yet they are not holy, because holiness is acquired by will and effort. “Blameless” may be said of one who has not committed sin, but “holy” of one who is full of virtues. Thus the holy are understood as the perfect, the blameless as the imperfect: holy through advancement in virtues; blameless through baptism from the sins of the world, and subsequently undefiled.

[Col. 1207C] Therefore God predestined us to become such, and this not in the vain estimation of human beings, but before the sight of him who beholds truth and considers hidden things. For if he sees that we are truly holy and blameless, whatever people may think of us, he himself will render us a reward. Conversely, if through hypocrisy we wish to feign holiness, though ignorant people judge us holy, he will nevertheless condemn us.

He chose us to be holy and blameless in his sight, and this in love: that we might advance toward that holiness and blamelessness not from fear of punishment, but from love of righteousness. It should therefore be noted that, in order to commend the greatness of grace, the apostle enumerates the benefits of that same grace which were given to the human race by God through [Col. 1207D] Christ.

For before the foundation of the world, when no one had merited anything because no one yet existed, God ordained that, in the time of grace, he would separate some from those to be lost and make them righteous and blameless; he ordained also that he would lead them to eternity. Of these predestinations, he fulfills one here, in making them holy; the other he will complete in the future, by granting immortality and blessedness. Thus, by predestining, he has already blessed us in heavenly places while we still remain on earth, just as, by predestining, he chose us before the foundation of the world while we did not yet exist. And he chose us not because we were going to be holy, but in order that we might be holy; that is, through grace he himself, in loving us, made us holy and blameless.

[Col. 1208A] “Who predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ unto himself, according to the purpose of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace, by which he made us gracious in his beloved Son. In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace, which abounded exceedingly in us in all wisdom and prudence, that he might make known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure, which he purposed in him, for the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth, in him.”

Predestination is the preparation of grace, while grace is the gift itself already given. And we rightly bless God, [Col. 1208B] who not only chose us beforehand in order to make us holy and blameless, but also predestined us for adoption as sons. He predestined—that is, he ordered beforehand and firmly. This is what *pre-* means: from a most ancient time. For *destinare*, “to appoint,” in itself indicates distance; the past tense indicates a remote time.

He predestined us for adoption as sons—that is, so that we might become sons according to a manifold conformity of his virtues expressed in us; namely, so that, insofar as human nature makes possible, we may be made conformed to our Father in holiness and righteousness, and that the image of his goodness may be expressed in us as far as possible. Our becoming sons is not from our merit but from his grace, by which he adopted us as sons. The apostle wished to note this by saying “adoption.”

What he says about God’s adopted sons is greater than what he had said about saints and blameless persons. He predestined us as sons, and did so through Jesus Christ the mediator, so that through him who is Son by nature he might make us adopted sons, tending toward Christ himself, that is, toward conformity with him through faith and good conduct. Or he made this predestination through Jesus Christ, that is, through his own power and wisdom, because the Father never did anything except through the Son, who is his power and wisdom. Hence the Son’s coeternity and equality with the Father are clear (Phil. 2).

And in predestining us, he acted according to the purpose of his will—that is, following the purpose which he set forth in the prophets, to whom he revealed and made known his will concerning [Col. 1208D] us. That is, just as he set it forth through the prophets, so he predestined it from eternity: he predestined our becoming sons from eternity neither less fully nor otherwise than he later set it forth in the prophets. Yet predestination did not precede purpose with respect to God himself, but with respect to us, because all things that pass for us through times or spaces are present to him.

This purpose was of his will, that is, not of our merits but of his gratuitous will. For freely he predestined from eternity; freely in time he set it forth and foretold it through the prophets. And he did all this to the praise of the glory of his grace. For eternal adoption is, as it were, the glory of his grace. He did this to the praise of the glory of his grace, that is, so that inwardly and outwardly we may praise the glory—that is, the abundance—of his grace by which he adopted us.

This abundance is called glory because it is so great and so abundant, and because honor is owed to it by us to the same degree as it has bestowed much of that glory upon us: what it foretold in the prophets, what it predestined before the ages. For by this it made us steadfast and certain. It was grace that predestined and chose us. And this grace abounded so greatly that it foretold through the prophets the things it had predestined. Therefore, because it foretold them, its grace is praised by us for that very abundance. For unless it had foretold through the prophets, whom it alone predestined, its predestination would not have been known to us. And if it had remained hidden from us, it would not have drawn us to praise of its grace.

From this it appears, then, that increased praise of his glory ought to arise from the abundance of his grace [Col. 1209B] by which he willed to disclose his predestination to us through the prophets. Therefore he is greatly to be glorified, since he both predestined us freely for adoption as sons and foretold this in the prophets.

What is said of his having predestined us differs from what was said above, that he chose us. For to predestine is one thing and to choose another: election is always considered among two or more, whereas predestination is not; and election is made only from among good things, while predestination concerns both good and evil. For the good are predestined in two ways, that is, to the first and second resurrection. But the evil are predestined simply to the recompense of unending punishment, which they will deservedly suffer for sins committed—yet God predestined no one to this. For no one is predestined by God to anything except that which God himself subsequently works in that person; for one cannot be predestined to something which cannot be found among God’s creatures. Thus it is plain that no one is predestined to sin, because it is established that no sin is created by God. But one is predestined to punishments, which God made so that the wicked may be punished justly.

God predestined us according to the purpose of his will—or rather, as it is read in Greek, according to the good pleasure of his will—because not everything that pleases can also please well. But “good pleasure” is used only where what has pleased is approved as having pleased rightly. God predestined us according to the good pleasure [Col. 1209D] of his will, not ours, lest in so great a benefit of grace we should glory in the pleasure of our own will.

In this very will he made us gracious, that is, made us pleasing to himself, so that we might give him thanks for his benefits. That is, not only do the benefits bestowed upon us proceed from his gracious will and not from our merit, but also the fact that we are grateful to him, ascribing everything to him because of those benefits. Thus *gratificavit*, “he made gracious,” is said from *gratia*, “grace,” just as *justificavit*, “he justified,” is said from *justitia*, “justice.”

He made us gracious, and did so in his Son, that is, in the activity of his own proper and natural Son, who is coeternal and consubstantial with him. Since the Son is of the same nature, this happened in his activity. And it could happen also in the Beloved, that is, because he is beloved by the Father [Col. 1210A] above all other sons, since he is Son from eternity and always remains and reigns with him.

Or, he made us—who formerly displeased him and were enemies—gracious to himself, that is, filled us with his grace; and this in his beloved Son, that is, through the death and resurrection of his Son, who is supremely loved by him because nothing in him displeases him. Or, “in his beloved Son” means that he made us gracious to himself in faith in that Son.

Nevertheless, Greek manuscripts do not read “in his beloved Son,” but simply “in the Beloved.” Since “God’s Beloved,” “the Father’s Beloved,” or “the Church’s Beloved” has not been added, but it is said absolutely, “in the Beloved,” it should be understood as supplied by all: he is beloved by all, because he is the highest good. Therefore every grace which we obtain, to the praise and glory of him who made us gracious, is completed in the Beloved—that is, in our Lord and Savior—because no good can exist except from the highest good and in the highest good, which every creature naturally loves and desires.

In him we have redemption, that is, manumission by God from Satan: we have been manumitted and set free from the devil’s yoke, which hindered in us the capacity to do good. He did not say “we had,” but “we have,” in order to indicate that we possess this manumission continually. And this is through his blood, that is, through the shedding of his blood, because his innocent blood, poured out, was the price by which we were redeemed and restored to freedom, having been held captive. By saying that his blood had such efficacy, he shows him to have been not only a sinless man [Col. 1210C] but also almighty God.

In him we have redemption. And what redemption? The forgiveness in baptism of original and actual sins. For the devil ruled over us through sins; but when our sins were forgiven, that evil one lost dominion over us. Thus the forgiveness of sins became for us redemption and liberation, so that in freedom we might serve our Redeemer.

Yet redemption and forgiveness are understood differently. Forgiveness produces redemption; redemption is manumission and the restoration of our freedom of choice for doing good, because even the righteous after death are held by no bond but enter the kingdom freely. Forgiveness, however, simply means the abolition of sins.

We have forgiveness of sins, and this according to the riches of his grace, that is, according to the rich and abundant grace of mercy—according to the multitude of his mercy freely bestowed upon us—which, being great and surpassing all understanding (Phil. 4), has likewise erased our manifold and innumerable sins.

I mean the grace that abounded exceedingly in us. Here he wishes to show what God graciously did concerning himself and the other apostles, so that through these things he may give weight to his authority and thus more effectively persuade them of what he has proposed. Up to this point he has spoken of what has been given to the whole Church of the saints; now he treats of what was granted especially to the apostles. For though grace had abounded, or does abound, in all saints, it nevertheless abounded exceedingly [Col. 1211A] in the apostles, because they received a more abundant generosity of it than the rest.

In all wisdom and prudence. The Stoics also hold that wisdom and prudence differ, saying that wisdom is knowledge of divine things, while prudence is knowledge only of mortal things. According to this distinction, we may take wisdom as faith concerning invisible things, but prudence as concerning things performed bodily by us, or concerning moral conduct and the management of temporal affairs.

Grace abounded exceedingly in the apostles in all wisdom and prudence because the Holy Spirit poured into them, more than into others, wisdom by which they knew the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit eternally proceeding from both; that the Son alone was incarnate, not the Father or the Spirit; and other mysteries of the incarnation, heavenly secrets, and also the gifts to be conferred upon the Church. The same Spirit also gave them prudence in overflowing measure concerning the ministries of the Church, so that they might provide for things which were to happen or be done in the Church; understand its future conditions and times of prosperity and adversity until the end of the age; understand how it was to be spread and exalted throughout the world, celebrate its rites honorably everywhere, and destroy all heresies.

For they knew more subtly than others concerning the Trinity and unity of the Godhead, and foresaw more keenly the mysteries of Christ’s incarnation and the state of the Church. Or let us understand prudence in relation to the governance of the Church. For they had greater knowledge of governing the Church than others. They knew how they ought to admonish each person, whom to rebuke, whom to entreat, and the like. And because all wisdom and prudence abounded exceedingly in them through heavenly grace, faith must be given to their teaching, by which they preach that Christ is God the Creator and true man.

The grace, he says, so abounded exceedingly in us that it made known to us—that is, disclosed to us—the sacrament, that is, the mystery, of his will: his mystical and hidden will, formerly concealed. I mean his will concerning the incarnation of the Son, the renewal of the human race, the state of the Church, the gifts to be conferred upon it, and its governance. For although the prophets knew these things in part, none of them saw all that the apostles saw, or saw it as clearly as the apostles. The prophets knew as persons concerned with the foretelling of events; the apostles as persons present at their realization.

I mean a will manifested not because of human merits, but according to his good and merciful good pleasure: because it mercifully pleased him to restore the human race. This good pleasure he purposed—that is, set forth far in advance, or fully established, or openly offered to all—in him, that is, in Christ; not to be fulfilled at another time, but in the dispensation of the fullness of times, that is, in the fullness of times divinely apportioned and ordered, when the times which he had previously ordained to be fulfilled had already been completed.

Or, he made known to us the mystery [Col. 1212A] of his will, and did this according to his pleasure—that is, according to what pleased him by his sole power—and that pleasure is good, that is, beneficial to us. Before he made this mystery known to us, he himself set it forth in the prophets: that is, he foretold through the prophets that mystery, for they sang beforehand of the mysteries of the Lord’s incarnation and the gifts which he would confer upon the Church. For if people had been wholly ignorant and not instructed beforehand even a little, they would not have received it.

This mystery was in him, that is, in Christ, in his death and resurrection. I mean a mystery directed toward the dispensation of the fullness of times: he set it forth in the prophets for this purpose, that in the fullness of time—that is, at the appointed time, the time of grace—that mystery might be distributed through the apostles. The Lord dispensed it because he granted some in the Church faith and knowledge of Christ’s incarnation, others virtues and charisms, and whatever the prophets had foretold would be apportioned and distributed.

And what was that mystery? To restore—that is, to bring back to the first state—all things destroyed through sin. And to make that restoration in Christ, that is, in Christ’s faith and grace, so that in him may be restored the things in heaven, that is, the number of blessed angels divinely established, after the reprobate angels had fallen from it; and the things on earth, that is, human beings. And all that he restored would remain in Christ himself without end, so as never again to fall.

For the things in heaven are restored in him when that which fell from among the angels is made up from human beings; and the things on earth are restored in him when those human beings who are predestined to eternal life are renewed from the oldness of corruption. The things in heaven are restored when humbled human beings return there, from which apostate angels fell through pride; the things on earth are also restored when sinners are converted to righteousness.

Or, the things in heaven were restored—that is, changed for the better—in Christ, that is, through Christ’s activity, because in the revelation of the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation the angels received a certain advancement for the better. Their joy also increased when they began to receive human beings into their fellowship. For Christ did not die for angels. But whatever among human beings is redeemed and freed from evil through his death is also done, in a sense, for angels, because after the hostilities which sins created between human beings and holy angels, human beings are in some manner restored to favor with them; and through the redemption of human beings the losses caused by that angelic fall are repaired.

Thus heavenly and earthly things are restored, but only those which were chosen and predestined in him before the foundation of the world. For those whom he chose from eternity always were and are in him. In saying *instaurare*, “to renew,” he did not speak properly except with regard to the things in heaven, because the things on earth are not *instaurated* but *restored*. For we say *instaurare* when something restored is renewed to something better, as good to better; but that is *restored* which, having been entirely destitute, is renewed, as evil into good.

[Col. 1213A] “In whom also we were called by lot, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, so that we might be to the praise of his glory, we who hoped beforehand in Christ.”

All things have been restored in Christ, in whom we too were called from unbelief to faith, and this by lot, that is, by grace alone and not by our merit. For grace is indicated by the name of lot, because in a lot there is no election but God’s will. Where it is said, “this person does” and “that person does not,” merits are considered; and where merits are considered, there is election, not lot. But when God finds no merits in us, he called us by the lot of his will, because he willed it, not because we were worthy.

The apostles also, in whom grace abounded exceedingly, were called by lot, lest they seem to have merited something better than the rest. We were called—I mean, we who were predestined, that is, prepared beforehand in his wisdom and ordained from eternity for life—and this according to his purpose, that is, according to what he afterwards foretold in the prophets. For the prophets foretold that the apostles would be converted to faith in Christ; and just as they foretold it, so God had predestined it. For they were predestined according to his purpose because, just as he foretold magnificently in the prophets that they would come to faith, so he had magnificently predestined them.

Or, we were predestined according to his purpose, that is, according to his firm and enduring ordinance. He also works in the apostles all things, even willing, according to the counsel of his will, so that no one may glory in personal merits. As if it were said: Why he chose us rather for the office of apostleship, we do not know; yet he does all things with counsel—that is, reasonably and providently, not rashly. For counsel is customarily taken in order that the matter concerning which counsel is taken may be done reasonably. And the counsel by which he does all things is that of his own will, not an external counsel; for he received counsel not from another but from his own will alone.

By this counsel he acts so that, entering eternal life, we may be for the praise of his glory: that is, so that in that life we may praise, through love and admiration, his ineffable glory—namely, himself, the glorious, praiseworthy, and admirable one—[Col. 1213D] we who hoped beforehand in Christ. That is, before we pass into that heavenly homeland, we placed our hope in Christ; or, we Jews, who before our conversion hoped in the coming Christ before he came. For from ancient times the Jews hoped in the coming Messiah, and Paul himself hoped in the same one before he was converted to the new faith.

That hope is placed in Christ shows that he is God. And because hope was placed in him before his advent, it is established that he has always been with the Father without beginning. For if he had not existed, all who hoped in him would have perished as persons hoping in nothing.

Or, we were called by lot for this end: that we might be for the praise of his glory, that is, that others might praise his glory through us, or that we ourselves might do so—we, I mean, who hoped in Christ before [Col. 1214A] you did. Therefore we are such that through us others may hope and praise. For the apostles believed before the rest.

“In whom you also, when you heard the word of truth, the Gospel of your salvation—in whom, having believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance, unto the redemption of the acquired possession, unto the praise of his glory.”

[Col. 1214B] Because he had said that he and the other apostles were called, lest he seem covertly to have said that the Ephesians were not called, he added, as though saying: “We were first called in Christ, in whom you too were afterward already called—if not directly, yet through his members and his precepts. You were called to a faith which you did not receive from any merit of your own, but from hearing alone; for when you had heard from my mouth the word of truth, then you were called.” In this the grace of God is greatly commended: they received it so easily, namely through hearing alone, because neither their merit nor the power of their own choice intervened, but hearing alone, so that they might receive grace unto faith. You believed because you heard a word not of falsehood, as formerly in the praise of idols, but of truth in the preaching of Christ, which is upheld by surpassing truth; that is, you believed because you recognized that what was said was true.

This word is the Gospel of your salvation, that is, good news, because in it salvation was announced to you: namely, forgiveness of sins, justification, and eternal life. And because they might have heard it without believing, he adds: “In this Gospel, when you believed, you were also sealed,” that is, set apart [Col. 1214C] from unbelievers by the Holy Spirit, whose grace you received. For the Holy Spirit seals believers, that is, distinguishes and separates them from other people, because he cleanses them from sins and adorns them with spiritual graces.

Or: in Christ you were sealed with his image; that is, you who had been disfigured by the fault of the first parent, and in whom the image and likeness of God had already perished, were sealed—that is, the image and conformity of God were impressed upon you. Restored to the capacity of acting well according to innocence and justice, you display the image of God the Father; namely, by the establishment of free choice you are impressed with God’s likeness in innocence and good works. And this is through the Holy Spirit, not through our merits, faith intervening. He indicated this when he said, “having believed,” etc. [Col. 1214D] As though he said: “Because you believed, you were therefore sealed with the Holy Spirit; that is, you received this sign by which you were distinguished from others: that you were filled with the Holy Spirit, whom unbelievers do not have.”

This Spirit is “of promise,” that is, promised by God, just as the Savior commanded his disciples not to depart from Jerusalem but to await the promise of the Father. And again he said of him: “I will send upon you the promise of my Father” (Luke XIV). Or, this Spirit is of promise because he promises eternal life to those whom he fills; and he does this because he himself is the pledge, earnest, and assurance of our inheritance which we shall receive from God—that is, the love which that Spirit has poured into us is the earnest of the future inheritance. Here “pledge” is used in the sense of an earnest.

For when a pledge is given, once that for which the pledge was given has been supplied, the pledge is taken away. But an earnest is when some portion of the price is first given, so that it may be a sign of the whole sum to be given. Thus the love given to believers through the Holy Spirit is the sign and earnest of the fullness of everlasting life which is to be given. For that for which the earnest was given will be fulfilled; nor will the earnest itself, that is, love, be taken away from us, but it will be completed when the full sum is rendered. [Col. 1215A]

“You were sealed with the Holy Spirit, and this unto the redemption of the possession”: so that the enemy may no longer rule over you, but Christ, who redeemed you with his blood, may possess you and not lose you. For here redemption means immortality, which will come through the resurrection. “Possession,” however, means that fellowship which seeks God. Therefore that Spirit will lead us [Col. 1215B] into the redemption of immortality and impassibility: namely, so that we may be redeemed and freed from the dead—that is, he will make us immortal through Christ’s death and resurrection. And that redemption will be such that it is “of possession,” because that immortality will so acquire us for God and unite us to him that we shall no longer be separated or lost from him, but shall always cling to him and be possessed by him. And this is “unto the praise of his glory,” namely, that with admiration, love, and participation we may praise his glory—that is, his blessedness. He said “his” in order to indicate that whatever good we have is from God.

> “Therefore I also, having heard of your faith which is in the Lord Jesus, and of your love toward all the saints, do not cease giving thanks for you, making remembrance [Col. 1215C] of you in my prayers, that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, the eyes of your heart having been enlightened, that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the saints, and what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of the might of his strength, which he worked in Christ, raising him from the dead and setting him at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality and authority and power and dominion and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come; and he subjected all things beneath his feet [Col. 1215D] and gave him as head over all things to the Church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all things in all.”

The Apostle invites them to the true steadfastness of the faith which they had received from him concerning the Lord Jesus: namely, that Christ is truly a creature in his humanity and truly Creator in his divinity—that is, true man and true God. For, that they might be strengthened and increased in this faith of theirs which works through love, he gave thanks to God for it, so that God himself, who had given it, might multiply and confirm it.

As though he said: “You were called, you heard the Gospel and believed, and you were sealed with the Holy Spirit. Therefore,” that is, for these reasons, “I give thanks, because not only your neighbors, but I too, though far away in a Roman prison, [Col. 1216A] hear of your faith”—as though it were now renowned and established among you, and proposed to many as an example for their conversion, because you are steadfast in it. And this is because it is “in the Lord Jesus”: firmly founded and abiding in the Lord and Savior, who made you subject to his lordship and saved you.

“I also hear that your love overflows toward all the saints”: that is, your charity, by which you love all the saints in such a way that you devote to them whatever you can piously do. Thus the works of charity which you perform for the saints cause your charity to be widely proclaimed, and many hold it forth as an example. Therefore, hearing these things, I do not cease giving thanks to God for you, because he bestowed this faith and love upon you. It was of great benefit to them that so great an apostle [Col. 1216B] gave thanks for them, because through this they were divinely confirmed and advanced in the faith and love which they had recently received through the Gospel preached to them.

“I give thanks,” he says, “for what you have already received, and I make prayers that you may be able to have what you do not yet possess. I make remembrance of you in my prayers, that God may grant you to understand what you have believed”—namely, that you may apprehend by knowledge, through discernment, that which you believed by faith. And may “the God of our Lord Jesus Christ” grant this to you: that is, the God of him whom we ought to revere, because we are his servants and he is our Lord; and he is Jesus, that is, our Savior; and he is Christ, that is, our king or priest. All this is said with respect to his human nature, because only according to his humanity is God the God of Christ, whereas according to his divinity [Col. 1216C] he is Christ’s Father. He who in time created him from a virgin had begotten him from himself before all times.

Hence he is called “the Father of glory,” because Christ himself, according to the excellence of his eternal divinity, is the glory of the Father: that is, his power, wisdom, and Word. Thus, by saying “the God of our Lord Jesus Christ,” he shows him to be true man; and by adding “Father of glory,” he signifies that he is true God from the Father’s substance.

And I pray that this Father may give you a spirit of wisdom concerning heavenly and divine things, and of revelation in the knowledge of him, so that you may know him—not obscurely, but without a veil—namely, Christ, as God omnipotent, without beginning or end, [Col. 1216D] and filling all things by his divinity. May he give you the Spirit of wisdom in the knowledge of him—that is, the Holy Spirit, through whom wisdom is poured into people—so that you may know him insofar as he can be known by those who still live in the flesh, and may know all that can be known about him in this life.

And may he give you the spirit of revelation concerning his humanity: the Holy Spirit, through whom he may reveal to you the mysteries of Christ’s humanity in the knowledge of him, so that you may plainly know his incarnation, not through a shadow, as did those who were before his coming. He therefore prays that God may give them this knowledge of Christ, because if they possess it, no adversity will overcome them away from faith and love of him.

He next explains what kind of wisdom and revelation he wants God to give them. “May he give you the eyes of your heart enlightened” [Col. 1217A]: that is, may he make the sight of your mind and reason clear and penetrating. This means: may he so enlighten your reason that, once the shadow of imagined appearances has been removed, your reason may clearly perceive what reward is hoped for from faith—namely, eternal life with the angels. And this is: “that you may know what is the hope of his calling,” that is, of faith in him.
