That is, may he so illuminate your inward eyes that you may understand what reward will be given for faith in him to those who persevere steadfastly in it, to which you were called through the Gospel.

Or, “what is the hope of his calling” means what kind and how great is the glory which you hope for and to which he has called you: how precious is the highest blessedness which you hope to attain through him who called you to his faith. And may you know “what are the riches of glory”—that is, the abundance of blessedness: how sufficient, manifold, and plentiful is the blessedness of that glorious inheritance which the saints, perfected in the completion of virtues, will possess jointly by secure right. For these riches will be among the saints. Or, may you understand that that blessedness is as great as it is among the saints: that is, as great as they themselves possess or understand it to be.

And may you know what and how great is the greatness of his power in us apostles: that is, how generously and abundantly his power came upon us, so that, enlightened by spiritual knowledge and strengthened by the power of the Holy Spirit, we feared nothing, but with great authority opposed kings and tyrants, preached the Gospel everywhere, worked miracles powerfully, and destroyed every error. This greatness of power and strength [Col. 1217C] which was given to us beyond others is surpassing—that is, remaining above others—because more excellent gifts have been given to us than to others, so that they too after us may strive to advance to lofty virtue. This greatness, so exalted, is in us apostles who believed, because we believed more intensely and firmly than others.

It was sent down from God into us “according to the working of the might of his strength”: that is, according to the work which the power of God—that is, the force of God—performed. I mean a power of might, powerful in all things. Or: we believed according to the working of the might of his strength, attending to the mighty work of his power. And what power? Namely, that which he powerfully worked in Christ, raising him so that he was far removed [Col. 1217D] from the dead—that is, so that he should never again die, but abide in the power of immortality. For in this work the might of his power was shown to us.

And he set him—that is, established him together according to soul and body—at his right hand: that is, in the heavenly places, placed in his more powerful dignity, preferring him above every creature. For the right hand of God is eternal blessedness, which is given to the saints; just as his left hand is rightly called perpetual misery, in which the ungodly are. Christ is in the heavenly places so that his dignity may also be shown by his place. And he is also in place above every principality, authority, power, and dominion, so that by this he may be shown to have a greater dignity and a fuller felicity and blessedness than any spirit in these orders, since [Col. 1218A] he was made higher than the heavens, that is, than the angelic spirits.

These four orders of angels are also numbered in ascending order according to the book of Dionysius the Areopagite, *On the Celestial Hierarchy*. Principality is below authority, authority below power, power below dominion. Above dominion, however, is the order called throne, because God sits upon it. Therefore, when Christ is said to be exalted above dominion, it is plainly shown that he sits on the throne with the Father.

“Principalities” are those who preside even over the good angelic spirits themselves. Since, having others subject to them, they arrange for them what must be done in carrying out divine ministries, they exercise principality. One of them, unless I am mistaken, appeared to Joshua and said that he was captain of the Lord’s host (Joshua V). “Authorities,” however, are understood to be of more worthy power [Col. 1218B] than principalities, so that they powerfully preside over the orders of angels subject to them and powerfully extend themselves toward divine contemplation above them. “Powers” are those spirits who, more firmly than the rest assimilated to the power of divine strength, prevail mightily to do whatever they will. “Dominions” are so called because they are the noblest in that heavenly court, and rule over and possess all who are subject to them as lords.

Christ, who is our head, has been exalted above all these according to his humanity, so that we too, his members, may attain even to their fellowship and equality. Hence what was said above—“that you may know what is the surpassing greatness of his power, which he worked [Col. 1218C] in Christ, raising him from the dead and setting him at his right hand in the heavenly places”—may be understood concerning our resurrection: so that, just as Christ was magnificently raised and elevated into heaven, so we too, at the end of the age, may according to our measure be magnificently raised and lifted to the heavenly places.

For a marvelous and surpassing greatness of power—that is, one remaining wholly above all others—will come to us from God when, “in the twinkling of an eye, we shall rise and be changed” (1 Corinthians XV), and “be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so shall always be with him” (1 Thessalonians IV). As stated, he was exalted above all the angelic orders mentioned and above the other higher ones. And, to speak generally, he is above every name—that is, above every order or person [Col. 1218D] of great renown and great name—“that is named not only in this age,” such as Michael and Gabriel, “but also in the future age”: such as certain persons among the blessed spirits of greater dignity in that heavenly kingdom, whose fame and name will never reach us while we remain upon earth. That is, his dignity surpasses the dignity of all the greater heavenly creatures.

And the Father not only exalted him above all choirs or persons of angels, but also “subjected all things beneath his feet” (Psalm VIII). This is said by comparison. For just as one who has been subjected is trampled beneath feet and cannot resist the one trampling him, so all things are subject to Christ’s command and power and cannot oppose him. He subjected all things, so that they might be “under,” that is, inferior. The further word “under” denotes complete subjection: namely, that they neither dare nor are able to oppose his command.

By “feet” we understand his humanity, because just as the feet are the lower part of our body, so humanity is the lower nature of Christ. His divinity is his higher nature. This knowledge is to be understood as referring to the future, when on the day of judgment all will know themselves subject to him: some receiving the reward of life, others enduring the sentence of eternal death. And he gave this Lord, so great, so powerful, and so exalted, not because of our merit but by his grace alone, as head over all the good things of the Church’s virtues, so that he might be the head and source of all the Church’s goods; or as head above all the Church’s members, so that he might be head of greater and lesser believers alike.

Or, as it is found [Col. 1219B] in other books, “above the whole Church,” namely of Jews and Gentiles, so that no one might belong to the Church who did not have him as head. For just as all the members of the human body are governed by the head—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—so all the Church’s spiritual senses are in Christ: so that in him it may see God, hear his Word, taste how sweet the Lord is (Psalm XXXIII), draw in the fragrance of his knowledge, and touch him spiritually, saying: “But for me, it is good to cling to God” (Psalm LXXII).

He is head of the Church in a way far different from any commander being head of an army, because it is his body. For bridegroom and bride are one, as head and body. I mean the Church, “his fullness”: that is, his complete body. For no member is lacking there which is ordinarily in the human body. There are those who provide for others, like eyes; those who minister, like hands; those who speak the word of salvation, like a mouth; and so with the remaining members.

Christ is filled up not in himself, for he is so full and perfect that he cannot be increased, but in all his believers. And in what is he filled up in them? In every good thing that is in them: love, humility, patience, chastity, and the like. For Christ is all these things in his elect. And as these increase and multiply in them unto fullness, he is indeed filled up in them. He will also in the future be happily filled up into himself, so that God may be all in all.

Or, he now fills all things in all [Col. 1219D] as his members make daily progress according to their measure; and as, when those who are now the Church’s eyes or mouth die, others succeed them in their place, and likewise with the remaining members, so that the full number of members remains intact and continually increases through succession.

All that has been said serves to confirm them in faith in Christ, so that they may believe him to be true man and God, and to give perfect salvation to believers. It follows:

## CHAPTER II

> “And you, when you were dead in your trespasses and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of this air, the spirit which now works in the children of unbelief. In which we too all once [Col. 1220A] lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the will of the flesh and of the thoughts; and we were by nature children of wrath, as also the rest. But God, who is rich in mercy, because of his exceeding love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together in Christ—by whose grace you have been saved—and raised us together and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, that he might show in the ages to come the abundant riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus. For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves. For it is God’s gift, not from works, lest anyone should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we might walk in them.”

[Col. 1220B] The Apostle begins to dissuade them from, and to show superfluous, the carnal observances which he foresaw would be introduced by heretics. He also recalls their former evils, so that they may be humbled in view of the good things they had already received; and so that it may be certain that, if these things were given to enemies, much greater things will be given to friends. Therefore, lest they be puffed up by good things, he shows from what condition they were called to what dignity, saying that all benefits were given to them, or to the apostles, or to the whole human race, by God’s grace alone.

The text is connected thus: He raised Christ from the dead and elevated him to his right hand; and he also raised you together and made you sit in the heavenly places. But he inserted below the words, “But God, who is rich,” [Col. 1220C] in order to dissuade them from carnal observances and humble them by the remembrance of their former faults. It is as though he said: “God bodily raised Jesus Christ from the dead, and spiritually raised you with him from inward death, when you were dead in soul through your trespasses and sins.” For just as righteousness is the life of the soul, so sin is its death.

Some wish “trespass” to be understood as the consent of an evil will, and “sin” as the performance of the act; or, trespass is when someone neglects to do what God commands, while sin is when he presumes to do what is forbidden. The grace of God made you alive though dead through trespasses and sins. This strongly argues against carnal observances, because if they came from the death of the soul to life not through those observances but through grace as their guide, there is no reason for them to need these observances after receiving life.

You were dead because once—that is, before your conversion—you walked in those trespasses and sins. And you walked in them from one thing to another “according to the age of this world”: that is, following and imitating worldly people who seek these worldly things. Or, you walked according to the wickedness of this world, which “lies wholly in the evil one” (1 John V). For the higher world, that is, the kingdom of heaven, has another age in which righteousness reigns. Or, you followed this age because, just as in this age one time succeeds another, so sin always succeeded sin in you; thus you were comparable [Col. 1221A] to the age in the uninterrupted sequence of your sins.

I mean the age of this corruptible and transitory world, whose followers are continually corrupted by diverse vices and swiftly fall into destruction. And you not only walked in the way of iniquity according to this age, but also “according to the prince of the power of this air”: that is, according to what the prince who has power in this air persuaded you, whether to tempt unbelievers or to stir the air itself. Those walk according to this prince of iniquity who sin according to his will.

He is prince of the aerial power because he rules over the host of demons, who are the power of the air because they can move about in it and provide suggestions to human beings. Or, Satan himself has power in this same dark air [Col. 1221B] near the earth, as we have said, to fly about in persuading people to evil or sometimes to stir storms to human harm, as he did against Job (Job I–II). And who is this prince? A spirit—that is, not a bodily substance but an incorporeal one. This also suggests that they were deeply involved in sins, because a spirit—an invisible thing against which they did not know how to guard themselves—attacked them. For a person is more dangerously attacked by an invisible thing than by a visible one, because if he saw his enemy, he might perhaps guard himself.

“This spirit now works in the children of unbelief”: that is, in those who wish to retain carnal observances, who distrust Christ, not believing that he suffices for righteousness and salvation unless they add carnal observances besides. They are called children of unbelief because the distrust of unbelief begot them in this error—that is, caused them to distrust. The devil works in them so that they may distrust Christ and now seek carnal ceremonies—that is, after Christ’s coming, who is the true light and removed the shadow of the old observances by the manifestation of truth.

It is as though it were said: Since the evil one works these things even after Truth has appeared—that is, since it is still his work to cause distrust—see that you do not perhaps distrust. This serves the argument. For if, while they were still entangled in so great and such a multiplicity of sins, they were freed by grace alone and not by carnal observances, it is clear that after liberation they would hold them superfluously.

Or, “in the children of unbelief” means in those who, [Col. 1221D] because of their many sins, distrust eternal goods and despair of their salvation: the devil now works in them, that is, after they had been snatched from his hand. Or, they are called children of unbelief because Mother Church distrusts their salvation, observing in them the working of the most wicked spirit.

But lest the Ephesians seem to have been entangled in such grave sins because they had not applied themselves to carnal observances, he shows that those serving these ceremonies were likewise implicated in a multitude of sins. And this is the point: “In these trespasses and sins, not only you who do not have carnal observances, but also we who kept them—we who are now such great apostles—we all,” he says, “once lived”: that is, we were occupied in every kind of vice before our conversion, in the desires of our flesh, that is, in its concupiscences. And we were doing the will of the flesh—that is, we fulfilled in deed what our carnality demanded, according to lust, gluttony, and the other things pertaining to the pleasure of the flesh—and doing the will of the thoughts, according to anger, pride, ambition, and the other vices which are in the heart and not in bodily pleasure.

If, however, “of our flesh” is read thus—

> **[Note: Col. 1221D. An obscure passage.]**

—I say that we were in trespasses when we remained in the desires of our flesh, that is, in the intensity of concupiscence supplied by the flesh. He wished “in desires” to indicate more than concupiscence: namely, the manifold and all-encompassing intensity of concupiscence which they incurred through the Law. Hence he says to the Romans: “For when we were in the flesh, the passions of sins which are through the Law were working in our members” (Romans VII). And again: “Sin, through the commandment, worked in me every concupiscence” (ibid.).

And therefore, coming under the curse of death, we were children of wrath: that is, children of vengeance, children of Gehenna; and this by nature, that is, by original sin, just as were the rest who had not received the Law. For all mortals are born under God’s wrath, and when the first man sinned, vice grew ingrained in place of nature. But through God’s grace some are made children of adoption from children of wrath; this cannot be accomplished through the Law. Therefore carnal Jews, though they had the Law, nevertheless remained children of wrath as they had been born, just like the other peoples of the earth who were without Law.

By this he wished to indicate that the Law had no power to relieve sins, since those who observed its legal precepts were liable to God’s wrath just as were those others who did not know the Law’s commands. All this is said of the Law alone, without the addition of grace. It all serves to commend grace, and thus to overthrow carnal observances: because, though they were dead through a multiplicity of sins while even serving those ceremonies, God’s grace made them alive together—a thing the Law could not do.

You were dead, and we likewise; and by corrupted nature we were children of wrath. But God, who is rich in mercy [Col. 1222D] (Romans V), because according to the abundant riches of his mercy he remitted through baptism all sins, original and actual—so that where sin abounded, grace might superabound—on account of his exceedingly great love toward us, surpassing all understanding, by which God loved us, when he caused his Son, coeternal with himself, to be incarnate and to die: while we were spiritually dead in sins, he made us alive together in Christ. That is, he gave us life together with Christ by forgiveness of sins, innocence, and the completion of virtues; just as he attributed to Christ perpetuity of life in eternal blessedness, so he granted us the true life of innocence and righteousness.

By the grace of this Christ, you Ephesians and the other Gentiles have been saved, as we also have been, through forgiveness, innocence, and righteousness. And he not only made us alive together, but also “raised us together”: that is, in hope he has already raised us with Christ, so that, just as Christ has risen, we may in the certainty of hope await our resurrection. He also “made us sit together”: that is, in hope he made us sit with Christ as judges in eternal blessedness, and this in heavenly places, or among heavenly beings. For sitting signifies judgment, because one who judges is accustomed to sit. He will therefore make us sit with Christ because he will make us judge with him. Indeed, he has already raised us with him and made us sit with him in the heavenly places, because although our body is not yet there, our hope [Col. 1223B] is already there. And all this is in Christ Jesus: that is, in his power, strength, and grace.

All these points greatly serve the argument, because, since grace alone, rich grace, gives all these things, carnal observances are vainly introduced afterward. Therefore, by his predestination and through our hope, he has already made us sit together, in order that he might show in the ages to come beyond these temporal ages—that is, in the ages of eternity, or in the ages that will come after us in this world—the abundant riches: namely, eternal blessedness, which will be so rich that no one there will lack anything; or the abundantly rich and copious gift of his benefits. I mean riches of his grace: given on account of his grace, and in his goodness, not in consideration of our merits, “for his mercy is better than lives” [Col. 1223C] (Psalm LXII).

And these great riches will be upon us: that is, far greater than we are worthy to receive. Or, they will be above us: that is, they will exceed every capacity of our understanding, because they will be so great and such as eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has the heart of man conceived (1 Corinthians II). For so much will be given as the mind cannot investigate. What understanding could sufficiently grasp how great are the joys of that heavenly city: to join the choirs of angels, stand in the glory of the Creator with the most blessed spirits, behold God’s present face, see unbounded light, be touched by no fear of death, and rejoice in the gift of perpetual incorruption?

All these things are given in Christ Jesus: that is, in Christ’s power, grace, and generosity. Why, then, should carnal observances be introduced after these things? Truly God’s grace possesses abundant riches, for by his grace you have been saved and cleansed from sins, and this through faith—that is, faith intervening—because you believed that you could be saved by grace. Yet this is not from yourselves, but from God who calls, because you received faith from hearing the Gospel. For faith itself, or your calling, is God’s gift; and not partly, but purely God’s gift, because it is not from your works—that is, there is no admixture of works in it—lest anyone boast that he has faith from works or has been saved by his own works without grace.

Here the Apostle seems to suggest that they boasted of works, not of God’s grace. But he especially wishes to boast of his own works [Col. 1224A] who seeks, or thinks he has received, faith and righteousness through carnal observances. And truly you have been saved by grace, not by your own works, which you have from yourselves, but only by those works in which he made you—that is, formed and created you (Genesis I). This is what is meant by: “For we are his workmanship, both we and you, created in Christ Jesus for good works”; not by that creation through which we were made human beings, but by the creation of which one who was certainly already a human being said: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Psalm L). This Apostle also praises the new creation elsewhere (Galatians VI).

Therefore we were made and created for good works, because, with the restoration of free choice, freedom to act well was given us: that is, we were made capable of acting well. This was done in Christ Jesus, that is, in his grace, not in [Col. 1224B] our merit. God prepared these good works beforehand by predestining them, preceding our choice. For every good has its origin in God’s grace. And he prepared them so that we might walk in them: that is, advance and progress from good to better. Since he saved us in these ways, it is clear that we have been saved by his grace. And if we have been saved by his grace, then carnal observances are introduced in vain.

> “Therefore remember that you were once Gentiles in the flesh, called ‘the foreskin’ by that which is called ‘circumcision,’ made in the flesh by hands; because at that time you were without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants, without hope of the promise and without God in this world. But now in Christ [Col. 1224C] Jesus you who were once far off have been made near in the blood of Christ.”

He had compared Jews and Gentiles, showing that both had been under sin. Now he shows that the Gentiles had been more unworthy and had endured the reproaches of the Jews, so that, now made equal with the Jews, they might be more indebted to the grace of God. It is as though he said: Since you are God’s workmanship, created in good works, do not forget from what baseness of vices to what height of virtues God has raised you, so that you may render him greater thanksgiving for such benefits as he has bestowed upon you. And this is: “Therefore,” that is, because God rescued you from evils and enriched you with good things, “remember that formerly,” that is, long ago before your conversion, [Col. 1224D] “you were Gentiles,” that is, such as you had been born; and not only according to origin, but also “in the flesh,” that is, according to the flesh—according to the will and appetite of the flesh—because you did everything that fleshly pleasure suggested.

I speak of you, who were sinners to such an extent that you were despised even by the sinful people of the Jews, who reproached you as being “the uncircumcision,” that is, uncircumcised. And this is: “who are called,” that is, who are called by this name of reproach, “the uncircumcision,” because by that member of the male more especially they are inflamed toward fleshly pleasure, stung by lust, and defiled by impurity; and this by that people which is full of sins, yet is truly called “circumcision in the flesh,” not in the spirit, and “made by hands,” not by God. For the flesh alone [Col. 1225A] was cut away, not the evil thought of the heart.

And you were rightly despised, because at that time you were conspicuous in wickedness, “without Christ,” that is, without faith in or knowledge of Christ. You were alienated and separated from “the commonwealth of Israel,” that is, from the Jewish people, because they disdained to live with you. And you were strangers to the covenants: that is, if any one of you came to Judaism, he was received in the Law as a guest and foreigner, and was considered insignificant among the Jews. He calls the Law “covenants” in the plural because of the many promises made to its worshippers, and because the New Testament was contained in the Old Testament.

I speak of you as not formerly having “the hope of promise,” that is, hoping in no promise, because you neither hoped for those things promised to Abraham (Gen. XXII), nor those promised [Col. 1225B] to David (Ps. CXXXI), nor those promised to the other fathers. Therefore the hope of that divine promise was not yours, because you were “without God,” that is, without knowledge of God the Father, in this world, so evil a world, which lies wholly in the evil one (1 John V). What he now says, “without God,” that is, without recognition and grace of God the Father, is what he had said, “without Christ,” that is, without knowledge and grace of Christ; because whoever does not know the Father does not know the Son either; or whoever does not have the Son does not have the Father; and whoever has the one has the other also.

Such you once were; but now, that is, after receiving grace, “in Christ Jesus,” that is, through Christ’s power and generosity, you who were formerly, before conversion, far from God—not in body, but [Col. 1225C] in heart and merits—have been made near to him, or to all the things mentioned above, from which you were far removed; and this “in the blood of Christ,” that is, through the power of Christ’s bloodshed. For that blood possessed such efficacy that through it all these things could be obtained. Unless it had flowed forth, none of the aforesaid good things would have come to us. You received all these things both through the power of Christ Jesus and through the efficacy of his shed blood, not through fleshly observances.

Therefore, if at that time, when you were so manifoldly distant from God, as has been noted, you had no need of fleshly observances but were saved by grace alone, in the grace and blood of Christ, much less do you need them now, when you have already received your salvation. Christ alone, therefore, is to be firmly held and loved by you: he rescued you from such great evils and made you equals and companions of the faithful Hebrews.

> “For he himself is our peace, who made both one, and, dissolving the middle wall of partition, the enmities in his flesh, abolishing the law of commandments by decrees, that he might create the two in himself into one new man, making peace; that he might reconcile both to God in one body through the cross, slaying the enmities in himself. And coming, he preached peace to you who were far off, and peace to those who were near; because through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father.”

Truly the blood of Christ has brought you near to God, in union with the Israelites and with the covenant and promises, because Christ himself is our peace: that is, he has made us at peace with God and [Col. 1226A] with the angels, and has made Jews and Gentiles—formerly discordant through their different rites—harmonious in faith. For peace makes persons peaceful, just as righteousness makes persons righteous. He himself is our peace, “who made both one,” that is, who made the Jewish and Gentile peoples unanimous in faith, in the worship of the one God, and in morals.

And how he did this is added: “dissolving the middle wall of partition.” By the wall he means circumcision, which divided the Jewish people from the Gentile. For just as a middle wall divides place from place, so circumcision separated people from people. At Christ’s coming this wall became a dry-stone wall (*maceria*), because circumcision, which before his coming could not be abolished, could easily be destroyed after he came. A *maceria* is so called, as it were, from a “thin row” (*macra series*). It is a heap [Col. 1226B] of stones with no cement binding them together, which collapses under a slight blow. A wall, on the other hand, is called a row of stones bound and fastened with cement, and it is not easy to cast it down.

Thus circumcision, confirmed by the Lord’s command until the time of reformation, could not be abolished; but at the time of reformation, weakened by God’s will, it was made subject to ruin. He fittingly says “dissolving the wall,” because circumcision, which before Christ’s coming was bound by the bond of a commandment, was dissolved at his coming: no command now compelled its observance. Nor did he make both one merely by dissolving circumcision, but also by dissolving “the enmities in his flesh.” He calls idolatry the enmities. For the Jewish people were hostile to the Gentile people serving idols, and the Gentiles to the Jewish people despising idols.

He rightly [Col. 1226C] called idolatry “enmities,” and not a wall, while calling circumcision a wall. For before the time of reformation circumcision belonged to the structure of the Law’s righteousness, because the Law commanded that circumcision be performed; but idolatry was never at all part of God’s structure, because it was always contrary to God. He destroyed the enmities, and this “in his flesh,” that is, through his incarnation: namely, because he became incarnate, idolatry was abolished. After he took flesh, he chose disciples to enlighten the Gentiles with the teaching of truth. And it was properly said that he “dissolved” idolatry, because the Gentiles had been constrained and bound by the chain of custom.

Or the obstacle of the Law is called the wall, because the legal observances were like [Col. 1226D] a wall separating Gentiles from Jews. I say, a wall of dry-stone construction, that is, one easily destroyed when grace came. This wall stood in the middle so that neither people agreed with the other. For while this wall stood, there was enmity, anger, and envy between them. Therefore it had to be destroyed, so that the enmities might be destroyed. And this was accomplished in Christ’s assumed or sacrificed flesh: appearing in the flesh and rising from the dead, he caused the whole Law to cease, and, removing every obstacle and disagreement, joined both peoples in his faith.

Or the wall was the obscurity of the Law and the prophets, blocking our way of life and placing itself between us and God. By his flesh and passion Christ dissolved the middle wall and the dry-stone barrier, that is, the obscurity of the ancient prophets, and [Col. 1227A] opened the sacraments of the entire ancient Law. Having dispersed the difficulty of proceeding, he revealed the way to the eyes of all, so that whoever wishes to go to God may be hindered by no barrier or frightened by the darkness of obscurity. Hence, when he gave up his spirit on the cross, the veil of the Temple was torn in the middle and the Holy of Holies was opened to all. That veil signifies the same thing as this wall.

Christ also dissolved, in the sacrifice of his flesh, the enmities between us and God. And he did all this by “abolishing,” that is, destroying and reducing to nothing, “the law of commandments,” that is, the other fleshly observances besides circumcision, since circumcision has already been discussed. Fleshly observances are aptly called commandments because they were not permanent but changeable, just as things commanded can [Col. 1227B] be and usually are altered. I say, abolishing them “by his decrees,” that is, by unchangeable ordinances firmly established on rational grounds—namely, the precepts of the New Testament, to which another covenant succeeds.

We are accustomed to call a decree that which is ratified and authorized by God, so that it is not lawful to change it. Therefore, since those were commandments, that is, transitory things, while these are decrees, that is, permanent things, those—namely, fleshly observances—are rightly abolished by these, namely, the precepts of the New Testament. Where the New Testament enjoins baptism and faith, there the Old Testament, according to its fleshly ceremonies, is abolished.

He himself did all this—dissolving the enmities and abolishing the Law—so that he might create, that is, join, the two peoples formerly divided by the Law so fully that both might go together “into himself,” [Col. 1227C] that is, into Christ: namely, so that both alike might tend toward the one new man who is Christ, have unity and newness in him, and together maintain conformity with him. I say, “making peace”: after destroying enmities between them, so that one may not trouble the other but may love the other as himself. For peace, that is, the removal of disturbance, is the stage by which one comes to the union of love.

What he says, “making peace,” differs from what he said above, “For he himself is our peace.” The former declares him to be peace itself, which makes those at discord peaceful; the latter, “making peace,” denotes that he is the mediator and author of peace. Further, each expression is used for a different purpose. That is, his being peace is stated [Col. 1227D] to show that those who were far away have been made near in Christ Jesus; whereas “making peace” is stated to show by what stage one reaches charity. And what he says—“that he might create the two peoples in himself”—differs from “who made both one,” which we understand according to faith; but we understand creating the two in himself according to charity.

Having thus shown how Christ joined each people to the other, he next wishes to show how he reconciled both to God. It is as though he said: He joined the two in himself so that he might reconcile both, placed in the one body of Christ, which is the Church, to God the Father. He did this “through the cross”: that is, the cross was the way by which reconciliation was attained. For unless Christ had [Col. 1228A] offered himself as a victim to the Father on the cross, our reconciliation with God would not have taken place.

“Slaying the enmities in himself.” This is as though it were said: When he reconciled us to God through the cross, he did not do this through a cross endured by another; rather, he did so as to slay, that is, blot out, the enmities which God justly had against us because of the fault of the first parent and the guilt of our sins. And he did this not in the body of another, such as a prophet or apostle, but in himself. For he himself made satisfaction to God for us, enduring sufferings and reproaches in our place, which we deserved to endure. Since reconciliation between us and God has been accomplished through him, fleshly ceremonies are therefore vainly observed after this.

And he not only makes peace on the cross, but, even before he ascended the cross, [Col. 1228B] “coming,” that is, appearing in the flesh, “preached peace,” that is, announced it well with his own mouth, to you Gentiles who were far from him—that is, who had departed into idolatry—and peace to those who were near, that is, to the Jews, because they worshipped one God. He preached this peace when he said, “I have other sheep,” and so forth, up to “and one shepherd” (John X); and likewise, “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John XIV).

He rightly proclaimed peace to us with one another and with God, because through him both peoples have access, that is, the ability to approach God the Father, and this “in one Spirit,” that is, in the united will of faith, religion, and charity, so that we may have one heart and one soul (Acts IV). Or “in one Spirit” means in the Holy Spirit, who is one and the same, though he distributes diverse gifts. We approach the Father according to conformity with his goodness, and in the future according to participation in his blessedness. [Col. 1228C] Since all these things have been done and are done through Christ, why should fleshly observances be introduced any further?

> “Therefore you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone. In him all the building, joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord. In him you also are built together into a dwelling-place of God in the Holy Spirit.”

Since you Gentiles have become one with the Jews in Christ and have equally been reconciled to God, therefore [Col. 1228D] from the time of faith you are no longer strangers to the covenants and foreigners, as you formerly were. The Gentiles were strangers and foreigners among those who possessed the covenants, either because, after the manner of guests, they came and departed for a time, or because those among them who converted to the Jewish rite were called foreigners, that is, proselytes. For guests are people in transit.

But now they were no longer strangers to the covenants, because they did not regard these covenants only in passing and then depart from them, but remained continually and were instructed in them, observing them as was fitting. Foreigners are those who, though not native-born, dwell in a place from which they do not originate. But once these people had become one with those who were, as it were, natives [Col. 1229A] of the covenants, they were reckoned no longer as aliens but as natives, so that they might be one with those among whom they were, because they possessed the covenants as naturally, so to speak, as those who had first possessed them. For divine grace granted the New Testament equally to both, and also the Old according to its spiritual sense. Moreover, Gentiles were no longer foreigners to the covenant but natives, because they had been regenerated through baptism, which is preached in both Testaments. For in one it is said, “I will pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements” (Ezek. XXXVI); in the other, “Go, baptize all nations” (Matt. XXVIII).

You are no longer strangers to the covenants—that is, pilgrims or inferior to the Hebrews in faith, as was formerly received under the Law—and foreigners, that is, outsiders and exiles; but you are “fellow citizens with the saints,” that is, of the same right and dignity in the city of God. You are citizens not of carnal Israel but of the saints, because you dwell in the one city which is the Church together with the saints. For you have fellowship with the saints in all the sacraments of the Church, though you were formerly alienated from the commonwealth of Israel.

You are not only fellow citizens with the saints, but also “members of God’s household,” that is, God’s familiars and friends in his house, according to the great perfection of knowledge and virtues and according to the great love which he has for you. For he loves his household members more intimately, reveals to them as friends the secrets of his mysteries, and grants them most abundant gifts. You, who were once without God, are now members of God’s household, built [Col. 1229C] in God’s building upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets—that is, upon the faith of Christ, upon which the apostles and prophets were first founded.

For Christ is the foundation of the entire divine temple or divine city, because every good thing begins from him and from his faith and grace, and he bears the entire spiritual building. Therefore he is the foundation of the apostles and prophets, because the apostles and prophets rest upon him and stand firm, and thereafter bear the whole structure of the holy building. He is the foundation: that is, his faith is the first firmness, the beginning, and the support of the entire structure of virtues and good works. Relying on this firmness of faith, you have been built upon in good works, [Col. 1229D] that is, you have advanced to higher things, growing from virtue to virtue.

And this was done in that chief cornerstone, namely Christ Jesus, who joins the two peoples in himself like two walls and is the strength of the whole building. He is a cornerstone in such a way that he is not only the foundation of the building—that is, not merely in its lower part—but is also supreme within the building itself. This stone is so supreme that no other cornerstone can be added above it. Those who seek to add fleshly observances and contend that they contribute to salvation wish to set another cornerstone above this one. But nothing can be placed above it. For he is the lower cornerstone according to faith, and also the supreme one according to the consummation of righteousness.

Or he is [Col. 1230A] the supreme stone, though he is the foundation, because the origin of this foundation occupies the highest place. As the foundation of a material structure is at the bottom, so the foundation of a spiritual structure is at the top. If we were being built toward the earth, the foundation would have to be placed below us. But because this is a heavenly structure, our foundation has gone before us into heaven.

In this foundation, in this chief stone, the whole building, both of Jews and Gentiles, constructed according to faith and reception of the sacraments, and according to innocence and righteousness, grows by advancing in virtues. For no one is so perfect that he cannot grow. Every one of the elect, great and small, grows as long as he is in this life. Indeed, one does not belong to the building of the elect, even if one bears the name of Christianity, [Col. 1230B] who does not strive to grow and increase in good things. Every building, whether of individual faithful persons or individual virtues, constructed in Christ, grows continually, going forward and advancing into a holy temple—that is, so as to become God’s holy and pure temple. And this whole thing is “in the Lord,” that is, through the Lord’s operation, because the Lord accomplishes it, not any fleshly observance.

In this Christ not only are Jews built up, but you Gentiles also are “built together”: that is, you are built with them in righteousness as equally as the Jews, and so fully that you may become a dwelling-place of God—that is, a house and sanctuary of God. And this is “in the Holy Spirit,” that is, through the operation of the Holy Spirit, not through fleshly observances.

## Chapter III

[Col. 1230C]

> “For this cause I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus for you Gentiles—if indeed you have heard of the dispensation of the grace of God which was given to me in you: because by revelation the mystery was made known to me, as I wrote above briefly, so that, when you read, you can understand my insight into the mystery of Christ, which in other generations was not made known to the children of men as it has now been revealed in the Spirit to his holy apostles and prophets: that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and fellow participants in the promise in Christ Jesus through the Gospel, of which I became a minister according to the gift of the grace of God [Col. 1230D] which was given to me according to the working of his power.”

“For this cause,” that is, for this thing pleasing to me—namely, that you may be built together—or in order to fulfil the grace of God in this matter (1 Cor. XV), “I, Paul, am a prisoner.” He states the means by which they have been built together: namely, because God revealed to him that salvation pertains to the Gentiles, sent him to preach to them, and causes him to suffer for them, so that they may be more grateful to God.

“I, Paul, am a prisoner of Christ Jesus,” that is, for the service and name of Christ; or I am a prisoner in his power and will, because whenever he wishes, he will release me. [Col. 1231A] Or, I am a prisoner for Christ’s Gospel, not for the devil, like those who are held in chains for their crimes. I am Christ’s prisoner, and this “for you Gentiles,” to whom I preached the way of salvation; or “for you,” because my being Christ’s prisoner tends to your benefit—that is, it is useful to you. For the merit of the shepherd brings advancement to the flock. At that time the Apostle was held in prison at Rome.

But since the shepherd’s merit will not benefit the sheep unless they conduct themselves as Christian religion requires, he adds: “if indeed you have heard” with the ear of the heart, that is, if you have understood “the dispensation of the grace of God,” namely the apostleship dispensed to me by God, who knows why he chose me for this office. Or, “dispensation” means the office of dispensing and preaching the grace of God, that is, God’s gratuitous benefit bestowed upon all. If you have understood my dispensing of God’s grace—that is, if you have understood that his gratuitous gifts which I have dispensed to you, namely remission of sins, innocence, virtues, [Col. 1231B] charisms, knowledge, faith, teaching, and the like—were freely bestowed upon you by God, not by any merit or by fleshly observances. For if you do not believe that these are freely given by God, you are not sound in faith. And if you do not have sound faith, my merit will avail you nothing.

It is as though he said: My imprisonment will benefit you if you understand that what I have dispensed to you is God’s free gift, so that you ascribe nothing to your merits and place no confidence whatever in fleshly observances. He used “you have heard,” not “you have believed,” in order to indicate that this point is so fitting and close to reason that it deserves not only faith but also understanding.

The dispensation truly is a free gift of God, freely bestowed upon you, because the dispensation itself was given to me: that is, the very [Col. 1231C] office of dispensing was given to me, and this for your conversion and edification, so that through my dispensing you might be converted and established in God’s building. Or the office of my dispensation is already abiding in you, since you have already received it, through God’s grace, with the ear of the heart and your inward hearing.

And if I have this dispensation only by grace, it is then plain that you have knowledge of God, remission of sins, justification, and the other things which I have dispensed to you only by grace. After this he gives an argument to demonstrate the same point—that he has freely received what he dispenses to them—and this indirectly. For when he shows that he has it freely, he proves that they likewise have it freely.

[Col. 1231D] It is as though he said: The dispensation was freely given to me, because “by revelation”—divine revelation, not human teaching nor my own powers—the mystery was made known to me: that is, something hidden of God was divinely revealed to me, openly communicated rather than obscurely. I have no knowledge of this matter beyond what God has revealed and uncovered to me; that is, I have nothing from myself, but everything from grace alone. And if I possess by grace whatever I dispense to you, then you too possess everything by grace.

God’s goodness revealed to me the sacrament, that is, a mystery hidden from many persons: namely, that you Gentiles were to be incorporated with the Jews in unity of faith and were to possess the same glory as the Jews. God made known the sacrament to me, [Col. 1232A] “as I wrote above briefly”: that is, it was divinely made known to me in the way I set out above when I said, “For he himself is your peace, who made both one,” and the other things there briefly said concerning the mystery of Christ and the fellowship of the two peoples. That is, I then wrote nothing about the mystery which had not been revealed to me by God through the spirit of prophecy, and which I therefore possess only from the grace of God.

It was made known to me “as you can understand when you read,” that is, insofar as you can perceive by attentive and sustained reading in the passage mentioned above: “For he himself is our peace,” and so forth—“my insight,” that is, the wisdom and understanding which I possess concerning the mystery of Christ. That is: the mystery was made known to me to the degree shown by the preceding passage, which demonstrates that I possess insight into Christ’s mystery, insofar as it directs diligent students toward understanding that mystery. For through that passage, though we may not know it, we can nevertheless be led to a manifold understanding of the mystery of Christ.

Perhaps the blessed Jerome may expound that passage in one way, Ambrose in another, and the great Augustine in another; and the Apostle was made aware of every understanding that may be drawn from it—namely, from that mystery of Christ. The whole point is as though he briefly said: The sacrament was made known to me to the extent—that is, with the multiplicity—with which it can be understood in that passage of Scripture: “For he himself is our peace,” and so forth. [Col. 1232B] He said this so that his authority might thereby be commended; and, once his authority had been commended, they might give greater [Col. 1232C] faith to his teaching, which dissuades them from the commandments of the Law.

This sacrament or mystery “was not made known,” that is, made closely and fully known, “to the children of men,” that is, rational human beings—whether carnal or spiritual sons of the patriarchs and prophets—“in other generations,” that is, in past times. Although the ancient saints knew that the Gentiles would come to faith, they did not know that they would come to the same height of life and glory to which the Jews, worshipping one God, would come. Moreover, this was hidden from them: that they would be saved without the Law.

This mystery was not made known to them so fully as now—that is, as it was revealed in the time of grace to those to whom it ought to be revealed, namely to his holy apostles, who were sent to preach it, [Col. 1232D] and to prophets under the new grace, among whom was Agabus (Acts II). And it was communicated to them “in the Holy Spirit,” that is, through the Holy Spirit.

What this mystery is he then adds: namely, that the Gentiles are “fellow heirs,” that is, together with the Jews they will possess one inheritance in heaven; “members of the same body,” that is, together with those Jews they will remain in the one present body of the Church, so that they may be members of the Church as honorable as the Jews; and “fellow participants in the promise” of eternal life, so that the promise may belong to Gentiles equally with Jews, and both may be raised equally in obtaining it.

All these things take place “in Christ Jesus,” that is, because Christ assumed flesh and enlightened the world through himself and the apostles. For the Gentiles have all these things [Col. 1233A] through the Gospel, that is, through receiving and observing the Gospel which I administer to them. Christ’s incarnation would not benefit them unless it were preached. “Of this Gospel I became a minister”; it is not mine. And my becoming its minister was not according to my merits, but according to “the gift of grace,” that is, God’s freely given gift of grace, which was given to me “according to the working of his power”: that is, according to the working of that power by which he raised Christ, in whom he might raise us all from the death of the soul and save us without works of the Law. Since I have the ministry of the Gospel by grace, it is plain that you too have by grace whatever you received through hearing the Gospel which I preached to you.

[Col. 1233B]

> “To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given: to preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to enlighten all as to what is the dispensation of the mystery hidden from ages in God, who created all things, so that through the Church the manifold wisdom of God may be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places, according to the predetermination of the ages which he accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord, in whom we have boldness and access in confidence through faith in him.”

Grace, he says, was given to me, the least of all the saints. Out of excessive humility he calls himself the least of all the saints, setting forth in himself a great example of humility; or he was the least of all the saints, [Col. 1233C] that is, more humbled—namely, afflicted by every kind of tribulation—than any other saint. For the Jews and Gentiles persecuted him far more than any of the others. To me, the least, this grace was given among the Gentiles, that is, the ministry; and this, as was said above, according to the working of His power, that is, so that the working of God’s power follows it, because, for the confirmation of my preaching, God works miracles through me. It was given to me, that is, freely granted by God for usefulness. This grace was given to me, namely, to preach the unsearchable riches of Christ: that is, His many gifts abundantly and lavishly bestowed upon us, which are so rich and great that they can by no understanding whatever be fully searched out—since God deigned to become man for human beings, Life to die [Col. 1233D] for the dead, and the Just One to be sacrificed for sinners; and to show the light of truth to all nations throughout the world, to give faith, and to grant sinners forgiveness, righteousness, gifts of grace, and other such things. It cannot be perfectly investigated how great these are and of what kind.

These riches are also unsearchable in this respect: they are given to some and not to others, and we cannot investigate why this happens. For when many are inwardly touched by the word of preaching and by the gift of heavenly grace in their minds so as to believe, while others are not touched, who but God alone can know why these are chosen and those left behind? Therefore the riches of Christ’s gifts are unsearchable.

Nor was I sent only to preach these riches, [Col. 1234A] but also to enlighten, that is, clearly and lucidly to teach everyone what—or how wondrous, and proceeding from how great a love—is the dispensation of the mystery: that is, how wonderfully the mystery of Christ’s incarnation, passion, and resurrection was arranged by God the Father, through which the Gentiles might become fellow-heirs, members of the same body, and fellow-partakers. This mystery had been hidden in the divine mind from the ages, that is, from the first beginning of the ages, when created things began together with the ages; for from the time that the ages took their beginning, it was revealed to no one as it has now been revealed to the apostles. He says this “in order to show that much credence ought to be given to one to whom so great a mystery has been revealed.”

By this same point he shows that this dispensation comes about by grace alone. This is evident from the fact that it had been hidden [Col. 1234B] from the ages, because neither human merits nor carnal observances could reveal it. It is rightly called a dispensation of the mystery because God apportions that mystery differently: He grants some a greater share in being fellow-partakers, fellow-members, and fellow-heirs, and others a lesser share.

I say, of the mystery hidden in God, because it remained in God in such a way that it did not proceed outside God, but lay concealed in the secrecy of His counsel. For God has within Himself hidden causes of certain deeds, which He did not implant in created things. He fulfills these not in that work of providence by which He established natures so that they might exist, but in that by which He administers them as He wills—the natures which He created as He willed. There is grace, through which sinners are saved. For in the world the rational causes of all things that will arise naturally are hidden, just as Levi was hidden in Abraham’s loins; but the causes of those things which are to come about through grace are hidden in God.

Thus too this mystery of our salvation, by which the Gentiles would be made equal to the Jews in holiness and glory, so that there would be no other future order at all, was hidden in God, who created all things, because He alone, the Creator, knew what He was going to do with His creatures. The grace of preaching was given to me so that my preaching might have effect in the Church, and through the Church—that is, through what is done among the manifold members, orders, or works of the Church—so that there might become known, that is, inwardly, more subtly, and more fully known, to the principalities and powers, that is, to the higher and more powerful orders of angels [Col. 1234C–D] who are in heaven, the manifold wisdom of God, with respect to the various and many works which He performs in the Church, not insofar as it is simple and unchangeable in God.

For they who stood before Him from the beginning knew it in this respect from the beginning. In itself this wisdom is not manifold but simple; yet, because of its many works which it wisely disposes, it is called manifold, because it adapts many forms of works. And in this respect the angelic spirits also advanced through the Church in knowledge of this wisdom, because, while Christ instructed the Church either through Himself or through the apostles, the angels learned many secrets which they had not known. Great, then, is the dispensation of the mystery, in which even the angelic powers learned or are learning; and great faith ought to be given to the words [Col. 1235A] of him who dispenses so great a mystery.

The wisdom is made known to the principalities, and this according to the foreordination of the ages: that is, it is made known to the extent that God foredetermined and preordained concerning the ages, that is, concerning the human beings who live in the ages—namely, those who were to exist from the first establishment of the Church until the consummation of the age. He calls them “ages” because they are mutable and transitory like the ages, that is, like the course of passing days. This foreordination He made in Christ Jesus: that is, God foreordained all these things in Christ, not in carnal observances or in any merit of ours.

Or the wisdom of God is manifold according to the foreordination of the ages, because, according to those things which He foreordained—that is, ordered beforehand to occur in the ages—it appears [Col. 1235B] manifold, since these vary manifoldly in their works. And God made this foreordination in Christ Jesus our Lord, since before the ages the Father determined beforehand in the Son what He would do in the ages; in whom we have confidence, that is, in whose help, Christ’s, we have hope and confidence of approaching the Lord—and not hope only, but the approach itself, both according to good works and according to reward.

In Him we have confidence to overcome tribulations or to obtain the heavenly inheritance, and, after the end of this present life, actual access to God; and this in confidence, that is, by the merit of the confidence held through faith in Him—namely, because through faith in Him, which we have kept undefiled, we have placed complete confidence in Him alone and have attributed nothing of our confidence [Col. 1235C] to our merits or to carnal observances.

> “Therefore I ask that you do not lose heart in my tribulations for you, which are your glory. For this reason I bend my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, that He may grant you, according to the riches of His glory, strength to be strengthened through His Spirit in the inner person, that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts; being rooted and grounded in love, so that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth; and also to know the love [Col. 1235D] of Christ which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled unto all the fullness of God.”

In Christ, as was said above, we have confidence and access to the Father in confidence through faith in Him. Therefore I ask you to be confident and steadfast in faith, through which you will attain so great a glory. As has often been shown above, you received all good things from the grace of God which went before you; it remains now for you, by the choice of your free will, to follow that same grace, persevering in it and doing good works. For I ask you on account of the choice of your will.

I ask that you do not fail in sincerity and steadfastness of faith and in perseverance in good works because of my tribulations; that is, the tribulations [Col. 1236A] which you have heard that I suffer for you, to whom I preached, must not be a cause of failing for you. Rather, stand firm in the grace which I announced to you, not being ashamed of my chains nor afraid of suffering similar things. Or, my tribulations are for you, that is, they pertain to your benefit and profit you. This matter—that I suffer tribulations for you—is your glory. For it is a glory to you, not a disgrace as unbelievers suppose, to have such a teacher. And you will be rewarded with a great reward of glory if you do not now despise me in tribulations but remain in firm faith.

I ask that you do not fail. Since you have freedom of choice, I ask. But because your own choice is insufficient to accomplish what I ask, for this reason—that is, so that you may not fail—[Col. 1236B] I bend my knees in prayer for you. For the Apostle offers prayer for them so that God may grant perseverance and an increase of virtues and knowledge. By the bending of the knees we understand the humility of the suppliant. For knees are customarily bent in prayer so that inward humility may be signified and the affection of prayer may be commended by a humbler entreaty. Perhaps the Apostle, bound fast in chains, was unable to bend the knees of his body; but if he was hindered from doing this bodily act, he bent the knees of his heart more humbly.

“I bend my knees,” that is, I humbly entreat in prayer the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that through His merit I may obtain what I ask. That is, I pray to Him of whom there is no cause for despair that He will hear, both because I bend my knees to Him [Col. 1236C] and because He begot Him who is our Lord and is Jesus and Christ—that is, our King and Priest. I bend my knees to the Father so that the Father may first hear me, from whom—that is, from whose likeness—every fatherhood is not merely said to exist, but is named.

For properly speaking, God alone is called Father; others, however, bear the name by likeness to Him. It should not be said of them that they are fathers in relation to God, but that they share in that name, in heaven—that is, among angelic spirits. There the higher beings who preside over others and have care for them are called fathers; and likewise on earth, that is, among human beings. For the intensity of God’s ineffable love loved us beyond all estimate; He loves and governs us, and therefore is called our Father [Col. 1236D] (Matt. 6; Luke 11). But we and the angels are called fathers through Him, in likeness of love and providence, because that very love and governance by which we are called fathers proceeds from Him.

Every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named from Him, because, as has been said, whoever are fathers and preside over others with paternal affection—whether in heaven, such as the dominations over the other subordinate orders; or on earth, such as bishops, abbots, and other prelates who preside over their subjects with paternal goodness—derive the title of fatherhood from imitation of Him. Or the angels of heaven who provide for us are called fathers in heaven, and the prelates of the Church fathers on earth. “Heavens” may be understood as spiritual persons, and “earth” as carnal persons.

He Himself is called Father either because He begot the Son from Himself or because He governs and rules creatures with kindly ordering. In likeness to Him, for the same reason, those are called fathers who either beget children from themselves or govern their subjects with kindly ordering and care. Since this Father is so good and loving toward us, there is no cause to despair that He will hear us. Therefore I bend my knees to Him, that He may grant you according to the riches of His glory—that is, according to the rich and abundant bestowal of the abundance of His majesty—the strength to be strengthened: that is, steadfastness of faith, which may make you robust and strong, inwardly and outwardly, against all tribulations. May He grant strength to be strengthened through His Spirit, that is, through the spirit of grace, through the working of the Holy Spirit in the inner person, that is, in the soul which cannot be reached by enemies [Col. 1237A–B].

And, in order that He may bestow this savingly upon you, may He grant Christ to dwell through faith in your hearts, according to perfection of virtues and steadfastness, and this through faith held concerning Him and made perfect. For some heretics are strong in enduring adversities, but it does them no good. Or, may He grant Christ to dwell in your minds and rational faculties by enlightening them: that is, may He enlighten your reason with Christ dwelling within it, and this through faith. For reason is not enlightened to understand unless faith comes first. Hence it is written: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isaiah, according to the Septuagint).

And may He enlighten your reason to such a degree that, being rooted and grounded in love, you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth.

Or, in accordance with what precedes, it may be continued thus: I ask that you do not fail, but persevere steadfastly—I mean you who are rooted and grounded in love. “Rooted,” that is, firmly planted after the manner of a tree which grows the more and bears fruit more abundantly the deeper it is fixed in the earth; and “grounded” like a building which is built upward more firmly the deeper its foundation is laid. For those who are vigorous in the active life are called rooted; love is their root, because just as a tree grows from a root and, as it grows, produces fruit for the benefit of others, so those who are in the active life grow from love in order to bear fruit, whether by providing bodily sustenance or spiritual nourishment. By those who are grounded, however, contemplatives are understood, [Col. 1237C–D] because they do not grow into this kind of fruit for others, but remain firm and unmoved, insofar as possible, in divine contemplation.

This means: whether you are in the active life or in the contemplative life, remaining always in love, may you be able—that is, may you have the capacity—to comprehend, that is, to grasp knowledge together with the execution of deeds, so that you may be able both to understand and to do, with all the saints. For you will not otherwise be saints unless you understand this mystery which all the saints understand.

May you be able to comprehend what is the breadth of the aforesaid building in which you are being built up, that is, of the temple of God. Its breadth is the expansiveness of the hearts of the saints, by which they love all persons, desire to benefit all, and, as far as they are able, do benefit them. Its length, which is also called long-suffering, is the joyful expectation of God’s promises. Its height is the heavenly life among the angels. Its depth, that is, the foundation of that building, is faith and baptism and other such sacraments of the Church. These four, therefore, the Apostle prays that we may comprehend in understanding and action.

Or these may be understood of the temple of the heavenly dwelling, that is, of the everlasting felicity of the kingdom. For the eternal glory of that kingdom will be so broad that no one there will be confined; so long and uninterrupted that it will never fail; so lofty and exalted that it will surpass every earthly good; and so deep and wonderful that in the present life no human voice can perfectly describe it and no human mind fully understand it [Col. 1238A].

Or again, these may be understood in God. For God has breadth because He extends His love even to the gathering in of persecutors. He has length because, by patiently enduring, He brings us to the homeland of life. He has height because He transcends even the understanding of those who have been received into the heavenly assembly. He has depth because He exercises intelligibly upon the condemned the judgment of His severity below. These four He exercises severally upon us while we are placed in this life: He manifests His breadth by loving; His length by enduring; His height by surpassing not only our understanding but even our desires; and His depth by sternly judging the hidden and unlawful movements of our thoughts.

But no one knows how unsearchable His height and depth are unless, either raised to the heights by contemplation [Col. 1238B–C], or resisting hidden movements, that person has begun to be troubled by the importunity of temptations.

These four may also be understood in the Lord’s cross and, through the cross, in the conduct of the saints. For the cross is broad in the transverse beam upon which the hands of the one hanging are stretched out; and this signifies good works in the breadth of love and cheerfulness of mind. It is long from the transverse beam to the ground, where the back and feet are fixed; and it signifies perseverance through the length of time unto the end. It is high at the summit, toward which the transverse beam extends upward; and it signifies the heavenly end to which all things are referred, since all things done in breadth must be done for the sake of the height of divine rewards. It is deep in that part which is fixed in the earth. There indeed it is hidden and cannot be seen. Yet all its visible and elevated parts rise from there, just as all our good things proceed from the depth of God’s grace, which cannot be comprehended or judged.

For the depth of the cross is the hidden will of God and the incomprehensibility of His judgments, whence this grace comes to humankind, preceding everyone and distributing all good things as He wills—thus to some, otherwise to others—choosing some and rejecting others. Why all these things happen thus is unsearchable. Yet the Apostle prays that we may be able rightly to comprehend these four in understanding and action, and this with all the saints, because all saints comprehend what these four are. For the comprehension of these things [Col. 1239A] is a kind of communion in the heavenly commonwealth.

“And I pray this also,” he says, “that you may be able to know the love of Christ which He had and has toward you.” This love is so great that it surpasses all knowledge and exceeds every understanding, because no one in this life is so wise as to be able perfectly to consider so great a love. But in the age to come this love will be known. For there is full and perfect love, without any endurance of evils: it does not by faith believe what it does not see, nor by hope desire what it does not possess, but will contemplate eternally the unchangeable form of truth. Its endless, tranquil occupation will be to praise what it loves and to love what it praises.

Thus may you be granted to know the love of Christ, surpassing knowledge and exceeding understanding, and this in such a way that you may be filled [Col. 1239B] unto all the fullness of God—not so that you may be full God, but so that you may be perfectly filled with God, so that God may be all in all.

> “Now to Him who is able to do all things superabundantly beyond what we ask or understand, according to the power that works in us—to Him be glory in the Church and in Christ Jesus, unto all generations, for ever and ever. Amen.”

“I,” he says, “bend my knees to God the Father that He may grant you all these things. But He is able to do superabundantly,” that is, far more lavishly and abundantly, “than we ask or understand”: that is, beyond every petition and understanding of ours He can bestow upon us [Col. 1239C] an abundance of gifts, according to the power of His grace, which works in us even certain things which no one would ask or understand.

Or, “according to the power which works in us,” that is, just as His power has worked magnificent gifts in us apostles, so He is able to accomplish in all of you for whom we pray. And to Him who can do these things, and will do them if He wills, to Him be glory and not to us—that is, supreme honor—and this in the Church, that is, in consideration of those things which He does in the Church, such as faith, innocence, and righteousness; and in Christ Jesus, that is, with reference to Christ, through whom all these things are done and in whose judgment and grace all these things exist.

And let glory be His not merely for an hour, but unto all generations of the age of ages: that is, in the future age, which will consist of all [Col. 1239D] generations born in these present ages. For the age of ages is eternity, whose parts are times and all ages. The “age of ages” may also be understood as this present age, taken together from the beginning of the world to its end, which is divided into many ages. And let the glory which the Father has in Christ and in the Church extend through all generations of this age of ages, so that from the beginning of the world to its end there may be no generation in which God is not glorified through Christ’s grace in the children of the Church. For no time ever passes or will pass without elect persons in whom the Father will be glorified through Christ. “Amen,” that is, truly or faithfully.

Here the Apostle concluded his treatment with a commendation of grace, in which he also rejected carnal observances [Col. 1240A], and passes to moral exhortation, saying:

## CHAPTER IV

> “Therefore I beseech you, I who am a prisoner in the Lord, that you walk worthily of the calling by which you were called (1 Cor. 7), with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, being diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. One body and one Spirit, just as you were called in the one hope of your calling. One Lord, one faith, one baptism. One God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in us all (1 Cor. 12).”

Thus far he has treated faith and grace, and has sufficiently shown that all things must be attributed to grace. Now he gives instruction concerning conduct: first to all in common, then according to the individual orders. Since you have been saved by grace alone, not by works or carnal observances, and have been made the dwelling-place of God, as was shown above, therefore I beseech you to live henceforth in such a way that you do not lose so great a grace bestowed upon you.

And this is what he means: “I beseech,” that is, through the sacred gifts of heavenly grace which you have received, “you”—I whom you ought to hear, because I am bound and imprisoned, not for theft but in the Lord, that is, in love of the Lord, namely, for His love and for His name, in which I remain fixed. And because I am bound, you ought to have compassion on me; my exhortation is not to be despised.

I beseech you that you “walk worthily of the calling by which you were called”: that is, walk worthily of the faith to which you were called by grace [Col. 1240B–C]; that is, walk worthily toward the heavenly homeland, as faith befits—the faith by which you will come to heavenly glory. “Walk,” that is, make progress and persevere by doing those things which befit faith leading to eternal salvation, namely, good works. For your faith requires good works. Or, because you were freely called to faith through my preaching, walk in faith and good works in such a manner that your manner of life accords with my preaching.

You will be able to walk worthily in this way: with all humility, that is, both held inwardly in the heart and shown outwardly, so that you presume nothing at all about yourselves in heart, word, or deed, nor prefer yourselves to others; and with gentleness, that is, mildness and teachableness, so that, like tame animals, you allow yourselves to be handled, being approachable and affable. The humble person is so called as though inclined toward the ground (*humi acclivis*); the gentle person as though accustomed to the hand (*manu assuetus*).

Many are humble who are not gentle, that is, mild and tranquil, but mingle a certain harshness and severity with humility itself, as though for the sake of justice. Therefore the Apostle now joins gentleness to humility, so that one who is humble may strive also to be gentle. Nor should you walk in the way of God only with humility and gentleness, but also with all patience, by which you endure tribulations for Christ in will and deed, because some do not at times suffer voluntarily. You will preserve this patience by bearing one another—that is, by having one person endure another in things that are burdensome and harsh. And [Col. 1241A] you will be able to do this if reciprocally you reckon yourselves as those who bear, that is, as inferiors. For one does not endure well who regards himself as superior.

Practice this varied forbearance in love, so that, while bearing with one another, you may love one another. For there are some who begin not to love those from whom they suffer insults or other such adversities. But love must not be abandoned because of adversities which we suffer. Or, bear with one another in love: that is, not insincerely, nor for earthly gain or loss, nor from fear of some powerful person, nor because of the exigency of the time, nor for empty glory, or anything of that kind, but for love alone, so that love alone may be the cause of your endurance. Do not be angry, nor let your heart be disturbed at the hour when you suffer these things; rather, remain in love and gentleness of spirit.
