I say, be diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit: that is, amid the adversities which you endure mutually, be diligent and attentive to preserve inviolate the unity of spirit, that is, unanimity of will, so that you may have one heart and one soul. And preserve this in the bond of peace: that is, let outward peace and concord be like a bond and joining of the inward unity of spirit.

Or otherwise: the Apostle begins to remove something opposed to love, namely, schism; and there is no doubt that it then existed among them because of spiritual gifts. For those who had gifts of grace despised others and broke themselves away from them, and thus schism existed among them. He wishes utterly to uproot it, saying: “Be diligent to preserve [Col. 1241B–C] the unity of the Spirit,” that is, by diligently putting aside every schism, preserve what you have not from yourselves—namely, unity, that is, the fact that you have become one according to faith—and preserve the other gifts, because that unity is of the Spirit, that is, granted to you by the Holy Spirit. It must therefore not be neglected but carefully retained.

You can preserve it in this way: in the bond of peace, that is, let peace be maintained among you in such a fashion that no one disturbs another, binding and joining you together. And may you all be one body through unity of faith and concord, although you seem devoted to diverse offices, like the different members of a body; and may you have one spirit, that is, one mind and will, just as all of you hope for one recompense of eternal life. This is what is meant by, “just as you were called by God in the one hope of your calling,” that is, in the one expectation of the heavenly reward to which you were called.

Or you ought for this reason to preserve unity of spirit, because the body of which you are members is one: namely, the Church, which is one and is the body of Christ. It is one body according to faith, love, and reception of the sacraments. And the Spirit of Christ, which gives life to this His body, is one. For one body consists of many members, and one spirit animates all the members. Behold: by the human spirit through which I myself am a human being, I unite and animate all my members. I command all my members to move; I direct my eyes to seeing, my ears to hearing, my tongue to speaking, my hands to working, my feet to walking. The offices [Col. 1241D–1242A] of the members are distributed, but the unity of the spirit holds all together.

What our spirit, that is, our soul, is to our members, the Holy Spirit is to the members of Christ, to Christ’s body, which is the Church. For although all Christ’s members are devoted to diverse offices, they are nevertheless animated by the one Spirit of Christ. Now if a member is cut off from the body, does the spirit follow it? By no means; yet it is still recognized as a member. Thus a person separated from the Church still retains the sacrament of baptism but has lost the Spirit. Therefore schism must be avoided and unity preserved. The Holy Spirit, who cannot be divided, is not lost by those who preserve unity, but remains one and fills those who preserve it. You ought to preserve this unity, just as you were called in the one hope of your calling: that is, just as you were called through faith into the one hope of eternal glory.

For this faith is the faith of calling, that is, of your calling; in other words, your faith is the cause of your hope, because it preceded that hope and gave it to you. This hope is one because it awaits one glory of eternal life. It is one because, although some there are as stars, others as the moon, and others as the sun, what they possess suffices for all. For those who are not in so exalted a brightness are so united in love with the greater ones that they reckon themselves to possess what the greater ones possess. So you too ought to do in this life: those who have less in gifts of grace and other gifts should, through the union of love, reckon themselves to possess what the greater ones possess, since the latter possess it for their benefit. In this matter, therefore, one ought not to envy another or despise another [Col. 1242B–C].

You ought also to preserve unity because Christ, who set you free and gave you life, is one Lord of you all. You do not have many lords, according to whose differing wills you would have to disagree, but one Lord, who commands unity among you. For unity contains no contrariety within itself, any more than does the Creator. But whatever is separated from unity and outside unity is already opposition and duality. For the Creator was indeed one; but as soon as creation followed, contrariety arose. Unity must therefore be preserved, so that one Lord may be served.

It must also be preserved because there is one faith. Although each believer has his own faith, it is nevertheless called one faith. For the faith in the mind of a believer is visible only to the person whose it is; although it is present in others, it is not the same faith numerically but a similar faith. It is one not in number but in kind. Nevertheless, because of similarity, we say it is one rather than many more than we do from any absence of opposition. When we see two human beings very similar, we say that they have one face, and marvel at them both. Thus the same faith of believers is called one, just as the same will of persons willing the same thing is called one, even though each of those who wills the same thing has a will visible to himself, while the will of another remains hidden, even though he wills the same thing.

For this reason too unity must be preserved: because baptism is one. It cannot be repeated; but whether given by a good person or a bad person, a Catholic or a heretic, according to the custom of the Church in the name of the Holy Trinity—namely, of the Father and [Col. 1243A] the Son and the Holy Spirit—it has equal efficacy for the remission of sins and the opening of the kingdom of heaven.

But unity must be maintained because God is one in His substance. His substance is not manifold but one and simple. Hence Moses also says: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6). He cannot be greater, He cannot be lesser, He cannot be numbered. God is one, Creator of all things; and He is one Father of all, loving and governing all with paternal affection. Therefore no one can prefer himself to another. This Father is called one because with one affection He cares for all things, like a loving Father.

He is above all, that is, He excels all creatures, whose dignity should invite us; and He is diffused through all things, because He is everywhere, and therefore is to be feared, since He can be avoided nowhere; and He is in all of us by grace, who preserve unity. For He is through all things by the power of His might and the wisdom of His ordering, but in us by the grace of His goodness. Or, He is above all by ruling and governing; He is through all things by supplying all the good things they possess; and He is in all of us by preserving the benefits bestowed upon us.

The word “through” in the phrase “through all” is ordinal, showing that if we examine all our things, passing through them in order, we shall find all of them supplied by Him. And because He rules over all, is present throughout all that is ours except sin, and preserves those things for us, we ought therefore to be diligent that, just as He is one, we too may be one and may always preserve unity.

[Col. 1243C]

> “But to each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift (Rom. 12; 1 Cor. 12). Therefore He says: ‘Ascending on high, He led captivity captive; He gave gifts to men’ (Ps. 67). Now that He ascended—what does it mean except that He first descended into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is the same who ascended above all the heavens, that He might fill all things (John 3). And He Himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, others as pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints (1 Cor. 12), for the work of ministry, for the building up of Christ’s body, until we all meet in the unity of faith and of the knowledge [Col. 1243D] of the Son of God, into a perfect man, into the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ, so that we may no longer be little children tossed about and carried around by every wind of doctrine, through the wickedness of human beings, through cunning unto the deception of error.”

We indeed are all one body and ought to preserve unity; yet we have not all received the gifts of heavenly grace equally, for grace has been given to each of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift. One person has one gift of grace, another a different one; what the latter has, the former does not. This measure is also a certain distribution of gifts, and harmony there makes one body. For just as in our body the hand receives one thing in order to work, the eye another in order to see, the ear another in order to hear, the foot another in order to walk—[Col. 1244A] while the soul is one, doing everything: in the hand, that it may work; in the foot, that it may walk; in the ear, that it may hear; in the eye, that it may see—so too the faithful, like members, have diverse gifts distributed to each according to a proper measure, while the grace of Christ which distributes them is one.

Therefore some ought not to envy others, nor should some pride themselves against others on account of gifts which are freely given by Christ, and which he measures and apportions as he knows to be expedient for each. For this reason much is given to one person: that through him many others may advance; and little to others: that in all things they may preserve humility toward all. And if Christ measures out much to one person in order that he may benefit many others who do not possess so much, then it is not right for those lacking it to envy those who possess it. Rather, they ought to reckon themselves to possess whatever [Col. 1244B] their superiors possess, because those superiors possess it for their benefit. Nor ought those who possess such gifts to despise those who do not possess them, since they possess them in order to serve those who lack them. Thus we ought to preserve unity amid the various gifts we receive, with every schism removed.

Therefore, to prove that Christ gives diverse gifts, the Holy Spirit says through the Psalmist: “Ascending on high,” etc. (Ps. 67). Yet, turning the expression toward Christ, the Psalmist says: “You ascended on high; you led captivity captive; you received gifts among men” (ibid.). Nor should it disturb us that the Apostle does not say, “You received gifts among men,” but “he gave gifts to men.” For the Apostle spoke with apostolic authority according to the fact that the Son is God with the Father. Accordingly, he gave gifts to men [Col. 1244C] by sending them the Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of the Father and the Son. But the Prophet, according to the sense in which Christ himself is understood in his body, which is the Church—and hence all the faithful are his members—said that he received gifts among men, because he himself receives whatever benefit is bestowed upon his members. Thus he is about to say: “When you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me” (Matt. 25).

But let us consider the meaning. Christ, ascending on high to heaven’s dwelling-place, “led captivity captive”; that is, by the power of his incorruption he swallowed up our corruption. Or, he led captivity captive because he conquered death, which held captives in its power and reigned in them. Or, those held captive in hell—[Col. 1244D] who can themselves be denoted by the name “captivity”—he led with himself to the heavenly kingdom. For just as, when “militia” is spoken of, those who serve as soldiers are understood, so by the designation “captivity” are understood those who were held captive in hell’s prisons. In this life also many were held captive by the devil in sins, and these likewise are called “captivity”; but Christ happily took them captive. For why should captivity not be happy, if human beings may be captured for good? Hence it was said to Peter: “From now on you will be catching men” (Luke 5). Therefore they were made captive because they were taken; and taken because they were subjected—that is, placed beneath Christ’s light yoke.

But this must be considered: being captives and earthborn, we had regarded this exile as our native country. But when Christ leads us to the heavenly kingdom, surely [Col. 1245A] our captivity is blessedly led captive by him. In these ways, then, he led captivity captive, ascending on high by his own power and will, not supported by the aid of anyone else.

And he gave gifts to men, because, sending the Spirit from above, he bestowed on some the word of wisdom; on others, the grace of powers; on others, the grace of healings; on others, kinds of tongues; on others, interpretation of utterances (1 Cor. 12). For not every individual possesses everything; rather, these have certain gifts and others different ones, as was said above, although all possess the gift itself from which distinct gifts are apportioned to each—that is, the Spirit. This part of the passage, where it says “he gave gifts to men,” serves to show that Christ gave each of us grace according to measure. He said the rest in order that the meaning might be more fully disclosed.

The Prophet said that he ascended. But what does it mean that he was said to have ascended, unless that he had previously descended? For the Word which in the beginning was God with God (John 1)—whither could he ascend, or how could he ascend, unless he had first descended? For he was above all things, or rather, he was everywhere. But he descended when he took the form of a servant (Phil. 2). He descended into the lower parts of the earth, that is, the aerial regions, in order to dwell among human beings. In his divinity he descended to us; but in the humanity which he assumed he ascended to heaven. And this is what the Apostle proves when he infers his descent from the statement that he ascended, saying: “But what is it that he ascended, except that he first descended into the lower parts of the earth?” That is, how or [Col. 1245C] why was it said that he ascended, unless in relation to a preceding descent?

The lower parts of the earth may be understood as the places of the dead, in which the saints were held. And Christ descended there according to the soul, not suffering ruin, a fall, or compulsion, but descending of his own will in mercy into those lower parts of the earth, in order powerfully to lead all his own out from there. First indeed he descended there; then, having resumed his body, he ascended into heaven. And lest anyone should suppose that the person who ascends was different from the person who descends, he adds: He who descended according to divinity, by taking humanity, and he who ascended according to humanity, to a place where he himself had never previously been in his humanity, is one and the same person.

He ascended not only above all material heavens, but also above [Col. 1245D] all orders of heavenly powers, surpassing every creature in place and dignity, in order that he might fulfil all that had been prophesied concerning him. For these things had not yet been fulfilled concerning him when he had not yet, in his humanity, sat at the right hand of paternal glory, reigning forever.

Or, by ascending he filled all things with his gifts, so that even the angelic creatures, which had previously been filled, might be filled further—that is, might receive a certain advancement. For not only human beings but angels too were advanced by his ascension. Or, he filled all things; that is, he perfectly and completely filled rational creation, namely the human race and the number of angels. For in the restoration of humankind the number of angels is made up, since it had been diminished by the fall of reprobate spirits. Thus, by completing the number [Col. 1246A] of the elect from angels and human beings, he fills all things. Or, he filled all the kingdoms of the world with his worship.

And in order to fill all things, he himself gave us, for instruction, four orders of rulers: namely, some to be apostles, such as Peter and Andrew (John 1), and the rest like them, who were greater than all others, having the office of preaching and themselves handing down teaching to others. In the Church, apostolic bishops, primates, and archbishops now hold their place. He gave others to be prophets, who foretold things to come even under the New Testament, such as Agabus and those like him (Acts 11). Their place is now held by those who, by interpreting the Scriptures, foretell through them to others the future joys of the righteous and punishments of the wicked.

He gave others to be evangelists, such as Luke and the rest, who handed down the Gospel in writing to posterity; or also those who preached the Gospel and held the office of serving the poor, as did the seven deacons under the apostles (Acts 6). For they supplied both kinds of sustenance, spiritual and bodily. All deacons ought still to act likewise. This is also why, even today, they read the Gospel at Mass. He gave others to be pastors and teachers, such as bishops or presbyters. For we understand pastors and teachers as one order of rulers, because he truly feeds God’s flock who teaches it. Therefore it is not said separately, “others pastors, others teachers,” but conjointly, “others pastors and teachers,” so that they might understand their teaching to be their office. Hence God also promised through the Prophet: “I shall give you pastors according to my heart, and they shall feed you with knowledge and teaching” (Jer. 3).

Yet if there can be any difference between these two, they seem to be called pastors in relation to the sheep—that is, the simple and dull—while teachers are so called in relation to those who are already instructed and have begun to understand rationally. Christ gave all these diverse gifts for the instruction of the Church. Therefore none of them ought to pride himself upon gifts received against those who do not possess them, or separate himself from them; rather, he should serve their salvation. Nor ought the lesser to envy them, but to venerate and love them as fathers. For the Savior gave these for the perfecting of the saints: that is, in order that they might bring to completion and perfection in holiness those who are already holy—namely, that they might [Col. 1246D] advance and perfect those who are holy through forgiveness of sins, innocence, and the beginning of good works, by increase of virtue and perseverance. And he gave them for the work of ministry, so that each might fully perform the ministry entrusted to him. For if one person did everything, he would not perform each thing perfectly. Therefore each received the particular work of ministry to which he was assigned.

And to what does the ministry of each of them tend? “For the building up of the body of Christ”: that is, in order that the body of Christ, which is the Church, may be built up, whether in virtues or in the conversion of unbelievers to faith. For this is the house which, as the Psalm sings (Ps. 126), is built after captivity, because the Church is built from those whom the devil held captive; and it is both the house and the body of Christ.

Christ gave such prelates to the Church, and will give them until we all meet: that is, until all who now are in one undivided faith and one undivided knowledge of the Son of God meet one another on the day of judgment from the different parts of the world, or meet Christ himself, as though running in desire toward joy—“unto a perfect man.” This means that each will be a perfect human being, because whether anyone is now lame, blind, or deprived of any member, in the resurrection he will possess the perfection of all members. And we shall meet “unto the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ”: that is, we shall rise neither below nor beyond youthful form, but at the age and strength which we know Christ attained here; that is, at the limit of age to which [Col. 1247B] a human being naturally grows, and beyond which nothing naturally increases, the age in which the Savior also had fullness of years and body when he departed from this world.

He did not say “the measure of the body” or “the measure of stature,” but “the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ.” For it is not permissible to say that, when the time of the resurrection of all has come, a bodily size will be added to any person which that person did not possess. But if we say that even bodies larger than the Lord’s body must be reduced to the measure of the Lord’s body, a great deal would perish from many bodies, though he himself promised that not even a hair would perish (Luke 21). It remains, then, that each will receive his own measure: either that which he had in youth, even if he died old; or that which he would have had, had he not died prematurely.

Or thus: Christ gave prelates [Col. 1247C] in the Church, who will endure as some succeed others, until we all meet in a perfect man; that is, until all of us are so assembled and united in charity that we are a perfect man. A man is called perfect when none of his members is still growing in quantity. For he is not perfect so long as he has room for growth. Thus the Church will then be in a perfect state, when none of her members can any longer increase through succession. For a hand grows daily when, after the death of one person who supplied necessities to the brethren, another succeeds him and does the same; and so with the other members. But after the number of the elect has been completed, this increase through succession [Col. 1247D] will cease. Then we shall be a perfect man, because none of the members will have any place for further growth, since the number of all will be complete.

“Until we all meet in a perfect man”: that is, until the Church is made a perfect man—when every member of the Church has its proper quantity. We shall all meet, and meet in such a manner that no member remains which does not receive its proper quantity. By saying “we meet” rather than “we assemble,” he shows that we shall be greatly inclined and eager for that love itself. For “to run” denotes greater speed than “to come.”

The whole meaning is this: He will give teachers and pastors as long as it is necessary, that is, until the Church is made a perfect man lacking nothing and requiring no subsequent addition in number or powers. And this will be when we meet unto the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ: that is, when the age measured by Christ is full. The measure will be full when Christ himself is full in his body, possessing all those who now grow individually, and when all in him are immortal and blessed. Beyond that, prelation will no longer be necessary, nor will it endure longer, though it is now necessary that it remain until that limit. Therefore it should not be borne heavily, since it will soon pass away.

But we shall meet unto a perfect man because we remain in the unity of faith—that is, because we hold one, not various, faith concerning the Son of God—and because we remain in unity of the knowledge of the Son of God—that is, because we acknowledge, or understand, [Col. 1248B] the same thing concerning the Son of God. That is to say, because we believe and understand the same thing concerning the Son of God. For those who do not believe the same thing in the Church, and do not understand the same thing, will not meet unto a perfect man. Nor do those tend toward understanding the same thing who wish to make a schism in the Church.

Or, as stated above, we shall meet Christ when he comes to judgment, and joyfully receive him—namely, we who now are in unity of faith, who hold the one faith of the Trinity and divine unity, and who are in unity of the knowledge of the Son of God: that is, who hold one harmonious knowledge of the Son of God in faith, believing him incarnate, suffering, risen, and exalted. For prelates were given to us so that, after the time of grace and after receiving spiritual teaching, we might no longer be children [Col. 1248C] in understanding but advanced in wisdom; and that we might not be wavering—that is, faltering through our weakness in good works or doubting in faith; that we might not be tossed amid the waves of temptations like a ship exposed to a storm, but firm and immovable; and that we might not be “carried about,” that is, carried round in the circuit of error, “by every wind of doctrine,” that is, every breath of empty teaching.

For the teaching of the wicked and heretics is like the wind of a tempest or whirlwind, because it overturns the settled state of the mind and leads it into the dizziness of errors; it is light and empty, without the weight of truth, and therefore must prudently be avoided. I mean doctrine which remains in the wickedness of human beings, since human wickedness is the seat of perverse teaching. For heresy exists only [Col. 1248D] in a soul subjected to sins, because sins committed are the causes for which God permits people to fall into the abyss of heresy. Such a doctrine of seduction also remains in craftiness. Craftiness denotes, if the expression may be used, deceitful knowledge, because the teaching of heresy abides in it, since it is both its cause and support. I mean craftiness tending toward the deceit of error: that is, striving to entrap the unwary and lead them into error. For through the fraud of deceit and craftiness heretics are accustomed to deceive many.

But we are safe from them through the teaching of truth preached by the prelates of the Church. For the Apostles and prophets of the New Testament who expound the Scriptures make us no longer children, but strong in understanding. Through the evangelists who preach the Gospel we are made not wavering [Col. 1249A] in faith but certain. Through pastors and teachers it comes about that we are not carried about by every wind of doctrine, but remain steadfast in faith and in the purpose of our religion.

> “But, doing the truth, let us grow in charity in every respect into him who is the head, Christ; from whom the whole body, fitted together and joined through every joint of supply, according to the working in the measure of each individual member, makes the body grow for the building up of itself in charity.”

We are not to be carried about by every wind of doctrine, but are to do the truth—that is, make true, firm, and rational arguments against their craftiness, against those who wish [Col. 1249B] to introduce heresy—and grow in him in all that we possess. That is, in everything we have already received, we are to increase in innocence, humility, patience, and the other virtues; and this is to take place in charity.

Or, let us do the truth: that is, let us act rightly according to the teaching of God’s commandments, of which it is said, “All your commandments are truth” (Ps. 118). And let us do this not in hypocrisy or fear, but in charity, so that charity alone may cause us to do these things. Thus let us grow and make progress in every good thing that we possess, whether in the faculties of the mind, good works, or words, in him who is our head—that is, who provides for and governs us. And who is he? Christ: that is, our king, or priest. And in [Col. 1249C] and under this head we ought always to grow and increase in all things, so that, as members follow the head, we may follow him and remain in him, who gave himself to us as a dwelling-place, saying: “Remain in me” (John 15).

Then the Apostle continues the metaphor of head and members, showing that none of the faithful can grow in any good unless he adheres to Christ the head. Likewise, in the human body, if a member is severed from its head, it no longer grows but withers. And this is the meaning: from this head, Christ, it comes about that the whole body—that is, the whole Church—is in every respect fitted together, that is, united in unanimity of faith, and joined by the bonds of charity. It is so fitted together by faith and joined by charity that, if we examine every joint of the members, we shall find [Col. 1249D] the whole there: namely, that the foot is joined not only to the leg but also to the hand, the head, and all the other members. Thus every joint is found there: the foot’s joint with the leg, the leg’s with the hand and head, and likewise in the other members.

This joint is one of supplying assistance, because those who become members of the Church are supplied to, and joined beneath, the elect who precede them through the offices of priests. It is a supply, I say, which exists worthily according to working, because the person worthily joined to the preceding members of the Church is the one who performs whatever good he can. And this working is according to the measure of each member, because each person performs good works according to his own capacity, and by these grows to the measure of his own quantity. For each person is called great or small according to what he [Col. 1250A] does.

Or, this joint is for supplying assistance: that is, in order that one may assist another. For this is why they are joined in the Church by faith and charity: that, just as in our body the eyes provide for the feet, so those who are eyes in the body of the Church may provide for those who are feet, and the other members may likewise act reciprocally. This assistance is rendered according to working, so that one person may serve another according to what he is able to do—that is, may render service to the extent of his ability to act. But those refuse either to minister or to be ministered to in the Church because they wish to create schism. And what else is it to create schism in the Church but to dissolve what Christ has fitted and joined together?

This working takes place according to the measure of each member, that is, according to [Col. 1250B] what each member is able to do. And thus this body, fitted together and joined, while members assist or are assisted by members, makes the body—that is, itself—grow: it increases in virtues and in number those who are already the body. And it does this for its own building up: that is, in order to build itself and construct itself as God’s temple, always placing in its own structure whomever it can convert. It does all this in charity, because it places them in God’s structure solely because of charity, and teaches them to remain and work in charity. Those who produce schism do the contrary and endeavor to diminish this sacred body and destroy the heavenly building.

The words, “according to the measure of each individual member, makes the body grow,” can also be understood otherwise. The body of the Church grows by advancing according to the measure of each member, so that each member may grow by succession to the extent that it ought to grow. The eyes grow in this body when, after one teacher has died, another grows and succeeds him. Yet the eyes are not said to be divided, because they do not become more numerous, but are increased. For one bishop always presides in a city, not several. The same should be understood of the other members. But when this succession and building has been completed, then the measure of the age of Christ’s fullness will be complete.

> “Therefore I say this and testify in the Lord (Rom. 1), that you no longer walk as the Gentiles walk [Col. 1250D] in the vanity of their mind, having their understanding darkened by shadows, alienated from the life of God through the ignorance which is in them because of the blindness of their heart; who, despairing, gave themselves over to unchastity, to the practice of every uncleanness in greed.”

He admonishes them to beware of the old habit of Gentile life. It is as though he said: Since you have been made members of so great a head, therefore I say and urge you that you should no longer live in the manner of those who do not belong to that head. I do not now entreat, as above, but “say”—that is, teach—and by my authority restrain old wickedness; and “testify,” that is, make myself a witness to this matter in the Lord, that is, in confirmation of the Lord’s truth and righteousness. Or, “I testify in the Lord” means that I assert this under the Lord’s testimony.

I say this, namely, that after your conversion you should no longer walk as you once walked; that is, should no longer act as you formerly acted, as the Gentiles who now exist walk, proceeding in the vanity of their mind—that is, possessing a mind full of vanity, because their mind thinks of nothing but transitory things, which are vanity, as it is written: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccl. 1). Therefore, because they know and seek nothing but passing and temporal things, they are said to walk in vanity of mind. They have also the natural understanding of reason darkened and dulled by the shadows of sins. Thus it is less surprising that they walk in vanity than it would be of you, who are enlightened and illumined by rays of inward light.

For past [Col. 1251B] sins have so darkened their mental understanding that it cannot exercise its own power, namely the power of discernment. And because they walk in vanity of mind, they are alienated from the life of God: that is, from the life which is in God, from the life which is God; separated from God, who is the life of the soul and to whom it is life to adhere. For as the soul is the life of the human body, so God is the life of the soul. Or, according to other manuscripts, they are alienated from the way of God, because they never walk in it. Their alienation from the life or way of God comes through the ignorance remaining in them. For they do not know the glory of heavenly life or the way of righteousness which leads to it; and therefore they remain strangers to both. That ignorance has a place in them because of the blindness of their hearts: they do not have the eyes of the heart open for the sight of the true light, having closed them against evangelical preaching, and so they have rightly been blinded.

For the soul which departs from the light of righteousness, the more it seeks what it may find contrary to righteousness, is repelled all the more from the light of truth and plunged into darkness. But this differs from what he said, “having their understanding darkened by shadows,” because that refers to the darkness of sins, whereas this refers to the blindness of ignorance.

And they are indeed blind: despairing of pardon and salvation because of their shamefulness—that is, not hoping for the reward of the riches of heavenly grace—they gave themselves over, under no compulsion but of their own accord, to unchastity which occurs with blood-relatives. That is, they gave themselves wholly as slaves to lust, so that they would not even [Col. 1251D] refrain from intercourse with female relatives. I mean those who fall into the practice of every uncleanness: those so degraded that they practise every form of fleshly uncleanness, whether in themselves, with one another, or with beasts. And they do this “in greed,” that is, in insatiability; for just as the greedy person never considers that he has enough, so they never attain satiety in fornication.

Or we may distinguish it thus: they have fallen into the practice of uncleanness because they defile themselves with pleasures of the flesh, all tending toward greed—that is, toward an immoderate love of possessing, whether in ambition for honors or for any kind of money.

> “But you have not so learned Christ, if indeed you have heard him and have been taught in him, as [Col. 1252A] truth is in Jesus. Put off, according to your former manner of life, the old man, who is corrupted according to the desires of error” (Col. 3).

The blinded Gentiles walk in works of this kind; but you ought not to walk in such a manner, because you have not so learned Christ. That is, you have not received from preachers the knowledge of Christ and his teaching in order to walk in it as the Gentiles shamefully walk in errors. I say that you have learned, but on this condition: if you have heard him—that is, if you have understood the preaching which is made concerning him, or have heard him speaking inwardly. For Christ speaks to a person when he inwardly enlightens and arouses that person’s reason. The person hears when he understands to what his reason [Col. 1252B] is being aroused and does what is divinely urged upon him.

And I say this again on this condition: if you have been taught in him, so as to know the things which you ought to know and do in his religion. If you have been taught in him, “as truth is in Jesus”: that is, in him is perfect and complete truth, with no admixture whatever of falsehood—the truth of faith, good action, wisdom, and salvation. Therefore the works of those who have begun to attend his schools and desire to attain in him the truth of eternal salvation ought truly to be good.

And what that truth in Jesus is follows: namely, that you put off the old man, that is, truly and not deceptively put off the old man—not according to the substance which you derived from Adam, but according to your former manner of life, which was in the oldness of the first [Col. 1252C] man, that is, according to the previous acts of your wickedness. Put off the old man: that is, the image and conformity of the old man, conformity to whose life leads to oldness and corruption. Put off, I say, the old man: that is, all wicked acts which flowed from him, and his wicked habits. This man is rightly put off because he is corrupted in his pleasures, whether of flesh or spirit, or of both. He is corrupted not only according to works, but also according to desires which belong to error: error, not the truth of the Lord Jesus, persuades these desires. Therefore, if you truly put off this man, put off also his desires, which either come from error or lead into error.

> [Col. 1252D] “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man” (Rom. 6), “who has been created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth.”

You ought not only to put off the old man, but also to be renewed: that is, be made new in respect to that which is behind, to the former newness which your father Adam possessed when he was created in the image of the Creator (Gen. 1). He was made in God’s image in mind, reason, and understanding, by which he could know God. But by sinning he became old, and this image was made ugly and discolored. Hence it is now renewed and re-formed by pursuing righteousness. Therefore, when it had been said, “Be renewed,” it was added, “in the spirit of your mind,” so that this renewal may be understood to take place in the mind.

By “the spirit of [Col. 1253A] your mind” he did not mean that two things are to be understood there, as though the mind were one thing and the spirit of the mind another; for every mind is spirit, but not every spirit is mind. For God too is spirit (John 4), and he can neither be renewed nor grow old. In a human being there is also said to be a spirit which is not mind, to which belong images resembling bodies; concerning it he says elsewhere: “If I pray with the tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful” (1 Cor. 14). For this happens when what is said is not understood, because it cannot be spoken unless images of bodily sounds in the mouth precede within the spirit’s thought. A person’s soul too is called spirit; likewise the spirit of an animal. Even wind, which is most evidently corporeal, is called spirit, according to the words: “He spoke, and the storm-wind stood” (Ps. 106).

Since, then, “spirit” is used in so many senses, he intended by “the spirit of the mind” that spirit which is called mind. And in this he commands that, even after the renewal of baptism, we be renewed daily by the exercise of divine fervor. For a mind refined by the fire of heavenly love always preserves in itself the brightness of beauty through the daily renewal of fervor. The mind which strives always to begin through desire does not know how to grow old through sluggishness. Be renewed, then, in the spirit of your mind.

And in order that you may be renewed in this way, put on the new man: that is, receive as a garment conformity to Christ’s manner of life, which may cover you so completely that nothing may appear in your habits except likeness to the works which Christ performed. He was created not through the operation of fleshly [Col. 1253C] concupiscence, but according to God: that is, conceived by the power of God alone and the power of the Holy Spirit, and thereby free from the stain of original sin. “Created” means conceived in righteousness and holiness of truth: that is, in true righteousness and true holiness, not in sins like other human beings, who were not preserved by a special privilege of God. Righteousness and holiness of truth belonged not only to his conduct but to his creation, distinguishing him from those who have false righteousness and feigned holiness. Therefore he is to be put on by you.

The order may be: “Put on the new man in righteousness and holiness of truth.” For Christ is put on in this manner. Righteousness is the observance of God’s commandments. Holiness, according to Dionysius, is purity free from every defilement, utterly uncontaminated, and most perfect. These ought truly to be in us according to our capacity, so that the newness of the new man may be our garment.

> “Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak truth, each one with his neighbor, because we are members one of another” (1 Pet. 2). “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4). “Let not the sun set upon your anger. Give no place to the devil” (Jas. 4). “Let him who stole steal no longer; rather let him labor, working with his hands what is good, that he may have something to give to one suffering need.”

You ought to put off the old human being and put on the new. Therefore, since this must be done, do the following. [Col. 1254A] For since the old human being must be put off, put away falsehood—that is, cease to lie—because “a lying mouth kills the soul” (Wis. 1). But since the new must be put on, speak the truth, which belongs to the new. Let each one speak truth with his neighbour—that is, with every human being. For every human being is a neighbour, since we have all been born from one parent. And we are all neighbours by the condition of earthly birth.

And in another sense: in hope of the heavenly inheritance, you ought to regard every person as your neighbour, even before he is a Christian. For you do not know what one who is now a Jew, a heretic, or a pagan will become before God. Perhaps through God’s mercy he will be so converted that he deserves to hold the first place among the saints. And according to this hope, [Col. 1254B] he may be reckoned, as it were, a member of the Church. For this is why we ought to speak truth to one another: because we are members one of another, so that one may in turn serve the other and love him as himself.

Put off the old human being. But if it should happen that you still do something according to the old manner, be angry with yourselves over it—that is, do penance—and cease thereafter from sinning. For what is a penitent person but one angry with himself? That he may receive pardon, let him exact punishment from himself. This may also be commanded to prelates: be angry with the faults of offenders—that is, show severity in correcting them—and do not sin—that is, do not act too harshly in this matter, lest by exceeding the measure you sin.

Or it may be said thus even to all: “Be angry”—that is, if perhaps you become angry, if a movement of the mind arises which, [Col. 1254C] because of the punishment for sin, is no longer within one’s power—“do not sin”: that is, at least let the mind and reason not consent to it. Even if it happens that you are angry, let not the sun go down upon your wrath; that is, do not retain it for long or preserve it until the next day, but before sunset cast it out of your heart. For *iracundia* [wrathfulness] is so called, as if it were hidden anger, because it is held in the mind for a long time.

But this saying is understood better in another way, because our sun is Christ, who is truth, wisdom, and righteousness, by whose light the human soul is illumined. Yet the mind ceases to see this light when it has been overcome, as though by a cloud, by the disturbance of wrathfulness. Then, as it were, the sun sets upon a person’s wrath, because when wrathfulness casts the darkness of confusion upon the mind, [Col. 1254D] God hides from it the ray of his knowledge. Therefore wrathfulness must be guarded against greatly, for through it the light of truth is lost. Once this light is lost, the devil, prince of darkness, finds a place for himself in a person. Hence follows: “Do not give place to the devil.”

For the angry person thinks evil thoughts and thus offers and opens himself to the devil, so that he may bring his thoughts to completion. He opens the door of the heart and permits the enemy to enter. But do not give him a place, when through the suggestion of evils he seeks to find in you a place of consent or delight. For whoever consents to his suggestions gives him a place in himself. The door of the heart must be shut, lest the tempter enter. The tempter does not cease knocking, in order to break in. If he finds it shut, he passes on. Therefore, since it is in your power to shut this door, do not [Col. 1255A] give place to the devil. For if he has entered and taken possession, either you shut it carelessly or neglected to shut it.

This door has, as it were, two leaves: desire and fear. Either you desire something earthly, and he enters by this; or you fear something earthly, and he enters by this. Therefore shut the door of desire and fear against the devil if you wish to be safe. For concerning the desire through which Satan enters, the text adds: “Let him who stole steal no more.” And this too, like the prohibition of the vices mentioned above, belongs to putting off the old human being. What follows—“but rather let him labour,” and so forth—belongs to putting on the New.

Here theft may be understood not merely as the secret taking of another’s goods, but also as whatever is acquired to another’s injury or by deception. Therefore, one who, while leading the old life, [Col. 1255B] stole another’s goods, after putting on the new human being must steal no more: that is, he must not take anything belonging to another by deceit or any contrivance of fraud; but rather—that is, instead—he should labour, not through slaves but with his own hands, that is, by his own work. And he should work not at work displeasing to God, but at what is good—that is, useful and without sin. He should labour, namely, so that he has not only what to live on but also what to give to one suffering necessity—that is, poverty. This is so that he may support the poor from righteous labour. Hence it is shown that almsgiving must be made from what is good—that is, what is justly possessed—not from what is unjustly possessed. It follows:

> “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but if any speech is good for the edification of faith, [Col. 1255C] let it give grace to those who hear. And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.”

Let no evil speech proceed—that is, let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, even if it has been conceived in the heart; rather restrain it lest it be able to come out, so that you never speak anything evil. Let no insulting, lascivious, murmuring, or other such speech leave your mouth. But if there is in your heart any good speech—that is, humble, charitable, and useful speech—let it proceed, not idly but for the edification of faith: that is, so fittingly that it builds others up in the faith which works through love, because that is true and saving faith.

Let good speech proceed for edification. [Col. 1255D] Here it is shown that not even good speech ought to be uttered except for edification. Hence the Psalmist says: “I became mute and was humbled, and I kept silence even from good things” (Ps. 38). Let what is good be spoken for this purpose, that it may give grace to those who hear—that is, that through it hearers may draw the sweetness of heavenly grace and advance in good works. Such speech proceeded from the mouth of the Lord’s mother when, at the voice of her greeting, Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit (Luke 1 [printed: XXXI]).

Do not utter evil speech. And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God by your evil conduct: that is, do not do such things as displease the Holy Spirit so that he withdraws from you, as though offended and grieved. “For, as it is written, the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful, and will withdraw himself from thoughts [Col. 1256A] without understanding, and will be reproved by the onset of iniquity” (Wis. 1). For in his substance the Holy Spirit cannot be grieved, since he himself is eternal and unchangeable blessedness; but he is said to be grieved by comparison with a person who leaves the house of one who has grieved him.

Or, one is said to grieve the Holy Spirit who by his depraved conduct grieves the saints in whom the Holy Spirit dwells. For just as saints rejoice at the progress of believers, so they grieve at their falls. Therefore the Holy Spirit is said to be grieved by those who act so that the saints are grieved by their deeds, for no other reason than that they possess the Holy Spirit, through whom they are so good that evil people sadden them—especially those whom they know or believe [Col. 1256B] to have been good. The Holy Spirit is said to be grieved because he inspires charity in his elect, by which he causes them to grieve over the losses of others.

Those saints who grieve in this way are especially the pious rulers of the Church. Therefore subjects are now commanded not to grieve them by their disobedience, because in them they would grieve the Holy Spirit. In order to aggravate the sin, the Apostle chose to speak in this way. For those grieve their rulers who despise their words and disdain to obey them.

You ought not to grieve this Spirit, in whom you have been sealed as wax, his image impressed upon you; or “sealed,” that is, distinguished from unbelievers. And this was done on the day of redemption—that is, when, after the night of unbelief and ignorance had passed, you were illumined by the light [Col. 1256C] of faith in baptism and redeemed from the devil’s slavery. For in baptism the Holy Spirit seals believers by faith, sacraments, and spiritual graces—that is, separates them from unbelievers.

> “Let all bitterness, wrath, indignation, clamour, and blasphemy be taken away from you, together with all malice. But be kind to one another, merciful, forgiving one another, as God also in Christ forgave you” (Col. 3).

Let all bitterness, which is indeed contrary to kindness—that is, rancour and harshness in words, deeds, or thoughts—be taken away from you; and wrath, that is, a sudden movement of the mind taking possession of the mind itself for some time; and indignation, that is, a vehement rage of mind accompanied by a certain fault of arrogance. This happens [Col. 1256D] often when a superior sees an inferior raised to some honour. For he is sometimes grievously indignant on account of this. And because clamorous words are accustomed to follow this impulse of mind, clamour is next added.

Here we understand clamour as occurring when people, in the frenzy of anger, utter evil and insulting words. And let blasphemy be taken away: that is, the utterance of words against God or his saints. For blasphemy is that by which false things are said about God himself or his saints. The Apostle commands that all these things be taken away from us, exhorting us to patience. And, as though all things outward had now been rightly ordered, he turns to inward things when he adds: “with all malice.” For malice properly belongs to the mind. [Col. 1257A] It is useless for indignation, clamour, and blasphemy to be removed from outward conduct if malice, the mother of vices, rules within. And outward wickedness is cut off from its branches in vain if it is preserved within at the root, ready to grow back more abundantly.

Therefore malice, the hidden root of vices, must be completely uprooted from the heart; and the sweetness of charity must be implanted, lest branches of vices break forth outwardly. For we ought so to endure those who inflict evils upon us that we also love them with a pure heart. When we remove these vices from ourselves, we put off the old human being; but we put on the new by doing what follows: “But be,” and so forth.

As though he said: Do not be bitter, but instead be kind to one another—that is, one toward another—having the good fire of pious sweetness. For kindness is serenity [Col. 1257B] of mind, when someone speaks clearly and cheerfully, gives what is his, and associates with another. As we have said, it is contrary to the vice of bitterness. And do not have wrath against anyone, but be merciful to one another—that is, having bowels of compassion, so that you always have the desire to do good to your neighbours, even if you lack something to give.

And do not cry out angrily against anyone, or bring before a judge, with clamour, the injury inflicted upon you; but be forgiving one another—that is, forgiving each other whatever injury or offence you have endured. Do this not falsely or partially, but as purely and perfectly as God in Christ forgave you: that is, as God through Christ forgave you all that you committed, without any regard to a vengeance yet to come, [Col. 1257C] so you too must always forgive one another without regard to any retaliation. Otherwise God will demand again what he had forgiven you.

## CHAPTER V

> “Therefore be imitators of God, as most beloved children; and walk in love, as Christ also loved us (John 13, 15), and gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, for an odour of sweetness.”

Since God in Christ forgave you the sins which you committed against him, therefore be imitators of God: that is, follow the example of his goodness, so that you too forgive your brothers whatever they commit against you. And do this as most beloved children; for if you do it, then you will be most beloved children of that Father. Hence [Col. 1257D] his Only-begotten says: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, pray for those persecuting and slandering you, that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon good and evil people, and rains upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5; Luke 6).

And be imitators of God not only in forgiving sins but also in love, so that you love those who oppose you. That is, established in love, walk—that is, advance and make progress in it—to such a degree that, if need be, you lay down your lives for those whom you love, as Christ also loved us and laid down his life for us (John 10). Great and inexpressible love: that the only Son of God should give himself up to death for us—the Lord for servants, the Creator [Col. 1258A] for the creature.

For in redeeming us, he gave up not a ram, not a goat, not even a prophet or apostle, but himself, who is God. He gave himself up—that is, he was not unwillingly led to death, but freely gave himself; and in this the power of love appeared. For he gave himself as an offering and sacrifice to God. An *oblatio* [offering] is so called when something is freely offered without anyone asking for it. Thus Christ, when no one dared ask it, offered himself on the cross as a sacrifice to God for us. But a *hostia* [sacrificial victim] is so called because it is offered for enemies, the defeated, or those to be overcome. Thus by Christ’s sacrifice the devil, demons, and sins were overcome.

Or Christ was an offering because by his death he acquired for us the gifts of virtues and divine grace; but a sacrifice because he freed us [Col. 1258B] from the enemy. Or he was an offering when he was wronged; a sacrifice when he was killed. He gave himself as such a sacrifice as might go up for an odour of sweetness—that is, as a sweet fragrance to God. For just as a pleasant and good scent is acceptable to someone, so is the sacrifice of the Lord’s flesh acceptable to God. The Father delighted in it not with respect to Christ’s bare death, but with respect to the fruit proceeding from it. For from it salvation now comes to the human race; and in this God indeed delighted.

The Father also delighted, as in a most sweet fragrance, in the Saviour’s intention and in the affection of his mercy when he permitted himself to be immolated for our redemption. For because the Just One was killed for righteousness, he gave forth from his death the finest fragrance. For just as sin breathes a stench, so righteousness breathes a good fragrance.

> [Col. 1258C] “But let fornication and every impurity or covetousness not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints; nor shamefulness, nor foolish talk, nor buffoonery, which is not fitting, but rather thanksgiving.”

Strive to imitate God. But let fornication, impurity, and covetousness be so completely cast away from you that they are not even named among you: that is, let the name of any of these vices be found in none of you; in other words, let no one even merely say that any one of you is such a person. Instead, be so irreproachable before God and human beings that you give no occasion for evil suspicion.

Fornication is named from arches, which are now also called sandpits. For there are theatrical arches [Col. 1258D] and places of prostitution in which prostitutes were found, with whom the most filthy persons had intercourse. But impurity is called every lack of continence pertaining to lust, however it may occur. Thus fornication is here understood in regard to women; impurity, however, in regard to what is done against nature, whether in oneself or with another.

Covetousness, moreover, is that pest of the mind which never says anything but “Take.” The Apostle places it with fornication and impurity in order to suggest that it is fornication of the soul, just as unlawful bodily action is fornication of the body. For as one who fornicates misuses not his own but another’s woman, so one contaminated by the pest of covetousness stretches out toward possessing another’s goods and strives to retain for himself everything he holds by robbery.

By placing a disjunctive conjunction between impurity and covetousness—which he had not done between impurity and fornication—[Col. 1259A] he intended to signify that fornication and impurity are of one kind, while covetousness is of another: the former are bodily, whereas the latter is of the soul. Let fornication, every impurity, or covetousness be not only absent from you, but not even named: that is, guard yourselves so carefully against these vices that none of you may even suffer their reproach, as is fitting for saints to be free both from vices and from the mark of infamy.

Nor let shamefulness, foolish talk, or buffoonery be named among you. Shamefulness is that by which the mind is inflamed to lust, as in kisses, embraces, and many other things of this kind. Foolish talk is a foolish utterance of words, containing no usefulness and no knowledge, made without skill or discernment. Buffoonery is the wit of jesting words, produced with a certain skill and artful ingenuity in order to move hearers to laughter. Although such buffoonery is pursued with great labour and study, it does not pertain to the matter—that is, to any usefulness—but only to vanity and the enervation of the mind.

Let these vices not be named among you; but rather—that is, instead—let thanksgiving [Col. 1259B] be named among you. That is, give God thanks continually for his benefits and devote yourselves to his praises, so that nothing may be said of you except that all your activity renders thanks to God. Namely, continually give thanks to the Saviour both in words and deeds.

> [Col. 1259C] “For know this, understanding it: that no fornicator, or impure person, or covetous person—which is the service of idols—has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.”

This is the reason why fornication and the rest ought not to be in you: because know without ambiguity that every fornicator, and so forth—every one, I say, with the individual parts of each one counted—will be found not to have an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God; that is, none will have by hereditary right a place in the kingdom of glory. And this is because it is Christ’s kingdom, against whose commands such people act, and the Father God’s, against whom they commit injuries.

This will be plain to you if you are understanding—that is, if you consider what must be considered: namely, what fornication and impurity are, how filthy a thing they are and worthy of every reproach; and likewise how utterly evil and perverse covetousness is, namely, that being covetous is not merely serving idols but is itself the service of idols. For the god of the covetous person is a coin. For just as one who serves idols assigns to an imagined creature the worship owed to the Creator, so the covetous person gives worship to coined money [Col. 1259D] when he ought to worship God, not money. Therefore the money he loves, venerates, and worships has become an idol to him, because he has placed his hope in it and has withdrawn from God’s worship for its sake. When he ought to go to church, he guards his chest; when he ought to pray to God, he seeks the marketplace in order to increase his profit. Therefore he is rightly judged an idolater.

Or it is also so because, just as idolatry commits robbery by taking away God’s honour and giving it to idols, so the covetous person robs the poor of those things which he heaps up superfluously for himself. The things which God wishes to serve the needy, he appropriates and stores away for himself. For reasons of this kind covetousness is the service of idols.

And, conversely, if you consider what that kingdom is—that is, how full of happiness it is, where there is no room for desiring anything except what each person has, because what each has wholly suffices him—and likewise if you consider what Christ is, that is, how holy, how free from every sin; and who God is, that is, how just a judge, and how great a good, namely the highest good: if you are willing to consider all these things, you will know that the fornicator and persons like him are excluded from the kingdom of God. For, as we read, nothing unclean [Col. 1260A] shall enter it (Rev. 21). Christ is named first and God afterwards, lest, according to the Arians, the Son should be thought inferior to the Father.

> “Let no one deceive you with empty words (2 Thess. 2; Matt. 24; Mark 13; Luke 21). For because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of unbelief. Therefore do not become their partners.”

Some were deceiving their hearers, promising them impunity through God’s mercy and persuading them that a person would not lose God’s kingdom on account of the foregoing sins. Against them the Apostle now says: “Let no one deceive you with empty words.” For the words of those who say or said that not every fornicator, impure person, or covetous person [Col. 1260B] is condemned are empty—that is, windy and devoid of all truth. They put forward this argument and say: “If every fornicator, impure person, and covetous person is condemned, then few people in the world are saved.” They judge this inconvenient and impossible, although it is fitting and possible. “For many,” as the Lord says, “are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20).

They sometimes also say that God’s mercy is so great that he will not permit even a fornicator or covetous person to be tormented eternally; and they proclaim it natural that one should serve these vices, saying: “Why did God make women, gold, silver, and things of this sort, except that we might use them?” But the Apostle cries the contrary: “Let no one deceive you with empty words”; that is, permit no one to lead you away from this conclusion, namely, that the fornicator and all such persons will have no share in God’s kingdom. [Col. 1260C] For all the arguments of those who wish to deceive you in this way are empty words.

And truly you ought not to be torn away from this sound understanding by words of this kind, because on account of these things the wrath of God comes—that is, divine punishment, so that they perish eternally—upon the children of unbelief: that is, upon those who, though they are children of the Church not according to a good life but solely according to participation in the sacraments, are nevertheless children of unbelief and despair, because we have no confidence in them on account of their wickedness. And because the wrath of divine judgment comes upon them at their death, therefore, lest you suffer like things, do not become their partners—either by saying the same things or by giving credence to them.

But according to the ancient history (Num. 21, 25, [Col. 1261A] 26), because of empty words, fornication, and similar things, the wrath of divine punishment came upon the Jews, casting down their corpses in the wilderness. They were children of unbelief because they distrusted the promises, not believing them to be true; and therefore they murmured and committed fornication, on account of which they also perished. Therefore do not act or speak similarly, lest you perish similarly.

> “For you were once darkness, but now light in the Lord. Walk as children of light. For the fruit of light is in all goodness, righteousness, and truth, proving what is pleasing to God.”

You ought no longer to become their partners, because you once—that is, before conversion—were darkness: the black obscurity of sins, both in yourselves [Col. 1261B] and in others, whom you blinded and hurled into error by your evil example. But now—that is, after you came to grace—you have become light according to faith, righteousness, and purity of life, because by the light and example of your conduct and knowledge you illuminate others. And this is not in yourselves, but in the Lord, because you were darkness in yourselves but are now light in the Lord, so that “he who glories may glory in the Lord” (Jer. 9; 1 Cor. 1).

You are light, but light that has been illumined, just as our eyes too are called light but illumined, because they cannot see unless either the sun shines by day or some lamp gives light at night. And because it is necessary that you, who are such light, be illumined by the true light who is God, you are not said to be light in yourselves but in the Lord. Therefore you can rightly be called children of light. [Col. 1261C] Since, then, you are light and children of light, do not now walk as children of darkness, but as children of light: that is, advance from bright works to yet brighter ones.

Reason urges you to walk thus because the fruit of light—that is, the useful work which light produces as a tree produces fruit—consists in every goodness, by which each person is good in himself; in every righteousness, by which he gives his neighbours what is just; and in every truth, by which he believes and speaks what is true. We may understand righteousness and truth as parts of goodness. Righteousness is maintained in the observance of good works; truth, in speech that is not false and in thoughts. All these things are good and therefore are parts of goodness. And the light that produces such fruits is a person [Col. 1261D] made luminous by the true light, who is Christ.

Walk as children of light, and do this by proving—that is, examining, striving to know, and discerning—what is pleasing to God: that is, what God especially wills, so that you may do what you have found most pleasing to him. For whatever we intend to do, before beginning it we ought to test whether it will please God. If we have found that it will please God, then let us do it; but if it will displease him, let us not do it. It follows:

> “And do not share in the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather rebuke them. For it is shameful even to speak of the things done by them in secret.”

Walk as children of light and do not share—that is, do not take pleasure in sharing, namely [Col. 1262A] in consenting to—the unfruitful works of darkness, that is, of those who are darkness: blinded in themselves and blinding others. For those works are unfruitful, bringing no benefit. Do not share in works of this kind, but rather—that is, instead—rebuke and correct them. For there are two ways in which the evil people with whom we live do not defile us: if we do not consent and if we rebuke them. Not to share is not to consent. For one shares with a sinner when one adds to his deed the partnership of one’s will or approval.

The Apostle, admonishing us of this, therefore says: “Do not share in the unfruitful works of people of darkness.” And because it was too little merely not to consent if negligence of discipline were involved, he says: “But rather rebuke them.” Observe that he has included both: “Do not share; but rather rebuke.” What is “do not share”? Do not consent, do not praise, do not approve. What is “rather rebuke”? Reprove, correct, restrain. This command is given especially to rulers. You ought not to share but rather to rebuke because it is shameful not only to do or see, but even to speak of the things which those darkened people do in secret [Col. 1262B]—that is, in hidden places—because they are ashamed to do such things openly. “Everyone who does evil hates the light” (John 3). It follows:

> “But all things that are rebuked are made manifest by the light. For everything that is made manifest is light. Therefore he says: Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ shall give you light.”

They do shameful things in secret. But all their works which are rebuked are made manifest to them by the light of that rebuke. Often a fault is unknown to the very person who committed it; but when he is reproved, it is made manifest to him. The consciences of those whom the Apostle now calls darkness have been so darkened by the habit of sinning that they no longer understand the things they do to be evil; or, if they understand, they count them as nothing and forget them. For sins committed are, as it were, covered and hidden under a certain darkness, so that they are either not understood or are not later recalled to mind. But when faults which they did not know are brought before the eyes of their hearts by one reproving them, and they are rebuked, then [Col. 1262C] they are made manifest by the light of truth to their minds, so that they may see, confess, and erase them through penance. See how great a benefit proceeds from rebuke.

And indeed they are made manifest by the light. For every sin that is made manifest is light—that is, evident and unambiguous; what has been openly stated cannot be hidden by excuse. Or every evil work made manifest through confession is light—that is, it illumines the conscience, because from consideration of the evils he has committed, the penitent person’s mind is illumined for doing good, so that he may see how greatly he ought to afflict himself in penance and with how much zeal he ought to labour in good works.

Therefore—that is, because everything made manifest becomes light—Isaiah says: “Arise, be illumined, for your light has come” (Isa. 40 [printed]). But the Apostle, in his customary manner and by apostolic authority, sets this saying in other words [Col. 1263A] and adds some things: “Awake,” he says, “you who sleep,” and so forth. The sleep of the soul is to forget its God. For whatever soul has forgotten its God sleeps. Just as a person who sleeps bodily, even though it is already day, is as though in night because he does not keep watch to see that the day has already risen, so in some people, although Christ is already present and truth already preached, there remains the sleep of ruin.

Therefore prophet or Apostle cries to each such person: “Arise, be illumined, for your light has come,” that is, Christ. Or: “Awake, you who sleep,” that is, you who lie sluggish in the darkness of heart, not remembering God or considering your sins, but fixing the eyes of your mind upon earthly desires: rise from that sloth through remembrance of God and recognition [Col. 1263B] of your faults; and rise—that is, rise wholly—through worthy penance, you, I say, lifted up and separated from the dead, that is, from those spiritually dead in soul through sins, so that you may no longer lie with them as similarly dead.

Or awake through confession and rise through satisfaction. Rise from the dead—that is, from sins—which in the Epistle to the Hebrews are called dead works (Heb. 6). Then Christ, who illuminates minds, will give you light: that is, he will so pour into your heart the light of his wisdom, truth, and grace that it remains with you, so that you do not lose it thereafter. For he conveys more by saying “will give you light” than if he had said “will illumine you.” For “will illumine you” would indicate that Christ pours the light of virtues into a person; but “will give you light” means not only that he spreads the radiance of virtues but also that he preserves it in him. For Christ would not illumine him—that is, for that person’s benefit—unless he preserved him in the light of virtues unto the end.

> “Therefore see, brothers, how carefully you walk: not as unwise persons, but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil (Col. 4). Therefore do not become imprudent, but understand what the will of God is (Rom. 12; 1 Thess. 4).”

You ought, as has been said, to walk as children of light and not to share in works of darkness, but rather to rebuke them. And because this is how you must act, therefore, brothers, see—that is, consider—how you walk carefully [Col. 1263D], that is, how prudently you act. For those walk carefully who proceed along the path of good works in such a way that they wisely guard themselves against the vices that lie in ambush. Those walk carefully who both do good things and are not stained either by their own vices or by those of others. Only those can do this who both live justly and do not consent to sinners, but rebuke them through the zeal of charity. Walk carefully, not as foolish persons: that is, not only guard yourselves from sin, but also from the appearance of sin. This means: guard yourselves in such a way that you seem in no respect to resemble the foolish.

For many walk carefully, keeping themselves, with God’s help, free from blameworthy sin, and yet they walk as foolish persons. For example, if a priest, while rebuking a prostitute, frequents [Col. 1264A] her house, he seems foolish, even if he has no intention of sinning with her. But it does not become saints, through their own negligence or lack of discernment, to give others a bad opinion of them. Do not walk the way of righteousness as foolish persons, but as wise persons: that is, so blamelessly that in your very manner of walking you appear wise. Or: do not walk as foolish lovers of the world, who make no provision for themselves for the future, but as wise persons, who strive to live in this world in such a way that they may possess eternal life in the world to come.

I mean you who are redeeming the time. To redeem the time is this: when someone brings a lawsuit against you, lose something so that you may give yourself to God rather than to litigation. For what you lose is the price of time. Just as you spend money to buy something for yourself, so spend money, or anything else whatsoever, to purchase for yourself [Col. 1264B] peace. For you will not have a peaceful heart; rather, you will be disturbed by thoughts of anger against your adversary. And so you will lose time. But it is better that you lose money and redeem time.

Or we redeem time when we restore by weeping the past life which we squandered in self-indulgence. For while we act wickedly, we lose the time in which we ought to be working well; but we redeem the loss of time if we so amend our life that we do both the good things which we formerly neglected to do and those which we ought now to do. Nor is it surprising that we have done less, since the days are evil: that is, the changing character of time is harmful, because it draws sinners toward a variety of pleasures. The days are evil because wickedness flourishes in them and [Col. 1264C] sin is easily committed in them, since time supplies material for evil action by presenting the variety of things which it brings with it.

For two things make days evil: wickedness and misery. Days are called evil because of human wickedness and misery. But these days, so far as the divisions of the hours are concerned, are ordered; they take their turns and carry out their courses. To whom are times burdensome, if people are not burdensome to one another? Therefore, as I have said, two things make days evil: wickedness and misery. But human misery is common to all; wickedness, however, ought not to be common. Since Adam fell and was expelled from paradise, there have never been days except evil ones. And because the days are evil, and we are placed on a slope toward sin, therefore do not become imprudent—that is, undiscerning or thoughtless—so that [Col. 1264D] you cannot prudently avoid evils and choose goods, or do all things with rational consideration; but be understanding what the will of God is: that is, what God wills, so that you may do it.

> “And do not become drunk with wine, in which is debauchery; but be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord; always giving thanks for all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God the Father, being subject to one another in the fear of Christ.”

Understand the will of God. And, so that you may be able to understand and do it, do not become drunk with wine. I do not forbid you to drink wine moderately, but do not exceed the measure. For I forbid drunkenness. Do not become drunk [Col. 1265A] with wine, in which, when drunk immoderately, there is debauchery: that is, debauchery lies in excessive drinking of wine. Debauchery is not in the nature of wine, but in the immoderation of drinking, lest anyone, perversely understanding this, attempt to show that God’s creature—namely wine—is evil, reasoning thus: “That whose effect is evil is itself also evil; but the effect of wine, namely debauchery, is evil; therefore wine is evil.” This reasoning does not hold, since wine is a creature of God. Therefore it must be said that in “becoming drunk” is debauchery.

Or certainly, by “wine in which is debauchery” we may understand desire and the other draughts of vices, which intoxicate and overthrow the mind. Of such wine Solomon says: “Wine is a thing of excess” (Prov. XX). Do not gorge yourselves with wine, but be filled—that is, strive [Col. 1265B] to be filled—with the Holy Spirit, who commendably intoxicates you by changing your minds and warming you with love of eternal things. You will be able to be filled with that Spirit in this way: if you think and understand in your mind those things which you sing with your mouth, and inwardly instruct yourselves from them.
