And this is what it means: “Be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to yourselves inwardly with attentiveness”; that is, understand what you utter with your lips. For it greatly pleases God that each person attends to what he says in psalms, which exhort to good works; and in hymns, which concern the praises of God; and in spiritual songs, which resound concerning eternal joy, and are therefore spiritual. For there are songs of worldly people, but they are not spiritual. And after speaking these things, be singing—that is [Col. 1265C] praising God and exulting in eternal things, as hymns and songs teach—and making melody in works, as psalms urge.

Sing, I say, and make melody in your hearts: that is, just as praises of the Lord resound in your mouth, so let them resound in your hearts. And do this not for vain glory or any other purpose, but for the Lord alone, that is, for his honor. Sing: that is, let heavenly things resound and desire them. For one who desires sings in the heart even if the tongue is silent. But one who does not desire, though he strike human ears with whatever clamor, is mute. For the desire and love of the heart is the sweet voice of one singing within. Thus sing in your hearts to the Lord.

I mean you who give thanks, not merely for an hour but always, for everything which he has given or will give, whether prosperous or adverse. Always give him thanks, [Col. 1265D] and do this in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all these things are given to you by the Father, so that the Son himself may be glorified in those thanksgivings. Give thanks, I say, to God who created you, and to the Father who adopted you as sons. I mean you who are subject to one another, humbly caring for each other and piously serving one another in turn. Do this in the chaste fear of Christ, who commanded the humility of this subjection in the present life and came not to be served, but to serve (Matt. XX).

> “Let wives be subject to their own husbands, as to the Lord, because the husband is the head of the wife (I Cor. XI; I Pet. III), as Christ is the head of the Church, himself the savior of his body. But as the Church is subject [Col. 1266A] to Christ, so also let wives be subject to their own husbands in all things.”

The Apostle turns to domestic precepts and commands each rank what it owes. Let wives be subject, by reverence and obedience, to their own husbands, not to strangers, as to the Lord: that is, only in doing good, just as we are subject to the Lord God in order to serve him by doing good, not evil. Or, “as to the Lord” means that they should serve their husbands in the simplicity and charity in which they would serve God. They ought to do this because the husband is the head of the wife: that is, her source, since woman was first made from man (Gen. II). He is also the head because he is her ruler. For woman is governed through her husband, as the body through the head. And it is fitting that the body be governed and subjected to the head—that is, the wife [Col. 1266B] to the husband.

The husband is the head of the wife in the same way that Christ is the head of the Church: because just as Christ governs and instructs the Church, so the husband ought to govern and instruct his wife; and just as Christ and the Church are spiritually one, so husband and wife are carnally one. As Christ is the glory of the Church, so a good husband is the glory of a woman. Christ is the head of the Church—he himself, I say, is the savior of his body, that is, of the Church—because he saves the whole body of the Church. For no member of the Church is saved except through Christ, who is the head and Savior of all the elect; and likewise, according to his measure, a husband ought to save his wife from every evil. For just as the Church has from Christ the cause of its life, so a woman has it from her husband, because, in order that she may stand, [Col. 1266C] she takes a husband.

Let wives be subject to their husbands, and not in just any manner, but as the Church is subject to Christ in all things, so let wives be subject to their own husbands in all things that are not contrary to God. The Church is so subject to Christ in all things that it prefers itself to him in nothing, lest it wish to be superior to him or even equal to him. In the same way, let wives be subject to their husbands, so as not to wish in any respect to rise above them.

> “Husbands, love your wives (Col. III), as Christ also loved the Church and gave himself for her, in order that he might sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word of life, in order that he himself might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of the sort, but that she might be holy [Col. 1266D] and without blemish. So husbands also ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his own wife loves himself. For no one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, as Christ also does the Church. Because we are members of his body, from his flesh and from his bones. For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and shall cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh (Gen. II). This is a great mystery, but I speak concerning Christ and the Church. Nevertheless, let each one of you love his own wife as himself. And let the wife fear her husband.”

“Husbands,” he says, “love your wives, whose head you are, as Christ also loved the Church, whose [Col. 1267A] head he is.” That is, love them with that goodness with which Christ loved the Church, so that you do not love sin in them but every good thing, and govern and cherish them justly. Christ loved the Church and, because of his exceeding love, gave himself over to death to redeem her. So you also, if necessary, give yourselves up for the salvation of your wives.

He gave himself so that he might sanctify her by his blood, since she was defiled by many sins. He himself, I say, cleansed her from all sins by the washing of water sanctified in the word of life—that is, by the washing of baptism. For Christ’s baptism is a washing of water in the word of life. Take away the water: there is no baptism. Take away the word: there is no baptism. By “word” he means the invocation of divinity uttered over the water by the baptizer. He cleansed her for this purpose: so that he, who [Col. 1267B] was able to do this well, might present to himself—that is, prepare for his own honor—the Church of the elect, glorious in the beauty of virtues, not having spot or wrinkle: that is, clean and simple.

For she has neither spot nor wrinkle who lacks both the ugliness of evil conduct and duplicity of speech: she is clean through righteousness and stretched taut through a simple intention. This is said by comparison with a garment, which is first washed and afterward stretched. For the Church is customarily called not only Christ’s bride but also Christ’s garment. It was cleansed so that it might have no spot; it was stretched so that it might have no wrinkle. In the elect it has no spot of crime and no wrinkle of deceit. It has no wrinkle in them because they do not know how to show one thing outwardly concerning themselves and [Col. 1267C] hold another inwardly.

Or it has no wrinkle in them because they are not bent toward love of earthly things, but are stretched out by hope and desire for heavenly goods. It has neither spot nor wrinkle, nor anything else of this kind, because it does not permit itself to be so burdened even by the habitual practice of venial sins that their multitude can be compared with any grave offense; rather, it is holy in good work and without blemish in abstaining from evil. “Without blemish” means without grave offense. For no one can be without sin in this life.

Or these words may be referred to the age to come. Christ cleansed the Church so that, after the day of judgment, he himself may present it to himself in eternal blessedness, glorious—that is, radiant in soul and body—because then the righteous will shine [Col. 1267D] like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matt. XIII; Wis. III). Then the Church will be wholly and perfectly without spot of sin, wrinkle of duplicity, or anything of this sort, because then it will also be truly glorious. For now, amid so many evils, so many scandals, such a mingling of utterly wicked people, and so many reproaches from the ungodly, it should not be called glorious. Rather, it will be glorious then, when, delivered from every evil, it will rejoice forever in good things with Christ. Then it will be truly holy and without blemish, because holiness alone will so reign in it that every stain of every kind of sin will be far from it. Or it will be holy through the transformation of the flesh and without blemish through the removal of corruption.

Christ, as has been said, loved the Church, which is his body. Thus husbands also ought [Col. 1268A] to love their wives as their own bodies: that is, as themselves, because wives are their bodies and they are their heads. Or, just as a person’s spirit loves, governs, and subjects to itself in good the body and flesh to which it is joined, so husbands should love, govern, and subject to themselves in good their wives. They ought to do this because one who loves his wife loves himself, since he and his wife are one body and the wife is his flesh. Thus a husband ought to love her, because no one has ever hated his own flesh.

For those who say that they would rather be without a body are entirely mistaken. They do not hate their body, but its corruptions and its burden. Therefore they do not want no body at all, but an incorruptible and most swift body. Nor do those who kill themselves hate [Col. 1268B] their own flesh; rather, they think that through death they will escape certain grievous troubles. Those who, by a certain continence and by labors, discipline their bodies—and who do this rightly—do not act in order to have no body, but in order to have it subdued and ready for necessary works. For they seek to extinguish, through a kind of arduous warfare carried out by the body itself, the lusts of those who misuse the body—that is, the habitual inclinations of the soul to enjoy inferior things. For they do not kill themselves, and they take care of their health.

Therefore no one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes it with food and drink and cherishes it with clothing, just as Christ spiritually nourishes the Church with the food and drink of his body and blood, or with the food of fuller understanding and the drink of easier teaching, and cherishes it with the garments [Col. 1268C] of virtues. Thus a husband ought to act toward his wife, who is his flesh. Christ cherishes the Church, which is his body. And truly it is his body, because all of us are members of this sacred body.

Because we are members of his body—that is, of the Church—from his flesh, that is, from its weakness, and from his bones, that is, from its strength. This means that some of us are weak and others strong in this body of his which is the Church. For just as the human body consists of flesh and bones, and its flesh is supported by its bones, so the Church consists of less perfect and more perfect persons, and the more perfect support the imperfect by their example and exhortation. Thus a woman, who is like fragile flesh, ought to be supported by her husband, who is like the firmness of bone [Col. 1268D] (I Cor. XII).

Or, whoever can say by his grace, “When I am weak, then I am stronger and powerful,” is from his flesh and from his bones. Whoever can say in imitation of him, “I became weak to the weak, in order that I might gain the weak” (I Cor. IX), is from his flesh and from his bones. Or we are from his flesh and from his bones because, receiving his flesh in the ministry, we join it to our own flesh, and by the power of his Spirit we are strengthened as though by inward bones. For just as Eve, made from Adam, drew flesh and bones from him, so the Church, brought forth from Christ, drew his flesh and Spirit into itself, as we have said.

Or we are from his flesh and from his bones because we have the same flesh and the same bones which he had, since he took flesh with bones from our mortality. It may also be understood as referring to a body composed of his flesh and bones—that is, of the strong and the weak. Because we are from his flesh [Col. 1269A] and from his bones, and because he loved the Church, it was prophesied of him from the beginning: “A man shall leave father and mother and shall cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Matt. XIX; Mark X; I Cor. VI).

“For this man, the mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (I Tim. II), was signified. He left his Father when he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. II). Thus he left the Father, not because he abandoned or departed from the Father, but because he did not appear to human beings in that form in which he is equal to the Father. He also left his mother, that is, the synagogue of the Jews, from which he had been born according to the flesh [Col. 1269B]. And he clung to his wife: that is, he associated and joined himself to the Church of the elect. And these two, Christ and the Church, are one flesh, because the Church daily receives, in the celebrations of the Mass, the flesh which he took from the Virgin.

Or they are one flesh because, as said above, he took flesh from our mortality and became our participant through flesh, so that we might be the body of that head. Thus there came to be, from two, one certain person: from head and body, from bridegroom and bride. Therefore the whole Christ is head and body, like a complete man, because woman was made from man and belongs to man. This is a great mystery concerning the union of Christ and the Church.

And lest anyone understand this greatness of the mystery as referring to every individual [Col. 1269C] person who has a wife, “but I,” he says, “speak concerning Christ and the Church.” I indeed interpret these words of Genesis allegorically concerning the marriage of Christ and the Church; but you, nevertheless, understand them morally and literally: and let each one of you love his own wife as himself. But we exhort the wife to fear her husband—that is, to love him with chaste fear, obey him in every good thing, and revere him.

## CHAPTER VI

> “Children, obey your parents in the Lord (Col. III). For this is just. Honor your father and your mother (Exod. XX; Ecclus. III; Matt. XV), which is the first commandment with a promise, [Col. 1269D] that it may be well with you and that you may be long-lived upon the earth.”

He commands children to obey their parents in the Lord: that is, in matters pertaining to God. For he does not advise obedience in things contrary to God. And parents ought to be obeyed because this is just: that children should obey them has the force of natural law. Nor is this merely natural law; it is also a commandment of the Lord, who says: “Honor your father and your mother” (Exod. XX).

This ought especially to be observed because it is the first commandment with a promise. Although this commandment is fourth in the Decalogue, it is first with a promise, because a promise was first added to this commandment, whereas none had been added to the preceding ones. For three commandments preceded this one [Col. 1270A], and they belong to the love of God, because God is Trinity. But the other seven, among which this is first, concern love of neighbor and teach how one ought to live among human beings. For that very number of seven commandments begins with the honoring of parents. “Honor,” he says, “your father and mother.” For a person opens his eyes to his parents, and his good life takes its beginning from friendship with them. But whoever does not render honor to parents, whom will he be able to spare?

This is the first commandment on the second tablet, which contains commandments concerning the love of neighbor. And it is with a promise. It may also be distinguished thus: that it is understood to be first on the other tablet, and to be with a promise. But it may more truly be said to be first in both respects: both on the tablet and in the promise. This promise is great. “Honor,” he says, “your parents, that it may be well with you”: that is, that through this you may obtain from God both bodily and spiritual goods; “and that you may be long-lived upon the earth”: that is, that you may have the length of eternity upon the stable dwelling-place of the heavenly homeland.

> “And you, fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and correction of the Lord.”

You children, obey your parents; and you parents, do not give them occasion for disobedience. Do not provoke them to anger: that is, do not do things to them on account of which they sin through anger, because you are their fathers and they are your children. But bring them up while they are young in the discipline of the Lord, lest they begin [Col. 1270C] to live without discipline; and in the correction of the Lord, so that you may correct them for the perversity of their conduct, according to God and with a good disposition, and lead them back to uprightness.

> “Slaves, obey your fleshly masters with fear and trembling, in simplicity of your heart, as Christ; not serving only under the eye, as those pleasing men, but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, serving with good will as the Lord and not men (Col. III; Tit. II; I Pet. II), knowing that whatever good each one does, this he shall receive from the Lord, whether slave or free (Matt. XVI). And you masters, do the same things to them, remitting threats, [Col. 1270D] knowing that both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no respect of persons with God (Rom. II; Jas. II).”

You slaves, obey your fleshly masters: that is, those who exercise temporal lordship over you according to bodily matters, not spiritual ones. For you also have an eternal spiritual Lord in heaven, who rules your minds; but he does not wish you, on his account, to disdain serving fleshly masters, to whom you are subjected by his ordering. Even if they are wicked or unbelieving, serve them until their wickedness passes away. For many religious persons serve wicked masters who are nevertheless not free, because “everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John VIII). And certainly it is happier to serve a human being than lust.

For God has so ordered the Church [Col. 1271A] that every power established in the world should receive some honor, even from those better than itself. Therefore obey your masters as is fitting, namely with fear and trembling. For fear is the cause of trembling. Let children obey their parents with the reverence of honor, but slaves with fear in the mind and trembling in the body: that is, so that bodily gesture and appearance may show inward fear. And do this not in pretence, but in simplicity of your heart: that is, in purity of intention. Although fear is to be maintained, intention must nevertheless remain simple, that is, without the duplicity of pretence, so that just as you outwardly show yourselves gladly obedient, so you may be inwardly disposed. That is, do not do this merely through fear of escaping temporal penalties, but with the pure intention of doing good.

Obey them as Christ [Col. 1271B]: that is, with the purity of intention with which you ought to obey Christ. For when, at Christ’s command, you serve human beings, you do not serve them but him who commanded it. Or obey them as Christ: that is, only in what is good. For they often command evil deeds, but in these matters they are not to be obeyed. Obey in simplicity of heart, not serving only under the eye: that is, do not be ready and diligent in service only when you are seen by your masters, while acting negligently in their absence. For this is what deceitful slaves do, who wish to please human masters whom they can deceive, not God, who sees all things.

Do not serve so falsely, as though pleasing human beings alone, but as servants of Christ: that is, in purity of heart [Col. 1271C] and truth, pursuing nothing except true righteousness. I mean you who in this do the will of God, who willed that you should serve fleshly masters, not unwillingly but from the heart; and not from an evil heart but with good will. Thus, even if you cannot become free, you may in some manner make your servitude free, serving not with deceitful fear but with faithful love. See: Christ did not make slaves free, but made bad slaves good slaves.

Serve from the heart with good will, as to the Lord God and not to human beings, by whose command you serve human beings. I mean you who know that whatever good each person does, he will receive this from the Lord, whether slave or free. That is, you ought therefore to serve your masters as is right, because you are certain that you will receive recompense from God not only for this but for every good that you do, whether you are slaves or free; for neither slavery hinders anyone from attaining the reward, nor does freedom render anyone ready for it—provided only that each does good. For God is the rewarder of all truly good works, whoever performs them.

And you masters, do the same things to them—not that you should serve them, but that you should treat them in simplicity of heart and good will according to God. That is, just as it befits them to render you due and just subjection by serving you, so exercise just and gentle authority over them by ruling humbly. Treat them more gently, remitting—that is, relaxing—your threats. I do not forbid threats, but command that they be made more mild. And if threats ought to be made more mildly, how much more so blows? [Col. 1272A] Treat them humanely, I say, knowing that both their Master and yours is in heaven. That is, although they are yours, yet you are their fellow-servants, having one Master. You are proud against his gift if you do not recognize as equal to yourselves by fellowship in nature those whom you hold subject by their social condition.

For if you treat them badly, I do not excuse your nobility. For there is no respect of persons with God: that is, he does not receive people on account of the dignities of their persons, since in his judgment loftiness of station contributes nothing to anyone, nor does lowliness of station harm anyone; but each receives, whether good or evil, according to his works, whether that person is free or a slave. Therefore both slaves and masters ought to strive to act justly.

[Col. 1272B]

> “For the rest, brothers, be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might. Put on the armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.”

Having completed his particular instructions for women and men, children and parents, slaves and masters, he returns to general exhortation and instructs all together for spiritual warfare. It is as if he were saying: “Until now some of you have thought that you could do some good by your own strength without the help of grace; but henceforth, brothers, if you wish to act with a good disposition, be strengthened not in yourselves but in the Lord.”

Or thus: “Up to now I have helped you, but for the remaining span of your life, be strengthened now in the Lord, so that without me you may become strong against the devil’s warfare.” Or again thus: “I have said many things to you up to this point, but as for what more I might say, do this one thing: for the rest, act thus—namely, be strengthened, that is, become strong against every assault of the adversary—in the Lord, that is, in view of the fact that you have a Lord by whose lordship you are protected; and be strengthened in the power of his might,” that is, in his might which can do all things.

And therefore you ought to be strengthened, both because you have a Lord and because he possesses mighty power in all things. And because you must be strengthened not by grace alone, but must also employ free choice, put on the armor of God. That is, do not merely be strengthened in the Lord, but, stirring up free choice, put on the armor of God: put on all the arms [Col. 1272D] by which one serves as a soldier of God. For “armor” includes all weapons. Put on the armor of God—this was said with respect to free choice—so that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.

For in this way you can resist his wiles, namely through the assistance of divine grace and the exercise of free choice, because no one can resist him either by grace alone or by free choice alone. Therefore first be strengthened in the Lord, and afterward put on the armor of God, because grace precedes free choice. For this reason you must put on the armor of God: so that, serving him courageously as soldiers, you may not yield or fall in battle, but may stand against the wiles of the devil, both because the devil is an accuser and because he acts deceitfully against you. For a battle fought by wiles is far more grievous than one fought by force. Human beings do not see the devil with whom they fight, but they nevertheless have an easy remedy: let them conquer themselves inwardly, and triumph over him outwardly. For this reason the armor of God must be put on. And what armor must be put on, if not progress in all virtues, by which we are defended from Satan’s darts?

> “For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the world of this darkness, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.”

Therefore we must be armed on every side with spiritual weapons, because our struggle is against spiritual enemies. For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, that is, against human beings who are flesh and blood. To the less perfect Galatians he prescribed another warfare, namely that against flesh and blood, saying: “For the flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5). But to the Ephesians, as though already spiritual, prevailing over the flesh’s concupiscence, and enduring outward persecution for righteousness’ sake, he says: Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood—that is, not against the human beings who seem to persecute us—but against the evil spirits who rule their minds and persecute us through them. And because this is so, we ought to love human beings, beware of demons, mercifully rescue human beings, and manfully overcome demons.

For just as, if an armed man from the opposing side comes against someone stationed in battle, riding a horse, he is angry not with the horse but with the rider, and strives as far as he can to strike the rider and take possession of the horse; so we must act against all evil people: not against them, but against him who incites them, must we labor with all our strength, so that when the devil is conquered, the unhappy persons whom he possessed may be set free. Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood—that is, against the people whom we see raging against us, who ought rather to be pitied than hated—but against their ruling demons, and against the wicked powers of evil spirits.

Those spirits are called “rulers” who rule in their own vices, which they customarily suggest in a particular way: such as the spirit of fornication, which attacks people by means of lust and rules over the lustful; and the spirit of pride, which attacks by means of pride; and the rest of this sort. Thus each one rules in its own vice. Those spirits are called “powers” which have the force and office of driving people into greater sins, because they preside over them by introducing greater and more grievous vices. Who does not understand how dangerous it is to fight against such beings? And how do we conquer enemies of this kind, whom we do not see, except because we feel our inward carnal motions, fight against them, and strike those enemies through them?

Or the “rulers” may be understood as those demons who rule other demons, and the “powers” as those who have authority over others. For some among them are more wicked than others and stronger in evil. Against these is our struggle, and against the rulers of the world—[Col. 1274A] that is, against those demons who, by God’s just judgment, rule those who are “the world,” namely those excessively attached to worldly things. These are they who persecute us through the people subject to them, since they rule them toward evil action and lead them from vice into vice. For they are rulers of the world because they rule worldly people, as has been said.

They are rulers not of the elements of the world—that is, heaven and earth, sea and air—but of this world of darkness: that is, of all these unbelievers and wicked people. Of this world it was said: “The whole world lies in the evil one” (John 8 [citation as printed]). And to converted sinners: “You were once darkness,” he says, “but now light in the Lord” (Wisdom 5 [citation as printed]). Evil spirits rule this world, which consists of such darkness—that is, darkened people. Our warfare is against these, not against those whom they rule; and likewise against spiritual beings, and so forth.

By this the great violence of the attack is shown. For a person is harassed by a much graver and more perilous conflict when attacked by an enemy not subject to the eyes, because he does not know from what quarter the adversary is assailing him. By “spiritual beings of wickedness” I mean beings of defect and of incapacity. For *nequitia* (“wickedness”) is so called from *nequam* (“worthless”), because through it one tends toward non-being; just as the reprobate angels deserted God, who alone truly is, and fell into everlasting ruin. These spiritual beings of wickedness are in the heavenly places—that is, in the dark dwelling-place of this lower air, where clouds also gather.

Or, “in the heavenly places” means that we endure assault from the most wicked spirits in the holy virtues of our mind. Or they fight against us “in the heavenly places,” that is, in order to take away our heavenly inheritance. Therefore the Apostle declares that we have a grave contest against rulers and powers, against the rulers of this world of darkness, and against spiritual beings of wickedness in the heavenly places.

The character of this contest itself should be understood thus: when losses, dangers, reproaches, and accusations are stirred up against us, the hostile powers do not seek merely that we suffer these things. Rather, through them they seek to provoke us either to great anger, excessive sorrow, or final despair; or—what is more serious—to compel us, worn down and defeated by weariness, to complain against God, as though he did not govern human life with equal justice. Thus they seek either to weaken us in faith, make us fall away from hope, force us away from the truth of doctrine, or persuade us to hold some impious opinion concerning him.

Such things were written concerning Job, when the devil asked God to grant him power over Job’s goods (Job 12 [citation as printed]). From these things we are also taught that we are not attacked by chance occurrences if losses of property strike us; nor is it by chance that one of our people is led away captive, or that houses collapse and beloved persons are crushed in them, or that anything of the kind happens. In all these things, or in any one of them, every believer should say to the adversary: “You would have no power against me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19). For he could do nothing against Job except insofar as God permitted him. So he will be able to do no more against any believer. We who fight against such adversaries must be instructed in this way.

> “Therefore take up the armor of God, that you may be able to resist in the evil day, and, having accomplished all things, to stand perfect. Stand therefore, having your loins girded in truth, and clothed with the breastplate of righteousness, and your feet shod in readiness for the Gospel of peace; in all things taking up the shield of faith, with which you may be able to extinguish the fiery darts of the most wicked one; and take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.”

The Apostle arms us with weapons of this kind: praiseworthy and invincible, unconquerable and splendid, spiritual and invisible, because we are fighting invisible enemies. [Col. 1275B] If you see your enemy, let your weapons be seen. But if you do not see the enemy, why should the weapons with which you attack him be visible? Because the conflict is so grave, so manifold, and so perilous, therefore take up the armor of God—that is, the weapons of virtues with which God arms his soldiers. Receive strong arms from the hand of the supreme commander, so that you may not yield to the enemies already mentioned but strongly resist them in the evil day: that is, in the hour of temptation, when they make it seem as though the day of prosperity smiles upon you by offering the pleasure of sin.

Or “in the evil day” means in the time when wickedness flourishes: in the time of diabolical assault, in the time of the present life, which is entirely temptation (Job 7). Thus you may not lie defeated, but stand perfect in all virtues—not perfect in some good virtues and imperfect in others, but perfect in all, insofar as this is permitted. Then you will be unable to be conquered from any side. Or, that you may stand perfect in every assault, which is more than merely resisting. Or, “in all things,” whether favorable or adverse.

Or again: “that you may be able to resist in the evil day” means on the day of judgment. It is called evil because it will be terrible with the devil’s accusations, so that when he has accused his own, you may defend yourselves by purity of conscience and may also stand perfect in all things with the elect.

You must stand against the enemies in the armor of God. Therefore stand with the loins of your mind girded—that is, stand in chastity, because this is the beginning of good action, and thus it is now placed first among the spiritual weapons described. So long as anyone is subject to lust, he can do no good, because nothing he does can please God. But once he has abandoned lust, he begins to work righteousness. Therefore we are first commanded to gird our loins and afterward to put on the breastplate of righteousness.

We gird our loins when, through continence, we restrain the fleshly lust that is in the loins. But because some pretend that they have their loins girded when they do not, we are commanded to have them girded in truth, not in pretense, so that our chastity may be real rather than feigned. Or let us gird the loins of the mind in truth, so that by the belt of chaste love for Christ we restrain ourselves from falsehood. For whoever speaks a lie, so far as lies in him, corrupts [Col. 1276A] truth and thus commits fornication. But whoever strives always to speak truth uses, as it were, a lawful marriage, having truth or wisdom as a wife, like the one who said: “I loved her and sought her from my youth, and I sought to take her as my bride” (Wisdom 8).

Thus your loins must be girded in truth, so that we may not go to a prostitute—that is, to falsehood—but delight in the lawful bride, who is truth, and beget children from her. Then it is added that we should also be clothed with the breastplate of righteousness: that is, fortified on every side by the strong garment of good action, so that nothing unjust may appear in our works, but everything may be righteous and equitable in every respect.

This righteousness of upright living is our breastplate because it does not allow our inward parts to be pierced, but defends our hearts on every side from all the enemy’s darts. For just as a breastplate is made from many links, so the garment of righteousness is joined together from many good works and virtues. Our inner person must put on such a breastplate, so that he cannot be wounded from any side.

Once we have conquered lust and clothed ourselves with the breastplate of righteous action, we shall then be fit to preach good things to others. Hence it follows: “Stand with your feet shod”—that is, having shod feet, namely the protected affections of your mind, so that they do not touch earthly things, that is, so that they do not rest upon earthly advantages—“in readiness for the Gospel of peace”: that is, by preparing the hearts of others for evangelical preaching, which announces peace between God and human beings.

Shoes are made from the hides of dead animals, and they signify the examples of the fathers already deceased. By these the feet of our mind—that is, the affections by which we advance, as by feet, to do something—are protected from every earthly injury. For the preacher’s foot is injured by the earth if his affection seeks earthly advantage from preaching: that is, if he preaches the Gospel for earthly gain rather than for the kingdom of heaven. Therefore let our feet be shod with the aforesaid shoes—that is, fortified by the examples of the fathers—so that, as the fathers preached the Gospel from zeal for a heavenly aim and not from desire for earthly advantage, so may we also do.

Its preachers must in no respect abandon the rule of faith. Hence he adds: “In all things taking up the shield of faith.” Faith must be taken up as a shield in every engagement, because it first resists evil spirits, receives their darts, and drives them back. The other virtues are protected beneath it, since it extends to every weapon of virtue, and the devil first undertakes to attack it.

In every battle and every temptation, take up the shield of faith, by which you may be able not only to repel but also to extinguish every dart of the most wicked devil—that is, all his most penetrating suggestions, by which he attacks in order to wound our hearts. These darts are fiery: that is, they kindle the fire of vices in human hearts. For they inflame human minds toward concupiscence and set them alight with the fire of all wickedness. These are the darts of the most wicked enemy: one who presumes even to attempt things which he cannot accomplish, and in which he labors in vain. But against these we are armed with faith in invisible things and overthrow the invisible adversary.

Put on these weapons, and also take up the helmet of salvation—that is, hope which awaits eternal salvation. It is called a helmet because, just as the helmet is in the upper part of armor, namely upon the head, so hope is higher than all the other virtues and always looks upward, breathing after heavenly things. For this reason he added “of salvation,” in order to show that hope attains what it desires, namely salvation.

Or, just as the shield of faith is faith, so the helmet of salvation is salvation. The remembrance or expectation of this perpetual salvation makes the head of the mind safe against every blow of demonic attack. Whoever diligently considers what eternal joys are easily rejects the pleasures of sin from his heart and conquers adversities. These are the weapons by which armed, you will never yield to the devil or to any member of his.

The weapons by which you may conquer him and his followers now follow: “And take the sword of the Spirit,” that is, the spiritual blade, “which is the word of God”: that is, the word of divine preaching. By it the devil is slain—that is, his assaults are brought to nothing—and by it you will conquer and subject to yourselves the tyrants of this age, heretics, who are members of Satan, and the rest of sinners. When it says, “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God,” “which” refers to the meaning, not to “sword.” Behold, these are the weapons by which God’s soldiers are armed and fight. It follows:

> “Through every prayer and supplication, praying [Col. 1277C] at every time in the Spirit, and in the same watching with all perseverance and supplication for all the saints and for me, that utterance may be given me when I open my mouth, boldly to make known the mystery of the Gospel, for which I discharge an embassy in a chain, so that in it I may dare to speak as I ought.”

Stand fortified with the weapons already mentioned. But because it is not in our power to be fortified by them unless God grants it, nor can you conquer by them unless he gives it, be praying through every prayer—that is, through all things which ought to be prayed for—so that our supplication may extend through every prayer that must be made: that is, leave out nothing among the things which should be sought in prayer. And not only through prayer, but also through supplication—that is, through the adjuration of all sacred things. For *obsecratio* indicates a more urgent form of praying than *oratio*, since *obsecratio* is prayer with adjuration or solemn appeal, while *oratio*, simply made, is a request.

Through every prayer and supplication be praying at every suitable time—that is, at all the hours appointed for prayer—or at every time, whether adverse or favorable. Let this prayer be in the Spirit, that is, in the mind, so that the mind’s affection may agree with the words of prayer spoken by the mouth; or pray in the Spirit, not in the flesh. For one prays in the flesh rather than in the Spirit when he prays with a defiled mind, intending to sin again, not accidentally but deliberately.

Or pray at every time in the Spirit—that is, in heartfelt devotion—so that, although the mouth cannot always pray, the spirit may nevertheless always pray inwardly through good desires. And in that same spirit be watching inwardly—that is, vigilant and attentive: as the eyes watch outwardly, so let the spirit act inwardly. Do this with all perseverance, so that spirit and body may persistently continue in vigils; and with every supplication, so that you may make supplication for all those for whom supplication ought to be made, namely the saints. For supplication seems to be fitting for the saints, and prayer for unbelievers, who have nothing sacred.

Watch, I say, and make supplication for all the saints—that is, for the perseverance and salvation of all saints—and especially for me, that tribulation may not blunt me, but that utterance may be given me when I open my mouth: that is, when I open my mouth, when I speak high mysteries and profound propositions. For this expression is not found in divine Scripture except where something great and profound is to be said. When I open my mouth to bring forth hidden meanings, may utterance be given me—that is, eloquence to express what I wish—so that I may expound these matters clearly: namely, boldly and not timidly making known the mystery of the Gospel, that is, the hidden secret of Christ’s incarnation and passion, so that I may disclose their hidden causes to the hearers (Ps. 50 [citation as printed]).

Since this mystery is hidden, it is necessary that I make it known. And I desire to do this because, in proclaiming it, I discharge an embassy in a chain. Even because of the chain I do not cease from my embassy. Although I am chained for the Gospel which I proclaimed, I nevertheless do not omit to preach it, as one sent by Christ. May utterance, I say, be given me for making known the mystery of the Gospel, so given that in the Gospel itself I may dare to speak to others without fear as I ought—that is, as is fitting for me, who was sent to do this.

In some manuscripts a verse of this kind follows here: “But the word of God cannot be bound.” As though the Apostle said: I am indeed bound for the Gospel, but I do not cease to preach, because the word of God, which must be proclaimed, cannot be delayed by any impediment.

> “But that you also may know the things concerning me, what I am doing, Tychicus, the most beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, will make everything known to you. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know the things concerning us [Col. 1278D] and that he may comfort your hearts.”

I said that you should pray for me, and that I am bound for the Gospel; but I did not say by what tribulations I am afflicted. Tychicus will report to you the troubles surrounding me, lest you be disturbed by my least adversities and, fearing them, withdraw from the faith. He will tell you what kinds of torments surround me—that is, are in my body, since they do not penetrate the inward parts of my mind—and what I am doing, that is, how steadfast I am.

Tychicus is not insignificant, but a most beloved brother—that is, a Christian—and not deceitful or deceptive, but faithful. Therefore listen to him, because he is a faithful minister in the Lord, that is, in the things belonging to the Lord. [Col. 1279A] You ought to trust him because I sent him to you, that he might tell you the pure truth about me and comfort your hearts: that is, soothe and console them, and moderate the sorrow which had increased upon hearing of my tribulations. Or, if you grieved over our tribulations, now receive consolation from him, knowing that I willingly endure far greater things.

> “Peace to the brethren, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption. Amen.”

Let peace with God be with the brethren—that is, Christians—and love, that they may love him with their whole heart. May this peace and love be given them together with sound faith from God the Father and his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. For through peace they will remain in love, which is in faith; and from him from whom peace and love come, faith also comes—that is, from God.

Faith is not to be said not to be God’s gift, nor to come from ourselves, because it is given before it is asked for by the person to whom it is given. For all good things are from God. Let grace, received in its general sense—the mother and nurse of all good things—be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ, the bridegroom of the Church, in incorruption: that is, with chaste love, like a bride who admits no corruption.

For those do not love Christ in incorruption whose faith is corrupted in any respect, or who love him for temporal and corruptible goods rather than eternal and incorruptible ones. But those who love Christ for Christ alone and for the hope of everlasting incorruptibility love him in incorruption, because in this way neither can their mind be corrupted now nor their flesh then.

## ON THE EPISTLE TO THE PHILIPPIANS

[Col. 1279]

## PREFACE

[Col. 1279C]

Philippi is a city in Macedonia, from which the Philippians take their name. The Apostle had preached to them, instructing them in the truth of faith and uprightness of conduct. They themselves persisted in faith and nobility of conduct in almost all respects according to apostolic teaching; but there was contention among them only concerning precedence, since some wished to set themselves above others, as though glorying in their merits.

For this reason the Apostle, writing to them especially from Rome, intends to call them back to humility: namely, that they should not glory in merits or set one above another, but should attribute to the grace of God whatever good they possess—whether forgiveness of sins or gifts of virtues—since from him they have everything and from themselves nothing.

They had sent him some material support to Rome through Epaphroditus, whom he sends back with this letter. Since he cannot be present, in it he fortifies them against a twofold warfare: that of tribulations and that of false preachers. They are to endure every adversity for Christ with humility, as Christ also did, and never accept the legal observances from false prophets.

Because he invited them to humility, he did not give the title of his office and authority, namely “Apostle”; perhaps also because they had never thought poorly of him or against him. At the beginning of the letter he adds Timothy with himself, because Timothy had been the Apostle’s companion in their conversion, was concerned with him for their salvation, and perhaps had asked him to write to them. Thus he begins.

## CHAPTER ONE

> “Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, [Col. 1280C] with the bishops and deacons: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

Paul and Timothy call themselves servants of Christ, which is a sign of humility, so that by their example they may commend humility to the Philippians. But since the Lord himself says, “I shall no longer call you servants, because the servant does not know what his lord does” (John 15), on what ground do they call themselves servants?

We should know that just as there is a servile fear, which perfect love casts out (1 John 4), and a chaste fear remaining for ever and ever, so there is a servant who does not remain in the house forever and a servant entering into the joy of his lord (John 8; Matt. 25). For together with the fear expelled by love, the servitude belonging to it must also be expelled. Paul and Timothy, then, were servants with respect to chaste fear, not servile fear; nor servants of any mortal ruler, but of Jesus Christ.

They address what follows to all the saints—that is, to the whole people cleansed from sins through baptism and sanctified not by their own merit but in Christ Jesus, that is, in the grace of Christ: namely, because God became human, suffered, and rose again. Courteously he calls them back to humility by showing that they are saints in Christ Jesus, not in themselves; and he specifies which saints, namely, those who are at Philippi, that is, in that city.

“Philippi” is interpreted “mouth of a lamp”; and those saints are at Philippi—that is, in the mouth of the lamp—who are in God’s most radiant illumination and spread it everywhere to others, as is said to these people later: “In the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine as lights in the world, holding fast the word of life.” This letter is therefore written to such saints wherever they live bodily.

“To all the saints who are at Philippi,” that is, to all those subject to authority, “with the bishops,” that is, the presbyters, “and deacons,” that is, the lesser with the greater. For in his customary way he used “bishops” for presbyters. There were not several bishops in one city, nor would he have omitted the presbyters in descending to the deacons. Rather, he declares the dignity and excellence of presbyters by showing that those who are presbyters are also bishops.

The later election of one person to be placed above the others was made as a remedy for schism, lest each person, drawing Christ’s Gospel to himself, should tear it apart. At Alexandria also, from Mark the Evangelist down to the bishops Heraclas and Dionysius, the presbyters chose one of their own, set him in a higher place and rank, and called him bishop; just as an army makes a commander, or as deacons choose from among themselves someone whom they know to be capable and call him archdeacon.

It is therefore established by apostolic institution that all presbyters are bishops, although now those of higher rank possess this title. For *episcopus* means “overseer,” and every presbyter ought to give attention to the care of the sheep entrusted to him. “To all,” he says, “the saints who are at Philippi, with bishops and deacons.” [Note: [Col. 1281D] This passage is obscure.] Because he places the lesser first, he invites them to humility. But because he also adds the lesser, he shows that no one is so perfect as not to need this admonition. [Col. 1281C] What follows—“Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ”—has been explained in the preceding epistles.

> “I give thanks to my God at every remembrance of you, always, in all my prayers for all of you, making my petition with joy because of your fellowship in the Gospel of Christ from the first day until now; being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it unto the day of Christ Jesus; as it is right for me to think this of all of you, because I have you in my heart, and in my bonds, and in the defense and confirmation of the Gospel, all of you being partners in my joy.”

Seeking to win their good will, he shows that the beginning of their good work was given them by God and that its completion must be given by the same God, so that they may not rely on themselves but attribute all their good things to God’s grace.

“I give thanks,” he says, “to my God, who accomplishes in you what I desire”: that is, I praise him who freely bestowed upon us such great spiritual benefits, because you came to the good of the Christian religion not through our merit but by his gift, and in it have also made great progress. I give thanks, I say, for all of you—that is, for the religious way of life of all of you given by him—at every remembrance of you: whenever I remember you. I mean remembrance not momentarily but always, namely in all my prayers, whenever I pray.

Or, I mean remembrance of you not made on behalf of only a part of you, but on behalf of all of you. For benefits previously bestowed upon you by God, I give him thanks, not with sorrow but with joy, because I do not grieve over your faults but rejoice over your holiness. I make petition—that is, I beseech God with my whole heart—concerning your fellowship, that is, that you may always have fellowship more and more, be of one mind, and have one heart in the Gospel of Christ, that is, in the faith and precepts of evangelical teaching.

Or, I make petition concerning your fellowship, that you may persist in what you have shared with me in the faith and works of the Gospel. I make this petition not only for the moment, but from the first day of your conversion until now: that is, from the time you began to believe, I have not ceased to pour out prayers for you. Or your fellowship was in the Gospel, because from the first day of your conversion until now you have made your goods common for its sake; and therefore henceforth you must stand all the more firmly in this.

I beseech God for you, confidently trusting in his goodness that he who, through prevenient grace, began a good work in you will, through subsequent and cooperating grace, complete it, giving perseverance until the day of Jesus Christ: that is, until the last day of each person’s life, when the soul leaves the body and is presented before Christ’s judgment-seat to be judged.

For God completes by cooperating in us what he begins by working, since in beginning he works in us that we may will, and in completing he cooperates with those who will. For he works that we may will without us. But when we will, and will in such a way as to act, he cooperates with us. He who began a good work in you will himself complete it. I am so confident; see to it that this confidence is not in vain. See to it that, through your own fault, the good work which God is ready to complete in you with you does not remain unfinished.

I hope this in firm confidence, as it is right for me to think and believe this concerning all of you. For it is not right that I should think otherwise of people so good. I ought to think this of you because I have you in my heart, not merely on my lips, since I continually hold you in my inmost heart with love; and because I have you in my bonds, because you too compassionately share the pain of my imprisonment, consider yourselves bound together with me, and because I have you in the defense of the Gospel, since you too defend it, as I do, by disputations against its assailants. And I have you in its confirmation because you too strive to establish it in the hearts of believers. Therefore it is right for me to think that all of you are partners in my future joy—that is, eternal gladness—as I now see you to be partners in my works and sufferings.

> “For God is my witness how I long for all of you in the affections of Jesus Christ. And this I pray: that your love may abound more and more in knowledge and in all discernment, that you may approve the things that are better, that [Col. 1283A] you may be sincere and without offense unto the day of Christ, filled with the fruit of righteousness through Jesus Christ, unto the glory and praise of God.”

As I said, I think and desire that you will be partners in the joy which I possess. For I desire that all of you may be received into the inward bosom of everlasting blessedness of Jesus Christ. And how—that is, with what ardent desire—I long for this, God is my witness, he who looks into the secrets of our hearts.

Or, as was said above, I make petition for you because, as God is witness, I desire that all of you may be in the affections of Jesus Christ: that is, in his innermost love, loved by him as though you were his very inward parts. For feeling is stronger in the inward parts than in another part of the body; therefore in Scripture “inward parts” are sometimes used for love.

I indeed desire such things for you. And that you may attain what I desire, I pray that your love, always making progress, may abound and increase more and more in knowledge of divine and profitable things, and in all prudence and discernment, so that you may approve the better things: that is, that you may know how to test and distinguish not only evil and good but also, among good things, what is better. Thus, after testing, you may be sincere—that is, without decay, so that some vice may not corrupt you as a worm eats wood from within—but may remain whole in goodness.

Be sincere [Note: [Col. 1283D] The etymology of this term was mentioned above.] with regard to yourselves, that is, without the corruption of vices; and without offense with regard to your neighbor, so that you do not offend him, until the day of Christ, that is, until the last day of life. Or, be sincere—that is, without the admixture of vices which are accustomed to mingle themselves with good works—and without offense, that is, without blame, walking in the steps of good works and desires until the day of Christ: that is, until the day of God’s just judgment, when he will reward you for your sincerity, without any admixture of evils.

Be also like good trees, filled with the fruit of righteousness: that is, abounding in good works through Jesus Christ, through Christ’s grace rather than through your own strength, unto the glory and praise of God—that God may thereby be glorified and praised, who makes you bear such fruit, rather than that you should gain empty glory from it as though you did such things through yourselves. Here the Apostle very fittingly commends humility to those who do good. Or, on the day of Christ may you be filled with fruit—that is, having received the reward of righteousness through Jesus Christ the judge—unto the glory and praise of God: that God may thereby be glorified and praised forever, and it may be said, “God is wonderful in his saints” (Ps. 67).

> “But I want you to know, brethren, that the things concerning me have turned out rather to the advancement of the Gospel, so that my bonds became manifest in Christ throughout the whole praetorium and among all the rest; and so that more of the brethren, trusting in the Lord because of my bonds, dared all the more without fear to speak the word of God. Some indeed preach Christ even because of envy and contention, but others because of good will. Some do so from love, [Col. 1284A] knowing that I am appointed for the defense of the Gospel. But others proclaim Christ from contention, not sincerely, supposing that they are raising affliction for my bonds. What then? So long as in every way, whether from pretext [or from truth, Christ is proclaimed; and in this I rejoice, yes, and I shall rejoice.]”

Because he had said above that he held them in his heart and in his chains, lest, on hearing that he was bound, they should think that the preaching of the Gospel was failing and yield to false apostles, he adds: “Now I want you to know,” etc. It is as though he said: I am indeed in chains, but the Gospel’s proclamation is not thereby diminished. I want you, brothers, to know that the things concerning me—that is, my chains and the torments which I suffer on every side, or [Col. 1284B] those that do not reach inward parts—have turned out more for the advancement of the Gospel than for its decline, as the wicked intended. Thus my chains became manifest in Christ: that is, they were made known everywhere in Christ’s name and proclamation, and through them Christ himself. For while talk of my chains flies everywhere, Christ, who is the cause of those chains, resounds on everyone’s lips.

They are manifest in the whole praetorium, where nobles and wealthy people assemble, and in every other place in Rome where the common people gather. It is known to all Romans, noble and lowly alike, that I am bound for the faith of Christ which I was preaching. And my chains have been so beneficial that more than before of the brethren—that is, of Christians—trusting not in themselves but in the Lord, dared, through my chains—that is, [Col. 1284C] through consideration of my chains—to speak the word of God publicly more abundantly than usual and without fear, thinking to themselves: “If this man speaks while bound, why should we not do so all the more?”

But when I said that more of the brethren, trusting in the Lord, proclaim the word of God because of my chains, I did not mean that all do so in this way. For some among them are hirelings and others are sons. Some indeed—that is, the hirelings—preach Christ even from envy and rivalry, because they envy my glory and strive to appropriate it for themselves, wishing to be famous and honoured among men as the apostles were. But some, differing from these in intention, namely the good sons, preach him after my example from good will: that is, with zeal to beget [Col. 1284D] children for eternal life. Some, who are themselves good, proclaim him from charity and love for me, knowing that I have been appointed by God for the defence of the Gospel, by disputing and proving it to be true and life-giving. Therefore, because they see that I am now held in chains and cannot fully exercise my office, they preach Christ in my stead and place, so that they may supply what I am now less able to do. These preach with a chaste intention.

But some, very different from them, proclaim Christ from contention—that is, through contention—because they seek thereby to inflict greater punishments on me: so that, if anyone should accuse them on account of their preaching, they might report that I am its author, [Col. 1285A] and thus turn the evil against me. Or “from contention” means from private hatred arising from the fact that they once disputed with me and were refuted. And lest they should seem to have been corrected, I add that they preach not sincerely—that is, not with a pure mind, but with one infected by malice—thinking in this way to stir up, that is, to move, affliction for my chains: namely, that I, though bound, may be oppressed by adversities. Thus, when Nero and his ministers see so many preachers of the Gospel in Rome, they may suppose that I am their cause and inflict greater torments upon me, or even death.

With such an intention they preach to others the salvation which they themselves do not possess; and while serving their earthly desires, they proclaim the kingdom of heaven, holding falsehood in their breast and truth on their tongue. Yet these also preach Christ and are not [Col. 1285B] forbidden, just as the good are not. For what does it matter with what intention Christ is preached, provided—that is, so long as—he is proclaimed in every manner of proclamation: whether from an occasion for stirring up tribulations among the faithful or gaining temporal profit, or through the truth of a pure conscience? And in this I rejoice: that all these preach, even those who contrive in this way to stir up affliction for my chains. Nor do I rejoice only now, but I shall always rejoice in this.

For it can happen that, while these men preach Christ on such an occasion as hirelings—whether from eagerness to stir up tribulations, or from desire to acquire money or temporal favour—believers may be born from hearing them, and God may work good from their evil. It is like the case in which a man enters into intercourse [Col. 1285C] not with the intention of begetting, but of satisfying lust, and yet a human being is born: a good work of God arising from the fruitfulness of seed, not from the foulness of vices. Therefore such hirelings must be tolerated (Matt. XX), while they proclaim Christ from occasion, since they too are useful in some respects: we should do what they say, but reject what they do. For Christ is truth. Truth is proclaimed by hirelings from occasion; truth is proclaimed by sons in truth. Sons patiently await the Father’s eternal inheritance; hirelings eagerly await the temporary wage of the one who hires them. Hirelings indeed proclaim Christ from occasion while seeking something else; but shepherds preach God for God’s sake.

> “For I know that this will turn out for my salvation [Col. 1285D] through your prayer and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ, according to my expectation and hope: that in nothing I shall be put to shame, but with all confidence, as always, so now Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether by life or by death. For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain. But if to live here in the flesh is fruit of work for me, then what I shall choose I do not know. Yet I am constrained by the two: having a desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, by far much better; but to remain in the flesh is more necessary because of you.”

As I said, I rejoice when ill-willed preachers proclaim Christ, even while stirring up affliction for me. [Col. 1286A] For I know that even this—that is, the stirring up of affliction—will turn out for my attaining eternal salvation in the future, not for oppression, as they suppose. And this will occur not through my merit alone, but through your prayer, which will aid me, and through the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ: that is, through the hidden bestowal of the Holy Spirit, who supports me beneath as a column or foundation, lest I fall. This Spirit is the source of all good things; therefore he is said to supply the saints, because from his fountain proceeds whatever benefits they receive.

This, I say, will turn out for me according to my expectation and hope: that is, according to what I await until it comes, and what I hope until I come. For my expectation will not disappoint me. And why? [Col. 1286B] Because in nothing am I put to shame: that is, I blush in no matter, since there is nothing in my conscience for which I should blush before God, nor can I be ashamed of the things which I outwardly suffer for Christ. Therefore I am certain that I shall attain what I hope for. For if the Apostle saw himself being put to shame or failing in anything, he could despair of salvation. But because he sees himself steadfast in all things, and sees that this grace of God has already been granted him, he therefore hopes for what is greater. I am not put to shame, so as to yield in anything, because both the hope is great and the matter true and honourable.

I am not put to shame, I say, like a fearful soldier, but with all confidence and with every boldness and steadfastness of mind by which I am accustomed to preach courageously. Just as from the time of my conversion the Lord [Col. 1286C] Christ has always been magnified in me, so now too—in this time, or in my chains—Christ will be magnified before all: that is, his fame and glory will be magnified even in my body, which is more frail, whether through life or through death. For as long as I live, I shall always magnify him by preaching and good works; and in death accepted for his name I shall glorify him as well.

For I live for no other reason than to magnify him, because Christ himself is life to me: that is, what I live is Christ; I have no life except Christ. I do not live as the old man, but as the new man, who has renewed my whole life. And to die is gain to me, because then I shall receive heavenly things for earthly, eternal things for temporal. To die is gain to me. But if living here in this present life [Col. 1286D] in the flesh is fruit of work for me—that is, fruitful and useful work, since while I live I do not cease to gain many for God through preaching—then I do not know what I should choose, namely, death or life. For if I could no longer bear fruit daily here, I would doubtless choose death, since I would have Christ as gain. But because I see that I am continually of benefit to many, charity toward them still holds me in the flesh.

For I am constrained—that is, bound and compelled—by these two things, death and life, because I would gladly die and patiently live. I do not love the present life, but endure it. It is wearisome for me to remain in the flesh, and I suffer anguish from the two alternatives, having a desire to be released from the fetters of mortality by which [Col. 1287A] I am bound, and to be with Christ present in the heavenly homeland—something far, far better for me than living in the present age. Yet to remain in the flesh is more necessary for me, not for my own sake, but for yours, to whom I minister the Gospel.

For when I am constrained by the two, I have the desire of one and the necessity of the other: namely, the desire to be released and be with Christ in heaven, but the necessity to remain in the flesh for others’ salvation. I desire to be released because I am bound. For bodily weakness and corruptibility are fetters to us, since the body weighs down the soul (Wis. IX). And when we are stripped of corruptible flesh, we are released, as it were, from the troublesome bonds by which we are now tied. We long already to be presented to God, but are still impeded by the obligation of a mortal [Col. 1287B] body. We are rightly called bound, because we do not yet have free movement of our desire toward God.

Hence the Apostle, now desiring eternal things but still bearing the burden of his corruption, cries out as one bound: “I desire to be released and to be with Christ.” For he would not seek release unless he undoubtedly saw himself to be bound. He desires to be released so that he may be with Christ, because the souls of perfect righteous persons, as soon as they leave the enclosure of this flesh, are received into heavenly dwellings. Yet he chooses that the joys of so great a blessedness should still be delayed, because of his exceeding love for those whom he can benefit by remaining in the flesh, when he adds:

> “And having this confidence, I know that I shall remain and continue [Col. 1287C] with all of you for your advancement and joy in faith, so that your rejoicing may abound in Christ Jesus in me, through my coming again to you. Only conduct yourselves worthily of the Gospel of Christ, so that, whether I come and see you or, being absent, hear about you, you stand in one spirit, of one mind, labouring together for the faith of the Gospel, and are in no way terrified by adversaries. This is for them a cause of destruction, but for you of salvation—and this from God—because it has been granted to you for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him, having the same conflict which you saw in me and now have heard of me.”

Behold, Paul, as was said, chooses not what is better for himself, but what benefits many: namely, to remain in the flesh, because of charity, which is greater than all other virtues. At first, uncertain, he had said: “What I shall choose I do not know.” But afterwards, upon deliberation, he is overcome by love for his disciples and declares that he will remain with them all. It is as though he said: It is necessary for me to remain in the flesh for your sake. And I, confident of this in the mercy of God—namely, that I shall yet live for your sake—know that I shall remain in the body; and not merely a little while, but shall continue for some time with all of you, greater and lesser alike, for your advancement: that is, that through me you may advance and grow in virtues; and for joy in faith: that is, that you may rejoice in the faith which you learned from me, when I shall still further confirm you in it by my presence; or that I may rejoice in [Col. 1288A] your faith. Thus your rejoicing may abound: that is, that you may give abundant thanks to God with joy in Christ Jesus, who has done you good in preserving me for you. That is, rejoice in Christ, through whom God has looked upon us by restoring me to you, namely through my coming to you again to confirm you.

I shall come again to you; only meanwhile do what I say: conduct yourselves worthily of the Gospel, that is, make your conduct such that it worthily accords with Christ’s Gospel. It is as though it were said: If you live in this way, then, according to your merit, life will be given to me for your benefit. Conduct yourselves worthily, I say, so that whether I come and see you, I may find you, as I said, such as I wish; or, if I do not come, I may hear while absent what I desire concerning you—namely, [Col. 1288B] that you do not succumb or yield, but stand bravely against every adversity and firmly maintain the state of uprightness in one spirit, being of one mind: that is, in the Holy Spirit, to whom no contrary spirit adheres. And just as he is one, so he makes you of one mind without dissension, so that what one wills, another also wills; labouring together for the faith of the Gospel: that is, all together exerting yourselves with all your strength to fulfil the demands of evangelical faith.

And while doing these things, do not be terrified: that is, do not fear adversaries in any danger, in any work of yours, or in anything whatever, lest through fear you fall away from your purpose. This fact—that they oppose you and inflict evils upon you—is a cause of eternal destruction to them, but a cause of everlasting salvation to you. For just as they will perish without end because they persecute you, so you will be saved eternally because you suffer from them for Christ. And you do not have this from yourselves—that you attain salvation through suffering—but from God, lest you begin to boast of merits. Even what you suffer is not from yourselves but from God, because among other graces this has been given to you by him: it has been granted to you, as though a reward, for Christ whom you love—that is, through the merit of Christ, who obeyed unto death on the cross—not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him, unto the fullness of glory. For both belong to God’s grace: the faith of believers and the endurance of sufferers, since both are God’s gift.

I say, suffer, having against adversaries the same—that is, a similar—conflict, [Col. 1288D] not with weapons but with faith, such as you saw in me while I was present among you and now have heard of me while I am absent. For among these people Paul and Silas were publicly beaten with rods, their tunics were torn, they themselves were shut up in prison, and their feet there fastened in stocks. And Paul had now suffered many things at Rome and was exhorting them to similar contests (Acts XVI). He then adds, exhorting and teaching:

## CHAPTER II

> “If then there is any consolation in Christ, if any comfort of charity, if any fellowship of the Spirit, if any bowels of compassion, fulfil my joy: that you think the same thing, having the same charity, of one mind, thinking the same thing; doing nothing through contention or vain glory, but in humility [Col. 1289A] considering one another superior to yourselves, each not looking to the things that are his own, but also to those of others.”

It is as though he said: Because you ought, as I said above, to stand united in one spirit and suffer for Christ as I do, therefore fulfil my joy, which I have begun to have from your good conduct, by thinking the same thing, having the same charity, and so forth. Do this if there is any consolation for you in Christ: that is, if through the charity which you have in Christ you can console anyone, because by doing this you will console me in my tribulations. For your good life will be my consolation.

Or: if there is any consolation for you in Christ—that is, if you wish to have consolation in the things of Christ, in forgiveness of sins and in other [Col. 1289B] gifts—if there is any comfort of common charity: that is, if you wish the charity of the other churches, who pray and do good for the brethren, to be a comfort to you in your adversities. Or, if you have any comfort of charity towards your neighbour, so that by brotherly love you may offer him comfort, that is, consolation in the sorrow of tribulation; if there is any fellowship of spirit for you: that is, if you have among yourselves any union of harmonious mind through the Holy Spirit, or if there is any fellowship of the Holy Spirit with your spirit. “For the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God” (Rom. VIII).

For fellowship belongs to him, by which you are made one body of the only Son of God. On account of this fellowship, those into whom the Holy Spirit first came spoke in the tongues of all nations (Acts II), because through languages the fellowship of the human race is more closely joined. Therefore the fellowship of spirit is that union of believers which the Holy Spirit gives them, by which all become one. “If any bowels of compassion”: that is, if there is in you any tender affection from which compassion toward me may proceed. If these things are in you, then fulfil—that is, bring to perfection—my joy which I have in your devotion. That is, lead a fully devout life, so that you think the same thing in faith and in other matters as is fitting; and let there not be a differing mind among you, but the same, though greater in some and less in others. Have the same charity toward all, so that you love all equally, as it is written: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (Matt. V; Lev. XIX). [Col. 1289D]

Or, have the same charity in this sense: let this person love that one as himself, and that one likewise this person as himself. Be of one mind, that is, of one will, so that you may have one heart and one soul (I Cor. XII); thinking the same thing: that is, all should regard each person’s evils as their own, and likewise each person’s goods, so that if one member suffers, all the members may suffer with it. Do nothing through contention, so that you do not contend with one another either in words or deeds. For there were among them, as appears from these words of the Apostle, some dissenting and unruly persons, contending for vain glory and breaking the peace of the Church. Therefore they are now warned to think the same thing: that is, to have no dissension and do nothing through contention, so that they may not contend either about precedence or about any matter. For even good things ought not to be spoken in contentious words, but rather kept silent; nor should they do anything for vain glory, that is, for the empty reputation of the age, seeking human favour from their works. Rather, let them do all things in humility, so that they always think humbly of themselves.

For this is commonly the distinctive mark of the elect: they always think of themselves as lower than they are. Therefore it is now added that they should consider one another superior to themselves.
