For because every wicked person judges everyone whom he considers beneath him to be inferior to himself, by contrast the righteous person should strive to regard every neighbour as superior. And lest, while one humbles himself before another, that humility should become an occasion of pride for the other, the Apostle admonished both parties, saying, “considering one another superior to yourselves,” so that in the thoughts [Col. 1290B] of the heart both I may prefer him to myself and he may prefer me to himself; thus, when the heart is pressed down on both sides, it is not puffed up by excessive honour.

We ought not to understand this in such a way that we do not really suppose it, but merely pretend to suppose it. Rather, we should truly suppose that something hidden may be in another by which he is superior to us, even though our good, by which we seem superior to him, is not hidden. These thoughts, which humble pride and increase charity, cause us to bear one another’s burdens not only with equanimity, but even most willingly. Hence it is added: “Each not looking to the things that are his own, but also to those of others.” For he teaches very well how they may avoid contention and vain glory [Col. 1290C] and how they may consider others superior: namely, if they consider not their own good things but those of others.

Or: let them not look to matters that pertain only to their own advantage, but also to those of others: that is, matters that concern others’ benefit. For Christ too sought not his own advantage but that of others. He did not exalt himself above others but lowered himself beneath all, though he was above all. Thus it follows:

> “For let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus: who, though he was in the form of God, did not consider being equal with God a robbery; but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross.”

[Col. 1290D] Here we are admonished that, just as he, in that the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us (John I), and though without sin took upon himself our sins, looked not to his own things but to ours, so we too, in imitation of him, should bear one another’s burdens and seek not our own benefit but that of others. Nothing makes this dutiful labour of bearing others’ burdens willingly undertaken except reflecting on how great were the things the Lord suffered for us.

Therefore, when the Apostle admonished them, saying, “considering one another superior to yourselves, each not looking to the things that are his own, but to those of others,” he immediately set before them the Lord’s example for imitation, saying: “For let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus.” That is, truly have and feel in yourselves [Col. 1291A] humility and patience for others’ salvation, as you perceive and understand them to have been in Christ. The Apostle first sets forth Christ’s lofty condition, from which he willingly inclined himself down to the lowest humility, so that once his sublimity has been seen, his humility too may appear greater; and so that human beings, in whom there is room for abasement, may not disdain to be humbled after the example of him who, though he was in the form of God—that is, in complete equality with the Father—did not consider himself equal to God to be robbery, that is, the usurpation of another’s property.

For it was not robbery for him, but nature, to possess equality with God, because he received it by being begotten, not by presumptuous pride. Yet he ascribes all that he has and can do not to himself but to the Father, because he is not from himself but from the Father. For he is equal to the Father, but even this he received from the Father. [Col. 1291B] Nor did he receive it in such a way as to become equal by increase; rather, he was equal by nature and eternity: as eternally begotten, so eternally equal. The Father therefore did not beget one unequal and then grant equality to one already begotten; rather, he gave equality in begetting him, because he begot an equal, not an unequal, Son. Thus the equality of the Son with the Father was not robbery but nature.

Therefore he did not consider being equal with God to be robbery. For he was equal, and it was without robbery because he was eternally begotten from the Eternal One. He was in the form of God because he was as great as the Father, such as the Father, and what the Father is: not the one who is the Father, but what the Father is. For the Father is God and the Son is God; the Father is almighty and the Son is almighty; the Father is immutable and the Son is immutable. He is what the Father is, not the one who is the Father, because the Father is Father and he is Son.

Thus he always was and is in the form of God: that is, in the full essence of the Father. And though naturally so great and without beginning, he did not consider himself equal to God through robbery—that is, through a violent invasion of another’s possession—because he knew himself to be truly and altogether equal by nature. For robbery is when someone violently appropriates another’s property, which does not belong to him. And by robbery the devil wished to appropriate equality with God, which in no way belonged to him, when he said: “I will ascend above the height of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV). But the Son did not suppose, through robbery, that he possessed the Father’s equality in pride; rather, as stated, he knew himself to be altogether equal by nature.

Or, according to other manuscripts: “He did not consider it robbery to be equal to God”; that is, he considered equality with God not alien but his own, because he did not judge that what he possessed by being begotten was foreign, but his own. He did not consider his equality with God robbery because he did not seize that equality, but possessed it naturally. Hence, while living bodily among human beings, he called God his Father, making himself equal to God, as we read in the Gospel (John X). He had not lost equality with the Father through assuming humanity, because the nature of divinity is not changeable, capable of being diminished or increased. He did not consider equality with God robbery—that is, something alien—but his own. Or, he did not consider himself equal to God by robbery—that is, by violent usurpation—but possessed it naturally. Nevertheless, for the salvation of the weak, he [Col. 1292A] emptied himself: that is, he temporarily withdrew from our sight the form of divinity which eyes cannot see, taking the form of a servant, that is, of a human being, seeking not his own things but ours.

Indeed, to empty himself was to show himself visible from the greatness of his invisibility, so that the servant’s form might conceal that which in his divinity penetrated all things without spatial limitation. He emptied himself because he did not appear to human beings in the form in which he is equal to the Father. He emptied himself not by losing the form of God but by taking the form of a servant. The form of a servant was added; the form of God did not depart. He did not lose or diminish what he was, but received what he was not. In this way he both became lesser and remained equal: made in the likeness of human beings, that is, passible and mortal like other human beings; and [Col. 1292B] found in appearance—that is, in clothed humanity—not for himself but for those to whom he appeared in humanity, as a man: that is, by having humanity, he was found to be a human being.

For he could not be found as a human being by those who had an unclean heart and could not see the Word with the Father, unless he assumed what they could see, and through it they might be led to that inward light. His “appearance” is the humanity with which he clothed himself as with a garment. For “appearance” is spoken of a thing that comes to us as something possessed. But although there are other things which come to us so as to form an appearance, the present discussion concerns that thing which, when it comes, is changed so as to form an appearance, but does not change that to which it comes—such as clothing. For once clothing is laid aside, it does not retain the shape which it takes when it is put on and fitted to the limbs; but the limbs themselves remain in their own state, both when clothed and when unclothed.

So Christ’s assumed appearance was taken in such a way that it was changed, ineffably, more excellently, and more closely than clothing is changed when it is put upon a human being, yet it did not change the one who assumed it. Therefore by the term “appearance” one must understand that the Word was not changed by assuming humanity, just as limbs are not changed by being clothed, although that assumption united what was assumed to the one assuming it in an ineffable manner. Thus the designation “appearance” shows how he was made in the likeness of human beings: not by being transformed into a human being, but by appearance, when he was clothed with humanity, which he in coming somehow made his own and conformed to himself, so as to associate it with immortality and eternity.

And not only did he so humble himself that he who was God became human, but he also humbled himself, being made obedient to the Father, though so exalted, so that we might be saved through his obedience, having perished through Adam’s disobedience. He was obedient not only unto insults and reproaches, but even unto death—and not just any death, but death on a cross, which was more shameful and bitter. Among all kinds of death there was nothing worse than that death. Indeed, where the sharpest pains torment, it is called *cruciatus* (“torture”), named from the cross. For those crucified, hanging on the wood and fastened by nails or wood through feet and hands, were killed by a prolonged death. To be crucified was not simply to be killed: rather, one lived long upon the cross, not because a longer life was chosen, but because death itself was extended, lest pain [Col. 1293A] should end too quickly. The Saviour chose so terrible a death in order to put to death every death of ours.

> “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of heavenly beings, earthly beings, and infernal beings, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, in the glory of God the Father.”

He humbled himself as greatly as possible; therefore God also exalted him as greatly as possible. For no greater humiliation or greater exaltation could occur. God exalted him according to his human nature; in this exaltation the divine nature too may be said to be exalted in respect of manifestation, because what it was began to be known, just as it is said to be emptied in the assumption of weakness. [Col. 1293B] Yet, because of the unity of person, divinity may be said to be exalted in the exaltation of humanity.

God exalted him by raising him from the dead and lifting him into heaven above all angels, at his right hand; and gave him the name above every name, so that in that very form he might be called the only-begotten Son of God. He had this even before the resurrection, but after the resurrection what he was became manifest, so that human beings and demons might know it and all bend the knee to him. [Note: [Col. 1293D] An obscure passage.]

After the cross there is made manifest what he received from the Father when he was begotten: when the creature began to know that the name of God was not given to a human being, but to one equal to God who emptied himself, whose all things are from the Father. Such an excelling name was given him that all things should be subject to him, so that at the name of Jesus every [Col. 1293C] knee should bend in exalting him, an evident sign of subjection: of heavenly beings, that is, angels; of earthly beings, that is, human beings; and of infernal beings, that is, demons, because they too tremble under his rule and are completely subject to him.

This does not mean that angels or demons possess knees to bend, as we do; it is spoken by analogy. When we see someone bend the knee to another, we believe him to show humility and reverence to the one before whom he bends. Thus heavenly and earthly beings—that is, blessed angels and holy human beings—willingly subject themselves to Christ with every affection of devout humility. Infernal beings too—that is, demons—tremble under his dominion as most wicked slaves and, compelled by fear, acknowledge themselves subject to him. But wicked human beings also will at the end perceive themselves subject to him. [Col. 1293D]

And not only was it granted him that every creature should subject itself to him, but also that every tongue should confess: that is, that the tongues of all the diverse nations of the world should proclaim in harmony that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father—that is, he is honoured with the same glory as the Father, being in every respect equal to the Father. All good and evil beings either willingly or unwillingly confess, or will confess, this.

> “Therefore, my most beloved, as you have always obeyed, not only in my presence but much more now in my absence, work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For God is the one [Col. 1294A] who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to his good will.”

As stated above, Christ humbled himself by obeying unto death and was therefore exalted. Therefore you too, my most beloved, following his example, humble yourselves by obeying God, so that you too may deserve, in your own measure, to be similarly exalted. As from the day of your conversion you have always obeyed God and me, or your superiors, so now act—not only as you acted in my presence, but strive much more to act now in my absence. Namely, work out your salvation: that is, by good works act so as to be worthy of eternal salvation.

And do this not proudly or presumptuously, but with the fear of inward humility. For one who always fears falling is humble; [Col. 1294B] and do it with trembling of body: that is, be altogether humble both inwardly and outwardly in the good things you do, attributing nothing to yourselves but everything to God’s grace, because it is not you who work, but God in you. Therefore there must be fear. For he is the one who works in you both to will what is good and to accomplish it, according to his own good will, not according to your merits.

When he commands them to work, their free choice is duly recognized. Yet he says “with fear and trembling” lest, by attributing their good works to themselves, they should be exalted by works as though those works were their own. Thus, as if the Apostle were asked, “Why did you say ‘with fear and trembling’?” he gives the reason for these words, saying: “For God is the one who works in you.” Lest they claim anything for themselves because he said, “Work,” he immediately added: “God is the one who works in you.” Therefore, with fear and trembling—that is, with humility. For if you fear and tremble, you will not exalt yourselves as though because of your own works, since God works in you.

You must fear lest what has been given to the humble be taken away from the proud. For he did not wish even the saints to glory in their own strength regarding perseverance in good, but in him: because he gives them not only assistance such as he gave to the first human being, without which they cannot persevere if they wish, but he also works willing in them. Since they will not persevere unless they both can and will, the capacity and the will to persevere are given them by the generous bounty of divine grace. Their will is so kindled by the Holy Spirit that they are able because they will in this manner, and they will in this manner [Col. 1294D] because God works in them that they may will. Thus God works willing in them, and, on account of the good will which he has worked, he also works accomplishment.

> “But do all things without murmurings and hesitations, so that you may be without complaint and simple children of God, without reproach in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine as lights in the world, holding fast the word of life, for my glory on the day of Christ, because I have not run in vain nor laboured in vain.”

I said that you should work out your salvation, that is, obtain eternal salvation for yourselves through good works. But whatever you do, do it without murmurings. Here [Col. 1295A] patience is joined to the humility mentioned above. For it was said earlier: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling”; and now they are commanded to do everything without grumbling, that is, to labor with an even mind in the good works enjoined upon them by their prelates. Do everything without murmurings, lest you be irreverent in the very good works that you do, or find the labor for your salvation burdensome; without hesitations, lest you waver in your heart whether or not to do the good which you wish to do. Rather, with firm resolve, readily complete every good thing which you have undertaken to do, lest you be unstable in mind. “For he who hesitates,” as James says, “is like a wave of the sea, moved and carried about by the wind” (James 1). Or, do not hesitate concerning the reward of good works. Or [Col. 1295B] do not hesitate to suffer for Christ, but be ready.

And do these things so that you may be without complaint, that is, so that your neighbor cannot complain of you; and, so far as concerns yourselves, may you be simple, that is, without duplicity of heart, because “a double-minded man is unstable in all his ways” (ibid.), and “no one can serve two masters” (Matt. 6; Luke 6). For he is double-minded who wishes to please both God and the world, wishing to be rich both in this world and in heaven. But you who have begun to be children of God, seek him in simplicity of heart, so that, just as he is one, you too may be simple in imitation of him and endeavor to please him alone. And even with regard to outsiders, be without reproach, so that unbelievers can find nothing blameworthy in you in the midst of a nation—that is, of Gentiles—who are not [Col. 1295C] reborn, but live carnally just as they were carnally born. I mean a nation crooked in its deeds and perverse through its various sects. Among these Gentiles you shine by the example of a good life like the moon and stars. Therefore it especially befits you to be without reproach. You shine like the lights of heaven, because, just as moon and stars do not lose their light because of the night but shine all the more, so you, with your minds fixed in heaven, though your manner of life is among dark and unbelieving people, are not darkened but shine all the more by doing good.

By this statement the Apostle both praises and strengthens his disciples, so that, knowing themselves to be such persons, they may strive more vigorously to persevere as such. For saints of this kind, from the heavenly manner of life which they possess, despise everything that wicked persons [Col. 1295D] do on earth. Just as night does not extinguish the stars of heaven, so worldly wickedness does not darken the minds of believers who cling to the firmament of Holy Scripture or to heavenly desires. For those whose minds are on high and who think of things above, as it is said, “Where your treasure is, there your heart also is” (Matt. 6), are made patient by their very thoughts of heavenly things; and whatever happens on earth they do not so care about, until they complete their journey, just as the lights of heaven do not concern themselves with how days and nights proceed, although they see so many evils done on earth. And just as the heavenly lights patiently bear whatever people imagine about them, so the righteous ought patiently to bear every false accusation made even against themselves. For whoever loses endurance is not bright like a light [Col. 1296A] from above, but is darkened and falls from heaven.

“You shine,” he says, “like lights in the world.” It is as though he said: “You are the light of this world” (Matt. 5); and you are also vessels of the Gospel, because you hold in your hearts the word of evangelical preaching, by which your soul lives, for you do not allow it to flow away from you. And you do this for my glory, not yet for your own, because I too shall receive glory from your good manner of life on the day of Christ, that is, on the day when Christ judges. And truly then I shall have glory, because I did not run in vain—that is, not without fruit, not fruitlessly—toward that end, since you and others believed through my preaching. I did not run in vain in the way of the Lord, nor labor in vain in his vineyard, which is the Church, since I shall receive a full reward. Or, I ran [Col. 1296B] among those whom I could convert easily; I labored among those whom I converted with greater difficulty.

> “But even if I am poured out upon the sacrifice and service of your faith, I rejoice and rejoice together with all of you. And in the same way you too rejoice and rejoice together with me.”

Your religious devotion will redound to my glory on the day of judgment, because I labored for you. Nor did I merely do this willingly; rather, even if I am offered in sacrifice—that is, killed for you—then I rejoice. That is, if I add the sacrifice of my body to the sacrifice and service of your faith. For I have already offered your faith as a sacrifice worthy of God, and I have sacrificed the service of your good works, by which you serve God. But if I too am offered for you, I rejoice, because I attain the crown; and I rejoice together, [Col. 1296C] that is, I give thanks together with all of you, because you are the cause to me of the death through which I enter life. Nor ought I alone to do this: you also, in the same way, rejoice—that is, if it should happen to you, rejoice to be sacrificed for me—and rejoice together, that is, give thanks to me, who am the cause that you become martyrs.

> “But I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon (Acts 16), so that I too may be encouraged when I learn the circumstances concerning you. For I have no one so like-minded, who will be sincerely concerned for you. For all seek what is their own (1 Cor. 13), not what belongs to Jesus Christ. But you know his proven worth, because [Col. 1296D] as a son with a father he served with me in the Gospel. Therefore I hope to send him to you as soon as I see how matters concerning me turn out. But I trust in the Lord that I myself also shall come to you soon.”

I am now sending you this letter through Epaphroditus; but I hope, not in myself but in the Lord Jesus—that is, in the Savior’s mercy—to send, that is, to direct, Timothy to you soon. Thus, as you will be encouraged when you learn what concerns me, so I too may be encouraged and rejoice when I learn what concerns you, whether adverse or prosperous. But I shall send Timothy rather than another because I have no one now so like-minded. At that time there were many hirelings with the Apostle, [Col. 1297A] but no sons or shepherds except Timothy. “I have no one with me now,” he says, “so like-minded,” that is, so in agreement with my will in this matter, who with sincere—that is, pure and unfeigned—affection of heart, that is, genuine charity, will be concerned for you, namely for your salvation. For many appear to be concerned for others, but are in truth not concerned for the persons themselves, but for their possessions, which they desire to have.

I rightly said that I have no one so like-minded; for all whom I now have seek among you what is their own, not the gains of Christ. Thus even now hirelings in the Church act, seeking their own interests. What is it to seek one’s own? It is not to love Christ freely, not to seek God for God’s sake, but to pursue temporal advantages, to hunger after gains, and to desire honors [Col. 1297B] from human beings. And when these things are loved by a superior, and God is served for their sake, whoever is such a person is a hireling; let him not count himself among the sons. For of such persons it is said that they “have received their reward” (Matt. 5). They do not seek those things which belong to Jesus Christ: the increase of the good flock, the devout manner of life of those subject to them, the salvation of souls. Therefore the Apostle did not wish now to send any of these, but Timothy, who, like a shepherd, would seek the salvation of the flock and would show, not only by word but also by example, how one ought to live.

I shall indeed send Timothy to you; but you should know his proven worth, that is, how I have found him faithful in every respect, in life and doctrine: for just as a son devoutly obeys his father, so he [Col. 1297C] served God with me in preaching the Gospel, in which he could be tested. And because he is concerned for you and has been approved by me, I therefore hope to send him to you not after a long interval of time, but as soon as I see what will happen in my case, that is, what outcome these matters will have, whether I shall escape from them or not. And I do not merely hope to send him; I also trust in God’s mercy that I myself shall come to you soon, that is, not after much time.

> “But I considered it necessary to send Epaphroditus to you—my brother and fellow-worker and fellow-soldier, but your apostle and minister to my need—because he longed for all of you and was distressed because [Col. 1297D] you had heard that he was ill. For he was indeed ill, even unto death; but God had mercy on him, and not only on him but also on me, lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow. Therefore I sent him all the more eagerly, so that, seeing him again, you may rejoice, and I may be free from sorrow. Receive him, therefore, with all joy in the Lord, and hold such persons in honor, because for the work of Christ he came near to death, giving up his life in order to supply what was lacking from you in your service to me.”

Timothy indeed, as I hope, I shall send to you, and I myself shall come; but meanwhile I considered it necessary to send to you with this letter Epaphroditus, a brother—that is, a Christian—and fellow-worker in preaching, [Col. 1298A] and my fellow-soldier in the war against demons and vices and against all who resist Christ’s kingdom; yet your apostle, that is, your particular teacher, and minister to my need, that is, one who supplied me with necessities, or ministered to the need arising from my poverty, whether from the labor of his own hands or from what he sought from other believers. I wished to send him because he desired to see all of you, and was distressed because you had heard that he had been ill. Perhaps because he had been beaten by unbelievers during his ministry. Nor did a false report of his illness reach you, for he was indeed sick with illness, as you heard; and this not lightly, but to the point of danger of death. Yet God mercifully healed him. And he had mercy not only on him in this respect, but also [Col. 1298B] on me, lest I have sorrow at his death in addition to the sorrow which I had had at his illness, which was harming you.

And because he longed for you, and you feared on account of his sickness, I therefore sent him more speedily than I would have done had this not happened, so that, when you see him, you may again rejoice—you who formerly rejoiced in him when he was among you—and so that I may be without the sorrow which I had because you were sorrowful. I send him for these reasons; you therefore receive him honorably, not irreverently but with all joy, so that you may have complete joy at his arrival. Let that joy be in the Lord, that is, not vain, wanton, or excessive, but devout and chaste. Nor should you receive him joyfully only at first; afterward, while he lives among you, hold in honor a man [Col. 1298C] of this kind, because he is your apostle. And he rightly ought to be honored, because he came near to death for Christ’s work—Christ who came not to be served but to serve (Matt. 20). This man came near to death for the work Christ had done because he ministered to me, from alms of other believers gathered through his own labor, deliberately giving up and exposing his soul—that is, his life—to the danger of death. He was willing rather to die and surrender his life than to abandon Christ’s work which he was carrying out in my behalf. And he did this in order to make up, in his service to me, what was lacking from you: because you had given me from your goods, but he strove to supply what you had done less fully; or because you had provided the thing, but from [Col. 1298D] among you someone to carry it was lacking, and he brought it; or because what you had sent was exhausted, and he ministered to me from alms given by others.

## CHAPTER III

> “Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord. To write the same things to you is not burdensome to me, but it is necessary for you. Beware of dogs; beware of evil workers; beware of the mutilation. For we are the circumcision, who serve God in the Spirit, and glory in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the flesh, although I too have confidence in the flesh.”

He now begins to deal with the sincerity of faith against false preachers, as though saying: Preserve in this way the things which I said above; but as for what remains to be said, [Col. 1299A] do this: rejoice in the Lord—that is, let all your joy be in God, not in carnal observances. Or thus: formerly you rejoiced in the world, but for the remaining span of life left to you, now rejoice in the Lord, so that, for as long as you henceforth live, all your joy may be in him. Do not rejoice in carnal and worldly things, as the pseudo-apostles urge, but in the Lord, as I have often told you. For to write to you the same things which I said when present, namely that you should rejoice in the Lord alone, is neither burdensome nor tiresome to me, and by writing they remain longer than a spoken utterance; but it is necessary for you against perverse teachers.

For beware of dogs: that is, recognize that they are dogs, namely, barking not by reason but by habit against an unfamiliar truth. For this is the nature [Col. 1299B] of dogs: they do not bark at those with whom they are familiar, whether they are good or bad; but at the sight of unfamiliar persons, even innocent ones, they are aroused. Thus the false teachers cling to the custom of the Law and irrationally bark and bite against the messengers of truth. Beware of evil workers: that is, mark and avoid those same false preachers, because in God’s field they sow the tares of error over the wheat. Beware of the mutilation: that is, those who are cut off and curtailed, because they have cut away the flesh but nurture vices, and have been cut off—that is, severed—from Christ. I call them mutilation, not circumcision, because we believers, not they, are the circumcision—not in flesh but in reason—that is, cleansed from superfluous vices. This [Col. 1299C] means that we are righteousness, who serve God in spirit, that is, with the whole affection of the mind, not by the carnal keeping of the letter of the Law; and we glory not in our merits or in carnal observances, but in Christ Jesus alone and in his grace.

We serve God not in flesh but in spirit. For he serves God in flesh who hopes to please God through carnal matters. But when even the flesh itself is subjected to the spirit for good works, we serve God in spirit, who tame the flesh so that the spirit may obey God. Or, according to other manuscripts, especially Greek ones, “we serve God in spirit,” in that service of which it was said: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him shall you serve” (Deut. 6, 10)—“for God himself is Spirit” (John 4), to whom such service is rendered by all saints. And, he says, we glory in Christ [Col. 1299D] Jesus and have no confidence in the flesh. He had in view certain persons who trusted in the flesh: these were the ones who gloried in circumcision of the flesh. We do not have confidence, that is, hope of salvation, in flesh—that is, in carnal observances or nobility of birth—although I too, if I wished, have ground for confidence and glorying in the flesh, that is, in nobility of birth and carnal observance of the Law.

> “If anyone else seems to have confidence in the flesh, I have more: circumcised on the eighth day; of the race of Israel; of the tribe of Benjamin; a Hebrew of Hebrews; according to the Law, a Pharisee (Acts 23); according to zeal, persecuting the Church of God; according to the righteousness which is in the Law, living without reproach.”

[Col. 1300A] “Do not suppose,” he says, “that I despise what I do not possess. For what great thing is it if a lowly person or an ignoble populace despises nobility? I possess these things, but I despise them; and therefore I teach you to despise such things, because you see that I possess what I despise. For if any other person”—that is, one different from me who seeks to deceive you—“seems to have confidence in the flesh, as though thereby righteous, I have more confidence than that false teacher.” And hear what confidence in the flesh I possess: I was circumcised on the eighth day, as the Law commanded (Gen. 17); that is, I was not a proselyte, not an outsider admitted to God’s people, not circumcised at an advanced age, but a Jew born of Jewish parents: I have circumcision on the eighth day. And I am of the race of Israel, not a foreigner; and not of an inferior tribe but of the tribe of Benjamin, which was more distinguished because it was descended from Rachel, Jacob’s beloved [Col. 1300B] wife. And when the ten tribes worshiped calves in Samaria, this tribe and the tribe of Judah did not depart from the Lord’s temple.

And I am a Hebrew of Hebrew parents, that is, not descended from an ignoble people, but from those born from Heber, son of Salah, son of Shem, Noah’s eldest son. I am also, according to the Law—that is, according to an eminent observance of the Law—a Pharisee, that is, one separated from others as more religious. For certain leading men were, as it were, set apart for Jewish nobility and were not mixed with the contemptible populace; they were called Pharisees, as though “the separated.” And according to the zeal that burned in me, I persecuted the Church of God, because I was not an indolent Jew, but bore impatiently and vigorously pursued whatever appeared hostile to my Law. And according to [Col. 1300C] the righteousness of the Law—which restrains the hand, not the mind, and is kept from fear, not love—I lived without reproach, that is, with no outcry raised against me, because no one could complain that I had wronged him by acting contrary to the Law’s carnal ordinances. This is nobility among Jews, but with Christ humility is sought.

> “But whatever things were gains to me, these I considered losses for Christ’s sake. Yet I consider all things to be loss because of the surpassing knowledge of Jesus Christ my Lord. For his sake I made all things loss and consider them as dung, that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having my own righteousness which is from the Law, but [Col. 1300D] that which is through faith in Christ Jesus: righteousness from God in faith, so as to know him and the power of his resurrection and the fellowship of his sufferings, conformed to his death, if somehow I may attain to the resurrection which is from the dead.”

Thus I can glory in the flesh in various ways, but I no longer glory in such things. Rather, all those carnal things which before knowledge of Christ were gains to me—that is, useful and dear—I considered, after faith, losses to salvation on account of Christ, who had been foretold in them. And if I still kept these things, I would indicate that his coming had not yet occurred. For things which signified that he would come, if they are still observed now, deny that he has come. Therefore they are losses, because [Col. 1301A] they wear away the truth of faith. Thus a little earlier the Jews were called “mutilation,” because carnal circumcision is a complete severing from Christ.

Not only for Christ’s sake have I considered these things losses; but also, that is, further, because of the knowledge of Jesus Christ my Lord which we have concerning him, surpassing every other knowledge—indeed, surpassing in him more than in others—I consider all those things loss, because they draw their adherents away from such surpassing knowledge. Or thus: these were once gains to me, but now I consider all of them loss and hindrance because of the exalted knowledge of Christ, through which it became known to me that he is God over all, so that by it I might understand the Scriptures. For even if I could not attain him himself, I would reject all those former things for the sake of his knowledge alone, which is so great and so preeminent.

For the sake of this venerable Christ, and out of love for him, I not only consider all those things loss, but have made them a loss to good things, by living spiritually and teaching, so that they might appear to others to be loss. And, what is more, I consider them not merely losses of good things but dung, that is, things that now defile the observer. And I do this in order that I may gain Christ—that is, have Christ as my reward in the future—and here be a member in him. This cannot happen otherwise, namely upon rational reflection, unless I be found in him as a faithful member, not having my own righteousness which is from the Law; for that righteousness fears punishment and does not love virtue. Rather, I have that righteousness which is through faith in Christ, which righteousness [Col. 1301C] is from God, not from human beings. I mean righteousness abiding in faith, because, just as it is born from faith, so it cannot exist except from faith.

Righteousness in faith is effective for knowing him. It is as though he said: He who thinks that he is justified in the Law does not know Christ; but I wish to be justified by faith, so that I may know him—why he was born, why he suffered—and may know the power of his resurrection, that is, the justification of believers, because “he rose again for our justification” (Rom. 4), and may know the fellowship of his sufferings, which he knows well who believes that through it he will attain the joys of heaven. Or, righteousness in faith is for knowing him, because faith brings it about that in that life he is perfectly known, who in this life is believed; and that the power of his resurrection, that is, immortality, may be possessed. For our resurrection is the power and efficacy of his resurrection. And faith brings it about in this life that we have fellowship in his sufferings, so that we too may suffer every adversity for him; for without faith no one would endure such great things, and may have conformity to his death, so that we may die as he did, if need be; or die once to vices, just as he died once in the flesh.

But the sentence is to be joined thus: “That I may be found in him, not having my own righteousness which is from the Law, but that which is through faith, conformed to his death,” that is, perfected through sufferings as he was, striving, if somehow I may joyfully attain the resurrection. “If somehow I may attain,” because it is difficult. “If somehow it may happen,” both through God’s mercy and through my merit, that I may meet Christ rejoicing [Col. 1302A] in judgment—which belongs only to the saints—coming to the resurrection which is not from the living, as now, but from the dead, so that they can die no more. The Apostle recalls that he acted, or acts, in this way so that they too, following his example, may despise all carnal rites of the Law and hasten through the righteousness of faith and fellowship in Christ’s suffering toward the kingdoms of heaven.

> “Not that I have already received, or am already perfect; but I pursue, if somehow I may grasp that for which I have also been grasped by Christ Jesus. Brothers, I do not consider myself to have grasped it. But one thing: forgetting those things which are behind, and stretching myself toward those which are before, I press on toward the goal, toward the prize of God’s upward calling in Christ Jesus. Therefore, all of us who are [Col. 1302B] perfect should think this; and if you think differently in any respect, God will reveal this too to you. Nevertheless, as far as we have attained, let us think the same thing and remain in the same rule.”

This man who had been caught up to the third heaven (2 Cor. 12), and shone with such great knowledge, was thought already to have grasped what others pursue; but he himself denies this. For, lest it seem superfluous to suffer so many adversities when he has faith and other goods, he adds, as though saying: I rightly labor so much for that glory, because I do not say that I have already received anything; for whatever glory I have received is nothing in comparison with the future, nor, if I have received any knowledge of Christ, do I say that I am already perfect in it. And if this is so of me, what of others? I have not yet received what I seek, [Col. 1302C] nor am I already perfect, as though nothing were lacking to me. I do not say, “What I have done is sufficient”; rather, I always add something, always walk, always make progress, always pursue what I labor to grasp, if somehow it may come about that I grasp it—that is, hold it perfectly in the manner in which I too have been grasped by Christ Jesus: that I may see Christ himself as he sees me and know him perfectly as I am known by him, so that, just as he fully sees and knows me, so I may fully know him in the human manner.

Or, that I may grasp him in whom I have also been grasped by him: that is, that I may see him in the splendor in which he appeared to me on the road when he grasped me (Acts 9). For this reason I pursue him. [Col. 1302D] His righteousness went before me; let mine follow him. Those who heard the Apostle saying, “Not that I have already received, or am already perfect,” began to wonder. “Brothers,” he says, “I do not consider myself already to have grasped it”: that is, do not be mistaken about me; I know myself better than you do; I know what is lacking to me, I know what is present. I do not consider myself to have grasped it.

But there is one thing which I do not consider myself to have grasped. I have many things, but I have not yet grasped one thing. “But one thing is necessary” (Luke 10)—“One thing I have asked of the Lord; this will I seek” (Ps. 26). And what is that? “That I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (ibid.). It is this one thing which I have not yet grasped. And insofar as it is lacking to me, so far am I not yet perfect, because I am not yet equal to angels.

What, then, do you do? What action do you teach by your example? Forgetting the things which are behind—that is, the earthly things which I left behind, removing them from the memory of my thought—and stretching myself in desire toward things before, that is, toward heavenly things which lift one up to divine things, I pursue them: that is, I follow them perfectly in mind and work. For eternal things are before us, temporal things behind us, because we find the former as we go forward, while the latter, as we withdraw from them, we leave behind our backs. Or, “the things which are behind” means my past merits, which I forget and count as nothing; and I stretch myself toward future merits, always adding something. For I am still making progress, still walking, still on the way, still stretching myself: I have not yet arrived.

I stretch myself toward the goal, that is, toward what God’s providence has [Col. 1303B] appointed and ordered for me, or toward that for which I have resolved to run. And I pursue, that is, I do not cease following until I come to the prize of God’s upward calling in Christ Jesus: that is, to the reward to be given in heaven, to which God calls me in his Son. And since I, who am so great, do not consider myself to have grasped it, but still pursue in case I may grasp it, all of us who are perfect should think this: namely, that we have not yet grasped it, but ought still to pursue and make progress.

The Apostle appears almost to contradict himself. For how can the statement stand that one who had said, “Not that I have already received, or am already perfect,” should say, “All of us who are perfect should think this”? But he speaks of two perfections, showing that every human being and all creation, even if it has come to perfection, nevertheless needs God’s mercy and possesses full perfection by grace, not by merit. Therefore the Apostle was perfect according to the measure of human possibility, but still awaited perfection from the gift of heavenly bounty, so that he might become equal to angels. He was perfect as a traveler, but not yet perfect as a possessor of the homeland. And every perfect person ought to think this of himself: remembering that he is a traveler and not an inhabitant, he should strive always to walk and make progress, lest perhaps he remain where he thinks that he has done enough.

This statement was very useful for some of the Philippians, who already considered themselves perfect, lest they think their perfection sufficient and begin [Col. 1303D] to act more laxly and perish. “You ought,” he says, “to think this: that we are imperfect by comparison with future perfection, and are striving toward it. And if you think otherwise as little children”—that is, if you already think that you have accomplished, are, or know something—“God will reveal even this to you,” namely that you do not think rightly. For whoever remains in Catholic peace, if he thinks otherwise than he ought in any respect, God will reveal it to the humble; if he defends it proudly, God will cast him off.

Or, if you think differently now from how you will think in the future, because you now see through a mirror, God will reveal even this: for he will cause you clearly to know both himself and all other things which you now see obscurely (1 Cor. 15). Or, “if you think otherwise,” that is, if you think that you have grasped perfect knowledge of Christ, God in his mercy will reveal to you that you think this wrongly. Likewise, he has delivered you from other errors because of your good life. Or thus: if you think otherwise now than you will in the future, both concerning God and concerning all things, God will reveal even this imperfect knowledge to you through his Spirit. Or, “if you think otherwise,” and if you devise something better for the worship of God, or interpret the Scriptures differently in accordance with the rule of truth, know that this too is God’s gift, because he himself has revealed it to you.

Nevertheless—that is, yet—let us all hold fast to that to which we have attained, so that we may think alike in believing and remain in the same rule of discipline, that is, rectitude of life: namely, that no one, because of some new discovery or interpretation of his own, should abandon the common understanding of faith or the rule of righteous living established by the fathers. Or thus: we all ought to think that we are not yet perfect and have not grasped full knowledge of God; but nevertheless let us hold with our whole mind that to which we have attained, namely the knowledge which we have reached, so that in the end we may think alike and remain in the same rule of life—that is, neither believe different things nor maintain differing ways of life, but all believe and live sincerely and purely in one manner.

> “Be imitators of me, brothers, and observe those who walk in this way, as you have our example. For many walk, of whom I often told you, but now even weeping I say it, that they are enemies of Christ’s cross (Rom. 16). Their end is destruction; their god is their belly; and their glory is in their shame—those who [Col. 1304C] think earthly things. But our commonwealth is in heaven, whence we await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humiliation so that it may be conformed to the body of his glory, according to the working of his power, by which he is able also to subject all things to himself.”

Likewise, as I have said, let us think the same thing and remain in the same rule of life. And in these matters—that is, in unity of faith and the rule of discipline—be imitators of me, brothers: that is, as you know me to think the same thing and to keep the same rule, so do you. And, like me, consign to oblivion the things that are behind—that is, past vices—so that, if vanity once pleased you, it may please you no longer; and always stretch yourselves forward, by devout desires and efforts, toward progress in virtues and eternal goods. [Col. 1304D] For the mind is stretched out by desire for joy not yet attained. And the whole life of a good Christian is a holy desire. In these and such matters imitate me; and observe—that is, consider carefully—and follow those who resemble me in the way of God, who thus walk—that is, advance in good works—according as you have our pattern: that is, as I delivered to you the pattern of walking rightly, either by the example of my conduct or by the word of preaching.

Those, I say, who thus walk, observe diligently; for there are many who proceed otherwise, and they are not to be imitated but avoided. Many walk the broad way of destruction—that is, many advance along the path of perverse conduct—whom I often told you, while I was present [Col. 1305A] with you, to be enemies of the cross of Christ; and now I say the same, weeping both for their destruction and for the overthrow of the simple whom they deceive. For pseudo-preachers are enemies of the Lord’s cross, because they say that Christ’s death does not suffice for believers’ salvation without the carnal observances of the law. Thus they strive to assail the Savior’s cross; and therefore they deservedly perish, “whose end is destruction,” that is, eternal death, because then they do not find the aid of the cross whose enemies they were.

“Their god is their belly,” because whatever they do, they do for their belly. Or they make foods, which belong to the belly, into their god, when they declare that such foods justify people and suppose the soul’s salvation to lie in foods; and “their glory is in their shame,” because they glory in things for which they might be confounded and blush: that is, in their [Col. 1305B] shameful circumcised members. They “think earthly things,” because in the law they understand nothing spiritually, but everything carnally.

These words also apply to evil Catholics. For they too are many, because an abundance of chaff fills the threshing-floor, and they walk in the broad way that leads to destruction. They are enemies of Christ’s cross, because they always act against the cross. For whereas Christ’s cross in all the elect afflicts the flesh and mortifies crimes, they, on the contrary, foster the flesh with pleasures and nourish vices. Therefore their end will be everlasting destruction, because, on account of faith alone—which they possessed without good works—they will not escape eternal punishments (James 2). “Their god is their belly,” because, just as they ought to venerate God with the highest honor [Col. 1305C] and offer him all the best things from their possessions, so they venerate their own belly, offering it costly kinds of food prepared with the utmost care. They are always devoted to serving the belly, worshipping it as god and not remembering their Creator. “Their glory is in their shame,” because, having now lost shame at sinning, they glory in those works of wickedness for which they ought to have blushed. They “think earthly things,” because in earthly matters they understand nothing except what they see; nor do they place the mind’s attention anywhere but in earthly things, but are always occupied in thought with what is lowest.

But our manner of life stands far apart from theirs, because already, according to faith and hope, it is in heaven. For if it is not in heaven, how do we have our heart above? In body we walk upon earth, but in heart we dwell [Col. 1305D] in heaven. For just as the dwelling-place of outward conduct is the building inhabited by the body, so the dwelling-place of our thought is whatever thing the mind inhabits through love. For whatever we love, we dwell in it as though resting there. Hence the Apostle, since he had fixed his heart on things above—though placed on earth, yet a stranger to earth—says concerning himself and those like him: “Our manner of life is in heaven”; that is, both in life and understanding we are like angels. From there—that is, from those heavenly things—besides the benefits which we already possess, we also await our Lord Jesus Christ, who will come for judgment: now the Savior of our souls, and then also [Col. 1306A] of our bodies.

For he then will refashion—that is, raise into a better form—the body of our lowliness, that is, of our vileness and abasement: namely, this vile and abject body of ours, now subject to so many miseries. He will refashion it so that in the resurrection he restores to it its former form in such glory that it may be conformed to the body of his glory: that is, made like his most glorious body, which he took from the Virgin, and that our body may have the same form of glory as his has, when “the righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13). And he himself will do this according to the working of his omnipotence, by which he can not only refashion the body but also subject all things to himself; for then will be wholly fulfilled: “You have subjected all things under his feet” (Ps. 109; [Col. 1306B] 1 Cor. 15).

## Chapter IV

> “Therefore, my most beloved and longed-for brothers, my joy and my crown, stand thus firm in the Lord, beloved.”

Because Christ will refashion the body of our lowliness and we shall attain so great a glory from so great a benefit, therefore, my brothers, stand in what you have begun, lest you lose so great a glory. I call you most beloved to me, because I hold you very dear; and longed-for, because I greatly long for you—or you for me; my joy, that is, those in whose faith and work I rejoice; and my crown in the future, because through you I shall receive the crown of glory. You who are such, [Col. 1306C] stand firm in the Lord thus: that is, as I taught you to stand and as you began; or as you know me and those like me to stand, because then you will be most beloved.

> “I entreat Euodia and I beseech Syntyche to think the same thing in the Lord. Yes, I also ask you, true yokefellow, help those women who labored with me in the Gospel, with Clement and the rest of my fellow-workers, whose names are in the book of life.”

Euodia and Syntyche were religious matrons, accustomed to receive preachers. Perhaps the Apostle had heard that they disagreed in faith; therefore he entreated them by name to think the same thing in the Lord as the rest did—that is, in his faith. As though he said: I exhort all to stand firm, but Euodia and Syntyche especially, [Col. 1306D] because I fear more for them. “Yes, I also ask you, true yokefellow”: that is, my fellow-worker in preaching, help them by strengthening them with your exhortations, instruction, and prayers, so that they may be able to stand united in faith. Nor are they to be lightly regarded, because they “labored with me in the Gospel”: that is, from their own labor they supplied me with support for preaching the Gospel. They labored, I say, with Clement, who labored in this, and with the others who helped me. This Clement was the third Roman pope. [Note: [Col. 1305] Third, if one begins not with Peter but with Linus.]

Or: help them together with Clement and the rest of my fellow-workers—that is, you and my other helpers who are at Philippi, help them. I mean helpers who [Col. 1307A] did not labor in vain to help me, because their names are written in the book of life: that is, they are held as assigned to life in the memory of divine predestination. For what is the book of life but God’s memory, in which are those who live forever? (Rev. 20, 22.)

> “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (1 Cor. 1; Jer. 9). “Let your moderation be known to all people. The Lord is near. Be anxious about nothing; but in every prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your petitions be made known to God. And may the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.”

The Apostle, rejoicing in their faith and works, exhorts them to rejoice in the Lord so that [Col. 1307B] they may eagerly advance in these things; and he repeats it, in order truly to show that he rejoices in them. “Rejoice,” he says: that is, make your heart glad, and establish for yourselves in the Lord, not outside him, every good in which one ought to rejoice. And this is so necessary for you that I say again, “Rejoice,” so that worldly sorrow may find no place in you, but spiritual joy may fill you wholly. Rejoice in the Lord, not at intervals—so that now you rejoice and now you do not—but rejoice always, whether in prosperity or adversity. And I do not say it once only, but again, that you may rejoice, confirming and impressing joy by repeated admonition. Rejoice, but in the Lord, not in the world.

For just as “no one can serve two masters” [Col. 1307C] (Matt. 6; Luke 16), so no one can rejoice both in the Lord and in the world. These two joys are contrary. For the joy of the world is unpunished wickedness: people may revel, fornicate at spectacles, trifle in drunkenness, gorge themselves in disgracefulness; and may neither hunger, fear of war or of anything else, illness, nor any adversity hinder these evils; but all may overflow in peace of the flesh and security of mind—and behold the joy of the world. Therefore do not rejoice in the world, but in the Lord: that is, not in iniquity but in truth; not in the flower of vanity but in the hope of eternity.

Let the joy of your mind be in the Lord; but let people see the moderation of your conduct, so that through your example they may learn to act moderately. *Modestia* (“moderation”) is, as it were, the standing of a measure, when measure is kept in all things. Moderation in the mind restrains desires; moderation in action regulates all acts, and likewise in words. Let this moderation shine so greatly in you that it may be known to all people: to believers, that they may imitate it; to unbelievers, that they may be unable to criticize it. Keep moderation of conduct, because the Lord is near, to help you continually, unless you fail through your own sluggishness. Although he ascended bodily above all the heavens, he did not withdraw in majesty. He who made all things is present everywhere. The Lord is near, ready to give you whatever you need in spiritual and bodily matters. Therefore cast away [Col. 1308A] the anxiety of empty fear, because the Lord will be present as your helper both in your good works and in the sufferings you endure for his name; nor will he deny you bodily food.

Therefore be anxious and fearful about nothing, as though concerning the future; but be free from worldly anxiety, keeping God’s promises before your eyes and asking everything from him. Do not be anxious, I say, but let your petitions for the things you wish to receive be so earnest and urgent that they may be made known to God: that is, may reach God; this means, may be acceptable to God, who knows all things, but is said to know those things which he has chosen and approved. Or let them be made known for you before God through endurance, not before people through boasting. Or perhaps they may be made known even to the angels who are with God, [Col. 1308B] so that in some manner they offer them to God and deliberate about them; and what they have learned, by God’s command, must be fulfilled, they report back to you either openly or secretly.

I mean petitions made in every prayer: that is, in prayer which omits none of the things that ought to be prayed for, but asks from God in prayer everything expedient; and in supplication, which is made with adjuration by sacred things; with thanksgiving for benefits received, because whoever wishes to obtain other things ought to be grateful for those already received. Or, according to others, prayer concerns past offenses and sins; supplication concerns the obtaining of future goods; thanksgiving concerns benefits bestowed; petition concerns specifically necessary matters. I exhort you to persist in such kinds of prayer, and I pray God—without whom human labor is useless—to grant the result: namely, that the peace of God, by which he is at peace in himself and by participation in which angels and human beings are made peaceful, may guard your hearts; the peace which surpasses every understanding, [Col. 1308C] that is, every intellect of human beings and angels. For the peace of God, by which God himself is at peace, we cannot know as God knows it—neither we nor the angels.

But because we too have become, according to our measure, partakers of his peace, the highest peace within us, between ourselves, and with him, as far as our highest capacity extends—[Note: [Col. 1307D] An obscure passage.]—the holy angels know it in this manner according to their measure; but human beings are now far below this knowledge, however greatly they may excel in advance of mind. “For now we see through a mirror, in an enigma” (1 Cor. 12). But when [Col. 1308D] we have become equal to the angels, then, like them, we shall see face to face—that is, openly—and shall have as great peace toward them as they have toward us, because we shall love as much as we are loved by them. Thus their peace will be known to us, because ours will be such and so great, and then it will not surpass our understanding. But God’s peace, which is theirs toward themselves, beyond any doubt surpasses both our understanding and theirs.

And may this peace of God guard your hearts—that is, your wills—and your minds in Christ Jesus, so that outside Christ you may desire or understand nothing. May it guard your hearts against the enticements of the world, and guard [Col. 1309A] your minds against the deceits of pseudo-preachers. May it guard hearts against all adversities, and minds against errors.

> “Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever are chaste, whatever are just, whatever are holy, whatever are lovely, whatever are of good report; if there is any virtue, if there is any praise of discipline: think on these things—those which you have learned and received and heard and seen in me. Do these things, and the God of peace will be with you.”

In conclusion the Apostle sets forth the things belonging to perfection. As though he said: Up to this point I have warned you against persecutors and pseudo-preachers; but now I shall briefly speak of another kind of exhortation, concerning the best conduct. Namely, think and do whatever things are true, and whatever are chaste, [Col. 1309B] so that you admit nothing false or lustful either in thought or action; but be truthful in every word, and chaste in mind and body, lest there be anything wanton even in your appearance. Likewise, think and do whatever things are just and whatever are holy. Just things concern one’s neighbor; holy things, one’s own life: that is, things to be observed justly toward one’s neighbor; holy things, that is, things sanctifying souls and bodies. Whoever always thinks and does what is just can wrong neither God nor human beings. And whoever constantly thinks and does holy things cannot be defiled by any stain.

Think and do whatever is lovely: that is, endeavor that your words and deeds may please people in a good way, so that by this you may draw them to imitate you and thus join them to God. Likewise think and do whatever is of good report, [Col. 1309C] lest an evil opinion be held of you, but a good one, so that it may benefit others. For the conduct of the saints ought also to take care that, if life is not evil through wantonness, reputation may not be evil through negligence.

Those should not be heard who, when rebuked for some negligence by which they fall under an evil suspicion—though they know their life to be far removed from it—say that conscience before God suffices them, recklessly and even cruelly despising people’s estimation. For they kill the souls of others: either those who blaspheme God’s life, to whom the life of the saints, though chaste, displeases according to their suspicion as though it were shameful; or those who, with an excuse, imitate not what they see, [Col. 1309D] but what they suppose. Therefore whoever guards his life from crimes of disgrace and wicked deeds does well for himself; but whoever guards his reputation is merciful also toward others. For our own life is necessary to us; our reputation, to others. And certainly what we mercifully minister to others for salvation also redounds to our own benefit.

If there is any virtue, pursue it; if there is any praise of discipline, possess it. Let virtue be in you, and let praise follow after it, so that people who praise your virtue may make progress. Or: think and do things of good report, if there is any virtue in them or any praise of Christian discipline. For good reputation regarding strength, knowledge, or other secular things is not to be sought. Think on these things, I say: that is, keep in memory all the things which you both learned, [Col. 1310A] while I taught; and received as worthy to be retained, because after learning them they were acceptable and pleasing to you; and heard to be in me, and saw. Do these things: that is, do not merely think them, but fulfill them in action. Then God, the giver of peace, will be with you, helping you to do them. For whoever lives thus will not only have peace with God, but will also be loved by almost all people.

> “But I rejoiced greatly in the Lord, because at last, after some time, you have flourished again in thinking of me, as indeed you did think of me; but you were occupied. I do not say this as though because of want. For I have learned to be sufficient in whatever circumstances I am. I know both how to be humbled and how to abound. Everywhere and in all things I have been instructed, both to be full and to hunger, both to abound [Col. 1310B] and to suffer need. I can do all things in him who strengthens me. Nevertheless, you did well in sharing my tribulation.”

He recalls their good deeds and gives thanks, in order to stir them up to do such things more zealously. As though saying: I exhort you to future zeal in religion, but I rejoice in the past zeal of your benefactions, and I rejoiced greatly—not in the gift which you promised, but in the Lord, who inspired this charity in you and will render recompense—because at last, that is, after a long time, at some time, since you could not do everything, you have flourished again: that is, you have resumed the former flower of generosity, so as to give me something as you formerly used to do. For generosity is a flower, because from it proceeds the fruit [Col. 1310C] of eternal life. You had withered from this flower through a certain barrenness and had become numb, as it were, in winter’s cold. But now, as though the south wind of the Holy Spirit were blowing, spring has returned to your hearts, and you have flourished again like good trees.

“You have flourished again in thinking of me”: that is, in having compassion on my account, because your compassion benefits me. To think of me means that you felt what pricked me, as formerly you felt it when you ministered to me. Nor did you suspend this for any evil reason, but you were occupied and hindered by certain adversities or duties. Above, he openly rebukes the Galatians for their imprudent sin, saying: “O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you?” (Gal. 3). But now he rebukes the faults of these ashamed people as though sympathizing with them, so that rebuke might expose the Galatians’ faults, while gentler speech might veil these people’s negligence. Likewise every ruler of the Church ought, according to the measure of the fault, to rebuke each person with rational discernment.

“I rejoiced, and you have flourished again.” I do not say this as though because of want: that is, I do not say that I rejoiced as though because of my own want, which you relieved; for I rejoice not because my distress has been eased, but because of your affection. Or, I do not say these things as though my want still needed relieving, in order that by these words I might endeavor to invite you to supply my need again. For I have learned, both from God and from daily experience, to be sufficient: that is, content with the circumstances in which I am, whether small or great. For I know how to be humbled by poverty, because [Col. 1311A] I am not broken by it; and I know how to abound in goods, because I am not exalted by them. Everywhere—that is, in every place, whether at Rome or elsewhere, whether I am placed before rulers or others—and in all things, that is, in every kind of circumstance, I have been trained and taught by God: to be full without fullness harming me; to hunger patiently; to abound humbly; and to suffer want moderately. I know these things and can carry them all out, with him strengthening me who taught me.

It is great knowledge to know how to be humbled and to abound, to be full and to hunger, to abound and to suffer need. Whoever is not broken by his need, not drawn away from thanksgiving, and not inflamed with desire for temporal things, knows how to be humbled. For in this place the Apostle calls suffering need “being humbled.” He immediately adds the contrary: “I know also how to abound.” [Col. 1311B] Whoever is not puffed up by goods received, does not twist them to the use of vain glory, and does not keep to himself alone what he has received, but mercifully shares it with the needy, knows how to abound. Whoever uses food received not for gorging the belly but for restoring strength, and grants the flesh no more than necessity demands, knows how to be full. Whoever endures lack of food without murmuring and, because of need for sustenance, does nothing by which the soul incurs the snare of sin, knows how to hunger. Therefore whoever is neither lifted up by pride in abundance nor provoked by greed in need knows how to abound and knows how to suffer need.

When the Apostle immediately added, “I can do all things,” he joined the words, “in him who strengthens me.” Behold, a branch is put forth on high; but because it holds itself in the root, it remains vigorous. For, rising upward, it would wither if it separated itself from the root. He attributes nothing to himself who confesses that he can do all things not in himself but in the Lord who strengthens him.

Indeed, he says, I know and can do all these things; nevertheless, as far as you are concerned, you did well in fulfilling what is right by sharing your goods in my tribulation. Your action pleases me because you acted well, ministering mercifully to me in my affliction, not because you sent me things of which I could have done without.

> “You Philippians also know that in the beginning of the Gospel, when I departed into Macedonia, no church shared with me in the account of giving and receiving except you alone; for even to Thessalonica [Col. 1311D] you sent once and twice for my need. Not that I seek the gift, but I seek fruit abounding to your account. But I have all things and abound; I am filled, having received from Epaphroditus the things you sent, an odor of sweetness, an acceptable sacrifice, pleasing to God. And may my God fulfill your every desire according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus. But to God, even our Father, be glory for ages of ages. Amen.”

You shared your goods with me both now and formerly, but others did not. For you Philippians, like other and many people, know that in the beginning of the Gospel—that is, when I first preached the Gospel to you—no church except yours shared with me in the account of giving and receiving: that is, so as reasonably to consider [Col. 1312A] that one who received spiritual things ought to give carnal things, according to the saying: “If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things?” (1 Cor. 9). You alone shared with me, because you did this not only while I was present among you, but also, when I was staying at Thessalonica—that is, in that city—you sent me from your goods for my use once and again.

The Apostle mentions this so that, as persons worthy of praise, they might devote themselves more eagerly to ministering to preachers, and lest they suppose that he had forgotten the charity often bestowed upon him. He did not reject these things from them because they did not give them in order to make him spare their vices. But he did not accept from the others, lest he diminish his authority to correct them, and lest perhaps it be burdensome to them to provide him with bodily food.

“I say,” he says, “that you acted well, not so that I may be filled, but lest you be empty.” And this is the meaning: I do not say it because I seek your gift, but I seek fruit from the gift abounding in your account, not mine. A gift is the actual thing expended, such as money, food, or clothing. But the fruit of a gift is when something is expended with a kindly mind and in pursuit of future reward. Thus we understand the gift as being in the thing, the fruit as being in the heart. Therefore this same fruit ought to abound in the account—that is, in the light of the heart. Or it ought to abound in their account, so that when they render an account of their actions to God, the fruit of righteousness may abound for them. Therefore, because the Apostle was fed more by the reward of his disciples than by their gift, he confesses that he seeks not the gift but the fruit. [Col. 1312C]

Accordingly, he immediately adds: “But I have all things and abound.” As though saying: I do not seek the gift, but I have all things, because I have God, in whom I possess all things; and I abound, not in one thing so that I lack another, but I am filled, because nothing is lacking to those who fear God. I am filled, even if you had given nothing; but I have received from Epaphroditus your gifts, which you sent me as an odor of sweetness, an acceptable sacrifice, pleasing to God: that is, gifts that please God like the most sweet odor of pure prayer. That prayer is an odor John testifies, where he reports that he saw elders holding golden bowls full of incense, “which are the prayers of the saints” (Rev. 5). But these persons’ gifts are also now called an odor of sweetness because the poor pray for them, as it is written: “Store up [Col. 1312D] alms in the heart of the poor, and it will pray for you against every evil” (Ecclus. 29).

They are also a sacrifice, because they were given by them in order that they might conquer their enemies, or because they had conquered them. And this sacrifice is acceptable and pleasing to God, because God accepted it favorably. You have filled me with your goods; may my God fill you with his. By his own example the Apostle shows that we ought to pray for those from whom we receive temporal goods. May God fulfill your every desire by granting all the goods that you desire, so that nothing of what you wish may be lacking to you. And may he do this according to his riches: that is, according to the fact that he himself is rich and can give more than anyone deserves. May he fulfill your desire, I say, not in earthly things but in the glory of heavenly blessedness, and this in Christ Jesus, so that [Col. 1313A] in him you may forever abound in delights. Let us not be ungrateful for his benefits, but always render him thanks and praise: namely, to God who created us and to our Father who adopted us as sons be glory, not for an hour but unto ages of ages—that is, forever. Amen.

> “Greet every saint in Christ Jesus. The brothers who are with me greet you; all the saints greet you, but especially those who are of Caesar’s household.”

“Greet,” he says, “every saint dwelling among you in Christ Jesus”: that is, one who is holy not in the law but in Christ, and has no holiness except in Christ and from Christ. But the brothers—that is, the children of the Catholic mother Church—who are with me, that is, who are staying with me, greet you. Nor do they alone greet you, but all the saints who are at Rome. All indeed greet you, [Col. 1314A] but especially those who are of Caesar’s household—that is, Nero’s. In this he greatly confirms them in faith, by showing that they are especially loved and specially greeted by those who now serve the Christian religion in Caesar’s household. Nor ought they any longer fear tribulations as though grievous and long-lasting, since the emperor’s advisers and friends are now Christians.

> “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.”

May the grace of Christ Jesus our Lord be with your spirit, so that what the spirit wills rightly through free choice, it may be able to accomplish with grace helping; lest you be “a generation that did not direct its heart, and whose spirit was not faithful with God” (Ps. 77). For our spirit must be faithful with God, because unless we believe that the spirit of our will can do nothing of itself without the help of God’s grace, we shall never be able [Col. 1314B] to do anything good. Amen.

# On the Epistle to the Colossians

[Col. 1313]

## Argument

[Col. 1313B]

There is a city in Asia named Colossae, from which the Colossians are called. The Apostle himself did not preach to them, but his disciples Epaphras and Archippus did, when they originated from [Col. 1313C] them. For Epaphras, preaching to them what he had learned from Paul, converted them and became their apostle; while Archippus received the episcopate over them. But when pseudo-apostles arrived and preached carnal observances, it was uncertain whom they ought rather to believe. Therefore Paul, whose authority was renowned, judges as an arbiter which side ought rather to be maintained. He describes Christ and his benefits, showing how he is sufficient for all things; but he wholly rejects carnal observances, so that henceforth they may hold Christ’s faith sincerely. He also instructs them morally, confirming what those men had taught. Hence this epistle has a great affinity and resemblance with that to the Ephesians. For in both, in like manner, the surpassing greatness of divine benefits is commended, [Col. 1313D] carnal observance of the law is overthrown, and the conduct of God’s people is instructed.

## Chapter I

> “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and Timothy the brother, to those who are at Colossae, holy and faithful brothers in Christ Jesus: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

Because Paul had been appointed apostle of the Gentiles, he simply calls himself an apostle in writing to these Gentiles, although he had not himself preached to them but had done so through his disciples. For he was their apostle as well. By contrast, in the epistle he wrote to the Hebrews, he did not call himself an apostle, because he was not apostle of the Hebrews but of the Gentiles.
