Paul, whose words are authoritative because [Col. 1314B] he is an apostle—that is, an envoy—of Jesus Christ, and this not through his own merits or human election but through God’s will, contrary to which pseudo-apostles act; and Timothy the brother, a man of great [Col. 1314C] authority, send what follows to those at Colossae: not indeed to idolaters, but to holy and faithful brothers, that is, to greater and lesser Christians. “Holy” means advanced in divine religion; “faithful,” those who already possess faith but have not yet advanced in holy conduct. Or, to the same persons as holy and faithful: that is, possessing good conduct and faith; and this in Christ Jesus—that is, in Christ’s grace, not in the observance of the law or in the powers of free choice. What do they wish or ask? “May grace and peace be to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

> “We give thanks to God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, always praying for you, having heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and of the love which [Col. 1314D] you have toward all the saints, because of the hope laid up for you in heaven, which you heard in the word of truth of the Gospel, which has come to you, just as it is in the whole world, and bears fruit and grows; as also in you, from the day when you heard and knew the grace of God in truth, as you learned from Epaphras, our most beloved fellow-servant, who is for you a faithful minister of Christ Jesus, and who also made known to us your love in the Spirit.”

He begins with thanksgiving, in order to make them well disposed toward him, and to kindle them always to give thanks to God for the benefits received. He writes, moreover, from Rome. “We give thanks,” he says, “I and Timothy,” that is, we render grateful praise to God, because he has given you all the good things that you possess [Col. 1315A]. Therefore we give thanks to him, not to you. We give thanks to God, that is, to the Creator of Jesus Christ insofar as he is man; and to the Father of the same Christ Jesus our Lord insofar as he is God, who through that same Mediator has bestowed all things upon you. I mean, we are always praying for you, that you may grow and make progress by day and by night; or, whenever we pray, we give thanks, having heard—that is, because we have heard—that your faith is in Christ Jesus, since your faith too is God’s gift. Otherwise thanksgiving would not be due for it. And because we have heard of the love which you have, not idle, but overflowing in good works, not toward certain saints, but toward all, since the benefits of your charity abound toward those whom you know to live holy lives. And therefore we render thanks to him [Col. 1315B] who inspired such charity in you.

And this is not for the sake of human praise, but because of the hope laid up for you in heaven: it does not now appear, yet it is kept for you in heaven in a secure place. That is, it is because of the everlasting life which you hope to obtain in heaven. But how is so hidden a thing hoped for? “Which you heard,” he says, that is, because you heard of it in the word of truth. Or, because you do not have hope from yourselves but from God: because it is in the word—that is, in the preaching—not of falsehood but of truth; nor of just any truth, but of the Gospel, that is, the good message by which it is announced that God became man in order to make human beings gods, that is, equal to angels. And lest they should pretend not to have heard the Gospel, as though it had not been preached to them but they had merely heard others speak a little about it, those to whom it had been preached, he adds: “Which Gospel has come to you”—understand, even if not through me, yet through those who had learned from me—and thus the truth has not escaped you.

Again, lest they should become proud, as though the Gospel had come to them and passed the other nations by, he adds: “It has come to you as also into the whole world”; that is, you alone have not heard it, but the whole world also, because there is no kingdom of the world in which Christ’s name has not been preached. Or: it has come to you as purely and truly as it came through me and others into the whole world, and still is and remains in it; that is, no less has been done for you than for the other churches. And since the Gospel is in the world, it bears fruit there through the good works of understanding and grows through an increase [Col. 1315C] of knowledge and in the number of believers. This is not because others have more than you, but because the same has been done for them as also in you. Therefore you ought neither to add anything nor alter anything, but to preserve the Gospel sincerely as you learned it, which the whole world preserves, lest you alone dissent from the entire globe.

As it is in the world, so it is also among you: it bears fruit and grows from the day on which you heard it, because you were not rebellious, but immediately began to believe and to bear fruit. Or, on that day—that is, in the illumination of the heart—you heard by believing and came to know by discerning the grace of God, that is, the forgiveness of sins and God’s other free gifts, in truth and not in pretence, because God truly gives them and does not pretend to give; or, you came to know them in the truth of the preaching, “as you learned from Epaphras.”

He now praises Epaphras [Col. 1316A] and says nothing of Archippus, because Epaphras was very fervent in zeal for charity, attentive, and their apostle; while Archippus was a bishop, but somewhat lax and lukewarm. You came to know the grace of God not as something you yourselves discovered by your own intelligence, but as you learned it from Epaphras, a teacher not of little worth but our most beloved fellow-servant, because he serves the Lord Christ with us in preaching. You ought not despise his teaching, but honor and observe it, because he is not deceitful but a faithful minister of Jesus Christ: that is, he ministers Christ’s gifts to you in preaching, or offers your good works to Christ. He is a faithful minister on your behalf, not for his own interests: he does not seek your possessions, but you; he does not desire to acquire your goods, but to join you to God. Desiring your salvation, he began to preach my teaching to you. He also informed us, by his report, that your love for God and neighbor is founded in the Holy Spirit; he made known to us your love, which is not in the affection of the flesh but in the grace of the Holy Spirit.

> “For this reason we also, from the day we heard, do not cease praying and asking for you that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, that you may walk worthily of God, pleasing him in all things, bearing fruit in every good work and growing in the knowledge of God; strengthened in all power according to the might of his glory, in all patience and long-suffering, with joy giving thanks to God the Father, who has made us worthy for a share in the lot of the saints in light; who has delivered [Col. 1316C] us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love.”

Epaphras reported to us your spiritual love. Therefore not Epaphras alone, but we also, from the day on which we heard this, do not cease praying with humble affection and devout devotion, and asking, as though assuming a certain boldness on account of your merits. This, indeed, is what we pray and ask unceasingly from God for you: that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will—that is, that you may fully know what he wills and what he does not will. It is a great thing fully to know what God wills in all matters of the active or contemplative life. Yet what he wills is now explained successively, point by point.

May you know, I say, his will [Col. 1316D] in all wisdom concerning the things of the active life, and in spiritual understanding, that is, knowledge of spiritual matters; or, in all wisdom concerning divine and heavenly things and in spiritual understanding of the Holy Scriptures. Thus may you walk worthily of God, that is, act so that you may be worthy to receive God’s reward; or, may you walk in such a manner that your conduct is fitting for God, pleasing him in all that you do. Namely, may you bear fruit, not in some good work but in every good work, manifoldly and increasingly; and through the merit of such good works grow in the knowledge of God, in spiritual perception of the Godhead, according to the saying: “From your commandments I have gained understanding” (Ps. 118 [119]). For good action illumines the understanding of the mind.

I mean, may you be strengthened in God with every power: made strong and steadfast [Col. 1317A] in charity, righteous in holiness, and in other such things; and this according to the might of his glory, that is, insofar as his glory can make you strong—the glory by which the minds of the elect are illumined, so that they may have a clear knowledge of God and be able clearly to discern all things. Thus they can no longer in any way be bent to consent to sin, but always do what is good.

I said that you should be strong in every virtue, namely in all patience, so that through patience you may courageously bear all adversities. For I do not ask that you be strong in merely some patience, patiently enduring some things and not others, but rather in all patience: that you may patiently bear for God every kind of trouble, and in all long-suffering, that is, in the long perseverance of the mind in enduring adversities [Col. 1317B] and awaiting the heavenly promises. For long-suffering must be added to patience, lest someone, after maintaining patience for some span of time, should fail amid adversity or grow weary of so prolonged an observance of patience and begin to act impatiently. Rather, through long-suffering, let him patiently endure all things to the end.

And preserve this patience and long-suffering with joy; or, do not be sad amid the adversities you suffer, but instead rejoice in hope while you are patient in tribulation. For you ought not be distressed but rejoice if it happens that you endure adversities for righteousness’ sake. I mean, give thanks to God the Father, who has bestowed such great benefits upon us as to make us companions of the saints. That is, do not murmur against God because he permits you to endure adversities in the present age [Col. 1317C], but always give him thanks, because he has deigned to count you among the number of the saints, so that you may reign with him eternally.

Give joyful thanks to him who, by his own act, has made us worthy to pass into a share—that is, a participation—in the lot, that is, the eternal inheritance, of the saints in light: in the brightness of the divine vision, so that we may be eternally illuminated by the splendor of his majesty. For an inheritance is called a “lot” when it is given not through human merits but through divine election, to the holy patriarchs and prophets. And God willed that we should have a share in this lot, so that with the holy fathers we might possess the inheritance in the light of the living.

Or, God’s will in the human race is a lot, with him in whom there is no injustice. For he does not show partiality (Rom. 2), but his hidden lot applies to each human being. By the name “lot” is signified the grace by which we are saved, because in a lot there is no choice, but God’s will. For where it is said, “This person does [it], and this person does not,” merits are considered. And where merits are considered, there is choice, not lot. But when God found no merits of ours, he made us by the lot of his will, because he willed it, not because we were worthy: this is lot. And he himself mercifully made us, who were unworthy, worthy for a share in this lot, because he called us to faith, not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles (Rom. 9). And he did this in the light [Col. 1317D] by which he illumined our minds, so that we might know him and understand the words of his preachers.

He made us worthy in this way [Col. 1318A]: namely, because he delivered us—that is, powerfully drew us out—from the power of darkness, that is, of the demons who ruled us inwardly while the blindness of unbelief and ignorance, or the darkness of sins, still remained in us. From the power of such darkness—that is, of the evil angels—God the Father delivered us, lest they possess us without end in the night of their condemnation. In baptism he erased our sins, through which they had power over us, and transferred us into the kingdom of his Son, into the Church of Christ, of which it was said: “The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all stumbling-blocks” (Matt. 13).

He transferred us, I say, into the kingdom of the Son of his love, so that through faith and good works his Son might reign in us. But what does “of his love” mean? If in the divine Trinity there is no love other than the Holy Spirit, then Christ in this place is found to be the Son not of the Father alone but also of the Holy Spirit. But since this is utterly absurd, it remains that love is not there the Holy Spirit alone. “The Son of his love” must be understood as nothing other than his beloved Son, or finally, the Son of his substance. For the charity or love of the Father, which exists in a nature ineffably simple, is nothing other than his very nature and substance. Therefore the Son of his charity or love is none other than he who is begotten from his substance.

He is said to have transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love [Col. 1318B] so that we may understand that he too will love us if we persevere in being the kingdom of his Son, whom [Col. 1318C] he naturally and ineffably loves; that is, if sin no longer reigns in us. For where sin begins to reign, Christ ceases to reign (Rom. 5).

> “In whom we have redemption and the forgiveness of sins, who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature.”

He transferred us into the kingdom of his Son, in whom we have redemption from the devil’s power and forgiveness of sins. For Christ’s blood was given as the price for us in this redemption. Having received it, the devil was not enriched but slain, so that we might be released from those bonds, and so that he might not drag with him, to the destruction of the second and everlasting death, anyone redeemed by Christ from every debt through the unjust shedding of his own blood, still entangled in the nets of sins [Col. 1318D].

For that blood, since it belonged to one who had absolutely no sin (2 Cor. 5; 1 Pet. 2), was shed for the forgiveness of our sins. Thus, although the devil justly held those whom he had bound by the condition of death as liable for sin, he should justly release them through him upon whom an undeserved penalty of death had fallen though he was guilty of no sin. By this justice and this bond was that strong one bound, so that his vessels might be snatched away, or the human beings whom he held might be freed (Mark 3). Thus in Christ we have redemption and forgiveness, which we received in baptism, the devil’s power having been destroyed and the freedom of our will restored.

Or, God transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, that is, he has already conveyed us into heaven through hope, because he raised us together and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ (Eph. 2). In him we likewise have redemption through hope, that is, release from the miseries and afflictions [Col. 1319A] that we now suffer; and through the actual bestowal we already have in him forgiveness of sins, because both once in baptism, through the pouring out of his blood, he erased our sins, and daily—if we sin—we have no need of other sacrifices. Hence it is evident that legal sacrifices ought no longer to be offered, because they now provide absolutely no benefit.

Christ, according to his divinity, is the image of the invisible God and the complete likeness of the Father, as he says: “Whoever sees me sees the Father” (John 14). For just as, through contemplating any image, we are given knowledge of the one whose image it is, even though that person is absent and has never been seen by us, so the apostles, seeing the Son, understood the Father, who did not bodily appear to them. We indeed are the image of God, but the Son is his image in another way. For as the emperor’s image is one thing on a coin and another in a son, so the image of God is one thing in the Son, who is consubstantial, coequal, and coeternal, and another in a human being, who is a creature.

And it should be noted that the Apostle wonderfully commends Christ’s excellence in each nature, now making a statement about his divinity and now about his humanity, in order to show that he alone is sufficient for justification and eternal salvation for all who believe, without works of the law [Col. 1319B–C]. For he made a statement concerning his divinity in saying that the Father transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love. He added one concerning his humanity in saying that in him we have redemption and forgiveness of sins. Again, according to the form of God, he said that he is the image of the invisible God. He now adds, according to the form of a servant, that he is the firstborn of every creature. For according to the form of God he is not firstborn but only-begotten; but according to the form of a servant he is firstborn among many brethren. In the substance of divinity he is only-begotten; in the assumption of humanity, firstborn in grace.

Therefore he is called the firstborn of every creature because, just as the firstborn among all brothers holds the primacy of rank among all the brothers, so Christ’s humanity holds the primacy of rank among all creatures, so that it may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory (1 Sam. 2) [Col. 1319D].

> “For in him all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers. All things were created through him and in him, and he is before all, and all things subsist in him. And he is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he himself may hold the primacy in all things (1 Cor. 15). For in him it pleased [God] that all the fullness of divinity should dwell, and through him to reconcile all things in him, [Col. 1320A] making peace through the blood of his cross, whether things in heaven or things on earth.”

It is not surprising if the humanity of the Son of God so surpasses all things that, with respect to it, he himself is the firstborn of every creature. For according to the power of his divinity all things were created—that is, made—in him, just as the Psalm is sung to the Father: “How magnified are your works, O Lord; you have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103 [104]), that is, in your Son. All things that are in heaven and on earth, visible, such as the sun and moon or human bodies, and invisible, such as angels and souls, were created in him. And the invisible things, which seemed less likely to have been made through him because of the greatness of their excellence, are set forth by parts.

All things, I say, were made in him: whether thrones, that is, those more worthy spirits in whom God sits; or dominions, that is, those nobler spirits who rule over the rest; or principalities, that is, those who preside over others and order what they ought to do; or powers, that is, those spirits who mightily excel the subordinate orders of others [Col. 1320B]. For those are called thrones in whom God always sits in order to exercise judgment. Since in Latin speech we call θρόνος (*thronos*) a “seat,” God’s thrones are said to be those who are filled with such great grace of divinity that the Lord sits in them and determines his judgments through them. Hence it is sung to him: “You sit upon the throne, judging righteousness” (Ps. 9). The thrones indeed surpass [the others] in the dignity of their higher place, leaving six other orders of angels beneath themselves.

Immediately after the thrones are the dominions: those spirits most noble in the court of the heavenly king, who rule over all subjected to them and possess them as lords. Also called principalities are those who preside even over the good spirits of angels. While they arrange whatever is to be done by their subjects for the fulfillment of divine ministries, they exercise rule. Yet the dominions wonderfully surpass the power of the principalities by a vast difference. For to rule is to stand first among the rest; but to exercise dominion is also to possess those subject to oneself.

According to Dionysius, powers also are believed to be of a rank more powerful than principalities, so that they mightily preside over the subordinate orders of the rest and mightily extend themselves upward to divine contemplation [Col. 1320C]. Or, according to blessed Gregory, powers are those who have received in their order, more powerfully than the rest, that adverse powers should be subject to their jurisdiction; by their power these are restrained, lest they prevail in tempting human hearts as much as they wish.

All these invisible ranks of heavenly and preeminent spirits were created in Christ, showing by this that he is not less than the Father. And not angelic spirits alone, but absolutely everything whatsoever that is or has been was created by the Father through him, as the Evangelist testifies: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1), that is, no creature. And all things were made in him, as we have already stated that the Psalmist sang: “You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103 [104]) [Col. 1320D–1321A]. Through him—that is, through the power of his omnipotence—and in him—that is, within the sign of the immeasurable greatness of his wisdom—all things were created. And according to the form of a servant, he is before all—that is, set above all—because no one is equal to him even insofar as he is human. And according to the form of God, all things subsist in him, because as he created all things, so he contains and governs all things.

All things subsist in him because, according to the immensity of his unbounded and incomprehensible divinity, all things are within him; and lest they return to nothing, they continue through him. And according to the form of a servant, he is the head of his body, namely the Church, because head and body are of one nature. The head of the Church is that man in whose assumption “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1) [Col. 1321B]; all the other members are the saints through whom the Church is perfected and completed.

Just as the soul animates and gives life to our whole body, although in the head it perceives by seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching, while in the other members it perceives only by touching—and therefore all things are subject to the head for action, while it is placed above for deliberation, because in a certain manner the head bears the role of the soul that deliberates for the body, for every sense is displayed there—so, for the whole people of saints as for one body, “the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2), is the head. Divine Wisdom did not assume this man as it assumed others, but far more excellently and sublimely, as it was fitting that it alone should be assumed in him in whom Wisdom would appear to human beings, as it was fitting for Wisdom visibly to be shown in one who would bear the person of Wisdom itself, through whom the others become wise [Col. 1321C].

He therefore is the head and the others are members, because all good things are in him as all the senses are in the head, while in the others particular shares of good things are distributed according to the measure of each member. He governs all the members, and all the members cling to him. According to the form of God, he is also the beginning, because he is God’s Wisdom which, abiding in itself, as it is written (Wis. 7), renews all things. For a beginning in a certain manner always begins and never fails, just as the Son has eternal birth from the Father. Or, as he himself said in John’s Apocalypse: “He is the beginning of God’s creation” (Rev. 3), because every creature has being from him. Or, he is for us the beginning of every virtue and every good, because no one can have anything good unless he receives it from him; and therefore he is rightly called the head.

And according to the form of a servant, he is the firstborn from the dead, because he rose first, never again to die (Rom. 6). For the resurrection of the dead itself is a kind of generation, as it is written: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit” (Matt. 19), and so forth. Therefore the remaining dead are still held in their mother’s womb—that is, enclosed in the bosom of the earth, they lie shut in tombs. But he has already come forth from his mother’s womb: that is, coming from the tomb, he rose like a giant, no longer to die, but to reign eternally with the Father [Col. 1321D–1322A] in heaven. Therefore he is first begotten from the dead, or firstborn of the dead: that is, begotten to immortality through resurrection. And this is so that he may hold the primacy—that is, dominion—in all things, because he can raise others too.

For just as he rose first of all—hence he is called “the first fruits of those who sleep” (1 Cor. 15)—so among all saints, both those before and those after him, he holds the primacy of dignity, power, and holiness. Or, he holds the primacy in all dignities because, as he rose first, so he first ascended into heaven, first saw the face of God, and surpasses all in every dignity. And rightly he has the primacy, not only because he is firstborn but also because it pleased the Trinity that in him all fullness [Col. 1322B] of knowledge and virtues should not merely be present but should dwell.

“For it pleased”—that is, it pleased the Father together with the Word and the Holy Spirit—“that all fullness should dwell in him”: that is, every way-perfect abundance of divinity, and of all graces (John 1), virtues, and good things. It pleased God that so great a fullness of good things should remain in that man to whom he gave the Spirit not by measure, as he customarily gives it to the other saints. And it pleased God through him to reconcile to himself all human beings placed in him—that is, Jews and Gentiles established in faith in him, who had previously been at discord both with one another and with God.

God, as stated, willed this: he, I say, making them at peace with one another, not through sacrifices of the law but through the blood of his cross, that is, through his blood shed on the cross; whether those things which are in heaven or those which are on earth, that is, angels and human beings. For at the hour when the blood of redemption came forth from the side of the Lord hanging on the cross, Adam’s sin was remitted to the human race and heavenly and earthly things were reconciled, because then entrance into the kingdom of heaven was opened to human beings [Col. 1322C].

For a great discord separated human beings and angels, because no one was so holy as to be received into the fellowship of angels; rather, all descended to hell because of the guilt of the first human being. But through Christ’s death such peace was made between humans and angels that now, when the souls of the righteous depart from their bodies, they immediately enter heaven while the angels rejoice. Or, through Christ’s blood those things which are in heaven—that is, the souls of the saints already in the kingdom of heaven, which formerly were at discord with God either through their own fault or that of their first parent—and those things on earth—that is, the elect who still journey in the exile of the present life—have been reconciled to God [Col. 1322D].

> “And you, when you were once alienated and enemies in disposition through evil works, he has now reconciled in the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy and spotless and irreproachable before him, provided indeed that you remain grounded and steadfast in the faith and immovable from the hope of the Gospel which you heard, which has been preached in all creation under heaven, of which I, Paul, have become a minister; who now rejoice in sufferings for you [Col. 1323A], and fill up in my flesh what is lacking of Christ’s sufferings for his body, which is the Church; of which I have become a minister according to God’s dispensation, given to me among you, that I may fulfill the word of God: the mystery that was hidden from ages and generations, but now has been revealed to his saints, to whom God willed to make known the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory. Him we proclaim, correcting every person and teaching every person in all wisdom, that we may present every person perfect in Christ Jesus; in whom I also labor, striving according to his working, which works in me with power.”

[Col. 1323B] He had said generally that all things were reconciled, and now he says specifically that they were reconciled—not through their own merits, nor through fleshly observances, but through Christ—so that they may be more zealous to submit to the dominion of so great a King and may not be ungrateful for such benefits. “It pleased God,” he says, “through Christ to reconcile all things to himself”; and he also willed to reconcile you, O Colossians, to himself through the same one, when formerly—that is, before faith—you were alienated from him, that is, having nothing in common with him, while you clung to alien gods; and you were his enemies, not by nature but in disposition, because by holding opinions contrary to him—thinking idols to be gods and loving what he hates—you were his enemies, continuing in evil works. For formerly you were indeed such; but now, that is, in this time of grace, God has reconciled you in the body [Col. 1323C] of his flesh, that is, in the body of Christ, which is flesh. For it is called “the body of flesh” to distinguish it from other bodies, which are not flesh.

God reconciled you to himself in the body of Christ’s flesh through his death, in order to present—that is, so that he might present—you holy in virtues, spotless from the filth of sins, and irreproachable, so that no evil may appear in you before him who sees all things. This cannot take place in this life, but will take place in the other, when the saints, now possessing no stain and nothing blameworthy, abiding before their Creator, will see his face forever. He himself will present you such before himself—that is, he will set you forth and offer you before the sight and presence of his glory—yet on this condition: if you remain [Col. 1323D] in the faith. Otherwise you cannot attain this glory. But you will then attain it if you now remain in the faith which you have learned, founded—that is, firmly rooted—and not wavering; and steadfast, that you may neither fall nor yield: that is, that you may neither be deceived by the fraudulent speech of pseudo-apostles nor withdraw from the constancy of faith through persecutions by the Gentiles. And if you remain unmoved from the hope of the Gospel—that is, if you persist in good works so firmly that nothing can move you away from the hope of eternal recompense promised by the Gospel—which you heard from your teachers. Therefore you ought to hold fast to it, because it would have been better not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back (2 Pet. 2).

This Gospel did not come to you alone [Col. 1324A], lest you become proud on that account or suppose that you alone have been deceived by it; rather, it has been preached “in every creature under heaven,” as the Lord commanded: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16). For by “every creature” every nation of the Gentiles under heaven throughout the whole world may be indicated. For there is no nation of the Gentiles in which the Gospel has not been preached. Or “every creature” signifies the human being, who has being in common with stones, life with trees, sensation with animals, and understanding with angels. Therefore, if the human being has something in common with every creature, then in one respect the human being is every creature. Thus the Gospel is found in every creature in the human being alone. Therefore the Gospel is preached to every creature [Col. 1324B] when it is preached to the human being alone, because he is taught for whose sake all things on earth were created, and from whom all things are, by a certain likeness, distinct.

Or “every creature” is the whole Church, spiritually created through new grace, according to: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Ps. 50), and so forth; “We are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Eph. 2). This creature is under heaven—that is, it still wanders in this valley of tears—but will finally be raised into heaven. For it is said that the Gospel has been preached in every creature that is under heaven. It is as though he said: You ought to hold this Gospel and this faith and evangelical hope, because the whole world of believers holds them in this manner.

The Apostle also commends this Gospel [Col. 1324C] by his authority, adding: “Of this Gospel I have been made a minister,” that is, a servant and preacher, I Paul, who am of such renown and authority. You may also know that it is true, and that you ought firmly to retain and obey it. I have become its minister, who now, bound in chains and held at Rome for its proclamation, rejoice in sufferings, because believers profit from them. I rejoice, I say, in sufferings endured for your confirmation in the truth of the Gospel; and I fill up in my flesh what is lacking of the sufferings of Christ—that is, what Christ suffered less in his own flesh, I endure in my flesh for the increase of his body, which is the Church.

For the sufferings [Col. 1324D] of Christ are not in Christ alone; indeed, the sufferings of Christ are nowhere except in Christ. If we understand Christ as head and body, the sufferings of Christ are nowhere except in Christ. But if we understand Christ as the head alone, the sufferings of Christ are not in Christ alone. For the Apostle says: “I fill up what is lacking of the sufferings,” not of my own sufferings but of Christ’s; in flesh, not now Christ’s flesh but mine. Christ, he says, still suffers sufferings—not in the flesh in which he ascended into heaven, but in my flesh, which still labors on earth.

Whoever you are among Christ’s members, whatever you suffer from those who are not among Christ’s members was lacking to Christ’s sufferings. Therefore it is added that it was lacking: filling up the measure, not overflowing it. You suffer only as much as, from [Col. 1325A] your own sufferings, had to be added to the total suffering of Christ, who suffered in our head and suffers in his members, that is, in ourselves. To this commonwealth, as it were, which is ours, each of us pays according to our measure what we owe; and by the suffering of our powers we contribute, as it were, the assessed portion of our sufferings. The full apportionment of all sufferings will not occur until the age has ended.

“I fill up,” he says, “what is lacking.” Lacking to whom? To Christ’s sufferings. And where is it lacking? In my flesh. For in the flesh of Christ, which the Virgin bore, no suffering is lacking; rather, all sufferings were completed in it. But there still remains a portion of his sufferings in my flesh, which I endure daily for his universal body, which is the Church. For if I ceased from instructing the faithful, I would not endure these sufferings [Col. 1325B] from unbelievers. But because I am always zealous to benefit the Church, I am always compelled to endure adversities.

I have been made a minister of this Church—that is, I have received the office of ministering to it the word of life—and this not by human arrangement, or by my own usurpation or merit, but according to God’s dispensation, that is, according to what God’s grace has appointed for me. Or, I have been made a minister of the Church according to God’s dispensation, that I may distribute to it the provisions of my Lord. This dispensation was given to me in you, because it amounts to the same thing that through my disciples I have distributed to you the food of life as if I had done it through myself. Or “in you,” because it was given to me among all the Gentiles, and you are Gentiles. It was given to me so that I might fulfill the word of God—that is, fulfill what God preordained [Col. 1325C] concerning you, and what in the secrecy of his counsel he spoke before the ages concerning your salvation, lest you suppose that salvation was not promised to the Gentiles. For in the secret of his wisdom, or in the prophets, he spoke good things concerning you. And I strive to fulfill this word while I urge you to hasten toward the promised salvation.

Or, “I fulfill the word of God,” that is, the word of preaching which Christ began to proclaim in person; I complete it through the ministry of my preaching, because in my teaching is brought to completion whatever had been stated less fully in the Holy Scriptures—that is, every perfection of righteousness and wisdom which mortals can attain is completed in my preaching. I fulfill the word, that is, the mystery: this is the hidden secret of human redemption through [Col. 1325D] the incarnation and death of the Son of God, through which the Gentiles were enlightened and joined to and made equal with believing Jews, while the remaining Jews were blinded.

This mystery was hidden from human beings from the ages—that is, from the time the ages began, when day began to succeed night and night day—and from generations, that is, from the time generation succeeded generation until the coming of the Lord. It was hidden throughout so long a span of the world from all, except for the few to whom God revealed it through the Holy Spirit (Luke 10; Matt. 11). For although some philosophers spoke many correct things concerning the divinity of the Son of God, they learned nothing concerning his incarnation and death, and our redemption through it. For God hid this from the wise and prudent and revealed it to little ones.

[Col. 1326A] Formerly, indeed, it was hidden; but now, in the time of grace, it has been revealed not to all people, but to his saints; nor to all of them, but to those whom God willed, from grace alone, to make known—that is, to disclose—the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles. In it are many things: faith, forgiveness, justification, the union of Jews and Gentiles, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and future blessedness; and therefore I called them riches. This mystery is Christ in you Gentiles, that is, Christ’s incarnation, passion, and resurrection, through which the human race was restored and Jews and Gentiles were made equal—something that the fleshly observance of the law could not accomplish. I mean Christ existing in you as the hope of glory: through him who dwells in your hearts, you hope for everlasting glory without the fleshly [Col. 1326B] works of the law.

Him—that is, such as he is—we proclaim to all: namely, that the Gentiles hope through him and will attain glory without the law. We preach him who is, for Gentiles believing in him, the hope of glory and eternal salvation, rebuking—that is, reproving and correcting—not you only, but every person who strays from the path of faith or right knowledge. We rebuke every person—that is, Jew and Gentile alike, noble and ignoble, rich and poor, free and slave, male and female alike—and we teach every person who is ignorant, teaching him, I say, in all wisdom commended in the Holy Scriptures, through which God is known and worshipped. We do this so that we may present—that is, prepare and render—every person perfect in faith and morals in Christ Jesus, not in the law; for “the law brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. 7).

[Col. 1326C] In this place are set forth the three stages of activity which the great Dionysius testifies exist not only in the ecclesiastical but also in the angelic hierarchy, that is, the sacred order of rule: purification, illumination, and perfection. Purification is in those who are rebuked; illumination in those who are taught; and perfection in those who are presented as perfect. For human beings are purified from sins and error, illuminated by the teaching of wisdom, and perfected by a more exalted attainment of virtues and wisdom. Angels also are purified from ignorance, illuminated by divine knowledge, [Col. 1326D] and perfected by a greater knowledge of that same science.

Therefore, indicating these stages of hierarchy—that is, of priestly activity—the Apostle says of himself and his companions that “we proclaim Christ,” rebuking every person who needs correction for whatever fault, and teaching in all wisdom concerning divine things every person who has already been corrected and purified from error or sins. For teaching in wisdom ought not to be delivered to a person before the vessel of his heart has been purified to receive it. Therefore we rebuke in this manner and then teach, so that we may present—that is, make—every person who has been corrected and taught perfect in Christ, that is, in the Christian religion. Or, in the heavenly homeland, we may present—that is, offer—him to God as a sacrifice [Col. 1327A] perfect in Christ Jesus, that is, perfectly full of every good thing.

In this—that is, for this purpose, namely, that I may rebuke, teach, and present every person perfect in Christ to God—I also labor, that is, I strive through laborious efforts, contending against the rebellious, aided by signs which God joins to my labor for confirmation, according to his operation, namely Christ’s, which he works in me through the power of miracles, or through the power of a mighty and effective word by the Holy Spirit, or through the power of inward strength, by which the Holy Spirit inwardly strengthened me for constancy in preaching and doing good.

## Chapter II

“For I want you to know what concern I have [Col. 1327B] for you and for those who are at Laodicea, and for all who have not seen my face in the flesh, so that their hearts may be comforted, instructed in charity, and unto all the riches of the fullness of understanding, unto the knowledge of the mystery of God the Father and of Christ Jesus, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. But I say this so that no one may deceive you by loftiness of speech. For although I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing and seeing your order and the firmness of your faith which is in Christ (1 Cor. 5). Therefore, as you received Jesus Christ the Lord, walk in him, rooted and built up in him, and confirmed in the faith, as you also learned, abounding in him in thanksgiving.”

[Col. 1327C] Therefore I tell you that I labor in order that I may rebuke and teach every person and present each one perfect, because I want you to know—that is, I want you to know—what concern I have for you, how solicitous I am for your salvation, and for those who are at Laodicea, that is, at that city neighboring yours, and for the rest, whoever they may be, who have not seen my face in the flesh. That is, do not suppose that I am less concerned for those to whom I did not preach in person than for those whom, while physically present, I instructed with my own mouth; or less concerned for those whom I do not see with bodily eyes than for those whom I foster by bodily presence. I am concerned for them so that their hearts may be comforted—that is, so that they may receive consolation when they learn that I have paternal concern for them.

I am concerned, I say, for those [Col. 1327D] who have not seen my face in the flesh, being instructed in charity—that is, those who have not seen me bodily and are instructed in the charity which God had toward us when he gave up his Son for us. Or, I am concerned so that their hearts—that is, their own hearts—may be comforted in you, being instructed in charity. Whoever considers this can console himself in this misery, because from it he judges that he can return to his homeland. Whoever considers this, I say, can console himself in the adversities which he suffers, because from it he judges how just it is that he should suffer scourges for his sins, when the Son of God suffered such great things without sin.

May their hearts be comforted, and this unto all the riches of the fullness of understanding [Col. 1328A], that is, as they tend toward every abundance of full understanding, so that they may have a perfect understanding of human and divine things, as also of the soul and the higher spirits; and thus may advance by stages into the knowledge of the mystery of God—that is, that they may know that secret, known by few, concerning the essence of God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. From this they may know that the substance of both is one, although the person of the Father is one and that of the Son another; and that the Father is neither earlier nor greater than the Son, nor the Son later or less than the Father, but both are coeternal and equal.

Therefore let them tend toward all the riches of the fullness of understanding, toward the knowledge of the mystery of the Father and his Christ, so that they may receive knowledge of God’s mystery in Christ, recognizing these to be the riches of wisdom and knowledge: that Christ, in the fullness of his deity [Col. 1328B], is to be worshipped with the Father. For the entire mystery of God’s sacrament is in Christ, so that whoever knows him may seem to possess knowledge of all things. For every principle of the knowledge of heavenly or earthly creation is in him who is the head and maker of all; so that whoever knows him should seek nothing further, because here is perfect power and wisdom, and whatever is sought elsewhere is found here perfectly.

Unbelievers do not think this, because they do not read in the Gospels and prophets astrology and other such things despised by God, since they contribute nothing to salvation but nourish error; and while they study these things, they take no care for the soul. But the person who knows Christ finds the treasure of wisdom and knowledge, because he knows what is useful for all things. In Christ, therefore, are all the treasures [Col. 1328C] of wisdom and knowledge. Wisdom concerns divine things, while knowledge concerns human things; and both of these—divine and human things—are in Christ.

Everything which the Word made flesh did and suffered for us in time and place belongs, according to this distinction, to knowledge and not to wisdom. But that the Word is coeternal with the Father without time and without place, and wholly present everywhere, belongs to wisdom. Thus the Word made flesh, who is Christ Jesus, possesses the treasures both of wisdom and of knowledge. Therefore all the treasures both of wisdom concerning divine and heavenly things and of knowledge concerning human and earthly things are in Christ. Yet some believers know these treasures in Christ more, others less; but unbelievers have wholly failed to know [Col. 1328D] them. For they are hidden in Christ. Therefore do not wonder if you are now in Christ and have not yet found them, or have so far found little of them, because they are not open to all, but only to those who ask and knock (Matt. 7).

But I say this to you concerning God’s mystery which is in Christ—that is, concerning the mystery of human redemption which God placed in Christ—and concerning the riches of the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in him, so that no one may deceive you by loftiness of speech; that is, so that neither any heretic, pseudo-apostle, nor Gentile may separate you from faith in Christ by exalted eloquence. For power lies not in the composition of words, but in their meanings. Let no one draw you away [Col. 1329A] from the hope that is in the Creator and Redeemer by arguments concerning worldly things; let no one separate you from God’s wisdom by arguments and verbal eloquence. I exhort you toward knowledge of the mystery of God so that you may not be deceived, because, although I am not bodily among you, I nevertheless have concern for you.

For though I am absent in body, yet—that is, nevertheless—I am with you in spirit, that is, in concern and the affection of love. By contrast, the hired man, though bodily present with the sheep, is nevertheless far from them in spirit when he flees at the wolf’s coming—not by changing his place, but by withdrawing comfort, because he hides himself in silence when he dares not oppose the ravager. I am with you in spirit, that is, in mind and concern; or by the Holy Spirit who dwells in me and is present everywhere and fills the whole world (Wis. 1), I am with you. For Elisha, though absent in body, was nevertheless present in spirit when Gehazi received gifts from Naaman the Syrian, or when the king of Syria devised plans against the king of Israel (4 Kgs. 5, 16).

Thus I am with you in spirit, observing whatever you do, so that you may now be ashamed to act perversely before my eyes and may be more ready to observe the Gospel. I am with you in spirit, rejoicing in your progress and seeing your order—that is, considering that you keep inviolate the order of sacred religion—and seeing the firmness of that faith of yours which is in Christ, that is, contemplating that you have firm faith in Christ. For I behold both the order of your holiness and the firmness of your faith. Therefore beware lest anything blameworthy [Col. 1329C] appear in you, since I see both your conduct and your faith.

And because I rejoice in the order you keep and the faith you hold, do not depart from them. Rather, as you received Jesus Christ as Lord and God from your good teachers—that is, as you learned from them how he ought to be believed in and worshipped—so walk: that is, make progress and increase, and press onward into the inner things in him, not outside him; and do not stray from the path of uprightness which you have begun to follow. You, I say, are rooted like good trees, so far as you bear the fruit of good work in the active life; and built up like God’s house, so far as contemplation is concerned, in him who is the true vine, from which all branches arise [Col. 1329D] (John 15), and the foundation upon which the whole building stands. For “you are God’s field; you are God’s building” (1 Cor. 3). And persevere confirmed—that is, made firm and steadfast in every respect—in the faith as you learned it, taught by Epaphras or Archippus, not as the pseudo-apostles wish to persuade you.

You, I say, are abounding in him in good works and virtues, in thanksgiving, so that you may always give God thanks for the good things you have already received from him and strive to abound more and more. For thus it will benefit you to be confirmed in faith. Otherwise, if faith does not have works, it is dead in itself (Jas. 2).

“See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world, and not according to [Col. 1330A] Christ; because in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily, and you are filled in him, who is the head of every principality and power.”

I exhort you to walk in Christ, and “see,” that is, beware with cautious watchfulness lest anyone deceive you, leading you astray into some error through earthly philosophy, which is composed through arguments and subtlety. It deceives when, through plausible reasons and invented notions, nothing is judged so true as what is perceived in the elements. It is ordained not by God but by human beings; and therefore it must be avoided, because it serves the world, not God. It draws one away from Christ, in whom is all perfection, because he possesses all that the Father has.

Therefore see that no one leads you astray through philosophy [Col. 1330B], that is, through worldly wisdom, which follows natural things and argues from them, and through the empty deceit of pseudo-apostles. For what they say about the law is deceit; it is empty because there is no usefulness in this falsehood, though false things sometimes have some usefulness. This deceit of fleshly observances is according to the tradition of human beings, that is, of the Pharisees, to whom the Lord says: “You have made void the commandment of God because of your tradition” (Matt. 15); according to the elements of the world, that is, according to the course of sun and moon, as in the observance of festivals and sacrifices performed at different times; and not according to Christ, because whoever thinks that the law must still be observed carnally departs from the truth of Christ. For those fleshly ceremonies can no longer be observed, lest Christ be promised in them as still to come, or lest it be believed that he was never promised in them. Therefore that fleshly observance is now not according to Christ.

Or, beware lest anyone deceive you through philosophy, that is, through a philosophical interpretation of idols; and through the empty deceit, that is, deceit void of every usefulness and every truth, of such assertions, which is according to the tradition of men—that is, of those regarded as wise—who expound idols as though more intelligently according to the elements of the world. “Juno,” they say, “is the air”; and they invite people to worship the sea in Neptune, the earth in the image of Tellus, and the air in Juno. These are the elements of which this world consists. Therefore I warn you to avoid not merely ordinary worshippers of images, but supposedly more learned interpreters [Col. 1330D] of symbols, because in such interpretations there is empty deceit that attempts to seduce the unwary.

For the philosophers, who in this passage are called “men” because they thought that they alone used reason, handed down that God cannot become a creature, nor can a human being be born of a virgin or rise again after death. They considered the elements—that is, these visible creatures—in which animals are generated through mixture, and that what dies does not live again. But advocates of such doctrines must be avoided, because, just as they reason about some creature by human arguments, so they reason about the Creator, seeing him as contained under human laws and not according to Christ—that is, not considering the power that was made manifest in Christ’s flesh.

[Col. 1331A] For in him dwells not some part of heavenly grace, as in the other saints, but the whole fullness of divinity—not shadowily, as in Solomon’s temple, but bodily [variant: “corporeal”], that is, solidly and truly. “Bodily” does not mean that God is corporeal; rather, either the Apostle employs a transferred expression, as though God had dwelt in a temple made by hands not bodily but shadowily, that is, by prefiguring signs. For he calls all those observances “shadows of things to come” (Heb. 10), likewise using a transferred term; for, as it is written (Acts 7), the Most High God does not dwell in temples made by hands. Or perhaps “bodily” is said because God dwells as in a temple in Christ’s body, which he assumed from the Virgin. Thus he said to the Jews concerning the temple [Col. 1331B] of his body: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2).

Although divinity dwells in any outstanding member, as in some great prophet or apostle, it nevertheless does not dwell in them as the whole fullness of divinity dwells in the head, which is Christ. For God, who is present everywhere and wholly present everywhere, does not dwell everywhere, but in his temple, to which he is gracious and favorable through grace. Those in whom he dwells receive him more fully in some cases and less fully in others. For in Christ, who is the head of all the righteous, the whole fullness of divinity dwells; but grace is distributed to the others according to measure.

For sensation exists in the individual members of our body, but not as much as in the head, where the whole fivefold faculty is entirely present. There are sight [Col. 1331C], hearing, smell, taste, and touch; in the other members there is touch alone. And besides this—that the whole fullness of divinity dwells as in a temple in that body—there is another difference between that head and the excellence of any member: of none of the saints can it be said, “The Word was made flesh” (John 1), nor does any of them receive the title “Only-begotten” by any presence of grace.

Thus in Christ the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily, that is, truly. Divinity, of course, is not a body. But because, as stated above, the Apostle calls the sacraments of the Old Testament shadows of things to come, he said that the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in Christ [Col. 1331D] (Heb. 10) by comparison with those shadows: all things signified by those shadows are fulfilled in him, and he is in some manner their body—that is, he is the truth of those figures and significations. Whoever says that fleshly observances are still necessary says that Christ is not the body of the shadows and that God is not sufficient for all things.

Indeed, the whole fullness of divinity remains bodily in Christ, and you are filled in him with the grace of divinity, through which you abound in virtues and holy works. Nor is it surprising that divine grace is poured into you through him, since he is of such excellence that he is the head of every principality and power. For there is no principality or power in heaven or on earth which does not descend from this head [Col. 1332A], is subject to this head, and is governed by this head.

“In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made by hand, in the stripping off of the body of flesh, but in the circumcision of Jesus Christ; buried with him in baptism, in which you also rose through faith in the operation of God, who raised him from the dead. And when you were dead in transgressions and in the uncircumcision of your flesh (Eph. 2), he made you alive together with him, forgiving you all transgressions, blotting out the written bond of the decree that stood against us and was contrary to us; he took it out of the way, fastening it to the cross; and stripping the principalities and powers, he led them forth boldly, openly triumphing over them in himself.”

The Apostle now begins covertly to show that the observances of the law are superfluous, and that faith in Christ alone is sufficient for salvation [Col. 1332B]. “You,” he says, “are in Christ, filled with spiritual goods, in whom you have also been circumcised.” For Christ’s resurrection—which occurred indeed on the third day from his Passion, but on the eighth day in the cycle of the week—has itself circumcised you. For Christ rose, took away your carnal desires, took away evil lusts, took away the excess with which you were born, and, much worse, that which you had added by living wickedly. You have been circumcised in Christ with a circumcision not performed carnally by human hand in the stripping off of the body of flesh—that is, in the removal of superfluous skin—but with the circumcision of Jesus Christ, which amputates not flesh but vices.

For he did not mean that two things should be understood, as though “flesh” were one thing and “the body of flesh” another [Col. 1332C]. Rather, because “body” is the name of many things, none of which is flesh—for apart from flesh there are many bodies, heavenly and earthly—he said “the body of flesh,” that is, the body which is flesh; just as elsewhere he says “the spirit of the mind,” that spirit which is mind. “You have been circumcised,” he says, “with a circumcision which is not by hand,” that is, not made by human action in the stripping off of the flesh of the body, that is, in the cutting away of superfluous flesh; rather, it has been made divinely in the circumcision of Jesus Christ, that is, in the cutting away of carnal vices and desires.

For Christ’s circumcision, performed on the eighth day, signified that through faith in his resurrection we were to be stripped of every excess of vice, and that in the eighth age of the world, through the resurrection of bodies, we are to be divested of every stain of mortality and corruption [Col. 1332D]. You have been spiritually circumcised with Christ’s circumcision (Luke 2), “buried with him in baptism.” For this is Christ’s circumcision in you: namely, that you are dead to vices, so that, having become sharers in his burial through baptism, you may also become sharers in his resurrection through incorruptibility of character and a new manner of life. For the triple immersion of baptism is an image of the Lord’s three-day burial, so that whoever is lowered into water as into a tomb may be wholly dead to sins and thus be able to rise to virtues.

“In whom,” that is, in Christ, “you have also risen” from the death of the soul after baptismal burial through the faith by which you believed that he rose and that you too would rise through him. You have risen, I say, “through faith in the working of God,” that is, through believing in the work which God performed in him—he who raised him from the dead—and who also made you alive together with him and raised you together with him, when you were spiritually dead in transgressions which you had committed by doing wrong, and in “the uncircumcision of your flesh,” that is, in the carnal uncleanness into which you had fallen [Col. 1333A]. For here “uncircumcision” denotes that which it signifies, namely sins of the flesh.

When you were thus dead, God made you alive with Christ; that is, by raising Christ bodily, he raised you spiritually with him, “forgiving,” that is, remitting to you all transgressions, both original and actual, himself “blotting out the handwriting of the decree which was against us.” For he not only forgave you Gentiles your transgressions, but also remitted to us Jews the violations arising from the law. And this is what is meant by “blotting out the handwriting,” and so forth.

A *chirographum* is a handwritten document made to preserve the record of some matter. Men divide such a document among those between whom the matter for which it is drawn up is settled, and each keeps his own portion. But the handwriting blotted out by God was the memory of sins arising from transgression of the law, which did not depart from the minds of Jews and evil spirits [Col. 1333B]. He therefore blotted out the handwriting of the decree—that is, the memory of transgression arising from the decree, that is, from the law. For our conscience and the devil possessed the memory of that transgression for accusation; and so this memory was against us, harming and tormenting us. But when this guilt has been blotted out through baptism, our conscience no longer fears, nor has the devil anything to bring as an accusation.

“The decree which was contrary to us” means the uprightness of justice ordained in the law, which was opposed to the perversity of our violations. But by the help of new grace we have come to agreement with our adversary, that is, the divine law, obeying its commands, as the Lord says: “Be quickly in agreement with your adversary while you are with him on the way.” That is: be harmonious with and obedient to the word of heavenly commandments, which opposes your perversities, while you are with it on the journey of this present life [Col. 1333C].

Or the handwriting—that is, that written by hand—was the commission of Adam’s transgression. It was against us, that is, it opposed our salvation and barred us from entering our heavenly homeland. The decree contrary to us, moreover, was the very sentence of our condemnation, adverse to all human beings. But God blotted out this handwriting, that is, the bond of the old guilt by which the devil held us as debtors to death. Therefore the handwriting itself was of the decree, that is, of our decreed condemnation, by which it was decreed that we should justly be held captive under the enemy to whom we had voluntarily subjected ourselves by consenting to iniquity.

Or God’s decree was: “Of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat” (Gen. 2). God blotted out the handwriting of this violated decree—that is, its memory—when he washed away the sin of the first parent through Christ’s blood and, as it were, consigned it to oblivion. And “he took it out of the way.” For this sin stood between God and us, separating us from God; but God took it out of the way so that we might cling to God [Col. 1334A]. He took it out of the way, “nailing it to the cross,” so that, just as it had begun from a tree, so it might end upon a tree. For when innocent Christ was crucified, Adam’s sin was put to death.

Or, if by “decree” we understand the law of Moses, God took it out of the way between Jews and Gentiles, so that they might no longer be separated by the law but might become one people in Christ, nailing it to the cross so that it might now cease, after all sacrifices had been fulfilled in the offering of the true Lamb. Just as he freed us from the law and from transgression of the law, so he also rescued the ancient fathers from hell, lest anyone suppose that they were saved through the law. And this is why, while speaking of the Father, he adds something concerning the Son: because the works of Father and Son are inseparable—“stripping principalities and powers, he led them forth confidently.”

For he stripped the principalities and powers of demons by taking away from them the souls of the righteous, whom they held in hell because of the guilt of the first parent; and he led them forth, that is, he led across hell to the heavenly kingdoms those souls of the saints rescued from hell. And he did this confidently, that is, with great assurance, not fearing the demons, since he had no sin [Col. 1334B]. Nor does the statement, “stripping principalities and powers,” conflict with the saying, “who is the head of every power,” because there the discourse concerns good principalities and powers, but here hostile ones.

For “principalities” are those wicked spirits who rule in the vices which they are especially accustomed to suggest: such as spirits of fornication, who rule the lustful, and spirits of pride, who dominate the proud [Col. 1334C]. “Powers,” however, are those spirits who have power to hurl into greater sins those people over whom they prevail through their inward desires. Thus the invisible powers hostile to us are conquered where invisible desires are conquered. Therefore, if within ourselves we conquer the desires for temporal things, we necessarily conquer within ourselves him who reigns in a human being through those very desires.

Christ therefore stripped these principalities and powers, snatching from them the people over whom they ruled, when through the gift of the Holy Spirit he extinguished worldly desires in the hearts of those people. And he led forth those same desires or principalities—that is, he expelled them from those converted to the faith—as he had said: “Now the prince of this world will be cast out” (John 12) [Col. 1334D]. And he did this confidently, knowing that his cause was just; and openly, that is, hanging on the cross before all the people, he triumphed—that is, gloriously conquered them—in himself, that is, in the Passion of his own body; and afterward he was to triumph also in his martyrs.

> “Therefore let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a festival day, or of a new moon, or of sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is Christ’s.”

And indeed you have been spiritually circumcised with Christ’s circumcision, through whom you do not need carnal circumcision. Therefore you ought to observe no other carnal observance of the law [Col. 1335A], since you ought not to receive even this one, which is the greater; especially because God has, as was said above, taken the handwriting of the decree—that is, of the law—out of the way between both peoples, nailing it to the cross, so that it now ceases as though dead. And through the triumph of the Lord’s Passion we have been freed from the power of demons, from which we could not have been rescued through the law.

Since these things are so, and you have been rescued from slavery to the law through the freedom of new grace, therefore let no one—that is, no false teacher—judge you, that is, declare you liable to judgment and blameworthy, in food or drink: that is, in distinguishing foods and drinks, as though some were to be taken and others rejected. For the foods which Jews avoid among animals, we avoid in our conduct; and the drinks which they shun in liquids, we avoid in the dispositions of the will.

Let none of those who boast that they are teachers of the law judge you concerning food or drink, as though some things were unclean and others clean; since “all things are clean to the clean, but to the defiled nothing is clean” (Titus 1) [Col. 1335B]. Nor let them judge you in respect of a festival day, treating some days as holy and others not holy, because for us who believe in the risen Christ there is continual and eternal festivity; nor in respect of a new moon, that is, the Kalends and the new month, when the waning moon comes to its end and is covered with the shadows of night, because the light of Christians is eternal and is always illuminated by the rays of the Sun of righteousness; nor in respect of sabbaths, by requiring that they do no servile work or carry burdens, because we have been endowed with Christ’s freedom and cease to bear the burdens of sins.

In Greek, **νέον** (*neon*) means “new” in Latin, and **μήνη** (*mēnē*) means “moon.” *Neomenia* means “new moon,” and observance of the new moon is the sanctification of new life [Col. 1335C]. The person who devotes himself to holy works in hope of future rest keeps the true, perpetual Sabbath; nor does he glory in his good actions as though they were his own and as though he had not received them, knowing that the one works in him who both works and is at rest.

For the Sabbath, interpreted as “rest,” signified the rest which the souls of the saints have from vices in the present life, and which, once divested of their bodies, they will have until they take up their bodies again. All these things are “a shadow of things to come” (Heb. 10), because nothing was observed carnally under the Old Testament which did not prefigure some spiritual reality to come, either in this Church or in that Church which has already begun to reign in heaven [Col. 1335D]. But the body—that is, the solid truth of this shadow—is Christ’s; that is, it pertains to Christ.

All those things are shadows of things to come, in which the Jews adhere to the letter and are held to the earth; but we, according to the Spirit, pass over to Christ, who is now called “body” in contrast to shadows. For just as truth is in the body and falsehood in the body’s shadow, so in spiritual understanding every food and drink is clean, all festivity is complete, the Kalends are perpetual, and eternal rest is to be awaited. The Apostle says all this against those who, having believed from among the Jews in the Lord Savior, wished to observe Jewish ceremonies (Matt. 24; Mark 13; Luke 21); and therefore he continues:

[Col. 1336A]

> “Let no one deceive you, choosing humility and the worship of angels, walking in things which he has not seen, vainly puffed up by the mind of his flesh, and not holding fast the head, from whom the whole body, supplied and built up through joints and ligaments, grows with the growth of God. Therefore, if you died with Christ from the elements of this world, why do you still make decrees as though living in the world: ‘Do not touch; do not taste; do not handle’—things which all perish in their use—according to human commandments and teachings, which indeed have an appearance of wisdom in superstition and humility and in not sparing the body, but not in any honor toward the satisfying of the flesh.”

Those who had come from circumcision and called themselves Christians did not abandon the habit of Judaizing, but labored to draw others into their error [Col. 1336B]. Therefore believers are warned concerning them. “Let no one deceive or overcome you”: that is, let no one draw you from truth into error; let no one fraudulently defeat you in the contest of disputation and thus take away from you the prize of heavenly recompense, “willing what he has not seen,” that is, wishing to maintain or recommend the carnal commandments of the law, which he has never understood in the humility of the letter and in the worship and cult of angels, so that you serve not spiritual understanding but the types of things to come.

For humility here is not that which Scripture praises, but that which depresses the understanding of the mind to earthly and carnal interpretation. Indeed, it is a truly humble understanding and a pitiable opinion to believe that the Lord delights in the blood of goats and bulls and in the odor of incense, which people often avoid. “The worship of angels” here means a cult rendered not to God but to evil spirits. For after what the Lord said came to pass—“Your house will be left desolate” (Luke 21; Matt. 23)—all worship connected with Jewish observances was destroyed. Whatever victims they offer, they offer not to God but to apostate angels, that is, unclean spirits [Col. 1336C].

Or “in humility and the worship of angels” means that followers of this kind commonly display in themselves humility and angelic religion, so that they may more quickly be believed as most holy. In this sense, “angels” means either heavenly spirits or holy preachers. Let no one who falsely presents himself as so religious deceive you, “walking vainly,” that is, doing vainly and without benefit whatever he does, since he does everything in unbelief; “puffed up by the mind of his flesh,” that is, understanding all things carnally, investigating the absurdities of Jewish traditions, swelling from knowledge of them, and not holding the head of all Scriptures and sciences—that is, Christ, who is God’s wisdom and the head of the Church of saints. Since he does not hold Christ, who is the head of all sacred understanding and the head of all the elect, it is evident that he is foolish and reprobate [Col. 1336D].

From this head the whole body of the Church, supplied and built up through joints and ligaments, grows with the growth of God. For we all are his body [Col. 1337A]. Through joints and ligaments the body is joined together: while the chest is joined to the head, the arms to the chest, the hands to the arms, the fingers to the hands, and the remaining members adhere to the members, the whole body is completed.

Thus the holy apostles, because they stood near our Redeemer, adhered to him as the chest to the head. Since martyrs followed them, the arms were joined to the chest. When pastors and teachers were joined to these through good works, the hands adhered to the arms. This whole body of our Redeemer is daily supplied and built up in heaven through joints and ligaments, because, as elect souls are brought to him there, his members are gathered to him. Hence it is rightly said that, “supplied and built up,” it “grows with the growth of God,” because God Almighty, our Redeemer, who has in himself nothing in which he can increase, nevertheless still daily receives increase through his members [Col. 1337B].

But whoever still preaches that the law must be observed carnally does not hold the head of this body, because he attacks its faith and grace and seeks to divide its thus-connected body. Therefore you must cautiously beware of him as an enemy of Christ and the Church, although he pretends to be Christian.

For you ought to beware not only of empty talkers and deceivers of minds, who chatter fabulous and vain things, promising in those vanities what seems like lofty knowledge against the rule of faith which you have received as Catholic; but you must also flee, as a plague more insidious than the rest, those who truly dispute concerning the unchangeableness of the divine nature or an incorporeal creature or the Creator, and who prove what they say by utterly certain evidences and arguments, yet endeavor to turn you away from the one mediator of God and humankind [Col. 1337C].

The following words, “If therefore you died with Christ from the elements of this world, why do you still make decrees as though living in the world?” appear to have this meaning: If you were baptized in Christ and died with him in baptism from the elements of the world, why do you not say with me: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6)? Why do you not listen to the Lord saying to the Father: “They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world” (John 17)? Instead, as though living in the world, you make decrees:

“Do not touch the body of a dead person, or the garment or stool upon which a menstruating woman has sat. Do not taste pork, hare, cuttlefish, moray eel, eel, or any fish which has no scales or fins; do not handle any of these things” [Col. 1337D].

Here the Apostle speaks to those who had already begun partly to keep the law carnally. Up to this point he had warned those who stood firm not to be deceived; now he addresses those who already kept certain things from the law. It is as though he says: “You, take care not to be deceived. But you others, tell me why you keep the law. If you have died with Christ,” and so forth.

“If,” he says, “when you received Christ’s faith, you died from the elements”—that is, were separated from every superstition and abstinence concerning the creatures of the world—“why do you still decree that some things are to be avoided and others accepted?” For he calls these visible creatures “elements,” because, considered in themselves as a whole, they are parts of the world. And these people, as was said, were dead from the elements—that is, separated from abstinence concerning creatures of the world, from which they had previously properly abstained under the law [Col. 1338A].

Or he calls “elements” those things which they themselves worshipped in idols, as the sea in Neptune and the air in Juno. But through faith in Christ they had been separated from these. For wherever we find someone to have become other than he was, a kind of death has taken place there. Death is not to be what one was. The soul is immortal, indeed, because it always lives; and its life is ever enduring, yet changeable. Therefore, according to the changeability of that same life, it can also be called mortal: if it once lived wisely and now is foolish, it has died for the worse; if it lived foolishly and becomes wise, it has died for the better [Col. 1338B].

Thus these persons were dead for the better, and to them it is now said: “If you died from the elements, why do you still make decrees as though living?” Associated with Christ through faith, they attained this praiseworthy death, and are therefore said to have died with Christ. Or they died with Christ because, while Christ suffered and died, they too suffered with and died with him—not at the time when he underwent death, certainly, but when they themselves received faith.
