And because they had once died to the world with Christ, they ought not again, as though living in the world, to issue carnal decrees, saying to one another or to their followers: “Do not touch a dead thing or a creeping thing, lest you be defiled by it; do not taste the flesh of animals which do not chew the cud; do not touch any such thing with your hand” [Col. 1338C].

These words must be spoken with a certain expression of face and tone of voice. For he states mockingly the words of those who say, “Do not touch; do not taste,” although all things are clean to the clean (Titus 1). All these things, “in their use”—that is, if one uses them according to the Jewish rite, abstaining from some and using others, believing oneself thereby justified—lead to destruction, that is, to the death of the soul, because they are according to human commandments and teachings, not God’s.

For after truth came, God no longer commands these things, but the Pharisees do. And because they command and teach these things on their own authority, or on God’s authority wrongly understood, their use and cult bring death, because they are commandments and teachings of human beings, not of God [Col. 1338D]. Hence Isaiah says: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29). “But they worship me in vain, teaching teachings and commandments of men” (Matt. 15; Mark 7).

For the Pharisees and scribes also added many things to what the law commands carnally, so that because of their inventions they often violated the law’s own carnal commandments. Hence the Lord rebukes them: “You have made void God’s commandment in order to establish your traditions” (Matt. 15). And although it is right that on Sabbath days everyone should sit in his own house and not go out or walk from the place where he lives, if we begin to press them according to the letter so that they neither walk, lie down, nor stand, but only sit if they wish to keep the commandments, they are accustomed to reply: “Barachias, Simeon, and Hillel, our teachers, handed down to us that we should walk two thousand feet on the Sabbath” [Col. 1339A].

They prefer these and other similar human teachings to God’s teaching, teachings which indeed have “an appearance of wisdom in superstition and humility.” In the Greek, “false religion” is read in place of “superstition”; and “humility” here is to be understood as that which thinks low and earthly things. Thus Jewish observances seem, to the uninstructed and the common multitude, to bear an image of rationality and human wisdom in false religion and humility—that is, in a low, carnal, and earthly understanding.

Or they indeed have “an appearance of wisdom in superstition,” that is, not in truth but in falsehood, which is excessive and has no usefulness, “and in humility,” that is, in abasement of soul [Col. 1339B]. But if this is applied to certain persons in the Church who boast of the virtue of abstinence, it should be noted that the Apostle joins an appearance of humility to superstition: because while the flesh is worn down through abstinence beyond what is necessary, humility is shown outwardly, but inwardly they are gravely proud of that very humility. Among the Jews, however, superstition reigns much more in the display of humility, because precisely from that by which they show themselves humbler than others, they become proud above everyone.

And the things they observe are “not for sparing the body, not in any honor toward satisfying the flesh.” Jews do not spare their bodies in their choice of foods, sometimes despising what they have and seeking what they do not have [Col. 1339C]. Because they do this, they sometimes contract weakness and illnesses from necessity. Nor do they honor themselves, since all things are clean to the clean (Titus 1), and nothing can be defiled which is received with thanksgiving (1 Tim. 4), and since it was created by the Lord in order to invigorate and sustain human limbs through the satisfaction and nourishment of the flesh.

By “the elements of the world,” from which he says believers have died, we may also understand the law of Moses and the entire Old Testament, through which, as through elements and first principles of religion, we learn God; just as letters are called elements, by which we combine syllables and words and proceed through long study to compose discourse. The art of music also has its elements, and geometry begins from the elements of lines [Col. 1339D]. Thus the childhood of holy men is instructed by the elements of the Old Testament, so that it may come to evangelical fullness (1 Cor. 3). Hence those Psalms which are marked with letters lead us through ethics to theology, and make us pass from the elements of the killing letter to the life-giving Spirit.

## Chapter III

> “Therefore, if you have risen together with Christ, seek the things which are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. Set your mind on the things above, not on those upon the earth.”

Since, if you have died with Christ from the elements of the world, you ought no longer, as though living in the world, to make carnal distinctions among worldly things, seeking one thing and rejecting another, therefore, if you have risen with Christ, you ought unceasingly to seek the heavenly things in which Christ already is, so that you may be able to possess them with him [Col. 1340A]. For just as, having died with Christ to the world, you ought to set worldly things aside, so it follows that, having been raised with Christ, you ought to desire heavenly things.

“Therefore, if you have risen together with Christ, seek the things which are above”—that is, heavenly goods—where Christ is now bodily seated at the right hand of God the Father. We have not, of course, risen as Christ rose; nevertheless, according to the hope which we have in him, the Apostle testifies that we have already risen with him: “For in hope we were saved” (Rom. 8) [Col. 1340B]. In Christ’s bodily resurrection we hold by hope the resurrection of our body, while the resurrection of the spirit we already possess in reality, so that henceforth we may walk in newness of life. For when our vices have been extinguished by the mystery and power of the Lord’s death, we have risen from the death of the soul through the grace of the Lord’s resurrection.

Or this is why it is rightly said now: “If you have risen with Christ, seek through good works and devout prayers the things which are above heaven, that you may deserve to find them, because everyone who seeks finds” (Matt. 7). And you ought to seek them because Christ, whom you desire to find, is already there at God’s right hand (Matt. 25). Rightly at the right hand, because the sheep are to be placed at the right, and it is fitting that the spotless Lamb should first occupy the place of the spotless flock [Col. 1340C]. For by “the right hand” eternal blessedness is signified.

And Christ now sits there; that is, he rests after the labor of his Passion. Sitting belongs either to one who reigns or one who judges. Christ sits at the right hand of the Father’s throne because he reigns with him forever. He is said, I say, to sit for this reason: because he now judges all things and will be seen as judge at the end. Seek, therefore, the everlasting goods in which he now sits according to his humanity; and savor the things above—that is, touch with the palate of your heart the sweet taste of heavenly goods—not those upon the earth, that is, earthly and temporal goods. For unless earthly things are sweet to you, you will be able to taste the sweetness of heavenly things. Unless you have earthly desires, you will be able to long for heavenly joys. Or, “set your mind on things above, not earthly things”: that is, possess wisdom and prudence concerning heavenly and eternal things, not temporal and passing things [Col. 1340D].

> “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. But when Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.”

You ought to set your mind on heavenly, not earthly, things because in mind you have died to this world. For we die according to the spirit and rise according to the spirit, so that afterward, having died according to the flesh, we may rise according to the flesh. For just as death according to the spirit precedes resurrection according to the spirit, so death according to the flesh will precede the resurrection which is to be according to the flesh [Col. 1341A].

For not doing what we did, nor believing what we believed, is a kind of death and resurrection within us. If one who served idols comes to know the one God, he has died to idolatry and risen in faith. If one who was drunken becomes sober, drunkenness has died and sobriety has risen. Thus all evil deeds which we cease to commit are a kind of death within us, because no longer being what we were is a kind of death.

“You have died,” he says, but you have died in appearance and are alive at the root, like trees in winter, because “your life is hidden with Christ in God” the Father and does not now appear to human beings. For you have died as trees seem in winter to be dry, as though dead. But lest you should wither: within is the root, within is life, within is love, because life is hidden with Christ in God [Col. 1341B]. Yet afterward your time will come, your summer will come, when you will be clothed with the dignity of leaves and filled with abundance of fruits.

But when Christ comes to judgment and appears—he who is your life—then you, not your adversaries, will appear with him in glory. Now is the season of winter; your summer will be Christ’s coming. Your winter is Christ’s hiddenness; your summer, Christ’s revelation.

It must be considered that holy men do not cease to mortify themselves with the sword of the sacred word against the importunity of temporal desires, the tumult of useless cares, and the clamor of resounding disturbances; and inwardly, before God’s face, they hide themselves in the bosom of the mind. Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “You will hide them in the hiding-place of your face from the disturbance of men” (Ps. 30) [Col. 1341C]. Although this will be perfectly accomplished afterward, it is now in great measure taking place, when their affections are drawn inward from the tumult of temporal desires, so that, while their mind is wholly directed in the love of God, it may not be torn by any useless disturbance.

Thus the Apostle, through contemplation, now saw disciples dead to outward life and hidden as though in a tomb; and to them he said: “You have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” They have died, namely, to carnal desires and the cravings of temporal things; and their life is hidden with Christ in God because, inwardly with God and Christ, the affection of their desires lives, so that, dead to the world, it lies concealed and hides itself from every disturbance of outward things within the bosom of inward love [Col. 1341D].

Truly it is hidden with Christ because it will be manifested with Christ: for when Christ appears to be your life—that is, when all at judgment see that Christ is your life and salvation—then you also will appear with him in glory. That is, you will appear before all people at his right hand with great honor and splendor, sharers in his glory.

It should be noted that John also explains this statement in other words: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. But we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3). For what Paul says—“You have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God”—is what John affirms when he says, “Now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be” [Col. 1342A]. And what Paul adds, “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory,” John follows with: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.”

This, therefore, will be to appear with Christ in glory: in his manifestation, to see the form of his divinity as it is, and from seeing him to receive his likeness, so that those who see him may become, according to their capacity, such as he himself is. These things are said to the perfect; then the Apostle says to the others who have not yet attained such perfection:

[Col. 1342B]

> “Therefore put to death your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and covetousness, which is the service of idols; because of which the wrath of God comes upon the children of unbelief. Among these you too once walked, when you lived in them. But now you also must put away all these: wrath, indignation, malice, blasphemy, foul speech from your mouth. Do not lie to one another.”

Because of the unity of the body: since both greater and lesser believers are members of the Church, although the Apostle’s discourse was being directed covertly as though there were no others but these same persons, he began to address the lesser members and drew from what he had said before the ground of his exhortation to them. “Because,” he says, “you ought to set your minds on things above, [Col. 1342C] not on things on earth; since in the greater members of the Church you have already died to this world and to its vices, therefore do in yourselves what has been done in them. Put to death, that is, in yourselves, the members which are upon the earth”: namely, extinguish your vices, which belong to the body of sin and flourish in earthly conduct, or exercise evil dominion over the earth of your body. The body of sin is conformity to the old man, and the members of this body are all vices and evil works. Therefore put to death these members of yours which belong not to human nature but to the body of sin: that is, extinguish not the members of your nature, which God created, but the members of the body of sin, which you yourselves have made, lest they live any longer in you. And I shall explain to you those members: namely, to put to death fornication, [Col. 1342D] that is, intercourse with prostitutes who stand for hire in the arches (*fornices*), from which fornication takes its name; and uncleanness, which is also called effeminacy and is perpetrated by one sex; and lust, which occurs with women who are not public women like prostitutes; and evil desire, by which one wrongly desires either a woman, or gold, or something else which it is not lawful to possess. Desire is here called evil, in distinction from good desire, of which it is said: “My soul longs and fails for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. LXXIII), and: “The desire of wisdom will lead to an everlasting kingdom” (Wis. VI).

Therefore you ought to put to death not only the acts of the aforesaid vices, but also desire for such things, so that [Col. 1343A] you may not even desire anything unlawful in your heart, but may keep your heart clean from every evil desire; and you should put to death covetousness, that is, the insatiable love of possessing. This covetousness is to be detested by every Christian (Gal. V; Eph. V), because it is the service of idols. For just as one who serves idols gives to an imagined creature the worship due to the Creator, so the covetous person, although he ought to worship God alone, worships money instead, on which the images of emperors are depicted. For each person has as his god that which he loves above all else and in which, above all else, he places hope and trust. And because the covetous person does this in particular with regard to money—that is, loves money more than anything else, thinks about money more than any other thing, and hopes and trusts in money more than [Col. 1343B] in anything else—therefore money is his god. He is rightly called an idolater, then, who does not worship God but idols, that is, the images of dead kings impressed upon coins.

You must put to death these aforesaid vices—fornication (*ibid.*), and so forth—lest, if they are found in you, you perish because of them. On their account the wrath of God already came long ago—that is, the execution of divine vengeance—upon the children of unbelief, that is, upon people whom unbelief had begotten into error; for, not believing in God, they turned themselves to practising these vices. Therefore they perished in the waters of the Flood and in the fire of the Sodomites (Gen. VII, XIX), or in the time of Moses (Num. II, XII, XIV, XVI, XXI, XXV), through various destructions in the wilderness. Beware, therefore, lest you too perish similarly, or more grievously, because of the same vices; [Col. 1343C] for even now, because of these things, wrath—that is, God’s vengeance—comes daily upon the children of unbelief: that is, upon those who, though they are children of the Church through reception of the sacraments, nevertheless do not firmly believe in the eternal condemnation of the wicked, and therefore dare to do such things.

And in these vices you too once walked: that is, you added act to act as step to step, formerly, when you lived in those vices, when you spent your lives in such things. But now, after you have died to such things through baptism, put off all vices, as the greater members also put them off. Put them off, that is, put them down below, so that they may not be over you but beneath you; so that they may not press upon you, but may [Col. 1343D] be pressed down by you. Put off wrath, namely the disturbed agitation of the mind against someone; and indignation, namely the vehement agitation of the mind, inflamed with a certain fault of arrogance to injure or despise someone; and malice, by which the mind is inwardly gnawed and seeks outwardly to harm a brother; and blasphemy, that is, the utterance of falsehood against God, against his saints, or concerning his saints. For blasphemy is that by which false things are said of God himself or of his saints. And beware not only of blasphemy, but do not utter from your mouth any shameful speech whatsoever, lest by it you defile both your own mouth and the ears and minds of those who hear. And do not lie to one another, so that one deceives another by speaking [Col. 1344A] falsehood to him as truth; but utter with your mouth the pure truth which your heart knows.

> “Putting off the old man with his deeds, and putting on the new, who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him. Where there is neither Gentile nor Jew, circumcision nor foreskin, barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free, but Christ is all things and in all.”

Put off the aforesaid vices, stripping yourselves, in putting them off, of the old man with his deeds: that is, the old life which is in sin, in which one lives according to Adam. And put on the new man: that is, the new life which is led in righteousness, [Col. 1344B] in which one lives according to Christ. Strip yourselves, therefore, of this old man, that is, unrighteousness; and put on the new man, that is, righteousness: namely, him who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him.

For the whole human being, that is, both the inward and the outward part, has grown old because of sin and has been made subject to the penalty of mortality. But now he is renewed according to his inward part, where he is re-formed according to the image of his Creator; in the resurrection, however, he will also be renewed according to his outward part. For just as after the fall into sin a human being is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him, so he was created in that knowledge itself before he grew old through transgression; whence he is again renewed in the same knowledge. [Col. 1344C]

For a distinction is said to exist between *notio* (“knowledge” or “notion”) and *agnitio* (“recognition”): *notio* concerns things which we did not previously know and then began to know; *agnitio*, however, concerns things which, having known them before, we afterwards cease to know and then remember. Thus humanity was created in the recognition of God, because at the beginning of creation it knew its Creator by reason; but afterwards, blinded through sin, it lost recognition of the Creator. Now, however, through the illumination of the Gospel and the infusion of the grace of the Holy Spirit, it recognizes again that same Creator; and immediately it is inwardly renewed, having contracted old age while it was ignorant of its Creator. Thus there comes about the renewal and re-formation of the mind according to the image [Col. 1344D] of God.

It is said “according to the image of God” so that the renewal may be understood to occur in that thing in which the image of God exists—that is, in the mind—just as we say that a faithful and righteous person who departs from the body is dead according to the body, not according to the spirit. For what do we mean by saying “dead according to the body” except dead in body or with respect to the body, not dead in soul or with respect to the soul? Or if we say that someone is beautiful according to the body, or strong according to the body, not according to the mind, what else does this mean than beautiful or strong in body, not in mind? We speak thus countless times. Therefore we should not understand “according to the image of him who created him” as though there were one image according to which he is renewed and another image which itself is renewed. For the very image of God is renewed in the human being—the image which [Col. 1345A] had grown old through transgression.

Put on, as I have said, the new man, that is, the way of life in which—namely, in this new man—there is neither Gentile nor Jew: that is, it accomplishes nothing, helps nothing, and harms nothing that the person who puts on this man is, by bodily origin, a Gentile or a Jew. Nor is there circumcision and foreskin: that is, circumcision, in which the Jews especially gloried, accomplishes no benefit there, and foreskin does no harm there. Nor is there a barbarian there: that is, no one’s barbarism harms him, because he becomes a fellow citizen of the saints and a member of God’s household (Eph. II). Or “barbarian” means someone so far removed and of such savagery that he could scarcely be conquered by the Romans; his barbarism does not prevent his admission into this new man. Nor is there a Scythian there, [Col. 1345B] that is, a people situated at the left edge of the world, fiercer than other barbarians and so warlike that they could scarcely ever be overcome by the Romans. Such a person is not helped by his savagery in the new man; rather, he must put off every savagery, in order to learn from Christ to be meek and humble in heart (Matt. XI). Nor is the slave more contemptible there, nor the free person more acceptable, because neither bodily slavery nor bodily freedom harms or assists in any respect there. Therefore neither nationality, nor fleshly rite, nor status, nor sex makes any difference, or has force, or accomplishes anything there; but in this new human being Christ is all things—that is, there is nothing in him except Christian piety and Christian religion. Christ is there holiness, righteousness, love, and every good thing; and Christ is [Col. 1345C] in all who have put on this new man, because whatever good they have, they have from Christ, and whatever good they do, they do through Christ.

> “Put on therefore, as God’s elect, holy and beloved, bowels of mercy, kindness, humility, modesty, patience; bearing with one another and forgiving yourselves, if anyone has a complaint against anyone; as the Lord forgave you, so you also.”

This is an inference from the whole. Since you ought to put on the new man, you ought therefore here to put on the ornaments of the virtues, which are, as it were, the members or parts of that same new man—that is, of the new way of life. Put them on as God’s elect: that is, foreknown by the wisdom of God, [Col. 1345D] separated from the mass of those destined to perish, and preordained to eternal life; and as holy, cleansed from sins by the sanctification of baptism; and thus already beloved by God, after you have been cleansed of the sins which God hates. Therefore, that you may deserve to be loved by him still more, put on the virtues which he himself loves.

Put on bowels of mercy: that is, clothe yourselves in outward action with an inward affection of mercy, so that the inward affection of devout conduct which you have in your heart toward your neighbours may appear everywhere in your works and adorn you on every side. For the garment with which we are clothed covers us on every side. Therefore you too ought to be covered on every side with bowels of mercy, so that in all your actions the bowels of mercy may shine forth—[Col. 1346A] those which your mind has conceived at the revelation of your neighbours’ misery. And likewise put on outwardly in works kindness: that is, the good fire of devout sweetness which burns in your heart. For kindness is a certain serenity of mind by which someone speaks cheerfully, gives of his own possessions for God’s sake, and lives with his neighbour.

Put on humility also, so that humility of mind may appear in all your words and works, in clothing, in gait, and in every movement of the body. And therefore clothe yourselves with modesty as with a garment, so that in all your words and deeds you keep due measure. For modesty is called, as it were, a “standing of measure,” because through this virtue an appropriate measure is kept in all things, governing all actions. And lest you exceed measure, [Col. 1346B] put on patience, by which, fortified on every side, you may endure with a tranquil mind all evils brought upon you by your neighbours. For it is impossible that one who lives among other people should not frequently suffer from them certain things which drive many to excess, unless he is surrounded by the virtue of patience as by a garment. But if he maintains patience on every side against all things that happen to him, he will always be able to preserve modesty.

Therefore put on patience, bearing with one another, so that each may endure the other in things that are burdensome and harsh. Bear with one another—that is, carry one another—so that those whom they have borne may be judged superior, and those bearing them inferior to those over whom they are superior. For one does not bear another patiently who regards himself [Col. 1346C] as superior to that other. And be forgiving to yourselves: that is, pardoning and remitting to one another, if perhaps anyone has a complaint against another for an insult or injury inflicted upon him. Forgive one another whatever injury or offence you have suffered, concerning which you could rightly complain. And do this not falsely or partially, but as the Lord forgave you, so do you also. That is, just as the Lord in baptism forgave you whatever injuries you had committed against him, without any regard to taking vengeance thereafter, so you too with a good mind always forgive one another everything, without regard to any revenge. For you ought not refuse to fellow servants what you rejoice to have received from the good Lord. [Col. 1346D] Otherwise, according to the Gospel parable, he will exact from you every debt that he had forgiven, if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts (Matt. XVIII).

> “But above all these things have love, which is the bond of perfection. And let the peace of Christ exult in your hearts, in which also you were called into one body; and be thankful. Let the word of Christ dwell in you abundantly. In all wisdom, teaching and admonishing yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing in grace in your hearts to the Lord. Whatever you do in word or deed, do all in the name of our Lord Jesus [Col. 1347A] Christ, giving thanks to God and the Father through him.”

Put on the aforesaid ornaments of the virtues; but above all these things have love, as a nobler ornament, which embraces and further adorns all the marks of the other virtues. For it surpasses and outshines all other virtues and is more pleasing in the sight of the immortal Bridegroom. This—that is, love (1 Cor. XIII)—is the bond of perfection, because through it all perfection of the virtues is bound together, lest, loosened, it flow away, fall apart, and perish. Love is the bond of perfection because every good which we do is bound through it lest it perish. For even any work whatsoever is more readily torn away by the tempter if it is found loose from the bond of love. But if the mind is guided by love and constrained by love of neighbour, whenever any movements of temptations suggest unjust things to it, that very love sets itself as an obstacle against them and restrains the vices [Col. 1347B] arising in the heart. Let love bind our good things together in perfection.

And let the peace of Christ—that is, the peace which Christ has and gives (John XIV, XVI, XX)—exult in your hearts. The peace of Christ is that by which we have been reconciled to God and to his holy angels; by which we love God and detest sin; by which we take care not to disturb ourselves; by which we trust one another that we love one another; by which we join our hearts to one another, so that we may be harmonious and have one heart in good will; and by which we subject the flesh to our spirit. Let this peace not lie dormant in your hearts, but let it exult [Col. 1347C] there in joy and dance, so that you may always be mindful of this peace and rejoice that you have attained it. In this peace you were also called by Gospel preaching into one body: that is, that you might be the one body of the Church, all preserving peace with one another, just as the different members of our body preserve peace and harmony with one another.

And in this exultation of peace do not be ungrateful to God, who gave it to you, but be thankful to him, so that for such great benefits you may always give him thanks in heart, words, and works. And so that you may be able to understand and preserve this peace, and always be thankful to God in it, let the word of Christ—that is, the teaching of the Christian religion—dwell in you: that is, remain in your heart and mouth not sparingly but abundantly, that is, richly and fully, so that you may both know and speak the word of sacred edification. [Col. 1347D]

I said that you should be thankful and have the word of Christ dwelling in you, teaching one another, or each one teaching himself, in all patience concerning divine things. This is the abundance of the word of Christ which ought to dwell in your hearts: namely, all wisdom, so that you may have perfect understanding in the knowledge of the divine Trinity and Unity, may know whatever pertains to its worship, may taste beforehand by devout desires the joys of its kingdom, and may seek them unceasingly by good works. In such matters consists all wisdom which a Christian ought to have in this life. Therefore be in all wisdom, teaching, as I have said, yourselves and one another—that is, each one teaching himself those things which you did not yet know—[Col. 1348A] and admonishing yourselves in those things which you already know, so that you may hold them firmly and fulfil them in deed. Teach, I say, and stir yourselves, so that you may both be instructed and aroused to do good. Do so in psalms, which admonish toward good action; and hymns, which are sung concerning the praises of God; and songs—not carnal but spiritual—which resound concerning eternal joy and are therefore spiritual. For carnal songs are also often sung by carnal people and pertain to pleasures of the flesh. But spiritual songs are contrary to these: they exhort us to delight and rejoice in the Creator alone. In such things teach and admonish yourselves—you, I say, singing in grace, that is, in thanksgiving, in your hearts to the Lord.

For not everyone who makes sound with his lips [Col. 1348B] sings to the Lord; rather, it is the one who, praising him with a devout heart, loves him and longs for his vision. For this joy is inward, where the voice of praise is sung and heard: by that voice he is praised who is to be loved freely with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole mind, and who kindles his lover within himself by the grace of his Holy Spirit. For that person sings to the Lord in grace who, kindled by the grace of the Holy Spirit, freely loves him whom he praises. Sing thus.

And whatever you do in word or deed—that is, whatever you say and whatever you do—do all in the name of the Lord: that is, invoke his name at the beginning of your speech and action, and always direct the words and deeds that follow to his glory. For then you will avoid sins of speech and action, and what you [Col. 1348C] say or do will be good. Do all in the name of the Lord, invoking and glorifying the Lord’s name in all things. Do everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom you have all that is given to you by the Father; and you, always give thanks for all things through him, through whom you receive all good things, to God who created you and to the Father who adopted you as sons. Or: to God, who created Christ according to his humanity, and to the Father, who begot Christ according to his divinity.

> “Wives, be subject to your husbands as is fitting in the Lord. Husbands, love your wives, and do not be bitter toward them. Children, obey your parents in all things (Eph. VI), for this is pleasing in the Lord. Fathers, do not provoke [Col. 1348D] your children to indignation, lest they become faint-hearted.”

Up to this point he instructed and admonished them generally. Now, however, he turns his exhortation specifically to family and domestic life, and subjects wives to husbands and children to parents. For there is also a natural order among human beings: women should serve men and children their parents, since for these too it is just that weaker reason should serve stronger reason. For in lordships and servitudes this is manifest justice: those who excel in reason should excel also in authority. Hence the Apostle now gives fitting commands.

“You,” he says, “wives, be subject to your husbands in all things, yet not in doing evil, but as it is fitting for you to be subject in the Lord”: that is, as it befits you, living in the Christian [Col. 1349A] religion, to be subject to them in all things except transgression of God’s commandments. And you, husbands, love your wives. It belongs to wives to fear and to love with fear, but to husbands only to love, because love belongs to the perfect. Husbands, love your wives and do not be bitter toward them. Even if they provoke you to anger and do things through which they deserve bitterness, nevertheless do not return bitterness to them in return.

You likewise, children, obey your parents in all things, whether bodily or spiritual parents. Obey them in all things, yet in the Lord: that is, only in matters which do not exceed the Lord’s commandment; for it is pleasing to God that you obey them in this manner. And you, fathers, do not provoke your children, whether bodily or spiritual, [Col. 1349B] to indignation by treating them too harshly, lest they become faint-hearted: that is, lest their spirit fail, unable to endure the excess of your severity, and they flee from you or do some evil through failure of spirit. Therefore take care not to give them an occasion for disobedience, lest they sin through anger and their mind be broken amid adversities and fail.

> “Slaves, obey in all things your earthly masters (Eph. VI; 1 Pet. II), not serving only before the eye, as pleasing men, but in simplicity of heart, fearing the Lord. Whatever you do, work from the heart, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the recompense of the inheritance (Lev. XIX). Serve the Lord Christ. [Col. 1349C] For whoever does wrong will receive what he has done unjustly, and with God there is no respect of persons” (Deut. I, X, XVI; 2 Chron. XIX; Job XXXII, XXXIV; Rom. II; Eph. VI; Acts X).

“You,” he says, “slaves, obey your earthly masters”—that is, those who rule you according to the body, not according to the spirit. Obey them in what is good in all things, not serving before the eye as pleasing men: that is, do not act well only when you are seen by them, and act negligently when you are not seen. Do not act so deceitfully, wishing fraudulently to please them by things which, when you stand before them, you seem energetically to do. Rather, serve them in simplicity of heart, not duplicity, so that what you show outwardly in deed you may have inwardly [Col. 1349D] in your heart, fearing the Lord, who is the searcher of hearts and the condemner of deceitful pretences.

And whatever you do, do it from the heart, that is, from the will. For God approves that innocence by which a person is innocent not from fear but from love of righteousness. For one who does not sin merely from fear, even though he does not harm the person whom he wishes to harm, nevertheless harms himself very greatly; and though he abstains from an unjust deed, he is guilty by the will of his mind alone. For feigned innocence is not innocence, and feigned equity is not equity; rather, the sin is doubled in which there are both injustice and pretence. Therefore whatever good you do, do it from the heart, not from pretence, doing it as for the Lord and not for human beings. You know that from this the Lord, who is the rewarder [Col. 1350A] of all good works, will give you the recompense of the eternal inheritance with the sons. Therefore serve our Lord Christ in all that you do. For if, on account of his commandment, you serve earthly masters with a good mind, you will serve Christ rather than them and will receive your recompense from him, even though you obtain no good reward from them.

Or, although you are occupied in the service of human beings, nevertheless serve the Lord Christ, so that on account of service to them you do not omit serving Christ. Nor let your minds be broken if they treat you badly. Whoever does injury, although he is powerful and noble in this world, will receive from God, the judge of the world, that which he has done unjustly. Therefore the sorrow of one who suffers injustice is better than the joy of one who commits injustice, because even a good person is often scourged on account of the malice of the wicked. The one who does injury [Col. 1350B] will receive what he has done, so that he who unjustly tortured another may himself be justly tortured. And this is so because with God there is no respect of persons: he does not spare nobles if they act unjustly while punishing the low-born who have acted wickedly. For by an equal judgment he judges all alike—masters and slaves, rich and poor—and renders to each according to what he has done.

## Chapter IV

> “Masters, provide to your slaves what is just and equitable, knowing that you too have a Master in heaven.”

Therefore you, masters, provide—that is, give to your slaves—that which is just, namely what they have earned by their service; and that which is equitable, namely what the law of nature or reason demands: that their necessities [Col. 1350C] be given to them even beyond what their service has earned. For there are many slaves who, because of illness or some other cause, do not earn by their labour the things necessary to them; nevertheless masters ought to supply them with what they need. You ought to provide these things to your slaves, knowing that you too have a Master in heaven, whose slaves you are and from whom you need to receive good things even beyond your merit. You also act proudly against him by means of his own gift if you do not recognize as your equals by sharing in the same nature those whom you hold subject by their condition.

For even the righteous who rule serve those whom they seem to rule, because they seek office not through a desire for domination but through the duty of care; not through the pride of commanding [Col. 1350D] but through the kindness of providing. And if our holy Fathers had slaves, they administered domestic peace in such a way that, with respect to temporal goods, they distinguished the lot of children from the condition of slaves; but with respect to worshipping God, in whom eternal goods are to be hoped for, they cared with equal love for all the members of their household.

> “Persist in prayer, watching in it with thanksgiving; praying also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I too am bound, that I may make it manifest as I ought to speak.”

He returns to a general exhortation. For this is fitting for everyone: that they should persist in prayer. And he rightly commands them to watch in it, so that when we stand in prayer every carnal and worldly thought may depart, and the mind may then think of nothing except that alone for which it prays. For the enemy often steals in and, subtly deceiving, calls our prayers away from God, so that we have one thing in the heart and utter another with the voice, whereas God ought to be prayed to with sincere intention, not by the sound of the voice but by the disposition of the mind. [Col. 1351A]

Persist in prayer, so that you may pray earnestly and without ceasing, watching in it with the lively attentiveness of the mind. And let this prayer be with thanksgiving, so that while asking benefits from God, you may return thanks to him for those which he has already granted you. Pray thus for yourselves, praying also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word: that is, may open our mouth, through which the word of preaching may go forth from us, to speak—that is, to discuss and expound—the mystery of Christ, namely the hidden secret of Christ’s incarnation and passion, so that we may disclose their hidden causes to our hearers and teach that the restoration of human salvation consists in them. On account of this mystery, because I preached it, I am bound: that is, I am held in chains at Rome, unable to go where I wish and evangelize more people. Pray that God may grant me to speak that mystery, that I may make it manifest and explain it to others as it is proper [Col. 1351B] and fitting for me to speak of so great a sacrament, since I was sent to proclaim it.

> “Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside, redeeming the time. Let your speech always be in grace, seasoned with salt, that you may know how [Col. 1351C] you ought to answer each person.”

You who are in the Church—that is, incorporated into the members of Christ—must all persist together in prayer as has been explained. But when you go out among those who are outside—that is, when you come to places where you are seen by those who have not yet entered the Church through faith—walk in wisdom: that is, act wisely, work prudently, set the step of your conduct cautiously, lest unbelievers observe anything foolish or blameworthy in you, and lest the Lord’s name be blasphemed by them because of you (Rom. II). You, I say, redeeming the time: that is, redeeming by repentance and good conduct the life previously lived badly, so that you may compensate for past losses by daily gains of merits. For we redeem the time when we repair by weeping the former life which [Col. 1351D] we squandered in self-indulgence.

I said that wisdom should shine in your conduct and actions; now I add that it should always appear also in your speech: namely, let your speech always be in grace—that is, in the sweetness of love—and seasoned with the salt of wisdom, like good food for the soul, so that it may contain nothing tasteless or corrupt. For food mixed with salt becomes savoury, and flesh well salted neither rots nor stinks. So also let your speech be such that it is received as savoury food by the mouth of the hearts of those who hear: let it not be tasteless through folly, corrupt through exhortation to fleshly delight, or spoiled through admixture of falsehood; but let it always be seasoned with the salt of spiritual wisdom, [Col. 1352A] uncorrupted in the integrity of truth, and breathing the fragrance of heavenly and incorruptible delight. And let your speech so possess within itself the seasoning of divine salt that you may know how you ought to answer each person: that is, through the prudence of measured discernment, know how one ought to answer a believer, an unbeliever, a rich person, a poor person, an old person, a young person, a man, a woman, and persons of the other ranks or conditions. For each person must be addressed in his own way, and each must be answered in his own way: one must answer his words, if he has spoken first; or answer his deed, if he has been silent in words. Each person must be corrected or admonished according to his own manner.

[Col. 1352B]

> “Tychicus, the most beloved brother, faithful minister, and fellow servant in the Lord, will make known to you all that concerns me. I sent him to you for this very purpose, that he may know what concerns you and comfort your hearts, with Onesimus, the most beloved and faithful brother, who is one of you. They will make known to you all that is happening here.”

Tychicus will make known to you all that concerns me. Since he had said that he was bound for the sake of the Gospel, lest they think that he was suffering more grievous things, he says that Tychicus will tell them everything about him, both adversity and prosperity. He is to be believed because he is a brother—that is, a Christian, and most illustrious before God or his saints by the merit of his life—and a faithful minister: that is, one who faithfully ministers the word of preaching without deceit. Or [Col. 1352C] “minister” means deacon, and “fellow servant” means one who serves with me in the Lord, that is, in things belonging to the Lord.

I sent him to you for this very purpose—that is, for this reason—that he may know what concerns you and report it to me. Therefore see to it that he finds among you nothing evil to report to me. I also sent him for this reason, that he may comfort your hearts, lest you have excessive grief about the things you suffer or about the things you have heard that I suffer. I sent him with Onesimus, the most beloved and faithful brother, not the most worthless and deceitful slave, as he once was. For this is Onesimus, the slave of Philemon, who, after committing theft against his master Philemon—or after he had consumed or squandered it—fled to the Apostle, heard from him the word of salvation, and was converted. [Col. 1352D] Therefore the Apostle commends him in this way, lest he be suspect to them in any respect.

From this it is plainly shown that the Apostle sent this epistle from Rome, from prison, just as he directed that one to Philemon. For in this letter and in that one he gives as greeters the same persons whom he declares to be with him and calls his fellow workers: namely Aristarchus, Mark, Epaphras, Luke, and Demas. Thus it is clear that both letters were sent from one and the same place, where the Apostle was held bound. For he begot Onesimus for Christ in chains (Philem. I). But the book of the Acts of the Apostles says nothing at all about his having endured chains at Ephesus. Therefore the opinion of those who say that the Apostle was bound [Col. 1353A] only at Ephesus and sent this letter to the Colossians from there is shown not to be true.

> “Aristarchus, my fellow captive, greets you, and Mark, Barnabas’s cousin (concerning whom you received instructions: if he comes to you, receive him), and Jesus who is called Justus. These alone are my fellow workers in the kingdom of God; they have been a comfort to me.”

Aristarchus was a Thessalonian, and is recorded to have followed the Apostle. Thus, to crown his glory, he deserved to be held captive with the same Apostle for Christ’s name. Mark, moreover, the cousin—that is, the kinsman—of the apostle Barnabas, is John surnamed Mark, on whose account disagreement arose between Paul and Barnabas (Acts 12). [Col. 1353B] “For Barnabas wished to take with them this Mark also. But Paul requested that one who had departed from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work of the Gospel ought not to be received. Thus disagreement arose between them, so that they separated from one another: Barnabas indeed, having taken Mark, sailed to Cyprus; but Paul, having chosen Silas, departed, having been commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord” (Acts 15).

Because this Mark, having placed himself in the very forefront of the battle-line, had stood far too faint-heartedly and, moreover, had sluggishly withdrawn from the line, Paul rightly rejected him, lest the strength of the others be corrupted, as it were, by his contagion. For a preacher ought to set before others in himself examples of courage, and to persevere manfully in the good things he has begun. But [Col. 1353C] because Mark had neither acted courageously nor persevered, Paul rightly did not wish thereafter to have him as a companion in the way of preaching. Fearing also that he might make others vain and idle by his example, he instructed his churches not to receive him. But afterward Mark was corrected and made worthy for Paul gladly to have him as a helper. This, then, is what he says: “Aristarchus, my fellow-prisoner, greets you, and Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, concerning whom you received instructions,” namely, that you should not receive him; “but now, if he comes to you, receive him,” since he has indeed been well corrected; “and Jesus, who is called Justus, greets you,” that is, one to whom, from the outcome of his holiness, this surname, Justus, meaning “the Just,” was given. [Col. 1353D] Mark and Justus, namely, “are of the circumcision,” that is, of Jewish stock. “These alone are my fellow-workers for the kingdom of God,” that is, in preaching the Gospel, concerning which the Lord says to the Jews: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. 21); or, in the kingdom of God, that is, in building the Church, concerning which the same Lord says: “The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all stumbling-blocks” (Matt. 13). These helpers, indeed, were a comfort to me in my tribulation.

“Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ Jesus, greets you, always earnestly concerned for you in his prayers, that you may stand perfect and complete in every will of God. For I bear him witness [Col. 1354A] that he has much labor for you, and for those who are at Laodicea, and those who are at Hierapolis.”

This is Saint Epaphras, of whom it was said at the beginning of this epistle: “You learned the grace of God in truth, as you learned it from Epaphras, our most beloved fellow-servant, who is a faithful minister of Jesus Christ for you” (above, ch. 1). Since, therefore, he had preached God’s grace to them, he continually implored God with anxious prayers that they might remain in the same grace, lest his labor become vain. For he had departed from them in bodily presence, and therefore commended them to God, who is absent nowhere. This is the meaning: “Epaphras greets you, who is from among you,” deriving his origin from you, “and is a servant of Christ Jesus,” that is, serving the Gospel commands; he, I say, [Col. 1354B] is “always earnestly concerned for you in prayers,” that is, always praying diligently and attentively for your salvation, in order that you may “stand,” that is, persevere. Hence it was said of the devil: “He did not stand in the truth” (John 8), because he was there but did not remain there. You, however, are in the Christian religion; therefore Epaphras prays that you may stand, that is, remain in it.

May you stand perfect in good action and complete in good will: perfect outwardly and complete inwardly, lest the mind be empty within while works appear perfect without. May you, I say, stand thus “in every will of God,” that is, in observance of every divine will, so that you may steadfastly fulfil all God’s will. He prays that this may be granted to you by God, without whose grace you can do nothing. For I bear him witness [Col. 1354C] that he labors greatly in prayer and watchfulness for you, that is, for your salvation, and for those at Laodicea, a city near you, and for those at Hierapolis, likewise a city situated not far from you.

“Luke, the most beloved physician, and Demas greet you.”

Luke was first a physician of bodies; afterward, converted to Christ, he became a physician of souls. Hence, more than the other Evangelists, he speaks of the Redeemer’s mercies, through which the sicknesses of sinners are driven away from human beings, and he depicts in Christ the person of a priest intervening for the sins of the whole world.

[Col. 1354D] “Greet the brothers who are at Laodicea, and Nympha, and the Church which is in her house. And when this epistle has been read among you, see that it is read also in the church of the Laodiceans; and that you also read the one which is from Laodicea.”

The aforementioned saints greet you. But you, in turn, greet your neighboring brothers at Laodicea; and among them, especially and by name, greet Nympha, that devout matron, and the Church in her house—that is, her household, or the multitude of believers assembled with her, whom she herself lodges and feeds. When this epistle has been read among you, see that it is read also in the church of the Laodiceans; that is, arrange for it to be recited in the assembly of the Laodiceans, because it was written secondarily for them, just as [Col. 1355A] it was written principally for you. Likewise, let the epistle “which is from Laodicea,” that is, the one which I sent to the Laodiceans, be read among you.

Although the Apostle wrote this as his fifteenth or sixteenth epistle, and apostolic authority confirmed it, as it did the others, nevertheless the holy Church recognizes no more than fourteen, so that by the very number of the epistles it might show that this eminent teacher had investigated the mysteries of the Law and the Gospel. For fourteen is four and ten: four signifies the New Testament on account of the four books of the Gospel; ten, the Old Testament on account of the Decalogue of the Law. Therefore, by this very number the holy Church wished to show that all the wisdom or perfection of the Old and New Testaments is briefly contained in these epistles; and for that reason it did not wish to exceed the number signifying these things.

“And say to Archippus: See to the ministry which you received in the Lord, that you may fulfil it.”

“Say,” he says, “to Archippus, your bishop, on our behalf: ‘See to the ministry which you received,’” that is, attend to and consider what sort of task you have undertaken, “in the Lord,” that is, in the Lord’s grace, or in the things that belong to the Lord. Do not be blind; do not turn your eyes away from the duty of your ministry, that is, from the exercise of your episcopacy. Rather, consider with earnest attention what ministry you have undertaken, so that you may fulfil it vigorously and not hold it idly vacant. Through them he admonishes [Col. 1355C] Archippus, their superior, that, having received charge of governing their Church, he should be concerned for them. The epistle is written for the people’s sake, and therefore is not directed to the ruler. Or, because he himself was acting faint-heartedly toward the pseudo-apostles, the Apostle admonishes him not directly but, to increase his shame, through his subjects, as though valuing them more highly.

“My greeting, in Paul’s own hand. Remember my chains. Grace be with you. Amen.”

“The greeting,” he says, “written in my hand, Paul’s,” that is, in my own hand, so that from my subscription you may know that the epistle was sent by me. “Remember my chains.” He urges them to remember his chains, either so that, taught by his example, they may learn to have patience in tribulations; or that they may pray [Col. 1355D] for him, so that he may be released more quickly and run freely about preaching; or—though this is less credible—that [Col. 1356A] they may give him something, since while in chains he was less able to procure necessities for himself. Then: “Grace,” he says, “of the Lord be with you,” so that, cooperating with it, you may be able to do good works.

Here ends the epistle sent to the Colossians. It seems fitting, moreover, for the readers’ information, to append the one addressed to the Laodiceans, which, as we have said, the Church does not use. It is as follows.

## EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE LAODICEANS, AS SOME SUPPOSE

Paul, an Apostle not from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ, to the brothers who are at Laodicea: grace to you and peace from God our Father [Col. 1356B] and the Lord Jesus Christ.

I give thanks to Christ in all my prayer, because you are remaining and persevering in good works, awaiting the promise on the day of judgment. Let not the empty talk of certain persons who accuse the truth disturb you, seeking to turn you away from the truth of the Gospel preached by me. And now God will cause those who are of me to serve fully the truth of the Gospel and to perform the kindness of works which belong to the salvation of eternal life.

And now my chains, which I suffer in Christ, are manifest, in which I rejoice and am glad; and this has become for me everlasting salvation through your prayers, with the Holy Spirit ministering. Whether through life or through death, life is Christ to me, and to die is joy; and he himself will show his mercy among you, so that you may have the same love and be of one mind.

Therefore, beloved, as you have heard the presence of the Lord, so think and act in fear, and you will have life forever. For it is God who works in you; and whatever you do, do without sin. And what is best, beloved, rejoice in the Lord Jesus Christ, and avoid every defilement in all gain. Let all your petitions be manifest before God. Be steadfast in the mind of Christ, and do whatever things are sound, true, modest, chaste, just, and lovely. Keep in your heart what you have heard and received, and peace will be with you. Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss. All the saints greet you. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen. [Col. 1356D] Cause this to be read to the Colossians, and the one to the Colossians to be read to you.

## ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS

[Col. 1355]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 1355D]

Thessalonica is a distinguished city in Macedonia. When Paul and Silas came there, because there was a synagogue of the Jews there, Paul entered among them according to his custom and reasoned with them from the Scriptures over three Sabbaths. Some of them believed and were joined to Paul and Silas, together with a great multitude of worshippers—that is, of proselytes and Gentiles—and not a few prominent women. But the Jews, being jealous and taking certain evil men from the rabble, formed a mob, stirred up the city, and, attacking Jason’s house, sought to bring them out before the people. When they did not find them, they dragged Jason and certain brothers before the city authorities, crying out: [Col. 1357A] “These are the men who are stirring up the city, and they have come here; Jason has received them, and all these act against Caesar’s decrees, saying that there is another king, Jesus.” They stirred up the crowd and the city authorities on hearing these things. After receiving security from Jason and the others, the authorities released them; but the brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Beroea.

Such was the conversion of the Thessalonians, and such things they at once began to suffer for the faith. For even after they had dismissed the apostles, they endured much for Christ’s name. Praising their constancy, the Apostle writes to them from Athens and intends to exhort them to remain immovable amid adversities and always to advance toward what is better. He then corrects the error of certain people who mourned their dead inconsolably, as if they would not rise again, [Col. 1357B] teaching that the common resurrection will truly come. He also instructs their life and conduct in many other respects. Since they were ready to obey, he does not state the title of his authority or office, but admonishes them as equals.

He associates Silvanus—that is, Silas—and Timothy with himself because they had shared his labor in their conversion, or because they were then with him at Athens. This epistle, unless I am mistaken, he wrote before all the others. For I find that before this one he had written nothing. It begins thus:

## CHAPTER ONE

“Paul and Silvanus and Timothy, to the Church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. [Col. 1357C] Grace to you and peace.”

Paul and his two companions, Silvanus and Timothy, send this epistle to the Church of the Thessalonians. The Jews’ assembly is properly called a synagogue, although it has also been called a church. But the apostles never called ours a synagogue; they always called it a Church, either in order to distinguish it, or because there is some difference between a gathering, from which *synagoga* derives its name, and a calling together, from which *ecclesia* derives its name. For cattle are accustomed to be gathered, and their herds are properly so called; but calling together belongs rather to beings who use reason, such as human beings.

Paul and his companions direct this letter to the Church of the Thessalonians, established in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, that is, in faith and love of the Father and the Son; the Holy Spirit is understood, by whom Christ was anointed. Or: Paul and his companions send this epistle in God the Father and the Son. “Grace,” he says, “and peace be with you.” He fittingly speaks first of grace and then names peace, because without God’s grace we cannot attain the peace of reconciliation; indeed, we can have nothing peaceful except through his grace. Grace is given freely, without preceding merits; and through it, while he remits sins, we approach the peace of reconciliation. It can also be understood thus: May grace and peace from God be yours, so that, though deprived of human favor and worldly peace, you may have grace and peace with God.

“We give thanks to God always for all of you, remembering you in [Col. 1358A] our prayers without ceasing, mindful of your work of faith and labor and love and endurance of the hope of our Lord Jesus Christ before God and our Father; knowing, brothers beloved by God, your election, because our Gospel did not come to you in word only, but in power and in the Holy Spirit and in much fullness, as you know what kind of persons we were among you for your sake.”

In his customary manner he begins with thanksgiving, because he sees God’s abundant grace shining forth in them. Therefore he first praises God, who gave them grace, and then them, who followed him in faith and works. It is as if he said: Hold fast what you hold; do what you do, because these things are such that we give thanks to God for them. For we give thanks and praise to God not for an hour [Col. 1358B] but always, for all of you—the greater, the middle, and the lesser; or men and women—because the grace which he first bestowed on you he still preserves and increases in you. For from him come all the good things that you possess, and therefore we give him thanks for them.

I mean: we remember you in our prayers, and this without ceasing; that is, whenever we pray, we never cease to remember you. For we are mindful of the work of your faith, that is, how your faith is not idle but always performs good work, and therefore we gladly pray for you. We are mindful, I say, of your work and of the labor which you undergo in that work; that is, we retain in mind how, while doing good, you labor; and of your love, that is, the brotherly affection which [Col. 1358C] you show in good works. Or, of the labor of enduring adversities, and of the love by which you love your enemies, and of the endurance—that is, the expectation—of the hope of our Lord Jesus Christ: because, while doing good and suffering evil, you long-sufferingly await that heavenly reward which you hope to receive from Christ when he comes.

You do all these things before God, because in them you do not seek human favor but attend to the presence of almighty God. You consider the Lord present, and recognize that you do everything before his sight. Or: we remember you in prayers before God—before God, who created us, and our Father, who adopted us. Thus we remember you, knowing [Col. 1358D] your election, that is, knowing that you are chosen and predestined to eternal life, O brothers beloved by God—that is, those whom God loves, because with fatherly scourges he trains you for the eternal inheritance. “For whom the Lord loves he corrects, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12; Prov. 3).

Or, we remember you, knowing your election, that is, knowing how God through our teaching chose you from the multitude of the rest who were left in unbelief. Truly God chose you while we preached, inwardly touching your hearts by the gift of the Holy Spirit, because our Gospel—that is, our preaching—did not come to you in word only, but also in the power of works, or the power of miracles, and in the Holy Spirit, because through the laying on of [Col. 1359A] our hands the Holy Spirit was given to you; and in much fullness, because we instructed you fully, filled you—God being the author—with spiritual graces, and wrought such things abundantly among you. You yourselves know and bear witness what kind of persons we were among you—how devout and wonder-working—for the sake of converting and instructing you, so that we might form you not only by the reasoning of our words but also by the example of our works.

“And you became imitators of us and of the Lord, receiving the word in much tribulation with the joy of the Holy Spirit, so that you became an example to all believers in Macedonia and Achaia. For from you the word of the Lord has been spread abroad, not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but in every [Col. 1359B] place your faith toward God has gone forth, so that we have no need to say anything. For they themselves report concerning us what manner of entrance we had to you, and how you turned to God from idols, to serve the living and true God and to await his Son from heaven—whom he raised from the dead—Jesus, who delivered us from the wrath to come.”

You yourselves know what kind of persons we were among you for the purpose of forming you. And you became imitators of us, and, what is more, imitators of the Lord, receiving the word of our preaching amid much tribulation, whether yours or ours, with the joy of the Holy Spirit—that is, the joy which the Holy Spirit inspired in you from hope of the heavenly reward. Therefore we rightly said above that we know your election, that is, that you are among God’s elect: for you are not chaff but grain.

For you became imitators not only of us but also of Christ, since no tribulation could call you back from receiving the heavenly word; rather, you rejoiced in tribulations for the word’s sake. For you received it—that is, received it reverently above all things, or apart from all things—in much tribulation inflicted upon you because of the word. Although your flesh bore tribulations, your spirit nevertheless rejoiced in the Holy Spirit. In these things you imitated the Lord and us, so that you became an example—that is, an example of persevering steadfastly in the faith amid adversities—to all believers in Macedonia and Achaia. Therefore, you who have become an example of faith and patience to so many others, see that you do not fail, [Col. 1359D] but always endure stronger in Christ.

You truly became an example to many, for the result shows it. For the word of the Lord—that is, the Lord’s preaching—going forth from you has been made widely known not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but your faith directed toward God has gone out and been heard in every surrounding place near you. It has become so widely known among all that we need say nothing about you, in order to commend your good life to others and provoke them by your example to faith and devout conduct. Truly we have no need to speak; for they themselves speak. For those dwelling round about report concerning us—that is, they tell one another—what kind of entrance [Col. 1360A] we had to you: with what power of miracles and abundance of spiritual gifts we came to convert you; and how easily, or how devoutly, you turned to God, and how readily our teaching entered your hearts.

You turned from images, that is, from the worship of idols, to God’s worship, “to serve”—that is, that you might serve—not a dead and false god, such as Jupiter or Hercules and the others whom pagans made gods from dead human beings, but the living and true God, because he is God by nature; and “to await”—that is, that, doing good works, you might patiently await without complaint and with devout longing his Son Jesus coming from heaven to render reward to his servants. The Father raised him from the dead; and the Son is therefore to be awaited by us as rewarder, because, by destroying our sins, he delivered us from the wrath to come, from the execution of future vengeance. God’s wrath is not disturbance but the judgment by which punishment for sins is inflicted.

## CHAPTER TWO

“For you yourselves know, brothers, our entrance to you, that it was not empty; but after suffering much and being shamefully treated, as you know, in Philippi (Acts 16–17), we had confidence in our God to speak to you the Gospel of God amid much anxiety. For our exhortation was not from error, nor from uncleanness, nor in deceit; but as we were approved by God to be entrusted with the Gospel, so we speak, not as pleasing men, but [Col. 1360C] God, who tests our hearts.”

Others report what kind of entrance we had to you; for you yourselves, brothers, know what it was like: it was not empty, that is, fruitless and trivial. But before coming to you, we suffered much and were shamefully treated at Philippi, the city of the Philippians, from which we came to you. There Silas and I were dragged insultingly before the magistrates, so that our tunics were torn; we were publicly beaten with rods, thrust into prison, and our feet fastened in the stocks. These and other things we suffered at Philippi before coming to you, as you also know.

Strengthened by enduring such afflictions and injuries, we had confidence and boldness, not in our own strength but in our God—that is, in his might and power—to speak to you, that is, to preach the Gospel of God amid much anxiety, lest before I had instructed you well I should be hindered by unbelievers. Yet we spoke to you confidently and boldly, because our exhortation is not from error, as though we were persuading anyone toward the error of any corrupt sect; nor from uncleanness, as though we were urging an unclean life in fleshly pollution; nor in deceit, as though we had one thing in the mouth and another in the heart. For even truth is preached deceitfully when it is not proclaimed for love of truth and the hearers’ benefit, but to gain glory or some profit.

Our exhortation is not from error, because we do not urge anyone to err from the truth; nor from uncleanness, because we persuade no one [Col. 1361A] to defile himself; nor in deceit, because we have no fraudulent pretence in our words. Rather, just as we were approved—that is, deemed upright—by God so that the Gospel might be entrusted to us, so we speak. That is: as those whom he approved and chose, not through error, uncleanness, or deceit, but through truth of faith, purity of life, and simplicity of heart, so we preach the Gospel to others—not as those seeking to please people, that is, not like those who seek human favor, but striving to please God, who tests, that is, searches and examines, our hearts and the secrets of our thoughts. For he who investigates the hidden things of hearts knows that we seek to please not people but him. And if we seek to please people, we do it not for ourselves but for their salvation.

“For we were never at any time in a word of flattery, as you know; nor under a pretext of avarice—God is witness; nor seeking glory from people, neither from you nor from others, although we could have been a burden to you as apostles of Christ. But we became little ones in your midst, as if a nurse should cherish her own children. So, longing eagerly for you, we were willing to impart to you not only the Gospel of God but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us.”

Truly, by our preaching we do not seek to please people but God. For we were never—that is, ever—in flattering speech, so as to please people by flattering words, either by pandering to their faults [Col. 1361C] or by praising them, as you know. Nor were we under a pretext of avarice; that is, we did not preach with the intention or under the pretext of gathering your possessions for ourselves. God is our witness in this, for he knows the secrets of the heart. Nor did we ever seek glory from people; and I demonstrate this by the various classes of people, since we sought it neither from you nor from others.

No one knows what power to harm the love of human glory possesses unless he has declared war upon it. For although it may be easy for someone not to desire praise while it is withheld, it is difficult not to delight in it when it is offered. But every righteous person either does not possess merely temporal glory, or, if he possesses it, breaks it beneath himself, so that he may rise free above his own honor and not, conquered by its delight, succumb to it. We did not seek any earthly thing from you, although we could have been a burden to you [Col. 1361D] by demanding maintenance from you, as the other apostles of Christ demand or receive it from their hearers.

We sought neither to be fed by your resources nor magnified by your praises. Rather, we became little ones in your midst: we humbled the glory of our apostleship before your eyes and lowered the greatness of our understanding to the smallness of your capacity, as though a nurse cherished her own children. She sits upon the ground, holds her children in her lap, nourishes them with milk, consoles them with affection, and by babbling teaches them to speak. Thus, for your sake, we were humbled; with maternal affection we bore you patiently, cherishing you in the bosom of compassion; we gave you the milk [Col. 1362A] of beginnings to drink; we comforted you by the sweetness of heavenly promises; and we lisped to you, as it were, concerning Christ’s humanity, in order to instruct you to speak the word of his divinity.

There are nurses who cherish children, but not their own; likewise, there are mothers who hand their children over to nurses, without cherishing them themselves. But the Apostle seems, with a genuine and rich affection of love, to assume both the role of a nurse by saying “cherish,” and that of a mother by adding “her own children.” Thus he compared himself to a nurse because he fed them; and he added “his own children” because he had begotten them, saying: “My little children, whom I am again in labor to bring forth” (Gal. 4). “We were like,” he says, “a nurse nurturing her own offspring, because, longing eagerly for you as a nurse longs for her own children, we were willing to impart to you not only the Gospel [Col. 1362B] of God but also our own souls”—that is, not only the preaching of truth but our whole life to expend for your salvation. This was because you had become most dear to us, owing to the merit of your holiness, which you at once embraced from the beginning of your conversion.

“For you remember, brothers, our labor and toil: working night and day so as not to burden any of you, we preached the Gospel of God among you. You are witnesses, and God also, how holily and justly and blamelessly we were among you who believed; as you know how we exhorted every one of you, as a father his own children, pleading with you, encouraging you, and charging you to walk worthily of God, who called you into his own kingdom and glory. [Col. 1362C] Therefore we too give thanks to God without ceasing, because when you received from us the word of God’s message, you received it not as a human word but, as it truly is, as God’s word, because it works in you who have believed in him.”

Truly we became little ones among you like a nurse, because we humbled ourselves in labor, as you know. Or thus: Truly we were prepared to impart our souls to you, as the result of our works showed, because we labored without ceasing for your benefit, as you remember. For you remember, brothers, the labor we had among you, and our toil. Labor is often without weariness, but our labor was not of that kind; nor was it light or momentary, but burdensome and continual. For we labored constantly both in preaching and in manual work; therefore, from the excess of unremitting labor we were worn out, yet we did not fail.

For, working with our hands night and day to obtain our livelihood, so as not to burden any of you by receiving maintenance from him, we preached the Gospel of God among you. By our example we sought to form you to work with your own hands for your living and to minister to the needy, and to reject false apostles who serve their bellies. For you are our witnesses, and God himself, who knows all things, how holily we were among you, with respect to the purity of a most clean way of life; how justly, with respect to preserving fairness toward neighbors by rendering what was due; and [Col. 1363A] how blamelessly—that is, innocently and irreproachably—we were among you who believed, because we did nothing to you of which you could complain against us.

Or, we were blameless among you because we never complained about you while bearing your weakness. In this way we conducted ourselves among you, that is, for your benefit. As you know—namely, you know these things just as you know the other matters which we add—how we affectionately admonished each one of you with such feeling as though a father were instructing his own children. We, I say, pleaded with you that you might advance toward what is better, and encouraged you in tribulations lest you fail. In doing this we charged you, that is, under the testimony of divine majesty or of the saints we adjured you, that you might walk upon the straight way, advancing and journeying toward the heavenly homeland; that you might walk, I say, worthily of God, that is, by a way worthy to lead to God, or as God’s elect ought to walk. He called you into his kingdom and glory, so that you might hasten to him by the path of virtues and remain with him everlastingly in his kingdom and glory. Or, he called you into his kingdom, that is, into the present Church, and afterward into his glory, that is, into fellowship with the angels.
