Because he called you to so great a blessedness and you gladly began to follow him who called, therefore not only you but we also give unceasing thanks to God, who accomplished this in you through the grace of his inspiration: because when you received from us the word of God’s message, that is, the Gospel in which you heard knowledge [Col. 1363C] of God, you received it not as a human word—that is, not uselessly and negligently, as human words are commonly received; or, not as a human word, that is, as though it came from wise persons—but as it truly is, God’s word; that is, with the reverence and honor due to what God has truly spoken.

The result shows this, because God himself works good works daily in you who have believed, advancing toward him by faith and longing. “We give thanks to God without ceasing,” he says, “because when you received,” and so forth. Why does he here give thanks to God? Surely it would be vain and empty to give anyone thanks for what that person had not done. But because this is neither vain nor empty, certainly God, to whom he gives thanks for this work, himself brought it about that those who had received from the Apostle the word of God’s message received it not as a human word but as what it truly is, God’s word.

He therefore says: By that calling according to his purpose, God works in human hearts, so that they do not hear the Gospel in vain, but, having heard it, turn and believe, receiving it not as a human word but as God’s word, as it truly is. Up to this point he has said much against the pseudo-apostles, showing that all the vices which he denied to be in himself and his companions were in them, and that they lacked all the goods of virtue which he demonstrated to be in himself and his companions. Now, lest the Thessalonians be troubled by their own tribulation or that of the apostles, he adds:

“For you became imitators, brothers, of the Churches [Col. 1364A] of God which are in Judaea in Christ Jesus, because you also suffered the same things from your fellow-countrymen as they from the Jews—who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets, and persecuted us; who do not please God and oppose all people, forbidding us to speak to the Gentiles so that they may be saved, in order always to fill up their sins. For God’s wrath has come upon them unto the end.”

Against the false apostles he had spoken covertly, so that they might not receive them; now he speaks openly against the Jews, so that they may not fear them. “Truly,” he says, “you have believed in him, because you have become imitators of the churches of God which are in Judea,” that is, in the land of the Jews, “in Christ Jesus,” that is, in the instruction of Christ himself [Col. 1364B]. You are imitators in this: that you too have suffered the same things which those churches suffered. You have suffered, I say, from your fellow-tribesmen, that is, from those from whose tribes you traced your descent, just as they did from the Jews. For your fellow citizens and friends or relatives persecuted you, just as their own persecuted them.

Nor is it surprising if the Jews, in their customary way, persecute the faithful: they killed both the Savior himself, the Lord Jesus, and earlier the prophets who foretold him; and afterwards they persecuted us apostles, who proclaimed to them that he had come (Acts VII). Therefore do not be amazed, but bear it patiently if they persecute you: they have always persecuted. And although they may seem to do these things out of zeal for the law, nevertheless they do not please God, whose grace they oppose. Nor are they rebellious against God alone [Col. 1364C], but they are also opposed to all people—that is, to the salvation of all people—preventing us, insofar as they can prevail, from speaking to the Gentiles, so that they may believe and be saved. Thus they are enemies of all, while they attempt to ensure that through us the word of salvation should come to no one, but that all should be left in perdition.

And they do this according to their custom, in order that they may always fill up their sins—that is, unceasingly heap sins upon sins until their fullness is complete, when for these things they will be sent into Gehenna (Matt. XXIII). They always fill up their sins because the wrath of God, so that they might be blinded, has come upon them—that is, it was long ago poured out upon their hearts, from the time when they rejected the Savior who had been sent to them [Col. 1364D]. For when their fathers said, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII), then the wrath of God came upon them; and it will endure until the end, when, through Elijah’s preaching, they will receive grace.

Or thus: “That they may always fill up their sins.” For forty years after the Lord’s passion, God gave the Jews time for repentance. When those years had passed and they were unwilling to believe, their sins were completed, so that they deserved to perish for them. But when the Apostle said this, Jerusalem was still standing, and their sins were not yet completed; yet they were completed when the Romans came. Hence he adds: “For the wrath has come”—that is, it came before they recovered their senses; it came before they expected it—the wrath of God came upon them, crushing them. The wrath of God is the vengeance wrought through the Romans. This wrath [Col. 1365A] endures upon them in captivity until the end of the age; or this temporal wrath is said to have come upon them in captivity because eternal wrath follows, when after this life they are punished without end in hell. The wrath of present vengeance has come, enduring upon them until the end; the wrath of future condemnation follows, enduring without end.

> “But we, brothers, having been bereft of you for a short time, in presence, not in heart, made more earnest haste to see your face with great desire; because we wished to come to you—I, Paul, indeed, once and again—but Satan hindered us. For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Are not you before our Lord Jesus Christ at [Col. 1365B] his coming? For you are our glory and joy.”

You have suffered much from your fellow citizens; but we, brothers, have been bereft of you—that is, made without consolation by separation from you. You did not make us bereft by the sorrow which we felt concerning your tribulations, before we learned of the steadfastness of your faith. We have been bereft for the time of an hour, because this bereavement of ours was, or will be, brief and not lasting. We have been bereft, I say, in speech, because we cannot speak to you in person; and in sight, because we do not see your face; but not in heart, because our heart always beholds you and is with you. Speech and sight cease, but the heart and its concern do not rest.

Thus bereft, we hastened more earnestly—that is, we hastened much more—to see [Col. 1365C] your face, lest it had changed; that is, lest perhaps you had failed amid the tribulations which you suffered from your fellow citizens. We hastened, I say, to see your face—that is, to see you face to face, to behold your presence—with great desire to exhort you; and we hastened to strengthen you in perseverance. Yet we could not accomplish what we hastened to do. For we all wished indeed to come to you, but we could not. I, Paul in particular, who labor more than the others and am more devoted, wished to come to you once and again; but I could not, because Satan hindered us. Satan means “adversary,” that is, the devil, who always opposes human salvation; he set obstacles before us. Therefore be more watchful [Col. 1365D] against his snares, lest he also impede your journey by which you press on toward the heavenly homeland.

Satan could by no means hinder the paths of so great an Apostle by himself; but while opposing, he unknowingly served the purposes of a hidden providence, so that Paul, being unable to go to others whom he wished to approach, might benefit those from whom he could not depart. “Therefore,” he says, “we wished to come to you, and therefore Satan opposed us, because what is our hope except you?” That is: for what do we now hope that we shall receive a reward in the future, if not for you? “Or what is our joy?” That is: from what do we rejoice now and in the future, if not from your holiness? “Or what is our crown of glory,” which shall be given to the victorious, “except you?” Are you not this for us before our Lord [Col. 1366A] Jesus Christ—that is, before the tribunal of the supreme Judge—at his coming? For before the righteous Judge we shall surely then find the glory which we now seek through zeal in preaching among your conduct; and because of your good way of life, prepared by our labor, we shall be crowned.

Truly, then, you will be for us a crown of glory, because even now you are our glory among the churches and our joy with us. For we glory before others in the progress of your faith and holiness, and we rejoice in our hearts. But in the world to come you will be for us eternal glory and enduring joy.

## Chapter III

> “Therefore, since we could endure it no longer, we thought it good to remain alone at Athens, and sent Timothy, [Col. 1366B] our brother and God’s minister in Christ’s Gospel, to strengthen and exhort you concerning your faith, that no one may be shaken by these tribulations. For you yourselves know that we are appointed for this. For even when we were with you, we foretold to you that we should suffer tribulations, as indeed happened, and you know it. Therefore I too, when I could endure it no longer, sent to learn of your faith, lest perhaps the tempter had tempted you and our labor should prove vain.”

I said that we have been bereft of you, who are our glory. Therefore I and Silvanus, unable to endure any longer because it was a heavy burden to us while we did not know how you were doing, thought it good that we two should remain alone at Athens; and we sent Timothy to you [Col. 1366C], that he might strengthen you in your purpose and bring us certain news concerning you. They did not send him only with this letter, but earlier; otherwise he would not have greeted them with them at the end. We sent Timothy, who is truly to be received and heard, because he is our brother—that is, he shares with us a portion in heaven—and is God’s minister in the Gospel: that is, one who ministers to the faithful the things of God in the preaching of the Gospel. We sent him to strengthen you, that you might stand fast in what you had already attained, and to exhort you, that you might advance to better things. We sent him to encourage and exhort you to hold and defend your faith, so that none of you might be moved from the constancy of sincere faith amid these tribulations, which [Col. 1366D] both we and you endure for a time in the exile of this present age.

Nor ought you to be moved from your purpose by these things, because you yourselves know that we are appointed for this: that we should endure temporal adversities. Hence the people of the elect say through Jeremiah concerning the ancient enemy: “He has set me as a target for an arrow” (Lam. III). For the faithful people are set before their enemy like a target for an arrow, because they are continually assailed as with arrows while afflicted by his persecutions. Whoever endures continual evils in this life, being set as a target, receives the arrows of the one who strikes.

Therefore the excellent preacher, while he himself endured the evils of persecution and groaned under the persecutor because of the adversary, consoled the tender minds of his disciples by his own afflictions, saying: “For you yourselves know [Col. 1367A] that we are appointed for this.” As though he said openly: “Why are you astonished at our wounds in this time, when, if we seek eternal joys, we came here for this very purpose: to be struck?” “You know this,” he says. For we say it not only while absent; even when we were present with you, we foretold and announced that we should suffer tribulations—that is, that we were about to suffer tribulations—as indeed happened afterwards, and you yourselves know it, because you prove this in yourselves by experience.

And just as we knew beforehand that we would suffer tribulations and did not flee, so you, who know that we are appointed for this, ought not to be shaken; rather, remain immovable in your purpose, patiently enduring everything. And because we have already suffered the foretold tribulations, therefore, lest you should be terrified on account of our tribulations [Col. 1367B], I also sent to you, since I could no longer endure uncertainty about you. For, being uncertain, I feared that our tribulations might be causes of the failure of your faith. I sent Timothy, not only with this letter but earlier, to learn of your faith—that is, that he might learn and report to me whether you remained in the faith, and whether that faith of yours was strong or weak—lest perhaps he who tempts had tempted you and, by tempting, overcome you: that is, the ancient deceiver, whose office is to tempt and seduce people.

“But God is not a tempter of evils” (Jas. I); he himself tempts no one in the sense, namely, of temptation which is deception or seduction. Yet in the sense of testing, God tested Abraham (Gen. XXII). But I feared lest that deceiver, who tempts in order to deceive, should tempt you, and our labor among you should become vain—that is, fruitless—the labor which we endured for you: namely, lest you should yield to the deceiver and all that we labored in your conversion and instruction should profit you nothing [Col. 1367C].

> “But now Timothy has come to us from you and has announced to us your faith and love, and that you have a good remembrance of us, always desiring to see us, as we also desire to see you. Therefore, brothers, we have been comforted in you in all our need and tribulation through your faith; for now we live, if you stand fast in the Lord. For what thanksgiving can we [Col. 1367D] render to God for you, for all the joy with which we rejoice before our God because of you, praying more abundantly night and day that we may see your face and complete what is lacking in your faith? But may God himself and our Father, and our Lord Jesus Christ, direct our way to you. And may the Lord multiply you and make you abound in love toward one another and toward all, just as we also abound toward you, to establish your hearts blamelessly in holiness before God and our Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints. Amen.”

Before we knew how you were doing, we were bereft of you. But now, with Timothy returning, whom we had sent to you, and reporting good things concerning you [Col. 1368A], we have been comforted. “But now,” he says, “Timothy has come to us from you and announced to us your faith and love”: that is, he has reported to us that you remain faithful amid adversities and have not abandoned the love by which you love God and your neighbors, even your enemies. And he reports that you have a good remembrance of us—that is, that you remember us and think nothing but good concerning us—always wishing to see us, just as we too desire to see you. Therefore, because we heard this concerning you, we have been comforted, brothers, in you, though we were previously bereft.

We have been comforted, I say, through your faith—that is, the steadfastness of your faith causes us to have consolation in every need, that is, the scarcity which we suffer in food and clothing, and in every tribulation [Col. 1368B] outwardly inflicted upon us by adversaries. And truly we have been comforted, because now, amid this misery, we live as though we were already in heaven and esteem ourselves as though already raised from the dead, if you stand—that is, if you perseveringly maintain the state of uprightness in the Lord. I do not say that you stand in us, but in the Lord, because “neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase” (1 Cor. III).

Oh, what tender inward affections the Apostle bore when he yearned for his children with so great a fervor of love that he said: “Now we live, if you stand fast in the Lord.” He greatly feared lest his disciples, seeing in their preacher the disgrace of so many persecutions, might despise the faith in him, so that the approaching insults of sufferings [Col. 1368C] might prevail against it. Therefore he grieved intensely amid torments, but feared even more for his children because of the testing occasioned by his torments. He made little of the wounds of his body in himself, while he feared wounds of the heart in his children. By suffering he received the wounds of torments; by consoling his children he treated their heart-wounds.

Let us therefore consider how great was his love: amid his own losses he sought his children’s salvation; amid his own pains he feared for others; and first of all he guarded their firmness of mind even by means of his own abasement. He was secure concerning his own reward even if his disciples fell; nevertheless, as though he would lose the reward of his labor if they fell, he said that he lived in their steadfastness—that is, that he possessed the reward of life. For he did not wish to live while they fell, but while they stood fast in the Lord, so that his fruit in them might be whole [Col. 1368D] and his reward before God full of joys.

“We have been comforted,” he says, “through your faith, for we cannot render worthy thanks to God for this.” For what thanksgiving can we render to God for you who stand well, being placed in all the joy with which we rejoice before our God because of you, whose eyes see the secrets of hearts openly? For our joy is not before human beings, since outwardly we appear as though sad because of the adversities surrounding us; but inwardly, before the Lord, we always rejoice over your progress. Nor do we merely give him whatever thanks we can for you; night and day we pray more abundantly that we may come to you and see your face, speak to you mouth to mouth, and complete what is lacking [Col. 1369A] in your faith—things which formerly we could not complete because you were little children and because we could not remain with you for a long time.

Since, therefore, though you have not yet learned the whole faith perfectly, you have striven to retain it firmly amid adversities, we desire to reach you and supply what is lacking in your faith. From this passage it is clear that when he said above, “so that there is no need for us to say anything” (above, I), he did not say this because they already knew all the mysteries of faith sufficiently. Rather, as we said, he said it because there was no need for him to say anything about them to others, since their renown celebrated them far and wide.

“We pray,” he says, “to see your face and instruct your faith fully; but may God accomplish what we pray.” May God himself, our Creator [Col. 1369B], who is able, and our heavenly Father, who wills what is good and loves and governs us with paternal affection, and the Lord Jesus Christ, who redeemed us from the enemy and made us subject to his lordship, direct our way to you—that is, make our way to you straight and free from obstacles. But may the Lord—that is, the Holy Spirit—multiply you in the number of believers and make you abound in love toward one another, that is, mutually among yourselves, and toward all, even those opposed to you; and may he do this as perfectly as he has made us abound in love toward you.

May he give you this abundance of love for the strengthening of your hearts—that is, so that through this love your hearts may be established in holiness, that is, in every purity and cleanness and the observance of good works—without complaint, that is, without fault, so that you may be so innocent that no one can justly complain of you. And may you be such before God—that is, in the eyes of God, who examines truth and from whom nothing is hidden. For there are those who appear holy before human beings, but not before God (Matt. XXIII). But you, be truly holy and without complaint—that is, irreproachable—before the eyes of God, who sees and created you, and of the Father who adopted us.

Strive to be such before God and our Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints—that is, when the Lord Jesus comes for judgment with all his saints. For as each person ends the present life, so that person will appear on the day of judgment. But those will not appear without complaint [Col. 1369D] against whom the Judge will complain, saying: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food” (Matt. XXV). Or: do what I have said together with all the saints, because all the saints do so. For confirmation of everything stated above, “Amen” is added; it means “truly” or “faithfully.”

## Chapter IV

> “Finally then, brothers, we ask and exhort you in the Lord Jesus that, as you received from us how you ought to walk and please God—as indeed you are walking—you may abound more.”

Up to this point he has urged patience amid one’s own or others’ tribulation; now he admonishes them to advance in good works [Col. 1370A] and teaches what kind of people they ought to be, whether in themselves or toward their brothers. Yet the preceding material, in which he urged patience in many ways, is more fitting for the perfect; what follows, in which purity and innocence are urged, is more suited to the imperfect. “Because,” he says, “you have lived well until now, as has been shown above, therefore for the rest—that is, for the remaining span of life—we ask you to spend it so as to abound more in good works.”

And this is what he means: “For the rest, for what remains, we ask you, brothers, and exhort you”—that is, we adjure you by sacred things in the Lord Jesus—“that, just as you fear and love him, so, out of reverence and love for him, do what we urge. We exhort you that, as you received from us”—that is, as you learned from our teaching how you ought [Col. 1370B] to walk if you wish to reach your homeland, how you ought to proceed by the way of righteousness and please God in all things—“as indeed you are walking,” because you began at once to do what we handed down to you concerning this walk, “you may abound more” in this walking of good works: that is, that from now on you may press more eagerly than before toward the heavenly homeland by carrying out God’s commandments.

Or, according to other manuscripts: “We exhort you that, as you received from us how you ought to walk and please God in that very walk, so you may walk,” advancing and persevering “from strength to strength” (Ps. LXXXIII), so that you may abound more and more daily.

> “For you know what commands I gave you through [Col. 1370C] the Lord Jesus. For this is the will of God: your sanctification, that you abstain from fornication; that each of you know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of desire, as also the Gentiles who do not know God; and that no one overreach or defraud his brother in a matter of business, because the Lord is an avenger in all these things, as we told you before and testified. For God did not call us to uncleanness, but to sanctification. Therefore whoever rejects these things rejects not a human being but God, who also gave his Holy Spirit in us.”

Therefore I exhort you to walk as you received from us, because you know what commands concerning walking and right living I gave you to bear and observe; and this was not through myself, but through the Lord Jesus. Although you know them, I shall nevertheless repeat them in part. For this is the will of God: your sanctification, which benefits you, not him. That is, God wills and requires of you that you be sanctified, that you abstain from fornication—that is, from every unlawful sexual union—lest, taking the members of Christ, you make them members of a prostitute (1 Cor. VI).

Or: this is the will of God and your sanctification: that you keep yourselves far removed from fornication, because while you abstain from an unclean deed, both body and soul are sanctified in you by chastity. Let your abstinence from fornication be such that each of you knows how to possess and keep under the dominion of the mind his own vessel—that is, his body, which is the vessel of the soul. For that person is said to possess his vessel who keeps his body under his own power, so that the mind does not serve the desires of the flesh, but the flesh serves the mind’s right intentions [Col. 1371A].

Let each of you know how to possess his vessel in sanctification—that is, in the purest cleansing—and honor, so that it is not dishonored by the reproach of shamefulness. For from abstaining from fornication arises the sanctification of chastity, and from this comes honor among human beings. Indeed, even in this age, one who leads a clean and chaste life is honored; whereas one who defiles himself by any fornication is regarded as infamous and disgraceful. Possess your vessels in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of desire—that is, when sin is desired but not carried out. “Not in the passion of desire” means that you should not even have the desire for fornication, which is a passion and an injury of the soul.

For the passion of desire consists in suffering inwardly the incitements of the flesh which arise from your desire. I do not command that you should not suffer the incitements of the flesh, because this is unavoidable; rather, see that they do not proceed from your desire—that is, do not, by premeditation, desire an unlawful sexual union, so that you do not afterwards suffer inwardly from desire and become subject to evil suggestions arising from desire, as do the Gentiles. There is no wonder concerning them; nor ought you to be like them, because they do not know God and therefore, without regard for divine fear or reverence, engage in wicked unions, not only with any women whatsoever but even with animals [Col. 1371B].

And this is the will of God: that none of you should overreach his brother in a business matter—that is, in trade, another Christian—so as to extort from him merchandise worth one hundred solidi for some lesser price; nor should he defraud him—that is, deceitfully mislead him, displaying to him a pile of cloth which is very beautiful and seemingly valuable on the outside but cheap within; or selling him gilded bronze as gold; or doing similar things. Overreaching occurs where something of greater value is obtained for a lesser price; defrauding, however, where through fraud a brother is deceived in the very act of selling or buying.

But refrain from these vices—from fornication, the passion of desire, overreaching, and defrauding a brother—because the Lord is avenger [Col. 1371C] in all these things: that is, he himself punishes all these things in his judgment, not only the act of fornication, but also the desire for an unlawful act and the injustice of unfair trading. He will take vengeance for all these things, as we foretold you—that is, as we announced beforehand to you concerning the judgment when we were with you—and testified: that is, proved by the testimonies of Scripture. Or, “we testified” means that, as witnesses of divine judgment, we asserted these things firmly.

These things are also to be avoided because God did not call us to uncleanness—that is, to lead an unclean and filthy life—but to sanctification: that is, to lead a manner of life wholly undefiled, pure, and full of virtues. Therefore through the law he cries: “You shall be holy, for I am holy” [Col. 1372A] (Lev. XI, XIX, XX; 1 Pet. I). And because God’s will is your sanctification, which must be maintained in the order we have set forth; and because God did not call us to live uncleanly but holily: therefore whoever rejects these things which we have now said about preserving holiness and purity and uprooting vices, rejects not a human being but God. That is, he rejects not me but God, whose commands I speak and whose will I announce; God who also gave his Holy Spirit in us—that is, in our hearts—so that we might speak and do all things through his Spirit. Therefore whoever rejects our words as though they were human words rejects the Holy Spirit through whom we speak all things, and God whose Spirit he is (Luke X).

There were among the Thessalonians some who remained in the above-mentioned vices and despised the Apostle’s words [Col. 1372B]. For their sake he speaks thus, showing that contempt for apostolic commands is directed rather against God than against the Apostle.

> “But concerning brotherly love, we have no need to write to you. For you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another (John XIII, 15; 1 John XXIV). For indeed you do this toward all the brothers throughout Macedonia. But we ask you, brothers, to abound more, and make it your aim to be quiet, to attend to your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you, so that you may walk honorably toward those outside and desire nothing from anyone.”

It was necessary to write to you concerning the matters mentioned above, because some of you are blameworthy in them. But concerning brotherly love—that is, the love by which you ought to love your brothers—we have no need to write to you: that is, it is not necessary for us to instruct you by letter. Truly, we have no need for this. For you yourselves have been taught by God—that is, taught by God’s Gospel—to love one another, because you have heard Christ saying, “This I command you: that you love one another” (John XIII, XV).

Or, you have learned this from God through inward inspiration, because as soon as the Holy Spirit has filled the human heart, he makes it add this love; nor can anyone ever learn love who does not have the Holy Spirit teaching within. You have learned this, as you show by your deeds [Col. 1372D]. For you do it toward all the brothers: that is, you love all Christians and show by works of love that you love them, not only in your own city but throughout Macedonia. You do this—that is, you love the brothers. Yet we ask you, brothers, to abound more in the love of the brothers: strive, therefore, to possess a still more abundant love for the brothers.

And make it your aim to be quiet, free from curiosity, which does not allow the curious person’s heart to be quiet. “Make it your aim.” It is as though someone said: “It is difficult to abandon a habit, but compel yourselves.” Strive that curiosity may no longer ravage the quiet of your mind. For curiosity, when it seeks to scrutinize another’s life, while always ignorant of its own inner condition, strives to think about outward things. Curiosity is indeed a grave vice [Col. 1373A]: while it leads the mind of any person outward to investigate a neighbor’s life, it always conceals that person’s own inner life from him, so that, knowing another’s affairs, he does not know himself. And the more skilled the curious mind becomes in another person’s worth, the more ignorant it becomes of itself.

Therefore it cannot possess quiet, while it continually labors to know others’ lives uselessly; and it often wanders through various places so that it may learn others’ deeds. But take pains to be quiet and to attend to your own business: that is, let each person, setting aside what belongs to others, carry out the duty that pertains to himself, because it is useful for you, in correcting your own lives, to act in this way. And work with your hands, so that you may have food and so that you may bestow benefits, as we commanded you while present with you; for manual work also helps one to remain quiet. For that evil comes from idleness.

Hence Scripture says, “Idleness has taught much wickedness” (Ecclus. XXXIII) [Col. 1373B]. And make it your aim to walk honorably—that is, to act irreproachably—toward those who are outside: that is, before unbelievers who are outside the Church, so that through the example of your honorable conduct they may be converted to honorable habits and to the faith. Therefore idleness is not to be pursued, but work is to be done, because it is honorable and like a light to unbelievers. And further make it your aim to desire nothing belonging to anyone—that is, no possession of any believer—much less to ask for it or take it; rather, let what you have suffice, or acquire through your just labor what you lack. For one who lives in idleness covets other people’s possessions. Therefore cast off idleness, so that you may overcome the appetite for others’ goods.

[Col. 1373C]

> “But we do not wish you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve as the rest do, who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus.”

Because some among them mourned their dead friends without understanding, as though they would rise no more, he teaches them that the resurrection of all is truly to come; therefore they ought not to grieve immoderately concerning the death of their own. It is as though he said: “You did not need to be taught by us concerning love, but you do need teaching concerning the resurrection of the dead.” Therefore, brothers, “we do not wish you to be ignorant”: that is, we do not wish you not to know, but we wish you to know what must be known concerning those who sleep—that is, the dead, who will rise easily as from sleep and with their bodies whole [Col. 1373D]. For just as a person wakes more quickly from sleep, so bodies will rise from death swiftly at the Creator’s command.

Therefore we do not wish you to be ignorant of these things, so that you may not grieve concerning the death of those dear to you as the rest—that is, unbelievers—grieve concerning their own dead, who have no hope: namely, hope of resurrection and eternal incorruption. The most truthful usage of Scripture also calls them “those who sleep,” so that, when we hear that they sleep, we may not doubt that they will awake. Hence the Psalm says: “Will not one who sleeps rise again?” (Ps. XL). For weak minds greatly fear the name of death, whereas the term “sleep” is not feared.

There is, however, a sorrow in some sense natural concerning loved ones who have died [Col. 1374A]. For it is not opinion but nature that recoils from death; and death would not have befallen humankind except as a punishment following sin. Therefore, if animals, which were created so that each dies in its own time, flee death and love life, how much more does the human being, who was created such that, if he wished to live without sin, he would live without end? Thus it is necessary that we should be sorrowful when those whom we love leave us by dying. For although we know that they do not leave us who remain here forever, but go before us for a while and are to be followed, nevertheless death itself, from which nature recoils, when it takes someone beloved, makes the affection of love sorrow within us.

Therefore the Apostle did not admonish us not to grieve, but not to grieve as the rest who have no hope [Col. 1374B]. We grieve, then, at the deaths of our own because we must lose them, but with hope of receiving them again. From one side we are distressed; from the other we are comforted. From one side weakness afflicts; from the other faith restores. From one side the human condition causes pain; from the other the divine promise heals. Therefore let devout hearts be allowed to grieve over the deaths of their beloved with a sorrow that can be healed, and let them shed consolable tears because of mortal condition; yet let the joy of faith restrain those tears, through which believers are understood, when they die, to depart from us for a little while and pass to better things.

“Truly,” he says, “you ought not to grieve inconsolably, like unbelievers, over the death of your loved ones, as though they would live no more and be with you no more. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so we ought certainly to believe [Col. 1374C] that God will bring with him to judgment, on the day of the resurrection of all, those who slept through Jesus”—that is, who died in Christ—“so that they may judge the world and reign with Christ.” Hence Zechariah also says: “And the Lord my God will come, and all the saints with him” (Zech. XIV).

Or, through Jesus the mediator, God will bring them with him, because their resurrection and their coming with Christ as judges will be received from God the Father only through Christ. “If we believe,” he says, “that Jesus died,” and so forth. Why does the excellent preacher call the Lord’s death “death,” while he calls the death of the Lord’s servants not death but sleep? Is it not because, considering the lowly hearts of his hearers, he applies the medicine of his preaching with marvelous skill? He does not hesitate to say that the one whom they already knew had risen was dead; but in order to instill hope of resurrection, he calls those who had not yet risen not dead but sleeping [Col. 1374D]. For he did not fear to call dead the one whom his hearers already knew had risen; but he feared to call dead those whom they scarcely believed would rise.

> “For this we tell you by the word of the Lord: we who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord, shall not go before those who have fallen asleep” (1 Cor. 15). “For the Lord himself, at a command, at the voice of an archangel, and at the trumpet of God, will descend from heaven; and the dead who are in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who remain, [Col. 1375A] will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air; and so we shall always be with the Lord. Therefore comfort one another with these words.”

Truly, those who now sleep in the sleep of death will come alive with Christ. For we say this to you not in our own word but in the Lord’s word: the discourse which we speak to you about this matter is not ours but the Lord’s, since we speak such things to you by his teaching and command, or as he speaks through our mouth. Namely, we say this: we who at that time live in the flesh, who remain after all the preceding saints—that is, whose life still remains in the body—shall not precede at the Lord’s coming those who have fallen asleep. That is, we shall not anticipate those who died long before, so as to meet the Lord before them; [Col. 1375B] rather, we shall meet him together with them.

The Apostle teaches this manner of resurrection because the living might seem able to meet the Lord more quickly than the dead. For the resurrection of all will occur so swiftly that the living will be unable to precede the dead. The Apostle now spoke in the person of the righteous who will then be found alive in the flesh, because he himself was righteous and lived in the flesh, and foresaw that the last saints would share his communion; therefore he used their words. But the Thessalonians, not understanding this, thought that Paul and those writing the letter with him said that they themselves would be found in the flesh on the day of consummation. They wavered amid various conjectures and [Col. 1375C] said: “If Paul is to be found in the body, the day of judgment is near.” Therefore he corrects them in the second Epistle.

For they thought the general resurrection would occur in their days because the Apostle had said, using the present tense, “we who are alive.” This was the chief reason that compelled him to write them another letter. As we have said, he called them “alive” and “remaining,” not because he wished it to be understood that he and his companions would be found in the body at the time of the resurrection, but because he said “we” in the sense of “the righteous,” among whose number he himself was. For they will be caught up to meet Christ, not sinners.

But we do not understand “the living” tropologically as saints who have not died to sin, but as all whom Christ will find in the body when he comes. And the following words, “we shall not [Col. 1375D] precede those who have fallen asleep,” are not to be referred to sinners who are stupefied by the sleep of negligence—for sinners will not be caught up with the righteous to meet Christ—but to those whom death had dissolved. We shall not precede in meeting the Lord those who have fallen asleep; rather, they themselves will first awaken—that is, rise again—before we begin to meet the Lord.

For the Lord himself will descend locally from heaven in his own person; or “from heaven” means “from concealment.” And this will be at the Father’s command. For he will descend as sent by the Father, not through any difference of power but through the judicial dispensation. Or he will descend at his own command, because he will command the dead to rise and to meet him. For he will not come humble and hidden as formerly, but exalted and manifest, with sovereign authority, so that everything [Col. 1376A] he commands may immediately take place; and he will come at the voice of an archangel, because the archangel will cry with a loud voice, awakening the dead before him. Of such a voice he himself says: “But at midnight a cry arose: Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him” (Matt. 25). And he will come with the trumpet of God, that is, with some great and public sound made by divine power. Again, he himself speaks of such a trumpet: “The hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God and will come forth” (John 5).

This trumpet will awaken all, terrify enemies, and summon Christ’s own people to battle, so that they may overcome their adversaries, who will flee from the Lord’s face and be cast into Gehenna. And just as the trumpet formerly summoned the people of the Hebrews to festivals (Num. 10, 29, 31), so this trumpet will summon the people [Col. 1376B] of the saints to the celebration of eternal joy. At God’s command, he says, and at the sounding of the archangel’s voice and God’s trumpet (Ps. 80), the Lord Jesus will descend from heaven into the air, not onto the earth. For since at the judgment there will be both those assumed into heaven and those left upon earth, the Lord will hold the judgment of both between heaven and earth—that is, in the air.

And as he descends, the dead who are in Christ—that is, those who ended their present life in the faith and love of Christ—will rise first, that is, before those then living meet Christ. Then—that is, after their resurrection—we who are alive, namely those among us who will then be found alive, who remain, that is, who among us will survive the torments of Antichrist, will together with them be caught up [Col. 1376C] by angels in clouds to meet Christ in the air. The Apostle joins himself to the last saints because of the unity of the Church, whose members include both the first and the last righteous; and because of similarity in suffering, since those last saints will resemble the apostles in their sufferings and for that reason will be most worthy.

Yet, though they are found alive, they will not precede the dead. So swiftly will the resurrection of the dead occur. But when the dead have been raised, they too will meet the Lord in their bodies, and those found alive in their bodies will do so as well—yet in such a way that what is corruptible and mortal will be transformed by glory into incorruption and immortality. Thus, just as the bodies of the dead will rise, so also the bodies of the living will be transformed into the same kind of substance.

Indeed, so far as the present words are concerned, [Col. 1376D] the Apostle seems to affirm that at the end of the age, when the Lord comes and the resurrection of the dead takes place, some will not die but will be found alive, suddenly transformed into the immortality also granted to the other saints, and caught up with them in the clouds. But let us see whether this sense is opposed by what the same Apostle writes to the Corinthians: “We shall all indeed rise,” or, “We shall all indeed sleep” (1 Cor. 15). If, therefore, we believe that the saints found alive at Christ’s coming and caught up to meet him are in that same catching-up to depart from mortal bodies and immediately return to the same bodies made immortal, we shall suffer no difficulty in the Apostle’s words when he says, “We shall all rise,” or, “We shall all sleep”; for neither will they be excluded from resurrection, which they will precede by a sleep, however brief, yet not nonexistent. [Col. 1377A]

For it must not be said that it is impossible for them, while they are borne upward through the air, both to die and to live again. And when he adds, “and so we shall always be with the Lord,” this should not be understood as though he had said that we would remain forever with the Lord in the air, for he himself certainly will not remain there. One goes out to meet one who is coming, not one who remains. Rather, we shall be with the Lord in this way: wherever we are with him, we shall possess everlasting bodies.

All the elect, both those awakened from the sleep of death and those found alive in the flesh, will be caught up in clouds to meet the Lord in the air; and so—that is, all together made immortal—we shall always be with the Lord, as he himself said: “Father, [Col. 1377B] those whom you gave me, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me, that they may see my glory” (John 17). Since we shall all rise and always be with the Lord, therefore comfort one another—that is, let each comfort the other concerning the death of friends—with these words which we have spoken about resurrection and the fellowship, or enduring glory, of all the righteous. Let sorrow perish where such great consolation exists. Let grief be wiped from the mind; amid such hope of glory, let faith drive out pain. For all the righteous will remain together with their friends, immortal and blessed without end, in Christ’s kingdom. Therefore you ought not mourn your friends who have died as though they were lost, for you have not lost them but sent them on before you.

## Chapter V

[Col. 1377C] “But concerning times and seasons, brothers, you have no need that we should write to you. For you yourselves know carefully that the day of the Lord will come just as a thief in the night” (2 Pet. 3). “For when they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them, as labor pains upon a woman with child; and they shall not escape.”

You needed to be taught through our letter concerning the resurrection. But concerning the times and seasons at which that resurrection itself will take place, you do not need us to write to you. “Times” means whether Christ will come in summer or winter, by day or night, in what month, or after how many years; “seasons” means at what hour of day or night [Col. 1377D] Christ will come. Brothers, you have no need—that is, it is not necessary—for us to write this to you, because knowing it would not benefit you.

There is no need to write of these things, because you yourselves, by searching the Scriptures or by being taught by us, carefully—that is, diligently—know that the day of the Lord, namely the day of judgment or the day of death on which the Lord will judge each person, will come secretly upon the unwary like a thief in the night. For it will come “in the night,” that is, in ignorance: it will come when no one knows or expects it; it will come suddenly and unexpectedly (1 Cor. 15). It will come as a thief who comes secretly while people sleep and steals everything, so that one who fell asleep rich awakens to find nothing. Thus it will happen to the complacent and negligent through the unexpected coming of the Lord’s day.

For this reason the Apostle began [Col. 1378A] to speak about times: that he might warn his disciples to beware lest they be thus overtaken. Therefore this is what must be known: those who do not wish to be caught by that day as by a thief at night must take care to be children of light and to watch with hearts prepared. For if knowledge of periods of time were needed to avoid this evil—that is, to prevent the Lord’s day from finding us unprepared like a thief—the Apostle would not say that there was no need to write this; rather, as a most provident teacher, he would judge it precisely what ought to be written.

But now he has shown that they did not need it: it was enough for them to know that the Lord’s day would come as a thief upon the unprepared and sleeping, and, knowing this, to remain watchful and ready however long it might be before it came. He also maintained his proper limit, so that the Apostle would not presume to teach others what he knew the Lord had said to the apostles: “It is not for you to know the times or seasons which the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts 1). Of these times and seasons, then, there was no need for him to write to them.

Truly, he says, that day will come as a thief upon lovers of the world. When they say, “We have peace, and in this peace security concerning the future, because we fear that no further troubles will happen to us,” then, when the Judge descends, sudden destruction will come upon them: the eternal death of body and soul. It will come as pain comes upon a woman carrying a child in her womb, because the evil of their conscience will suddenly begin to torment them when, at the Judge’s coming, it begins to be compelled to come into the light—that is, to appear before all. [Col. 1378B]

For a pregnant woman at last expels with pain what she carried for a long time in her womb as a burden. So too the reprobate will, before the Judge’s presence, disclose to all with grievous torment the evil which lay hidden for a long time within their conscience and weighed it down. A woman conceives that burden with pleasure but, as has been said, expels it with pain. So too the reprobate willingly committed sin with pleasure, but before the strict Judge they will unwillingly disclose it with much bitterness. When she does not expect it, a woman begins to be pressed by sudden pains in order to give birth. So, when they do not foresee it, the reprobate begin to be compelled by sudden torments to bring forth publicly before the tribunal of the eternal Judge the hidden evils which they possess within. Thus they will begin to be tortured inwardly with sudden pains, like a pregnant woman, [Col. 1378C] and they will not escape. For the woman does escape; they will not.

The Lord announces that near the end of the age there will be very great tribulation (Luke 21), and says that people will wither from fear and expectation of what will come upon the whole world. But the Apostle testifies that they will say, “Peace and security.” The Lord speaks this concerning the elect, but the Apostle concerning the reprobate. Therefore we should understand that what the Lord foretold is not now being fulfilled, but will rather happen then, when tribulation will affect the whole world in such a way that it belongs to the Church suffering tribulation throughout the world, not to those who persecute it. For they will say, “Peace and security,” so that sudden destruction may come upon them and the Lord’s coming may seize them like a thief in the night, [Col. 1378D] while, on the contrary, the one who loves the Lord’s appearing will rejoice and exult.

This also should be noted: after Antichrist’s death, forty-five days will be granted for the amendment of those predestined to life who fell during Antichrist’s persecution. But those not foreordained to life will not be corrected even by the death of their leader. Rather, clinging with all their heart to worldly things, they will rejoice, take wives, hold banquets, and build houses, saying: “We have peace and security, although our leader has died.” And when they suppose themselves thus peaceful and secure, the Judge will suddenly appear and condemn all such people.

> “But you, brothers, are not in darkness, so that [Col. 1379A] that day should seize you like a thief. For you are all children of light and children of the day; you are not of the night nor of darkness.”

The Lord’s day will be unexpected for them, so that, because of their hearts’ blindness, it may entrap them unto death. But you, brothers, are not in the darkness of ignorance, unbelief, or worldly desires, so that that day may seize you like a thief unto death. For those are in darkness and do not watch against the thief’s coming who, presuming upon their desires and dissolving in this world’s delights, swell with pride and rise up against the humble, while insulting the saints who understand and keep the narrow way leading to life (Matt. 7; Luke 13). But you are not such, because the desires of the world do not blind you.

For you are all children of light—that is, of Christ, who says: “I came as light into the world, that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness” (John 12)—and children of God, that is, of the Church of saints, which Christ, the sun of righteousness, illuminates. Truly you are children of Christ and of the Church, because you are not children of night—that is, of the devil, who is night, concerning which holy Job says: “May a dark storm possess that night” (Job 3)—nor children of darkness, that is, of unbelievers and the wicked, who, if converted, will hear: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5). [Col. 1379B]

Or: you are all children of light, namely faith, and children of day, namely holy conduct. And lest anyone suppose one can be partly of day and partly of night, I add that you are not of night—that is, ignorance or unbelief—nor of darkness, that is, evil deeds. For children of night and darkness are unbelievers and the wicked. They are children of night and darkness, I say, who perform every evil deed; and they are so much children of night that they fear to be seen doing what they do. Those who perform such things publicly are indeed in the sunlight, but in the darkness of their hearts.

> “Therefore let us not sleep, as the rest do, but let us watch and be sober. For those who sleep sleep by night, and those who get drunk get drunk by night. But we who belong to the day should be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love, and the helmet, the hope of salvation. For God has not appointed us for wrath but for obtaining salvation through our [Col. 1379C] Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us, so that whether we watch or sleep, we may live together with him. Therefore comfort one another and build up one another, as you also do.”

Since we are not of the night, therefore let us not sleep—that is, let us not become sluggish amid worldly goods—as the rest do, namely unbelievers who belong to the night. Rather, let us watch: let us await with wakeful hearts the coming of the hidden Judge, recognizing that all these things are transitory and soon to perish. And let us be sober, that is, let us use these things soberly, not as our own goods, but as things given for our support.

Let us not sleep: let us not be complacent and idle, as though it were sufficient for us simply to have embraced the Christian religion and we might therefore act negligently. Rather, let us watch: let us drive away from ourselves the darkness of bodily indulgence and negligence, and keep the eyes of the mind open for the sight of the true light. And let us be sober: let us avoid the intoxication of worldly desires.

It is right that we, who do not belong to night, flee sleep and drunkenness. For those who sleep—that is, who take delightful ease and rest in present things—sleep by night, that is, they delight in wickedness. Those who are drunk—that is, whom love of the world intoxicates so that they use transient things without restraint—are drunk in the night of the heart. For wickedness is night, in which they fell asleep and became intoxicated by desiring these earthly things. All these apparent felicities of the world are dreams of sleepers. [Col. 1379D] As one who sees treasures in dreams is rich while asleep but poor when awake, so all these vain things of the world in which people rejoice appear in sleep and are seen in drunkenness. Lovers of such things will wake and become sober when they do not wish to, if they do not now wake and become sober when this is beneficial; and they will find that those things were dreams and passed away like a shadow.

Those who belong to night sleep and become drunk. But we who belong to day should be sober: let us use temporal things moderately, and not forget, because of present goods, to seek future—that is, eternal—goods. We should be sober, I say. We shall be able to be so if we are clothed with the breastplate of faith and love—that is, if faith and love, like a breastplate, fortify us on every side against all the devil’s darts, namely every temptation of vices. For as a breastplate protects the vital organs, so faith and love protect our heart lest it be wounded by onrushing vices.

Although the Apostle now calls faith a breastplate, elsewhere he calls it a shield of faith (Eph. 6). Faith is therefore a shield because it receives and repels the weapons of enemies. It is also a breastplate because it does not permit our inward parts to be pierced. Likewise love is our breastplate, because it does not allow the darts of evil spirits to penetrate into our inmost heart. Let us also be clothed with the helmet, namely the hope of salvation, so that hope, reaching upward toward eternal salvation, may envelop—that is, protect—the head of the inner person, namely our mind, lest it be wounded by the blows of enemies, that is, by demonic temptations in this [Col. 1380A] conflict with vices. For hope protecting the head of the mind is our helmet; and it is called the hope of salvation because through hope we come to salvation.

And it is rightly called hope of salvation, because God has not appointed us for wrath but for obtaining salvation. That is, he has not placed us in hope for the purpose of going into the wrath of condemnation, but in order that we may obtain salvation by doing good works. Salvation is not given to the idle, but to those who obtain it through the merit of good works. And this comes through our Lord Jesus Christ, because no merit of righteousness could obtain salvation for us except through the mediator between God and human beings.

Or, we should be sober and put on the weapons of virtues because God has not appointed us for wrath but for obtaining salvation. That is, he has not ordered and determined us for the purpose of exercising wrath [Col. 1380B] upon us, but to obtain us for salvation through Christ the mediator, who died for us—that is, who by his death redeemed us from eternal death—so that whether we watch, that is, live in the body, or sleep, that is, rest in death’s sleep, we may live together with him. That is, may our mind always be and live with him, whether we live in this world or sleep in the grave.

Therefore—that is, because this is our hope, that Christ died for us for a time so that we may always live with him—comfort one another. Let each among you comfort another amid the adversities of present tribulations or at the death of loved ones. Build one another up: mutually build yourselves up in virtues through good conversations and good examples, so that both individually and collectively you may be built into a temple for the Lord. Build up, I say, as you also do. He commends them so that he may increasingly stir them to zeal in doing good.

Up to this point he has spoken generally to all. But now he turns particularly to admonish subjects to honor and love their prelates; afterward he will admonish prelates to correct their subjects. Since they were humble and ready to obey, he imposes upon them what he wishes them to do not by commanding but by entreating. Thus at the beginning of the Epistle he did not call himself an apostle, because they did not need to be compelled by apostolic authority. So also now, prelates of the Church ought humbly to entreat good subjects that they may advance to what is better, rather than imperiously compel them to do good unwillingly. For see what the Apostle adds:

> “But we ask you, brothers, to recognize those who labor among you, preside over you in the Lord, and admonish you; and to hold them in more abundant love, and because of their work be at peace with them.” [Col. 1380C]

All of you comfort and build up one another, as we admonish. But you, brothers who are subjects, we ask you to recognize—that is, to show through reverence and honor that you recognize—those who labor among you in ecclesiastical government, who preside over you in the Lord, that is, by the Lord’s ordination or in matters pertaining to the Lord, and who admonish you to avoid evil, do good, and advance to better things. Recognize them in such a way that you hold them in more abundant love: love and honor them more than others, and support them with bodily goods.

For I wish you to honor presbyters out of love and show them reverence. And because of their work—that is, because they rebuke you or sometimes even punish you, seeing that it ought to be done—be at peace with them. Do not murmur; do not abandon the friendship of peace if they cut away your vices. Instead, preserve peace more firmly for that very reason, because they correct you not from hatred but from love.

The Apostle aptly confronts the perversity of those who, when rebuked or beaten for their faults, cast away the peace which they had with their prelates and cause discord and murmuring. He commands them to have peace with their prelates because of the prelates’ work. Or it may be divided thus: “Hold them more abundantly in love because of their work,” that is, love more those who admonish and correct you, as it is written: “Reprove the wise man, and he will love you” (Prov. 9); and “be at peace with them,” so that you never disagree with them, even if they sharply rebuke or beat you.

> “But we ask you, brothers: correct the disorderly; comfort the faint-hearted; support the weak; be patient toward all. See that no one returns evil for evil to anyone, but always pursue what is good toward one another and toward all.” [Col. 1380D]

Now his address is to prelates. We asked subjects to honor their superiors and be at peace with them. But you, brothers who preside, we ask you: correct the disorderly—that is, discipline the meddlesome, those who disturb the peace of quietness, the undisciplined and the wandering. Correct them, lest you be hirelings. For one who refrains from correcting such people because he fears losing the gift he was accustomed to receive from them, or fears suffering hostility from them, is a hireling, not a shepherd.

Also comfort the faint-hearted: those whose courage is slight in bearing present adversities and who grieve over evils happening to them, or those who fail in hope because of the greatness of their sins. Support the weak: do not reject those weak in their conscience or conduct, but receive them for healing [Col. 1381A] as spiritual physicians. And if, in carrying out this duty, you suffer some injury from your subjects, be patient toward all who trouble you.

Also see to this—that is, attend with careful consideration—that no one returns evil for evil to another. Not only should you yourselves not return evil for evil, but see that no one else does so. You too return evil for evil if you do not provoke to repentance those who inflict evil upon you. For in this place we should understand that evil is rather returned for evil when someone who ought to be corrected is not corrected but is neglected through a perverse indulgence.

Sometimes people think those who correct them are their enemies. Thus, after saying, “Correct the disorderly,” he added, “Comfort the faint-hearted.” For if someone begins to lose heart and is troubled because of correction, then he must be comforted. Support the weak, lest they fall through weakness. If weakness has made someone stagger, let love receive him in its bosom. And then: “See that no one returns evil for evil to anyone.” Therefore correction, when it is done, is not evil. But one returns evil for evil to the person from whom he withholds correction. See that no one ever does this to anyone; rather, always pursue among yourselves, mutually, and toward all others what is good and right.

> “Always rejoice in the Lord; pray without ceasing; give thanks in all things. For this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for all of you.” [Col. 1381B]

These things are said generally to all. Although you often suffer adversities, nevertheless do not grieve, but always rejoice, in prosperity as well as adversity. But since it is evil to rejoice in worldly joy, I add that you should rejoice in the Lord, not in the world or in yourselves. Rejoice in the Lord, so that your joy and glory may be within, in him.

Pray without ceasing: that is, do not omit the fixed times of prayer on any day. But the continual desire of the heart is also continual prayer. For can we bend the knee, prostrate the body, or raise the hands without ceasing, so that this may be said to us: “Pray without ceasing”? But whoever now wishes to interrupt praying should not interrupt desiring. Thus Moses prayed: though silent, the Lord said to him, “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exod. 14). [Col. 1381C] For he cried in his heart although he said nothing with his mouth. Thus abiding desire and unceasing love are the continual prayer of the saints.

Give thanks to God in all things. True humility in believers is neither to be proud in anything, nor to murmur in anything, nor to be ungrateful or complaining, but to give thanks to God and praise him in all God’s judgments, whose works are all either just or benevolent. Therefore, in everything that happens to you, give thanks to God. And you ought not do these things unwillingly—that is, always rejoice, pray, and give thanks—because this is God’s will: God wills you to do these things. This will is in Christ Jesus, because through Christ’s benefaction the will of God has granted human beings the power to do these things. And this will of God is for all of you: God wills all of you, greater and lesser alike, to do these things.

> “Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies. But test everything; hold fast what is good; abstain from every appearance of evil.” [Col. 1381D]

Because some among them had spiritual gifts but were prevented by others, through envy, from exercising them and were not permitted to prophesy, while their prophecies were scorned by rivals, the Apostle now says: “Do not quench the Spirit,” and so forth. This is not because the Holy Spirit can be quenched, but because those who act as though they wish him quenched are rightly called, so far as lies in them, his extinguishers.

“Do not quench the Spirit,” he says. Then, as if explaining what he meant, he added: “Do not despise prophecies.” Therefore, in relation to themselves, those who despise prophecies quench the Spirit, because they attempt to extinguish and nullify the fire of the Holy Spirit which illumines and inflames prophets to speak. Do not quench the Spirit: that is, if the Holy Spirit reveals something to someone, do not forbid that person to speak what he perceives. And do not despise prophecies: do not suppose false, or neglect, what the saints have foretold through the Holy Spirit; rather, believe it true and receive it reverently.

Yet, according to John: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are from God” (1 John 4). Hence he adds here: “But test everything; hold fast what is good.” Honor prophecies, but do not indiscriminately receive the sayings of everyone. Test everything—that is, examine all things by reason, whether they are good or evil; retain whatever is found good. After examining each thing and discovering by certain testing what each is, retain what you know to be good. Conversely, abstain from every appearance of evil: that is, abstain not only from what is truly evil, but even from the very semblance of evil. If something has an evil appearance and suggests something evil, even if it is not evil, nevertheless abstain from it, lest by its evil appearance you give people an evil example. For you ought not give people occasion for evil suspicion concerning you, even when you possess no evil conscience. [Col. 1382A]

> “May the God of peace himself sanctify you wholly, so that your spirit and soul and body may be preserved entire, without complaint, for the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Faithful is he who called you, who will also do it.”

I indeed admonish you thus to live and devote yourselves to holiness, but may God himself accomplish in you what I admonish. May the God of peace—that is, the God to whom we have been reconciled through Christ, who is our peace, and who can remove the disturbance of present tribulations—sanctify you inwardly and outwardly in every respect, so that no part of you may be without sanctification.

May he sanctify you in such a way that your spirit may be preserved entire—that is, that by which you understand; your soul—that by which you live; and your body—that by which you are visible and tangible. For there are three things of which a human being consists: spirit, soul, and body. Yet the first two are distinguished, since soul is often named together with spirit. A certain rational part of the soul, which beasts lack, is called spirit. Therefore our ruling part is spirit. Then the life which joins this to the body is called soul. Finally, the body itself, because it is visible, is our outermost part.

That by which we reason, understand, and know is called spirit in such a proper sense that it is not the whole soul but something belonging to it: namely our rational part, by which the soul itself perceives and understands. It is not perceived by bodily senses, but is that inward sense from which *sententia* (“meaning,” “judgment”) receives its name. [Col. 1382B] In this respect we are undoubtedly set above animals, because they lack reason. For they do not possess spirit—that is, understanding and the faculty of reason and wisdom—but soul only. And if the spirit of animals is called “spirit” in the Scriptures, “spirit” is used there for soul.

Therefore let your spirit be whole, that is, wounded by no consent to sin; your soul whole, that is, not wounded by fleshly pleasures; and your body whole, that is, not injured by committing sin. Thus may the whole substance of your nature be preserved whole for the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that, when the Lord comes, he may find in you no wounds of sins. Let it be preserved whole until the Lord’s coming, that is, until the end of this present life; for as each person departs from this life, so that person will appear at the coming of the Judge. And let it be preserved without complaint, that is, so innocent that no one can justly complain of it.

For it is one thing to be without sin, which in this life is said only of the Only-Begotten [Col. 1382C] (1 Pet. 2; Luke 1; Phil. 3); it is another thing to be without complaint, which could be said even in this life of many saints. There is indeed a manner of good life concerning which no just complaint can be made even within this human life. For who could justly complain of a person who wishes evil to no one, faithfully gives counsel to those whom he can help, and does not retain the desire to take vengeance for anyone’s injuries, so that he can truthfully say: “As we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6; Luke 11)? And yet, in saying again, “Forgive as we forgive,” he declares that he is not without sin.

Therefore may you be preserved without complaint until the Lord’s coming, that is, until the end of this life, so that no one can make a complaint against you. And truly you will be preserved whole and without complaint, because God is faithful—that is, true in his promises—who called you to life and who will also bring it about that you arrive there whole.

> “Brothers, pray for us. Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss. I adjure you by the Lord that this letter be read to all the holy brothers. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Amen.”

Pray, brothers, he says, for us, that by the help of your prayer we may be delivered from evils and attain the good things we desire; and, for your part, greet all the brothers, so that by this greeting they may be filled with greater [Col. 1386B] grace and be more warmly kindled in love for us. Greet them with a kiss not wanton or feigned, but holy—that is, chaste and full of true love. I also adjure you by the Lord: if you should neglect to do these things because of a simple command, then at least do them because of the solemnity of this adjuration. I adjure you that this letter which I send you be read to all the holy brothers—that is, those sanctified by baptism—so that all may be edified and confirmed by it; or “holy,” that is, perfect, so that they too may make progress. And that you may be able to do all these things: May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you, by whose help you may accomplish them. Amen.

## ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS

[Col. 1385]

## PREFACE

[Col. 1385C]

To the Thessalonians, who were persevering or exercising themselves amid great tribulations, the Apostle writes another letter. Again he urges them to patience, showing that by God’s just judgment the good attain, through present tribulations, the glory of everlasting rest; while the wicked, because of the injuries they inflict upon the saints, undergo eternal punishments. He also shows that the day of the Lord was not imminent in their time, as they supposed because of certain of his words concerning the resurrection which he had set down in the preceding epistle. For when he said, “The dead who are in Christ shall rise first; then we who are alive, who remain, shall together be caught up with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air” (1 Thess. IV), they did not understand this and were troubled, thinking [Col. 1385D] that the Lord would come in the days of those then living. For this reason especially, writing this second letter to them from Athens, the Apostle intends to destroy such an opinion: lest, when the period in which they believed the Lord would come had passed and they did not see him come, they should judge that the other promises too had been falsely made to them and despair even of the reward of faith. For if the Apostle were thought to have lied in this matter, he would be rejected in every respect; and thus the devil would mock and deceive them through such an opinion.

Therefore the Apostle corrects this error of theirs and shows that certain definite signs must appear before the day of judgment comes: namely, first an apostasy must come, and the man of sin, who is Antichrist, must be revealed. Having removed this error, he proceeds in his customary way to moral exhortation, in which he sharply rebukes the restlessness of certain persons. Thus he begins.

## CHAPTER I

“Paul and Silvanus and Timothy, to the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

These matters have been explained above. After the greeting he begins thus:

“We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is fitting, because your faith grows exceedingly and the charity of each one of you toward the others abounds, so that we ourselves glory in you among the churches of God because of your patience and faith in all your persecutions and tribulations which you endure, as an example of the just judgment of God, that you may be counted worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you also [Col. 1387A] suffer; if indeed it is just with God to repay tribulation to those who afflict you, and to grant rest with us to you who are afflicted, at the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven with the angels of his power, in a flame of fire, inflicting vengeance upon those who have not known God and who have not obeyed the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

He begins from their great praise, so that by praising them he may strengthen and nourish them. Yet before all that he praises in them, he gives thanks to God, signifying that they have from God all that he praises, or for which he praises them, lest perhaps they should be puffed up by what they had received from God as though they possessed it from themselves. For pride is often born from good accomplishments.

“We ought,” he says, “O brothers, always to give thanks to God for you [Col. 1387B] magnificently, as is fitting; for great blessings call for great thanksgiving. For your faith does not diminish amid tribulations, but grows exceedingly—that is, it becomes greater daily and overcomes adversities; or it advances so greatly that it accomplishes more than we commanded. Likewise, the charity of each of you toward the others—that is, among yourselves—abounds, overflowing abundantly. And because your faith thus grows exceedingly and your charity abounds, we ought therefore to give thanks to God for you, not praise you as though you had this from yourselves.

“Your faith and charity grow and abound so greatly that we ourselves, who would not glory in a small matter, glory in you among the churches of God—that is, among the churches of the faithful, to whom we give your example. See, then, that you do not become an example of failure. We glory [Col. 1387C] among the churches of the saints in you—that is, in the good things that are in you and are increasing. We glory, namely, because of your patience and faith: because you neither fail nor murmur, but are patient and keep the faith amid all your persecutions from place to place, and amid tribulations—that is, torments and afflictions—which come upon you in one place. You endure these as an example of the just judgment of God.

“It is as if he said: While you, who act so rightly, endure such harsh things, what do you give except an example of God’s just judgment? For from your punishment one must infer how he strikes those with whom he is angry, if he permits you to be afflicted thus when he delights in you; or how he will strike those upon whom he executes just judgment, if he even torments you thus, whom he cherishes while correcting you mercifully. From this one understands [Col. 1387D] how he will not spare the wicked, as branches cut off for burning, when he does not spare the righteous because their purification must be completed. Hence Peter also says: “It is time for judgment to begin from the house of the Lord” (1 Pet. IV). But if it begins first with us, what will be the end of those who have not believed the Gospel of God?

“This is an example of the future Judgment, now seen in the affliction of the godly. But if they are now severely judged for their slight sins, the wicked will be judged far more severely at the end for their crimes. You therefore endure the lashes of present tribulations so that, purified through this, you may be counted worthy in the kingdom of God—that is, in eternal blessedness, into which no unclean person will enter, because he is unworthy. But through these [Col. 1388A] sufferings you are made worthy of that kingdom, for which you also suffer—not for human favor, nor for any crime. For your mind seeks nothing else in return for these sufferings except the kingdom of God, and you have committed no crime for which you should suffer such things.

“I said that you endure them as an example of the just judgment of God, by which your adversaries are punished and you are counted worthy in God’s kingdom.
