Yet this will occur on the condition that it is just before God to give punishment to them and rest to you: that is, if their works are so wicked that God judges it just to repay them eternal torments for these things, and if your works are truly so good before him that he judges it just to recompense you with everlasting rest. For God judges differently from man: he often approves what we disapprove, [Col. 1388B] and condemns what we praise. For God’s judgments are subtle and just.

“Therefore, lest these persons become too secure regarding their future salvation and begin to act negligently, and lest, being too certain of their adversaries’ damnation, they begin to despair of their conversion, the Apostle gives a fittingly balanced statement about both. ‘You endure,’ he says, ‘as an example of the just judgment of God, that you may be counted worthy in his kingdom—provided, however, that it is just before God to repay eternal tribulation to those who temporarily afflict you, and to grant everlasting rest with us to you who are afflicted temporarily.’ This rest will be not in the present life but at the revelation of the Lord Jesus: that is, when the Lord is revealed and openly appears before all, to render to each according to his work [Col. 1388C] (Matt. XIX).

“I mean the Lord coming from heaven with the angels of his power—that is, those through whose ministry he will show his power when through them he chooses the good and casts the wicked out—and coming in a flame of fire. Not that he is surrounded by flame, but in effect, because he will burn up his enemies. I mean a fire inflicting vengeance—that is, bringing punishment—upon those who have not known God, namely unbelievers; and upon those who have not obeyed the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, namely those who had faith but neglected to keep the Lord’s commands. He who knows sins more gravely than one who does not know.

“Yet no one should therefore flee into the darkness of ignorance in order to seek excuse there. For it is one thing not to know and another to have been unwilling to know. For the will is condemned in the man of whom it is said: ‘He would not understand, that he might act well’ [Col. 1388D] (Ps. XXXV). But that ignorance which belongs not to those unwilling to know, but to those who simply do not know, excuses no one so as to prevent his burning in everlasting fire if he did not believe because he had not heard what he should believe—though perhaps he may burn more mildly. And if those who did not know God are to be burned in eternal fire, what will happen to those who persecuted God’s preachers or servants because of his name? Or if those who did not obey the Gospel they had received are to suffer forever, what will those suffer who knowingly and willingly transgressed the very commands of that Gospel?”

“They shall pay eternal penalties in destruction, away from the face [Col. 1389A] of the Lord and from the glory of his power, when he comes to be glorified in his saints and to be made admirable in all who have believed, because our testimony was believed among you on that day. For this reason we also pray always for you, that our God may count you worthy of his calling and fulfill every desire for goodness and every work of faith in power, so that the name of our Lord Jesus Christ may be glorified in you, and you in him, according to the grace of our God and of the Lord Jesus Christ.”

That fire will inflict vengeance—that is, will bring punishment for their sins—upon unbelievers who have not known God and upon vain believers who have not obeyed the Gospel of the Lord. Both will pay—that is, endure—penalties not for an hour but eternally; not merely with excessive pain, but in destruction—that is, [Col. 1389B] in everlasting death—far removed from the face, that is, from the presence of the Lord’s vision and from the glory of his power, lest they see that glory which his power will manifest in himself and give to the saints, as it is written: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God.”

For at the judgment both good and wicked will see the form of the servant; then, once the wicked have been hurled into Gehenna, the good will be raised up to behold the brightness of his divinity. Then, for their ignorance and disobedience, the wicked will pay eternal penalties, cast away from the face of the Lord, when he comes to be glorified in his saints—that is, to fill and illuminate his saints with his glory, so that, seeing him as he is (1 John III), they may become like him and he may appear glorious in them—and to be made admirable, that is, to be shown worthy of admiration and [Col. 1389C] praise in all, even the lesser ones, who have believed with the faith that works through love (Gal. V).

He will then be made admirable in those who believed: the wicked will marvel at the great salvation of the righteous whom they despised here, and the righteous themselves will marvel at their own salvation (Wis. V). Therefore, as was said, he will then grant you rest with us because our testimony—that is, whatever we testified to you concerning what would take place on that day, namely the glory of the good and the punishment of the wicked—was believed by you, although it was above you—that is, beyond your understanding. For although what we said was beyond comprehension and your understanding could not grasp it, nevertheless you gave faith to our testimony.

Or it was “over you,” that is, ruling over you, since you did not seek reasons. Or, as if speaking from a higher place, we uttered testimony over you, which you believed concerning those things that will happen on that day. On that day, that our God may count you worthy—that is, may deem you worthy—of his calling, we also pray always for you. That is, we have not merely instructed you concerning that glorification of the righteous and damnation of the wicked, but we pray constantly for you that you may attain that glory: namely, that our God may count you worthy by his calling, that is, judge you worthy to be called to the kingdom, saying, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” [Col. 1389D] (Matt. XXV), and that he may fulfill every desire of your goodness—that is, fully accomplish whatever good things you desire.

Or, meanwhile in this age, may he fulfill in you every desire for goodness—that is, may he make you fully desire every good thing—and fulfill in you the work of faith, that is, every good work which faith requires, and this in the power of effective action. Or confession is properly the work of faith: that what the mind believes, the tongue may confess. May he fulfill in you the work of faith, that is, confession, and this in the strength of steadfastness, so that you may in no way be turned from the confession of faith. May he fulfill this in you in such a way that, in the present life, the name of our Lord Jesus Christ may be glorified in you—that is, may appear clear and glorious in your good works—and that you may be glorified in him in the other life. And this according to the grace of God our Father and of the Lord Jesus Christ: that is, according to what the Father and the Son, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, freely bestow in goodness upon their elect beyond what they can merit.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 1390B]

“Now we beseech you, brothers, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together to him, that you not be quickly moved from your understanding or alarmed, neither by a spirit, nor by a word, nor by a letter supposedly sent by us, as though the day of the Lord were imminent.”

Having won their good will and praised them, he confidently comes to his principal purpose: the removal of the error by which they had been especially troubled. It is as though he said: “You indeed, brothers, patiently endure all things because of the recompense you hope for from God; but we beseech you that you be moved in no way from the understanding of the catholic faith.”

“Now we beseech you,” [Col. 1390C] he says, “brothers, not by some slight matter but by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, if you wish it to benefit you, and by the coming of our gathering together to Christ himself, if you wish to be among it, when all of us who are elect shall meet and be gathered together unto the Savior himself: that you not be quickly moved—that is, that you not quickly waver—from your understanding, that is, from the understanding of catholic truth, or from the pure understanding which you have hitherto possessed. Do not be quickly moved. For if you are moved, it is quick, because nothing is brought upon you that endures long; nor be alarmed as though by the near danger of impending judgment.

“Do not be moved or alarmed by a spirit: that is, if an evil spirit, appearing in a vision as an angel of light (2 Cor. XI), persuades you that the day of the Lord is imminent in your days; or if anyone says that he has learned this through the Holy Spirit, do not believe him. Nor be moved or alarmed by a word: that is, if anyone present among you should seek to establish this in a public discourse and among other matters, never believe him. Nor by a letter from anyone absent, as though [Col. 1390D] sent by us—that is, sent by our command or under our name—do not be deceived. Or: do not be troubled by the letter which we previously sent you; that is, do not suppose that our letter says that Christ will come in your days.

“Do not be frightened by all these things as though the day of the Lord were imminent—that is, as though the day were near at hand in which the Lord will show his power by punishing the wicked and saving the good. The Apostle does not say this because he wishes them to grow dull in security, act negligently, and remain unprepared; rather, he says it lest, in the very disturbance of expecting the Lord’s most speedy coming, they might be deceived into receiving the devil in place of Christ. For this was what the devil sought: to cause himself to be worshipped under Christ’s name, as he also wished to persuade blessed Martin.

“That this might not happen, the Apostle describes the time and signs of the Lord’s coming. For their minds had been moved and troubled into hoping that Christ would then come in his majesty by either an occasion arising from the epistle which he himself had sent them, which they had not understood; or a false revelation that had deceived them in a dream; or the conjecture of some who interpreted for that time the words of Isaiah, Daniel, and the Gospels foretelling Antichrist. The Apostle remedies this error and explains what must be awaited before Christ’s coming, so that when those things have occurred, Christ may then be expected. [Col. 1391B]

“Yet sparing their modesty or tenderness, he does not openly rebuke them because they had been moved, but beseeches them not to be moved, and first praises them greatly. For we often correct the fainthearted more effectively if we recall their good deeds and, concerning whatever they have done disorderly, do not rebuke it as already committed but forbid it as though it were not yet to be committed. Thus the favor bestowed by what we approve increases those things, while against what we rebuke a modest exhortation more strongly prevails among the fainthearted.

“Hence the outstanding teacher, as has been said, when he perceived that the Thessalonians, persevering in the preaching they had received, were troubled in a certain faintheartedness about the nearness of the world’s end, first praises in them what he sees to be strong; then, by cautious admonition, strengthens what is weak. For after saying many things worthy of praise, he added what we are discussing: ‘Now we beseech you, brothers, by the coming of the Lord,’ and so forth. For the true teacher acted so that they should first hear praised what they recognized in themselves, and afterward hear what they should follow when exhorted; thus the praise given beforehand might steady their minds, lest the admonition following should shake them.

“And since he knew that they had been disturbed by suspicion of the near end, he did not rebuke them now as already disturbed, but, as though unaware of what had passed, forbade them still to be disturbed; so that, while they believed themselves unknown to their preacher in the very instability of their agitation, they might become more blameworthy in proportion as they feared being known by him.”

[Col. 1391D] “Let no one deceive you in any way” (Matt. XXIV; Eph. V). “For unless the apostasy comes first and the man of sin is revealed, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above every being called god or worshipped, so that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself as though he were God—do you not remember that, while I was still with you, I told you these things? And now you know what restrains him, so that he may be revealed in his own time. For the mystery of iniquity is already at work; only let him who now restrains continue to restrain, until he is removed from the midst. And then that lawless one shall be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus shall kill with the spirit of his mouth” (Isa. XI), “and destroy by the brightness of his coming—him whose coming is according to the working of Satan, with every power and with lying signs and wonders [Col. 1392A] and with every deception of iniquity for those who are perishing, because they did not receive the love of truth in order to be saved. Therefore God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe a lie, in order that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity.”

“See,” he says, “that no one deceives you in any way—that is, that no one draws you into error, whether by a spirit, or by a word, or by a letter, or by any other manner of deception, so that you believe the day of the Lord to be imminent. For it will not be imminent unless first the apostasy comes: either so that all nations subject to the Roman empire depart from it; or so that the multitude of churches depart from the Roman pontiff; or so that a multitude of persons depart from the faith. And unless there is revealed—that is, made manifest and shown—the man of sin, foretold by the words of all the prophets: namely Antichrist. He is not the God of righteousness, as he will pretend, but a man of sin, in whom is the source of all sins; and the son of perdition—that is, of the devil, who is the destruction of all—or the son of perdition, born in order to destroy others and at last to be destroyed himself.

“This pestilential man opposes Christ, and therefore is called Antichrist, that is, contrary to Christ. Or he opposes the salvation of all and exalts himself—that is, raises himself—above every being called god or worshipped: above those who are gods by title rather than essence, and above him who is God by nature. For even a human being may sometimes be called “god,” as it is said of Moses: “Behold, I have made you God to Pharaoh” [Col. 1392C] (Exod. VII). But a mere human being cannot be worshipped as God. Since Antichrist raises himself both above all holy persons and above the very power of divinity, by exacting for himself the name of glory, he attempts to surpass both what is called God and what is worshipped as God.

“And he will so exalt himself that he will sit and command himself to be worshipped in the temple of God (2 Cor. VI), perhaps the temple which is in Jerusalem. Or rather, he will sit in the temple of God—that is, in the minds of Christians whom he will deceive, who had been God’s temple. For according to this sense it is said in the Psalm: ‘O God, the nations have entered into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple’ (Ps. LXXVIII). For the nations defiled God’s temple when pagans compelled certain Christians in persecution to sacrifice to idols. In a temple of this sort Antichrist will sit, showing himself as though he were God. That is, he will raise himself by the arrogance of worldly glory above the minds of those whom he can deceive, so that, although he is a sinful man, he scorns to be considered a man and falsely declares himself God over human beings.

“Unless the Roman empire has first thus been laid waste and Antichrist has thus manifestly preceded, Christ will not come; for he is to come in order to destroy Antichrist. Do you not retain in your heart that I used to tell you these very things which I now write in a letter, when I was still with you, speaking in person: namely, that Christ would not come unless Antichrist came first? You should have firmly retained this and not wavered through suspicion of the Lord’s near coming. I said in person that Antichrist would come first.

“And now you know what restrains him: that is, you know very well what cause prevents Antichrist from coming now. Because he said that they knew, he did not wish to say it openly here; and therefore we, who do not know what they knew, can with difficulty, if at all, attain to what he meant in this place. Yet it is understood concerning the Roman empire. He seems for this reason not to have wished openly to say that it would be destroyed: those who ruled it thought it eternal, and he did not wish to stir them up against the Christian name. For if he had openly and boldly said, ‘Antichrist will not come unless the Roman empire is first destroyed,’ a just cause of ruin might seem to arise against the Church, then newly born.

“Therefore he veiled what he said in a certain obscurity, lest he provoke the Romans to persecute the Church or hinder them from receiving the faith. ‘You know,’ he says, ‘what now restrains him, so that he does not come now.’ What restrains him is this: that the things which must occur before his coming must first occur—namely the apostasy, so that nations depart from the Roman empire, as we see has already happened. And an even more grievous apostasy must first occur: a vast multitude of those who bear the name of Christianity must depart from religion, or from the Christian faith itself, so that when Antichrist comes they may readily receive him. These and similar things are what still restrain and delay him. For he ought not and cannot come unless the human race has become so depraved that, when he comes, it immediately receives him.

“You know what now restrains him—that is, what is the cause of his delay—so that he may be revealed, that is, appear more manifestly to all, in his own time: that is, at a time suitable to him, when Satan is loosed and released with all his powers against the Church. For then will be Antichrist’s time, because then he will reign when he does whatever he wishes; therefore he will then be openly revealed.

“For the mystery of iniquity is already at work in his members. That is to say: through the many evils and sins by which Nero, the most impure of the Caesars, oppresses the world, the coming of Antichrist is being brought forth; and what he will do later is partially fulfilled in Nero. Thus in Nero, whose works seemed like those of Antichrist, and in others like him, that adversary has already, from the very time of the apostles, worked the mystery of iniquity; for Nero and others of this kind prefigure him, just as Abel, Isaac, and David prefigured Christ. Only this remains: that he who now rules should rule until he is removed from the midst—that is, until he is taken away from the midst.

“Only let the Roman empire, which now holds almost all nations, hold them until it is removed from the midst—that is, until that power is taken away from the midst of the world, because people from every direction flocked to Rome as to a head. Or ‘be removed from the midst’ means that that power is taken away from common possession; for to be removed from the midst is to be taken out of the common sight of people. And then that lawless one will be revealed, whom no one doubts to signify Antichrist.

“Or thus: you know what now restrains him—perhaps this, that not all are yet so depraved that they would immediately receive him—so that he may be revealed in his own time, when people are ready to receive him. For the mystery of iniquity is already at work. It is as though he said: Then Antichrist will be seen manifestly; for even now he secretly works his hidden designs in the hearts of the wicked. In the evil and deceitful who are in the church, the mystery of iniquity is already at work. It is called a mystery because it appears hidden: such workers present themselves as ministers or servants of Christ, whereas in truth they are ministers of Antichrist. For their iniquity is mysterious—that is, veiled by the name of piety—and under the appearance of good they commit evil.

“Only let him who now holds the faith of the Christian religion hold it—that is, persevere firmly in it—until the mystery of iniquity is removed from the midst of the Church, though now hidden, and becomes manifest, when all who belong not to Christ but to Antichrist openly go out from the Church. And then the lawless one will be revealed.

“Or: let the Roman pontiff, who now holds the churches, hold them until iniquity is removed from the midst—that is, until there proceeds from the Roman Church itself, which is the center and heart of the churches, an iniquity on account of which many churches depart from it. These very obscure words of the Apostle are understood in various ways; yet he discloses no span of time. For he says, ‘that he may be revealed in his own time,’ but does not say after how long this will happen. He adds, ‘for the mystery of iniquity is at work,’ but does not state how long it will work.

“Likewise, what follows—‘only let him who now restrains continue to restrain, until he is removed from the midst; and then that lawless one will be revealed’ [Col. 1394C]—teaches us that Antichrist will become manifest. But the Apostle says nothing, not even obscurely, about after what time he is to be revealed. For what ‘he who now restrains’ should restrain may mean, or what ‘until he is removed from the midst’ intends, each person can so adapt as to understand or at least suspect something. Yet however one reads the text, how long he is to restrain, or after what intervals of time he is removed from the midst, is entirely silent here.

“But however long or short this interval may be, all the things that must first occur will occur within it; and then Antichrist, the source of all iniquity, will be openly revealed. He is not to be feared either now in his members or then in himself, because the Lord Jesus himself will kill him by the spirit of his mouth—that is, by the invisible [Col. 1394D] power of his Spirit, proceeding from himself as from the Father, namely by divine power and the command of his majesty, whose commanding is doing—not by a multitude of armies, not by the strength of soldiers, not by the assistance of angels. But as darkness is driven away by the rising of the sun, so the Lord will destroy and annihilate him by the brightness of his coming.

“Moreover, as we understand from the book of Daniel (Dan. XI), he will be killed on the Mount of Olives, in his pavilion upon his throne, namely in that place from which the Lord ascended into heaven (Acts I). After his killing, forty-five days will be granted for repentance to those predestined to life who passed through that persecution not without stumbling. But whether, after those forty-five days are completed, the Lord comes at once, or whether some little time still remains [Col. 1395A], we do not know at all.

“Therefore the statement, ‘The Lord Jesus will kill him by the spirit of his mouth and destroy him by the brightness of his coming,’ should not be understood as though he were to be killed and destroyed at the very coming of the Judge, but beforehand. For the brightness of his coming can fittingly be understood as some splendor announcing his coming, so great that, upon seeing it, that pestilential one immediately dies from fear.

“Therefore the Lord will destroy him whose coming is according to the working of Satan: that is, who, when he comes, will do all things at the devil’s instigation, though not without understanding like madmen, who bear no blame for the evils they do. For as God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself (2 Cor. V), so the devil will be in Antichrist, deceiving the world. And as Christ says, ‘The Father abiding in me, he himself does the works’ (John XIV), so the devil abiding in Antichrist will do whatever seems good to him to do.

“His coming, then, will be according to the working of Satan in every power, because Satan will then be released to work through him in all his power. He will work by signs, which at any time signify something, and wonders, which signify something only in the future; or by lesser signs and greater wonders. These signs and wonders will be lying—that is, false—either because he will deceive mortal senses by magical phantasms, appearing to do what he does not do, or because even if they are wonders, they will draw those who believe toward falsehood.

“Therefore Satan will work through him [Col. 1395C] and through his followers in every power of opposing might, in signs and wonders of false miracles or tending toward falsehood, and in every deception of iniquity. For he will pretend to be religious in order to deceive under the appearance of piety; indeed, he will say that he is God, cause himself to be worshipped, and promise heavenly kingdoms. He will corrupt some by gifts of temporal riches; he will crush others by tortures, threats, and terrors. In every art of deception he will employ his frauds against those who perish—that is, those not predestined to life, but proceeding to destruction.

“Therefore that temptation of Antichrist will appear greater than all preceding temptations, when a godly martyr submits his body to torments and yet the torturer works miracles before his eyes. For what unbeliever will be converted to faith when even the faith of one already believing would tremble and be shaken, while the persecutor of piety also becomes a worker of power? The very man who rages with torments so that Christ may be denied will provoke by miracles so that Antichrist may be believed. Yet the Spirit of God is able to preserve the hearts of his own even amid such grievous trials.

“For by these signs and wonders those will be deceived who deserve to be deceived: namely the Jews or other unbelievers, because they did not receive the love of truth—that is, the Spirit of Christ—in order to be saved. For the Holy Spirit is called love, and Christ is truth (ibid.). Therefore, as we said, the love of truth is the Spirit of Christ. But the Jews did not receive this love [Col. 1396A] in order that they might be saved; therefore they will be deceived so that they may perish.

“Or: they did not receive the love of truth, so that they might desire not spiritual goods but carnal ones. And because they do not know how to rejoice in hope of invisible goods, they are about to rush into the snares of Antichrist, so as to believe the lie that, under his leadership, as though in the sight of their visible enemies who had visibly taken them captive, they will have visible glory. Therefore, because they did not receive the truth’s love so as to love invisible goods, which alone are true, and to be saved by receiving the Savior, God will send—that is, permit to come upon—them not the worker but the very operation, that is, the source, of error, so that they may believe the lie; for “he himself is a liar and its father” (John VIII).

“So that all who did not believe the truth of Christ but consented to the iniquity of Antichrist may be judged—that is, condemned at the coming of the Judge. God will send them the operation of error because, by his own just judgment, he will permit the devil to do these things, although the devil does them through the wicked counsel of evil persons. ‘So that all may be judged,’ he says, ‘and the rest.’ Accordingly, they will be deceived because they are to be judged, and, having been deceived, they will also be judged.

“But those to be judged are deceived by those judgments of God which are secretly just and justly secret, by which he has never ceased to judge since the beginning of the sin of rational creation; yet those deceived will be judged in the final and most manifest judgment. Indeed, if Antichrist had been born of a virgin and had come first into the world, the Jews could have had an excuse and said that truth came afterward, and so they could at first have received falsehood as truth. But since this is not so, they are to be judged—indeed, beyond doubt condemned—because, having despised Christ’s truth, they will afterward receive falsehood, that is, Antichrist.

«But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brethren beloved by God, because God has chosen us as firstfruits for salvation, in sanctification of the Spirit and faith in the truth, to which he also called you through our Gospel, for the obtaining of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.»

Those who reject the truth and embrace falsehood will be condemned; but we and you, who have embraced the truth, shall be saved, and therefore we ought to give thanks. This is what he means: We ought always to give thanks to God for you [Col. 1396D], whom he called to knowledge of himself, O brethren beloved by God, either on account of the merit of your holiness, or beloved by him freely before you had deserved anything good; and thus called through his preceding love, because he himself first loved us. We ought, I say, to give thanks to God because God chose us apostles from eternity in the counsel of his providence or wisdom; and chose us as firstfruits, that is, as the first and chief, not in the dangerous last time, but at the beginning of evangelical grace; and this for eternal salvation, in order that he might lead us into it, established in sanctification by the Spirit, who sanctifies in baptism, and in faith in the truth, not in error: for whatever our faith believes is true, nor is it deceived by the opinion of any error, as are those who follow Antichrist. [Col. 1397A] Into this faith he also called you: that is, he not only first called us, but afterwards also called you through our Gospel which we preached to you, for the obtaining of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ—that through faith you may obtain the glory which Jesus possesses. Or, “for the obtaining of Christ’s glory,” that is, that Christ might acquire you for himself, to glorify himself, so that you might be a people of acquisition and might glorify him by living well (1 Pet. 2).

“Therefore, brethren, stand firm and hold the traditions which you have learned, whether by word or by our letter. Now may our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God, even our Father, who loved us and gave eternal consolation and good hope in grace, exhort your hearts and strengthen you in [Col. 1397B] every good work and word.”

Since God has converted you to faith, so that through it you may attain glory, and since the day of the Lord is not yet at hand: therefore, brethren, stand firm in faith and do not be moved from your conviction, so that you may be able to stand steadfastly in faith and preserve the condition of uprightness in good works. Hold in heart and in works the traditions which you learned, either through our word while we were present, or through the letter which we sent you while absent. We indeed admonish you by words and letters to remain in the good; but may God himself, through his inward grace, inwardly exhort your hearts. For we labor outwardly in vain if he has not worked within. And therefore may our Lord Jesus Christ himself [Col. 1397C], who in mercy made us his own under his dominion; and God, who created us, and our Father, who adopted us as sons and loved us with fatherly affection, giving his Only-begotten for us, and through the Holy Spirit the Paraclete, which is interpreted “Comforter,” gave us eternal consolation—when amid the adversities of this present misery we already begin to taste beforehand eternal joys—and good hope, by which in grace, that is, in his gratuitous gift, since we had not deserved it, we await our return from exile to our homeland: may he, I say, the Son and the Father, who has already bestowed upon us so many and such great gifts, exhort your hearts, that is, spur your wills toward better things, and strengthen you against assailants in every good work and every good word.

## Chapter III

[Col. 1397D]

“Finally, brethren, pray for us, that the word of God may run and be glorified, as it was also among you; and that we may be delivered from troublesome and evil people. For faith does not belong to all. But the Lord is faithful: he will strengthen you and guard you from evil. But we have confidence concerning you, brethren, in the Lord, that you both do and will do the things which we command you. May the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God and the patience of Christ.”

We have spoken and instructed you concerning those matters which concern you, regarding how you ought to act. But finally—that is, concerning what pertains to others—brethren, pray for us, that the word of God which we speak may run without hindrance among all nations, so that many may be converted quickly. [Col. 1398A] “May it run,” that is, may it hasten without obstacle to reach everyone; and “be glorified,” that is, become clear and intelligible to those hearing it, just as it ran and was glorified among you. And pray that we may be delivered, lest we be detained by troublesome and evil people—that is, unbelievers who resist us—so that we may freely travel everywhere to preach. May we be delivered from troublesome persons, that is, unbelievers who resist the truth, dispute against it in words, persecute us through malice, and torture us with torments. I say, “that we may be delivered,” because faith does not belong to all: that is, faith does not pertain to everyone; not all have yet received the faith who will receive it. Or, pray that we may be delivered, because faith does not belong to all: it does not pertain to everyone; not all will believe, [Col. 1398B] even though you pray, but only those who have been preordained. For the capacity to have faith, like the capacity to have charity, belongs to human nature; but having faith, like having charity, belongs to the grace of believers. God makes unbelievers believe through the prayers of the faithful in order to show that he himself does it. For no one is so unskilled, so carnal, or so slow in understanding that he does not see God doing what he commanded people to ask him to do. Faith does not belong to all; nevertheless, do not fear those who lack faith, because the Lord is faithful, that is, true in the promises which he made to his elect, saying: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). He is faithful—that is, faithfully fulfilling what he promised—who will strengthen [Col. 1398C] you in the good and guard you from evil. He will strengthen you, that is, make you firm and stable, lest you be “tossed about and carried around by every wind of doctrine in the wickedness of men” (Eph. 4); and he will guard you from evil, not so that you suffer no adversity, but so that nothing may harm you.

We said that you should hold our traditions and fulfill the other things which we commanded; and I do not think this was in vain, but we have confidence concerning you, brethren, in the Lord, who works in you, that you both now do and always will do the things which we command you. But lest we have this confidence concerning you in vain, may the Lord—that is, the Holy Spirit—direct your hearts, that is, make your wills upright, abiding in the love of God the Father, so that you may love him with all your heart; and in the patience [Col. 1398D] of Christ, so that you may be ready willingly to suffer for Christ, as he suffered for you. The whole Trinity is declared in this brief statement. For “the Lord” is placed first; he, as we have said, is the Holy Spirit. He is rightly called Lord, like the Father and the Son, because he breathes where he wills (John 3), does whatever he wills, governs all things, and is not governed, so that all things serve him. Thus also in the preceding epistle the Apostle similarly called him Lord, saying: “May the Lord multiply you” (1 Thess. 3), and so forth. After this he treats of the meddlesome, when he adds:

“But we command you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to withdraw yourselves from every brother walking disorderly, and not according to the tradition which [Col. 1399A] they received from us. For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us (2 Cor. 11). For we were not disorderly among you; neither did we eat bread from anyone without payment, but in labor and hardship, working night and day, lest we burden any of you. Not as though we did not have the right, but in order that we might give ourselves to you as an example for imitating us. For even when we were with you, we gave you this command: if anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat. For we have heard that some among you walk disorderly, doing no work, but acting as busybodies. Now those who are such we command and exhort in the Lord Jesus Christ that, working quietly, they may eat their own bread.”

[Col. 1399B] You, indeed, as we trust, do and will do our commands; but withdraw yourselves from whoever does not do them. And this we command you, brethren: that is, concerning this matter we bring you a divine message in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, by the authority of his name, or in his glory—so that, out of reverence for his name or for the glory of his name, you may do what we say: namely, withdraw and separate yourselves from every brother, that is, every Christian, who walks disorderly—that is, who lives not as the order of nature or the order of Christian religion requires—and who walks not according to the tradition of walking, that is, of living or working, which they received from us.

Withdraw yourselves from every brother who thus walks [Col. 1399C]: that is, do not associate with him in food, drink, trade, conversation, or any other matter, except for the purpose of correcting him, lest you share in his sins. Rather, avoid him, lest you seem to encourage his perversity; thus he may be ashamed and corrected when he sees that all avoid him. Withdraw yourselves from those who do not walk according to our tradition. For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us: that is, there is no need for me to explain that tradition to you, because you know it. You know, namely, how those who wish to walk rightly ought to walk on the path upon which we walk—that is, to follow our examples. For we were not disorderly among you, like those who concern themselves with other people’s affairs, idly wandering here and there, abandoning the divine office, needlessly scrutinizing the lives [Col. 1399D] of individuals, speaking ill of brothers, and fostering murmurings, dissensions, or scandals. For while they are idle and do no work, the cunning enemy occupies their empty minds with such things, because, as it is written, “idleness has taught much wickedness” (Ecclus. 33). But we were not disorderly in this way.

Neither did we eat “without payment,” that is, without the recompense of just labor—not, I say, luxurious foods, but not even bread itself received from anyone. Rather, we worked with labor of our hands and hardship, because we labored to the point of weariness, working night and day so that we might have means of support, lest we burden any of you—that is, lest we become a burden to any of you by accepting wages. Nor did we labor as though we lacked the right to receive what was yours: that is, we did not seek sustenance by our own labor because we could not receive provisions from you, but in order that [Col. 1400A] we might give ourselves to you as an example, for you to imitate us—that you might abandon idleness and imitate us in work. For if we, though we could obtain support from preaching, preferred to live by our labor, much more ought you to prepare your bread in the sweat of your face (Gen. 5).

The Apostle labored at work among the righteous for one reason, and among the Corinthians for another. The Corinthians were grasping and occupied with many vices; and if they had given anything to the Apostle, it would have seemed to them that the Apostle ought to act more mildly toward them, not rebuke them sharply, but flatter them because of their gifts. [Col. 1400B] These people, however, were accustomed to live in idleness; and therefore the Apostle gave them in himself an example of working with their own hands, so that they might have means from which to live and to provide alms for those in need.

Therefore, it should be known that the blessed Apostle wished servants of God to perform bodily works that would end in a great spiritual reward, so that they themselves might lack neither food nor clothing and might procure these for themselves with their hands. Nor is the Apostle’s command and example contrary to what the Lord says: “Do not be anxious, saying, What shall we eat? or What shall we drink? or With what shall we be clothed?” (Matt. 6). The Lord did not forbid his servants to procure, insofar as necessity requires, the means by which they might [Col. 1400C] live honorably; rather, he forbade the superfluity of excessive concern for luxurious foods and clothing. For he did not say, “Do not be anxious for your soul, that you may eat,” but, “what you may eat”; nor, “for your body, that you may be clothed,” but, “what you may wear.” Thus he forbade excessive fastidiousness in choosing clothing and food, not the labor of work or moderate concern for necessary things.

“We gave ourselves,” he says, “as an example to you, that you might imitate us in the labor of work; for we also said this to you.” That is, not only now, while absent, do we say this to you; but even when we were present among you, we declared and commanded you that if anyone is unwilling [Col. 1400D] to work, neither should he eat. We did not say, “If anyone does not work, let him not eat,” but, “If anyone is unwilling to work, let him not eat,” because there are some who would be willing but cannot; and therefore, though they do not work, they are nevertheless blameless, because on earth there is peace for people of good will (Luke 2). But those who can and will not are rightly blamed, and even bodily food is forbidden them.

For this reason we have mentioned our labor, commanded you to act likewise, and above instructed you to withdraw yourselves from every brother walking disorderly: because we have heard—that is, it has been reported to us—that some among you walk disorderly, that is, wander from place to place throughout the day, doing nothing with their hands that is useful either to themselves or to others, but acting as busybodies. That is, with a certain superfluous and useless concern and zeal, they inquire of others what the king of the Franks is doing, what the price of grain is, [Col. 1401A] what kind of weather this year will bring, or similar matters. For here he briefly rebukes many vices: restlessness, idleness, curiosity, and excessive talk, “in which sin will not be lacking” (Prov. 10). For restlessness, while it anxiously goes about other people’s houses or curiously investigates others’ actions, falls into many offenses. Those act as busybodies who devote themselves to being able to say or hear something new.

But those who are such we command and further exhort—that is, we entreat them adjuring them by sacred things—in the Lord Jesus Christ, that at least from reverence for him they may do what we say: namely, that they may not speak or inquire curiously what this or that person is doing, nor remain idle and live from another’s labor, but, working quietly—that is, restraining their tongues [Col. 1401B] and exercising their hands in work—may eat not another’s bread but their own, that is, bread prepared by their own labor, not given to them by others.

“But you, brethren, do not grow weary in doing good. And if anyone does not obey our word through this letter, take note of that person and do not associate with him, so that he may be ashamed. Yet do not regard him as an enemy, but correct him as a brother.”

Because of the needs of the saints who, although they obey the Apostle’s commands to work quietly and eat their own bread, may nevertheless for many reasons need some supplementary support of this kind, lest those who had resources from which to provide necessities for God’s servants become negligent under this pretext, [Col. 1401C] he immediately added in foresight: “But you, brethren, do not grow weary in doing good.” We have admonished, he says, the talkative and idle to keep silence and work with their hands so that they may have sustenance. But you, brethren, who possess the substance of this world, must not, because of what we have said, grow weary of doing good to them; rather, support them from your goods. For even if they work, they may nevertheless need certain things—indeed, many things—since perhaps they are of weak and delicate constitution. We command them to work as much as they can.

“But if anyone does not obey our word”—that is, this command, or indeed any other command which we give you through this letter—“take note of him,” that is, impose upon him a mark of rebuke. Or, “take note of him through the letter”: that is, notify me by letter [Col. 1401D] who he is. “And do not associate with him,” that is, do not communicate with him, but excommunicate him and separate him from yourselves, so that, rejected by you, he may be ashamed—that is, blush when he sees himself shunned by all—and thus may be corrected and obey, even out of shame. And although I command that you not associate with him, nevertheless do not regard him as an enemy: that is, do not hate him, thinking that he is an enemy; rather, correct him with loving affection as a brother, because he has one Father with you. It is as though he said: Break outward peace with him, but preserve inward peace toward him from the depths of your heart, so that your discord may strike the mind of the sinner in such a way that peace does not depart from your hearts as something renounced.

For although dealings in common ought to be maintained with outsiders, even pagans, so that [Col. 1402A] by this they may be drawn to love our religion, dealings in common ought sometimes not to be maintained with brothers, so that they may be corrected. Outsiders should be attracted to good conduct by kindness; brothers, if they have sinned deliberately, should be corrected by measured severity.

“May the Lord of peace himself give you everlasting peace in every place. May the Lord be with all of you. The greeting is in my own hand—Paul’s—which is the sign in every letter. So I write. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all of you. Amen.”

I admonished you to correct a disobedient brother outwardly and yet to keep peace toward him inwardly within yourselves. But because you can do this only through the gift [Col. 1402B] of heavenly grace, may the Lord himself, who is giver and lover of peace and concord, give you peace not for an hour but everlasting—that is, peace having no end. May he give you peace, that is, brotherly concord; or relief from the tribulations which you suffer from adversaries; or rest from the assault of vices; or peace with God and the holy angels, which may never end or be interrupted. May he give it to you in every place: that is, both among those of your household and among outsiders, and in this age and in the age to come. And that you may have peace, may the Lord be with all of you, to defend you from evil and preserve you in good.

My greeting follows, written in Paul’s hand—that is, in my own hand, not in the hand of a secretary—which is the sign in every letter, so that by this it may be known to be mine: “Thus [Col. 1402C] I write.” Lest some impostor put his own name at the beginning in place of Paul’s name and say that the letter was his, Paul was accustomed to place this sign at the end, by which it might be recognized as coming from him. Yet this is not found in every one of his letters, but in this one, in that to the Colossians, and in the First Letter to the Corinthians. To the Galatians the same thing is said thus: “See with what large letters I have written to you with my own hand” (Gal. 6). And to Philemon: “I, Paul, have written with my own hand” (Philem. 19).

Therefore, when he says that this sign is in every letter, it should not be understood as meaning that this precise wording occurs in absolutely every one, but in many; for “every” does not always signify complete universality, but sometimes [Col. 1402D] a certain multitude. For when it is said to the Corinthians, “All the saints greet you” (2 Cor. 13), one must by no means suppose that all the saints in the whole world then greeted them through that letter, since many did not know that the letter was being written. Likewise, when it is said to the Romans, “All the churches of Christ greet you” (Rom. 16), this is not understood of all the churches throughout the world. So, where we read that “all nations told of the battles of Judas” (1 Macc. 3), we do not at all believe that every nation in Scythia, India, or remote islands was then speaking of the battles of the Maccabee. Many similar passages are also found in Holy Scripture, in which “every” does not signify universality. [Col. 1403A] Therefore the Apostle did not lie when he said that this sign was in every one of his letters, although he did not put it in each individual letter, because he spoke according to the customary language of Holy Scripture.

Then, “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ,” he says—that is, Christ’s general help and gift for all things—“be with all of you,” both greater and lesser, men and women. Or, if what [Col. 1404A] he now says, “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all of you,” is the greeting which he testifies that he writes with his own hand in every letter as a sign, then “every” may truly be understood as signifying complete universality, because this is found at the end of each letter. For all the letters which he wrote end in a prayer for grace. Amen.

## On the First Epistle to Timothy

[Col. 1403]

### Argument

[Col. 1403B]

As Luke relates, after Paul had separated from Barnabas, he traveled through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches, and came to Derbe and Lystra (Acts 15 and 16). And behold, there was there a certain disciple named Timothy, the son of a faithful widowed woman, with a Gentile father. The brethren at Lystra and Iconium bore good testimony concerning him. Paul wished him to travel with him, and, taking him, circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places. For they all knew that his father was a Gentile. Paul did not circumcise him because he thought that Timothy would receive any justification from circumcision, but lest the Jews, because of him, should be delayed in receiving the faith if he were uncircumcised.

Afterwards, when Paul had left him in Asia as bishop of the Ephesians [Col. 1403C], the false apostles, who strove to introduce carnal observances, drew strength against him from this circumcision. He himself resisted them less firmly than he ought. Therefore the Apostle writes to him, showing in some measure the arguments which he should raise against them. He also writes concerning the episcopal office: how he should instruct the Church; what sort of presbyters or deacons he should ordain; what sort of widows he should honor; how he should conduct himself in the Church and govern it. And thus he begins:

## Chapter I

“Paul, an Apostle of Jesus Christ according to the command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope, to Timothy, beloved son in faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God our Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.”

[Col. 1403D]

Paul writes to Timothy, and Paul is to be believed because he is an Apostle of Christ Jesus—that is, an envoy of the saving King—and, armed with this authority, Paul resists the false apostles. Paul is an Apostle not by his own presumption but according to God’s command. Therefore, whoever resists him resists God’s command (Rom. 13). The Holy Spirit commanded: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work to which I have called them” (Acts 13). And now Paul himself says that he is an apostle according to God’s command, because the command of the Holy Spirit is the command of God the Father, since the will and operation of the Trinity are inseparable.

Paul is an apostle according to the command of God our Savior and of Jesus [Col. 1404B] Christ our hope: that is, according to the command of the supreme Father, who saves us, and of the Son, in whom is the hope of our salvation and glory, not in carnal observance. Paul, who possesses such authority, sends this letter to Timothy, his beloved son in faith—that is, one whom he begot not in the flesh but in faith. Although Timothy was already faithful and had good testimony when Paul found him, he was nevertheless so instructed by Paul in that same faith and religion that he is rightly said to have been begotten by him in faith. Or, he writes to him “in faith” against corrupters of the faith. And he greets this son, saying: May grace be yours—that is, the gift of the Holy Spirit, with which ministers of God, that is, bishops, are armed; and mercy, through which you may be divinely delivered from the misery of this age or from every evil (1 Pet. 4); and peace, that is, tranquility of mind and a foretaste of eternal peace, so that, with vices and enemies overcome, you may rest in a peaceful Church. And may this be yours from God our Father, who created us and loves us with fatherly affection; and from Christ Jesus our Lord, that is, from him whom God anointed and appointed Savior, who also mercifully made us his own under his dominion.

“As I urged you to remain at Ephesus when I was going into Macedonia, so that you might instruct certain persons not to teach otherwise, nor to give attention to fables and endless genealogies, which provide disputes rather than the edification which is in faith.”

May grace, mercy, and peace be yours, just as I urged you to remain at Ephesus—that is, to reside as bishop among the Ephesians. Or the sense is implied: Do as I urged you [Col. 1404D] to do when I was going into Macedonia—namely, remain at Ephesus, acting in my stead in person and ordering the Church at Ephesus, which I, being absent, could not govern sufficiently—in order that you might instruct certain persons: that is, act as God’s messenger to certain persons, whose names the Holy Spirit, speaking in me, does not know, that they should not teach otherwise than we do, nor should their hearers attend to their fables and endless genealogies—that is, accounts of generations and drinking-parties, which are endless because of their length, since their end cannot be found. They are to be rejected because they produce contentious questions—that is, generate disputes—rather than, indeed more than, the edification of morals and righteousness which is in faith, not in [Col. 1405A] carnal observance.

First comes the command to repel the false teachers and their hearers, so that, once they have first been driven away, the purity of Catholic truth may then be preached and heard. He calls “fables” what elsewhere he calls traditions: things which the Jews maintain apart from the lawful and prophetic Scriptures, which they do not have in writing but retain by memory and pass from one person to another in speech; these they call *deuterosis*. There they even dare to say and believe that God created two women for a man, from which they weave genealogies truly, as the Apostle then says, endless, producing most unfruitful questions. And the false apostles, who wished to be partly Jews and partly Christians but were heretics, taught at Ephesus not only the carnal observances of the Law but also these Jewish traditions, alien to the prophetic and lawful books; and some Ephesians attended to their words. But Timothy was left at Ephesus in order to correct or expel hearers and teachers of this sort.

“But the end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith. From these things some, having wandered away, have turned aside into empty talk, wishing to be teachers of the Law, without understanding either what they say or the things concerning which they make assertions.”

They teach fables and that the Law must be fulfilled carnally; but the end of the commandment—that is, the fullness of the Law—is charity. Here “end” means not the consumption of the commandment but its completion. Thus the end of every commandment [Col. 1405C] is charity: that is, every commandment is referred to charity and fulfilled through charity. For charity, by which we love God and neighbor, securely possesses the whole greatness and breadth of the divine utterances. Therefore the end—that is, the completion—of every commandment read in either the Old or the New Testament is charity: not charity of any sort, but that which proceeds from a pure heart.

For those who live wickedly are entangled with one another in fellowship of a ruined conscience. They are said to love one another, not to wish to leave one another, to be reconciled through their conversations, to long for one another when absent, and to rejoice in each other’s presence. But this love is infernal. Therefore, in order that true Christian charity may be distinguished from such love, it is said to proceed [Col. 1405D] from a pure heart. For robbers and others of that sort do not have charity from a pure heart. A heart is pure in charity when a person is loved according to God, and nothing is loved except what ought to be loved. “A good conscience” is added because of hope; and he uses “conscience” in place of hope. For one who bears a good conscience hopes; but one whom an evil conscience stings recoils from himself and expects for himself nothing but condemnation.

Third, he says, is “faith unfeigned.” For if our faith is free from falsehood, then we neither love what ought not to be loved nor incorrectly believe what we hope, and we hope what we believe, so that our hope is not deceived in anything. But those who imagine that they believe and hope—as heretics, Jews, or Gentiles do—[Col. 1406A] have feigned faith, and therefore cannot have the charity which fulfills the commandment. He too has feigned faith who indeed believes rightly but, through fear, shame, or any other cause, does not confess what he believes, but in some way pretends not to believe.

But that charity fulfills every commandment which proceeds from a pure heart, which loves nothing except what ought to be loved; from a good conscience, that is, from the good hope borne by the conscience of one who acts well; and from unfeigned faith, that is, faith drawn not from human invention but from divine utterances; or unfeigned, that is, faith not concealed in the heart through fear but freely expressed in oral confession. From these virtues—that is, from charity out of a pure heart, from the hope of a good conscience, and from true faith—some have strayed far away [Col. 1406B], supposing that they loved God and neighbor with a pure heart when they did not love purely; supposing that they had the hope of a good conscience without the merit of religious action; and supposing that they had unfeigned faith when they had confidence but were deceived.

Such were those who preached carnal observances. They thought that they loved God, when they did not love him, as their conduct showed: they thought that they fulfilled his commands, but rather transgressed them. They thought they had a good conscience, as though because of observance of the Law, and judged that they had unfeigned faith drawn from divine utterances; whereas they had a fabricated faith, believing God to take delight in the blood of goats and bulls and in the smell of incense, which we human beings [Col. 1406C] often avoid. This is what is meant when it says that some, wandering away from charity, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith, have turned aside into empty talk: they speak vainly about the Law, desiring to be teachers of the Law while teaching that it must be observed carnally. They do not understand the words which they teach—namely, neither the things which they themselves say, that is, the words they teach and the commands of the carnal ceremonies which they themselves teach. For they do not understand what the Sabbath, circumcision, the sacrifice of goats or bulls, or anything of that kind is—that is, they do not know what is signified in these things. Nor do they understand the things concerning which they make assertions—that is, the authorities and testimonies which they employ in attempting to maintain that those ceremonies ought to be fulfilled carnally according to the letter. [Col. 1406D] For they do not perceive the intention of the Scriptures and their spiritual sense; and therefore they speak vainly, wishing to be teachers of others when they themselves know nothing.

Or, they understand neither what they say nor the things concerning which they make assertions: that is, neither the questions they propose nor the arguments by which they prove them. Heretics, or any rash presumptuous persons, act similarly when they begin to be rebuked and refuted for their perverse and false opinion. In defending what they have said with the lightest rashness and the clearest falsehood, they attempt to produce holy books to prove it, or even recite from memory many words from them which they think may serve as testimony, without understanding either what they say or the things concerning which they make assertions. [Col. 1407A] Having refuted his adversaries with these words, the Apostle immediately approves his own position, adding:

“But we know that the Law is good, if anyone uses it lawfully, knowing this: that the Law is not laid down for the righteous, but for the unjust and unsubmissive, the impious and sinful, the wicked and defiled, murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers, murderers, fornicators, men who lie with males, kidnappers, liars and perjurers, and whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine, which accords with the Gospel of the glory of the blessed God, entrusted to me.”

They themselves do not understand the law which they wish to teach, and therefore speak vainly about it; but we understand it, and therefore speak truly about it. For we know that the law is good, that is, useful, if anyone uses it lawfully, that is, as the law itself intends: namely, so that through it one may flee to grace, knowing that the law is not laid down for the just, but for the unjust.

The law is not laid down for the just, though it is good if anyone uses it lawfully. By joining these two statements, as though they were contrary to one another, the Apostle warns the reader to investigate and resolve the question. For how is the law good, if anyone uses it lawfully, if it is not laid down for the just? For who uses the law lawfully except the just person? Yet the law is not laid down for the just, but for the unjust. Must not even the unjust person, in order to become just, use the law lawfully, being brought through it, as through a pedagogue, to grace (Gal. III), by which alone he can fulfil what the law commands? For by that grace he is justified freely, that is, with no preceding merits from his own works. “Otherwise grace is no longer grace” (Rom. II); for it is given not because we have done good works, but so that we may be able to do them—not because we have fulfilled the law, but so that we may be able to fulfil the law.

Therefore the unjust person uses the law lawfully in order to become just. When this has happened, he no longer uses it as a pedagogue, once he has been instructed. For in what way is the law not laid down for the just, if it is necessary also for the unjust—not in order that the unjust may be brought by it to justifying grace, but in order that one already just may use it lawfully?

Or the person already just uses the law lawfully when he imposes it with threats upon the unjust, so that, when in them the disease of inbred concupiscence begins to increase through the stimulus of prohibition and the accumulation of transgression, they may flee through faith to justifying grace; and, delighted by the sweetness of righteousness through the gift of the Spirit (*donum Spiritus*), may escape the punishment threatened by the letter. Thus these two statements will not be contrary or at war with each other: the just person may use the good law lawfully, and yet the law may not be laid down for the just. For he was not justified by the law, but by the law of faith through which he believed.

He uses the law lawfully who, understanding why it was given, flees through its threatening to liberating grace. Therefore the law is good for him, because it greatly benefits him while it brings him to grace. But anyone who is ungrateful for this grace by which the ungodly person is justified, trusting, as though for fulfilling the law, in his own powers, ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish his own righteousness, is not subject to God’s righteousness (Rom. X). Therefore the law becomes for him not an aid to absolution but a bond of guilt; and so it is not good for him—not because the law is evil, but because sin through what is good works death in such people (Rom. VII). For through the commandment one sins more grievously who knows through the commandment how evil is what he commits.

But the law is not laid down for the just, that is, it is not imposed upon him as something above him. Rather, he is in it than under it, because he does not live his own life; the restraining law is imposed upon one who lives his own life. But the unjust person is under it, because he lives his own life, upon whom the restraining law is imposed. For, so to speak, he in some fashion lives the law itself who lives justly with delight in righteousness, enjoying not a private or passing good, but the common and enduring good. But everyone lives under the law insofar as he is a sinner, that is, insofar as he has not been changed from the old man.

For he lives his own life, and therefore the law is above him, because one who does not fulfil it is beneath it. But the pseudo-apostles, not understanding this, did not use the law lawfully; and therefore they wished to impose it upon the just, that is, upon Christians living justly through grace.

Nor is this contrary to the Apostle’s statement: the Psalmist, certainly just, prays, “Set before me, O Lord, the law, the way of thy justifications” (Ps. CXVIII), because he asks this concerning the grace of the New Testament, whereas the Apostle says, concerning the hardness of the letter of the Old Testament, that the law is not laid down for the just but for the unjust. For one who of his own accord does what the law morally commands, or more, why should the necessity of law be imposed upon him? What he does, he does in freedom, not from necessity. But the unjust person, who did not willingly choose to do good, must be compelled by the necessity of law.

Therefore, lest he seem to blame the law, the Apostle says that it is good if anyone uses it lawfully. And again, lest he seem to introduce it, he says that it is not laid down for the just, to rule over him, but for the unjust: that is, for those who did not keep the natural law; and for the unsubmissive, that is, the obstinate, who, when something is forbidden to them, do it all the more out of a certain pride. It is also laid down for the ungodly, that is, those who do not possess the piety of right faith; and for sinners, that is, those who sin grievously even under that faith.

Then it is explained in detail for which sinners: namely, the wicked, such as robbers, thieves, and shedders of blood; and the defiled, such as those who pollute themselves by lust, or foul themselves by shameful speech, drunkenness, and dishonourable banquets. The law is also laid down for patricides and matricides, that is, for those who kill father or mother, so that, because the law of nature has been dissolved in them, it may be restored through the law written in letters; also for murderers, that is, killers of human beings; and for fornicators, that is, those who have intercourse with prostitutes; for men who lie with males, that is, those committing the Sodomite abomination; and for kidnappers, that is, assassins, or those who inflict wounds with any sword; for liars, who speak falsehoods; and for perjurers, who swear falsely.

The law is imposed upon those who do such things, and upon those who commit anything else of this kind: “if there is anything else opposed to sound doctrine,” that is, to the moral teaching of natural or written law, which heals the understanding of the mind. This doctrine accords with the Gospel—that is, it agrees with the Gospel of the glory of the blessed God, the Gospel which proclaims or gives glory to God, who is blessed naturally from himself, since he himself is eternal blessedness; and this Gospel was entrusted to me by God, as to a faithful steward.

> “I give thanks to him who strengthened me, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he judged me faithful, appointing me to the ministry, though formerly I was a blasphemer and persecutor and insolent man. But I obtained God’s mercy, because I acted ignorantly in unbelief. And the grace of our Lord overflowed, with the faith and love which are in Christ Jesus.”

God entrusted the Gospel to me, that is, he committed to me the preaching of the Gospel. Therefore I give him thanks, that is, I devoutly offer him praise for this gratuitous gift of his, because the law had placed no good merit in me. He shows that he had been full of many sins under the law, but was justified after withdrawing from it.

“I give thanks,” he says, “to him,” that is, to God the Father, “who strengthened me,” that is, made my mind strong in Christ Jesus our Lord, and so rendered me strong that neither death nor life can separate me from Christ; but that I may be strong both for doing good and for enduring evil. Thus he strengthened me, and therefore I give him thanks. And it is right that I return thanks to him, because “he judged me faithful,” that is, he foresaw me as faithful when I had been unfaithful under the law. He judged me faithful, I say, “appointing me to the ministry” of preaching, because he foreknew that I would faithfully administer the Gospel, withholding nothing and adding nothing alien to it.

For formerly under the law I was “a blasphemer,” that is, one speaking wickedly about Jesus of Nazareth; and “a persecutor” (Acts IX) of his saints; and “insolent,” that is, inflicting many insults by words and deeds upon Christians. But I obtained the mercy of God, that is, remission of sins from God, because I did this not from a purpose of malicious mind, but ignorantly: that is, not knowing that I acted wrongly. For, burning with zeal for the law, I persecuted the preachers of grace and thought that I thereby pleased God, as the Lord foretold: “The hour is coming,” he says, “when everyone who kills you will think that he renders service to God” (John XVI).

Although pardon is often also granted to those who knowingly sin, I nevertheless obtained mercy much more readily for this reason: because I sinned not through malice but through ignorance, living in unbelief, because I did not know that it was evil to persecute Christians, nor did I believe that Jesus was the Christ. Nor did I merely obtain mercy, by which my sins were forgiven; but the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ “overflowed,” that is, exceeded all the enormity of my sins. The new grace which came upon me was greater than my fault had been, so that holiness conquered preceding sins.

The grace, I say, overflowed in me with the faith and love which are in Christ Jesus: that is, with the faith by which I believed in Christ, and the charity by which I loved Christ, or my neighbour in Christ. With this faith and love the abundance of heavenly grace overflowed in me, so that I abounded in divine gifts.

> “The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance: Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first. But for this reason I obtained mercy, that in me first Christ Jesus might display all patience, for the instruction of those who are to believe in him unto eternal life. But to the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.”

Christ’s grace overflowed in me. For the saying which I speak concerning this matter is faithful, that is, true; and it is worthy of every acceptance of heart and work, because it saves body and soul. Therefore it is worthy to be accepted in every way by all people, both Jews and gentiles. And what is that saying? Namely, that Christ Jesus—that is, the saving king—came into this world to save sinners: that is, to save them from sins or to free them from sins. For he had no cause for coming to us except to save sinners.

All sinned, either in themselves or in the first parent. But one came without sin, who might save them from sins. He came to save sinners, “of whom I am the first,” not in time, but in the magnitude of my offences, by which I am worse than all. For “first” is meant as “better,” as when, among craftsmen, one who wishes to build says, “Who is the foremost builder here? Who is the foremost artisan?” Or, if he wishes to be treated, he says, “Who is the foremost physician?” He is certainly not asking who is earlier in age or in profession, but who is foremost in skill. As those are first in skill, so this man is first in wickedness and outstanding in sins.

“But,” he says, “although in evil deeds I had surpassed the rest, being the chief of persecutors, for this reason I obtained mercy: so that in me first”—that is, in the greatest sinner who had obtained mercy—“Christ Jesus might display all patience,” by which he bears with sinners for a long time so that at last they may be converted; and might display it for the instruction of those who are to believe in him in order to attain eternal life. That is, he might instruct them toward repentance by the example of my conversion, when they saw with how great patience he waited for me in order to convert me, and with how great grace he endowed me when at last converted, so that no one might thereafter despair that whatever sins he had would be forgiven, since I had received pardon for such great crimes.

Rather, every sinner might say to himself: “If Saul is holy, why do I despair? If so desperate a patient has been healed by so great a physician, shall I not desire those hands for my wounds? Shall I not hasten to those hands?” That people might say this is why Saul was made an apostle from a persecutor. For when a physician comes seeking to gain a reputation, he seeks out some desperate sick person and heals him. And if he finds one who is very poor, he does not seek payment there, but commends his skill. Thus Christ displayed in Saul the power of his particular spiritual medicine, so that thereafter all might know that he can heal every infirmity of all who flee to him.

Then, he says, I obtained mercy for such a cause. But from this let there be honour and glory to the King of the ages: that is, to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, who reigns from eternity to eternity through all ages, and, as Creator, is Lord and King of all things. I call him King, “immortal,” that is, unchangeable. For where you find one thing and then another, a kind of death has occurred. For death is not to be what one was. Therefore God is truly immortal, because he is never changed but always remains the same (Ps. CI).

And he is invisible in his substance, because divinity cannot at all be seen by human sight. He is called invisible because that by which a human being sees bodies cannot see him—not because the minds of the pious are deprived of his vision, since it is written: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V). Or God is invisible because no one can comprehend his greatness even with the mind, since even his peace surpasses all understanding.

And he alone is God, because there is no other besides him. Yet someone might be troubled how, concerning this one God who is the Trinity itself, it is said, “to the only invisible God,” when there are also certain invisible creatures, because all things visible and invisible were created by Christ. But because there are visible false gods, it is said: “to the only invisible God be honour and glory.” For there is also an invisible creature, which nevertheless is not God to us. Therefore honour and glory belong to God alone, who is the invisible God: honour from creatures, and glory in his own essence. Or honour in the good conduct of the saints, and glory in their increase, enduring for ages of ages: that is, through the length of all times, or rather through the immeasurable expanses of eternity. Amen.

> “This charge I commit to you, son Timothy, according to the prophecies which went before concerning you, that by them you may wage the good warfare, holding faith and a good conscience; which some, rejecting, have suffered shipwreck concerning the faith. Among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I delivered to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme.”

After recalling what and how great are the benefits of the Father and Christ toward sinners, he wishes to encourage Timothy to act well: namely, that as a good soldier he may fight against vices and against false apostles, and may defend and teach the people entrusted to him.

“This charge,” he says, “I commit to you, son Timothy.” In calling him son, he shows that he ought willingly to obey a father who commands. In using his name, he makes him more attentive and awakens him to a great desire concerning himself. He appropriately calls him Timothy when urging him to act well, because *Timothy* is interpreted “beneficent.” “This charge I commit,” that is, I command and impress upon you by every means in my power, “according to the prophecies which went before concerning you”: that is, according to the knowledge of the Scriptures of the prophets which has long been in you, or according to what the prophetic Spirit has shown me concerning you.

I especially command this above the other commands: that among them—that is, among the others entrusted to you—you may “wage the good warfare”; that is, that in God’s camp, like a brave soldier, you may fight against all enemies of God’s people and conquer them with spiritual weapons, so that neither false teachers nor malignant spirits nor vices may prevail against you or the people whom you govern. Wage the good warfare, holding right faith and a good conscience, so that you may be conscious of no perverse consent, but your heart may see that in everything you wish to act well. For this is why you can fulfil what I say, to wage the warfare well: because you have faith and a good conscience, by which God’s warfare is carried on. Therefore strive always to retain them.

Some, rejecting this conscience of purity, good will, and humility, and choosing to consent to sins—so that “he who is filthy may be filthy still” (Rev. XXII)—were driven by the wind of pride and suffered shipwreck: that is, they dashed the ship of the soul upon the rocks of errors and sank themselves and others in the sea of this age.
