Thus they suffered shipwreck concerning the faith, as though travelling around the truth: neither wholly departing from the faith nor remaining within it.

Among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander. They lost the faith and suffered shipwreck in error because they refused to possess a conscience of good humility. For pride plunged them into the dangers of errors while they wished to appear teachers. “Whom I delivered to Satan”: that is, I permitted them to be excommunicated and harassed by the devil, so that, instructed even by torments, they might learn not to blaspheme—that is, might be corrected and return to salvation.

Although the first persuasion to sin came from Satan and he is the author of all sins, some are nevertheless delivered to him for correction, so that Satan’s work may be excluded by Satan’s work. For no creature—whether it remains in truth, giving glory to God, or did not stand in truth, seeking its own glory—fails, willingly or unwillingly, to serve divine providence. That creature serves willingly which voluntarily does what is good. But from that which does not wish this, what is just is brought about.

For if even the transgressing angels, with their prince the devil, could not rightly be called administrators or agents of divine providence, the Lord would not call the devil the prince of this world (John XII, XIV, XVI), nor would apostolic authority deliver blasphemers to him in order that they might be corrected from blasphemy. But this prince, under so great an Emperor, does nothing except as much as is permitted him; and these administrators do nothing except as much as the Lord allows.

For nothing is hidden from him as from a human being, nor is he less powerful in any matter, so that the administrators and agents who are in his power may effect anything among the things subject to them, according to their rank, whether he does not permit it or does not know it. Yet they are not rewarded according to what is justly done through them, but according to the intention with which they themselves act, because he considers the intention with which they act. For God neither denied free will to his rational creature nor relinquished to another the power by which he justly orders even the unjust. Therefore some are rightly delivered to Satan to be corrected, because Satan cannot do to them anything except what is divinely ordered.

Thus far the Apostle has dealt with pseudo-preachers; now he adds teaching concerning all people.

## CHAPTER II

> “I exhort, therefore, first of all, that entreaties, prayers, petitions, thanksgivings be made for all people: for kings and all who are established in high office, that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life in all piety and chastity. For this is good and acceptable before God our Saviour, who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.”

Here he urges prayer for all. “Because,” he says, “Christ came to save sinners, and you must wage warfare in this matter, therefore teach them to pray, that what must be done may be obtained.” “I exhort,” that is, I ask with solemn adjuration, “first of all,” that is, chiefly before all else, that there be made by you or by those subject to you, or by all the saints, “entreaties,” that is, requests with the adjuration of holy things, for a more emphatic expression of asking; “prayers,” that is, petitions simply offered; “petitions,” by which God’s benefits to be granted to the human race are requested; and “thanksgivings,” by which thanks are returned to God for benefits already received.

Or the order of the Mass is shown in these words: entreaties are those which we make in the celebration of the sacraments, in the commemoration of holy things, before that which is on the table of our Lord begins to be blessed; prayers are made when it is blessed and consecrated and broken for distribution; petitions are made when the people are blessed by the bishop. For petitions are asked as though by right, with a certain confidence or earnestness; thus the petition is made there with confidence, that what is performed here may be fulfilled in eternal life. When these things have been completed and the whole sacrament received, thanksgiving brings all to a conclusion.

The Apostle’s principal reason for saying these things was that, after these matters had been briefly prescribed and indicated, what follows might not be judged negligible: “for all people, for kings and all who are established in high office.” No one, given the weakness of human thought, was to suppose that these things should not be done for those from whom the Church suffered persecution, since Christ’s members were to be gathered from every class of humanity. Hence he adds: “For this is good,” and so forth.

Or “entreaties” are made with adjuration for difficult matters, such as the conversion of the ungodly or the removal of evils; “prayers,” when virtues and goods are requested for those already converted; “petitions,” when heavenly glory is requested for them; “thanksgivings,” for goods received or accomplished. And prayers of this kind should be made for all people, so that no one may be such a sinner that he is not prayed for, since Saul too was converted through Stephen’s prayers (Acts VII).

And they should be made also for those for whom it seemed least likely: namely, for kings, even if they are evil and hostile to the saints, and for all who are set in the high places of secular offices, such as consuls and commanders. For persons from every class of humanity are converted to religion and attain salvation, including those who, through the pride and exaltation of secular power, seem to shrink from faith and humility. Thus we see that even kings themselves, abandoning the idols for which they persecuted Christians, have come to know and worship the one true God; and therefore prayer ought to have been made for them even while they persecuted the Church.

Prayer should also be made for rulers so that we who are under them may lead a quiet life, free from persecution, and a tranquil life in peace; and this in every piety of divine worship and chastity of faith. Thus, when rulers are converted, gentiles may not dare to trouble us by raising persecutions on account of the ungodliness of idolatry, nor may heretics presume to disturb our tranquillity, wishing to corrupt the chastity of some persons’ faith.

In the peace of rulers, the quiet and kingdom of the Churches are preserved. For in their wars and discords tranquillity is scattered, piety grows cold, and discipline or strictness is loosened. When this is loosened, the chastity of the weak is violated. Therefore prayer must be made for rulers lest these things happen through their dissension. Hence through Jeremiah the Lord commanded the Jews held captive in Babylon, saying: “Seek the peace of the city to which I have caused you to be carried away, and pray to the Lord for it, because in its peace you shall have peace” (Jer. XXIX).

Babylon, however, which is called “confusion,” signifies the society of the wicked. But the Jews are citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem, who in this age live as pilgrims among the evil, pay tribute to kings and rulers, and render the other things which secular government requires without detriment to God’s worship. Therefore they ought to pray for the rulers’ peace, because in their peace they will have peace—certainly a temporary peace, common to good and evil alike.

Thus we too use Babylon’s peace; through faith and desire for the heavenly homeland, God’s people will so rejoice in it as nevertheless meanwhile to live as pilgrims in it. But our own proper peace is here with God through faith, and eternally with him through sight. “Pray,” he says, “for the peace of rulers and for the salvation of all, because this is good”—that is, useful to the Church—“and acceptable,” that is, pleasing and agreeable before God our Saviour, who, just as he saves us, “wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth,” as we have already come.

Although it is certain to us that not all are saved, we must not for that reason detract anything from God’s most omnipotent will. Rather, we should understand the statement, “who wills all people to be saved,” as though it said: no person is saved except one whom he wills to be saved; or, no one becomes saved except one whom he wills. Therefore he must be asked to will it, because it is necessary that it happen if he wills it. For the Apostle was dealing with praying to God when he said this.

So we understand what is written in the Gospel: “who enlightens every human being” (John V), not because there is no human being who is not enlightened, but because no one is enlightened unless by him. Therefore he wills all who are saved to be saved, and all who come to the knowledge of truth to come, because no one is saved or approaches the knowledge of truth unless he wills it.

Or certainly, “who wills all people to be saved” is said in this way: not because there is no human being whom he does not will to be saved—he who was unwilling to perform miracles among those of whom he says that they would have repented if he had performed them (Matt. XI; Luke X)—but so that by “all people” we understand every class of humanity, distributed through whatever differences: kings and private persons, noble and low-born, exalted and humble, learned and unlearned, sound in body and weak, quick-witted and slow of heart, wise and foolish, rich and poor, persons of moderate means, males and females, infants, children, adolescents, young people, old people, the decrepit; people in all languages, all customs, all arts, all professions, all dispositions, and the innumerable variety of consciences, together with whatever other differences there are among human beings.

For what, I ask, is there among them in respect of which God should not will, through his only-begotten Son, that people in all nations be saved—and therefore bring this about, because the Omnipotent cannot will in vain whatever he wills? The Apostle had commanded that prayer be made for all people, and had particularly added kings and those established in high office, who might be thought, through secular arrogance and pride, to shrink from the humility of Christian faith. Therefore, saying, “For this is good before the Saviour”—that is, that prayer should be made even for such persons—he immediately added, in order to remove despair: “who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.” For God judged this good: that through the prayer of the humble he should deign to grant salvation to the exalted.

> “For there is one God, and one mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a redemption for all, a testimony in its own times, in which I was appointed a preacher and apostle. I speak the truth; I do not lie: a teacher of the gentiles in faith and truth” (II Tim. I).

Because it had been said that God wills all people to be saved, lest anyone say that there could be a way of salvation through good conduct and worship of the one omnipotent God without participation in the body and blood of Christ: “For there is one God,” he says, “and one mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.” Thus the statement, “he wills all people to be saved,” is to be understood as accomplished in no other way than through the mediator—not God, who was always the Word, but the man Christ Jesus, when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I).

For human beings were mortal and sinners; but God, to whom they had to be reconciled in order to be saved, was immortal and without sin. A mediator between God and human beings had to possess something like God and something like human beings, lest he be like human beings in both respects and far from God, or like God in both respects and far from human beings; and thus not be a mediator.

Therefore between mortal sinners and the immortal Just One appeared one mortal with human beings, just with God, so that, since peace is life’s wage, through righteousness joined to God he might abolish the death of the ungodly who are justified—a death which he did not wish to share with them. And because all human beings, so long as they are mortal, must also be miserable, a middle one had to be sought who was not merely human but also God, so that the blessed mortality of this middle one, intervening, might lead human beings from mortal misery to blessed immortality.

Therefore the mediator between us and God had to possess transient mortality and enduring blessedness, so that through what passes away he might be suited to those dying, and might transfer them from the dead to that which endures. But good angels cannot be intermediaries between miserable mortals and blessed immortals, because they too are blessed and immortal. Evil angels, however, can be intermediaries, because they are immortal with the latter and miserable with the former.

Opposite to them is the good mediator, who, against their immortality and misery, both willed to be mortal for a time and could remain blessed in eternity. Thus he destroyed in them both the immortally proud and the miserably harmful, lest, through boasting of immortality, they should seduce human beings into immortal misery; and by the humility of his death and the kindness of his blessedness he destroyed them in those whose hearts he cleansed through his faith, freeing them from their utterly unclean domination.

For the immortal and miserable intermediary places himself between us for this purpose: that he may not allow a passage to blessed immortality, because that which obstructs remains—namely, misery itself. But the mortal and blessed one placed himself between us for this purpose: that, mortality having passed, he might make the dead immortal, as he showed in himself by rising again, and the miserable blessed, from which condition he himself never departed.

Therefore one intermediary is evil, separating friends; another is good, reconciling enemies. And for this reason there are many separating intermediaries, but one good mediator, because the multitude that is blessed becomes blessed by participation in the one God. By deprivation of this participation, the miserable multitude of evil angels, which opposes itself as an impediment rather than placing itself between as an aid to blessedness, even makes a kind of clamour through its multitude, lest one be able to reach that one source of blessedness. To bring us to it we needed not many mediators, but one, and such a one that by participation in his divinity we might become blessed.

For he did not free us from mortality and misery in order to bring us to immortal and blessed angels, so that through participation in them we too might become immortal and blessed; but he brought us to that Trinity, by participation in whom angels also are blessed. For he is mediator not between the Father and humanity, but only between God and human beings. God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; human beings are sinners and mortals. Between that Trinity and human weakness and iniquity, a mediator was made: a human being not iniquitous but weak, so that in being not iniquitous he might be joined to God, and in being weak he might draw near to us, and so exist as mediator between God and human beings.

But let us consider the Apostle’s words. “Truly,” he says, “he wills all to be saved, because there is one God, the creator of all, by participation in whom all who will be saved shall be saved; and there is one mediator of God and human beings, who joins all to the one God so that they may be saved. Christ Jesus is this mediator, not according to that whereby he is God, but according to that whereby he is human. He gave himself upon the cross as a redemption for all, excluding no one who wished to be redeemed unto salvation.

“For in this is revealed how greatly God loves human beings and wills them all to be saved, unless their perversity prevents it: the mediator God, whom God set between himself and human beings, endured death for all in order to redeem all from death. Therefore those who are not saved have no grounds to complain against God or against the mediator, but against themselves, because they did not wish to receive either the redemption which the mediator gave or the salvation which God offered.”

But he gave himself as a redemption, and gave himself as a testimony of the salvation of all the elect in its own times, because in rising from death and ascending into heaven, at the time of resurrection and the time of ascension, he presented himself as the example and confirmation of our salvation to come. For in rising and ascending he testified, as it were, that his members will rise and ascend; indeed, he himself was the testimony.

He also gave himself as a testimony of the future condemnation of those who will not be saved, when he struck down his persecutors with one utterance (John XVIII). For his coming and whatever he did or endured in the flesh are for the reprobate a testimony of condemnation, but for the elect a testimony of salvation.

In some manuscripts it is read: “whose testimony was confirmed in its own times.” This is understood thus: the testimony which the prophets gave concerning Christ, or which Christ himself set forth concerning himself—namely, when or how he would suffer or rise—was truly confirmed by fulfilment at the appropriate times. In confirming and proclaiming this testimony, I was appointed by God a preacher and apostle: that is, herald and envoy, in order to testify to all that he himself wills all to be saved. *Preacher* is a title of authority; *apostle*, a title of dignity or power, which is greater.

And I must be believed in the preaching of this testimony, because I speak truth concerning this and do not lie in this respect. Therefore all ought to believe me, because I endeavour to teach all people faith and truth, as a teacher in faith and truth. Faith is to believe what you do not see; truth is to see what you have believed. Faith leads to truth. If one remains in what is believed, one also arrives at what is seen.

> “Therefore I will that men pray in every place, lifting up pure hands without anger and disputation. Likewise also women, in modest dress, with shamefastness and sobriety, adorning themselves not with braided hair (I Pet. III), or gold, or pearls, or costly clothing, but—as befits women professing piety—through good works.”

Since I am a teacher of the Gentiles and a master of the churches, I therefore will that men pray—that is, that men [Col. 1418A] pray to God—not only in church, but in every place, because God is everywhere; and that they pray, lifting hands pure from the filth of sins toward heavenly things, not lowering them toward earthly things. For lest hands lifted to God be put to shame, they must be pure from sins and exercised in good works. We are commanded to lift pure hands, so that, when you lift your hands to God, your works may come to mind. Since these hands are lifted in order that you may obtain what you desire, consider that these very hands must be exercised in good works, lest they blush to be lifted to God. And let them be lifted without anger, so that you do not retain anger in your heart against your neighbour, but may say with a free conscience: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI; Luke II). And without disputation—that is, without litigation in legal matters—lest [Col. 1418B] you still retain in your heart a will to contend in judgment against your brother; rather, remit whatever it may be, so that your sins too may be remitted by God when you pray. Or, “without disputation” before God: do not dispute in your heart or judge concerning the unsearchable mysteries of God’s secrets, nor hesitate in faith. Likewise, let women pray in becoming dress, so that their clothing may display religion, and their undisciplined exposure may not provoke lust. Let them be with modesty, so that in humility they may be heard while praying; and with sobriety, so that they may keep moderation in food and drink. I mean women adorning themselves not with braided hair—that is, hair artificially curled—nor with gold, pearls, or costly clothing, because by such ornaments they stir those who look upon them to lust; but let them profess godliness not by [Col. 1418C] boastful words but by good works, as befits women. For it is fitting that they should show the godliness of their minds not by words but by works, and should not clothe themselves in luxurious ornaments.

> “Let a woman learn in silence with all subjection. But I do not permit a woman to teach, nor to exercise authority over a man, but to be in silence” (I Cor. XIV). “For Adam was formed first, then Eve” (Gen. I, II, III). “And Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, was in transgression. Yet she shall be saved through the generation of children, if she remains in faith and love and sanctification with all sobriety.”

Let a woman learn not in a clamorous voice but in silence, [Col. 1418D] lest her voice move her hearers to lust. And let her learn not uprightly, but with all subjection, because on account of the guilt of the first transgression she is subjected to man by a servitude of condition rather than of love (Gen. III). But I do not permit a woman to teach, because indeed on one occasion, when she taught, she separated man from eternal wisdom. Nor do I permit her to rule over a man, though she may rule over another woman; for man is of a stronger nature and ought to have dominion over woman. Rather, I will that she be silent, so that she does not even converse idly with her neighbour. Let her keep silence, because while she speaks she both incites and is incited more readily to lust.

And lest the woman’s condition, reduced so completely to servitude under her husband, should seem harsh, the Apostle returns to the ancient and original example: Adam was made first, [Col. 1419A] then Eve from his rib; the devil could not deceive Adam, but did deceive Eve; and after offending God, she was immediately subjected to the man. Those are deceived who do not think that what they do is sin. Adam, however, knew that what he was doing was evil; but, being inexperienced in divine severity, he could be mistaken in thinking that the offense committed was pardonable. Thus, although the woman was deceived, he was not deceived in that respect; yet he was mistaken about how the matter would be judged which he was to state: “The woman whom thou gavest me as a companion, she gave to me, and I ate” (ibid.).

For just as Aaron did not consent, when the erring people were being led to make an idol, but yielded under constraint (Exod. XXIII); nor is it credible that Solomon thought it no error to serve idols, but was compelled to those sacrileges by feminine blandishments [Col. 1419B] (III Kings XI): so it must be believed that that man, in transgressing God’s law at the urging of his woman, was not deceived into believing her speech true, but complied because of the bond of companionship. For the woman received as true what the serpent had told her; but he was unwilling to be separated from their sole fellowship, even in fellowship of sin. Yet he was no less guilty if he sinned knowingly and deliberately. For he did not wish to grieve his wife, whom he believed might waste away without his consolation if he were estranged in mind from her, and indeed might perish altogether through that discord—not overcome by a lust of the flesh, which he had not yet felt in the law of his members resisting the law of his mind, but by a certain friendly goodwill, by which it often happens that [Col. 1419C] God is offended lest a human being become an enemy from being a friend.

Therefore, in some other fashion he too was deceived; but he could in no way be deceived by that serpentine fraud through which the woman was deceived, since, endowed with a spiritual mind, he could not believe that God had forbidden him the fruit of that tree out of envy. For the Apostle properly called this “deception,” because what was urged, though false, was believed true: namely, that God had forbidden them to touch that tree because he knew that, if they touched it, they would become like gods—as though he, who had made them human, begrudged them divinity. Adam, therefore, was not deceived; but the woman was deceived into transgression, so that through her the man also transgressed.

“But she shall be saved through the generation of children,” and so forth. That is, the woman joined in marriage and once reduced to [Col. 1419D] Eve’s condition will erase the ancient error through the begetting of children—provided, however, that she educates those children in faith, love of Christ, sanctification, and chastity. For the reading is not *sobriety*, as Latin manuscripts incorrectly have it, but *chastity*, as Jerome testifies. Thus, where marriage seemed to be commended as conferring salvation, virginity is commended. For if a woman is saved in the generation of children, and the number of children is the salvation of mothers, why was it added: “if the children remain in faith and love and sanctification with all chastity”? Therefore a woman will then be saved if she bears children who remain virgins; if she recovers in her children what she herself lost, and compensates the loss and decay of the root by flower [Col. 1420A] and fruit; if she nourishes and instructs her children in religion, so that they hold the faith, do not abandon charity, and preserve with all chastity of mind and body the sanctification received in baptism. Or, according to the Latin manuscripts, “with all sobriety,” that is, with temperance against the heat of vices. Although a woman is not permitted to preach publicly, she ought nevertheless to instruct children, the household, or young women at home.

In this place man may signify the rational spirit, and woman the flesh or sensuality. Adam was formed first, then Eve, because rational perception was made principally in the human being, and flesh secondarily. That Adam was not deceived but Eve was signifies that, whenever we sin, rational perception in us is not so deceived [Col. 1420B] as to think sin not evil, though it consents because of its friendly association with the flesh; but the flesh is so deceived into delight that it does not even think evil what it commits pleasurably. But she will be saved through the generation of children, because through the production of good works she will be joined to everlasting salvation. Such good works are especially practiced in offices of mercy. Yet works of mercy profit neither pagans nor Jews who do not believe in Christ, nor heretics nor schismatics, where faith and love are not found. Therefore this woman—that is, the flesh—will be saved through the generation of children and the performance of good works only if those works remain in the Catholic faith, in twofold love, and in sanctification with all chastity of body and [Col. 1420C] soul, or sobriety. For “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI); nor does the branch of a good work possess any greenness if it remains in the root of love; nor does anything done without sanctification profit, nor is anything a good work without chastity.

## CHAPTER III

> “The saying is faithful: If anyone desires the episcopate, he desires a good work. Therefore a bishop must be blameless, the husband of one wife, sober, prudent, orderly, chaste, hospitable, a teacher; not given to wine, not violent, but gentle; not contentious, not covetous; but one who governs his own household well, having children in subjection with all chastity. For if anyone does not know how to govern his own household, how shall he have care of the Church of God [Col. 1420D]? Not a novice, lest, lifted up in pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil. Moreover, he must have a good testimony from those outside, lest he fall into reproach and into the snare of the devil.”

The saying which I now speak is faithful—that is, true: “If anyone desires the episcopate, he desires a good work.” A work, not a dignity; labour, not delights. A work by which he may grow in humility, lest he swell with exalted station. He did not wish to explain what the episcopate is, because it is the name of a work, not of an honour. For it is a Greek word, derived from the fact that one set over others oversees those whom he governs, namely by taking care of them; for *episkopein* [ἐπισκοπεῖν] means “to oversee.” Therefore *episkopos* [ἐπίσκοπος] is interpreted “overseer,” so that one may understand that he is not a bishop who loves to preside rather than to benefit others. Nor is he to be judged to desire the episcopate who desires his own profit or honour rather than the salvation of the people. For it is not said, “He who desires the episcopate desires a good rank,” but “he desires a good work”: one who is placed in a higher order may, if he wishes, have an opportunity to exercise virtues. He himself therefore bears witness against himself that he does not seek the episcopate if he seeks not the ministry of good work but the glory of honour.

He does well who desires the episcopate—that is, to oversee others and bear concern for the salvation of many. Therefore a bishop must be blameless, so that he is enslaved to no vice; and the following enumeration of virtues makes clear what that blamelessness is. It is as though such aspirants were told: “I praise what you seek, but first learn what you seek, lest, while you neglect to lie to yourselves, your blameworthiness be exposed all the more foully because you hasten to be seen by all upon the height of honour.” It should also be noted that when the Apostle said this, whoever presided over congregations was the first led to the torments of martyrdom. Thus it was then praiseworthy to seek the episcopate, when by it one seemed to hasten almost to martyrdom and there was no doubt that one would come, if not to death, at least to harsher punishments. But now a higher place, without which the people cannot be governed, even if held and administered as it ought to be, is nevertheless sought improperly. [Col. 1421C] If, however, this burden is imposed, it must be accepted because of the necessity of the flesh (Ecclus. XXXIII). For in action, in this life, honour or power ought not to be loved, since all is vanity under the sun; rather, the work itself which is done by that honour or power, if it is done rightly and usefully—that is, if it avails for the salvation of subjects according to God.

And since the bishop’s office is such, he must be blameless: such that no fault can be observed in him which could be blamed. This is almost contrary to nature. For every vice, even in an idle word, deserves blame (Matt. XII; Jas. III). And who is there who cannot be blamed even in the things he says? Yet a future shepherd of the Church must be chosen of such a kind that, in comparison with him, the rest may rightly be called the flock, so that when he rebukes others, he himself cannot be rebuked by anyone. For one loses the authority to correct when the person corrected can reproach him with his own faults. He must be the husband of one wife—that is, a man who has had one wife, not a second, such as blessed Hilary or Germanus of Auxerre; sober, or watchful. For priests who minister in the temple of God are forbidden to drink wine and strong drink, lest their hearts be weighed down in feasting and drunkenness (Judg. XIII; Luke XXI), and so that the faculty of perception which renders service to God may always be vigorous and keen; prudent, so as to exclude those who excuse the foolishness of priests under the name of simplicity. For unless the brain is sound, [Col. 1422A] all the members will be diseased; orderly in good works and honourable conduct, so that he may be found wise in these things. For some people do not know their own measure and are so foolish and irreverent that, in gesture, gait, and ordinary speech, they make observers laugh; chaste—that is, modest or continent—lest he be shameless or violate chastity; hospitable, that he may imitate Abraham (Gen. XVIII, XIX), receive Christ with strangers—or rather, in strangers—and have been accustomed to do this even before becoming bishop; a teacher, that is, one possessing the grace to teach. For it is of no benefit to enjoy the consciousness of virtues if one cannot also instruct the people entrusted to oneself and refute opponents. For an innocent manner of life, without speech, benefits as much by example [Col. 1422B] as it harms by silence. The rage of wolves must be driven away by the barking of dogs and the shepherd’s goad.

Not given to wine, not violent. He sets vices against virtues. He has said what sort of person a priest ought to be; he also says what sort he ought not to be. Let him not be given to wine, but drink in such a way that it cannot be known whether he has drunk. Drunkenness belongs to buffoons and revellers, and a belly heated with wine soon boils over into lust. Let him not be violent: that is, not so irascible and disturbed in mind as to strike, when he ought to be patient and imitate him who gave his back to the scourge and did not return curses to those cursing him (I Pet. II). Or, “not violent” means that he should not strike the consciences of the weak by word or bad example. It does not befit him to be given to wine and violent, but gentle, so that gentleness may restrain drunkenness and anger [Col. 1422C] and he may act moderately in all things; not contentious, that is, not habitually quarrelsome. Nothing is more imprudent than the arrogance of certain people who mistake chattering for authority and, ever prepared for quarrels, thunder at the flock subject to them with swollen words; not covetous, because through greed for gifts he would quickly turn aside from justice, like the sons of Samuel (I Kings VIII). Samuel himself taught by his example that greed or covetousness must be avoided by a priest, proving before the people that he had taken nothing from anyone (I Kings XII); likewise the poverty of the Apostles, who accepted from the brethren relief for their expenses and desired nothing beyond food and clothing (below, VI); governing his own household well, not in order to increase wealth, [Col. 1422D] but so that he may first require from his household what he will command to the people, having his children in subjection with all chastity.

His discipline is tested in his children, if they are well subject and obedient to their father. Such chastity is required of him that, if his children are not chaste, he cannot be bishop; and he offends God by the same fault by which Eli the high priest offended him. Eli had indeed rebuked his sons because they slept with women in the vestibule of the temple; but because he had not cast out the offenders, he fell backward and died (I Kings IV). As has been said, he ought to govern his own household well, so as to rule it according to God. But if someone does not know how to govern his own household, which is small in comparison with the Church, how will he take care of the Church of God? That is, how will he know how to exercise concern [Col. 1423A] so as to govern diligently the Church, which is far greater than his household and must be governed with greater prudence?

He must not be a novice—that is, an inexperienced person. Let not one newly converted to the faith be ordained bishop, lest, puffed up with pride—that is, considering himself worthier than the rest, as though the Christian religion needed him—he fall into the judgment of the devil; that is, be condemned for pride like the devil, who judged himself better than all and became lower than all (Isa. XIV). Nor should one newly baptized, or newly separated from secular affairs or wickedness, become bishop, because every such person is a novice. Nor is it fitting that one who was a catechumen yesterday should be a bishop today; yesterday in the amphitheatre, today in church; in the circus in the evening, at the altar in the morning; recently a supporter of actors, now a consecrator of virgins. A priest made in a moment does not know humility and gentleness; he does not know how to despise himself. He is transferred from one dignity to another. He has not fasted, wept, often reproved his own conduct and corrected it by continual meditation, or distributed his substance to the poor. The devil’s judgment and downfall are arrogance. Those fall into it who, in an instant of time, are teachers though not yet disciples.

The person being ordained must not only possess the virtues already mentioned and lack the vices already mentioned, but must also have a good testimony from those outside. The conclusion corresponds to the beginning of the statement. One who is blameless is praised with one voice not only by those within the household, but also by outsiders. Outsiders are Jews, Gentiles, and heretics outside the Church. [Col. 1423C] Therefore Christ’s bishop must be such that not even those outside dare to disparage the religion of his life; lest, if he is blameworthy, he fall into reproach, so that his vices are cast in his teeth. Thus, despised, he falls into the devil’s snare, hating those by whom he sees himself despised. For it commonly happens to those scorned by others that they in turn scorn those who scorn them; and so they fall into anger and hatred, and the devil’s other snares. Therefore a bishop must be such that no one can reproach him with any former stain. But if, after embracing the faith, he has adopted things contrary to the virtues now described, he is not to be admitted to the episcopate.

> “Likewise, deacons must be chaste, not double-tongued, not devoted to much wine, not pursuing shameful gain, [Col. 1423D] holding the mystery of faith in a pure conscience. And let these also first be tested; then let them minister, having no crime. Likewise women must be chaste, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things. Let deacons be husbands of one wife, governing their children and their households well. For those who have ministered well will acquire for themselves a good rank and great confidence in the faith which is in Christ Jesus.”

Since, passing over presbyters, he immediately adds the discussion of deacons after the description of the bishop, he makes it understood that by the name “bishop” he designated both the high priest and the presbyter; and everything said of the bishop is secondarily to be observed concerning the presbyter. For a presbyter too is a bishop, that is, an overseer of the Church [Col. 1424A] which he governs. But the former is the greater bishop, the latter the lesser. And just as it was previously said that a bishop must be chaste, so likewise deacons must be chaste—that is, continent; not double-tongued, that is, not speaking in two ways, so as to speak well of someone in his presence and ill of him in his absence; not devoted to much wine, lest they become drunk. For whoever gets drunk is both dead and buried, and drunkards shall not possess the kingdom of God (I Cor. VI); not pursuing shameful gain, as greedy people do who buy and sell at a higher price, or take interest; holding in a conscience pure from the filth of vices the mystery of faith, that is, holding in a clean heart what concerning faith is hidden from others: such as that Christ was born of a virgin, that he committed no sin, that by dying [Col. 1424B] he destroyed death, that the bread consecrated on the altar truly becomes his body, and the other mysteries of faith.

Such must deacons be. But these too must first be tested. Here it is implied that bishops also must be tested. Let them first be tested, and if they are found to be such as we have described, let them minister at the sacred altars, having no—not merely sin, but—crime. For no human being is without sin, but many are without crime. A crime is a grave sin most deserving of accusation and condemnation, such as homicide, adultery, theft, sacrilege, or some impurity of fornication (Heb. XI). Women—that is, deaconesses—likewise must, like deacons, be chaste, so that purity of chastity may reign in them; not slanderers, that is, not seeking by speech [Col. 1424C] to diminish anyone’s good reputation; but sober, that is, free from every kind of drunkenness; and faithful in all their words and deeds, so that they keep faith with God and with human beings.

Let deacons be husbands of one wife: that is, let no deacon be ordained who has had two or more wives, but one who has had only one; and after he has been ordained, let him not have intercourse with her. Thus let deacons be men of a single wife, governing well the children they may previously have begotten, educating them in the discipline of the Lord, and governing their households well. It is right that they govern their children and households well, because those who have ministered well in small matters will acquire for themselves a good rank, that is, a higher rank in goodness; and they will acquire great confidence [Col. 1424D] in the faith which is in Christ Jesus—that is, they will receive or give assurance that they will conduct themselves faithfully in greater things and instruct others in the Christian faith. Or they should govern their children and households well so that, having first become accustomed to this, they may later know how to minister well in the Church; for those who have ministered well in the office of deacon will acquire a good rank for themselves, so as to deserve promotion to the episcopal rank, and will acquire for themselves great confidence of eternal recompense in faith, which is in Christ, who deserved to be exalted through the humility of obedience (Phil. II).

> “I write these things to you, son Timothy, hoping to come to you soon. But if I delay, [Col. 1425A] it is so that you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of truth. And manifestly great is the mystery of godliness: which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, was preached to the Gentiles, believed in throughout the world, and taken up in glory.”

Hold and keep all these things firmly, for I write them to you, son Timothy, hoping to come to you soon, so that in my presence I may instruct you still more fully. Therefore in the meantime you must observe more diligently the things which I add for you, so that you may not be ashamed when I see you. I shall come quickly, as I hope. But if I delay, I write these things so that meanwhile you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, in order that you may benefit all who are in it and know how you ought to instruct each one. This house in which God dwells is the Church, gathered from many faithful persons, who must be taught in various ways. It is the Church of God, who lives eternally and therefore eternally does good to those who keep his will, and, conversely, eternally punishes those who despise his commands.

And his Church itself is, in the perfect, a pillar—that is, lofty, upright, immovable, sustaining and raising up the younger members—and in those same perfect persons it is the foundation of truth, because by words and examples it establishes in the hearts of the weak the truth of faith and of God’s commandments. And manifestly great in it is the mystery of godliness, in which human salvation consists. A mystery is a hidden thing, that is, something mystical. Here may rightly be understood the mystery concerning which it was said to the Colossians: “The mystery which was hidden from ages and generations, but now has been manifested to his saints, to whom God willed to make known the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory” (Col. I).

For it is a mystery of godliness because the Son of God, through the inward parts of his mercy, visited us—the Dayspring from on high—to give light to those sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death (Luke I). The mystery of godliness consists in this: the Only-begotten of God mercifully deigned through grace to become human, in order to acquire brothers who might possess with him the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven. And this mystery is manifestly great, because all the faithful know it to be so great that [Col. 1425D] no one can suffice to conceive its magnitude. It “was manifested in the flesh,” Christ’s flesh, because in his assumption of flesh we understand that all the elect are his members or brothers and will therefore reign together. It “was justified in the Spirit,” because that singular man whom the Virgin bore was made righteous in his mother’s womb by the Holy Spirit; that is, in his very conception and creation the Holy Spirit made him righteous, and afterwards preserved him without sin in this present life. We too, when we become members, are justified in the Holy Spirit through baptism.

And this mystery of such great godliness “appeared to angels,” that is, became known to apostles and preachers, who are designated by the name of angels because they announce the glory of the heavenly kingdom. Hence John in the Apocalypse [Col. 1426A] writes to seven angels—that is, to the bishops of the seven churches of Asia. Through angels of this kind, that is, through messengers of truth, this mystery was preached to the Gentiles; and through their preaching it was believed throughout the world. As for the following phrase, “taken up in glory”: in our head it has already been perfectly fulfilled, but in his members it will not be wholly fulfilled until all the elect, having received their bodies, have entered together into the kingdom of heaven.

## CHAPTER IV

> “But the Spirit plainly says that in the last times some shall depart from the faith (II Tim. III; II Pet. III; Jude I; Ecclus. XXXVI), giving heed to spirits of error and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy and having [Col. 1426B] their conscience cauterized; forbidding marriage, and requiring abstinence from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who have known the truth. For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving. For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer.”

The Church indeed is the pillar and foundation of truth; nevertheless the Holy Spirit plainly says in me, or through me, that in the last times—that is, when Antichrist reigns, or before then—certain notable persons will depart from the faith. On account of such a departure it is said: “Unless the departure comes first” (II Thess. II). Since such persons will arise, vigilance is necessary lest they arise in our times, or, if they have arisen, lest they deceive others. For they will depart from the faith of truth, giving heed to spirits of error—that is, demons—which will speak to them or appear to them by the art of deception, and give them certain apparently good things so that they may cause them to err or keep them in error. This, we know, happened to the Agimnensian heretics: demons appearing to them at night in the form of horses carry them through the air wherever they wish, supply them with an abundance of temporal goods, and imbue them with depraved doctrines. Or, “spirits of error” means heresiarchs, in whom evil spirits will speak and teach error.

And they give heed to doctrines of demons—that is, of persons having demons—speaking lies in hypocrisy, that is, with feigned [Col. 1426D] religion, so that they may deceive more effectively, and having their own conscience cauterized: that is, corrupted and rotted, continually emitting its rot with stench. I mean demons who forbid marriage and require those who marry to abstain from foods which God created. This is what the Agimnensians and Manichees do, and some others have done. For the one who forbids marriage is the person who says it is evil, not the person who prefers something better to this good. There is therefore a great difference between those who urge virginity, setting a greater good before a lesser good, and those who forbid marriage by more violently accusing intercourse for procreation, which alone is properly marital.

Likewise, there is a great difference between abstaining from foods for a sacred signification or the discipline of the body, and abstaining from foods which God created by saying that God did not create them. For our first fathers too abstained from certain foods, not in order to condemn them but for their signifying function. And now the faithful abstain, not because they consider foods unclean, but for the subduing of the body, in order that the soul may be more deeply humbled in prayer: they abstain not only from meats but also from certain fruits of the earth, either always, as a few do, or on specified days and seasons, as almost everyone does during Lent. But the Manichees denied that creation itself was good and said that it was unclean because the devil produced meats. They abstained from such foods not because of their symbolic meaning, but because they were evil and unclean by nature. In this they undoubtedly blasphemed their Creator, [Col. 1427B] which belonged to the doctrine of demons.

For God created foods to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful—that is, to be received with thanksgiving by those who rightly believe concerning those foods, even though they do not yet understand what they believe—and by those who have known the truth, that is, those who understand what they believe concerning the same foods. They have known this truth: every creature of God is good in its own nature, and no food is to be rejected—that is, abhorred and spurned as naturally evil or unclean—when it is received, as it is customarily received, with thanksgiving; that is, so that thanks are given to God by the recipient. For everything which exists naturally is good in its own order; and no one sins in such things except one who, by failing to preserve his own order in obedience to God, disturbs their order also through evil use.

But our fathers who pleased God held their own order in that obedience, so that whatever God distributed by command at fitting times they observed in the manner in which he distributed it. Thus not only did they refrain at that time from certain meats given for food—though all were, or are, clean by nature—which were then declared unclean for a certain signification, when they were commanded not to eat them, so that the future revelation of realities might be prefigured by such signs; but they also observed unleavened bread and the other things of this sort in which there was a shadow of things to come. They would have been guilty, as persons belonging to that time and that people, if they had scorned to observe them—when those things had to be done in that manner and the things now revealed had to be foretold in that manner—as we would be foolish if, now that the New Testament has been revealed, we thought those prophetic observances could benefit us in any way.

Therefore no food is to be rejected which is received with thanksgiving. For the food itself is sanctified through the word of God, which is in the act of thanksgiving, and through prayer, which is added so that the devil may not harm through it. For the word sanctifies, prayer obtains, but the devil tempts through food.

> “By setting these things before the brethren, you will be a good minister of Christ Jesus, nourished by the words of faith and sound doctrine which you have followed. But avoid foolish and old-womanish fables; rather, exercise yourself unto godliness. For bodily exercise is profitable for a little [Col. 1428A]; but godliness is profitable for all things, having promise of the life which now is and of that which is to come. The saying is faithful and worthy of every acceptance. For for this we labour and are reviled, because we hope in the living God, who is the Saviour of all human beings, especially of the faithful.”

Setting before the brethren these things which I have said concerning foods and created things, for them to observe, you will be a good minister of Christ Jesus—you, I say, nourished either by your mother or by other believers in the words of faith, that is, words which teach faith, and in words of sound doctrine as regards good conduct, which you have followed from infancy, seeking it earnestly and finding it. Hold and teach the sound doctrine which you have attained; but avoid foolish old-wives’ tales, that is, Jewish traditions, [Col. 1428B] because they are foolish, that is, without fitness; and “old-wives’,” that is, poured into younger hearts by the sayings of old women; and they are tales, that is, empty words devoid of truth and usefulness. This is not said of the divine utterances, but, as I have said, of traditions which the Jews received from their elders besides the books of the Law and the Prophets, and of the foolish talk of heretics, who forbid marriage and prohibit foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving.

Avoid tales, indeed; but exercise yourself in godliness. That is, shun the tales of the ungodly and train yourself in godliness: let this be your study, that you may be religious in mind, devoted to the worship of God, and sincere in the godliness of faith. Therefore I exhort you to strive to be godly in mind toward God and neighbour, because bodily [Col. 1428C] exercise—which consists in fasts, vigils, manual labour, and many forms of bodily affliction, in which you weary yourself—is useful only to a small extent; that is, it has little usefulness in comparison with the great usefulness possessed by the godliness of a religious mind. For that bodily exercise is found even in hypocrites and heretics, whereas the godliness of a devoted and kindly heart is found only in the elect. Bodily exercise is useful to a small extent, but godliness is useful for all things, because it pursues every good, having the promise of the life which now is and of that which is to come. For God has promised the godly the life possessed in this age by the souls of the righteous, or temporal aids, and the life of future blessedness, saying: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, [Col. 1428D] and all these things shall be added unto you” (Matt. VI; Luke XII). And through Solomon, speaking of wisdom: “Length of days is in her right hand; and in her left, riches and glory” (Prov. III). The right hand signifies everlasting life, the left the present life.

Or, exercise yourself in godliness, that is, in compassion toward neighbours and in works of mercy. Godliness is useful for all things, because it benefits both the future and the present age, giving temporal and eternal remedies. It has the promise of the life which now is and of that to come, because to one who bestows the benefits of godliness on the poor, God gives in the present the means by which to live temporally, and in the future everlasting life. And this saying concerning godliness is faithful, that is, true: namely, that godliness is useful for all things, and what is promised to it is faithfully [Col. 1429A] fulfilled—that it may have present and future life. This saying is faithful, deceiving no one, and worthy of all acceptance, so that it should be wholly received by all people. Truly godliness has the promise of present and future life; for to this end we labour, that we may attain this promise, and we are reviled by the ungodly and blasphemers. To this end we labour, because we hope in the living God: that is, we toil in works of godliness and righteousness because we hope for the life which the living God has promised to those who act godly. He is the Saviour of all people, because he makes his sun rise upon good and evil and sends rain upon just and unjust alike (Matt. V), and commonly provides bodily preservation in this life for good and evil alike; yet he is especially the Saviour of believers because, beyond [Col. 1429B] the temporal preservation which they share with the reprobate, he gives them eternal salvation, which they may possess with the angels.

> “Command these things and teach them. Let no one despise your youth, but be an example to believers in word, in conduct, in charity, in faith, in chastity. Until I come, attend to reading, exhortation, and teaching. Do not neglect the grace which is in you, which was given you through prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. Meditate on these things; be occupied with them, so that your progress may be evident to all. Attend to yourself and to doctrine; persevere in them. For by doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you.”

[Col. 1429C] Command those who know, and teach those who do not know, these things which I have said concerning the avoidance of tales and the pursuit of godliness. Command these things to be done, and teach how they are to be done. And, so that your command and teaching may be received, let no one despise your youth: that is, live in such a way, and show yourself mature in conduct, that no one can despise you as a young man; nor let your life make your age blameworthy. Although you are young in body, if you do anything blameworthy you are rebuked more boldly and, as it were, held in contempt.

It may also be referred to those subject to you, so that it means: let none of those to whom you will give commands and whom you will teach despise your youth. For in sacred speech *adolescentia* sometimes denotes youth, Solomon bearing witness when he says: “Rejoice, young man, in your youth” (Eccl. [Col. 1429D] XI). For if he did not judge the two to be one, he would not call the one whom he exhorted “in youth” a young man. Thus here also *adolescentia* is understood as youth, so that holy Timothy, in the authority of preaching, may be even of mature age. Let no one despise your age; but be an example to believers in speech, so that they may speak good things by your example; in conduct, so that by your example they may conduct themselves well and honourably; in love of God and neighbour, in integrity of faith, and in purity of chastity.

And so that you may thus offer others an example of good works, attend to the reading of the divine Scriptures until I come. For among human words the heart readily flows away. Since it is beyond doubt that the heart, driven by the tumult of outward occupations, falls away from itself, [Col. 1430A] it must strive without ceasing to rise again through the study of instruction. Attend, I say, to reading; and after reading attend to exhortation of those already willing, and to instruction of those who do not know. For you ought to act so that you do what reading has taught should be done; admonish your subjects to do the same; and teach those who do not know it.

Act thus, and do not neglect the grace of the episcopal office which is in you. For God freely set you over that people for this purpose, that you might act thus. This grace was given to you through prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. The Apostle appears to call “prophecy” the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, through which he knew beforehand what he was going to do concerning Timothy and the others. Or certainly the bishop specially [Col. 1430B] prophesied concerning what ought to be done—whether the Apostle himself or some other holy person. By the laying on of hands he means that which took place in Timothy’s ordination. This laying on of hands was that of the presbytery, because through it he received the presbyterate, that is, the episcopate. For bishop is often called presbyter by the apostles, and presbyter bishop.

Or this laying on of hands was that of the presbyter—called in Latin *senior*—because the Apostle himself, who in this sense is understood as a presbyter, laid his hands upon Timothy’s head when consecrating him bishop. Peter (1 Pet. V) and John in their epistles call themselves elders (2 John I; 3 John I), that is, presbyters, on account of their grave maturity in conduct and wisdom, or also on account of age. Then, he says, meditate on these things: [Col. 1430C] that is, examine and turn over in your mind the things which I enjoin upon you, since you have been made a bishop for this purpose; and be continually occupied in these actions and meditations, so that, when you have lived and taught as I have said, your progress may be evident to all—that is, that all may openly know that you make progress in all things.

And so that you may profit both yourself and others, attend to yourself: that is, frequently turn the gaze of your mind back upon yourself and carefully consider how you live. If you find anything in yourself that must be corrected, correct it at once, and always strive for better things. And persevere in doctrine among them: that is, teach diligently those committed to you. You ought gladly to do both, because in doing this you will bear a twofold fruit: you will save both yourself and those [Col. 1430D] who hear you. You will save yourself if you attend to yourself, and your hearers if you persevere in doctrine. Thus a ruler must seek his own salvation without abandoning the common salvation, and seek the common advancement without neglecting his own. For he will be required to render an account to Christ the Judge concerning his subjects, just as he is compelled to render one concerning himself.

## CHAPTER V

> “Do not rebuke an elder, but entreat him as a father; younger men as brothers; older women as mothers; younger women as sisters, in all chastity.”

I said that you should persevere in teaching; nevertheless, do this with discernment, teaching or admonishing each person as is fitting. For younger people must be admonished differently from older people. Since the severity of rebuke commonly [Col. 1431A] directs the former toward improvement, gentle entreaty disposes the latter toward better things. Therefore do not rebuke an elder, but, for the honour due to godliness, entreat him reverently as a father, so that through kindly entreaty he may more readily receive your admonition. For he is offended and ashamed if he is harshly corrected. But admonish younger men with the affection of love, as brothers.

In sacred Scripture, moreover, “elders” are called not those mature merely by the length of time, but those mature by the venerability of their character. Younger men are those not weighed down by the gravity of counsel; and such persons can therefore be understood here as well. An elder, then, who has advanced in maturity: if he has acted otherwise than he ought in anything, do not rebuke him, but gently entreat him to amend himself and henceforth make progress toward better things. [Col. 1431B] But younger men, driven by levity of character, rebuke kindly, if they have sinned, as brothers. Likewise admonish older women, advanced either in age or in good character, reverently as mothers; but admonish younger women in age or character as sisters, and this in all chastity. In speaking with younger women, a young man is most rightly admonished concerning all chastity, so that he may not be stirred toward them by even the slightest arousal of the flesh.

> “Honour widows who are truly widows. But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let her first learn to govern her own household piously and to repay her parents in return. For this is acceptable before God. But she who is truly a widow and desolate hopes in God and continues in entreaties and prayers night and day. For she who lives in pleasures is [Col. 1431C] dead while living. Command these things also, that they may be beyond reproach. But if anyone does not have care for his own, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.”

“Honour widows,” he says, “who are truly widows”: that is, those deprived of all assistance from their own people, unable to work with their hands, weakened by poverty and worn down by age, for whom God is their hope and prayer their entire work. From this it is understood that younger widows, except those excused by infirmity, should be assigned either to their own labour or to service of their children or relatives. Here honour means alms or a gift. For where it is elsewhere said, “Honour your father and mother” (Exod. [Col. 1431D] XX; Eph. VI), this should be understood not in the sound of words—which can frustrate the parents’ want by empty flattery—but in supplying the necessities of life.

Therefore honour widows: that is, support them from the funds of the Church; yet not all widows, but those who are truly widows, that is, who have no aid save that of God alone. But if a widow has children or grandchildren, let her first learn to govern her own household piously; in this she will be tested. Let her learn this first—that is, before she comes to the Church to be honoured by the Church’s support. Let her learn to govern her household and repay in return the parents who supported her, so that by the same rule she may support others. Not only parents, but children, grandchildren, and other relatives are called *parentes* (“kindred”); whence an entire line of descent is called a *parentela* (“kindred group”). In secular law too, one relative is [Col. 1432A] commanded to succeed another by degree and kindred.

Therefore one repays parents in return, as was said, when one who has been nourished by elders nourishes younger people, and spends upon successors what one has received from predecessors. Or one repays parents in return when one gives assistance back to children and relatives who render services. Let the good widow do this, because it is acceptable before God. Yet she is not truly a widow who has relatives who are a comfort to her. But she who is truly a widow—that is, deprived of every worldly aid and bereft of every earthly consolation—hopes in God: seeing that she has no refuge from any quarter, she clings to God with her whole mind, from whom alone she hopes for the aid of life and salvation. Therefore she persists night and day in entreaties for the removal of evils alone, [Col. 1432B] and in prayers for the attainment of good things.

Such was holy Anna, who did not depart from the temple, serving with fasts and entreaties day and night (Luke II). Widows above all ought to devote themselves to prayers, because when the Lord exhorted people always to pray, he mentioned the widow who, by repeatedly pressing the unjust judge to hear her case, moved him (Luke XVIII). Therefore, since destitution and desolation are marked in widows, every soul should understand itself in this world to be destitute and desolate, so long as it is away from the Lord; assuredly it commends its state of widowhood to God its defender by constant and most earnest prayer.

[Col. 1432C] Mystically, either the Church or every soul which understands itself to be left without all aid except that of God alone is a widow. For why is a woman a widow? Because she has no help other than God alone. Those who have husbands, however, as it were take pride in the help of their husbands. Widows appear abandoned, but their aid is stronger. Thus the whole Church is one widow: whether in men or women, in the married, in married women, in young people, old people, or virgins. The whole Church is one widow, abandoned in this world, if it feels this and knows its widowhood; then aid is at hand for it. But let us again understand “widow” simply as a woman, as above.

For she who is truly a widow and desolate persists in prayers and becomes close to God. But, conversely, she who lives in pleasures—that is, [Col. 1432D] who indulges her flesh luxuriously and does not afflict it at all by prayers and fasts—is dead in soul while alive in the common life, because God, who is the life of the soul, has departed from her. Thus blessed Job says of wisdom, which is God, that it “is not found in the land of those who live pleasantly” (Job XXVIII): that is, in the mind of those who serve the pleasures of this life. For to be dead while living is not to have God abiding in one’s mind. Therefore, lest one be dead while living, let spiritual delights succeed carnal delights in holy chastity: namely, prayer, fasting, good thought, and frequent good works. For when a widow, instead of the marital pleasures which she was accustomed to have in her husband’s flesh, adopts the use of other carnal delights as though for consolation, then she is dead [Col. 1433A] while living.

For just as, in the bodily senses themselves, those who do not see hear more sharply and distinguish many things by touch, while those who use their eyes do not touch with such liveliness—one does not understand, from hearing alone, namely from the sense of hearing, [Note: [Col. 1433D] An obscure passage.] that, when the intention of perceiving lights is restrained, it exercises itself in the other senses with a keener faculty of recognition, as though it strove to supply by one sense what is denied by another—so too the desire of the flesh, often restrained from the pleasure of intercourse, extends itself with greater appetite into the pleasure of money; and, turned away from that, it directs itself here with a more burning impulse. Death itself is the delight of enjoyment when someone gains what he has desperately desired. Therefore the widow who lives in pleasures is dead, for pleasures are reached through desires as through gates of death.

[Col. 1433B] Therefore command widows not to live luxuriously. And this is what it means: command them to be irreproachable—that is, to beware of doing things deserving blame. I said above that, if a widow has children or grandchildren, she should learn to govern her household. But if she neglects to do this, she has lost the faith; because if anyone does not have care for his own, and especially for members of his household, so far as he can to provide them with necessities, he has denied the faith in deeds, though not in words, because he does not love his neighbour and acts faithlessly toward that person.

Or, widows ought not to seek to amass pleasures; rather, their children or other relatives should supply them with what is necessary. But if anyone is unwilling, he has denied the faith which he promised in baptism, when he renounced the works of the devil; and he is worse than an unbeliever, who has never had faith. [Col. 1433C] For this person has known the truth and promised to act well; the unbeliever has not yet known it or made the promise. But this person promised and refused to fulfil it; therefore he is worse than the one who has not yet received faith. For a sin committed knowingly is much more serious than one committed in ignorance; and it is much worse to promise good works and not do them than neither to promise nor to do them. Therefore everyone ought to bestow care on his own, and especially on members of his household, because when one begins to wish to benefit those whom one can, care for one’s own is first present. For one has a more convenient and easier access to assisting them, both by the order of nature and by that of human society itself. Even an unbeliever has care for his own; therefore one who lacks it is worse than an unbeliever.

> “Let a widow be enrolled who is not less than sixty years old, [Col. 1433D] who has been the wife of one husband, having testimony in good works: if she has brought up children, if she has received strangers, if she has washed the feet of the saints, if she has supplied the needs of those suffering tribulation, if she has pursued every good work.”

Here he gives a general command concerning those widows supported by the Church’s provisions. Accordingly, an age is prescribed, so that only those may receive the food of the poor who are now unable to work and have maturity alike of character and age. Consider also that a woman who has had two husbands, even if old, even if decrepit, even if needy, does not deserve [Col. 1434A] to receive the Church’s alms. I said above that true widows should be honoured from the Church’s resources. A widow to be thus honoured should be enrolled if she is not less than sixty years old, when the fuel of lust has already been extinguished, and if she has been the wife of one husband—that is, has had only one husband—and, after his death, has testimony in good works: namely, if she has nourished the children whom she had; if she has received the poor as guests; if she has washed the feet of holy preachers, whom at that time it was dangerous to receive.

When brothers are received as guests, a custom has arisen among many holy persons that their feet should be washed; and in this act humility receives great commendation, lest a Christian disdain to do what Christ first did (John XIII). When the body bends down to a brother’s feet, the disposition of humility is also stirred in the heart itself, [Col. 1434B] or, if already present, strengthened. A widow should be enrolled who has testimony of having done all these things; and if she has supplied such good things as she could to those suffering tribulation—that is, prisoners or persons afflicted in any manner—and, to conclude briefly, if she has pursued every good work. Such a woman should be supported from the Church’s provisions and, if she has the strength, should serve the priest.

> “But avoid younger widows. For when they have become wanton, they wish to marry in Christ, having condemnation because they have made void their first faith. At the same time they also learn to be idle, going about from house to house; and not only idle, but also garrulous and meddlesome, speaking things which they ought not. Therefore I want younger women to marry, bear children, [Col. 1434C] be heads of households, and give the adversary no opportunity for reproach. For already some have turned back after Satan. If any believing man or believing woman has widows, let such a person support them, and let the Church not be burdened, so that it may suffice for those who are truly widows.”

I said that a widow should be enrolled who is not less than sixty years old, once all wantonness has been restrained. But avoid younger widows, whose blood still boils, for service in the Church. And why? Because, when they have become wanton, they wish to marry in Christ. That is, it often happens that, abandoning their purpose of chastity, they become wanton through many lovers, or engage in the luxury of foods and pleasures; and after much wantonness they wish to marry—that is, to be joined to husbands in Christ, that is, through lawful marriage—as though it were then no sin to marry.

I say that they have eternal condemnation because they have made their first faith void: that is, because they vowed chastity to the Lord and did not fulfil it. For those who vow virginity or widowhood, not only marrying but even wishing to marry is condemnable. Thus they have condemnation because they have made their first faith void, even if not by marrying, yet by wishing to marry. Not because marriage itself is judged to be condemned as an evil; rather, the deceit of their purpose is condemned, and the pledged faith of their vow, once broken, is condemned. The adoption of an inferior good is not condemned, but the falling away from a superior good. Finally, such women are condemned not because they subsequently enter into marital fidelity, [Col. 1435A] but because, wishing to marry, they have made void their first pledge of continence. For the will which has fallen away from its purpose is condemned, whether marriage follows or does not follow.

Therefore the will of a good purpose must be preserved steadfastly in the heart, lest any man or woman look back (Luke IX, XIII) and become like Lot’s wife. For what happened to Lot’s wife? She was delivered from Sodom and placed on the road; she looked back (Gen. XIX). Where she looked back, there she remained: she became a pillar of salt, so that people might be seasoned by looking upon her, might have sense and not be foolish, and might not look back—lest, by giving an evil example, they themselves remain and season others. “At the same time they also are idle,” and so forth. These women do not merely do the things we have mentioned; added to those evils is the fact that they are idle, doing nothing with their hands. And through the wandering of their minds they become unstable even in body, because they do not remain in their own houses but learn—that is, become accustomed—to go about other people’s houses without reasonable cause, which is hostile to religious life.

[Col. 1435B] Nor are they merely idle, but also garrulous: that is, abundant in the excessive speech of tales and useless talk. Nor merely garrulous, but also meddlesome: that is, investigating the actions of others, neglecting their own, and always eager to hear something. They speak things which they ought not: shameful things and things pertaining to lust, or things otherwise contrary to religious life. Since certain widows, after promising God continence and religious conduct, commit such evils, I therefore wish younger widows not [Col. 1435C] to vow continence which they cannot preserve, but to marry and bear legitimate children—lest, if they bear any through fornication, they destroy them through fear and shame—and I wish them to be heads of households. Let them marry, lest they wander through other people’s dwellings; but, placed under husbands, let them have a restraint by which they may be governed. Let them bear children and be heads of households, so that they are not idle, but are occupied in useful actions: the nurture of children and the administration of households. For it is good to marry, good to bear children, and good to be heads of households. Therefore let them do these good things, lest perhaps they commit the evils mentioned above.

I wish them to do this and to give the adversary—that is, the unbeliever—no opportunity for reproach, that is, no cause for evil speech. This means: I do not wish them to give any occasion to the unbeliever who opposes us [Col. 1435D] and takes great pleasure in speaking ill of us, so that he may be able to say anything abusive about them. Perhaps they would give such an occasion, as some have already given it, for some have already turned back from the good of continence which they had undertaken, going after Satan, who turned back and perished. The Apostle added this so that we might understand from these words that those whom he wished to marry could more advantageously have remained continent than married, but that it was better to marry than to turn back after Satan: that is, to fall and perish by looking backward from that excellent purpose of virginal or widowed chastity.

I said that younger women should marry. But if any desire to marry, let their own people provide for them. This is what it means: if any believing man or believing woman has widows—that is, sisters or female relatives bereft of husbands, who belong to him by some line [Col. 1436A] of kinship—let that person supply them with necessities, and let the Church not be burdened by them, so that it may provide food for those who are truly widows, that is, deprived of all assistance. Here the Apostle shows that believers must provide necessary things for themselves and for others for the future. Thus we understand that when the Lord commands that one should not be anxious about tomorrow (Matt. VI), his command does not mean that holy people should save no money at all, but that God should not be served for the sake of such things, nor righteousness abandoned through fear of want.
