> “Let the presbyters who govern well be held worthy of double honour, especially those who labour in word and doctrine. For Scripture says: ‘You shall not muzzle the ox treading out the grain’ (Deut. XXV; 1 Cor. IX), and ‘The labourer is worthy of his reward’ (Matt. X; Luke X). [Col. 1436B] Do not receive an accusation against a presbyter except on the testimony of two or three witnesses.”

Let it be done concerning widows as I have shown thus far. But concerning good presbyters it is otherwise: those who govern the Church well should be held worthy of double honour, so that in the present they receive from their subjects the honour of provisions, and in the future from God the honour of everlasting glory—especially those who labour in the word for those who know, and in doctrine for those who do not know: that is, who endeavour to admonish those who know and teach those who do not know. And since double honour, that is, twofold reward, is due to such persons, I prove one honour, which subjects owe them in the offering of provisions. For the Scripture of the Law says: “You shall not muzzle the ox treading out the grain”: that is, you shall not prohibit the preacher from receiving food from the Church. And the Scripture of the Gospel according to Luke says: “The labourer is worthy of his reward” (ibid.): that is, the preacher is worthy of the provision of expenses.

The Apostle took this sentence from Luke’s Gospel, establishing it by his authority. The labourer is worthy of his reward, because the very provisions of maintenance are already a reward for labour; thus the reward for the labour of preaching begins here and is perfected there by the vision of truth. In this matter we should consider that two rewards are owed to our one work: one on the way, the other in the homeland; one sustaining us in labour, the other rewarding us in the resurrection. For good presbyters are worthy of double honour. The reward received in the present [Col. 1436D] ought to make us strive more strongly for the following reward. For every true preacher ought not to preach in order to receive a reward in this temporal life, but to receive a reward in order that he may continue preaching. Whoever preaches in order to receive here either the reward of praise or of a gift undoubtedly deprives himself of eternal reward.

But whoever desires that he himself or what he says should please people so that, when what is said pleases, not he himself but the Lord may be loved; or who receives earthly support in preaching so that he may not be worn out by want and cease from preaching—nothing at all prevents such a one from receiving his reward in the homeland, because he has received provisions on the way. For a human being gives food to a worker during labour so that he may be able to work, and after [Col. 1437A] labour pays him his reward. Much more, then, will God honour—that is, reward—his worker in two ways.

Therefore do not readily receive an accusation against a presbyter, because a person of so exalted a title should not readily be accused. Do not receive an accusation against him unless the accuser produces two or three witnesses so suitable that the accusation may rest upon them—that is, that the witnesses themselves are superior to the accuser, so that their manner of life is not inferior to that of the accuser. For witnesses, as Isidore says, are considered in respect of status, nature, and life: in status, whether free rather than enslaved, for often a slave, through fear of his master, suppresses the testimony of truth; in nature, whether male rather than female, for “woman is ever changeful and mutable” (*Aeneid* IV); in life, whether innocent and blameless in conduct. For if good life is lacking, faithworthiness will be lacking. Justice cannot have fellowship with a wicked person.

There are two kinds of witnesses: those stating what they have seen and those producing what they have heard. Witnesses sin in two ways: when they either utter falsehoods or cover truths with silence. For among the ancients it was no lesser fault to be silent about truth than to speak a lie.

> “But rebuke those who sin before all, so that the rest also may have fear. I charge you before God and Christ Jesus and the elect angels to keep these things, doing nothing without prejudice, inclining to one side.”

Act toward a presbyter as I have said. But rebuke those who sin [Col. 1437C] before all, so that the others who wished to sin may fear and not presume to do such things. The Lord says: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him alone” (Matt. XVIII); yet now the Apostle commands that sinners be rebuked before all. But there is no contradiction between these two commands, because at times a person must be corrected between yourself and that person alone, and at times rebuked before all. He is to be admonished privately when he sins against you—that is, when you know that he has sinned. Since it was secret when he sinned against you, seek secrecy when correcting what he has done. For if you alone know that he has sinned against you and wish to correct him before all, you are not a corrector but a betrayer. Therefore those things which are done more secretly should be corrected more secretly; but those done before all should be rebuked before all.

Then, to confirm the observance of all the commands, he adds: “I charge you before God.” It is as if he said: God is my witness that I have delivered my soul by saying what I ought to say; take care for yourself, lest you perish by transgressing what I have commanded. And I charge you before Christ Jesus, who will judge, and before the elect angels, [Col. 1437D] who will separate evil from good (Matt. XIII, XXIII). I charge you to keep these things which I have now commanded concerning not lightly receiving an accusation against a presbyter, the public correction of manifest sinners, and also the other commands given throughout the epistle above and still to be given below. Keep these things, never doing anything without prior judgment—that is, without considering beforehand whether it should or should not be done—and inclining to no side other than that which you have found just by prior consideration.

Or: keep these things without prejudgment, that is, without blame, doing nothing by inclining to the side which I have not commanded—that is, to the side of left-hand action. Or: keep what I have said concerning accusation against a presbyter, doing nothing without prior examination, and do not depart from that examination toward anything other than what examination has found.

> “Lay hands hastily on no one, neither share in other people’s sins. Keep yourself chaste. Do not continue to drink water, but use a little wine, because of your stomach and your frequent infirmities. The sins of some people are manifest, going beforehand to judgment; [Col. 1438B] but those of others also follow after. Likewise good deeds are manifest, and those which are otherwise cannot be hidden.”

Because the case of a presbyter must be handled with such gravity, first consider carefully who the man is whom you are about to ordain presbyter. For he ought not easily to be ordained who cannot easily be deposed from his rank; and therefore, in ordaining him, do not hastily lay hands on anyone, but test him for a long time beforehand, because by delaying you will be able to know his manner of life. Nor, by consenting, share in the sins of others, if you ordain a sinner without consideration. For whoever ordains an unworthy man shares in his sins. And so that you may be able to exclude worthless persons from ordination, keep yourself chaste, as though it were said: You who wish to repel the unworthy must keep yourself [Col. 1438C] in purity of life. And you who judge others, take care lest you be judged by others for a perverse deed: whoever avoids others’ sins, let him avoid his own.

I say that you should keep yourself chaste; nevertheless, do not still drink only water, as you were formerly accustomed, but use a little wine, since when taken moderately it does not harm chastity. And I prescribe this because of your stomach, which is distressed by long abstinence and is the seat of weakness; and because of your frequent infirmities, that is, those that often come upon you. Because he has admonished him concerning chastity, he takes this occasion to prohibit the immoderate abstinence Timothy had undertaken, and commands that a little wine be taken because of infirmities—more by the counsel of a physician than of an apostle, though the apostle is a spiritual physician—[Col. 1438D] lest Timothy, overcome by weakness, be unable to fulfill the work of preaching. Yet even for these necessities the drinking of wine is scarcely conceded, because wine and youth are a double fire of pleasure (Prov. XX). But stomach-pain and frequent weakness in holy Timothy restrained the fuel of lust.

Therefore, when the Apostle was instructing his beloved disciple concerning the appointment of the offices of the Church, lest he perhaps advance persons disorderly to sacred orders, he said: “Do not hastily lay hands on anyone, nor share in the sins of others. Keep yourself chaste.” Then, turning immediately to the weakness of his body, he says: “Do not still,” etc., as far as, “your infirmities.” And he immediately added: “The sins of certain men are manifest, going before them to judgment, [Col. 1439A] but those of others follow after.” What relevance to his forbidding a sick man to drink water has what he adds concerning the sins of certain men and their manifest character, except that, after inserting the statement about his infirmity, he returns at the end to what he had said above, “Do not hastily lay hands on anyone,” etc.? For, to show with what concern these same sins ought to be refuted, he inserted an admonition of prudent discernment against the annoyance of infirmity, and immediately afterward stated that in some men sins are exposed and in others hidden, saying: “The sins of certain men,” etc.

A similar insertion is found in the book of the Lord Job, where it is said of the reprobate: “From morning until evening they are cut down, and because no one understands, they perish forever” (Job IV); and immediately something is added concerning the elect: “but because they shall have been left behind, they shall be taken away from them” (ibid.); and again, directly afterward, it is said of the reprobate: “They shall die, and not in wisdom” (ibid.). But in other places of the Holy Scriptures such insertions are frequently found.

Therefore, since Timothy, or any bishop, ought not hastily to lay hands on anyone, lest he share in another’s sins if he ordains a sinner, the reason is added when it says: “The sins of certain men are manifest, going before them to judgment.” That is, certain persons’ sins are so open that their reputation or notoriety comes before them to the judgment—that is, to the place where persons are examined—before the notorious men themselves come to be ordained. But some persons’ sins follow them to judgment, because they first become manifest when those to be ordained are examined. [Col. 1439C] This must be understood of certain sins; for not all are disclosed in that examination, but very many sometimes remain hidden.

Nor are only certain sins manifest in this way, while others are gradually uncovered in examination or conduct; certain good works also are similarly manifest, going before a person to judgment, so that there is no need to prove that they are good. And other works, though also good, “are otherwise situated,” that is, are not so openly displayed; they cannot be hidden even in the examination itself, and therefore must be tested.

Jerome: What he says is of this sort. Some sin so freely and openly that, before you have seen them, you immediately know them to be sinners; but others, who cunningly conceal their vices, we recognize from their subsequent conduct. Likewise, good works in some are in plain view; in others we learn them through long experience.

Augustine: He calls those things manifest about which it is clear with what intention they are done. These go before judgment, because, if the judgment has followed such things, it is not rash. But those things which are hidden follow after, because neither will they remain concealed in their own time. This must likewise be understood concerning good works. Therefore let us judge what is manifest, but leave judgment upon what is hidden to God, because such things too, whether evil or good, cannot remain hidden when the time comes for them to be disclosed.

## CHAPTER VI

> “Let all who are servants under the yoke consider their masters worthy of all honor, lest the name [Col. 1440A] of the Lord and the doctrine be blasphemed. But those who have believing masters should not despise them because they are brothers, but should serve them all the more, because they are believers and beloved, and sharers in the benefit.”

What is commanded concerning the Hebrew servant—that he should serve for six years and in the seventh be sent away free without payment—might have led Christian servants to demand this from their masters. Therefore apostolic authority now commands servants to be subject to their masters, lest the name of the Lord and the doctrine be blasphemed. For the false teachers said that servants could not lawfully be kept except for six years, or rather that no one ought to be another’s servant, but that all should equally be free, because all had descended from one father, Adam, and Christ by redeeming them had set all free.

The Apostle opposes their perverse persuasion, saying that Christian servants ought to serve all masters well, whether pagan or Christian, because Christ commanded this when he said: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Luke XX). This means: Christian servants oppressed under the yoke of unbelieving masters—whoever those servants may be, whether just or wise—should nevertheless consider their masters worthy of every honor, by serving them well, lest, if they disdain to serve, the name of the Lord be blasphemed by their masters on their account, as though it were invading what belongs to another, and Christian doctrine be blasphemed as though it preached unjust things and decreed against worldly law.

Thus should those act who have unbelieving masters. But those who have believing masters should not therefore disdain to serve them, as the false apostles taught, because they are brothers—[Col. 1440C] that is, equal to their masters in Christ, since they are indeed Christians—but should serve them all the more, that is, with greater affection, because they are believers, sharers in the sacraments of the Church; and they are beloved by God because they share in his present and future benefit.

> “Teach and exhort these things. If anyone teaches otherwise and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the doctrine that accords with godliness, he is proud, knowing nothing, but sickly about questions and disputes over words. From these arise envies, strife, blasphemies, evil suspicions, conflicts of men corrupted in mind and deprived of the truth, who suppose [Col. 1440D] godliness to be gain.”

Teach these things which I have said about servants to those who do not know them, and exhort those who do know them. Do this when anyone teaches otherwise—that is, when someone preaches a liberty common to all in Christ, saying that all ought to be free. Then, on the contrary, command—that is, preach—that servants should consider their masters worthy of all honor and should not disdain to serve them.

Indeed, it is always advantageous to teach these things, but especially when a perverse man teaches otherwise, preaching that all should be free, and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ when Christ’s saying is set before him, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Luke XX); nor to the command given to Peter to give, for himself and for Christ, the stater found in the fish’s mouth to those demanding tribute (Matt. XVII); nor again to the saying, “Learn from me, because I am meek” (Matt. XI). Nor does he assent to our doctrine, which accords with godliness—that is, which does not make Christianity hateful by teaching insolence.

The man who does not assent to these and similar words of the Lord and to this doctrine, but teaches otherwise, is proud: pride, not reason, leads him. He is proud, that is, unwilling to be defeated or turned from his own opinion. And although he thinks himself learned, he knows nothing; rather, he is always sickly about questions—that is, ineffective and hindered in resolving them, unable to attain the investigation of truth—and likewise sickly about disputes over words, that is, about an apparent contradiction in certain words [Col. 1441B] of Scripture, though their meaning agrees. For example: “If the Son sets you free, you will be truly free” (John VIII); and again, “Whoever wishes to be first among you shall be servant of all” (Mark IX; Matt. XX). These words appear contradictory to this fool: that the Son makes us free, and yet one who wishes to be first becomes a servant, although the first among us ought especially to be free if we are free.

Or he is sickly about disputes over words, that is, debates in which disputants fight one another with words. From such questions and verbal disputes arise envies, strife, blasphemies, and evil suspicions. For because of the words of false apostles preaching such liberty, those who have servants envy the Christian name, contend against believers, blaspheme God as though he takes away what belongs to others, and suspect evil of us, as though we had invented this liberty for gain.

And from this arise conflicts against them from men corrupted in mind—that is, false preachers whose understanding or reasoning is corrupted by error, so that it cannot possess knowledge of inviolate truth in a true apprehension of things. Or they are corrupted in mind because, even if their flesh through a simulation of holiness is intact, their inward mind nevertheless delights in the impurities of lusts, in shameful acts, or in the love of money. They are deprived of truth because, although they may at one time have known in some measure the truth of Catholic doctrine, through the errors they have implanted in their minds they have utterly lost that knowledge. I mean men who suppose godliness—that is, the worship of God—to be gain in temporal things, because the false teachers thought that Christ was to be worshiped for the advantages of the present life, not of the future, since they themselves preached for the acquisition of present profit.

> “But godliness with sufficiency is great gain. For we brought nothing into this world, and without doubt we can carry nothing away. But having food and the means of covering ourselves, we are content with these.”

They think that the godliness of our religion is gain in carnal advantage; and it is indeed true that Christian godliness is gain, yet not a small gain that acquires only temporal things, as they think, [Col. 1442A] but a great one, acquiring eternal goods of body and soul. Godliness with sufficiency is great gain: that is, godliness to which its small possessions suffice, and which does not desire to possess more than is necessary. Whoever wills this sufficiency wills it fittingly only if he does not will more. Otherwise he does not will sufficiency itself, and therefore does not will it fittingly.

The man who prayed, saying, “Give me neither poverty nor riches; grant only what is necessary for my sustenance” (Prov. XXX), desired this sufficiency. These necessities ought to suffice us, because it is incongruous that we who brought nothing here and will carry nothing away from here should seek to possess much here. We brought nothing into this world when we were born; and there is no doubt that we can carry nothing away from it when, dying, we depart from the world. “Naked he comes forth from his mother’s womb, and naked he departs from the world” (Job I). Thus there is one entrance into life for all and a like departure. Why then does one man seek in this life to become richer than another? Or why does the rich man swell against the poor, when each has come without riches and will depart without riches?

Therefore let us not seek to multiply riches, which we cannot carry with us from here; but, having food with which we may be fed and clothing with which we may be covered, let us be content with these, seeking nothing further in this age, because cold and hunger can be driven away by simple clothing and food.

> “For those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and the snare of the devil, and into many useless and harmful desires, which plunge men into destruction [Col. 1442C] and perdition. For covetousness is the root of all evils. Some, desiring it, have wandered from the faith and entangled themselves in many pains. But you, O man of God, flee these things. Rather pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, charity, patience, meekness. Fight the good fight of faith; lay hold on eternal life, to which you have been called, and have confessed the good confession before many witnesses.”

For us apostles, whom others ought to imitate, food and coverings suffice; and they ought to suffice all Christians. For those who wish to become rich fall into temptation. I do not speak of those who are rich, but of those who wish to become rich. For it is one thing to be rich, another to wish to become rich. Here covetousness is accused, not gold, not silver, not riches. The rich man is commanded to distribute to the poor, not to desire riches.

For those who wish to become rich, even if they do not become so, nevertheless by that very desire fall into temptation and into the snare of the devil: that is, they consent to the devil’s suggestion, loving riches, the love of which he suggests; and they are bound by him through consent to wicked persuasion and through a perverse act. They fall into many useless and harmful desires, because these profit nothing but greatly harm, harming in such a way as to plunge men into the destruction of their bodies and the perdition of their souls.

And I rightly said that through desire for riches they fall into many desires, for covetousness is the root of all evils: that is, there is no kind of evil which does not at some time proceed from some covetousness. By it the first angel fell (Isa. XIV), who certainly did not love money but his own power. By it the first human beings were cast down (Gen. III), who proudly desired not gold but a divinity not granted to them. For desiring to possess more than they had received, they lost what they had received. Since pride is the beginning of all sin (Ecclus. X), covetousness is rightly called the root of all evils.

Or avarice is understood here in a general sense, by which anyone desires something more than he ought, for the sake of his own excellence and a certain love of what belongs to him. Such perversity of mind is appropriately called either pride or covetousness. Since, therefore, there is a particular covetousness which may more commonly be called the love [Col. 1443B] of money, the Apostle, now naming covetousness, has signified the genus by the species and intended universal covetousness to be understood when he says: “Covetousness is the root of all evils.” It indeed secretly arises in the mind, but openly produces in action the prickings of every sin. These prickings, rising from this root, the outstanding preacher immediately indicated, adding: “Some, desiring it, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many pains.” For, in saying “many pains,” he made known the prickings or thorns growing, as it were, from this root.

Some through covetousness have wandered from the faith and entangled themselves in many pains, as those who worshiped idols for the gifts of rulers and afterward, having in this age become despised by all, suffered many miseries. Even now many wander from the faith through covetousness, since avarice is the service of idols (Eph. V; Col. III), and pierce themselves with many pains, since their minds are continually pricked by the thorns of anxieties over acquiring or preserving riches, and their bodies are worn down by manifold labor.

They fall through irrational covetousness into so many evils. But you, O man who uses reason, because you belong to God rather than to covetousness, flee these evils if they should ever seek to seize you through some pleasure of human frailty. Flee these things indeed, but pursue righteousness, so that the observance of righteousness may never escape you, but you may always follow it through all the paths of its actions. Pursue righteousness by doing for each person what justice demands, not what covetousness demands.

And pursue godliness, so that by compassion you may condescend to one in need or affliction and mercifully assist him as necessity requires, giving without avarice what is needed. And pursue faith, so that, believing in invisible goods, you may despise visible ones. For the man who has true faith concerning God and future blessedness does not care to become rich here in exile with the ungodly, nor does he esteem the world above God. Pursue charity toward God and neighbor, which the avaricious man wholly lacks, because he neither loves God, whose command concerning giving alms he despises (Luke XI, XII), nor is proved to love his neighbor, to whom he imparts nothing from his possessions.

But, so that you may be able to pursue charity, add patience, by which you may bear with equanimity what is inflicted on you by your neighbors, lest you be inwardly bitten by any pain of indignation against those who inflict these things on you, but preserve a serene and tranquil heart toward them. For you must bear much from your neighbors with equanimity if you do not wish often to lose charity. And especially toward those from whom you suffer adversity, pursue meekness, so that you repay them with no harshness or bitterness, but remain gentle and tractable toward them. The covetous man, however, neither patiently endures adversities nor preserves meekness toward anyone.

Fight also—that is, contend for your soul in the contest of this present life—and receive the crown at the end. Fight not an evil fight, like the avaricious, who contend to surpass others in riches; or like heretics, who contend to separate believers from the faith. But fight the good fight of faith, that you may graciously strive to surpass others in faith and goodness and bring unbelievers under the faith. Or fight the fight of faith—that is, the fight which faith requires—so that in martyrdom, in the contest for righteousness, against the enemies of faith, or against whatever vices, you may fight continually.

And through victory in this contest lay hold—that is, take to yourself by a certain force—of eternal life. You ought manfully to lay hold of it because you were called to it by God through evangelical preaching, or through the purpose of the divine will; and you confessed the good confession of faith and righteousness before many witnesses when you were baptized or when you were consecrated bishop. Therefore strive to lay hold of the fruit of this confession, namely eternal life.

> “I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, [Col. 1444C] and before Christ Jesus, who gave testimony under Pontius Pilate to the good confession, that you keep the commandment spotless and irreproachable until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, which in its own times the blessed and only powerful King of kings and Lord of lords will reveal (Apoc. XVII, XIX), who alone has immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen nor can see (John I; 1 John IV); to whom be glory, honor, and everlasting dominion. Amen.”

That you may be able to lay hold of eternal life and keep your good confession, I charge you before God, who gives life to all things that are made alive, and before Christ, who in his Passion gave the good confession, that you keep the commandment. For you will not attain eternal life except through him who gives life to all things; and therefore I now invoke him as witness of my charge, that he may grant you life if you obey. Nor will you keep your good confession unless you imitate Christ, who, just as under Pilate he gave the good confession, so you also should not fear to confess the truth before the authorities of this age. Therefore I deliver this command to you before Christ.

God the Father gives life to all things, though not without the Son, because whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does. “For as the Father raises the dead and gives life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills” (John V). Nor is this giving of life accomplished without the Holy Spirit, because, as the same Son says: “It is the Spirit who gives life” (John VI). Not the Father alone, but the whole Trinity, which is one God, gives life to all things.

But what follows, “and before Christ Jesus, who gave testimony under Pontius Pilate to the good confession,” is properly understood of the Son, because under Pilate we know that the Son alone suffered in the form of a servant—not the Father or the Holy Spirit. Then the Son himself gave good testimony because he said that he was a king, although he knew that he would die for it; and that testimony was the good confession of truth. He gave this testimony and confession when he answered Pilate: “You say that I am a king. For this I was born and for this I came into the world, that I might bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice” (John XVIII). So you also must not, through any fear of tyrants, be silent concerning the confession of truth.

Therefore I charge you before God, who is Trinity, and before Christ, who is “the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (above, II), that you keep spotless from criminal sin the commandment of right action and right teaching which I give you; and keep it irreproachable—that is, so that it affords no basis for rebuke because of any appearance of dishonesty. Keep it thus until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, of whom he himself says: “Watch, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come” (Matt. XXIV): that is, until your death.

Or, in Timothy this is commanded to every ruler of the Church, because one will succeed another until the final coming of the Lord: that he keep this commandment free from the stain of crime and from the reproach of dishonorable appearance. The Lord Christ—or the coming of the Lord—will be revealed “in his own,” that is, fitting and appointed, times (ibid.): that is, God the Trinity will set him openly before all as visible. He is blessed naturally in himself and from himself, which belongs to no creature. For no creature can be blessed except by participation in the blessedness of its Creator (Rom. XIII). He alone is powerful, because by himself and naturally he can do all things. If creatures have any power, they receive it from him, for “there is no power except from God.” He is King of kings because all who reign do so under his rule; and Lord of lords because all who exercise dominion over others serve him, willingly or unwillingly.

These things, as we have said, are said of the whole Trinity, which is one God. He alone has immortality because he alone is unchangeable. For in every mutable nature, change itself is in some respect death, because it causes something not to be what it was. Accordingly, even the human soul, which is called immortal because in its own fashion it never ceases to live, nevertheless has, in accordance with its own condition, a certain death of its own. For if it lived righteously and sins, it dies to righteousness. If it was sinful and is justified, it dies to sin. To say nothing of its other changes, about which it would take long to dispute, even the nature of heavenly creatures could die, [Col. 1446A] because it could sin. For angels sinned and became demons; and those who did not sin were able to sin. And whenever a rational creature is granted inability to sin, this does not belong to the creature itself but to God’s grace.

And for this reason God alone has immortality: not by anyone’s grace but by his own nature he neither could nor can be changed by any conversion; neither could nor will be able to sin by any change. He also “dwells in inaccessible light.” But if the light in which he dwells is inaccessible, how are we told: “Draw near to him and be enlightened” (Ps. XXXIII)? It is inaccessible to our own powers, but one draws near to him by his gifts. For Moses approached the darkness in which God was (Exod. XIX). That darkness is this light called inaccessible here, because even any bodily light which cannot be looked upon because of the excess of its brightness may rightly be called darkness and inaccessible.

Dionysius wrote thus concerning the darkness to which Moses approached: “The divine darkness is inaccessible light, in which God is said to dwell, being invisible because of surpassing brightness and inaccessible because of the superexcellent outpouring of superessential lights. Everyone worthy to know and see God comes into this darkness by neither seeing nor knowing, truly becoming beyond vision and knowledge, knowing this very thing: that he is beyond all things sensible and intelligible; and seeing prophetically: ‘Your knowledge has become wonderful from me; it has been strengthened, and I shall not be able to attain it’ (Ps. XIII).”

Therefore this light, or darkness, in which God dwells, is called inaccessible because of the surpassing excellence of its splendor; in beholding it, the inward eye of the rational creature is darkened. For, as the same Dionysius says elsewhere concerning him, he leads beyond both word and understanding, into a darkness beyond every word and understanding, superessentially, as the superessential and superdivine reality; neither is he name nor word, but he is exalted above all.

> **[Note: Col. 1445D]** An obscure passage.

This exaltation is that inaccessibility of light. “No human being has seen him, nor can see him” (John I), because of his surpassing brightness, which exceeds and overwhelms human sight. Divinity can in no way be seen by human vision, but is seen by that vision by which those who have already seen are no longer human beings but are beyond [Col. 1446D] human beings. For Sacred Scripture customarily designates all followers of carnal things by the name of humanity. Hence it was said to the Corinthians: “Since there is zeal and strife among you, are you not carnal and walking according to man?” (1 Cor. III); and shortly afterward: “Are you not men?” (ibid.). In his customary manner the Apostle both here and there called “men” those who think human things, because those who think divine things are above human beings.

Therefore we shall see God if, through heavenly conduct, we are worthy to be above human beings. To him be glory in the increase of the faithful, honor in their constancy of good conduct, and dominion in the complete humility of their hearts. I say everlasting dominion, [Col. 1447A] so that he may reign forever in their good hearts. Or glory, honor, and everlasting dominion exist in him naturally, permanently in himself, without beginning, end, or mutability; by that everlasting dominion his will is eternally fulfilled. For he did not begin to possess dominion when he began to create creatures, but from eternity possesses everlasting dominion. Amen: that is, all these things have been spoken faithfully.

> “Charge the rich of this world not to think highly of themselves, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who supplies us abundantly with all things to enjoy; to do good, to become rich in good works, to give readily, to share, to lay up for themselves a good foundation for the future, that they may lay hold of the true life.”

[Col. 1447B] Above he showed the dangers that happen to those who wish to become rich. Therefore, lest Timothy despair of the salvation of the rich and avoid them, he teaches him how to show them the way of salvation. “Charge,” he says, “the rich of this world,” that is, those who have worldly riches, “not to think highly,” that is, not to think proudly.

It should especially be noted that the teacher of humility, when mentioning the rich, does not say, “Ask,” but “Charge.” For although charity or compassion ought to be given to weakness, honor is not owed to arrogance. Thus what is rightly said to such persons is commanded all the more rightly, inasmuch as they swell in lofty thought over transitory things. For nothing in riches is so much to be feared as pride. The Apostle did not fear riches, but the disease of riches; and the disease of riches is pride. Great indeed is the soul which, amid riches, is not tempted by this disease. Great, therefore, is the rich man who does not think himself great because he is rich. But the man who thinks himself great for this reason is proud and needy.

“Charge the rich of this world.” He would not add “of this world” unless there were other rich persons who are not of this world. They are those whose prince and head is he of whom it was said: “For your sake he became poor when he was rich, that by his poverty you might become rich” (2 Cor. VIII). Christ’s poverty brought us not money but righteousness. Whence came his poverty? From becoming mortal. Therefore true riches are immortality. For there is true abundance where there is no want. Whoever therefore possesses these riches is rich, but not rich in this world.

Yet the rich of this world are not despised; rather, they are shown how they can possess true riches. “Charge the rich of this world not to think highly,” that is, so that loftiness may not taste sweet and pleasant to them; “nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches,” that is, not to hope in riches, concerning which they have no certainty how long they will possess them or what will come to them because of them. Just as fruits or trees have their worms, so riches have their worm. The worm of riches is pride. Therefore the rich are commanded not to cast away riches, but not to think proudly. The worm is excluded; the use of riches is permitted.

The rich man takes pride because he hopes in the uncertainty of riches. For if he prudently considered their uncertainty, he would never be proud but would always be afraid; and the richer he was, the more anxious he would become, even in this life. For many poor people have been safer amid the disturbances of this age. But many have been sought out, seized, tortured, or killed because of their riches. Many who were rich yesterday awaken poor when robbers come and take everything away. Therefore one must not hope in the uncertainty of riches but in the living God. Lest they think that their hope has been taken away, it is added: “but in God.” Let them hope in God, who supplies us abundantly with all things, temporal and eternal, to enjoy. Yet eternal things are more properly for enjoyment, temporal things for use: temporal things as for travelers, eternal things as for inhabitants; temporal things by which we may do good, eternal things by which we may become good.

The rich ought thus to act and do good: that is, to labor at good works and become rich in good works, so that they may be filled with the riches of good works. Let them hope in the Lord, who gives all things abundantly for enjoyment: that is, who himself will be all things for our enjoyment. For I do not think that “who gives us all things abundantly to enjoy” is said except of himself. For using seems to be one thing and enjoying another. We use things for necessity; we enjoy them for delight. Therefore he gives these temporal things for use, but gives himself for enjoyment. If, then, he gives himself, why is “all things” said, except in accordance with what is said: “that God may be all in all” (1 Cor. XV)?

“Become rich,” he says, “in good works; give readily.” Let riches benefit them in this way, so that giving may not be difficult for them. The poor man wishes to give but cannot; the rich man wishes to give and can. Therefore, because he can give readily, let him readily give to those in need. For the rich ought to share—that is, make their goods common with holy poor persons—and lay up for themselves a good foundation: that is, the firmness of enduring stability for the future, where they are truly rich, but not rich in this world.

For when I say that they should give readily and share, I do not wish to strip them or leave them empty. I do not teach loss when I say that they should lay up treasure for themselves. I do not urge them to lose their riches; I teach them where to send them ahead. Let them send their treasures ahead to the place where true life is, so that they themselves, following afterward, may lay hold of it. Otherwise, if they lay up treasure here, they may be deceived by the falsity of this life, [Col. 1448D] like the rich man clothed in purple, who was unwilling to give crumbs to Lazarus and therefore, afterward delivered to flames, could not obtain a drop of water (Luke XVI).

> “O Timothy, guard the deposit entrusted to you, avoiding profane novelties of speech and oppositions of falsely named knowledge. Some, professing this, have fallen away from the faith. Grace be with you. Amen.”

When the Apostle had enjoined many things upon Timothy, after all the rest he commands him to guard the deposit—that is, the treasure of knowledge entrusted to him, namely the talent received from the Lord—carefully, so that he may return it multiplied. For this reason he addresses him by his own name, to make him more watchful and attentive in preserving what he is admonished to preserve. “O Timothy,” he says, “guard the deposit,” that is, the treasure of wisdom which God and I entrust to you, lest anyone steal it from you through novel verbal inventions. Therefore guard it, “avoiding profane novelties of speech,” that is, those outside religion.

For not all novelties are to be avoided—those which accord with the teaching of religion are not. Such, for example, is the very name “Christians,” which began after the Lord’s ascension, when the disciples were first called Christians at Antioch (Acts 11); yet the reality itself existed before the name. And against the impiety of the Arians the Fathers added the new term ὁμοούσιον, “of one substance”; but they did not mark a new reality by that name. For what is called ὁμοούσιον is this: “I and the Father are one” (John 10), namely, of one and the same substance. For if every novelty were profane, neither would the Lord have said, “I give you a new commandment,” nor would the testament have been called “new” (John 13). But novelties of speech are profane whenever heretics invent some new error and presume to speak differently from others.

Avoid such novelties, if you wish to guard the deposit; and beware “oppositions of knowledge falsely so called,” that is, objections which may be raised against Christian teaching from the supposed knowledge of heretics, who boast that they know though they are ignorant; or from secular knowledge, [Col. 1450A] which is called knowledge under a false name, since its true name is ignorance, error, or incompetence. From it many objections are raised against evangelical preaching: for example, that a Virgin could not give birth; that God could not die; that one who was dead could not raise himself; and similar things which are objected to us through the lack of understanding of natural philosophers or heretics.

But avoid objections of this kind, which arise from a knowledge falsely called knowledge, because it is not knowledge but ignorance. Some, promising to impart this knowledge to others, “have fallen away,” that is, have fallen altogether into errors, always moving about around the faith and never entering within it. For nothing do such people love so much as promising knowledge, while ridiculing as ignorance the faith in true things which little ones are commanded to believe.

“Grace be with you”; as though he said: I have enjoined many things upon you throughout the course of this epistle; but, that you may be able to keep them all, may the grace of God be with you—that is, remaining with and cooperating with the powers of your free will. “Amen”: that is, all that is contained in this epistle has been spoken faithfully. For just as “amen,” answered at the end of a prayer, confirms the whole prayer, so “amen,” written at the end of an epistle, confirms the epistle.

## ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO TIMOTHY

[Col. 1449]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 1449C]

Paul, held in bonds at Rome and about to depart from the world, writes again to Timothy, wearied by weaknesses and adversities, that he may labour steadfastly in the grace of God entrusted to him. In many ways he exhorts him to martyrdom. He strengthens him against false preachers, instructs him concerning the rule of all truth, concerning what will come to pass in the last times, and concerning his own suffering. Thus he begins.

## CHAPTER I

> “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, according to the promise of the life which is in Christ Jesus, to Timothy, most beloved son: grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.”

Paul writes to Timothy, he who is an apostle—that is, an envoy of Christ Jesus, sent by the Saviour-King to preach the way of salvation—and is an apostle not by his own usurpation, but through the will of God the Father. He is, I say, an apostle, sent to preach according to the promise of life which is in Christ Jesus, [Col. 1450C] that is, to announce to believers the promise made by God of that incorruption which is already in Christ, raised from the dead: namely, that God promised to the members that life which is already in the Head.

And he who is such an apostle writes to Timothy, not as to a worthless but as to a most beloved son, begotten in holiness and wisdom. To this son may there be grace—that is, the gift of the Holy Spirit, by which whatever he does may be sanctified; and mercy, by which he may mercifully be delivered from sins, enemies, and all miseries; and peace, which Christ left to his own in the observance of brotherly love, and which he will give them in the repose of blessed eternity. May these be his from God the Father, who created us and adopted us as sons, and from Christ Jesus our Lord, who is our king, saviour, and ruler.

> [Col. 1450D] “I give thanks to my God, whom I serve from my forefathers in a pure conscience, as without ceasing I remember you in my prayers night and day, desiring to see you, mindful of your tears, that I may be filled with joy, receiving remembrance of that unfeigned faith which is in you, which first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice. And I am certain that it is also [Col. 1451A] in you. For this reason I remind you to rekindle the grace of God which is in you through the laying on of my hands. For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power and love and sobriety.”

I give thanks for you to my God, whom I serve with a pure conscience from my forefathers—that is, from Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and the other holy Hebrew fathers, from whom I take the example of divine service. Or, if this is understood of his fleshly father and mother: from the time when I came forth from them and began to understand, I have always served God with a conscience pure from evil intention. Even in the persecution which, out of zeal for the Law, I inflicted upon Christians, I had a pure conscience, since I thought that by this I was greatly pleasing God, just as Christ himself foretold to them: “The hour comes,” he says, “when everyone who kills you will think that he renders service to God” (John 16).

Thus, always possessing purity of conscience—that is, a clean intention of heart, free from disgrace—I do not cease to serve God. To him I now give thanks for how continually I remember you. That is, constantly considering how mindful I am of you, I give thanks to God, who has made you such that you are worthy always to remain in the memory of my mind. Or, according to other manuscripts, it is more easily read thus: “I give thanks to God, whom I serve from my forefathers in a pure conscience, that I have unceasing remembrance of you”—namely, that because of the merit of your holiness you are worthy always to be in my heart. This is a wise exhortation toward better things.

I have unceasing remembrance of you in my prayers; that is, whenever I pray, I never cease to remember you, so as to pray for you night and day. And therefore I mingle you thus with my prayers, because I desire to see you, that I may have some consolation in the sight of your presence, being afflicted by so many evils in this prison. I desire, I say, to see you, mindful of your tears, which you poured forth abundantly when I left you at Ephesus, because it was exceedingly hard for you not always to be with me. Therefore I desire to see you, so that, seeing you whom I love so greatly, I may be filled with joy. For it will be great joy to me if I can still see you before I die.

I said that I am mindful of your tears. And I remember them while receiving recollection of that [Col. 1451D] unfeigned faith which is in you—not feigned, simulated, or fictitious, but true and adorned with good works. It admonishes you to act bravely, since it was firm even in women; for it first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice. For your father was a Gentile (Acts 16). Faith dwelt in them; but I too am certain—that is, I know for certain—that the same faith dwells in you, whose example you received from them. Therefore preserve it diligently.

For this reason—that is, because you possess faith from good parents as if by hereditary right, and have hitherto been so good that you cannot be removed from the memory of my heart—I remind you to rekindle the grace of God which is in you through the laying on of my hands: that is, by preaching, to exercise the episcopal office which you received when I laid hands upon you in your ordination, an office which is as though dead in you through fear of martyrdom. For the grace of the episcopate admonishes him to rekindle it, that he may preach the word of God more confidently, neither fearing earthly powers nor being ashamed to call himself servant of the Crucified One and disciple of one in chains.

For he had become somewhat negligent and timid in this matter, because he was wearied by adversities. But the mention of his grandmother and mother, who were women and held the faith steadfastly while it was still newer and believers were few, is placed first so that he may consider that he, being a man and having been nurtured under them, ought much more now—when the multitude of believers is already abundant—to hold and preach faith and grace manfully.

“I admonish you,” he says, “to rekindle the grace of God which has in some measure fallen dormant in you through fear of tribulations.” You can and ought to do this, because God has not given us a spirit of fear, but a spirit of power: that is, he has not given us a spirit which makes us fear the adversities of this age, but one which makes us strong against every adversity, so that through the strength of constancy we may always overcome the adversity of fear.

We have not received that spirit of fear of which the Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matthew 10), lest we deny him through that fear by which Peter was troubled (John 18). Rather, we have received that spirit of fear of which he immediately adds: “Fear him who has power to destroy both body and soul in Gehenna” (Matthew 10). For greater freedom is necessary against so many and such great temptations, so that this world may be conquered together with all its attractions, terrors, and errors. This the martyrdoms of the saints have taught: granted by him from whom they received not a spirit of fear, by which they might yield to persecutors, but one of power, love, and sobriety, by which they might overcome all things that threaten, change, or torture.

Of power, that they may be strong against adversities; of love, that they may love God above all things; of sobriety, that they may flee being intoxicated by the desires of the age.

> “Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner; but labour with the Gospel according to the power of God, who delivered us and called us with his holy calling, not according to our works but according to his purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal times, but has now been manifested [Col. 1452D] through the illumination of our Saviour Jesus Christ, who indeed destroyed death but illuminated life and incorruption through the Gospel, in which I have been appointed preacher, apostle, and teacher of the Gentiles. For this reason I also suffer these things, but I am not ashamed. For I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to guard my deposit unto that day.”

Since you have not received a spirit of fear but of power and love, therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord Jesus Christ. That is, do not merely fail to fear, but do not be ashamed to preach Christ crucified, because he rose again; and therefore the glory of the resurrection utterly removes the shame of the cross. Since he himself is our Lord, whom we all ought to serve, do not be ashamed of his testimony: do not be ashamed to preach as immortal God the one who, for all, deigned in assumed flesh to taste death for a time, lest you incur that threat by which he said: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed when he comes in his majesty” (Luke 9).

Nor be ashamed of me, his prisoner, because there is no shameful disgrace in suffering bonds for righteousness. There is nothing in this matter of which to be ashamed. Therefore do not, because of the taunts of unbelievers, be ashamed that I am bound for Christ; but labour together—that is, labour with me—for the Gospel, that is, for the advancement of the Gospel, according to the power of God, given to us by God. He delivered us through Christ’s blood [Col. 1453B] from the yoke of the devil, just as formerly through the blood of the lamb he delivered the children of Israel from Pharaoh’s power; and through evangelical preaching he called us who had turned away.

He called us with his calling, that is, one fitting to himself alone; a calling, I say, holy—that is, tending to make us holy. The Apostle repeats “calling” in order to suggest that we have been called by God through the Son and the apostles. He called us, I say, and not according to our works, because we had done no works for which we might deserve to be called by him, but rather to be condemned. Rather, without preceding good works on our part, he mercifully called us according to his purpose: that is, according to what he had purposed, to save through mercy those whom he could, and to condemn through justice. He called us according to his grace—that is, according to the gratuitous gift of God—which was given, that is, foreseen to be given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal times: before these times began with the world, which revolve and pass in their appointed spans.

For before the world there was no time, but *aevum*, an age; time began with the world, as we have said, when the mutability and alternation of day and night began. And in that age, after the world was made, this grace was given us in the counsel of divine Providence through Christ. But now it has been manifested in the fulfilment of our calling and salvation through the illumination of our Saviour Jesus Christ—that is, through the illumination of the new knowledge brought by the Saviour, by which he enlightened us, opening our understanding that we might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24).

“He destroyed,” and so forth. This is that grace: namely, that the Saviour destroyed our death, but by his resurrection illuminated—that is, made manifest in clear light—life and incorruption, so that there may be life and incorruption of soul and body, toward which he willed us to strive. And he effected this illumination through the Gospel, that is, through the manifestation of the Gospel, in which those things that were veiled in the Law are uncovered.

In this Gospel I have been immovably appointed as preacher—that is, as a herald crying aloud—apostle, that is, an envoy possessing authority, and teacher of the Gentiles, that is, one daily teaching the nations. For this reason—because I preach the Gospel—I now suffer so many adversities at Rome; yet I am not ashamed, that is, I do not blush amid all the insults and tortures which I endure, knowing that through them I acquire glory. For I know whom I have believed: that is, I know who he is to whom I entrusted my faith. I am certain that he can do all things and is able to guard my deposit, that is, the treasure of my merits which I entrusted to him for secret keeping.

He is able to preserve this precious deposit of my righteousness, deferring it until that notable day of judgment, so that then he may restore it to me and return the riches of righteousness which I entrusted to him. Until that day of judgment, of which I frequently speak and think, he is able to guard the treasure of my spiritual riches entrusted to him, so that then he may return it to me more abundantly and fill me with great riches.

> [Col. 1454B] “Holding the pattern of sound words which you heard from me, in the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus, guard the good deposit through the Holy Spirit who dwells in you.”

Christ will guard the deposit which I entrusted to him; and you, guard the deposit which Christ entrusted to you. Holding the pattern of sound words—that is, the rule of words in which there is nothing unsound but pure health of heart—which you heard not from just any teacher but from me, in the faith and love which are in Christ Jesus, that is, as Christ Jesus established them, guard the good deposit: the treasure of knowledge entrusted to you by Christ, or the office committed to you. Guard it not through your own industry, but through the Holy Spirit who dwells in [Col. 1454C] us—that is, in you as in me.

> “You know this: that all who are in Asia have turned away from me, among whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes. May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chain; but when he came to Rome, he diligently sought me and found me. May the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day. And how much he ministered to me at Ephesus, you know better.”

Therefore you must diligently guard the good deposit entrusted to you by God or by me, because you know that all the false persons in Asia have turned away—that is, departed—from me; and from them you especially must beware, lest they steal your deposit. Those in Asia who had been with the Apostle in a feigned spirit, pretending [Col. 1454D] to be his friends, deserted him when they saw him under constraint. He now mentions them for this purpose: that Timothy may beware lest he too turn away from him in the same manner.

“All have turned away from me,” he says—not indeed all who are in Asia, but all those Asians among whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes: that is, those in Asia who are such as these two. Those hypocrites, finally disclosing what they were, turned their backs upon me; but Onesiphorus, or his household, did not act thus.

The benefits of Onesiphorus are recalled so that Timothy may imitate him, return favour to him, and have confidence in him, since he is an Ephesian or Asian. When he came to Rome—whether to the emperor, as one most noble and of great rank, or for some other reason—he asked where the Apostle was. When he learned that he was in prison, he did not disdain to come to him, but consoled him and supplied what he needed. This is what the Apostle recalls as a great matter. And because the merciful will obtain mercy, he prays that mercy may be repaid to him by the Lord (Matthew 5).

“May the Lord grant mercy to the household,” that is, the family, “of Onesiphorus,” because not he alone but also the household which came with him often refreshed me by conversation and consolation, by alleviation of my punishments, and by provision from their goods. And he was not ashamed of my chain, as were the aforementioned hypocrites who turned away from me. Rather, when he came to Rome, he diligently sought me [Col. 1455B] in order to bring me help, and found me.

Here it is shown that believers who are held in prison, sickness, or some other affliction caused by necessity ought to be diligently sought out and refreshed by those who expect mercy from God. May the Lord Christ grant him—that is, Onesiphorus, who was so merciful to me—to find mercy from God the Father on that day of judgment of which I so often think. “May the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord.” Such is the statement read in Genesis: “The Lord rained fire and sulphur from the Lord upon Sodom” (Genesis 19).

These things which I have said Onesiphorus did for me at Rome. And how much he ministered to me at Ephesus, you know better than these things which I write, because you saw them.

## CHAPTER II

> [Col. 1455C] “Therefore you, my son, be strengthened in the grace which is in Christ Jesus. And the things which you heard from me through many witnesses, entrust these to faithful people who will be fit also to teach others. Labour as a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, that he may please him to whom he has proved himself. For one who competes in the contest is not crowned unless he has competed lawfully. The labouring farmer ought first to receive from the fruits. Understand what I say; for the Lord will give you understanding in all things.”

Since Onesiphorus, when others departed, sought me and ministered much to me not only at Rome but also at Ephesus, therefore you, my son, be strengthened by his example. “You”: as though he said, Be strengthened because others have failed. Be strengthened in the grace which is in Christ, so that you may not merely remain in it, but daily become stronger in it for doing and preaching good things and overcoming evil through patience.

And the words which you heard from me through many witnesses—that is, confirmed by the testimony of many prophets—entrust these to faithful persons. Or: through many witnesses entrust these to faithful persons; that is, appoint fellow-workers for yourself through whom you may entrust to the faithful the things which I taught you: to persons of sound faith, acting faithfully without deceit, who by life, knowledge, and eloquence will be fit also to teach others, as they themselves are taught by you or your helpers. Thus the teaching of virtue will multiply and religion will increase.

Entrust these [Col. 1456A] to faithful persons. And in exercises of this kind labour as a good soldier of Christ Jesus. And that you may be able to act in the manner of a valiant soldier of Christ, hear how such a soldier acts: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs,” because “no one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6; Luke 16), that is, God and the world.

A cleric is bound by this saying. For if, not content with the stipends which, at the Lord’s command, he receives from the altar, he carries on trade, sells advocacy or intercessions, or gladly accepts the gifts of widows, he can more rightly be regarded as a trader than a cleric. Still less is it permitted to a monk to be a trader in secular merchandise or entangled in secular cares.

Therefore the definition of a good soldier of Christ is this: serving wholly the one God, who cannot be divided, he does not entangle himself [Col. 1456B] in secular affairs—that is, he does not involve himself in the cares and actions of the world for earthly gain, knowing that many snares of sins lie hidden there—so that, freely devoting himself solely to divine things, he may please him to whom he has proved, that is, devoted, himself.

And truly, apart from his king’s service, a good soldier ought to do nothing if he wishes to please the same king under whose standards he has resolved to serve; for the contestant who seeks a crown must complete his contest lawfully. This is the meaning: one who competes in the contest—that is, who struggles with an opponent in competition—is not crowned, that is, does not obtain the victor’s reward, unless he has competed lawfully, that is, as the law of the contest requires.

So also the athlete of Christ, who struggles with the devil in the contest of this present life, will not receive the crown of eternal glory unless he is victorious according to the law of Christian combat. Let the greatness of the rewards therefore delight the mind, but do not let the struggle of labours frighten it; for great rewards cannot be attained except through great labours. Nor does the advancement of believers arise without temptation; nothing becomes known about oneself except through the test of trial. No one will be crowned unless he conquers; no one will conquer unless he competes; and no one will compete unless he has an enemy and resists temptation. The labours of contests therefore benefit the righteous, because through them they merit to be crowned.

I said that a soldier of God does not entangle himself in secular affairs, nor does a righteous contestant transgress the law of the contest. Yet “the labouring farmer”—that is, the preacher—ought first, that is, before others, to receive from the fruits of the field in which he labours, [Col. 1456D] that is, from the material goods of the Church.

This Timothy, following the Apostle’s example, wished to live by the labour of his own hands and receive nothing from those to whom he preached the word of salvation. Thus he suffered great want, because he was weak and could not devote himself to manual work. The Apostle therefore admonishes him under the figure of a farmer not to disdain receiving, from the field which he cultivates, fruit by which he may be sustained.

Since he knew him to be infirm in body and unable to labour at bodily work, he tells him that a soldier of God does not entangle himself in secular business, lest perhaps, when he lacked daily food, he might wish to seek from those to whom he ministered the Gospel some business concerns by which the attention of his mind would be entangled. For it is one thing to work bodily with a free mind, as a craftsman may do if he is neither fraudulent nor greedy nor covetous of private property; it is another to occupy the mind itself with the concerns of gathering money without bodily labour, as merchants, estate-managers, or contractors do. They preside through care, not work with their hands; and therefore they occupy the mind itself with anxiety for acquisition.

Thus, lest Timothy fall into such things, since because of bodily weakness he could not work with his hands, the Apostle exhorts and consoles him in this way: “Labour,” he says, “as a good soldier,” and so forth, until “unless he has competed lawfully.” Then, lest he suffer distress, saying, “I cannot dig; I am ashamed to beg” (Luke 16), he immediately adds: “The labouring farmer ought first to receive from the fruits,” according to what he had said to the Corinthians: “Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruits?” [Col. 1457B] (1 Corinthians 9).

He therefore made him secure, not so that he might sell the Gospel, but so that he might receive the necessities of this life from those to whom he ministered the Gospel and whom he cultivated as a vineyard or field—necessities which he could not provide for himself with his own hands. “The labouring farmer ought first to receive from the fruits,” and so forth: that is, the one who labours in the word of preaching and in governing the Church ought, as he is first, first to receive from the goods of the Church and then distribute to the others.

“Understand”—that is, discern—what I say, even though I seem to speak inconsistently and contrary to what I myself do. For you are weak, and therefore ought to receive; but if I received, I would cause scandal. You will be able rightly to understand these things, because the Lord will give you understanding not only in these matters but in all things.

> [Col. 1457C] “Remember that Jesus Christ has risen from the dead, of the seed of David, according to my Gospel, in which I labour even unto bonds as an evildoer; but the word of God is not bound.”

That you may strive lawfully toward the crown, remember that Jesus Christ rose from the dead: that is, diligently turn over in your mind that Christ reached the glory of resurrection through the labour of his passion, and that you likewise will rise to glory at the fitting time if you do not now reject the bitterness of sufferings for his name.

Faith in Christ’s resurrection will distinguish them from pagans and Jews; for they believe that he was crucified, but we believe that he rose on the third day. They readily believe the disgrace of the cross but refuse to confess the glory of the resurrection; therefore they will endure everlasting dishonour. But after the cross and burial we joyfully confess the glory of the resurrection, so that by his example, through contests of spiritual warfare, we may deserve to receive the everlasting crown of victory.

He is of the seed of David because his incorrupt mother drew the true origin of her flesh from the line of David. For the Son of God, through whom we were made, also became Son of Man by assuming flesh, in order to die for our offences and rise for our justification (Romans 4). And this is according to my Gospel, because the authentic truth of my preaching affirms both that Christ was incarnate from [Col. 1458A] David’s line and that after death he rose again, although the perverse deny it.

In this Gospel I labour even unto bonds, and you likewise ought to act. I labour unto bonds in the Gospel, because in evangelical preaching I endure all preceding labours and, finally, bonds, being treated as an evildoer. In my body I indeed bear chains, but the word of God is not bound, because it proceeds freely from my mouth. Nor do I instruct only those present by speech, but also strengthen those absent by letters. For I may be bound by those who oppose truth, but not the truth itself which I speak. So you too, amid those punishments, ought not cease from preaching the truth.

> “Therefore I endure all things for the elect, that they also [Col. 1458B] may obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus, with heavenly glory. The saying is faithful: for if we have died with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him; if we deny him, he too will deny us; if we do not believe, he remains faithful; he cannot deny himself. Keep reminding them of these things, testifying before the Lord.”

I said that the word of God cannot be bound. Therefore, because I cannot be restrained from preaching the truth, I willingly endure all evils inflicted upon me for this reason; and I do this for the elect, because it greatly benefits those predestined to life that no severity of punishments breaks me from the persistence of preaching.

Or, because I remember that Christ rose again, I therefore patiently endure all things for the elect, who are to be formed by my example, so that they too, enduring as I do, may obtain true salvation which is in Christ Jesus, and obtain it with heavenly glory: that they may receive together eternal salvation and heavenly glory. And this saying concerning the attainment of salvation and glory by those whom God has already chosen in his predestination is faithful—that is, true and containing nothing false. And this saying will indeed be fulfilled faithfully.

For if we have died with Christ—that is, if, in imitation of his death, we were in baptism made dead to vices, so that we no longer live in them—we shall also live with him in eternal blessedness. If we endure adversities for his name, as he endured for our salvation, then we shall also reign with him, sharing his kingdom. But if we deny him through fear of sufferings, he also will deny us in the future judgment, saying: “I do not know where you are from; depart from me, workers of iniquity” (Matthew 7, 25). This is what he himself threatened when he said: “Whoever denies me before men, I too will deny him before my Father” (Matthew 10; Luke 12).

And if we do not believe concerning him those things which must be believed, he remains faithful—that is, true in those things which he has said concerning himself—and cannot deny himself. Dionysius the Areopagite argues concerning this matter as follows: “The negation of oneself is a falling away from truth. But truth is ὄν [being], and a falling away from truth is non-ὄν [non-being]. Ὄν is interpreted as ‘existing,’ or ‘that which is.’ If, therefore, truth is ὄν, and the negation of truth is non-ὄν, a fall from ὄντος [being] is to fall away from ὄν [being]. God cannot fall away and become non-ὄν [non-being].” It is as though someone said: “He cannot be unable, and he does not know by privation.” These are from the sayings of Dionysius.

If, therefore, God cannot deny himself and cannot lie or do anything unjust, how is he omnipotent, unless because to be able to do these or similar things is not power but impotence? For one who can do such things can do what is not advantageous to himself and what he ought not to do. The more he can do these things, the more adversity and perversity have power over him, and the less he has against them. Thus one who can act in this way does so not through power but through impotence.

But God is truly omnipotent precisely because he can do nothing through impotence, and nothing can do anything against him. Therefore it is rightly said of the Almighty [Col. 1459B] that he cannot deny himself. For we also read of the Jews that they could not believe because Isaiah said: “He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart” (Isaiah 6; John 12). Yet “they could not” is said where we must understand “they would not,” just as it is now said of God that he cannot deny himself. Therefore, just as the Lord’s inability to deny himself is praise of the divine will, so their inability to believe is blame of the human will.

Keep reminding them to attend to and preserve these things, testifying—that is, affirming them as a suitable witness—before the Lord, that is, in the sight of God, who beholds us as present.

> “Do not contend with words. For it is useful for nothing except the overthrow of the hearers. But diligently [Col. 1459C] take care to present yourself approved to God, a worker unashamed, rightly handling the word of truth.”

Up to this point he has given reasons why he ought to be steadfast in preaching. And lest, through zeal for steadfastness, he should wish to serve disputes in the manner of chatterers, he says: Do not contend with words. He does not say, “Do not contend with arguments,” for that is good; but, Do not contend with words, where there is impudent babbling. Therefore do not contend with words, because to contend in this way is useful for nothing; that is, such contention accomplishes nothing except the overthrow of the hearers. For hearers are overthrown by it, thinking that the opponents have some reasonable case when they observe them shouting thus. Abandon contentious words, and conquer your adversaries [Col. 1459D] by good works. And this is what follows: Be diligent to present yourself to God as approved, that is, praiseworthy: namely, present yourself such in God’s sight that he may approve you. And present yourself as a worker unashamed—or, according to other manuscripts, irreproachable, which means the same thing. For shame arises from rebuke in the one rebuked; and one who cannot be reproved is not ashamed. Present yourself, therefore, as a worker unashamed, that is, irreproachable: make yourself such in all your works that in none of them you incur the shame of disgrace; that you cannot be reproved in anything, nor can anyone cast up against you anything worthy of shame. And present yourself as one rightly handling the word of truth, [Col. 1460A] so that you neither give what is holy to dogs nor cast pearls before swine (Matt. 7), but proclaim the word of God as is fitting according to the character of each individual person, and mix into it nothing of perverse interpretation. For heretics do not handle the word of truth rightly, but perversely, because they try to bend it to the perversity of their own understanding. Of their teaching he continues:

> “But avoid profane things and empty talk. For they make great progress toward impiety, and their speech spreads like cancer. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have fallen away from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already taken place, and they overthrow the faith of some. But the firm foundation of God stands, having this seal: ‘The Lord has known those who are his,’ and, ‘Let everyone who names the name [Col. 1460B] of the Lord depart from iniquity.’”

Handle rightly, as I have said, the word of truth. But avoid profane things—that is, the words of heretics, alien to the religion of godliness—and their empty talk, that is, their sayings void of all usefulness. And why? Because, if heard, they make great progress toward strengthening and increasing the impiety of unbelief, since they destroy the godliness of faith; and their speech spreads like cancer: that is, it increasingly occupies, devours, and defiles the minds in which it has begun to take root, just as the disease called cancer continually spreads farther, defiles, and devours the part of the body in which it arises. Or, as the creature called a crab (*cancer*) moves not forward but backward, so their speech does not lead its hearers toward God but draws them away from God and [Col. 1460C] causes them to apostatize.

Among those who speak thus are Hymenaeus and his companion Philetus, who have fallen away from the truth of faith in which they had been placed, imitating the devil, who did not stand in the truth (John 8), saying that the resurrection has already occurred in the hearts of those who have believed, and that no other resurrection will occur hereafter. By such sayings they overthrow the faith of some, so that they do not believe in the resurrection of bodies.

For all sects that have presumed to implant some religion among people have not denied this resurrection of minds, lest it be said to them: “If the soul does not rise, why do you speak to me? What do you wish to do in me? If you do not make the worse person better, why do you speak to me? If you do not make the unrighteous person just, why do you speak to me? But if [Col. 1460D] you make the unrighteous just, the ungodly godly, the foolish wise, you confess that my soul rises again if I obey you, if I believe you.” Therefore, all who established a sect of any—even false—religion, wishing to be believed, could not deny this resurrection by falsehood. All agreed about this; but many denied the resurrection of the flesh. They said that the resurrection had already taken place in faith.
