For, observing the words the Apostle continually says—namely, that we have died with Christ and have risen with him—and not understanding why these things are said, they supposed that the resurrection had already taken place and that no resurrection was further to be hoped for at the end of the ages. The same Apostle now resists such persons. [Col. 1461A] “Among them,” he says, “are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have fallen away from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already taken place, and they overthrow the faith of some.” They said that the resurrection had already occurred, but in such a way that no other was to be hoped for; and they rebuked those who hoped for the resurrection of the flesh, as though the promised resurrection were fulfilled in the mind by believing.

“They have overthrown,” he says, “the faith of some.” And as though someone should say to him, “Who can resist them?” he immediately adds: But the firm foundation of God stands. The faith of some who are weak and do not belong to the lot of the elect is overthrown by heretics; but the firm foundation of God—that is, the firm faith which God has founded [another reading: established] by the Holy Spirit in the hearts of his elect—stands: that is, [Col. 1461B] it can in no way be overthrown or inclined. It has this seal, that is, this imprint as of a seal: namely, “The Lord has known those who are his,” and “Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity.”

A good person has this seal impressed upon the heart: that is, this thought firmly fixed in the mind, so as to say within himself: “What would it profit me if outwardly I pretended to be just or faithful, but inwardly were wicked? Nothing. For he who examines the hearts of all knows who are his.” Therefore I strive truly to appear faithful or just in his sight, so that I may belong to the lot of those who are his. Such a thought is the imprint of the divine seal. By this also one avoids heresies and everything contrary to salvation, because one knows that all who call upon the Lord [Col. 1461C] ought to depart from iniquity.

This imprint of the seal, therefore, by which they are distinguished from the others who are overthrown, is in God’s firm foundation—that is, in the robust faith of God’s elect—because the Lord knows who belong to his inheritance. And while others fall away from the faith, those who are predestined cannot fall away; or, if they have fallen away, they must return. Nor should it trouble anyone that the devil often deceives even those who, regenerated and now in Christ, enter upon the ways of God: for the Lord knows who are his. From these he deceives no one into eternal damnation. The Lord knows them thus, as one from whom nothing is hidden, even things to come.

For there are also some of their number who still live wickedly, or even lie in heresies or in the superstitions of the Gentiles; yet even there the Lord knows who are his. For in that ineffable foreknowledge of God, many who appear outwardly to be outside are within, and many who appear outwardly to be within are outside. And lest anyone should say, “I no longer care what I do, because I am secure that, if the Lord knows me to be his, I cannot perish; and conversely, if he knows me not to be his, I cannot attain salvation,” a useful admonition is added: let everyone who knows the name of the Lord depart from iniquity. For the Lord has given us free choice, so that by the choice of our own will we may depart from iniquity and be among those whom he knows to be his, or remain in iniquity and be among those whom he knows not to belong to him.

For this also is that seal which will appear impressed upon the foundation of our [Col. 1462A] faith, if of our own accord we have departed from iniquity. For we cannot depart from unjust persons, because chaff is mixed with wheat until the threshing floor is winnowed. A remarkable comparison. For behold: on the threshing floor itself, the wheat withdraws from the chaff when it is stripped, but it does not withdraw from the threshing floor when it is threshed. But when will it be completely separated? When the winnower comes. Therefore the threshing floor is now throughout the world. If you make progress, you must live among the unjust, because Abel cannot exist without being exercised by Cain’s malice. You cannot depart from unjust persons; you can depart from injustice.

For Jerusalem, captured by the Babylon of this age, ought to be held in the heart as firmly and immovably as by the impression of a seal: after the course of time it will be delivered, and none of it will perish, because whoever [Col. 1462B] perishes was not of it. Therefore let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity, because unless one departs from it, the naming of the Lord’s name will profit him nothing. For “not everyone who says to Christ, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of his Father” (Matt. 7).

> “But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also wooden and earthenware vessels; and some indeed are for honor, but others for dishonor. If, therefore, anyone cleanses himself from these, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified and useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work.”

Let the one who names the Lord’s name depart from iniquity. But, as we have said, one cannot depart from unjust persons, [Col. 1462C] because in the great house—the Church spread throughout the whole world—there are not only golden and silver vessels, that is, righteous persons endowed with wisdom and eloquence, but also wooden and earthenware vessels, that is, sinners to be burned and broken.

Since wisdom or charity is customarily signified by gold, and eloquence by silver, by gold—which is more precious than all metals—are now understood those whom charity, preferred to all the other virtues, or wisdom adorns. By silver, which gleams with wonderful brightness, are understood those who shine in the instruction of many by the brilliance of keen eloquence. These are rightly called golden and silver vessels, suitable for the service of the highest King in his great house. Wooden and earthenware vessels, however, signify carnal persons, whom the fire of vices easily kindles and the force of adversity breaks. But on the day of the Lord these wooden vessels will be burned in the blaze of penal fire, and the earthenware ones will be broken by him to whom the iron rod has been given.

Nevertheless these vessels are now together with golden and silver vessels in the great house, because the reprobate are now mingled with the elect in the Church. And some vessels there are appointed for eternal honor, like the golden and silver ones; but others are suited for the disgrace of everlasting reproach, like the wooden and earthenware ones. And since in this house there are also vessels assigned to honorable uses, if anyone cleanses himself from these vessels of dishonor, so as to render himself free from their contamination, he will be a vessel appointed for honor and sanctified: that is, a holy dwelling-place for the Lord in this house. [Col. 1463A]

For just as, in a great human house, its master does not rest in every place whatever, but certainly in some more secluded and honorable place, so our Lord does not dwell in all who are in his house. He does not dwell in vessels of dishonor—that is, in those who serve the shamefulness of vices—but in vessels of honor: those who lead a life honorable before God and human beings. Whoever cleanses himself from these vessels of dishonor, so as not to share in their defilement, will be a vessel for honor, sanctified for the honorable use of upright action, and useful to the Lord: that is, bringing usefulness to the Lord’s house, prepared for every good work, so that he does not refuse to undertake whatever good work is enjoined upon him, or whatever difficult [another reading: of whatever kind] [Col. 1463B] sacred action or word of preaching he is suited for. This will benefit both himself and others, or enable him to hold any rank of sacred orders.

> “But flee youthful desires; pursue righteousness, faith, charity, peace with those who call upon the Lord from a pure heart. But avoid foolish and undisciplined questions, knowing that they produce quarrels. And the servant of the Lord ought not to quarrel, but to be gentle toward all, teachable, patient, correcting with modesty those who resist the truth, lest perhaps God grant them repentance for acknowledging the truth, and they recover their senses from the devil’s snares, by whom they are held captive to do his will.”

I said that in God’s house there are vessels of honor and vessels [Col. 1463C] of dishonor. But lest you become a vessel for dishonorable use, flee youthful desires, which pursue you while you are young, lest they seize you into consent with perverse delight. Flee these, I say; but pursue righteousness, lest it escape you. Pursue it—that is, follow it frequently along the paths of righteous actions in which it goes before you—so that you may overtake it. Likewise pursue faith, lest in any part the rule of faith be able to remain hidden from you or escape you.

But since the practice of righteousness and the truth of faith profit nothing without charity, pursue charity also, so that through it your faith may work the work of righteousness. For saving faith is faith that works through charity. And pursue peace with the good, so that you may never disagree with them or disturb them.

Or thus: pursue righteousness, doing to each person what justice requires; and faith in invisible goods—not invisible honors, which youth is accustomed to desire; and charity, so that you may love God more than yourself and your neighbor as yourself, which youth often neglects; and peace, to which the desire of youth plainly opposes itself. Pursue peace, I say, not with the perverse, but with those who call upon the Lord from a pure heart: that is, those who have purified their heart, who ask through devout prayers that God may come into it.

Pursue these things, as I have said; but beware of foolish and undisciplined questions. Foolish questions are those which are insoluble and seek secrets forbidden to the human race. Undisciplined questions are those not asked humbly and modestly, and those in which the questioner does not wish to learn [Col. 1464A] but to quarrel. Avoid questions of this kind, so that you do not answer them, knowing that they produce quarrels. But the servant of the Lord ought not to quarrel, because quarrelling produces hatred; rather, he ought to be gentle—that is, as though accustomed to the hand (*manu assuetus*), namely approachable, that is, mild or kind toward all, so that he may be harsh toward no one, as though wild; and teachable—that is, capable of being easily taught.

For this is the distinction between *docilis* and *docibilis*: *docilis* is one who can teach others, whereas *docibilis* is one who can easily be taught. Hence it is said: “They shall all be teachable by God” (John 6), that is, they shall easily be taught by God. The servant of the Lord ought not to quarrel, because a clear and simple eye is needed if the way of wisdom is to be found—a way against which the great deceptions and errors of evil and perverse people raise such clamor. One must escape them all, that is, come to the most certain peace and unshakable stability of wisdom.

For one must fear greatly lest, through a zeal for debating or disputing, a person fail to see what can be seen by few, unless the clamor of contradictors is slight and they also raise no clamor against themselves. It is rightly said, therefore, that the servant of the Lord ought not to quarrel, but to be gentle toward all, teachable, and patient. And lest anyone infer from this that correction of another’s error should cease, it is added that he ought to correct with modesty those who resist. Thus we ought neither fail in correcting our brothers nor devote ourselves to strife.

How do we correct with modesty except by retaining gentleness of heart and sprinkling some sharpness of medicine into the word of correction? [Col. 1464C] Peace and love, therefore, must be retained in the heart; but the measure of speech, whether spoken more sharply or more gently, must be regulated as the welfare of the person corrected appears to require. Those who still resist impudently ought to be corrected modestly, lest perhaps God grant them repentance. For the usefulness of correction—which is now greater, now less, and is beneficially applied according to the diversity of sins—is salutary when the heavenly physician looks upon it. For it accomplishes nothing unless it brings someone to repent of his sin; and who grants this except him who looked upon Peter denying him and made him weep? Therefore his mercy is necessary not only when repentance is being performed, but also in order that it may be performed.

[Col. 1464D] This expression, *nequando*, is used here in the sense of *si forte*, “if perhaps”; it was used in ancient times but is now considered obsolete. “Correcting,” he says, “those who resist, *nequando*”—that is, “if at any time,” or “if perhaps,” God grants them repentance.

Or this sentence may also be understood thus. Let us not despair of the salvation of those who still resist, but let us correct them, lest, while we do not correct them, God should at some time grant them repentance by himself, and we should be ashamed who despaired of their salvation. For this reason we ought to endeavor to convert them to repentance, so that we may gain a reward thereby, lest perhaps God grant them repentance without us through inward inspiration, and we receive no reward from it. May he grant them repentance for their error, so that they may acknowledge the truth of Catholic [Col. 1465A] doctrine, which they opposed in ignorance; and may they recover their senses from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive to fulfill his will.

To “recover one’s senses” (*resipiscere*) is, as it were, to “taste rightly again” (*resapere*): when someone returns from what he tasted wrongly to what he had formerly tasted rightly, or ought to have tasted rightly.

## Chapter III

> “But know this: that in the last days dangerous times will come, and people will be lovers of themselves, greedy, arrogant, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, without peace, slanderers, incontinent, harsh, without kindness, traitors, insolent, swollen with pride, lovers of pleasures rather than of God, having indeed an appearance of godliness but denying its power.”

Those held ensnared by the devil may perhaps someday recover their senses; but know this: such persons will abound in the last days, that is, in the final age. For then dangerous times will come, in which many souls will be endangered; and they will be dangerous because people will then be lovers of themselves. For by some inexplicable principle, whoever loves himself and not God does not love himself; and whoever loves God and not himself does love himself. For one who cannot live surely dies from himself by loving himself. Therefore one who loves himself in order not to live does not love himself.

But when the one from whom one lives is loved, the person who does not love himself for that reason, in order that he may love him from whom he lives, loves himself more by not loving himself. Since, however, near the end of the age there will abound especially those who, neglecting love of God and of their brothers, will wrongly love themselves and thus perish by loving themselves, dangerous times will therefore come then.

People will be lovers of themselves, because they will care for nothing except themselves; they will seek only their own profits, advantages, honors, and glories. And from this as from a fountain—that is, from being lovers of themselves—many streams of vices will flow. For because they will wrongly love themselves according to the present life, they will be greedy for money, puffed up in body, proud in mind, blasphemers—that is, speaking false and impious things about God; disobedient to parents, whether natural or spiritual; ungrateful to benefactors; wicked, that is, passing beyond the bounds of sin and grievously falling into atrocious deeds; without affection, that is, without [Col. 1465D] the inward feelings of compassion; without peace, that is, discordant and restless; slanderers, that is, fastening accusations upon good people; incontinent, that is, not restraining lust; harsh, that is, rough and quarrelsome; without kindness, that is, merciless; traitors, that is, revealing to the adversaries of good people the secrets which they have learned should be concealed; insolent, that is, impudent; swollen with the wind of pride; lovers of carnal pleasures more than of God, as he himself said: “Light came into this world, and people loved darkness more than light” (John 3). They have, indeed, in outward appearance and words, like false monks, an appearance of godliness, that is, a likeness of religion; but they deny its power—that is, its reality—by their deeds and habits.

But blessed Augustine, especially endeavoring to remove these faults from pastors of the Church, says:

“Let those who feed Christ’s sheep not be lovers of themselves, lest they feed them as their own rather than his; nor let them seem to seek from them their own profits, like lovers of money; or to lord it over them, like the arrogant; or to glory in the honors they receive from them, like the proud; or progress so far as even to create heresies, like blasphemers; nor yield to the holy fathers, like those disobedient to parents; nor return evil for good to those who wish to correct them because they do not wish them to perish, like the ungrateful; nor kill their own souls and the souls of others, like the wicked; nor tear apart the maternal bowels of the Church, like the irreligious; nor show compassion to the weak, like those without affection; nor allow others to rest, like those without peace; [Col. 1466B] nor attempt to stain the reputation of the saints, like slanderers; nor restrain their most evil desires, like the incontinent; nor engage in quarrels, like the harsh; nor know how to help, like those without kindness; nor reveal to enemies of the godly things which they have learned ought to be concealed, like traitors; nor disturb human modesty by shameless invention, like the insolent; nor be puffed up by proud knowledge, like the swollen; nor prefer carnal joys to spiritual joys, like lovers of pleasures more than of God; nor simulate religion while failing to possess it in truth, like those who have an appearance of godliness but deny its power.”

For these and similar vices, whether all happen to one person or some rule in some and others in others, spring in some manner from that root: people being lovers of themselves. This vice must especially be avoided by those who feed Christ’s sheep, lest they seek their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ, and devote to the service of their own desires those for whom Christ’s blood was shed. [Col. 1466C]

> “And avoid these. For among them are those who enter houses and lead captive little women laden with sins, who are led by various desires, always learning and never arriving at the knowledge of truth.”

In the last days there will be people such as I have described; avoid them, because many of them have already appeared. For among them are those who enter houses, and so forth. He does not say, “They will enter,” as foretelling the future, as above he had said, “Dangerous times will come”; [Col. 1466D] but he says, “They enter houses and lead captive little women.” He does not say, “They will lead,” or “They are going to lead”; but, “They already lead.” Nor should it be thought that here he used present-tense words in place of future-tense words, since he was warning the person to whom he wrote to avoid them.

Nor, however, did he say in vain, “Dangerous times will come in the last days”; and, showing from this that they would be dangerous, he foretold that such people would arise, because they will be more numerous and abound more as the end draws nearer. We therefore see that such persons now abound. But what if they are more numerous after us, and utterly most numerous when the end itself is now, now at hand?

Among them already are heretics who enter houses, that is, they go in [Col. 1467A] to speak secretly with those inside. Or “houses” means the consciences of the hearers, which they wickedly penetrate with deceptive words. And they lead captive “little women,” that is, foolish, weak, lowly, and unstable souls—whether of men or women—drawing them into the captivity of errors. I mean souls burdened with sins, and therefore worthy of being deceived, who are led by various desires: they now desire one thing, now another; wearying of what they already possess, they continually seek other things and delight in novelties. Such persons easily abandon Catholic truth and gladly lend an ear to the words of new errors: always learning, yet never arriving at the knowledge of truth.

Those are always learning and never arrive at the knowledge of truth who seem to have zeal in learning but do not come [Col. 1467B] to discern truth from falsehood, good from evil. Such are the disciples of heretics and the Jews (Rom. 1). For in this life they are always learning and do not attain knowledge of the truth. But when they depart from this life, they will no longer be learning, but receiving the reward of their error. For “always learning and never arriving at the knowledge of truth” is said as though one said, “Always walking and never arriving at the road.” For they not only do not arrive where the road leads, but do not even arrive at the road itself. But let us always walk on the road until we come to where the road leads. Let us never remain upon it until it brings us where we may remain.

> “Now just as Jannes and Mambres resisted [Col. 1467C] Moses, so these also resist the truth: people corrupt in mind, rejected with regard to the faith. But they will not advance further, for their folly will become evident to all, as theirs also did.”

Such people do not arrive at the knowledge of truth, but rather resist the truth preached by Catholic teachers, just as Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses as he preached the truth (Exod. 7). These were Pharaoh’s magicians, whose names the Apostle now gives, though they are not read in Exodus. This is the meaning: Just as Jannes and Mambres under Pharaoh resisted Moses, lest he lead God’s people out of Egyptian slavery, so these heretics resist the truth of the preachers, lest by it the faithful be freed from the darkness of ignorance and the slavery of sin.

These, I say, are people corrupt in mind, because their mind has been corrupted by the adulterer, the devil, having lost the chastity that is in Christ. And they are rejected with regard to faith: that is, turned back from uprightness, moving about on the outside of faith but not remaining within. Such persons lead captive little women—that is, wretched and dull souls—and resist the truth; but they will not advance further in the seduction of people. For their folly, now hidden while they are thought wise, will be made evident to all through the Apostle John, just as the folly of those others was through Moses. For in Asia, through John, the folly of their error will be exposed and destroyed, just as that of the others was made manifest through Moses in Egypt.

The boldness of heretics is always restless. The Apostle now declares that they have the enterprise of Pharaoh’s magicians when he says: “Just as Jannes,” and so on, through “as theirs also did.” For since through this very corruption of mind they were most restless, they failed at the third sign, confessing that the Holy Spirit, who was in Moses, was against them. For when they failed, they said: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. 8). But just as the Holy Spirit, when reconciled, grants rest to the meek and humble in heart, so the contrary and hostile evil spirit agitates the harsh and proud with restlessness. That restlessness was signified by those exceedingly small flies, beneath which the magicians, as has been said, failed, saying: “It is the finger of God.” Their folly becomes evident to all when they are openly shown to be foolish before all, [Col. 1468B] so that they can no longer deceive any whom at first they deceived by the promise and display of outstanding wisdom.

> “But you have followed my teaching, manner of life, purpose, faith, long-suffering, love, patience, persecutions, sufferings—the things that happened to me at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra; the persecutions I endured; and from them all the Lord delivered me. And all who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution.”

Heretics resist the truth and are rejected regarding faith. But you have followed my teaching: that is, you have learned what I teach and know how to hand it on to others. You have followed my manner of life: that is, the way I established [Col. 1468C] my life or instructed others. You have followed my purpose, because you have resolved to live as I had resolved: namely, to fast and keep vigil in the same manner or at the same time as I, and to do other things likewise. You have followed my faith, because you believe as I do; my long-suffering, because you have learned, as I have, to await God’s promises patiently amid adversities without murmuring; my love, because you have learned, like me, to love even adversaries; and my patience, by which you bear with an even mind the evils done by others, like me, and do not grieve against the one who has inflicted them upon you.

You have followed my persecutions from city to city, because you have sometimes endured these with me; and my sufferings, that is, my afflictions and torments, because you have become their participant and know them. You have followed—that is, known and shared—the adversities that befell me [Col. 1468D] at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra, and the persecutions I endured there or elsewhere. And I was not abandoned in anything so that I should fail; but from them all the Lord delivered me, and likewise he will not forsake you but will deliver you.

At Antioch in Pisidia, the Jews stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas and expelled them from their territory (Acts 13). But they shook the dust from their feet against them and came to Iconium. There, when an attack by Gentiles and Jews with their rulers arose to abuse and stone them, they learned of it and fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra and Derbe. But some Jews came from Antioch and Iconium; after persuading the crowds, they stoned Paul [Col. 1469A] and dragged him outside the city, supposing him to be dead (Acts 14). And he now recalls that he endured these things at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra.

And lest anyone think that he can please God without enduring tribulations, he adds: And all who desire, and so forth. “I,” he says, “endured persecutions; and all who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus—that is, who desire to lead a religious and devout life in faith in Christ—will suffer persecution.” Persecution never fails those living godly lives, because even when there seems to be tranquility from those who are outside and not raging, there are many within who torment the hearts of the godly by their ruined conduct, since through them the Christian name is blasphemed. The dearer that Christian name is to those who wish to live godly lives in Christ, the more they grieve that, through evil people among them, it is loved less than the minds of the godly desire.

Heretics too, when they attempt to have the name, sacraments, Scriptures, and profession of Christians, cause great grief in the hearts of the godly; for many who wish to be Christians are compelled to hesitate because of their dissensions, and many blasphemers find in them material for blaspheming the Christian name, because they too are in some fashion called Christians. By these and similar evil habits and errors of people, those who desire to live godly lives in Christ will suffer persecution, even though no one attacks and no one harasses their bodies. For they suffer this persecution not in their bodies, but in their hearts. Godly sorrow is to be troubled by the vices of others, not entangled in them; to grieve, not cling; [Col. 1469C] to be contracted by sorrow, not drawn by love. This is that persecution which all who desire to live godly lives in Christ suffer.

For what here so persecutes the life of the good as the life of the wicked? It does not compel the godly person to imitate what displeases him, but it compels him to grieve over what he sees. For one who lives impiously, though he does not bind one who refuses consent, torments one who perceives it. The devil too ceaselessly persecutes the godly, and the more dangerously the more secretly. The enemy persecutes them, I say, “to whom belong a thousand names and a thousand arts of harming” (Vergil). This world persecutes them too with its enticements; the host of innumerable vices persecutes them; their own flesh persecutes them; their own unlawful thoughts persecute them.

[Col. 1469D]

> “But evil people and seducers will progress from bad to worse, deceiving and leading others into error. But remain in the things you have learned and which have been entrusted to you, knowing from whom you learned them; and because from infancy you have known the sacred writings, which can instruct you for salvation through the faith that is in Christ Jesus. Every Scripture divinely inspired is useful for teaching, for refutation, for correction, for training in righteousness, so that the person of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work.”

The godly will suffer persecutions, whereas evil people and deceivers will enjoy prosperity. They are evil in relation to themselves, deceivers in relation to others. Those are called deceivers who, as though under the appearance of sweetness, pour in the poison of deadly persuasion. Evil people and deceivers will progress [Col. 1470A] from bad to worse; that is, they will have success in their errors and will reach graver things, themselves wandering and leading others into error. Yet they will not progress for long, as Paul said above: they will not progress further. Such persons will wander and will prosper, and will draw others after themselves. But do not go after them into error; rather, remain always in those good things which you learned from me and which were entrusted to you by God, knowing from what teacher you learned them—that is, how truthful, how great in authority, and how devoted to you I, your teacher, am. Remain in them also because you know the sacred writings; that is, from childhood you have been instructed in the sacred writings, namely the Law and the writings of the prophets. These writings can instruct you—that is, make you sufficiently learned—for attaining eternal salvation, [Col. 1470B] and this through the faith which is in Christ Jesus. For the sayings of the Old Testament do not instruct toward salvation but toward death, if Christ is not understood in them and faith in him is not held.

I rightly said that the sacred writings can instruct you toward salvation, to be sought both by you and by others. For all Scripture is divinely inspired—that is, produced by the divine Spirit—and is useful for this purpose. Those Scriptures possess the summit of authority which were uttered through the Spirit of God and are called canonical. All Scripture which God breathed—that is, which has been composed through divine inspiration—is useful for teaching the ignorant; for refuting, that is, convincing those who resist; and for rebuking—that is, reproving—or, according to other manuscripts, for correcting, that is, reforming [Col. 1470C] those who sin; and for instructing the untrained, so that they may advance to perfect understanding in righteousness, that is, in the observance of righteousness. Thus the person of God who is so instructed may be perfect in conduct, equipped through the Scriptures for every good work to be done—that is, carefully knowing how each good work ought to be done. Such a man is rightly called a person of God, because, set apart from the wickedness of those who serve vices, he has become the possession of his Creator.

## CHAPTER IV

> “I charge you before God and Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom: preach the word; persist in season and out of season; refute, exhort, rebuke, in all [Col. 1470D] patience and teaching.”

Because you are instructed in the sacred writings, I therefore charge you—that is, I adjure you—not to cease preaching. For to charge solemnly is to adjure, because one who adjures sets a witness in the adjuration itself. I charge you before God the Father—that is, in the presence of God, who is everywhere and sees all things. I adjure you and call him himself as witness; and before Christ Jesus—that is, before the Mediator of God and human beings, who, like the Father, fills heaven and earth in his divinity—I entreat you to preach.

You ought not to disregard the testimony of this Mediator, because he himself is to judge all. “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son as they honor the Father” (John 5). He himself is to judge the living—that is, those who will be found alive in the flesh when he comes (1 Thess. 5)—and the dead, that is, those whose souls have already departed from their bodies. And I charge you—that is, I make a witness and employ as testimony to this my adjuration toward you—by his appearing, in which each will receive according to what he has done (2 Cor. 5), and by his kingdom, in which the righteous will reign perpetually.

And what is it that I so forcefully charge under such great and fearful witnesses? Namely this: preach the word of the Gospel; and do not do so by the hour only, but persist—that is, be constant in preaching. Do this in season for those who are willing, and out of season for those who are unwilling. It is in season when you find hearers who gladly receive your words; out of season when you find those who despise your admonitions. Or, “in season, out of season” means: suitably display persistence; for persistence destroys itself in the hearer’s mind by its very worthlessness, if it does not know how to make its persistence timely.

Refute those who resist, so that, convicted by arguments, they may yield; exhort those who act rightly, so that they may advance toward what is better; rebuke offenders, so that, put to shame, they may correct themselves. Do this in all patience—that is, patiently awaiting their amendment and not immediately rejecting them if they are disobedient—and in all teaching, that is, by teaching them attentively, not by being angry or indignant with them.

Or the passage can be divided thus: “Persist in season,” so that “out of season, refute” has a separate sense; then let the remainder continue: “exhort, rebuke, in all patience and teaching,” so that you may be regarded as timely when you persist in building up; but when you destroy by refuting, you are not blamed even if you appear untimely. [Col. 1471B] Thus the following two commands may severally be referred to the two above: exhort when you persist in season; rebuke when you refute out of season. Then the remaining two are likewise referred, but in reverse order: “in all patience,” to endure the indignation of those whom you pull down; and “teaching,” to instruct the efforts of those whom you build up.

We must consider how we speak, because words which call one person back to salvation often wound another. Hence the Apostle, who now admonishes Titus, saying, “Rebuke with all authority” (Titus 2), exhorts Timothy, saying: “Refute, exhort, rebuke, with all patience.” Why did he prescribe authority to one and patience to the other, unless he perceived one to be of a gentler spirit and the other of a more ardent one? To the gentle man the severity of speech had to be enjoined through the authority of command; but the man who was fervent in spirit had to be tempered through patience, lest, growing more zealous than was right, he should not bring the wounded back to health but wound those who were sound.

For these reasons the Apostle dispenses his teaching with such skill: he sets authority before one and patience before the other because, as has been said, he saw Titus to be of a gentler spirit and Timothy of a somewhat more ardent one. He inflames the former through zeal for emulation; he tempers the latter through the mildness of patience. To the one he adds what is lacking; from the other he removes what is excessive. He endeavors to drive the one forward with a spur; he restrains the other with a bridle. For the great cultivator of the Church entrusted to him waters some branches so that they may grow; others, when he sees them growing beyond measure, [Col. 1472A] he prunes, lest by failing to grow they bear no fruit, or by growing without moderation they lose the fruit they have borne. It follows:

> “For the time will come when they will not endure sound teaching, but, according to their own desires, they will heap up teachers for themselves, having itching ears. And indeed they will turn their hearing away from the truth, but will turn aside to fables.”

Therefore, he says, you must devote yourself to preaching with such urgency, because a time will come in which the preaching of truth will not be accepted. Therefore hasten to forestall that time while your preaching can have effect. The time will not end before the things I say take place; but there will still be a time when people will not endure sound teaching—that is, teaching conducive to the health of the soul—but will cast it from their shoulders as though it were a heavy burden.

They will not endure this teaching, but, in order to fulfill their own desires, will heap up teachers for themselves—that is, they will gather for themselves a heap of teachers to teach them the things they desire. They themselves will have itching ears, that is, ears spiritually committing fornication and afflicted with an itch, just as bodily chastity is corrupted in the flesh by a certain itch of lust. For just as flesh which itches always wants to be scratched, so their ears will always desire to hear words which teach errors and entice them to pleasures. They will turn their hearing away from the truth—that is, they will flee from hearing the discourse of truth, which will be harsh to them because it will not flatter them in their wickedness—but will turn aside to fables, in order to hear them, that is, false [Col. 1472C] and idle speeches.

Nor will they turn only to such fables as are recited in theaters or frequently told by frivolous people, but also to such as heresiarchs may devise against the Lord. Isaiah also spoke of those whom the Apostle now foretells:

> “For this is a people provoking to anger, lying children, unwilling to hear the law of God; who say to those who see, ‘Do not see’; and to those who behold, ‘Do not behold for us things that are right. Speak pleasant things to us; show us errors. Remove the way from before me; turn the path away from before me; let the Holy One of Israel cease from before our face’” (Isa. 30).

Those who leave the Church and follow Antichrist when he reigns will speak in this manner especially. They will not endure the sound teaching of Christian [Col. 1472D] preaching; they will turn their hearing away from it and turn to Antichrist’s fables. Yet almost all these things occurred long ago in the times of the heretics. Even now there are many who are unwilling to endure the teaching of sound morality and who disdain to hear the truth preached in the Church, but gladly listen to actors’ tales.

> “But you, be vigilant; labor in all things; do the work of an evangelist; fulfill your ministry; be sober. For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course; I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will render to me on that day—and not to me only, but also to all who love his appearing.”

They will reject the truth of Catholic doctrine and receive the fables of errors; but you, be watchful, prudently attending to the truth and rejecting every error. Labor in all your actions, and do the work of an evangelist, that is, of a Gospel preacher. For the work of an evangelist is to live well and teach well, instructing those subject to him by conduct and words. Fulfill your ministry—that is, your office—so that it may not be empty of your good action, but that you may fully carry out whatever you ought to do in it. Be sober: let no error, love of the world, greed, or any other vice intoxicate your mind.

For this reason I urge you to keep watch against the snares of demons, heretics, errors, and vices; to labor well; and to do the work of an evangelist: because I, who until now have kept watch and fulfilled [Col. 1473B] the work of an evangelist, am already being poured out—or, according to other manuscripts, am being sacrificed, which means the same thing. For *delibatio*, which is the tasting of sacrifices, here signifies sacrifice—that is, the offering of one’s own body. I am already being poured out; that is, I have already begun to be offered in sacrifice, and through suffering to be offered as a sacrifice pleasing to God for the people entrusted to me. The time of my departure is at hand—that is, the time is now near and imminent when I shall be released from the bonds of this body and fly freely to heaven.

“I have fought the good fight.” This is said according to Greek idiom, as though one said, “I have waged a strenuous campaign,” or “I have served a faithful service.” For Latin speech would say, “I have fought with a good fight.” “I have fought the good fight,” he says: that is, I have fought well; I have contended well and without failing against the assailants of the faith and against transitory evils. I have finished the course of my good action, by which I was hastening toward the heavenly prize; I have kept the faith inviolate.

How could he say this when there still remained for him the great struggle of his own suffering, which he had just said was impending for him—such a grievous and great contest? Or did little remain toward finishing his course when that still remained, where his enemy would be fiercer and more cruel? If, then, he rejoiced with such words, certain and secure, because the one who had already revealed to him that the same passion was imminent had made him certain and secure about victory in the future contest, he says this not in fullest actuality but in firmest hope; and what he confidently expected would happen he declared as though it had already happened. [Col. 1473D] “I have completed the course,” he says.

And henceforth—that is, in the interval that remains from now into eternity—there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness: that is, in a secret and secure place there is being kept for me the crown which I have justly earned. The Lord Jesus will not give it but render it to me as something owed, on that notable day of the universal judgment, of which I think diligently; or on that desired day of my departure. He will render it to me because he is a righteous judge, rendering to each according to his work (Matt. 16; Rom. 2). Yet he will render such a crown not only to me, but also to those who love his appearing—that is, to all who know themselves to be conscious of good works. For no one loves the coming of the Judge unless he knows that his own case possesses the merit of righteousness. Therefore whoever does not love but fears his coming should correct his life, so that, having a good case, he may be able to desire his coming and hope for a crown from him rather than condemnation. [Col. 1474A]

> “Make haste to come to me soon. For Demas has deserted me, loving this present age, and has gone to Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia. Luke alone is with me. Take Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me in ministry (Col. 4). But I have sent Tychicus to Ephesus. When you come, bring with you the cloak which I left at Troas with Carpus, and the books, but especially the parchments.”

Because the time of my departure is at hand, make haste to come to me soon—that is, quickly, before I am released by death—so that I may instruct you more fully still, or so that you may be a comfort to me, since I have remained alone. For Demas, whose name means “silent,” has fallen silent from preaching or confessing the truth through fear of death. He deserted me in adversity, loving this present age with its allurements; and, leaving Rome where he feared to die, he went to Thessalonica, where he could live.

Crescens—that other disciple—went to Galatia, not deserting me but sent by me for some reasonable and necessary cause. Titus likewise was sent by me to Dalmatia. Luke the evangelist alone is with me, for he has always been accustomed to remain close to me. I said that you should come quickly to me; and when you come, take Mark and bring him with you. This is Mark, the writer of the Gospel; or, as we believe more probably, this is Mark, the cousin [Col. 1474C] of Barnabas (Col. 4), whom the Apostle now commands to be brought because he has been corrected, though formerly Paul rejected him when he was negligent and lukewarm. “For he is useful to me,” he says, “in the ministry of preaching,” though once he was useless for this purpose.

Titus went, as stated, to Dalmatia; but I sent Tychicus to Ephesus, perhaps with the letter addressed to the Ephesians. Also, when you come, bring with you the *paenula*, that garment so called, which I left at Troas with Carpus, my disciple who remains there. Let us recount what we have found said by others about this *paenula*. The *paenula* was a consular garment, worn by Roman consuls when entering the senate-house.

But perhaps someone asks how such a type of clothing came to blessed Paul. The answer is that, before Christ’s incarnation, when the Romans were acquiring the monarchy of the whole world, they had this custom: whatever people met them with peace and crowns, they granted such liberty that they were called the Romans’ brothers and Roman citizens. They gave them authority to build a senate-house and have consuls as the Romans did. Therefore the father of blessed Paul migrated from the town of Giscala in Galilee, of which he was a native, to Tarsus of Cilicia, after the Romans had captured that town.

At a certain time, when Romans were passing through Cilicia, he met them, together with others who came out to meet them, as one regarded as noble among them, and received them peacefully. Then the Romans granted them the freedom mentioned above: namely authority to build a senate-house [Col. 1475A] and have consuls like themselves, to wear consular garments, and, clothed in *paenulae* after the Roman custom, to enter the senate-house. There the distinctive *paenula* was given by the Romans to the father of blessed Paul when he was received as an ally and a Roman citizen.

These things were written before our time; let the credibility of their truth rest with those who wrote them. For we do not read in our histories all that has happened, and there are known to be many histories that we do not know. Indeed, the fact that Paul is frequently read in the Acts of the Apostles to have called himself a Roman strongly accords with these things, especially where the tribune asked him: “Tell me, are you a Roman?” and he said, “Yes.” The tribune replied, “I acquired this citizenship for a great sum,” and Paul said, “But I too was born” (Acts 16, 22, 23).

For how can it be literally true that Paul was born from the Roman citizenship unless he was born of a Roman citizen? Far be it from us to think that he lied in this statement. Therefore he was born in Roman citizenship—that is, in the household of parents who were Roman citizens. But also, in the spiritual understanding, when he said that he had been born in the city of Rome, he foretold by a prophetic spirit that the birthday of his passion would be in that city, using a past tense verb in place of a future tense.

If, then, what we have related concerning the *paenula* is true, it is easy to see why the Apostle commanded it to be brought: namely, that by means of it he might claim liberty among the Romans, if only for a short time, [Col. 1475C] so that he could freely go wherever he wished to preach and convert many persons to the faith in different places. Thus he says: “When you come, bring the *paenula* which I left at Troas with Carpus.” Dionysius greatly praises this Carpus in the Letter to Demophilus, relating a most remarkable vision of his. “Bring the *paenula*,” he says, “and the books,” which perhaps he himself had left there, “but especially the parchments”—that is, skins suitable for writing, though Jerome interprets them differently.

> “Alexander the coppersmith has shown me many evils; the Lord will repay him according to his works. Avoid him also, for he strongly opposed our words.”

Know that Alexander the coppersmith—that is, a worker in bronze or keeper of a treasury—has shown, that is, done, many [Col. 1475D] evils to me. But he will not go unpunished, because the Lord will repay him according to the works which he performed against me. Avoid him also, lest he become an obstacle to you, because he strongly opposed our words and will be able to oppose yours still more. He does not say, “He strongly opposed us,” but “our words,” that is, the preaching of the Gospel—a far more serious matter, because he opposed not human beings but the Gospel of God. Nor does he say, “May the Lord repay him according to his works,” but “The Lord will repay him,” which is the word of one declaring, not of one cursing.

> “At my first defense no one stood by me, but all deserted me; may it not be charged against them. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the preaching might be fulfilled and all the nations might hear; and I was delivered from the lion’s mouth. The Lord will [Col. 1476A] deliver me from every evil work and will bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom. To him be glory for ages of ages. Amen.”

“Many times,” he says, “I was brought before Nero in defense of the faith; but at my first defense—that is, when for the first time I defended the Gospel before that tyrant—no one, that is, none of my disciples, stood by me to help me defend Christian doctrine before Nero. Rather, all deserted me through fear of punishments. May this not be charged against them by God, but may they be forgiven.”

He did not pray for Alexander, who had sinned by attacking the brotherhood out of envy. But for those who had not broken off love, but had succumbed to fear, he prays that they may be forgiven. There is indeed a great difference between a person who, after knowing God through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, attacks the brotherhood and is driven by the torches of envy against the very grace by which he has been reconciled to God—as Alexander is understood to have been—and a person who has not withdrawn his love from a brother but, through some weakness of mind, fails to render the duties owed to brotherhood. Thus the disciples deserted Paul through fear at his first defense, or the apostles themselves deserted Christ in the Passion (Matt. 26; Mark 14), though they did not cease to love him.

Therefore he does not pray for Alexander, who, ungrateful for God’s grace, was sinning unto death by attacking grace itself and persecuting brotherly love; for John says, “There is sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (1 John 5). But he prays for those who withdrew from him not out of malice [Col. 1476C] but fear, because the same John says: “If anyone knows that his brother is committing a sin not unto death, he should ask, and life will be given to the one sinning not unto death” (ibid.).

“All deserted me,” he says, “but the Lord stood by me when I had been deserted by human beings”: he consoled me through his inner inspiration, spoke through my mouth, softened the tyrant’s fury, and strengthened me—that is, made me steadfast—so that I would not cease teaching the truth, but might powerfully overcome the tyrant by arguments so that he would release me; so that the Gospel preaching might be fulfilled through me and all nations might hear, not only in Italy but even as far as Spain. And so, through the Lord who stood by me, I was delivered from the lion’s mouth—that is, from the rage of the lion that wished to devour me, namely the rage of Nero, lest he immediately kill me.

And the Lord will still deliver me from every evil work, so that by no one’s tortures may I be compelled to commit an evil deed. Thus, brought to completion by martyrdom, he will bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom. To this Lord be glory for all these things for ages of ages—that is, for eternal ages. Amen.

Eusebius writes in his *Ecclesiastical History*: Festus was sent by Nero into Judea to succeed Felix. After his case had been heard before him, Paul, bound, was sent to Rome with Luke and Aristarchus, whom he calls his fellow prisoner (Acts 24, 28). There, remaining for two years, he preached the word of God without anyone hindering him. But the account confirms that he was there, defended himself before Nero, and then again departed for the work [Col. 1477A] of preaching; after this he returned once more to the aforesaid city, where he was completed in martyrdom. Then, being in chains, he wrote the Second Epistle to Timothy, in which he indicates both the first defense and his present suffering:

> “At my first defense no one stood by me, but all deserted me; may it not be charged against them. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the preaching might be fulfilled and all the nations might hear; and I was delivered from the lion’s mouth.”

By these words he most clearly indicates that at first, in order that the preaching begun through him might be completed, he was delivered from the lion’s mouth—meaning Nero as a lion because of his cruelty. But foreseeing his own consummation in the Spirit, he added: “The Lord will deliver me from every evil work and will bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom,” thereby signifying that he was soon to be crowned with martyrdom.

Therefore Paul did not undergo martyrdom at the time when Luke wrote the Acts of Paul in the city of Rome; for it could have happened that Nero, still milder as an enemy, did not receive Paul’s defense of our doctrine with harsh disdain. Bede likewise, on the final verse of the Acts of the Apostles, where it is said that Paul taught for two years without hindrance, added:

> Not only was he not hindered at Rome, but, since Nero’s power had not yet been strengthened, nor had he yet burst into such crimes as the histories recount about him, Paul was released to preach Christ’s Gospel also in the regions of the West, as he himself says to the Romans: “Now therefore I shall go to Jerusalem to minister to the saints” (Rom. 15); and a little later, “When therefore I have completed this, I shall go by way of you into Spain” (ibid.).

Later, that is, in Nero’s final year, he was detained by him and crowned with martyrdom. Both matters he explains in the Second Epistle to Timothy, which he dictated from prison while about to suffer: “At my first [Col. 1478A] defense,” he says, and so on through “from the lion’s mouth,” most clearly signifying Nero as a lion because of his cruelty. Then in what follows, “and he will save me and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom,” he signifies that martyrdom was then felt by him to be imminent.

> “Greet Prisca and Aquila, and the household of Onesiphorus. Erastus remained at Corinth; but I left Trophimus sick at Miletus. Make haste to come before winter. Eubulus, Pudens, Linus, Claudia, and all the brothers greet you. The Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Grace be with you. Amen.”

“Greet,” he says, “Prisca and Aquila, my friends, with whom I was often accustomed to stay.” [Col. 1478B] Prisca and Aquila were wife and husband; yet Prisca is often named first. From this it is clear that she excelled her husband in outstanding merits, although both were of great merit before God. Greet also the household of Onesiphorus, which showed me such great kindness. If you wish to know where Erastus is, he himself remained at Corinth. I left Trophimus sick at Miletus; he later became bishop of Arles.

I told you to come to me soon, and now I say that you should hasten to arrive before winter, lest winter’s difficulty delay the matter, because perhaps you would not find me alive. Those remaining at Rome greet you: Eubulus, Pudens, and Linus—this Linus was the first bishop of the Roman see—and Claudia. Nor do these alone greet you, but all the brothers as well. May the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, so that by the presence of his divinity he may guard the thoughts of your mind and direct your good will toward every good work. And may the grace of the same Lord be with you, so that, by his help, both you and those subject to you may be able to avoid evil and do good.

## ON THE EPISTLE TO TITUS

[Col. 1477]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 1477D]

The Apostle had left Titus as bishop among the Cretans, so that he might govern and teach the whole of Crete. Therefore he now instructs him by letter concerning what kind of bishops he ought to ordain and how he should repel false preachers who wished to introduce legal ceremonies. He teaches how Titus ought to admonish each person and instructs him concerning spiritual conduct, writing to him from Nicopolis, which is situated on the Actian shore.

## CHAPTER ONE

> “Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of God’s elect and the knowledge of truth which accords with godliness, in the hope of eternal life, which God, who does not lie, promised before worldly times, but has manifested in his own times his word in the preaching entrusted to me according to the command of God our Savior—to Titus, beloved son according to the common faith: grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior.”

Paul, a servant of God, writes to Titus; not, however, a servant by that service which arises from servile fear, but rather by that which is produced by love and chaste fear. A servant of God is one who is not a servant of sin. “For everyone who commits sin is a servant of sin” (John 8), etc. “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. 6; Luke 6). Therefore Paul, who was not a servant of sin, was rightly called a servant of God. Here “God” is understood to mean the Father, or even the whole Trinity.

Paul indeed is a servant of God, but an apostle of Jesus Christ—that is, ambassador and chief officer of the Mediator. For the phrase “apostle of Jesus Christ” is like saying, “prefect of the praetorium of Augustus Caesar,” or “master of the army of the emperor Tiberius.” For as the judges of this world receive their titles from the kings whom they serve and from the rank in which they take pride, in order to appear more noble, so too the Apostle, claiming for himself a great dignity among Christians, identified himself in the heading as an apostle of Christ, so that by the authority of the very title he might strike fear into his readers, showing that all who believed in Christ ought to be subject to him.

“I am an apostle,” he says, “according to the faith of God’s elect”: that is, there is no discord between my apostleship and the faith of those who are not merely called by God but chosen. I am an apostle, he says, according to the faith of God’s elect, and according to a faith which possesses knowledge of truth. For the Savior spoke to the Jews who had believed in him: “If you remain in my word, you will know the truth” (John 8). They therefore possessed faith, but had not attained knowledge of the truth.

I mean knowledge of truth which accords with godliness—that is, with devout religion. For example, someone may know grammar or dialectic, so as to possess the method of speaking correctly and to distinguish falsehood from truth. But knowledge of truth according to godliness is to know the Law, understand the prophets, believe the Gospel, and not be ignorant of the apostles. This truth, whose knowledge accords with godliness, is founded in the hope of eternal life, because as soon as someone has known it, it gives him hope of immortality.

God, who does not lie, promised this before worldly times. How did he promise, when he surely promised to human beings who did not yet exist before worldly times, unless because in his eternity and in his Word coeternal with himself, that which would come to pass in its own time was already fixed by predestination? Or to whom did he promise, if not to his Wisdom, promising that all who would believe in it would possess eternal life? He promised before worldly times, or, according to another translation, before eternal times.

From the time when, according to the narrative of Genesis (Gen. 1), the world was made, and times were established through the succession of nights and days, months and years, worldly times have flowed in this course and cycle, beginning with the world. Before these—that is, before the world began—he promised eternal life to the elect whom he knew would exist. But before these times of the world, one must believe that there was a certain eternity of times, called the *aevum*, because it was not altered by changes. For the difference between the *aevum* and time is this: the *aevum* is stable, whereas time is changeable. And before eternal times—that is, before the *aevum*—God promised unending life to his elect. For as we read: “All wisdom is from the Lord God, and has always been with him and is before the *aevum*” (Sir. 1). Thus in this Wisdom, which is with him before the *aevum*, that is, before eternal times, he promised life to the elect before eternal times.

He who does not lie made this promise, not because he could lie but refuses to burst into words of falsehood, but because, being the Father of truth, he has no falsehood in himself. Since he can never lie, we should therefore believe without hesitation that what he promised is true, and we should endeavor to prepare ourselves so that we may be worthy to receive it. He did indeed promise eternal life before worldly or eternal times; but in his own times—that is, fitting times—he manifested it, namely his Word, in preaching. The life which he promised manifested his Word. Therefore the life which he promised is itself the Word which “was in the beginning with the Father, and the Word was God, and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1), and which said: “I am the resurrection and the life. … I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 11, 14).

God manifested this life and this Word to the world in fitting times in the preaching [Col. 1480B] of the Gospel entrusted to me, so that I might faithfully announce it to the nations, and in accordance with the command of God our Savior, who wished us to be saved, fulfilling what he had promised. Paul, who is such an apostle and herald of so great a salvation, writes to Titus, his beloved son—that is, a son better and more genuine than the rest—not according to the flesh, but according to the faith common to him and the Apostle, or common to all who believe rightly. This faith is called *katholikē* in Greek, “universal,” because just as there is one baptism, so there is one faith. Heretics, who have turned aside into various errors, are separated from this common—that is, Catholic—faith.

Titus, however, is the Apostle’s son not according to the private sect of any such persons, but according to the common faith of all the elect, because he rightly teaches the Catholic truth which he learned from the Apostle. May Titus possess the grace of the Holy Spirit, which may consecrate all the works of his priestly office, and peace, which may grant him rest when enemies and vices have been subdued and enable him always to remain in harmony with God and the holy angels. And may this be from God the Father and his Son, Christ Jesus our Savior.

> “For this reason I left you in Crete: that you might correct what is lacking and appoint presbyters in every city, as I directed you. If anyone is without reproach, the husband of one wife, having faithful children, not accused of dissipation or unsubmissive. [Col. 1480D] For a bishop must be without reproach, as God’s steward: not proud, not quick-tempered, not given to wine, not violent, not greedy for shameful gain; but hospitable, kind, sober, just, chaste, holy, self-controlled, and holding fast the faithful word which accords with teaching, so that he may be able both to exhort in sound teaching and to refute those who contradict.”

After Paul had softened the hard hearts of the Cretans to faith in Christ, and had subdued them both by speech and by signs, so that they believed no longer in Jupiter but in Christ, he left his disciple Titus in Crete, to strengthen the first elements of the nascent Church and to correct whatever seemed lacking, while he himself went on to other nations, that he might lay Christ’s foundation among them as well [Col. 1481A]. This is what he says: “For this reason,” that is, for the sake of this matter, “I left you in Crete, that you might correct what is lacking.” For when he says, “that you might correct what is lacking,” he shows that they had not yet come to the full knowledge of the truth and that, although they had been corrected by the Apostle, they still needed correction. For everything that is corrected is imperfect. “That you might correct what is lacking,” he says; that is, that what has been corrected by me but has not yet been brought into the full line of truth may be corrected by you and receive the standard of evenness. And because you alone would not be sufficient to do this, “appoint presbyters in the cities,” that is, bishops, “as I directed you”: namely, such persons as I designated to you, not such as perhaps your fleshly inclination might desire or men might persuade you to choose.

“Appoint presbyters,” he says; and a little later he adds that a bishop must be blameless, showing that the presbyter is the same as the bishop. For before, through the instigation of the devil, factions arose in religion and people said, “I belong to Paul,” “I to Apollos,” “I to Cephas,” the churches were governed by the common counsel of presbyters (1 Cor. 1) [Col. 1481B]. But after each person began to regard those whom he had baptized as his own rather than Christ’s, it was decreed throughout the world that one chosen from among the presbyters should be set over the rest, to whom the whole care of the Church should belong and by whom the seeds of schisms might be removed.

For elsewhere it is written: “Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, with bishops and deacons” (Phil. 1) [Col. 1481C]. Philippi is one city of Macedonia, and certainly there could not be several bishops in a single city. But because at that time those whom they called presbyters were the same persons as bishops, he spoke of bishops as though of presbyters without distinction. And in the Acts of the Apostles he says to the priests of one church: “Take heed to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops” (Acts 20).

We have said this in order to show that among the ancients presbyters and bishops were the same; but gradually, in order that the nursery-plants of dissension might be uprooted, all responsibility was transferred to one person. Therefore, just as presbyters know that by the custom of the Church they are subject to the one set over them, so bishops should know that they are greater than presbyters more by custom than by the truth of the Lord’s ordinance [Col. 1481D]. And they ought to govern the Church in common, imitating Moses, who, though he had the power to preside alone over the people of Israel, chose seventy men with whom he might judge the people (Exod. 18).

Let us therefore see what sort of presbyter or bishop ought to be ordained. “Appoint presbyters in the cities,” he says, “as I directed you. If anyone is blameless”—understand, appoint him. This does not mean that at the time he is to be ordained he must be free from every accusation and have erased former stains by a new manner of life, but that from the time when he was reborn in Christ he is not stung by the consciousness of any grave offense. A *crimen* is a serious sin, most worthy of accusation and condemnation. The first freedom is to be without grave offenses [Col. 1482A]. Many believers, indeed, are without grave offense, but no one in this life is without sin. Therefore the Apostle, in specifying who is to be ordained, did not say, “If anyone is without sin”; if he had said this, every human being would be rejected and none ordained. Rather, he says, “If anyone is blameless,” as with murder, adultery, some unclean act of fornication, theft, fraud, sacrilege, and other such offenses. When a person does not possess these—though every Christian ought not to possess them—he begins to lift his head into freedom. Therefore let the person ordained be free from every grave offense, so that with an untroubled countenance he may rebuke the offenses of others and no one may be able to cast his own against him.

“And let him be the husband of one wife”: of one whom he has had, not one whom he presently has. Many, more superstitiously than truthfully, think that even those who, while Gentiles, had one wife and, after losing her, married another after Christ’s baptism, ought not to be chosen for the priesthood. Yet, if this rule is to be observed, those ought all the more to be excluded from the episcopate who previously indulged wandering desire among prostitutes and, after regeneration, took one wife [Col. 1482B]. For it is much more detestable to have fornicated with many women than to have had one wife. Thus Jerome.

Augustine, however, says: They understood “the husband of one wife” more acutely who judged that even a man who had had another wife while a catechumen or pagan ought not to be ordained. For the matter concerns the sacrament, not sin; sins are forgiven in baptism. But because of the sanctity of the sacrament, just as a woman—even if she was defiled while a catechumen—cannot after baptism be consecrated among the virgins of God, so it has not seemed unreasonable that one who has exceeded the singular number of wives has not committed some sin, but has lost a certain norm of the sacrament, necessary not for the merit of a good life but for the seal of ecclesiastical ordination [Col. 1482C]. Accordingly, just as the several wives of the ancient fathers signified churches to come from all nations, subject to one husband, Christ, so our bishop, the husband of one wife, signifies unity from all nations, subject to one husband, Christ.

“Having faithful children, not accused of debauchery or insubordination”: that is, not outside their father’s control. Let us suppose that someone has rightly trained his children and from their earliest age has always instructed them in the Lord’s commands. If later they give themselves to debauchery and, overcome by vices, loosen the reins for lust, will their fault be imputed to the father, and will the father’s holiness be stained by his children’s wickedness? For Isaac must be believed to have instructed his son Esau well, though Esau nevertheless later proved to be sexually immoral and profane (Gen. 25–28) [Col. 1482D]. Samuel also had sons who turned aside after greed and perverted judgment for gifts (1 Sam. 8). Therefore, if at that time an election of priests were being held, Isaac on account of Esau and Samuel on account of his sons would be considered unworthy of the priesthood.

But one should know how holy the name of the priesthood is: even things placed outside ourselves are reckoned against us, not because we do not become bishops on account of our own faults, but because on account of the incontinence of our children we are to be reproved [variant: excluded; Col. 1483A] from this rank. For with what freedom can we rebuke and teach other people’s children what is right, when the person reproved can immediately say to us: “First teach your own children”? Or with what face do I rebuke a stranger who fornicates, when my own conscience answers me: “Then disinherit your fornicating son; cast away your children who serve vices”? While a wicked son remains in the same house with you, do you dare to remove the speck from another’s eye while not seeing the beam in your own? (Matt. 7.)

Thus the righteous person is not defiled by the vices of his children; rather, the Apostle reserves freedom for the ruler of the Church, so that such a person may be appointed as does not fear, on account of his children’s faults, to rebuke outsiders. Hence those who swell with pride over the episcopate should consider that bishops are not immediately better than all those who were not ordained bishops [Col. 1483B], since some have failed to attain the priesthood precisely because their children’s faults hindered them. But if the sins of children prevent a righteous person from the episcopate, how much more should each person, considering himself, withdraw from this office, which is not so much an honor as a burden, and not covet another’s place, which those more worthy ought to occupy?

Works are also customarily designated by “children,” so that he is understood to be fit for ordination who has his works in his own power and does not allow them to be stained by any taint of creeping vices. “Therefore,” he says, “I said that he is to be ordained if anyone is blameless, because a bishop must be blameless as God’s steward,” who is without sin, so that he may in some respect imitate the purity of his Lord; for what he administers is not his own but God’s [Col. 1483C].

And he must be “not proud,” that is, not puffed up or self-pleased because he is a bishop, but, like a good steward, seeking what benefits the greater number. He must also be “not irascible.” The irascible person is one who is always angry and is moved like a leaf by the slightest breath of an answer. Nothing is indeed uglier than an enraged instructor: though he ought to be gentle, patient, and wise, he resounds with shouting, with grim face, trembling lips, wrinkled brow, uncontrolled abuse, and a countenance changing between pallor and redness; and by his savagery he precipitates the erring not so much toward good as toward evil. Yet one who is angry on occasion is not irascible, but one who is frequently overcome by this passion [Col. 1483D].

He must also be “not given to wine.” For what kind of thing is it to see a bishop drunk, so that, with his judgment impaired, he either raises an unseemly laugh against the dignity of his office, or guffaws with loosened lips, or, somewhat sad as though he remembered some matter, breaks into sobs amid his cups and sheds tears, or does something else still more senseless? Wherever fullness and drunkenness are found, there lust rules. Look at the belly and the genitals, for the order of the vices follows the order of the members.

Next it is added that a priest must not be “a striker.” Even understood simply, this edifies the hearer: he should not readily stretch out his hand to strike, nor, madly, burst forth to beat another’s face. But it is better to call “not a striker” the person who, being gentle and patient, knows in due season what ought to be said and what ought to be kept silent, and does not strike the consciences of the weak with useless speech [Col. 1484A]. For the Apostle, in forming the ruler of the Church, does not forbid him to be a boxer who physically injures others with bodily blows; even in an ordinary layperson or any pagan this would be condemned. Rather, as we have said, he forbids him to be abusive and talkative, lest he destroy by insults and chatter one whom he could have corrected by modesty and gentleness.

He must also be “not greedy for shameful gain,” so that he does not desire to accumulate money; rather, having food and clothing, he should be content with these. Thus far the Apostle’s speech has described what a bishop or presbyter must not be; now, conversely, it shows what he ought to be. “But hospitable,” he says, “kind, sober, just, chaste, holy, self-controlled, and holding fast,” and so forth.

Before all else, hospitality is prescribed for the future bishop. For if every person desires to hear, “I was a stranger and you received me” (Matt. 25), how much more does the bishop, whose house ought to be a common lodging for all? A layperson, by receiving two or a few, fulfills the office of hospitality; but a bishop, unless he receives everyone, is inhumane [Col. 1484B]. Let him also be kind, loving everyone kindly and bestowing whatever good he can, both bodily and spiritually. Let him be sober, so that bodily drunkenness is far from him and neither worldly desire, anger, nor any other vice intoxicates his mind; rather, with keen judgment he discerns all things, as the spiritual person does (1 Cor. 2).

Let him also be just, exercising justice among the people over whom he presides, rendering to each what he deserves and showing no partiality in judgment [Col. 1484C]. The difference between the justice of a layperson and of a bishop is this: a layperson may appear just in a few matters, but a bishop must practice justice toward as many persons as he has subjects.

Let him also be chaste (1 Cor. 7). For if laypeople are commanded to abstain from intercourse with their wives for the sake of prayer, what should be thought of the bishop, who is to offer unblemished sacrifices to God for his own sins and those of the people? Therefore, just as hospitality, kindness, and justice ought to be especially present in the bishop and preeminent among all laypeople, so also should his chastity—or, so to speak, priestly purity—be distinctive: he should abstain not only from an unclean act, but his mind, which is to consecrate Christ’s body, should also be free from the dart of the eye and the wandering of thought [Col. 1484D].

Hence it is added that he be holy. Holiness, so far as concerns us, is to be called purity free from every defilement, most complete and utterly undefiled. Let him also be self-controlled, not only from the embrace of a wife but from every disturbance of the mind: lest anger stir him up, sadness cast him down, fear agitate him, or excessive joy exalt him. For self-control is necessary not only in the work of the flesh and in desire of the mind, but in every matter: lest we seek honors not due to us, be kindled by greed, or be overcome by any passion.

Finally, let him be “holding fast the faithful word which is according to doctrine,” so that, just as the word of God is faithful and worthy of all acceptance, he too may show himself such that everything he says is considered worthy of trust, his words are a rule of truth, and he embraces with the desire of love such a word by which hearers may be taught, so that he may be able in sound doctrine to exhort them to do good [Col. 1485A].
