It is called “sound doctrine” in distinction from weak and infirm doctrine. He must also be able “to refute those who contradict”: that is, heretics, Jews, and the wise persons of this age, or even bad Catholics, who contradict by their conduct—not by speaking, but by living badly. For they are commanded not to fornicate, yet they fornicate; commanded not to seize, yet they seize; and so they do the other evils from which they are forbidden. Thus they always contradict holy doctrine not by tongue but by life.

The preceding qualities set forth among the bishop’s virtues concern life; but the statement that he must be able to exhort in sound doctrine and refute those who contradict pertains to the work of preaching [Col. 1485B]. For if a bishop’s life alone is holy, he can benefit himself by living in that way; but if he is educated in doctrine and speech, he can instruct others as well. Nor does he merely instruct his own people, but he repels adversaries; for unless they are refuted and convicted, they readily seek to pervert simple hearts.

This passage is against those who, giving themselves over to idleness, leisure, and sleep, think it sinful to read the Scriptures or neglect to read them; and who despise as useless chatterers those who meditate on the law of the Lord day and night (Ps. 1), not observing that the Apostle, after the catalogue of a bishop’s conduct, likewise commanded doctrine [Col. 1485C].

> “For there are many insubordinate persons, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision, who must be rebuked, since they overthrow whole households, teaching what they ought not for the sake of shameful gain. One of themselves, their own prophet, said: ‘Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies.’ This testimony is true. For this reason rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith, not giving heed to Jewish fables and commandments of people who turn themselves away from the truth.”

Therefore the person ordained bishop must be able to refute those who contradict, because there are many [Col. 1485D] who walk the broad way leading to destruction and are disobedient to divine commands. Whoever is to become a ruler of the Church should therefore have eloquence joined to integrity of life, lest works be mute without speech or words blush because deeds fail them. This is especially so because they are not few but many; not compliant but insubordinate; “empty talkers,” that is, preaching empty tales [perhaps *factas*, “made-up”]; and deceivers, that is, drawing others after themselves from truth into error. But those especially act in this way who are “of the circumcision,” that is, those who came from the Jews to baptism but did not abandon the fleshly observances of the Law. At that time they were striving to overthrow Christ’s nascent Church and introduce legal precepts [Col. 1486A].

For their chatter would have no credibility without the authority of Scripture, when they seemed to support their perverse doctrine by divine testimonies. “They must be rebuked”: that is, teachers of the Church ought to overcome such people by reasoning from the Scriptures and impose silence on them by the weight of testimonies. They overthrow not one or a few households but whole households with their masters and families, that is, they cast them down from the standing of faith, teaching what they ought not for the sake of shameful gain. Under the appearance of giving counsel, they pursue a business of deception for profit; they teach what they ought not, namely distinctions of foods, the leisure of the Sabbath long ago abolished, and the offense of circumcision. Would that they taught such things through zeal for faith! In some respect they might be forgiven, and one could say that they had zeal for God, though not according to knowledge (Rom. 15) [Col. 1486B]. But because their god is their belly (Phil. 3), they wish, for shameful gain, to make disciples their own, so that as masters they may be supported by their followers or receive money.

“Shameful gain” can also be understood otherwise. All heretics, while teaching perversely, commonly claim to be gainers of people, though to kill the souls of those deceived is not gain but destruction. Conversely, one who rebukes an erring brother according to the Gospel (Matt. 18), if that man is converted, has gained him. What gain can be greater or more precious than gaining a human soul? Therefore every teacher of the Church who rightly persuades people to faith in Christ is an honorable gainer [Col. 1486C]. And every heretic who deceives people by fraudulent words speaks what he ought not for the sake of shameful gain.

It follows: “One of themselves,” and so forth. So far as the wording and coherence of the passage are concerned, the statement, “One of themselves, their own prophet,” seems to refer to those of whom it was said above: “especially those of the circumcision, who must be rebuked, who overthrow whole households, teaching what they ought not for the sake of shameful gain”; so that the sequence is: “One of themselves, their own prophet, said: ‘Cretans are always liars,’” and so forth. But since this hexameter verse is found in one of the prophets who prophesied in Judaea [Note: [Col. 1485D] Epimenides.],

[Col. 1486D] “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies” (Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσται, κακὰ θηρία, γαστέρες ἀργαί), let it be referred, if one wishes, to the earlier words, where it was said: “I left you in Crete, that you might correct what is lacking,” so that the sequence is: “One of themselves, their own prophet,” that is, a prophet of the Cretans. But because much intervenes, and this perhaps seems absurd, it should be connected differently with the preceding and less remote words. We should read:

“For there are many insubordinate persons, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision; these many insubordinate persons, empty talkers, and deceivers, together with those of the circumcision, must be rebuked, since they overthrow whole households, teaching what they ought not for the sake of shameful gain [Col. 1487A]. One of themselves, their own prophet, said: ‘Cretans are always liars.’”

Thus the phrase “their own prophet” is not referred particularly to the Jews and those of the circumcision, but to the many insubordinate persons, empty talkers, and deceivers, who, since they were in Crete, must be considered Cretans. A certain prophet of their own foretold that they were empty talkers by saying, “Cretans are always liars.” And that they are deceivers and overthrow households he added in the words, “evil beasts.” And that they teach what they ought not for the sake of temporal profit he added, “lazy bellies.” For they are liars, evil beasts, and lazy bellies because they persuade falsehoods, thirst after the blood of those whom they deceive in the manner of wild beasts, and, rather than working quietly and eating their own bread, have the belly as their god (Phil. 3), with glory in their shame [Col. 1487B].

This verse is said to occur in the oracles of Epimenides, the Cretan poet, whom the Apostle now calls a prophet either by allusion—because such Christians deserve to have such prophets as the prophets of Baal and whatever idle prophets Scripture mentions (Jer. 2, 23)—or truly because he had written concerning oracles and responses, which themselves foretell future things and proclaim long beforehand events that are to come. Indeed, even at that time there existed a certain book of Epimenides, marked with the title *Oracles*. Because it seemed to promise something divine, I suppose that the Apostle examined it to see what it promised [Col. 1487C], and at the proper time used the little verse in writing to Titus, because he was in Crete, so that he might crush the false teachers of the Cretans by an author native to their own island.

Nevertheless, he did not confirm Epimenides’ entire work, which he had written concerning oracles, by one verse; rather, he rebuked the Cretans alone as liars through a fault of mind, their inborn readiness to lie, refuting them by an author of their own nation. For there is no assassin, parricide, or poisoner so great that he has not at some time done some good. If we praise him on seeing one good act, must we necessarily praise all the other things that he does badly? Far from it! And if an enemy quarrels and shouts against us, does he not, amid words of hostility and dispute, say something true which we, even though he speaks it against us, do not entirely condemn? Thus Epimenides did not say everything true that is contained in his poems because the remaining matters are false; rather, he is proved to have spoken truly in this one point only: that he expressed the fault of the Cretans’ inborn lying and called them evil beasts for their cruelty and lazy bellies for their feasting and idleness [Col. 1487D].

Accordingly, the Apostle speaks thoughtfully and carefully when he adds: “This testimony is true.” Not the whole poem from which the testimony was taken, not the entire work, but only this testimony, this little verse. For one who agrees with a poem in one part only must be considered to have rejected the rest. “This testimony,” he says, “is true, because the Cretans are such as he testifies them to be,” though not all of them [Col. 1488A].

“For this reason,” that is, because they are such, “rebuke them,” not gently, as you are accustomed, but sharply, so that a sharp rebuke may penetrate their hard hearts, “that they may be sound in the faith”: that is, that their mind may not be weak in faith but may grow strong and drive every weakness of unbelief far from its faith. Let them, I say, be sound in purity of faith, which wastes away under no weakness of unbelief, “not giving heed to Jewish fables,” as though they were teachers of the Jews who teach without the authority of Scripture and without any proof of reason, “and commandments,” not of God but of people, that is, of Jews who are wise only in human and fleshly matters and turn themselves away from the truth of spiritual understanding.

If anyone after Christ’s coming is mutilated, he is not circumcised but serves Jewish fables and commandments of people who turn themselves away from the truth [Col. 1488B]. “For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly; nor is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter” (Rom. 2). If anyone keeps Passover not in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, so as to expel from his soul all the old leaven of malice and wickedness (1 Cor. 5), that person gives heed to fables and follows shadows while neglecting truth. If anyone does not rise with Christ or seek the things above, but those upon the earth (Col. 3), and says, “Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle—things all destined to perish by use—according to the commandments and doctrines of people” (Col. 2), that person is intent on fables and observes human commandments, holding the shadow [Col. 1488C] and turning his back upon truth.

Hence it is added:

> “All things are clean to the clean; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean; rather, both their mind and their conscience are defiled. They profess to know God, but deny him by their deeds, being abominable, unbelieving, and unfit for every good work.”

Because above he had said, “For there are many insubordinate persons, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision,” and had then added concerning those deceived by them, “rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith, not giving heed to Jewish fables and commandments of people who turn themselves away from the truth,” and because they supposed there to be a distinction among foods, so that some were clean and others unclean, he therefore now adds: “All things are clean to the clean.” That is, all kinds of food are clean according to nature, and among those who believe in Christ and know that every creature of God is good and that nothing is to be rejected if received with thanksgiving, they contain no uncleanness [Col. 1488D].

To the clean all things are indeed clean; but to the defiled, that is, those who understand the Law carnally, and to the unbelieving, that is, those who do not distinguish the time of grace from the time of the Law, no food is clean, because they use neither what they reject nor what they consume in a holy and just manner. Rather, their mind—that is, their reason—and their conscience—that is, the secret place of their heart—are defiled by the stench of unbelief. Therefore even things clean by nature become unclean to them, because according to the character of those eating, what is clean becomes clean to the clean and unclean to the defiled [Col. 1489A].

Thus it is within us whether we eat clean things or unclean things. If we are clean, creation is clean to us. But if we are defiled and unbelieving, all things become unclean to us, whether because of heresy dwelling in our mind or because of consciousness of sins. Nothing is clean to such persons, who profess only by voice that they know God but deny him by deeds, being abominable—that is, deprived of humanity by living like beasts—and untrustworthy, that is, unworthy of belief because they have so often been caught lying.

These persons, whose mind and conscience are polluted, profess God in words but deny him by deeds, according to that saying of Isaiah: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29) [Col. 1489B]. For just as someone honors with lips and departs in heart, so someone who confesses God in speech denies him in works. Such a person is deservedly called abominable, that is, persuaded by no reasoning of truth; untrustworthy, that is, unwilling to believe and obey divine commands; and unfit for every good work, so that even the good things he may perhaps have done under the compulsion of natural goodness are not good, since they are unfit through the perversity of his mind. For such people either do things that are wrong, or pursue right works with an unright heart. They seek not everlasting rewards for their works but passing favor, or perform what they do with heretical understanding.

Some suppose that God is denied only if someone, seized by Gentiles in persecution, denies that he is a Christian. But behold: the Apostle declares that God is denied by every perverse act [Col. 1489C]. God is love (1 John 4), and love is denied through hatred. Christ is wisdom, justice, truth, holiness, strength, and the like: wisdom is denied through folly, justice through injustice, truth through lying, holiness through shamefulness, strength through weakness of mind. And as often as we are conquered by vices and sins, so often we deny God; conversely, as often as we do something good, so often we confess God. Nor should it be thought that on the day of judgment only those who denied Christ in martyrdom will be denied by the Son of God. In all deeds, words, and thoughts Christ, denied, denies; Christ, confessed, confesses [Col. 1489D].

## Chapter II

> “But speak what accords with sound doctrine. Let older men be sober, modest, prudent, sound in faith, in love, and in patience. Let older women likewise be reverent in bearing, not slanderers, not enslaved to much wine, teaching what is good, so that they may teach younger women prudence: to love their husbands and cherish their children; to be prudent, chaste, sober, attentive to their households, kind, subject to their husbands, so that the word of God may not be blasphemed. Likewise exhort younger men to be sober in all things. Show yourself an example of good works—in doctrine, integrity, chastity, seriousness, sound and irreproachable speech—so that the opponent [Col. 1490A] may be ashamed, having nothing evil to say about us. Let servants be subject to their own masters in all things (Eph. 6; Col. 3; 1 Pet. 2), pleasing them, not contradicting, not defrauding, but showing all good faith in all things, so that they may adorn in every way the doctrine of God our Savior.”

They teach, as has been said above, what they ought not; but you speak what it is fitting for you to speak—sound doctrine, which has in itself no sickness of error or vice, like the doctrine of heretics or philosophers, which, while it draws people away from some vices, often drives them toward others. Christian doctrine alone heals every sickness of vices and errors.

The Apostle had given Titus a general command concerning what he himself ought to say to all, when he said, “But you speak what accords with sound doctrine”; and now he explains, under the individual categories, what befits each age. First he sets forth what is suitable for elderly men; then what befits elderly women; third, what is appropriate for young people, both males and females—although, in his command concerning old women, he appended instructions concerning young women, in order to explain not so much what he himself should teach young women as what they should be taught by old women. Finally, he gives commands concerning slaves. Through the respective ages and conditions he establishes precepts so fittingly that his discourse is a rule of life and morals.

“Speak,” he says, “what it is fitting for you to speak, since you have been appointed a teacher of Christ’s Church”: namely, that elderly men be sober—that is, moderate in food and drink—so that the dignity of their age may possess dignity of conduct, know how to preserve measure, and be chaste, lest in their final years they be wanton, and, when their blood has already grown cold for lust, become an example of ruin to young people; and that they be prudent in rejecting or avoiding evils and choosing and doing good things, so that they may do everything with careful discernment.

Let them also be sound in faith, so that they may not be weakened by any sickness of unbelief or faithlessness, but be strong in faith, like “the righteous person who lives by faith” (Hab. II; Rom. I; Heb. X; Rom. IV), and like Abraham, who was not weakened in faith and did not waver through distrust at the promise, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, fully knowing that he was able also to perform whatever he had promised [Col. 1490D]. And let them be sound in love. He is sound in love who loves God with his whole heart, whole soul, and whole mind, and his neighbour as himself (Deut. VI). He who is sound in love “does not envy, is not puffed up, does not behave improperly, does not act dishonourably, is not provoked to anger, thinks no evil, does not rejoice over injustice, but rejoices with the truth; bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, awaits all things” (I Cor. XIII). The sickness of love, however, is when charity grows cold because iniquity abounds (Matt. XXIV). Amnon too grew cold with this chill of charity toward his sister Tamar (II Kings XIII). We must therefore fear lest we too at some time waste away through this infirmity of love.

For it sometimes happens that at first we have a holy love for a virgin, or for any woman whatever; but when the mind has been softened toward affections, little by little the health of charity grows pale with sickness, begins to weaken, and carries the one who loves to utter death [Col. 1491A]. Hence the Apostle cautiously commanded Timothy to exhort young women with all chastity. For all chastity is in body, spirit, and soul: lest the eye be scandalized; lest we linger upon the beauty of a woman’s face; lest it delight us to hear flattering words; lest, at each conversation, a mind once firm first wither. Let not only young men, then, but old men also beware lest, through the health of love, the disease of lustful love enter in; and lest an unholy love arise through holy affection, drawing them down to Gehenna.

Let them also be sound in patience, so that when they endure adversities they may not be weakened by any sickness of impatience or murmuring, but may glory in tribulations and count it all joy when they fall into various trials (I Cor. XII).

“Teach the elderly women likewise.” Although the Apostle Peter warns that men should render honour to their wives as to the weaker vessel, it must not be supposed that a wife whose bodily vessel is weak is therefore immediately weaker in soul. Hence they too are now commanded that the Apostle’s saying may be fulfilled in them: “Power is perfected in weakness” (II Cor. XII). They are said to possess all the qualities commanded generally for elderly men, in the words “elderly women likewise”: that is, like elderly men, that they be in every respect sober, chaste, prudent, and sound in faith, love, and patience.

[Col. 1491C] In accordance with their sex, let them have this special quality: that they be “reverent in demeanour,” so that their very bearing, dress, walk, movements, expression, speech, and silence may display a certain dignity of sacred adornment. And because this kind of little old woman is usually talkative, it is added: “not slanderers,” that is, not speaking ill of others. Let those who have now passed beyond youth not discuss the age and affairs of young women, saying, “She dresses like this; she arranges her hair like that; she goes about in this manner; she loves him; he loves her.” Even if these things are true, they ought not so much to defame them before others as to correct the woman herself privately in the charity of Christ, teaching her rather not to do it than publicly accusing her for having done it.

These ages, moreover, since bodily wantonness has grown cold, though some become no more modest for that reason, commonly seek to soothe their desire with wine. Therefore they are forbidden excessive drinking, because what lust is among the young, drunkenness is among the old; and it is expressly said, “not enslaved to much wine.” It is indeed a kind of slavery and an extreme condition for a person’s senses to be occupied by wine, so that one belongs not to oneself but to wine.

Since, therefore, he has taught what old women ought first to be, setting forth both what they share with elderly men and what is peculiar to them—that they be reverent and holy in bearing, neither slanderers nor persons who surrender their senses to wine—he now accordingly loosens the reins of their teaching, so that, being such persons, they may have freedom to teach. Thus they should be teachers of good things: teaching prudence [Col. 1492A], that is, discernment of good and evil, so that good may be done and evil avoided; and they should teach this prudence to young women.

Although elsewhere he said, “I do not permit women to teach” (I Tim. II), this must be understood to mean that teaching men is withheld from them. Young women, however, they should teach as though they were their daughters: to love their husbands and cherish their children. What sort of teaching is this, to love husbands, when this is established not in the speech of the instructor but in the heart of the one who loves? He therefore wishes them to love their husbands chastely; he wishes there to be chaste affection between husband and wife, so that with modesty, shame, and, as it were, the necessity of sex, the wife should render the marital due to her husband rather than herself demand it from him, and should believe that she is carrying out the work of producing children before the eyes of God and angels.

They love their children rightly if they bring them up in the discipline of God [Col. 1492B]. But not wishing to grieve them by teaching what is good, and giving them freedom to sin, is not loving children but hating them. Let old women also teach young women to be prudent, so that, though young in body, they may yet be keenly discerning in mind through the sharpness of prudence. Let them teach them to be chaste, because the enemy wages war more fiercely against chastity at the flowering age, and all his power against women is in the navel of the belly (Job XL); and sober, lest through immoderate drinking they become more inflamed toward lust; and careful for the household, diligently managing everything in the home; and kind—that is, gentle and merciful.

For it could happen that care of the household might be administered with harshness, and that through this apostolic command a stern matron might become more severe toward her little servants. He therefore joined “kind,” so that she should believe that she governs her husband’s household well if she obtains this from the servants by kindness rather than fear. Let them also teach them to be subject to their husbands, lest, swollen with wealth and noble birth, they forget God’s sentence by which they have been subjected to husbands. For he says to the woman: “You shall be under the power of your husband, and he shall rule over you” (Gen. III).

[Col. 1492C] Here the prudence of Holy Scripture must be considered. The Lord did not say to the man, “You shall rule over your wife,” but said to the woman herself, “the man shall rule over you,” so that he might leave her the reward of obedience, since it lies in her power, if she wishes to obey God’s command, to serve her husband and be subject to her spouse. Thus her service would in some sense be free and full of affection: serving her husband because she fears to offend him.

But since the husband is the head of the woman, and Christ is the head of the husband (I Cor. II; Eph. V), every wife who is not subject to her husband—that is, to her own head—is guilty of the same fault as a husband who does not submit to Christ his head. Therefore let women be subject to their husbands, so that because of them the word of God may not be blasphemed. The word of God is blasphemed either when it is despised and God’s first sentence is counted as nothing, or when Christ’s Gospel is defamed. For it is contrary to the law and faith of nature if a woman who is Christian and, under God’s law, subject to her husband wishes to rule him, when even Gentile women serve their husbands in accordance with the common law of nature.

“Exhort the young men likewise.” As, in the preceding command, where he said “reverent in demeanour” [Col. 1493A], we said that the likeness of elderly women is to be referred to elderly men, so now, in saying “exhort the young men likewise,” we think that the likeness of young men should be adapted to elderly women and, through elderly women, to elderly men: that they possess the sobriety of old men; are chaste, prudent, and sound in faith, love, and patience like them; and possess the holiness of elderly women, neither being slanderers nor enslaved to much wine, but teachers of good things.

Their special trait, however, should be that they be sober in all things—that is, observing measure and pursuing no excess, as young men often do. Or, according to other manuscripts, “let them be chaste in all things”: namely, in mind as well as body, in deed as well as thought, so that in a young man there may be no suspicion of disgracefulness.

Teach these things as they have so far been set forth [Col. 1493B]; and, so that your teaching may be effective, present yourself as an example of good works: live in such a way that you are a pattern of right living to all, and that those who see you may read in your works, as in a book, what they ought to do. For it is of no advantage for someone to be practiced in speaking and to have worn out his tongue in talk, unless he teaches more by the example of his conduct than by speech. Indeed, if a person is unchaste, however eloquent he may be in exhorting his hearers to chastity, his speech is weak and lacks authority to exhort. Conversely, however uncultivated and slow of speech he may be, if he is chaste, he can by his example impel people to a similar life.

“Present yourself,” he says, “as an example in teaching,” so that others may teach what is right by your example; “and in integrity,” so that the integrity [Col. 1493C] of your mind may be corrupted neither by love of human praise nor by receiving money nor by anything else, and so that others likewise may preserve, through your example, the uncorrupted integrity of their minds; “and in chastity,” so that others may preserve chastity through your example.

Or “in integrity” may mean the untouched integrity of the body, so that others too may preserve perpetually, through your example, the integrity of virginity; and “in chastity” may refer to others who are not virgins, so that, even after the loss of integrity, they may preserve the purity of chastity. From this I judge that Titus, having received baptism as a believer in the Gospel before he was engaged in a work of the flesh, remained a virgin; and that he is therefore now admonished by the Apostle to make himself an example in integrity. We do not see the same integrity in Timothy.

For when he said to Timothy, “Let no one despise your youth, but be an example to the faithful in word, conduct, charity, faith, and chastity” (I Tim. IV), he was silent about integrity and mentioned chastity alone [Col. 1493D]. Chastity, however, may be understood in celibacy even without virginal integrity. Be also an example to others in gravity, so that the seriousness of maturity may always be evident in your speech, walk, and conduct; and make your word sound and irreproachable, so that the speech of your preaching—or even of ordinary conversation—may contain no sickness of vice and may be beyond anyone’s reproach.

This does not mean that anyone is of such eloquence and prudence as never to be reproached: the Apostles and Evangelists are reproached by heretics and Gentiles. Rather, it means that he should say or do nothing worthy of reproach, even though opponents are ready to criticize. Or, according to other manuscripts: by sound and irreproachable speech present yourself as an example to believers, and do this so that one who is on the opposing side—that is, any unbelieving and spiteful person—may fear to sink his teeth into us, having nothing evil to say about us: finding nothing evil to say concerning us; terrified by the soundness of our life and teaching, not daring to accuse us—that is, unable to invent anything plausible in accusation.

Even to this day, in some churches, though they are found more rarely, there are persons of such gravity and self-control that they receive testimony even from opponents [Col. 1494A]. For no one is of such unrestrained shamelessness that he can accuse the rays of the sun of darkness or cover clear light with the gloom of night. “One who is on the opposing side” may also be understood as the devil, who is the accuser of our brothers, as we read in the Apocalypse of John (Apoc. XII). When he finds nothing evil to bring against us, the slanderer will blush and will be unable to slander. For *diabolus* means “accuser.”

Teach slaves also to be subject to their masters, lest, because of the spiritual freedom they have obtained in Christ, they rise against their earthly masters; rather, let them humbly submit to them in all things. Since the Saviour, who said, “Come to me, all who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. II), excludes no condition, age, or sex from access to blessedness, the Apostle now establishes commands also for slaves, as a part of the Church and members of Christ. As he previously explained what Titus ought to teach elderly men and women, young women and young men, he now shows what commands he should give to slaves.

First, that they be subject to their masters in all things [Col. 1494C] that are not contrary to God. If an earthly master commands things not opposed to God, the slave should submit to his master; but if he commands contrary things, the slave should obey the master of spirit rather than of body. And let them be pleasing, which in Greek means that they should be pleased with themselves, so that God’s sentence may not seem unjust to them because of their condition.

But just as the poor person can be saved according to his measure, and a woman is not excluded from the kingdom because of the weakness of her sex, and every condition can attain blessedness according to its order, so slaves too should be pleased that they are slaves. Let them not therefore think they cannot serve God because they are subject to human beings; rather, let them believe that they please God’s will if they are subject to their masters in all things and are content with their condition. Let them not contradict their masters’ commands, for it is commonly a great fault of slaves to contradict masters and mutter when something has been ordered. Such a disposition must be removed from Christian slaves. For if a slave must carry out what the Lord commands, why should he not do it with good will, rather than offend the Lord and yet do what is commanded?

Nor should they defraud, for this too is commonly a fault of slaves: to deceive their masters by stealing their property and serving them faithlessly [Col. 1495A]. Let them not defraud—that is, deceitfully diminish anything from their masters’ goods—but show good faith in everything, so that it may be clear that they act faithfully in all respects. This is so that they may adorn in all things the teaching of God our Saviour. For if they are faithful in the least things before earthly masters, greater things will begin to be entrusted to them before God. He adorns God’s doctrine who does what is suited to his condition; conversely, he disgraces it who is not subject to people, who is displeased with his condition, who is contentious and deceitful, and who shows good faith in nothing. For how can he be faithful in God’s substance—that is, in his doctrine—who could not show faithfulness to an earthly master?

Or the addition, “that they may adorn the teaching of God in all things,” should not be referred only to slaves, but also to all those named above, from the words “that elderly men be sober”; so that elderly men and women, young women and young men, and slaves may adorn the teaching of our God as though with pearls—with good works.

> “For the grace of God our Saviour has appeared to all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly desires, and to live soberly, justly, and piously in this age, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity and cleanse for himself an acceptable people, pursuing [Col. 1495C] good works.”

After the catalogue of instruction to Titus, in which he had described what he ought to admonish elderly men, elderly women, young women, young men, and finally slaves, he rightly adds that the grace of God the Saviour has appeared or shone upon all people. For there is no distinction between free and slave, Greek and barbarian, circumcised and uncircumcised, male and female; rather, we are all one in Christ, all are called to God’s kingdom, and after our offense we must all be reconciled to our Father—not through our merits, but through the Saviour’s grace.

Either Christ himself is the living and subsisting grace of God the Father, or this is the grace of Christ God the Saviour: that we are saved not by our merit, according to what is said elsewhere, “You will save them for nothing” (Ps. LV). Therefore slaves must adorn God’s doctrine by living well, because the grace of God, through which this doctrine can be fulfilled, has appeared to all people—and hence also to slaves. Or, you ought therefore to exhort people of every age, sex, and condition to live well, because the grace of God the Saviour—that is, the freely given Son of the Father, who wills to save the human race—has appeared through faith to all people: elderly and young, male and female, free and slave; and has excluded no one from knowledge of himself.

Or the grace of God the Saviour—that is, the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, who desires freely to save the human race through baptism—has appeared through the illumination of the Gospel to all people [Col. 1496A], excluding no one and passing over no one who is willing to open the eyes of the heart. I mean grace training us: making us advance from being unformed persons and perfectly instructing us to renounce ungodliness—that is, the unbelief of pagans and the faithlessness of heretics—and worldly desires, that is, cravings for the pleasures of this age, which deceive many Catholics.

For ungodliness exists where the piety of faith is absent; worldly desires are those suggested by the ruler of this world, and, though they belong to the age, they pass away with this age’s cloud. Whoever was formerly ungodly but, converted to Christ, has become pious, has renounced ungodliness. Whoever was lustful but changed his life to continence has renounced the desires of the age. Whoever was greedy but has ceased coveting and learned to give away his own possessions, though he formerly seized those of others, has renounced the desires of the age.

For those who hunger and thirst for righteousness (Matt. V), because they seek the joys of the heavenly homeland, have indeed now renounced the alluring desires of the present age which they once pursued. Therefore, renouncing ungodliness and worldly desires, let us live in this very fragile age soberly and justly, against the desires of the age, and piously, against ungodliness: soberly with respect to ourselves; justly toward our neighbour; and piously toward God. Let us live soberly—that is, moderately—preserving measure and abstaining from vices; justly, performing works of righteousness by keeping God’s commandments; and piously, persevering in the piety of faith, or possessing a devout heart of compassion toward the afflictions of neighbours.

We are, I say, awaiting in return for these things [Col. 1496C] the blessed hope of heavenly recompense: that is, awaiting the blessedness for which we hope because of good works. All of us ought to observe this abstinence in the time of the present life as though during Lent. For a great and universal fast is abstinence from errors and unlawful pleasures of the age, so that, renouncing ungodliness and worldly desires, we may live soberly, justly, and piously in this age. A reward is attached to this fast when he says, “awaiting the blessed hope.” Thus in this age we celebrate, as it were, the forty-day fast of abstinence when we abstain from ungodliness and unlawful pleasures and live well. But because this abstinence will not be without a reward, we await that hope of blessedness.

Let us not, then, seek recompense in the present life; rather, let us await with all our heart the blessed hope of eternal reward and the appearing in glory of the great God, when he will come in the clouds with great power and glory (Matt. XXV), and the great God will be recognized—he who at his first coming was seen as a small human being. Let us await the appearing of this great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ, because he who will be perceived as the great God by the reprobate will deign to be our Saviour.

There is also this ordering of meanings: “awaiting the appearing in glory of Jesus Christ, the great God and our Saviour.” We ought to await him and hope for salvation from him because he who found us held captive by the devil gave no other price for us but himself, so great as he is, in order to redeem us by his precious blood, because we were his own [Col. 1497A]. For we are said to buy what belongs to others, but to redeem what is our own.

He redeemed us from every iniquity, so that no iniquity—that is, no sin—might henceforth rule us, as John says: “Everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity, and sin is iniquity” (I John III). And he cleansed for himself a people: that is, he not only redeemed us from the yoke of the devil and of iniquity, but also cleansed us by washing away the stains of our sins in baptism, and thus made us a people acceptable to himself, or, “as the Greek has it,” a peculiar people: a people, I say, pursuing—or, as the Greek has it, emulating—good works. Therefore he redeemed us by his blood in order to make the Christian people his own peculiar and acceptable people, and to make it a pursuer of these works, persevering in them.

[Col. 1497B]

> “Speak these things, exhort, and rebuke with all authority. Let no one despise you.”

Speak these things that have been said concerning the appearing of grace, the renunciation of ungodliness, and the Lord’s giving himself as a ransom for us, in order to free us from iniquity and cleanse for himself a peculiar people pursuing good works. Speak them to the ignorant; exhort those who know them to live accordingly; and rebuke—that is, convict—the contemptuous or resistant. Do these things with all authority, that is, with commanding authority.

By “authority” he does not urge domination by power but the authority of a virtuous life. For teaching is given with authority when what is said has first been done. The conscience weakens the confidence of teaching when it hinders the tongue [Col. 1497C]. He therefore does not suggest to Titus the power of eloquent speech but the confidence of good conduct. Hence it is written of the Lord: “For he was teaching as one having authority, and not as the scribes and Pharisees” (Matt. V; Mark I). He alone, uniquely and supremely, spoke good from authority, because he committed no evil from weakness. By divinity he possessed the power which he imparted to us through the innocence of his humanity.

For this reason Titus too is commanded to speak, exhort, and rebuke with all authority, because he was very gentle, and through excessive mildness his speech might have been ineffective unless he were more fervently enjoined through the authority of command. That “authority” principally signifies authority of life, as we have said, is made clear by what is immediately added: “Let no one despise you”—that is, “I do not wish you to present yourself in such a way that you may deservedly be despised by someone.”

Or: “Let no one despise you,” that is, let none of those in the Church, while you act negligently, live in such a way as to think himself better than you and despise you as inferior. What kind of edification can a disciple have if he realizes that he is greater than his teacher? Hence not only bishops, presbyters, and deacons must take great care to precede in conduct and speech all the people over whom they preside, but also those of lower rank—exorcists, readers, church attendants, and absolutely all who serve God’s house—for it greatly destroys the Church of God when laypeople are better than clerics.

## Chapter III

[Col. 1498A]

> “Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities, to obey commands, to be ready for every good work, to blaspheme no one, not to be quarrelsome but gentle, showing all meekness toward all people.”

Because above he had said only that slaves ought to be subject to their masters, someone might perhaps suppose that those not of servile condition ought to be subject to no one. Therefore he now says: “Remind them,” although they are free from servile condition, nevertheless to be subject—that is, subject to rulers, namely kings, because they are the first and greatest heads of peoples; and to authorities, namely governors, consuls, tribunes, and the like, who exercise power over others.

Perhaps he gives these commands also because in that period the teaching of Judas the Galilean still flourished and had many followers; it is mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts V). Among other things, this man advanced as though probable from the Law the proposition that no lord except God alone should be called lord, and that those who brought tithes to the Temple ought not to pay tribute to Caesar. This heresy had grown so greatly that it disturbed a large part both of the Pharisees and of the people; thus this question was even brought to our Lord: “Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not?” To them he prudently and cautiously replied: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. XXII; Mark XII; Luke XX).

In accord with that answer, the Apostle now teaches that believers ought to be subject to rulers and authorities, even if they are unbelievers to whom believers considered it unworthy to submit, and that they should obey their command, lest they have to be compelled by force. Because those who feared tortures could find an occasion for denial while maintaining, under the Apostle’s instructions, that they must be subject to rulers and authorities and do what they command, he therefore added, “ready for every good work.” If what the emperor or governor commands is good, he says, let one be ready to obey the commander. But if he commands what is evil and against God, answer him that “one must obey God rather than men” (Acts V).

Understand the same thing concerning slaves in relation to masters, wives in relation to husbands, and children in relation to parents, whether earthly or spiritual: they ought to submit to them only in matters not contrary to God’s commands [Col. 1498D]. Or the wording may be divided thus: “to obey commands for every good work,” and then a separate meaning follows: “to be ready.” They should be ready in the sense that they should mentally anticipate everything that can possibly happen; when it occurs, they should endure nothing as though it were new, but be prepared for everything.

“Remind them to blaspheme no one,” because the common people often speak against their ruler and speak ill of him. But believers too ought not blaspheme a perverse ruler, lest they be oppressed and afflicted by him. Yet “to blaspheme no one” is not to be taken simply. He did not say, “blaspheme no human being,” but absolutely, “no one”: that is, not a human being, not an angel, not any creature of God [Col. 1499A]. For all things made by God are very good, and it does not at all become Christ’s disciples to blaspheme or curse anyone.

“Not quarrelsome, but gentle.” If we are children of peace, wish peace to rest upon us, and have come to the heavenly Jerusalem, which received its name from peace, let us have peace with those who hate peace (Ps. CXIX); and, so far as it depends upon us, let us be at peace with all people, not only with the gentle but also with the contentious, since it is no virtue to bear with the gentle. Let us give place to wrath. Christians ought therefore not be quarrelsome but gentle—that is, self-controlled—lest, bursting forth in anger, they blaspheme someone, call an unbeliever a dog or a child of the devil, or say or do anything of that sort in anger.

“And showing all meekness”: so that they may not only be meek in heart—that is, gentle and tractable—but also openly display every meekness outwardly, in their walk, words, and deeds. Let them display it not merely toward some people but toward all, both good and bad: toward the good, so that it may perfect them; toward the bad, so that they may repent. This does not mean that, out of desire for empty glory, we ought to show ourselves meek to all; rather, because when we bear with everyone and do not repay injury in kind, the deeds themselves become known to all. Someone may, through ostentation, concern for public opinion, and popular applause, feign meekness and simulate goodness before certain persons. But where there is no true, genuine, and solid meekness, I do not know whether anyone can be persuaded that he is meek toward all people [Col. 1499C].

> “For we too were once foolish and unbelieving, wandering, enslaved to various desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another.”

They ought therefore to blaspheme no one, quarrel with no one, preserve gentleness, and show meekness to all, because those who now seem to act perversely may perhaps turn from their wickedness, just as we have turned. For we too were once—that is, formerly or at some time—foolish, not possessing the wisdom of divine knowledge; unbelieving, not believing what ought to be believed concerning God; and wandering, believing what is not true of God, regarding light as darkness and darkness as light (Isa. V), judging falsehood true and truth false.

We were enslaved—that is, obedient—to our desires, because we followed our lusts and unlawful desires, satisfying them as far as we could; and we served various pleasures: the pleasures of flesh, gluttony, soft clothing, and similar things. We lived in malice toward others—that is, performing evil actions against others—and in envy, that is, ill will. If we could not do evil, we were at least ill-disposed and envious toward others as much as we could be, desiring their evil and detesting their good. We were therefore hateful—that is [Col. 1500A], liable to be hated, worthy to be hated by others—and hating one another, because we hated others and others hated us.

Such were not only Gentiles before faith but also unbelieving Jews after the Lord’s resurrection, after they cried, “Crucify, crucify him”; “We have no king but Caesar”; and “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Luke XXIII; John XIX; Matt. XXVII). From that time they were foolish, not possessing the wisdom of God, which is Christ; unbelieving, unwilling to believe that Christ had come in the flesh; wandering, awaiting Antichrist instead of Christ; enslaved to carnal desires and pleasures; and doing the other things described.

Was not Saul foolish, unbelieving, and wandering when he had zeal for God, but not according to knowledge, persecuted the Church, and guarded the clothes of those stoning Stephen (Acts VII)? So inflamed was he, stirred up to hatred against the Saviour, that he obtained letters from the priests and went to Damascus (Acts IX) to bind those who had believed in Christ. Could he extinguish the burning flame of pleasures when he was not a temple of God? What greater malice and envy could there be than to obtain letters against those absent, devastate Christ’s disciples everywhere, refuse salvation for oneself, envy others who could be saved, hate Christians, and consequently deserve hatred from all?

> “But when the kindness and love for humankind of God our Saviour appeared [Col. 1500C], he saved us, not from works of righteousness which we had done, but according to his mercy, through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Saviour, so that, justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.”

Such were we before the knowledge of Christ, as we have described: therefore we had deserved condemnation; but by God’s grace, in the knowledge of Christ, we found salvation. For he saved us when there appeared—that is, when there shone upon us—the kindness, that is, the liberality with which mercy is bestowed, and the love for humankind, that is, the merciful disposition, of God our Father and Savior. By “kindness” [Col. 1500D] he means the manifestation of the works of divine mercy; by “love for humankind” (*humanitas*), the very benevolent disposition of that same mercy. Love for humankind is spoken of in God by analogy with ourselves. For among us that person is called humane who is disposed humanely and mercifully toward human beings, since *humanitas* is itself an effect of mercy.

According to faith and understanding, the love for humankind and kindness of God our Savior appeared to us when we learned that God the Father is compassionate and merciful. And then he saved us, though by our merits we were worthy of destruction. For this salvation did not proceed from works of righteousness which we ourselves had done, since we had performed no works of righteousness by which we might have deserved salvation; rather, according to his own mercy, he saved us. He gave us this salvation not according to our merits [Col. 1501A], but through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit—that is, through baptism, in which we were regenerated and renewed when the Holy Spirit came upon us, through whom forgiveness of sins was given to us.

Indeed, in baptism there was given to us the hope of future salvation, not the salvation itself which is promised; yet, because the hope is certain, that same salvation is said to have saved us as though it had already been given. Elsewhere he says that “we were saved in hope” (Rom. I). Therefore he saved us not yet in actuality, but already by certain hope—that is, through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit he gave us the eternal salvation of body and soul: through the washing of baptism, in which we have been washed from the stains of sins, spiritually [Col. 1501B] begotten anew after carnal generation, and, having put off the old person, renewed by the Holy Spirit. Thus in baptism we might again receive the newness of innocence which we had received in the first parent before he sinned, and thereafter walk in newness of life.

God the Father poured out this Holy Spirit upon us—that is, poured him forth outside upon us—because we are still exiles outside Paradise, so that his greater mercy toward us might be shown. He poured him out abundantly, that is, sufficiently for the remission of all sins and for the bestowal of virtues. Or “abundantly” means making us abundant in his spiritual gifts. And he did this through Jesus Christ our Savior—that is, through the working of Jesus Christ, who by his blood saved us from our sins and will still save us from all evils. To this end the Father poured out [Col. 1501C] this Spirit upon us—that is, into our inward parts—that we might be justified through him; and, justified not by our merits but by his grace, whether that of the Father or of the Holy Spirit, we might already, according to hope, be heirs of eternal life, though not yet according to actual possession: that is, we already possess eternal life by hereditary right in certain hope.

> “The saying is trustworthy. And concerning these things I want you to insist, so that those who believe God may take care to lead in good works. These things are good and useful for people. But avoid foolish questions, genealogies, disputes, and quarrels about the Law, for they are useless and empty.”

This saying which I have set forth—that, justified by his grace, we may become heirs according to the hope of eternal life—is trustworthy. The saying about God’s inheritance [Col. 1501D] and the hope of eternal life is worthy of faith. “And concerning these things I want you to insist,” that is, concerning the matters stated above I want you not to be doubtful but certain; and, that others may believe, I want you to confirm them—that is, that you may confirm others concerning the matters already mentioned: grace, justification, inheritance, the hope of eternal life, and such things.

Or: “I want you to insist concerning these things,” that is, I want you to speak insistently about them and affirm them strongly, so that those who hear you may believe you and may take care to lead—that is, may endeavor to go before others—in good works. Those who believe these things to be true must necessarily take care for good works, through which God’s inheritance and the hope of eternal life are prepared. Let them take care to lead others in good works, that is, with utmost concern and greatest diligence let them labor to do good works, by which they provide others an example of right conduct; and let those who believe God strive thus to act [Col. 1502A], adorning faith by works, because these things are good—that is, just and holy—and useful, that is, conferring upon people the benefit of eternal reward.

Concerning these things, I say, I want you to confirm those who believe God, because they are good and useful. But avoid foolish questions, because, on the contrary, they are empty and useless. Foolish questions are those in which foolishness is plainly evident, as in many of the questions which heretics raise concerning Christ or other matters in order to disparage Catholics; but avoid questions of this kind. Avoid also genealogies—that is, calculations of generations—which the Jews make. They boast in this and think they have knowledge of the Law if they retain the names of every individual, and run through from Adam to the last Zerubbabel the generations of all persons [Col. 1502B] rapidly and from memory; and in reckoning years and recounting grandchildren, great-grandchildren, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers, they imagine themselves teachers.

Avoid also the disputes of those who argue through the techniques of dialectic, not with reason but with the heated temper of litigants, devoting themselves to this by day and night: questioning or answering, offering or accepting a proposition, making assumptions, proving, and drawing conclusions. If, then, those whose special art is disputation do this, what ought a Christian to do except flee contention altogether? Avoid also quarrels about the Law. For it frequently happens that we engage in disputes about the Law, not from desire for truth but from ostentation and desire for glory, while we wish to be considered learned by our hearers, or while we pursue shameful gain from this little traffic [Col. 1502C].

For what benefit is there in babbling with foaming lips and the barking of dogs, when a simple and temperate answer, if true, can satisfy you, or, if false, can be gently and peaceably corrected by you? Altercations arose concerning the Law when some said that one must abstain from certain foods because this had been commanded in the Law; and others replied that the Gospel had permitted them, the Lord saying: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person” (Matt. XII). Others contended that the whole Law itself ought to be understood and observed carnally; others, however, replied and said that it ought now to be observed and understood not carnally but only spiritually. But such questions, genealogies [Col. 1502D], disputes, and quarrels are to be avoided because they are useless—that is, they benefit neither speakers nor hearers—and empty, that is, void, because they possess only the appearance of knowledge.

> “Avoid a heretical person after a first and second admonition, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment.”

The Greek word *hairesis* (“heresy”) is derived from choosing, because each person chooses for himself what seems better to him. Hence Stoics, Peripatetics, Academics, and Epicureans were called adherents of this or that *hairesis*. A heretic, therefore, is one who, abandoning the teaching of the universal Church, chooses for himself an error of perverse doctrine which he follows in a distinctive manner. And he is a heretic because [Col. 1503A] he is a person who thinks merely human thoughts and disputes concerning God according to human reasonings.

But such a person should be corrected, and if he persists in error, avoided; just as the Lord commands that false teachers be left to their own choice, knowing that they can with difficulty be drawn to the truth: “Leave them,” he says; “they are blind, and guides of the blind” (Matt. XV). Hence the Apostle now also commands that a heretic be avoided. “Avoid,” he says, “not only the questions and genealogies mentioned above, but also a heretical person after one and another correction or admonition.”

It is as though he said: “If you see someone wandering from the faith, admonish him reasonably, that he may hold the catholic faith; and if he delays, correct him still more sternly for the perversity of his error. It is not enough merely to correct or admonish him once [Col. 1503B]; a second correction must also be applied, so that every word may stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (II Cor. XIII; Deut. XVII). “If, after twofold correction or admonition, he refuses to come to his senses, then avoid him henceforth, having no participation or fellowship with him, nor continuing to admonish him, knowing that he is perverted.”

For one who, corrected once and twice and having heard of his error, does not wish to be corrected, considers the one correcting him to be in error; and, preparing himself instead for fights and wranglings of words, wants to gain over the very person from whom he is taught. Therefore one who is of this kind—that is, of so perverse an error and so wicked an obstinacy—is “perverted”: turned away from contemplation of the things above toward looking at lower things, so that he always contemplates earthly things and savors nothing except what is earthly and infernal [Col. 1503C] (*sic*). And he sins—that is, he abandons the truth more and more—while condemned by his own judgment: that is, given over, body and soul together, to the loss of everlasting condemnation.

He is said to be condemned by his own judgment because fornicators, adulterers, murderers, and other criminals are expelled from the Church by priests; heretics, however, pronounce sentence upon themselves by departing from the Church of their own choice. Such a departure appears to be the condemnation of their own conscience. Between heresy and schism there is this difference: heresy holds a perverse doctrine, whereas schism separates itself from the Church because of disagreement with a bishop. Yet there is no schism which does not devise some heresy for itself, in order that it may appear to have departed rightly from the Church [Col. 1503D].

> “When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, hasten to come to me at Nicopolis, for I have decided to spend the winter there. Diligently send ahead Zenas, the lawyer, and Apollos, so that they may lack nothing. Let our people also learn to lead in good works for necessary needs, that they may not be unfruitful.”

Keep for the present these things which I write; and when I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, then hasten to come to me at Nicopolis, in order that you may preach elsewhere as well, because I have decided—that is, firmly resolved—to winter there, that is, to remain during the winter.

It was said at the beginning of this letter: “For this reason I left you in Crete, that you might set right what remains and appoint presbyters in the cities” (above, I). Since the Cretans had recently believed, Titus was left behind when Paul departed [Col. 1504A] for other churches, so that they might not be abandoned as orphans but might have an apostolic man to correct what seemed lacking. Since Titus, after the foundation of other churches, was necessary to lay the substructure of the building, Paul writes to him that, when he had sent Artemas or Tychicus—one of the two who had been with him—to Crete to fill his place, he himself should come to Nicopolis, declaring that he would winter there. From this we see Paul’s paternal affection for the Cretans, among whom the seeds of idolatry had first sprung up. Although Titus was necessary for the ministry of the Gospel, Paul does not wish him to come to himself before Artemas or Tychicus has arrived as his successor, by whose teaching and comfort the Cretans may be nurtured.

Nicopolis [Col. 1504B] is the city which received its name from Augustus’s victory, because there he overcame Antony and Cleopatra: *Nikopolis* (νικόπολις) in Greek is called in Latin, as it were, “the city of victory.” I said, “Come to me,” and beforehand diligently send Zenas, the expert in the Law, and Apollos, so that they may lack nothing—that is, may lack none of the necessities, but may bring with them whatever they need, since I have no means of providing for them. Here he intimates that he is poor and does not long to accumulate earthly things.

Concerning this Apollos it was said to the Corinthians: “Each of you says: ‘I indeed am of Paul; but I of Apollos; and I of Cephas’” (I Cor. I; Acts XVIII). He was an Alexandrian man from among the Jews, very eloquent and learned in the Law, bishop of the Corinthians. Because of the dissensions which existed at Corinth [Col. 1504C], he is thought to have crossed over to the neighboring island of Crete with Zenas, a teacher of the Law; and, once the dissensions of the Corinthians had been settled by Paul’s letter, to have returned again to Corinth. But of Zenas, the expert or teacher in the Law, we cannot say from another passage of Scripture who he was—only that he was an apostolic man, holding the task which Apollos had, of building up Christ’s churches.

Paul therefore commands Titus, since they were about to sail from Crete to Greece, not to let them lack purses, but to ensure that they have what is necessary for the journey. And because a hidden objection might arise—so that not so much Titus as any reader of the letter might say, “And from where was Titus to give [Col. 1504D] travel provisions to those who had none?”—he resolves this question and, as though crushing any objection, says: “Let our people also learn to lead in good works for necessary needs, that they may not be unfruitful.”

By “our people” he means his own, those who believed in Christ. Because they belonged to Christ, they rightly deserved to be called both Paul’s and Titus’s; having food and clothing, they were content with these. And lest they perhaps readily despise either Paul’s letter (I Tim. VI) or Titus’s command, he calls unfruitful all who do not minister to evangelists. “Let them not,” he says, “be unfruitful. For every tree which does not bear good fruit will be cut down and cast into the fire” (I Matt. III). Therefore whoever is unwilling to provide necessities for holy preachers is an unfruitful tree and, on account of its barrenness, worthy of burning.

The text is read thus [Col. 1505A]: “Send them ahead.” But “let our people also”—that is, those whom I converted to Christ and left with you to be instructed longer—learn, under your teaching, to lead in good works for their necessary needs: that is, always to be ready to minister to preachers the things necessary for them. Or, let them learn “to lead,” that is, to go before others in good works performed for the necessary needs of preachers, so that they may not be unfruitful by failing to provide them with needed expenses.

> “All who are with me greet you. Greet those who love us in the faith. The grace of God be with you all. Amen.”

“All who are with me,” he says, “greet you,” that is, they pray for your welfare. Or he uses the customary form, saying that Titus is greeted by all who were with him [Col. 1505B]; or perhaps this applies particularly to Titus, because he was such a man as to deserve the affection of all those with Paul. It is indeed great praise for Titus to be greeted by all through Paul.

“They greet you,” he says, “and you, on our behalf, greet those in Crete who love us in the faith, not in the flesh.” For not everyone who loves, loves in faith. Many love [Col. 1506A] without faith: mothers love their children, indeed, but do not love in faith; wives love their husbands, but that love is not the love of faith. The love of saints alone loves in faith, so much so that, even if the person loved is not in the faith, the saint nevertheless loves him in faith. For the saint loves in faith because he believes in him who promised that he would repay a reward for fulfillment of the commandment; and he loves the unbeliever with the intention that he may become a believer.

Then he invokes the grace of God upon Titus and the others who were with him, saying, “May the grace of God be with you all. Amen.” And just as the patriarch Isaac blessed his son Jacob (Gen. XXVII), and Jacob himself the twelve patriarchs (Gen. XLIX), and the Apostles, when entering a house, said, “Peace to this house” (Matt. X)—and if the house was worthy, the Lord’s peace rested upon it (Luke X), but if it showed itself unworthy, it returned to those who had uttered the blessing—so now, at the end of his letter, the Apostle invokes grace upon believers. This invocation had effect together with the wish, and it lay in the believers’ power if the person blessed was willing to show himself such as the one blessing prayed that he might be [Col. 1506B].

## ON THE EPISTLE TO PHILEMON

[Col. 1505]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 1505C]

The Apostle sends a familiar letter to Philemon from a Roman prison, asking on behalf of his servant Onesimus. Onesimus had stolen his property and fled to Rome so that he might not be apprehended by him; but there, having gained the Apostle’s friendship, he received Christ’s baptism and corrected himself so thoroughly, and learned apostolic teaching, that he became a suitable preacher of Christ. Therefore the Apostle seeks to obtain his pardon from Philemon, sending him back with this letter.

## SOLE CHAPTER

> “Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, to Philemon our beloved and fellow-worker, and to Apphia our dearest sister, and to Archippus our fellow-soldier [Col. 1505D], and to the church which is in your house: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, writes to Philemon. By placing first his own very celebrated name, he indicates to him that he ought not to deny to so great a man what he asks. Yet he does not call himself an apostle, because, since he intends to obtain pardon, he ought to use only conciliatory words and not put forward a name of authority. He does not command, but asks. Yet it seems a mark of greater dignity to call himself a prisoner of Jesus Christ than an apostle (Acts V). For the Apostles gloried that they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus Christ.

But the authority of his chains is necessary [Col. 1506C]. For, since he was going to ask on behalf of Onesimus, one ought to make the request who could obtain what he sought and who, by mention of his own sufferings, might bend Philemon to mercy, lest he add sorrow upon sorrow by denying pardon to Onesimus. Not everyone who is bound is a prisoner of Jesus Christ; only the one who suffers chains for Christ’s name and confession is so bound, just as only blood shed for Christ’s name makes a martyr.

He therefore writes to Philemon while imprisoned at Rome, at the time when the letters to the Philippians, Colossians, and Ephesians seem to have been dictated. The letter to the Philippians is first similar for this reason (Phil. IV): he writes it with Timothy alone, as he does in this letter [Col. 1506D]. Then he says that his chains for Christ had become known throughout the whole praetorium. What the praetorium is he indicates at the end of that letter: “All the saints greet you, especially those of Caesar’s household.” Sent by Caesar to prison, he became known to Caesar’s household and made the house of the persecutor a church of Christ.

Moreover, the beginning to the Colossians is similar: “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and Timothy our brother” (Col. I). And at the end he says: “Remember my chains” (Col. IV). The same Onesimus who is now commended to Philemon was also the bearer of that letter. Thus we read: “Tychicus, the beloved brother, faithful minister, and fellow-servant in the Lord, whom I have sent to you for this very purpose, will make known to you all things concerning [Col. 1507A] me, that he may know the things concerning you and comfort your hearts, with Onesimus, the beloved and faithful brother, who is one of you” (*ibid.*).

Now this Philemon, to whom this letter is written, is Onesimus’s master—or rather, he began to be his brother in the Lord. The Colossians are told that Onesimus is one of them; therefore reason itself and the sequence lead us to conclude that Philemon also was a Colossian, and that Onesimus bore the letter addressed generally to the whole church at the same time as he received private letters of commendation to his master concerning himself.

There is also another indication: in this same letter Archippus is named, to whom, together with Philemon, the letter is here written. “Say to Archippus,” he says, “See to the ministry which you received in the Lord, that you fulfill it” (*ibid.*). What is the ministry which Archippus received from the Lord [Col. 1507B]? In the letter to Philemon we read, “and to Archippus our fellow-soldier.” To the Ephesians he also writes that he is a prisoner in the Lord (Eph. III, VI), and at the end says: “That you may know the things concerning me, Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful minister, whom I have sent to you for this purpose, will make all things known to you, that you may know the things concerning me and that he may comfort your hearts” (Col. IV).

Tychicus, however, is the one sent to the Colossians with Onesimus; and he had Onesimus as his companion at the same time that Onesimus was bearing letters to Philemon [Col. 1507C]. At the beginning of those letters Paul associates Timothy with himself, so that the letter, not written by one person alone, might have greater authority, and Philemon might do what was requested not only for the Apostle’s sake but also for Timothy’s, who was familiar to him.

Paul and Timothy our brother write to beloved Philemon; and because he is beloved by them, he ought for their sake to grant pardon to Onesimus. In the Greek, however, “beloved” is not found, but “lovable” (*diligibilis*). The difference between “beloved” and “lovable” is this: one who does not deserve love may be called beloved; but lovable applies only to one who is deservedly loved. Thus we are commanded to love our enemies (Matt. V; Luke VI): they are beloved, but not lovable. For we love them not because they deserve to be loved, but because the Lord commanded this. Philemon, however, is both beloved and lovable, because he is loved and deserves to be loved.

“To Philemon,” he says, “our beloved and fellow-worker”—that is, one who through his preaching assists us in spreading Christ’s Gospel; and therefore he is beloved by us because he labors in the same work of holy preaching as we do. “And to Apphia our dearest sister,” who has in herself nothing of false or feigned sisterhood; “and to Archippus our fellow-soldier,” whom I suppose, fighting with Paul and Timothy against adversaries for Christ’s name, to have emerged victorious. Therefore he now calls him fellow-soldier because he had overcome in the same contest and warfare, or because he was still serving with them [Col. 1508A] in continual preaching and the repulse of enemies.

What the Apostle says in writing to the Galatians (Gal. III)—that in faith in Christ it makes no difference whether someone is Gentile or Jew, male or female, slave or free—is clear in this passage also. For Apphia’s name is inserted between two apostolic men, between Paul’s fellow-worker and his fellow-soldier, so that, supported by such company on either side, she may seem to have not the rank of her sex but that of merit.

Some understand Apphia to be Philemon’s wife and Archippus his son. This seems quite fitting: the letter is sent principally to Philemon as master of the household, then to Apphia his wife and Archippus his son, and also to the church—that is, the assembly of believers—which is in his house, that is, in his household [Col. 1508B], or which he himself feeds and maintains in his house for Christ’s name. The Apostle greets the wife, son, and household church so that all may intercede for Onesimus and forgive him from the heart, because they too had been offended by him.

“Grace,” he says, “and peace be to you from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.” Grace is that by which we are saved without any merit or work; peace is that by which we have been reconciled to God through Christ. But because grace and peace are asked from the Father and from Christ, the one nature or power of the Son and the Father is shown, since the Son can grant what the Father grants, and the Father is said to grant what the Son grants. Thus far Paul and Timothy address Philemon and the others; from here Paul alone speaks to Philemon alone until the end of the letter [Col. 1508C].

> “I give thanks to my God, always making mention of you in my prayers, hearing of your love and faith which you have in the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints, so that the sharing of your faith may become evident in the knowledge of every good thing which is in us in Christ Jesus.”

He praises Philemon in many ways so that afterward he may more easily bend him to grant what he will request. “I give thanks,” he says, and so forth—as though saying: “O Philemon, you ought to forgive Onesimus and no longer retain any resentment or hatred against him in your heart, since you are a man of outstanding love and faith; therefore I give thanks to my God.” For how will so charitable a man not extend his love even to a servant who has been rightly corrected? Or how will one so faithful not pardon him who now shares the same faith?

“I give thanks to God for you” [Col. 1508D]—to God, I say, who is mine as though especially my own, because with a certain special excellence I serve him above others. I always give thanks to him, making mention of you in my prayers. It is ambiguous whether he always gives thanks to his God or always makes mention of Philemon in his prayers; both can be understood. For one who commands others to give thanks to God in all things could not be driven by any distress not to give thanks to God himself always. But if he always prayed for saints and all the better persons, it is credible that he always prayed for Philemon, that his faith and love might be preserved by Christ’s mercy [Col. 1509A].

“I always give thanks,” he says; or, “I always make mention of you in my prayers”—that is, whenever I pray for myself, I mingle prayer for you as well. “I give thanks, hearing”—that is, because I frequently hear of your love and faith which you have in the Lord Jesus and toward all his saints. For this reason I give thanks and pray for you: because I am often told that you have love in the Lord Jesus, by which you love him above all things, and love toward all his saints, whom you love as yourself. Therefore you ought also to love Onesimus, because he is now one of his saints.

You also have faith in the Lord Jesus and in his saints, as we read in Exodus (Exod. XIV), that the people believed God and Moses his servant. Whoever believes God [Col. 1509B] cannot receive faith in him otherwise than by believing also his saints—that is, the preachers and authors of the holy Scriptures. Nor is love and faith toward God genuine when one maintains hatred and unbelief toward his ministers.

You have such love and faith that the sharing of your faith may become evident in good works. Or, “I pray for you so that the sharing of your faith”—that is, your faith’s conviction that everything you possess ought to be held in common with all the saints—“may become evident,” that is, may outwardly appear in action, so that what it believes inwardly it may show outwardly in performing deeds. And may it do this, advancing in the knowledge of every good thing, so that by believing rightly and acting rightly it may reach the point of knowing every good thing as far as is possible in this life: that is, understanding it [Col. 1509C], distinguishing it from evil, and knowing what it is.

For there are many simple persons who perform works of righteousness yet do not possess knowledge of what they themselves do. But you, understand every good thing that you do, so that the sharing of your faith may become evident in the knowledge of every good thing—good, I mean, which exists in Christ Jesus. With how many stages and advances does apostolic discourse rise toward higher things! Someone has love and faith in God and his saints, but perhaps does not distribute it to all in an equal balance.
