Perhaps he shares with all, but does not fulfill his intention in deed. Another fulfills it in deed, but cannot have full knowledge of his actions. There may also be someone who possesses both work and knowledge, but does not possess every good thing. For though he performs many things justly, gently, and diligently, he falls short of his own virtues in some respect.

But Philemon is not such a person. For he has the sharing of faith and love that works, made evident toward God and toward all his saints, in the knowledge of every good thing. Since this knowledge is in the Apostles, we should not suppose that it is perfect merely because it is similar; rather, its whole perfection lies in this, that it belongs to Christ. Thus whatever good is praised in Philemon and drawn from the Apostles’ example is good because it is drawn from Christ’s fountain [Col. 1509D].

> “For I had great joy and consolation in your love, because the hearts of the saints were refreshed [Col. 1510A] through you, brother. Therefore, though I have great confidence in Christ Jesus to command you concerning what is fitting, yet because of love I rather entreat you, being such a one as Paul—an old man, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ. I entreat you for my child, whom I begot in chains, Onesimus, who formerly was useless to you, but now is useful both to me and to you. I have sent him back to you; but receive him as my own heart.”

He more fully impresses and explains what he had said: “I give thanks to my God always, making remembrance of you in my prayers.” “For this reason,” he says, “I give thanks: because, having heard of your charity, which you exercise toward the saints, I have found in it joy—not merely any joy, but great joy—and consolation. For I had experienced a certain desolation and sorrow [Col. 1510B], fearing that, if Onesimus returned to you, he might suffer some harm from you. But when I heard that your charity overflowed toward all the saints, I had consolation and joy, believing that you would grant pardon also to Onesimus, who is now one of the saints. Therefore I received joy and consolation in your charity, because it is so great that the inward parts—that is, the hearts—of the saints, whom you have often received as guests, have been refreshed through you, good brother. That is, you have bestowed such great outward benefits upon them that even their inward affection rested in the goodness of your charity.

“For the mind and will of the saints are refreshed through those who pursue works of mercy, just as they are afflicted through those who act perversely. And it was fitting to give thanks to God for the charity of Philemon [Col. 1510C], who, by receiving the saints, had refreshed the inward affection of their hearts and the deep recesses of their souls. The Apostle has this customary usage: he always calls them ‘inward parts,’ wishing to express the fullness of the mind’s charity. Thus, rejoicing with those who rejoice (Phil. IV), and believing himself refreshed together with those who had been refreshed, he possesses a joy not passing or slight, nor such as may happen by chance, but great—corresponding to the eminent charity found in Philemon. This joy was increased by consolation concerning that same charity of Philemon, descending from the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation (II Cor. I).

“From this point he begins gradually to come to the matter, adding: ‘Therefore’—that is, because the inward parts of the saints have often been refreshed through you—‘I, having in Christ Jesus, for whose sake you do such great things, much confidence to command you,’ that is, much certainty that, if I wished, I could command you concerning that which pertains to the matter, namely, to your advantage and mine; yet, because of charity, I do not wish to command—that is, to compel you by authoritative force—but, setting command aside, I rather beseech you, that is, I entreat you by sacred things: I ask you by faith, by your charity, to do what I request. ‘I beseech you,’ he says, ‘since you are such as Paul the aged,’ that is, because you are such as I, Paul the aged, am—advanced in bodily age as I am. Therefore I do not command you but beseech you, because old men are not to be compelled by command but asked by entreaty, as it is said in another epistle: ‘Do not rebuke an elder, [Col. 1511A] but beseech him as a father’ (I Tim. V).

“In this very respect the Apostle calls himself an old man and compares Philemon with himself in old age, making it plain that Philemon ought not to offend an old man by refusing what he can and ought to do, since he himself is old. ‘I am old,’ he says, ‘and not only old, but now also bound’—that is, constrained by chains in old age. Therefore you ought the more readily to consent to my request, so that in some measure you may lighten the burden of my chains. ‘I am bound,’ he says, ‘and bound for Jesus Christ,’ that is, given over to chains for his Gospel. Therefore do not grieve me, lest you also offend him whose prisoner I am.

“After first setting before Philemon many praises, since the matter for which he was about to ask was advantageous both to the one granting and to the one asking, Paul could more properly command than [Col. 1511B] request. And this arose from that confidence: one who had performed such great works for Christ could surely not be deficient in other matters. Yet he wishes rather to request than command, having set forth the great authority of the petitioner, through which the Apostle, an old man and a prisoner of Jesus Christ, makes supplication.

“The whole matter for which he asks is this, as we have already touched upon in the introduction. Onesimus, a slave, added theft to flight: he took certain goods of his master and, going to Italy so that he could not easily be apprehended nearby, squandered his master’s money wastefully. When Paul was in prison because of his confession of Christ, this man believed in the Lord Jesus; baptized by him, he wiped away the stains of his former life through worthy repentance, so thoroughly that the Apostle became the witness of his conversion—the Apostle who [Col. 1511C] had once rebuked Peter for not walking with a straight foot in the truth of the Gospel (Gal. II).

“So far as the sin and crime by which he injured his master are concerned, he does not deserve pardon. But in view of the testimony of the Apostle, who knows that he has been fully converted, great weight is brought to bear upon the person asked not to refuse pardon to one who, from a runaway and thieving slave, had become a minister of the Apostle. What other ministry did the Apostle have than that of the Gospel of Jesus Christ? Thus he was to be forgiven, not as from a master, but as from a convert and fellow-preacher of the Gospel—a servant of Christ and likewise a minister. This, then, is what he asks, adding: ‘I beseech you for my son,’ and so forth.

“It is as though he said: ‘I had said, “I rather beseech you because of charity,” and had not disclosed [Col. 1511D] for whom or for what I beseech you. But now know that I beseech you for my son’—that is, one who is my own and, as it were, singularly beloved—‘whom I have spiritually begotten while in chains. And because he did not shrink from my chains but received the faith more courageously, he should be forgiven his former error.’ He now first names the son for whom he makes request, after giving many reasons why he ought to obtain what he asks for him: ‘I beseech you,’ he says, ‘for Onesimus.’ He then adds why he should be entreated for him: ‘Who was once unprofitable to you.’ ‘For this reason,’ he says, ‘I beseech you for him: because he was once—that is, formerly—unprofitable to you, seeking not your benefit but your loss, when he stole your money and fled. But now he is useful [Col. 1512A] both to you and to me; therefore you ought to forgive him, whom I have sent back to you so that he may ask pardon from you, make satisfaction to you, and devote himself to your service.’

“He had previously been unprofitable only to his master. For a slave who was a thief and a fugitive harmed no one but his master. Now, on the contrary, by a compensation of usefulness, through which he is useful both to his master and to Paul, and to others through Paul, he deserves more charity than he formerly deserved hatred. Hence he says, ‘Who was once unprofitable to you.’ ‘To you alone,’ he says, ‘not to others; but now useful both to you and to me.’ He is useful to his master because he could serve Paul on behalf of his master. He is useful to Paul because, while Paul is detained in prison and chains, he could minister in the Gospel—that is, preach the Gospel abroad on Paul’s behalf.

“At the same time, one must admire the greatness of the Apostle’s soul [Col. 1512B] and the fervour of his mind toward Christ. He is held in prison, bound with chains, confined by bodily squalor, separation from loved ones, and penal darkness; yet he does not feel the injury, is not tortured by grief, and knows nothing except to think upon Christ’s Gospel. He knew that a slave, a fugitive, formerly a thief, had been converted to the faith of Christ. It is a great labour for such a person to persevere in what he has begun. Therefore he repeatedly calls him his son, the son of his chains, and the minister of the Gospel while he himself is in chains, so that Philemon—prudently and judiciously praised to this extent in the preface—would not dare to refuse, lest he seem unworthy of his own praises.

“‘I have sent him back to you,’ he says—that is, I have again sent him to you, from whom he had departed—because I did not wish [Col. 1512C] to make use of another’s slave. But do not reject or afflict him; receive him, that is, take him up: receive him honourably. I mean him who is my inward parts. As we said above, ‘inward parts’ signifies the inner affection of the heart and the full disposition of the soul, when everything that is in us is taken up by the petitioner. Otherwise, all children are the inward parts of their parents.

> “Whom I had wished to keep with me, that he might minister to me on your behalf in the chains of the Gospel. But without your counsel I wished to do nothing, so that your good might not be as if from necessity, but voluntary.”

“I have sent back to you the one whom I had first wished to keep with me—I, an Apostle of such name and authority [Col. 1512D], who by my authority could sufficiently have kept him. I wished to keep him, I say, so that he might supply my necessities on your behalf, that is, in your place, since you used to minister to me. The service which he rendered to me I would have credited to you, and you would thereby gather the fruit of eternal reward. I mean, rendered to me while I am in chains and therefore greatly in need of his service—in the chains of the Gospel, that is, the chains which I suffer for the Gospel, not for any crime of my own.

“For these reasons I had wished to retain him. But afterward, reflecting with myself, I wished to do nothing concerning your slave without your counsel—that is, without your consent and common will—so that your good might not be as if from necessity; that is, so that your good might not be unwilling but voluntary, proceeding from your own [Col. 1513A] will. Philemon’s good was the service which his slave rendered to the Apostle on his behalf. The Apostle could indeed have retained Onesimus in his service even without Philemon’s consent. But if he had done this without Philemon’s will, it would have been good, certainly, but not voluntary. What is not voluntary is shown, in another respect, not to be good. Nothing can be called good unless it is freely undertaken.

“From this the prudence of the Apostle must be considered: he sends the fugitive slave back to his master in order that he may benefit his master, whom he could not benefit if he were kept while his master was absent and unwilling. From this passage, too, there may be answered a question often asked by many: why, when God made man in his image and likeness, he did not make him such that he could not be evil. For if God is good voluntarily and not by necessity, then, in making man in his image and likeness, he ought to have made him good voluntarily and not by necessity. But those who maintain that man ought to have been made such that he could not admit evil say this: he ought to have been made such that he was good by necessity and not by will. But if he had been made such that he performed good not by will but by necessity, he would not have been like God, who is good because he wills, not because he is compelled. Thus it is plain that they seek a thing contrary to what they assert. For when they say, ‘Man ought to have been made like God,’ they ask that he should be made of free will, as God himself is. But when they add, ‘He ought to have been made such that he could not admit evil,’ [Col. 1513C] in imposing upon him a necessity of goodness, they wish that man should not be made like God.

“This question, then, is resolved: God could have made man good without his will. But if he had done so, that good would not have been voluntary but necessary. What is good by necessity is not good, and is shown in another respect to be evil. Therefore, in leaving us to our own choice, he made us more according to his image and likeness. For to be like God absolutely is good.

> “For perhaps he departed from you for a time for this reason: that you might receive him for ever, no longer as a slave, but, instead of a slave, as a most beloved brother—especially to me. But how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord?”

[Col. 1513D] “Sometimes evil becomes an occasion of good, and God turns the wicked designs of men toward what is right. What I say will become clearer by an example: ‘Joseph’s brothers, stirred by the goads of envy, sold him to the Ishmaelites’ (Gen. XXXVII); this was the beginning of every good thing for his father, his brothers, and all Egypt. Indeed, Joseph himself later said to his brothers: ‘You intended evil against me, and God turned it to good’ (Gen. L).

“We may understand something similar in Onesimus: evil beginnings became occasions for a good result. If he had not fled his master, he would never have come to Rome, where Paul was held prisoner. If he had not seen Paul in chains, he would not have received the faith of Christ. If he had not possessed the faith of Christ, he would never, having become Paul’s [Col. 1514A] son, have been sent into the work of the Gospel. From this it is inferred step by step that Onesimus became a minister of the Gospel because he fled from his master. This is what is said: you ought to receive him honourably and willingly, because perhaps for this reason he departed from you for a time—that is, for a brief period—so that you might receive him for ever.

“By adding ‘perhaps,’ he suitably moderates the statement. God’s judgments are hidden, and it is rash to pronounce as certain what is doubtful. ‘Perhaps,’ he says, ‘he departed for this reason,’ speaking cautiously, timidly, and hesitantly, not asserting everything with fixed step; for, if he had not said ‘perhaps,’ all slaves would have had to flee in order to become apostolic men. Perhaps, then, he departed from your service not for long but for a time—that is, as though for the space of one hour—so that, in exchange for so brief an absence, [Col. 1514B] you might receive him for ever: one who would remain with you eternally, whereas he would only have remained with you temporarily if he had not departed. That is: perhaps God foresaw this and, by hidden counsel, willed that he should depart from you for a time, that is, for a brief period, so that you—who would not have him dwelling with you eternally if he had not departed to come to me and receive the faith—might receive him, to dwell with you not for an hour but for eternity.

“For since he holds the same faith and religion as you, he will always be with you both here and hereafter; whereas he would have been separated from you for ever and handed over to punishments, if he had not departed for a time in order to cast off unbelief. Although the Apostle said this as if doubtfully, it nevertheless came to pass as truly as he declared. For this Onesimus, as we have learned from the writings of the Fathers, later became a bishop and a glorious martyr. ‘That you might receive him for ever,’ he says, now—that is, after he received the Spirit of freedom in baptism—not as a slave as before, but instead of a slave as a brother, because he began to have the same Father as you in heaven.

“Not merely any brother, but one most beloved by all the children of the Church who know the holiness he now possesses; but especially—that is, far more than others—beloved by me, who know better whom I ought to esteem as dearer and who know his perfect conversion better than others do. To me, indeed, he is so outstandingly dear on account of spiritual brotherhood alone; but how much more—that is, far more—ought he to be most dear to you, both [Col. 1514D] in the flesh, in respect of the flesh, because, as a slave, he owes you bodily service; and in the Lord, in respect of the Lord, because through faith he has become his son and will be a fellow-partaker with you in his kingdom.

“In his saying, ‘that you might receive him for ever,’ it should be noted that no one is an eternal master of his slave. For a master’s power and the condition of both alike end in death. But Onesimus, through faith in Christ, was made eternal to eternal Philemon; and, having received the spirit of freedom, he ceased to be a slave and began, from being a slave, to be a brother—a brother most beloved because of his holiness, an eternal brother to eternal Philemon, to the Apostle himself, and to his own master. Formerly the condition of the flesh joined Onesimus to him; afterward the Spirit joined him. While Onesimus was subject to Philemon in the flesh, he was not joined to him in the Lord; now, however, [Col. 1515A] he is joined to him both in the flesh and in the Lord. From this we understand that a slave who has believed in Christ, if his master is a believer, is bound to that same master by a double law: he is joined to him temporarily by the necessity of the flesh, and joined to him eternally by the Spirit.

> “If, therefore, you hold me as a partner, receive him as myself. But if he has harmed you in anything or owes you anything, charge it to me. I, Paul, have written it with my own hand: I will repay it—not to say to you that you owe even yourself to me. Yes, brother, let me have joy of you in the Lord; refresh my inward parts in Christ.”

“Since Onesimus has been so well corrected and has become so dear to me, therefore receive him reverently as myself—that is, with the same care, hospitality, and affection with which you would receive me if I came to you. Receive him, I say, if you have—that is, if you wish to have—me as your partner, that is, your companion and friend. Otherwise I shall not be your partner. Philemon desired to have Paul as his partner; and, believing in Christ, he surely wished to make such progress as to become like Paul and share with him in chains.

“Let us consider, therefore, how greatly Onesimus is praised here and how much progress he is shown to have made, since he is to be received as the Apostle and his master ought to desire partnership with Paul. In brief, his meaning is this: if you wish to have me as your companion, have Onesimus, whom I have as companion, son, and my inward parts. If you do not receive him and do not wish to have him, know that you cannot have me. ‘Receive him,’ he says, ‘as myself.’ But if he harmed you in [Col. 1515C] anything by destroying your property—for example, uprooting a vineyard, burning a house, or committing some other such act, which fugitives often do—or if he owes you anything, that is, if he took some of your money with him which he ought to restore, charge to me the harm or debt which he caused: reckon the injury and debt as being in me, not in him, so that I may repay it to you for Onesimus, as Christ also in his passion paid for us what he did not owe.

“I, Paul, of such renowned name and so proved in truthful speech, have written this letter not through a secretary but with my own hand, in which I promise to repay what he owes: I myself will repay it. I say this so as not to mention something else [Col. 1515D] which I might justly say: namely, that you owe even yourself to me. That is, you owe me not only your possessions but, what is greater, even yourself; so that, if necessary, you ought to give yourself for me by dying, because whatever good is in you is wholly through the faith which you learned from me. Therefore every good thing in you is owed entirely to me.

“His meaning is this: ‘What Onesimus took by theft, I pledge myself to repay. This letter and this handwritten signature are the witness of my pledge; I did not dictate it in the customary manner, but wrote it myself with my own hand. Believe me, then, as I promise for Onesimus.’ Yet he says this as though speaking to a stranger. But if I return to my own right, you owe even yourself to me because of the word of Christ which I preached to you and by which you became a Christian. If you are mine, then all that is yours is mine. But if all that is yours is mine, Onesimus also, who is yours, is mine. I could therefore use him as my own; but I leave him to your will, so that you may have the reward of forgiving him.

“When he says, ‘I will repay,’ this is not to be understood of a monetary but of a spiritual repayment: that is, through his intercession he will obtain from the Lord an everlasting recompense of spiritual goods for the temporary loss Philemon suffered through Onesimus. ‘Receive him,’ he says, ‘as myself, because what he owes I will repay spiritually.’ Thus, brother, in that heavenly recompense, let me have joy of you—that is, let me delight in you in the Lord, in the glory of blessedness which the saints have in the Lord. Therefore now refresh my inward parts [Col. 1516B]—that is, kindly cherish Onesimus—and do this in Christ, that is, in Christ’s charity. Or: ‘Refresh my inward parts,’ that is, renew my inward affection and fulfil my desire in Christ, by granting pardon to Onesimus and henceforth treating him honourably.

“The word translated ‘Yes’ is, in Greek, as it were an adverb of affectionate entreaty, but cannot properly be expressed in Latin. It conveys the feeling of one making a request. ‘Let me have joy of you in the Lord,’ he says. When one enjoys a human being in God, one enjoys God rather than the human being; for one enjoys that by which one is made blessed, and rejoices that one has come to God, in whom one places hope of arriving. He rightly says, therefore, ‘Let me have joy of you in the Lord.’ If he had not added ‘in the Lord,’ but had simply said, ‘Let me have joy of you,’ he would have placed the hope of his blessedness in Philemon.

“Nevertheless, ‘to enjoy’ is also used, very nearly, for ‘to use with delight.’ When what is loved is present, it necessarily brings delight with it. If someone passes beyond that delight and refers it to the one in whom he must remain, he uses it; and then he is said improperly, not properly, to enjoy it. But if he clings to it and remains there, placing in it the end of his joy, then he is truly and properly said to enjoy it. This should be done only in that Trinity which is the highest and unchangeable good. Therefore the Apostle enjoys Philemon in the Lord, having him with himself in that contemplation of the Creator in which lies the perfect fulfilment of delight and the joy of the righteous.

“He also wishes his inward parts—Onesimus, whom he had called by the same name above—to be refreshed through Philemon. [Col. 1516D] The statement is ambiguous: whether Onesimus is Paul’s inward parts in Christ, or whether Onesimus, Paul’s inward parts, is to be refreshed by Philemon in Christ. If we take the former interpretation, Onesimus is rightly called Paul’s inward parts in Christ, since Paul begot him in Christ’s chains. If the latter, Onesimus is to be refreshed in Christ by Philemon, so that he may be instructed by Philemon’s words in Christ.

> “Confident in your obedience, I have written to you, knowing that you will do even beyond what I say.”

“You ought to refresh my inward parts, for I wrote to you concerning Onesimus, confident in your obedience—that is, having complete confidence and being certain that you will obey me in this matter, as you have always been accustomed to obey in other matters—so that you may forgive and receive him as myself. [Col. 1517A] ‘I have written these things to you,’ he says, ‘knowing that you will do even beyond what I say’: you will either give more than I ask, or do beyond what I request and grant more than I demand. One who presumes concerning the person from whom he is about to ask, by that very presumption in some sense prejudges what he asks. Moreover, if the petitioner knows that the one asked will do more than has been requested, he asks greater things in God, so that the person asked may have a willing disposition and a greater reward from his service.

“If Philemon does this at the command of a man, how much more will he do it from love of God? Hence he is rightly praised in the Apostle’s words because he has anticipated his commands by deed and can say: ‘Let the freewill offerings of my mouth please you, O Lord’ (Ps. CXVIII), so that, by doing more than is commanded, he surpasses those who do only what is commanded. For virginity too will be crowned with a greater reward (I Cor. VII), because it has no command of the Lord and extends itself beyond what is commanded.

> “At the same time, prepare lodging for me also. For I hope that through your prayers I shall be granted to you.”

“Not only receive Onesimus as myself, but also prepare lodging for me at the same time. For I hope that God will yet grant me to you through your prayers, so that, released from this prison, I may return to you and again teach you and others. I do not think that the Apostle was so wealthy or encumbered with so much baggage that he needed lodging to be prepared, or that, not content with one cell, he sought very spacious houses. Rather, while Philemon expects him to come, he will more readily do what he has been asked, lest perhaps he blush when Paul arrives. But if anyone thinks that this command to prepare lodging for him is not judiciously adapted to the purpose but literal, lodging ought to be prepared for the Apostle rather than merely for Paul.

“For one who was going to a new city to preach the Crucified One and bring an unheard-of doctrine knew that very many would flock to him. First, therefore, the house had to be in a notable part of the city, easily accessible for gathering; next, it had to be free from every inconvenience and spacious enough to contain many hearers; not near places of public spectacles, lest its disgraceful and detestable neighbourhood offend; and finally, it had to be situated preferably on level ground rather than in an upper room. For this reason, I think, he also stayed for two years in hired lodgings at Rome; and the lodging was not small, in my opinion, since crowds of Jews frequently gathered there. [Col. 1517D]

“‘I hope,’ he says, ‘that through your prayers I shall be granted to you.’ God grants the Son to the Father when asked, and a brother is often saved by a brother’s prayer. But the Apostle is granted through the prayers of the whole Church for the benefit of those who will hear him. This gift is said to be not so much to him, who is delayed from martyrdom though ready for it, as to those to whom the Apostle is sent.

“That Paul was frequently in prison and released from chains, he himself says elsewhere: ‘in prisons more abundantly’ (II Cor. XI). From these he was sometimes released by the Lord’s help and often because his persecutors found nothing in him worthy of death. For decrees of the senate against the Christian name had not yet been issued, nor had Nero’s sword yet been consecrated by Christian blood. Rather, because of the novelty of the preaching, the people were stirred to frenzy either by jealous Jews or by those who saw their own idols being overthrown; they were sent to prison and, when the violence and fury subsided, were released. That these things were so is attested by the Acts of the Apostles: Agrippa says to Festus that Paul could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar (Acts XXVI); and Festus says to Agrippa that he found no charge except certain questions concerning their own religion and a certain Jesus whom Paul declared to be alive (Acts XXV). From this we perceive that they could likewise have been released by other judges, the Lord so arranging it that the new preaching might be spread throughout the whole world. Therefore the Apostle now says [Col. 1518B] that he hopes he may yet be granted to the faithful through their prayers.

> “Epaphras, my fellow-prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you, as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow-workers.”

“What we said at the beginning—that the Epistle to the Colossians was written at the same time and conveyed by the same bearer of letters as this Epistle to Philemon—is also shown by the names of those introduced as sending greetings. For the former likewise concludes: ‘Aristarchus, my fellow-prisoner, greets you, and Mark, Barnabas’s cousin, and Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ’; and a little later: ‘Luke, the most beloved physician, and Demas greet you; and say to Archippus: See to the ministry [Col. 1518C] which you received in the Lord, that you may fulfil it’; and: ‘Remember my chains’ (Col. IV).

“If anyone does not think the letters were written together because a few names occur in the Epistle to the Colossians which do not occur here, let him know that not all persons are either friends or acquaintances of all others, and that it is one thing to write a private letter to one person and another to write a public letter to the whole Church. ‘Epaphras, my fellow-prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you,’ he says. Of this Epaphras it was said to the Colossians: ‘You learned the grace of God in truth, as you learned it from Epaphras, our beloved fellow-servant, who is a faithful minister of Christ Jesus for you, and who also made known to us your love in the Spirit’ (Col. I). The Apostle now calls him his fellow-prisoner in Christ [Col. 1518D], because he was held at Rome with Paul, captured and bound in chains for Christ’s Gospel.

“As for Mark, whom he next mentions, we would believe him to be the one who wrote the Gospel, were he not called Barnabas’s cousin in the Epistle to the Colossians. Therefore we rather believe that this is the Mark over whom Paul and Barnabas formerly disagreed: John, who was surnamed Mark. Through his association with Barnabas he improved sufficiently to be worthy of attachment to Paul, by whom he had once been rejected.

“Aristarchus, whom the Apostle also calls his fellow-prisoner in the Epistle to the Colossians (Col. IV), was a Thessalonian. He accompanied Paul when he went up to Jerusalem, and from there he and Luke were sent with him to Rome, as ecclesiastical history also records. Demas is the same man concerning whom the Apostle complains to Timothy: ‘Demas has deserted me, loving this present age, and has gone to Thessalonica’ (II Tim. IV). Perhaps afterward, led by repentance and strengthened in Christ, he returned to the Apostle; or, if he did not return to him, it is clear that this letter was written before the Second Epistle to Timothy. Luke, the most beloved physician, is that glorious brother ‘whose praise is in the Gospel throughout all the churches’ (II Cor. VIII). Leaving the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles to the churches, he was transformed, as the Apostles became fishers of people from fishers of fish, from a physician of bodies into a physician of souls. Whenever his writings are read in [Col. 1519B] the churches, his medicine never ceases.

“The conclusion of this Epistle is as follows:

[Col. 1520A]

> “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.”

“As the people of Israel are counted from the better part of a human being, that is, the head, Scripture saying, ‘according to their heads,’ so the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ is indeed in the whole person and every part of the saints; but by synecdoche, it is spoken of the whole person from the greater and better part, namely the spirit: ‘The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.’ When the Lord’s grace is in the spirit, it makes the whole person spiritual, so that the flesh may serve the spirit and the soul not be overcome by the flesh; and, reduced together into a spiritual substance, the person may cleave to the Lord, since ‘he who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit.’

# ON THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS

[Col. 1519]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 1519B]

Paul, while in Italy, wrote this Epistle in the Hebrew language and sent it to Jews converted to faith in the Lord Jesus, who were living in Judaea after acknowledging the truth. His principal intention was to confirm them in the purity [Col. 1519C] of Christian faith and wholly detach them from the legal observances by which they were still held. They believed that faith in Christ alone, without the addition of legal ceremonies, was in no way sufficient for the attainment of blessedness; rather, they said that both together were necessary for salvation. They considered no one worthy of everlasting life either in faith in Christ without legal observance, or in observance of the Law without faith.

Their blessed Apostle Peter permitted them still to live under legal ceremonies, fearing that if he entirely removed bodily observances from them and withdrew them from the works of the Law in which they had always lived, they would abandon faith in the Lord Jesus rather than abandon the Law. He considered that, if they were converted to faith in the Saviour and, after faith and the merit of truth, the uselessness of signs and shadows were made manifest to them, they could more easily be recalled from that error than if, at their first hearing, they were told to cease entirely from works of the Law. What Peter then foresaw could be done, Paul now undertakes to do.

For he feared lest their faith, which was exceedingly imperfect, and their conversion itself should become empty and superfluous. Therefore he writes to them, through many arguments, concerning Christ’s pre-eminence and the uselessness of the Law, and finally instructs them concerning conduct. As has been said, he labours to persuade them that faith in the Saviour without bodily observances is sufficient for eternal life, and that they should no longer persist in bodily observances but place the confidence of their justification and salvation in faith in Christ.

The reason why this Epistle lacks the customary superscription, “Paul [Col. 1520B] the Apostle,” is that the Hebrews were prejudiced against Paul’s name, so that they would not receive his words. He therefore prudently avoided it, lest, as soon as the name of Paul was seen at the beginning, the reading should be rejected. Moreover, Paul is said by the almighty Lord to have been sent especially to the Gentiles, not to the Hebrews. Thus, out of humility, Paul, appointed to the Gentiles, does not call himself an Apostle to the Hebrews—either out of honour for the Lord, who said that he had been sent to the sheep of the house of Israel (Matt. XV), or because Paul seemed to be Apostle of the Gentiles and not of the Hebrews. For he had contributed neither faith nor anything else to them.

“Hebrews” is interpreted as “crossers over” or “those passing through.” Whoever have not planted the root of their heart in love of the present world, but pass over to things above in continual longing; whoever do not love earthly pilgrimage as a homeland to dwell in, but seek the true homeland—these are truly Hebrews and should believe this Epistle written to themselves. In it the Apostle first proposes that Christ’s words must be heard, comparing him with the prophets: for God spoke in him as in the prophets, yet he is greater than they. Thus he says:

# CHAPTER ONE

> “God, who at many times and in many ways formerly spoke to the fathers in the prophets, has in these last days spoken to us in the Son.”

“**In many and various ways**,” that is, by many kinds of speech: at one time openly, at another obscurely; at one time literally, at another figuratively; at one time through an angel, at another through hidden inspiration; at one time in Hebrew, at another in Chaldaic; at one time soothingly, at another terrifyingly—God spoke. And “**in many ways**,” that is, by diverse and varied kinds of actions, because not only the sayings of the prophets, but all their deeds as well, foretold those things which were to come in our times [Col. 1521A]. And who could easily know how varied and how numerous are the deeds of the prophets reported in the Scriptures? In all those deeds of the fathers he spoke of future things. For concerning their words—which are many, and uttered in different and manifold kinds of speech—there can be no doubt that he himself spoke them.

Thus God, speaking in many portions, in many ways, and with many modes long ago—that is, in ancient times—to the fathers who begot us carnally and left us their faith concerning Christ; and speaking to them in the prophets, because he himself spoke in their hearts whatever they outwardly spoke to human beings, whether by words or deeds. Nor is it without purpose that he says, “speaking long ago,” and joins the present to the past. For all that he spoke to the fathers in the prophets, he speaks to us in the Scriptures even to this day [Col. 1521B], so that, as they did, we too may attain eternal life by believing these things and fulfilling them in deed.

It can also be understood of words alone that he says, “in many portions and in many ways.” “In many portions,” that is, in many utterances; “in many ways,” that is, in many qualities of speech. God the Father, speaking long ago to the fathers who begot us in flesh and faith, has at the last—that is, at the end of the ages, when no further speech of God follows, since every perfection of holiness and righteousness is contained in this one—in these days, that is, in the time of these people who still live in the flesh, spoken to us in his Son. For whatever Christ outwardly spoke to human beings, the Father was speaking inwardly in him.

God was in the prophets according to the indwelling [Col. 1521C] of grace and the revelation of the will of his wisdom; but in the Son he remained wholly and altogether, illuminating his mind and understanding in every respect, so that nothing was lacking to him for the perfection of his soul, since the wisdom of God was personally united to him. And he who spoke in the prophets—what he spoke through them to our fathers—has at last spoken this to us in his Son. Therefore the words of the Son are not of lesser authority than those of the prophets, but of greater: for they are servants, whereas this one is the Son in whom the Father spoke; and this speech is final, because after it no other will come.

For the speech made to Moses was not final, because it was established only until the time of correction. Therefore, as long as this final speech—that is, the New Testament—endures, our faith will certainly endure [Col. 1521D], because it cannot be changed into another thing more effective for our obtaining heavenly life (below, ch. IX). And, so that what the Son spoke may be observed more diligently, the Apostle turns to commendation of him according to both natures, saying:

> “Whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the ages. Who, being the brightness of his glory and the figure of his substance, and upholding all things by the word of his power, having made purification of sins, sits at the right hand of Majesty on high.”

He shows how great is the Son, in whom the Father [Col. 1522A] spoke to humankind, so that, once the dignity of his greatness is known, faith in him may be recognized as sufficient for eternal salvation. The Father, according to his humanity, appointed him the now unchangeable heir of all things—that is, possessor of all creatures and Lord of the whole world—so that Jacob alone might no longer be the portion of his inheritance, but what is written might be fulfilled: “I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession” (Ps. II). From this it is clear that all ought to believe in him.

And through him, insofar as he is the Word of the Father, the Father made not only eternal things, which are less known even to us, but also the ages—that is, all changeable things which we see vary through time. For an age (*saeculum*) is so called from following, because it is always [Col. 1522B] in motion: something always goes before and something else follows. Since the ages were made through the Son, it is manifest that he is the Creator of humankind and of all other things made in heaven.

This Son, after the toil of his warfare and obedience, sits—that is, rests, suffering no further labor—at the right hand of the Father’s majesty. And rightly, according to his humanity, he was exalted to the Father’s right hand, since according to divinity he is coeternal and coequal with the same Father. For he is “the brightness of his glory and the figure of his substance.” The brightness of glory is as light from light; for the Father is glory, as the same Son sings to him in the Psalm: “My glory, and the one who lifts up my head” (Ps. III). The Son is the brightness of this glory—that is, of the Father—because he is from the Father, as brightness is from the sun; and he is coeternal with the Father, as brightness is coeval with the sun.

For, just as nature does not allow there ever to be a sun without brightness or fire without heat, so the Father could never be without his wisdom. And just as the sun is not from brightness, nor fire from heat, so the Father is not from the Son, but the Son from the Father. And just as brightness displays that of which it is brightness, so the Son manifests the Father, whose wisdom he himself is. And just as brightness is substantially in the sun and the sun in brightness, so the Son is substantially in the Father and the Father in the Son.

And because he might be coeternal and yet not of the same substance, he adds: “and the figure of his substance,” by which he is shown to be consubstantial with the Father. For he is the figure of his substance—that is, his express likeness [Col. 1522D]—not according to outward features but according to substance. He is the figure of his substance, that is, the form and image of his substance: for as great as the Father is, so great is he; such as the Father is, such is he; of whatever substance the Father is, of that same substance is he; what the Father is, that he also is.

For the Son, who is the wisdom of the Father, expresses the figure of his substance by revealing and making him known, when that same wisdom first describes itself and thus manifests the Father.  
[Note: [Col. 1521D] An obscure passage.]

For when the eternity of the Father is perceived by us, insofar as the capacity of our weakness permits, his image is presented to the eyes of our mind. For when we truly strive toward the Father, we see him, insofar as we receive him, through his image—that is, through the Son [Col. 1523A]. And through that form which was born from him without beginning, we endeavor in some way to behold him who neither began nor ends. This is the express figure of God’s substance. Hence the same Son says: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John XIV); and, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (ibid.).

He also “upholds all things”: that is, he holds them aloft, lest they fall and return to nothing, from which they had been created by him. He sustains them not by labor or difficulty, but “by the word of his power”—that is, by the command of his might, namely by his will alone, which in him is power and omnipotence. From this it is clear that he is equal in power to the Father. And he is “making purification of sins,” because by his blood he cleanses us from sins.

The Apostle recalls [Col. 1523B] his cross, and immediately his resurrection and ascension. For after he shed his blood on the cross in order to make purification for our sins, he was raised from the tomb and lifted into heaven. There he now sits—that is, rests, reigns, and judges—exalted at the right hand, that is, in equality and honor, of Majesty, that is, of the Father, who is Majesty, meaning the greater power, because he is greater than all powers. At his right hand the Son is in the same seat as his equal, lest, if he sat on another side, he might seem lesser. And he sits “on high,” that is, above every creature, among the most exalted angelic spirits, who are called “throne,” that is, the seat of God.

> “Having become so much better than the angels, as he has inherited a more distinct name than they. For to which of the angels did he ever say: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’? (Acts XIII; Ps. II.) And again: ‘I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son’? (II Kings VII; II Chronicles XXII).”

Here he compares him with the angels and sets him above them, as far as the passage where he says, “Therefore we ought more abundantly.” He sits on high, having become so much better—that is, more worthy—than the angels according to his humanity, according to which he had been made a little lower than the angels; insofar as he inherited—that is, possessed by hereditary right—a more differing name, namely “Son.”

While he was mortal, he had a differing name, because angels ministered to him; nevertheless, an angel is recorded as strengthening him in his passion. But after [Col. 1523D] he became immortal, he had a more differing name, because angels may still minister to him, but can no longer strengthen him (Matt. IV; Luke XXII). Before his passion, although he was sometimes called Son of God, he was almost always called Son of Man; after the resurrection, however, he is called Son of God.

And in that he has a more excellent name, he is before them, not after them. For although angels are sometimes called sons of God, this name signifies that they were created by God, not that they have the same substance as God; rather, that they were made by God’s will alone. But in Christ it signifies that he is naturally begotten from the Father, is of the same substance as the Father, and that his humanity is personally united to the same only-begotten Son of God. Therefore [Col. 1524A] even his humanity deserved the designation “Son of God.” Thus this name, “Son,” is in Christ more excellent and far more unlike what it is in angels, and he is far above them.

Or Christ has the name before them because he was made more honorable than they when he rose and ascended. And truly he has the name above them. For to which angel did God say what he said to Christ? Nor did he ever say this even to the greatest angel—that is, neither at creation nor after they were confirmed in heavenly things. Likewise, no angel is so exalted that God is ever read to have said to him what he said to Christ: “You are my Son, consubstantial with me, because today”—that is, in the day of eternity, which lacks beginning and end and has an ever-present present without past or future—“I have begotten you from my substance.”

He said, “I have begotten you,” and not “I beget you,” lest the Son appear imperfect and lest God’s same only-begotten Son be thought newly made, contrary to the prophet. For if he had said, “Today I beget you,” this begetting might be thought to have begun today. But in saying “I have begotten,” he shows that it is today, but that it did not begin today. Thus it is declared that it had no beginning.

Nevertheless, if we consider Paul’s words in the Acts of the Apostles, we shall see that he referred this statement to the Lord’s resurrection. For he said of the Father: “Raising Jesus Christ, as it is written in the second Psalm: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’” (Acts XIII). According, then, to this testimony of the Apostle, the Father said to him on the day of resurrection [Col. 1524C]: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you,” so that the resurrection which the Father effected may be understood as a kind of generation.

For our resurrection too is called regeneration, when it is said: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty” (Matt. XIX). And again it is said of the elect that in the age to come they are sons of God, since they are sons of the resurrection (Luke XX). Therefore Christ, according to his humanity—while mortal, he was Son of Man—by putting on immortality in the resurrection became Son of God, yet without ceasing to be Son of Man, because he remained a true human being. But he received the glory which he did not have according to his humanity. Thus that man whom the only-begotten Son of God had assumed into his own person heard at the resurrection [Col. 1524D]: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” This was never said to any angel, because no angel, by any promotion ever granted to him, was worthy to hear it.

And again, to which angel was what God said of the Son of Man personally united to the Word of God ever said: “I, who am always the Father of my Word, will be to him a Father”—that is, I will be Father to that man whom my Word will assume—“and he, that man, will be to me a Son” (II Kings VII), that is, he will be my son? This was said of no angel, nor was it said to any angel. But this man, because of the unity of person of Word and flesh, became Son of the same Father whose Son the Word also is. Thus the Virgin is called Mother of God because she bore not only a human being but also God [Col. 1525A] (Ps. XCVI). For flesh communicates with the higher things, just as divinity communicates with the lower.

> “And when he again brings the Firstborn into the world, he says: ‘Let all the angels of God worship him.’ And indeed to the angels he says: ‘He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire’ (Ps. CIII). But to the Son: ‘Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the sceptre of righteousness is the sceptre of your kingdom’ (Ps. XLIV). ‘You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.’ And: ‘You, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They shall perish, but you shall remain; and all shall grow old as a garment; [Col. 1525B] and as a cloak you shall change them, and they shall be changed; but you are the same, and your years shall not fail’ (Ps. CI).”

Having shown by authorities that Christ inherited a more excellent name than the angels, he shows by other authorities that he is better and more eminent than the angels. As if he said: Before the Son of God became human, God promised that he would be Father to that same man. And again, when he brings into the world—that is, into this world—the Firstborn among many brothers, he says of him that he is to be worshipped by all the holy angels.

He brings him in again as visible through assumed flesh, though formerly he was invisible in the world. This assumption is called an going forth from the Father and an introduction into the inheritance. Or “he brings in” means that he leads him inwardly [Col. 1525C] even into human hearts, so that he may be known by those for whose salvation he put on flesh, and into the world—that is, for the restoration of the human race existing throughout all lands.

This Son, according to divinity, in which he has no brothers, is called only-begotten; but according to humanity, in which he deigned to have brothers, he is called Firstborn. The angels are exhorted to worship him in this humanity, because in his divinity they did not need exhortation to worship him. Since the man united to God is worshipped by angels, it is evident that he is far better than angels.

This testimony is read in the Song of Deuteronomy according to the Septuagint translators as follows: “Rejoice, heavens, together with him, and let all the angels of God worship him” (Deut. XXXII). Here it should be noted that the translation of the Septuagint was authoritative for the Hebrews to whom the Apostle wrote, since they knew both Greek and Hebrew. Since, therefore, the heavens rejoice with the man whom the Son of God assumed, and all God’s angels worship him, it is manifest from this how far he is set above the angels; and it is also manifest from what follows, because he says concerning the angels: “He makes his angels,” and so forth.

For what was said above refers to the Son, showing him to be better than angels; while what follows refers to angels, showing them to be inferior to him whom they serve and minister to. This, then, is what Scripture says concerning angels: namely, that the Son makes his angels—that is, the messengers and envoys of his will to humankind—his heavenly spirits [Col. 1526A]. For “angel” is the name of an office, not of a nature; “spirit” is the name of their nature. Those holy spirits of the heavenly homeland are always spirits, but they are not always angels. They are angels only when they announce something.

Those whom Christ always has as spirits, therefore, he makes angels when he wills, by sending them to announce what he commands. And he makes his ministers “a flame of fire”—that is, seraphim, which is interpreted “the burning ones,” because they are wholly inflamed with the fire of divine love, and are before all others—so that they may minister and serve him. That is, he makes the foremost heavenly spirits minister to himself. This was indeed said concerning angels, to show their subjection; but what follows is said concerning the Son, to declare his excellence:

“Your throne, O God the Son” (Ps. XLIV)—that is, your royal seat—remains for ever and ever, that is, eternally. For God could not have a temporal throne. He calls him God, so that his divinity may be made known to all who saw that he was human. By “throne,” that is, royal seat, his kingdom is designated. This throne endures for ever and ever because his kingdom shall have no end (Luke I); and elsewhere it is said: “The Lord shall sit as king for ever” (Ps. XXIII).

Likewise, by the rod—that is, the sceptre—the insignia of one reigning is expressed. This rod is of righteousness, as it is also said through the prophet concerning him: “Behold, a king shall reign in righteousness” [the printed text reads: “injustice”] (Isa. XXXII). Or the throne may be understood as the judicial seat, and through it the judgment itself. That throne endures for ever and ever because Christ’s final judgment will stand forever. Hence he says: “These shall go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. XXV).

By the rod of righteousness may be understood the uprightness of his judicial sentence, because he will strike the reprobate. This rod is strength in vengeance and most upright equity. Or certainly, “the rod of your kingdom”—that is, the discipline and rule by which you govern the good and chastise the evil—is a rod of righteousness, that is, a straight and inflexible rule. Nor is this surprising, because you “loved righteousness,” that is, you possessed every good not under compulsion but by love; and, conversely, you “hated iniquity,” that is, every evil. For, as John says in his Epistle: “Everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity, and sin [Col. 1526D] is iniquity” (I John III).

You did not possess both at once—that is, good and evil—but held one in love and rejected the other in hatred. And therefore—that you might love good and hate evil—God, your God, O God the Son, anointed you himself, not through ministers. For in the phrase, “God, your God, has anointed you,” as is evident in Hebrew and Greek, the first name “God” must be understood in the vocative case and the following one in the nominative: “God, your God has anointed you.”

He anointed you according to your humanity, because divinity had no need of anointing. For God who was anointed had become human; and therefore God was anointed because he was human. He was anointed with oil, that is, with the gift of the Holy Spirit. But he was anointed above his companions, because all of us first exist in sin and afterward are sanctified through the anointing [Col. 1527A] of the Holy Spirit. But he, existing as God before the ages, was conceived as human through the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin; and at the end of the ages he was there anointed by the same Spirit where he was conceived.

He was not conceived first and anointed afterward; rather, his very conception from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin’s flesh was his anointing by the Holy Spirit. The name of Christ could not be expressed more plainly than by calling him “anointed God.” For *Christos* is Greek, while *unctus*, “anointed,” is Latin; and “anointed” signifies either king or priest. God was anointed with oil, but spiritual oil. Visible oil is a sign; invisible oil is in the sacrament.

He was anointed “with the oil of gladness,” that is, with the grace of the Holy Spirit, which made his conscience glad, causing there never to be any sin whatever in it, but every holiness without exception. Therefore he was anointed above his companions, because no one is without sin except this one alone, and no one can possess so much holiness. For no one can have any good unless he has received it from this one. Since all saints receive from him whatever they possess, they are called his companions, as we read later in this epistle: “For we have become companions of Christ” (below, ch. III).

Therefore he himself is called Christ, while they are called Christians; in this designation it is declared that he alone was anointed with greater grace above all. For God did not give the Spirit to him by measure (John III), but bestowed the whole Holy Spirit upon him; to us, however, he gave according to measure.

These things were said concerning the Son, in which the excellence of his humanity [Col. 1527C] is shown. And again the Prophet (Ps. CI), indicating the eternity of his divinity, says to him: “O Lord the Son, you founded the earth at the beginning of the world,” that is, by your will and ordering you caused it to rest immovably [variant: “to subsist”]. You founded it in the beginning because you already existed before every beginning, and in the beginning gave being to creatures. “And the heavens are the works of your hands,” because by your hands—that is, by the power of your command—you made the heavens.

Those heavens, though so enduring, shall perish on the day of judgment. Yet this is not to be understood of the higher heavens, but of the lowest, which are near the earth and in which birds fly. They will perish according to the extent and dimensions of this air, when the fire of judgment occupies as much of the air’s expanse [Col. 1527D] as the floodwaters occupied. They shall perish from the form they now have, in order to be changed into a better form.

“But you shall remain,” because, just as before all things you remained unchangeable in your eternity, so after they have perished you shall always remain—that is, eternally. And all those airy heavens shall grow old like a garment: that is, through long duration they shall gradually become worse. We see this being fulfilled daily in the present alteration of the air and the barrenness of the earth. For this is likewise to be understood of the earth.

“And as a cloak you shall change them.” The heavens are compared to a cloak because they cover and surround the earth. “As a cloak you shall change them,” that is, as easily as a cloak is spread out and folded. Thus the heavens and earth shall perish so as to be changed, not so as to cease to exist altogether. For they shall be cleansed by fire from the form they now possess [Col. 1528A], yet will always remain in their own nature.

Creatures indeed shall be changed, but you remain unchangeable, as you said elsewhere: “I am the Lord and I do not change” (Mal. III); and, “I am who I am” (Exod. III). You are always the same, equally unchangeable, and your years shall not fail—that is, your eternity. Our years fail daily and do not stand at all; but your years do not fail because they always stand. And because they stand, those years that stand are one year; and that year which stands is one day, because that one day has neither rising nor setting, but always stands and shines. These are the years that do not fail but endure.

By these words, therefore, it is plainly shown that the Son of God remains eternally unchangeable in his divinity, without beginning and end; that he is Creator of all things; and thus that faith in him is fully sufficient for eternal salvation. In the Psalm these prophetic words may be interpreted mystically, but here they are better understood according to the letter, because in this sense the eternity and power of the Son—which the Apostle now seeks to show—are declared more clearly.

For in this epistle, “You, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth,” and so forth, is said of the person of the Son, not of the Father, although in the Psalm these words may fittingly be said of the Father, or rather of the whole Trinity. But the Apostle now intends to demonstrate, through prophetic testimonies, the excellence of the Son alone, who seemed lesser to the Jews because of his assumption of flesh. He therefore adds:

> [Col. 1528C] “But to which of the angels did he ever say: ‘Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet’? (Ps. CIX.) Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for ministry on behalf of those who shall inherit salvation?”

Again he speaks of the glory of Christ’s humanity, showing him to be far more worthy than angels. As if he said: Not only is he shown to be greater than angels by the foregoing statements, but also by this: to which angel, however great his excellence, did the Father ever—in any state of theirs, whether before the fall of the proud or after the confirmation of the humble—say what he is read to have said to Christ: “Sit at my right hand”?

For it is written of the most excellent angels that seraphim stood around him (Isa. VI; Rev. VII). Seraphim stand as ministers; the Son sits as Lord. Seraphim stand around him; the Son is at his right hand. For on the day of his ascension, the Father offered the victorious Christ a share in his own seat, saying: “Sit at my right hand,” that is, rest and reign in my higher places, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet, that is, completely subject them to you.

By the feet, eternal stability is signified: there, as though his footprints were set down, he stands by the power of omnipotence. Or certainly, the feet signify his humanity; and his enemies are daily subjected to these feet, either by voluntary conversion or by just condemnation (I Cor. V). But when all have been subjected—that is, at the end of the age—then it will be evident to all [Col. 1529A] that he will sit perpetually at the right hand of the Father.  
[Note: [Col. 1529D] An obscure passage.]

Therefore it was necessary now to say that he himself will sit there after the day of judgment, but only “until” that day because of those who do not yet believe that he sits there. This was said to no angel: “Sit at my right hand.” For it is not for a minister to sit at the right hand of the one whose minister he is; rather, it is for the Son to sit at the right hand of the Father.

For all angels are his ministers; and this is said interrogatively, as though in rebuke: “Are not all angels, both great and small, ministering spirits”—that is, fitted for ministry, so that each may minister to God in his own office? They are ministering, that is, they have an office of ministry. And since one could have an office of ministry without actually ministering—just as the king’s steward is called his minister even when he is not ministering—the text adds: “sent for ministry,” supply, “to be actually performed.” That is, they both have the office of ministry and do minister: in ministering they serve.

They do this not for themselves but for human beings. Though these people are lesser, angels serve them at Christ’s command, in order to help them in good works and defend them from evil spirits: those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation, that is, shall attain the inheritance of the heavenly homeland, where they shall have the perpetual salvation of soul and body. Angels are therefore sent here for our sake, either by the Lord or by greater angels.

For from the lower companies of angels, angels or archangels [Col. 1529C] come forth for external ministry, that is, for human aid. The higher companies never depart from the inner places, because those which are preeminent do not perform external ministry. Hence Daniel says: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. VII). For it is one thing to minister and another to stand before. Those minister to God who go forth to us in announcing; those stand before him who enjoy inward contemplation and are not sent forth to perform outward works.

This must therefore be understood of the lower orders, which are sent for ministry on behalf of people who will receive the inheritance of salvation. For nowhere do we read that dominions or thrones are sent for ministry. Yet they may be called ministering spirits, because they minister to God inwardly as well, while they impart to lower beings the divine knowledge they have received from him and lead them to higher contemplation.

But those who go outward also always stand before him, because even when they come to us, they so perform their outward ministry that they never fail inwardly through contemplation. Hence the Savior says concerning little ones—that is, the humble—“that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father” (Matt. XVIII). They are therefore both sent and stand before him, because although the angelic spirit is circumscribed, the highest Spirit, God himself, is not circumscribed. Angels are thus before him even when sent, because wherever they come when sent, they move within him.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 1530A]

> “Therefore we ought more abundantly to observe the things that we have heard, lest perhaps we drift away. For if the word spoken through angels proved firm, and every transgression and disobedience received a just recompense of reward, how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation? Which, having begun to be spoken by the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard him, while God also testified by signs and wonders and various powers and distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his will.”

Up to this point he has shown by many authorities that the Son is better than the angels; and now, accordingly, he maintains that his words are to be observed more carefully than those of the angels. [Col. 1530B] God had spoken in the prophets; he had also spoken through angels; but in these last days he has spoken to us in the Son. Therefore, since he is so much more worthy than they, we must observe and fulfil in deed more abundantly the things we have heard from him than those which we heard from the prophets or from the angels who were ministers of the Law. “More abundantly,” that is, we ought to keep more liberally and diligently the words which God spoke in Christ than those which he spoke through angels: the commandments of the Gospel rather than those of the Law. For it is certain that the angels spoke the things which God is reported to have said to Moses (Acts 7).

But someone says: Why then is it written, “The Lord said to Moses,” rather than, “An angel said to Moses”? Because, when the herald proclaims the words of a judge, [Col. 1530C] the records do not say, “That herald said,” but, “That judge said.” Thus the angels spoke the words of the Law. Yet we ought more carefully to observe the words of the Gospel which Christ spoke, lest perhaps we “flow away,” that is, be punished. For we flow away, because, like a river, we are in flux and change: from infancy to childhood, from childhood to youth, from youth to old age, and thence to decrepitude. We flow out when, in death, we are dissolved in soul and body. We flow out—that is, flow outside—when we breathe out the soul. We utterly flow away if, separated perpetually from the true being of God, we perish through diverse torments without end. And lest this happen to us, let us observe Christ’s words at least through fear of punishment, if the love of righteousness does not yet reign in us.

Or, [Col. 1530D] we flow through the sufferings of mortal nature; we flow out by adding sin; we utterly flow away in eternal condemnation. Or thus: to flow is to die; to flow out is to suffer punishments, whether in this age or in the age to come; to utterly flow away is to suffer harsher torments perpetually—and these things must be avoided by us. But, morally understood, to utterly flow away is to flow wholly away from the inward intention of desiring inward and eternal things, by thinking of and desiring only outward and temporal things. This happens to those whose minds are wholly abandoned by God’s grace, and who, because they neglect to keep it, are deservedly deserted by the Holy Spirit on account of their perversity, so that they may follow their own desires and perish.

Therefore he immediately adds, terribly, concerning the punishment of their future condemnation, [Col. 1531A] by comparison with the punishments formerly inflicted upon transgressors of the Law: “For if the word spoken through angels,” etc. For if those who despised the words of angels were punished, how much more severely will those be punished who despise Christ’s words? This is proved from the lesser case.

Or, according to the earlier sense, the connection is as follows: We shall indeed utterly flow away amid torments unless we keep what was spoken to us by the Son. For how shall we escape the punishments of eternal vengeance if we neglect so great a salvation of the new grace, when even those did not escape who neglected the old Law? This is what is meant: if the word of God spoken to Moses through angels—that is, through the ministry of angels—was made firm, that is, ratified and stable both in threats and promises, because whatever the Law threatened and whatever it promised was fulfilled; and if every transgression and disobedience, etc. Transgression is doing what is forbidden, whereas disobedience is failing to do what is commanded. And not only did every transgressor, who was guilty of many things, but every transgression—that is, every fault of violation, so that vengeance might be exacted for individual offenses—and every fault of disobedience, which despised the performance of the Law’s commands, receive a recompense for its deeds: a recompense, I say, of desert, that is, of merit, just, that is, proportionate—not a great punishment for a slight fault, nor a slight one for a great fault, but justly measured, [Col. 1531B] as an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth (Exod. 21; Lev. 34; Deut. 16).

“Transgression and disobedience” is better phrased than “transgressor and disobedient person,” because by this, as we have said, it is shown that punishment was inflicted for each individual transgression and act of disobedience. For a transgressor is described not in relation to one matter only, but many; and if “transgressor” had been used here, one might understand that a person was punished not for one offense but for many. If, I say, the word of angels was made so firm that our forefathers were compelled by such necessity to fulfil it in deeds, since anyone acting otherwise could not escape, how shall we escape the due vengeance if we now neglect so great a salvation—that is, the eternal blessedness offered to us in keeping the commandments of the New Testament? We shall in no way escape punishments if we treat this inestimable salvation lightly.

For the salvation in the Old Testament [Col. 1531C] was not as great as this which the Son has brought us. That was temporal; this is perpetual. That promised earthly riches; this promises heavenly ones. That promised victory over fleshly enemies; this grants victory over spiritual enemies. That gave a happy temporal life; this bestows an eternally blessed one. Therefore it must at least not be neglected, which is less than transgressing it. For a more severe vengeance will be taken on those who neglect this salvation than was taken upon those who transgressed the word of angels. There there was a word; here, salvation: there only the letter commanding, but here the Spirit assisting.

But because the Jews might reply: “It does not follow that, if those who transgressed the Law given through angels were punished, we too shall be punished if we neglect the things [Col. 1532A] spoken by the Son of God; for they saw and heard angels, whereas we neither saw nor heard the Son,” he adds: “Which salvation was confirmed to us by those who heard.” It is as if he said: You will not escape punishment because perhaps you did not hear him present in the flesh, since you heard those who heard him. This salvation and everlasting life of the elect, having received through the Lord Jesus a beginning not of establishment—for it is eternal—but of proclamation, because the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, himself declared it, was confirmed by those—that is, by the apostles—who heard from his mouth. It was proclaimed with effective assurance, passing into us, that is, reaching the seat and understanding of our soul.

It was confirmed to us by those who heard, not merely at the end [Col. 1532B] of the Lord’s preaching, but from the beginning, when that salvation began to be declared—that is, clearly and openly declared by the Lord, rather than wrapped in figures, as it had formerly been through the prophets. It was confirmed, I say, with God bearing witness—that is, God testifying with them to whatever they said. And how did God bear witness, that is, give testimony and certainty to their preaching? By signs—that is, lesser miracles, such as the raising of the lame man—and by wonders, that is, greater and astonishing marvels, such as the healing of all infirmities by Peter’s shadow (Acts 3, 14). Or the signs were signs because they signified something else (Acts 5): for example, the raising of that same lame man signified the raising of the limping Jewish people; and the wonders were portents because they foreshadowed something else: for example, the healing of infirmities beneath Peter’s shadow [Col. 1532C] foreshadowed the healing of all the soul’s spiritual sicknesses in the present Church, which is figured by Peter’s shadow, just as the heavenly Jerusalem is figured by his body.

By such signs and wonders God testified that what the apostles taught was true; and by various powers, namely other miracles which were not so mystical. Or by the various virtues of the soul—that is, charity, humility, chastity, and other such virtues—which God caused to shine forth in their conduct, so that their life might accord with their preaching: thus, while teaching humility, they were humble; while preaching generosity, they were generous. By these virtues, indeed, God testified that their teaching was true; and also by distributions of the Holy Spirit—that is, gifts of the Holy Spirit given in different ways, [Col. 1532D] so that one possessed kinds of tongues, another interpretation of speeches, another prophecy, and others other gifts. These distributions, I say, were made not according to merit but according to his own will, that is, according to the good pleasure of his mercy. According to the will of the same Spirit, because he distributes to each as he wills (1 Cor. 12). Or according to the will of God the Father, because the will of the undivided Trinity is one.

> “For God did not subject to angels the world to come, of which we speak. But someone has testified somewhere, saying: ‘What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the Son of Man, that you visit him? You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honour, and appointed him [Col. 1533A] over the works of your hands. You subjected all things beneath his feet’ (Ps. 18; 1 Cor. 15). For in subjecting all things to him, he left nothing not subject to him. But now we do not yet see all things subject to him. But we see Jesus, who was made somewhat lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death, so that by God’s grace he might taste death for everyone.”

He said above that we ought to observe more abundantly the things heard from Christ than those (Phil. 3) which we heard from angels—that is, carnal ceremonies—and now explains why more abundantly: because power to judge us in the future age and to reign over all things was given, not to angels, but to Christ. For God the Father did not subject to angels, but to Christ, [Col. 1533B] the world to come—that is, the world which will exist after the day of judgment, when there will be a new heaven and a new earth. We now speak of that world yet to come, not of the one we presently see. For this present world still partly refuses to be subjected to Christ; but that one will be wholly subjected to him.

The world was not then subjected to angels but rather to Christ, because the prophet so affirmed in the psalm. I withhold his name from you, not out of any desire to conceal it, but because you know the psalms by heart and know that they were composed by King David. One of the prophets testified to this, who, because of his acknowledged excellence, is understood without a personal name and recognized from authority alone. He testified in a certain place of Scripture—that is, a distinguished and notable place—so that by the witness and by the place it may be clear without ambiguity that what he said is true. He testified, saying, “What is man,” etc.

Every son of man is a human being, but not every human being is a son of man. Adam, indeed, was a human being, but not a son of man. Thus “man” in this passage is earthly, whereas the Son of Man is heavenly; the former is far removed from God, whereas the latter is present to God. Therefore he is mindful of the former as one far off, but visits the latter whom he illuminates by his countenance. Of him, on account of the weakness of the flesh and the humility of the Passion, it is rightly said: “You made him a little lower than the angels”; and on account of the glorification by which he was raised and exalted into heaven: “You crowned him with glory and honour,” etc.

Accordingly, the words “What is man?” must be read contemptuously: “O Lord God [Col. 1533D] the Father, what is man”—as though fragile, despised, and sinful—“that you are mindful of him,” when you forgive sins? Or: “What is”—that is, how great in dignity and excellence—“the Son of Man,” namely Christ, who was born not from two parents but from the Virgin alone, “that you visit him,” raising him from the tomb? In the former case you are mindful, showing mercy from heaven to the patriarchs; in the latter you visit, because the Word was made flesh.
