Or the whole verse may be read of Christ and spoken admiratively: “What”—that is, how great and wonderful—is the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, “that you are mindful of him”? That is, although he lives upon earth, you nevertheless never forget him so that he sins; rather, you are always mindful of him, causing him always to remain free from every sin and full of all holiness. Or, “What is”—that is, how glorious is—the Son of Man, namely the same Christ, a man born from a human mother, [Col. 1534A] “because you visit him,” raising this seemingly weak one. For all others are sons of men because they derive their origin from the union of two persons; but Christ is the Son, as we have said, of a human being alone, because he was born from the Virgin without a fleshly father. Therefore he is something great and incomparable before God. “Because you visit him,” he says, as a physician in his weakness, and by the resurrection drive from him every infirmity of mortality, passibility, and corruption.

And he needed visitation because “you made him lower.” For he was and always is consubstantial and coeternal with you; but you made him lower when, emptying himself, he took the form of a servant (Phil. 2). Lower than angels because he was made mortal; a little lower because he was without sin. For he was lower than angels because of the humility of fleshly birth and Passion, not because of the nature of humanity. For the nature of the human mind, made in God’s image, if it lacks sin, is equal to angels. Christ, therefore, was lower than angels in body, not in mind, and in a body that was mortal and capable of suffering.

When it says, “a little lower than the angels,” the word “than” [Col. 1534B] indicates that he should not be understood as lower in such a way that angels possess in any respect the nature in which he is said to be lower; rather, it signifies that it is wholly removed from them. These words do not prove that all things are subject to him; rather, they indicate certain stages and merits by which he arrived at having all things subjected to him, so that, through what has already been fulfilled, we may believe that what has not yet been fulfilled will also be fulfilled.

“You made him lower,” I say—that is, you made the greater one lesser: you united the human being to the Word in unity of person. And after the obedience of his Passion had been completed, you crowned him—that is, surrounded him in the manner of a crown, which encircles the whole head—with glory in respect of the soul, so that all its inward powers were glorified; and with honour in respect of the body, so that it was immortal and most radiant.

For there are three powers in the soul: reason, sensation, and vegetation. In respect of reason, he received nothing in the resurrection, because he received neither greater wisdom nor more intense love of God and neighbour. But he received in respect of vegetative power and sensation, because [Col. 1534C] by the resurrection the soul animated its body in such a manner that it could be subject to no corruption; and likewise endowed it with sensation, making all bodily senses so vigorous that it could in no way be restrained or suffer anything distressing. That body was then made so beautiful that it could not be made more beautiful, both in the comeliness of its colour and in the fitness of the body itself.

Or, in the resurrection and ascension he was crowned with glory, after the likeness of a conqueror, and with honour in his sitting with the Father; or with glory, that is, the radiance of immortality, and with honour because every knee is bent to him. “And you also appointed him,” that is, you set him firmly, so that he may reign there forever over the works of your hands—that is, over angels and human beings. You are said to have made both with hands because they are more worthy than the other creatures.

[Col. 1534D] Nor did you appoint him only over angels and human beings, but also over all things, since you subjected to him all things in heaven, on earth, in hell, and in the whole creation, so that they are beneath his feet—that is, so that they can in no way be compared with him, but lie beneath him so as to worship him. Therefore, because the Father subjected all things to him and not to angels, we ought more abundantly to keep what we heard from him than what we heard from angels in the Law. By “all things” he shows that the things stated are sufficient for salvation without fleshly observances. And if we do not keep his commandments from love, let us at least keep them from fear of judgment, since all things are subject to him, or will shortly be subject to him. For the prophet used the past tense for the future.

The Father subjected all things to him. When he says “all,” he excludes neither earthly nor heavenly things. For in subjecting all things to him, he left nothing in the whole creation not subject to him. The prophet uttered this universal statement with the intention of making no exception, but of showing either the willing or the necessary subjection of all things.

The prophet said that the Father subjected all things to him. But now—that is, at this time—we do not yet see all things subject to him, because this whole prophecy has not yet been fulfilled, although its greater part has already been fulfilled. For here we see only the willing subjection of those who believe in him; but in the future we shall see the unwilling overthrow of the proud. [Col. 1535C] Some are subjected every day, but not all until the judgment. That all things are to be subjected to him is clear because the remaining words of the prophecy have already been fulfilled. For we do not yet see all things subjected to him; yet already we see—that is, understand as clearly as though we saw with bodily eyes—him who is great and conspicuous in the nature of divinity, who was made somewhat lower than the angels: that is, who was made a little lower than angels because of the suffering of death, being able to suffer and die, which the blessed angels cannot do.

Him, I say, who was made such—namely Jesus, that is, the Saviour who can save without fleshly observances—we see with the eyes of faith crowned with glory and honour in soul and body; and he was crowned because of the suffering of death, that is, because he was obedient to the Father even unto death. Here the Apostle begins to show that Christ’s words are to be heard not merely because of power or vengeance, but rather because of the love by which he loved us, so as to die for us.

I say that he was made lower, and this for the purpose that he might taste death—that is, a brief death rather than a long one, passing through it as though tasting something—for all predestined to life; or for all, because the price of his blood is sufficient for all. And this was done by grace—that is, by God’s free gift—because human beings did not deserve it. Or Christ himself is the grace of God, who tasted death for the salvation of all, since it was not owed to us that the Son of God should die for us. He [Col. 1536A] died for all because, although not all believe, he nevertheless did what belonged to him.

> “For it was fitting for him, for whom are all things and through whom are all things, who had brought many sons to glory, to perfect through suffering the author of their salvation. For he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one; for which reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying: ‘I will proclaim your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I will praise you’ (Ps. 21); and again: ‘I will put my trust in him’ (Ps. 17); and again: ‘Behold, I and the children whom God has given me’ (Isa. 8). Therefore, since the children shared in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same, so that through death he might destroy him who held the power of death, that is, the devil, and might free those who through fear of death were subject to slavery throughout their whole life” (Hos. 13; 1 Cor. 15).

Christ is the grace of God, that is, his gratuitous gift, because he gave him to us freely, no one having merited it. He gave him to us so that he might taste death for us in a brief draught. For it was fitting that God the Father should do this, because in doing it he did nothing contrary to his honour; rather, it became him to assist lesser beings through his greater Son. This is what is meant by “it was fitting for him,” that is, the Father, for whose glorification are all things and because of whose supreme being all things are lower; and through whom are all things, because through him stability and perseverance have been bestowed upon all things. He had already brought many adoptive sons into the glory of heavenly blessedness by predestination, [Col. 1536C] though not yet in actuality. It was fitting for him, I say, to perfect—that is, to make supreme over all things at once, namely to exalt above all through Passion and resurrection—the author of their salvation, that is, his Son, who is the author of the salvation of all the adopted, because no one has salvation except through him. Therefore it was fitting that the Father should hand him over to death for the salvation of all.

Or, according to other manuscripts, let us say that it was fitting for him—that is, Christ—to be perfected through suffering: Christ for whom all things exist to give praise and through whom all things exist as creator, who had already brought many sons—that is, brothers adopted to himself—into glory by predestining them; who made things that are future, as the prophet testifies. I mean him, the author of their salvation, who would not be the author of salvation unless he suffered. Thus the predestination concerning their being brought in would be false; nor would he be glorified in those things made for his glorification, but all things would have been made in vain, since the human being to whom other things are subject would have perished.

Therefore it was fitting that he should be perfected through suffering. It might seem unbecoming that the author of salvation should suffer. But it is not dishonourable, because he depends upon God and is subject to him, like other human beings; and therefore it was fitting for him to suffer. For Christ himself, who sanctifies the predestined by his blood, and those who are sanctified through him, are all from one Father, God, who is one and unique and to whom none is equal. That is, all depend upon him and have from him all their good. But Christ is from him as his proper Son, while the others are from him as adopted sons. And because he is so great and of such power that he can sanctify others, while the others are so weak that they need sanctification, it was more fitting that he rather than another brother should undergo the Passion.

[Col. 1537A] All are from one, for which reason—that is, because both have the same Father—he is not ashamed, that is, he does not blush, to call them brothers. For *confundi* is understood as “to blush,” because when someone blushes, the humours of the face are mingled together. When he says that he is not ashamed to call them brothers, he shows that our brotherhood is not of his nature but, according to his divinity, of his mercy. And he proves by prophetic authority that he calls us brothers, lest this seem new, saying (Ps. 21): “After my resurrection I will proclaim throughout the whole world to my brothers, whom you will adopt for me, your name, which is Father, so that they may know you as Father, who in fatherly affection call them as sons to the inheritance of heavenly blessedness.”

Or, “your name, which is God,” that is, the report and glory of your divinity, so that they may know your omnipotence and know that you are their Creator. And I, existing in the midst of the Church like a pillar, so that all may be summoned from every side to faith upon me and have me as their support, “will praise you,” that is, will cause you to be praised, kindling all around me to praise you. Or, “in the midst of the Church,” so that I may be present among all alike, advise them, and assist them. Or, “in the midst,” that is, in the hearts of believers, I shall praise you.

And again—if this authority does not suffice you—he says elsewhere [Col. 1537C] (that is, in Isaiah) something that confirms the same point, namely that he who sanctifies and those sanctified are from one: “I,” he says, “will be as a man trusting in him” (Ps. 17), namely in the Father. That is, I shall become man, and I shall not trust in my own powers, but shall trust in him: my confidence will not remain in myself but will wholly pass to him, because every good comes to me from him, just as it does to other human beings. In saying that he trusts in him, he plainly declares that he is from him and needs his help. And while showing that he is from and dependent on him, he, who is greater, openly teaches those far inferior to himself that they ought to place their confidence not in human beings but in God.

And again, that is, he says repeatedly in Isaiah [Col. 1537D] (ch. 8) what shows that he and the other faithful are from one: “Behold,” he says, “we are plainly before you, to offer examples of right conduct to other human beings: I, who have deigned to humble myself thus, and my children”—that is, those made pure from crimes through me—“whom I do not have from myself, but whom God the Father gave to me by his free will.” Hence it is clear that both they and I are from him. Therefore he is rightly received and honoured by us who, though he is the author of our salvation, so humbles himself as to call himself our brother both in the prophets and in the Gospel. For he according to his humanity, and all the saints, are from one race and from one God.

Therefore, because the children—that is, those whom he wished to make humble and pure from vices—shared in flesh and blood, that is, all alike possessed flesh and blood, being corruptible human beings composed of body and soul, which is here understood by “blood,” for this reasonable cause he too, so great in divinity, likewise partook of the same—that is, flesh and blood—just as his children who were to be sanctified did, because he likewise assumed a mortal and passible human nature. [Col. 1538A] See how he truly deigned to become our brother.

“Blood” here stands for the soul, because Moses testifies (Lev. 17) that the blood is said to be the seat of the soul: “the soul of the flesh is in the blood.” And because the Lord’s blood is the redemption of the human race, and he offered his flesh for us upon the altar of the cross and shed his blood, it was signified that he redeemed the whole human being—that is, delivered the bodies and souls of his faithful from original sin. He also wished to signify this in the sacrament of his body and blood, which, apart from fleshly observances, was alone wholly sufficient for our redemption.

Therefore it is said, “they shared,” that is, he and his children had a common nature, since he assumed the nature common among human beings in order to redeem all in common whose nature he deigned to share. Yet this redemption benefits unto life only his children predestined to life, who preserve the purity of a clean manner of life. And because he and his children are from one race, or from one God, and the children all alike possessed flesh and blood, [Col. 1538C] therefore he too likewise became a participant in flesh and blood, because he possessed the same fragile nature as they did, except for sin. And he assumed such a nature in order to give it to death for them and, by dying, to kill the devil.

For unless a human being overcame the devil, human beings would be taken from him not justly but violently. Therefore he wished to die, so that through the death of his innocent self he might destroy the prince of death. He sought no other weapons with which to fight the author of death except death itself. And through it he destroyed him—that is, cast down and overthrew, like some building, the height of his pride and the strength of his power—him who held the dominion of death. For since through Adam he had made captive the free will of the human race, he exercised a certain power: that is, he persuaded human beings to things leading to death, namely sins; and no one could resist him, because no one was able entirely to reject sin.

For he is said to have had dominion and power over death for no other reason than that he persuaded people to sin, from which death arose. Therefore he who deigned to die without any sin, whether original or personal, by his innocent death destroyed and deprived of power this prince of wickedness and death—that is, the devil, whose name means “flowing downward,” because he himself always flows down to the depths through wickedness and causes those who consent to him to flow down until they fall into hell. Thus he has dominion of death over them.

But let us, on the contrary, strive upward, whither Christ [Col. 1539A] calls us, who by his death also freed us from the prince of death. Nor did he wish to die only in order to destroy this enemy, but also to free from the yoke of fear and from the slavery of the Law those—namely, the Jews—who were subject to slavery: that is, to remove from them the fear of punishment and to pour into them through the Holy Spirit the love of righteousness, so that they might serve God in freedom. They were subject to the slavery of the Law not for an hour but throughout the whole duration of the present life, slavishly fulfilling its fleshly observances through fear of death of body and soul. For they feared being bodily killed if they violated the Law, and, after death, being tortured in hell, since in the Law they had learned that Abiron and Dathan with their companions fell alive into hell (Num. 16), and in the prophets they had heard more clearly of the eternal punishments of the reprobate.

But Christ, by dying, freed them both from the yoke of the Law and from hell; and now his elect desire death in order to pass into the kingdom. See how great are the goods wrought by death through Christ’s grace. He certainly could also have granted believers that they would not experience even the death of this body. But if he had done this, a certain felicity of the flesh would have been added, while the strength of faith would have been diminished. For human beings fear this death in such a way that they would call Christians happy for no other reason than that they could not die at all. In consequence, no one would hasten to Christ’s grace for the sake of that life which will be blessed after death, through the virtue even of despising death itself; rather, people would believe in Christ too self-indulgently for the sake of removing the distress of death.

[Col. 1539C] Therefore he bestowed more grace upon his faithful. For what great thing would it have been, on seeing that believers did not die, to believe that one would not die? How much greater it is to believe in such a way as to hope that, though one will die, one will live without end! Faith is feeble and weak—indeed, it ought not be called faith at all—if human beings obtain visible rewards by believing; that is, if immortality in this age is granted to the faithful. Thus the Lord himself wished to die, so that, as has been said, through death he might abolish him who had the power of death and rescue the Jews from the slavery of the Law.

> “For he nowhere takes hold of angels, but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham. Hence he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people. For in that in which he himself suffered and was tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted.”

It has been said that he shared in flesh and blood so that he might die, and thus destroy the angel who is prince of death. And it was rightly said in this way, because nowhere—in no place of the sacred Scriptures—did he take hold of the angels who had departed from him. Nowhere in Scripture is it found that he wished to take hold of, that is, to take back to himself and restore, the angelic nature that had perished, since all the Scriptures speak in agreement about the restoration of human beings. For he had made two creatures capable of understanding themselves: namely, the angelic and the human. Pride struck down both and broke them from the state of innate uprightness. But one possessed the covering of flesh; the other bore nothing infirm from flesh. For the angel is spirit alone, whereas the human being is spirit and flesh. Therefore the Creator, in his mercy and in order to redeem, ought to restore to himself that creature which, in committing sin, is known to have had some share of weakness; and he ought all the more to reject the apostate angel, who, when he fell from the strength to persevere, bore nothing infirm from flesh. [Col. 1540A]

There is yet another reason why fallen humanity had to be restored while the proud spirit could not be restored: namely, the angel fell through his own malice, whereas the human being was overthrown by another. Therefore nowhere—that is, in no place, as we have said, of the Scriptures—or nowhere—that is, neither in heaven, nor in the air, nor on earth, nor in the abyss—did he take hold of apostate angels; rather, he entirely abandoned them. [Col. 1540B] But he took hold of Abraham’s seed, because he mercifully pursued and took hold of us as though we had withdrawn from him and fled far away; and he joined to himself, in one person, the nature of our frailty.

By “seed” he means the children of Abraham. The Apostle more suitably used “seed” than he would have done had he said “children,” because “seed” is spoken both of remote and of near ancestors, whereas “children” are more especially called near descendants. He omits the Gentiles because he is speaking to Jews; and his expression “Abraham’s seed” is sufficient for his purpose. Moreover, by this he makes them more indebted to Christ, who was sent not to the Gentiles but to the Jews, as he says: “I was sent only to the sheep that were lost of the house of Israel” (Matt. XV). Or again, Gentiles converted to the faith are Abraham’s seed, because, when they believed in Abraham’s [Col. 1540C] seed—that is, in Christ—they became the children of him to whose seed they are united. Hence it is said to them: “But if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s seed” (Gal. III). Whether, therefore, believers are from Jews or Gentiles, they are Abraham’s seed, which Christ took hold of.

“Wherefore”—that is, for this reason, because he took hold not of angels but of human beings—he had to be made like his brethren, so as to become a human being, which they were. For the very nature that was to be delivered had to be assumed. Therefore our Redeemer became not an angel but a human being, because that which he redeemed unquestionably had to be made so: that, by not taking hold of the lost angel, he might abandon him, while by taking hold of humanity in himself he might restore it. He took hold of Abraham’s seed—that is, flesh from Abraham—in order to save his children. [Col. 1540D]

For this reason he had to be made like his brethren in all things except sin: likewise mortal and capable of suffering, possessing all other things that naturally belong to a human being. He was made like them in all things, because he was born, reared, grew, suffered, and died. If he had appeared otherwise, how would he have led human beings back to salvation not under compulsion but willingly? They would have had no one whom they could follow by imitation unless they saw a human being like themselves in every respect whom they could imitate.

For this especially he had to be made like us: that he might become merciful—that is, that the God who had always been merciful and had held an affection of compassion toward his creature might have a human body, so that our misery and weakness might pierce his heart; [Col. 1541A] as the Gospel relates that he frequently groaned and wept for us, truly sympathizing with us and grieving over our miseries. And because he could sympathize with us through sharing the same mortal nature, yet might not thereby be able to deliver us from miseries, it follows: “and a faithful high priest before God.” For he became a faithful high priest in order faithfully to build for us a bridge over the waves of this world to the land of the living (Mark VII, VIII; Luke XIX; John XI). He deceives no one; rather, he faithfully leads to God all who walk across the bridge which he himself made.

For he made a bridge by giving us the power to tread down and overcome worldly waves, to cross over them to the homeland of life, and to come to our Creator: by restoring free choice to us, granting us the aid of his grace, and giving himself as mediator, “that he might make propitiation for the sins of the people”—that is, remove the negligences and faults through which the people were forsaking God. [Col. 1541B] *Repropitiare* is formed from *re*, *prope*, and *cieo, cies*.

The faults by which we sin—that is, by which we forsake God and draw away from him—are, as it were, drawing near to God when they grow importunately before his eyes and provoke his anger. But our kindly high priest and mediator makes propitiation for them—that is, he drives them back (*retro ciet*) from that in which they had been near; that is, he removes them from the face of God, mercifully interceding for us and blotting them out. He can indeed make propitiation for our sins because he can also preserve us from sin in temptations.

For in that in which he suffered—that is, in the lower substance, namely his humanity, [Col. 1541C] in which he appeared lesser—he is able to assist us in temptations. In that, namely as a human being, in which he suffered under Pilate (John XIX; Matt. XXVII; Mark XV), while in his divinity he always remained incapable of suffering, he who had previously also been tempted three times by the devil is able to help those who are tempted. That is, he is able to assist those who after baptism are tempted either by the devil or by the return of a corrupt habit, lest they fall and return to the very sin from which they were delivered by the grace of God.

For this reason he deigned first to be tempted: that he might overcome our temptations by his own temptations, just as he had come to overcome our death by his death. It should be noted that “tempted,” in its proper sense, may also be said of the Lord himself, [Col. 1541D] because the devil greatly despised him when he judged him unable to make bread from stone and attempted to persuade him to avarice (Luke IV; Matt. IV).

Thus far the Apostle has dwelt on the point that we ought to observe more diligently the things we have heard from Christ and his disciples than those heard from angels, because all things are subject to him, as has been proved by prophetic authority. Now he begins to make a comparison between Christ and Moses, in order to show that Christ’s words are to be observed more than Moses’ words, and thus persuade them more and more that everything Christ preached must be maintained; and that he did or taught nothing which had not [Col. 1542A] been commanded him by the Father. This is what follows.

## Chapter III

> “Therefore, holy brethren, sharers in the heavenly calling, consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession, who is faithful to him who made him, as Moses also was faithful in all his house (Num. XII). For this man has been considered worthy of greater glory than Moses, by as much as the builder of the house has greater honor than the house. For every house is built by someone; but he who created all things is God. And Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, for a testimony to the things that were to be spoken; but Christ as a Son in his own house. [Col. 1542B] We are that house, if we hold fast our confidence and the glory of hope, firm unto the end.”

It was said above that Christ is our high priest before God, that he suffered for us, and that, even according to his humanity, he can assist us in temptations. Therefore—that is, from all these foregoing things, or because of all these things stated above—O brethren, begotten from faith as your mother, and through that same faith holy—that is, cleansed from sins and instructed in good works—and also sharers in the heavenly calling, because you too have been called to heavenly things so that you may possess there with Christ an eternal inheritance: for this reason you owe much submission and obedience to him who called you to heaven by his grace and raised your minds to the excellence of his new promises. [Col. 1542C]

You, I say, O brethren, children of one heavenly Father and of one mother, the Church, for all these reasons “consider”: that is, look attentively with the eyes of your hearts upon the apostle whom God sent to you, namely his only-begotten Son. Paul rightly did not call himself an apostle in writing to those to whom he now calls Jesus an apostle, because Jesus is their apostle by special prerogative, as he says: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. XV). And if fleshly observances could suffice for heavenly dwelling and calling, one so great and so worthy would never have been sent to them. For Ἀπόστολος means “one sent.”

Therefore consider this apostle by loving and imitating him and doing his will; and consider this same one as high priest—that is, as intercessor and the one making a road for us to the land of the living—because he both intercedes for us and provides us the means to cross over the waves of the world and all transient things to the heavenly homeland. I call him the high priest [Col. 1542D] “of our confession”: that is, the one whom all Christians confess and whom we acknowledge as Jesus, that is, Savior. We all confess that we have him as the giver of salvation and need no other, because he alone entirely suffices for salvation.

He is faithful to him who made him—that is, to the Father who created him according to his humanity—because he faithfully fulfilled everything the Father commanded him. He sought not his own glory but the Father’s; he concealed none of the Father’s commands; and he came not to do his own will but the Father’s. Therefore, if he abolished fleshly ceremonies, in this he did not oppose the paternal will but instead faithfully obeyed it. He is faithful to the Father, just as Moses had been faithful in all his house—that is, in the whole people of the Jews.

Moses was faithful in his house—that is, the house of Jesus or of the Father—because he was a minister, not the Lord. Whatever the Lord commanded Moses to punish, he punished; whatever the Lord enjoined on him, he did or taught in its entirety; and he compelled the Jews to perform works conforming to the Lord’s will. So Christ is faithful to the Father, doing all his will in his whole house—that is, in his entire Church, of Jews as well as Gentiles. Thus he is faithful in this house, not only abolishing idolatry among the Gentiles but also annulling fleshly observances [Col. 1543A] among the Jews.

I said that you should consider this apostle, as you ought to do, because he is above Moses—that is, greater than Moses; and consider this. For if Moses could suffice for you unto righteousness and salvation, one so great would never have been sent to you. For this one has been regarded by the Father as worthy of greater glory than Moses—that is, of greater honor and crown than Moses. According to the usage of Latin speech he ought to have said, “worthy of greater glory”; but following Greek usage he says, “worthy of greater glory’s.” Or, this one has been regarded and accounted as of greater glory than Moses because he is worthy by merit to be regarded as of greater glory. He has this not through grace or nature alone, but also through the merit of righteousness. He is above Moses in glory and merit.

For this one is the Son, whereas Moses is a servant; this one sanctifies, whereas Moses is sanctified; this one is free from every sin, altogether complete in every good. Moses, however, was not without sin and could always grow in some good. Christ was judged by the Father worthy to have greater glory and exaltation after this life in proportion to his having in this life greater veneration among believers and those subject to him than Moses had among his own. [Col. 1543B] Moses was accounted God’s servant, God’s good minister, God’s faithful steward, whom those under him were to honor not as God but as a teacher. But those under Christ honor him as God, their Creator, the true God, sufficient to keep his flock—a thing not to be thought of Moses.

And thus this one is of greater glory than Moses, “by as much as the builder of the house has greater honor than the house”—that is, greater honor from or in the house than the one who administers in it. This must be understood of the spiritual house, namely the people of God, of which Moses is recognized as steward but Christ as builder. For he built—that is, founded in faith and built up in good works—the house of God, which is the Church, in the saints of old and the new saints; and therefore he is honored in it far more highly than Moses.

I say that he built God’s house. For every house—that is, every soul which becomes a temple of God—is built by someone else, because it cannot build itself unless it is built by another who is above it. It can possess no good by itself alone. [Col. 1544A] But he who created every good of virtue in the elect is God; and Christ has always been accustomed to do this by the power of his divinity. For he created us not only that we might exist, but also that we might be good, if we are already good. But if we are not yet good, we must ask him, who made us human beings, to make us good.

Therefore he is the builder of this holy house and consequently is to be honored in it differently from Moses. Both indeed, as has been said, were faithful, because each fulfilled well the office assigned to him; yet there was a difference between them. Moses was faithful as a servant, but Christ as Son and Lord in the Father’s house. This is the meaning: “And Moses indeed was faithful”—that is, faithfully fulfilling whatever was divinely commanded him. He was faithful in the house not his own but that “of him,” namely of the Father or Christ; and in all that house—that is, throughout the Jewish people—rebuking and punishing the wicked, exhorting the good, and always advancing them to better things, not as Lord but as a servant. For he did not call himself God, but said that he was serving him who sent him; nor was Moses loved by God as the Lord was, whose own house was that house in which Moses was faithful. [Col. 1544B]

And this was “for a testimony to the things that were to be spoken”: that is, in order to bear witness to and confirm what was fitting to be said to fleshly persons, who were not yet able to grasp spiritual things—not in order to bestow grace. For he faithfully declared to the people what God commanded. By these statements he gave testimony through many arguments, signs of miracles, and various proofs.

I say that Moses was as a servant in the Lord’s house; but Christ was not as a servant, but as a Son who is heir by right, and as Lord in a house not alien but his own, because it belonged to him as properly as to the Father. It is as though he said: Even if both were set over the house of God and each proved faithful in his ministry, there is nevertheless a great difference: Moses was in the Lord’s house as a servant, whereas Christ was in the Father’s house as Son, heir, and Lord. And since Christ is so much greater, he must altogether be received; Moses, however, being lesser, must be set aside in respect of fleshly observances. Moses without Christ will not benefit; Christ alone suffices for all things.

Someone might now say: What does it matter to us whether Moses or Christ is in the house? For we do not know [Col. 1544C] what that house is, nor is Christ commended to us by this; for even if human beings were that house, those who lived in the times of Moses or Christ ought rather to be believed to have been that house, not we who live now. The Apostle seems to answer: “We are that house.” It is as though he said: Do not despair concerning the house, for we are God’s house. We believers in this present time, like our fathers before us, are that house which Christ built by his death.

Yet I say that we are the house of the divine dwelling on this condition: if we retain confidence—that is, if we do not lose the most certain hope he has given us, but hold it firmly and without doubt. That is, if we hope with complete certainty for salvation in Christ without fleshly observances, then we are the house in which he dwells by faith. [Col. 1544D] For “confidence” is here understood as hope.

And because no one can hope unless hope arises from a good conscience, he adds also “the glory of hope”: that is, if we retain also a good conscience, which is the cause of hope and the mind’s adornment and glory, by which we are raised into hope. Thus, as the same Apostle says: “Our glory is the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I). And because some possess the consciousness of a good work, through which they can glory in God and hope, yet have it wavering, he adds “firm.” And because they might have it firm for a month or a year, he adds “unto the end”: that is, unto death, for “he who has persevered unto the end shall be saved” (Matt. XXIV).

Or, let us retain confidence lest, as some unbelief stealthily enters, we lose confidence that we can be saved through Christ, seeking the help of salvation in fleshly observances. Rather, without these, let us trust without doubt that Christ alone suffices for everything. For Christ was shown to be far nobler than Moses so that we may hold Christ alone, in whom we shall possess all things, and “the glory of hope”: that is, a glorious hope, because it concerns heavenly joy; firm—that is, enduring unto the end of life, when what is now hoped for shall be received. [Col. 1545A]

> “Wherefore, as the Holy Spirit says: Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts (Ps. XCIV), as in the provocation, according to the day of temptation in the wilderness, where your fathers tempted me, tested me, and saw my works for forty years. Therefore I was angered with this generation, and said: They always err in heart. But they did not know my ways; so I swore in my wrath: ‘If they shall enter into my rest.’”

Now he again invites them to faith through fear, lest through unbelief they lose eternal rest, as their fathers did in the wilderness; for because they were unbelieving, they lost their promised land, which signified that rest. We are God’s house if we do not lose confidence through unbelief but maintain confidence through certain faith. Therefore do not harden your hearts through unbelief. And I admonish this in the same way as the Holy Spirit says: that is, I now have in correcting you the same intention which the Holy Spirit had when he spoke this through David’s mouth. Nor do I alone urge this; the Holy Spirit likewise urges the same thing. [Col. 1545B]

And I offer you the same good, if you obey—or the same evil, if you harden your heart—which the Holy Spirit promised when, directing his voice to you and to others who would live in the time of grace, he said: “Today, if you hear his voice,” and so forth. For the Holy Spirit, foreseeing the hardness of the Jews’ hearts, that they would harden their hearts in unbelief against the voice of the Lord Jesus, and therefore wishing by his authority to call them back from hardness of heart and invite them to the integrity of faith in Christ—namely, that after the coming of truth they should suppose no salvation to lie in fleshly observances—said: “Today,” and so forth.

By this the Apostle strongly calls back the Jews who possess this prophecy, since he shows that the Holy Spirit had foretold so long beforehand exactly what is now said to them in the time of grace. “Today”—that is, on this distinguished and noble day, namely in this time of grace, remarkable and glorious among all other ages, in which God has shown human beings a greater affection of compassion than in other times—“if you hear his voice,” that is, the new preaching of Christ, let no sign of unbelief remain in you. He who formerly spoke through heralds now speaks in person. If you were hard then, be gentle now.

When he says, “if you hear his voice,” he does not doubt that they will hear it; rather, by this he makes them more attentive to hearing, as though he makes them uncertain and expectant lest perhaps it happen that they do not hear. “Do not harden”: that is, do not make hard against him your hearts, which are your own—that is, subject to your own choice—[Col. 1546A] as your fleshly fathers hardened theirs (Exod. XVI, XVII, XXXII; Num. II, XXV) “in the provocation”: that is, in the sharpest offense, by which they made God bitter toward themselves when they did not believe that God would give them the land of promise, as he had promised, nor the heavenly rest signified by it.

Do not, I say, harden your hearts now “according to the day of temptation in the wilderness”: that is, by following and imitating the day and time in which your fathers tempted me and, in their distrust, asked for bread and said with hesitation: “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?” (Ps. LXXVII), and other such things. They did this in the wilderness after they had been led out of Egypt, where they ought not to have tempted God, whose many and great works they had already seen: namely, themselves led out of Egypt by a mighty hand through the Red Sea on dry ground, and their enemies drowned in the sea (Exod. XIV), besides many other mighty deeds. [Col. 1546B]

Therefore afterward they ought not to have distrusted the protection of his grace because of any enemies. When they heard from the scouts (Num. XIV) that the inhabitants of the promised land were strong in battle, they forgot God’s power, tested so many times, and did not believe that he was able to subject that land to his people. For this reason they were unworthy to enter it. But take care that, by doing likewise, you are not excluded from the true homeland of the saints.

For you too have been led out of Egypt spiritually—that is, delivered from the darkness of ignorance and the oppression of vices—with your enemies, the devil with all his pomp and the army of vices, submerged in your baptism. And under the Lord’s guidance you have been advanced to understand that this world and the dwelling of this present age are a wilderness, a place of dread, a pilgrimage, and an exile. Therefore you ought no longer to tempt God by any distrust, supposing that without fleshly observances you cannot be saved through Christ. For then you will not enter the homeland of the elect. Instead, believing with most certain faith that you will be saved through him, keep his commands alone. [Col. 1546C]

But because he spoke of “the day of temptation” and did not say by whom that temptation had been made, he now explains who tempted God in the wilderness: “where”—that is, in which wilderness—“your fathers tempted me,” whose temptation and provocation you are children and imitators of while you doubt in faith. Therefore you must fear lest, having them as fathers in guilt, you imitate them in the same punishment. Let such men therefore no longer be your fathers; do not imitate them. They were your fathers, but if you do not imitate them, they will not be your fathers.

“They tested me”: that is, from curiosity they investigated whether I could do what they requested. “And they saw my works for forty years,” because for so long a span of years I performed miracles before them through Moses, and they hardened their hearts more and more. I kept company with them for forty years in order to show that such a kind of human beings, always provoking me, would exist until the end of the world; for in those forty years the whole duration of this age was signified. They tempted me by their unbelief. [Col. 1546D]

“Therefore I was angered”—that is, wrathful against—“this generation,” so perverse, which also represented that kind of rebellious people who would always exist in the Church until the end of the world. And although they offended me, nevertheless I always said of them: “They err in heart.” That is, through Moses and Aaron I mercifully declared and strove to correct the error which they held in their heart knowingly and willingly, saying: “They err in heart,” that is, by their own deliberate decision, because they sin in earnest and, though they know they act badly, do not desist.

I indeed recalled them with paternal kindness, but “they did not know my ways”: that is, they did not understand the mercy by which I strove to correct them, nor the truth by which I intended to condemn them if they persisted in evil; for all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth (Ps. XXIV). Or, “they did not know my ways”: that is, they did not understand my commandments, by which one comes to me, because I spoke spiritually—“for we know that the law is spiritual” (Rom. VII)—but they understood carnally. [Col. 1547A]

Thus they did not know my ways, as I, because of their deserts, swore—that is, immutably confirmed—and I did this “in my wrath,” that is, in the determination to exact vengeance: “If they shall enter into my rest,” that is, they shall not enter the land of promise, in which I intended to make them rest; nor the kingdom of heaven, which is signified by it, where rest is perpetual. He notes two things: that he inflicted punishment upon them and that he denied them rest. For in the wrath by which he denied them rest, he exacted vengeance.

The broken construction also indicates the force of wrath when it is said, “If they shall enter into my rest,” although God’s wrath is not like a human being’s—that is, a disturbance of an agitated mind—but the tranquil disposition of one simply established in justice. For he threatens vehemently when, as though from excessive wrath, he leaves the sentence incomplete, saying: “If they shall enter into my rest.” He also threatens this with an oath. This threat, therefore, is greatly to be feared. For it is a great thing for God to speak; how much more for God to swear. You ought to fear a human being when he swears, lest because of the oath he do what is contrary to his will. How much more God, who can swear nothing rashly? [Col. 1547B]

Historically, he here recalls that they sent men to inspect the land; and, when they heard that invincible men were there, forgetting God’s power so often proved, they said: “Let us return to Egypt” (Num. XIII, XIV). Therefore the Lord swore that they would not enter that land, which is rest from labors; and so all died in the wilderness except two. And just as they lost through unbelief and distrust the land prepared for their rest, so you, if you doubt Christ’s faith or are disobedient to him, shall not enter the true homeland of the righteous.

Thus far he has spoken through fear, lest they be unbelieving toward Christ as their fathers were toward Moses, and so lose the true rest of perpetual blessedness, as their fathers lost the rest of the promised land. From here he begins to admonish them gently, lest they lose that rest; [Col. 1548A] and he urges the opportune time, so that they may hasten toward it, adding:

> “Take heed, brethren, lest perhaps there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, departing from the living God. But exhort yourselves every day, while it is called ‘today,’ lest any of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. For we have become partakers of Christ, provided that we hold fast the beginning of his substance firm unto the end, while it is said: ‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in that provocation.’ For some who heard provoked him, though not all who went out of Egypt through Moses. But with whom was he angered for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, [Col. 1548B] whose bodies lay fallen in the wilderness? And to whom did he swear that they would not enter into his rest, except those who were unbelieving? And we see that they could not enter because of unbelief.”

It begins gently with admonition, so that they may receive the admonition more willingly. “Take heed,” he says, “O brethren,” as though to say: You ought to yield to me, who admonish you with brotherly love. Take heed—that is, beware by rational consideration—lest any one of you have an unbelieving heart and be excluded from the eternal rest of the faithful. But some wish to connect the foregoing “wherefore” with this admonition thus: “We are the house of God, if we retain confidence and the glory of hope.” [Col. 1548D] Therefore take heed, brethren, lest you distrust.

Take heed lest perhaps—“perhaps,” I say, because it lies in your own choice and may go either way—there be in any one of you (for I do not doubt concerning many, who are perfect) a heart of unbelief, so as not to believe that Christ is sufficient for salvation; for such a heart is evil, since it thus falls into a great abyss of sins and afterwards into death. For such a heart is a heart—that is, a will—of departing, that is, of turning aside and fleeing by diverse paths from the living God, that is, from Christ, who, as we read, is the true God and eternal life. For whoever walks a path different from his, departing from life, tends toward death. Some among them did this when, doubting in the faith of Christ, they did not believe that he could suffice for righteousness and salvation without carnal observances; and thus, [Col. 1549A] regarding his faith as a small thing, they would readily have wished to depart from it. And it is a lesser thing to depart from God through another fault than to set him wholly aside through unbelief. For whoever casts away faith departs altogether from God; but whoever departs from him through another fault still hopes to return.

By his saying “a heart of unbelief,” “an evil heart” and “a heart of departing from the living God” could have been understood. But he used these words because they have greater force to frighten them away. Do not have a heart of unbelief; rather, exhort—not strangers, not persons of another nation, but yourselves—one another. For his saying “yourselves” shows that their mutual exhortation was so necessary among them that it need not be extended to others. Exhort one another to believe sincerely and to live piously and [Col. 1549B] holily; and do this “day by day,” that is, daily, and not for merely one or two years, but “while it is called Today,” that is, so long as days together are called “today.” For by saying “while it is called Today,” he intended to mark the multitude of days in the time of grace.

That time is “Today,” that is, great and manifest; and it is a day, that is, light after the darkness of error and ignorance. While it is called Today—that is, while the time of grace endures—exhort yourselves concerning the increase of faith and of the other virtues, because you can progress no less now than when Christ was present. Or, “while it is called Today” means while this present life remains to each person, in which it is always said, “today”: exhort yourselves always toward better things. For if anyone has sinned, [Col. 1549C] while it is Today, he can return. Therefore let no one despair while he lives. Yet neither should he become carelessly secure, because he does not know when this “Today” will be determined for him.

Therefore exhort yourselves, so that none of you may be hardened—that is, become hard and unbelieving against the admonition of the Holy Spirit, who wishes to make his heart soft, so that he may write his words in it as in wax. Let none be hardened; for I do not fear this concerning many. For one is hardened against the faith by the deceitfulness of sin: that is, by the error of sin deceiving him under the appearance of virtue, if, together with faith in Christ, he thinks the Law necessary for salvation because it was given by God. For thus he will be deceived by sin—that is, he will act wrongly while thinking that he acts well—because by observing the Law he will offend God, whom he thinks that he pleases [Col. 1549D] by that same observance of the Law. For whoever still observes the Law denies that Christ has come. Therefore none of us ought to be hardened by such deceit, so as, under the pretext of legal observance, to depart from Christ and nullify his faith.

For we have become partakers of Christ. For there cannot be a departure where there was not first a union. But we are now joined to Christ; therefore let us not depart from him. We have become partakers of Christ in name and grace, because we are called Christians and receive his grace; through him we have obtained whatever good we possess—namely faith, remission of sins, innocence, righteousness, and so forth. Or: we have become partakers of Christ, that is, in hope we are already partakers of the same incorruption and glory which [Col. 1550A] Christ possesses. It is as though he said: You ought to exhort one another and not be hard, because by grace we have become what we were not, having a share with Christ in the inheritance.

Yet I say this on the condition that we retain “the beginning of his substance,” that is, faith, which is the beginning of the words, through which God exists in us, through which we are made divine and partake of the divine substance. For faith is the beginning of substance—that is, of incorporation into him—because it is the foundation and origin of virtues through which he is established in us and we become his members. And we must retain this beginning not waveringly but firmly and immovably; not for a month or a year, but until the end of this present life, so that we may never abandon the faith.

And lest they should say, “Only you apostles and Christ’s contemporaries were commanded [Col. 1550B] to keep the faith,” he adds: “while it is said, Today,” etc. As though he said: It was commanded not only to those who heard Christ speaking that they should retain faith and not harden their hearts; the same injunction is laid also upon you and upon all others while it is said—that is, as long as it is said—“Today, if you hear his voice,” throughout the whole time of grace or present life.

Or thus: Not only Christ’s hearers were bound to give faith to his words, but you also, so long as it is said, “Today, if you hear his voice”—that is, so long as you can hear the voice of divine preaching in this age—must not unbelievingly harden your hearts against the voice of the Lord’s admonition, as your fathers hardened theirs in that notable and great provocation. Do not [Col. 1550C] follow the examples of the wicked, but of the good. For some of them, hearing in the wilderness God’s voice promising that he would bring them into the land of promise, in which eternal rest was also prefigured, doubted that God could do these things; and thus by their hesitation they provoked him—that is, made him bitter and harsh toward themselves. This statement shows that it is not enough to hear of that rest, because they all heard, but not all arrived there.

For you too now hear that Christ promises that rest to you if you believe. If you doubt that he can bring you into it without carnal observances, you will provoke him as your fathers did, and you will not enter it. For it is worse to provoke than to test.

“Some provoked him, but not all who went out of Egypt through Moses,” that is, under Moses’ leadership. For among them were Caleb and Joshua, who did not offend; these you ought to imitate. For you also, under the leadership of the true Moses, that is, Christ, have been brought forth from the darkness of ignorance and error. Therefore you ought no longer to provoke God by unbelief and evil conduct, but by faith and good works hasten to the land of perpetual blessedness promised to you. By saying that some provoked him, but not all, he intimates that he understood some among them to be doubting and others not doubting.

I say that some provoked him, but not all. But against which of these was he angry for forty years? That is, against those who provoked him or against those who did not provoke him? [Col. 1551A] Was it not against those who sinned? Certainly against them. This appeared from the effect, because their corpses were “cast down”: that is, strewn far from the camp and from every dwelling-place, in the wilderness; and because of their multitude their bodies lay unburied, exposed to beasts and birds—that is, their bodies, like the carcasses of brute animals, were left in the wilderness and not committed to burial. In this the wrath of God appeared.

Moreover, as was said above, the forty years signify the whole present life, or the span of time until the end of the world. During it, whoever after baptism provokes God either by unbelief or by criminal conduct is not worthy to reach the land of the living; rather, in the wilderness of this world he is torn like a corpse by beasts and birds, that is, by evil spirits, and is carried off to eternal punishments.

Jerome, in the sixth book on Ezekiel: “My eye,” he says, “spared them, so that I should not kill and destroy them, nor consume them utterly” (Ezek. 20). Here one asks how he spared those whose corpses fell in the wilderness and of whom, except Jesus son of Nave and Caleb son of Jephunneh, none entered the land of promise. From this we understand that they live, are not reserved for eternal punishments, have not been blotted out from the book or land of the living, and have not been consumed before the face of the Lord. For if they are to be believed to have perished because they were not brought into the land of promise, then Moses perished, since he only saw the land of promise and did not enter it. He indeed struck down sinners into bodily death, but denied the rest of the soul after [Col. 1551C] death to unbelievers.

And this is what is said interrogatively for the rebuke of these persons who still doubted in faith: “But to whom did he swear that they should not enter into his rest”—the eternal rest signified by the land of promise, or the land of promise itself—“except to those who were unbelieving” toward the voice which promised that very rest? It is as though he said: He swore this not to others but to them. And we see, by plain reasoning, that they could not enter into that everlasting rest, just as neither into the land of promise, because of their unbelief. For God fulfilled the threat of his oath, by which he said that unbelievers would not enter his rest; and he will act similarly toward all unbelievers.

## Chapter IV

[Col. 1551D] “Let us therefore fear, lest perhaps, while the promise of entering into his rest remains, any one of us should be thought to have fallen short. For the good news has been proclaimed to us as to them; but the word heard did not profit them, because it was not mixed with faith in those things which they heard. For we who have believed shall enter into rest, as he said: ‘As I swore in my wrath, if they shall enter into my rest’ (Ps. 94), although the works were finished from the foundation of the world. For he said somewhere concerning the seventh day thus: ‘And God rested on the seventh day from all his works’ (Gen. 2); and again in this place: ‘If they shall enter into my rest.’ Since therefore it remains for some to enter into it, and those to whom it was first announced did not enter because of unbelief, [Col. 1552A] again he appoints a certain day, Today, saying in David after so long a time, as has been said above: ‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.’ For if Jesus had given them rest, he would never afterwards speak of another day. Therefore there remains a sabbath-rest for the people of God. For he who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his. Let us therefore hasten to enter into that rest, lest anyone fall into the same example of unbelief.”

And because they lost rest through unbelief, therefore let us fear—that is, let us be anxious—lest we too lose it similarly through unbelief; so that, if not through love, at least through fear, we may flee unbelief. [Col. 1552B] Let us fear, because there is cause for fear, lest perhaps—“perhaps,” I say, because it lies in your choice and may go either way—while the promise remains: that is, lest, despising, neglecting, and abandoning the repeated promise which God made us, or which we made God in baptism, of entering through faith and works into the rest which is his—that is, which belongs to his power, because he can give it to whom he wills—any one of us should be thought to fall short.

God promised that rest to us who believe. Let us not abandon his promise, but hold it with certain faith, believing that, without carnal observances, we shall receive it by Christ’s promise alone. Let us fear lest any one of us—that is, from our own so religious fellowship—abandoning this promise, wavering in his heart and faltering in faith, [Col. 1552C] give others an evil opinion of his salvation, so that he may be judged to have fallen short of that rest because of his unbelief, like the ancient fathers. For every person ought to strive to be so firm in faith and good conduct that, when he dies, there may be no doubt that he has attained that rest. But one who, while living, wavered in faith and was negligent in conduct is thought after death to have fallen short of it. And this is to be feared, lest it happen to any of us.

For we too are concerned to be anxious concerning that rest, just as our fathers were concerned. For in the time of grace it has been announced to us through the Son, just as it was announced to them through the servant by the figure of the land of promise. Therefore we cannot make an excuse concerning it on grounds of ignorance, because that rest has been preached not only to those fathers but also to us. Nor have we been taught of it only in the Gospel, but also before the Law and under the Law. It was announced to us as also to them.

But it did not profit them; may it profit us. The word did not profit them—that is, that prior announcement of rest—because they saw it only in word; and therefore the word did not profit them because it was heard only and not fulfilled. And it was truly only heard, not acted upon or believed. For it was not mixed with faith, so that word and faith might be joined and blended together: I mean faith arising from what they had heard from their scouts. For they did not derive faith from the scouts’ words, but rather lost it. Or, from what they heard from the scouts, it came about that the word [Col. 1553A] which they had previously heard concerning that rest was not mixed with their faith, but was considered false. For when they heard that the land of promise was surrounded by mountains, had very strongly fortified cities, and inhabitants of great strength, they despaired of entering that rest, which also signifies the rest to come; and, with the hope of present rest lost, they doubted concerning that which was prefigured in it.

I said that it was announced to us as well concerning that rest, and the result proves this, because we shall enter it. For we would not have known the way of entering unless it had been announced to us. Or thus: It did not profit those who did not believe, because it will profit us who believe. For we who believe shall enter that rest, just as he says conversely concerning unbelievers, “if they shall enter into my rest.” From this it is clear that those who believe will enter. We shall enter by believing, just as they lost it by not believing.

“They have not known,” he says, “my ways,” just as I showed them wrath which they deserved. Thus they were blind in knowing my ways, just as I firmly threatened them that they would not enter my rest, whether of the region of Palestine or of the heavenly dwelling; and just as it was taken away from them because they did not believe, so it is promised to us if we believe.

But because he had said that rest had been announced, he shows when and how it was announced: namely, before the Law, after the completion of the works; under the Law, when it was signified through the land of promise; and in the time of grace, in David. For he mentions three rests: one of the Sabbath, a second in Palestine, and a third in heaven. [Col. 1553C] Rest was announced first by deeds and then by words. For when God’s works, which he had made on the individual days from the foundation of the world—that is, from when he began to establish the world—were completed, that rest was announced, when God is said to have rested.

Augustine, in the sermon *On the Ten Strings*, says: “In the Holy Spirit—that is, in the house of God—everlasting rest is promised to us. For since he is called the Holy Spirit, God therefore sanctified the seventh day, when he made all his works, as we read written in Genesis. There you do not find sanctification named except on that day on which it is said: ‘God rested from his works’ (Gen. 1). For God was not weary, so that it might be said, ‘God rested [Col. 1553D] from his works’; rather, in that word he promised rest to you who labor.”

Or, because he made all things very good and, as it is said, God rested, understand also that after good works you will rest, and rest without end. For all the earlier works which were mentioned—that is, the earlier days—have an evening. But this seventh day has no evening. Where God sanctified rest, there it is said, “Morning came,” so that that day might begin. It was not said, “Evening came,” so that the day might end; rather, “Morning came” was said, so that there might be a day without end. Thus our rest begins as though in the morning, but does not end, because we shall live eternally. Whatever we do, if we do it with this hope, we keep the Sabbath.

God never ceased from a new work until man was made; but once man was made, [Col. 1554A] he rested from every work. By this he signified that he would make no other creature after man, to which man might be subject and for whose service man might be created. For because he rested when man had been made, we understand that he had made all things for man. Therefore rest was promised to man when the works had been completed; and Scripture shows that rest and blessedness were promised to him.

For in a certain notable and excellent place the Holy Spirit said concerning the seventh day, by which eternal rest was signified—because it is not described as having had an evening—thus, that is, in these words: “And God rested on the seventh day.” For why would he say that, after the day on which man was created, on the following day he rested and ceased from work, unless by this he wished to intimate that the one [Col. 1554B] after whose creation he rested was made for rest and blessedness? For six days from that creation he did not rest, because he saw nothing complete until man, lord and possessor of all things, was created. But when man was completed, all things were completed; and then at last he ceased from every work, because then all things were complete, having the man for whom they had been made.

God rested from all his works—that is, he ceased from new creation, so that he would make nothing further except from the material already made there, or in likeness to things which he had already made there. He worked for six days and rested on the seventh. So too man was born into the world for labor in the sixth age. He suffered on the sixth day and at the sixth hour of the day; on the seventh he rested in the tomb. By this he taught us that, after our works, which are performed through the six [Col. 1554C] ages—infancy, childhood, adolescence, youth, old age, and decrepitude—we ought to rest in the seventh age, as on the seventh day.

The first age, as I said, is infancy, to be nourished at the breast with milk. The second is childhood, now fitted for solid food. The third is adolescence, sufficient for begetting offspring. The fourth is youth, strong and suited to honors. The fifth is old age, when the ardor of youth has cooled and been extinguished, because, when the heat of the flesh is moderated, life is led in tranquillity. The sixth is decrepit age, when the person who once was perishes, when, strength having been lost, he is now placed at the entrance of death. After the end of these ages, death follows.

In the same way six ages may be identified in the spiritual life. Infants [Col. 1554D] are those weak in understanding who defend themselves by authority alone, humbly yielding in their faith without any reasoning to the authorities of the Fathers. Children are those whose understanding has now been somewhat exercised, who do not remain satisfied with authority alone, but are advanced by certain reasons and inquiries toward the rational basis of faith. Adolescents are those whose sensuous nature is now subject to reason, so that they are sufficient for the generation of good works, laboring and being moved to act well. Youth is when the mind not only generates through good action, but its virtue has become so hardened and strengthened that neither death nor life can separate it from the love of God, and it does not fear to undergo martyrdom if necessary.

Old age is when the mind [Col. 1555A] so prevails over the sensuous nature that it is not only not overcome by it, but is not even assailed by it, so that the flesh now consents to the spirit, insofar as this is possible in the present life, and desires the same rest and purity of soul. Decrepit age is that of those who, now enjoying contemplation of the Lord insofar as is permitted, live in the likeness of angels. They are no longer to be called children of this world; they already live in the heavenly realm, so that no traces of human conduct may now be seen in their deeds.

After these six moral ages follows the seventh day, promised eternally to all who live thus; in it true rest and perpetual joy will be given them, so that they will no longer be subject to any labor or misery. God signified this to us when, after the work of six days, he willed to rest on the seventh. [Col. 1555B] In that passage of Scripture it was shown that rest is promised to man, and it was announced there before the Law concerning it. Again, under the Law, the same rest was announced and promised in this passage through the figure of the land of promise, when the Holy Spirit said concerning unbelievers: “If they shall enter into my rest,” that is, into the land which Moses promised, which signified the true rest prepared by the Holy Spirit; and therefore they will not be able to enter even that true rest.

For where a threat was made to unbelievers that they would not enter it, there it was declared that it had been promised to some human beings. If it had been promised to no one, neither would anyone have been foretold to enter it. Nor would there have been cause for the threat that they would not enter if no one was going to enter. Nor would it have harmed them greatly if he threatened to remove something of which they could have had no hope or certainty. Behold, rest was marked and promised twice: by the Sabbath day and by the land of promise.

And because the Holy Spirit, who can neither be deceived nor lie, marked, announced, and promised it, and prepared it for some, since he would not have made it superfluously, therefore it remains—that is, after the promise it remains—for some, that is, the excellent and elect, to enter that everlasting and true promise. And since it remains for some to enter, and those to whom it was first announced that they should enter did not enter, because of unbelief, into the true rest which the land of promise prefigured, a rest which they did not attain, therefore again—that is, under the designation of the same rest—[Col. 1555D] the Holy Spirit appoints and distinguishes a certain day on which the things announced may be fulfilled: namely, the excellent time of grace at Christ’s coming, saying “Today” in David, that is, speaking through David, because David himself was not speaking, but the Holy Spirit in him; and this was after so long a time from the entry of the children of Israel into the land of promise.

From this it is clear that he did not then speak of that land, which had long since been possessed, but of the true rest still awaited. For entry into the land of promise could no longer then be taken away from them. But from the threat made in the wilderness which says, “If they shall enter into my rest,” a great interval elapsed until David’s time. From the time of that threat to the entry into the land of promise, however, there was only a short time. Therefore it is established that David spoke of the promise of true rest, which, after so long a time, he made to those who were to be in the New Testament, since his contemporaries had already entered.

Therefore he appoints the day on which we may enter true rest. For no one would ever enter unless the time of grace had been defined, in which the kingdoms of heaven would stand open to believers. Therefore he appoints the day of entering, because it remains for some to enter. And unless he saw that some would enter, he would not appoint it. Though living under the Law, he was nevertheless in heart placed in the time of grace. By saying “Today,” he announces for the third time the rest to be consummated in that time; in David he appoints the day by saying “Today,” which “Today” must be understood as was said above: [Col. 1556B] “Today, if you hear his voice.”

For he had used “Today” in different senses when he said, “Today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2), and when he again said, “Today, if you hear his voice” (Ps. 94). Therefore he had to define what meaning “Today” now has, lest it be understood otherwise: Today—that is, in this bright time of grace, of which John writes (1 John 2) that the darkness has passed and the true light now shines—if you hear the voice of his preaching. For not all who are in the time of grace hear it, just as even now many pagans have not been reached by evangelical preaching. Do not harden your hearts against his voice, lest the time of grace pass by you in vain, because afterward there will be no time in which you can enter into rest.

Someone might say: You say that those to whom it was first announced did not enter, yet we see that they entered, since through Jesus son of Nave they obtained it. The answer is: They did not enter, through their unbelief, the rest promised to man. For if Jesus son of Nave—that is, Joshua son of Nun—had given them that rest in the division of the land of promise, he would not afterwards have spoken of another day on which entrance into rest would be open.

Or it may be continued thus: It remains for some to enter, as David appoints. For if Jesus—that is, Joshua, who led them into the land of promise—had given them rest, that is, complete rest, so that no other was to be hoped for, never—that is, at no time—would David or the Holy Spirit afterwards [Col. 1556D] speak of another day, that is, another time in which rest would be given. But because he spoke afterwards, he plainly shows that the rest of which he said “Today” is different from that into which Joshua had led them. Therefore it is certain that the rest to which Christ leads is another, the rest prefigured by that one under Joshua.

Therefore a sabbath-rest remains for the elect. Since that rest was not true, but the Holy Spirit promised another afterward, it remains—that is, it is reserved by God for those to come—because the unbelieving fathers were unable to attain it. What remains is not merely rest; rather, to express it more fully, it is a *sabbatismos*, that is, Sabbath leisure and joy. For *sabbatismos* was called the preparation, joy, and festivity of the Sabbath, and “Sabbath” is interpreted “rest.” Therefore *sabbatismos* signifies not only true and complete rest, but also unutterable joy and an abundance of spiritual riches.

This sabbath-rest is not reserved for a few, but for a people—that is, a great multitude; yet not for every people, but only for the people of God. Therefore, if anyone wishes to keep sabbath, let him belong to the people of God. And this sabbath-rest will be far different from the rest which Joshua gave. For he who has entered into God’s rest—that is, the tranquil dwelling of the heavenly kingdom, like the servant to whom it was said, “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25)—has attained true and perfect rest, because he too has rested perpetually and perfectly from his works, by which he labored here, as God rested from [Col. 1557B] his works, though he made them without labor.

For as the Sabbath on which God rested is not read to have had an evening, so the rest of the righteous will have no end. For as God ceased from works, so they will cease perpetually from every work, wholly free from every anxiety of labor. But those to whom Joshua divided the land rested little and endured many labors and many afflictions.

Since, therefore, that rest is so great, has been promised to us, and now in the time of grace it remains for some to enter, let us hasten to enter it and not linger in these earthly things which hinder us. Let us hasten by faith and good works—what those do not do who still carnally observe the Law and are negligent concerning faith and spiritual conduct. Let us hasten, I say, to enter that rest, so great, so noble, so glorious, and so often promised to us. Let us also hasten to that rest in order to escape everlasting punishments.

And this is the meaning: “lest anyone fall”—that is, lest anyone fall inwardly in the heart, where the fall is more grievous—someone notable in unbelief—into that into which the fathers fell; and thus into it, as into the very same thing: not dissimilarly, but in every respect in the same manner, falling into what the fathers fell into, namely the example of unbelief. That is, lest he fall into unbelief after their example and be excluded from divine rest. For they did not believe that God was sufficient to give even the rest of the land of promise; and these likewise did not believe that Christ was sufficient to give [Col. 1557D] everlasting rest without carnal observances. Therefore they barred for themselves the entrance to rest by the same reasoning by which their fathers had previously done.

Or, “lest anyone fall into the same example of unbelief,” that is, into the same condemnation which your fathers underwent because of their unbelief—a condemnation or punishment which is an example to you, because if you are unbelieving, the same will happen to you. For God’s vengeance, which was inflicted upon them so greatly that it can serve as an example to others, is aptly called an example of unbelief, lest they presume to be unbelieving. Or, as we have set forth, the fathers’ unbelief is an example to you not to be unbelieving; and therefore you will sin worse than your fathers unless you beware of unbelief.

For all these reasons, breaking through every impediment of unbelief [Col. 1558A] and worldly allurements, let us hasten as greatly as possible to that rest in which we shall rest forever.
