“For the word of God is living and effective, and more penetrating than every two-edged sword; it reaches to the division of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow; and it is a discerner of the thoughts and intention of the heart. No creature is invisible in his sight, but all things are naked and laid open to his eyes. To him we must give account.”

Let us hasten, as I said, toward that rest. For the word of God—that is, Christ, the Word of the Father—who may help us as we hasten and crown us when we arrive, is living: that is, he is true life in himself and sufficient for the enlivening of others [Col. 1558B], and thus we shall live in him. The word of God, who preached that rest, is living by his own life, that is, giving life to others. “For as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5).

Or, in the assumed humanity in which he chose to die, he is now living: that is, he has attained eternal life and likewise causes his followers to live, because he has become immortal and will make you immortal. And he is effective: that is, he fully accomplishes whatever he wills, whether by saving believers or condemning unbelievers.

Or it may be connected thus: Beware lest any one of you fall into the example of the fathers’ unbelief, that is, into a punishment like that which they deserved through unbelief; for the word of God—that is, the Son, who judged them and will judge you [Col. 1558C]—is living. And as he lives eternally, so his judgment remains eternally. For those whom he condemns, a living punishment will torment forever; and those whom he saves, he will make to live forever. For he is effective for both.

Nor is he only effective in both respects—that is, powerfully doing whatever he wills—but he is also more penetrating than every two-edged sword, because he penetrates all things. Do not suppose that the hidden things of hearts escape him, and that he therefore judges less justly. For if he did not penetrate human consciences, he could not truly judge who was faithful and who unfaithful, or who had a good or bad conscience; and then he could not render to each a fitting recompense, because he would lack the power to see human secrets [Col. 1558D]. But in order that he may be effective powerfully in all things, he penetrates all things by his sight; and he is keener and more discerning than every two-edged sword, than every subtlety of the discourse of divine preaching.

This Word, who is God—for “the Word was God”—is more penetrating than every two-edged sword, because he penetrates human consciences more deeply than any discourse of preaching. For the word of doctrine is a two-edged sword, that is, sharp on both sides, because it speaks of temporal things and speaks of eternal things. In both it proves what it says keenly and subtly, and separates from the world the person whom it strikes. It could not do this unless it penetrated that person’s mind. But this Word, who is God, is much more penetrating.

And he also reaches—that is, by consideration he arrives—unto the division of soul [Col. 1559A] and spirit. Our spirit is not the whole soul, but something belonging to it: namely, that by which we reason, understand, and have wisdom, and by which we are set above cattle, because they lack reason. For they do not have spirit, that is, the understanding of reason and the sense of wisdom, but only soul. For it was said even of them: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls”; and: “Let the earth bring forth a living soul” (Gen. 1). Therefore, by spirit we understand with the angels; by soul we live with beasts.

But the Word of God reaches—that is, touches perfectly, because he touches in every respect, leaving nothing untouched by his knowledge—unto the division of soul and spirit, that is, unto the distinction between sensibility and rationality. For by unconquerable knowledge he knows how sensibility is divided from reason and how much one differs from the other.

Or, he reaches unto the division of the soul because he sees how the soul—that is, sensibility—differs from itself: when it is more devoted to lower things, it is lower; when recalled from them, it is worthier. And he reaches unto the division of the spirit because he observes how rationality is divided from itself: whether it longs for God, or on a lower level considers heavenly things, or again, lower still, reflects upon rightly ordering worldly matters [Col. 1559B].

For the soul thinks only about worldly things or matters belonging to the body, in which it scarcely differs from beasts. Something in it is lower, such as thoughts of food, drink, and the like. But something is, as it were, higher in it, as when it thinks of honorable matters, such as glory, renown, power, and things of that sort. And the Word of God knows this division well, nor is it hidden from him when the soul does one thing or another.

The rational spirit, however, is in its higher part when it thinks of its Creator and burns to attain him through love alone. But it is occupied in its lower part when, leaving sublime contemplation, it meditates on the lesser virtues pertaining to good action. The Word of God considers this division, discerning what in it is higher and what lower.

Soul and spirit are divided from one another because, as has been said, the soul concerns itself with worldly and bodily things, whereas the spirit with heavenly and spiritual things. Therefore what is lower in the spirit surpasses what is higher in the soul. And the living Word of God touches and searches this division [Col. 1559C] of soul and spirit.

He also knows the division of joints and marrow: that is, of the junctures of soul and spirit. For he sees how the junctures of the soul are divided, at what time they are divided, and when it passes from one juncture to another; and likewise with the spirit. The junctures of the soul are the increases it receives at each age. For a person is wiser in adolescence than in childhood, wiser again in youth than in adolescence, and likewise more mature in adulthood than in youth. Similarly, the spirit advances through stages of growth.

We call these increases “joints” (*compages*), because one seems to be added to another by a certain joining without distinction of time; and the divisions of these joints are the changes corresponding to different ages [Col. 1559D]. “Marrow,” however, because it is interior, denotes whatever is more inward or subtler in soul or spirit. For as marrow in bodies is subtler and hidden in secret parts and in the very innermost places, so whatever is subtler and more concealed in soul or spirit is here called marrow. The Word of God also knows the division of such marrow of the mind, because he distinguishes among themselves those things in us which are most subtle.

Hence it is added that he is “a discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” For he discerns thoughts and separates them from one another, that is, good from evil, whether in the same person or in different persons. He also discerns their intentions: that is, whether each tends toward good or toward evil. And because some intentions are compelled—for example, if someone, forced by fear, dug a field and intended to finish the work, yet not from the heart—the word “of the heart” is added, so that compelled intentions, which are easy to recognize, may be excluded [Col. 1560A].

That is, he knows how to distinguish what intention a person has in a thought that is of the heart: voluntary and not yet outwardly displayed, but hidden within the heart’s secret places.

Or, where he says that he reaches “unto the division of joints and marrow,” he may be understood to have called the joints the connections of thoughts and the marrow their intentions. For by joints bones are joined to bones. Often, while we do something with a right thought, we suddenly turn aside to a love of praise and do for praise what we had first begun to do for truth. Thus, because thoughts are joined to thoughts, certain joints, as it were, arise in the spirit [Col. 1560B]. But the bones joined in these joints have marrow, that is, subtle intentions. The Apostle expressed this more plainly when he said: “a discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart.”

For our joints are thoughts joined together when one follows another; but marrow is intention. And the Word of God is a discerner of joints and marrow, that is, of thoughts and intentions. If one thought is joined to another, he knows which is according to God and which according to the world; he also knows toward what their intention inclines. For we often think one thing and intend another through our thought.

For if someone, with the reward of gifts in view [Col. 1560C], defends the case of an orphan or widow and perhaps, entering a church, says to God in his prayers, “You see that I defend the cause of the orphan and widow,” such a person undoubtedly knows what he is thinking, but he does not know toward what his thought intends. For he thinks one thing and intends another. He does not seek the defense of the orphan and widow, but the payment of gifts. Remove the temporal reward, and he does not defend the orphan and widow.

Therefore the Word of God is a discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart, because he sees not merely what you think within yourself, but rather, through the marrow of the joint—that is, through the intention of the thought—what you seek to obtain for yourself.

And, to say more and conclude briefly: there is no earthly or heavenly creature, bodily or incorporeal [Col. 1560D], invisible—that is, unable to be seen—in the sight of so great a wisdom. Nothing is invisible to him; rather, all things are naked, that is, uncovered, and open, that is, exposed, to his eyes, who sees everything both outwardly and inwardly.

If someone has a book covered by some wrapping, it may indeed be called visible, but not naked. Again, if the wrapping were removed, it could be called naked, but not open. Yet again, if it were opened and all its inner contents displayed, then everything hidden in it would be entirely seen. Thus all things are visible, naked, and open to the Word of God, because, as has been said, he fully sees everything both outwardly and inwardly. By his “eyes” is understood his power of sight.

“To whom we must give account”: we must give him an account at judgment for our deeds. We must have dealings with the living and effective Word of God [Col. 1561A], who sees all things, because we shall speak before him and render an account of everything we have done or thought. Therefore we must always take every care lest we offend him by words, deeds, or thoughts.

Thus far the Apostle has spoken in a frightening manner, calling the Jews back from unbelief by the example of their fathers, to whom eternal rest was denied because of unbelief; and declaring the Son of God living and powerful, so as to reward them if they reject him, and effective, so as to punish them if they neglect him. From this point he wishes again to call them back by gentler arguments, commending Christ’s high priesthood, in order that, once it has been commended, he may show it sufficient for salvation and prove carnal observances superfluous [Col. 1561B]. Thus he adds:

> “Therefore, since we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our confession. For we do not have a high priest unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one tempted in every way according to our likeness, yet without sin. Therefore let us approach his throne of grace with confidence, that we may obtain mercy and find grace for timely assistance.”

He begins, as has been said, to treat of Christ the high priest: how he is sufficient, how he is worthier than the old priesthood—which he changes, together with the law under it, through his better law—and how he is necessary.

Because the Word of God is living and effective and such as we have described, therefore let us hold fast our confession, so that neither terror [Col. 1561C] nor torture may take from our mouths the confession of his faith which we bear in our hearts. And it is right that we should hold it, since we have a high priest: that is, because we have a great high priest. For the same Word of God, inasmuch as he is human, is our high priest, who offered the sacrifice of his own body for us and does not cease to intercede for us.

Thus he makes for us a bridge and access to the Father, so that, leaving beneath our feet temporal things—which run, slip away, and pass on like a river—we may hasten toward the land of the living. We have a great high priest above all high priests, who did not enter the Holy of Holies of Solomon’s Temple but, by ascending, passed through the heavens, so that we too may be able to follow him. Moses, indeed, was then unable to enter the land of promise; but this one passed through the heavens [Col. 1561D], that is, by his entrance he opened them.

We have a high priest—and whom? Jesus, that is, Savior, who can save us without carnal observances. I say Jesus, the Son of God: not adoptive, but consubstantial; not lesser, but equal. Other high priests neither pass through the heavens nor can save, nor are they sons of God by nature. Therefore this one is rightly preferred above all of them, as the Apostle has now begun to prove by many and lengthy arguments.

“Let us hold fast,” he says, “our confession”: let us profess his faith with our mouths, or let us also strive to confess our sins, because we do not have an unmerciful high priest. This is said against those who despaired because of their fall and distrusted that they could appease his wrath, as though they said: “Confession is of no use to us, because this high priest, so exalted as to be raised above the heavens and to be the Son of God, will not receive it or condescend to our weakness” [Col. 1562A].

It is as though the answer to them were: You who have fallen must not despair or abandon confession, because we do not have a stern or disdainful high priest, but a merciful one; not one remote from us, but a participant in our nature. For we do not have a high priest unable to sympathize with our weaknesses: that is, unable to condescend to our frailty and have mercy on those who sin through human weakness. Although he is so exalted, he has not therefore cast us away; rather, he mercifully condescends to our weakness and feels compassion even for one who falls through the weakness of the flesh.

Yet he can no longer suffer any pain. But because our misery and fall displease him, and because he gives help that we may rise and intercedes for us, this is called his compassion. He cannot fail to sympathize with us; he has the power of this compassion because he experienced our weakness, since he endured temptation in every respect without acquaintance with sin [Col. 1562B].

For he was tempted in our flesh and experienced our miseries apart from sin. He was tempted in every kind of temptation, because all temptations are contained in the three temptations which he underwent from the devil. Or, in the single temptation in which the devil showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory (Matt. 4; Luke 4)—in which are contained all things by which human hearts are tempted—he may be said to have been tempted through every kind of sinning. Or, because he endured every temptation: he was mocked, crucified, and suffered all the rest.

He was tempted according to the likeness which he took from us: that is, according to that nature in which he was like us, mortal and capable of suffering; nevertheless he was without sin, although like other human beings. Or, he was tempted in all things without sin because, though he endured every kind of temptation, he did not succumb, nor did he take delight in any enticement to evil. Therefore he can rightly free from sin and temptation.

For when the Apostle says that he was tempted in all things and not overcome, he shows that confidence in his aid must be placed in him; and this because he was made like us. He is not remote from us, but was tempted in that nature of his [Col. 1562C] in which he is like us. Therefore we must believe that he both wills and is able to help in our temptations.

And because we have so great a high priest, willing to sympathize with us and able to help our weakness, therefore with every hope and confidence let us approach his throne of grace: that is, let us come to him, who presides on the judicial throne, by will, prayers, amendment of life, and good works. For a throne is a judge’s seat. But Christ’s throne is a throne of grace for those who, while they are in this present life, come humbly repenting, that they may receive the judgment of penitence; for others, after this life, it is a throne of justice.

Although we are sinners, therefore, let us not despair of pardon, but with confidence of obtaining mercy let us approach his throne of grace [Col. 1562D]: that is, the judge not of severity and strict justice, but of mercy and pardon, because he is not a judge who punishes confession but one who rewards humility.

Let us approach him, I say, that we may obtain mercy from him: that is, remission of past sins; and henceforth find grace from him, that is, the capacity for an innocent manner of life and advancement in goodness, in assistance: that is, that he may help us against the assaults of temptations and cooperate in the completion of good works.

I say assistance that is timely: that is, suitable and necessary, because help sometimes occurs that is neither timely nor suitable. But Christ’s help is timely for us, that is, fitting and necessary, because without it we can do nothing good, and eternal life cannot be possessed without good works [Col. 1563A]. For now is the time of help, while it is the time for action.

Or, his throne is his high-priestly seat and therefore a throne of grace, because he sympathizes with us and intercedes for us. Therefore let us sinners approach the throne of our high priest with confidence of pardon; let us fall at his feet in prayer, so that through him we may obtain from the Father mercy, that is, forgiveness of sins and the grace of a good manner of life.

## Chapter V

> “For every high priest, chosen from among human beings, is appointed on behalf of human beings in matters pertaining to God, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins [Col. 1563D], being able to sympathize with those who are ignorant and who go astray, because he himself is surrounded by weakness. And therefore he must offer for sins, as for the people, so also for himself. And no one takes this honor for himself, but only one called by God, as Aaron was (2 Chron. 26). So also Christ did not glorify himself in order to become high priest, but he who said to him: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’ (Ps. 2), as he also says in another place: ‘You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek’ (Ps. 109).”

He argues from the lesser that this our high priest can obtain mercy and grace for us, since the high priests of the Old Testament in some way obtained mercy by sacrifices and prayers [Col. 1564A], though they were merely human and sinners. It is as though he said: We can obtain mercy through him, because this also occurs through every other high priest.

For every high priest, whether greater or lesser in Aaron’s order, chosen from human beings—that is, taken from the number of human beings to something more honorable, so as to preside over others—is appointed, that is, established by the common judgment of all, for human beings: that is, for their salvation, that through him they may obtain benefits from God. He is appointed in matters that pertain to God and lead subjects toward him: that is, in the offering of gifts, victims, and prayers, which lead to God, so that he may offer—that is, bring them before God and, as it were, set them against the onset of his indignation to restrain and appease it.

Or, because God mercifully condescends when something is offered to him with a sincere heart [Col. 1564B], the priest brings gifts before his mercy—such as firstfruits of crops and the like—and sacrifices from animals, such as oxen and birds, for the removal of human sins.

And if the one who is only from human beings—that is, in no respect unlike human beings, and thus chosen from among them—cleanses his subjects by gifts and sacrifices and directs them to God, then much more must we go to the throne of grace of our high priest, who is not only from human beings but is God and human, who has no sin and does not need to offer for himself, who is sufficient in himself to do that in which others are held back by human weakness.

A high priest chosen from human beings is such a one as is devout and merciful, able, out of habitual goodness, to sympathize—that is, to have an affection of compassion—with the weakness of his subjects [Col. 1564C]: with those who are ignorant, that is, sin through ignorance, and those who err, that is, after the way of truth has been shown, sin as though knowingly through their own error. And he ought to sympathize with them compassionately, because not only they but also he himself, though greater and apparently stronger, is surrounded by the weakness of the flesh, through which he necessarily also sins.

Christ, however, is no longer surrounded by weakness and therefore can help more than that priest. And because he is enclosed by weakness, he consequently ought—that is, is compelled by an obligation of right—to offer sacrifice for sins, that is, for the expiation of sins, as for the people: that is, with as much necessity and supplication as he offers for the people, so also and no differently he offers for himself, that his own sins may be forgiven [Col. 1564D]. Christ, however, need not offer for himself, but only for his faithful people.

Everything now said concerning the high priest of the Old Testament must be observed in the election of the Church’s high priests and in their conduct and actions, although the sacrifices offered by ours are different. I said that the high priest is appointed for human beings and set over the rest. And no one, however noble or wise, takes the honor for himself, so as to claim it as his own and seek to be honored. He does not attribute the honor to himself but to God who calls him; nor does he thrust himself forward to receive the honor, but is chosen by divine direction.

This statement strikes those who desire to seize ecclesiastical honors to which they are not called by God. For whoever thrusts himself forward and seeks his own glory does not receive the honor if he becomes a high priest or prelate in the Church [Col. 1565A]; rather, by making a robbery of God’s grace, he usurps another’s right. Therefore he receives not blessing but a curse.

No one takes that honor by himself, but the one called by God. For the person rightly and canonically elected is called by God. That person receives honor before God and people who is called by God to this prelacy through the Church’s administrators and faithful men, worthily and sincerely, as Aaron was: he did not attribute it to himself nor thrust himself forward in any way, but was chosen through Moses at God’s command. Korah, however, wished to take the honor for himself and therefore experienced divine vengeance. But Aaron was raised to the priesthood because God called him (Exod. 7:27; Num. 17).

Thus Christ likewise did not glorify himself by his virtues so as to take that honor for himself, becoming high priest [Col. 1565B]. He did not glorify himself, but glorified the Father, because in all things he sought not his own glory but the Father’s. He did not glorify himself as one distinguished from the rest, that is, make himself illustrious by raising himself to the honor of the high priesthood; rather, the Father glorified him, in order to appoint him high priest and show him as teacher of the whole world, when he said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. 17).

It is as though he said: Until now you have heard teachers of the law and other high priests; but from now on listen to him, the true high priest. For by saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased,” he glorified him nobly. And he showed that he glorified him in order to appoint him high priest when he added, “Listen to him.”

But the Apostle did not wish to bring forward this statement of glorification against the Jews, because either they did not possess the Gospel or they considered it of lesser authority; therefore he presented testimonies to them from their own books [Col. 1565C]. For this glorification had long before been foretold through the Prophet: “You are my Son.” He did not glorify himself; rather, the Father glorified him by the testimony of his own voice and by many miracles, he who also spoke to him in the Psalm:

“You are my natural and coeternal Son, because I today—that is, in the light of my eternity, which always endures—have begotten you from my own substance.”

By these words the Father glorified him in order to appoint him high priest, just as—that is, as—he also says to him elsewhere: “You are a priest,” that is, one giving sacred things through yourself and your own, “forever” [Col. 1565D], that is, as long as this age endures, because Christ’s priesthood will not pass away for another to succeed it, as the Levitical priesthood passed away.

“You are a priest,” and this “according to the order of Melchizedek,” because, as he offered bread and wine to Abraham returning from the slaughter of kings (Gen. 14), so you will give your body and blood under the form of bread and wine to those victorious over vices. Or, you are priest forever because by one offering you perfected forever those who are sanctified; or because without end you intercede for them by that same sacrifice which you offered once. By this authority it is made clear that God the Father appointed him priest and high priest.

Therefore, if other high priests, who need to offer for themselves, can assist others because they are called by God, then this one can much more assist us and obtain every good for us [Col. 1566A]: he who never needed an offering for himself, who did not glorify or thrust himself forward, but was glorified by the Father and chosen for the high priesthood.

> “Who, in the days of his flesh, offering prayers and supplications with loud crying and tears to him who could save him from death, was heard because of his reverence; and indeed, although he was the Son of God, he learned obedience from the things that he suffered; and, having been perfected, he became the cause of eternal salvation to all who obey him, having been named by God high priest according to the order of Melchizedek.”

He said that Christ was made high priest not by himself but by the Father’s will. Now he begins to show [Col. 1566B] that he performed the service of a high priest, because he did everything that becomes a high priest. “Who in the days of his flesh,” and so forth.

These words further show that through him we can obtain mercy, since he now sits at the Father’s right hand and does not cease to intercede for us, if he was so heard while he was still living on earth and mortal. In the days of his flesh—that is, of his mortality and passion, when the nature of flesh appeared because he endured hunger, thirst, weariness, and pain—he offered prayers as a true high priest.

For the Gospel often records him praying, especially Luke (Luke 6, 11, 22, 23), who described in him the character of a priest. Moreover, everything that he did in the flesh was prayer and supplication for human beings. Throughout his entire life he prayed to the Father concerning the resurrection of his own flesh and our salvation; and when the Passion was at hand he offered supplications, that is, most humble and earnest prayers, with the utmost devotion and affection of heart, when “being in agony, he prayed more earnestly, and his sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground” (Luke 22) [Col. 1566C].

And he offered these prayers and supplications: that is, he brought them before the Father, who met him by hearing him. He offered them to him who could save him from death: that is, raise him again; to him whom he knew sufficient to save him, that is, to make him immortal and incapable of suffering by delivering him from death, so that neither his soul should remain in hell nor his flesh decay in the tomb.

And he offered them with a loud cry: that is, with a most vehement and effective intensity of devout devotion, as when he prayed more earnestly; and also with tears, because we should believe that he shed tears in that prolonged prayer, since drops of blood ran down from his body as sweat. And he was heard, because in the resurrection he received what he sought.

He was heard: that is, he was heard apart from the number of all others, since after the warfare of his labor he was exalted by the Father above every creature; and this because of his reverence [Col. 1566D], that is, because, as the Son of God, he is worthy of reverence and veneration.

Or, “because of his reverence toward God”: that is, because above all things he revered and honored the Father. Or, “because of his reverence”: that is, as his religious devotion deserved. The shedding of his blood may likewise be understood as the loud cry in which he was heard because of the reverence of that same Passion. His reverence consists in his suffering without sin, for love alone.

Therefore greater confidence should be placed in him, because he did what no other high priest did when he offered himself as a victim for us. And indeed, while he was in the time of lesser status—that is, although according to divinity he was the Son of God—he learned obedience according as he is human. That is, he not only offered prayers and supplications but learned obedience in the Passion: he experienced in himself the labor of obedience. For one who has not experienced affliction cannot know the labors of the afflicted.

But Christ, insofar as he is human, learned obedience because he endured and sensibly underwent all the labors of obedience [Col. 1567A]. From the things that he suffered—that is, from the bitterness of the torments he endured—he learned obedience: that is, he came to know by experience the labor of obedience.

And “having been perfected”: that is, ended by the Passion; or “having been perfected”: that is, brought to the highest point, because he was raised to the Father’s right hand. He became the cause of eternal salvation, that is, of everlasting life, for all who obey him: that is, who obey his will, because he is sufficient for salvation for all without any carnal observances.

By his being heard, the resurrection is indicated; by his perfection, his exaltation. Or, he was perfected in every work of holiness when, after completing every act of his obedience, he said: “It is finished,” and gave up his spirit (John 19) [Col. 1567B]. Thus he became the cause not of just any salvation, but of eternal salvation; not for a few, but for all—yet on this condition, that they obey him. For otherwise they cannot obtain salvation.

And he can rightly be the cause of salvation for others, because he was named by God high priest, just as he himself truly showed this in his deeds. For because he fulfilled the office of high priest, was in all things obedient to the Father, and attained in himself so great a perfection of all good things that he was sufficient even for the salvation of others, therefore he was named by God high priest, and this according to the order of Melchizedek: namely, so that every order of divinity that could be discerned in Melchizedek might be discerned in him.

> “Concerning whom we have much to say, and difficult to explain, because you have become weak in [Col. 1567D] hearing. For although by this time you ought to be teachers, you again need to be taught what are the elementary principles of the beginning of God’s words; and you have become such as need milk, not solid food. For everyone who partakes of milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, for he is a child. But solid food belongs to the perfect: those who through practice have their senses trained to distinguish good and evil.”

Of this—that is, of the matter of how he is high priest according to the order of Melchizedek—we have a weighty discourse: that is, there remains another subtle discourse, containing profound mysteries, lengthy and great, and requiring interpretation, that is, having many expositions of sacraments and allegories to be set forth [Col. 1568A] for you, who are of limited capacity and would not otherwise understand unless it were interpreted. It is weighty and needs interpretation, not in relation to me, but in relation to you, who are weak in understanding profound mysteries, because you have become feeble—that is, without the spiritual staff by which your inner person may be supported, lest it stagger or fall. You are feeble in hearing, that is, in understanding, because the weight of these statements can easily cast you down, since you are not upheld by the strength of mature understanding. He inserts a rebuke concerning their weakness, so that they may strive to understand the lofty matters concerning Christ.

Truly, you are feeble in hearing. For although you ought to be teachers of others and adequate for their instruction, and this because of the time—that is, the length of time [Col. 1568B] already passed since you received the faith, and because it was preached to you before the rest—you again need to be taught, just as at the beginning when you came to faith, like children to whom the first elements of letters are given for understanding. Or, because of the time, you ought to have been teachers of others, since you had always been exercised in the Law and the Prophets concerning Christ. Yet again, as from the beginning, you need to be taught by others what are the elements of the beginning of the words of God: that is, that the works first learned when someone begins the words of God may be shown to you.

For those parts from which the discourse of God is first woven are called “elements”: namely, the incarnation, passion, resurrection, universal judgment, condemnation of the wicked, crown [Col. 1568C] of the righteous, and the rest, which are first proclaimed to converts. The beginning of the words is the Creed of the Christian faith, which these people not only did not understand, but did not even know the very text in which it is recited from memory. The beginning of the words is simple teaching. Its elements are the first matter of faith, such as Christ’s birth, passion, and so forth.

And through your own negligence you have also become such persons as, in the manner of infants, need milk—that is, humble and elementary instruction—and not solid food, that is, perfect doctrine. Milk, indeed, is a brief presentation of faith and an easy observance of morals. Solid food, however, is the rationale of faith itself and a perfect ordering of life. The solid food of wisdom is: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1); but milk is: “The Word was made flesh.” [Col. 1568D]

Truly, you do not need the solid food of wisdom, since you are nursing infants; for no nursing infant needs it. For everyone who partakes of milk, as you do—that is, whose portion is milk, and who is so tender that he cannot take in even the whole milk of simple doctrine, but only a part—is “without experience,” that is, without a share, in the word of righteousness which befits the righteous and perfect: that is, in the doctrine that pertains to those who have made good progress in understanding, possessing great capacity and the righteousness of religious conduct. He is without a share in this word because he is unable to comprehend or practice even a part of it.

Therefore the nursing infant does not grasp the word of righteousness because he is a little child in understanding; and just as a child in age does not distinguish foods and perishes by taking harmful ones, so [Col. 1569A] one little in mind—that is, unlearned—does not distinguish good from evil and sins by doing evil. You indeed need milk, as has been said, not solid food. But solid food—that is, the pattern of faith and instruction in morals—belongs to the perfect in understanding and action. Therefore, after drinking milk, you too ought to advance to the robust food of wisdom. This food belongs to those who have senses—that is, understandings—trained through the practice of reading and study in many Scriptures. They have their senses trained for the discernment of good and evil: that is, so that they may distinguish good from evil, good from another good, and evil from another evil, judging one greater and another lesser.

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 1569B] “Therefore, leaving the discourse of the beginning of Christ, let us be carried on to perfection; not again laying the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith toward God, of baptisms, teaching, and also the laying on of hands, and the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. And this we shall do, if indeed God permits.”

I said that solid food belongs to the perfect. Therefore let us be carried on to perfection, that we may be fed with solid food—I mean, leaving the discourse of Christ’s beginning, that is, the beginning of faith. For since we ought to have senses trained in the law of the Lord, let us therefore pass beyond the discourse of beginning and advance our understanding to further things.

The discourse of Christ’s beginning is the beginning of faith, by which Christ begins [Col. 1569C] to exist in us in understanding and action. For just as one introduced to the study of letters must first hear the elements, so a Christian must first of all be instructed in the Catholic faith, which is the foundation of our salvation. But leaving behind the discourse of this beginning, let us be carried on to perfection—we by teaching, you by hearing. Let us be carried thus: not again laying the foundation of repentance; that is, let us not repent negligently and thoughtlessly, as formerly. Repentance ought to be a foundation upon which good action and perfection are built and rise aloft.

For one lays the foundation of repentance—that is, does not set it firmly and orderly, but places it negligently as though it were a matter not well considered [Col. 1569D]—when he grieves and repents in such a way that he returns again to what he has not adequately mourned as committed. We have already laid a foundation in this manner, and therefore it has been destroyed: that is, our former repentance has perished and been rendered void by the return of those sins for which we had repented. But now, as we press toward perfection, let us repent perfectly, so that we may not again be laying—that is, negligently and carelessly placing—a foundation which may be scattered as before; rather, let it remain firm and stable, and no further foundation need be laid.

I mean the foundation of repentance from dead works: that is, repentance because the good works which formerly lived in us have died through the admixture of sin. For when someone falls into a grave sin, his prior good works are put to death [Col. 1570A] and perish. Hence the Lord threatens: “Even if I say to the righteous that he shall surely live, and, trusting in his righteousness, he does iniquity, all his righteous deeds shall be given over to forgetfulness” (Ezek. 33).

Or sins are dead works: that is, having nothing living in them, wholly lacking the life of righteousness, killing their authors. A settled repentance must be undertaken for all these things: that is, both for good things lost and for evil things committed. And let us not again lay the foundation of faith leading to God: that is, do not again negligently place faith in your hearts, as formerly, but place it firmly, so that it may no longer waver or fall as before, when you did not think it sufficient for righteousness and salvation without carnal observances.

Nor let us again lay the foundation of baptisms, so that [Col. 1570B] you seek to be washed again by the water of baptism—which is impossible. Rather, preserve the cleansing from sins which you received once in it, no longer seeking it through carnal observances. For he holds baptism wrongly who does not believe that all sins are washed away in it unless carnal observances are added. He said “baptisms” in the plural because there is baptism in water, baptism in the tears of repentance, and baptism in the blood of martyrdom.

Nor let us again lay the foundation of the teaching delivered to you at the beginning through the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, as though you had to begin again to be imbued with it. Nor let us again lay the foundation of bishops’ laying on of hands in the confirmation of the newly baptized, but hold it firmly. For whoever does not believe that through the laying on of hands [Col. 1570C] the Holy Spirit is given for remission and strengthening is not founded. Such is anyone who thinks that carnal observances help toward receiving the Holy Spirit, who is received through the laying on of hands.

Nor let us again lay the foundation of the resurrection of the dead, but hold firmly what we once believed about it: namely, that through Christ’s resurrection the dead shall rise. For whoever does not believe that Christ’s resurrection brings about the resurrection of the dead has no foundation upon which to build. If you knew that all sins are forgiven in baptism and that the Holy Spirit is given through the laying on of hands, the Law would seem superfluous to you; nor would you seek anything apart from Christ if you knew that through him [Col. 1570D] the dead will rise and be judged.

For neither ought we again to lay the foundation of eternal judgment, but hold firmly in our heart what has once been laid, so that we may expect a judgment only concerning faith in Christ and the virtues, without ceremonies of the Law. That judgment will be eternal, because whatever is decided there will endure forever. Whoever does not believe this judgment is without a foundation and can build nothing. Unless all these things have first preceded in the foundation, no one can act rightly.

For whoever converts anyone to faith makes him repent, believe in God, be baptized for the remission of sins, be taught what he ought to believe, be confirmed through the laying on of hands, and await the resurrection and the day of judgment, so that upon these things he may be able to build the structure of a good manner of life [Col. 1571A]. Therefore it is said of these things, “laying” all of them—that is, as a stone is laid in a foundation—not again, that is, not as formerly, nor so that, having fallen before, they may fall again; or, “not again laying,” that is, laying them now in such a way that it will no longer be necessary to lay them again.

All these things above have been called by the name of milk because the infancy of believers is nourished by them. Yet God wills that they be nourished with milk in such a way that they do not remain there, but, growing through milk, arrive at solid food. For if you feed with milk, feed so that there may be growth; grow in such a way that you eat bread.

I said, “Let us be carried on to perfection,” both in understanding and in progress of morals. We shall do this if God permits: that is, if he grants it by the nod of his will and the favor of his grace, because no one can advance to this perfection from free choice alone [Col. 1571B], unless God’s grace assists him. Let us be carried on to perfection in understanding and morals, not again laying the foundation of repentance, because it is impossible for those who have fallen gravely after becoming perfect to be renewed unto repentance. Let no one now oppose our words, but let him wait patiently a little while for us to explain these matters. For it follows:

“For it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, and have tasted also the heavenly gift, and have become partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have likewise tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and have fallen away, to be renewed again unto repentance, crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and holding him up to scorn. For the earth, often drinking the rain coming upon it and producing useful vegetation for those by whom it is cultivated, receives a blessing from God; but that which produces thorns and briars is rejected and near to a curse, whose end is in burning.” [Col. 1571C]

He says, “Let us be carried on to perfection,” not henceforth repeating the foundation of repentance, because the perfect cannot be renewed unto repentance after their fall. For those who have once been enlightened through faith—that is, who have received within themselves the light of faith, which is given once to believers—and have also tasted the heavenly gift—that is, have inwardly anticipated the light of faith, which is a heavenly gift; or, through its sweetness and savor as it were, have felt upon the palate of the heart the remission of sins given from heaven in baptism—and have become partakers of the Holy Spirit: that is, desiring a share in spiritual grace through the laying on of hands, or partakers of spiritual charisms, such as kinds of tongues and prophecy; and have tasted—that is, have perceived as savory in the mouth of the heart—the good word of God, no less than we, or no less than spiritual grace, concerning which he himself says: “My heart has uttered a good word” (Ps. 44 [45]); I do not mean according to which this Word was made flesh (John 1), but according to which it is the unchangeable supreme Good, by participation in which other words are good. They have tasted this such word: that is, have touched it with the taste of the heart, so that it tasted sweet to them; or they have sensed as savory and delightful the word of evangelical preaching [Col. 1572A].

They have also, as it were, tasted beforehand with the taste of the mind the powers of the age to come—resurrection, immortality, and impassibility—understanding those future powers of the body, that beauty and charity and lightness of the flesh, and the virtues to be in body and soul, and the blessed life with angels forever. Those who have reached such perfection and then, neglecting all these things, loving iniquity, have fallen away—that is, have voluntarily plunged into grave sins and lie delighting in them—it is impossible for them, after recovering all those good things which they lost, to be renewed again unto repentance, returning: that is, to put off through repentance the old nature which they have again assumed, and put on again the new person.

This is not because we approve here the heresy of Montanus [Col. 1572B] or Novatus, who contend that those who have crucified the Son of God for themselves cannot be renewed through repentance. But we say that it is impossible for such persons to be renewed because they do not wish to be renewed. For if they wished, it would certainly be possible. Therefore, their inability to be renewed is not an excuse based on their weakness, but the fault of their own will: they prefer to remain old rather than be renewed.

For their mind has become so cold toward the love of virtues and so inflamed toward the love of vices that by no reasoning do they consent to leave the sins to which they have obstinately clung. Therefore, by a most just judgment, they are left in their perversities by him who said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15); they are not helped by him, but are taken up by the devil, so that by him they may be [Col. 1572C] bound and burdened still more. Thus it comes about that they cannot return to repentance.

This is not because people, while they are in this world, cannot be changed for the better; rather, because, while they love vices from the depths of their heart and neglect virtues, they are neither divinely assisted nor can in any way be converted, but are oppressed by the ancient deceiver. Such are those who first advanced to the heights of virtue and afterward fell into the depths of vice: that is, fell utterly, or fell far away, or fell far from their former state, so that they lie for a long time in the very vices into which they fell.

We must not now understand by “those who have fallen away” devout persons who suddenly fell into some grave sins and quickly rose again, but those who, through long deliberation and long practice, have clung to vices and departed from purity of virtues; for it is rare that any such person is found to have done repentance, if indeed one is found anywhere. Therefore David is not understood as having fallen away in the commission of adultery and homicide, for which he quickly repented (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 2); but Solomon is understood in his love for foreign women, through whom he was separated from the faith and was unwilling to come to his senses, though divinely warned once and again (3 Kings [1 Kings] 2). [Col. 1572D]

Likewise Aaron is not understood as having fallen away when, through fear of the people or wishing to please them, he made the calf, since at Moses’ first word he repented (Exod. 32); but Balaam fell away through avarice: he loved the wages of iniquity and gave counsel as to how the people of Israel might offend their Creator, forgetting what he had previously prophesied and what he had heard from God (Num. [Col. 1573A] 22, 23, 24). He counted everything as nothing in order to satisfy his avarice.

Peter too did not fall away in that denial, because he immediately wept bitterly; but Judas did, through avarice, in that betrayal which he planned for a longer time and afterward carried out, and for which he did not perform suitable repentance (Matt. 26, 27). Thus we understand as having fallen away devout persons who, by a plan long devised, voluntarily subject themselves to wickedness and remain in it for a long time.

Such, moreover, are some today in monasteries: “having indeed a form of godliness, but denying its power”; and therefore they cannot repent, because they glory only in their outward habit and think themselves holy because they wear the garment of holiness. Rightly, then, it is said of such persons that it is impossible for them to be renewed [Col. 1573B] unto repentance, because either never, or rarely, is any one of them renewed. The Apostle therefore uttered this terrible sentence in order through fear to awaken to the pursuit of virtues the hardened minds of the Hebrews, who, after illumination and reception of the Holy Spirit, had relapsed into their former vices.

“They cannot,” he says, “be renewed, but are again crucifying the Son of God for themselves and holding him up to scorn,” that is, to mockery, because they extinguish and mock Christianity in themselves. For they crucify the Son of God in themselves and hold him in contempt while, despising his grace, they lie in sin. Such persons, as we have explained, cannot return to repentance; persisting in their perversity, they hasten toward eternal death.

For, by contrast, the good earth which produces good fruit deserves an eternal [Col. 1573C] blessing. This is the meaning: the earth—that is, the mind or the Church of faithful subjects—which, like soil, is cultivated by the plowshare of doctrine, drinking the rain of preaching and heavenly grace, that is, eagerly drawing in what comes down from heaven upon it through the mouths of preachers; and this often, because if it came rarely it would not suffice, while if it descended continually it would become cheapened. The earth, I say, which receives this rain in this way and produces vegetation—that is, brings forth good action—fitting for those by whom it is cultivated, that is, for the preachers by whose plowshare of doctrine it is broken and renewed, so that the action of subjects may accord with the words of teachers: this earth receives from God a blessing, that is, an increase of virtues in [Col. 1573D] this age and everlasting reward in the future, when it hears: “Come, you blessed,” and so forth (Matt. 25).

This earth indeed is blessed; but the one that produces harmful vegetation is cursed. But that which brings forth, so that they are visible, thorns—that is, graver sins—and briars—that is, lesser sins, or those more numerous and more sharply pricking, for a briar wounds with three points—is rejected by God, although it too receives the rain of doctrine and in place of good plants germinates briars and thorns. It is rejected, that is, has goodness behind it, like the one to whom God says: “You have cast my words behind you” (Ps. 49 [50]); and it is near to a curse, that is, to eternal condemnation, so as to hear: “Depart from me, [Col. 1574A] you cursed,” and so forth (Matt. 25).

It is not yet under the curse, but is near it, because return is still permitted; and unless it takes heed for itself, it is close to being condemned. Its consummation, that is, its end, if it persists in evil, will lead to burning, so that body and soul may be burned together without end.

Up to this point the Apostle has spoken terribly and harshly, in order to provoke the hard and sluggish minds of the Hebrews to repentance and the pursuit of virtues. But lest, by terrifying them, he cast them into despair and so make them remain in evil all the more, he then soothes them with gentle words and exhorts them to do good, saying:

“But, beloved, we are persuaded better things of you, and things nearer to salvation, though we thus speak. For God is not [Col. 1574B] unjust so as to forget your work and the love which you showed in his name, in that you have ministered to the saints and do minister. But we desire every one of you to show the same diligence unto the full assurance of hope, unto the end, that you may not become sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience shall inherit the promises.”

“I have spoken,” he says, “in order to draw you back from sins and make you more cautious through fear of despair.” [Note: [Col. 1573D] Perhaps *damnationis* (“of damnation”) should be read.] “Yet I am confident of better things concerning you. I do not say this because I think you are such people, but because I fear that you may be such; I frighten you with words lest you fulfill them in reality.

“We have spoken harshly, but we are confident concerning you, O beloved, whom we admonish out of excessive love [Col. 1574C], not from any obligation of superiority. We are confident, I say, of better things than that you should have fallen away, producing thorns and briars; and of things nearer to salvation than belong to those who cannot be renewed unto repentance and are near to a curse. We have a better confidence concerning you, although we speak so harshly in frightening and rebuking you.

“We are confident before God concerning you because formerly you did many good works, for which God will do good to you if you repent of evil things. For God is not unjust so as to forget your work. It would indeed be great injustice in God if he punished sins alone and did not accept good works. He will not forget your work so as to leave it unrewarded: you made your goods common to the saints, and this because of your love [Col. 1574D], through which you performed that work; for love of the saints stirred your heart to minister to them (Matt. 6).

“You did not conceal this love fruitlessly within, but showed it outwardly by good works as an example to others. Nor did you do these things for human favor, like hypocrites, but in his name, that is, for the honor of God. Thus you outwardly displayed to others in action the love which you retained in your heart, so that your light might shine before people, and that, seeing your good works, they might glorify not you but your Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5).

“You demonstrated love by work, because you ministered: that is, humbly, as subjects and servants, you supplied from your own resources what was necessary [Col. 1575A] to the saints, who had laid their goods at the feet of the apostles; and you still minister to them, persevering in the same good work. From these things you may know that God will not forget this, but will reward it.

“By these words it is clear that the preceding rebuke and the present consolation are not directed to the perfect, who had left everything and had one heart and one soul (Acts 4), but to the rest, who were unwilling to leave secular things and lived negligently and laxly. By the few good things that they had done, the Apostle attracts and restores their spirits and strengthens them.

“You have indeed ministered and you do minister; yet we do not want you to cease from this ministry as though what you have done thus far were now sufficient. Rather, we desire you to persevere in this action until the end. [Col. 1575B] We desire, that is, with great affection of charity we long for every one of you—so that not one may be lacking, but all may apply yourselves together—to display, that is, frequently to show others an example, the same diligence in ministering to the saints: that is, an eager readiness, so that you may act skillfully and promptly; and not merely for an hour, but until the end of your life.

“And this is unto the fulfillment of hope: that what you hope for may be wholly fulfilled in you in receiving eternal blessedness. We desire you thus perseveringly to minister to the saints until the end, so that you may not become sluggish—that is, without fire—in this diligence. That is, do not be torpid and lacking the fire of holy fervor; rather, do not fail ardently to love the saints upon whom you bestow bodily benefits, [Col. 1575C] but be imitators of those to whom you minister, and of the other saints, who will inherit—that is, possess by hereditary right—the promises: namely, the manifold gifts of everlasting blessedness, often promised. They will obtain them not through nobility of birth, but through faith and patience, because they gave faith to the promises themselves and, patiently awaiting them, suffered many adversities in the meantime.

“For when God made promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself, saying: ‘Surely I will bless you, and I will multiply you’ (Gen. 22). And thus, bearing patiently, he obtained the promise. For people swear by one greater than themselves, and an oath is the end of every dispute among them for confirmation. In this, God, willing more abundantly to show to the heirs [Col. 1575D] of the promise the unchangeableness of his counsel, interposed an oath, so that through two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge to hold fast the hope set before us may have the strongest consolation. We have this hope as an anchor of the soul, secure and firm, and entering even within the veil, where Jesus entered for us as a forerunner, having become forever a high priest according to the order of Melchizedek.”

He explains the promises which those who preserve faith and patience will inherit—namely, those which God made to Abraham. In these no room for doubt is left to us [Col. 1576A], when he promised them to Abraham and swore to him, and likewise to all his imitators in faith and patience. As though he said: From this you may see that those who have faith and patience will inherit the promises, because Abraham, who first began to hear them, thus obtained them. For God, promising Abraham—that is, making him a promise of future glory—swore, that is, firmly and unchangeably established it, by himself, that is, by his own unchangeableness. He swore by himself because he had no one greater than himself by whom to swear; for, if there were something greater, he would have shown the immovability of his promise by that.

He swore, I say, saying: “O Abraham, unless I continually bless you in your spiritual children, who shall be as the stars, I will bless you with an increase [Col. 1576B] of virtues; and unless I continually multiply you in your carnal children, who shall be as the sand, I will multiply you in future blessedness.” As though he said: Unless I do this, let no one henceforth believe me. For the incompleteness of the expression indicates the forcefulness of the assertion. Or: “Unless, by blessing you—that is, enriching you with virtues—I bless you,” that is, advance you so that you act in accordance with them; “and unless, by multiplying you—that is, enlarging you through a still more abundant fullness of virtues—I multiply you,” that is, make you blessed in the heavenly homeland with manifold recompense.

God thus promised by oath; and so, because God promised so firmly, Abraham, certain of the promise, did not immediately seek to receive it, nor did he murmur against God because of the delay. Rather, enduring patiently amid many adversities and waiting faithfully, he at last obtained [Col. 1576C] the promise—that is, what had been promised him. Or, “the promise,” because many things had been promised him in one promise. Likewise, therefore, those who keep faith and patience unto the end will inherit the promises, as has been said.

After this a reason is given why God swore in the promise, when it is said: “For men swear by one greater than themselves.” God swore because he was speaking to human beings, and human beings swear. For with God merely to promise is as firm as to swear. But he wished by an oath to make human unbelief certain. He swore by himself, since he had no greater one, because people swear by one greater than themselves—that is, by someone greater than themselves. For a person swears by that which he can find greater [Col. 1576D] than himself. Human beings swear, and an oath is the end of all their controversy—that is, dispute—when one affirms and another denies; for by an oath the dispute is ended. It is an end effective for the confirmation of the other party, that is, for producing complete certainty, because after the oath has been taken the matter is then certain and established for both parties.

And if a human being, who is a liar, is believed because of an oath, how much more God, who cannot lie? In this—that is, in consideration of the fact that he observed that every controversy is ended and confirmation produced by an oath—God interposed an oath: that is, he placed between himself and human beings a middle thing in which they might believe; or he placed an oath between the promise and the fulfillment of that promise. He, I say, [Col. 1577A] wishing from his own goodness to show more abundantly by swearing—for he shows abundantly by promising, but more abundantly by an oath—wishing, I say, to show the immovability of his counsel, that is, his secret rational ordering, known to few, since scarcely anyone knows that human beings are saved through faith in Christ; and wishing to show it to the heirs of the promise—that is, to those who will possess, by hereditary right and securely, the promise so often made.

Wishing to show these the firmness of his counsel still more abundantly by an oath than he had shown it without an oath, he interposed an oath among the promises, accommodating himself to human custom so that they might believe more fully and certainly what he had unchangeably ordained concerning them. Therefore he swore in the promise, so that through two immutable things—that is, promise and oath—which cannot be changed, by which he who is God is bound so that his counsel becomes immutable, because it is impossible for God to lie—that is, for him to lie in these two things, although he cannot lie in anything whatever—we may have in every tribulation the strongest consolation against pain and anxiety.

Or, “through two immutable things,” namely, that God swore and that he swore by himself; in neither of these can he lie, since he never lies. May we have most powerful consolation, that is, that which makes us strong in every adversity, willing to suffer for a time in order to reign eternally. [Col. 1577C] For when we suffer tribulation, if we look to the future glory promised us, we have refreshment of mind and alleviation of distress in the furnace of tribulation.

I mean us who, while tribulations pursue us and seek to assail us in every way, flee—that is, flee wholly—to hold fast the hope of the future rest, blessedness, and glory promised to us: not abandoning it because of adversities, but holding it firmly with all the strength of the soul. This hope is offered to all; or it is “set before” us, having been openly placed before us from ancient times in Abraham and the other fathers as an example. Whoever despises all tribulations in hope of blessedness flees to this hope; and it is useful for us to flee to it and hold it, which we have [Col. 1577D] as an anchor—that is, as a restraint and support—of our soul, lest it be shattered on the rocks of adversities in the sea of this world.

For as an anchor holds and steadies a ship, lest it be submerged by the violence of winds and the rising storm of the sea, becoming the sport of sea and waves, so our hope, fixed in heavenly things and irrevocably clinging to the glory it desires, holds the faithful soul and strengthens it against all such assaults as against storms at sea. It fortifies the soul in its purpose, lest it fail, as though broken upon the rocks of adversities and tribulations; and it restrains it from sinking through consenting to wickedness. This hope, I say, is safe, that is, fearing nothing; and firm, that is, unshaken, so that it does not even waver. For hope in heavenly things strengthens the mind so that it is not shaken by the waves [Col. 1578A] of earthly disturbances.

That is to say: hope exercises in us the likeness of an anchor, which holds a ship lest it be shattered on rocks, makes it safe so that it does not fear submersion, and firm so that it cannot even waver. And I call this hope “entering,” that is, introducing us by hope even to the inner places beyond the veil: to the heavenly and hidden things themselves, which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the human heart (1 Cor. II; Isa. LXIV). These are still veiled to us while we live in the flesh—that is, covered by the veil of our ignorance—and yet our hope penetrates even to them.

The sands to which an anchor is fixed and clings are hidden and cannot be seen; nevertheless sailors are secure, although they cannot see the things to which the arms of their anchors [Col. 1578B] have firmly adhered. So also we, set amid the waves of this world, do not see heavenly things; yet through hope we are so joined to them that no assault of fear can move us.

It should also be noted that, when he says “entering even to the inner places beyond the veil,” he alludes to the history which relates that there was a veil between the two tabernacles, veiling the hidden things of the inner tabernacle. Into this the high priest entered once each year, and it prefigured the secret of inward blessedness. Into these inner places and secrets of the eternal homeland Jesus entered according to his humanity—Jesus, that is, our Savior, who according to his divinity is always everywhere. He entered for us, that is, for our salvation, to intercede for us, as the high priest entered the Holy of Holies to pray for the people. And he entered [Col. 1578C] as a forerunner for us, so that we too might run thither after him. He is a runner because no sin hindered him; a forerunner both in time and in dignity; forerunner for us, who are to be brought in.

He, I say, was made by God high priest: that is, making for us a bridge and access to the Father by interceding for us, offering the obedience of his passion, and presenting himself before the Father for the salvation of the human race. And this he does forever: not only while the present age endures or while we live, but he also performs the work of high priest in the future—not then offering for our sins, since there will be none, but so that the good which he has wrought in the good may remain unfailing and stable. He is high priest, not according to the order of Aaron, but according to the order of Melchizedek [Col. 1578D], who alone was king and priest and exercised the office before circumcision, so that not the Gentiles should receive priesthood from the Jews, but the Jews from the Gentiles. Nor was he anointed with oil as Moses ordained, but with the oil of gladness and purity of faith. Nor did he sacrifice animals, but consecrated Christ’s priesthood with bread and wine. It is therefore clear that Christians are superior to Jews and possess a sacrifice better than animal victims: namely, rational service, which leads to heaven.

## Chapter VII

> “For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of the most high God, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings (Gen. XIV) and blessed him—to whom Abraham also apportioned a tenth of everything—first, indeed, being interpreted king of righteousness, and then also king [Col. 1579A] of Salem, which is king of peace; without father, without mother, without genealogy; having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God, he remains a priest forever.”

After the Apostle had warned them to advance toward perfection, so that they might become capable of that great and interpretable discourse, and had urged them toward this in many words, he returns again to his subject and to that great discourse concerning Christ’s high priesthood. Thus he may set Christ above all the high priests of the Old Testament, and gradually proceed to show that carnal observances ought to cease through the transfer of the priesthood.

First he explains what order preceded in Melchizedek, and how Christ was made high priest forever according to his order. Once the order of Melchizedek has been expounded and commended, it may appear how worthy is Christ’s priesthood, which is so great that Melchizedek’s priesthood foreshadowed it—not as an equal, but as a shadow. For when a great shadow is shown to have preceded, it is sufficiently evident that the great reality of the body follows. As though he said: I rightly compare Christ’s high priesthood to Melchizedek’s order, because this Melchizedek was king of Salem.

But Salem, we should not believe—as Josephus [Note: [Col. 1579D] Book I of *Antiquities*, ch. 1.] and very many of our writers suppose—to be Jerusalem, but a town near Scythopolis, which even today is called Salem. Melchizedek’s palace is shown there, its ruins displaying ancient magnificence by their size. Concerning it Genesis later says: [Col. 1579C] “Jacob came to Succoth and crossed into Salem, a city of the region of Shechem” (Gen. XXXIII). For Salem, a town of the metropolitan district of Shechem, rather than Jerusalem, lay on Abraham’s route as he returned from the slaughter of enemies whom he pursued as far as Dan, now called Paneas. Of it we also read in the Gospel: “John was baptizing at Aenon near Salem” (John I).

Melchizedek was king of this city; he was also priest, so that he might prefigure the kingship and priesthood of Christ, who also made us a royal and priestly race (1 Pet. II). He was priest not of idols but of God, because, although he was a Gentile and not of Jewish descent, he was priest of God—not of Jupiter or Apollo, but rather of the most high God, Creator of all things [Col. 1579D], who is above all. And Christ is priest of God the Father, who once offered the victim of his body and blood on the cross (John XIX), just as Melchizedek is read to have offered bread and wine.

He, I say, met—that is, went out to meet—Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings, when Abraham was held by people to be of the greatest dignity: in the very moment of triumph, returning not from flight but from slaughter, not of one king but of many. Hereby Melchizedek’s great dignity is shown: Abraham, a stranger in that land, recognized him as so exalted that he judged him worthy to approach, although he was both king and priest [Note: [Col. 1580D] An obscure passage.], and to give him tithes from all the spoils [Col. 1580A], and to turn first to him, from whom he was to receive a blessing, rather than to his own home.

Melchizedek not only met this triumphant man, but also gave him a blessing. Abraham, having received the blessing, apportioned to him a tenth of all that he had brought with him from the slaughter of the kings. By Lot, who, after losing his goods, was led into captivity, is signified the soul bowed down by the burden of vices through the five bodily senses and enslaved to the lord of hostile power. Abraham strives to loose its bonds when reason, recognizing the soul’s captivity, arms itself with the shield of faith, the helmet of hope, and the sword of God’s word; and, taking up a band of virtues as though household servants, vigorously attacks the battle-lines of vices. It fights until, having overcome its enemies, it frees the soul.

After the kings are slain, Abraham returns with Lot, rejoicing as he goes back to his own country. He finds Melchizedek meeting him on the way, offering sacred food and blessing him. For after vices have been extinguished, rational strength hastens to bring the freed soul back to the joys of paradise and the home of the heavenly homeland; but before it arrives there, it finds Christ, the true king and priest, coming to meet it and offering it the food and drink of his body and blood, and the blessing of heavenly grace—that is, granting an increase of virtues. For he joyfully comes to meet those victorious over vices, to receive them and refresh them with sacred nourishment; and he blesses—that is, advances and multiplies them in virtues and increases them with spiritual gifts.

No one but a victor ought to receive his food; for no one should presume to approach the Eucharist [Col. 1580C] unless he has first defeated the kings against whom he fights—that is, unless, with the Lord’s help, he has overcome the vices that have fought within him. Otherwise he eats and drinks judgment upon himself (1 Cor. II). Abraham, however, gave the priest Melchizedek tithes of all that he had taken from the enemies. So every faithful person, rejoicing after victory in his struggle, offers tithes to Christ: that is, he ascribes the perfection of all his good works and the completion of his virtues to divine grace. But if he sees anything imperfect or less suitable in himself, he retains that for himself—that is, he attributes it to himself.

For ten, beyond which the number does not proceed but repeats, signifies perfection; just as the nine parts which Abraham retained for himself [Col. 1580D] signify imperfection. Whatever is first, best, and perfect is signified by ten, in which number is first completed. Everything chief and perfect in us must be attributed to God; everything imperfect must be ascribed to ourselves.

“First, indeed,” and so forth. The Apostle notes the very words in order to show that all these things are in Christ in the order in which they preceded in Melchizedek. He is first interpreted “king of righteousness,” but then also “king of Salem,” which is “king of peace.” This fittingly applies to Christ, who reconciles the things in heaven and the things on earth (Col. I), who governs his own by righteousness amid the storms of the age [Col. 1581A], reigns in their righteous conduct, and afterward does not cease to govern them and reign in them in eternal peace.

Melchizedek is first, for us, king of righteousness and afterward king of Salem, because he first rules us in righteousness and afterward will rule us in peace. First he obtains in us now the kingdom of righteousness; then after this life he will possess in us the eternally tranquil kingdom of peace.

Melchizedek, I say, was “without father, without mother.” This does not mean that he was without father and mother, since Christ too had both father and mother according to his two natures. Rather, it means that he is suddenly introduced in Genesis as meeting Abraham returning from the slaughter of enemies (Gen. XIV), and neither before nor afterward is his name recorded. Hence he is said to be without genealogy, although perhaps he had a wife and children; and without beginning [Col. 1581B] or end, although without doubt he had a beginning by birth and an end by death. He is said to lack all these things because Scripture says nothing of them concerning him.

Or, genealogy is the account of preceding fathers; he lacks this because it is not discovered from which fathers he descended. The Holy Spirit chose, by a higher counsel, to be silent about this concerning him, so that he might in every respect bear the figure of the Lord. For Christ is without father according to the flesh, because he was born from a virgin without male intercourse; and without mother according to divinity, because that ineffable generation remains in eternity. He is without genealogy—that is, without the begetting of children—because he had no children of the flesh; but he remains without offspring, without any carnal succession. Or because he had no preceding fathers [Col. 1581C] in his divinity. He has neither beginning of days nor end of life, but exists coeternally with the Father according to divinity.

This too should be noted: when Melchizedek is said to be without father and without mother, priests of the New Testament are to be chosen not for the nobility of their parents but for the merit of their own lives. Attention should not be paid to what parents they had, but to what merit they possess. Melchizedek is also without genealogy because priests of the New Testament and ministers of the altar may not have wives. If they wish to have them, let them profess themselves priests of Jewish institution, not Christian.

Melchizedek has neither beginning of days nor end of life because his priesthood—that is, the priesthood [Col. 1581D] of Christ and the Church—is eternal both toward the past and toward the future. But Aaron’s priesthood—that is, that of the Jewish people—had both beginning and end. Christ’s priesthood lacks beginning and end because we were chosen in him before the foundation of the world, and he intercedes for us without end (Eph. I).

Such and so great is Melchizedek; but in all the respects mentioned he was made like the Son of God, because in all things he bore the shadow of the truth that shines in Christ, and he remains priest forever. This does not mean that he is still alive exercising priesthood, but that Scripture does not recount the end of his priesthood (Num. XX). For of other priests we read when they died and that others succeeded them in their place; for example, we learn how Aaron died and who succeeded him as high priest [Col. 1582A]. But we do not read that Melchizedek ever died or lost his priesthood. For just as Moses was silent concerning his death, so he nowhere reported that Melchizedek ever ceased to hold or lost his priesthood.

Therefore he remains priest forever because no other priesthood succeeds his priesthood, as another succeeds the Levitical priesthood; rather, his institution will remain as long as the world stands. For he offered bread and wine to God for Abraham, and every day priests offer bread and wine to God for the salvation of believers. The bread and wine themselves become Christ’s body and blood and remain forever, so that they confer eternal life upon worthy recipients.
