For these reasons Melchizedek is rightly said to remain a priest forever: because no other rite will be instituted by which his offering is changed, and because he signifies Christ perpetually interceding for us.

> “Consider now how great this man was, to whom Abraham the patriarch gave even tithes from the choicest spoils. And indeed, those of the sons of Levi who receive the priesthood have a command to take tithes from the people according to the law (Num. XVIII), that is, from their brothers, although they too came forth from Abraham’s loins. But he whose descent is not counted among them took tithes from Abraham (Gen. XIV), and blessed him who had the promises; and without any contradiction, what is lesser is blessed by what is better.”

The Apostle dwells upon the commendation of Melchizedek’s dignity, setting him above Abraham, whom the Jews [Col. 1582C] exalt and glory in, and whom they wish to set before Christ, saying: “Are you greater than our father Abraham?” (John VIII). As though he said: From what has been said above, you have seen what Melchizedek was like. But now consider—that is, consider inwardly—how great he is. Consider, that is, with inward sight and great diligence, as you inspect some great thing, how great in dignity, holiness, and perfection this man must be understood to be. Abraham, who was patriarch—that is, prince of fathers, whose holiness the fathers imitated—gave him not only many other marks of reverence, but also tithes. He gave him tithes not of inferior things but of the chief and better things, such as horses, garments, breastplates, and other things that might seem chief among the rest [Col. 1582D].

Hence he appears to be of supreme and immeasurable greatness, since the father of other fathers gave him tithes, regarding himself as far inferior to him and him as the better man, to whom he offered the better and choicest things. As I said, Melchizedek received tithes from Abraham, whereby he is preferred to Abraham, and thus to all the sons of Levi, that is, the priests of the old law.

Indeed, it is thus apparent how much he surpasses all those priests: not all the sons of Levi, but certain of his sons, receiving the priesthood through the election and consecration of others, have a command to take tithes; otherwise they would not dare to do so. They have this command according to the law—that is, according to the law’s institution—without whose authority they would never presume to act. Thus “according to the law” means not otherwise than the law commands: namely, that they receive neither more nor less, nor in another manner, than is decreed in the law.

They receive from the Hebrew people—that is, from their brothers. That is, they receive from people whom they do not surpass in dignity except because they were appointed priests under the law. For so great is the excellence of priesthood that even those alike in descent are much more worthy than their brothers. They took tithes, I say, from the people, yet not from inferiors, such as proselytes, but from their brothers according to the flesh, who were not inferior; although those brothers who gave the tithes also came from Abraham’s loins [Col. 1583B], that is, descended from Abraham’s stock. Thus, although both priests and people were equal in the origin of their lineage, the people were compelled by the precept and authority of the law to pay tithes to them.

But Melchizedek received neither priestly office nor consecration from any human being, nor did he have a command to take or demand tithes from anyone. And whereas Levi’s sons received tithes not from inferiors but from equals, namely their brothers, he received from Abraham not as from an equal or brother but as from an inferior, because he was not of that stock. For Abraham would not have given tithes to an uncircumcised foreigner unless he knew him to be more excellent—a person to whom even the Levitical priests paid tithes.

Levi’s sons received from brothers; but he whose genealogy—that is, whose posterity of children, because there is none, or even if there were, it is not counted among them—is not numbered among the sons of Levi, nor said to have any blood relationship with them [Col. 1583C], took tithes from Abraham. He so surpassed Abraham in all respects that no compulsion can be understood to have occurred when Abraham paid him tithes from all things, as the Jewish people were compelled by a certain force and necessity to give tithes to their priests.

The sense of these words is briefly explained thus: Melchizedek is shown to be worthier and greater than Levi’s sons because he took tithes from Abraham, greater than all of them, as from an inferior; whereas the Levitical order received not from those inferior to itself but from brothers. For if Levitical priests were superior even to those equal in descent, that is, to their brothers, by the consecration of priesthood and institution of the law, because they received tithes from them, then Melchizedek is still more worthily preferred to Abraham, from whom he received tithes as a priest from a layman, and to Levi’s sons, whom he tithed in Abraham’s loins.

Yet Melchizedek and Abraham are not read to have been of the same descent, so that they could even be equals in lineage. And if Melchizedek, who was sign and shadow, is preferred to Abraham and all Levitical priests, how much more Christ, who is truth and body? He said that Melchizedek took tithes from Abraham and also blessed him, by which his great excellence is declared: he blessed so great a patriarch, one who had—that is, so firmly believed as though he already possessed—the promises [Col. 1583D], namely, the divine promises repeatedly made to him. He blessed—that is, consecrated—him: he blessed the man to whom God had promised blessing.

Abraham was made more holy by Melchizedek’s blessing; he did not bless Melchizedek, but gave him tithes as an inferior gives to a superior. Abraham received a blessing from him; and without any contradiction it is true that what is lesser is blessed by what is greater or better. No one can contradict this reasoning; all know it to be established that everything which is blessed is less than the one blessing it. For everyone who receives blessing from another is proved, by that very reception, to be lesser. But Abraham, as has often been said, received blessing from Melchizedek at the time of his greatest dignity, when he returned triumphantly from battle. Therefore he cannot be denied to be lesser. And if the type of Christ, namely Melchizedek, is greater than him who had the promises, how much greater is Christ himself!

[Col. 1584B]

> “And here indeed dying men receive tithes; but there Scripture testifies that he lives. And, so to speak, through Abraham even Levi, who receives tithes, was tithed; for he was still in his father’s loins when Melchizedek met him.”

Consider also the dignity of Melchizedek for another reason. Here indeed—that is, in this passage of Scripture where Levitical priests are discussed—dying human beings receive tithes: human beings daily tending toward death through many miseries. That is, Scripture speaks of them as human beings, some of whom die and others succeed them. But there, where the discourse concerns Melchizedek, Scripture testifies that he lives, since it speaks of his life and says nothing of his death. By this he is sufficiently shown to be worthier than all other priests. For the whole Scripture concerning him together testifies that he lives. And since Levi’s sons are dying while he lives, it is apparent which is to be preferred.

It is still further clear in another way that he is greater than Levi’s sons: Levi, who received tithes, paid tithes to Melchizedek himself. That is, Levi—that Levitical tribe from which God chose priests—and the chosen order itself, which received tithes from all others, was tithed by Melchizedek, that is, paid tithes to him through Abraham. Levi himself did not personally, as a circumcised priest, give tithes to an uncircumcised man. But, if this expression be accepted as stated, he was tithed not in himself but through an intermediary—namely, Abraham, his father. Levi, the father of the priestly line, was still in his father’s loins [Col. 1584D], that is, had not yet come forth from them by generation, when Melchizedek met Abraham.

Therefore the whole Levitical order was bound to Melchizedek in the same obligation and subjection in which Abraham its father was bound. Levi was still one thing with Abraham, because he was afterward begotten from him. Therefore he necessarily is subject to the one to whom his father was subject before he begot him. Hence it is clear that the priesthood of the Jews is subject to the priesthood of Christians. For Levi was tithed through Abraham by Melchizedek, because he was still in the loins of the father who gave tithes.

For just as those who were in Adam’s loins sinned when Adam sinned, so those who were in Abraham’s loins were tithed when Abraham gave tithes [Col. 1585A]. But this does not follow in Christ, although he was in the loins of Adam and Abraham, because he did not proceed from them according to the concupiscence of the flesh. For he too was not tithed there, whose flesh derived from that source not the heat of the wound but the material of the remedy. Since the tithing itself belonged to prefiguring the remedy, that was tithed in Abraham’s flesh which was healed, not that from which healing came. Thus Christ is not inferior to Melchizedek, because he was not tithed by him as the Levitical order was, which paid him tithes through Abraham.

The same flesh of not Abraham only but of the first human being himself had together both the wound of transgression and the remedy [Col. 1585B] for the wound. The wound of transgression was in the law of the members resisting the law of the mind (Rom. VII), which is transmitted, as it were, by a seminal principle through all flesh propagated from there. But the remedy for the wound was in that which, without the act of concupiscence, was taken from there in bodily matter alone from the virgin through the divine manner of conception and formation, for participation in death without iniquity and for an example of resurrection without falsehood.

> “Therefore, if perfection were through the Levitical priesthood—for under it the people received the law—what further need was there for another priest to arise according to the order of Melchizedek, and not to be called according to the order of Aaron? For when the priesthood is transferred, there must necessarily be a transfer of the law.”

Up to this point he has preferred Christ’s priesthood, which is according to the order of Melchizedek, to the Levitical priesthood; and now he adds that Christ’s priesthood destroys the Levitical priesthood, and that, once this has been destroyed, the law according to carnal observances must also be destroyed. As though he said: Since it was said above that Christ is priest according to the order of Melchizedek, and all who possess the law know this was to happen, what necessity was there for this new priest to arise not according to Aaron but according to Melchizedek, under whom perfect righteousness would be given?

If consummation—that is, perfection of righteousness—was through the Levitical priesthood, that is, was given or accomplished through it, why was another new priest still prophesied to arise according to another order [Col. 1585D]? For if the Levitical priesthood, as the Jews supposed, brought perfection, another priest according to Melchizedek would arise in vain. But another does arise, and not in vain, since he was foretold by a divine oracle. Therefore the former did not bring perfection.

But why it seemed to bring perfection is explained by the addition of a reason: “for under it the people received the law.” Since the law was given under that priesthood, and perfection was thought to lie in observance of the law, perfection was thought to come through that priesthood, because the law was both given under it and administered by it. Yet perfection was not through it. For if it had been, another priest would never have been sought, one who would give perfection according to another order.

This is the point. If perfection of righteousness, as the Jews supposed, was through the Levitical priesthood, then after that old priesthood had given perfection, what further need was there—what cause, what benefit—for God to say through David that another priest would arise, when he sang: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX), and did not say “according to the order of Aaron”? This is the true priest, because he both frees from sin and supplies every completion of righteousness, which those priests were utterly unable to do.

Therefore it was necessary that another should arise after them, according to another rite and another manner. The people received and held the law under that priesthood, and the old priesthood is changed when the new priesthood comes. Hence the law likewise must be changed. For once the priesthood [Col. 1586B] has been transferred into a new priesthood, a transfer of the law into a new observance must necessarily follow. Since both were given together, by the same giver and under the same pledge, what is said of one must be understood of the other. For the law cannot remain without priests to administer it; once the priesthood is destroyed, the law also is destroyed, since it can stand only under that priesthood. But the priesthood has been destroyed or transferred.

> “For he of whom these things are said belongs to another tribe, from which no one attended at the altar. For it is evident that our Lord arose from Judah, concerning which tribe Moses said nothing about priests. And this is still more evident, if another priest has arisen according to the likeness of Melchizedek, who was made not according to the law of a carnal commandment, but according to the power of an indissoluble life. For Scripture testifies: ‘You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.’”

It shows that the priesthood has been transferred, and thus that a transfer of the law has consequently taken place. Truly the priesthood has been transferred, since it has passed both to another tribe and to another rite. For he concerning whom—namely, in consideration of whom—these things are said, that is, the Lord Jesus, for whose commendation we undertake these arguments, is not from the tribe of Levi but from another tribe, from which no one ever stood ready at the altar; that is, neither lesser nor greater person from that tribe approached the altar according to the law in order to minister by priestly right [Col. 1586D].

Truly this new priest, who possesses an eternal priesthood, is from another tribe: namely, Judah. And it was fitting that he who was to abolish the sacrifices performed according to the order of Aaron in the Levitical priesthood should be from another tribe, not from the Levitical one, lest the cleansing of sins which he accomplished by the offering of his true sacrifice—himself—should seem to belong to that priesthood which was temporarily the shadow of things to come. He is from another tribe. For it is manifest that this same Lord of ours sprang from Judah, that is, from the tribe of Judah, so that the same tribe might be royal and priestly, as Melchizedek was king and priest. In that tribe Moses said nothing concerning priests; that is, he did not say that anyone from it should be a priest or possess anything priestly [Col. 1587A].

Therefore, since the Lord Jesus, who is from another tribe, received the priesthood, it is clear that the priesthood has been transferred and can no longer remain in the tribe of Levi; and consequently the carnal observances given under it can have no further standing after this. “I have given,” he says, “above, a sufficiently clear and fitting reason; and besides this I now give another, from which it will be still more manifest and evident to everyone that the priesthood has been transferred.” It is manifest that it has been transferred through the tribe, and it is still more manifest through the rite, because this is the clearer and firmer proof. More abundantly—that is, more widely and clearly—it is manifest that the priesthood has been transferred if it is observed according to another rite: namely, if another priest has arisen according to the likeness of Melchizedek [Col. 1587B]; that is, if the Lord Jesus arose above all others in order by his offering to cleanse his people from all sins, which no other was able to do. And just as Melchizedek gave Abraham consecrated bread and wine, so this priest also gave his disciples his body and blood under the same species.

He was not made priest according to the law of a carnal commandment—that is, according to what the law commands carnally—because he was not anointed priest with material oil, nor were carnal sacrifices offered for his ordination; but according to the power of an indestructible life, that is, eternal life, which can neither be dissolved nor corrupted nor destroyed, and which is given through the Holy Spirit, by whom Christ was invisibly anointed priest. And truly he was anointed priest according to the power of an indestructible life [Col. 1587C], because he remains forever. For the prophet, or God the Father, bears witness together with me: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

> “Indeed, there is a setting aside of the preceding commandment because of its weakness and uselessness. For the law brought nothing to perfection; but there is the introduction of a better hope, through which we draw near to God—and this, so far as it goes, not without an oath.”

He had given reasons why the priesthood was transferred; now likewise, as followed from this, he sets forth the cause and reason for the transfer of the law, saying: “Indeed, there is a setting aside of the preceding commandment,” that is, of the ancient law, because of its weakness, that is, its feebleness and incapacity. For it had to be shown why the old commandment [Col. 1587D], which commanded carnal ceremonies to be observed, was rejected although God had given it, and why a new one was substituted. Therefore there is a setting aside—that is, a repudiation—of the preceding commandment, because it was weak and ineffectual. For the preceding commandment is set aside in order that there may be room for the grace which follows. It is called “preceding” because another was to follow. The old preceded the new as a shadow precedes a body. But as the shadow passes away and is reduced to nothing when the body comes, so does the old commandment when the new comes.

For that commandment of carnal observances was weak, that is, insufficient in itself to confer justification. For what cannot by itself alone accomplish righteous things is judged weak. Such was the law, which could justify no one without the help of grace. It was also useless [Col. 1588A], that is, unable to confer true benefit, because it could not give the kingdom of heaven to its worshippers; and now it is wholly useless—that is, conveying no benefit whatsoever, indeed harmful—if it is observed after Christ’s coming. Truly it is rejected because of weakness, because the law brought nothing, that is, no human being, to perfection. For even if some were perfect under it, they did not receive perfection from it but from grace. For although the law accomplished something, it did not fully justify. It could neither wholly overthrow the kingdom of sin, nor give perfect innocence or perfect righteousness, nor procure eternal life; it could only promise temporal goods.

[Col. 1588B] It instilled fear of death but did not give love of righteousness; nor did it reign in the depths of the heart, although it was observed outwardly in works. Therefore it was rightly rejected. That law was indeed rejected, but in its place comes the introduction of a better hope: that is, grace of the new law penetrates our heart and is introduced into it to reign there, granting us hope of eternal life, which the ancient law could not give. That law promised temporal things; this promises eternal things. This hope also bestows the completion of virtues, making a person hope not for a security that soon passes away, nor for abundance of temporal riches, nor for a multitude of children, but rather for eternal life, unfailing salvation, and God being all in all. Through this hope we draw near to God, because, while we despise earthly things [Col. 1588C] and desire heavenly things, we approach God in mind, reform his image within us, and desire to cleave to him, so that we may become one spirit with him.

There is the introduction of a better hope; and how great and wonderful it is that this occurs not without an oath but with an oath. For when God swears that Christ is priest forever, who will intercede for us without end, he grants us a better hope with an oath.

> “Others indeed were made priests without an oath; but this one with an oath, through him who said to him: ‘The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever.’ Thus Jesus has become the guarantor of a better covenant.”

It is a great thing that God gave us such hope in Christ’s priesthood [Col. 1588D] with an oath. For the others—that is, the Levitical priests, far different from him—were made without an oath, as though subject at some time to change; but this one, who was never to be changed, was made with an oath through him who can do all things, namely God the Father, who said to him with an oath: “You are a priest forever.” This is the sense. But, to show more plainly that God swore, he inserts the very words of the prophet affirming it: “The Lord has sworn,” that is, he has established it by unshaken truth, “and will not repent,” that is, he will not alter this priesthood for any reason.

For God does not repent as a human being repents. Yet any alteration by him of something he had instituted, which was thought to remain [Col. 1589A], is called God’s repentance. Accordingly, when he says, “He will not repent: You are a priest,” and so forth, he sufficiently shows that he did repent of the institution of the former priesthood—that is, that he willed to change the priesthood which he had established according to the order of Aaron. Hence it is sufficiently apparent how much worthier this priest is than all those priests. The Lord swore concerning this one that he should remain forever; to that extent Jesus himself became the guarantor of a better covenant, that is, the promiser of a better inheritance than they. For through the Old Covenant they promised an earthly and temporal inheritance; but through the new covenant he promises a heavenly and eternal one.

A testament, indeed, was called the written instrument of an inheritance which one who was dying left to the person whom he appointed as heir after himself. And the Lord Jesus [Col. 1589B], dying, left us the New Covenant, in which he promised that we should be heirs of the kingdom of heaven; and he willed himself to be priest and mediator of that same covenant. But the Old Covenant was dedicated with the blood of brute animals, and therefore promised an earthly inheritance to old humanity. Jesus the priest is therefore far better than those former priests: he has a better covenant and a better promise.

> “And the others indeed were made priests in greater number because they were prevented by death from remaining. But this one, because he remains forever, has an everlasting priesthood. Hence he is able to save forever, approaching God through himself, ever living to intercede for us.”

In the fact that the others were made priests without an oath, while this one was made with an oath [Col. 1589C], his excellence appears, as has been said; it also appears in this: the others are many because they die, whereas this one is one because he lives always. For the others—that is, the Levitical priests, greatly unlike him—were made priests, not one but many through many successions, while some died and others succeeded, because they were prevented by death; that is, because death prevented them from remaining in this life. They were therefore established in succession, one after another, because the necessity of death intervened and prevented them from remaining in their office—that is, from remaining altogether. Each of them did remain for a time, but none remained permanently. But this one [Col. 1589D], of whom we speak, remains; this one whom we intend to magnify has an everlasting—that is, eternally enduring—priesthood: the office of giving sacred things to the people and of interceding for them.

For no one now succeeds him in the priesthood, nor does his priesthood have an end, because he himself remains forever. “For, having risen from the dead, he dies no more; death will no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. VI). Thus, because he remains and possesses an enduring priesthood, he can save forever. The Apostle shows that his priesthood destroys the old priesthood and the old law, and now commends his activity. “Hence,” he says—that is, he who has the everlasting priesthood, which the whole multitude of priests does not possess—“is able not only to intercede for us but also to save,” that is, to give salvation [Col. 1590A] to those whose high priest he is, not temporarily but forever.

Here the folly of those who thought that Christ could not suffice for salvation without carnal observances plainly appears. He can save eternally, because even his name indicates it: Jesus, that is, “Saviour.” He, I say, approaches God not through some intermediary—not through an angel or through another creature worthier than himself—but through himself, entering into participation in the divine secrets, in order that he might know the Father’s will and render him gracious and favorable toward sinners. This is said after the likeness of someone wise and powerful who is admitted to a king or other great person not through another but enters in his own person and accomplishes whatever he wills.

Rightly, then, he approached through himself [Col. 1590B], since all others approach through him, as he himself says: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John XIV). Or, he approached God to propitiate him for us not through others’ victims but through himself, offering himself upon the altar of the cross. He, I say, lives always after the resurrection in order to intercede for us, because everlasting life was given him for this purpose: that he might always intercede with God the Father as a good mediator for our life and glory. Although he lives for his own glory and as the reward for his obedience, yet he also lives in order always to offer himself—that is, to show himself to the Father—for our glory and exaltation. From that nature in which he is high priest, namely the human nature which he brought into heaven, he intercedes and pleads for us. Therefore, because he approaches God through himself and always lives [Col. 1590C] to intercede for us, and always has a living priesthood, it is clear that he can save us forever. Other priests, however, neither live forever nor can save.

> “For such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens.”

I said that he approaches God through himself and lives always to intercede. For it was fitting—that is, appropriate—that we, his children, should have such a high priest. Servants, however, had others. Ours had to be holy, that is, complete in himself in every perfection of virtues; innocent with respect to his neighbor, never doing anything harmful to anyone; and undefiled, that is [Col. 1590D], one whose holiness and purity was never defiled by consent to or delight in any sin; and separated from sinners, that is, set apart from the company of sinners, so that he was held by no stain of sin among their company, being conceived and born without carnal concupiscence through the Holy Spirit.

Or: holy inwardly, innocent in his hands, undefiled in body, separated from sinners—that is, free from every sin and separated from the company of the other priests, among whom none is without sin—and made higher than the heavens, in order that he might minister there at the heavenly altar. Or, he is separated from sinners because his dwelling is no longer among mortals, who, as long as they are in this life, cannot be without sin; and he was made higher than the heavens, that is, elevated above all heavenly creatures [Col. 1591A], so that his greatness or sublimity surpasses the greatness of the highest angels to such a degree that no comparison can be made between him and the angels in greatness and excellence.

> “He has no need, as the priests do, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people; for this he did once, by offering himself. For the law appoints as priests men who have weakness; but the word of the oath, which came after the law, appoints the Son, perfected forever.”

He further shows him to be worthier than the Levitical priests and powerful to save. Since he is such as he has described, he has no need to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins, as those priests [Col. 1591B] had to do because they sinned daily and required daily cleansing. He says that he has no need to offer daily, not because he intends us to understand that this one ever had such a need, but in order to remove from him what belonged to them. He has no need, as they did, to offer on each day first for his own sins and then for the sins of the people. He does not need to offer daily, because he did this once—not for his own sins, but for the people’s sins.

Nor did he do this by offering a bull or goat, but himself, because no other victim was to be found that could worthily be offered for the people’s expiation; nor any other priest worthy to offer it. For what priest was so righteous and holy as the only Son of God, who had no need to cleanse [Col. 1591C] his sins by sacrifice, neither original nor actual sins? And what could be offered for human beings more fittingly than human flesh? What was more suited to immolation than mortal flesh? What was more pure against the worldly vices of mortals than flesh born in a womb and from a virginal womb without any contagion of carnal concupiscence? And what could be more acceptably offered and received than the flesh of our sacrifice, made the body of our priest?

Thus, since four things are considered in every sacrifice—what is offered, to whom it is offered, by whom it is offered, and for whom it is offered—the same one true mediator, reconciling us to God by a sacrifice of peace, remained one with him to whom he offered; made one in himself those for whom he offered; and was himself both the one offering [Col. 1591D] and what he offered. He offered this once, because repetition was unnecessary. It was sufficient for all, and therefore need not be repeated. For this sacrifice is so great that, although it is one and was offered once, it suffices for eternity.

I said that the priests needed to offer daily not only for the people’s sins but also for their own. This was because the law appointed as priests men who were not yet immortal but still had weakness: that is, men frail with respect to sin and, through the very corruption of nature, mortals inclined toward it—mere human beings, unable to escape the condition of human frailty. Therefore, as was said, it was necessary for them to offer for their own sins as for the people’s. Phinehas needed this remedy (Num. XXV), Jehoiada needed it (II Chron. XXIV), Zechariah needed it, Aaron himself needed it, and any others who lived laudably and righteously in the former priesthood [Col. 1592A]. Our priest alone was free from this necessity.

The law indeed appointed such men (Exod. XXVIII), but the word of the oath spoken after the law by the prophet David—that is, the Father’s promise made with an oath—appoints as priest not a weak human being inclined to sin, but the Son, equal [to the Father] and perfect in every holiness, so that this perfection never has defect or end but remains forever. For he was perfect whom frailty did not cause to sin. And he remains perfected forever because his perfection can never be diminished; or because he was appointed priest forever, not temporarily like the other priests. The word of the oath [Col. 1592B] is after the law, lest, if it had been in the law, the Jews should say that the oath was fulfilled in the law through their priesthood. It is after the law, therefore, so that the law may thereby be shown insufficient. For if it had been sufficient, nothing else through which it was to be fulfilled would have been proclaimed after it. This also shows that this priest belongs to another rite and priesthood than that according to the law. From all these things it is clear that he can approach God through himself and save forever, and that the law’s carnal observances are superfluous.

## CHAPTER VIII

> “Now the chief point concerning the things being said is this: we have such a high priest, who sat down at the right hand of the throne of Majesty in the heavens, a minister of the holy things and of the true tabernacle, which God pitched, and not a human being.”

[Col. 1592C] From the point at which he said, “Hence he is able to save forever,” he demonstrated by many reasons that he is able to save. Now also, by a brief, summarizing argument, he wishes to prove the same thing and add something more certain. It is as though he said: “I have said much about him, but now I make a summary of these matters—that is, a brief comprehension.” A *capitulum* is a brief compendium of many things, so called because it briefly contains the whole sum. For its diminutive form, *capitulum*, denotes brevity; and its derivation from *caput* (“head”) or *capio* (“I contain”) signifies that it contains a great meaning and is a brief head of many matters that are discussed at length.

“I speak,” he says, “in many ways about Christ’s high priesthood; but what I now add is the chief point [Col. 1592D] concerning the things I have said thus far about him.” That is, this brief statement which I am now going to make surpasses the many things said above, because it contains a worthier praise of Christ and declares more firmly and certainly that he is able to save forever. For although it was said above that he had been made higher than the heavens, it was not thereby necessarily proved that he had been exalted above the heavens in such a way that he could not be elevated higher. But this is now plainly stated in the summary, so that we must understand him to have been exalted so greatly that he cannot ascend higher, cannot become greater, and sits with the Father on the throne of majesty, when it says: “We have such a one,” and so forth. For here the summary begins.

“We have such a high priest,” that is, one so glorious, so exalted, so powerful, [Col. 1593A] “who sat down,” that is, sits with the Father on the royal throne of majesty—namely, reigns, judges, and rests with the Father. And this is “at the right hand of the throne of Majesty in the heavens,” that is, he sits with the Father in such a way as to remain in equality with the Father’s kingdom: he is equal to the Father in kingship and possesses the greatness of the kingdom’s glory with the Father in heaven, that is, in the heavenly homeland, so that all the powers of heaven may glorify him as they glorify the Father. Therefore, he who is known to be equal to God in kingship and in the governance of all creatures is well able to save his own forever and bring them to eternal life.

Or, “sat down” means that he sits according to both soul and body—that is, rests and remains—at the right hand of the throne of Majesty in the heavens: that is, in the superior share of the rest of God, who is greatness in the heavens [Col. 1593B], that is, in the holy angels, since he makes them great by dwelling in them. And the Father himself, who is the greatness of the heavens, could not magnify him more than by exalting him above all things in eternal blessedness.

Since this high priest so worthy and so powerful always works our salvation, it fittingly follows: “a minister of the holy things.” For he begins already in the present to minister to us the eternal blessedness signified by the Holy of Holies, giving charity and perseverance; and in the future he will minister it more perfectly. “For he will gird himself and, passing by, will minister to those whom he has made recline in the kingdom” (Luke XI). The heavenly kingdom is called the Holy of Holies, that is, the worthiest of all the other holy things, because there holiness is lived perfectly [Col. 1593C], where life exists in us without awareness of sin. There, indeed, nothing is done that displeases God or offends the eyes of majesty.

Christ ministers this Holy of Holies to us when he now grants a religious life, so that we can say: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III); and afterward introduces us into that very hidden place of eternal blessedness, saying: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. XXV). Or, he is minister of the holy ones and priest appointed by the Father to minister every good thing to those who are already in the Holy of Holies, that is, in the sanctuary of perpetual blessedness. Or rather, he ministers to God as the true high priest for us in the Holy of Holies, while he always shows the Father the flesh assumed for us and presents the remembrance [Col. 1593D] of his passion, that he may incline him toward mercy for us.

Thus he is minister of the holy things and of the tabernacle—not a shadowy or prefiguring tabernacle, but the true tabernacle, that is, the tabernacle signified: namely, the eternal sanctuary signified by Moses’ tabernacle. But because that earlier tabernacle was in a way also true, that is, furnished with real skins and curtains, it is added: “which God pitched,” that is, established and founded as firm and inviolable, “and not a human being,” that is, so that human activity was not mixed into it. For when Moses, helped by God, pitched the old tabernacle, God pitched it there with a human being. But this true tabernacle—that is, this blessed and serene dwelling and glory of the eternal sanctuary—God alone pitched; God prepared it from the beginning [Col. 1594A] for his elect.

There he is now high priest, interceding for them without interruption, just as formerly the high priest alone entered once a year into the Holy of Holies of the old tabernacle in order to pray for the people. That high priest was a minister of the holy things, prefiguring this our Redeemer, the minister of eternal blessedness. Into that blessedness he entered with the flesh which he made a sacrifice for us, in order there to pray for the salvation of the people. This has been said concerning the summary. After its conclusion, there follows:

> “For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices. Hence it is necessary for this one also to have something to offer. Therefore, if he were on earth, he would not even be a priest, since there are those who offer gifts according to the law, who serve a copy [Col. 1594B] and shadow of the heavenly things, as Moses was instructed when he was completing the tabernacle: ‘See,’ he says, ‘that you make everything according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain’” (Exod. XXV).

I said that Christ is a minister. For every high priest is appointed to minister: every high priest, greater or lesser, is appointed according to the law to offer gifts—such as the firstfruits of crops and the loaves of presentation—and sacrifices, such as the slaughtering of bulls and goats. That is, every high priest was appointed for this purpose, that he might offer and through the offering obtain for the people what he requested. Hence, because everyone is ordinarily appointed to offer, it is necessary that this our high priest also have something with him in heaven [Col. 1594C] which he may continually offer for us.

This is to say: because every high priest is a minister, it follows necessarily—unless the universal assertion is false—that this one too is a minister. For, when we say that everyone offers, we understand that everyone ministers; for this is his office, to offer and minister to the Lord. And because this one also must have something to offer for the salvation of the world, therefore, if that thing were on earth—that is, if something could have been found in this world which could worthily be offered for the sin of the whole world—not even any priest would be worthy to offer that sacrifice, although there were those who offered according to the rite of the law. Therefore Christ, the pure priest, offered himself as a pure sacrifice.

Or, better thus: since he sits at the right hand of the throne in heaven and is [Col. 1594D] there a minister and, after the manner of a high priest, offers, therefore if he were still on earth—that is, if he had not yet entered into the Holy of Holies, namely the inner places of heaven—I would not say that he would be high priest, but that he would not even be a priest. This necessarily proves that, if the high priest who can save forever offers and intercedes for us in heaven, then the Jews’ sacrifice is no longer necessary for us. Since the sacrifice offered once upon the altar of the cross is sufficient for the washing away of all sins, carnal shadows are therefore superfluous, since truth acts for us in truth.

Since he is high priest and minister in the true tabernacle, and entered through his own blood into the true Holy of Holies, if after his resurrection he had remained on earth and wished to exercise the priesthood [Col. 1595A] in the shadow, he would not be called a priest, because he would be performing the priestly office superfluously; nor could one from another tribe become a priest under the law. He would not, I say, be a priest while there were still many other priests from the tribe of Levi performing their priesthood according to the commandment of the law. The shadow and the priesthood of the law had to remain only until the true priest should offer the true sacrifice in the tabernacle signified and in truth. He could not perform the true priesthood on earth, nor acquire the priesthood of the law, while many others were offering victims and gifts according to the law. For one born from another tribe would not be admitted to the priesthood under the law, and he would offer carnal things superfluously while those of the tribe of Levi were sufficient [Col. 1595B] to offer such things.

Nor could he in any way be priest “on earth,” that is, in carnal things, lest he might seem to offer those same things more worthily. Therefore it adds concerning those priests, “who serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things”: that is, they serve earnestly and zealously, fulfilling everything completely; and thus he himself would assume this priesthood in vain. They still today “serve a copy and shadow,” not because the copy and shadow remain in reality, but with respect to the representation of Scripture, which still treats the order of their priests as though their office were presented before our eyes.

They serve and are subject to the law, offering sacrifices and performing carnal observances according to the law’s commandment. These were a copy and a kind of figure of heavenly things. [Col. 1595C] And because there is some pattern in which a greater reality exists than in the thing of which it is the pattern—as Christ is the pattern of all the faithful and even of heavenly things—the text sets the shadow of earthly things under God in order to show that the copy is less worthy. The old tabernacle is called a copy of heavenly things, that is, of the Church, one part of which is in heaven and the part yet to come journeys on earth, because the spiritual Church was made in likeness of it. And as a shadow is inferior to a body, so that tabernacle was a shadow and empty in comparison with the Church.

“They serve a copy,” he says, that is, figures; and because a copy is sometimes a reality rather than a figure, as a book according to whose likeness another book is made, he adds, “and shadow.” For all the things done in that tabernacle were only [Col. 1595D] a shadow of truth, soon to pass away when Christ came. They serve a copy, that is, the old tabernacle, which is a copy of heavenly things, just as Moses was instructed—not when he began, because he had already expressed many things in figures, but when he was completing the tabernacle. For, unable to complete it by himself, he consulted the Lord, who taught him concerning the figures as concerning the truth.

“See,” says the Lord, that is, consider carefully, “and make all things necessary for the tabernacle in such a way that in everything you follow the pattern of heavenly things shown to you on Mount Sinai” (Exod. XXV; Acts VII). A *pattern* (*exemplar*) is that according to whose likeness something is made; an *example* (*exemplum*) is the likeness derived from it. On the mountain the Lord showed Moses the reality; but because the carnal [Col. 1596A] people could not grasp it, he commanded that Moses represent it in figures, so that, nurtured by them, that childish people might someday come to the truth. Thus the thing first shown is called the pattern of the figures made in accordance with it.

Again, the figures are called the pattern of the truth afterwards fulfilled in the Church, as they prefigured it; for whatever was there signified either the heavenly or present Church, or the virtues of the saints now existing. The shadowy Jewish priests served this pattern of heavenly things—that is, the figures of true realities. Since those things were patterns of the heavenly and spiritual realities which have now been and are being accomplished in the Church through Christ, the pattern and shadow are no longer necessary.

Yet it should not be passed over carelessly that the pattern of heavenly things is said to have been shown to Moses on the mountain [Col. 1596B]. For, remaining forty days on Mount Sinai with the Lord, he saw the sublime life of angelic purity and immortality. He was commanded to establish human conduct on earth in its likeness, insofar as mortals could imitate it, so that, by devoting ourselves on earth after their example to mutual love directed toward God, divine praise, unanimous peace, sincere chastity, and other such virtues, we might merit to be their companions also in heaven.

Moses therefore showed us, through the precepts of the law, a pattern of the angelic way of life which he saw on the mountain of contemplation, through the observance of which we too, born from earth, may arrive at fellowship with the angels in heaven. He likewise set before us a pattern of a more perfect life and blessed recompense in the figure of the tabernacle and of priestly and Levitical ministry [Col. 1596C]. Therefore, as has been said, the angelic purity shown to Moses was the pattern of the figures which he fashioned in constructing the tabernacle; and in turn those figures were the pattern of ecclesial religion and salvation. Therefore Christ, who is truth, could not possess a priesthood in figures and shadow.

> “But now he has obtained a more excellent ministry, inasmuch as he is also mediator of a better covenant, which has been established upon better promises.”

He said above that Jesus could not be a priest on earth, that is, in connection with earthly and legal sacrifices. And the reality itself shows this to be so, since the Lord Jesus never held a priesthood under the Law. But now, [Col. 1596D] that is, in the time of grace, in this last age, he has obtained—meaning that he did not presumptuously seize it by usurpation, but received it freely from God the Father by the election of divine grace—a better ministry of priesthood, inasmuch as his law too is better than the old law.

The Apostle now passes from priesthood and sacrifice to the difference between the Testaments, in order to show how greatly the New surpasses the Old. The ministry which Jesus has now obtained at the end of the Law is so much better and more beneficial than the ministry of the former priests as he himself is mediator of a better Testament, that is, of the new Law. That is: just as you see that the Testament of which he is mediator is more effective for eternal life than the Old, so you can see that his ministry is better than that of the former priests, who profited their [Col. 1597A] subjects but little. Moses was mediator of the Old Testament, which he received from God and delivered to humankind, as he himself said: “I stood as an intermediary and mediator” (Deut. V). But the Lord Jesus is mediator of the New Testament because, standing between God and human beings, he gave it by reconciling us to the Father.

This Testament is better than the Old because it gives better commandments and supplies the aid of grace by which they may be fulfilled. For in the Old Testament, on account of the weakness of the Jews, it was permitted that a man should put away his wife if she displeased him and should hate his enemy (Deut. XXIV); but in the New no reason is permitted for putting away a wife except fornication, and we are commanded to love our enemies and to do good to those who hate us (Matt. XIX). Hence it is clear that Christ [Col. 1597B] gave a better and more perfect Testament, more efficacious for eternal blessedness.

That Testament is holy, that is, ratified and confirmed so as to endure. And in what is it ratified? In better promises. For this reason it is more binding and firm than the old one, because it promises better things to those who fulfil it. For earthly things are promised in the former, heavenly things in this one. The commandments of both Testaments are, indeed, found to be almost entirely the same. For “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; honour your father and mother” (Exod. XX; Matt. XIX; Mark X), and other such things, are commanded to us as well. But the sacraments are not the same, nor are the promises the same. The commandments are the same because according to them we ought to serve God. [Col. 1597C] The sacraments are not the same because some sacraments give salvation, while others promise salvation. The sacraments of the New Testament give salvation; those of the Old promised the Saviour. The promises likewise are not the same, because there earthly things are promised, while here heavenly things are promised.

Finally, everything promised to the Jews has been taken away. For where is their kingdom? Where their Temple? Where their anointing? Where their priest? Where among them now is a prophet, since he has come who was preached through the prophets? In that nation none of these things now remains. Hence it is clear that the Old Testament, according to its carnal observances and earthly promises, is now nothing.

“For if that first had been free from fault, surely no place would have been sought for a second. For, finding fault with them, [Col. 1597D] he says: ‘Behold, days shall come, says the Lord, and I shall consummate over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah a new testament’” (Jer. XXXI), “not according to the testament which I made with their fathers on the day when I took their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt” (Exod. XIII, XIV), “because they did not remain in my testament, and I neglected them, says the Lord. For this is the testament which I shall establish for the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: giving my laws into their mind, and I shall write them upon their heart. And I shall be their God, and they shall be my people. And no one shall teach his neighbour, [Col. 1598A] and no one his brother, saying: Know the Lord; because all shall know me, from their least unto their greatest, because I shall be merciful toward their iniquities, and I shall remember their sins no longer.’”

He proves that Christ’s Testament is better than the Old. For the former is not free from fault; this one is. If it had been free from fault, a second would not have been given. But it is given. Thus it appears that the former was imperfect, this one perfect. The former was not free from fault, that is, it was not without sin, because it did not perfectly cleanse its observers. For it virtually contained the fault itself when it commanded without grace and made transgressors. And because it was kept through fear of punishment rather than love of righteousness, it did not justify their minds. [Col. 1598B]

Moreover, in outward action it allowed them certain criminal things to be pardonable because of their weakness: for example, to put away a wife when she displeased them; and if anyone beat his male or female slave even to death, provided that the slave survived for two or three days, he would be judged innocent (Deut. XXIV; Exod. XXI). Therefore it was not free from fault: that is, it did not render its observers blameless, much less fully justify them. For if it had been wholly free from fault, so that none of its worshippers had fault in them but were fully justified, there would not have been sought a place—that is, an opportunity—for a second Testament. And I say this “surely,” that is, in the truth of the matter.

It was burdensome to the Jews that a New Testament should be sought for the destruction of the Old; therefore the Apostle makes this assertion [Col. 1598C] to restrain their unbelief. But God sought the fitting place and time at which he ought to give the second. [Note: [Col. 1597D] An obscure passage.] For, wisely ordering all things, he first gradually instructed, guided, and advanced them through what had gone before, so that afterward he might give the perfect Testament. “A place for a second would not be sought,” that is, throughout all that had preceded there would not be inquiry into when it could suitably be given, unless it were better. But such inquiry is made.

For God, through Jeremiah, finding fault with those who served the Law—that is, reproaching them with their defect—says: “Behold,” that is, it is manifest, “days are coming,” that is, the time of grace gradually draws near, in which the faithful will be enlightened with manifold brightness. And, says the prophet, I do not say this on my own authority, but the Lord says it, whom you do not dare to contradict. [Col. 1598D] Therefore he prefaced this with the Lord’s authority, because he was about to speak concerning the change of the Old Testament, which the Jews were unwilling to hear.

The Lord says that days are coming—that is, the bright time of grace—and in those days “I shall consummate,” that is, by completing and perfecting it, I shall give the New Testament. For it will be so complete and perfect in all its commandments and ordinances that it will have nothing deserving rebuke and will contain every perfection of righteousness. Thus it will be supreme, that is, above all other Scriptures, because it will advance its observers to the height of utmost perfection. This is called New, while the other is Old. For the former Testament is called Old because of the fault of the old human being, which was by no means healed through the letter that commands and threatens; [Col. 1599A] but this one is called New because of the newness of the Spirit, which heals the new human being from the defect of oldness.

“I shall consummate this Testament over the house of Israel and the house of Judah,” that is, over the Jews, who after Solomon were divided into two kingdoms (III Kings XII). For the ten tribes who lived in Samaria were called the house of Israel, whereas the tribes of Judah and Benjamin were called the house of Judah. I shall consummate the New Testament over these, so that it may rule them and have them subject to it.

Or the house of Israel and Judah are the children of Abraham, of whom it was said to him, “For in Isaac your seed shall be called” (Gen. XII). “For not those who are children of the flesh are children of God; but the children of promise are reckoned as seed” (Rom. IX). This is the house of Israel and the house of Judah, on account of Christ who came from the tribe of Judah: the household of the children of promise, that is, not of their own works but of God’s beneficence. [Col. 1599B]

The interpretation of the names also agrees: Israel is called “most upright of God,” or “a man seeing God”; Judah, however, “confession.” The house of Israel is the family of the perfect, who are God’s house and dwelling-place because they maintain the highest uprightness in action and in some measure behold God in contemplation. But the house of Judah belongs to those who, by confessing their sins, cleanse the house of their own breast so that it may become God’s dwelling-place. Over all these the New Testament is consummated, so as to hold them entirely subject to itself and to surpass their understanding and perfection. For no one is so perfect [Col. 1599C] that in this Testament he cannot find means to make continual progress as long as he lives.

“I shall give them,” he says, “a New Testament, and I shall do this not according to that Testament which I made with their fathers,” because in it I shall not follow the rite of the Old, so as to command carnal things and promise earthly things. Behold: it was prophesied that that Testament would not endure but that another, New Testament would come. Yet it is foretold as to be destroyed not according to its spiritual sense but according to its carnal sense.

But because God had made a spiritual testament with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, he specifies: “Which I made,” he says, “on the day when I took their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt”; that is, at the time when, showing them the light of my knowledge, I took the hand of those unable to rise from the mire by themselves, just as a nurse takes the hand of a small child, or as one draws someone out of a pit by the hand or leads him along. [Col. 1599D] I took them thus in order to lead them out of the land of Egypt, that is, out of the place of slavery and affliction, from which they could not escape by themselves.

He calls that whole period one day, from the time when he began through Moses in Egypt to provide for them and care for their salvation until he brought them into the land of promise. Rightly, indeed, does he signify the whole span of that time by the name of one day, because he always appeared to them and always dealt mercifully with them. And during part of that day he gave them the Law among his other benefits, after he had powerfully freed them from Pharaoh’s hand.

Therefore, he says, [Col. 1600A] I shall give a New Testament, not according to that which I then gave their fathers, because “they did not remain,” that is, did not remain in every respect, “in my Old Testament.” For although they observed it carnally through fear of punishment, nevertheless they did not understand it spiritually nor fulfil it out of love for righteousness. Or, “they did not remain” means they did not persevere, because they made the calf at Horeb (Exod. XXXII), afterward worshipped Baal-peor, and then served many idols (Num. XXV). And because they did not diligently keep my law, I too, repaying them in kind, neglected them: that is, I did not care for their protection and salvation, but regarded them as nothing or of little account. Nor need you doubt, he says, if I say that they were neglected, because the Lord says it.

When he says that they did not remain in the Testament, [Col. 1600B] and so forth, he finds fault with them, as the Apostle had previously stated, and shows that the first Testament was not free from fault. For he attributes to their fault the fact that they did not remain, lest the Law itself should appear blameworthy.

Truly, I shall now give a Testament not according to that which I gave their fathers, because “this is the Testament which I shall establish,” that is, which I shall arrange in different ranks: so that some in it may leave everything and follow me; others may lawfully use worldly things; some may be continent; others married; and each may keep the form of his own order. This I shall establish for the house of Israel, that is, for Abraham’s seed, namely the children of promise, “after those days”: that is, not now in the time of the perfection of these people, but after the completion of those days which have been prescribed and [Col. 1600C] preordained with me. And this says the Lord, that is, he who is almighty, to whose will nothing is impossible and to whom all things are subject.

I shall establish this Testament in this way: namely, by giving my laws—or, I shall give my laws—not on tablets of stone as before, but into their mind, so that they may be written there not with ink but with the Holy Spirit, and portrayed in their understanding and in the good will of their soul. For they will fulfil my Testament out of love for righteousness and delight in virtues, and will understand my will in all things; nor will they have a veil over the face of their heart. But the Jews did not understand what had been laid upon them; they always kept the Law through fear of punishment and unwillingly.

“And I shall write them”—namely, the laws—“upon their heart”: that is, I shall place them so that they remain there as though written, cannot be removed from it, but endure in their understanding and will, and as it were remain above and rule them. But what are these laws written in hearts by God himself except the very presence of the Holy Spirit, who is “the finger of God” (Exod. VIII)? By his presence love is poured out in our hearts (Rom. V), and this is the fulfilment of the Law and the end of the commandment.

For since the promises of the Old Testament are earthly and external, now the good of the heart itself is promised: the good of the mind, the good of the spirit, that is, intelligible good, when it is said, “I shall give my laws into their mind,” and so forth. Thus he indicated that they would not fear a Law terrifying them externally, but, having it inwardly, would love the righteousness of the Law itself.

Then he added the reward: “And I shall be their God, and [Col. 1601A] they shall be my people.” This is what another prophet says: “But for me, it is good to cling to God” (Ps. LXXII). What is better than this good? What is happier than this happiness: to live for God, to live from God, “with whom is the fountain of life, and in whose light we shall see light” (Ps. XXXV), so that in him may be reward, in him the end, in him the perfection of blessedness?

Accordingly he immediately added: “And no one shall teach his neighbour,” and so forth. For there it will not be necessary for one to teach another, because no one there will be ignorant; all will behold God himself, the fountain of knowledge. For then they will see him not through a mirror in an enigma, but face to face (I Cor. XIII), as he is in the beautiful form of his own substance (I John III); and in him they will possess every good and every delight.

Thus all will then be perfectly [Col. 1601B] wise, so that no one will any longer teach his neighbour whom he loves, nor his brother whom he loves more, saying to him, “Know the Lord.” Why will one not tell another to know the Lord? Because no one will be ignorant of him, nor will a teacher be needed, for “all shall know me from their least unto their greatest”: that is, neither their greater nor their lesser ones will be ignorant of me. He calls them lesser and greater because there each of the saints will be judged greater or lesser according to the measure of his merit: “for star differs from star in glory” (I Cor. XV).

Or he intended “the lesser” to mean those later in time, and “the greater” those earlier in time. For all will receive the promised contemplation of God at the same time; and therefore those who arrived later are found, as it were, prior because they have been delayed less, as is shown by the parable of the Gospel denarius, which those who came later to the vineyard received first (Matt. XX). [Col. 1601C] Hence it is by no means now said, “from the greater unto the lesser,” but “from the lesser unto the greater, all shall know me.”

This, then, is the difference between the Old and the New Testament: the former is written on stone, the latter in the heart; there the reward is land, here the vision of God. Between God and human beings nothing separates except sins, which are remitted only through this same grace. Therefore, after saying that all will know me from their least unto their greatest, he immediately adds: “because I shall be merciful toward their iniquities, and I shall remember their sins no longer.” As though he said: They will truly know me by manifest [Col. 1601D] vision, because I shall remove the wall that stood between me and them and separated them from my face.

“Because I shall be merciful toward their iniquities”: that is, through the gift of my grace I shall mercifully forgive them all the things that they have done unjustly—that is, unequally—against their neighbours; and I shall no longer remember the sins which they have committed in themselves without offence to their neighbours, because I shall neither reproach them for these nor punish them on their account nor hold them in lower esteem.

This propitiation may also be understood in reference to this life, as if he said: They will come to such great glory in the future age and, entering the kingdoms of heaven, will be raised to behold my majesty, because while they still live here, I shall be merciful toward their iniquities, blotting them out through the grace of the New Testament [Col. 1602A]; and I shall no longer remember their sins then, after their expiations.

“But by saying ‘new,’ he has made the first old. And what is becoming old and ageing is near to destruction” (Heb. VIII.13).

God said, “I shall consummate a New Testament over the house of Israel.” But by saying “New”—that is, in saying “new”—he made the first old: he taught that the Old was to end in this way. For he would not have said “New” except in relation to the Old. Or, “he made the first old” means that it became old and was weakened by a kind of old age; and from the time of Jeremiah, when the Holy Spirit said that he would give a New Testament, he had already made the first old.

But what becomes old—that is, whatever begins to become old among inanimate things—and ages—that is, begins to possess old age [Col. 1602B] among living things—is near destruction: that is, it is now only a little distance from death. For antiquity and old age foretell death. This may be seen in all animate and inanimate things. When they become old and age, they are near death. But the first Testament was already becoming old when Jeremiah, in the promise of grace, named another as New; and thus it was already near destruction. Therefore, when Christ came much later, it was necessary that it should perish in its carnal observances, since it had drawn so near to death long before.

## CHAPTER IX

“The former Testament indeed also had ordinances of worship and an earthly sanctuary. For the first tabernacle was made, [Col. 1602C] in which were the lampstands, the table, and the presentation of the loaves, which is called the Holy Place (Exod. XXV, XXXVII). But behind the second veil was the tabernacle called the Holy of Holies, having a golden censer and the ark of the testament, covered on every side with gold, in which were a golden vessel containing manna, Aaron’s rod which had budded, and the tablets of the testament; and above it were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy-seat (Num. XVII). Of these things it is not now necessary to speak individually.

“But when these things had thus been arranged, the priests continually entered into the first tabernacle, performing the offices of the sacrifices. But into the second, the high priest alone entered once a year, not without blood, which he offered for his own ignorance and that of the people; [Col. 1602D] the Holy Spirit thereby signifying that the way into the holy places had not yet been revealed while the first tabernacle still retained its standing. This is a parable of the present time, according to which gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot make the worshipper perfect with respect to conscience, being imposed only with regard to foods, drinks, various washings, and ordinances of the flesh, until the time of correction.”

We have said that the former covenant grew old and failed through old age, so that the new might arise, in which perfect righteousness would be given; and this is indicated by the thing itself and cannot be denied. For that former covenant once indeed had ordinances of worship, but now has them no longer; it also had a worldly sanctuary, that is, a tabernacle or temple [Col. 1603A], which it now lacks. Hence it is manifest that the covenant itself has failed through age.

Or it may be connected thus. The New Testament, which is written in the heart, justifies perfectly. Yet the former covenant also gave a certain righteousness, because it too once had ordinances of worship—that is, it made some of its worshippers righteous insofar as it restrained their hands from committing sin and caused them to perform some good deeds; but it was never able inwardly to justify the conscience. And it had a holy place, that is, a sanctuary. It was called holy because it had been consecrated to God’s honour. But it was worldly, that is, composed of worldly and transitory things. For gold and silver, precious stones and wood, and the rest from which that sanctuary was made, are things [Col. 1603B] belonging to this world, passing away with the world and containing no permanence in themselves. The Old Testament possessed all these things; but now, as we have said, it possesses none of them. For when it is said, “It indeed had,” it is understood, “but now it does not have”; for the word *indeed* suggests this. It lacks both tabernacle and temple, and can no longer justify its worshippers, but rather repels them from righteousness and makes them sinners.

“A first tabernacle was made, in which were the lampstands and the table and the presentation of the loaves, which is called the Holy Place.” Now he explains that worldly sanctuary. Truly the former covenant had a worldly sanctuary. For a first tabernacle was made, and so forth. It is called the first tabernacle in relation to the second. Moses, at the Lord’s command and according to his specification, made both first and second [Col. 1603C]; nevertheless, the two were one tabernacle, divided by a curtain suspended in the middle. This tabernacle was thirty cubits long, ten broad, and ten high, having a flat roof throughout, as houses are customarily built in Egypt and Palestine. But in the middle hung a curtain, by which the sanctuary and the Holy of Holies were divided, arranged so that twenty cubits of the length belonged to the first chamber and ten to the second. Thus what the Apostle now calls the first tabernacle was twenty cubits long and ten broad, while the second was ten cubits long and ten broad.

In the first tabernacle, on the south side [Col. 1603D], was a lampstand with seven branches, which the Apostle now calls “lampstands”; and on the north side stood a table, upon which were the twelve loaves of presentation. Outside, before the entrance of the tabernacle, stood the altar of burnt offering. This tabernacle, together with the things in it, was called “the Holy Place”; that is, both that tabernacle and the objects within it were called holy because they had been consecrated for prayer, the worship of God, and praise. But beyond the curtain—that is, beyond the curtain hanging in the middle—was the second tabernacle, called “the Holy of Holies”; that is, this tabernacle itself with the objects in it was called the Holy of Holies, holy through God, so that the things in the first tabernacle might not seem holy in comparison with them.

And that second [Col. 1604A] tabernacle contained a golden censer, in which the high priest burned incense for the people’s welfare. It also contained the ark of the covenant—that is, the ark which held the covenant, namely the ten commandments of the law—covered with gold all around, that is, on every side, exterior and interior, since it was gilded not only outside but also inside. In this ark, namely, was a golden jar containing manna, because Aaron is read to have placed in the tabernacle a vessel full of manna, so that those who were to be born might know the food by which their fathers had been fed in the wilderness for forty years. In the same ark was Aaron’s rod which had budded (Num. VII). When Aaron was considered less worthy of the priesthood, and some men from other tribes seemed more worthy, Moses, at God’s command, received [Col. 1604B] twelve rods, one from each tribe, and placed them in the tabernacle. Returning the following day, he found that Aaron’s rod, in the tribe of Levi, had flowered and borne fruit. By this miracle Aaron was proved worthy of the priesthood, and that rod was carefully kept in the tabernacle.

The two tablets of the covenant, on which the ten commandments of the law had been written by God’s finger, were also contained in that ark, because Moses himself had placed them there. And above it were two cherubim of glory—that is, gloriously adorned—overshadowing, with wings outspread, the mercy-seat above the same ark: a golden plate of the same length and breadth as the ark. Upon this plate, which was called the mercy-seat, those two cherubim stood on either side, inclined toward the mercy-seat [Col. 1604C] and looking at one another. That plate was called the mercy-seat because, from above it, God spoke graciously to Moses or to the high priest, declaring the goodness of his will.

Of all these things it is not now necessary to speak in detail in this epistle, because it would be lengthy to discuss each item. What we have said suffices for our purpose, since through these matters it will be clear that other things also are to be understood allegorically and are not to be retained in the present time. Some, however, have thought that, because of the greatness of the mysteries, the Apostle declares that no span of the present life is adequate to explain them. If this is true, how shall we, so insignificant, be able to expound them? Yet let us attempt to say something about them briefly.

The first and second tabernacles signify the present and future Church [Col. 1604D]. For the Church itself is in part still a pilgrim on earth and in part already reigning in heaven. Its pilgrim portion is represented, as we have said, by the first tabernacle; the portion which reigns, by the second. The intervening curtain which divided the first tabernacle from the second signifies heaven, which by its interposition still separates us who labour on earth from the kingdom of the saints at rest.

The first tabernacle, as we have said, was twenty cubits long, ten broad, and likewise ten high. The ten cubits of breadth signify the expansive activity of the faithful in God’s commandments, commonly indicated by the Decalogue of the law. The twenty cubits of length signify perseverance in that same [Col. 1605A] good activity through the assistance of the twofold love; for, on account of that living love which alone causes one to act rightly, the number ten is doubled to make twenty, since no one can persevere in observing God’s commandments without charity. The ten cubits of height signify expectation of heavenly blessedness: namely, the denarius which those who laboured in the vineyard are said to have received (Matt. XX).

In this tabernacle were golden lampstands. He uses the plural “lampstands,” because, though there was one, it nevertheless had seven branches. Its central shaft bore three branches on the right and three on the left. The first tabernacle, as we have said, is the present Church, in which service is rendered to God and the sacrifice of good action is offered before one comes [Col. 1605B] to heaven. In it is the lampstand, that is, Christ, shining with the light of divinity in the midst of the faithful. They too are golden lampstands, because they shine with wisdom, which is signified by gold, and with the brightness of good works.

Christ himself is the central stem, bearing three branches on the right and three on the left, because “he is the true vine, from which fruitful branches proceed” (John XV). He is the source, concord, and head of all the righteous, making the saints of the Old and New Testament adhere to himself on either side. For all rise from this foundation and are governed by so great a ruler, by this central good and common light of all.

The three branches on the left are the three men Noah, Daniel, and Job; that is, the three orders of the faithful in the Old Testament: [Col. 1605C] rulers, continent persons, and married persons. For rulers are figured by Noah, who guided the ark amid the waters (Gen. VII–VIII); abstinent and continent persons by Daniel, whose remarkable abstinence is recorded (Dan. I); and married persons by Job, who had a wife and children (Job I, XLII). Likewise the other three branches on the right are the three chosen disciples Peter, John, and James, who saw the glory of the Transfigured One on the mountain (Matt. XVII); that is, the three orders of saints who will see his glory in the heavenly kingdom: rulers, continent persons, and married persons. These are on the right—that is, more worthy in the time of grace than those who were before grace, who are therefore on the left, that is, less worthy. Peter signifies the rulers of the Church, John the celibate, and James [Col. 1605D] the remainder, that is, those who use marriage. All these shine either through teaching or through examples of good works, and diffuse their light to others.

The lower part of the branches proceeding from the shaft was like golden reeds; then came cups, then small spheres, and finally, at the top, forms like lilies (Exod. XXV). The reeds are saints nourished in the moisture of the fountain of divine wisdom, hollow so as to send forth a sweet sound into the ears of many, resounding God’s praise and saying: “He put in us my new song, a hymn to our God” (Ps. XXXVI). They are cups when they offer others the wine of knowledge with which they themselves are filled, so as to make them spiritually drunk and inflame them with desire for heavenly blessedness. Then come the small spheres: that is, they are rounded, perfect, and mobile. A sphere rolls in every direction, because the minds of the elect can neither be held back by any adversities of the world nor corrupted by prosperity; in all that befalls them, they advance toward God through holy desires. Thus at last they reach the lilies: that is, the heavenly homeland, springing with eternal flowers—namely, holy souls and every delight [Col. 1606A]. These and such things are the lampstands which the Apostle now indicates to be in our tabernacle.

There was also a table made of shittim wood, overlaid with the purest gold; upon it were twelve loaves set before God, made of fine flour. The brightest frankincense was laid upon them; they were changed every Sabbath, and belonged to Aaron and his sons, that they might eat them in a holy place. The table made of shittim wood is divine Scripture, constructed from the strong words and deeds of the holy Fathers.
