Since it shows us what the joys of eternal blessedness are and how they are attained, it surely supplies us with the food of salvation and life. It is overlaid with the purest gold because it shines brightly with the meaning of heavenly wisdom.

The twelve loaves upon it are the twelve apostles and their successors [Col. 1606B]. They are rightly called loaves of presentation because they always stand ready in public view to refresh the minds of the faithful with the nourishment of the heavenly word. And these loaves were rightly made not from just any flour but from fine flour, because all who minister the word of life to others must first apply themselves to the fruits of virtues, so that they may commend by their deeds what they urge in preaching. The placing of the brightest frankincense upon them signifies the power of pure prayer, by which those teachers commend to the Lord both the ministry of their preaching and the devotion of their work.

They were rightly changed every Sabbath [Col. 1606C]. For the loaves which had remained on God’s table through the six days of labour are changed for us on the Sabbath when, after the time of their holy labour has been completed, the teachers of the holy Church receive the reward of eternal rest in heaven and leave others after them to labour in the same work of the word under the hope of the same recompense. Thus God’s table never remains without loaves: when the old are taken away, new loaves are immediately substituted. Aaron with his sons ate the loaves removed from that table because Christ, our high priest, receives his elect, taken from this life, into the increase of his body which is in heaven—that is, into that supreme multitude of the elect (Col. II).

The table stood on the north side, but the lampstand on the south [Col. 1606D]. By the north may be understood the coldness of unbelief or malice, and by the south the fervour of charity and holy devotion. It was fitting, therefore, that the table should stand on the north side, because, lest the malice of temptations coming from the left overcome us by finding us weak, we need to be fed and strengthened by the bread of heavenly teaching. But if, fervent through zeal for charity, we pass to the right side—that is, to the exercise of virtues—then we shall be illuminated by the lights of the lampstand: by the brightest examples and sayings of the saints, so that we may see everything that ought rightly to be done [Col. 1607A].

We have touched briefly on these matters concerning the first tabernacle. The second tabernacle, signifying the heavenly Jerusalem, was ten cubits long, ten broad, and likewise ten high. Therefore John says in the Apocalypse of that same heavenly Jerusalem: “The city is laid out as a square; its length is as great as its breadth” (Apoc. XXI). For it has ten cubits in length, breadth, and height: that is, the evangelical tenfold perfection of blessedness, because it possesses blessedness in the breadth of fraternal charity, in the length of everlasting life, and in the height of divine contemplation. That heavenly dwelling is rightly called the Holy of Holies because nothing is done or thought there that might offend God; only what pleases God is done there [Col. 1607B]. Its blessedness is so great that no one there either can or wishes to sin.

Between the two tabernacles was placed the curtain by which the sanctuary and the Holy of Holies were divided, because the holy Church, consisting of angels and human beings and in part still on pilgrimage in the lower regions while in part already reigning in the eternal homeland above, still has its citizens separated from one another by the dividing curtain of heaven.

Within this Holy of Holies is the golden censer: that is, Christ’s precious humanity, free from all sin and possessing most perfect holiness. Filled with the fire of the Passion, it gave forth from itself for us a most sweet fragrance to God; and now, by the continual remembrance of that Passion, it constantly intercedes for us and does not cease to offer such incense, as though saying: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight” (Ps. XIV) [Col. 1607C].

The same mediator of God and humanity, who alone knows the Father’s hidden mysteries, is signified by the ark of the covenant. For he himself gave the New Testament; he kept the Old Testament closed as long as he wished; and when it pleased him, he brought forth its meaning from the secret treasury of his mysteries. This ark is in the Holy of Holies because the Saviour himself, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. II), after his resurrection ascended above all heavens and sits at the Father’s right hand.

Concerning the construction of this ark Moses was told: “Make an ark of shittim wood, two and a half cubits [Col. 1607D] in length, a cubit and a half in breadth, and likewise a cubit and a half in height; and you shall overlay it with the purest gold within and without” (Exod. XXV). Shittim wood is said to be light and incorruptible in nature, not greatly different in quality from white thorn. Thus the ark was made of shittim wood because the Lord’s body consisted of limbs free from every stain of vice. These woods resemble thorns because, although he did not come in sinful flesh, he came in the likeness of sinful flesh.

The length of the ark is the longsuffering patience of that same Redeemer in his life among human beings. It measured two cubits because of the teaching and action in which he shone. The half—that is, the half-cubit—added to this signifies the slowness of his disciples’ human frailty [Col. 1608A], which was not yet able, as it ought, to grasp his exalted words or deeds; and he bore this patiently. The breadth of the ark is the extent of the charity with which Christ loved us. In our head himself it had a whole cubit because it was perfect and sought to give life to his elect, saying: “That all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be one in us” (John XV). But the half-cubit signifies our imperfection, since, while placed in this life, we are not yet able perfectly to love God or to comprehend the love which he has for us.

Its height was hope of future exaltation, through which he foresaw that after the Passion he himself would be glorified and would glorify his own. The ark had a full cubit in height [Col. 1608B], because the Lord, while still living in corruptible flesh, knew most fully what glory was reserved in the future both for himself and for his members, who are ourselves. It also had half a cubit of height because he gladly receives into his body the devotion of our smallness, who love the future life with a devout intention but are not yet able perfectly to grasp its felicity.

The ark was overlaid within and without with the purest gold because the human nature assumed by the Son was inwardly full of the power of the Holy Spirit and outwardly displayed plainly to human beings the works of the Holy Spirit. This is what the Apostle means in affirming that it was covered with gold on every side: in the thought, speech [Col. 1608C], and action of our Redeemer, nothing appeared but pure truth and wisdom.

The golden jar in the ark containing manna is the holy soul in Christ, possessing within itself all the fullness of divinity, by which angels are fed and by which the fathers lived in the wilderness, as it is written: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. LXXVII). Aaron’s rod, which when cut off had budded, is the unconquered power of his priesthood, concerning which the Prophet says: “A rod of equity is the rod of your kingdom” (Ps. XLIV). After it was seen for a time to have been cut down through death, it was found at the dawn of resurrection to have flowered again more vigorously; and it became known that it would remain forever inviolable and unfading.

For, as we said above, when neither Aaron’s priesthood—he being from the tribe of Levi—was being disparaged [Col. 1608D], nor was his tribe believed worthy to offer burnt offerings, twelve rods corresponding to the twelve tribes were commanded to be placed in the tabernacle. And behold, the rod of Levi became green (Num. XVII) and showed what gift of power Aaron possessed. What else is signified by this sign except that all of us who lie in death until the end of the world remain in dryness like the other rods? Yet while all the rods remained dry, the rod of Levi returned to flower: for the body of the Lord, our true priest, laid in the dryness of death, burst forth into the flower of resurrection. By this flower Aaron is rightly known to be a priest, because by this glory of resurrection our Redeemer, sprung from the tribe of Levi and Judah, is shown to be an intercessor for us. Therefore Aaron’s rod, [Col. 1609A] as we have said, is Christ’s priestly power.

The tablets of the covenant in the ark signify all knowledge in Christ both of the Father’s hidden mysteries and of the power of judgments. For on the tablets of the covenant were written faith in the eternal divinity which created and governs the world; the commandments by which God must be served; and the distinction of judgment by which he justly condemns those who hate him and mercifully rewards those who love him with a worthy reward.

But when another apparently conflicting statement of Scripture is brought to mind, a very serious question arises from these words of the Apostle. In the third book of Kings (chap. VIII), when Solomon dedicated the temple, it is reported that there was nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets which Moses had put into it. How then can it be true that in it there was, or had been [Col. 1609B], not only the tablets but also the jar of manna and Aaron’s rod?

When I asked some persons about this matter who seemed knowledgeable, they replied that after the time of that dedication the rod and jar were placed in the ark; but they could establish this neither by the authority of the holy Scriptures nor by the account of any history. Yet the following seems not unsuited to support this interpretation: King Josiah is found in Chronicles to have said to the Levites, “Put the ark in the sanctuary of the temple which Solomon son of David, king of Israel, built” (II Chron. XXXV); “you shall no longer carry it.” These words clearly indicate that after the temple’s dedication the ark was removed from the sanctuary and carried by the Levites and [Col. 1609C] priests. Perhaps then the rod and jar were put into it.

For in the books of Moses we read that they were placed in the tabernacle, but not in the ark as the tablets were. Moses says in Deuteronomy: “I placed the tablets in the ark which I had made, and they remain there to this day, as the Lord commanded me” (Deut. X). And in Exodus he says to Aaron: “Take one vessel, put into it as much manna as a gomor can hold, and set it before the Lord to be kept through your generations” (Exod. XXVI). And the Lord says to Moses in the book of Numbers: “Return Aaron’s rod to the tabernacle of testimony, that it may be kept there” (Num. XVII).

Perhaps, because the rod and jar were placed beside the ark in the sanctuary, the Apostle says that they were in the ark, using place for place, as the Evangelist says: “Jesus walked in the temple, in Solomon’s portico” (John X) [Col. 1609D]. What he had said, “in the temple,” he explained by adding, “in Solomon’s portico,” showing that he called that portico the temple because it adjoined the temple. So too the Apostle, by the same manner of expression, could call the place adjoining the ark, which contained the jar and rod, “the ark.”

Again, the order of blessed spirits in which God specially sits is called the throne; yet the Psalmist prays, “You who sit above the cherubim, manifest yourself before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh” (Ps. LXXIX). Although, in the distinctions of the angelic ranks, the order of the holy cherubim is joined to the thrones, God is nevertheless said to sit above the cherubim because of the equality of the neighbouring rank. So too something may be said to have been in the ark because of proximity of place [Col. 1610A], when it was beside the ark. We ourselves frequently use expressions of this kind, naming a thing by another neighbouring thing, or one place for another.

Thus it may not unsuitably be understood that the Apostle has here put the place near the ark for the ark itself, since he was looking chiefly to the spiritual sense, understanding the ark to signify Christ, in whom spiritually, as has been said, are the tablets of the covenant, Aaron’s rod, and the jar with manna. Let whoever can resolve this question better do so; but whoever cannot resolve it better should not disdain to retain whichever solution of our two preceding proposals seems more probable.

Above the ark was the mercy-seat, also called the oracle. This mercy-seat signifies none other than the same Saviour, but more particularly his compassionate affections [Col. 1610B], of whom the Apostle says: “Whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood” (Rom. III). It is placed above because “mercy exalts itself above judgment” (James II). Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord is gracious to all, and his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. CXLIV).

Concerning the cherubim overshadowing the mercy-seat, Moses was told: “You shall also make two golden, hammered cherubim from each side of the oracle. Let one cherub be on one side and the other on the other; let them cover both sides of the mercy-seat, spreading their wings and covering the oracle, and let them look at one another with their faces turned toward the mercy-seat which I shall give you. From there I shall command and speak to you, namely from above [Col. 1610C] the mercy-seat and from the midst of the two cherubim which will be over the ark of testimony, all that I shall command through you to the children of Israel” (Exod. XXV).

Cherubim is a particular order of angelic powers; nevertheless, all holy angels in general are sometimes signified by this name, as here. In the singular the word is *cherub*, in the plural *cherubim*, and it is masculine in gender. Greek usage, however, treats *cherubim* as neuter, changing the letter *m* into *n*. Hence the Apostle here says, following the Greeks, *cherubin gloriae obumbrantia propitiatorium*—“cherubin of glory overshadowing the mercy-seat”—not *obumbrantes*, “overshadowing” in the masculine plural; whereas in Moses we read, “two golden cherubim,” not “two golden cherubim” in a neuter form.

*Cherubim*, or *cherub*, is interpreted “a multitude of knowledge,” because angelic spirits are filled with the more abundant knowledge [Col. 1610D] insofar as they are continually illumined by purer rays of divine illumination. They are two, to signify the fellowship of angelic charity, because charity is especially found between two; golden, because the virtues of angels shine by the grace of the highest brightness; hammered or extended, because their blessedness is extended—that is, prolonged—eternally. In this sense of extension it is also said of Christ’s kingdom: “There I shall cause David’s horn to spring forth” (Ps. CXXXI). They stand in each Testament because by their ministry the prophets foresaw what shepherds later came to know as accomplished through those same angels (Luke II). They cover both sides of the mercy-seat because in both Testaments many heavenly secrets are hidden from mortals which they understand.

Moses fashioned them with wings, among other features, to signify that angels have their dwelling on high and can range everywhere in something like light flight [Col. 1611A], with no slowness preventing their immediate presence wherever they wish. Therefore they spread their wings and cover the mercy-seat, because angels devote all the power of their nature—having merited to dwell on high and to traverse every place in that heavenly country by a light and joyful course—to the service of their Creator. They gaze upon and overshadow the mercy-seat, that is, honour it by veiling it, because they ascribe their entire condition of perpetual felicity to the grace of him from whom they received the power to will no evil. They look at one another, with faces turned toward the mercy-seat, because in glorifying the divine vision they harmonize with one another.

The cherubim are placed above the mercy-seat in the way that Christ’s city—that is, the holy Church—is said to be established upon a mountain, that is, upon Jesus Christ: not because his city can be higher than he is (Matt. V; Apoc. XXI), but because it makes progress sustained by his aid [Col. 1611B]. God was accustomed to speak above the mercy-seat and from the midst of the two cherubim because through Christ, “who is the propitiation for our sins” (I John II), and whom angels stand ready to serve, as it were on both sides before and after his advent, God the Father has graciously deigned to disclose his will to humankind. In Christ’s humanity the Father is above him, but not in Christ’s divinity, in which he is equal to the Father. That mercy-seat was called the oracle because God spoke there.

These were the things within the Holy of Holies, after those which were in the first sanctuary. Of them, he says, it is not now necessary to speak so fully that our discourse should proceed by discussing every one individually. Or: in the present life it is not possible to speak of them—that is, the depth of these mysteries cannot be opened in every detail. Of each thing that was there or was done there, it is not now necessary to speak.

With these two tabernacles thus arranged—or, as we have briefly indicated, joined together—it must be said that priests always entered the first tabernacle, that is, daily or continually, completing the duties of sacrifices. These were the ordinances of worship which I said above that the Old Testament possessed. All priests entered the first sanctuary [Col. 1611D] whenever they wished. But only the high priest entered the second, and this once a year; nor did he enter without blood, but carried with him blood which he might offer for his own ignorance and that of the people—that is, for sins committed unknowingly by himself as well as by the people.

The priests’ daily entry throughout the year into the first tabernacle with sacrifices signifies that, in the present Church, the saints who serve the Lord without interruption expiate the daily errors of their frailty—which they can in no way be without in this life—by daily victims of good works and daily libations of their tears, as true priests. But the high priest, who once a year entered the Holy of Holies [Col. 1612A] with the blood of victims, signifies Christ, who, once in the fullness of time, having been offered for our sins, himself priest and victim, entered through his own blood into heaven itself—that is, into the true Holy of Holies—so that he may now appear before God’s face for us. And for his own—that is, for the ignorance of his own prelates and of all his people—he offers within the blood that was poured out without: that is, he presents to the Father in heaven the remembrance of the Passion which he endured in this world.

The year may signify the whole time from the incarnation of the same Saviour to the end of the age. Of this year he said through Isaiah: “That I might proclaim the year acceptable to the Lord” (Isa. LXI). Ignorance may be called any sin, because it blinds the heart [Col. 1612B] and makes a person wander when it persuades that the pleasure of sin is pleasing. The high priest’s entry into the Holy Place being repeated every year signified that perfection had not yet come.

Only the high priest entered, the Holy Spirit—who instituted that this should be done—thereby signifying that the way of the saints had not then yet been disclosed and opened: that is, the path by which human beings might reach the Holy of Holies, entering the secrets of heaven, had not yet been made accessible, because Christ had not yet come to disclose this way to believers, while the former—that is, shadowy—tabernacle still retained its standing in carnal observances. That is, access to eternal blessedness had not yet been open to human beings because the shadow of the old tabernacle had not yet yielded but stood and endured; nor could the truth shine openly for all unless the shadow were removed. For Christ, ascending first, opened for us the entrance of heaven, so that souls stripped of their bodies may enter there.

Here the “former tabernacle” is not called former in relation to the second, as above; rather, both are called former in relation to the new Church and the supercelestial Jerusalem. Or, just as when the high priest entered the Holy of Holies the people could not enter with him, so we mortals cannot follow Christ into heaven, the Holy Spirit signifying by that solitary entry of the old high priest that in our time the way of the saints—that is, the entrance into the heavenly kingdom—has not yet been publicly opened for those clothed in flesh [Col. 1612D], while the former tabernacle, that is, the present Church, retains its standing.

For the first tabernacle will be destroyed and the second will remain, because the present Church, according to the manner of life which it now has, will be dissolved; but the heavenly Jerusalem, in the manner of life which it has in the angels, will endure without end. So long as the present Church, which is the first tabernacle, remains in its present condition, heaven is inaccessible to our bodies, just as before the Saviour’s ascension it was inaccessible to the souls of the righteous. We must therefore await patiently the general resurrection, when, after the dissolution of the present Church, we shall be permitted to enter the dwelling of the heavenly kingdom with body and soul, just as the souls of the perfect have been permitted to do after the Redeemer’s ascension.

“This parable,” that is [Col. 1613A], this mystical likeness concerning the two tabernacles and the things contained or done within them, “is of the present time”; that is, all those things performed there prefigured those things which are openly enacted in this time of grace. A parable is a representation of an event performed in order to signify something else. Thus all the things then done are represented to us by Scripture in order to signify those things occurring in our time. From this it is clear that the people’s inability then to follow the high priest into the Holy of Holies was a sign that we still cannot follow Christ bodily into heaven.

“In accordance with this parable gifts”—such as offerings from produce—“and sacrifices”—such as offerings from animals—“are offered,” or were commanded to be offered, “which cannot make perfect in conscience the worshipper” [Col. 1613B]. For even if someone fulfilled outwardly everything commanded, inwardly he could not perfectly fulfil the law. Although the law said, “You shall not covet” (Exod. XX; Rom. VII), it did not take away covetousness; rather, by its very prohibition it stirred people toward covetousness. And although someone might seem, according to the flesh, to be cleansed from sin through those sacrifices, he could not thereby be fully cleansed in conscience.

Nevertheless, even then there were many spiritual persons who, justified by faith and possessing the help of grace, pleased God by fulfilling the spiritual law. “For we know that the law is spiritual” (ibid.). But because it was observed carnally, [Col. 1613C] it could not make perfect in conscience the worshipper, occupied only with foods and drinks,
and in various baptisms, and in ordinances of the flesh imposed until the time of reformation—that is, upon the person who did nothing there spiritually, but served the law in this only according to the surface of the letter: so that he rejected certain foods or drinks as though unclean, chose others as though clean, observed various baptisms, that is, diverse washings, and various ordinances not of the spirit but of the flesh, because they justified not the soul but the flesh, insofar as they restrained the hand from perverse action and the tongue from blasphemy through fear of punishment, but did not cleanse the heart from an evil will.

And all these things—that is, the observance of distinctions among foods and drinks, the frequent washings of bodies or garments, and the shadowy [Col. 1613D] justifications of the flesh, together with the rest of this sort—were imposed upon them as a burden, to restrain transgressors, not that they might continue forever, but that they might endure until the time of reformation; that is, until the time of grace, by which they would be corrected for the better and these things would cease. For what that law accomplished imperfectly, and was unable to bring to fulfilment in all who observed it, the newly intervening grace corrected and brought all its impossibility to perfection: by removing carnal rites, it transformed them into spiritual observances.

> “But Christ, standing by as high priest of the good things to come, entered once for all into the holy places through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made by hands—that is, not of this creation—and not through the blood of goats or calves, [Col. 1614A] but through his own blood, having found eternal redemption.”

The high priest alone entered once a year into the second tabernacle which Moses had constructed; but Christ entered a nobler and eternal tabernacle, where he performs the office of high priest, standing before God to intercede for us, as Stephen saw him standing for him at the Father’s right hand (Acts 7). For then he was interceding for Stephen; and thus, in a sense, he stands before God for each one of the elect while he intercedes for them. For he is also said to sit and to stand, so that at one time his power, at another his mercy, may be described. Certainly, he is said to sit in the capacity of king or judge because of his authority; he is represented as standing because of the kindness of an intercessor.

I say, he is high priest not of carnal and temporal [Col. 1614B] goods, but of spiritual and eternal—that is, future—goods; because by his intercession and the offering of himself he obtains for us not temporal but eternal goods, which will be so present that they will always be future—that is, never failing. Or, he is high priest of future goods, namely present righteousness and eternal blessedness, which in their proper time were still to come.

He entered the true tabernacle, that is, heaven, through a greater one—that is, perfectly and altogether greater, because it holds more than that earthly one—and a more perfect one, because perfect righteousness and blessedness are there. I mean a tabernacle not made by hand, like that which Moses made; that is, not of this creation, of which that erected by man in the wilderness was a part. It was not made by human hand but by God’s right hand, nor composed of corruptible material [Col. 1614C] like that which Moses made from curtains, skins, gold, and silver, but completed with wondrous solidity and beauty.

He did not enter that narrow, imperfect tabernacle constructed by human hands, but entered through one of greater extent in every respect and greater perfection, fashioned by the supreme Maker; nor did he enter the Holy of Holies through the blood of goats or calves, as the high priest formerly used to do under the Law, but through his own blood. For he found nothing clean in humankind which he might offer on behalf of humankind; and therefore he himself, the priest, offered himself as a clean victim. He brought his gracious blood, shed for us, into the Holy of Holies, [Col. 1614D] that is, into heaven; and he did this once—that is, not yearly like the Levitical high priest, but only on one occasion. For the offering of his blood so pleased God that no further repetition is needed, because through the humility of that sacrifice whatever the first human being committed was erased; and he brought all those for whose salvation he shed his blood to complete perfection. Therefore it need not be repeated, because it is perfect.

Through his blood he entered once into the Holy of Holies, having obtained eternal redemption; and this was so because through that offering, made once, the redemption of all was obtained—a redemption which could not be found in the whole human race. For when all people were held captive by the devil, what could be found among them that might be given as the ransom of so many [Col. 1615A] captives? But Christ found in his own blood the redemption of all: not temporal but eternal, because the price he gave was so great that it restored eternal freedom to those redeemed. For he erased both original and actual sins, supplied every justification, and opened the kingdom of heaven.

> “For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled upon the defiled, sanctify for the purification of the flesh, how much more did the blood of Christ—who through the Holy Spirit offered himself without blemish to God—cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God?” (Lev. 16; 1 Pet. 1; 1 John 1; Rev. 1)

Truly, by offering his blood once he obtained our redemption, and there was no need for a repetition of such [Col. 1615B] an offering. For his blood cleansed our conscience, so that we are no longer conscious of consenting to any evil; and this is truly to be free. As though someone were to say: Through Christ’s blood spiritual and eternal redemption and liberation are possible. For if the blood of the shadowy sacrifices of the Law sanctified persons in the flesh—that is, purified their flesh and rendered it clean—much more powerfully Christ’s blood cleanses and sanctifies our souls, so that they may remain clean and free forever. This is what is meant by: “For if the blood of goats,” and so forth. If a shadow purifies the flesh, how much more does the truth sanctify the soul?

Those purifications were shadows of the purifications performed under grace; and the animals by whose blood cleansing was effected bore the figure of Christ. The blood [Col. 1615C] of the goats and bulls which were sacrificed was sometimes sprinkled upon those who were to be cleansed, or seven times before the veil on their behalf, so that they might be sanctified. Christ, who cleansed us by the sprinkling of his blood, was signified by goats because of the likeness of sinful flesh and because he was offered for the sin of the world. For a goat was always sacrificed for sin; and he was signified by bulls because of strength, since by the horns of power he scatters his enemies.

But the heifer more clearly prefigured him. It was burned so that its ashes, mixed with water, might become a purification for unclean persons. It would take far too long to say everything about it, but let us say something briefly:

> “Command the children of Israel,” he says, “to bring you a red cow, of full age, in which there is no blemish and which has borne no yoke; and you shall deliver her to Eleazar the priest. He shall lead her outside the camp and sacrifice her in the sight of all; dipping his finger in her blood, he shall sprinkle it seven times before the doors of the tabernacle. And, with all looking on, he shall burn her, delivering to the flame both her skin and flesh, her blood and dung. The priest shall also cast cedarwood, hyssop, and scarlet material twice dyed into the flame that consumes the cow.” (Num. 19)

The cow signifies Christ’s flesh by its female sex, because of bodily weakness; it is red, that is, stained with the blood of the Passion. It is of full age because he was thirty years old, or a little more, when he was crucified. In him there was no stain of iniquity, [Col. 1616A] for he had borne no yoke of sin. The fact that it was commanded to be delivered not to Aaron the high priest but to his son Eleazar signifies that the Lord’s Passion was to reach not the age then present, but the successors of that priesthood, of whom Eleazar now bears the type. Those who led him outside the camp—that is, outside the city—sacrificed him by crucifying him in the sight of all.

Then Eleazar changes his signification and represents the true priests of the New Testament, namely the apostles, when, dipping his finger in the heifer’s blood, he sprinkles it seven times before the doors of the tabernacle. For the apostles sprinkled the blood seven times with the finger, because, commending Christ’s Passion by their works, they preached to the peoples the entrance of faith through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 1616B] “And he shall burn her,” it says, “with all looking on.” Burning is a sign of resurrection, for it is the nature of fire to move upward, and what is burned is changed into it. Therefore the cow was burned in the sight of all, because Christ rose again and all faithful people throughout the world behold the glory of his resurrection.

What follows—“both her skin and flesh, her blood and dung delivered to the flame”—signifies that not only the mortal substance of Christ’s body, intimated by the mention of skin, blood, and flesh, but also the reproach and rejection by the people, signified by the name “dung,” would be changed into glory, which the flame of burning signifies. Cedarwood, which rises high, is hope, [Col. 1616C] which ought steadfastly to dwell in things above. Hyssop, because it clings to rock by its roots, is faith founded in Christ. Scarlet twice-dyed is fiery love, dyed with love of God and neighbor. These three things the priest—that is, every Christian—ought to cast into Christ’s resurrection, as into the midst of that burning, so that his life may be hidden with Christ in God (Col. 3).

“A clean man,” however, “shall gather the ashes of the cow and pour them out beyond the camp in a most clean place, so that they may be kept for the multitude of the children of Israel and be used for water of sprinkling, because the cow was burned for sin.” What are we to think the cow’s ashes are but the report which followed Christ’s Passion and resurrection? For it was ash because he was despised by unbelievers as though dead; yet [Col. 1616D] it cleansed because believers believed that he had risen. And because this report shone most brightly among those who were among the other nations and were not joined to the community of the Jews, it was therefore said that a clean man would gather the cow’s ashes—clean, certainly, from Christ’s killing, which had defiled the Jews—and pour them out in a most clean place, that is, in the most clean heart of believers, outside the camp, that is, beyond the observance of Jewish custom. These ashes are thus handled so that they may be for the multitude of the children of Israel—that is, Christians—a safeguard for the heavenly commandments and water of sprinkling, that is, the washing of baptism. For sprinkling-water is purification.

From all these things was made the water of sprinkling, by which persons were cleansed from contact with the dead, [Col. 1617A] which indeed signifies cleansing from the iniquity of this dying or death-dealing life [Note: [Col. 1617D] An obscure passage.].

> “Whoever touches a human corpse,” he says, “and is therefore unclean for seven days, shall be sprinkled with this water on the third and seventh days, and thus shall be cleansed. If he has not been sprinkled on the third day, he will not be able to be cleansed on the seventh.” (Num. 19)

Whoever touches a human corpse—that is, whoever shares in evil deeds—and is therefore unclean for seven days, that is, in soul and body, shall be sprinkled with this water. The uncleanness of seven days is said with reference to soul and body, because a human being has a sevenfold constitution in soul and body: the former consists in three movements, the latter in four elements. Hence it is also said through Amos: “For three crimes of Israel, and for four, I will not turn [Col. 1617B] him back” [or: “I will not revoke it”] (Amos 1).

He shall be sprinkled with this water on the third and seventh days and thus be cleansed: that is, by the water of baptism in faith in the Trinity and the confirmation of the Holy Spirit. “If he has not been sprinkled on the third day, he will not be able to be cleansed on the seventh”: that is, unless he has been washed by baptism performed in faith in the Trinity, he cannot receive sevenfold grace. Many other kinds of uncleanness are also described, all of which are commanded to be cleansed by the sprinkling of this water. But let us return to the Epistle, since it is now clear how this heifer prefigured Christ.

For the blood of goats and bulls, and the sprinkled ashes of this heifer, sanctified—that is, cleansed—those defiled by some of the uncleannesses which the Law describes. It sanctified them not for the cleansing of the soul but for the cleansing [Col. 1617C] of the flesh, so that the flesh might now be judged clean and the person so cleansed might be received into the fellowship of others. If animal blood or ashes could accomplish this in the flesh, how much more can Christ’s blood effect purity and sanctification in our soul? Hence it was said of him in the Law, under the figure of bodily victims:

> “The life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you that you may make expiation upon my altar for your souls; and the blood shall be for the expiation of the soul.” (Lev. 27)

Accordingly, Christ’s blood, as the Law had prophesied and decreed, cleansed our conscience—that is, it wholly cleansed our soul—so that it was no longer conscious of any sin or unlawful consent. It cleansed it from dead works, that is, from the guilt of the sins [Col. 1617D] we had committed, by which it had been defiled. For works of sin are dead, that is, altogether devoid of the life of righteousness. Whoever touches them is defiled, just as one who touched a dead person was defiled; nor does such a person enter heaven, just as the other did not enter the temple. Christ cleansed our heart from such dead things so that no defilement of consent might remain in us; and he cleansed us in order that we might serve the living God, whom one cannot serve while serving dead works, that is, sins. “For everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8), and “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. 6; Luke 6).

[Col. 1618A] But Christ did two things: he cleansed us from sins and, restoring freedom of choice, made us serve God, who truly lives and grants true life to those who serve him. Nor is it surprising that Christ’s blood accomplishes such things, since he offered to God for us not the victims of brute animals but himself, without blemish, because he had neither original nor actual stain. This occurred through the Holy Spirit, who created his flesh without seed in the virgin’s womb and always preserved him free from sin. Or, he offered himself through the Holy Spirit because the Holy Spirit prompted him to do this.

> “And therefore he is mediator of the New Testament, so that, death having intervened for the redemption of those transgressions which were under the former testament, those who are called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance.”

[Col. 1618B] I say that he offered himself to God for us, and therefore he himself is the Mediator of the New Testament: that is, the intermediary between God and human beings in the giving of the new Law, better than Moses had been in the giving of the Old. For discord had arisen between us and God, and therefore we could not become heirs of his kingdom, because we did not even know how we ought to return to peace with him. For this reason, through God’s mercy, this Mediator was given to us: that he might reconcile us to God and interpret his will to us, so that we might know what he wished us to do; and, having become his friends, might obtain through the New Testament the inheritance of his kingdom, just as the Jews obtained the inheritance of the land of Canaan through the Old Testament.

And this is what is meant: he is Mediator of the New Testament so that those who are called—that is, [Col. 1618C] chosen by God from eternity, of whom it is said elsewhere, “Blessed are those called to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Rev. 19)—may receive through that Testament the promise of the eternal inheritance; that is, may attain as their inheritance eternal blessedness, which has many times been promised them in the Scriptures. This occurs with his death intervening between the testament and the inheritance. He gave them the New Testament precisely so that, when his death intervened, those who possessed the New Testament might receive the inheritance, as is customary in all testaments.

For whenever a householder makes a testament for his heir, it benefits the person for whom it is made only after the maker has first died. Here we call a testament a document made for someone concerning the obtaining, after another’s death, [Col. 1618D] of an inheritance. Sometimes it is made simply; sometimes with a condition, as if someone said: “Do this, and after me you will have my inheritance; but if you do not do it, you will not have it.” He leaves that person a written instrument concerning this agreement, just as Christ made us a conditional testament concerning the inheritance of everlasting life, saying: “If anyone keeps my word, he shall not see death forever” (John 8). Then he interposed his death, so that by keeping his word we might attain the inheritance of eternal life.

“Death having intervened for the redemption of those transgressions which [Col. 1619A] were under the former testament”: that is, his death intervened for the purpose of redeeming his own from those transgressions which they committed while they were still under the old Law. That Law pressed them down in the slavery of fear and did not release them into the freedom of love; and therefore it did not sanctify them but rather made them transgressors. He says “under the testament” because the Law was like a certain heavy burden upon them. He says nothing of the sins of the Gentiles, which were likewise erased by Christ’s blood, because he is speaking to Hebrews, who supposed themselves justified through the Law. He shows that they had never lived under the Law without transgressions; and therefore they too had to be redeemed by Christ’s death from the guilt of their transgressions, so that they might become worthy of the eternal inheritance.

[Col. 1619B]

> “For where there is a testament, the death of the testator must intervene. For a testament is confirmed in the dead; otherwise it is not yet valid while the one who made the testament lives. Hence not even the first was dedicated without blood.”

I said that he is the Mediator of the New Testament so that, with his death intervening, we might attain possession of the inheritance written in the Testament; and it was necessary that his death should intervene if we were to attain the inheritance. For this is how it occurs in all testaments. Wherever a testament is made, the death of the testator must intervene: that is, the one who made the testament must first die before the person designated heir in the testament can possess the inheritance. For that person can never obtain it [Col. 1619C] otherwise.

And because this is necessary in every testament, our Testator, who made a testament for us in which he appointed us to be heirs of eternal life, interposed his death, so that we might come without obstacle to possess the inheritance and could not reach it otherwise. And indeed the testator’s death must intervene in every testament. For every testament is confirmed, so that it may be valid, in the dead—that is, in the testator’s death. The Apostle speaks according to secular laws, in which it is decreed that a testament is not valid while the testator is alive but receives firmness from his death, so that it can no longer be altered. Otherwise—that is, unless the testator’s death intervenes—it is not yet valid, that is, the testament itself is not yet [Col. 1619D] firm, while—that is, as long as—the one who made the testament lives. For while he lives, he can, if he wishes, alter it: he can remove the one whom he had written as heir and enter another in writing. But at his death it is so confirmed that it can no longer be altered, and the heirs who are recorded receive the inheritance.

So too Christ’s testament was confirmed in his death, so that those whom he designated heirs in it might receive the inheritance without alteration. For not others, but those alone “whose names are in the book of life” (Phil. 4), obtain that inheritance accordingly. I said that every testament is confirmed by death; hence—that is, because death confirms every testament—not even the first testament was dedicated without blood. Rather, at its dedication, [Col. 1620A] that is, when it was received into authority by the children of Israel, animals were sacrificed, and it was confirmed by their blood, as a sign of the New Testament, which was dedicated by Christ’s blood. This is what is meant: “Not even the first”—supply, “like the second”—“was dedicated without blood.” For it had to be confirmed by death in order to be valid and authoritative.

> “For when Moses had read every commandment of the Law [Col. 1620B] to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying: ‘This is the blood of the testament which God has commanded for you.’ And he likewise sprinkled the tabernacle and all the vessels of ministry with blood; and almost all things are cleansed in blood according to the Law, and without the shedding of blood there is no remission.” (Exod. 24)

Truly, the first testament too was dedicated with blood. For after Moses had read every commandment of the Law, so that nothing in the Law might lack authority but all its commandments might be dedicated and made authoritative in blood for all the people—who were likewise wholly cleansed by blood—after Moses had read through all the Law’s commandments in the people’s hearing, he took the blood of calves and goats with water and scarlet wool and hyssop. That is, mixing blood and water and making a sprinkler from wool and hyssop, he sprinkled with that blood not merely the other things but the very book of the Law and all the people. And so that they might receive it with greater devotion, he said: “This is the blood of the testament, [Col. 1620C] which God commanded through me for you.” It is as though he said: “I do not sprinkle you without purpose, for this blood by which I purify you confirms the testament which God commanded me to bring to you.”

He sprinkled not only the book and people but also the tabernacle and all the vessels of ministry—that is, those made for service in it—with blood in the same way as the people. Moses cleansed all those vessels with blood and through the sprinkling of blood made them fit to serve God, just as he had cleansed the people and the remaining things with blood. Taking that as an example and its authority thereafter, priests cleanse almost all things in blood according to the Law—that is, according to what the Law commands and Moses instituted—and without the shedding [Col. 1620D] of blood there is no remission, because under the Law no sin is remitted without sacrifice.

The Apostle does not say, however, that human sins were remitted by the blood of brute animals; rather, he indicates that not even those under the Law were forgiven except by Christ’s blood. Moses’ first teaching the Law and then sprinkling the book and people with blood prefigured that Christ would first preach and then sprinkle his preaching and the people of believers with his blood. For the book of the New Testament is sprinkled with Christ’s blood: it recalls his Passion more clearly and more frequently, and it was confirmed by his death, so that it may be held in authority and what is written in it may be fulfilled without alteration. Thus, because Christ [Col. 1621A] died for us, we may love his commandments—he who obtained for us through death the grace by which we are able to fulfill them.

The sprinkling of the entire people declared that all who belong to the people of God have redemption and sanctification in Christ’s blood, which the blood of goats and calves prefigured. Christ, in figure, is a calf because of the power of the cross, by whose horns he scatters the ungodly (Ps. 43). He is a calf, however, not an ox, because he had nothing of oldness but brought us the newness of grace. He is also called a goat because of the likeness of sinful flesh, “that he might condemn sin concerning sin” (Rom. 8); and there the blood of calves and goats prefigured Christ’s blood, as we have said.

Water was mixed with the blood because from Christ’s side came forth [Col. 1621B] not blood only but water also (John 19). Hence there is also the custom of mixing water with the wine in the sacred chalice that is to be consecrated in the Mass. This may also be referred to the sacrament of baptism, because our baptism, prefigured by the Red Sea, is red with Christ’s blood. Therefore Moses mixed blood and water.

He sprinkled that blood and water with scarlet wool because Christ, in wondrous love, brought forth from his side the blood and water by which he would sanctify us. Scarlet color signifies the redness of the most ardent love by which Christ loved us. Wool also is warm, and a garment to repel cold may be made from it. Therefore we ought to take Christ’s love as warm wool and make from it for ourselves a garment of righteousness, with which we may be clothed and adorned in all our words and deeds and defended from the cold of every wickedness. [Col. 1621C] Hyssop, moreover, a lowly herb which drives away swelling of the lungs, signifies Christ’s humility, by which he mercifully “humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Phil. 2). With this humility he sprinkled his gracious blood upon us. We too ought to imitate it according to our measure, lest we be found to have received in vain the grace of that sprinkling. For what benefit is his blood to us unless we utterly drive the swelling of pride away from ourselves?

Moses sprinkled the book and the people, saying: “This is the blood of the testament which God commanded for you” (Exod. 14). So too Christ, about to sprinkle the new [Col. 1621D] Law and the whole world with his blood, said to his disciples at supper: “This is my blood of the New Testament, which shall be shed for many” (Matt. 26; Mark 14; Luke 22). See how harmoniously the two testaments correspond to one another. See how fittingly Moses foretells the words which the Savior uses at supper.

He also sprinkled with blood the tabernacle—that is, the Church of the faithful, concerning whom God said, “For I shall dwell in them and walk among them” (Lev. 26)—and all the vessels of ministry—that is, all the saints who serve at the altar, such as deacons, presbyters, bishops, and those who administer in the Church the consecrated food of holy preaching. For Christ cleansed and consecrated with his blood the whole Church together, and all its holier members as well as the ordinary people. [Col. 1622A] According to the Law almost everything is cleansed by blood, so that it may appear that everything ought to be cleansed by Christ’s blood. He said “almost everything” because certain vessels were washed with water alone to be cleansed, and people were purified by sprinkling-water from certain contaminations, such as contact with the dead, and did not need blood for their cleansing (Lev. 13, 15). But in the Gospel nothing at all is cleansed without Christ’s blood. This also is maintained in the Law: without the shedding of blood in some sacrifice, there is no remission of sin, thereby showing that absolutely no sin can be remitted without Christ’s Passion.

> “It was therefore necessary that the copies of the heavenly things [Col. 1622B] should be cleansed by these; but the heavenly things themselves by better sacrifices than these.”

Since Moses acted in this way and the Law so commanded, it was necessary that the copies of heavenly things—that is, the tabernacle and its vessels, and so forth, which were figures of heavenly things, namely, which prefigured the Church that can say, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3)—should be cleansed by the aforesaid things, namely, the blood of calves and goats, and water with wool and hyssop. The copies of heavenly things had to be cleansed by such sacrifices; but the heavenly things themselves—that is, people already belonging to heaven, whom the ancient shadows prefigured—had to be cleansed by better sacrifices than these, that is, than the blood of calves and the rest.

For it was not fitting that the victims of brute animals should be slain for rational [Col. 1622C] human beings. Since brute animals were not worthy victims for a rational creature—that is, for a human being—a human had to be sought who should be offered for human beings, so that a rational victim might be slain for the rational sinner and erase the guilt of the first parents. But what of the fact that no sinless human being could be found? And when could a victim offered for us cleanse us from sin if it itself did not lack the contagion of sin? What is defiled cannot cleanse those who are defiled.

Therefore, for the victim to be rational, a human had to be offered; but for that human to cleanse humanity from sins, he had to be human and without sin. But who could be a human being without sin if he descended from the union of sin? [Col. 1622D] Accordingly, for our sake the Son of God came into a virgin’s womb. There, made human without sin for our sake, he made his own body a sacrifice for us; for sinners he presented a victim without sin, able both to die by his humanity and to cleanse by his righteousness. This, I say, is what is meant when the heavenly things—that is, human beings destined to become companions of the heavenly powers—are said to have had to be cleansed by better sacrifices, namely, by Christ’s humanity. It is designated in this passage by the plural term “sacrifices,” because it was prefigured by all the aforesaid sacrifices and accomplished more than all of them.

> “For Jesus did not enter holy places made by hands, copies of the true ones, but heaven itself, that he might now appear before the face of God for us; nor in order to offer himself often, as the high priest [Col. 1623A] enters the Holy of Holies every year with another’s blood. Otherwise he would have had to suffer often from the foundation of the world. But now, once at the consummation of the ages, he has appeared for the abolition of sin through his own sacrifice. And just as it is appointed for human beings to die once, and after this comes judgment, so Christ too, having been offered once to take away the sins of many, will appear a second time, without sin, for salvation to those who await him.” (Rom. 5; Pet. 3)

He proves both points: that heavenly things were cleansed by sacrifices, and that they were cleansed by better sacrifices—which are one sacrifice, namely Christ. As though he said: The true Christ cleansed the heavenly things, that is, cleansing human beings by his blood, he made the heavenly to share in heavenly things. [Col. 1623B] For Jesus himself—that is, our Savior—who is the true sacrifice, signified by all preceding sacrifices, did not enter holy places made by human hands, because these were copies of the true holy places, which are in heaven; rather, he entered heaven itself, which was signified by the second tabernacle. The handmade holy places were copies—that is, figures and shadows—of the true holy places which are in heaven; and therefore the true priest, Jesus, had to enter not the shadowy things but the true ones. He would indeed have entered the handmade holy places if he had wished to cleanse them—that is, if he had wished to sanctify them so that those entering them might receive from them cleansing from sins. But by not entering them, he indicates that no one will now be able there to attain purity of soul. [Col. 1623C] For this reason he disregarded them and did not sanctify them: because, as was said, they are copies and likenesses of the true things, not themselves the true things.

But he entered heaven—heaven itself, I say, that which was signified by those things. But why should Jesus, that is, he who sought our salvation in all that he did, enter heaven, unless by that ascent he wished all to be cleansed so as to become heavenly, in order that he who ascended for these purposes might dwell in them as though in heavenly beings, “that he might now appear before the face of God for us”—that is, that he alone might intercede for the salvation of us all, just as formerly the high priest alone prayed for all in the Holy of Holies. Now he does this while we do not see him. Or “now,” that is, in the fullness of the time of grace, after the completion of the works which he performed while living among human beings, he appears before the face—that is, the presence and benevolent favor—of God the Father, interceding with him for us, showing the scars of the wounds which he suffered for our redemption and perpetually setting forth how greatly he labored for our salvation. [Col. 1623D]

For in a wonderful and ineffable order, the Lord Jesus continually reminds him who can never forget anything and who is always ready to have mercy, how fitting it is that he should have mercy upon human beings, whose fellow-participant in suffering and passion the very Son of God truly became, and for whom he, struggling himself, overthrew by dying the dominion of death. Thus he often intercedes for us.

Yet he does not do this in such a way as to offer himself often upon the altar of the cross and suffer often, because, having been offered once, he was sufficient for all, and no repetition is needed. Hence it is clear that his sacrifice is worthier and more effective than all others: those entered often without bringing perfection, whereas this one, offered once, leads to the homeland. He did not enter heaven in order to offer himself often through the shedding of his own blood, as the legal high priest enters the Holy of Holies each year, doing so because he cannot effect completion and perfection. And he does this not with his own blood but with another’s; and he does it each year. Christ, however, does not do so often but once; that priest does so with another’s blood, Christ with his own. That priest immediately leaves the holy places; Christ remains perpetually in the Holy of Holies, standing before the face of God and always interceding for us. [Col. 1624A]

Therefore he did not enter as that high priest did, to leave afterward and afterward return, offering the sacrifice of his passion as the other offered the blood of brute animals. Rather, he offered his own blood once and penetrated heaven. Otherwise—that is, if he acted differently, if he offered himself often—it would then be necessary for him to suffer frequently, beginning from the foundation of the world, so that he might suffer in every generation, redeeming his own in each generation. For if he often offered himself upon the altar of the cross, he would do so because he was by no means sufficient for the redemption of all. And when he had redeemed those whom he found alive in the flesh, it would again be necessary for him to die for the redemption of others who would be born afterward. Thus it would have to occur in every generation.

And since Abel, Noah, Abraham, Job, David, and the other righteous people predestined to life [Col. 1624B] had to be redeemed in the same manner as those whom, appearing in the flesh, he justified, and since in the former the same necessity and cause preceded which followed in the latter: therefore, if he wished to redeem all and could redeem only his contemporaries, he would have had to begin suffering from the first righteous man—that is, from the time of Abel—which would be a great absurdity. Therefore he was offered not often but rather once upon the altar of the cross. This is now established, because it has been shown by the aforesaid absurdity.

Or thus: He did not suffer frequently from the foundation of the world, but now once at the consummation of the ages. If, having been offered once, he were not sufficient to take away the sins of all who believe in him, it would be necessary for him to suffer more often from the foundation of the world. To prevent this, he suffered once at the consummation of the ages, [Col. 1624C] that is, in the final age of the world, in which all things are completed and fulfilled that were imperfect in the ages gone by. Therefore there was no need for him to begin suffering from the foundation of the world. For if he suffered so many times, he would be more pitiable than all human beings.

He did not begin to suffer at the beginning; rather, now at the consummation of the ages he appeared in the Holy of Holies before the face of the Father, having entered there once through his sacrifice, slaughtered on one occasion, “for the putting away of sin”—that is, in order to place sin beneath, so that it might no longer be over us but under us; that is, so that it might no longer rule us, but we might trample it underfoot. No other sacrifice could accomplish this. And because his sacrifice, offered once, overthrew the kingdom of sin, and sin no longer prevails over us through consent or action, [Col. 1624D] there was no need for it to be offered again.

I said that he appeared once before God through his sacrifice, entering the Holy of Holies. And for this reason he suffered once: because human nature possesses this condition in all people, that they die once. And just as—that is, by what necessity and natural condition—it has been appointed for all human beings to die once, that is, to die only once, but after this, that is, after death, judgment remains for them, in which they receive according to what they have done; that is, it does not remain for them to rise again and die again, but only to come to judgment to receive rewards or punishments—so also, that is, by the same necessity and immutable law of nature, Christ, as a true human being, was offered once and no more upon the altar of the cross, and afterward he will conduct judgment. That is: just as for human beings after death nothing necessarily remains except that they be judged, so for Christ after death nothing remains except that he judge. [Col. 1625A]

For if after his resurrection he could die again, he would not possess in himself the nature of other human beings. And thus he would benefit us in no way, since he would not be a true human being. But in order that he might be proved a true human being, just as he was once born from a virgin mother, so once, dying on the cross, he was offered to the Father as a sacrifice “to take away”—that is, wholly to remove and abolish—sins. I do not say the sins of all, because not all believe, but of many, that is, of those predestined to life. Other sacrifices were not sufficient for this, because, although they diminished sins in some manner, they nevertheless did not take them away. That is, he came once, and by that coming [Col. 1625B] took away all the sins of his own; but at his second coming he will appear, not in order to suffer again, but in order to judge.

For he will appear “without sin,” that is, without a sacrifice for sin; for then he does not offer a sacrifice for sins, but condemns those who persevere in sins. For it is the custom of the Law to call the sacrifice offered for sins “sin.” And according to that custom the Apostle calls it “sin,” because he speaks to Hebrews, among whom such terms were familiar through their knowledge of the Law. As though he said: Be afraid, because no sacrifice will henceforth be slain for you. For then there will be no sacrifice, but justice in rewarding or condemning. He will appear to those who await him—that is, to those who, because they are conscious of the merit of their good works, await his coming with a certain confidence; or to those who now await him patiently, persevering to the end in good works and lifting the gaze of their hearts toward his coming. [Col. 1625C] He will appear to them for salvation, because the vision of him will be their everlasting salvation, so that they will no longer experience any evil, whether of body or soul, but will rejoice without end in his sight.

## Chapter X

> “For the Law, having a shadow of good things to come, not the very image of the things, can never, by the same sacrifices which they offer continually year by year, make those who approach perfect. Otherwise they would have ceased to be offered, because the worshippers, once cleansed, would have had no further consciousness of sin. But in those sacrifices a remembrance of sins is made year by year. [Col. 1626A] For it is impossible for sins to be taken away by the blood of bulls and goats.”

He sufficiently proved that Christ ought to die only once, and now gives the reason why it was necessary for him to die once. For the Law could not bring about perfection, and therefore he who could bring about perfection had to die. Or the connection may be made thus: he proved Christ to be the better sacrifice by showing that those things which were in him were worthier than the earlier sacrifices. He now does the same thing again from another side, rejecting the sacrifices of the Law and showing that they were insufficient. For just as he is shown to be a better sacrifice by his own excellences, so likewise, conversely, he appears better when the weakness of legal sacrifices has been shown. For he proved that Christ took away the sins [Col. 1626B] of his own, both in their actions and even in the consent of their minds—something which the sacrifices of the Law could not do, though the Jews wished it.

Christ truly took away sins and made people perfect, because the Law could do neither. It can never—that is, at no time, neither in the time of Moses nor in the time of others—make perfect the high priests who approach the Holy of Holies. But why can it not? Because it has and contains a shadow of future things—that is, it has and commands those things which are a shadow of future good things. For whatever the Law commanded, such as the vessels of the tabernacle, sacrifices, and other things of that sort, were not the truth but a shadow of true things; and thereby it may be judged incapable of bringing anyone to perfection.

Or, the Law has a shadow of future good things—that is, a certain remote likeness of the things that were to come. That is, it shows future good things as dubiously and remotely as a shadow represents to our eyes the body of which it is the shadow. [Col. 1626C] And because the Law might in part have a shadow of future good things and in part the true image itself, he adds: I say that it has a shadow of future good things in such a way that in no part of itself does it possess the true image of the things. For an image represents a thing more truly and distinctly than a shadow. By an image we come in some manner to know both the qualities and the quantities of that of which it is an image; but through a shadow we have nothing certain, nothing definite.

If Moses or Melchizedek had been offered for the people of God, perhaps he would appear to be an image of Christ; but the goat and calf, and the other things which signified Christ, were not an image but a shadow. The Law itself, I say, can never make perfect—that is, make the high priests blessed and complete in the perfection of virtues—when they approach the Holy of Holies year by year with sacrifices. It cannot make them perfect by those very sacrifices which they always offer, for they are shadows, foretelling the grace by which we are justified, and human beings are not justified in them. [Col. 1626D] The high priests cannot be perfected in justice through them or in them; that is, they cannot truly be justified through them, even though they offer them continually as each year returns.

And because they might remove sins year by year over a period of twenty years, but then afterward let them remain, he adds “continually,” that is, perseveringly. As though he said: Although the high priests offered continually in the Holy of Holies year by year, nevertheless the Law could not make them perfect. And because the Law, through all its sacrifices, being shadows, led no one to perfection, something had to be offered through which the perfection of righteousness might be given to the human race.

The Law cannot make them perfect by such sacrifices, so that their conscience may be free from every stain of consent. Otherwise—that is, if it had done otherwise, if it could make them perfect—those sacrifices would already have ceased to be offered. That is, there would have been neither any need nor even any reason why they should afterward be offered; and thus they would have ceased, because the worshippers—that is, the sacrificers—once cleansed, that is, purged from every sin by one offering of them, would no longer have a consciousness of sin. [Col. 1627A] They would not be conscious in themselves of any sin, but would remain clean both in heart and in works; and therefore they would no longer need a sacrifice, since they would be perfect. This the Law could not accomplish.

But the one sacrifice of Christ makes people perfect. His body, once offered, perfectly cleansed and cleanses all his own, because that sacrifice will be sufficient for all unto cleansing until the end of the age. And even if they sin a thousand times, they need no other sacrifice, because this one is sufficient for all things and washes every conscience from sin. For it first purifies them through baptism, and, if they afterward sin, cleanses them again through repentance and restores them to the completion of virtues. And if we offer it daily, it is a remembrance of his death; and this sacrifice is one, not many, because it was offered only once. Nor are many Christs offered by many people, [Col. 1627B] but one Christ, everywhere and always whole, one body everywhere. Once offered, he is not consumed. What we do is a remembrance of the sacrifice; it is not repeated because of any weakness in it, since it perfects a human being, but because of our weakness, since we sin daily.

It was said above that the legal sacrifices would have ceased to be offered if they could effect the perfection of cleansing, because they would be offered superfluously when the worshippers, having been cleansed by them, knew that they had no stain of sin. But we see that they do not cleanse them. For in the sacrifices themselves, offered year by year, a remembrance of sins is made: a remembrance, not an absolution; an accusation of weakness, not a display of strength. For while they recall and confess their sins and offer those sacrifices for them, it is clear that they have sins. [Col. 1627C] Nor is this surprising: for it is impossible that sins should be taken away by the blood of bulls, goats, or other cattle. Even if outward action is removed through those sacrifices, inward guilt and consent remain. For sins are blotted out only by the blood of Christ, even for those who formerly, under the Law, seemed to receive remission through those sacrifices.

> “Therefore, entering into the world, he says: ‘Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but you prepared a body for me; whole burnt offerings and offerings for sin did not please you. Then I said: Behold, I come. In the beginning of the book it is written of me, that I should do your will, O God’ (Psalm XXXIX). Saying above that sacrifices and offerings and whole burnt offerings and offerings for sin [Col. 1628A] you did not desire, neither were those things pleasing to you which are offered according to the Law, then I said, ‘Behold, I come, that I may do your will, O God’: he takes away the first in order to establish that which follows. In this will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.”

Since the sacrifice of Christ’s body was sufficient to take away the sins of many, whereas the Law could not make even the high priests themselves perfect, therefore, to confirm this truth, the Son of God says these things as he enters the world—that is, as he assumes flesh. This is said with reference to the time when he was about to enter the world by assuming flesh. Through the prophet, as he considered the weakness of the Law and the necessity of offering his body, he says: “O Father, you did not desire a sacrifice made from cattle [Col. 1628B] or an offering made by the shedding of blood.”

For God was not truly delighted by such sacrifices; rather, he commanded them to signify the true sacrifice of Christ and to restrain the Jewish people from sacrifices to idols. Nor was he ever delighted by those odors except in the faith and devotion of those offering them. And especially from the coming of the Lord onward, he did not desire those sacrifices, since all of them were like the words of one promising, words that make a promise; when that which they promise has come, they must be set aside. A person remains a promisor until he gives; when he has given, he changes his words. He no longer says, “I shall still give,” which he had said he would give, but says, “I have given.”

Therefore those sacrifices, as words making a promise, were removed because the promised truth was presented—namely, the sacrifice of Christ which they promised; [Col. 1628C] and this was the reason why God first commanded them and afterward did not desire them. “You did not desire sacrifice,” he says, “and offering.” What then? Are we now, in this time, left without sacrifice and offering? Far from it. “But you prepared a body for me.” You did not desire those things because you prepared this for me. The fulfillment of the promise removed the words of the one promising.

You no longer desired those things in the time of grace; but you prepared a body for me—that is, you gave me a fitting and suitable body, because it was without sin, capable of suffering, and mortal, able to be offered for the redemption of all. “Whole burnt offerings” also—that is, those sacrifices which seemed worthier than all others because they were wholly burned upon the altar—“did not please you” when offered for some sin, because through them you did not pardon sin. And then, that is, when I see that all these things displease you [Col. 1628D] and that a body fit for sacrifice has been given me, I said: “Behold”—that is, without delay—“I come”; that is, I willingly approach to offer myself, because I regard this as the only sacrifice that will please you.

For in the beginning of the book of Psalms it is written of me that I should do your will, O God, where it says: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly,” and so forth (Psalm I). And this prophecy had to be fulfilled in me. There are also those who call all the canonical Scriptures one book, because they agree in a most marvelous and divine unity. In the beginning of this book it is written of me that I should do your will, because in the early parts of the book of Genesis, which is the beginning of the Scriptures, it is read prophetically that “a man shall leave [Col. 1629A] his father” (Genesis II)—that is, the Son of God, clothing himself in humanity, will come from the Father’s seat—and “shall leave his mother,” that is, the synagogue, “and shall cleave to his wife,” that is, the Church.

Or, “the beginning of the book” is the proclamation of divinity, than which nothing higher is found in the Scriptures. And in the beginning of the book it is written of me, because the holy Scriptures show me to be God over all, when they say: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Psalm XXXII), “and the Word was God” (John I), and other things of this sort. And I, who am found so great in the most exalted beginning—that is, in the loftiest proclamation of divinity—in the book of Scripture, mercifully assuming the form of a servant, willed, O God, that I should do, or that I should perform, your will, becoming obedient unto death (Philippians II). [Col. 1629B] For I made my will, which I had according to the nature of my humanity, wholly harmonious with your divine will: so that, just as you willed the human race to be redeemed through the sacrifice of my body, so I too might will it, and might desire in all things to fulfill your will.

Christ spoke these words in the Psalm, and now the Apostle explains to us what he himself thinks of them. Namely, that this authority not only shows that the old sacrifices made no one perfect, and that Christ’s sacrifice alone sufficiently accomplished or accomplishes this for all believers; but also, if these words are carefully observed, it demonstrates both the removal of the Old Testament offering and the establishment of the New. For Christ himself, saying above, “You did not desire those things,” and adding, “Then I said: Behold, I come,” takes away the first sacrifice and with it the Old Testament, and establishes a new sacrifice, that it may remain firm, and with it the New Testament. [Col. 1629C]

And this is the meaning: the Son himself, saying above that you did not desire sacrifices and offerings and whole burnt offerings, even offerings for sin, showed that carnal sacrifices, and with them all carnal observances, were rejected. “You did not desire those sacrifices”; and lest those which were not offered according to the institution of the Law should seem to displease you, it is added: “Neither were those things pleasing to you which are offered according to the Law.” And then, when all those things displeased you and you desired another sacrifice, I said: “Behold, I come to be sacrificed, that I may do and fulfill your will, O God,” whom I worship and serve according to my humanity.

In saying these things, the Lord takes away the first sacrifice in order to establish that which follows. For by saying, “You did not desire sacrifices and offerings,” he takes away the first—that is, he shows the removal of the first; and by adding, “Behold, I come to do your will,” he establishes that which follows—that is, he shows that the new thing will be stable and firm. “The first” and “that which follows” may be understood either as sacrifice, as we have said, or as testament. [Col. 1629D] For we see both fulfilled. The old sacrifice has been wholly removed from the people of God, and the succeeding sacrifice of the Lord’s body has been substituted. Likewise, the first testament, with its carnal observances, has been removed, and the Gospel has succeeded it.

“I said, ‘Behold, I come to do your will,’” that is, that I may be sacrificed as you wish and establish a new law. “In this will”—that is, in this sacrifice of himself made according to the Father’s will—we believers have been sanctified: that is, not only cleansed from sins but perfected in virtues. And this has occurred through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ made on the cross for us, once and no more; and therefore that which follows has been established, because through it we have been sanctified. But the first was cast down or removed because it led no one to perfection. [Col. 1630A]

> “And indeed every priest stands ready, ministering daily and often offering the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins.
