But this man, offering one sacrifice for sins, sits forever at the right hand of God, henceforth awaiting until his enemies are made the footstool of his feet” (Psalm CIX; I Corinthians XV).

[Col. 1630B] Question: Someone might say, “The blood of goats and bulls, offered once a year by the high priest, led no one to perfection; but those sacrifices which were performed daily rightly made priests perfect, because they sacrificed continually and always implored God’s grace.” He responds, as it were, by showing that, just as high priests were not sanctified through their sacrifices, neither were priests, although by some legal observance they might be sanctified while offering continually.

As though he said: Every high priest offers year by year and does not arrive at any completion; and in the same way every priest always offers, yet is never made complete through those offerings. And every priest “stands ready,” that is, standing prepared to fulfill his office, ministering daily at the altar and often [Col. 1630C] offering the same sacrifices which he had already offered—that is, ones like the former: so that he who offered a bull yesterday may offer a bull today and a bull tomorrow. Although these sacrifices are the same and frequently repeated, and although they are offered by a priest who stands ready, always and diligently at his office, however often they may be offered, they can never—that is, at no time—take away sins.

The priest offers many sacrifices and is always devoted to such service, yet he wears himself out in fruitless labor. But this our true priest, of whom we speak and whose sacrifice we intend to show sufficient, offers not often, nor many sacrifices, but one sacrifice, which alone was sufficient to blot out the sins of all believers. After completing the obedience of his passion, he sits—that is, he rests, reigns, and judges—at the right hand of God, [Col. 1630D] that is, in the Father’s higher dignity, remaining there forever. For he has no need to labor again or offer again, nor is there any need for him to suffer anything because of any imperfection in himself or his own.

For his sacrifice was of such perfection and efficacy that there is no need for it to be offered again for anyone’s sins. And though we offer it daily, Christ no longer feels the pain of his passion; rather, we make a memorial of his passion. We would be greatly afflicted in this flesh unless we lived under pardon until its laying aside. Therefore grace was bestowed upon us through the mediator, so that, polluted by the flesh of sin, we might be cleansed through the likeness of flesh—that is, through the sacrifice of his body, which is offered in the celebration of Masses.

Therefore, since although he himself suffers no more, [Col. 1631A] he has not ceased to offer that same sacrifice through his priests, it is aptly now said that, “offering one sacrifice for sins, he sits at the right hand of God.” For “offering” is in the present tense, because, as we have said, he still offers it through his priests, because he offered it once through himself. For of his passion it was said that his sacrifice was offered once, although it is still offered in the ministries.

The legal priest ministers, but this one sits, because ministering belongs to servants, while sitting belongs to lords. And he sits at the right hand of God, in order that it may be apparent that he can well perfect his own, because he merited such exaltation. “Henceforth,” that is, as to what remains—namely, the glorification of bodies, since with sins forgiven this alone remains. Or rather, “henceforth,” that is, as to what remains: awaiting the glory of the good and punishment of the evil, until his enemies are made his footstool. [Col. 1631B] That is, until the time when those who still oppose and contradict him are wholly subjected to him: some meanwhile through faith, others in the future through condemnation.

There is a reason why, though already glorified, he does not yet glorify his own, or why, though judged in his passion, he does not yet judge his enemies: because some of his enemies will still become friends and acquire for themselves the best place beneath his feet. For it is necessary that each person have there a place either of grace or of punishment; and therefore judgment is delayed, so that each may seek what place he will have there.

> “For by one offering he has perfected forever those who are sanctified. And the Holy Spirit also testifies to us. For after he said: ‘This is the testament which I shall establish for them after those days, says the Lord: I shall place my laws in their hearts and write them upon their minds; and I shall remember their sins and iniquities no more’ (Jeremiah XXXI; above, VIII). But where there is remission of these things, there is no longer an offering for sin.”

I said that he offered one sacrifice for sins. And why one, rather than many? Because it was sufficient for all things. For by one offering—that is, the shedding of his own blood—he perfected those who are sanctified: that is, cleansing them from sins through baptism, he sanctified them; and having sanctified them, he perfected them, that is, advanced them to the highest perfection [Col. 1631C] of virtues insofar as a human being can attain the completion of righteousness in this life. And he perfected them forever, because they will possess that completion of righteousness without end in the kingdom of everlasting blessedness, and their perfection will never be changed.

Nor do I alone say this; the Holy Spirit also testifies with us through Jeremiah (chapter XXXI), that is, testifies together to the same thing which we testify concerning sanctification and perfection. He truly testifies. For after he said, “This is the testament,” and so forth, there he testified to that which we maintain. After he said this, he testified to that—that is, from the fact that he said this, it follows that he testifies with us to what we testify concerning the sanctification and perfection of believers in the New Testament.

For because that perfection comes not through the Old but through the New Testament, the Spirit himself makes mention of that same New Testament when he promises this perfection, saying: “This is the testament,” and so forth. [Col. 1631D] As though he said: I shall not teach the Old Testament, I shall not proclaim carnal observances; rather, this is the spiritual testament which I shall establish and affirm, speaking to and approaching them. And I shall do this after those days which have been predetermined by me, says the Lord through Jeremiah, not Jeremiah himself.

And I shall not establish this New Testament for them as I established the Old, writing upon stone tablets for their hard fathers; but rather in another and more useful manner, namely, by placing my laws in their hearts—that is, by making my will known to their inward faculties through the Holy Spirit, who will pour wisdom and charity into them, so that they may understand those laws and fulfill them with delight. And I shall write those laws which I give upon their minds, because the new commandments will be of such dignity that the judgment of their minds will be exceeded, and no one will be sufficient of himself to fulfill them; rather, his weakness will be helped and strengthened by the aid of grace, so that he may fulfill them. [Col. 1632A]

Here it is indicated that he would perfect them in virtues forever; and concerning the sanctification which he would give, it is added that he will no longer remember their sins, insofar as they were committed against himself, nor their iniquities, insofar as they were committed against their neighbor, from the time of baptism onward. For he will neither impose upon them any penance for these in this age nor inflict any punishment upon them for them in the age to come.

Thus the Holy Spirit promised through the new grace that sins would be forgiven. But where there is remission of these things, an offering of the Law for sin is no longer to be made; rather, it ought to cease among Christians, whose sins have been forgiven in baptism. But even if someone sins after baptism, forgiveness comes through repentance, and they do not need a legal offering. Or, in the age to come, when all sins have been altogether forgiven, Christ’s offering will no longer be offered for any of their sins, because there will be none.

> “Therefore, brothers, having confidence to enter the holy places through the blood of Christ, by the new and living way which he inaugurated for us through the veil, that is, his flesh, [Col. 1632D] and having a great priest over the house of God, let us approach with a true heart in the fullness of faith, our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with clean water. Let us hold fast the unwavering confession of our hope. For he who promised is faithful; and let us consider one another unto the stirring up of charity and good works, not forsaking our assembly, as is the custom of some, but encouraging one another, and so much the more as you see the Day approaching.”

In many ways having commended Christ’s high priesthood, demolished that of the Jews, shown that Christ was a better sacrifice and sufficient for the remission of sins, and that the law with its sacrifices was powerless for this end, he now concludes his discussion of these matters and begins to exhort them [Col. 1633A] to hold fast to faith in Christ alone together with the practice of good works. From all that he has said above, ever since he began to discuss Christ’s priesthood, he now draws this inference. It is as though he said: Since Christ is a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, has opened heaven by his own blood, and by one offering sanctified and perfected us, along with the other matters treated above, therefore, brothers, let us draw near to him by faith and good works—from whom we were far removed through unbelief and evil conduct. I mean us, who have confidence, that is, the most certain hope, by which we need not despair if we have wandered, but may confidently draw near: having confidence for entry into the holy places, that is, for entering the Holy of Holies, namely heaven, into which we understand that [Col. 1633B] our High Priest has gone before us.

We have confidence that we shall enter those holy places, not through legal sacrifices but through Christ’s blood, which he shed precisely so that, redeemed by it, we might draw near there and enter those holy places. He inaugurated for us that way—that entrance now made into a well-trodden road to the homeland—being himself the first of all believers to enter; he first walked by it, and granted his faithful the power to walk it after him. I call it a new way, that is, one by which no one had walked before him; and a living way, that is, enduring and permanent, awaiting us who have been sanctified, because thereafter it is always open to believers. Or it is living because it makes all who enter it live [Col. 1633C]. It is living because no one enters by it except one whom life leads.

Through the veil—that is, through that which was signified by the veil dividing the two tabernacles, namely through his flesh—the way into the Holy of Holies, that is, into the heavenly Jerusalem, has been opened to us. Thus, when he died on the cross, “the veil of the temple was torn” (Matt. XXVII), signifying that by his death the way into the Holy of Holies had been opened to us. Through the veil, that is, through Christ’s flesh by which his divinity was veiled, that way remains passable, because believers receive Christ’s flesh as provision for their journey and, departing this life, enter the gate of heaven. Through the veil, that is, through his own flesh, he inaugurated that way for us, because, veiled in flesh, he was the first to pass through it. He inaugurated it through flesh because, unless he had assumed flesh, [Col. 1633D] he would not have inaugurated it for us. For through flesh, not through divinity, one can go from place to place; and therefore through the flesh with which he had veiled himself, he inaugurated for us the journey to heaven, as the Psalmist sings to him: “You make the cloud your ascent” (Ps. CIII). For he made the cloud his ascent because he ascended in flesh, not in divinity. What the Apostle here calls a veil, the Psalmist calls a cloud.

Or, according to the view of some, Christ’s flesh, which we receive from the altar, is called a veil because it is veiled to our senses in the sacrament. For our senses report one thing and faith another. Sight persuades us that there is merely bread under the appearance of bread; faith, however, teaches that it is living and life-giving flesh. Taste reports bread in its flavor; [Col. 1634A] hearing likewise reports the same in the breaking; but faith teaches that believers receive the whole Lamb without any injury to him. For we receive not lifeless flesh but flesh living through consecration and divine operation. That is, in the sacrament we receive Christ and the Lamb offered for us—not in order that he himself should suffer any insult or injury in the sacrament, but so that what he endured for our life might be brought before our remembrance.

Through this veil of the Lord’s flesh a new life was inaugurated for us, because through the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood entry into the kingdom of heaven began to be opened to believers in the New Testament, whereas under the old law it was open to no one. “And having,” he says, “a great priest,” Christ praying to the Father for us. For through his sacrifice [Col. 1634B] he entered the Holy of Holies, where he always lives, offers sacrifice, and intercedes for us. I mean a priest appointed over God’s household, that is, over the Church, to govern it and defend it against every assault.

The whole sense is as if it were said: We have confidence of entering the Holy of Holies, into the vision of heavenly peace: first, because through Christ’s blood humankind has put off slavery; secondly, because he himself entered first; thirdly, because he strengthens and nourishes his faithful with the food of his flesh and the drink of his blood; fourthly, because he intercedes for us; and fifthly, because he governs and protects the Church. We, he says, having confidence through all these things that have been said, let us draw near to him—that is, by steps of devotion and the course of religious [Col. 1634C] conduct, let us become ever nearer to him for entry into the holy places.

Let us draw near not with a feigned but with a true heart, so that we may seek him with a heart not counterfeit but pure and true, as it is written: “Seek him in simplicity of heart” (Wis. I). Let us do this in the fullness of faith: that is, let our faith concerning him be complete and lack nothing that it ought to have, lest we should still unbelievingly suppose that without carnal observances he is less than sufficient for salvation. I mean us, whose hearts have been sprinkled and purified from every evil conscience, and whose body has been washed with clean water, that is, baptism, by which all the stains of sins are cleansed. This means: let us draw near to him with a true heart in the fullness of faith—we whose hearts have been sprinkled, that is, whose [Col. 1634D] hearts have been sprinkled in baptism with the dew of the Holy Spirit and by this cleansed from an evil conscience, that is, from every guilt of conscience; and whose body has been washed, that is, who have a body washed and cleansed from sin by the clean water of baptism. For in baptism all sins, inward as well as outward, are blotted out.

Therefore, because by baptism we have been made free from sin, freedom of choice has been restored to us, grace has been given to us, and we have no excuse, let us, as has been said, draw near to him who has bestowed such benefits on us. Let us love him with a true heart, keep whole faith toward him, believe him with full faith, and confess with our mouth what we believe in our heart: namely, let us hold fast the confession of our hope. That is, let nothing be so burdensome [Col. 1635A] or harsh as to take from our mouth the confession which is the cause of hope, making us hope for heavenly blessedness—that is, the confession which proceeds from hope. For unless someone hoped for future goods, he would not confess that for which he might lose present goods.

Let us hold this confession, which makes us hope for eternal goods, without wavering: that is, let us hold it so firmly that it may not bend downward toward desire for or fear of earthly things, but may always stretch upward toward desire for heavenly things. And we ought steadfastly to hold this confession of hope because the Lord is faithful in his promises and cannot lie—he who promised beforehand, that is, who many times through the Scriptures promised us the eternal goods for which we hope.

Thus far [Col. 1635B] the Apostle has exhorted them with respect to God. Then he urges them to be diligent concerning their neighbors’ good and admonishes them to charity and good conduct. This exhortation seems chiefly to concern, or to rebuke, those who, thinking themselves of a better life, forsook the fellowship of others. It is as though he said: Let us hold faith and confession with regard to ourselves and to God; and let us consider one another—that is, let us carefully and attentively observe each other, not in order to envy or plot against one another, but for the provoking of charity and good works: that each may have a greater fervor of love and be stirred up to every good work.

Thus the perfect should consider the imperfect, exhorting them to love of God and neighbor and to the fruit of love, [Col. 1635C] that is, good works. The imperfect, however, should consider the perfect, taking from them an example of benefit to imitate. And so they will stir one another up to charity and good works. Or, in every respect let us consider what is useful for our brothers, doing this reciprocally: just as we are concerned for others’ salvation, so they too, in turn, may be concerned for ours, so that none among us may be idle and fruitless. Since it says, “let us consider one another,” this exhortation belongs to each individual.

Let us do these things, he says, not forsaking our assembly—that is, those gathered with us into the faith—as is the custom of some among you, who, having no charity and glorying as though in the singularity of their merits, separate themselves from the rest. He touches upon and rebukes those who rend the unity of charity, as though they could not live among others because of their holiness, whereas they ought rather by their example to console others. To console one who is laboring is to persist together in the labor, because relief from labor is the sight of a fellow laborer; just as, when a companion joins one on a journey, the road itself is not shortened, but the toil of the journey is lightened by the companion’s society. And this all the more, he says, as you see the Day drawing near. It is as though he said: Let labor increase in proportion as the rewards of labor now draw near.

Or, if tribulation and persecution by unbelievers should press upon the brothers, do not forsake your assembly—that is, those associated with you through the sacraments of faith [Col. 1636A] in the one body of the Church—but rather console them in adversity by the sweetness of your exhortation. I say: do not forsake Christ’s poor in tribulation, as some do, who, seeing anxieties threatening the saints, withdraw from them the support of aid. Do not withdraw yourselves from your companions in the contest of martyrdom by denying them the comfort of your exhortation; but be those who console them in their very sufferings. And do this all the more as you see harsher punishments impending, through which their end draws near—the end at which they will pass from the darkness of this age to the day of perpetual brightness—lest anyone ever be absent from that most blessed day through the withdrawal of your exhortation.

Or even in peace, you who seem holier should not forsake the assembly of the brothers on account of [Col. 1636B] your own religious devotion because they appear less devout; rather, through your dwelling and conversation among them, offer them consolation, lest they despair of their salvation on account of their own irreligion when they see themselves abandoned by you who are holy. Console them by promising forgiveness, raising them into hope, and admonishing them to do good. Do this more and more daily, as you see the day of death drawing near. It is as though he said: Do not delay, for each person’s death is near and becomes nearer every day; pursue this all the more earnestly as you see that singular and fearful day drawing near.

> “For if we sin willfully after receiving [Col. 1636C] the knowledge of truth [above, ch. 6], there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a certain fearful expectation of judgment and a zeal of fire which is to consume the adversaries.”

Truly, you ought not to sin by neglecting and forsaking the assembly of the brothers, because for us Christians who sin willfully—that is, who offend God deliberately, not through ignorance or weakness but by conscious transgression—after receiving the knowledge of truth, that is, after we have been inwardly enlightened and have known without doubt what is to be chosen and what rejected, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, as under the old law sacrifices were commanded to be offered repeatedly for sins. For Christ is not to be sacrificed again [Col. 1636D] for sins: this was done once, and need not be done a second time. Rather, we must remain in faith and good works.

I do not exclude repentance, but speak according to baptism. I do not say there is no further repentance or remission, but no further sacrifice—that is, no second cross—because one was sufficient. We should not expect another, but repent, because we cannot be rebaptized into Christ’s death. For one who repeats baptism repeats Christ’s death, so that from its repetition there may be a repeated remission. But this is impossible. No such sacrifice remains for us if we have defiled ourselves after baptism.

Or, “for those sinning willfully” means those who remain in the will to sin: for us no sacrifice for sins remains—that is, the sacrifice [Col. 1637A] of the Lord’s body can confer no benefit. For sacrifice and offering are daily offered to God for the sins of penitents, not for the sins of those unwilling to abandon their very sins. If it should please us to continue in sin so persistently and continuously, no sacrifice for sins remains for us; rather, there remains for us a certain notable expectation of judgment, which is fearful—that is, fitted to terrify, because it can greatly terrify us. This punishment is inward, since outwardly too everlasting fire will rage. For fear of judgment itself is a punishment for evil persons at the resurrection, indescribable and more grievous than Gehenna.

When the Judge says, “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV), the fire of zeal will immediately seize them—that is, violent hostility—because with an excessively inflamed zeal it will punish them forever, and will, as it were, envy them, since it will always burn for this purpose: unceasingly to consume them. This intensely burning zeal is indeed to consume—that is, perpetually devour—the adversaries of Christ, so that they may always fail in torments and, failing, never reach an end: those who now oppose Christ either through unbelief or through evil conduct [Col. 1637B].

> “Anyone who makes void the law of Moses dies without any mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deut. XVII; Matt. XVIII; II Cor. XIII). “How much worse punishments, do you suppose, will he deserve who has trampled the Son of God underfoot, regarded as defiled the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace? For we know him who said: ‘Vengeance is mine, and I will repay’” (Deut. XXXII; Rom. XII). “And again: ‘For the Lord will judge his people’” (Ps. CXXXIV). “It is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God.”

Certainly, for us who sin voluntarily and willingly after being enlightened by the knowledge of truth, no hope of future salvation remains while we wish to lie in sin; rather, the punishment of everlasting condemnation remains. This is clear from the lesser case: anyone making void the law of Moses—that is, transgressing any precept of the old law—dies by the death decreed by the law: he is stoned, burned, or destroyed by another kind of death, without any mercy, [Col. 1637D] that is, without any mitigation of punishments. I mean one convicted by two or three witnesses, who testify that he has transgressed the law in some point. Such a person was indeed killed for transgression of that law, in which those who observed it did not receive divine grace.

Therefore, how much more ought you to think that he deserves worse and more bitter punishments against whom the holy angels and his own conscience will bear witness at judgment that he has trampled the Son of God underfoot. Under the law two or three witnesses are produced, but there the multitude of angels and saints will be witnesses, along with the sinner himself against himself. Then punishments will receive him—that is, penalties folding, bending, and crushing him beneath themselves. I call these punishments worse [Col. 1638A] because they terrify and crush him more than the torments of the law.

He who now tramples the Son of God underfoot and regards the blood of the covenant as defiled will feel so terrible a vengeance, and forever. That is, he despises it so greatly that he believes it insufficient for salvation if he thinks brute animals slaughtered according to the law still necessary for salvation. For he tramples underfoot the Son of God who does not believe that the faith and rule of life which Christ gave to people are sufficient for eternal life, but trusts in carnal observances more than in Christ’s new precepts. He tramples Christ underfoot who, after receiving Christianity, sins freely without fear and repentance, and who partakes of him unworthily.

He also regards as defiled the blood of the New Testament—that is, Christ’s blood, the confirmation of the Gospel and pledge of the new inheritance—who believes that it does not at all cleanse humankind from sins but instead defiles all who believe in Christ. For necessarily, if it did not cleanse, it defiled; and it made them sinners because it caused the carnal observances and justifications of the law to cease. Everything that defiles was first defiled in itself; and this blood would be defiled in itself and would defile us if it withdrew us from that in which remission of sins existed—that is, if it separated us from carnal observances when remission of sins could be effected through them.

But, to show that one who thinks so wrongly of this blood is to be punished more severely, he adds: “by which he was sanctified,” that is, by which he received remission of sins. Thus [Col. 1638C] he sins more gravely against it and proves ungrateful. For this reason he will be punished more, because he believes that the means by which he was cleansed is unclean. Yet that person also regards this blood as defiled who, cleansed by it, returns to his vomit and neglects to repent (II Pet. II). And he insults the Spirit of grace—that is, the Holy Spirit who has been thanked or who gives grace—who ascribes to carnal observances the remission which that Spirit works, or who rejects him from himself by evil living.

Whoever does these things will rightly die without mercy, as was proved in the lesser case by the law’s vengeance, where a transgressor is punished without mercy. For if the transgressor of the law is put to a death he deserves for a single precept transgressed once, how much more severely will he be punished [Col. 1638D] who offends God in the three ways stated above: trampling his Son underfoot, regarding his blood as defiled, and inflicting insult upon the Holy Spirit?

Certainly, every such person will be punished. For we know him who said—that is, we know how truthful and how powerful is he who said—“Vengeance is mine, and I will repay.” It is as though he said: People take vengeance in the present upon their enemies, and I too will exact vengeance for myself in the future; that is, I will avenge myself upon my adversaries, who now trample me underfoot and provoke me with insults, though they live under Christian profession. Where we read in Ezekiel, “The visitations of the city have drawn near” (Ezek. IX), the Seventy translated: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay,” says the Lord.

And again, to prove the same point—that the one [Col. 1639A] who tramples the Son of God underfoot will be punished—Moses (Deut. XXXII), or the Psalmist, says: “For the Lord will judge his people” (Ps. CXXXIV). That is, he will not leave the sins of his people unpunished, but will judge even each of the faithful according to his ways. Therefore let no one flatter himself concerning impunity if he sins because he is now among the Christian people; rather, let him know that the criminal will not possess the kingdom of God. For those who now, by evil living in the Church, trample the Son of God underfoot are to be cast out of it. “For many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX). The Lord will judge his people, and those whom he finds condemnable among them he will condemn severely.

For it is dreadful—that is, to be feared and guarded against with utmost dread—to fall into the hands of the living God: the God who is always living and [Col. 1639B] inflicts punishments that always live upon those whom he condemns. He falls into God’s hands who does not provide for himself but is suddenly caught: that is, one who does not foresee the coming calamities comes, without repentance for sins and without the adornment of virtues, before the judgment of the eternal Judge and will experience the fall of condemnation. “Hands” stand for power: just as one who falls perhaps into an enemy’s hands is held fast so that he can never escape uninjured, so every person to be condemned is compelled by God’s powerful judgment to suffer the punishments he has deserved. If that God should ever die, the punishment which he decreed might cease. But because he always lives and is omnipotent, whatever has been decreed in his judgment remains forever.

> “But remember the former days, in which, after you were enlightened, [Col. 1639C] you endured a great contest of sufferings. Sometimes you were made a public spectacle by reproaches and tribulations; at other times you became companions of those so treated. For you had compassion even on those in bonds, and accepted with joy the plundering of your possessions, knowing that you have a better and abiding substance. Therefore do not lose your confidence, which has great recompense. For you have need of patience, so that, doing the will of God, you may receive the promise.”

He had sternly terrified them, restraining them from sins by speaking of eternal punishment; now he restores those who have been frightened, praising them for the past and exhorting them [Col. 1639D] to persevere in the good things they had begun. For it is shameful and worthy of rebuke if those who lived devoutly while they were still untrained in the faith now offend God by acting wickedly; and if those who, at the beginning when they came to faith, bore various persecutions magnanimously should later become fainthearted and fail in tribulations.

“But remember the former days,” and so forth. He shows that it had been long since they came to faith, and that consequently they ought more fully to have advanced in religion and been trained to endure persecution. It is as though he said: Do not forsake our assembly in tribulation, nor by evil living continue to trample the Son of God underfoot; rather, remember your steadfastness and perfection in former days. This is what “remember” means: bring [Col. 1640A] the former days back to mind; consider what you were like in those days, lest you now be worse, when by the length of time you ought to be much better.

Consider the days in which, enlightened by the light of faith, you endured a great contest of sufferings: that is, you did not fail under endurance, but fought magnanimously, holding faith in heart and mouth, which the persecutors strove to force from you. For by saying “you endured a great contest of sufferings,” he signifies more than if he had simply said, “you endured great sufferings.” The word *contest* shows that they did not fail but fought steadfastly. This would not be signified if *contest* were not added. Or he called it a contest of sufferings because the sufferings themselves fought against them, in order to force patience and [Col. 1640B] faith from them, but could not do so.

Therefore, those who stood so bravely at the beginning of their conversion ought not now, through fear of persecution, to forsake the assembly of brothers who need their comfort. Or he used the phrase “contest of sufferings” because suffering that is inflicted is one thing, while the difficulty of suffering that struggles against reason and urges one to set faith aside is another. Thus he praises them in two ways: first, because they endured sufferings and blows outwardly; secondly, because inwardly they fought most invincibly against the sufferings themselves. It is as though he said: You did two things in one, because you suffered one thing outwardly and another inwardly.

“And in one respect,” that is, in what you endured outwardly, “you were made a spectacle”—that is, an object of astonishment [Col. 1640C] to all the people—“by reproaches,” which they uttered against you, because everyone mocked you and called you mad and senseless. Reproach is grievous indeed, but it is more grievous when someone becomes a spectacle to people rather than being reproached in private. You became a spectacle through reproaches because, while all the people watched, many insults and dishonorable words were inflicted upon you; and through tribulations because you were publicly scourged and endured various punishments. In this he shows their very great steadfastness: though they were a spectacle, they did not nevertheless fail in faith.

For it is no slight reproach to become a spectacle, suffer people’s taunts, and—as though becoming a spectacle were not enough—to have verbal reproaches added; and to the reproaches, verbal tribulations. These things you endured “in one respect,” that is, in one part of the contest, which, as stated, was active outwardly. “But in the other respect”—what was inward, namely the other part of the contest, which was carried on in the heart—you fought in such a way that by compassion you became companions of those so treated. He says “in one respect” and “in the other” in order to show that these are the two parts of the contest and thus that they endured every kind of conflict. By sharing their suffering and supplying necessities, you became companions of those so treated: that is, of the apostles and the like, who passed their whole life enduring adversities for Christ, and by whose example you too ought to persevere in the practice of patience.

Truly, you became their companions. For you had compassion on those in bonds [Col. 1641A]: if they suffered for Christ’s name, you grieved for this as though you yourselves were bound with them, and you showed the grief of your heart by works, providing them support from your possessions because, being held by chains and prisons, they could not seek what was necessary for themselves. You had compassion on them by serving them, and for this reason the unbelievers took away your own possessions: namely, because you were providing from them for the saints. You received this plundering of possessions not with sorrow but with joy and gladness of heart. This is what he says: “You had compassion on those in bonds; and you received with joy the plundering of your possessions”—that is, you grieved over the tribulations of the saints as though you suffered them in your own body, and rejoiced at the loss of your possessions inflicted upon you because of your support for them.

You joyfully received the loss of your resources as a gift of God, knowing—that is, because you knew—that you thereby possessed a substance far better than these things and abiding: not transitory but eternal. That is, with most certain hope you trusted that through the loss of temporal things you would gain eternal goods; through transitory labor, eternal rest; and through earthly loss, a heavenly treasure. Since you had a certain hope, that is, confidence in heavenly recompense, therefore, do not lose your confidence—that is, do not fail. The inference follows from his statement that they had borne such great things and expected eternal life from them, namely an abiding substance. It is as though he said: Since at the beginning of faith [Col. 1641C] you suffered so many adversities and from them confidently hoped for eternal reward, therefore do not lose your confidence—your firm hope—by failing in the patience of faith, because through loss of patience you will also lose hope of eternal life.

And lest loss of hope seem a slight loss, he adds: “which has great recompense.” Therefore hope with certainty for that ineffable reward which eye has not seen nor ear heard (I Cor. II; Isa. LXIV), as though you already possess it. Or, it possesses that reward in divine predestination. Truly, through impatience you ought not lose confidence in everlasting recompense. For patience is necessary for you: that is, it is necessary that you now patiently endure adversities for God if you wish afterwards to reign with him, for “if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” [Col. 1641D] (II Tim. II).

It is necessary so that through it, doing God’s will—that is, bearing with equanimity all injuries inflicted on you, since this pleases God; or doing God’s will, that is, keeping his commandments and willingly enduring whatever adversity occurs on their account—you may receive the promise. That is, just as you now bear for God the burden of adversity, so afterwards you will carry away the burden of blessed recompense which the heavenly God has often promised. “For this momentary and light tribulation of ours in the present works in us beyond measure an eternal weight of glory in the heights.” Therefore strive through present patience then to receive that weight of glory [Col. 1642A] which God has promised beforehand.

> “For yet a little while, and he who is to come will come and will not delay. But my righteous one lives by faith” (Hab. II). “And if he draws back, my soul will not be pleased with him. But we are not children of drawing back unto destruction, but of faith unto the gaining of the soul.”

Patience, as I have said, must be maintained, for it is neither long nor severe, but small and very slight, lest it seem long and hard to you to preserve it. For the end of each person is near, and soon you will rest from labor and receive glory when Christ judges. For according to Habakkuk’s prophecy, there remains yet a little while: that is, patience must still be preserved for a short time; [Col. 1642B] and it is very slight: that is, there is no severe or great thing to suffer, but whatever must be endured in this age will be of small extent. The patience of this time is momentary and must be reckoned as of no severity when compared with what is to be given in eternity and highest glory.

“There remains,” he says, “yet a little while, a very little, and afterwards the Judge will come,” who will undoubtedly come at some time and will not delay his coming, but will come quickly to give you the promise already mentioned, if for the present, keeping patience, you do his will. There will be no delay in giving the reward; the Rewarder will soon come. In the meantime, however, “my righteous one lives in the soul by faith,” because faith is now the life of the heart until he comes who will give eternal life to both soul and body. And whoever is my righteous one is justified through faith, not [Col. 1642C] through works of the law. For one justified through works of the law is not my righteous one but his own, because he is justified not by me but by himself, and glories not in me but in himself. But one justified through faith is my righteous one because he is justified by the gift of my grace; he does not attribute his righteousness to himself but reckons it to my grace.

And in the meantime he lives by faith, until, when Christ comes, he is brought into my vision and lives eternally by sight. Or he lives afterwards by the faith he now possesses, because what he now believes he will then receive. “He lives by faith.” But if he draws himself back from faith—either abandoning faith through fear of persecution or, seeking righteousness in works of the law, beginning inwardly to withdraw from faith—my soul, that is, my will, will not be pleased; and therefore he [Col. 1642D] cannot live, but will instead deserve condemnation because he offends me by withdrawing himself from faith and grace. The Lord spoke these things through the prophet. Whoever withdraws himself displeases God.

“But we are not such.” We are not apostates who withdraw ourselves from faith. It is as though he said: We ought not to apostatize by withdrawing ourselves, but to advance toward what is better. The Apostle counts himself among them in order to persuade them more effectively; and he does not say that they are such as he does not wish them to be, so that by gentle admonition he may keep them from withdrawing themselves, because they had not yet wholly apostatized but still remained partly in faith—that is, retained a part of faith.

“We are not,” he says, “children of drawing back,” that is, of apostasy leading us to destruction; rather, we are [Col. 1643A] children of God leading to the gaining of the soul. That is, we have not been begotten by apostasy, which draws its children into destruction; rather, faith has begotten us, leading to the gaining of the soul, so that through faith each of us may gain his soul and not lose it through drawing back. For as the soul is gained through faith, so it is lost through withdrawal. It is gained so that we may possess it freely in eternal blessedness, lest through withdrawal it pass out of our power and become, in torments, the possession of demons.

## Chapter XI

> “Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not appearing. For by it the elders obtained testimony.”

Because they were very stubborn with respect to faith, the Apostle therefore gives a lengthy treatment of faith, in order wholly to bend their obstinacy toward faith, showing that all the saints, their fathers, pleased God through faith. I said that you are children of faith. This faith is not concerned with things that are seen, but with things unseen and hoped for. But faith is the substance of things hoped for: that is, faith is the cause why the things to be hoped for will at some time subsist in us; it is for us the cause of attaining eternal things, which now are to be hoped for and desired. Faith is properly called the substance of things hoped for because it underlies them. For just as substance underlies form, making it to be, so faith underlies the things hoped for by placing them within us. The things hoped for are glory, blessedness, rest, eternity, and the like; and faith is called their substance because it already makes them subsist in our heart through the certainty of belief. It makes them subsist—that is, to be, or as it were to stand before our gaze, and to remain immovable as eternal things. The same faith is also the evidence of things not apparent: that is, certainty concerning things which do not appear, and, if anyone doubts them, proof—for example, the resurrection still to come is proved because the prophets, apostles, and other saints believed thus.

For when such things do not appear, they are either past, as in the creation of the world; or present, as in the Lord Jesus seated at the right hand of the Father; or future, as in the day of judgment. Faith is the evidence—that is, the certainty and proof—of all these things. Faith, therefore, is evidence of those things which cannot appear. Things which are apparent do not have faith, but knowledge. Even if things seen are said to be believed, as each person says that he has believed his own eyes, this is not the faith which is built up in us. Rather, from things that are seen we are led to believe things which are unseen, as Thomas saw the man and believed the God (John 20).

Thus faith is the substance—that is, the foundation, firmness, and essence—of hoped-for goods; and it is the evidence of things not apparent, namely a certain and rational proof of invisible things and a fore-indication of things to come. For an argument is called a reason which produces conviction regarding a doubtful matter. Faith truly is the substance of things hoped for, making them subsist in the hearts of believers and thereby justifying their heart; for in this faith the elders received from the Lord the testimony of righteousness. God himself was witness to their pure conscience and testified that they were righteous, as he said to Noah: “I have seen thee righteous before me in this generation” (Gen. 7). And if through faith they received the testimony of righteousness, while righteousness is the cause and merit of future goods, then faith is the substance of things hoped for. By “elders” he means the ancient fathers, because they possessed maturity of conduct and faith and lived in ancient times. Hence it is clear that faith is not a new thing, nor one to be abandoned, but one to be retained: the faith which their predecessors retained, through which they were justified, and through which they received from God the testimony of goodness which they sought.

[Col. 1644B] “By faith we understand that the ages were fitted together by the word of God, so that visible things were made from invisible things” (Gen. 1).

He proves that faith is the evidence of things not apparent. For by faith we understand that the ages were fitted together, and so forth. Or, as though they might say, “How can we place faith in future things, when no one sees them?” he shows by analogy that faith may rightly be had concerning future things because it is had concerning past things which no one saw when they were made, and yet are believed to have been made. For we did not see that God made the world, and yet we believe that he made it.

Since we did not see him performing these works, nevertheless by faith we understand that the ages—that is, all transient things—were fitted together: that is, were suitably composed by the assumption of qualities and forms, through the Word and Wisdom of God, which is Christ, since “all things were made through him” (John 1). They were so fitted together that visible things came to be from invisible things: that is, formed from unformed elements. Before forms were given to things, there were darkness and invisible elements; but through their separation light arose. Unformed matter, which God made from nothing, was at first called heaven and earth. Thus it was said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1), not because these already were so, but because they could become so. For all the elements were confusedly contained in that unformed matter, called *chaos* by the ancients, and from it all things were formed. Then, as darkness gave way through the rising of new light, visible things were made which previously could not be seen.

Or visible things were made from invisible things: that is, from the intelligible world. For the invisible world existed in the wisdom of God, and this visible world was made in its likeness. We understand by faith that all these things were made thus.

“By faith Abel offered to God a more abundant sacrifice than Cain” (Gen. 4), “through which he received testimony that he was righteous, God bearing witness to his gifts” (Matt. 23); “and through it, though dead, he still speaks.”

He now shows in detail how the elders received through faith testimony to their uprightness. He begins with the first righteous man, who was found righteous because of his faith and was made for us an example of righteousness and faith. Truly the elders received testimony in faith. For Abel was the first to receive it: by faith—that is, through faith—he offered God a more abundant sacrifice, that is, one of greater value or more acceptable, than his brother Cain. Through faith he received testimony that he was righteous: that is, testimony that he was righteous, God bearing witness to his gifts by showing that he received them, sending fire from heaven to consume them.

For when God did not kindle Cain’s gifts, but consumed Abel’s gifts by fire sent from heaven, he gave a clear testimony by these very gifts both that he had accepted them and that their offerer was righteous and had offered faithfully. He received such testimony through faith while he lived. And though dead, he still speaks through it: that is, by the example of his faith he urges all posterity to possess faith together with good works. Or, because Scripture is still read, in which God says to Cain: “The voice of thy brother’s blood cries to me from the earth” (Gen. 4), that cry of blood is the speech of the dead man. Or “though dead, he speaks” means that he makes us speak of him as dead; he provides us with matter for speaking, so that from his great faith we may give an example to others. Death did not extinguish the renown of his faith, but rather spread it everywhere.

“By faith Enoch was translated so that he should not see death, and he was not found because God translated him” (Gen. 5; Ecclus. 11). “For before his translation he had testimony that he pleased God. But without faith it is impossible to please God. For one who approaches God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him.”

Faith must be possessed on the example of another elder. For Enoch was translated by faith: that is, because he possessed faith and upheld righteousness, he was translated into Paradise, from which Adam had been cast out. He was translated so that he should not see death: that is, not only that he should not experience death in himself, but that he should not even see it in another, being removed far from the earth of the dying and dwelling in the region of the living. For he was not translated merely to some other part of the earth uninhabitable by men; rather, he was separated from all fellowship with mortals. He was not found when his people carefully sought him in many places. He could not be found because God translated him, and God was able to conceal him so that he might not be found by anyone.

For God placed him in another hidden region, where he might live in great repose of flesh and spirit, until, near the end of the age, he comes with Elijah to convert the remnant of Israel to faith. Truly he was translated because of the merit of faith. For before his translation he had testimony that he pleased God, because, as Scripture relates, “Enoch walked with God, and Enoch lived three hundred years after he begot Methuselah” (Gen. 5). He greatly pleased God, living so holy a life that for three hundred years he walked with God in the way of righteousness. Since God made him so continually to walk with him in the path of uprightness, he gave him evident testimony that he pleased him.

He had testimony that he pleased God. But without faith it is impossible to please God: that is, no one can ever advance so far as to please God unless the merit of faith comes first. It is therefore clear that Enoch also pleased God through faith and deserved through faith to be translated. The faith so praised by the Apostle must be understood as that which “works through charity” (Gal. 5). And truly no one will please God unless he has first shown the merit of faith, because one approaching God must believe: that is, whoever wishes to draw near to God, to become near to him and please him, must first possess faith. Faith is the first step on which one establishes one’s mind when intending to approach God.

He must believe that God is: that is, that he alone properly possesses being, as he says to Moses: “I am who I am” (Exod. 8). Other things do not possess true being, because they are changeable. But he alone is, who is never changed but always is what he is. Whoever desires to overcome the variability of his own changeableness should approach God and believe that he is unchangeable and frees those who cleave to him from changeableness. One must believe this, and also that he is a rewarder of those who seek him: that is, that in the future he gives rewards to those who now seek God alone through what they do—that is, whose heart’s intention seeks nothing other than God through the works which they outwardly display. Whoever wishes to approach him must believe that such persons are rewarded by him.

“By faith Noah, having received an answer concerning things not yet seen, moved by fear, prepared an ark for the salvation of his household” (Gen. 6), “through which he condemned the world and was appointed heir of the righteousness which is through faith.”

Josephus relates that Adam foretold that the destruction of all things would come twice, once through the power of fire and once through a multitude of waters. From this Noah perhaps consulted God and received the answer that a flood was then to come, and that it was right for him to build an ark. He faithfully believed God and performed what had been commanded him.

Thus Noah, having received a divine answer, by faith—that is, through faith—was moved by fear concerning things not yet seen: namely, the inundation of the flood, which was not yet discernible, because the air was still clear and no sign of this event appeared. He prepared—that is, suitably constructed—an ark for the salvation of his household: that through it he might save from the flood his wife and his sons with their wives.

When the text says “moved by fear concerning things not seen,” it commends his faith: he already feared what he did not yet see, believing what God had foretold him. So we too must believe without doubt that all things which God promises or threatens will come to pass, and in the present serve his commandments, if we wish by the example of holy Noah to attain salvation. Though he saw no outward sign of what was to come, he believed solely on hearing God’s voice that the world’s submersion would occur. Yet we see many signs of the end of the age and of the future judgment, and nevertheless one rarely finds anyone who now fears that judgment as holy Noah feared the flood.

[Col. 1647A] He prepared the ark, through which he condemned the world, because people had a greater sin in proportion as they saw his greater diligence in building the ark and did not believe. For when they saw him labor for a hundred years in constructing the ark, they ought to have recognized the calamities to come and fled to repentance. Since they did not do this, they acquired for themselves a more severe condemnation. This is the first praise of his faith: that he condemned the unbelieving world. And he was appointed by God heir of the righteousness which is through faith; after the flood he obtained by hereditary right the religious manner of life which faith produces, and which his righteous predecessors had possessed.

For the flood had been brought about so that an end might be put to vices and the righteousness which Abel, Enoch, and the other saints had upheld might remain. Blessed Noah became its heir. Thus he received testimony in faith, because he inherited the righteousness of faith.

“By faith Abraham, who is called, obeyed to go out into the place which he was to receive as an inheritance; and he went out, not knowing where he was going” (Gen. 12, 13). “By faith he sojourned in the land of promise as in a foreign land, dwelling in huts with Isaac and Jacob, fellow-heirs of the same promise. For he awaited the city which has foundations, whose architect and builder is God.”

Again, by an example he shows that faith must be possessed and that the elders received testimony in it. He who was first called Abram and afterward called Abraham by God (Gen. 17:5) gives us an example of faith. For faith was the reason for the enlargement of his name: he who had first been called Abram, “high father,” afterward, upon receiving the promise that all nations would follow his faith and have him as their father, was called Abraham (Gen. 17), “father seeing a multitude,” because, made in faith the father of believers, he saw the multitude of all nations that would come to his faith.

He who for such a reason is called Abraham obeyed God by faith; for he would not have obeyed unless he believed. He obeyed the command: “Go out from thy land and from thy kindred, and come into the land which I shall show thee” (Gen. 12). Thus he obeyed to go out: that is, in obedience he left the land of his fathers and came into that place—the land of Canaan—which he was to receive as an inheritance in his children, not in himself. Having heard God’s command, he immediately went out from his land, not knowing where he was going, desiring only to obey and believing that he would receive from God things far better than those he left in his native country.

For if he had known a definite place to which he might proceed, while leaving a definite homeland, his faith would not have been so admirable. And if, on arriving, he had found even an empty place where he was directed, so that he could possess that land, his faith would not have been so praised. But he found the place full of Canaanites and remained among them as a stranger. This is what follows: “By faith he sojourned in the land of promise,” that is, the land promised to him not once but many times, not as a possessor but as a stranger, as in a foreign land and not as his own.

By faith in a better land he lived there as a pilgrim, and did not return to his paternal soil. Wishing to obey, he remained where he had been commanded, dwelling not in splendid and large houses but in huts and cottages. He did not build great edifices, but small shelters sufficed him, because his mind was directed elsewhere and he always considered himself an exile wherever he was placed in this present world. Thus he dwelt with Isaac and Jacob, for, as may be gathered from Genesis, Jacob was fifteen years old when Abraham died (Gen. 25). These two, Isaac and Jacob, were fellow-heirs of the same promise, because God made to them the same promise of the land of Canaan, in which the heavenly inheritance was prefigured.

Why then did Abraham, with his son and grandson, remain like a poor man and stranger in huts rather than build great houses? Because he awaited the city: namely, the heavenly homeland, the Jerusalem above, which has foundations—that is, the permanence of its various rewards, which will never fail or be overthrown. God is the architect and builder of this city because by the art of his wisdom he designed it and afterward established it in manifest reality. That is, Abraham endured to dwell humbly as a stranger in huts because he desired not that land but the eternal city, which God, not man, made and established, and which he expected God to give him.

[Col. 1648C] “By faith Sarah herself, though barren, received power for the conception of seed, even beyond the age of life, because she believed him who had promised to be faithful” (Gen. 17, 18, 21). “Therefore also from one man—and he as good as dead—were born descendants as the stars of heaven in multitude, and innumerable as the sand which is by the shore of the sea. All these died according to faith, not having received the promises, but seeing and greeting them from afar, and confessing that they are strangers and sojourners upon the earth” (Ps. 38). “For those who say such things make clear that they seek a homeland. And indeed, if they had remembered that land from which they went out, they certainly had time to return. But now they desire a better, that is, a heavenly homeland. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them.”

Not Abraham alone was proved by faith, but Sarah also. She herself—that is, in her own person, not through a substitute—received through faith power for the conception of seed: she was made capable of conceiving, even beyond the age of life, having long since lost in her cold blood the power of conception. In her decrepitude she received this, though she had always been barren from youth. Although these two things appeared impossible—barrenness and extreme old age—Sarah herself, who had both, received power for conception of seed: namely, so that she might receive the man’s seed by the power of heat together with her own seed. This was accomplished by faith, not nature, because she believed that he who had promised and promised again was faithful: she believed God truthful in his promises and did not doubt that all things were possible to him. At first she laughed, though from joy; yet not with full faith. But after the Lord’s word she was strengthened in faith (Gen. 18).

Therefore, because Abraham believed and Sarah did not doubt God’s faithfulness, many were born from one father. This was remarkable, since it would not have been so remarkable if so many children had been born from many fathers. But because so many were born from one, it is very wonderful; and, more wonderfully still, from one who was as good as dead—that is, wholly dead according to the nature of old age, because his inward parts were cold and dead and unable to emit seed. We must understand “as good as dead” not in every respect but in some respect: namely, with regard to generation. For if he had been dead in every respect, he would not have been an old man but deceased.

An innumerable multitude arose from such a man. Or they were born from Sarah’s one womb. They were born from one, and that one as good as dead: as good as dead with respect to an elderly husband. For if a woman is so advanced in age that her customary female flow still continues, she may bear by a young man but cannot by an old man; although the old man may still be able to beget by a young woman, as Abraham after Sarah’s death was able to beget by Keturah, because he found her age vigorous. But Sarah was barren and already deprived of menstrual blood; therefore she could no longer bear, even if she had not been barren. Yet faith worked against all these obstacles, so that Sarah’s barren and as-good-as-dead womb conceived from an elderly man as good as dead.

Thus children were born not from many but from one; and not from a young man but from one made as good as dead by old age, so that the miracle might be greater. They proceeded in multitude “as the stars of heaven”: that is, they are compared to the stars in the light of holiness and their multitude, because they are both bright and innumerable; and “as the sand which is by the shore of the sea, innumerable”: that is, they are compared to sand in heaviness, fruitlessness, instability, and multitude.

But what is signified by the sea except the Gentile world? And what by the shore of the sea except a manner of life adjacent to Gentile practice? Some Jews were unstable at the shore of the sea and not in the sea itself, while they adhered to Gentile customs by living perversely and worshipping idols, yet were not Gentiles because they were circumcised. Such persons were not such through the faith of Abraham or Sarah, but through their own fault. Faith did not merit to have children of this kind; rather, after they had been begotten from him, they degenerated from his faith and uprightness by their own wickedness. Faith, therefore, never merited anything evil.

What follows, “all these died according to faith,” must be understood only of those compared to the stars, and not only of the children but also of the patriarchs themselves. For all these did not possess faith for a moment, but retained it always until death, always lived according to it, and died according to it. While they lived, they always ordered their conduct religiously as faith requires; and when they died, they awaited the divine promises, as Jacob said when dying: “I will await thy salvation, O Lord” (Gen. 49). These all died not having been removed from faith through doubt or evil conduct, but persisting according to it, without receiving the promises on earth. Therefore they awaited them in heaven, knowing that God who had promised was faithful. They believed that these promises had not been made concerning earthly things, but hoped for what had been promised concerning heavenly things. In this faith they died.

Through all this the Apostle exhorts the Hebrews to retain unshaken faith after the example of the fathers, if they recognize themselves as their children. They died without yet receiving the promises, but seeing and greeting them from afar: that is, considering with the eyes of faith that they would receive them after death, yet not immediately but after long periods, at Christ’s coming, when he was to prepare the kingdoms of heaven. For at that time all the righteous descended into hell, and there, resting, awaited the Redeemer’s coming. Therefore at death they saw the heavenly promises not nearby but from far away: their longing in contemplation extended far forward to receive them. They greeted them—that is, they greatly desired those things in which they believed they would obtain salvation.

Or they greeted them—that is, joyfully acclaimed them. The expression is drawn from sailors who, seeing from far away the cities toward which they sail, greet them for joy. Since they awaited after death the promises of the heavenly homeland, they confessed that they were strangers upon the earth: that is, not dwelling in their own land. Yet because they could be strangers while remaining a long time, the text adds “and sojourners” to exclude a prolonged stay. A sojourner is one who immediately departs and does not seek to remain long; a pilgrim is one who does not dwell in his own country, even if he remains long in a foreign one. Thus, by calling themselves pilgrims, they showed that they judged themselves to dwell in a foreign land; by confessing themselves sojourners, it appears that they believed they would depart soon and regarded the hour of death as daily uncertain.

That they confessed themselves pilgrims and sojourners is clear not only from the Apostle’s statement but also from their own words. Jacob said to Pharaoh: “The days of the pilgrimage of my life are one hundred and thirty years, evil and painful, and they have not reached the days of my fathers, in which they were pilgrims” (Gen. 17). But lest anyone think the patriarchs were called pilgrims merely because they dwelt in the promised land as in a foreign land, since neither they nor their children had yet received it as an inheritance, let him consider what David, who held kingship there, said to the Lord: “For I am a stranger with thee and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were” (Ps. 38).

This pilgrimage of the holy fathers was that of which the Apostle says: “As long as we are in the body, we are pilgrims away from the Lord” (2 Cor. 5). For this reason they called themselves pilgrims and sojourners as long as they were upon earth: that is, until their bodies were buried beneath the earth and their souls migrated away. Or they were upon the earth because they trod earthly things underfoot. Hence it is evident that they considered themselves exiles and sought the homeland whose citizens they already were.

For those who say such things—namely, who confess themselves pilgrims and sojourners—by saying this make clear that they seek a homeland. They confessed themselves pilgrims in order to signify that, in all they did, they were seeking their true homeland and sighing toward it with devout groaning. And lest anyone think that they sought the land from which they had gone out, he adds: “And indeed, if they had remembered that,” and so forth. As though he said: They sought a homeland. If they had remembered the homeland from which they went out—that is, if they had recalled and desired the land of their birth, and called themselves pilgrims in relation to it—they certainly had time and opportunity to return to it, and no one hindered them from returning. But because they did not return there, it is clear that they sought another homeland. They would have returned to it if they had sought it.

But now, since it is evident that they did not seek that homeland, it is clear that they desire—or desired—a better homeland, namely the heavenly one. Therefore, because they did not set their hearts upon earth but yearned with all their desires for the heavenly homeland, God is not ashamed—that is, he does not blush—to be called their God, when he says: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob; this is my name for ever” (Exod. 3). A master can be ashamed when he is said to have a useless servant; but if he has a good servant, he is honored through him. If God were called the God of Cain as he is called the God of Abraham, he would receive not honor but disgrace from such a servant.

But since these three patriarchs were excellent servants, God chose, by a certain intimacy and privilege, to be called their God, as though he were God of them alone, though he is God of all creation. He gave them such honor not without reason, but because he knew their sincere and outstanding charity, and because in these three he completed the wondrous mystery of the people to come.

For through free women they begot both into freedom—as Isaac through Sarah—and into servitude—as Esau through Rebekah, to whom it was said: “Thou shalt be servant of thy brother” (Gen. 27). Through maidservants they begot not only into servitude—as Ishmael through Hagar—but also into freedom—as Dan and Naphtali through Bilhah, and Gad and Asher through Zilpah (Gen. 30). So too in the people of God, through spiritual men persons are born to faith not only into praiseworthy freedom, those who imitate them, to whom it is said: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 4, 11), but also into condemnable servitude, as Simon Magus through Philip (Acts 8). Through carnal men are born not only those who imitate them into condemnable servitude, but also those into praiseworthy freedom, to whom it is said: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23).

Whoever prudently recognizes this mystery in the people of God preserves the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace to the end, cleaving to some and tolerating others. For reasons such as these God wished to be called the God of those patriarchs, in whose posterity was prefigured the whole propagation of good and evil persons who are in the Church. Nor is it surprising if God deigns to be called their God, he who is God of angels, because he prepared for them a city, namely the heavenly Jerusalem, in which to receive them. He is not ashamed of them because they are fellow citizens of the angels. In them he is honored, just as conversely he is blasphemed because of the wicked (Isa. 52; Jer. 36).

“By faith Abraham offered Isaac when he was tested, and he was offering his only-begotten son” (Gen. 22), “in whom he had received the promises, to whom it had been said: ‘In Isaac shall thy seed be called’” (Gen. 21), “reckoning that God is able even to raise from the dead. Hence he also received him in a parable.”

Again, Abraham’s example shows that faith must be possessed, because he had such great faith that he was prepared even to offer his son, and yet did not doubt that the promise divinely made to him concerning seed in that son was true. He did not hesitate that the son who could be given when not hoped for could also be restored after being sacrificed. God tested him: that is, he who knew him showed what he was, for the example of others.

Inflamed by faith, Abraham offered upon the altar Isaac, whom he loved more, not Ishmael, who had been born of a maidservant. He offered the only-begotten son whom he had through a free wife, and in whom he had also received promises of posterity, when it was said to him: “In Isaac shall thy seed be called” (ibid.). Although Isaac was his only-begotten, and he had no other son through whom the promises of seed might be fulfilled, he nevertheless offered his son, doubting neither of these things: neither did he doubt concerning the promises.

The Lord himself spoke to him, not to another who might tell him: that is, the Lord did not command him through another but said directly to him, “In Isaac shall thy seed be called,” meaning: in Isaac’s posterity there will be the name of thy seed, because those who descend from Isaac will be called thy children. Although Ishmael, Esau, and the sons of Keturah were from Abraham’s stock, they were not counted as sons. God promised Abraham posterity in Isaac alone. The promise would have been less authoritative if God had spoken it to another and that person had afterward reported it to Abraham.

Yet, when ordered to offer Isaac, Abraham did not raise a question for himself as if God’s words were contrary and opposed to one another, saying: “You promised me seed in Isaac, and now you command Isaac to be killed?” Rather, his heart always possessed faith unshaken and in no way failing. He considered that he who had given Isaac birth from elderly parents when he did not exist could also restore him from death. This is what the Apostle adds: “Reckoning that God is able even to raise from the dead,” that is, not only able to rescue him from sacrifice so that he should not be killed, but also able to restore him to life after he was killed. He believed either that God would deliver him from sacrifice or that, once sacrificed, he would immediately raise him up, and thus fulfill in him the promise concerning future seed.

This is clearly shown in Abraham’s words when he said to the servants: “Wait here with the ass; I and the boy, hastening thither, will return to you after we have worshipped” (Gen. 22). He did not say, “I shall return to you,” but “The boy and I shall return.” Hence, because he believed so firmly in all things, he received him unharmed from the altar, since he was not sacrificed. He also received him in a parable: that is, as a likeness of Christ, whose divinity remained impassible although his humanity endured the Passion.

For Abraham, leading his only son to sacrifice, signified God the Father, who “did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8). Isaac carried himself the wood to the place of sacrifice, upon which he was to be laid; Christ likewise carried his cross. Isaac was bound and placed upon the altar, because Christ too was bound in the Passion and placed upon the cross. Isaac left the altar unharmed, but a ram was sacrificed in his place: because, as we have said, Christ’s divinity, signified by Isaac, remained impassible, but his humanity, figured by the ram, was subject to death.

That ram was caught by its horns among brambles, because Christ was crucified among the wicked and sinners, signified by the brambles, so that his hands, pierced by nails, clung to the horns of the cross, as it is written: “Horns are in his hands” (Hab. 3). Likewise, all the other details of Isaac’s sacrifice must mystically be referred to Christ’s Passion.

“By faith Isaac also blessed Jacob and Esau concerning things to come. By faith Jacob, dying, blessed each of Joseph’s sons and worshipped the top of his staff. By faith Joseph, dying, remembered the departure of the children of Israel and gave command concerning his bones” (Gen. 27, 48, 49).

Abraham was thus tested in faith. Isaac too, by faith, blessed his sons Jacob and Esau concerning things to come; that is, by his blessing he invoked good things upon them, believing that they would indeed come to them in the future. For in blessing Jacob he said: “May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth, abundance of grain and wine” (Gen. 27), etc. And again he promised Esau: “In the fatness of the earth and in the dew of heaven from above shall your blessing be” (ibid.), etc. Unless, therefore, he believed that these things would come to them, he would by no means have promised them in a solemn blessing.

Jacob likewise, when dying, although he was consigning all else to oblivion, by faith blessed Joseph’s two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, giving each his own blessing [Col. 1653D], because he believed it would benefit them; and he worshipped the top of his staff. This is found in the old translation at the place where in the new we read that Israel worshipped God, turned toward the head of his bed. For this holy man, devoted to God and weakened by old age, had his bed so placed that his posture while lying down could readily become one of prayer. But according to another translation, he worshipped upon the head of his staff, that is, his son’s staff, or upon the summit of his staff. It is understood that he had taken Joseph’s staff, and, over the top of the same staff which he held, bowed himself to worship God.

But the Apostle, drawing the meaning toward a mystical understanding, does not say that he worshipped upon the summit [Col. 1654A], but rather the summit and top of his staff itself. For Joseph’s staff, which he bore as a sceptre to signify his authority by which he ruled all Egypt, prefigured Christ’s staff of power, by which he was to reign over the whole world. Christ was foreshadowed through Joseph, while by the top of his staff was signified the height of Christ’s royal power, of which it was said: “A staff of uprightness is the staff of your kingdom” (Ps. 44). Therefore, in true faith he worshipped the top of his son’s staff, signifying that with all devotion he submitted himself beneath the exalted dominion of Christ, whom he foresaw would be born from his own flesh. For if he had not understood Christ in Joseph, it would not be called faith if he worshipped the top of that staff.

Joseph also, when dying, by faith made mention [Col. 1654B] of the departure of the children of Israel, saying: “After my death God will visit you and cause you to go up from this land to the land which he swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (Gen. 50). He had heard this from his father, and now, dying, recalled it in faith. For unless he believed it would happen, he would not have recalled it. He also gave command concerning his bones, saying: “Carry my bones with you from this place” (ibid.). This too he commanded in faith, because he believed that Christ would be born in the land of promise, would rise after the Passion, and that he himself would rise again with him, one among the other saints destined to be raised at his Passion.

“By faith, Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw a beautiful [Col. 1654C] child, and they did not fear the king’s edict” (Exod. 2).

Faith is still to be maintained by the example of the elders, since Moses, when born, was hidden for three months by the faith of his parents, because they saw the child was beautiful. For they believed that God would accomplish something great through him, since he was of such beautiful appearance.
