From birth a great grace of beauty had been infused into him, not by nature but by God’s gift. Therefore they did not fear the king’s edict (ibid.), who had commanded that all male infants of the Hebrews should be killed as soon as they were born; but, trusting in God by faith, they preserved the child.

“By faith Moses, when grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to be afflicted with the people of God than to have the pleasure of temporary sin, [Col. 1654D] considering the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasure of the Egyptians. For he looked to the reward. By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the king’s anger. For he endured as though seeing him who is invisible. By faith he celebrated the Passover and the sprinkling of blood” (Exod. 12), “lest he who destroyed the firstborn should touch them. By faith they crossed the Red Sea as though over dry land; when the Egyptians attempted this, they were swallowed up” (Exod. 14).

Further examples of faith shine forth in Moses. When he was a child, he was adopted as a son by Pharaoh’s daughter, who, according to Josephus, was called Thermut and had no lawful offspring. Therefore she wished that Moses should succeed to the kingdom after her father. But when Moses had grown up, fired by faith and despising the kingdom [Col. 1655A] of Egypt, he refused, according to the Apostle, to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, and rejected royal rank, choosing rather—that is, preferring—to be afflicted and subjected to injuries with the people of God, who laboured in mud and brick, than to enjoy temporary and passing sin. That is, faith persuaded him to prefer and choose above all things to suffer for God for a time rather than to live in the enjoyment of those things in which there was sin and which quickly pass away. For he judged it sinful to rejoice in the court while his brothers were afflicted.

Yet Moses’ books do not report that he denied being Pharaoh’s daughter’s son; but it is not doubted that he did this at the time when he also did what we read there: after he had grown up, he went out to his brethren, the children of Israel, and saw their affliction. He, I say, considered the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasure of Egypt [Col. 1655B]. The reproach of Christ means what he would suffer for Christ; or what signified the reproach that would be inflicted upon Christ after long ages; or what he suffered from his own people, as Christ afterwards did from his own. He chose this reproach more highly, and valued Egyptian works less, because through it he believed that he would be enriched with eternal riches if he bore insults and reproaches for Christ. For in full faith he looked to the eternal recompense which Christ was to give to those suffering for him. That is, he therefore chose to be poor and despised temporarily among people because his heart was set above, and he thought of the eternal honours which he hoped to obtain through poverty and endurance.

And by faith [Col. 1655C] he left Egypt, leading the children of Israel out from there, because he believed they would escape safely. He did not fear the king’s fury, who had conceived great anger against him; but, trusting in God’s help, he withdrew the people of Israel from that king’s yoke. And truly, by faith, he did not fear the king. For he endured—that is, he was not broken in heart, but endured as one truly strong. He held fast in the steadfastness of his mind to the invisible one, that is, God, whom he did not see, as though seeing him, as if he beheld him there present. For a soldier is accustomed to fight more carefully when the king is present than when he is absent. But Moses fought for God, whom he did not see, and endured for him—that is, awaited his help—as though he saw him [Col. 1655D] present before him and helping him with bodily eyes.

Therefore the Lord said to him, though he uttered nothing with his mouth: “Why do you cry to me?” (Exod. 14). For he cried in his heart while he was silent with his mouth, because with devout desires he implored and awaited the help of the divine majesty. And before he left Egypt, he celebrated the Passover; and he did this in faith—that is, he made solemn and festive the passage, or rather kept a night for the Passover, that is, for the departure from Egypt, because he did not doubt that they would truly depart. Therefore, made joyful by faith, before they went out he held a solemn feast for their passage.

For he celebrated the Passover, that is, he made solemn and common the eating of the lamb, which was called *Pascha*, “passage,” because it was the cause of their passage from slavery to freedom. And by faith he celebrated the sprinkling of blood, lest the angel [Col. 1656A] who destroyed the firstborn—that is, who killed Egypt’s firstborn—should touch them; for he firmly believed that the destroying angel would not enter those houses which had the lamb’s blood on the lintel and on both doorposts. By faith also all the children of Israel crossed the Red Sea unharmed, as if they were travelling over dry and parched ground, because they believed that God could lead them through the sea just as through dry land. When the Egyptians, who possessed not even a share of faith, tried and wished to make that crossing of the sea, they were swallowed by the waters, that is, completely engulfed. Or, attempting to discover whether that crossing happened by faith or by chance, they were swallowed by the waves. For if the Israelites had crossed by chance, the Egyptians would have had a like passage. But because faith had prepared such a way for them, [Col. 1656B] unbelievers perished in it.

“By faith the walls of Jericho fell after they had been encircled for seven days” (Josh. 2, 6). “By faith Rahab the harlot did not perish with the unbelievers, having received the spies in peace.”

Faith not only divided the sea but also threw down Jericho’s walls. For the Lord had commanded: “Let all the warriors go around the city once a day. Thus shall you do for six days. On the seventh day the priests shall take seven trumpets and go before the ark of the covenant; you shall go around the city seven times, and the priests shall sound the trumpets. When the sound of the trumpet has grown longer and sharper and has struck your ears, all the people shall shout with a great cry; [Col. 1656C] and the city’s walls shall fall utterly, and each man shall enter by the place opposite which he has stood.”

The children of Israel, trusting this divine command and the promises, did as they had been ordered, and in this manner took the city. But in that city was Rahab, who by faith deserved not to perish with the unbelieving citizens. For all perished by the sword except those who were in her house. She had received the two spies in peace, whom Joshua had sent, and hidden them so that the king of Jericho would not find and kill them; for upon seeing them she believed that the children of Israel would possess the land by God’s power. Thus she said: “I know that the Lord has given you the land” (Josh. 2). “For your terror has fallen upon us, and all the inhabitants of the land have melted away. [Col. 1656D] For the Lord your God, he is God in heaven above and on earth below.”

By this faith she saved the spies and secretly sent them out through her house’s window. Therefore, when the rest later perished, she herself lived among the people of Israel with all her kindred. Previously, indeed, she had been a harlot; but after being joined to God’s people she lived lawfully, so that she was even placed in the genealogy of the Saviour (Matt. 1). And since even a harlot deserved by faith to be justified and saved, let every man be ashamed to be unbelieving, lest through unbelief he be burdened with every sin and perish.

“And what more shall I say? For time would fail me in recounting Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets who through faith conquered [Col. 1657A] kingdoms, practised righteousness, and obtained promises.”

“I have brought you many examples,” he says, “of the ancients concerning the necessity of faith, and I could bring you still more. But what more shall I say? That is, what deed of what person should I further adduce as an example of faith? For I have produced so many examples that they should suffice for all toward faith. And if I set forth all the others that could be set forth, perhaps they would produce weariness rather than benefit. Nor should I linger longer upon these, because, having fixed the time in which I may write to you, if I consume it in producing examples of the faith of the ancients, I shall not be able to complete within the prescribed time the other things which I ought to write to you.”

And this is what follows: “For time would fail me.” [Col. 1657B] As though he said: “It is not useful for me to supply every example I could, because time which I assigned for writing to you would fail—that is, abandon—me while I am recounting them, that is, relating each clearly and individually; nor could all that I have decided to write to you be expounded within it.” That is, the shortness of time, by which I am occupied with other matters, does not allow me to give a full account of these things. Or, the time of my life would fail—that is, leave—me if I wished to pursue everything. Therefore it must be passed over, because time would fail me while I recount, that is, while I recount fully, or externally and openly, Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets. That is, if I wished in the brief time of this epistle [Col. 1657C] or of my life to expound all their mighty deeds and those of others which they performed by faith, I could not do so.

For great are the things these men did. They conquered—that is, they conquered by casting down and subjecting—kingdoms, that is, kings with all those subject to them. And this was not through their own powers, but through the faith by which they believed God and trusted in God. Through the same faith, by which they believed him to be the rewarder of good works, they practised righteousness, that is, performed works of righteousness. And through the faith in which they persevered, they obtained the promises, that is, the rewards of heavenly blessedness which God promised and promised again in the Scriptures to workers of righteousness. This does not mean that they received them immediately upon dying, because Christ had not yet made a way for them and they were in darkness because of original sin; but because, when the Apostle wrote these things, Christ had suffered, they already possessed the promises according to the soul. For he had drawn them from the underworld and clothed each with robes [Col. 1657D] (Rev. 6).

Or, they obtained promises of temporal goods which the Law had made to its observers. For Gideon, Barak, and the others are said to have received, because of their observance of the Law, not only eternal life but also temporal riches and the subjection of enemies (Judg. 6). Gideon, indeed, conquered kingdoms through faith, because, by God’s command and permission, with three hundred men whom he armed not with iron but with jars and lamps, he overcame the Midianites, the Amalekites, and other eastern peoples, whose multitude contained one hundred and thirty-five thousand fighting men [Col. 1658A]; and he captured and killed their kings. He also practised righteousness, because he destroyed Baal’s altar, built an altar to the Lord, and delivered the people of Israel. He obtained the promises of life because he died in a good old age.

Barak likewise conquered kingdoms through faith. God said to him through Deborah the prophetess: “Go and lead the army to Mount Tabor; take with you ten thousand fighters from the children of Naphtali and the children of Zebulun. I will bring to you at the brook Kishon Sisera, commander of Jabin’s army, with his chariots and all his multitude, and I will give them into your hand” (Judg. 4–5). Barak did as the Lord commanded and went up the mountain. When Sisera heard this, he assembled [Col. 1658B] nine hundred scythed chariots and all his army from Harosheth of the Gentiles to the brook Kishon. Barak came down from Mount Tabor with ten thousand fighters. The Lord terrified Sisera, all his chariots, and the whole multitude before Barak by the edge of the sword, so that Sisera leapt down from his chariot and fled on foot. Barak pursued the fleeing chariots and army as far as Harosheth of the Gentiles, and the whole multitude of the enemy fell to complete destruction. On that day God humbled Jabin, king of Canaan, until they destroyed him.

Thus Barak conquered kingdoms through faith. He also practised righteousness in that he delivered the children of Israel from that king, who had grievously oppressed them for twenty years; and he did not claim the victory for himself [Col. 1658C] but sang a song to God concerning these things. Therefore he was worthy to obtain the heavenly promises.

Samson also conquered kingdoms through faith (Judg. 13, 16), because although he was one man, he had within him the Spirit of the Lord, who strengthened him. Many times he inflicted great slaughter upon the Philistines, and none of them could possess strength enough to resist him. He also practised righteousness, because he judged Israel for twenty years and afflicted the Philistines, their oppressors; and he was a Nazarite—that is, consecrated—from his mother’s womb, drinking neither wine nor strong drink and eating nothing unclean (Luke 2). Yet in the end, when he crushed himself together with his enemies, he can be excused only on the ground that the Spirit who worked miracles through him secretly commanded this; just as the Spirit had earlier inspired him to take a wife from the daughters of the Philistines, although the Law prohibited this [Col. 1658D]. For just as in taking a foreign wife he did, by God’s will, what the Law forbade and did not sin, so it may be believed that the Holy Spirit commanded him to destroy with himself that vast multitude of enemies who praised their idol because of his humiliation and, for greater reproach, made him play while drunk—especially since that Spirit had already begun to restore his former strength to him, signifying the recovery of his former grace. Therefore the Apostle now places him among those who obtained the promises.

Jephthah likewise conquered kingdoms through faith, because the Spirit of the Lord came upon him; and, going around Gilead and then passing on [Col. 1659A] to the children of Ammon, he made a vow to the Lord, saying: “If you give the children of Ammon into my hands, whoever first comes out from the doors of my house and meets me as I return in peace from the children of Ammon, I shall offer that person as a burnt offering to the Lord.” Jephthah passed over to the children of Ammon to fight against them, and the Lord gave them into his hand. He struck twenty cities with an exceedingly great blow, and the children of Ammon were humbled before the children of Israel. But when Jephthah returned home, his only daughter came out to meet him with tambourines and dances. When he saw her, he tore his garments and said: “Alas, my daughter, you have deceived me, and you yourself have been deceived. For I have opened my mouth to the Lord, and I cannot do otherwise.” And he did to her as he had vowed (Judg. 11).

It is rightly asked [Col. 1659B] whether his sacrificing her should be considered as done by God’s command. For Abraham was not merely free from blame for cruelty, but was even praised under the name of piety because he wished to kill his son not wickedly but obediently. Jephthah, however, is not read to have received such a command to kill his daughter. Yet because Scripture reports that the Spirit of the Lord came upon him, and that he then made such a vow for victory and obtained victory, he does not seem to have vowed rashly, since the Holy Spirit presided over him; nor does he seem to have made an unjust vow, since he obtained the victory for which he made the vow. The obtaining of victory bears witness that the vow did not displease God. For the Lord knows the hidden reasons for which such a sacrifice could have pleased him.

Jephthah himself [Col. 1659C] rather sacrificed himself spiritually in this matter, because, having no son or daughter except this one, he overcame all his affection for her by the rigor of his vow and conquered the grief of compassion by the ardour of faith. He also practised righteousness, because he assumed leadership quite reasonably and justly, argued his case justly through envoys against the king of the children of Ammon, justly undertook war, and judged the people of Israel for six years according to the Lord’s Law. Therefore he is believed to have obtained the promises of heavenly rewards.

With regard to David, I consider it superfluous to show how he conquered kingdoms through faith [Note: [Col. 1659D] 1 Sam. 16, passim.], since it is clear that, with the Lord’s help, he killed so many impious kings. He practised righteousness [Col. 1659D] in such a way that God said of him: “I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my own heart, who will do all my wills.” He also obtained promises not only concerning eternal life but also concerning Christ’s coming: for he himself possesses eternal blessedness, and Christ, the eternal king, has been raised up from his seed.

Samuel too [Note: [Col. 1660D] 1 Sam. 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, passim.] conquered the kingdoms of the Philistines through faith. When the satraps of that people had assembled against Israel with their armies, Samuel offered a burnt offering and cried to God for Israel, and the Lord heard him. For at the very hour of sacrifice it happened that the Philistines began battle against Israel. The Lord thundered with a great crash [Col. 1660A] over them and terrified them, and they were struck down before Israel. The hand of the Lord was against them throughout all Samuel’s days, and the cities which they had taken from Israel were restored. Thus Israel was delivered from their hand.

Samuel also practised righteousness so fully that he is never found blameworthy even in the smallest matter. Therefore, without any doubt, he obtained the promises of eternal blessedness. Some of the following prophets also conquered kings either by their prayers or merits. Thus, while Isaiah prayed with King Hezekiah, an angel struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian camp, and King Sennacherib withdrew shamefully from Judah (Isa. 37; 2 Kgs. 19). Elisha also obtained by his merits that Ben-hadad, king of Syria (2 Kgs. 7), who had long besieged Samaria [Col. 1660B], should flee in terror with his whole army. For the Lord caused the Syrians to hear in their camp the sound of chariots, horses, and a great army; they fled and left their tents, horses, and donkeys, together with gold and great wealth. The children of Israel plundered all these things, so that a measure of fine flour sold for one stater and two measures of barley for one stater at the gate of Samaria. Holy prophets did many such things through faith against impious kings; they maintained righteousness throughout their conduct and obtained the divine promises in the kingdom of heaven.

“They stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, recovered from weakness, became strong in battle, put foreign armies to flight, and women received their dead by resurrection” [Col. 1660C].

The saints of old had victory through faith not only over people but also over beasts as fierce as lions, and over insensible elements such as fire. That is: they stopped—made blocked and closed—the mouths of lions, so that even hungry lions did not touch them while faith preserved them. Thus Daniel (Dan. 6, 14), whom faith preserved unharmed in the lions’ den for the space of one night; and on another occasion, shut for six days in the den with seven hungry lions, he remained without injury. For here the plural number is understood to have been used for the singular in the phrase, “they stopped the mouths of lions,” unless David’s deed is also understood as recalled in this statement [Col. 1660D]: while he was feeding his flock, a lion and a bear came and carried off a ram; he pursued and struck them, rescued the sheep from their mouths, and when they rose against him, seized their jaws, choked, and killed them (1 Sam. 17).

Others, by the dew of faith, quenched the violence of fire—that is, a most violent fire rushing upon them with force—such as Moses. For when the Hebrews murmured (Num. 11), the Lord’s fire was kindled against them and devoured the outer part of the camp. When the people cried to Moses, Moses prayed to the Lord and the fire was extinguished. Similarly Aaron on another occasion quenched the violence of fire [Col. 1661A] (Num. 16), when, taking a censer, he ran into the midst of the multitude which the conflagration was destroying, offered incense, stood between the dead and the living, prayed for the people, and the plague ceased.

The three boys in Babylon also quenched the violence of fire through faith. The angel of the Lord descended with them into the furnace, drove the fiery flame out of the furnace, made the furnace’s interior like a wind blowing dew, and the fire did not touch them at all (Dan. 3). Others escaped the edge of the sword, as Isaac too did when his father, taking up the sword, wished to sacrifice him, but an angel forbade him to strike (Gen. 22); and as David did when, while he played upon a stringed instrument with his hand before Saul, Saul held a spear and threw it, thinking he could pin him to the wall. But David moved aside [Col. 1661B] from before him (1 Sam. 19). The same thing happened similarly on another occasion, in David’s escape from the stroke of the spear (1 Sam. 20).

Or “they escaped the edge of the sword” means that through faith they put to flight an army girded with swords, as Gideon did the armed Midianites under arms (Judg. 7), and Judas Maccabaeus often did almost innumerable multitudes of enemies with a few men (1 Macc. 3). Others recovered from weakness through faith, that is, were healed of bodily sickness, like Job and Hezekiah (Job 42). Others through faith became strong and unconquerable in battle, as Joshua, David, and Judas Maccabaeus did (2 Kgs. 20). Some put foreign camps—that is, camps of aliens who came against them—to flight, like Judith (Judith 13) and Gideon, so often mentioned (Judg. 7).

It should be noted that putting camps to flight is one thing, since this can occur even without battle; putting to flight an army equipped with the sword is another, since that occurs by battle [Col. 1661C]. The ancient fathers attained such things through faith and obtained temporal prosperity; but under the New Testament this is not the time for such things. Formerly the Lord gave such things; now he gives better ones. It is as though he said: “Learn, people, through the grace of the New Testament to desire everlasting life. Why do you want so greatly to be delivered by the Lord from death, as your fathers were delivered, when the Lord was teaching that there was no giver of even earthly prosperity apart from himself? That prosperity belongs to the old man, whose truth began from Adam. But I am Christ, not Adam. You were old from the old one; from the New One be new [Col. 1661D] even unto death.”

Therefore Christ himself wished to suffer this before his enemies, so that they might think him abandoned, in order that the grace of the New Testament might be commended, through which we learn to seek another happiness, which now exists in faith but will afterwards exist in sight. Yet under the Old Testament it was necessary that temporal goods also should be divinely given to the saints. Therefore they were delivered from various dangers when they shut the mouths of lions, quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, and recovered from weakness. They also obtained strength and victories from God, because they became strong in battle and put foreign camps to flight. They obtained great things too by prayer, because women received their dead through resurrection. For the woman of Zarephath, when Elijah prayed, received her son coming back from resurrection [Col. 1662A] (1 Kgs. 17); and through Elisha the Shunammite received her child restored to her by resurrection (2 Kgs. 4).

“But others were stretched out under torture, not accepting deliverance, so that they might obtain a better resurrection. Others suffered mockery and scourging, and moreover bonds and prisons; they were stoned, sawn asunder, tested, and died by slaughter with the sword.”

He has shown how great were the deeds the saints accomplished through faith; now he shows how great were the things they suffered for faith, so that he may strengthen by the imitation of many sufferings what he had urged through the many examples of faith. Some of the fathers in their lifetime were delivered through faith from various adversities. But others of them were also stretched out under torture for faith [Col. 1662B], that is, their limbs were extended in punishments, not accepting deliverance—that is, escape from the penalties inflicted upon them—so that they might obtain in another age a better deliverance than the present one which they rejected.

This was done by the seven noble brothers with their mother, whom King Antiochus, torturing with whips and thongs, compelled to eat pork contrary to the Law (2 Macc. 7). When they said, “We are ready to die rather than violate the ancestral laws of God,” the angered king ordered the tongue of the first speaker to be cut out, the skin of his head stripped off, and his hands and feet cut off at their extremities. When he had been mutilated in every part, he ordered fire to be applied and the man, still breathing, to be roasted in a frying-pan. Thus he did to the second, and then consumed all seven and their mother, the eighth, with such torments [Col. 1662C]. Thus they were stretched out under various punishments, extending their hands and feet to receive penalties and putting forth their tongues. They refused to be redeemed from the punishments because, though they were urged to eat unlawful meats and escape the penalties, they did not consent. For they desired a better resurrection, as they said to the tyrant: “You indeed, most wicked man, destroy us in this present life; but the King of the world will raise us, who have died for his laws, into the resurrection of eternal life.”

These men endured such things in faith. But others, by endurance, experienced mockeries and scourgings, because they were mocked and beaten; for example Jeremiah, who said: “I have become a mockery all day long; everyone derides me” (Jer. 20), and of whom it is written [Col. 1662D] that Pashhur struck Jeremiah the prophet and put him in the stocks (ibid.). And as if it were too little to have suffered mockeries and scourgings, they also endured bonds and prisons. In saying “moreover,” he indicates that these four things were inflicted upon the same persons.

Jeremiah endured bonds and prisons, because, as stated, Pashhur put him in the stocks; King Zedekiah confined him in the court of the prison; and again, when he wished to go to the land of Benjamin (Jer. 32) and had reached Jerusalem’s gate, the gatekeeper seized him, saying: “You are deserting to the Chaldeans!” He led him to the princes. Therefore the princes, angered against Jeremiah, beat him and put him in prison; he entered the house of Jaci and the dungeon and remained there many days (Jer. 37). Thus Jeremiah is read [Col. 1663A] to have suffered mockeries and scourgings, and moreover bonds and prisons.

Micaiah likewise is read to have suffered scourgings, prison, and mockeries. For when King Ahab wished to go to battle against the Syrians at Ramoth-gilead and had consulted his prophets, whom he had gathered to the number of about four hundred, they all answered the king that he should go, since the outcome would be favourable to him. At length Micaiah was brought in and, when questioned, answered: “The Lord has given a lying spirit into the mouth of all these prophets of yours who are here.” Then Zedekiah son of Chenaanah came up and struck Micaiah on the cheek, saying: “Has the Spirit of the Lord then left me and spoken to you?” (1 Kgs. 22). Here are mockery and scourging: he was ridiculed before the king and struck without trial. “And the king said: Take [Col. 1663B] Micaiah and put him in prison, and sustain him with bread of affliction and water of distress, until I return in peace” (ibid.). Here is prison, where there may perhaps also have been bonds.

Others were stoned, like the one of whom it is written that the Spirit of the Lord clothed Zechariah, son of Jehoiada the priest. He stood before the people and said to them: “Thus says the Lord: Why do you transgress the Lord’s commandment, which will not benefit you, and abandon the Lord, so that he abandons you?” They gathered against him and, by King Joash’s command, threw stones at him in the courts of the Lord’s house and killed him (2 Chron. 24). Naboth the Jezreelite too was unjustly stoned (1 Kgs. 21).

In the phrase that follows, “they were sawn asunder,” the plural number is believed to be used for the singular, since it is understood to refer only to Isaiah’s suffering: the Hebrews most certainly hand down that he was sawn with a wooden saw by King Manasseh [Col. 1663C]. Others were tested by the enticements of pleasures or promises of worldly goods, to see whether they could be torn away from the justifications of faith: as holy Joseph, to whom his unchaste mistress said, “Sleep with me” (Gen. 39); Judith, to whom Holofernes said, “You shall be great in Nebuchadnezzar’s house, and your name shall be named throughout the whole earth” (Judith 11); and the last of the seven brothers mentioned above, whom King Antiochus not only urged by words but also affirmed by oath that he would make him rich and happy and would regard him as a friend transferred away from the ancestral laws (2 Macc. 7).

Others died [Col. 1663D] by slaughter with the sword, such as the eighty-five priests of the Lord whom Saul unjustly massacred because of David (1 Sam. 22), and the prophets of the Lord whom Queen Jezebel killed (1 Kgs. 18).

“They wandered about in sheepskins, in goatskins, needy, distressed, afflicted—of whom the world was not worthy—wandering in deserts and mountains, and in caves and hollows of the earth.”

“**They went about in melotas, in goatskins, etc.**” A *melota*, as they say, is a garment made from camel’s hair or from goatskins. It is difficult to discover openly in the writings who in the ancient people of the Jews used this clothing; but John the Baptist, who may be meant in this passage, is read to have used it (Matt. 3; Mark 1). Judith, however, had sackcloth [Col. 1664A] upon her loins (Judith 9); and it was said to Isaiah: “Untie the sackcloth from your loins” (Isa. 20), that is, the sackcloth garment. We believe that Elijah too used this clothing (4 Kings 1), as did certain prophets.

It is also reported that the skin of an animal called *taxus* or *taxo* is called a *melota*. Religious men, subduing their flesh, did not wear soft and costly garments, but used sackcloth and rough animal skins, such as those of badgers and goats. Or, thus clothed, they went about many places, like Elijah, who is reported to have travelled through various places at the Lord’s command (3 Kings 19), and like John the Baptist, who came into the whole region of the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance (Luke 3). These men, I say, were needy of bodily necessities because they possessed nothing; distressed by anxiety of mind because [Col. 1664B] they mourned the sins of the people; afflicted with hardships because they endured persecution for righteousness’ sake.

Lest they should seem contemptible because of their poverty and afflictions, it is added: “**Of whom the world was not worthy**”; that is, they were of such dignity that the world was not worthy of their manner of life. Thus Elijah was taken alive into heaven (4 Kings 2), and John was more quickly brought to completion by martyrdom (Matt. 14; Mark 6). Those too were needy, distressed, and afflicted of whom it is related that, when Jerusalem was occupied by the Antiochenes, Judas Maccabaeus withdrew into a desert place; there, among wild beasts, he lived with his followers in the mountains, feeding on grass, and remained there lest they should share in defilement (2 [Col. 1664C] Macc. 5). These men had separated themselves from the wickedness of the world; and therefore the world was not worthy of them. Of them is understood what the Apostle adds: “wandering in deserts and mountains.”

Others, assembling in nearby caves and secretly observing the Sabbath day, were, when betrayed to Philip, the king’s officer, set on fire, because through reverence for religion and observance they feared to offer themselves assistance by force. Of these the Apostle now says that they remained “in caves and in caverns of the earth.” Caves are natural; caverns are those made by human hands or by some accident. Elijah had formerly been in deserts, mountains, and caves. Fleeing Jezebel, he came to Beersheba of Judah, went one day’s journey into the desert, and then travelled forty days and forty [Col. 1664D] nights to Horeb, the mountain of God. When he arrived there, he stayed in a cave; and, having heard the words of the Lord there, he returned by the same route through the desert (3 Kings 19). Those also remained in caves or caverns of whom Scripture says that, when Jezebel was killing the prophets of the Lord, Obadiah took one hundred prophets, hid them fifty by fifty in caves, and fed them with bread and water (3 Kings 18).

Up to this point the Apostle has used examples of those who received testimony in faith. Earlier, before beginning his treatment of faith, he used arguments throughout almost the whole epistle (Rom. 1). For the outstanding teacher, debtor both to the wise and to the foolish, seeing among the Hebrews some wise persons and some rather slow ones, overcame the wisdom of the wise by arguments; but drew the slowness of the simple by examples alone, so that victorious reasoning might break the former, while gentle imitation might persuade the latter to ascend to greater things.

> “And all these, approved by the testimony of faith, did not receive the promise, God providing something better for us, so that they should not be made perfect without us.”

Thus far I have mentioned many; and all these whom I have brought forward as examples, whether named expressly or with their names unspoken, were approved by the testimony of faith—that is, they were proved so steadfast in faith that they have good testimony from it. In his conclusion he returns to what he had stated at the beginning: that the elders received testimony in faith. And although they were approved in faith, [Col. 1665B] nevertheless they did not receive the promise. What does this mean? Was it not said a little above that some of them by faith conquered kingdoms, worked righteousness, and obtained promises?

But those saints both obtained promises and await the promise: they possess the blessedness of their souls, but await the resurrection of their bodies. Hence it was well said above that they “obtained promises,” in the plural and as various; but now it is said that they did not receive “the promise,” in the singular, since there are various ranks of dignity which souls have received according to the distinction of their merits, whereas bodily incorruption is one thing, which they all await together. Therefore they have not received the promise, because the resurrection of the bodies [Col. 1665C] which God promised to his saints is still delayed, so that we may all rise together, and in the common joy of all, each person’s joy may become greater.

Thus they still wait until we too hasten to join them, while God provides and wisely ordains something better for us: namely, that they should not be made perfect—that is, should not receive the complete blessedness of soul and body—without us, rather than being perfected before us. For since they still await us for their own consummation, they desire our deliverance all the more ardently; and, both for themselves and for us, they intercede for us that we may be delivered sooner from the misery of this present age. We too, even if we are lazy concerning ourselves, ought at least not to make them wait longer, but should hasten; we should run more eagerly for this reason also, because we shall not wait [Col. 1665D] as long as they waited.

For such reasons God arranged something better for us: that they should wait for us unto perfection. Therefore the patriarchs, the prophets, and all the spirits of the prophets who have passed into the blessed life eagerly await our rejoicing with them; nor is their joy altogether complete while in some manner they grieve for our errors. Indeed, saints departing from here do not immediately receive the full rewards of their merits, but wait even for us, though we delay and are sluggish, so that with us they may receive perfect blessedness. For this reason also that mystery of the judgment deferred until the last day is preserved: for it is one body that awaits justification [Col. 1666A]; it is one body that is said to rise for judgment.

## Chapter XII

> “Therefore we also, having such a great cloud of witnesses set over us, laying aside every weight and the sin that surrounds us, let us run with patience toward the contest set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and finisher of faith, who, for the joy set before him, endured the cross, despising shame, and sits at the right hand of the throne of God.” (Eph. 4; Col. 3; 1 Pet. 2.)

Having set forth examples of the saints’ faith and patience, by which faith has been strengthened in the hearts of the hearers, he adds that which must be joined to faith: that is, he begins to exhort them to endure adversities, so that, just as [Col. 1666B] the fathers overcame every adversity by enduring through faith, we also may do the same. It is as though he said: “Our predecessors accomplished and endured so much by faith. Therefore let us too endure for the faith in like manner, imitating them.”

We, I say, have set over us for protection and shade such a great cloud of witnesses: that is, such a multitude of saints who, rising from the earth like clouds, flew upward to the heights of heavenly life, free from every burden of earthly desire. As clouds, by their example, they give us the refreshment of consolation in the heat of tribulation and pour down upon us the abundance of their teaching. They are called witnesses because they bore witness to faith by word and suffering. For witnesses are called *martyres* [μάρτυρες] in Greek. They were also witnesses of good works, because in their deeds they testified that works of this kind ought to be done.

Their cloud—that is, their dense multitude—is set over us to protect us and nourish us by its examples. And we, having this light cloud above us, should lay aside—that is, cast downward—every weight, namely every heaviness of worldly desire and whatever presses our mind down among low things, so that, made light, we may fly up to the cloud that is over us and be joined to it. Let us also lay aside the sin surrounding us; that is, let us be raised to what is high and leave below the sin which wickedly attacks and encircles us while we keep our heart among low things. So Zacchaeus, who could not see Jesus because of the crowd, climbed a tree to see him (Luke 19). For the crowd, taller than little Zacchaeus, [Col. 1666D] does not allow him to see Jesus when the ingrained habit of vices, which has mastered us and grown above us, and the tumult of perverse thoughts, which has subjected our heart to itself, does not allow us to behold the light of divinity.

But Zacchaeus climbs the tree, leaving the crowd below, because we ought to climb the tree of the cross, crucifying our flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. 5), and raise our heart to things above, if we desire to behold Jesus without the hindrance of the harmful crowd. Thus let us lay aside every weight and the sin surrounding us. The weight may also be understood as the burden of sins we have committed, which, like a heavy load, has weighed us down. But the sin which surrounds us is the temptation to sin, [Col. 1667A] which threatens us on every side and besieges us from every quarter (Ps. 37).

But by confession let us lay aside every burden of sins by which we are weighed down; and by an exalted manner of life let us leave below every sin which surrounds and attacks us in low things. Then, having cast off the weight and overcome the obstacles, made light and uplifted, let us run—that is, without the delay of hesitation, let us quickly pass through patience to the contest of martyrdom set before us by unbelievers, who have proposed either to separate us from faith or to torture us with various torments. Or it has been set before us by God, who through the immeasurable benefits of his grace has granted not only that we should believe in him but also that we should suffer for him (Phil. 1).

Thus, without murmuring or hesitation, let us run through patience to the contest of martyrdom, looking to the author of faith: that is, considering how much he endured for us, he who both gave and increased the faith for which he urges martyrdom upon us. It is as though he said: “Let us run toward the contest set before us, both because of the many examples of the fathers who have gone before, and because of love for faith and for Jesus its finisher. He is so great; from him we received the faith for which we suffer, and from him we hope for its completion in full blessedness.” For he is both author and finisher of faith: by his authorship we have faith, and by his finishing we shall attain to the sight of that which faith now believes.

Let us look to him, lest we fail amid adversities: he who, for the joy set before him, endured the cross—that is, who set before his heart the eternal joy to which he was to pass through [Col. 1667C] suffering, and so most willingly bore the punishments of the cross, despising shame, that is, disregarding every disgrace while he was mocked as he hung on the wood. Or, when the crowds set joy before him by wishing to make him king, he refused such joy (John 6); but later he endured the cross, mockery, and reproaches, despising all human shame. For he despised every earthly good, so that happiness might not be sought in such things. He endured the cross and therefore sits at the right hand of God’s throne: “for he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2), and for this reason God also exalted him.

Therefore he had not set before himself in vain the joy of resurrection and ascension while he suffered and was mocked, [Col. 1667D] but attained that joy. Accordingly, just as he, for the joy set before him, endured the cross, despising shame, and attained the confession of faith, so we too, with eternal joy set before us, ought to endure everything for his faith and despise every shame of reproaches, that we may deserve to attain a share in his throne. For he says: “To the one who conquers I shall grant to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sit with my Father on his throne” (Rev. 3).

> “For consider him who endured such contradiction from sinners against himself, so that you may not grow weary, failing in your souls. For you have not yet resisted unto blood, fighting against sin; and you have forgotten the consolation which speaks to you as to sons, saying: My son, do not neglect the discipline of the Lord, nor grow weary when you are rebuked by him. For whom the Lord loves he chastens; moreover, he scourges every son whom he receives.” (Prov. 3; Rev. 3.)

I said that we ought to look to the author of faith crucified for us. And it is right that this should be done. For “consider” means: think constantly upon what and how great he is, who endured such contradiction—that is, contradiction so disgraceful and violent—when men contradicted him and said: “He has blasphemed” (Matt. 26; John 19), and, “According to the law he must die, because he made himself the Son of God.” He endured this not from just anyone, but from sinners [Col. 1668B], which is more unworthy; nor was it directed merely against his members, but against himself.

Constantly consider him for imitation: though so holy, so free from sin, and so great, he patiently endured sinners who contradicted and mocked him, and afterward crucified him. Consider him, I say, so that, weighing what and how great were the things he endured, you may not grow weary in any adversities, failing in your souls: that is, even if you fail in body, nevertheless remain strong and unconquerable in mind. Nor ought you to fail, because what you have endured thus far is slight. Why should you incur the guilt of failing when you are not enduring the severe force of suffering? Why should you be corrupted by failure in faith when you still lack the shedding of blood? For even if you have already lost your possessions, nevertheless you have not yet resisted unto blood—that is, to the shedding of blood—fighting, that is, fighting repeatedly, not, I say, against sinners, that is, against people, but against the sin which they urge upon you when they attempt to call you back from faith or urge you to do something unlawful. You have not yet reached the shedding of blood.

And already, made sluggish by weariness, you have forgotten the consolation which God’s Wisdom offers you through Solomon amid adversities. It is as though he said: “You are blameworthy because you do not hold that consolation continually in memory.” Or it may be read as a question: “Have you not yet resisted unto blood, and have you already forgotten the consolation?” You ought not to have forgotten it. This consolation is read to you—that is, [Col. 1668D] consolatory words are directed to you through God’s Wisdom, which is Christ, from whom consolation comes. It speaks to you not as to servants, nor even merely as to friends, but rather as to sons, which is sweeter. For Christ is the father of believers, as he himself shows when he says: “Can the sons of the Bridegroom fast while the Bridegroom is with them?” (Mark 2).

Therefore he speaks in Proverbs to each faithful person suffering adversity: “My son, do not neglect.” “My” is an adverb of endearment. “Do not neglect,” that is, do not be willing to neglect—namely, to make light of—discipline, that is, the tribulations through which you can learn why God wills you to suffer tribulation: so that you may, like gold, be tested in the fire of tribulation. Or you can learn there that, if he does not spare you now although you are his son, how much less will he spare his adversaries in judgment. Since it is discipline, you ought not to disregard the tribulation you suffer; and since it is God’s discipline, you ought not disregard it. For to neglect God’s discipline is to refuse tribulation as useless when the necessity of suffering it presses upon one. “Nor grow weary,” that is, do not fail by becoming exhausted, when you are rebuked—that is, reproved—by him who is Lord both of you and of all.

Though you are adopted as a son, you must nevertheless acknowledge your Lord. You must patiently endure adversity, because by adversity itself you are rebuked and reproved by the Lord for the evils you have done, so that you may recall and correct them. Therefore humbly ascribe to your sins whatever adversity you suffer. Nor [Col. 1669B] ought you to grow weary when you are thus rebuked, because the Lord chastens—that is, makes chaste: through tribulations he makes chaste from vices the person whom he loves. And he not only chastens and corrects by blows the faithful person whom he loves, but also scourges every son whom he receives—that is, whom he calls back to himself after the fault of the first parent. He scourges every son, both greater and lesser, whom he receives.

Perhaps you say, “I shall be an exception.” If you are exempted from the suffering of scourges, you will be excluded from the number of sons. Do not hope to be without the scourge unless perhaps you mean to be disinherited. For no one is otherwise received into the eternal inheritance. He scourges everyone whom he receives. No one will be exempt; no one will be without the scourge. He scourges everyone so fully that he scourged even his only Son. That Only Son, although without sin, was nevertheless not without the scourge. It is clear, therefore, that he who scourges his Only Son without sin does not leave adopted children with sin immune from scourging. He scourges everyone in whatever way: through evil people, evil angels, loss of possessions, bodily illness, or some other adversity.

> “Persevere in discipline. God offers himself to you as to sons. For what son is there whom his father does not correct? But if you are without discipline, of which all have become partakers, then you are bastards and not sons. Furthermore, we had indeed the fathers of our flesh as instructors, and we revered them. Shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits and live? For they indeed instructed us for the time of a few days according to their own will, but he for what is useful, in receiving his sanctification.”

Because every son is scourged in order that he may be received into the inheritance which he lost through Adam, therefore persevere in the discipline you have begun, that is, in enduring adversities. For no one can be trained without labour, because “power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12). By these scourges of discipline you are being trained for a great thing, because God offers himself to you as to sons: so that, when you have been well trained by his scourges, you may possess him eternally as Father, and he may possess you as sons.

In other manuscripts *himself* is absent, and the reading is: “God offers to you as to sons.” This has the same meaning. Because he offers himself to you as to sons, so that you may persevere in discipline and attain the inheritance, and because in giving discipline he shows himself to be Father: “I shall visit their iniquities with a rod,” he says, “and their sins with blows; but I shall not take my mercy away from them” (Ps. 88). Therefore his mercy is not only that of one who calls, but also of one who strikes and scourges. Let the fatherly hand, then, be upon you, even if you are good sons. Do not reject his discipline. Let him give discipline, provided that he does not withdraw mercy. Let him strike the stubborn, provided that he restores the inheritance. If you have recognized the Father’s promises, do not fear to be scourged, but fear to be disinherited. It ought not to be as bitter to you that he scourges as it is sweet that he receives.

For how does the Lord who guards little children not scourge those whom he seeks as adult heirs? Nor is it surprising that he scourges them, because every father does this to the son whom he loves and desires to be wise. For what son is there whom his father does not correct when he sees him go astray in some matter? We see people doing this to their sons. Sometimes they allow their sons, now despaired of, to live as they please. But those in whom they have hope they scourge. Those whom they see to be wholly hopeless and untamed, they allow to do as they please. But those who permit them to do as they please do not intend to admit them to their inheritance. The son whom they scourge, however, they preserve the inheritance itself for him.

Therefore, when God scourges a son, let that son run beneath the hand of his scourging Father, because while he scourges, [Col. 1670C] he trains him for the inheritance. Let him not be of such vain and childish mind as to say, “My father loves my brother more, because he allows him to do whatever he wishes. If I stir myself against my father’s command, I meet with lashes.” You should rejoice under the lashes, because the inheritance is being kept for you. He corrects for a time lest he condemn eternally. Another, however, spares for a time, but will condemn them eternally.

Every father scourges his son and chastens him with the blows of discipline. But if you are outside the discipline of fatherly blows, in which discipline all sons have become partakers, then you are bastards and not sons. That is: since no son is without his father’s discipline, if you do not remain in God’s discipline, by which he chastens you with fatherly goodness, then you are not God’s sons, but rather offspring of the adulterous corrupter, who is the devil and is not rightly called a father. For one who has begotten through adultery cannot rightly be called a father. God is indeed the lawful father of believers; but the devil is not a father, but a corrupter, and therefore begets not sons but bastards. Such are those who do not endure God’s scourge in this present life, though they bear the name of Christianity.

For these reasons you ought to remain in discipline. Further, for this reason: we had fathers indeed, but instructors of our flesh, and we revered them—that is, we showed them reverence in submission and obedience. Therefore, shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits? That is, shall we not obey God, who is our spiritual Father? For obedience alone is the virtue which reconciles a human being to God, just as pride—that is, disobedience—separates one far from God. What else is disobedience except unwillingness to be subject to God—that is, willingness to be under one’s own power?

Shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits—that is, God, who formed the human being from the mud of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life? (Gen. 2.) For he did not make the human spirit from matter as he made the body, but created it from nothing by his breath, and thus in some manner showed himself to be Father of the spirit. He is also called Father of spirits because in baptism he begot us according to the spirit. We ought to obey him more than carnal parents because, in doing so, we shall live eternally.

Carnal fathers can offer little benefit. What could your father give you by correcting or beating you? Could he grant you eternal life? What he could not grant himself, when could he grant it to you? For the sake of whatever small amount of money he gathered by labour, he trained you with lashes so that you might not squander by evil living what he left to you. He left you what he could neither retain here nor carry away. For he did not leave you anything that could remain his own. He yielded place for you to succeed him.

But your God, your Redeemer, your Chastener, your Father, trains you to receive an inheritance: not that you may possess something apart from the Father, but that you may have the Father himself as your inheritance. You are trained for this hope, and yet you murmur. “Then God will be all in all” (1 Cor. 15). There will be no misery to test us, but happiness alone to nourish us. He himself will be our shepherd, our Lord, our harbour, our riches. Whatever various things we seek here, he alone will be all things to us. We are subdued for this hope, and the one who subdues us is thought unbearable.

For carnal fathers formerly subdued us, and they indeed trained us with blows according to their own will—that is, in what they desired, namely in vain and passing things—for the time of a few days, while we were children. But he, namely the Father of spirits, trains us for what is useful—that is, for faith and good conduct—in receiving his sanctification: that is, when we receive his discipline, which not only cleanses us from sins but also sanctifies us.

> “Now every discipline indeed seems at present not to be of joy but of sorrow; yet afterwards it will yield to those exercised through it the most peaceful fruit of righteousness. Therefore lift up the hands that hang down and the feeble knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that no lame person may go astray, but rather may be healed.”

He urged them to persevere in discipline. But since they could object that discipline is heavy and harsh, he himself responds beforehand, anticipates their thoughts, and resolves the objection. It is as though he said: “I exhort you to stand firm in discipline, but I acknowledge the truth that it is harsh.” For every discipline—that is, affliction—which anyone suffers for his sins in order to be corrected, at present, that is, amid the pains of distress themselves, seems to the sufferer to be not [Col. 1672A] of joy but of sorrow, because by striking the body it disturbs gladness.

Our Scriptures customarily use *disciplina* where instruction through hardships is to be understood, as in this passage; the Greeks call it *paideia* [παιδεία]. Indeed, this passage of the epistle has *paideia* in Greek. But discipline, which is named from learning, by which any matter is learned so that it may be known, is called *epistēmē* [ἐπιστήμη]. Discipline which corrects by scourging seems to bring sorrow; but it will not seem so if one considers the future. To those who think only of present things it seems unbearable, but to those who think of eternal things it becomes desirable. It now seems to be sorrowful, but afterward—that is, in the other life—it will render fruit, that is, fruitful reward: the fruit, I say, of righteousness, that is, the fruit which righteousness deserves. [Col. 1672B] And that fruit will be most peaceful, because it will be possessed in complete peace without any bodily or spiritual adversity.

And to whom will it be given? “To those exercised through it”: that is, through discipline. In other words, those who are now trained by fatherly discipline will then enjoy lofty peace without distress. Therefore, because such rest in the future age is gained through exercise in present discipline, you who, overcome by sorrow because of the lashes of discipline, had grown slack in good works, now eagerly lift up for good action and the heavenly reward your hands that hang down—that is, hands sluggish in almsgiving. Or “hands that hang down” means: lift up to God your sudden desires. And lift up your feeble knees—that is, raise lax habit to the standing of uprightness—and make straight paths for your feet, that is, for your actions.

For unless lax habit is raised to the state of virtue, toward which desire looks, the steps do not effectively follow in works [variant: *follow*]. Make straight paths of good works with your feet—that is, with the affections of your thoughts—so that action may follow where intention calls, lest anyone go astray from the straight way of faith by limping: that is, wavering in the course of thoughts or actions, like one who wished to keep at once the carnal observances of the Law and the Gospel, or like one who now wished in the future age to be without the scourge. Let no one limp in that way, for then he would stray from the path of uprightness; but rather let him be healed from every weakness of the feet of the heart, so that he may walk strong and upright [Col. 1672D] upon the way of righteousness.

> “Pursue peace with all and holiness, without which no one shall see God; watching lest anyone fall short of the grace of God, lest some root of bitterness springing up hinder you, and through it many be defiled; lest there be any fornicator or profane person like Esau, who for one meal sold his birthright. For know that afterward, when he wished to inherit the blessing, he was rejected. For he found no place for repentance, though he sought it with tears.” (Rom. 12; Gen. 25; Gen. 27.)

He instructs them how they should live with other people. “Pursue peace,” he says, “not with some, but with all”; that is, pursue the obligations of peace toward all persons [Col. 1673A], so that you maintain peace even with those who persecute you. For there are some who, while striving to be wiser than is necessary, recoil from peace with their neighbors, despising them as dull and foolish. What we have said concerning these two virtues ought also to be understood concerning all the others. Against the evil of discord, therefore, the Apostle rightly now warns: “Pursue peace with all,” that is, never depart from the peace of concord so as to begin to have discord with anyone; and pursue holiness, that is, chastity of mind and body, or holiness, that is, perfection in good works, without which peace or holiness no one will see God.

The Apostle frightens greatly, but only lovers. For he did not say, “Pursue peace with all [Col. 1673B] and sanctification; whoever lacks it shall be tortured in eternal fire”; rather, he said, “without which no one will see God.” He wished you to be a lover of good, not a fearer of evil, and frightened you precisely by that which you desired. For if you love to see your God, if in this pilgrimage you sigh with longing for his love, behold, your God tests you. It is as though he said to you: “Behold, do what you wish; satisfy your desires; extend your wickedness; enlarge your luxury; consider whatever pleases you permissible. I do not punish you for this; I do not send you into Gehenna; I shall merely deny you my face.” If you were afraid, you loved. If, when it was said that your God would deny you his face, your heart trembled—if you judged not seeing God to be a great punishment—you loved freely. Therefore let us pursue peace, without which no one will see God. [Col. 1673C] For we shall not possess the means by which we see God if, by strife, we extinguish in ourselves the very eye.

How foolish would two people be who wished to see the rising sun, if they disputed with one another as to from what quarter it would rise and how it could be seen, and, a controversy arising between them, fought, and by fighting struck one another, and by striking extinguished their own eyes, so that they could not see that sunrise? Therefore, in order that we may be able to see God, let us cleanse our hearts by faith, heal them by charity, and strengthen them by peace; for the very thing by which we love one another is already from him whom we desire to see. But without holiness likewise no one will see God. Hence, when John had said, “We know that, when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” [Col. 1673D] (1 John 3), he immediately added: “And everyone who has this hope in him sanctifies himself, just as he is holy” (ibid.). We must therefore strive for peace and holiness, so that we may be fit to see him.

“Pursue,” he says, “these two virtues, so that you may be holy, and, because of your holiness, may not depart from the peace of the perfect; but have care for them, watching lest any one of them or of you fall short of the grace of God,” which is present with you, so that by it you may pursue peace, holiness, and the other goods. For it is very wrong if any of you withdraws himself from the grace of God when grace itself offers itself to all of you. He withdraws himself from it through sin, and rejects it from himself, who consents more to his own pleasure than to heavenly grace.

Hence it is added: “Watching [Col. 1674A] lest any root of bitterness”—that is, lest some beginning of delight in sin—“hinder” that grace. This delight in sin is more truly called bitterness, and therefore must be avoided. “Lest any root of bitterness,” that is, any beginning of delight, and any thought of wickedness “springing up,” that is, breaking out into action, hinder your way to heaven. For the root is understood as evil thoughts, while the shoot is evil deeds and words, because what is hidden in the root is displayed in the shoot. This root is understood either as unbelief, or as delight in sin arising in the heart, or as any other affection for wickedness. And one must carefully watch lest, springing up into action or speech like tares, it impede the wheat of virtues in the one in whom it has thus sprouted, and thereafter [Col. 1674B] many be defiled through it, taking from him an example of wickedness or unbelief. For this is why care must be taken lest such a root sprout: what sprouts in one person spreads to others.

Then the Apostle shows these shoots of bitterness in detail and marks out certain Jews. “Watching,” he says, “lest any be a fornicator or profane person,” that is, alien from the assembly of believers, “like Esau” (Gen. 25), who, because of his love for Gentile women, separated himself from the seed of Abraham, offended his father and mother, and, for one food, that is, for the lentils his brother had cooked, sold him his *primitiva*, that is, his birthright: namely, the dignity due to him because he had been born first, on account of which he ought also to have received his father’s blessing. But he was so [Col. 1674C] profane, that is, far from religion, that for the greediness of his belly he sold the blessing. Although he had been born of holy parents, he nevertheless degenerated by living wickedly, separated himself, as was said, from Abraham’s seed, and did not inherit the promises made to Abraham.

So likewise the Apostle is understood to have seen in the Spirit, among the Hebrews of his own time, certain followers of Esau in fornication, neglect of religion, and greediness of the belly. For those whom the Law restrained from the wickedness of fornication by fear now, under grace, committed fornication as though freely, because they were not immediately punished but were awaited for repentance. Or a fornicator was anyone among them who held the carnal observance of the Law together with faith as though it were a concubine; while a profane person [Col. 1674D] was anyone who entirely neglected faith, and thus sold his *primitiva*, that is, the preeminence which he might have possessed with God, to his younger brother—that is, he allowed the Gentile people coming to faith to receive it—while taking the red food of lentils, that is, delight in sin, which is customarily signified by blood. Thus, degenerating after Esau’s manner from the faith and religion of the spiritual fathers, from whom he had been begotten in Christ through the Gospel, he was not worthy to obtain the promises of the heavenly inheritance.

Fearing this, therefore, the Apostle gently warns them lest there be among them any fornicator or profane person like Esau, who, for the desire of one cheap food, gave up the dignity of his primacy. “And you ought not,” he says, “to be like that man who was rejected. For know that afterward,” that is, after he had sold his birthright [Col. 1675A], “when he desired to inherit the blessing due to the firstborn, he was rejected by God.” For although his father wished to bless him, it nevertheless came about by divine dispensation that he blessed his brother in his place. Thus he was divinely rejected from receiving the blessing, although his father had chosen him for blessing.

“For he then found no place for repentance, although he sought it with tears.” For when he returned from hunting and recognized that Jacob had received the blessing which he himself expected, he grieved deeply and wept because he had previously lost his birthright and now his blessing. But although he wept abundantly, he found no opportunity for repentance through which he might recover the birthright he had long ago sold, or receive for himself the blessing [Col. 1675B] which his brother had received, because he wept too late and sought repentance too late. For it was now impossible to alter what had been done. So you also must beware lest, when after death you ought to receive the blessing, you be rejected and then find no place for repentance, if you now lose the primacy of your dignity for some brief pleasure. For repentance is sought too late in that age, when we have learned that our brothers have received the blessing for which we hoped, and that we have been left without blessing. Now is the time for repentance, not then.

> “For you have not come to a tangible and approachable fire, and whirlwind, and darkness, and storm, and the sound of a trumpet, and a voice of words [Col. 1675C] which those who heard begged that no word be spoken to them (Exod. 19–20). For they could not bear what was commanded: ‘Even if a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned’ (ibid.). And so terrible was what was seen that Moses said: ‘I am terrified and trembling.’”

He said, “Lest any of you fall short of the grace of God,” for it is prepared for you. For you have not come to the harshness of the Law now described, so that, by contrast, the sweetness of grace may be understood. You have not come to the fire burning on Sinai’s summit, tangible, that is, able to be touched, and approachable, that is, one could approach it by bodily movement; but to the Holy Spirit, who is a fire consuming sins and kindling charity in the mind, [Col. 1675D] who is not touched bodily because he is spirit, and whom one approaches not by bodily movement but by the affection of the heart, because he is nowhere locally confined.

“You have not come to fire, and whirlwind, and darkness,” and so forth. These things occurred at the giving of the Law so that the hearts of the Jews might be shaken and they might not dare to transgress the Law. But it was not so at the reception of the New Law. For all things are presented to us gently and sweetly, so that we may serve not from fear but from love. “And you have not come,” he says, “to a whirlwind.” A whirlwind is a violence of winds with hail and rain, and it signified the onslaught of vices, which were more severely condemned by the Law. But now, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, one comes to the serenity of virtues. “And you have not come to darkness,” that is, to the obscurity of the Law, but to clear understanding. [Col. 1676A] “And you have not come to the storm” which then occurred, but to tranquillity. For a storm, that is, a tempest greater than a whirlwind and driving everything before it [variant: “wherever it drives”], is the slavery of sin according to its operation, which drew people along through the Law. But now the perfect rest from vices; and you have not come to the sound of a trumpet. For the sound of a trumpet, which is the signal for movement to war, is the stirring of pleasure, which is lulled and extinguished not by the Law but by grace.

“And you have not come to a voice of words,” which those who heard begged that no word be spoken to them by the Lord, when terrified and shaken with fear they stood far off, saying to Moses: “Speak to us, and we will hear; let not the Lord speak to us, lest perhaps we die” (Exod. [Col. 1676B] 20). Such a voice is the command and threat of the Law, which the people considered burdensome and unbearable, because it was command alone, without assisting grace. “For they could not bear what was commanded,” because without grace they were insufficient for keeping the commandments.

Fire may be understood as the wrath of the Law: “For the Law produces wrath” (Rom. 4). The whirlwind is the threat expressed in the saying: “If anyone does this or that, let him surely die.” Darkness is the obscurity of ignorance that was in the Law. The storm is the punishment of guilt imposed by the Law. The sound of the trumpet is the coming of the Judge, who will descend from heaven with a trumpet (1 Thess. 4). The voice of words is the Judge’s harsh utterance by which he will accuse sinners. This voice was therefore rightly judged unbearable, because no one can endure the weight of that judgment if he is judged strictly. [Col. 1676C] “For they could not bear what was commanded,” because the word of that Judge is unendurable for those judged without mercy.

But what was commanded which seemed unbearable? Namely this: “Even if a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.” Thus the Lord commanded, as though saying: “Stand far off, for even if a beast touches the mountain, it shall be crushed by stones.” Therefore, through fear, they could not bear the voice of the Lord speaking terribly, because they feared they would immediately die. Spiritually, however, the mountain is the height of divine contemplation; the beast is the absence of reason. This occurs when a word of blasphemy is uttered against God, or when one irrationally strives toward his contemplation. Therefore he touches the mountain like a beast [Col. 1676D] who offends against the divinity through his irrationality, while rashly [variant: shamelessly] thinking or saying about God what ought not to be thought or said. A beast touches the mountain when a mind subjected to irrational desires raises itself to the heights of contemplation. But it is struck by stones because, unable to endure what is above, it is slain by the very blows of the heavenly weight.

Thus, when the Law is received, the people are kept from the mountain, so that those who still desire earthly things with weak minds may not presume to contemplate lofty things. For the mind must first be cleansed of the appetite for temporal glory and every delight of carnal concupiscence, and only then raised to the keenness of contemplation. God, speaking in fire, threatened that even a beast would be stoned if it touched the mountain. “And so terrible was what was seen” [Col. 1677A], because the mountain appeared to burn; and the children of Israel said to Moses: “We have heard the voice of God from the midst of the fire, and today have proved that, when God speaks with a human being, the human being may live. Why then shall we die? This great fire will devour us. For if we hear further the voice of the Lord our God, we shall die” (Deut. 5). What is all flesh, that it should hear the voice of the living God speaking from the midst of fire, as we have heard, and be able to live? So terrible was what was seen—and truly terrible. For Moses said: “I am terrified and trembling.” For what could terrify Moses was exceedingly terrible. And if he so feared, what should be thought of the rest? Moses was terrified because the severity was so great that even the perfect were frightened, since there was no assisting grace. But now the command is not burdensome even to the imperfect, [Col. 1677B] because Christ’s yoke is sweet and his burden light (Matt. 9). It follows:

> “But you have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to the gathering of many thousands of angels, and to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and to God the judge of all, and to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and to Jesus, mediator of the New Testament, and to the sprinkling of blood that speaks better than Abel.”

“You have not come,” he says, “to tangible fire and to the other things which he has described up to this point.” You have not come to those harsh things, but rather to Mount Zion. He does not set down the opposites which are understood by contrast, but the reward which follows from them, in order by this means more strongly [Col. 1677C] to urge the preservation of grace. “You have come to Mount Zion,” that is, to the height of heavenly blessedness in which God is seen. For “mountain” signifies sublimity, while Zion, which means “watchtower” or “place of viewing,” signifies contemplation. You have come to it through faith and the merits of virtues—that is, you have already been made near, so that afterward you may arrive at it—according to the saying: “They shall go from strength to strength; the God of gods shall be seen in Zion” (Ps. 83). You have come thus by making progress, for now our salvation is nearer than when we believed (Rom. 13). Therefore, by arranging ascents in your hearts, you have indeed drawn near, although you have not yet arrived at Mount Zion, that is, the height of that ineffable blessedness [Col. 1677D] in which the saints behold God; and at the city of the living God, which receives from his vision the gift that it too may live without end as he does.

To the city of God, namely the heavenly Jerusalem, which is called “vision of peace,” because in that kingdom of heaven they see no disturbance among themselves, but everlasting rest and peace; and you have come to the gathering of many thousands of angels, who happily inhabit that city. You will be companions of all these, because blessedness will be greater among many, where each rejoices in another as in himself, truly loving his neighbor as himself. “And you have come to the assembly of the firstborn,” that is, the apostles and the other saints of that time, who have already migrated to the heavenly places and are enrolled in heaven—that is, written among those who are [Col. 1678A] in heaven; in other words, they belong to their order, being assigned a place among the angels. Therefore do not doubt that you will come to the gathering of angels, to which your predecessors have already come.

“And you have come also to God, judge of all,” so that you too may become judges with him and then render to your persecutors a just recompense of punishments; “and you have come to the spirits,” that is, the souls of righteous persons made perfect, who have already departed from this world, since they too reached the heavenly kingdom after the apostles. For all righteous persons who are perfect in deeds, words, and thoughts are brought into heavenly dwellings as soon as they send forth their souls from their bodies. You have come to their spirits because you have drawn near to their blessedness, since you are already their companions in faith and [Col. 1678B] deed.

To come to all these things is already a great reward, since one comes to them not by the movement of feet but by progress in virtues, through Christ, who has become for us the way to them. Hence it follows: “and to Jesus, mediator of the New Testament.” You have come to Jesus, through whom you could come to all the things mentioned above, because he is mediator of the New Testament: that is, through himself the giver of the Gospel received from the Father, so that through it we may arrive at the eternal inheritance. For Moses, as we said far above, was mediator of the Old Testament, in which a temporal inheritance was promised; he says: “I stood as intermediary and mediator between the Lord and you at that time, to declare his words to you” (Deut. 5). But the Lord Jesus, in the time [Col. 1678C] of grace, was intermediary between the Father and us, declaring his words to us, reconciling us to him, and through himself as mediator giving us access to him and to all the things noted above.

“And you have come to the sprinkling of his blood,” he says, by which you were cleansed and sanctified from your sins, just as certain things in the Law which had to be cleansed and sanctified were sprinkled with the blood of sacrifices in order that they might be cleansed and sanctified. Thus all of us too have been sprinkled with the blood of this true sacrifice, through which we have not only been cleansed from sins, but have also received sanctification and justification. I mean the sprinkling “speaking better than Abel.” For the sprinkling of Christ’s blood speaks because it intercedes with the Father for us. Therefore it speaks better than Abel’s blood, of which it was said, “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the ground” (Gen. 4), because Abel’s blood sought the death of his fratricidal brother, whereas Christ’s blood obtained life for his persecutors.
