[Col. 1678D] Abel’s blood demands vengeance; Christ’s blood demands mercy. The former harmed one person; the latter benefited many. Therefore it speaks better. Or “speaks better” means: it makes people speak that Jesus is the Son of God, by whom we have been redeemed.

> “See that you do not refuse him who speaks. For if they did not escape who refused him who spoke on earth, much more shall we not escape if we turn away from him who speaks to us from heaven. His voice shook the earth then; but now he promises, saying: ‘Yet once more [Col. 1679A] I will shake not only the earth but also heaven’ (Hag. 2). And this phrase, ‘yet once more,’ declares the removal of things that can be shaken, as things made, so that the things that cannot be shaken may remain. Therefore, receiving an unshakable kingdom, let us have grace, through which we may serve God acceptably with fear and reverence. For our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4).

The Lord Jesus to whom you have come speaks, as was said, through his blood, because he both intervenes for us with the Father and urges us to imitate his passion. See, therefore, that you do not refuse him who speaks while he exhorts you to follow his footsteps. You will also refuse him speaking if, while he intercedes for you, you seek to please [Col. 1679B] God through carnal observances. For this too he speaks through his blood: that all sacrifices of the Law must now cease and that his sacrifice alone must remain, while he forbids carnal things and commands spiritual things. Therefore attend carefully, lest you refuse him who speaks; rather, embrace him with such desire of mind in all that he says.

For if they—that is, the ancient Jews—did not escape their deserved vengeance when they refused him who spoke on earth, that is, Moses, who, although filled with Christ, was nevertheless only a human being and not also God, and who lived among people to whom he delivered God’s commandments, much more shall we not escape if we turn away Christ speaking to us from the hearing of our heart. For he who warns us concerning conversion now sits in heaven; and if those who despised Moses, though mortal and placed on earth, suffered deserved punishments, what shall we suffer if we despise Christ, immortal and seated in heaven?

Or Moses spoke “upon earth” because he gave carnal commandments to earthly people and promised earthly goods. He spoke upon earth because he did not lay his law upon a righteous person, but upon any sinner, to whom it was said: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3). But Christ speaks from heaven, that is, of heavenly and spiritual things, because he promises spiritual—that is, eternal—goods. But if those did not escape who despised Moses commanding carnal things, how shall we escape if we neglect to hear Christ commanding spiritual things? [Col. 1679D]

His—Christ’s—voice shook the earth then, when Moses spoke upon earth, because he himself gave the Law to Moses on Mount Sinai and uttered the Decalogue of that same Law in a great voice from the mountain summit, while all the people heard; and in order to strike greater fear into them, he shook the earth. Then indeed, in order to threaten them lest they refuse his words, he moved the earth by his voice alone; but now he not only does not threaten but persuades gently and promises. Therefore we ought much less to refuse him.

Now he promises again and again, or promises as a reward, concerning the last day on which all the elements will be shaken; or, after that movement of the earth which occurred at the giving of the Law—when heaven too is understood to have been moved—he promises through the prophet Haggai [Col. 1680A] (ch. 2), saying: “Yet once more,” and no more thereafter, namely on the day of judgment, “I will shake not only the earth but also heaven.” But this heaven is not the ethereal heaven, but the airy one; not the higher, but the lower; not the firmament, but that through which winds and clouds pass.

The Apostle explains the meaning of this statement when he adds: “And this phrase, ‘yet once more,’” and so forth. He says, “I shall yet once more shake,” as though saying: “They have already been moved, but I shall move them once more.” But his saying “yet once more” declares the removal of things that can be shaken. For by “once” he indicates that afterward they will not be moved further, but will thereafter be unshakable. By saying “I will shake,” the transformation of heaven and earth is declared, that is, their change into another state, so that a new heaven and a new earth may be made from this old heaven and old earth (above, ch. 1). Hence it is said: “They shall grow old like a garment, and like a covering you shall change them, and they shall be changed” (Ps. 101). [Col. 1680B] Therefore other things will not be made; these very things, made from the beginning, will be renewed by the fire of judgment and will then remain without end.

Thus he declares the transformation of things that can be shaken, that is, the changing of the face of the earth and the heavens, meaning this windy air, not the higher heavens where the sun, moon, and other stars are placed. But what is said in the Psalm—“The heavens are the works of your hands; they themselves shall perish” (Ps. 101)—seems to leave no heaven remaining, since it does not say that any of them will not perish; for just as it made none of them exempt from God’s work, so it made none exempt from destruction. This is similar to what is said here: “the removal of [Col. 1680C] things that can be shaken, as things made.” For they are not merely not immovable, but also movable, things made by God among created beings.

Therefore, lest the whole world be believed to be perishing, the part must, as we said, be understood from the whole in the phrase “they themselves shall perish,” since only the lowest heavens will perish, while the higher ones are preserved and remain in their integrity, in whose firmament the stars are set. Similarly, here “as things made” is understood of those things that are movable and to be transformed. But the things to be transformed are called made by God in order to show that they can fittingly be changed into another state, since they could be made from nothing. Thus he declares the removal of movable things as things made by him: namely, the lower heavens which formerly perished in the Flood, and the elements existing [Col. 1680D] in this one stormy and turbulent part of the world, so that there may remain forever the things that are immovable: the higher heavens with their inhabitants, and the earth after it has been changed by fire.

Or he declares the transformation of movable things so that those things which now exist and change may, after they have been transformed, remain eternally immovable. For after that transformation heaven and earth will be immovable, as appears from the fact that they are said to be moved once. And since movable and temporal things perish, while immovable things remain, therefore the kingdom of God, which is immovable, will remain forever; and we, already receiving it in hope, have the grace of God, without which we could not reach it. Therefore let no one fall short of the grace of God which has offered itself to us.

[Col. 1681A] We have grace, in which we receive faith, hope, and charity in good action, through which we may serve God acceptably. “Let us serve,” he says, “and this with fear, because he is God, and reverence,” that is, trembling awe, “because he is Father.” Truly, through the grace we have received, we ought to serve with fear and reverence. “For our God is a consuming fire,” whom we wish to serve, as Moses also said previously (Deut. 4). God is called a consuming fire because by this fire the rust of sins is consumed. For the rust of vice cannot be consumed except by the fire of punishment.

Fire has four functions: it cleanses, burns, illuminates, and warms. Thus the Holy Spirit cleanses the filth of vices; burns the loins and heart, drying the moisture of lusts; illuminates the mind by knowledge of truth; and warms it with the burning of charity. [Col. 1681B] Through all these things he makes one pleasing to God. Therefore, through the grace received, let us serve him acceptably. Or let us serve with fear and reverence because our God is a consuming fire, who at judgment will consume those who now neither fear nor revere him. Not that God is fire, but that he appears as fire to those enduring punishments. For just as he will illumine the righteous, so he will burn up the wicked.

## Chapter XIII

> “Let brotherly charity remain among you, and do not neglect hospitality” (1 Pet. 4; Rom. 12). “For by this some have pleased God, having received angels as guests. Remember those in bonds as though bound with them, and those who suffer as though you yourselves also dwell in the body. Marriage is honorable in all things [Col. 1681C], and the marriage bed undefiled; but God will judge fornicators and adulterers.”

He now gives moral instruction. Since God is a fire kindling charity in the heart, by which not only God but also one’s neighbor is loved, see therefore that the charity of the brethren, which that fire has kindled in your hearts, is not extinguished or withdrawn from you; but let brotherly charity continually remain in you—that is, always love the brotherhood, namely, brothers reborn of water and the Spirit (John 3), as you yourselves are. Let there never be anything that can take their love from your hearts. And do not forget hospitality, which you formerly practiced before you were despoiled of your possessions, because of your present need; rather, [Col. 1681D] be frequently mindful of it in deed, so that you may offer lodging with charity even if you cannot provide an abundance of food.

Nor ought you through disuse to forget hospitality, because through it certain most distinguished fathers—Abraham and Lot (Gen. 18–19)—pleased God, having received angels as guests. For because they habitually welcomed guests with devout zeal, they deserved to provide hospitality even to angels. They thought them human beings while offering them food, but afterward understood that they were angels, either when the angels went up to heaven before their eyes or through other indications which they saw in them.

Besides guests, remember those in bonds—that is, be mindful of those held in prisons or chains for the Lord’s name, who cannot seek [Col. 1682A] assistance for themselves. Therefore think compassionately of them and provide what is necessary. Do not let them be forgotten by you, although they are shut away in hidden confinement; remember them as though bound with them—that is, think continually of them, sympathize with them and assist them as if you were bound alongside them. As you would wish to be aided if you were in chains, so strive to aid them. And remember those who suffer, that is, those burdened either by bodily weakness or by some necessity. Remember them frequently by doing them good, as persons who are yourselves capable of suffering and of feeling the burden of affliction; this is what is meant by “as though you yourselves also dwell in the body.” Through dwelling in the body, you have learned by your own experience what sufferers need; and it may happen that you too will endure a harder suffering [Col. 1682B] than they do and will wish to be helped by others. Therefore be the first now to help them, so that you too may be helped, if it becomes necessary.

I also make known to you that marriage is honorable: that is, lawful marriages are honorable in every respect, and there is nothing in them lacking honor; and the marriage bed of such spouses is undefiled, that is, without the stain of sin. But God will judge fornicators, who have intercourse with prostitutes, and adulterers, who violate other men’s wives; that is, at the last judgment he will condemn them perpetually. For adultery is committed with another’s spouse. But fornication here is understood not only as intercourse with other women, but also as that practiced after the manner of the people of Gomorrah, or whenever chastity is voluntarily violated in any way. [Col. 1682C] God will judge all who defile themselves with any kind of lust.

The day of judgment is indeed far off, but the last day of each individual cannot be far off; and because life is short, and that very brevity is always uncertain, so that none of us knows when his final day will be, whoever is stained by any uncleanness of lust should strive quickly to be cleansed through repentance while it is still possible, lest he begin to wish for it when he can no longer do so and fall under the judgment of the eternal God.

> “Let your conduct be without avarice, content with what is present. For he himself has said: ‘I will not leave you nor forsake you’ (Josh. 1), so that we may confidently say: ‘The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man may do to me’ [Col. 1682D] (Ps. 117). Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you; considering the outcome of their manner of life, imitate their faith. Jesus Christ yesterday and today, the same also for ever.”

After they had lost their possessions, they wished to gather them again. This is what the Apostle now forbids. “Let your conduct,” he says, “be without avarice,” that is, let avarice not mingle itself with your manner of life. Rather, let your holy conduct be guided without an immoderate love of money, being content with what is present, so that you do not scheme for future gains or heap up wealth for yourselves for future times. But lest they should say, “What if necessities fail us?”, he adds consolation. You ought not greedily to gather possessions, as though fearing that God might permit you to lack necessities, [Col. 1683A] because he who cannot lie has said to everyone who hopes in him: “I will not leave you nor forsake you.” To give us greater confidence, he repeated the promise of not abandoning us, saying: “I will not leave you nor forsake you.” He said this to Joshua (ch. 1), who bore the figure of the Lord Jesus Christ, and in Christ to every member of Christ. Thus he promised that he would not forsake us, and thus he is with us, so that each of us may confidently say: “The Lord is my helper in all my labours and tribulations; therefore I shall not fear what man may do to me,” even if he takes away my possessions, even if he afflicts my body with punishments. Properly speaking, the devil is our adversary; but more often he inflicts evils upon us through a human being. Therefore, through God’s help we do not fear the wicked person through whom the devil works.

But that [Col. 1683B] you may overcome avarice and fear no evil person, remember your departed leaders, who spoke to you the word of God; that is, consider how perfectly they left everything for the Gospel, and how steadfastly and fearlessly they trod underfoot every adversity through patience. Remember them so that you may imitate them; and then you will fear neither poverty nor persecution, “considering the outcome of their way of life”—that is, inwardly observing how they departed from their present manner of life and with what end they concluded their temporal life, passing into eternal joys. Imitate their faith, which they maintained even unto death, so that you too may likewise die in faith and attain the rewards of faith.

And lest you doubt that the divine [Col. 1683C] help which was with them is present with you, know that Jesus Christ was yesterday, is today, and will be the same for ever. It is as though he said: The same Christ who was with them is with you, and will be with those who are to come, “until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). Yesterday he was with the fathers; today he is with you; he himself will be with your descendants for ever. “Yesterday” belongs to past time; “today,” to present time. But that which remains for ever seems to have no end. “Yesterday,” then, signifies all past time and the whole extent of eternity that was before the world’s origin; “today,” all present time; and enduring “for ever,” the whole expanse of time and infinity that is to come. Thus Jesus Christ was yesterday, because “in the beginning [Col. 1683D] was the Word” (John 1); and from eternity to our own times he is himself today also—that is, he exists in our time. And he will be for ever, because he will remain eternally. Hence John says of him: “He who was, and who is, and who is to come” (Rev. 1). For “he who is to come” may be understood as he who will be through all ages. These things, indeed, are said in accordance with the weakness of human understanding. But his boundless divinity simultaneously comprehends and possesses all fullness: nothing future is absent from it, nor has anything past flowed away, because his being is whole and always is; it knows no change, having neither ever begun nor ever to cease—a certain unconquerable and endless sea of being, enclosed by no bounds or limits, surpassing every sense, [Col. 1684A] every time, and every nature. It follows:

> “Do not be carried away by various and strange teachings. For it is best for the heart to be established by grace, not by foods, which have not profited those who walk in them.”

Because Jesus Christ always was, is, and will be, do not be led away from his faith by the various teachings of false preachers—that is, teachings diverse from one another, differing and discordant in many ways, while one teaches one error and another another, and they proclaim mutually contrary things—or by strange teachings, that is, teachings alien to Catholic truth. Therefore do not be led away by such teachings; that is, do not be separated from the integrity of faith and the purity of Christian religion. Nor ought you to be led astray by the deceptive words of liars, because it is best for the heart to be established in the grace of faith and holiness, so that it [Col. 1684B] may steadfastly remain in it, be led into no error, but abide in the grace of God which it has received.

The heart ought to be established by grace according to the Gospel, not by foods according to the teaching of false preachers. For it is implied that there were some among them who taught as doctrine that it was no sin to devote oneself to foods. Since through grace it is lawful to use all foods, they preached that it was not blameworthy but good to abound in foods. Against them the Apostle says: “Do not be carried away by the various teachings of fools”—that is, teachings different from ours—“and strange,” that is, foreign. For you ought to strengthen your heart by grace, which by releasing from the law gives freedom, and not devote yourselves to foods; for they have not profited for salvation—not, I say, those who sustain themselves by them, but [Col. 1684C] those “who walk in them,” that is, those who conduct their lives in banquets and feasts.

Or: establish your hearts by evangelical grace, so that your mind may abide and labour in it, not in the foods which the law teaches are alone to be eaten, prohibiting the others as unclean, though they are creatures of God, “who made all things very good” (Gen. 1). These legal foods, after the Lord’s coming, did not profit but rather harmed those who walked in them; that is, those who conducted their life in observing distinctions among them.

> “We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no right to eat. For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the Holy Place by the high priest for sin are burned outside the camp (Num. 9). Therefore Jesus also, [Col. 1684D] that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate. Let us therefore go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach. For we do not have here an abiding city, but seek the one to come” (Mic. 2).

He touches upon the custom of the law and recalls it to spiritual understanding. For it was a commandment of the law that on the tenth day of the seventh month, namely at the feast of propitiation, they should take a calf and a goat and sacrifice them within the camp; their blood the high priest alone was to carry into the Holy of Holies, praying for the whole people; but their flesh was to be burned outside the camp, and no one serving the tabernacle was permitted to eat of it.

Christ is that calf on account of the new strength which he showed in [Col. 1685A] the resurrection; and he is that goat on account of the likeness of sinful flesh. This calf or goat was sacrificed for the sin of the whole people. The priests received him for sacrifice by command of the law, because according to the law they thought that they were killing Christ, since, in their view, he broke the Sabbath. They sacrificed him in the camp—that is, they killed him by their words in the house of Caiaphas, saying, “He is guilty of death” (Matt. 26); or in Pilate’s house, crying, “Crucify him” (John 19). But afterwards his flesh was burned outside the camp—that is, outside Jerusalem it was consumed by the fire of suffering.

Or burning belongs as a sign to the resurrection, because it is the nature of fire to move upward, and that which is burned is transformed into it. For the word *cremare*, “to burn,” itself is drawn into [Col. 1685B] Latin from Greek, from suspension.

> [Note: *κρεμάζω* (*kremázō*), or *κρεμάω* (*kremáō*), or *κρέμαμαι* (*krémamai*), means “to hang” or “suspend.” Hence the author supposes that *cremo* is derived from this word.]

But his blood was brought into the Holy of Holies by the high priest—that is, by Christ himself, who carried it into heaven, entering there to intercede for us. The altar upon which he was burned outside the camp is the altar of the Church, where his body is consecrated. Those who serve the tabernacle—that is, the shadow of truth—have no right to eat from it. Or by “tabernacle” the body is understood; and those who serve the tabernacle, that is, bodily pleasures, such as gluttons, drunkards, fornicators, and the like, have no right—that is, no permission—to eat from our altar, that is, to receive the Lord’s body.

For he had said that one ought not devote oneself to foods, and immediately fittingly added that we have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no right [Col. 1685C] to eat—that is, those who live voluptuously and satisfy carnal desires. For just as that calf and goat were burned outside the camp and were not eaten by any who served the tabernacle, so the memorial of Christ’s passion is celebrated among those who have gone outside bodily pleasures, and his body is received by them. It cannot be received by those who remain in fleshly pleasures and serve the tabernacle of the body.

The elect too may be understood through the goat and the calf: through the goat, because they strive to slay in themselves the sins of the flesh; through the calf, because they strive to offer God the sacrifice of righteousness. They are burned outside the camp because, kindled by the Holy Spirit, they consume outside the manner of life of worldly people [Col. 1685D] whatever is carnal in them, while devoutly afflicting themselves with fasts and other labours. For the blood of those animals—that is, their praiseworthy life—is brought into the holy place by the high priest, that is, presented to God through Christ; and this is for their sin, because they live praiseworthily not only that they may please God, but also that they may redeem their former sins.

Or their blood—that is, their souls—is brought into the holy place, that is, into heaven through Christ the high priest; their bodies are burned upon the altar of the heart. Those who serve the tabernacle—that is, carnal people who love the world and serve bodily pleasures—cannot approach this altar because of their irreligion. The bodies of those animals whose blood is [Col. 1686A] brought into the Holy Place by the high priest are burned outside the camp. In order to fulfil this mystery Jesus too suffered outside the gate of Jerusalem, that he might sanctify the people truly through his blood, just as the blood of those animals sanctified in shadow.

Or, by a double allegory, one of the Old and the other of the New Testament, he proved that Christ’s body ought not to be eaten by those who serve the tabernacle. For this purpose the bodies of animals were burned outside the camp, and for this reason too Christ suffered outside the gate: so that we who wish to be cleansed from sins by his body and blood may abandon the delights of the tabernacle, being about to suffer reproaches and hardships. Hence it is immediately added: “Let us therefore go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach.” Whoever wishes [Col. 1686B] to receive his body and blood ought to approach the place of his passion, so that, leaving behind the honours and riches of the tabernacle, he may not refuse to bear reproaches and poverty for Christ’s name; and, going out from the camp and the city, he may come to the cross—that is, abandoning the perverse customs of the multitude who follow the broad way of the world, he may take up the narrow way which leads to life (Matt. 7).

For Christ’s suffering outside the gate indicates that, through the redemption of his passion, he gathers those who have departed from fleshly desires in imitation of his passion. Therefore let us go out to him outside the camp—that is, leaving the common wickedness of worldly people who serve the pleasures of the flesh—so that we may no longer linger with them in unlawful pleasures, but, abandoning fellowship in their depravity, hasten to Christ’s cross, bearing his reproach, so that we too may be mocked with him by the ungodly and sinners of the world. Let us go out to him—that is, let us direct ourselves with devout concern and action towards the end of the present life, by which we pass to him. We ought always to fix the eyes of the heart upon the end and meditate without ceasing on when we shall leave this present life, so that we may reach Christ. And daily we ought thus to go out to him with devout desires, mentally meditating on our departure, because we do not have here an abiding city—that is, an abiding body in this condition—but seek the city to come, [Col. 1686C] that is, we desire to possess the incorruptible and impassible body which will exist after the resurrection.

Or, let us go out in heart and deed from the camp—that is, from the midst of the multitude of those who love the world—so that we may be poor and despised with Christ, whose kingdom is not of this world (John 18). For we do not have here an abiding city—that is, we are not citizens of Babylon, which has planted the root of its heart in love of the present world—but we are strangers and sojourners in this world (Gal. 4), and seek the city to come, that is, the heavenly Jerusalem, which is our mother; we seek it inwardly, that we may find its inner blessedness. “For blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.”

> “Through him, therefore, let us always [Col. 1687A] offer to God a sacrifice of praise, that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name. And do not forget beneficence and sharing; for by such sacrifices God is won.”

Christ offered himself as a sacrifice for us; and therefore through him let us always offer to God the Father a sacrifice of praise, because he, the high priest, has made all of us priests, if we are his members. Let us offer a sacrifice not of cattle but of praise, so that we no longer offer and sacrifice the flesh of brute animals, but do what is written: “Sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 49); that is, let us praise him by loving him, so that we may worship him not slavishly but willingly.

For people who feared God in the Old Testament, because of the letter that terrifies and kills, [Col. 1687B] not yet possessing the life-giving Spirit, ran to the temple with sacrifices. Although these sacrifices were a figure of the future blood by which we are redeemed, yet, not knowing what they prefigured, they sacrificed bloody victims. Now, through the grace of the New Testament, the terror of the law having been removed and the Holy Spirit given, those carnal sacrifices have been rejected, and spiritual ones established in their place. Thus a person need no longer seek outside himself what to offer God, but may offer him the devout devotion and love of his own mind as a sacrifice of praise.

“Let us always offer,” he says, “to God a sacrifice of praise”; that is, let us praise him unceasingly with heart and mouth, like him who says: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. 33). Let us offer a sacrifice of praise, that is, “the fruit [Col. 1687C] of lips confessing his name”: the fruit which our lips bring forth when we confess his name, namely when, praising him with devout devotion, we render to him a confession of praise and thanksgiving. Therefore let us always offer this sacrifice of praise—that is, this fruit of the lips, namely the affection of inward love uttered by lips praising God—so that what the mind always loves, the mouth may speak in fruitful praise; “for with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10).

Be such in confession and praise of the Lord’s name; but towards the saints do not forget beneficence and sharing. That is, although you were once despoiled of your goods because you ministered to the saints from them, nevertheless do not forget your customary beneficence [Col. 1687D] and sharing; but from what you have subsequently acquired, do good to needy saints and share with them what you have, as you did before. You ought to share your goods with the saints in almsgiving, because by such sacrifices—that is, alms given to saints—God is won: that is, God himself is the reward which you acquire by such sacrifices. Therefore offer to God not now the sacrifices of the law but sacrifices of almsgiving, he who says: “For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice” (Hos. 6).

For what is called sacrifice among human beings is a sign of the true sacrifice; mercy, however, is the true sacrifice. Therefore whatever is read in the mystery of the tabernacle or temple as divinely commanded in many ways concerning sacrifices [Col. 1688A] refers to signifying love of God and neighbour. “On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets” (Matt. 22). God therefore does not desire slaughtered cattle, but desires the sacrifice of almsgiving, as we have already shown him saying: “For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice.”

> “Obey your leaders and submit to them. For they keep watch as those who must render an account for your souls, so that they may do this with joy and not groaning; for this is not advantageous to you.”

He had warned them not to forget beneficence and sharing, but always to remember to do good to the saints and share their possessions with them. This was said especially to subjects, who ought to do these things [Col. 1688B] most of all for their prelates. Hence he now says still more plainly to the same subjects: “Obey your leaders,” that is, comply with their commands in all things, unless perhaps they command some evil; for evil is not to be done in obedience. In all other matters, even if they do not seem good, do not compare yourselves with them or set yourselves above them in pride; but humbly submit to them and show due reverence.

You certainly ought to do this because they must render an account to God the judge for your souls, and they keep watch: that is, they watch in every respect, always watching—that is, they are concerned for you as those who must render an account for your souls, which they have received into their care. And because they strive to lead you rightly along the way of righteousness, [Col. 1688C] so that, when they bring you before Christ’s tribunal, they may not be accused of having led you wrongly, therefore obey them now, lest you too then be accused of having departed from the way which they commanded you to follow.

Therefore obey and submit to them, so that they may do this—that is, watch over you—with joy at your progress and not groan at your loss; for it is not advantageous to you that they should be grieved because of you. Leaders watch with joy when they see their subjects advancing in God’s word. For the farmer too labours with joy when he looks at a tree and sees its fruit, when he looks at the crop and sees its abundance bearing fruit. He sees that he has not laboured without cause, not bent his back without cause, not worn out his hands without cause, not endured cold [Col. 1688D] and heat without cause. So it is with spiritual farmers, that is, with prelates of the Church: they rejoice in their labour when they see those whose conduct they cultivate making progress. This is what he says: “that they may do this with joy and not groaning. For this is not advantageous to you.” He did not say, “This is not advantageous to them”; rather he said, “This is not advantageous to you.” For when those leaders are saddened by your evils, their very sadness is advantageous and beneficial to them, but it is not advantageous to you. Therefore let prelates and subjects alike work good in the Lord’s field, so that together they may rejoice in the reward.

> “Pray for us. For we are confident that we have a good conscience, desiring in all things [Col. 1689A] to conduct ourselves well. But I especially beseech you to do this, that I may more quickly be restored to you.”

The Apostle seeks the aid of their prayer, either that he may be freed from prison and return to preaching, or that, perfected by martyrdom, he may pass to Christ. “Pray,” he says, “for us,” using the plural number for the singular, asking that prayer be made either for himself or for those detained with him. And you ought to pray for us because we are confident that we have a good conscience. For conscience does not accuse us; therefore do not think anything unfavourable about us.

The Apostle was accused of neglecting his own people, but he showed that he had affection for all Jews and Gentiles. Some also said that he taught differently from the other apostles, and that he was an enemy of the Jewish law and temple, [Col. 1689B] because he rejected circumcision and carnal observances more strongly than the others. But he showed that he had a good conscience, that he did whatever he did from zeal to please God, and that he had not sinned in what he taught. “We are confident,” he says, “that we have a good conscience”; that is, we know certainly that our conscience does not rebuke us for what we have done or taught since we came to faith. And why? Because “we desire in all things to conduct ourselves well”; that is, we are not double-minded but single-minded. We are not willing to conduct ourselves well in some matters and not well in others, but well in all things. That is, we strive to live well not in part but wholly; therefore conscience does not reproach us.

I said that you should pray for us. But “I especially beseech you to do this,” [Col. 1689C] that is, to obtain by your prayers that I may more quickly be restored to you. That is, I especially beseech you to pray for me for your salvation rather than mine, because I ask that this be accomplished through your prayers: that, released sooner from prison, I may be restored not to myself but to you—that is, restored to my former office of preaching, so that travelling freely into different regions I may instruct both you and others more diligently.

> “Now may the God of peace, who brought again from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep in the blood of the eternal covenant, our Lord Jesus Christ, fit you for every good work, that you may do his will, working in you what is pleasing before him, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever and ever. [Col. 1689D] Amen.”

I have indeed thus far admonished you and urged patience and good works upon you; but may God, who is powerful, himself make you do what I have admonished. The God of peace, who gives his people peace and rest when he knows it fitting, calming all persecutions and assaults of vices, and after this life gives them the peace of eternal tranquillity when they have patiently endured adversities for his name—the God, I say, who brought again from the dead, that is, raised up, separating from the company of the dead, the great shepherd of the sheep: that is, him who feeds and preserves his sheep, namely all the elect souls.

For bishops and the other guardians of the Lord’s flock are lesser shepherds, because each feeds the part of the same flock of believers entrusted to him. [Col. 1690A] But this one is the greatest shepherd because he preserves and feeds the whole flock. He feeds them not only with the word of teaching, but also with his body and blood. Hence he is now said to be shepherd “in the blood of the eternal covenant,” because he feeds with the sacrament of his flesh and blood the sheep whom he redeemed. This blood confirms not a passing but an eternal covenant; that is, not the old law which passed away, but the new, which remains. The New Testament is called eternal because no other will succeed it, as the New succeeded the Old.

Or God brought Christ from the dead “in the blood of the eternal covenant,” because just as it is said to Christ through Zechariah: “You also, in the blood of your covenant, brought forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water” (Zech. 9), that is, from hell, [Col. 1690B] so Christ himself was brought forth from the dead in that same blood. For such was the power of his blood that it not only delivered the righteous who were held bound in hell, but also raised our Lord Jesus Christ himself from the dead.

May the God who does these things fit you—that is, make you fit and willing—in every good work, so that, acting well in all things, you may do and fulfil his will in deed. I say, he who works in you what is pleasing before him, because unless he works in you, you can do nothing that is pleasing in his sight. This is grace, which precedes and helps the mind, so that a person may add the service of his will and action; and this was said lest they should presume upon the powers of their free will and think that they could do these things well as though from themselves.

[Col. 1690C] May he thus work in you what pleases him, and this not through carnal observance of the law but through Jesus Christ, through whom, as mediator, all good things are given to us by the Father. To Christ be glory, not for a short time but for ages of ages—that is, for the eternal ages succeeding temporal ages. To him whom the Jews mocked in the passion belongs glory that endures not for a few days but for eternal ages. Amen: that is, truly.

> “But I beseech you, brothers, bear the word of consolation. For I have written to you very briefly.”

I have sent you this epistle; but lest it be wearisome to you, O brothers—that is, those for whom I care with brotherly love—I ask you to bear the word of consolation which [Col. 1690D] I have spoken to you in it, because the discourse of this epistle is consolatory, providing you comfort in tribulation lest you fail. And you ought to bear without weariness whatever I say in this letter, because I have written to you “very briefly,” that is, in few words throughout. For in all that I have discussed in it, what I have said is little, because much could be said concerning each individual point.

Here the excellent teacher teaches us by his own example to state what we think both very humbly and without wearisome prolixity. For he has thus far spoken much humbly to the Hebrews, but by humble exhortation he strives to appease them still more humbly, saying: “But I beseech you,” etc. Hence, if a disciple ever rightly understands something, let him infer how humbly he ought to speak to his teacher. If the teacher of the Gentiles, in matters which he preaches with authority, [Col. 1691A] humbly entreats his disciples, then let everyone infer from this that he should humbly tell those from whom he receives examples of good living what he understands well or better than they do—if Paul submitted himself to them in a humble voice, though he himself had raised them to life.

Care must also be taken concerning how much we speak, lest by speaking at too great length to one unable to bear much, we lead him into weariness. This is particularly fitting for the weak: they should hear few things, indeed, and such as they are able to grasp, but things which may pierce their mind with repentance and sorrow.

> “Know that our brother Timothy has been released; with him, if he comes sooner, I shall see you. Greet all your leaders and all the saints. [Col. 1691B] The brothers from Italy greet you. Grace be with all of you. Amen.”

Know our brother Timothy: know how great his holiness is and how much reverence is owed him. I mean Timothy, “released,” that is, setting out on the journey he wished; or released in order to preach, as he desired; [Col. 1692A] or perhaps freed from prison. “With him, if he comes sooner, I shall see you,” because if he hastens to come more quickly, I shall have the opportunity of going with him to you. In this promise he makes them attentive and more obedient, lest, if he comes, he find them disobedient to the admonition of this epistle and acting wrongly.

And then he says: “Greet all your leaders,” that is, the priests and others who preside over you in the Lord, “and all the saints,” that is, all the subjects who have received the sanctification of baptism. When he adds, “The brothers from Italy greet you,” he shows that he wrote from Italy. Moreover, in saying above, “I beseech you to do this, that I may more quickly be restored to you,” he made clear that he was held in chains while writing; and it is inferred that he sent the epistle from Rome, [Col. 1692B] where he was held in bonds. “Grace,” he says, “be with all of you,” so that through the help of grace you may be able to live well—you who could not please God through the law. May we too be made participants in that grace, that through it we may be justified and deserve to attain eternal life. Amen.

## In the Year of the Lord 1150: Hildebrand the Younger

[Col. 1691]

## Notice

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. III, p. 259)

Hildebrand the Younger, writer of commentaries on Matthew. The *Little Book on Contemplation*, published by E. Martène from a manuscript codex of the monastery of Himerad, about 500 years old, in vol. IX of the *Amplissima Collectio*, p. 1237, appears to be by the same Master Hildebrand.

[Col. 1691]

# The Little Book on Contemplation of Master Hildebrand

(Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. IX, p. 1237, from a Himerad manuscript codex about 500 years old.)

[Col. 1691C] From the Gospel reading of Matthew which begins, “When Jesus was born,” etc., where the faithful and devout visitation of the Lord Jesus by the blessed three kings is commended, three things present themselves to subtle investigation under grace’s guidance. When these are rightly and orderly distinguished, and each divided into three members—together making nine—[Col. 1692C] there may be found, though only by one who truly languishes with love for the beloved Jesus, the state and manner of true contemplation.

The first is the faithful and devout seeking of the child Jesus by the three kings; for he could not be sought except by faithful and devout persons. Thus you have: “Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying: Where is he who [Col. 1693A] has been born king of the Jews?” The second is the joyful and welcome finding of the same Lord Jesus, because truly it is wholly full of every joy to find and behold the maker of humanity as a human being. Of this it is said: “When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy; and entering the house they found the child.” The third is his humble and discerning adoration; for vows are not acceptable to God except those of humble and discerning souls. Hence it follows: “And falling down they worshipped him, and opening their treasures,” etc.

2. It should therefore be noted that seeking has desire, finding joy, and adoration with offering service. From the desire of seeking arises the joy of finding, and the joy of finding is followed by the service of adoration. Desire is [Col. 1693B] a certain movement of the rational soul, which it has in its concupiscible power. This movement is caused by the desired object, as the philosopher says: the desired object moves desire. The object of our desire ought to be none other than he who is wholly desirable, into whom even angels desire to look, and of whom the prophet says: “Behold, the Desired One of all nations shall come” (Hag. 2:8); and the Psalmist: “As the deer desires the springs of water, so my soul desires you, O God” (Ps. 41:2). If our mind’s desire has been caused and moved well and rightly by the desired object, namely God, it will appear to contain all things within itself.

3. First is the fervent and devout confidence of hope. For nothing is sought with desire unless it is truly hoped for; [Col. 1693C] and whatever is hoped for is desired and sought. Hope, suspended upon him because it concerns not present things but future things, must, if it is true, possess a sure expectation of itself, together with confidence of attaining him; otherwise it would not be true. The confidence of hope in attaining him must also have an inward stretching forth. This extension of hope toward what is hoped for, because it is delayed, afflicts the soul and keeps it restless about the business of seeking until it finds what is desired, as Augustine says: “Lord, you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.”

4. The second follows rightly: the anxious and restless exercise of the mind in seeking. For [Col. 1693D] the more desire is moved by the object desired or hoped for, the more the spirit is exercised in the business of seeking. Hence the Psalmist says: “My soul refused to be comforted” (Ps. 76:3), because I do not have present the one whom I seek and desire. “I remembered God and was delighted” (ibid.), namely in the hope of finding him, as blessed Bernard says: “Meanwhile, while his presence is delayed, memory is sweet.” And I was exercised in the office of seeking, and indeed my spirit failed, unable to endure the delay of such prolonged expectation. For truly, to a desiring soul nothing comes quickly enough; the desired object is never made present too swiftly.

This diligent exercise of the spirit seeking God is commended in the Song of Songs, where it is said: “I will arise and go about the city; [Col. 1694A] through the lanes and streets I will seek him whom my soul loves” (Song 3:2). For the bride, seeing that the bridegroom could by no means be found in the bed of the body and negligence, fervently extended herself into the exercise of diligent and laborious seeking. But because this restlessness of the soul is concerned not with many things but with the one thing which alone is necessary, and disdains to be occupied with outward and transitory things—which commonly hinder and draw back the mind that longs for eternal and enduring goods—the third is fittingly set down: contempt and forgetfulness of the world and of all worldly things.

5. For temporal and eternal things cannot be loved at the same time. Since, therefore, God is a good both eternal and supreme, both incomprehensible and unchangeable, [Col. 1694B] how can one who hastens to comprehend him incline himself to love something changeable? He alone, not for one person but for all, is sufficient. Let him alone be enough for you, without whom all things are nothing. Without him, nothing is for you not merely enough, but even anything at all. Who will grant me to be deprived of all things that are from him, and to be endowed eternally with him alone? There is nothing, Lord Jesus, that I should wish or ought to wish to possess if I do not possess you; without you nothing is pleasant to me, nothing abundant. It is better for me not to be than to be without you. May I will what you will, and not will what you do not will. You will that I should will you alone: may I never be able to will anything more. May my willing be free toward you, subject to nothing alien to you. Yet if I truly and effectually will you, I shall be unable to will anything outside you.

Sweetest [Col. 1694C] Jesus, let your sweetness, gentle and true, become sweet to me. Let the honeyed savor of your divinity flow into my soul; let it draw from my inmost heart everything that tastes of temporal things. Before the sweetness of your most longed-for vision, let every inclination toward passing delight become worthless to me. My soul has longed to desire you; if desiring you according to you is not enough, let it desire more of you, as much as it pleases. My soul has chosen suspension from the circuit or love of temporal things, O beloved Jesus, and my bones have chosen death. Draw me after you; do not leave me about myself. If you leave me, I shall sin; and I know certainly that, if I sin, you leave me. Therefore do not leave me, lest I sin; but if I sin, that is mine, not yours. But if I do not sin, it is yours, not mine. Act, gracious Jesus: [Col. 1694D] I place my whole self in the bosom of your mercy. From you, the Good, if you grant it, I can be good. Guard the good deposit. For I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that you are able to preserve my deposit unto that day.

Therefore one who seeks the Lord needs contempt for this world, and for all things that are in it and belong to it, as John says: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world” (1 John 2:15). And Paul says: “Forgetting what lies behind, I stretch forth toward what lies ahead” (Phil. 3:13). Whoever you are, then, who seek God with fervent hope and diligent exercise, if you are not less entangled in earthly occupations and affections for earthly things, then, just as you are shown not to possess an altogether true desire in seeking, so neither can you attain the fullness of finding.

[Col. 1695A]

6. Let us therefore turn the eyes of the mind toward the three matters set forth, which proceed from the movement of true desire; and it will readily appear that each rightly follows the other. For hope, through love of what is hoped for, stretches itself fervently toward seeking; diligent exercise of the mind furnishes perseverance in seeking; discriminating forgetfulness of temporal things removes an impediment to seeking. The first, namely hope, excludes distrust; the second, that is, earnest exercise, drives away negligence; the third, namely contempt for the world, utterly destroys every resistance.

Come, blessed Jesus, my hope, my expectation, my love: a word from me to you, a word concerning you, a word full of sorrow and misery. You who are the Word, the only-begotten of the unbegotten Father, made flesh for my sake; Word uttered from the Father’s heart; [Col. 1695B] Word whom God spoke once; Word through whom your heavenly Father has spoken to me in these last days: deign to hear the word of my heart, uttered toward you, the Word of God, in the fullness of desires. Hear and see that my soul is sad and troubles me, while it is said to me daily: “Where is your God?” I have nothing to answer; I fear that you are absent, and I do not feel you present. My heart burns; I desire to see my Lord. For where are my waiting and my patience? You are, Lord, my God—and what shall I do? I seek and do not find; I long and do not see; I follow and do not grasp. What is my strength, that I should endure? Or what is my end, that I should act patiently? What is sadder for my soul? What more miserable? [Col. 1695C] What more burdensome?

Do you think, Beloved, that my sadness will be turned into the joy of your vision? My misery into fellowship with your dwelling? My trouble into the play of possessing you? Speak to the heart of my soul. Speak, Lord, for your servant hears. I shall hear what you speak in me, Lord my God. Say to my soul: “I am your salvation.” Say further, Lord, and say it so that I may hear: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (Luke 15:31). Come, Word of God the Father: this is what I wished to hear. “I rejoiced at the things spoken to me.” Let this voice of yours sound in my ears. For truly this voice is sweet—indeed, sweeter than every voice of harpists playing upon their harps. May this blessed voice grow strong in the innermost parts of my soul, and there shall be nothing outside which I would wish to hear. It will be enough for me [Col. 1695D] if I know that you will say concerning me to those blessed servants and messengers of my joy: “Go and bring him to me.”

Yet I shall desire and hope that your word, full of every desire, may be fulfilled concerning me—the word which you spoke to your holy apostles: “I shall come and receive you to myself.” I myself who spoke: “Behold, I am here”; I shall come, I shall receive you, so that where I am you also may be. These pleasing promises and consolations of yours have gladdened my soul. Meanwhile, while you delay, I shall wait for you, although, if I speak as I feel, truly my exile has been prolonged exceedingly: dwelling, indeed, with the dwellers of Kedar, knowing and very frequently recalling that, just as the dwelling-place of those who rejoice is in you, so a valley of tears weighs upon me, a place of affliction torments me, and the shadow of death occupies me.

[Col. 1696A] Many are my causes of grief and sadness; but there is one cause of consolation and joy, if you sweetly and gently repeat more often to my soul that word—the good and sweet word: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.” Meanwhile, because I cannot know, and perhaps ought not to know, when I shall come and appear before your face—which indeed I desire to be hastened—although for me, Christ, to live is you and to die is gain, I shall console myself in these promises of yours, which exceed every desire; and I shall seek you joyfully, find you more joyfully, and grasp you most joyfully.

For in this life there is a certain possessing of you, full of grace, which is indeed followed by that possessing which shall be full of glory. Since, therefore, I do not reckon that I have yet comprehended, I shall follow on, if somehow I may comprehend. Thus, Lord my God, [Col. 1696B] I have placed all my hope in you; I have suspended in you the desire of my restless mind; for love of you I have despised the kingdom of the world and all the adornment of the age. Therefore do not put me to shame in my expectation, but grant that I may receive what I ask, find what I seek, and at last, as I knock, have opened to me the most longed-for inner chambers of your divinity.

Finally, concerning the three matters which I mentioned regarding the desire of seeking, although I could have adduced many authorities and examples, yet because it was not my intention to say much, let these few things suffice. It remains, therefore, to consider the second member of the division: the joy of finding.

7. But since joy, properly speaking, is one of the four affections of the soul which, according to Augustine, Bernard, and Boethius, are the seeds of vices [Col. 1696C] and virtues; and since, according to its name, it may be predicated generally of the state or distinction of a threefold joy—namely, that which belongs to this world and to the outward person alone; that which belongs to the spirit rejoicing in the Lord and to the inward person alone; and that which belongs to glory and the higher homeland: concerning the first you have in the Gospel of John, from the Lord’s words, “The world indeed shall rejoice” (John 16:20), etc.; concerning the third likewise there: “But I shall see you again, and your heart shall rejoice” (ibid., 22). Concerning the second, however, Proverbs says: “A heart which knows the bitterness of its own soul—no stranger shall mingle in its joy” (Prov. 14:10). And Ecclesiasticus: “There is no delight beyond the joy of the heart” (Ecclus. 30:16).

[Col. 1696D] It is neither the subject of my present material nor my purpose to treat of the first, because that would presently be superfluous, nor of the third, because it is too lofty. But I intend to deal with the second, because this is necessary for estimative contemplation.

8. With Blessed Bernard I call “estimative contemplation” that which stands between dispensative and speculative contemplation. Dispensative contemplation is that by which one who loves God administers the outward senses in the business of contemplation, and makes good use of them for the purpose of meriting God. Estimative contemplation is that by which the powers of the soul, detached from the body yet attached to bodily organs, and not obscured by phantasms, wholly raise themselves to the knowledge and love of God. It is this of which we now speak. Speculative contemplation is that by which a person longs, as far as it is granted, to behold God in himself and through appearance, [Col. 1697A] and to be wholly united with him, as far as possible. It is given very rarely, and only to the perfect at once; it belongs rather to the homeland than to the way, and can never exist except in true ecstasy.

9. The first is motive, the second cognitive, the third affective. According to Blessed Bernard, the first labors, the second worships, the third tastes. The first belongs to beginners, the second to those making progress, the third to those who have, as it were, already arrived and are wholly pleasing. The first finds God, the second knows him, the third possesses him. Yet the second does not exist without the first, nor the third without the first and second. For the first raises the mind toward the beloved; the second directs it to him; the third admits it into him.

But although I have defined the middle kind, namely the estimative, according to the manner in which I propose to treat it, [Col. 1697B] it might nevertheless be more conveniently and simply described, for simpler readers, from the force of its name: it is that which is found in the exercise of the apprehensive and motive powers of the rational soul—namely reason, will, free choice, and the rest—insofar as they are proportioned to and attached to bodily organs. Speculative contemplation, on the other hand, is that of the powers of the soul which have no obligation to the body: the intellect unmixed with phantasms, and synderesis. For wayfarers may sometimes possess this latter; the former, however, only rarely, and only those who have attained. The signs and properties of these contemplations, perhaps, if God grants it, we shall explain later more clearly.

10. Let us return, then, to our subject. And certainly [Col. 1697C] since there are three motive powers of the soul—the rational, the concupiscible, and the irascible—according to which the soul will indeed be endowed and rewarded; and since philosophers attribute the second and third to the sensitive soul, while John Damascene and most others place will in the rational soul in place of the concupiscible faculty, and spirit in place of the irascible; since reason also often stands for intellect; and since the joy of the inward person is a certain pleasant affection caused by these three powers: we may rightly say that three things are required for such joy—namely, a godlike illumination of the intellect, a good-form devotion of the will, and a light-form and pleasant exultation of the spirit. In the intellect, godlikeness; in the will, goodness of form; in the spirit, tranquil and peaceful light-likeness.

[Col. 1697D] For how can you rejoice in the beloved Jesus whom you have found, or possess signs of having found him, unless he has been understood godlike, according as it has been granted you from above, willed in a good-like manner, and tasted in a light-like manner? For if you understand and know him keenly, you can will nothing other than him; and if you will him in a good-like manner, you will desire nothing other than to taste him in a light-like manner. I call that intellect godlike which is obscured by no cloud of sensible things; that will good-like which delights in no changeable good; that spirit light-like which is disturbed or troubled by no accidental evil. Such are the intellect, will, and spirit of God and of those who enjoy him. [Col. 1698A] You will find these three commended in various places, if you understand rightly, in Dionysius’s *Hierarchy* and in the book *On the Divine Names*.

Therefore, if you wish to rejoice with him and in him, you ought to give yourself to him alone, to see him alone, to taste and savor him alone: to give yourself over in order to know, to see in order to will, to taste in order to be pleased. Hence the Psalmist: “Be still, and see” (Ps. 45:11), etc. And again: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33:9). Therefore, when true contemplation is suspended upon God, you know and understand him alone; you will and desire him alone; you taste and savor him alone. You behold nothing passing, embrace nothing superficial, fear nothing contrary. You flee every counterfeit glory of the world, despise every recollection of deceptive good, forget every injury done. For these [Col. 1698B] and many others are signs of the true finding of the Lord Jesus, and of the pleasant exultation over him when found. Yet I shall set down still more on this matter.

11. Since, therefore, as was shown above in part, contemplation is the sharp vision of the mind, suspended with wonder at the spectacle of wisdom, the first member of this division is rightly placed as illuminated understanding. Since from such understanding there properly follows devotion of a good will, which is a sweet affection extended toward God, the second is fittingly the good-form of the will. For these two indeed require a tranquil and placid affection toward everything that belongs to God; thus the third is rightly placed as the serene and light-form exultation of the spirit.

[Col. 1698C] The intellect, illuminated in a godlike manner, because it is the apprehension of the true good in itself, seizes and draws you into God and makes you know him. The will, affected in a good-like manner, makes you love him; for love is an act of the will. The peaceful exultation of the spirit causes you to reject everything contrary to the knowledge and love of God. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). And immediately follows: “Blessed are the peacemakers” (ibid., 9). For neither God without one’s neighbor, nor one’s neighbor without God, can truly be known and loved.

[Col. 1698D]

12. Let us return, then, to the first part of this love, and in it let us endeavor to contemplate God, according as he himself grants it. Who will grant me, sweet Jesus, that you may be my brother, nursing at my mother’s breasts, so that I may find you outside and kiss you, and no one may now despise me? (Song 8:1.) May I find you outside through true knowledge; may I kiss you through full love; may no one despise me because of a compassionate affection shared with all. I am outside, Lord—outside I shall find you, as you deign to grant it. Behold, I stand at the door and knock. Lord, Lord, open to me: glorious things have been said to me concerning you. As I have heard, I desire to see. Within, with you, is what I seek outside. I have not yet entered—alas, alas!—into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, unto the house of God.

[Col. 1699A] Meanwhile, with you favorable to me, I shall endeavor, remaining as far as may lawfully and possibly be in the outer watch, to understand and know you. Send forth, Lord, wisdom from the throne of your greatness, that it may be with me and labor with me, so that I may know you and what is pleasing before you. For I know that no intellect can comprehend you fully: who you are in nature, what you are in grace, how great in glory. Incomprehensible in nature, immeasurable in grace, unthinkable in glory. In nature beautiful, in grace abundant, in glory precious. In nature white and ruddy; in grace lovable and delightful; in glory overflowing and abundant. In nature white with the brightness of divinity, ruddy with the redness of humanity assumed and suffered; in grace lovable and delightful. For grace has been poured forth upon your lips—indeed, poured out from your lips—and your name is oil poured out, namely the oil of grace and joy; therefore the young women have loved you. Precious in glory: for if a man gave all the substance of his house for the acquisition of your glory, he would despise it as though it were nothing.

[Col. 1699B] I have rightly called you incomprehensibly beautiful, whose beauty sun and moon marvel at. Your works, indeed, are beautiful, but not as you are. And all that heavenly and blessed household of yours marvels too, gazing with unsated eyes and longing upon your ineffable beauty, crying in wonder: “Truly, my Lord, you are wonderful, and your face is full of graces.” And surely also your most blessed mother, with a voice of rejoicing: “Behold,” she says, “you are beautiful, my beloved son, and fair.” Indeed, turning even to the companions of her glory, she reverently glories that she is the mother of such and so great a son, saying: “I am the mother of fair love,” etc. (Ecclus. 24:24).

[Col. 1699C] Not only this: your heavenly Father also, delighting most joyfully in you as in the image of his most divine glory, sounds forth most sweetly: “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased” (Matt. 17:5). O surpassing beauty, in which is reflected the splendor of the Father’s glory, which is the brightness of eternal light and the spotless mirror of the divine majesty; in the contemplation of whom Father and mother delight, between whom you sit, differing from neither, God and man: God from God the Father; man from a human mother; the same Son, God with God and from God the Father; the Word of the Father, God; the art of the Father, God; the wisdom of the Father, God; the image of the Father, God; the power of the Father, God.

Being such and so great, so beautiful and so fair, you feed and refresh the angels and citizens of your heavenly court delightfully with the glory of your beauty; you refresh earthly people and the children of humankind, guilty and miserable, by the grace and mercy of your compassion. Who, O most beautiful of the children of men, would not delight to behold you, so delightful and so desirable? How shall I not rejoice when I see you thus—indeed, I do not know how to say what you are? Who will grant that the desired day may come, so that I may be allowed to see? Who will grant me that I may die for you by whatever kind of death, so that I may somehow gain you, so beloved and so chosen? Every pain, every misery, every sadness is joy to me, for the sake of meriting you alone.

[Col. 1699D] Meanwhile, merciful Jesus, may the splendor of your brightness illumine my heart’s inmost recesses and drive away every darkness of unbelief and impiety. While you shine upon me, let nothing foul, nothing dark, remain in me. Grant that I may and may wish to behold and contemplate you keenly, as far as is possible to a mortal; for there is no other light than you by which I can be enlightened so as to see you, and, seeing you, rejoice. For the best manner of seeing will be that, when I see you, I shall lack nothing, content in you for everything that I wish.

[Col. 1700A] In you, through you, it will be granted me to see whatever is from you. The brightness shining forth in you will reveal to me all that you are and everything that is from you. I cannot, I say, any more than I can satisfy myself from myself, enlighten myself from myself; for in your light we shall see light: in your light, Son of God, we shall see the light of God the Father; and we shall see the light of the Holy Spirit of God. Yet we shall not see three lights of God, but shall see, in three distinct persons, one undivided light, God: your Father, light and God; you, the Father’s Son, light and God; and the Holy Spirit, [Col. 1700B] proceeding naturally and equally from that same God the Father and from you, light and God. For, not only enlightened in a godlike manner by your light, shall we see you, the divine uncreated light; but also, both now and then, we shall see how greatly the illumination of your countenance is upon us, and to what degree it has made us created lights shining before the Lord.

Since, therefore, I hope—I speak it with your peace—that “the light of your countenance has been marked upon us,” and that you have given joy in my heart, I have said these things concerning the beauty of both your divine and your human nature, Jesus Christ, adornment and beauty of my soul, although not as worthily, fittingly, or fully as I desired. But, with you favorable to me, I shall speak more fully and joyfully before the throne of your glory, when I am made a contemplator, a “templator” [reading uncertain], and a possessor of your divinity, [Col. 1700C] insofar as I now see more keenly and happily.

I shall also behold you, the Word of God, full of grace and truth, from whose fullness we all have received; and I shall delight in the remembrance of your innumerable graces and benefits. I neither wish nor ought to be ungrateful to you, knowing that a benefit received by an unworthy person does not make that benefit welcome to its giver unless the recipient himself renders it so. O, O, O—how immeasurable a grace it is, most merciful Jesus, that you, one living and true God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, created me, when I was nothing, in the image of your one supreme divinity; that you decreed me to be a fellow citizen of angels, a dweller in heaven, [Col. 1700D] and a citizen of your ineffable joys.

Alas for sorrow! Made by you, for you, and according to you, I did not remain with you; but I withdrew from you, abandoning and losing you. Since I unjustly abandoned your justice, that same justice judged me cast out from you; nothing remained to me but guilt and punishment. And not undeservedly: by nature deformed through the forbidden—and truly accursed—food of those first parents; emptied of grace; stripped of glory; not only unhappily deprived of so great a blessedness, but also miserably exiled and assigned to everlasting punishments. Alas, miserable me! There was none to redeem, none to recognize, none to seek my soul.

But you at last, Father of mercies and God of all consolation, [Col. 1701A] unable in your wrath to restrain your mercies, because you are truly rich and abundant in mercy, did not allow me to be subject eternally to such sufferings. Acknowledging yourself as Creator and not refusing to be Redeemer, remaining what you were—God, Son of God—you became what you were not: man, son of man. Thus you restored, by the reproach of your cross and death, to the authority of the Father’s glory, me—the son of ruined humans through the merits of the first transgressing humans; made a companion of demons, servant of vices, fuel for everlasting fires.

O my Jesus, a death worthy of my death, by which, lest I should die to you, you willed to die! I would altogether have died, unless you had died for me. The fault of my death gave you cause of death: how, then, will you not be the cause of love for me, when I was for you the occasion of such bitter sorrow? My love brought upon you causes of pain: how will your pain not furnish me causes of love? If, in loving me, you had not suffered for me, I could not, in suffering for you, have loved you; nor is your pain without love, nor my love without pain. The more violent was your pain as you died for me upon the cross, the more ardent surely will be my love as I recall your pain.

[Col. 1701B] The water flowing from the side of my beloved, who on the cross binds me in most powerful and vehement embraces; the blood springing from his heart; the spirit departing from his body—these have become for me the means of knowing that no pain and love are like your pain and love. May those pains of your most holy Passion, most loving Jesus, and those rose-red bruises of your most venerable wounds, always cling to my affections. May they be present to my senses; may they be to me the material of continual pain and love; may they provoke me to love you, stir me to praise you, and assist me in meriting you.

O wondrous condescension of your compassion toward me! I was nothing, and you made me—and not merely some thing, but your image. I was evil, and you remade me—not merely for some good, but for contemplating with the holy angels the delightful vision of your supreme divinity. [Col. 1701C] Nor, content with these things, you poured your whole self into me and retained nothing of yourself for yourself. Having become man for my sake, you gave yourself to me as the dearest companion in the exile of my pilgrimage; as the most effective price upon the cross of redemption; as the sweetest food upon the altar of spiritual refreshment; and you will be for me, indeed, in my departure, the most desired viaticum; in my journey, the safest protection; and in heaven, the happiest reward.

[Col. 1701D] That supreme and divine power by which you preside in heaven and command the angels, condescending to me, you extend yourself as brother and companion; you weigh yourself out as a price; you bestow yourself as a drink. And, that I may speak somewhat more fully, as your grace permits me to feel and understand, about the dispensation of your most abundant goodness: you deign to show me such compassion that, wondrously and ineffably, in the very sweetest hour of your immolation, at the word of your priest you become for me and to me priest and sacrifice, guest and banquet, food and feeder, gift and giver.

O truly venerable sacrifice of my redemption, by which the only-begotten Son of God is joined to my soul in a wondrous union; the Father is reconciled; the Holy Spirit is propitiated; the heavens are opened; angels are made companions to me; the prayers and merits of the saints are shared with me; sins are forgiven; the enemies of my salvation are destroyed; virtues are given; gifts are heaped up; rewards are multiplied; and finally an utterly full abundance of every good is supplied!

[Col. 1702A] O living bread descended from heaven, indeed formed by the hand of the Holy Spirit in the womb of the glorious Virgin, baked upon the altar of the cross by the fire of passion, which you, God, prepare in your sweetness for the poor upon the table of your holy altar as a most delightful banquet, possessing every delight and every savor of sweetness: when my soul has loved it, it cannot but be gracious; when it has touched it, beautiful; when it has tasted it, delightful; when it has received it, glorious!

[Col. 1702B] O truly blessed worthy taster of such a banquet, in whose blessed administration and reception the whole Trinity glories; whom that blessed heavenly household serves with wonder and reverence; by whom the souls of those triumphant in heaven are honored, those still fighting on earth are aided, and those suffering in purgatorial torments are freed! This is my Passover, good Jesus, which with desire I have desired to eat with you until I die; and, made already a guest of the heavenly table, may I eat it new in the kingdom of your Father: namely, no longer beneath the veil of the sacrament, but without any covering of a veil.

And, O most precious blood, flowing most abundantly with rosy color from the lily-white body of my beloved dying for me upon the cross: lest your outpouring should afford me no benefit if I descended [Col. 1702C] into corruption, and lest I should be unable to remain in the perfection jointly received by the benefit of redemption, because I sin daily, you are daily poured out through the ministry of priests for the remission of my sins. Moreover, when you grant that I receive you, you enter into my soul with such fullness of divine gifts that I can no longer know what I lack for sufficiency. For, having given me drink from the torrent of divine delight, you have so enriched me with riches, delights, and heavenly joys, that, now borne above myself, I sometimes seem to myself to be admitted into a certain unfamiliar affection, turned toward I know not what sweetness. If it is perfected in me, I do not know what it will be which this life will not be. Meanwhile, suspended in the desire of that sweetness, I almost wholly fail through weariness at the delay!

[Col. 1702D] O wondrous sweetness of the precious cup! O holy fruitfulness of the delectable draught! O surpassing sweetness of noble blood! Truly my soul has thirsted for you; and the more fittingly and reverently it drinks you, the more ardently it thirsts. For when you flow into it, you cleanse it that it may be worthy of you; adorn it that it may please you; strengthen it lest it perish; intoxicate it lest it fail; sustain it that it may advance; delight it that it may cling to you—until, led into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, unto the house of God, it sees the beloved face to face and enjoys him in his full and wondrous sweetness.

Thanks to you, beloved Jesus, who, though Creator and Redeemer, do not refuse to be the giver of such a banquet. Truly blessed is the banquet in which you give me your whole self and nothing other than yourself; and, entering into me, you transform and change me, and by so wondrous and sweet a union connect and join me to yourself, making me one spirit with you. What then? “Why are you sad, O my soul, and why do you trouble me?” (Ps. 41:12.) Why do you complain of the absence of your bridegroom? What if he is more present than you are present to yourself? He is certainly with you, within you, beneath you, around you, above you. He does not come empty, for he is full of grace and truth. He brings grace, which empties out your guilt; truth, by which he enlightens ignorance.

[Col. 1703A] What more, then, ought he to have done for you and has not done? It is no longer possible to say: “Why, Lord, have you withdrawn far away? Why have you turned away your face?” (Ps. 10:1.) Behold, he is with you. He does not depart from you unless perhaps you depart from him; he does not turn away if you do not turn yourself away. Say, say, my soul; rejoice and say: “I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine.” Embrace him with sweetest and strongest affections, and hold him whom you have. Make use of him as you please; strive, hasten; ascend, enter into the beloved, and he will show you the immeasurable beauty of his nature, the sweetness of grace, the fullness of glory. You will see and overflow; you will marvel and be enlarged. You will see him, your mind divinely illuminated; you will overflow in him, sweetly affected; you will marvel, yourself sublimely exalted through him; you will be enlarged in him, enriched in many ways.

Therefore, O my soul, you will call yourself blessed if you are grateful to your most beloved bridegroom for all these things, and do not fall away from the graces received or render yourself unworthy of graces yet to be received. Meanwhile exult and rejoice in the bridegroom whom you have on earth in the sacrament, and whom you shall possess and see in heaven [Col. 1703C] without a veil.

Act now, most merciful Jesus: what return worthy of these benefits of yours shall I make? What shall I render to you for all that you have rendered to me? I know certainly that, just as I am nothing without you, so I cannot merit you without you. [Col. 1704A] Whatever benefit you bestow upon me is not owed but gratuitous.
