To deem the unworthy worthy belongs not to justice but to grace. It redounds to your glory, mighty one, not to punish the unjust when you are able. You show yourself more merciful by sparing the impious than by punishing them. By giving yourself as a benefit to one who does not merit it, you have acted generously; you will act more mercifully with me when you exact from me the service owed. If you decree to save me, you do not contend with me in judgment: for if you sit in judgment and grant no place to mercy, I shall cry out my miseries forever; but if you do grant it, I shall sing your mercies forever.

Behold, now I bind my soul to you by the bond of your sacrament, reckoning myself secure if you fortify me with the new and eternal blood of the covenant. Embrace one joined to you by the covenant of faith; [Col. 1704B] guard one fed, strengthened, and sanctified by your most sacred body. Look upon one made to drink, adorned, and sealed with your most sweet blood. Let there be nothing that drives you from one who follows you, nothing that tears away one who clings to you and trusts most fully in the name of your glory, which is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

13. Moreover, I have said these things briefly for the commendation of God’s grace, so that you, loving reader, may have words to warn and advance you toward the joy of the inward person. For the things which I have set down, spoken attentively and meditated upon intently, together with other similar matters which study and practice will discover and unction will suggest, ought to be yours in the exercise of estimative contemplation. For what inward imagination does for the more perfect, outward utterance commonly does for the less [Col. 1704C] perfect; because what breath does to charcoal, utterance does to devotion.

## Aimon, Abbot of Saint-Pierre-sur-Dive, and Peter the Monk, in the Year of the Lord 1150

[Col. 1703]

## Notice

(*Literary History of France*, vol. XII, p. 357)

### I.

Aimon, a religious of Saint-Pierre-sur-Dive, in the diocese of Séez, succeeded Richard as abbot of the same monastery. [Note: [Col. 1703] Mabillon, *Annals*, book LXXVIII, no. 67; *Pious Neustria*, p. 503.] The year of his election is uncertain, but it must fall between 1140, when Richard began the rebuilding of his church, and 1143, when we first see Aimon exercising abbatial functions. Two years after the latter date, he completed [Col. 1705] the building begun by his predecessor. The other particulars of his life are unknown; its end has likewise remained forgotten. The Chronicle of Robert of Mont tells us only that Warin had succeeded him by 1150. [Note: [Col. 1705] Mabillon, *ibid.*, book LXXX, no. 46.]

We have from him a long letter to his brethren at Teuksburi [Note: [Col. 1705] Mabillon, ibid., book LXXVIII, no. 67], now in the county of Gloucester in England. Its purpose was to urge them to give thanks to God for a new form of devotion that had taken hold of the people of Normandy—a form so extraordinary, it was said, that one would seek examples of it in vain in past ages. This devotion, which had arisen at Chartres, consisted in men and women, nobles and commoners alike, without distinction of sex or rank, dedicating themselves to the building of churches. In every diocese of Normandy there was a confraternity of these devotees, whose patroness was the Blessed Virgin and over which a devout person presided. To enter it, one had to have confessed, received penance, and been reconciled with one’s enemies. This last condition was very important in an age when nobles almost always had arms in hand in order to destroy one another.

As soon as the brethren learned that a church was to be built somewhere, they went there in a body and performed not merely the work of laborers but even that of draught animals. “What an unheard-of wonder,” says our author, “to see tyrants, men powerful in the world, puffed up by their birth and riches; women accustomed to a soft and luxurious life—fastening themselves to a cart with harnesses and themselves carrying, in place of animals, wine, wheat, lime, timber, stones, sand, and in general every food-supply and every material necessary for the construction of the sacred building. Yet still more astonishing is this: amid these labours, in which sometimes a thousand persons, men and women, draw the same cart together—for such is the weight of the load placed upon it—there reigns so profound a silence that not the slightest word or murmur is heard; so that, without the testimony of one’s eyes, one would think that there was not a soul in the whole multitude. When they halt on the road, then they speak; but of what? Of their sins, which they confess publicly, with tears and prayers to obtain their forgiveness. Then the priests address these penitents, exhorting them to stifle hatreds, banish dissensions, remit debts, and strengthen among themselves the bonds of unity and peace. Is anyone found hardened enough not to wish to forgive his enemies, or to refuse submission to the counsels given him by the priests? Immediately he is detached from the cart, his offering is removed from it as impure, and he himself is expelled with disgrace from the holy society.”

The author then describes various miracles by which God made known that He approved this devotion. After that he relates in what order the brethren proceeded to these labours. “When the faithful people,” he says, “have set out at the sound of trumpets and preceded by banners, they continue their journey with the most remarkable ease, without either the height of steep mountains or the depth of waters encountered before them causing the least delay. You would think you saw the Hebrews crossing the Jordan under Joshua’s leadership when our pilgrims cross a river lying in their way, so confidently do they enter it and so readily reach the farther bank. Indeed, several of them affirm that, when they were at the port of Sainte-Marie, the waves of the sea coming toward them suddenly stopped, so as to leave them free to pass … Having arrived at the place where the church is to be built, they form an enclosure around it with their carts, in order to establish a kind of spiritual camp, where, throughout the following night, the army keeps watch, singing hymns and spiritual songs. On each cart candles and lamps are lighted, after the infirm and sick have been placed upon it; relics of the saints are brought to them in order to procure relief for them. Prayers are offered for them, and processions are held, the clergy at their head and the people following, to ask God and His blessed Mother for the healing of their ailments.”

Aimon concludes his account by saying that this observance had passed from the church of Chartres into the territory of Saint-Pierre-sur-Dive, where it had been confirmed by a great number of wonders; from there it spread through almost all Normandy, but it had occupied especially the places dedicated to the Mother of Mercy. It was through such assistance that the church of Saint-Pierre-sur-Dive was raised. If facts so incredible were attested by Aimon alone, criticism would find it difficult to yield. But Hugh of Amiens, metropolitan of Normandy, gives them the same testimony [Note: [Col. 1705] Mabillon, ibid., no. 66] in a letter to be presented under his entry. Ralph de Diceto attests the same thing under the year 1144.

Suger, who was building the church of Saint-Denis at the same time, reports something similar in speaking of the manner in which the columns destined for that building were drawn from the quarries of Pontoise. We have a translation of Aimon’s letter, published at Caen in a duodecimo volume in 1671 by Dom Jean-Bernard Planchette (not Blanchet, as Père Le Long writes [Note: [Col. 1705] *Bibl. Fr.*, p. 253]); but Aimon’s original text has not yet appeared. Dom Mabillon, who gave the extracts just reported, had promised to insert it in the appendix to the sixth volume of his *Annals*. This undertaking was not fulfilled by Dom Martène, editor of that volume.

Our author is also credited with the Martyrology of Saint-Pierre-sur-Dive, which remains in manuscript.

## II.

Under Aimon’s government there lived a religious named Peter who practised versification. At the advice of Milon Crispin, monk of Bec, mentioned above, he composed in heroic verse a historical eulogy of the first seven abbots of that monastery. It is the only work of his pen that has reached us. It was published by Dom Martène in the sixth volume of his great Collection (p. 93). The seventh abbot celebrated by our author is Roger de Bailleul, whose rule began in 1149. He speaks of him as still alive and, without entering into detail about his deeds, is content to praise his good qualities. Dom Ruinart esteemed Peter’s versification. In some manuscripts Peter is called *Petrus Augiensis*, because the abbey of Saint-Pierre-sur-Dive lay in the district of Auge in Normandy.

[Col. 1707]

## Aimon’s Letter to the Brethren Living at Totesberia in England

(Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictines*, book LXXVIII, no. 67.)

[Col. 1707A] From the year of Christ 1040, when the monastery of Blessed Mary in the town of Saint-Pierre-sur-Dive had been begun, the basilica had not yet been completed, down to the time when Abbot Aimon, successor of Richard of l’Aigle, put the finishing hand to it. When his design was understood, the townspeople of Dive and the surrounding peoples, stirred by the piety of the people of Chartres [Note: [Col. 1707] See the letter of Hugh, bishop of Rouen, to Theodoric of Amiens, below, under Hugh. EDITOR], not only commoners but nobles also, of every sex and age, themselves conveyed from afar, in carts and in complete silence, a mass of stones, timber, and sand, without any help from horses or oxen.

Aimon, the abbot who presided over the work, should be heard on this matter in the little book on this subject which he wrote to his brethren living at Totesberia (*Tuttebery*) in England, in order to encourage them to give thanks to God, who, amid so great a corruption of the age, established [Col. 1707B] a new kind of piety, a piety hitherto unheard of in all ages. For who has ever seen, or heard in all generations past, tyrants, princes powerful in the world, swollen with honours and riches, noble-born men and women, submitting proud and haughty necks, fastened with harnesses to carts, and drawing like brute animals to Christ’s refuge carts laden with wine, wheat, oil, lime, stones, timber, and other things necessary either for the uses of life or for the building of a church?

But still more wonderful is what the same author adds: “In drawing,” he says, “it is marvellous to see that, although sometimes a thousand or more men or women are fastened to a cart—for the mass is so great, the machine so large, and the load imposed so heavy—yet they proceed in such silence that no voice, indeed no whisper, is heard; and unless you saw it with your eyes, you would suppose that no one was present in so great a multitude. But when they halt on the road, nothing is heard except confession of sins and humble, pure prayer to God for the obtaining of forgiveness of offences. There, while the priests preach peace, hatreds are soothed, discords driven away, debts remitted, and unity of hearts restored. But if anyone has advanced so far into evil that he refuses to forgive one who has sinned against him, or to obey the priests in what he is piously admonished, his offering is immediately cast down from the cart as unclean, and he himself is separated, with much shame and disgrace, from the fellowship of the sacred people.”

This devotion of the faithful seemed so pleasing and acceptable to God that, at their prayers and the invocation of Blessed Mary, countless miracles occurred and sinners were converted to repentance. [Col. 1708A] “There,” Aimon says, “at the prayers of the faithful you may see all kinds of sick persons weakened by diverse ailments rise healthy from the carts upon which they had been placed; the mute open their mouths in praise of God; and those vexed by demons recover sounder minds. You may see priests of Christ, presiding over individual carts, exhorting all to repentance, confession, tears, and the resolution of a better life; and people prostrate on the ground and leaning upon their whole bodies, kissing the earth for a long time; old men together with young men and tiny children crying out to the Mother of the Lord and directing especially to her sobs and sighs from their inmost hearts, together with words of confession and praise.”

The same author explains the order in which all advanced to the work as follows: “But when the faithful people—to return to what I had begun—have taken to the road at the blare of trumpets and the raising of banners going before them, the matter proceeds, wonderful to say, with such ease that nothing delays them on their journey: neither the steepness of mountains nor the depth of intervening waters. Rather, as we read of that ancient people of the Hebrews that they entered the Jordan in their companies, so, when each comes to a river to be crossed, they immediately enter it directly, with the Lord leading them, without hesitation. Indeed, it is faithfully asserted that the waves of the sea, at the place called the Port of Saint Mary, came toward them and stood still while they were crossing … When they have reached the church, the carts are arranged round about it like a spiritual camp, and throughout the following night watches are observed by the whole host in hymns and songs. Then candles [Col. 1708C] and lamps are lit on each cart; then the infirm and weak are placed upon each; then the pledges—that is, relics—of the saints are brought for their aid; then the offices of processions are performed by priests and clerics, the people likewise following most devoutly and earnestly imploring together the mercy of the Lord and of His blessed Mother for the restoration of the weak.”

All these things appear so new and singular that I have thought them worth reporting at somewhat greater length. “The rite of this sacred institution,” says the same author, “was begun at the church of Chartres, then confirmed in ours by innumerable miracles; finally it flourished far and wide through nearly all Normandy, and especially occupied the several places dedicated to the Mother of Mercy.” Something similar occurred, according to Suger's testimony, in extracting from the quarry of Pontoise immense columns for the construction of the new basilica of Saint-Denis. [Col. 1709A] Thus the basilica of Blessed Mary at Dive was finished and brought to its completion; it remains even today, inferior to scarcely any sacred building in the country.

[Col. 1709]

## Deeds of the Seven Abbots of Bec, by Peter of Dive

(Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. VI, col. 93, from two manuscripts: one from Bec, the other belonging to the Queen of Sweden.)

### Preliminary Observation

Two ancient codices supplied us with the metrical account of the deeds of the first seven abbots of Bec, composed by Peter of Dive: one, from Bec, was most obligingly copied for us by our colleague Dom Richard Houssaye; the other, belonging to the Queen of Sweden, was discovered at Rome by Mabillon. We compared its transcript with the Bec codex.

The author, Peter of Dive—that is, a monk of the monastery of Saint Peter above the Dive in the diocese of Sées—was also called Peter of Auge, after the district of Auge where that monastery is situated. When he had at some time lodged as a guest with our monks of Bec, he undertook this work at the urging of the most noble Milon Crispin, monk and cantor of Bec. Moreover, the codex of the Queen of Sweden contains, together with the aforesaid deeds, the Chronicle of Bec, previously published by Acheri at the end of Lanfranc’s works.

Peter of Dive writes thus in verse concerning the first builders and chief masters of Bec.

[Col. 1709B]

1. Since Bec has now begun to exist,  
from whom or through whom it first came into being,  
by what men it was nobly founded,  
and by what persons enriched and made illustrious;  
how many abbots preceded, who they were,  
and for what length of time they ruled and fostered Bec—  
these things I have resolved to sketch in metrical verse,  
so that they may be marked in brief speech and in such order.

Not because I should be judged presumptuous for this work:  
rather, I have often been driven to it by the repeated urging  
of Lord Milon Crispin,  
who with all his wishes likewise pressed for it.

Having thus touched upon these matters and placed them at the beginning,  
I shall undertake this work, though unequal to it in strength.  
May that same Spirit, who makes infants’ tongues eloquent,  
[Col. 1709C] now be present with me as I hasten to it.

### Saint Herluin, First Abbot of Bec

2. In the year one thousand, three tens, and four besides,  
when God Himself brought forth from a mother’s womb  
the Word of the Father, our body, and shone upon the world,  
when William the Elder subdued  
the swelling necks of the Normans and ruled over them,  
there was a certain noble and prudent man, great of heart,  
as appears in the monastic construction of Bec.  
He was called Herluin from the sacred font.  
God inspiring him and the fear of death spurring him on,  
though he had been especially vigorous in many campaigns  
and highly honoured among his own men,  
and was therefore sufficiently esteemed among the foremost of his country,

he despised the world, now applauding, compliant, and favourable to him,  
[Col. 1710B] and immediately withdrew himself.  
Made a monk and touched by the holy breath,  
with Heribert, bishop of the city of Lisieux,  
cutting his hair and at the same time giving him the cowl,  
he at once gave himself and all that was his to the church  
which he himself had earlier built on his paternal estate,  
not far from the river called Bec,  
from which the place itself thereafter took the name Bec.

Having associated with himself very many brethren,  
they strove more strictly to become fit for blessedness,  
keeping watch with sweet hymns and ample praises,  
subduing their bodies by rough garments and scanty fare;  
eating raw herbs and drinking water,  
with bread sometimes added, made of rye;  
reading often, speaking little according to a fixed rule,  
[Col. 1710C] avoiding evil and following what is right along the straight path;  
moreover approving the commands of Paul the Teacher,  
and constantly working with their own hands at whatever they did.

Such, small, humble, and very lowly,  
was the beginning and first movement of Bec.  
There was no murmuring there, no deceit, nor bitter wrath;  
but within was abundant peace and marvellous concord.

### Lanfranc Comes to Bec from Italy

3. While they thus lived their hidden life within,  
their fame gradually began to spread.  
It now rose from the bottom of the valley to the heights.  
Wherefore many, stirred and summoned by it,  
came from regions known and remote alike;  
they sought Bec and gathered there,  
submitting themselves to Father Herluin’s rule.

[Col. 1711A] Among them was a great man, gentle as a lamb,  
born in Italy, in the city called Pavia;  
not low in lineage, of noble birth and family;  
a magnificent rhetorician, a teacher known everywhere,  
whose name was Lanfranc, sufficiently renowned  
among the French, Italians, and Greeks as well.  
Through disputing in learned studies and teaching marvels,  
he had visited cities and travelled through regions.  
He was famous among all, peerless because rare—  
for Tully says that all excellent things are rare.

Seeing all these things as vain and superfluous,  
and because the world passes away, together with all seen in it,  
Lanfranc, inflamed by the fire of divine love,  
having utterly trampled down the summit of earthly honour  
and resolved to undergo Christ’s poverty  
[Col. 1711B] so that he might happily enter the riches of heaven,  
at last came to Bec, Christ being his guide—  
Christ who had foreknown him before time and prepared him  
as a pure vessel for the Church, and one to be worthy.

### He Assumes the Monastic Habit

4. When he saw the desired poverty of the place,  
the simplicity of the Father, and the marvellous life of the brethren,  
he joyfully cast off the costly garments in which he had been clothed  
and was invested with the cheap monastic tunic.  
Joined to the brethren and attaining his desire,  
he chose to appear more abject before all  
than to be held exalted in the houses of sinners,  
keeping fixed before his eyes and deep in his heart this saying:  
“The greater you are, the more humble be.”

What joy, I ask, did Father Herluin feel  
[Col. 1711C] when he knew that he had received, as he desired,  
one by whose teaching Bec, still unlearned within,  
would be instructed and trained?  
Though he often wished to yield precedence to Lanfranc, as was fitting,  
Lanfranc declined it, rendering this honour rather to him.  
The one feared to be subject to so great a teacher;  
the other reverenced the abbot so dear to him.

The man of such noble birth rejoiced sufficiently  
to be unknown and removed from recognition.  
He restrained and pressed himself more severely within,  
lest he should soon lose the quiet he loved.

### Lanfranc Becomes Prior

5. When he had completed three years in monastic life  
under the guidance of Father Herluin, to whom he had come,  
[Col. 1711D] lest the lamp that had hitherto been hidden  
in the midst of the valley under a bushel should remain concealed,  
he was made prior, chosen by the company of brethren.  
Thus, by the splendour of his understanding and wisdom,  
they might be illuminated by the lofty light of being,  
as might this renowned house and all Neustria itself.  
Although he declined it, he finally assumed the charge  
and under that position devoted himself to benefiting all,  
assigning to the brethren what they ought rightly to follow  
and no less showing them what they ought properly to avoid.

He always had teaching ready to hand,  
with which he watered the hearts of his companions in excellence.  
He was pleasing to all, for he did everything wisely.  
He fed some with solid food, others with milk,  
giving to all according to what he thought fitting for each.

### As His Fame Spreads, a Great Crowd of Nobles and Scholars Comes to Him

[Col. 1712A]

6. But when his flying fame increased and filled the earth,  
concerning the novelty of the place, its religious life,  
and knowledge of the great man Lanfranc,  
many nobles, wealthy persons, and sons of counts,  
as well as many others—scholars, to be sure, swollen with pride—  
flocked to Bec, desiring to know Lanfranc  
and more ardently wishing to be instructed by so great a teacher.

Established in his lucid philosophy,  
some of these were pierced to their inmost hearts  
and suddenly anointed with the fervour of the Holy Spirit.  
Having cast down the pride of the world and the guile of the flesh,  
they hastened to submit their necks to Christ’s gentle yoke,  
remaining altogether there through love of Him.

[Col. 1712B] But many others, pursuing philosophy under the same master,  
instructed and well trained in the noble arts,  
went forth from the school of Bec, speaking wonders,  
and became heralds of those arts throughout the regions.  
Thus the arts which had been wholly annihilated  
in these parts since the time of Rollo  
came to be known as restored through Lanfranc’s effort—  
a work which should certainly be credited to his praise.

### Bec Flourishes and Abounds in Everything

7. Then Bec, previously poor and lowly,  
began to be enriched, to increase, and to bear fruit  
in gold, riches, religious persons,  
vines and lands, and precious ornaments.

Happy church, pleasing and dear to Christ,  
which knows that it has Him alone as patron through all these things!

### Lanfranc Becomes Abbot of Saint Stephen at Caen

[Col. 1712C]

8. As time passed, when Bec was already flourishing greatly  
and shining almost throughout the whole world,  
Lanfranc dispensing teaching within  
and Herluin managing outward affairs,  
William, duke of the Normans, at the praise of his people  
took Lanfranc, deservedly revered by all,  
not without much sobbing and great mourning  
of the brethren and of Father Herluin, now old.

He made him abbot of his church then being built at Caen,  
for the advantage of the church itself  
and likewise of the new monastery and the region.  
For by his remarkable understanding and action  
Lanfranc instructed, adorned, ordered, and made it illustrious  
in rule, teaching, chant, and philosophy.

[Col. 1712D] Although he had watched over it for not many years,  
he was removed from the care of the monastery  
and afterwards promoted to an episcopal see.  
Yet the marks of his unfading teaching remain  
and are still sufficiently evident within to all.

### He Then Becomes Bishop of Canterbury

9. But after the aforesaid duke, called by right to reign,  
had defeated the English in close battle,  
possessed the land as king, and sat enthroned in his rule,  
he wished to renew the churches of the conquered kingdom,  
which had been greatly neglected and grown up in vices.  
Following the counsel of the nobles and his magnates,  
he removed Lord Lanfranc, abbot of the monastery at Caen,  
at the Almighty’s command,  
[Col. 1713A] though Lanfranc resisted greatly and long refused.  
At last, pressed by the entreaties of many—  
especially overcome by the bond of Father Herluin,  
whom he obeyed as Christ’s agent and mouth—  
he brought him to the illustrious city called Canterbury  
and appointed him chief priest over it.  
The clergy and people received him  
with amplified praises and joyful hearts.

10. Having attained the summit of such honour,  
he did not devote himself to the material construction of castles,  
nor to dogs, nor to birds in lay luxury,  
as is known to be the custom of English bishops;  
for he was wholly removed from such things.  
But, as a pious shepherd, he diligently attended  
to spiritual construction through episcopal discipline,

[Col. 1713B] building barbarous minds by teaching  
and recalling them from evil and disgraceful practices.

There is no need now to proclaim in many speeches  
how greatly he benefited the whole English nation.  
For the condition of the kingdom and of its churches testifies  
that, by his immense care and constant effort,  
it was then restored under the rule of justice.

O how happy and flourishing was the people then,  
when an illustrious king secured peace for them  
and so great a bishop supplied instruction!  
The former restrained rebels with the drawn sword:  
no retainer could stand against him.  
The latter everywhere renewed the dwellings of the blessed,  
appointing and consecrating chosen governors throughout the land.  
The former restored ancient churches by new laws.

[Col. 1713C] Then Britain blossomed; then it grew green again;  
then it was illustrious because endowed with worthy leaders;  
then rich in goods, because desired peace crowned their heads—  
that peace from whose excessive sweat and great labour  
all who are wealthy in this world and powerful  
take the material for foolish swelling pride.

But since I have wandered somewhat from the order begun,  
I must return there by taking up the path again.

### Herluin, Worn Down by Years, Chooses Anselm as His Successor

11. But Father Herluin, whose mind knew the truth,  
when he saw himself now bereft of Lanfranc,  
whom he rejoiced to have ready as successor  
and upon whom he had transferred all the care of his house,  
chose Anselm, approved in life and studies,  
[Col. 1713D] and determined that he should be placed in Lanfranc’s position.

### Anselm’s Origin and First Studies; He Comes to Lanfranc, Becomes a Monk at Bec, and Is Appointed Prior after Lanfranc

12. This Anselm was born in the city of Aosta,  
and was nevertheless distinguished by a sufficiently famous lineage in the world.  
After the years of childhood had passed,  
he applied himself to studies and was trained in the arts.  
First in the trivium, as the order of schools requires,  
then in the quadrivium, at which every common person marvels,  
he soon equalled the greatest teachers.

While he flourished in study in those regions,  
moved by the far-famed report of the marvellous renown  
of Master Lanfranc—then a widely known prior  
[Col. 1714A] at Bec in the time of its first shepherd—  
he spurned his father’s house, rejected acquaintances and country,  
and, having travelled through many Italian regions,  
at last happily reached the haven he had desired.

Having found the man, remarkable in life and speech,  
and having experienced both his religious life and wisdom,  
he is said to have embraced him with so great love of heart  
that he no longer wished to depart from his presence.

Having therefore assumed the garment of religious life,  
he is said to have attained such virtue in a short time  
that he was in no respect second to any of the brethren.  
After Lanfranc’s notable departure—  
when Lanfranc, because of his pre-eminent upright life,  
had been transferred from this church to become abbot at Caen—  
Anselm was charged, according to custom, with performing the office of prior.

[Col. 1714B] He was not exalted by this, nor marked by levity,  
for, as the saying goes, honours often change character.  
Rather, he strove to be the least among those whom he governed,  
because by the law of ministry he was bound to serve each one.

### Herluin Departs This Life

13. Abbot Herluin, now weakened by old age,  
after he had completed nine five-year periods less one year  
since, fleeing the world, he had joined himself to Christ,  
after all that his mind had desired had been fulfilled  
in human affairs and his eyes had performed their task;

then, because the basilica too had been splendidly completed  
and consecrated by Lanfranc, now supreme archbishop,  
with manifold pomp and marvellous splendour;  
since nothing remained for the fulfilment of his desires  
except that he wished to be dissolved and see Christ—

[Col. 1714C] like a veteran soldier, cleansed of every stain,  
strengthened by the Body and partaking of Christ’s Blood,  
he gave his soul, supported on every side by virtues, to heaven,  
and returned his body to the earth from which it is known to have first arisen.

How great was the weeping there! For sorrow filled everything.  
How great the groaning, because so great a shepherd had died!  
Many common people hastened there along with the wealthy:  
some weeping for their lord, others calling for their father.  
So great was the cry of mourners and their anguish  
that, because the doors were forced back by the crowd,  
the psalm-singers could scarcely be heard, scarcely approached.

### Saint Anselm Succeeds Him; His Virtues

14. But after the obsequies had been performed as befitted so great a man,  
not without frequent sobbing,  
the brethren, now bereft of their father, gathered together,  
[Col. 1714D] united in one resolve and not divided by schism.  
They established Anselm as abbot and paid the honours due to him.  
Such a continued succession is certainly not believed  
to have been manifested without God’s will.

For he was so great, though young in years,  
that he was most worthy to be placed over so great a flock.  
Gentle in speech, but gentler still in service,  
he was to all joined with him in the monastery.  
For to the healthy he was a father, and to the sick a mother;  
indeed, to both alike he was father and mother.  
Touched by divine inspiration, he had become all things to all  
that he might win for Christ those whom he sought to gain.

Thus, trusting well in the sobriety  
and likewise in the upright life of the brethren,  
[Col. 1715A] he more diligently attended outward matters entrusted to him  
and more carefully devoted himself inwardly to their concerns,  
watching over the instruction of his own through teaching,  
at times gathering the fruits of contemplation,  
at times lingering in the giving of counsel.

Who was ever so discerning and so widely known that anyone able to enjoy Anselm’s conversation would have consulted it as though it were a divine oracle?  
For such grace rested on his lips  
that almost every people delighted in his words.  
He was not unwelcome to kings, to the chief men of the land,  
to those of middling estate, or to the lowly;  
rather, he was beloved and precious.

15. Under him Bec flourished and grew exceedingly through his care;  
nor did Normandy alone, but distant and neighbouring regions also,  
[Col. 1715B] breathe fragrance from his good odour through divine favour.  
Stirred by this, eminent and learned men came to Bec,  
giving themselves and their possessions to Christ:  
lands with villages and many estates under them;  
gold with precious gems and stones;  
abundant silver with valued garments—  
all these they solemnly subjected and assigned to Him.

### Anselm Goes to the King of England on Affairs of His Church

16. Bec was now powerful and thus continued,  
always growing and advancing for the better  
in rule, riches, its religious community,  
and moreover in numbers, merits, and increase.

But after Anselm had ruled mature Bec well  
for fifteen years,  
[Col. 1715C] constrained by the entreaty of the brethren and finally overcome by command,  
because very many affairs of the church had arisen,  
he crossed the sea and went to address the king about them  
and to give him certain admonitions.  
Received and revered by him with sufficient honour,  
he obtained, as desired, what he had gone to request.

### He Is Carried Off to the See of Canterbury

17. At that time the renowned English city of Canterbury—  
alas!—had been bereft of its excellent patron in merits  
for almost four complete years  
since beloved Lanfranc had departed the world.

When the king had often been urged in this matter  
to provide for the mourning church,  
[Note: [Col. 1715D] William II, king of England, called Rufus.] Rufus had long delayed and dissembled.  
But then he was softened and at last his fury was stilled.

[Col. 1715D] Persons of various religious orders in the realm,  
as well as princes pressing him on this matter,  
secured his consent that an episcopal election should take place  
and that legal contention should be kept far away.

Therefore, since all together with the king desired the same man  
and repeatedly cried this demand aloud,  
Anselm, abbot of Bec—worthy of so great an honour,  
distinguished, wise, and of great sweetness—  
was sought, seized, and dragged away by force,  
although he had tried very vigorously to resist them.  
He was established as supreme bishop of the Church of Canterbury,  
a worthy successor of the Italian [Lanfranc].

[Col. 1716A]

18. Raised to the honour of the archbishopric,  
he sought not his own interests but Christ’s, out of love for Him.  
A diligent guardian of the churches of the whole realm,  
he stood by them and relieved them;  
fair in judgment to great and small,  
ready to help widows and orphans alike;  
generous to natives and no less unstinting toward foreigners,  
he was wholly and continually poured out for the needy.

Compassionate toward the sorrowful, he did not spare the proud.  
Yet he was a help to all in common.  
Moreover, scattering the seeds of the divine word,  
he did not hide in the earth what had been entrusted by the Lord;  
rather, what he had heard he taught aloud from the rooftops,  
as an eminent shepherd and faithful steward.

Adorned with such virtues, this blessed man  
[Col. 1716B] rightly undertook the charge of so worthy a pontificate.  
Therefore he was sufficiently loved by the clergy  
and greatly revered by the people:  
because he was a powerful defender of the clergy  
and a diligent provider for the people.

### William, Third Abbot of Bec: His Country, Character, and Learning; Robert of Meulan, His Kinsman

19. Once Anselm had been consecrated and installed in his see,  
this news could no longer remain hidden.  
The community of the brethren of Bec gathered together,  
lamenting their shepherd who had been taken away  
and discussing the restoration of a new one.

At the counsel of the kindly Bishop Anselm,  
a certain William was immediately chosen by them,  
born of Montfort and set over them.  
[Col. 1716C] He was adorned with virtues and approved in religious life:  
gentle, generous, patient, and a lover of peace.  
He was powerfully instructed in the divine law,  
knowing reverently how to bring forth things new and old.

The honour, mirror, and manifest rule of monks,  
he shone like a lily among flower-buds.  
He was dear and acceptable not only to neighbouring brethren  
and to those born near him,  
but also to those far off, to the exalted, and to strangers.  
Having attained this virtue, during his time many gave much to Bec,  
enriching it with wealth and cultivating it.

And Count Robert of Meulan, a memorable man,  
closely related to the abbot by kinship,  
especially increased Bec, through his love, with substantial revenues  
[Col. 1716D] under the honour of the Mother of God.  
Yet the inner rule was not weakened under him;  
rather, it was firmer in moderation.  
Nor was inward observance relaxed in any respect;  
indeed, it increased somewhat and was bowed under no burden.

For Bec at that time was not inwardly in need;  
it already abounded and was already renowned abroad.

### William Ruled Thirty Years; Concerning Boso, Fourth Abbot of Bec

20. But after he had presided as abbot over the Church of Bec  
for about thirty completed years,  
having first kept watch with pastoral care  
[Col. 1717A] and beautifully fulfilled his office,  
William, touched by bodily sickness, at last set aside worldly cares.  
Full of days, he fell asleep and rested in the Lord,  
and was laid with his fathers and buried.

Boso, previously prior of the church, succeeded him,  
being placed in the pastor’s seat by the brethren’s choice.  
He was shrewd, wise, subtle, and keen.

By counsel, care, writings, and philosophy.

Who, I ask, approached that man in sorrow  
and did not immediately leave him rejoicing?

For eminent men, however distant and remote,  
sufficiently instructed and cheered by his discourse,  
would return to him seeking counsel;  
admiring him, they marvelled at the power of his speech.

[Col. 1717B] But what shall I say of his religion,  
or what declare concerning the integrity of his mind?  
Who was so closely joined to the venerable Anselm  
that he could scarcely, or only late, be parted from him?

He kept those subject to him in such great peace,  
and moreover governed them with such an art of gentleness,  
that the Holy Spirit dwelling in his heart  
became known, clearer, and more manifest.

He shone forth in many diverse regions of the world,  
with magnificent understanding and wonderful weight of words;  
and the marks of supreme devotion made him known  
to kings and to the foremost men of every far-off land.

Striving to keep the flock entrusted to him,  
now he gave them drink by instructive examples,  
now he fed them with spiritual doctrine,  
[Col. 1717C] yet did not exclude them from material nourishment.  
Indeed, he generously supplied what was fitting for each,  
binding the novice to himself by a wonderful affection of Christ.

Thus Boso, an outstanding and experienced shepherd,  
keeping watch over the Lord’s camp for twelve years,  
a well-taught man clad in the breastplate of righteousness  
and girded with the sharp sword of the Holy Spirit (*pneumatis*),  
safe behind the shield of faith and the helmet of salvation,  
acted within as a strong athlete, not sluggishly;  
he strove to preserve his own from the enemy’s assault.

When the course of this present life was completed,  
he passed to Christ, under the condition of death;  
and rightly was his spirit borne above the heavens,  
for to him to die was gain, and to live was Christ.

[Col. 1717D] **Theobald, fifth abbot of Bec**

21. In his office there arose a certain man of noble birth,  
and, formerly prior of the place, received the care of the sheepfold.

He was called Theobald, and was plainly  
distinguished in character and worthy in birth,  
trained in excellent arts, and even in higher things.

After two full years had passed,  
with six additional months counted thereafter,  
while he governed Bec itself with considerable diligence,  
receiving from without what he knew was fitting for the house  
and assigning within what accorded with the divine law,  
he was pleasing to all and joined to them in affection;  
yet he was taken from them and, Christ so ordaining, transferred with remarkable honour to the English;  
[Col. 1718A] he became supreme prelate of the church of Canterbury,  
to which the distinguished island of Albion is subject.

**Theobald is made Archbishop of Canterbury; he suppresses various disturbances in England; above all he protects Bec’s English possessions.**

22. In his time—his character itself attests it—  
England, which had formerly been most rich in resources,  
on the one hand in diverse wealth, on the other in powerful peoples,  
alas, was deprived and despoiled by foreigners;  
overwhelmed, it languished, and was seen almost overthrown  
by the envy of the magnates, powerful men of kingdom and country,  
raging with swords, flames, and treachery.

To ward off and repress the frenzy of this disaster,  
which then flared more savagely even in ravaging churches,  
passing scarcely any by,  
[Col. 1718B] this man endured such opposition from proud men  
that he often incurred danger even to his life.

But Christ preserved him unharmed and delivered him from all these things, restoring him to peace. For just as Joseph himself, by God’s ordering, is said—and Scripture teaches it—to have been sent into Egypt so that, at the fitting time, he might make recompense to his brothers, father, and indeed all his people, so this man, by God’s will, was advanced to the primacy of the whole English kingdom, and to the greater dignity, so that, with freer power and compassion for his mother, he might aid his brethren and his own people, and moreover become protector of the possessions that belonged to Bec in that distant land.

Making good return for these things and reflecting on them in his heart,  
[Col. 1718C] he often honoured his mother with worthy gifts,  
raised her up, and reverently gave her humble assistance.  
Preserving inviolate whatever belonged to Bec,  
he defended it unsullied from the enemy’s hands,  
at a time when all were known to be moved to every outrage.

**Letard, sixth abbot of Bec**

23. After him succeeded a man of supreme devotion,  
hostile to vices and zealous for virtues,  
named Letard, fragrant like Indian nard.

He was, however, advanced in age, for he possessed great gravity  
and a mind cultivated exceedingly well:  
prudent, mature, patient, and chaste in body,  
showing his disciples by a sufficient example  
what he commanded them openly to observe.

[Col. 1718D] After he had happily completed twice five years  
from the time he undertook the government of the monastery of Bec,  
he ended this present life and so died;  
he passed on, and came forth a virgin from his mother’s womb,  
having exceeded his sixty-fifth year.

**Roger of Bailleul, seventh abbot**

24. Immediately after him, from the simple flock of the convent, came a certain Roger, born at Bailleul, a man of excellent character and himself an investigator of wisdom; quick in intellect and well polished in speech. He was imbued not merely with those human teachings by which each empty person puffs himself up, but with divine instruction. He who is deprived of knowledge of these is like an ass, though adorned with laurel.

## In the year of the Lord 1150: Guy of Cherlieu, Abbot

[Col. 1719]

### Notice

(Oudin, *Script. eccles.*, II, 1417)

Guy, abbot of Cherlieu, a Cistercian house in Burgundy on the Seine, to whom Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, wrote two letters, composed at about this same time—that is, around the year 1150—a *Treatise on the Correction of the Chant of the Cistercian Order*. John Mabillon published it under Saint Bernard’s name in his edition of the works of the divine Bernard, on the authority of John Bona, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and a most learned man.

The manuscript used by John Bona misled him. He thought it was a treatise by the divine Bernard because he saw a letter of Saint Bernard prefixed to the said treatise. But the manuscript codex which I have here at Bucilly, containing various treatises concerning music and ecclesiastical chant, bears at the head of the work the name of Guy, abbot of Cherlieu, and lacks that extraneous letter of Saint Bernard which had persuaded the cardinal that this treatise should be attributed to Bernard; for it certainly belongs to Abbot Guy. John Mabillon nevertheless maintains that Saint Bernard certainly also contributed his assistance to this reform of chant, as proved by definite arguments. No one known to me has ever mentioned this writer.

[Col. 1719]

### Treatise on the Correction of the Chant of the Cistercian Order

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXV, col. 1121; *Works of St Bernard*, vol. I.)

## About the year 1150: Heribert, Monk

[Col. 1719]

### Notice

(*Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. XII, p. 446)

While the heretic Henry, this restorer of Manichaeism in France, was infecting Languedoc and Provence with his errors, one of his disciples, named Ponce or Ponne, assisted him in Périgord and made a great number of proselytes there. Their doctrine and morals are set out in a letter by the monk Heribert, addressed to all the faithful as a denunciation.

Nothing is known about this writer personally. He was probably from Périgord, since he speaks as an eyewitness of what he recounts. It appears that this good monk was somewhat credulous and readily deceived by the misleading appearances of false miracles. Nevertheless, the candour pervading his writing testifies in favour of his sincerity. He is an author who ingenuously reports what his senses had taught him, with no distrust of the reliability of their testimony.

His letter must precede 1147, the date of Saint Bernard’s mission to Périgord. First published by Dom Mabillon in the third volume of his *Analectes* (p. 467), it was reprinted with some corrections in the first volume of Dom Martène’s *Anecdotes* (p. 453). Both editions agree that the heretics in question bent their knees a hundred times daily, not merely seven times, as Father Pagi says (under the year 1163).

[Col. 1721]

### Letter of the Monk Heribert concerning the Heretics of Périgord

(Martène, *Anecdot.*, I, 453, from the Elnone manuscript.)

[Col. 1721A] I, the monk Heribert, wish it to be known to all Christians that they should guard themselves carefully against false prophets, who strive to corrupt Christianity. For very many heretics have arisen in the region of Périgord, who say that they lead an apostolic life. They do not eat meat; they do not drink wine except very sparingly every third day; they bend the knee a hundred times a day; and they do not accept money.

But their sect is very perverse. They do not say “Glory be to the Father,” but, instead of “Glory be to the Father,” say: “For yours is the kingdom, and you rule over all creation for ages of ages. Amen.” They hold almsgiving to be nothing, because nothing ought to be possessed from which it might be given. They regard the Mass as worthless and say that Communion ought not to be received, but only a fragment of bread.

If one of them sings Mass, he does so for the sake of deception; [Col. 1721B] he neither says the Canon nor receives Communion, but throws the host beside or behind the altar, or into the missal. They do not adore the cross or the Lord’s image, but forbid those who do adore them, so that before the Lord’s image they say: “O how wretched are those who adore you!”—the psalm saying: “The idols of the nations,” etc. [Col. 1722A]

By this deception very many have already been drawn in: not only nobles who abandon their property, but also clerics, priests, monks, and nuns. No one is so uncultivated that, if he joins them, within eight days he will be so learned in letters that he can no longer be overcome either by words or by examples.

They cannot be detained in any way, because, if they are captured, no bonds can hold them: the devil releases them. All of them are such that they hope and desire to find persons who will torment them and hand them over to death. They also perform many signs. For if anywhere they are bound with iron chains or fetters and put into a wine-cask, with its bottom turned upward and the strongest guards appointed, they are not found on the following day until they present themselves voluntarily. After a little of their own wine has been poured into an empty wine-vessel, it is found full the following day. [Col. 1722B] They perform very many other remarkable things. Their leader is called Ponne.

## In the year of the Lord 1151: Bartholomew, Bishop of Châlons

[Col. 1721]

### Notice

(*Gallia Christiana*, new ed., vol. IX, col. 881)

Bartholomew, formerly dean of the Church of Paris, became bishop of Châlons in 1147. In that year, on 26 October, he was present at the dedication of his church, reportedly celebrated by Pope Eugenius III; together with the bishops of Paris, Auxerre, and Nevers, he purified it within and without by sprinkling holy water.

In the same year he obtained a royal diploma concerning the inheritance of the bishops of Châlons who died intestate; it may be found in the proofs to the *Liberties of the Gallican Church*, vol. I, p. 595, and in Martène, *Collectio Amplissima*, vol. I, p. 803. In the following year he attended the Council of Reims against Gilbert of Poitiers. Bartholomew’s letter to Abbot Suger appears in Du Chesne, *Historia Francorum*, vol. IV.

Bartholomew died in 1151 during a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, according to the chronicles of Alberic and of Saint Peter of Châlons; according to the necrologies, either on 25 or 26 December.

[Col. 1721]

### Letter of Bartholomew to Abbot Suger

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXVI, under Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis.)
