[Col. 1723]

### [Three Letters]

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CLIII, col. 885.)

## In the year of the Lord 1151: Saint Rainard, Fifth Abbot of Cîteaux

[Col. 1723]

### Notice concerning Rainard

(*Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 985)

Rainard, son of Milo, count of Bar-sur-Seine, was taken from being a monk of Clairvaux and made abbot of Cîteaux in 1133 by Walter, bishop of Chalon-sur-Saône. In that year he is mentioned in a charter of Walter himself for the monastery of Saint Peter. [Note: [Col. 1723] *Proofs for the History of Chalon*, p. 50.]

He established very salutary statutes in the following year, or rather collected the statutes of the general chapters. In 1128 he instructed Saint Peter of Tamié, the first abbot in Savoy, to accept the archbishopric of Tarentaise offered to him. Near the end of September 1140, he reconciled Peter Abelard with Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux.

At about the same time he wrote to Pope Innocent II on behalf of Humbert, bishop of Autun, against the monks of Vézelay. Since general assemblies were held at Cîteaux in that very year, he made an agreement with Hugh and the monks of the Premonstratensian order: neither order might receive monks of the other into its own, nor found abbeys except at a distance equal to that separating the Premonstratensian monastery and Saint-Médard of Soissons. It further stipulated that mutual complaints were not to be entrusted for settlement to anyone other than monks of the two orders, according to the cartulary of Boulbonne.

Peter the Venerable writes to him in book V, letter 25; he is also discussed in the *Cistercian Exordium*, book I, chapter 28, and by Vincent in the *Mirror of History*, book XXVII, chapter 27. In 1148 he was visited by Pope Eugenius III at the general chapter, and the pope consecrated the abbey cemetery there. Rainard attended the consecration of the church of Saint Lazarus at Autun, performed in 1146 by Humbert, bishop of the diocese.

Finally, after founding very many monasteries to the great benefit of religious life, he fell asleep in Christ in 1151, on 16 December, as stated in the Supplement to Sigebert from the Cistercian martyrology. Saint Bernard mourned at his death: “The abbot of Cîteaux,” he says in letter 270, “has left us—a great wound to the Order. For me, a twofold cause of grief is laid upon me, since in one man I have lost both a father and a son. And now we have in his place Lord Gozwin, abbot of Bonnevaux.”

A contemporary writer of the life of Blessed Stephen, abbot of Obazine, book II, chapter 11, also speaks of Rainard thus: “At that time the Cistercians were governed by an abbot named Rainard, a man … scarcely comparable to anyone: for in elegance of person, nobility of birth, the adornment of humility, and fervour of religion, he surpassed all the abbots whom he governed; he burned with the vigour of holy religion so that he surpassed fire in ardour, and outwardly he excelled in such sweetness that he overcame the pleasantness of honey.” See vol. II of Baluze’s *Miscellanea*, p. 117 ff., and the Cistercian *Menologium* for 16 May.

[Col. 1725]

## Institutions of Saint Rainard, Fifth Abbot of Cîteaux, for the General Chapter of the Cistercian Order

(*Nomasticon Cisterciense*, or the more ancient customs of the Cistercian Order. Paris, 1664, folio.)

### Prefatory Notice

This is the first collection of definitions of the General Chapter of the Cistercian Order from the time of the *Charter of Charity*. Its author is believed to have been Saint Rainard, son of Milo, count of Bar-sur-Seine, [Note: [Col. 1725B] Orderic Vitalis, book VIII of the *History of the English*.] first a monk of Clairvaux and afterwards the fourth abbot of Cîteaux, whom Saint Christian saw among the choirs of angels. [Note: [Col. 1725B] *Greater Exordium of Cîteaux*, book I, chapter 28.] Saint Bernard pursued his death with tears as a great wound to the Order, as Bernard himself calls it. [Note: [Col. 1726B] Saint Bernard, letter 270.]

This collection, divided into eighty-seven chapters, contains various definitions issued in general chapters from the beginning of the Order to the year 1134, when it was itself published.

### Prologue of Saint Rainard

The *Charter of Charity* contains among other things that every year all abbots of monasteries established by God’s grace in diverse provinces are to assemble at the church of Cîteaux, and that there they are to deliberate most diligently on the observance of the holy Rule, the whole ordering of their life, and the preservation of unbreakable peace among themselves. Thus, the rule of life, often repeated and confirmed by the authority of the divine Scriptures, may not readily grow lax but may remain vigorous through the long span of many years.

Accordingly, assembled in the aforesaid place, they established these chapters and decreed that they should be observed throughout the brotherhood of all our communities.

## Institutions

Of the General Chapter of the Cistercian Order. [Note: [Col. 1726B] In the year of the Lord 1134; the thirty-sixth year of Cîteaux.]

### Chapter I. In what places monasteries are to be built

[Col. 1725A]

No monasteries of ours are to be built in cities, castles, or villages, but in places removed from human intercourse.

### Chapter II. On unity of observance in divine and human matters

In order that indissoluble unity may endure perpetually among abbeys, it is first established that the Rule of Blessed Benedict shall be understood in one way and observed in one way by all; then that there shall be everywhere the same books, insofar as concerns the divine office, the same food, the same clothing, and finally the same customs in all things.

### Chapter III. Which books may not differ

[Col. 1725B] The Missal, Epistolary, Gospel-book, Collectary, Gradual, Antiphonary, Rule, Hymnal, Psalter, [Col. 1726A] Lectionary, and Calendar are to be held uniformly everywhere.

### Chapter IV. On clothing

Clothing is to be plain and cheap, without furs, shirts, or woollen undergarments, such as the Rule describes.

### Chapter V. From what source monks’ sustenance ought to come

The sustenance of monks of our Order ought to come from the labour of their hands, the cultivation of lands, and the keeping of livestock. Thus we may possess for our own use waters, woods, vineyards, meadows, lands remote from secular habitation, and animals—except those which tend more to excite curiosity and display vanity than to provide any usefulness, such as deer, cranes, and [Col. 1726B] other animals of that kind. For working, tending, and preserving these things, near or far, though not beyond [Col. 1727A] a day’s journey, we may have granges to be kept by lay brothers.

### Chapter VI. A monk must not live outside the cloister

[Note: [Col. 1727D] Rule of Saint Benedict, chapters 4, 66, and 67.]

Although a monk, whose proper dwelling according to the Rule ought to be the cloister, may go to the granges whenever he is sent, he must by no means reside there for a longer time.

### Chapter VII. Cohabitation with women is prohibited in our Order, and they are denied entrance through the monastery gate

Setting aside every occasion, whether for increasing or preserving provisions, for washing any things belonging to the monastery when this may at some time be necessary, or indeed for any other necessity whatever, cohabitation with women is altogether prohibited to us and [Col. 1727B] our lay brothers. Therefore they are not to be permitted either to lodge within the yards of the granges or to enter the monastery gate.

### Chapter VIII. On lay brothers

Work at the granges is to be done by lay brothers and hired labourers. With episcopal permission, we receive these lay brothers as necessary helpers and assistants under our care, just as we receive monks; and we regard them as brothers and participants in our spiritual and temporal goods equally with the monks.

### Chapter IX. We are not to have revenues from others’ property

Churches, altars, burial rights, tithes from another’s labour or livestock; villages, villeins, rents from lands, revenues from ovens and mills, and all similar things contrary to monastic purity, are excluded by the institution of our name and Order.

### Chapter X. What may or may not be possessed in gold, silver, gems, and silk

Altar linens and ministers’ vestments are to be without silk, except for the stole and maniple. The chasuble, moreover, may only be of one colour. All ornaments and utensils of the monastery are to be without gold and silver, except the chalice and communion tube (*fistula*); these two alone we permit to be of silver and gilded, but in no way of gold.

### Chapter XI. No one is to receive a person wishing to go to another church

If a monk, cleric, or layperson wishes to come to one of our churches to remain there, no other church is to dissuade or retain him, even if he wishes to remain, because it is written: “What you do not wish done to you, do not do to another.” After he has come to the place in which he intends to live, however, and has changed his mind and does not wish to remain there, [Col. 1728A] he may depart freely.

If he has lived in the novices’ cell and is expelled through his own fault or leaves of his own accord, he is not to be received by any church of our brotherhood without letters of recommendation, because from such a cause fuel for discord may arise among the churches. We decree the same concerning a travelling monk received at one of our houses who leaves by whatever means.

### Chapter XII. How a new church is to be provided with an abbot, monks, and other necessities

Twelve monks together with an abbot as thirteenth are to be sent to new monasteries. Yet they are not to be assigned there until the place has been furnished with books, buildings, and other necessities: with the books, namely, a Missal, Epistolary, Gospel-book, Rule, book of Usages, [Note: [Col. 1727D] Observe here the mention of a book of Usages, as already written and to be possessed and observed everywhere by all.] Psalter, Hymnal, [Col. 1728B] Collectary, Antiphonary, Lectionary, and Gradual; and with buildings—an oratory, refectory, guest-house, and porter’s cell—as well as temporal necessities, so that they may both live there and immediately be able to observe the Rule.

### Chapter XIII. On book-fasteners

We forbid gold, silver, silvered, or gilded clasps—commonly called fasteners—from being used on church books, and we forbid any codex to be covered with a cloth covering.

### Chapter XIV. On daily bread

As in ecclesiastical and other observances we take care not to be found discordant, so difference in daily food must likewise be avoided, lest brothers overcome by weakness of flesh or spirit reject coarser bread and begin to desire finer. Therefore we establish that white bread is not to be made in our monasteries, not even on the chief festivals, but coarse bread, that is, bread made with a sieve.

Where wheat is lacking, bread may be made with *scatio* [uncertain cereal or flour], a rule which does not bind the sick. White bread is also set before such guests as seem appropriate, and before those being bled at their bloodletting, as prescribed in their regulation. [Note: [Col. 1727D] See the *Book of Usages*, chapter 70, “On bloodletting.”] This white bread supplied to those being bled, like the ordinary daily ration, is not to weigh more when placed on the scale, but is to be weighed in equal balance. [Col. 1728C]

### Chapter XV. On cowls and under-tunics

In our churches cowls are not to be fringed on the outside; [Note: [Col. 1727D] By “fringed cowls” he forbids those which Saint Bernard also censures among the Cluniacs in his *Apology* and in his letter to Robert: namely, cowls broad and overflowing with superfluity of cloth, not those in which there were fringes or more prominent tufts of wool, as Ángel Manrique understands in his *Annals*, under the year 1134, chapter 6. In that sense our Fathers would have been opposed to Saint Benedict, who in his Rule allowed shaggy cowls to his monks in winter. Our men therefore admitted no cowls or tufts except simple and narrower ones, as Peter the Venerable acknowledges in letter 28 and in book IV, letter 17.] and daytime under-tunics are not to be of goatskin or Cordovan leather, but of cowhide. [Col. 1728D]

### Chapter XVI. On fugitive monks or lay brothers

If a monk or lay brother leaves any church through his own fault and comes to another, he is to be urged to return. If the abbot or prior of that [Col. 1729A] place learns that he does not wish to return to his own house, he is not to allow him to remain there for more than one night, and is to command the religious habit to be taken from him—unless it is established that he had been a monk before he came to our Order. A lay brother, however, is to be allowed to retain nothing from the monastery’s possessions except plain and cheap clothing.

### Chapter XVII. A travelling monk must be received or depart within a short time

If a travelling monk comes to a monastery to live there but cannot be received because of proximity to or acquaintance with his own church, he is not to be kept longer in the guest-house. This is so that, during this delay, he may not be wrested from his own abbot, either by some contrivance or by the request [Col. 1729B] of certain ecclesiastical or secular persons, which is unquestionably coercive.

### Chapter XVIII. All monasteries are to be dedicated in honour of Blessed Mary

Because our predecessors and fathers first came from the church of Molesme, built in honour of Blessed Mary, to the place of Cîteaux from which we too sprang, we decree that all churches of ours and of our successors shall be founded and dedicated in memory of that same holy Mary, Queen of Heaven and Earth.

### Chapter XIX. Rich supplementary dishes are not to be served in the refectory at Cîteaux during the General Chapter

[Note: [Col. 1729D] By the name *pitantiae*, mentioned here and often elsewhere, are meant certain dishes more luxurious than the regular pottages, as we have already said above. Thus, according to James of Vitry and Stephen of Sainte-Geneviève, our monks’ pottages were made from [Col. 1730D] vegetables and legumes; the *pitantiae* from eggs and fish. See what we have said on these matters in the book *On the First Manner of Life of the Cistercians*, above at chapter 17 of the *Book of Usages*. (*Patrologia*, vol. CLXVI, under Saint Stephen.)]

We ten abbots, coming to Cîteaux at that time as we usually do after a year, [Col. 1729C] asked Lord Abbot Stephen and the brothers not to set before us in the refectory the customary supplementary dishes after the two regular courses of pottage. For in the refectory, in the distribution of these things, there seemed to be a certain disturbance among the brothers, and during that delay a reduction in their sleep. Therefore, with the consent of that abbot and the brothers, we established that these things should no longer be done at that time.

### Chapter XX. On carvings, paintings, and wooden crosses

We forbid carvings or paintings to be made in our churches or in any workshops of the monastery, because while attention is given to such things, the benefit of good meditation or the discipline of religious seriousness is often neglected. [Col. 1729D] We do, however, have painted crosses, provided they are wooden.

### Chapter XXI. No dwelling is to be maintained outside the gate

It is not fitting that any dwelling for people be built outside the monastery gate, except for animals, because danger to souls can arise from this.

### Chapter XXII. Animals marked by the vice of frivolity are not to be kept

It is certain that we who have embraced monastic warfare [Col. 1730A] ought to devote ourselves in our monasteries to honourable gravity and regular discipline, not frivolities or amusements. Therefore stimulants of vice must be removed from holy places: namely deer, bears, cranes, and other such incitements to frivolity.

### Chapter XXIII. On clerics and laypeople who build monasteries; and that no one is to become a monk without probation

If clerics or laypeople build a place in honour of God and wish to grant it to one of our monasteries so that it may develop into an abbey, and the abbot from whom they seek counsel judges the place suitable, he may receive it if he wishes.

If the clerics or laypeople themselves wish to submit to the yoke of the holy Rule, they are either to wait for an abbey to be established in [Col. 1730B] that place or enter the novices’ cell at the monastery of the aforesaid abbot, that they may be tested according to the Rule. If they choose to withdraw to any other of our churches, or to do anything else as they choose, they may do so freely. Yet we must take great care that neither these persons nor any others are in any way joined to our community without regular probation, except monks whom Blessed Benedict receives.

### Chapter XXIV. No one within the monastery is to eat meat or fat

Within the monastery no one is to eat meat or animal fat, except those wholly infirm and hired craftsmen. Likewise, this is not permitted within the yards of the granges, except for the same reasons and also for hired labourers.

### Chapter XXV. On which days we eat only Lenten food

[Col. 1730C]

Throughout Advent, except the first Sunday; on the Monday and Tuesday before the beginning of the fast; on the vigil of Pentecost; during the September Ember fast; and on the vigils of Saints John the Baptist, Peter and Paul, Lawrence, the Assumption of Blessed Mary, the apostle Matthew, Simon and Jude, All Saints, and the apostle Andrew, we eat only Lenten food.

### Chapter XXVI. Monks are not to give or receive a half-share or *cressementum*

We are not permitted to enter into any partnership with secular persons in raising livestock or cultivating lands, namely by giving or receiving a half-share or *cressementum*.

### Chapter XXVII. Whom we receive for confession, Communion, and burial

For confession, Holy Communion, and burial, we receive no outsider except our guests and hired labourers who die in the monastery. Nor do we receive outsiders for the offering at conventual Mass, except on the Purification of Saint Mary. For burial, however, we receive only two persons, chosen by us from our friends or dependants, together with their wives. [Col. 1731A]

### Chapter XXVIII. What is to be done concerning persons who give themselves to one of our churches for monastic life and die before appearing in chapter

If anyone rejects the world and desires monastic life, and, coming to one of our abbots, reveals his desire and gives himself to him or to a monk of his church, then if he dies before his request has been formally made in chapter, he is not to be regarded as a novice but as a dependant.

### Chapter XXIX. No abbot of our Order is to bless a nun

[Note: [Col. 1731D] It was determined in the General Chapter of 1241 that this blessing of nuns is to be understood not of that which they receive at their profession, but of the consecration that belongs to bishops.]

It is forbidden for any of our abbots to presume to bless a nun, [Col. 1731B] baptize an infant, or even hold one at baptism, except perhaps at the point of death or where a priest is unavailable.

### Chapter XXX. How cases arising at the General Chapter are to be decided

If any matter, whether voluntarily confessed or raised by complaint, arises at the General Chapter of Cîteaux, it is to be decided, if this can be done harmoniously, by the common consent of all the abbots. But if, owing to the capacity of each person’s understanding—as often happens—they disagree among themselves, the Father of the monastery of Cîteaux is to direct four abbots suited to this task to decide it. Whatever they judge more useful is to be upheld without reconsideration by the assembly of the whole holy multitude.

### Chapter XXXI. On privileges

[Col. 1731C] We establish that no one may presume to obtain a privilege contrary to the institutions of our Order. What our holy predecessors established, and what those of the present day still establish with sound counsel, is to remain ratified and stable. If anyone presumes contrary to the statutes of the Chapter to acquire, buy, or build anything, then, with all dispensation removed, the buildings are to fall, and the expenditures and labour are to be lost.

### Chapter XXXII. A daughter-house is to visit its mother church once each year

The community of Cîteaux has ordained with diligent foresight, for the sake of humility, that a daughter-house shall visit its mother church at least once a year through its abbot, if he is in health.

### Chapter XXXIII. What penalty is to be imposed on those neglecting the institutions

[Col. 1731D]

If any abbot of our General Chapter neglects its institutions, he is to be publicly called out and admonished to amend. If he does not correct himself in that year and the matter becomes known at the following Chapter, he is to be subject to the lighter fault, wherever and for as long as the Chapter of Cîteaux decrees.

### Chapter XXXIV. On an archbishop or bishop

No one may presume to omit the General Chapter on an archbishop’s or bishop’s command. If he is healthy, he should strive to come, setting aside other occasions. This is not because we deny due obedience to our prelates, but because we must observe what we have established to maintain in our Order. Therefore, as we have written elsewhere, when any abbot wishes to establish an abbey, this chapter and the others must first be carefully shown to the archbishop or bishop. [Col. 1732A]

### Chapter XXXV. On pillows

Pillows are not to exceed one and a half feet in any dimension.

### Chapter XXXVI. On the election of an abbot or monk as bishop

If an abbot or monk of our Order is elected bishop, he is never to consent without the assent of his own abbot and the Chapter of Cîteaux, unless perhaps compelled by the lord pope. [Col. 1732B]

### Chapter XXXVII. Monks or lay brothers are not to seek anything at another abbey

Monks and lay brothers of our Order, sent by their own abbots on business to another abbey of our Order, are not to request anything without their abbot’s authorization except food, repair of footwear, and shoeing of horses, unless some misfortune befalls them on the road.

### Chapter XXXVIII. In what manner a travelling monk is to be blessed

A travelling monk received into a monastery of our Order is to be blessed in the manner in which a novice is blessed, if he has not previously been blessed. [Col. 1732C]

### Chapter XXXIX. Who may carry a quilted mattress

[Note: [Col. 1731D] Here too the aforesaid Ángel Manrique errs when he understands by *puncta culcitra* a cushion laid upon a riding saddle. For here, as is evident from the text of the chapter, *culcitra* must mean a mattress stuffed with tow and wool-flocks, laid beneath those who sleep.]

[The supplied source ends here, with the heading and note for Chapter XXXIX but without the chapter’s surviving body.]

No one shall carry with him on a journey a padded mattress for lying down, unless this has been granted to him in chapter.

### CHAPTER XL. How many companions an abbot coming to the chapter ought to be content with

An abbot coming to the general chapter shall not bring a monk within the abbey, nor more than two horses; but he shall be content with one lay brother or one servant.

### CHAPTER XLI. Where monks or lay brothers ought to be bled

A monk or lay brother ought not to be bled except at abbeys of our Order, nor at granges unless grave necessity presses.

### CHAPTER XLII. Concerning those who are to communicate

[Col. 1732D]

On those days on which the monks are to communicate, the ministers may communicate at private Masses. The abbot may also distribute monks, novices, and lay brothers among the altars for communion, as he judges expedient.

### CHAPTER XLIII. That no abbot may speak in the general chapter except while standing

No abbot except the Abbot of Cîteaux may call out or speak in the hearing of all unless standing, while all the others listen seated. If any other wishes either to object or to say something else, he shall rise while the other is seated.

### CHAPTER XLIV. That no one may claim another’s land or rights of use upon it

If any abbot possesses land, rights of use, or any agreement concerning it, no abbot shall seek that land or rights of use upon it without that abbot’s consent.

### CHAPTER XLV. How an abbot shall make satisfaction if he has not arrived by the *Gloria* of the first psalm

If an abbot has not arrived by the *Gloria* of the first psalm, he shall make satisfaction at the step, as a monk does; except that, after making satisfaction, he shall return to his seat without another’s permission, unless another abbot is in choir.

### CHAPTER XLVI. When Cistercian monks ought to leave the general chapter

> [Note: Col. 1733D] This chapter makes it plain that, at that time, all abbots took part in framing definitions and in discussing other matters in the general chapter; although now, according to present practice—or rather abuse—only the definers take part, as though abbots were now in a worse position than the former priors who then acted in their stead.

[Col. 1733B]

On the first day of the chapter, after the absolution of the dead, let *Our help* (*Adjutorium nostrum*) be said, and let all monks depart except the priors who are present in the place of abbots. The same shall be done on the other days after the exposition of the Rule.

### CHAPTER XLVII. Concerning extraordinary psalms and prayers

It is forbidden that psalms or any other prayers be said in the community for any necessity whatever, unless perhaps for the conventual Mass, another Mass for an impending distress, or the collect at conventual Mass.

### CHAPTER XLVIII. Concerning the mixture for younger brethren

[Col. 1733C]

On those fast days on which younger brethren are permitted to take a mixture (*mistum*), they shall always take it before Terce.

### CHAPTER XLIX. Concerning fairs

It is indeed dangerous and less than honorable for religious to frequent the named fairs; but because our poverty requires that we sell our goods or buy necessities, those upon whom such necessity rests may go to market or fair, though not farther than three days’ journey, or at the most four. Nor may more than two monks or lay brothers from one abbey go; and we judge that the English Channel ought not to be crossed for the sake of fairs. Yet those who are near a seaport may cross in order to buy or exchange necessities for their house; but not for fairs, nor may they proceed more than two days’ journey from the port where they land.

Whoever, then, monk or lay brother of our Order, comes to the named fairs, shall, as long as he is at the fair, receive no provisions for himself or his horses from any religious house, but shall rather live from his own resources, and in the measure becoming a man of his Order. For he ought not to buy fish for himself [Note: Col. 1734D: Observe here that fish are not counted among the dishes allowed to our monks.], [Col. 1734A] or seek luxuries; nor may he drink wine unless it is well diluted with water, and he shall be content with two dishes. They shall neither buy nor sell anything for the benefit of secular persons.

### CHAPTER L. Concerning taverns

It shall not be lawful for us to sell our wine for a tavern, whether through a monk, a lay brother, or any other person—whether, as it is commonly said, “by the broc,” or, in the German tongue, “by the *tapa*”—whether in our own houses or in others’ houses, nor anywhere at all.

### CHAPTER LI. Concerning abbots sitting outside while the general chapter is in session

Any abbot who is outside while the general chapter is in session shall abstain from wine that day.

### CHAPTER LII. Concerning the measure of oats

[Col. 1734B]

For monks or any other members of our Order coming to our abbeys or their places, the measure of oats established at the Cistercian chapter shall suffice for their horses.

### CHAPTER LIII. Concerning guests coming to the general chapter

On the day on which the abbots assemble annually at Cîteaux for chapter, and on the remaining days on which they stay there, it is to be understood that it has been established in the general chapter of those same abbots that no arriving guest is to be received. If, however, such a person should arrive to whom this absolutely cannot be refused, neither his horses nor his horse are to be received in any way. For they judged that this must be carefully guarded against, lest they incur any hindrance, through such receptions, to the matter for which they assemble from provinces so far distant—namely, that they may attend to [Col. 1734C] their Order.

### CHAPTER LIV. Concerning the measure of dishes

Let there be the same measure, as for bread and wine, throughout all abbeys, by which dishes are distributed equally both in abbeys and in granges.

> [Note: Col. 1734D] *Pulmenta* were the regular dishes, that is, dishes permitted and prescribed by the Rule. According to Stephen of Tournai, in his letter to Hugh of Pontigny, the field formerly supplied our monks with them from legumes, or the garden from vegetables.

### CHAPTER LV. Who may carry a chalice and the other things necessary for singing Mass

Wherever abbots of our Order go, they shall not carry a chalice and the other things necessary for singing Mass, except those to whom this has been granted in the annual chapter of abbots.

### CHAPTER LVI. Whether anyone may compose new books

Nor may any abbot, monk, or novice make books, unless this has perhaps been granted to someone in the general chapter.

### CHAPTER LVII. Concerning herds or flocks

No abbot of our Order shall allow either herds or flocks to range so far from pasture during the day that they do not return at night within their own boundaries and lands. Yet those who live in the Alps or near the Alps shall not be bound by this rule, but only with respect to flocks of sheep.

Concerning swine, however, it is permitted to keep them at a distance from the abbey or grange of two leagues, or even three if necessary; and they may range as far as needed around that house, provided that they return at night. The daily sustenance of the keepers of sheep or livestock shall come from nowhere but their own abbey or that grange. But if any persons in other regions should perhaps be unable to keep this rule because of the barrenness and dryness of the places, they shall not be bound by it; rather, the chapter may dispense with it in their case so that they may live, if they can demonstrate this by the testimony of neighboring abbots.

### CHAPTER LVIII. Concerning lawsuits

Abbots, monks, and lay brothers of our Order ought not to attend lawsuits except their own or those of others [Col. 1735B] belonging to our Order. If one of them happens to be present for other reasons, nevertheless he shall not be a judge or spokesman there, nor shall he go to the counsel of the parties or to judgment.

### CHAPTER LIX. Concerning bishops from our Order

Bishops chosen from our Order shall maintain our custom in the quality of food, the form of clothing, the observance of fasts, and the office of the canonical hours. Except that those who wish may have a mantle of cheap cloth and sheepskin, and a similar or a plain cap; nevertheless, wearing these things, they shall by no means enter the cloister or attend our communities, because of the dissimilarity.

> [Note: Col. 1735] Observe the original simplicity, modesty, and holiness of the Order, even in its bishops.

From our houses, each bishop may be given assistance consisting of up to two monks and three [Col. 1735C] lay brothers, if so many are necessary; nevertheless, no secular business or care shall be imposed upon any of them. On account of bishops of our Order, when they lie in the infirmary, their infirmary attendants may, if necessary, remain away from the canonical hours; likewise, their companions who attend them constantly. But no other person shall omit any canonical hour for the sake of any bishop, and none of his monks shall eat with him, but in the refectory, unless he is ill.

### CHAPTER LX. Concerning extra portions

An abbot who is in the infirmary shall not send an extra portion to the community, except to the abbot of the place. Nor shall any abbot who eats in the refectory provide an extra portion, except the one who sits at the *nola*, unless perhaps for the person sitting beside him.

### CHAPTER LXI. What spices we do not use

In the community we use neither pepper, cumin, nor spices of that kind generally, but common herbs such as our land produces.

### CHAPTER LXII. Concerning grave faults

It is known that, at the annual Cistercian chapter, archbishops of our Order have specifically excommunicated thieves, conspirators, and arsonists. Therefore any of our brethren found guilty of such acts shall be subjected to the graver fault. If any such persons leave on that account or are [Col. 1736A] expelled, they shall by no means be received back except under the same sentence. This itself shall be extended or intensified for each person according to the nature of the fault.

Attention must also be paid to ensuring that the dinner hour is later and the food allowance smaller than for one placed under a lighter fault. Nevertheless, the abbot shall consider both bodily health and the kinds of faults; and when he has been received in chapter, he shall not be restored to his rank on the same day. The vessels he uses shall either be broken or distributed to the poor. He shall lie prostrate at the doors of the oratory without his cowl upon his head. Whenever Mass or the office of the dead follows a canonical hour without interval, he shall not prostrate himself until the community leaves the church; nevertheless, all are not compelled to leave on his account. Those who do leave shall pass before him. Likewise, when he has been received in chapter, while the work of God is being completed, he shall prostrate himself upon the ground.

### CHAPTER LXIII. Concerning lighter faults

Brethren who are under a lighter fault shall eat outside the refectory, in a place the abbot judges fitting. After the servants’ meal, they shall neither go to drink with the others, nor shall those who are doing penance for having missed the third verse; rather, they shall go into the refectory after the others.

### CHAPTER LXIV. In what rank a fugitive ought to be received

If a fugitive returns within eleven days, he may be restored to the rank he held before. But if he returns after more than eleven days, he may indeed be received, provided that he remains forever in the rank in which the last person is received.

### CHAPTER LXV. Concerning the summoning of abbots for the election of a new abbot

When an abbot has died, the Father Abbot shall be summoned, together with any abbots whom that house has produced. The nearer abbots shall likewise be summoned together for the day prescribed by the Father Abbot; and, at the Father Abbot’s discretion, the abbots present from that house and its monks shall elect an abbot together. In the house of Cîteaux, which is the mother of us all, the abbots present who came forth from Cîteaux and the Cistercian monks shall elect together.

### CHAPTER LXVI. Concerning the care of granges

We forbid any abbot to entrust his granges, or any one of them, to any monk except the cellarer, who, according to the authority of the Rule, is to have charge of all things at the abbot’s will. He shall be supplied, as necessary, with helpers by whom he may be assisted in the matters to be done.

### CHAPTER LXVII. What the Abbot of Cîteaux ought to inquire into in the general chapter

If, in any year, an abbey has not been visited by its father abbot—the abbot of the house from which it issued—either personally or through another, its abbot shall make this known in the common chapter of Cîteaux when the presiding officer asks this question publicly. Inquiry shall also be made whether any abbot is absent; and, after the excuses have been heard of those who perhaps could not come because of illness, henceforth no one shall [Col. 1737A] conceal it if he knows that one of those who ought to have come that year is absent; nor shall the matter be passed over without severe censure.

### CHAPTER LXVIII. How disputes arising between abbots ought to be settled

If any dispute should arise between certain abbots of our Order, they shall summon neighboring abbots of our Order and make peace by their counsel. If it cannot be settled even thus, their case shall be reserved for the annual chapter at Cîteaux, and there it shall be settled according to the judgment and decision of the chapter of Cîteaux. Nor may an appeal be made in any way to another hearing.

### CHAPTER LXIX. Concerning houses situated in towns

Monks or lay brothers shall not live in houses situated in villages, castles, or cities.

### CHAPTER LXX. Concerning monks or lay brothers coming to their own granges

[Col. 1737B]

When monks or lay brothers come to their own granges, they shall eat as the brethren of the granges eat; nor shall they speak with the brethren except with the master and the hospitaller.

### CHAPTER LXXI. Concerning false voices

It becomes men to sing in a manly voice, and not, in a feminine manner, with tinkling or, as is commonly said, “false” voices, imitating the theatrical wantonness of performers. We therefore establish that moderation be maintained in singing, so that it may convey gravity and preserve devotion.

### CHAPTER LXXII. Whether anyone may go to Rome

No one of our Order shall go to Rome except with a bishop of the Order.

### CHAPTER LXXIII. Concerning abbots who leave their abbeys

[Col. 1737C]

Abbots who leave their abbeys shall return to the rank of their conversion.

> [Note: Col. 1737D] In subsequent general chapters, abbots of this kind were granted a place after the other abbots. *Novellarum Definitiones*, distinction 8, chapter 2.

### CHAPTER LXXIV. That monks or lay brothers coming to the general chapter shall be beaten

From the ninth hour on the day preceding the Exaltation of the Holy Cross until the ninth hour on the day when the abbots depart from the general chapter, any guest monk or lay brother found in the monastery or the granges of Cîteaux shall be brought to the general chapter and there beaten before all the abbots. Nor may even the Abbot of Cîteaux offer any excuse on behalf of those who are beaten.

### CHAPTER LXXV. That the infirmarian may speak with his assistant

[Col. 1737D]

Whoever is master of the infirmary may speak with his assistant, if the abbot nevertheless sees that this is necessary; and this shall be done in the place and manner he himself provides. A lay brother may also be kept in the infirmary as the infirmarian’s assistant.

### CHAPTER LXXVI. Concerning boys learning letters

No boy shall be taught letters within the monastery or in the monastery’s places unless he is a monk or a novice received for probation; they may learn during the time of reading. It should also be noted that no one may be placed under probation until after [Col. 1738A] his fifteenth year.

### CHAPTER LXXVII. Concerning the punishment of an abbot who despises the Father Abbot

A son abbot who despises his abbot when the latter corrects him concerning his observance shall, when accused in the chapter of Cîteaux, be subjected to a lighter fault, either in his own abbey or in the place appointed by the Abbot of Cîteaux.

### CHAPTER LXXVIII. When and to whom the chief cellarer ought to render accounts

The chief cellarer shall render account to the abbot, or to those whom he orders, once each month—or more frequently if the abbot wishes—of everything he receives. Other officials, whether grange-masters or those presiding over any workmen, shall do likewise in the presence [Col. 1738B] of the cellarer, or of those whom the abbot orders to be with him. The person whom the abbot orders shall keep the resources of the monastery in coin or other money; the abbot himself shall keep with him some of his monks who are privy to the money.

### CHAPTER LXXIX. Concerning the punishment of those speaking at table

At all times, according to the precept of the Rule, a monk ought to cultivate silence, but especially during the night hours and at table. We therefore ordain that neither monk nor lay brother speak at table, unless perhaps he is travelling and has no one who understands his signs: then, by saying individual words—such as “water,” “bread,” and “wine”—he may briefly and silently request only those things necessary for eating. Whoever acts otherwise shall abstain from wine at that meal; and if [Col. 1738C] he has no wine, he shall lack one dish, if he has two.

### CHAPTER LXXX. With how many monks an abbot who is a guest may speak at once

We establish that no abbot coming to another house may, without permission, keep a monk away from work, nor speak at once with more than two. Visiting abbots alone may summon monks to speak with them in the hearing-room, or in a place near the monks’ hearing-room. Moreover, excepting, as we have said, visitors, no one may lead a monk through the court, infirmary, or beyond the boundaries without the abbot’s permission, or the prior’s if the abbot is absent. While an abbot speaks with two, should a third arrive, he may speak briefly while standing, if necessary; but, even if invited, he shall not presume to sit down.

### CHAPTER LXXXI. Concerning letters and glass

Letters shall be made of one color and not painted. Glass windows shall be white, without crosses or pictures.

### CHAPTER LXXXII. Concerning the church lamp

Whoever wishes and is able may keep a lamp burning in the oratory both by day and by night.

### CHAPTER LXXXIII. Concerning kinds of clothing

“Those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses”: such things do not become a monastery. Let us put away delicate garments; henceforth let no one use Isembrun, *saia*, Valembrun [Col. 1739A], or materials of that kind, nor finer cloths, whether new or old.

### CHAPTER LXXXIV. On whose behalf we may write to the lord pope

No one shall write to the lord pope except concerning his own causes and those of his fellow abbots, bishops, archbishops, kings, and princes.

### CHAPTER LXXXV. Concerning *wandagiae*

> [Note: Col. 1739A] *Vandengiae* or *vendagiae* are leggings, a kind of garment covering the legs and feet.

Those sent on a journey may, if they wish, have *wandagiae* to avoid [Col. 1740A] mud or to ward off cold.

### CHAPTER LXXXVI. That a prostrate monk shall not pray

It is not our custom that a monk or lay brother pray lying prostrate with his whole body in the oratory, but upon his knees and standing.

### CHAPTER LXXXVII. Concerning writing rooms

> [Note: Col. 1740A] *Scriptoria* were cells in which monks devoted themselves to copying books.

In all writing rooms wherever monks customarily write, silence shall be kept as in the cloister.

[Col. 1739]

## LETTER OF SAINT RAINARD TO INNOCENT II

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXIX, col. 671, among the letters of Innocent II.)

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1151: HUGH OF MÂCON, FIRST ABBOT OF PONTIGNY, AFTERWARDS BISHOP OF AUXERRE

[Col. 1739]

## NOTICE

*Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. XII, p. 408.

> [Note: Col. 1739] Manrique, *Annals of Cîteaux*, under the year 1112, ch. 2, no. 2. Le Nain, *History of Cîteaux*, vol. I, p. 155.

Hugh, of the house of the counts of Mâcon, formed, from his earliest youth, a close friendship with Saint Bernard, whose cousin he was and whose approximate equal he was in age. When Bernard left the world, he did not think that he ought to leave this dear kinsman amid the reefs he himself was avoiding out of fear of shipwreck. He urged him to follow him to Cîteaux. Hugh resisted for some time; but at last he allowed himself to be overcome, and was one of the thirty companions whom Bernard took with him into that holy retreat.

The rapid progress he made there in virtue led Abbot Saint Stephen to place him at the head of the colony which he sent in 1114 to found the abbey of Pontigny in the diocese of Auxerre. Under Hugh’s government, that house itself became the mother of several others. Hugh is said to have been the first to add the words *salvo ordine nostro* (“with our Order preserved”) to the profession of obedience which Cistercian abbots made to their diocesan bishop.

> [Note: Col. 1739] Here is the form of the oath of obedience made by abbots of the Order of Cîteaux to their bishop: “I, N., abbot of the Cistercian Order, promise that I shall perpetually maintain toward you, Lord Bishop, and your canonically appointed successors, and toward the Holy Apostolic See, the subjection and obedience established by the holy Fathers according to [Col. 1740] the Rule of Saint Benedict, without prejudice to my Order.” (Sirmond, notes on letter 7, book II of the Letters of Geoffrey of Vendôme.) This addition later proved beneficial to the Order.

Having gone in 1127 to the general chapter at Cîteaux, he saw Stephen of Senlis, bishop of Paris, arrive there. The latter had been obliged by the vexations of King Louis the Fat to abandon his church. Moved by the prelate’s situation and softened by his prayers, the assembly deputed the abbots of Clairvaux and Pontigny to the monarch, in order to induce him to end this kind of persecution.

The following year Hugh attended the Council of Troyes, where he gave proofs of his ability. Theobald the Great, Count of Champagne, informed of his merit by the bishops of Auxerre and Troyes, chose him in 1135, together with Andrew of Beaumont, a monk of Clairvaux, to establish regular canons in the church of Saint-Loup at Troyes, [Col. 1741] previously served by secular clerics. After discharging this duty, the two commissioners gave the new canons special statutes, which Pope Innocent II confirmed.

Hugh’s wise governance caused the abbey of Pontigny to grow daily, until Providence removed him from it in order to place him on the episcopal see of Auxerre, vacant through the death of Hugh of Montaigu in 1136.

> [Note: Col. 1741] Mabillon, *Annals*, book LXXVI, no. 95.

He was ordained in the same year by Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres and papal legate, at the abbey of Ferrières in the diocese of Sens.

> [Note: Col. 1741] Le Nain, ibid., p. 83.

The funeral poem reproduced below succinctly states the virtues that characterized his episcopate.

In 1141 he introduced the Premonstratensians into Auxerre and endowed them from his own funds. Called to the great Council of Reims held in 1148, he demonstrated his theological learning by combating the errors of Gilbert de la Porrée.

> [Note: Col. 1741] *Annals of Cîteaux*, vol. I, p. 411, no. 6.

Hugh was one of the three commissioners whom the French prelates of that assembly charged with drafting their profession of faith against these novelties, for presentation to the Pope and Sacred College.

> [Note: Col. 1742] Villefore, *Life of St Bernard*, book VI, ch. 5; Le Nain, ibid., no. 18; Martène, *Anecdotes*, vol. IV, p. 141.

This venerable prelate died on 10 October 1151. His body, buried in the church of Pontigny near the high altar, was found in 1560 as whole as on the day it had been put into the ground. Taking it, from this sign, to be the body of Saint Edmund, the Calvinists carried their blind fury so far as to burn it and reduce it to ashes. Simon Chevredor, a Regular Canon of Saint-Victor and his contemporary, adorned his tomb with the following epitaph:

> Pre-eminent as bishop in the city of Auxerre,  
> Ascending in mind to heaven, he left his body on the earth.  
> Distinguished in sex, lineage, goodness, renown, and honor,  
> Hugh was generous in name, speech, and hand.  
> Both rich and poor—poor for himself, rich toward the needy—  
> Inferior to none, and no one was his equal.  
> Service, fear, favor, gifts, and prayers  
> Could not recall him from the standard of justice.  
> In him alone the virtue of piety triumphed,  
> When, after justice, he had to be merciful.  
> As first Father of this Church, he enlarged  
> Its renown, achievements, place, by renown, vigor, and benefactions.  
> As October closed twice five days,  
> He closed the end of his days, now possessing a day without end.

Despite this praise, we shall not conceal that Hugh’s will stains his memory. Instead of bequeathing everything he possessed to the poor and to churches, this prelate left them only a small portion, giving all the rest to one of his nephews, a young layman who had nothing to recommend him except the honor of being related to him.

> [Note: Col. 1742] Bernard, letter 276.

It was said that he gave him as many as seven churches that he had acquired, together with their tithes and meadows in the bishop’s own forest, not counting his gold and horses. The young man used these in going to Rome to have the will confirmed. When Saint Bernard was informed of this, he hastened to warn Pope Eugenius by a letter, asking him to annul this act, which he called fraudulent, because it had been procured from the prelate by his deacon Stephen during one of the spells of weakness frequent in the final period of his life. He even suspected that the deacon had had it drawn up without Hugh’s knowledge. This, he said, was all the more likely because, during a dangerous illness the preceding year, Hugh had been made to give a church to this same nephew—a gift of which, after his recovery, he declared he had no recollection.

Although M. Le Beuf, in his *Memoirs for the History of Auxerre*, did not judge it proper to rank our prelate among authors, he nevertheless left works from his pen that seem to deserve that title. Dom Charles de Visch, in his *Bibliotheca of Cîteaux*, names a treatise by him entitled *On Preserving the Privileges of the Church*. This work has not yet appeared, and we do not know in what repository it exists. The same bibliographer, with considerable plausibility, is inclined to attribute to him the *Little Exordium of Cîteaux*.

There are moreover two letters of his to Suger: one urging him to establish a truce between Hugh of Marinis and Hugh of Borne, who were waging implacable war against one another; the other commending to him the widow and children of the physician Robert, whom Suger had honored with his esteem and protection while he lived. We might also add the letter written in his name and in Saint Bernard’s to Pope Honorius II, complaining of the haste with which he had lifted the interdict imposed by Stephen of Senlis, bishop of Paris, upon the lands of King Louis the Fat. He is the author of the Statutes of the Abbey of Saint-Loup at Troyes, and he participated in the Constitutions of the nuns of Hières. Finally, Dom Martène published, in the first volume of his *Anecdotes* (p. 402), a charter by him concerning the goods possessed by Hugh du Til.

We shall nevertheless take care not to attribute to our prelate the poem by a Hugh of Mâcon entitled *On the Remarkable Deeds of Knights*. The author of that work had nothing in common with the man who concerns us except the similarity of names; and it is certain, as will be shown in its proper place, that he flourished only toward the end of the fifteenth century.

[Col. 1741]

## TWO LETTERS OF HUGH TO SUGER

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXVI, under Suger.)

[Col. 1743]

## CHARTER OF HUGH, BISHOP OF AUXERRE, CONCERNING THE GOODS POSSESSED BY HUGH DE TILIO  
*(Year 1147)*

(Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. I, col. 402.)

[Col. 1743A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, I, HUGH, bishop of Auxerre, wish it to be known to those present and future that Hugh de Tilio, while laid low by the illness in which he died, declared before us and other religious and secular persons that William, grandfather of William, Count of Nevers, who withdrew to the Charterhouse to serve God, possessed during his life, for many years, the lordship of Giriac and the castle of Luperciac, with the appurtenances belonging to it, except Bolum; and that, at his death, he left the aforesaid things peacefully to his grandson William.

This William likewise possessed them in the same peace until he granted them in inheritance to the aforesaid Hugh de Tilio, both as recompense for his love and service and also in exchange for the land of Forges and money given on that account. Hugh himself had possessed these same things peacefully [Col. 1744A] until the day on which he made this declaration.

He also declared that he had acquired many other things from Hugh Sajet, with the approval of Hugh’s wife Amelina and their children; and that, after the acquisition, he had possessed them quietly until that day. He declared that he had acquired all the above-written things, except Bolum, in such a way that he could rightfully leave them—and did leave them—to his wife Sarah, who was present, and to the children he had begotten by her, for possession by hereditary right.

Present with me at this act were Pontius, abbot of Vézelay; Peter, abbot of Boniradius; Stephen, abbot of Reigny; Geoffrey, abbot of Les Roches; Itherius of Totiac; Nargodus; Seguinus of Crux; Gauterius of Montescot; Ernaudus of Totiac; Hugh of Prii; Rainaldus; Morellus; and many others.
